In this context, the term "faculty" (*indriya*) refers to the locus of support and does not denote the essential nature of the faculty itself;
how, then, would this contradict my position?
Their statement to that effect is likewise unreasonable.
Because it contradicts other sūtras. That is to say,
another sūtra records that the brahmin Jātiśroṇa went to the Blessed One and addressed him, saying:
The Venerable Gautama said, "How many faculties (indriya) are there?
The Buddha replied,
"I teach that there are twenty-two faculties."
Regarding what is called the eye-faculty,
and so forth, as explained at length:
does that sūtra not also state the basis upon which the faculties rely?
In these two sūtras, the meaning of the term "faculty" (indriya) is no different;
one refers to the essential nature of the faculty itself,
while the other refers to its basis.
This is not universally established;
it is merely one's own false attachment.
Therefore, one must certainly admit that the five faculties, such as faith and the rest, also pertain to the outflowing (sāsrava) realm.
Question: If they also include those with outflows (*sāsrava*), how should that cited sūtra be interpreted?
Answer: The five faculties, such as faith and so forth, actually do include those with outflows.
That sutra speaks exclusively of the untainted (anāsrava).
Why is this? Because the distinctions among noble ones (ārya) are established based upon the untainted faculties (indriya).
Some say that the sutra speaks only of the noble path. Why is this so?
The distinctions among noble beings (ārya) are explained based on the noble path (āryamārga), not according to worldly convention.
It is asked: That sutra further states, "If these five faculties, such as faith, were entirely non-existent..."
I say that they abide in the category of external worldlings (*bāhya-pṛthagjana*).
How, then, is this to be reconciled?
The answer is: those who have severed their roots of goodness (*samucchinna-kuśalamūla*) are called external worldlings.
That is to say, there are generally two types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*):
first, those internal, and second, those external.
These are those who have not severed their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Those who possess [wholesome roots] are called "internal";
those who have severed their wholesome roots are called "external."
The intent of that sutra is to say:
"If one is entirely devoid of these five faculties, such as faith,
I declare them to be those who have severed the roots of goodness."
Therefore, the scripture cited poses no difficulty for us.
Alternatively, it is said that this is what was taught by the Sautrāntikas.
That is to say, the Sautrāntika masters also speak these words in order to refute the conceptualists who hold views as previously described.
The Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma) have the five faculties as their nature;
it is not merely that much. Some say:
This is the tenet of the Vātsīputrīya school.
The masters of that school maintain that the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) have the five faculties, such as faith (*śraddhā*), as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Only these five faculties are intrinsically wholesome (*kuśala-svabhāva*).
Because other [faculties] are mixed with these,
they also receive the designation "wholesome.
It is by means of these five faculties that the distinctions among all noble beings (ārya) are established, and not by means of any other faculties.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"If one possesses the five faculties that are intensified, sharp,
balanced, and perfected through extensive cultivation, one becomes one liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta)."
From this point, by further diminishing [the faculties], one becomes liberated through wisdom (prajñā-vimukta);
next, by further diminishing, one becomes a bodily witness (kāyasākṣin);
and next, by further diminishing, one becomes one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Next, by further diminishing [the faculties], one becomes a *śraddhādhimukta*;
next, by further diminishing them, one becomes a *dharmānusārī*;
and next, by further diminishing them, one becomes a *śraddhānusārī*.

Question: What connection does the tenet system of this treatise have with the Vātsīputrīya school such that their doctrine is mentioned? Answer: It is for the sake of enabling those who doubt to attain certainty;
that is to say, [it concerns] the tenets established by them and by this [treatise].
Although they are largely the same, there are slight differences. Specifically,
that school maintains that the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) has as its nature only the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*),
and that the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is invariably defiled (*kliṣṭa*).

This means that it has as its intrinsic nature the ten types of latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) which are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya).
The essence of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) is a dissociated formation (viprayukta-saṃskāra).
There are three kinds of nirvāṇa:
namely, that of the learner (śaikṣa), that of the non-learner (aśaikṣa), and that which is neither of the learner nor the non-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
The asuras are established as the sixth realm of rebirth (*gati*) among persons (*pudgala*),
and their substantial existence is real.
Such categories as these— whether six or seven— are different from this [system].
The rest are mostly similar; do not harbor doubts, for they are all identical to this.
Although their tenets are described, there are differences in what is negated and what is revealed.
Now one should question them:
if only the five faculties are wholesome by their very nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*),
what is the intrinsic nature of the remaining wholesome phenomena?
If it is argued that those [five faculties] are also called "wholesome" because they are mixed with the wholesome, unwholesome,
and indeterminate [faculties], then why are these five faculties not also called unwholesome or indeterminate when they are mixed with those?
However, the five faculties beginning with faith and the remaining factors share the same basis and the same mode of activity.
They have the same object of cognition,
arise together, abide together,
cease together, share the same fruit, and possess the same outflow.
They share the same maturation (vipāka),
yet the five faculties are said to be wholesome by nature;
the others are designated as "wholesome" only figuratively because they are associated with them.
However, to follow mere deluded sentiments would be contrary to correct principle;
lest such an error occur,
one should therefore state that the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) possess both the nature of faculties (*indriya*) and the nature of non-faculties (*anindriya*).
The Venerable Dharmatrāta spoke thus:
"All minds and mental factors are specific manifestations of volition (*cetanā*);
therefore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) has volition as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."
The Venerable Buddhadeva speaks thus:
"The essence of all minds and mental factors is mind itself;
therefore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma has mind as its intrinsic nature."
Those two venerable ones spoke thus:
"Faith and the other mental factors of volition differ before and after; they do not function simultaneously.
The five faculties, such as faith, serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)."
Regarding those who enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
this statement is made based on the sense that it is possible for them to do so; thus,
the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are able to enter the path of seeing.

That is to say, either one enters the path of seeing immediately after a mind of faith accompanied by the mental application of faith, or even one enters the path of seeing immediately after a mind of wisdom accompanied by the mental application of wisdom.
If that were so, then one would also have to enter the path of seeing immediately after a factor dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-dharma*).
He says this: "Even if it were granted, what fault would there be?
It is as you, Venerable Sir, have stated regarding the essence of the mind being both prior and posterior."
Although they are not associated, they possess an object of cognition and can serve as the immediate precursor for entering the Path of Seeing;
our own school holds the same view.
Thus, although faith and the other [faculties] are mental states that lack the quality of association by their very nature, [they function in this way].
Since there is an object of focus,
one is able to enter the path of seeing immediately;
what fault is there in this?
There is a great fault.

Why is this? If one believes that the mind of reflection (*cintā-citta*) serves as the equal-and-immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), [it would contradict the established doctrine].
Since there would be no diligence, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom,
it would follow that laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, and faulty wisdom could enter the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
This applies even to the case where the mind associated with wisdom (*prajñā*) serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for entering the path of vision.
If there were no faith, diligence, mindfulness, and concentration, then lack of faith,
laziness, forgetfulness, and distraction would have to be able to enter the path of vision;
how could such a thing not constitute a great error?
In order to refute such various divergent attachments, it is further stated:
"In this context, if the mind and mental factors enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth as an equal-and-immediate [condition]..."
This is called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Regarding the phrase "in this matter," it means being non-erroneous with respect to this.
This is the school, this is the treatise;
this is the aggregate, this is the section, this is the category;
this accords with the sūtras.
It is thus within the meaning accepted by myself and my fellow practitioners of the holy life.
The Venerable Kātyāyanīputra wished to demonstrate that,

according to his own school, the *laukikāgra-dharma* (the supreme mundane dharma) has as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) the mind and mental factors associated with the faculties and non-faculties, together with their concomitant states.

Question: Regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) and the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma concerning Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), is it called "entering the Path of Seeing" because the former serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the latter,
or is it only after the former has ceased that one is said to have entered?
Is this stage of abiding itself called "entry"?
If it were only after this [stage] has ceased that one could be called "entered," why is it not stated here that one has already entered?
If this state of abiding were itself called "entry," then ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) would become confused. Some have said:
Cessation is termed "entry.
Question: If that were so, this text should state "has already entered," because at that time the path of seeing (darśanamārga) is said to have already arisen.
Regarding the statement "having promised, he enters and speaks upon entering," this uses the term for the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) to refer to the ultimate state,
just as the expression "he has come" refers to the fact that he has already arrived.
As it is said in the world:
"Great King, from where have you come now?
Although he has already arrived, one says, "He comes now."
This is also like that.
It is also like saying one is currently abandoning what has already been abandoned, as the Sūtra says: "abandoning pleasure and abandoning pain."
...and so on, as explained at length.
At the time of becoming free from the defilement of desire,
the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) has already been abandoned.
Now, when one emerges from the third dhyāna,
it is said that the faculty of defiled pleasure is abandoned at the moment it is severed.
Is it not that what was already abandoned is said to be abandoned now,
and likewise, what was already liberated is said to be liberated now?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The mind is liberated from the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsava*), existence (*bhava-āsava*), and ignorance (*avijjā-āsava*).
At the time of being freed from the defilement of desire, the mind has already attained liberation from the outflow of desire;
now it is freed from the defilement of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).
When the mind attains liberation from the outflows of existence and the outflow of ignorance,
it is then said to be "liberated. Furthermore,
regarding that which is already liberated, it is said to be "now liberated."
Furthermore, it is as when one speaks of "present experiencing" regarding that which has already been experienced.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is: 'I am experiencing a pleasant feeling,'" and so forth, as explained at length.
That [feeling] was already experienced and is now being described as "experienced," because it cannot be cognized at the very moment of its experience.
This case is also like that.
Although they have already entered [the path], it is said that they are entering now.
Other masters state that this passage should read:
"Immediately thereafter, one enters rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma)."
That statement is irrational.
Since they enter the immediate [state] from the immediate [state],
what difference is there in the meaning of "entering"?
According to this explanation,
abiding in the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) is termed "entry."
Question: If that were so, ordinary beings would be noble ones, because they enter the noble path.
Answer: There is no such fault.
When the Supreme Mundane Dharma reaches the stage of abiding,
the Patience of the Dharma-knowledge of Suffering is in the state of being about to arise;
because it is not yet accomplished, one is not called a Noble One (ārya).
Although the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) has not yet arisen,
because it is currently in the process of arising, it is termed "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*);
at that time, the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) serve as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Therefore, it is called "entry.
For this reason, it is said:
if the mind and mental factors enter into the state of correctness and departure from birth as their immediate antecedents (*samanantara-pratyaya*), [they constitute entry].
This is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Question: If the mind and mental factors have already entered the state of correctness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), [how can they be mundane?].
"Or when one is about to enter [the path], is that also the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma)?
Answer: It is also."
Question: If that is so, why is this not stated here?
Answer: If one speaks of "correctly entering," it should be understood that this includes both having already entered and about to enter.
If one speaks of the present,
it should be understood that one is speaking of the past and the future as well,
because their characteristics are identical.
The proponents of the theory of the differentiation of the mental factor of volition (*cetanā*) state as follows:
"If one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) through the mental factor of volition associated with faith (*śraddhā-sahagata-cetanā*),
then that volition associated with faith serves solely as a homogeneous immediately preceding condition (*sabhāga-samanantarapratyaya*)."
In this manner, up to the point where if the mind of wisdom-contemplation enters the path of seeing as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
that mind of wisdom-contemplation serves solely as a homogeneous immediately preceding condition.
Proponents of the theory of similar succession state as follows:
mental states and mental factors serve only as equivalent and immediate conditions for those of their own kind;
that is, a mind serves as such a condition for a [subsequent] mind, but not for mental factors.
Mental factors are neither mental factors nor mind;
among all mental factors,
feeling is neither feeling nor anything else.
The same applies to perception and the other mental factors;
however, these mental concomitants do not always function in association,
but arise only when encountering specific conditions.
That is to say: if one delights in a preceding object, pleasant feeling arises;
if one feels aversion toward a preceding object, painful feeling arises;
if one is neutral toward an object, [neutral feeling arises].
It gives rise to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
If one wishes to experience something, feeling arises;
if one wishes to apprehend an image, perception arises.
If one wishes to perform an action, volition arises;
and so on, up to if one wishes to make a definitive discernment, wisdom arises.
Therefore, the mental factors do not always associate [with the mind].
If that were so, then all mental states and mental factors that have already arisen would not necessarily function as equivalent-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*). To this, they reply:
All [factors] can serve as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*),
yet they are not necessarily immediate,
as your own school maintains.
When emerging from the state of non-conception,
although there have been no mind or mental factors for five hundred kalpas,
one nevertheless employs the mind and mental factors belonging to the stage of entry [into that state].
It serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for those currently arising;
our own school holds the same view.
Although dharmas of the same kind are frequently interrupted by long intervals, that which precedes acts as the equal-and-immediate condition for that which follows.
What fault is there in this?
That statement is irrational. Why is this so?
Because the meanings of "having a mind" and "being without a mind" are distinct;
furthermore, among associated dharmas,
there are those that have already yielded their fruit and those that have not yet yielded their fruit.
Because it would be illogical;
minds and mental factors that have not yet arisen cannot be equal-and-immediate conditions.
It is unreasonable to pre-arrange those conditions;
furthermore, that would contradict the explanation in the *Prakaraṇapāda*, which asks: "What are the dharmas that arise immediately after the mind?
and answers: "The subsequent minds and mental factors."
Either already arisen or currently arising,
as well as the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation,
either already arisen or currently arising.
Furthermore, if that were the case, there would be another distinct fault:
namely, if immediately following the mind and mental factors of a stage characterized by both vitarka and vicāra,
there were [a state] of a stage characterized by no vitarka and only vicāra.
Alternatively, when states of mind and mental factors belonging to a stage without applied thought or sustained thought (avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ) are present,
the mind and mental factors that have already arisen in the preceding stage [also persist].
It should not be the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the subsequent stages and so forth,
because they are dissimilar;
this applies even if [the mind] arises from a stage that is without applied thought or sustained thought (*avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ*).
Immediately following the mind and mental factors,
there are stages that are without vitarka and with only vicāra,
or stages with both vitarka and vicāra.
The same explanation applies to the manifestation of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
This refers to the immediate succession of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate mind and mental factors.
The fault is likewise:
if the former were not the equal-and-immediate condition for the latter,
then the latter would have no condition at all.
It should not arise.
If it is argued that a subsequent arising occurs because of an interval created by preceding factors,
[we reply that] this applies equally to all dharmas of the same kind as immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This is also not the case,
because it would be illogical for [the object] to serve as a condition by being separated [from the mind] during a state of mental engagement.
Furthermore, regarding the first untainted [state] and the superior tainted states that have never arisen since beginningless time, since these have not previously arisen,
[they cannot be produced by the power of prior cultivation].
The homogeneous and other immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*) would then be unable to arise.
Furthermore, what they have stated involves a grave error:
namely, that greed should constantly arise immediately after [any state], including greed itself.
There would never be a time to subdue greed and give rise to the contemplation of impurity;
if anger were immediate, one would always give rise to anger and never have a time to subdue anger and give rise to the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion.
If delusion were to arise immediately after [the cessation of] delusion, it would arise constantly;
there would never be a time for subduing delusion through the cultivation of causal analysis,
nor for the arising of the view of self and so forth— this should be understood according to reason.
Because there is no proximate condition for the arising of a different category [of mind],
and because this superior wholesome [mind] has never arisen before,
it follows that a wholesome mind would have no means of arising.
If that were so, there would be no possibility of attaining liberation. To avoid such various faults,
one must therefore admit that a preceding collection of mental states serves as the equal-and-immediate condition for a subsequent collection of mental states.
Whether they are equal or unequal,
their power to open the way for what arises later is the same as that of a heap of grain or beans.
Question: When the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) is present before one,
what future mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) are being cultivated?
Is that dharma also the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*)?
Some say that it is not the supreme mundane dharma.
Why is this so? Because it is stated therein that if the mind and mental factors serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
one enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
This is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
As for that which is future,
it cannot function as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Therefore, that is not the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Furthermore, if that were the supreme mundane dharma,
then there would have to be multiple minds constituting the supreme mundane dharma.
This would contradict the subsequent passage,
which states that the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) should be described as a single moment of mind, not many moments of mind.
If it were said thus,
then that dharma would either be the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) or it would not be the supreme mundane dharma;
in the latter case, it would contradict what is stated in the *Jñānaskandha*.
As it is said: "If, when a path not previously attained manifests in the present, one cultivates other future paths of that same category;
if one maintains that these are not the 'supreme mundane dharmas' (laukikāgradharma)."
What is meant by "the path of that same category"?
Question: Since it cannot serve as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), how can it be called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)?

The answer is: although it does not act as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), it can nevertheless be conducive [to the arising of the mind] because its acquisition (*prāpti*) arises;
this is, for example, like a bhikṣu granting his consent (*chanda*) to the Saṃgha.
This refers to when the Saṃgha performs the *poṣadha*,
and although there are certain bhikṣus who are not present in the assembly,
they nonetheless participate in the *poṣadha* by means of granting their consent (*chanda*).
Other monastic affairs can likewise be established.
In this way, although the types of cultivation to be practiced in the future cannot act as an immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), [they still function].
If it arises, it conforms to the attainment of its own manifest characteristic;
even if it does not arise, it conforms to the attainment of the manifest characteristic.
This [latter case] cannot function as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This can serve as a condition because it accords with the power of that [state];
for that state possesses a powerful, unimpeded force toward the arising of the Noble Path.
Question: If that is also the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma), why is this so?
Regarding this, why does the root treatise not state it?
One should know that when something ought to be stated but is not,
the meaning therein is incomplete.
Furthermore, if there were that which could act as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
it would be stated here that such a thing cannot act as an equal-and-immediate condition.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, that which functions within the world is explained herein;
since that [subject] does not function within the world, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, that which is capable of grasping a fruit and giving a fruit is what is discussed here;
since those [other factors] are incapable of grasping or giving a fruit,
they are not mentioned.
Furthermore, if something were obtained through nourishment and yet remained within the body,
that would be discussed here;
however, although it is obtained through nourishment, it does not remain within the body.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, if there is power capable of cultivating the future,
it is mentioned herein.
Because that [state] lacks the power of cultivation,
it is not mentioned. Furthermore, if a mind is the cause of another mind, and that mind is its effect,
then within this context, it is said that those dharmas are not otherwise.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, if a dharma repays its cause and is also able to grasp its fruit while abiding in the body and engaging with objects, [it is so designated].
In this context, it is precisely those factors that are not so [characterized] which are not mentioned.
Furthermore, if both types of cultivation are present, they are mentioned here.
Since that [cultivation] consists solely of the meaning of cultivation without application (*anabhisamskāra-bhāvanā*), it is not mentioned here.
Furthermore, only that which possesses an active function (*kriyā*) is discussed in this context.
It has no functional activity;
therefore, it is not mentioned.
Question: If that is so, why does the subsequent text state that the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) do not consist of multiple moments of mind?
In response, it is said that those who claim there is activity in the present world speak only of a single mind, not of all minds;
if one were to speak of all [minds], there would indeed be many minds.
In future ages, because there are many categories that are of the same kind, even those not currently being cultivated may still be called the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*);
how much more so, then, for those that are actually being cultivated? How could they not be such?
Therefore, it is asked:

"Is there a case where the 'worldly supreme dharmas' (*laukikāgradharma*) are associated [with the mind] yet do not serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the 'patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering' (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*)? The answer is: "Yes.
That is to say, those of the same category that are cultivated in the future."

Question: Regarding the factors that arise concomitantly with the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*)— namely, matter (*rūpa*) and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*)—
are these also the Supreme Mundane Dharma?
Some say that these are not the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*),
because it is stated therein: "If [there are] mind and mental factors..."
That which serves as the immediately preceding condition for entering into the state of rightness and departure from birth is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
It cannot itself function as an immediately preceding condition [for that very same state].
Therefore, it is not called the "supreme mundane dharma.
According to this explanation,
that dharma is also indeed the supreme mundane dharma.
Question: Since it does not function as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), how can it be called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)?
Answer: Although it does not function as an immediately preceding condition, it is able to act as a conforming condition (*anuloma*).
Because that [mind] and these mental factors arise together,
abide together, cease together,
share the same fruit, the same outflow, and the same maturation.
Because it is extremely closely related.
Question: If that is so, why is this not stated here?
Answer: That which ought to be stated but is not stated [is as follows].
One should know that this meaning is not exhaustive.
Furthermore, whatever dharma can act as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
it is precisely this that is being discussed here.
Those dharmas are not like that;
therefore, they are not mentioned.
Furthermore, if a dharma is acquired through nourishment by causes and possesses an object of perception (ālambana), [it is so stated].
In this context, it is said that those phenomena are not so;
therefore, they are not mentioned.
Furthermore, if phenomena are associated,
they possess a basis, possess an aspect,
possess an object, and possess alertness.
This is explained herein;
that dharma is not so,
and therefore it is not mentioned.
Therefore, it is asked:

"Is there any present supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) that is not the immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and so forth? The answer is: "Yes;
namely, the matter (*rūpa*) that evolves concomitantly with it."
Mental Factors Dissociated from Thought.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 2; *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 3. (As expounded in the *Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*).
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;
translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, who received the Imperial Decree.

Section One of the First Aggregate on Miscellaneous Topics: The Sub-section on the Supreme Mundane Dharma (Loka-agra-dharma), Part Two. Question: The Supreme Mundane Dharma has already been understood.
The secondary factors of arising, abiding, aging,
and impermanence are also the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
Are those [secondary factors] also considered to be the supreme mundane dharmas?
Whether this is correct or incorrect, what fault is there in either case?
If that attainment were also the "supreme mundane dharma," then after one has attained the fruit of an Arya, [it would follow that one must attain it again].
The aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) should manifest repeatedly.
If those attainments were not the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*),
why would they be considered the attainment of the fruits of śrāmaṇya?
Is this the fruit of śramaṇaship?
Is it attained through the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma),
or not through the supreme mundane dharma?
Answer: That attainment is certainly not the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Once the noble fruit has been attained, the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) do not arise again.
Question: Why is it that while the attainment of the fruits of śrāmaṇya is the fruit of śrāmaṇya,
the attainment of the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) is not?
Is it not the state of supreme mundane dharma?
Answer: Because it is manifested by the accomplishment of the fruits of śrāmaṇya;
the attainment of the fruits of śrāmaṇya is itself the fruit of śrāmaṇya.
The state of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) is manifested by way of being an equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya).
Since that attainment is neither an equal-and-immediate condition nor does it conform to the arising and so forth of that [dharma] in the same manner, [it is not the same].
Therefore, those [attainments] cannot be the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*). Nor can they be the Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), or Patiences (*kṣānti*),
because once one has attained the Noble [Path], it would be improper for the Heat and so forth to manifest again.
Some say that its acquisition (*prāpti*) is also the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). Question:
If that were so, then after having attained the fruit of an noble one (*āryaphala*), [what would happen]?
The aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) should manifest repeatedly.
Answer: It is accepted that there is no fault even if only a portion of them manifests;
that is to say, for those that are associated (*saṃprayukta*), they do not manifest repeatedly.
Regarding those that are dissociated, there is a re-manifestation [of the roots].
It is the same for the attainment of Heat, Summits, and Patience.
Other masters say:
The acquisition (*prāpti*) that arises simultaneously with them is also the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*);
since that which arises subsequently is not [the Supreme Mundane Dharma], the aforementioned fault does not apply.
The same holds true for "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the other stages.
The commentary states:
Whether they arise simultaneously with it or arise subsequently,
all such acquisitions are not the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma).
Because their categories are identical,
the same applies to "Heat" (ūṣmagata) and the others;
therefore, the initial explanation is logically sound.
Question: Why is it that the arising, abiding, aging,
and impermanence of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) are also not considered to be the Supreme Mundane Dharma?
Answer: Birth and the others share the same fruit as that [conditioned phenomenon];
they proceed in mutual association and are inseparable;
they are always conjoined, being neither prior nor posterior.
The characteristic and that which is characterized have never been separate;
for this reason, it is also the "supreme worldly dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
However, its attainment (*prāpti*) does not share the same fruit as that dharma.
They do not proceed together;
by their very nature they are separate and do not combine,
whether one precedes or follows the other.
Acquisition (*prāpti*) and that which is acquired (*prāpya*) may at times be separated from one another;
for example, tree bark may sometimes be separated from the tree.
Therefore, acquisition is not the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
The attainment of the stages of Heat, Summits, and Patience is likewise.
Question: How many applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) does the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) possess?
Answer: In the present moment, it possesses only one.
The application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that takes mixed objects has all four [applications] in the future, because it resembles the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Question: How many conditions does the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) have?
Answer: There are four conditions, namely:
the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Regarding the causal condition:
That is to say, the dharmas that are associated with it, co-existent with it, and of its own kind, act as the cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
As for acting as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
it means that [the dharma] acts as the equal-and-immediate condition for the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
As an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
it means that it serves as the object-condition for those minds and mental factors that take it as their object.
As a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya),...
That is to say, excluding its own nature, it serves as the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Question: How many conditions does the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) possess?
Answer: There are four conditions.
Regarding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), it refers to factors such as those associated with it, those co-existent with it, and those of the same class.
Regarding the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*):
it refers to the already-arisen superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): [it refers to the objects of that patience].
This refers to the five aggregates of the desire realm.
Regarding the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*),
it refers to all dharmas other than its own nature.
Question: Although the text does not explicitly state it, the meaning must necessarily exist.
What is the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*)?
Answer: It is the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
This means that it can sustain all noble paths (*āryamārga*).
Other masters say that it is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*).
This means that it is able to attain the fruit of the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Some say that the first knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is this.
This means that it can sustain all dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Alternatively, some say it is anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This means that among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), this is the most excellent.
Furthermore, some say it is the realm of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇadhātu*).
This means that among all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, this is the most supreme.
Some say it is the final moment of the noble path of an arhat.
That is to say, just as the final momentary mind in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*),
so too the final momentary untainted mind (*anāsravacitta*) of an Arhat is called the "Supreme Supramundane Dharma" (*lokottarāgradharma*).
Some say it is the final mind of an arhat; that is to say,
just as the final mind of the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma).
Such is the final mind of an Arhat;
it is the supreme mundane dharma (*lokottara-agra-dharma*).
The commentary states:
That person should not make such a statement,
because the final mind of an arhat is not a supramundane dharma.
Among these various explanations, the first is the correct one.
Because it is able to sustain all noble paths (*āryamārga*),
for what reason is it called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)?
[The following] is explained at length.
Question: For what reason was this treatise composed?
Answer: Although the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) has been explained previously, the reasons for its designation have not yet been stated.
Because I now wish to speak of it:
for example, when a person is universally acclaimed as preeminent in the world,
it is logically appropriate that they be described as such.
Regarding the causes for establishing such names, is it based on lineage,
or on physical appearance, strength, wealth, nobility, or retinue? Which is considered the most preeminent?
This treatise is composed for this very reason.
Why is it called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)?
Answer: Because such mental states and mental factors [are so designated].
Among all other worldly dharmas,
it is the most supreme, the most excellent,
the longest-lasting, and the most venerable.
Because it is supreme and most excellent,
it is called the "Highest Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
This refers to the mind and its mental factors.
Is it called "foremost" because it is preeminent over all other worldly dharmas,
or is it called "foremost" because it is preeminent [only] in comparison to others?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
If it were called "foremost" simply because it is superior to all else,
how could this possibly surpass the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of direct realization (*abhisamaya-pṛṣṭhalabdha-saṃvṛti-jñāna*)? Yet,
it is precisely that conventional knowledge cultivated at the conclusion of direct realization [which is so].
This is an attendant and subordinate factor of the path of seeing;
the wisdom of the path of seeing possesses superior power,
whereas this dharma does not.
Furthermore, how could this surpass the mixed cultivation of dhyāna?
Nevertheless, those meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the births they induce are not shared with ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
This dharma is not like that.
Furthermore, how could this surpass the roots of goodness cultivated at the time of the initial knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
Nevertheless, when cultivating that [knowledge], one is purified from the basis of all obstructions.
This dharma is not like that.
Furthermore, how could this be superior to emptiness-of-emptiness or the wishlessness-of-wishlessness?
The signless-signless,
the three samādhis;
yet even they are still able to feel revulsion toward the noble path.
How much more so for that which is with outflows?
This dharma is not like that.
If it were called "foremost" merely because it is superior in some respect, [then other dharmas would also deserve such a name].
The stages of Heat (ūṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), Patience (kṣānti), and so forth,
should also be called "foremost," because each is superior to the wholesome roots of its respective lower stage.
Some have stated this as follows:
This dharma is called "foremost" because it is preeminent in every respect;
however, this is said with reference to its ability to open the gateway to the Noble Path,
and not on the basis of all qualities.
This refers to the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamaya-prsthalabdha-saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and so forth;
although they possess the superior qualities previously described,
they all lack the power to open the gateway to the Noble Path.
This dharma alone is capable;
therefore, it is entirely superior. Some may say:
This dharma is called "foremost" because it excels all other matters; that is to say, all superior matters,
such as the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), are accomplished by means of this.
Why is this so? Because if these dharmas did not open the gateway to the Noble Path, those various superior qualities would not even be cultivated in their essence.
Moreover, there is a superior function;
it is only by means of this dharma that one opens the gateway to the Noble Path,
and only when one cultivates its essence does it possess such a superior function.
Since those various superior qualities are established by virtue of this [wisdom],
it is therefore superior to all other things;
so say some other masters.
This dharma is called "foremost" because it is superior to its own category.
Question: If that is so, then stages such as "Heat" (ūṣmagata) should also be called foremost, since each is superior to the wholesome roots of their respective lower levels.
The answer is: because neither of these two parts is supreme.
That is to say, worldly wholesome dharmas generally comprise two parts:
first, those based on ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Second, regarding the noble ones:

although the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) are not called "supreme" in relation to the conventional wisdom (saṃvṛtijñāna) and so forth of the noble ones, [they are so called in relation to other mundane states].
And regarding ordinary beings,
the meditative concentrations,
immeasurables, and liberations that they have attained.
The bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
up to the attainment of the foremost [attainments],
as well as volition and the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*).
Mindfulness of breathing, the various foundations of mindfulness,
the threefold contemplation of meaning, and proficiency in the seven bases [occur] within the stages of Heat, Peak, and Patience.
All of these are supreme;
the stages of "Heat" and so forth are not so.
Therefore, this alone is designated as the "Supreme Mundane Dharma."
Question: In what sense is this called "foremost"?
Answer: Because it is most excellent and because it can induce the foremost.
Because one attains the foremost fruit and because one proceeds toward the foremost nature,
it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Some say that this is the ultimate truth (paramārtha) because it can subdue the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
Other masters say:
Because this is the final mind of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*),
it is like the top of a tall banner from which nothing higher exists;
this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Question: Is that which is spoken of herein the most excellent, the most preeminent,
the longest-lasting, or the most venerable?
Which is superior and more excellent?
What is the distinction between them?
Some teachers say:
There is no distinction,
for all of these are expositions of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, there are those who say:
There are also distinctions.
For instance, there is a distinction in their names;
that is to say, this name is supreme.
It is even called "sublime.
Furthermore, there are also distinctions regarding its relation to the various roots of goodness;
that is to say, in relation to those produced through hearing, this is called the most excellent.
In relation to that which is accomplished through reflection (*cintāmayī*), it is called "superior" (*viśiṣṭa*).
In relation to the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhā-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), and the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it is called "vast" (*vipula*).
In relation to "heat" (*uṣmagata*), it is called "venerable" (*guruka*).
In relation to the Summits (mūrdhan), it is called "superior" (uttama);
in relation to Patience (kṣānti), it is called "excellent" (praṇīta).
Furthermore, there is also a distinction based on the supporting stages (bhūmi).
That is to say, based on the *anāgamya* (preliminary concentration), it is called "supreme";
based on the first *dhyāna*, it is called "excellent";
and based on the intermediate *dhyāna*, it is called "vast."
Based on the second dhyāna, it is called "venerable";
based on the third dhyāna, it is called "superior";
based on the fourth dhyāna, it is called "sublime."
Furthermore, there is also a distinction based on the difference in meaning:
it is called "supreme" (agra) because it reaches the ultimate limit (koṭi).
It is called "superior" because it is subsumed within the highest grade;
it is called "long" because it brings about auspiciousness;
it is called "venerable" because its essence is one of upward progression.
It is called "superior" because its nature is firm and stable;
it is called "wondrous" because it fulfills all aspirations.
Furthermore, there is a distinction between its essence and its function.
There is also a distinction:
namely, because this serves as the immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and so forth,
it is called "supreme."
It is called "superior" because it surpasses all the roots of goodness of ordinary beings;
it is called "long" because it outshines all mundane roots of goodness.
Because he is able to attain supreme virtues,
he is called "Venerable" (Guru).
Because he is indivisible, he is called "Supreme" (Uttara).
It is called "sublime" because it resembles the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, there are differences in its characteristics and functions,
and thus distinctions exist as well.
This refers to the final mind of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*);
thus, like the tip of a tree, it is called "the foremost," for it is capable of opening the gateway to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
Therefore, it is called "superior" (*viśeṣa*).
Because its faculties are sharp and keen, it is called "prolonged" (*āyata*).
This is because, among all the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), this is the most supreme.
Therefore, he is called "Venerable.
Because he subdues all enemies that are the afflictions,
he is called "Supreme."
It is called "excellent" because it leads to desirable results.
Other masters say that these six phrases [are as follows].
The subsequent section explains what preceded it;
thus, there is a distinction.
That is to say, because this is the most excellent, it is called "the foremost."
It is called "supreme" because it is victorious;
it is called "victorious" because it is preeminent;
it is called "preeminent" because it is honored.
It is called "supreme" (vara) because it is superior;
it is called "excellent" (agra) because it is sublime.
For these reasons, it is termed the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma).
Furthermore, these mental states and mental factors,
acting as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
cause one to relinquish the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) and attain the nature of a noble one (*āryatva*).
Abandoning the nature of error and attaining the nature of correctness,
one is able to enter the state of rightness and emergence from birth;
therefore, it is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Regarding "abandoning the state of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*):
it refers to these mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) that are able to abandon the state of an ordinary person.
Question: Who is it that truly abandons the state of an ordinary person?
[If it were so,] would it be the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma),
or would it be the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti)? If that were the case, what fault would there be?
If the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) were truly able to abandon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*),
how could one abide in it while abandoning it?
If the Receptivity to the Knowledge of Suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*) were truly able to abandon the nature of an ordinary person...
In what stage does this occur?
Is it abandoned at the time of arising, or is it abandoned at the time of ceasing?
If it were abandoned at the time of arising, [then...]
How can that which is future be capable of performing an action?
If it were to relinquish [its nature] at the time of cessation,
then its very nature would have already been relinquished.
Furthermore, what is it that is abandoned?
Some say it is the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (laukikāgradharma).
It is precisely capable of abandoning the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Question: Since this [nature] is itself a dharma of an ordinary person, how can one abide in it while being able to abandon it?
Answer: There is no fault in abiding in that [state] and relinquishing that [state],
just as a trainer mounts an elephant to train the elephant and mounts a horse to train the horse.
He boards the boat and steers the boat;
he mounts the chariot and drives the chariot,
like a victorious warrior who ascends [his mount] to overcome and harm his enemies.
Just as a woodcutter climbs a tree to fell it,
so too is the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*):
relying upon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), it is able to abandon it.

Some say that the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is precisely what abandons the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*); that is to say,
at the very moment it arises, it abandons the state of being an ordinary person.

At the stage of its actual cessation, it is able to sever the ten types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
This is like a lamp: when it arises, it emits light and dispels darkness;
when it ceases, it consumes the wick, heats the vessel, and exhausts the oil.
Question: How can that which is future be capable of performing an action?
For a single dharma to have two functions—how could such a principle possibly be correct?
Answer: There is no contradiction with the meaning; even if this is accepted, what fault would there be?
That is to say, all phenomena possess functional efficacy regarding the future.
In total there are three categories.
The first is internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*),
such as the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*).
The second is external phenomena,
such as the light of the sun and so forth.
The third is internal-external phenomena.
Just as with the characteristics of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*),
it is commonly known in the world that a single lamp serves many purposes;
what fault is there in the two functions of the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*)?

Other masters say that the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) and the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) mutually support one another to abandon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
That is to say, although the Supreme Mundane Dharmas are constantly opposed to the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*),
they cannot abandon it alone because their power is inferior.
From this, the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is induced;
together with its auxiliary power, it abandons the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
It is, for example, like a weak man who relies upon a strong man.
By mutually assisting one another, they are able to subdue their enemies;
for this reason, the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are like the Path of Uninterrupted Succession (*ānantaryamārga*).
The patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is like the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*);
it abandons the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Therefore, [it follows that] the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukika-agra-dharma*) [are the path of preparation].
The possession of the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) ceases simultaneously with the acquisition [of the path];
the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises simultaneously with the non-possession of the state of being an ordinary person.
"Attaining the noble nature" refers to these mental states and mental factors that are able to attain the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Because it is able to sustain all noble dharmas,
it is for this reason designated as the "noble nature" (*āryatva*).
Furthermore, although other paths of the noble ones are also subsumed within the noble nature, [this specific one is so designated].
However, because it is not attained through this [path], it is not mentioned.
Some say that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is entirely of a noble nature (*āryatva*).
Other masters say that all noble paths (āryamārga) are of a noble nature (āryatva). If this were not so,
[the following would occur].
In the paths of cultivation and no-more-learning, one would not possess the nature of an noble one (*āryatva*);
thus, such a person should not be called a noble one (*ārya*).
[This concerns] the question regarding the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
It can only induce the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering;
it cannot even attain the dharma-knowledge of suffering itself,
much less anything else.
Why is it said that this attains the nature of an ārya?
The answer is: all noble paths (āryamārga) that are capable of making one an ārya are termed the "nature of an ārya" (āryatva).
Because they belong to the same category, the attainment of a portion of those [dharmas] by the Supreme Mundane Dharmas is also called "attainment," just as it is said that one "burns a garment."
Regarding "abandoning wrong nature":
this refers to these mental states and mental factors being able to abandon three kinds of wrong nature.
First, the perversity of action;
second, the perversity of destination;
third, the perversity of view.
The perversity of karma refers to the five deeds of immediate retribution.
The perversity of rebirth refers to...
This refers to the three evil destinies.
"Seeing what is of wrong nature" refers to the five inverted views.
Question: In this stage, the karma that leads to a wrong destination was not previously accomplished;
at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna), [it is accomplished].
Having abandoned the nature of wrong views,
one then attains the ultimate.
How can it be said that this stage is able to abandon the three natures of perversity?
Answer: This stage is called "equanimity" (upekṣā) due to three conditions.
First, it is called equanimity because of non-action;
that is to say, the absence of the perversity of karma.
Second, it is called "abandonment" by virtue of not proceeding,
namely, by entering into wrongness (*mithyātva*).
Third, it is called "abandonment" by virtue of not practicing.
This refers to seeing the nature of falsity.
Question: Since the three conditions have already been fulfilled at the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), why is it said that one abandons falsity only at this stage?
Answer: Now, because that basis is refuted, it is said that one abandons it.
Question: What is meant by "that basis"?
Answer: It is the state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva), which is unobscured and neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
This refers to the fact that the various afflictions rely upon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*);
they harm all sentient beings,
causing them to undergo various sufferings within birth and death.
Like a lion king,
relying upon an unobscured-neutral cave,
he is able to slay various kinds of animals and other such beings.
Because the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is able to abandon that basis, which is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*),
it is said to "abandon them."
Other masters say that the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) is its antidote.
Because the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma) draw forth and cause [the Path of Seeing] to arise,
it is said that one abandons those [mundane dharmas].

Question: Since the nature of the wrong course of karma is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), how can the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) act as its antidote?
Answer: The patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering...
It can serve as five kinds of antidotes, namely:
the antidote of relinquishment, the antidote of abandonment, the antidote of maintaining, the antidote of non-action, and the antidote of non-approaching.
Regarding the antidote of relinquishment:
This means that it is able to abandon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). As for the "counteractive abandonment" (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*),
it means that this is able to sever the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
The antidote of maintenance refers to its ability to maintain all subsequent stages of the noble path.
The antidote of non-action refers to its ability to ensure that the five deeds of immediate retribution are never committed again.
"Not proceeding toward [the opposite]" means that this causes one to ultimately not proceed toward the three evil destinies.
"Attaining the right nature" means:
That is to say, these minds and mental factors are able to attain the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*),
because they are capable of upholding all true dharmas (*saddharma*).
Therefore, for the time being, that [state] is described as the "right nature" (*samyaktva*).
Furthermore, although other noble paths (*āryamārga*) are also subsumed under the right nature,
they are not mentioned here because they are not what is attained by this [attainment].
Some say that the entire path of seeing is the right nature (*samyaktva*).
Other masters say:
All noble paths are of right nature;
were it otherwise,
there would be no path of cultivation or path of no-more-learning.
One would not possess the state of correctness (samyaktva);
thus, one should not be called a noble one (ārya).
[This concerns] the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma).
It can only induce the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*); it cannot even attain the dharma-knowledge of suffering itself,
much less anything else.
Why is it said that this attains the state of correctness (*samyaktva*)?
The answer is: because all noble paths (*āryamārga*) are free from inversion (*viparyāsa*), they are all states of correctness.
Because they belong to the same category,
the attainment of even one part of those [dharmas] by means of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) is also called "attainment.
This is as when it is said that "the garment is burned."
"Those capable of entering the state of right determination and transcendence" refers to these mental states and their associated factors that are able to enter the path of seeing.
Question: All noble paths are both of right nature (*samyaktva*) and of emergence from birth (*niyāma*).
Why is it that here only the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is specifically mentioned?
Answer: All afflictions, or various forms of craving,
prevent the maturation of all roots of goodness and cause the arising of faults through the moistening and conjoining of the various realms of existence (*bhava*).
Although all are termed "arising" (*jāti*) and are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),
regarding this explained meaning of arising,
the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is able to serve as its ultimate antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Therefore, it is specifically regarding the path of seeing that one speaks of "separation from birth," for all false views must necessarily be abandoned by means of the path of seeing.
Because it is able to bring about ultimate severance, it is called "right nature" (*samyaktva*).
Since it is induced immediately after the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*),
it is said that one is able to enter "right nature and departure from birth" (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Furthermore, all afflictions or various forms of craving can prevent the roots of virtue from reaching maturity,
and cause the moistening and coalescence of the various realms of existence (bhava) to arise as faults.
All these are termed "births.
Once the Path of Seeing has arisen, it subdues their power so that they no longer produce the fault of being predominant births.
For this reason, the path of seeing alone is termed "separation from birth" (*vairāgya*).
The meaning of the phrase "entering into the state of rightness" (*samyaktva-niyāma*) is as explained previously.
On account of this principle, the Venerable Ghoṣaka made the following statement:
When the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of sentient beings have matured, they are able to enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
therefore, the path of seeing is called "leaving birth" (*niyāma*).
Furthermore, regarding the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya-kleśa*):
It causes all sentient beings to fall into the evil destinies and undergo various intense sufferings,
just as raw food remaining in the body for a long time can produce all manner of extreme pain and affliction.
Therefore, these afflictions are said to be "birth.
Because the Path of Seeing can extinguish them, it is called "separation from birth.
This is what is meant by the phrase "entering into the state of rightness."
It is also as previously explained.
Furthermore, because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other such [afflictions] are stubborn and difficult to subdue—
like a wild beast that is headstrong— they are called "born" (*jāti*).
It is called "born of separation" (*vairāgyaja*) because the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is capable of extinguishing [the defilements].
The expression "entering into rightness" (*samyaktva-niyāma*) is also as previously explained.
Furthermore, in this context, the term "birth" (*janman*) signifies the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Because it is capable of giving rise to violent and evil afflictions and karmas,
and because those are abandoned upon the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), it is called "born of detachment" (*vairāgyaja*).
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, the aggregates of afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation assist one another in succession,
drawing forth an infinite series of births;
once the path of seeing has arisen, it destroys their power.
This prevents the fault of inviting an infinite succession of births;
therefore, the path of seeing alone is called "leaving birth.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, within the body of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
afflictions and evil karma are extremely unruly; therefore,
it is called "birth" (*jāti*).
The various practitioners of yoga sink into this;
the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) pulls them out and places them within the state of the noble ones (ārya),
and is therefore called "leaving birth" (vairāgya).
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, the afflictions to be abandoned through insight are like the roots of a tree.
It would entail the fault of birth being endless;
because the path of seeing (darśanamārga) eradicates it forever,
it is called "freedom from birth" (vairāgya).
The rest is as previously stated.
Other masters say that this text should state "entering into the determination of correctness" (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Why is this so? It is because at this time, one enters and exits from the group of the indeterminate (aniyata-rāśi) into the group of those fixed in rightness (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi).

Furthermore, at that time, the practitioner abandons the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva), which is the basis for the group of those fixed in error (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi), and enters the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), which is the basis for the group of those fixed in rightness.
Therefore, this is called "entering into the certainty of the right nature.
Furthermore, at that time, the practitioner abandons the five commonalities and enters the eight commonalities.
As for the five commonalities:
This refers to the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) of all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
It is based upon that [homogeneity] that one is able to commit the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*).
Regarding the eight types of homogeneity:
This refers to all noble ones (*ārya*);
because they rely upon that homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) to attain the four fruits of the paths,
at that time they abandon the category of wrong certainty (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*) and enter the category of right certainty (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*).
For this reason, it is called "entering the determination of the correct nature" (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Furthermore, the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) that is entered is not the group of those fixed in error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*);
therefore, it is called the "correct nature."
It is called "definite" because it is not the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*).
Some say that this term indicates entry into and the maintenance of the state of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Because this term *niyama* also expresses the sense of "sustaining," it is like the place where cattle, horses,
and so forth are fed and protected.
Just as one maintains those types [of beings] so that they do not become heedless,
so too it is with the practitioners of yoga;
having entered the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), they never again fall into negligence.
The term "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) is said to signify "entry into the correct nature" (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The masters of the Dārṣṭāntika school explain it thus:
this term indicates entry into the "correct nature of dissociation" (*samyaktva-visaṃyoga*).
By the term "niyama," the sense of restraint (*niyama*) is also indicated;
that is to say, "restraint" (*ni-*) also indicates the sense of separation (*-yama*).
All noble paths are eternally free from bondage;
this is called *niyama*.
The rest is as previously explained.
The proponents of phonology say:
This sound "ni" indicates entering the state of correctness and not departing;
for the sound "nir," which means "departing," also indicates the meaning of "not."
This means that it both prohibits [unwholesome conduct] and reveals its lack of meaning;
for when practitioners of yoga have attained the Noble Path, [they no longer engage in such things].
Ultimately, one does not go to the destinies of non-virtuous persons;
therefore, the noble path is called *nyāya*.
The rest is as previously explained.
Some say that this passage should state:
"One enters into the correct nature of reality;
all noble paths [are included therein]."
Because it accords with principle,
it is called "in accordance with principle" (*yoniśas*).
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this passage should state:
"one enters into the state of right determination from the stage of equality.
The stage of equality is precisely the time of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
The term "right nature" (samyaktva) indicates the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and so forth.
From the state of the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*),
one is able to enter the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Therefore, it is called "entry.
Question: Are those who are equanimous also of the right nature?
Answer: This should be treated as a "consequent-to-the-latter" (anuloma-paścāt-sūtra) formula.
That is to say, all that is "right-natured" (samyaktva) is indeed "equal" (sama);
however, there are things that are "equal" which are not "right-natured."
This essence is precisely the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma).
Question: For what reason is the Supreme Mundane Dharma "equal" (samatā) yet not "the true nature" (bhūtatā)?
Answer: Since beginningless time,
the mind and mental factors have become non-upright due to being afflicted and disturbed by various afflictions, unwholesome actions, and inverted views.
Because the Supreme Mundane Dharmas subdue and eliminate those [afflictions], they cause the mind and mental factors to function with rectitude; therefore,
they are called "equanimity."
However, because it is associated with outflows (*āsrava*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is not termed the "Right State" (*samyaktva*).
Furthermore, the lineages of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas,
and Śrāvakas are identical in this stage.
Because it abides in the highest degree of the highest degree,
it is called "equality.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, they are called "equal" because their manifestation and so forth are equal;
that is to say, within this state, all practitioners are equal.
Because they all manifest within a single kṣaṇa.
Furthermore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) occupies a middle position.
It is called "equilibrium" because it is like the cord of a suspended scale.
Just as when a scale weighs an object with the cord hanging between its pans,
if there is any partiality in weight, the balance will be uneven, tilting low on one side and high on the other.
The Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are likewise.
Situated between the noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), once the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) has arisen,
they belong exclusively to the category of the noble ones.
If the supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) is in the process of ceasing,
one abides exclusively in the category of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Therefore, this alone is the state of equality (*samatā-bhūmi*).
Question: At that time, one is still categorized within the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
Why, then, is it called "abiding in the state of equality"?
Answer: Although at that time one remains within the stage of an ordinary person, [one abides in equality].
Yet, by turning one's back on the state of an ordinary being and seeking the stage of a noble one,
it is called "equality. Others are not so.
Furthermore, because the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) and the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) are equal in four respects,
they are termed "equal."
First, regarding the stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth:
this means that based upon whichever stage one gives rise to the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*),
one likewise relies upon that very same stage for the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
Second, the equality of faculties (*indriya*),
meaning that if the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is associated with these faculties.
The same applies to its association with the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
Third is the equality of aspect (*ākāra*),
which means that if this aspect is the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), [the subsequent moments share that same aspect].
This very mode of activity constitutes the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Fourth, regarding the equality of the object (*ālambana*):

that is to say, if one gives rise to the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) by taking this object as its focus, one likewise gives rise to the Supreme Mundane Dharma by taking this very same object as its focus.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this:
some recite the name as "entry into rightness and departure from birth" (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
This is because the noble paths eternally extinguish perversions; therefore, they are called "rightness."
It is also called "born of separation" because it arises from being separated [from the antidotes].

That is to say, since beginningless time, the two categories of afflictions—those abandoned through seeing and those abandoned through cultivation—have been mutually combined and have performed various evil deeds;
because their nature is rigid and stubborn, they are said to be "birth."
Once the Path of Seeing has arisen, it severs a portion of those [afflictions] and causes them to become eternally estranged from one another;
because the Supreme Mundane Dharmas serve as the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for this portion, they are called "entry."
Some recite that this is called "entry into the determination of correctness" (*samyaktva-niyāma*), meaning the uncontaminated continuity during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Because there is necessarily no other interruption, it is called "determination"; subsequent stages are not so.
The rest is as previously explained.
Regarding the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*),
it should be stated that they belong to the desire realm, and so forth, as extensively described.

Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed? Answer: Although the causes and conditions for establishing those names have already been explained, they have not yet been analyzed according to which realm (*dhātu*) they belong to; we now wish to analyze them.
It is like when a person says "superior," having already stated the reasons for its superiority.
Furthermore, because it was not known in which country or city he resided,
this treatise was composed for that reason as well.
Moreover, it is intended to refute the divergent tenets held by other schools.
This refers to the tenet held by the Mahāsāṃghika school:
that the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) pertain to both the desire realm and the form realm. Why is this so?
That is to say, according to the Vātsīputrīya school's tenet, if a given stage possesses the conventional wisdoms (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that arise at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
then that stage must also possess the "highest mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*).
The Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma) pertain to both the realms of form and formlessness. Why is this?
It is because those [realms] are grounds where the various noble paths exist.
In this stage, there is the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma).
According to the tenets of the Mahīśāsaka school,
the supreme mundane dharma pertains to all three realms of existence.
Why is this? It is because they say that when the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) arises on a particular stage,
the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) cultivated therein [are abandoned].
In this stage, there is the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
According to the tenets of the Dharmaguptaka school,
the supreme mundane dharma pertains to both those factors bound to the three realms and those that are unbound.
Why is this so? Because these so-called "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgra-dharma) are called "mundane," they pertain to the bonds of the three realms;
yet, because they are called "supreme," they also pertain to that which is unconditioned (anāsrava).
Within that same school, there is another distinct tenet:
the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgra-dharma) are neither bound to the three realms nor are they unbound. Why is this so?
He says that because these "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) are called "supreme," they are not bound to the three realms;
yet because they are called "mundane," they are also not unbound.
