This treatise is composed in order to refute the distinct tenets of other schools and to reveal our own school’s position.
Regarding the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*):
should they be said to belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
It is stated that [the Supreme Mundane Dharmas] are bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*). This indicates that the Supreme Mundane Dharmas are exclusively bound to the realm of form.
Although this statement exists, one must further explain the reason for it.
Why should this dharma not be said to be bound to the desire realm?

Answer: It is not by means of a path of the desire realm that one can sever the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and restrain the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), so as to prevent the envelopments of the desire realm from arising again.
Thus, by means of the path of the form realm, one is able to sever the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and restrain the fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
causing the fetters of the desire realm not to manifest again. If,
by means of the path of the desire realm, one is able to sever the hindrances and restrain the fetters...
It causes the fetters of the desire realm not to manifest again;
thus, the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) should be said to be bound to the desire realm.
However, it is not by means of the path of the desire realm that one can sever the hindrances and restrain the fetters so as to prevent the fetters of the desire realm from arising again;
rather, it is by means of the path of the form realm that one can sever the hindrances and restrain the fetters.
It causes the fetters of the desire realm not to manifest again;
therefore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) should not be said to be bound to the desire realm.
In this context, the expression "restraining so that they do not manifest again" indicates the sense of ultimate restraint such that they do not arise.
This is because the path of the desire realm cannot ultimately sever the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and restrain the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) so that they never arise again.
Therefore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) does not exist [therein];
because the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) is not like this, it exists there.
Question: Why is it not present in the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu)?
Is there a path that is ultimately characterized by cessation and non-arising within the form realm?
Answer: No; the desire realm is not a state of meditative concentration (samāhita-bhūmi).
It is neither a stage of cultivation nor a stage of freedom from passion;
therefore, there is no path of ultimate abandonment that prevents [the defilements] from arising.
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) is a stage of meditative concentration (samāhitabhūmi).
This is the stage of cultivation and the stage of detachment from passion;
therefore, this path exists.
Furthermore, regarding the desire realm:
Because the unwholesome roots are strong and the wholesome roots are weak, this path does not exist [in the desire realm].
Because the wholesome roots are strong and there are no unwholesome roots, this path exists [in the form realm].
Furthermore, in the desire realm, the predominant causes of the unwholesome are nurtured.
The wholesome is not so;
it is nourished by the superior causes of wholesome dharmas of the form realm,
as there is no unwholesome therein.
Furthermore, in the desire realm, unwholesome states are like a powerful host,
whereas wholesome states are like guests lacking influence.
In the form realm, wholesome states are like a powerful host.
Because there is no unwholesomeness [in that state].
Furthermore, unwholesome states of the desire realm can sever the roots of goodness,
whereas wholesome states do not.
The wholesome dharmas of the form realm sever the unwholesome roots because there are no unwholesome states there.
Furthermore, in the desire realm, modes of deportment do not involve mutual respect or deference, being like those of husband and wife.
In the form realm, the modes of deportment are mutually respectful and difficult to transgress, like those between a mother and her child.
Furthermore, in the desire realm, the modes of deportment lack such restraint,
being like that of a prince compared to the son of an elder.
Because they share the same prison,
those in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) maintain a sense of decorum and restraint,
just as a prince behaves toward one who has committed an evil deed.
Because they share the same prison.
Furthermore, the roots of goodness of the desire realm [are opposed] to the afflictions of the desire realm.
They must be bound by the same fetter and lack the power to sever it;
just as a person who is bound cannot free themselves, much less harm another,
so it is in this case as well.
Because the wholesome roots of the form realm and the afflictions of the form realm differ in their levels of bondage and their specific bases, [the former] can even sever those of its own realm;

how much more so could it not sever those of lower realms? Furthermore, the wholesome roots of the desire realm are necessarily defiled by the craving of the desire realm and thus cannot be permanently abandoned.
Just as one does not abandon a friend even if they are inferior,
so too there are roots of goodness belonging to the form realm that are not objects of craving for the form realm.
Because the stages (*bhūmi*) to which one is attached differ,
one is even able to permanently sever craving for one's own realm;
how much more so, then, could one not sever the cravings of the lower stages?
Furthermore, when severing afflictions by means of the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*),
one cultivates delight in one's own stage while cultivating revulsion toward and the severance of what is below.
This is because in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no lower stage toward which one could cultivate revulsion and severance.
There is no path capable of ultimately severing and restraining [the defilements] so that they do not arise,
because within the form realm there are lower [levels] that can be loathed and severed;
thus, there exists a path capable of ultimately severing and restraining them so that they do not arise.
Other masters say that the statement regarding the restraint of non-arising in this context indicates the meaning of a temporary restraint from arising.
Since even the path of the desire realm cannot temporarily sever the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) or restrain the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) so that they do not arise again,
how much less could it do so ultimately?
Therefore, there is no "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
It is not so in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Therefore, therein exist both temporary restraint from arising and ultimate restraint from arising.
In this way, there is that which has parts and that which lacks parts;
that which has shadow and that which lacks shadow;
that which has subsequent bondage and that which lacks subsequent bondage.
One should know that it is likewise in the case of crushing the branches and trunk, uprooting the root,
subduing the entanglements and stains, and eliminating the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Question: It may be that the desire realm lacks the path of ultimate cessation through restraint that prevents [defilements] from arising;
but could it also lack the path of temporary cessation through restraint that prevents them from arising?
Answer: Although such a path exists.
And it is not to be trusted. Why is this?
Because it is not firm, does not endure for long, and does not flow on continuously.
It is not predominant, lacks continuity,
and does not persist for long;
the mind quickly grasps and quickly relinquishes its object.
Because they lack the superior power to subdue the afflictions,
they are unable to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma),
just as duckweed and other weeds float upon the surface of a pond.
If one throws small stones into a pond of frogs,
although they may momentarily separate at first, they soon follow one another back together;
such is the nature of the desire realm.
Although there are paths that temporarily sever the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth,
they are not to be trusted;
this is explained at length as previously stated.
Within the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
there is not only the path that brings about ultimate cessation and non-manifestation,
but there is also the path that brings about temporary cessation and non-manifestation, which is deeply worthy of confidence.
Why is this? Because that path is firm,
enduring, continuous, and preeminent.
Continuing in succession for a long time, it persists;
the mind does not quickly grasp or abandon its object;
possessing superior power, it subdues all afflictions.
Therefore, one is able to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth.
It is like when duckweed and other such things float upon the water of a pond,
and a great elephant or a massive stone is thrown into it.
Once long separated,
it is difficult to reunite;
likewise, in the form realm as well, there are paths that temporarily sever the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
And it can be relied upon with confidence.
As explained extensively before,
one should therefore know that in the desire realm there is no path for severing the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth.
It is not so for the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Therefore, it should be stated that the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma) are exclusively bound to the form realm and are not bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Question: The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) cannot sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Why, then, is it said that "if one uses the path of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one can sever the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and restrain the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*)"?
It causes the fetters of the desire realm to no longer manifest.
Thus, the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) should be described as being associated with the desire realm, and so forth.
Answer: Although the "Dharma Supreme in the World" does not sever the fetters, this root of goodness is supreme, wondrous, and foremost;
it resides in a profound and remote state.
One ought to abide in the same stage as that path capable of severing the fetters; therefore,
one should realize it by means of this very path.
Furthermore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) necessarily induces the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) and resides in the same stage as that Path of Seeing.
Since the Path of Seeing is capable of severing all afflictions (kleśa), [the Supreme Mundane Dharma must likewise be so].
Therefore, the path that severs the fetters can serve as this proof.
Furthermore, since the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) has already produced the utmost revulsion toward the desire realm, [it follows that the subsequent path must be supramundane].
It should reside in the same stage as the path that serves as the antidote to the afflictions of the desire realm; therefore,
it can be drawn from there.
[The opponent] asserts that this dharma exists.

[The proponent] asks: If that were so, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) would exist only in the stage of the Not-Yet-Arrived (anāgamya), because it is only in the Not-Yet-Arrived stage that one can abandon the afflictions of the Desire Realm.
The higher stages should not exist.
Answer: There are two kinds of antidotes.
First, the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*).
Second is the antidote of repudiation (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*).
In the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-bhūmi*),
both types of antidotes are present regarding the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Although the five higher stages lack the antidote of abandonment with respect to the desire realm,
they possess the antidote of revulsion; therefore,
they also possess the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*).
The Venerable Ghosaka has stated that within the six levels of the form realm (rūpadhātu),
there exist both types of antidotes for the afflictions of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
It is not that the paths of the five higher stages are incapable of abandoning [defilements];
rather, because they have already been abandoned previously by the *anāgamya* stage,
although these [higher paths] possess the power to abandon, there is nothing further to be abandoned.
For example, it is like six people who share a common enemy and deliberate together, saying: "Wherever [he may be]..."
The one who catches them is then harmed;
among them, one person is caught first and killed,
while the remaining five, though they possess the power to harm, cannot be harmed.
Furthermore, it is like six people each holding a lamp who enter a dark room one after another;
when the first lamp enters, all the darkness is dispelled.
Furthermore, although other [lights] possess power, there is no darkness they can dispel.
Moreover, throughout the initial, middle, and final phases of sunlight,
there is never a moment when it does not contradict the darkness of night.
When the sun first rises,
it destroys all darkness;
though other lights may possess power, there is no darkness remaining for them to destroy.
In this way, although the sixth stage is able to sever all afflictions of the desire realm,
the detailed explanation is as previously stated.
Question: How is it known that the six stages of the form realm possess both types of antidotes for the afflictions of the desire realm?
He spoke as follows:
"Those who enter the path of seeing based on the five higher stages realize the abandonment of conceptual discrimination within the desire realm."
Because a separate acquisition of untainted dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) arises;
if this were not the case, then for the five higher stages regarding the afflictions of the desire realm,
there would be no antidote for their abandonment.
The critique states:
One should not speak in such a manner;
for he has attained the ultimate cessation of afflictions within the desire realm.
Because there is no one capable of severing it,
who says that there is the acquisition of the untainted (anāsrava-prāpti) in that stage?
It is the abandonment of conceptualization in the desire realm that is realized.
Furthermore, do you cite that [scriptural passage] to prove this point?
Therefore, what was stated previously is logically sound.
Question: From this discussion, another question arises.
Regarding the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*):
why is it unable to sever the various afflictions?
Answer: At that time, those roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are still minute.
Although the dharma-body has not yet grown, it possesses majestic power.
Because the roots of goodness are slight and the dharma-body has not yet grown, one cannot sever the afflictions;
yet because there is majestic power, one is not overwhelmed or subdued by the afflictions.
Just as a lion cub, though its body is small and not yet fully grown, possesses majestic power;
because its body is small and not yet fully grown, it cannot harm other beasts,
yet because it possesses majestic power, it is not harmed by any of those beasts.
Some say: "Because the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) lasts for only a single moment, it cannot effect abandonment.
Question: "The Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) also lasts for only a single moment; how then can it effect abandonment?"

Answer: Although the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) lasts for only a single moment, it is able to sever the afflictions because it arises in a continuous succession;
the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukika-agra-dharma*) lack such a quality and therefore cannot sever them.
Other masters say that because the Supreme Mundane Dharmas are subsumed under the Path of Preparatory Practice (prayoga-mārga), they cannot effect abandonment.
Because it can only be abandoned by means of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Within this context, there is further analysis.
Question: For what reason is the "highest mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) [so designated]?
Is it bound exclusively to the realm of form?
Answer: Because that realm of form can serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the three paths, the three stages, and the three faculties;
and because it can also induce the category of the initial Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) and subsequently the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
The other realms are not so;
therefore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is exclusively bound to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Question: For what reason is it certain that the Supreme Mundane Dharma is not bound to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
Answer: It is not the realm of desire, nor the realm of non-concentration, nor the realm of non-cultivation, nor the realm of non-detachment from passion;
for it is only in the realm of concentration, the realm of cultivation, and the realm of detachment from passion that the Supreme Mundane Dharma exists.
Furthermore, the desire realm is a base realm, a realm of coarse heaviness, and an inferior realm;
it requires a noble and superior realm,
a realm of subtlety and lightness.
In the supreme and wondrous realm,
there exists the "Dharma Supreme in the World" (laukikāgradharma).
Furthermore, if the Dharma Supreme in the World were bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), [it would follow that it could not serve as the immediate precursor to the path of seeing].
For there would then be the fault that it could take its own nature as an object.
That is to say, if it were bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta),
it would take its own nature as its object.
It cannot take [itself] as an object.
If it were to take its own nature as an object, there would be the fallacy of contradicting reason,
because a nature cannot apprehend its own nature.
If it were unable to take this as its object, it would contradict the original treatise,
as stated in the subsequent passage:
"If one takes this dharma as an object, the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering arises."
Taking these very dharmas as its object, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) arises;
specifically, the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Suffering of Dharmas (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti) takes the five aggregates of the desire realm as its universal object.
This should also be the case here.
Therefore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) is definitely not bound to the desire realm.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume Three [continued as] Volume Four,
composed by five hundred Great Arhats and others.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Section One of the First Aggregate of Miscellaneous Matters: The Sub-section on the Supreme Mundane Dharma (Laukikāgradharma), Part Three. Why is this dharma [so called]?
One should not say that it is not associated with the formless realm.

Answer: Upon entering the state of right determination and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one first realizes the suffering of the desire realm as suffering through direct insight (*abhisamaya*).
Subsequently, one combines the present observation of suffering in the form and formless realms as suffering.
When the Noble Path arises, it first accomplishes the task of the desire realm,
and subsequently accomplishes the tasks of the form and formless realms by combining them.
If one enters the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma),
one first realizes the suffering of the formless realm as suffering through direct insight,
and subsequently realizes the suffering of the desire and form realms as suffering through combined direct insight.
The Noble Path first accomplishes the tasks of the formless realm and subsequently accomplishes the tasks of the desire and form realms;
such is the nature of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
One should say that it belongs to the formless realm;
however, when entering the state of rightness and departure from birth,
one first realizes the suffering of the desire realm as suffering.
Subsequently, one combines the present observation of suffering in the form and formless realms as suffering.
When the Noble Path arises, it first accomplishes the task of the desire realm,
and subsequently accomplishes the tasks of the form and formless realms by combining them.
Therefore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) should not be said to be bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
It is within this [state] that one enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
First, one directly realizes the suffering of the desire realm as suffering;
subsequently, one realizes the suffering of the form and formless realms as suffering collectively.
This refers to the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
First, one separately realizes the truth of suffering in the desire realm through the aspect of suffering;
subsequently, one realizes the truth of suffering in the form and formless realms collectively through the aspect of suffering.
Question: Within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one contemplates all four truths;
why, then, is it said that one contemplates only the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*)?
Answer: Within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one first contemplates the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*);
because its characteristics are coarse and manifest, it is specifically mentioned here.
Question: Since all four aspects of practice realize suffering through direct insight (*abhisamaya*),
why is it said that there is only the aspect of suffering?
The answer is: that which ought to be stated in full but is not stated should be understood as an elliptical statement (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*).
Some say that this passage should have been stated only in such a manner.
One first realizes the suffering of the desire realm through direct observation (*abhisamaya*),
and subsequently realizes the suffering of the form and formless realms in combination;
it should not be said that [the latter] constitutes [a separate] suffering.
Furthermore, what is the intention behind stating that [the aggregates] are suffering?
The answer is: because among the four aspects [of the Four Noble Truths], suffering comes first;
therefore, by speaking of the category of suffering, the other three are implicitly revealed.
Some say that it is because the aspect of suffering has been transmitted for a long time;
for all past Tathāgatas, Arhats,
and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have designated it by the name "suffering" at the very beginning of their teaching on the truths.
Some say that because the characteristic of suffering belongs exclusively to the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya), it is mentioned specifically;
whereas the characteristic of impermanence (anityatā) is common to all three truths.
Because the aspect of emptiness and non-self applies to all phenomena,
some say that this aspect of suffering can oppose all forms of existence and enable one to abandon birth and death.
Because these superior modes of practice accord with a mind inclined toward renunciation.
Even when an infant has obtained various kinds of excellent food and drink,
just as he is about to eat, someone says to him:
Because this food is bitter, one immediately discards it;
for this reason, it is specifically mentioned.
Some say that because its characteristic is suffering, it is easily accepted with conviction.
This means that both those within and outside the Buddhist path—whether old or young, foolish or wise—all believe that suffering exists;
therefore, it is taught specifically.
Some say that the characteristic of suffering is coarse and manifest, easily known by wisdom, and understood as soon as it is mentioned.
Therefore, it is explained in a partial manner,
just as knowledge relates to the object of knowledge,
or awakening relates to the object of awakening.
The mode of activity [operates] upon its object;
the faculty [operates] upon its objective field;
and the cognitive subject [operates] upon its object of cognition.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Question: For what reason does the practitioner [attain this] during the stage of the path of seeing?

Question: Does one first realize the suffering of the desire realm through direct observation (*abhisamaya*), and subsequently realize the suffering of the form and formless realms through combined realization?
Answer: Because they differ in terms of coarseness and subtlety.
This means that because the suffering of the desire realm is coarse and easy to observe, it is realized first;
the suffering of the form and formless realms is subtle and difficult to observe, and thus it is realized later.
It is like an archer who first shoots at coarse objects and later shoots at the tip of a hair.
This is also the case here.
Question: If it is so that the suffering of the form realm is coarse and the suffering of the formless realm is subtle, why does the practitioner realize them both simultaneously?
The answer is: because the practitioner of contemplation gives rise to clear realization (abhisamaya) regarding the distinction between the two realms—the determinate and the indeterminate.
That is to say, because the suffering of the desire realm is subsumed under the indeterminate realm, it is realized separately.
Because the realms of form and formlessness are comprised within the realm of concentration associated with suffering, they are combined in the clear observation (*abhisamaya*),
just as the realms of the concentrated and the unconcentrated,
and the realms of the cultivated and the uncultivated.
It should be understood that the same applies to the realms of those who have abandoned passion and those who have not.
Some say that for a practitioner, the suffering of the desire realm [is perceived as such].
Because it currently manifests as an affliction like a heavy burden,
the practitioner first contemplates the suffering of the form and formless realms.
Therefore, it is not the case that subsequent clear observation occurs later.
Some say that because the suffering of the desire realm is what the practitioner currently grasps and experiences, its clear observation occurs first,
whereas that of the form and formless realms does not.
Therefore, it is not so; rather, there is subsequent clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

Some say that because the suffering of the desire realm produces immediate pain and affliction for the practitioner, it is realized first, whereas the suffering of the form and formless realms does not do so, and is therefore realized subsequently.
Some say that because the suffering of the desire realm is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), it is realized first;
whereas the suffering of the form and formless realms is not so, it is realized later.
Question: If the suffering of the form and formless realms is not directly perceived, [how can it be realized]?
How does the practitioner realize that?
The answer is: there are two kinds of direct perception.
First, direct perception as apprehension (*upātta-pratyakṣa*).
Second, there is the direct observation through detachment from defilements.
For that practitioner, regarding the suffering of the desire realm, both types of direct observation apply;
however, regarding the suffering of the form and formless realms, there is only the direct observation through detachment from defilements.
It is just as a merchant who has two loads of wealth:
one he carries himself,
and the other he causes another person to carry.
Regarding what one carries oneself,
there are two kinds of direct perception:
namely, the direct perception of lightness and heaviness, and the direct perception of wealth and goods.
In the case of another person carrying a load, only one kind of material object is directly perceived;
this [case] is also like that.
Some say that because the suffering of the desire realm is proximate, it is realized first.
Because suffering in the form and formless realms is remote, it is realized later;
this is just as with what is near or distant, or what is concomitant with the body or not concomitant with the body,
and likewise for what resides in one's own body or in the bodies of others.
Some say that the suffering of the desire realm is of three kinds—
namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral— and therefore it is realized first;
[the suffering of] the form and formless realms follows.
There are only two types, namely the wholesome and the indeterminate; therefore, they are realized subsequently.
Some say that when a practitioner of meditation is about to enter the state of an Arya, [they realize them].
One necessarily achieves the state of being an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) of the desire realm,
but does not achieve the state of being an ordinary being of the form or formless realms. This is because,
by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), that which is to be achieved arises first.
It arises subsequent to that which has not yet been accomplished.
Some say that when one sees the suffering of the desire realm, one abandons two kinds of fetters—
namely, the unwholesome and the neutral— and thus realizes them first.
When one perceives the suffering of the form and formless realms, because one severs only the indeterminate fetters (*avyākṛta-saṃyojana*), it is a subsequent clear observation (*paścād-abhisamaya*).
This is like the case of unwholesome and indeterminate [states],
which may have or not have maturation (*vipāka*).
Producing two fruits or producing one fruit;
associated with shamelessness and lack of dread,
or dissociated from shamelessness and lack of dread.
One should know that it is likewise so.
Some say it is like when one, while in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
slanders the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
First one slanders the suffering of the desire realm,
and subsequently one slanders the suffering of the form and formless realms;
now, upon entering the stage of the noble ones, one has faith in the truth of suffering.
Likewise, one first believes in the suffering of the desire realm and subsequently believes in the suffering of the form and formless realms;
this is like the sequence of denial, belief, delusion, awakening, doubt, and resolution.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Therefore, regarding the suffering of the desire realm, one first realizes it individually;
regarding the suffering of the form and formless realms, one subsequently realizes it collectively.
Regarding the statement that the Noble Path first accomplishes the tasks of the desire realm and subsequently accomplishes the tasks of the form and formless realms:
this refers to the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
First, one separately accomplishes the tasks to be performed in the desire realm;
subsequently, one collectively accomplishes the tasks to be performed in the form and formless realms.
This is the question regarding the accomplishment of the task of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
What is the distinction?
Some say that this non-distinctive realization is itself the task to be accomplished.
Some say that there is indeed a distinction,
and that the name itself constitutes the distinction;
namely, this is called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*).
This is called the accomplishment of the task.
Furthermore, thorough penetration of the object of focus is clear realization;
the abandonment of all afflictions is the accomplishment of the task.
Furthermore, "clear realization" (abhisamaya) refers to the clear realization of wisdom;
"accomplishing the task" refers to the clear realization of the objective.
Furthermore, "clear realization" refers to the thorough knowledge of wisdom.
The "one who effects abandonment" refers to thorough knowledge through abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
Just as with thorough knowledge through wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*), the thorough knowledge through abandonment is the realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) by means of wisdom.
One attains realization;
it should be understood that the same applies to the path of clear liberation and its fruit.
Furthermore, "clear realization" (abhisamaya) refers to that which is performed by the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga).
"Accomplishing the task" (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna) refers to...
That is to say, it is that which is performed by the path of liberation,
just as that which is performed by the uninterrupted path is performed by the path of liberation.
One severs the fetters and realizes dissociation;
one eliminates faults and cultivates virtues;
one emerges from the base and enters the sublime.
Abandoning that which is meaningless and attaining that which is meaningful,
and exhausting the oil of craving to receive the bliss of freedom from fever—
this should be understood to be likewise.
Furthermore, there are those who say that a single moment (kṣaṇa) is the direct realization (abhisamaya),
while the continuity [of moments] is the accomplishment of the task.
Just as [the moments of] a continuum are included in the count of "entrances," one should know that the entrances themselves are likewise so.
This applies to those who have entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and so forth.
On the contrary, you raise an irrational objection;
[we reply that] this conforms to and establishes the correct meaning.
Question: Just as suffering in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is not previously realized (*abhisamaya*), [so too is it here].
Furthermore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) belongs to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Likewise, although [the truth of suffering] regarding the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) has not previously been directly realized, [it is subsequently realized].
What prevents the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) from being bound to the formless realm?
The answer is that within the form realm there exists pervasive-cognition wisdom (*pariṣpharaṇa-jñāna*),
which is able to take its own level as an object and also take the levels above and below as objects.
Therefore, although the suffering of the form realm is not previously realized, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) is nonetheless associated with the form realm.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is no knowledge that takes everything as its object;
although it takes its own level and higher levels as objects, it does not take lower levels as objects.
Therefore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) is not bound to the formless realm.
Furthermore, one enters the formless attainments and eliminates the perception of form.
It is not by eliminating the perception of form that one can know the desire realm.

If, taking this dharma as an object, one gives rise to the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), then one immediately takes that same dharma as an object and gives rise to the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
Question: In this context, it is logically improper to state [the sequence] again.
One should simply say: "Entering the formless attainments, one eliminates the perception of form," and so forth, as explained at length.
Why is this? Because it is a single gateway.
Others, clarifying the meaning of this passage, should state it as follows:
For what reason should this dharma not be said to be "bound to the formless realm"? Answer:
Because upon entering the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one eliminates the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*).
...and so forth, as explained at length. Why is this?
Because this constitutes the fundamental answer to the question asked.
Therefore, one should state it in this way;
what is the intention behind not stating it so?
Answer: Now, the establishment of discourse on the Dharma is of two kinds:
first, the expedient means;
second, the fundamental.
What was previously stated was discourse concerning skillful means;
what is being stated now is...
This is the fundamental discourse,
because it is the fundamental alternative means (*upāya*).
Furthermore, it is said that the method of skillful means (*upāyadharma*) comes first.
It should be explained according to the text.
Some say that there are two types of paths discussed in the treatise.
First is permitting;
second is prohibiting. Of these, the former category refers to the following.
This is the path of discursive argumentation through affirmation;
the subsequent section is the path of discursive argumentation through negation.
Consequently, there is no error in the meaning of this original text.
Other masters say:
Here, the former formulation shows that the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) takes only the desire realm as its object;
the latter formulation shows that the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*) and the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering have the same object of focus.
That concentration is certainly not bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
because the formless attainments involve the removal of the perception of form (*rūpasaṃjñā*) and necessarily do not take as their object any contaminated form belonging to a lower realm.
Excluding the meditative attainment of the perception of form (*rūpa-samjñā-samāpatti*),
it is included within the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) and their three upper preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
This has been stated in many places.
The phrase "removing the perception of form" means that it is stated here that one enters the formless attainments by removing the perception of form.
...and so forth, as explained at length in the Mahābhūta-skandha.
What is the removal of the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*)?
That is to say, there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to such a resolute conviction (adhimukti),
and so forth, as explained at length.
Pāruyaṇa also spoke thus:
"All those who eliminate the perception of form are able to eliminate the entire body."
Regarding internal and external phenomena, there is nothing that is not seen;
this is also stated in the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* (The Chapter on the Multitude of Meanings).
Regarding perception, there is neither perception nor the departure from it; it is neither non-perception nor the removal of perception.
Thus, by equally removing the perception of form, one is free from attachment to its causes and conditions.
Such are these various teachings.
What is the difference in meaning?
The answer is: within this aggregate, it is taught that the "perception of form" (rūpa-saṃjñā) refers to the various forms that flow forth without taking lower stages as their object.
The *Mahābhūta-skandha* states that the removal of the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) consists in causing the accumulated matter (*saṃcita-rūpa*) to no longer appear.
This is explained in the *Pāramārtha-arthavarga*.
The severance of craving for the form realm is called the removal of the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*).
Some say that this "removal of the perception of form" in this context applies to all four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
This is stated in the *Mahābhūta-skandha* [treatise] regarding the removal of the perception of form.
The *Pāramārthika-saṃgraha-parivarta* states that the application of mindfulness to the body alone is for those who have eliminated the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*).
Regarding the mindfulness of phenomena alone (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), some say that this stage excludes the perception of form (*rūpasaṃjñā*).

It is comprised within seven stages: namely, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) and the three preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) above them; this is explained in terms of the aggregate of primary elements (*mahābhūta-skandha*).
Regarding the "removal of the perception of form," it is included within the fourth dhyāna;
this is stated in the *Pāramārthika-saṃgraha-paṭala*. As for the "removal of the perception of form":
It is also subsumed within the seven stages,
namely: the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four dhyānas,
and the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka*).
Some say that the mention of "excluding the perception of form" (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) in the *Mahābhūta-skandha* [sūtra] is because it is unique and exists only within our own school.
The remaining three are common.
Other masters say that among those mentioned in this aggregate, the term "perception" (saṃjñā) excludes form (rūpa).
Because this [first] is shared with both internal and external paths,
the other three are unshared.
Thus, these are called the differences in the meanings of the various explanations.
Within this context, there is further analysis. Question:
For what reason is it called "the supreme mundane dharma"?
Is it not connected with the formless realm?
Answer: No, because it is not a field [of merit] and so forth;
that is to say, the formless realm [is not a field] for the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
It is not a field, nor a vessel, nor ground;
it cannot produce the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Therefore, it does not exist therein.
Furthermore, if a stage possesses other factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
that stage may possess the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), however, there are no other factors conducive to penetration.
Therefore, there is no such thing as the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma).
Furthermore, if it were a meditative concentration,
it would have to be possible for it to universally contemplate the four truths of the three realms.
That concentration can certainly possess the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma),
whereas in the formless concentrations (ārūpyasamādhi) these roots of goodness do not exist;
therefore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma is absent there.
Furthermore, if a concentration could possess the aspect of the "selflessness of all phenomena" as its object,
then the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) would exist in that stage; however,
within the formless concentrations (ārūpyasamādhi), this aspect does not exist.
Therefore, there is no such thing as the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma).
Furthermore, if a stage can cultivate the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna), [then it cannot be the Supreme Mundane Dharma].
That stage may possess the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma),
but such a thing does not exist within the formless stages (ārūpyabhūmi);
therefore, those [stages] lack the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
Furthermore, if there were a path of seeing (darśanamārga) on the level of the form realm (rūpadhātu),
the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma) could exist; however,
within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is no path of seeing.
Therefore, there is no "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma).
A question arises from this discussion:
for what reason is there no path of vision (darśanamārga) in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)?
The answer is as previously stated: the absence of the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) serves as this proof.
Furthermore, there is another reason:
because śamatha is predominant in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
It is on the stages where vipaśyanā predominates that one can attain the path of seeing; others, however,
exclude both [the path of seeing and the path of cultivation] from these two realms.
This means that because the desire realm is extremely coarse and the formless realm is extremely subtle,
neither possesses the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Furthermore, because the roots of goodness in the desire realm are extremely weak and inferior,
and because the roots of goodness in the formless realm are extremely dull and obscure,
neither possesses the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Furthermore, because the desire realm is extremely agitated and the formless realm is extremely tranquil,
neither possesses the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma).
Furthermore, if a stage possesses both universal-object knowledge and the path for severing fetters,
that stage may contain the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
Although the desire realm possesses knowledge that universally objects to all phenomena,
it lacks the path for severing the fetters;
although the formless realm possesses the path for severing the fetters, [it lacks knowledge that universally objects to all phenomena].
Yet there is no wisdom that takes [all] as its universal object.
Therefore, both lack the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
Question: Are there perhaps two types of noble beings?
Being born in the same place,
they both achieve the "highest mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) simultaneously.
Is there one that is not accomplished?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, one based on the first dhyāna.
One enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
First, one relies on the second dhyāna to enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth.
When both have passed away and are reborn in the second dhyāna,
those who rely on the first dhyāna do not possess the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
Because one has transcended the stage [of the first dhyāna],
one who relies on the second dhyāna still accomplishes the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
Because they are born from their own stage.
Question: Is it possible for two Arhats, both residing in the desire realm, [to arise] in the state of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) simultaneously?
Is it that one is accomplished and one is not?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, one relies on the first dhyāna to enter into rightness and departure from birth,
while another relies on the second dhyāna.
Entering the state of rightness and freedom from birth,
they both pass away together and are reborn in the second dhyāna.
There are those who, while not yet free from desire for the desire realm,
simultaneously attain the fruit of arhatship based upon the first dhyāna.
One does not achieve the supreme mundane dharmas because they are abandoned upon transcending the stage;
this refers to one who relies on the second dhyāna.
One accomplishes the supreme mundane dharma because it arises from its own stage;
this is the supreme mundane dharma.
"It should be said that they possess vitarka and vicāra," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Although it has already been stated that they belong to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), their specific stage (*bhūmi*) has not yet been distinguished;
this is now intended to be distinguished.
Just as one might know the country or city where a person dwells,
yet remain unaware of the specific house or dwelling they inhabit,
so it is with this case; therefore, this treatise is composed.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of enabling those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
That is to say, it was previously stated:
"The Supreme Mundane Dharmas."
It is bound exclusively to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Within the realm of form, however,
there are three levels (bhūmi).
1. The stage with vitarka and vicāra;
2. The stage without vitarka and with only vicāra;
3. The stage without vitarka and without vicāra.
However, it has not yet been shown in which stage the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is definitively situated.
There are certain roots of goodness that exist only in the stage with vitarka and vicāra,
such as the analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*).
There are certain roots of goodness that exist only in the stage free from applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ*),
such as the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*).
The latter four spheres of mastery and the former eight bases of totality possess various roots of goodness.
In the stages with applied thought and sustained thought,
as well as in the stage without applied thought and sustained thought,
it is like the immeasurable joy.
Some say that it is also like the first two liberations and the first four bases of mastery.
Do not give rise to doubt:
the Supreme Mundane Dharmas exist in only one stage.
Alternatively, [some] may hold that it exists in two stages;
however, since we now establish that this concentration definitely exists in three stages,
we have composed this treatise.
Regarding the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*),
should they be said to be with vitarka and vicāra,
or without vitarka and with vicāra only?
Is it without vitarka and without vicāra?
One should answer: "It is either with vitarka and with vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra only."
Or [it is] without vitarka and without vicāra.
Question: For what reason is it shown that the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) exists in three stages?
Answer: To refute the tenets of other schools.
This root of goodness exists in only one stage;
that is to say, some maintain that the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma) [belong to this category].
It is characterized only by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*),
possesses signs (*nimitta*) and alertness (*prabodha*),
is not in meditative equipoise (*asamāhita*), belongs to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and takes conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as its object.
Only those with vitarka and vicāra exist,
because they involve the activity of conceptual construction;
those with nimitta exist, because they arise by taking names as their object.
Because it involves alertness,
because it requires effort,
and because it proceeds as a continuum that is not in a state of meditative equipoise.
It belongs to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
because it is attained by ordinary beings.
It takes conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as its object.
Because it has conditioned phenomena as its object,
this root of goodness is revealed in order to stop that attachment.
These are present throughout three stages.
What is "with vitarka and vicāra"?
Answer: It is when one relies on a samādhi that possesses both vitarka and vicāra.
One enters into the state of right determination and transcendence of birth. That which is attained is the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma),
which relies upon the threshold concentration (anāgamya) and the first dhyāna.
Regarding "one who has entered the state of rightness and separation from birth":
this refers to the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgra-dharma) that have been attained.
Question: What is the meaning of the term "basis" (āśraya) used here?
What phenomenon is intended to be revealed? Some say:
this innate concentration is specifically designated as "dependence" (*niśraya*).
That is to say, the concentration associated with the supreme mundane dharmas is spoken of by way of its support;
this refers to the simultaneous support.
There is textual evidence for this,
as stated in the *Jñānakāya*:
"If one relies on the samādhi of emptiness..."
One enters the state of rightness and departure from birth.

That [state] is designated by the term "sound" because it is a meditative concentration associated with the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
This is also like that.
Other masters say that these [conditions] are fixed as immediate conditions (samanantara-pratyaya).
It is called "reliance" (*niśraya*); that is,
the meditative concentration associated with superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*),
which is expressed by the term "reliance."
To speak in this way,
those very three stages are designated as the "basis."
The basis described later should be understood in the same way.
What is "without vitarka and with vicāra only"?
Answer: If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on a samādhi that is without vitarka and with only vicāra,
the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgra-dharma) attained therein—

This refers to the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) attained by one who enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based upon the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
What is the state of being without applied thought and without sustained thought?
Answer: It is when one enters into rightness and departure from birth by relying on the concentration that is without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Regarding that which he has attained, the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*):
this refers to entering into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based upon the second, third, or fourth *dhyāna*.
Regarding the worldly supreme dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) that has been attained:
if one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-samādhi*), [it is so].
He cultivates one stage:
the stage of the path of seeing and the supreme mundane dharmas.
The conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realization of the second stage:
if one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth based on the first dhyāna.
He cultivates two stages:
the stage of the path of vision and the stage of the supreme mundane dharmas.
The conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realization on the third stage;
if one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth based upon the intermediate dhyāna.
He cultivates three stages:
the stage of the path of seeing,
and the supreme mundane dharmas.
The conventional knowledge at the edge of clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of the fourth stage:
if one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the second dhyāna,
they cultivate [the conventional knowledge] of four stages.
The path of seeing constitutes one stage;
the supreme mundane dharmas constitute five stages;
and the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realizations constitutes five stages.
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth by relying on the third dhyāna,
they cultivate the five stages.
The path of seeing constitutes one stage;
the supreme mundane dharmas and the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realizations constitute six stages.
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth based on the fourth dhyāna,
they cultivate six stages.
The path of seeing constitutes one stage;
the supreme mundane dharmas constitute seven stages;
and the conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization constitutes seven stages.
Other masters say:
if one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth based on the first dhyāna, they cultivate two stages.
The two stages of the path of seeing,
the supreme mundane dharmas,
and the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realization of the three stages.
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth based on the intermediate dhyāna,
they cultivate three stages.
The three stages of the path of seeing,
the supreme mundane dharma,
and the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realization of the fourth stage.
Why is this? Because those three stages are all one and the same stage.
Because of the single underlying tendency (*anuśaya*),
and because wholesome dharmas therein act as causes for one another;
it relies on other stages as previously explained.
The critique states: He should not make such a statement. Why is this?
Because if he were to make such a statement...
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth based on the intermediate dhyāna,
they should attain the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) of two stages.
That is to say, there are states with both vitarka and vicāra,
as well as those with no vitarka and only vicāra.
If that were so, it would contradict this very text.
What is it that is taught?
It is with vitarka and vicāra;
if one relies upon a samādhi that is with vitarka and vicāra.
One enters into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Regarding that which has been attained, the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgra-dharma*):
how is it that there is no applied thought (*vitarka*) and only sustained thought (*vicāra*)?
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth by relying on a samādhi that is without vitarka and with only vicāra,
the worldly supreme dharmas attained therein—
Let there be no such error;
therefore, what was stated previously is logically sound.
Question: For what reason is it the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)?
Regarding the cultivation of the stages of oneself and others:
when cultivating the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*),
does one cultivate only those of one's own stage?
Answer: Because the untainted liberation and dissociation of the path of seeing (darśanamārga) are not like that of the supreme mundane dharmas (laukikāgradharma).
Furthermore, although the path of seeing exists within the stages (bhūmi), it does not fall within the realms (dhātu).
Because the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) both belongs to a stage (*bhūmi*) and falls within a realm (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is cultivated by virtue of three conditions:
first, because of the nourishment of its causes.
Second, because they accomplish the same task;
third, because they share the same antidote.
Regarding "nourished by causes":
This refers to the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the six stages,
which serve as causes for one another in accomplishing the same task.
That is to say, the tasks to be performed by the path of seeing of a higher stage [are accomplished] by the path of seeing of a lower stage.
It can also accomplish this.
That which shares the same antidote refers to the path of seeing (darśanamārga) of the higher stages.
The afflictions that are the objects of counteraction can also be countered by the path of seeing of the lower stages.
The cultivation of the path is also practiced across one's own stage and other stages due to the three aforementioned conditions.
As for "nourishment by causes," this refers to the cultivation of the path within the nine stages.
They function as causes for one another in turn.
Furthermore, when the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm,
one also cultivates the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
This is solely due to one condition, namely, being nourished by the cause.
"Performing the same task" refers to the tasks that ought to be performed through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) in the higher stages.
The path of cultivation of the lower stages is also capable of accomplishing this.
Furthermore, it is like the task to be performed by the knowledge of suffering,
up to and including the knowledge of the path.
These can all be accomplished as well.
Regarding "having the same counteractive," this refers to the afflictions that are the objects to be countered by the path of cultivation in the higher stages.
The path of cultivation of the lower stages can also serve as an antidote.
Furthermore, when this wisdom manifests in a single moment,
it enables one to cultivate immeasurable moments of mindfulness in the future.
The supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are not nourished by causes,
because the various stages (*bhūmi*) cannot serve as causes for one another.
Nor is it the same as accomplishing the task,
because one cannot realize the abandonment of the afflictions [thereby].
Nor is it a direct antidote,
because it cannot permanently sever the various afflictions.
Furthermore, regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*):
It is bound to the continuity [of rebirth].
Since the Path of Seeing is not like this,
furthermore, [this applies to] the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
It is capable of producing maturation (*vipāka*);
the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is not so.
Furthermore, regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Because they are bound by craving,
whereas the vision of the Path is not so.
Furthermore, regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*):
It is stained and faulty;
it is poisonous and thorny;
it is defiled and turbid.
The path of seeing is not like this.
Furthermore, the supreme mundane dharma relies upon the body of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
and the dharmas of an ordinary person's body do not cultivate other stages.
The path of seeing relies exclusively upon the body of a noble one (*ārya*),
because the dharmas of a noble one’s body cultivate [the factors] of both their own stage and other stages. Now,
regarding the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*):
Since it is likewise contaminated (*sāsrava*), like the conventional cognitions (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamaya-prānta*),
why is that cognition [distinguished]?
The cultivation of one's own stage and other stages occurs during the mundane supreme dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), whereas during the mundane supreme dharmas themselves,
there is cultivation only of one's own stage.
Answer: The conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (abhisamaya-antya-saṃvṛti-jñāna) is an attendant of the path of seeing;
it is cultivated based upon the path of seeing.
Just as one sees the paths of one's own stage and other stages during the path of seeing,
so too is that knowledge; however, the Supreme Mundane Dharmas are not like this.
Furthermore, regarding the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛti-jñāna*):
based upon the person of a noble one (*ārya*),
the noble one is able to cultivate [this knowledge] pertaining to their own stage as well as other stages.
The supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are not like this.
Furthermore, there is the conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Based on the bodies of those who practice through faith-following or dharma-following,
they are able to fully cultivate the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) of both their own stage and other stages.
It is not so. Furthermore, regarding the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
one has no enemies or adversaries who possess power.
Because of the existence of enemies and adversaries,
one practices on the stages of both oneself and others;
because of a lack of personal power, one practices by relying on the power of others.
The Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) is free from enmity and possesses great power;
because it is free from enmity, [it is so called].
One cultivates only that which belongs to one's own level,
because it possesses the necessary power; thus,
one cultivates by relying on one's own strength.
Furthermore, the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization is attained without effort,
following the power of the path of vision.
The cultivation of one's own and others' stages,
up to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*),
is attained through the application of effort.
Therefore, one can only cultivate [the path] belonging to one's own level.
Question: For what reason does the path of vision (darśanamārga) arise only in the six levels?
Question: Why is it that those in higher stages can cultivate the lower, while those in lower stages do not cultivate the higher?
Answer: Because the dharmas of the higher stages are superior.
When it is present before one,
one is then able to cultivate the lower;
the dharmas of the lower stages are inferior.
When it is present before one,
one cannot cultivate what is superior;
just as the inferior does not precede the superior, nor does the superior precede the inferior.
This is also the case here.
Furthermore, those in lower stages possess inferior power and thus practice by relying on those above,
just as a person of weak strength relies upon one who is strong.
The power of the higher stages is superior; thus, one does not rely on the lower stages for cultivation, just as a person of superior strength does not depend upon those who are inferior.
Furthermore, the lower stages are subordinate to the higher ones.
Those in higher stages can cultivate those of lower stages,
because the higher stages do not belong to the lower; however,
those in lower stages cannot cultivate those of higher stages.
Just as a person who is subject to another is driven by that other's commands,
whereas one who is not subject to another cannot be enslaved by them;
furthermore, if one relies upon a higher stage.
One enters the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
Since one has already attained detachment from the lower stages, one is able to cultivate the lower [stages].
If one enters the state of rightness and separation from birth by relying on a lower stage, [one can likewise cultivate the lower].
He has not yet attained freedom from passion regarding the higher stages;
even if he has already attained such freedom, he does not possess mastery over them,
because he has not relied upon them to enter into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
For this reason, those in the lower stages cannot cultivate the higher ones.
Furthermore, if one enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) in a higher stage, [one does not descend].
Because they have already attained the lower stages, they are able to cultivate [the factors] therein;
however, if one enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on a lower stage,
because they have not yet attained the higher stages, they do not cultivate them.
Even if they have attained them, they do not possess mastery over them,
because they have not relied upon those [attainments] to enter the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Furthermore, because one seeks the higher stages from the lower stages, one cultivates the lower stages while in the higher.
Because those in higher stages do not seek what belongs to lower stages, those in lower stages do not cultivate what belongs to higher stages.
Furthermore, because those in lower stages can abandon what belongs to higher stages,
those in higher stages can cultivate what belongs to lower stages.
Because the higher stages do not abandon the lower, one does not cultivate the higher while in the lower.
Furthermore, because the lower is capable of accomplishing the tasks of the higher,
the higher must cultivate the lower.
Because those above cannot accomplish the tasks of those below, those below do not cultivate what belongs to those above.
Furthermore, it is like the six kinds of protective dharmas,
namely those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Fearing the asuras,
he deployed his sixfold army to protect himself.
First were the nāgas who dwell in the ocean.
Second, the Deva Dṛḍhahasta;
third, the Deva Mālādhāra;
fourth, the Deva Nityapramudita.
Fifth, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;
sixth, the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
and the asuras.
When he departs from his own palace,
intending to engage in battle and strife with the various devas,
he relies upon the nāgas who dwell in the ocean.
First, they engage in battle;
if the nāgas are able to defeat the asuras,
the remaining five classes of celestial armies remain at ease.
If they cannot prevail,
the celestial army of Dṛḍhapāṇi assists them with its strength;
if the two can prevail, [they do so].
The remaining four celestial armies remained there without incident.
If they were unable to prevail,
the Mālādhāra celestial army would further assist them with its strength.
If the three [gods] are victorious,
the armies of the other three heavens remain at ease;
if they are not victorious, [the situation is otherwise].
The gods of the Heaven of Constant Pride further assist their forces;
if these four are victorious,
the remaining two heavenly armies remain inactive.
If they cannot prevail,
the armies of the Four Great Kings further assist them with their strength;
if the five can prevail, [the conflict ends].
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven dwell there without concern.
If they are unable to prevail,
the Trāyastriṃśa gods join with the first five armies.
They assist one another in battle and strife,
causing the asuras to retreat in defeat and flee;
thus they perceive the Path.
In order to counteract the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), six stages are established:
first, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*) up to the sixth [stage], which is the fourth dhyāna.
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the threshold concentration, [it is so].
In the future, one cultivates only a single stage;
through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one is able to permanently sever the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya-kleśa*).
The remaining five stages remain inactive.
If one enters the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on the first dhyāna,
one then cultivates two stages in the future;
for the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) assists in the permanent abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing.
The remaining four stages abide without activity.
If one enters the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on the intermediate dhyāna,
one then cultivates three stages in the future.
The path of seeing, aided by its associates, permanently abandons the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing;
the remaining three stages abide without such activity.
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the second dhyāna:
In the future, one cultivates four stages;
with the assistance of the path of seeing, one permanently abandons the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing,
while the remaining two stages remain inactive.
If one enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the third dhyāna,
one then cultivates the five stages in the future;
the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) assists in the permanent abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing, while the fourth dhyāna remains without further activity.
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the fourth dhyāna,
one then cultivates six stages in the future;
the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) acts as an auxiliary to bring about the permanent abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
Therefore, one can cultivate the lower stages by relying on the higher stages,
but one cannot cultivate the higher stages by relying on those lower stages.
Furthermore, it is just as there are six successive ponds based upon a mountain.
That is to say, from the mountain peak down to the base,
there are six springs and ponds flowing in succession;
the water of the uppermost stream flows through all six ponds.
In the second round it pervades five, in the third round four,
and so on until in the sixth round it pervades only a single pond;
such is the path of vision (darśanamārga) arising from the six stages.
Those in higher stages can cultivate lower [stages], while those in lower stages do not cultivate higher ones.
Question: Is there such a thing as the "highest worldly dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) that is associated with vitarka but not with vicāra?
Is it associated with vicāra but not with vitarka?
Or is it associated with both vitarka and vicāra?
Or is it dissociated from both vitarka and vicāra?
Answer: That which is associated with vitarka but not with vicāra refers to the vicāra of the threshold concentration (anāgamya) and the first dhyāna;
for vicāra is not associated with its own intrinsic nature.
Regarding those associated with sustained thought (*vicāra*) but not with applied thought (*vitarka*):
this refers to applied thought itself, the intermediate dhyāna (excluding sustained thought),
and all other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
Those associated with both vitarka and vicāra refer to the remaining mental states and mental factors within the threshold concentration (anāgamya) and the first dhyāna,
excluding vitarka and vicāra themselves.
Those that are dissociated from both vitarka and vicāra are:
the vicāra of the intermediate dhyāna,
as well as the mind and mental factors of the three higher dhyānas.
And all matter that evolves in accordance with the mind (citta-anuvartin-rūpa), as well as the formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).
Question: Is there any such thing as the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma)?
Is it not with vitarka and vicāra?
Is it not without vitarka and with vicāra only?
Is it not without vitarka and without vicāra?
Answer: There are.
Namely, the vicāra of the threshold concentration (anāgamya) and the first dhyāna.
These are not accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
Why is this so? As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"What are the phenomena with vitarka and vicāra?"
Answer: If a phenomenon is associated with both vitarka and vicāra, then although that vicāra is associated with vitarka, it is not itself vitarka;
nor is it the case that there is no vitarka and only vicāra.
Why is this so? As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"What are phenomena that are without vitarka and with only vicāra?"

Answer: If a dharma is associated with vicāra but not with vitarka, that vicāra is associated only with vitarka and not with vicāra; therefore, it is also neither without vitarka nor without vicāra. Why is this so?
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"What are phenomena that are without vitarka and without vicāra?
Answer: Those phenomena that are dissociated from vitarka and vicāra."
Because that vicāra is exclusively associated with vicāra and not with vitarka.
Question: Is there perhaps a state of the "highest mundane dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma) that is dissociated from both vitarka and vicāra?
Is it not the case that there is no vicāra?
Answer: There is;
namely, the vicāra of the intermediate dhyāna.
Although it is not associated with vitarka and vicāra,
it is not without vicāra. Why is this so?
Because it has vicāra as its intrinsic nature.
Question: Is there any "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) that exists in the stage with both vitarka and vicāra, which is associated with vicāra but not with vitarka?
Answer: Yes.
This is because it is said that they are associated exclusively with *vitarka* (applied thought).
Question: Is there such a thing as the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)?
In the stage of being without vitarka but with vicāra,
are these associated dharmas not associated with vicāra?
Answer: There is.
It refers to the intermediate dhyāna;
it has vicāra [as its mental factor] and that which is its own nature.
Because they are not associated [with one another].

Question: Is it possible for the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) to exist within the stage characterized by both applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-bhūmi*), while yet possessing three types?
That is to say: with vitarka and vicāra,
without vitarka and with vicāra only,
or without both vitarka and vicāra?
Answer: That which is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra refers to the threshold concentration (anāgamya) and the first dhyāna.
Excluding vitarka and vicāra,
the remaining mental states and mental factors are "without vitarka and with vicāra only";
vitarka itself is said to be "without vitarka and with vicāra only."
That which is without vitarka and without vicāra refers to matter that evolves in accordance with the mind and formations dissociated from the mind.
Question: Is there perhaps a state of the highest mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) that exists on the level of "without vitarka and with vicāra only" (*avitarko vicāramātraḥ*),
and yet is of two kinds?
That is to say, is it that there is no vitarka but only vicāra, or is it that there is neither vitarka nor vicāra?
Answer: There is that which has no vitarka but only vicāra.
This refers to the mental states and mental factors, excluding vicāra, that exist in the intermediate dhyāna;
these are those that are without vitarka and without vicāra.
That is to say: the vicāra of that stage,
as well as the matter that arises concomitantly with the mind,
and the formations dissociated from the mind.
The Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) should be said to be associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya),
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Although the distinctions among the stages upon which they depend have already been explained, it has not yet been analyzed with which [mental factors] they are associated.
I now wish to analyze this:
it is just as when one already knows the house where a person dwells, yet does not yet know their friends and companions;
this case is likewise so.
Therefore, this treatise is composed. Some have said:
"Although it has already been shown that the 'supreme mundane dharmas' (laukikāgradharma) pertain to all three stages."
Although it has not yet been stated that those [supernormal powers] pertain to the six stages,
this now clarifies their association with the three faculties,
intending to make known that they pertain to the six stages.
It is clearly perceived as if looking at a fruit in the palm of one's hand;
for this reason, this treatise was composed concerning the "Dharma Supreme in the World" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Should it be said that it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*),
or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
It is associated with either the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*),
or the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*),
or the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Since it has already been stated that they are not bound to the desire realm,
it is known that they are not associated with mental grief or physical pain;
therefore, the treatise is composed based solely on the three faculties.
Although those three faculties have been described in general as being associated [with the mind],
their specific modes of association have not yet been revealed; therefore,
their distinct characteristics must be explained further.
What is associated with the faculty of pleasure?
Answer: If, relying on the third dhyāna, one enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
That which he has attained is the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) of the third dhyāna.
This is the supreme mundane dharma of the third dhyāna.
It is either associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) or dissociated from it.
As for that which is associated with the faculty of pleasure:
This refers to all other mental states and mental factors, excluding the faculty of pleasure,
as well as the dissociated phenomena.
That is to say: the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
as well as matter that evolves in accordance with the mind (*anuparivartin-rūpa*),
and formations dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Now, let us first discuss other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta).
