Abandonment occurs either by transcending a realm or level,
or by relinquishing the homogeneous class of beings;
it does not occur through falling back.
Furthermore, what further benefits are there?
Namely, one never regresses and does not commit the deeds of immediate retribution.
One does not fall into the evil destinies.
Regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharmas,
they are both attained and relinquished.
Acquisition occurs by means of preparatory application;
relinquishment occurs by means of transcending a realm or stage,
not by means of falling away.
Nor does it do so by means of relinquishing the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Furthermore, what further excellence (*viśeṣa*) could there be that would enable it to serve as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
One enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Other masters say that "heat" (*uṣmagata*) is both acquired and abandoned, as previously explained.
Having abandoned this "heat," one may also commit an act of immediate retribution and fall into the miserable destinies.
What are the benefits?
It can serve as the definitive cause for nirvāṇa,
and it can ensure that one’s roots of goodness are never ultimately severed.
If that were so, Devadatta would not have attained "Heat" (*uṣmagata*),
because he gave rise to wrong views and severed his roots of goodness.
As previously stated, the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) is both attained and lost.
Having abandoned this summit, one likewise falls into the evil destinies;
what further benefit is there?
One does not commit the deeds of immediate retribution.
Patience is both attained and relinquished as previously described.
Furthermore, what further benefit does it possess?
It is ultimately non-retrogressive.
They do not fall into the evil destinies, nor do they cling to a self.
Question: If that is so, Upāli, [what about] Śrīgupta?
Aṅgulimāla, Satyavādī, and others—
these should not yet have attained *kṣānti*,
for they maintain the existence of a self (*ātman*).
Because they resist the Buddha,
when they wish to engage in debate,
they falsely posit the existence of a self.
In reality, one does not cling to the "highest mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) or to such matters as attainment and relinquishment.
All is as previously explained.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume Six of the *Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*;
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree, based on the work of five hundred Great Arhats and others.

Section One of the First Aggregate of Miscellaneous Topics: The Sub-section on the Supreme Mundane Dharma (Laukikāgradharma), Part Six. The Venerable Ones of the West distinguish these four [dhyānas] by means of seventeen categories, as stated in the following verse:

The underlying intention (*abhiprāya*), the basis (*āśraya*), the cause (*hetu*), the object (*ālambana*), the fruit (*phala*), the outflow (*niṣyanda*), the maturation (*vipāka*), and the excellence (*viśeṣa*);

the aspect (*ākāra*), the two types of objects (*ālambana*), wisdom (*prajñā*), concentration (*samādhi*), and definition (*vyavasthāna*); the investigation (*vitarka*) and so forth, the faculties (*indriya*), the mind (*citta*), and the regression (*parihāṇi*)—these constitute the subsequent questions.
What is the underlying intention regarding "Heat" (*uṣmagata*)?
Answer: It refers to all the roots of goodness previously cultivated and accumulated,
namely those arising from giving.
Up to and including proficiency in the seven bases,
all are dedicated toward liberation;
this is their underlying intent.
Question: Upon what does "heat" (ūṣmagata) arise?
Answer: It arises based on the meditative concentration (samādhi) of its own level (svabhūmi).
Question: What serves as the cause for heat?
Answer: It is the wholesome roots of the same category belonging to one's own stage from a previous life.
Question: What serves as the object of focus for "Heat" (*uṣmagata*)?
Answer: The Four Noble Truths.
Question: What is the fruit of "heat" (ūṣmagata)?
Answer: Its proximate virile fruit (puruṣakāraphala) is "summit" (mūrdhan).
Question: What is the outflow (niṣyanda) of "heat"?
Answer: It produces subsequent roots of goodness of the same category within its own stage.
Question: What is the maturation (*vipāka*) of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*)?
Answer: The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).
Question: Do the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) also have the power to project a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*)?
Some say they do not.
Why is this? Because it involves a turning away from existence;
that is to say, these roots of goodness.
Aversion toward all forms of existence within a particular class of beings can only bring them to completion;
it cannot project them [into a new birth].
Some say that it can also project them.
This means that although these roots of goodness turn away from and loathe existence,
they are nonetheless capable of drawing one toward it.
It conforms to the noble path;
it is the fruit of the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga), meaning the fruit of the homogeneous class induced by this [path].
It is increasingly intense,
subtle, and sublime;
it is free from calamities and obstacles, and is conducive to the categories of supreme virtue.
Question: What is the benefit of *ūṣmagata*?
Answer: It serves as the definitive cause for attaining *nirvāṇa*.
Some say that upon attaining *ūṣmagata*, one certainly does not sever the roots of goodness.
Question: How many aspects (ākāra) does "Heat" (uṣmagata) possess?
Answer: It possesses sixteen aspects.
Question: Is "Heat" a condition by way of name, or is it a condition by way of meaning?
Answer: It takes both name and meaning as its object.
Question: Is "Heat" (uṣmagata) produced by hearing (śrutamaya) or produced by reflection (cintāmaya)?
It is produced through cultivation.
Answer: It is produced solely through cultivation.
Question: Is "heat" (ūṣmagata) bound to the desire realm?
Is it bound to the realm of form?
Is it bound to the formless realm?
Answer: It is bound exclusively to the realm of form.
Question: Does "Heat" (ūṣmagata) exist within meditative concentration, or does it not exist within meditative concentration?
Answer: It exists only within meditative concentration.
Question: Is "Heat" (ūṣmagata) accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra,
or is it without vitarka and with only vicāra,
or is it without both vitarka and vicāra?
Answer: It possesses all three.
Question: Is "heat" associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), or is it associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*)?
It is associated with the faculty of equanimity.
Answer: It is associated with three faculties.
Question: Is "heat" (uṣmagata) a single moment of mind?
Question: Is there a plurality of minds?
Answer: There is a plurality of minds.
Question: Can the stage of "heat" (uṣmagata) be lost?
Regarding the statement "it is not subject to regression," the answer is that it is indeed subject to regression.
This is the intended meaning of the "Summit" (mūrdhan) stage.
This means that from generosity up to the fruit of "heat," patience serves as the immediate human effort result (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The Victorious One does not sever the roots of goodness;
some say he also does not commit an act of immediate retribution.
The rest is as explained for "Heat" (ūṣmagata).
As for the intended meaning of "Patience" (kṣānti),
it refers to [the progression] from generosity (dāna).
Regarding "up to the fruit of the summit":
the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) serves as the immediate human-effort fruit (puruṣakāraphala).
The Victorious One does not regress;
he does not commit the deeds of immediate retribution,
nor does he fall into the evil destinies.
Some say that one also does not grasp at a self;
the rest is as explained in the section on the "Summit.
As for the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) of the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*):
That is to say, from generosity up to the object of focus for patience,
these are exclusively the fruits of the Truth of Suffering.
Taking the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering as its proximate virile fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*),
it is superior.
Regarding the aspect of entering the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) immediately [thereafter]:
it consists of the four aspects of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Regarding "one mind" and "many minds," it should be said that there is but one mind;
the rest is as explained in the section on patience (*kṣānti*).
At the initial stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), one takes the three truths as objects;
while practicing the present application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), one cultivates all four applications of mindfulness for the future.
When one aspect is cultivated in the present, the future aspects are also cultivated;
these four aspects are cultivated as being of the same category,
for they do not take the Truth of Cessation as an object in a manner that is of a different category.
When the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is cultivated in the present, one also cultivates it in the future;
furthermore, one cultivates only the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
When a single aspect (*ākāra*) is cultivated in the present, one cultivates it in the future.
The cultivation of the four aspects is likewise a cultivation of similar types,
not of dissimilar types. Why is this so?
Since one cannot cultivate the path that takes the aggregates as its object by first contemplating the cessation of the aggregates,
one increases the "heat" stage (*uṣmagata*),
which consists of any one of the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) taking the three truths as its object.
Now, one cultivates the future;
this cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness is both of the same kind and of a different kind.
When one aspect is cultivated in the present, the future [aspects] are cultivated;
sixteen aspects are cultivated,
taking the Truth of Cessation as their object.
In the present cultivation of the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), one cultivates the four mindfulness-establishments in the future;
in the cultivation of a single aspect (*ākāra*) in the present, one cultivates [all aspects] in the future.
One cultivates the sixteen aspects.
Question: For what reason is it that at the initial stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata), one cultivates only those of the same category and not those of different categories?
Can one who increases the stage of "heat" (uṣmagata) cultivate both similar and dissimilar [roots]?
Answer: At the initial stage of heat, one has not yet attained the spiritual lineage (gotra), because one is first learning to contemplate the truths (satya).
One cultivates only those of the same kind;
having increased the "heat" (ūṣmagata) stage, one increases the lineage already previously attained and becomes habituated to the contemplation of the truths.
Therefore, even though it is of the same category, its cultivation is not of the same category.
At the initial stage of the Summits, one takes the Four Truths as the object;
in the present moment, one cultivates the mindfulness of dharmas with respect to the future.
One cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness;
one cultivates one aspect in the present for the sake of the future,
and cultivates the sixteen aspects.
The increase of the summit has as its object any one of the four foundations of mindfulness among the three truths;
it is cultivated in the present with regard to the future.
One cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness:
practicing one aspect in the present for the sake of the future,
and cultivating the sixteen aspects while taking the truth of cessation as the object.
In the present cultivation of the mindfulness-establishment of dharmas, one cultivates the four mindfulness-establishments in the future;
in the present cultivation of a single aspect, one cultivates [all aspects] in the future.
One cultivates the sixteen aspects of the truths.
At the initial stage and during the increase of patience (*kṣānti*), one takes the four truths as objects;
this constitutes the cultivation of the present and future applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding dharmas.
One cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness:
one cultivates one aspect in the present for the sake of the future,
and cultivates the sixteen aspects.

Question: Why is it that in the stages of Patience (*kṣānti*) and its increase (*vṛddhi*), only the present application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is cultivated, whereas this is not the case for the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*)?
Answer: Because Patience is proximate to the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
It is similar to the path of seeing;
as in the path of seeing, one arouses only the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
The same applies to patience (*kṣānti*).
The Venerable Ghosaka has stated this regarding initial patience and increasing patience.
As it was explained regarding the initial warmth and the increasing warmth,
so it is with the wholesome roots of the form realm:
they have never before attained the lineage.
Furthermore, because they have already attained the spiritual lineage (gotra),
they should not say that these four roots of goodness [are newly acquired].
Because all [of these] are produced through cultivation in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Patience (*kṣānti*) is proximate to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
because it arises as the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), just like the path of seeing.
Question: Does one who increases patience at all times cultivate the sixteen aspects?
Answer: No; sometimes there are sixteen.
Sometimes there are twelve, sometimes eight, or sometimes four.
Why is this? Because, in accordance with the gradual condensation of the objects of observation (ālambana) regarding the truths (satya).
In this way, through such a brief description of the characteristics of practice,
one gradually becomes able to approach the path of seeing (darśanamārga),
just as it is with the path of seeing itself.
Regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*):
one cultivates the present mindfulness of dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and cultivates the four mindfulnesses of the future.
When one aspect is cultivated in the present, the future [aspects] are cultivated;
specifically, four aspects are cultivated,
and this cultivation is exclusively of the same kind.
It is not that they are of a different class.
Question: Regarding the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*), has the lineage (*gotra*) already been attained?
Regarding the cultivation of the contemplation of the truths through repeated practice: for what reason does one cultivate only those of the same class,
and not those of a different class?
Answer: Regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), there are only so many aspects (*ākāra*) that can be cultivated;
there are no other aspects.
It is like a person who possesses only a single garment;
once it has been taken away, there is nothing further to take.
This case is likewise, and therefore one should not ask such a question.
Furthermore, the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma) are proximate to the Path of Seeing;
because they resemble the Path of Seeing, [they are so designated].
Furthermore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma opens the gateway to the Path of Seeing and leads to the arising of the Path of Seeing.
Because it is like the path of seeing.
Question: Regarding the four noble truths, are the initial stages of heat (ūṣmagata), summits (mūrdhan), and patience (kṣānti) observed as a continuous sequence?
It is not a continuous succession;
some say it is a succession,
as in the fifteen moments of mind during the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).
The sequential realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*) regarding the four noble truths is also like this; however,
some say it is not sequential.
That is to say, having contemplated the Noble Truth of Suffering in the desire realm,
one immediately comes to rest; subsequently,
one initiates the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Having contemplated the Noble Truth of Suffering in the realms of form and formlessness,
he then abides in equanimity;
it is the same for the remaining truths.
Regarding this statement,
it is not definitive;
for it may be viewed as a continuous succession or as non-continuous.
Because it proceeds by the power of that preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Question: Immediately after which mental attention (*manasikāra*) does this occur?
Does it induce "Heat" (*uṣmagata*)?
Answer: It is included within the aspects (*ākāra*) of practice produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
With a sense of weary detachment and yearning,
with loathing and longing,
one applies the mind continuously to give rise to "heat" (*uṣmagata*).
Immediately following "Heat" (uṣmagata), one brings forth "Summit" (mūrdhan);
immediately following "Summit," one brings forth "Patience" (kṣānti);
and immediately following "Patience," one brings forth the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma).
Question: This may be so for one who is already free from the defilement of desire;
but how is it for one who is not yet free from the defilement of desire?
Answer: Within the desire realm as well, there exists a mental attention that resembles that [of the higher realms].
Included within the mental aspects (ākāra) accomplished through reflection (cintāmayī) are:
weariness and detachment, yearning and aspiration,
loathing and contempt, and longing and remembrance.
For one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire,
this mental attention immediately gives rise to "heat" (*uṣmagata*);
the rest is as previously explained.
Question: Suppose one who has completed the cultivation of "heat" (ūṣmagata) dies just as they are about to give rise to "summit" (mūrdhan).
In their subsequent rebirth, [what will happen?]
Does it arise immediately upon [encountering the conditions], or does it arise from its original source?
Answer: If one encounters an enlightened teacher.
It arises according to those [conditions].
As for the explanation of its limits:
it is precisely that which can give rise to the *mūrdhan* (Summits).
If it were not so, one would return to the beginning;
however, one can arise [from meditative attainment] quickly,
unlike when first practicing.
Question: If one gives rise to the "summit" (*mūrdhan*) in another lifetime, from what kind of mental attention (*manasikāra*) does it arise immediately after?
Answer: It is like the mental attention present at the time of giving rise to "heat" (*uṣmagata*).
As it is said that from "heat" (ūṣmagata) one arises in "summits" (mūrdhan), so too is it from "summits" that one arises in "patience" (kṣānti).
Question: If this is so, why is that?
If one asks: "Does the 'Summit' (mūrdhan) arise immediately after the 'Heat' (uṣmagata), and does the 'Patience' (kṣānti) arise immediately after the 'Summit'?
The answer is: This is stated with reference to those that arise in a continuous succession within a single continuum of existence.
However, this is not the case for all.
Question: If one has fallen away from *ūṣmagata* and subsequently gives rise to *ūṣmagata* again, does one obtain the *ūṣmagata* that was previously obtained?
He promised that he would not follow those whom he had delivered;
having withdrawn, he was born again,
and thus it was those very ones he delivered.
It is attained anew with each new moment. Why is this?
Because it is extremely difficult to attain.
Because it has not been previously practiced,
and because it is accomplished through exertion,
as is the case with the Prātimokṣa vows.
To whatever extent they have been delivered,
having relinquished it, they receive it again;
to that same extent they are delivered.
It is attained anew with each new moment;
this is also like that.
As it is said regarding "Heat," so it is for "Summits" as well.
The "Heat" and "Summits" stages arising from the fundamental dhyānas are also necessarily non-retrogressive,
because the meditative concentration upon which they rely is sovereign and firm.
The "Heat" and "Summits" produced in dependence on the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) or the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) are not fixed,
because they are subject to regression.
Question: Regarding the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata), Peak (mūrdhan), and Patience (kṣānti):
by relying on the lower stage, one gives rise to the middle; by relying on the middle, one gives rise to the upper.
After the middle-upper grade [state], does the lower-middle grade arise?
Answer: It certainly does not arise.
Why is this? Because one who dwells in the stage of superior progress does not take delight in what was previously attained.
Question: From the arising of "Heat" (uṣmagata) onwards, is there detachment from defilements?
Some say this:
they do not delight in the departure from defilement. Why is that?
He would rather give rise to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) than take pleasure in generating the volition for the Summit of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
let alone the meditative concentrations of the lower stages.
Regarding what has been said in this way,
it is not definitive.
If that practitioner...
If one knows that one has the power to produce the "summit" (*mūrdhan*),
one immediately produces it;
if one knows that one lacks the power to produce the summit, [one does not].
Then one seeks to become free from defilement.
Why is this? Because if one attains freedom from defilement, [one realizes liberation].
One will be born in a superior realm because one has departed from the lower realms;
this applies to the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and so forth.
Regarding the distinctions of types,
there are seventy-three.
What are their specific matters?
This refers to the complete abandonment of all defilements in the desire realm;
there are ten instances of being bound by all fetters,
each serving as the abandonment of one category of defilement.
Up to the abandonment of the ninth [category],
these together with the preceding constitute ten;
these pertain to the defilements of the first dhyāna.
There are nine [levels] from being free from one [defilement] up to being free from nine;
there is no separate category for those who are bound by all fetters,
as they are subsumed within the tenth [level] of the desire realm.
The subsequent stages are likewise so.
Thus it continues, up to and including attachment to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
There are nine [levels] from the abandonment of one up to the abandonment of nine;
it is within these various stages that the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and other factors arise.
There are seventy-three types of distinctions.
Question: Regarding that which arises in accordance with one [instance], how does it relate to that which arises in others?
Are they one or different?
Some say they are one.
Question: If that is so, for what reason?
It is said that there are seventy-three kinds of distinctions.
The answer is: although their essence is one, their states differ;
these are distinguished according to their respective states.
Therefore, it is said that there are that many.
Some say they are each distinct,
referring to those who are bound by all fetters.
The arising that is distinct differs from one category;
this is explained in detail, up to and including the distinction from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The ninth is the difference arising from the one who is defiled;
however, regarding those bound by all fetters,
[it is] with respect to those bound by all fetters.
The "heat" and other stages that have arisen are both acquired and present in the body;
they are both accomplished and manifest.
In one who is free from bondage,
the stages such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) that arise must necessarily exist within the body.
It is neither accomplished nor manifested.
For one who has abandoned the first grade of defilement of the desire realm,
[this applies] regarding one who has abandoned the first grade of defilement of the desire realm.
The "Heat" and other stages that have arisen are both acquired and present in the body;
they are both accomplished and manifest.
In those who are still bound by all fetters,
the "Heat" and other stages that have arisen are attained but do not abide in the body; they are neither accomplished nor manifest.
Regarding those [defilements] that arise elsewhere,
they cannot fail to exist within the body;
yet they are neither acquired nor present before one.
To speak at length, up until:
one who is free from the ninth grade of defilement of the sphere of nothingness also attains the "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) and other stages that arise within themselves.
It is both present in the body and accomplished,
and it is also manifest;
as for the other [factors] that arise, such as "Heat" (ūṣmagata) and so forth.
Having attained it, it does not abide in the body;
it is neither accomplished nor manifest before one.
It relies upon the fundamental dhyānas.
Regarding those who have generated "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the other stages:
they will certainly enter the state of rightness and transcendence (*samyaktva-niyāma*) in their present body. Why is this so?
Because he induces "heat" and the other stages by means of the noble path,
he relies upon the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna, and the [four] dhyānas.
Regarding those who give rise to "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the other stages,
this is not fixed. Why is that?
Because those [levels], such as "Heat" (uṣmagata), induce the Noble Path.
Question: If one relies upon this stage...
Does one enter into rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) while relying on that very same stage upon which the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) arose?
Some say: "If one relies upon a particular stage to give rise to the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya)..."
Relying precisely upon this stage,
one enters the state of right determination and departure from birth; thus it is said.
This is not fixed;
it may depend on this very stage,
or it may depend on another stage.
"Or those who rely on this very stage" refers to those of the śrāvaka lineage who,
relying on the *anāgamya* concentration, give rise to the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage.
That is, based on this very stage, one gives rise to the stages of Peak, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma,
entering the state of rightness and departure from birth;
and so on, up to if one gives rise to Heat based on the fourth dhyāna.
That is to say, based on this very stage, one gives rise to the stages of Peak, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma,
and enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth;
or alternatively, one may do so based on another stage.
This refers to those of the śrāvaka lineage:
if they generate "heat" (ūṣmagata) based on the preparatory stage (anāgamya),
they do so based on the first dhyāna.
One generates the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas,
and enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth;
this is likewise for each stage up to the fourth dhyāna.
If one gives rise to the stages of Heat and Summits based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya),
they give rise to the stages of Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas based on the first dhyāna.
One enters the state of rightness and departure from birth;
this remains the same up to the fourth dhyāna.
If one relies on the threshold concentration (anāgamya), [the same applies].
One gives rise to Heat, Summits,
and Patience; based on the first dhyāna,
one gives rise to Patience and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas.
One enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
This remains the same up to the fourth dhyāna.
Some say that if one generates "heat" (*uṣmagata*) based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), [it is likewise].
Relying on the first dhyāna,
he gives rise to the summit, patience, and the highest mundane dharmas,
and enters into rightness and the departure from birth.
The same applies up to the fourth dhyāna.
If one generates the levels of Heat and Summits based on the *anāgamya* concentration,
they do so by relying on the first dhyāna.
One gives rise to the stage of patience and the supreme mundane dharmas,
enters into rightness and departure from birth,
and so on up to the fourth dhyāna; it is likewise for all [the stages].
If one relies on the *anāgamya* concentration to give rise to *uṣmagata*,
*mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti*, those rely on the first *dhyāna*; if one gives rise to *kṣānti* and the *laukikāgradharma*, they likewise rely on the first *dhyāna*.
One enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
This applies likewise up to the fourth dhyāna.
Some say that if one generates "heat" (*uṣmagata*) based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), [the same result follows].
Based on the first dhyāna, he gives rise to the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas,
and enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth;
this is likewise true up to the fourth dhyāna.
If one gives rise to the stages of Heat and Summits based on the *anāgamya* concentration,
they give rise to Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas based on the first dhyāna.
One enters the state of rightness and departure from birth;
this applies likewise up to the fourth dhyāna.
If one gives rise to the stages of Heat, Summits, and Patience based upon the threshold concentration (anāgamya), [the same applies].
Relying upon the first dhyāna,
he gives rise to the stages of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas,
and enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth.
This also applies up to the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
after the medium and superior stages:
It does not arise from the lower or middle stages.
Why, then, is it said now that it arises in this way?
Answer: It does not arise from within its own stage.
Arising occurs from a different stage (*bhūmi*).
Such is the teaching regarding the śrāvaka lineage.
Now, what is the case for the bodhisattva?
Some say that if a bodhisattva generates "heat" (ūṣmagata) based on the preparatory stage (anāgamya),
they generate "heat," "summit" (mūrdhan), and "patience" (kṣānti) based on the first dhyāna up to the third dhyāna.
Relying on the fourth dhyāna,
one gives rise to the stages of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas,
thereby entering the state of rightness and departure from birth.
If one gives rise to the stages of Heat and Summits based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya),
or gives rise to Heat, Summits, and Patience based on the first dhyāna up to the third dhyāna.
Based on the fourth dhyāna,
one gives rise to the stages of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas,
thereby entering the state of rightness and departure from birth; if based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the same occurs.
One generates the stages of Heat, Peak,
and Patience based on the first dhyāna up to the third dhyāna;
one likewise generates Heat, Peak, and Patience based on the [lower] dhyānas as well.
Relying on the fourth dhyāna,
one gives rise to the stages of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas,
and enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth.
Question: Regarding the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
once the medium and superior grades have arisen,
the lower and medium grades do not arise again.
Question: Why is it stated at this time that [a mind] does not arise from the same level?
Answer: Because [a mind] does not arise from its own level.
It can arise in a different stage (*bhūmi*).
Some say that śrāvakas cannot cause it to arise,
whereas bodhisattvas can.
Others, in order to avoid such faults,
state as follows: "If a bodhisattva,
relying on the *anāgamya* concentration, gives rise to 'heat' (*uṣmagata*)."
The same applies up to the fourth dhyāna.
If one gives rise to the "summit" based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya),
the same applies up to the fourth dhyāna.
If one gives rise to patience based on the *anāgamya* concentration,
it is likewise for all stages up to the fourth dhyāna;
that is, based precisely upon the fourth dhyāna.
One who gives rise to the stage of patience and the supreme mundane dharmas enters into rightness and departure from birth;
thus it is said.
The bodhisattva relies solely upon the fourth dhyāna to give rise to the stages of heat,
summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas,
thereby entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
Why is this? Because all the sublime qualities of a bodhisattva are induced solely by relying upon the fourth dhyāna.
That is to say, from the contemplation of impurity up to the knowledge of non-arising.
Question: What is the case for a pratyekabuddha?
Answer: Regarding the rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddhas, they are as described for bodhisattvas; regarding the group-practicing pratyekabuddhas, they are not fixed, as described for śrāvakas.
Question: Did the Bodhisattva ever, in other previous lives, give rise to the roots of goodness conducive to penetration?
If so, what fault would there be?
If they have already arisen,
why is it said that the bodhisattva’s extraordinary roots of goodness consist of those beginning with the contemplation of impurity?
Up to the knowledge of non-arising,
all are attained in a single sitting;
provided that one does not rise [from that seat].
For ninety-one kalpas, the bodhisattva does not fall into the evil destinies.
By whose power is this?
Some say that in previous lives,
the Bodhisattva had already produced the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
By the power of patience,
for ninety-one kalpas,
he did not fall into the evil realms.
Question: If that is so, why is it said that a bodhisattva attains all roots of goodness in a single sitting?
Answer: Those which were previously aroused.
This belongs to another lineage,
not to one's own lineage;
it is that which is attained in a single sitting.
This explains one's own spiritual lineage;
therefore, there is no contradiction.
Some say that [the seeds] do not arise.
Why is this? Because the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva do not pass through the succession of worlds.
Because he attained [enlightenment] by sitting once under the Bodhi tree.
Question: If that is so, then regarding the Bodhisattva—
For ninety-one kalpas,
one does not fall into the evil realms.
By whose power is this?
Answer: It is capable of obstructing rebirth in the evil destinies;
it does not necessarily depend on the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Why is this so?
Whether it be generosity, ethical discipline, hearing, or reflection;
or whether it be the levels of Heat or Summits—
these are capable of obstructing rebirth in the evil destinies.
If one is of dull faculties,
only upon attaining patience can they be capable; yet,
when Bodhisattvas perform even a single act of giving, [they do so with such power].
It also encompasses ethical discipline and wisdom.
When practicing a single form of ethical discipline,
it likewise encompasses generosity and wisdom.
When practicing a single wisdom,
one also encompasses generosity and ethical discipline;
by means of this, one can obstruct tens of millions of rebirths in the evil realms.
How much less could it fail to obstruct [rebirth in] the three evil destinies?
Thus it is said:
"All the sublime roots of goodness possessed by a bodhisattva..."
This means that from the contemplation of impurity up to the knowledge of non-arising,
all are induced within a single sitting in this very life, based upon the fourth dhyāna.
This is not even the case for other stages within this very life, let alone in previous lives.
The same applies to the rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddhas.
As for the group-practicing pratyekabuddhas, their roots of virtue are indeterminate.
As stated regarding the śrāvakas,
there are six distinct types of spiritual lineage for each of the stages of heat (ūṣmagata), summits (mūrdhan), patience (kṣānti), and the supreme mundane dharmas (laukikāgradharma).

That is to say: the lineage of those subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*), the lineage of those who reflect (*cetayitadharman*), the lineage of those who protect (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), the lineage of those who abide (*sthitākampya*), the lineage of those capable of penetration (*prativedhanādharman*), and the lineage of the immovable (*akopyadharman*).
Among these, one may transform the lineage of those subject to regression at the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
One gives rise to the heat of the *cetana-dharmin* lineage,
up to the heat of the *prativedhanādharmin* lineage;
one gives rise to the heat of the *akopya-dharmin* lineage.
The "heat" stage of the śrāvaka lineage may be transformed into the "heat" stage of the pratyekabuddha or buddha lineage;
the "heat" stage of the pratyekabuddha lineage may be transformed into the "heat" stage of the buddha or śrāvaka lineage.
The stage of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) within the Buddha-lineage is irreversible;
as it is said regarding warmth, so it is regarding the "summit" (*mūrdhan*).
However, the stage of "patience" (*kṣānti*) within the Śrāvaka-lineage can be transformed.
One gives rise to the patience of the pratyekabuddha lineage;
one does not transform the patience of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha lineages,
but is able to give rise to the patience of the buddha lineage.
Why is this? Forbearance opposes the evil destinies,
yet bodhisattvas make vows to be born in the evil destinies.
Nor can one transform the receptivity of the pratyekabuddha lineage into the receptivity of the śrāvaka lineage. Why is this?
Because of the non-retrogression of patience (*kṣānti*).
Some say that the *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti* of the śrāvaka lineage can give rise to the *uṣmagata*,
*mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti* of the pratyekabuddha lineage.
If one has generated the *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan* stages of the Pratyekabuddha lineage,
one cannot also generate the *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan* stages of other vehicles. Why is this?
The roots of goodness of a Pratyekabuddha range from the contemplation of impurity up to the knowledge of non-arising.
Because it is attained in a single sitting.
The critique says: He should not make such a statement. Why is that?
The lineage of the rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddha attains its roots of goodness in a single sitting; however,
the lineage of the group-practicing pratyekabuddha is not fixed, as explained in the case of the śrāvakas.
Therefore, regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma),
there are six types of spiritual lineages (gotra) as well as the lineages of the three vehicles (triyāna).
None of these can be turned back, because they last for only a single moment.
[Question: Regarding the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
From where does it arise?
Answer: It arises from the desire realm (kāmadhātu), not from the form or formless realms (rūpadhātu and ārūpyadhātu).
In the desire realm, humans and devas are able to give rise to it,
but not those in the three evil destinies,
because they lack superior roots of goodness.
It can arise among humans in the three continents, but not in Uttarakuru;
although it can arise among the gods,
it arises later and not at the beginning.
This means that having previously arisen among humans and later regressed to be born among the desire-realm devas,
one is able to give rise to it again through the force of prior habituation.
Question: Why can [the path] not first arise among the gods?
Answer: Because in those realms there is no superior attention (*manasikāra*) such as that of revulsion (*nirveda*).
Question: In the miserable destinies (*apāya*), there is superior attention such as that of revulsion.
Why do these roots of goodness not arise?
The answer is: because in the evil realms there is no superior physical basis (*āśraya*).
If there were superior mental orientations such as renunciation (*nirveda*), [the roots of goodness would arise].
Furthermore, there are those with superior physical bases who are able to first give rise to this kind of wholesome root;
although such superior physical bases exist among the gods of the desire realm, [they cannot do so].
Yet there is no superior attention characterized by revulsion and so forth;
and although such superior attention as revulsion exists within the miserable realms,
there is no superior physical basis [for it].
In the human realm, both [conditions] are present;
therefore, one is able to first initiate [the path].
Question: What about the form and formless realms?
Why do these roots of goodness not arise?
Answer: They arise in those places where one can enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Since the realms of form and formlessness cannot admit entry into the state of rightness and departure from birth, [the roots of goodness do not arise there].
Therefore, it cannot arise.
A question arises from this discussion:
for what reason [do these afflictions not arise] in the form and formless realms?
"Is it not possible for them to enter the state of rightness and transcendence?
He replied, "They are neither a field nor a vessel," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Furthermore, wherever patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) can arise, one can enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Although knowledge can arise in the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*),
because patience does not arise there, one cannot enter the state of rightness and departure from birth.
Furthermore, wherever the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) can arise,
in those places one can enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
Although the subsequent knowledge arises in the form and formless realms, [one cannot enter the state of rightness there].
Because they do not give rise to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), they are unable to enter the state of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*).
Furthermore, wherever there is a superior physical basis (*āśraya*) and the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*),
in that place one is able to enter the state of right determination.
Although the form and formless realms possess superior physical bases,
because they lack painful sensation,
one cannot enter the state of right determination and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
Question: Upon what kind of body do these stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas arise?
Answer: They arise upon the bodies of men and women.
Question: Is the "heat" (ūṣmagata) that arises based on a female body and directed toward obtaining a female body also obtained when it arises based on a male body?
Answer: It is obtained.
As with attaining *uṣmagata*, so it is for attaining *mūrdhan* and *kṣānti*.
Question: Does the *uṣmagata* arising from a male body depend upon that male body?
"Can one also obtain the 'heat' (*uṣmagata*) arising from the female body?
Answer: "One obtains it just as one obtains heat;
the same applies to obtaining the 'summit' (*mūrdhan*) and 'patience' (*kṣānti*)."
In the case of a female body, the heat generated within that female body is both acquired and present in the body;
it is both accomplished and manifested.
The heat produced in relation to a male body is attained,
yet it is not established within that body,
nor does it manifest.
As it is said regarding *ūṣmagata*, the same applies to *mūrdhan* and *kṣānti*.
When a male body gives rise to *ūṣmagata* within a male body,
it both is acquired and resides therein.
It is both accomplished and present before one.
Regarding the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) that arises in a female body,
it is attained but not accomplished within that body.
It does not manifest before one.
As it is said regarding *ūṣmagata*, the same applies to *mūrdhan* and *kṣānti*.
The *ūṣmagata* that arises from a female body...
It serves as the cause for the heat (*ūṣman*) arising from the female body,
and it also serves as the cause for the heat arising from the male body.
As it is said regarding heat, so it is for the summits (*mūrdhan*), the patiences (*kṣānti*), and likewise for the others.
The heat produced by a male body serves as the cause for the heat produced by a male body;
it does not serve as the cause for the heat produced by a female body.
Why is this? Because that which is superior cannot be caused by that which is inferior, as the latter is itself inferior.
As it is said regarding "warmth," so it is for "summits" and "patience" as well.
Question: Having already given rise to the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) based on a male body,
is it possible to subsequently receive a female body?
Answer: They may further be received.
However, only the first three are not the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*). Why is this so?
Because it lasts for only a single moment.
Question: Once one has produced the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), can one again become a *śaṇḍha* or a *pandaka*?
Is it not the case that those with no sexual organs or with both sexual organs cannot [attain it]?
Answer: It can be further received;
however, only those in the *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan* stages, and no others.
Why is this? Because once one has attained patience (kṣānti),
one then turns away from the evil destinies.
Those such as the *śaṇḍha* have bodies that are base and loathsome;
they are among the evil destinies within the human realm.
Yet, if they should attain superior roots of goodness such as *kṣānti*, [they may transcend them].
Because they will certainly not again receive a body of that same class.
Question: Regarding an ordinary person who has attained *kṣānti* (receptivity) at the moment of death—
When one abandons the homogeneous group (nikāyasabhāga), does one also abandon patience (kṣānti)?
If so, what would be the fault?
If one were to abandon it, one would fall into the miserable destinies (apāya).
For what reason is it said that if one attains patience (*kṣānti*), one does not fall into the evil destinies?
Furthermore, if it is abandoned,
why is it abandoned at the time of the death of another being?
The Noble One is not so.
If he does not relinquish [them],
for what reason are they included in the aggregate of karma?
And why are the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the aggregate (*skandha*) not both mentioned,
as when it is said that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) dwells in the womb and so forth?
It is only the body that is accomplished, not bodily action.
To this, one should reply: "It is relinquished."
Some say it is not relinquished;
some say it is indeterminate;
others say it is sometimes relinquished and sometimes not.
Each of these points will be explained in detail,
as set forth later in the section on "Harming Living Beings" within the *Karmaskandha*.
According to this explanation,
when a sentient being dies, they necessarily abandon patience because their roots of goodness are inferior.
When an ordinary person relies on a particular stage and gives rise to this type of wholesome root,
if they die and are reborn again in that same stage, [they will possess it].
Since one abandons even the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*), how much more so these roots of goodness,
which are dharmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
Having taken birth in the desire realm, one should not abandon [this practice].
Question: What are the characteristics of the preparatory stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata) when it is cultivated?
Answer: To state it briefly, its characteristic consists of the three types of wisdom;
namely, the wisdom consisting of hearing.
The wisdom resulting from reflection and the wisdom resulting from cultivation.
Question: How does one cultivate the wisdom resulting from hearing?
Answer: When a practitioner of meditation encounters an enlightened teacher who briefly explains for them the essential points of all phenomena.
There are only the eighteen elements (dhātu),
the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha);
or one may personally recite the Sūtra Piṭaka.
Having brought the Vinaya Piṭaka and the Abhidharma Piṭaka to full maturity, he forms this thought:
The textual and doctrinal content of the Tripiṭaka is exceedingly vast.
If one were to constantly memorize and maintain it, the mind would become weary;
therefore, the essentials taught within the Tripiṭaka are simply the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
Having formed this thought,
he first observes the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
At the time of that observation, he establishes them in three categories.
That is to say, by way of name, by way of specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and by way of general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
"Name" refers to designating that this is the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to and including that this is the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
"Specific characteristic" refers to...
That is to say: "This is the specific characteristic of the eye-element," and so on, up to "this is the specific characteristic of the mind-consciousness-element.
As for the common characteristic:
That is to say: the sixteen aspects,
the eighteen elements as the objects of observation,
and the sixteen kinds of common characteristics.
Taking these realms as objects, he cultivates wisdom and serenity.
Having cultivated wisdom and serenity regarding the eighteen realms,
he again gives rise to weariness and reflects thus:
These eighteen elements (dhātus) are identical to the twelve bases (āyatanas).
Therefore, they should be subsumed within the twelve bases by means of abbreviation;
that is to say, the ten material elements.
That is, the ten bases of form;
the seven elements of mind are the base of mind;
and the element of phenomena is the base of phenomena.
When he contemplates these twelve bases,
he establishes them in three categories:
namely, by way of name, by way of specific characteristic, and by way of general characteristic.
"Name" refers to designations such as "this is called the sense-base of the eye," up to "this is called the sense-base of mental phenomena.
"Specific characteristic" refers to...
That is to say: "This is the specific characteristic of the eye-base," and so on, up to "this is the specific characteristic of the mental-object-base.
As for the common characteristic:
That is to say: the sixteen aspects,
the twelve bases as the objects of observation,
and the sixteen kinds of common characteristics.
Taking these bases as his object, he cultivates wisdom and serenity.
Having cultivated wisdom and serenity regarding the twelve bases,
he again becomes weary and reflects thus:
These twelve bases,
excluding the unconditioned— which constitutes the five aggregates—
should be subsumed under the five aggregates as follows: the ten material bases.
Furthermore, the form included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*);
the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*);
and the feeling within the sphere of mental objects is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*).
Perception is the aggregate of perception;
the remaining mental factors and formations dissociated from mind are the aggregate of formations.
When he contemplates these five aggregates in this manner, [he understands them as they truly are].
It is established as threefold:
namely, by way of name, by way of specific characteristic, and by way of general characteristic.
"Name" refers to this designation "aggregate of form."
Up to this point, it is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
As for its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*):
it means that this is the specific characteristic of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
This is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
As for its general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*),
it consists of twelve modes of activity (*ākāra*).
Regarding the five aggregates as the object of observation,
one cultivates wisdom and serenity by taking those twelve types of common characteristics of these aggregates as the focal point.
Having cultivated wisdom and tranquility regarding the five aggregates,
he further gives rise to weariness and reflects thus:
"These five aggregates, together with the unconditioned,"
This is because they are the four foundations of mindfulness;
one should therefore briefly enter into the four foundations of mindfulness.
That is to say, the aggregate of form is the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
The aggregate of feeling is the application of mindfulness to feelings;

the aggregate of consciousness is the application of mindfulness to the mind; and the aggregates of perception and formations, together with the unconditioned, [are the application of mindfulness to phenomena].
This is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
When he contemplates these four foundations of mindfulness,
he establishes them in three parts.
That is to say: by way of name, by way of specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and by way of general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
"By way of name" means: this is the application of mindfulness on the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), up to and including this is the application of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*): this refers to "this is the specific characteristic of the mindfulness-establishment of the body," and so on,
up to "this is the specific characteristic of the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena."
The common characteristics refer to the sixteen aspects of the four foundations of mindfulness that are observed.
Regarding the sixteen kinds of common characteristics,
one takes them as objects and practices mindfulness-establishment,
cultivating wisdom and cultivating tranquility.
Having cultivated wisdom and tranquility within the four foundations of mindfulness,
he again gives rise to weariness and reflects thus:
"These four foundations of mindfulness..."
Excluding space and non-analytical cessation,
since these are precisely the four noble truths,
they should be subsumed within the four noble truths.
That is to say, the fruit-portion of contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) is the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*);
the cause-portion is the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*);
and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
The remedy is the Truth of the Path.
When one contemplates these Four Noble Truths,
they are established as three parts.
That is to say: by way of name, by way of specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and by way of general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
"By way of name" means that this is named the Truth of Suffering, up to and including this being named the Truth of the Path. "Specific characteristic" refers to...
That is to say: "This is the specific characteristic of the truth of suffering," up to "this is the specific characteristic of the truth of the path.
As for the common characteristic:
This refers to four aspects:
the four common characteristics of the Truth of Suffering as it is observed—
namely, (1) suffering, (2) impermanence, (3) emptiness, and (4) non-self.
The four aspects through which the truth of origination (samudaya-satya) is observed are its four common characteristics:
first, cause; second, origination; third, production; and fourth, condition.
The truth of cessation, as observed through its four aspects, has four common characteristics:
first, cessation; second, tranquility; third, excellence; and fourth, detachment.
The four aspects through which the Truth of the Path is observed are its four common characteristics:
first, the path; second, the right method; third, practice; and fourth, renunciation.
Taking these truths as objects, they cultivate wisdom and cultivate serenity;
while cultivating wisdom and serenity regarding the four noble truths,
it is just as in the path of seeing.
One contemplates the truths progressively;
that is, first one contemplates the suffering of the desire realm individually,
and subsequently contemplates the suffering of the form and formless realms collectively.
First, one contemplates the origin of the desire realm individually;
subsequently, one contemplates the origin of the form and formless realms collectively.
First, one contemplates the cessation of the desire realm individually.
Subsequently, one contemplates the cessation of the form and formless realms collectively;
first, one contemplates the path of the desire realm individually, and later, one contemplates the path of the form and formless realms collectively.
When observing the Four Noble Truths in this manner:
It is like viewing various forms and images through a fine silk screen;
only when one practices to this extent is the wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) fully perfected.
Based on this, the wisdom arisen from reflection is produced;
once that has been perfected through cultivation,
the wisdom arisen from meditation is subsequently produced.
This is called "Heat.
Following Heat, "Summit" arises;
following Summit, "Patience" arises.
Following patience, the Supreme Mundane Dharma arises;
following the Supreme Mundane Dharma, the Path of Seeing arises;
and following the Path of Seeing, the Path of Cultivation arises.
Following the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) arises.
In this sequence, the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are brought to fulfillment.
There are three kinds of roots of goodness.
1. The stage conducive to merit;
2. The stage conducive to liberation;
3. The stage conducive to penetration.
Wholesome roots conducive to merit refer to planting the seeds for birth as a human or birth in the heavens.
Regarding the seeds for birth as a human:
That is to say, this seed is capable of producing rebirth among humans in a high-ranking and noble family,
with abundant wealth and treasures, and a complete circle of kinsmen.
With a countenance that is dignified and a body that is delicate and soft, they may even become a universal monarch (cakravartin).
As for the "seeds for birth in the heavens," this refers to these very seeds.
They are able to be born among the gods of the desire, form, and formless realms,
where they experience superior and wondrous fruits;
or they may become Śakra, Māra-rāja, or Brahmā-rāja.
Possessing great majesty and authority over many,
those with the roots of goodness conducive to liberation are said to have planted the seeds of certain liberation.
Therefore, it is determined that one will attain parinirvāṇa.
The roots of goodness conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) refer to the stages of heat (uṣmagata),
summits (mūrdhan), patience (kṣānti), and the supreme mundane dharmas (laukikāgradharma).
In this context, the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) should be analyzed in detail.
Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these roots of goodness?
Answer: They have the actions of body, speech, and mind as their intrinsic nature.
However, mental action (manas-karma) is predominant.
Question: Do these roots of goodness (kuśala-mūla) reside in the level of the mind (manobhūmi), or do they reside in the five groups of sensory consciousness (pañca-vijñāna-kāya)?
Answer: It resides in the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*), not in the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*).
Question: Are these roots of goodness obtained through preparatory effort (*prayoga*) or obtained through the removal of defilements (*vairāgya*)?
Is it acquired through birth?
Answer: It is acquired solely through application (*prayoga*).
Some say: [it is so].
This is also acquired at birth (*upapattiprātilambhika*).
The critique states:
the former explanation is superior.
Because it arises from preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Question: Are these roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) produced by hearing (*śrutamaya*) or produced by reflection (*cintāmaya*)?
Is it produced by cultivation?
Answer: It is produced by hearing and reflection, not by cultivation.
Some say it is also produced by cultivation.
The commentary states:
The former explanation is superior,
because [the afflictions] are bound exclusively to the desire realm.
Question: In what place do these roots of goodness arise?

Answer: They arise in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), not in the form or formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*). Within the desire realm, they arise among human beings, not in other destinies (*gati*).
Among humans, they arise in the three continents, not in Uttarakuru.
Question: At what time are these roots of goodness planted?
Answer: At the time when a Buddha appears in the world;
for it is only when there is the Buddha-dharma that one is able to plant them.
Other masters say that even if the Buddha-dharma does not exist,
if one encounters a pratyekabuddha, [one may still attain it].
They are also able to plant these roots of goodness.
Question: Upon what kind of body do these roots of goodness arise?
Answer: They arise upon both male bodies and female bodies.
Question: For what purpose did they plant these roots of goodness?
Answer: Either through giving, or through ethical discipline, or through hearing the Dharma.
Yet it is not fixed. Why is this?
Because their intentions differ.
That is to say, there may be someone who, by giving even a single morsel of food,
or even a single tooth-stick,
is able to plant the seed of liberation.
For example, Cāṇḍāla and others,
whatever they may give, all say these words:
"May I, by means of this, certainly attain liberation."
There may be those who, although they establish a great unrestricted assembly (pañcavārṣika), are unable to plant the seeds of liberation—
such as those who are not free from violence and the like—
and who, in accordance with whatever they give, seek only worldly wealth, honor, and fame.
They do not seek liberation.
Yet, there are those who, by observing the eightfold precepts for a single day and night,
are immediately able to plant the seeds of liberation.
There may be some who uphold the Pratimokṣa precepts with full understanding and distinction,
yet fail to plant the seeds of liberation;
or there may be some who recite even a single four-line verse of the Gāthās.
One is thus able to plant the seeds of liberation;
yet there may be those who are well-versed in both the words and meanings of the Tripiṭaka,
yet are unable to plant the seeds of liberation.
Question: Who is definitively able to plant these roots of merit conducive to liberation?
Answer: One who possesses a superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Those who joyfully seek nirvana and feel aversion toward saṃsāra will, accordingly,
give rise to even a small measure of generosity, ethical discipline, learning, and virtue.
One will then be able to decisively plant these roots of goodness;
however, this cannot be achieved without a superior intention that aspires for and seeks nirvāṇa.
Those who are averse to birth and death,
although they may give rise to a great deal of merit through generosity, ethical discipline, and learning,
are nonetheless unable to plant these roots of goodness.
Question: If one has planted these roots of goodness, how long will it take before they are able to attain liberation?
Answer: If they are extremely swift, [it will be as follows].
It requires three lifetimes:
namely, planting this seed in the first lifetime,
and bringing it to maturity in the second lifetime.
In the third birth, one is able to attain liberation immediately;
for others, it is not fixed.
That is to say, there may be some person who, having already planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*), [attains it later].
They may wander through birth and death for one kalpa, or a hundred kalpas, or even a thousand kalpas.
Yet they are unable to give rise to the levels conducive to penetration;
or again, there are those who,
having already given rise to the roots of goodness conducive to penetration...
They may undergo transmigration through birth and death for one lifetime, or for a hundred lifetimes, or for a thousand lifetimes.
Yet one cannot enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) also consist of six types.
That is to say, from the lineage of those subject to regression up to the lineage of those who are immovable.
One transforms the *mokṣabhāgīya* of the *parihāṇadharman* lineage into the *mokṣabhāgīya* of the *cetanādharman* lineage, and so on,
up to transforming the *mokṣabhāgīya* of the *prativedhanādharman* lineage.
One generates the factors conducive to liberation of the immovable dharma-lineage;
one transforms the factors conducive to liberation of the śrāvaka lineage;
and one generates the factors conducive to liberation of the pratyekabuddha and buddha lineages.
One transforms the stage of the factors conducive to liberation of the pratyekabuddha lineage,
and gives rise to the stages of the factors conducive to liberation of the śrāvaka and buddha lineages;
once the stage of the factors conducive to liberation of the buddha lineage has been produced, [it cannot be transformed].
This is because it cannot be turned back, as it is extremely intense.
Question: Within the preparatory stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), there is the contemplation of arising and ceasing (udayavyaya-vipaśyanā).
What is the nature of this preparatory practice of the contemplation of arising and ceasing?
Answer: When the various practitioners of yoga are about to contemplate arising and ceasing,
they first apprehend the signs of emergence and decline within and without.
Returning to one's place of residence,
one should harmonize body and mind,
and contemplate the arising and ceasing of the body throughout its single lifetime, from birth until death.
Next, one contemplates the stages: by year, by season, by month,
by half-month, and by a single day and night.
Next is the muhūrta;
next is the lava;
next is the tatkṣaṇa.
Next, it gradually diminishes until,
regarding all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma),
one contemplates that two moments arise and two moments perish.
This is called the fulfillment of the preparatory application.
Next, one further contemplates conditioned phenomena as arising in one moment and ceasing in the next moment.
This is called the accomplishment of the contemplation of arising and ceasing.
Question: Regarding this contemplation of arising and ceasing, when one contemplates arising and ceasing—
Is it observed by a single mind?
Or is it observed by two minds?
If it is observed by a single mind, [then...]
Is it to be understood as one [meaning],
or is it to be understood as two?
If it is to be understood as one:
Just as one contemplates arising as arising,
one should likewise contemplate cessation as arising;
contemplating arising as arising may be called right contemplation.
To contemplate cessation as arising would be a false contemplation;
just as one contemplates cessation as cessation, one should likewise contemplate arising as cessation.
To contemplate cessation as cessation may be called right contemplation.
To contemplate arising as cessation would be a false contemplation;
how can a single interpretation be both correct and false?
If one were to propose two interpretations,
there would necessarily be two entities:
a single mind and two entities.
This is impossible.
If one were to observe with two minds,
it would be observing the arising of a single mind.
One should contemplate cessation with a single mind;
one should not contemplate arising and cessation.
What, then, is meant by "contemplation of arising and cessation"?
Answer: For two moments;
with one mind one contemplates arising, and with one mind one contemplates cessation.
This is called the contemplation of arising and ceasing with reference to the continuum (*saṃtāna*),
not with reference to the moment (*kṣaṇa*);
therefore, there is no error.
Some say that one mind simultaneously contemplates both arising and ceasing,
yet without the faults mentioned previously.
One infers the existence of cessation by observing the time of arising,
because any phenomenon that arises must necessarily cease.
If one perceives the moment of cessation, one infers that there was arising,
because a phenomenon that undergoes cessation must necessarily have had an arising.
The critique states:
That explanation is irrational.
How could a single mind possess two distinct modes of understanding?
For the natures of the two means of valid cognition—direct perception and inference—are different.
The previous explanation is correct.
Question: Is this contemplation of arising and ceasing an act of attention consisting of resolute conviction (adhimokṣa-manasikāra)?
It is for the sake of true mental attention (*bhūta-manasikāra*).
Some say that it is true mental attention.
Question: If that is so, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) truly have no coming or going.
How can it be real when one perceives coming and going?
Answer: This perception has not yet been perfected; thus, one perceives coming and going.
When it is accomplished, one perceives only arising and ceasing;
one does not perceive any characteristic of coming or going,
like a single dancer performing on stage.
If one moves slowly, coming and going are perceived; if one moves rapidly, they are not perceived.
This is illustrated by the analogy of a whirling firebrand and the analogy of a potter’s wheel.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Some say it is the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
Question: If this is so, how should one reconcile what is stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, as it says:
If there is knowledge and vision that can exhaust the outflows, how could they be exhausted without knowledge and vision?
One who is able to contemplate the arising and ceasing of the aggregates—that is the liberation of the mind from afflictions.
It is not through the mental application of resolve that one can sever the afflictions.
Answer: It is explained according to the principle of a causal lineage, like the succession from father to son;
that is to say, it refers to the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
It induces true mental attention;
through true mental attention,
one abandons all afflictions.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Seven; *Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Eight.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;
translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
Section One of the First Aggregate on Miscellaneous Matters: The Chapter on the Supreme Worldly Dharmas, Part Seven. These twenty phrases.
Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*):
how many are views of a self and how many are views of "mine"?
[The answer] is explained at length, and so forth.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras;
that is to say, within the various sūtras...
The Buddha taught that there are twenty propositions of the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Venerable Śāriputra,
[this was stated] in the *Saroopama-sūtra*.
Although these twenty phrases of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) have been briefly analyzed,
it has not yet been stated how many among them are views of "I" and how many are views of "mine.
That sutra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which has not yet been explained therein, I now wish to explain; for this reason, I compose this treatise.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of others and manifesting the correct meaning.
That is to say, the Dārṣṭāntikas assert that the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) has no real objective referent.
He spoke thus: "The view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) conceives of 'I' and 'mine';
however, in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is neither 'I' nor 'mine'."
It is like a person who sees a rope and thinks it is a snake,
or sees a tree stump and thinks it is a human;
this case is likewise, and therefore there is no objective referent.
To stop that attachment and to demonstrate that this view actually has an object of perception,
this treatise was composed.
Question: Since in the ultimate sense there is neither self nor what belongs to a self, how can this view have a real object?
Answer: It is the view of a transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Based on the five aggregates of clinging, one conceives of them as "self" and "what belongs to self," just as one might perceive a rope or a tree stump as a snake or a person;
although the mode of apprehension is inverted, it is not without an objective referent.
Since the five aggregates of clinging are substantially existent,
of these twenty phrases of the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
how many are views of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and how many are views of what belongs to a self (*ātmīyadṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: There are five views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
That is to say, one regards form as the self;
one regards feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as the self.
Fifteenth is my own view:
namely, to regard with equal contemplation that "I have form; form is mine."
"I am in form; I have feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are mine."
Within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness,
I ask: what is the mode of activity of my view that takes the five aggregates of clinging as its object?
There are five modes of the view of "mine," and since they take the five aggregates of clinging as their object, there should likewise be five;
why, then, is it said that there are fifteen?
Answer: The mode of activity of the view of a self (ātmadṛṣṭi) has only five types,
because it takes the five aggregates of clinging (pañcopādānaskandha) as its object without distinction.
The aspects of my own view of practice are fifteenfold,
due to the distinctions among the five aggregates of clinging that serve as their objects.
This means that regarding each and every aggregate (skandha),
the self and its requisites possess three distinct characteristics;
such is this view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Alternatively, one should say it is one,
namely the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) among the five views;
or alternatively, one should say it is two.

That is to say, the conceptual distinctions regarding the modes of activity concerning "self" and "what belongs to self" are termed the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of what belongs to self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).
Alternatively, one should speak of three [views].
This is because there are distinctions among the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness;
alternatively, one should speak of five,
because there are distinctions based on the five aggregates as objects of perception.
Alternatively, one should say there are six,
because in each of the three realms there are both views of self and views of what belongs to self.
Alternatively, one should say there are nine.
This refers to the nine levels from the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
due to their distinctness;
alternatively, one should speak of ten.
This means that because there are views of self and views of what belongs to self (ātmagrāha and ātmīyagrāha) directed toward each of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), [the self-view] is tenfold.
Alternatively, one should say it is twelvefold,
because there are distinctions based on the objects of the twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana).
Alternatively, one should say there are eighteen,
because in each of the nine stages there are both views of self and views of what belongs to self,
and furthermore, because there are distinctions based on the objects of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
Alternatively, one should speak of twenty [aspects],
namely: the discrimination of the aggregates as objects,
and the discrimination of the characteristics and modes of the self.
Without discriminating the place from which it arises,
one contemplates accordingly:
"Form is self" or "I possess form."
Form is mine; I am in form.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Since there are four [aspects] for each of the five aggregates, there are twenty;
alternatively, one should say there are twenty-four,
namely, those that take the twelve bases as their objects.
Because each possesses the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of what belongs to self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*),
they should rather be said to be thirty-six; that is,
taking the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) as their objects.
Because each possesses the view of self and the view of what belongs to self,
one should perhaps speak of forty-eight [types],
namely, the distinctions regarding the objects of conditions.
I possess the distinctions of the characteristics of practice;
I do not discriminate regarding the place from which they arise,
observing them as they truly are.
"The eye-base is my self; I possess the eye-base.
The eye-base belongs to me;
I am within the eye-base."
The same applies to the remaining eleven bases (*āyatana*).
Since there are four for each of the twelve bases, there are forty-eight;
alternatively, one should say there are sixty-five.
This refers to the discrimination of the aggregates as objects;
it is the discrimination of the distinctions of my own possessed characteristics of activity,
as well as the discrimination of the locus from which they arise.
Thus, one regards it with equanimity:
"Form is the self; feeling is the self;
my ornaments are the self."
The servants are my vessels;
as there are three types of sensation,
so too are perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The four [types of views] regarding the thirty-two [parts of the body], together with the view that form is the self,
total thirteen. Just as there are thirteen [views] when one regards form as the self, so it is for each of the other aggregates.
Feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are also like this. Five sets of thirteen make sixty-five.
Alternatively, one should say there are seventy-two,
namely the distinctions of the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the distinctions of the characteristics of my own practice.
Without discriminating the place from which it arises,
one contemplates accordingly:
"The eye-faculty is my self," or "I possess the eye-faculty."
The eye-element is mine;
I am within the eye-element.
The same applies to the remaining seventeen elements.
Since each of the eighteen elements has four [aspects], there are seventy-two;
alternatively, one should say there are four hundred and eighty,
namely, when distinguishing the objects of cognition.
I fully understand the distinctions among the characteristics of formations,
as well as the bases from which they arise,
