just as I observe them accordingly.
"The eye-base is my self;
the form-base is my self;
the necklace is my self."
The servants are my vessels.
Just as there are three [types] in the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*),
so it is for the remaining ten spheres (*āyatana*).
There are eleven types of triads,
totaling thirty-three;
together with the contemplation that the sense-base of the eye is the self.
In total there are thirty-four.
For example, if one views the eye-base as the self, there are thirty-four [possibilities];
the same applies to the remaining eleven bases.
Twelve kinds multiplied by thirty-four make four hundred and eight;
alternatively, one should say nine hundred and thirty-six.
That is to say, one discriminates the elements as objects of perception,
thinking, "I possess the various characteristics of conditioned formations," and one also discriminates the locus from which they arise.
Thus, one regards accordingly:
"The eye-element is my self;
the form-element is my self."
The necklace is the self;
the servant is the vessel.
It is like the three [realms] within the form realm.
The same applies to the remaining sixteen elements.
There are three types of seventeen and fifty-one [factors].
Furthermore, one contemplates the eye-element as the self;
in total there are fifty-two [factors],
comprising eighteen types and fifty-two [instances].
This results in nine hundred and thirty-six [varieties].
Such are the aspects of the conditioned aggregates (*saṃskāra-skandha*) when distinguished by way of their elements (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*).
The objective basis and its mode of activity;
the classification by realm and stage;
and the objective basis, realm, and mode of activity.
The classification by realm and level; whether by continuity,
by time-period, or by moment.
Through conceptualization, there are immeasurable forms of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Here, however, we shall speak only of the conceptual differentiation of the characteristics of the aggregates as the basis for the notion of "I" and "mine," because we do not differentiate the specific locations from which such notions arise.
There are only twenty propositions of the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Question: Why, in this context, are only twenty propositions of the view of a personal identity taught based on the aggregates as their object?
"Are they not elements (dhātu) or bases (āyatana)?
Answer: It is because the author of that treatise intended it to be so.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Furthermore, it should also have been stated in terms of the elements (dhātu) and bases (āyatana),
yet it was not so stated.
One should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, because the aggregates (skandha) come first, the explanation is given primarily in terms of the aggregates;
this is not the case for the elements (dhātu) and bases (āyatana).
Furthermore, in this context,
one should not question the author of the treatise,
for the author composed the treatise based upon the sūtras.
In the sūtras, the Buddha speaks of the twenty modes of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) solely in reliance upon the aggregates (skandha).
Therefore, the author of this treatise composes his work based on that. [Question: If that is so, let us set aside the author of the treatise.
One should ask:
For what reason, Blessed One,
do you state that the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) consists of twenty positions based solely upon the aggregates?
Is it not the case that they are neither elements (*dhātu*) nor bases (*āyatana*)?
Answer: This is because [the Buddha] considers those to be converted.
That is to say, the Buddha observes the sentient beings who are to be converted.
If one explains the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) based on the aggregates (skandha), it consists of twenty items;
by this, one attains understanding and is able to accomplish what is to be done,
which is not the case when based on the elements (dhātu) or bases (āyatana).
If one relies upon the elements and bases,
one will attain understanding and be able to accomplish what is to be done;
the Buddha has also taught this.
But it is not so; therefore, it was not taught for them.
Furthermore, the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) mostly takes the aggregates as its object.
It is taught specifically because it is not [subsumed under] the elements (*dhātu*) or bases (*āyatana*). Question:
Why, in this context, is only the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) said to have twenty phrases?
Is it not the case that other views are not mentioned?
Answer: It is because the author of that treatise intended it to be so.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this statement is incomplete;
one should also state that there are twenty types of views of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
There are eighty types of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*);
the same applies to the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
There are forty types of grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
That which is not mentioned should be understood as being incomplete.
Furthermore, among the five views,
the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the foremost.
Therefore, it is explained partially.
Furthermore, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the specific counteragent to the ten kinds of emptiness.
The reason for explaining the ten kinds of emptiness specifically is as follows:
namely, internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).
Emptiness of the external;
emptiness of the internal and external;
emptiness of the conditioned.
The emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). The emptiness of dispersion and disintegration (*vibhava-śūnyatā*).
The emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
The emptiness of the limitless,
the emptiness of the ultimate truth,
and the emptiness of emptiness.
Question: Regarding the "twenty phrases," what is the meaning of "phrase" (pada)?
Answer: It means "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva).
This view has twenty intrinsic natures.
It asks: what is meant by "contemplating form as self," and "feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as self"?
"What is meant by 'contemplating form as self,' or 'feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as self'?
The answer is: whatever form there is."
Whether it be the four great elements or that which is derived from the four great elements,
one regards all of them equally as "self."
This should be stated for each of the aggregates up to consciousness as appropriate.
Question: Why is the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) exclusively conditioned by outflows (sāsrava) and not unconditioned by outflows (anāsrava)?
They take as their object their own realm and level, not other realms and levels;
even within their own realm and level, they do not take everything as an object simultaneously.
For what reason, then, is it said that "he contemplates all of those as 'I'?"
The answer is: this term "all" refers to a partial all, not an absolute all;
therefore, there is no fault.
Furthermore, this entire statement is made in reference to the sphere of one's own practice;
therefore, there is no fault.
Question: Is there anyone who, with respect to a single aggregate (skandha), clings to it as "self" or "mine"?
Answer: There is. That is, within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) and the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
Each possesses many phenomena,
yet they grasp one as "self" and the rest as "mine."
Although the aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness do not consist of many types,
they possess various distinct intrinsic natures.
Therefore, one may also reckon that "this is I" and "the rest is mine.
Regarding the detailed exposition beginning with "observing accordingly that 'I have form,'" and so forth:
What is meant by "observing that the self possesses form"?
Answer: Having successively grasped one among the other four aggregates as being the self, [one observes it thus].
Thereafter, one clings to form as "I am," just as a person possesses wealth, necklaces, and so forth. How, then,
does one contemplate form as "mine" through equal conformity?
Answer: Regarding the other four aggregates,
once one has successively clung to one of them as "I," one subsequently clings to form as "mine."
Just as a person has attendants, such as servants and the like;
how is it that one observes "I am in form"?
Answer: [One observes] with respect to the other four aggregates.
Having thus successively clung to one [of the aggregates] as "I," they subsequently cling to form as the vessel for the self and the locus of the self,
just as oil exists within sesame seeds.
Fat within a lump;
a snake within a basket;
a sword within its scabbard.
Ghee exists within curd;
blood exists within the body, and so forth.
Thus, one should observe that matter possesses these three kinds accordingly.
It should be understood that this applies equally up to the contemplation of consciousness.
Question: It may be granted that the grasping [of the aggregates] and so forth exist within form as the self.
However, [the claim that they exist] in consciousness is not tenable.
Since form is coarse while feeling and the other aggregates are subtle,
how could it be possible to hold that "I am form" existing within feeling and the others?
Because coarse phenomena should not exist within subtle ones.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"In principle, one should not blame the ignorant and blind for falling into a pit."
Other masters say:

If one holds that form (*rūpa*) is the self existing within feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, they hold that form is subtle while feeling and the rest are coarse; therefore, the Venerable Vasumitra said:
Throughout the body composed of the four great elements and their derived matter,
wherever it comes into contact with touch, sensation is produced.
What is the meaning of this statement?
This explains that contact can arise throughout the entire body,
and sensation is likewise produced throughout it;
he then reflects as follows:
Since sensation is present throughout the body from the feet to the crown of the head,
it is known that the self consisting of form exists within sensation.
The Venerable One said:
All parts of the body are capable of producing feeling.
He reflects thus:
"Feeling exists throughout the entire body; it is one part of the body."
This is me and not another;
therefore, within feeling (*vedanā*), one apprehends a self characterized by form (*rūpa*).
As it is with feeling, so it is for the others up to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Question: Is it possible for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) to arise with a single atom as its object?
If so, what would be the fault?
If it were possible, this [view] would have to be right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) rather than the view of a self-identity.
Why is this? It is because one must first possess the wisdom of authentic practice in order to perceive the ultimate atom (paramāṇu).
If [the self] does not exist, how should one reconcile what is stated in the *Ṣaḍdharmaka-śāstra*?
As that treatise states:
Because atoms are eternal and abide separately;
this separate abiding is not a cause for impermanence.
Therefore, atoms are definitely eternal.
How do they explain this?
They claim that this perception has atoms as its object.
That [opponent] asserts that the view of extremes takes atoms as its object;
this proves that the view of a self-identity also takes atoms as its object,
because the objects of the two views— the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes— are one and the same.
Answer: It is impossible for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) to arise with respect to a single atom as its object.
Question: If that is so, how are you to explain the statement in the *Ṣaḍdharmaka-sūtra*?
Answer: What is stated in that treatise does not accord with correct reasoning.
One cannot cite this as proof that atoms are the causal condition;
for that treatise further states many other reasons that are inconsistent with reason,
and thus cannot serve as valid evidence.
Other masters say that there is a view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) that arises having a single atom as its object.
Question: If that were so, this would have to be right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) rather than a view of a self-identity.
Answer: This is said to exist in terms of its object of perception (*ālambana*), not in terms of its actual manifestation.
The critique states:
That statement is irrational. Why is this so?
How can this view [be maintained]?
Although it is able to abide upon its object,
it cannot give rise [to cognition]; therefore,
what was stated previously is superior in terms of logical principle.
Question: Is there a simultaneous, collective grasping of the five aggregates as a self?
If so, what fault would there be?
If there were, it would contradict the *Ṣaḍdharmaka-sūtra*.
How should this be reconciled?
As that treatise states:
"The essence of the self is singular; it does not exist in five ways."
If there were someone who simultaneously and collectively apprehended the five aggregates as a self,
that self would have to be fivefold;
however, the specific characteristics of the aggregates are five distinct types.
The characteristics of the self as conceived by them are without distinction,
because the self as conceived lacks subtle parts and thus possesses no differentiating features.
It is eternally abiding and unchanging,
for it cannot be destroyed by birth, old age, sickness, or death.
If it did not exist, how could one reconcile this with the *Satyavāda-sūtra*?
As that sutra states: Satyavādī,
an outsider, addressed the Buddha,
saying, "Gautama."
I say that form is the self;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self.
There are those who speak thus.
There is no one who simultaneously takes all five aggregates as a collective object and clings to them as a self.
Question: If that is so, then the *Ṣaḍdharmaka-vibhaṅga-śāstra* would be well-explained.
How should one interpret the *Satyavādin-sūtra*?
The answer is: that was spoken unreasonably out of pride;
in reality, such a tenet does not exist.
Furthermore, wishing to test the Buddha, he spoke such irrational words;
that is to say, having heard that the Buddha possessed superior wisdom and vision,
his mind did not yet believe it with certainty.
He formed this thought:
"I shall now test whether such a thing exists," and thus he spoke these words.
Furthermore, because that mind was struck with alarm and fear,
he made such an irrational statement,
namely, that he had previously employed various skillful means.
He came to where the Buddha was with the desire to engage in debate;
having seen that the World-Honored One’s body possessed the marks of a preeminent great master of discourse—
such as a jaw-mandible like that of a lion— he [was struck].
His eyelashes are like those of a bull king;
his teeth are fine and sharp, numbering forty;
and his Brahma-voice is deep and wondrous.
This causes people to delight in hearing it.
Having seen this, he feared falling into a position of defeat and, giving rise to great terror, made this statement.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power eclipsed his mind.
Therefore, he intentionally made this irrational statement:
that those non-Buddhists came to the Buddha’s presence for the sake of debate,
and upon seeing the World-Honored One’s blazing majesty and virtue...
Even Brahmā, Śakra, and the World-Protectors cannot behold it;
having seen it, they were struck with alarm and thus spoke these words.
Furthermore, there are devas, nāgas, and yakṣas.
By the power of their majestic spiritual authority,
they cause such irrational speech to be uttered,
namely that there are those who believe in the Buddha, such as devas, nāgas, and yakṣas.
He formed this thought:
"This wicked outsider has devised these words intending to vex and disturb the Buddha;
I shall use my power to agitate his mind."
This causes those who speak contrary to reason to quickly fall into a position of defeat.
For example, when Upāli intended to come and revile the Buddha,
a deva used its supernatural power to disturb his mind.
It is turned into praise;
this case is also like that.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
At one time, there is the arising of self-grasping by taking all five aggregates as its object collectively.
Question: If that is so, the *Satyavādin-sūtra* (Discourse on Truthful Speech) is well-explained;
however, how should one explain the *Ṣaddharma-śāstra* (Treatise on the Six Dharmas)? Answer: That [treatise] refers to the arising of a notion of a single unity with respect to the five aggregates.
There is no fault, because they grasp [it] as a single self.
Question: If that is so, what do they grasp as "mine"?
Answer: If they grasp the internal aggregates as the self.
Those who grasp at external aggregates as "mine" must,
if they grasp at external aggregates as "self," necessarily grasp at internal aggregates as "mine."
Therefore, there is likewise no fault.
Question: Is there an external grasping at a self apart from the five aggregates?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If it were the case that [the self] exists,
how would one reconcile this with what is stated in the sūtras? As the sūtra says:
Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas posit a self,
all do so based upon the five aggregates of clinging.
If it does not exist, how can one speak of a sixth view of self?
Answer: There is no one who clings to a self apart from the five aggregates.
Question: If that is so, why is it said that there is a sixth view of self?
Answer: It refers to the view of self arising with respect to the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) and the view of self arising with respect to other aggregates of formations.
Because they are established individually, there are six types.
Question: The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* speaks of sixty-two views.
All [views] have the view of a self-identity as their root.
The *Siṃhanāda Sūtra* states:
"There are certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas..."
Various divergent views all rely upon two views,
namely, the view of existence and the view of non-existence.
What is the distinction between these two statements in the sūtras?
Answer: It is said that all views have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their root based on their origination;
it is said that there are various divergent views based on the investigation of existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is able to give rise to various speculative views (*dṛṣṭigata*),
while the view of existence and non-existence (*astitva-nāstitvadṛṣṭi*) is able to protect those various heterodox views.
This is what is called the distinction between the two sūtras.
If one views what is impermanent as permanent,
under which of the five views is this subsumed?
"What is abandoned by vision?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: These various views, within the cycle of birth and death, act as a great fetter for all sentient beings;
they constitute a great calamity and a great subjugation.
Because this exists,
sentient beings repeatedly undergo much suffering and affliction within the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, transmigrating through birth and death;
they remain far removed from the light of wisdom and enter the womb.
Dwelling between the stomach and the large intestine, one undergoes various oppressions,
like a person of heavy crime confined in a prison.
Desiring to cause sentient beings to realize the faults of such views and to strive diligently for liberation, [the Buddha taught this].
Therefore, this treatise has been composed.
Just as in the world, if one does not recognize the places of bondage, decay, affliction, and subjugation,
one is unable to avoid them from afar.
If a person knows this, they will be able to avoid it from afar;
this case is likewise so.
This treatise consists of the Miscellaneous Aggregate, the Wisdom Aggregate, and the View Aggregate.
All views are sought and examined by means of two things:
first, by way of their intrinsic nature;
second, by way of their antidotes.
Regarding "by way of intrinsic nature":
this refers to seeing [the self] in such a manner; as for which of the five views it is subsumed under. Regarding "by way of antidote": [it refers to the view that perceives the non-self as self].
That is to say, such a view.
What [view] is abandoned by insight?
This is discussed in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
One should also seek out and examine these two points regarding their views,
as that treatise states concerning the heretics' slander of the Buddha: [text follows].
"The śramaṇa Gautama is a great magician who deceives the world; however,
the World-Honored One’s Way has already transcended illusion."
He said: "To say 'this is an illusion' is a false view that slanders the Path;
it is to be abandoned by the vision of the Path."
Regarding those with the wrong view of slandering the path,
this reveals their essential nature;
for they slander the World-Honored One’s path that transcends illusion.
Regarding those [afflictions] to be abandoned by the path of seeing:
this indicates their counteractive path,
because when the patiences (kṣānti) and knowledges (jñāna) arise, they are permanently severed.
Furthermore, that treatise states:
Someone says, "For what reason did the Blessed One [say this]?"
"Avarice, O Arhat;
yet the Blessed One’s path has already transcended avarice," he said.
This stinginess is a false view that slanders the Path, which is to be abandoned through the vision of the Path.
In this regard, two matters should be understood as previously explained.
Furthermore, in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* concerning questions and discourses:
Furthermore, one seeks out the underlying views by means of a single method:
namely, by investigating from what such a view arises.
This is the general summary.
One then seeks out and examines these views by means of three things:
first, by way of their intrinsic nature.
Second, by way of counteractive;
third, by way of origination.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
One should not seek out such views in this manner;
it would be like blaming one who is ignorant and blind for falling into a pit.
The critique says:
One should seek out views by means of three matters.
Why is this? Because if one seeks out views by means of these three matters, [they will be understood].
Then even ordinary beings bound by all fetters would never arise [again],
just as one has eternally severed and fully known [the afflictions] through the Noble Path.
In this regard, the causes and conditions concerning the true Dharma teacher should be explained in detail.
That is to say, formerly, in this land of Kaśmīra,
there was a certain forest hermitage.
Various yogācāras gathered in one place and discussed various views.
They speak thus:
"O Noble One, regarding these immeasurable faults and calamities,
as well as these various evil views..."
Never manifesting again—
this is most rare.
At that time, within that assembly...
There was a Dharma master named Dalabha,
who said to the multitude:
The Noble One has already abandoned and fully understood these various evil views;
they shall never again manifest.
What is so extraordinary about me,
who am now an ordinary person still bound by all fetters?
By means of these three matters,
one seeks out and examines views;
even if I were to continue transmigrating through birth and death until the end of time.
Just as throughout the number of kalpas traversed since the beginningless past,
these views shall no longer manifest.
This is indeed rare.
At that time, there was an arhat among the assembly who had this thought:
One who is an ordinary person still bound by all fetters is thus able to let out a lion’s roar amidst this assembly of noble ones.
This is truly rare.
At a later time, I shall verify whether what he has said is true or not.
Yet all accumulated wealth must inevitably come to an end;
all who are high and noble must inevitably fall;
and all unions must inevitably result in separation.
All life must inevitably return to death.
This was indeed the Dharma Master;
after his life came to an end, he passed away.
He was reborn in his native country into a brahmin family.
An arhat, seeing this with his divine eye,
went to that house several times to inquire after his well-being.
In this manner, as time passed and he grew to adulthood,
an Arhat tested him by taking his ornaments and asking him about them.
"Whose view is this?
He remained silent and did not answer.
His mother said to him:
"Why does the boy not answer his teacher's question now?
He said to his mother,
"As for what the teacher asked..."
"If it does not exist in the world, how should one answer?
The mother asked,
'What things are there that do not exist in the world?'"
He said: "There is no self. Why is this so?"
Because all conditioned phenomena are without self,
without a sentient being, without a life-principle,
and without a person.
That which is unarisen has no nourisher;
it has no agent and no experiencer.
Since it is merely a collection of empty formations, it should not be answered.
At that time, having heard this, the Arhat sighed and said:
"This is truly rare;
although they have passed through birth and death,"
Yet, even now, various views do not manifest before you;
you have let out the lion’s roar among the assembly of noble ones in previous lives,
whereas ordinary beings remain bound by all fetters.
If one seeks out these views through three methods,
they will not manifest even after many eons;
thus, these words are true.
Therefore, one should seek out views by means of the three matters already explained;
this will be of great benefit.
If one views what is impermanent as permanent, [it is a wrong view].
Among the five views, which view does it subsume?
By which view is it abandoned?
Answer: It is subsumed under the view of extremes, specifically the eternalist view.
[This is] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Question: What is meant by "impermanence"?
Answer: All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Question: For what reason do non-Buddhists conceive of those [phenomena] as permanent?
Answer: Due to two reasons.
First, because they see that all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) continue in a similar succession.
Regarding "the two views [arise] because they recollect past events regarding mind and mental factors,
and because they see the similarity and continuity of all material phenomena":
this means that those non-Buddhists perceive the form of old age as being similar to the form of childhood.
Seeing that the color of today resembles the color of yesterday,
one forms this thought:
"The color of childhood has thus transformed into the color of old age."
Regarding the statement, "The form of yesterday transitions to today;
seeing the mind and mental factors, one recollects past events," this refers to those non-Buddhists seeing what was done, practiced, and experienced during childhood.
When old, one is able to recall and see what was done,
practiced, and experienced yesterday;
being able to recall it today, one then forms this thought:
The mind and mental factors at the time of old age are the very same mind and mental factors as those at the time of youth;
they are the mind and mental factors of this very day.
That is to say, the mind and mental factors of yesterday.
Due to these two conditions, those non-Buddhists falsely conceptualize the five aggregates of clinging as permanent.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this as follows:
Because those non-Buddhists are obscured by the similar continuity of the five aggregates of clinging,
they do not know that [existence] is impermanent;
because they are obscured by grasping and concealing, they do not know that it is suffering.
Because it is covered by the adornment of the thin skin,
one does not know its impure functions;
because it is covered by the grasping at a self (*ātman*), one does not know non-self (*anātman*).
From this, non-Buddhists give rise to views such as eternalism.
Among these, the fact that the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) is subsumed under the view of permanence reveals its intrinsic nature;
for it is subsumed under the extreme of permanence within the two extremes of permanence and annihilation.
"Those abandoned through the vision of suffering" indicates their antidote,
because they are permanently severed at the time of seeing the Truth of Suffering.
That is to say, when there arise such types of improper reflection and improper discrimination regarding the patience and knowledge concerning the truth of suffering.
Perverted views and unbalanced grasping are forever severed and stilled,
like dew on the tips of grass that evaporates when struck by the sun.
They too, in this same way, through delusion regarding suffering, give rise to [the view that] suffering exists, and thus they sever it.
One asks: Do those who speak the Good Dharma also assert that all phenomena possess a permanent substantial essence, characteristics, and a personal self?
For what reason are those views not called "evil"?
The same applies to the non-Buddhists;
why are they alone designated as having "evil views"?
Answer: One who speaks the Dharma well,
although they may speak of all phenomena as having substantial reality and so forth,
[acknowledges that] they lack functional activity.
The teachings of the non-Buddhists include [the notion of] functional activity.
Some say that those who preach the Dharma well [do not admit this].
Some say that [the Sautrāntikas] teach that all phenomena (dharma) merely exert their activity for a brief moment,
whereas they [the Vaibhāṣikas] teach that all phenomena repeatedly exert their activity. Others say:
The one who skillfully teaches the Dharma proclaims that all phenomena are born by birth and aged by aging.
They are extinguished by that which is to be extinguished;
it is said that all phenomena are not produced by production,
nor aged by aging.
It is not that which is extinguished by extinction.
Some say: "One who speaks the Dharma well."
It is taught that all phenomena circulate through the three periods of time;
yet it is also said that those phenomena do not pass through the periods of time. Some say:
Those who skillfully expound the Dharma proclaim that all phenomena arise through the combination of causes and conditions;
yet they claim that those phenomena do not arise from causes and conditions.
Some say that one who expounds the Dharma well proclaims the arising and ceasing of all phenomena in accordance with reality.
They possess causes, possess conditions, and are conjoined with conditioned characteristics;
yet they say it is not so.
This is due to various such causes and conditions.
The views of those who skillfully expound the Dharma are not evil;
it is only the views arising from non-Buddhists that are uniquely called evil views.
Question: If one gives rise to the view of permanence regarding that which is impermanent, they certainly slander the causes and conditions of impermanence.
Why is such a view not called wrong view?
Answer: It is called "false view" because it functions with a non-existent mode of apprehension (*ākāra*).
Since that [view] does not perceive in such a manner, it is not false view. Some say:
The term "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is established for that which destroys real entities;
since this [view] instead performs an exaggeration (*samāropa*), it is not a false view.
Question: For what reason is this view called the "view of extremes" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: Because one clings to the extreme of permanence, both the views of annihilationism and eternalism deviate from the Middle Way and are thus called "extremes.
Clinging to these two extreme views is termed "view of clinging to extremes" (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
As the Blessed One told Kātyāyana:
If one contemplates the world as "origination" (samudaya) with right knowledge,
the statement that "nothing exists" no longer applies;
for such a statement of non-existence is precisely the view of annihilationism (uccheda-dṛṣṭi).
If one contemplates the world with right wisdom as subject to cessation,
the notion that "there is something existing" no longer arises;
for such a notion of existence is precisely the view of eternalism.
This means that because one contemplates the arising of future aggregates, it is not annihilation;
and because one contemplates the cessation of present aggregates, it is not eternalism.
Furthermore, regarding those who give rise to the view of a self:
This is already a vulgar and base view censured by the world;
how much more so is it when one clings to me as being subject to annihilation or permanence?
Because this clinging is vulgar, base, and utterly censurable, it is called the "view of extreme adherence" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
If one holds the view that what is permanent is impermanent,
among the five views, under which view is it subsumed,
and by the abandonment of which view is it eliminated?
Answer: It is subsumed under wrong view and is abandoned by the vision of the cessation [of suffering].
Question: What is meant by "permanence"?
Answer: It is the quiescent nirvāṇa.
Question: For what reason do the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon that it is not eternal?
Answer: Because the non-Buddhists cling to four types of liberation.
The first is named Bodyless;
the second is named Boundless Mind;
the third is named Pure Accumulation.
There are four worldly stūpas.
That which is bodiless refers to the sphere of infinite space.
"Boundless mind" refers to the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
"Pure accumulation" refers to...
That which is called the "base of nothingness" refers to the worldly stūpa;
that which is called the "base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" refers to the [supramundane] stūpa.
However, although they have long remained in the four formless attainments, they eventually fall back from them. They then think:
"Since we have already fallen away from our liberation,"
One should know that even the nirvāṇa spoken of by the Śākyas can involve falling back;
thus, one gives rise to the view of impermanence regarding nirvāṇa.
This is what is subsumed under wrong view herein.
This reveals their intrinsic nature,
because they deny the permanence of nirvana;
these are those to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
This reveals their antidote;
because they are permanently severed at the time of seeing the Truth of Cessation.
The rest is as previously explained.
Question: Is there a wrong view that can give rise to the aspect of impermanence toward the quiescent nirvana?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
If it did exist, how would one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
As it has been said:
What is wrong view?
It refers to the denial of cause and the denial of result.
To slander [the Buddha's] activity is to destroy the reality of things;
this is what is being discussed here regarding those who possess patience, delight, wisdom, and insight, were they not to exist.
How should this be reconciled?
As it is said:
"If one views what is permanent as impermanent, this is subsumed under wrong view."
Regarding that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation, one should say:
there exists this false view.
Question: How should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
Answer: That text does not exhaustively describe the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of wrong view;
it means that there are other modes of activity belonging to the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because it was not mentioned by him.
Some say that it is included within what he did mention.
That is to say, one who slanders the cause slanders the Truth of Origination;
one who slanders the result slanders the Truth of Suffering;
and one who slanders functional activity slanders the Truth of the Path.
Those who deny real entities slander the Truth of Cessation.
Some say that those who deny the cause, the result, and the activity [also slander it].
Each [of these views] slanders three truths;
however, those who destroy actual reality slander only the truth of cessation.
Other masters say that such wrong view does not exist.
[The author] asks: what is being stated here?
How should this be reconciled?
The answer is: within *nirvāṇa* there is the characteristic of permanence.
If one slanders it by claiming that *nirvāṇa* does not exist, [one commits an offense].
This also slanders the characteristic of permanence.
It is like having four parts within a finger; if one were to deny the existence of the finger [by denying its parts], [it would be a false view].
This also negates the four bases (*āyatana*).
Some say that this statement was made by implication of the meaning.
This means that while the various non-Buddhists maintain only that the aggregates (skandhas) are permanent phenomena,
they hold that nirvana is not an aggregate; therefore, by logical implication,
they must certainly deny its existence.
Thus, it is said that there are views of permanence and impermanence;
yet, there is no wrong view regarding the quiescent nirvana.
If one perceives suffering or pleasure regarding the actual arising of the aspect of impermanence,
under which of the five views is this subsumed?
What is abandoned by insight?
Answer: To take inferior phenomena as superior;
this is subsumed under the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
[They] are abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Question: What is meant by "suffering"?
Answer: All contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Question: For what reason do the non-Buddhists reckon that [state] to be happiness?
Answer: Because they are deluded by the fact that for a short time their minds find satisfaction, just as when one who is exhausted finds temporary rest.
When cold, one briefly attains warmth;
when hot, one briefly attains coolness;
when hungry, one briefly attains food.
Having briefly obtained a drink when thirsty,
one then thinks:
"I am now experiencing pleasure."
However, within the aggregates, there exists a small portion of pleasure;
to apprehend it according to its actual measure is not a perversion.
It is only when outsiders superimpose upon this [pleasure] and apprehend it as being identical to ultimate bliss that it becomes a perversion.
Thus, it constitutes a perversion.
In this context, grasping inferior phenomena as superior is subsumed under the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which reveals its intrinsic nature.
Because one grasps at suffering, suffering-as-suffering, and so forth as being sublime pleasure,
that which is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering is revealed as its antidote;
for when the Truth of Suffering is seen, those [afflictions] are permanently severed.
The rest is as previously explained.
Question: Why is it that grasping at suffering as pleasure is called "grasping at views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), whereas grasping at the impermanent as permanent is not?
Answer: Regarding those who take suffering to be pleasure,
because they invariably take inferior phenomena to be superior,
it is called "adherence to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
Regarding the grasping of the impermanent as permanent:
this is not the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), because it does not exclusively grasp an inferior phenomenon as superior.
This is because within the category of permanent phenomena, both superior and non-superior phenomena are taken together as a single aggregate.
Just as space and analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) are neutral (avyākṛta), they are not called "excellent dharmas" (viśeṣa-dharma).
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Within the aggregates there is a slight degree of pleasure;
because one perceives them through that [pleasure], taking suffering to be pleasure is called the "view of grasping" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
It is not, however, because one can perceive any degree of permanence within the aggregates.
To grasp at the impermanent as permanent is also called the "clinging to views.
Why is this? Because the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, are momentary in nature.
Because its nature is illusory,
because it abides only for a moment,
and because it is on the verge of disintegration.
As it is said:
"What is a phenomenon at the time of cessation?
It refers to present phenomena."
Therefore, to take what is impermanent to be permanent is called a view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*),
not a grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
If one holds the view that pleasure is suffering,
among the five views, under which view is it subsumed,
and by the abandonment of which view is it eliminated?
Answer: It is subsumed under wrong view and is abandoned through the vision of cessation.
Question: What is meant by "pleasure"?
Answer: Ultimate happiness is exclusively nirvāṇa.
Question: For what reason do the non-Buddhists claim that nirvāṇa is suffering?
Answer: They speak as follows: [text continues]
If even when a single sense faculty perishes one still experiences suffering,
how much more so when all faculties perish within nirvāṇa?
Therefore, nirvāṇa must be the ultimate suffering.
To that Venerable Vasumitra, it was said:
"The faculties (indriya) are the cause of suffering."
If even a single faculty can produce suffering,
how much more so when many faculties are present?
Only within nirvāṇa do all the faculties cease.
Because it lacks the cause of suffering, it is indeed the Ultimate Bliss (*sukhāvatī*).
Herein, that which is subsumed under wrong view reveals its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
because it slanders *nirvāṇa*.
"Those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation" indicates their antidote,
because they are permanently severed at the time of seeing the truth of cessation.
The rest is as previously explained.
It is asked: Is the Truth of the Path also pleasant?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The path depends on the provisions;
nirvāṇa depends on the path,
because of the joy found in the path.
One attains the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Why, then, is it said that [the afflictions] are abandoned only by seeing cessation?
One should know that this statement is incomplete (sāvadeśika).
It should be stated as follows:
if the view that pleasure is suffering is subsumed under false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*),
this is of two kinds.
If one were to claim that cessation is suffering, it would be abandoned through the vision of cessation;
if one were to claim that the path is suffering, it would be abandoned through the vision of the path.
That these are not so stated is because there is a specific underlying intention.
This means that although the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) is also pleasant, it belongs to two categories:
that which belongs to the category of pleasure because it attains *nirvāṇa*,
and that which belongs to the category of suffering because it is impermanent (*anitya*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Because it is impermanent, it is suffering.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
The Truth of the Path is not pleasure;
it is metaphorically designated as pleasure because one attains nirvāṇa through it.
As it is said:
Because one proceeds from pleasure to the pleasure of nirvāṇa, it is said here that [this ignorance] is abandoned only by seeing cessation.
Question: Is there a false view capable of giving rise to the aspect of suffering toward nirvāṇa?
If this were the case, what fault would there be?
It is difficult to provide a satisfactory explanation for this;
the details are as extensively explained previously regarding impermanence (*anityatā*).
If one views the impure as pure, among the five views, under which view is it subsumed, and by which path of abandonment is it abandoned?
Answer: Taking an inferior dharma to be superior is subsumed under the view of attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
It is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Question: What is meant by "impurity"?
Answer: All contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Question: For what reason do the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon those things to be pure?
Answer: Because they are deluded regarding the fact that these things are pure for only a brief period, such as when one cleans one's hair, nails, teeth, or skin.
Causing the visible form to appear momentarily fresh and pure,
one then forms this thought:
"My body is pure."
However, within the aggregates there is a small portion of purity;
to apprehend it according to its measure is not erroneous.
It is the non-Buddhists who, regarding this, engage in conceptual superimposition and thus apprehend it erroneously.
Because it takes that which is equally ultimate and pure to be so, it constitutes a perversion.
In this context, taking inferior phenomena to be superior is what is subsumed under the view of holding to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); this reveals its essential nature.
Because one takes things such as excrement and filth to be truly pure;
those [afflictions] abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) are shown to be its antidote,
for they are permanently severed when the Truth of Suffering is seen.
The rest is as previously explained.
Question: Since we directly perceive that the nine orifices constantly discharge impurities, how can the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to the body as being pure?
The answer is that they think:
"That which has already been discharged is impure,
but that which has not yet been discharged must necessarily be pure."
Just as when the flowers of the *śirīṣa* tree are red like flesh,
a jackal crouches down, looks at them, and thinks:
"I shall certainly eat this meat now."
After a short while, some of those flowers fell to the ground;
he ran to smell them and realized they were not flesh.
He then thought to himself:
Although that which has already fallen to the ground is not meat,
the remainder that has not yet fallen must necessarily be meat;
the same applies to the non-Buddhists.
Because they are deluded by ignorance, they form such attachments.
All contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) are called "impure" for two reasons.
First, by way of afflictions;
second, by way of objects.
All defiled phenomena possess both of these meanings.
Non-defiled phenomena [are so called] solely by virtue of their objects.
Question: If that is so, why are tainted wholesome phenomena also termed "pure"?
Answer: Because they possess a small degree of purity.
That is to say, although it possesses stains, faults, poisons, and turbidity,
it opposes the afflictions (*kleśa*), is unmixed with the afflictions, and destroys the afflictions.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
All untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) are the ultimate purity (*paramārtha-śuddhi*).
Tainted wholesome phenomena (*sāsrava-kuśaladharma*) are also called "pure" because they lead toward that [ultimate purity].
Question: What is one who teaches the Dharma well?
Regarding contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), it is also said that they possess purity;
for example, the three types of pure karma are not called evil.
Why, then, do the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) designate such [purity] as "pure" and yet call it an "evil view"?
Answer: Those who preach the Dharma well teach that only sublime conduct constitutes purity;
the non-Buddhists, however, generally claim that both sublime and evil conduct constitute purity.
Furthermore, those who preach the Dharma well teach that only the roots of goodness constitute purity;
the non-Buddhists, however, generally teach that both the roots of goodness and the roots of unwholesomeness constitute purity.
Furthermore, those who preach the Dharma well teach only the antidotes.
The fetters (*saṃyojana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are considered pure by those [who hold such views].
Non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also claim that the fetters and so forth are pure.
Furthermore, one who teaches the Dharma well explains that among the contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), there is a small portion that is pure;
whereas the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) claim that those [phenomena] constitute ultimate purity.
Therefore, what is taught by the non-Buddhists is evil;
those who skillfully teach the Dharma are not said to hold evil views,
whether their views concern the pure or the impure.
Among the five views, which view does it subsume?
By which view is it abandoned?
Answer: It is subsumed under false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This is of two kinds:
if one regards cessation as impure, it is abandoned through the vision of cessation;
if one regards the path as impure, it is abandoned through the vision of the path.
Question: What is meant by "purity"?
Answer: The two truths of cessation and the path.
Question: For what reason do non-Buddhists consider the truths of cessation and the path to be impure?
The answer is: That [opponent] asserts that the afflictions are truly impure;
thus, when they are severed by the Noble Path, [the path] becomes impure, and even the cessation attained through the path becomes impure.
Just as a blade or water that has cut or washed filthy objects becomes impure,
yet that same blade or water may be used to cut or wash other things.
It would also become impure;
since cessation and the path are likewise [of that nature], they too should be impure.
Herein, that which is subsumed under wrong view reveals its intrinsic nature.
Because slandering the cessation and the path is impure,
that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path is revealed as their antidote;
for when cessation and the path are seen, those [afflictions] are forever severed.
The rest is as previously explained.
Question: Is there a type of vision that can give rise to the aspect of impurity regarding the two truths of cessation and the path?
If so, what fault would there be?
The difficulty in reconciling this is as explained extensively above.
