Section One of the First Aggregate on Miscellaneous Topics: The Sub-section on the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (Loka-agra-dharma), Part Eight. If there is no self, yet there is the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Among the five views, under which view is it subsumed?
By which view is it abandoned?
Answer: It is subsumed under the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
It is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Question: What is meant by "non-self"?
Answer: All phenomena (*dharmas*).
Question: For what reason do the non-Buddhists conceive of a self (*ātman*) therein?
Answer: Because they are deluded regarding the functions of coming, going, and so forth;
they form this thought: [that there is a self].
If there is no self,
who goes and who comes?
Who stays and who sits?
Who bends and who stretches?
Who rises and who lies down?
Who sees, hears, smells, tastes, touches, remembers, and cognizes?
Because there is a self, these various phenomena exist;
therefore, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) postulate a self therein.
In this context, the inclusion [of the self] within the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) reveals its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Because one clings to a self within the five aggregates of grasping,
that which is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering reveals its antidote;
for when the truth of suffering is seen, those [afflictions] are permanently severed.
The rest is as previously explained.
Question: The view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) has two modes of activity, namely: the mode of activity of "I" and [the mode of activity of "mine"].
The characteristics of "what belongs to me" (mamakāra) are subsumed within the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi) and the view of what belongs to self (ātmīya-dṛṣṭi). Why, then,
is only the view of self mentioned here, and not the view of what belongs to self?
The answer is: because it was the intention of the author of this treatise to proceed in this way, as explained at length.
Some say: "One should also have mentioned that [point], yet it was not mentioned."
It should be understood that this is an incomplete statement.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
since the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) has already been mentioned here, it should be understood that the view of what belongs to the self (*ātmīyadṛṣṭi*) is also thereby mentioned.
Why is this? Because there is a self, there arises "what belongs to the self.
Because there is the view of a self, there arises the view of what belongs to the self.
Because there is the view of a self, there arises the view of what belongs to a self.
Because there are five views of a self,
there arise fifteen views of what belongs to a self.
Because there is attachment to a self, there can be attachment to what belongs to a self.
Because there is delusion regarding a self, there can be delusion regarding what belongs to a self.
Other masters say:
I see that the view of self is the root and is of the nature of perversion;
therefore, it is specifically discussed here.
The view of "mine" is not the root.
Because it is not of a perverted nature, it is not discussed herein.
Question: Those who preach the Dharma well also assert that all phenomena possess a permanent substantial essence and characteristics.
To regard the self as an object is not an evil view.
Why, then, do the non-Buddhists consider the assertion that a real self exists to be an evil view?
Answer: There are two kinds of self.
First is the self of phenomena (dharma-ātman);
second is the self of the person (pudgala-ātman).
These are the well-expounded teachings.
I teach only that the self of phenomena (dharma-ātman) truly exists;
because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) truly exists and one sees it as it really is, this is not called a wrong view.
The non-Buddhists also claim that the person (pudgala) truly exists as a self; however,
the person does not possess the nature of true existence.
Because it is a false perception, it is called a "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Question: Why is the view of self (*ātman*) and non-self (*anātman*) not mentioned?
Answer: Because the self does not truly exist.
If one perceives that which is non-self as such, this constitutes right view.
Herein, only various types of wrong views are discussed;
therefore, the views of self and non-self are not mentioned.
If it is not the view of a cause regarding causes,
under which of the five views is it subsumed,
and by which view is it abandoned?

Answer: That which is not a cause but is taken as a cause is comprised within the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Question: What is meant by "that which is not a cause"?
Answer: [They hold] Maheśvara and others to be an unequal cause.
Question: For what reason do the non-Buddhists regard what is not a cause as a cause?
Answer: Because they associate with evil friends.
When they hear it said that all phenomena arise from such things as the Lord (Īśvara), self-nature (svabhāva), the primal spirit (puruṣa),
time (kāla), or space (ākāśa), it is like farmers who, upon harvesting a bountiful crop in autumn, speak thus:
I have been granted many things by the gods and others;
if a son or daughter is born,
they will further say this.
This was bestowed by the devas such as Nanda.
For those with mastery over faith,
if they give birth to sons or daughters.
He then spoke these words:
"It has been granted by the deity Viṣṇu,
the god Kubera, and other such celestial beings."
Such categories as these are instances of regarding what is not a cause as a cause.
However, those categorized as sentient beings are produced by their respective individual karma,
whereas those not categorized as sentient beings are produced by collective karma.
It is not produced by false causes such as Īśvara and so forth;
herein, that which is "not a cause" is designated as the "cause," and it is subsumed under the clinging to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
This reveals its intrinsic nature:
it clings to what is not a true cause as being a true cause.
Briefly stated, there are two types of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
First, regarding what is not a cause as being a cause;
second, regarding what is not the path as being the path.
Here, only the first—regarding what is not a cause as being a cause—is discussed.
"Those abandoned through the vision of suffering" indicates their antidote,
because they are permanently severed when the Truth of Suffering is seen;
the rest is as previously explained.
Question: Why is this view not abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*)?
Answer: Because it functions with respect to the fruit (*phala*).
Question: Regarding that which is not a cause, [viewing it] as a cause—
It is also a denial of the causes of all phenomena.
Why is this view not subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: That which functions with a [specific] mode of activity (*ākāra*) is called wrong view.
Because this functions with a positive mode of activity (*ākāra*), it is not termed wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, others say that what functions by destroying real entities is called wrong view.
Because this functions as an augmentation, it is not termed wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The Venerable Vasumitra stated:
"If one denies the existence of causes, that is called wrong view."
This is not called wrong view because it is a conception of what is not a cause as being a cause;
rather, it is because one regards what is not a true cause as being a true cause.
If it were a view of a cause as a non-cause, [it would be wrong view].
Among the five views, by which view is it subsumed?
By which view is it abandoned?
Answer: It is subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
It is abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
Question: What is meant by "cause"?
Answer: Karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and so forth.
Question: For what reason do the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain that internal and external phenomena arise without a cause?
Answer: Because they do not understand the principle of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) regarding the internal and the external.
They form this thought: [as follows].
Who dug the rivers and seas?
Who piled up the mountains and plains?
Who fashioned the thorns and brambles?
Who painted these birds and beasts?
According to this principle, all things arise without cause;
thus, that verse says:
"Who dug the rivers and seas? Who piled up the mountains and plains? Who fashioned the thorns and thistles, or painted the birds and beasts?
There is no independent creator in the world; therefore, know that all things are without cause.
This [view] is subsumed under wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This reveals their intrinsic nature,
because they involve the denial of the causes from which all phenomena arise;
these are abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
This reveals its antidote;
because it is permanently abandoned when the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) is seen, the rest is as previously explained.
Question: Why is the false view that denies the cause (hetu-apavāda-mithyādṛṣṭi) abandoned by the vision of the Truth of Origination?

In the *Dṛṣṭivarga*, it is stated that the false view which denies causes (*hetu-apavādikā mithyādṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
The answer is: this is because the author of the treatise intended it thus, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, this is not a definitive teaching (*neyārtha*).
That is a teaching of definitive meaning;
this has a further underlying intention,
whereas that has no further underlying intention.
This teaching has a remainder; that teaching is without remainder.
This teaching relies on the conventional (saṃvṛti);
that teaching relies on the ultimate (paramārtha).
Furthermore, this explains only a portion of causes,
whereas that explains all causes;
this speaks only of the cause of suffering.
That [text] explains the causes of suffering and non-suffering;
this [text] explains only the causes of inversion;
that [text] explains the causes of both inversion and non-inversion.
This [view] speaks only of the cause that produces an effect;
that [view] speaks of both the cause that produces an effect and the cause that does not produce an effect.
Furthermore, the wrong view that denies the origin (samudaya) negates both the substantiality of the cause and the causal function.
The false view that slanders the Path negates only the substance of the cause, not the meaning of the cause;
for to say that Nirvana has no cause is correct and not false.
Therefore, it is only the false view that slanders the cause that is discussed here.
That which is abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and not abandoned by the path of vision (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*):
if there is a view of existence or non-existence, under which of the five views is it subsumed,
and by the vision of what is it abandoned?
Answer: It is subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
There are four types of this:
if one asserts that there is no suffering, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
If one claims there is no origination, it is abandoned through the vision of origination;
if one claims there is no cessation, it is abandoned through the vision of cessation;
if one claims there is no path, it is abandoned through the vision of the path.
Question: What is meant by "existence"?
Answer: The Four Noble Truths.
Question: For what reason do non-Buddhists deny the Four Truths?
Answer: Because they cling to the existence of a self, they consequently deny the Four Noble Truths.
They assert that the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, are the self and not suffering;
thus, they deny the Truth of Suffering.
If one holds that the self has no cause, one negates the truth of origination (samudaya-satya).
If one holds that the self is eternal and does not perish, one negates the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya).
If one holds that the self has no antidote, one negates the truth of the path (mārga-satya).
Just as a skilled teacher of the Dharma knows that the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, are suffering and not the self, one thus gains faith in the Truth of Suffering;
knowing that this suffering has a cause, one gains faith in the Truth of Origination.
Believing that this suffering can be extinguished, one gains faith in the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Believing that there is an antidote to suffering, one gains faith in the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
Among these, those comprised by false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are as follows:
This reveals their intrinsic nature:
because they deny the existence of the four noble truths as real entities.
There are four such types.
To speak at length, up to:
if one were to claim that there is no Path,
then [the defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of the Path would not exist.
This reveals their antidote, for they are permanently severed when the Four Truths are realized.
The rest should be understood as previously explained; herein, those who deny the Truth of Suffering [are addressed].
There are two kinds of denial:
first, denial of the substance;
second, denial of the meaning of the result.
Regarding the denial of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*),
there are two kinds of denial:
first, the denial of its substantial entity (*dravya*).
Second is the meaning of slandering the cause.
Regarding the slander of the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya),
one slanders only the substantial entity and does not slander the meaning of the fruit.
There are those who say that this also slanders the meaning of the fruit;
it slanders the Truth of the Path.
It is only the substance of the object that is denied,
not the meaning of its cause. Some say, however,
that the meaning of the cause is also denied.
Some say that this also slanders cause and effect;
others say: [as follows].
One who slanders the Truth of the Path slanders only its functional activity.
Question: For what reason do wrong views not take space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as their objects?
Answer: If a phenomenon is an aggregate (*skandha*), the cause of an aggregate,
the cessation of an aggregate, or the antidote to an aggregate,
then false view takes as its object space (*ākāśa*) or non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
It is not the aggregates, nor the cause of the aggregates;
because it is neither the cessation of the aggregates nor the antidote to the aggregates, it does not take them as its object.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is suffering or the cause of suffering...
This is the cessation of suffering; this is the antidote to suffering.
Wrong view, however, takes as its object space and non-analytical cessation.
It is neither suffering nor the cause of suffering;
because it is neither the cessation of suffering nor the antidote to suffering, it does not take that as its object,
just as [it does not take] the suffering of suffering or its causes, and so forth.
One should know that illness, abscesses, arrows, afflictions, burdens, and their causes are likewise.
Furthermore, whatever phenomena constitute matters of defilement or purification,
false view takes them as its object.
Space and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) are not objects of cognition because they are neither defiled nor purified phenomena;
furthermore, if a phenomenon is an object of untainted right view,
it is then an object of wrong view.
Space and analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) are not objects of uncontaminated right view; therefore, that [view] does not take them as its object.

Just as uncontaminated right view serves as the antidote to false view, it should be understood that uncontaminated wisdom, clarity, decisive faith, and so forth, likewise serve as antidotes to non-wisdom and the like.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is like a boat or raft on this shore, the far shore, or in midstream,
then false views take it as their object; however,
because space and non-analytical cessation are not like a boat or raft on this shore, the far shore, or in midstream, they are not taken as objects by them.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon possesses the sense of cause and effect,
wrong view takes it as its object; however,
because space and non-analytical cessation lack the sense of cause and effect, wrong view does not take them as its objects.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is an object of either attraction or aversion,
wrong view takes it as its object;
since space and non-analytical cessation are not objects of attraction or aversion, wrong view does not take them as its object.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is capable of causing benefit or harm,
wrong view takes it as its object;
since space and non-analytical cessation cannot cause benefit or harm, they are not taken as objects by it.
Question: Upon what phenomena does one who denies space and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) take as their object?
Answer: They take as their object the very names "space" and "non-analytical cessation. Why is this so?
Those who deny it lack a profound and respectful mind, just as those who slander the phenomena of affliction and purification.
Question: What kind of knowledge is this?
Answer: This is the wisdom that takes as its object the aspect of unobscured-neutral misconduct among those things to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm.
Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings:
Some say there are two kinds:
first, substantial existence (*dravyasat*),
which refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth.
Second is existence by designation,
which refers to things such as male and female;
some say there are three kinds.
First, existence through mutual dependence:
this refers to a phenomenon that exists in dependence upon another.
Because it depends on that [other factor], it does not exist [independently];
yet it exists through the conjunction of the two.
That is to say, such is the case.
"It exists here but does not exist there;
it exists during three periods of time.
Such is the case.
That which exists at this time does not exist at that time.
Some say there are five kinds;
the first is called "existence" (bhāva).
The first refers to such things as tortoise hair, rabbit horns, and garlands of flowers in the sky.
The second refers to real existence,
meaning that all phenomena each abide in their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Third, conventional existence (*prajñaptisat*),
which refers to things such as jars, clothing, vehicles, armies, forests,
and houses. Fourth, collective existence (*samudāyasat*).
This refers to the designation of a *pudgala* (person) based on the collection of the aggregates (*skandha*).
There are five kinds of relative existence (*apekṣā-sat*), namely: this and that, long and short, and so forth.
If there is no view, among the five views, under which view is it subsumed?
By which view is it abandoned?
Answer: This is not a view; it is false knowledge (mithyājñāna).
Question: If this is not a view (*dṛṣṭi*), why does it say, "if there is no view"?
Some explain that one should ask here: "If there is no view, in which of the five views is it included?"
What is abandoned by vision?
Answer: That which is comprised within the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*).
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"In this context, one should ask:
if wisdom were absent, which of the five views would it be subsumed under?"
What is abandoned by insight?
Answer: This is not insight; it is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
Alternatively, some say that in this context one should state as follows:
If there were no such thing as "viewing this as not seeing," it would not be mentioned among the five views;
thus it is said.
It should be explained according to the text.
Why is this? Because it is for the purpose of question and answer.
In order to establish the dialogue,
although this principle does not exist,
it is stated as such.
As it is asked in the *Daśamukha-varga*:
"Among the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*),
how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase in association?"
He replied:
"There are no underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that increase [in this state].
This case is also like that."
Question: What is this wrong knowledge?

Answer: It is the knowledge characterized by wrong conduct that is non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) among those things to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Just as one might perceive a person in a tree stump,
or perceive a tree stump in a person,
or perceive a path where there is no path.
To conceive the notion of what is not the path regarding the path—
thus have other masters taught.
Such is false wisdom.
There is also a defiled class of pride that can arise;
while dwelling here, the Brahmā King speaks thus:
"I am Mahābrahmā, the most honored among all Brahmās."
To say, "I am able to create and bring forth the world;
I am the father of the world," is irrational.
Why is this? Because the mind abandoned through seeing cannot give rise to bodily or vocal karma.
For this reason, what was stated previously is logically sound.
This refers to the knowledge of the aspect of non-obscured neutral wrong conduct among those things to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret what is stated in the *Jñānaskandha*?
As it is said:
What is wrong knowledge?
It is defiled wisdom.
Answer: There are two kinds of false wisdom:
first, the defiled;
second, the non-defiled.
That which is defiled is associated with ignorance;
that which is non-defiled is dissociated from ignorance,
such as when one conceives the notion of a person in relation to a tree stump.
As for the defiled [afflictions], both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are able to exhaust them completely and they no longer manifest.
As for the non-defiled [afflictions],
although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are able to exhaust them completely, they still manifest.
Only the Tathāgata never arises again,
because the habitual tendencies of afflictions have been forever severed; for this reason,
he alone is called the Truly and Fully Awakened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
Defiled wrong knowledge is called "wrong knowledge" from the perspective of ultimate truth;
that which is undefiled is not so called.
One receives the designation of "wrong knowledge" by way of conventional truth,
not by way of ultimate truth,
because it is not associated with afflictions or false phenomena.

Regarding the claim that the "false knowledge" (*mithyājñāna*) mentioned in the subsequent *Jñānaskandha* [chapter] refers to the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no contradiction here, as it is currently being discussed in terms of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).

**The Section on Knowledge (Jñāna-nikāya), Part One:** In the first section of the *Miśraka-skandha* of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the second part of the *Jñāna-nikāya*: Is there a single knowledge that knows all phenomena?
Having thus comprehended these chapters and the meaning of the explanations within them,
one should next provide a detailed exposition.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the tenets of other schools and clarifying one’s own position.
That is to say, there are some who hold [the following view]:
The mind and mental factors are able to cognize their own intrinsic nature;
as the Mahāsāṃghikas state,
this is because cognition and so forth have the capacity to cognize as their very nature.
It is able to cognize both itself and others,
because its intrinsic nature is like that of a lamp which, being capable of illuminating,
can illuminate both itself and others.
Alternatively, there are those who hold that the mind and mental factors can cognize their own associated [factors],
as the Dharmaguptaka school asserts.
Wisdom and the other [mental factors] are able to cognize their associated sensations and so forth;
or again, there are those who maintain that mind and mental factors [are self-cognizing].
It can understand them as co-existent.
As the Mahīśāsaka school says:
"Wisdom is of two kinds."
They arise simultaneously:
first, those that are associated;
second, those that are dissociated.
There are those who maintain that associated wisdom knows what is dissociated,
and dissociated wisdom knows what is associated.
Alternatively, there are others who hold such a view.
The *pudgala* is able to cognize all phenomena.
As the Vātsīputrīyas assert,
it is the *pudgala* that knows, not cognition (*jñāna*).
In order to cease such heterodox attachments of other schools and to clarify what has been taught by ourselves:
that all minds and mental factors do not perceive their own intrinsic nature.
Since the nature of a person (pudgala) cannot be found as being either associated with or co-existent [with the aggregates],
this treatise is composed.
Furthermore, one should not merely aim at refuting others or establishing one's own position;
rather, the characteristics of all phenomena ought to be analyzed according to reason.
This treatise was composed for the benefit of sentient beings.
Is there perhaps a single cognition that knows all phenomena?
Answer: No.
If this wisdom arises that all phenomena are non-self, what is it that this wisdom does not know?
Answer: It does not know its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor the phenomena associated with it or co-existent with it.
In this context, "not knowing the intrinsic nature" refers to the refutation of the Mahāsāṃghika tenet;
"not knowing the associated dharmas" [refers to the same].
This immediately refutes the tenets of the Dharmaguptaka school.
As for those who do not understand that phenomena coexist,
this immediately refutes the tenets of the Mahīśāsaka school.
The statement that "consciousness knows" serves to refute the tenets of the Vatsīputrīya school.
Furthermore, within this context, there is a question and an answer.
There are objections and there are resolutions.
"Is there perhaps a single cognition that knows all phenomena?"—
this is the question.
The answer “none” is the response.
The objection is: “If this wisdom arises that all phenomena are non-self, what is there that this wisdom does not know?”
Answer: Not knowing the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and those factors associated with and co-existent (*sahabhū*) with it constitutes the "penetration" (*uttara*).
Question: In this context, who asks and who answers?
Who poses the challenge and who provides the penetration?
The Vaibhāṣika asks;
the Sautrāntika answers;
the Vaibhāṣika objects.
The proponents of the *Abhidharmakośa* (the "Exponents of Reasoning") maintain that this applies universally.
Some say it refers to a disciple asking a question and a teacher answering.
The disciples challenge the Master’s thorough understanding.
Some say that within this context, there is no separate person who poses the questions and challenges.
However, the Master of the Treatise,
in order to distinguish the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), provisionally establishes the roles of interlocutor and respondent;
herein, there is one wise person.
This refers to a cognition of a single moment;
by means of this, one does not know its own nature,
nor the associated and co-existent dharmas.
If one were to ask this question:
"Among the ten knowledges (*jñāna*),
is there perhaps even a single knowledge that knows all phenomena (*dharma*)?"
One should answer that they exist,
namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Thus, when asked regarding the nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, or one types of knowledge:
Is there any single knowledge that knows all phenomena?
Answer: There is;
namely, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
If, within this very conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), one were to ask:
"Is it possible to know all phenomena within the duration of two moments?"
Answer: There is.
That is to say, at the very first moment of this wisdom, with the exception of its own nature, its associated factors, and its co-existent factors.
All others it can know.
In the second moment,
it likewise knows the preceding factors of its own nature, as well as those associated and coexistent with them.
Therefore, [in the previous case] he answered "it exists.
Now, this question concerns only knowledge of a single moment;
therefore, he answered "it does not exist."
Question: For what reason does intrinsic nature not know its own intrinsic nature?
Answer: Lest there be the confusion of cause and effect, or of agent and acted-upon.
The means of accomplishment and that which is accomplished;
the inducer and that which is induced;
the producer and that which is produced.
The subject and the object;
the transformer and the transformed;
the characteristic and the characterized.
If there were no distinction between the perceiver and the perceived, it would entail the logical error [of identity];
therefore, intrinsic nature does not know intrinsic nature.
Some say that intrinsic nature neither benefits nor harms itself.
Without nourishment and without harm;
without formation and without destruction;
without increase and without decrease.
It has no accumulation and no dispersion;
it has no cause and no equal-and-immediate condition;
it has no object of cognition.
There is no supremacy;
the intrinsic nature of all phenomena does not observe its own intrinsic nature.
However, it is only within the nature of another that various conditions can function;
therefore, self-nature does not know self-nature. Some say:
It is commonly observed in the world that the tip of a finger cannot touch itself,
and the edge of a blade cannot cut itself.
The pupil does not see itself;
a strong man does not carry himself on his own back.
Therefore, intrinsic nature does not know intrinsic nature.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"For what reason does intrinsic nature not know its own intrinsic nature?
He replied: "Because it is not its objective domain."
Furthermore, if intrinsic nature were to know intrinsic nature,
the Blessed One would not have established that two conditions give rise to the six consciousnesses—
namely, that with the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises.
Up to: with mind and mental objects as conditions, mind-consciousness arises.
Furthermore, if self-nature were to know self-nature, the Blessed One would not have established the contact of the threefold conjunction.
That is to say, with the eye and visible forms as conditions,
eye-consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three,
contact occurs, and so forth, as explained in detail.
Furthermore, if intrinsic nature were to know itself,
the Blessed One would not have established wrong view;
for if that wrong view could know itself, "I am wrong view," it would thereby become right view.
As it is said:
"If wrong view were able to observe itself as being wrong view,
it would have to be called right view, not wrong view."
Furthermore, if intrinsic nature were to know intrinsic nature,
one could not establish that an evil mind is entirely unwholesome,
because its own essence would not be deviant.
Furthermore, if intrinsic nature were to know intrinsic nature,
one could not establish the distinction between the grasper and the grasped,
or the knower and the known.
The grasper and the grasped;
the object and that which possesses the object;
the aspect and the focal point.
The meaning of each faculty and so forth is equal.
Furthermore, if the intrinsic nature were to know the intrinsic nature,
then the four foundations of mindfulness would have no distinction between them.
Because the application of mindfulness to the body is itself the application of mindfulness to phenomena,
and so on up to the application of mindfulness to the mind being itself the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
Furthermore, if intrinsic nature were to know intrinsic nature, [it would follow that it knows itself].
The knowledge of the four noble truths would then be without distinction,
because the knowledge of suffering would be identical to the knowledge of the path,
and so on, up to the knowledge of cessation being identical to the knowledge of the path.
Furthermore, if intrinsic nature were to know intrinsic nature,
then the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) should not be said to exist,
because that [knowledge] would already know present phenomena.
Furthermore, if intrinsic nature were to know intrinsic nature,
then the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) should not be said to exist,
because that too would be knowing what belongs to one's own mind.
The Venerable One said:
"If intrinsic nature were to know intrinsic nature,
then it would not know extrinsic nature."
Because it functions with respect to its own nature.
If the own nature were to know another nature,
then it would necessarily not know its own nature.
Because it transforms into the nature of another.
If one knows both self-nature and other-nature,
how does one know them?
If one knows that intrinsic nature is intrinsic nature,
does one know extrinsic nature in the same way?
And if one knows that extrinsic nature is extrinsic nature, [is it likewise]?
Is it that the knowledge of self-nature is likewise? If,
as you say, the knowledge of self-nature is itself the self-nature,
then the knowledge of other-nature is likewise so.
Thus one knows that self-nature is indeed self-nature,
which is correct;
one knows that other-nature is self-nature, which must be erroneous.
If one knows that the nature of another is the nature of another,
and knows the nature of oneself in the same way,
then one knows that the nature of another is the nature of another.
However, if that which is the nature of correct knowledge were to be another nature, it would necessarily be erroneous.

If that were so, there would be no distinction between the essential characteristics of the two types of cognition—correct and erroneous—if one were to know the nature as being the nature itself at one and the same time.
If that which is known as other-nature were itself other-nature,
then a single cognition would necessarily possess two distinct modes of comprehension;
and because these modes of comprehension are distinct, their essential natures would likewise have to be distinct.
Since their entities are distinct, they should not be a single cognition.
It would contradict correct reasoning for two cognitions to arise simultaneously within the body of a single sentient being; let there be no such error.
Therefore, intrinsic nature does not know intrinsic nature.
Question: If that is so, how do you account for the analogy cited by the Mahāsāṃghikas?
Answer: It is not necessary to account for it.
Because it is not included within the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Abhidharma;
furthermore, one cannot challenge the dharmas of the noble ones (ārya) with worldly examples,
for the dharmas of the noble ones are distinct and the worldly dharmas are distinct.
If it must be explained away,
one should point out the fault in the analogy;
since the analogy already possesses this fault.
The analogy is not established.
For example, a lamp has no roots and no objects of cognition, and it does not belong to the category of sentient beings;
wisdom should likewise be so.
Just as a lamp is composed of material atoms (rūpa-paramāṇu),
so too should cognition be;
yet it is not so.
What serves as the analogy?
Furthermore, do you admit that a lamp is of the nature of illumination?
If it is of the nature of illumination, why would it require further illumination?
If it did not possess the nature of illumination, its essence would be darkness and it could not be called a lamp.
Since a lamp is defined by its ability to destroy darkness, how could it not possess the nature of illumination?
Therefore, one should not maintain that a lamp can illuminate itself.
For this reason, the analogy also fails to be established.
Question: For what reason are the associated dharmas not known?
Answer: Because they have the same object of cognition and arise simultaneously.
That is to say, the mind and mental factors of a single sentient being.
When [multiple consciousnesses] operate simultaneously upon a single object,
it is logically impossible for them to serve as mutual objects for one another;
it is like many people gathered in one place.
Whether they both observe the lower realm or both observe emptiness,
logically they must be unable to see one another's faces.
It is the same for the mind and mental factors as well.
If wisdom can know the associated feeling,
does that feeling take its own self-essence as its object?
If it were to take itself as its object,
then there would be the previously mentioned fault of taking its own nature as an object;
if it cannot take itself as an object, [then how could it know itself?]
In that case, the mind and its mental factors would have to arise simultaneously;
yet, since they do not share the same object of perception (*ālambana*), this fault must be avoided.
Therefore, one cannot know the associated dharmas [simultaneously].
Question: For what reason are co-existent dharmas not known?
Answer: Because they are extremely close together.
It is like when a wooden stick dipped in añjana ointment is placed in the eye.
Because they are extremely close, the eye cannot see them; this case is also like that.
Question: What are called the "co-existent dharmas"?
Answer: These are the derivative forms (anuvartaka-rūpa) that follow along.
Regarding this and the concomitant formations dissociated from mind,
the masters of the West (the Westerners) speak thus:
it is the continuity of the aggregates that arise together with wisdom.
That which is comprised within itself refers to co-existent dharmas;
that assertion is unreasonable. Why is this so?
If that were so, visual consciousness would be unable to apprehend its own constituent forms,
and the same would apply to other types of consciousness.
They explain it as follows:
The five consciousnesses can apprehend objects within their own domains, whereas the mental consciousness cannot.
If that were so, it would follow that the mental consciousness could not apprehend all objects, which would be unreasonable.
Furthermore, there is another fault:
the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* would not be a direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the continuity of the aggregates (*skandha*) co-arising with itself.
If that were the case, it would follow that there is only a partial realization of the objects of one's own truth (*sva-satya*).
He says this:
there is no fault in [the claim] that the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is a partial realization (*parokṣa*) of its own objective truth.
Because the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) arises through the full realization (*parijñā*) [of the truth of suffering].
Just as the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharmajñānakṣānti*) does not incur any fault,
even though it constitutes only a partial realization with respect to its own objective sphere (*svasatyālambana*).
Their statement is unreasonable because it claims that the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path arises from the full comprehension (*parijñā*) [of cessation]. Why is this so?
Because the meanings of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) regarding the path to suffering differ:

that is to say, each instance of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) collectively denies the entire category of the path consisting of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
Regarding the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna-kṣānti*):
even if one attains clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the path within only a single category of dharma-knowledge,
one is also able to completely sever the false views that slander it.
Moreover, setting aside its intrinsic nature, its association, and its coexistence,
all other [factors] are the present realization of the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) with respect to the five aggregates of clinging.
Grasping at a self and what belongs to a self,
whether collectively or individually,
[is abandoned] by the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
If one has not fully realized the truths regarding oneself,
there must be a distinct object-condition for the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
for at that time, one has neither severed nor fully realized that which is grasped as its object.
If the view of a self-identity were not completely abandoned, then all other afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, which take that view as their primary leader,
would likewise not be abandoned.
If that were so, one could not be said to have attained true direct realization regarding one's own truths.
If one does not attain direct realization regarding the truth of suffering,
one likewise would not attain it regarding the truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
In this way, there would be no ultimate liberation.

To avoid this fault, one should not say that the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) does not observe the various co-arising phenomena within one's own body.
Furthermore, if that were the case,
it would contradict what was previously stated in the root treatise, as it says:
If one gives rise to the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) by taking these dharmas as objects,
one immediately gives rise to the supreme mundane dharma (laukika-agra-dharma) by taking those same dharmas as objects.
Since the supreme mundane dharma is able to take the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) of the desire realm as its object in their entirety, [it follows that it takes all dharmas as its object].
What is it that the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* cannot do?
Therefore, one should know that what was stated previously is correct.
Question: For what reason does the *pudgala* not know?
The answer is that they are as unobtainable as the horns of a rabbit;
that is to say, all phenomena are devoid of a self, a sentient being,
a person, a life-force, a living being, or a nourisher.
The agent and the recipient are merely a collection of empty formations; therefore, there is no *pudgala*.
"One who is able to know all phenomena—
could there be a single consciousness that comprehends all phenomena?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of others and clarifying one's own position.
That is to say, there are some who hold [the following view]:
"Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is itself wisdom (*jñāna*); it merely adds one character, namely the syllable *vi*.
This is to refute that school's position and to demonstrate that the essence of consciousness and wisdom are distinct, as stated in the Sūtra:"
Consciousness associated with wisdom may be held to have distinct objects for each of the six consciousnesses,
just as the objects of the five groups of sensory consciousness are distinct.
In this way, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes only the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) as its object.
To refute that school's position and demonstrate that the mental consciousness takes all twelve spheres as its objects,
it is said in the Sūtra:
All things are objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Some maintain that while cognition (*jñāna*) can take all phenomena as its object, consciousness cannot;
to refute that position and demonstrate that both consciousness and cognition are capable of taking all phenomena as their objects—both collectively and individually—[this treatise is composed].
There are some who maintain that while wisdom (*jñāna*) takes both specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its objects,
consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes only specific characteristics as its object.
To refute their position and demonstrate that both wisdom and consciousness take both types of characteristics as their objects, [the author] says:
There are some who maintain that while cognition (*jñāna*) takes both homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and heterogeneous (*tatsabhāga*) objects as its domain,
consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes only homogeneous objects as its domain.
To refute that position and demonstrate that both cognition and consciousness take both parts as their domain, [the author] says:

There are some who maintain that while cognition (*jñāna*) takes as its objects those of the three times as well as the non-temporal, consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes only the present as its object. In order to refute that position and demonstrate that both cognition and consciousness take as their objects those of the three times as well as the non-temporal, [the author states]: "The Blessed One said... and so forth. This means that the Blessed One taught that both cognition and consciousness take as their objects those of the three times and the non-temporal. Thus, it is established that cognition and consciousness are not distinct in terms of their objects. Furthermore, because they are not distinct in terms of their objects, they are also not distinct in terms of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, it is established that cognition and consciousness are one and the same. This concludes the section on the refutation of the distinction between cognition and consciousness. Next, the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of omniscience: there are some who maintain that the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) knows all phenomena, whereas the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) does not know all phenomena. In order to refute that position and demonstrate that both know all phenomena, [the author states]: "The Blessed One said... and so forth. This means that the Blessed One taught that both the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of the paths know all phenomena. Thus, it is established that these two types of omniscience are not distinct in terms of their objects. Because they are not distinct in terms of their objects, they are also not distinct in terms of their intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is established that the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of the paths are one and the same. This concludes the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of omniscience. Next, the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of wisdom: there are some who maintain that the wisdom of the Buddhas knows all phenomena, whereas the wisdom of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas does not know all phenomena. In order to refute that position and demonstrate that both know all phenomena, [the author states]: "The Blessed One said... and so forth. This means that the Blessed One taught that both the wisdom of the Buddhas and the wisdom of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas know all phenomena. Thus, it is established that these two types of wisdom are not distinct in terms of their objects. Because they are not distinct in terms of their objects, they are also not distinct in terms of their intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is established that the wisdom of the Buddhas and the wisdom of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are one and the same. This concludes the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of wisdom. Next, the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of vision: there are some who maintain that the vision of the Buddhas sees all phenomena, whereas the vision of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas does not see all phenomena. In order to refute that position and demonstrate that both see all phenomena, [the author states]: "The Blessed One said... and so forth. This means that the Blessed One taught that both the vision of the Buddhas and the vision of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas see all phenomena. Thus, it is established that these two types of vision are not distinct in terms of their objects. Because they are not distinct in terms of their objects, they are also not distinct in terms of their intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is established that the vision of the Buddhas and the vision of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are one and the same. This concludes the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of vision. Next, the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of hearing: there are some who maintain that the hearing of the Buddhas hears all phenomena, whereas the hearing of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas does not hear all phenomena. In order to refute that position and demonstrate that both hear all phenomena, [the author states]: "The Blessed One said... and so forth. This means that the Blessed One taught that both the hearing of the Buddhas and the hearing of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas hear all phenomena. Thus, it is established that these two types of hearing are not distinct in terms of their objects. Because they are not distinct in terms of their objects, they are also not distinct in terms of their intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is established that the hearing of the Buddhas and the hearing of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are one and the same. This concludes the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of hearing. Next, the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of mindfulness: there are some who maintain that the mindfulness of the Buddhas remembers all phenomena, whereas the mindfulness of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas does not remember all phenomena. In order to refute that position and demonstrate that both remember all phenomena, [the author states]: "The Blessed One said... and so forth. This means that the Blessed One taught that both the mindfulness of the Buddhas and the mindfulness of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas remember all phenomena. Thus, it is established that these two types of mindfulness are not distinct in terms of their objects. Because they are not distinct in terms of their objects, they are also not distinct in terms of their intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is established that the mindfulness of the Buddhas and the mindfulness of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are one and the same. This concludes the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of mindfulness. Next, the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of concentration: there are some who maintain that the concentration of the Buddhas is able to enter into all meditative absorptions, whereas the concentration of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is not able to enter into all meditative absorptions. In order to refute that position and demonstrate that both are able to enter into all meditative absorptions, [the author states]: "The Blessed One said... and so forth. This means that the Blessed One taught that both the concentration of the Buddhas and the concentration of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are able to enter into all meditative absorptions. Thus, it is established that these two types of concentration are not distinct in terms of their objects. Because they are not distinct in terms of their objects, they are also not distinct in terms of their intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is established that the concentration of the Buddhas and the concentration of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are one and the same. This concludes the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of concentration. Next, the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of liberation: there are some who maintain that the liberation of the Buddhas is able to liberate all sentient beings, whereas the liberation of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is not able to liberate all sentient beings. In order to refute that position and demonstrate that both are able to liberate all sentient beings, [the author states]: "The Blessed One said... and so forth. This means that the Blessed One taught that both the liberation of the Buddhas and the liberation of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are able to liberate all sentient beings. Thus, it is established that these two types of liberation are not distinct in terms of their objects. Because they are not distinct in terms of their objects, they are also not distinct in terms of their intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is established that the liberation of the Buddhas and the liberation of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are one and the same. This concludes the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of liberation. Next, the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of power: there are some who maintain that the power of the Buddhas is able to overcome all Māras, whereas the power of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is not able to overcome all Māras. In order to refute that position and demonstrate that both are able to overcome all Māras, [the author states]: "The Blessed One said... and so forth. This means that the Blessed One taught that both the power of the Buddhas and the power of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are able to overcome all Māras. Thus, it is established that these two types of power are not distinct in terms of their objects. Because they are not distinct in terms of their objects, they are also not distinct in terms of their intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is established that the power of the Buddhas and the power of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are one and the same. This concludes the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of power. Next, the section on the refutation of the distinction between the two types of fearlessness: there are some who maintain that the fearlessness of the Buddhas is able to subdue all adversaries, whereas the fearlessness of the Śrāvakas and Pr
There are some who maintain that while the wisdom of supernormal power (*abhijñā*) takes as its object both the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and non-aggregate objects,
consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes only form (*rūpa*) as its object.
To refute that school and demonstrate that both wisdom and consciousness take as their objects both the five aggregates and non-aggregate objects, [this passage is stated].
There are some who maintain that while cognition (*jñāna*) takes both one's own continuum and the continua of others as its objects,
consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes only one's own continuum as its object.
To refute that position and to demonstrate that both cognition and consciousness take both self and other as their objects, [the author] says:
There are some who maintain that wisdom takes both internal and external bases as its object,
whereas consciousness takes only external bases as its object.
To refute their position and demonstrate that both wisdom and consciousness take both internal and external bases as their objects, [the author] says:
There are some who maintain that while wisdom (*jñāna*) takes both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as its objects,
consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes only the contaminated as its object.
To refute their position and demonstrate that both wisdom and consciousness take both types as their objects, [the author] says:
There are some who maintain that wisdom takes both the conditioned and the unconditioned as its object,
whereas consciousness takes only the conditioned as its object.
To refute their position and demonstrate that both wisdom and consciousness take both types as their objects, [the author] says:
Some maintain that wisdom (*jñāna*) alone constitutes the members of the path (*mārgāṅga*),
while consciousness (*vijñāna*) alone constitutes the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*),
as is the case with the Vātsīputrīyas.
Because the sūtras state that right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is the path,

and because it serves as the object-condition for the consciousness that constitutes the members [of the path], this is to refute their position and demonstrate that both wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) pertain to both members.
This is merely stated according to the stronger position;
for there are those, such as the Dārṣṭāntikas, who maintain that wisdom (jñāna) and consciousness (vijñāna) do not coexist.
To refute that school's position and to demonstrate that wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) arise simultaneously, this treatise was composed for this reason.
Question: Why is consciousness mentioned after wisdom here?
The answer is: because it was the intention of the author of this treatise to proceed in this manner, as explained at length.
Some say that this is the established method of the sūtras and śāstras.
That is to say, a sutra states:
the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was staying.
First, ask:
"Why is the wise one called 'wisdom'?
Afterward, ask: "Why is consciousness called 'consciousness'?"
Śāriputra said:
"It is called wisdom (jñāna) because it is able to know;
it is called consciousness (vijñāna) because it is able to discern."
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* first explains the "knowable" (*jñeya*) and subsequently explains the "cognizable" (*vijñeya*).
It first explains the gateway of wisdom (*jñāna-mukha*) and subsequently explains the gateway of consciousness (*vijñāna-mukha*).
Dharmadinnā also spoke in this manner.
If, in this context, there is the transformation of wisdom-consciousness (*jñāna-vijñāna*),
one should know that there will necessarily be the accomplishment of a superior feat;
for this reason, consciousness is also mentioned after wisdom.
Some say that both are fundamental dharmas; that is to say,
within all categories of the pure, wisdom is the fundamental [dharma].
Consciousness is the root of all categories of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
Because it is preeminent among the categories of purification (*vyavadāna*), it was explained first. Some say:
Because both are foremost dharmas.
As the Sūtra says:
"With clarity as the foremost, immeasurable wholesome dharmas all attain growth."
With consciousness as the primary factor, all various defiled phenomena are able to arise and grow;
because it is the most excellent among all wholesome phenomena, it was mentioned first. Some say:
Because both are objects of reliance.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One should rely on wisdom and not rely on consciousness."
It is further stated:
"The five faculties each have their own respective range and their own respective objects."
The mental faculty (manas) is capable of experiencing all those objects of its range;
the mental faculty is that upon which they all depend.
Because the excellence of the basis for wisdom is paramount, it was mentioned first.
Some say that because both are possessed of an object of cognition (*sālambana*),
two among the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are possessed of an object of cognition.
This refers to the sense base of mind (manāyatana) and the sense base of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Here, "knowledge" is taught,
which collectively indicates that the sense base of phenomena possesses objects of cognition.
To speak of consciousness (vijñāna) is to manifest the sense base of mind (manāyatana) and the sense base of phenomena (dharmāyatana), as these [bases] are manifold;
therefore, it was mentioned earlier. Some say:
This is because it speaks here of both mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
That is to say, if one speaks of "knowledge" (*jñāna*), it generally indicates all mental factors;
if one speaks of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), it indicates that both mind and mental factors are predominant.
Therefore, it was previously asked:
"Is there any single consciousness that comprehends all phenomena?
The answer is: No.
If this consciousness arises [with the realization that] all phenomena are not-self, what is it that this consciousness does not understand?
Answer: It does not understand its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor the mental factors associated with it and those that coexist with it.

Regarding the refutation of attachments herein, the questions, answers, and difficult points for clarification concerning the main text and so forth should be explained according to the preceding [sections].
Question: What is meant by "conditioning all phenomena" as stated here?
The aspect of non-self.
By what sūtra is it known that there exists such an aspect of non-self that takes all phenomena as its object?
Answer: As stated in a sūtra:
"When one observes with wisdom that all phenomena are non-self, at that time one can become weary of suffering; this is the path to attaining purification.
From this sutra.
Knowing that there is such a mode of apprehension (ākāra) as the non-self nature of all phenomena conditioned by [the four truths],
one asks: does this sutra teach the mode of apprehension of the non-self nature of all phenomena conditioned by [the truths],
or does it teach the mode of apprehension of the non-self nature of the Truth of Suffering?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If it is said that the aspect of the practice is "non-self" with respect to all phenomena,
how can it further be said that at that time one feels weary of suffering?
If it is said that one contemplates the aspect of non-self with respect to the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*),
how can it be said that one contemplates all phenomena as non-self? Some say:
In this sutra, it is taught that all phenomena are characterized by the aspect of non-self.
Question: Why, then, is it said that at that time one becomes weary of suffering?
Answer: This refers to the first half of the verse.
It is said that the first part [of the verse] teaches the aspect of non-self with respect to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*),
while the latter half teaches the aspect of non-self with respect to the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). Others say:
The first half explains the time of cultivating contemplation (*bhāvanā*),
while the second half explains the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Some say:
The first half explains the wisdoms consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
the second half explains only the wisdom consisting of cultivation. Some say:
The first half explains wisdom with outflows (*sāsrava-prajñā*);
the second half explains wisdom without outflows (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
As it is with wisdom having outflows and without outflows, so it is for the rest.
Worldly and supramundane;
with flavor and without flavor;
based on attachment and based on renunciation.
One should know that the same applies to those bound to a realm and those not bound to a realm,
as well as to those conducive to grasping and those not conducive to grasping.
Some say that the first half explains the attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*),
while the second half explains the attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*).
Other masters say:
"This sutra speaks only of the aspect of non-self (*anātman*) as a condition for the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Question: "How then does it speak of contemplating all phenomena as non-self?"
Answer: There are two kinds of "all": namely, all-in-all and partial-all.
In this context, "all" refers only to a limited portion;
elsewhere as well, "all" is spoken of as referring only to a limited portion,
as the Blessed One has said:
All things are ablaze;
there is no sense of being ablaze in regard to untainted (anāsrava) phenomena,
and it is the same in this case as well.
Although the aspect of "non-self" regarding all phenomena as objects is not explicitly mentioned here,
other sūtras state it,
as the Blessed One said:
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
all dharmas are without self;
nirvana is tranquility.
The commentary states:
Depending on whether there is scriptural evidence or no scriptural evidence.
Nevertheless, there definitely exists a mode of apprehension that takes all phenomena as its object and perceives them as non-self;
that is to say, when a practitioner of yoga gives rise to this mode of apprehension during the stage of meditative cultivation.
Therefore, it is said herein:
Question— Is there also a mode of activity of emptiness that can take all phenomena as its object?
Why is this not mentioned here?
The answer is: because it was the intention of the author of this treatise to do so, and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say: "That which should have been stated but was not stated,
one should know that its meaning is incomplete."
Some say that the aspect of non-self has a definitive meaning; therefore,
it is specifically mentioned.
This means that the meaning of the aspect of emptiness is not definitive,
because all phenomena possess intrinsic meaning,
and emptiness is predicated upon the nature of other-dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Because there is existence;
because "not empty" refers to intrinsic nature (svabhāva);
and because the aspect of non-self is not indeterminate.
Because, in brief, both self and other are devoid of self;
for this reason, the Venerable Vasumitra said:
"I do not definitively state that all phenomena are empty."
It is definitively taught that all phenomena are without self.
Question: If they are not characterized by the aspect of selflessness, are they then characterized by the aspect of emptiness?
Regarding the statement that both can take all phenomena as their objects:
what is the difference between these two modes of activity (*ākāra*)?
Answer: The mode of activity of non-self (*anātman*) serves as the antidote to the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Emptiness serves as the antidote to the view of "mine," just as it serves as the antidote to the view of "self" and the view of "what belongs to self.
It likewise serves as the antidote to the view of "I" and the view of "what belongs to I."
There are five views of "I" and fifteen views of "mine.
These consist of the aspect of "I," the aspect of "mine," the grasping at "I," and the grasping at "mine."
"I love what I love;
I am deluded by what I am deluded by.
One should know that it is likewise so.
Some say that contemplating the aggregates as non-self is the aspect of non-self.
Contemplating that there is no self within the aggregates is the characteristic of the practice of emptiness;
it is like contemplating that the aggregates are not the self and that there is no self within the aggregates.
One should know that it is likewise when observing within each element and when observing within each location.
Some say that observing non-existence as non-existent is the aspect of "non-self" (anātman).
To observe existence as non-existence is the characteristic of emptiness;
so it is said by some.
To contemplate non-existence within that which is non-existent is the aspect of "not-self" (anātman);
to contemplate non-existence within that which is existent [is the aspect of impermanence].
This is the characteristic of emptiness.
Some say it is the contemplation of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
This is not the aspect of my practice;
observing that which is practiced as empty is the aspect of emptiness.
Some say that observing the essence as not being self-governing is the aspect of "not-self."
To observe that there is no person within is the characteristic of emptiness;
this is called the distinction between these two types of characteristics.
Question: Why is it that the impure (sāsrava) aspect of non-self takes all phenomena as its object,
whereas the pure (anāsrava) aspect of non-self does not?
Does it take only the Truth of Suffering as its object?
Answer: It takes the aspect of the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) non-self;
for it is not an antidote to the afflictions (kleśa).
It can take all phenomena as its object;
it is the aspect of "outflow-free" and "non-self," because it is the antidote to the afflictions.
It does not take all phenomena as its object,
because not all phenomena possess a nature conducive to affliction. Some say:
The aspect of "impure" and "non-self" can take all phenomena as its objects, because it is not an antidote to cognitive inversion.
The aspect of the outflow-free (anāsrava) non-self (anātman) does not take all phenomena as its object, because it serves as the antidote to cognitive inversion (viparyāsa).
It is not because all phenomena conform to the nature of inversion.
Some say that there is a mode of apprehension regarding the non-self (anātman) aspect of contaminated phenomena (sāsrava).
Because it takes objects without limitation,
it can take all phenomena as its objects;
it possesses the aspect of being untainted and non-self.
Because it has a limited object,
it does not take all phenomena as its object;
rather, it takes the object of the view of self as "non-self."
Some say that because the aspect of "non-self" regarding contaminated phenomena is superior at the time of practicing contemplation.
It can take all phenomena as its object,
because when practicing contemplation, one contemplates all phenomena as being non-self;
thus, it possesses the aspect of the untainted non-self.
Because it is superior at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), it does not take all phenomena as its object.
This is because, at the time of clear realization, one takes only the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) as non-self;
for during the stage of clear realization, one contemplates each truth individually.
By virtue of these causes and conditions,
the aspect of "outflow-tainted non-self" is able to take all phenomena as its object.
The aspect of non-self that is untainted takes only the truth of suffering as its object.
Question: What about the aspect of non-self that is tainted?
Nor can it take all phenomena as its object,
because it cannot take its own nature, its associated factors, or its coexistent factors as objects.
How, then, can it be said that it takes all phenomena as its object?
Answer: There is no fault, because this is stated according to the majority.
That is to say, the objects of perception are like the great earth and the four great oceans.
Mount Sumeru and the extent of the great void;
those who do not take these as objects of perception.
It is like a single drop of water from the great ocean compared to a mustard seed;
a single mote of dust on Mount Meru;
or a mosquito in the vastness of space.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Some say that this is by means of the aspect of "this is with outflows" and "this is not-self."
Because it takes all phenomena as its object for the duration of two moments,
this statement is made;
it is not like the aspect of "non-self" (anātman) in the case of the untainted (anāsrava).
Although it lasts for many moments,
it still cannot take all phenomena as its object in their entirety.
Some say:
The aspect of impermanence regarding the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) is also able to take all that is to be known as its object within a single moment.
The intrinsic nature of the dharmas that serve as conditions,
as well as the associated and co-existent dharmas,
are not objects of perception.
One should not be reproached for this reason; by means of these causes and conditions,
there is thus the aspect of the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) as non-self (anātman).
Although it is said that all phenomena are non-self,
this is not a misconception.
From the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-mahāvibhāṣā*, Volume Nine.

2. The second part of the second section, the "Section on Wisdom" (*jñāna-nikāya*), within the first chapter, the "Miscellaneous Aggregates" (*saṃgīti-paryāya*). Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the mental aspect (*ākāra*) that takes all phenomena as non-self?
Answer: Wisdom (*prajñā*) is its intrinsic nature.
Just as with the aspects of the self, the substance, and the characteristics,
so it is with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The intrinsic nature has already been explained.
Therefore, it shall now be explained.
Question: Why is it called the aspect of non-self that takes all phenomena as its object?
Answer: Because this wisdom arises with respect to all phenomena by way of the aspect of non-self.
It is named the mental aspect of "non-self" that takes all phenomena as its object.
As for its realm, this mental aspect exists only in the desire realm and the form realm, and not in the formless realm.
There are also instances where this mode of activity (*ākāra*) cannot take all phenomena as its object;
this will be explained in detail later.

As for the "stages" (*bhūmi*), this mode of activity exists in seven stages, namely: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
And the four fundamental dhyānas.
This is the general explanation.
To explain them specifically:
The wisdom derived from hearing exists only in five stages,
namely: the desire realm and the four dhyānas.
The wisdom resulting from reflection exists only in the desire realm.
The wisdom resulting from cultivation exists only in six stages;
that is, within the seven stages previously mentioned, excluding the desire realm.
The four formless stages also possess this mode of activity,
yet they cannot take all phenomena as their object.
That is to say, the sphere of infinite space,
characterized by the aspect of non-self,
takes the four formless spheres as its object.
They arise through that cause and cease through that cause;
this includes all paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) as well as the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the four formless attainments.
The entire category of the path of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and all unconditioned space (*ākāśa-asamskrta*)—
some may wish to consider these as a single entity.
Alternatively, one may wish to take these many objects as the object of cognition;
this mode of activity (ākāra) exhausts all that can be so perceived.
The Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana) takes the mode of activity of non-self (anātman).
It takes the three higher formless attainments as its object;
it has those as its cause and cessation,
and consists of all paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

the rest is as previously explained,
