Question: For what reason is this so regarding the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Is it the case that all phenomena are without objective conditions and are characterized by non-self?
Answer: If within a given stage there are factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
And its preparatory stage possesses similar roots of goodness;
in that stage, there can be a mode of apprehension (ākāra) that takes all phenomena as its object and is characterized by non-self (anātman).
The formless realms are not so; therefore, they do not exist in those stages.
Some say: if a stage contains the roots of goodness pertaining to the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya), [then the Path exists there].
Such characteristics may exist in that stage [the form realm],
but it is not so for the formless [realm]. Some say:
If a stage possesses the conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*),
that stage may have such mental aspects; the formless [stages] are not like this.
Some say: if a stage contains the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the preparatory stage for the path of seeing (*darśanaprayoga*),
then that stage possesses such mental aspects (*ākāra*).
It is not so for the formless realms. Some say:
if a stage excels in insight (*vipaśyanā*), this aspect exists there; because the formless realms excel in tranquility (*śamatha*), it does not exist in those stages.
As for its basis:
this aspect of non-self relies upon the bodies of the desire and form realms.
Its initial arising depends on a body belonging to the desire realm.
As for its mode of activity,
it performs the mode of activity that is the contemplation of non-self.
As for the object of focus,
it takes all phenomena as its object.
As for the foundations of mindfulness:
This is the application of mindfulness to phenomena with mixed objects.
"Wisdom" here refers to conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
It may be accompanied by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or not accompanied by meditative concentration.
Regarding association with faculties, it is associated with three faculties:
namely, pleasure, joy, and equanimity.
Question: Is there also a wholesome faculty of grief that can take all phenomena as its object?
Why is this mode of activity not associated with that?
Answer: Because they are mutually contradictory;
that is to say, this [state] proceeds as a mode of joyful activity.
Because that [non-concomitance] functions as a mode of mental distress, it is not associated;
as for "time," this mode of activity falls within the three periods of time.
Regarding those conditioned by the three times and that which is beyond time—
whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—
the wholesome [factors] take as their objects all three types [of phenomena] within the three realms.
Regarding "bound" and "unbound":
those bound to the realms of desire and form take as their objects that which is bound to the three realms as well as that which is unbound.
The learner, the one beyond learning, and that which is neither learner nor beyond learning:
this is that which is neither learner nor beyond learning.
They have as their objects the three types [of phenomena]: those abandoned by seeing, those abandoned by cultivation, and those not abandoned.
Those not abandoned have as their objects the three types. Regarding "having names as objects" and "having meanings as objects":
[the former refers to conceptualization, while the latter refers to direct perception].
It takes both name and object as its conditions;
it takes as its conditions those within one's own continuum, those within the continua of others,
and those that do not constitute a continuum.
All three types take all three as their objects.
Those consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation pertain to all three [levels].
Acquisition through application,
acquisition through detachment from defilements,
and acquisition through birth.
It may be said that [this] applies to all three types;
this is the general explanation.
If explained specifically:
The aspect of non-self (anātman) consisting of that which is produced by hearing and reflection (śrutamayī and cintāmayī) in the desire realm is acquired solely through application (prayoga).
The aspect of non-self consisting of that which is produced by hearing (śrutamayī) in the form realm is likewise so acquired.
It may be said that it is acquired through application, and it may be said that it is acquired by birth.
How can it be said that it is acquired through application?
It refers to when one here [in this world] is well-versed in the specific and general characteristics of things.
One who has cultivated [the path] attains it upon being born there;
if one has not, one does not attain it upon being born there.
How, then, can it be said that it is "attained at birth"?
This means that although one has practiced well here [in this world],
if one has not yet been born there, one will ultimately be unable to attain it;
only upon being born there can one attain it.
That mental aspect of non-self consisting of what is produced through hearing must necessarily depend upon the preparatory application cultivated here in this world,
for it arises from that [application].

The aspect of non-self (anātman) cultivated through meditation in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) is obtained through application (prayoga-prāpta) and obtained through detachment from defilements (vairāgya-prāpta);
it may also be said to be obtained by birth (upapatti-prāpta).
Question: If one dies in the desire realm and is born in the second dhyāna,
or dies in the second dhyāna and is born in the first dhyāna—
Does he attain the first dhyāna through the aspect of non-self?
Answer: If he has previously practiced it well, he attains it;
otherwise, he does not.
The same applies up to being born in the fourth dhyāna.
Question: If one passes away from the desire realm and is born in the formless realm?
When one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the first dhyāna,
does that person attain the first dhyāna through the aspect of non-self?
Some say that it cannot be attained because it is too distant.
Regarding this teaching:
it is attained by those who have previously practiced well;
otherwise, it is not attained.
The same applies up to being born in the fourth dhyāna.
Question: If one passes away from the first dhyāna and is born in the second dhyāna...
When one passes away from the second dhyāna and is reborn in the first dhyāna,
does that person attain the first dhyāna through the aspect of non-self?
Answer: If one has previously cultivated it well, one attains it;
otherwise, one does not.
The same applies when one is born in another stage.
Question: What kind of person (pudgala) attains this mode of practice?
Is it only noble ones (ārya), or does it extend to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) as well?
Some say that only noble ones attain it,
and not ordinary beings.
Regarding this statement, it applies to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) as well.
Question: There are two kinds of ordinary beings.
That is to say, internal phenomena and external phenomena.
Regarding which ordinary beings attain this mode of activity,
some say as follows:
Those who attain it are those of the internal dharma,
not those of the external dharma;
for the latter are attached to a self.
If one says that they are unable to cultivate the view of emptiness and non-self,
then even ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) regarding external phenomena would likewise obtain this mode of activity.
However, it differs from the internal [dharmas].
That is to say, as for internal dharmas,
they are obtained both through application and through birth.
They are both acquired and present in the body, and they are also accomplished and manifest.
This applies to external phenomena and to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
It is obtained only at birth and does not exist as a bodily attainment;
it does not manifest before one because of attachment to a self.
Question: How does one give rise to the aspect of non-self?
Answer: If one is born in the desire realm, one gives rise to the aspect of non-self regarding the desire and form realms.
Both are able to take all phenomena as their objects.
If one is born in the first dhyāna and gives rise to the aspect of non-self (anātman) within the first dhyāna.
Those who are not concentrated can take all phenomena as objects;
those who are concentrated take only [phenomena] from the first dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as objects,
giving rise to the aspect of non-self (*anātman*) within the upper three dhyānas.
Furthermore, it can only take as its object [realms] from the first dhyāna up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
If one is born in the second dhyāna,
one gives rise to the aspect of non-self (*anātman*) pertaining to the second dhyāna.
The indeterminate [attainments] can take all phenomena as their objects;
the determinate [attainments] take only those from the second dhyāna up to the peak of existence as their objects,
arising with the aspect of non-self (*anātman*) in the third and fourth dhyānas.
Furthermore, it can only take as its object [the states] from the second dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
If one is born in the third or fourth dhyānas,
it should be explained accordingly.
If one is born in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm,
and gives rise to the aspect of non-self pertaining to the formless realm,
the scope of the phenomena as its object is as previously explained.
Question: Regarding the aspect of non-self (*anātman*) in both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), which has more objects of cognition (*ālambana*)?
Answer: The aspect of non-self in the form realm.
If it is indeterminate,
the objects of focus are equal to those of the desire realm and so forth;
if it is determinate, the objects of focus are fewer than those of the desire realm.
This means that it cannot take as its object the matter that evolves concomitantly with itself;
for in the desire realm, there is no such concomitant matter within the aspect of non-self.
Because it can take all forms as its object,
some say that there is a "foundation of mindfulness on the body."
The mindfulness of body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) takes as its object all forms (*rūpa*) that are devoid of feeling and mind.
The mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) takes as its object all feelings, minds, and phenomena.
Question: This [mindfulness of phenomena] takes all phenomena as its object through the aspect of non-self (*anātman*).
Is it with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava)?
Answer: It is with outflows, not without outflows. Why is this so?
There is a mundane aspect of non-self that cannot even take all phenomena as its object,
such as the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
How much more so for the untainted aspect of non-self,
which is able to take all phenomena as its object?
This is because this aspect takes the truths individually as its objects.
Just as those with false views do not even for a single moment perceive both truths simultaneously,
how much less could they perceive many?
As it is with that which is to be countered, so it is with its antidote.
Question: Can the aspect of "outflow-tainted" (sāsrava) and "non-self" (anātman) sever the afflictions (kleśa)?
Answer: It cannot sever them.
Question: If that is so, for what reason does a noble one (ārya) arise [in meditative absorption]?
Answer: It is in order to cause the faculties (indriya) to become sharper and enter the Noble Path (āryamārga).
Furthermore, a noble one arises [therein] due to four conditions.
First, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life;
second, for the sake of contemplating what was previously done;
and third, for the sake of sporting with spiritual qualities.
Fourth, it is for the sake of enjoying the noble wealth.

Is it associated with a mind of aversion?
If so, what is the fault?
If it were associated with a mind of joy, [what would follow]?
What is the object-condition for phenomena that are to be reviled?
It is when [the mind] is accompanied by the mental attention of revulsion.
What is the object-condition for phenomena that are to be welcomed?
It is agreed that it is so stated.
It is associated with a mind of joyful attention (*prāmodya-manasikāra*).

Answer: Because that yogin generates appreciation for phenomena worthy of appreciation,
even amidst an immeasurable mass of things worthy of aversion.
If there is even one thing to be delighted in, joy arises;
how much more so when there are many?
It is like placing a single gold coin upon a heap of copper coins.
Thus, one generates a general sense of delight toward this collection;
this case is likewise,
and therefore there is no fault.

There are some non-Buddhists who,

They speak as follows:
One currently observes that the spring gushes forth;
subsequently, the later [waters] press against the earlier ones,
causing them to surge and flow.
In this context, the subsequent water serves as the cause for the preceding water.
Likewise, when these phenomena proceed through the three periods of time,
the future period impels them to enter the present.
The present world, being pressured, causes [the future] to enter the past;
therefore, the future world serves as the cause for the present,
and the present, in turn, serves as the cause for the past.
To refute that school's position and clarify that a subsequent dharma is not the cause of a preceding dharma:
if it were indeed the cause,
it would contradict the principle of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) regarding all dharmas, both internal and external.
Regarding the contradiction with the internal dependent origination:
this refers to the principle that ignorance conditions formations,
and so on, up to birth conditioning old age and death.
Parents are the cause for a child;
the eye and visible forms are the causes for visual consciousness,
and so on, up to the mind and mental phenomena being the causes for mental consciousness.
Furthermore, [the claim that] the kalala is the cause of the arbuda,
and so on up to the mature body being the cause of old age,
contradicts the dependent origination of external phenomena.
That is to say, it would follow that the seed is the cause of the sprout,
and so on, up to the flower being the cause of the fruit;
such [a view] entails further great fallacies.
This would mean that one would experience the fruit before having performed the karma,
and only after experiencing the fruit would one perform the karma.
How could such a thing be?
One should first experience the maturation of pleasure and pain,
and only afterwards perform wholesome or unwholesome actions;
one would thus obtain the fruits of restraint and non-restraint prior to attaining them.
One may first receive the vows of restraint or non-restraint,
and later fall into hell; one may first become a wheel-turning monarch, and later create those [karmic] actions.
One would first attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and only thereafter cultivate the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
If one were to experience the fruit before having performed the action, [this contradiction would follow].
What ought to have been accomplished would instead be lost and destroyed;
thus, there would be no liberation or transcendence.
Therefore, that which comes later cannot serve as the cause for that which precedes it.
For this reason, this treatise is composed:

This demonstrates that for a single person (pudgala) throughout the three periods of time,

This serves to refute the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) attachment to the idea that a subsequent state acts as the cause for a preceding one,

Since this treatise proceeds solely on the basis of the five causes, it answers by saying "no."

In this way, there are two feelings, two perceptions,

or the patience regarding origin (samudaya-kṣānti) and the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna).
Regarding that past mass of wrong views,
one gives rise to the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, as well as cause,
accumulation, arising, and condition.
In this way, these two minds take each other as objects in turn.
It should be understood that herein, momentariness is excluded and the continuous flow is excluded,
but temporal duration is not excluded.
It does not obstruct the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga),
nor does it obstruct that which has existed since beginningless time;
it obstructs only the momentary.

This means that it is absolutely impossible for one who has given rise to wrong views and slandered the Noble Path in the preceding moment to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) in the second moment; thus,
the continuous flow [of defilements] is obstructed.
That is to say, it is absolutely impossible for anyone within a single stream of existence to first give rise to wrong views that slander the Noble Path,
and subsequently enter the state of right determination and transcendence of birth.
Regarding "not obstructing the time period," this refers to the first watch of the day when one gives rise to wrong views and slanders the Noble Path.
At the time of the middle part of the day,
one is able to enter the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma).
At the time of the middle part of the day.
Having given rise to wrong views and slandered the Noble Path,
at the time of the latter part of the day,
he was immediately able to enter the state of right determination and transcendence from birth.
The same applies to the three parts of the night.
Thus, none of the stages—day, night, half-month, month, season, year, and so forth—are obstructed;
how much less so the homogeneous character (nikāya-sabhāga)?
Since beginningless time,
it should be understood that false views, doubt, and ignorance are likewise;
for they share the same object as the [noble] path.
If there is an arising of mind, there is a future path;
that mind then contemplates this arising as a second mind.
Question: For what reason is this treatise further composed?
Answer: It was previously stated that the mind of right view takes impure minds as its objects in a reciprocal manner;
now, we wish to explain the mind of right view itself.
This treatise is composed because the untainted mind (anāsrava-citta) serves as a reciprocal object for itself;
that is to say, one first gives rise to a single moment of right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).
Either one gives rise to a mental aspect directed toward the future untainted mind alone,
or toward the future untainted aggregates as a whole.
The subsequently arising noble path either focuses solely on the past aggregate of right view,
or it takes as its object the totality of the past contaminated aggregates.
The aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, as well as cause,
origin, production, and condition, arise; in this manner,
these two minds take one another as their objects.

It should be understood that herein, those who maintain that the noble path arises immediately after the attention to common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra) refute the [notion of arising] at a single moment (kṣaṇa),
but do not refute [its arising] as a continuous stream (pravāha).
Regarding the exclusion of the moment:
this possesses the mental activity of the future path,
because it is a mental attention directed toward specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*).
As for those who maintain that both types of attention arise immediately prior to the Noble Path,
they likewise do not deny [the possibility of] successive moments,
just as there are two knowers of others' minds.
Those two minds take each other as their respective objects.
Question: For what reason is this treatise further composed?
Answer: Because the preceding discussion concerned the mind within one's own continuum.
[The mind] takes as its object the minds within its own continuum in a reciprocal manner.
Now, I wish to explain how the mind within one's own continuum takes as its object the minds within the continua of others in a reciprocal manner.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
Question: What kind of "two knowledges of others' minds" are spoken of here?
Do those two minds take one another as their objects?
Answer: Herein, the faculties, the stages, and the paths are explained.
Regarding the two types of knowledge of others' minds, those two minds take each other as their mutual objects.
"Faculties and so forth" refers to those with sharp, medium, and dull faculties.
"Stages and so forth" refers to...
This refers to those who share the same basis,
from the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna;
as for "the paths and so forth," it means:
That is to say: they are alike in being contaminated,
alike in being uncontaminated,
and alike in the category of dharma-knowledge.
Regarding the category of knowledge of similarity (*sabhāga-jñāna*), there are those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Question: How do these two types of mind take one another as objects?
Answer: It takes that mind as its object alone;
it does not take that mind’s objects or its cognitive modes (*ākāra*) as its objects.
If it were to take that mind’s objects and cognitive modes as its objects, [it would follow that]...
In that case, there would be the fault of self-referential causation (*sva-saṃtāna-pratyaya-doṣa*).
Question: There are also other cognitions that mutually condition one another;
why, then, is it stated only in relation to those associated with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?
Answer: This is because the author of this treatise intended it to be so;
thus it is explained at length.
Some say: "When something that ought to be stated is not stated,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete."
Some say: "In this context, only those [knowledges] that are clear, unmixed, and easy to discern are mentioned;
other types of knowledge are not so."
Question: There are many kinds of knowledge of others' minds.
Which of these is being discussed here?
Answer: It refers to that which is acquired through application and that which is acquired through the removal of defilements.
Question: Why are others not mentioned?
Answer: Because it was the intention of the author of this treatise to do so, and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say: "When something that ought to be stated is not stated,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete."
Some say that herein only those names and meanings that are superior are mentioned; that is to say,
those acquired through preparatory effort (*prayoga-prāpta*).
That which is obtained through the removal of passion is produced by cultivation;
it is comprised of the supernormal knowledge and consists of four or five factors.
Regarding the fruit of the supreme dhyānas,
some say that this knowledge is free from error with respect to its object.
The others are not so; therefore, they are not mentioned.
Now, by means of this text, I shall stir the ocean of *jñeyārṇava*.
As it is said:
"Two minds take each other as their reciprocal objects;
one should know that the same applies to the mutual objectification of the mental factors, such as sensation (*vedanā*) and the rest."
Furthermore, one should also explain the mutual object-conditioning of the various mental states categorized by their classes (*nikāya*), elements (*dhātu*), wholesomeness (*kuśala*),
and so forth. As for "class," it refers to the mind that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
They mutually serve as objects for minds abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origination,

and through cultivation. A mind abandoned through the vision of origination serves as an object for minds abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origination, and through cultivation.
They are mutually conditioned in turn.
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of cessation,
the outflow-tainted minds that take [cessation] as their object are mutually conditioned in turn.
Those abandoned by the path of seeing are outflow-tainted states that take objects;
these minds, which have outflow-tainted objects, mutually condition one another,
and they too are abandoned by the path of seeing.
The mind that takes the untainted as its object and the untainted mind mutually take one another as objects;
it should be understood that untainted minds also mutually take one another as objects.
It should be understood that the mind abandoned by cultivation takes other minds abandoned by cultivation as its reciprocal objects,
and the mind abandoned by cultivation takes the untainted mind as its reciprocal object.
Regarding the mind abandoned by cultivation:
Those that mutually serve as objects for minds abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin are:
the wholesome, the unobscured-neutral,
and the untainted mind.
Regarding mutual conditionality, it is exclusively wholesome.
As for the realms, it refers to a mind of the desire realm [conditioning] minds of the desire and form realms, as well as unconditioned (unbound) minds.
They are mutually conditioned by one another.
A mind belonging to the form realm is mutually conditioned by minds of the form realm, the formless realm,
and those that are unconditioned (unbound).
The mind of the formless realm takes as its object the mind of the formless realm and the mind that is unconditioned (unbound),
and these take each other as objects in turn.
It should be understood that when a mind of the formless realm takes a mind of the form realm as its reciprocal object,
this refers to the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the Sphere of Infinite Space.
Regarding "wholesome and so forth":
this refers to wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate minds,
each of which is associated with three types of mind.
They function as mutual objects for one another,
with the sole exception of unwholesome resultant [states],
because those exist only within the body of the five sensory consciousnesses.
Other non-obscured neutral minds have the sense of being mutually conditioned by one another;
furthermore, this is what is stated herein.
Regarding those with wrong views who slander causes and slander effects,
there are four distinct categories.
That is to say, some may slander the effect based on [denying] the cause.
Either they slander the cause by relying on the effect,
or they slander the effect by not relying on the cause,
or they slander the cause by not relying on the effect.
Regarding those who deny the fruit based on the cause:
as it is said,
"There is no fruit or ripening for wholesome or unwholesome conduct."
Denying the cause by means of the effect is,
for example, as it is said:
"All pleasure and pain experienced by persons (pudgala) and individuals have no cause and no condition."
Denying the effect by not relying on the cause is,
for example, as it is said:
"There are no spontaneously born sentient beings."
Denying the cause by not relying on the fruit is,
for example, as it is said:
"There are no wholesome or unwholesome actions."
Question: There are four kinds of conditions.
Why, in this context, are only the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) mentioned, and not the other two?
The answer is: because it was the intention of the author of this treatise to state it thus, and so forth, as explained at length. Some say:
Regarding that which should have been stated but was not:
one should know that this meaning is incomplete. Some say:
Those two are also included within what is here explained; that is to say,
when the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is mentioned,
it should be understood that the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) has already been mentioned as well.
Just as two minds do not serve as causes for one another in succession,
nor do they serve as equal-and-immediate conditions (samanantara-pratyaya) for one another;
so it is when speaking of the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
It should be understood that the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) has already been explained;
for just as two minds can serve as objects (*ālambana*) for one another,
so too can two minds serve as dominant conditions for one another.
"For what reason is there not a single *pudgala*?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason was this treatise further composed?
Answer: This is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of others and clarifying one's own position.
That is to say, there may be those who maintain that the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) [is the sole cause of consciousness].
Since its substance is not truly existent,
this is intended to refute that view and to demonstrate that the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) does indeed exist as a real entity.
Some maintain that two minds arise simultaneously in a single *pudgala*; to refute this emphatically and to demonstrate that there is only one mind at a time,
it is said:
This text concerns the discourse on animals.
It was previously stated that there is no single *pudgala* who exists neither before nor after.
The two minds arise simultaneously;
the reason for this has not yet been explained,
and it is now intended to be explained.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
Why is it that no single *pudgala* has two minds arising simultaneously, neither before nor after?
Answer: Because there is no second immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
That is to say, the arising of mind and mental factors necessarily depends upon the immediately preceding condition;
since there is no second such condition, [they do not arise].
Therefore, there is certainly no single person (pudgala) for whom two minds arise simultaneously, neither before nor after. This,
moreover, should be questioned.
For what reason is there no second immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
To this, he further replies:
"Because the mental continuum of sentient beings proceeds one by one."
That is to say, the minds of sentient beings,
by their very nature, proceed as a single continuous succession;
they are neither two nor many.
This is the meaning of successive mutual responses.
Some say that this text provides a repeated answer to a previous question, namely, that which was asked first: [the question].
For what reason is there no single person in whom two minds arise simultaneously, neither before nor after?
To this, he now answers again:
The mental continuum of each sentient being evolves one by one;
that is to say, by the power of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
each individual sentient being possesses only a single mental continuum that evolves.
Why is this? Because a future collection of mental states necessarily arises through the conjunction of the present.
If there is no conjunction, then [the mind] does not arise.
Because there is only a single conjunction in the present,
it causes each successive future mind to arise one by one.
It is like many people traveling along a narrow path;
they pass one by one, for there is not even room for two to go side by side,
let alone for many.
Furthermore, just as the gates of a pen for cattle or sheep are narrow, such that they pass out one by one—
neither two at once nor in a multitude—
so too is the future collection of minds of sentient beings.
They arise one by one based on present conjunctions;
even if there are many conjunctions in the present world,
this is for the purpose of establishing their sequential order.
In that case, many minds would have to arise simultaneously;
however, since this does not occur, they arise one by one.
Furthermore, because their conjunction occurs sequentially, [they cannot arise at once].
If the path of cultivation were to arise first and be joined with it,
and the path of vision were to arise later, then one would have to cultivate the path of cultivation first;
however, since the path of vision arises first, this [proposed] situation does not exist.
First, the path of seeing arises;
consequently, there is no individual who does not [attain it] either before or after [the others].
The two minds arise together.
Regarding this point, there is further analysis:
why is it that there is no single *pudgala*?
The two minds do not arise simultaneously, neither before nor after.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"Within a single moment of the body..."
There is only one mind;
because it functions in dependence upon that [life-faculty], there are not two.
Furthermore, at a single moment, the life-faculty consists of only one mind.
Because it evolves in dependence upon that [object], there are no two [distinct entities].
Furthermore, in a single moment,
there is only one type of mind belonging to a particular homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Because it arises in dependence upon that, there are not two.
The Venerable One said:
"When a phenomenon arises, its causal conjunction is singular and non-dual."
Because it is impossible for two fruits to arise from a single conjunction;
furthermore, in a single moment of mind, there is only one [fruit].
Moreover, some say:
If two minds were to arise simultaneously,
they would be impossible to subdue;
yet now, this single mind is stubborn and unruly.
If it is difficult to tame even a single mind, how much more so two minds?
If the mind cannot be tamed,
then there is no possibility of attaining liberation.
Therefore, within a single continuum, two minds do not arise simultaneously.
Some, however, say:
"If two minds were to arise simultaneously within a single continuum..."
Then there would be the fault of defilement and purification arising simultaneously;
that is to say, a single mind would be both defiled and pure at once.
If the mind were pure in this way,
there would be no principle for attaining liberation;
furthermore, one would have to be born simultaneously in both the good and evil realms.
Furthermore, if two minds were to arise simultaneously within a single continuum,
what would prevent there being three?
If there were three, [what would prevent four, and so on?]
One would have to experience the maturation (*vipāka*) of the three realms simultaneously;
in that case, the realms would be destroyed and there would be no liberation.
Furthermore, if three minds were to arise together within a single continuum (*saṃtati*):
What prevents there being four?
If there were four, one would have to experience the maturation of the four types of birth simultaneously.
In that case, there would be neither birth-and-death nor liberation.
Furthermore, if four minds arise simultaneously within a single continuum,
what prevents there being five?
If there were five [aspects],
one would have to experience the maturation of the five destinies simultaneously;
in that case, the destinies would be destroyed and liberation would be impossible.
Furthermore, if five minds were to arise simultaneously within a single continuum,
what would prevent there being six?
In that case, the six consciousnesses should arise at once, and they should simultaneously apprehend all objects.
Furthermore, if six minds arise simultaneously within a single continuum,
what prevents there being a hundred?
If there can be a hundred, what prevents there being a thousand?
Furthermore, what prevents an infinite number [of dharmas] from arising simultaneously?
If that were the case, all dharmas would have to arise at once from the future.
If they were to perish simultaneously in the present age,
then there would be no future or present, because one observes the future and the present [precisely] by means of them.
It is said that the past exists;
yet because the future and present do not exist, the past likewise does not exist.
If the three periods of time do not exist, then conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) do not exist.
If there were no conditioned phenomena, there would be no unconditioned phenomena.
In that case, all dharmas would be non-existent;
this would constitute a great error.
Therefore, there is no simultaneous arising of two minds.
Other masters say:
"If within a single continuum, two minds arise simultaneously..."
In that case, mental factors such as feeling and so forth would also arise simultaneously with both [the mind and its object];
consequently, there would be ten aggregates in a single moment,
and thus sentient beings would be destroyed.
Because sentient beings perish, the body that serves as their basis perishes.
Because the basis perishes, the five categories perish.
Because the five categories perish, the antidotes perish.
If the antidote were destroyed, then thorough knowledge would be destroyed;
if thorough knowledge were destroyed, then all things such as the fruits of the śramaṇa would be destroyed.
Let there be no such fault.
Therefore, within a single continuum, two minds do not coexist.
Question: Just as there are multiple mental factors (*caitta*) in a single moment without the aforementioned fault, the same should apply to the mind (*citta*).
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"Although mental factors are numerous, they are identical to the mind in that they are both produced by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)."
Just as the mind is one, so too are feeling and the other [mental factors] one;
therefore, there is no fault.
The Venerable One said:
The mind arises in a single harmonious conjunction with sensation and the other factors;
just as the mind is one, so too are sensation and the others one.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the mind arises together with feeling and the other [mental factors] through a single act of attention (*manasikāra*);
just as the mind is one, so too are feeling and the others one.
Although all are termed mental factors (*caitta*), their essential natures and categories differ;
therefore, there is no error.
Question: As previously stated...
What is the essential nature of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
Answer: It consists of all other past and present mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), excluding the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat.
This is called the essential nature of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Question: Why are the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat not considered an equal-and-immediate condition?
Answer: If those minds and mental factors were the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
then subsequent minds and mental factors would necessarily arise.
If that were so, there would be no ultimate liberation.
Other masters say that it is also an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
As for the fact that those subsequent minds and mental factors do not arise,
it is due to other conditions; they are not the obstruction.
Even if it were to arise, it would still serve as a condition for it,
just like the faculty of mind (manas-indriya), the sphere of mind (mano-dhātu), and the base of mind (mana-āyatana). Therefore,
one should not make such a statement.
Why is this? Because the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) is established based on its functional activity.
If a phenomenon acts as an equal-and-immediate condition for another phenomenon, [it is so designated].
There is no phenomenon, no sentient being,
no incantation, and no medicinal herb or the like that can create an obstacle to prevent them from arising.
The sense faculty of mind (manas-indriya), its element (dhātu), and its sphere (āyatana) are established based on the characteristic of the faculty; thus,
even though subsequent consciousnesses do not arise [from them], they are still established as such.
Because it possesses the characteristics of faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, it is designated as a faculty and so on.

Question: Why is it that the final mind of an Arhat possesses the characteristics of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) and so forth, yet lacks the characteristic of being an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
The answer is that the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) and its sphere (*dhātu*) and base (*āyatana*) do not necessarily observe subsequent dharmas; therefore,
the observation of mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth is established.
It is also called the "equal-and-immediate condition" (samanantarapratyaya) because it is established by observing that subsequent phenomena do not arise [if this condition were absent].
It is not said to be a condition.
Furthermore, within dharmas that do not arise,
there exists the characteristic of mental consciousness.
Therefore, the final mind consists of the mental faculty (*manas*) and so forth;
among those dharmas that do not arise, there is no characteristic of equal and immediate antecedence (*samanantara*),
because they abide in a state of confusion.
For this reason, the final moments of consciousness and so forth are not established as equivalent-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
[The following] asks about the equivalent-immediate condition.
What constitutes its characteristic?
Answer: The essence itself is the characteristic;
the characteristic itself is the essence.
One should not seek its characteristic apart from its substance.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"Its meaning is that which is capable of opening up and making way."
This is the characteristic of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, the meaning of "succession" is the characteristic of the equal-and-immediate condition.
Furthermore, the meaning of performing a function is the characteristic of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Furthermore, it is the meaning of being able to produce the mind.
This is the characteristic of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, the capacity to induce the arising of the mind is the characteristic of the immediately preceding condition.
Furthermore, the meaning of being able to awaken the mind is the characteristic of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, the meaning of enabling the continuity of the mind [is its characteristic].
Regarding the characteristics of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
the Venerable One says:
it is that which has the sense of being able to induce the arising of an immediately succeeding mind.
Regarding the characteristics of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
the Venerable Bhāradvāja stated:
"It is that which enables an unarisen mind to succeed an arisen mind."
Regarding the characteristics of this immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the Abhidharmikas state:
it is the sense of being able to cause individual phenomena, each with its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), to arise without interval.
The characteristics of these immediately preceding conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) are the individual specific characteristics of phenomena;
that is to say, the mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
Furthermore, since the specific characteristics of minds are distinct,
it is impossible for two to arise simultaneously.
Other masters say:
The meaning of causing similar dharmas to arise in immediate succession is the characteristic of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Its essential nature has already been explained.
Therefore, it shall now be explained.
Question: Why is it called the "equal-and-immediate condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
Answer: Because this condition can induce dharmas that are equal and immediate.
For this reason, it is called the "equal and immediate condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Question: Regarding preceding and succeeding moments—
Regarding the various mental factors (caitta-dharma),
which are more or fewer in number,
what is meant by "equality" (samatā)?
Just as mental factors of the desire realm are many but those of the form realm are few,
mental factors of the form realm are many but those of the formless realm are few,
and wholesome mental factors are many but unwholesome ones are few.
Since unwholesome mental factors are mostly not indeterminate,
and tainted mental factors are mostly not untainted,
how can it be said that these conditions can induce the immediately preceding dharmas?
Answer:
It is spoken in accordance with the entities and so forth,
not in accordance with the numbers and so forth.
Therefore, there is no fault.
If within a single moment of mind there were one perception,
two feelings, and so forth, they could not be called "equal."
Within a single moment of mind, the mental factors such as feeling arise according to their respective conditions,
each occurring only once; therefore,
they are called "equal" (samā).

Question: Does the mind serve as an equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) only for the mind, and do sensation and the other [mental factors] serve as such only for sensation and the others?
Is it not so? The Śramaṇas who advocate for similar continuity state:
"The mind serves only as an equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) for the mind."
The same applies to sensation (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors];
each acts as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for its own kind.
They should not make such a statement.
Why is this? If that were necessarily the case,
then a wholesome mind should give rise to another wholesome mind.
An unwholesome mind gives rise to another unwholesome mind;
an indeterminate mind gives rise to another indeterminate mind;
and a mind of greed gives rise to another mind of greed.
From a mind of hatred, a mind of hatred arises;
from a mind of delusion, a mind of delusion arises.
In this way, there is no ultimate liberation.
Furthermore, among the various mental factors (caitta),
some are few and some are many;
when they arise, the few give rise to the many.
Consequently, there would be a deficiency of conditions;
much would be produced for only a brief duration,
and the fruit would accordingly diminish.
In this way, within a single collection of mental states,
there are those that arise from conditions and those that do not arise from conditions.
There are those that act as conditions and those that do not act as conditions;
furthermore, there is the collection of outflow-free (anāsrava) minds.
It should arise without an object.
One should state it thus:
"The mind and the mind, as well as the feeling and so forth [arise]."
Feeling and feeling itself, like the mind,
act as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
The same applies to the other mental factors (*caitasika*).
Question: Does mind act as the immediate antecedent condition (samanantarapratyaya) for mind, but not for feeling and so forth?
And do feeling and so forth act [as such] for feeling and so forth?
Is it not the case that [the preceding moment] acts as the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the subsequent state,
rather than being the mind itself? Thus says the Śramaṇa Saṃtati-sadṛśa.
The mind acts as the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the mind, but not for feeling and the other [mental factors].
Feeling and the other [mental factors] act as the immediate antecedent condition for feeling and the other [mental factors], but not for the mind and the other [factors].
He should not make such a statement.

Why is this? Because it was previously stated that the characteristic of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is the sense of being able to open up space for [the subsequent moment].
Within the sense of "making way," there is no distinction between far and near; therefore,
it should be explained in this manner.
There is no distinction between a preceding mental aggregate and a succeeding mental aggregate in their functioning as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Like a heap of beans, etc.

Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;
translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, who received the Imperial Decree.
Section One of the *Saṃgītiparyāya*, Chapter Two on Wisdom (*Jñāna-nirdeśa*), Part Three. Question: Is there an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) in the future world?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
If it existed, future dharmas would have to abide in succession,
and the cultivation of correct application would become useless.
Why is this so? Because if a phenomenon abides here without interruption,
that phenomenon will necessarily arise from this without interruption.
Furthermore, what would be the purpose of corrective application?
Moreover, there would be no sense of subduing the afflictions or giving rise to their antidotes;
thus, there would be no ultimate liberation.
How, then, is the statement in the *Dṛṣṭiparyāya-skandha* to be reconciled? As it says:
"If a dharma acts as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for another dharma..."
Is it ever the case that one does not act as a condition for those dharmas?
Answer: When this dharma has not yet arisen or has already perished.
If it does not exist, why is it that [the path] immediately following the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) [is not so]?
Only the dharma-knowledge-patience regarding suffering arises;
[the subsequent knowledges] up to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising do not arise.
This is stated in the *Aṣṭāṅgika-sūtra*.
Furthermore, how is this reconciled?
As it is said:
"When such a person has performed this karma..."
Either for thirteen kalpas,
or fourteen kalpas,
or even up to twenty kalpas.
One does not fall into the evil destinies.
Furthermore, how is it established?
It is that which is to be experienced in the present life.
Are there three types of karma: that to be experienced in the next life, that to be experienced in subsequent lives, and that to be experienced in the third life or later?
Answer: There is no equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for that which is future.

Question: If that is so, why is it that immediately after the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), only the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises?
Is it from non-arising up to the knowledge of the exhaustion of non-arising?
Answer: This refers to a determination of number, not a determination of specific characteristics.
Why is this so? Regarding the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti),
one does not yet know which of the six stages it belongs to.
It should arise in association with three faculties.
As for which faculty it is associated with,
it should arise with four aspects of mental application.
It is unknown what kind of activity will arise in immeasurable moments;
it is unknown which moment will arise.
Up until the stage of abiding in superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*),
the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is fixed with respect to only three matters.
That is to say, while there is determination regarding the stage, the faculty, and the aspect,
there is still indeterminacy regarding two matters:
namely, indeterminacy regarding the moment.
The immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) is not fixed;
however, when one abides in the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma),
it is fixed with respect to all five matters.
Furthermore, it is not necessary for there to be an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for all phenomena to arise in a sequential succession. Why is this so?
If a phenomenon is dependent upon another phenomenon,
it arises immediately after that phenomenon;
other phenomena do not do so.
Just as external things, although lacking an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
arise in a sequential order through mutual dependence, such as the sequence of seed,
sprout, stalk, branches, twigs, flowers, and fruit.
That which is dependent on it arises immediately after it; others do not.
In this way, although internal phenomena do not exist in the future world and thus lack an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
those that depend upon them arise immediately following them.
The others are not so; the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) is dependent upon and belongs to the supreme mundane dharmas (laukikāgra-dharma).
The dharma-knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledges are not like this;
therefore, immediately after the supreme mundane dharmas,
only the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering arises.
From non-arising up to the knowledge of the exhaustion of non-arising.
Furthermore, future dharmas arise depending upon present dharmas.
If present phenomena come together,
they arise; if they do not come together, they do not arise.
Although such a case does not exist, for the sake of analytical distinction,
even if the conditions for the arising of the path of cultivation were to coincide beforehand,
it would still have to arise first.
However, such a thing does not exist;
rather, it is only the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) that arises through the conjunction with the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
Because the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) and so forth depend upon other combinations [of conditions],
therefore, immediately after the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*),
only the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises.
From non-arising up to the knowledge of the exhaustion of non-arising—
how, furthermore, are the *Aṣṭāṅgika-sūtra* and other such texts to be reconciled?
Some say that the Blessed One, relying on the past and the present,
infers the future.
Therefore, this statement was made:
that the Blessed One, observing past and present,
[saw] individuals of such a kind.
Having performed such karma,
for that many eons, such a person (pudgala) does not fall into the evil destinies.
One performs such karma and experiences its fruit in the present life;
one performs such karma and experiences its fruit in the next birth;
one performs such karma and experiences its fruit in subsequent lives thereafter.
From this direct observation,
one infers that a person of such a kind who performs such an action will experience its result in the future.
Throughout those kalpas, such a person will not fall into the evil destinies;
such a type of *pudgala*, having performed such karma,
shall experience its fruit in the present life.
"When one performs such karma, one shall experience its fruit in the present life;
when one performs such karma, one shall experience its fruit in a future life.
Other masters say:
Within the bodies of sentient beings there are such signs;
these are subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from thought (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
The Blessed One observed them.
He then knows that such a person will not fall into the miserable realms for that many eons throughout the future,
and he also knows the various karmas performed by such a person.
Some are to be experienced in the present life,
some are to be experienced upon rebirth,
and some are to be experienced in subsequent lives.
The critique states:
One should not speak in such a manner.
If one were to speak thus:
This would imply that the Blessed One possesses only inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*) regarding future events and lacks direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*),
which is unreasonable.
It should rather be stated as follows:
The Buddha knows the future through direct perception rather than inference;
that is to say, because the Buddha’s wisdom-vision is luminous, pure, sharp, and penetrating,
he perceives all phenomena of the future.
Although they dwell in a disordered manner without any sequence,
one is able to know them directly as being of such a type of *pudgala*.
Having performed such karma,
for that many eons in future worlds, such a person (pudgala) will not fall into the evil destinies.
Having created such karma,
one shall experience its results either in the present life,
or in a future birth.
Or it will be experienced in a future life;
this is clear and unerring.
Other masters say:
There are also equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) in the future.
Question: If that were so, all dharmas in the future would exist in a sequential order, and the cultivation of correct application (*prayoga*) would become useless.
Furthermore, there would be no sense of subduing the afflictions (*kleśa*) through the arising of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
In such a case, there would be no ultimate liberation (*mokṣa*). [Objection:
Although future phenomena possess the nature and characteristics of being an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), [the response is as follows:]...
Yet there is no fixed sequence of priority and posteriority;
that is to say, in the state where mind and mental factors have not yet arisen,
there are dharmas that ought to arise immediately following them, yet they lack a sequential order of precedence.
Once they have reached the stage of having already arisen,
there are dharmas that must arise immediately after them,
and these likewise possess a sequential order and arrangement.
It is like many śramaṇas who,
though they may be arranged in a disordered manner and their seniority and juniority already fixed,
have not yet formed a formal procession.
If they abide in sequence, their large and small dimensions are fixed,
and their arrangement is also fixed;
since this case is likewise so, there is no error.
Corrective application is not rendered useless,
because there are two moments of mind in uninterrupted succession within a single moment of mind;
that is to say, in the future, there is a single moment of mind followed by another in immediate succession.
There are two types of mental abidings: first, the wholesome, and second, the defiled.
If one practices correct application in the present life, then the wholesome mind arises and the defiled mind does not arise.
If one engages in improper application in the present life, then a defiled mind arises and a wholesome mind does not arise;
it is like a single seed from which two things would have to arise: both a sprout and ash.
If the conditions for a sprout are assembled, then the sprout arises and the ash does not;
if the conditions for ash are assembled, then the ash arises and the sprout does not.
This case is also like this.
By this means, there is also the sense of subduing the afflictions and giving rise to their antidotes;
through this gradual process, one then realizes ultimate liberation.
One might ask: how, then, is the teaching in the *Dṛṣṭiparyāya-skandha* to be reconciled?
As it is said:
"If a phenomenon acts as the equal-and-immediate condition for another phenomenon,
is there ever a time when it does not act as such a condition for that phenomenon?"
Answer: When this dharma has not yet reached the state of having already arisen, the answer is that it is explained based on the fixed sequence of preceding and succeeding moments;
it is not explained based on its being fixed as a causal condition (*pratyaya*) by way of its essential nature (*lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
The critique says:
one should state it in this way.
In the future, there is no equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). Why is this?
Because the equal-and-immediate condition does not abide in a state of confusion.
Because the dharmas of the future exist in a state of disorder,
the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) abides in a sequential order; however,
because the dharmas of the future lack such sequence, [the equal-and-immediate condition does not apply to them].
The equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) is established based on the sense of "making way" (avakāśa);
because dharmas of the future lack this sense of making way, it is not established for them.
Furthermore, if future dharmas possess the condition of immediate antecedence (samanantarapratyaya),
then one who wishes to cultivate what is wholesome should always perform what is wholesome,
and one who wishes to commit what is unwholesome should always commit what is unwholesome.
However, we currently observe that those who intend to cultivate virtue subsequently commit evil deeds,
such as Devadatta and others.
One who intends to commit evil may subsequently perform good deeds,
as in the case of Aṅgulimāla and others;
therefore, in the future, there will certainly be no such thing as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Question: For what reason are material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) not equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
Answer: Because those phenomena that are associated (*samprayukta*) possess a basis (*āśraya*) and possess mental aspects (*ākāra*).
There are states that possess alertness and have an object;
those dharmas can be established as having the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Material dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*) are not like this.
It is not an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Some say that the equal-and-immediate condition is present without confusion.
Because material phenomena (rūpadharma) are subject to disorder,
they do not constitute an equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya);
that is to say, [this applies] to a single moment.
One gives rise to matter of the desire realm and matter of the form realm;
or, for a single moment,
one gives rise to matter of the desire realm and matter that is unconditioned (unbound).
Or, in a single moment,
one may give rise to both matter belonging to the form realm and matter that is unconditioned (unbound).
The Venerable Vasumitra says:
While the continuity of one type of maturation-form has not yet ceased,
there arise further continuities of nurtured-form and outflowing-form,
which are produced in many varieties simultaneously.
Therefore, it is not an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
The Venerable One says:
"Because few material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) arise immediately after many."
Because many arise immediately after few,
they are not equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*).
[However,] when few arise immediately after many, [they are].
It is like the time of summer rains,
when from a few clouds there arise, without interval,
immeasurable clouds that completely cover the sky.
From a small seedling grows the extremely tall and great *nyagrodha* tree;
from a tiny *kalala* is produced a vast body and form.
It is common for the few to arise from the many.
It is like a great heap of grass that, when burned, becomes but a small amount of ash.
Question: If that is so, do mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) also arise from many immediately preceding moments as few, or from few as many?
One should not establish the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for cases where many [mental states] arise in immediate succession from few,
such as when proceeding from a stage characterized by both vitarka and vicāra.
Entering the stage of being without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicārā bhūmiḥ*).
Regarding "a small [number] arising uninterruptedly as many":
this is like entering the stage with applied and sustained thought (*savitarkasavicārā bhūmiḥ*) from the stage without applied and sustained thought.

Answer: This is stated based on the equality of number between preceding and succeeding moments within the same stage (*bhūmi*), and not based on different stages; therefore, there is no fault. Some say:
This is stated in reference to the equality of number among similar types occurring in succession;
since it does not refer to dissimilar types, there is no error.
That is to say, within a single moment of mind:
If two [moments of] feeling or the like were to arise immediately after one [moment of] feeling or the like,
or if one [moment of] feeling or the like were to arise immediately after two [moments of] feeling or the like,
such a fault would ensue.
However, because such a thing does not exist, it is distinct from matter (*rūpa*).
This is because the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of various material phenomena,
being of the same class, arise together in great numbers within a single aggregate.
Therefore, it is not possible to establish [the existence of] an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Such a thing does not exist for mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
Question: Why is this not the case for the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*)?
It is not an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Answer: If a phenomenon is associated (*samprayukta*), it possesses a support (*āśraya*) and possesses an aspect (*ākāra*).
That which possesses alertness and has an object can be established as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*);
the dissociated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) are not so.
Therefore, it is not an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Some say that the equal-and-immediate condition is present without confusion.
Because non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra) manifest with confusion,
they are not equal-and-immediate conditions (samanantara-pratyaya);
that is to say, within a single moment.
There are those that arise pertaining to the three realms as well as those that are unconditioned (unbound),
because they are dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The remainder follow as appropriate.
As explained extensively above,
the Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra contains the following statement:
What are the dharmas that are the equal-and-immediate [condition] of mind?
Answer: Those other minds and mental factors that arise immediately after a mind.
The already arisen and presently arising [states],
as well as the already arisen and presently arising [states] of the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation.
This is called the "mental state that is immediately contiguous" (*cittānantara-dharma*).
Question: Why is the maturation of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya-vipāka*) not mentioned here? Some say:
Regarding that which should have been stated but was not:
one should know that this meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*). Some say:
Regarding the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*):
it is said that they are attained through application (*prayoga*), effortful exertion (*sābhisamskāra*), and diligent labor.
The fruition of non-conception is the opposite of this;
therefore, it is not mentioned there. Some say:
The two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) are mentioned because they are wholesome (*kuśala*);
the fruition of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) is not mentioned because it is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Some say:
If, by the power of the mind, [a phenomenon] is produced immediately thereafter without confusion,
it may be called a mental state that is an equal-and-immediate antecedent (cittasamanantaradharma).
The maturation of non-conception is produced by the power of the ripening cause;
it proceeds spontaneously and is not induced by the force of the mind that enters that state.
Therefore, they are not termed "dharmas that are immediate antecedents of mind.
Question: If that is so, then the resultant minds and mental factors are also produced by the power of their retributive causes.
If it were to proceed spontaneously, it should not be called a "dharma that is the equal-and-immediate antecedent" (samanantarapratyaya) of the mind.
Answer: It possesses a superior power to induce its own kind.
Because they are not different from one another,
and because they all possess association, a support, and so forth,
they are said to be of the same category.
Question: For what reason are the two mindless attainments (asaṃjñi-samāpatti and nirodha-samāpatti) states that are the equal-and-immediate [successors] of mind (citta-samanantara-dharma),
yet not the equal-and-immediate conditions (samanantara-pratyaya) for mind?
Answer: Because they are obtained through the exertion and effort of mental application (*citta-prayoga*),
they are called "mental equal-and-immediate dharmas" (*cittānantara-dharma*).
Because it is contrary to the mind and obstructs the mind,
it is not a mental equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). Some say:
Because they are produced by the power of the mind,
they are called "mental dharmas that arise immediately after" (cittānantara-dharma).
The dissociated (viprayukta) [conditioned factors] have no support.
It lacks the aspect of activity and lacks alertness because it has no object of cognition; therefore,
it is not a mental equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Some say that it increases by the power of the mind,
because it possesses functional activity.
It is called a dharma that is immediately antecedent to the mind because it diminishes the mind,
preventing it from performing its function; therefore,
it is not an immediately antecedent condition for the mind.
Question: Why is it that although the two mindless attainments arise in succession with similar preceding and succeeding states without interruption,
the former is not the equal-and-immediate condition for the latter?
Answer: It is induced by the power of the mind entering meditative absorption, not induced by the power of the preceding thought-moment;
therefore, the former is not the equal-and-immediate condition for the latter.
Question: If that is so, then the resultant (*vipāka*) mind and mental factors are induced by the power of the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) and proceed spontaneously.
Question: Should that which precedes not be the equal-and-immediate condition for that which follows?
Answer: Mental states and mental factors are associated and possess a basis.
Because it possesses an aspect (*ākāra*), possesses alertness (*prabodha*),
and possesses an object (*ālambana*),
the preceding thought has superior power over the subsequent one.
Because they induce and clear the way,
all [conditioned phenomena] are subsequent equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*);
non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), however, are the opposite of this.
This cannot be taken as a general rule.

Question: When entering or emerging from the meditative attainments of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the interval between these states may last for half an eon or even a full eon.
How can it be said that they are "immediately contiguous" (samanantara)?
The answer is: because there is no intervening mind to separate them.
This means that although the moments of entering and exiting [meditative absorption] may be distant from one another, [they are contiguous].
Because no other mental factors intervene between them,
the latter is called "immediately preceding" (samanantara) in relation to the former;
it is like two people traveling together along a long road.
One went in front and the other behind, traveling some distance apart.
Someone asked them,
"Do you have a companion?"
He replied, "There are.
Subsequently, they arrived;
although there were birds and beasts between the two of them, [they did not cause harm].
Because there is no intervening person, it is called "immediately following";
this case is likewise:
because there is no intervening consciousness, it is termed "equal and immediate" (samanantara).
Question: If a dharma is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for mind and so forth, is it also the immediate [condition] for mind?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are dharmas that have mind as their immediate antecedent,
but do not have mind as their immediate [successor];
namely, with the exception of the first moment [of those states] and the two mindless absorptions.
Furthermore, there are the mind and mental factors during states of consciousness,
all other continuities,
the two mindless attainments, and the mind and mental factors upon emerging from those attainments.
There are dharmas that are the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) of mind,
but not the equal-and-immediate antecedent condition of mind.
These are the first moment of the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*).
Furthermore, regarding the states of mind and the mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) that possess mind,
there are the phenomena of birth, aging, duration, and impermanence;
these are dharmas that are both the equal-immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya) of the mind and the immediate antecedent of the mind itself.
This refers to the first moment of the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*),
as well as the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) during states with mind;
there are dharmas that are neither immediately preceded by mind nor immediately followed by mind.

This refers to the characteristics of birth, aging, duration, and impermanence, excluding those of the first moment [of arising], the two mindless attainments, and the mind and mental factors during states of consciousness.

In all other continuities, there are the two mindless attainments (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti* and *nirodha-samāpatti*), as well as the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of the mind and mental factors upon emerging from those attainments.
Question: If a dharma is the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the mind and so forth...
Is it also immediately followed by the mindless meditative attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*)?
One should respond that there are four possible cases (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are phenomena that are the equal-and-immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) of the mind.
It is not immediately following the two mindless attainments;
that is to say, it refers to the first moment of the two mindless attainments,
as well as the mind and mental factors during states possessing mind.
There are dharmas that are immediately preceded by the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*),
but are not the equal-and-immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the mind;
these are, namely, all [moments] except for the first moment.
The two mindless attainments,
as well as the mental states and mental factors during states with mind,
and all other successions characterized by birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
The two mindless attainments,
as well as the mental states and mental factors at the moment of emerging from those attainments,
along with their birth, aging, subsistence, and impermanence.
There are dharmas that are both the equal-and-immediate antecedent of mind and the equal-and-immediate antecedent of the mindless attainments;
namely, with the exception of the first moment of the two mindless attainments.
Furthermore, there are the mind and mental factors during states where the mind is present;
all other successions [of moments]; the two mindless attainments;
and the mind and mental factors upon emerging from those attainments.
There are dharmas that are neither immediately preceded by mind and mental factors,
nor immediately preceded by the mindless attainments;
namely, the first moment of the two mindless attainments.
Furthermore, regarding the states of mind accompanied by mental factors,
there are three kinds of attention associated with their arising, aging, duration, and impermanence.
That is to say: attention to specific characteristics,
attention to common characteristics,
and attention through resolute conviction.
Regarding attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*):
one contemplates that form has the characteristic of being subject to transformation and resistance,
and sensation has the characteristic of experiencing.
Perception has the characteristic of grasping images;
volitional formations have the characteristic of conditioning;
consciousness has the characteristic of discerning.
Earth has the characteristic of solidity;
water has the characteristic of moisture;
fire has the characteristic of warmth.
Wind is characterized by motion;
such are the examples.
Regarding "attention to common characteristics":
Regarding the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika-manasikāra*),
it is like the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) or the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), such as the sixteen aspects of the [four] noble truths.
Regarding the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*):
among these three types of mental attention (*manaskāra*),
how many are immediate?
When the noble path manifests,
immediately following the noble path,
how many kinds manifest?
Some say that there are three kinds of immediate succession when the Noble Path manifests before one.
Immediately following the Noble Path,
three types [of consciousness] manifest;
thus, this is correctly understood as being in accord with what is taught in the Sūtras.
Accompanied by the contemplation of impurity,
one cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness,
relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation.
It is dedicated toward relinquishment.
In this context, the word "both" (ubhaya) signifies the sense of "immediate succession."
Some say that there are two kinds of immediate succession when the noble path manifests before one.
Immediately following the attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) and the noble path (*āryamārga*),
three [types of attention] manifest. Some say:

Only immediately after the attention directed toward general characteristics does the Noble Path manifest; and immediately after the Noble Path [does the attention directed toward specific characteristics manifest].
Regarding the three types [of faculties] that manifest before one:
how should the statements in the sūtras be reconciled?
As it is said:
"One cultivates the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness accompanied by the contemplation of impurity.
The answer is: this statement is made because they function as successive causes for one another.
Because they arise in succession like the lineage of father and son;
that is to say, attention consisting of resolute belief (adhimokṣa-manasikāra) gives rise to attention consisting of common characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-manasikāra).
Some say that the attention to common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra) gives rise to the Noble Path.
Immediately after the mental attention to common characteristics,
the Noble Path manifests; immediately after the Noble Path, [the mental attention to specific characteristics manifests].
The mental attention to common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra) manifests before him.
Question: If that is so, for one who enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna), [how does this occur]?
When emerging from the noble path,
one may give rise to the attention to common characteristics pertaining to the desire realm;
this applies if one relies on a higher stage.
When one enters the state of right determination and departure from birth,
at the moment of emerging from the noble path,
that mind of the desire realm cannot arise.
Because it is extremely distant,
