and furthermore, because they have not yet attained the attention to the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they,
although having already attained the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), [do not attain the higher stages].
Yet, after the noble path has arisen, it does not manifest again.
By means of what kind of attention to common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra) does one emerge from the noble path?
The answer is: In the intermediate stage of the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
one has already cultivated and attained such a mode of activity (*ākāra*),
namely, that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent.
"All phenomena are non-self;
nirvana is tranquility," and so forth—
now, having emerged from the noble path, one gives rise to that mental attention.
The critique says:
He should not make such a statement;
it is better as previously stated.
That is to say, when the noble path manifests, three types [of states] manifest immediately following it;
and when the noble path is present, three types [of states] manifest immediately following it.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of attention (*manasikāra*) in the desire realm:
namely, attention consisting of what is heard (*śrutamaya*),
and attention consisting of what is reflected upon (*cintāmaya*).
There is the attention acquired at birth.
Within the form realm, there are three types of attention, namely:
the attention consisting of what is heard.
There are two types of attention in the formless realm: that produced through cultivation and that acquired at birth.
That is to say: the attention consisting of cultivation,
the attention acquired at birth,
and one type of untainted attention.
This refers to the attention consisting of cultivation.
Herein, in the desire realm,
there is only that which consists of reflection immediately following.
When the Noble Path is present before one,
immediately following the Noble Path,
three types [of minds] are present before one.
In the form realm, the noble path manifests immediately after that which is produced solely through cultivation;
and immediately after the noble path, [that which is produced solely through cultivation manifests].
When two types [of paths] manifest, excluding those acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*),
in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), only the path consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*) immediately precedes the manifestation of the noble path (*āryamārga*).
Immediately following the Noble Path, there likewise arises only that which is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*) as it manifests before one.
Question: Why is this so immediately following the Noble Path?
Is it that the innate [attainment] of the desire realm manifests, but not the innate attainments of the form or formless realms?
Answer: The innate attainment of the desire realm is sharp and intense.
In the form and formless realms,
[the faculties] are not acquired through birth with such intensity; therefore,
if one relies on the *anāgamya* concentration...
They attain the fruit of arhatship.
They may emerge from the noble path with a mind of the desire realm,
or they may emerge from the noble path with a mind of the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
If one attains the fruit of arhatship based on the sphere of nothingness,
one may emerge from the noble path with a mind belonging to the sphere of nothingness.
Alternatively, one may emerge from the noble path with a mind belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
or, if relying on another stage,
one attains the fruit of arhatship.
He emerges from the noble path solely by means of a mind belonging to his own level.
Furthermore, the first dhyāna is of three kinds:
namely, that associated with relish (*āsvādana-samprayukta*), the pure (*śuddha*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
In this manner, up to the sphere of nothingness,
there are likewise three types;
as for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is the same.
There are only two kinds;
that is, excluding the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Among these, immediately following that which is associated with relish (*āsvādana-samprayukta*), there is—
When two types [of minds] manifest, excluding the untainted (*anāsrava*),
three types manifest immediately after the pure (*śuddha*).
Immediately after the untainted, two types manifest.
Excluding those associated with flavoring,
the pure first dhyāna further has four types,
namely: the portion conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*).
The stage conducive to abiding,
the stage conducive to progress,
and the stage conducive to penetration.
In this manner, up to the sphere of nothingness,
there are likewise four types in each case.
In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
there are only three types,
excluding the stage conducive to superior progress.
In this context, immediately following the stage conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*),
two types manifest: namely, that which is conducive to decline and [that which is conducive to stability].
And the stage conducive to abiding.
Immediately following the stage conducive to abiding,
three types manifest in the present.
That is to say, excluding the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
three types [of moments] manifest immediately following the aids to advancement (*viśeṣabhāgīya*).
That is to say, with the exception of the stage conducive to decline,
two types [of factors] manifest immediately following the stage conducive to penetration.
That is to say, the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and the aids to advancement (*viśeṣabhāgīya*).
Question: What if one is born into the second, third, or fourth dhyāna?
When first entering the various groups of consciousness of the dhyānas, how many minds enter immediately after which minds, and from how many minds do they emerge?
Answer: It depends on the place of birth.
If one has not yet abandoned the defilements,
those various groups of consciousness manifest immediately following three kinds of mind.
Immediately following those various groups of consciousness,
three kinds of minds manifest:
namely, the wholesome, the defiled, and the neutral.
It is unobscured-neutral.
For one who has already become free from passion,
it arises immediately after two kinds of minds.
When those various groups of consciousness manifest,
immediately following those groups of consciousness,
two kinds of mind manifest.
That is to say, excluding the defiled,
there are twelve minds in the desire realm: four are wholesome and four are unwholesome.
There are three types each for the form and formless realms: obscured-neutral, unobscured-neutral, and [the other two].
This means that among the aforementioned four, unwholesome [factors] are excluded.
There are two types of untainted [factors]:
namely, those of the learner (śaikṣa) and those of the non-learner (aśaikṣa).
Question: Regarding these twelve types of consciousness,
how many consciousnesses arise immediately after each one,
and from how many consciousnesses does each one arise immediately?
Answer: A wholesome mind of the desire realm arises immediately after nine minds:
namely, four of the desire realm and two of the form realm.
The wholesome and the obscured-unspecified [factors] each have one [type] in the formless realm:
the obscured-unspecified.
As well as the minds of those in training and those beyond training.
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after eight minds;
namely, the four of the desire realm.
From the two wholesome minds of the form realm, the obscured-unspecified mind,
and the minds of those in training and beyond training,
four minds arise immediately after an unwholesome mind.
This refers to the four minds of the desire realm.
These minds, in turn, arise immediately after ten minds,
namely the four of the desire realm.
The three minds of each of the form and formless realms are like the unwholesome mind;
the obscured-neutral mind of the desire realm is also like this.
Immediately following an unobscured-neutral mind of the desire realm, seven minds arise:
namely, four of the desire realm,
two of the form realm (the wholesome and the obscured-neutral), and one of the formless realm.
The obscured-unspecified mind. This mind,
in turn, arises immediately after five minds,
namely the four [minds] of the desire realm.
And one wholesome mind of the form realm.
Immediately following a wholesome mind of the form realm,
eleven minds arise.
That is to say, among the twelve types of mind,
excluding the unobscured-neutral mind of the formless realm,
this mind arises immediately after nine minds.
That is to say: three in the form realm;
two in the desire realm—the wholesome and the non-obscured neutral;
and two in the formless realm.
The wholesome, the obscured-unspecified,
as well as the minds of those in training and those beyond training,
and the obscured-unspecified mind of the form realm— immediately following these, six minds arise.
This refers to the three [minds] of the form realm and the three [minds] of the desire realm— excluding the unobscured-neutral mind.
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after eight minds.
That is to say, there are three each in the form and formless realms, and two in the desire realm: the wholesome mind and the unobscured-neutral mind.
Immediately following an unobscured-neutral mind of the form realm, six minds arise.
That is to say: three minds of the form realm;
two minds of the desire realm—the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified;
and one mind of the formless realm—the obscured-unspecified mind.
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after three minds—
namely, the three minds of the form realm.
A wholesome mind of the formless realm arises immediately after nine minds.
That is to say: three in the formless realm;
two in the desire realm—the unwholesome and the obscured-unneutral;
and two in the form realm—the wholesome and the obscured-unneutral.
And the minds of those in training and those beyond training—
these minds, in turn, arise immediately after six minds,
namely the three of the formless realm.
From the single wholesome mind of the form realm,
as well as from the minds of those in training and those beyond training,
seven minds arise immediately after the obscured-unspecified mind of the formless realm.
That is to say: three in the formless realm,
and two in the desire realm—
the unwholesome and the obscured-unneutral.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are two types of mind: the wholesome and the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after seven minds.
That is to say: three in the formless realm,
and two each in the desire and form realms—
namely, wholesome and non-obscured neutral minds.
Immediately following an unobscured-neutral mind of the formless realm, six minds arise:
namely, three of the formless realm and two of the desire realm.
The unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified [minds] of the form realm: one,
the obscured-unspecified mind.
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after three minds—
namely, the three minds of the formless realm.
A mind of one in training (śaikṣa) arises immediately after five minds.
That is to say, the wholesome minds of the three realms,
as well as the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
These minds, in turn, arise immediately after four types of minds.
That is to say, the wholesome minds of the three realms and the mind of one in training (śaikṣa).
Immediately following the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), four minds arise:
namely, the wholesome minds of the three realms and the mind of one beyond training.
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after five minds— namely,
the wholesome minds of the three realms, as well as the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa)— making twenty minds in total.
Within the desire realm, there are eight.
That is to say: acquired through application (prāyogika-kuśala),
acquired at birth (upapatti-lābhika-kuśala),
unwholesome (akuśala), and obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
The [minds] arising from deportment (*airyāpathika*), those of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), and those of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*)—
these six [types of mind] belong to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
That is to say, among the aforementioned eight types of mind, [these six are included].
Excluding the unwholesome and the arts and crafts,
there are four [types] in the formless realm,
namely, the preparatory wholesome.
Wholesome states acquired at birth,
obscured-unspecified states,
and states born of maturation.
The untainted [minds] are two, namely, the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Question: Regarding these twenty minds...
How many minds arise immediately after each [type of mind], and from how many minds do they arise immediately?
Answer: Immediately after a wholesome mind of application (*prayoga-kuśala*) in the desire realm, ten minds arise.
That is to say: the seven [minds] of the desire realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition;
one preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm;
and the minds of those in training and those beyond training.
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after eight minds;
namely, the four of the desire realm,
excluding the four neutral-unobscured (anivṛtāvyākṛta) states.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are two:
the wholesome mind of application (prayoga-kuśala), the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) mind, and the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Other masters say: [there are three].
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after eleven minds:
namely, the aforementioned eight, as well as the minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*),
craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and maturation (*vipākaja*) belonging to the desire realm.
Why is this? Because for one who has thoroughly cultivated the virtuous mind of preparatory application (*prayoga*), [it arises] from its own realm (*svadhātu*)— namely,
from the paths of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).
Immediately following a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
it also manifests.
Immediately following a wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*) in the desire realm, nine minds arise.
That is to say: seven [minds] of the desire realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition;
one each from the form and formless realms;
and the obscured-unspecified mind.
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after eleven minds;
namely, the seven minds of the desire realm,
excluding the mind of supernormal fruition.
In the form realm, there are two:
the wholesome produced by application, the obscured-unspecified,
and the minds of those in training and those beyond training.
The unwholesome mind arises immediately after seven minds—
namely, the seven minds of the desire realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition.
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after fourteen minds.
In the desire realm, there are seven [minds],
excluding the mind of supernormal fruition.
In the form realm, there are four.
Excluding the preparatory wholesome mind and the mind resulting from supernormal powers,
there are three [minds] in the formless realm;
excluding the preparatory wholesome mind.
As with the unwholesome mind,
so it is with the obscured-unspecified mind of the desire realm.
Immediately after a mind of deportment in the desire realm, eight minds arise.
This refers to six [minds] of the desire realm—
excluding the preparatory wholesome mind and the mind resulting from supernormal powers—
and one each from the form and formless realms.
Regarding the obscured-neutral mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*),
other masters state that nine minds arise immediately after it.
This refers to the aforementioned eight [minds] and the preparatory wholesome mind of the desire realm,
because one who has practiced them extensively is able to bring them into manifestation.
Furthermore, this mind arises immediately after seven minds.
This refers to the seven [minds] of the desire realm,
excluding the mind of supernormal fruition;
it is like the mind of deportment in the desire realm.
The same applies to the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) in the desire realm.
A mind of the artisan stage (*śailpasthānika*) gives rise to six minds immediately thereafter;
namely, the six minds of the desire realm, excluding the mind of applied virtue (*prāyogika-kuśala*) and the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala*).
Other masters say that seven minds arise immediately after this mind:
namely, the aforementioned six, plus the preparatory wholesome mind of the desire realm.
Because that which has been thoroughly cultivated can manifest before one,
this mind in turn arises immediately after seven minds;
namely, the seven [minds] of the desire realm.
Excluding the mind of supernormal fruition,
the mind of supernormal fruition in the desire realm gives rise immediately to two types of minds:
namely, the mind of supernormal fruition in the desire realm and [the mind of supernormal fruition in the form realm].
And the preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm;
this mind, in turn, arises immediately after two minds,
namely, the supernormal fruit mind of the desire realm.
And the preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm.
Immediately following the preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm, twelve minds arise;
that is to say, the six [minds] of the form realm.
In the desire realm, there are three:
the wholesome produced through application, the wholesome acquired at birth, and the resultant of supernormal powers.
In the formless realm, there is one.
The preparatory wholesome mind, as well as the minds of those in training and those beyond training—
this mind, in turn, arises immediately after ten minds;
namely, the four [minds] of the form realm.
Excluding the minds of deportment and those born of maturation,
there are two [types] in the desire realm:
the wholesome mind of application and the mind of fruition.
In the formless realm, there are two types:
the wholesome resulting from application and the obscured-unspecified,
as well as the minds of those in training and those beyond training.
From the wholesome mind acquired at birth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
eight minds arise immediately thereafter; that is, the five [minds] of the form realm,
excluding the fruition-of-superknowledge mind (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).
In the desire realm, there are two:
the unwholesome and the obscured-unneutral.
In the formless realm, there is one.
The obscured-unspecified mind.
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after five minds;
namely, the five [minds] of the form realm.
Excluding the mind that is the fruition of supernormal powers and the obscured-unspecified minds of the form realm,
nine minds arise immediately thereafter, namely the five minds of the form realm.
Excluding those resulting from supernormal powers,
there are four types of wholesome states in the desire realm: those acquired through application and those that are naturally wholesome.
The innate wholesome mind,
the unwholesome mind, and the obscured-unspecified mind—
these minds, in turn, arise immediately after eleven minds.
This refers to the five [minds] of the form realm,
excluding the mind of fruition from supernormal powers,
and the three [minds] of the desire realm.
The wholesome states acquired at birth, those of the modes of deportment, and those born of maturation—
these three exist in the formless realm,
excluding the wholesome mind of application.
Immediately after a mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) in the realm of form, seven minds arise:
namely, the four minds of the realm of form,
excluding the wholesome mind of application (*prayoga-kuśala*) and the mind of fruition (*vipākaja*).
In the desire realm, there are two:
the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified;
in the formless realm, there is one.
The obscured-unspecified mind arises immediately after five minds;
namely, the five minds of the form realm.
Excluding the mind of fruition resulting from supernormal powers,
the mind of deportment in the form realm is the same as the mind born of maturation in the form realm.
Immediately after a mind of supernormal power (abhijñā-phala-citta) in the realm of form, two minds arise:
namely, a wholesome mind of preparatory application (prayoga-kuśala) in the realm of form,
and a mind of supernormal power.
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after two types of minds:
namely, the preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm and the mind of supernormal power.
The preparatory wholesome mind of the formless realm gives rise to seven minds in immediate succession:
namely, four of the formless realm and one of the form realm.
The preparatory wholesome mind, as well as the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), arise immediately after six minds;
namely, the three [minds] of the formless realm.
Excluding one [type of mind] born of maturation in the form realm—
namely, the preparatory wholesome mind— and the minds of those in training and those beyond training,
the wholesome mind acquired at birth in the formless realm gives rise immediately after it to seven types of mind.
That is to say: the four [mental factors] of the formless realm,
and the two— unwholesome and obscured-unspecified— of the desire realm.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there is one [type of mind]:
the obscured-unspecified mind (nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta). This mind, in turn, arises immediately after four minds.
This refers to the four minds of the formless realm.
Immediately following a mind that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) in the formless realm, eight minds arise;
namely, the four [minds] of the formless realm.
In the desire realm, there are two:
the unwholesome and the obscured-unneutral.
In the form realm, there are two.
The preparatory wholesome mind and the obscured-unspecified mind—
these two minds, in turn, arise immediately after ten minds;
namely, the four [minds] of the formless realm.
In the desire and form realms, there are three types each:
the innate wholesome, the deportment, and the resultant mind.
In the formless realm, the resultant mind gives rise immediately to six minds.
This refers to the three [minds] of the formless realm—
excluding the preparatory wholesome mind—
and the two [minds] of the desire realm: the unwholesome and the obscured-neutral.
In the form realm, there is one [type of mind]: the obscured-unspecified mind.
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after four minds.
That is to say, from the four minds of the formless realm,
six minds arise immediately after a mind of one in training (śaikṣa):
namely, two from the desire realm.
The wholesome states of application (prayoga-kuśala) and those acquired by birth (upapatti-lābhika-kuśala) each exist once in the form and formless realms; these,
along with the minds of application and those of the learner (śaikṣa) and the non-learner (aśaikṣa).
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after four minds:
namely, one from each of the three realms,
as well as the wholesome mind of application and the mind of one in training (śaikṣa).
Immediately after the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-citta), five minds arise:
namely, two from the desire realm—
the wholesome acquired through application (prāyogika-kuśala) and the wholesome acquired by birth (upapatti-labdha-kuśala).
There is one each in the form and formless realms:
the wholesome mind of application and the mind of no-more-learning.
This mind, in turn, arises immediately after five minds.
That is to say, there is one each for the three realms,
plus the wholesome minds of application, as well as the minds of those in training and those beyond training.
Since a *pudgala* (person) cannot be apprehended, [it does not exist].
Furthermore, since there is no preceding mind that transfers to a succeeding mind,
by what principle could one remember what was originally done?
This is explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To refute the tenets of other schools and to clarify one's own position.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that the *pudgala* (person) exists.
The self-essence exists substantially,
as the Vātsīputrīyas maintain;
they speak as follows.
I allow that there is a self,
because one is able to recollect past deeds;
for what was previously experienced by oneself is now recollected by oneself.
If there were no self,
by what cause could one remember past deeds? Or,
there may be those who hold such a view.
The intrinsic natures of things conceal one another;
as it is said:
"The characteristics of all phenomena conceal one another."
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) assert this:
all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) possess divisions of day and night;
they conceal one another, such that at night the day enters [into it].
The nature of day exists during the night,
yet it is present without manifesting;
at the time of day, the night enters [into it].
The nature of night exists during the day,
yet it remains unmanifest;
in this way, one may still remember what was done previously.
Within the divisions of day and night,
because there are nights and days,
[one performs] what is to be done during the times of night and day.
If one is able to remember throughout the day and night, yet were it not so,
for what reason could one remember things done in the past?
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that the characteristics of the nature of things undergo transformation,
as it is said:
"The characteristics of all phenomena undergo transformation."
The non-Buddhists (tīrthika) maintain this view:
that at the stage of the kalala,
it transforms into the stage of the arbuda.
Even so, the stage of firmness transforms into the stage of senescence,
just as a green leaf transforms into a yellow leaf.
In this way, it is possible to recollect what was previously done,
because there is no difference in the essential nature of the preceding and succeeding states; thus,
what was performed in the preceding state can be recollected in the succeeding state.
If it were not so, by what cause could one remember things previously done?
Or again, there are those who hold [the following view]:
The natures and characteristics of things interact with one another,
as it is said:
"All dharmas interact with one another."
The non-Buddhists (tīrthika) maintain this view:
that the kalala proceeds and enters into the state of the arbuda.
Even when one has reached a firm state and entered the stage of old age and decay,
it is still possible to remember what was done in the past.
Because the preceding state exists within the subsequent state,
what was performed in the preceding state can be remembered in the subsequent state;
otherwise, this would not be possible.
For what reason is it able to recollect past deeds?
Question: Regarding the transformation of the characteristics of the nature of things and their movement, how do the two types of attachments held by the non-Buddhists differ?
Answer: This is the position held by the Transformationists (Vaiśeṣika),
who maintain that a preceding state transforms into a succeeding state,
such that the preceding state no longer exists within the succeeding state.
The characteristic moves toward the externalist position.
Since the characteristic from the preceding stage moves to the succeeding stage, once it has reached that succeeding stage, its characteristic is not destroyed;
rather, it increases simultaneously with the succeeding stage.
Some say that the former [position] is the attachment of the Tīrthikas who maintain the transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*),

while the latter is the attachment of the Tīrthikas who maintain that characteristics go forth [from the substance], asserting that the subsequent is neither identical to nor different from the preceding.
The subsequent [moment] and the preceding one are both identical and different.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that the nature of cognition is a single unity.
As it was said regarding the preceding and the succeeding:
the proponents of a single awakening (ekabuddhavādin) speak as follows.
The former is the awareness of having performed an action,
and the latter is the awareness of recollection;
although their characteristics and functions differ, their nature is one and the same.
In this way, it is possible to recollect what was previously done,
because the essence of consciousness remains one throughout its prior and subsequent stages; thus,
what was performed in a prior stage can be recollected in a subsequent stage.
If it were not so, by what cause could one remember things previously done? Or,
there are those who hold this view:
The mind-element is eternal.
Just as those who maintain the doctrine that the mind-element is eternal speak thus:
Although the six consciousnesses arise and perish, the mind-element (manodhātu) is permanent;
thus, it is possible to remember what was done previously by the six consciousnesses.
Because the mind-element (manodhātu) is capable of recollecting; if it were not so,
for what reason would one be able to recollect things previously done?
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that the aggregates are of two kinds:
first, the fundamental aggregates; [and second, the derivative aggregates].
Regarding the two aggregates of activity:
the former aggregate is permanent,
while the latter aggregate is impermanent.
He asserts this:
although the two aggregates of fundamental activity are distinct,
they combine together to constitute a single sentient being.
In this way, it is possible to recollect what was previously done,
because the fundamental aggregates (*mūla-skandha*) are able to recollect the work performed by the active aggregates (*kāritra-skandha*).
If it were not so, by what cause could one remember things previously done? Or,
there are those who maintain [the following]:
The preceding thought informs the subsequent thought, saying:
"I have performed this deed; you should remember it.
The latter then says: [I remember].
The mind is subtle and attuned to the profound;
whatever was done previously is necessarily known by what follows,
such that one can thus remember what was originally done.
If it were not so, by what means could one remember past actions?
Yet, although Buddhas and their disciples, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, have not taught that a *pudgala* exists, [the memory of past deeds would otherwise be impossible].
Nor does it say that there is a substance with characteristics of concealment or transformation that migrates.
The nature of a single awakening is the mental realm (manodhātu), which is eternal;
the fundamental aggregates (mūla-skandha) are distinct from the functional aggregates (kāritra-skandha).
The preceding mind informs the subsequent mind,
such that there is the capacity to recollect what was previously done;
this principle is certain.
It is subtle, profound, and difficult to realize;
it is for the purpose of demonstrating such certainty,
subtlety, and profundity.
It is difficult to realize the nature and characteristics of all phenomena,
as well as to refute the irrational assertions of other schools.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.

Question: In this context, it should be fully explained that since a *pudgala* cannot be found, there is likewise no substance, no characteristic of concealment, no characteristic of transformation, and no going.
The single awakened nature of the mental faculty (manas) is eternal;
the fundamental aggregates differ from the functional aggregates.
The preceding mind informs the subsequent mind.
For what reason is it possible to remember past actions?
Why is it said that since a *pudgala* cannot be found,
and furthermore, there is no principle by which a preceding mind travels to a subsequent mind?
The answer is: that which is stated here regarding the non-apprehension of a *pudgala* specifically refutes the first type of *pudgala* theory;
furthermore, there is no entity of a preceding mind that migrates to a subsequent state of mind.
This collectively refutes the latter seven treatises.
Some say: "Since it is stated here that a *pudgala* cannot be found," [it follows that...]
This refutes the theory of the first *pudgala*.
Furthermore, since there is no entity of a preceding mind that travels to a subsequent mind,
it also refutes the eighth theory concerning a preceding mind going to inform a subsequent mind.
Since the first and the last have already been refuted,
it should be understood that the six intermediate theories have likewise been refuted.
This means that the Master of the Treatise briefly cites the beginning and the end so that his disciples may easily receive and uphold [the teaching].
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Volume Eleven.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Twelve.
Composed by five hundred Great Arhats and others.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
4. In the second part of the first section on Knowledge within the Miscellaneous Aggregates, Part Four:
Since a person (pudgala) cannot be apprehended, and furthermore, there is no principle by which a preceding mind travels to a subsequent mind.
For what reason is one able to recollect past actions?
Answer: Sentient beings, through the power of habitual practice regarding phenomena, attain such a cognition of commonality (*sabhāgatā*).
One can know things in this way according to whatever experiences one encounters.
Question: Previously it was stated that there is no *pudgala*;
why is it now said again that sentient beings [exist] in relation to phenomena?
Answer: Previously, it was manifested based on the designation of "noble" (ārya);
now, it is manifested based on the designation of "worldly" (laukika). Previously, it was manifested through speech based on the noble; [now, it is manifested through speech based on the worldly].
Now, this is presented by relying on worldly discourse;
previously it relied on the ultimate truth,
whereas now it relies on the conventional.
Some say: for the sake of conforming to the text;
even if the teaching conforms to the dharma and the meaning, [it may still not conform to the phrasing].
It is not consistent with the phrasing.
If one speaks of sentient beings,
it is consistent with both the phrasing and the meaning of the Dharma.
Because sentient beings exist according to conventional truth,
some say [the Buddha] spoke [of them] for the sake of generating understanding;
if one were to speak of dharmas, the disciples would not comprehend those dharmas.
If one says that a sentient being remembers a phenomenon,
the disciple understands that the sentient being remembers the phenomenon;
this is because the sentient being [remembers] the phenomenon through the power of habitual practice.
One who has attained such knowledge of the homogeneous class (sabhāgatā-jñāna) refers to a sentient being’s cognition that is definitively habituated toward the phenomena to be known.
Because they are similar in their preceding and succeeding states according to one's desires and mastery,
they are called "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
Those who are able to know things in this way according to the objects they encounter [are so named].
That is to say, one is able to recollect in this way according to what was originally seen and according to what was originally experienced. Some say:
This passage should be stated as follows:
"In accordance with whatever phenomenon can be known in this way— that is,
in accordance with its original essential nature."
All marks, all selves,
and all things.
All natures and all parts can be recollected in this way.
Some say that this passage should be stated as follows:
"In accordance with the object upon which one dwells, one is able to know it thus."
That is to say, one is able to recollect the primary colors as they originally appeared,
as well as the shapes and other characteristics as they originally appeared.
In order to make this meaning clear,
an analogy from worldly experience is cited:
it is like two people who have each made a seal.
They are able to discern the seal-syllables created by themselves and others,
even though those two individuals do not go to ask one another,
"How did you create this syllable?"
Nor did they reply to me, "I created these letters in this way";
rather, by the power of habitual practice,
those two persons attained such a shared cognition.
One is able to discern the seal-syllables created by oneself and others;
sentient beings are likewise so,
through the power of habitual practice.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Among these, those who are able to write are all called makers of seals (*mudrā*).
Just as those two people neither question nor answer one another, [so it is here].
Through the power of habitual practice, one attains such a cognition of commonality that one is able to discern the seal-syllables created by oneself and others,
even being able to read and understand letters sent from beyond the seas.
Sentient beings are likewise:
although there is no truly existent *pudgala*,
nor is there a principle by which a preceding mind travels to a subsequent mind.
Furthermore, through the power of habitual practice, one attains such knowledge of commonality (*sabhāgatā-jñāna*),
whereby one is able to know things exactly as they have been experienced;
moreover, this is done so that the meaning may become even more distinct and clear.
He cites the second analogy:
"Furthermore, it is like two knowers of others' minds who mutually know each other's thoughts,
even though those two persons do not go to ask one another."
"How do you know my mind? He did not answer me.
"In this way, I know your mind."
Yet those two individuals, through the power of habitual practice,
attain such a commonality of cognition that they know each other's minds;
sentient beings are likewise.
"By the power of habitual practice," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Regarding this, one who knows the minds of others:
This refers to one who has attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds;
although those two individuals neither question nor answer each other,
it occurs through the power of habitual practice.
Having attained such knowledge of the homogeneous class (sabhāgatā-jñāna), they know one another's minds;
even beyond a hundred yojanas, they likewise know one another's minds.
It is the same for sentient beings as well.
"Although there is no truly existent *pudgala*, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: If it were something other than the mental factors that could remember by means of a different mind, [what would happen]?"
Why is it that Devadatta cannot remember what Yajñadatta has experienced, yet Yajñadatta can remember what Devadatta has experienced?
The answer is: because their mental continuums are distinct.
The preceding mind and the succeeding mind continue in succession without difference;
one should not raise an objection to this. Some say:
Since those minds, when compared to one another, lack the sense of being causes for each other,
it should not be difficult to accept that a preceding mind can serve as the cause for a subsequent mind.
Some say: because those two [bodies] are not mutually connected in body and mind,
whereas the preceding and succeeding bodies and minds are indeed successively connected.
Therefore, what was previously experienced can later be remembered.
Question: If it is the case that memory occurs because the mind is connected [to the object], why is it that upon seeing a different cow one does not remember that previous cow?
Answer: If one perceives now what was previously experienced as being similar [to it], then one is able to remember it;
even if it was previously experienced, [if it is not perceived as similar, one cannot remember].
If one does not perceive a similarity now, one cannot remember;
yet what was experienced during the first part of the day can be remembered during the latter part of the day,
and what was experienced during the latter part of the day can be remembered during the first part of the day.
Because the bodies perceived before and after are similar.
Furthermore, all minds and mental factors are fixedly established upon their respective objects of perception.
This is the ultimate fundamental answer to the question asked.
Why is this so? It is as explained in the *Dṛṣṭiskandha*.
If a phenomenon serves as an object-condition for another phenomenon, is there ever a time when it does not so serve?
Answer: There is no time when it is not an object-condition.
Because the mind and mental factors are fixed upon their objects,
they abide securely on those objects without being able to shift;
therefore, they are able to recollect things previously done.
That is to say, regarding a single object of focus, there are immeasurable clusters of mind and mental factors;
these revolve around this single object of focus according to this principle, this category, and this method.
It acts as the objective referent for the assembly of one mind and its mental factors;
it likewise acts as the objective referent for other immeasurable assemblies of minds and mental factors.
Just as a single mind and its associated mental factors,
by this principle, by this nature, and by this method,
experience this object of perception.
The same applies to the experience of this object by the remaining immeasurable clusters of mind and mental factors;
it is like a single person who has a hundred sons.
Just as this one person performs the duties of a father toward his only son,
so too does he toward his other sons;
and just as that only son performs the duties of a son toward his father, so it is likewise.
The same applies to other sons regarding their father.
In this context, from eye-consciousness and its associated mental factors being fixed upon visible forms as their object,
up to and including mind-consciousness and its associated mental factors.
Regarding the concentration on the objects of all phenomena:
this form serves as the object for the eye-consciousness and its associated mental factors.
There is no time when it is not an object of cognition;
that is to say, until this dharma becomes an object of the mental consciousness and its associated mental factors.
There is no time when [a dharma] is not an object-condition (*ālambana*),
because all minds and mental factors each individually experience their own respective objects.
Consequently, there is no other collection of mind that could experience [an object] and another collection of mind that could subsequently remember it.
Question: What are the mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma)?
Regarding the concentration on the object of focus, does it consist in concentration on the location,
concentration on the blue color and so forth,
or concentration on the moment?
Regarding this, some say that it is restricted only to the sense bases (āyatana). Why is this so?
There are no immeasurable minds or mental factors, because they abide in the state of non-arising.
Question: What is meant by "certainty regarding the bases" (*āyatana-niyama*)?
Answer: Visual consciousness and its associated mental factors are definitively established within the sphere of visible forms;
likewise, up to tactile consciousness and its associated mental factors are definitively established within the sphere of tangibles;
and mental consciousness and its associated mental factors are definitively established within the sphere of mental phenomena.
Just as with a single visual consciousness:
if it encounters the conjunction of blue appearing before it, it arises taking blue as its object;
if it encounters the conjunction of yellow or other colors appearing before it, it arises taking yellow or those others as its object.
In this way, the other consciousnesses are also restricted solely to their respective objects.
They should not make such a statement. Why is that?
If that were so, a single cognition would possess multiple cognizing natures;
it is not logical for a single dharma to have multiple entities.
How, then, is the statement in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* to be reconciled? As it says:
"Past visual consciousness takes only past form as its object."
It is not the case for the future or the present.
Others, wishing to avoid such a fault,
assert that the mind and mental factors are fixed upon their respective objects.
Furthermore, it is not fixed with respect to blue and so forth, nor is it fixed with respect to moments. Why is this?
Lest there be an infinite number of minds and mental factors.
Because one abides within the state of non-arising dharmas.
Question: How can there also be meditative concentration (*samādhi*) upon blue and so forth?
Answer: The mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that take blue and so forth as their objects are each distinct in essence.
If it encounters the conjunction of blue appearing before it, then it arises,
taking as its object the mind and mental factors associated with blue.
If it encounters the conjunction of yellow and so forth appearing before it, then it arises.
They should likewise not say that it takes mental states and mental factors such as yellow as its object.
Why is this? Because blue has many varieties.
That is to say, there are blue roots, blue stems, blue branches, blue leaves, blue flowers, and blue fruits;
the same applies to yellow and the other colors.
Thus, the cognition that takes the root as its object would be the very same cognition that takes the stem and so forth as its object.
If that were so, a single cognition would possess multiple natures of apprehension;
it would be illogical for a single dharma to have multiple entities,
and this would also contradict what is stated in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*, as previously mentioned.
Regarding those who speak thus, they maintain that the mind and mental factors are fixed with respect to three things.
Question: If this were so, then there would have to be immeasurable minds and mental factors abiding in a state of non-arising.
What fault is there in this answer?
Is the future world so vast that it has no room [for them]?
Yet they have always already possessed their own dwelling places.
Therefore, one should not raise such an objection.
It is asked: Are the mind and mental factors as fixed with respect to their objects?
Nor is it fixed with respect to its basis.
If that were so, what fault would there be?
If it were also fixed with respect to its basis, [then...]
Why is it that in this context only concentration with respect to the object (*ālambana*) is mentioned,
and not concentration with respect to the basis (*āśraya*)?
Furthermore, how is the statement in the *Prakaraṇapāda* to be reconciled?
As it is said:
"What are the co-existent dharmas?
Answer: All contaminated (sāsrava) dharmas."
Furthermore, regarding the co-arising of untainted phenomena with tainted phenomena:
if they are not fixed with respect to their basis (*āśraya*),
why would they be fixed with respect to their object (*ālambana*)?
Is it indeterminate with respect to its basis?
Answer: It is also determinate with respect to its basis;
however, as for the mind and mental factors...
In the future, it is distant from its basis;
in the present, they are simultaneous;
and in the past, it is again distant.
Some say that [dharmas] in the future world are distant from their basis,
while those in the present and past are co-existent with their basis.
Some say that all [phenomena] of the three time periods coexist with their bases.
Question: If that is so, then...
Why is this not mentioned here?
The answer is: herein, one merely wishes to speak of recollecting what was previously done;
that which is recollected is as follows.
Because this is an object of cognition (*ālambana*) but not a basis (*āśraya*).
Question: How then should one interpret the statement in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
Answer: That text should have stated it as follows.
What are the co-existent dharmas?
The answer is: all conditioned dharmas.
As for why this is not explicitly stated [in the definition]:
That passage demonstrates that the noble path is functional;
since it does not state that it is non-functional, there is no contradiction.
Some say that the passage demonstrates the noble path.

Because that which arises through the power of others is obtained by depending on the power of others, it is said that [the mind] arises simultaneously with only those dharmas that are tainted (*sāsrava*).
Question: If this refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*),...
Regarding that which is fixed with respect to the object and also fixed with respect to its basis:
at what stage does it apprehend the object—at the time of its arising or at the time of its cessation?
If this were so, what fault would there be?
If it occurs at the time of arising, then the time of arising exists in the future;
how then can a dharma that is in the future perform any action?
If it occurs at the time of ceasing...
At the time of cessation, all phenomena decline and disintegrate.
How, then, can they apprehend an object at this stage?
One should reply: "At the time of cessation."
Question: How can phenomena that are subject to decline and disintegration apprehend an object?
Answer: Because all conditioned phenomena are by nature weak and inferior, and because they do not depend upon themselves.
Because it arises in dependence on others,
because it lacks autonomous activity,
and because it is not self-governing.
In whichever state one may be,
if the conjunction of the basis and the object occurs, it occurs in that very state.
The grasper and the object of cognition are conjoined only at the time of cessation;
some say that the time of arising belongs to the future.
Because future dharmas lack functional activity, they cannot apprehend an object;
at the time of cessation, they belong to the present.
Because present dharmas possess functional activity, they can apprehend an object.
If, at the time of cessation, the mind and mental factors did not grasp their objects, they would ultimately be unable to grasp objects at all;
let there be no such error.
Therefore, at the time of cessation, one is able to apprehend the object;
furthermore, because the power of the cause— the mind associated with feeling—
is strong, mindfulness does not forget.
It should be understood that herein, the preceding collection of mental states is designated by the term "mind" (manas),
while the succeeding collection of mental states is designated by the term "attention" (smṛti).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of mind that experience.
First is the mind that experiences the mode of activity;
second is the mind that experiences the object.
For instance, regarding superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), there are two types of mind.
One experiences its aspect but does not experience its object;

that is, there are two moments of mind associated with the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*).
One experiences its object but does not experience its aspect.

This refers to the three moments of mind associated with the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (*samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*).
They take on those mental aspects (*ākāra*) and also take on those objects (*ālambana*).

That is to say, they are associated with the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*), and the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*).
Other minds do not take those aspects (ākāra),

nor do they take that object (ālambana); that is to say, other minds associated with patience (kṣānti) or knowledge (jñāna) are like [the case of] other minds [at the stage of] supreme patience (adhimātra-kṣānti).
The detailed explanation should be understood accordingly in the same way:
feeling recollects the aspect, the experienced object, and the object of experience;
and feeling recollects the object of experience, the experienced aspect, and the aspect of experience.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of intention:
first, the defiled;
second, the non-defiled.
Each and every experience is of two kinds;
furthermore, there are three types of minds capable of recollecting them, namely:
wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Each and every experience can be recollected in three ways.
Furthermore, there are four types of mental objects:
namely, the wholesome, the unwholesome, the obscured-unspecified, and the unobscured-unspecified.
Each and every experience can be recollected through four modes.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of mental objects (ālambana):
namely, its cause, its immediately preceding condition, its object-condition, and its dominant condition.
Each and every experience can be recollected through four types [of mindfulness].
Furthermore, there are five kinds of mental objects, namely:
those abandoned by seeing suffering, up to those abandoned by cultivation.
Among these, that which has been experienced by what is abandoned through the vision of suffering can be recollected in five ways;
the same applies to that which has been experienced by what is abandoned through the vision of the origin and through cultivation.
That which has been experienced by what is abandoned through the vision of cessation can be recollected in four ways.
Excluding those abandoned by the path of seeing,
the four kinds [of objects] experienced and remembered by what is abandoned by the path of seeing exclude those abandoned by the vision of cessation.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of mental states:
namely, the wholesome, the unwholesome, the obscured-unspecified,
and the unobscured-unspecified induced by correct reasoning.
It is neither-conducive-to-reason nor obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Regarding this, some say that two kinds [of objects] experienced by the wholesome can be recollected.
That is to say, wholesome [states] induced by correct reasoning,
as well as non-obscured neutral states induced by correct reasoning— those which are experienced are likewise [remembered].
Unwholesome states, when experienced, can be remembered in three ways.
That is to say: unwholesome [states], obscured-unspecified states, and non-obscured-unspecified states induced by improper mental application;
likewise, the objects experienced by those non-obscured-unspecified states induced by improper mental application are also thus.
According to this teaching,
each and every experienced object can be recollected in five ways;
furthermore, there are six types of mental objects.
This refers to visual consciousness up to mental consciousness.
What has been experienced by the five consciousnesses can be recollected by the mental consciousness;
what has been experienced by the mental consciousness can be recollected by the six consciousnesses.
Furthermore, there are twelve kinds of mental states.
In the desire realm, there are four:
namely, the wholesome, the unwholesome, the obscured-unspecified, and the unobscured-unspecified.
The realm of form has three [types of feeling],
namely the previous four with the exclusion of the unwholesome.
The same applies to the formless realm.
The untainted [consciousness] is of two kinds:
namely, that of the learner (śaikṣa) and that of the non-learner (aśaikṣa).
The wholesome [consciousness] of the desire realm can recall twelve types of objects.
The same applies to what is experienced by unwholesome [minds] and wholesome [minds] of the form realm.
Regarding what is experienced by obscured-unspecified [minds] of the desire realm, eight types can be recollected;
that is to say, excluding the obscured-unspecified [minds] of the form realm and the three [types] of the formless realm.
The same applies to what is experienced by the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states of the desire realm.
In the form realm, ten types [of consciousness] can recollect what is experienced by the obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) states,
excluding the two neutral types of the desire realm.
The same applies to what is experienced by wholesome states of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Ten types [of objects] can be recollected by unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states of the form realm,
excluding the two neutral states of the formless realm.
The nine types of objects experienced by the obscured-neutral [mind] of the formless realm can be recollected;
this excludes the two types of neutral [objects] of the desire realm and the unobscured-neutral [objects] of the form realm.
The same applies to the objects experienced by the unobscured-neutral [mind] of the formless realm.
The eleven types of experienced objects that can be recollected by those in training (śaikṣa) exclude the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) states of the desire realm.
Regarding those in no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), if they are of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharman), the explanation is the same as for those in training.
If one is of the non-retrogressive type (*aparihāṇadharman*), seven kinds [of minds] can be recollected—
excluding the learner’s mind (*śaikṣa*) and the four defiled minds—
because the power of the causal force of the preceding experienced intention is strong.
Regarding the phrase "producing a subsequent moment of mindfulness toward that object so as not to forget":
this means the mind is neither deranged nor oppressed by suffering.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
One recollects what was previously done due to three causes and conditions.
First, because one has properly grasped the preceding signs.
Second, because the homogeneous continuity proceeds;
third, because mindfulness is not lost.
For these reasons, although there is no *pudgala*, [the continuity of karma and its results is established].
Furthermore, there is no principle by which a preceding mind travels to a subsequent mind to enable the recollection of past actions.
For what reason, then, do sentient beings forget and yet later remember?
Answer: When the continuum of a sentient being's homogeneous class (sattva-sabhāgatā) evolves, one is able to give rise to a cognition and vision that perceives the interconnectedness of phenomena.
In this context, "forgetting" means the loss of mindfulness (smṛti-pramoṣa).
It is not that there is no meaning to "non-recollection. Why is this?
Because there is not even the slightest dharma that can be named "non-recollection."
There are three kinds of homogeneity (sabhāgatā):
namely, homogeneity of application (prayoga-sabhāgatā), homogeneity of object (ālambana-sabhāgatā),
and homogeneity of conformity (anuloma-sabhāgatā).
Regarding those of similar application (*prayoga-sabhāga*):
for example, there is one who previously recited the Sūtra Piṭaka but subsequently forgot it.
Later, through the application of effort as previously described, he regains his memory;
the same applies to his prior recitation of the Vinaya and Abhidharma Piṭakas.
In this way, he first gives rise to the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Having forgotten it in the interim,
one later regains the memory through the same preparatory application (*prayoga*) as before.
The same applies to the preliminary method for initiating mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
It has been heard that there was once the son of a brahmin who had previously mastered the four Vedas,
but later forgot them.
He recited it again and again with all his skill, yet he was unable to master it.
He then went to his teacher and related the circumstances in detail.
The teacher immediately asked him:
"When you previously recited it, what preparatory practice did you employ?
He replied,
"At that time, I recited it orally while holding a string in my hand."
The teacher said,
"You should perform the preparatory practices as you did originally.
He followed the teacher's instructions and remembered them all.
Regarding "having a similar objective referent" (ālambana-sabhāga):
for example, one might previously have seen such things as gardens, groves, springs, ponds, mountain valleys, or walking paths,
but subsequently forget them.
Later, when one sees similar gardens and so forth, one recollects them all.
Regarding those that accord with one's lot (*nikāya-sabhāga*):
it is like obtaining food, drink, clothing, bedding, dwellings, teachers, and so forth that are conducive [to one's needs].
Thus, one is able to recollect events previously experienced.
It is said that there was once a bhikṣu who had previously mastered the four Āgamas.
Having forgotten the middle portion, he recited it again from memory; though he exhausted every means, he could not master it fluently.
He then went to where the Venerable Ānanda was.
When asked about the cause and conditions for this,
the Venerable One replied,
"You should now go and bathe in the warm bathhouse after anointing your body with oil."
When seeking requisites such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, dwellings, and teachers who speak the Dharma,
the bhikṣu follows the instructions and becomes fully proficient in them all.
In this way, when the homogeneous continuity (nikāya-sabhāga) proceeds, it functions in such a manner.
One is able to give rise to the knowledge and vision of mutual connection regarding phenomena.
Question: To what does this connection arise?
Answer: There are three types of distinctions within the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*).
The recitation states that one is able to give rise to continuous wisdom and vision regarding phenomena;
this means giving rise to wisdom and vision that flow and continue for a long duration.
Furthermore, another recension says:
To be able to give rise to sequential knowledge and vision regarding phenomena means to give rise to knowledge and vision of their respective successive arrangements. Furthermore,
there is another recension which says:
To be able to give rise to unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding phenomena means to give rise to knowledge and vision that is unhindered, unattached, and uninterrupted.
Furthermore, there is another recension which says:
Regarding phenomena, one is able to give rise to unobstructed knowledge and vision;
this means giving rise to the knowledge and vision that is free from hindrances and overcomes the powerful enemy of the discordant factors.
Furthermore, because the power of the mental faculty (*manas*) as the cause is strong, mindfulness does not forget.
It should be understood that herein, the preceding collection of mental states is designated by the term "mind" (*manas*),
while the succeeding collection of mental states is designated by the term "attention" (*manasikāra*).
The explanation of the term "mental attention" (*manasikāra*) is as previously interpreted.
Because the causal force of the preceding volition is strong,
it induces the subsequent moment of thought with respect to that same object.
Although one may forget in the interim and later remember again,
the term "not forgetting" is explained as before.
For what reason do sentient beings remember and yet subsequently forget?
Answer: When the continuity of a sentient being’s distinct states evolves, one does not give rise to a cognition or vision of connection regarding those phenomena;
this is what is meant here by "forgetting."
This is the meaning of "loss of mindfulness.
A detailed explanation is as given previously.
There are three types of "distinctive factors" (*vibhāga*).
That is to say: difference in application,
difference in object,
and difference in conformity.
Regarding the differentiation of preparatory application:
for example, one who has previously recited the Sūtra Piṭaka may forget it in the interim.
Having set it aside, he then recited the Vinaya or the Abhidharma-piṭaka,
but later he could remember none of it.
The same applies to first reciting the Vinaya and Abhidharma Piṭakas.
Likewise, one may first give rise to the contemplation of impurity and then forget it midway.
Having relinquished it, one again gives rise to mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
Alternatively, after the application of the elements (*dhātuprayoga*), one does not recollect anything at all.
It is the same when one first gives rise to mindfulness of breathing and the application of the elements.
Regarding the diversity of objects of focus (*ālambana-vibhāga*):
for example, one might previously have seen such things as gardens, groves, springs, ponds, mountain valleys, and places for walking meditation,
but subsequently forgets them.
Later, one no longer perceives that similar appearance,
nor can one recall what was previously experienced.
This refers to that which conforms to a different category.
Just as when one cannot obtain things such as food, drink, clothing,
or other necessities, one can no longer recall what was previously possible;
so it is when the continuity of a different state evolves.
One does not give rise to the cognition or vision of mutual connection regarding phenomena (*dharma*).
Question: With respect to what is there no arising of mutual connection?
Answer: Regarding the three kinds of homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*), there are also four different recensions on this point.
The opposite of the preceding should be explained in detail.
Furthermore, when the power of the causal force of the feeling (*vedanā*) is weak, mindfulness (*smṛti*) is lost;
it should be understood that in this context, the preceding complex of mental states (*citta-kalāpa*) is designated by the term "mind" (*manas*).
The subsequent collection of mind is explained by means of recollecting the sound.
The mental verbalization of feeling (*vedanā*) is as previously explained;
however, because the causal force of the preceding feeling of the mind was weak.
Regarding that object of focus, no subsequent thought arises;
although one may remember it in the interim, one subsequently forgets it again.
"Forgetting" refers to the mind being deranged and oppressed by painful sensations.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"Mindfulness is lost due to three causes and conditions:
first, because one has not properly grasped the preceding signs."
Second, because it manifests as a continuity of distinct parts;
third, because of the loss of mindfulness.
Furthermore, he says this:
Mindfulness is lost due to eight causes and conditions.
First, at the time of birth, mindfulness is lost because one is oppressed by the suffering of birth.
Second, at the time of death, mindfulness is lost because one is oppressed by the suffering of death.
Third, because idle chatter is frequently practiced;
fourth, because their faculties are dull and they rely on inferior wisdom;
fifth, because they are born in undesirable realms and oppressed by painful sensations.
Sixth, because the five faculties scatter toward their objects without ceasing due to excessive heedlessness;
seventh, because the heavy afflictive obstructions frequently manifest;
eighth, because the mind is distracted due to not frequently cultivating meditative concentration.
One forgets what has been brought to mind.
Question: Regarding the forgetting of what has been brought to mind, by which type of knowledge does this occur—is it that consisting of what is heard (*śrutamaya*)?
Is it that which is produced through reflection?
Is it that which is produced through cultivation?
Or is it that which is acquired at birth, and so forth?
Some say that what is produced through hearing and reflection, as well as that acquired at birth and so forth, may be forgotten once it has been experienced; however,
this is not the case for what is produced through cultivation.
Because it is sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
there is no loss of mindfulness. Some say that even that which is experienced through the cultivation of wisdom (*bhāvanāmaya*) may be lost.
Because the body is weak.
That is to say, there are those who have attained meditative concentration but whose bodies are weak;
because the body is weak, the mind is also weak.
That which has been experienced by him may also be forgotten.
Question: Where does forgetfulness occur?
Answer: In the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
It does not exist in the form or formless realms.
Within the five destinies, forgetfulness exists in all of them;
some say that there is no forgetfulness in the hells.
Because it is constantly forgotten.
Question: What kind of *pudgala* possesses forgetfulness?
Answer: Both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) possess forgetfulness.
Among the noble ones— stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas—
all possess forgetfulness,
with the sole exception of the Blessed One.
Because the Buddha has accomplished the quality of non-forgetfulness.
How is this known?
Answer: Because the sūtras are the authoritative source.
As it is said:
"Śāriputra, suppose a community of bhikṣus were to carry me along on a couch for a hundred years."
It is impossible for the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed wisdom and eloquence to suffer even the slightest decline; therefore,
one knows that the Buddha possesses the quality of non-forgetfulness.
As in the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint,
it is said in the Sūtra that Śāriputra spoke as follows:
If the internal sense base of the mind is unimpaired,
and external phenomena are present and the mental attention capable of producing them correctly arises,
at that time, the mental consciousness arises.
Question: In what sense is there destruction?
Answer: There are three kinds of destruction:
first, temporary destruction.
Second, the destruction of the homogeneous life-span;
third, ultimate destruction.
Regarding temporary destruction:
That is to say, when an unwholesome or indeterminate mind manifests immediately after a wholesome mind,
at that time it is called the "temporary impairment" of the wholesome mind.
Even until, immediately after an indeterminate mind,
a wholesome or unwholesome mind manifests;
at that time, it is said that the indeterminate mind is temporarily interrupted.
In this way, immediately after a mind of the desire realm,
a mind of the form realm that is unconditioned by the realms manifests;
at that time, it is said that the mind of the desire realm is temporarily destroyed.
Even until the unbound mind is momentarily interrupted and a mind belonging to the three realms manifests,
at that time it is called the "temporary destruction" of the unbound mind.
This occurs when one enters the meditative attainments of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

At that time, it is said that "the entire mind is momentarily destroyed" and "the entire homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga) is destroyed," which refers to those who have severed their roots of goodness (kuśala-mūla).
The wholesome mind ceases when the *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous life-constituent) is destroyed;
the unwholesome mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is free from the defilement of desire [ceases] when the *nikāyasabhāga* is destroyed, and so forth.

"Ultimate destruction" refers to the ultimate destruction of the minds abandoned through the vision of suffering within the three realms, occurring when the knowledge of suffering has already arisen but the knowledge of origination has not yet arisen.
Up until the time when the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,
the minds of the three realms to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation are completely destroyed.
For a stream-enterer, the minds of the three realms to be abandoned through vision are completely destroyed.

The non-retrogressive once-returner has completely eliminated the defilements abandoned through seeing in the three realms, as well as the sixth category of defilements abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
The non-retrogressive non-returner...
The defiled minds abandoned through seeing and abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm are ultimately destroyed for those of non-retrogressive nature (*aparihāṇadharman*) who are Arhats.
The defiled minds abandoned through seeing and abandoned through cultivation in all three realms are ultimately destroyed [for such Arhats].
For a non-returner who is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and free from the defilements of the desire realm,
the defiled minds of the desire realm are completely destroyed;
this continues up until they are free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The defiled mind of the eighth stage is ultimately destroyed.
The Venerable Vasumitra says:
"If the mental faculty encounters harmonious conditions, it is not called 'destroyed'."
If they do not encounter the conditions for conjunction, they are said to be "disintegrated.
Furthermore, it is said:
if the mind is not obstructed by contrary causes, it is not said to be "disintegrated."
If it is obstructed by a contrary cause, it is termed "ruined.
For what reason does an offering made to a preta reach that realm and not other destinies?
This is explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To explain the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra:
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Buddha and said to him, "Gotama,
a relative of mine has passed away, and I wish to offer food for his sake."
"Will he obtain my food?
The World-Honored One replied,
"This matter is not fixed."
Why is this? Because among the various classes of sentient beings, there are distinctions between the five destinies.
If your kinsmen have been born into the hells, [how can you feel attachment?]
They consume the food of the hells to sustain themselves;
they cannot partake of your food.
It is likewise for those born in the realms of animals, gods, or humans.
If your kinsmen are born among the hungry ghosts, [you should likewise cultivate compassion].
"Then they would be able to receive the food and drink you offer.
The brāhmaṇa said,
"If my kinsmen were not born in the realm of ghosts..."
"Who shall receive the food and drink you have offered?
The Buddha said to them,
"Within the realm of hungry ghosts."
"It is impossible that you have no kinsmen," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Although that sutra makes this statement, [it does not contradict our position].
Yet it does not state for what reason offerings made to hungry ghosts reach them specifically and not others;
that sutra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
As for what is not stated therein:
It should now be explained;
therefore, this treatise is composed.
[The author] questions that Brahmin:
Why did he not ask the Buddha for what reason offerings made to hungry ghosts reach them specifically and not others?
He replied: "There are two reasons:
namely, that they may be of sharp faculties or of dull faculties."
If one possesses sharp faculties, one can understand by oneself without needing to ask the Buddha.
If one possesses dull faculties, one is unable to give rise to doubt and thus does not ask the Buddha.
Why is this so, World-Honored One?
It is not taught that they are merely hungry ghosts who have reached the conditions for [liberation].
The answer is also due to two conditions:
namely, that they may be of sharp faculties or of dull faculties.
If one possesses sharp faculties, they can understand it by themselves without needing the Buddha’s teaching;
if one possesses dull faculties, they are not vessels for the Dharma,
and thus the Buddha does not teach them.
For what reason do offerings made to hungry ghosts reach them, while they do not reach those in other realms?
Answer: It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of that realm that such a state is attained;
the matter arises as part of their own being (*ātmiya*).
Therefore, one arrives at [this realm] through sacrifice and not by other means.
Herein lies the intent of the question: does one arrive at this destiny because of being lowly and base, or because of being noble and exalted?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
If one were to go there because of being lowly and base,
then one should also go to the hells and the animal realm when performing sacrifices for them.
If one were to go there because of noble status,
then those who perform sacrifices to humans and devas should also go there.
The intended meaning of the response here is that one does not go there because of lowly status.
Nor does one arrive there by virtue of being noble;
rather, it is due to two conditions:
first, because that destination is its own inherent nature (*dharmatā*).
Second, by way of the maturation of karma:
herein, first, the natural state (*dharmatā*) of that realm is revealed;
that is to say, it is the natural state of the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*) to obtain such a place.
Since the arising of the ritual action belongs to my own sphere,
the sacrifice reaches [the deity] and nothing else.
This is stated in order to make this meaning clear.
To cite worldly examples:
just as geese, swans, peacocks, parrots, śāris, and jīvajīvaka birds,
though they fly through the sky with sovereign ease according to their will, [are nevertheless subject to the laws of nature].
Yet their supernatural power and majesty are no greater than those of humans; rather,
it is the nature of that realm that they obtain such a place,
and by the occurrence of this event within my own sphere, I am able to fly through the air.
The realm of hungry ghosts is likewise;
by the power of the natural law (*dharmatā*), the sacrificial offerings reach them,
whereas this is not the case for other realms.
This refers, for example, to geese, swans, peacocks, and other such beings within the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*),
who, by the natural power of their own destiny, are able to fly through the air and remain there for long periods,
sporting in a manner that transcends humans except through the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), mantras, or medicinal herbs.
They wished to remain suspended in the air at a height of four finger-widths above the ground;
yet after a brief moment, not one was able to do so.
Nevertheless, their supernatural power and majestic virtue were no inferior to those of humans.
The same applies to hungry ghosts (preta).
By the inherent power of their destiny,
they arrive at the sacrificial offering and no others.
In order to make the preceding meaning even more clear and distinct,
a second analogy is cited:
"Furthermore, it is like a certain class of hell-beings."
They are able to recollect their past lives and also know the minds of others;
[they perceive] one class of animals and one class of hungry ghosts.
They are able to recollect past lives and know the minds of others;
they can also produce smoke and flames,
raise clouds and bring forth rain, and create cold and heat.
Although they are able to perform such deeds,
their supernatural power and majesty are no greater than that of humans;
nevertheless, by the very nature of that realm, they obtain such a place.
When an action arises within my own sphere, I am capable of performing that action;
the realm of hungry ghosts (preta) is likewise.
By the power of the nature of things (dharmatā), the sacrificial offering reaches them.
It is not so for other realms of existence.
Among these, there is a certain class of hell-beings who are able to recollect their past lives.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"The sentient beings in the hells have this thought:
