they are able to make their bodies invisible to others.
Animals, hungry ghosts, and devas also possess this knowledge acquired at birth that causes the body to become invisible; however,
this does not exist among those in the human realm.
Question: Among these four types of powers, including the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which can cause which others not to appear?
Answer: The supernormal powers can cause all others not to appear, because they are the most supreme.
Question: Who has the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) to cause whom to become invisible?
Answer: The Buddha can cause everyone else to become invisible.

A Pratyekabuddha, with the exception of the Buddha, can cause all others to become invisible. Śāriputra, with the exception of the Buddha and the Pratyekabuddha, can cause all others to become invisible.
Except for the Buddha, the Pratyekabuddhas, and Śāriputra,
[the power] does not manifest in others; likewise,
it does not manifest in those of dull faculties except for those of sharp faculties.
It is not manifested to others.
Regarding the phrase "except for spells" (*mantra*) and "except for supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*):
it asks which spell causes non-manifestation to what [person], and by what means.
The answer is: there are mantra-arts that are complete and those that are incomplete;
there are mantra-arts that are sublime and those that are not sublime.
As for those that are both complete and sublime:
Regarding all things that are neither complete nor excellent, they do not manifest;
except for those that are complete and excellent, the others do not manifest.
Except for medicines, supernatural powers, and incantations, he cannot manifest other abilities.
Why is this? It is because of the power of incantations.
Because medicinal substances can bring about results through the power of spells rather than the power of the substances themselves.
Question: Which medicine can cause what to become invisible?
Answer: A superior medicine can cause an inferior one to become invisible.
Wisdom is attained according to one’s place of birth.
With the exception of the previous three types, it does not manifest in others because they are most inferior.
Question: Who can cause what not to manifest?
Some say that hell-beings can only cause [themselves] to become invisible to other hell-beings, and so on,
up to gods who can only cause themselves to become invisible to other gods.
Some say that hell-beings can cause [the Buddha] to become invisible only within the hells;
animals, within two [realms]; hungry ghosts, within three; and gods, within four.
It can cause [beings] to not appear within the five destinies.
As it is said: hell-beings can cause themselves to not appear within the five destinies, and even devas can likewise cause themselves to not appear within the five destinies.
This is called "not manifest and not past.
"Not manifest" refers to the second type of non-manifestation.
"Not past" means it is not either of the two types of the past.
Because that which has been obscured abides in the present,
there is also that which is past yet not manifest;
namely, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have already arisen and have already originated.
That which has already arisen has already been produced; that which has already turned has already manifested.
That which has already accumulated has already appeared and has already passed away.
It has already been exhausted, ceased, and detached from transformation.
This refers to the past of the past, which is subsumed within the past time.
All such phrases collectively demonstrate the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the past;
"past" here refers to the world that has passed away.
"Not manifest" refers to that which is not manifest in the world.
There are things that are neither past nor not manifest;
these are cases other than those previously described.
In this context, the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) applies to that which is named;
that is to say, all phenomena that fall under the first three categories and are manifested by names are entirely excluded.
Those not yet manifested constitute the fourth category. What, then, are these?
They refer to all dharmas of the past, excluding those within the present body of a Buddha and those that have become obscured.
One takes all other present, future, and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas.

Question: Just as the subsequent exhaustion and cessation are also formulated in four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) with reference to the abandonment of fetters (*saṃyojana*), why is this not done here with reference to the abandonment of fetters?
Is this presented as a fourfold proposition?
Answer: There are places where it is stated that the severance of fetters is called "exhaustion" (kṣaya) and "cessation" (nirodha).
Because it is nowhere stated that the abandonment of the fetters (saṃyojana-prahāṇa) is called "non-manifestation" (anabhyavakāśa).
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Thirteen; *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Fourteen. (From the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda school.)
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;
translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Section Two, Part Six of the First Aggregate on Miscellaneous Topics: "Wisdom"—Do all those things that are past become exhausted?
It is agreed that there are four propositions.
Regarding the past, there are two types,
as previously explained.
Exhaustion also has two kinds,
as previously explained.
Herein, the discussion is conducted based on both types.
The past and exhaustion (kṣaya) differ in their respective scopes;
therefore, four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) are established.
There is that which is past but not exhausted.
This refers to what the Venerable Udāyin said:
"All fetters have passed away," and so forth,
as explained at length.
That which is "past" refers to the second past;
that which is "not exhausted" is not the first exhaustion,
because the Buddha’s body has already been completely severed and exhausted in the present.
There is that which has been exhausted but is not past;
as the Buddha said:
"This noble disciple has already exhausted the hells."
The animal realm has been exhausted;
the realm of hungry ghosts has been exhausted;
all treacherous and evil pits of miserable destinies have been exhausted.
Regarding the phrase "those who have already exhausted hell" mentioned herein,
it indicates that the noble disciples have already exhausted hell; regarding "those who have already exhausted the animal realm," it likewise indicates they have exhausted that state.
"Having exhausted the realm of animals" means that this has already exhausted the animals.
"Having exhausted the realm of hungry ghosts" means that this has already exhausted the hungry ghosts.
Regarding the phrase "having already exhausted all the treacherous pits of the evil destinies," what further exhaustion does this indicate?
The answer is that it indicates the same three [aspects] mentioned above; however, while they were explained extensively previously, they are stated concisely here.
The former is specific while the latter is general; the former is gradual while the latter is sudden;
the former involves discrimination while the latter is non-discriminative. Some say:
"Having exhausted the hells, the animal realm,
and the hungry ghosts" reveals that these three evil destinies have been exhausted in their essential nature.
"Having exhausted all the treacherous pits of the evil destinies" [is likewise explained].
Having explained this, it is said that those who have exhausted [rebirth in] the hells and so forth exist within that intermediate state (antarābhava). Some say:
"Those who have exhausted the hells and so forth..."

"Having manifested that hell and the others have been exhausted" means having manifested that all the treacherous pits of the miserable destinies (*durgati*) have been exhausted. "Having manifested that [the states of] humans who are *śaṇḍha*,
*paṇḍaka*, sexless, or hermaphrodite have been exhausted" means having manifested that these have been exhausted.
Because they are precipices and pits of perilous evil destinies among humanity.
Some say that the preceding [passage] has already revealed those who have exhausted [rebirth as] hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
The latter [verse] reveals that one who has already exhausted [the lifespan] remains in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*),
because such a person is destined to fall into the precipitous pit of the miserable destinies (*durgati*).
Some say that the former [verse] reveals those who have already exhausted [the lifespan] in the hells, among animals, or as hungry ghosts (*preta*).
The latter [verse] reveals that he has already exhausted the commission of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*),
because he falls into hell in the very next life.
Some say that the former [verse] reveals that he has already exhausted [rebirth as] hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
This subsequently clarifies those who have completely severed their roots of goodness;
for one who has severed these roots is like a pit in a treacherous and evil realm,
and because if they do not reconnect their roots of goodness, they will inevitably fall into hell upon death.
Some say that the former [verse] reveals that the fruits of hell and so forth have already been exhausted,
while the latter reveals that the causes of hell and so forth have already been exhausted.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "O Bhikṣus,
if you see one who practices evil deeds of body, speech, and mind..."
One should know that they have already seen the hells or other evil destinies.
Some say that the preceding [passage] has already manifested the exhaustion of the hells, the animal realm, and the hungry ghost realm.
The subsequent statement, "having already exhausted all that is perilous," further clarifies that the hells have been exhausted,
because within the hells there are no virtuous fruits.
The "evil destinies" (durgati) further clarify those who have already exhausted [their karma as] hungry ghosts (*preta*),
because they are constantly impoverished and lack the necessary resources.
The "pits" (*garta*) further clarify those who have already exhausted [their karma as] animals (*tiryagyoni*).
Because their body and mind have fallen into that state from which it is difficult to emerge;
they are born during the kalpa of formation and only pass away at the time of the kalpa of destruction.
Some say: the former statement reveals that one has already exhausted [rebirth as] hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts;
the latter statement, "having further exhausted all the treacherous pits of the evil destinies," reiterates this.
This further clarifies that the fruits of the three evil destinies have been exhausted;
for these three evil destinies are all extremely perilous,
being pits into which one enters and falls due to various evils.
Question: There are still various cauldrons of boiling water, furnaces of burning coals, and countless instruments of torture such as hell-wardens within the hells now;
how can you say they have all been exhausted?
Answer: It is called "exhaustion" because there is no further going and no further arising.
That is to say, the noble disciple no longer goes to those places, nor does he arise again within those aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
This is because they have already attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of those [states].
Question: Since there are also ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who attain the non-analytical cessation of the hells and so forth, why is it said here only of the noble disciples (*ārya-śrāvaka*)?
Answer: Because all noble disciples (ārya-śrāvaka) have already exhausted [them], whereas among the class of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), there are those who have not yet exhausted them;
therefore, it is not mentioned.
Question: Since the noble disciples also exhaust [rebirth among] humans and devas, why is it said here only that they exhaust the hells and so forth?
Answer: In this context, the term "all" refers specifically to those [lower realms].
Because the noble disciples still have [karmic results] remaining within the realms of humans and devas, these are not mentioned; this is called "exhaustion.
That which is not the exhaustion of the past is the second type of exhaustion.
That which is not past is not the initial past;
there is that which is past and yet has ceased,
namely, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have already arisen and originated.
...and so on, as explained at length.
All of these demonstrate past formations (*saṃskāra*).
"Past" refers to that which has passed away in time; its exhaustion is likewise [past].
There is that which is neither past nor exhausted, namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Herein, the meaning of the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is as explained previously in detail.
Furthermore, what does this mean?
That is to say, excluding all dharmas of the past, the present body of the Buddha,
and the future aggregates, elements, and bases of the noble disciples in the hells and so forth;
one takes all remaining present, future, and unconditioned dharmas.
This constitutes the fourth alternative.
Furthermore, if this is explained in terms of the abandonment of fetters (*saṃyojana*),
the word "based upon" (*niśritya*) here indicates the sense of that which serves as a support.
In the first four statements,
the term "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) is spoken in reference to worldly exhaustion and the exhaustion of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣaya*).
In the present four statements:
The designation "exhaustion" (kṣaya) is established based on the attainment of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) through the abandonment of afflictions; however,
there are fetters (saṃyojana) that are past but not yet exhausted.
That is to say, the fetters are past; they have not been abandoned,
not fully understood, not extinguished, and not vomited out.
That which has not been abandoned is not established as the thorough knowledge of abandonment;
that which has not been fully known is not established as the thorough knowledge of cognition;
and that which has not been extinguished has not attained analytical cessation.
"Those not yet transformed or vomited forth" means they have not yet been discarded;
some say it means those not yet severed, i.e., not yet severed by the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
"Those who have not fully understood" means they have not fully understood by means of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
"Those who have not abandoned" means they have not yet realized the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyogaprāpti*) from those [afflictions].
"Those who have not disgorged" means they have not yet relinquished the acquisition of bondage (*bandhanaprāpti*) to those [afflictions].
Some say that all four of these phrases reveal the meaning of not yet having abandoned. How is this so?
That is to say, for ordinary beings who are bound by all fetters,
there are the past fetters of the three realms to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation;
or for those who have already become free from the defilement of desire but have not yet become free from the defilement of the first dhyāna.
For one who has abandoned the defilements of the eight stages,
from those to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation up to those who have already become free from the taints of the sphere of nothingness,
there are past fetters to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation pertaining to one stage.
If a noble one who is still bound by all fetters enters the state of the certainty of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*),

at the moment of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the fetters to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation belonging to the three realms in the past have been eliminated;
the dharma-knowledge of suffering has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen.
The fetters of the past belonging to the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering,
up to those of the three realms to be abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, and through cultivation,
as long as the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen.
The fetters of the past that are abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) in the realms of form and formlessness,
as well as the fetters abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the three realms;
for a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), these are the fetters abandoned through cultivation in the three realms belonging to the past.
The once-returner [abandons] the three categories of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the past desire realm,
as well as the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms.
As for the non-returner, if they have not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna...
The fetters abandoned through cultivation belonging to the past eight stages,
up to those belonging to the past one stage for one who has already become free from the defilement of the sphere of nothingness.
This is called a fetter that is past but not exhausted.
There are fetters that are exhausted but not past;
namely, those fetters of the future that have been abandoned, fully understood, ceased, and vomited out.
That which has been abandoned is established as the thorough knowledge of abandonment;
that which has been fully known is established as the thorough knowledge by wisdom;
that which has been extinguished is the attainment of analytical cessation.
That which has already been transformed and vomited up is that which has already been discarded.
Some say: that which has already been severed is that which has already been severed by the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
That which has been fully known is that which has been fully known by means of the path of liberation.
That which has been extinguished is that for which the acquisition of dissociation has already been realized.
That which has been vomited out is that for which the acquisition of bondage has already been abandoned.
Some say that all four of these phrases reveal the meaning of having already abandoned. How so?
This refers to the fetters of the three realms to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation that remain in the future for an Arhat;
or, for a Non-returner who has already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness,
it refers to those fetters of the three realms to be abandoned through seeing that remain in the future.
And the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation on the eighth stage,
up until one has not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna;
these are the future [fetters] of the three realms to be abandoned through seeing.
And the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the first stage;
if one is a once-returner, [they abandon] the future fetters to be abandoned through vision in the three realms,
as well as the six categories of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
If it concerns a stream-enterer regarding future fetters to be abandoned through vision within the three realms;
or if it concerns one practicing in accordance with faith or in accordance with dharma,
when the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path has already arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen.
The fetters of the future three realms to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation,
as well as those to be abandoned through the vision of the path in the desire realm,
[persist] until the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of suffering has not yet arisen.
The future fetters of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering;
and, for those ordinary beings who have already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness,
the future fetters of the eight stages to be abandoned through both vision and cultivation.
Up to the point where one has already abandoned the defilements of desire but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna,
there are future fetters to be abandoned through both vision and cultivation belonging to a single stage;
these are called "the exhaustion of fetters that is not past."
There are fetters that are past and also exhausted;
that is to say, fetters that are past, already abandoned, already fully understood, already ceased, and already vomited out.
The phrases "already abandoned" and so forth are explained in detail as previously stated.
What, moreover, is this?
It refers to the fetters of the past, belonging to the three realms,
which were to be abandoned through insight and cultivation by an Arhat.
To speak at length, up to:
if an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) has already become detached from the defilements of the desire realm but is not yet detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
they possess the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation belonging to one stage in the past.
This is called a fetter that is both past and exhausted.
There is a fetter that is neither past nor exhausted;
namely, a fetter that is future, not yet abandoned, not yet fully known, not yet ceased, and not yet relinquished.
The phrases "and having bound [the defilements] of the present" and "not yet abandoned," etc., are explained in detail as previously stated.
Furthermore, what does this mean?
It refers to those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who are fully fettered (*sakalabandhana*).
Regarding the fetters of the three realms to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the future,
explained at length up to:
if one who is a non-returner has already become free from the defilement of the sphere of nothingness.
The fetters to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the future stage,
as well as all present fetters—
these are called fetters that are neither past nor exhausted.
Are all those things that are past necessarily ceased?
One should respond by formulating four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are two kinds of the past.
As previously stated,
cessation is also of two kinds: first,
cessation by way of time.
Second is obscured cessation (*nivṛta-nirodha*).
Herein, the discussion is based on both types [of cessation].
Between the past and cessation, there is a mutual relationship of greater and lesser scope.
Therefore, four propositions are established.
There is that which is past but not ceased;
as the Venerable Udāyin said:
"All fetters are past," and so forth,
as explained at length.
"The past" refers to the second type of past.
That which is not subject to cessation does not possess the two kinds of cessation,
because the Buddha-body is present and not hidden.
There is cessation that is not of the past.
This refers to relying upon conventional small streets, small houses, small vessels, and small eyes,
and speaking of "the extinction of the street" up to "the extinction of the eye.
That is to say, people in the East, seeing a small street and so forth, say, "This has been extinguished."
Based on this meaning, one may say:
"Is it possible for an eye that has ceased to see forms?
The answer is: "Yes."
This refers to the present-world homogeneous small eye; this is called cessation.
That which is not the cessation of the past is the second cessation.
"Not of the past" means not the first past.
There are those that are past and have ceased;
namely, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have already arisen and originated,
and so forth, as explained at length.
All of these demonstrate past conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
"Past" refers to that which has passed away in time; its cessation is likewise [past].
There are, however, those that are neither past nor ceased.
This means excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Herein, the term "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) is also as previously explained,
and so on at length.
What, then, is this? It refers to all phenomena of the past,
excluding the present body of the Buddha, small streets, and so forth.
Taking all other present phenomena, as well as all future phenomena and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*),
these constitute the fourth category.
Furthermore, if one speaks in terms of the abandonment of the fetters (*saṃyojana*):
In this context, the meaning of the term "basis" (*āśraya*) is as previously explained.
In the first four statements, the term "cessation" (*nirodha*) is used in reference to cessation through worldly destruction and cessation through disappearance.

In the present four statements, the designation "cessation" is established in reference to the cessation consisting of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is attained through the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).
There are fetters that are past but not yet extinguished;
that is to say, those fetters that are past, yet have not been abandoned, have not been fully understood,
have not been extinguished, and have not been cast out.
To speak at length, up to:
there are fetters that are neither past nor ceased;
namely, fetters that are future—unabandoned, not fully known, unceased, and not vomited out—as well as fetters that are present.
In this regard, all meanings are as previously explained.
Among these five sets of four statements thus described,
the first three sets of four are spoken in reliance upon worldly designation (*loka-prajñapti*) and noble designation (*ārya-prajñapti*).
It is spoken by means of worldly language and noble language;
it is spoken by means of the conventional and the ultimate.
Based on the sūtras and what is directly perceived,
it is said that the latter two sets of four propositions rely solely on the noble ones' designations and noble speech as taught in the sūtras of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
Regarding these latter two sets of four propositions:
Why is it that only the fetters (saṃyojana) are mentioned, and not the phenomena that constitute fetters?
Answer: It is because the author of that treatise intended it to be so.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Regarding those who say that what ought to have been stated was not stated,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Some say: "The fetters have already been explained;
it should be understood that the phenomena which constitute fetters have likewise already been explained."
Why is this? Because the dharma of "fettering" (saṃyojana-dharma) is established based upon the fetters themselves;
furthermore, because they share the same antidote (pratipakṣa).
Some say that the intrinsic nature of the fetters is severed;
once severed, they are no longer possessed.
Therefore, it is so stated.
As for the phenomena of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), because they are not fixed, they are not mentioned. Some say:
The various fetters (*saṃyojana*) possess many faults;
because they are firm, difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend, they are so designated.
The phenomena of the fetters are not like this, and therefore they are not so called.
Some say: "The various fetters (saṃyojana) are contrary to the noble path (āryamārga),
but the phenomena that constitute the fetters are not so."
Because wholesome states with outflows can enter into and emerge from the Noble Path,
and because non-obscured neutral states can serve as the basis for the Noble Path.
However, because it is intermingled with the fetters (*saṃyojana*),
it is also abandoned by the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
It is like a lamp which, when destroying darkness, also consumes the wick and so forth.
When a king breaks another's army, he also inflicts damage upon his own troops.
Some say that the fetters (saṃyojana) are both fetters and the objects of the fetters (saṃyojanīya-dharma).
Therefore, it is so described. As for the phenomena that are fetters (*saṃyojana-dharma*) and those that are not fetters, they are not so described,
just as in the case of the fetters themselves.
The phenomena that are fetters;
the phenomena that are underlying tendencies;
the phenomena that are secondary afflictions.
The same should be understood for the *paryavasthāna* (envelopments) and the *mala* (stains).
If one gives rise to doubt regarding suffering, thinking, "Is this suffering?
Is this not suffering?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra:
A Brahmin who maintained the theory of causality came to where the Buddha was and asked him this:
"Śramaṇa Gautama, [what is your view?]"
"Doubt is indeed extremely rare and difficult to cross over, not easily crossed.
The World-Honored One replied, "So it is, so it is."
The brahmin was deeply skeptical, thinking, "This is most extraordinary and difficult to master;
it is not easily mastered. Why is this?
Because there were ancient brahmins who composed the *Vidyā* treatises.
There are ten foremost practitioners of incantations:
first, Aṭṭhakas; second, Vāmakas.
3. Sambhavati; 4. Viśvāmitrā; 5. Jamadagnī.
Sixth, Aṅgīrasa;
seventh, Varadāśa;
eighth, Vasistha.
Ninth, Kāśyapa;
tenth, Bṛhaspati.
Such were the various brahmins.
Although people in the world revere them, none of them passes beyond doubt before their lives end.
Therefore, one knows that doubt is exceedingly difficult to overcome.
Although the sūtras state this, they do not provide a detailed analysis.
That sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies;
what was not explained therein shall now be explained here.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
If one should harbor doubt regarding suffering, asking: "Is this suffering?"
Is this not suffering?
Should it be said that it is a single mind or many minds?
One should say that it is many minds.
That is to say: "Is this suffering?
is the first thought;
"Is this not suffering? is the second thought.
The same applies to the arising of doubt regarding the origin, cessation, and path.
Herein, the term "wrong" (*mithyā*) serves to clarify the meaning of doubt.
If it were merely said, "This is suffering," [doubt would not arise].
To regard this as not suffering constitutes wrong view;
the same applies up to the [Noble Truth of] the Path.
Because of the statement regarding false sounds, a state of doubt arises.
Thus, from suffering up to the path,
there are two minds for each, totaling eight minds.
This is said to be the minimum speed.
For one who has sequential doubt regarding the Four Noble Truths, there are these eight moments of mind,
as at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
From the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) up to the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna), there are sixteen moments;
so say some.
These eight [moments] do not constitute eight distinct kṣaṇas,
because each individual moment of mind arises and ceases with such extreme rapidity.
If one were to think thus:
"Is this suffering? Thus, in the interim, hundreds of thousands of births and deaths have already occurred;
it is the same for the remaining moments of mind.

Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the sake of enabling those who doubt to attain certainty.
That is to say, the Abhidharmikas maintain that there is a single mental collection (*citta-kalāpa*).
There are many dharmas that arise together.
That which arises in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and is characterized by hesitation is called doubt (*vicikitsā*);
that which is characterized by certainty is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
There are mental factors that are neither doubt nor certainty, namely the remaining mental concomitants;
let there not arise the suspicion that what is "without doubt" is simply a mind that possesses doubt.
This refers to one who possesses doubt; it is for the sake of bringing certainty to this doubt.
This treatise was composed because it is shown that the state of having doubt is distinct from the state of being without doubt.
"Is there perhaps even a single mind that has doubt and yet no doubt?
He replied, "No.
[The Buddha] asked this question.
Is this stated with reference to a collection of minds,
or is it stated with reference to the objects of cognition?
If it is stated with reference to a collection of minds, then...
Thus, within a single mental aggregate, there may be both doubt and non-doubt,
as has already been explained previously.
Why, then, do you say that they do not exist?
If explained in terms of the object of focus,
then there may be doubt regarding the mind of a single Buddha; however,
for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there is no such doubt.
It means that even the Noble Ones should not say it does not exist.
Why, then, did he answer that it does not exist?
The answer is: this was answered as "non-existent" with reference to the collection of mental factors (*citta-kalāpa*).
That is to say, among the various collections of mind, those that possess doubt are called "doubtful minds," while those that lack doubt are called "non-doubtful minds. Therefore,

However, regarding the statement here that one who is free from doubt does not arise [with such views],
this means that with respect to the Four Noble Truths, whether one apprehends them as existing or denies them as non-existent,
it is not merely that [such views] do not arise in dissociation from doubt.
Why is this so? It is because regarding the Truth of Suffering, if one asks, "Is this suffering?
[one must answer accordingly].
This mind harbors doubt;
if one says, "This is suffering," this mind is free from doubt.
If one says, "Is this not suffering?
there is doubt in this mind.
If one says, "This is not suffering."
This mind is without doubt;
one should know that it is likewise regarding the origin, cessation, and path.
One should know that within this there are sixteen minds.
Because there are four [factors] for each of the Four Noble Truths;
that is to say, eight are doubt and four are right view.
The fourth is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The first four types of doubt induce the four right views (*samyagdṛṣṭi*),
while the latter four types of doubt induce the four wrong views.
That is to say, "This is suffering" and so forth is right view, whereas "This is not suffering" and so forth is wrong view.
Question: What kind of person can doubt lead to the arising of right view?
What kind of person does doubt lead to the arising of wrong view?
Answer: If one is inclined to dwell together with those of this Dharma, that doubt leads to the arising of right view;
if one is inclined to dwell together with non-Buddhists, [that doubt leads to the arising of wrong view].
That doubt gives rise to wrong view.
Furthermore, for one who delights in practicing the internal treatises,
that doubt gives rise to right view.
If one delights in practicing external treatises,
that doubt will give rise to wrong views.
Furthermore, if one loves to associate with virtuous persons and listens to the true Dharma, [doubt will not arise].
If that doubt leads one to draw near to virtuous persons and listen to the true Dharma,
it gives rise to right view; if it leads one to draw near to unvirtuous persons and listen to what is not the true Dharma,
it gives rise to wrong view.
Furthermore, if the powers of cause, application, and heedfulness are predominant,
doubt will lead to the arising of right view;
if the powers of cause, application, and heedfulness are not predominant, [doubt will not].
That doubt gives rise to wrong view.
As it is said in a sutra:
"There are three kinds of darkness that envelop the body."
This refers to doubt and hesitation regarding the three periods of time.
Question: Since the intrinsic nature of that which obscures the body should be ignorance (*avidyā*), why is it called "doubt" (*vicikitsā*)?
The answer is: because it is similar to that.

This means that among the various afflictions (*kleśa*), there is none that does not have an aspect of activity (*ākāra*) similar to that of ignorance (*avidyā*), just as is the case with doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Therefore, it is called doubt.
Some say that the nature of the body’s obscurity is in fact ignorance (*avidyā*).
Doubt is the dwelling place and abode of ignorance; therefore, it is called doubt.
As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
"Doubt is the dwelling place and abode of non-knowing."
Some say that because doubt dwells in close proximity to ignorance—
meaning that wherever there is doubt, there must necessarily be ignorance.
Just as people in the world say of a relative,
"That is me," or "He is I," it is for this reason that doubt is spoken of. Some say:
Because doubt (*vicikitsā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are similar in their characteristics;
that is to say, both operate with respect to an object by not being determined and by wavering between two alternatives, and for this reason it is called doubt. Some say:
That sutra was intended to establish whether [the self] is a conditioned phenomenon or not.

That is to say, it states that ignorance is the intrinsic nature of the "dark body" (mṛtyu-kāya), but it does not state that it exists as a self-established entity; rather, it implies that there is also the sense of a "dark body" which is subject to doubt.
However, because this is not explicitly clarified, it is explained selectively.
Question: Why does the Blessed One speak only of doubt regarding the conditioned world as being the "darkness of the body," and not speak of doubt regarding the unconditioned?
Regarding those who agree to speak but do not speak,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*). Some say:
That sutra speaks according to the majority of cases;
that is to say, this "dark body" (ābhāsvara-kāya) arises mostly with conditioned phenomena as its object,
while it rarely takes unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) as its object, and for this reason it is not mentioned there.
Some say: conditioned phenomena are coarse and manifest; among them, one may give rise to doubt.
That which is censured by the Noble Ones is called "darkness."
Because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is subtle and difficult to discern, one may harbor doubts regarding it;
since the Noble Ones do not censure such doubt, they do not speak of it.
It is like a person who stumbles during the day and is censured by the world as being blind.
If one stumbles at night, the world does not reproach them;
it is the same with that [person]. Some say thus.
Non-Buddhists give rise to superior delusion regarding the world;
because they harbor doubt and hesitation, this is taught specifically.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Did I exist in the past, or did I not exist?
What was it that existed in the past?
How was there existence in the past?
Will I exist in the future, or will I not exist in the future?
What will exist in the future?
How could there be such a thing? One would have internal doubt:

What is there that exists?
From where do such sentient beings come when they are born,
and to where do they go when they pass away?
Because non-Buddhists give rise to such excessive doubt regarding worldly enumerations,
they are specifically mentioned.
Some say: Whether foolish or wise, whether belonging to the inner or outer paths,
and even including worldly disputants down to mere children, all know that the world exists.
This means that while they all understand the existence of the past, future, and present, they harbor doubts regarding them;
because these doubts are profoundly blinding, they are called the "body of darkness.
Nirvana is free from characteristics and is extremely difficult to realize.
Even those of sharp and penetrating intelligence cannot exhaustively fathom it;
therefore, because of doubt regarding it, it is not discussed here. Some say:
The Buddha, observing the future,
saw that there would be disciples who deny the existence of the past and the future;
therefore, he said that those who give rise to doubt and confusion regarding the world are called "dark-bodied" (mingshen).
As stated in the sūtra,
there are five kinds of mental obstructions:
the first is doubt regarding the Buddha.
Second is doubt regarding the Dharma;
third is doubt regarding the precepts;
fourth is doubt regarding the teachings.
Fifth is anger toward the Saṃgha.
As that sūtra states,
there are five mental obstructions.
What are the five?
They are doubt and hesitation regarding the Great Teacher, the Dharma, and the teaching of the Vinaya;
failing to penetrate them; lack of faith and understanding; and the obstruction of the mind.
Regarding the disparagement of wise fellow-practitioners (sabrahmacārin) praised by the Buddha—
such as through anger, reviling, insulting, or provoking them—
one asks: what constitutes the essence of these five mental obstructions (cittakhila)?
The answer is that anger (*dveṣa*) constitutes its essence.
Of the preceding four, the first four are doubt (*vicikitsā*), and the fifth is anger.
[Objection: It may be so for anger.
What is doubt?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"There are three kinds of stumps."
They are greed, hatred, and delusion.
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* also states this:
"What is hatred?"
That is to say, regarding sentient beings, one inflicts harm and creates obstacles; since there is no place for doubt to be spoken of, it is held that the obstacle is the very nature [of the mind].
Why is this stated here?
The answer is that they are similar; for among the various afflictions (*kleśa*),
there is none that does not possess the intrinsic nature of a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) while performing the function of a fetter,

As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*:
"Doubt obscures the mind,

One does not even allow the mind to attain false certainty,

it is like a fertile field that has not been plowed or tilled.
Even if it were hard and full of stumps and brushwood,
foul weeds would not grow there,

Some say that because doubt and ill-will are similar in their respective modes of activity (*ākāra*),

Regarding similarity of aspect:

Regarding similarity of object: [because they take the same object].
Because both are characterized by a state of delight.
Question: Why is doubt regarding the Buddha designated as a "stump of the mind" (*cittakhila*), while doubt regarding the Saṃgha is not?
Answer: To give rise to groundless suspicions where they do not belong is called a "stump of the mind.
Since the Buddha is free from all evil conduct and faults, to harbor such suspicions is to act in an improper place.
One should know that the same applies to the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the teachings.
If one suspects that the Saṃgha has even a slight fault or transgression of conduct,
such a suspicion arising in that situation is not called a "stump of the mind."
Question: For what reason is anger toward the Saṃgha designated as a "mental wasteland" (*cittakhila*), but not anger toward the Buddha?
Answer: Because the Saṃgha possesses some degree of faults consisting of unwholesome conduct.
Because the nature of anger arising from such conditions is necessarily more severe, it is called a "mental thicket.
Since the Buddha is free from all evil conduct and faults, any anger that might arise would be slight; therefore, he is not said to have them.
One should know that it is likewise with respect to the Dharma, the precepts,
and the teaching. Other masters say that the "stump of the mind" (cittakhila) is designated in relation to grave transgressions.
To harbor doubt toward the Saṃgha is a grave transgression;
because it arises in relation to those who ought to be relied upon and is difficult to sever, it is not termed a "mental thicket" (*cittakhila*).
Although the Buddha is free from all faults, to give rise to anger toward him is by nature even more severe and difficult to sever, yet it is likewise not a "mental thicket."
It is the same regarding the Dharma, the precepts, and the teachings.
