Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is because the author of this treatise intended it to be so;
[this is] explained at length, up to...
Some say: it is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras,
as the sūtra says:
"O bhikṣus, you should know that when a Tathāgata appears in the world,
there appear in the world the collections of names, phrases, and syllables."
Although this has been stated, it was not analyzed.
What are the name-body (*nāmakāya*), phrase-body (*padakāya*), and syllable-body (*vyañjanakāya*)?
Now, wishing to analyze them, I compose this treatise.
Some say:
it is for the sake of enabling those who harbor doubts to attain certainty;
that is to say, this treatise analyzes various kinds of profound and subtle meanings.
There may be those who raise doubts or arguments;
although they have attained skill regarding the meaning, they may lack skill regarding the phrasing. In order to bring such doubts to a definitive resolution, [the following is stated].
This treatise was composed because [the author] has attained skill in both the words and their meaning;
some say it was written to refute the doctrines of others and to clarify one's own position.
That is to say, some maintain that the collections of names, phrases,
and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) are not substantially real entities, as the Dārṣṭāntikas do; or again,
there are those who maintain that the collections of names, phrases, and phonemes [are substantially real].
For those who maintain that sound is the intrinsic nature [of names],

in order to refute that attachment and to demonstrate that the "bodies of names" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth are substantially existent phenomena (*dravyasat*) subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayuktasaṃskāraskandha*), this treatise is composed.
Some say:
This is intended to demonstrate that the arduous efforts exerted by the World-Honored One over three incalculable eons yield a great fruit.
This means that although the Buddha should have attained parinirvāṇa countless kalpas ago,
he nevertheless spent three incalculable aeons cultivating hundreds of thousands of difficult practices and ascetic austerities.
It is solely for the benefit of others.
Now, as for benefiting others,
it must necessarily involve the body of names, the body of phrases, and the body of syllables.
They all attain skillfulness;
by virtue of this skillfulness,
they are able to explain the aggregates, elements, bases, and so forth to others.
To cause [beings] to attain nirvana, which is the ultimate benefit, is called the "great fruit.
Some say it is for the purpose of establishing the dominant conditions for the three types of enlightenment.
That is to say, if one employs superior discerning wisdom,
one perceives the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables as the Buddha’s bodhi;
if one employs middling discerning wisdom, [one perceives them as such].
To awaken to the sets of names, phrases, and syllables is called the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
If one awakens to the sets of names, phrases, and syllables with an inferior degree of awakening-wisdom, it is called the enlightenment of a śrāvaka.
Some say that this is intended to reveal that the Buddha is an infinitely and boundlessly eloquent teacher; that is to say,
the Buddha has thoroughly mastered the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables.
He is able to preach the Dharma for sentient beings inexhaustibly.
Some say this is intended to distinguish the World-Honored One from the Pratyekabuddhas.
This means that both Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas are able to awaken by themselves without relying on a teacher;
however, regarding names and so forth, only the Buddha possesses perfect knowledge,
whereas the Pratyekabuddha does not.
Some say: it is for the purpose of illuminating and making known to others the natures and characteristics of the two dharmas— defilement and purity.
This means that the group of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth are the fundamental basis for illuminating both defilement and purity;
if these names and so forth did not exist, defilement and purification could not be manifested. Some say:
This is intended to demonstrate the observation of the sets of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth;
for failure to observe them leads to great disadvantage and great loss.
That is to say, for the practitioner:
If one can observe the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables, then one will be able to subdue them—
just as a mountain of accumulated afflictions and evil conduct is subdued—
because one is able to endure even when subjected to insults and humiliation.
If one does not examine the sets of names, phrases, and syllables,
then afflictions and unwholesome conduct will flow on without interruption,
like a river. As it was said when rebuking Prince Vīraśikha:
"How can this slave-girl ascend my Śākya hall?
Because he was unable to discern these four or five syllables,
he led countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to fall into the great hells.
Question: When that practitioner is reviled by others, how does he observe so that anger does not arise?
Answer: Regarding what was said about the *krośa-māna* (the one who is full of pride): [it refers to the following].
This is to revile me.
If one were to omit the character "A" (阿), it would merely be calling out to me;
if one were to omit the character "Man" (縵), it would simply be the sound of reviling.
If both syllables are removed, it is simply called "calling out.
When that practitioner is reviled by another,
they should then carefully examine these various syllables.
If there is no "a," why should I become angry when you call me?
If there is no "man," it is merely a sound of abuse;
since it does not concern me, on what basis could I become angry?
If both words are absent, it is simply called "calling out.
Why should I suffer and give rise to anger?
Furthermore, when a practitioner is reviled by another, [he should reflect as follows:]
He then carefully examines these various syllables:
"This one is an insult; that one is a praise.
If I were to give rise to anger or sorrow toward this [insult]," he reflects.
If one gives rise to greed and joy regarding others,
then one will be constantly sorrowful, constantly joyful, constantly angry, and constantly greedy.
Who could have such exhaustion and suffering as I do?
Through this observation, aversion does not arise.
Furthermore, when a practitioner is reviled by others,
they carefully observe that there is no other distinct character besides those who praise them.
However, regarding the syllables used in reviling me,
their sequence is merely inverted; since these words for praise and revilement are neither fixed nor certain,
one should not give rise to sorrow or joy within them.
Consequently, one does not give rise to anger when reviled.
Furthermore, when a practitioner is reviled by others,
they should carefully examine such verbal karma.
By whom is this accomplished?
Is it the one who reviles,
or is it my own self?
He immediately recognizes that this is the accomplishment of the reviler and thinks:
"That person is reviling themselves; what concern is it of mine?"
Therefore, one does not give rise to anger.
Furthermore, when a practitioner is reviled by another,
they should contemplate all phenomena within the body of the reviler.
Whether one scolds me frequently or scolds the Dharma frequently,
one immediately knows that the Dharma which is scolded comprises only a single element (dhātu),
a single base (āyatana), and a small portion of a single aggregate (skandha).
The non-abusive dharma (adūṣaṇā-dharma) comprises seventeen elements (dhātu),
a portion of one element, eleven bases (āyatana), a portion of one base,
four aggregates (skandha), and a portion of one aggregate.
One should form this thought:
"Of those who revile me,
they revile my qualities to a small degree, but fail to revile my qualities to a great degree."
Why should one give rise to anger toward the many things forgotten rather than the few?
Furthermore, when a practitioner is reviled by another,
they should contemplate each single syllable for the duration of a single kṣaṇa.
It certainly cannot constitute an act of abuse.
There are no multiple syllables or multiple moments of thought that arise simultaneously;
when the preceding syllable arises, the subsequent syllable has not yet occurred.
If the subsequent word has arisen while the preceding word has already ceased,
there is no basis for it being an insult at all;
it is merely a false discrimination to claim that it is an insult, and therefore one should not become angry.
Furthermore, when a practitioner is reviled by others,
they should contemplate that both their own body and the reviler perish moment by moment,
being just about to undergo conceptual differentiation.
Both the one who reviles and I have already ceased to exist;
toward whom, then, should anyone give rise to anger?
Through this contemplation, anger does not arise.
Furthermore, when a practitioner is reviled by others,
they should contemplate that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are devoid of self and what belongs to a self (ātman-ātmīya),
and that neither an agent nor an experiencer can be found.
"Why should one give rise to anger toward a mere collection of empty formations?
Some say that this treatise was composed for this reason.
This is to demonstrate that this treatise is complete in its exposition of meaning;
that is to say, within this treatise, the differentiation of the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena is called the "completeness of meaning."
In this context, the analysis of the sets of names (nāmakāya), phrases (padakāya), and phonemes (vyañjanakāya) is called the "explanation of the phrasing" (vyañjana).
Some say it is for the purpose of demonstrating that the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes possess great utility.
That is to say, it reveals the immeasurable gateways of meaning concerning the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields through names and so forth,
and is able to praise and describe the boundless merits of the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
For these various reasons and conditions,
this treatise is composed.
What is meant by "multifarious name-group" (*nāmakāya*)?
Answer: It refers to many names, synonyms, alternative expressions, designations, conceptualizations, conventional designations, and provisional establishments;
this is called a "group of many names" (*nāmakāya*).
In this context, the proponent is skillful regarding the phrasing.
Because many phrases collectively manifest a single name, as they are all distinct names for that same name. Question:
Why, in this context, is the "body of multiple names" (nāmakāya) asked about?
"And why does it not inquire about names and name-bodies?
The answer is: "Because this is the intention of the author of the treatise," and so on, as explained at length.
Some say that regarding those things which ought to be asked but were not,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Some say that both "name" (nāman) and "name-body" (nāmakāya) are subsumed within the "multitude of name-bodies" (bahunāmakāya).
The question concerning "multiple name-bodies" (nāmakāya) is a comprehensive inquiry.
Some say that this is what was taught in the Sūtras.
One should not ask this.
The author of the treatise [states] that the sūtra asks only about the "body" (kāya) because it possesses many names.
The proponent cannot increase or decrease anything therein.
Question: If that is so, why is it asked whether there are many "name-bodies" (nāmakāya)?
Yet one answers by means of names.
The answer by name is the root;
the fulfillment of names constitutes the "name-body" (nāmakāya).
Because a "name-body" (nāmakāya) consists of many names,
it is called a "body.
Some say that this statement is made based on the principle of successive causality (pāramparyahetu).
It is according to the principle of descendants:
that is to say, based on a name there is a "name-body" (nāmakāya),
and because based on a name-body there are many name-bodies.
Question: What is the nature of names?
Answer: They are subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*);
the same applies to phrases.
Question: For what reason is it called "name" (nāma)?
Answer: "Name" is so called because it conforms to naming;
it is called "name" because it functions as a summons, and it is called "conforming" because it accords with that [naming].
Whatever one performs, it immediately accords with that;
for this reason, the term "summoning" (āhvāna) is established.
It is like seeking that which is destined to be joined; when the opportunity arises, they should naturally unite.
Following its formation, it turns so as to accord with meaning.
In this context, it is called "name" (*nāman*) because it possesses three meanings: it conforms to, it summons, and it is named.
Mental states and mental factors possess these qualities of conforming and summoning.
Because it lacks the sense of "conjoining," it is not called a "name.

Other non-associated factors, material phenomena, and unconditioned phenomena also lack the sense of "summoning," even though they possess "concomitance" or "conjoining"; therefore, they are likewise not names.
Question: What is the meaning of "name-body" (*nāmakāya*)?
Answer: It has the meaning of a collection of two names;
therefore, a single name is not called a "name-body."
Question: What is the meaning of "multitude-body" (*nāma-kāya*)? Answer: It means an accumulation of many names.
For instance, one elephant or two elephants are not called a "multitude-elephant-body";
it is only when there are many elephants that they are called a "multitude-elephant-body."
The same applies to horses and so forth.
It is likewise for the group of phrases (*padakāya*), the group of multi-phrases, the group of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*), and the group of multi-phonemes.
Within this, there are names (*nāman*).
There are name-bodies;
there are many name-bodies;
and there are those produced by a single syllable.
There are names produced by two syllables and names produced by many syllables.
Among those produced by a single syllable:
Regarding the fact that a single syllable has only a name, while two syllables have a "name-body" (nāmakāya) and many syllables have a "phrase-body" (padakāya):
some wish to base this on three syllables,
while others wish to base it on four syllables.
Regarding the names produced by two syllables:
while there is only a "name" (nāman) in the case of two syllables, there is a "name-body" (nāmakāya) and a "multiple name-body" (bahunāmakāya) in the case of four syllables;
some maintain that these should be based on six syllables.
There are those who maintain that it depends on eight syllables:
within a name consisting of three syllables,
there is only a "name" (nāman), whereas within six syllables, there is both a "name-body" (nāmakāya) and a "multiple-name-body" (bahunāmakāya).
Some maintain that it relies on nine syllables;
others maintain that it relies on twelve syllables.
This refers to the names arising from four syllables.
Regarding the four syllables, there is only the name; regarding the eight syllables, there is the name-body (*nāmakāya*) and the multiple-name-body (*anekanāmakāya*).
Some maintain that these depend upon twelve syllables.
Some maintain that [the name] is based on sixteen syllables;
one should know that other names with many syllables are likewise understood through this gateway.
Other masters say:
Within that which is designated by a single syllable,
when one syllable is uttered once, there is merely a name;
when that same syllable is uttered a second time, there is a "name-body" (nāmakāya).
Regarding this very syllable, it has many names and many bodies when pronounced three or four times.
It should be understood that the same applies to the names and so forth produced by two syllables.
What is a multi-word body (*padakāya*)?
The answer is that the various phrases fulfill meanings that have not yet been fulfilled;
the conjunction of these within [a single expression] is called a "phrase-aggregate" (padakāya).
To establish this meaning, a scriptural passage is cited as proof.
As the Blessed One has said:
"Commit no evil; practice all that is good; purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
These four lines are each capable of being fully realized.
The connection therein of meanings that have not yet been fully satisfied is called a "group of many phrases" (padakāya).
In this way, each of these four phrases is capable of fulfilling [the meaning].
Regarding the connection of meanings that are not yet complete within each individual phrase:
this refers to each of the four phrases being distinct from one another.
The combination of various syllables manifests the meaning of being incomplete;
alternatively, the combination of various phrases manifests the meaning of forming a verse as a multi-phrase body.
In each and every phrase, there is both a thesis and an explanation:
"all evils" is the thesis,
and "do not commit them" is the explanation.
Up to the phrase "these Buddhas," this constitutes the thesis;
"the teaching" constitutes the explanation.
Therefore, within this verse, four matters are fulfilled.
First is the heading, second is the explanation, third are the phrases, and fourth are the verses.
If one speaks of various evils, it is complete in the heading,
but incomplete in the explanation, the phrases, and the verses.
Furthermore, it is said that if the three types of names— the summary, the explanation, and the sentence— are complete,
yet the verse itself is not yet complete; furthermore,
it is said that if all the virtuous qualities are complete within the summary, the explanation, and the sentence of the general verse.
If, regarding individual phrases, the designation is complete and not otherwise;
and even further, when it is said "these Buddhas," if, regarding the summary verse, the designation and the explanatory phrases are complete;
and if, regarding individual phrases, the designation is complete and not otherwise.
Furthermore, it is said that all teachings are complete.
In this verse, eight characters form a line,
and thirty-two characters constitute a stanza.
Many verses in the various sūtras and śāstras rely on this system;
even the calculation of written characters follows this system.
Furthermore, from six syllables up to twenty-six syllables, all may constitute a verse-line (*pāda*).
Now, that which consists of six syllables is called the initial phrase;
that which consists of twenty-six syllables is called the final phrase;
and that which has fewer than six syllables is called a short phrase.
That which exceeds twenty-six syllables is called a long verse.
What is a "multitude of phonemes" (vyañjana-kāya)?
Answer: A collection of various syllables is what is meant by a multitude of phonemes.
To establish this meaning, a scriptural passage is cited as proof, as the Blessed One said:
"The desire [for expression] is the basis of the verse; the text is the syllable; the verse depends upon the name."
Regarding the composer of the verse, "desire" here refers to the aspiration,
joy, and delight in composing the verse.
As for the basis of the verse, this desire is the cause, the collection, and the condition for its arising.
Regarding the statement "the *vyañjana* (phoneme) is the *akṣara* (syllable)":
it is called a *vyañjana* because it skillfully and clearly manifests [meaning];
this is precisely the *akṣara*, for it is without transition or exhaustion.
This demonstrates that the verse which serves as the manifestor has syllables as its essence.
Regarding the statement "the verse depends upon names":
the verse is a conventional existence established in dependence upon names.
Furthermore, it is based on the words and phrases that one speaks provisionally by relying on names;
here, the term "based on" (niśritya) is like a forest being based on its trees,
as well as for the sake of composing verses.
One who reflects and observes while composing various gāthās is called a "maker of verses" (kāraka).
Just as a snake relies on its hole and water relies on its spring, and milk relies on the udder, the verse relies upon its maker;
thus, the support and that which is supported differ in name.
It should be understood that herein there are names, name-bodies, and multiple name-bodies;
there are phrases, phrase-bodies, and multiple phrase-bodies.
There are syllables (*vyañjana*), there are bodies of syllables (*vyañjanakāya*), and there are multiple bodies of syllables.
Within a single syllable, there is a name (*nāman*) but no body of names (*nāmakāya*) and no multiple bodies of names.
There are no phrases (*pada*), no bodies of phrases (*padakāya*), and no multiple bodies of phrases.
There are phonemes (*vyañjana*) but no phoneme-body (*vyañjanakāya*), nor a plurality of phoneme-bodies.
Regarding two syllables (*akṣara*), there is a name (*nāman*) and a name-body (*nāmakāya*), but no plurality of name-bodies.
There are no phrases (*pada*), no phrase-body (*padakāya*), and no plurality of phrase-bodies.
There are syllables (*vyañjana*) and groups of syllables (*vyañjanakāya*), but no plurality of groups of syllables.
Within four syllables, there is a name (*nāman*) and a group of names (*nāmakāya*), but no plurality of groups of names.
There are no phrases (*pada*), no groups of phrases (*padakāya*), and no plurality of groups of phrases.
There are syllables (*vyañjana*) and groups of syllables (*vyañjanakāya*), and there are many groups of syllables.
Within eight syllables, there is a name (*nāman*) and a group of names (*nāmakāya*), and there are many groups of names.
There are phrases (*pada*), but there is no group of phrases (*padakāya*), nor are there many groups of phrases.
There are syllables (*vyañjana*) and collections of syllables (*vyañjanakāya*), and there are many collections of syllables.
Regarding the sixteen characters, there are names (*nāman*) and collections of names (*nāmakāya*), and there are many collections of names.
There are phrases (*pada*) and collections of phrases (*padakāya*), but there are no multiple collections of phrases.
There are syllables (*vyañjana*), groups of syllables (*vyañjanakāya*), and multiple groups of syllables.
Among the thirty-two letters, there are names (*nāman*), groups of names (*nāmakāya*), and multiple groups of names.
There are phrases (*pada*), groups of phrases (*padakāya*), and multiple groups of phrases.
There are syllables (*vyañjana*), there are bodies of syllables (*vyañjanakāya*), and there are multiple bodies of syllables.
By means of these, one should understand, according to reason, the extent of what has been taught regarding the various collections of phonemes (*akṣara*).
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Fourteen. At the end of the sixteenth leaf of the Song edition of this fascicle, the text "Furthermore, when the practitioner attains...

follows immediately, yet the subsequent portion beginning with "When one is reviled by others" is missing from the upper part of the manuscript. From there, it proceeds through a detailed examination up to the sixty-eight lines consisting of twenty characters and four-character phrases; these are now supplied based on the two extant editions.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Fifteen.
Composed by Five Hundred Great Arhats and others;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
7. In the first section of the *Saṃyukta-skandha*, the second sub-section on "Wisdom" (Jñāna-nikāya), part seven: Question:
Is [the state] bound to the stage according to the expression, or is it bound to the stage according to the person (*pudgala*)?
Some say that names are bound to the stage of speech;
they speak as follows:
One born in the desire realm,
if they produce speech of the desire realm,
possesses that body of the desire realm.
Speech of the desire realm;
names of the desire realm;
the meaning expressed is either bound to the three realms or unbound.
If one speaks the language of the first dhyāna,
that body belonging to the desire realm produces the speech and the designation of the first dhyāna.
The meaning of what has been said is as previously explained.
Regarding one who is born in the first dhyāna:
if they produce speech belonging to the first dhyāna, that is the body of the first dhyāna.
The speech of the first dhyāna;
the name of the first dhyāna;
the meaning of what is spoken is as previously explained.
If one produces speech of the desire realm with a body of the first dhyāna,
that speech belongs to the desire realm and its designation is "desire realm";
the meaning of what is spoken is as previously explained.
For one born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna,
if they produce speech belonging to the desire realm,
that body of theirs belongs to the second, third, or fourth dhyāna.
Speech of the desire realm is named "desire realm";
the meaning of what is spoken is as previously explained.
If one produces speech of the first dhyāna, [it is named "first dhyāna"].
The body of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas,
as well as the speech and names of the first dhyāna,
have meanings as previously explained.
Question: If that is so, do the three higher dhyānas have names?
Some say: [they do].
No. Some say there is.
Yet it cannot be so stated.
The critique says:
He should not have made such a statement.
It is better to say that it does not exist than to say that it exists,
yet it cannot be said [to exist] because it serves no purpose; so some say.
It is said that this belongs to the level (bhūmi) associated with the person (pudgala).
They explain it thus:
one who is born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
If one utters speech belonging to the desire realm,
that speech of the desire realm, the name of the desire realm,
and the meaning expressed therein are as previously described.
If one produces speech of the first dhyāna,
that speech of the first dhyāna belonging to a body in the desire realm is designated by the name "desire realm."
The meaning of what has been stated is as previously explained.
One who is born in the first dhyāna, if they produce speech of the first dhyāna,
[is said to speak with a voice of the first dhyāna].
Its body belongs to the first dhyāna, its speech belongs to the first dhyāna,
and its name belongs to the first dhyāna;
the meaning of what is spoken is as previously explained.
If one produces speech of the desire realm,
that speech of the desire realm belonging to a body of the first dhyāna receives the designation "first dhyāna.
The meaning of what is spoken is as previously explained.
For one who has been born into the second, third, or fourth dhyāna,
if they produce speech belonging to the desire realm,
that body of theirs belongs to the second, third, or fourth dhyāna.
The speech of the desire realm and the names of the second, third,
and fourth dhyānas have meanings as previously explained.
If one utters speech belonging to the first dhyāna,
that speech of the first dhyāna belongs to the bodies of those in the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
The names of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas have meanings as previously explained.
Question: If that is so, then...
Is there a designation for the formless realm?
Some say there is not.
Some say that it exists,
yet it cannot be described.
The critique states: He should not make such a statement.
It would be better to say that it does not exist rather than saying that it cannot be said to exist;
for it is impossible to speak of it because it serves no purpose.
As it is said regarding names, so it is with phrases and syllables.
Question: Are names and so forth included within the category of sentient beings?
"Are they not included among non-sentient things?
Answer: "They are included among sentient things.
Question: "Are names and so forth appropriated?"
Is it non-appropriated?
Answer: It is non-appropriated.
Question: Are name and so forth considered nurtured (aupacayika)?
Is this a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*), or is it born of maturation (*vipākaja*)?
Answer: It is a result of outflow.
They are neither nurtured (*aupacayika*) nor born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Question: If the name-aggregates (*nāma-kāya*, etc.
are not born of maturation, how is this reconciled with the Sūtra?
As it is said:
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"I also say this."
The name arises from karma; it is the fruit of that karma.
The answer is that the name is also the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) of karma, and therefore it is stated thus:
that is to say, by performing wholesome karma, one also obtains a good reputation.
However, it is not a maturation (vipāka).
Question: Are names and so forth wholesome or unwholesome?
Is it indeterminate?
Answer: It is indeterminate, because it is not a karmic action.
Because they arise from volition, like the four great elements.
Question: Who accomplishes [the possession of] names and so forth?
Is it the speaker or the spoken?
If so, what is the fault?
If it were the speaker, then it would be the Arhat.
One would have to accomplish defiled dharmas;
one who is free from the defilement of desire would have to accomplish unwholesome dharmas;
and an ordinary worldling would have to accomplish noble dharmas.
One who has severed the roots of goodness should still be endowed with wholesome dharmas,
because it is also said that Arhats and others possess defiled dharmas and so forth.
If this is what is being asserted:
If that were so, then external objects and even unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) should also achieve [the status of] names and so forth, since they too are things that are spoken of.
The answer is: only the speaker is able to achieve names and so forth.
Question: If that is so, the latter objection is well resolved;
how, however, is the former objection resolved?
Answer: Although Arhats and others do possess names such as "defiled" and so forth, [they are not so in reality].
Yet, it does not accomplish afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and other such dharmas, because names such as "afflicted" all refer to dharmas that are non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Question: Can a single moment of mind give rise to a single utterance?
Question: Can a single moment of speech express a single syllable?
Answer: A Buddha’s mind can produce a single utterance in a single moment;
a single moment of speech can express a single syllable.
The minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can produce a single utterance in a single moment,
yet a single momentary utterance cannot express a single syllable;
for when they pronounce the sound "a," it necessarily takes many moments.
For this reason, the Buddha alone possesses speech that is swift and incisive, with a flawless melodic resonance and supreme eloquence.
Question: Do all phenomena of the three periods of time each possess their own respective names for those three periods?
Answer: There are.
Those past phenomena that possess the designation "past" are, for example, the past Buddhas.
By means of such names,
past phenomena and all past dharmas are spoken of;
there are also those that have future names.
Just as a future Buddha, by such names,
speaks of past phenomena and all past dharmas.
There are those who have names in the present,
such as the Buddhas of the present,
by whom they are designated with such names.
He speaks of past phenomena, future phenomena, and present phenomena;
the detailed exposition is likewise so. Question: Do all names manifest their meanings?
Answer: All names manifest their meanings.
Question: If these names are used to manifest [the refutation of] eternalism and nihilism,
then what of a second head, a third hand, a sixth aggregate,
a thirteenth base, or a nineteenth element?
What does this name signify?
Answer: This name signifies the notions of annihilationism and eternalism, and so forth.
Question: If this name signifies that all phenomena are without self, [how is it so?]
What is it that this name does not manifest?
Some say: except for its own nature (svabhāva) and its co-existent dharmas (sahabhū-dharma).
Others can all be manifested.
Some say that,
with the exception of its own nature, everything else can be manifested.
Some say that,
with the exception of four characters, all others are able to manifest [the meaning];
others say that all of them manifest it entirely.
That is to say, herein *sa* manifests *na*,
*na* manifests *sa*;
*da* manifests *ma*.
Polishing can bring about manifestation; therefore,
although everything is manifested herein,
there is no fault of manifesting an intrinsic nature where none exists.
Question: Between names and meanings, which is more numerous?
Answer: Meanings are many and names are few. Why is this so?

In terms of meaning (*artha*), it subsumes seventeen elements (*dhātu*), a portion of one element; eleven bases (*āyatana*), a portion of one base; four aggregates (*skandha*), and a portion of one aggregate.
In terms of name (*nāman*), it subsumes one element, one base, and a portion of one aggregate.
Some say that the names are many while the referents are few. Why is this so?
Because each individual meaning has many names,
as established in the ancient Nighaṇṭu lexicon,
where each single meaning has a thousand names.
Subsequently, these were further abbreviated;
for each individual meaning, only one hundred names were retained,
and now, for each individual meaning, only ten names are retained.
Furthermore, because a speaker of the Dharma explains a single meaning through immeasurable names,
such a speaker has many meanings but few words. Why is this so?
Because names are also meanings;
even if names were not meanings, meanings would still be more numerous,
as they encompass seventeen elements (*dhātus*) and a portion of one element.
...and so on, as explained at length.
How much more so the name itself,
since it is also manifested by other names.

Thus, while "meaning" (artha) encompasses the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha), "name" (nāman) encompasses only a small portion of one element, one base, and one aggregate.
Question: If "name" is also "meaning," [why is there this distinction?]
What is the distinction between name (*nāman*) and meaning (*artha*)?
Answer: That which can manifest is the name; that which is manifested is the meaning.
Furthermore, the name is non-material (*arūpa*).
The meaning [of "name"] applies to both the material and the non-material;
its designation is exclusively invisible.
Its meaning applies to both the visible and the invisible.
The name [nāman] is exclusively non-obstructive;
its referent [artha] extends to both the obstructive and the non-obstructive.
The name is exclusively with-outflows [sāsrava].
The meaning [of "name"] applies to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);
the designation (*nāman*) applies only to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). The meaning [of "designation"] applies to both the conditioned and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, names are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta), whereas referents (artha) pertain to all three categories: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Names alone fall within the three periods of time.
The meaning [of "name"] extends to those belonging to the three time periods as well as those transcending them;
however, the designation [of "name"] is restricted to being bound to the realms of desire and form.
The meaning [of "name"] extends to being bound to all three realms as well as being unbound.
The name refers exclusively to that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
its meaning, however, extends to the learner, the non-learner, and that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
The name refers exclusively to that which is abandoned through cultivation.
The meaning [of the term] applies to that which is abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*), that which is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and that which is not abandoned (*aheya*).
Furthermore, the name refers exclusively to what is non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*),
whereas the meaning applies to both the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and the non-defiled.
Just as with the defiled and the undefiled,
the culpable and the blameless,
the obscured and the unobscured, so too are there those that involve regression and those that do not.
The same applies to black dharmas and white dharmas.
Furthermore, while the term "without maturation" (avipāka) is used,
its meaning extends to both those with maturation (savipāka) and those without maturation.
The name "non-resultant" (avipāka) applies specifically to that which is not a maturation; its meaning, however, extends to both the resultant and the non-resultant.
The name "dissociated" (viprayukta) applies generally.
The meaning applies to both associated and dissociated [dharmas].
Just as with associated and dissociated [dharmas],
there are those that have a basis and those that lack a basis.
There are those with an object of focus and those without an object of focus;
there are those with mental aspects and those without mental aspects;
and it is the same for those with alertness and those without alertness.
Furthermore, names are subsumed solely within the truths of suffering and its origin;
their referents (artha) pertain to all four truths as well as that which is not subsumed under the truths.
It is by means of such [distinctions] that [the classification is established].
Regarding the distinction between names and meanings:
one asks whether meaning can be expressed or whether it cannot be expressed.
If that were the case, what fault would there be?
If it could be so stated,
then stating "fire" should burn the tongue.
If one speaks of a knife, it should cut the tongue;
if one speaks of impurity, it should defile the tongue;
if one speaks of drink, it should quench thirst.
"Speaking of food should eliminate hunger," and so forth.
If such things were inexpressible, [how could this be so?]"
What is meant by "seeking in a perverted manner"?
It is like seeking an elephant and obtaining a horse,
or seeking a horse and obtaining an elephant.
How are such statements as these to be reconciled with what is taught in the sūtras?
For example, it is said:
The Dharma I teach is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end;
its words and meaning are skillful and subtle,
and its ultimate meaning is ineffable.
Question: If that is so, the previous objection has been well resolved.
How then is what was sought not erroneous?
Answer: At the beginning of the kalpa, human beings...
The conventional designations and concepts for elephants and so forth are established in common;
having been transmitted from one to another,
they ensure that what is sought is not erroneous.
Some say: speech can give rise to names, and names can manifest meanings;
although speech cannot directly express the attainment of meaning, it does so through a successive sequence.
Because it follows the principle of "son and grandson," there is no error regarding what is sought in relation to elephants and so forth.
Question: How then should one interpret the statement in the Sūtra? As it says:
"The Dharma I teach is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end;
its phrasing and meaning are exquisite.
Regarding this, the Venerable Vasumitra offers the following explanation:
Speech is able to give rise to phonemes, and phonemes are able to manifest meaning;
therefore, this statement is made.
Furthermore, it is said:
This statement was made in order to distinguish [the Buddha's teaching] from that of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
That is to say, the teachings expounded by the various non-Buddhists are either deficient in meaning or entirely devoid of meaning.
The Blessed One’s teachings possess both meaning and manifold significance;
therefore, it is said:
"The Dharma I have taught is skillful in both its phrasing and its meaning."
Furthermore, it was said:
"The words and meanings spoken by the non-Buddhists are contradictory,
whereas the words and meanings spoken by the World-Honored One are consistent."
This statement is made in order to distinguish it from those [other categories].

Question: Since the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*) are subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāraskandha*), for what reason does the Buddha state that the four aggregates are called "name" (*nāman*)?
Answer: The Buddha establishes two general categories for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*):
namely, form (*rūpa*) and non-form (*arūpa*).
Form constitutes the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
That which is not form consists of the four aggregates beginning with sensation (*vedanā*).
Within this non-material aggregate,
there exists that which can manifest the names of all phenomena.
Therefore, it is not that a collection of matter is collectively designated as "name.
Some say that because material phenomena are coarse and manifest, they are designated as "matter" (rūpa).
It is not that form is subtle and hidden;
rather, it is called "name" because it is manifested by names.
In reality, however, names and so forth are subsumed solely within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
Names are of six kinds:
first, names of qualities;
second, names of genus.
1. Names according to the three time periods;
2. Names according to one's wishes;
3. Names arising from karma.
Sixth is the name based on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the name based on qualities (*guṇa*), this refers to establishing a name in reliance upon qualities,
as explained.
Those who recite the Sūtras are called masters of the sūtras;
if they understand them, or those who recite the Vinaya, are called masters of the discipline (vinayadhara).
If they understand it...
Those who recite the Abhidharma are called masters of treatises (śāstrin).
Those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry are called stream-enterers (srotāpanna),
and so on, up to those who have attained the fruit of arhatship, who are called arhats.
Regarding such categories as these,
"names based on genus" refers to names established in reliance upon a genus.
Just as one born in a city is called a city-dweller,
one born in a village is called a villager,
and one born into the kṣatriya caste is called a kṣatriya.
Even those born among the Śūdra caste are called Śūdras;
such are the cases.
Regarding the designation based on time:
this refers to designations established in dependence upon specific periods of time,
such as being called a "child" during one's childhood.
Up until the time of old age, one is called an "elder," and so forth.
These are names used according to one's desire.
This refers to establishing a name according to one's wishes,
such as at the time of birth,
or by one's parents and so forth.
Or śramaṇas and others may establish names for them;
such are the cases.
Regarding names derived from karma:
these are names established based on one's performed actions,
such as calling a skilled painter a "painter."
One who smelts gold and iron is called a smith of gold and iron;
such are the designations based on their defining characteristics.
This means that names are established based on characteristic marks (*nimitta*).
For example, one who holds a staff is called a "staff-bearer," and one who holds a parasol is called a "parasol-bearer."
And so forth.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of names:
first, conventional designations (prajñapti-nāman).
Second, names according to function;
third, names according to benefit;
fourth, names derived from abbreviation.
Regarding metaphorical names:
for example, calling a person who is poor and lowly "wealthy and noble," and so forth.
Regarding names according to function:
for example, that which moves with its belly is named a "belly-crawling insect," and so forth.
Regarding those names derived from benefit:
for example, one who obtains [a name] from a celestial deity is called Devadatta (God-given);
one who obtains it through a sacrificial offering is called Yajñadatta (Sacrifice-given).
Such as these. Regarding abbreviated names:
for example, one who possesses five qualities is called "one of five virtues" (pañcaguṇa).
Those who are bound to and dependent upon a king are called "king's men" (rājapuruṣa), and so forth.
Furthermore, names are of two kinds.
First is the name of birth;
second is the name of action.
Regarding the name of birth:
Regarding those who create names, such as Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas:
this refers to the naming performed by parents and others.
Some say that "birth-name" refers to the name assigned by parents and others at the time of birth;
"created name" refers to...
This refers to the names established by friends and acquaintances at a later time.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of names:
first, names that possess characteristics (sanimitta-nāman).
Second, names of the signless.
Names of the characterized refer to such things as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth.
Regarding names without characteristics:
for example, when there are human beings with mental and emotional states such as arising and so forth,
if a Buddha appears in the world, then names with characteristics are many and names without characteristics are few.
If [the Tathāgata] does not appear in the world, then there are no designations; thus, those with designations are few.
Question: Is the designation "fire" characterized by signs (*sanimitta*) or is it signless (*animitta*)?
Answer: If one says "Śikhin," it is a name with characteristics;
if one says "Agni," it is a name without characteristics.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of names:
first, common names;
second, unique names.
Non-common names are,
for example, "Buddha," "Dharma," "Saṃgha," "skandhas," "dhātus," and "āyatanas.
Common names are...
This refers to names established in common by other worldly people.
Other masters say that there are no names that are not shared.
Because a single dharma can establish all names,
and all dharmas can be established by a single name,
all names are common, just as common and uncommon names are.
The same applies to the name "never having been.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of names:
first, fixed names; second, [provisional names].
Second, names that are not fixed.
Fixed names are,
for example, Sumeru, the great ocean, islands, and so forth.
Regarding the term "indeterminate" (aniyata):
it refers to names established by worldly convention among others.
Other masters say:
There is no fixed name.
Why is this? Because [names such as] Sumeru and so forth...
In border regions, various names are also applied;
here in this land, the verses of the text are likewise given other names.
Thus it is said that Sumeru and the others have fixed names.
Since names such as Sumeru were already established at the time of the initial formation of the eon,
it is asked: when all things were destroyed during the preceding period of dissolution,
who transmitted those names once this eon had been formed?
Answer: There are certain rishis who have attained the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), and they remember the events of previous kalpas and transmit those names.
Alternatively, it may be due to the natural power of the laws of existence (*dharmatā*) for the people at the beginning of a kalpa.
As one thinks, that name suddenly appears before the mind.
One asks: regarding all names that exist, do they all pre-exist through successive oral transmission, or are they newly established?
Answer: Names such as Sumeru and others existed previously;
other names are not fixed, for some are newly established.
Furthermore, names are of two kinds:
first, those that express the essence;
second, those that express function.
Names that express the essence (svabhāva) are,
for example, "fruit in a basin" or "person in a house.
Names that express function (kāritra) are...
Regarding those such as the reciter and the chanter,
some say that the name denotes the essential substance.
Those that express functions through their names are like solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion;
those that express functions through their actions are like supporting, gathering, maturing, and growing.
Some say that names which express the essence refer to things such as the various evils,
while names which express function [refer to...]
This refers to "do not act" and so forth.
Question: Is "name" (nāma) something that has a limit?
Some say as follows:
It is called "limitless" because dharmas are limitless;
for each and every dharma has many names.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
It is called "having a limit" because only a Buddha can know it and no one else can;
because the Buddha can know the limit of names, he is called the "Omniscient One."
Some say that only Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas know the limit of names;
others cannot know it.
Some say that the Buddhas,
the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Śrāvakas who have reached the further shore know the limit of names,
whereas others cannot know it.
The commentary states:
The former explanation is superior;
only a Buddha can know the ultimate limit of its nature.
Because all others lack omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Question: Whether a Buddha exists or not, the world always possesses the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*).
For what reason, then, does the Sūtra say:
When a Tathāgata appears in the world, various types of name-aggregates (nāmakāya) and so forth appear in the world.
Answer: This statement is made based on his unique (asādhāraṇa) names.
Just as the names "Buddha," "Dharma," and "Saṅgha," as well as the aggregates,
elements, and sense-bases, only come into existence when a Buddha appears in the world.
Some say that only when a Buddha appears in the world do there exist [teachings] conducive to liberation and conducive to emptiness and selflessness.
It opposes the suffering of birth and death and opposes the notions of "I" and "mine.
It severs all views, gives rise to awakening-intention (*bodhicitta*),
turns away from afflictions, and inclines toward the essential path of liberation.
Cessation of delusion gives rise to wisdom;
severing doubt gives rise to certainty;
weariness with birth and death leads to delight in nirvana.
They disparage non-Buddhist paths and praise the True Dharma;
such as these, the collections of names,
phrases, and syllables appear in the world.
At other times it is not so; therefore, this statement was made.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There are three bases for speech."
There is no fourth or fifth.
What are the three?
They are called "formerly existing dharmas" based on the past.
Based on the future, one speaks of "future dharmas";
based on the present, one speaks of "present dharmas.
The question asks: by what is their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) established?
The *Prakaraṇapāda* states:
"It is comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
It further asks: "That which is speech is precisely this; its basis is called 'name' (*nāman*)."
It should be comprised of only one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*).
Why, then, is it said to be comprised of eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates?
The answer is that that treatise should have stated this.
When it is said that [the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates] are subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate,
yet are also said to be subsumed under eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates,
this statement is made on the basis of their mutual causal relationship.
That is to say, speech proceeds in dependence upon names, and names proceed in dependence upon meanings.
Within these meanings, the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas) are fully present; for meaning is the ultimate basis upon which words revolve.
Both the speaker and the listener do so for the sake of the meaning;
therefore, that treatise, relying on indirect causes,
speaks of "relying on intrinsic nature."
Some say that the basis of speech consists of names and the meanings they express;
therefore, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth are fully present,
because speech proceeds in dependence upon both names and their referents.
Question: Why are only the phenomena of the three periods of time designated as the bases of speech (*vāda-niśraya*), while unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are not?
Answer: Unconditioned phenomena should also be designated as the bases of speech.
That this was not mentioned should be understood as indicating that the meaning is incomplete.
Some say that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are included within the category of the present.
Because one attains the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) by means of present dharmas.
Some say that [the teaching] mostly proceeds in dependence upon conditioned (saṃskṛta) dharmas.
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are not said to be bases of reliance (*pratisaraṇa*).
Some say that the three bases of reliance were taught in order to stop the excessive delusion of sentient beings.
Because ignorance regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is largely predominant;
some say it is because sentient beings mostly harbor doubt regarding the three periods of time.
The Buddha taught the three bases of speech (trīṇi vāgvastūni).
Some say that these three bases of speech were taught in order to stop the non-Buddhists' adherence to a self (ātman).
That is to say, the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) say:
"If there is no self (ātman), upon what does the word 'self' depend?
Therefore, the Buddha taught three kinds of bases for speech.
I say that it is because [the three times] arise based solely on the three periods of time.
Some say that the three terms "based" are stated in order to refute the denial of the two periods of past and future,
and furthermore to refute the attachment to the present as being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Since the *āśraya* (basis) is a phenomenon that possesses both substance and function, it cannot necessarily lack substance;
because unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena lack function, they are not called *āśrayas*.
Some say that conditioned phenomena are coarse and numerous, and thus are believed to exist.
Because it is easy to give rise to verbal expression, conditioned phenomena are established as the basis for speech.
Unconditioned phenomena are subtle and few; since it is difficult to give rise to verbal expression regarding their existence, they are not the basis for speech.
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke thus:
"Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are divided into two aggregates.
If within those aggregates three things can be found..."
That is to say, speech, names, and meanings are established as the bases of expression (*vāg-āśraya*).
Although meaning exists within the collection of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*),
because the other two [speech and names] are absent, it is not a basis of expression.
The Venerable One said:
"If a phenomenon has a function such that it can take or give a fruit, one may establish it as a basis for designation;
since the unconditioned has no function, it is not so described."
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"Conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) are established as the basis for expression because they possess the sense of existing simultaneously with verbal expression;
unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) are not so, and therefore they are not so described."
Question: If one speaks of future and present phenomena based on the past;
speaks of past and present phenomena based on the future;
and speaks of past and future phenomena based on the present.
To which of the bases of speech (vāg-āśraya) does that belong?
Some say it is not included within the three bases of speech;
others, however, say:
If one speaks of the future and the present based on the past,
they are subsumed within the past; likewise,
if one speaks of the past and the future based on the present.
This is then subsumed within the present.
Other masters say:
if one speaks of the future and the present based upon the past, [it is likewise subsumed].
That which is future is subsumed within the future;
that which is present is subsumed within the present, and so forth,
even when the past and future are explained in reliance upon the present.
The past is subsumed within the past, and the future is subsumed within the future;
for it was previously stated that their essence consists of their referents (*artha*).
Question: If both time periods are taught simultaneously at one time, [how is this possible]?

Alternatively, regarding the question of why the three times are said to be included within the bases of expression (*vāgvastu*), some say that they are not included among those three bases of expression.
Others say that it is according to what can manifest the name.
In which world are they included?
It is said that they are included in the world to which they depend.
Other masters say:
In whatever time the meaning thus manifested is subsumed,
it is said to be subsumed in that very time;
this is because the previously mentioned "basis of expression" (vāgvastu) has meaning as its essence.

Question: Since it is stated in the sūtra that there are only three types of speech and that this is sufficient with respect to their meaning, why does it further state that there is no fourth or fifth?
Answer: The absence of a fourth excludes a fourth time period.
It is feared that there might be those who cling to the existence of a fourth time;
[the mention of] "no fifth" excludes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*),
for it is feared that one might cling to the idea that unconditioned phenomena are a basis for designation (*adhivacana-adhiṣṭhāna*).
Some say that the two terms [“worldly” and “linguistic”] are used with emphasis to preclude other interpretations,
so as to ensure that the meaning of what is taught is determined.
This is because the sūtra establishes its discourse based on the world, taking the world as its linguistic foundation.
It is said that there are three, not four, nor five.
If one establishes the basis of speech (*vāg-āśraya*) based on appropriate attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
it should be said that there is one, and not a second or a third.
The absence of a second excludes the presence of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
The absence of a third excludes those phenomena not subsumed under proper mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
If one establishes [the path] based on serenity and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), it is said to be "based" [on them].
It should be said that there are two [bases], and no third or fourth, as explained previously.
If one establishes the statement "based on" according to the three doors of liberation,
it should be said that there are three, and no fourth or fifth, as explained previously.
If the basis for discourse is established according to the Four Noble Truths,
it should be said that there are four [bases] and no fifth or sixth, as previously explained.
If the basis for discourse is established according to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), [it should be said that there are five bases].
It should be said that there are five [foundations of mindfulness] and no sixth or seventh, as explained previously.
If one establishes the statement "relying" based on the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*),
it should be said that there are six and no seventh or eighth, as explained previously.
If one establishes the basis of speech by relying on the seven factors of enlightenment,
it should be said that there are seven and no eighth or ninth, as previously explained.
If one establishes the basis of speech by relying on the eightfold noble path...
It should be said that there are eight [stages] and no ninth or tenth, the meaning of which is as previously explained.
If one establishes the teaching based on the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*),
it should be said that there are nine and no tenth or eleventh, the meaning of which is as previously explained.
If one establishes the basis of speech by relying on the ten powers of the Tathāgata,
it should be said that there are ten [bases], with no eleventh or twelfth, as explained previously. Likewise,
if one establishes the basis of speech by relying on other dharmas, it should be explained accordingly.
This sutra establishes its discourse based on worldly conventions;
therefore, it speaks only of three [bases], not four or five.
It is stated thus within this very sutra:
One should examine a person (pudgala) by means of four criteria to determine whether that venerable one is someone with whom one may converse or with whom one may not.
What are these four?
First, the possible and the impossible;
second, the treatise on knowledge;
third, analytical discernment.
Fourth are the tracks of the path.
If one is well-established in these four,
that person may be spoken with.
One who is contrary to this cannot be spoken with.
Question: What is the distinction between these four matters?
Answer: Regarding the improper abiding in what is non-factual (asthāna): [it refers to] that which is unwholesome.
This refers to not knowing, as it truly is, what is possible and what is impossible;
and for one who does not skillfully abide in the treatises on knowledge,
it refers to not knowing, as it truly is, both knowledge and the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
Those who do not dwell securely in discernment are those who do not know the conventional and the ultimate as they truly are;
those who do not dwell securely on the path are...
This refers to not knowing, as it truly is, the practice leading to the origin of suffering and the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
Some say that this is not "improperly abiding in what is a proper basis" (sthāna); rather, it is "what is not a proper basis" (asthāna).

This refers to not knowing, as it truly is, that visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms, up to mental consciousness arising conditioned by the mind and mental phenomena; and that visual consciousness arises conditioned by the ear and so forth.
Furthermore, it is impossible for consciousness to arise with the eye and so forth as conditions for one who is not well-established in wisdom and treatises;
that is to say, one who does not know the distinctions among the ten types of knowledge as they truly are.
Those who do not dwell securely in discernment are those who do not know,
as it truly is, the sūtras of definitive meaning and the sūtras of interpretable meaning.
Those who do not dwell securely on the path are...
This refers to not knowing the four types of tracks as they truly are.
Some say that this means not being well-established in the possible and the impossible;
that is, not knowing, as it truly is, what is logical and what is illogical.
One who is not well-established in the wisdom of treatises refers to one who does not know the correct treatises of the noble ones as they truly are.
One who is not well-established in discernment refers to...
This refers to not knowing conventional designations and discursive speech as they truly are;
it refers to one who is not well-established on the path of practice,
meaning one who does not know the meaning of others' words and phrases as they truly are.
One responds immediately by distinguishing between the beginning, middle,

and end. Some say that one who does not properly abide in the principles of what is possible (*sthāna*) and what is impossible (*asthāna*) is one who cannot establish a thesis (*pakṣa*) as it truly is.
One who is not well-established in the treatises on knowledge (*jñāna-śāstra*) is one who cannot withstand the challenges and interrogations posed by others.
One who is not well-established in discernment (*vibhāga*) is one who does not properly understand the distinction between the deceptive and the real.
"One who does not dwell securely on the path" refers to one who is unable to accomplish superior awakening-wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
Some say it refers to one who does not dwell securely in the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*).
This refers to one who speaks while failing to properly establish either their own position or the opposing position;
such a person is one who does not properly establish knowledge or treatises.
This refers to not understanding that another person’s critique is preceded by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and thus being unable to properly maintain one's analytical position;
it refers to not understanding the sequential coherence of another person’s discourse.
"One who does not dwell properly on the path" means one who is unable to fulfill the superior goals they seek.
Some say it refers to one who does not dwell properly in what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).
This refers to those who do not correctly understand what is perceptible and what is imperceptible,
and who do not properly abide in the treatises on knowledge;
that is to say, they stubbornly cling to what they have previously heard and refuse to relinquish it.
Not wishing to examine the virtues and faults of what precedes and follows,
and being poorly established in discernment,
means harboring doubt in one's mind regarding the correct speech of others.
Just as one cannot distinguish whether this is rice or ghee,
so too is one who does not dwell properly on the path of practice;
that is to say, they do not understand through prior inquiry and investigation based on direct perception, inference, and authoritative scripture.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"Not being well-established in what is possible and what is impossible means not having a thorough understanding of the objects of knowledge."
One who is not well-established in the treatises on knowledge refers to one who does not properly understand the wisdom that is capable of knowing;
one who is not well-established in discernment refers to the same.
This means not correctly understanding the false and the authentic teachings;
"not abiding well in the path" means not correctly understanding false and authentic practice.
The Venerable Saṅgharakṣa said:
"Not being well-established in what is possible and what is impossible refers to that which is taught in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*."
One who does not properly understand the meaning of what is possible and what is impossible,
and who is not well-established in the treatises on knowledge,
is said to be one who does not properly understand the matters of the forty-four knowledges and the seventy-seven knowledges.
Those who do not dwell well in discernment are those who lack thorough understanding of affliction and purification;
those who do not dwell well in the path are likewise so described.
This refers to not correctly understanding the course leading to the cessation of form, up to the course leading to the cessation of consciousness.
That which is the opposite of this is called "well-established.
Furthermore, in this very sutra it is said:
One should examine a person (pudgala) by means of four criteria to determine whether that venerable one is fit for conversation or unfit for conversation.
What are these four?
First, there are questions that should be answered categorically;
second, there are questions that should be answered by way of analysis;
third, there are questions that should be answered by means of a counter-question.
Fourth, there are questions that should be set aside and not answered.
If one can answer these four types of questions as they require, one may engage in discourse with that person;
otherwise, if it is contrary to this, one should not engage in discourse.
What is meant by a question that should be answered categorically?
It is because such a question should be answered with a categorical response.
For example, suppose someone asks: "Is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?"
Is the Dharma well-expounded? Is the Saṅgha of noble conduct?
Are all conditioned phenomena impermanent?
Are all phenomena without self?
"Is nirvāṇa tranquility?
To this, one should give a categorical answer that it is indeed so in every respect.
Why should this question be answered categorically?
This question leads to meaningful benefit, leads to wholesome qualities,
accords with the holy life, gives rise to awakening and wisdom, and leads to the attainment of nirvāṇa; therefore,
this question should be answered categorically.
What is meant by a question that should be answered with analysis?
It is a question that ought to be answered through analysis, such as when someone requests:
"Please teach me the Dharma."
One should tell them: "The dharmas are of many kinds.
There are those of the past, the future, and the present;
there are those that are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate."
There are those bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form realm, and those bound to the formless realm.
There are those who are in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training.
There are those to be abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Regarding the teaching on non-abandonment of desire: what is it?
How is it that a question is called one to be answered by counter-interrogation?
It is because this question should be answered by means of a counter-interrogation.
That is to say, if someone asks, "Please teach me the Dharma," one should counter-interrogate them by saying, "The Dharmas are manifold;
which among these manifold Dharmas do you wish to ask about?"
That is to say, the past and so forth are as explained extensively above.

Question: What is the difference between a discourse that should be answered through analysis (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇīya*) and a discourse that should be answered with a counter-question (*paripṛcchā-vyākaraṇīya*)?
Answer: Although the underlying intention is without distinction, the purpose of the questions differs.
That is to say, some who ask questions do so for the sake of understanding and comprehension, while others ask for the sake of causing provocation or offense.
If one asks for the sake of understanding, one should tell them: "The dharmas are of many kinds;
there are past, future, and present," and so forth, as explained at length.
There are those abandoned by seeing, those abandoned by cultivation, and those that are not abandoned; which of these do you wish to speak of?
If one says, "Speak of past dharmas for my sake," one should tell them: "Past dharmas are also of many kinds."
There are wholesome states, unwholesome states, and indeterminate states.
If one wishes to explain which of these is intended, and someone says, "Please teach me the wholesome dharmas," one should tell them: "Wholesome dharmas are also of many kinds."
Regarding the statement that there is form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, what is intended to be explained?
If one says, "Explain the dharma of form for me," one should tell them: "The dharmas of form are also of many kinds."
Regarding the statement "there is abstention from taking life" up to "there is abstention from frivolous speech," what is intended to be explained?
If one says, "Teach me the abstention from taking life," one should tell them: "There are three kinds of abstention from taking life."
That is to say, it arises from non-attachment,
arises from non-hatred,
and arises from non-delusion.
What is intended to be said?
If one says, "Tell me that which arises from non-attachment," one should reply to them:
"That which arises from non-attachment is further of two kinds."
Regarding what is intended by the terms "manifest" (vijñapti) and "unmanifest" (avijñapti):
if one asks these questions for the sake of understanding,
then one should answer by distinguishing them in this manner.
If he asks for the purpose of causing annoyance, one should counter-interrogate him by saying: "The dharmas are manifold; which of them do you ask about?
One should then explain that there are past [dharmas], and so on, up to those that are non-interrupted.
If one says, "Speak to me of past phenomena," one should counter-interrogate him, saying:
"Past phenomena are many; which one do you ask about?
One should then explain to him the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
If someone says, "I shall explain the wholesome dharmas for you," one should counter-interrogate them, saying:
"Wholesome dharmas are many; which ones do you wish to ask about?
One should then explain them, beginning from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
If someone says, "Speak of material phenomena (rūpadharma) for my sake," one should counter-interrogate them by saying, "Material phenomena are also many; which one do you ask about?
One should then explain [the answer] as being from abstaining from taking life up to abstaining from frivolous speech.
If someone says, "Speak for me on abstaining from taking life," one should counter-interrogate them by saying, "Abstaining from taking life is also manifold; which among these do you ask about?
One should then explain [the types] from those arising from non-attachment up to those arising from non-delusion.
If one says, "Speak for me of that which arises from non-greed," one should counter-interrogate: "That which arises from non-greed is also manifold; which among them do you ask about?
One should not simply explain both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
If one asks a question for the purpose of provocation or vexation,
one should counter-interrogate them in this general manner until their questioning is exhausted or they provide the answer themselves.
Just as one asks questions for the sake of understanding conditioned phenomena,
and asks questions because of being afflicted by conditioned phenomena,
so too does one ask questions for the sake of seeking what is wholesome regarding conditioned phenomena.
Some ask in order to test the depth or shallowness of another's awakening-wisdom;
some ask in order to seek the meaning;
some ask in order to defeat another.
There is questioning because of straightforwardness;
there is questioning because of flattery and crookedness;
there is questioning because of gentleness and pliancy.
Because of the presence of arrogance, one should know that questioning is likewise [to be understood].
This is called the distinction between the two types of debate: the analytical and the counter-interrogative.
What is meant by a question that should be set aside?
It is a question that should be answered by being set aside.
That is to say, there was a non-Buddhist who came to where the Buddha was staying.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama, is the world eternal? and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding the fourfold set of propositions, beginning with "Is the world finite?
and so forth, as explained at length, the Blessed One replied:
"None of these should be declared."
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One not answer this question?
Answer: Those non-Buddhists who cling to the existence of a real self call it the "world.
Having approached the Buddha, they asked such a question.
The Buddha thought to himself: "In truth, a self certainly does not exist.
If I were to answer that it does not exist, they would say:
'I am not asking whether it exists or not.'"
If one were to answer that it is permanent or impermanent and so forth,
this would not accord with reason; since the real self was originally non-existent,
how could it be said to be permanent or impermanent?
Suppose someone were asked about the son of a barren woman:
"Is he respectful, filial, and kind-spoken?
That person would think, "A barren woman has no son."
If he answers that they do not exist, one should say to him:
"I am not asking whether they exist or not.
If I answer by saying [they consist of] respect, filial piety, and kind speech, [then it is so].
This would not be reasonable; for instance, since a barren woman has no son, how could one say that she possesses respect and so forth?
This [case] is likewise subject to the same inquiry.
Because it would not be logical for that which is neither existent nor true nor real to exist, the Buddha did not answer.
Furthermore, another non-Buddhist approached the Buddha and said to him, "Gautama."
"Is the life-principle (jīva) identical to the body, or is the life-principle different from the body?
The World-Honored One replied:
"In both cases, this question should not be answered."
Why did the Blessed One not answer this question?
The answer is that those non-Buddhists who cling to the existence of a real self, which they call the "life-principle" (jīva),
came to the Buddha and asked such a question.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"In truth, there is certainly no self.
If I were to answer that there is none, they would say this:"
I do not inquire whether [the self] exists or does not exist.
If I were to answer that it is identical to the body,
or that it is different, it would be unreasonable.
In reality, the self does not exist at all;
how, then, can it be said to be either identical to or different from the body?
It is like asking someone else whether the horns of a rabbit and the horns of an ox are similar or not.
He thinks to himself, "A rabbit's horn does not exist from the outset.
If one answers, "It does not exist," he will then say this:
I do not inquire whether [they] exist or not.
If I were to answer that they are similar or dissimilar,
it would be unreasonable.
Since a rabbit’s horn does not exist at all,
how can one say whether it is similar or dissimilar to a cow’s horn?
This is the same as the question being asked here.
Because it is neither existent, nor true, nor real,
and because it would not accord with reason, the Buddha did not answer. Furthermore,
another non-Buddhist approached the Buddha’s dwelling and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama, regarding whether the Tathāgata exists or does not exist after death, and so forth— the four propositions.
The Blessed One replied:
In all such cases, one should not provide a definitive answer.
Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One not answer this question?
Answer: Those non-Buddhists maintain that there exists a real self, which they designate as the Tathāgata.
They maintain that this self was originally non-existent, yet they ask:
"Does the Buddha exist after death, or does he not exist? and so forth, as explained at length.
The Buddha had this thought:
"Thus, that which was originally non-existent now exists;
yet a real self ultimately has no substance."
If one answers, "Even now I am still non-existent," that person should say:
"I am not asking whether you exist now or not."
If I were to answer that there is existence after death and so forth, it would be unreasonable.
Since such a real self does not even exist now,
how could it be said that there is existence after death and so forth?
The question posed was neither existent, nor true, nor real;
because it was not logically tenable, the Buddha did not answer.
Furthermore, another non-Buddhist came to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
