Do the subsequent births and so forth also include the associated dharmas?
Answer: One should know that the preceding births and so forth should also have been said to include the associated dharmas, yet they were not mentioned.
This is an incomplete statement.

Furthermore, it is in order to refute the views of those śramaṇas who hold that there is a similar continuity [of the afflictions] that they assert the existence of universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
They are the universal causes (sarvatraga-hetu) only for the latent dispositions (anuśaya).
Those associated dharmas are the universal causes only for the dharmas associated with those latent dispositions.
This is intended to exclude that [other] view and to clarify that the universal cause refers specifically to the universal latent dispositions.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and their associated dharmas (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) act as universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) for one another;
those associated dharmas and the dharmas associated with the latent dispositions, as well as the latent dispositions themselves, likewise act as universal causes for one another.
Therefore, this statement was made.

Question: Regarding the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*), are they also universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) with respect to the co-existent dharmas (*sahabhū-dharma*) and so forth associated with those proclivities?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If it is also [a cause], why is it not mentioned here?
If it is not, why is it a cause with respect to associated factors (*saṃprayuktaka-dharma*), yet not a cause with respect to coexistent factors (*sahabhū-dharma*) and the like?
It may be said that it is also [a universal cause].
This is because it serves as a universal cause for all defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*).
Question: If this is so, why is it not mentioned here?
Answer: The associated dharmas and those latent dispositions (anuśaya) share the same object of cognition (ālambana) and the same mode of activity (ākāra);
they are extremely proximate, and for this reason it is said that [the latter] give rise to [the former]. This is not the case for birth and so forth; therefore, they are not so described.
Regarding "one's own realm":
this means that the desire realm serves as a universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu) only for the desire realm;
it should be understood that the same applies to the form and formless realms.
As it has been stated regarding one's own realm (*dhātu*) and one's own level (*bhūmi*), so it is with regard to the distinctions of bondage.
That is to say, the first dhyāna serves as the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) only for the first dhyāna;

this should be understood to apply likewise up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Within one's own level, this holds true across the various locations and divisions.
Furthermore, they may also function as pervasive causes (sarvatraga-hetu) for one another because their bondage is identical.
The mention of "past" and so forth is intended to demonstrate that the substance of the past and future is substantially real.
Because the present is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
it is as stated regarding those things abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and those abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*);
this is because their essential nature (*svabhāva*) and category (*jāti*) are identical.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the universal latent proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*)?
Answer: There are eleven in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), namely:
the five views (*dṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
One should know that the false view, adherence to views, doubt,
and ignorance abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the form and formless realms each likewise consist of eleven [factors].
Among these, as for "ignorance" (*avidyā*):
This refers to the five views associated with doubt, as well as non-associated ignorance;
so it is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda* among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Thirty-three are universal;
sixty-five are non-universal. Question:
Regarding the ignorance abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin [of suffering]...
There are those that are universal (sarvatraga) and those that are not universal.
Why, then, does he state that thirty-three are universal and sixty-five are not universal?
The answer is: this is according to the version recited by the Venerable One of the West.
Among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), twenty-seven are universal (*sarvatraga*).
Sixty-five are not universal.
Six should be analyzed further.
This refers to ignorance abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin;
some of it is universal, while some is not universal. What is universal?
This refers to those abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin that are dissociated from non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
How is it that ignorance (*avidyā*) is not universal?
This refers to the ignorance associated with non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin.
What has been stated in this way is correct in meaning.
If one were to say this: what is the universal [ignorance]?
It refers to the ignorance associated with the universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin.
Consequently, it would not include the unshared ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
Therefore, that explanation is superior in meaning.
Question: If this is so, for what reason [is it stated otherwise]?
The masters of Kaśmīra do not recite this;
the answer is that one should indeed recite it as such,
yet the fact that they do not do so is due to a specific underlying intention.
Because for the most part they are universal;
that is to say, there are ten types of ignorance abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Seven are universal: namely, those associated with the five views and doubt, as well as the unshared ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
Three are non-universal: namely, the ignorance associated with greed, hatred, and pride.
There are seven types of ignorance to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
The fourth [category] consists of the universal factors (*sarvatraga*), namely: the two views, doubt (*vicikitsā*) associated with them, and non-associated ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*).
The third category consists of the non-universal factors, namely: ignorance associated with greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and pride (*māna*).
Furthermore, according to the recitation of this country, thirty-three [factors] are universal.
Sixty-five [types of ignorance] are not universal;
all such ignorance is said to be "unshared" (āveṇika),
because they arise through their own power, whether they are universal or non-universal.
There are eighty-three types of ignorance associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*):
namely, twenty-seven universal (*sarvatraga*) and fifty-six non-universal (*asarvatraga*).
These are associated with the latent dispositions and depend upon their power.
Because it is present before one, it is said to be associated;
furthermore, because its nature is indeterminate, it is not mentioned separately.
Thus, its intrinsic nature has been explained.
Therefore, it shall now be explained.
Question: Why is it called a "pervasive latent tendency" (sarvatraga-anuśaya), and what is the meaning of "pervasive" (sarvatraga)?
Answer: The meaning of "pervasive" is the sense of taking everything as its object.
The meaning of being sustained by the power of conditions is the meaning of being omnipresent (*sarvatraga*).
"Sustained by the power of conditions" means that it is able to take a vast range of objects.
Furthermore, it has been so from the very beginning.
Because they arise in relation to everything, they are called "universal" (sarvatraga).
Regarding the first "everything," this refers to the arising of all nine grades [of afflictions] from time immemorial.
"All that is within" refers to the fact that from time immemorial, there is not a single sentient being who does not give rise [to these afflictions].
"All that is subsequent" refers to...
This means that it arises by universally taking all contaminated phenomena as its object from time immemorial;
thus, the *Prajñapti-śāstra* states:
"There has never been an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) since the long course of saṃsāra..."
Regarding contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), one does not cling to them as a self,
nor as belonging to a self,
nor as subject to annihilation or permanence.
Either they deny it as non-existent,
or they grasp at it as pure, liberation, and transcendence,
or they grasp at it as venerable, supreme, and foremost.
Either doubt and hesitation arise,
or ignorance and lack of knowledge arise; therefore,
from the very beginning, all [these] arise in every way and in every respect.
It is called "pervasive" (sarvatraga).
Furthermore, when a dharma manifests for even a single moment,
it is able to take the five categories as its objects and serves as the cause for those five categories.
That which causes the five categories of dharmas to be deluded regarding their objects is called "pervasive" (sarvatraga).
Question: Regarding pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya):
How does one cause delusion regarding the object of those dharmas that have the untainted as their object?
Answer: If one clings to [the notion of] a self and so forth, one thereby slanders the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
thus, one first becomes deluded regarding the antidote to that [slander].
Thereafter, because one negates that [object] as being non-existent;
furthermore, when a phenomenon manifests for even a single moment.

That which can take the five categories as its objects and serves as the cause for those five categories, increasing in accordance with all dharmas of the five categories, is called "pervasive" (sarvatraga).
Question: Regarding the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) and their associated and co-existent dharmas...
Is it also a universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*)?
If so, what is the fault?
If it were also one, why are only thirty-three [factors] said to be universal?
If that is not the case, why is it that among associated and co-existent dharmas,
some are universal causes while others are not?
Some say that those [latter] are not universal causes.
Question: If that is so, why is it that among associated and co-existent dharmas, some are universal causes while others are not?
Answer: It is just as with associated and co-existent dharmas.
There are those that are latent dispositions (anuśaya) and those that are not latent dispositions;
likewise, there are associated and co-existent dharmas that are universal causes (sarvatraga-hetu) and those that are not universal causes.
Furthermore, what fault would there be?
The critique states that one should say this:
it is because the meaning of "cause" (hetu) applies to that as well, since it is also a universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu).
Because they are associated, co-existent, and share the same fruit.
Question: If that is so, why are only thirty-three [factors] said to be universal?
Answer: That statement was intended merely for the sake of analytical distinction.
Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
how many are universal (*sarvatraga*) and how many are non-universal?
This does not contradict [the previous teaching], as it was not intended to provide a general definition of the meaning of the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*).
Furthermore, the pervasive latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) are called "pervasive" because they possess three characteristics:
first, because they increase in accordance with [the afflictions] throughout all five categories of phenomena;
second, because they are able to take all five categories of phenomena as their objects.
Third, because they act as causes for all five categories of phenomena, they are explained in this comprehensive manner.
As for the associated factors, they possess only two functions, excluding pervasive increase (*anuśaya*).
As for the co-existent factors, they possess only one function.
It is said that because [the acquisition] is universal as its cause, it is not mentioned by him.
Question: Are the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) also universal causes?
The Venerable Saṃghavasu replied:
If the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a universal dharma were not itself universal,
then the acquisition of a non-universal dharma would have to be universal;
therefore, the acquisition of a universal dharma is also a universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*).
That objection is unreasonable.
For example, since the acquisition of form (rūpa-prāpti) is neither form nor the acquisition of form,
how could it be form?
Therefore, it is logically sound that universal [factors] can have non-universal factors as their causes.
Question: Why is it that the universal characteristics, such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth, are universal causes, yet those [characteristics] themselves do not have them as their causes?
Answer: Because the characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth share the same fruit as the universal factors (*sarvatraga-dharma*),
constantly accompany them without separation, and are extremely intimate with no priority or posteriority,
they are also obtained through the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
It does not share the same fruit as the universal [mental factors],
yet it does not constantly accompany them nor is it dissociated from them;
it may precede or follow them, but it is not extremely intimate.
Just as bark is to a tree, therefore that [defilement] cannot be a universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).

Question: Why is it that universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are established only with respect to those phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*)?
Is it not the case for those dharmas abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path?
The masters of the ancient Abhidharma say:

"Because these belong to the same category as those [dharmas] abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin. This refers to all dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin.
These are the lineage, the root, the birthplace, and the dwelling of the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
It is said that they are not among those dharmas abandoned through the vision of cessation or the path. Some say:
In this context, because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are extremely firm and stable—
meaning that those latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin all share a single intention and a single function.
Therefore, they are extremely firm;
because they are firm, the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) can be established within them.
However, the phenomena abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) and the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*) do not share a single underlying intention.
Because their functions are distinct, they are extremely weak;
because they are extremely weak,
universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) are not established among them.
Just as when the people of a city or town share a single intention and a single undertaking,
neither the city governor nor other enemies can subdue them;
yet if those people do not share a single intention and their undertakings differ from one another, [they are easily overcome].
In this case as well, it is thus subdued.
Some say that this is because it is sustained by the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
That is to say, where there is the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
the continuity of tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) becomes intensely flourishing, and thus it can be established as universal (*sarvatraga*).
Although the view abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*) lacks the view of self, it nonetheless possesses the quality of nourishment (*puṣṭi*).
I see that among all phenomena, there is no such thing within those phenomena abandoned through the vision of cessation or the path.
Some say this is because [the view of self] universally takes as its object the causes and effects of all contaminated (sāsrava) things.

This means that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin are established as "universal" (*sarvatraga*) because they are all capable of universally taking all contaminated causes and effects as their objects; others are not so.
Some say that this is because [the defilements] definitely increase with respect to their objects; that is to say,
the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin all take contaminated phenomena as their objects.
Following conditions, these outflows gradually increase;

it is like a person observing the moon who thereby enhances their visual faculty. As for the latent tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of cessation or the path, they may take either contaminated (sāsrava) or uncontaminated (anāsrava) phenomena as their object.
Those [defilements] conditioned by the untainted (*anāsrava*) decrease gradually in accordance with their respective objects,
just as a person’s visual faculty diminishes when gazing at the sun because it is not fixed; therefore,
universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) are not established in this case.
Some say that there are two kinds of latent dispositions (anuśaya) here: namely,
those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and those to be abandoned through the vision of the origin.
Both function as latent dispositions (anuśaya) by means of two doors:
first, by way of the object (ālambana),
and second, by way of association (samprayoga).
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path perform their function as latent dispositions either by way of two doors,
or solely because their association is not fixed.
It is not possible to establish the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
Some say that because two feet are fixed here with certainty, the meaning is as previously explained.
Some say that because each of the four categories possesses two types of paths—
namely, within the categories to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin [of suffering].
There are those that are universal and those that are not universal.

Within the categories of what is abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, there are those with outflow-objects (*sāsravālambana*) and those with outflow-free objects (*anāsravālambana*); therefore, one should not criticize the statement that they exist.
Because all latent dispositions (anuśaya) fall within these two [truths];
that is to say, all latent dispositions are subsumed under the truths of suffering (duḥkha-satya) and origination (samudaya-satya),
and it is only within these that the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) exist.
Some say that if one perceives suffering and its origin as being the fruit and cause of outflows (*sāsrava*),
then one perceives that the various phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path are fundamentally weak and inferior; therefore,
they do not establish the existence of universal underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
Some say that because they should not be held accountable,
those which are universal latent tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) necessarily and universally take all objects as their cognitive range.
There are no factors abandoned by the vision of the cessation or the path that possess universal object-conditions (*sarvatraga*).
Question: For what reason are greed, hatred, and pride abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin not universal?
The answer is that they all lack the characteristic of being universal (*sarvatraga*).
That is to say, while universal factors are able to take everything as their object, those three are not so.
Some say that these three are included among the afflictions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*).
That is to say, only those afflictions subsumed under the category of "universal" (sarvatraga) can be established as such.
How, then, are these three all subsumed under the category of "particular-characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) afflictions?
It is because one who gives rise to desire may do so toward that body and not toward this body.
Or [it may arise] in this body but not in that body;
likewise, it arises separately with respect to each individual part of the body.
Therefore, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and so forth exist as specifically characterized phenomena (svalakṣaṇasat).
Within a single moment, regarding all things within a single realm, a single destiny, birth, and so forth,
one either clings to them as "I" or clings to them as "mine";
furthermore, because they arise from ignorance and delusion, they constitute a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
Some say it is because they are difficult to inflame; that is to say,
greed, hatred, and pride are difficult to cause to blaze up intensely.
Because they flourish when supported by wives, wealth, enemies, or inferior adversaries,
the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) are easily set ablaze;
they flow on spontaneously and continuously like a river.
Some say that view,
doubt, and ignorance can take the four truths as their objects;
among these, they may be established as universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
Greed, hatred, and pride do not possess these three characteristics;
therefore, they are not established as universal underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
Question: Why are greed, hatred, and pride abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*) and the path (*mārga-darśana*) [not considered universal]?
Are the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) not objects of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) cognition?
Answer: Because they are not to be censured;
because they lack the characteristic of enmity or harm; and because their nature is gentle and supple.
Because they are supreme and because they are pure,
greed and the other [afflictions] do not have the uncontaminated as their object.
In the desire realm, there are eleven universal underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Nine have objects that extend across other realms, while two have objects restricted solely to their own realm;
these two are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Question: Why do these two views not take other realms as their objects?
Answer: Because they possess only such limited power regarding their objects;
furthermore, because these two views operate only with respect to coarse phenomena (*audārika-dharma*).
That is to say, these two views pertain only to the coarse and manifest;
they consist of grasping at a self and what belongs to a self within the directly perceived aggregates,
as well as the reckoning of annihilationism and eternalism.
If one is born in the desire realm, one cannot directly perceive the subtle aggregates of the form and formless realms; therefore,
one does not grasp them as "self" or "what belongs to self," and so forth.

Question: If that is so, why do those born in the form realm (rūpadhātu) not grasp as self or belonging to self the coarse and manifest aggregates (skandha) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) that they clearly perceive?
Answer: Because they have already become detached from such defilements (kleśa).
This refers to those born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
because they have already attained detachment from the aggregates (*skandha*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
although they perceive them directly, they do not grasp them as "I" or "mine," and so forth.
Furthermore, because the afflictions of the higher stages do not take the lower stages as their objects.
Question: Following from this discussion, why is it that the afflictions of the higher stages do not take the lower stages as their objects?
Answer: Because one has already become detached from the defilements of those lower stages.
That is to say, only one who has already become detached from the defilements of a lower stage gives rise to the manifestation of afflictions belonging to a higher stage;
since they have already become detached from the dharmas of the lower stage, [the afflictions of that stage do not arise].
How could afflictions of a higher stage possibly take those [lower stages] as their objects?
Question: How is it known that the afflictions of a higher stage can only manifest once one has abandoned the defilements of the lower stage?
Answer: As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, there are six types of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*);
that is, two types for each of the three realms of existence.
One is associated and two are dissociated.
When non-restraint associated with the desire realm manifests,
one possesses six types of non-restraint and four types of non-restraint also manifest.
That is to say, in the desire realm there are two [types], and in the form and formless realms they are each non-associated;
when non-restraint associated with the form realm is present,
four types of non-restraint are accomplished.
Third, there is that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint and is also present before one;
namely, when the two [types of] non-restraint belonging to the form realm and the dissociated [non-restraint] belonging to the formless realm,
as well as the associated non-restraint belonging to the formless realm, are present before one.
Second, there is non-attainment of restraint that is also present before one;
this refers to the two [types] of the formless realm.
In this context, defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are termed "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*).
From this it is known that only when one has abandoned the defilements of the lower realms do the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the higher stages manifest.
Question: Why are the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) able to take the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*) as their objects?
Do the afflictions of those two realms not take the desire realm as their object?
Answer: The desire realm is an indeterminate realm;
it is not a stage of cultivation.
Without being in a stage free from passion,
one cannot subdue the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of one's own realm; therefore,
it is able to transcend and take as its object the realms of form and formlessness.
The form and formless realms are the realm of meditative concentration, the stage of cultivation, and the stage of freedom from passion;
because they are able to thoroughly subdue the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of their own respective realms,
they cannot transcend objects belonging to lower stages.
Just as when a person is unable to restrain their wife or concubines,
they may commit unlawful acts with others;
yet if one restrains them well, such things cannot even occur.
To cast a glance with the eye while disregarding what is not in accordance with the Dharma is likewise so.
Furthermore, for one born in the desire realm regarding the aggregates of the two higher realms:
Is this suffering or is it not suffering?
Is this its origin or is it not its origin?
Is this the foremost or is it not the foremost?
"Is this pure or impure?
Because of such lack of understanding, the afflictions of the desire realm take the higher realms as their object.
However, if one is born in a higher stage, there is no doubt regarding the aggregates of the lower stages, as they have already been directly perceived.
Therefore, higher-level afflictions do not take lower levels as their objects.
Furthermore, if the afflictions of the form and formless realms were to take the desire realm as their object, they would necessarily increase in accordance with it.
If they were to increase in accordance with it, the distinctness of the realms would be confounded.
Therefore, those afflictions do not take the desire realm as their object.

Question: Just as the afflictions of the desire realm, though they may take the higher realms as objects, do not increase in accordance with them, why is it that the afflictions of the higher realms are not like this?
Answer: Although the aggregates of the higher realms give rise to afflictions of the desire realm when they are taken as objects, those afflictions do not increase in accordance with them.
The aggregates of the desire realm are inferior to those of the higher realms;
thus, if the afflictions of the higher realms take them as objects, they immediately increase in accordance with them.
Just as an inferior person,
though able to see a superior being face-to-face, cannot harm them,
whereas a superior being, upon seeing an inferior person, is able to harm them.
This is also the case here.
In the form realm (rūpadhātu), there are likewise eleven universal underlying tendencies (anuśaya);
nine of these have other realms as their objects.
The second category consists of those that take only their own realm as an object.
Within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are likewise eleven universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya),
all of which take only their own realm as an object and none that take another realm as an object.
Because there is no higher realm and because it does not take a lower realm as its object.
Some say that there are also [mental states] taking other realms as objects;
however, while such taking of objects is possible, their actual manifestation is certainly not fixed.
The critique states:
He should not make such a statement.
Since there is no higher realm to serve as an object of cognition, how could there be a meditative absorption capable of cognizing it?
Therefore, it is logically sound to say that they do not exist [in those higher stages].
From the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), there are eleven universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) in each;
nine of these extend to other stages as objects of cognition.
The second type takes only its own level as its object.
The non-percipient and non-non-percipient realm (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) also possesses eleven universal underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
all of which take only their own level as their object.
Because it is the unsurpassed stage and because it does not take the higher stages as its object.
Some say that there are also instances where it takes other stages as its object;
however, while the capacity to take them as objects exists, they are certainly not manifest at that time.
The critique states:
He should not make such a claim; since there is no higher stage that can be taken as an object, how could there be a meditative concentration capable of taking it as its object?
Therefore, it is better to say that [the self] does not exist from a logical standpoint.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 19 (continuation of Volume 18).
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;
translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
Section Eleven of the Second Chapter on Knowledge within the First Aggregate of Miscellaneous Topics: Wrong Views to be Abandoned through Seeing Suffering and Origin in the Desire Realm.
It is able to take the suffering and origin of the three realms as its objects, but not simultaneously;
that is to say, it takes the desire realm as its object in one moment,
and the form and formless realms in another moment.
Question: Why does one not, in a single moment, simultaneously take as objects the three realms, whether they be suffering or its origin?
Answer: Because those [afflictions] also increase in accordance with their objects within the desire realm.
Because they do not increase in accordance [with the defilements] when taking the form and formless realms as their object.
Question: Why is it that they increase in accordance when taking the desire realm as their object, yet do not increase in accordance when taking the form and formless realms as their object?
Answer: Because the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is the locus where those [defilements] increase, whereas the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*) are not such loci for their increase.
Furthermore, the desire realm is their dwelling place.
Because the form and formless realms are not their dwelling places.
Furthermore, the desire realm possesses those results of outflow and maturation,
whereas the form and formless realms lack those results of outflow and maturation.
Furthermore, the desire realm possesses those five categories of pervasive results;
however, because the form and formless realms lack those five categories of pervasive results,
and furthermore, because the desire realm lacks their ultimate antidote.
Because there exists an ultimate antidote to those [afflictions] in the realms of form and formlessness.
Furthermore, if one were to suddenly take as an object the suffering or the origin of all three realms in a single moment, [it would be impossible].

In what way does it take [them] as objects? Is it the case that, just as it takes the desire realm as its object and increases accordingly, it likewise takes the form and formless realms as its objects and increases accordingly?
Or is it the case that, unlike when taking the form and formless realms as its objects, it does not increase accordingly?
Is it the same regarding the objects of the desire realm?
If it were so, what would be the fault?
If it were as with the objects of the desire realm, then [the defilements] would increase accordingly.
If it were the case that [defilements] do not increase in accordance with their objects in the realms of form and formlessness, then the realms would become confused.
If it were the case that they do not increase in accordance with their objects in the realm of desire as well, then it would be unreasonable.
This is because there are no afflictions that take phenomena of their own realm as objects and yet lack both objective and associative increase;
for those taking phenomena of their own stage as objects must necessarily possess both objective and associative bondage.
If, in a single moment, one simultaneously takes as objects the suffering or the origin within the three realms,
and if among those objective conditions there were some upon which [defilements] increase and others upon which they do not increase,
then it would likewise follow that among the associated mental factors there would be some upon which [defilements] increase and others upon which they do not increase.
This would contradict the principle of this cause and also destroy the coherence of associated dharmas.
To avoid such an error,
the principle that conditions operate at different times and across both one's own realm and other realms is well established.
Thus, the wrong view abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin within the first dhyāna can take the suffering and origin of eight stages as its object, yet not all at once; that is,
it takes the first dhyāna as its object in one distinct moment.
A different moment [of wrong view] takes the upper seven stages as its object.

In this manner, even up to the wrong view abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin within the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), it can take the suffering and origin of two stages as its object, though not simultaneously;
that is, it takes its own stage as its object at a different moment.
A wrong view abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception takes as its object only the suffering and origin of its own level,
whereas [a wrong view] taking a higher level as its object arises in a different moment.

The false view abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavyā mithyādṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm takes as its object only the cessation of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm.

Question: For what reason can the false views abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) in the desire realm take the suffering and origin of all three realms as their objects?

Does the false view abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering] in the desire realm only take the cessation of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm as its object?
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"If a phenomenon is that which is clung to by craving in the desire realm, and which the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) grasps as 'self' or 'mine'..."
These dharmas, being ceased, should be the objects of the false views to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the desire realm;
it is not the case that those afflictions can take other realms as their objects, and this [case] is likewise so.
Some say that because the truths of suffering and its origin are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), they mutually induce one another across their own and other stages;
therefore, those false views can take other stages as their objects.

However, the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); since there is no principle of mutual induction between one's own stage and other stages for what is unconditioned, it cannot be so.
Therefore, that wrong view does not take other stages as its object.
Likewise, the wrong view abandoned through the vision of cessation within the first dhyāna takes as its object only the cessation of the formations belonging to the first dhyāna.
Up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
the false view abandoned through the vision of cessation takes as its object only the cessation of the conditioned phenomena of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

The false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) takes as its object only the counteractive factors (*pratipakṣa*) of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm.

Question: Why is it that the false views to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) in the desire realm can take the suffering and origin of the three realms as their objects?
Does the false view abandoned through the path of seeing in the desire realm only take as its object the counteragents to the various formations of the desire realm?
The Venerable Pārśva replied:
"If a phenomenon is clung to by craving in the desire realm, and the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) grasps it as 'self' or 'mine'..."
This dharma, as its antidote, should be the object of the false views abandoned by the path of seeing within the desire realm;
it is not the case that those afflictions can take other realms as their objects, and this [dharma] is likewise so.

Some say that because the objects of the wrong views abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin in the desire realm are not their antidotes, those views can take other stages as their objects;

however, because the objects of the wrong views abandoned through the vision of the path in the desire realm are indeed their antidotes, they cannot take the antidotes of other stages as their objects.

Regarding this, some say that the false views to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm take as their object only the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge within the stage of the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
"Only that [path] is the antidote for the abandonment of this [defilement].
The critique says: It should be stated thus.
Because the types of paths within the category of dharma-knowledge that take these as objects are identical across the six stages,
and because both are antidotes to the destruction of the desire realm;
such is the false view abandoned through the path of seeing in the first dhyāna.
It can take as its object the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) across nine stages,
up to and including the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
It can take as its object the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge across nine stages.

Question: Why is it that the false view abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) can only take as its object the cessation of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of its own level, whereas the false view abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) can take as its object the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*) across six levels?
Or does it take as its object the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) across nine stages?
Answer: The cessations (*nirodha*) of one's own stage and other stages are not mutual causes, because the noble paths (*ārya-mārga*) of multiple stages serve as causes for one another.

Question: If that is so, since the paths belonging to the categories of Dharma-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge (dharmajñāna-pakṣa and anvayajñāna-pakṣa) are also mutual causes for one another, why is it that the false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned by the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) do not take them as their collective object?
Some say that the false views abandoned by the Path of Seeing are also able to take the paths of the Dharma-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge categories as their collective object.
Because they serve as mutual causes,
and because the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñānapakṣa*) is also capable of acting as an antidote to the two higher realms.
The critique says:
He should not say this,
because the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is not an antidote to the phenomena of the desire realm;
and although the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) is an antidote to the two higher realms, it is neither the primary nor the complete antidote.
Furthermore, because of the distinctions among the categories of Dharma-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna),
some say that the path belonging to the category of Subsequent-knowledge in the nine stages serves as the antidote for the abandonment of the eight higher stages; thus,
it is the object of the false views abandoned by the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) of those respective stages, and not the object of other paths of knowledge.
The critique states:
He should not make such a statement,
because there are many kinds of antidotes.
Furthermore, because the categories of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) act as causes for one another and share the same nature,
it is asked: how can a single moment of latent disposition (*anuśaya*) universally take all things as its object,
given that there is no principle for such universal increase (*anuśayana*)?
Why is it called "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*)?
The answer is: there is no fault, because it is spoken of in reference to that which continues as a series of its own kind.
However, regarding pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and pervasive objects (*ālambana*), one should formulate four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are not pervasive causes;
namely, future pervasive latent dispositions.
There are pervasive causes that are not pervasive latent dispositions.
This refers to those past and present phenomena that are associated with and co-existent with the pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
There are also cases where the pervasive latent dispositions themselves constitute a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*),
namely, the past and present pervasive latent dispositions.
There are underlying tendencies that are neither universal nor universal causes.
If one does not speak in terms of those specific categories, it should be stated as follows:
namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
If one speaks according to that specific category, one should say: "future pervasive latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) and their associated and co-existent factors.
Question: Are all defiled phenomena (kliṣṭa-dharma) caused by factors to be abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya)?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
If all defiled phenomena take those abandoned by insight as their cause,
then both the unabandoned and the already abandoned would act as causes.
What is the difference between that which has not yet been abandoned and that which has already been abandoned?
Furthermore, if this were the case,
why would the defiled dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation by the noble ones [still exist]?
Is there that which arises and that which does not arise? That which does not arise refers to non-existence-craving (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*),
the various types of conceit (*māna*), and the extreme fetters of hatred (*pratighaparyavasthāna*).
"Arising" refers to other forms of greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance.
Furthermore, if that were the case,
how would one reconcile this with the statement in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*?
As it is asked: "Is there any unwholesome dharma that has only the unwholesome as its cause?
The answer is: "There is."
This refers to when a noble one is retrogressing from the defilement of desire,
and the first defiled volition manifests;
this applies to all defiled phenomena.
If not all [factors] take factors abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) as their cause, how should one reconcile this with the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, which states:
[The passage from the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"As it is said..."
What are the phenomena that have as their cause those factors to be abandoned by insight?
They are all defiled phenomena,
as well as the maturation of those phenomena to be abandoned by insight.
Furthermore, if that were so, it would contradict that statement:
"What are the phenomena that have the indeterminate as their cause?"
That is to say, it refers to indeterminate conditioned phenomena and all unwholesome phenomena.
Furthermore, if that were the case:
Furthermore, this contradicts that statement:
"There may be a Truth of Suffering that has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause,
but does not serve as the cause for the view of a self-identity."
This refers to all other defiled truths of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and so forth— excluding those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present,
and extending broadly to exclude future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (the view of a self-identity) along with its associated factors,
as well as birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
Furthermore, if that were the case,
how would one reconcile the statement in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*? As it says:
Unwholesome eye-consciousness,
up to and including unwholesome mind-consciousness,
all have unwholesome and indeterminate states as their causes.
It is agreed that one should speak thus:
all defiled phenomena have those abandoned by vision as their cause.
Question: If that is so, and both the unsevered and the severed can serve as causes, what is the distinction between them?
Answer: Their very names constitute the distinction.

That is to say, the preceding stage where [the afflictions] have not yet been abandoned is called the "cause of non-abandonment," while the subsequent stage where they have already been abandoned is called the "cause of abandonment.
Furthermore, in the former stage, [the afflictions] have not yet been destroyed by their antidotes.
Although the subsequent state also functions as a cause,
it has already been destroyed by its antidote.
Furthermore, in the preceding state, [the afflictions] are able to obstruct the Noble Path within one's own continuum.
Although the subsequent stage also acts as a cause,
it does not obstruct the noble path within its own continuum.
Furthermore, regarding the preceding stage within its own continuum:
It is capable of producing [the acquisition] like smoke and flame;
although it also serves as a cause in the subsequent stage,
it can no longer produce [the acquisition] like smoke and flame within its own continuum.
Furthermore, in the preceding stage, one performs acts that are censurable and loathsome,
as well as defiled acts within oneself;
although these also serve as causes in the subsequent stage, [the latter is distinct].
Furthermore, within one's own person, one is no longer capable of performing acts that are censurable, loathsome, or defiled. Moreover,
in the preceding stage, one was able to accomplish the tasks that ought to be performed within one's own person.
Although the subsequent stage also serves as a cause,
it can no longer accomplish the tasks that ought to be performed within its own continuum.
Furthermore, regarding the preceding stage within its own continuum:
It is capable of performing the functions of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Although it also serves as a cause in its subsequent state,
it is no longer capable of performing the functions of a homogeneous cause or a pervasive cause within its own continuum.
Furthermore, in the former stage, [the cause] is able to produce both the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) within its own continuum;
although it also serves as a cause in the subsequent stage, [it does not produce these fruits].
Furthermore, within its own continuum, it can no longer produce either a flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) or a ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
Moreover, in the preceding stage, it was capable of both taking up a fruit and giving forth a fruit within its own continuum.
Although the subsequent state also acts as a cause,
it can no longer take up or yield its fruit within its own continuum;
this is what is meant by the distinction between the "unsevered" and the "already severed."
Question: If that is so, why is it that among the defiled phenomena abandoned through cultivation by the noble ones, some arise while others do not?
Answer: Because the phenomena abandoned through seeing either serve as the immediate cause for the continuity of those [defiled phenomena] or do not.
Or it serves as a remote cause for non-continuity;
if it were to serve as an immediate cause for continuity with that [result],
the noble one would not arise.
If it were a remote cause for non-continuation with respect to that [state],
then even noble ones would still give rise to it;
furthermore, if one has already attained its non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), [it would follow].
Noble ones do not give rise to it.
If they have not yet attained its non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*),
noble ones still give rise to it.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that the arising of that [state] depends on the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*):
it does not arise for noble ones (*ārya*).
If it were not so determined, [the following would occur].
The Noble One still arises.
Furthermore, if that arising were capable of obstructing the state of a Noble One,
the Noble One would not arise.
If it were not so, the noble ones would still arise [in rebirth].
One might ask: why do the noble ones not give rise to craving for existence (*bhavarāga*)?
The answer is: because it is nurtured by the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), and because it manifests immediately following that view of annihilationism;
since all noble ones (*ārya*) have already abandoned the view of annihilationism, it does not arise in them.
Question: For what reason do noble ones (ārya) not give rise to the various types of conceit?
Answer: Because they are nurtured by the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and because they manifest immediately following that view of a self-identity.
Because all noble ones have already abandoned the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), that [affliction] does not arise in them.
Question: For what reason do noble ones not give rise to the obsession of extreme hatred?
Answer: Because it is nourished by false views (mithyādṛṣṭi).
Because it manifests immediately after wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and because all noble ones (*ārya*) have already abandoned wrong view, it does not arise in them.
Question: If that is so, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*?
As it is said:
"Is there any unwholesome dharma that has only the unwholesome as its cause?"
Answer: There is.
[The passage] continues at length.
Answer: Because that was stated in reference to causes that have not yet been abandoned, there is no contradiction.
That is to say, there are two kinds of causes for the initial arising of unwholesome volition:
first, those already abandoned;
second, those not yet abandoned.
That treatise speaks solely based on causes that have not yet been abandoned.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction because it speaks based on unwholesome causes;
that is to say, when an unwholesome volition first arises, it has two kinds of causes.
First, the unwholesome;
second, the indeterminate.
That treatise speaks only in reliance upon unwholesome causes.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction because that [explanation] is stated according to the causes within its own school (sva-nikāya).
That is to say, when unwholesome volition first arises, it has two kinds of causes:
first, its own school; [and second, external conditions].
Second, regarding other schools:
that treatise speaks solely based on causes belonging to its own school.
Furthermore, because it speaks based on non-universal causes (*asarvatraga-hetu*), there is no contradiction.
That is to say, when that initial unwholesome volition arises, there are two kinds of causes:
first, universal;
second, non-universal.
That treatise speaks only in reliance upon the non-universal cause (*asarvatraga-hetu*).
Furthermore, there is no contradiction because it speaks in reliance upon the unique cause (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*).
That is to say, when that initial unwholesome volition first arises, it has two kinds of causes.
There are two types: common and uncommon.
That treatise explains [the matter] based solely on the uncommon cause.
Question: When a noble one had not yet abandoned the defilements of desire, those defiled volitions were also caused by the unwholesome.
Why, then, does that treatise state [that they arise] at the time of falling back?
Answer: At that time, that thought, which was previously unestablished, is now established;
what was previously without bondage is now bound;
and what was previously dead is now born.
Therefore, it is explained selectively.
Question: Since subsequent defiled volitions (*cetanā*) also have the unwholesome as their cause, why does that treatise speak only of the initial arising?
Answer: At that time, what was previously severed is now continued;
what was previously without function now has function;
what was previously dead is now born.
Therefore, it is taught selectively. Some say:
"All defiled phenomena [are associated with the afflictions]."
Not all [factors] have factors abandoned through seeing as their cause.
Question: If that is so, how do you explain what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* and the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*?
How should this be reconciled?
The answer is: that was stated in terms of general characteristics.
If explained specifically:
One should say:
there is defiled matter that has factors to be abandoned by insight as its cause.
Not all defiled matter,
up to and including defiled consciousness,
has dharmas to be abandoned by seeing as their cause.
"It is not all defiled consciousnesses.
[The Critic] says:
He should not have made such a statement.
For that treatise states that all defiled phenomena have factors abandoned through seeing as their cause,
and all unwholesome phenomena have neutral factors as their cause.
All other afflicted truths of suffering and so forth have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause;
all unwholesome sixfold consciousnesses have the unwholesome and the indeterminate as their causes.
The previous explanation is correct.
However, the Venerable Śamathadeva distinguishes the defiled phenomena differently;
he states as follows:
There are dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering that have only those abandoned through the vision of suffering as their cause;
there are dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering that have only those abandoned through the vision of origin as their cause.
Non-duality is the cause.
It is the same for those dharmas abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
This is stated as a conceptual distinction, for such a thing does not exist in reality.
Suppose a noble one, having already realized suffering but not yet realized its origin, arises from the noble path;
for those phenomena abandoned by the vision of the origin that arise at that time, only those abandoned by the vision of the origin serve as their cause.

When dharmas abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) arise and manifest, having as their cause those dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya),
they do not arise and manifest [again],
because their causes have already been severed.
There are dharmas abandoned through the vision of cessation that have only those abandoned through the vision of cessation as their cause;
there are dharmas abandoned through the vision of cessation that have only those abandoned through the vision of suffering as their cause.
There are phenomena abandoned through the vision of cessation that have only those abandoned through the vision of origin as their cause.
There are phenomena abandoned through the vision of cessation that have only those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin as their cause.
There is no such thing as having three [factors] as causes.
It is likewise for defiled phenomena abandoned through the path of seeing and those abandoned through cultivation;
these are spoken of only by way of conceptual discrimination, for in reality, such a case does not exist.
Suppose that a noble one has already realized cessation but has not yet realized the path;
having emerged from the noble path, for those phenomena abandoned by seeing the path, which take only those abandoned by seeing the path as their cause.

Those [dharmas] that arise and manifest have as their cause only those dharmas to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of origin; those [dharmas] to be abandoned by the vision of the path do not arise and manifest.
Because the causes have already been severed,
it is thus that for a noble one, among the defiled dharmas to be abandoned through the path of cultivation,
those which have only the factors to be abandoned through cultivation as their cause [are so designated].
Defiled dharmas abandoned through cultivation that arise and manifest have only those abandoned through seeing suffering and the origin as their causes.
Because the causes for their manifestation have already been severed.
However, when noble ones (*ārya*) become free from the defilements of desire, the afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*) of the desire realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)—
if they have only those [afflicted phenomena] to be abandoned by cultivation as their cause— [do not arise].
If one were to abandon only those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin by combining them into a single aggregate and severing them in nine stages,
then at the time of subsequent retrogression, the defiled dharmas of the desire realm abandoned through cultivation would [arise].
That which has only what is to be abandoned by cultivation as its cause remains accomplished, whereas that which has only what is to be abandoned by seeing as its cause is not accomplished,
because its causes have already been severed.
Furthermore, at that time, it has only what is to be abandoned by cultivation as its cause.
Among the defiled dharmas abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), those that are future are still possessed,
whereas those that are past are not possessed,
because it is impossible for them to arise and manifest again subsequently.
The critique states:
He should not make such a statement.
How could it be that afflictions to be abandoned by the same antidote [could be so different]?
When those [faculties] are subsequently lost, there are cases where they are reacquired and cases where they are not;
furthermore, this cannot be reconciled with the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* and the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*.
Therefore, what was stated previously is correct.

Question: Since craving is equally and completely severed across all realms, stages, and categories, why is it that the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) can increase in subsequent categories but not in other realms or stages?

Answer: Universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) are able to increase [their influence] over dharmas of other categories because they possess either outflow fruits (niṣyanda-phala) or retribution fruits (vipāka-phala).
They do not increase [their influence] over those of other realms or stages because they lack both outflow fruits and retribution fruits therein.
Furthermore, because [factors] of one's own level and other categories are similar in their coarseness or subtlety, they can increase accordingly;
however, because those of a higher level are subtle, they cannot increase accordingly.
Question: Do universal (sarvatraga) and non-universal (asarvatraga) retributive (vipāka) factors act as causes for one another?
Some say: universal maturation acts as a cause for non-universal maturation,
but not all non-universal maturations act as causes for universal maturation.
Just as universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) serve as causes for non-universal latent dispositions,
so too it is that latent dispositions of other categories which are non-universal cannot serve as the cause of maturation (vipāka-hetu) for universal latent dispositions.
The critique says:
He should not make such a statement;
the dharmas of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) are distinct.
The dharma of maturation (vipāka) is distinct [from its cause],
because the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belong to five categories while maturation is abandoned only by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Thus it should be stated.
Universal resultant [dharmas] act as causes for both universal resultant [dharmas] and non-universal resultant [dharmas].
Non-universal resultant [dharmas] act as causes for non-universal resultant [dharmas].
It also serves as the cause for universal and retributive [dharmas], because they share the same level, the same category, and similar nature.
Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature of the universal cause?
Answer: All past and present universal proclivities (*anuśaya*),
as well as the various phenomena associated with and co-existent with them—
their intrinsic nature has already been explained.
Therefore, it shall now be explained.
Question: Why is it called the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*)?
What is the meaning of "universal" (*sarvatraga*)?
Answer: The meaning of being a cause for everything is the meaning of "pervasive" (sarvatraga).
Furthermore, the meaning of being able to take everything as an object is the meaning of "pervasive.
Furthermore, the meaning of increasing everywhere [through affliction] is the meaning of "pervasive."
This universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu) exists only in the two time periods of the past and the present, and its result is exclusively a flow-on result (niṣyanda-phala).
What, then, is the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu)?
[The text continues] at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To refute the tenets of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that apart from volition (*cetanā*), there is no cause for karmic maturation (*vipāka-hetu*).
There is no maturation fruit apart from feeling,
as the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain;
in order to refute that position, it is shown that both the cause of maturation and the fruit of maturation pertain to all five aggregates.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that only the mind and mental factors possess both the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) and the retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*),
such as the Mahāsāṃghikas.
To stop that attachment and clarify this cause and effect,
it also applies to all material forms (*rūpa*) and non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*).
Alternatively, there may be another attachment.
Only mind, mental factors, and all material phenomena possess the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) and the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*);
this is stated in order to refute that [limited] position and to demonstrate that these also extend to the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Alternatively, there are those who hold the view that the fruit of a ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) only matures once its own substantial entity (svabhāva) has been relinquished;
they speak as follows:
All retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*) must enter the past before they yield their fruit;
since the past has already ceased, it is argued that it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
To refute this position, it is shown that the retributive cause still possesses substantial reality (*dravya-sattva*) at the stage when the fruit matures.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that the substance of the various ripening causes and effects exists constantly as long as they have not yet matured,
but once those effects have matured, their substance is then destroyed.
As the Kāśyapīya school asserts:
"Just as when a sprout has not yet emerged, its substance exists constantly, but once the sprout is produced, it perishes;
so too it is with all retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*)."
To stop that adherence, it is shown that although the fruit has already matured, its substance still exists.
Or again, there is another adherence:
This treatise was composed in order to refute the attachment of certain non-Buddhists who hold that the wholesome and unwholesome actions one performs do not yield fruits of suffering or pleasure,
and to demonstrate instead that such actions do indeed produce fruits of suffering and pleasure.
What is the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*)?

Answer: All mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), as well as the resultant matter (*vipāka-rūpa*), mental states and mental factors, and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
These mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) serve as the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu) for that maturation (vipāka).
Herein, "all mental states and mental factors" refers to all unwholesome (akuśala),
wholesome (kuśala), and tainted (sāsrava) mental states and mental factors.
This statement also includes the derivative matter (anuvartaka-rūpa) that accompanies them,
because non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra) share the same fruit as the mind and mental factors.
As for resultant matter (vipāka-rūpa):
This refers to the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha),
namely the five sense faculties beginning with the eye, as well as visible forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
As for "mind" (citta):
This refers to the aggregate of consciousness,
namely the six consciousnesses of the eye and so forth.
As for mental factors (caitta-dharma):
This refers to the three aggregates,
namely feeling, perception, volition, and so forth,
as well as the formations dissociated from mind.
This refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), namely the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), and so forth.
This indicates that both the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) and the retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*) pertain to all five aggregates.
Furthermore, regarding all bodily and vocal actions—
namely, the resultant matter, the mind and mental factors, and the formations dissociated from mind—
these bodily and vocal actions serve as the ripening cause for those resultant states.
Question: Since it has already been stated previously that bodily and vocal karma follow the mind because they share a single fruit with the mind,
why is it stated here once again that these are "bodily and vocal karma"?
What dharma is being described?

The answer is: wholesome and unwholesome informative acts (*vijñapti*), as well as the non-informative acts (*avijñapti*) produced in dependence upon informative acts that do not follow the mind—the two types of bodily and vocal karma.
This is because they are definitely capable of bringing about a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Some say that this refers to the fact that the bodily and vocal informative acts (*vijñapti*) and the non-informative act (*avijñapti*) produced in that same moment have the same fruit.
That statement is irrational.
The bodily and vocal informative actions arise simultaneously with them;
however, the bodily and vocal non-informative actions do not share the same result,
because they do not serve as simultaneous causes for one another.
Some say that although manifest karma and the unmanifest karma of body and speech— which arises based on the manifest— are not of a single fruit,
they nonetheless simultaneously receive their ripening fruits because they arise from a single moment of mind.
That explanation is unreasonable.
Since they are not simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) in relation to one another,
how can it be definitively stated that they receive their retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*) at the same moment?
However, because manifest and unmanifest karma do not serve as simultaneous causes for one another, their ripened fruits are distinct.
Within manifest karma, the seven branches of bodily and vocal action differ;
each one individually brings about its own distinct ripened fruit.
Each individual factor (*aṅga*) and so forth consists of many atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Each atom has distinctions across the three periods of time (*adhvan*),
and within each period there are many moments (*kṣaṇa*).
Because each moment of the maturation fruit is distinct and not a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the same applies to unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*).
However, the seven branches of unmanifest karma that follow the mind (*citta-anuvartin*) can mutually serve as co-existent causes for one another; therefore, they share the same maturation fruit.

The informative and non-informative karma described herein also includes their concomitant factors, such as arising and so forth, because they share the same fruit; the maturation experienced by these should be understood as previously explained.
Furthermore, among the various formations dissociated from mind— namely, the matter that is maturation, the mind, and mental factors—
the formations dissociated from mind act as the ripening cause for those maturations.
This is called the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Question: Regarding the various mental states and mental factors, manifest and unmanifest karma, and their concomitant arising and so forth, as has already been explained previously.
Because they share the same fruit.
What, then, are the presently explained non-associated formations?

Answer: They are now explained as the attainment (*prāpti*) of the meditative absorption of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), all unwholesome and wholesome contaminated states, and the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) such as birth (*jāti*) that arise concomitantly with them.
Because it has not been explained previously.
Question: What kind of ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) does the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) receive? Some say:
The fruit of maturation for the attainment of non-perception consists of non-perception and form;
its life-faculty and group-homogeneity are the fruits of maturation of karma with mind belonging to the fourth dhyāna.
The maturation of those remaining aggregates is a common fruit (*sādhāraṇa-phala*).
Some say that the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) receives the maturation fruits of non-perception and form.
The maturation of its life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the fruit of karma with mind belonging to the fourth dhyāna.
The maturation of those remaining aggregates is a common fruit.
Some say that the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) receives the maturation fruits of both non-conception and form.
The maturation of those remaining aggregates is a collective fruit (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*).
Some say that while the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) yields only the maturation fruit of non-perception itself, the maturation of its remaining aggregates is a collective fruit.
Question: If the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is also a non-karmic maturation fruit (*avipāka-phala*),
how should one reconcile this with the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*,
which states as follows?
There is one dharma that is the maturation of karma (*vipāka*) but is not itself karma: namely, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Answer: All life-faculties are exclusively maturation;
all maturations are manifested by means of karma.
It is with this underlying intention that such a statement was made;
however, in reality, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not produced by karma.
Furthermore, that treatise speaks according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
That is to say, when people in the world see one of short lifespan, they immediately say,
"This person performed actions that lead to a short lifespan";
and when they see one of long lifespan, they likewise say:
This person performs karma that results in long life.
Some say that even during the state of mindlessness in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), one experiences the karmic fruit of the fourth dhyāna while possessing a mind.
One also experiences the fruit of the attainment of non-conception while in a state of mind.

Question: If one experiences the fruit of a state with mind while in a state without mind, and likewise experiences the fruit of a state without mind while in a state with mind, [then what is the distinction?]
How is it that cause and effect are not inverted?
Answer: For instance, there is material karma that also receives immaterial fruit, and there is immaterial karma that also receives material fruit.
And thus there is no fault of the inversion of cause and effect;
this case is also like that.
The Venerable Śamadatta said:
The fruit of maturation for the attainment of non-perception consists of the state of non-perception itself and the homogeneous character (nikāya-sabhāga).
Its life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and its form (rūpa) are the fruits of karma with mind belonging to the fourth dhyāna.
Those minds, mental factors, and other formations dissociated from mind are all not maturation (*vipāka*).
The critique says:
He should not speak in that way,
because the homogeneous character of the maturation (vipāka-nikāya-sabhāga) is the fruit of karma.
Those minds and mental factors, as well as other formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra), are also of the nature of maturation.
Therefore, the Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"The attainment of non-conception receives the fruit of maturation that is non-conceptual;
it consists of the life-faculty and the group-homogeneity."
This is the mental karma-result of the fourth dhyāna;
the maturation of its remaining aggregates is the common result.
The critique states:
He should not speak in that way;
for the five faculties, such as the eye, are the fruits of karma.
He should speak thus:
The maturation of the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) is exclusively the fruit of the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Its life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), category-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*),
and the five material sense-faculties are maturations that are exclusively the fruits of karma associated with mind in the fourth dhyāna.
The maturation of those remaining aggregates is a common fruit.
Question: What kind of maturation fruit does the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) receive?
Answer: It receives the maturation fruit of the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Excluding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), for they are exclusively the fruit of karma.
Question: What kind of ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) do these acquisitions (*prāpti*) receive?

Answer: It refers to the maturation fruits (*vipāka-phala*) obtained by all acquisitions (*prāpti*), feeling (*vedanā*), form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
As for "form," it refers to visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility;
it does not refer to the five material sense organs (*indriya*).
Due to the fruit of that karma,
the mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) refer to painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,
as well as their associated factors and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).
This refers to the acquisition (*prāpti*) of birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
The Venerable Saṃghavasu stated:

"Acquisition can also experience the five faculties, such as the eye, as well as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the commonality of group (*nikāyasabhāga*), which are the fruits of maturation (*vipākaphala*)."
He asserts this:

although each [of these acquisitions] individually lacks the power to project the acquisition of a common destiny (*nikāyasabhāga*) and so forth, when they gather together, they are able to project it; however, that [result] only brings about a body of dull faculties.
For example, earthworms and the like obtain the nine bases of form that are produced by their own karma, excluding sound.

Mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta) pertain to the three groups of feeling; non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra) include the generic similarity of beings (nikāya-sabhāga), the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), the various acquisitions (prāpti), and the characteristics of arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
The critique states:
He should not make such a claim;
the various acquisitions (prāpti), when compared to one another, are not simultaneous causes (sahabhū-hetu).
Even if one were to assemble ten million [causes], what benefit would there be?
Since they do not produce a single fruit, they cannot collectively project the commonality of existence (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and so forth.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka has stated this as follows:
When karma that cannot project the commonality of a group (nikāya-sabhāga) and so forth induces the projection of such a commonality,
