it can only bring about the acquisition of visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects within the locations of the sense organs, such as the eye.
The critique states:
He should not make such a statement,
lest it imply that there is no acquisition of the fruit of maturation in the formless realm.
Therefore, one should know that the initial explanation is correct.
Question: What is the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) as explained in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
What is the difference between all unwholesome and wholesome contaminated dharmas and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) as explained in this treatise?
The answer is: this is of provisional meaning while that is of definitive meaning;
this has a further underlying intention while that has no further intention;
this has a further underlying cause while that has no further cause.
This is based on the conventional truth, while that is based on the ultimate truth.
This involves manifesting with a shadow, whereas that is without manifesting a shadow.
Furthermore, this explains the cause of maturation that has already arisen.
The former explains the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) in terms of that which has already produced its fruit and that which has not yet produced it;
this explains the ripening cause in terms of its actual yielding of fruit.
The former explains the ripening cause in terms of that which has already yielded its fruit and that which has not yet yielded its fruit.
Furthermore, this explains the results of new karma,
whereas that explains the results of both new and old karma.
Furthermore, this explains past ripening causes (*vipāka-hetu*).
He speaks of the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) across the three time periods.
Furthermore, this refers specifically to the ripening cause that is currently yielding its fruit;
he speaks of the ripening cause that has already yielded, is currently yielding, or will yield its fruit.
This is what is meant by the distinction between "this teaching" and "that teaching.
Question: Why is it that in this context only the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) that is currently yielding its fruit is mentioned?
Answer: Because the characteristics of that which is currently yielding its fruit are most manifest.
Furthermore, because those fruits are manifested as the designation of sentient beings within the five destinies;
furthermore, at that time, this cause reaches its ultimate function and thus correctly bestows its fruit.
This demonstrates both the causes that are currently yielding their fruit and those that have already yielded their fruit; however,
for the sake of convenience regarding the meaning,
only the causes currently yielding their fruit are discussed here.
Furthermore, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are four types of maturation causes (*vipāka-hetu*) that yield a single fruit:
namely, wholesome and unwholesome mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), along with their arising (*jāti*) and so forth.
There are also two types of maturation causes that yield a single fruit.
This refers to wholesome or unwholesome bodily and vocal actions, as well as their arising and so forth.
There is one case where a single aggregate that is a ripening cause produces a single fruit;
namely, acquisition (*prāpti*) and its arising and so forth.
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are five types of maturation causes (*vipāka-hetu*) that yield a single fruit:
namely, those accompanied by derivative matter (*anuvartaka-rūpa*), consisting of mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), as well as their [characteristics] such as arising (*jāti*).
There are four types of maturation causes that yield a single fruit, consisting of the four aggregates (*skandha*).
This refers to wholesome minds and mental factors that lack concomitant matter, along with their arising and so forth;
these two aggregates have a single fruit through the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*).
This refers to wholesome bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*), along with their arising and so forth.
There is one case where a single aggregate that is a ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) produces a single fruit:
namely, the attainment of the meditative absorption of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and its [concomitant] arising and so forth.
In the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu), there are four cases where aggregates that are ripening causes produce a single fruit.
This refers to wholesome mind and mental factors, as well as their arising and so forth.
There is one case where a single maturation cause produces a single fruit:
namely, the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and its arising and so forth.
Furthermore, there is karma that results in maturation in only one location;
namely, the karma that acquires the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and the homogeneous character of a group (nikāyasabhāga).
That karma results in maturation in the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) alone.
There is karma that ripens in only two bases (*āyatana*).
That is to say, there is karma pertaining to the mind base (*manāyatana*);
such karma ripens only in the mind base and the phenomena base (*dharmāyatana*).
Karma that results in the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) also brings about the maturation (*vipāka*) of two spheres,
namely the sphere of tangibles and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Karma that results in the sphere of the body (*kāyāyatana*) brings about the maturation of three spheres.
That is to say, the sense bases of body, tangibles, and mental phenomena;
the acquisition of the sense bases of visible form, odor, and taste; and their karma are likewise.
Each receives its own respective maturation within the sense bases of body, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
Karma that results in the acquisition of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) brings about the maturation (*vipāka*) of four bases:
namely, the eye-base, the body-base (*kāyāyatana*), the contact-base (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), and the mental-object-base (*dharmāyatana*).

Karma that results in the acquisition of the ear-, nose-, or tongue-base is likewise; each brings about the maturation of its own respective base, as well as the body-base, the contact-base, and the mental-object-base.
Other masters say that all great elements produce both visible form and sound,
and that no visible forms in the desire realm are devoid of odor or taste.
He asserts this:
the karma that acquires the eye base undergoes maturation as seven bases,
namely, the maturation of the eye base, the body base, and the bases of visible form, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena.
The same applies to the karma that results in the acquisition of the sense bases of the ear, nose, and tongue;
that is, each receives the maturation of its own respective base, as well as the sense bases of body, visible form, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena.
Karma that results in the acquisition of the sense base of the body receives the maturation of six sense bases.
That is to say, the maturation of the sense base of the body and the sense bases of visible form, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
One who has acquired the karma for the sense base of visible form experiences the maturation of five sense bases;
that is to say, the maturation of the sense bases of visible form, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
The same applies to the karma that results in the acquisition of the spheres of odor, taste, and tangibles;
that is, one respectively experiences the maturation of the spheres of visible form, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
What has been stated thus far refers to those [karmas] whose results are necessarily acquired.
Those whose attainment is indeterminate are indefinite in number.
Nevertheless, there are karmas capable of experiencing maturation in eight locations,
and there are karmas capable of experiencing maturation in nine locations.
There is karma that can experience the maturation in ten bases;
there is karma that can experience the maturation in eleven bases—
both excluding the base of sound.
Question: Why is it that some karma can experience maturation in many locations, while other karma can experience maturation in few locations?
Answer: If a karma possesses various capacities and thus attains various fruits, [it experiences maturation in many locations].
If karma possesses various functional capacities, one experiences maturation in many locations; if karma lacks such diverse capacities and does not yield various fruits,
one experiences maturation in few locations.
Just as external seeds possess various capacities and thus yield various fruits—
such as rice, sugarcane, grapes, and lotus roots—
those that lack various capacities do not yield various fruits.
It is like the case of Śuklodana, the son of Maitrāyaṇīputra,
and others. This refers to a grass found in marshes called *śuklodana*,
which grows in single stalks, each reaching several feet in height.
At its top there are few leaves, their shape like a parasol.
There is a tāla tree over a hundred cubits high;
at its top there are also few leaves, their shape like a parasol.
Although the trunk may be tall, the fruits are very few;
karma is likewise.
Nevertheless, the karma of one lifetime yields fruit across three lifetimes.
There is no case where karma from the three periods of time yields a fruit in a single period;
nor does karma of a single moment yield a fruit over many moments;
nor does karma spanning many moments yield a fruit in a single moment.
Because karma has results that are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral;
and because the resulting fruit does not diminish the cause.
Question: Do those who perform actions first create the karma that projects a particular homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*)?
Is it that one first creates the karma that fulfills the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*)?
Regarding this, some say:
"One first creates the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) and subsequently creates the fulfilling karma (*paripūraka-karma*)."
If one does not first draw the outline, there will be nothing to fill in later;
it is just as a painter first establishes the layout and then fills it with various colors—
this case is likewise so.
Other masters say that one first creates the completing karma (*paripūri-karman*) and subsequently creates the projecting karma (*ākṣepa-karman*). For example,
after a Bodhisattva has first created the completing karma throughout three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), [he then creates the projecting karma].
If it is said that the projecting karma is only created during the final hundred great eons,
this is not fixed.
There are cases where one first creates the projecting karma and later creates the completing karma;
there are also cases where one first creates the completing karma and later creates the projecting karma,
because these arise according to the intentionality of the agent.
Furthermore, there are three types of karma that ripen as feeling:
first, karma to be experienced in the present life;
second, karma to be experienced in the next life.
Third, karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Regarding karma to be experienced in the present life:
it is karma that is performed and accumulated in this very birth.
One experiences the ripening fruit in this very life,
not in another birth.
As for karma to be experienced in the next birth:
If karma is performed and accumulated in this life,
its ripened fruit is experienced in the immediately subsequent life,
and not in any other life.
Regarding karma to be experienced in subsequent lives:
if karma is performed and accumulated in this life,
it will be experienced in the third life, the fourth life, or thereafter.
They experience the results of maturation (vipāka) in their respective order.
However, the term "maturation" is used to express various meanings;
in some instances, even that which is a result of uniform outflow (niṣyanda) is designated as "maturation."
As it is said that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the branch of feeling (*vedanā*);

in some places, nourishment is called maturation, as when it is said that food, drink, and various medicines result in the maturation of pleasure; and in some places, dream-events are called maturation, as when it is said that one sees such and such kinds of maturation in dreams.
In some instances, abundance and scarcity are designated as "maturation" (vipāka),
as it is said:
"The constellations travel along this path."
There are indeed such ripened results (vipāka) of abundance and scarcity;
in some places, the Brahmā King refers to them as "ripened results," as it is said:
"O Great Sage, I shall not depart yet; let me observe what ripened result this radiance possesses."
In some instances, the term "vipāka" (maturation) refers to the locus of maturation;
as it is said here, the results of maturation, such as form and so forth, are themselves called "vipāka.
There are two kinds of maturation.
First, those of the same class;
second, those of different classes.
Regarding those of the same class that ripen:
This refers to the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*):
namely, that from the wholesome arises the wholesome,
and from the unwholesome arises the unwholesome.
When an indeterminate [cause] produces an indeterminate [result],
this is a maturation of a different category;
that is, the ripening fruit (vipākaphala).
This means that wholesome and unwholesome [actions] produce neutral (avyākṛta) results.
Because these neutral results arise from causes of a different class—namely, the wholesome and unwholesome—they are called "maturation" (vipāka).
Question: If it is the case that maturation is so named because it ripens from a cause of a different class, then...
For what reason are the miserable destinies (durgati) called "non-ripened" (avipāka)?
Answer: They are indeed maturation (vipāka);
however, because they are base and lowly, they are designated as "non-ripened."
For example, inferior villages, cities, and so forth are called "non-villages" and so on.
Furthermore, that which has over-ripened is called "unripe," just as when an unskilled potter fires various earthenware vessels.
Much fuel and grass are wasted, and all the vessels become scorched and melted;
being unfit for trade or use, they are also called "unrefined.
The same applies to the evil destinies.
It is called "non-ripening" (*avipāka*) because its painful fruit is excessive.
Furthermore, it is called "non-ripening" because there is no virtuous ripening (*kuśala-vipāka*) therein.
Question: Do animals and hungry ghosts also experience the fruits of virtue?
Why are all the miserable realms (durgati) called "non-maturation" (avipāka)?
Answer: Because their wholesome fruits are so few, they are also called "non-existent.
It is like a river with very little water being called "waterless."
Furthermore, although those realms possess wholesome fruits,
one cannot cultivate other superior wholesome dharmas; therefore,
they are called "immature."
For example, if a farmer harvests very little, it is also called "unripe," yet in reality, there are indeed results of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) in the evil destinies.
Question: Why do unwholesome and wholesome tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena have results of maturation?
Do indeterminate (avyākṛta) and untainted (anāsrava) dharmas lack a ripened fruit (vipākaphala)?
Answer: They differ according to three types—those whose intrinsic nature and various conditions are complete, those whose conditions are deficient, and others—just like external seeds.
Just as when a firm and solid seed is placed in fertile soil,
watered with moisture, and covered with manure and earth,
the sprout will immediately emerge once the power of these causes and conditions is complete.
In this way, unwholesome and wholesome tainted phenomena possess a firm and solid intrinsic nature.
When placed within the field of existence, watered with the water of craving, and covered by other fetters,
they produce the sprout of existence once the power of causes and conditions is complete.
Just as a solid seed placed in a granary cannot sprout if the conditions of water and manure are lacking, so too,
although the substance of untainted conditioned wholesome dharmas is solid, [they do not produce further results in the absence of conditions].
Yet, because the moisture of craving is absent and the remaining fetters provide no nourishing cover, the sprout of existence does not arise;
it is like a rotten seed that, though placed in fertile soil, watered, and covered with manure, will not grow.
Yet, due to the deficiency of causal power, it cannot produce a sprout.
In the same way, although these neutral conditioned phenomena are moistened and covered by the water of craving and other fetters, [they do not ripen].
However, because their physical constitution is weak and inferior, the sprout does not arise.
Question: For what further reason do all untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas lack a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*)?
Answer: Because they are neither a field (*kṣetra*) nor a vessel (*bhājana*).
...and so forth, as explained at length.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon can cause the continuous succession of birth, aging, sickness, and death within the various realms of existence and destinies, it possesses a ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
Because the untainted (*anāsrava*) causes the ultimate cessation of birth, aging, sickness, and death within the various realms of existence and destinies, it has no ripening fruit.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon can cause the various realms of existence (*bhava*) and destinies (*gati*) to gradually increase, it possesses a ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Because the untainted (*anāsrava*) causes the various realms of existence and destinies to gradually diminish, it lacks a ripening fruit.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon is suffering and is a process of arising, aging, sickness, death, and the convergence of the various realms of existence for all beings in the world, it possesses a ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*).

Because the untainted (*anāsrava*) is suffering that is a process of the cessation of arising, aging, sickness, death, and the various realms of existence for all beings in the world, it has no ripening fruit.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is the object of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the object of perversion (*viparyāsa*),
the object of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and the object of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*;
*vāsana*), it is defiled, poisonous, impure, and turbid.
Those who fall into the truth of suffering and the truth of origination and are subject to the three realms of existence possess the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
Because all untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are unlike those, they lack the fruit of maturation.
Furthermore, if untainted phenomena were to have a fruit of maturation, [it would follow that they are tainted].
Thus, one would obtain an inferior fruit from a superior cause;
for the cause is an untainted (anāsrava), wholesome, conditioned dharma,
whereas the fruit is a tainted (sāsrava) and indeterminate (avyākṛta) dharma.
Furthermore, if untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) were to have maturation (vipāka),
they would cause the continuity of existence (bhava-saṃtati) by means of the Noble Path (āryamārga).
This would contradict the principle that the Noble Path brings about the cessation of existence.
Furthermore, if untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) were to possess maturation (*vipāka*),
where would this maturation be experienced?
If it were in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it would be unreasonable.
Because untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) are not bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu),
they are like karma belonging to the form or formless realms;
if [this karma] were in the form realm, it would likewise be illogical.
Because untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are not bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-vīta-rāga*),
it would likewise be unreasonable for them to exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), just as [it is unreasonable] for karma belonging to the desire or formless realms [to exist there].
This is because untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are not bound to the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*),
just like the karma of the desire and form realms;
furthermore, it would also be illogical for them to exist outside the three realms.
Because there is no other place apart from the three realms.
Furthermore, the untainted noble path serves as the antidote to both the matured result (*vipāka*) and its cause;
if it were also capable of producing a matured result, [it would contradict its nature].
Furthermore, that which serves as the counteragent must itself be countered;
because it is untainted (*anāsrava*),
one must again cultivate the Noble Path to counteract the ripening (*vipāka*) it induces.
That noble path itself would then produce further karmic maturation (*vipāka*), and thus, through such successive cycles, it would become infinite.
In that case, there would be no liberation or deliverance; let there not be this fault.
Therefore, untainted phenomena have no ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, if untainted phenomena were to produce a ripened fruit,
one would never attain nirvāṇa.
Noble ones should not apply themselves with diligence to its cultivation,
for it is a phenomenon that produces birth, death, and saṃsāra;
consequently, it is untainted and lacks any ripened fruit.
Question: For what reason do all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas lack a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*)?
Answer: Because they are neither a field (*kṣetra*) nor a vessel (*bhājana*), and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, if indeterminate dharmas possess a ripened fruit (vipākaphala),
is this ripened fruit itself indeterminate, or is it wholesome or unwholesome?
If it were indeterminate, [it would follow that]...
Why is it called "maturation" (vipāka)? Because it is the ripening of a different class [of cause].
If it were both wholesome and unwholesome, it would not be maturation either, because the fruit of maturation is indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Furthermore, if indeterminate dharmas were to possess maturation,
then because this matured fruit is itself indeterminate, it would necessarily have its own maturation;
that maturation, in turn, would be able to produce further matured fruits.
If this were to continue in such a succession, it would be infinite;
thus, there would be no liberation or transcendence.
To avoid this fault, it is held that indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas have no ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
By virtue of such various causes and conditions,
only unwholesome and wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena constitute the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*).
