Section Twelve of the Second Sub-section on Wisdom within the First Aggregate of Miscellaneous Topics: Question: Does a single momentary action only have the power to project a single homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*)?
Can it also project multiple *nikāya-sabhāga*s?
If so, what fault would there be?
If a single moment of karma could project only a single *nikāya-sabhāga*, [what would follow]?
How should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*?
For instance, it says: "There are sentient beings who have previously existed among humans, having been either kings or ministers."
Possessing great power, they unjustly harmed immeasurable sentient beings,
seizing their wealth and resources to provide for themselves and their retinues;
due to these evil karmas, they died and fell into hell.
Having endured great suffering for immeasurable time,
they pass away from that state and, due to the remaining karma, are born in the great ocean,
taking the body of a fierce beast of immense size.
They devour immeasurable beings of water and land,
while they themselves are also devoured by immeasurable beings;
[the parasites] adhere all over their bodies like *kośa* bristles.
Having undergone such suffering, unable to endure it,
they rub their bodies against the crystal mountains (*sphaṭikaparvata*); the worms within their bodies are all likewise destroyed,
causing the seawater— extending for hundreds of thousands of *yojanas* in length and breadth— to turn entirely into blood.
Furthermore, if that were so, how would one reconcile the account given by the Venerable Aniruddha in the *Itivṛttaka*?
As it is said:
"Venerable sir,
because I gave a single meal as an offering to a field of merit,
I was born seven times in the heavens as a great celestial king."
He was born seven times among humans as the sovereign of a great kingdom.
Furthermore, if this is so,
how are the past events (*pūrvayoga*) described by Mahākāśyapa to be reconciled?
As it is said:
"Venerable One,
because I gave a single vessel of millet rice as an offering to the field of merit."
A thousand times he was born in that northern continent of Uttarakuru, where clothing and food are provided spontaneously;
a thousand times he was born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, experiencing great bliss.
Furthermore, if this were so...
How, then, is the *Sāṃyuktāgama Sūtra on Salt* to be reconciled? As it says:
"A certain type of person performs and accumulates such evil karma that they must experience its retribution in hell."
Or [karma] may be experienced in the present life;
yet there are cases where that which ought to be experienced in the present life is instead experienced in hell.
If even a single moment of karma can project many *nikāyasabhāga*s (homogeneous classes of beings), how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
As it is said:
"By the power of the various distinctions of karma,
the various distinctions of the realms of existence (gati) are established."
Based on the power of the various distinctions among the destinies (*gati*),
the various distinctions among births (*jāti*) are established.
Based on the various differentiated powers of arising,
the various differentiations of maturation (*vipāka*) are designated;
based on the various differentiated powers of maturation, [the various differentiated powers of arising are designated].
The various distinctions among the faculties are established;
and by the power of these various distinctions among the faculties,
the various distinctions among individuals (pudgala) are established.
Furthermore, if that were the case,
how would one reconcile the statement in the *Sūtra on Thorough Penetration*? As it says:
How should one understand the distinctions among various karmas?
It is said that distinct karmas lead to birth in the hells,
and distinct karmas lead to birth among animals.
Through distinct karmic actions one is born as a hungry ghost;
through distinct karmic actions one is born in the heavens;
through distinct karmic actions one is born among human beings.
Furthermore, if that were so,
how could the distinctions among the three types of karma— such as that to be experienced in the present life and so forth—
be established? Moreover, if that were so...
How, then, is the statement in the *Prakaraṇapāda* to be reconciled? As it says:
"One performs and increases the karmic action of superior killing."
When their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the Avīci Hell;
having been born there, they are subsequently born in other places, and from those they are born yet again in others,
and so forth, as explained at length.
It is agreed that this should be stated thus:
a single moment of karma can project only one *nikāya-sabhāga*.
Question: If that is so, [what follows]?
How should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*?
For instance, it says:
"There are sentient beings who have previously existed among human beings."
...and so on, as explained at length.
The answer is: it is due to residual karma and due to karma leading to other destinies;
that is to say, one who has committed and accumulated karma for the two evil destinies of hell and the animal realm while among humans.
Having experienced the retribution for hellish karma within the hells,
the remaining animal karma causes one to be born in the great ocean; therefore,
this "remaining sound" does not refer to a single karmic action.
Question: How then should one reconcile the account of the former life related by the Venerable Aniruddha?
As it was said:
"O Āyuṣmat..."
"Because I have offered a single meal as a gift to the field of merit," and so forth,
as explained at length.
This answer was stated because it reveals the primary cause.
This means that because they previously gave a single meal as an offering,
they were born into a wealthy and noble family with abundant riches and treasures;
this was due to their recollection of past lives or the power of their original vows.
Furthermore, he bestowed hundreds of thousands of offerings of wealth and food.
Thus, through many successive lifetimes,
he constantly delighted in giving and enjoyed great wealth and happiness.
Relying on the first cause, he makes this statement:
it is like a farmer who, with a small amount of seed, plants for many years;
through successive growth, it reaches a yield of hundreds or thousands of bushels.
They utter these words:
"I have planted a small seed and now obtained hundreds of thousands.
It is like a merchant who, with a single gold coin, engages in trade over a long period until it reaches ten million.
He spoke these words:
"I used a single coin to seek growth through trade,
and now it has reached ten million."
All of these statements are made based on the initial cause;
the Venerable One was likewise so.
Furthermore, it may be that during his lifetime, the Venerable One first gave a single meal and subsequently gave many more.
By this, he initiates the causes for many humans and devas;
it is based on that initial [act] that he makes such a statement.
Furthermore, when that venerable one gave a single meal, he gave rise to many thoughts and aspirations.
By this, one brings about many fruits of maturation (vipāka-phala) among gods and humans.
Furthermore, it may be that the Venerable One, by giving a single meal, gave rise to three grades of wholesome karma: inferior, middling, and superior.
By means of inferior karma, he was born among humans and became a ruler of men;
by means of middling karma, he was born in the heavens and further became a celestial king;
and by means of superior karma, in his final birth, he was born into the Śākya clan.
Having been abundant in wealth and jewels, he left the household life to practice the path and became an Arhat.
By this reasoning, the original account spoken by Mahākāśyapa has already been explained and resolved.
Question: How is the *Salt Simile Sūtra* to be reconciled? As it says:
"A certain type of person..."
...and so on, as explained at length. Some say:
"That [text] states that those two persons perform two kinds of karma and experience two distinct maturations (*vipāka*)."
It refers to two persons who both take life.
One does not diligently cultivate the body, ethical discipline, mind, and wisdom;
because his merit is slight, he goes to hell to undergo this karmic ripening fruit.
First, one diligently cultivates the body, ethical discipline, mind, and wisdom.
Because of that great merit, one receives this maturation of karma among human beings.
The Sūtra speaks of it as being "to such an extent."
What meaning does this express?
The answer is: it is called "that much" because it is either less, equal, or similar [to that].
Other masters say:
They assert that a single person performs two kinds of karma and experiences two types of maturation;
that is to say, there is a person who takes the lives of two beings,
where one karma is capable of projecting the maturation of the hells.
A single karma can lead one to experience maturation within the human realm;

if that person does not cultivate the body, ethical discipline, mind, and wisdom, they will instead go to hell to undergo the maturation of other karmas. However, if they can diligently cultivate the body, ethical discipline, mind, and wisdom...
Thus, one receives the distinct ripening fruits of various karmas among human beings.
Furthermore, there are those who say that a single person creates a single type of karma and experiences two types of ripening results.
This refers to a person who takes the life of one sentient being;
this karma can induce the retribution of the hells and,
simultaneously, can also induce the retribution of the human realm.
If he does not cultivate the body, ethical discipline, mind, and wisdom,
he will go to hell to undergo the ripening fruit;
as for the ripening fruit among humans, it remains within the state of non-arising.
If one can diligently cultivate the body, ethical discipline, mind, and wisdom,
one will receive the ripening fruit among human beings;
as for the ripening fruit of the hells, it shall abide in the state of non-arising.
The critique states:
He should not make such a statement,
lest there be the fault of the destruction of karma and the destruction of the realms of rebirth.
Regarding the destruction of karma:
it refers to a single karma that is both hellish karma and human karma.
Regarding the destruction of the destination (gati):...
It should be said that a single maturation is both the destiny of hell and the destiny of humans, because the fruit resembles its cause.
Thus it should be stated:
that person creates a single type of karma and experiences a single maturation.
This refers to a person who takes the life of another being;
this karma can induce the retribution of rebirth in hell.
If that person is unable to apply themselves diligently to the cultivation of the path and attain arhatship, [they will experience that retribution].
He will then go to hell to undergo the karmic fruit of this action.
If that person can apply themselves diligently to the practice of the Path and become an Arhat,
they will then be able to draw forth and experience the sufferings of hell.
This karma is experienced within the human body;
it cannot project the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga),
because karma that projects the homogeneous class cannot be experienced as a deposit.
For this reason, the Venerable Vasumitra said:
"Is it possible for an event that would lead to the suffering of hell to be experienced among human beings?
He replied: "It is possible."
This means that it is one who has realized the fruit of arhatship who is able to perform this deed, because their body has been cultivated by the excellence of meditative concentration and wisdom;
neither those still in training (śaikṣa) nor ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) are able to do so.
It is like a cook who, having soaked his hands in water, does not burn them even when handling hot rice;
yet if he did not soak his hands, he would be burned.
This case is also like that.
Therefore, only those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are capable of this.
Other masters state that even a single moment of karma can project many types of homogeneous existence (nikāyasabhāga).
Question: If that is so, the previous objection has been well resolved.
How, then, is the subsequent objection to be resolved?
Answer: The categories of karma created by sentient beings are not fixed.
There is karma that is disordered and can be transformed;
there is karma that is not disordered and cannot be transformed.
If it is disordered and subject to change,
it is as previously cited;
if it is not disordered and not subject to change, [it is otherwise].
As will be cited below,
both of these preceding and following difficulties are thus resolved.
The critique states:
He should not speak thus, lest there be the fault of the destruction of karma and the destruction of the realms of rebirth (*gati*).
One should rather say this: a single moment of karma can only project a single homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Furthermore, one is born in the hells solely through unwholesome karma that projects a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).

Once born there, one experiences only the maturation (*vipāka*) of unwholesome phenomena: matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Form consists of the nine bases excluding sound.
Mental states and mental factors consist of painful feeling and its associated phenomena.
Non-associated formations are as follows:
The life-faculty, the homogeneous class, and [the states of] birth, aging,
subsistence, and impermanence arise solely through unwholesome karma that projects rebirth within the realms of animals and hungry ghosts.
Having been born there, one experiences the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas:
the maturation of unwholesome dharmas consisting of matter, mind, mental factors, and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*). Regarding "matter":
[it refers to the following].
Excluding sound, there are nine bases.
As for the mind and mental factors,
they consist of the sensation of suffering and its associated phenomena.
The factors dissociated from mind are:
the life-faculty, the group-homogeneity, and the acquisitions of birth, subsistence, aging, and impermanence;
as well as the form that is the maturation of wholesome dharmas.
The four bases:
namely, visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects.
As for the mind and mental factors:
Pleasant feeling, equanimity, and their associated and dissociated factors undergo birth,
aging, duration, and impermanence.
Other masters say that within the realms of animals and hungry ghosts, wholesome dharmas do not have resultant matter;
they possess only resultant mind, mental factors, and non-associated formations.
Question: If that is so,
why is it that among the realms of animals and hungry ghosts,
we observe some with exquisite forms while others are hideous?
Answer: That unwholesome karma may have wholesome karma as its concomitant,
or it may have unwholesome karma as its concomitant.
If one takes virtuous karma as one's retinue,
one's physical form will be exquisite and beautiful,
for one has effectively subdued the power of unwholesome, base, and evil forces.
If one takes unwholesome karma as a companion, one’s physical form and appearance will be ugly and coarse,
because that unwholesome karma increases the power of such debased and evil states.
The commentary says:
It is not logically contradictory that wholesome karma can also induce the maturation of matter within those realms of animals and hungry ghosts.
Therefore, one should know that the first explanation is correct:
it is solely by virtue of karma that leads to a homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) which is wholesome that one is born among humans or gods in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Having been born there, one experiences the maturation of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas:
matter, mind, mental factors, and formations dissociated from mind.
Regarding the maturation of wholesome dharmas as matter:
With the exception of sound, there are nine bases.
As for the mind and mental factors,
these consist of the feelings of pleasure, joy, and equanimity, along with their associated phenomena.
Regarding those factors dissociated from the mind:
the life-faculty, the homogeneous character of beings, and the acquisitions, as well as birth, aging, duration, and impermanence;
and the matter that is the maturation of unwholesome dharmas.
The four bases:
namely, visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects.
As for "mind and mental factors":
Painful feeling and its associated factors,
as well as dissociated formations,
undergo birth, aging, subsistence, and impermanence.
Other masters say that in the realms of humans and gods, unwholesome dharmas do not have resultant form;
they possess only resultant mind, mental factors, and non-associated formations.
Question: If that is so, why is it that among the realms of humans and devas, we currently observe some with ugly forms and others with beautiful ones?
Answer: It is due to their wholesome karma.
Either unwholesome karma constitutes its retinue,
or wholesome karma constitutes its retinue.
If unwholesome karma constitutes its retinue, [it leads to suffering].
Their physical form is ugly and coarse because they lack the power to subdue the unwholesome and manifest the beautiful through virtue; yet,
if they were to take wholesome karma as their retinue, [they would be otherwise].
The form and color are exquisite and beautiful;
this is because wholesome karma increases the power of that beauty.
The commentary states:
It should be understood that among these, the first explanation is correct, as it does not contradict reason.
Question: We clearly observe in the human realm those who possess both sexual organs.
Is this the maturation of a wholesome karma,
or is it the maturation of an unwholesome karma?
Regarding this, some say:
That is the maturation of unwholesome karma.
Other masters say that it arises as a single form according to the place and the time.
This is the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome karma.
Regarding the statement that a second form arises at an improper place or time, this is the maturation of unwholesome karma; thus it is evaluated.
It should be stated thus:
the physical basis of the male and female faculties in those who possess both sexual organs is the result of wholesome karma.
Regarding the maturation (vipāka): the visible forms, odors, tastes,
and tangibles in those locations are the maturation of unwholesome karma.
However, it is solely through karma that leads to a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) by means of the wholesome that one is born within the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).
Having been born there, one experiences only the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome phenomena:
namely, matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Matter consists of the seven bases, excluding sound, odor, and taste.
Mind and mental factors consist of the feelings of pleasure, joy, and equanimity, as well as their associated phenomena.
Non-associated formations consist of the life-faculty, the homogeneous character of beings, the state of non-perception, acquisition, birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
However, it is solely by virtue of karma that draws one toward a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) through wholesome [roots] that one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Once born there, one experiences only the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome phenomena:
namely, the mind, mental factors, and formations dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Regarding the mind and mental factors:
these consist of the sensation of equanimity and its associated factors;
as for the dissociated formations: [they are as follows].
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya), the group-homogeneity (nikāyasabhāga), and [the factors of] birth, aging, duration,
and impermanence arise. Furthermore,
some say that one is born in hell solely by means of a superior unwholesome karma that projects the group-homogeneity.
Having been born there, they experience only the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those superior unwholesome dharmas;
however, it is by means of karma of middling strength that projects a common destiny (*nikāya-sabhāga*) that they are born into the animal realm.
Once born there, they experience only the maturation fruit of those medium-grade dharmas;
however, it was solely due to an unwholesome karma of inferior grade that drew them into the destiny of hungry ghosts as a commonality of rebirth.
Once born there, one experiences only the maturation fruit of those inferior dharmas;
other masters say that this occurs solely through superior unwholesome karma.
Karma that projects one into a commonality of rebirth leads to birth within the hells;
having been born there, one experiences the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those two grades of unwholesome dharmas—the superior and the middling.
The realms of animals and hungry ghosts are as previously described.
Alternatively, some say that one is born in hell solely by virtue of karma of an intense degree of unwholesomeness that projects a homogeneous life-span;
once born there, one experiences the ripening results of all three degrees of unwholesome dharmas.
However, it is solely by means of karma of middling strength that is unwholesome and which projects a common destiny (*nikāyasabhāga*) that one is born into the animal realm;
having been born there, one experiences the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) of those two types of dharmas—the middling and the inferior.
The realm of ghosts (*preta-gati*) is as previously explained.
Some say that one is born in the hells solely by means of karma of an extremely superior degree of unwholesomeness (*adhimātra-akuśala*) that projects a commonality of kind (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Having been born there, they experience the ripened fruit of those three grades of unwholesome dharmas;
however, it is specifically by means of a karma of medium-grade unwholesomeness that draws forth the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) that they are born into the realm of animals.
Having been born there, one experiences the maturation fruit of those three grades of dharmas;
yet, it is solely by virtue of an unwholesome karma of the inferior grade that projects the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) that one is born into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Having been born there, one experiences the maturation fruit of those two grades of dharmas—the inferior and the medium.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one is born in hell solely by virtue of karma of an intense grade of unwholesomeness that projects a homogeneous life-span;
once born there, one experiences the ripened fruit of all three grades of unwholesome dharmas.
It is solely by means of karma of middling unwholesomeness that draws one toward a common destiny (*nikāya-sabhāga*) that one is born in the realm of animals;
once born there, one experiences the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those three grades of dharmas.
It is solely by means of karma of inferior unwholesomeness that draws one toward a common destiny that one is born within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Having been born there, one experiences the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of those three grades of dharmas.
The critique states that this should be explained as follows:
there are three grades of unwholesome karma that project rebirth in the hell realm; through any one of these, one is born within the hellish homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Once born there, they experience the ripened fruit of those three grades of unwholesome dharmas according to their respective correspondence.
There are three grades of unwholesome karma that project rebirth in the animal realm; by whichever one of these it may be, one is born into the animal realm.
Once born there, they experience the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) of those three grades of dharmas according to their respective correspondence.
There are three grades of unwholesome karma that project rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*); by whichever one of these is operative, one is born into the realm of hungry ghosts.
Having been born there, one experiences the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those three grades of dharmas according to their respective correspondence.

Furthermore, some say that one is born in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) solely through karma of the highest grade of goodness belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) which projects a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Having been born there, they experience only the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those superior dharmas;

however, it is solely by means of karma of medium strength wholesome roots from the desire realm that draws forth the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) that they are born into the five lower heavens.
Once born there, one experiences only the maturation fruit of those intermediate-grade dharmas;
however, it is solely due to karma of a low-grade wholesome nature from the desire realm that draws one’s *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class) to birth within the human realm.
Having been born there, one experiences only the maturation fruit of those inferior dharmas.
Question: If one is born into the human realm by means of an inferior wholesome karma, and experiences the maturation fruit of inferior dharmas, [how is this so?]
How is it that a bodhisattva’s wholesome karma is also experienced among humans as being of the highest grade?
Furthermore, what is the difference between a bodhisattva’s wholesome karma and the wholesome karma of the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*)?
Answer: Regarding what was stated—that the lower-grade wholesome karma of the desire realm is experienced among human beings—this excludes the karma of Bodhisattvas;
therefore, such a statement was made, but it does not refer to all cases.
Due to other conditions, the karma of a bodhisattva is superior;
for the body of a bodhisattva is the basis for boundless qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*),
whereas the body of a Paranirmita-vaśavartin deva lacks such attributes.
Due to other conditions, the karma of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods is superior;
for the bodies of those gods are pure and subtle like the flame of a lamp,
whereas the birth-body of a Bodhisattva still possesses various impurities such as excrement and urine.

Other masters say that one is born in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations solely through karma of the highest grade of goodness in the desire realm that draws forth a homogeneous life-stream;
having been born there, one then experiences the maturation fruits of the dharmas of the upper and middle grades.
The five lower heavens of the realm of humans and gods are as previously described.

Alternatively, some say that one is born in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations solely through karma of the highest grade of goodness within the desire realm that projects a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Having been born there, they experience the matured fruit (*vipākaphala*) of those three grades of dharmas;
however, it is solely by virtue of karma of medium-grade goodness belonging to the desire realm that draws the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) that they are born into the five lower heavens.
They experience the ripening fruits of those two lower and middling grades of dharmas.
Regarding the human realm, it is as previously explained. Some teachers say:

However, it is solely by virtue of karma that draws a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) through superior wholesome states of the desire realm that one is born in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
Having been born there, one experiences the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those three grades of dharmas.

However, it is solely through karma of the desire realm that is wholesome and of a certain degree which draws one into a particular homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) that one is born into the five lower heavens;
having been born there, one then experiences the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those three types of dharmas.
It is solely through the karma that draws the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*)—a wholesome action of the inferior grade belonging to the desire realm—that one is born among human beings;
having been born there, one then experiences the maturation results (*vipāka-phala*) of those two grades of dharmas, namely the inferior and the intermediate.

Furthermore, there are those who say that one is born in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations solely through karma of the highest grade of goodness within the desire realm that projects a homogeneous life-span (*nikāya-sabhāga*);
having been born there, one then experiences the matured fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those three grades of dharmas.
However, it is solely by means of karma of middling strength that is wholesome within the desire realm which draws one into birth in the five lower heavens;
having been born there, one experiences the maturation of those three types of dharmas as their fruit.
It is solely through the karma that draws one’s *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous class) from a low-grade wholesome state of the desire realm that one is born into the human realm;
having been born there, one then experiences the ripened results (*vipākaphala*) of those three grades of dharmas.
The commentary states:
It should be explained as follows.
There are three grades of wholesome karma that lead to rebirth in the common lot (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods.
Depending on a single grade [of wholesome karma], one is reborn in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
Having been born there, one experiences the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those three grades of dharmas as appropriate.
There are three grades of wholesome karma that project the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the five lower heavens.
Depending on a single grade [of karma], one is born into any of the five lower heavens.
Having been born there, one experiences the maturation results (*vipākaphala*) of those three grades of phenomena as appropriate.
There are three grades of wholesome karma that lead to rebirth in the human realm within the commonality of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
According to whichever single grade [of karma] one is born into the human realm,
having been born there, one experiences the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) of those three grades of dharmas as appropriate.
Furthermore, there are three grades of wholesome karma that project a non-distinct commonality of group (*nikāyasabhāga*) for the first dhyāna.
Depending on which single category [of wholesome action] gives rise to the first dhyāna,
once it has arisen therein, one accordingly experiences the ripened fruit of those three categories of non-distinct wholesome dharmas.

However, it is solely by means of an inferior grade of wholesome karma that draws forth the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the second dhyāna that one is born in the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*).
Once born there, one experiences only the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of that inferior grade of wholesome dharma.

However, it is solely by means of karma of middling strength that draws forth the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the second dhyāna that one is born among the Gods of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābhā*).
Once born there, one experiences only the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those middling wholesome dharmas.
However, it is solely by virtue of karma of superior-grade goodness that draws forth the group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the Second Dhyāna that one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven;

once born there, one experiences only the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those superior-grade wholesome dharmas. Furthermore, it is solely by virtue of karma of inferior-grade goodness that draws forth the group-homogeneity of the Third Dhyāna that one is born in the Parīttaśubha Heaven.
Having been born there, they experience only the maturation fruit of those inferior wholesome dharmas;

however, it is solely by means of karma of middling-grade wholesomeness that draws the generic similarity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the third dhyāna that they are born among the gods of Immeasurable Purity (*Apramāṇaśubha*).
Once born there, one experiences only the maturation fruit of those intermediate wholesome dharmas;
however, it is solely through the karma of superior wholesome roots that projects the homogeneous group (nikāya-sabhāga) of the third dhyāna that one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
Once born there, one experiences only the matured fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those superior wholesome dharmas;
however, it is solely by means of an inferior wholesome karma that draws forth the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the fourth dhyāna that one is born in the Anabhraka heaven.
Once born there, they experience only the maturation fruit of those inferior wholesome dharmas;

however, it is solely by virtue of karma of medium-grade wholesomeness that draws the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the fourth dhyāna that they are born in the Heaven of Merit (*Puṇyaprasava*).
Once born there, one experiences only the maturation fruit of those intermediate wholesome dharmas;
however, it is solely by virtue of karma that induces the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga) of the Fourth Dhyāna through superior wholesome states that one is born among the Bṛhatphala devas.
Once born there, they experience only the matured fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those superior wholesome dharmas;

however, it is solely by means of the karma that draws the generic similarity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the fourth dhyāna through the practice of mixed meditation (*vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna*) at a low degree that they are born in the Avṛha heaven.
Having been born there, one experiences only the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those inferior levels of mixed meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
However, it is by means of karma that induces the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the fourth dhyāna through medium-level mixed meditative absorption that one is born in the Atapa Heaven.
Once born there, one experiences only the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those intermediate meditative absorptions mixed with dhyāna;
however, it is by means of the karma that draws the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the fourth dhyāna through superior mixed meditative absorption that one is born in the Sudṛśa Heaven.
Having been born there, one experiences only the ripening fruit of that superior practice of meditative absorption (dhyāna-viśeṣa-bhāvanā).

It is solely by means of the karma that draws forth the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga) of the fourth dhyāna through the superior-of-the-superior practice of meditative absorption that one is born in the Sudarśana Heaven.
Having been born there, they experience only the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of those superior-superior (*adhimātrādhimātra*) dhyānas mixed with the formless attainments.
It is solely by means of the karma that projects the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) of the fourth dhyāna through these superior-superior mixed dhyānas that they are born in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Having been born there, one experiences only the ripening fruit of those superior, most excellent dharmas of the mixed meditative absorptions (*dhyāna-vyavakīrṇa*).
There is a threefold wholesome karma that draws forth a distinct *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class) for the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Accordingly, one is born into the Sphere of Infinite Space through any one of its three grades; having been born there,
one experiences the ripened fruit of those three grades of wholesome dharmas as appropriate.
There are three grades of wholesome karma that project the consciousness-infinity-sphere (vijñānānantyāyatana) with no distinction in its homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga).
Whichever single grade [of karma] brings about birth in the consciousness-infinity-sphere,
once born there, one experiences [the results] accordingly.
One experiences the maturation fruit of those three grades of wholesome dharmas.
There is karma of three grades of wholesomeness that draws forth a non-distinct *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class) of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Depending on whichever single grade [is predominant], one is born in the sphere of nothingness.
Having been born there, they experience the ripened fruit of those three grades of wholesome dharmas according to their respective correspondence.
There are three grades of wholesome karma that project a non-distinct commonality of group (nikāya-sabhāga) for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Depending on whichever single grade [of karma] gave rise to birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
once born there, one experiences the ripened fruit of those three grades of wholesome dharmas as appropriate.

Question: Why is it that the three grades of wholesome karma in the first dhyāna result in a non-distinct ripened fruit, whereas the three grades of wholesome karma in the three higher dhyānas result in distinct ripened fruits?
The answer is: In the first dhyāna, there are beings with lords who dwell in a state of confusion;
this is not the case in the three higher dhyānas.
Other masters say: [the reason is that]...
In the first dhyāna, there is vitarka and vicāra, as well as the various groups of consciousness and the production of bodily and vocal intimation (vijñapti-karma) belonging to its own level;
these things do not exist in the three higher dhyānas.
Furthermore, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), unwholesome karma has a maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) that lasts for one eon (*kalpa*);
wholesome karma is not like this.
Within the desire realm, unwholesome karma has maturation fruits across the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
Wholesome karma is not like this.
Question: Why is it that in the desire realm, unwholesome karma has a maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) lasting for one eon (*kalpa*), whereas wholesome karma does not?
Answer: The desire realm is an indeterminate realm;
it is not a stage of cultivation, nor is it a stage of freedom from defilement.
Unwholesome karma is superior because wholesome karma is inferior.
Furthermore, within the desire realm:
Unwholesome phenomena are difficult to sever,
difficult to shatter,
and difficult to transcend.
Because the wholesome is not so;
furthermore, within the desire realm, the unwholesome roots are strong while the wholesome roots are weak.
Furthermore, within the desire realm,
unwholesome states are like the host,
while wholesome states are like guests.
Furthermore, within the desire realm, the causes of unwholesome dharmas constantly increase,
whereas the causes of wholesome dharmas do not.
Furthermore, within the desire realm:
The unwholesome roots are capable of severing the wholesome roots,
whereas the wholesome roots cannot sever the unwholesome roots.
Furthermore, within the desire realm, modes of conduct are intermingled and disordered.
It is like a husband and wife;
for unwholesome qualities increase while wholesome qualities decrease.
Furthermore, within the desire realm, there is no intermixture of deportment.
It is like the son of a caṇḍāla being imprisoned together with the sons of thieves;
for unwholesome dharmas increase and wholesome dharmas diminish.
Furthermore, within the desire realm (kāmadhātu), there is no vessel capable of receiving wholesome karma.
Because it is the maturation (*vipāka*) of one kalpa.
Question: Is there not the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) consisting of the continents, Mount Sumeru, the seven golden mountains, and so forth, which lasts for one kalpa?
Answer: Those are sovereign fruits (*adhipati-phala*), not maturation fruits (*vipāka-phala*).
This statement is made based on the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, even among the wholesome karmas of the desire realm,
those that are most predominant can also induce a ripening for one eon.
Such wholesome karma must be attained by abandoning the ninth grade of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
once defilement has been abandoned, such karma certainly cannot project the fruit of a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Therefore, in the desire realm, no wholesome state is capable of producing a maturation lasting for an entire kalpa.
Furthermore, among all wholesome dharmas,
the most superior is the untainted (anāsrava) wholesome.
That has no ripening;
among the contaminated wholesome states, the most superior is the wholesome state of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
That is not the desire realm;
therefore, there is no maturation of wholesome karma in the desire realm that lasts for an entire eon.
As for unwholesome karma, it is only the highest grade [of such karma] that [does so].
This refers to karma that projects a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) without interruption;
therefore, it has a maturation (*vipāka*) lasting for one eon (*kalpa*).
Question: Why is it that exceptionally superior wholesome karma can induce eighty thousand great eons in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)?
Do unwholesome [karmas] only result in a single intermediate kalpa?
Answer: Wholesome karma is cultivated across many realms and many stages, whereas various unwholesome karmas are not so.
Question: For what reason do unwholesome karmas in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have the five destinies (*gati*) as their matured fruit (*vipākaphala*), whereas wholesome karmas do not?
Answer: All that has been stated previously constitutes this reason.
This means that within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), unwholesome karma is predominant.
Furthermore, there is a unique cause for this:
namely, that the desire realm is the field (*kṣetra*) for unwholesomeness.
Just as it is difficult for fine crops to grow in a poor field while weeds easily flourish,
so it is with the desire realm:
wholesome karma finds it difficult to thrive, whereas unwholesome karma arises with ease.
Therefore, unwholesome karma receives its maturation fruit throughout one entire realm and a portion of four realms;
wholesome karma receives its maturation fruit only in a portion of four realms.
Other masters say that because wholesome and unwholesome actions each have their own distinct effects, one should not find fault with them;
that is to say, the results of unwholesome karma are experienced within the five destinies and do not pervade all three realms.
Wholesome karma is pervasive throughout the three realms, yet its fruition is not pervasive across all five destinies.
Regarding the matter of their shared pervasiveness:
both wholesome and unwholesome karma are pervasive across the four modes of birth, wherein they receive their respective matured fruits (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, both are capable of experiencing the maturation (vipāka) of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Karma is the cause of the eye."
The Abhidharma states that the great elements (mahābhūta) are the cause of the eye;
it further states that the eye itself is the cause of the eye.
Thus, there are these three statements.
Is this not contradictory?
Answer: There is no fault of contradiction, because it is based on the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
The sūtra states:
"Karma is the cause of the eye;
it is the cause of its arising."
Because they serve as the cause of dependence, the cause of abiding, the cause of support, and the cause of nourishment,
the Abhidharma states that the great elements (mahābhūta) are the causes of the eye;
this is because they function as homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu).
That same [text] further states that the eye is the cause of the eye.
Question: If the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the eye are also causes of the eye, why does the Sūtra state only that karma is the cause of the eye?
Answer: Because karma is the fundamental cause.
As it is said:
"By the diverse powers of the various distinctions of karma."
One designates the various distinctions among the realms of existence;
even up to the point where, by the power of the various distinctions among the faculties,
one designates the various distinctions among individuals (*pudgala*).
Furthermore, karma is the cause for the differentiation among sentient beings;
that is to say, it is by virtue of karma that there are distinctions among sentient beings such as beauty and ugliness, or nobility and lowliness.
Furthermore, karma is the cause for the differentiation among the seven classes of practitioners.
That is to say, it is by virtue of karma that there are distinctions in the conduct of monastics and others;
furthermore, because karma can differentiate between desirable and undesirable fruits;
and furthermore, because karma is the manifest characteristic of both the ignorant and the wise.
Furthermore, karma distinguishes sentient beings by means of its "seal.
Furthermore, the differentiation of the faculties arises from the distinction of karma,
just as the differentiation of sprouts arises from the distinction of seeds.
Furthermore, the increase and decrease, the advancement and retreat, and the rise and fall of the lifespan of all sentient beings are entirely due to karma.
Furthermore, the distinctions among the various realms, destinies, and modes of birth are all due to karma.
Due to various causes and conditions such as these,
the sūtra states only that karma is the cause of the eye,
as the sūtra says:
By repeatedly practicing and extensively propagating the sin of taking life,
one shall fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts;
subsequently, if born among humans, one’s lifespan will be short.
Question: Is it by this very same karma that one falls into the evil destinies, and by this very same karma that one’s lifespan is short?
Regarding this, some say:
Due to this evil karma, one falls into the various miserable realms;
by that very same karma, one returns among human beings with a short lifespan,
for that sutra does not state there is any other cause.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one falls into the various evil destinies due to the preliminary application (*prayoga*) of killing,
and is born among humans with a short lifespan due to the fundamental act (*maula*) of killing.
Furthermore, there are those who say that falling into the various evil destinies is the ripened fruit of killing,
while being born among humans with a short lifespan is the subsequent result.
This is the flow-on result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of killing.
Furthermore, some say that by taking life,
one falls into the various evil destinies (*durgati*).
By eating that flesh, one will subsequently be born among humans with a short lifespan.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the killer of living beings incurs two faults.
First, one gives rise to undesirable painful sensations there;
second, one cuts off the lifespan that is cherished there.
Because of giving rise to those undesirable painful sensations, one falls into the various evil destinies.
Because they have severed the lifespan that was dear to them, their lifespan is short when they are later reborn among humans.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"Those whose lifespan among humans is short..."
It is not the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) of the karma of killing;
for since the eight faculties, such as the life-faculty, in the realms of humans and gods are ripened,
they are exclusively the ripened fruits of wholesome karma.
However, as for the agent: formerly, while among human beings, they first created karma that leads to a human lifespan;
subsequently, they further created the karma of taking life.
This latter karma causes harm to the former [karma].
One's prior karma would have resulted in a lifespan of twenty years;
however, due to subsequent harm, one receives only ten.
Therefore, the shortening of human life is not the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of that [prior] karma.
As stated in the sūtra:
because people at the time when the human lifespan was ten years were able to undertake and practice the paths of wholesome action,
the sons and daughters born to them lived for twenty years.
Question: There is no principle that one person creates karma while another receives its fruit.
Why is it that when parents who have practiced virtue for ten years give birth to a child, that child’s lifespan is twenty years?
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke thus:
"Because those who are ten years old cultivate wholesome deeds together,
at the end of their lives they are reborn as twenty-year-old sons."
Therefore, there is no fault of one person performing an action while another receives its result.
The Venerable One said:
"The maturation results of karma are each distinct and determined."
This means that karma with a lifespan of twenty years brings about a fruit of twenty years,
and so on up to karma with a lifespan of eighty thousand years bringing about a fruit of eighty thousand years;
however, this occurs because the parents have cultivated wholesome karma.
This ensures that the karma created by a son can yield its fruit.
Although there is no principle whereby one person creates karma and another receives its fruit,
there exists the sense of karma and fruit being mutually related through their functioning as conditions for one another.
Question: When one reaches the age of ten, do actions such as not killing constitute a path of action (*karmapatha*)?
Some say: "Those are not paths of action;
rather, they are merely communal regulations (*samādāna*) for not harming living beings and so forth."
Because one undertakes and maintains [the precepts] such as non-killing with a resolute mind of superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Other masters say that these are also courses of action (*karmapatha*), because they too involve a mutual undertaking of abstention through a focused mind directed toward one another.
Furthermore, the Prajñapti-śāstra states that there are four kinds of death:
first, death due to the exhaustion of the life-span, but not due to the exhaustion of wealth.
For example, there may be a certain class of persons who possess both karma for a short lifespan and karma for great wealth.
At a later time, one dies because their lifespan is exhausted, not because their wealth is exhausted;
another dies because their wealth is exhausted, not because their lifespan is exhausted.
Suppose there is a certain class of person who possesses both the karma for limited wealth and the karma for long life.
At a later time, that person dies because their wealth is exhausted, not because their lifespan is exhausted;
or they die because both their lifespan and their wealth are exhausted.
Suppose there is a certain class of persons who possess karma for a short lifespan and karma for meager wealth;
they die at a later time because their lifespan has been exhausted and because their wealth has been exhausted.
Fourth, there are those who die neither because their lifespan is exhausted nor because their wealth is exhausted.
For example, there may be a certain class of beings who possess karma for long life and karma for great wealth;
yet, at a later time, although both their wealth and lifespan are not yet exhausted,
they encounter adverse conditions and die prematurely.
The author of that treatise made this statement because he wished to demonstrate the existence of untimely death; thus,
although the Buddha had not yet exhausted either his wealth or his lifespan, he entered parinirvāṇa.
Nevertheless, it is not an untimely death,
because it is accomplished through the power of the meditative concentration on the limit (*prāntakoṭi-samādhi*),
and because the majesty of its merit has not yet been exhausted.
Other sentient beings have their power exhausted at the point of death,
but the Buddha is not like this.
Furthermore, the *Prajñapti-śāstra* states:

Is there a case where one does not experience the maturation of karma to be experienced in the present life, yet experiences the maturation of karma to be experienced in the next life or in subsequent lives?
Answer: There is.
This means that while the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma to be experienced in the present life does not manifest,
the maturations of karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*) and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) do manifest.
Is it possible for there to be no manifestation of the maturation of karma to be experienced in the next life?
"And does one experience the maturation of karma that is to be experienced in the present life as well as karma that is to be experienced in subsequent lives?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, when the maturation of karma to be experienced in the next life does not manifest in the present."
When the maturation of karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*upapadyavedanīya* or *aparaparyāyavedanīya*) manifests,

is it possible for one to experience the maturation of karma to be experienced in the present life and karma to be experienced in the next life, while not experiencing the maturation of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives?
Answer: Yes.

This refers to the case where the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives does not manifest, while the maturation of karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*) do manifest.
This essential point is that such a phenomenon occurs only upon the realization of the fruit of arhatship, and not for those who have not attained it.
Question: Should not such a phenomenon also occur for those in training (śaikṣa) and for ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana)?
Why does that treatise speak only of the arhat?
The answer is: only the arhat possesses the capacity [for such feats] because his body has been cultivated by superior concentration and wisdom;
those still in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) do not possess such qualities.
Furthermore, only an Arhat is able to thoroughly know his own karma—whether it is proximate or remote, and whether it is reversible or irreversible.
Regarding those karmas that are reversible, he transforms them through the power of cultivation.
If it cannot be turned back, one brings forth the experience of the present life so as not to undergo future existence.
It is like a person who wishes to travel to another country, but all his creditors come before him; that person immediately turns back to repay them.

This explains that such a thing may occur regarding the karma of completing actions (*paripūri-karman*), because the karma for the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is not experienced simultaneously.
Furthermore, it is because there is no interruption in a single continuum (*saṃtati*).
Other masters say:
There is karma from previous lives that, although its maturation has already been experienced, still has a remainder;
at this time, upon realizing the fruit of arhatship, one brings it forth for experience in the present through the power of superior cultivation and the power of decisive discernment.
Because only Arhats possess such a capacity, they are specifically mentioned.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*)?
Answer: It consists of all unwholesome (*akuśala*) and wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*) phenomena.
The intrinsic nature has already been explained;
its reason for being so shall now be discussed.
Question: For what reason is it called the "ripening cause" (vipāka-hetu)?
What is the meaning of "ripening" (*vipāka*)?
The answer is: ripening in a different category is the meaning of ripening.
That is to say, wholesome and unwholesome causes have the indeterminate as their fruit.
The meaning of "fruit" (*phala*) as that which has ripened has already been explained previously.
This cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) definitely extends across the three time periods and possesses a fruit of maturation.
"What is the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*)? and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To refute the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that when phenomena arise, they do so without a cause, like the various non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
To refute their position and demonstrate that the arising of all phenomena necessarily possesses a cause, [the author] says:
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that although phenomena arise from causes when they are produced,
they do not cease due to causes when they perish, such as the Dārṣṭāntikas.
To stop that attachment, it is shown that the arising and ceasing of all phenomena do not occur without causes.

Alternatively, there may be those who hold the view that only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) can function as efficient causes (*kāraṇahetu*), and not unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
To stop that attachment, it is shown that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) can also act as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Alternatively, there may be those who hold the view that all efficient causes possess an activity (*vṛtti*) of grasping and giving results.
To refute that attachment, it is shown that even a productive cause (kāraṇa-hetu) may be incapable of grasping or yielding its fruit;
nevertheless, it is established as a cause simply by not acting as an obstacle.
Alternatively, there are those who hold the following view:
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is also a productive cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) with respect to itself;
however, in order to refute that attachment, it is shown that the intrinsic nature is not a productive cause with respect to itself.
Or again, there is another attachment:
All unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) also possess the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
This is stated to refute the attachment [to the contrary] and to demonstrate that conditioned phenomena possess the efficient cause, whereas unconditioned phenomena do not.
Alternatively, there may be those who hold the view that a subsequent phenomenon is not an efficient cause for a preceding one.
In order to refute those attachments and to demonstrate that the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) can serve as a cause for dharmas that precede, follow, or coexist with it—
and in order to refute these various divergent attachments and reveal the correct cause— this treatise was composed.
What is the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*)?
Answer: With the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
This eye-consciousness [arises] by means of those eyes and visible forms, their associated mental factors (*samprayuktadharma*), and their co-existent factors (*sahabhūdharmas*).
And likewise for the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness; the nose, odors, and nose-consciousness; the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness; the body, tangibles, and body-consciousness;

and the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness—including those that are material or immaterial, visible or invisible, resistant or non-resistant, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned, and so forth.
All phenomena serve as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), with the exception of their own nature.
This applies likewise to visual consciousness, as well as auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness.
This is called the efficient cause.
Regarding "the factors associated with it" and "the factors coexistent with it" herein:
this refers to all factors that are associated with and coexistent with visual consciousness.
Question: What are the six pairs of factors previously mentioned, such as the eye and visible forms?

Alternatively, since the meaning of the six triads of dharmas is already sufficient for well-designating, well-explaining, establishing, and revealing the essential nature of all phenomena as acting causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
why are the five pairs of dharmas, such as "with form" and "without form," further taught?
The answer is: the former is an extensive explanation and the latter is a concise explanation;
the former is a specific explanation and the latter is a general explanation;
the former is a detailed explanation and the latter is a non-detailed explanation.
The former is the gradual teaching and the latter is the sudden teaching;
thus it is shown that their meaning is clear. Question:
Why, in this context, does one not simply state, "How can [all] phenomena act as efficient causes? Answer: [Because... all phenomena.
Answer: If one were to speak in this way, it would follow that a nature acts as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for itself.
Question: If that is so, why is it not stated in this manner?
What is the efficient cause? Answer: All phenomena, with the exception of their own nature.
Answer: If one were to speak in this way, then unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) would also possess the nature of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), because there would be no distinction made.
Question: If that is so, why is it not stated in this way?
What is the efficient cause? Answer: All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), with the exception of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Answer: If one were to speak in this way, then unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) would not be acting causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Question: Why is it stated here that only the six consciousnesses take remaining phenomena as their acting cause, and not other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)?

Answer: Because consciousness is the most preeminent among all phenomena, the six causes mentioned here are all stated in terms of their preeminence and do not exhaustively cover the entire principle.
Question: If that is so, then for visual consciousness, with the exception of its own nature, all other phenomena are efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*).

Why is it that in this context, the eye and visible forms are explained first, followed by their associated and co-existent dharmas, and finally all other dharmas such as the ear and so forth? The answer is:

because the eye and visible forms possess a stronger functional efficacy in the sense of acting as the support (*āśraya*), the object (*ālambana*), and the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) for visual consciousness.
Because associated and co-existent dharmas exert a direct and proximate influence as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) upon visual consciousness, whereas the ear and other [faculties] do not;
for this reason, they are mentioned later.
Question: Why is it that a nature is not an efficient cause with respect to itself?

Answer: If a self-nature were the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) of itself, then there would be no distinction between cause and effect, the producer and the produced, the inducer and the induced, the characteristic and the characterized, the transformer and the transformed, or the continuity and the continued; [in short], cause and effect and so forth would be indistinguishable.
Since there is a distinction between these two, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not an efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) with respect to itself.

Furthermore, because the intrinsic nature neither benefits nor harms itself, neither increases nor decreases, neither establishes nor destroys, and neither advances nor retreats, it is therefore not an efficient cause.
Furthermore, intrinsic nature is not a cause for itself;
it is not an equal-and-immediate condition,
nor is it an object-condition.
Because it is not predominant, it is not a creative cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Furthermore, if a self-nature were a creative cause for itself,
it would contradict all empirical facts perceived in the world.
That is to say: a fingertip cannot touch itself;
the eye cannot see itself;
a blade cannot cut itself.
All such things cannot be carried by even those who possess great strength.
Furthermore, because intrinsic nature has no sovereignty over itself and lacks dependence, it is not a productive cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Furthermore, because intrinsic nature does not depend upon itself, it is not a productive cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
It is like a person who can stand by relying on a staff;
once the staff is removed, they fall.
There is no such principle that an intrinsic nature acts upon itself.
Furthermore, the non-obstructive aspect constitutes the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*);
however, because the intrinsic nature of phenomena obstructs its own intrinsic nature, it is not an efficient cause.
There are two kinds of obstructions:
first, the conventional, such as a person on a bed obstructing others;
second, the ultimate.
Just as intrinsic nature obstructs intrinsic nature and renders it non-sovereign;
furthermore, if intrinsic nature were the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) for itself,
one would have to say that "ignorance conditions ignorance" and so forth, rather than "ignorance conditions formative forces" and so forth.
It should be said that visual consciousness arises with visual consciousness itself as its condition, and not that visual consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as its conditions.
Therefore, it is a settled principle that a self-nature is not the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) for itself.

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section 13 of the Second Sub-section on Wisdom within the First Aggregate of Miscellaneous Topics: The nature of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is identical to the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Because all phenomena have [the nature of] self-nature as their essence,
yet there is a difference in meaning:
that is to say, "many" refers to the meaning of the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The meaning of non-obstruction is the meaning of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).

Question: If the meaning of "predominance" (*adhipatya*) is the meaning of the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), then the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) should also be called "predominant."
Their substance also encompasses all phenomena,
as explained in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*.
This is because both of these conditions take all phenomena as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Answer: If based on the continuity (*saṃtāna*), these two conditions are similar in their breadth and narrowness;
however, if based on the moment (*kṣaṇa*), the nature and meaning of the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) are more extensive and superior.
This refers to when the aspect of non-self (*anātman*) regarding all phenomena manifests before one.
Among all phenomena, that which is not an object-condition (*ālambana*) refers to its own nature (*svabhāva*),
its associated factors (*samprayukta*), and its co-existent factors (*sahabhū*).
That which is not a dominant condition (*adhipati*) is solely this own nature.
Because the various phenomena that are associated and co-existent with this [mind] are its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and not its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Question: If the meaning of "non-obstruction" is the meaning of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), then...
In that case, the essence of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) would not encompass all phenomena;
for if a single sentient being gives rise to the aggregates, elements, and bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*) of one destiny,
that same sentient being could never again give rise to a second set of aggregates, elements, and bases.
If visual consciousness arises based on a single eye,
no second consciousness can arise therein,
just as it cannot arise in a single location.
If there is one tree, there is no second tree;
if there is one house, there is no second house.
In this way, all phenomena obstruct one another.
How is it that this cause encompasses all phenomena?
Answer: Although this is the case, there is no contradiction in principle.
That is to say, if for a single sentient being there arises the sense of the aggregates, elements, and bases belonging to even one realm of existence; [then all phenomena are encompassed].
He said to the remaining aggregates, elements, and sense bases:
"I shall not create an obstacle for you; I will arise together with you.
Even if I were to become an obstacle for you," [he continued].
You would not be able to arise therein.
If visual consciousness manifests in dependence upon one eye,
this consciousness is designated by the term "other visual consciousness."
I shall not act as an obstacle for you, but will arise in accordance with your births.
Even if I were to become an obstacle for you,
you would be unable to manifest before me.
The analogies of the tree and the house should be explained accordingly.
Furthermore, regarding those very things that act as obstacles,
they do not obstruct when [the object] arises.
Therefore, when a single dharma is about to arise,
all other dharmas do not act as obstructions.
Should there be even a single dharma that obstructs it, [it would not arise].
Because those [other] dharmas would not be able to arise at that time,
the meaning of non-obstruction is the meaning of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Furthermore, the efficient cause encompasses all dharmas.
Question: All phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions;
all phenomena cease through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
There is no time when causes and conditions are not in conjunction.
"How is it that all phenomena do not arise and perish at every moment?
To this, the Venerable Vasumitra replied:
"Because they arise through the conjunction of conditions, all phenomena arise."
Because the conjunction of conditions ceases, all phenomena cease.
Since the conjunction of arising and ceasing is neither dual nor manifold,
how could all phenomena be subject to constant arising and constant ceasing?
Furthermore, he spoke these words:
"Once phenomena have arisen through the conjunction of causes and conditions,
they subsequently continue in succession for immeasurable moments."
Even if one were continuously drenched and weighed down by pressure, one could not rise again.
It is like a person who has fallen from a cliff and is further covered layer after layer with soil;
even at that time, such a person cannot even move, let alone rise up.
The Venerable One said:
"Since the causal conditions for conjunction exist only momentarily,
how is it that all phenomena are constantly arising and ceasing?"
The Venerable Buddhadeva asserts this:
the arising and ceasing of all phenomena each occur at but a single moment;
consequently, there would have to be a functional activity such that what has already arisen arises once more.
If they were to cease again after having already ceased, they would be rendered useless.
Therefore, the arising and ceasing of all phenomena is not constant.
Question: When all phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions...
Are the functions of causes and conditions many or one?
If you say they are only one, how can they depend upon many?
If you say they are many, how can they be combined into a unity?
Answer: It can be said to be one, and it can also be said to be many.
This is because it accomplishes a single task while depending upon multiple entities.
Furthermore, it is because the functional capacities of its causes and conditions accord with one another.
It may be said to be "one" because it gives rise to many dharmas;
furthermore, it may be said to be "one" because the functional capacity of its causes and conditions is identical in causing all those dharmas to arise.
Because they give rise to distinct functions such as form and sensation, they can be said to be manifold.
If those capacities were not of many kinds,
there would be no distinction between the functions they produce, such as form and non-form.
Therefore, regarding the functional capacity of the causes and conditions of all phenomena, one cannot definitively state whether it is manifold or singular.
Question: Just as all phenomena arise by virtue of causes and conditions...
"Is it also by way of causes and conditions that all phenomena cease?
To this, the Venerable Dṛṣṭāntika replied:
"Arising depends upon causes and conditions, but cessation is not so."
Just as when a person shoots, the arrow requires force to be launched but not to fall;
or as when a potter’s wheel is spinning, it requires force to turn but not to stop.
Thus say the masters of the Abhidharma treatises.
All phenomena arise and cease in dependence upon causes and conditions, because both cessation and arising are functional activities.
Question: How should one interpret the analogies previously mentioned?
Answer: It is not necessary to interpret them, as they do not belong to the Tripiṭaka.
However, the dharmas of ordinary beings and sages differ and cannot be treated as identical.
Furthermore, both the arrow and the wheel come to rest due to causes.
The cause for the arrow’s descent consists of such things as the shield or the target.
If there were no other causes, then the bending of the bow and so forth would also be its cause.
If it had not been previously shot, by what means would it now fall?
As for the causes that bring the wheel to rest, these refer to the hand, a staff, and so forth.
If there were no other causes that could cause it to turn, then those [causes] would also be its cause.
If it did not previously turn, by what means would it now cease?
Question: If one removes obstacles such as hands and so forth from an arrow or a wheel, causing them to fall and stop.
How does it act as a *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient cause) for that?
Answer: By displacing objects such as hands, it removes obstacles to its movement and progression.
What logical flaw is there in considering non-obstruction and the state of not falling [due to support] as a *kāraṇa-hetu*?
Question: If phenomena arise and cease only by depending on causes and conditions,
and since these causes and conditions for arising and ceasing exist at all times,
why does that which is in the process of arising not also cease, and that which is in the process of ceasing not also arise?
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke thus:
"The two moments of arising and ceasing are distinct in their conjunction;
therefore, at the time of arising there is no ceasing, and at the time of ceasing there is no arising."
Because a single cause cannot have two effects.
Furthermore, it is said that at the time of arising,
the causal conditions accord with that dharma.
When they cease, the causal conditions act as an adversary to those phenomena;
although the essence of those conditions remains identical before and after,
their functions of benefit and harm differ according to time.
It was like a bhikṣu who, having completed his summer retreat,
took up his robes and bowl and traveled from monastery to monastery;
a thief saw him, first offered him salutations and respect, and then followed him with deference.
Later, when he reached a wilderness, [the thief] seized his robes and bowl, humiliated him, and departed.
The causal conditions for birth and cessation are likewise thus.
The Venerable One said:
Since the two phenomena of arising and ceasing are mutually contradictory, how can they exist simultaneously?
The Venerable Ghosaka stated:
"When dharmas arise, their activity has not yet occurred; what, then, would there be to cease?"
When all phenomena are in the process of ceasing, they have already performed their function; what further could be produced?
Question: Since a single phenomenon serves as the efficient cause for many phenomena, do many phenomena also serve as the efficient cause for a single phenomenon?
When a single dharma acts as a creative cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for multiple dharmas,
is it like a single dharma acting as a cause for multiple dharmas,
or is it like multiple dharmas acting as causes for multiple dharmas?
When many dharmas act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for a single dharma,
is it like many dharmas acting as causes for a single dharma,
or is it like a single dharma acting as a cause for a single dharma?
If that were so, what fault would there be? When this single dharma acts as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for multiple dharmas,
if it were like [the case where] one dharma is the cause for multiple dharmas,
why would the effect not also become a single entity because of that single cause?
If multiple phenomena serve as causes for multiple phenomena,
why does the cause not also become multiple because the effects are multiple?
When these multiple phenomena act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for a single phenomenon, [why is it not so]?
If multiple dharmas serve as causes for a single dharma,
why does the result not also become multiple because its causes are multiple? If,
on the other hand, a single dharma serves as the cause for a single dharma...
How is it that because the effect is one, the cause is also established as one?
It should be answered thus:
when a single dharma acts as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for multiple dharmas.
It is also like multiple dharmas acting as causes for a single dharma;
when multiple dharmas act as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for a single dharma,
it is likewise like a single dharma acting as a cause for multiple dharmas.
Question: If that were so, the one would become many, and the many would become one.
Answer: I say that the one becomes many and the many also become one;
this is based on functional activity (*kāritra*), not on substantial reality (*dravya*).
I have taught that all causes take functional activity as their fruit, not substantial entity as their fruit.
Furthermore,
I have taught that all fruits take functional activity as their cause, not substantial entity as their cause.
The substantial nature of all phenomena is eternally without transformation because it is neither cause nor effect.
Nevertheless, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are designated as "efficient causes" (*kāraṇa-hetu*);
however, they merely do not constitute an obstacle and are not capable of producing an effect.
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena serve as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for conditioned phenomena,
and they likewise take those [conditioned phenomena] as their dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Conditioned phenomena do not serve as the efficient cause for unconditioned phenomena.
Nor is it taken as its dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) do not act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) for unconditioned phenomena,
nor are they taken as their dominant fruit.
Although unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) serve as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*),
they do not take them as their dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*),
because they lack the functional capacity to either grasp or yield a fruit.
