Even when they have not yet been abandoned, they can be said to possess a characteristic by virtue of their nature of "increasing" (*anuśayana*).
If it were in the state of having already been abandoned, because it would be extremely remote, its characteristic existence would not be mentioned.
Herein, the name "existence" (bhava) is established based on its immediate and powerful [connection],
unlike the establishment of names such as "having an object" (*sālambana*).
The Venerable Vasumitra stated as follows:
"Because the associated latent dispositions (saṃprayukta-anuśaya) defile the mind,
whereas the object-referent latent dispositions (ālambana-anuśaya) do not."
Furthermore, because the associated latent dispositions (saṃprayukta-anuśaya) do not depart from the mind,
whereas the object-referential latent dispositions (ālambana-anuśaya) are not like that.
Furthermore, because the associated latent dispositions obscure the mind.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take objects as their basis are not like this.
Furthermore, the latent dispositions that are associated with the mind follow the mind in its transformations;
the latent dispositions that take objects as their basis are not like this.
Furthermore, because the associated latent dispositions (saṃprayukta-anuśaya) disturb the mind,
whereas the object-referent latent dispositions (ālambana-anuśaya) do not do so. Furthermore,

the associated latent dispositions share with their associated mind the same basis (āśraya), the same object (ālambana), the same aspect (ākāra), the same fruit (phala), the same outflow (niṣyanda), and the same maturation (vipāka).
They arise together, abide together, change together,
and cease together because of their extreme intimacy; however,
the latent dispositions (anuśaya) regarding the object of perception do not function in this way.
The Venerable One said:
"The associated latent dispositions cause the associated mind to become rigid and obstinate;
the wise revile and loathe them, for they are difficult to escape."

Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take an object as their support, the Venerable Ghoṣaka has stated that such dispositions do not exist within the mind that serves as their object; rather,

it is the associated latent dispositions that cause the associated mind to give rise to defilement, acting as an obstruction to the attainment of the noble fruit, just as smoke and flames obstruct the flame itself.

Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take an object as their support, Venerable Buddhadeva has stated that such dispositions do not exist within the mind that takes that object as its support; rather,
it is the associated latent dispositions that cause the associated mind to be deluded and lack clear comprehension regarding the objective sphere.
Because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take an object do not exist within the mind that takes that object as its focus,

it is by virtue of such various causes and conditions— specifically regarding the states of whether the associated latent dispositions have been abandoned or not— that the mind is always designated as "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*).
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with their objects: only when they are in an unsevered state can a mind be designated as "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*).
If they have already been severed, it is not so designated.

Furthermore, if a latent disposition increases within a mind, is that mind called "possessing latent dispositions" solely by virtue of that specific disposition? The answer is: either by virtue of that [specific one] and not others, or [by virtue of all].
It arises either from that [state] or from others. How is it from that and not from others?
It means that this mind has not yet been severed.
What is meant by "by that and by others"?
It refers to when the knowledge of suffering has already arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen;
if the mind views that which is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering as being the origin.
Regarding the objects of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are to be abandoned: herein,

"by those and not by others" means that a mind possessing underlying tendencies (*sānuśaya-citta*) is so called because the underlying tendencies increase within that mind solely through those [objects], and not by others.
A mind is not called "possessing latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) merely because other latent dispositions do not increase within it;
rather, this refers to a mind that has not been abandoned.
If a mind has not been abandoned, it is necessarily called "possessing latent dispositions" only because those [specific] latent dispositions increase within it.
A mind is called "possessing latent tendencies" (sānuśaya) not because other [tendencies] increase within it, but because [the tendencies] do not increase [within it].
Some say that this passage should be stated as follows:
This refers to the defiled minds of those who are bound by all fetters.
One should not say that;
for it is possible for both those bound by all fetters and those not bound by all fetters to have both defiled and non-defiled minds.
One should simply state this:
that is to say, when this mind has not yet abandoned [the defilements], all minds that have not yet been abandoned are called "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*).
This is solely because the latent dispositions increase (*anuśerate*) within the mind, and not because of anything else.
"By that and by others" means:
a mind with latent dispositions (*sānuśaya*) is so called because those latent dispositions increase within it;
furthermore, it is also called a mind with latent dispositions because other latent dispositions do not increase within it.
Regarding the statement "the knowledge of suffering has already arisen," and so forth in detail:

at that time, the mind which is subject to latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering is [abandoned] by means of that [knowledge] which is to be abandoned by the vision of origin.
A mind is said to be "with latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) because the universal latent dispositions increase within it;
furthermore, it is called "with latent dispositions" because other latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering, though associated with it, do not increase within that mind.
This refers to the mind abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
In this state, it is called a "mind with latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) because those latent dispositions belonging to other categories increase within the mind,
and because the latent dispositions belonging to its own category do not increase within the mind.
Question: Why, in this context, are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of other categories called "those" (*tad*), while the latent dispositions of one's own category are called "others" (*anya*)?

Answer: Because it was previously asked: "If a latent disposition increases within the mind, is that mind called 'possessing a latent disposition' (*sānuśaya*) solely by virtue of that specific latent disposition?"

Therefore, the present answer states that a mind abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in this state is called "a mind accompanied by latent tendencies" (*sānuśaya*) not only because of those pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) which increase with respect to this mind, but for other reasons as well.
Furthermore, because other [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering do not increase in association with this mind,
it is called a "mind with latent tendencies" (sānuśaya-citta).
Thus, that which was the subject of the question is designated as such.
That which is not the primary subject of inquiry is termed "the rest.
At that time, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of other schools have not yet been abandoned;
because they continue to increase [in strength], they are the primary subjects of inquiry.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) of one's own category have already been abandoned at that time;
because they no longer increase [in the mind], they are not the subject of the current inquiry. Some say:
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) of one's own category are said to be "residual" because they have shifted from their previous state;
that is to say, those previously unsevered have now been severed. Some say:
Previously, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of one's own category had attained mastery and could act according to one's will;
now, because they have been abandoned, they no longer possess mastery.
Since they are incapable of acting, they are described as "residual" (avaśeṣa).
Some say that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of one's own school are originally established,
but because they are not currently established, they are described as "residual" (avaśeṣa).

Some say: because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of one's own school have now been ultimately severed by the Noble Path and are different from what they were previously, they are described as "residual" (*avaśeṣa*).
Others say: [the same].
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) of one's own category have already been definitively severed by the Noble Path;
they differ from those of the other four categories, which were previously severed gradually and simultaneously with them, and are therefore designated as "the remainder."
Question: The mind abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) also possesses this same meaning.

That is to say, when one has abandoned from the first grade up to the eighth grade, the defiled mind is called "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) because those [defilements] have not yet been abandoned, while others have already been abandoned.
Why is it not stated?
The answer is: because the intention of the author of this treatise was such.
This is explained at length.
Furthermore, when something that ought to be stated is not stated,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Moreover, if one school [is considered] for the sake of another school, or for the sake of others;
Regarding the mind abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) mentioned herein:
although this principle applies, it is not stated here because [the text] pertains specifically to its own school and excludes other schools.
Furthermore, what is discussed here refers only to that mind abandoned through cultivation from which one never again falls back once it has been severed.
Although this principle exists, it is not mentioned because, even after those [defilements] have been abandoned, there may still be regression. Question:
How do the various latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase with respect to their objects (ālambana), and how do they increase with respect to their associated factors (samprayukta)?
The masters of the West (Pāścātyas) maintain this view:
because they possess the nature of bondage,
they increase in accordance with their objects of perception (*ālambana*).
Because they share the same nature as their companions,
they increase in accordance with their association;
thus say the masters of the Abhidharma from Kaśmīra.
Because they adhere to and superimpose [unrealities] upon their respective objective referents through distinct modes of activity,
they are said to "increase" (anuśerate) with respect to the object.
Because they cause associated factors to conform to and superimpose their own faults, they are said to increase with respect to the associated dharmas.
The name [of a latent tendency] increases in accordance with its association.
Other masters say that the various latent tendencies increase in relation to their objects just as they do in relation to their associations.
Regarding the increase [of defilements] through association, it is the same as regarding the object.
Question: If this is so, how should one interpret the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, which says:
How does the latent tendency of sensual desire increase?
It refers to that which is lovely, desirable, pleasing, and agreeable;
it lacks the capacity to take those as objects in association with them.
Why is it also said that there are "desirable" [objects] and so forth?
Answer: This reveals the characteristic of craving (*rāga*).
That is to say, because the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) possesses the characteristics of being desirable and so forth, this statement is made.
The distinct characteristics of the objects of focus (*ālambana*) and their association (*samprayoga*) are not explicitly revealed.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are said to possess the quality of "proliferating" (*anuśayana*) due to four factors.
First, because of falling into an evil state of mind:
just as when one person commits an evil act in a great assembly, it causes all those many people to fall into an evil state of mind,
so too does a single latent disposition (anuśaya) arise within a single category of associated factors.
It causes all these mental states and their associated factors (citta-caitta-dharma) of this stage to fall into a state of evil intention.
This is because they are like fire's heat;
it is like placing a small vessel of water into a pot of heated iron.
Just as the vessel and the water within it are both entirely heated,
so too, when a single affliction arises within the factors of a single mental state,
it causes all mental states and their associated mental factors to become afflicted with feverish distress.
Third, because they are like smoke and so forth.
Just as clothing that has been besmeared by smoke, dust, or filth becomes entirely defiled and foul, so too,
when a mental state (citta-prakāra) possesses even a single latent disposition (anuśaya), it becomes entirely afflicted (kliṣṭa).
Fourth, because they are to be reviled and loathed.
Just as when one person among a monastic community commits an offense, the entire assembly incurs reproach,
so too within a mental complex (*cittapakṣa*), even a single latent tendency (*anuśaya*) may be reviled and loathed, just like its associated states (*saṃprayukta*).
These four factors are said to be "concomitant increase" (anuśaya).
Because these four also increase with respect to the object of perception (ālambana), they are called "concomitant increase.
That is to say, if the object of perception increases these four, it is said that the afflictions (kleśa) increase concomitantly with respect to that object.
Question: Do the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the past and future also increase?
Answer: They also increase.
If those latent dispositions did not increase, [the following would occur].
In the state where an undefiled mind is present, there would be no underlying tendencies (anuśaya),
which would contradict the scriptural teaching as it says:
The Buddha said to Māluṅkyamātā:
"An infant lying on its back cannot yet distinguish between the excellence and inferiority of sensual objects."
How much less could they give rise to the fetters of sensual desire that bind the mind?
Nevertheless, they are bound by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of sensual desire.
Question: Since the past and future lack functional activity, [how can there be such binding]?
How can it be said that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase?
Answer: Because they are able to give rise to [their corresponding states] and bring them into manifestation.
Just as fire can produce smoke even when it is not manifest,
so too, the Venerable Ghosaka has stated that although those [faculties] lack the activity of apprehending an object, they still exist.
However, because they possess a binding function with respect to their objects and associated dharmas as if they were present,
those latent dispositions (anuśaya) have the sense of "increasing along with" (anuśerate).
The Venerable Śamathadeva stated:
Due to five reasons, it can be said that past and future latent dispositions (anuśaya) possess the sense of "increasing" (anuśerate).
First, because their causes have not yet been exhausted;
second, because their acquisitions (prāpti) have not yet been severed.
Third, because its basis has not yet been transformed;
fourth, because its object of focus has not yet been fully understood;
fifth, because its antidote has not yet been attained.

When various minds are called "minds with underlying tendencies" (sānuśaya) because they are accompanied by underlying tendencies, will those underlying tendencies be abandoned in relation to those minds?
Answer: They may be abandoned, or they may not be abandoned.
How should it be abandoned?
It means that those latent dispositions take this mind as their object.
How should it not be abandoned?
This means that those latent dispositions (anuśaya) are associated with this mind.

Here it is shown that while the latent dispositions can be said to be abandoned with respect to their objects of perception (ālambana), they cannot be so said with respect to their association (samprayoga).
That is to say, [they are abandoned] with respect to the object.
One may restrain the afflictions so that they do not manifest and thereby commit various transgressions;
however, one cannot restrain the afflictions within their associated states so that they no longer associate with the mind and its concomitants.
It can be said that [defilements] are to be abandoned with respect to their objects (*ālambana*),
but not with respect to their associated factors (*samprayukta*). Some say that this passage should be stated as follows:
How is it that they should be abandoned?
It means that those underlying tendencies (anuśaya) have not yet been abandoned with respect to this mind as their object.
How is it that they should not be abandoned?
That is to say, those latent dispositions (anuśaya) have already been abandoned with respect to this mind and are associated with this mind.
Their explanation is unreasonable. Why is that?
Previously, it was asked whether those minds are called "minds with latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) by virtue of being associated with latent dispositions;
[the question was] whether those latent dispositions are to be abandoned in relation to this mind.
Now, one should simply state [the answer].
How should it be abandoned?
It means that since those latent dispositions (anuśaya) have already taken this mind as their object, they are satisfied with respect to their objective;
why then need one further state that they are not yet abandoned?
If that [defilement] has already been abandoned, it is not a matter for inquiry whether the mind possesses latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) by virtue of that [abandoned defilement].
Therefore, there is no need to further state that it is "not yet abandoned.
Furthermore, it is logically inconsistent to speak of "having abandoned" this mind while simultaneously speaking of "latent dispositions directed toward the mind."
Since that which has already been abandoned is not a subject for inquiry,
one should simply state:
"In what way should it not be abandoned?"
That is to say, it is already sufficient for the meaning that those latent dispositions (anuśaya) are associated with this mind;
however, what is stated here is that the various latent dispositions are to be abandoned with respect to their objects (ālambana), not with respect to their association (samprayoga).
The designation "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) is explained based on the sense of being associated with the mind,
not based on the sense of "increasing along with" (*anuśayana*).
This is because, according to the sense of "increasing along with," [the latent dispositions] would be subject to abandonment simultaneously [with their objects].
By what cause are the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned?
Answer: The meaning previously revealed by way of their objects and conditions is now presented in its textual form;
that is to say, through the power of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), those latent dispositions are rendered such that they no longer give rise to faults with respect to their objects.
It can be said that they should be abandoned.
It is like a person restraining their child and not allowing them to enter taverns, brothels, gambling dens, and the like;
it is impossible for latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be separated from their associated mental states (*saṃprayukta-dharma*).
Therefore, it is said that for those associated phenomena, there is no sense of abandonment.
You say that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) should be abandoned by means of their objects (ālambana). Answer: Yes.

If that were so, then as for those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) which take contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) as their object, by what means would those latent dispositions be abandoned?
If one says they are abandoned simultaneously with the abandonment of [the object], this is not reasonable in either case.
Answer: They are abandoned because they are the causes and objects of the untainted (anāsrava) latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path.
Because these are abandoned, those are also abandoned.
This is the intended meaning here.
It is through the vision of wisdom that the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) which take afflictions as their object are finally severed.
To establish this principle,
the following questions and answers are provided to resolve potential difficulties.
Regarding your statement that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) should be abandoned through their causes and objects (*ālambana*):
this question, though briefly addressed previously, was not yet definitively settled.
It is impossible to point out a fault in another's position without first having definitively established what that position asserts.

The answer "it is so" means that it is established as a certainty that the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) which are the objects of the afflictions (*kleśa*) can only be severed through the vision of wisdom;
because there is no other way, it is said, "it is so."

If that were so, how would those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have contaminated objects (sāsrava-ālambana) and are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana) or the path (mārga-darśana) be abandoned?
If you say they are abandoned simultaneously with this [abandonment], that too is unreasonable.
This is the intent of that objection:

it asks by what means those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take contaminated objects (*sāsravālambana*) and are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) should be abandoned?
If it is said that they are abandoned because one abandons them through wisdom (*prajñā*) by seeing this suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), [then...]
This reasoning is incorrect,
because these [afflictions] have not yet been abandoned at the time of seeing suffering and its origin.
If it is argued that they are abandoned because one sees their cessation and the path through wisdom, [that too is untenable].
This reasoning is also incorrect, because cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are not the objects of focus for this [defilement].

Answer: Because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, they take those [cessation and the path] as their causal objects.
The statement that "by the abandonment of this, that is also abandoned" refers to a general principle (*sāmānya*). The intended meaning of this principle is as follows:

the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take contaminated objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) and the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*) grow and develop by depending upon those latent dispositions that take uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*).
Because when one perceives the truths of cessation and the path, these untainted (anāsrava) objects of the latent tendencies (anuśaya) are abandoned;
consequently, those tainted (sāsrava) objects of the latent tendencies that are to be abandoned by the perception of cessation and the path are also abandoned along with them.
It is like a weak person who stands up by leaning on a staff.
When the staff is removed, it immediately falls;
this case is likewise.

A question is raised regarding the established tenet of the preceding section: that the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which take defilements as their objects must first be seen through wisdom before they can be abandoned.
Now, you say that because the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is severed, the subject that cognizes it (*ālambaka*) is accordingly severed.
Is this not contradictory?
Answer: There is no fault of contradiction.
If even the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned when their objects are seen by wisdom, how much more so when the objects themselves are abandoned?
It is like fruit on a tree: if it falls when the tree moves, how much more so when the tree has already toppled? Would the fruit not fall?
This case is likewise. Furthermore,

regarding what was stated previously— that the latent tendencies (anuśaya) which take as their object the afflictions abandoned through the vision of wisdom are only then severed by means of the vision of wisdom—

it was not said that the latent tendencies which take as their object the afflictions abandoned through the vision of what is to be abandoned [by cultivation] are only then severed by means of the vision of wisdom.

However, it is taught that the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) which take the objects of the afflictions as their basis are severed only through the vision of wisdom; thus, there is no contradiction.
This is because one sees, by means of wisdom, the cessation and the path, which are the objects of those afflictions that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have contaminated objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path are also abandoned.
By this principle, the dharmakṣāntis regarding suffering and its origin can abandon the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) that take higher realms as their object.

Within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the two knowledges of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the path (*mārga-jñāna*) are able to abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the nine stages.
Other masters say:

Regarding the statement that "latent dispositions (anuśaya) are abandoned by means of their objects (ālambana)," this indicates that latent dispositions are abandoned only when the objects of the afflictions (kleśa) are abandoned.
To establish this principle, the following question and answer address potential difficulties.
Do you say that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) must be abandoned by means of their causes and objects?
[He] answers: "Yes.

If that is so, then as for those latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path that have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object—by what means should those latent dispositions be abandoned?
If it is argued that this [defilement] is abandoned because its associated [factors] are abandoned,
that reasoning is incorrect;
for it was previously stated that latent dispositions (anuśaya) cannot be said to be abandoned with respect to their associated factors.
If it is argued that [the afflictions] are abandoned because their objects are abandoned,
this is also logically untenable;
for the Path, which is the object [of the antidote], is free from all defects and thus cannot be abandoned.

Answer: Because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take contaminated objects (*sāsravālambana*) and are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path are abandoned, these [dispositions] are also abandoned accordingly.
Question: Your previous established position stated that latent dispositions are abandoned only when their objects (*ālambana*) are abandoned.
Now, it is said that because the afflictions which act as objects of cognition are abandoned, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are then abandoned.
Is this not contradictory?
Answer: There is no fault of contradiction.
This means that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) which have uncontaminated objects arise and grow in dependence upon those latent dispositions which have contaminated objects;
because the latter sustain the former, allowing it to continue,
when the latter are abandoned, the former are also abandoned accordingly.
Just as the trunk and other parts of a tree depend upon the root for their existence,
and if the root is severed, the trunk and other parts fall down accordingly,
so it is in this case as well.
That explanation is irrational,
for it contradicts the preceding thesis; furthermore,
it is difficult to reconcile with this fundamental treatise, as it differs from it.
Because there are cases where the object of cognition (*ālambana*) has been severed while the subject of cognition (*ālambaka*) has not yet been severed;
and there are cases where the subject of cognition has been severed while the object of cognition has not yet been severed.
Alternatively, some say:

Regarding the statement that "latent dispositions (anuśaya) are abandoned by means of their objects," this intends to say that latent dispositions are abandoned only when they possess an object through which the path [is realized].
That explanation is irrational.
Because the Blessed One has taught that this Noble Eightfold Path is able to sever all suffering— past, future, and present—
and to relinquish, vomit out, exhaust, become free from passion for, extinguish, pacify, and lead to Nirvana.
Therefore, it should be stated that both the path with an object and the path without an object are capable of severing the afflictions.
Furthermore, this will be explained later.
Since both the objection and the resolution are inconsistent, that [position] is irrational.
The Venerable Śamadatta stated:
"The various latent dispositions (anuśaya) are abandoned by way of four factors."
First, by the abandonment of the object of cognition (*ālambana*),
as in the case of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) with outflow that take cessation and the path as their objects.
Second, by the abandonment of the subject that cognizes (*ālambaka*).
Just as with latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have external realms as their objects,
these three are abandoned through the simultaneous abandonment of both [the object and the subject],
like non-universal latent dispositions abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin.
Fourth, it is because of the attainment of the antidote;
as with other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), when their respective antidotes are attained, they are accordingly abandoned.
Thus spoke the Venerable Vasumitra.
The various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are abandoned through five factors.
First, they are abandoned by seeing their objects,
such as the latent dispositions that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, as well as those universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions that take their own realm as their object.
Second, they are abandoned because their objects (*ālambana*) are abandoned,
such as the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) with outflow that take cessation and the path as their objects.
Third, they are abandoned because their subjects (*ālambaka*) are abandoned.
Just as pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take other realms as their object are abandoned because the four [factors] they depend upon are abandoned; likewise,
non-pervasive latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin are abandoned in the same manner.
Fifth, they are abandoned through the attainment of their antidotes,
such as the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation;
even if these latent dispositions are to be abandoned from the mind, [they are so abandoned].
Is this mind called "a mind with latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) solely because of those latent dispositions?
Answer: It is so either because of those alone and not others, or because of both those and others.
How is it that [the mind] is defiled by that [affliction] alone and not by others?
It refers to the mind that is undefiled yet to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
How is it that [the mind] is defiled by both that [affliction] and others?
This refers to the defilement of the mind.
Herein, "non-defiled" distinguishes it from that which is defiled;
"to be abandoned by cultivation" distinguishes it from that which is untainted (*anāsrava*).
This refers to wholesome minds associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) and non-obscured neutral minds (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
These minds are "minds with underlying tendencies" (*sānuśaya*) because the underlying tendencies increase in accordance with them by taking these minds as their objects.
"Not by others" means that a mind is not called "possessed of latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) by virtue of being associated with them;
for there are no latent dispositions associated with this mind.

Regarding "a defiled mind is [said to be] with latent dispositions (sānuśaya) by virtue of them": because the latent dispositions increase in accordance with this mind as its object, it is called a mind with latent dispositions;
and "and by others" means that it is also called a mind with latent dispositions by virtue of other associated latent dispositions.
Question: Why is it that here the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the object are mentioned, while those associated with the mind itself are mentioned as "the rest"?
Answer: Because the previous question stated: "Suppose the latent dispositions were to be abandoned in the mind."
Is it only because this mind is accompanied by those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that it is called "a mind with latent dispositions"?

It was stated previously that latent dispositions have the sense of being "to be abandoned" only with respect to their objects (*ālambana*), and not with respect to their associated [mental factors] (*samprayukta*).
Therefore, that statement refers only to the fact that one should abandon the latent dispositions (anuśaya) regarding their objects;
since it is these very latent dispositions that are the subject of the question, they are referred to as "those."
Because the associated latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are not the actual subject of the inquiry, they are designated as "the rest.
Question: For what reason are such questions and answers formulated?
Answer: It is for the sake of enabling those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
That is to say, there may be those who doubt that [the latent tendencies] should be abandoned solely by means of [insight];
because the mind is so designated on account of them, it is said to be "possessing latent tendencies" (*sānuśaya*),
since the associated latent tendencies (*samprayukta-anuśaya*) are not to be abandoned.
The mind is not called "possessing latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) merely because of those [dispositions];
rather, in order to resolve this doubt,
it is shown that a defiled mind is also called "possessing latent dispositions" by virtue of being associated with them.
Alternatively, there may be doubt that associated latent dispositions (saṃprayukta-anuśaya) should also be abandoned; therefore,
it is now further clarified that associated latent dispositions lack the sense of being "to-be-abandoned" (prahātavya).
Furthermore, for those who harbor doubts regarding why latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are called "existence" (*bhava*),
[it is] solely on the basis of their nature of increasing [the defilements].
Now, moreover, it is demonstrated that they are so called on the basis of their nature of being concomitants (*sahāya*).
That is to say, an undefiled mind is called "possessing latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) solely by virtue of the nature of their increase through association;
whereas a defiled mind possesses them by virtue of both natures.
Is there a case where latent dispositions are abandoned, yet wisdom does not perceive their object?
It can be answered in four propositions.
There are cases where latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are abandoned, yet wisdom does not perceive their objects.
This refers, for example, when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) become detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
One abandons the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take the higher realms as their object and those that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object.
When noble ones (ārya) realize the truths of suffering and its origin within the desire realm,
they abandon the latent dispositions that take other realms as their object.
When one realizes the truths of cessation and the path,
one abandons the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with outflows that take cessation and the path as their objects and are to be abandoned by the vision of those truths;
furthermore, through the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path, one becomes detached from all latent dispositions to be abandoned by cultivation.
There are those who, though possessing wisdom and seeing the objects of their perception, do not sever the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) at the time they are becoming detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*);
[this includes] the various categories of underlying tendencies that were previously or subsequently abandoned.
When one is free from the defilements of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness,
the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take other levels as their object— ranging from the desire realm up to the sphere of infinite consciousness— are [abandoned].
Furthermore, when noble ones (ārya) realize the truths of suffering and its origin pertaining to the form and formless realms...
Regarding all latent dispositions (anuśaya) in the desire realm that have objects belonging to other realms,

they are abandoned at the time of the clear realization of the truth of suffering; as for those latent dispositions with objects belonging to one's own realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of the truth of origin, they are likewise abandoned at that same time.

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take contaminated objects as their conditions and are abandoned through the vision of the truths of cessation and the path, as well as all latent dispositions abandoned through cultivation;
and when one realizes the truth of origin,
the latent dispositions that take objects within one's own realm and are abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering.

One sees the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, as well as all latent dispositions abandoned through cultivation.
This occurs when one becomes detached from the defilements abandoned through cultivation by means of the knowledge of suffering and origin, as well as conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

When one abandons the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) objects of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by seeing, as well as the latent dispositions to be abandoned by cultivation belonging to preceding and subsequent categories, through the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), at that time,
the latent dispositions with uncontaminated objects (anāsrava-ālambana) [are also abandoned].
Furthermore, when all other ordinary beings and noble ones perceive the objects of the afflictions without having severed those afflictions,
all latent dispositions (anuśaya) [arise].
There are latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned by wisdom and whose objects are also seen;

namely, all latent dispositions of one's own level that take their own category as an object when ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) become free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
When noble ones realize the truths of suffering and its origin,

they perceive the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with their own realm that are to be abandoned through the realization of suffering and its origin; when they realize the truths of cessation and the path, [they perceive those to be abandoned through the realization of cessation and the path].
Regarding the untainted objects (anāsrava-ālambana) abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path:
they are abandoned by means of the knowledge of suffering and origin, as well as conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna),
at the time of becoming free from the defilements abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation within one’s own stage and category, even when they are not yet abandoned, wisdom does not perceive their objects—
provided the aforementioned conditions are excluded. Is there, however,
a single moment in which the latent dispositions are abandoned, yet wisdom still does not perceive those objects?
It should be stated that there are four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
However, there are many such positions;

that is to say, in each of the stages of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering and its origin (duḥkha-samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti), as well as the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of cessation and the path (nirodha-mārga-anvayajñānakṣānti), there are four propositions.
Regarding the four propositions concerning the stage of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*):

the first proposition refers to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with objects in other realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm; the second proposition...
This refers to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm that take their own realm as an object and are abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering];
the latent dispositions with outflows (sāsrava) that take [other objects] as their basis and are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path;
and the latent dispositions abandoned through cultivation.
The third phrase refers to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and which take their own realm as an object.
The fourth phrase [refers to those not so specified].
That is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics,
the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) for the stage of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of origination (samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) are likewise according to their respective applications.
This also applies to the stages of the receptivities to the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge of cessation and the path (nirodha-mārga-dharma-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti).
If, while previously in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one has partially or completely separated from the defilements of the desire realm,
and has likewise partially or completely separated from those of the seven higher stages,
four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) can be established.
Furthermore, regarding the four propositions concerning the stage of the patience of the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñānakṣānti*):

the first proposition refers to the previously unabandoned latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) with outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the desire realm; the second proposition...

The third case refers to those latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the cessation of suffering within the desire realm that have already been abandoned and which take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object.
The fourth case refers to those latent dispositions associated with the cessation of suffering within the desire realm that have not yet been abandoned and which take the untainted as their object.

The fourth clause refers to those latent tendencies (anuśaya) with outflow-objects (sāsrava-ālambana) abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya) within the desire realm that have already been abandoned previously; or,
alternatively, it excludes the aforementioned characteristics.

The fourfold permutation applies accordingly at the stages of the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñānakṣānti*) and the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*). Furthermore,
when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) become detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), [the same fourfold permutation applies].
Within each and every uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) can be formulated.
The first proposition refers to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take their own category (*svapakṣa*) or another stage (*bhūmi*) as their object.
The second clause refers to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take their own stage as an object across preceding and succeeding categories.
The third clause refers to the latent dispositions that take their own category and their own stage as an object.

The fourth alternative refers to latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take other stages (*bhūmi*) as their objects across preceding or succeeding categories, or which exclude the aforementioned characteristics.

Is it possible for there to be the attainment of the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*) without relinquishing it, or the non-attainment of its relinquishment; or likewise, both attainment and relinquishment, and neither attainment nor relinquishment?
Answer: There is.

One who attains but does not relinquish refers to those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) when they become detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Regarding those noble ones who, when abandoning the afflictions— excluding the moment of attaining the fruit—
abandon [the acquisition] but do not obtain it:
this refers to ordinary beings who, having fallen away from detachment, die in a lower stage and are reborn in the second dhyāna or above.
When those who have passed away from the two upper realms are reborn in the desire realm,
if they are noble ones who have regressed from their progress toward the middle [fruit],
they both acquire and relinquish [the faculties].
This refers to ordinary beings who die in a higher realm and are reborn in the first dhyāna or above;
as well as noble ones when they refine their faculties to attain a fruit,
or when they fall away from a fruit.
That which must necessarily be relinquished refers to the exclusion of the aforementioned characteristics.
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Volume 22.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-three,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Fifteen of the Second: The Chapter on Knowledge (*jñāna-nikāya*) within the First: The Miscellaneous Aggregate (*saṃgīti-paryāya*). Is there a case where one personally realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) with the body, yet wisdom does not perceive that cessation?
It can be answered with four propositions.
There are those who have realized the cessation of latent dispositions within their own bodies, yet their wisdom does not perceive that cessation;
this refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) when they become free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
All latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to one’s own level and category are extinguished;
furthermore, when a noble one (ārya) realizes suffering (duḥkha),
those latent dispositions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering are extinguished.
At the time of the clear realization of origination (*samudaya-abhisamaya*), one sees the cessation of all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of origination;
at the time of the clear realization of the path (*mārga-abhisamaya*), one sees the cessation of all latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the path.

During the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one [sees the cessation] by means of the knowledge of suffering, origination, and the path, as well as conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), according to what is appropriate for each case.
When one becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
there is the cessation of all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of one's own level and category that are to be abandoned through cultivation. Furthermore,

when one attains the fruits of the path or refines one's faculties (*indriya*) as appropriate by means of the knowledge of suffering, origin, the path, or conventional knowledge, there is the cessation of those already-abandoned latent dispositions that are realized at that time.
There is one who possesses wisdom and perceives that cessation, yet does not personally realize it through bodily experience.

This refers to the time when, during the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of cessation, one perceives the cessation of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with suffering, its origin, the path, and those to be abandoned through cultivation.

Furthermore, it refers to the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), when one uses the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) to become free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Excluding the state of having attained the fruit,
it refers to the cessation of all latent dispositions (anuśaya)— both those already abandoned and those not yet abandoned— according to what is currently being observed;
as well as the time when other ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) or noble ones (ārya), who have not yet realized analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), perceive cessation.
That is, one sees the cessation of those very latent dispositions (anuśaya) that were previously observed.
There is also a wisdom that realizes the body as the cessation of latent dispositions and perceives that cessation;
namely, at the time of the clear realization of cessation (nirodha-abhisamaya), one perceives the cessation of all latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation.

In the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), when one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), there is the cessation of the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are realized and observed;
or, when one refines one's faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) by means of the knowledge of cessation.
Regarding the cessation of the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have been realized and observed:
there are those who do not personally realize the body of the cessation of latent dispositions, nor do they perceive that cessation;
this refers to cases other than the aforementioned characteristics.
Is there any moment during which one realizes the cessation of the underlying tendencies within the body, yet wisdom does not perceive that cessation?
One should respond by establishing four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*):
namely, when one attains the fruit of the Once-returner through the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*).
There are those who realize the cessation of the underlying tendencies within their own bodies, yet their wisdom does not perceive that cessation;
this refers to the cessation at that time of all underlying tendencies in the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned by insight.
There is one who possesses wisdom that perceives the cessation of those [defilements] but does not personally realize it with the body;
this refers to the cessation of the final three categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm.
There is also one who personally realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions with the body and whose wisdom likewise perceives that cessation.
This refers to the cessation of all latent dispositions (anuśaya) in the desire realm that are to be abandoned by insight and the first six categories of those to be abandoned by cultivation.
There are those who do not personally realize this cessation within their own bodies, nor do they perceive that cessation through wisdom.
This refers to the cessation of all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the realms of form and formlessness.
For example, when one attains the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) by means of the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodhadharmajñāna*),
there are four propositions within a single moment.
Thus, when a stream-enterer, once-returner, or non-returner transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) at the moment of the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*),
all four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established within a single instant.
How is it that consciousness is abandoned by means of its object?
Answer: When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen,
if a mind perceives that which is to be abandoned by the vision of origin while having as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering—
this is called consciousness abandoned by means of the object.
In this context, when the cause of a consciousness is severed and its object is severed,
yet the consciousness itself is not yet severed, it is called "a consciousness whose cause and object have been severed.
For those who maintain that the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and their associated and co-existent factors do not serve as non-universal causes within their own category:
He speaks as follows:
"When the knowledge of suffering has already arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen,
if the mind views that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin while having as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering."

This consciousness is called "consciousness whose causes and objects are severed" because its causes are entirely severed and its objects are entirely severed, even though its own substance has not yet been severed.

At that time, if the mind takes as its object [defilements] abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), or those abandoned by the vision of the origin, cessation, and the path (*mārga-bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Although the causes of this mind have been completely severed, its objects have not yet been severed;
therefore, consciousness does not cease because its objects have ceased.

At that time, if the mind perceives objects abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), or objects abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), or those abandoned by the cultivation of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Although the causes of this mind have been completely severed, its objects are both severed and not yet severed;
therefore, it is not the case that consciousness ceases because its objects cease.
This is for those who maintain that the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), as well as the associated and co-existent dharmas, also function as universal causes within their own category.
He speaks as follows:
when the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen,
if a mind takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin and is itself to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
In this case, although the causes belonging to its own category have not yet been severed, the causes belonging to other categories are entirely severed and the objects are entirely severed;
because its own substance has not yet been severed, it is called "consciousness whose causes and objects are severed.
At that time, if the mind takes as its object [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of origin, or those to be abandoned by the vision of origin, cessation, the path, or by cultivation.

Because this mind has some factors that have been abandoned and some that have not been abandoned, and because its objects have not been abandoned, it is not the case that consciousness is abandoned by virtue of the abandonment of its objects.

At that time, if the mind perceives [factors] abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), or those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), origination, cessation (*nirodha*), the path (*mārga*), or those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), [it does not abandon them].
Because this mind is simultaneously present with its object and is either abandoned or not yet abandoned, it is not the case that consciousness is abandoned by means of the object.
Having already clarified the intrinsic nature of consciousness abandoned by means of the object,
one should next clarify how the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with it.
Question: How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in association with this consciousness?
Answer: Nineteen.
Question: Is it in a single moment of mind?
Answer: It is not so.
What is the reason?
It refers to one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of sensual desire.
When the knowledge of the dharma of suffering has already arisen but the knowledge of the dharma of origination has not yet arisen,
if a mind is associated with the views to be abandoned by seeing origination and takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by seeing suffering in the desire realm,
this consciousness is abandoned by means of its object.
The seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin of suffering increase with respect to this [consciousness].
Four of them increase with respect to it both as associated factors and as objects;
namely, false view, adherence to views, doubt, and ignorance.
Third, regarding this consciousness, only the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of craving, aversion, and pride increase by way of their objects (*ālambana*).
This refers to one who is already free from the defilement of desire (*kāmarāga*) but not yet free from the defilement of form (*rūparāga*).
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen,

if a mind belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and takes as its object that which is abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),
this consciousness is abandoned by means of the abandonment of its object.
The six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] increase in the form realm;
four [underlying tendencies] increase with respect to this consciousness by way of association and object,
as explained for the desire realm.
Second, regarding this consciousness, only the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and pride (*māna*) increase by way of their objects (*ālambana*).
Question: Is it not also the case for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire?
Why is it said that one must be free from the defilements of desire?
The answer is given here:
it is taught that for those [mental states] capable of manifesting, one must necessarily be free from the defilements of the lower stages.
This statement is made because afflictions of the higher realms only become manifest [at this stage].
One has already abandoned the defilements of the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*),
and while the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen.

If the mind has as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) or that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
then this consciousness is abandoned by means of its object;
six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin in the formless realm increase therein.
Fourth, in this consciousness, latent dispositions increase both through association and through their objects;
second, in this consciousness, latent dispositions increase solely through their objects,
as explained in the case of the form realm.
Regarding this, some recite: "one who has already become detached from the defilements of form but not yet from those of the formless.
That should not be recited;
for it has already been shown that as long as the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) has not arisen, one has not yet become detached from the defilements of the formless realm.
Question: Within those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), can one also establish the abandonment of consciousness through the abandonment of its causal objects?

That is to say, when those [defilements] ranging from the highest-of-the-high (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) down to the low-of-the-middle (*mṛdu-madhya*) grades have already been abandoned, the mind that has not yet been abandoned—ranging from eight grades down to a single grade—is [still present].
This mind takes as its object that which has already been abandoned in one grade up to eight grades;
because the causes of those one up to eight grades have already been abandoned,
it should also be called "consciousness whose objects are abandoned by way of their causes."
Why is it not mentioned?
The answer is: although it should also have been mentioned, the fact that it was not mentioned indicates that this teaching is incomplete.

Furthermore, it is explained herein that if a consciousness of one category takes a cause and an object from a different category, yet its causal and objective conditions are severed while its substance remains unsevered,
this refers to a mind abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which takes its own category as both cause and object.
Although it is abandoned due to its object, it is not said to be a consciousness abandoned due to its object.
Furthermore, in this context, "cause" refers to the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), because it is exclusively defiled; other causes are not fixed.
In this context, "consciousness" refers exclusively to those minds associated with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), as these alone are defiled.
For this reason, the consciousness that ceases due to the abandonment of its objects exists only within the three realms and is abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin.
Question: For what reason are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) explained after the causes?
Answer: Because the meaning of the Abhidharma-piṭaka should be understood through fourteen matters:
namely, the six causes, the four conditions, inclusion, association, possession (*prāpti*), and non-possession (*aprāpti*). If one [examines] by means of these fourteen matters—
One who understands the Abhidharma without error is called an Abhidharmika;
it is not merely one who recites and maintains the texts.
Other masters say that the meaning of the Abhidharma-piṭaka should be understood through seven matters,
namely: skill in causes and skill in conditions.
Skillfulness regarding specific characteristics,
skillfulness regarding common characteristics,
and skillfulness regarding what is included and what is not included.
Skillfulness regarding the associated and the non-associated, and skillfulness regarding accomplishment and non-accomplishment—
if one understands the Abhidharma through these seven matters without error, [one is proficient].
One who is called an Abhidharma master is not merely one who recites and upholds the texts;
therefore, there is no fault in meaning in subsequently explaining the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
3. The Section on Persons (*Pudgala-varga*), Part One of the First Aggregate of Miscellaneous Topics in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Section Three of the Pudgala-varga, Part One: The Person.
Having already mastered these chapters and their commentaries, such as:
"Regarding this life, how many of the twelve links of dependent origination are past, how many are future, and how many are present? and so forth.
Next, it should be explained in detail.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the tenets of other schools and revealing the correct meaning; that is to say, there are some who maintain that the substance of the past and future is not truly existent.
Although the present exists, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
this is to refute their tenet and demonstrate that the essence of the past and future is substantially existent (*dravyasat*),
whereas the present is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and thus subsumed within the world of phenomena.
Furthermore, there are those who maintain that dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), such as the Vibhajyavādins.
One asks them: for what reason do they hold such a view?
The answer is: because of that sutra.
That is to say, the sūtra states:
"Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, phenomena abide in their dharma-nature."
The Buddha, having attained equal enlightenment himself, revealed it to others and explained it at length;
thus, one should know that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
This was stated in order to refute that school's position and to demonstrate that dependent origination is a conditioned dharma (*saṃskṛtadharma*), as it falls within the three periods of time.
Unconditioned phenomena do not fall within the three periods of time.
Question: If dependent origination is not unconditioned, how do you reconcile this with the sūtra passage that was cited?
Answer: Because the Sūtra teaches the definitive meaning of cause and effect.
That is to say, whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, ignorance is definitively the cause of all formative activities (*saṃskāra*).
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are definitively the fruit of ignorance (*avidyā*).
In this manner, up to birth (*jāti*), which is definitively the cause of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*),
and aging and death, which are definitively the fruit of birth.
The "abiding of phenomena" (dharmasthiti) and the "nature of phenomena" (dharmatā) have the meaning of being determinate;
they do not have the meaning of being unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Such is the intent of the sūtra.
If it were not so, the Sūtra would also state:
"Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world..."
The Dharma abides in its own nature: form is always the characteristic of form, and so on up to consciousness being always the characteristic of consciousness;
earth is always the characteristic of solidity, and so on up to wind being always the characteristic of motion.
Harītakī is always bitter in taste;
kaṭukarohiṇī is always pungent in taste.
Could it be that the five aggregates and so forth are likewise unconditioned?
Since those are conditioned,
dependent origination is likewise;
that is to say, regarding the five aggregates and so forth, whose specific characteristics are determined, it is stated as follows:
Dependent origination is also determined by cause and effect;
it is thus stated.
This treatise is composed in order to establish correct reasoning and to refute such heterodox views held by other schools.
In this context, the proponent of the treatise should clarify five points regarding the initial argument presented:
first, for what reason is only one *pudgala* mentioned;
second, which kind of single *pudgala* is being referred to.
Third, for what reason is only this birth mentioned?
Fourth, what kind of birth is being described? Fifth, what kind of present is being described?
And why is only a single *pudgala* mentioned?
To avoid the fault of excessive prolixity in the treatise:
if one were to speak of all *pudgalas*, the treatise would likewise be unnecessarily prolix;
for by speaking of one, it is understood that the others are likewise so.
As for what is meant by "a single individual" (pudgala):
it refers to one who traverses these twelve links as if ascending a staircase;
this is what is being described here.
That is to say, if ignorance and volitional formations arose in the past,
they induce present consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases,
contact, and feeling; furthermore, craving, clinging, and becoming arise in the present.
That which draws forth future birth, aging,
and death is this single *pudgala* spoken of here; it is that which,
having arisen in the past, produced ignorance and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
That which induces present consciousness up to feeling,
and that which does not further give rise to craving, grasping, and becoming in the present to induce future birth, aging, and death—
this is not what is being discussed here.
As stated in the *Jñānakāya* (The Compendium of Knowledge),
one who is endowed with the eight branches is called a practitioner of training (*śaikṣa*).
What is meant by "training" as it is described therein?
If there is one who traverses the *samāpattis* as if ascending a ladder,
that is what is being described: namely,
if one first enters the meditative absorption with applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*).
Next, he enters the concentration without applied thought and sustained thought;
next, he enters the formless concentrations;
next, he enters the attainment of cessation.
Regarding the arising of a contaminated mind (*sāsrava-citta*) upon emerging from the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), that is explained therein:
if one has previously entered the meditative concentration with applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-samādhi*).
Next, he enters the concentration without applied thought or sustained thought;
next, he enters the formless attainments;
next, he enters the attainment of cessation.
That an untainted mind manifests upon emerging from the meditative attainment of cessation is not what they [the opponents] assert;
furthermore, as it is said in the Sūtra:
First, one sees a woman whose appearance is upright and graceful, youthful and full of vitality;
next, one sees her aged, decrepit, and emaciated;
and finally, one sees her suffering from a grave illness and in great distress.
Next, one again sees that corpse having been dead for one day up to seven days;
next, one again sees it bloated, festering, and putrid;
next, one again sees its bones and joints separated, devoid of flesh, blood, and so forth.
Later, one again sees those skeletons decayed and rotten, the color of pigeons.
If a woman passes through all the stages as described above,
this is what that scripture teaches.
If it were not so, it would not be what was taught by him;
the same applies here.
It merely speaks of traversing the twelve links and does not speak of anything else.
Why is it said that "only this birth" is mentioned?
Because by mentioning the present birth, one knows that the past and future are likewise;
therefore, no others are mentioned. What is meant by "this birth"?
The homogeneous character of a group (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is said to be this "birth.
As for what is said to be "present," it refers to the present homogeneous character of the group.
We do not speak of the present in terms of moments (*kṣaṇa*) or the present in terms of states (*avasthā*).
Regarding a single person (*pudgala*) in this life, how many of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are past, how many are future, and how many are present?
Answer: Two are past, namely ignorance and formations;
two are future.
These are birth, old age, and death.
The eight present factors are consciousness,
name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, and becoming.
Question: These twelve links exist fully in the past, future, and present.
Why, then, is it said that there are two links each in the past and future, while there are eight in the present?
Answer: Those who lack the eye of wisdom infer future results from present causes and infer past causes from present results;
thus, it can be known that there is indeed intentional action, and for this reason, such a statement was made.
That which constitutes the present causes refers to craving, grasping, and becoming;
that which projects the future results refers to birth, aging, and death.
Regarding those that are present fruits:
these refer to consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.
Regarding the inference of past causes: [these refer to ignorance and volitional formations].
This refers to ignorance and volitional formations.
The Blessed One, wishing to enable those who lack the eye of wisdom to infer the existence of the past and future through present causes and effects, [taught this].
By means of this, one is able to accomplish what is to be done;
the fruit of the past and the cause of the future can also be known through this gateway.
Therefore, this proponent merely makes this statement:
furthermore, by stating that the two past members exist, he refutes the attachment that cyclic existence was originally non-existent and now exists;
by stating that the two future members exist, he refutes the attachment that cyclic existence, having existed, returns to non-existence.
It is said that there are eight present members [of dependent origination] which establish the continuity of the causes and effects of birth and death.
Thus, because the Tathāgata’s work of transformation was already complete, he made this statement.
Furthermore, by stating that there are two past members, he refutes the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
By stating that there are two factors in the future, he refutes the view of nihilism;
by stating that there are eight factors in the present, he reveals the Middle Way.
Thus, because the Tathāgata’s work of transformation was complete, he made this statement.
Furthermore, to say that there are two past links reveals that birth and death have a cause;
to say that there are two future links reveals that birth and death have a result;
and to say that there are eight present links reveals the continuity of cause and effect.
Because sentient beings are thereby able to accomplish what is to be done, this statement is made.
Furthermore, it is said that there are two past links which eliminate delusion regarding the prior limit,
and two future links which eliminate delusion regarding the posterior limit.
It is said that there are eight present factors [of dependent origination] in order to eliminate delusion regarding the middle period;
this is stated because by means of these, sentient beings are able to accomplish their tasks.
Furthermore, herein only the causes and effects of a single lifetime are discussed.
The meaning of cause and effect regarding other births can be understood by analogy;
therefore, this statement was made.
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* speaks as follows:
What is the dharma of dependent origination?
It refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Question: How does this differ from what is taught in that other treatise?
The answer is: this teaching is of provisional meaning (neyārtha), whereas that teaching is of definitive meaning (nītārtha);
this is a teaching that is incomplete (sāvaśeṣa).
That is a teaching without remainder;
this teaching has an underlying intention (*saṃdhi*),
whereas that teaching is without an underlying intention.
This teaching asserts that there is a distinct cause;
that teaching asserts that there is no distinct cause.
This teaching is conventional.
That [system] speaks of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This [system] speaks only of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) pertaining to sentient beings.
That [system] speaks generally of dependent origination pertaining to both sentient and non-sentient beings.
This [text] speaks only of the dependent origination of phenomena possessing faculties (*sendriya*),
whereas that [text] speaks generally of the dependent origination of both phenomena possessing and lacking faculties.
This [text] speaks only of the dependent origination of phenomena possessing mind (*sacittaka*).
That [text] explains the dependent origination of both states with mind and without mind;
this [text] explains only the dependent origination of the appropriated.
That [text] explains the dependent origination of both the appropriated and the non-appropriated.
Furthermore, there are four types of dependent origination:
first, the momentary;
second, the continuous.
Third, the states;
fourth, the distant continuity.
This explains the distant continuity of the states.
He speaks of the momentary and the continuous [dependent origination].
Question: Why does this treatise speak only of dependent origination pertaining to sentient beings?
Answer: Because it is the intention of the author of the treatise to do so.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, one should not reproach the intention of this author of the treatise,
for the author composed the treatise based upon the sūtras.
The sūtras speak only of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) as pertaining to sentient beings; this [treatise] is likewise.
A question arises from the discussion:
why does the Blessed One speak only of dependent origination as pertaining to sentient beings?
Answer: It is because he observes those to be converted.

That is to say, the Buddha observes that for those sentient beings to be converted, it is appropriate to teach only the dependent origination of phenomena belonging to the category of sentient beings.
Thus, it is said because one is able to understand and accomplish what is to be done.
Furthermore, it is because it accords with the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*);
that is to say, for those included among sentient beings, its meaning is most preeminent in accordance with the factors of existence.
The phenomena comprised within the category of sentient beings have, from beginningless time, circulated through the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*) in an uninterrupted succession.
According to one interpretation, that which is most preeminent is designated as "existence" (*bhava*).
Because the phenomena comprised within the category of sentient beings conform to this existence, they are called "limbs of existence" (*bhavāṅga*).
Therefore, the Blessed One taught only the dependent origination of sentient beings;
this treatise, relying upon that, likewise teaches only the dependent origination of sentient beings.
Furthermore, all classes of sentient beings have, since beginningless time, transmigrated through birth and death, undergoing great suffering and affliction.
