translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, in accordance with the Imperial Decree. Section One: Miscellaneous Aggregates; Chapter Three: The Sub-section on the Person (Pudgala); Part Five. Just as the mental continuum of sentient beings possessing form proceeds in dependence upon the body.
...and so forth, as explained at length. Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the sake of enabling those who have doubts to attain certainty.
That is to say, some may doubt that because the realms of desire and form possess material form (*rūpa*), the continuity of the mind (*citta-saṃtati*) depends upon matter for its operation.
Since there is no form in the formless realm, the mental continuum would presumably lack a basis for its operation;
in order to resolve this doubt, this treatise was composed to demonstrate that even in the formless realm, the continuum of mind and so forth likewise operates with a basis.
Just as the mental continuum of sentient beings with form evolves in dependence upon the body, upon what does the mental continuum of sentient beings without form evolve?
Answer: It evolves in dependence upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character of the group (*nikāyasabhāga*).
And other such formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
What are these other dissociated formations?
They are acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), impermanence (*anityatā*), and so forth.
Question: The mental continuum in both the desire and form realms also proceeds in dependence upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*), and so forth.
Why, then, is it said here that it depends only on the body? Should it not also be stated that it proceeds in dependence upon those [other factors]? Why is this not mentioned?
This is an incomplete explanation.
Others have said this because the meaning [of the teaching] is manifold.
This means that within the mental continuum of the desire and form realms,
the sense organs (*indriya*) serve as the basis for the body in a more significant sense than the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth.
This is because immeasurable material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), such as the eye-faculty and others, serve as the bases for visual consciousness and the other types of consciousness.
Other masters say that because the body is coarse, it is mentioned alone as the support;
whereas the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth are subtle and difficult to demonstrate.

If one is born in the desire realm and visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is present, this consciousness takes the eye and the immediately preceding ceased mind (*manas*) as its support (*āśraya*) and its basis (*niśraya*).

The great elements upon which the eye-faculty depends, as well as the body-faculty and the great elements upon which the body-faculty depends, along with the life-faculty and the group-homogeneity (nikāya-sabhāga),
take birth, aging, subsistence, impermanence, and so forth as their support, but they do not serve as their basis.
It should be understood that the same applies to the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, and tongue as it does to the visual consciousness.
When tactile consciousness is present,
this consciousness takes both the body and the immediately preceding ceased mind as its support (āśraya) and its basis (niśraya).

When the mental consciousness manifests, it takes as its support— rather than as its objective basis— the great elements that serve as the physical basis for the body-faculty, along with the life-faculty and the group-homogeneity (nikāya-sabhāga),
as well as birth, aging, duration, impermanence, and so forth.
This consciousness takes the immediately preceding ceased mind as its support (*āśraya*) and basis (*niśraya*).
It takes the body-faculty, the primary elements upon which the body-faculty depends, the life-faculty, and the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*),
along with birth, aging, duration, and impermanence, as its supports but not its bases.
As it is for those born in the desire realm,
so it is for those born in the form realm.
The difference is as follows:
For one who lacks nose-consciousness and tongue-consciousness, if consciousness arises in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is present,
this consciousness takes the immediately preceding ceased mind as its support and basis,
and relies upon the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and the group-homogeneity (nikāyasabhāga).
Birth, aging, subsistence, impermanence, and so forth function as supports, not as supported objects. Some say:
if one is born in the desire realm...
When visual consciousness is present,
this consciousness takes the eye and the immediately preceding ceased mind as its support (*āśraya*) and basis (*niśraya*).
It also takes the body-faculty, visible forms, odors, tastes, tangibles, the life-faculty, and the homogeneous character of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) as its supports.
Birth, aging, subsistence, and impermanence, etc., are obtained as the support (āśraya) and not as the supported (āśrita).
It should be understood that this is likewise for eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, and tongue-consciousness.
If body-consciousness manifests, [the same applies].
This consciousness takes the body and the immediately preceding ceased mind as its support (*āśraya*) and basis (*niśraya*).
It takes visible form, odor, taste, tangible objects, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*),
and [the characteristics] such as birth, aging, duration, and impermanence as its supports, but not as its bases, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is present.
This consciousness takes the immediately preceding ceased mind as its support (*āśraya*) and basis (*niśraya*).
It takes the body-faculty, visible form, odor, taste, tangible objects, the life-faculty, the group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*),
and [the characteristics] such as birth, aging, duration, and impermanence as its supports, but not as its bases.
As it is for those born in the desire realm,
so it is for those born in the form realm.
The difference is as follows:
They lack nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, as well as odors and tastes;
their birth in the formless realm is as previously explained.
Other masters say:
If, being born in the desire realm, visual consciousness is present before one,
this consciousness takes the eye and the immediately preceding ceased mind as its support (*āśraya*) and its basis (*niśraya*);
it takes the four co-arising aggregates as its support, but not as its basis.
It should be understood that the same applies to the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, and body as it does to eye-consciousness.
When mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is present,
this consciousness takes the immediately preceding ceased mind as its support (āśraya) and its basis (niśraya).
Taking the four co-emergent aggregates as a support, they are not the supported;
as it is for one born in the desire realm,
so it should be understood for one born in the form realm.
As for the distinction:
those [beings] lack nose-consciousness and tongue-consciousness;
when consciousness belonging to the formless realm arises and manifests before them.
This consciousness takes the mind that has just ceased as its support (*āśraya*) and basis (*niśraya*);
it takes the three co-emergent aggregates as its support, but not as its basis.
Question: Is the essence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) a single entity or multiple entities?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If it were a single entity, why is it that one does not die when the hands and such are severed,
yet dies when the head or waist is severed?
If life were composed of many entities, why would there be no life when the hands and other limbs are severed from the body?
One should answer that the essence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is a single entity.
Question: If that is so, why does one not die when the hands, feet, and so forth are severed?
Answer: There are two kinds of life-faculty (jīvitendriya):
first, that which depends on a complete body;
second, that which depends on an incomplete body.

When the hands, feet, and so forth are severed and separated from the body, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) ceases in dependence upon the complete body and arises in dependence upon the incomplete body.
Furthermore, the body that serves as the basis for life is also of two kinds.
When the hands and other limbs have not yet been severed, it is called a complete body;
when the hands and other limbs are severed, it is called incomplete.
Once the hands and other limbs have been severed, that which was complete ceases to exist.
Because they arise when [the conditions] are incomplete, life and the body revolve in mutual dependence.
Question: For what reason does one die immediately upon having the head or the waist severed?
"Is it that one does not die even when the hands, feet, and so forth are severed?
He replied: "The head and the waist are the two primary vital points; therefore, death occurs immediately upon their severance.
This is not the case with the hands and other limbs."
Furthermore, sentient beings in the desire realm subsist on edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra).
The throat serves as the passage for edible food,
and the stomach is the locus of its sustenance.
Therefore, when the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of these two locations is severed, it is immediately cut off.
Furthermore, the head is the locus of support for the eye and other sense-faculties; if it is severed, the eye and other faculties are destroyed.
The abdomen is the locus where the vital winds (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*) reside.

Because when the waist and abdomen are severed, the breath is destroyed and there is no basis [for life], the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is cut off at those two locations; it is not so for the hands and other limbs, thus they cannot be used as an objection.
Some say:

The substance of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) consists of multiple entities, for the life-faculty has distinct bases within the hands, feet, and so forth, corresponding to the number and quantity of those which it supports.
Question: If this is so, why is there no life when the hands, feet, and other members are severed and separated from the body?
The answer is: Because the hands, feet, and so forth are bound to the body, if they were separated from the body, life would not arise.

Just as when the hands, feet, and so forth have not yet been separated from the body, this body is called a "sentient being" because it is the basis for the sense-faculties; once separated from the body, it is not so.
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is likewise.
Therefore, when it is separated from the body, life does not arise.
[The] critique says:
It should be said that the essence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is a single entity; because there is one life,
there is a "living being," just as because there is one mind, there is a "sentient being."
When there is the cessation of one mind, it is called "mindless";
likewise for one feeling, one perception, and one volition.
Similarly, when a sentient being possesses one life-force, they are called "possessing life."
And this life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is exclusively a maturation (*vipāka*) and a dissociated formation (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*).
Just as with the mind and feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, within a single sentient body at a single moment, there is only one and not two.
What is the homogeneous character of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*)?
It refers to the homogeneous character of sentient beings, which—like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)—is a single entity that serves as the basis for all parts of the body;
it is comprised within the formations dissociated from thought (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
It is exclusively non-obscured and neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta), and being exclusively with outflows (sāsrava), it pervades all three realms.
Question: Is this group-homogeneity (nikāyasabhāga) a result of nourishment (aupacayika) or a result of uniform outflow (naiṣyandika)?
It is a maturation (vipāka).
Answer: It is both a maturation and a flow-on (niṣyanda), but not a nurtured (aupacayika) phenomenon.
Because it is not a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*).
"Maturation" (*vipāka*) refers to the commonality of destiny (*gati-sabhāgatā*) and so forth.
Just as sentient beings in the hell realm resemble one another,
so it is for those in the heavenly realms and others alike.
As for "outflow" (niṣyanda):
This refers to the homogeneity of realms (*dhātusabhāgatā*) and so forth;
for example, sentient beings of the desire realm are mutually similar,
and this likewise applies to sentient beings up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Some say that what is called "maturation" (vipāka) is acquired at the moment of birth,
such as the mutual resemblance one has with one's parents and so forth.
Regarding "outflow" (niṣyanda):
it means that it is obtained only at a later time,
such as when one gradually comes to resemble śramaṇas, brahmins, and others.
One should understand, according to reason, that the commonality of sentient beings (*sattva-sabhāgatā*) extends to continents, regions, lands,
and clans. Other masters say:
The homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) of sentient beings is comprised within the categories of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
Specifically, the homogeneous character of sentient beings who are candidates for or have attained the four fruits of the path is comprised within the wholesome category;
the homogeneous character of sentient beings who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) is comprised within the unwholesome category.
All other [types of] homogeneous character (sabhāgatā) are subsumed under the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
The critique states:
one should not make such a statement.
Although dharmas are of three kinds, the *sabhāgatā* of sentient beings is comprised solely within the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
From this, one should know that the previous statement is a valid question: "If one acquires a *nikāyasabhāga*, does one then abandon that *nikāyasabhāga*?"
It is agreed that this conforms to the preceding statement:
namely, if one obtains a homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), one necessarily abandons that homogeneous class;
however, there are cases where one abandons a homogeneous class without obtaining another homogeneous class.
This refers to the time when an Arhat enters parinirvāṇa.
Question: When one dies here and is born there, is it certain that one abandons the *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous character) and acquires a [new] *nikāyasabhāga*?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold logical alternative (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are cases where one dies here and is born there, yet does not relinquish the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) nor acquire a [different] homogeneous class—
such as dying in hell and being reborn again in hell,
or even dying among the gods and being reborn again among the gods, and so forth.
There is the relinquishing of one *nikāyasabhāga* and the acquisition of another *nikāyasabhāga*,
yet this does not constitute dying here and being born there;
namely, [this occurs] in such states as entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
There are cases where one dies here and is born there, both relinquishing the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) and acquiring a new homogeneous class;
this refers, for example, to dying in the hells or similar realms and being born in another destiny (*gati*).
There are also cases where one neither dies here nor is born there, neither relinquishing the homogeneous class nor acquiring a new one.
That is to say, setting aside the aforementioned characteristics,
should craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) be said to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Thus it is explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
That is to say, the sūtra states:
There are three kinds of craving:
first, craving for sensory pleasures;
second, craving for existence.
Third is the craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).
Although the Sūtra states this, it does not provide a detailed analysis,
nor does it specify whether the craving for non-existence is to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) or through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The sūtras are the foundation of this treatise;
that which was not stated therein shall now be explained.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of refuting divergent views and elucidating the meaning of the sūtras.

That is to say, some claim that the "craving for non-existence" (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) mentioned in the sūtras pertains to both what is abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) and what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Just as in the case of the Vibhajyavādins,
in order to refute their tenet, it is shown that what the Sūtra teaches regarding "craving for non-existence" (vibhavatṛṣṇā) is that it is abandoned solely through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
Should craving (*tṛṣṇā*) be said to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
It should be said that it is abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding "non-existence":
it is the impermanence of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Craving that takes this as its object is called craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*).
Therefore, this craving is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
because the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is abandoned through cultivation.
Some have said as follows:
The craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*) is either abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned through insight?
It refers to the craving for non-existence directed toward phenomena that are to be abandoned through insight.
What is that which is to be abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to craving for non-existent things among those phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation.
Question: Who made this statement?
Answering the Vibhajyavādin,
he says: They state that the impermanence of the three realms is designated as "non-existence."
The craving that takes that [impermanence] as its object is called "craving for non-existence.
Since impermanence is common to both what is abandoned by seeing and what is abandoned by cultivation,
the craving that takes it as its object likewise pertains to both types.

That is to say, within this treatise which follows the non-erroneous meaning of the sūtras, there is no *tṛṣṇā*;
it should simply be said that [this craving] is abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding this, some say:
if one explains according to the literal meaning of the sūtra, the craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) is abandoned only through cultivation;
if one explains according to the ultimate meaning, the craving for non-existence is abandoned by both [the path of seeing and the path of cultivation].
Why is this so? It is because a sutra states:
"Suppose there is a certain class of people who, being tormented by the suffering of fear and dread, form this thought:"
"If, after my death, I were to be annihilated and cease to exist,
would that not be a joy?
This sūtra states that their *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous class) is impermanent at a later time.
It is called "non-existence.
Since such non-existence is abandoned solely through cultivation,
craving for non-existence is not abandoned through insight.
In this context, the Master of the Treatise explains the meaning according to the sūtras.
Because he contends with the Vibhajyavādins in interpreting the meaning of the sūtras,
he states that craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
If one follows the actual meaning as will be explained later,
the impermanence of the three realms is termed "non-existence.
This impermanence of the three realms is common to both categories of what is to be abandoned.
Therefore, craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) also pertains to both types. Some say:
"This craving for non-existence follows either the ultimate meaning (*tattvārtha*) or the literal meaning of the sūtra (*sūtrārtha*)."
In both cases, it should be stated that they are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Although impermanence in the three realms pertains to both types [of abandonment],
the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) toward it is abandoned only through cultivation.
Because non-existence-craving (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) arises based on weariness with suffering,
it is merely craving for the future vessel of suffering;
it is to be abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
This is a vessel for manifold suffering;
therefore, the craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Although the view of non-existence (*vibhavadṛṣṭi*) takes the five categories as its object, it does not [itself] constitute existence.
However, craving does not function as a pervasive condition;
it conditions only the severance of the future *nikāyasabhāga*.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghosaka said:
Regarding the person who has given rise to craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*):
they arise solely by taking the appropriated aggregates, elements, and bases as their object;
being oppressed by those [aggregates], they give rise to craving directed toward their future cessation and destruction.
Because there is no craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) that oppresses sentient beings in such a way as to cause them to sever their affection for them,
craving for non-existence is exclusively abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Thus far, it has been briefly stated that craving for non-existence is abandoned solely through cultivation.

Answering "it is not so," the proponent of the reasoned argument (yuktivādin) negates that question to demonstrate that there is no contradiction in the meaning. [The opponent] asks:

Answer: Because they have seen the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
That is to say, because a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) sees that the nature of all phenomena consists in the continuity of cause and effect, they do not desire their cessation.
Furthermore, it is because they have faith in the ripening of karma and its results.
This means that because a stream-enterer has deep faith in the continuity of the results of karma from beginning to end, they do not desire its cessation.
Furthermore, it is because they have realized emptiness;
that is, the stream-enterer attains the gate of liberation of emptiness and knows there is no self or what belongs to a self.
Now, because there is a subsequent cessation, craving and greed do not arise; rather, they are extinguished by that subsequent cessation.
Furthermore, this absence of craving is not nurtured by the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*);
it manifests only after the view of annihilationism has been abandoned.
Because all stream-enterers have already abandoned the view of what is to be abandoned, they do not give rise to this craving.
Furthermore, because all stream-enterers have attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of craving for existence, it will certainly never arise again.
Listen to what I say: if craving were to exist only as something to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),

it would follow that one must say a stream-enterer gives rise to such a thought.
If, after my death, I were to be annihilated and cease to exist, would that not be peace and happiness?
A stream-enterer does not give rise to such a thought as,

Then one should not say that craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);

that destination belongs to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Because the Noble Ones are not ordinary beings;
for those [ordinary beings] have an evil disposition,
whereas the Noble Ones have a virtuous disposition.
Those realms abound in the breaking of precepts and evil karma;
because the noble ones have accomplished pure morality, they do not seek rebirth there.
Furthermore, because all noble ones have attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding those realms, they do not desire birth therein.
