translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Four of the Fourth Sub-section on Affection and Veneration within the First Aggregate of Miscellaneous Topics: Thus, analytical cessation is also called Nirvana.
It is also called "of a different category," "not an aggregate," and "not manifest."
They are also called "Most Excellent," they are also called "Thoroughly Penetrating," and they are also called "Arhats."
It is also called "not associating with," it is also called "not cultivating," and it is also called "delightful."
It is also called "proximate," it is also called "sublime," and it is also called "renunciation."
Question: For what reason is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) also called *nirvāṇa*?
Answer: *Nir* means "to go out" and *vāṇa* means "destiny" (*gati*).
Because it is the eternal departure from all destinies, it is called *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, *pari* means "stench" and *nir* means "non-existence.
Because there is forever no stench of the defilements (*kleśa*) and karma, it is called *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, *pari* means "dense forest" and *nir* means "eternal departure."
It is called *nirvāṇa* because it is eternally free from the dense forest of all the three fires, the three marks, and the aggregates (*skandha*).
Furthermore, *vaṇa* means "weaving" and *ni* means "not";
herein, there is eternally an absence of the threads of afflictions and karma.
It is called *nirvāṇa* because it is not woven from the silk of the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of birth and death;
the rest is as previously explained.
Question: For what reason is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) also called "of a different class" (*visabhāga*)?
Answer: Because there is no homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu), and because it is also not a homogeneous cause.
The rest is as previously stated.
Question: For what reason is analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) also called "non-aggregate" (apratisaṃkhyāta)?
Answer: Because it is free from all aggregates (skandha).
That is to say, it refers to those who assert that conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) lack the characteristic of abiding (sthiti-lakṣaṇa).
He asserts that conditioned phenomena necessarily consist of four components coming together:
namely, the entity itself and its three characteristics.
If one says that conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*), [then...]
He says that conditioned phenomena necessarily consist of a collection of five categories:
namely, the intrinsic nature itself and the four characteristics.
Furthermore, all realms, destinies, births, aggregates, worlds, and sufferings are termed "assemblages."
Because analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is distinct from those [conditioned phenomena], it is called "non-aggregate" (aprakaraṇa).
Question: Why is analytical cessation also called "non-manifest" (apradarśana)?
Answer: "Manifest" refers to the praising of the qualities of nirvāṇa, which is universally established among the wise.
It is called "non-manifest" because it does not depend upon praise.
Furthermore, because the merits of nirvāṇa are boundless, they cannot be praised.
As it is said:
Because this person’s skill is boundless and beyond praise, it is called "non-manifest.
Furthermore, "manifest" refers to the ultimate perfection of the merits of nirvāṇa, which are here disparaged.
Just as a mani jewel is perfectly round, luminous, pure, and beyond reproach, it is therefore called "non-manifest.
Furthermore, the merit of nirvāṇa is ultimately and securely established;
like the substance of a mani jewel, it neither increases nor decreases.
Because it abides securely wherever it is placed and cannot be disparaged, it is called "non-manifest.

Furthermore, "manifest" refers to the explicit teaching that nirvāṇa is realized through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the noble ones; because it cannot be explicitly described, it is called "non-manifest."
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena possess causes and possess effects;
thus, one may explain their effects by means of their causes,
and likewise explain their causes by means of their effects.

Nirvāṇa is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), without cause, and without fruit; because it cannot be manifested through verbal expression, it is called "non-manifest. Furthermore, "manifest" means to reveal.
Nirvāṇa is quiescent (*śānta*); there are no distinctions of caste such as Brahmin or Kṣatriya that can be revealed therein.
Furthermore, it possesses no characteristics such as blue, yellow, red, or white that can be manifested;
therefore, it is called "non-manifest.
Moreover, "manifest" refers to being made evident.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are either material in essence and thus manifest in appearance, or, although not material, they depend upon matter and can likewise be manifested.
Nirvāṇa is not like this; therefore, it is called "non-manifest" (*anidarśana*).
Question: For what reason is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) also called "supreme"?
Answer: Because it is sublime and excellent.
Just as in the world, superior clothing, food, drink, ornaments, and so forth are termed "supreme."
Nirvana is likewise so.
The Venerable Ghosaka has stated that among all phenomena,
the nirvana of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is the most supreme dharma.
Among all meanings, it is the most supreme meaning;
among all phenomena, it is the most supreme phenomenon;
among all principles, it is the most supreme principle.
Among all fruits, this is the most excellent fruit;
therefore, it is called "most excellent.
Question: For what reason is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) also called "penetration" (*prativedha*)?
Answer: "Thorough penetration" refers to wisdom; because nirvāṇa is the fruit of wisdom, it is also called thorough penetration.

This is just as the nine types of full knowledge are also called full knowledge because they are the fruits of knowledge, or as the six sense bases are said to be "former karma" because they are the fruits of karma.
Furthermore, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is *nirvāṇa*, is called "penetration" (*abhijñā*) because it is the fruit of penetration;
just as the divine eye and ear are also called "penetrations" because they are the fruits of penetration.
Question: For what reason is analytical cessation also called "Arhat"?
Because they have consented to receive offerings.

That is to say, the term "Arhat" generally conveys the sense of being worthy; there is no sublime offering in the world that the one who has attained cessation through analytical discernment (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), namely Nirvāṇa, would not accept.
Furthermore, "Arhat" means "one who should not.
The syllable *a* signifies "not.
Because the nirvāṇa of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) should not flow through the various realms and destinies, it is called "that which should not [flow]."
Furthermore, an Arhat is called a "thief" and is also called an "enemy.
The word "A" signifies "non-existence."
In nirvāṇa, there are no afflictions or enemies.
For this reason, analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is called arhatship.
Question: Why is analytical cessation also called "non-association" (anupasevana)?
Answer: Because it is free from proximity to the source.
This means that those who are in proximity to conditioned phenomena do so out of craving for their fruits;
they are like those who, craving the shade, flowers, leaves, and fruit, remain in proximity to a tree.
Since nirvāṇa has no fruit that could cause one to crave it, it is called "not to be approached.
Question: For what reason is it said that the wise should approach nirvāṇa?
Answer: The wise person...
This refers to the Buddha and his disciples.
Because they understand, give rise to, and realize [the truth], they are said to be "intimate" with it;
yet because they do not crave its fruit, they are also said to be "non-intimate."
Question: For what reason is analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) also called "not to be cultivated" (abhāvya)?
Answer: Because it does not exist within the continuum (saṃtāna).
If something exists within the continuum, it manifests repeatedly and gradually increases.
It is called "to be cultivated.
Nirvāṇa is not like this, and therefore it is also called "not to be cultivated.
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret the verse?
Beneath the *jambu* tree, through meditative concentration and heedfulness,
one will before long tread the tracks of the Path;
"Nirvāṇa is in the mind" means that because it is attained by relying upon the mind, it is said to be "in the mind."
It is not meant that *nirvāṇa* has the sense of being something to be cultivated.
Question: For what reason is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) also called "desirable"?
Answer: Because it is what the noble ones desire and delight in.
It means that the noble ones fear all forms of suffering,
while the noble ones cherish nirvana because it is free from suffering.
Furthermore, the noble ones are weary of saṃsāra.
Because it is devoid of birth and death, it is cherished by the noble ones;
that is to say, within nirvāṇa, one is forever free from all matters of saṃsāric flux.
Furthermore, the noble ones loathe the breaking of precepts.
Because he is free from the breaking of precepts, he is beloved by the noble ones;
that is to say, within nirvāṇa, one is forever separated from all matters of violating the precepts.
It is because of nirvāṇa that the Buddha taught the untainted (anāsrava) morality.
It is called the "precept beloved by the noble ones" (*āryakānta-śīla*), because this precept can realize the abandonment of and the cessation of immoral conduct.

For this reason, it is also called the "timely liberation beloved by time," because one attains Nirvana through a timely delight. Question: Why is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) also called "proximate"? Answer: Because those who have attained the Noble Path realize it through direct manifestation. As stated in the Sūtra: [omitted].
One who accomplishes fifteen factors through diligence is said to tread the path of training and draw near to nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, this is because they realize [the goal] without selecting a specific mental continuum.
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is called "near.
This means that those capable of cultivating the path, such as Kṣatriyas and Brahmins, all realize *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, cessation through deliberation is called "near" because it is realized without selecting a specific location.
That is to say, whether one practices the Noble Path in a city or in a forest hermitage (āraṇya), one attains nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, through the power of resolute conviction (adhimukti), analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is said to be "near";
this refers to when the patience toward extinction and the knowledge of extinction (nirodha-kṣānti and nirodha-jñāna) manifest before the Noble Ones.
Because it is clearly visualized as if before one's eyes through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Furthermore, just as something near is called "near," so too is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) called "near," meaning that it can be realized wherever one may be.
As stated in the Prakaraṇapāda:
"What are distant phenomena?
They are past and future phenomena."
What are the proximate dharmas?
They are present dharmas and all unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas.
Furthermore, because it is obtained through proximity, analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is called "proximate."
That is to say, the present world is called "near.
Because one gives rise to the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) and realizes analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) based upon the present world, it is called "near.
Furthermore, because one abandons what is near in order to enter [the state of cessation], analytical cessation is called "near."
That which is said to be the "near Dharma" refers to the present life.
By relinquishing this near Dharma, one enters Nirvana;
therefore, Nirvana is also called "near."
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"Those who diligently cultivate the Path proceed directly toward Nirvāṇa;
therefore, it is called 'proximate'."
Furthermore, there are distinctions among the bases upon which the noble path relies.
Because nirvāṇa is not fixed [in location], it is called "near";
for all those who can cultivate the path attain it.
Question: The Noble Path is also sublime, as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
What is the sublime Dharma?
This refers to the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Why is nirvāṇa alone designated as "sublime" (praṇīta)?
The answer is: because nirvāṇa is the most sublime among all that is sublime. Furthermore, although the Noble Path is sublime, it is interspersed with impermanence.
Nirvāṇa is not like this, and therefore it alone is called "sublime.
Furthermore, although the noble path is sublime, there are counteragents to it,
namely the wholesome dharmas of "emptiness-of-emptiness" and so forth, which involve a sense of wearying detachment.
Nirvāṇa is not like that; therefore, it alone is called "sublime.
Question: The Noble Path is also a dharma of transcendence, as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
What is the dharma of renunciation?
It refers to the wholesome precepts of the desire realm,
as well as the wholesome meditative absorptions arising from detachment in the form and formless realms.
This includes both the learned (*śaikṣa*) and the unlearned (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Why is *nirvāṇa* alone termed "renunciation" (*niḥsaraṇa*)?
Answer: Because *nirvāṇa* is itself renunciation; it is not something from which one must renounce.
The Noble Path is both the departure and that which possesses departure,
because at the time of parinirvāṇa one departs from it;
furthermore, because nirvāṇa is the dharma of true departure.
It is said that there are two kinds of relinquishment regarding contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*):
first, relinquishment through abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); second, relinquishment through discarding (*tyāga*).
Although uncontaminated conditioned phenomena lack abandonment through severance, they do possess relinquishment;
whereas only analytical cessation lacks both types of relinquishment,
and is thus termed "true transcendence."
Furthermore, nirvāṇa is the ultimate merit of transcendence.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One transcends desire by means of form; one transcends form by means of the formless."
One departs from the formless realms by means of the noble path;
one departs from all conditioned phenomena by means of nirvāṇa.
Question: It is already known that the essence of non-analytical cessation is not dissociation.
One should explain: why is it called "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?

Answer: It is called cessation not through deliberation because this cessation is not obtained by means of the wisdom of deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-jñāna*), and because it is not the fruit of such deliberation.

Furthermore, this cessation is called "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) because it is not attained by means of exclusive exertion, exclusive application, or exclusive effortful discernment of phenomena.
Furthermore,
this cessation does not necessarily result from the repeated discernment of suffering and so forth; therefore, it is called "cessation not through discernment" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: If that is so, by what means is this cessation attained?
Answer: It is attained through the absence of conditions, just as when one faces a single direction.
When objects such as visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles existing in other locations cease,
the mental states and mental factors that take them as objects will never arise again due to the absence of their objective conditions.
From this, non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) arises.
Question: In which time period do phenomena attain non-analytical cessation?
Some say as follows:
One attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding all phenomena of the three times because they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Question: If that is so, with respect to what is this cessation not attained?
What further difference is there between attainment and non-attainment? Other masters say:
"Non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is attained only with respect to past and future dharmas, not with respect to present ones."
Because present phenomena exist within the body and its activities.

Question: If that were so, this cessation would have to be attained and then relinquished in each successive moment, and having been relinquished, attained once more—namely, when future phenomena enter the present.
Once that non-analytical cessation has been attained, it is relinquished when present dharmas enter the past;
having been relinquished, that non-analytical cessation is attained once again.
However, non-analytical cessation does not possess such a characteristic.
Some say that non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is obtained only with respect to future dharmas,
and not with respect to past or present ones.
Why is this? Because past dharmas have already been practiced within the body,
and present dharmas are being practiced within the body.
Question: If that were so, one would have already abandoned the acquisition (prāpti) of this cessation when a future dharma enters the present,
because the acquisition of its non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) has already been abandoned at that time.
However, non-analytical cessation does not possess such a meaning.
The critique states:
this non-analytical cessation is attained only with respect to dharmas that will not arise in the future.
Why is this? This cessation fundamentally intends to prevent conditioned phenomena from ever arising again.
If a phenomenon does not arise, then this attainment (prāpti) occurs.
Just as the dharma of "giving consent" (chanda-dāna) is connected to sentient beings, so too do present, past, and future occurrences of its actual practice all possess the sense of arising.

Therefore, regarding those dharmas, this cessation [of the path] cannot be attained. Now, between analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), which is more numerous?
Some say that analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is more numerous,
while non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is fewer.
Why is this? Because cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is acquired with respect to dharmas of the three time periods,
whereas cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is acquired only with respect to dharmas that will not arise in the future.
Other masters say that non-analytical cessation is more numerous,
while analytical cessation is fewer.
Why is this so? Because non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is attained with respect to both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava) phenomena,
whereas analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is attained only with respect to contaminated phenomena.
The commentary states:
One should say this:
non-analytical cessation is abundant, while analytical cessation is scarce.

Why is this? Because non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) exists in the same measure as conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma), whereas analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) exists only in the measure of contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma).
If it were otherwise, then regarding those phenomena capable of arising, if they were to not arise, one would not obtain non-analytical cessation.
Although the extent of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of these two types of cessation (*nirodha*) is thus, regarding their acquisition (*prāpti*),
one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*).
There are dharmas for which there is the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) but not the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This refers to those past, present, and future conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) that are subject to outflows (sāsrava),
for which there is non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and no analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
It also refers to those future, non-arising, uncontaminated phenomena (anāsravadharma).

There are dharmas for which both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are obtained; these are future impure (*sāsrava*) dharmas that are not destined to arise.

There are dharmas for which neither analytical cessation nor non-analytical cessation is obtained; these are past and present dharmas, as well as future pure (*anāsrava*) dharmas that are destined to arise.
Question: Regarding all classes of sentient beings, do they all attain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) collectively or individually?
Answer: This is not fixed.
Regarding the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of shared phenomena, it is attained collectively;
regarding the non-analytical cessation of unshared phenomena, it is attained individually.
As for the various classes of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), if they abide in a single destiny (*gati*).
Regarding the phenomena of other realms,
one attains non-analytical cessation moment by moment,
because objects such as forms perish from instant to instant.
Because that eye-consciousness and so forth ultimately do not arise,
it is as if one were abiding in a single course;
the same applies to a single realm, a single stage, and a single location.
Question: By means of which wholesome dharmas do practitioners attain the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the various evil destinies?
Answer: Either by means of generosity (*dāna*), or by means of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Whether by means of the wisdom derived from hearing,
the wisdom derived from reflection, or the wisdom derived from cultivation,
practitioners attain the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding the various evil destinies.
Regarding the giver:
there are those who, although they have kept their doors open for great giving for twelve years, do not attain non-analytical cessation regarding the miserable realms.
This is because, like Vairambha, Kṛkī, and others, they are unable to cultivate revulsion toward saṃsāra.
There are those who, by giving even a single gift of a mouthful of food, attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the evil destinies,
because they are deeply able to weary of saṃsāra.
Conversely, there are those who, though observing the *prātimokṣa* vows for the duration of their lives, do not attain non-analytical cessation regarding the evil destinies.
As previously stated: there are those who,
although able to maintain the precepts for one day and night, attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the miserable destinies (*apāya*),
as previously stated.
Regarding those who possess wisdom derived from hearing:
there are some who, although they fully understand both the words and the meaning of the Tripitaka, do not attain non-analytical cessation regarding the miserable realms,
as previously explained.
There are those who, although they have understood a four-line verse, attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the miserable destinies (*apāya*),
as previously stated; this is by means of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
There are those who, despite possessing reflection upon external and internal treatises, do not attain non-analytical cessation regarding the miserable realms,
as previously stated. There are also those who,
though reflecting on only a small portion of the contemplation of phenomena, do attain non-analytical cessation regarding the miserable realms.
As previously stated,
this refers to the contemplation of impurity, mindfulness of breathing, and the various foundations of mindfulness,
which are practiced by those possessing wisdom derived from cultivation.

There are those who, although they have fully attained the worldly concentrations (*laukika-samādhi*) of the eight stages, do not attain the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the miserable destinies (*apāya*).
This is as previously stated;
namely, the outsiders such as the son of Mṛgī and others.
There are those who, although practicing only a limited portion of the meditative gateways, attain non-analytical cessation regarding the evil destinies,
as previously stated;
these are those of the extremely dull faculties among those at the stages of Heat, Summits, and Patience.
When one attains the lower grade of patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), one obtains the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding all miserable destinies (*apāya*).

The Venerable [Vasumitra] says: "One must first realize dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) before obtaining the non-analytical cessation regarding the miserable destinies."
Because one cannot transcend the various evil destinies apart from the Noble Path.
The critique states:
He should not have made such a statement.
A bodhisattva does not fall into the evil destinies for ninety-one kalpas;
this must be explained as being due to their awakening to dependent origination through untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā).
Whether through generosity, ethical discipline, or even the lower stage of patience (*kṣānti*), one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the evil destinies.
Question: Is this non-analytical cessation of the three evil destinies attained simultaneously?
Is it acquired separately?
Some say that it must be acquired simultaneously.
Question: If that is so, how is it that Devadatta has already attained the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of two evil destinies, yet not of the hell realm?
Answer: He has [already] excluded only one further birth in hell.
All other births and both evil destinies are simultaneously attained as non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: Since one birth has already been excluded, is this not a separate attainment?
Other masters say that if [the qualities] such as generosity, ethical discipline,
and learning attain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) within the miserable realms (apāya), [they are not abandoned].
Whether individually or collectively, those who attain the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) necessarily attain them collectively.
Question: Does Devadatta not also attain the aids to penetration?
The commentary states:
It should be said that one attains them collectively at the stage of patience (*kṣānti*),
whereas in the preceding stages, it is not fixed.
Having already explained the attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the evil destinies,
one should now explain its attainment regarding the happy destinies.
At the stage of the supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one attains it with the sole exception of seven births among humans and gods in the desire realm.
In each of the individual realms of the form and formless worlds, there is one birth;
for all other births, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is the case when a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) is proceeding toward the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
For one who does not emerge from meditative absorption,
the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the six [desire-realm] births is acquired during the stage of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*).
For one who does emerge from absorption, it is required that they reach the sixth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Regarding the desire realm, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) in six births;
furthermore, for a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) proceeding toward the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*),
it is attained at the time of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) when not emerging from meditative concentration.
Regarding the desire realm, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) for that single lifetime.

If one enters meditative absorption, it is only upon reaching the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that one attains non-analytical cessation for that single lifetime in the desire realm.
At that time, one attains the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of all births in the desire realm.

For one who is of the nature of non-retrogression (*aparihāṇadharman*), this occurs at the time of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) when they have not yet arisen from meditative absorption while abandoning the defilements of the first dhyāna.
Regarding the first dhyāna, there is the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the two types of birth.

For one who enters meditative absorption, it is only upon reaching the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) that the non-analytical cessation of the two types of birth in the first dhyāna is attained; at that time, all births in the first dhyāna attain analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
If one who is subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman) becomes free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
whether they have emerged from meditative absorption or not.
When one reaches the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one attains the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of all births in the first dhyāna,
but does not attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Because they are subject to falling back and being reborn;
this should be understood to apply likewise up to the point of becoming free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

As for those of the non-falling nature (*aparihāṇadharman*), it is at the time they become free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
For one who does not emerge from meditative absorption,
non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is attained during the stage of the preparatory path (prayoga-mārga).
For one who does emerge from absorption, it is only upon reaching the ninth uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) that it is attained.
When one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
at that moment one attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding all future births.
This applies even to one of the "nature of falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*) when they become free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
For one who does not enter meditative absorption,
the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is acquired regarding the eight stages during the stage of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*).
For one who does enter meditative absorption, it is required that they reach the ninth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
In the eighth stage, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
At that time, one attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding all births.
Thus has been explained the attainment of non-analytical cessation regarding the places of birth.

It should be stated that the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of afflictions occurs at the stage of supreme patience (*adhimātrākṣānti*); specifically, at that time,
there is the non-analytical cessation of the acquisition of the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms.
Upon reaching the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one attains the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of those [defilements] according to the uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*).
As for the noble ones who possess the quality of non-retrogression (*aparihāṇadharman*) during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
at the time they become free from the defilement of desire (*kāmarāga*):
For one who does not emerge from meditative absorption,
the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm is attained during the preparatory path (prayoga-mārga).
For one who does emerge from absorption, it is attained at the time of each respective uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) reached therein.
At that time, one attains the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of those afflictions.
If it is one of the "subject to falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*) who is free from the defilement of desire,
it occurs when they emerge from meditative absorption.
If one does not emerge from meditative absorption,
one attains the analytical cessation of those afflictions at the very moment each respective path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) occurs.
One does not attain the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of those [states],
up to and including detachment from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana);
this should be explained according to what is appropriate in each case.

Question: At what time do those of a nature subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman) obtain the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya)?
Regarding this, some say:
When one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) transforms their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) and attains the state of "one who has attained vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
and when one who is liberated by time (samayavimukta) transforms their faculties and attains the state of the "immovable" (akopyadharman),
they obtain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) that have already been abandoned.
The commentary states:
It should be said thus:
if one has attained certainty and shall no longer fall back.
When those afflictions arise, one attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) with respect to them.
Question: At what time does one attain that non-analytical cessation?
Is one also said to obtain the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of those [dharmas]?
One should respond by formulating four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are dharmas for which non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is obtained first, and analytical cessation is obtained later.
This refers to the afflictions of the three realms abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*),

as well as the afflictions of the three realms abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) which do not arise for those of non-retrogressive nature (*aparihāṇadharman*) due to their attainment of meditative absorption.
There are thus dharmas that first obtain analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and subsequently obtain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This refers to one of the "nature of falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*) who, while detached from the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the three realms,
simultaneously attains both non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

This refers to one of the "nature of not falling away" (*aparihāṇadharman*) who, when entering meditative absorption, becomes detached from the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation of the three realms.
If one is of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) and has abandoned the first eight grades of defilement of the desire realm,
then at the time when the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) corresponding to those grades manifests,
the five consciousnesses— eye-consciousness and the others— are defiled by those respective grades of affliction.
Regarding the associated dharmas and so forth,

one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) with respect to present objects, as well as their analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), at the time of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the ninth grade of defilement of the desire realm.
The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, along with their associated mental factors— whether they are defiled, wholesome, or neutral—
attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) with respect to their present objects of perception.
When the eight grades of defilement prior to the first dhyāna are being abandoned,
as each respective path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) manifests,
the eye-consciousness and the other three consciousnesses, along with their associated dharmas, become defiled by those respective grades of defilement.
Regarding the present object of focus,

one attains both non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and its analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) at the time of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the ninth grade of defilement of the first dhyāna.
The three consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, along with their associated mental factors— whether defiled, wholesome, or neutral—
attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) with respect to present objects of perception.
There are dharmas that are at times not acquired with respect to both types of cessation;
this refers to cases other than those previously mentioned.
Thus has been explained the non-analytical cessation of the acquisition of afflictions.
It should be said that the noble path attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
One who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārī*) attains non-analytical cessation regarding the path of one who follows by dharma (*dharmānusārī*).

One who follows by dharma attains non-analytical cessation regarding the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) at the time when one who follows by faith becomes one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).
If one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) attains the fruit of arhatship by relying definitively on the path of liberation through faith,
they attain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding the path of those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Conversely, one who has attained vision attains non-analytical cessation regarding the path of liberation through faith at the time [of attaining that fruit].
If one who is "liberated by occasion" (samaya-vimukta) attains finality by relying definitively on the path of liberation-by-occasion,
they attain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding the path of non-occasional liberation (asamaya-vimukta).
Conversely, one who is "non-occasionally liberated" attains non-analytical cessation regarding the path of liberation-by-occasion.
When one of the śrāvaka lineage attains certainty in the śrāvaka path,
non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is attained with respect to the paths of the Buddha and the pratyekabuddha.
When one of the pratyekabuddha lineage attains certainty in the pratyekabuddha path, [non-analytical cessation is attained with respect to the paths of the Buddha and the śrāvaka].
The lineage of the Buddha attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the path of the Buddha’s śrāvakas;
when the lineage of the Buddha becomes fixed upon the path of the Buddha,
it attains non-analytical cessation regarding the paths of the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas.

Regarding the fruit of arhatship, there are six types of dispositions (*gotra*). If one who possesses the disposition of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) reaches the ultimate state by means of the path of falling away, they attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) with respect to the five higher paths.
If one of the *cintāmayī-gotra* (lineage of those who attain through reflection) reaches the ultimate by means of the path of reflection,
they obtain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the four higher paths and the one lower path.
This continues up to the *prativedhanā-dharman-gotra* (lineage of those capable of penetration), which, if it reaches the ultimate by means of the path of penetration...
One attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) with respect to the one higher path and the four lower paths;
one of immovable lineage (*akopya-gotra*) attains non-analytical cessation with respect to the five lower paths.
Question: Is it when one is progressing toward excellence that one attains non-analytical cessation?
Why is this cessation not the fruit of the path?
The answer is: because the path is cultivated not for the sake of this cessation.
That is to say, one diligently cultivates the path for the sake of nirvāṇa and for the sake of detachment from defilements.
Because one cultivates the path, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) with respect to the evil destinies and so forth.
If one were to cultivate the path for the sake of this cessation,
one would not attain this cessation with respect to the evil destinies and so forth.
One cannot attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the miserable destinies without having a profound sense of weary revulsion toward birth and death;
therefore, non-analytical cessation is not called a fruit of the Path.
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*: [text follows].
What are resultant phenomena?
They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
What are non-resultant phenomena?
This refers to space and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: Of which mind is the acquisition (*prāpti*) of analytical cessation the fruit?
Some offer this explanation:
This acquisition of cessation (*nirodha-prāpti*) is the fruit of the mind that projects the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Other masters say that this acquisition of cessation is the fruit of the mind at rebirth (*pratisandhi-citta*).
The commentary states:
One should speak thus:
whichever state of mind one abides in, non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is attained accordingly.
It is said that this attainment is the fruit of that mind.
Question: With respect to which phenomena is non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) attained?
Answer: It is attained with respect to phenomena associated with the three realms and those not so associated.
Those born in the desire realm attain [the acquisition] of four dharmas;
it should be understood that the same applies to those born in the form and formless realms.
The acquisition of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is bound to the specific level (bhūmi) in which it arises.
It is comprised solely within the category of non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) nature;
it is exclusively a result of outflow (niṣyanda),
because this acquisition arises by the power of its basis.
Question: In which phenomena does the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) gradually increase?

Answer: If one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the acquisition of non-analytical cessation with respect to the fivefold body of sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*) bound to the desire realm gradually increases.
There are also instances where mental consciousness definitely takes the present as its object;
in such cases, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) regarding these phenomena also gradually increases.
However, because it is difficult to discern, it is not specifically indicated.

Regarding the three groups of consciousness associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as well as the dharmas such as the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
and within the dharmas of the spheres of totality belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) gradually increases.

If one is born in the form realm, the acquisition of the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the five bodies of sensory consciousness associated with the desire realm gradually increases;
likewise for the three bodies of sensory consciousness associated with the form realm.
Furthermore, regarding the dharmas such as the immeasurables, the liberations, the bases of mastery,
and the bases of totality, the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) gradually increases within the dharmas of the bases of totality of the formless realm.
For one born in the formless realm, [there is non-apprehension] regarding the five groups of sensory consciousnesses associated with the desire realm,
the three groups of sensory consciousnesses associated with the form realm,
and the dharmas such as the immeasurables, the liberations, the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality.
Within the dharmas of the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) of the formless realm, the acquisition of analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) gradually increases.
Question: When a noble one (*ārya*) is born in the form realm, which dharmas of the desire and form realms do they attain through analytical cessation?
Answer: If one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the first dhyāna,
with the exception of the category of transformation-minds arising in a higher stage based on the desire realm and the dharmas produced thereby,
[one possesses] all other dharmas of the desire realm.
Furthermore, all dharmas of the form realm that arise based on the desire realm attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the second dhyāna, [non-analytical cessation is attained] with the exception of the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
Based on a higher stage, there arise the classes of transformational minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) that are the fruits of the three higher dhyānas and the phenomena produced by them;
furthermore, based on a higher stage, there arise the four groups of consciousness (*vijñāna-kāya*) and so forth belonging to the first dhyāna.
With respect to other phenomena of the desire realm and the first dhyāna,
as well as the phenomena of the higher stages of the form realm that arise based on the desire realm and the first dhyāna,
one attains their non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one dies in the first dhyāna and is reborn in the second dhyāna, excluding those belonging to the first dhyāna,
one gives rise to the classes of transformation-minds (nirmāṇa-citta) that are fruits of the three higher dhyānas and the phenomena produced by them, based upon the higher stages.
Furthermore, the four bodies of consciousness and so forth arise in the first dhyāna based on a higher stage;
these, along with other phenomena of the first dhyāna and phenomena of higher or lower stages that arise based on the first dhyāna, [are all included].
All attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the third dhyāna,
[non-analytical cessation is attained] with the exception of the desire realm and the first two dhyānas.
Based on a higher stage, there arise the category of transformation minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) that are the fruits of the two higher dhyānas and the phenomena produced by them;
furthermore, based on a higher stage, there arise the four groups of consciousness (*vijñāna-kāya*) and so forth belonging to the first dhyāna.
Regarding other phenomena of the desire realm and the first two dhyānas,
as well as the phenomena of the upper levels of the form realm that arise based on the desire realm and the first two dhyānas,
all attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one passes away from the first dhyāna and is reborn in the third dhyāna,
with the exception of the classes of transformation minds and the phenomena produced by them that arise in the higher stages based on the first and second dhyānas, [one possesses all others].
Furthermore, the four bodies of consciousness and so forth arise in the first dhyāna based on a higher stage;
as do other dharmas of the first and second dhyānas,
as well as dharmas of lower and higher stages arising based on the first and second dhyānas.
All [of these] attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one passes away from the second dhyāna and is reborn in the third dhyāna,
with the exception of the category of transformation-minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) belonging to the two higher dhyānas that arise based on the second dhyāna, as well as the phenomena produced by them.
Regarding the dharmas of the other second dhyāna and the dharmas arising from the second dhyāna that belong to higher or lower stages,
one attains their non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) when passing away from the desire realm and being reborn in the fourth dhyāna.
Excluding the first three dhyānas of the desire realm,
there arise, based on the fourth dhyāna, the category of transformation-minds (nirmāṇa-citta) that are the fruit of the fourth dhyāna and the phenomena produced by them;
as well as the four groups of consciousness (vijñānakāya), etc., which arise based on the first dhyāna while relying on the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding other phenomena of the desire realm and the first three dhyānas,
as well as phenomena of the fourth dhyāna that arise based on the desire realm and the first three dhyānas,
all of them attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one dies in the first dhyāna and is reborn in the fourth dhyāna,
with the exception of the first three dhyānas,
one gives rise to the category of transformation-minds (nirmāṇa-citta) that are the fruit of the fourth dhyāna, as well as the phenomena produced by them, based upon the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, the four bodies of consciousness and so forth belonging to the first dhyāna arise based on the fourth dhyāna;
as do other dharmas of the first three dhyānas,
as well as dharmas of higher and lower stages that arise based on the first three dhyānas.
All [of these] attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).

If one dies in the second dhyāna and is reborn in the fourth dhyāna, with the exception of the category of the transformation mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the fourth dhyāna and its produced phenomena that arise based on the fourth dhyāna—specifically those belonging to the second and third dhyānas—one attains non-analytical cessation.
Regarding the dharmas of the second and third dhyānas, as well as the dharmas of the higher and lower stages arising in dependence upon the second and third dhyānas,
one attains their non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is the case when one passes away from the third dhyāna and is reborn in the fourth dhyāna.
Excluding the third dhyāna,
based on the fourth dhyāna, one produces the category of transformation-minds that are the fruit of the fourth dhyāna, as well as the phenomena produced by them;
[this applies] to all other phenomena of the third dhyāna.
Furthermore, all dharmas of the higher and lower stages that arise based on the third dhyāna attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: When a noble one (*ārya*) is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), [what occurs]?
Regarding which phenomena in the desire, form, and formless realms attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
the answer is: when one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*),
there is the non-analytical cessation of phenomena belonging to the desire and form realms, as well as those formless-realm phenomena that arise based upon the desire and form realms.
All attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one passes away from the first dhyāna and is reborn in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*),
[one attains non-analytical cessation] regarding the dharmas of the four dhyānas and the dharmas belonging to the higher and lower realms that arise in dependence upon the four dhyānas.
All attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one passes away from the second dhyāna and is reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Space,
[one attains it] regarding the dharmas of the subsequent three dhyānas.
Furthermore, one attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding all dharmas of higher and lower stages that arise based on the three higher dhyānas.
If one passes away from the third dhyāna and is reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāśānantyāyatana), [one attains non-analytical cessation regarding those dharmas].
Regarding the dharmas of the latter two dhyānas,
as well as the dharmas of the higher and lower stages that arise based on the latter two dhyānas,
all obtain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one passes away from the fourth dhyāna and is reborn in the sphere of infinite space,
[one possesses] the dharmas of the fourth dhyāna,
as well as the dharmas belonging to the higher and lower stages that arise based upon the fourth dhyāna.
They all attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Whether one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn as far as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
regarding the dharmas of the lower three formless realms within the desire and form realms:
Furthermore, those who give rise to the dharmas of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) based on the desire realm, the form realm, or the lower three formless realms,
all attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This applies whether one passes away from the first dhyāna or is born as far as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Regarding the dharmas of the three lower formless realms within the form realm,
as well as the dharmas of higher and lower stages that arise based on those same three lower formless realms,
all obtain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
...up to the point where, having passed away from the sphere of nothingness, one is reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
regarding the phenomena of the sphere of nothingness,
as well as the phenomena of the Peak of Existence that arise based upon the sphere of nothingness.
All attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: Once a noble one (*ārya*) has been born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), does he attain the non-analytical cessation of the dharmas belonging to the desire and form realms?
Answer: He does not.
Because it has already been obtained previously.
Question: Does a noble one who has been born in a higher stage of the formless realm obtain the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the dharmas belonging to the lower stages?
Answer: No, they do not.
Because it has already been attained previously.

Question: Is there more non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) attained by one who attains parinirvāṇa earlier, or is there more non-analytical cessation attained by one who attains parinirvāṇa later?
Answer: Those who attain parinirvāṇa earlier obtain a greater number of analytical cessations (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), while those who attain parinirvāṇa later obtain a smaller number.
For example, those who attained parinirvāṇa during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha obtained a greater number of analytical cessations.
Those who attain parinirvāṇa during the time of the Buddha Śāntamati obtain a small amount of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
those who attain parinirvāṇa during the time of the Buddha Śāntamati obtain a great amount of non-analytical cessation;
those who attain parinirvāṇa during the time of the Buddha Maitreya obtain a small amount of non-analytical cessation.
Question: Among which Arhats, at the moment they abide in their final mind,
is the attainment of the greatest number of non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—
those of the desire realm?
Is it the form realm?
Or the formless realm?
Answer: The formless realm.
When an Arhat abides in their final moment of consciousness,
they possess the greatest number of non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
because all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) no longer manifest.
At that time, although there was nothing previously unobtained that is now for the first time obtained as a non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*),
there are immeasurable instances of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation that are currently present; thus, it is said that one "possesses many."
Others formulate a question and answer regarding this, saying:
"Is it possible that there are aggregates, elements, and bases that do not continue in succession and are eternally extinguished,
yet for which one does not obtain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?"
Answer: Yes.
This refers to when an Arhat in the formless realm dwells in their final moment of mind;
although there are immeasurable aggregates, elements, and bases, they cease forever without further continuity.
Yet, in that case, one ultimately does not attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The critique states:
One should not speak in such a manner.

Why is this? Because there is no aggregate, element, or sense-field that does not continue in succession and yet undergoes permanent cessation such that it does not attain non-analytical cessation therein.
Question: At the moment an Arhat in the formless realm dwells in his final thought-moment...

Regarding the aggregates, elements, and bases that have been eternally extinguished without further continuity, is it not the case that one does not attain their non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)? Answer:
Although it is not attained at this time, it is said to be "accomplished" (*samanvāgata*).
Because it has already been obtained previously;
that is to say, when an Arhat of the formless realm is certain to enter parinirvāṇa,
with the exception of the present moment arising in the future life.
One attains the cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding the remaining aggregates, elements, and bases.
As the Sūtra says:
"There are two realms of nirvāṇa."
That is to say, there is the realm of nirvana with remainder and the realm of nirvana without remainder,
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the sake of extensively analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
That is to say, the sūtra states:
There are two realms of nirvana:
first, the realm of nirvana with a remainder of substrate;
second, the realm of nirvana without a remainder of substrate.
Although the sūtra makes this statement, it does not explain in detail:
what is the nirvāṇa-element with remainder (sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu),
and what is the nirvāṇa-element without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu)?
That is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies;
that which was not analyzed therein shall now all be analyzed.
Furthermore, as previously stated:
What is analytical cessation?
It refers to those cessations that are dissociation;
this dissociation is nirvāṇa.
However, there are two kinds of nirvāṇa:
first, that with a remainder of support;
second, that without a remainder of support.
Now, I wish to distinguish between these two differences.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of refuting other schools and revealing the correct doctrine;
that is to say, there are some who maintain the following view:
The nirvāṇa-realm with remainder has intrinsic nature,
whereas the nirvāṇa-realm without remainder lacks intrinsic nature;
in order to refute that attachment, it is revealed that both types of nirvāṇa-realm possess intrinsic nature.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that the nirvāṇa-realm with remainder is contaminated (sāsrava),
while the nirvāṇa-realm without remainder is uncontaminated (anāsrava).
To refute that attachment, it is shown that both types of nirvāṇa-realm are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Alternatively, there may be those who hold that the nirvāṇa-realm with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The nirvāṇa-realm without remainder is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
To refute that attachment, it is shown that both types of nirvāṇa-realms are unconditioned.
Alternatively, there are those who hold the following attachment:
The nirvāṇa-realm with remainder is wholesome,
while the nirvāṇa-realm without remainder is indeterminate.
To refute that attachment, it is shown that both types of nirvāṇa-realm are of a wholesome nature.
Alternatively, there are those who hold the view that the nirvāṇa-realm with remainder is the path but not the fruit of the path,
while the nirvāṇa-realm without remainder is the fruit of the path but not the path itself.
This is to refute that attachment and demonstrate that both types of *nirvāṇadhātu* are fruits of the path.
Alternatively, there may be those who hold that only the *nirvāṇadhātu with a remainder of support* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*) is the fruit of the path.
The nirvāṇa-realm without remainder is not the fruit of the path;
in order to refute that attachment, it is shown that both types of nirvāṇa-realms are fruits of the path.
Alternatively, there are those who hold that the nirvāṇa-realm with remainder is subsumed under the [Noble] Truths.
The realm of nirvana without remainder is not included among the truths;
in order to refute that attachment, it is shown that both types of nirvana realms are included among the truths.
Alternatively, there are those who hold the following attachment:
The nirvāṇa-realm with remainder belongs to those beyond training (aśaikṣa),
while the nirvāṇa-realm without remainder is neither in training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
To refute that attachment, it is shown that both types of nirvāṇa-realm are neither in training nor beyond training.
For these various reasons thus explained, this treatise is composed.
What is the nirvāṇa-element with remainder?
Answer: It is when an arhat’s outflows are forever exhausted.
Life-span still persists;
the continuity of the primary elements and derived matter has not been severed;
and the continuity of body and mind proceeds in dependence upon the five sense faculties.
Because there remains a substratum of clinging (*sopadhiśeṣa*),
the permanent exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the attainment of its realization is called the realm of nirvana with a substratum remaining (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
Within this, "life-span" (*āyus*) refers to—
It refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Question: Why is the homogeneous character of a group (*nikāyasabhāga*) not mentioned?
Answer: Because it was the intention of the author of this treatise to proceed in this manner.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, when something that ought to be stated is not stated,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, because both the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) are fruits of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*),
and because the life-faculty is exclusively a maturation (*vipāka*),
it is mentioned specifically here.
Based on these, other forms, mind, and so forth continue to evolve;
among them, the primary elements (mahābhūta) are mentioned first because they serve as the basis.
Derived matter arises depending on these primary elements;
the mind and mental factors arise depending on derived matter,
because the mind is the sovereign.

In this context, the specific mention of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) generally indicates the material body; the mention of the continuity of mind and body based on the five sense faculties indicates the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*);
it also includes the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth.
Because they are difficult to comprehend and because they pertain to the aforementioned phenomena,
they are not explained separately.
In this way, when the continuity of these phenomena has not been severed, the various fetters (saṃyojana) attained therein are forever exhausted.
This is called the realm of nirvana with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
Some say that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) constitute the body and the five sense faculties.
This continuity of the faculties and the mind is the awareness of this body;

as long as the continuity of the awareness of the faculties has not been severed, yet all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are forever extinguished, it is called the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
The state in which the faculty of the body has been realized but not yet severed is called nirvana with remainder.
Regarding the phrase "because there is a remainder," there are two kinds of remainders.
First, the basis of afflictions;
second, the basis of the birth-body.
Although this arhat lacks the basis of afflictions, he still possesses the basis of the birth-body.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of bases:
first, the defiled basis;
second, the non-defiled basis.
Although this Arhat lacks a defiled basis, because he possesses a non-defiled basis,
the permanent exhaustion of all fetters attained therein is called the realm of nirvana with remainder.
One attains direct realization.
Although the words differ, they all reveal the same meaning.
What is the realm of nirvana without remainder?
The answer is: It refers to the Arhat whose outflows are forever exhausted;
whose lifespan has already ceased and the continuity of the great elements and derived matter has been severed;
and in whom the body and mind no longer function in dependence upon the five sense faculties.
Because there is no remaining support (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
The eternal exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) is called the realm of nirvāṇa without remaining support (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
In this context, the phrase "the life-span has already ceased" indicates that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character of the group (*nikāyasabhāga*) have already ceased.
Since both are the results of projecting karma,
take the life-faculty as an illustration;
one should know that this also refers to the continuity of the primary elements and derived matter of the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga).
"Those who have already severed" generally indicates that the continuity of the material body has been severed.
"The body and mind no longer function based on the five sense faculties" indicates that the mind and mental factors no longer continue in succession.
The meanings of "arising" and so forth are not explained here as they were previously.
Some say that "the primary elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādāyarūpa)" refers to the body.
The five faculties and the body manifest the sense organs;
the continuity of mind manifests cognition.
Thus, there are the material body, the mind, and the mental factors.
Alternatively, when the continuity of the perception of the body-faculty has been severed and all fetters are eternally exhausted, this is called the realm of nirvana without remainder;
that is to say, when an arhat is about to enter parinirvāṇa.
Wind arises within the body, causing it to become unbalanced.
Because of this imbalance, the internal fire becomes weak.
Because the fire is weak, what has been eaten is not digested.
Because food is not digested, the desire for food does not arise.
Because there is no desire for food, one no longer eats or drinks.
Because one does not eat or drink, the primary elements (mahābhūta) diminish.

Because there is great diminution, the derived material faculties also undergo diminution accordingly; because the faculties are diminished, the mind and mental factors have no basis and no longer continue in succession.
Because the mind and mental factors do not continue in succession, [the continuum is severed].
The life-faculty and so forth are severed;
because the life-force and others are severed, one is said to enter nirvana.
"Because there is no remaining support" means that the two kinds of supports are absent.
First, there is no basis for affliction;
second, there is no basis for the body of birth. Furthermore, first, there is no basis for defilement;
second, there is no basis for non-defilement. Because there is no remainder of support, all fetters are eternally exhausted.
This is called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Question: Why are terms such as "attaining," "obtaining," or "realizing" not mentioned here?
Answer: Terms such as "attaining" and so forth are spoken in reference to present attainment.
It is not mentioned here because it has already been attained and abandoned in the present.
Furthermore, the designation of "attainment," "acquisition," or "realization" is established in dependence upon a *pudgala*;
however, herein there is no *pudgala*, there is only the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, it is not so stated.
Is there perhaps an Arhat who does not abide in either the realm of nirvana with remainder or the realm of nirvana without remainder?
Answer: Although it does not exist in principle, it does exist in accordance with what is taught herein.
That is to say, it is taught here that that which possesses three factors is called the realm of nirvana with remainder.
The state in which these three things are all absent is called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
An Arhat born in the formless realm does not abide in the realm of nirvana with remainder because they lack a physical body.
Because the mind continues to function, he does not abide in the realm of nirvana without remainder;
because the mind no longer functions once an Arhat born in the realm of form has entered the meditative attainment of cessation,
he does not abide in the realm of nirvana with remainder.
Because he possesses a physical body, he does not abide in the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*). Furthermore,
because an Arhat born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) lacks certain faculties,
he does not abide in the realm of nirvana with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*), as he is incomplete in his five faculties.
Because he possesses a physical body, he does not abide in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Some say that this passage should be stated as follows:
What is the realm of nirvāṇa with a remainder of substrate?
Answer: It is when an arhat’s lifespan still remains, yet all fetters are forever exhausted, and he has attained and realized [this state].
What is the realm of nirvāṇa without a remainder of substrate?
Answer: It refers to an Arhat whose lifespan has already ceased and whose fetters are eternally exhausted.
If one were to speak in this way, it would imply that there are Arhats born within the three realms who possess a physical body.
Whether there is no form-body,
or whether there is the turning of the mind,
or the non-turning of the mind.
Whether they possess the five faculties or do not possess the five faculties,
as long as they have life, they are all said to abide in the realm of nirvana with remainder.
Once their life-span has ceased, they are all said to abide in the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
This is how it should be stated;
however, the master of this treatise spoke thus because he wished to benefit his disciples by making the meaning easy to understand.
Question: Regarding the disconnections (visamyoga) attained by ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and those in training (śaikṣa), to which of the two types of nirvāṇa-realm (nirvāṇadhātu) do they belong?
Answer: They are not subsumed under either of the two types of nirvāṇa-realm.
That is to say, the dissociation (visamyoga) attained by ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) should only be termed abandonment (prahāṇa),
detachment (viveka), cessation (nirodha), and truth (satya);
it is not termed thorough knowledge (parijñā).
It is not called the fruit of śrāmaṇya;
it is not called the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder;
it is not called the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
If the dissociation attained by those in training is termed abandonment, detachment, cessation, and truth,
it is termed thorough knowledge when it occurs at a specific stage.
There are states that are not designated as "omniscience" (sarvajñatā).
There are states designated as "fruits of the śramaṇa" (śrāmaṇyaphala),
and there are states not designated as "fruits of the śramaṇa."
It is not called the realm of nirvana with remainder,
nor is it called the realm of nirvana without remainder,
[referring to] the dissociation from bondage attained by those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa).
It is called abandonment, detachment, cessation, truth, and full comprehension;
it is called the fruit of śrāmaṇya.
At times, it is called the realm of nirvāṇa with a remainder of support.
At times it is called the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
In the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* with the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, Volume Thirty-two, from the seventh line of the seventh page of the Song edition onwards, there are three passages of text.
The textual passage is interrupted and the meaning is severed.
First, at the beginning of the first three lines of the seventh panel, after the words "Other teachers say" (*anye āhuḥ*), it abruptly states: "Answering this, it is not determinate," and so forth.

Second, at the fourteenth or fifteenth line of the eighth panel, immediately after the words "either patience or precepts" (*kṣāntir vā śīlaṃ vā*) and continuing down to "not" (*na*), it abruptly states: "Regarding past and future dharmas, one attains non-analytical cessation" (*atītānāgateṣu dharmeṣv apratisaṃkhyānirodhaṃ prāpnoti*), and so forth.

Third, regarding the first four lines of the tenth scroll, immediately below the phrase "Is it not obtained exclusively? (不共得耶), it states: "Patience [leads to] the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of all [births] in the evil destinies, and so forth.
Now, upon examining the Guo and Dan editions, it appears that the Song edition has erroneously transposed the phrase "Is it not obtained exclusively? [to this location].

Below the phrase "In response to this, it is not determined... and continuing through "...or patience, or morality, even down to the lower grades," totaling thirty-six lines of text, [the scribe] wrote them forward; however, below the phrase "Other masters say, 'But... and specifically below the phrase "But... regarding past and future dharmas, one attains non-analytical cessation... or is it exclusively attained? totaling thirty-five lines of text, [the scribe] wrote them backward, placing them below the phrase "...or morality, even down to the lower grades."

Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

However, it has not yet been stated whether nirvāṇa is training (*śaikṣa*), beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or neither-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
This is what is now intended to be explained.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of others and manifesting the correct meaning.
That is to say, there are those who maintain that *nirvāṇa* is both "in training" (*śaikṣa*), "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), and "neither in training nor beyond training," such as the Vātsīputrīyas.
To refute their position and to demonstrate that *nirvāṇa* is exclusively "neither in training nor beyond training," this treatise was composed.
Should nirvāṇa be described as belonging to the stage of training (śaikṣa), the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa), or neither training nor beyond training?
Answer: Nirvāṇa should be described as neither training nor beyond training, because the meanings of "training" and "beyond training" are not applicable to it.
It is called "training" (*śaikṣa*) because one clearly progresses toward a distinct fruit;
when this progress is fulfilled and there is no further distinct fruit toward which to progress,
it is of the same category as training but is not that [training] itself, and is therefore called "beyond-training" (*aśaikṣa*).
Nirvāṇa is called "neither-learner-nor-non-learner" because it possesses neither of these two meanings.
Some maintain that nirvāṇa is of three types:

For example, the Vātsīputrīyas maintain this:
"The intrinsic nature of nirvāṇa has three characteristics."
There are three: the learner (śaikṣa), the one beyond learning (aśaikṣa), and neither-learner-nor-one-beyond-learning.
What is the learner?
It refers to one who has attained the abandonment of all fetters (saṃyojana) through the attainment of a learner, having reached and realized it.
What is that which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to the attainment of the severance of all fetters (*saṃyojana*), its acquisition, and its realization through contact.

It is said that there is a fault in asserting that one attains the severance of the various fetters through contaminated acquisitions (*sāsrava-prāpti*) and realizes them through contact;

A single dharma ought not to possess three distinct essential natures (*svabhāva*), as they would be identical to its own essence.

That is to say, in the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), one possesses three [kinds of knowledge] and attains one;
upon reaching the stage of training (śaikṣa), one possesses three and attains two;
and upon reaching the stage of no-more-training (aśaikṣa), one likewise possesses all three kinds.
If one possesses all three, one should possess the acquisitions of those in training (*śaikṣa*);
if one possesses only two, one should not be complete in the acquisition of nirvāṇa.
If, in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), one attains all three types [of fruits] by means of the attainment of no-more-learning,
then those in the stages of learning (śaikṣa) and so forth should likewise be so;
in that case, one should not say that the abandonment of the fetters attained through learning is called "learning" (śaikṣa).
The attainment of the severance of all fetters by one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is called "beyond training.
The attainment of the severance of all fetters by one with outflows (sāsrava) is called "neither-training-nor-beyond-training.
If it is argued that although each stage possesses all three [types of attainment],...
Because they are attained individually, each is designated as "one.
In that case, nirvāṇa would undergo transformation according to its attainment,
and it would consequently incur the fault of impermanence, as previously explained.
Therefore, this statement is also illogical. If it were so,
