it would result in a threefold division [of phenomena], and because phenomena would not be determinate, there would be confusion.
This means that one should not posit the definitive nature and characteristics of all phenomena.
[The author] refutes the two preceding views in their entirety by means of correct reasoning;
namely, the views of the Vibhajyavādins.
One school asserts that nirvāṇa is indeterminate according to its stages;
another school asserts that the three natures of nirvāṇa are fixed. Thus, the essence of nirvāṇa would possess both permanence and impermanence, resulting in a bifurcation.
Furthermore,
that which was stated subsequently also possesses the sense of transformation according to its capacity for attainment.
Because their transformations are not identical, they are called "two.
If they were not transformed according to what is attained,
how could it be said that there are three types of nirvana?
If a single nirvāṇa were subject to transformation upon its attainment,
then all phenomena would necessarily be indeterminate;
if they were not determinate, there would be confusion and disorder.
If there were such confusion, one could not establish the definitive characteristics of natures such as permanence or impermanence;
nor would the Buddha have taught that *nirvāṇa* possesses the nature of being either with-training (*śaikṣa*) or beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*).
This collectively cites the sacred teachings to refute the two preceding positions;
for it is never stated in the sūtras that nirvāṇa is either with-training (śaikṣa) or beyond-training (aśaikṣa).
What he has stated is certainly unreasonable;
for although there is no place where it is said that *nirvāṇa* is exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
it is nonetheless inconsistent with the meaning of "learner" (*śaikṣa*) and "non-learner" (*aśaikṣa*).
It is determined that this is of a nature that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
for nirvāṇa is eternally neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
and all dharmas are definitively free from confusion.
Nirvana is eternally abiding in its own nature and never relinquishes its own nature;
it is permanently constant and without change.
Therefore, nirvana should be described as neither a learner nor one beyond learning.
Having already explained that other schools possess faults,
he now demonstrates that his own school is free from all such faults,
because nirvāṇa is of only one kind.
The nature and characteristics of all phenomena are definitively established without confusion;
nirvana is eternally abiding and without change—
this principle is well-established.
The meaning of "attainment" (*prāpti*) herein shall be analyzed in detail later in the section on attainment within the *Samāpatti-skandha*.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"He has accomplished the aggregate of the precepts of one beyond training, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of providing a detailed analysis of the meaning of the sūtra.
As the sūtra says:
"He accomplishes the aggregate of precepts of one beyond training."
...and so on, as explained at length.
Although the sūtra makes this statement, it does not provide a detailed analysis:
what is the aggregate of the morality of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-śīlaskandha*), up to the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñānadarśanaskandha*)?
That is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies;
that which was not analyzed therein shall now be analyzed in its entirety.
Furthermore, although the fruit of the path was previously mentioned, the path itself has not yet been explained;
it is now intended to be explained.
Moreover, the unconditioned fruit of arhatship was previously discussed.
The conditioned fruit of arhatship has not yet been explained;
it is now intended to be explained.
Furthermore, nirvāṇa was previously discussed.
The awakening (bodhi) has not yet been explained; it is now intended to be explained, and for this reason this treatise is composed.
Question: Is there also the accomplishment of the aggregates of training (śaikṣaskandha), or the aggregates that are neither of training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣaskandha)?
Why does the sūtra not state this?
One should know that when something ought to be stated but is not,
the meaning therein is incomplete.
Furthermore, this is a concise teaching by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, for his disciples.
Moreover, this is taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, according to what is preeminent;
that is to say, among all dharmas, the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) are preeminent.
Among all sentient beings, those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are supreme;
therefore, they are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, these are the World-Honored Buddha’s own eldest sons, whom he praises.
Therefore, this statement was made:
that the Buddha at times praises the eldest son,
and at other times praises the middle son.
At times he praises the younger son,
and at times he praises the elder son,
as it is said in a gāthā:
The Arhat is most blissful, for he has forever severed craving and forever severed all conceits;
having torn asunder the net of ignorance,
he is at times praised as the "Son of the Middle."
Just as the Buddha praised the seven destinations of the virtuous person (*saptasatpuruṣagati*),
or at times praised the "young son," or as the *Anupada-sūtra* (the Pool Simile Sūtra) extolled the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).
Now, because he praises the eldest son,
he speaks only of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore:
If there is the aggregate of ethical discipline that is not destroyed by unwholesome discipline,
the aggregate of concentration that is not disturbed by distraction,
and the aggregate of wisdom that is not obscured by faulty wisdom.
It is explained here that the aggregate of liberation is not disturbed by afflictions,
and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation is not obscured by ignorance.
Regarding the aggregates that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
there is no such meaning [in this context], and therefore they are not mentioned. What,
then, is the aggregate of precepts of one beyond training?
Answer: It refers to the bodily restraint, the vocal restraint, and the purity of livelihood of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Among the factors of the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣāṅga*), right action is precisely the bodily restraint herein;
right speech is precisely the vocal restraint herein;
and right livelihood is precisely the purity of livelihood herein.
The Sūtra states:
"These three are collectively termed the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha).
Question: Apart from bodily and vocal actions, there is no separate right livelihood (samyagājīva).
How are three types established herein?
Answer: They are established by way of the opposition between the two dharmas of black and white.
That is to say, among the first seven unwholesome paths of action:
Bodily action arising from hatred and delusion is called wrong action;
verbal action arising from hatred and delusion is called wrong speech;
and bodily and verbal action arising from greed is called wrong livelihood.
Because of wrong livelihood;
being far removed from these three is called right action, right speech, and right livelihood. Some say:
If one performs unwholesome bodily and vocal actions for the sake of livelihood or for the purpose of entertainment, it is called wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
If one performs unwholesome bodily and vocal actions for any other purpose, it is called wrong action (*mithyākarmānta*) and wrong speech (*mithyāvāc*).
To remain far removed from these three is called "right livelihood" and so forth.
Some say: if one performs medical or incantational acts for the sake of making a living, [it is not right livelihood].
The arising of unwholesome bodily and vocal karma is called wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
If one gives rise to unwholesome bodily and vocal karma for other purposes, it is termed wrong action (*mithyākarmānta*) and wrong speech (*mithyāvāc*).
To distance oneself from these three is called right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), and so forth.
Some say that if unwholesome bodily and vocal actions arise due to four kinds of craving,
they are termed wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
If unwholesome bodily or vocal karma arises due to other matters, it is called wrong action (*mithyākarmānta*) and wrong speech (*mithyāvāk*).
To be free from these three is called right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), and so forth. Some say:
If unwholesome bodily or vocal karma arises by means of the five [factors] such as guile and deceit, it is called wrong livelihood;
if it arises by means of other matters, it is not.
The arising of unwholesome bodily and vocal karma is called wrong action and wrong speech;
the avoidance of these three is called right livelihood and so forth. Some say:
Bodily and vocal actions that constitute prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) are called wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*);
bodily and vocal actions that constitute natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) are called wrong action (*mithyākarmānta*) and wrong speech (*mithyāvāc*).
To distance oneself from these three is called right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), and so forth.
Some say that unwholesome bodily and vocal karma consisting of the preliminary (prayoga) and subsequent (pṛṣṭha) stages is called wrong livelihood (mithyājīva);
unwholesome bodily and vocal karma consisting of the fundamental paths of action (mūlakarmapatha) is called wrong action (mithyākarmānta) and wrong speech (mithyāvāc).
Being far removed from these three is called "right livelihood" and so forth.
Question: Why is this aggregate called *śīla*?
Answer: *Śīla* has the meaning of "coolness."
Because it is far removed from the distress and affliction of breaking the precepts.
Furthermore, *śīla* (ethical discipline) has the meaning of training and study.
Because this [morality] stands at the beginning among the three trainings,
as it is said:
"Through the observance of morality, one is without remorse."
...and so on, as explained at length.
The untainted bodily and vocal actions within the continuum of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are called the aggregate of morality (*śīlaskandha*) of one beyond training.
What is the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*) of one beyond training?
Answer: The three samādhis of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), namely emptiness (śūnyatā), wishlessness (apranihita), and signlessness (animitta).
Question: The essence of meditative concentration (samādhi) is but one.
This refers to samādhi among the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
How are its three distinctions established?

The answer is: because it serves as the immediate antidote to three types of hindrances. Specifically, the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) serves as the immediate antidote to the view of a self-entity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
The wishless samādhi is the proximate antidote to the clinging to rules and observances;
the signless samādhi is the proximate antidote to doubt.
Furthermore, this is because their modes of activity (ākāra) differ.
That is to say, the emptiness samādhi is accompanied by three aspects: namely, emptiness and non-self.
The wishless samādhi is accompanied by ten aspects: namely, suffering and impermanence, and the four aspects each of origin and the path.
The signless samādhi is associated with four aspects, which take the four aspects of cessation as their object.
Furthermore, it is due to three reasons:
first, by way of being an antidote.
Second, by way of intention;
third, by way of the object of focus;
and fourth, by way of the antidote, the emptiness samādhi is established.
That is to say, the practice of non-self serves as the antidote to the view of self,
and the practice of emptiness serves as the antidote to the view of "mine," just as the views of self and "mine" have been seen and what has been seen by them.
There are fifteen views of "I" and likewise fifteen views of "mine.
Furthermore, the practice of non-self serves as the antidote to self-love,
while the practice of emptiness serves as the antidote to the love of "mine."
Just as with "I" and "what is mine," so it is with "the conceit of I" and "the conceit of what is mine.
It is on account of this mental inclination that the wishless samādhi is established.
This means that because of their noble intention (*āśaya*),
the noble ones do not desire existence nor the noble path. Why is this so?
Because the noble ones, by virtue of their intention,
do not wish for saṃsāra or the suffering of the aggregates and the world; rather,
they rely upon the noble path through [the understanding of] saṃsāra and the suffering of the aggregates and the world.
Nor does one aspire for the aspects of the path as objects;
although it is not that one does not aspire [to liberation],
it is given the name "wishless" (apraṇihita) because of the underlying intention.
Question: For what purpose does a noble one cultivate the Noble Path?
Answer: For the sake of nirvāṇa;
that is to say, apart from the Noble Path.
Since there is no other dharma capable of attaining nirvāṇa,
the cultivation of this [signless state] is not undertaken out of intrinsic inclination;
rather, the signless samādhi is established by virtue of its object of focus.
This means that within the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya), there are no ten characteristics;
therefore, it is called "signless" (animitta). The five sense objects, male and female, and the three conditioned characteristics are designated as the "ten characteristics."
Furthermore, because within the truth of cessation there are no superior, middling, or inferior grades, nor the characteristics of the aggregates or the world, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).
Because the four aspects of cessation serve as its objective referent (*ālambana*),
it is called "signless."
What is the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
The answer is: the wisdom of right view of one beyond training; this recension is considered superior.
There is another recension which states: the eight knowledges of one beyond training.
This means that the recitation of those four categories is too general,
as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are also included therein.
There is another recitation which says:
The thorough discernment and supreme discernment of phenomena associated with the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
and so forth, up to *vipaśyanā*, as well as the further recited statement: "the wisdom, vision, clarity, awakening,
and clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of one beyond training"— these too are the great summary.
Since the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are also included herein, what is the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training?
Answer: It is the mind associated with the mental attention of one beyond training.
Has been resolved upon,
is being resolved upon,
and will be resolved upon.
This refers to the resolve associated with the right view of an adept regarding exhaustion and non-arising;
because it is comprised within these aggregates, it is not unconditioned liberation.
That is to say, among all phenomena, two factors are termed "liberation."
The first is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*).
The second is resolute confidence (*adhimokṣa*), which is conditioned liberation (*saṃskṛta-vimukti*).
These are designated as "liberation" because they consist in mastery over their respective objects.
It does not refer to dissociation (*visamyoga*).

What is the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)? Answer: It is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Question: Why are these two types of knowledge called the aggregate of liberation, knowledge, and vision?
Answer: Because they alone exist within the body of liberation, and because they are most capable of definitively discerning the matters of liberation.
What is the difference between the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation?
Answer: The knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of its origin belonging to one beyond training constitute the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training.
Because it takes as its object the phenomena that constitute bondage,
the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path in one beyond training (aśaikṣa) constitute the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation in one beyond training.
Because it takes as its object the phenomena that constitute liberation.
Furthermore, the knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation belonging to those beyond training (aśaikṣa) constitutes the aggregate of wisdom of those beyond training.
This takes as its object the liberation from the conditioned and the unconditioned,
because it does not take as its object the untainted knowledge that takes liberation as its object.
The knowledge of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārgajñāna*) is the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣavimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*).
This takes as its object the untainted (*anāsrava*) conditioned liberation,
and also takes as its object the untainted knowledge that cognizes that liberation.
Furthermore, the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path belonging to one beyond training (aśaikṣa) constitutes the aggregate of wisdom (prajñā-skandha) of one beyond training,
because it does not take the disjoined dharmas (visamyoga-dharma) as its object.
The knowledge of cessation belonging to one beyond training constitutes the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha) of one beyond training.
"Because it has as its object the phenomena that are dissociated from fetters.
This is called "distinction";
this refers to the distinction of coarse characteristics in conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
If one speaks of the distinction between the ultimate and the conventional truth,
it should be as previously stated:
namely, that the wisdom of the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is the aggregate of wisdom (prajñā-skandha) of one beyond training.

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) constitute the aggregate of the wisdom of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana-skandha*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore,
that which counteracts false wisdom constitutes the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*) of one beyond training.
The antidote to ignorance is the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, it is that wisdom which is sharp and intense, characterized by persistent application in investigation and inquiry.
This is the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
If wisdom is not intense, not sharp, not penetrating, not seeking, not investigating, and not searching, and if its application has ceased,
this is the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*) of one beyond training.
These five aggregates and elements are not bound to the three realms.
As for the "ground," the aggregate of ethical discipline resides in six grounds:
namely, the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), and the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara).
The remaining four aggregates exist in nine stages, namely, the aforementioned six stages plus the three lower formless realms.
Question: Do these five aggregates possess distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior grades?
Answer: Within a single continuum, there is no such distinction.
It exists in different continuums:
that of the Buddha is superior,
while that of the Pratyekabuddha is middling.
The śrāvaka is of the inferior grade;
furthermore, those with sharp faculties are of the superior grade,
while those with middling faculties are of the middling grade.
Those of dull faculties are of the inferior grade.
Although conditioned merits (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*) are immeasurable,
these five are established as aggregates (*skandha*) because they are the most preeminent.
As the Blessed One has said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is only one ultimate goal; there is no other ultimate goal."
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in the sūtra:
"There is only one ultimate; there is no other ultimate.
Although this was stated, it was not further analyzed.
Whether it be the ultimate perfection of diligent effort or the ultimate accomplishment of a task, these sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Since those [sūtras] have not been explained, I now wish to explain them; for this reason, I have composed this treatise.
Question: There are two types of ultimate attainment (*niṣṭhā*).
How can you say there is only one?
The Venerable Pārśva replied:
Because these two ultimates are each singular, they are spoken of as a single word;
that is to say, there is only one ultimate of exertion,
and no other distinct ultimate of exertion exists.
Furthermore, there is only one thing that constitutes the fulfillment of perfection;
there is no other separate thing that constitutes the fulfillment of perfection,
as the Blessed One has said.
There is only one truth and no second;
because each of those is also of only one kind, it is spoken of as "one word," meaning there is only the single Truth of Suffering.
There is no second Truth of Suffering distinct from it,
and so on, up to: there is only the single Truth of the Path,
and no second Truth of the Path distinct from it.
This is also like that;
therefore, a single word is spoken. Some say this:
To refute the heterodox paths and false liberations of the non-Buddhists, he spoke these single words:
namely, that various non-Buddhists falsely cling to such practices as nakedness, self-starvation, lying on ashes, breath-control, and turning with the sun.
Some consume only water, eat fruits, or eat excrement;
they wear robes of discarded rags and sleep upon wood, pebbles, or stones;
they throw themselves from cliffs, leap into fire, and practice the conduct of cattle and other such asceticisms.
Regarding this as the true path,
the Buddha spoke these words to refute them:
"That is a false path practiced by the ignorant."
The true path is unique and has no second;
it is the ultimate of diligent effort.
Furthermore, various non-Buddhists falsely cling to diverse things—such as bodilessness, boundlessness, the purification of the mind, or worldly stūpas—as being true liberation.
The Buddha spoke thus to refute them:
"That is merely a place of birth, not true liberation;
true liberation is but one."
This refers to the ultimate accomplishment of the task.
Other masters say that there is only one ultimate application of effort capable of severing the cause of birth and death.
There is only one thing that brings about the ultimate ability to abandon the suffering of birth and death;
therefore, it is said that a single word is not devoid of two aspects. Some may say:
Ultimate singularity refers to the ultimate accomplishment of the task;
for the sake of realizing this, one practices the ultimate application of diligence.
Therefore, it is said that the ultimate is solely one and non-dual. Furthermore,
there are those who say that the non-Buddhists each give rise to the notion of ultimacy regarding their own respective tenets.
The Buddha spoke thus to refute them:
"In the poorly taught Dharma, there is no true ultimate;
for what is practiced by the foolish cannot bring about the permanent abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion."
Within the well-expounded Dharma, there is true ultimate liberation;
for when practiced by the wise, it enables one to forever transcend greed, hatred, and delusion.
Alternatively, some say:
It is not that the Buddha intended to reveal the ultimate truth by speaking of "only one," but rather to demonstrate the faults of the non-Buddhists;
for these non-Buddhists engage in mutual disputes and polemics.
Those who give rise to the view of annihilationism cling to annihilation as ultimate and repudiate the view of permanence as false.
Those who give rise to the view of eternalism cling to permanence as ultimate and repudiate the view of annihilation as false.
To reveal that error, the Buddha spoke these words:
"If annihilation were ultimate, the view of permanence would be untenable;
if permanence were ultimate, the view of annihilation would be untenable."
Because it is ultimately one and without a second,
both the extremes of annihilation and permanence that are clung to are not ultimate.
In this context, what dharma is called "ultimate"?
Answer: The World-Honored One sometimes uses the term "ultimate" with respect to the Path, and sometimes uses the term "ultimate" with respect to Cessation.
Because both the supramundane cause and the supramundane fruit are ultimate, he uses the term "ultimate" with respect to the Path.
As the Blessed One has said:
"A certain class of people, clever yet arrogant, cannot know the ultimate;
because they have not realized the path, they die unsubdued."
As for "one class":
this refers to those non-Buddhists who are actually deluded,
yet consider themselves wise.
One who gives rise to conceit is called "one who is arrogant about their cleverness.
"Ultimate" refers to the culmination of diligent effort;
such a person does not know or see this culmination as it truly is.
Names cannot know it.
The Noble Eightfold Path is called the "path," yet they are unable to realize this path.
They die unsubdued;
that is to say, they are born with afflictions and they die with afflictions,
because they have not attained the true path of subduing.
Regarding the expression of "ultimate" in relation to abandonment,
as the Blessed One said:
"One who has reached the ultimate is without fear, doubt, or regret."
Because he has forever uprooted the arrow of existence, he dwells in his final body;
this is the ultimate goal, the unsurpassed path of peace,
the pure track of deathlessness, for all marks have been exhausted.
"Ultimate" means that the task has reached its completion;
one who has already been able to reach that state is called "one who has arrived."
"Being without fear" means having thoroughly mastered the dharma of dependent origination and having well cultivated the gate of liberation that is emptiness.
They do not fear the suffering of the evil realms or of birth and death.
"Being without doubt" means that,

unlike non-Buddhists who abide in improper discipline and false views and thus give rise to various hesitant discourses, doubting what they have realized for themselves, these practitioners are not like that.

One who is without regret is so because they have already abandoned and fully understood the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and because they have already given rise to ultimate knowledge (*niṣṭhājñāna*); thus, they possess no change of mind or remorse.
One who possesses the arrow...
This refers to two kinds of "arrows":
first, the arrow of craving;
second, the arrow of views.

Because one has well cultivated the noble path, attained the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇaparijñā*), relinquished [the defilements], and vomited them out so that they never recur, it is called "permanently uprooted.
The final physical existence is called the "body of the last limit" (*paścimaka-deha*).
Having eternally severed the causes and conditions, they will no longer undergo future birth and death;
therefore, it is said that they abide in their final body.
This is the ultimate consummation.
This means that because the task has reached its ultimate completion and surpasses even the culmination of diligent effort,
it is called the "supremely unsurpassed path of tranquility."
Because the three fires have been extinguished, it is called "knowledge of tranquility.
Because it establishes a station, it is called a "path.
Because it is supreme among paths, it is called "unsurpassed."
Regarding the "trace of the deathless that is pure":
the term "trace" is as explained previously;
it is so called because it is free from all afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
It is called "pure.
It is named "immortal" because it is eternally abiding and unchanging;
and it is said that "all characteristics are exhausted" because within nirvāṇa, the various characteristics of afflictions, karma, and suffering have all ceased.
Furthermore, a sutra states that there was a brahmin named Maudgalyāyana who came to the place where the Buddha was and questioned him, saying:
The Venerable Gautama instructed and exhorted the bhikṣus; having received these instructions,
they [acted accordingly].
"Are they all able to realize the most ultimate realm of parinirvāṇa?
The Blessed One replied, "This is not fixed; some are able to realize it."
A certain class [of beings] is unable [to do so].
Here too, the term "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*) is used in reference to abandonment,
because nirvāṇa is the ultimate state of abandonment.
Furthermore, there is diligence,
there is the perfection of diligence,
and there is the accomplishment of tasks.
There are matters that reach completion.
What is diligence?
What is the culmination of diligence?
What is the accomplishment of the task?
What is the ultimate accomplishment of the task?
Answer: The path of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is one of diligent exertion.
It is not the culmination of diligent effort;
that which is abandoned by it is an accomplished fact,
yet it is not the culmination of the accomplishment of that fact.
The noble path is diligence; it is the culmination of diligence.
That which is abandoned through its attainment is an accomplished fact; it is the culmination of the accomplished fact.
Furthermore:
The path with outflows is the ultimate of diligent effort, but not the ultimate of non-diligent effort;
that which is abandoned through it is the ultimate of the accomplishment of the task,
but not the ultimate of the non-accomplishment of the task.
The untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) is diligence and the perfection of diligence;
that which is abandoned through it is the accomplishment of the task and the perfection of accomplishing the task.
Furthermore, the path of approach (*pratipannaka-mārga*) is diligence.
It is not the culmination of effort;
the abandonment attained therein is the accomplishment of the task,
yet it is not the culmination of the task itself.
The path of fruition is diligence, but it is not the culmination of diligence.
That which is abandoned through it is the accomplishment of the task, but it is not the culmination of the accomplishment of the task.
Furthermore, the path of training is diligence, but it is not the culmination of diligence.
The abandonment attained by him is the accomplishment of the task,
yet it is not the ultimate accomplishment of the task.
The path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) is diligence, and it is the ultimate diligence.
That which has been abandoned by him is accomplished; this matter is brought to its ultimate fulfillment.
As it is said in the Sūtra, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
There are certain non-Buddhists who,
although they likewise establish the abandonment and knowledge of all grasping,
are unable to establish it in its full completeness.

This means that they merely designate the abandonment and knowledge of the grasping for sensual pleasure (*kāma-upādāna*), the grasping for views (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*), and the grasping for precepts and vows (*śīla-vrata-upādāna*), but not the grasping for a doctrine of self (*ātma-vāda-upādāna*). What is the meaning of this?
Why was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of providing a detailed analysis of the meaning of the sūtra.
That is to say, the sūtra states that the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are certain non-Buddhists..."
This is stated at length in the sūtras;
however, although the sūtras make such a statement,
they do not extensively analyze its meaning.
That [work] is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Since there are matters not explained therein that must now all be explained, this treatise has been composed.
Within this, the intent of the inquiry is threefold.
First question: The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) truly do not understand the meaning of abandoning all grasping (upādāna);
why, then, does the Blessed One say that they are identical to him in the designation of having abandoned and known all grasping?
Second question: The non-Buddhists truly cannot speak of having abandoned and known all grasping.
World-Honored One, for what reason do you teach that one should establish the abandonment and knowledge of the three graspings?
Since non-Buddhists are also able to partially abandon the grasping at a self-theory (*ātmavādopādāna*),
why not establish that as well, rather than speaking only of abandoning these three?
Among these three, the middle question is answered first:
namely, since the various non-Buddhists are truly unable to speak of the abandonment and knowledge of all grasping (*upādāna*),
for what reason did the Blessed One say that they establish the abandonment and knowledge of the three graspings?
Some say: "This was the Blessed One preaching the Dharma impulsively. They should not say this.
Why is this? Because the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is not entirely without cause,
nor does it arise from a deficient cause.
This means that what they have said is a slander against the Blessed One;
therefore, it should be restrained, rebuked, and opposed. Why is this so?
Because the Blessed One is forever free from meaningless speech;
because what he speaks is measured and necessarily beneficial;
and because, relying upon the field and the vessel, he rains down the rain of Dharma.
Because he teaches the Dharma only when there is a great causal condition,
all the words spoken by the Blessed One cause sentient beings to obtain great benefit and happiness.
Therefore, what they have said is a slander against the Blessed One.
Furthermore, there are those who say that these words reveal that he has abandoned only a small portion [of the afflictions].
One should not make such a statement.
Why is that? Because even ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are capable of severing a small portion of the grasping at self-identity (*ātmavādopādāna*).
That which they have stated does not accord with correct reasoning;
therefore, it must be refuted, censured, and rebuked. Why is this so?
For example, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is in the state of being free from the defilements of desire (*kāmarāga*), they completely sever the grasping for sensual pleasure (*kāmopādāna*).
From the state of being free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the state of being free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
they are able to partially sever the grasping for views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*) and the grasping for precepts and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*).
In this way, during the stages of detachment from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness,
one is also able to partially abandon the grasping for the doctrine of self (ātmavādopādāna).
If it were to be designated [as the abandonment of the four graspings] upon such partial abandonment, [then the following would occur].
One should also establish the abandonment of the grasping at the doctrine of self (ātmavādopādāna);
therefore, what they have said does not accord with correct reasoning.
However, the Buddha, the World-Honored One...
For the sake of the immeasurable great assembly of devas, humans, and others, he extensively expounded the essential teachings of the Dharma.
He revealed them without error, enabling each being to understand according to their own kind.
Among them were various followers of external paths.

I have heard that the Buddha spoke of the names of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), hindrances (nīvaraṇa), foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), and so forth up to the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga);
some of these are complete, while others are incomplete.
If any of these non-Buddhists should hear that one seeks to grasp at desire,
they will say: "I also establish the abandonment and knowledge of grasping at desire."
If there are those who hear or see the term "clinging to views," they will say: "I,
too, establish the abandonment and knowledge of clinging to views."
If there are those who hear the name "clinging to precepts and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa), they will say:
"I too shall establish the abandonment and knowledge of clinging to precepts and observances."
This is the author of the treatise’s response based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It does not contradict reason, nor does it misrepresent the Buddha;
for when the Blessed One had not yet appeared in the world, [the following occurred].
The various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) and others obtained much fame and profit;
once the Buddha appeared in the world, he eclipsed all the non-Buddhists,
just as when the sun has risen, the glow of fireflies vanishes.
As his followers gradually diminished in number regarding fame and profit,
they gathered in one place and deliberated together, saying:
"Before the Gautama clan appeared in the world..."
"All worldly fame and profit belonged to us;
now that he has left the world, they have suddenly returned to him.
Yet, Gautama possesses no real virtues superior to our own."
He is well-versed in the sūtras and śāstras,
and his physical appearance is so dignified and majestic that we cannot equal it;
though his appearance is difficult to surpass, [it is not the cause of his excellence].
Furthermore, their sutras and treatises are easily susceptible to plagiarism.
We thought that if we were to obtain them, we would again attract fame and profit;
thus, we deliberated together and said:
"Susīma and the others are wise and possess powerful memories; if they are sent to the presence of Gautama to seek admission as disciples,
he will surely explain the sūtras and śāstras to them in detail."
Having heard this, he returned and recounted it for our sake.
After deliberating, we went together to the place where Suśīma was,
to comfort him and exhort him.
He then accepted the instruction and went to the Buddha’s presence, intending to surreptitiously obtain the Dharma.
By means of his ten powers and four fearlessnesses, the Buddha [responded].
While he was extensively expounding the essential teachings of the Dharma amidst the great assembly,
those non-Buddhist practitioners were walking nearby;
desiring to steal his teachings, their minds became hollow and timid.
They are unable to fully receive what has been taught in its entirety;
or, though they are able to receive it in its entirety, they do not understand its meaning.
Nevertheless, these are the essential points of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Some are complete and some are incomplete;
yet regarding the task at hand, there is nothing that is not complete,
as stated in the Sūtra.
If sentient beings are able to dwell in the contemplation of the body within their own internal bodies—
as [rare] as the soil on a fingernail—
and if sentient beings do not dwell in the contemplation of the body within their own internal bodies.
As with the soil of the great earth,
what is taught in this sutra,
although called "complete" regarding the task to be accomplished, [is not so].
However, regarding the names mentioned therein, they are not exhaustive,
as stated in the Sūtra:
"There are four foundations of mindfulness."
Both of these are fully present in what is taught in this sutra,
as stated in the sūtras regarding the six elements,
the five hindrances, the seven factors of enlightenment, and so forth.
Although that which is to be done is said to be complete, what is stated therein is not complete,
as it is said in the Sūtra:
The eighteen elements, the ten hindrances, the fourteen factors of enlightenment, and so forth—
both of these are fully contained within what is taught in this sutra.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Some may be complete and some incomplete;
yet those non-Buddhists are unable to receive them in their entirety,
or even if they do receive them completely, they do not understand their meaning.
According to what they have received and maintained, they falsely establish [their own views].
To prove this point, he further cites a sūtra,
such as when many bhikṣus assemble in one place.
There were certain non-Buddhists who came and spoke thus:
"Just as Gautama proclaims the essentials of the Dharma to his disciples..."
That is to say, he spoke thus:
"O bhikṣus, you should abandon the five hindrances; these five hindrances defile the mind, weaken the power of wisdom, harm the factors of enlightenment, and obstruct nirvāṇa."
One should well establish the mind in the four foundations of mindfulness and diligently cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment. We,
too, are able to explain this essential teaching to our disciples.
"In that case, what difference is there between the essential teachings of the Dharma expounded by Gautama and those of my own?
Why is it that you all have returned to him alone?"
Yet those non-Buddhists cannot even recognize the names and characteristics of the five hindrances,
much less understand how to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness and cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment.
Nevertheless, they have fabricated this teaching by surreptitiously appropriating the Buddha’s words.
One should know that the designation of "abandoning grasping" is likewise:
namely, those non-Buddhists who are born together with the hindrances and die together with the hindrances.
Since they do not even recognize the canopy,
how much less could they know that it is the applications of mindfulness and the factors of enlightenment that serve as its remedy?
To clarify this principle, another scriptural authority is further cited.
Furthermore, it is like the non-Buddhist Makkhali Gosāla,
who did not understand that his own body was a collection of various ailments,
impermanent from moment to moment, suffering, empty, and non-self.
He approached the Buddha and, drumming his belly, said:
"This body of mine is now free from all illness;
you should know that this is itself ultimate nirvāṇa."
He does not even know the name or characteristics of being free from illness,
much less can he comprehend ultimate nirvana; yet,
he has fabricated this statement by misappropriating the Buddha’s words.
One should know that the designation of "abandoning grasping" is likewise so.
That is to say, those non-Buddhists regard the absence of physical pain as being free from illness,
and they regard obtaining fine food and drink as attaining nirvāṇa.
They do not even know that the harmony of the four great elements is called "freedom from illness," much less can they realize that the harmony of the mind is called "nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, they do not even know that the untainted noble path is called "freedom from illness."
How much less could they understand that the ultimate fruit of the path is called nirvāṇa?
They merely pilfer the Buddha’s words and fabricate such claims;
one should know that their conceptualization of "abandoning grasping" is likewise [false].
Having answered the preceding question,
he next answers the subsequent question:
"For what reason do the non-Buddhists only establish the abandonment and knowledge of the three types of clinging, but not of clinging to the doctrine of self?"
This question could also be answered to some small extent by the non-Buddhists;
why then is no answer provided? It is because they have, for a long night, clung to the existence of a real self, a sentient being, a life-principle, a soul, a nourisher, and a person (*pudgala*).
Since they already maintain that there is a truly existent self,
how could they possibly propose the abandonment of the grasping at the doctrine of a self?
This refers to those non-Buddhists who hold the self as their fundamental tenet.
If one were to posit the abandonment of the grasping at a self-theory (*ātmavādopādāna*),
one would then renounce one's own school and take refuge in the views of others;
therefore, one does not posit the abandonment of the grasping at a self-theory.
Furthermore, because those non-Buddhists cling to a self, they fear selflessness as if approaching a deep pit;
therefore, they do not establish the abandonment of the grasping to the doctrine of a self.
Furthermore, those non-Buddhists conceive this thought:
Because there is a self, one lives. If there were no self,
then because there would be no living being, one would not live.
Therefore, one does not establish the abandonment of the grasping to the doctrine of self (ātmavādopādāna).
Furthermore, those non-Buddhists (tīrthika) think as follows:
"If I were to establish the abandonment of the grasping to the doctrine of self..."
"Even my fellow practitioners of the holy life (sabrahmacārin) despise me and abandon me;
how much more so others who fear such contempt?
Therefore, having answered the subsequent question, I did not posit the 'clinging to views' (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*) as being the 'clinging to self-theory' (*ātmavādopādāna*)."

Next, in response to the first question, it is stated that the abandonment and knowledge of all grasping (*upādāna*) is taught through conventional designation (*prajñapti*). What is the meaning of this?
The intent of this question is to say that those non-Buddhists do not truly understand the meaning of abandoning all forms of grasping.
Why did the Blessed One state that the abandonment and knowledge of all grasping (*upādāna*) are designated in the same way?
Answer: This is because the Buddha, the Blessed One, followed their own terminology;
that is to say, those non-Buddhists themselves claim to have fully understood [it].
The Blessed One stated that this was not his own intentional teaching;
in order to prove this point, he further cited a sūtra,
as the Blessed One said:
Those non-Buddhists postulate that sentient beings truly exist and undergo destruction;
however, from the perspective of ultimate truth,
there are no real sentient beings, and one merely follows their words.
And it is said thus:
"This case is also like that.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Not merely repeating the words of others,
lest one become identical to them.
*Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Thirty-three.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Thirty-Four,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section 4 of the First Aggregate on Miscellaneous Matters (Saṃyukta-skandha), Part 6: On Loving-Regard. As stated in the Sūtra:
"There are two types of thorough knowledge."
That is to say, the thorough knowledge of wisdom and the thorough knowledge of abandonment;
this is explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of providing a detailed analysis of the meaning of the sūtra.
That is to say, the sūtra states that there are two types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*):
namely, thorough knowledge as wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*) and thorough knowledge as abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
Although the sūtra makes this statement,
it does not extensively analyze its meaning;
that [sūtra] is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which was not stated by him should all now be explained.
Furthermore, although it was previously stated that one must abandon and know all forms of grasping (*upādāna*),
the meaning of abandoning and knowing grasping has not yet been analyzed.
Now, wishing to provide a detailed analysis, this treatise is composed.
What is the thorough knowledge through wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*)?
The answer is: all forms of wisdom (*jñāna*), vision (*darśana*), clarity (*vidyā*), awakening (*buddhi*), and clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
This is called the thorough knowledge of wisdom.
In this context, all these names express a single meaning;
however, because the author of the treatise has attained mastery over the meanings of various terms, he provides these diverse explanations.
That which counteracts ignorance is called knowledge (*jñāna*);
that which counteracts wrong views is called vision (*darśana*);
and that which counteracts nescience (*avidyā*) is called clarity (*vidyā*).
It is called "awakening" (*bodha*) because it counteracts false awakening;
it is called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*) because it counteracts false clear realization.
Question: Among these, what kind of knowledge and so forth is designated as "thorough knowledge by knowledge" (*jñānaparijñā*)?
Some say this: it is because only the untainted (anāsrava) is called "clear observation" (abhisamaya). Why is that?
Conventional knowledge cannot be termed "clear observation" (*abhisamaya*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that the term "knowledge of full comprehension" (*jñānaparijñā*) refers generally to both contaminated and uncontaminated knowledges.
Why is this? Because it is the thorough knowledge of all phenomena;
for the sūtras frequently speak of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Question: Is conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) also called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*)?
Answer: The meaning of clear realization is that of clear and thorough observation;
[this applies] within conventional wisdom.
One who is able to clearly and thoroughly examine the dharmas is also said to possess clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
It is not only that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) that receives the name "clear realization";
therefore, the *Nagaropama-sūtra* speaks thus:
When I had not yet realized unexcelled perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi),
I directly perceived through insight that old age and death have birth as their condition;
it was not the case that there was already an observation of dependent origination prior to my realization of unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
True, untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*) may be called "clear observation" (*abhisamaya*).
By this, it is known that conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is also termed "clear observation.
Question: What kind of conventional wisdom is also termed "thorough knowledge by wisdom" (*jñānaparijñā*)?
Answer: With the exception of conventional knowledge associated with attention through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*),

all other conventional knowledges that clearly perceive the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) through the insights of hearing, reflection, and cultivation are also termed "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*).
It is also called "knowledge through universal comprehension.
Regarding wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*),
it is, for example, the contemplation of the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
Wisdom arisen from reflection refers to such practices as mindfulness of breathing and the four foundations of mindfulness;
wisdom arisen from cultivation refers to...
For example, the levels of heat (*uṣmagata*), summits (*mūrdhan*), patience (*kṣānti*), and the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
These, together with untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*), are collectively termed "knowledge and full comprehension" (*jñānaparijñā*).
What is "abandonment and full comprehension" (*prahāṇaparijñā*)?
Answer: All greed is forever severed;
hatred and delusion are forever severed;
all afflictions are forever severed.
This is called the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).

Question: Since "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) is established based on the ability to thoroughly know the object of focus (*ālambana*), why is it called "thorough knowledge" when there is no longer an object of focus and no further function of thorough knowing in relation to abandonment?
Answer: Because abandonment is the fruit of knowledge, it is also termed "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*);
just as an Arhat is also said to possess "liberation" because it is the fruit of understanding.
Because the divine eye and the divine ear are the fruits of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are also called "supernormal powers.
Because the six internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) and so forth are the fruits of karma, they are called "karmic results.
This case is likewise.
This abandonment is the fruit of knowledge and is also termed "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
Question: Since abandonment through cultivation is the fruit of knowledge, it may be called thorough knowledge.
Since that which is abandoned through seeing is the fruit of patience (*kṣānti*),
how can it be called "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*)? The Venerable Saṃghavasu said:
This is called "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) because it is the fruit of wisdom.
That is to say, there are two kinds of thorough knowledge:
first, that which has wisdom as its intrinsic nature.
The nature of these two is wisdom.
They should not say this;
the Sūtra merely states that there are two types of thorough knowledge (parijñā).
First is the thorough knowledge of wisdom;
second is the thorough knowledge of abandonment.
Regarding the thorough knowledge of wisdom, its intrinsic nature is wisdom itself.
The thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) has abandonment as its intrinsic nature.
Because abandonment is the fruit of wisdom, it is called "thorough knowledge.
Nowhere else is it stated that wisdom itself is thorough knowledge.
Because "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) is a designation for the function of wisdom,
the Venerable Pārśva said:
"One should say that this abandonment is called the 'thorough knowledge of relinquishment' (prahāṇa-parijñā)."
Because one abandons birth and death by attaining this abandonment,
the Venerable Ghosaka has stated that this abandonment should be called "thorough knowledge through principle" (*yukti-parijñā*).
One perceives the most excellent Dharma and the most excellent ultimate principle;
because one attains this ultimate, supreme abandonment,
both of these [previous] teachings are of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
Because neither [of these] explains the term "abandonment" as being "thorough knowledge," the Venerable Buddhapālita stated:
"Although abandonment has no function of thorough knowledge with respect to the object."
Furthermore, it is also called "thorough knowledge" by way of its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
For example, although the eye of the past or the future does not see forms, it is nevertheless designated as "the eye" by way of its defining characteristic.
It should be understood that the same applies to the ear up to the mind,
as well as to all mental factors;
this case is also like that.
To claim that "abandonment" is called "thorough knowledge" because it is the characteristic of wisdom is unreasonable. Why is this so?
Because this abandonment lacks the function of universal knowledge (*parijñā*) at all times.
Other masters state that the abandonment effected by the receptivities (*kṣānti*) is also called "universal knowledge," because it is the fruit of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
That explanation is unreasonable.
It may be so for the realms from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness.
Regarding the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by insight within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
how can it be said to be the fruit of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?
For conventional knowledge lacks the function of permanent abandonment with respect to that [level].

Furthermore, while at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), when one abandons the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) of the lower eight stages by means of the worldly path (*laukika-mārga*), it is not yet called "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
When the stage of the path of insight (*darśana-mārga*) is reached and thorough knowledge is established, there is no longer any worldly wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*).
How can this be said to be the fruit of conventional knowledge?
Furthermore, there are those who say that the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing is untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Because it is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), it is also called "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).

That is to say, when untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) serves as the sixth path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) for abandoning [the defilements of] the desire realm and one realizes the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*),
one simultaneously attains the abandonment of those things to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) across all three realms.
The abandonment of the six categories of afflictions in the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation constitutes the fruit of once-returner;
this abandonment is effected by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
At the time of realizing the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) via the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the desire realm, [the same applies].
One attains the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through seeing in the three realms,
as well as the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
thereby realizing the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala).

When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, one simultaneously attains the abandonment of what is to be eliminated through the paths of seeing and cultivation across the three realms;
this constitutes the fruit of arhatship.
Therefore, that abandonment is also termed "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*).
He also should not speak in such a manner,
for it would follow that the six thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are not thorough knowledges.
One should rather speak as follows:
Patience is the retinue of wisdom;
because it is of the same lineage as wisdom, it is also called wisdom.
Abandonment is its fruit, and is therefore termed "thorough knowledge" (parijñā).
Just as one born into the Gautama clan is called "Gautama," so it should be here as well.
Question: Is the abandonment of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) also called "thorough knowledge" (parijñā)?
For what reason is it said that the permanent abandonment of all craving, up to the permanent abandonment of all afflictions, is called "thorough knowledge of abandonment" (prahāṇa-parijñā)?
Answer: Although the abandonment of even a single fetter (saṃyojana) is also called thorough knowledge, [it is designated as such only when all are abandoned].
However, it is here that complete thorough knowledge is taught,
for it is only when all fetters are exhausted that one is said to possess complete thorough knowledge of abandonment.
Furthermore, O Blessed One:
At times, the term "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) is used with reference to wisdom;
at times, it is used with reference to abandonment.
Regarding its use with reference to wisdom:
As a gāthā says:
The noble Māṇava is serene; He benefits all the world.
Possessing wisdom, he fully understands That craving gives rise to manifold sufferings.
"The wise should speak what ought to be done;
they should not speak of what ought not to be done. The wise should understand this thoroughly:
when there is speech but no action, one seeks many reasons for the king. This is the root verse.
It is said that in the past there was a king named Much-Seeking (Bahudāna),
who by nature was fierce and violent, and whose greed for acquisition knew no satiety;
he plundered all the wealth and treasures belonging to the people of the land.
Thereupon, the ministers and aides deliberated together and withdrew him [from the throne],
installing his younger brother, Shao, to succeed to the royal position.
At that time, many sought the king to go to the border towns of the kingdom.
He weaved grass into sandals to sustain himself in this manner for a long time. Then,
his younger brother, the king, suddenly remembered him.
He asked his ministers,
"Where is my elder brother?
The ministers replied:
He heard that [his brother] was living by making shoes in a border town.
Upon hearing this, the king became distressed and thought to himself:
"Since my elder brother is in such a state..."
"What use have I now for the position of king? he thought.
He immediately summoned him and granted him a district as a fief.
Many people then attached themselves to him, so that food was no longer supplied to [the king].
In this manner, he successively conferred the seals of office upon two districts, three districts, and even half the kingdom;
yet he remained unsatisfied.
He subsequently raised an army once more, killed his younger brother, and established himself as ruler.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing this, thought to himself:
"This wicked king does not recognize kindness or righteousness;
I should now go and deceive and vex him."
He then transformed himself into the likeness of a Brahmin,
wearing a cap, draped in a shawl, holding a water-pot and a staff;
he went before the king and spoke words of auspicious blessing.
Having offered praises and prayers for blessings, he stood to one side.
The king said,
"Brahmin!"
"From where have you come?
The brahmin replied,
"From beyond the great ocean."
The king asked,
"What is happening beyond the sea? He replied,
"I have seen a certain kingdom."
It was peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, with vast multitudes of people;
rare and extraordinary treasures filled the kingdom.
The king said:
"Can I obtain it by my own power?
The brāhmaṇa replied,
"If you go, you will certainly obtain it."
The king asked again,
"Who guided you?
He replied:
"I am able," [he replied]. The King asked,
"In how many days will you be able to set out on the journey?"
The brahmin said,
"Seven days hence," and having spoken, he departed.
At that time, King Bahudatta assembled his troops and prepared all necessary provisions; on the seventh day,
he set out in full ceremonial procession.
Having searched for a brahmin, he was unable to find one.
The king then became distressed and troubled, thinking to himself:
"If he were to come, great benefit would be gained."
Because he had lost that which he had expected, his purpose was not fulfilled; he entered a chamber of sorrow and sat there in distress and resentment.
No one in the entire kingdom understood the poison of his grief.
At that time, Śākyamuni Bodhisattva was born in that country in a village of great brahmins.
Having come to the royal capital for a minor reason,
he heard these matters and felt compassion in his heart;
he said to the ministers:
"I can untie the knot of sorrow in Your Majesty's heart.
The ministers, filled with joy, led him before the king;
he offered words of auspicious praise and benediction, then stood to one side.
For the king, he proclaimed these verses from the *Arthavargīya*:
"Those who pursue various desires always give rise to longing;
if their desires are fulfilled as they wish, their minds become greatly delighted."
Those who pursue various sensual desires always give rise to longing;
if their desires are not fulfilled, they are tormented and ruined as if struck by an arrow.
Having thus explained these verses from the Chapter on the Censure of Desire in their entirety for the sake of the King, [he continued]:
At that moment, the Bodhisattva himself became free from the defilement of desire.
Upon hearing this, the King was relieved of the poisonous grief in his heart and immediately spoke the first verse for the Bodhisattva.
"The wise Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta is tranquil," and so forth,
as extensively explained.
The meaning of this verse is clear and requires no further analysis.
The Bodhisattva spoke the second verse to the king:
"The wise person should act," and so forth,
as explained at length.
The first half of this verse rebukes Śakra.
It means that those who possess wisdom say that once one has promised another to do something, one must certainly carry it out;
if one does not wish to do it, one should not have made the promise at all.
The latter half rebukes the king,
stating that a wise person should fully understand that if someone speaks words they do not act upon with the intent to cause disturbance or vexation,
yet there is no actual substance to it.
"O King, why do you so stubbornly believe those empty words?
Who could possibly come from beyond the sea,
and who again could go to the other side of the ocean?"
I pray that Your Majesty will not seek matters beyond your station.
Regarding the term "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) in the context of abandonment,
as it is stated in the Sūtra:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I shall explain to you the phenomena to be fully known (*parijñeya-dharma*), the intrinsic nature of full knowledge (*parijñā-svabhāva*), and that which is capable of full knowledge (*parijñātṛ*).
As for the phenomena to be fully known:"
It refers to the five aggregates of clinging.
Full comprehension of their intrinsic nature means the permanent abandonment of craving.
Hatred and delusion are forever severed;
all afflictions are forever severed.
One who is able to fully know this—
This refers to the Arhat whose outflows are forever exhausted,
who does not grasp at such indeterminate matters as whether the Tathāgata exists after death.
In this context, the phenomena to be fully understood are the five aggregates of clinging.
Question: Based on what kind of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is this statement made?
Is it thorough knowledge as wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*), or is it thorough knowledge as abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*)?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If it were taught based on the thorough knowledge through wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*),
then one should have stated that all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) are the objects of thorough knowledge.
Why is it that only the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are mentioned?
This would also be illogical if explained in terms of the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇaparijñā*),
because the five aggregates of clinging pertain to both types of thorough knowledge.
Since it is that which is to be fully known (*parijñeya*), one should not say that it refers solely to the full knowledge through abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
Some maintain that here it refers solely to the full knowledge through wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*).
Question: If that were so, one should say that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are what are to be fully known (*parijñeya*).
Why, then, do you say only the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are?
Answer: It is as in the case of the Four Noble Truths.
It is simply stated that the Truth of Suffering is to be fully known;
that explanation of the reason is precisely this cause.
Other masters say:
This [explanation] is stated here solely in reliance upon the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).

Question: Since these five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*) are objects of thorough knowledge (*parijñeya*) that pertain to both types of thorough knowledge, one should not state this by relying exclusively on the thorough knowledge of abandonment.
Answer: As in the case of the Four Noble Truths, it is simply stated that the Truth of Cessation is what should be realized;
the explanation for why that is so constitutes this very reason.
Furthermore, there is another unique cause herein: namely,
that the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) is obtainable only with respect to the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*),
and does not constitute the intrinsic nature of other types of thorough knowledge.
This refers to the permanent abandonment of greed, the permanent abandonment of hatred and delusion, and the permanent abandonment of all afflictions.

Question: Other sūtras state that the cessation, detachment, and extinction of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are called the realm of cessation, detachment, and extinction (nirodha-virāga-nirodha-dhātu).
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are precisely all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). Why, then,
is it said here that only the permanent abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*) is called "thorough knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-parijñā*)?
The answer is: that sutra is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and an exhaustive teaching;
this one is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and an incomplete teaching.
As the Blessed One said:
Because all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) preceded by afflictions (*kleśa*) are forever severed;
furthermore, because afflictions are difficult to sever, difficult to destroy, and difficult to transcend, they are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, because all afflictions possess many faults and calamities—
losing sight of the correct principle and obstructing nirvāṇa as well as the various noble paths—
they are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, because the various afflictions are abandoned by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*), they are no longer possessed after being abandoned;
whereas other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are not abandoned by way of their intrinsic nature, and thus they are still possessed even after being abandoned.
Therefore, it is specifically said that the afflictions (*kleśa*) are eternally severed.
Furthermore, because the various afflictions are directly and mutually contradictory with the Noble Path (*āryamārga*),
whereas other contaminated wholesome states and non-obscured neutral states are not so, it is therefore specifically said [of the afflictions].
Just as light and darkness are mutually exclusive,
it is not the vessel, oil, or wick that does so;
rather, when the lamp is lit, it is precisely that which can dispel the darkness.
It is also like a vessel of hot oil that exhausts the wick;
in this way, because the Noble Path and the various afflictions are mutually antagonistic,
when the Noble Path manifests, it directly severs the afflictions.

It also causes the remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena to be abandoned, because they share the same antidote as the afflictions (*kleśa*). One who is able to fully comprehend them is called an Arhat;
this is explained at length, and so forth.
Question: Since those in training (śaikṣa) are also capable of full comprehension, why is it said that only the Arhat [is so]?
Answer: Because the statement is made with reference to the most eminent.
That is to say, among all dharmas, the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) are the most excellent;
among all persons (pudgala), the person beyond training is the most excellent.
Therefore, it is taught selectively.
Furthermore, although those in training possess thorough knowledge, they have not yet been able to abandon everything;
those beyond training, however, both possess thorough knowledge and are also able to abandon everything.
Therefore, it is explained selectively.
Furthermore, regarding the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) mentioned here,
the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) attains its fulfillment and ultimate perfection therein.
The learner (*śaikṣa*) is not so;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, it is called "thorough knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇaparijñā*) because it involves the universal abandonment [of defilements].
It is not so for those in training;
therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, as previously stated, the permanent abandonment of all afflictions is termed "thorough knowledge of abandonment" (prahāṇaparijñā).
It is now stated that only an Arhat achieves this thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
Regarding the question, "What is it that those who take refuge in the Buddha actually take refuge in? and so forth at length:
for what purpose was this treatise composed?

The answer is: for those who conceive the notion of taking refuge in that which is not a true object of refuge, this [teaching] reveals the true object of refuge so that they may abandon the former and resort to the latter.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Driven by fear, many people take refuge in mountains,
groves, forests, solitary trees, and shrines;
yet such refuge is not supreme, and such refuge is not noble.
One cannot be liberated from all suffering by relying on these;
But by taking refuge in the Buddha, And by taking refuge in the Dharma and the Sangha,
One should constantly observe the Four Noble Truths with wisdom.
Knowing suffering, knowing the origin of suffering, knowing the eternal transcendence of all suffering,
and knowing the Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the secure state of Nirvana—
this refuge is supreme; this refuge is most venerable.
One must surely take refuge through this, for it can liberate one from all suffering.
Furthermore,
[this is taught] for those who are deluded or confused regarding refuge.
This is for the purpose of enabling them to attain correct understanding and be free from hesitation.
That is to say, there may be some who claim that one who takes refuge in the Buddha [takes refuge in the physical body].
One takes refuge in the Tathāgata’s body, which is composed of the head, neck, belly, back, hands, feet, and so forth;
yet it is now revealed that this body, produced and grown by parents, consists of impure (*sāsrava*) phenomena and is not an object of refuge.
That which is the object of refuge is the Buddha’s state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), the dharma of having realized *bodhi*,
which is the *dharmakāya*. Alternatively,
there are those who say that taking refuge in the Dharma means taking refuge in the three truths.
Or [it concerns] phenomena such as the wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;
or it concerns the training rules (śikṣāpada) prescribed by the Bhikṣus,
namely, what should be done and what should not be done, and so forth.
Now this dharma is revealed:
that which is conditioned and tainted is not the refuge;
that which is the refuge is as follows.
That is to say, it is solely the extinction of craving within the Truth of Cessation, which is Nirvana;
or alternatively, there are those who say that taking refuge in the Sangha means:
Regarding the monastics who have left the household life from the four castes:
I shall now reveal that their deportment and physical appearance are all characterized by outflows (*sāsrava*) and are therefore not objects of refuge.
That which is the object of refuge refers to the dharmas of the Saṃgha, both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
For this reason, this treatise is composed.
Regarding those who take refuge in the Buddha, in what do they take refuge?
Answer: In whatever phenomena are real, manifest, and are designated by names, concepts, designations, and verbal expressions.
That which is called "taking refuge in the Buddha" refers to taking refuge in all those dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that constitute the attainment of enlightenment.
In this context, if these dharmas were substantially existent,
it would manifest that the substantially existent essence of the Buddha has these dharmas as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This statement is intended as a refutation of those who claim that the Buddha is merely a name,
merely a concept, merely a conventional designation, and lacks any substantial reality.
"Existing now" (pratyutpanna) reveals that the Buddha's essence exists as it is present, rather than having existed previously.
"Equal perception" (samasaṃjñā) reveals that one's perceptions directed toward the Buddha are equal [to those directed toward other Buddhas].
"Perception" (saṃjñā) indicates that this perception arises together with all [other mental factors].
"Designation" (prajñapti) refers to the designation of names based upon perception.
"Discourse" (abhilāpa) refers to the turning of speech based upon names and expressions.

Question: If those who have attained the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) and perfected the factors for awakening (bodhi-dharma) are truly Buddhas, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the sūtras?
For example, as it is said:
"Elder, what is meant by 'Buddha'?
It refers to a son of the Śākyas who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and gone forth from home with right faith;
one who is endowed with all-encompassing wisdom—this is called a Buddha."
Answer: Since the supporting body is used to manifest the supported phenomenon, there is no contradiction in principle in making this statement.
Question: If that is so, [what of the case where] an evil mind draws blood from the Buddha’s body?
Why does he incur the offense of immediate retribution?
Answer: Because by destroying the physical basis (the body), he causes that which relies upon it (the mind) to be destroyed as well.
One incurs the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).

Furthermore, because one gives rise to an evil mind toward those who take the dharmas that constitute enlightenment as their object of focus while they are in the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one incurs the offense of immediate retribution.
Because he harbored hatred for the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma), he harmed the Buddha’s body and incurred an immediate transgression (ānantarya-karma).
It was not merely the arousal of the intention to draw blood from his body that constituted the offense.
For those who take refuge in the Dharma, what is it that they take as their refuge?
Answer: If a phenomenon (dharma) truly exists and is designated by perception, conceptualization, convention, and verbal expression, it is called taking refuge in the Dharma.
Such is the exhaustion of craving, its detachment, cessation, and nirvāṇa.
This is called taking refuge in the Dharma.
In this context, if the Dharma were substantially existent,
it would manifest that nirvāṇa is substantially existent.
This statement is intended to refute those who assert that what is called nirvāṇa is merely the cessation of all suffering and lacks any real substantial entity;
it is made in order to demonstrate that nirvāṇa possesses a real intrinsic nature.
"Existing now" indicates that nirvāṇa exists as a reality, not as a mere conventional designation.
The remainder is as explained previously.
There are some versions that state only:
"Taking refuge in the exhaustion of craving, detachment, cessation,
and nirvana is called taking refuge in the Dharma," without mentioning such expressions as "truly existing" or "presently existing."
What is the meaning of this?
It means that the essence of nirvāṇa is quiescent and free from characteristics;
it is beyond the reach of conceptualization, names, and verbal expression.
To hold that there is nothing within this [nirvana] and thus to regard it as non-existent is unreasonable;
for it would be a false view to deny the cessation of nirvana, which is actually attainable.
This should simply have been stated;
however, it was omitted by the reciter.
