Section Five, Part Three of the First Chapter on the Miscellaneous Aggregates (*Saṃyukta-skandha*), titled "The Sub-section on Shamelessness and Lack of Remorse" (*Ahrīkyānapatrāpya-nirdeśa*): What are the superior roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) in the desire realm?
"What are the roots of goodness that proceed in conjunction with the subtle?
... [as explained at length] ...
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?"
Answer: It is for the purpose of extensively analyzing the meaning of the sūtra.
That is to say, the sūtra states that they still possess subtle co-arising roots of goodness that have not been severed;
from these, other wholesome dharmas will arise, by means of which there is purification.
Although the sūtra makes this statement, it does not extensively analyze its meaning,
nor does it explain what the superior roots of goodness of the desire realm are,
or what the roots of goodness that proceed with the subtle are.
The Sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which was not analyzed therein shall now be analyzed in detail; for this reason, this treatise is composed.
Question: Why are the intermediate roots of goodness not mentioned here?
Answer: Because it is the intention of the author of this treatise to do so, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, when something that ought to be stated is not stated,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Furthermore, by stating the beginning and the end, the middle is already revealed.

Just as it was at the beginning, so it should be understood that the same applies to the subsequent stages, the upward and downward movements, the entry, the emergence, and the culmination of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, if something is coarse, manifest, easy to understand, and easy to designate, [it is considered accessible].
That which is easy to manifest and easy to explain is explained herein.
It is not so with the middle grade; therefore, it is not explained.
Furthermore, because the middle grade is subsumed within the upper and lower grades, it is not explained separately.
Furthermore, because the superior and inferior grades are rare in the world, they are specifically mentioned;
the middle grade is extremely common and not considered rare, and is therefore omitted from discussion.
Question: Why is it that here only the wholesome roots of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are mentioned, and not those of the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*)?
The answer is: because it was the intention of the author of this treatise to proceed in this manner;
this is explained at length.
Furthermore, when something that ought to be stated is not stated, one should know that the meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, the wholesome roots of the form and formless realms take the wholesome roots of the desire realm as their gateway, their preparatory practice, and their path of entry.
Since these [higher realms] have already been explained by this [explanation of the desire realm], they need not be discussed separately.
Furthermore, in this context, only the immediate antidotes are discussed.

That is to say, the two unwholesome roots mentioned immediately prior have as their immediate antidotes the two kinds of wholesome roots of the desire realm; therefore, these alone are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, because the increased and subtle roots of goodness in the desire realm are easy to manifest, easy to understand, and easy to designate, they are explained herein.

Although the superior roots of goodness in the form and formless realms are likewise easy to manifest, easy to understand, and easy to designate, their subtle counterparts are not so; therefore, they are not mentioned here.
Because the two upper realms lack the quality of severing the roots of goodness, it is difficult to designate the characteristics of their subtle roots of goodness.
What, then, are the superior roots of goodness in the desire realm?

Answer: They are the conventional wisdom at the limit of clear observation (*abhisamaya-antya-saṃvṛti-jñāna*) in the desire realm, which is attained when a bodhisattva enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Furthermore, when the Tathāgata attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), he acquires wholesome roots of non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion pertaining to the desire realm.
Because such wholesome roots are the most preeminent among all wholesome roots bound to the desire realm, they are called "supreme" (*adhipati*).
What are the subtle concomitant roots of goodness?
Answer: They are those which are abandoned last at the time when the roots of goodness are severed;
it is by abandoning them that one is said to have severed the roots of goodness.
Such roots of goodness, being included within the inferior-inferior grade of innate goodness bound to the desire realm, are called "subtle and co-arising.

Question: Why, in this context, is the distinction made by contrasting the roots of goodness obtained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) with the conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*)?

Some say: herein, the distinction is not made by comparing the wholesome roots obtained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) with the conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*);
rather, the distinction is made by comparing one conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization with another conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization.
This means that regarding conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), it is inferior for śrāvakas,
middling for pratyekabuddhas,
and superior for bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, one distinguishes the differences between the roots of goodness obtained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the roots of goodness obtained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion by way of comparison:
that is to say, the roots of goodness obtained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion by a śrāvaka are inferior.
Among the pratyekabuddhas,
the Tathāgata is supreme;
thus say some other masters.

In this context, the distinction is also made by comparing the wholesome roots obtained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) with the conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*);
that is to say, the conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization possessed by a bodhisattva is inferior.
The wholesome roots obtained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) are superior;
the same applies to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, there is the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) at the conclusion of the Bodhisattva’s clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

The mundane conventional knowledge at the limit of the solitary realizer’s clear realization is superior to the roots of goodness obtained at the time of the solitary realizer’s knowledge of exhaustion,
because it is superior to the roots of goodness obtained by a śrāvaka at the time of their knowledge of exhaustion.
Some say that herein one does not intend to distinguish between the two differences, but merely to clarify that these two are equal and without distinction;
namely, that both arise by transcending the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and attaining the conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Because it transcends the acquisition of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) which is to be abandoned by insight; thus,
at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), one obtains wholesome roots that transcend the acquisition of the Peak of Existence which is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā).
Question: Since the two vehicles are likewise [incapable], why is this not stated?
Answer: Because they cannot transcend the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) abandoned through seeing and cultivation, and thus it is not predominant for them.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
In this context, there is no intention to speak of the distinction between the two or their equality; rather,
it is simply said that [this refers to] the conventional knowledge at the limit of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the desire realm attained by a bodhisattva,
as well as the roots of goodness in the desire realm obtained at the time of a Tathāgata’s knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
This is because the superior roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) in the desire realm are more excellent than those attained by the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*).
Question: If that is so, do the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas not possess superior roots of goodness?
Answer: Their roots are designated as "superior" only in comparison to other inferior classes; they are not superior when compared to the supreme vehicle (*anuttarayāna*).

Question: Since conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*) is only acquired after one has entered the state of rightness and departure from corruption (*samyaktva-nyāma*), why is it said that it is acquired "at the time of entering"?
Answer: Although logically one should say it is acquired only after having entered, it is stated that it is acquired "at the time of entering" [for the sake of brevity].
This refers to the expression "entering" when one has already entered; it is a case of using a term for proximity to denote distance.
It is like saying, "Where has Your Majesty come from now?
even though [the King] has already arrived, yet one says he is "coming now."
As it is said: "When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it really is that one is experiencing a pleasant feeling," and so forth;
here too, the state of having already experienced [the feeling] is designated as the time of experiencing.
This is as it is said: "Having abandoned pleasure and abandoned pain, one enters the fourth dhyāna."
This too is called "abandoned" when suffering has already been abandoned.
Just as it is said that one enters the meditative attainment of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*) by contemplating a certain object,
this too is called "entered" once one has already entered it.
As it is said that the mind of an arhat is liberated from the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*),
and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), and that it is called "liberated" because it is already liberated even from the outflow of desire—
here, too, it is the same.
"Having entered" refers to the time of entry.

Furthermore, there are those who say that one should properly state that at the moment a bodhisattva enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma), they attain the conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (abhisamaya-antika-saṃvṛti-jñāna).
Because all initial cognitions regarding the truths are termed "entry into the state of correctness" (*samyaktva-nyāma*), while the various "patiences" (*kṣānti*) are termed "entry" itself.

That is to say, when one enters the subsequent cognitions (*anvaya-jñāna*) of suffering, origin, and cessation through the patiences of suffering, origin, and cessation, it is called the attainment of conventional cognition at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamaya-anta-saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

Just as the time when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests is called the time of attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), so it is with this [knowledge] as well.
Question: Why is this knowledge called "the limit of clear realization" (*abhisamaya-anta*)?

Answer: Because it is the limit of the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha*), the limit of the clear realization of origin (*samudaya*), and the limit of the clear realization of cessation (*nirodha*).
Because one attains this wisdom, it is called "the limit of clear observation" (*abhisamayāntika*).
Some say that because it is attained as a secondary practice when various yogins contemplate the Noble Truths, it is called "the limit of clear observation. The Venerable Ghosaka says:
Because this wisdom is proximate to clear realization (*abhisamaya*), it is called "at the edge of clear realization" (*abhisamayāntika*).
It is like how things near a village are called "on the outskirts of the village.

Question: What is the nature of these mundane wholesome dharmas cultivated at the edge of clear realization? They have the four aggregates or the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Why is it that only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is mentioned?
The answer is: because knowledge predominates, it is designated as "knowledge.
It is just as the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), which constitute the intrinsic nature of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), are called "seeing" because seeing predominates.
The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) has the four aggregates or five aggregates as its intrinsic nature;
it is called "concentration" because concentration is predominant.
The four types of practice (*pratipad*) have the four aggregates or five aggregates as their intrinsic nature.
It is called "pervasive" (*abhisamaya*) because it penetrates and increases;
this [case] is also like that.

Question: Between the conventional knowledge of the desire realm at the conclusion of the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya-anta*) and the conventional knowledge of the form realm, which is superior?
Answer: The form realm is superior because its realm is superior; the same applies to the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realization of cessation.

Question: Between the conventional knowledge of the desire realm at the conclusion of the clear realization of origin and the conventional knowledge of the form realm at the conclusion of the clear realization of suffering, which is superior?
Answer: Those of the desire realm are superior because their basis is superior;
those of the form realm are superior because their realm is superior.
The same applies when one asks about cessation regarding suffering and its origin.

Question: Between the conventional wisdom of the desire realm at the conclusion of the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*) and the conventional wisdom of the form realm at the conclusion of the clear observation of origination (*samudaya-abhisamaya*), which is superior?
Answer: That of the form realm is superior because it excels in two respects.
First is the excellence of the realm (*dhātu*), and second is the excellence of the basis (*āśraya*).
It is the same when one asks about cessation by means of suffering, or asks about cessation by means of origination.

Regarding the conventional knowledge of the desire realm at the conclusion of the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya-antya*) and the conventional knowledge of the desire realm at the conclusion of the clear realization of origination (*samudaya-abhisamaya-antya*), which of these is superior?
Answer: It is superior because it is at the limit of the realization of the origin (samudaya-abhisamaya-anta). Since the basis is superior, one asks about cessation by means of suffering;
likewise, one asks about cessation by means of the origin.
As it is with the desire realm, so it is with the form realm.
Question: For what reason is conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛti-jñāna*) not cultivated at the time of the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*)?
Answer: Because for that [conventional knowledge], dharma-knowledge is neither a field nor a vessel, and so forth, as explained at length.

Furthermore, because this wisdom is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), it is called "conventional wisdom at the conclusion of clear realization" (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*).

If it were also cultivated during the time of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), it should be called "conventional wisdom within clear realization" (*abhisamayamadhye-saṃvṛtijñāna*) rather than "conventional wisdom at the conclusion of clear realization."
Furthermore, it was previously stated that this knowledge is attained because it transcends the abandonments through vision belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);

it is not the case that one does not cultivate this knowledge at the time of the Knowledge of Phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), for it is precisely at that time that one is able to transcend the abandonments through vision belonging to the Peak of Existence.
Furthermore, one is able to cultivate this knowledge when the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for each individual truth has been completed and has ceased;
whereas while abiding in the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), much remains to be done and the preparatory application has not yet ceased.
This means that at the time of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), although one knows the suffering of the desire realm, one has not yet known the suffering of the form and formless realms;
and although one has abandoned the origin of the desire realm, one has not yet abandoned the origin of the form and formless realms.
Although one has realized the cessation of the desire realm but has not yet realized the cessation of the form and formless realms,
one does not cultivate this knowledge at the time of the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).
Furthermore, one can cultivate this knowledge when the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of each individual truth is completed and when the objects abandoned by seeing have been completely eliminated.
When abiding in the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), such a thing does not exist; therefore, it is not cultivated.
Question: Why is this knowledge not cultivated at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)?
Answer: For the subsequent knowledge of the path, this [knowledge] is neither a field nor a vessel.
...and so forth, as explained at length.

Furthermore, this wisdom is an adjunct to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and is connected to it; since the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) belongs to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one does not cultivate this wisdom [at that stage].
Furthermore, this knowledge belongs to the retinue of the path of application (*prayogamārga*) and is connected to the path of application;
because the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is the resultant path, one does not cultivate this knowledge.

Furthermore, this knowledge exists within the mental continuum of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*) at the time when they cultivate the subsequent knowledge of the path.
Those whose mental continuums consist of faith-resolve (śraddhādhimukta) or those who have attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) do not cultivate this knowledge.

Furthermore, because this knowledge is called "at the edge of clear realization" (abhisamayāntika) and the term "edge" (anta) applies to it with respect to the three truths, one cultivates this knowledge.
As it is said: the limit of the suffering of the personal identity (satkāya),
the limit of the origin of the personal identity,
and the limit of the cessation of the personal identity.

However, because the "edge" (*anta*) of the path of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is not mentioned, this knowledge is not cultivated at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
Question: Following from the discussion, why does the term "edge" (*anta*) apply to the three [other] truths but not to the truth of the path?
The answer is: because while there is one who can know all suffering,
abandon all origination, and realize all cessation,
there is none who can cultivate the entire path.
The Buddha also does not exhaustively cultivate or practice even upon the Path; therefore, his voice proceeds boundlessly.
Furthermore, if the truths were such that both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) paths could perform their functions [exhaustively], then his voice would proceed with limits.
Because only the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) path within the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) is capable of performing its function, the term "unlimited" (*apramāṇa*) is applied.
This is just as [the distinction is made between] contaminated and uncontaminated paths,
or mundane and supramundane paths.
The path with relish and the path without relish,
as well as the path based on attachment and the path based on renunciation,
should be understood in the same way.
Furthermore, the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is both existence (*bhava*) and that which has existence as its fruit; regarding that existence, the term "existence" is applied.
That is to say, the truths of suffering and its origin (*samudayasatya*) are both existence and have existence as their fruit.
Although the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is not existence, it nevertheless has existence as its fruit.
Because the Truth of the Path is neither a [limited] existence nor a fruit of existence, the term "infinite" (ananta) is applied to it;
this is because no limit is predicated of the Truth of the Path.
At the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna), one does not cultivate this knowledge.
Furthermore, from the unknowable limit of the past onwards, through the mundane path,

one has previously engaged with the three truths by thinking, "I am this path. Now, when the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) manifests, [one realizes that those were merely conventional].
Because they have seen the true path, they feel shame; therefore, they do not cultivate [such views].
It is like a village or town where no leader has yet been established, and someone who considers themselves noble claims the title of leader for themselves.
Furthermore, when a leader is later established, those who were previously self-important feel shame and depart; this is also like that.
Moreover, the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realization (abhisamaya) is both an existence and possesses a fruit.
The truth of the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudayasatya*) is both existence and the fruit of existence.
Although the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is not existence, it is the fruit of existence; therefore, when one perceives it, one cultivates conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
As for the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), it is neither existence nor the fruit of existence.
Seeing that at that time one does not cultivate this wisdom;
furthermore, because the truths of suffering and its origin have boundless faults,
while the truth of cessation has boundless benefits.
When seeing that [Truth of Cessation], one cultivates conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*);
because the Truth of the Path has neither infinite faults nor infinite benefits,
when seeing it, one does not cultivate this knowledge.
Furthermore, since beginningless time, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) has already possessed efficacy regarding the three truths;
that is to say, it knows and abandons [afflictions], yet it is not ultimate,
because it lacks efficacy with respect to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Now, at the time of attaining clear realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the three truths, because it is ultimate,
one rejoices as if the dharma of desire were arising and becoming manifest;
for this reason, one practices.
Since beginningless time, there has been no functional capacity regarding the Noble Truths of the Path;
that is to say, because it has not yet been cultivated, this knowledge is not cultivated at the time of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Furthermore, at the time of attaining the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, its origin, and its cessation, the true Path has not yet been seen.
Conventional wisdom still considers itself to be the path, and for this reason it is cultivated.

However, when one attains the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Noble Truth of the Path, one perceives the true path; because this conventional wisdom then knows itself to be not the path, it is no longer cultivated.
In this regard, the analogy of the crow and the peacock should be explained.
Furthermore, at the time of seeing the three truths, one has not yet permanently abandoned the false view that slanders the path,
nor has one yet permanently abandoned the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) which regards what is not the path as the path.
Because various conventional knowledges still claim to be the Path, they are cultivated for that reason;
however, once the Truth of the Path has been seen, those [conventional knowledges] are forever abandoned, and thus these conventional knowledges are no longer cultivated.

Question: When one attains the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), just as one abandons the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), is this conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*) also abandoned?
Answer: It is not abandoned. Why is that?
Because the paths with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*) differ in their modes of relinquishing factors,
it is said that the path without outflows is relinquished by way of three conditions:
first, through falling away (*parihāṇi*).
Second, because of attaining the fruit;
third, because of refining the faculties.
One abandons [the path] through the four conditions of the contaminated path.
First, because of falling back;
second, because of transcending the realm and stage;
third, because of severing the roots of goodness.
Fourth, because it involves abandoning the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*):
at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), since none of the four conditions for abandoning the outflows (*sāsrava*) are present,
one does not abandon this knowledge at that time.

Furthermore, because the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) and the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) are mutually contradictory both in terms of their manifestation and their possession, it is abandoned at that time; whereas,

although the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛti-jñāna) is contradictory in terms of its manifestation, it is not contradictory in terms of its possession, and thus it is not abandoned at that time.
Question: For what reason does this wisdom not manifest during the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga)?

Answer: This conventional wisdom at the conclusion of clear realization (abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna) is an attendant of the path of seeing (darśanamārga) and is bound to the path of seeing; therefore, it necessarily does not manifest during the path of cultivation.
Furthermore, this knowledge belongs to the retinue of the path of application and is connected to the path of application;
because it is associated with the fruit during the path of cultivation, it does not manifest.
Furthermore, this knowledge relies upon the continuity of those who practice through faith or through dharma.
Because this continuity does not exist within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it does not manifest.

Furthermore, although this wisdom is compatible with the path of cultivation in terms of its attainment (*samanvāgama*), it is incompatible in terms of its actual functioning (*samudācāra*); therefore, it does not arise.
Furthermore, because this knowledge is extremely similar to the objects, aspects, and modes of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
it certainly does not manifest during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Regarding the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of this clear realization (*abhisamaya*), its realms are exclusively the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Question: Why is this wisdom not [associated] with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Answer: Because the formless realm is neither a field nor a vessel for this wisdom, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, if a realm possesses the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), that realm possesses this knowledge (*jñāna*).
Since there is no path of seeing within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this knowledge is likewise absent there.
Question: Following from this discussion, why is it that there is no path of seeing in the formless realm?
Answer: The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is neither a field nor a vessel for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, if a realm possesses the aspect of non-self (*anātman*) directed toward all phenomena as its object, then that realm possesses the path of seeing.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is no path of seeing (darśanamārga) because it lacks the aspect of non-self (anātmanākāra) that takes all phenomena as its object.
Furthermore, in whichever realm the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) regarding the truths of practice exist, in that realm the path of seeing exists.
Because the wholesome roots of the truth of practice (*pratipad-satya*) do not exist within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) there.
Furthermore, in whichever realm the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) exist, in that realm the path of seeing exists; [this is not the case] in the formless realm.
Because the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) do not exist within that realm, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is absent there.
Furthermore, if a realm possesses both patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), that realm possesses the path of seeing;
since the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) possesses knowledge but lacks patience, the path of seeing is absent there.
Furthermore, if a realm possesses both dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), that realm possesses the path of vision (darśana-mārga).
Although subsequent knowledge exists within the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu), because dharma-knowledge is absent there, the path of vision does not exist.
Furthermore, if the elements (dhātu) are balanced in calm abiding and insight,
or if insight is predominant,
then that element possesses the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) because it involves neither increase (*vṛddhi*) nor contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Furthermore, in whichever realm there is knowledge that takes [all objects] as its universal object (*sarvālambana-jñāna*), that realm possesses the path of seeing;
since there is no such universal-object knowledge in the formless realm, there is no path of seeing there.

Because there is no path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) there, the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) cultivated by it is likewise absent. Furthermore, even if this knowledge were to exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it could not be cultivated; thus, it would be useless. Therefore, it is said that it does not exist there, for the cultivation of this knowledge necessarily depends upon the path of seeing.
Because the path of seeing can only cultivate its own level and lower levels, but cannot cultivate higher levels, even if such [higher levels] were to exist, they could not be cultivated.
Furthermore, in the formless realm there is no cause for the path of seeing; accordingly, there is simply no cause for this knowledge there.
As for the stages (*bhūmi*), this wisdom exists within seven stages:
namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the four dhyānas.
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the threshold concentration; [this wisdom is present].
He cultivates the conventional knowledge at the edge of the clear realization of two stages within the path of seeing of one stage.
If he enters the state of rightness and departure from birth based on the first dhyāna,
he cultivates the conventional knowledge at the edge of the clear realization of three stages within the path of seeing of two stages.
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on the intermediate dhyāna,
they cultivate the mundane knowledge at the limit of clear observation (abhisamaya-antika-saṃvṛti-jñāna) belonging to the three stages and the path of seeing (darśana-mārga).
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth by relying on the second dhyāna...
If one enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the third dhyāna,

they cultivate the conventional knowledge at the limit of clear observation (*abhisamaya-antya-saṃvṛti-jñāna*) belonging to five stages while on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and six stages in total.
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on the fourth dhyāna,

they cultivate the mundane knowledge at the limit of the clear observation (abhisamaya-antya-saṃvṛti-jñāna) belonging to six stages of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) and seven stages of the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).
As for its basis:
This wisdom relies upon a body in the desire realm, not on those in the form or formless realms.
Question: Does this wisdom rely upon the body of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana)?
Is it based on the body of a noble one? If so, what is the fault?
If it were based on the body of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), why would it not be called an ordinary person's dharma?
If it were based on the body of a noble one (ārya),
why would the noble one not manifest it?
Some say that this knowledge does not depend upon the body of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
Nor does it rely upon the body of a noble one (ārya), being entirely without reliance.
The critique states: One should not speak thus.
How can that which is called a "wholesome root" (kuśalamūla) be without reliance? It should be stated as follows:
This is because it is cultivated and attained by relying on the bodies of noble ones who follow through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow through the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
Question: If this is so, why does it not manifest?
Answer: Because this wisdom is incompatible with the actual functioning (*samudācāra*) of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Because there is no possibility for it to arise once one has passed the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Even if, during the path of seeing, the path of seeing were not manifest for even a moment, this knowledge would nonetheless arise;
for the path of seeing does not have the characteristic of being interrupted from moment to moment.
Therefore, it is impossible for this knowledge to manifest.
Question: If it does not manifest, how can it be said that this [knowledge] relies upon the bodies of those who practice through faith or through dharma?
Answer: Those bodies are of two kinds.
First, it is the basis for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Second, it is the basis for the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Regarding the path of seeing, it is acquired within the body that serves as its basis; it is both accomplished within that body and manifested therein.
The conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*) is acquired in that body but is neither accomplished nor manifest within that body.
The conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization is both acquired in the body upon which it depends and accomplished within that body, and it is also manifest.
The path of seeing is attained within that body, yet it is not accomplished therein nor is it manifest.
Even if the body upon which this conventional knowledge relies were present during the stage of the path of seeing:
Thus, while this wisdom is accomplished and also manifests in the present, the path of seeing (darśanamārga) is accomplished only in the future;

nevertheless, because one must necessarily give rise to the body that serves as the basis for the path of seeing during the stage of the path of seeing, the accomplishment of the path of seeing also manifests in the present.
This wisdom is accomplished only in the future. If,
at the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one were not to give rise to the body that serves as the basis for the path of seeing,
then there would be no sense of "seeing the noble truths" through the path of seeing, and one would consequently not be a noble being (*ārya*).
Therefore, it necessarily arises as the basis for the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
By means of this, that body attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
consequently, this knowledge never arises again.
Regarding the aspects (*ākāra*):
this wisdom possesses twelve aspects in total.
Specifically, that which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of suffering constitutes the four aspects of suffering.
That which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization of origination functions through the four aspects of origination;
that which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization of cessation functions through the four aspects of cessation.
As for the object:
This wisdom takes as its object the three truths of the three realms.
That which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of suffering takes the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) of the three realms as its object;
that which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear observation of origination (*samudayasatya*) takes the truth of origination of the three realms as its object.
That which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of cessation takes the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) of the three realms as its object.
Question: Does this take [the objects] collectively or individually?
Answer: Individually.
This means that those belonging to the desire realm take as their objects the three truths of the desire realm as appropriate;
those belonging to the form realm take as their objects the three truths of the form and formless realms as appropriate. Some say:
Regarding "collectively taking the desire realm as object":
this refers to taking whichever of the three truths of the three realms is appropriate as an object;
the same applies to the form realm.
Of these two explanations, the former is superior.
This is because, like untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), the factors of the dharma-classification (*dharmapravicaya*) take their respective objects individually.
As for the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*):
This knowledge cultivated at the conclusion of the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of suffering and its origin pertains to all four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*);
that cultivated at the conclusion of the clear observation of cessation pertains only to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
As for this "knowledge," it is exclusively conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Regarding concentration: this wisdom does not coexist with concentration.
Regarding association with faculties:
this wisdom is generally associated with three faculties, namely the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity.
Regarding the past, future, and present:
this knowledge—specifically that cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization of suffering and its origin—takes the three time periods as its object;
that cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization of cessation takes that which is beyond the world (the supramundane) as its object.
Regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate:
this knowledge is exclusively wholesome.

That which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization of suffering and its origin pertains to the three types [of objects] for the desire realm, and pertains to the wholesome and indeterminate for the form realm.
That which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization of cessation (nirodha-abhisamaya) takes only the wholesome as its object.
Regarding its connection to the three realms or its non-connection:
this knowledge is connected to the desire realm and the form realm.
That which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization of the origin of suffering pertains to the desire realm and takes as its object that which is bound to the desire realm;
that which pertains to the form realm takes as its object that which is bound to the form and formless realms.
That which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization of cessation takes as its object that which is unbound.
Regarding those that are neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee:
this knowledge is neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee,
and it takes as its object that which is neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
Regarding those [factors] to be abandoned by seeing, those to be abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned:
this knowledge is abandoned only by cultivation;
that which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of suffering and origin takes as its object those factors to be abandoned by both seeing and cultivation.
That which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization of cessation takes only the non-interruption as its object.
Regarding the statement "taking names as objects and taking meanings as objects":
this wisdom, cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization of suffering and origination, takes both names and meanings as its objects.
That which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization of cessation (nirodha-abhisamaya) takes only the object (artha) as its focal point.
Regarding those that take one's own continuum, another's continuum, or that which is not a continuum as their focal points:
this wisdom cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization of suffering (duḥkha) and origination (samudaya) takes both one's own and others' continua as its focal points.
That which is cultivated at the conclusion of the clear observation of cessation takes non-continuous [objects] as its object.
Regarding those obtained through application, obtained through detachment from defilements, and obtained by birth:
this knowledge is obtained solely through application.
Regarding those produced through hearing, reflection, and cultivation:
this wisdom in the desire realm is produced through reflection,
not through hearing, because it is superior [to the latter].
It is not produced by cultivation because it is indeterminate;
that which belongs to the form realm is produced by cultivation and not produced by hearing because it is superior;
nor is it produced by reflection because there is no wisdom of reflection therein.
Since it enters meditative absorption when one reflects, it belongs to the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
If it were in the five consciousnesses, this wisdom would not belong to the mental level,
because there is no preparatory wholesome state (*prayoga-kuśala*) within the five consciousnesses.
Question: Does this wisdom have maturation (*vipāka*), or is it without maturation?
Answer: It has maturation, because it is wholesome and contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Question: In what place does this wisdom receive its matured fruit?
Answer: Those belonging to the desire realm [attain it] in the desire realm;
those belonging to the form realm in the form realm;
and those in the first dhyāna in the first dhyāna.
Regarding those who have attained up to the fourth dhyāna, [the text states] "in the fourth dhyāna.
Question: It may be so for śrāvakas, since it is possible for them to possess a continuum belonging to the form realm (rūpadhātu);
but how can this be the case for Buddhas and pratyekabuddhas?
It is not that only Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas can have the continuity of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-saṃtāna*) to undergo this maturation (*vipāka*).
The answer is: those individuals (*pudgala*) of that lineage (*gotra*) also previously possessed the continuity of the aggregates, elements, and bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*) of the form realm.
In that way, they successively undergo this maturation (*vipāka*).
Question: If that is so, how can a cause accomplished within the continuum (*saṃtati*) of a noble one (*ārya*) produce a fruit within the continuum of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)?
Answer: It is without fault to accept that such principles constitute cause and effect, as stated in the *Karmaskandha-pāda*:
"If one is bound by both types of fetters—those to be abandoned through vision and those to be abandoned through cultivation—one may go to the evil destinies."
All stream-enterers do not go to the evil destinies because they lack the fetters and bonds to be abandoned by insight, possessing only those to be abandoned by cultivation.
This is because there are two kinds of causes for the evil destinies.
There are two types of fetters: those to be abandoned by seeing and those to be abandoned by cultivation.
Since the fetters to be abandoned by cultivation possessed by stream-enterers are the cause for rebirth in the miserable destinies.
Is it not the case that a cause accomplished within the continuum of an Ārya produces an effect within the continuum of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)?
Therefore, there is no fault in what has been said here.
This statement—that such a thing might occur if the cause and effect are non-arising, but not if they are subject to arising—is correct.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas also possess a continuum of the aggregates, elements, and bases of the form realm, like that of the Śrāvakas, through which they successively receive this maturation fruit of wisdom.
The critique states: Neither of those [positions] should be stated in such a manner.
One should state it thus:
because conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*) is contaminated (*sāsrava*) and determinate (*vyākṛta*), it is said to have maturation (*savipāka*).
Since there is no sense of having already experienced [feeling] or of being about to experience it, one should not question why they do not receive a body as karmic maturation. Question:

Is it possible for two noble ones (*ārya*) born in the same stage to have one who has attained and another who has not attained the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*)?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, one enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth based on the first dhyāna;
another enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth based on the second dhyāna.
Upon the end of that life, they are born together with the second dhyāna.
Those who rely on the first dhyāna do not accomplish this knowledge because they have abandoned it by transcending that level;
those who rely on the second dhyāna do accomplish it.
Because this wisdom arises from its own stage and is not relinquished,
is it possible for two Arhats dwelling in the same stage to have one who has attained conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) while the other has not?
Answer: There are.
That is to say, previously one person, relying on the first dhyāna, entered into the state of rightness and departure from birth;
another, relying on the second dhyāna, entered into the state of rightness and departure from birth.
Upon the end of that life, he is reborn together with the second dhyāna;
while abiding in the intermediate state (antarābhava), he attains the fruit of arhatship.
This is not accomplished by relying on the first dhyāna.
Because this wisdom transcends the stages through relinquishment (*tyāga*),
it is accomplished by relying on the second *dhyāna*.

Because this wisdom arises without relinquishing its own stage, when Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas attain the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), they all cultivate the wholesome roots of the nine stages within the three realms.
Regarding this, why is it said that only the roots of goodness in the desire realm attained by the Tathāgata are mentioned, and not those of others?

The answer is: although in reality all [roots of goodness] are attained, here one intends to speak specifically of the predominant roots of goodness in the desire realm; therefore, those attained by the two vehicles or in other stages are not mentioned.
Question: Do all Arhats, at the time they attain the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), cultivate the wholesome roots of the nine stages within the three realms?
Answer: This is not fixed.
If one born in the desire realm attains the knowledge of exhaustion, they are able to cultivate the [wholesome roots] of the future of the nine stages within the three realms.
When one born in the first *dhyāna* attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), they can cultivate the future [paths] of two realms and eight stages;
this is because when born in a higher stage, one does not cultivate the contaminated (*sāsrava*) states of lower stages.

This continues until, if one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), upon attaining the knowledge of exhaustion, they can cultivate the future [paths] of one realm and one stage.
In this context, because the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) are predominant, they are mentioned specifically;
however, in reality, one cultivates all four aggregates (skandha) or five aggregates.
Question: Is that which is thus cultivated obtained through preparatory effort (prayoga-prāpta), obtained through the removal of defilements (vairāgya-prāpta), or obtained by birth (upapatti-prāpta)?
Answer: It is obtained through detachment from defilements (*vairāgyalābha*) as well as through application (*prayogalābha*),
because it is attained at the time of becoming detached from the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
and because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas also bring it forth through application.
However, it is not acquired by birth, because that [birth-acquired state] is not superior.
Question: Is that which is cultivated here produced through hearing (*śrutamaya*) or produced through reflection (*cintāmaya*)?
Is it produced by cultivation?
Answer: All three types exist.
That is to say, those belonging to the desire realm are produced by hearing and reflection.
That which belongs to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is produced from hearing and cultivation;
that which belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is produced from cultivation alone.
Question: Why is the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*) not produced from hearing?
Are there roots of goodness cultivated at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that are produced through hearing (*śrutamaya*)?
Answer: They are not produced through hearing, because they are the retinue of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), being exclusively intense and cultivated by means of the swift path.

This is the retinue of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); because the knowledge of exhaustion seeks cessation and is a path of composure, it is able to universally cultivate all conditioned wholesome states (*prayoga-kuśala*).
Question: Are such roots of goodness situated in the mental level (*manobhūmi*)?
[Question: Does it exist within the five consciousnesses?
[Answer: It exists only in the mental ground (manobhūmi), because there is no preparatory wholesome state (*prayoga-kuśala*) among the five consciousnesses.
Although there are wholesome states acquired at birth that are not cultivated by this [path], they are therefore exclusively of the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
Question: If these roots of goodness belong exclusively to the mental level, how should one interpret the statement in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*?
As it is said, once an Arhat has attained the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), do the six modes of constant abiding (ṣaḍ-āvenika-dharmāḥ) exist or not?
If they exist, how do they exist?
If they do not exist, how do they not exist?
If they exist, how many are accomplished in the past,
how many are accomplished in the future,
and how many are accomplished in the present?
The answer is: It is said that after an Arhat has seen forms with the eye, he is neither glad nor sad, but dwells constantly in equanimity, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension;
this is explained in detail up until: after he has cognized mental phenomena with the mind.
Neither joyful nor sorrowful, his mind dwells constantly in equanimity, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Once that Arhat has attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), if at first a wholesome visual consciousness arises and becomes present before him.
He accomplishes one of the past, six of the future, and one of the present;
having ceased, he does not abandon it.
If a wholesome ear-consciousness arises and manifests before him, [he accomplishes those same].
He accomplishes two of the past, six of the future, and one of the present.
Once this has ceased and he does not abandon it— up until the point when a wholesome mental consciousness arises and becomes manifest—
he accomplishes six of the past and future and one of the present.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"If, for the first time, a wholesome eye-consciousness arises and manifests before one, that [consciousness] does not exist in the past;
rather, one possesses six in the future and one in the present."
Once this has ceased, it is not relinquished.
If a wholesome ear-consciousness arises and becomes present, he accomplishes one of the past, six of the future, and one of the present;
once this has ceased, it is not relinquished.
Even up to the point where a wholesome mental consciousness arises and becomes present,
one accomplishes five past, six future, and one present [dharmas];
once these have ceased, they are not abandoned.

If, moreover, a wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) or another consciousness arises and becomes manifest, one accomplishes six [consciousnesses] in the past and future, and one in the present.
How is this statement to be reconciled? The answer is: this refers to that which has arisen and ceased within the body of one whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya-viśuddha*).
It is not said that [the roots of goodness] have arisen and ceased since beginningless saṃsāra;
however, what is here stated does not entail the fault of contradiction with the wholesome roots cultivated at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).

Furthermore, there are those who say that the six modes of constant abiding (*ṣaḍ-ābhoga-vihāra*) belong exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmi*), because it is taught that after having seen forms with the eye, up to having cognized phenomena with the mind, one neither rejoices nor grieves, but dwells constantly in equanimity (*upekṣā*) endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension (*smṛti-samprajanya*).
Question: If that is so, why is it further stated that when a wholesome eye-consciousness and so forth are present, one is endowed with one [consciousness] of the present?
Answer: It should be understood that this refers to the constant application (*prayoga*) rather than the constant entity (*bhāva*); therefore, there is no contradiction.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the six modes of constant abiding (*ṣaḍ-ākāra-satata-vihāra*)?
Answer: Their intrinsic nature consists of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
How is this known to be so? As it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Arhats whose minds are well-liberated possess the six modes of constant abiding."
What are the six? They are:
having seen forms with the eye, and so forth up to having cognized phenomena with the mind, one is neither glad nor sad, but dwells with equanimity, possessing mindfulness and clear comprehension.
If one includes the associated and co-existent factors, its intrinsic nature consists of the four aggregates or the five aggregates.
The intrinsic nature has already been explained;
its reason for being so shall now be discussed.
Question: Why is it called "constant abiding"? What is the meaning of "constant abiding"?
Answer: All Arhats constantly abide in these [states] and never depart from them; therefore, they are called "constant abodes.
Question: Do all Arhats possess these six dharmas of constant abiding?
Some maintain this view:
not all arhats possess these six [knowledges].
Specifically, only those who are liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*), having attained the ultimate fourth dhyāna and the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*), possess these six.
The commentary says:
It should be stated that all arhats possess these six.
How is this known to be so?
These six constant abodes all have mindfulness and wisdom within the pure body of one whose outflows are exhausted as their essence.
This is because there are no Arhats who do not achieve this mindfulness and wisdom.
Question: In which realms and stages do these six constant abodes reside?
Some say that these six exist in the desire realm and the form realm, specifically in two stages:
namely, the desire realm and the first dhyāna, as they pertain to the mental stage (*manobhūmi*).
Furthermore, because it enters into and emerges from the same states as wholesome visual consciousness and so forth,
it does not exist in the higher stages. Others, however, say that it exists in five stages.

This means that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) belonging to the desire realm and the five stages of the four dhyānas enters into and emerges from the same objects as the visual consciousness and the others.
The critique states:
one should speak thus.
These two pervade the three realms and eleven stages;

that is to say, because the mental consciousness, mindfulness, and wisdom of the desire realm, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna, the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments are present throughout all these stages.
Question: Are there distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior among these six constant abidings?
Answer: There are.
That is to say, the Tathāgata is the superior.
Among the pratyekabuddhas,
those of the śrāvaka lineage are inferior;
furthermore, those of the immovable dharma lineage are superior.
Those of the *parihāṇadharman* lineage are inferior;
those of the other four lineages are middling.

Question: If both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also accomplish the six constant abidings (*ṣaḍ-ananyathā-vihārāḥ*), why are the three applications of mindfulness (*trayaḥ smṛtyupasthānāḥ*) said to be the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of the Buddha?
Answer: The Buddha constantly proclaims the essential points of the Dharma for the sake of the assembly; because he specifically guides sentient beings, he speaks of them with particular emphasis.
Since śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not possess this function, he does not say they have them.
Furthermore, although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess a small degree [of such qualities], they are not established [as such] because it is not ultimate.
Furthermore, although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have severed greed and anger, they still possess residual habitual tendencies.
If, when the assembly encounters either adversity or favor, one gives rise to corresponding greed, anger, sorrow, or joy, then the three foundations of mindfulness are not established.
Furthermore, there is a difference in the establishment of the six constant abidings compared to the three foundations of mindfulness.
That is to say, the three foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are established based on the assembly [of practitioners],
whereas the six modes of constant abiding (ṣaḍ-ābhoga-vihāra-dharma) are established based on the object.
It is easier not to give rise to sorrow or joy regarding the object.
Because it is difficult [to maintain] among a multitude,
the śrāvakas and others possess the six constant abidings but lack the three applications of mindfulness.
Question: Why is it that at the moment one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), one suddenly cultivates the future wholesome roots of the three realms, and not at other times?
Answer: At that time, the afflictions of the three realms are forever exhausted, and there is nothing further to be done.

Because one must utilize the conventional minds that enter and emerge from meditative absorption to enjoy the various concentrations, at this time one cultivates the roots of goodness of the three realms.
Furthermore, at this time, one permanently abandons the previously unabandoned aggregates of afflictions.
Furthermore, because one has attained for the first time the previously unattained mass of all meritorious qualities,
one is able to suddenly cultivate the roots of goodness of the three realms.
Moreover, at this time, the mind attains the sovereign rank of a king, and the head is bound with the auspicious white silk of liberation.
The roots of goodness of the three realms all come to offer tribute,
just as when one ascends the royal throne for the first time and ties the ceremonial silk band, all the kingdoms come to offer tribute.
Furthermore, at this time, one is able to destroy the enemies of affliction that were previously indestructible.
The roots of goodness of the three realms all come to welcome and congratulate him,
just as when a person has defeated an enemy nation and returns to his own country,
all the people of the land come to welcome and congratulate him.

Furthermore, at that time, the power-wielders of the afflictions—which had previously remained unsubdued—are overcome; consequently, all the roots of goodness within the three realms join in celebration and praise.
It is like a great assembly where, when a powerful wrestler who had never before been defeated is finally subdued, the entire multitude rejoices and offers their acclaim.
Furthermore, at this time, because liberation is ultimately fulfilled,
one is able to cultivate the roots of goodness of the three realms in a transverse manner.

That is to say, from the path of seeing (darśanamārga) gradually up to the diamond-like concentration (vajropamasamādhi), while liberation is not yet fulfilled, one can only cultivate a small portion of those [roots] as appropriate.
When one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), because liberation is perfected, one is able to concurrently cultivate the wholesome roots of the three realms.
It is like a person drawing water to irrigate a field: once one furrow is filled, they proceed to the next, continuing until all the furrows are saturated.
Once all [the roots of goodness] have been filled, the water overflows and flows everywhere to other places.

Furthermore, at this time, because the afflictions that bind them have been exhausted, the roots of goodness of the three realms all attain liberation; their power and function increase and flourish, and for this reason, they are cultivated all at once.
This means that from time immemorial, the wholesome dharmas of the three realms have been constantly bound by afflictions, lacking autonomy and functional power.
Therefore, they cannot be fully cultivated; even when a practitioner becomes free from the defilement of desire, they attain only slight liberation while the remaining fetters are still many.
Even when one is freed from the bonds of the eight grades of afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), although there is much liberation, some slight bondage still remains.

However, when one is freed from the ninth grade of the Peak of Existence, all bonds of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of the three realms are severed; because one has attained mastery, one cultivates everything instantaneously.
It is just as when nine strands of silk or similar materials are bound together: even if one, two, or up to eight are severed, the bundle does not disperse;
only when the ninth is severed does the bundle finally come apart. This case is also like that.

Furthermore, since time immemorial, all wholesome dharmas within the three realms have collectively viewed the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) with revulsion; yet, despite employing many skillful means, they have been unable to sever them.
Now that they are attained and completely severed, one therefore practices them all at once.
Furthermore, through the power of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), which is exceedingly intense, all afflictions (*kleśa*) are forever extinguished;
the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) induced thereby also enables the attainment of all liberations (*vimukti*).
Therefore, in this stage, one is able to cultivate the wholesome roots of the three realms in their entirety.
At the time an Arhat of occasional liberation attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), they are able to cultivate two knowledges and thirty aspects (*ākāra*).
That is to say, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) consists of fourteen aspects, excluding emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and non-self (*anātman*).
The wisdom of the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi-jñāna*) consists of sixteen aspects.

If one has not yet attained the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), or the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), one cultivates each of the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) with all thirty aspects respectively.
If one practices only the thirty aspects of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) within the three formless attainments,

then at the time an Arhat of the "not-timely-liberated" (*asamayavimukta*) type attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), they are able to cultivate three knowledges across forty-four aspects.
That is to say, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) each possess fourteen aspects (*ākāra*);
the knowledge of the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*) possesses sixteen aspects;
and this occurs in each of the four dhyānas, the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
One cultivates forty-four aspects for both the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
If one is in the three formless realms, one cultivates only the forty-four aspects of the subsequent knowledge.
This is called the cultivation of untainted wholesome roots (*anāsrava-kuśalamūla*).
