translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Five, Part Four of the First Aggregate on Miscellaneous Matters: Regarding Shamelessness and Fearlessness. Question: If a mind has passed away, has that mind undergone transformation and disintegration?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was in order to refute the tenets of other schools and to reveal the correct meaning.
That is to say, there are some who hold the view that the past and future lack real substance, while the present is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Because they are deluded and ignorant regarding the three periods of time, they give rise to such a misconception. To refute that view and to reveal that the past, future, and present truly exist as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), [this treatise] is composed.
Furthermore, there are certain non-Buddhists who maintain that when conditioned phenomena proceed through time, their substantial nature and characteristics are merely concealed;
and there are other non-Buddhists who maintain that when conditioned phenomena proceed through time, their substantial nature and characteristics undergo transformation.
There are certain non-Buddhists who maintain that when conditioned phenomena proceed through time, it is their substantial nature (*dravya*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) that move.
To refute this attachment and to demonstrate that conditioned phenomena cease before they arise again, this treatise was composed.
The disintegration of all phenomena is, briefly stated, of two kinds: first, disintegration through time;
second, disintegration through external conditions.
Second is the transformation through principle.
Regarding transformation through time:
this refers to the fact that what was in the past is now transformed and designated as "past."
That which is contrary to principle refers to defiled phenomena,
because all defiled phenomena are in opposition to principle.
A defiled mind of the past possesses both types of transformation;
a non-defiled mind of the past possesses only temporal transformation;
and a defiled mind of the future or present possesses only logical transformation.
A mind that is not defiled is not said to be "transformed and corrupted.
This is the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
Are all minds that have passed away transformed and corrupted?
Answer: All minds that have passed away are subject to transformation and decay.
Specifically, a defiled mind is called "transformed and decayed" because it possesses both types of transformation and decay;
a non-defiled mind is called "transformed and decayed" solely because it undergoes transformation and decay through the passage of time.
There are cases where a mind undergoes corruption, yet that mind is not past;
namely, a future or present mind associated with greed or hatred.
Such a mind is termed a "corrupted mind" solely because it is corrupted by way of its intrinsic nature (*yukti*).
To further substantiate this meaning, another sūtra is cited as spoken by the Blessed One:
"O bhikṣus, even if you are seized by hostile bandits who saw your bodies apart at the joints or sever your various limbs."
You should not allow your minds to become corrupted;
you must also guard your speech and refrain from uttering harsh words.
For if the mind becomes corrupted or harsh words are spoken, they will constitute a profound obstacle to that which you seek for yourselves.
This proves that a mind of hatred is called "corrupted.
"Enemy" refers to an adversary, and "thief" refers to one who robs and steals.
Question: Why is it said only that the limbs of the body are sawn apart?
Answer: This is to demonstrate that [the sword] serves as a cause for manifold suffering.
That is to say, when the body is injured by weapons such as swords and spears, there is pain upon entry but not upon exit, or there is pain upon exit but not upon entry.
If one is being sawn apart, both the entering and exiting of the saw cause suffering;
even toward such extreme suffering, one should not give way to anger,
much less toward minor suffering.
That which one seeks for oneself is a happy rebirth and nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus, you should not give rise to thoughts of transformation or corruption regarding the objects of exquisite sensual desire."
This proves that a mind of desire is called "subject to transformation.
"Exquisite sensual objects" refers to the five types of exquisite sensual pleasures.
A "mind subject to transformation" refers to a mind of sexual desire.

Question: If it is said that when the present reaches the past, the phenomena of the past are called "the world's transformation and decay," then why, when the future reaches the present, are the phenomena of the present not called "the world's transformation and decay"?
Answer: If that which has already undergone transformation and disintegration does not undergo further transformation and disintegration, it is called "worldly transformation and disintegration.
That which is currently undergoing transformation and disintegration will also undergo transformation and disintegration;
therefore, it is not designated as "worldly transformation and disintegration."
Furthermore, if a world possesses both temporal change (*adhvan-pariṇāma*) and the destruction of its functional activity (*kāritra-vināśa*), it is called a "world subject to transformation.
Although the present world possesses temporal change, it lacks the destruction of its functional activity.
Because present phenomena possess functional activity, they are not termed "worldly transformation and decay.
Furthermore, it is commonly accepted in the world that only phenomena already passed and ceased are called "worldly transformation and decay," while the present is not so described.
Therefore, the present is not a transformation through destruction.
Question: Since there is no affliction that does not contradict principle, all should be termed "transformation through principle.
Why, then, do you speak only of the two minds of greed and hatred as being "transformations"?

Answer: This is because the intention of the author of this treatise was such; [this continues] at length until it says: some claim that within this context, one should also state that a mind associated with other afflictions is called "corrupted" (*vipariṇata*).
As for the fact that this is not stated, one should know that the meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Some say that one should not question the intention of the author of the treatise,
because the author composed the treatise based upon the sūtras.
In the Sūtra, it is stated only that a mind associated with greed and hatred is called "corrupted" (*vipariṇata*);
other afflictions are not so described, and for this reason they are not mentioned.
Question: Why did the Blessed One, the author of the treatise, state only that a mind associated with greed and hatred is called corrupted, and not others?

Answer: The Buddha observed that those to be converted would attain awakening and accomplish their tasks upon hearing that the mind associated with greed and hatred is called "subject to transformation and decay" (vipariṇāmadhamma).
Therefore, he spoke of these two specifically, rather than other afflictions.
Furthermore, the Buddha observed these two—the basis for transformation and the object of perception—and therefore spoke of them specifically.
Regarding the basis for the transformation of greed:
when greed is present, the body becomes supple, light, buoyant, and joyful.
Regarding the object of transformation and decay:
when a beloved object appears before one,
at the time when the mind and mental factors are immersed in and attached to it, the basis [of those states] becomes empty, like an insentient thing.

Regarding the basis for the transformation caused by hatred: when hatred manifests, the body becomes coarse, rigid, heavy, and haggard. Regarding the perception of impure objects as pure and exquisite:
[this refers to the transformation caused by attachment]. When hatred is present, the body becomes coarse, rigid, heavy, and withered.
Regarding the object of transformation and decay:
when an object that is loathed appears before one,
the mind and mental factors feel aversion toward it.
One does not wish to face it, much less look upon it;
among what was once beautiful, one now perceives only the loathsome.
Furthermore, the Buddha observed these two states of transformation and decay in color and form, and therefore spoke of them specifically.
Regarding "the color of greed being transformed and corrupted":
when greed becomes manifest, it causes the body that serves as its basis to turn yellow. Regarding "the form being transformed and corrupted":
[it likewise causes the form to change].
If intense greed repeatedly manifests,
the male form disappears and a female form appears;
as for those whose color is transformed by hatred:
If hatred manifests, it causes the body that serves as its basis to change into a different color and to undergo physical disfigurement;
this occurs when predominant hatred repeatedly arises.
The human form perishes and the serpent form arises.
I have heard that there was once a Nirgrantha outsider who,
although he had gone forth as a monk under the Buddha, did not abandon his original views and teachings.
The disciples of the Buddha speak of the various faults within that teaching;
they give rise to intense hatred, and because of this hatred, they transform into venomous snakes.
Furthermore, the Buddha contemplates these two states of transformation and their respective *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class), and for this reason, he speaks specifically of them.
Regarding the stage of transformation through desire:
by the power of desire, there are said to be the distinctions between males and females, as well as between youth, middle age, and old age.
Regarding the transformation of the *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous class), as the Blessed One has said:
There is a class of gods in the desire realm called "Forgetful in Play.
They become so absorbed in their amusements that their bodies grow utterly exhausted and their minds lose mindfulness.
Due to this loss of mindfulness, they pass away.
Regarding the state of transformation through aversion:
by the power of aversion, one also speaks of the distinctions between male and female, as well as childhood, middle age, and old age.
Regarding the transformation of the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class), as the Blessed One said:
There is a class of gods in the desire realm called Manas-krodha (Mind-Anger).
Because of their anger, they stare at one another with eyes like horns;
through this mutual staring, their anger increases further, and after a long time, they pass away.
Furthermore, the Buddha observed that these two [cravings] cause the transformation and decay of one's own body, the bodies of others, and all their requisites;
because they exceed other afflictions in this regard, he spoke of them specifically.
Furthermore, the Buddha observed that these two can give rise to various faults associated with both adverse and favorable conditions.
These are taught specifically because they surpass all other afflictions.
Furthermore, the Buddha observed that these two are the root of strife and dispute, surpassing all other afflictions; therefore, he taught them specifically.
Moreover, they constitute the various profound and heavy faults of the world.
It is primarily because of attachment and aversion that these two are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, these two underlying tendencies (anuśaya) pervade all six consciousnesses and arise through their own power;
for this reason, they are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, these two underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are the root of all afflictions of joy and grief;
moreover, they can give rise to various faults and manifold sufferings based upon the body and mind. For this reason, they are specifically mentioned.
"Does the mind that is defiled by attachment undergo transformation? and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed?
Answer: Because it was previously stated [only] regarding the objects of exquisite sensual desire (*kāmaguṇa*).
One should not give rise to attachment;
one should not give rise to aversion toward the dissolution of the body’s limbs.
Do not claim that only the attachment and aversion abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm are termed "transformation and decay."
This treatise was composed to demonstrate that craving for the three realms and the five classes of craving and hatred are all termed "transformation and disintegration" (*vipariṇāma*).
Do all minds that are defiled by attachment undergo transformation and disintegration?
Answer: All minds that are defiled by attachment undergo transformation and disintegration.
That which is past is called a "changing mind" because it undergoes transformation through both time and principle;
that which is future and present is called a "changing mind" solely because it undergoes transformation through principle.
There is a mind that undergoes transformation and deterioration, yet that mind is not defiled;
this refers to a past mind that is dissociated from greed.
If it is a defiled mind, it is called a "transformed mind" because it undergoes transformation by way of two factors.
That which is non-defiled is called a "corrupted mind" solely because it is corrupted by worldly conditions;
furthermore, a future or present mind associated with hatred is also called a "corrupted mind" because it is corrupted by its very nature.
To prove this point, another sūtra is cited,
as the Blessed One said: "O bhikṣus, even if you are beset by enemies and bandits," and so on at length,
"it constitutes a profound obstacle to what you yourselves seek."
In this context, because it is abbreviated, only the principle of attachment is stated;
one should also say that there is a mind of aversion.
Does every mind that is averse undergo transformation?
Answer: All minds that harbor aversion toward others are corrupted.
Specifically, those of the past are called "corrupted minds" because they are corrupted by two factors;
those of the future and the present are called "corrupted minds" solely because they are corrupted by principle.
There is a mind that undergoes corruption, yet that mind is not characterized by aversion;
this refers to a past mind that is dissociated from hatred.
If it is defiled, it is called a "corrupted mind" because it is corrupted by two factors.
That which is undefiled is called a "corrupted mind" solely because it is corrupted by worldly conditions;
furthermore, a future or present mind associated with greed is also called a "corrupted mind" because it is corrupted by its very nature.
To prove this point, one should also cite a sutra.
As the Blessed One said: "O bhikṣus, you should not give rise to a mind of transformation and decay toward the objects of exquisite desire."

Although all defiled minds are termed "corrupted" (*vipariṇata*), because it is as previously stated, only two types are mentioned. What is "restlessness" (*auddhatya*)? [The passage continues] at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is in order to bring certainty to those who harbor doubts.
That is to say, when the Blessed One taught that restlessness (auddhatya) and remorse (kaukṛtya) are established together as a single hindrance (nīvaraṇa), some may give rise to the doubt:
"Is there no remorse apart from restlessness, or is there no restlessness apart from remorse?"
In order to bring certainty to this doubt,
this treatise was composed to demonstrate that remorse exists apart from restlessness, and that restlessness exists apart from remorse.
What is restlessness?
Answer: When various states of mind are not tranquil, do not cease, and are flighty and agitated—this restless nature of the mind is called *auddhatya* (restlessness).
Herein, the author of the treatise, being skilled in the meanings of synonyms, provides these various explanations.
Although their designations differ, their essence is not distinct.
What is "regret" (*kaukṛtya*)?
Answer: The nature of the mind that is parched, distressed, agitated, and transformed by remorse—that is what is called regret.
The definitions of these terms are as previously explained.
Regarding the question of whether all minds characterized by restlessness (*auddhatya*) are associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*),
the answer is that this should be analyzed through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Because these two have mutually varying scopes of meaning:
there is a state of mind that possesses restlessness (*auddhatya*) but is not associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*),
namely, a mind devoid of remorse yet characterized by agitation.
Namely, the five categories of defiled minds in the form and formless realms;
the four categories of minds abandoned through seeing and the five categories of defiled consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm;
and the defiled mental consciousness dissociated from regret.
There is a state of mind that is associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*) but not with restlessness (*auddhatya*);
namely, a non-defiled mind characterized by regret.
This is often found in those such as bhikṣus who observe the precepts.
For instance, there is this mind when one fails to put away items such as beds and stools that ought to be put away,
or fails to close doors that ought to be closed; furthermore,
such a mind arises based on both merit and non-merit.
In this context, there are four general categories of remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
First, there is remorse that is wholesome arising in regard to what is unwholesome.
Second, there is remorse that is unwholesome arising in regard to what is wholesome.
There are three types of regret that arise in relation to wholesome states;
there are four types of regret that arise in relation to unwholesome states.
Regarding the first category:
It refers, for example, to someone who, having committed an evil deed, feels remorse in their heart, thinking:
"What I have done was not well done; for what reason did I commit this unwholesome act?"
Just as monks who observe the precepts feel regret when they transgress them;
the second case refers to someone who,
having performed a virtuous deed, feels remorse in their mind.
"What I have done was not well done; for what reason did I perform such a useless act?
It is like a preeminent householder who, after giving food to a pratyekabuddha, felt regret in his heart.
"I would rather give this food to my slaves and laborers than bestow it upon those shaven-headed śramaṇas.
As for the third case,
it refers to someone who, having performed a small amount of merit, subsequently feels regret in their heart.
"What I have done was not well done; why did I not perform more of this virtuous deed?
As the Venerable Aniruddha said:
"If I had known that he possessed such majestic power, I should have given even more; what difference does it make whether it is much or little?"
Regarding the fourth case:
it refers, for example, to someone who, having committed a minor evil, feels remorse in their heart, thinking, "What I have done was not well done;
why did I not do less of such a thing?"
For example, butchers and the like, having committed a small evil, repent and do not commit it much again.
Among these four phrases, the first and third are states of mind that possess remorse (*kaukṛtya*) but are not associated with restlessness (*auddhatya*).
There is a state of mind associated with both restlessness (*auddhatya*) and remorse (*kaukṛtya*);
that is, a defiled mind characterized by regret.
This refers to the second and fourth phrases among the aforementioned four.
Question: Why is it that here [in this context] one does not say that a restless mind possesses the quality of remorse, but rather says only that a defiled mind possesses the quality of remorse?
Answer: It is because wherever there is a defiled mind, there is necessarily restlessness; this is established without needing to be stated.
If one speaks of a "restless mind," then there arises doubt as to whether a defiled mind possesses restlessness;
therefore, it is simply said that the defiled mind [itself] is [restless]. For this reason, the second clause of the preceding section states that a non-defiled mind possesses the nature of remorse.
The meaning of non-agitation is not stated as being self-evident.
If one were to say that a non-agitated mind possesses the quality of remorse, then it would follow that doubt is undefiled,
because it may possess agitation.
Previously, only the non-defiled mind was mentioned.
There is also a state of mind that is without restlessness (*auddhatya*) and not associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*), namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Herein, the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is used in its literal sense.
If a phenomenon has already been established and its name already proclaimed, it constitutes the first three phrases;
if its name has not yet been established and not yet proclaimed, it constitutes the fourth phrase.
Therefore, it is said that "the preceding characteristics are excluded."
What, then, is this? It refers to these four propositions within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
The first proposition concerns taking up a mind that is without remorse (*kaukṛtya*) but possesses agitation (*auddhatya*).
The second phrase refers to a mind that is without restlessness but possesses remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
The third phrase refers to a mind that possesses both restlessness and remorse.
Excluding these, the fourth phrase refers to a mind that is neither restless nor possessed of remorse. As for the question, "What is lethargy (*styāna)? and so forth, it is explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the sake of enabling those who harbor doubts to attain certainty, as the Blessed One has said:
Stolidity and drowsiness are established together as a single hindrance because there may arise doubt as to whether there is drowsiness apart from stolidity,
or stolidity apart from drowsiness;
it is for the sake of resolving this doubt.
This treatise is composed because it is shown that there is sleep when one is free from lethargy, and lethargy when one is free from sleep.
What is lethargy?
The answer is: the state of heaviness of the body.
The nature of heaviness of mind;
the body is not pliant,
and the mind is not pliant.
The body is dazed;
the mind is dazed. The body is distressed;
the mind is distressed.
The state of mental dullness and heaviness is called *styāna* (torpor). Herein,
the author of the treatise, being skilled in the meanings of various synonyms, provides these diverse explanations.
Although the descriptions differ, their essence is not distinct.
"Heaviness of the body" (kāya-styāna) reveals the torpor associated with the five sensory consciousnesses;
"heaviness of the mind" (citta-styāna) reveals the torpor associated with the mental consciousness.
By this, it should be understood that the remaining phrases are likewise.
The state of mental torpor and heaviness (*styāna*) indicates that these are all of the nature of mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
What, then, is sleep (*middha*)?
Answer: When various states of mind proceed in a state of sleepiness, torpor, and subtlety, such that the mind is dull and its nature is abbreviated, this is called the "sleeping mind.
By the term "sleeping," it is shown that this [state] is associated exclusively with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The phrase "that which turns toward dullness and subtlety" distinguishes it from the time of awakened cognition and from the meditative attainments without mind.
The phrase "the nature of mental obscurity and contraction" reveals that its intrinsic nature is a mental factor (*caitta*).
By specifying "contraction," it excludes those associated with the five sensory consciousnesses.
Setting aside the various meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and the conceptualizing mind (*manovijñāna*),
if a certain state of mind is characterized by lethargy (*styāna*), is that mind associated with sleep (*middha*)?
One should respond by means of four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Because these two have mutually varying degrees of breadth and narrowness,
there are cases where the mind possesses *styāna* (sloth-torpor) but is not associated with *middha* (drowsiness);
that is to say, there is a state of mind without drowsiness that nonetheless possesses the nature of *styāna*.
Namely, all defiled minds of the form and formless realms,
as well as all defiled minds during the waking state in the desire realm;
there are states of mind that possess sleep but are not associated with torpor.
This refers to a non-defiled mind that possesses the nature of sleep;
specifically, it is the mental consciousness associated with sleep that is wholesome or unobscured-neutral within the desire realm.
There is also a state of mind that possesses both lethargy and is associated with sleep.
This refers to a defiled mind possessing the nature of sleep;
that is, the defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the desire realm associated with sleep.
The question and answer regarding this are as previously explained in the section on restlessness (*auddhatya*) and remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
There is a state of mind that is without lethargy and is also not associated with torpor;
this refers to the exclusion of the aforementioned characteristics.
Herein, the term "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) is used as a synonym for "mark" (nimitta).
If a phenomenon has already been established and its name already proclaimed, it constitutes the first three phrases;
if its name has not yet been established and has not yet been proclaimed, it constitutes the fourth phrase.
Therefore, it is said that "the preceding characteristics are excluded."
What, then, is this? It refers to these four permutations within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
The first [permutation] concerns a mind that possesses lethargy (*styāna*) but lacks sleep (*middha*).
The second phrase refers to a mind that has sleep but lacks torpor;
the third phrase refers to a mind that has both torpor and sleep;
excluding these, the remaining minds that have neither torpor nor sleep constitute the fourth phrase.
"Should sleep be said to be wholesome? and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Because it was previously stated that sleep has the nature of mental dullness and contraction (*samkṣepa*).
It has not yet been stated whether this is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Now, wishing to explain this, the following treatise is composed:
Should sleep be said to be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
Answer: Sleep should be said to be either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
This is because, at the time of sleep, the mind and mental factors are of these three types.
How is it wholesome?
This refers to the state in which a wholesome mind proceeds in a manner that is drowsy, subtle, and faint, characterized by a dull and abbreviated nature.
Because one habitually practices and engages in various wholesome deeds while awake, the mind continues to function accordingly even during sleep and dreams.

Just as one who, while in the state of existence (pūrvabhava), was accustomed to and fond of practicing various wholesome deeds will continue to follow that inclination even in the state of death (maraṇabhava) or the intermediate state (antarābhava),
so it is in this case as well.
Question: Are the wholesome dharmas that arise during sleep and dreams acquired through application (*prāyogika*) or acquired by birth (*upapattilābhika*)?
Answer: They are exclusively acquired by birth, because [the mind] is dull and subtle.
Other masters say:
It is also a wholesome state of application (*prayoga-kuśala*), because it involves the discernment of both words and meanings.
What is unwholesome?
It refers to the nature of mental dullness and contraction that arises when an unwholesome mind functions in a state of sleep, torpor, or faintness.
Because one habitually engages in unwholesome deeds during the waking state, these tendencies continue to manifest even within dreams;

just as one habitually engages in unwholesome deeds while in the state of existence (*pūrvabhava*), those same tendencies continue to manifest within the state of death (*maraṇabhava*) or the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
This case is also like that.
Question: Are the unwholesome states arising within this sleep and dream abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) or abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
Answer: They are abandoned by both.
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to the state in which the indeterminate mind proceeds in a state of sleep, torpor, and subtlety, characterized by a nature of mental dullness and contraction.
Because one was habituated to engaging in indeterminate matters during the waking state, the mind continues to proceed accordingly even within dreams.

Just as one who, while in the state of existence (*pūrvabhava*), habitually practices and delights in recording things that do not exist, continues to act accordingly within the state of death (*maraṇabhava*) or the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
so it is here as well.
Question: Regarding this neutral state that arises during sleep and dreams, is it obscured (*nivṛta*) or unobscured (*anivṛta*)?
Answer: It possesses both types.
Regarding the obscured-unspecified:
this refers to sleep associated with the two views of self-identity and extremes within the desire realm.
Regarding the unobscured-unspecified: [it refers to...]

This refers to those [actions] belonging to the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*), the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), but not those that are the fruit of supernormal powers (*abhijñāphala*).
Regarding the modes of deportment:
these are, for example, when one in a dream thinks to oneself that one is walking and so forth.
Regarding the "sphere of craftsmanship" (śailpasthānika),
it is, for example, like when one in a dream thinks they are painting and so forth.
Regarding that which is "born of maturation" (vipākaja):
In the state of sleep or dreaming, there occurs the transformation of other neutral [states] besides those previously mentioned;
some other masters say that it is exclusively of the nature of maturation (*vipākaja*).

In this state of sleep, because it is an unobscured-neutral state and the mind is so clouded that it does not initiate bodily or vocal actions, there are no modes of deportment (īryāpatha) nor any craftsmanship (śailpasthānika).
Regarding the question of whether merit increases during dreams, and so forth, the full explanation is as follows.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was stated previously that sleep can be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;
however, it has not yet been explained how merit increases during dreams and so forth.
Now, wishing to explain this, I have composed this treatise.
One should ask: can it be said that merit increases within a dream?
"Does non-merit increase?
Does neither merit nor non-merit increase?
Answer: "In a dream, one should say [they do not]."
Either merit increases,
or non-merit increases,
or neither-merit-nor-non-merit increases.
In some places it is said that "attainment" (prāpti) is called "increase" (vṛddhi);
in other places it is said that "arising" (utpāda) is called "increase.
In which place is it said that attainment is called increase?
As stated in the *Skandhaprakaraṇa*:
Why is it that when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) falls away, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through both seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*) increase,
whereas for a disciple of the Blessed One (*bhagavataḥ śrāvaka*), when falling away, only the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation increase?
In that context, it is said that "increase" (vṛddhi) is so named.
Where is it said that "arising" (utpāda) is named "increase"?
As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*: [text follows].
When the latent tendency of sensual desire arises in an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), five factors necessarily arise:
first, the latent tendency of sensual desire;
second, the growth and production of the latent tendency of sensual desire.
1. The underlying tendency of ignorance;
2. the arising and growth of the underlying tendency of ignorance;
3. restlessness.
In that context, "arising" is termed "growth.
Here, however, the volition capable of grasping agreeable and disagreeable fruits and so forth is termed "growth," because it is able to grasp its respective fruit accordingly.
Regarding the increase of merit:
it is as when one performs meritorious acts such as giving, observes the fast and precepts,
or engages in any other such form of merit within a dream, whereby that merit continues to evolve.
What is that matter?
At the time of his subsequent realization, through the power of his excellent resolve,
it manifests in his dreams as if those virtuous events were occurring once again.
Therefore, just as during the waking state one is said to "increase" by being able to grasp the fruit of what is loved—
namely, if during the waking state one practices giving well,
whether by means of food and drink, or clothing, bedding, medicine, dwellings, and so forth.
One gives gifts to others;
through the power of familiarity with this resolute conviction, even in dreams, it manifests as if one were performing such deeds again.
If one performs meritorious actions well during the waking state, [the same occurs].
Some diligently attend to the affairs of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, as well as roads, bridges, groves, flowers, fruits, ponds, and merit-houses;
others delight in tending to the sick and serving those of virtue.
Or, one may cultivate merit such as by organizing a five-year great assembly;

through the power of familiarity with this resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), it will manifest in dreams as if such deeds were being performed. Furthermore, if during the waking state one observes the eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*) and various other precepts.
This refers to the seven classes of discipline, such as that of the bhikṣus.
Due to the power of familiarity and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) gained through this practice, these activities appear in dreams as if they were being performed.
If, during the waking state, one delights in reciting, listening, questioning, explaining, teaching, reflecting upon, and discerning the words and meanings of the Tripiṭaka;
Due to the power of familiarity with this resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), even within dreams, it manifests as if those very practices were being performed.
This applies whether one cultivates the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) during the waking state,
or engages in other contemplative practices such as mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) or the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
By virtue of the power of familiarity with this resolute conviction (*adhimukti*),
that which was cultivated appears as such even within dreams.
Through the power of such resolute conviction, meritorious karma also increases within dreams.
Regarding the increase of non-merit:
for example, as if in a dream one commits the taking of life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, or drinking intoxicants;
or otherwise, any one of these non-meritorious acts continues to evolve within the mental continuum.
What is the meaning of this?
Because at the time of awakening from sleep, the power of that negative resolve causes the dream to appear as if those same negative events were occurring again;
thus, just as grasping at undesirable results during the waking state is said to be "growth," so it is here.
That is to say, when awake, one delights in taking the lives of others, such as a butcher of sheep;
or in taking what is not given, such as a robber;
or in sexual misconduct, such as an adulterer.
Or they may deliberately speak falsehoods, such as giving false testimony;
or drink various intoxicants, like those addicted to wine;
or engage in other acts such as beating, reviling, and slandering others, acting as buffoons, singing, and consuming flesh and blood, being greedily attached to the five desires.
One increases such things as malice toward the Triple Gem, arrogance, wrong views, and envy;
because of the power of familiarity with these through the force of one's resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), they manifest in dreams as if being performed once again.
Therefore, even non-meritorious actions increase within a dream.
Regarding the increase of that which is neither meritorious nor non-meritorious:
what is the nature of the continuous succession of states that are neither meritorious nor non-meritorious occurring within a dream?

Because at the time of subsequent realization, by the power of one's resolute conviction (adhimukti) that [the dream] was neither virtuous nor non-virtuous, it manifests again in the dream as resembling that very object;
therefore, just as during the waking state, the grasper is said to increase when it can take as its fruit that which is neither undesirable nor not undesirable.
That is to say, when one is awake, whether engaged in the modes of deportment,
the arts and crafts, or tasks such as plowing, sowing, and carrying loads,
through the power of familiarity and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), these activities continue to manifest in dreams as if they were being performed.
Therefore, even non-meritorious and non-non-meritorious karma can increase within a dream.
Question: If merit increases within a dream, why did the Buddha say that for a fool, there is no fruit or ripening while asleep?

Answer: Just as a person, while awake, is able to perform various tasks such as farming and sowing, but cannot do so while asleep, so too, while awake, one is able to cultivate various kinds of superior wholesome karma.
This refers to the ability to read, recite, hear, explain, and bestow [the teachings], as well as the discernment of the words and their meanings;

it includes the cultivation of the meditation on impurity, mindfulness of breathing, and so forth—the individual and collective foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

One enters into the determination of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) to attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), up to and including the attainment of the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*),
or is able to cultivate the superior karmas of humans and devas;
since none of these can be accomplished during sleep, it is said that there is no ripening of fruit (*vipāka*) during sleep.
Therefore, the Venerable Vasumitra said:
"Because the meritorious karma performed during sleep yields little fruit, it is said to be 'fruitless,' but this does not mean it is entirely without fruit.
Question: If non-merit does not increase within a dream, why did the Buddha say, "It would be better to sleep than to give rise to evil thoughts"?

Answer: It is like a person who, while awake, frequently gives rise to various kinds of predominant unwholesome thoughts, which do not occur while asleep; it is for this reason that such a statement was made.
It does not mean that no demerit whatsoever increases during dreams.
Question: Can virtuous or non-virtuous karma performed in a dream project a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*)?
Answer: It cannot.
This is because it is clear karma that can project a homogeneous class of beings, whereas that [karma performed in a dream] is obscure and weak.
Some say that it can also [do so];
that is to say, it can induce the inferior *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous class) of creatures such as grubs and earthworms, but not other superior ones.
The critique states: "Those who speak thus [are correct]."
One should not speak in this way;
it is better as previously stated:
during sleep, one can only create completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*), not projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*).
Because its nature is dull and inferior as it evolves under the power of others,
it nevertheless attains the maturation of the five aggregates of the desire realm.
What dharma is designated by the name "dream," and so forth, as explained at length?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Although the function of dreams was previously explained, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) had not yet been discussed; it is now intended to explain that.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of refuting the positions of other schools and to reveal the correct meaning.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that dreams do not truly exist;
for instance, the Dārṣṭāntikas (Dṛṣṭāntavādins) assert this.
In a dream, one sees oneself eating and drinking until full, with all the sense faculties satisfied and joyful;
yet upon waking, one is hungry and thirsty, and the body’s strength is exhausted and frail.

In a dream, one sees oneself surrounded by kinsmen and entertained by the sounds of the five musical instruments, experiencing joy and pleasure; yet upon waking, none of it remains, and one dwells alone in sorrow and emaciation.
While dreaming, one sees oneself surrounded by the fourfold army and running hither and thither, yet upon waking, one is at ease.
From this, it should be known that the dream is not truly existent.
This is to refute their attachment [to the dream] and to demonstrate that the dream does indeed exist.
If dreams were not real, they would contradict the sūtras.
As a sūtra says: "When I was a bodhisattva, in a single night I had five great dreams.
Furthermore, another sūtra says: "The Great King Prasenajit, in a single night, had ten great dreams."
The Vinaya states that King Kṛkī had fourteen dreams in a single night. Furthermore,
a sūtra records that the mother of Nandika came and addressed the Buddha, saying:
After my husband had passed away due to his violation of the precepts, he appeared to me in a dream at night.
Manifesting in the form of his former body, he said to me, "You are my wife;
you should perform our former duties."
“World-Honored One, at that time I had no thoughts of any other kind whatsoever; not for a single moment did I comply with his mind.
The World-Honored One said, “Excellent, excellent!
You are one who has attained the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmin); how could you again be defiled by such matters of desire?”
Furthermore, a sūtra states: "You should sever those phenomena that are like a dream.
What are these phenomena? They are the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
Furthermore, a verse from the Gāthās says:
"Just as one does not see the people encountered in a dream upon waking,
so too, after death, one no longer sees those who were beloved."
If dreams were not real, they would contradict what has been stated here.
For this reason, this treatise is composed.
What phenomenon is designated by the term "dream"?
Answer: During sleep, the mind and mental factors operate upon their objects.
Having awakened, one subsequently recollects them and is able to say to others, "I have seen such and such things in a dream"; this is what is called a dream.
Question: If one sees something in a dream and does not remember it upon waking, or even if one remembers it, cannot describe it to others—is that still considered a dream?
Answer: That too is a dream, but it is incomplete.
If it is complete, it is as described here.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a dream?
Answer: Its intrinsic nature consists precisely of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) at the time of dreaming.
Some say that its intrinsic nature is the mind (*manas*), because by the power of the mind, the mental factors (*caitta*) arise and apprehend dream-objects.
Other masters say that its intrinsic nature is mindfulness (*smṛti*), because by the power of mindfulness, one recollects after having awakened and explains it to others.

Some say that the five aggregates of clinging constitute its intrinsic nature, because at the time of dreaming, the various aggregates mutually support one another to bring about the dream-object. Others, however, say:
Because all phenomena have the nature of a dream, as they are all objects perceived by the dreaming mind.
The critique states:
although each of these explanations has its own meaning, the first explanation is superior in terms of logical principle.
This is because it is stated therein that during sleep, the mind and mental factors operate with respect to their objects.
This indicates that when the mind and mental factors operate clearly toward their objective referents during sleep, this is called a dream; no other state is so described.
Question: Since dreams occur in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and not in the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñānakāya*), how can one see forms and other objects within a dream?
Some offer this explanation:

these spirits and deities first manifest signs of good or bad fortune to the person; although [the dreaming mind] occurs in the mental consciousness, it takes forms and other objects as its objective conditions (*ālambana*).
The Venerable Ghosaka spoke thus:
"By the very nature of things, one is able to see signs of future auspiciousness or inauspiciousness within a dream;
having mastered the matter of dreams, he composed a manual on dreams."
The various sages speak thus.
The Venerable One says:
although the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, do not exist within a dream and cannot see forms and so forth, it is nevertheless by means of the mental ground [that they occur].
When the force of sleep has weakened, one sees forms and so forth in dreams,
such as the dream events seen by the mother of Nandika.
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke thus.
One sees the events of a dream due to five causes and conditions,
as stated in that verse:
"Due to doubt, habitual practice, conceptualization, previous experience, and recollection."
Nor is it induced by a person; one should know that dreams arise from five conditions.
The *Āyurveda* states that one sees forms and so forth in dreams due to seven causes.
As that verse says:
"Through what was previously seen, heard, or experienced; through longing, as well as conceptualization;
and through future existence and various illnesses—these seven conditions, one should know, give rise to dreams."
One should explain that there are five conditions for seeing things in a dream:
first, being induced by others.
This refers to dreams induced by gods, sages, spirits, ghosts, incantations, medicinal herbs, the thoughts of those who are powerful, or by noble and holy beings.
Second, by way of prior experience:
that is, having previously seen, heard, perceived, or known such a thing,
or having formerly habituated oneself to various activities, one now sees them in a dream.
Third, by way of what is to come:
that is to say, when auspicious or inauspicious events are about to occur, it is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that one first sees their signs in a dream.
Fourth, by way of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*): that is to say, if one contemplates, yearns for, or harbors doubt regarding something, one then sees it in a dream.
Fifth, due to various illnesses:
that is to say, when the great elements (mahābhūta) are out of harmony, one sees in dreams things corresponding to whichever element has increased.
Question: In which realms, destinies, or locations do such dreams occur?
Answer: Dreams exist in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), not in the form or formless realms, because sleep does not exist there.
Within the desire realm:
Some maintain this view:
dreams exist in the four destinies, with the sole exception of the hells,
because beings there lack sleep due to the oppression of suffering.
One should say that dreams can also occur in the hells,
as stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
"In the Saṃjīva hell, although beings are oppressed by heat until their flesh and bones are scorched and putrefied, there are times when they are fanned by cold winds."
Or, perhaps when the hell-wardens cry out "Live!", they immediately return to life and their flesh and bones are restored;
their experience of suffering pauses briefly and a small measure of pleasure arises.
From this, it is known that sleep can indeed occur, and by means of this, dreams may arise.
Question: What kind of *pudgala* experiences dreams?
Answer: Both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) experience dreams.
Among the noble ones, everyone from those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) up to arhats and pratyekabuddhas likewise all experience dreams.
Except for the World-Honored One. Why is this?
A dream is like an inversion; since the Buddha has already completely severed all inversions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), he has no dreams.
Just as the mind and mental factors function without inversion during the waking state, so it is also during sleep.
Question: Does the Buddha also experience sleep?
Answer: He does.
How is this known to be so?
Because it is stated in the sūtras. As the sūtra states:
The Vatsiputriyas came to where the Buddha was and asked this question:
"Venerable Gautama, do you experience sleep?
The Blessed One replied:
"O Aggivessana, you should know that when I am extremely hot, I eat to relieve my exhaustion and also sleep for a while.
He then addressed the Buddha again:
"In this world, there is a class of śramaṇas and brahmins who speak as follows:"
"One who possesses sleep is one who is deluded;
will such a thing not apply to the Venerable Gautama?
The Blessed One replied:
If one sleeps while the outflows (*āsrava*), defilements (*saṃkleśa*), and the subsequent fruits of suffering—
birth, old age, sickness, and death— have not been abandoned or fully understood, such a person may be called deluded. Regarding these outflows, defilements,
and the subsequent fruits of suffering— birth, old age, sickness, and death— the Buddha [has already abandoned them].
Because it has been abandoned and fully understood,
even though sleep is present, it is not termed delusion (*moha*).
Nevertheless, there are briefly two kinds of sleep.
First, those that are defiled;
second, those that are non-defiled.
As for all defiled [phenomena], the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and others have already abandoned them and fully understood them.
Because those who are undefiled act for the sake of self-discipline, even the Buddhas appear before them, let alone others who have not yet awakened;
thus we know that even the Buddhas possess sleep.
Therefore, sleep exists throughout all five realms of existence;
it also exists in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, even for those within the womb or egg whose sense faculties and bodily parts are already fully developed, sleep is present.
Question: Are the things seen in a dream those previously experienced (*anubhūta*) or not previously experienced?
If so, what is the fault?
If they were previously experienced, [what follows]?
How is it that one dreams of a person with horns?
Has there ever been a time when a person was seen to have horns?
Furthermore, how are the statements in the sūtras to be reconciled?
As it is said, a bodhisattva once had five great dreams in a single night:
first, he dreamed that his body lay upon the great earth with his head resting on Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains,
while his right hand stirred the western great ocean.
With his left hand he stirred the eastern great ocean,
and with his two feet he stirred the southern great ocean;
second, in his dream he saw auspicious grass named "Firm."
From the center of his navel it emerged, gradually rising higher and expanding until it completely covered the void.
Third, he dreamed that various insects and birds with white bodies and black heads crawled up the Bodhisattva’s feet as far as his kneecaps, only to fall back down again.
Fourth, he dreamed that four-colored birds came from the four directions to the Bodhisattva’s side and all became a single color.
Fifth, he dreamed that he was walking back and forth upon a mountain of excrement and filth without being defiled.
At what point did the Bodhisattva previously experience such a thing that he could see it in a dream?
If the matter seen in the dream was not previously experienced,
how is it that the Bodhisattva is not subject to delusion?
Some say that all things seen in a dream have been previously experienced. Question:
If this is so, how is it that one sees a person with horns in a dream?
"Has it ever been seen that a person has horns?
He replied, "In the waking state, one sees the person in one place and sees the horns in another place."
There is no fault, because one sees [the object] as being in a single location due to the confusion of dreaming.
Furthermore, there are creatures in the great ocean that resemble humans and have horns upon their heads; such things have been seen before.
Now, returning to the dream, it was seen that because all types of sentient beings pervade the great ocean, it is called the "great ocean.
One asks: how, then, are the five dreams of the Bodhisattva to be reconciled?
Has a bodhisattva ever performed such an act before?
Answer: Yes, there have been two instances.
First, one that was witnessed.
Second is "having previously heard it.
Although the Bodhisattva had not previously seen [these things] in the past, because he had previously heard of them, he now sees them in a dream.
Question: When did the Bodhisattva hear of such matters?
Answer: In the past, he practiced the holy life under the teachings of various Buddhas.
Those Buddhas also once saw this matter in dreams and expounded it for him; because he heard it from them, he now sees it in a dream.
Some say that even at the beginning of the eon, there were people who dreamed of such things,
and from their oral tradition the Bodhisattva heard them.
For this reason, one now dreams of them once again.
Furthermore, some say that what is seen in a dream is not necessarily something previously experienced.
Question: If that is so, how is it that the bodhisattva is not subject to inversion?
Answer: Because this is a precursor to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is not subsumed under inversion.
Question: By whom were the various manuals on dream interpretation composed?
Answer: They were composed by sages.
They composed these books by recollecting past events through the power of the knowledge that recollects former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*).
Question: That wisdom cannot observe future objects;
observing future objects is the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna).
That [wisdom] lacks the knowledge resulting from aspiration.
How is it that one can compose manuals for interpreting dreams regarding future events?
Answer: It is because they infer future dream-events through analogy;
that is to say, they observe that those who have seen such dreams in the past experienced such-and-such results.
The same is true now.
By this inference, one knows that those who have such dreams in the future shall likewise experience such results;
therefore, they are able to compose various manuals on dream interpretation.
Some say that there are also sages who have attained the knowledge of sublime aspirations (praṇidhijñāna),
and it was they who composed this book for the sake of enabling sentient beings to avoid dangers and calamities.
Question: Between the objects of dreams and the objects of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), which is more numerous?
Answer: Dream-objects are more numerous;
they are not the objects of the knowledge of recollecting past lives in the fourth dhyāna.
Why is this? Because the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) in the fourth dhyāna can only recollect up to three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*),
whereas in a dream one can know the events of incalculably incalculable great eons (*asaṃkhyeyāsaṃkhyeya-mahākalpa*).
Someone asked: "Is it possible to know the events of countless, countless great eons without entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) or giving rise to supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*)?
He replied: "It is possible;
namely, by means of dreams. As the Blessed One said: "You should sever those phenomena that are like dreams."
What is this phenomenon?
It refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
For what reason are the aggregates of clinging said to be like a dream?
Answer: Because they are momentary in nature;
because they do not endure for long;
and because they deceive sentient beings.
Because they are subject to destruction;
because their nature is emptiness;
and because they are difficult to satiate.
Explained as being like a dream.

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Five: The Remainder of the Chapter on Shamelessness and Lack of Remorse within the First Aggregate of Miscellaneous Topics. As stated in the Sūtras, there are five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
The various hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are subsumed within the five hindrances;
the five hindrances, in turn, are subsumed within the various hindrances, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is in order to enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
As stated in the Sūtra, there are five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*):
first, the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*).
2. The hindrance of ill will;
3. The hindrance of sloth and torpor;
4. The hindrance of restlessness and remorse.
Regarding the five hindrances of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*): some may raise the objection that there are only five hindrances and that ignorance (*avidyā*) is not one.
This is intended to ensure that this doubt is resolved with certainty.
This demonstrates that, in addition to the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), there is a sixth,
namely the hindrance of ignorance (*avidyā-nīvaraṇa*).
For this reason, this treatise was composed.
Are the various hindrances subsumed by the five hindrances?
Are the five hindrances subsumed by the various hindrances?
Do the various hindrances and the five hindrances mutually subsume one another?
The five hindrances do not encompass all hindrances; what, then, is not encompassed?

It refers to the hindrance of ignorance (*avidyā-nīvaraṇa*). Because the hindrances are manifold, they can encompass the five hindrances; because the five hindrances are few, they do not encompass all hindrances.
Just as a large vessel can cover a small vessel,
but a small vessel cannot cover a large one,
so too, although the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) is also an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*).
Because it is weighty, it is not included among the five hindrances;
the Blessed One established it separately as the sixth hindrance.
This is because the power of the preceding five hindrances is equal [to one another].
Because ignorance is predominant, it is explained separately.
To substantiate this meaning, another sutra is cited,
as the Blessed One said:
Covered by the veil of ignorance and bound by the fetter of craving, both the foolish and the wise alike experience such a conscious body.
[Question: Is ignorance both a veil and a fetter?
Craving is both a fetter (*saṃyojana*) and an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*).
Why, then, is it said here that ignorance (*avidyā*) is only an obscuration,
while craving is only a fetter?
Answer: Ignorance (*avidyā*) should also be called a fetter (*saṃyojana*) and should also be called an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*);
that it is not so stated should be understood as an incomplete teaching (*sāvasesa-vacana*).
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to manifest various literary styles and various explanations.
If one employs various literary styles and various explanations, the meaning will be easy to understand and easy to receive and uphold; otherwise, it would be cumbersome and confusing.
Furthermore, it is intended to manifest two gates, and so forth, as explained at length.
Just as ignorance is described as an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*),
craving (*tṛṣṇā*) should be understood in the same way.
Just as craving is taught as a fetter (*saṃyojana*), so too should ignorance (*avidyā*) be understood;
this is to demonstrate two aspects, and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, ignorance is taught specifically as an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*).
Craving is designated only as a fetter (*saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, because ignorance has many meanings of "obscuration" (*nīvaraṇa*) and few meanings of "fetter," it is described only as an obscuration;
whereas craving has many meanings of "fetter" and few meanings of "obscuration," it is described only as a fetter.
Furthermore, because the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*) is heavy while the meaning of fetter (*saṃyojana*) is light, it is described only as a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).
Because the meaning of the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) is heavy while the meaning of hindrance is light, it is described only as a fetter.
Furthermore, the meaning of "covering" (*chādana*) is the meaning of "hindrance."

Among all afflictions (*kleśa*), there is no second affliction capable of obscuring the eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*) of sentient beings as much as ignorance (*avidyā*); therefore, it is designated as a "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*).
The meaning of "binding" (*bandhana*) is the meaning of "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).

Among all afflictions (*kleśa*), there is no second affliction that binds sentient beings to remain long in birth and death (*saṃsāra*) like craving and attachment; therefore, it is called a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).
All classes of sentient beings are blinded by the veil of ignorance (*avidyā-āvaraṇa*) and bound by the fetter of craving.
They are unable to abandon the cycle of birth and death to head toward nirvana;
it is like a person who encounters two enemy bandits,
one of whom binds their hands and feet.
Second, they smear their eyes with dust;
thus bound, the person’s vision is obscured,
and they are unable to escape to a place of safety.
Sentient beings are likewise:
shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving,
they are unable to abandon the cycle of birth and death to head toward nirvana.
In this regard, two parables concerning enemies and robbers should be told.
Formerly, there were two robbers:
one was named Ilī and the other was named Śeṣa.
They constantly traveled and stayed together.
When they encountered a wealthy man, one bound his hands and feet while the other blinded him with dust, and they took his wealth and departed.
The man was thus bound and could see nothing.
In that very place, they suffer until death;
sentient beings are likewise,
for being shrouded and bound by ignorance and craving, they sink and wander in saṃsāra.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghosaka said:
"All classes of sentient beings, blinded by ignorance and bound by craving,
dwell for a long time in saṃsāra, increasing unwholesome dharmas."

Therefore, it is for this reason that ignorance (avidyā) is specifically designated as an "obscuration" (nīvaraṇa), while craving (tṛṣṇā) is specifically termed a "fetter" (saṃyojana); thus, their respective definitions are well-established.
However, because the power and function of the obscuration of ignorance are particularly predominant—being superior to the other five—the Buddha did not include it among the five obscurations.
Because the power of the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is equal in all respects.
[The sūtra asks: "Do the hindrances cover those [states]? and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed?
Answer: Previously, based on the principles of the *Vinaya* (Pātimokkha), the sixth hindrance, ignorance (*avidyā*), was established separately from the five hindrances.
Now, however, based on the principles of the *Abhidharma*, it is asserted that all afflictions (*kleśa*) are none other than hindrances.
Because the meaning of "obscuration" (*nīvaraṇa*) is the sense of covering and obstructing,

all afflictions (*kleśa*) are capable of obscuring and obstructing both the Noble Path and the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) that serve as the preparatory application for the Noble Path; therefore,
they are all termed "hindrances."
For this reason, the following treatise is further composed:
Are all hindrances (nīvaraṇa) also obscurations (paryavasthāna)?
One should respond by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
In this context, "hindrances" (nīvaraṇa) are explained according to their essential nature and characteristics.
The five, beginning with sensual desire,
whether past, future, or present, are all without exception of the nature and characteristics of the five hindrances as established.
All are termed "obscuring factors" (nīvaraṇa).
Among these, "concealment" (mrakṣa) is explained in terms of its function:
because all afflictions possess the function of concealing when they are present, it is called concealment.
Because past and future [states] lack an unobscured function (*anivṛta-kāritra*), they are not termed "obscuring" (*nivṛta*).
Since these two categories differ in their mutual breadth and narrowness, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established.
There are those that are hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) but not obscuring.
This refers to the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) of the past and future.
Because they possess the essential characteristic of being hindrances, they are called "hindrances";
however, because they do not perform the function of obscuring, they are not called "obscurations" (paryavasthāna).
Because the activity of the past has already ceased and the future has not yet arisen.
Question: Does the past conceal the past continuum?
The future obscures the continuity of the future,
and the present obscures the continuity of the present. Why,
then, is it said here that the past and the future are obscurations (*nīvaraṇa*) rather than concealments (*chādana*)?

Answer: If explained in terms of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena, concealment (*paryavasthāna*) pervades the three periods of time, because the intrinsic nature of phenomena pervades the three periods of time.
If explained in terms of the person (*pudgala*), concealment pertains only to the present.
Because the *pudgala* exists only in the present;

that is to say, the *pudgala* is established only with respect to the phenomena of the present aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), and not with respect to those of the past or future.
This is because those [past and future phenomena] fall under the category of "phenomena" (*dharma*) and are not sentient beings (*sattva*).
Now, because the meaning of *mrakṣa* (concealment) is established solely in dependence upon that *pudgala*, it exists only in the present.
Furthermore, since it has already been stated previously that *mrakṣa* is established based on its functional activity (*kāritra*), this should not be raised as an objection.
There are obscured [states] that are not hindrances;
this refers to the manifestation of all other afflictions with the exception of the five hindrances.
Furthermore, what are these?
This refers to all afflictions of the form and formless realms;
and in the desire realm, those envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) that are not subsumed under the views, pride, ignorance, or the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), when they manifest before one.
These are called concealment (*mrakṣa*) but not hindrances.
Question: Why is it said that only present afflictions are concealment (*mrakṣa*), and not others?
Answer: If one speaks of the present, it should be understood that the past and future are also included, because their nature and characteristics are identical.
However, because the obscuring function exists in the present world, it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, present afflictions obscure and obstruct the Noble Path and the roots of goodness that serve as the preparation for the Noble Path within one’s own continuum.
The past and future are not so; therefore, the present is mentioned.
Furthermore, present afflictions give rise to various karmas within one's own continuum;
the past and future do not do so; therefore, the present is mentioned.
Furthermore, present afflictions take and give results within their own continuum;
since past and future ones do not do so, it is said that they are "present.

Moreover, present afflictions can act as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), pervasive causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*) within their own continuum, thereby taking resultant-flow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) and retributive fruits (*vipāka-phala*).
Because the past and future are not so, it is said to be "present.
Furthermore, present afflictions are able to defile one's own continuum; they are currently censurable, causing one to sink into the mud and fall into improper states.
The past and future are not so; therefore, the present is specified.
Furthermore, present afflictions cause burning distress and inflict harm within one's own continuum;
the past and future do not do so; therefore, the present is specified.
Furthermore, present afflictions produce delusion regarding their own nature (*svabhāva-moha*) and delusion regarding their objects (*ālambana-moha*) within their own continuum;

past and future ones do not, and for this reason the present is mentioned. Furthermore, present afflictions delude [the mind] regarding the three times and phenomena that transcend time (*lokottara-dharma*) within their own continuum.
Because the past and future are not so, it is said to be the present.
Furthermore, the afflictions of the present obstruct the basis, the object, and the mental aspect, preventing liberation;
because the past and future are not so, it is said to be the present.
Due to such various causes and conditions as these,
it is taught that only present afflictions are called *paryavasthāna* (obsessions);
those which are also *nīvaraṇa* (hindrances) are likewise *paryavasthāna*.
That is to say, when any one of the five hindrances manifests before one.
Specifically, when the hindrance of sensual desire manifests,
three hindrances manifest during the state of wakefulness.

That is to say, when one is in a state of sleep, four hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are present: namely, the three previously mentioned, together with torpor (*middha*). These are sensual desire, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-agitation, and sleep.
As it is with the hindrance of sensual desire,
so it is with the hindrances of ill-will, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt.
When the hindrance of lethargy-and-drowsiness manifests, [the same applies].
In the state of wakefulness, two hindrances are necessarily present:
namely, lethargy and restlessness.
In the state of sleep, three hindrances are necessarily present.
That is to say, the two preceding [hindrances] together with torpor (middha).
As it is with the hindrance of lethargy (styāna) and the hindrance of restlessness (auddhatya),
so it is when the hindrance of torpor manifests.
Three hindrances necessarily manifest:
namely, torpor, lethargy, and restlessness.
When these five hindrances thus manifest, [one is obstructed].
They are also called "obstructions" (*nīvaraṇa*) because they possess the characteristic nature of being obstructions;
they are also called "coverings" (*chādana*) because they possess the functional activity of covering.
There are, however, those that are neither obstructions nor coverings.
This means excluding the aforementioned characteristics.

Herein, that which is designated by the term "characteristic" refers to those phenomena for which a name has already been established and which have already been verbally expressed; these constitute the first three phrases.
That which has not yet been given a name or designated by speech constitutes the fourth alternative;
therefore, it is said that "the preceding characteristics are excluded.
What, then, does this mean?
This refers to the formulation of four propositions within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
The past and future five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) constitute the first proposition;
all other present afflictions (*kleśa*), excluding the five hindrances, constitute the second proposition; and the present five hindrances constitute the third proposition.
The remaining associated and dissociated formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), as well as the four [other] aggregates in their entirety,
together with the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), constitute the fourth alternative.
Are all those latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) necessarily unwholesome (*akuśala*)?
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To show that ignorance (*avidyā*) is also of the nature of an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*).
That which has not yet been clarified as unwholesome is now intended to be clarified.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of refuting the positions of others and establishing the correct doctrine;
that is to say, there are some who maintain that all afflictions (*kleśa*) are unwholesome.
As the Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"All afflictions are unwholesome because they are sustained by an unskillful wisdom.
To refute that position, it is shown that among the various afflictions, some are unwholesome while others are indeterminate.
Question: Since all afflictions are sustained by unskillful wisdom (*akuśala-prajñā*), they should all be unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Why, then, is it also said that some are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Answer: They are called unwholesome because they bring about undesirable results (*aniṣṭa-phala*).
This is because it is not the case that it is not sustained by skillful means (*upāya*).
If it were otherwise,
the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) would have to be unwholesome (*akuśala*), because within its nature there is also that which lacks skillful means.
Furthermore, there are those who hold that all afflictions of the desire realm are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*),
while all afflictions of the form and formless realms are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

To refute that position, it is shown that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with them, are also indeterminate.
For this reason, this treatise is composed.
Are all those latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) necessarily unwholesome (*akuśala*)?
Answer: All unwholesome latent tendencies of ignorance are indeed bound to the desire realm.
There are unwholesome latent tendencies of ignorance bound to the desire realm that are not themselves unwholesome;
namely, the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm.
Question: For what reason are the view of a self-identity, the view of extreme adherence, and the factors associated with and co-existent with them in the desire realm not unwholesome?
Yes. Answer:
If the nature of a phenomenon is itself lack of shame and lack of remorse, or if it is associated with them.
Whether they coexist with it or are produced by it, those [factors] are unwholesome; however,
factors such as the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) are not unwholesome because they are contrary to them.
The detailed explanation of the remainder is as found in the subsequent *Anuśaya-skandha*, in the section on the unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Are all those latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) bound to the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpya-dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed?
Answer: The preceding [section] has already demonstrated that ignorance possesses the nature of unwholesomeness (*akuśala*).
Since it has not yet been clarified that [the latent tendencies] are also indeterminate, this treatise is composed again to clarify it:
Are all those latent tendencies of ignorance bound to the realms of form and formlessness indeterminate?
Answer: All latent tendencies of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) bound to the realms of form and formlessness are indeterminate (avyākṛta).
However, there are indeterminate latent tendencies of ignorance that are not bound to the realms of form and formlessness.
That is to say, it refers to the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme attachment (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) bound to the desire realm. Question:
Why are the afflictions bound to the form and formless realms, as well as the phenomena associated with and co-arising alongside them, not unwholesome?
Answer: If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is lack of shame and lack of dread,
or if it is associated with them,
or co-existent with them.
Alternatively, that which is produced by them is unwholesome; however,
the afflictions and other dharmas bound to the two higher realms are not unwholesome because they are contrary to those [afflictions].
The detailed explanation of the remainder is as found later in the "Chapter on Aggregates," in the section on unwholesome factors.
Are all those latent tendencies of ignorance abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin necessarily universal?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Because it was previously stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) is either unwholesome (*akuśala*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
However, it has not yet been stated whether those [defilements] are universal (*sarvatraga*) or non-universal.
Now, wishing to explain this, the following treatise is composed:

Are all the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) necessarily universal?
Answer: All pervasive (sarvatraga) latent tendencies of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) are abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin (duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-prahātavya).
However, there are latent tendencies of ignorance abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin that are not pervasive.
This refers to the ignorance associated with the non-universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin;
that is, the ignorance associated with the latent dispositions of attachment, aversion, and pride abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin.

Are all the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) non-universal (*asarvatraga*)?
Answer: All latent tendencies of ignorance abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path are indeed non-universal.
There is non-universal ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) that is not abandoned by the vision of cessation or the path;
