If a sentient being’s body perishes and a non-sentient being’s body arises, the sign of a corpse does appear.

Furthermore, if that which possesses appropriation ceases and that which possesses appropriation arises, the appearance of a corpse will not manifest; if that which possesses appropriation ceases and that which lacks appropriation arises, the appearance of a corpse will manifest.
Furthermore, through the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, after death there appears the characteristic of a corpse.
This is because sentient beings must utilize its skin, flesh, tendons, bones, hair, fur, nails, teeth, hooves, horns, and so forth.
Due to the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, while they are alive, no signs of a corpse yet appear;

that is to say, in a single day and night, there are a total of sixty-four billion, ninety-nine thousand, nine hundred and eighty moments (*kṣaṇa*) of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
If the appearance of corpses were to manifest in every single moment, there would be no space on the great earth to contain the corpses of even a single sentient being.
Since they could not be buried or interred and are utterly loathsome, all classes of sentient beings would have no way to escape them.
Due to the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, no signs of a corpse appear while they are alive.
Question: Why is it that for spontaneously born (*upapāduka*) sentient beings, no signs of a corpse appear after the end of their life?
The answer is that at the time of taking birth and at the time of death, one suddenly acquires or abandons the sense faculties and the constituent parts of the body.
This is like a person who briefly emerges from and briefly submerges in water;
it is impossible to know where they have gone when submerged or from where they emerge when they surface.
Therefore, after death, no appearance of a corpse manifests. Furthermore, the bodies of beings born by transformation are light and subtle;
like a flame, a cloud, mist, or a flash of lightning, they leave nothing behind when they cease, and thus no corpse appears.
Furthermore, when the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are predominant, there is no corpse;
because the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is predominant there, there is no corpse.
Furthermore, when the sense faculties (*indriya*) are not predominant, there is a corpse at death.
Because those beings possess many root-elements (*indriya-dharma*), they have no corpses.
Furthermore, those who possess many discardable elements (*prahāṇa-dharma*), such as hair, body hair, and nails, have corpses at the time of death;
because spontaneously born (*upapāduka*) sentient beings possess few discardable elements, they have no corpses.
Furthermore, those who form a body by means of gathered semen, blood, and so forth have a physical corpse at the time of death;
those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) are not like this, and therefore they have no corpse.
Question: When all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise...
Does it arise because its essence is a phenomenon subject to arising,
or does it arise because it is conjoined with the characteristic of arising?
If this were so, what would be the fault?
If it is because the essence itself is a phenomenon subject to arising that it arises,
then the characteristic of arising would be useless.
If it is because it is conjoined with the characteristic of arising that it arises, [then...]
If that were so, then unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) would also be subject to arising, because they are conjoined with the characteristic of arising.
One should answer:
They arise because their essential nature (*svabhāva*) is that of a phenomenon subject to arising.
Question: If that were so, the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) would be useless.
Answer: Although its essence is a dharma subject to arising, if it were not conjoined with the characteristic of arising, it could not arise.

Therefore, at the time of its arising, it arises by virtue of being conjoined with the characteristic of arising; for the characteristic of arising is the predominant cause of that arising, just as a dharma that is to be destroyed depends on a destructive cause to destroy it, and a dharma that is to be severed depends on a severing cause to sever it.
Therefore, the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) can give rise to a dharma that is subject to arising. Some say:

"Because it is conjoined with the characteristic of arising, [the dharma] arises. If this were so, one might ask: "In that case, since unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are also conjoined with the characteristic of arising, they too should be subject to arising."
Answer: The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot arise because it lacks the meaning of conjunction with the characteristic of arising, as in the case of space and so forth;
nor can it be destroyed because it lacks conjunction with a cause of destruction.
Because it is not conjoined with the cause of cessation, it cannot be ceased;
because it is not conjoined with the characteristic of arising, it cannot arise— one should know that the same applies here,
for the characteristic of arising has never been conjoined with it.
It should be understood that the two questions regarding the abiding and the alteration of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are likewise to be treated in this manner. Question:

When conditioned phenomena perish, do they perish because their essence is an impermanent phenomenon, or do they perish because they have conjoined with the characteristic of impermanence? If it were the latter, what fault would there be?
If it were to perish because its essence is an impermanent phenomenon (*anityadharma*), then the characteristic of impermanence would be rendered useless.

If it were to perish because it is conjoined with the characteristic of impermanence, then unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) would also be subject to perishing due to their conjunction with impermanence. One should therefore state: it perishes because its essence is an impermanent phenomenon.
Question: If that were so, the characteristic of impermanence would be useless.
Answer: Although its essence is an impermanent phenomenon, if it were not conjoined with the characteristic of impermanence, it could not be extinguished.
Therefore, at the time of its cessation, it is conjoined with impermanence;
for impermanence is the predominant cause of that cessation, just as the cause of arising produces a dharma that is subject to arising. This case is exactly like that.
Some say: "It ceases because it is conjoined with the characteristic of impermanence.
Question: If that were so, then the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) would also be subject to cessation, as it would be conjoined with impermanence.
Answer: Because the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) lacks the sense of being conjoined with impermanence, it cannot be extinguished.
Just as space and the like cannot arise because they lack conjunction with the characteristic of arising, so too is this [unconditioned] case:
since impermanence has never been conjoined with it, it cannot be extinguished.
Other masters say:

the nature of conditioned phenomena consists of arising, abiding, change, and cessation; if these four characteristics did not exist, they could not be known, just as a jar, a garment, or other objects cannot be perceived in the dark.
If there were no lamp to illuminate it, it could not be known;
this case is likewise.
Therefore, the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) serve as the revealing cause (*vyañjanahetu*) for them.
The commentary states:
It should be understood that the initial statement constitutes a skillful inquiry, as in the question:
"If conditioned phenomena possess the characteristics of the conditioned, do unconditioned phenomena likewise possess the characteristics of the unconditioned?"
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If it exists, how can the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) be called a non-aggregate phenomenon (aprāptidharma)?
If it does not exist, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
As it is said: "What are the phenomena that are unarisen, non-abiding, and non-ceasing?

They are all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). One should answer thus: "All unconditioned phenomena lack the characteristics of being unconditioned. [Objection: If this is so, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
Answer: This statement is made in contrast to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
That is to say, conditioned phenomena possess arising, abiding, and ceasing;
the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), being different from those, is said to be non-arising and so forth.
It is not meant that there are separate characteristics such as non-arising and so forth, as stated in the sūtra.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You all have birth, you have old age, you have death; you have existence, but you do not have transcendence."
Why is this so? Because all your conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are like illusions, mirages, and the like.
Question: What is the distinction between "arising" (*utpāda*) and "death-existence" (*cyuty-upapatti*) as explained here?
Some say there is no distinction:
birth is itself emergence, and death is itself disappearance,
because everything is of the nature of momentariness.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated:
"Entering the mother’s womb is called 'birth' (utpāda); emerging from the mother’s womb is called 'emergence' (niryāṇa);
and when the aggregates (skandhas) reach maturity, it is called 'passing away' (astaṅgama)."
The relinquishing of the aggregates is called death.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"The acquisition of the aggregates of the intermediate state (antarābhava) is called birth."
The moment of relinquishing [the aggregates] is called "disappearance.
The moment of acquiring the various aggregates that constitute birth is called "birth";
the moment of relinquishing them is called "death."
The Venerable Ghosaka stated it thus:

when the aggregates of those born from a womb, an egg, or moisture arise, it is called "birth" because the sense faculties gradually develop; when they perish, it is called "death" because there remains a physical carcass.
When the aggregates of those born by transformation arise, it is called "emerging" because the sense faculties emerge all at once;
when they perish, it is called "subsiding" because no physical remains are left behind.
The Venerable One said:
The initial moment of taking birth within the various realms of existence is called "birth.
The exhaustion of the life-faculty is called "death.
The moment-by-moment arising of the intermediate aggregates is called "emergence."
The moment of destruction at the time of cessation is called "passing away.
The Venerable Buddhadeva has stated:
"For sentient beings possessing form, the time of arising is called 'birth'."
The time of death is called "death.
For formless sentient beings, the time of birth is called "emergence," and the time of death is called "disappearance."
This is called the distinction between birth and death. 7.
The Section on Meaninglessness (Anarthavarga), the first part of the seventh section within the first *Skandhaka* of the *Saṃyukta-āgama*. As the Blessed One said:
One should know that practicing various other ascetic penances is devoid of meaning;
one gains neither benefit nor peace therein. This is like rowing a boat on dry land.
Having thus understood these chapters and their meanings, [one should proceed].
Next, it should be explained in detail.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing and elucidating the meaning of the sūtras.
Although all treatises are intended to explain the sūtras,
this section (*nāśika*) explains the meaning of many sūtras. Specifically,
a sūtra states that the Blessed One was staying by the side of Lake Uruvilvā, on the bank of the river Nairañjanā, beneath the Bodhi tree.
Not long after attaining Buddhahood, he briefly taught the essential Dharma to the śrāvakas, addressing the bhikṣus:
"I have been liberated from meaningless ascetic practices; that I have attained liberation is most excellent."
Because he has swiftly realized unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment through the power of his own right aspirations,
at that time the bhikṣus, hearing what the Buddha had said, were filled with joy and exultation, and they paid him respectful homage.
With a concentrated mind and ears attentive, he listened to and received the essential points of the Dharma. At that time, the Evil Māra thought to himself:
"Now that Śramaṇa Gautama is teaching the Dharma to the assembly beneath the Bodhi tree."
"All those śrāvakas are listening with reverence;
I should now go there to create obstacles for them.
He then transformed himself into the body of a young brahmin (maṇava).
Approaching the Buddha, he spoke these verses:
"O Benevolent One, you have now abandoned asceticism, The ancient, truly pure path of the seers;
Yet you practice another, defiled way, Which will surely not bring about purity."
The meaning herein is as follows:
that evil Māra conceives the notion of true purity regarding the bodies of the gods,
and regarding the ascetic practices formerly cultivated by non-Buddhist outsiders.
Because he conceived the thought that he could realize the path of true purity,
he said to the Buddha:
"O Benevolent One, for what reason do you now abandon the ancient sages' wondrous path of asceticism capable of attaining true purity?"
"Are you practicing other base, defiled, and indolent paths?
You will certainly not attain purity through these; you should abandon them immediately.
Therefore, for their sake, the Buddha spoke this verse: 'Practicing various other ascetic penances...'"
...and so on, as explained at length.
The meaning of this verse is that it was not because I was unable to practice those ascetic austerities of the non-Buddhists that I abandoned them.
However, upon careful examination,
I see that such ascetic practices are ultimately unable to sever the various afflictions or attain the benefit of true meaning; therefore,
I shall abandon them and cultivate instead the sublime practice of the Middle Way, which is truly authentic.
By means of this, one has already realized unsurpassed bodhi and is able to uproot the intense suffering of birth and death for sentient beings.
The meaning of this verse is as follows:
regarding the various ascetic practices cultivated by non-Buddhists, [it is said:]...
Because they are outside of the True Dharma,
it says "all others. Some say that one should instead speak of "lowly ascetic practices."
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of ascetic practices:
first, the superior,
which refers to the Noble Eightfold Path and its attendants.
Second is the base and lowly.
This refers to the ascetic practices cultivated by various non-Buddhists;
because they are mixed with self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*), they are designated as "base and lowly. Furthermore, those ascetic practices cultivated by the non-Buddhists...
Because they seek the fruits of birth and death within the mundane world,
and because those fruits are inferior, they are given the name "lowly.
Some say that one should instead call them "austerities of immortality" (*amṛta-tapas*).
The term "Immortal" (Amarā) is a specific name for the devas;
thus, the celestial Māra is called by the name "Immortal.
This is because Māra venerates such ascetic practices of the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika).
This is called the "Immortal Asceticism.
Furthermore, because various non-Buddhists seek the exquisite sensual pleasures of the heavens and practice this asceticism for that purpose,
it is called "Immortal Asceticism."
Next, regarding the statement "one should know that it is accompanied by the meaningless":
when practicing those ascetic penances, one should know that they are called "accompanied by the meaningless" because they lead to various forms of ruin and loss in both this life and future lives.
Furthermore, the statement that "they do not obtain benefit and peace" reiterates the previous meaning;
"benefit" refers to spiritual welfare (*hitam*).
"Peace" refers to peace and happiness; for those various ascetic practices cannot permanently sever the afflictions,
nor can they induce superior virtue,
and thus one does not attain ultimate benefit and happiness.
It is like one who wields a boat oar on dry land;
though they exert themselves with great toil, in the end nothing is achieved.
You should know that the ascetic practices of non-Buddhists are likewise.
Although he practiced with diligence, he did not obtain benefit or peace.
Then that celestial Māra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If this asceticism does not result in benefit or peace,"
"What path did the Buddha cultivate to attain true purity?
The World-Honored One replied:
"I cultivated the path of precepts, concentration, and wisdom—the truly pure path that abides in the middle."
Although the sūtras state that one attains the fruit of ultimate purity and unsurpassed bodhi, they do not analyze their meaning.
These sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which was not analyzed by him should now be analyzed in its entirety; for this reason, this treatise is composed.
Why did the Blessed One speak thus?
[He said it] because practicing other ascetic practices is devoid of meaning and accompanied by suffering.
The answer is: those practices lead toward death, approach death, and culminate in death; such ascetic practices cannot transcend death.
This is because sentient beings cultivate those ascetic practices for the purpose of transcending the ocean of old age and death.
However, because those ascetic practices arise from dogmatic views and cause one to sink even deeper into the ocean of old age and death,
the Buddha taught that cultivating them is accompanied by meaninglessness.
Birth, old age, and death pervade all states of existence.
Old age and death are precisely what sentient beings loathe; because the loathing toward death is particularly intense, these alone are mentioned.
The Venerable Ghosaka stated:
"All cyclic existence is termed 'meaningless'."
All cessation and reversal are termed "having meaning.
Such ascetic practices arise from views and tendencies; they contradict cessation and reversal, and instead conform to the process of saṃsāra.
Therefore, it is said that cultivating those [unwholesome states] is accompanied by what is meaningless (*anartha*).
The Venerable [Vasumitra] says:
"The suffering of the three evil destinies is all termed 'meaningless'."
The higher realms and liberation are both termed "meaningful.
Such ascetic practices arise from wrong means and are contrary to the higher realms and so forth.
Because they lead toward the suffering of the evil destinies,
it is said that cultivating them is accompanied by what is meaningless.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this as follows:
Such ascetic practices cause sentient beings to fall into the cycle of birth and death,
where they constantly undergo the manifold sufferings of the various elements, destinies, births, and locations;
therefore, it is said that practicing them is associated with what is meaningless.

Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "One should sit cross-legged, straighten the body, set the intention correctly, and dwell with mindfulness directed toward the front," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra: "There are certain bhikṣus who dwell in the araṇya."
Whether beneath a tree or in a quiet chamber, he sat cross-legged,
with body upright and aspiration correct, dwelling in mindfulness directed toward the presence before him.
This is explained at length in the sūtras;
however, although the sūtras state this,
they do not analyze its meaning.
The Sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Since those [Sūtras] did not explain certain matters, I now wish to explain them; therefore, I have composed this treatise.
Question: Can one cultivate wholesome qualities within all modes of deportment?
Why is it said that one sits in the full lotus posture?
The answer is: because this is the constant deportment of the noble ones (*ārya*).

That is to say, all Buddhas and their disciples, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, throughout the past and future, have entered meditative absorption while abiding in this very deportment.
Furthermore, such modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*) accord with the category of the wholesome (*kuśalapakṣa*).
That is to say, if one walks or stands, the body quickly becomes fatigued;
if one leans or lies down, drowsiness and sleep increase.
Only by sitting cross-legged are such faults avoided;
thus one is able to cultivate sublime wholesome qualities.
Furthermore, such a posture is contrary to unwholesome dharmas.
This means that other postures are conducive to lust and various unwholesome states,
whereas only the full-lotus posture (paryaṅka) can oppose them.
Furthermore, such a posture leads humans, devas, and others into the True Dharma.
This means that other modes of conduct cannot lead humans, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and so forth,
to enter the Buddha-dharma in the same way as the mode of conduct consisting of sitting cross-legged.
Furthermore, such deportment gives rise to respectful and faithful minds among humans, devas, and others;
that is to say, other forms of deportment cannot inspire respectful and faithful minds in humans, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and so forth.
Because he maintains the deportment of sitting cross-legged,
even if this deportment gives rise to unwholesome discursive thoughts, he should still remain in it for the sake of generating virtue in others;
how much more so when it naturally conduces to the arising of his own superior wholesome qualities?
Furthermore, it is because one realizes unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment (anuttara-buddha-bodhi) by relying exclusively on this specific deportment (*īryāpatha*).
That is to say, while one may also realize the enlightenment of the two vehicles (*dviyāna-bodhi*) by relying on other modes of deportment, [this is not the case for supreme enlightenment].
Because one cannot realize the Buddha’s bodhi thereby.
Furthermore, by abiding in this posture, one terrifies the armies of Māra;
that is to say, in the past, beneath the Bodhi tree, the Buddha sat cross-legged and defeated the two armies of Māra.
This is because it causes the hosts of Māra, including Maheśvara and all the afflictions,
to see these majestic deportments and become terrified, for the most part retreating and dispersing.
Furthermore, this is a teaching not shared with non-Buddhists.
This means that while other modes of deportment are also found among non-Buddhists,
the full lotus posture (paryaṅka) alone is not;
furthermore, the full lotus posture is conducive to the cultivation of meditative concentration (samādhi).
This means that while all scattered wholesome states can be cultivated while remaining in other postures,
if one cultivates concentrated wholesome states, sitting cross-legged is most conducive.
It is for such various reasons as these.
Therefore, it is simply called "sitting cross-legged.
Question: What is the meaning of "sitting cross-legged"?
Answer: It means to sit securely with the body perfectly rounded.
The proponent of phonetics said:
"He sat upright in meditation with his legs crossed,
placing one foot upon the other thigh, like a coiled dragon."
For this reason, it is called "sitting in the full lotus posture" (*paryaṅka-bandha*).
The Venerable Upagupta said:
"To stack the two feet one upon the other, crossing them left and right, while correctly contemplating the object of meditation, is called sitting in the full lotus posture."
Because this posture alone is conducive to the cultivation of meditative concentration,
the Venerable One said:
"This is called the 'cross-legged posture' (paryaṅka) because it is the auspicious seat of the noble ones."
Question: What is the meaning of "straightening the body"?
Answer: It means sitting with the body upright and composed.
Question: What is the meaning of "right aspiration"?
Answer: This refers to the meaning of directing the mind in accordance with the category of wholesome factors (*kuśalapakṣa*).
Question: What is the meaning of "dwelling in mindfulness directed toward the presence" (*mukhābhimukha-smṛti*)?
Answer: "Presence" (*mukha*) refers to the object of meditative concentration (*samādhi-viṣaya*).
"Facing" (abhimukha) means direct observation.
This mindfulness causes the mind to observe the object of concentration directly;
because it is unerring and clear, it is called "mindfulness facing [the object]" (abhimukhī-smṛti).
Furthermore, "face" (*mukha*) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), and "opposing" (*pratimukha*) refers to their antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
This mindfulness serves as the antidote to the primary afflictions of birth and death; therefore, it is called "mindfulness directed toward the face" (*pratimukhā smṛtiḥ*).
Furthermore, "face" refers to one's own face.
"Facing" means directing the mind toward it; thus, this mindfulness causes the mind to face its own face while observing other objects, and is therefore called "mindfulness of facing the face."
Question: For what reason does one fix the mindfulness upon one's own face?
Answer: Since beginningless time, men have been captivated by the beauty of women, and women by the beauty of men.
For the most part, one contemplates one's own face based on the face to subdue the various afflictions.

Furthermore, because the greedy mind of sentient beings arises mostly in relation to the face—specifically the eyes, eyebrows, lips, teeth, ears, and nose—and not in relation to other parts of the body.
Contemplate one's own face to subdue and eliminate desire.
Furthermore, the face has seven orifices from which impurities constantly flow;
thus, one should develop a sense of revulsion toward it that exceeds that felt for other parts of the body.
Therefore, one contemplates one's own face and cultivates disenchantment and equanimity.
Furthermore, because one sees one's own face rarely and does not give rise to much attachment toward it, one fixes the mind on the face and not elsewhere;
for when it is not reflected upon, one does not see it.
Furthermore, practitioners who cultivate insight generally delight in observing the characteristics of the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*).
Since there are always nine distinct locations on the face,
they observe them accordingly.
It is also said that this refers to both "abiding with one's back turned" and "being opposed"; there is no contradiction between these two meanings.
Why is this? Because by the power of this mindfulness, one turns away from and abandons all defilements.
Because it is oriented toward purity,
one turns away from birth and death;
because it is oriented toward nirvāṇa, one turns away from saṃsāra.
Because it turns its back on saṃsāra and faces toward nirvāṇa,
it turns its back on the five desires.
Because it is directed toward the object of meditative concentration,
it turns away from the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
because it is directed toward the liberation door of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
It turns its back on the grasping at a self because it is directed toward non-self;
it turns its back on false teachings.
Because it is directed toward the True Dharma,
there is no logical contradiction between this and being turned away from [unwholesome states].
One who abides in this mindfulness...
This is called "abiding in mindfulness facing [the object].
