translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang in compliance with the Imperial Edict. Section One of the *Saṃyukta-skandha*, Chapter Seven: The Sub-section on Meaninglessness, Part Three. As it is said in the Sūtra:
When the Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma, the bhikṣus such as Kauṇḍinya perceived the Dharma.
The earth-dwelling yakṣas raised their voices and proclaimed everywhere:
"The World-Honored One is now at the Deer Park of the Ṛṣis in Vārāṇasī."
"The Wheel of Dharma was turned three times, complete with twelve aspects," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
That is to say, a sūtra states:
"The Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma."
The earth-dwelling yakṣas raised their voices and proclaimed it everywhere;
although the sūtra makes this statement,
it does not analyze its meaning.
It is not said that the earth deity possesses independent wisdom and vision;
rather, it is through dependence on others that she knows and raises her voice to proclaim it everywhere.
This sutra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which he did not previously state shall now be explained.
Furthermore, it is taught in the Sūtra in order to enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
The Earth Deity raised her voice and proclaimed everywhere:
"The Buddha is at the Deer Park, turning the Wheel of Dharma for the third time.
Some, however, gave rise to doubt.
The earth deity possesses direct perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*) that knows such matters as they truly are.
In order to bring this doubt to a definitive conclusion,
it is shown that he possesses only inferential knowledge (*anumānajñāna*) and the knowledge acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhikajñāna*).
Because the turning of the wheel of Dharma is not within the range of direct perception,
for this reason and by these causes and conditions, this treatise was composed:
To inquire whether those earth deities possess right knowledge and vision such that they know when the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma and whether the bhikṣus have seen the Dharma.
Answer: No.
This matter is extremely profound and is not within their domain;
how, then, could they know it?
Answer: It is due to five conditions.
First, because of faith in the World-Honored One;
that is to say, when the Buddha gave rise to a conventional thought, thinking, "I have turned the wheel of Dharma, and the bhikṣu has seen the Dharma."
From this, he knows that if the Buddha arouses an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) or a conventional mind (*saṃvṛti-citta*) never before attained,
no sentient being whatsoever is able to know it.
When he gives rise to a conventional mind that has been previously acquired,
there are sentient beings capable of knowing it;
that is to say, when the Buddha gives rise to this conventional mind.
If one wishes to cause those of dull faculties to also understand,
then even Sarpadāsa and others would be able to comprehend it;
if one wishes to cause those of sharp faculties not to understand, [they likewise would not].
Thus, even when Śāriputra and others enter the fourth dhyāna of the ultimate limit and give rise to the sublime knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*),
they cannot know [it]; yet, if one were to cause even those in the evil destinies to know it,
then even monkeys and the like would be able to understand it.
If he had wished for even those in the happy realms not to know,
then no humans or devas would have been able to know it.
Now, because the Buddha wishes for the earth deities to know, [he speaks thus].

When the Buddha gave rise to the thought, "I have turned the wheel of Dharma; the bhikṣus have seen the Dharma," which was a previously acquired worldly mind, the earth deities, having perceived this, raised their voices and proclaimed it everywhere.
They then asked the Buddha, "For what reason did you give rise to this worldly thought?"
Answer: Having practiced and accumulated various difficult ascetic practices over three incalculable eons for the benefit of sentient beings, he has now turned the wheel of Dharma;
thus the bhikṣu has seen the Dharma.
This mind arises because one feels profound joy at having now attained the fruit for the first time after those former preparatory practices.
Furthermore, it arises because one previously made great vows.
One gives rise to this mind because one has now finally attained the fruit for the sake of benefiting others.
Furthermore, it is because of the great vows previously made.
This mind arises because one has now finally attained the fruit for the sake of rescuing others.
Furthermore, it refers to the intended ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This mind arises because the goal of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings has now been newly accomplished;
or secondly, because the Buddha told others, "I have turned the wheel of Dharma, and the bhikṣus have seen the Dharma."
Therefore, they are able to hear it.
That is to say, if one has attained skill regarding the mind, as soon as the Buddha arouses his mind, that person can immediately understand;
whereas if one has attained skill only regarding words, [they cannot].
Only after the Buddha has informed others can they fully understand.
Question: For what reason does the World-Honored One inform others so that they may know?
Answer: The World-Honored One wishes to manifest that within the well-spoken Dharma, what is stated is truthful, singular in vision, and singular in joy.
Because the assembly all gave their consent, he informed others.
Furthermore, having practiced many ascetic austerities throughout three incalculable eons for the benefit of sentient beings,
he has now first attained the fruit.
Because he gave rise to profound joy, he informed others.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One manifested for himself that among the ninety-six paths and dharmas, he was the most honored, the most supreme, and beyond compare.
Therefore, he informs others.
Furthermore, he informs others because he wishes to demonstrate that the Buddha-dharma is truly capable of leading to liberation and possesses great miraculous power.
Furthermore, the Buddha, wishing to manifest the true merits of Kauṇḍinya and the others,
and also to demonstrate them as a field of merit for the world,
informed others so that they might know.
Furthermore, it is because he wishes to inspire deep respect and faith in the Buddha’s holy teaching among devas and humans that he informs others so they may know.
Moreover, it is so that the World-Honored One may manifest his own freedom from the stinginess regarding the Dharma.

Furthermore, because there is no teacher’s closed fist regarding the marvelous Dharma, he informs others so that they may know it; moreover, the Buddha wishes to manifest that he possesses the qualities of a Great Being unlike those of other paths, and thus he informs others so that they may know it.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One, in order to manifest for himself the mark of intelligence—which is not shared by other paths—instructed others so that they might know it.
As stated in a sutra:
"There are three marks of those who are intelligent."
First, one has well-considered what is to be considered;
second, one has well-performed what is to be done;
third, one has well-spoken what is to be spoken.
Third, some have heard it from great virtuous celestial seers (*mahā-ṛṣi*).
This refers to the five bhikṣus who saw the Dharma when the Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma.
One asks: what are these "great virtuous celestial seers"?
Some say these are the Śuddhāvāsa deities;
other masters say they are deities of the desire realm who have already seen the truths.
Furthermore, there are those who say that a certain long-lived deity once witnessed the manner in which past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, turned the wheel of Dharma; now,
seeing that the World-Honored One possesses such a manner, [he recognizes him as a Buddha].
Filled with joy and exultation, he informed others so that they might know.
Upon hearing this, the earth deities raised their voices and proclaimed it everywhere.
Fourth, perhaps those venerable ones, such as Kauṇḍinya and the others, gave rise to worldly thoughts.
"The Buddha has turned the wheel of Dharma; we have seen the Dharma.
From this, he knew. [The interlocutor] asked:
"For what reason did the Venerable One give rise to a worldly thought?"
The answer is: because the twenty kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* have already been destroyed;
because all causes for the evil destinies have already been severed;
and because the boundless cycle of birth and death now has a limit.
Because the boundless ocean of suffering now has a limit;
because the Noble Truths have been seen;
and because one has entered the assembly of those fixed in rightness.
Deep joy arises;
therefore, this mind is generated.
Furthermore, because the great vows of universal resolve previously initiated and all the ascetic practices have now reached their fruition.
They give rise to this mind because they experience profound joy.
Fifth, it may be that the earth deity informs others, who then hear of it.
Question: For what reason did the Venerable One inform others so that they might know?
Answer: The Venerable One wished to demonstrate that what is spoken within the well-expounded Dharma is truthful, singular in its vision, and singular in its joy;
because the assembly all agreed with this, he informed others so they might know.
Furthermore, it is to manifest that the World-Honored One, having practiced many ascetic austerities throughout three incalculable eons,
has now first attained the fruit and thus informs others.
Moreover, it is to manifest that the Buddha-dharma is the most honored and supreme among the ninety-six paths of practice.
Therefore, he informs others.
Furthermore, wishing to demonstrate that the Buddha-dharma truly possesses the power of renunciation and great miraculous transformations,
he informs others.
Furthermore, desiring to cause devas and humans to develop deep reverence and faith in the Buddha’s holy teaching, he informs others so that they may know it.
Furthermore, he does so with the desire to inspire in immeasurable sentient beings a mind that delights in the Dharma.
Therefore, he informs others so that they may know.
Furthermore, he informs others so that they may know, desiring to inspire diligent perseverance in immeasurable sentient beings who are indolent.
Furthermore, it is because he wishes to demonstrate that the Tathāgata’s relinquishing of extreme ascetic practices yields great fruit,
and thus informs others so they may know this.
Furthermore, it is because he wishes to demonstrate that his own taking of refuge in the Buddha and the Dharma is not in vain.
He informs others so that they may know.
The meaning of "turning the wheel of Dharma" will be explained in detail later in the *Prativedha* section of the *Samāpatti-skandha*.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
There were certain bhikṣus who had attained arhatship and whose outflows were exhausted.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven frequently gathered in the Sudharmā Hall and proclaimed:
"In such-and-such a place, there is a certain venerable one."
Or his disciples,
having shaved off their hair and beards and donned the saffron robes,
left the home life out of right faith and diligently cultivated the Noble Path.
With all taints exhausted, he has realized the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom;
in this very life, he has personally attained,
realized, and dwells in the fulfillment of that state.
Furthermore, he knows for himself:
"Birth has been exhausted;
the holy life has been established."
"What was to be done has been accomplished;
there will be no further existence," and so forth,
as extensively explained.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
That is to say, it is stated in the *Pārijāta* Sūtra: [text continues].
There are bhikṣus who have attained arhatship and whose outflows are exhausted;
from the Trāyastriṃśa gods down to [the other realms], as explained at length in the sūtras—
although the sūtras speak thus.
Yet they do not analyze its meaning.
They do not say that the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven possess their own wisdom and vision, but rather that they know it because of others; thus, in the Sudharmā Hall, they discuss these matters.
The Sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies;
those points not stated therein shall now be explained.
Furthermore, it is intended that those who harbor doubts may attain certainty.
This means that there may be those who harbor doubts;

[the Buddha] desires to bring such doubts to a definitive resolution by showing that the devas themselves possess direct perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*) that perceives these matters as they truly are.

This is to show that there exists only inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*), because the knowledge attained through birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-jñāna*) does not have the quality of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) as its direct object.
For this reason, this treatise was composed.
"Do those gods possess right knowledge and vision such that they know whether the bhikṣus have attained arhatship and exhausted all outflows?
"No. "This matter is exceedingly profound; it is not within their domain."
How is this known?
The answer is: by way of five conditions.
First, because of faith in the World-Honored One.
That is to say, when the Buddha gives rise to a conventional mind, those bhikṣus know that they have attained arhatship and that their outflows are exhausted;
however, if the Buddha gives rise to an untainted mind or a conventional mind not previously attained, they do not know this.
No sentient being is able to know it; however,
when a conventional mind previously attained arises,
there are sentient beings who are able to know it.
This means that when the Buddha gives rise to this conventional mind—
as explained at length previously—
up until now, it is because the Buddha wishes to make those devas understand.
Having arisen with a previously acquired mundane mind, those bhikṣus attained arhatship and their outflows were exhausted.
When that deva learned of this, he gathered [the assembly] in the Hall of Good Dharma and proclaimed the matter.
Question: For what reason does the Buddha give rise to this conventional thought?
Answer: Because that reality accords with the Buddha’s intention;
that is to say, if a bhikṣu has forever severed future existence.
This is truly and appropriately in accordance with the Buddha’s intention.
Because these bhikṣus have exhausted all outflows and forever severed future existence,
they are all truly and appropriately in accord with the Buddha’s intention.
First, he gives rise to a mundane thought so that the devas may know of it and gather to proclaim it.
Second, the Buddha informs others:
"These bhikṣus have attained arhatship; all their outflows are exhausted."
Therefore, they are able to hear it;
that is to say, if one is skilled regarding the mind,
as soon as the Buddha has aroused his mind, one can immediately understand it.
If one were merely skilled in words, one would only be able to understand after the Buddha has told others;
[one might then ask: "Why does the World-Honored One tell others so that they may know?"
Answer: The World-Honored One wishes to manifest that what is spoken within the well-expounded Dharma is truthful, singular in its vision, and singular in its joy;
because all beings consent to this, he informs others.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One manifests for himself that among the ninety-six paths and dharmas, he is the most honored, the most supreme, and unsurpassed; therefore, he informs others.
Furthermore, wishing to demonstrate that the Buddha-dharma truly possesses the power of transcendence and great miraculous transformations, he informs others;
furthermore, the Buddha wishes to manifest the true merits of those bhikṣus.
Furthermore, he informs others so that they may know him as a sublime field of merit for the world.
Moreover, he informs others so that devas and humans may develop deep reverence and faith in the Buddha’s holy teaching.
Furthermore, the Buddha, wishing to encourage other practitioners to develop a mind of courageous exertion, informs others so that they may know:
thirdly, [he has heard it] from great and virtuous celestial sages (*deva-ṛṣi*).
This refers to that bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted.
Question: What is meant by "virtuous celestial seers"?
Answer: Those who have realized arhatship among the gods.
Question: Do all those Arhats know this matter and inform others of it?
Answer: Not so.
Those with superior faculties such as the [five] roots can know this,
but not the other four. Alternatively,
that venerable one may have given rise to a conventional thought, thinking, "I have exhausted the outflows and attained arhatship."
From this, he knew.
He asked: "For what reason did the Venerable One give rise to a conventional mind?
He replied: "Because that Venerable One’s afflictions have been intensely burning and his body and mind tormented since beginningless time, and he has now attained coolness."
The cycle of birth and death, which has continued from time immemorial, is now forever severed.
Having abandoned the stifling heat, one attains refreshing coolness;
having abandoned the relish for existence, one attains the state free from such relish.
By abandoning indulgence, one attains liberation;
by abandoning defilement, one attains purity.
It is because of giving rise to profound joy that this mind is produced.
Fifth, he may inform others and the various devas hear it.
If one asks why the Venerable One informs others so that they may know, the answer is:
the Venerable One wishes to demonstrate that what is spoken within the well-expounded Dharma is truthful, singular in its vision, and singular in its joy.
Because the assembly had all given their consent, he informed others of this.
The rest should be understood as appropriate, as explained in the accounts of the Buddha informing others and of Kātyāyana informing others.
Furthermore, he wished to ensure that those who had previously provided the Venerable One with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine [would continue to do so].
When the various donors hear this, they give rise to joy;
their merit increases further,
and thus it is made known to others.
Furthermore, it is in order to inspire reverence and faith in those who previously lacked them that he informs others;
furthermore, it is to demonstrate that the diligent practice of asceticism by one who has left the household life yields superior fruits that he informs others.
Question: Are there other devas besides these who are also said to have attained the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)?
Answer: It should be said that there are.
Question: For what reason is it said that only the Trāyastriṃśa devas [are mentioned]?
The answer is: because those devas frequently assemble to discuss matters of good and evil, they speak of them specifically.
That is to say, on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of each half-month—whether the bright or dark fortnight—those devas regularly gather.
In the Hall of Accumulated Goodness (Sudharmā), they weigh the amount of good and evil in the world.
Furthermore, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three constantly observe those who perform good and evil deeds;
seeing those who perform good, they immediately protect them.
When they see those who commit evil, they immediately join in disparaging and reviling them;
for this reason, it is mentioned specifically.
Furthermore, because the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven see people performing wholesome deeds and rejoice in praising them, it is mentioned specifically.
Furthermore, because the Pārijāta tree in the Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods is used as a metaphor for the Arhat, it is specifically mentioned there.
Question: Is it also commonly said among the inhabitants of the Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods that there are those still in training (śaikṣa)?
The answer is that they likewise proclaim it together.
If those who are still in training (śaikṣa) and all sentient beings, when filially supporting their parents, still proclaim it; how much more so for others?
How much more so for those still in training? Question:
If this is so, why does the sūtra state that they merely agree to call him an arhat?
Answer: This is because it is spoken of in terms of what is preeminent.
That is to say, both the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) and the person (pudgala) who possesses them are superior to those of one still in training (śaikṣa);
therefore, they are mentioned specifically.
Furthermore, because the Pārijāta tree bears many similarities to those who have exhausted their outflows (āsravakṣaya),
it can serve as a metaphor;
for this reason, it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, it is because those who have exhausted the outflows (āsravakṣaya) are supremely delightful,
free from all faults,
and utterly pure.
Because it is free from fault;
because it is extremely difficult to obtain;
and because it is beyond reproach.
Because they are worthy of offerings,
they are specifically so designated.
Furthermore, it is because the Arhat possesses the perfection of liberation and the fullness of all meritorious qualities.
It is specifically so designated because it brings about the eternal exhaustion of all birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Furthermore, when an Arhat appears in the world,
the realms of gods and humans become filled while the evil destinies diminish.
Just as when a virtuous king appears in the world,
he is therefore spoken of specifically;
furthermore, it is the same when an Arhat appears in the world.
The hosts of devas increase and the hosts of asuras decrease,
just as the great ocean overflows when the moon is full.
Therefore, it is spoken of in this partial manner.
Furthermore, if an Arhat appears in the world,
then the armies of the devas will be victorious.
Asura: It is because, at the time of battle, they saw the devaputra Suyāma;
therefore, he is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, if an Arhat appears in the world and a deity born subsequently possesses a lifespan,
physical form, and renown superior to those of the previous birth,
it is like a person of low status and poverty who gives a mere dregs of rice-gruel as an offering, yet excels other donors.
Therefore, it is taught selectively.
Furthermore, if an Arhat appears in the world,
one obtains a great fruit by giving even a small thing as a gift.
For instance, when the Venerable Kāśyapa gave a single coarse meal to Aniruddha,
humans and devas subsequently received many times over superior and wondrous fruits; therefore,
this case is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, if an Arhat appears in the world, he can cause those who see him to give rise to even a slight degree of pure faith and attain rebirth in heaven to experience bliss;
yet, like a dog or a frog, one might still harbor malice through the emission of poisonous breath.
Therefore, it is taught selectively.
Furthermore, if an Arhat appears in the world,
many are liberated from the prison of birth and death.
It is like when a king fathers a son and grants a general amnesty throughout the realm;
for this reason, it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, if an Arhat appears in the world...
The paths to the good and evil realms appear with perfect clarity,
just as the rising sun illuminates both the safe and the perilous places; therefore,
this is explained specifically.
Furthermore, when an Arhat appears in the world,
he is able to cause the various devas not to lose their celestial stations,
just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, eliminates the signs of his own decline.
Therefore, it is explained in this partial manner.
Furthermore, if an Arhat appears in the world,
he causes the celestial palaces to be filled with devas and ṛṣis.
Just as one who is sustained by a virtuous friend becomes filled with merit,
for this reason it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, if an Arhat appears in the world...
It can cause the various devas to become weary of the pleasures of the five desires;
just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and King Yama, the Wheel-Turning Monarch,
are able to give rise to weary detachment when exquisite desires appear before them.
Therefore, it is explained in this partial manner.
Furthermore, if an Arhat appears in the world,
he is able to cause the world to hear the True Dharma.
The jewels of the factors of enlightenment are all abundant therein;
like a sea-going treasure ship, it reaches wherever it may go,
and for this reason, it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, when an Arhat appears in the world,
all sentient beings experience happiness,
just as when sweet rain falls, the crops flourish and ripen.
Therefore, it is taught selectively.
Due to various causes and conditions such as these,
the devas speak only of those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Question: Is it said that all arhats [reside] in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, or only a small portion?
Regarding this, some say:
He spoke of them all,
for those devas delight in praising the virtues of others;
"The Arhats have accomplished what was to be done— this is truly marvelous."
Therefore, they all speak of them;
yet there are also those who do not speak of everything.
Why is this? There are Arhats—
whether by the hundreds or by the thousands— who,
relying upon mountain valleys, have entered into parinirvāṇa.
If even those who dwell together with him do not understand this, how much less could other devas and humans, who hear of it from afar, proclaim it?
[The interlocutor] asks: "Which kind of arhat is being proclaimed?"
Answer: As it is stated in such a sutra, it refers to an Arhat who performs and increases actions that bring about renown;
it is of such a person that this statement is made.
If one does not perform deeds that bring renown,
or even if one does perform them, they do not increase;
such a person does not speak of them.
Furthermore, if there are those of noble and high status who have gone forth,
they are praised as being like King Śuddhodana and others.
Furthermore, if there are those who are immensely wealthy and possess great merit,
they are praised accordingly,
such as Aniruddha and others.
Furthermore, if there are those of great wisdom who tirelessly benefit others,
they are praised as being like Śāriputra and others.
Furthermore, if one is able to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma, which is the refuge to which all turn together,
others will proclaim that person’s name,
as they did for Kāśyapa and others.
Furthermore, if there is one who at the time of birth causes heaven and earth to tremble and manifests great radiance,
they shall proclaim it.
Furthermore, if there is one who has gone forth from home and practices diligent asceticism.
Those who are able to perform what is difficult to do and protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma for the benefit of devas and humans—
of them he speaks; of other arhats, he does not speak.
Question: Do the various devas know those who possess overweening pride?
Some explain it thus:
There are those who know and those who do not.
This means that while the gods do not recognize one who gives rise to overweening pride based on superior qualities,
they do recognize one who gives rise to overweening pride based on inferior qualities.
The devas know [this].
Furthermore, if one gives rise to overweening pride based on subtle and exquisite virtues,
the devas do not know it.
If one gives rise to overweening pride based on coarse and superficial merits,
the devas will know it;
furthermore, if one gives rise to overweening pride based on the merits of the higher realms, the devas will not know it.
If one gives rise to overweening pride based on the merits of the desire realm,
the gods will know it;
so say other masters.
Those with overweening pride are not known by the devas. For example, when Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
sees an outsider dwelling alone in seclusion at a time when no Buddha exists in the world, [he does not recognize him as such].
He then went to that place, observed it, and paid homage, thinking it was the Tathāgata.
If even Śakra acted thus,
how much more so would the other hosts of devas?
Question: Do the devas know those who have transgressed the precepts?
Answer: Some know, while others do not.
That is to say, if one violates a coarse or grave precept,
the devas will know it;
if one violates a subtle precept, they will likewise know it.
The devas do not know this,
as it is stated in the Sūtra:
"The various ministers and assistants of the kingdom of Magadha..."
Or they are disciplined through transformation;
or they practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma;
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
Specifically, the *Śrī-vijaya-sūtra* states as follows:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kūṭāgāraśālā forest in the town of Nādikā.
At that time, eighty-four thousand ministers of the kingdom of Magadha passed away simultaneously.
Some say they died because of an epidemic;
others say...
He was killed by Ajātaśatru;
that is to say, after Ajātaśatru had killed his father, the king,
he also killed eighty-four thousand ministers.
Those attendants went to where Ānanda was and spoke to him as follows:
"In various kingdoms and towns, there are those who have faith in the Buddha;
when their bodies perish and their lives end, the Tathāgata has prophesied that they will all be reborn in such and such places."
The eighty-four thousand ministers who previously served the former kings of Magadha were also all followers of the Buddha;
they have now passed away,
yet the World-Honored One has not yet granted a prediction regarding the places where they have been reborn.
"Please request this for me.
Ānanda consented and went to the presence of the Tathāgata during the first part of the day.
Having prostrated at his feet, he stood to one side;
with palms joined in reverence and an expression of affection, he spoke these words of request:
"In various kingdoms and towns, there are those who have faith in the Buddha."
When his body perished and his life ended, the Buddha predicted the place of his rebirth.
There were also eighty-four thousand ministers of King Kṛkī of Magadha who likewise believed in the Buddha;
they have now passed away, yet the Tathāgata has not made a prediction concerning them.
Those attendants felt sorrow and distress in their hearts;
had the Buddha not predicted their place of rebirth,
they feared that those attendants would give rise to feelings of resentment.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and grant us this prediction.
Furthermore, it was here in this land of Magadha that the Buddha attained equal and perfect enlightenment.
That land was graced by his kindness.
Furthermore, King Śibi,
who possessed profound faith in the Triple Gem, made offerings and paid them respect without ever failing for even a moment.
Therefore, the World-Honored One ought certainly to grant him a prediction.
Out of compassion for him, the Buddha silently consented.
He then took his robes and bowl and entered Nadika.
He went on his alms-round in accordance with the Dharma.
Having finished eating, he returned to the Kuṇḍadhāna forest;
after putting away his robes and bowl and washing his feet, he entered the dwelling where he stayed.
He spread out his seat and sat down;
settling his body and composing his mind,
he focused his mindfulness and contemplated the birthplaces of the various ministers of Magadha.

Question: Since the Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom and vision arise spontaneously at the mere moment he directs his mind toward any phenomenon, why did he enter his room to engage in focused contemplation?
Answer: It was because he wished to demonstrate that the ripening of karmic results is extremely profound and subtle.
Because it is most subtle,
because it is difficult to perceive,
and because it is difficult to manifest clearly.
Because it is difficult to perceive directly,
the Vinaya-piṭaka among all three collections of the Tripiṭaka is the most profound;
for it extensively elucidates the various characteristics of karmic causes and their effects.
Among all the sūtras, the sections concerning karma and its results are the most profound.
Within the twelve links of dependent origination, the two links of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are the most profound.
Among the ten powers of a Buddha, the power of knowing the diversity of one’s own karma is the most profound.
Among these eight aggregates, the fourth—the aggregate of karma—is the most profound.
Among the four things that are difficult to conceive, the karmic fruits of sentient beings are the most profound;
therefore, the Buddha entered his room to contemplate and investigate with focused diligence.
Furthermore, the Buddha wished to demonstrate that for the ministers of Magadha, regarding the causes and effects of body and mind,
the obstacles and their remedies, death and rebirth,
each possesses various distinct differences.
Therefore, he enters his chamber to contemplate with focused diligence.
Furthermore, because those who are to be converted have not yet assembled;
for the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma is not intended for a single person alone.
Just as a great dragon king’s rain necessarily moistens all things universally,
he entered his chamber to contemplate with focused mindfulness for the sake of waiting upon immeasurable sentient beings who were to be transformed through his emanations.
Furthermore, because the Devaputra Jayasena had not yet arrived—
namely, King Dṛḍhacchāya, who, having been killed by his son, was reborn in the Hall of the Learned (Tuṣita) under the name Jayasena.
Having heard the Tathāgata speak of the differences in the birthplaces of his attendants,
he will surely come to listen and receive the teaching;
therefore, waiting for him, he entered his room once more.
Furthermore, it was because he wished to inspire Ānanda’s reverence for the Dharma;
for if one were to preach the Dharma to him with casual indifference,
he would not develop deep reverence for the Dharma.
Desiring that those who hear [this teaching] with longing and thirst for it should certainly uphold it, contemplate it according to the principle, and explain it extensively to others,
he therefore enters his room to engage in focused contemplation.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of severing the pride and arrogance of foolish people.
This refers to those who, being actually ignorant of what they know,
harbor pride in their supposed cleverness;
when others question them, they fail to discern the depth or shallowness of the matter and answer haphazardly.
Because the Buddha wishes to sever their prideful minds,
he manifests his own wisdom and vision as operating spontaneously toward all phenomena;
even when questioned by others, he still reflects with deliberation before responding with composure.
How much more so for one who lacks wisdom, yet answers when questioned.
Furthermore, the Buddha wished to manifest the qualities of a true spiritual friend (*satpuruṣa*);
that is to say, all true spiritual friends possess three characteristics.
That is to say, he has already well-considered what was to be considered;
therefore, without waiting for a question, he answers with ease.
Furthermore, it is because the Buddha wishes to manifest the characteristics of a wise person himself.
That is to say, the wise speak only after careful reflection;
therefore, the Buddha, having attained [enlightenment], maintains mindfulness and contemplation when questioned. Some say this:
The Buddha wished to enter his chamber to sport in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Because Ānanda had asked a question that he had not yet answered,
at that time, in the afternoon, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and went forth into the midst of the assembly.
He sat down composedly upon the seat as usual.
The Venerable Ānanda approached the Buddha,
prostrated at his feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
The Tathāgata’s face and eyes are now pure, his movements are composed,
and his faculties are tranquil; he must surely be dwelling in meditative concentration, experiencing the bliss of the present dharma.
"As for what you previously requested,
I only wish that you would explain it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is so, it is so, just as you have said.
Listen closely, listen closely, and reflect upon it well;
I shall speak for you."
Of the eighty-four thousand ministers and assistants of the kingdom of Magadha who have passed away,
some were disciplined through the transformative Dharma,
while others practiced in accordance with the Dharma.
They all severed the three fetters,
attained the fruit of stream-entry,
and would no longer fall back into lower states.
They are destined for enlightenment and will undergo rebirth at most seven times;
after wandering and transmigrating seven times among humans and devas, they will bring an end to suffering.
A certain class is born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
In this manner, up to and including one class of beings born within the homogeneous group (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods;
thus it is explained at length.
Question: What is the meaning of the term "ministerial assistants" (*pārṣadya*)?
Answer: They are called "assistants" because they constantly protect and uphold the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, ensuring that they do not decline.
Furthermore, they are all internal attendants of Bimbisāra.
Therefore, they are called "ministers" (*pāricāraka*).
Furthermore, because they all assisted Bimbisāra in governing and nurturing the people of the kingdom,
they are called "ministers."
Furthermore, that was a name established in a previous life;
namely, there was once a king who possessed the seven treasures and ruled over the four continents.
The general was assisted by eighty-four thousand followers as they traveled through the air in sport;
at that moment, the precious wheel and the other treasures suddenly halted and would not proceed.
The king was then struck with terror and said to his ministers,
"Is it not that I have lost my throne,
or that my life has come to an end?"
The deity of the Bodhi tree looked up and addressed the king, saying:
"Not far below here is the Bodhi tree;
it is upon this that all Buddhas rely to attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment."
"One should not travel through the air above a superior vehicle.
Upon hearing this, the king quickly descended, prostrated himself, and apologized with remorse.
Together with his ministers and attendants, he respectfully circumambulated him to the right.

When he had made these offerings and departed by another path, the Wheel-turning King was none other than the present King Bimbisāra; and those eighty-four thousand ministers were those who have now been executed by Ajātaśatru.
Therefore, it is known that "assistant" (*pārṣada*) is an epithet from a previous life.
Although the Sūtra speaks thus, it does not analyze its meaning;
for the Sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which he did not explain should now be explained;

therefore, this treatise is composed to address these questions: What is meant by "subduing through transformative teachings" (*nairmāṇika-dharma-vinaya*), and what is meant by "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharma-pratipatti*)?
Answer: If one perceives the Dharma while among the devas, it is called "conversion through the transformative Dharma" (*dharmānuśāsana-vinaya*).
If one perceives the Dharma while among humans, it is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmanudharmapratipatti*).
Furthermore, if one perceives the Dharma without having undertaken the precepts, it is called "conversion through the transformative Dharma."
If one upholds the precepts and perceives the Dharma, this is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (dharmānudharmapratipatti).
Furthermore, if one plants various roots of goodness among human beings and brings them to maturity,
such that one subsequently attains liberation upon being born among the devas, this is called "subduing through the transformative Dharma" (nairmāṇikadharmavinaya).
If one plants various roots of goodness among human beings and brings them to maturity,
such that one attains liberation while among humans, this is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (dharmānudharmapratipatti).
Furthermore, if one cultivates the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) while among human beings...
Those who attain realization after being reborn among the gods are said to be "tamed by the transformation of the Dharma" (*nairmāṇika-dharmanirvāṇa*).

Those who cultivate the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) while among humans and attain realization while still among humans are said to practice "the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipanna*).

Furthermore, if one cultivates the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) while among humans and subsequently enters the state of rightness and freedom from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) after being reborn among the gods, this is called "subduing through the transformative Dharma" (*nairmāṇika-dharmavinaya*).
If one cultivates the path of preparation while among humans...

Those who, while among human beings, enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) are called those who practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipanna).

Furthermore, if one cultivates the roots of goodness regarding the Truths while among human beings and subsequently attains the clear realization of the Truths (satyābhisamaya) after being born among the gods, this is called conversion through the teaching (avavādavinīta).

If one cultivates the roots of goodness of the truths among human beings and thereby attains the clear realization of the truths while among human beings, this is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, if one cultivates and refines the roots of goodness while among human beings...
Those who, having been born in the heavenly realms, perceive purity therein are said to be disciplined by transformation-dharma (*nairmāṇika-dharma-vinaya*).

Those who cultivate the roots of goodness while among humans and perceive purity therein while among humans are said to be practitioners of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharma-pratipanna*).
Furthermore, if one receives the conventional precepts while among humans and later,
upon being born among the devas, attains the precepts beloved by the noble ones, this is called "taming through the transformative Dharma.
If one receives the conventional precepts while among humans...
That which consists in obtaining the precepts beloved by the noble ones among human beings is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is when one obtains the prātimokṣa and dhyāna restraints among human beings.
Those who, after being reborn among the gods, attain the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) are called "those disciplined by transformation through the Dharma" (*nairmāṇika-dharmavinīta*).
Those who, while among humans, attain either the prātimokṣa or dhyāna restraint,
and subsequently attain the untainted restraint while still among humans, are called "those who practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipanna*).
Furthermore, if one receives the precepts of mental attention while among humans and subsequently attains the natural precepts (*dharmatā-śīla*) upon being born among the gods,
this is called "subjugation through the transformative Dharma" (*nairmāṇika-dharma-vinaya*).
If one receives the precepts of mental attention while among humans...
One who attains the naturally inherent precepts (dharmatā-śīla) among human beings is said to practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharma-anudharma-pratipanna).
Furthermore, if one attains the training in higher ethics (adhiśīla-śikṣā) and higher mind (adhicitta-śikṣā) among human beings.
Those who, having been reborn in the heavenly realms, attain the training in higher wisdom are called "those disciplined by transformation through the Dharma.
Those who, while among humans, attain the training in higher virtue and higher mind,
and subsequently attain the training in higher wisdom among humans, are called "those who practice in accordance with the Dharma."

Furthermore, if one cultivates the factors conducive to stream-entry while among humans and subsequently attains the fruit of stream-entry after being reborn among the devas, this is called "subduing through the transformative Dharma.
If one cultivates the factors conducive to stream-entry while among humans...
Those who attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) among human beings are called "practitioners of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipanna*).

Furthermore, those who attain mundane faith while among humans and later attain verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) upon being born in the heavens are called "those disciplined by the transformative Dharma" (*nairmāṇika-dharma-vinīta*).
If one attains mundane faith while among human beings,
and thereby attains verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) among human beings, this is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, if one cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) while among human beings...
Those who are born in the heavenly realms and attain full realization are called "tamed by transformation.
Those who cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment while among humans and attain full realization therein are called "practitioners of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma."

Question: Why is one who attains the vision of the Dharma among the devas called "tamed by the transformative teaching" (nairmāṇika-dharmanirvāṇa), whereas one who attains the vision of the Dharma among humans is called "one who practices in accordance with the Dharma" (dharmānudharmapratipanna)?
Answer: If one attains the vision of the Dharma among the devas, the cultivation of preparatory application is slight;
if one attains the vision of the Dharma among human beings, the cultivation of preparatory application is extensive.
This is because those who attain the vision of the Dharma among human beings [require more effort].
First, diligently honor and make offerings to one’s teachers and friends;
recite the Sūtras, study the Vinaya,
and listen to and receive the analytical determinations of the Abhidharma.

To refute that attachment and to demonstrate that the intrinsic natures of these two are also distinct, this treatise is composed.

Furthermore, there are those who say that here it specifically refers to the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*).
This refers to the discrimination of the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena,
the establishment of the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena,
and the removal of delusion regarding the substance of things and delusion regarding the objects of cognition.
Among all phenomena, there is neither increase nor decrease.
Alternatively, some say that what is here primarily taught is the cognition obtained through birth.
That is to say, regarding the Three Piṭakas and the twelve divisions of the teachings,
they receive, uphold, recite, and ultimately disseminate them.
The commentary states:
It should be stated thus:
herein, all *prajñā* is spoken of in general;
whether it be that which is innate (*upapatti-labdha*).
Whether it be that which is accomplished through hearing,
that which is accomplished through reflection,
or that which is accomplished through cultivation.
Whether it be the penetration of the truths,
whether they be with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
Whether it occurs in the mental ground (manobhūmi) or in the five sensory consciousnesses,
all are termed "deliberation" (vitarka),
because all possess the characteristic of observation. What, then, is the distinction between [the two types of] deliberation?
