This refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and [the other views],
excluding only false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*);
for one who has attained receptivity (*kṣānti*) does not repudiate the Four Noble Truths.
The masters of the West say:
"Only the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) is termed 'view' (dṛṣṭi) in this context,
because one who has attained patience (kṣānti) no longer clings to a self."
The critique says:
One should state this:
they, too, cling to a self.
Therefore, it is best to explain it here in this initial manner:
although one momentarily grasps at a self, one does not grasp at [the extremes of] annihilation or permanence;
and although one momentarily conceives of purity, one does not grasp at it as supreme.
However, due to five causes and conditions,
the various afflictions do not manifest even though they have not yet been permanently severed.
First, by the power of śamatha.
Second, by the power of vipaśyanā;
third, by the power of virtuous teachers and friends;
fourth, by the power of a favorable dwelling place.
Fifth, due to the power of the thinness of the afflictions by nature;
herein, for the sake of brevity, only the first two types of patience are mentioned,
namely, the mental application of *vipaśyanā*.
This refers to śamatha.
Because it is sustained by two roots of goodness, views and doubt do not arise;
even if they were to arise, one would not perceive them, because the afflictions are subtle.
"Because their wisdom is inferior,
they form this thought," and so forth, as explained at length; this refers to those who,
through tainted patience (*sāsrava-kṣānti*), contemplate the truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).
One who claims to have already attained the untainted true vision when it has not yet been attained is said to possess the pride of overestimation (*adhimāna*).
This arises from the view of suffering (*duḥkha-dṛṣṭi*).
That which has suffering as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) takes suffering as its object; that which arises from the view of origination takes origination as its object-condition.

Although those taintless patiences (anāsrava-kṣānti) are able to contemplate the truths of suffering and origination both collectively and individually, [they do so by taking them as their respective objects].
However, those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) can only take specific objects;

that is to say, those [afflictions] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) take only the dharmas to be abandoned through the vision of suffering within their own stage as their objects.
As for those [defilements] abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they take as their object only the factors abandoned through cultivation within their own stage. Question:

Should this overweening pride (*adhimāna*) also be able to take as its object the mind and mental factors associated with the category of receptivity to suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-kṣānti*)?
Why is it that only the conditions for suffering and its origin are mentioned?
The answer is: although they should also have been mentioned, their omission should be understood as an intentional ellipsis within this context.
Furthermore, those [instances of pride] that take the categories of patience (*kṣānti*) as their object are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Those that take suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) as their objects pertain to all five classes of pride.
Since this section speaks only of those [prides] that can take everything as their object, it does not mention the overweening pride (*abhimāna*) that takes patience as its object.
Furthermore, the category of tainted patience (*sāsrava-kṣānti*) is also subsumed under suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
For this reason, it is said here that [this pride] takes suffering and its origin as its object.
The statement that it takes suffering and its origin as its object precludes the attachment that conceives of this pride as being without an object.
This also excludes the possibility that this pride takes other stages (*bhūmi*) or other schools (*nikāya*) as its object.
Other masters say:

"That which takes suffering (*duḥkha*) or origin (*samudaya*) as its object is the patience regarding suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-kṣānti*), not [the knowledge] regarding suffering and origin."
That explanation is unreasonable.
Since it is not stated that [the pride] based on the subsequent [attainment] regarding cessation or the path takes cessation or the path as its object,
it does not contradict reason for it to take suffering or origination as its object.
If one gives rise to overweening pride, thinking that the extinction of the view of self is extinction, or that the path of seeing is the path—what is the object of this [pride]?
The answer is: suppose there is a certain class of people who associate with virtuous persons.
By hearing the true Dharma and attending to it correctly,
one attains the patient acceptance that accords with the truths (*satyānulomikī kṣānti*).
This refers to the stage at the conclusion of the clear realization of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya-anta*).
Regarding the patience and delight toward cessation, one clearly realizes it as cessation;
regarding the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika*), through patience and delight toward the path, one clearly realizes it as the path.
This is because they maintain these through the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of that patience.
Alternatively, due to a lack of mental attention (amanasikāra) in the interim, views and doubt do not arise.
Even if they were to arise, one would not perceive them and would instead think:
"I see cessation as cessation," or "I see the path as the path."

From this, having already given rise to conceit (*māna*), or conceiving conceit, or being about to conceive conceit, there is the uplifting of the mind, the haughtiness of the mind, and the grasping at a self;
this is called overweening conceit (*adhimāna*). This takes those very minds and mental factors as its object.
The meaning of the various phrases herein is as previously explained.
Regarding the phrase "this is that which takes those mental states and mental factors as its object":

when one possesses contaminated patience (*sāsrava-kṣānti*) and contemplates the truths of cessation and the path, one might claim to have already attained the untainted true vision (*anāsrava-bhūta-darśana*).
To claim to have attained what has not yet been attained is called the pride of overestimation (*abhimāna*).
Regarding those arising from the cessation of views:

these are the mental states and mental factors of the category of outflow-free patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) that take the cessation of the object and the subject as their condition. Regarding those arising from the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*): [these are the mental states and mental factors of the category of outflow-free knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*)].
Taking as objects the mental states and mental factors belonging to the category of outflow-tainted patience (*sāsrava-kṣānti*) regarding the path and its objects,

those outflow-tainted patiences, although they take cessation and the path as their objects, involve overweening pride (*abhimāna*) that takes only the mental states and mental factors of the category of patience as its object.
Because the cessation and the path are states of tranquility and are not objects of conceit,
the phrase "having the mind as its object" and so forth serves to refute the attachment that conceit has no object of perception.
This also excludes the possibility that this pride takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) or the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object.
Question: Is this overweening pride (*adhimāna*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) or bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
If it were so, what would be the fault?
If the receptivity (*kṣānti*) that is part of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) belonging to the desire realm has no object within the desire realm,
then how could a person belonging to the form realm who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire be free from this pride?
Some say that this pride is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-saṃprayukta*).
If that were so, one might ask: would a person (*pudgala*) who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire (*kāmarāga*) be without this pride?
Answer: Here, it is briefly stated that this applies to those who have abandoned the defilements of desire.
Some say, however, that even those who have not abandoned the defilements of desire may give rise to overweening pride (*abhimāna*) regarding the *anāgamya* stage.
He should not speak thus,
because one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of a lower stage necessarily does not give rise to the afflictions of a higher stage.
Furthermore, there are others who say:
This conceit is also bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Question: If that is so, and there is no patience (*kṣānti*) of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) in the desire realm, what is its object?
Answer: Although the aids to penetration do not exist in the desire realm, [the conceit] has that as its object.
Furthermore, there are similar roots of goodness;
this overweening pride arises based upon them,
because the desire realm possesses all qualities that resemble [those of the higher realms].
"If one gives rise to overweening pride [thinking], 'Birth for me has been exhausted,' and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed?
Answer: The preceding text spoke only of the overweening pride arising in ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Now, I shall explain in general the overweening pride (*adhimāna*) arising in both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).

Just as with ordinary persons and noble ones, it should be understood that there are those who have not yet seen the truths (*adṛṣṭasatya*) and those who have already seen them (*dṛṣṭasatya*), and those who have not yet realized through direct insight (*anabhisamita*) and those who have already realized them (*abhisamita*).
The same applies to those in the indeterminate group and those in the group of right determination,
as well as to those who lack the noble path and those who possess it.
Furthermore, the preceding text spoke only of overweening pride in those who have not yet attained the fruit.
Now, I wish to explain generally the overweening pride (*adhimāna*) of those who have not yet attained the fruit and those who have already attained it.
Furthermore, while the preceding text spoke only of overweening pride arising based on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
I now wish to explain generally the overweening pride arising based on the paths of seeing, cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Furthermore, the preceding passage spoke only of conceit arising based on the path of training (*śaikṣamārga*);
now, we wish to speak generally of conceit arising based on both the paths of training and no-more-training (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Moreover, the preceding passage spoke only of conceit belonging to the desire and form realms (*kāmadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*).
Now, wishing to provide a general explanation regarding the overweening pride (*adhimāna*) within the three realms, this treatise is composed.
If one gives rise to overweening pride thinking, "Birth for me has been exhausted," what is the object of that [thought]?
Answer: It is as when a certain class of persons thinks and says:
"This is the path, this is the practice.
By relying on this path and this practice,
I have fully understood suffering."
Having permanently abandoned the origin [of suffering], having realized cessation,
and having cultivated the path,
my births are now exhausted.
From this, pride arises—past, present, and future—a state of mental inflation and self-exaltation called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This is precisely dependent origination.
Within this, there is "this is the path" and "this is the practitioner."
Wherever one forms the perception of the path, having fully understood suffering up to having cultivated the path;
wherever one forms the perception of the origin, cessation, and path of suffering.
Regarding the phrase "birth has been exhausted":
whichever aggregate one perceives as "birth," that itself is what is conditioned by birth.
That which has its arising exhausted by conditions is precisely the contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*).
Question: This overweening pride (*abhimāna*) should also be able to take pride itself as its object;
why, then, is it said that what is grasped [by this pride] is only the practice of the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga-caryā*) that has its arising exhausted?
The answer is that it should also have been stated;
the fact that it was not stated should be understood as an elliptical expression.

Furthermore, regarding those who practice by taking the Path as their object, the conceit that arises from what is to be abandoned through cultivation alone takes all five categories [of suffering] as its object.
In this context, only those [factors] that are able to take [everything] as their object are mentioned.
Furthermore, because the practice of the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*) is also comprised within "arising," it is said to have arising as its object.
Other masters say:
The path of practice as it is grasped is called "arising" because it can give rise to conceit;
however, this conceit takes only the path capable of exhausting arising as its object.
That [previous] explanation is irrational, for later, regarding conceits such as "I have already established the holy life," it is not said that they take arising as their object.
Because this conceit has as its object that which is exhausted by birth, it does not contradict reason.
If one gives rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), thinking "my holy life (*brahmacarya*) is established," what is the object of this?
Answer: It is as when a certain class of persons thinks to themselves:
"This is the path; this is the practice.
Relying upon this path and this practice, I have fully understood suffering and have permanently abandoned its origin."
Cessation has been realized;
the path has been cultivated.
My holy life has been established.

From this, having already given rise to conceit, or conceiving oneself as conceited, or being about to conceive oneself as conceited, the mind becomes uplifted and haughty, taking it as a self-designation; this is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This takes those very mental states and mental factors as its object.
The meaning of the various phrases herein is as previously explained.
Regarding the phrase "my holy life has been established":
wherever one forms the perception of the holy life,

the Arhats— having already established themselves in the name of the path of training (śaikṣa) and now established in the name of the path beyond training (aśaikṣa)— take as their object those very mental states and mental factors.
This overweening pride (adhimāna) takes as its object the practice of the contaminated path (sāsrava-mārga) which they grasp;
for the untainted holy life (anāsrava-brahmacarya) is not within their domain.
If one gives rise to overweening pride thinking, "What was to be done by me has been accomplished," what is the object of this [pride]?
Answer: Suppose there is a certain class of people who think thus:
"This is the path; this is the practice.
Relying upon this path and this practice..."
Suffering has been fully understood;
its origin has been permanently abandoned;
its cessation has been realized.
The path has been cultivated;
I have already severed the latent tendencies;
I have destroyed the afflictions.
The knots have been cast off;
the outflows have been exhausted;
what was to be done has been accomplished.
From this, having already given rise to conceit (*māna*), or conceiving conceit in the future, the mind’s inflation and self-exalting is called "overweening conceit" (*adhimāna*).
This takes those very mental states and mental factors as its object.
The meaning of the various phrases herein is as previously explained.
Regarding those who have already severed the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and so forth, up to those who have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), the author of this treatise,
being skilled in the meanings of various synonyms, has thus provided these diverse explanations.
Although the phrasing differs, the essence is no different;
all are intended to demonstrate the cessation of afflictions,
such as the severing, harming, vomiting out, and exhausting of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The meanings established through mutual correlation are not contradictory.
That is to say, the cessation of afflictions is termed "that which is to be done" (*kṛtya*);
because its realization is fulfilled, it is called "already accomplished" (*kṛta*).
Regarding the phrase "this refers to those very minds and mental factors":
this overweening pride takes as its object the practice of the contaminated path adhered to by that [pride];
since the cessation of all afflictions is not its objective domain, if one gives rise to overweening pride, thinking, "I shall not undergo further existence," [it is erroneous].
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed?
Answer: It is because [the previous section] discussed the overweening pride (*adhimāna*) that arises in those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*).
I now wish to explain the overweening pride (abhimāna) that arises based on non-timely liberation (*asamaya-vimukti*).
Furthermore, while previously I explained the overweening pride that arises based on the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*),
I now compose this treatise because I wish to explain the overweening pride that arises based on the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
If one gives rise to overweening pride, thinking, "I shall not undergo further existence," what is the object of this [thought]?
Answer: It is as when a certain class of people thinks to themselves, "This is the path; this is the practice."
By relying on this path and this practice,
I have fully understood suffering and have permanently abandoned its origin.
Cessation has been realized;
the path has been cultivated;
my births have come to an end.
The holy life has been established;
what was to be done has been accomplished;
there will be no further existence.
From this, pride arises—past, present, and future; the elevation of the mind, the reliance upon it, and the grasping at a self are called "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*).
This has as its object that [attainment] which exists; the meanings of these various phrases herein are as previously explained.
Furthermore, the statement "my births are exhausted" and so forth reveals that the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) arises based upon the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
Just as the aforementioned knowledge of exhaustion arises based upon the practice of the path (*mārga-caryā*), it is therefore called the practice of the path.
"One who does not undergo further existence" refers to one who has attained the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) and no longer falls back into receiving further existence;
this is precisely what takes existence as its object.
This overweening pride takes as its object that which is not accepted [as existing].
The question and answer regarding this should be understood as before,
because the meanings of "existence" (bhava) and "arising" (jāti) are similar.
Some versions state that because the conditioning of mind and mental factors reveals the non-existence of future existence, this is itself the cessation and the path.
To the question, "Why is it not the case that 'my births are exhausted'?
the answer is: that too should be understood in the same way; it is merely stated in a reciprocal manner.
Question: Who gives rise to how many kinds of overweening pride (*adhimāna*)?
Some say that ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) give rise to five kinds of overweening pride;
namely, regarding superior contaminated roots of goodness (*sāsrava-kuśalamūla*) and the four fruits of the śramaṇa, such as stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
The stream-enterer gives rise to four, excluding the first;
the once-returner gives rise to three, excluding the first two;
the non-returner gives rise to two, excluding the first three.
The various Arhats are free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Question: How is it that those such as the Stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) give rise to pride regarding their own fruit?
Answer: They give rise to overweening pride regarding their superior faculties (*indriya*).
Some say that ordinary beings give rise to nine kinds of overweening pride (*abhimāna*):
namely, [pride] regarding superior contaminated roots of goodness,
as well as [pride] regarding the four paths and four fruits of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phala) gives rise to seven [knowledges], excluding the first two.
The candidate for the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka) gives rise to six, excluding the first three.
The fruit of once-returning gives rise to five, excluding the first four.
The candidate for the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmipratipannaka) gives rise to four [knowledges], excluding the first five.
The fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) gives rise to three, excluding the first six.
The candidate for the fruit of arhatship (arhattvapratipannaka) gives rise to two, excluding the first seven.
The fruit of arhatship is free from overweening pride;
there is no sense in which one on the path of stream-entry could give rise to overweening pride.
The critique states:
The noble ones also give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*) regarding superior contaminated wholesome states;
therefore, each of the six noble ones adds one more [type of pride] to those previously mentioned.
Question: How can ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) give rise to overweening pride regarding an Arhat?
Answer: There are two types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*):
first, those who follow by way of craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*), and second, those who follow by way of views (*dṛṣṭi-carita*).
If one who is dominated by craving practices the contemplation of impurity,
they subdue the afflictions belonging to the category of craving so that they do not manifest; however,
those whose nature is such will not give rise to the afflictions belonging to the category of views.
He then considers himself to have attained the fruit of arhatship.
If he sees a practitioner cultivating mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti),
which suppresses the afflictions of the category of views so that they do not manifest, [he likewise considers himself to have attained it].
Because those whose nature does not give rise to the afflictions of the category of craving, they claim for themselves the fruit of arhatship.
Question: Does this overweening pride arise only based on the existence of a locus?
"Does it also arise based on the non-existent?
Answer: "It arises based on both.
That is to say, when ordinary beings give rise to overweening pride (*abhimāna*) regarding contaminated wholesome states, it arises based on the existent."

Regarding the arising of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) with respect to untainted wholesomeness (*anāsrava-kuśala*), it arises based on what is non-existent; regarding the arising of overweening pride with respect to the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) and tainted wholesomeness (*sāsrava-kuśala*), it arises based on what is existent.
Regarding the stage of one entering the stream (srotāpatti-pratipannaka) up to the fruit of arhatship, one gives rise to overweening pride (abhimāna);
this arises based on what is non-existent.
To speak at length, this extends even to one entering the fruit of arhatship regarding that very fruit of arhatship and regarding wholesome states with outflows (sāsrava-kuśala).
The arising of overweening pride (adhimāna) occurs based on what exists;
the arising of overweening pride regarding the fruit of arhatship occurs based on what does not exist.
Question: Can one who has not yet attained the fundamental meditative absorptions (mauladhyāna) of the form and formless realms also give rise to such overweening pride?

Some say that it does not arise, because those afflictions are bound to the fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*) of that specific level. It should be said, however, that this is not fixed;

for one who has not yet attained [the higher level] at all cannot give rise to it, since the afflictions of a higher level do not manifest for one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of a lower level.

If one has already attained [a higher stage] but has not yet manifested it, it is possible for that pride (*māna*) to arise, because the afflictions such as pride also exist in those preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
How is it that one considers oneself inferior and yet gives rise to pride? This is explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to bring certainty to those who harbor doubts.
Specifically, there are those who doubt whether one who exalts oneself and disparages others can truly be said to possess pride (*māna*).
If one feels inferior toward oneself and superior toward others, it should not be called pride (*māna*).
However, in order to resolve the doubts of others and to demonstrate that such a state constitutes the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*), this treatise was composed.
What is meant by "conceiving oneself as inferior and yet giving rise to pride"?

Answer: Suppose there is a certain class of person who, seeing another who is superior to themselves in terms of lineage, clan, wealth and status, arts and skills, fields and houses, and so forth, thinks to themselves:
"He is slightly superior to me, and I am slightly inferior to him.
Yet, one is actually inferior to that other person by many hundreds of thousands of times.
From this, pride arises—past, present, or future—a loftiness of mind, a state of self-conceit, and a grasping at oneself.
This is called conceit arising from considering oneself inferior. In this context, "caste" refers to the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and so forth;
"clan" refers to the Kāśyapas, Gautamas, and so forth.
"Clan" refers to one's paternal and maternal lineages;
"kind" refers to categories such as white or black;
and "wealth" refers to gold, silver, and so forth.
"Rank" refers to kings, nobles, and the like;
"crafts" refers to skills and arts and the like;
"arts" refers to calligraphy, mathematics, and the like.
"Field" refers to the place where crops are sown and harvested;
"dwelling" refers to the place where humans and others reside;
"and so forth" refers to other matters such as eloquence and the like.
Regarding such matters, because one perceives others who are superior to oneself as being many while claiming them to be few, one forms the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*).
If one were to weigh [the situation] correctly, it would not be called pride.
Furthermore, there are seven types of pride (*māna*).
1. Pride (māna).
2. Excessive pride (atimāna).
3. Pride beyond pride (mānātimāna).
4. Pride of self (māna).
5. Arrogant pride (adhimāna).
6. Inferiority pride (ūnamāna).
Seventh is false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
Pride consists of regarding oneself as superior when one is inferior, or regarding oneself as equal when one is equal.
Based on this, there arises pride, past pride, and future pride; it is the inflation of the mind, the mind’s self-reliance, and its self-appropriation.
Excessive pride (*atimāna*) consists in regarding oneself as superior to those who are equal,
or regarding oneself as equal to those who are superior;
the arising of pride based on this is explained at length as previously described.
*Abhimāna* (conceit beyond conceit) is the claim of being superior when one is actually inferior;
the arising of conceit from this is explained at length as before.

*Asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") is the notion of "I" and "mine" with respect to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*); the arising of conceit from this is explained at length as before.
Those with overweening pride claim to have attained what they have not attained,
to have acquired what they have not acquired, and to have realized what they have not realized regarding superior qualities.
To claim realization when one has not yet realized it gives rise to pride, as explained in detail previously.
As for inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*), it is to consider oneself slightly inferior when others are far superior.
Arrogance arising from this is explained at length as before.
As for false pride (*mithyāmāna*), it is when one who actually lacks virtue claims to possess virtue;
arrogance arising from this is explained at length as before.
Question: Since both overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and false pride (*mithyāmāna*) arise based on what has not been attained, how do they differ?
Answer: Overweening pride arises with respect to both what exists and what does not exist, whereas false pride arises only with respect to what does not exist.
Furthermore, overweening pride (*adhimāna*) arises with respect to both what has been attained and what has not yet been attained,
whereas false pride (*mithyāmāna*) arises only with respect to what has not yet been attained.
Furthermore, overweening pride arises with respect to qualities that are equal or superior.

False pride arises in relation to that which is entirely devoid of merit. Furthermore, overweening pride arises in relation to what appears to be merit or actual merit, whereas false pride arises in relation to that which is entirely devoid of merit.
Furthermore, overweening pride (*adhimāna*) arises in both non-Buddhists and Buddhists alike,
whereas false pride (*mithyāmāna*) arises only among non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, overweening pride arises in both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
The pride of false superiority arises only in ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
this is the distinction.
Question: Among these seven types of pride, how many are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
How many are abandoned through cultivation?
Some say that one is abandoned solely through seeing.
That is to say, the pride of "I am" (asmimāna) is abandoned solely through cultivation; the pride of inferiority (ūnamāna) is also abandoned solely through cultivation;
the remaining five types of pride are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation.
Other masters say that two are abandoned only by insight— namely, the conceit "I am" and false conceit—
and one is abandoned only by cultivation— namely, inferiority conceit.
The remaining four [supernormal powers] are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation.
The critique states:
one should speak thus.
The seven types of pride are all subject to abandonment through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Question: How is it that the pride of self (asmimāna) and the pride of wrongness (mithyāmāna) are also subject to abandonment through the path of cultivation?

Answer: Following the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of nihilism (mithyādṛṣṭi), which grasp at the five aggregates as "self" and "mine" or deny them as non-existent, [the pride of self and the pride of wrongness arise]. Thus, they are subject to abandonment through the path of cultivation.
Either conceit (*asmimāna*) and false conceit (*mithyāmāna*) arise taking as their object phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*),
or they even arise taking as their object phenomena abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). Therefore,
these two types of conceit are both abandoned through cultivation.
Question: How is it that the view of inferiority (*ūnamāna*) is abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
Answer: It is as when those who hold the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) have mutually questioned one another regarding the characteristics of the view of self.

There is one who, having perceived that another’s view is superior to his own, yet considers himself only slightly inferior to those who are much superior, and thus gives rise to the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*).
These forms of the pride of inferiority are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). Question: Of these seven types of pride, how many are bound to which realm (*dhātu*)?
Some say that the desire realm possesses all seven [pride-afflictions],
while the two upper realms possess only six, excluding the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*).
Because there is no comparison of lineage and so forth in those realms.
The commentary states:
the form and formless realms also possess all seven types of pride.
Question: Since they lack the sense of comparing their lineage and so forth, how could they possibly have inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*)?
Answer: Although they lack the comparison of lineage and the like, they do possess inferred merits such as meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, it first arises in relation to others while one is still in the desire realm;
subsequently, through the power of repeated practice, it is induced when one is born in the higher realms. Some say this.
Although one born in the higher realms does not give rise to the conceit of inferiority,
such conceit arises in the desire realm; for example,
as in the case of two who have attained meditative concentration in the higher realms.
Through successive rounds of inquiry and response, one attains a specific sign of meditative concentration (*samādhi-nimitta*).
Based on this, one may engage in comparative evaluation and give rise to the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*).
The critique states:
One should state it thus:
[the pride of inferiority] and so forth do not arise by inferring the superiority or inferiority of others;
rather, they arise due to the power of repeated practice since beginningless time.
Even though they arise in the higher realms, they also manifest there;
therefore, all three realms possess the seven types of pride.
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 43.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Forty-four,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Eight of the First Aggregate on Miscellaneous Matters, Sub-section Three:
As stated in the Sūtra, if one gives rise to thoughts of desire, thoughts of malice, or thoughts of harm...
Either harming oneself,
or harming others,
or harming both.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was for the purpose of extensively analyzing and elucidating the meaning of the sūtras.
That is to say, a sutra states that the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Before I had realized unexcelled perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi),
I occasionally gave rise to thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harm."
Or they give rise to thoughts of renunciation,
thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-harming;
even when thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and harming arise, they do not become heedless.
Then he reflects:
"If thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, or cruelty arise,
they may lead to my own harm."
Whether it harms others,
or harms both [self and others],
although the sūtra states this, it does not analyze its meaning.
The Sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Since those [points] were not explained therein, they shall now be explained; thus, this treatise is composed.
How does the pursuit of sensual desire lead to self-harm?
Answer: It is as when a certain class of persons, due to the arising of the fetter of greed,
experiences physical exhaustion and mental exhaustion,
and physical burning and mental burning.
The body is feverish and the mind is feverish;
the body is parched and the mind is parched.
Furthermore, by reason of this, one will experience for a long night the ripening fruits that are unlovely, unpleasant, joyless, and disagreeable—thus harming oneself.
In this context, "physical exhaustion" and so forth indicate that desire,
discursive thought, and the like are the outflowing fruits [of] greed, hatred, and delusion, because they drive and employ one,
causing body and mind to become exhausted like a blazing fire.
It is able to burn the body and mind, making them hot and parched;
one shall undergo these for a long night, etc.—
this reveals the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of sensual desire and discursive thought.
Because one will experience the undesirable fruits of the miserable realms.
How does the pursuit of sensual desire harm others?
Answer: For instance, there is a certain class of persons who, being bound by the fetter of greed, gaze upon the wives of others.
Upon seeing this, that husband gives rise to anger, resentment, hatred, and distress;
thus he harms another.
One might ask: since observing another's wife also brings about bitter fruit, should it not be called "harming both"?
Why is it said that this [covetousness] harms only others?
Answer: Because the fault observed is slight, and since her husband has not yet been subjected to manifest humiliation or injury, it is not so described.
How do sensual thoughts harm both?
Answer: Suppose there is a certain class of person who, having given rise to the fetter of greed, defiles and seizes another's wife.
Once the husband has become aware of this, he subsequently beats, binds, or takes the life of both that wife and that person.
"Or they seize their wealth and treasures; thus they harm them both. Question:
"If that husband harms others and also incurs bitter fruits for himself, he should be called one who commits 'three harms. Why then is he called one who harms 'both'? Answer:
"Because that person does not encounter punishment or penalties in the present life, but is instead praised; therefore, he is not so described."
Furthermore, because it is also harmful to others, it is called "harmful to both.
How does the thought of ill will harm oneself?
Answer: It is as when a certain class of persons gives rise to the fetter of anger.
Therefore, the body is fatigued and the mind is fatigued;
the body is consumed by fire and the mind is consumed by fire;
the body is feverish and the mind is feverish.
The body is tormented and the mind is tormented;
furthermore, by reason of this, one shall experience for a long night the ripening fruits that are unlovely, unpleasant, joyless, and disagreeable.
Thus is one's own destruction.
Regarding these, the two fruits should be understood as previously explained.
How does one harm others through malicious thought?
Answer: It is when a certain class of person gives rise to the obsession of anger.
Regarding "taking the life of another" and "thus harming another":
if one who takes the life of another also incurs a bitter fruit [of suffering], they should be called "harming both.
Why, then, is it said that this refers only to "harming another"?
Answer: Regarding the taking of a thief’s life and so forth, because there is currently no punishment and, on the contrary, one is even praised for it, these are not mentioned.
How is it that harmful thought (vyāpāda-vitarka) causes harm to both?
Answer: For example, there is a certain class of persons who,
because they give rise to the fetter of hatred, take the lives of others,
and are likewise themselves deprived of their lives by others.
Thus, both are harmed. Question:
Since the killer who inflicts harm also incurs bitter fruit, it should be called a "threefold harm"; why then is it called "both"?
Answer: One who executes and harms others is commonly praised by the world and experiences no immediate suffering or retribution; therefore, this is not mentioned.
Furthermore, because they also harm others, they are called "harming both.
How does harmful thought harm oneself?
The answer is: it is as when a certain class of persons gives rise to the fetter of harmfulness (*vyāpādasaṃyojana*).
The body is weary and the mind is weary;
the body is scorched and the mind is scorched;
the body is feverish and the mind is feverish.
The body is consumed by fire and the mind is consumed by fire;
furthermore, due to these conditions, one shall experience for a long night the ripening fruits that are undesirable, unpleasant, joyless, and disagreeable.
Thus is one's own destruction.
Regarding these, the two fruits should be understood as previously explained.
How does harmful thought harm others?
Answer: It is when a certain class of persons, due to the arising of the obsession of harmfulness, beats or binds others.
If it is thus harmful to others, one might ask:
since striking and binding others also brings about bitter fruits, they too should be called "harming both.
Why, then, is this described as being "only harmful to others"?
Answer: Because striking and binding wicked people are universally praised by the world and do not result in suffering in the present life, they are not mentioned.
What is meant by "harmful thoughts that involve harming"?
Answer: It is when a certain class of persons, due to the arising of the obsession of harmfulness (*vihiṃsā-paryavasthāna*), strikes and binds others.
Furthermore, they may be beaten and bound by others; thus, they are harmed in both ways.
Regarding this, the question and answer should be understood as before. Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these three types of unwholesome discursive thought?
Answer: Sensual vitarka has as its intrinsic nature the vitarkas associated with greed that coexist with the five categories and six groups of consciousness of the desire realm.
Hostile vitarka likewise has as its intrinsic nature the vitarkas associated with hatred that coexist with the five categories and six groups of consciousness.
Regarding harmful investigation (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*),
there is a teaching that its intrinsic nature consists of the investigative thought associated with a portion of hatred (*dveṣa*),
because harmfulness is itself hatred.
Question: If that is so, what is the difference between ill-will (*vyāpāda-vitarka*) and harmful intent (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*)?
Answer: Hatred (*dveṣa*) is of two kinds:
first, the desire to terminate the life of sentient beings.
The first two involve the desire to strike and bind sentient beings;
the former is called anger (*krodha*) and the latter is called harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of hatred (*dveṣa*).
First, it arises toward an object where anger is appropriate;
second, it arises toward an object where anger is inappropriate.
The former is termed *pratigha* (hostility), and the latter is termed *vihiṃsā* (harmfulness).
Because those two types of vitarka are termed "vitarka of ill-will" (*vyāpāda-vitarka*) and "vitarka of cruelty" (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*), there is a distinction between them.
Some say that the vitarka of cruelty has as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) the vitarka associated with a portion of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because harm is none other than ignorance.
As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
"For what reason does delusion increase?"
That is to say, regarding the element of harm (*vihimsā-dhātu*), the perception of harm (*vihimsā-saṃjñā*), and thoughts of harm (*vihimsā-vitarka*):
if one practices, cultivates, or frequently engages in them, the thoughts associated with those are called "thoughts of harm" (*vihimsā-vitarka*).
The critique states:
It should be stated thus:
there is a distinct mental factor called harm (*vihiṃsā*),
which is not anger (*dveṣa*).
It is not ignorance;
it is not a latent tendency (anuśaya).
Its intrinsic nature is induced by hatred.
These are the outflows and concomitants of hatred;
arising after hatred,
they are called the defilements (kleśamala).
It is associated only with the mental consciousness that is abandoned through cultivation;
this associated vitarka is the intrinsic nature of harmful vitarka.
Because these three are unwholesome, they are called "evil vitarkas."
Furthermore, there are three types of wholesome thoughts: first, the thought of renunciation;
second, the thought of non-ill will;
and third, the thought of non-harming.
Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these three wholesome thoughts?
Answer: All have as their intrinsic nature the thoughts associated with all wholesome states of mind.
That is to say, the three unwholesome thoughts arise individually, each having a distinct intrinsic nature.
They do not coexist with any unwholesome mind.
These three wholesome vitarkas have no distinct intrinsic natures; they are all associated with every wholesome mind.
Question: If this is so, what is the difference between these three?
Answer: Their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not distinct, yet their meanings differ.

Because these three are the immediate antidotes to unwholesome thoughts (*akuśala-vitarka*), it is said that wholesome thoughts which oppose thoughts of sensual desire are called "thoughts of renunciation" (*naiṣkramya-vitarka*).
Because it opposes thoughts of ill will, it is called "thought-free from ill will";
because it opposes thoughts of harmfulness, it is called "thought-free from harmfulness.
As stated in the Sūtra: "When I had not yet realized unexcelled perfect enlightenment..."
Although he gives rise to thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harm, he does not become negligent.
Question: At that time, if the bodhisattva is not negligent, how can he still give rise to these three unwholesome thoughts?
The Venerable Vasumitra stated as follows:
"Although a bodhisattva gives rise to these three unwholesome thoughts, he is called 'heedful' because he diligently cultivates the wholesome.
Furthermore, although he gives rise to unwholesome thoughts, he is called 'heedful' because he is able to quickly recognize them as unskillful."
Furthermore, although [the afflictions] arise, one is able to immediately feel weary of them, cast them off, and relinquish them; this is called heedfulness (*apramāda*).
Furthermore, being able to cultivate their antidotes as soon as they momentarily arise is called heedfulness.

Furthermore, non-negligence (*apramāda*) is defined as the ability to sever [afflictions] immediately upon their arising, to recognize the deficiency of their causes, and to understand the faults of their objective conditions.
Furthermore, afflictions manifest due to three causal conditions.
First, by the power of the cause;
second, by the power of the object;
third, by the power of application.
When a bodhisattva gives rise to these three unwholesome thoughts,
being able to suppress the other two solely through the power of the cause is called heedfulness (*apramāda*).
The Venerable One says:
Although a bodhisattva may give rise [to such thoughts], they are able to quickly subdue and eliminate them;
this is called "heedfulness" (apramāda), like a single drop of water falling upon hot iron.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
To arise [from such states] and swiftly abandon them, as if extinguishing a fire on one's head, is called heedfulness (*apramāda*).
Question: Where does a bodhisattva give rise to the three types of unwholesome seeking (*vitarka*)?
The Venerable Pārśva replied:
Due to the power of causes, [the afflictions] arise wherever they may be without requiring a fixed location for their retribution;
just as a blind man stumbles or a fool is deluded,
it is the same wherever he goes— how could there be a fixed place?
Some say: "The Bodhisattva renounced the position of a wheel-turning monarch,
left the city to become a renunciant, and sought unsurpassed enlightenment."
Seeking out his teachers and friends, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha.
During the first part of the day, he entered the city to beg for alms,
surrounded by hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who gazed upon him with reverence.
He prostrated and offered praise without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
When the Bodhisattva first gave rise to thoughts of desire, he was obstructed and hindered by the surrounding crowd;
furthermore, being tormented by the fire of hunger, he again gave rise to thoughts of anger.
As the mind of anger gradually subsides, harmful thoughts arise once more;
in an instant, he becomes aware and gives rise to profound shame and remorse.
Other masters say: [text continues].
The Bodhisattva abandoned the city of Kapilavastu and sought supreme enlightenment in a secluded forest; the King,
his father, consequently dispatched five Śākya men to follow and attend upon him.
Among them, some hold that purity is attained through pleasant practices;
as soon as they see a bodhisattva practicing asceticism, they immediately depart. Furthermore, there are others who hold that purity is attained through ascetic practices.
Later, when he saw that the Bodhisattva had abandoned his ascetic practices, she also took her leave.
At that time, there were two daughters of brahmins named Nandā and Nandabalā;
because they offered him milk-rice and saw that he had no attendant, they remained to provide for his needs.
The woman’s hands were soft and supple as she touched the Bodhisattva;
the Bodhisattva then gave rise to thoughts of desire and immediately thought to himself:
"Previously, it was because my attendants did not abandon me that no woman could come near me;
now, they have again given rise to thoughts of resentment."
When the mind of anger subsides slightly, harmful thoughts arise once again;
he then awakens to this himself and gives rise to great shame and remorse. Some say:
Before the Bodhisattva had left the household life,
his father, King Śuddhodana, betrothed five hundred jade-like maidens to him as consorts and ladies-in-waiting,
intending to provide him with pleasure so that he would not renounce the world.
After the Bodhisattva had abandoned them and gone forth into homelessness,
the various kings sent messengers to demand that the women be returned to their kingdoms.
King Śuddhodana said:
"My son has renounced the world, and my heart is filled with profound grief and distress.
When I see his queen and her attendants, they serve only to comfort my heart for a moment; yet, at present, I am unable to release him to return to his own kingdom.
Upon hearing this, each of the kings gave rise to indignation.
They mobilized their armies and came together to wage war and inflict punishment.
The father king, filled with anxiety and fear, sent word to the Bodhisattva: "It is because of you that I am now beset by these enemies.
Some say that a celestial deity came to inform the Bodhisattva.
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva first gave rise to thoughts of desire toward his father the king;
then, thoughts of malice toward the five hundred kings;
and subsequently, he gave rise to thoughts of harm toward their military hosts.
After a short time, he became aware of this and felt deep shame and remorse.
Furthermore, there are those who say that when the Bodhisattva had left the household life and was practicing austerities, [he experienced this].
Recalling the pleasures of the five desires he had previously experienced gave rise to thoughts of sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*).
Later, hearing that the lifespan of the devas was ending and his own palace was in disarray, thoughts of ill will (*vyāpāda-vitarka*) arose.
Furthermore, regarding those who acted as go-betweens for him, thoughts of harmful intent (*vihiṃsā-vitarka*) arose.
In a brief moment, he attained awakening and gave rise to great shame and remorse.
Alternatively, there are those who say that while the Bodhisattva was practicing austerities for six years, he experienced this.
Māras follow them, seeking to create obstacles;
at times they manifest desirable forms and images,
and the bodhisattva gives rise to thoughts of desire toward them.
At times he manifests a terrifying form,
and the bodhisattva gives rise to thoughts of malice toward him;
at times he manifests a form that mocks and derides.
The Bodhisattva gave rise to thoughts of malice toward him,
but after a short time, he felt remorse and gave rise to a profound sense of shame and dread of blame.
The Venerable Ghosaka spoke thus.
First, the bodhisattva uses the two types of wisdom arising from hearing and reflection within the desire realm to suppress the various afflictions.
Because of attachment to this wisdom, they give rise to thoughts of desire (*kāma-vitarka*).
Upon momentarily awakening to the fact that these are increasing afflictions, they give rise to thoughts of ill-will (*vyāpāda-vitarka*) because of their aversion toward them.
Gradually, his [afflictions] subsided and thinned, and he gave rise to harmful thoughts;
later, upon realizing this, he felt deep shame and remorse.
The Venerable One said:
In the past, when the Bodhisattva was dwelling beneath the Bodhi tree,
a māra-maiden came during the first watch of the night to seduce and disturb him.
At that time, the Bodhisattva briefly rose with the intention of seeking her out.
In the middle of the night, the hosts of Māra came together to harass and afflict the Bodhisattva.
He briefly gave rise to thoughts of malice, which gradually subsided;
then he again gave rise to thoughts of harm.

In an instant, he became aware and immediately entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), causing the hosts of Māra’s soldiers to be defeated and cast down, as described in the sūtras.
After the bodhisattva had given rise to these three unwholesome thoughts, [he realized his error].
He then understands for himself that these [thoughts] can cause harm to oneself, harm to others, and harm to both.
He asks: how is it that the thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and harmfulness arising in a bodhisattva can constitute these three types of harm?
Answer: Although there is no harmful function [in this case], it is explained according to its characteristics.
This is because unwholesome vitarka necessarily possesses the three characteristics of harm.
Furthermore, when unwholesome vitarka arises, one’s own welfare is distanced; therefore, it is called "harming oneself."
Because the welfare of others is remote, it is called "harming others.
Because the welfare of both is remote, it is called "harming both. Furthermore, when unwholesome thoughts arise, because the welfare of oneself is destroyed, it is called "harming oneself."
It is called "harming others" because the welfare of others is destroyed;
it is called "harming both" because the welfare of both is destroyed.
Furthermore, when unwholesome thoughts arise, the mind intent on one's own benefit ceases, which is therefore called "harming oneself."
The cessation of the intention to benefit others is called "harming others.
The cessation of the intention to benefit both is called "harming both.
Furthermore, when unwholesome thoughts arise, they are called "harming oneself" because they take and yield results within one's own continuum.
Because it causes donors to give the four requisites without obtaining great fruit, it is called "harming others.
The combination of these two is termed "harming both.
Furthermore, when unwholesome thoughts arise, they produce innate ignorance within one's own continuum.
Because one is deluded regarding the object of focus, it is called "harming oneself.
Because one causes donors to give without great fruit, it is called "harming others.
The combination of these two is termed "harming both."
Furthermore, when unwholesome thoughts arise, they afflict one's own continuum and are thus called "self-harm.
They afflict the continua of others and are thus called "harming others.
Taken together, these two are termed "harming both."
Furthermore, when unwholesome thoughts arise, they cause one's own continuum to be separated from the bliss of the noble ones;
therefore, they are called "self-harming. They also cause others to be separated [from that bliss];
therefore, they are called "harming others. Taken together, these two are termed "harming both."
The Venerable Vasumitra says:
When unwholesome vitarka arises, it causes one’s own continuum to distance itself from the fruit of dissociation; therefore, it is called "self-harming.
It causes those to be converted to distance themselves from the fruit of dissociation; therefore, it is called "harming others."
Thus, these two together are termed "harming both.
The Venerable Ghosaka said:
"When unwholesome thoughts arise, they cause one's own continuum to distance itself from superior virtues; therefore, they are called 'harming oneself.'"
Because it causes those being converted to lose their superior merits and virtues from afar, it is called "harming others.
These two together are termed "harming both.
The Venerable One said:
When unwholesome thoughts arise, they prevent the swift realization of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); therefore, they are called "self-harming.
Because they cause those to be converted not to quickly obtain benefit, they are called "harming others."
Thus, these two together are termed "harming both.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"When unwholesome thoughts arise, the body and mind are afflicted by feverish distress; therefore, it is called 'harming oneself.'"
Because one loses the benefit of transforming others, it is called "harming others.
Thus, these two together are termed "harming both.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
When unwholesome thoughts arise, one's body and mind become uncomfortable; thus it is called "harming oneself.
Because celestial deities reprimand one, it is called "harming others.
Taken together, these two are termed "harming both."
As stated in a sutra,
the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When I first attained Buddhahood, I frequently gave rise to two types of vitarka."
That is to say, the thought of tranquility and the thought of seclusion.
Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature of these two thoughts?
Answer: The thought of tranquility has the thought of renunciation as its intrinsic nature.
The abandonment of discursive thought has non-hostile and non-harming discursive thought as its intrinsic nature;
some say it is the opposite of this.
Furthermore, peaceful discursive thought serves as the antidote to sensual discursive thought.
The discursive thought of seclusion is the antidote to the discursive thoughts of ill will and harm;
some say it is the reverse of these.
Furthermore, the discursive thought of tranquility is associated with the wholesome root of non-attachment.
It is free from applied thought (*vitarka*), associated with non-aversion and non-delusion, and linked to wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*).
Some say it is the opposite of this.
Furthermore, the "tranquil applied thought" (*praśānta-vitarka*) is the antidote to the applied thought associated with craving (*rāga*).
The thought of seclusion is the antidote to thoughts associated with hatred and delusion;
some say it is the opposite of these.
Furthermore, the thought of peace is associated with loving-kindness and compassion.
It is dissociated from vitarka, prīti, and upekṣā;
some say the opposite.
Furthermore, it is associated with the knowledge of the origin of suffering (duḥkha-samudaya-jñāna) and with vitarka that is peaceful (praśrabdha).
It is dissociated from vitarka and associated with the knowledge of the path of cessation;
some say it is the opposite of this.
Furthermore, it is associated with the samādhis of emptiness regarding the thought of security, and of wishlessness regarding suffering and its origin.
It is associated with the signless concentration (animitta-samādhi) that is free from applied thought, as well as the wishless concentration (apraṇihita-samādhi) of the path;
some say it is the opposite of this.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
Thoughts associated with the defects of saṃsāra are called thoughts of security;
thoughts associated with the virtues of nirvāṇa are called thoughts of renunciation.
The Venerable Buddhadeva says:
The investigation associated with seeing the merit of cessation is called the "investigation of tranquility.
The investigation associated with seeing the faults of cyclic existence is called the "investigation of detachment.
As the Venerable One has said:
The investigation associated with the intention for boundless benefit is called the investigation of tranquility (*kṣema-vitarka*).
The investigation associated with the intention for boundless happiness is called the investigation of seclusion (*viveka-vitarka*).
The Venerable Pārśva said:
The application of thought associated with the intention for boundless peace and happiness is called the "thought of security.
The application of thought associated with the intention for boundless benefit is called the "thought of seclusion.
The Venerable Vasumitra stated:
That which arises from the intention of boundless compassion is called the thought of tranquility (*kṣema-vitarka*);
that which arises from the intention of boundless benevolence is called the thought of seclusion (*viveka-vitarka*).
Question: Why does one who has first attained Buddhahood predominantly give rise to these two thoughts?
Answer: Because these two types of vitarka serve as the preliminary practice and the path of purification for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, they serve as the antidote to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures experienced previously while living as a householder.
Immediately after attaining Buddhahood, he frequently gave rise to thoughts of seclusion as an antidote to the profitless suffering experienced during his practice of asceticism;
immediately after attaining Buddhahood, he gave rise to thoughts of peace and security.
Furthermore, after first attaining Buddhahood, because he rejoices in his own virtues, he frequently gives rise to thoughts of tranquility (*anurakṣaṇā-vitarka*);

because he desires to deliver others, he frequently gives rise to thoughts of renunciation (*viveka-vitarka*). As for wisdom (*jñāna*), is it more numerous, its objects (*ālambana*) more numerous, or both?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To refute the doctrines of other schools and to manifest the correct meaning.
That is to say, there are some who hold the view that there is cognition of the non-existent,
such as the Dārṣṭāntikas; they speak as follows:

If it were the case that cognitions such as those of a magical illusion, a city of *gandharvas*, a whirling firebrand, or a mirage all take non-existent objects as their referents, this would refute their [the opponents'] position;
therefore, it is shown that all cognitions take existent objects as their referents.
Alternatively, there may be those who maintain that while consciousness exists,
it does not take an object as its condition, and that which possesses an object is not consciousness taking an object as its condition.
To refute that position, it is shown that all consciousness is capable of taking an object as its condition.
This demonstrates that all objects are the objects of cognition.
Furthermore, it is to show that because non-Buddhists possess inversions, there is a discrepancy between their objects and their cognition;
whereas it is to show that because followers of the inner path (Buddhists) are free from inversions, their objects and their cognition are in accord.
Furthermore, some say that it is cognition (*jñāna*) that is manifold,
not the object (*viṣaya*), because there are multiple cognitions upon a single object. Now,
wishing to demonstrate that it is the object that is manifold, not the cognition, this treatise is composed for this reason.
Which is more numerous: the knowledges (*jñāna*) or the objects (*viṣaya*)?
Answer: The objects are more numerous, not the knowledges. Why is this so?
Wisdom is also an object; that is to say,
wisdom comprises only a small portion of one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha),
whereas its objects comprise eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
Some say that cognition is not primarily an object. Why is this?
For example, the single momentary feeling of the lowest-of-the-low grade in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is known by the ten knowledges of the desire realm;
that is to say, by the knowledge of the category associated with the universal underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the nine non-homogeneous realms.
And it is known by the wholesome conventional knowledge (*sāṃvṛtijñāna*).
It is known by the ten knowledges of the desire realm;
the same applies up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is known by sixteen types of knowledge:
namely, the knowledge of the category associated with the eleven universal underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
as well as the knowledge associated with greed, pride, and ignorance abandoned through cultivation, and the unobscured-neutral and wholesome conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Thus, there are ninety-six cognitions in total; together with untainted cognition (*anāsrava-jñāna*), these ninety-seven cognitions know that single feeling.
One should understand the remaining feelings and remaining phenomena accordingly.
Therefore, one should know that it is not the case that cognition is manifold while its object is not.
That assertion is irrational. Why is this so?

Since the factors associated with and coexistent with that wisdom, as well as the intrinsic nature of wisdom itself, are all objects, even if one were to grant that wisdom is not an object, its objects would still be many; how much more so when wisdom itself is also an object—how could its objects not be many?
Question: If both cognition (*jñāna*) and its object (*viṣaya*) are [mental], what is the distinction between them?
Answer: That which knows is cognition; that which is known is the object.

Furthermore, cognition is exclusively non-material (*arūpa*), invisible (*anidarśana*), non-obstructive (*apratigha*), conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), associated with mental factors (*samanvāgata*), possessed of a basis (*sāśraya*), possessed of an object (*sālambana*), and possessed of an aspect (*sākāra*).
The objective sphere (ālambana) encompasses both the material and the non-material;
the visible and the invisible; the resistant and the non-resistant; the conditioned and the unconditioned;
the associated and the dissociated; that which has a basis and that which has no basis; and that which has an object and that which has no object.
There are those with mental aspects and those without mental aspects.
Furthermore, wisdom is comprised solely within the three time periods and the three truths;
its objects, however, extend across the three time periods as well as the non-temporal, and are comprised within all four truths.
These are called the distinctions between objects and cognition.
Is cognition more numerous, or are consciousnesses more numerous?
And so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the tenets of other schools and elucidating the correct meaning.
That is to say, there are some who hold [the following view]:
Since the two dharmas of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) are mutually associated, and since patience (*kṣānti*) is itself wisdom,
[the author] refutes that attachment by demonstrating that while all wisdom is associated with consciousness,
not all consciousness is associated with wisdom.
Because the various untainted patiences (anāsrava-kṣānti) are not of the nature of knowledge (jñāna).
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that knowledge is exclusively untainted, whereas consciousness (vijñāna) is exclusively tainted.
Since they are not mutually associated,
this is to refute that attachment and demonstrate that consciousness (*vijñāna*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) both pertain to two types [of association],
possessing the sense of being associated.
Other masters maintain that since wisdom (*jñāna*) is merely a specific state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of consciousness (*vijñāna*),
there is no sense in which wisdom and consciousness are associated (*samprayukta*).
In order to refute that attachment and to demonstrate that consciousness (*vijñāna*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) have distinct essences and functions yet possess the sense of being associated,
this treatise was composed for these reasons.
Which is more numerous: wisdom or consciousness?
Answer: Consciousness is more numerous, not wisdom. Why is this so?
All cognitions (jñāna) are associated with consciousness (vijñāna),
but not all consciousnesses are associated with cognition;
for consciousness associated with receptivity (kṣānti) is not associated with cognition.
Question: Why are the various untainted patiences (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) not considered cognitions (*jñāna*)?
Answer: Because they have not yet repeatedly contemplated the objects perceived.
That is to say, since beginningless time, one has not yet seen the Four Noble Truths with untainted, true wisdom (*anāsrava-bhūta-prajñā*).
Although there is an initial perception now, it is not yet called "knowledge" (jñāna) because it has not been repeatedly observed;
for knowledge is only established when a corresponding wisdom (prajñā) repeatedly observes the object.
There is not a single sentient being who,
since beginningless time, has not repeatedly contemplated all phenomena with outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*);
therefore, all outflow-tainted wisdom is subsumed under knowledge (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, patience (*kṣānti*) consists of the inferential deliberation and acceptance regarding the Noble Truths;
because it is not yet ultimate, it is not subsumed under knowledge (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, because patience coexists with the acquisition of the doubt that is to be abandoned, it is not subsumed under knowledge.
Even if it does not coexist with doubt, it belongs to that same category;
because the uncontaminated path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is not a true antidote [to doubt],
it is still considered knowledge (*jñāna*), even though it may coexist with doubt.
Because untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) is not subsumed under wisdom (*jñāna*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) is said to be predominant.
Furthermore, consciousness is subsumed within seven elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*);
whereas wisdom is subsumed only by a small portion of one element, one base, and one aggregate. Therefore, wisdom is minor.
"Are contaminated formations more numerous, or are uncontaminated formations more numerous?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is given in order to refute the positions of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that the Buddha’s birth-body (*janma-kāya*) is untainted (*anāsrava*),
such as the Mahāsāṃghikas, who speak as follows:
The Sūtra states: "The Tathāgata is born in the world and dwells long in the world;
whether walking or standing, he is not defiled by worldly dharmas.
From this, it is known that the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) of the Tathāgata is likewise untainted (*anāsrava*).
To refute that attachment, it is shown that the Buddha’s birth-body (*janma-kāya*) is necessarily contaminated (*sāsrava*).
If the Buddha’s birth-body were uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
then women of incomparable beauty would not give rise to desire for his body.
Aṅgulimāla should not give rise to hatred; a noble person should not give rise to pride;
and Ulūka should not give rise to delusion.
Since love, hatred, pride, and delusion arise from conditions, the Buddha’s physical body (nirmāṇakāya) is certainly not untainted (anāsrava).
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret the sūtra cited by that school?
Answer: That statement was made with reference to the *dharmakāya*.
When the sūtra says, "The Tathāgata is born into the world and dwells in the world," this is said with reference to the *janmakāya* (the body of birth).
If one is neither walking nor standing and is not defiled by worldly dharmas, this is explained according to the *dharmakāya*;
therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, it is said that one is undefiled because one does not conform [to worldly dharmas].
It is said that the eight worldly dharmas conform to the world,
and because sentient beings also conform to them, they are called defiled;
yet the eight worldly dharmas also conform to the Tathāgata.
Because the Buddha does not conform to them, he is said to be unstained.
Furthermore, although the Tathāgata’s birth-body (*janmakāya*) is subject to outflows (*sāsrava*), it is said to be unstained because it transcends the eight worldly dharmas.
Question: In what way does the Tathāgata also transcend the eight dharmas, such as gain and so forth?
"Profit" refers to when, out of compassion for the brave and wealthy elder, he accepted three hundred million sets of robes in a single day.

"Decline" refers to when he entered the village of Mahāśālā to beg for alms but returned with an empty bowl. "Defamation" refers to the slander by the Brahmin woman Ciñcā and Sundarī, the sound of which spread throughout the sixteen great kingdoms.
Regarding renown: when the Tathāgata was born, his voice reached the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations;
upon attaining Buddhahood, his voice reached the Akaniṣṭha Heaven;
and when turning the wheel of Dharma, his voice reached the Brahma world.
The brahmin Varadāśa praised the Buddha face-to-face with five hundred verses;
so too did the great masters of debate, such as the heterodox Upāli and others.
With hundreds of thousands of verses, they gazed upon and praised the Buddha.
The Venerable Ānanda joined his palms and praised the Buddha’s various marvelous qualities;
the Venerable Śāriputra reverently praised the Buddha’s unsurpassed qualities.
All such cases are as follows:
"Censure" refers to when the brahmin Vālodaka reviled the Buddha in person with five hundred verses;
"Suffering" refers to when the Tathāgata experienced back pain at times.
Gravel, stones, and poisonous thorns wound the toes and so forth.
"Happiness" refers to the happiness of pliancy possessed by the Tathāgata,
as well as the most supreme feeling of pleasure within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
How does the World-Honored One transcend the eight worldly dharmas?
Answer: Although the Tathāgata encounters the four dharmas beginning with gain, he gives rise to neither elation nor joyful attachment;
although the Tathāgata encounters the four dharmas beginning with loss, he gives rise to neither dejection nor sorrowful resentment.
It is called "untainted" (asaṃkliṣṭa) because it transcends [defilement],
not because the term "untainted" is established for that which is untainted (anāsrava).
It is like Mount Sumeru, which rests upon the golden wheel.
Just as the fierce winds from the eight directions cannot shake [a mountain], so too are the Buddhas;
abiding in pure ethical discipline (*śīla*),
they cannot be shaken by the eight worldly concerns.
Therefore, in order to refute the divergent tenets of other schools and to demonstrate the correct principle, this treatise is composed. [Question:
Are contaminated formations more numerous, or are uncontaminated formations more numerous?
[Answer: Contaminated formations are more numerous; uncontaminated formations are not.
Why is this? Because contaminated formations comprise ten bases (*āyatana*) and a small portion of two bases,
whereas uncontaminated formations comprise only a small portion of two bases.
Some say this: "Untainted formations are for the most part not tainted formations. Why is that?"
Just as that which is bound to the desire realm and comprised within the lowest-of-the-low grade is taken as an object by four kinds of untainted wisdom in a single moment: first,
the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
2. Dharma-knowledge of suffering;
3. Receptivity to dharma-knowledge of origin;
4. Dharma-knowledge of origin.
The remaining forms and remaining factors should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, because there are these other various untainted (anāsrava) factors, untainted formations (anāsrava-saṃskāra) are certainly predominant.
Other masters say:
Defiled formations are numerous.
Why is this? For example, a single pure formation serves as the object for four types of defiled formations.
First, wrong view;
second, doubt;
third, ignorance.
The four wholesome mundane knowledges (*laukika-jñāna*) and the remaining untainted formations (*anāsrava-saṃskāra*) should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, there are these other remaining tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Therefore, contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) are certainly more numerous.
The critique states: one should speak thus;
although both contaminated and uncontaminated formations (*anāsrava-saṃskāra*) are equally infinite.

Furthermore, this master of the treatise explains for the time being by way of categorization according to the bases (*āyatana*) that contaminated (*sāsrava*) formations are numerous, while uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) ones are not.
Moreover, although this master of the treatise does not inquire about or answer regarding the quantity of conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, [he proceeds as follows].
Furthermore, according to the principle, there should be a question: "Are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) more numerous, or unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) more numerous?
The answer is: conditioned phenomena are more numerous, not unconditioned phenomena. Why is this so?
Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) comprise eleven bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base,
while unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) comprise only a portion of one base;
the critique states that this should be explained in such a manner.
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are more numerous than conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Why is this?
For as many entities as there are in contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), there are an equal number of unconditioned cessations through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
There are as many entities as there are in the untainted path;
the quantity of the unconditioned state of non-analytical cessation is likewise.
Furthermore, there are others corresponding to the number of entities in tainted phenomena, whether they be few or many.

Because the various non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and the unconditioned space (*ākāśa-asamskṛta*) are unconditioned phenomena (*asamskṛta-dharma*), unconditioned phenomena are for the most part not conditioned phenomena (*samskṛta-dharma*).

Nevertheless, following the previous method and speaking provisionally by way of their bases (*sthāna*), it is said that the number of unconditioned phenomena is small. What is the perfection of conduct (*caryā-sampad*), and so forth, as explained at length?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
That is to say, a sūtra states:
The community of the Buddha’s disciples is perfected in ethical discipline and perfected in meditative concentration.
