Perfection of wisdom,
perfection of conduct,
and perfection of protection.
Although the sūtra makes this statement,
it does not analyze its meaning nor explain how the perfection of conduct is maintained.
The sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Since he has not explained this, and I now wish to explain it, I have composed this treatise.
What is the perfection of conduct?
The answer is: the untrained (aśaikṣa) restraint of body, restraint of speech, and purity of livelihood.

Question: Since there is also restraint for those in training (*śaikṣa*) and for those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), why is it that only those beyond training are mentioned here?
Answer: Because the teaching is given based on what is preeminent.
This refers to those factors or persons who are both beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and preeminent; for this reason, they are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, it refers to those who possess restraint (*saṃvara*) that has not been impaired by non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
The trainings and so forth are not like this.
The bodily action of one beyond training is called bodily restraint;
the vocal action of one beyond training is called vocal restraint.
The bodily and vocal actions of one beyond training are collectively termed "purity of livelihood" (*ājīva-śuddhi*);
these are precisely right action, right speech, and right livelihood.
The Sūtra speaks of them as "precepts."
It is sometimes called śīla,
sometimes called conduct (caryā),
and sometimes called the feet (pāda).
It is also called a "casket.
The term *śīla* carries the meaning of "coolness," in that evil causes the body and mind to suffer the distress of feverish heat.
Because the precepts can bring about peace and comfort, they are called "cooling.
Furthermore, evil can invite the heat and affliction of the miserable realms, whereas the precepts invite the happy realms; therefore, they are called "cooling."
Furthermore, *śīla* has the meaning of "peaceful sleep.
This means that because one who upholds the precepts attains peaceful and secure sleep and constantly experiences auspicious dreams, it is called *śīla*.
Moreover, *śīla* has the meaning of "repeated practice," as one constantly practices wholesome dharmas; thus, it is called *śīla*.
Furthermore, *śīla* has the meaning of "attaining concentration," because for one who maintains the precepts, the mind easily attains concentration; thus it is called *śīla*.
Moreover, *śīla* has the meaning of "a foothold."
As a gāthā says:
The pool of the Buddha’s Dharma is cool and refreshing;
With ethical discipline as its steps, the noble ones bathe therein without wetting their bodies, And thus attain the merit of reaching the further shore.
Furthermore, *śīla* has the meaning of "ornament.
There are ornaments that are beautiful when one is young, but not when one is in middle age or old age;
there are ornaments that are beautiful when one is in middle age, but not when one is young or old.
There are ornaments that are beautiful when one is old, but not when one is young or in the prime of life;
however, the ornament of ethical discipline (śīla) is always beautiful at all three times.
As a verse in the Gāthā says:
The adornment of the body with ethical discipline (*śīla*) is suitable for the young, the middle-aged, and the old alike;
dwelling in faith and wisdom is a treasure that no one can steal.
Furthermore, "ethical discipline" (*śīla*) carries the meaning of a "clear mirror."
Just as a clear and pure mirror reflects images within it,
so too does the image of selflessness appear within one who abides in pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Furthermore, *śīla* carries the meaning of a staircase.
As the Venerable Aniruddha said:
"I tread upon the steps of ethical discipline (śīla) to ascend the palace of supreme wisdom.
Furthermore, ethical discipline carries the sense of "preeminence" (adhipati).
Whatever beings possess power within the trichiliocosm, it is all due to the power of their ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Formerly, in this land of Kaśmīra, there was a venomous dragon.
He was named Wuqiejù (Fearless).
By nature he was violent and malevolent, frequently causing harm.
Not far from there was a monastery (*vihāra*) that was repeatedly tormented by that nāga.
In the monastery there were five hundred great arhats.

They deliberated together and entered meditative concentration, wishing to expel that dragon by exhausting their supernatural powers, but they were unable to send it away. At that time, an arhat arrived from outside.
The resident monks explained the aforementioned matter to them.
Then, the newcomers arrived at the dragon’s dwelling and snapped their fingers, saying:
Bhadramukha departed at once.
Upon hearing his voice, the nāga immediately fled far away.
The arhats, finding this strange, asked: "Why did he leave?"
"What meditative power do you possess that you have dispatched this nāga?
He replied to the assembly,
"I have not entered meditative absorption, nor have I exercised supernormal powers."
It is solely because of guarding the *śīla* that such power exists.
Since I guard even minor offenses as if preventing grave prohibitions, it causes the evil dragon to depart in terror;
therefore, this *śīla* possesses the sense of being "preeminent" (*adhipati*).
Furthermore, *śīla* has the meaning of "head" or "chief.
Just as when there is a head,
one is able to see forms, hear sounds, smell odors, taste flavors, feel tangibles, and cognize mental phenomena.
One who possesses ethical discipline (śīla) is able to see the forms of the Four Noble Truths and hear the sounds of previously unheard name-sets (nāmakāya) and so forth.
They smell the fragrance of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
they taste the flavor of the tranquility of renunciation and supreme enlightenment;
and they experience the contact of meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
Because one knows the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates, bases,
and elements, śīla has the meaning of "foremost.
As the Sūtra says:
Precepts are called "practice" because the world designates precepts by the name of practice.
When people in the world see one who upholds the precepts, they say, "That person possesses practice";
when they see one who violates the precepts, they say, "That person lacks practice."
Furthermore, the pure upholding of the precepts is the root of all practices because it can lead to nirvāṇa; therefore, it is called "practice.
As the sūtras state that the precepts are called "feet," it is because they enable one to go to the happy realms and reach nirvāṇa.
Just as one who has feet is able to avoid dangerous places and reach a secure location,
so too one who possesses pure precepts is able to transcend the evil realms and be born among gods or humans,
or even to transcend birth and death and reach the shore of nirvana; therefore, it is called "feet."
The Sūtra states that ethical discipline is called a "casket" because it sustains all dharmas of merit.
This means that one who maintains the precepts sustains their meritorious qualities so that they do not decline or dissipate,
just as a casket holds jewels.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka has explained it in this way.
The name of the precepts shall not be impaired. Why is this?
Just as when the feet are not impaired, one can travel freely to a place of peace and security.
One who possesses pure ethical discipline is likewise able to reach nirvāṇa.
In this context, the pure ethical discipline of body and speech of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is called the perfection of conduct, as it is the ultimate within all forms of conduct.
What is the perfection of restraint?
The answer is: the restraint of the faculties of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
It should be understood that herein, the faculties are that which is to be restrained.
By the power of mindfulness and wisdom, one guards the sense faculties, such as the eye, so that they do not give rise to faults regarding their objects;
this is like using a hook to restrain an elephant so it does not bolt away.
Therefore, the right mindfulness and right knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are called the perfection of guarding.
As it is said in a gāthā:
"The various torrents of the world can be guarded against by right mindfulness;
if they are to be severed forever, the merit lies solely in clear comprehension."
Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) and non-restraint of the sense faculties?
Answer: Restraint of the sense faculties has right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right situational awareness (*samyak-samprajanya*) as its intrinsic nature.
The non-restraint of the faculties has lack of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension as its intrinsic nature.
How is this known?
Because the sūtras are the authoritative source.
As it is said in a sutra:
A deva addressed a bhikṣu,
"You should not now yourself open this festering wound."
The bhikṣu replied,
"I shall cover it.
The deva spoke again, saying:
"The ulcerous leak is no small matter; how can it be covered?
The bhikṣu replied, "I shall cover it with right mindfulness and right situational awareness."
The deva said, "Excellent!
This is true concealment.
Thus one knows that these two are the restraint of the faculties and the restraint of concealment."
Because they share the same meaning and because the non-restraint of the faculties is established as the opposite of the former, these constitute lack of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension.
Question: If right mindfulness and right clear comprehension constitute the restraint of the faculties, [then...]
How should one interpret what is stated in the sūtras?
For instance, it says: "Because mindfulness and wisdom are fulfilled, the restraint of the faculties is fulfilled.
Does this mean that because the self-nature is fulfilled, the self-nature is fulfilled?
Answer: Mindfulness and wisdom are of two kinds:
first, the nature of cause;
second, the nature of fruit.
The nature of the cause is called mindfulness and wisdom;
the nature of the fruit is called restraint of the faculties.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of mindfulness and wisdom.
First, innate goodness;
second, acquired goodness.
Innate goodness is termed mindfulness and wisdom.
The wholesome state of preparatory application is called "restraint of the faculties.
Furthermore, mindfulness and wisdom are of two kinds:
first, those that are wholesome but not fixed.
There are two types of wholesome states:

those that are not fixed in concentration and those that are fixed in concentration. Those that are not fixed in concentration are called mindfulness and wisdom; those that are fixed in concentration are called the restraint of the faculties.
Furthermore, mindfulness and wisdom are of two kinds:
first, mundane wholesomeness;
second, supramundane wholesomeness.
Mundane wholesomeness is called mindfulness and wisdom;
supramundane wholesomeness is called restraint of the faculties.
Furthermore, mindfulness and wisdom are of two kinds:
first, those of training (śaikṣa);
second, those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
For those in training, it is called mindfulness and wisdom;
for those beyond training, it is called restraint of the faculties.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of mindfulness and wisdom.
First, the lineage of dull faculties;

second, the lineage of sharp faculties. The lineage of dull faculties is termed mindfulness and wisdom, while the lineage of sharp faculties is termed restraint of the faculties; therefore, this does not contradict or conflict with the sūtras.
Some say that restraint of the sense faculties has heedfulness as its intrinsic nature,
while non-restraint of the sense faculties has heedlessness as its intrinsic nature.
Other masters say that restraint of the faculties has the six constant abidings as its intrinsic nature,
while non-restraint of the faculties has the afflictions and karma that are the opposites of these as its intrinsic nature.

Some say that the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) has as its intrinsic nature both the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of those dharmas regarding the six sense faculties that have been abandoned and fully known,
and the possession (*prāpti*) of their counteractive path (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).
Non-restraint of the faculties has as its intrinsic nature the state of possessing those factors that have not been abandoned and not fully understood regarding the six faculties,
as well as the state of not possessing their counteractive path.
Furthermore, there are those who say that restraint of the faculties has as its intrinsic nature the growth, development,
and expansion of all sublime conduct and roots of virtue at the time when the six faculties have been abandoned and fully understood.
Non-restraint of the faculties has as its intrinsic nature the growth and expansion of all evil conduct and unwholesome roots while the six faculties have not yet been severed or fully understood.
Some say that restraint of the faculties has all wholesome dharmas as its intrinsic nature,
while non-restraint of the faculties has all defiled dharmas as its intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, some say that sense-faculty restraint (*indriya-saṃvara*) has as its intrinsic nature all wholesome dharmas and non-obscured neutral dharmas conducive to the wholesome;
whereas sense-faculty non-restraint (*indriya-asaṃvara*) has as its intrinsic nature all defiled dharmas and non-obscured neutral dharmas conducive to defilement.
Formerly, in this land of Kaśmīra, there was a monastery named Śrīkaṇṭha where two arhats once resided;
both had realized the three types of supernormal knowledge (traividya).
He is endowed with the eight liberations and has attained the analytical knowledges;
he is a master of the Dharma and is my own brother.
The father’s name was Nanda, of the Brahmin caste.
They both spoke thus:
"Regarding the restraint of the faculties and the lack of restraint of the faculties."
All of these have as their intrinsic nature the discipline and non-discipline within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind that are unobscured and indeterminate.
Question: If these are all included within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind that are unobscured and indeterminate, [how is there a distinction between them?]
What is the distinction between these two natures?
The answer is: that which accords with defilement is called non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), while that which accords with purification is called restraint (*saṃvara*).
This is called the distinction.
The critique states:
among these various explanations, the first is the best.
The Sūtra states that mindfulness and wisdom are able to guard the sense faculties.
Furthermore, these same mindfulness and wisdom, depending on their specific state, may also receive the name "restraint through abandonment" (*prahāṇasaṃvara*).
Based on the distinctions between these various states, multiple types are established.
Furthermore, regarding the restraint that abandons the outflows (sāsrava-prahāṇa-saṃvara):
this refers to the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation;
for it is by means of the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya-bhūmi) that one can become detached from the outflows of the desire realm.
Within the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), the two factors of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).
If the factors to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*) of the first dhyāna are to be relinquished,
this is accomplished by means of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna.
Within the nine paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), the two factors of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).
This applies up to the factors abandoned through seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*) belonging to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
This is because the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is capable of detaching from the sphere of nothingness.
Within the nine paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), the two factors of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃvara*).
If one speaks of the untainted restraint of abandonment (*anāsravaprahāṇasaṃvara*),
it refers to the phenomena of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the paths of seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Because the stage of "not-yet-reached" (*anāgamya*) can bring about detachment from the desire realm,

within the various untainted paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), the two factors of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).
This applies to those phenomena of the first dhyāna that are to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
By relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), and the first dhyāna, one is able to abandon the three stages of the first dhyāna;
within the various untainted paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), the two factors of mindfulness and wisdom constitute the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃvara*).
Regarding the dharmas to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the second dhyāna:

within the untainted paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) across the four stages— including the first three stages and the second dhyāna— which are capable of abandoning the second dhyāna,
the two factors of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).

Regarding the dharmas to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the third dhyāna, the five stages—consisting of the four preceding stages and the third dhyāna itself—are able to abandon [them].
Within the various untainted paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), the two factors of mindfulness and wisdom constitute the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃvara*).
The dharmas to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the fourth dhyāna,
as well as the dharmas to be abandoned through seeing in the formless realm,
are abandoned by means of the first five stages and the fourth dhyāna, which are capable of relinquishing the fourth dhyāna and so forth.

Within the various uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the six stages that are free from outflows (*anāsrava*), the two factors of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).
Regarding the factors to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*),
one is able to detach from the sphere of infinite space by means of the preceding six stages and the sphere of infinite space itself.

In the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the seven stages, the two dharmas of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*) regarding the dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

Because the first seven stages and the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness are capable of abandoning [the defilements of] the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the two dharmas of mindfulness and wisdom within the nine uninterrupted paths of the untainted (*anāsrava*) eighth stage constitute the restraint of abandonment.
Regarding the dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*):
by means of the first eight stages and the sphere of nothingness, one can become detached from two stages, making nine stages in total.
In the nine untainted paths of immediate succession (*anantarya-mārga*), the two dharmas of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 40; *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Fascicle 44 of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Eight, Part Four of the First Aggregate on Miscellaneous Topics, entitled "The Section on Volition": What is the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was composed in order to refute the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct meaning.

That is to say, some maintain that the ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm constitute the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Such is the case for the Vātsīputrīyas,
who assert that the nature of an ordinary person is bound to the desire realm.
This [nature] is defiled and is to be abandoned by insight;
it is comprised within the aggregate of formations associated with consciousness.
This is stated in order to refute that [erroneous] attachment and to demonstrate that the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is bound to the three realms.
It is to be abandoned by cultivation;
it is non-defiled;
and it is subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) lacks substantial reality;
in order to refute their position, it is demonstrated that the intrinsic nature of the state of an ordinary person is substantially real.
In order to refute the various divergent tenets of these schools and to demonstrate the correct principle,
this treatise was composed. Within this fundamental treatise,
the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is explained.
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* explains the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
As it says: "What are the dharmas of ordinary beings?"
That is to say: the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the northern continent of Uttarakuru, and the heaven of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*).
Their karma and their birth—these are called the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Question: For what reason is this stated in this fundamental treatise?
Does the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* state that the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is not the dharmas of an ordinary person?
Or does it state that the dharmas of an ordinary person are not the nature of an ordinary person?
Answer: Because it is the intention of the author of this treatise;
furthermore, because both of these are incomplete statements;
and furthermore, because each of these two treatises explains one aspect so as to mutually clarify the other.
Furthermore, the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is superior, not the qualities of an ordinary person;
this treatise speaks according to what is superior.
Since this treatise has already explained the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*),
the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* does not repeat it; however,
this treatise has not yet explained the dharmas of an ordinary person.
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* speaks of the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
This indicates that that treatise was composed after this one. Some have said:
Since that treatise has already explained the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are not repeated here.
However, since that treatise has not yet explained the state of being an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*), this treatise explains it.
This indicates that that treatise was composed prior to this one.
Question: Why is it called "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke as follows:
Because it causes sentient beings to give rise to views of different kinds, afflictions of different kinds, and karmas of different kinds,
thereby experiencing results of different kinds and births of different kinds,
it is called the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Furthermore, it is because it causes sentient beings to fall into different realms,
to go toward different destinies,
and to undergo births as different types of beings.
It is called the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Furthermore, it causes sentient beings to place their faith in teachers other [than the Buddha],
and it produces a distinct characteristic.
Because they receive different dharmas,
because they practice different conducts,
and because they seek different fruits.
It is called the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). The Venerable One says:
it is that which causes sentient beings to rely upon a different class of realm, destiny, birth, or mode of existence.
They give rise to various inverted afflictions and perform and increase karma that leads to future existence; thus,
they revolve in birth and death without limit.
It is called "the nature of an ordinary person" (pṛthagjanatva). The masters of the Abhidharma say:
because it is a portion of an ordinary person and because it is the essence of an ordinary person, it is called "the nature of an ordinary person."
The Venerable Ghosaka stated it thus:
"Because they are of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is called 'the state of being an ordinary being' (*pṛthagjanatva*).
The Venerable Pārśva said:
Because ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) rely on faults and thus obstruct the nature of an ārya, they are called "the state of being an ordinary being" (pṛthagjanatva).
Question: Why are they called "dharmas of an ordinary being"?
Answer: Because ordinary worldlings possess these phenomena, they are called "phenomena of ordinary worldlings.
This is, for example, like what are known in the world as the laws of kings and the laws of ministers.
Question: Since the dharmas of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) also exist for noble ones (ārya),
why are they designated solely by the name "dharmas of ordinary beings"?
Answer: For the most part, the dharmas of ordinary beings do not exist in noble ones;
even if they exist to a slight degree, they are not called "noble dharmas.
This is because while noble ones have attained them, they are neither present in their bodies nor manifested before them.
Only ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) obtain these [dharmas], and because they are both accomplished within their bodies and manifest before them, they are called "dharmas of ordinary beings.
Furthermore, ordinary beings accomplish those dharmas.
Because they are able to cause those dharmas to grasp and yield their fruits,
they are called "dharmas of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana-dharma*).
Although noble ones (*ārya*) may possess those dharmas, [they do not grasp or yield their fruits].
Because it is not so, it is not called a noble dharma (*āryadharma*). Furthermore,
ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) accomplish those dharmas,
which cause them to go to different destinies, realms, and locations, and to receive different fruits as ordinary beings.
These are called the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Although noble ones (*ārya*) also possess these dharmas, they do not do so in that manner;
therefore, they are not called the dharmas of noble ones.
Furthermore, the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is contaminated (*sāsrava*);
because those dharmas are also contaminated, they are called "dharmas of an ordinary person.
The nature of a noble one (*āryatva*) is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*); because those dharmas are not uncontaminated, they are not called "noble dharmas."
Furthermore, because ordinary beings are obscured by them,
bound by them, and deceived by them.
They are called the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Because the noble ones (*ārya*) are not like this, they are not called noble dharmas.
Furthermore, because the various classes of ordinary beings conform to those dharmas and cause those dharmas to grow, [they are so named].
These are called the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Since the noble ones (*ārya*) are not so, they are not called noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
Question: What is the nature of being an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*), and what are the dharmas of an ordinary being?
What is the distinction?
Answer: The state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is exclusively non-material (*arūpa*);
the dharmas of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanadharma*) pertain to both the material and the non-material.
The state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is exclusively non-visible;
the dharmas of an ordinary person are both visible and non-visible.
The state of being an ordinary person is exclusively non-resistant.
The dharmas of ordinary beings (pṛthagjanadharma) include both the resistant (sapratigha) and the non-resistant (apratigha).
The state of being an ordinary being (pṛthagjanatva) is exclusively dissociated (viprayukta).
The dharmas of ordinary beings include both the associated (saṃprayukta) and the dissociated.

The state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is exclusively without a basis (*āśraya*), without an object (*ālambana*), and without mental aspects (*ākāra*). All dharmas of an ordinary person, however, pertain to both types [of defiled and non-defiled].
The state of being an ordinary person is exclusively non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*);
it is blameless (*anavadya*) and without karmic maturation (*avipāka*).
The dharmas of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana-dharma) all pertain to both types.
Furthermore, the state of being an ordinary being (pṛthagjanatva) is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta),
whereas the dharmas of ordinary beings pertain to the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
The state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) pertains to all three realms;
the dharmas of an ordinary person pertain only to the desire and form realms;
and the state of being an ordinary person is abandoned only through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
The dharmas of ordinary beings (pṛthagjanadharma) are common to both those abandoned by seeing and those abandoned by cultivation.
Furthermore, the state of being an ordinary being (pṛthagjanatva) is the cause,
while the dharmas of an ordinary being are the result.
As it is with cause and effect, so it is with the agent and the acted-upon.

Furthermore, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is subsumed under the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
The dharmas of an ordinary person are subsumed under the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).

Furthermore, the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is abandoned at the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*); the dharmas of an ordinary person are abandoned at other times.
Such categories as these are called the distinctions.
As the Blessed One has said:
those who practice through faith or through dharma transcend the stage of ordinary beings;
until they have attained the fruit of stream-entry, they certainly will not die.
Question: Why is one called an "ordinary person" (pṛthagjana)?
Answer: All noble ones (ārya) are called "those of common birth.
Because this [state] is different from them, it is called "ordinary birth" (pṛthagjanatva).
The stage that accommodates ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is called the "stage of ordinary beings.
Question: If that is so, since noble ones (*ārya*) are distinct from ordinary beings, they too should be called "ordinary beings."
Answer: All noble ones (ārya) equally assemble at the truth;
because they share the same view and the same aspiration, they are called "those of equal birth" (sabhāga).
Ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are not so.
One should not raise an objection [to this], for the name "ordinary person" (pṛthagjana) is established because they are to be loathed and despised.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated it thus.
It is possible for divergent views and heterogeneous afflictions to arise;
it is possible to create diverse karma;
and it is possible to fall into different realms.
Because one undergoes rebirth in other realms of existence and so forth,
it is called the "ground of ordinary beings" (pṛthagjanabhūmi).
Furthermore, one who is capable of placing faith in a teacher different [from their own]—
as explained at length up to the point of seeking a different fruit—
is called a person of the stage of differing natures (*pṛthagjanabhūmi*).
The Venerable One said:
"Because one takes birth in a manner that is distinct from the True Dharma and the Vinaya."
They are called "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*).
The ground upon which these ordinary beings are born and grow is called the "ground of ordinary beings. What is the nature of being an ordinary being?
The answer is: it is [the absence of] noble dharma, noble warmth, noble vision, noble patience, noble desire, and noble wisdom.

The non-acquisition of all [dharmas] that have already been acquired, are currently being acquired, or will be acquired in the future—this is called the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Question: Is it the non-acquisition of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) that constitutes the nature of an ordinary person?
Is it the case that the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) consists in not having attained any of the noble dharmas?
If so, what fault would there be?
If the nature of an ordinary person were defined as not having attained the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), [what would follow]?
When the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has already arisen, one abandons the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*);
at that time, the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering should be the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
In that case, those who abide in the path of cultivation or the path of no-more-learning would also have to be called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
If the state of being an ordinary being consists in not attaining any of the noble dharmas, [then this fault follows].
In that case, all sentient beings should be called ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*),
because no noble one (*ārya*) could be said to possess all noble qualities (*āryadharma*).
For even a Buddha does not possess the noble qualities of the two vehicles.
Furthermore, those who study the teachings of their own vehicle should also be called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Some have made this statement:
The state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is the non-acquisition of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).

Question: If that is so, when the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has already arisen and one has relinquished the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering, at that time there would be no acquisition of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering.
It must be the state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva).
If that were so, then those abiding in the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) or the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga) would also have to be called ordinary persons.
Answer: At the moment when the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti) arises.
It is the non-acquisition of that harm,
because it ensures that [the harm] will never again arise within one's own continuum for those who abide in the path of cultivation or the path of no-more-learning.
Although one does not yet possess the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*),
it is neither called "not obtained" nor is it called "obtained."
For example, when the eye-faculty arises, it destroys its non-possession (*aprāpti*),
causing it never again to arise within one's own continuum; thus,
even though the eye-faculty has ceased and is no longer possessed, [the non-possession does not arise].
Nor is it called "not obtained," nor is it called "obtained"; this case is also like that.
Therefore, there is no fault as previously stated.
Furthermore, once the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has arisen,
although one does not yet possess the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*),
one nevertheless possesses its outflow-result (*niṣyandaphala*).
They are not called "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that the nature of being an ordinary being consists in not attaining any of the dharmas of the noble ones (*āryadharma*).
Question: If that were so,
then all sentient beings should be called ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*),
because no noble one (*ārya*) possesses all the qualities of a noble one.
Answer: Although there is no noble one who fully accomplishes all the dharmas of a noble one,
they are nonetheless not an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
because their non-acquisition is not mixed with the acquisition of a noble one.
That is to say, if within a person's continuum there is the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of noble dharmas that is not mixed with their acquisition,
this constitutes the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Because the non-acquisition of noble dharmas within the continuum of a noble one is mixed with the acquisition of those noble dharmas, it does not constitute the state of being an ordinary person.
Because that non-acquisition (aprāpti) is always co-nascent [with its object].
Furthermore, there are two kinds of that non-acquisition:
first, the common [non-acquisition].
The second is the uncommon.
The uncommon refers to the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*);
the common refers to that which is not the nature of an ordinary person.
The non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the noble dharmas within the body of a noble one is exclusively common [to all], and thus the aforementioned fault does not apply.
Furthermore, that non-acquisition is of two kinds.
First, those not yet harmed; second, those already harmed.
Those not yet harmed are of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*);
those already harmed are not of the nature of ordinary beings.
Since the non-acquisition (aprāpti) of the noble dharmas within the body of a Noble One has already been destroyed, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
Furthermore, there are two types of non-acquisition of all noble dharmas.
First, it manifests based on the continuum of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);
second, it manifests based on the continuum of a noble one (*ārya*).
The former is the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

Since it is not the case that [the state of] being a non-ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) exists subsequently, there is no fault of implying that a noble one (ārya) would be called a non-ordinary person.

Question: What is the distinction between the noble factors (āryadharma), noble warmth (āryanuṣṇatā), noble vision (āryadarśana), noble forbearance (āryakṣānti), noble desire (āryacchanda), and noble wisdom (āryaprajñā)?
Some say that among these,
all six phrases collectively reveal the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*;
the first one is the general [statement].
The latter five are specific;
the first one is concise,
while the latter five are detailed.
The first is non-discriminative;
the latter five are discriminative.
That is to say, because the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering causes the seeds of the aggregates to wither away entirely, it is called "Noble Heat" (*ārya-uṣmagata*).
Investigating the principle of the truths is called noble vision (*ārya-dṛṣṭi*).
Accepting the principle of the truths is called noble patience (*ārya-kṣānti*).
Delighting in the principle of the truths is called noble desire (*ārya-chanda*).
It is called noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*) because it definitively discerns the principles of the truths.

Furthermore, it is called noble heat (*āryanuṣma-gata*) because the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) causes all seeds of existence to wither away.
It is called noble view (*āryadṛṣṭi*) because it functions by means of investigative inquiry.
Patience is called "noble patience" because it can be practiced and transformed;
noble desire is so called because it delights in liberation;
and noble wisdom is so called because it awakens to and realizes the principles of the truths.
Some say that the "patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) of the sixth stage is precisely what is manifested by these six phrases herein.
Some say that the six types of patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) are precisely what is revealed by these six phrases herein.
Furthermore, there are those who say that these six phrases collectively demonstrate all noble dharmas (*āryadharma*). That is to say,
the meaning of the noble dharmas possesses both general and specific aspects.
The first is the general [explanation],
while the latter five are the specific ones.
Among these five, it should be understood that two are explained as previously [stated].
Some say that the sixfold noble qualities (ṣaḍāryavaṃśa) of all noble ones are precisely what is revealed by these six phrases herein.
Some say that the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training within the three vehicles are precisely what is revealed by these six phrases herein.
Other masters say that this passage reveals two kinds of noble dharmas: the real and the counterfeit.
As for the counterfeit noble dharmas:
These are the four aids to penetration, beginning with "heat.
As for "noble dharmas," this refers to the true noble dharmas, namely the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Noble warmth refers to the stage of warmth (*uṣmagata*).
Noble vision refers to the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*).
Noble patience refers to the lower and middle stages of patience (*kṣānti*).
The "noble desire" refers to the stage of supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), and the "noble wisdom" refers to the stage of the highest mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
If one has not yet cultivated and attained the four [stages] beginning with "heat" (*uṣmagata*),
it should be known that such a person is a full-fledged ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*).
If one attains "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the other stages, they are also called noble ones (*ārya*).
As the Blessed One said:
"If there is one who accomplishes the roots of goodness such as heat..."
I call such a person a "semblance-noble one" (*ābhāsa-ārya*).

However, since the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is merely the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the truly noble dharmas—and not their acquisition—others [who possess it] should not be said to have attained the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the other stages.
Regarding this state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) associated with the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, should it be called wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral?
It should be said to be neutral;
that is, because its nature is non-obscured neutrality (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), as it is of the nature of non-possession (*aprāpti*).
All non-acquisitions (*aprāpti*) are subsumed under the category of the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Question: Among the four types of unspecified [states], such as those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and so forth, under which one is this [non-acquisition] subsumed?
Answer: It is not subsumed under any of the four.
However, it is an outflow (niṣyanda) that is non-obscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
Question: Why is this not obscured-indeterminate (nivṛtāvyākṛta)?
Answer: Because its nature is not abandoned at the time of detachment from defilements (vairāgya).
Why is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) not wholesome?
The answer is: wholesome dharmas are acquired either through preparatory effort (*prayoga*) or through other conditions.
One does not intentionally apply effort to seek the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, at the time when the roots of goodness are severed, all wholesome dharmas are relinquished,
and one acquires the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of all wholesome dharmas.
If the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) were of a virtuous nature,
then one who has severed the roots of virtue would not be an ordinary person.
It is not merely by words that their meaning is established;
therefore, further questions and answers are provided to clarify why they are not "wholesome" and so forth.
Regarding this, some say:
Regarding "wholesome dharmas that are acquired either through application":
this indicates those various wholesome states arising from application;
or "that are acquired through other conditions."
This reveals the various future virtues that one cultivates.
Furthermore, regarding those wholesome dharmas obtained through application (*prayoga*),
this reveals the wholesome [dharmas] obtained by application.
"Or obtained through other conditions" indicates that wholesome states are acquired by being free from defilement (*vairāgya-lābhika*).
Furthermore, "or obtained through application" refers to wholesome states acquired through preparatory effort (*prayoga*).

The phrase "manifested as acquired through application among the wholesome [states], specifically those conducive to progress and those conducive to penetration" indicates that within the wholesome states acquired through application,
there are also those conducive to decline and those conducive to maintenance, which are obtained due to other conditions.
Question: If that is so, why are the wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*) not mentioned here?
Answer: They should have been mentioned, yet they are not.
One should know that this meaning is not exhaustive.
Furthermore, herein only those wholesome states that are difficult to obtain are mentioned;
those wholesome states acquired at birth, which are easily obtained and inferior, are not mentioned.
Furthermore, all states of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) are acquired at birth.
If what is discussed here were "wholesome [states] acquired at birth," it would not differ from that [definition].
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, there are those who say that wholesome dharmas arise either through application (prayoga).
"Thus it is acquired" indicates that it is acquired through preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
"Or it is acquired by other conditions" refers to [the case where it is acquired] through other circumstances.
This reveals the wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*). Furthermore, regarding those wholesome dharmas obtained through application (*prayoga*),
this reveals the various wholesome states attained during the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gamana*).
"Or obtained due to other conditions" refers to the various wholesome states acquired at times such as during a regression; herein,
one should apply a fourfold logical analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are wholesome dharmas that are acquired through application (*prayoga*) and not by other conditions; such as heat (*uṣmagata*),
summits (*mūrdhan*), patience (*kṣānti*), and the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*),
as well as the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realization of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-abhisamaya-antya-saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The path of subsequent knowledge (*mārgānvayajñāna*), unshakable liberation of mind (*akopya-cetovimukti*),
the absence of contention (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the meditative absorption of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*), and so forth—
there are some wholesome dharmas that are acquired through other conditions rather than through deliberate application (*prayoga*).
Just as with innate wholesome states,
there are some wholesome dharmas that are acquired through application and also through other conditions,
such as the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.

Regarding the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), formless attainments (ārūpya), the immeasurables (apramāṇa), liberations (vimokṣa), spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana),
there may be wholesome dharmas that are not obtained through application (prayoga);
however, there are none that are obtained neither through application nor by other conditions.
The phrase "there is no application of effort to seek to become a worldling" indicates that the nature of being a worldling is not something acquired through effort;
that is to say, there is certainly no one who was previously not a worldling.
This is because one subsequently seeks to realize that state of being lowly;
because one has been an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) since beginningless time;
and because when the roots of goodness are severed, all wholesome dharmas are abandoned, and so forth.
This demonstrates that the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is not a virtue acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*).

That is to say, when one severs the roots of virtue, it is precisely the virtue acquired at birth that is severed, and not that produced through application (*prāyogika*), because [the latter] is not yet present.
If one who has severed the roots of virtue were not an ordinary person, [this would be impossible].
This is in great contradiction with correct reasoning,
for that [view] is extremely evil;
let there not be such faults as those previously mentioned.
Therefore, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is definitely not wholesome.
Why is the state of being an ordinary person not unwholesome?
Answer: At the time of becoming free from the defilement of desire, all that is unwholesome is abandoned.
One attains the state of non-accomplishment regarding unwholesome dharmas.
If the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) were unwholesome,
then ordinary beings who have abandoned the defilements of desire would no longer be ordinary beings.
If they were not ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), they would not be reborn in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) thereafter;
for once noble ones (ārya) have become detached from the defilements of desire, they certainly do not undergo further birth in the desire realm.
Furthermore, if that were the case:
If it were so, there would be no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the form and formless realms,
which would entail a great error. Therefore,
the nature of being an ordinary being is certainly not unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Therefore, that [state] is exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Should this nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) be said to belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*),
or to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
Are they bound to the formless realm?
One should answer: "Either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm."
Alternatively, it may be bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Since its meaning is not established merely by stating it directly in words,
one should therefore engage in question and answer to further clarify this point.
Why is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) not restricted solely to the desire realm?

Answer: When one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all dharmas of the desire realm are abandoned, and one acquires the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of those desire-realm dharmas.
If the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) were exclusively bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*),
then those ordinary persons who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) would no longer be ordinary persons.
If they were not ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
then those born there would necessarily be free from falling back;
for a noble one (*ārya*) born in a higher realm can never fall back and undergo birth in a lower stage.
Although one who passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the form realm also abandons the dharmas of the desire realm,
they do not abandon them entirely.
Since they still possess the transformation-minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of the desire realm and so forth,
it is for this reason that only birth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is mentioned here. Why,
then, is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) not restricted solely to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)?

Answer: When one dies in the form realm and is reborn in the formless realm, all dharmas of the form realm are abandoned, and one acquires the state of non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the dharmas of the form realm.

If the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) were exclusively bound to the form realm, then ordinary persons who die in the form realm and are reborn in the formless realm would no longer be ordinary persons.
If it were not so, those such as the son of Mṛgāra would not be born as ordinary beings (pṛthagjana),
for the noble ones (ārya) are not like that;
this remains true even for one who dies in the form realm (rūpadhātu) and is born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
One also abandons the dharmas of the form realm,
yet does not abandon them entirely,
because one still possesses the afflictions and other such dharmas of that realm.
For this reason, it is said that one is merely born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Why, then, is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) not exclusively bound to the formless realm?
The answer is: because one enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
First, one realizes the suffering of the desire realm through direct insight;
subsequently, the noble path arises that realizes the suffering of the form and formless realms simultaneously.
Thus, one first accomplishes the task of the desire realm.
Subsequently, it also encompasses the affairs of the form and formless realms;
therefore, the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is not restricted solely to the formless realm.
Such is the principle of dharmas.
If one accomplishes the state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) of this stage,
one must first realize the Truth of Suffering (duḥkhasatya) of that stage.
Furthermore, since the arising of the Noble Path is for the purpose of counteracting the state of being an ordinary person, it is stated thus.
Question: If that were so, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) would be bound only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Answer: Only if it were bound to the desire realm would there be the aforementioned fault.
Therefore, it should be said that this belongs to all three realms of existence.
Should this state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) be said to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*),
or abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
It is agreed that [the afflictions] are abandoned through cultivation;
however, the meaning is not established merely by stating it in words.
Therefore, this meaning should be further clarified through a series of questions and answers.
Why is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
Answer: Because all factors abandoned by insight are defiled (*kliṣṭa*), whereas the state of being an ordinary person is undefiled (*akliṣṭa*).
All defiled factors are gradually abandoned according to their respective categories and stages, resulting in their non-attainment (*aprāpti*).
The state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is abandoned all at once simultaneously with the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Because it is severed all at once by the power of the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) of each respective stage, it is not defiled.

Furthermore, when the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is in the process of ceasing and the Patience of the Dharma-knowledge of Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) is in the process of arising,
at that moment one abandons the nature of an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) of the three realms.
One attains that state of non-accomplishment because,
at that time, there is no abandonment of the factors to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
If the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) were to be abandoned by insight, [it would follow that it is not attained].
If, within this stage, one has not yet abandoned that nature,

then an individual bound by all fetters (sakalabandhana) dwelling in the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) would necessarily possess the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva).
Because one fully possesses the factors to be abandoned by vision,
those abiding in this stage would have to be called both "Noble Ones" (ārya) and "ordinary beings" (pṛthagjana),
which would result in confusion.
Therefore, the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).

Question: At that time, one should abandon only the nature of being an ordinary person belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because the nature of being an ordinary person belonging to the two higher realms was not previously possessed.
How can it be said that one abandons the three realms?

It should be answered that at that time, one abandons any one of the states of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) within the three realms and attains the state of non-possession (*aprāpti*) thereof.
As for the statement that one abandons the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) of the three realms,
this is said so as to complete the number three; that is to say,
the state of being an ordinary person of the two upper realms was not previously accomplished [by the practitioner].
Now, having further abandoned the state of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) of the desire realm, the three counts are fulfilled; therefore, this statement is made. Some say:
Although the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) in the two higher realms was not previously attained and is likewise not attained now,
it is nevertheless said to be abandoned.
What does it mean for something that was previously unaccomplished to be unaccomplished again?
It means because it has become further removed. Some say:

Because the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) of the desire realm can support and induce the nature of an ordinary being of the two higher realms, serving as their gateway and preliminary application (*prayoga*);
therefore, when one abandons the nature of an ordinary being of the desire realm, it is said that one also abandons those [higher natures].
Some say that when one accomplishes the state of being an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) of the desire realm,
one simultaneously accomplishes the states of being an ordinary being of the form and formless realms.
Because it is capable of arising and serves as the basis and support for that [state],
when one abandons the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) in the desire realm,
it is also said to be abandoned because the path of its arising has been severed.

Some say: At that time, because the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) within the three realms attains cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), this statement is made;

for at that moment, one simultaneously attains the cessation not through deliberation regarding the state of being an ordinary person across all nine stages of the three realms. It is for this reason that a question is asked: [text continues]
Is there any dharma that is abandoned at one time and severed at nine times?
Answer: There is.

That is to say, the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is abandoned at one time, which refers to the moment when the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises.
Regarding "severance at the ninth stage":
this refers to the abandonment of the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
each occurring at the time of the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Is there anyone who has attained the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), but has not yet attained its non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
One should answer that this involves four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There may be one who, regarding the state of an ordinary person...
One has already attained cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) but has not yet attained cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already become detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Alternatively, there may be those who have already attained cessation not through deliberation regarding the state of being an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*), but have not yet attained cessation through deliberation.
This refers to those noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm;

some among them have already attained the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
This also refers to those noble ones who have already abandoned the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

There may be those who have not yet attained either analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) or non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
That is to say, there are ordinary persons who have not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Is it possible for such an ordinary person to have the state of being an ordinary person unsevered yet not be possessed of it?
It can be answered in four propositions.
There may be cases where the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) has not been abandoned, yet it is not possessed.
This refers to those ordinary persons born in the desire realm who have not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
Although the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) regarding those higher eight stages has not yet been abandoned, it is no longer possessed;
he has already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
but has not yet become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna.
Although the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) of the seven higher stages has not yet been abandoned,

it is no longer possessed [by one who has already abandoned the defilements up to the level of the sphere of nothingness]. Likewise, although the state of being an ordinary person of the stage immediately above that has not yet been abandoned, it is no longer possessed [by one who has already abandoned the defilements up to the sphere of nothingness].
If one is born in the first dhyāna and has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna,
although the state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) regarding the seven higher stages has not been severed, it is not yet possessed.
Having already become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna,
but not yet free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
one has not abandoned— though one does not possess— the state of an ordinary being (pṛthagjanatva) pertaining to the six higher stages.
Up to the point where one has already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) of the higher stage is neither abandoned nor possessed.
This continues up to the case where one is born in the sphere of nothingness.
Those in the higher stages have not yet abandoned the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) of that stage, yet they do not possess it.
Likewise, if noble ones (*ārya*) have not yet become free from the defilements of the desire realm,
they have not yet abandoned the state of being an ordinary person of those nine stages, yet they do not possess it.
Having already abandoned the defilements of the desire realm but not yet having abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna,
one has not abandoned the state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) regarding the eight higher stages, yet does not possess it.

Up to the point where one has already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) but has not yet become free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
the state of being an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) of that higher stage is not yet abandoned, yet it is no longer possessed [by him].
There may be those who possess the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) but have not yet abandoned it;
that is to say, when various ordinary beings born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have already become free from the defilements of the desire realm,
they still possess the nature of an ordinary being of the desire realm and have not yet abandoned it.
Even up to having been born in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one has already become free from the defilements of that sphere;
yet, one still possesses the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) of that sphere, which has not yet been abandoned.
There are cases where the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) has not been abandoned and is also currently possessed.
This refers to those ordinary persons who have not yet become free from the defilements of the desire realm;
for them, the state of being an ordinary person of the desire realm has not been abandoned and is also currently possessed.
Up until one is born in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and has not yet abandoned the defilements of that sphere,

one has neither severed nor abandoned the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) of that sphere of nothingness, and thus remains possessed of it. If, however, one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), [one is likewise possessed of the state of being an ordinary person of that sphere].
They have not yet abandoned the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor have they [yet] attained it.
Alternatively, there may be those who are ordinary persons for whom the state of being an ordinary person has neither been unabandoned nor is it attained;
namely, those ordinary persons born in the desire realm who have already become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
For one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna,
the state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) of the first dhyāna is neither unsevered nor possessed;
this continues up until one has already abandoned the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
The state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) regarding the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) is neither unsevered nor possessed [by him].
This applies if one is born in the first dhyāna and has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna.
That state of being an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) in the desire realm has neither been abandoned nor is it possessed;
one has already become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna,
but has not yet become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
For one who has not yet abandoned the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) of the second dhyāna of the desire realm, nor has yet attained it,
and so on up to one who has already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
the state of being an ordinary person of the second dhyāna of the desire realm up to that of the sphere of nothingness is neither un-abandoned nor attained.
Even if one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
the state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness is neither unsevered nor possessed.
If noble ones have already become free from the defilements of the desire realm but have not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
their state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) of the desire realm is neither unsevered nor possessed.
Having already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
but not yet having become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna,
that ordinary being (pṛthagjana) neither has the state of an ordinary being of the desire realm or the first dhyāna severed, nor does he possess it.
Up to the point where one has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
that state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) belonging to the nine stages of the three realms is neither unsevered nor possessed.
Is there any case where the state of being an ordinary person has been severed yet is still possessed?
It should be formulated as four propositions:
that is, the former second proposition becomes this first proposition,
and the former first proposition becomes this second proposition.
The former fourth phrase becomes this third phrase;
the former third phrase becomes this fourth phrase—their characteristics should be understood according to what was previously stated.
What dharma is designated as "the state of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
Answer: It refers to the formations dissociated from mind within the three realms that are non-defiled.
Question: For what reason is this treatise further composed?
Answer: It is because one wishes to bring about certainty for those who harbor doubts.
It was stated previously that the failure to attain the dharmas of an ārya is termed "the nature of an ordinary person" (pṛthagjanatva).
However, some may harbor the doubt that this failure to attain the dharmas of an ārya does not possess a real ontological substance.
Just as with wealth not yet obtained,
in order to bring certainty to this doubt,
it is shown that the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is a substantially existent phenomenon (*dravyadharma*) included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Therefore, this treatise is composed.

Some have said: "Although the characteristics of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) have already been revealed previously, its essential substance (*svabhāva*) has not yet been distinguished."
I now wish to explain this, and therefore compose this treatise.
Other masters say:
although the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) has already been revealed previously, [it is here further elucidated].
Their characteristics have not yet been distinguished;
wishing now to explain them, I have composed this treatise. Some may say:
The preceding [section] revealed the antidote to the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*);
now, wishing to explain the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of that ordinary beinghood, this treatise is composed.
By stating "the three realms," it is excluded that the nature of an ordinary being is restricted solely to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Non-defiled" means that it excludes the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), which is a defiled dharma and is abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*).
"Dissociated from mind" means...
The nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is a mental factor (*caitta*).
A practitioner negates that this nature of an ordinary person is a substantially existent phenomenon (*dravyasat*), because,
according to the principle of conventional phenomena (*prajñaptidharma*), it is not subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
This negates the attachment to [the view that] they are different and reveals the nature of the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
The Venerable Ghosaka says:
"The state of being an ordinary person is simply the generic similarity (*nikāyasabhāga*)."
Just as the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) of cattle, sheep,
and so forth is designated as the "nature" (*svabhāva*) of cattle, sheep, and so forth,
likewise the essence of the homogeneous character of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is called "the state of being an ordinary being" (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Other masters say:
there is a distinct dharma that is non-defiled,
which is subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
Just as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth are termed "the nature of an ordinary being" (*pṛthagjanatva*),
in order to refute that [erroneous] attachment, it was previously stated that the name "nature of an ordinary being" refers to the non-acquisition of noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
This "non-acquisition" is precisely the state of non-possession (*aprāpti*).
Question: For what reason do you not accept that the very *nikāya-sabhāga* of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
or a distinct dharma named "ordinariness" (*pṛthagjanatva*), is [ordinariness],
but instead accept that the state of non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) is called "ordinariness"?
Answer: It is the commonality of the group of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā*).
Because it is not a relative [quality] and because it contradicts the noble Dharma, there is a distinct dharma that cannot be known [by other means].
It is not merely the state of not possessing the noble dharmas; rather,
there exists a definable characteristic that directly contradicts the noble dharmas, which is known as the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
It is logically well-established that when various phenomena are associated with wrong view,
those phenomena are also associated with wrong reflection;
and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason are the factors of wrongness (*mithyā-aṅga*) explained after the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
Answer: Because these two mutually support one another;
that is to say, the nature of an ordinary person supports the factors of wrongness.
Furthermore, these factors of the wrong path can also sustain the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Moreover, because the practitioner, weary of the nature of an ordinary person and the eight factors of the wrong path,
cultivates the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
Following the analysis of the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), one further analyzes the factors of the wrong path.
Regarding those phenomena that are associated with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*),
are those phenomena also associated with wrong intention (*mithyāsaṃkalpa*)?
It is answered in four statements:
among these, wrong view exists in all stages,
but it is not present in all defiled minds.
Because [wrong view] such as the view of a self-identity does not exist within that cluster [of afflictions],
whereas wrong reflection exists in all defiled minds,
though not in all stages.
Because these do not exist from the intermediate dhyāna upward,
four great permutations (catuṣkoṭi) are established in comparison to one another.
There are dharmas associated with wrong view that are not associated with wrong intention.
This refers to wrong intention associated with wrong view,
as well as other factors associated with wrong view that are not associated with wrong intention.
Among these, "wrong intention associated with wrong view" is as follows:
This refers to the vitarka associated with wrong view in the desire realm, the *anāgamya* concentration, and the first *dhyāna*.
That [vitarka] is associated only with wrong view and not with wrong thought (*mithyā-saṃkalpa*),
because a factor is not associated with itself due to three reasons.
First, because two thoughts do not arise simultaneously;
second, because preceding and succeeding thoughts are not conjoined;
and third, because the intrinsic nature of phenomena does not observe itself.
This refers to those phenomena that arise dependent on others rather than their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
and which are associated with wrong view while being dissociated from other forms of erroneous conceptualization; specifically,
it refers to the phenomena associated with wrong view from the intermediate dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
That is to say: the nine universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma),
the nine universal defiled mental factors (kleśa-mahābhūmika-dharma),
lethargy (styāna), and discursive thought (vicāra).
There are phenomena associated with wrong reflection but not with wrong view;
namely, those phenomena associated with both wrong reflection and wrong view,
as well as other phenomena associated with wrong reflection that are not associated with wrong view.
Among these, wrong view associated with wrong attention refers to wrong view in the desire realm,
the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the first dhyāna.
That [wrong view] is associated only with wrong attention, not with wrong view.
Because intrinsic nature and intrinsic nature are incompatible with the three types of causes and conditions previously explained,
as well as with other factors associated with wrong thought that are incompatible with right view.

This refers to the factors associated with wrong intention within the remaining defiled aggregates—excluding the cluster of wrong views—in the desire realm, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the first dhyāna; namely:

the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), and non-specific ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
Within the category of associated aggregates (*saṃprayukta-skandha*),
those factors associated with wrong reflection (*mithyā-saṃkalpa*) should be understood accordingly as the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) and so forth.
There are factors that are associated with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and are also associated with wrong reflection.
That is to say, excluding the wrong intention associated with wrong view,
and excluding the wrong view associated with wrong intention,
it refers to all other phenomena associated with both wrong view and wrong intention.
