This refers to the factors associated with wrong view and wrong intention within the category of wrong views in the desire realm, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the first dhyāna;
namely, the nine universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and the nine universal defiled mental factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*).
There are states that are not associated with wrong view and also not associated with wrong intention, namely: wrong intention that is not associated with wrong view;
as well as lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, drowsiness, and discursive thought.
There is wrong view dissociated from wrong reflection,
as well as other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta), matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra).
Among these, there is wrong reflection that is dissociated from wrong view.
This refers to wrong thought (*mithyāsaṃkalpa*) within other defiled aggregates in the desire realm, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*),
and the first dhyāna— excluding the group of wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This is because it is dissociated from those [other factors], as that specific aggregate lacks wrong views.
Because intrinsic nature is not associated with intrinsic nature.
Regarding the non-association of wrong view with wrong reflection:
this refers to wrong views from the intermediate dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Neither of those two is associated with the other,
because a self-nature is not associated with itself,
and because that stage lacks discursive thought (avitarka).
As for the various other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*),
these refer to those from the intermediate dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
excluding the cluster of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi-kalāpa*).
This includes all other afflicted minds and mental factors, as well as all wholesome and non-obscured neutral [phenomena],
and form, unconditioned phenomena, and mind-dissociated formations—
namely, all form, unconditioned phenomena, and mind-dissociated formations.
In this way, these dharmas are all mutually non-associated;
for that aggregate lacks false view,
and that stage lacks discursive thought.
Because they are non-defiled and because they are not associated dharmas;
[yet] all dharmas are associated with false view.
Is that dharma associated with wrong diligence?
One should respond by formulating four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Among these, wrong view exists in all stages (*bhūmi*).
Not all defiled mental states possess wrong diligence, nor does it exist in all stages or in association with all defiled mental states.
Based on these mutual relations, one should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena associated with wrong view but not with wrong effort;
that is to say, wrong effort associated with wrong view.
Regarding this, what is wrong effort associated with wrong view?
This means that within the category of wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), laziness (*kausīdya*) is associated only with wrong views and not with wrong effort (*mithyāvīrya*),
because a factor cannot be associated with itself. There are,
however, factors that are associated with wrong effort but not with wrong views.
This refers to wrong view and those factors associated with wrong effort that are not associated with other wrong views.
Regarding "wrong view" herein:
This means that all wrong views are associated with wrong effort, but wrong view itself is not [associated] with it;
for within that collection there is necessarily wrong effort,
and a self-nature cannot be associated with itself.
As for those factors associated with wrong diligence that are not associated with wrong view,
they exist in all stages,
excluding the category of wrong view itself.
From among the remaining defiled aggregates, one takes up those factors associated with wrong effort.
There are factors that are associated with wrong view and also associated with wrong effort;
specifically, these are all factors associated with wrong view, excluding wrong effort itself.
Regarding all other phenomena associated with wrong view,
those associated with wrong effort are excluded here;
this is because the categories of wrong effort are extremely numerous.
Among these, only those associated with wrong view are excluded;
since there is no overlap with others, they are not excluded here.
As for all other phenomena associated with wrong view:
This refers to the collection of wrong views, excluding the factors of wrong effort and the essence of wrong view itself;
it comprises the remaining mental states and mental factors associated with them,
namely, the nine universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).
The eight universal factors of affliction (*kleśa-mahābhūmika-dharma*):
shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), torpor (*styāna*), drowsiness (*middha*), vitarka, vicāra, and the mind itself.
There are factors that are neither associated with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) nor with wrong effort (*mithyāvīrya*).
This refers to wrong effort dissociated from wrong view, as well as all other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta),
matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra).
Among these, "wrong effort dissociated from wrong view" means:
This refers to wrong diligence associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth;
it is not associated with that [view],
because wrong view is absent within that aggregate.
Because intrinsic nature does not associate with itself,
and as for all other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*),
this refers to all wholesome and non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) mental states and mental factors, which are not defiled.
Matter that is unconditioned and dissociated from mind refers to all matter that is unconditioned and dissociated from mind.
Such phenomena are both dissociated and non-defiled.
Because they are not associated factors (*asaṃprayukta-dharma*).
Just as wrong view is paired with wrong effort,
so too is it paired with wrong mindfulness and wrong concentration.
In this context, one should formulate two sets of four propositions (catuṣkoṭika) for wrong mindfulness and wrong concentration,
just as with wrong effort, because they exist throughout all stages and within all defiled minds.
Just as with wrong view in relation to wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration,
so it is with wrong intention in relation to wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. In this context,
one should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) for each of these three.
Because wrong reflection does not pervade all stages,
just as wrong view does not pervade all defiled minds; thus,
all phenomena are associated with wrong diligence.
Are those factors associated with wrong mindfulness?
One should respond that there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Among these, two factors pervade all stages (*sarvabhūmi*).
All defiled minds possess this;
by comparing these in relation to one another, four minor tetralemmas are formed.
There are factors that are associated with wrong effort but not with wrong mindfulness.
This refers to wrong mindfulness (*mithyāsmṛti*).
In this context, wrong mindfulness must be associated with wrong diligence (*mithyāvīrya*), because wrong mindfulness does not always coexist [with all other factors],
and because a factor cannot be associated with itself.
There are phenomena that are associated with wrong mindfulness but are not wrong exertion;
namely, wrong exertion itself.
In this context, wrong exertion is necessarily associated with wrong mindfulness.
Because it is not the case that wrong diligence is always co-existent [with it],
and because a factor cannot be associated with itself;
there are factors that are associated with wrong diligence and are also wrong mindfulness.
This refers to those factors associated with wrong effort and wrong mindfulness.
Within this context, excluding the essential natures of wrong effort and wrong mindfulness themselves,
one takes the remaining defiled mental states and mental factors.
Namely, the nine universal mental factors (mahābhūmika),
the eight universal factors of defilement (kleśamahābhūmika),
and the ten minor factors of defilement (parīttakleśabhūmika).
Lack of shame and lack of dread,
greed, hatred, pride, doubt, lethargy, drowsiness, regret, fear, applied thought,
sustained thought, and the mind— these various factors are defiled.
Because these two are associated and always coexist.
There are factors that are neither associated with wrong effort nor with wrong mindfulness;
namely, all other mind and mental states, as well as matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
Among these, "all other mental states and mental factors" refers to all wholesome and non-obscured neutral mental states and mental factors;
they are not defiled.
The rest is as previously explained.
Just as with wrong effort in relation to wrong mindfulness,
so it is with wrong effort in relation to wrong concentration.
Just as with wrong effort in relation to wrong mindfulness and wrong concentration,
so it is with wrong mindfulness in relation to wrong concentration; herein,
two minor sets of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) should be formulated.
They pervade all stages because all defiled minds possess them; herein,
the three [unwholesome paths] beginning with wrong speech are not mentioned.
Because they are not associated [with consciousness].
Question: Of these eight factors of the wrong path (*mithyā-aṅga*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
How many are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta)? How many are bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta)?
Answer: False view, false diligence, false mindfulness, and false concentration are bound to all three realms.
Wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood are bound only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they exist only in the first dhyāna;
they do not exist in the higher stages.
Some say that there is also no wrong livelihood in the form realm,
because beings there do not produce bodily or vocal karma for the sake of sustaining their lives.
The critique states:
Among these, the former explanation is superior,
because the two types of karma— bodily and vocal— arising from that greed are designated as "wrong livelihood."
Question: Of these eight factors of the wrong path, how many are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Answer: One is abandoned by vision.
That is to say, wrong view;
three are abandoned through cultivation,
namely wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood.
The remaining four [superknowledges] are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation.
Question: Within this "Miscellaneous Aggregate" (saṃkīrṇa-skandha), why are the pure phenomena (viśuddhi-dharma) explained first, followed by the defiled phenomena (saṃkleśa-dharma)?
Answer: This is to demonstrate that the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*) consists in this:
the Supreme Mundane Dharmas are able to induce the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), thereby permanently severing false views.
This is its result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Purity refers to the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) and so forth;
defilement refers to the eight branches beginning with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, in accordance with the Imperial Decree. 2. The Aggregate of Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha). 1. The Section on the Unwholesome (Akuśala-nikāya). 1. The First Part of the First Section on the Unwholesome within the Second [Chapter] on the Aggregate of Fetters: From the three fetters up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
Having thus mastered these chapters and their meanings,
one should next provide a detailed explanation of these three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth,
as all are taught in the sūtras— with the exception of the five fetters and the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
In this context, these two types of treatises should be excluded.
Why is that? Because all Abhidharma exists solely for the purpose of explaining the Sūtras.
Since these two treatises are not what was spoken in the sūtras,
they should therefore be excluded.
For this reason, the Venerable Ghoṣaka made the following statement:
All Abhidharma is for the purpose of explaining the Sūtras;
based on such and such sūtras,
such and such treatises are composed.
Whatever is not taught in the sūtras should all be eliminated.
Some say that these two treatises should not be eliminated.
Why is this so? Because those two are also taught in the sūtras;
specifically, in the Ekottarika Āgama.
The five fetters were taught within the Five Dharmas,
and the ninety-eight underlying tendencies were taught within the Ninety-Eight Dharmas;
as time passed through vast ages, both were lost and forgotten.
The Master of this treatise, through the power of his vows and wisdom, recollects and contemplates [this matter],
and thus provides an explanation by restating it here. Some say:
Although these two are not mentioned in the sūtras, they should not be excluded.
Question: Since the five fetters (*pañca-saṃyojana*) are likewise not mentioned in the sūtras, why are they not excluded?
Answer: All treatises follow the author's intention;
provided they do not contradict the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one may compose them as one wishes.
This refers to the teaching herein on pervasive fetters (*sarvatraga-saṃyojana*), non-pervasive fetters, and both pervasive and non-pervasive fetters.
The pervasive fetters are exemplified by the three fetters;
the non-pervasive fetters are exemplified by the five fetters.
Regarding the explanation of pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and non-pervasive (*asarvatraga*) fetters (*saṃyojana*), it is as in the case of the nine fetters.
For this reason, although these five fetters are not mentioned in the Sūtras, they should not be excluded.
Question: Since the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are likewise not mentioned in the Sūtras, why are they not excluded?
Answer: The Abhidharma exists for the purpose of explaining the seven types of latent dispositions (anuśaya) taught in the Sūtras.
Now, the author of this treatise analyzes them extensively according to their modes of activity (ākāra), realms (dhātu), and categories (nikāya).
Therefore, this treatise also should not be excluded.
Question: For what reason are the chapters established here at the outset?
Answer: It is because one wishes to reveal the meanings of the various gates.
If topical headings are not established,
the meaning cannot be made manifest;
it is like a painter who cannot paint upon empty space.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to ensure that this treatise remains long in the world.

For even among hundreds or thousands of people, there might be but a single individual capable of fully reciting and upholding this treatise— which, though well-established in its sections on the aggregates (*skandha*), chapters (*varga*), and topical headings (*mukha*)— let alone one for a treatise that is not so well-established.
Who would be able to recite and uphold such disordered phrases? Lacking anyone to recite and uphold them, they would quickly vanish.
Furthermore, if chapters were not established, [the teaching] would be empty.
There is nothing that is not asked;
for a question must necessarily arise based on something upon which it relies.
Why, then, does the commentator establish chapters by relying on the sūtras?
Answer: All treatises that have been composed are intended to explain the sūtras.
Therefore, all the various seemingly inconsistent meanings found within the sūtras are now established as the "Miscellaneous Aggregate" (Kṣudraka-skandha) for the purpose of this explanation.
Up to the point where "view" is established as the aggregate of views (*dṛṣṭiskandha*).
However, each individual aggregate possesses all these meanings.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of demonstrating that the meaning of the sūtras is immeasurable.
It is not like the texts of non-Buddhist traditions, which contain many words but little meaning, or no meaning at all;
for example, the *Rāmāyaṇa* consists of twelve thousand verses,
yet explains only two matters.
The first clarifies that Rāvaṇa went away;
the second clarifies that Rāma brought him back.
The Buddhist sūtras are not like this.
The words and the meanings are immeasurable and boundless.
They are "immeasurable" because their meaning is difficult to fathom;
they are "boundless" because their words are difficult to comprehend.
For example, the great ocean is immeasurable and boundless;
"immeasurable" refers to its depth,
and "boundless" refers to its breadth.
Furthermore, it is to demonstrate that the sūtras are capable of withstanding inquiry and debate,
unlike non-Buddhist treatises which cannot withstand such inquiry and,
when subjected to it, only increase in meaninglessness.
Just as a monkey cannot endure being struck or touched,
and will void excrement whenever it is struck or touched,
the Buddha’s sutras are not like this.
It is capable of withstanding interrogation.
When interrogated, it gives rise to the pure color of ethical discipline and the sublime touch of wholesome roots,
like a fine cotton cloth produced in Vārāṇasī that is resilient to beating and contact.
When struck or touched, it emits a fresh, pure color and an exquisite, sublime touch.
Furthermore, this is intended to show that according to the sūtras, emission is excellent;
that is to say, there are three matters for which concealment is excellent.
If these are initiated, they are not excellent:
first, a fool; second, a woman; third, the books and treatises of non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, there are three things whose initiation is excellent.
If it is concealed, it will not be excellent.
These three are: first, wise persons; second, the sun and moon; and third, the Buddha’s sūtras, treatises, and commentaries.
Furthermore, this is intended to demonstrate that the sūtras are worthy of investigation and analysis.
It is not like the non-Buddhist scriptures, which are unfit for investigation;
for when one investigates them, they cause the eye of wisdom of sentient beings to diminish,
just as a person looking at the sun causes their faculty of sight to deteriorate.
The Buddha-dharma is not like that;
it is capable of being investigated through discernment.
When one investigates, the eye of wisdom increases.
It is like a person who, by observing the moon, causes the faculty of the eye to increase.
Question: For what reason is the chapter established first and the inquiry formulated later?
Answer: Because it is according to the method of constructing a house.
Just as one who wishes to build a house first establishes the foundation and only afterwards constructs the structure,
so too does the Venerable One, wishing to build the house of the Dharma,
first establish the chapters according to the principle of the foundation.
The gate is constructed last because it follows the method of structural assembly.
Furthermore, it is like the method for planting trees:
just as one first prepares the ground before planting a tree.
Thus, the Venerable One, wishing to plant the tree of the Dharma,
first established the chapters according to the method for preparing the ground,
and subsequently composed the sections according to the method for planting.
Furthermore, it is according to the method of stringing a garland.
Just as one who wishes to string a garland first passes the thread through and then binds the flowers,
so too does the Venerable One wish to string the garland of the Dharma.
Because it is like the method of weaving thread, the chapters are established first;
because it is like the method of stringing flowers, the sections (dvāra) are composed afterward.
Furthermore, it is like the method of painting with colors.
Just as one who wishes to paint a picture must first create a sketch before filling it with various colors,
so too does the Venerable One, wishing to paint the image of the Dharma,
first establish the chapters according to the method of creating a sketch.
It is like the method of applying colored pigments; therefore, the doors are made last.
Furthermore, it is like the method of carving and engraving.
Just as one who wishes to carve must first prepare the raw block and only then carve the various limbs and features.
In this way, the Venerable One wished to engrave the image of the Dharma.
Just as when carving a wooden statue, one first establishes the general outline;
and just as when carving the limbs and body, one subsequently creates the details, so too did he first establish the chapters and later compose the sections.
Furthermore, just as in the method of contemplative practice, where a yogin first establishes the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*),
and subsequently analyzes them into atoms (*paramāṇu*) and moments (*kṣaṇa*),
so too does the Venerable One.
Just as the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) were established first, this chapter was established first;
just as they were subsequently analyzed by means of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and moments (*kṣaṇa*), these gateways were subsequently composed.
Furthermore, it is because the Buddha taught the Dharma in such a manner.
Just as the Buddha’s teaching first presents a heading and subsequently provides an explanation—
namely, first stating that the six elements, the six bases of contact, the eighteen mental applications, and the four supports are designated as "sentient beings."
Later, he further explains:
"Thus they are called the six elements," and so on,
up to "thus they are called the four bases of reliance."
The Venerable One is likewise:
because he first indicates the doctrine, he first establishes the chapters;
because he subsequently explains the doctrine, he subsequently constructs the gates.
Furthermore, it is in order to manifest two kinds of skillful methods:
first, by establishing the chapters,
one manifests skillfulness regarding the meaning.
Later, he composed a gateway [of teaching],
manifesting skill in expression;
just as there is skill in meaning, so too is there skill in expression.

One should know that the power of meaning and the power of phrasing constitute the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) and the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
These culminate in the analytical knowledge of meaning.
The same applies to the ultimate mastery of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, it is to demonstrate that one’s own wisdom and vision are free from error;
for if one’s wisdom and vision were erroneous, [the teaching would not be authoritative].
The treatises he composed were likewise confused;
he was unable to establish the aggregates (*skandha*), sections (*nirdeśa*), or topical headings (*mukha*).
If his wisdom and vision were free from confusion, [he would not have acted thus].
The treatises he composed are likewise free from confusion;
he is able to skillfully establish the aggregates (*skandha*), sections (*varga*), and topical divisions (*mukha*).
Because the Venerable One wished to demonstrate that his own wisdom and vision were unerring, he first established the chapters and subsequently composed the topical divisions.

Question: For what reason is the arrangement of the chapters established such that it first relies on the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and subsequently extends even to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)?
Answer: It is because the author of this treatise intended it to be so.
This means that the author composed this treatise according to his own intention;
since it does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), he should not be held accountable.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
All give rise to doubt, meaning that whether it be the prior mention of the three unwholesome roots,
or even the prior mention of the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
there is likewise doubt in every case.
For what reason is this chapter established based on that [prior section]?
Therefore, what has been stated does not contradict the characteristics of the dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Whether it comes first or later, there is no fault in either case.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the Abhidharma should be sought through its characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and one should not demand a sequential order of priority.
Some may say that within this context,
the sequence could also be explained according to minor causes and conditions;
however, the principles of the Abhidharma are profound and vast.
If one were to further explain this, it would become overly prolix and confusing;
since it is difficult to uphold, I shall not explain it further.
Some have said as follows:
In this context, it is intended to demonstrate the progressive increase of dharmas;
that is to say, first three are mentioned,
then four, and then five.
Finally, up to the last point, ninety-eight [defilements] are taught.
Furthermore, because they demonstrate the gradual growth of the tree of afflictions,
the three fetters are taught first.
...up until the later teaching of the ninety-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*).
Other masters say that this was taught in order to demonstrate that the fruits of śrāmaṇya are realized through the gradual abandonment of those [proclivities].
This refers to the abandonment of the three fetters and the realization of the first fruit;
for this reason, the three unwholesome roots were explained first.
By doubling the abandonment of the outflow of desire, one attains the second fruit;
by exhausting and abandoning that very [outflow], one attains the third fruit.
Therefore, it is explained next.
The remaining two outflows are abandoned upon attaining the fourth fruit;
therefore, they are mentioned last.
As for the floods, yokes, graspings, bodily fetters, and hindrances, there is no separate abandonment or realization for them.
All of these are taught for the purpose of further elucidating the three outflows (*āsrava*).
Therefore, within this [treatise], it first explains the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and concludes by explaining the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
There are three fetters:
namely, the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the fetter of adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these three fetters?
The answer is that they have twenty-one things as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

That is to say: the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) has three things, being abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms;

the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*) has six things, being abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms.
The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) consists of twelve matters abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path within the three realms.
These twenty-one matters constitute the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the substantial entity (*dravya*),
the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), the individual essence (*ātman*), and the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) of these three fetters.
The intrinsic nature has already been explained;
its purpose shall now be discussed.
Question: For what reason is it called a "fetter" (saṃyojana)?
What is the meaning of "fetter" (*saṃyojana*)?
The answer is: the meaning of binding is the meaning of fetter;
the meaning of conjoining with suffering is the meaning of fetter; the meaning of being mixed with poison is the meaning of fetter.
Regarding the statement that "the meaning of being bound here is the meaning of fetters" (*saṃyojana*):
this means that the fetter itself is the binding.
How is this known to be so?
As stated in the sutra:
the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was.
He asked: "Venerable sir, does the eye fetter form, or does form fetter the eye?
This applies likewise to the questions concerning the mind and mental phenomena."
Śāriputra said:
"The eye does not fetter form;
form does not fetter the eye."
In this context, sensual desire is called a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*);
this applies likewise up to the mind and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
It is like a black and a white ox tied together by a single yoke.
If someone were to ask:
"Is one bound by the black bound by the white,
or is one bound by the white bound by the black?"
One should answer correctly:
"The black is not bound by the white;
the white is not bound by the black."
In this context, the "yoke" (praśvāsa) is called the "bond" (bandhana).
From this, it is known that the fetter (*saṃyojana*) is itself the bond.

Regarding the meaning of "fetter" as the sense of "conjunction with suffering": this means that the fetters of the desire realm cause sentient beings of the desire realm to conjoin with the suffering of the desire realm, rather than with pleasure.
The fetters of the form realm cause sentient beings of the form realm to be joined with the suffering of the form realm, not with happiness.
The fetters of the formless realm cause sentient beings of the formless realm to be joined with the suffering of the formless realm, not with happiness.
The meaning of "mixed with poison" is the meaning of "fetter.
This refers to excellent births as well as contaminated meditative absorptions (*sāsrava-samādhi*),
such as the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Because they are mixed with afflictions, the noble ones feel weary of them and renounce them, just as one avoids food mixed with poison;
though it may be delicious,
the wise keep far away from it.
As the Blessed One has said:
"By the permanent abandonment of the three fetters, one realizes the fruit of stream-entry;
having attained the state of being fixed in the Dharma, one is destined for enlightenment."
At most, one undergoes seven more existences—seven births in the heavenly realms and seven births among humans—wandering back and forth until reaching the end of suffering.
Question: As stated in the Abhidharma, one realizes the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) through the permanent abandonment of the eighty-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
The *Anupada Sūtra* states that one realizes the fruit of stream-entry through the abandonment of immeasurable sufferings. Why, then,
is it said here that one realizes the fruit of stream-entry through the permanent abandonment of the three fetters?
It is agreed that this was spoken thus.
This is the Blessed One’s concise teaching with intentional omissions for the sake of those beings to be converted.
Furthermore, the Blessed One observes the inclinations and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the sentient beings to be converted in order to teach the essential points of the Dharma.
"Intention" refers to the roots of goodness;
"latent tendencies" refers to the afflictions.
One thus examines such intentions and latent tendencies.
He briefly expounds the essential points of the Dharma to sever those afflictions;
what he teaches is measured, being neither too much nor too little.
To speak too little cannot sever those afflictions.
To speak much to them would be in vain.
It is like a skilled physician who examines a patient’s illness and its cause,
and then prescribes a medicinal formula.
That which is bestowed is measured so as to be neither too little nor too much;
for if it were too little, it could not eliminate their suffering and illness,
and if it were too much, it would be a mere waste for them.
Furthermore, the teachings that are expounded are both concise and detailed.
The concise version refers to the teaching on the permanent abandonment of the three fetters and the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
The detailed version refers to the teaching on the permanent abandonment of the eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
And it speaks of the abandonment of immeasurable suffering and the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.

Thus, there are brief explanations and extensive explanations; non-discriminative explanations and discriminative explanations; general explanations and specific explanations; non-distinct explanations and distinct explanations; non-universal explanations and universal explanations; and sudden explanations and gradual explanations.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Furthermore, for those of sharp faculties, it is taught that by the permanent abandonment of the three fetters, one realizes the fruit of stream-entry.

For those of dull faculties, it is taught that by the permanent abandonment of the eighty-eight underlying tendencies and the abandonment of immeasurable suffering, one realizes the fruit of stream-entry.
Just as it was taught for those of sharp faculties and dull faculties,

so too should one understand what is taught for those who rely on the power of causes and conditions, internal power and external power, the power of their own reflection and the power of the teachings heard from others;
likewise for those who are open-minded and those who are wise.
Furthermore, in order to entice those disciples who are timid and weak,
he demonstrates that the practice is easy to perform,
just as one might lead them by the hand; for those who are timid fear extensive practice.
To encourage progress, this is explained by contrasting the much with the little;
herein, one should explain the analogy of the bhikṣu Kṛṣṇa regarding how one who has heard much may yet practice only a little.
That is to say, there was a bhikṣu named Kṛṣṇa.
While the Tathāgata was in the world, having gone forth into the Buddha-dharma,
more than two hundred and fifty rules of training had already been established.
At the time when the Prātimokṣa Sūtra was being recited during the fortnightly night, [he said:]...
Upon hearing it said that those sons of good family who cherish themselves and delight in training in the precepts should train in this way,
they become timid and weak, thinking:
"Who is able to fully practice and observe such a multitude of rules of training?"
He then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and said, "World-Honored One,
I am now unable to guard such a multitude of precepts.
I beg to return home and resume my former worldly occupation."
The World-Honored One, out of compassion, rebuked him with gentle words and further exhorted him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Vāsiṣṭha-putra, are you able to train in the three bases of training?
That is to say: the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom."
Hearing that the number was small,
he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness;
he then addressed the Buddha, saying:
I am able to train in those trainings;
when one trains in these three types of training,
one has already trained in all points of training.
In this way, World-Honored One, if you were to speak of the permanent abandonment of the eighty-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
or of the realization of the fruit of stream-entry through the abandonment of immeasurable sufferings,
then the minds of the sentient beings to be converted would become timid and weak.
Who can uproot these eighty-eight kinds of great trees of affliction?
Who can cross over these eighty-eight kinds of great rivers of affliction?
Who can dry up these eighty-eight kinds of great oceans of affliction?
Who can shatter these eighty-eight kinds of great mountains of affliction?
Who can cultivate the remedies for these eighty-eight kinds of afflictions?
It is because the Blessed One has taught that by permanently severing the three fetters, one realizes the fruit of stream-entry.
Upon hearing that the number was small, he rejoiced and leaped for joy;
he then diligently practiced the cultivation of the remedies for the three fetters.
When the three fetters were severed, all those things to be abandoned by insight were also permanently eliminated.
Because they share the same antidote.
Furthermore, the Blessed One spoke of these as preeminent matters here;
that is to say, among the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are the most preeminent.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghosaka said:
"Among the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing, the three fetters are the most preeminent;
all others are subordinate to them."
For example, greed, hatred, pride, and so forth arise because of views.
Furthermore, the Blessed One spoke of these as being "foremost," meaning that these three fetters are the foremost among the afflictions abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
Just as a valiant general always stands at the front of the army,
by this power the afflictions to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) are difficult to subdue when they arise.
Furthermore, the Blessed One spoke of these as supreme virtues because they overcome the supreme enemy.
"Supreme merit" refers to the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
"Victorious over enemies" refers to these three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, the Buddha spoke of this here because it is a dharma that closely obstructs the three samādhis.
That is to say, the view of a self-identity is the proximate obstacle to emptiness;
the clinging to precepts and observances is the proximate obstacle to wishlessness;
and doubt is the proximate obstacle to signlessness.
Furthermore, because these three fetters (*saṃyojana*) frequently manifest for those who are close to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
as stated in the *Saṃyuktāgama*,
when one maintains the attention of receptivity (*kṣānti-manasikāra*), views and doubt do not arise; even if they were to arise, they are not perceived.
Because their afflictions are subtle and their discerning wisdom is inferior,
"views" refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*);
"doubt" (*vicikitsā*) is simply doubt itself.
Furthermore, these three fetters are difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend;
for this reason, they are specifically mentioned.
Moreover, the faults and afflictions of these three fetters are particularly intense, firm, and numerous.
Therefore, it is explained selectively:
namely, that the fetter of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the root of the sixty-two types of speculative views,
and these various speculative views are the roots of all other afflictions.
The remaining afflictions are the root of karma;
all karmas are the root of the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Depending upon the fruit of maturation, all wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral phenomena are able to grow and develop.
The fetter of adherence to rules and observances gives rise to various meaningless ascetic practices;
the fetter of doubt causes sentient beings to doubt the past, doubt the future, and doubt both the past and the future.
Internally, one hesitates, wondering:
"What is this? How is this thing?
Who currently exists? Who will exist?"
In this way, from where do these sentient beings come when born, and to what place do they go when they die? Furthermore,
once these three fetters have been abandoned and fully understood,
even up to the stage of an Arhat, they continue to proceed in a similar manner.

This means that at the time of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) has already been abandoned and fully understood;
yet, Arhats still manifest in a similar manner,
making such statements as follows.

"My bowl, my robe, my co-residents, my disciples, my dwelling, my requisites"—these notions of "I" within what is selfless are the fetter of clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*);
they are abandoned and fully understood at the moment of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*).
The various arhats still conduct themselves in a similar manner:
they wash their hands and feet, dwell in forest hermitages (āraṇya),
maintain only the three robes, and constantly practice alms-gathering.
...up to fully undertaking and maintaining the twelve dhūta-guṇas,
thereby attaining purity.
It has been heard that the Venerable Rumaṅgaka once said:
Although they are arhats, there are many of this class who believe that daily bathing constitutes purification.
Such doubts have already been abandoned and fully understood at the moment of the patience associated with the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti).
Even the various Arhats still function in a similar manner;
that is to say, when an Arhat sees a vertical object from a distance,
doubt arises as to whether it is a tree stump or a person.
Whether they are men or women,
if they see two paths, they will likewise harbor doubt, wondering:
"Is this the right path or not the right path?"
Seeing the two robes and the alms bowl, he also harbored doubt,
wondering whether they were his own or belonged to another;
such was the case with everything.
Furthermore, all yogācāras take the abandonment of the three fetters as their primary focus,
because they collectively realize the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of all fetters to be abandoned through insight.
Furthermore, all yogācāras take the abandonment of the three fetters as their primary focus.
This is because it is the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
Furthermore, these three fetters are "factors conducive to the lower realm" (*avarabhāgīya*) because they pertain to all three realms;
although sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) are indeed factors conducive to the lower realm, [they are not included here].
However, they do not pertain to all three realms.
Although views of extremes, false views, clinging to views, pride, and ignorance do pertain to all three realms,
they are not mentioned as being abandoned because they are not conducive to the lower [realms].
Furthermore, regarding those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) among the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),

it is said here that they have already permanently abandoned two of the seven latent tendencies. Thus, within the seven latent tendencies, those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry have already permanently abandoned two.
This refers to views and doubt.
Views are of two kinds,
distinguished by whether they take their own level or another level as their object.
Regarding the statement that "one preeminent [fetter] is mentioned for each among them":
furthermore, this is stated because, among the nine fetters, those that have been permanently abandoned by those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) are being discussed here.
This means that among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) has already abandoned three fetters:
namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). For this reason, the Venerable Ghosaka said:
This sutra should state that one who has eternally severed the three fetters realizes the fruit of stream-entry—
namely, the view of grasping at views, doubt,
and [attachment to precepts and vows]. Furthermore, among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), those which have been eternally severed by those in the fruit of stream-entry are as follows:
Because it is stated therein:
"The ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya) consist of the five views."
Doubt, greed, hatred, pride, and delusion.
Among these ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the stream-enterer has already permanently abandoned six:
namely, the five views and doubt.
Regarding the fact that only the permanent abandonment of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) is mentioned here and not the six,
it is because only the primary [fetters] are stated.
That is to say, among these six, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the primary, while the view of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is the secondary derivative.
The clinging to rules and observances is the turning;
the clinging to views is the following-turning;
and doubt is the turning.
Wrong view is a derivative [of the primary defilements].
Since the primary transformation has already been explained, it should be understood that the derivative has also been explained.
Therefore, only the permanent abandonment of the three fetters is mentioned.
Furthermore, this sutra briefly presents the stages of the gateway;
that is to say, among the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*),
there are those belonging to only one category (*nikāya*), those common to two categories, and those common to four categories.
If it is said that there is the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
one should know that this refers collectively to only one category.
If it is said that there is the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa)...
It should be understood that when it is said in general that [a certain factor] pervades both categories,
although there is no other separate underlying tendency (anuśaya) that pervades both,
the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) is nonetheless termed "pervading both categories."
Alternatively, it may be said that they are associated and co-existent.
If one speaks of "doubt," it should be understood as a general statement encompassing all four categories.
Furthermore, among the fetters to be abandoned by insight,
some are universal within their own realm,
while others are universal across other realms.
If one speaks of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
it should be understood as referring collectively to the universal [afflictions] within one's own realm.
If one speaks of the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) and doubt (vicikitsā), it should be understood as referring collectively to the universal [afflictions] of other realms.

Question: Why is it that the universal [defilements] of one's own realm are described as only one fetter (*saṃyojana*), whereas the universal [defilements] of another realm are described as two fetters?
Answer: Because the universal [defilements] of another realm pertain to both those conditioned by the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and those conditioned by the non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*).
If one speaks of the clinging to precepts and observances,

it should be understood as a general designation for the fetters that have outflows as their object; if one speaks of doubt, [it should be understood as a general designation for the fetters that have outflows as their object].
It should be understood that, in general, these are called the fetters with uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*).
They are like the universal [fetters] of one's own realm and the universal [fetters] of other realms;
likewise, they are the universal [fetters] of one's own stage and the universal [fetters] of other stages.
One should know that it is likewise so.
Furthermore, among the fetters to be abandoned by insight,
there are those that have outflowing objects as their conditions.
There are those that have the untainted as their object.
If one speaks of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*),
it should be understood that these are spoken of collectively as fetters having the tainted as their object.
If one speaks of "doubt," it should be understood as a general designation for the fetters that have untainted objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*).
Question: Why are two fetters said to have tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*), while only one is mentioned for those with untainted objects?

Answer: Among the fetters (saṃyojana) that have outflowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana), some have as their object [factors] of their own realm (sva-dhātu) and their own stage (sva-bhūmi), while others have as their object [factors] of another realm (para-dhātu) and another stage (para-bhūmi).
This is the case when referring to the view of a self-identity (satkāya-dṛṣṭi).
It should be understood that when it is said to have its own realm and its own stage as its object,
this refers generally to the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*);
when it is said to have other realms and other stages as its object, this should likewise be understood as referring generally to that same grasping.
For example: those with outflows as their object and those without outflows as their object;
those with contention as their object and those without contention as their object;
those with the mundane as their object and those with the supramundane as their object.
There are conditions associated with the relish of craving and conditions not associated with the relish of craving;
conditions based on attachment and conditions based on renunciation;
conditions that lead to falling into the realms and conditions that do not lead to falling into the realms.
Conditions that accord with fetters and conditions that do not accord with fetters;
conditions that accord with grasping and conditions that do not accord with grasping;
conditions that accord with entanglements and conditions that do not accord with entanglements.
It should be known that it is likewise.
Furthermore, among the fetters to be abandoned by seeing,
there are those that have conditioned phenomena as their object.
There are also fetters conditioned by the unconditioned.
If one speaks of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*),
it should be understood that these are spoken of collectively as fetters conditioned by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If one speaks of doubt (*vicikitsā*),
it should be understood as a general designation for fetters conditioned by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding the reason why fetters conditioned by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) are said to be twofold, it should be understood as previously explained.

It should be understood that the same applies to those conditioned by the conditioned, those conditioned by the unconditioned, those conditioned by the permanent, those conditioned by the impermanent, those conditioned by the constant, those conditioned by the non-constant, those conditioned by the subject to change, and those conditioned by the not subject to change.
Furthermore, among the fetters to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), some possess the nature of view (*dṛṣṭi-svabhāva*) while others do not.
It should be understood that when the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*) are mentioned,
these are collectively said to be fetters possessing the nature of view.
If one speaks of "doubt," it should be understood as a general designation for fetters that are not of the nature of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
The reason why those fetters that are of the nature of views are spoken of as two is as previously explained; this should be understood accordingly.

Just as with the nature of views and the non-nature of views, so too should one understand the nature of seeing and the non-nature of seeing, the nature of investigation and the non-nature of investigation, the nature of seeking and the non-nature of seeking, the nature of delighting in seeking and the non-nature of delighting in seeking, the nature of delighting in turning back and the non-nature of delighting in turning back, the nature of firm attachment and the non-nature of firm attachment, and the nature of repeatedly grasping objects and the non-nature of repeatedly grasping objects.
Furthermore, among the fetters abandoned through seeing, some are unwholesome and some are indeterminate.
If one speaks of the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*),
it should be understood that these refer collectively to all unwholesome fetters.
If one speaks of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it should be understood as a general designation for all neutral fetters (*avyākṛta-saṃyojana*).
Regarding the fact that all unwholesome fetters are said to be of two kinds, the reason should be understood as previously explained.
Just as there is a distinction between the unwholesome and the neutral in terms of having or not having maturation (*vipāka*), so it is here.
Experiencing two fruits; experiencing one fruit.
Associated with shamelessness and lack of dread;
dissociated from shamelessness and lack of dread.
One should know that it is likewise so.
Furthermore, among the fetters to be abandoned by seeing, there are those that function with a mode of joyous activity and those that function with a mode of dejected activity.

If it is said that there are the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), one should know that these are spoken of collectively as functioning with a joyful mode of activity (saumanasya-carita).
If it is said that there is doubt (vicikitsā), one should know that this is spoken of collectively as functioning with a dejected mode of activity (daurmanasya-carita).
The reasons for explaining the two modes of activity of joy should be understood as previously stated.
Furthermore, these three fetters obstruct the three pure aggregates;
therefore, they are specifically mentioned: namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) obstructs the aggregate of pure ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*).

Some say that the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) within the aggregate of concentration obstructs the aggregate of pure concentration. Others say: [the grasping at rules and observances within the aggregate of view obstructs the aggregate of pure concentration].
The fetter of doubt obstructs the aggregate of pure ethical discipline, and it obstructs the aggregate of pure wisdom.
Just as these three aggregates are obstructed, one should know that the obstructions to the three trainings, the three cultivations, and the three purities are likewise.
Furthermore, these three fetters obstruct the eightfold noble path.
Therefore, it is explained selectively;
namely, that the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) obstructs right speech, right action, and right livelihood. Some say:
They obstruct right mindfulness and right concentration.
Some say that the grasping of rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa) obstructs right mindfulness and right concentration.
It obstructs right speech, right action, and right livelihood;
doubt obstructs right view, right thought, and right effort.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of enabling those who doubt to attain certainty.
It is taught that the fruit of stream-entry involves the permanent abandonment of the three fetters,
namely: doubt regarding the world, [doubt regarding the Dharma],
and having already attained the state of a noble one.
They still cling to the notion of a self;
they still cling to notions of fortune and misfortune;
they still harbor doubts and perplexities.
Therefore, the World-Honored One taught that by permanently severing these three,
one realizes the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna),
because the fruit of stream-entry is the first fruit of the noble ones (ārya).
Question: Is one called a "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) because they have first attained the Path, or because they have first attained the Fruit?
If so, what would be the fault [in either case]?
Both positions entail faults.
If one is called a "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) because they have first attained the Path,
then the eighth noble person (the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry) should also be called a stream-enterer.
The eighth noble one refers to those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).
They are designated as the eighth when counted from the superior perspective.
Because he has first attained the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*),
if one were to be called a "stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*) merely by first attaining the fruit,
then those who have partially abandoned desire-taints (*vītarāga*) as well as those who have completely abandoned desire-taints would also be [so called].
Upon entering the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and reaching the stage of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*),
one should be designated as a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), because at that time one realizes the first of the four noble fruits.
Some have said this.
Because one first attains the Path, one is called a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
Question: Should not the eighth noble person also be called a Stream-enterer?
Answer: Only when one first attains the Path and possesses the knowledge of the path as its object is one called a Stream-enterer.
Although the eighth noble one has initially attained the Path,
they are not yet called a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) because they have not fully acquired the knowledge of the path as an object (*mārgālambana-jñāna*).

Furthermore, if the initial attainment of the Path were the fruit of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) comprised within the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*), [it would follow that they were already Stream-enterers].
This is what is called "stream-entry.
The eighth [moment] is not so.
Furthermore, if one first attains the path by means of three conditions:
This is called "Stream-enterer" (srotāpanna).
First, one abandons what has already been attained;
second, one attains what has not yet been attained.
The third is the attainment of the severance of fetters through a single taste (*ekarasa*).
"Having abandoned and attained the Path" means having abandoned the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
"Attaining what has not yet been attained on the Path" refers to attaining the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
"Attaining the single flavor of the severance of the fetters" refers to the attainment [of the fruit].
This refers to obtaining the attainment of the single-flavored abandonment of the fetters to be abandoned by insight within the three realms;
the eighth [liberation] is not like this.
Furthermore, if one first attains the path while possessing five conditions:
This is called "Stream-enterer" (srotāpanna).
First, one abandons what has already been attained;
second, one attains the path not yet attained; third, one attains the single flavor of the severance of the fetters.
Fourth, one simultaneously attains eight knowledges;
fifth, one cultivates the sixteen aspects at one time.
This is not the case for the eighth [knowledge].
Furthermore, if, having first attained the Path, one has already severed all fetters to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*),

and is one whose afflictions are to be abandoned by the patience regarding the non-existence of things (*vastu-śūnyatā-kṣānti*) and who possesses the nature of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), such a person is called a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
The eighth is not so.
Furthermore, if one who has first attained the Path possesses signs and designations such that they can engage in discussion with others,
only then is they called a Stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
The eighth is not so.
Furthermore, if one who has first attained the Path is subject to death and rebirth, they are called a Stream-enterer;
the eighth is not so.
Other masters say that one is called a "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) because of first attaining the fruit.
[This applies even to] those who have partially abandoned the defilements of desire or those who have completely abandoned them.

One who enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) and reaches the stage of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) should be called a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
Answer: This applies if one first attains the fruit through gradual progression and not by means of transcendence (vyutkrāntaka).
One is then called a stream-enterer; others are not so.
Furthermore, if one first attains the fruit and realizes the first liberation, [one is a stream-enterer].
This is the first attainment of deliverance;
one who abides in the first fruit is called a Stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
The others are not so. Furthermore, if one first attains a fruit by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*)—
having previously either partially abandoned or completely abandoned the defilements of desire (*kāmarāga*)— and thereby attains that fruit;
This is what is called "stream-enterer";
others are not so. Furthermore, if one first attains the fruit [of the path], [one is a stream-enterer].
One who, prior to this, has not yet realized the fruit by means of the mundane path—
having either abandoned six grades or nine grades of the dharmas of the desire realm—
is called a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
The others are not so. Furthermore, if one first attains a fruit,
it is the very first fruit among these four fruits.
This is what is called "stream-enterer";
others are not so. Furthermore, if one first attains the fruit [of the path], [one is a stream-enterer].
Among these four paths and four fruits,
that which is the very first fruit is called "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna); the others are not so.
Furthermore, if one first attains a fruit among these four pairs of eight types of individuals (*pudgala*),
that which is the very first fruit is called "stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*).
The others are not so. Furthermore,
if one has definitively attained both the path and the fruit at their initial acquisition,
one is then called a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
This means that although the stage of the fruit of once-returning is fixed, the path is not fixed,
because both contaminated and uncontaminated paths can attain it.
For the stage of the fruit of non-returning, neither the path nor the stage is fixed.
Because both the contaminated and uncontaminated paths of the six stages can achieve it,
although the path to the fruit of arhatship is fixed, its stage is not;
for it can be achieved by relying on any of the nine stages.
The path and the fruit of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) are both fixed;
this is because they are attained solely by means of the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) based on the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna).
Furthermore, there are those who say:
One is not called a "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) merely because of first attaining the Path,
nor is one called a stream-enterer merely because of first attaining the Fruit;
rather, one is called a stream-enterer by virtue of having accomplished the fruit of stream-entry.
The designation "pudgala" (person) is established based on the dharmas,
just as one speaks of a "butter-jar," an "oil-jar," "medicine," or "water.
For what reason is this so?
Is he called a "Stream-enterer"?
The answer is: "stream" refers to the noble path;
"entering" refers to having entered it.
Because he has entered the noble path, he is called a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
Question: Since the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and the arhat also enter the noble path, they too should be called stream-enterers.
Answer: Even according to this interpretation, we do not exclude that [designation].
However, because it is the first instance of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), it receives its name;
the others receive different designations based on their distinct qualities.

Question: Since once-returners, non-returners, and arhats also attain the state of being non-falling, why is it said that only those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry attain the state of being non-falling?
Answer: It should also be said of the others, but it is not mentioned.
It should be understood that this sutra is an incomplete teaching (sāvaśeṣa-vacana).
Furthermore, each fruit has its own specific ultimate meaning (paramārtha) and manifest meaning (vyañjana-artha):
namely, the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) is the non-falling dharma in terms of its ultimate meaning, and the non-falling dharma in terms of its manifest meaning.
Therefore, it is said that he does not fall.
Because he does not fall into the evil destinies,
the fruit of once-returning, the dharma of once-returning, and the excellence of the dharma of once-returning are manifested.
Therefore, one is called a "once-returner" because they return only once more.
The state of non-returning and the qualities of non-returning are superior; the qualities of non-returning are thus made manifest.
Therefore, it is called "Non-returner" (*anāgāmin*),
because one does not return to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In the fruit of Arhatship, the excellence of the dharma of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma*) is manifested.
Therefore, it is said that they are "unborn," because they do not undergo further existence. For this reason,
the stream-enterer alone is specifically said to be "not subject to falling."
Question: Since ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) also possess the quality of not falling away from the Dharma, why are they not mentioned in this context?
Answer: Although they should have been mentioned, they were not.
One should know that this meaning is not exhaustive.
Furthermore, because it is indeterminate:
namely, among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there are those who attain and those who do not attain the state of being "not subject to falling" (*avinipāta-dharman*).
All those who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) are certain not to fall [into the lower realms];
therefore, they are specifically mentioned here.
"Certainty" refers to abiding in the fixed group of those destined for rightness (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi).
Because all stream-enterers are certain to attain parinirvāṇa, they are said to be "fixed";
this is because their conditions have already transformed,
just like a clay vessel.
He threw it from atop a three-storied pavilion onto the ground;
before it had even reached the earth,
although it was said not yet to have broken, [it shattered].
Because it must necessarily destroy [the afflictions], it is also called "destruction.
For one who proceeds toward enlightenment, the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows and the knowledge of non-arising are termed "enlightenment" (*bodhi*).
He aspires to, delights in, and accepts that enlightenment.
Revering, cherishing, and following after sensual desires constitutes "inclination" (*nati*).
Reaching this point is called "inclination.
As for "one who returns at most seven times" (*saptakṛtvah-parama*):
This means that one experiences only seven existences.
Question: One should rather say fourteen existences, or twenty-eight existences.
If this were explained solely on the basis of what exists inherently (*sahaja*),
one should speak of fourteen existences (*bhava*),
because there are seven existences each among the gods and among humans.
If one speaks according to the theory that the intermediate state (antarābhava) exists inherently,
then there are twenty-eight states of existence,
because gods and humans each have fourteen states of existence.
This refers to seven existences as the fundamental state (*mūlabhava*) and seven existences as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Why is it said that there are at most seven existences?
The answer is: just as a "seven-leaf tree" does not exceed seven leaves, so too it is said that there are at most seven existences.
This means that both gods and humans possess seven [types] each in their fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*) and intermediate existence (*antarābhava*),
as stated in other sūtras:
"The Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma through four truths, three turnings, and twelve aspects."
It is not merely three turns with twelve aspects; rather,
it should be said that there are twelve turns with forty-eight aspects—
namely, for each of the four truths, there are three turns and twelve aspects.
However, each individual truth possesses three turnings and twelve aspects;
because they do not exceed these three turnings and twelve aspects, this statement was made.
Other sūtras also state this.
There are seven points of proficiency and three contemplations on meaning;
by means of these, one can swiftly exhaust all outflows within the Noble Dharma and Vinaya.
One should not say that there are only seven bases of mastery;
rather, one should say there are thirty-five bases of mastery, or even immeasurable bases of mastery.
It is spoken of as "seven" because they do not exceed that number.
That is to say, because there are seven points of proficiency regarding each of the five aggregates or other phenomena,
this case is likewise.
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"Bhikṣus, I shall now teach you two dharmas.
The two are: the eye and forms, up to the mind and mental objects."
One should not say that there are two;
rather, one should state that there are twelve.
Because they do not exceed two, the expression "two dharmas" is used.
This case is also like that.
A question was asked: "Why does a stream-enterer transmigrate through and come back from rebirths exactly seven times, neither more nor less?
Venerable Pārśva replied:
Whether there is increase or decrease, doubt arises in both cases.
However, because experiencing only seven existences does not contradict the nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one should not find fault with this.
Furthermore, it is because the power of that ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) remains sufficient to produce only that much ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
Furthermore, by the power of that karma, one is able to undergo seven existences;
yet by the power of the Noble Path, one does not reach an eighth.
It is like being bitten by a venomous snake that can only travel seven paces.
By the power of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), he was able to walk seven steps;
by the force of the poison, he did not reach the eighth.
Furthermore, had he been subject to eight existences (*bhava*), [he would have reached it].
That eighth birth would lack the Noble Path;
for it is the nature of the Noble Path not to rely upon an eighth body in the desire realm.
If that eighth birth were devoid of the Noble Path, [it would follow that one could not attain parinirvāṇa there].
Having already seen the truths, they again fail to see the truths;
having attained the fruits of sanctity, they again fail to attain those fruits;
having entered into clear observation (*abhisamaya*), they again fail to observe clearly.
Once one has become an noble one (ārya), one does not revert to being an ordinary person (pṛthagjana);
lest such an error occur,
there are only seven existences.
Furthermore, if one were to undergo eight more existences, one would transcend the three periods of time;
thus, regarding the Dharma and Vinaya of the Samyaksaṃbuddhas—more numerous than the sands of the Gaṅgā—one would not be among the inner retinue of the Tathāgata.
Just as those beyond seven generations of kin are no longer considered relatives, so too,

at the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one has already eliminated seven births among humans and gods in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and one birth in each distinct location of the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*).
In all other births, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Since a dharma for which non-analytical cessation has been attained will never again manifest, there are only seven [existences].
Furthermore, it possesses the sense of taking birth in the seven locations above and below within the desire realm.
The seven locations refer to humans and the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because beings transmigrate back and forth among them with humans and gods alternating, they undergo seven existences (*bhava*).
Furthermore, because there are differences in the strength of the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) within the desire realm, they undergo those seven existences.
Furthermore, because he has cultivated the seven factors of enlightenment throughout seven existences and attained their perfection,
he undergoes only seven more existences. Furthermore,

because he has cultivated the seven bases of power, the seven types of meditative concentration, and the sevenfold noble path throughout seven existences and attained their perfection, [he undergoes only seven more existences].
They undergo only seven existences.

Furthermore, because they have perfected the path that counteracts the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) throughout those seven existences, they undergo only seven existences—neither more nor less.
Regarding the statement "seven times reborn in the heavens and seven times reborn among humans," this is spoken with reference to a perfected stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*); thus,
such a person experiences seven births equally among humans and devas.
However, there is a distinction regarding the rebirths of stream-enterers:
namely, some take seven births among gods and six among humans,
while others take seven births among humans and six among gods.
Either six devas and five humans,
or six humans and five devas, or five devas and four humans,
or five humans and four devas.
Either four gods and three humans,
or four humans and three gods,
or three gods and two humans.
Or there may be three humans and two gods;
or two humans and one god;
or two humans and one god.
In this context, since we are speaking of those who undergo the maximum number of births, it is said that the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) takes seven rebirths each among gods and humans.
Question: Regarding one who has fulfilled the requirements for a stream-enterer, where do they complete the seventh birth?
Is it in the heavenly realms or among humans that they experience the seventh existence and attain parinirvāṇa?
Regarding this, some say:
if one attains the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) in a particular birth, that birth is said to be included within the count of the seven existences.
They explain it as follows:
If one attains the fruit among humans, then after completing seven full lifetimes in the heavens, one enters parinirvāṇa.
If one attains the fruit in the heavens, then after completing seven full lifetimes among humans, one enters parinirvāṇa.
Some say: "If one attains the fruit of stream-entry based on this birth, it is not said that this birth is counted among the seven existences.
This is what they say.
If one attains the fruit among humans, one returns to the human realm and attains parinirvāṇa after completing seven [lifetimes];
if one attains the fruit in the heavens, one returns to the heavenly realm and attains parinirvāṇa after completing seven [lifetimes].
It should be understood that the first explanation among these is unreasonable,
because those born in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) upon attaining a fruit are entirely comprised within the class of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Consequently,
it would follow that a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) could only be said to undergo twenty-seven existences.
However, the *Prakaraṇapāda* states that because a stream-enterer puts an end to suffering by transmigrating and returning through twenty-eight existences,
one should not say that the first birth after attaining the fruit is counted among those seven existences.
Question: Do those who are destined to undergo seven more existences give rise to the Noble Path during the first six births? Some say they do not.
If they were to give rise to it, they would enter parinirvāṇa.
Some say that they also arise;
because they are sustained by the power of karma, they do not enter parinirvāṇa.
Question: If seven existences are completed and no Buddha has appeared in the world, can one who is a householder attain arhatship?
Some say it is not possible;
they must go forth from home, receive other dharma robes, and then attain arhatship.
Others say that one may attain arhatship while remaining a householder.
Later, he will certainly leave the household life and receive the remaining dharma-robes.
According to this teaching,
it is by becoming a disciple of the Buddha through the natural law of his own nature that he attains the ultimate fruit.
For example, five hundred sages were practicing the path on Mount Isigili;
originally śrāvakas who had appeared during a world without a Buddha,
a monkey manifested the appearance of a Buddha’s disciple for them.
They all train to realize the fruit of a solitary buddha (pratyekabuddha) and, being beyond training (aśaikṣa), do not assume the marks of non-Buddhists.
As for those who transmigrate back and forth, when their lifespan in the heavens is exhausted, they come to be born among humans.
When the lifespan in the human realm is exhausted, one is reborn in the heavens,
like a wealthy person strolling through a garden.
"Flow" refers to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), and "turning" refers to the fundamental existence (*pūrvabhava*).
"One who makes an end of suffering" means one who realizes the limit of suffering.
Question: Does this limit of suffering exist within suffering or outside of suffering?
If it were within suffering, it could not be the limit.
If it were outside of suffering, how could worldly analogies be reconciled?
For example, just as a golden tally-stick is gold from its beginning to its middle to its end,
so too the limits of suffering should themselves be suffering.
Some say that the "limit of suffering" refers to being within suffering itself;
it is the very substance of the final aggregates of an Arhat.

Although this is suffering, it is not the cause of future suffering; because it does not produce future suffering and future suffering does not continue, it is called the "limit of suffering" (*duḥkhānta*).
Other masters say that the limit of suffering refers to that which lies outside of suffering, namely, *nirvāṇa*.
It is called the "limit of suffering" because one emerges from suffering forever.
As for the worldly examples provided, they need not necessarily be reconciled with the Dharma, for they are not included within the Tripiṭaka and do not require interpretation;
this is because the principles of worldly phenomena and noble dharmas are each distinct.
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume Forty-Six;
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Forty-Seven.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, who received the Imperial Decree. Section Two: The Aggregate of Fetters (*Saṃyojana-kāya*), Part One: The Sub-section on the Unwholesome (*Akuśala-nikāya*), Second; there are three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
That is to say: the unwholesome root of greed,
the unwholesome root of hatred,
and the unwholesome root of delusion.
