The Venerable Ghosaka also spoke thus:
"Because two fetters have not been abandoned and have not been fully understood, one does not emerge from the desire realm;
because three fetters have not been abandoned and have not been fully understood."
Because they lead to rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
these five are specifically designated as the "fetters conducive to the lower realm" (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
The Venerable Vāśpa also spoke in this way.
Second, because they bind one, one does not transcend the desire realm;
third, because they have not been severed, one falls back into the desire realm.
Therefore, these five alone are established as the fetters conducive to the lower realms (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, because this section manifests the gate, manifests the summary, and manifests the entry,
these five are specifically designated as the "lower fetters" (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
This means that among the various afflictions (*kleśa*), some belong to only one category, while others pertain to both categories.
It may pertain to four categories or five categories.
If it speaks of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
one should know that this is said collectively as belonging to only one category.
If one speaks of the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa),
it should be understood as a general statement encompassing both categories. If one speaks of doubt (vicikitsā),
it should be understood as a general statement encompassing all four categories.
If it is said that greed and hatred should be understood as collectively referring to those that pervade all five categories,
then they are thus exclusively abandoned through vision.
They are abandoned through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation;
they are both universal and non-universal;
and they manifest only in ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
It should be understood that this applies equally to both ordinary beings and noble ones when they manifest [these states],
whether they proceed with a mode of joy or a mode of sorrow.
Furthermore, among all the afflictions abandoned through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation,
only greed and hatred exist independently across all six consciousnesses;
this is the case only among those afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing.
Only the three beginning with the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) function as the primary movers and leaders;
therefore, these five alone are specifically established as the fetters conducive to the lower realm (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana).
Furthermore, if one asks why the first two fetters are established as being conducive to the lower realm:
This should be answered in detail as in the section on the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
If it is asked why the last three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are established as "conducive to the lower realm" (*avarabhāgīya*), this should be answered in detail as in the section on the three fetters.

By means of these two questions and answers, all other afflictions (*kleśa*) are collectively excluded; for what reason, then, are the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) not "conducive to the lower realm"?
The response is: "That too should be among the fetters conducive to the lower realms (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana), yet it is not mentioned.
One should know that this is an intentional omission;
there are those who say this is the Blessed One’s concise teaching for the sake of those to be converted (vineya). Furthermore, others say: [text continues].
If they cause rebirth in the lower realms and among lower sentient beings, they are established as "fettering to the lower" (*avarabhāgīya*).
Since the various secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) cannot effect rebirth, they are not established as fetters to the lower.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"You should receive and uphold the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni) previously revealed by me.
At that time, Māluṅkyāputra rose from his seat in the assembly, bared one shoulder, and placed his right knee on the ground.
He bowed toward the Bhagavān with palms joined and said:
"Bhagavān,
I have already received and upheld the five lower fetters taught by the Bhagavān."
The World-Honored One asked,
"How do you receive and uphold it?
He replied:
Greed itself is the latent tendency of sensual desire that binds the mind; it is a lower fetter.
The Blessed One has already revealed this, and I have accepted and upheld it.
This applies extensively to the fetter of doubt as well.
The Buddha said:
"Foolish people, non-Buddhists, and followers of other teachings will, upon hearing what you say, rebuke and interrogate you,
like a sick infant lying on its back upon a bed."
He does not even clearly comprehend the objects of desire such as form, much less can he manifest a mind bound by the fetter of sensual craving;
nevertheless, he still possesses the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of sensual craving.
This applies extensively to all [the fetters] up to the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-bandhana*).
Question: As the Buddha has taught, one who fully accepts and upholds the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīyāni) ought to be censured.
Answer: What is censured is the meaning grasped, not the name by which it is grasped;
what is censured is the meaning understood, not the name by which it is understood.
What is being refuted is the meaning of the statement, not its name.
That is to say, when that venerable one says that the arising of afflictions is called "conducive to the lower realms" (*avarabhāgīya*) and not their non-arising,
the Buddha taught that when afflictions have not yet been abandoned, they are termed "conducive to the lower realms," even if they do not necessarily manifest at present.
Furthermore, they claim that afflictions must be in active manifestation (*samudācāra*) to be called "factors conducive to the lower realm" (*avarabhāgīya*).
The Buddha, however, taught that even when these are merely possessed (*prāpti*), they may likewise be termed "fetters conducive to the lower realm.
Furthermore, they claim that afflictions must be present in the current moment to be called "factors conducive to the lower realm."
The Buddha taught that all three time periods are designated as the fetters conducive to the lower realms (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).

Furthermore, he taught that afflictions are called "conducive to the lower realms" only when they actively envelop the mind; however, the Buddha also taught that both their state as active envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and their state as latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) may be designated as the fetters conducive to the lower realms.

As it is said, when the fetters of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not correctly abandoned, they are called the lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
This applies in detail to the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*) as well.
There are five higher-tier fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
That is to say: the fetter of attachment to form that leads to the higher realms, the fetter of attachment to the formless that leads to the higher realms,
the fetter of restlessness that leads to the higher realms,
and the fetter of conceit that leads to the higher realms.
Ignorance is a fetter conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these five fetters conducive to the higher realms?

Answer: Their intrinsic nature consists of eight factors. Specifically, "craving for form" (*rūparāga*)—that is, the attachment to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) regarding the realm of form—is one factor.
Attachment to the formless realm refers to the single entity of craving abandoned through cultivation within the formless realm.
Restlessness, pride, and ignorance refer to the six entities consisting of restlessness, pride, and ignorance abandoned through cultivation within both the form and formless realms respectively.
These five higher fetters (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana) have eight factors as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Having already explained their intrinsic nature, their etymology shall now be explained.
Question: Why are they called "higher fetters"?
What is the meaning of "fetter leading upward" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*)? The answer is:
it means causing one to proceed upward, causing one to ascend, and causing the continuity [of existence] to arise in a higher realm.
This is the meaning of the "fetter conducive to the higher realms" (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana).

Question: If the meaning of "tending toward the higher" constitutes the meaning of the fetter conducive to the higher realms, then the fetter conducive to the higher realms should not be identical to the "floods" (ogha).
Because falling, drowning, and so forth constitute the meaning of "flood" (ogha).
Answer: The meaning of "flood" is distinct from the meaning of "factors conducive to the higher realms" (ūrdhva-bhāgīya).
That is to say, the factors conducive to the higher realms are established in dependence upon the realms and stages (dhātu-bhūmi).
Because they cause sentient beings to ascend to higher realms,
they are established as floods (*ogha*) based on the path of liberation.
Although one may be born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), these [floods] cause sentient beings to sink into saṃsāra, preventing them from reaching liberation and the noble path.

Question: Why are the attachments to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) each established separately as fetters leading upward (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), while the other three are established as one for both realms?
Answer: The other three should also be established separately according to the distinction of the realms.
If it were not so, one should know that there is more to be said.
Furthermore, because he wishes to make the meaning of what is taught easy to understand, he speaks using various words and various phrases.
Moreover, the Blessed One intends to manifest two doors, two summaries, two stairways, two steps, two lamps, two torches, two texts, and two shadows.
Just as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is established as two fetters (*saṃyojana*) based on the distinction between the realms,
so too should restlessness (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) each be established as two.
Just as craving is established as two by combining it with the two realms, such should also be the case for restlessness and the others.
In this way, it should correspond to the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Whether eight or four are mentioned, two gates are presented; even down to two shadows, they are spoken of in this manner so that they may mutually illuminate one another.
Furthermore, craving differentiates realms, stages, and categories; craving is able to increase all afflictions.
Since craving has many faults as described regarding its objects of attachment, it is established as two fetters based on the differentiation of realms.
Because the three [fetters], such as restlessness (*auddhatya*), do not possess these characteristics, those belonging to the two higher realms are combined and established as one. Question:
Why are only those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) established as the fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: They are called "factors conducive to the higher realms" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*) because they cause one to proceed toward rebirth in the higher [realms].
Since the fetters abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya-saṃyojana*) also cause one to fall back into the lower [realms], they are not established as factors conducive to the higher realms.
Furthermore, that which is practiced by those who have ascended is called "conducive to the higher."
The noble one (ārya) is not an ordinary person (pṛthagjana);

because the fetters to be abandoned by insight (darśana-prahātavya-saṃyojana) arise only in ordinary persons, they are not established as the fetters conducive to the higher realms (ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana).
Among the noble ones, only those fetters that arise in a non-returner (anāgāmin) are established as the fetters conducive to the higher realms.

Question: From this discussion, another question arises: why are the fetters (saṃyojana) produced by those who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) not classified as "fetters conducive to the higher realms" (ūrdhvabhāgīya)? Answer:

Those termed "conducive to the higher realms" refer to those that lead to rebirth in the upper [realms]. Since the fetters produced by Stream-enterers and Once-returners also cause rebirth in the lower [realms], they are not established as "fetters conducive to the higher realms."
Furthermore, if one were to attain the fruit even by merely transcending a realm, then the fetters arising therein would be established as "factors conducive to the higher realms" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
However, although stream-enterers and once-returners do indeed attain the fruit, they have not yet transcended the realm [of desire]. Therefore, [those fetters] are not so designated.
What arises therein is not conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
Furthermore, if one transcends the realms and also completely abandons unwholesome afflictions (*akushala-kleśa*),
the fetters (*saṃyojana*) that arise therein are established as being conducive to the higher realms.
Because both [the fetters] of the stream-enterer and the once-returner are absent,
the fetters they give rise to do not belong to the category of those conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
Furthermore, if one transcends the realm and the fetters conducive to the lower realms (*avarabhāgīya*) are also completely severed, [then...]
The fetters arising therein are called "conducive to the higher realms" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
Because both [the stream-enterer and the once-returner] lack these two conditions,
the fetters they give rise to are not conducive to the higher realms.
Furthermore, the bases for the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) and the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) are distinct.
If these higher fetters arise within one's continuum, the lower fetters will certainly not arise therein.
If the fetters conducive to the lower realms arise within one's person, those conducive to the higher realms will certainly not arise;
for it is possible for the fetters conducive to the lower realms to arise within the person of a stream-enterer or a once-returner.
They will certainly not give rise to the fetters conducive to the higher realms.
Furthermore, if they no longer give rise to karma resembling that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
the fetters they do give rise to are established as being conducive to the higher realms.

Since even stream-enterers and once-returners still manifest karma resembling that of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), the fetters they give rise to are not conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
How is it that they manifest karma resembling that of ordinary worldlings?

This refers to being addicted to various colorful decorations, incense, and flowers; accepting and storing gold, silver, rare curios, and precious objects; employing others as servants and laborers while still inflicting beatings and punishments;
and sharing a single bed with men and women, or touching their corpses.
They give rise to perceptions of smoothness and tactile pleasure,
and furthermore, they engage in unchaste conduct without shame or remorse;
these are called the karmas resembling those of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, if there is one who is not to be born again,

having increased the *kalala* from the drop of blood and entered the mother’s womb to dwell between the receptacle for the undigested and the receptacle for the digested, the fetters arising therein are called the "fettering to the higher realms" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
Since it is possible for such a matter to occur for those in the stages of Stream-enterer and Once-returner,
the fetters they give rise to are not conducive to the higher realms,
as stated in that sutra.
The householder Citra addressed his kinsmen and friends:
"You should know this:
I shall certainly not be reborn again in the blood-drops of the Kakutstha."
Having entered the mother's womb and dwelling between the two sacs— the raw and the cooked—
I have forever severed the five lower fetters and shall no longer return to undergo rebirth in the desire realm.
The Venerable Ghosaka also spoke thus:
"I declare that one who is liberated from the fetters of sensual desire and ill will is liberated regarding the matter of entering the mother's womb."
Question: Among the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*), is the intrinsic nature of restlessness (*auddhatya*) itself a fetter (*saṃyojana*)?
If it were so, what would be the fault?
If these are fetters (*saṃyojana*), how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
For example, it asks: "What are the phenomena that are fetters?"
This refers to the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*). What are the phenomena that are not fetters?
They are all other phenomena, excluding the nine fetters.
If they were not fetters, how would one reconcile what is stated in this sutra?
For example, it asks:
"What are the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*)?"
That is to say: attachment to form, attachment to the formless, restlessness, pride, and ignorance.
It should be stated that these are fetters (*saṃyojana*).
[Objection: How then should one reconcile this with what is taught in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
Answer: The recitation of the masters of foreign lands differs from this.
They recite: "What are the fettering factors (*saṃyojana-dharma*)?
They are the nine fetters (*nava-saṃyojana*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) among the fetters pertaining to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*)."
What are the non-fettering phenomena (*asaṃyojana-dharma*)?
They refer to all other phenomena, excluding the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the restlessness (*auddhatya*) among the fetters pertaining to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Question: For what reason do the masters of Kaśmīra not recite it in that manner?
The answer is that this case should also be understood as being like the previous recitation, where the fact that it is not recited has a specific underlying intention.
This is because that restlessness (*auddhatya*) is indeterminate as to whether it is a fetter (*saṃyojana*) or not;
that is to say, only a small portion of the nature of restlessness constitutes a fetter.
Regarding those in the two upper realms,
a small portion are not fetters; regarding those in the desire realm,
some are indeed fetters, namely those arising from the noble ones.
There are cases where what is not a fetter (saṃyojana) arises as something distinct;
there are cases where what is a fetter arises in a state where a noble one (ārya) has already abandoned desire-taint (rāga-kleśa);
and there are cases where what is not a fetter arises in a state where a noble one has not yet abandoned desire-taint.
Question: Why is restlessness (*auddhatya*) a fetter (*saṃyojana*) in the two higher realms, but not a fetter in the desire realm?
Answer: Because the desire realm is not a realm of meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
It is not a stage of cultivation;
it is not a stage of freedom from defilement;
it lacks superior concentration and wisdom.
Because restlessness is understood to be a matter of agitation, it is not established as a fetter (*saṃyojana*).
The realms of form and formlessness are the realm of meditative concentration;
they are the stages of cultivation.
This is a stage free from defilement,
possessing superior concentration and wisdom;
because it can perceive restlessness as a source of disturbance, it is established as a fetter.
Just as in a village or town, even a loud sound does not cause distress,
whereas in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*), even a small sound is considered a disturbance.
Furthermore, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are many unrighteous afflictions (*kleśa*).
Just as anger, resentment, and so forth obscure and obstruct restlessness (*auddhatya*) such that it is not clear, they are not established as fetters (*saṃyojana*).
In the realms of form and formlessness, there are not many such unwholesome afflictions (*kleśa*) that obscure and obstruct restlessness.
Because they are clearly manifest, they are established as fetters (*saṃyojana*).
It is like this: although there may be many bhikṣus of evil conduct in a nearby village, they go unnoticed;
whereas although there may be few bhikṣus of evil conduct in a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*), they are easily noticed.
Question: Dullness (styāna) and restlessness (auddhatya) both pertain to all three realms,
both pervade the six consciousnesses,
and both pertain to all five categories.
It is associated with all defiled minds.
For what reason is restlessness established as a factor conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*), and not lethargy?
The answer is: because that restlessness (auddhatya) is an excessively fierce, heavy, and excessive fault, the Buddha established it as an upper-tier fetter (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana).
It is also for this reason that it is established among the ten universal mental factors of affliction (kleśamahābhūmika-dharma).
Furthermore, for this reason, the *Prakaraṇapāda* recited in foreign lands states: "What are the fettering dharmas?
They are the nine fetters (*nava-saṃyojana*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) among the fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).

Moreover, for this reason, it has already been stated in the *Saṃyuktāgama*: "What is the non-common latent tendency of ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā-anuśaya*)? What is the non-common entanglement of restlessness (*asādhāraṇa-auddhatya-paryavasthāna*)?"
Furthermore, for this reason, the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states that when the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) arises in an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), five factors arise:
first, the latent tendency of sensual desire;
second, the latent tendency of sensual desire... [and so forth].
In accordance with birth, there is the increase of the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*);
[and] the three latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*),
[which constitute] the four latent tendencies of ignorance.
In accordance with their arising, they are recited as the increase of the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*).
The five types of restlessness (*auddhatya*) and lethargy (*styāna*) are not so; therefore, they are not established as fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*).

Furthermore, because the manifestation of the fetter of restlessness (*auddhatya-paryavasthāna*) is sharp and its activity swift, it disturbs the five factors and four factors of concentration and wisdom;

therefore, the Buddha established it as an upper-tier fetter (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*). As for lethargy (*styāna*), because its manifestation is obscure and its activity sluggish, it resembles concentration and can accord with it; moreover, since one who possesses lethargy can quickly induce concentration, it was not established as an upper-tier fetter.
Furthermore, since lethargy (styāna) is an outflow of ignorance (avidyā),
and ignorance is itself a fetter conducive to the higher realms (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana),
it obscures and covers lethargy, preventing clarity.
Therefore, *styāna* (sloth-torpor) is not an upper-tier fetter (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
Question: Since the higher realms also possess the three—*śāṭhya* (dissimulation), *māyā* (deceit), and *mada* (pride)—why are they not established as upper-tier fetters?
Answer: Because the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are coarse and mobile, they are easily stilled; their function as fetters (*bandhana*) is inferior.
Therefore, they are not established among the "collections of bonds" (*saṃyojana-rāśi*).
It is for this reason that the Venerable Pārśva said:
The Buddha knows the nature, characteristics, and functional power of all phenomena;
if something is capable of being established as a fetter (*saṃyojana*), he establishes it as a fetter, and if it is not so, he does not establish it as one.
Therefore, one should not hold him accountable for this.
The Venerable Ghosaka also stated this: "Deceit, guile, and arrogance are coarse and volatile, and are easily stilled;
because they do not accord with the meaning of 'fetter' (*saṃyojana*), they are not established as fetters.
Among all the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), only a small portion may be established as fetters."
There are five views:

namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these five views?

The answer is that their intrinsic nature consists of thirty-six factors: namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), each being abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms, thus constituting six factors;

false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), each being abandoned through the vision of four categories (*catur-nikāya*) within the three realms, thus constituting twenty-four factors; and the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), being abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms, thus constituting six factors.
These five views have thirty-six factors as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Having already explained their intrinsic nature, we shall now explain the reason [for their designation].
Question: For what reason are they called "views" (*dṛṣṭi*)?
What is the meaning of "view" (*dṛṣṭi*)? It is answered that it is called a view for four reasons:
first, because it is a thorough seeing;
second, because it is an inferential deliberation.
Third, because of firm adherence;
fourth, because of penetratingly entering the object of focus.
Regarding "seeing through": [it refers to]...
It is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) because it is capable of seeing through [its object].
Question: Since this view is both false and inverted, why is it called "seeing"?
Answer: Although it is false and inverted, its nature is wisdom (*prajñā*), and because it is capable of seeing its focal object (*ālambana*), it is also called "seeing."
Just as when a person perceives an object, whether it be clear or dim, both are termed "seeing.
Regarding "because of deliberation," this means that because one is able to deliberate, it is called "seeing."
Question: How can one perform such investigation within a single kṣaṇa?
Answer: Because their nature is sharp and acute, they are also capable of performing such investigation;
this is because they are firmly attached.
It is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) because it is able to grasp firmly.
This view is a perverse and stubborn attachment to its object that cannot be relinquished except by the blade of noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*).
It is only when the Buddhas and their disciples take up the blade of noble wisdom and sever the sprout of that view that it can finally be abandoned.
It is like a sea creature named Śiśumāra;
whatever it bites cannot be severed by a blade.
This is because when it bites grass, trees, or the like, it will only let go once it has cut through their sprouts.
As a verse says:
"Whatever object is carried by a fool and held in the mouth of a fish is bitten by Śiśumāra;
it cannot be released except by a sword."
Regarding "because of penetrating deeply into the object of focus":
this means that because its nature is sharp and intense, it penetrates deeply into the object of focus, like a needle falling into mud; therefore, it is called "viewing."
Furthermore, it is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) for two reasons:
first, because of observing;
second, because of determining.
Furthermore, it is called "view" for three reasons:
first, because it possesses the characteristic of viewing;
second, because it accomplishes what is to be done.
Third, because it is unimpeded regarding its object.
Furthermore, it is called "vision" (*darśana*) for three reasons:
first, by way of intention (*āśaya*).
Second, because of clinging;
third, because of investigation.
Furthermore, it is called "view" (dṛṣṭi) due to three factors.
First, due to intention;
second, due to application;
third, due to ignorance.
"By way of intention" means one whose intention is corrupted;
"by way of application" means...
That is to say: those whose preparatory application has failed;
those who fail due to ignorance;
and those who fail in both respects.
Furthermore, "due to intention" refers to one who practices concentration erroneously;
"due to application" refers to [the same].
This refers to those who engage in improper seeking;
"due to ignorance" refers to those who have heard the Dharma incorrectly.
The general meaning of the various views has already been explained.
Their individual specific meanings shall now be explained.
Question: Why is it called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: This view arises with respect to the body of existence (satkāya), and is therefore called the view of a body of existence (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Question: Other views also arise with respect to the body of existence;
should they not also be called the view of a body of existence?
Answer: This view operates with respect to one's own body and not another's body;
it operates toward that which possesses a body and not toward that which lacks a body. Therefore, it is called the "view of a self-identity" (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Other views may operate with respect to one's own body or with respect to another's body.
Because it operates with respect to the existence of a body,
or because it operates with respect to the non-existence of a body, it is not called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
As for its operation with respect to one's own body:

That which takes its own realm and level as its object refers to [cognition] functioning with respect to one's own body; that which takes another realm and level as its object refers to [cognition] functioning with respect to the bodies of others.
"Operating with respect to the body" means having outflows as its object or conditioned phenomena as its object;
"operating without respect to the body" means...
That is to say, it takes uncontaminated objects as its condition, or it takes unconditioned phenomena as its condition.
Question: The view of extremes also operates with respect to one's own body and not another's body;
it operates with respect to that which possesses a body and not that which lacks a body.
That [view] should be called the "view of a self-identity" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); although the meaning of both names is present, the former name is established first,
while the latter name is subsequently applied according to other meanings—
namely, because it specifically clings to the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
According to this meaning, it is called the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, because this view operates upon the basis of personal existence (*satkāya*) by grasping at "I" and "mine," it is called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Although other views also operate upon the basis of personal existence, [only this one receives that name].
Because one does not grasp at a self or what belongs to a self,
it is not called the view of a personal body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, this view operates upon the personal body by functioning with the aspect of grasping at a self and what belongs to a self.
It is called the view of a personal body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Although other views also operate with respect to the personal body, they are not called the view of a personal body because they do not function with the mode of apprehension that conceives of "I" and "mine."
Furthermore, this view operates with respect to the body of existence (*satkāya*) by conceiving of it as "I" and "mine," and as that which acts and that which experiences;
therefore, it is called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Although other views also operate with respect to the body of existence, they do not conceive of it as "I" and "mine," nor as that which acts and that which experiences.
It is not called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, because this view operates toward the self-identity and accords with [the practice of] giving, morality, and cultivation, it is named the view of a self-identity.
Although other views also operate toward the self-identity, [they are not so named].
Furthermore, because it does not accord with [the practice of] giving, morality, and cultivation,
it is not called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Moreover, this view operates within the context of a self-identity without contradicting the relationship between karma and its fruit.
It is called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Although other views also operate with respect to the self-identity,
they are not called the view of a self-identity because they contradict [the principles of] karma and its fruit.
The Venerable Vasumitra stated as follows:
This view arises only with respect to one's own body; therefore, it is called the "view of a self-identity" (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
That which is called "one's own body" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (pañcopādānaskandhāḥ).
Question: For what reason are the aggregates of clinging called "one's own body"?
Answer: Because they are produced by the power of their own causes and conditions, and because they are the fruits obtained through one's own karma and afflictions.
The questions and answers regarding the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are as before.
Question: Why is it called the view of extremes?
Answer: Because this view clings to two extremes, it is called the view of extremes.
This means that it functions by turning away from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
As stated in a sūtra:
"Kātyāyana, if one knows and sees the arising of the world as it truly is with right wisdom..."
To not grasp at the world and instead regard it as non-existent is nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
That is to say, when one perceives the arising of a future body, one forms this thought: [the self does not exist].
In this way, sentient beings die here and are born there; it is certainly not a matter of annihilation.
If one knows and sees the cessation of the world as it truly is with right wisdom, one does not grasp at what exists as being existent.
This is the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).
That is to say, if one perceives the various aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) as distinct continuities, one forms the thought:

"In this way, sentient beings undergo birth and cessation; they are certainly not eternal. Furthermore, because this view clings to an extreme and base position, it is called the view of clinging to extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
It is said that even those non-Buddhists who cling to the existence of a real self are already considered foolish and vulgar;
how much more so those who cling to the self as being either annihilated or eternal—who could fail to regard them as utterly base?
Furthermore, because this view clings to the most extreme limits, it is called the "view of clinging to extremes" (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).

This means that while the various non-Buddhists already stand far removed from the principle of selflessness because they cling to a real self, how much more so is this the case for those who cling to the self as being either annihilated or eternal? They are not merely distant; they are utterly remote.
Furthermore, this is called the "view of extremes" because it functions by way of grasping at two extremes; that is,
it functions by way of grasping at the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism,
as stated in the Sūtra.
"O bhikṣus, you should know this:
I do not dispute with the world;
rather, it is the world that disputes with me."
Question: What is the meaning of what is taught in this sutra?
Venerable Vasumitra replied:
Because the Blessed One has definitively taught that cause and effect exist.
This refers to when the Buddha encounters eternalist non-Buddhists who assert that all phenomena have effects but no causes;
because there are no causes,
they claim that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is eternally present.
The World-Honored One said:
"As for what you say exists as a fruit, I also say it exists.
As for what you say is without cause, that is the doctrine of the ignorant."
“World-Honored One, if one encounters an outsider who holds the view of annihilationism, they claim that all phenomena have causes but no results;
because there are no results, everything will be annihilated in the future.
The World-Honored One replied:
Regarding your statement that causes exist, I also say they exist.
Your statement that there is no fruit is a doctrine of ignorance.
The Buddha, in regard to these two doctrines, grants a portion to each while avoiding the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, thereby teaching the Middle Way.
Therefore, I say this:
"I do not dispute with the world;
rather, it is the world that disputes with me."
Furthermore, the Blessed One is a proponent of the Dharma,
whereas the various non-Buddhists are proponents of what is not the Dharma.
It is the nature of things that those who propound the Dharma are free from dispute.
Those who propound what is contrary to the Dharma naturally possess contention.
Furthermore, while the Buddha accords with the world in terms of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), they do not accord with the Buddha in terms of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Moreover, because the Blessed One has thoroughly severed the two roots of contention.
Regarding the two roots of dispute:
these are craving and views.
Because the Buddha has eternally severed them, he is said to be without dispute.
Because it has not been severed in the world, it is said to be "with contention.
The Venerable One says:
"The Blessed One is one who speaks according to reality (*yukti-vādin*)."
The various non-Buddhist practitioners are not proponents of reasoned argument.
It is the nature of those who follow reasoned argument to be free from contention;
it is the nature of those who do not follow reasoned argument to be contentious, just as a horse crossing a precipice has its steps rise and fall.
If one travels on level ground, there is no deviation or error.
Furthermore, because the Buddha perceives the meaning, perceives the Dharma, perceives the good, and perceives harmony and gentleness, he is said to be "without strife.
The world is not so; therefore, it is said to be "with strife."
Question: Why is it called "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: Because it is a false inference (*mithyā-vitarka*), it is called wrong view.
Question: If that is so, all five views are false inferences.
Why is this alone designated as "wrong view"?
Answer: Because this name is established based on its specific mode of activity (*paryāya*).
As for its specific mode of activity:
This refers to the absence of objective characteristics (*nimitta*). If names were not established based upon this,
then all five types [of views] would have to be called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Because all five views involve erroneous conceptualization (*vitarka*), yet among them, none has a mode of activity (*ākāra*) with more grave defects than this;

therefore, it is based solely on this that the name "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is established. Furthermore, if an erroneous conceptualization also results in the destruction of reality, it is designated as "false view."
Although the remaining four views involve erroneous speculation, they do not subvert the actual facts; therefore, they are established as distinct categories.
Furthermore, if one speculates erroneously by slandering cause and effect, that is termed "wrong view" (mithyādṛṣṭi).
Although the remaining four views involve false conceptualization, they are given distinct names because they do not deny cause and effect.
Furthermore, if false conceptualization is diametrically opposed to the practice of giving, morality, and cultivation, it is termed "wrong view."
Other views are not like this, and therefore they are established separately by name.
Furthermore, if one engages in false speculation and also slanders the past, future, and present perfect enlightenment, as well as the Three Jewels, this is called wrong view.
Other views are not like this, and therefore they are established separately by name.

Furthermore, if one falsely speculates and destroys the two kinds of grace, it is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); other views are not like this, and therefore they are established separately by name.
As for the "two kinds of grace": [they are] the grace of parents and the grace of the Buddha and Dharma.
This refers to the debt of gratitude toward the Dharma and the debt of gratitude toward one's parents. To destroy the debt of gratitude toward the Dharma means to fail to practice giving.
There is no love or delight;
there is no sacrifice, no sublime conduct,
and no evil conduct.
There is no result or maturation of wholesome or unwholesome karmic actions;
there is no this world,
and there is no other world.
One who destroys the debt of gratitude for birth refers to one who has neither father nor mother,
and [denies] the existence of sentient beings born by transformation in the world of sentient beings.
"There is no true arhat who has attained rightness and practices rightly," and so forth,
as extensively explained.
Furthermore, if one gives rise to the two types of enmity through false deliberation, this is called wrong view.
Because other views are not like this, they are established separately by name.
Regarding the arising of two types of enmity:
first, the arising of enmity toward the Dharma.
Second is the arising of enmity.
Regarding the arising of enmity toward the Dharma,
it refers to saying that there is no giving, and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding "giving rise to enmity":
this refers to saying that there are no parents, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, if one engages in false conceptualization that subverts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The other views are not like this, and therefore they are established separately by name;
it is like a person who has fallen into a pit of blazing fire,
yet deceives the world by saying, "I am experiencing pleasure."
Sentient beings with wrong views are likewise in this regard.
Dwelling amidst the various aggregates, elements, and bases of suffering, their minds are entangled by wrong views as they say, "I have no suffering.
Those who speak thus—
This is termed the subversion of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, if one engages in false conceptualization, it is called "violence" and is designated as "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
As stated in the Sūtra: "O Bhikṣus, you should know this."
Whatever bodily actions, verbal actions, intentions, pursuits, vows, and practices belong to those with wrong views,
as well as everything of that same category, are all capable of bringing about results that are undesirable, unpleasant, disagreeable, and contrary to one's will.
Why is this so? Because that wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is a violent and evil view;
whereas the remaining four views, though they involve erroneous deliberation, are not violent or evil, and thus are given distinct names.
Question: Why is it called "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)?
Answer: Because this clinging seizes upon various views, it is called clinging to views.
Question: Does this also pertain to the grasping of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*)?
Why is it called only "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)?
Answer: Because this [clinging] takes all views as its object by way of grasping the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), it is called only "clinging to views.
Furthermore, by what characteristic is the name "clinging to views" established?
That is to say, if one grasps at views or grasps at other aggregates and clings to them as supreme, it is termed "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, this should properly be called "clinging to views and so forth" (*dṛṣṭyādiparāmarśa*);
however, by omitting the word "and so forth," it is simply called "clinging to views."
Furthermore, because this [view] grasps excessively, it is called "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Question: Why is it called "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?
Answer: Because this clinging grasps various precepts and observances, it is called "clinging to precepts and observances."
Question: Since this [grasping] takes all five aggregates of clinging as its object, why is it called only "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?
Answer: Because this [grasping] takes the five aggregates as its object specifically by means of precepts and observances.
It is simply called the "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, it is called the "clinging to precepts and observances" by virtue of its mode of activity (*ākāra*);

that is to say, clinging to precepts and observances, or clinging to other aggregates (*skandha*) while grasping them as being capable of purification, is called the clinging to precepts and observances.
Furthermore, this view should properly be called "clinging to precepts and observances, etc.";
however, because the word "etc. has been omitted, it is simply termed "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, because this involves grasping at many rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it is called "clinging to rules and observances.
Question: Why are both [of these] views collectively termed "clinging" (*parāmarśa*)?
Answer: Because these two views function through the mode of grasping (*parāmarśa*), they are both termed "grasping" (*upādāna*).
That is to say, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) clings to "self" and "what belongs to the self"; the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) clings to annihilation or permanence;
and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) clings to non-existence.
Because one grasps these various views as being supreme, they are called "clinging to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
Because one grasps various precepts and observances as being able to bring about purification, they are called "clinging to precepts and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
Furthermore, because the three preceding views involve the estimation of their objects with intense and sharp mental force, they are termed "views."
The latter two views are called "grasping" (*upādāna*) because they possess a sharp and intense force as the subjective grasper.
There are six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*), namely:
the group of craving born of eye-contact, and so forth.
The group of cravings born from contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—
such a group of cravings should be described as a single type,
just as among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), all cravings belonging to the three realms are collectively established as the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*).
Alternatively, one should speak of two:
just as among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), craving belonging to the desire realm is established as the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānuśaya*),
while craving belonging to the form and formless realms is established as the underlying tendency of existence-lust (*bhavarāgānuśaya*).
Alternatively, one should speak of three,
as stated in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know."
The three rivers of craving refer to the craving of the three realms;
alternatively, one should speak of four.
As stated in the Sūtra:

there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others who, on account of robes, food and drink, and bedding, give rise to craving for existence and non-existence; when it arises, they arise with it; when it abides, they abide with it; and when they are attached to it, they remain attached.
Alternatively, one should say there are five:
namely, craving to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as that to be abandoned through cultivation.
Or, one should say there are nine.
This refers to craving ranging from the highest-of-the-high grade down to the lowest-of-the-low grade;
alternatively, it should be stated as eighteen,
corresponding to the eighteen modes of craving.
Alternatively, one should speak of thirty-six,
as in the case of the thirty-six modes of craving;
or one should speak of one hundred and eight.
Just as there are one hundred and eight modes of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), if one were to analyze those present within the body moment by moment, there would be immeasurable cravings.
[The interlocutor] asks the World-Honored One: "For what reason do you extensively explain only one craving and so forth?"
Why are the immeasurable types of craving summarized and taught as the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*)?
Answer: This is based on their respective supports (*āśraya*).
That is to say, from a single instance of craving up to immeasurable instances of craving.

There is nothing that does not arise based on the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), the six gates, the six steps, the six stairways, the six tracks, the six paths, and the six groups, because they are associated with the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*); therefore, only six are taught.

Question: Hatred (*dveṣa*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) also rely on the six faculties and, as extensively explained, are associated with the six consciousnesses up to the sixth. Why are they not mentioned?
“World-Honored One, for what reason do you speak of the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*) but not of the six groups of aversion or the six groups of ignorance?
[The Buddha replied: “When something should be stated but is not stated, one should know that this meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).”

Furthermore, since it has already been stated that craving constitutes a "body" (*kāya*), one should know that this also applies to the bodies of hatred and ignorance, as they likewise serve as the bases for [the aforementioned functions].
Furthermore, craving is called a "body" because it pervades all three realms, functions independently, and operates throughout the six consciousnesses.
Although hatred (*dveṣa*) also occurs independently and pervades all six consciousnesses, it does not extend throughout the three realms;

and although ignorance (*avidyā*) does extend throughout the three realms, it does not occur independently and pervade all six consciousnesses. Therefore, they are not designated as "bodily" [afflictions].
Furthermore, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) pervades the three realms, functions independently, and operates throughout the six consciousnesses;
because it manifests in both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*), it is designated as "the body" (*kāya*).
Although hatred (*vyāpāda*) also functions independently and operates throughout the six consciousnesses, [it is not so designated].
Both ordinary beings and noble ones may manifest [these],
yet they do not pertain to all three realms;
although ignorance also pertains to all three realms.
Because it manifests in both ordinary beings and noble ones, and because it does not function alone but pervades all six consciousnesses, it is not designated as the "body.
Furthermore, craving is established as the "body" because it can differentiate between various realms, stages, and categories, and because it is capable of generating all afflictions.
Because hatred and ignorance lack such characteristics, they are not called "bodies.
Question: For what reason is it called a "body" (kāya)?
Answer: Because it is a great accumulation of craving, it is called a body.
That is to say, a single moment of craving produced by eye-contact is not called a "body of craving produced by eye-contact";

rather, it is many moments of craving produced by eye-contact that constitute a "body of craving produced by eye-contact," and this applies likewise up to the "body of craving produced by mind-contact."
Just as a single elephant is not called an "elephant army," but only when many elephants are assembled is it called an "elephant army," so too should one understand the cavalry and the infantry.

Therefore, it is because craving is manifold that it alone is called "craving for the body" (*kāyatṛṣṇā*). Question: Since views such as the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) are also manifold accumulations, they too should be called "body.
Why is it that only craving is so designated?
Answer: Views such as the view of a self should indeed also be called "body."
That it is not so stated constitutes an incomplete teaching (*śeṣavāda*).

Furthermore, because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the other [afflictions] exist only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-bhūmi*) and not in the five sensory consciousnesses, they are not called "bodies" (*kāya*).

Question: Since lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*) also pertain to all six consciousnesses, why are they not called "bodies"?
The answer is that it should also be called "body" (*kāya*), yet it is not so stated;
one should know that this is an incomplete explanation.
Furthermore, what was previously described as pervading the three realms, functioning independently, and extending throughout the six consciousnesses is designated as "body."

Although lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) pertain to all three realms, they are not called "groups" (*kāya*) because they do not function independently across all six consciousnesses.
Furthermore, shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are not called "groups" because both of their defining characteristics are deficient.
Furthermore, because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) possess subtle yet powerful and intensified activity, they may be called "bodies" (*kāya*);
whereas the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and impurities (*mala*) are coarse and agitated, and their activity is weak and inferior, they are not so called.
Furthermore, as previously stated, because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is able to differentiate the various realms (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), and categories (*nikāya*), it is designated as a "body."
Even the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and others do not possess such a meaning [of "body"] as to be called a "body";
how much less so the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and impurities (*mala*). *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 49.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 55.
Composed by the Five Hundred Great Arhats and others;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
In the first section on the Unwholesome (*akuśala-nikāya*) within the second aggregate of fetters (*saṃyojana-skandha*), there are seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

They are: the underlying tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of ill will (*pratigha-anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of existence (*bhavarāga-anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*), and the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).
Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these seven latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)?
Answer: They have ninety-eight entities as their intrinsic nature.

That is to say, the latent dispositions of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and aversion (*pratigha*) each consist of ten entities, being the five categories (*pañca-varga*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*) consists of ten items, comprising five categories each in the realms of form and formlessness.
The latent tendencies of pride (*māna*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) each consist of thirty items, comprising five categories each across the three realms.
The latent tendencies of view consist of twelve types in each of the three realms, totaling thirty-six items.
The latent tendency of doubt consists of four types in each of the three realms, totaling twelve items.
Thus, these seven latent tendencies have ninety-eight items as their intrinsic nature.
The intrinsic nature has already been explained; now its meaning shall be discussed.
Question: Why is it called *anuśaya*?
What is the meaning of *anuśaya*? Answer: The meanings of subtlety (*sūkṣmatā*), increase (*anuśayana*), and binding (*bandhana*) constitute the meaning of *anuśaya*.
Regarding the statement that "the meaning of 'subtle' is the meaning of 'latent tendency' (*anuśaya*"):
the seven modes of activity, such as sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), are subtle,
just as seven atoms (*paramāṇu*) combine to form a single minute material form.
Regarding the meaning of "proliferating" (*anuśaya*) as the meaning of "latent tendency":
the seven [types of latent tendencies], such as sensual desire and so forth, proliferate universally throughout all subtle outflows (*sāsrava*),
even down to a single infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*).
Alternatively, because all seven, such as sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), increase concomitantly within a single moment,
the meaning of "concomitant bondage" (*anuśayana*) is the meaning of "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*).
This is like the way a shadow follows one who moves through the air or water.
Those that travel through the air are birds;
those that travel through the water are fish.
A bird, by the power of its wings, desires to cross the great ocean.
In the water there are fish that skillfully observe its signs and form this thought:
"No flying bird is able to cross the great ocean,
except for the courageous and swift King of Birds, Suparṇa."
The bird immediately pursued its shadow; exhausted, it fell into the water and was swallowed by a fish.
In this way, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) constantly manifest throughout all states, giving rise to improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
If, at the time of manifestation, it immediately experiences a result of outflow or a result of maturation; furthermore, if the meaning of "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) is the sense of being subtle;
or if the meaning of "latent tendency" is the sense of increasing in accordance with its own nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the statement that "the meaning of 'proclivity' (anuśaya) is defined according to its function as 'binding'":
this is said with reference to that [function].
Furthermore, if the meaning of "latent tendency" (anuśaya) is "subtlety," it is stated in terms of its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
If the meaning of "latent tendency" is "increasingly adhering" (anuśayana), [it is stated in terms of its activity].
Regarding the statement that the meaning of "proclivity" (*anuśaya*) is "binding according to the continuity," this is said in reference to the firmness of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, if the meaning of "proclivity" (*anuśaya*) is "subtlety," this is said with reference to past proclivities.
If the meaning of "proclivity" is "increasingly adhering" (*anuśayana*), [this refers to present proclivities].
When it is said that the meaning of "proclivity" (anuśaya) is "binding" (anubandha), this refers to proclivities in the present.
When it is said that the meaning of "proclivity" is "binding," this refers to proclivities in the future.
Furthermore, if the meaning of "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) is the sense of being subtle,
it is explained in terms of its mode of activity (*ākāra*).
If the meaning of "latent tendency" is the sense of increasing (*anuśayana*), [it is explained in terms of its object].
If the meaning of "proclivity" (*anuśaya*) is explained according to the sense of being bound by way of the object (*ālambana-bandhana*),
it refers to the binding by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
Furthermore, if the meaning of "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) is the sense of being subtle and increasing,
this is stated with reference to associated latent tendencies (*saṃprayukta-anuśaya*).
If the meaning of "latent tendency" is the sense of binding, [this refers to the dissociated latent tendencies].
This is stated with reference to the dissociated latent dispositions (*asamprayukta-anuśaya*).
Question: Since all latent dispositions are associated (*samprayukta*) with the mind and its concomitants, how can it be said that they are explained with reference to what is dissociated?

The answer is: here, the name "proclivity" (anuśaya) is established with respect to acquisition (prāpti); because it is an acquisition that follows along [with the defilement], it is called a "proclivity.
This is the explanation given by the masters of the Western Regions (Bahirdeśaka).
It is called "latent tendency" (anuśaya) by virtue of four meanings:
namely, the meaning of subtlety, the meaning of following along, the meaning of increasing, and the meaning of binding;
these constitute the meaning of "latent tendency."
The meaning of "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) is the meaning of "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*);
that is to say, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and their modes of activity (*ākāra*), such as sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and so forth, are both extremely subtle.
The meaning of "following along" (*anu-pra-veśa*) is the meaning of "latent tendency."
This means that desire-attachment and the like enter into the continuum of existence without being anywhere incomplete,
just as oil is pervasive within sesame seeds and grease is pervasive within a ball of dough. Thus,
the meaning of "pervasive increase" (anuśaya) is the meaning of "latent tendency" (anuśaya).
This means that desire, greed, and so forth increase progressively within the continuum [of a person],
like a nurse to an infant.
The meaning of "binding" (anu-bandha) is the meaning of "proclivity" (anuśaya).
Just as a bird in the sky is followed by its shadow, so too,
furthermore, when the meaning of "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) is understood in the sense of being "subtle," it is explained in terms of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If the meaning of "conforming entry" (anupraveśa) is the meaning of "latent tendency" (anuśaya),
it is explained in terms of association (samprayoga).
If the meaning of "increasing along with" (anuśayana) is the meaning of "latent tendency," [it is explained in terms of object].
Regarding the explanation based on their modes of activity (*ākāra*):
if the meaning of "proclivity" (*anuśaya*) is the sense of "binding according to [its object]," then one should understand all proclivities by means of three factors.
First, by way of intrinsic nature;
second, by way of result;
third, by way of the person (pudgala).
Regarding their intrinsic natures:
the latent tendency of sensual desire is like food mixed with *kunkuma*; the latent tendency of aversion is like pungent and spicy food;
the latent tendency of craving for existence is like the clothing of a wet-nurse.
The latent tendency of pride is like an arrogant person;
the latent tendency of ignorance is like one who is blind;
the latent tendency of views is like one who has lost their way.
The latent tendency of doubt is like being at a crossroads.
As for "because of the fruit":
it refers to the latent tendency of sensual desire when it has been practiced, cultivated, or frequently performed.
If one habituates, cultivates, or frequently practices the latent tendency of hatred (*dveṣānuśaya*), one will be reborn among pigeons, sparrows, mandarin ducks, and the like;
if one habituates, cultivates, or frequently practices [hatred], one will be reborn among bees, scorpions, venomous snakes, and the like.
If the latent tendency of sensual desire is practiced, cultivated, or frequently performed, one will be reborn in the realm of form or the formless realm.
If the latent tendency of conceit is practiced, cultivated, or frequently performed, one will be reborn into a lowly or base lineage.
If the latent tendency of ignorance is practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed, one will be born into a lineage of the ignorant and blind.
If the latent tendency of views is practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed, one will be born into a lineage of non-Buddhists.
If the latent tendency of doubt is practiced, cultivated, or frequently performed, one will be born into a lowly or outcaste lineage.
Regarding this in terms of the *pudgala* (person):
the latent tendency of sensual desire is exemplified by Nanda and others.
The latent tendency of hatred (*pratighānuśaya*) is like Āṭavika, Aṅgulimāla, and others;
the latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*) is like Aśvajit, Arjuna, Udraka, and others;
the latent tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*) is like Mānastabdha and others.
The latent tendency of ignorance is like Ulūka, Piṅgala, Kāśyapa, and others;
the latent tendency of views is like Sunakṣatra and others;
the latent tendency of doubt is like Mālukyaputra and others.
Question: Why are envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) not established as latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)?
Answer: Because those two lack the characteristics of a latent disposition.
Furthermore, latent dispositions are subtle, whereas those two are coarse and agitated.
Furthermore, while the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are subtle, those two are particularly heavy;
furthermore, while the latent dispositions are sharp and intense, those two are frequently active;
furthermore, while the latent dispositions are the root afflictions, those two are the outflows of the afflictions.
That is to say, envy is an outflow of hatred (*dveṣa*), while stinginess is an outflow of sensual greed (*kāmarāga*).

Furthermore, the latencies (*anuśaya*) and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are so firm that they are like the heat remaining in the ground long after a mountain of wood has been burned; although the fire has long since been extinguished, the ground remains hot.
Those two types of habitual tendencies are not firm;
they are like the ground where grass and birch bark have been burned:
as soon as the fire is extinguished, the ground becomes cool again.
Furthermore, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are difficult to subdue,
whereas those two are easy to subdue;
therefore, those two are not established as latent dispositions.
The remaining fetters (*paryavasthāna*) and stains (*mala*) should be explained by analogy with these two.
There are nine fetters (*saṃyojana*):

namely, the fetter of attachment (*anunaya*), the fetter of aversion (*pratigha*), the fetter of pride (*māna*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā*), the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi*), the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa*), the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*), the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*), and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya*).
Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these nine fetters (*saṃyojana*)?
Answer: They have one hundred things as their intrinsic nature;
namely, the fetters of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Each of the three realms has five categories, making forty-five matters in total.
The fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) belongs only to the five categories of the desire realm, making five matters.
The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) comprises eighteen matters.

That is to say, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), each being abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms, constitute six items.
False views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), being fourfold in each of the three realms, constitute twelve items.
The fetter of views regarding what is held as supreme (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) consists of eighteen matters.
Specifically, the view of holding [inferior things] as supreme comprises twelve matters, being four categories for each of the three realms.
The view of holding [wrong] precepts and observances as supreme comprises six matters, being those abandoned through the vision of suffering and the path within each of the three realms.
The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) consists of twelve matters, being four categories for each of the three realms.
The fetters of envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) each consist of two matters, being abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Thus, these nine fetters have one hundred matters as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The reason for their intrinsic nature has already been explained; now it shall be explained.
Question: For what reason are they called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*)?
What is the meaning of "fetter"?
Answer: The meaning of binding (*bandhana*), the meaning of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and the meaning of being mixed with poison (*viṣasaṃsṛṣṭa*) constitute the meaning of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The detailed explanations for the remaining [fetters] have already been explained in the section on the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*).
Now, the general meaning of all fetters and their individual intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) shall be explained in detail.
What is the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*)?
It refers to greed within the three realms.
However, greed within the three realms is established collectively as the fetter of craving among the nine fetters.
Among the seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya), two are established:
namely, greed belonging to the desire realm is called the underlying tendency of sensual greed (kāmarāgānuśaya),
and greed belonging to the form and formless realms is called the underlying tendency of existence-greed (bhavarāgānuśaya).
In other sūtras, three types of craving are established:
namely, craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmatṛṣṇā*), craving for form (*rūpatṛṣṇā*), and craving for the formless (*ārūpyatṛṣṇā*).
Question: What is the distinction between these three?
Answer: The faculties transformed by the World-Honored One are of three grades.
For those of sharp faculties, he taught the single fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*);
for those of middling faculties, he taught the two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
For those of dull faculties, he teaches craving for the three realms.
Furthermore, there are three types of cultivation for those transformed by the Blessed One;
for beginners, he teaches the single fetter of craving.
For those who have already matured their practice, he teaches the two types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
for those who have transcended mental attention (*manasikāra*), he teaches craving for the three realms.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of delight among those to be converted by the Blessed One.
For those who prefer brevity, one fetter of craving is taught;
for those who prefer detail, craving of the three realms is taught;
and for those who prefer both brevity and detail, two underlying tendencies are taught.
Furthermore, the meaning of "conjoining suffering" is the meaning of "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).
Because craving belonging to the three realms conjoins sentient beings with suffering rather than with happiness, a single "fetter of craving" (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) is established.
The meaning of "increasing in accordance" is the meaning of "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*).
Because greed for the desire realm increases through external objects,
while greed for the form and formless realms increases through internal objects, two types of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are established.
The meaning of "staining the object" is the meaning of "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).
Because there are distinctions among the objects of attachment— namely, those of the desire, form, and formless realms—
the craving for these three realms is established.
What is the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
That is to say, it is the desire to cause harm toward sentient beings.
Question: If one also desires to cause harm toward non-sentient things, that too should be anger (*vyāpāda*).
Why is this not mentioned?
Answer: This is stated according to what is predominant.
That is to say, this fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) mostly intends to cause harm toward sentient beings, and only rarely toward non-sentient things.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, it is because it is taught according to gravity;
that is to say, the offense of intending to cause harm to sentient beings is extremely grave.
It does not apply to non-sentient things;

therefore, it is not mentioned. Furthermore, because this is explained from the perspective of its fundamental nature, it means that this fetter of ill-will necessarily intends to cause harm toward sentient beings.
Only then do they arise even with respect to non-sentient things;
therefore, they are not mentioned.
Furthermore, it is because [the teaching] is spoken in reliance upon conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).
This means that even if one gives rise to the fetter of malice toward that which is insentient,
one nevertheless conceives the notion of a sentient being with respect to that object;
therefore, it is said that [the fetters] arise only toward sentient beings.
What is the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*)?
It refers to the seven types of pride:

first, pride (*māna*); second, excessive pride (*atimāna*); third, pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*); fourth, the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*); fifth, overweening pride (*adhimāna*); sixth, inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*); and seventh, false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
Pride (*māna*) is defined as the exalting of the mind by regarding oneself as superior when one is inferior,
or regarding oneself as equal when one is equal.
Excessive pride (*atimāna*) refers to considering oneself superior to those who are equal, or considering oneself equal to those who are superior, thereby causing the mind to become haughty.
Pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*) refers to considering oneself superior to those who are actually superior, thereby causing the mind to become haughty.
*Asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") refers to the inflation of the mind by regarding the five aggregates of clinging as "I" or "mine.
*Abhimāna* (overweening conceit) refers to the inflation of the mind by claiming to have attained superior qualities that one has not yet attained.
Inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*) is the exaltation of the mind that thinks oneself only slightly inferior when others are far superior.
False pride (*mithyāmāna*) is the claim of possessing virtues when one actually lacks them entirely.
These seven types of pride are collectively termed the fetter of pride (*mānasaṃyojana*).
What is the fetter of ignorance?
It is well said that it refers to the lack of knowledge regarding the three realms.
If one were to say that it is the lack of knowledge conditioned by the three realms, [that would be incorrect].
It would then follow that the untainted (anāsrava) objects of ignorance would not be included.
What is the fetter of views?
It refers to the three views: namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), and false view (mithyādṛṣṭi).
These are collectively termed the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
What is the fetter of clinging (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*)?
It refers to the two types of clinging: namely, the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*).
These are collectively termed the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
Question: Why, among the five views, are three views established as the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), while two views are established as the fetter of grasping?
Answer: It is because of the names and so forth associated with the time of union.
That is to say, the first three views share the same female name, while the latter two views share the same male name.
Because one perceives this female voice and grasps it as a male voice; furthermore,
because at the time of the conjunction with suffering, the objective basis (vastu) and so forth are equal.
This means that the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) each comprise eighteen matters.
Furthermore, it is because they are equal in their inclusion of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*);
that is, within the ninety-eight latent dispositions, the fetter of views and the fetter of grasping each comprise eighteen.
Furthermore, because the first three views involve inferential judgment (*vitarka*) but not grasping (*parigraha*),
they are established together as the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
Because the latter two views involve both inferential judgment and grasping, they are treated separately.
The fetters of grasping and attachment are established together.
Furthermore, because the first three [fetters] involve the conceptualization of objects,
the fetter of views is established as a single category.
The latter two views are established together as the fetter of grasping because they involve speculative deliberation (*tarka*).
What is the fetter of doubt?
It refers to doubt regarding the truths (*satya*).
Question: For what reason is this described as doubt regarding the truths?
Answer: It is because one wishes to enable those who are doubtful to attain certainty.
This refers, for example, to when someone sees an upright object from afar and gives rise to doubt:
"Is it a tree stump or a person? Even if it is a person, is it a man or a woman?
Or, upon seeing two paths, one gives rise to doubt.
Is this the path to be taken, or is it not?
Upon seeing the two robes and bowl, he also gives rise to hesitation, wondering whether they are his own or belong to another.
Or perhaps he suspects that these are [the objects of] the fetter of doubt; thus, he desires to bring certainty to that which is currently doubted.
This now clarifies that this doubt has as its essence merely unobscured-neutral wrong knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) of the desire realm,
and is not the true fetter of doubt.
The true fetter of doubt refers to hesitation regarding the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering and the others.
What is the fetter of envy?
It refers to the mind’s jealousy.
What is the fetter of avarice?
This refers to the mind’s stinginess and its protective guarding.
Question: For what reason are these two characteristics explained as distinct?
Answer: It is because one wishes to enable those who are doubtful to attain certainty.
This refers to how people in the world mistake envy for stinginess and stinginess for envy.
Regarding "mistaking envy for stinginess":
it is, for example, when one sees another person obtain something desirable.
To give rise to envy and jealousy is what is termed stinginess;
however, in reality, envy and jealousy are *īrṣyā* (envy), not *mātsarya* (stinginess).
To claim that stinginess is envy is [an error].
If one sees another being stingy and protective toward their wife and so forth, one might think this is envy (*īrṣyā*);
however, in reality, such stinginess and protectiveness are avarice (*mātsarya*), not envy.
To resolve such doubts and establish certainty, the distinction between the two characteristics of envy and avarice is explained.
