Regarding the meaning of "establishing the thesis first" as being "preceding," it refers to first establishing the categories of what is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The indeterminate category is established later.
As for the meaning of the prior response— that it is the meaning of "preceding"—
it was first answered by means of the category of what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
He subsequently answered with an indefinite statement:
"What is abandoned through cultivation?
It is the unwholesome root of greed that is abandoned by the various knowledges of those in training who have seen the tracks."
This is abandoned through cultivation.
That is to say, the unwholesome root of greed is found across five categories, namely:
those abandoned through the vision of suffering up to those abandoned through cultivation.
The path of seeing arises with the power to abandon the unwholesome roots of greed that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering up to the vision of the path;
however, regarding the unwholesome roots of greed to be abandoned through cultivation,
this path of seeing lacks the power to abandon them.
It remains stationary and does not progress;
only later, when the superior cultivation of the path manifests, can it be abandoned.
Among these, the unwholesome root of greed is definitively its intrinsic nature.
For one who has attained the vision of the path, it is certain that they are a person capable of abandoning [the afflictions];
for those with wisdom, it is certain that they possess the path of antidotes;
and for those who have abandoned [them], it is certain that this is the function of that path.
If the unwholesome root of greed possesses an unmixed antidote, a definitive antidote, and a unique antidote,
it is abandoned by noble ones and not by ordinary beings;
it is abandoned through the path of cultivation and not through the path of vision.
That which is abandoned by wisdom but not by patience is what is here described.
As for the rest: if it is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they abandon what is to be abandoned by cultivation;
if they are a disciple of the Blessed One (*śrāvaka*), they abandon what is to be abandoned by seeing.
What are the remaining ones?
They refer to the first four types of unwholesome roots of greed, which are abandoned through the vision of suffering up to the vision of the path;
if they are abandoned by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The abandonment by noble ones is through the path of seeing;
the abandonment by ordinary beings is through the mundane path;
the abandonment by noble ones is through the untainted path.
The abandonment by ordinary beings is through knowledge;
the abandonment by noble ones is through receptivity.
The abandonment by ordinary beings occurs through the nine grades [of the path] abandoning the nine grades [of afflictions].
The noble ones abandon [the afflictions] by abandoning one grade at a time until all nine grades are abandoned;
ordinary beings abandon them through repeated arising and ceasing.
The abandonment of the noble ones is an abandonment that does not arise again.
Ordinary beings abandon [afflictions] without observing the truths;
noble ones abandon them by observing the truths.

Question: Regarding what is stated here—that the unwholesome roots of greed abandoned by the various knowledges of those in training who have seen the path are abandoned through cultivation—how is this so?
This reveals that within the body of a noble one (ārya), there is the unwholesome root of greed to be abandoned through cultivation;
whereas others who are ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) abandon what is to be abandoned through cultivation,
and the disciples of the Blessed One (bhagavat-śrāvaka) abandon what is to be abandoned through vision.
The unwholesome root of greed to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) within the bodies of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) has already been revealed;
as for the remaining unwholesome root of greed to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) within the bodies of ordinary beings,
why is it not mentioned here?
Regarding that which was promised but not yet spoken,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, it has already been explained within what was previously stated.
Why is this? Because afflictions are established according to their categorical distinctions,
rather than being defined by the specific afflictions present within an individual's continuum.
The categories consist of five and not six.
When the Noble One’s Path of Seeing is present, they abandon what is to be abandoned by seeing;
subsequently, when the Path of Cultivation is present, they abandon what is to be abandoned by cultivation.
When the path of cultivation of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) manifests, they abandon all five categories [of afflictions] collectively.
This is because ordinary persons are unable to distinguish between the specific differences of the five categories; they can only abandon them as a whole.
By stating that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) abandon what is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
this has already accounted for them, so they are not mentioned separately.
Furthermore, by stating that those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have seen the path abandon [defilements] through various knowledges (*jñāna*), [this is likewise accounted for].
Since these have already been explained, they are not mentioned separately;
for those factors to be abandoned through cultivation within the bodies of ordinary beings are precisely those abandoned by the knowledge of the learner who has seen the path.
Just as with the unwholesome root of greed,
so too are the unwholesome roots of hatred and delusion,
and among the three outflows, the outflow of sensual desire.
Among the four floods and yokes, it is the flood and yoke of sensual desire;
among the four graspings, it is the grasping for sensual pleasure;
and among the four bodily fetters, it is the fetter of sensual desire and ill will.

Among the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), excluding restlessness-remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*); among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*);
among the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), the fetters of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and aversion (*vyāpāda*);
and among the seven latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), the latent dispositions of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and aversion (*pratigha*).
The same applies to the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) among the nine fetters,
because their intrinsic natures are identical and both pertain exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and encompass all five categories (*pañca-varga*).
Regarding the outflow of ignorance associated with the outflows (*āsrava*), when preceded by views (*dṛṣṭi-pūrvaka*), there are three propositions.
Some are abandoned by seeing, some are abandoned by cultivation, and some are abandoned by both seeing and cultivation.
Question: What is the meaning of "preceding" (*pūrvagama*)? Answer: The meaning of "preceding" is that which establishes the thesis first, or that which provides the initial response.
Regarding the statement that "establishing the thesis first" means "preceding action":
one first establishes the categories of what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*),
and subsequently establishes the categories of what is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The indeterminate category is established later.
As for the meaning of the prior response being the meaning of "preceding," it was first answered by means of the category of what is abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*).
Next, it is answered with the category of what is abandoned through cultivation;
finally, it is answered with the category of the indeterminate.
What is abandoned through seeing?

If there are outflows of the taints and the taint of ignorance, bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which are abandoned by the various patiences at the limit of clear realization for those practicing through faith or through dharma,
these are abandoned by vision.
That is to say, the outflow of the taints (āsrava) is found from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
the outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava) is found from the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

The mundane path gives rise to [the knowledge] that can sever the outflows of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness— namely, the outflow of sensual desire up to the outflow of ignorance pertaining to the sphere of nothingness—
as well as the outflow of existence and the outflow of ignorance pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This mundane path lacks the power to sever [the defilements];
thus, one remains stationary and does not progress.
Only later, when the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) manifests, is one able to sever those factors to be abandoned by seeing.
Among these, the outflows of the taints (āsrava) and the outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava) are definitively their own intrinsic nature;
those bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are definitively of that stage.
Those who practice according to faith or according to dharma are definitively the individuals capable of abandoning [the afflictions].
The various patiences at the limit of clear realization are definitively their path of antidotes.
Abandonment is definitively the function performed by that path.
Regarding the outflows of the fluxes and the outflow of ignorance, there exist unmixed antidotes, definitive antidotes, and unique antidotes;
these are abandoned by noble ones and not by ordinary beings,
and they are abandoned by the noble path and not by the mundane path.
It is said that what is abandoned by the path of seeing is not abandoned by the path of cultivation,
and what is abandoned by forbearance (*kṣānti*) is not abandoned by knowledge (*jñāna*).
What, then, is abandoned by cultivation?
If the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) are abandoned by the various knowledges of one who has entered the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*),
they are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
This means that those outflows of existence and the outflow of ignorance consist of five categories (*pañca-varga*).
When the path of seeing (darśanamārga) is present, it abandons the four preceding categories [of afflictions].

Regarding the outflows of the outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava) that are to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), this path of seeing lacks the power to abandon them; thus, it remains stationary and does not progress.
Only when the subsequent superior path of cultivation manifests can those [outflows] be abandoned.
Among these, the outflow of existence (bhava-āsrava) and the outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava) are definitively its intrinsic nature;
the learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭapada) is definitively the person (pudgala) capable of abandoning them.
The wise are certain that this is the path of antidotes capable of abandoning;
they are certain that abandonment is the function performed by that path.
Regarding the outflows of the taints and the outflow of ignorance, there are the unmixed antidote, the definitive antidote, and the unique antidote.
What is abandoned by the Noble Ones is not abandoned by ordinary beings;
what is abandoned by the path of cultivation is not abandoned by the path of seeing;
and what is abandoned by knowledge is not abandoned by receptivity—this is what is being stated here.
As for the "others": if they are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), they have abandoned what is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
if they are disciples of the Blessed One (*śrāvaka*), they have abandoned what is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*). What, then, are these "others"?
This refers to the outflows with taints (*āsrava*) from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness;
the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness;
and the five categories [of afflictions] within the bodies of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding the four categories within the continuum of a noble one (*ārya*):
if they are abandoned by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);
if abandoned by a noble one, they are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The abandonment by ordinary beings is through the mundane path;
the abandonment by noble ones is through the untainted path.
The abandonment by ordinary beings is through knowledge.
The noble ones abandon [the afflictions] by means of a single moment of patience (*kṣānti*).
Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) abandon them by means of nine grades [of abandonment]. The noble ones abandon the nine grades by means of a single grade.
Ordinary beings abandon them through repeated arising [of the antidote].
The abandonment of noble ones is an abandonment through non-arising;
the abandonment of ordinary beings is an abandonment that does not contemplate the truths,
whereas the abandonment of noble ones is an abandonment that contemplates the truths.
Just as there is the outflow of the taints (*āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*),
so among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*) there is the flood and yoke of ignorance;
and among the four clingings (*upādāna*) there is the clinging to self-theory (*ātmavādopādāna*).
Among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), there are the fetters of greed and pride;
among the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*), there is the group of craving born of mental contact;
and among the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), there are the latent dispositions of greed, pride, and ignorance.
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*),
the fetters of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) are likewise;
because their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are identical, they all pertain to both the nine and eight stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, because it penetrates the five families,
there are three types of preliminary practices (*pūrvagama*).
First, the uncommon preliminary practice.
Second is the ultimate preliminary;
third is the initial preliminary.
As for the uncommon preliminaries, they are such as the three fetters and so forth.
Those that precede ultimately are like the three unwholesome roots and so forth;
those that precede initially are like the outflows of contaminated ignorance and so forth.
If the various afflictions are bound to all three realms and are abandoned solely through the path of seeing, [they are as described above].
There are two phrases concerning that which has "view" as its precursor,
such as the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth.
If various afflictions are bound exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they pertain to all five categories (*pañca-nikāya*).
There are two phrases concerning that cultivation as a preliminary practice,
such as the three unwholesome roots and so forth.
If the various afflictions pertain to all three realms and also pertain to all five categories, [they are to be abandoned by cultivation].
There are three phrases preceded by "seeing that":
namely, the outflow of impurity (*āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), and so forth.
This is the brief *Vibhāṣā* on this point.
The hindrance of regret (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*) is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
because both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) abandon it by means of the nine grades of knowledge (*jñāna*).
This is like the hindrance of regret and the fetters of envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The five fetters binding one to the higher realms (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*);
the first five among the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ tṛṣṇākāyāḥ*);
and likewise, the fetters of envy and avarice (*īrṣyā-mātsarya-saṃyojane*) among the nine fetters (*nava saṃyojanāni*).
Since both are abandoned by the wisdom of the nine grades,
the hindrance of doubt is abandoned through cultivation by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
whereas it is abandoned through seeing by the disciples of the Blessed One (*śrāvaka*).
This refers only to the first four categories of the Desire Realm.
Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), twenty-eight are abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*);
these are the first four categories of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Ten are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
namely, the categories abandoned through cultivation within the three realms.
As for the remainder, if they are abandoned by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they are abandoned through cultivation.
The disciples of the World-Honored One abandon those [defilements] to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), namely the first four categories (*pakṣa*) of the lower eight stages (*bhūmi*).
Question: If there are twenty-eight [defilements] to be abandoned by insight...
Ten are abandoned through cultivation;
as for the remaining indeterminate ones,

why does the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* state that among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), eighty-eight are abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and ten are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Answer: This passage is of definitive meaning (nītārtha), whereas that passage is of non-definitive meaning (neyārtha).
This passage possesses no ulterior intention (abhiprāya).
That text has a distinct underlying intention;
this text lacks any such distinct cause or condition.
That text possesses a distinct cause and condition.
This passage is spoken in accordance with ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
while that passage is spoken in accordance with conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Furthermore, that treatise is explained based on those who proceed gradually, who are bound by all fetters, and who do not transcend [the stages] through leaping.
This treatise is explained based on those who do not proceed gradually, who are not bound by all fetters, and who are leapers.
Furthermore, that treatise relies solely upon noble ones who are free from defilement; it concerns the functioning of the noble path, not the conventional discourse of ordinary beings.
This treatise explains the functions of the noble path and the mundane path— both for noble ones and ordinary beings—
in a general sense. Furthermore, this treatise provides a definitive explanation,
whereas that treatise explains by way of alternative formulations.
This refers to one who, having previously abandoned the defilements from the realm of desire up to the sphere of nothingness, enters into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Within that path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), they also realize the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) regarding the factors to be abandoned by vision belonging to the eight lower stages.
Therefore, this statement was made:
eighty-eight [defilements] are abandoned through vision, and ten are abandoned through cultivation.
The Venerable Ghosaka also spoke thus.
The exposition in this treatise is based on the principle of definitive certainty.
As for the statement in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* that eighty-eight [defilements] are abandoned through vision (*darśana-prahātavya*),
this is said in reference to the attainment of untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*).
Or [this is] said with reference to those who attain the fruits through gradual stages.
Question: Why is it called "to be abandoned by seeing" (*darśana-heya*), and why is it called "to be abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
Seeing is not separate from cultivation, and cultivation is not separate from seeing.
How, then, are the two categories of what is to be abandoned established?
Answer: Although within the path of seeing there is also cultivation that accords with reality, [the distinction is made based on the predominance of each].
Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is also that which can be obtained as seeing according to reality (*yathābhūta-darśana*).
Here, "seeing" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), while "cultivation" refers to non-negligence (*apramāda*).
"According to reality" carries the sense of expansion and increase.
Alternatively, it means "intense.
In the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant and heedfulness (*apramāda*) is slight;
in the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), heedfulness is predominant and wisdom is slight.
Therefore, that which is abandoned is said to have distinctions.
Furthermore, "as it truly is" (yathābhūta) means equality,
or it means similarity.
Although there is such a measure of wisdom within the path of seeing,
there is also such a measure of heedfulness;
within the path of cultivation, there is likewise such a measure of heedfulness.
There is likewise that same amount of wisdom;
however, within the path of vision (darśanamārga), the function of wisdom is predominant,
while the function of heedfulness (apramāda) is weak.
Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because the function of non-negligence (*apramāda*) is predominant while the function of wisdom (*prajñā*) is weak,
the abandonments effected therein are designated with distinct differences.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this:
although one abandons all afflictions by contemplating the Four Truths,
it is not possible to distinguish which are abandoned through seeing and which are abandoned through cultivation.
Those [defilements] that are abandoned, cast off, and spat out by the power of vision are called "abandoned by vision" (*darśana-heya*),
as in the case of one who has already attained the Path.
If, through practice, cultivation, or frequent application,
one gradually causes [the afflictions] to become attenuated and ultimately brings them to total exhaustion,
these are termed "abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Some say that what is abandoned through seeing is also called abandoned through cultivation,
because there is also cultivation according to reality within the path of seeing.
That which is to be abandoned by cultivation is also called "to be abandoned by seeing," because within the path of cultivation there is likewise seeing according to reality.
Within this context, that which is abandoned, cast out, and rejected through the power of seeing—
It is called "to be abandoned by vision.
It is like one who has already attained the Path,
whether through practice, cultivation, or frequent application.
That which is gradually made thin and subtle through its various categories and stages until it is ultimately and completely severed is called "to be abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Question: What is the meaning of this statement?
The answer is: This explains that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is a sharp and intense path;
it can, in a single moment of its temporary presence, sever the nine grades of afflictions.
The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), however, is not a sharp or intense path.
The nine grades of afflictions are severed only after repeated cultivation over a long period of time.
This is like two knives, one sharp and one dull, cutting the same object:
the sharp one severs it instantaneously, while the dull one severs it gradually. Those that are severed by a mere glimpse are called "abandoned by seeing" (*darśana-prahātavya*).
That which is abandoned through cultivation is called "abandoned by cultivation.

Furthermore, that which is abandoned by means of the path of vision as the predominant factor is called "abandoned by vision," while that which is abandoned by means of the path of cultivation as the predominant factor is called "abandoned by cultivation."
Furthermore, if that which is abandoned by the path characterized by the two aspects of vision and wisdom is called "abandoned by vision" (darśana-heya),
and if that which is abandoned by the path characterized by the three aspects of vision, wisdom, and [subsequent] knowledge is called "abandoned by cultivation" (bhāvanā-heya).
Furthermore, if that which is abandoned by the path characterized by the four aspects of eye, clarity, awakening, and wisdom is called "abandoned through seeing" (darśana-heya),
and if that which is abandoned by the path characterized by the five aspects of eye, clarity, awakening, wisdom, and knowledge is called "abandoned through cultivation" (bhāvanā-heya).
Furthermore, that which is abandoned by the various patiences (kṣānti) is called abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya);
that which is abandoned by the various knowledges (jñāna) is called abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Furthermore, that which is abandoned by a single grade among the nine grades is called abandoned through seeing.
If the nine grades are abandoned by means of the nine grades, they are called abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, if they are abandoned by means of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), they are called abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*);
if they are abandoned by means of the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), they are called abandoned through cultivation.

Furthermore, if it is severed like splitting a stone, it is called abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*); if it is severed like snapping a lotus fiber, it is called abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, if it opposes resolute determination, it is called abandoned by insight.
If they are abandoned through further application [of practice], they are called abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, those abandoned by contemplating the truths while not yet having seen them are called abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*);
those abandoned by contemplating the truths again after already having seen them are called abandoned by cultivation.
Furthermore, that which is abandoned by means of a single path of cause is called "abandoned through vision" (*darśana-heya*).

That which is abandoned by means of two paths of cause is called "abandoned through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*). Furthermore, that which is abandoned like a strong man donning armor is called "abandoned through vision"; that which is abandoned like a weak person driving a donkey-cart is called "abandoned through cultivation."

Furthermore, when those [defilements] are abandoned while one is cultivating only the aspects of the truths as they are personally observed, they are called "abandoned by seeing" (*darśana-prahātavya*).

When those are abandoned while one is also cultivating the aspects of the truths as they are observed by others, they are called "abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). Furthermore, if they are abandoned by means of the path of approach (*prayoga-mārga*) before the fruit has been accomplished, they are called "abandoned by seeing."
If that which is abandoned by means of a path already established in its direction toward the fruit is called "abandoned through cultivation" (bhāvanā-heya),
furthermore, if that which is abandoned by means of a path of undifferentiated categories is called "abandoned through seeing" (darśana-heya).
If it is abandoned by means of a path characterized by distinct categories and limits, it is called "abandoned through cultivation.
Furthermore, if it is abandoned by means of the path of those who follow faith or the path of those who follow the Dharma, it is called "abandoned through seeing."

If that which is abandoned by means of the path of those with faith-resolve (śraddhādhimukta), those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), or those who have realized through the body (kāyasākṣin) is called "abandoned through cultivation" (bhāvanā-heya).
Furthermore, if it is abandoned by means of the path that arises suddenly at the beginning, it is called "abandoned through vision" (darśana-heya).
If they are abandoned by means of a path arising through subsequent application, they are called "abandoned by cultivation.
Furthermore, if their dissociation is included within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, they are called "abandoned by vision."
If those disconnections (visaṃyoga) are comprised within three, two, or one of the fruits of śramaṇaship, they are called abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Furthermore, if the dharmas to be abandoned have non-existent things as their objects, they are called abandoned by vision (darśana-heya).
If the dharmas to be abandoned have objective referents (*savastuka*), they are called "abandoned through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, if, once abandoned, they never regress, they are called "abandoned through vision" (*darśana-heya*).
If, once abandoned, they may either regress or not regress, they are called "abandoned through cultivation."
Furthermore, that which, once liberated, is not bound again is called abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
That which, once liberated, may be bound again or may not be bound again is called abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, that which, once disjoined from its fetters, is never again bound, is called abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
That which, once disjoined from its fetters, may either be bound again or not bound again, is called abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Furthermore, when those [defilements] are abandoned, if patience (*kṣānti*) serves as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) serves as the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), they are called "abandoned by seeing" (*darśana-prahātavya*).

When those are abandoned, if knowledge serves as the path of uninterrupted transition and knowledge serves as the path of liberation, they are called "abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Furthermore, when those [defilements] are abandoned, if wisdom serves as the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), patience (*kṣānti*) serves as the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), and wisdom serves as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they are said to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
If, when abandoning them, wisdom serves as the path of preparation...
The path of liberation immediately following [the path of preparation] is called "abandoned by cultivation.
Furthermore, if a dharma first attains non-analytical cessation and subsequently attains analytical cessation, it is called "abandoned by seeing."
If a phenomenon is first attained as non-analytical cessation and later attained as analytical cessation,
or first attained as analytical cessation and later attained as non-analytical cessation,
or both cessations are attained simultaneously, it is said to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, when those [defilements] are abandoned by cultivating a path that takes a single truth as its object, they are called "abandoned through seeing" (darśana-heya).
When those [defilements] are abandoned by cultivating a path that takes all four truths as its object, they are called "abandoned through cultivation" (bhāvanā-heya).
Furthermore, when those [afflictions] are abandoned by means of cultivating the path with four aspects, they are called "abandoned through seeing" (darśana-heya).
When they are abandoned by means of cultivating the path with sixteen aspects, they are called "abandoned through cultivation" (bhāvanā-heya).
Furthermore, if at the time of their abandonment one cultivates only a path that resembles [the affliction], they are called abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
If at the time of their abandonment one cultivates both a path that resembles and one that does not resemble [the affliction], they are called abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, if at the time of abandoning those [defilements] one cultivates two or one samādhi, they are called abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya);
if at the time of abandoning them one cultivates all three samādhis, they are called abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Furthermore, if at the time of abandoning them, no [further] abandonment arises, they are called abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
If at the time of abandoning them, either further abandonment arises or does not arise, they are called abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume Fifty-one;
