translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, who received the Imperial Decree. Section Two: The Aggregate of Fetters (*Saṃyojana-kāya*), Part One: The Sub-section on Unwholesome States (*Akuśala-nikāya*), Chapter Seven. The three fetters up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
"How many are abandoned through the vision of suffering, up to how many are abandoned through cultivation?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Although the previous section has already refuted the notion of simultaneous abandonment according to the perspective of the śramaṇas, [this treatise is composed to further clarify].
However, this has neither refuted the position of those who maintain that realization occurs instantaneously,
nor has it clarified the meaning of gradual realization.
Now, I wish to refute the former and clarify both instantaneous and gradual realization.
Some say: Although the preceding section has already refuted the notion of simultaneous realization (sakṛt-abhisamaya),
it has also already revealed the meaning of gradual realization (anupūrva-abhisamaya).
Yet it was not coarse, manifest, clear, or perceptible;
now, it is made coarse, manifest, clear, and perceptible. Some say:
Now, I shall demonstrate the five classes of afflictions and their five antidotes.
The five classes of afflictions refer to those abandoned through the vision of suffering, up to those abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding the antidotes for the five categories:
the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) are the antidotes for what is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering;

and so on, up to the patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the path (*mārga-jñāna*), which are the antidotes for what is to be abandoned through the vision of the path.
The truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), are the antidotes for what is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
For this reason, this treatise was composed.
Answer: Among the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Question: Why is the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) abandoned only through the vision of suffering?
Answer: Because this view operates only with respect to the sphere of suffering;
when one contemplates suffering, this view is thereby abandoned.
Furthermore, because this view operates only with respect to the fruit,
it is severed when the fruit is scrutinized.
Moreover, the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has inversion as its intrinsic nature.
All perversions are abandoned through the vision of suffering.
When the perversions are abandoned, these views are also abandoned,
because they share the same antidote.

Furthermore, these afflictions are coarse; they are abandoned forever when the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* (receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering) manifests during the first path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
If the afflictions are subtle, they can only be completely exhausted when the "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests during the final path of uninterrupted transition.
Just as when a garment has stains that do not adhere firmly,
it becomes clean with merely washing;
but if they adhere firmly, one must use strong lye and the like.
One must apply effort to wash it before it can become clean.
It is also like an earthenware vessel where grease does not penetrate deeply;
with a rinse of water, it becomes clean.
If grease has penetrated deeply,
it may be purified by boiling in hot water or by burning with fire;
thus did the Venerable Ghosaka also say.
Because this view is coarse, it is permanently severed as soon as the first path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) manifests.
The two analogies of the garment and the vessel are also as explained previously.
Furthermore, this root of view does not penetrate deeply into the sphere of its object.
Because they do not penetrate deeply, their nature is weak and inferior;

thus, when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) within the initial path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) manifests, these are immediately and permanently severed.
This is the case even if the roots of the afflictions have penetrated deeply into the spheres of existence.
Only when the subsequent path of immediate succession, the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), manifests can [the afflictions] be completely severed.
It is like a tree root that has not been planted deep in the earth;
even a slight breeze will cause it to topple over.
"Only when its roots are deeply embedded can it be toppled by a great wind," so said the Venerable Vasumitra.
This view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises with the five aggregates as its object.
When one views the five aggregates of clinging as they truly are, this view is abandoned.
Furthermore, this view of a self-identity arises from the notions of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self;
when these four notions are abandoned, this view is abandoned.
The Venerable One said:
"This view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises conditioned by the self-identity; thus it is called the 'view of a self-identity.
If one contemplates this self-identity as being without a self or what belongs to a self, this view is then severed."
Therefore, the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is abandoned only by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
As it is with the fetter of the view of a self-identity,

so it is also with the fetter of the view of a self-identity among the five lower-tier fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), and with the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) among the five views (*pañca dṛṣṭayaḥ*).
Because their intrinsic nature is identical and because both are deluded regarding suffering,
there are two types of the fetter of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
It is either abandoned by seeing suffering or abandoned by seeing the path.
Question: For what reason is the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) not abandoned by seeing the origin or the cessation [of suffering]?
The answer is that non-Buddhists give rise to this adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) solely with respect to the path of suffering.
That is to say, these non-Buddhists are also able to regard the origin of suffering (*samudaya*) as a place of impurity,
and they are also able to regard cessation (*nirodha*) as a place for bathing.
They say that because origination (*samudaya*) is a place of defilement, they do not conceive a longing for it;
yet they say that because cessation (*nirodha*) is a place of purification, they falsely conceive a longing for it.
Because of this false longing, they initiate various kinds of useless ascetic practices (*duṣkaracaryā*).
To the extent that one undertakes ascetic practices that yield no benefit,
to that same extent the stains of the afflictions increase, defiling the body and mind and distancing one from nirvāṇa;
it is like a person who, in order to remove dirt from their body, bathes in foul water.
Just as when one bathes, the filth and impurities increase all the more;
therefore, the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) pertains only to two categories.
Furthermore, this clinging to rules and observances operates only with respect to the two locations of suffering (*duḥkha*) and the path (*mārga*).
That which functions regarding the sphere of suffering is abandoned through the vision of suffering;
that which functions regarding the sphere of the path is abandoned through the vision of the path.
Furthermore, this clinging to precepts and observances functions only with respect to the two spheres of the impure and the pure.
That which functions regarding impure objects is abandoned through the vision of suffering;
that which functions regarding pure objects is abandoned through the vision of the path.
Furthermore, this clinging to rules and observances is of only two kinds.
This refers to the distinctions arising from the internal and external paths.
Those arising from the internal path are abandoned through the vision of suffering;
those arising from the external path are abandoned through the vision of the path.
Furthermore, this clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is of only two kinds:
namely, regarding what is not a cause as a cause, and regarding what is not a path as a path.
Regarding what is not a cause as a cause is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*).
Regarding that which is not the path as the path is abandoned by the vision of the path;

it is like the fetter of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*), which is the attachment to precepts and observances among the four types of clinging (*catvāra upādānāni*).
Among the four fetters of the body (*kāyagrantha*), there is the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Among the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), there is the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances.
Among the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), it is likewise the adherence to precepts and observances.
Because their intrinsic natures are identical,
there are four types of the fetter of doubt:
those abandoned through the vision of suffering, up to those abandoned through the vision of the path.
Question: Why is there no doubt (*vicikitsā*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
Answer: When one has not yet perceived an object, the mind harbors hesitation;
once that object has been perceived, the hesitation is immediately eliminated. Therefore, there is no doubt to be abandoned through cultivation.
As for the fetter of doubt, it is the flood and yoke of views among the four floods and yokes;
it is the clinging to views among the four clingings;
and it is the fetter of grasping at this as real among the four bodily fetters.
Among the five hindrances, it is the hindrance of doubt;
among the five fetters conducive to the lower realms, it is the fetter of doubt;
and among the five views, it is wrong view and the grasping at views.
Among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the underlying tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*);
likewise, among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*)— are also thus,
because their essential nature and category are identical.
The three unwholesome roots are of five types: they are either to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, or even up to being abandoned by cultivation.
This is because greed, hatred, and delusion exist within all five categories [of the afflictions].

Just as with the three unwholesome roots, so it is with the three outflows (*āsrava*), the four floods (*ogha*), and the four yokes (*yoga*): from these, one excludes the floods and yokes consisting of views;
furthermore, among the four graspings (*upādāna*), there are the grasping for sensual pleasure (*kāmopādāna*) and the grasping for self-theory (*ātma-vādopādāna*).
Among the four bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*), there are the fetters of sensual desire and ill will;
among the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), there are the remaining hindrances excluding restlessness-remorse and doubt;
and among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), there are the fetters of greed, hatred, and pride.
1. Among the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), it refers to the fetters of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
2. Among the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ tṛṣṇākāya*), it refers to the group of craving born of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja-tṛṣṇākāya*).
3. Among the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), it refers to all latent dispositions except for those consisting of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetters of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) are likewise so;
for their essential natures and categories are identical.
Although it is stated generally that these all pertain to the five classes (*pañca-varga*).
Furthermore, they are separately distinguished as being of one, two, four, or five types.

Among the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and so forth, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), parsimony (*mātsarya*), anger (*krodha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*) belong to only one category.
The adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) belongs to only two categories.
False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) belong to only four categories.
This is because craving (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), and so forth, pertain to all five categories.
The hindrance of regret (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*) is abandoned through cultivation and abandoned by wisdom,
just like the fetters of envy and avarice among the five fetters,
and the five higher-tier fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).
Among the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*), the first five groups of craving are likewise [included],
as are the fetters of envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) among the nine fetters (*nava-saṃyojana*);
this is because they function in dependence upon the same objects and are equal in their categories.
Among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
twenty-eight are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),
because they operate with respect to the object of suffering.
Nineteen are abandoned through the vision of the origin,
because they function within the sphere of the origin.
Nineteen are abandoned through the vision of cessation.
Because they function in relation to the cessation [of suffering],
twenty-two [factors] are abandoned by the path of vision;
because they function in relation to the path.
Ten are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they function based on objective entities (*vastu*).
Question: Among these, which are called those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*)?
Furthermore, what is meant by "abandoned through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
The answer is: those for which the antidote is fixed and the object of focus is fixed are called "abandoned through the vision of suffering" up to "abandoned through the vision of the path."
If the antidote is not determined and the object of the antidote is not determined,
it is called "to be abandoned by cultivation.
Furthermore, if the location is determined and the object of the antidote is determined, [it is called "to be abandoned by seeing"].
Those [defilements] whose antidotes and objects are determined are called "abandoned through the vision of suffering" up to "abandoned through the vision of the path.
Those whose locus is not determined and whose antidotes and objects are not determined are called "abandoned through cultivation."
Furthermore, if the receptivity to suffering (duḥkha-kṣānti) and the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) serve as the antidotes,
they are termed "to be abandoned by the vision of suffering" (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya);
this continues up until, if the receptivity to the path (mārga-kṣānti) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) serve as the antidotes.
Those abandoned by the path of seeing are so named;
if suffering, origin, cessation, the path, and conventional knowledge serve as their antidotes,
they are said to be abandoned by cultivation.
Furthermore, if that which is abandoned by the patience regarding the dharma and subsequent knowledge of suffering is called "abandoned through seeing suffering," and so on,
up to if that which is abandoned by the patience regarding the dharma and subsequent knowledge of the path [is called "abandoned through seeing the path"].
Those abandoned by the path of seeing are called "abandoned by insight.
Those abandoned by the four dharma-knowledges, subsequent knowledges, and conventional knowledge are called "abandoned by cultivation."
Furthermore, if something is abandoned through the contemplation of the truth of suffering,
it is called "abandoned by seeing suffering" (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*);
likewise, up to if it is abandoned through the contemplation of the truth of the path, it is called "abandoned by seeing the path" (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
If one abandons [afflictions] by contemplating the truth of suffering,
or even up to the truth of the path, or by contemplating other matters,
these are called abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Furthermore, if one opposes the contemplation of the truth of suffering,
it is called "to be abandoned by the vision of suffering";
likewise, up to if one opposes the contemplation of the truth of the path, it is called "to be abandoned by the vision of the path."
If one violates the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths or violates the contemplation of other matters,
these are termed "to be abandoned through cultivation."
Regarding the three fetters up to the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*):
how many are views (*dṛṣṭi*) and how many are non-views?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting other schools and revealing the correct meaning.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that all afflictions are of the nature of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Why is this so? Because the term "view" (dṛṣṭi) refers to a mode of activity that is sharp and intense.
All afflictions are each sharp and intense in their own respective modes of activity.
For example, the view of a self-identity has a mode of activity that is intensely sharp in its grasping at "I" and "mine";
the view of extremes has a mode of activity that is intensely sharp in its grasping at annihilationism or eternalism;
and false views have a mode of activity that is intensely sharp in their grasping at non-existence.
The mode of grasping at views as supreme is characterized by intense vehemence;
the mode of grasping at precepts and observances as purifying is characterized by intense vehemence;
and the mode of doubt is characterized by intense hesitation.
The mode of activity of greed and attachment is intense; the mode of activity of hatred and aversion is intense;
the mode of activity of pride and arrogance is intense;
and the mode of activity of ignorance and non-comprehension is intense.
Therefore, some maintain that all afflictions are of the nature of view (*dṛṣṭi*),
while others hold the position that not all afflictions are of the nature of view.
Why is this so? Because the thorough comprehension of all phenomena is what is termed "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
Since all afflictions lack such thorough comprehension regarding their own respective objects, they do not possess the nature of "view."
To stop such misconceptions and to clarify that among the various afflictions some possess the nature of views while others do not, this treatise was composed.
It is answered that, among the three fetters, two are views and one is not a view.
The two views refer to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The one that is not a view refers to doubt (*vicikitsā*).
The rest are explained in detail as in the original treatise.
The detailed explanation of the meaning of "views" has already been stated as before;
that is to say, the five bases of views,
the three fetters, and so forth, up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
How many have both vitarka and vicāra?
How many have no vitarka and only vicāra?
How many have neither vitarka nor vicāra?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of other schools and revealing the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who hold the following view:
From the desire realm up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there are both vitarka and vicāra,
according to the Dārṣṭāntikas.
Why do they hold this position?
Based on the sūtras;
for a sūtra states:
"The coarse nature of the mind is called vitarka."
The nature of subtlety of mind is called *vicāra*.
However, since the natures of coarseness and subtlety can be found from the desire realm up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*),
it is known that both *vitarka* and *vicāra* exist throughout all three realms.
The Venerable One said:
"The explanations of the Abhidharma masters are unreasonable. Why is this so?"
The nature of mental coarseness and subtlety exists throughout all three realms.
The Sūtras state that these are precisely vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought),
yet it is said that vitarka and vicāra exist only in two stages.
That is to say, [it refers to] the desire realm and the Brahma-world;
therefore, what the Abhidharmikas have stated is unreasonable.
It is also called "badly explained" and "badly upheld."
They are not called "well-spoken" or "well-retained.
The Abhidharma masters say:
"What we have spoken and what we have retained is wholesome, not unwholesome."
Why is this? Because there are many ways of designating the coarse and the subtle.
That is to say, it is stated in some places:
The outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) are coarse and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are subtle;
herein, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are neither coarse nor subtle,
because these two are neither outbursts nor latent dispositions.
In some places it is said that the aggregate of form is coarse while the other four aggregates are subtle; herein,
vitarka and vicāra are subtle rather than coarse because they are subsumed within the aggregate of formations.
In some places it is said that the desire realm is coarse and the first dhyāna is subtle. In this context,
both vitarka and vicāra pertain to both the coarse and subtle levels, as both vitarka and vicāra are present in each.
In some places it is said that the first dhyāna is coarse and the second dhyāna is subtle; herein,
vitarka and vicāra are coarse, not subtle.
Because there is no vitarka or vicāra above the first dhyāna,
one should not dogmatically insist that the categories of "coarseness" and "subtlety" applied to such states are fixed; rather,
the nature of coarseness is called vitarka, and the nature of subtlety is called vicāra.
Furthermore, one should not maintain that both vitarka and vicāra exist throughout all three realms.
Nevertheless, the Sūtra states that vitarka and vicāra are the coarse and subtle natures of the mind.
This is explained based on the coarse and subtle natures of the mind that can be disturbed in the two lower stages;
because the mind from the second dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is free from disturbance, it lacks vitarka and vicāra.
Furthermore, since it has already been stated that from the second dhyāna upward there is neither vitarka nor vicāra,
how are the three stages— namely, those with vitarka and vicāra, and so forth— established as distinct?
They explain it as follows:
The wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured neutral states of the desire realm and the first dhyāna,
as well as those of the intermediate dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence— including the defiled minds and so forth— are called the stage with vitarka and vicāra.
The wholesome and non-obscured neutral minds of the intermediate dhyāna are called the stage of "without vitarka and with vicāra only.
The wholesome and non-obscured neutral minds from the second dhyāna up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra) are called the stage of "without vitarka and without vicāra."
If that is so, how should one interpret the sūtra?
As it is said in the sūtra:

"With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, entering and abiding in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and bliss born of concentration."
He asserts this:
"This sutra teaches the stilling of vitarka and vicāra based on the wholesome and the non-obscured neutral, not based on the defiled."
That explanation is irrational. Why is this?
For what reason would the entry into the second dhyāna involve only the cessation of wholesome and neutral vitarka and vicāra, rather than their defiled counterparts?
It is better to say that the pacification of defiled vitarka and vicāra is neither wholesome nor neutral. Why is this?
Because all defiled phenomena are abandoned at the time of detachment from defilement.
This is because wholesome and neutral dharmas are abandoned only when one transcends their respective realms or stages;
however, the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain that these are the fruits of ignorance, the fruits of darkness, and the fruits of a lack of diligent application.
Therefore, it is correctly stated that while both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) exist throughout all three realms,
vitarka and vicāra are present in the two lower stages but absent in the upper seven stages.
This treatise is composed in order to demonstrate the correct principle and to refute the assertions of other schools.
It is answered that the three fetters are of three types:
namely, those accompanied by vitarka and vicāra; those without vitarka but with vicāra; and those without either vitarka or vicāra.
Or there is that which has no vitarka but only vicāra,
or that which has neither vitarka nor vicāra.
What is that which has both vitarka and vicāra?
This refers to [the states] in the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
What is "without vitarka and with only vicāra"?
This refers to the intermediate dhyāna.
What is the absence of vitarka and vicāra?
It refers to the three higher dhyānas and the four formless attainments.
The rest is explained in detail as in the original treatise.
Question: In this context, what is called "with vitarka and vicāra"?
What is called "without vitarka and with only vicāra"?
And what is called "without vitarka and without vicāra"?

Answer: If it is accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra, associated with both vitarka and vicāra, and arises from vitarka and vicāra and is driven by vitarka and vicāra, it is called "with vitarka and with vicāra.
If it is not accompanied by vitarka but is accompanied by vicāra alone, [it is called "without vitarka and with vicāra"].
That which is not associated with vitarka but is associated only with vicāra;
that which does not originate from vitarka but originates only from vicāra;
and that which, with vitarka already stilled, proceeds only by means of vicāra—this is called "without vitarka and with only vicāra."
If it is neither accompanied by vitarka and vicāra,
nor associated with vitarka and vicāra,
nor arisen from vitarka and vicāra.
That which does not proceed by means of vitarka and vicāra is called "without vitarka and without vicāra.

Furthermore, if there is various seeking (vitarka) and various investigation (vicāra), it is called "with vitarka and with vicāra"; if there is no various seeking but there is various investigation, it is called "without vitarka and with only vicāra."
If there is no various seeking (*vitarka*) and no various investigation (*vicāra*), it is called "without vitarka and without vicāra.
Furthermore, if there is repeated seeking and repeated investigation, it is called "with vitarka and with vicāra."
If there is no frequent vitarka but there is frequent vicāra, it is called "without vitarka and with only vicāra.
If there is neither frequent vitarka nor frequent vicāra, it is called "without vitarka and without vicāra."
Regarding the three fetters up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
how many are associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
and how many are associated with the faculties of pain (*duḥkha*), joy (*saumanasya*), grief (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the tenets of other schools and elucidating the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who hold the following view:
When all phenomena arise, it is gradual and not instantaneous,
as the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain;
thus the Bhadanta said:
When all phenomena arise, they arise sequentially; there is no principle of simultaneous arising.
As the Sūtra says: "Just as when many merchants pass along a narrow path one by one, there is not even the possibility of two passing at the same time."
How much more so for those that exist in multiplicity?
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are likewise:
each arises from its own characteristic of arising (*utpādalakṣaṇa*).
"Conditioned phenomena arise through distinct combinations and do not arise simultaneously.
The masters of the Abhidharma say:
"Because there are causes and conditions, it is said that conditioned phenomena arise through distinct combinations."
Because each arises from its own characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*),
and because there are causes and conditions, it is said that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) arise through a single conjunction.
"Not separated" means they arise simultaneously.
This means that when speaking in terms of the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) arise through distinct combinations;
however, when speaking in terms of moments (*kṣaṇa*), conditioned phenomena arise through a single combination,
because those that are inseparable must necessarily arise together.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that the meaning of "power" and "lack of power" constitutes the meaning of "conjunction" and "non-conjunction."
That is to say, if a phenomenon arises through the power of another,
it is said that this phenomenon is associated with that other;
if a phenomenon does not arise through the power of another, [it is not so associated].
Although they arise simultaneously, there is no sense of association (*saṃprayoga*);
nevertheless, just as this mind arises by virtue of the power of that [other] mind,
one may say that this mind is associated with that mind.
Furthermore, because mental factors (caitta) are produced by the power of the mind (citta),
it can be said that mental factors are associated with the mind.
Moreover, because the mind is produced by the power of mental factors, [it is likewise associated with them].
It can be said that mental factors (caitta) are associated with the mind (citta),
because the mind arises by virtue of the power of the mental factors;
however, it cannot be said that the mind is associated with the mental factors.
To refute that intention, it is shown that the mind is associated with mental factors,
and mental factors are also associated with mental factors.
Mental factors...
Furthermore, it can be associated with the mind;
however, there is no principle of association between one mind and another mind,
because two minds do not arise simultaneously within a single body.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that all phenomena are associated with their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and not with the intrinsic nature of others.
He asserts that the meaning of "conjunction" (saṃprayoga) is the sense of mutual affection and esteem;
for there is no dharma that esteems another dharma as much as it esteems itself,
namely its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Therefore, [the objection] holds that [a dharma] is associated only with its own nature (*svabhāva*).
To refute that intention, it is shown that [a dharma] is associated only with other natures (*parabhāva*),
because the meaning of "association" (*saṃprayoga*) is established by way of distinct entities being mutually related.
Just as the mind and mental factors, when viewed in relation to one another,
share the same support, the same object, and so forth, and are termed "associated" because they do not abandon one another;
or again, there are those who hold [the following view].
All phenomena neither possess the sense of being associated with their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor are they dissociated from it.
The reason they do not possess the sense of being associated is that all phenomena arise without depending upon an intrinsic nature.

It is not that they are non-associated; rather, because "being extremely fond of one another" carries the meaning of association, this treatise was composed to refute that view and to demonstrate that all phenomena are associated without confusion.
Question: Why is it asked only regarding association with feeling (*vedanā*)?
Answer: It is because the intention of the author of this treatise was such.
That is to say, since the author composes the treatise according to his own intent without violating the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), he should not be held accountable for this.

Furthermore, because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of feeling (*vedanā*) and the mental factors associated with feeling (*vedanā-samprayukta-dharma*) are distinct, and while they do not contradict [the presence of] their possession (*prāpti*), they do contradict their actual manifestation (*samudācāra*), the question is asked specifically regarding them.
As for "not contradicting possession," it is because within a single body, the possession of all five faculties of feeling (*pañca-vedanendriya*) is possible.
Regarding their contradictory manifestation:
it is because two feelings can never manifest simultaneously.
Furthermore, feeling arises by conforming to the transformations of the sense faculties.
The five faculties are established within the single basis of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), whereas other phenomena are not; therefore, he asks specifically about sensation.
Furthermore, sensation occupies the position of the hub within the wheel of the twelve links of dependent origination;
for this reason, he asks specifically about it.
Furthermore, because all phenomena ultimately converge upon sensation (*vedanā*), this question is asked specifically regarding it. Moreover,
if one were to ask with which faculties [other] than sensation they are associated,
and were to answer that they are associated with the eight faculties beginning with the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), that would be irrational, as such a connection would not hold.
If one asks whether [the mind] is associated with the five faculties such as faith and so forth, or with the three untainted [faculties],
that too is unreasonable, because [those states] are exclusively wholesome.
If one asks whether it is associated with other defiled [states] or with mental factors such as perception (saṃjñā) and volition (cetanā), [that is reasonable].
This is also unreasonable,
because it lacks the characteristics of a faculty (indriya) and because some [of these] are of the nature of afflictions (kleśa).
If it is asked whether [the mind] is associated with mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom,
this too is unreasonable,
because [such a state] lacks the characteristics of being associated with the afflictions and lacking roots.
Alternatively, it may be because [the mental faculty] is of the nature of affliction (*kleśa*).

If one asks why, it is because it would also be illogical for the mental faculty (*manas*) to be established based on the mind (*citta*), since it is a factor associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta-dharma*);
furthermore, there would be no distinction between the mind and its associated factors.

Question: Since the characteristics of the faculties associated with feeling are not themselves the essence of afflictions, yet they are capable of producing afflictions, with which [faculties] do they correspond?
Answer: Among the three fetters, the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the fetter of adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) correspond to three faculties.
Excluding the faculty of suffering and the faculty of grief.
Question: For what reason is the faculty of suffering excluded here?
Answer: The faculty of suffering exists within the five sensory consciousnesses.
Because these two fetters belong to the mental level (*manobhūmi*), they are not associated [with the faculties].
Question: Why is the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) excluded here?
Answer: Because it functions with the aspect of sorrowful dejection (*daurmanasyākāra*).
Because these two fetters function through modes of activity that are mutually exclusive, they are not associated with one another.
Taken collectively, these two are said to be associated with three faculties.
To distinguish them specifically: if they occur in the desire realm or the first two dhyānas, they are associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
If it is in the third dhyāna, it is associated with both pleasure and equanimity;
if it is in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realm, it is associated with equanimity alone.
Therefore, it is said in general that it is associated with three faculties.
The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) is associated with four faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
Question: Why is the faculty of suffering excluded here?
Answer: Because the faculty of suffering exists in the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), whereas doubt exists in the mental ground (*manobhūmi*); therefore, they are not associated.
In summary, the fetter of doubt is associated with four faculties.
To distinguish them specifically: if it occurs in the desire realm, it is associated with the faculties of mental grief (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*);
if it occurs in the first or second dhyāna, it is associated with the faculties of joy (*prīti*) and equanimity.
If it is in the third dhyāna, it is associated with both pleasure and equanimity;
if it is in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realm, it is associated with equanimity alone.
Therefore, it is generally said to be associated with four faculties.

Question: Why is it that the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*), when in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), is not associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), whereas when in the first and second dhyānas, it is associated with the faculty of joy?
Answer: Because the modes of activity of joy and dejection are mutually incompatible.
That is to say, doubt in the desire realm functions with a mode of activity characterized by dejection, whereas the faculty of joy functions with a mode of activity characterized by joy.
Since their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are distinct, there is no sense of association (*samprayoga*).
However, in the first and second dhyānas, doubt (*vicikitsā*) is associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), because it functions through a mode of activity characterized by gladness;
for the meaning of "equality" (*samatā*) constitutes the meaning of association.
Furthermore, because joy (*prīti*) in the desire realm is coarse while doubt (*vicikitsā*) is subtle, they are not associated.
Question: Why is joy in the desire realm coarse?
Answer: Because sentient beings in the desire realm give rise to that which they ought not to give rise to.
Regarding matters of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one should not give rise to [such states], yet they do arise.

Why is it that sentient beings of the desire realm should not give rise to them but do so? It means that sentient beings of the desire realm are by nature suffering, and upon this further suffering is added; they ought to give rise to revulsion and detachment, yet instead they leap about with joy—is this not indeed coarse?
What is meant by "arising [a thought] toward objects of the desire realm that should not be arisen"?

It refers to seeing another person stumble, err, or go astray, and instead of giving rise to compassion, one laughs with delight—is this not a coarse form of the fetter of doubt regarding the desire realm? For it is subtle because it involves deep reflection.
Since the coarse and the subtle are distinct, there can be no sense of association (*samprayoga*).
In the first and second *dhyānas*, doubt and joy are both subtle, and therefore they may be associated.
Furthermore, because the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) in the desire realm is heavy and stable, while the faculty of joy (*prīti-indriya*) is light and restless, they are not associated.
In the first dhyāna, both are present and stable, and thus they are associated. Furthermore,
because the fetter of doubt in the desire realm operates within the internal door,
while the faculty of joy in the desire realm operates through the external door, they are not associated.
The first and second dhyānas are associated [with joy] because they both function internally.
Furthermore, doubt (vicikitsā) in the desire realm is like a host, whereas the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) is like a guest; therefore, they are not associated.
In the first and second dhyānas, both [factors] are associated because they are like their respective masters.
Furthermore, although the fetter of doubt in the desire realm is not associated with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*), it is associated with the feeling of grief (*daurmanasya*).
If the fetter of doubt in the first and second dhyānas is not associated with the feeling of joy (*prīti*), it would then be without feeling;
for joy is the intrinsic feeling of those stages.

If one were to claim that the aggregate of doubt is entirely devoid of feeling (*vedanā*), it would contradict the principles of mutual dependence (*āśraya*) and association (*samprayoga*); let there be no such error.
Therefore, the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) is associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) in the first two dhyānas.
Among the three unwholesome roots, the unwholesome root of greed is associated with three faculties, excluding the faculties of pain (*duḥkha*) and grief (*daurmanasya*).

This is because the faculties of pain and grief function through a mode of activity characterized by despondency, whereas the unwholesome root of greed functions through a mode of activity characterized by joy; therefore, they are not associated.
The unwholesome root of hatred is associated with three faculties, excluding the faculties of pleasure and joy.

This is because the faculties of pleasure and joy function through a mode of activity characterized by gladness, whereas the unwholesome root of hatred functions through a mode of activity characterized by dejection; therefore, they are not associated.
The unwholesome root of delusion (*moha-akuśalamūla*), as well as the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), are associated with five faculties (*indriya*).
This is because they all operate through the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*) by way of both pleasant and unpleasant modes of activity.
The outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) is associated with three faculties, excluding the faculties of pain (*duḥkha*) and grief (*daurmanasya*).
Because the realms of form and formlessness lack the faculties of sorrow and suffering,
those [faculties] that serve as the causes for sorrow and suffering will be explained in detail in the *Skandha* section.
With the exception of wrong view, the rest are explained at length as in the original treatise.
False view is associated with four faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
This is because the faculty of suffering exists in the five sensory consciousnesses, whereas false view belongs to the mental level (*manobhūmi*); therefore, they are not associated.

Generally stated, false view is associated with four faculties; however, to distinguish them specifically: if it occurs in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is associated with three faculties, excluding the faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
If it is in the first or second dhyāna, it is associated with the faculties of joy and equanimity;
if it is in the third dhyāna, it is associated with the faculties of pleasure and equanimity;
if it is in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realm, [it is associated with the faculty of equanimity].
It is associated exclusively with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Question: Among the wrong views of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which are associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and which are associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)?
Answer: There are some who from the outset have no inclination for giving, no inclination for affection, and no inclination for making offerings.
Later, if he encounters non-Buddhist practitioners of wrong views who preach that there is no giving,

no affection, no sacrifice, no wholesome conduct, no unwholesome conduct, and no ripening of the fruits of wholesome or unwholesome karmic actions— having heard this, he rejoices and thinks to himself:
"From time immemorial, I have not been fond of giving, nor even of performing sacrifices, as these are truly futile matters;
for they bear no fruit and no karmic maturation.
Such a wrong view is associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
There may be some who from the outset are inclined toward giving, inclined toward affectionate joy, and inclined toward sacrificial offerings.

Later, if they encounter non-Buddhist outsiders who hold wrong views, they hear it said that there is no giving, no affectionate joy, and no sacrificial offerings; that there is no good conduct and no evil conduct, and no ripening of the fruits of good or evil karmic actions.
Having heard this, he became sorrowful and dejected, thinking to himself:
"All my acts of giving from time immemorial, even up to my sacrificial offerings, have been utterly in vain,
for they bear no fruit and no karmic maturation."
Thus, the detailed explanation of the meaning of association regarding the faculty of grief associated with wrong view has already been explained among the six causes.
This applies from the three fetters up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

How many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
Why was this treatise composed? It is answered:
in order to refute the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.

This means that there are some who hold the view that all the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) found in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) also exist in number and substance within the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*).
To refute that intention, it is shown that the desire realm is an indeterminate stage (*aniyata-bhūmi*) characterized by a multitude of afflictions and secondary afflictions.
Because the form and formless realms are states of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*), they possess few afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
This is because [afflictions] such as the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*) and remorse (*kaukṛtya*) do not exist in those realms.

Alternatively, there may be those who hold the view that the outflows (*āsrava*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and grasping at self-identity (*ātmavādopādāna*) exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as well, because various afflictions arise therein with internal objects as their conditions and thus receive those names. To refute such an intention, it is shown that while the outflows and so forth do not exclusively pertain to the desire realm, the defilements of the two upper realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*)—which are subsumed under the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and largely arise with internal objects as their conditions—definitely receive those names.
Alternatively, there are those who hold that the two fetters of envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) also exist in the Brahma-world,
as the Vibhajyavādins do.
Question: For what reason do they hold this position?
Answer: Because it is based on the sūtras;
that is, the sūtra says:
The Great Brahmā King addressed the assembly of Brahmās:
"We need not go to the place of the śramaṇa Gautama to pay him homage and listen to the Dharma.
While remaining right here, we shall cause you all to transcend birth, old age, and death, and realize eternal quiescence."
That statement was made because the Brahmā King’s mind was entangled by the fetters of envy and avarice;
it was intended to refute that view and demonstrate that the fetters of envy and avarice exist only in the desire realm.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that the Brahma-world possesses the obscuring fetter (*nivṛti-kaṣāya*).
One might ask: for what reason do they hold this view?
Answer: It is based on the sūtras.
That is to say, a sūtra states:
"The Great Brahmā King, failing to understand the question posed by the Venerable Aśvajit, feared that the Brahma assembly would find out."
Using skillful means, he drew him out with gentle words and apologized;
the Brahmā King, because of the entanglement of concealment (*mrakṣa*), had drawn him outside the assembly and only then expressed his lack of understanding.
To refute that intention, it is shown that the entanglement of concealment exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
However, because the Great Brahmā King’s mind was obscured by pride, flattery, and deception, he spoke these words.
For this reason, this treatise was composed.
The answer is: the three fetters are of three kinds, or they are bound to the desire realm.
Either bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) or bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
The rest is explained in detail as in the original treatise.
Question: Why are they called "bound to the realm of desire," "bound to the realm of form," and "bound to the formless realm"?
Answer: It is called "bound to the desire realm" because it is bound to the desire realm;
it is called "bound to the form realm" because it is bound to the form realm;
it is called "bound to the formless realm" because it is bound to the formless realm.
Just as oxen, horses, and the like, when tied to a pillar or a stake, are said to be "tied to a pillar" and so forth;
furthermore, because they are bound by the fetters of the desire realm, they are called "bound to the desire realm."
They are called "bound to the realm of form" because they are fettered by the fetters of the realm of form;
they are called "bound to the formless realm" because they are fettered by the fetters of the formless realm.
"Fetters" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), as a verse says: "The conduct of the Buddha is boundless and without fetters."
Who will go?
Just as a person who has feet can travel freely throughout the eight directions, whereas one without feet cannot do so;
likewise, sentient beings who possess the "feet" of afflictions are able to travel through the various realms, destinies, and births.
It is not so for those whose feet are free from afflictions,
because the Buddhas have eternally severed the feet of affliction; thus,
they no longer undergo transmigration within the realms, destinies, or births.
However, because the spheres of activity of meditative concentration and wisdom are boundless;
furthermore, because it is comprised within and stored in the cave-dwelling of the desire realm,
and because it is grasped and adhered to by the self-clinging of the desire realm, it is called "bound to the desire realm" (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
Because it is subsumed within and stored in the cave-dwelling of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
and because it is grasped and adhered to by the self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) of the form realm, it is called "bound to the form realm" (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Because it is subsumed within and stored in the cave-dwelling of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), [it is called "bound to the formless realm"].
It is called "bound to the formless realm" because it is that which is grasped by and attached to the self-grasping of the formless realm.
"Cave-dwelling" refers to craving;
"self-grasping" refers to views.
Furthermore, it is called "bound to the desire realm" because it is moistened by craving for the desire realm and is clung to by the views of "I" and "mine.
It is [also] moistened by craving for the form realm.
Because they are clung to by the view of self and what belongs to self, they are said to be bound to the form realm;
because they are moistened by craving for the formless realm and clung to by the view of self and what belongs to self, they are said to be bound to the formless realm.
Furthermore, because it is firmly attached to the desires and cravings of the desire realm, it is called "bound to the desire realm" (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
Because it is firmly attached to the desires and cravings of the form realm, it is called "bound to the form realm" (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
Because it is firmly attached to the desires and cravings of the formless realm, it is called "bound to the formless realm" (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
"Desire" refers to craving; "view" refers to [wrong] views.
Furthermore, because one is bound by the birth and death of the desire realm, it is called "bound to the desire realm";
because one is bound by the birth and death of the form realm, it is called "bound to the form realm."
It is called "bound to the formless realm" because it is fettered by the birth and death of the formless realm.

Furthermore, it is called "bound to the desire realm" because it is defiled by the impurities of the desire realm, harmed by its poisons, and stained by its filth; likewise, it is bound to the form realm because it is defiled by the impurities of the form realm.
Because it is harmed by poison and defiled by impurities, it is called "bound to the realm of form" (*rūpadhātu-saṃprayukta*).
Because it is stained by the defilements of the formless realm, harmed by poison, and defiled by impurities, it is called "bound to the formless realm" (*ārūpyadhātu-saṃprayukta*).
All afflictions (*kleśa*) are termed "impurities" (*kaṣāya*), not merely anger; therefore, they pervade all three realms.
Furthermore, because they are bound by the afflictions of the desire realm, they are called "bound to the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
They are called "bound to the realm of form" because they are fettered by the afflictions of the realm of form;
they are called "bound to the formless realm" because they are fettered by the afflictions of the formless realm.

and so forth, as explained at length.
In this context, "falling" (*pāta*) is of six kinds.
1. Falling into a realm;
2. falling into a destiny; 3. falling into a person;
4. falling into a station.
Fifth is falling into the outflows;
sixth is falling into one's own nature.
Regarding "falling into the realms":
As it is said therein: "The fetters that fall into the desire realm—those fetters exist in the desire realm," and so forth.
The intended meaning here is that if a phenomenon belongs to a particular realm, it is designated as "falling into" that realm.
If a phenomenon belongs to the desire realm, it is called "fallen into the desire realm.
If a phenomenon belongs to the form realm, it is called "fallen into the form realm.
If a phenomenon belongs to the formless realm, it is called "fallen into the formless realm."
Regarding "falling into the realms of existence":
it is as when a Dharma-preacher, while practicing the gift of Dharma, makes this aspiration, saying:

Regarding individuals who have fallen away,

there are three types of individuals who, though having fallen away, remain within the count of the Saṃgha and cause the Saṃgha to remain in harmony.
Regarding those that are included [in the aggregates]: as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*, what is the aggregate of form?
It refers to the ten bases of form and the form included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Regarding those subject to outflows and falling [into saṃsāra], as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"What are the dharmas that fall? They are the dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava*)."
Regarding "falling into its own nature," it is as explained in the *Mahābhūta-skandha*.
What is the meaning of "appropriated" (*upātta*)?
Answer: This refers to phenomena (dharma) that fall within their own intrinsic nature as manifested by this designation.
Among the six types of falling, the discussion here concerns only falling according to the realms (dhātu).
Within this context, there are four kinds of "being present."
First, the existence of the self-substance;
second, the existence of the vessel-world;

Regarding "existence in four ways," as for "existence by way of its own essence," it means that all phenomena each abide within their own essence, their own self, their own substance, their own characteristic, their own portion, and their own intrinsic nature.

This refers to one who, while bound by the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), passes away from the form realm and arises as an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the desire realm.

thus, the place where the death-existence (*mṛtyubhava*) ceases is where the intermediate existence manifests.
Just as a sprout appears at the very place where the seed has perished,
so too, from the moment of death-existence until the intermediate existence,
one or another of the thirty-six latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm manifests, causing the continuity of birth to arise.
Furthermore, because the Evil Māra dwells in the Brahma-world and is bound by the fetters (*paryavasthāna*), he reviles and rejects the Tathāgata.

Answer: Because it was cited by Brahmā, as stated in a sūtra:

They give rise to wrong views, thinking:

you should reflect that those Brahmās of the past who fell into the desire realm were like flowers or fruits that have fallen.

he took no pleasure in discourse and thought to himself:
"Who could possibly debate as an adversary against the Buddha?

Immediately, by means of his supernormal power, he led him and placed him in the Brahma world, transforming it into a realm of desire, and settled him there.

"This place is eternal," and so forth, as extensively described.

They are driven out by means of swords, staves, and the like;

"You should respectfully follow what the Brahmā has said.
They further addressed the Buddha, saying,

He respectfully followed his words and did not dare to disobey them.
The Buddha then told him:

This is indeed an evil Mara;
devoid of shame or remorse,
he comes unprovoked to disturb you.
At that time, Māra the Evil One, knowing that the Buddha had awakened,

Section Two: The Aggregate of Fetters (*Saṃyojana-khandha*). Chapter One: The Sub-section on Unwholesome [Fetters]. Section Eight. There are fetters that exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), yet those fetters do not themselves fall within the desire realm.
This refers to one who, while enveloped by the *paryavasthānas*, dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and arises as an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Such a person, dying in the desire realm and being born in the form realm,
includes both ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
The intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of that form realm arises in the desire realm; the principle should be understood as follows:
where the death-existence (*cyutyabhava*) ceases, the intermediate existence manifests there, just as where a seed ceases, the sprout manifests.
When that [being] passes from the existence at death (*cyuty-bhava*) to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
if they are an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one or another of the thirty-one latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm manifests,

causing the continuity of birth; if they are a noble one (*ārya*), one or another of the three latent dispositions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the form realm manifests, causing the continuity of birth.
And when the fetters of the form and formless realms manifest while one dwells in the desire realm—
meaning, while dwelling in the desire realm without dying or being reborn, the fetters of the form and formless realms manifest.
That [attainment] is common to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
If it is an ordinary being, it is when any one of the sixty-two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms is manifest—
namely, craving, views, doubt, or pride in those who have ascended to the dhyānas.
If, for an Ārya, any one of the six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the form or formless realms becomes manifest—
namely, craving or pride in those who have ascended to the higher dhyānas—
then a defilement will necessarily manifest subsequent to that meditative concentration.
The defilements (kleśa) necessarily manifest immediately after [the attainment of cessation];
this is called having fetters (saṃyojana) in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) without being included within the desire realm.
Regarding those who exist in the desire realm, there are three types of existence, excluding the existence of one's own self.
Because they do not manifest within their own realm;
they do not belong to the desire realm,
as they belong to the form and formless realms.
This realm belongs to that [desire] realm and not to others.
There are fetters that belong to the desire realm, and those fetters also exist within the desire realm;

namely, when one who is bound by the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) dies in the desire realm and arises as an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) or a birth existence (*upapattibhava*) in the desire realm.
Regarding those who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the desire realm:
this applies to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
Ordinary beings are unimpeded in taking birth within the five destinies.
The Noble One is unimpeded regarding rebirth in the two destinies—
namely, among humans and devas—
from the moment of death-existence until the intermediate state.
If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) manifests any one of the thirty-six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm, it causes them to arise and continue in the stream of existence.

If a noble one (*ārya*) manifests any one of the four latent dispositions of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), it causes them to arise and continue in the stream of existence.
The same applies from the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*).

Furthermore, regarding those abiding in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm manifest—meaning, while abiding in the desire realm, neither dying nor being reborn, yet the fetters of the desire realm manifest.
That [attainment] pertains to both ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
If it is an ordinary worldling, any one of the thirty-six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm is present;
if it is a noble one, any one of the four latent dispositions of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is present.
This is called having fetters that cause one to fall into the desire realm and also being situated within the desire realm.
"Falling into the desire realm" refers to falling into the realm itself and not falling into anything else.
"Also being situated within the desire realm" means possessing all four bases, because they are present in their own realm.
There are fetters that do not belong to the desire realm, and those fetters do not exist within the desire realm either.

This refers to one who, while bound by the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), passes away from the form realm and arises in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) or the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) of the form realm;
as well as one who passes away from the form realm and is reborn in the form realm.
This applies to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
If an ordinary being is born in a higher realm, they may also be born in a lower realm;
thus, there are many births for each respective location.
If an Ārya is born in a higher realm and not in a lower one,
there is only a single birth in each location;
this refers to the period from the existence at death (maraṇabhava) until the intermediate existence (antarābhava).
If for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), any one of the thirty-one latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) manifests and causes the continuum to arise;
or if for a noble one (*ārya*), any one of the three latent dispositions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the form realm manifests and causes the continuum to arise.
The transition from the intermediate state to the state of birth is likewise.
When one passes away from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
this also applies to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
From the moment of death-existence until the moment of birth-existence:
if it is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), any one of the thirty-one latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm manifests and causes the continuity of existence to arise;

if it is a noble one (*ārya*), any one of the three latent dispositions of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) manifests and causes the continuity of existence to arise.
One who passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the formless realm includes both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
If an ordinary being is born in a higher [formless] realm, they may also be born in a lower one.
In each location there may be multiple births; however,
if an noble one (ārya) is born in a higher realm, they do not take birth in a lower one,
and in each such location there is only a single birth.
From the moment of death-existence until the moment of birth-existence,
if it is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), any one of the thirty-one latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm manifests and causes the continuity of existence to arise;

if it is a noble one (*ārya*), any one of the three latent dispositions of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) manifests and causes the continuity of existence to arise.
One who passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the form realm is exclusively an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
From the moment of death-existence (*cyutibhava*) until the time of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), [they remain an ordinary person].
Any one of the thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) manifests and causes the continuity [of existence] to arise;
furthermore, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the form and formless realms manifest while dwelling in the form realm.
That is to say, while dwelling in the form realm—neither dying nor being reborn—the fetters of the form and formless realms manifest.

That [attainment] is common to both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*). If it is an ordinary person, any one of the sixty-two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms is manifest, namely:
craving, views, doubt, and pride—[the latter] being those who have ascended to the higher dhyānas.
If for an noble one, any one of the six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the form or formless realms becomes manifest—
namely, craving or pride in those who have attained the higher dhyānas—
then that affliction will necessarily manifest after the [meditative] attainment has ended.
After the afflictions, one definitely manifests and dwells in the formless realm;

the fetters of the formless realm manifest while dwelling in the formless realm—meaning that while dwelling in the formless realm, neither dying nor being reborn, the fetters of the formless realm nevertheless manifest.
That [defilement] pertains to both ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) and noble ones (ārya).
If it is an ordinary person, any one of the thirty-one latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm is manifest;
if it is a noble one, any one of the three latent dispositions of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) is manifest.
This is called a fetter that neither falls within the desire realm nor resides in the desire realm.
That it does not fall within the desire realm is because it falls within the form and formless realms.
This realm belongs to those who have fallen [into it], not to others, nor does it belong to those residing in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
because it manifests for those in the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*). Thus,
it may possess all four states of existence.
Furthermore, because they manifest within their own realm, one might ask:
"Are all fetters that belong to the form realm (rūpadhātu) necessarily present in the form realm?

views (dṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), or pride (māna)— [it is so].

This realm belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and not to others, because this fetter (*saṃyojana*) belongs to the formless realm.
Question: Why is the "non-phrase" (*na-vākya*) established in this context?
Answer: This is because the intention of the author of this treatise was such.

That is to say, since the original master of the treatise composed it according to his own intent without violating the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), he should not be held accountable.
Furthermore, it is intended to demonstrate that mastery has been attained over speech.
This means that one who has attained mastery over discourse can establish what is not a [valid] proposition;
whereas one who lacks mastery over discourse cannot even compose a treatise based on such a proposition, much less establish what is not a proposition.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to cause disciples to give rise to the faculty of awakening that a treatise is composed based on non-words; by doing so,
the disciples are able to give rise to the faculty of awakening.
That is to say, regarding the nature of all phenomena, this may be so and that may also be so, without mutual contradiction. Furthermore,
there are non-terms (*apada*) distinct from these terms,
as will be explained later in the *Pudgala-viniścaya* chapter.
A phrase consists of four, three, or two [syllables];
a non-phrase consists of five, six, or four.
Since this is not the case here, it is established as a non-phrase.
"A disciple of the World-Honored One who possesses right view," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the positions of others and clarifying one's own doctrine.
That is to say, there are those who maintain that the nine grades of form are severed gradually and part by part, such as the masters of foreign lands (bahirdeśaka), who speak as follows:
Just as the nine grades of defiled mind and mental factors are gradually abandoned, so too should it be with form;
this is stated in order to refute that [opinion] and to demonstrate that the nine grades of defiled mind and mental factors are indeed gradually abandoned.

The contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome and non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds and mental factors of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are abandoned all at once by the power of the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*).
Question: For what reason are the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) minds and mental factors abandoned gradually in nine grades?
Are the tainted wholesome and non-obscured neutral states of mind and mental factors belonging to the realm of form abandoned all at once by the power of the ninth path of uninterrupted transition?
Answer: Because clarity and ignorance are mutually contradictory.
This means that the arising of the lowest-of-the-low clarity (*vidyā*) eliminates the highest-of-the-high ignorance (*avidyā*),
and so on, up to the arising of the highest-of-the-high clarity eliminating the lowest-of-the-low ignorance.

Furthermore, the outflowing wholesome (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) are not mutually incompatible with either clarity or ignorance.
However, light and ignorance serve as the basis and support for one another;
they are mutually contradictory like a lamp and darkness.
Yet, the vessel, oil, and wick are not contradictory to these two, while being able to serve as their basis and support.
Furthermore, defiled minds and mental factors are abandoned by their very nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*) because they are incompatible with the Path.
When a path belonging to a particular category (*pakṣa*) manifests, those [defilements] of that same category are abandoned;
one loses their possession (*prāpti*) and attains non-possession (*aprāpti*).

The contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome and non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) forms of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are not abandoned by their own nature (*svabhāva-prahīṇa*), nor do they directly contradict the Path.
As for all defiled (*kliṣṭa*) forms, their possession (*prāpti*) has already been lost at the time of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*).

When most of the contaminated wholesome states and the non-obscured neutral states have been severed, yet they are still possessed [by the practitioner], at the moment of the ninth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) corresponding to each respective stage, one correctly severs the defiled mind and mental factors.
Because the bonds of the objects of perception—such as form—are exhausted, these are also said to be "abandoned.
Phenomena such as form are like the light of a lamp:

they are primarily capable of dispelling darkness, while simultaneously being able to heat the vessel, burn the wick, and exhaust the oil. Furthermore, let there be no stopping others merely to manifest the tenets of one's own school.
This treatise is composed solely to reveal the correct principles of all phenomena and to bring enlightenment to students.
Question: What is excluded by the term "possessing vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*)?
Furthermore, what is excluded among the disciples of the Blessed One?
The answer states that the term "one who possesses vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) is used to distinguish [the noble ones] from those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
The term "disciple of the Blessed One" (*bhagavataḥ śrāvakaḥ*) is used to distinguish them from ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Question: Why are those who follow by faith or by dharma not called "those who possess vision"?
Answer: If, within the continuum, one has already fully realized the Four Truths and has already abandoned the four types of false views, one is said to be "one who has fully realized.

Those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) have not yet fully realized the Four Truths, but because they are about to fully realize them, they are so designated.
Because one has not yet abandoned the four wrong views,
though they should have been abandoned, one is not said to possess right view (*dṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, if within the continuum the four kinds of ignorant darkness have been abandoned and the four kinds of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) have arisen, one is said to possess right view.
Because those who follow by faith and those who follow by Dharma have not yet abandoned the four kinds of ignorance and delusion,
which they ought to have abandoned;
and because they have not yet given rise to the four kinds of untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna).
Because it has already arisen, it is not called "possessing vision.
Furthermore, if within the continuum the fourfold net of hesitation and doubt has been destroyed,
and the fourfold certain noble knowledge has already arisen, one is said to possess vision.
Those who follow by faith or follow by dharma have not yet broken the fourfold net of hesitation and doubt, though they should have;
nor have they yet given rise to the fourfold definitive noble wisdom.
Because it has already arisen, it is not called "possessing vision.
Furthermore, if within the continuum there are no afflictions, evil conduct, or inverted views—such as frost, hail, or other calamities—one is said to possess vision.
Those who practice by following faith or by following the Dharma still possess these [defilements] and are therefore not said to be "endowed with vision.
This is just as various crops that suffer from calamities are not said to be "complete."
This is also the case here.
Furthermore, those who have already conquered the continents of the Four Truths are said to be "possessed of vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
This applies to both those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by Dharma (dharmānusārin).
Because they have not yet brought the continents of the Four Noble Truths under subjugation, they are not said to possess right view.
Question: For what reason are ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) not called disciples of the Blessed One?
Answer: If they hear the Buddha’s teaching on the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths...
Those who possess definitive faith and acceptance are called disciples of the World-Honored One.
Ordinary worldlings, upon hearing the teachings on the Triple Gem and the Four Noble Truths, may either believe or not believe; therefore, they are not called disciples of the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, those who worship only the Buddha and do not worship other deities are called disciples of the World-Honored One (*bhagavant*).
Ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), because they may worship either the Buddha or other deities, are not called disciples of the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, those who have attained verified clarity regarding the Three Jewels are called disciples of the Blessed One;
ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) are not so, and therefore they are not called disciples of the Blessed One.
Furthermore, those whose minds do not waver from the Buddha’s Dharma, remaining as firm as a door-sill, are called disciples of the Blessed One.
Ordinary worldlings have minds that are light and fickle toward the Buddha’s teachings, like willow catkins or layers of cotton; therefore, they are not called disciples of the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, even if they have heard the true Dharma...
One who is not corrupted by false teachings is called a disciple of the World-Honored One.
Ordinary worldlings, even after hearing the true Dharma,
are not called disciples of the World-Honored One because they may be corrupted by false teachings.
Question: What is meant here by "the Blessed One’s disciples who possess vision"?
Answer: Here, the stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats are called the Blessed One’s disciples who possess vision.
"Are all forms that have not been abandoned bound by those forms?
and so forth, as explained at length.
In this context, whenever forms are said to be "abandoned," they are simultaneously "disengaged" from their bonds.
When there is dissociation from the fetters, it is at that very moment called "abandonment.
