There is no such case where abandonment occurs first and dissociation later, or where dissociation occurs first and abandonment later;
this applies to all defiled minds and mental factors.
Either disjunction occurs after the afflictions have been severed,
or disjunction occurs at the very moment they are severed;
these consist of nine grades.
That is to say, from the highest-of-the-high down to the lowest-of-the-low:
for the first eight grades, there is first abandonment and subsequently dissociation;
however, at the moment the lowest-of-the-low grade is abandoned, dissociation occurs simultaneously.
That is to say, even after the highest-of-the-high grade has been abandoned, one is still bound by it as an object of perception for the remaining eight grades;
and so on, until after the first eight grades have been abandoned, one is still bound by them as objects of perception for the lowest-of-the-low grade.
Because the nine grades within the same stage serve as mutual objects of attachment for one another, when the ninth grade is abandoned, all nine grades attain dissociation from bondage;
thus, the bondage regarding the objects of the preceding eight grades is completely exhausted.
Because those fetters associated with it have already been exhausted, one is said to have attained dissociation (*visamyoga*).
Since both types of fetters are exhausted in the ninth category, one attains dissociation.
This is the summary of the *Vibhāṣā* regarding this point, including its full exposition.
“Is it the case that for the disciples of the Blessed One, whatever forms have not been abandoned are bound by those forms?
Answer: “It is so.
“If forms are bound, have those forms not been abandoned?”
The answer is: so it is.
As previously stated, regarding all forms (*rūpa*), at the very moment they are said to be "severed," they are simultaneously "disengaged" (*visamyukta*);
and at the very moment they are disengaged, they are simultaneously said to be severed.
First there is abandonment, and subsequently there is dissociation;
it is impossible for dissociation to occur first and abandonment later,
because all form is abandoned by the final uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*).
At that time, because one is said to have attained dissociation [from the defilements],
the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) are bound by the various forms (*rūpa*) of the five stages which they have not yet abandoned;
the non-returner (anāgāmin), who has not yet become free from the defilement of the first dhyāna, is bound by the various forms of the four stages which he has not yet abandoned.

One who has already abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna is bound by the forms of the three stages, which have not been severed.
One who has already abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna [is likewise bound].
In the second dhyāna, various forms are not yet abandoned but remain as fetters;
one has already become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
but has not yet become free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna.
All forms of the first stage are not yet abandoned and are bound.
For a disciple of the Blessed One who possesses right view, are their feelings, perceptions, formations,
and consciousnesses— being unabandoned— also bound?
The answer is as follows:

namely, the stream-enterer and once-returner have not yet abandoned the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that are to be abandoned through cultivation within the three realms, and are thus bound by them;
likewise, the non-returner has not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
There are cases where the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness to be abandoned by cultivation in eight stages are unabandoned and constitute a fetter:
namely, when one has already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna but has not yet become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna.
There are cases where the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness to be abandoned by cultivation in seven stages are unabandoned and constitute a fetter.
Up to the point where one has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
there is a stage wherein the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) have not yet been severed and thus constitute a bond;
yet, while there is feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that constitute that bond, those very feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are not themselves unsevered.
That is to say, for one who is a *kulaṅkula*, a *sakṛdāgāmin*, or an *ekavīcika*,
the superior and medium grades of fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm have already been abandoned and fully known;
yet they remain bound by the inferior grades of fetters associated with that [state] regarding feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
Among these, one who is "from family to family" (kulaṃkula) has already abandoned the first three or four categories of fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm,
as well as the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with them.
Nevertheless, those associated feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are still bound by the objects of the last six or five categories of fetters of the desire realm.
A once-returner has already abandoned the first six grades of fetters of the desire realm,
as well as the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with them;
yet those associated feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are still bound by the objects of the remaining three grades of fetters of the desire realm.
An ekabījin has already abandoned the first seven or eight grades of fetters of the desire realm,
as well as the corresponding feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Nevertheless,
those corresponding feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are still bound by the objects of the last two or one grade of fetters of the desire realm.
This refers to one who is bound but not yet free from [the fetters], yet possesses right view— a disciple of the Blessed One—
for whom all forms have been abandoned.
Are those forms dissociated from him?
Answer: It is so.
If form is dissociated, has that form already been abandoned?
Answer: It is so.
It was previously stated that regarding all forms (*rūpa*), the moment they are termed "severed" (*prahīṇa*), at that very moment they are "disjoined" (*visamyukta*);
and the moment they are disjoined, at that very moment they are termed severed.
It is not the case that they are severed first and then become disjoined.
There is no such case where disjunction occurs first and abandonment follows later;
for all forms (*rūpa*) are abandoned by the final uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*),
and at that very moment, one is said to have attained disjunction.
This refers to a non-returner who has already become free from the defilements of the form realm;
having abandoned and become detached from the forms of the five stages, they have become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
yet have not yet become free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, having abandoned and become detached from the forms of those four stages.

One who has already abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna has already severed and become detached from all forms belonging to those three stages.
One who has already abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna [is likewise described].
The various forms of the second dhyāna have already been abandoned and dissociated from;
however, one has not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
The various forms of that single stage [the first dhyāna] have already been abandoned and dissociated from.
Regarding the disciples of the World-Honored One who possess right view:
have their feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness been severed?
Are those feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness dissociated [from defilements]?
The answer is: it is the dissociation from feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;
those feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousness have already been abandoned.

That is to say, for an Arhat, the feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousness to be abandoned through vision and cultivation within the three realms have already been abandoned and dissociated.
The non-returner has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness;

the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that are to be abandoned through the vision of the three realms and through cultivation across the eight stages have been abandoned and disjoined from their fetters.
Having already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite consciousness but not yet having become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness,

one has already abandoned and is dissociated from the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that are to be abandoned by insight into the three realms and those to be abandoned by cultivation in the seven stages.
Up until one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna, the feeling, perception, formations,
and consciousness that are to be abandoned through seeing and the cultivation of the [lower] three realms have been abandoned and are dissociated;

however, for a stream-enterer or a once-returner, while the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness to be abandoned through seeing the three realms have been abandoned and are dissociated, there remains feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that have been abandoned but are not yet dissociated.
This refers to those who are "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula), "once-returners" (sakṛdāgāmin), or "one-interval" (ekavicika) practitioners,
who have already abandoned and fully understood the superior and intermediate grades of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm;
they remain bound only by the inferior grades of fetters associated with the corresponding feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
In this context, one who is a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) has already abandoned the first three or four grades of fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm,
as well as the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with them.

Nevertheless, those associated feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are still bound by way of being objects (*ālambana*) for the remaining six or five grades of fetters of the desire realm.
A once-returner has already abandoned the first six grades of fetters of the desire realm,
and has also abandoned the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with them;
yet those associated feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness remain bound by the objects of the final three grades of fetters of the desire realm.
An ekabījī has already abandoned the seven or eight grades of fetters of the desire realm,
as well as the corresponding feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Nevertheless,
those corresponding feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are still bound by the objects of the two or one remaining grades of fetters of the desire realm.
This is called "already abandoned but not yet dissociated.

Question: When those who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) abandon the highest and highest degrees (adhimātra-adhimātra) of fetters (saṃyojana) in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), do they also simultaneously abandon the associated feelings (vedanā) and so forth?
Those associated factors, such as feeling and so forth, are still bound by the objects of the eight grades of fetters.
When one abandons the upper and middle grades of fetters of the desire realm,
one also abandons those associated factors, such as feeling and so forth.
Since those associated [factors] such as feeling and so forth are still bound by the seven categories of fetters as their objects,
why is the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) not mentioned here?

It is only said that those who go from family to family (*kulaṃkula*), those who return once more (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and those who have one interval remaining (*ekavicika*) are bound [by fetters], but it is not said that those whose [fetters] have not been abandoned or those whose [fetters] have been abandoned are not disjoined [from them].
One should know that this meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*), for what ought to have been stated was not stated.
Furthermore, for those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the characteristics of their destruction are not fixed;
therefore, this is not mentioned.
That is to say, such a principle does not apply to those who are bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*).
This principle applies to those who are not yet free from all fetters (*abandhana*).
It likewise applies to the three types of practitioners, such as those who go from family to family (*kulaṃkula*) and so forth;
it is taught because their characteristics are unimpaired and certain.
Furthermore, regarding those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*):
if they sever one or two categories of fetters belonging to the desire realm,
this is not mentioned because there is no possibility of death and rebirth [within that same existence].
It is as when one has severed five categories [of afflictions].

That is to say, once a practitioner of yoga has attained the first fruit and initiates the great preparatory effort (*prayoga*) to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm abandoned through cultivation,
it is absolutely impossible for death or rebirth to occur while even a single category of fetter remains unsevered.
Just as when five grades [of fetters] have been severed,
there is necessarily no possibility of death and rebirth while the sixth grade of fetter remains unsevered;
since the three types such as *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) do involve death and rebirth, they are specifically mentioned here.
Question: In the eight stages of the form and formless realms, there are also cases where feelings and so forth have been abandoned yet lack the status of being dissociated from their fetters;
and there are also cases where they remain bound despite not having been abandoned, such as when one grade has been abandoned but the remaining eight grades still bind.
Up until the eighth grade has been abandoned, one remains bound by the ninth grade. Why, in this context, is only the desire realm mentioned and not the form realm and the formless realm?

It should have been stated, yet it was not; [the reason is as follows: [The answer: Although it should have been stated, it was not. This is because the abandonment of the afflictions in the form and formless realms occurs simultaneously with the abandonment of the afflictions in the desire realm. Furthermore, since the afflictions of the higher realms are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) in the same manner as those of the desire realm, they are subsumed within that discussion. Moreover, because the afflictions of the desire realm are the most coarse and prominent, they are specifically singled out for mention. Finally, the teaching is intended to demonstrate that the abandonment of the afflictions of the desire realm serves as the foundation for the subsequent abandonment of the afflictions of the higher realms. Therefore, although it should have been stated, it was not.
One should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, herein we have merely shown the initial entry into the preparatory stage (*prayoga*);
by speaking of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), we have also spoken of that [higher realm].
Furthermore, by gradually abandoning the fetters of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation, various types of *pudgalas* are established.
Specifically, those who have abandoned three or four [fetters] are called "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*);
if they have abandoned the sixth, they are called "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
If one has abandoned seven or eight [categories of defilements], they are called a "One-Interval" (ekāvacara).
Since there is no such principle for the gradual abandonment of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the higher realms, it is not so stated.
Question: Regarding the abandonment of the inferior grade of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, which is equivalent to a single interval,
there are cases where they have already been abandoned yet lack the status of dissociation (*visamyoga*),
as well as cases where they remain bound and thus have not been abandoned.

In this context, why is it stated that only the abandonment of the superior and medium grades of fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm is mentioned?
Furthermore, the associated feeling, perception, formations,
and consciousness also possess the sense of being bound by superior and medium grades of fetters.
If one has abandoned the eight highest grades [of defilements], one is still bound;
if one has abandoned the seven middle-high grades, one is still bound;
if one has abandoned three, four, six, or five [grades], one is still bound.
Why is it that only the fetters of the inferior grade are mentioned?
The answer is: although they should also have been mentioned, their omission should be understood as an abbreviated statement made with the intention of leaving something unsaid.
This is intended to increase the power of reflection for the wise.
Herein, the "one who goes from family to family" (kulaṃkula) is a distinction of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna);
the "one with one interval" (ekavīcika) is a distinction of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
There are two types of "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula):
namely, the distinction between those who are reborn in two families and those who are reborn in three families.
Those reborn in two families are those who have abandoned the first four grades of fetters of the desire realm.
There remain the seeds of the two types of existence in the desire realm for one who is born into three families;
that is to say, for one who has severed the first three grades of fetters in the desire realm,
there remain the seeds of the three types of existence in the desire realm.
Question: Why is it that one who has severed five grades of fetters is not designated as a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family)?
Answer: Because if the fifth grade is severed, the sixth must necessarily be severed, thereby becoming a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
This is because the nature of the sixth grade of fetter is weak and inferior; it cannot alone obstruct the realization of the fruit of a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Just as a single strand of thread cannot restrain an elephant,
so too is one who is "one-interval" (ekavicika):
this refers to one who has severed the first seven or eight grades of fetters within the desire realm.
There remains one seed of existence in the desire realm.
Question: Since they may still have two categories of fetters remaining, why are they called "one-interval" (ekavīcika)?
Answer: It is not because a single grade of affliction remains that one is called a "single-interval" (ekavīcika);
rather, it is because he possesses the seed of one existence that he is named a single-interval.
Other masters say that one who has not yet abandoned eight grades [of afflictions] is called a single-interval.
Why is this? Because if the eighth [grade of fetters] is severed, the ninth must necessarily be severed, thereby constituting the state of a Non-returner (anāgāmin).
This is because the nature of the ninth grade of fetters is weak and inferior; it cannot alone obstruct the realization of the fruit of Non-returning.
Just as a single strand of thread cannot restrain an elephant,
so it is with one who has severed five [fetters] and is called a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula).
According to the true meaning:
One who has abandoned eight grades [of afflictions] is called an "ekavicika" (one-interval);
one who has not abandoned five grades is called a "kulankula" (family-to-family). Why is this so?
Once the five categories [of afflictions] have been abandoned, if one abandons the sixth, one realizes the fruit of a Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).

At that point, although there still exist in the desire realm, within one's own level, karmas capable of projecting a homogeneous class of beings (nikāyasabhāga) and karmas destined for maturation, their capacity to yield results does not constitute an extreme obstruction.

Because the nature of the sixth category of fetters is weak and inferior, it cannot by itself obstruct the realization of the fruit of once-returner; therefore, there is no mention of "one who has abandoned five" among those called *kulaṃkula*.
Once the eighth category has been abandoned, if the ninth is abandoned, one realizes the fruit of non-returner.
It is certain that there is no principle for the karma belonging to one's own level— which projects the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga) and is destined to ripen—
to yield its fruit when one has resolved not to be born in the desire realm;
such a state constitutes an extreme obstruction.

Although the fetters of the ninth category are weak by nature, they can assist those [fetters] that obstruct the fruit of Non-returner; therefore, one who has abandoned eight of them is called an "Ekavīcika" (One-Interval).
For this reason, it is said that for sentient beings in these three stages, karma that must necessarily ripen creates an extreme obstacle.
First, those who are about to enter the stage of patience from the summit;
second, those about to realize the stage of the non-returner;
third, those about to attain the stage of the arhat.

This means that when one is about to enter the stage of *kṣānti* from the stage of the *mūrdhan*, there is a sense in which all karma that leads to rebirth in the miserable destinies (*durgati*)—which is certain to ripen and project a new existence (*nikāyasabhāga*)—is utterly obstructed. The meaning of the statement is:
"If you attain the stage of *kṣānti*, you will certainly not undergo birth in the three miserable destinies."
"In whose body shall I receive the maturation [of this karma],
such that I create such an extreme obstacle for them?
This was when the Noble One was about to become free from the defilements of the desire realm.
This means that the karma which draws forth a common lot (*nikāya-sabhāga*) in the desire realm and is destined to ripen acts as an extreme obstacle;
it implies that if you realize the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), you will certainly not undergo birth in the desire realm again.
"In whose body shall I receive the maturation [of this karma],
such that I create such an extreme obstacle for them?

When a Noble One is about to become free from the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the two realms (*dhātu*) possess the projecting force for the commonality of the group (*nikāyasabhāga*).
The meaning of the statement that "karma to be experienced in a fixed state acts as an extreme obstacle" is this:
"If you were to become an Arhat, you would certainly not undergo further rebirth;
in whose body, then, would I receive the maturation [of this karma]?"
Because this creates extreme obstacles for them,
those who have abandoned five [fetters] are called "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula);
those who have abandoned the eighth are called "one-interval" (ekavicika).
There are two types of "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula): namely, the family-to-family among gods and the family-to-family among humans.
Regarding the family-to-family among gods, this refers to those who undergo either two or three births within the celestial realms.
They may undergo two or three births in one celestial realm, or two or three celestial realms;
or they may undergo two or three births in one celestial family, or two or three celestial families.
Regarding the phrase "a person of many births":
this refers to one who, among human beings, undergoes two or three births;
or who, in one continent, or two continents, or three continents, undergoes two or three births.
One may receive two or three births in one household, or two or three households, or three households.
There are two types of "one-interval" (ekāvacara):
namely, the one-interval of the devas and the one-interval of humans.
"One interval in the heavens" means that one receives only a single birth in the celestial realms—
either among the Gods of the Four Great Kings or among the Thirty-three Gods.
Either the Yāma Heaven,
or the Tuṣita Heaven,
or the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
Or one who has received this single birth among the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods;
such is the "one-interval" person (ekavicika).
That is to say, among human beings, one receives only a single birth,
whether in Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, or Aparagoyānīya.
Experiencing this single birth,
one is established as a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner due to three conditions.
First, it is by reason of karma.
Second, by way of the faculties;
third, by way of the fetters;
and by way of karma. Regarding "by way of karma":
This refers to having previously performed and accumulated karma for two or three existences (*bhava*) within the desire realm.
Regarding "by way of the faculties" (*indriya*):

it means that such a person has already attained the untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) which serve as the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to three or four grades of fetters (*saṃyojana*) belonging to the desire realm.
Regarding "by way of fetters": this refers to one who has already abandoned three or four categories of fetters belonging to the desire realm;
if any one of these three conditions is not fulfilled, they are not called a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family).
An ekabijin is established by way of three conditions:
first, by way of karma;
second, by way of the faculties (indriya).
Third, by way of fetters.
Regarding "by way of karma," it refers to having previously performed and accumulated karma for a single existence within the desire realm.
Regarding "by way of the faculties" (indriya):

this refers to those who have already attained the untainted faculties (anāsravendriya) that serve as the antidote to seven or eight grades of fetters (saṃyojana) belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Regarding "by way of fetters":
this refers to one who has already abandoned seven or eight grades of fetters pertaining to the desire realm;
if any one of these three conditions is not fulfilled, they are not designated as an *ekavīcika*.
Question: Does a noble one (ārya) create karma that projects the homogeneous character (nikāyasabhāga) in the desire realm? Some say he does not. Why is this?
Because the desire realm abounds in many faults and calamities.
Therefore, noble ones do not create karma that projects a homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) in the desire realm;
they only create karma that completes a homogeneous class in the desire realm.
Question: If this is so, how should one interpret what is stated in the Sūtra?
As stated in a sutra,
when the Buddha was praising Maitreya’s attainment of buddhahood,
there were among those in the assembly some who were still in training and had not yet abandoned desire.
Having heard this, he made a vow:
"May I pass into parinirvāṇa only after I have seen those sublime and wondrous things.
The answer is that because his resources were abundant and he had not yet encountered heavy suffering, he temporarily made this vow.
If they encounter heavy suffering,
they immediately become weary of and detached from all existence,
thinking to themselves:
If such a thing were possible— just as a frightened bird swiftly flies into the sky—
I too would now swiftly hasten toward parinirvāṇa; therefore,
he did not create karma that leads to rebirth in the common lot of the desire realm.
He asserts this:
the karma for two or three existences in the "house-to-house" (kulaṃkula) stage is created during the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), not during the state of an noble one (ārya).
The fetters of three or four categories are abandoned either in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or in the stage of an noble one (*ārya*).
Karmas that lead to one more birth (*ekavicika*) or one existence (*ekabhavika*) are created only in the stage of an ordinary person.

Regarding the fetters of seven or eight categories, they are abandoned either in the stage of an ordinary person or in the stage of an noble one; some say that noble ones also create karma that projects a homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) within the desire realm.
The fruit of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) induced by that karma is of intense power,
exceptionally sublime and exquisite,
pure and brilliantly white.
Free from all faults and afflictions,
free from all calamities and misfortunes,
it accords with wholesome qualities.
They state this:

for those who go from family to family (*kulaṃkula*), the karma for two or three existences is created either in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or in the stage of a noble one (*ārya*); and the four or three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned either in the stage of an ordinary person or in the stage of a noble one.

The karma of one who is bound to one more birth (*ekavīcika*) or of one existence (*ekabhavika*) is created either in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or in the stage of a noble one (*ārya*).
Seven or eight grades of fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned either in the stage of an ordinary person or in the stage of a noble one.
Question: What of a noble one who has undergone rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
Furthermore, could one be reborn in the two higher realms? If one were not, what fault would there be?
There are faults in both cases.
If one were reborn [there],...
How should one interpret the statement in the *Ekottarika Āgama*?
As it says: "There are five kinds of persons:
those who plant the seeds here and reach final realization here."
1. Those who have at most seven more rebirths;
2. those who go from family to family;
3. those who return only once.
Fourth, those with one interval;
fifth, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life.
These are those who plant the seeds in this very life.
This refers to entering the state of rightness and departure from birth while in the desire realm.
"Reaching the ultimate in this interval" means attaining the exhaustion of all outflows while in the desire realm.
There are five types of persons (*pudgala*).
Sowing the seeds here and reaching completion there:
first, attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state;
second, attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth.
Third, parinirvāṇa through application;
fourth, parinirvāṇa without application;
fifth, parinirvāṇa by ascending the stream.
"Those who sow the seeds in this interval" refers to those in the desire realm who enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
"Those who reach the ultimate in that interval" refers to those same individuals.
If it is said that one attains the exhaustion of all outflows while in the realms of form or formlessness,
how then should one interpret the verse from the *Devapraśna-sūtra* which states: "If one does not take birth"?
As it is said in that verse:
Three know the Dharma here; Two advance therein;
having attained such advancement, Both ascend to the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers.
Regarding that second explanation,
how is it further to be reconciled?
As it is said:
"Venerable sir, if you would instruct me in accordance with the Dharma,
I shall practice it and bring an end to suffering right here.
If you do not so instruct me, I have heard that the Akaniṣṭha Heaven is most excellent."
"I shall be reborn there after my life ends. [Objection:
If that is so, a noble one (ārya) who has passed through births in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) can no longer be reborn in the form or formless realms (rūpārūpyadhātu).
[Question: If this is the case, how are you to reconcile this with the verse from the *Devaputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*?
Answer: Although those two ascended to the Brahma-world, it was not through death and rebirth.
There was a maiden named Gopikā who had three bhikṣus who would regularly enter her house and preach the Dharma to her with exquisite voices.
Having heard the Dharma, she conceived pure faith in her heart;
weary of her female body, she vowed to become a man.
At the end of her life, she was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
He was the son of Śakra, handsome and exquisite;
the devas gave him the name Gopaka.
At that time, three bhikṣus, out of attachment to their own voices, [acted as follows].
At the end of his life, he was reborn among the gandharvas.
As for the gandharvas,
they are celestial musicians who constantly provide music for the devas day and night.
When Gopaka saw him, he recognized him and said, "In the past,
I heard your voice teaching the Dharma and became weary of this female body;
I vowed that as a man, upon the end of my life, I would be reborn here in the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
As a son of Śakra, you will be dignified and most exquisite.
Having practiced the unsurpassed holy life,
would you rather be born among the lowly gandharvas?
When the three *nandana* deities heard those words, two of them were deeply ashamed;
having become free from the defilement of desire, they ascended to the Brahmā-purohita heaven by means of their supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
One remained here as before. Therefore, although those two ascended to the Brahma-world, it was not a case of death and rebirth.
Some say that although those two undergo death and birth, it does not contradict reason;
namely, that one who previously among humans had merely cultivated and attained the *nirvedhabhāgīya* [aids to penetration] dies and is born among the *gandharvas*.
Because Gopaka mocked them, the two felt extreme shame;
they entered the path of seeing, became free from the defilements of the desire realm,
realized the fruit of non-returning, and at the end of their lives were reborn among the Brahmapurohita devas.
Therefore, the existence of birth and death does not contradict reason.
Question: How, then, is that second explanation to be reconciled?
As it is said:
"Venerable sir, I practice according to the principle," as explained at length above.
Answer: Śakra did not understand the Abhidharma;
because he did not know that noble ones who have been reborn in the desire realm cannot be reborn in higher realms, he spoke these words.
Question: He uttered words contrary to reason in the presence of the Buddha.
Why did the World-Honored One not reprimand and prohibit this?
The answer is: The Buddha knew that although those words violated reason, they did not obstruct the Path; therefore, he did not reprimand or prohibit them.
Later, upon entering the dharma-nature, he will naturally understand it himself; fearing that he might feel shame, [the Buddha] does not rebuke him.
Some say that noble ones who have undergone births in the desire realm can also be born in the form and formless realms.
Question: If that is so, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Ekottarika-āgama*,
such as the passage beginning, "There are five types of persons," and so forth, at length?
Answer: There are two kinds of noble ones (ārya):
first, those who possess confusion and transition;
second, those who are free from confusion and free from transition.
Regarding that which is disordered and subject to transference,
it should be understood as explained in the *Ārya-rājapraśnīya-sūtra*.
Regarding that which is neither disordered nor subject to transference:
It should be understood as explained in the *Ekottarika-āgama*.
By this principle, both explanations are well-integrated.
The critique states:
If a noble one (*ārya*) who has undergone rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) does not, as a rule, take birth again in the form or formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*). Why is this?
Because for a noble one who has undergone rebirth in the desire realm, three things necessarily do not exist.
First, non-retrogression;
second, non-transformation of the faculties;
third, not being born in the form or formless realms.
Because the Noble Path abides for a long time within that continuum and is extremely firm,
and fearing that the suffering in the two upper realms might likewise endure for a long duration as it does in the desire realm,
[this was stated]. *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 53.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 54,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Two: The Aggregate of Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha), Chapter One: The Sub-section on the Unwholesome (Akuśala-nikāya), Part Nine. There are five types of persons (pudgala).

That is to say: those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those who follow by Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and those who have realized the body (*kāyasākṣin*).
This is explained at length.
Question: For what reason does the Venerable [Kātyāyanīputra] compose this treatise on the Aggregate of Grasping (*upādānaskandha*) based upon these five types of persons (*pudgala*)?
In the subsequent section on the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), the treatise is composed based on seven types of persons (*pudgala*).

That is to say, to these five [types], the one liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*) and the one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*) are added; this is because such is the intention of the author of the treatise.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Furthermore, within this *saṃyojana-skandha*, the discussion is conducted based on those who possess fetters (*saṃyojana*); therefore, the latter two [fetters] are not mentioned.
Within the *jñāna-samādhi-skandha*, the discussion is conducted based on those who possess knowledge and concentration (*jñāna-samādhi*); therefore [the others are not mentioned].
Those who possess fetters and those who are free from fetters should both be discussed.
Furthermore, since this treatise on the aggregate of fetters (saṃyojanaskandha) is composed based on those who possess afflictions (kleśa), the latter two [categories] are not mentioned.
Since this treatise is composed based on those who possess wisdom and meditative concentration within the aggregate of wisdom and concentration,
it should speak of both those with afflictions and those without them.
Furthermore, in this aggregate of fetters, the *pudgala* (person) is taken as the subject matter.
Because the afflictions serve as the gateway, the latter two [aggregates] are not mentioned; however,
within the aggregates of wisdom and meditative concentration, the *pudgala* (person) serves as the chapter heading,
and because wisdom and concentration serve as the gateway, the latter two are also mentioned there.
Therefore, this treatise was composed based on five [categories] and seven types of persons (*pudgala*).
What is the person who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārin*)?
It refers to a certain class of individuals.
By nature, he possesses much faith, much affection, much kindness, much joy, much compliance, and much resolute conviction;
he does not delight in deliberation, investigation, or discernment.
It is because his nature is characterized by such abundance of faith and the like that [he is thus].
At times, they may encounter a Buddha or a disciple of the Buddha who expounds the essential points of the Dharma through instruction and admonition,
extensively elucidating the meanings of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth.
He thinks to himself:
"It is most excellent that for my sake he has explained the meanings of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and so forth;
he desires that I cultivate such contemplative practices."

I should diligently and unerringly train myself in those practices; having trained in the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and so forth, once they have reached full maturity, I shall gradually give rise to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Next, there arises the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
From this point, all fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are termed "followers by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*).
This person who is a follower by faith (*śraddhānusāri-pudgala*)...
Or they are stream-enterers-in-training,
or once-returners-in-training,
or non-returners-in-training.
That is to say, whether one is still bound by all fetters or has already abandoned up to five grades of fetters and entered the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma),
such a person is termed a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-pratipannaka) during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga).
If, having abandoned six grades or even up to eight grades of fetters, one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma),
one is termed a candidate for the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka) during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga).
If, having abandoned the defilements of the realm of desire, or even up to the realm of nothingness, one enters into right determination (samyaktva-niyāma),
one is termed a "candidate for non-returner" (anāgāmipratipannaka) during the fifteen moments of mind in the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
What is a person who practices in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusārī-pudgala)?
It refers to a certain type of individual who,
by their original nature, possesses much reflection, much deliberation, much investigation, and much discernment.
They lack faith, affection, aspiration, compliance, and resolute conviction,
because by their very nature they are prone to excessive reflection and the like.
Occasionally, however, they may encounter a Buddha or a disciple of the Buddha who explains the essential points of the Dharma and provides instructions and admonitions.
He extensively expounded for him the meanings of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and so forth.
He then thought:
"The meanings of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and so forth have been taught to me."
I should investigate whether this is real or false; having investigated it thoroughly and known it to be without error,
I further reflect as follows:
"Excellent indeed!
Since you wish to have me cultivate such contemplative practices,
I shall apply myself with unerring diligence to their cultivation and study."
The remaining details are explained at length as in the case of the *śraddhānusārin*.
What is a person of *śraddhādhimukta*?

It refers to one who, having followed the *śraddhānusārin*, attains the knowledge of the category of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and thereby abandons the state of being a *śraddhānusārin* to attain the state of being a *śraddhādhimukta*. Regarding this, what is it that they abandon and what do they attain at that time?

Answer: "Abandoning the name" means abandoning the name of a follower by faith (śraddhānusārin); "attaining the name" means attaining the name of one resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta). It is called "abandoning the path" because one abandons the name;
it is called "attaining the path" because one attains the name.
One who abandons the path abandons the path of seeing;
one who attains the path attains the path of cultivation.
This refers to the person characterized by faith and resolve (śraddhādhimukta).
Or they may be stream-enterers;
or those practicing for the fruit of once-returning;
or those who have attained the fruit of once-returning.
Either one who is a candidate for the fruit of non-returning,
or one who has attained the fruit of non-returning,
or one who is a candidate for arhatship.
That is to say, one who abides in the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) but has not yet progressed to a higher stage is called "abiding in the fruit of stream-entry.
If one progresses from this state, they are called "entering the path toward once-returning" (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*).
If one abides in the fruit of once-returning but has not yet progressed to a higher stage, they are called "abiding in the fruit of once-returning."
If one progresses from this stage, it is called the "candidate for the fruit of non-returning" (anāgāmipratipannaka).
If one abides in the fruit of non-returning without yet progressing further, it is called the "fruit of non-returning" (anāgāmiphala).
If one progresses from this fruit, it is called the "candidate for arhatship" (arhattvapratipannaka).
What is the person who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta-pudgala*)?

It refers to one who, having practiced according to the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), attains the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) and thereby relinquishes the status of practicing according to the Dharma.
One attains the state of "seeing and reaching.
Question: What does one abandon and what does one attain at that time?
Answer: One abandons the name and attains the name; one abandons the path and attains the path.
"Abandoning the name" means abandoning the name "follower by dharma" (dharmānusārin).
"Obtaining the name" means obtaining the name "attainer through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
"Abandoning the path" means abandoning the path of vision (darśanamārga).
One who has attained the path attains the cultivation of the path;
this person of "attainment through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta-pudgala) is either one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna).
Up to and including those who are candidates for arhatship (*arhattvaprati-pannaka*),
their characteristics should be explained as in the case of those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).
What is a person who is a bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin*)?

That is to say, one who is either resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) or attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), having physically realized the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) but not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) through wisdom,
abandons the state of being resolved through faith or attained through vision and attains the realization through the body (*kāyasākṣin*).
Question: What is it that is abandoned and what is attained at that time?
The masters of foreign lands (bahirdeśaka) explain it thus:
"Abandonment" means attaining the name [of abandonment], and "attainment" means attaining the path.
Regarding the abandonment of names: one abandons the name "one liberated through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) or "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Regarding the acquisition of names: one acquires the name "bodily witness" (*kāyasākṣin*).
Regarding the abandonment of the path: one abandons the path of "one liberated through faith" or "attained through vision."
One who has attained the Path attains the realization of the Path within their own body.
The masters of the treatises in Kaśmīra say that this is designated by the name "abandonment" and the name "attainment."
One does not attain the Path by abandoning the Path.

This is because when those with faith-based liberation (śraddhādhimukta) and others attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), they neither abandon nor newly acquire the untainted path (anāsravamārga).
What, then, is a person liberated through wisdom (prajñāvimukta)?
That is to say, one who is either liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) or attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) exhausts all outflows (*āsrava*) solely by means of wisdom,
yet has not yet physically realized the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
Upon relinquishing that state of being liberated through faith or attained through vision, such a person attains liberation through wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*).
Question: At that time, what is it that is abandoned and what is it that is attained?
Answer: One abandons the name and attains the name; one abandons the path and attains the path.
Regarding the abandonment of names: one abandons the names "one liberated through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) or "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Regarding the acquisition of names: one acquires the name "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*).
Regarding the abandonment of the path: one abandons the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
One who has attained the path attains the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
What is a person liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*)?
It refers to one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), or one who has reached through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), or one who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*).
Having personally realized the eight liberations with the body and exhausted all outflows through wisdom, he attains liberation through wisdom by means of equanimity;
he may be one who has attained through vision, one who has attained through reaching, or one who has attained through bodily realization, thereby becoming doubly liberated.
If one first attains the fruit of arhatship and subsequently attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti),

that person relinquishes the designation of "liberated by wisdom" (prajñāvimukta) and acquires the designation of "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta); it is merely a matter of relinquishing one name and acquiring another.
It is not that one attains the path by abandoning the path, as it is said regarding the attainment of bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin*) by abandoning faith-understanding (*śraddhādhimukta*) and so forth.
If one first attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and subsequently attains the fruit of arhatship,
one abandons the state of bodily witness and attains the state of one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
"Abandoning names and attaining names; abandoning paths and attaining paths.
"Abandoning names" means abandoning the body to realize the name.
"Attaining names" means attaining the name of "liberation through both parts" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
Those who abandon the path abandon the path of cultivation;
those who attain the path attain the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
When bodhisattvas realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), they abandon the state of one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
One attains both-fold liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukti*).
Regarding the abandonment of names and the attainment of names: "abandoning the path" means abandoning the name of "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
This is because the stage of cultivation for a bodhisattva is designated as "one who has attained vision."
Regarding the attainment of a name: one attains the name "liberated in both ways" because all Buddhas are liberated in both ways.
Regarding the relinquishing of the path: this refers to relinquishing the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
One who attains the Path attains the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
The masters of the West (the Western teachers) say that during the stage of training (*śaikṣāvasthā*),
a bodhisattva first gives rise to the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and subsequently attains enlightenment (*bodhi*).
Having relinquished the body, he realizes both forms of liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukti*).
The masters of the Kaśmīra school state that one attains enlightenment in thirty-four moments of thought (*cittakṣaṇa*).
Because a Bodhisattva in the stage of training has not yet produced the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),

at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), they necessarily abandon the attainment of the "one who has attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and become one liberated by both parts (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).

This is because it is impossible for one of dull faculties who has not yet obtained the meditative attainment of cessation to become one liberated by both parts at the moment of attaining the knowledge of exhaustion.
Regarding those who attain liberation through both [tranquility and insight] without relying on the resolution of faith (*śraddhādhimukta*):
Question—Why is it called "liberation through both"?
Answer—Because there are two portions of obstacles.
First, the hindrance of afflictions;
second, the hindrance to liberation.
Because the mind is liberated from these two types of hindrances, they are called "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).

Question: If one first attains the fruit of arhatship and subsequently attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), from which hindrance to liberation is that mind liberated—is it with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava)?

Some say that because the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) [factors] are already liberated when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is attained by means of an outflow-free (*anāsrava*) mind, [therefore only the untainted are liberated].
The critique states: one should say this:
both the outflow-tainted and the outflow-free attain liberation.
Why is this? There are two kinds of liberation.
The first is mundane liberation.
Second, regarding liberation while in the body:
when one has not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the mind that enters and emerges from that absorption cannot function within the world.
Because it does not function within the world, it cannot be said to exist "in the body."
If one attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), because the mind that enters and emerges from this state functions within the body, it is called "liberation.
Therefore, both the contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava) minds attain liberation.

Just as the name "one liberated through both parts" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) is established based on its meaning, the names of the preceding five [types of practitioners] should likewise be established based on their meanings.
Question: Why is one called a "follower by faith" (śraddhānusārin)?
Answer: Because they rely on faith and practice in accordance with faith, they are called "followers by faith" (śraddhānusārin).
That is to say, relying on contaminated faith, they practice in accordance with uncontaminated faith;
relying on faith that is bound, they practice in accordance with faith that is liberated.
One follows the faith that is bound by existence and the faith that is dissociated from it;
because one first gains entry into the Noble Path through faith,
such a person has, from the very beginning, possessed a nature characterized by a predominance of faith.
If one hears others exhorting them, "You should engage in agriculture to sustain yourself," they do not reflect upon whether what they are doing is appropriate or inappropriate,
or whether they are capable of doing it or incapable of doing it.
If it is appropriate for them to exist, they will act as if they do not exist;
having heard this, they act accordingly.
Or, they may hear others exhorting them, saying, "You should engage in trade."
Some should serve kings,
while others should study various arts and crafts such as writing, arithmetic, and seal-engraving to provide for their own livelihood;
yet they do not reflect upon this.
To speak at length, up to:
having heard this, they act upon it immediately;
or, when hearing others exhort them, "You should go forth into homelessness," they likewise do not reflect or examine it.
Whether one should leave the household life or should not; whether one is able to leave it or unable to leave it;

whether one is able to maintain the precepts or unable to maintain them; whether there is favorable opportunity or no favorable opportunity—having heard the exhortation of others, one immediately leaves the household life.
Once you have gone forth,
if you hear others exhorting you, "You should recite and study that," do not examine whether it should or should not be recited and studied.
Whether one is able to recite and study it or unable to recite and study it;
whether it is suitable or unsuitable;
and whether it is a sūtra.
For the Vinaya and for the Abhidharma;
having heard the exhortations of others, he immediately began to recite and study them.
Or, upon hearing others exhorting him to attend to the affairs of the Saṃgha,
he does not reflect or examine whether what he is to do is appropriate or inappropriate,
or whether he is capable of doing it or incapable.
If it is suitable, they act as if it were unsuitable;
having heard [the instruction], they act immediately.
Or, upon hearing others exhorting them to dwell in an araṇya, they do not even reflect upon it.
"Should I abide or should I not abide?
Am I able to abide or am I unable to abide?
Is there an opportunity or is there no opportunity?"
Having heard this, he remained [in that state].

As he gradually cultivated the preparatory practices for the Noble Path, they successively induced the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), which immediately gave rise to the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma regarding Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
From this point, during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing, one is called a "follower by faith" (śraddhānusārin).
Question: Why is one called a "follower of the Dharma" (dharmānusārin)?
Answer: Because they practice in accordance with the Dharma and follow the Dharma, they are called a follower of the Dharma.
That is to say: practicing in accordance with untainted phenomena based on tainted phenomena;
and practicing in accordance with liberated phenomena based on bound phenomena.
Based on phenomena associated with existence, they proceed toward phenomena dissociated from existence;
through wisdom as their primary acquisition, they first enter the Noble Path.
This is because such a type of person has, from the very beginning, possessed a nature characterized by abundant wisdom.
If he hears others exhorting him, saying, "You should engage in agriculture to sustain yourself," he then reflects and examines:
"Is this something I ought to do, or is it something I ought not to do?"
Whether an action can be performed or cannot be performed,
whether it is appropriate or inappropriate,
one should examine and investigate thoroughly before acting.
The rest is as extensively explained previously regarding the faith-follower (*śraddhānusārin*).

As they gradually cultivate the preparatory application for the noble path, it successively induces the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), which immediately induces the Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma concerning Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
From this point, during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing, one is called a "follower of the Dharma" (dharmānusārī).
Regarding the follower by faith (śraddhānusārī), it is said that as much faith as they possess, so much wisdom do they possess.
As for the follower of the Dharma:
If there is such an amount of wisdom, there is likewise such an amount of faith.
For what reason is one called a "follower by faith" (śraddhānusārin) and another a "follower by dharma" (dharmānusārin)?

Answer: Either one enters the noble path by practicing through mere faith in others' successive guidance, or one enters the noble path by practicing through one's own contemplation of their successive guidance.
One who enters the noble path by practicing through mere faith in others' successive guidance is called a "follower by faith" (śraddhānusārin).
If one enters the noble path through successive cultivation by means of personal reflection, they are called a "follower of the Dharma" (dharmānusārī).
Furthermore, there are those who enter the noble path through the power of causes, the power of application, or the power of heedfulness, none of which are extensive.
Alternatively, one enters the noble path through all three powers being fully extensive.
If one enters the noble path through none of the three powers being extensive, this is called "following by faith" (śraddhānusārin).
If one enters the noble path through all three powers being fully developed, this is called "Dharma-follower" (dharmānusārī).
Furthermore, one may enter the noble path either by way of the practice of tranquility (śamatha) or by way of the practice of insight (vipaśyanā).
If one enters the noble path by way of the practice of tranquility (śamatha), they are called a follower by faith (śraddhānusārin).
If one enters the noble path by way of the practice of insight (vipaśyanā), they are called a follower of the Dharma (dharmānusārin).
Furthermore, some delight in śamatha.
Those who delight in vipaśyanā and delight in śamatha are called followers by faith (śraddhānusārin).
Those who delight in vipaśyanā are called followers of the Dharma (dharmānusārin).
This is also the case for those who delight in zeal (chanda).
Furthermore, one may enter the noble path preceded by serenity (śamatha),
or one may enter the noble path preceded by insight (vipaśyanā).
If one enters the noble path preceded by serenity, such a person is called a follower by faith (śraddhānusārin).
If one enters the noble path preceded by insight (vipaśyanā), they are called a Dharma-follower (dharmānusārin).
Furthermore, there are those for whom śamatha is predominant and those for whom vipaśyanā is predominant; those for whom śamatha is predominant are called faith-followers (śraddhānusārin).
One for whom vipaśyanā predominates is called a "follower by dharma" (dharmānusārī).
Furthermore, either the mind is perfumed by śamatha and attains liberation through vipaśyanā,
or the mind is perfumed by vipaśyanā and attains liberation through śamatha.

If one attains liberation by means of the mind being permeated by calm abiding (*śamatha*) and relying upon insight (*vipaśyanā*), they are called a follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); if one attains liberation by means of the mind being permeated by insight and relying upon calm abiding, they are called a follower of the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
Furthermore, there are those with dull faculties and those with sharp faculties.
Those with dull faculties are called followers by faith (śraddhānusārin);
those with sharp faculties are called followers by dharma (dharmānusārin). Furthermore, there are those who speak of knowledge and those who open up knowledge.
Some say that those with dull faculties are called "followers by faith" (śraddhānusārin), while those with keen faculties are called "followers by dharma" (dharmānusārin).

Furthermore, one may enter the noble path either through the power of conditions or through the power of causes; if one enters the noble path through the power of conditions, they are called a follower by faith.
If one enters the noble path by the power of the cause, they are called a "Dharma-follower" (dharmānusārī).
Furthermore, there may be those who have attained the higher mind of śamatha, but not the higher wisdom of vipaśyanā.
Some attain superior insight (*vipaśyanā*) but not superior concentration (*samatha*).
The former is called "one who follows by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*);
the latter is called "one who follows by dharma" (*dharmānusārin*).
Furthermore, as the Blessed One has said, two causes and two conditions can give rise to right view:
first, externally hearing the sound of another's Dharma;
second, internally applying correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
If one hears many external sounds of the Dharma from others, they are called a follower by faith (śraddhānusārin).
If one has much internal correct mental attention (yoniśomanasikāra), they are called a follower of the Dharma (dharmānusārin).
Furthermore, as it is said in the Sūtra:
There are four qualities by which a person accomplishes much:
first, associating with virtuous persons;
second, hearing the true Dharma.
Third, proper mental attention;
fourth, practice in accordance with the Dharma.
One who frequently associates with virtuous persons and hears the true Dharma extensively is called a follower by faith (śraddhānusārin).
If one has much correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) and practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmanudharmapratipatti*), they are called a "follower of the Dharma" (*dharmānusārī*).
Furthermore, there may be those who frequently abide in the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*),
or those who frequently abide in the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha*).
Those who predominantly abide in the wholesome root of non-attachment are called followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*).
Those who predominantly abide in the wholesome root of non-delusion are called followers of the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
Furthermore, there may be sentient beings who possess external faith.
Those who internally contemplate the true Dharma while externally placing faith in sentient beings are called "followers by faith" (śraddhānusārin).
Those who internally contemplate the true Dharma are called "followers by Dharma" (dharmānusārin).
Question: For what reason is one called "resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*)?
Answer: Because one attains resolution through faith by relying upon faith, one is called "resolved through faith.
That is to say, by relying on the faith comprised within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one attains the resolution through faith comprised within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Based on the faith included within the path of approach and the faith included within the path of attaining the fruit, there is the resolution through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).
Furthermore, because that person, preceded by faith, has liberated the mind from the three fetters, they are therefore called one resolved through faith.
Question: For what reason is one called "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*)?
Answer: Because by relying on vision, one attains vision, one is called "attained through vision.
That is to say, by relying on the vision subsumed under the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), one attains the vision subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
It refers to the vision included within the path of approach and the vision included within the path that has reached the fruit.
Furthermore, because that person’s liberation from the three fetters is preceded by vision, they are called "one who has attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).

Question: Since those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta) should also be called those who have reached [the fruit] through faith (śraddhāgata), and those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) should also be called those resolved through vision (dṛṣṭyadhimukta), why is one designated as "resolved through faith" and the other as "attained through vision"?
Answer: Just as one who is liberated through faith is called "liberated through faith," so too should one who has attained through vision be called "liberated through vision.
And just as one who has attained through vision is called "attained through vision," so too should one who is liberated through faith be called "attained through faith."

If it were not so, one would desire to manifest distinct characteristics and distinct gateways in teaching the Dharma, so that wise persons might delight in receiving and upholding it without confusion.
Question: For what reason is it called the "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*)?
Answer: Because he has personally realized the eight liberations with his body, yet has not exhausted all outflows through wisdom, he is called a "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin).
Question: For what reason is one called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñāvimukta)?
Answer: Because they have exhausted all outflows through wisdom but have not yet personally realized the eight liberations with the body, they are called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñā-vimukta).
The term "doubly liberated" (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta) has already been explained as before.
Question: Just as two types of individuals (pudgala) are established based on the distinction between those of sharp and dull faculties within the path of seeing—
namely, the follower by faith (śraddhānusārin) and the follower by dharma (dharmānusārin)—
are two types of individuals likewise established based on the distinction between those of sharp and dull faculties within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga)?
This refers to those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who have attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Why is it that within the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), two types of persons (*pudgala*) are not established based on the distinction between dull and sharp faculties,
but are instead collectively described as one?
Is it one liberated by wisdom or one liberated both ways?
Answer: From the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness, there may be the path with outflows that serves as the antidote for abandonment.
Alternatively, the untainted path serves as the antidote for abandonment;
because the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception has only the untainted path as its antidote for abandonment,
a single *pudgala* is established in total.
Furthermore, among those in the preceding stage, there may be some who predominantly practice with desire, or others who do not;

yet, when they become free from the defilement of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, because their bodies and so forth are free from desire, they are collectively established as one type of *pudgala*.
Furthermore, among those in the preceding stage, there may be some who are predominantly characterized by delusion (*moha*),

or others who are not. When they become detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), because their bodies and so forth are free from delusion, they are collectively established as one type of person (*pudgala*).
Furthermore, in the preceding stage, there may be those who predominantly practice with pride or those who do not.

When they become free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, because their bodies and so forth are devoid of pride, they are collectively established as a single type of person (pudgala).
Furthermore, because liberation in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is equal, one person (*pudgala*) is established in total.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The liberation of the Tathāgata is equal and without distinction from the liberation of an Arhat Bhikṣu."
Furthermore, those in the stage of no-more-learning are alike in having cut the heavy topknots of the afflictions of the three realms,
alike in having severed the necks of the afflictions at the peak of existence (bhavāgra),
and alike in having transcended the final barriers and fords of the three realms.
Because they equally abandon all craving and desire within the three realms,
one person (pudgala) is established in total. Some say this:

Within the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there are likewise two types of persons (*pudgala*), namely: those liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) and those not liberated by time (*asamayavimukta*).
Question: If this is so, then only two types of persons should be established.
That is to say, there are the dull-witted and the sharp-witted.
Alternatively, one should establish six types of *pudgalas*,
namely two for each of the stages of the seeker (*śaikṣa*), the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those in the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
From the faith-follower (*śraddhānusārin*) up to the sixth type, the one liberated at an improper time (*asamayavimukta*).
How are the seven types of persons (*pudgala*) established?
Answer: They are established as sevenfold by virtue of five conditions.
First, by way of application;
second, by way of faculties; third, by way of meditative concentration;
and fourth, by way of liberation.
Fifth, by way of concentration and liberation.
Regarding "by way of application," this refers to those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).
In terms of faculties, this refers to those with faith-resolve (śraddhādhimukta) and those who have attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
In terms of meditative concentration, this refers to the bodily witness (kāyasākṣin).
"By way of liberation" refers to those liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta).
"By way of both concentration and liberation" refers to those liberated in both ways (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta).
As for the follower by faith (śraddhānusārin), one might say that he is [liberated] in one way.
That is to say, among the seven types, they are called "followers by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*).
Alternatively, one should speak of three based on their faculties (*indriya*), namely: inferior, medium, and superior.
Or, one should speak of five based on their spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
From those of the nature of falling back (*parihāṇadharman*) up to those capable of reaching the ultimate (*prativedhanādharman*),
or rather, fifteen [types] should be stated, by way of the paths.

This refers to the stages from the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) up to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Alternatively, one should state seventy-three,
by reason of the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*).
That is to say, there are ten [levels] for those bound by all fetters in the desire realm who have abandoned from one up to nine grades of defilement;
and there are nine [levels] for those who have abandoned from one up to nine grades of defilement in the first dhyāna.
The tenth [category] of the desire realm—
that is, those bound by all fetters (sakalabandhana) in the first dhyāna— is not mentioned separately;
subsequent cases should be understood accordingly.
Up to the abandonment of one grade up to nine grades of defilement in the sphere of nothingness, there are nine; these combined with the previous total make seventy-three.
Alternatively, it should be stated that there are six hundred and fifty-seven.
This refers to the basis (*āśraya*).
Specifically, for each of the three continents and the six heavens of the desire realm, there are the seventy-three types previously mentioned as bases.

If one combines these with the faculties (*indriya*), lineages (*gotra*), paths (*mārga*), and stages of freedom from defilement (*vairāgya-bhūmi*)—taken two at a time, three at a time, four at a time, or five at a time—the number increases accordingly; this should be reflected upon according to the principles.
If analyzed according to the moments of its existence within the body, it should be said to be immeasurable.
Among these, those who follow by faith are collectively described as "one who follows by faith.
As it is with those who follow by faith, so it is with those who follow by dharma.
Because they share the same basis for the faculties, the path, and the detachment from defilements,
and because those who follow by Dharma (dharmānusārin) are exclusively subsumed under the immovable lineage (akopya-gotra),
one might argue that those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta) should also be said to be of a single type.
That is to say, among the seven types, they are called "those resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*);
alternatively, one should speak of three [categories],
namely, by way of their faculties (*indriya*).
Alternatively, one should speak of five [categories], namely by way of lineage (*gotra*);
or one should speak of eighty-one, namely by way of freedom from defilement (*vairāgya*).

That is to say, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are ten [categories] consisting of those who are bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) and those who have abandoned one up to nine grades of defilement.
There are sixty-three [defilements] consisting of one through nine grades of defilement for each stage from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

There are eight [defilements] consisting of one through eight grades of defilement for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Combined, these total eighty-one.
Some say that because of the abandonment of defilement, one should speak of eighty-two;

that is to say, by adding the moment of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the ninth grade of defilement of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) to the previously mentioned eighty-one.
Alternatively, one should state that there are four hundred and five.
That is to say, by way of their bases (*āśraya*), there are eighty-one bases in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and seventy-two bases in the first dhyāna.
The second dhyāna has sixty-three bases;
the third dhyāna has fifty-four bases;
and the fourth dhyāna has forty-five bases.
The bases for the sphere of infinite space consist of thirty-six;
the bases for the sphere of infinite consciousness consist of twenty-seven;
and the bases for the sphere of nothingness consist of eighteen.

There are nine bases for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; namely, those who are bound by all fetters and those who have abandoned from one grade up to eight grades of defilement, making nine, which together total four hundred and five.
Some say that this should be stated as four hundred and fourteen;
namely, there are eighty-two bases in the desire realm and seventy-three bases in the first dhyāna.
The basis for the second dhyāna consists of sixty-four;
the basis for the third dhyāna consists of fifty-five; and the basis for the fourth dhyāna consists of forty-six.
The basis for the sphere of infinite space consists of thirty-seven;
the basis for the sphere of infinite consciousness consists of twenty-eight;
and the basis for the sphere of nothingness consists of nineteen.
There are ten bases for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
These consist of nine states: those who are bound by all fetters, and those who have abandoned from one grade up to eight grades of defilement;
the tenth is the state at the time of the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) that abandons the ninth grade.
This is based on the classification of the supports according to the nine stages (*bhūmi*).
If one classifies them according to the twenty-nine locations of the supports, their number— whether many or few— should be considered as appropriate,
since the count is further increased by combining the faculties (*indriya*), lineages (*gotra*), and the bases of freedom from defilement (*vairāgya-āśraya*) in groups of two, three, and four.
If one were to analyze them according to their moments while abiding in the body, they should be said to be immeasurable.

Here, those with faith and resolution (śraddhādhimukta) are collectively referred to as "one with faith and resolution"; the same applies to those who have attained vision through insight (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
