Because they are based on the faculties (*indriya*) and the detachment from passion (*vairāgya*),
and because their specific lineage (*gotra*) is distinct— since those who have attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) are comprised solely within the immovable lineage (*akopyadharman*).
As for the "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*), one might say that there is only one, namely, that which is called "body-witness" among the seven types.
Alternatively, one should speak of three,
namely by way of faculties; or one should speak of six, namely by way of lineage,
from the dharma of falling away up to the immovable dharma.
Alternatively, one should speak of nine [types], namely:

by virtue of being free from defilement, there are nine [stages] ranging from those bound by all fetters in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to those who have abandoned one grade up to eight grades of defilement.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this should be stated as ten;
namely, the aforementioned nine, with the addition of the moment of emerging from the ninth path of immediate succession as the tenth.
Alternatively, one should speak of twenty-seven [types],
based on their supports (*āśraya*). That is to say,
there are nine supports belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
There are nine bases for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and nine bases for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
these belong exclusively to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
It is not the three formless realms,
because those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) are not reborn there.
Some say that this should be stated as thirty.
This refers to the time when the ninth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) is added for each of the three realms.
This is a classification based on the supports (*āśraya*) of the three realms;
if classified according to the specific locations of the stages (*bhūmi*), one should reflect upon the number [of paths] as appropriate.

If one calculates by combining the faculties, lineages, states free from passion, and bases—namely two, three, four, and two—the number increases further. If analyzed according to the moments in which they exist within the body, they are immeasurable.

Herein, those who have realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*) are collectively described as "one who has realized through the body. As for those liberated through wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), they may also be described as "one," meaning that among the seven types [of arhats], they are designated as "liberated through wisdom."
Alternatively, one should speak of three,
namely by way of the faculties;
or one should speak of six.
That is to say, it is by way of lineage (*gotra*).

Alternatively, one should speak of nine [types] by way of the basis (*āśraya*), namely, from the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the differentiation of the bases according to these nine stages.
If categorized according to the twenty-nine bases, they become twenty-nine;
if calculated by combining the two or three bases of the faculties and the spiritual lineage, one should reflect accordingly.

If one were to analyze those who possess liberation through wisdom (prajñā-vimukti) moment by moment while remaining in the body, there would be immeasurable such individuals; yet, herein they are collectively referred to as "one" liberation through wisdom.
As it is with liberation through wisdom, so it is with both types of liberation (ubhayatobhāga-vimukti).

Regarding their distinctions: it is said that because their basis—the one liberated through both parts—does not reside in the three lower formless realms, these five types of persons [are distinguished] with respect to the three fetters up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
"How many are accomplished and how many are not accomplished?

In this context, the Venerable One formulated this question and answer by taking the *pudgala* (person) as the subject and the various afflictions (*kleśa*) as the categories: "For one who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), as long as the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, all three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are accomplished."
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*) has arisen, two are accomplished and one is not accomplished.
The two that are accomplished are the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*),
because these pertain to both realms and four categories (*pakṣa*).
The one that is not accomplished is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
because it pertains exclusively to the three realms and is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*), those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire (*kāmarāga*) accomplish them all.
Those who have already abandoned the defilements of desire do not possess these three at all,
because these three are exclusively bound to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It should be understood by analogy that those who have already abandoned the defilements of desire had previously abandoned them while in the state of an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*).
Those who have not yet abandoned desire-taint regarding the three taints possess all of them.
Those who have already abandoned desire-taint possess two and do not possess one.
The two they possess are the taint of existence and the taint of ignorance.
One is not accomplished [in] the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
Regarding the four floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and graspings (*upādāna*), those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire are accomplished in all of them;
those who have already abandoned the defilement of desire are accomplished in three and not accomplished in one.

Three are accomplished: namely, the flood, yoke, and grasping of views, as well as the grasping of ignorance, the flood and yoke of views, and the grasping of rules and observances and the theory of self.
One is not accomplished: namely, the flood, yoke, and grasping of sensual desire.
Regarding the four bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*), those who have not yet abandoned desire for the realm of passion (*kāmarāga*) possess all of them.
Those who have already abandoned desire for the realm of passion possess two and do not possess two.
The two they possess are the fetter of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the fetter of grasping at this as real (*parāmarśagrāha*).
Regarding the two non-attainments, namely the fetters of sensual desire and ill will:
one possesses both as long as one has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire regarding the five hindrances and the path-knowledge of dharma (dharmajñāna) has not yet arisen.
When the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path has already arisen, four [factors] are accomplished and one is not accomplished.
Those who have already abandoned the defilements of desire do not accomplish any of them,
because the five hindrances are exclusively bound to the realm of desire.

Regarding the four that are accomplished, these refer to the first four hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); the one not accomplished is the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*), because it has already been abandoned once the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) has arisen.
Regarding the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire accomplish all of them.
One who has already become free from the defilement of desire accomplishes two and does not accomplish three.
The two that are accomplished are the fetters of greed (*rāga*) and conceit (*māna*),
because they pertain to the bonds of all three realms.
The three that are not accomplished are the fetters of anger, envy, and stinginess,
because they are bound exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire and for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen accomplishes all of them.
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*) has arisen,
four are accomplished and one is not accomplished.
Regarding the accomplishment of the four, this refers to two at the beginning and two at the end.
One that is not yet accomplished refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
For one who has already become free from the defilement of desire but in whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, three are accomplished and two are not.
Those that are accomplished refer to the final three.
Regarding the two that are not accomplished, this refers to the first two.
Once the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*) has arisen, three are accomplished and two are not.
Regarding the two that are accomplished:
This refers to the latter two.
Regarding the three that are not accomplished,
this refers to the first three.
Regarding the five fetters binding one to the higher realms (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*): those who have not yet abandoned passion for the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*) possess all of them.
Those who have already abandoned passion for the realm of form possess four and do not possess one.
As for the possession of the four:
That is to say, with the exception of desire for form (*rūparāga*). The one that is not accomplished is desire for form.
Regarding the five views, as long as the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen, one possesses all of them.
Once the subsequent knowledge of suffering has arisen, one possesses three and does not possess two.
As for the three that are possessed:
This refers to the latter three.
Regarding the two that are not accomplished,
this refers to the first two.
Those who have not yet abandoned desire for the six bases of craving (ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya) possess all six.
Those who have already abandoned desire for these but have not yet abandoned desire for the Brahma-world possess four and do not possess two.
Regarding the four who have attained accomplishment,
there are two at the beginning and two at the end;
as for the two who have not attained accomplishment:
This refers to the group of cravings born from nose-contact and tongue-contact.
Having already become detached from the defilements of the Brahma-world,
one accomplishes five [factors] and does not accomplish one.
One is accomplished;
that is, the sixth.
Five are not accomplished.
That is to say, regarding the first five [latent dispositions],
those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire for the seven latent dispositions possess all of them;
those who have already abandoned the defilement of desire possess five and do not possess two.
The five who possess [them] refer to those with desire and so forth;
the two who do not possess [them] are as follows.
That is to say, regarding desire-greed and ill-will:
among those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire, all nine fetters are fully present;
for those who have already abandoned the defilement of desire, six are present and three are not.
The six that are established refer to the six beginning with craving;
the three that are not established are as follows.
This refers to ill-will, envy, and stinginess;
regarding the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), it concerns those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire and for whom the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* has not yet arisen.

"Accomplishing all" means that for one who is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), at the moment of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*), there is no underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) that is not accomplished.
The rest is explained in detail as in the original treatise.
Question: Why is it not stated that "the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) has arisen"?
Answer: Because if that had already arisen, one would no longer be a follower by faith (śraddhānusārin);
therefore, it is not so stated.
As it is for those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by Dharma (dharmānusārin), so it is here as well.

Regarding these two, whether in the path or in birth, there is no difference in their basis for the abandonment of defilements; they are entirely equal, with the sole exception that their faculties (indriya) differ.
This means that those of dull faculties are called "followers by faith" (śraddhānusārin),
while those of sharp faculties are called "followers by dharma" (dharmānusārin).
One who is resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta) does not possess any of the three fetters (saṃyojana), because those [fetters] are abandoned solely through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga).

Regarding the three unwholesome roots, those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire possess them all; those who have already abandoned the defilement of desire do not possess them at all, because they are exclusively bound to the desire realm.
As for those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire:
This refers to those in the stage of entering the fruit of stream-entry, those in the stage of entering the fruit of once-returning, and those in the stage of entering the fruit of non-returning;
as well as those who have already abandoned the defilement of desire,
namely, those in the stage of the fruit of non-returning and those in the stage of entering the fruit of arhatship.
Whether one has already become free from the defilement of desire while in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
or only becomes free from it upon reaching the stage of a noble one (*ārya*), the subsequent cases should be understood accordingly.
In all three outflows (*āsrava*), as long as one has not yet become free from the defilement of desire, they are fully possessed.
Having already become free from the defilement of desire, two are accomplished and one is not accomplished.
The two that are accomplished are the outflow of the taints of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Regarding "one is not accomplished":
this refers to the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) within the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*).
For one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire, three are accomplished and one is not accomplished.
Three are accomplished, namely:
the flood, the yoke, and the craving for existence, and ignorance.
One is not accomplished.
This refers to the floods and yokes of views.
One who is already free from the defilement of desire accomplishes two and does not accomplish two.
As for the accomplishment of the two: [text continues].
This refers to the flood and yoke of ignorance.
Those who do not possess these two refer to the flood and yoke of sensual desire and views.
Regarding the four types of clinging (*upādāna*), those who have not yet abandoned desire-taint (*rāga*) for them accomplish two and do not accomplish two.
The two that are accomplished are namely:
clinging to sensual pleasure (*kāmopādāna*) and clinging to self-theory (*ātmavādopādāna*).
Regarding the two that are not accomplished:
this refers to the views of *dṛṣṭi* and *śīlavrataparāmarśa*.
One who is already free from the defilement of desire accomplishes one and does not accomplish three.
One is accomplished,
namely the last one;
three are not accomplished.
This refers to the first three.
Regarding the four bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*), those who have not yet abandoned desire for them accomplish two and do not accomplish two.
As for accomplishing two: [text continues].
This refers to the former two.
The non-attainment of these two refers to the latter two.
Those who have already abandoned the defilements of desire do not possess [these] at all;
for the first two are bound exclusively to the desire realm,
while the latter two are abandoned exclusively through the path of seeing.
Regarding the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire, four are accomplished and one is not accomplished.
The four that are accomplished refer to the first four;
the one that is not accomplished refers to the last one.
Those who have already become free from the defilement of desire do not possess [these fetters],
because the first four and the last one are all bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Regarding the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), those who have not yet become free from the defilement of desire possess them all.
One who has already abandoned the defilement of desire accomplishes two and does not accomplish three.
The two that are accomplished are the fetters of greed and pride.
The three that are not accomplished are anger, envy, and stinginess;
these are among the five fetters that bind one to the lower realms.
One who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire accomplishes two and does not accomplish three.
The accomplishment of two refers to the first two.
Regarding the three that are not accomplished:
this refers to the latter three,
which are all not accomplished by those who have already become free from the defilement of desire.
The first two are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*);
the latter three are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
Among the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), [the first two are as described above].
Those who have not yet abandoned attachment to the realm of form possess all [of these].
Those who have already abandoned attachment to the realm of form possess four and do not possess one.
As for the possession of four:
That is to say, with the exception of desire for form.
The one that is not accomplished refers to desire for form.
Regarding the five views, none are established [in these beings], because they are abandoned solely by the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*).
Regarding the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*), those who have not yet abandoned desire-attachment (*kāma-rāga*) possess all of them.
Those who have already abandoned desire-attachment but have not yet abandoned attachment to the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*) possess four and do not possess two.
Regarding the four who have attained accomplishment:
this refers to two at the beginning and two at the end.
Regarding the two who have not attained accomplishment: [this refers to the remaining two].
This refers to the two intermediate [dhyānas].
Having already become free from the defilements of the Brahma-world, one accomplishes five and does not accomplish one.
As for the one accomplished:
This refers to the last one.
Regarding the five that are not accomplished:
this refers to the first five.
Regarding the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire accomplishes five and does not accomplish two.
As for the five that are accomplished:
These are sensual desire, ill will, desire for existence, pride, and ignorance.
Two are not possessed: namely, views and doubt.
One who is already free from the defilement of desire possesses three and does not possess four.
The three accomplishments refer to greed, pride, and ignorance. The four non-achievements refer to...
[the four non-accomplishments].
This refers to the remaining four.
Regarding the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), those who have not yet abandoned desire for the realm of form possess six and do not possess three.
As for the possession of six: [the list follows].
These are the fetters of attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, envy, and avarice.
The three that are not established are the fetters of views,
grasping at views, and doubt.
One who has already abandoned the defilement of desire accomplishes three and does not accomplish six.
The three that are accomplished are craving, conceit, and ignorance.
The six non-acquisitions refer to the remaining six [categories] among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
One who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire accomplishes ten and does not accomplish eighty-eight.
Regarding the accomplishment of ten,
these refer to those [factors] to be abandoned through cultivation within the three realms.
Regarding the eighty-eight non-attainments:
this refers to those abandoned through the vision of the three realms.
For one who is already free from the defilement of desire but not yet free from the defilement of form, six are attained and ninety-two are non-attained.
Six are accomplished,
namely those abandoned through cultivation in the realms of form and formlessness;
ninety-two are not accomplished.
That is to say, those abandoned through seeing in the three realms,
as well as those abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm;
one who has already become free from the defilement of form possesses ninety-five and does not possess [the remaining] ones.
Regarding the three attainments:
these refer to the ninety-five factors abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm that are not attained.
This refers to those abandoned through seeing in the three realms,
as well as those abandoned through cultivation in the desire and form realms.
The same applies to those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
These two paths of cultivation are the basis for detachment from defilement;
whether in meditative concentration or in rebirth, they are entirely equal,
differing only in their faculties (*indriya*).
That is to say, those of dull faculties are called "resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*),
while those of sharp faculties are called "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
As for the body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*), they do not possess any of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) or the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
Because the three fetters are abandoned solely through the path of seeing;
because the three unwholesome roots are bound exclusively to the desire realm;

and because one who has realized the body must have already become detached from what is abandoned through the path of seeing in the three realms, as well as from the eight lower stages abandoned through the path of cultivation.
Regarding the three outflows, two are accomplished and one is not accomplished.
As for the accomplishment of the two,
it refers to the existence of the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
The first non-attainment refers to the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*) among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*).
There are two types of accomplishment and two types of non-accomplishment.
Regarding the two accomplishments,
they refer to the presence of ignorance.
Regarding the two non-attainments:
this refers to the desire to see.
Among the four graspings, one is attained and three are not attained.
One is established,
namely the grasping at the doctrine of self;
three are not established.
This refers to the remaining three types of clinging (*upādāna*).
They do not possess any of the four bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*) or the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*),
because the first two bodily fetters and the five hindrances are bound exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because the latter two bodily fetters (*kāyasaṃyojana*) are abandoned solely by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), one accomplishes two of the five fetters (*saṃyojana*) and does not accomplish three.
Regarding the accomplishment of two: [text follows].
The fetters of greed and pride are what is meant;
the three that are not accomplished are the fetters of anger, envy, and stinginess.
One does not possess any of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*),
because the first two are bound exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*),
and the latter three are abandoned exclusively through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*).
Regarding the five fetters pertaining to the higher realms (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*),
four are accomplished and one is not accomplished. That which is not accomplished is:
This refers to craving for form (*rūparāga*).
As for the four attainments (*siddhi*),
they refer to the remaining four [realms].
Regarding the five views, he does not possess any of them, because he has long since been detached from those abandoned by insight.
Regarding the six groups of craving, he possesses one and does not possess five.
As for the one he possesses:
The sixth refers to the sixth [consciousness].
The five non-attainments refer to the first five [consciousnesses].
Regarding the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), three are accomplished and four are not accomplished.
As for the three that are accomplished,
they are sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Regarding the four non-attainments:
this refers to the remaining four.
Among the nine fetters, three are attained and six are not attained.
The three factors that are established are craving, pride, and ignorance.
The six factors that are not established are:
That is to say, among the remaining six [categories],
regarding the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
three are established as possessing ninety-five and are not established as possessing the others.
The three that are accomplished refer to those abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm;
the ninety-five that are not accomplished refer to those abandoned through insight in the three realms.

Furthermore, regarding the question of whether there are noble ones who possess all ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)—those to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire and form realms—the answer is: yes.

This refers to one who is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) at the moment of entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and abiding in the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Question: Is there any noble one who has already abandoned eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), yet has not abandoned ten underlying tendencies and has not attained the fruit?
Answer: There is.

This refers to the time when one who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and abides in the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*);
at that moment, there are thirty-six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm and thirty-one latent dispositions of the form realm [to be abandoned].
The twenty-one underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the formless realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation have already been abandoned;

however, because they have not yet attained the fruit and remain on the path of approach (pratipannaka), the seven underlying tendencies of the formless realm to be abandoned through the vision of the path and the three to be abandoned through cultivation have not yet been abandoned.
Question: Is it possible that one has already abandoned the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) yet has not yet attained the fruit of Arhatship?

Answer: Yes; for example, one who is already detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) but is not yet detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
He has already abandoned thirty-six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the desire realm,
thirty-one underlying tendencies of the form realm, and thirty-one underlying tendencies of the three lower formless realms;
yet, not having attained the fruit of arhatship, he may still be an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
Or perhaps because they are non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
The critique states: one should not say this, for the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are established in relation to the realms (*dhātu*), not in relation to the stages (*bhūmi*).
For this reason, one should answer that there is none when asked.
