Section Two on the Aggregate of Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha), Chapter One on Unwholesome Factors (Akuśala-nikāya), Part Ten: How many conditions does the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) serve as a condition for the view of a self-identity?
How many conditions do the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*),
up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), serve as for [those same factors]?

Furthermore, how many conditions does the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm serve as for the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm?

How many conditions does the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) serve as a condition for the latent tendency of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) up to the latent tendency of conceit (*māna-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm? ...
[and so on,] explained in detail.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the tenets of other schools and clarifying one's own position.
That is to say, there are some who hold [the following view]:
Regarding the claim that conditions lack intrinsic nature, as illustrated by the analogy:
if one asks why those masters hold such a position,
the answer is that they form this conviction based upon the sūtras.
That is to say, the Sūtra states that ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
They [the opponents] say:
"Ignorance has no distinct characteristic."
Conditioned phenomena have distinct characteristics.
How could a phenomenon without distinct characteristics serve as a condition for a phenomenon with distinct characteristics while possessing a real intrinsic nature?
The Venerable One replied:
The various masters provisionally designate "conditions" (pratyaya) according to conceptualization, yet these do not possess a real nature.
To refute their attachment and to demonstrate that conditions do indeed exist as real entities, this treatise was composed.
This is because if one were to hold that conditions lack a real nature, [it would contradict the truth].
All phenomena should be understood as lacking any real intrinsic nature,
because the four conditions encompass all phenomena.
That is to say, the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) encompasses all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma).
The immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) comprises all other past and present mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta),
excluding the final mind and mental factors of a past or present Arhat.
The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) collectively encompass all phenomena.
Furthermore, if the nature of these conditions were not substantially real, then all phenomena would lack profound meaning.
That is to say, when all phenomena are being revealed,
if they are not subsumed within the analysis of conditions (*pratyaya*), they are coarse and shallow, and thus easily understood; however,
if they are subsumed within conditions and analyzed, [they are profound].
It would then be exceedingly profound, surpassing the four great oceans,
and could be known only by the ultimate wisdom of a Buddha.
Furthermore, if the nature of all conditions were not substantially existent, [how could they produce effects?]
One should not establish three kinds of bodhi;

that is to say, observing the nature of conditions with superior wisdom is called the bodhi of a Buddha, while observing the nature of conditions with middling wisdom is called the bodhi of a Pratyekabuddha.
If one observes the nature of conditions with inferior wisdom, this is called the enlightenment of a śrāvaka.
Furthermore, if these various natures of conditions were not substantially existent,
the awakened intellect would have no basis for functioning in its three grades.
That is to say, all forms of discerning wisdom should always remain inferior when they are inferior,
always remain middling when they are middling,
and always remain superior when they are superior.
However, since all levels of cognitive wisdom can be considered "middling" by those below them,
and "superior" by those above them,
it follows that the nature of all objects of cognition must possess a determinate, real essence.
Because they possess functional efficacy.
For this reason, the Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"If the nature of conditions were not substantially existent..."
The teacher should not be able to cause the disciple’s wisdom to be inferior at first and superior later;
likewise, the disciple should never become a teacher in turn.
However, this is because the nature of all conditions exists as a reality.
The teacher causes the disciple’s wisdom to increase gradually;
at times, the disciple succeeds in grasping the meaning of the teacher’s doctrine.
Therefore, the nature of all conditions is definitively and truly existent.
Question: If the nature of all conditions (*pratyaya*) were substantially existent (*dravyasat*), how would one reconcile this with the sūtra cited?
Answer: Although the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) has no distinct characteristics, the functions it performs do possess distinct characteristics.
This refers to immeasurable gateways and immeasurable rungs [of the ladder],
whose distinct functional capacities serve as conditions for the process of practice. It is,
for example, like a single person who possesses five different skills.
Although its substance is one, its functions are fivefold.
Furthermore, it is intended to demonstrate that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are weak by nature and lack self-mastery.
Relying upon others and lacking independent agency,
I have composed this treatise not out of my own desire, but in accordance with their wishes.
Regarding "those that are weak by nature":
this refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) are given the name "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) because their very nature is to arise from conditions. Some say:
Conditioned phenomena are weak by nature because they are subject to arising and ceasing.
Some say that conditioned phenomena are weak by nature because they arise from conditions.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that form is impermanent."
The various causes and conditions that can produce form are also impermanent.
Since form arises from causes and conditions that are themselves impermanent, how could it be permanent?
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
Because they are weak and inferior,
conditioned phenomena arise from four conditions, three conditions, or even two conditions;
yet there is not even a single condition that is capable of producing them independently.
How much more so for that which is without conditions;
therefore, conditioned phenomena are weak and inferior by their very nature,
like one who is frail and ill.
Sometimes four people support him, sometimes three,
or sometimes two must support him before he can rise and stand;
yet there is not even one person who can make him rise and stand alone.
How much more so for that which lacks a person and lacks self-mastery;
this refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise without having any power or efficacy of their own.
"Dependent upon others" means that all conditioned phenomena must depend on others in order to function; they possess no autonomous activity.
"Lacking autonomous activity" means that all conditioned phenomena cannot initiate their own discriminative functions.
"Who created me, and whom have I created?
refers to those conditioned phenomena that do not follow their own desires;
that is, there are no conditioned phenomena that can achieve their wish, "May I not arise; may I not cease."
Furthermore, this treatise is composed in order to reveal the correct principle of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) for those who are deluded regarding it; that is to say,
there are some who hold [the following] views.

Only the sequence from "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise" up to "with birth as condition, aging and death arise" constitutes the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
It is for the sake of causing those who are deluded to attain understanding that it is revealed that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are dependently originated.
Regarding what is said by the multitude of worldly people, this should be explained here.
Furthermore, let it not be for the sake of refuting others merely to manifest one's own tenet.
I have composed this treatise solely with the desire to reveal the correct principle of dependent origination so that others may attain understanding.
The answer is: the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) serves as four, three, two, or one condition for another view of a self-entity.
Question: Why is it asked here how many conditions the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) serves as a condition for the view of a self-identity?
Answer: It is said that it serves as four, three, two, or one condition.

Later, in the Section on Knowledge (jñānaskandha), it is asked how many conditions the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) serves as a condition for the knowledge of phenomena; the answer states: "As a cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya), an immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), and a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya)."
The answer is: because it is the intention of the author of this treatise to be thus, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, although these two should be identical, there is a difference.
The author of this treatise employs various explanations and diverse literary compositions to adorn the meaning,
ensuring it is not confused and is easy to receive and uphold.
Furthermore, he does so with the desire to manifest two gates, two summaries, two stairways, two rungs, two torches, two lights, two texts, and two shadows.
What has been stated here should likewise apply there,
and what has been stated there should likewise apply here;
therefore, this is said.
Furthermore, this teaching is of definitive meaning (nītārtha), while that teaching is of non-definitive meaning (neyārtha).
This teaching has no ulterior intent, whereas that teaching possesses an ulterior intent.
This teaching has no underlying cause, whereas that teaching possesses an underlying cause.
This is said to be the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), while that is said to be the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
Furthermore, this treatise is composed based on four types of analysis (*vibhaṅga*):
first, the analysis of the elements (*dhātu-vibhaṅga*).
Second, the analysis of the world;
third, the analysis of moments;
fourth, the analysis of the equal-and-immediate condition.
The treatise composed by him relies on a partial analysis,
namely, it analyzes only the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*);
therefore, what he says differs from this [present work].
Regarding the "four" herein, what are these four?
For example, when a view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises immediately after another view of a self,
one contemplates how that preceding life serves as four conditions for the subsequent life.
That is to say, immediately after the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) in one moment,
the view of a self manifests in the second moment;
what subsequently arises takes that preceding [moment] as its object.
That [condition] functions as all four conditions— namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*),

the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)— both prior to and subsequent [to the effect]. Regarding the causal condition:
This means that the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arising in a prior life serves as two causes for the view of a self arising in a subsequent life—
namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*).
As for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*):
This means that the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arising in a subsequent life is produced immediately after the view of a self-body in a preceding life.
As for the object-condition (ālambanapratyaya),
it means that the view of a self-body arising in a subsequent life arises by taking the view of a self-body in a preceding life as its object.
The dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) refers to that which,
in relation to what follows, either merely does not obstruct or does not hinder its arising.
Among these, the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) is like the nature of a seed.
The equal-and-immediate condition is like the dharma of opening and yielding;
the object-condition is like the dharma of the leaning staff;
the dominant condition is like the dharma of non-obstruction.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in a subsequent life is able to function in the world, grasp its fruits,
perform its actions, and cognize its conditions, because it is sustained by the four conditions provided by the view of a self-identity in the preceding life.
Regarding these three, what are the three?

For example, when a view of self-identity arises immediately after another view of self-identity, one does not reflect upon the former arising as a condition for the latter; these constitute the three conditions.
Regarding the exclusion of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
immediately after a moment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), a second moment of the view of a self-identity manifests.
That which arises subsequently does not take the preceding [moment] as its object.
That is to say, it either takes form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as its object;
or, excluding the aforementioned view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it takes the remaining aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as its object.
In these cases, the former [view] and the latter [formations] act as only three conditions (*pratyaya*).
That is to say, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
An explanation of these three conditions is as previously set forth in detail.
Subsequently arising views of a self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) are sustained by the views of a self-existence arising in a prior life through the inclusion of these three conditions.
It is capable of functioning in the world, capable of grasping results, capable of performing actions, and capable of cognizing conditions.
Alternatively, after a view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has arisen without interval, other minds may arise, followed by another view of self-existence;
this [subsequent view] takes that preceding birth as three conditions for the subsequent birth, excluding the condition of immediate antecedence (*samanantarapratyaya*).

That is to say, immediately following a moment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), in the second moment, the view of a self-identity does not manifest; rather, one of the following manifests:

the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), wholesome states associated with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*), or non-obscured neutral states (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*).
Thereafter, when the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises again, it takes the previously arisen view of a self-body as its object.

That former [view] and this latter one function as three conditions for one another: namely, the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), the object condition (ālambana-pratyaya), and the predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
These three conditions are explained in detail as previously stated.
Subsequently, the view of a self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arising in a later life is sustained by the view of a self-existence arising in a prior life through these three conditions;
thus, it is able to function in the world, grasp its fruit, perform its activity, and cognize its objects.
Regarding these two, what are the two? For example,
when a view of a self-identity arises after another mind has arisen immediately following a previous view of a self-identity,
one does not reflect upon those preceding and succeeding moments as being two conditions.
This refers to causal predominance:
that is, when self-view (satkāyadṛṣṭi) exists in one moment,
self-view does not manifest in the immediately subsequent second moment.
Alternatively, when views of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) up to an unobscured-neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛtacitta*) manifest,
following this, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises again, but it does not take the previously arisen view of a self-identity as its object.
That is to say, whether taking as objects form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, or—
excluding the view of a self-identity— the remaining formations, the former and the latter serve as only two conditions:
namely, the causal condition and the predominant condition.
The explanation of these two conditions is as previously set forth in detail.
Because the view of a self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arising in a subsequent life is sustained by the view of a self-existence arising in a preceding life through these two conditions,
it is able to function in the world, grasp its fruit, perform its activity, and cognize its conditions.
In this context, what is meant by "one"?
It refers to the view of a self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arising later taking as its object the view of a self-existence that arose previously,
such that it functions as an object-condition (*ālambanādhipati*).

It does not function as a single object-condition or a single dominant condition, because there is no sense of a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) or an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) between the subsequent and the preceding.
Question: Why is it that in this context one question is asked and two answers are given?
Answer: Respondents employ various methods when composing treatises and establishing doctrines;
some first provide a refutation and then an answer, while others first provide an answer and then a refutation.
Regarding the method of first negating and then answering, as stated here:
if one takes an object-condition (ālambana) as being predominant by way of its object-condition, this negates [the possibility of it being] both conditions.
"Not acting as an object-condition for one [condition] while being its predominant condition" is the answer regarding the single object-condition (*ālambana*).
This method of answering first and then negating is as explained in the *Ekavyavahārika-varga*.
If that which arose previously has not been abandoned, then one is bound; this is the answer regarding bondage.
If it has not arisen previously, or if having arisen it has been abandoned, then one is not bound; this is the negation of non-bondage.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
These are both answers.
That is to say, if the latter serves as an object-condition for the former, it constitutes two conditions and answers the first two questions;
if it does not serve as an object-condition, it constitutes only one condition and answers this one question.
Of the two points addressed in the previous response, only one part was answered;
that which remained unanswered is now answered here.
Subsequently, future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* should be explained according to this same principle, in relation to past and present *satkāyadṛṣṭi*.
If it acts as an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), it does so by way of being an object-dominant condition (ālambanādhipati);
it does not act as a single [condition] without being an object.
This applies to future and present satkāyadṛṣṭi in relation to past satkāyadṛṣṭi.

If it functions as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it does so by way of being a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); it does not function as a predominant condition alone without being an object-condition.
Question: Does the currently existing view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) have the capacity to take an object while its activity is actually present?
If the activity of past *satkāyadṛṣṭi* has already ceased, how can it serve as an object?
Regarding this, it is said that if it functions as an object, it does so by way of being an object-condition (*ālambanādhipati*).
The answer is: although past *satkāyadṛṣṭi* existed at a previous time, it was already extinguished when it served as the object in the present.
Although this has now passed, it is spoken of as such by recounting its function from the past.
Question: Regarding what was previously stated here concerning the view of a self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arising in a later life and the view of a self-existence arising in a prior life—
If it acts as an object of focus,
it is predominant as an object;
if it does not act as an object of focus, it is predominant in one [other] way.

It is stated that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) belonging to a future subsequent birth and the view of a self-identity belonging to a past prior birth share two common objects (*ālambana*).
Why, then, is it not stated that a view of a self-identity belonging to the future and a view of a self-identity belonging to the future share two common objects?
Regarding that which was promised to be explained but has not yet been explained,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, in this context, only those [dharmas] that possess a temporal sequence have been discussed.
Because they lack priority and posteriority, they are omitted here.
Question: Is there not priority and posteriority between the stage of future birth and that which has not yet been born?
Answer: Because there is no distinction in time, they are not designated as prior or posterior.

Question: If that is so, since there would be no distinction between past, prior-born, and posterior-born [dharmas] in terms of their temporal status, they should not be considered as having a sequence of before and after.
Answer: Because those dharmas previously existed at times such as the present, they possess the sense of temporal distinction; thus, the sequence of before and after is established.
Because it is not so in the future, it is omitted and not mentioned.
The view of a self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm serves as a single dominant condition for the view of a self-existence in the form and formless realms;
that is, the view of a self-existence in the desire realm [is the dominant condition] for the view of a self-existence in the two higher realms.
Alternatively, it is a single dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) because it is merely unobstructed or does not hinder arising;
it is not a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) because the cause and effect are severed by differences in realm (*dhātu*) and level (*bhūmi*).
Regarding those that are not equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*):
this is because the afflictions of a higher stage do not manifest immediately after the afflictions of a lower stage.
Regarding those that are not object conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*): [this is because...]
This means that because the afflictions of the determined, unsurpassed stages take those of the lower stages as their objects,

the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) belonging to the form and formless realms acts as an equal-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the view of a self-body belonging to the desire realm,
and as an equal-immediate dominant condition (*samanantarādhipatipratyaya*).
It does not function as an equal-and-immediate or a single predominant condition;

that is to say, if one dies while abiding in the form or formless realms with a mind associated with the view of a self-identity, and is reborn in the desire realm with a mind associated with the view of a self-identity.

The meaning of how the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the form and formless realms serves as the equal-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*)—but not the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*)—for the view of a self-body in the desire realm is as explained previously.
Regarding that which is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
this refers to the various views of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) which do not take other stages as their objects.

Furthermore, if one dies with a mind associated with the view of self-existence belonging to the form or formless realms, and is reborn with a mind associated with the view of self-existence belonging to the desire realm, [the former is not the object-condition for the latter].
The view of a self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the form and formless realms serves as only a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the view of a self-existence in the desire realm,
and not as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This is because the view of a self-existence in the desire realm does not arise immediately after the view of a self-existence in the form and formless realms.
The meaning of the other two conditions is as previously explained.

The view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) serves as a single predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the view of self-existence belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as previously explained.

The view of a self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the formless realm and the view of a self-existence in the form realm [are related such that] if they act as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
they serve as both the equal-and-immediate condition and the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*);
if they do not act as an equal-and-immediate condition, they serve as only one [predominant] condition.
The meanings herein should be understood by analogy with what precedes,
as in the case of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of a self-identity.
One should know that the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and all other non-universal [factors] are related to all non-universal [factors];
all non-universal [factors] and all other non-universal [factors] are likewise related;
and so too are all universal [factors] and all non-universal [factors].
That is to say, there are ten categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*):
namely, the five views and the five non-views.
As for the five views:

The views consist of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The five that are not views are doubt (*vicikitsā*),
attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Among these, five are universal (sarvatraga):
namely, wrong view, adherence to views, adherence to precepts and observances, doubt, and ignorance.
Five are non-universal (asarvatraga).
That is to say: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), greed, hatred, and pride.

Among these, although the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes are called "universal" (*sarvatraga*) because they universally take their own level as an object, they are also called "non-universal" because they do not take other levels as objects.
By this, they are included among the non-universal [mental factors];
just as with the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of a self, it should be understood that the view of a self and all other non-universal [factors] are likewise related.
Just as there is a certain number [of instances] where the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) serves as a condition for the view of a self-identity,
so too is it with the view of a self-identity serving as a condition for all other views of extreme adherence (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), greed, hatred, and pride.
Regarding the statement that "it is the same for all other non-universal [factors] with respect to all other non-universal [factors]," this means:
just as there is a certain number of conditions by which *satkāyadṛṣṭi* serves as a condition for *satkāyadṛṣṭi*,
so it is for *antagrāhadṛṣṭi* with respect to *antagrāhadṛṣṭi*, greed, hatred, pride, and *satkāyadṛṣṭi*.
Greed serves as a condition for greed, hatred, pride, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Hatred serves as a condition for hatred, pride, the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, and greed.
Pride serves as a condition for pride, the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, greed, and hatred; the same applies to the number of conditions for each.
The same applies to all universal factors and all non-universal factors:
just as there is a certain number of conditions for the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) by which it serves as a condition for itself, so it is for false view (mithyādṛṣṭi),
the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), the grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), doubt (vicikitsā), and ignorance (avidyā).
The number of instances in which each [of these] serves as a condition for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), greed, hatred, and pride is likewise.
The view of a self-identity serves as a condition for the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in four,
three, two, or one way.
Regarding the "four" herein, what are these four?
For example, when the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is immediately followed by the grasping of precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa),
one contemplates how that former birth serves as four conditions for the subsequent birth.
That is to say, immediately after a moment of the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), a moment of the adherence to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) manifests.
What arises subsequently takes that which preceded it as its object.
Thus, the former and the latter mutually function as four conditions for one another.

These are the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Regarding the causal condition:
it means that the previously arisen view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) serves as two causes for the subsequently arisen grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
This refers to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Regarding the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*):
it means that the subsequently arising grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arises immediately after the previously arisen view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
it refers to the arising of the subsequently produced grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) conditioned by the previously produced view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
As for the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*):
That is to say, the former either merely does not obstruct or does not hinder the arising of the latter.
Among these, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is like the nature of a seed;
the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is like the nature of making way.
The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is like the law of the leaning staff;
the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is like the law of non-obstruction.

This is because the later-arising grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is sustained by the four conditions through its dependence on the earlier-arising view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
It is capable of proceeding through the world, capable of grasping results, capable of performing actions, and capable of cognizing conditions.
Among these, what are the three?
For example, as when the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) arises immediately followed by the grasping of precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
One does not contemplate that the preceding birth and the subsequent birth serve as three conditions— excluding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya)—
such that a moment of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is immediately followed by the manifestation of a moment of the adherence to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
The subsequent view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that arises thereafter does not take the prior view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its object.
That is to say, it either takes form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as its object, or—
excluding the view of a self-identity— it takes the remaining aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) as its object.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) from a previous life serves as three conditions for the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in a subsequent life—
namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). These three conditions are explained in detail as previously stated.

The subsequent arising of the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is due to its being sustained by the preceding arising of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) through three conditions;
thus, it can function in the world, grasp results, perform actions, and cognize conditions.

Or, after a view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has arisen without interval, and other minds have subsequently arisen, there may arise the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
One then contemplates that the preceding birth and the subsequent birth function as three conditions for one another, excluding the condition of immediate contiguity (*samanantarapratyaya*).
That is to say, immediately following a moment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the moment of the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) does not manifest.

Rather, there manifests either the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), wholesome states with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*), or non-obscured neutral states of mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*).
Subsequently, the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arises, taking as its object the previously arisen view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
That previously arisen view of a self-identity serves as only three conditions for the subsequently arisen grasping at precepts and observances.
This refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
These three conditions are explained in detail as previously stated.
Subsequently arising grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is sustained by the previously arisen view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) through these three conditions.
It is capable of functioning in the world, capable of grasping results, capable of performing actions, and capable of cognizing conditions.

Within this context, what are the two? How are they two? Just as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises immediately followed by another mind, and subsequently the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arises.
One does not contemplate those two conditions— the preceding birth and the succeeding birth—
namely, the causal condition and the dominant condition.
That is to say, the moment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not immediately give rise to the moment of the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Alternatively, when a view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) up to an unobscured-neutral mind is present before one,
it is only after this that the grasping of rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) arises, rather than taking the previously arisen view of a self as its object.
That is to say, whether taking as its object form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness— or,

excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), taking other formations as its object— the previously arisen view of a self-identity acts as two conditions for the subsequently arisen adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
This refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). The explanation of these two conditions is as previously detailed at length.
Subsequently arising grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is sustained by the previously arisen view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) through these two conditions.
It is capable of proceeding through the world, capable of grasping results, capable of performing actions, and capable of cognizing conditions.
Among these, what is meant by "one"?
It refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arising in a later life and the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arising in a prior life.
If it functions as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it does so by way of being an object-dominance (*ālambanādhipati*);
it does not function as a single dominance [in other ways],
because there is no sense of a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) or an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) between what follows and what precedes.
In this regard, the question and answer should be understood as before:
future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* [serving as] an object for past and present *śīlavrataparāmarśa*,
when acting as an object, functions as an object-dominance (*ālambanādhipati*).
When not acting as an object-condition, it is a single predominant condition;
when future and present satkāyadṛṣṭi acts upon past śīlavrataparāmarśa as its object, it is an object-predominant condition.
It does not have a single dominant condition as its object.
Regarding this, the question and answer should be understood as before.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm has the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the form and formless realms as its single dominant condition.

This means that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm serves as a single dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the two higher realms—
either because it merely does not obstruct them or because it does not hinder their arising—
but it is not a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*).
This means that because the realms and stages are distinct, there is a severance of cause and effect.
Regarding the absence of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*):
it means that the afflictions of a higher stage do not manifest immediately after the afflictions of a lower stage.
Regarding that which is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
it means that, as a matter of certainty, there are no afflictions of a higher stage that take a lower stage as their object.
This refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) in the form and formless realms taking the precept-and-vow attachment (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) of the desire realm as its object.
If it acts as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but not as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it functions as an object-dominant condition (*ālambanādhipati*).

This refers to the case where one dies with a mind associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) belonging to the form or formless realms, and is reborn with a mind associated with the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) belonging to the desire realm.
This view of precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) in the desire realm conditions the arising of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) in the form and formless realms;
that view of a self-identity in the form and formless realms [is conditioned by] the view of precepts and observances in the desire realm.
It serves as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
As for why it is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the meaning is as previously explained.
As for why it is not an immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*):
This means that the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) of the desire realm arises immediately after [the view of a self-identity] of the form and formless realms;

thus, while it acts as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), it does not act as an object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*). As an equal-and-immediate condition, it functions as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

That is to say, if one dies with a mind associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) while abiding in the form or formless realms, and is reborn with a mind associated with the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) belonging to the desire realm,
this grasping at precepts and observances of the desire realm does not arise taking the view of a self-identity of the form or formless realms as its object.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the form and formless realms serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the desire realm;
it does not serve as a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*), the meaning of which is as explained previously.
That which is not an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) does not take that as its object;
however, if it acts as an immediately preceding condition (samanantara) and an object-condition,
it functions as an immediately preceding, object, and dominant condition (adhipati).

That is to say, if one dies while abiding in the form or formless realms with a mind co-arising with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and is reborn with a mind co-arising with the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) belonging to the desire realm—
this grasping at precepts and observances of the desire realm arises conditioned by the view of a self-identity of the form and formless realms.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the form and formless realms acts as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the desire realm;
however, it does not act as a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*), the meaning of which is as explained previously.
It does not function as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) or an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); it functions as one dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

That is to say, if one dies with a mind associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) belonging to the form or formless realms, and is reborn with a mind associated with the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) belonging to the desire realm.
This grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) of the desire realm does not arise by taking the existence-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of the form and formless realms as its object;
rather, that existence-view of the form and formless realms serves merely as a single dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for this grasping at rules and observances of the desire realm.
The meaning of the other three conditions is as previously explained.

The sense that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) serves as a single predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is as previously explained.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the formless realm and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the form realm,
when acting as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), function as object-dominance (*ālambanādhipati*) without being an immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);
when acting as an immediately antecedent condition, they do not act as an object-condition.

It functions as the equal-and-immediate and the predominant conditions. If it acts as both the equal-and-immediate and the object condition, it functions as the equal-and-immediate, the object, and the predominant conditions;
if it does not act as the equal-and-immediate or the object condition, it functions as one predominant condition alone.
The meanings herein should be understood according to what was previously stated.
Just as it is with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*),
so too should one understand the relationship between the view of a self-identity and all other universal (*sarvatraga*) factors.
The universal [factors] with the universal [factors];
and likewise, the other non-universal [factors] with the universal [factors],
just as it is with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
It should be understood that the same applies to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and all other universal factors (*sarvatraga*).
Just as there is a certain number of conditions provided by the view of a self-identity for the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*),
so too is the number of conditions provided by the view of a self-identity for false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Regarding the statement that "it is the same for all-pervasive [factors] with respect to all-pervasive [factors]":
just as there is a certain number of conditions provided by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) for the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*),
so it is for false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) with respect to false view, the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the grasping of precepts and observances, doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
The grasping at views is associated with the grasping at views, the grasping at precepts and observances, doubt, ignorance, and false view;
the grasping at precepts and observances is associated with the grasping at precepts and observances, doubt, ignorance, false view, and the grasping at views;
and doubt is associated with doubt, ignorance, false view, the grasping at views, and the grasping at precepts and observances.
The same applies to the number of conditions for ignorance, as well as for ignorance, false view, adherence to views, adherence to precepts and observances, and doubt.
It is likewise for all other non-universal factors in relation to all universal factors.
Just as there is a certain number of conditions for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in relation to the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*),

so too is it for each of the views of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), greed, hatred, and pride in relation to false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the clinging to precepts and observances, doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Regarding all phenomena,
if one asks about their inclusion, one should distinguish them according to the elements (dhātu);
if one asks about their knowledge, one should distinguish them according to the truths (satya).
If one asks about consciousness, it should be analyzed according to its bases;
if one asks about the afflictions, they should be analyzed according to their categories.
When analyzing the characteristics of phenomena in this manner:
Thus, it is easy to demonstrate and easy to establish.
Herein, because the afflictions are being questioned, they should be analyzed according to five categories.
These five categories are:
This refers to those [afflictions] abandoned through the vision of suffering, those abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding the afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering, there are two types:
first, the universal [defilements].
The two non-universal [afflictions] are likewise abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
The afflictions abandoned through the vision of cessation are of two kinds.
First, those with outflow as their object;
second, those without outflow as their object.
The same applies to the afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing.
The afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation are of only one type,
namely, those that are non-universal (*asarvatraga*).

Among these, the universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) serve as four conditions for the universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
That is to say: the causal, the immediately antecedent, the object-conditioned, and the dominant conditions.
Regarding the causal condition, there are four types of causes:
namely, the associated cause, the co-existent cause, the homogeneous cause, and the pervasive cause.
Regarding the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*):

it refers to the manifestation of universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering immediately after [the cessation of] universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Regarding the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):

This means that the universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering arise conditioned by the universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
it refers to the fact that this [result] arises merely without obstruction from that [cause].
The universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) act as four conditions for the non-universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Regarding the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), there are two types of causes: namely, the similar-type cause (sabhāga-hetu) and the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu).
Regarding the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*):

it refers to the manifestation of non-universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering immediately after universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering [have ceased].
Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):

it refers to the non-universal afflictions (*akliṣṭa-kleśa*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), which arise conditioned by the universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering.

Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), as previously explained, the universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering act as four conditions for the universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
As for the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is the single cause known as the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
As for the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*):
This refers to the immediate succession of the universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering,
followed by the manifestation of the universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of the origin.
As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):

This means that the universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) arise conditioned by the universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained.
[Furthermore,] the universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the non-universal afflictions (*asarvatraga-kleśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin—

Furthermore, all afflictions abandoned through the cultivation of the truths of cessation and the path serve as three conditions [for the arising of subsequent afflictions], with the exception of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
As for the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): [it consists of the six causes].
The sole cause refers to the universal [cause].
As for the equal-and-immediate condition:
This means that immediately after the universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),
those various afflictions manifest;
the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained.
Regarding those that are not object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
because those various afflictions (*kleśa*) cannot take other categories as objects when they are not universal (*asarvatraga*).

Afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) that are not universal serve as four conditions for afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering that are also not universal.
Regarding conditions (*pratyaya*), there are three causes.
These are the associated condition (*samprayuktaka-pratyaya*), the co-existent condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*), and the similar-type condition (*sabhāga-pratyaya*).

As for the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), it refers to that which follows immediately after the non-universal afflictions (*asārvatrika-kleśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding the object-condition for the manifestation of non-universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering:
it refers to those non-universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering.
It arises conditioned by the non-universal afflictions (*akliṣṭa-kleśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously explained: the non-universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering serve as the four conditions for the universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering; specifically, they function as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The sole cause refers to the homogeneous cause;
as for the equal-and-immediate condition:

This refers to the immediate succession of non-universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering, followed by the manifestation of universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering.
As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): [it is as follows].
This refers to the universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

They serve as a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the non-universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, arising [from them] as previously described regarding the non-universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
It serves as three conditions for the universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya), excluding the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya).
As for the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya): [it is as follows].
This refers to the case where, immediately following the non-universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),
the universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) manifest.
As for the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):

This refers to the universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), which arise conditioned by the non-universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously explained; it is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Non-universal factors do not serve as causes for the afflictions of other categories.
Non-universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering [serve as causes] for non-universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of origination.

Regarding the seeing of cessation and the path, and all afflictions abandoned through cultivation, they serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). As for the equal-and-immediate condition:
it refers to that which occurs immediately after the non-universal afflictions abandoned through the seeing of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
When those various afflictions manifest,
the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained;
it is not the other two conditions.
Because non-universal factors (*asarvatraga-dharma*) are definitely not causes for defiled factors of other categories;
and because non-universal afflictions are definitely unable to take factors of other categories as their objects.

This is just as the two types of afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) serve as conditions for the nine types of afflictions, according to the degree of their respective influence.

It should be understood that the two types of afflictions abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) function as conditions for the nine [types of] afflictions in the same manner.
Regarding the afflictions with outflows (*sāsrava*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*):
They serve as four conditions for the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*).

Regarding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), there are three causes: namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
As for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*):

This refers to the immediate manifestation of afflictions with outflow conditioned by cessation that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, following immediately upon [the abandonment of] those same afflictions with outflow conditioned by cessation that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): [it is as follows].

That is to say, the defiled afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of cessation arise conditioned by those very defiled afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of cessation that take [those same] objects;
the dominant condition is as previously explained.

The outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) objects-of-consciousness (*ālambana*) afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) serve as three conditions for the untainted (*anāsrava*-object) afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of cessation,
excluding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
As for the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is the single cause,
namely the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
As for the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*):

This refers to the case where, immediately after a defiled (sāsrava) object-conditioned affliction to be abandoned by the vision of cessation has ceased, an undefiled (anāsrava) object-conditioned affliction to be abandoned by the vision of cessation manifests.
Regarding the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya), it is as previously explained; however, it is not an object-condition (ālambanapratyaya).
This means that the outflow-free (anāsrava) objects of the afflictions abandoned by the vision of cessation are exclusively the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha),
because they are not themselves afflictions.

The outflow-afflicted (sāsrava) objects of the afflictions abandoned by the vision of cessation serve as three conditions for the universal (sarvatraga) afflictions abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin.
Excluding the cause-condition and the equal-and-immediate condition:
this refers to the immediate succession of afflictions with outflow that have the cessation [of suffering] as their object— which are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation—
and the manifestation of pervasive afflictions that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin [of suffering].
Regarding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya):
it refers to the universal afflictions (sarvatraga-kleśa) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin,
which arise conditioned by the outflow-tainted afflictions (sāsrava-ālambana-kleśa) abandoned through the vision of cessation.
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained.

Regarding that which is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): it is because there is no sense of "causelessness" for non-universal factors (*asarvatraga-dharma*) with respect to the defilements of other categories.
This refers to the outflow-afflicted (*sāsrava*) objects of the afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*).

It serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the non-universal afflictions (*akliṣṭa-kleśa*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, as well as for all afflictions abandoned through the vision of the path and through cultivation.
It is neither a cause nor an object-condition.
As for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
it refers to that which follows immediately after the outflow-tainted afflictions (*āsrava*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Those various afflictions manifest before one;
their status as a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained,
and the meaning of their not being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is also as explained above.
Regarding those that are not object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
because those various afflictions (*kleśa*) are not universal (*asarvatraga*), they do not take other categories as objects;
this includes the afflictions with uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*).
With the outflow-free (anāsrava) objects of the afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, they act as three conditions,
excluding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
As for the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), there are three causes.
Regarding the associated, coexistent, homogeneous, and immediately preceding conditions:
this refers to the immediate succession of the outflow-free object-afflicted afflictions abandoned through the vision of cessation,
wherein the outflow-free object-afflicted afflictions abandoned through the vision of cessation manifest.
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained.
It is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
because that condition— analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)— is not an affliction (*kleśa*).

The untainted (anāsrava) objects-of-consciousness afflictions abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya) serve as four conditions for the tainted (sāsrava) objects-of-consciousness afflictions abandoned through the vision of cessation.
As for the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), it consists of only one cause.
Regarding the homogeneous and immediately preceding conditions:
this refers to the state immediately following the afflictions that have the untainted as their object and are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
Regarding the manifestation of outflow-tainted afflictions associated with the cessation of suffering (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) as objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
this refers to those outflow-tainted afflictions associated with the cessation of suffering that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
It arises conditioned by the outflow-free objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) of the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
The predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained.
[This refers to] the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of cessation that have outflow-free objects.
It serves as three conditions for the universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin;
excluding the causal condition,
it acts as the equal-and-immediate condition.
Immediately after the untainted object-afflicting afflictions abandoned through the vision of cessation,
the universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin manifest.
As for the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):

The universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin give rise to the outflow-free object-afflicted afflictions (*anāsrava-ālambana-kleśa*) abandoned through the vision of cessation.
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained.
Regarding those that are not causes:
pervasive afflictions do not serve as causes for the defilements of other categories;
likewise, the untainted-object (anāsrava-ālambana) afflictions abandoned through the vision of cessation [do not serve as causes].

It serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the non-universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, as well as for all afflictions abandoned through the vision of the path and through cultivation.
It is neither a cause nor an object-condition.
As for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
it refers to the state immediately following the afflictions that take the untainted as their object and are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
Those various afflictions manifest before one;
their predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained.
As for what is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*):
Because non-universal afflictions have no causal basis for [arising from] the defilements of other categories,
they are not object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Since those various afflictions are not universal, they do not take other categories as their objects.
Just as the two types of afflictions abandoned through the vision of cessation serve as conditions for nine types of afflictions in varying degrees,
so too do the two types of afflictions abandoned through the path of vision.
It should be understood that the number of afflictions with which they serve as conditions is likewise.
Afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) serve as four types of conditions for other afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation.
Regarding the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), there are three causes.
That is to say, the associated, co-existent, and homogeneous [conditions],
as well as the equal-and-immediate condition,
refer to the immediate succession of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding the object-condition for the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation that manifest:
it refers to the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation.
It arises conditioned by the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained:
the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.

It serves as three conditions for the universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, with the exception of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Regarding the equivalent-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*): [it is as follows].
This refers to the case where, immediately following the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
the universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*) manifest.
As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
This refers to the universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin,
which arise by taking as their object the afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained.
Regarding those that are not causes by way of conditions:
because non-universal dharmas do not serve as causes for defiled dharmas of other categories,
[they are not causes] for the afflictions abandoned through cultivation.

It serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the non-universal afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, as well as for all afflictions abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path.
It is neither a cause nor an object-condition.
As for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
it refers to that which occurs immediately after the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
When those various afflictions manifest,
the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained;
it is not the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
This is because non-universal dharmas do not serve as causes for the defiled dharmas of other categories.
Regarding those that are not object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
this is because not all non-universal afflictions are able to take dharmas of other categories as their objects. Furthermore, there are fifteen categories of afflictions.
That is to say, each of the three realms has five categories, from those abandoned through the vision of suffering up to those abandoned through cultivation.
Within these, one should reflect according to reason on how many of these fifteen categories serve as conditions for each individual category.
Furthermore, the afflictions of each individual realm are divided into five categories, which further constitute nine types;
thus, there are twenty-seven in total.
One should reflect according to reason upon how many of these serve as conditions for each of the others among the twenty-seven.

Chapter Two: The Section on the Single Path (Ekayāna-nirdeśa). Within the second part of the Second Aggregate of Bonds (Saṃyojana-skandha), the first section of the Section on the Single Path, there are nine bonds (saṃyojana).
This refers to the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) up to the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*).
If, regarding a particular object, there is the binding of the fetter of craving, is there also the binding of the fetter of hostility (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
Such are the sections [of the text] and the explanations of their meanings.
Having already grasped this,
one should next provide a detailed explanation.
Regarding the "matter" herein:
There are five kinds of entities (vastu):
first, the entity of intrinsic nature;
second, the entity of the object-condition (ālambana).
Third, the matter of the three fetters;
fourth, the matter of causes;
fifth, the matter of appropriation.
Regarding the entity of self-nature,
it is as explained in the discourse on the aggregates (*skandha*).
If an entity can be thoroughly penetrated, can that entity also be fully known?

If one is able to fully know a phenomenon, is one also able to penetrate that phenomenon? When the term "phenomenon" (*vastu*) is used to refer to the intrinsic nature of the various patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*), does that same phenomenon, once attained, constitute its accomplishment?
If a thing is accomplished, has that thing already been attained?
Regarding this, some say that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is expressed by the term "thing" (*vastu*).
Some say: if a phenomenon has acquisition (*prāpti*), it is spoken of by way of its objective basis (*vastu*);
that which is the objective basis is the object of cognition (*ālambana-vastu*).
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*,
all phenomena are known by wisdom according to their respective natures.
What does "according to their respective natures" mean?
That is to say, whatever dharma is the objective sphere of this wisdom is designated by the term "entity" (vastu) with respect to its object;
yet, as the Sūtra says:

Regarding the statement, "I shall explain to you the forty-four matters of knowledge and the seventy-seven matters of knowledge," the masters of the Abhidharma say that this sutra speaks of the nature of the entities themselves (*svabhāva-vastu*).
The Venerable Ghoṣaka states that the various patiences and knowledges which take the members of existence (bhavāṅga) as their objects are expressed by the term "thing" (vastu);
that sutra speaks of the "thing" that is the object of cognition.
That is to say, the objects of the various patiences (kṣānti) and knowledges (jñāna) among the members of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) are expressed by the term "entity" (vastu).
Regarding the "binding entity," it is as explained here.
"If, regarding this object, there is a bond of attachment (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), is there also a bond of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
and so forth, as explained at length.
In this context, the "five categories of phenomena" (*pañca-vastuka-dharma*) are expressed by the term "object" (*vastu*).
This refers to the phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation;
because these are the objects bound by the afflictions of the five categories, they are called "objects of bondage.
As for "causes":
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"What are phenomena with a basis (*savastuka*)?
What are phenomena without a basis (*avastuka*)?"
His intention is to state that there are both conditioned phenomena (*sa-hetuka-dharma*) and unconditioned phenomena (*a-hetuka-dharma*).
Furthermore, a verse from the *Gāthā* says:
"O Bhikṣu, when the mind is tranquil, One can forever sever all conditioned things (*vastu*)."
"Because his birth and death are exhausted, he does not undergo further existence.
The meaning of this verse is that all birth and death depend entirely upon causes.
Because there is a cause, there is birth and death;
because the cause is severed, birth and death are exhausted.
By this means, one no longer undergoes the appropriation of the three types of future existence.
As stated in the sūtra:
"One should abandon the mind that clings to fields, houses, and wealth;
one should distance oneself from the karmic activity of clinging to fields, houses, and wealth."
Furthermore, a verse states:
"If one desires fields, wealth, cattle, horses, and the like,
as well as male and female servants and kinsmen, that person is said to be extremely greedy."
Furthermore, householders speak thus:
"I take charge of this matter; I maintain this matter.
Such instances as these are called "appropriated matters."
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, the matter of the realm;
second, the matter of the location.
Third, the matter of the three aggregates;
fourth, the matter of the four worlds;
fifth, the matter of the moment.
Regarding these ten matters,
this treatise is composed based solely upon the matter of "bondage" (saṃyojana),
and not based on the other nine.
The Abhidharma masters state:
"The objects to which one is bound are real, and the fetters that bind are also real;
the *pudgala* (person) is a mere designation."
The Vātsīputrīyas say:
"The object to which one is bound is real,
and the fetter that binds is also real."
The *pudgala* is also real.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say that the fetters which bind are real, while the things bound are conventional; the *pudgala*, too, is conventional.
Question: For what reason does he say that the objects to which one is bound are merely provisional?
Answer: He says that because the distinction between objects that are subject to defilement and those that are not is not fixed, he knows that these objects are not real.
That is to say, suppose there is an upright woman, beautifully adorned with various ornaments, who enters an assembly;
some who see her give rise to reverence, some give rise to desire,
and some give rise to anger.
Some views give rise to envy;
some views give rise to revulsion; some views give rise to compassion;
and some views give rise to equanimity.
It should be understood that among these, those who regard him as a son give rise to reverence upon seeing him;
those addicted to desire give rise to lust;
and those who harbor enmity give rise to hatred.
Those who shared her husband's feelings saw her and gave rise to jealousy;
those who practiced the meditation on impurity saw her and gave rise to revulsion;
and the sages free from desire saw her and gave rise to compassion.
They form this thought:
"This exquisite form will before long be destroyed by impermanence.
Seeing it thus, the Arhats give rise to equanimity.
For this reason, it is known that objects lack substantial reality.
That [previous] explanation is irrational. Why is this so?
If the object were not real,
it should not serve as a condition for the arising of mind and mental factors. If that were so,
there would be no phenomena belonging to the categories of affliction or purification.
The *pudgala* (person) is certainly not substantially existent,
for the Buddha taught that there is no self and nothing belonging to a self. Furthermore,
some afflictions are associated with the five sensory consciousnesses.
There are those associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
and those associated with the five [sensory] consciousnesses.
If they are past, they are bound to past objects.
If it exists in the present, it is bound to present phenomena;
if it exists in the future as a dharma subject to arising, it is bound to future phenomena;
if it is a dharma not subject to arising, it is bound to phenomena of all three times.
Regarding that which is associated with mental consciousness:
whether it belongs to the past, the future, or the present,
it is capable of being bound to the three periods of time.
Furthermore, the afflictions associated with visual consciousness act as objects of attachment (*ālambana-bandhana*) toward the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*),
