Regarding the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of grasping (*parigraha-saṃyojana*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm, both have already been abandoned.
However, because the fetter of grasping abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) has not yet been abandoned,
one remains bound to the phenomena of the desire realm abandoned through the vision of suffering by way of taking them as objects (*ālambana-bandhana*).

Although the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm has not yet been abandoned, it does not constitute a bond through being an object (*ālambana-bandhana*) with respect to those phenomena of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),
because it is not universal (*asarvatraga*).
Because that which is bound by non-associated [factors] belongs to another category,
for those who have not yet abandoned the fetters of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) regarding the dharmas of the form and formless realms,
there may be eight stages of the fetters of grasping that remain unabandoned.
...up to the point where there may be one category of fetters of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) not yet abandoned in a particular stage;
or within that stage, there may be four categories of fetters of grasping not yet abandoned;
up to the point where there may be even a single category of fetters of grasping not yet abandoned.
Because it has not been abandoned, there is the fetter of grasping (upādāna-saṃyojana) but no fetter of ill-will (vyāpāda-saṃyojana),
since that [ill-will] is absent;
or alternatively, both may be present as fetters.
This means that for one who is bound by all fetters, there are two types of fetter-bondage regarding the phenomena of the desire realm to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
Among these, for one bound by all fetters, regarding the phenomena of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering:
There is one category bound by the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and two categories bound by the fetters of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
The same applies to those dharmas in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding those dharmas in the desire realm abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*):
There is one portion bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and three portions bound by the fetters of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
It is the same for the factors of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Regarding the factors of the desire realm abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is one portion bound by the fetter of ill-will and two portions bound by the fetters of grasping.
Furthermore, for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire,
when the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen,
there are two fetters binding them to the phenomena of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through cultivation.
In this context, regarding the phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*),
there is bondage by one portion of the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and bondage by one portion of the fetter of attachment (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
Regarding the phenomena of the desire realm abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*):
Each is bound by one portion of the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and two portions of the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
Regarding the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
there is binding by one portion of the fetter of ill-will and one portion of the fetter of grasping.
At that time, regarding the phenomena in the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),
although there is the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), there is no fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*); therefore,
this is not mentioned here.
Furthermore, when the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen,
there are two fetters binding one to the phenomena of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path;
herein, one has also not yet become free from the defilement of desire.
Regarding the dharmas of the desire realm abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path,
each has one portion bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and one portion bound by the fetter of attachment (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
At that time, regarding the dharmas of the desire realm abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
Although there is the fetter of ill-will (vyāpāda-saṃyojana), there is no fetter of grasping (upādāna-saṃyojana);
therefore, this is not mentioned.
Furthermore, when the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) has already arisen but the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) has not yet arisen.
Regarding the dharmas to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the desire realm, there are two fetters that bind one;
herein, one has likewise not yet become free from the defilement of desire regarding those dharmas to be abandoned through the path of seeing.
There is a case where one is bound by the fetter of aversion (pratigha-saṃyojana) and bound by the fetter of grasping (parāmarśa-saṃyojana).
At that time, although there is binding by the fetter of aversion toward the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), there is no binding by the fetter of grasping.
Therefore, this is not mentioned.
Alternatively, there may be cases where both are unbound,
namely when one has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire.
When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen,
there is no bondage by the two fetters regarding those phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination,
nor regarding those phenomena abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms.
When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,
there are no two fetters (saṃyojana) binding one to the phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin,
and cessation, nor to the phenomena of the form and formless realms abandoned through cultivation.
A disciple of the World-Honored One who possesses right view,
but has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire,
with respect to those phenomena to be abandoned by seeing.
Furthermore, there are no two fetters binding to the factors abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms.
There are no two fetters binding to the factors of the desire realm for one who has already become free from the defilement of desire.
There are no two fetters binding to the factors of the desire and form realms for one who has already become free from the defilement of form.
Having already become free from the defilements of the formless realm, one is not bound by the two fetters regarding the phenomena of the three realms;
because within these, both the fettering factors and the fettered objects have been abandoned, one is entirely free from the two fetters.

This means that because one is liberated from both the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*). If, regarding a certain object, there is the binding of the fetter of ill-will, is there also the binding of the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: If, regarding that object, there is the binding of the fetter of envy.
There must be the fetter of ill-will (pratigha-saṃyojana).
Alternatively, there may be the fetter of ill-will without the fetter of envy (īrṣyā-saṃyojana);
that is to say, when the fetter of ill-will toward those dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by insight (darśana-prahātavya) has not yet been severed.

Among these, the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) belongs exclusively to the desire realm, pervades all five categories, and has only outflowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*), but is not universal (*asarvatraga*).
The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) belongs exclusively to the desire realm, is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), has outflowing objects, and is not universal.
For those who are bound by all fetters regarding matters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
if there is bondage by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), there is also bondage by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*); and if there is bondage by the fetter of envy,
[there is also bondage by the fetter of ill-will].
There is also the case where one is bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) regarding matters to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
yet is not bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*).
This applies to those who are not fully bound (*asamagra-bandhana*) and have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire (*avītarāga*).
Regarding matters abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm, there is bondage by both types of fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Regarding matters abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) in the desire realm, wherever they have not yet been abandoned, there is bondage by the fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), but no bondage by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*).
If there is no bondage by two fetters regarding that which has already been abandoned;
and if one is already free from the defilement of desire, there is no bondage by two fetters regarding the five categories of objects in the desire realm,
nor regarding the five categories of objects in the form and formless realms.
Whether one is bound by all fetters or not bound by all fetters, at no time are there two fetters simultaneously binding,
because the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha*) is long while the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*) is short. Therefore,
the question should be answered with a "consequent" formula (*paścāt-pādaka*).
If there is a binding by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) regarding this object, there is necessarily a binding by the fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*).
This refers to objects in the desire realm that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) but from which one has not yet attained dissociation.
Alternatively, there may be a binding by the fetter of malice without a binding by the fetter of envy.
This refers to the fact that among the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), the fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) has not yet been abandoned.
Within this, there may be four categories of the fetter of malice that have not been abandoned,
up to and including one category of the fetter of malice that has not been abandoned.
Because it has not been abandoned, there is the bond of the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) but no bond of the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*).
Why is this? Because the category of factors to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) lacks the fetter of envy.
As it is with the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*), so it is with the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*).

That is to say, both envy and avarice are exclusively abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); they have outflowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and are not universal (*asarvatraga*).
If, regarding this matter, there is bondage by the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana), is there also bondage by the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana)?
Answer: If, regarding this matter, there is bondage by the fetter of views, there must necessarily be bondage by the fetter of ignorance.
"Or there may be one who is bound by the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana) and bound by the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana)," and so forth, as explained at length.

In this context, the fetter of ignorance pertains to all three realms, all five categories, and has both outflowing (sāsrava) and non-outflowing (anāsrava) objects; it includes both universal (sarvatraga) and non-universal factors.

The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) pervades all three realms and consists solely of the four categories; it includes both those with outflow (*sāsrava*) and those without outflow (*anāsrava*), as well as universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal (*asarvatraga*) objects.
For those who are bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), this applies to the five categories of objects within the three realms.
If one is bound by the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana), one is also bound by the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana);
if one is bound by the fetter of views, one is also bound by the fetter of ignorance.
This is because for those who are not fully bound, the fetter of ignorance is predominant while the fetter of views is subordinate.
The question should be answered by means of a *pṛṣṭhottara* (subsequent-phrase) response:
if there is bondage by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) regarding a given object, there must necessarily be bondage by the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*).
That is to say, regarding objects belonging to the five categories within the three realms where the fetter of views has not yet been abandoned.
There may be those who are bound by the fetter of ignorance and bound by the fetter of views;
that is to say, when the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen,
they are bound to those phenomena associated with the fetter of views that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path.
Furthermore, regarding the factors to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there is the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) that has not yet been severed.

Among these, the factors dissociated from the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*) and the path (*mārga-darśana*) refer to the collection of factors—both associated and dissociated—that are dissociated from the intrinsic nature of those wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), as well as from the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), and non-common ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*).
Because the fetter of ignorance has not been severed regarding these phenomena, there is the binding of the fetter of ignorance.
For him, this constitutes both an objective-binding (ālambana-bandhana) and an associative-binding (samprayoga-bandhana) with respect to his own group [of aggregates].
If it pertains to another's group, it is an objective-binding but not an associative-binding; nor is there the binding of the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-bandhana).
Why is this? Because those pervasive fetters of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) that take the five categories as their object have already been abandoned;
as for the remaining unabandoned ones, they are dissociated from these phenomena (dharma) that are not associated with the fetter of views.
It is not bound by way of the object, because it has the untainted as its object;
it is not bound by way of association, because it belongs to a different category;
and self-nature is not associated with itself.
Because they have not yet abandoned the fetter of ignorance regarding the factors to be abandoned by cultivation, they are bound by the fetter of ignorance;

that is, there may be cases where the fetter of ignorance of the nine stages has not been abandoned, up to and including cases where the fetter of ignorance of even a single stage has not been abandoned.
Within this stage, there may be nine grades of the fetter of ignorance that have not yet been abandoned,
up to and including the case where even a single grade of the fetter of ignorance remains unabandoned and one is bound by the fetter of views.
Why is this? Because the pervasive fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana), which takes the five categories as its object,
has already been abandoned by him.
Because the category of factors to be abandoned by cultivation lacks the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, when the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) has not yet arisen,
one is dissociated from the factors to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) that are associated with the fetter of views.
Furthermore, regarding the factors to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there is the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) that has not yet been severed.
Among these, the factors dissociated from the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are as previously explained.

Regarding these various factors and the factors to be abandoned through cultivation, the state of being bound by the fetter of ignorance and the state of not being bound by the fetter of views are also as previously explained.
Furthermore, among the disciples of the World-Honored One who possess right view,
there may be those for whom the fetter of ignorance regarding the factors to be abandoned through cultivation has not yet been severed;
among these, there may be some for whom the fetter of ignorance pertaining to the nine stages has not yet been severed.
...up to the point where there may be an unsevered bond of ignorance regarding a certain stage (*bhūmi*).
Within that stage, there may be nine grades of the bond of ignorance that are unsevered,
or even down to a single grade of the bond of ignorance that remains unsevered.
Because they have not been abandoned, there is the fetter of ignorance and the fetter of views. Why is this?
Because all fetters of views have already been abandoned by them.
As it is with the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*),
so it is with doubt (*vicikitsā*). That is to say,

just as the fetter of views pertains to all three realms, consists of only four categories, and encompasses both impure (*sāsrava*) and pure (*anāsrava*) objects, as well as universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal [factors].
The fetter of doubt is likewise.
Therefore, as with the fetter of ignorance in relation to the fetter of views,
if there is the bondage of the fetter of ignorance regarding a given object, is there also the bondage of the fetter of grasping?
Answer: If there is the bond of grasping (upādāna-saṃyojana) with respect to this object, there is necessarily the bond of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana);
however, there may or may not be the bond of ignorance [with respect to other objects].
"There is no fetter of grasping," and so forth, as explained at length.

Among these, the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) pertains to all five categories (*pañca-nikāya*) across the three realms; it has both outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) objects, and is both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal (*asarvatraga*).

The fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*) pertains to all three realms and consists of only four categories: those with outflows as objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*), including both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal (*asarvatraga*).

For those who are bound by all fetters, regarding the five categories of phenomena within the three realms, if they are bound by the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), they are also bound by the fetter of grasping.
If there is a binding by the fetter of grasping (upādāna-saṃyojana), there is also a binding by the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana).
For one who is not fully bound, the fetter of ignorance is long while the fetter of grasping is short;
thus, the question should be answered with a "consequent" (paścāt-pādaka) formula.
If there is bondage by the fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*) regarding a given object, there is necessarily bondage by the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*).
That is to say, regarding objects within the five categories of the three realms where the fetter of grasping has not yet been abandoned;
or, conversely, there may be bondage by the fetter of ignorance without bondage by the fetter of grasping.

That is to say: when the knowledge of origination has already arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, there remains the fetter of ignorance regarding the phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation;
or when the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen.
Regarding the phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation, there exists the fetter of ignorance that has not yet been severed.
Even for a disciple of the Blessed One who possesses right view,
regarding the phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation, there exists the fetter of ignorance that has not yet been severed.
In this regard, there may be those for whom the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) has not yet been severed across nine stages,
or even those for whom it has not yet been severed in a single stage;
within that stage, there may be those for whom the fetter of ignorance has not yet been severed across nine grades.
Even if there remains a single category of the fetter of ignorance that has not been abandoned,
because it is not abandoned, one is bound by the fetter of ignorance and the fetter of grasping. Why is this so?
Because the universal fetters of grasping (*pariṣaṇṇa-grahaṇa-saṃyojana*) that take the five categories as their object have already been abandoned;

and because the non-universal fetters of grasping that have not yet been abandoned cannot act as a bond with respect to phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), since they have already been abandoned.
Because the category of factors abandoned by cultivation lacks the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
If there is the binding of the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) with respect to a given object, is there also the binding of the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: If there is the binding of the fetter of envy with respect to that object, there must necessarily be the binding of the fetter of ignorance.
There may be those who are bound by the fetter of ignorance but not by the fetter of envy;
that is to say, regarding the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned by insight,
as well as the factors of the form and formless realms, the fetter of ignorance has not yet been abandoned.

Among these, the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) pertains to all three realms, all five categories, and has both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) objects; it includes both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal factors.
The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) belongs exclusively to the desire realm, is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), has contaminated objects, and is non-universal.
For those who are bound by all fetters, regarding matters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm:
if they are bound by the fetter of ignorance, they are also bound by the fetter of envy;
if they are bound by the fetter of envy, they are also bound by the fetter of ignorance.
Regarding the objects of the four categories to be abandoned through vision in the desire realm,
as well as the objects of the five categories in the form and formless realms,
there is bondage by the fetter of ignorance, but not by the fetter of envy.
One who is not yet free from bondage, if they have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire,
possesses the bonds of both types of fetters regarding the objects to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm;
and regarding the four categories of objects to be abandoned through insight in the three realms.
In states where one has not yet become dissociated from fetters, there is the bondage of the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana) but not the bondage of the fetter of envy (īrṣyā-saṃyojana);
in states where one has already become dissociated, neither of these two fetters is present.
This applies to matters abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) within the realms of form and formlessness.
There are those bound by the fetter of ignorance but not by the fetter of envy.
Having already abandoned the defilement of desire, they are not bound by either of these two fetters with respect to the five categories of objects in the desire realm;
nor are they so bound with respect to the five categories of objects in the form and formless realms.
In accordance with the state of not being dissociated from fetters,
there is the bondage of the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana) but not the bondage of the fetter of envy (īrṣyā-saṃyojana);
if one has already become dissociated from that state, there is no bondage by either of these two fetters.
Because the fetter of ignorance is long and the fetter of envy is short,
the question should be answered by means of a *pṛṣṭhottara* (subsequent) formula:
if one is bound to this object by the fetter of envy, one is necessarily bound to it by the fetter of ignorance.
This refers to matters in the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation and from which one is not yet disengaged;
such matters may be bound by the fetter of ignorance,
but are not bound by the fetter of envy.

This refers to the fact that regarding the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), there exists the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) which has not yet been abandoned;
herein, there may be four categories of the fetter of ignorance that have not been severed, up to and including one category of the fetter of ignorance that has not been severed.
Regarding the phenomena of the form and formless realms, there is the fetter of ignorance that has not yet been abandoned;
herein, there may be the fetter of ignorance of eight stages that has not yet been abandoned,
up to and including the fetter of ignorance of a single stage that has not yet been abandoned.
Within this stage, there may be some for whom the fetters of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana) of five categories have not yet been abandoned,
up to those for whom even one category of the fetters of ignorance has not yet been abandoned;
and within that category, there may be some for whom nine grades of the fetters of ignorance have not yet been abandoned.
Even if there remains a single category of the fetter of ignorance that has not been severed,
because it has not been severed, one is bound by the fetter of ignorance and bound by the fetter of envy. Why is this so?
Because the category of factors to be abandoned by insight (darśana-prahātavya) lacks the fetter of envy (īrṣyā-saṃyojana),
and because envy is likewise absent in the form and formless realms;
as it is with the fetter of envy, so it is with others.
The same applies to the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*).

That is to say, envy (*īrṣyā*) and stinginess both belong exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and have out-flowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) that are not universal (*apratighāna*).
If there is a binding by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) regarding a given object, is there also a binding by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: If there is bondage by the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) regarding this object, there is necessarily bondage by the fetter of grasping (parāmarśa-saṃyojana);
however, there may be bondage by the fetter of grasping without bondage by the fetter of views, and so forth, as explained at length.

Among these, the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) pertains to all three realms, consists of only four categories, and includes both those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*), as well as universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal [defilements].
The fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) pertains to all three realms, consists of only four categories, has outflows as its object, and includes both universal and non-universal [defilements].
For those who are bound by all fetters regarding the five categories of phenomena within the three realms,
if there is bondage by the fetter of views, there is also bondage by the fetter of grasping;
if there is bondage by the fetter of grasping, there is also bondage by the fetter of views.
One who is not fully bound possesses factors dissociated from the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path;
such a person is bound by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) but not bound by the fetter of views.
This is because the fetter of views is short while the fetter of grasping is long.
The question should be answered by following the preceding formula:
if there is bondage by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) regarding a given object, there must necessarily be bondage by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
That is to say, regarding those objects within the five categories of the three realms from which one has not yet become free from the bondage of the fetter of views.
There may be one who is bound by the fetter of grasping but not bound by the fetter of views;
that is to say, when the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen,
there exists within phenomena dissociated from the fetter of views— which are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path— the fetter of grasping which has not yet been severed.
When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,

there remains the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) that has not been abandoned regarding those factors dissociated from the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing.
Among these, the factors dissociated from the fetters of views to be abandoned through the paths of seeing cessation and the path are as previously explained.
Because the fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*) has not yet been abandoned regarding these phenomena, there is the bondage of the fetter of grasping.
For him, it constitutes both an object-condition bondage (*ālambana-bandhana*) and an association bondage (*samprayoga-bandhana*) with respect to his own group (*svakalāpa*).
If it pertains to another group, it constitutes an object-condition bondage but not an association bondage, and there is no bondage of the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
Why is this? Because those universal fetters of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) that take the five categories as their object have already been abandoned.

As for the remaining unabandoned [fetters], they do not bind this dissociated dharma through the mode of being an object (ālambana-bandhana), because they take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object.
Because that which is bound by association belongs to a different category,
and because a self-nature does not associate with itself.
If there is binding by the fetter of views regarding a given thing, is there also binding by the fetter of doubt?
It shall be explained in four statements.

Herein, the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) pertains to all three realms, consists of only four categories, and encompasses both impure (*sāsrava*) and pure (*anāsrava*) objects; it includes both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal factors.
The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) is likewise.
For those who are bound by all fetters regarding the five categories of phenomena within the three realms,
if they are bound by the fetter of views, they are also bound by the fetter of doubt;
and if they are bound by the fetter of doubt, they are also bound by the fetter of views.

For one who is not bound by all fetters (*asakalabandhana*), the two fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are "long" because each has a binding connection (*saṃyojana*) within its own category (*sva-nikāya*),
and they are "short" because each lacks a binding connection within the other's category (*para-nikāya*).
Therefore, the question should be answered by establishing four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) based on their respective categories.
There may be one who is bound by the fetter of views but not by the fetter of doubt;
that is to say, when the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen,
there remains an unsevered fetter of views regarding those phenomena associated with the fetter of views that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path.
When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,
there remains unabandoned fetter of views regarding those phenomena associated with the fetter of views that are to be abandoned through the path of seeing.
Among these, "phenomena associated with the fetter of views to be abandoned through the path of seeing cessation or the path" refers to...
This refers to the mind and mental factors associated with that wrong view.
Because the fetter of views has not been abandoned, there is a bond of association with them;
however, there is no bond of objectification, because [the fetter] takes uncontaminated objects as its focus.
The fetter of doubt has no connection whatsoever with that [state].
Why is this? Because the pervasive fetter of doubt, which takes the five categories as its object, has already been abandoned.

As for those remaining fetters that have not yet been abandoned: they are not bound to the dharmas associated with the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) by way of being an object (ālambana-bandhana), because [those dharmas] take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object; nor are they bound by way of association (saṃprayoga-bandhana), because they belong to a different group (nikāya).

Alternatively, there may be binding by the fetter of doubt (vicikitsā-saṃyojana) without binding by the fetter of views, namely when the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) has already arisen but the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) has not yet arisen.
Regarding those factors associated with the fetter of doubt abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, the fetter of doubt remains unabandoned;

when the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, the fetter of doubt remains unabandoned regarding those factors associated with the fetter of doubt abandoned through the vision of the path.

Among these, the factors associated with the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path refer to those mental states and mental concomitants associated with that doubt;
for the fetter of doubt possesses an association-bond (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) toward them because it has not yet been abandoned.
Because there is no bondage by way of an object for those [factors] that take the untainted as their object;
thus, the fetter of views has no sense of bondage toward them at all. Why is this so?
Because the pervasive fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) that take the five categories as their objects have already been abandoned;

as for the remaining unabandoned ones, they are not bound by way of being an object (*ālambana-bandhana*) toward those factors associated with the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*), because [those factors] have uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*), nor are they bound by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*), because they belong to a different group (*anya-kalāpa*).
There may be cases where both [types of fetters] bind.
That is to say, for one who is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), there are two types of fetter-bondage regarding the phenomena to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.

Among these, for one bound by all fetters, regarding the phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, there is bondage by the two categories of the fetter of views and the two categories of the fetter of doubt.
The same applies to the phenomena abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding the phenomena associated with the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*),
there is bondage by the fetter of views belonging to three categories and bondage by the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) belonging to two categories.
Regarding those factors associated with the fetter of doubt to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*),
there is bondage by the three categories of the fetter of doubt and bondage by the two categories of the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding those factors dissociated from the single fetter of either view or doubt to be abandoned by the vision of cessation:
There is the fetter of views belonging to two categories and the fetter of doubt belonging to two categories.
It is the same regarding the factors abandoned by the path of vision.
Regarding the factors abandoned by cultivation: [the same applies].
There are two types of fetters of views and two types of fetters of doubt that bind.
When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen,
there are two fetters binding the phenomena to be abandoned through the cultivation of the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
In this context, when the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origination has not yet arisen,
regarding those phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of suffering,
there is bondage by one portion of the fetters of views and bondage by one portion of the fetters of doubt.
The same applies to the factors abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding the factors associated with the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*),
there is bondage by the two categories of the fetter of views and bondage by one category of the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*).
Regarding those phenomena associated with the fetter of doubt to be abandoned by the vision of cessation,
there is bondage by two categories of the fetter of doubt and bondage by one category of the fetter of views.
Regarding those phenomena dissociated from both the fetter of views and the fetter of doubt to be abandoned by the vision of cessation:
There is one category bound by the fetter of views and one category bound by the fetter of doubt;
it is the same for those dharmas abandoned through the path of vision.
Regarding those dharmas abandoned through cultivation:
There is one class bound by the fetter of views and one class bound by the fetter of doubt;
or there may be those bound by neither,
namely, those for whom the knowledge of origination has already arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen.
Regarding the phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin,
as well as those phenomena dissociated from the two fetters of views and doubt to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path,

and furthermore regarding the phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation— wherein the knowledge of destruction has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen— the two fetters are no longer bound.
Regarding the phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation,
as well as the phenomena dissociated from the two fetters of views and doubt abandoned through the vision of the path,
and furthermore regarding the phenomena abandoned through cultivation, there is no bondage by these two fetters.
A disciple of the World-Honored One who possesses right view has no two fetters binding them regarding phenomena to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation;
one who is already free from the defilement of desire has no two fetters binding them regarding phenomena of the desire realm.
Having already abandoned attachment to form, one is no longer bound by the two fetters regarding the phenomena of the desire and form realms.
Having already abandoned attachment to the formless, one is no longer bound by the two fetters regarding the phenomena of all three realms.
Since, herein, both the fettering factors and the fettered objects have been completely severed, one is liberated from both fetters.
This means that because one is simultaneously dissociated from the fetters of views and doubt,
the factors dissociated from both the fetters of views and doubt— which are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path—
remain bound by their own respective categories even though they have not yet been dissociated from them.
Because the two fetters of views are not bound to that [object], it is called "being without the bondage of the two fetters.
If there is bondage by the fetter of views regarding this object, is there also bondage by the fetter of envy?
It is agreed that there shall be four propositions.

Among these, the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) pervades all three realms and consists exclusively of four categories; it encompasses both the outflow-possessing (*sāsrava*) and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) objects, and includes both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal [factors].
The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) belongs exclusively to the desire realm, is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), takes only outflow-possessing objects, and is non-universal.
For those who are bound by all fetters, regarding matters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm:
if there is bondage by the fetter of views, there is also bondage by the fetter of envy; and if there is bondage by the fetter of envy, [there is also bondage by the fetter of views].
There are also cases where there is bondage by the fetter of views regarding the four categories of objects to be abandoned through vision in the desire realm,
as well as the five categories of objects in the form and formless realms; in these cases, there is bondage by the fetter of views, but no bondage by the fetter of envy.
For one who is not yet free from the bonds— that is, one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire—
if the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen,
then with respect to the four categories of objects to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms:
Regarding matters to be abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms,
there is bondage by the fetter of views but no bondage by the fetter of envy;
regarding matters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, both fetters are present.
When the knowledge of origination has arisen and ceased, or when the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,

there is bondage by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) but no bondage by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) regarding objects to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm;
and there is bondage by the fetter of views regarding those factors associated with views that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation or the vision of the path within the three realms.
There is the state of being bound by the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) but not by the fetter of envy (īrṣyā-saṃyojana).

This applies to those phenomena in the three realms abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, as well as to those phenomena dissociated from the fetter of views abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path; these are not bound by either of the two fetters.
If one has already become free from the defilement of desire, there is no bondage by the two fetters regarding the five categories of objects in the desire realm.
Regarding the five categories of objects in the form and formless realms,
for one who has not yet abandoned the fetter of views, there is bondage by the fetter of views, but there is no bondage by the fetter of envy.
If one has already become detached from the fetter of views (dṛṣṭisaṃyojana), there is no bondage by these two fetters,
because these two possess the sense of being mutually long and short.
To the question asked, one should respond by means of a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
There may be one who is bound by the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) but not bound by the fetter of envy (īrṣyā-saṃyojana);

that is, one for whom the fetter of views regarding the factors to be abandoned by insight (darśana-prahātavya-dharma) in the desire realm, as well as those in the form and formless realms, has not yet been abandoned.
In this context, regarding those in the desire realm for whom the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) among the factors to be abandoned by seeing has not been severed,
there may be four categories of the fetter of views that have not been severed,
up to and including one category of the fetter of views that has not been severed.
Regarding those for whom the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*) has not yet been abandoned with respect to the phenomena of the form and formless realms:
there are some for whom the fetter of views has not been abandoned in eight stages,
and so on, up to those for whom it has not been abandoned in even a single stage.
Within this stage, there may be those who have not yet abandoned four categories of fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*),
or even those who have not yet abandoned one category of fetters of views.
Because they have not yet abandoned them, they possess the bond of the fetters of views but lack the bond of the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*).
Why is this? Because among those [factors] to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), as well as in the two higher realms, there is no fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*).
Alternatively, there may be the binding of the fetter of envy without the binding of the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
This refers to one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire:
having already produced the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) but not yet produced the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna),
such a person has not yet severed the fetter of envy (īrṣyā-saṃyojana) regarding the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,
there is a fetter of envy regarding the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation that has not been severed,
even for a disciple of the Blessed One who is possessed of vision.

For one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire, there remains the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) regarding the factors to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Among these, there may be nine grades of the fetter of envy that have not been abandoned,
up to and including even a single grade of the fetter of envy that has not been abandoned.
Because it has not been abandoned, there is the fetter of envy and the fetter of views.
Why is this? Because those universal fetters of views that take the five categories as their object have already been abandoned.

Those [afflictions] not yet abandoned cannot act as fetters with respect to dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they do not have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object;
furthermore, the category of dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation lacks the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
Alternatively, there may be cases where one is bound by both.

This means that for one who is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), there are two types of fetter-bondage (*saṃyojana-bandhana*) regarding the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Among these, for one bound by all fetters, there is bondage by two categories of the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) and bondage by one category of the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) regarding the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation.
Furthermore, for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of sensual desire,
when the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen,
there are two fetters binding them to the phenomena of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation.
Among these, those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire may have nine grades [of fetters] unabandoned, or even down to one grade unabandoned;
for them, the knowledge of suffering has already arisen, but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen.
Regarding the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
there is one class bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) and one class bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*);
or there may be those bound by neither.
This refers to one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire,
for whom the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) has already arisen but the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) has not yet arisen,
regarding those phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination.
Furthermore, regarding those phenomena dissociated from the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) which are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path,
as well as the phenomena of the form and formless realms abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there is no bondage by two fetters.
This is the case when the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) has not yet arisen.
Regarding the phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation,
as well as the phenomena dissociated from the fetter of views abandoned through the vision of the path,
and furthermore regarding the phenomena abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms, there is no bondage by the two fetters.
A disciple of the World-Honored One who possesses right view,
but has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire,
with respect to those phenomena to be abandoned by seeing.
Furthermore, there is no bondage by two fetters regarding the factors abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms.
For one who has already become free from the defilement of desire, there is no bondage by two fetters regarding the factors of the desire realm.
For one who has already become free from the defilement of form, there is no bondage by two fetters regarding the factors of the desire and form realms.
Having already become free from the defilements of the formless realm, one is not bound by the two fetters regarding the phenomena of the three realms.
Among these, some are not bound because they have already been abandoned,
while others are not bound because they were originally non-existent.
As it is with the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*),
so it is with the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*).

That is to say, both envy and stinginess belong exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and have impure objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) that are not universal (*apracaraka*).
Just as the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) forms a single category following its classification,
so too does the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*).

This is because both views and doubt pertain to all three realms, consist of only four categories, and encompass both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) objects, as well as both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal factors.
If, regarding this matter, there is bondage by the fetter of grasping (upādāna-saṃyojana), is there also bondage by the fetter of doubt (vicikitsā-saṃyojana)?
Answer: If, regarding this matter, there is bondage by the fetter of doubt, there must necessarily be bondage by the fetter of grasping.
"Or there may be one who is bound by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) but not bound by the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*)," and so forth,
as explained at length. In this context,

the fetter of grasping pertains to all three realms, consists of only four categories, has outflowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*), and includes both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal [defilements].

The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) pervades the three realms; it consists of only four categories, and its objects include both the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), as well as both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal factors.
For those who are bound by all fetters, this applies to the objects of the five categories within the three realms.
If one is bound by the fetter of grasping (*upādāna*), one is also bound by the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*);
if one is bound by the fetter of doubt, one is also bound by the fetter of grasping.

However, for those who are not fully bound, there are phenomena dissociated from the fetter of doubt that are to be abandoned through the vision of the cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-darśana-heya*).
There are those who are bound by the fetter of grasping (upādāna-saṃyojana) but not by the fetter of doubt (vicikitsā-saṃyojana),
because the fetter of grasping is long while the fetter of doubt is short.
To the question asked, one should provide an answer according to the subsequent clause (paścāt-pādaka).
If there is a binding by the fetter of doubt regarding a given object, there is necessarily a binding by the fetter of grasping.
That is to say, regarding objects within the five categories of the three realms from which one has not yet abandoned the fetter of doubt,
there may be a binding by the fetter of grasping without a binding by the fetter of doubt.

That is to say: when the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, there is the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) that has not been abandoned regarding those phenomena dissociated from the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path.

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, there is the fetter of grasping that has not been abandoned regarding those phenomena dissociated from the fetter of doubt to be abandoned by the vision of the path.

Among these, the factors dissociated from the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path refer to the collection of factors associated with and dissociated from the intrinsic nature of that doubt,
as well as the views of holding to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), holding to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), greed, hatred, pride, and non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
Because the fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*) has not yet been abandoned regarding these phenomena, there is the bondage of the fetter of grasping.
For that [person], it constitutes both an object-condition bondage (*ālambana-bandhana*) and an association bondage (*samprayoga-bandhana*) with respect to their own group;
however, with respect to another's group, it constitutes an object-condition bondage but not an association bondage.
There is no bondage by the fetter of doubt. Why is this?
Because those universal fetters of doubt that take the five categories as their object have already been abandoned.
Regarding those other [defilements] not yet abandoned, they are not associated with this dharma of the fetter of doubt;
they are not bound by way of being an object, because they take the untainted as their object,
nor are they bound by way of association, because they belong to a different category.
Because intrinsic nature does not associate with itself.
If there is the binding of the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) regarding a certain object, is there also the binding of the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*)?
One should answer that this constitutes four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Among these, the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) pertains to all three realms; it consists of only four categories, has objects that are tainted (*sāsrava*), and includes both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal [defilements].
The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) pertains only to the desire realm; it is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), has tainted objects, and is non-universal.
For those who are bound by all fetters regarding matters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
if they are bound by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa*), they are also bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*);
and if they are bound by the fetter of envy, they are also bound by the fetter of grasping.
Regarding the objects of the four categories abandoned through seeing in the desire realm, as well as the objects of the five categories in the form and formless realms:
there is bondage by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) but no bondage by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*).
For one who is not fully bound—if they have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire—this applies.
When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen,
there is the bondage of the fetter of grasping with respect to the four categories of things abandoned through vision within the three realms,
as well as the things abandoned through cultivation within the form and formless realms.
There is no bondage by the fetter of envy.
Regarding matters in the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation,
there is bondage by both fetters when the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation or the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen.
Regarding objects to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
there is bondage by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) but no bondage by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
Regarding objects to be abandoned through the vision of cessation or the path in the three realms, [the same applies].
There is bondage by the fetter of grasping (*upādāna*) but not by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*).
Regarding objects to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin within the three realms, there is bondage by neither of these two fetters,
provided one has already become free from the defilement of desire.
Regarding the objects of the five categories in the desire realm, there is no bondage by the two fetters.

Regarding the objects of the five categories in the form and formless realms, for one who has not yet abandoned the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), there is bondage by the fetter of grasping but no bondage by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*); for one who has already abandoned the fetter of grasping, there is no bondage by either of these two fetters.
Because these two possess the sense of being mutually long or short,
the question should be answered by means of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There may be the case where one is bound by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) but not bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*).

This refers to the fetters of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*) that have not yet been abandoned regarding the factors to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm, as well as regarding the factors of the form and formless realms.
Among these, "the fetters of grasping regarding the factors to be abandoned by insight within the desire realm have not yet been abandoned" means:
There may be those who have not yet severed the fetters of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*) in four categories,
or even those who have not yet severed them in one category;
and regarding the phenomena of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*), there may be those for whom the fetters of grasping have not yet been severed.
There may be those who have not yet severed the fetters of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*) in the eighth stage, or even those who have not yet severed them in the first stage;
within these stages, there may be those who have not yet severed the fetters of grasping belonging to four categories.
Furthermore, there may be a certain class [of beings] for whom the fetter of grasping (*parigraha-saṃyojana*) has not yet been abandoned.
Because it has not been abandoned, they possess the bond of the fetter of grasping but lack the bond of the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*). Why is this?
Because the fetter of envy does not exist among those factors to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), nor does it exist in the two higher realms.
There may be one who is bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) and bound by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).

This refers to one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire (*kāma-rāga*), for whom the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen,
and who has not yet abandoned the fetter of envy regarding the factors of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, there exists in the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation the fetter of envy that is not yet severed,
in the case of a disciple of the Blessed One who possesses vision but has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire.
Regarding the factors to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there exists the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) that has not yet been abandoned;
herein, there may be nine grades (*navaprakāra*) that have not been abandoned,
or even as few as one grade that has not been abandoned.
Because it has not been abandoned, there is the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*). Why is this?
Because those universal fetters of grasping that take the five categories as their object have already been abandoned.
Those [fetters] that remain unsevered cannot act as bonds with respect to phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
because they do not have them as their objects (*ālambana*) and because the category of phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation lacks the fetters of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*).
There may be cases where both are bound;
that is, for one who is fully fettered (*sakalabandhana*), there are two fetters (*saṃyojana*) regarding the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
In this context, for one who is fully fettered, [there are two fetters] regarding the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation.
There are two types of fetters of grasping that bind one to one category, and the fetter of envy binds one.
Furthermore, for one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire, when the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen,
there are two fetters binding one to the phenomena of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation.

Among these, there may be those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire, ranging from those who have not yet abandoned nine grades down to those who have not yet abandoned even a single grade; for them,
the knowledge of suffering has already arisen, but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen.
Regarding the dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
there is one class bound by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) and one class bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*);
or there may be those that are bound by neither.
This refers to one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of sensual desire,
for whom the knowledge of origination has already arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen,
regarding those phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination.
Furthermore, regarding the factors abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms, there is no bondage by the two fetters;
this occurs when the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,
with respect to the factors abandoned through seeing suffering, origin, and cessation.
Furthermore, for those disciples of the Blessed One who possess right view, there are no bonds of the two fetters regarding the factors to be abandoned by cultivation in the form and formless realms;
nor are there any [bonds] regarding the factors to be abandoned by seeing in those who have not yet abandoned desire-taint.
Furthermore, there are no two fetters binding one to the dharmas abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms.
One who has already abandoned desire for the realm of desire has no two fetters binding them to the dharmas of that realm.
One who has already abandoned desire for the realm of form has no two fetters binding them to the dharmas of the realms of desire and form.
Having already become free from the defilements of the formless realm, one is not bound by the two fetters regarding the phenomena of the three realms;
herein, some are unbound because they have already been abandoned,
while others are unbound because they were originally non-existent.
The application regarding the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) is the same as that regarding the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*).

That is to say, both envy and stinginess belong exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and have outflowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) rather than being universal (*asarvatraga*).
If one is bound by the fetter of envy toward a certain object, is one also bound by the fetter of stinginess toward that same object? Answer: It is so.
If there is the bondage of the fetter of stinginess (mātsarya-saṃyojana), is there also the bondage of the fetter of envy (īrṣyā-saṃyojana)?
Answer: It is so.
This is because both the fetters of envy and stinginess are exclusively to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) within the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The answer to the question should be formulated as follows:
If one has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire, one is bound by two fetters regarding the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation,
and regarding the factors of the three realms to be abandoned through insight.

Furthermore, regarding the dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms, once one is bound by two fetters, when one has already become free from the defilement of desire, there is no binding by those two fetters with respect to any dharmas of the three realms;
because their length and brevity are similar, it is said to be "thus."
Question: The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) operates in dependence upon others, whereas the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) operates in dependence upon oneself.
For what reason do they ask each other these questions and both answer in this same way?
Some offer this explanation:
The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) arises manifestly with respect to the objects of others' faculties,
but does not arise manifestly with respect to the objects of one's own faculties.
The fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) arises manifestly with respect to the objects of one's own faculties.
It does not arise as an object for the cognition of others.
This is stated thus based on the nature of the cognizing subject.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Both of these arise in relation to both oneself and others.
Question: It is understandable that the fetter of envy arises in relation to others;
how can it arise in relation to oneself?
Answer: Suppose there is a donor who provides the requisites for two bhikṣus;
one of them obtains excellent ones while the other does not.
The one who did not obtain excellent ones sees this and gives rise to envy.
One forms this thought:
"How wonderful it would be if those means of subsistence were as I have obtained them!
This envy can also arise with respect to oneself.
Question: It may be granted that the fetter of stinginess arises with respect to oneself;
however, how does it arise with respect to others?
Answer: For example, there is a certain class of persons who, upon seeing another person giving, [experience stinginess].
He immediately gave rise to a mind of stinginess and thought:
"What use has that person for giving things to others?
As for the object given, he himself shall have no share at all."
This stinginess can also arise by taking another as its object;
thus, there is no contradiction with reason.
