there is the dharma to be abandoned by cultivation for which the fetter of craving that arose previously has not yet been abandoned, once the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) has already arisen.
There may be one who is bound by the fetter of craving (rāga-saṃyojana) of the past,
as well as bound by the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) of the past and future, but not of the present.
This refers to a case where, regarding this particular object, the fetter of craving that arose previously has not yet been abandoned.
Furthermore, there are cases where the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*) has not been abandoned but is not currently manifest.
In this context, the phrase "the fetter of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) that was previously produced and not yet abandoned" indicates the existence of past craving.
The statement that "the fetter of views has not been abandoned" indicates that the past and future fetters of views exist,
while the phrase "but do not manifest in the present" excludes the existence of the present fetter of views.
There may be one who is bound by the fetter of craving (anunaya-saṃyojana) of the past,
and also bound by the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) of the past, future, and present;
that is to say, regarding this object, the fetter of craving that arose previously has not yet been abandoned.
There is also the case where the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) is present;
herein, the mention of the fetter of craving (tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana) that was previously arisen and not yet abandoned indicates the existence of past craving.
The phrase "there is also the fetter of views present" indicates that the fetter of views exists in the present;
its existence in the past and future is established by implication without needing to be stated.
Since the presence of the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) in the present necessarily entails its existence in the past and future,
if there is bondage by the fetter of views in the past, future, and present,
is there also bondage by the fetter of craving (tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana) in the past?
Answer: If that which arose previously has not been severed, one is bound;
if it had not arisen previously, or if it arose but has since been severed, one is not bound.
The meaning and intent herein are as explained extensively before.
As it is with the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), so it is with the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*),
because all three are exclusively abandoned through the vision [of the truths] within the three realms. Therefore,
craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is contrasted with them to form the "small sevenfold set" (*sapta-kṣudraka-vākya*).
As explained regarding the view [of self],
there is also a slight distinction therein: namely,
that the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) exists only when the knowledge of the path category (*mārga-jñāna*) has already arisen.
Regarding those dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) for which the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) has arisen previously but has not yet been severed:
there is past craving,
but no grasping (*upādāna*) across the three periods of time.

It is not as in the case where, once the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) has arisen, there are factors dissociated from the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path,
for which the previously arisen fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) has not yet been abandoned.
There are also cases where there is past craving but no views regarding the three periods of time;
because the distinction in meaning is slight, this is not mentioned.
This is like the treatment of the fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*) when contrasted with the subsequent "small seven" [set].
This applies up to the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*), which, in relation to the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), forms a "small seven" according to its respective correspondence;
the same holds true for the others as well. Herein, regarding what is "according to its respective correspondence":
only pride (*māna*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) pertain to all three realms and all five categories (*pañca-nikāya*).
Because only those with outflows (*sāsrava*) are not universal (*asarvatraga*),
the sevenfold major set of propositions is formulated in relation to the latter;
all are explained as in the case of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) pervades all three realms and all five categories (*pañca-varga*).

It has both outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) objects; it is both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal; and it is associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*). It pervades all three realms and consists only of four categories; it has both outflowing and non-outflowing objects; and it is both universal and non-universal.
The two types of grasping (*upādāna*) pertain to all three realms and consist of only four categories.
Their objects are tainted (*sāsrava*), and they include both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal factors.
Hostility (*pratigha*) pertains only to the desire realm and consists of five categories.
Only those with outflows (*sāsrava*) as their object are not universal (*asarvatraga*).

Envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) belong exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), have only outflows as their object, and are not universal.
Thus, these various fetters (*saṃyojana*) differ in their breadth and narrowness.
Regarding the last seven phrases, there are differences;
therefore, it is necessary to state the words "as appropriate.
As with the small seven, so too is it with the great seven; such is their distinction.
From pairing two against one up to pairing eight against one:
that is, taking past fetters of craving and hostility,
first pair them against past fetters of conceit.
Next, it is applied to the future;
next, to the present;
and next, to both the past and the present.
Next, they are correlated with the future and the present;
next, with the past and the future;
and finally, with the past, the future, and the present.
The fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*) forms seven propositions, just as [it was done] with the past fetters of craving (*rāga*) and aversion (*pratigha*).

Likewise, when contrasted with the fetters of ignorance (*avidyā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), grasping (*parāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*), each also forms seven propositions in the same manner.
Next, the fetter of craving is eliminated.
Having previously addressed the fetters of aversion and pride with respect to the past fetter of ignorance,
one next addresses them with respect to the future.
Next, it corresponds to the present;
next, it corresponds to the past and present;
next, it corresponds to the future and present.
Next, they are paired with the past and future; subsequently,
they are paired with the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana) of the past, future, and present to form seven propositions,
just as was done with the fetters of ill-will (pratigha-saṃyojana) and pride (māna-saṃyojana) regarding the past.
Regarding the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), seven propositions are formulated.

Regarding the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), grasping (*parigraha-saṃyojana*), doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*), envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*), and avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), each likewise has seven propositions formulated.
Next, the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) is excluded.
By means of the past fetters of conceit and ignorance,
one first confronts the past fetter of views,
and subsequently the future.
Next, it corresponds to the present;
next, it corresponds to the past and present;
and next, it corresponds to the future and present.
Next, [the fetters] are paired with those of the past and future;
subsequently, they are paired with the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) of the past, future, and present to form seven propositions.
This is just as when the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) of the past are paired with the fetter of views to form seven propositions.
The same applies to each of the fetters of grasping (*parāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and stinginess (*mātsarya*), each forming seven propositions. Next,
excluding the fetter of pride (*māna*),
one [considers] the fetters of past ignorance (*avidyā*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*).
First, one takes up the fetters regarding the past;
next, regarding the future;
and finally, regarding the present.
Next, [the past] is paired with the present; next, [the past] is paired with the future and the present;
next, [the past] is paired with both the future and the past;
finally, [the past, future, and present] are paired with the past, future, and present as they take up the fetters (*saṃyojana*), forming seven propositions.
Just as one forms seven propositions by contrasting the fetter of ignorance and the fetter of views with the fetter of grasping,
so too does one form seven propositions for each of the fetters of doubt, envy, and avarice.
Next, one eliminates the fetter of ignorance.
By means of the fetters of views and grasping regarding the past,
one first confronts the fetter of doubt regarding the past.
Next, it corresponds to the future; next, to the present;
and next, to both the past and the present.
Next, [the doubt] is correlated with the future and the present;
next, it is correlated with the past and the future;
finally, it is correlated with the past, the future, and the present as the fetter of doubt, forming seven propositions.
Just as the view-fetters (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) and the grasping-fetters (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) are correlated with the doubt-fetter (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) to form seven propositions,
it is likewise for each of the envy-fetter (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) and the stinginess-fetter (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*).
Next, the view-fetter is excluded.
By means of the fetters of attachment to the past and the fetter of doubt,
one first confronts the fetter of envy regarding the past,
and subsequently regarding the future.
Next, it corresponds to the present;
next, it corresponds to the past and present;
next, it corresponds to the future and present.
Next, [the fetter of envy] is paired with the past and future;
subsequently, it is paired with the past, future, and present fetters of envy to form seven propositions.
This is just as when the past fetters of grasping and doubt are paired with the fetter of envy to form seven propositions.
The seven propositions regarding the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) are likewise; however,
with the exception of the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*),
they are applied using the past fetters of doubt (*vicikitsā*) and envy (*īrṣyā*).
First, with respect to the past, one contemplates the fetter of stinginess;
next, with respect to the future;
and finally, with respect to the present.
Next, [the fetter of stinginess] is paired with the past and present; next, it is paired with the future and present;
next, it is paired with the past and future;
and finally, it is paired with the past, future, and present, forming seven propositions.
Just as two fetters are contrasted with one fetter,
so too are three, four, five, six, seven, and eight fetters contrasted with one fetter; likewise,
there are seven [fetters] beginning with past craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Furthermore, beginning with craving (*tṛṣṇā*) of the past, future, and present, there are likewise seven [factors] for each.
Thus, it should be understood that there are forty-nine phrases (seven times seven).
Regarding this, some say that [the sequence begins] with past craving and so forth.
First, one contemplates anger and the other [afflictions] with respect to the past;
next, with respect to the future;
and finally, with respect to the present.
Next, [the present] is contrasted with the past;
next, with the future and the present;
and next, with both the past and the future.
Subsequently, with past hatred and so forth as the initial seven phrases,
one first correlates past craving and so forth with future hatred and so forth.
Next, it corresponds to the present;
next, it corresponds to both the past and the present;
next, it corresponds to both the future and the present.
Next, they are paired with the past and the future;
next, they are paired with the past, the future, and the present;
finally, they are paired with past anger and so forth to form the second set of seven propositions.
By means of past craving and so forth,
one first opposes present hatred and so forth,
and subsequently opposes both the past and the present.
Next, [it is] correlated with the future and the present;
next, with the past and the future;
and next, with the past, the future, and the present.
Next, with reference to the past; subsequently,
with reference to the future, taking ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and so forth as the third set of seven propositions,
using past craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth.
First, one contemplates past and present anger and so forth;
next, past and future; and finally, past and future.
Next, they are correlated with the past, future,
and present; first with the past,
and then with the future.
Subsequently, with past craving and so forth as the basis, one faces present hatred and so forth;
this constitutes the fourth set of seven propositions.
First, one faces future hatred and so forth with past craving and so forth as the basis.
Next, it is correlated with the past and the future;
next, with the past, the future, and the present;
and finally, with the past.
Next, it corresponds to the future;
next, it corresponds to the present; and finally, it corresponds to the past and the present anger and so forth, constituting the fifth sevenfold set of propositions.
By means of past craving and so forth,
one first applies them to past and future hatred and so forth;
subsequently, one applies them to the past, future, and present.
Next, it corresponds to the past; next, to the future;
and next, to the present.
Next, [the past] is contrasted with the present;
subsequently, the future and the present [states of] ill-will and so forth are contrasted as the sixth and seventh phrases.
By means of past attachment and so forth,
one first relates them to past, future, and present aversion and so forth;
next, one relates them to the past.
Next, it corresponds to the future; next, to the present;
and next, to both the past and the present.
Next, [the verse] refers to the future and the present;
finally, it refers to past and future ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and so forth,
forming the seventh set of seven propositions.
This is called the "small sevenfold" [set of afflictions], because past desire, hatred,
and so forth first correspond to past pride and so forth.
Next, it corresponds to the future; next, to the present;
and next, to both the past and the present.
Next, [the pride] directed toward the future and the present;
next, directed toward the past and the future;
finally, directed toward the past, the future, and the present. These constitute the first seven propositions, beginning with pride (*māna*).
Based on past attachment, aversion, and so forth,
one first relates them to future pride and so forth,
and subsequently to the present.
Next, [the present] is contrasted with the past;
next, with the future and the present;
and next, with the past and the future.
Next, [the second sevenfold set] consists of the subsequent [set] where past pride and so forth are correlated with the past, future, and present.
This constitutes the second sevenfold set.
Based on past attachment, aversion, and so forth,
one first correlates them with present pride and so forth,
and subsequently correlates them with both the past and the present.
Next, it is correlated with the future and the present;
next, with the past and the future;
and finally, with the past, the future, and the present.
Next, with respect to the past; subsequently,
with respect to the future, pride and so forth constitute the third set of seven propositions,
based on past craving, aversion, and so on.
First, [the pride] takes the past and present as its objects;
next, it takes the future and present as its objects;
and finally, it takes the past and future as its objects.
Next, they are correlated with the past, future,
and present; first with the past,
and then with the future.
Subsequently, with respect to present pride and so forth,
there is the fourth sevenfold set;
[this is] by means of past craving, hatred, and so forth.
First, [the conceit] is directed toward the future and the present;
next, toward the past and the future;
and finally, toward the past, the future, and the present.
Next, it corresponds to the past; next, to the future;
and next, to the present.
Subsequently, regarding past and present pride (*māna*) and so forth,
there is the fifth sevenfold set;
this is because of past craving (*tṛṣṇā*), aversion (*pratigha*), and so forth.
First, [the pride] is directed toward the past and future;
next, it is directed toward the past, future, and present;
and finally, it is directed toward the past.
Next, it corresponds to the future; next, to the present;
and next, to both the past and the present.
Subsequently, regarding future and present pride (*māna*) and so forth,
these constitute the sixth and seventh phrases;
[the latter] refers to past craving (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and so forth.
First, one applies this to pride and so forth regarding the past, future, and present;
next, to the past; and then, to the future.
Next, it corresponds to the present;
next, it corresponds to the past and present;
next, it corresponds to the future and present.
Subsequently, regarding the pride directed toward the past and future and so forth,
these seven sets of seven constitute what is called the "Great Seven.
Thus, what has been explained here is a futile expenditure of effort.
It is of no benefit to the phrasing and of no benefit to the meaning,
because it is a redundant repetition.
Furthermore, it is not only the seven sets of seven phrases that should be stated in this manner.
By means of past craving and so forth,
one first applies them to past hatred and so forth,
and subsequently to the future.
Next, it corresponds to the present;
next, it corresponds to the past and the present;
next, it corresponds to the future and the present.
Next, [the afflictions] are paired with the past and future;
subsequently, they are paired with past, future, and present anger (*vyāpāda*) and so forth,
forming the first seven propositions.
By means of future craving and so forth,
one first opposes future hatred and so forth,
and subsequently opposes the present.
Next, they are correlated with the past and the present;
next, with the future and the present;
and next, with the past and the future.
Next, [the past, future, and present] are correlated;
subsequently, [the past] is correlated with hatred and so forth,
forming the second set of seven propositions.
By means of present craving and so forth,
one first opposes present hatred and so forth,
and subsequently opposes those of the past and present.
Next, they are correlated with the future and the present;
next, with the past and the future;
and finally, with the past, the future, and the present.
Next, with regard to the past;
subsequently, with regard to the future,
anger and so forth constitute the third set of seven propositions.
Using past and present craving and so forth,
one first applies them to past and present hatred and so forth,
and subsequently to future and present [hatred and so forth].
Next, it is correlated with the past and the future;
next, it is correlated with the past, the future, and the present;
next, it is correlated with the past.
Next, [the analysis] is applied to the future;
subsequently, it is applied to the present.
This constitutes the fourth set of seven propositions.
By means of future and present craving and so forth, one first opposes future and present hatred and so forth;
next, one opposes past and future [hatred]; and finally, one opposes past, future, and present [hatred].
Next, it corresponds to the past; next, to the future;
and next, to the present.
Subsequently, regarding past and present anger and so forth,
this constitutes the fifth sevenfold set;
[the sixth] consists of past and future craving and so forth.
First, one contemplates ill will and so forth with respect to the past and future;
next, with respect to the past, future, and present;
and finally, with respect to the past.
Next, it is applied to the future;
next, to the present;
and next, to both the past and the present.
Subsequently, with regard to future and present hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth,
they constitute the sixth and seventh phrases;
likewise, with regard to past, future, and present craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth.
First, one contemplates ill-will and so forth with respect to the past, future, and present;
next, with respect to the past;
and finally, with respect to the future.
Next, it corresponds to the present;
next, it corresponds to the past and the present;
next, it corresponds to the future and the present.
Subsequently, regarding past and future anger and so forth,
there is a seventh set of seven phrases;
this is called the "small seven."
Based on past attachment, aversion, and so forth,
one first confronts past pride and the like,
and subsequently confronts those pertaining to the future.
Next, it corresponds to the present;
next, it corresponds to both the past and the present;
next, it corresponds to both the future and the present.

Next, [the pride] directed toward the past and future constitutes the first seven propositions; subsequently, [the pride] directed toward the past, future, and present constitutes the [remaining] propositions, beginning with pride (*māna*) and so forth.
Based on future craving, hatred, and so forth,
one first applies them to future pride and so forth,
and subsequently to the present.
Next, [the present] is correlated with the past;
next, it is correlated with the future and the present;
next, it is correlated with the past and the future.
Next, [the second set] is contrasted with the past, future, and present;
subsequently, [the third set] is contrasted with past pride (*māna*) and so forth,
constituting the second group of seven propositions.
Based on present craving, hatred, and so forth,
one first correlates them with present pride and so forth,
and subsequently with the past and present.
Next, they are correlated with the future and the present;
next, with the past and the future;
and finally, with the past, the future, and the present.
Next, the [pride] directed toward the past;
subsequently, the pride and so forth directed toward the future constitute the third set of seven propositions.
By means of past and present attachment, aversion, and so forth,
one first applies them to past and present pride and so forth;
next, one applies them to future and present [pride].
Next, it is correlated with the past and the future;
next, it is correlated with the past, the future, and the present;
next, it is correlated with the past.
Next, [pride] directed toward the future;
finally, [pride] directed toward the present, such as pride and so forth—
these constitute the fourth set of seven propositions.
By means of future and present craving, hatred, and so forth,
one first opposes future and present pride and so forth;
next, one opposes [them] with respect to the past and future.
Next, they are correlated with the past, future,
and present; first with the past,
then with the future.
Next, it corresponds to the present;
subsequently, it corresponds to past and present pride (*māna*) and so forth,
forming the fifth sevenfold category.
Based on past and future craving and aversion,
one first correlates them with past and future pride and so forth;
subsequently, one correlates them with the past, future, and present.
Next, it corresponds to the past; next, to the future;
and next, to the present.
Next, [the first five] are contrasted with the past and present;
subsequently, pride and the others are contrasted with the future and present,
forming the sixth and seventh phrases.
By means of past, future, and present attachment and aversion,
etc., one first opposes past, future, and present pride,
etc.; next, one opposes the past.
Next, it corresponds to the future; next, to the present;
and next, to both the past and the present.
Next, [pride] directed toward the future and present;
finally, [pride] directed toward the past and future, and so forth—
these constitute the seventh set of seven propositions.
If one speaks in this way, the effort will not be in vain;
it is beneficial for both the phrasing and the meaning,
as it avoids redundant repetition.
Furthermore, there are only seven sets of seven phrases.
What is the distinction between the single sequence that traverses six small sevens and one great seven?
Answer: The names themselves constitute the distinctions.
That is to say, one name applies to a single category, while another name traverses six categories.
It is called the "Small Seven" and the "Great Seven.
Furthermore, it is called "Single Practice" because questions and answers are formulated based on a single practice.
It is called "traversing the six" because questions and answers are conducted based on the sixfold scheme.
It is called the "small seven" because questions and answers are conducted based on the sevenfold scheme with one [term] paired against one.
[Furthermore, it is called the "large seven"] because questions and answers are conducted based on the sevenfold scheme with two [terms] paired against one.
Furthermore, because eight [factors] are paired with one, it is called the "Great Seven. Moreover,
because questions and answers are formulated by pairing dissimilar phenomena with dissimilar phenomena,
rather than according to worldly conventions, it is called the "Single Path" (Ekamukha).
One formulates questions and answers by means of similar dharmas corresponding to similar dharmas;
because they are fixed according to the world, this is called "traversing the six.
One formulates questions and answers by means of dissimilar dharmas corresponding to dissimilar dharmas.
Because the worldly determination pairs one with one, it is called the "small seven.
Because questions and answers are formulated by pairing dissimilar dharmas with dissimilar dharmas,
the worldly determination pairs two with one.
Up to the point where eight [units] are paired with one, it is called the "Great Seven.
One practice traverses six "Small Sevens" to reach the "Great Seven";
this is what is meant by their distinction.
Regarding the three fetters up to the ninety-eight proclivities:
within these ninety-eight proclivities,
how many proclivities are subsumed by each one?
Answer: All [points] should be analyzed.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To refute the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct meaning.
That is to say, some may claim that all phenomena are subsumed under the nature of others and not subsumed under their own nature,
such as the Vibhajyavādins.
He speaks thus based on the sūtras of provisional designation and based on conventional discourse.
Regarding "based on the sūtras of provisional designation":
As stated in the sūtras:
"The central point of all things such as platforms and canopies serves as the foundation for those platforms and canopies;
it is that upon which all the constituent materials depend, capable of supporting them so that they do not scatter or fall."
Therefore, it is said that the central part can encompass those [other parts].
Yet, since that central part is distinct from the various constituent materials while being described as capable of encompassing them,
we know that all phenomena encompass the nature of others, not their own nature.
Other sūtras also state that among the five faculties, the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) is the most preeminent.
The faculty of wisdom is able to encompass all the other four faculties;
yet, although that faculty of wisdom is distinct from the four faculties, it is said to be able to encompass them.
Thus, one should know that all phenomena are comprised within the nature of others and not comprised within their own nature.
Furthermore, another sutra states:
the World-Honored One addressed the householder Hasta, saying:
“By what dharma do you gather your own followers?
How do your followers receive your guidance?
The householder Hasta replied:
"World-Honored One, please explain to me the four means of integration:
first, giving;
second, kind speech."
Third is beneficial conduct;
fourth is cooperation.
By means of these four methods of attraction, I gather my own followers.
The followers thereby come to be included within my own following.
However, since the Elder Hastaka’s followers were distinct from his own, he spoke of "including the assembly.
Thus we know that all phenomena include other-natures, not self-nature.
Other sūtras further state:
Right view, right thought, and right effort are subsumed under the aggregate of wisdom;
right mindfulness and right concentration are subsumed under the aggregate of concentration.
However, right thought and right effort differ from the aggregate of wisdom,
and right mindfulness differs from the aggregate of concentration;
yet it is said that they are included therein.
Thus, one should know that all phenomena are comprised by the nature of others and not comprised by their own nature.
Regarding what is said according to conventional discourse:
this refers to worldly expressions such as "the door hinge comprises the door leaf," "the thread comprises the garment," or "the attachment comprises the firewood."
The householder says,
"I am able to provide for my fields, livestock, wealth, servants, and family"; the renunciant says,
"I provide for my assembly and their requisites, robes, and bowls."
In this way, the grasper and the grasped are distinct;
therefore, one knows that all phenomena grasp the nature of others.
To refute that view and reveal that all phenomena grasp their own nature—which is the ultimate mode of grasping—[the following is stated].
If the inclusion of the nature of others were the ultimate truth,
then the self-nature of a single phenomenon would be all phenomena;
and when a single phenomenon arises, all phenomena should arise.
When one dharma ceases, all dharmas should cease.
Furthermore, there is another error:

that which is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering would then be subsumed under what is to be abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through cultivation.
When that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering is being abandoned, the afflictions abandoned through the vision of the origin and so forth should also be abandoned.
If this were the case, then the subsequent paths of counteraction cultivated later would become useless.
To avoid this fault, it is held that all phenomena are subsumed under their own nature alone; this is the ultimate subsumption.
Question: If all phenomena are subsumed under their own nature alone as the ultimate subsumption and not under other natures, then...
How should one interpret the sūtras cited by the Vibhajyavādins as conventional discourse?
The answer is: the sūtras they cite are of provisional meaning (neyārtha);
they are spoken by way of conventional designations (prajñapti) with a specific underlying intention.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The very center of all things such as platforms and canopies serves as the platform and canopy;
it is that upon which the various materials depend and by which they are supported."
To prevent them from falling away or dispersing,
it is said that the mind which can grasp those [objects] is metaphorically designated by the term "grasping" (saṃgraha) in the sense of "sustaining" (dhāraṇa),
because it sustains them so that they do not fall away or disperse.
This is a conventional designation for inclusion,
not an ultimate inclusion.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
Among the five faculties, the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) is the most excellent.
As for the statement that the faculty of wisdom can "encompass" the other four faculties,
the term "encompassing" is used metaphorically in the sense of skillful means (upāya).
Wisdom acts as the skillful means that causes the other four faculties to also operate swiftly and be able to accomplish the great task; thus,
the name "inclusion" is provisionally established,
but it is not inclusion in the ultimate sense.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Regarding those who gather a following by means of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*),
the term 'gathering' is metaphorically established for that which leads them so as not to cause dissension."
The name "attraction" is established as a conventional designation for that which is induced by means of the four bases of attraction;
it is not attraction in the ultimate sense.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
Right intention and right effort are also subsumed under the aggregate of wisdom;
as for right mindfulness being subsumed under the aggregate of concentration,
the term "subsumption" is applied metaphorically in the sense of being conducive to it.
Because right thought and right effort accord with the aggregate of wisdom,
and right mindfulness accords with the aggregate of concentration,
they are provisionally designated by the name "comprehension."
Furthermore, that which is not included within the ultimate truth, as well as the conventional discourse it induces—
such as a door hinge including the door leaf, or thread including a garment, or fuel being included by its support—
is designated with the term "inclusion" (saṃgraha) based on the sense of "sustaining" (upastambha).
It is not included within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Those who live at home speak of being able to sustain fields and so forth;
those who have left the home life speak of sustaining their disciples and so forth.
The designation "inclusion" is used metaphorically in the sense of providing benefit;
it is not inclusion in the ultimate sense.
As for the inclusion of other-nature (parabhāva), the designation of inclusion is established in dependence upon time and causes.
This is not a definitive inclusion.
Regarding "waiting for the time," it means that there is a time when one is able to include [them].
"Sometimes it is not included;
that which awaits causes means there is a cause capable of including it."
Because there are causes that are not subsumed [within it],
it is not ultimate. As a verse says:
Because there is a cause, attachment arises; because there is a cause, aversion arises.
In the world, nothing occurs without a cause; those who experience attachment and aversion are governed by their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
There is the sense of inclusion that does not depend on time;
this is ultimate inclusion.
"Not depending on time" means:
All phenomena are never at any time not comprised within their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
because they never abandon their own essence at any time.
Regarding "not depending on causes," it means that all phenomena are comprised within their own intrinsic nature without depending on causes.
Because it possesses an intrinsic nature that does not depend on causes and conditions.
If one wishes to examine all phenomena,
one should first observe the meaning subsumed within that intrinsic nature.
Question: When observing the inclusion of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, what benefit is there and what merit is attained?
Answer: One eliminates the notion of a self and the notion of a composite whole.
Cultivating the perception of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*) and the perception of distinctness (*prthaksaṃjñā*) is easily fulfilled.
This is because if sentient beings possess the notion of a self (*ātmasaṃjñā*) or the notion of a unified whole (*ekasaṃghātasamjñā*),
their afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion will increase and flourish.
Because of this intensification, one cannot be liberated from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and the various calamities and afflictions.
If one eliminates the notion of a self and the notion of a composite whole, [one may attain liberation].
He then contemplates material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) as being like a heap of flour, soon to be dispersed;
he contemplates immaterial phenomena (*arūpadharma*) as not coexisting from beginning to end, soon to be extinguished.
Thus, he contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) in their entirety.
It is like a handful of sand scattered and destroyed by the wind;
through this, one obtains seeds similar to the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*),
because one contemplates conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) as empty and non-self (*anātman*).
Consequently, they develop a profound lack of aspiration for and delight in birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
By means of this, they further obtain seeds similar to the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).
Because they do not aspire to or take delight in birth and death, [they attain this state].
They then develop a deep-seated aspiration for nirvāṇa.
By means of this, they further obtain seeds that resemble the gate of signless liberation (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).
Regarding these three types of samādhi:
Relying on the lower [stage], one gives rise to the middle; relying on the middle, one gives rise to the upper; and relying on the upper, one develops wisdom.
Free from the defilements of the three realms, one attains the three types of enlightenment and realizes eternal quiescence.
When observing the time of the inclusion of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena:
One thereby attains such victorious merits and virtues.
For this reason, this treatise has been composed.
Regarding all that should be analyzed herein:
This refers to the three fetters up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Since the underlying tendencies subsumed within each one are distinct,
all of them should be analyzed individually.
Regarding the statement that among the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) comprises three:
this means that within the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), this fetter comprises three underlying tendencies— namely,
the underlying tendencies of the view of a self-identity to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the three realms.
This is stated in terms of their general categories, which include the three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
If distinguished individually, those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) include the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of the desire realm,
and those belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) include the view of a self-identity of the form realm.
The formless realm includes the view of a self-identity within the formless realm.
Each of these realms is distinguished by the three periods of time.
That which is past includes the past view of a self-identity.
That which is future subsumes the future view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
that which is present subsumes the present view of self-existence.
Furthermore, each of these consists of many moments (*kṣaṇa*).
The mutual inclusion of each should be understood accordingly hereafter.

Regarding the fetter of clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*), it comprises six of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*); that is to say, this fetter includes six underlying tendencies among the ninety-eight.
That is to say, the latent tendencies of attachment to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the path within the three realms.

Regarding the statement that the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) comprises twelve [factors]: this means that within the ninety-eight latent tendencies, this fetter comprises twelve latent tendencies.
These are the latent tendencies of doubt abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path within the three realms.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots, the unwholesome roots of greed and hatred each comprise five;
that is to say, they comprise the greed and hatred of the five categories of the desire realm.
Regarding the statement that "the unwholesome root of delusion subsumes four [categories] and a portion of one":

this refers to its subsuming the last four categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as well as the unwholesome ignorance (*avidyā*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding the three outflows (*āsrava*), the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) subsumes thirty-one [factors].
This refers to the thirty-one latent dispositions (anuśaya) among the thirty-six of the desire realm, excluding the five types of ignorance.
Regarding the fifty-two included within the outflowing [states]:
this refers to the fifty-two latent dispositions among the sixty-two of the form and formless realms, excluding the ten types of ignorance.
Regarding the inclusion of fifteen [factors] within the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*):
this refers to the inclusion of the five categories of ignorance from each of the three realms.
Regarding the four floods (*ogha*), nineteen [factors] are included within the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*).
This refers to the inclusion of the five categories of greed, hatred, and pride, along with the four categories of doubt, from the desire realm.
Regarding the inclusion of twenty-eight factors within the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*):
this refers to the inclusion of the five categories of greed and pride, along with the four categories of doubt, from each of the form and formless realms.
Regarding the inclusion of the thirty-six [factors] within the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*):
this refers to the inclusion of twelve views from each of the three realms.

Specifically, there are twelve [views] consisting of one view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and one view of extreme adherence (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) for each realm; two types of clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); and four types each of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). Thus, they constitute twelve [per realm].
Regarding the statement that "the flood of ignorance comprises fifteen [factors]":
this means it comprises the five categories of ignorance from each of the three realms.
As with the four floods and the four yokes, it is likewise.
Although their names and meanings differ, they are identical in essence.
Regarding the fact that twenty-four [factors] are subsumed under "grasping at sensual desire" (*kāma-upādāna*) among the four types of grasping:
this refers to the inclusion of the five categories of greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance, as well as the four categories of doubt, belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) comprises thirty [factors],
meaning it comprises ten views from each of the three realms. That is to say,
among the twelve views previously mentioned, excluding the two types of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the remaining ten views constitute this category.
The six types of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) comprise two types from each of the three realms.
The thirty-eight types of adherence to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*) comprise...
This refers to the inclusion of the fivefold greed, pride, and ignorance, as well as the fourfold doubt, belonging respectively to the form and formless realms within each category.
Among the four bodily ties (*kāyagrantha*), the bodily ties of sensual desire (*abhidhyā*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) each include five factors.
This means that the fetter of greed and hatred comprises the five categories of the desire realm.
As for the fetter of the attachment to precepts and observances comprising six,
this means it comprises two instances of the attachment to precepts and observances from each of the three realms.
Regarding these twelve factors subsumed under the fetter of adherence to a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*):
this refers to the inclusion of four views from each of the three realms within the view of grasping at extremes (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*).
Among the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda*) each include five factors.
This means that the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) subsumes the five categories of greed and hatred belonging to the desire realm;
the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā*) subsumes four,
meaning it subsumes the four categories of doubt belonging to the desire realm.
As for the remaining hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) that are not included [in the other categories]:

*styāna* (torpor), *middha* (drowsiness), *auddhatya* (restlessness), and *kaukṛtya* (remorse) are of the nature of *paryavasthāna* (envelopments), and thus are not included among the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of greed (*rāga*) and the fetter of pride (*māna*) each include fifteen [factors].
This means that [the fetters] subsume the five categories of greed and pride from each of the three realms.
As for the fetter of aversion subsuming five,
it means it subsumes the aversion of the five categories of the desire realm.
Regarding the fetters of envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) that are not included [within other categories]:
these two fetters are not of the nature of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Among the five fetters conducive to the lower realm (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), the fetters of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) each include five [of the ten fetters].
This means that the fetter of greed and hatred encompasses the five categories of the desire realm;
the fetter of the view of a self-identity encompasses three,
meaning it encompasses one instance of the view of a self-identity from each of the three realms.
The fetter of clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana) comprises six,
meaning it includes two instances of clinging to precepts and observances from each of the three realms.
The fetter of doubt (vicikitsā-saṃyojana) comprises twelve.
This refers to the inclusion of the four categories of doubt for each of the three realms.
Regarding the statement that "among the five fetters of the higher realm (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*),
the fetter of attachment to form (*rūparāga*) includes a small portion," this means it includes a small portion of attachment abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the form realm.
Regarding the statement that "the fetter of sensual desire for the formless realm subsumes a small portion of one [fetter]":
this refers to its subsuming a small portion of the desire abandoned through cultivation within the formless realm.
As for the fetter of restlessness (*auddhatya*), it is not subsumed by any [of the nine fetters].
Because they are not of the nature of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Regarding the statement that the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*) comprises two partial portions:
this refers to the inclusion of a portion of the pride to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within each of the form and formless realms.
Regarding the statement that the fetter of ignorance comprises two partial portions:

this refers to the inclusion of a partial portion of the ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in each of the form and formless realms; and among the five views, the inclusion of three views each from among the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
This means that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) each comprise one [set] from each of the three realms;
as for the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), each comprises twelve,
meaning they each comprise four from each of the three realms.
Regarding the inclusion of the six types of clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*):
this means that they include two types of clinging to precepts and observances from each of the three realms.

Regarding the inclusion of two portions each within the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ tṛṣṇākāyāḥ*)—namely, the groups of craving born of eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact: [this refers to the following].
This means that each [of these] comprises a small portion of the greed to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire and form realms;
as for each comprising a small portion of the group of cravings born of nose-contact and tongue-contact,
this means that each comprises a small portion of the greed to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
Regarding the statement that "the aggregate of craving born from mental contact comprises thirteen [categories] and a small portion of two":
this means it comprises the first four categories of each of the three realms,

as well as the greed abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and a small portion of the greed abandoned through cultivation in both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Among the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the latent tendencies of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and hostility (*pratigha*) each comprise five;
that is to say, they comprise the five categories of desire and hostility belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The latent tendency of attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*) comprises ten.
This means that the latent tendencies of greed (*rāga*) and conceit (*māna*), as well as ignorance (*avidyā*),
each comprise fifteen [types] within the five categories of both the form and formless realms;
that is, they comprise the conceit and ignorance of each of the five categories within the three realms.
The thirty-six [factors] subsumed under the latent tendency of views (dṛṣṭi-anuśaya) refer to the twelve views in each of the three realms.
The twelve [factors] subsumed under the latent tendency of doubt (vicikitsā-anuśaya) are as follows:
This refers to the inclusion of the four categories of doubt for each of the three realms.
Regarding the fact that among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetters of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), conceit (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) each comprise fifteen:
this refers to the inclusion of greed (*rāga*), conceit, and ignorance for each of the five categories within the three realms.
The fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) comprises five [categories],
namely, it comprises the five classes of hatred and views belonging to the desire realm.
The fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) each comprises eighteen.

This means that the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) comprises one view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), one view of extreme attachment (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and four types of wrong views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) for each of the three realms.

The fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) comprises two types of clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and four types of clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) for each of the three realms.
Regarding the statement that "the fetter of doubt (vicikitsā-saṃyojana) subsumes twelve," this refers to its inclusion of the four categories of doubt from each of the three realms.
As for the fetters of envy (īrṣyā) and avarice (mātsarya), they are not so subsumed.
Because they are not of the nature of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions, from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of the desire realm— which subsumes the view of a self-identity of the desire realm—
up to the ignorance (*avidyā*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
Regarding the inclusion of the ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*):
each [category] includes its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Question: In what way do all phenomena include their own intrinsic natures?
Answer: Because self-nature exists within self-nature, is real, and is obtainable, it is said to be "inclusion.
Because self-nature is not different from, not external to, not separated from, and not distinct from self-nature, and is eternally non-empty, it is said to be "inclusion."
Because intrinsic nature is not non-existent in relation to itself in the past, not non-existent in the present, and not non-existent in the future, it is called "comprehension.
Because intrinsic nature neither increases nor decreases in relation to itself, it is called "comprehension."
When all phenomena encompass their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
it is not like grasping the index finger with the hand or pinching a garment; rather,
because each one individually maintains its own essence so that it does not disintegrate, it is called "encompassing."
The term "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*) is established in the sense of grasping or holding;
therefore, inclusion in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) consists solely in the inclusion of one's own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 59.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Sixty-Five.
Composed by the Five Hundred Great Arhats and others;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
5. Within the second section on "Single Modes" (Ekavidha-nikāya-saṃgraha) of the second aggregate on the fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha), part five:
Regarding the three fetters up to the ninety-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya), does the former include the latter, or does the latter include the former?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: It was composed in order to more emphatically refute the proponents of the *Vibhajyavāda* who maintain that [the aggregates] are subsumed under the nature of others (*parabhāva*), and to more clearly elucidate the assertions of the proponents of the *Yuktivāda* that they are subsumed under their own nature (*svabhāva*), thereby making them manifest.
Regarding the answer that the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*) do not mutually include one another:
this is because their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are each distinct.

As for the mutual inclusion of the three fetters and the three outflows (*āsrava*), where the three fetters and two portions of the three outflows include one another while the remainder do not: [this is as follows].

This means that the three fetters— namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)— are mutually inclusive within the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*) and the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*),
because their intrinsic natures are identical.
They are not mutually inclusive with the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*) or with a portion of the two [other] outflows.
Because their intrinsic natures (svabhāva) differ,
the subsequent cases should be understood by analogy.
The three fetters (saṃyojana) and the four floods (ogha)— specifically the three fetters and a portion of the four floods— mutually include one another.
Regarding those that are not mutually inclusive:

the three fetters (trisaṃyojana) are mutually inclusive with the flood of desire (kāma-ogha), the flood of views (dṛṣṭi-ogha), the latent tendency of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi-anuśaya), the grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), and doubt (vicikitsā).
They are not mutually inclusive with the flood of ignorance (avidyā-ogha) or with a portion of the other three floods.
As it is with respect to the four floods (*ogha*), so it is with respect to the four yokes (*yoga*), for their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are identical.

Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), the four graspings (*upādāna*), and the three fetters and one grasping: these three [categories] partially include one another, while the remainder do not mutually include one another.
This means that the three fetters, along with the clinging to precepts and observances and the other three types of clinging, mutually include the view of a self-identity and doubt;
however, they do not mutually include a portion of the other three types of clinging.
The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the four bodily ties (*kāyagrantha*)—one fetter and one bodily tie—are mutually inclusive;
those that are not mutually inclusive are as follows:

the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*) and the bodily tie of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-kāyagrantha*) are mutually inclusive.
The other three fetters (saṃyojana) do not mutually include one another.
Three fetters, five hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and a portion of one fetter and one hindrance do mutually include one another;
the remainder do not mutually include one another.

This means that among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), those that are unwholesome are mutually inclusive with the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*), but they are not mutually inclusive with the other four hindrances.
As for the three fetters and the five fetters being mutually non-inclusive: [the same principle applies].
Because their intrinsic natures differ,
the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the five lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), as well as the three fetters and the three lower-tier fetters,
mutually include one another; those that remain are not mutually included.

This means that among the three fetters and the five lower fetters, the fetters of identity view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) mutually include one another;
they do not, however, mutually include the remaining two fetters.
The three fetters (saṃyojana) and the five higher-tier fetters (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana) do not mutually include one another because their intrinsic natures (svabhāva) are distinct. However,
the three fetters and the five views (dṛṣṭi), as well as two of the fetters and two of the views, do mutually include one another.
Regarding those not mutually included:
among the three preceding fetters and the five views, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) are mutually inclusive,
whereas they are not mutually inclusive with the other three views.
The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the six groups of craving (*tṛṣṇākāya*) do not mutually include one another because their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are different.

Regarding the three fetters, the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the three fetters as a single underlying tendency: these mutually include one another’s respective portions, while the remainder do not include one another.

This means that among the three fetters, the latent tendency of doubt, and the latent tendencies of views, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) mutually include one another;
however, they do not mutually include the remaining five latent tendencies nor the other three views among the latent tendencies of views.

The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the nine fetters are mutually inclusive in part: the three fetters and one fetter among the nine fetters, as well as two portions of other fetters, are mutually inclusive.
As for those that are not mutually inclusive:

among the three fetters and the nine fetters, the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)—specifically the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*)—and the fetter of grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*) are mutually inclusive.

The [three] fetters (*saṃyojana*) do not mutually include the other six fetters, nor the remaining two views within the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*), nor the view-grasping (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) within the fetter of view-grasping.
However, the three fetters and the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do mutually include the three fetters and the twenty-one underlying tendencies.
Regarding those that are not mutually inclusive:

among the three fetters and the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the three types of identity view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the six types of adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the twelve types of doubt (*vicikitsā*) underlying tendencies are mutually inclusive.
They are not mutually inclusive with the other seventy-seven latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
In this manner, up to the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) and ninety-eight latent dispositions,
the seven fetters and the ninety-eight latent dispositions are mutually inclusive.
Regarding those not mutually included:
among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the first seven are mutually included with the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
whereas the latter two fetters are not mutually included with the underlying tendencies.
Because these two are not, in either case, of the nature of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Herein, the first three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the last nine fetters are cited to briefly explain their inclusion (*saṃgraha*) with those explained extensively later.
As for the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*) up to the seven latent dispositions, their inclusion with those explained later is omitted from brief mention.
Because they are easy to understand:
among the three fetters up to the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*),
how many cause the continuity of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and how many cause the continuity of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
"How many [factors] cause the continuity of the formless realm?
Answer: "All [of them] should be analyzed.
Question: "For what purpose was this treatise composed?"
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of others and clarifying one’s own position.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that even an undefiled mind causes the continuity [of existence] to persist, such as the Vibhajyavādins.
One asks: for what reason do they hold this view?
The answer is that he holds this view based on a sutra, which states:
"A bodhisattva enters the mother’s womb with full awareness."
He dwells in the mother’s womb with full awareness;
he emerges from the mother’s womb with full awareness.
Since he possesses such full awareness, [he is called a Bodhisattva].
Regarding one who enters the mother's womb:
it is because they possess correct awareness while remaining in an undefiled state of mind;
furthermore, this undefiled state of mind also causes the continuity [of existence] to persist.
This treatise is composed to refute that intention and to demonstrate that it is only a defiled mind that can cause the continuity of existence.
Question: How is the sūtra cited by them to be reconciled?
Answer: The term "clear comprehension" (*saṃprajanya*) is spoken with reference to non-erroneous perception.
It is said that sentient beings generally enter the mother’s womb while giving rise to perverted perceptions.
When a male enters the womb, he conceives desire for the mother and aversion toward the father;
when a female enters the womb, she conceives desire for the father and aversion toward the mother.
This is because they are either favorable or unfavorable to him.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva enters his mother’s womb, his mind is free from delusion;
he perceives the father as a father.
Regarding one's mother, one perceives her as a mother;
although both [mother and son] share mutual affection, there is no divergent thought.
Because there is affection, the mind is defiled.
Because it is an unerring perception, it is called "correct knowledge" (saṃprajanya).
Therefore, that sūtra does not contradict my position.
Furthermore, the reason for composing this treatise is as follows:
That is to say, there are some who maintain that only craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and aversion (*pratigha*) cause the continuity of existence (*bhava-saṃtati*), as the Dārṣṭāntikas do.
One asks: for what reason do they hold this view?
Answer: It is based on the sūtras.
That is to say, the sūtras state that entry into the mother’s womb occurs through the conjunction of three factors:
first, the union of the parents in mutual passion; [the second is the presence of the intermediate being (antarābhava); and the third is the mother’s season].
Second, at that time, the mother’s body is in a state of fitness;
third, the gandharva is present before her.
At that time, two minds arise alternately in the gandharva.
This refers to being accompanied by both craving and aversion.
From this, it is known that only craving and aversion cause the continuity of existence (*bhava*).
To refute that view and to demonstrate that all afflictions (*kleśa*) cause the continuity of existence, this treatise was composed.
Question: How do you reconcile this with the sūtra cited by the opponent? Answer:
The sūtra states that at the moment the mind is about to take rebirth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is not only through craving or aversion [that this occurs].
Therefore, what I have said does not contradict that sūtra.
Furthermore, the reason for composing this treatise is as follows:

there are some who hold the view that rebirth in the miserable realms occurs only through a mind of hatred (*dveṣa*), while rebirth in the happy realms occurs only through a mind of attachment (*rāga*).

To refute such a position, it is shown that in every location within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), each of the thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) manifests to cause the continuity of existence.
This treatise is composed because, in every sphere of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), each of the thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) manifests and causes the continuity of existence to arise;

likewise, in every sphere of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), each of the thirty-one underlying tendencies manifests and causes the continuity of existence to arise. Thus, this discussion is undertaken.
Furthermore, this treatise was not composed to refute others and display one's own position;
rather, it was written to reveal the correct principles of all phenomena and to bring sentient beings to enlightenment.
Now, the term "all" (*sarva*) expresses many different meanings.
Here, "existence" (bhava) refers to the homogeneous character (nikāyasabhāga) and the five aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings that correspond to that homogeneous character.
As it is said: "All those who die and are reborn in the desire realm all undergo the existence of desire," and so forth.
He also speaks of the *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneity) and the five aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings (*sattvagaṇa*) that follow that homogeneity;
as when it is said that those bound by the *paryavasthānas* (obsessions) undergo existence in hell,
he likewise speaks of the *nikāyasabhāga* and the five aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings that follow that homogeneity.
As it is said regarding the time one experiences desire, how many roots produced by karma are first acquired;
that also refers to the homogeneous character (nikāyasabhāga) and the five aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings (sattvasaṃkhyāta) that correspond to that homogeneous character.

As it is said, there are four types of existence (bhava): existence at birth (upapattibhava), existence at death (maraṇabhava), intermediate existence (antarābhava), and existence as the fundamental state (pūrvakālabhava).

These are also explained as the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) belonging to the category of sentient beings, both in terms of their commonality of group (nikāyasabhāga) and that which conforms to such commonality.

As it is said: "Regarding those who abandon the existence of desire and undergo the existence of desire, is it the case that all phenomena of the desire realm cease and phenomena of the desire realm manifest before them? and so forth.

He also explains that it consists of the commonality of group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the five aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings (*sattvākhya*) that correspond to that homogeneity.
This is as it is said: "What are the existent phenomena (*bhava-dharma*)?
They are all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*)."
He says that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are called "existence" (*bhava*).

Just as it is said that "Potalaka, you should know that the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) can cause future existence to arise," he says that the mind of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi-citta*) and its attendants are called "existence."
As it is said, Ārāḍa, one should know that if karma can cause the continuity of future existence,
it is called "existence" (bhava).
That [teaching] states that the volition capable of projecting future existence is what is termed "existence."
Regarding the statement that "existence (bhava) is conditioned by grasping (upādāna)," the Abhidharma masters say:
"What they call 'existence' refers to the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) at that particular time."
The Venerable Ghosaka spoke thus:
"He asserts that those karmas which lead to future existence are called 'existence' (bhava),
just as it is said regarding the seven existences."
First, the existence of hell-beings;
second, the existence of animals;
third, the existence of the realm of hungry ghosts.
There is existence as the four gods,
existence as the five persons,
and existence as the six karmas.
Seventh is existence-in-the-intermediate-state (*antarābhava*).
They explain that the five destinies (*gati*) along with their causes and their means are called "existence" (*bhava*);
that is to say, the existence of hell and so forth are the five destinies.
Karmic existence (*karmabhava*) is its cause;
intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) is its means.
As it is said: "What is desire-existence (*kāmadhātu-bhava*)?"
This refers to those karmas bound to the desire realm which, taking grasping as a condition,
lead to future rebirths;
and so forth, as extensively explained.
He states that karma and its maturation (vipāka) are called "existence" (bhava), but he does not state that grasping (upādāna) is the condition for it.
Question: If that is so, [what is the condition for existence?]
How should the explanations in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* be reconciled?
For instance, it is said: "In the realm of desire, all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the realm of desire increase;
in the realm of form, all latent dispositions of the realm of form increase."
In the formless existence (ārūpyabhava), all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm increase;
this may be so for the desire existence (kāmadhātu). Why is that?
The karmas of the five categories within the desire realm are all capable of producing maturation (vipāka),
because they are susceptible to being increased by all the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the desire realm.
How could this be possible for the form and formless realms?
Why is this so? Because in that realm, there are only karmas to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) that produce maturation (*vipāka*).
This is answered in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
It should be said that in the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu-bhava*), all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase;
in the existence of form (*rūpadhātu-bhava*), the universal latent dispositions and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the form realm increase;
and in the existence of the formless (*ārūpyadhātu-bhava*), the universal latent dispositions and those to be abandoned through cultivation of the formless realm increase.
If it were not so, there would be a different underlying intention:
namely, that the mind associated with the fivefold fetters possesses its own retinue.
Therefore, they are also conventionally described as existing.
Thus, it is said that all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase accordingly. Some say:
That treatise consists of chapters and sections.
Within the chapters, it speaks only of karma and its maturation (vipāka), using the term "existence" (bhava) but not mentioning "grasping as a condition" (upādāna-pratyaya).
Within the sections, it fully explains that karma and its maturation, as well as grasping as a condition.
Therefore, it is said that all underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase accordingly.
The critique states:
"One should not make such a statement."
Why is this? That master first established the meaning of the chapters and subsequently applied the gates to them.
How could the explanation within the gates differ from that of the chapters?
Therefore, what was stated previously is logically sound.
Question: For what reason is it called "existence" (bhava)?
Answer: It is called existence because there is increase and decrease.
Question: If that is so, the Noble Path also undergoes increase and decrease; should it not likewise be called "existent" (*sat*)?
Answer: That which, through increase and decrease, is able to nourish, benefit, and sustain its possessor, is said to be "existent."
Although the Noble Path undergoes increase and decrease,
it diminishes, opposes, harms, and destroys all forms of existence;
therefore, it is not called "existence."
Furthermore, if there were increase or decrease, yet it still caused birth, old age, sickness, and death to continue without interruption for all beings, that would be called "existence" (*bhava*).
Although the Noble Path involves increase and decrease, [it does not function in this way].
Furthermore, because it causes all beings to sever birth, old age, sickness, and death so that they do not continue, it is not called "existence" (*bhava*).
Moreover, if there were increase or decrease, it would likewise be a movement toward the accumulation of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya-gati*).
The Noble One explains that "existence" (bhava) refers to the process of proceeding toward birth, aging, sickness, and death within the world;
although the Noble Path undergoes increase and decrease,
it is not called "existence" because it is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering and the practice leading to the cessation of birth, aging, sickness, and death within the world.
Furthermore, whatever involves increase or decrease is also the domain of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
the domain of perversions, the domain of craving, and the domain of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
it is the basis upon which greed, hatred, and delusion are established.
That which is with defilement, with poison, with fault, with thorns, with turbidity, and which leads to existence and leads to the suffering of the Truth of Origination is called "existence" (bhava).
Although the Noble Path possesses increase and decrease,
it is contrary to all these characteristics and therefore is not called "existence."
Furthermore, there are those who say that it is called "existence" (bhava) because it is something to be feared.
Question: If that is so, then...
Nirvana can also be feared;
it should likewise be called "existent," as stated in the Sūtra.
"O bhikṣus, you should know that unlearned worldlings,
due to their ignorance, fear nirvāṇa."
That is to say: "In this regard, 'I' do not exist;
'mine' does not exist; and 'I shall not exist.'"
"Even 'mine' shall not exist. In response:
if one who possesses fear gives rise to right view, it is said that there is nirvāṇa;
although there is fear, because it arises from wrong view, it is not so called.
Furthermore, if there were fear arising from both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*), it would be said that "nirvāṇa exists.
Although such fear exists,
because it arises only in ordinary persons and not in noble ones, it is not said to exist [in the latter].
Some say: "It is called 'existence' (bhava) because it is a vessel for suffering.
Question: Existence is also a vessel for pleasure.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Mahānāman, you should know that if form were exclusively suffering and not pleasure..."

"Mahānāman, you should know that if pleasure were not accompanied by [pleasure], and if no slight pleasure or joy were to follow after it, there would be no sentient beings who, for the sake of seeking pleasure, become stained with attachment to form."
Because form is not exclusively suffering, but is also pleasure and accompanied by pleasure, and because it is pursued by slight pleasure and joy,
there are sentient beings who, for the sake of seeking pleasure, become attached to form.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that the three feelings are established definitively without confusion: first, pleasure; [second, pain;
and third, neither-pain-nor-pleasure].
Second is suffering;
third is neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
The Path relies upon its requisites, and Nirvāṇa relies upon the Path; because one delights in the Path, one realizes the bliss of Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, all that exists is not merely a vessel of suffering.
How could one possibly explain the term "existence" (bhava) as being a vessel of suffering?
Answer: Although there is a slight degree of pleasure within the phenomena of birth and death, because suffering is so predominant, they are designated by the name "vessels of suffering.
Therefore, all states of existence are merely called vessels of suffering.
It is like a jar of poison into which a single drop of honey has been placed;
it is not called a "honey jar" because of this,
but is simply called a "poison jar."
Because poison is so prevalent,
existence is likewise so:
it is the basis for manifold suffering.
It is merely called an "instrument of suffering.
Furthermore, there are briefly five types of continuity (*saṃtati*):
first, the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Second, the continuity of birth;
third, the continuity of temporal divisions;
fourth, the continuity of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Regarding the fivefold succession of moments,
that which constitutes a "succession in the intermediate state" refers to the cessation of the aggregates of the death-existence and the arising of the aggregates of the intermediate existence.
In this context, the aggregates of the intermediate state (antarābhava) continue into the aggregates of the existence at birth (upapattibhava);
therefore, it is called the continuity of the intermediate state.
As for the continuity of the existence at birth:
That is to say, when the aggregates of the intermediate state cease, or the aggregates of the death-existence cease, the aggregates of the birth-existence arise.
These aggregates of the birth-existence continue from the aggregates of the intermediate state,
or they continue from the aggregates of the death-existence.
Therefore, this is called the continuity of birth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
As for the continuity of time-periods,
it refers to the cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*) from the stage of the *kalala* up until the period of full maturity.
The aggregates from the *arbuda* stage up to the period of old age arise;
