these aggregates from the *arbuda* stage up to the period of old age continue the aggregates from the *kalala* stage up to the period of full maturity.
Therefore, it is called the continuity of temporal phases (*kāla-bhāga-saṃtati*).
As for the continuity of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-saṃtati*),
it refers to the arising of unwholesome or indeterminate phenomena immediately following wholesome phenomena.
These unwholesome dharmas or neutral dharmas follow immediately after preceding wholesome dharmas, unwholesome dharmas,
or neutral dharmas; the detailed explanation is likewise for all such cases.
Therefore, it is called the continuity of the dharma-nature.
As for the continuity of moments (kṣaṇa),
it means that each preceding moment arises without interval into each succeeding moment.
Each subsequent moment follows each preceding moment;
therefore, it is called the "continuity of moments.
These five continuities can also be subsumed within two types of continuity.
Because the first three do not depart from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) due to the two modes of momentary continuity,
the nature of phenomena can also enter into moments;
for all things are of the nature of moments.
Regarding these five realms of continuity:
the desire realm possesses all five,
while the form realm possesses only four.
Excluding the intermediate state and the period of time,
the formless realm consists of only three;
excluding the intermediate state and the period of time.
Regarding the destinies (*gati*), hell possesses only four;
excluding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
the other four destinies all possess all five.
Regarding "beings," all four modes of birth (*yoni*) possess five kinds of continuity.
Here, however, the treatise is composed based solely on the continuity of the two existences (*bhava*) within the birth-process (*upapatti-bhava*).
That is to say, it concerns how the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) cause the continuity of the three existences.
This is stated according to their general categories.
However, these three fetters pertain to all three realms of existence;
those bound to the desire realm cause the continuity of existence in the desire realm.
That which is bound to the realm of form causes the continuity of existence in the realm of form;
that which is bound to the formless realm causes the continuity of existence in the formless realm.
This is because rebirth-linking occurs through the manifestation of one or another [existence] at the very first moment of the intermediate state (antarābhava).
The remainder should be understood according to the principles of the original treatise.

Question: It is the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that cause the continuity of existence (*bhava*), and not the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) or impurities (*mala*), because these latter are not firmly established.
The afflictions of the mental level cause the continuity of existence, not those of the five groups of sensory consciousness,
because at the precise moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*), there is necessarily mental consciousness and no sensory consciousnesses. For what reason, then,

does the fundamental treatise state that the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*)— envy and stinginess— and the fetters (*saṃyojana*) consist of the group of cravings born from nose-contact and tongue-contact?
Does it cause the continuity of existence in the realm of desire?
Does the group of cravings born from eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact cause the continuity of existence in the realms of desire and form?
And does the restlessness that is a fetter conducive to the higher realms cause the continuity of existence in the realms of form and formlessness?
Answer: The original treatise should state that the hindrances of sensual desire, ill-will, and doubt cause the continuity of existence in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*);
whereas the fetters of greed for the higher realms, pride, and ignorance cause the continuity of existence in the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The aggregate of craving born of mental contact causes the continuity of the three realms of existence;
the other two hindrances, the fetters of envy and avarice, the bond of restlessness, and the first five aggregates of craving born of contact do not cause the continuity of existence.
As for the fact that this statement is not made,
one should know that this passage has a specific underlying intention (*abhiprāya*): namely,
that those who have not yet been liberated from the other two hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth, upon the end of their life, will still be reborn in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and so on.
The statement that they "can continue the existence of desire" and so forth refers to this;
however, at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), it is not by their power alone.
Furthermore, it is said that the various afflictions (*kleśa*) cause existence to continue due to three conditions.
First, because it has not yet been abandoned;
second, because it is capable of producing a retributive fruit (*vipākaphala*);
and third, because at the time of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), it is able to moisten existence (*bhava*).
All unwholesome latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the mental level possess all three conditions;
neutral latent dispositions cannot induce existence and thus possess only two conditions.
The unwholesome latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) present in the five sensory consciousnesses cannot moisten existence;
they possess only two conditions.
As for the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) latent dispositions, they possess only the condition of being unabandoned, lacking the other two conditions.
The unwholesome fetters and stains have only two conditions and are unable to moisten existence;
the indeterminate fetters and stains have only one condition,
namely, that they have not yet been abandoned.
Because the hindrance of torpor and so forth have not been abandoned,
or because they bring about existence (*bhava*),
it is said that they can continue existence but cannot moisten existence.
This does not contradict reason.

Regarding the question of which meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) brings about the cessation of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), why was this treatise composed?
It is answered: it is because one wishes to reveal that when the Buddhas appear in the world, there are extraordinary events.
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* states that surrounding Jambudvīpa there is a road for the wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*) one *yojana* in width;
when no wheel-turning king exists, it is submerged by the ocean waters such that no one can see it.
When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world,
the waters of the great ocean recede by one yojana,
and only then does this path of the Wheel-Turning King appear.
It is strewn with golden sand and adorned with various jewels;
it is sprinkled with sandalwood-scented water.
When a Wheel-Turning Sage King tours the continents, he travels along this path together with his fourfold army.
Thus, when these Buddhas have not yet appeared in the world,
those who rely on the fundamental stage are unable to see [the truth],
while all those who have severed their fetters rely on the peripheral lands.
When the Wheel-Turning King endowed with the ten powers appears in the world,
he emerges based upon the fundamental ground;
the dharmas conducive to enlightenment are spread everywhere like golden sand.
Adorned with various merits and a multitude of precious jewels,
it was sprinkled above with four kinds of pure, clear water.
The Buddha was there together with an immeasurable and boundless retinue.
We both travel this path toward the city of Nirvāṇa;
for this reason, I have composed this treatise.
Furthermore, it is to refute the proponents of conceptual analysis who maintain that the various afflictions are not extinguished by relying upon meditative concentration.
He asserts this:
if there is a noble one born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
it is impossible for the Noble Path to manifest before him.
When their lifespan is exhausted, their afflictions are also exhausted, and they become arhats;
this is called "level with the crown of the head.

This treatise was composed to refute that attachment and to demonstrate that there are no afflictions [remaining] and that [liberation] is not achieved by depending on meditative absorption for cessation.
In this context, "concentration" (samādhi) indicates the path of antidote;
that is, the path of antidote is sometimes called concentration and sometimes called the path.
It is sometimes called the antidote (pratipakṣa),
sometimes called attention (manasikāra),
and sometimes described as practice (caryā).
Although the expressions differ, their meaning is no different.
Herein, "cessation" (nirodha) indicates permanent abandonment;
that is, this permanent abandonment is sometimes called cessation.
It is sometimes called "exhaustion," sometimes named "detachment from passion," and sometimes named "separation from fetters."
It is sometimes called "liberation" (vimukti);
although the terminology differs, the meaning is no different.
Formerly, within this Dharma, there were two masters of treatises.
The first was named Upavīra,
and the second was named Goṣavarma.
The Venerable Upavīra spoke as follows:
In this context, it is said that there is abandonment without remainder, ultimate abandonment, and abandonment such that not even a trace remains.
Such abandonment belongs to the noble ones (ārya) and not to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana);
it is accomplished by the noble path (āryamārga) and not by the mundane path (laukikamārga).
Why is this so? Because this treatise was composed based on the Sūtra on the Seven Reliances;
that sūtra speaks only of the seven fundamental stages (mūlabhūmi).
This refers to the four dhyānas and the lower three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Since there is no mundane path (*laukikamārga*) in these fundamental stages capable of severing afflictions (*kleśa*),
it is known that only noble ones (*ārya*) employ the supramundane path (*anāsravamārga*) to sever them.
The Venerable Ghoṣavarma spoke thus:
"In this context, it is said that there is abandonment without remainder, abandonment that is ultimate, and abandonment such that not even a trace remains.
Such abandonment belongs to both noble ones (ārya) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana)."
This noble path is also capable of being a mundane path.

Question: Does this treatise not rely on the Sūtra of the Seven Reliances? How then can an ordinary person, relying on a fundamental stage, give rise to a mundane path that has the sense of permanent abandonment?
Answer: For this reason, it is said that the Abhidharma illuminates the sūtras and other scriptures like a bright lamp;
that which was not previously explained within the sūtras and other texts is explained herein.
That which has not yet appeared is now manifested herein.
While that [system] speaks of "with remainder," this [system] speaks of "without remainder.

Therefore, both noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), relying upon the seven fundamental stages and the eight neighboring stages, are able to permanently sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) through both the noble path and the mundane path.
Thus, both explanations are well-supported, as this fundamental treatise allows for two meanings.

Regarding the answer that the three fetters are either abandoned based on the four [dhyānas] or based on the *anāgamya* (threshold concentration): [This refers to the fact that while the first three fetters are generally abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) associated with the *anāgamya*, they may also be abandoned through the paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) associated with the four dhyānas.]
The "four" refers to the stages of the four dhyānas.
"Not-yet-attained" (anāgamya) refers to the stage of not-yet-attained and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara),
as both are designated by the name "not-yet-attained stage."
Question: Why is this stage named "the Not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*)?
Answer: Because it is able to manifest before one has yet entered the fundamental [dhyāna] and can sever all afflictions, it is therefore called "the Not-yet-attained.
Question: The Sūtra speaks only of the fundamental [dhyāna] as the basis, not of the stage of the Not-yet-attained.
Regarding this, why is it said that the three fetters are abandoned either by relying on the four [dhyānas] or by relying on the *anāgamya*?
The answer is: in this context, one should say they are abandoned either by relying on the four or by relying on the *anāgamya*;
one should not say they are abandoned by relying on the *anāgamya* alone.
As for the statement that it "depends on the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage] for its cessation," there is a specific underlying intention: namely,
that the subsequent mention of "dependence" is a reiterative reference to the fundamental [stage].
The meaning here is that the three fetters are either abandoned based on the four cessations,
or they are abandoned based on the cessation of the four fundamental dhyānas, or based on the cessation of the *anāgamya* (threshold) concentration,
or they are abandoned based on both the *anāgamya* and the four fundamental dhyānas.
For example, if someone were to ask another:
"Did you do this while having entered the city,
or did you do this before entering the city?"
In this context, one city is mentioned twice, both before and after;
the same applies to the word "relying" (*niśritya*).
This does not contradict reason.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "based on words," there is both a general and a specific sense.
The specific sense refers only to the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*), as in the *Saptaniśraya-sūtra*.
The general sense applies to both the fundamental and the peripheral stages (*prāntakoṭika*).
As it is stated therein,
this reliance on words does not contradict reason. Furthermore,
these three fetters can be found based on the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The desire realm ceases based solely on the *anāgamya* (threshold concentration).
The first dhyāna ceases either based on the first dhyāna or on the *anāgamya*.
The second dhyāna ceases either based on the second dhyāna or on the *anāgamya*.
Those in the third dhyāna either rely on the three dhyānas or rely on the threshold concentration (anāgamya) for cessation.
Those in the fourth dhyāna and the four formless attainments (ārūpya) either rely on the four dhyānas or rely on the threshold concentration for cessation.
Why is this? Because the three fetters are forever severed— severed without remainder, severed ultimately, and severed so that not even a trace remains—
and this must necessarily be through the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
However, all paths of seeing rely exclusively upon six stages, namely:
the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), and the intermediate dhyāna.
If one enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth by relying on the threshold concentration...
In this way, these three fetters are abandoned based on the *anāgamya* [preliminary stage];
up to the point where, if one enters rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the fourth dhyāna,
these three fetters are abandoned based on the fourth dhyāna.
Although only the fourth dhyāna and the three stages of the formless realm possess the three fetters,
and these may be abandoned based on either the fourth dhyāna or the threshold concentration (anāgamya),
they are described here according to their general category.
There is no fault in this either.
Although one may partially sever the three fetters by relying on the mundane path arising from the limits of the eight stages,
it is not a permanent severance.
Therefore, this is not mentioned here.
However, the permanent abandonment of these three fetters occurs exclusively at the moment of the *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti* (patience regarding subsequent knowledge of the path).

If they were to be explained individually, the permanent abandonment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) occurs exclusively at the moment of the *duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti* (patience regarding subsequent knowledge of suffering).
Therefore, it is said that the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*) cease in the stage of *anāgamya*;
as for the three unwholesome roots and the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), they cease before arising,
because they are permanently abandoned at the time one becomes free from the defilement of desire.

Whether they be ordinary persons or noble ones, whether by means of the contaminated path or the uncontaminated path, all rely on the "not-yet-attained" (anāgamya) stage because it is through this that one becomes detached from the defilements of desire.
As for the outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava), whether contaminated or uncontaminated, it is either extinguished by relying on seven stages or by relying on the "not-yet-attained" stage.
The seven refer to the four dhyānas and the lower three formless attainments; these constitute the seven.
"Based on concentration" refers to the *anāgamya* (preliminary) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), as both are designated as the *anāgamya-bhūmi* (the stage of the preliminary).
Among these, the outflow of impurities (āsrava) is found from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
The outflow of ignorance (avidyāsrava) is found from the desire realm (kāmadhātu) up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Both of these are permanently severed only when one is free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
That freedom from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is attained by means of the path belonging to the ninth stage.
Therefore, it is said that [the outflows] are either abandoned by relying on the seven [stages] or by relying on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage.
However, the *avidyā-āsrava* (outflow of ignorance) belonging to the desire realm is abandoned only by relying on the *anāgamya*.
The *āsravas* and *avidyā-āsravas* belonging to the first dhyāna are abandoned by relying on either the first dhyāna or the *anāgamya*.
One who dwells in the second dhyāna relies on the second dhyāna or on the threshold concentration (anāgamya) for cessation; likewise,
one who dwells up to the sphere of infinite consciousness relies on the four dhyānas, the first two formless attainments, or on the threshold concentration for cessation.
Regarding the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
they may be based on the four dhyānas and the lower three formless attainments, or they may be based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya) or cessation;
they may also be described according to their general categories.
The others are either based on the seven [dhyānas] or on the *anāgamya* for their cessation;
however, only this [first category] is mentioned here because it refers specifically to the two locations of permanent abandonment (*atyantaprahāṇa*),
which are severed only by the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) of the noble ones (*ārya*).
This is precisely the final *vajropama-samādhi*.
The remaining details should be understood as appropriate according to the original treatise.

One should understand, in accordance with reason, the distinctions regarding the permanent abandonment [of afflictions] by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) through mundane (*laukika*) noble paths.
Regarding the various fetters that have passed away:
were those fetters already bound?
[And so on, as explained at length.]
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed? Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the tenets of other schools and revealing the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who claim that the past and the future do not possess real substantial entities.

Alternatively, there are those who claim that once afflictions have been abandoned, they never regress; to refute this claim, it is shown that the past and future truly exist, and it is further demonstrated that there is indeed regression even after afflictions have been abandoned.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
It should be understood that herein, "already bound" refers to the past, "to be bound" refers to the future, and "now bound" refers to the present.
Furthermore, regarding this matter, some have made the following statement:
The application of the term "bond" (*bandhana*) refers to "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).
Some say that it is because they are fetters that they are called bonds.
However, there are three types of acquisition regarding the fetters:
first, like a bull king, the acquisition precedes;
second, like a calf, the acquisition follows.
The three cases are as follows: like a physical form and its shadow, they are obtained simultaneously;
like a bull-king, it is first bound and then obtained;
like a calf, it is first obtained and then bound.
Regarding those with physical form, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and their acquisitions (*prāpti*) arise together.
If various fetters are past, have those fetters already bound?
Answer: If various fetters are past, those fetters have already bound, meaning that when the fetters are in the past, their acquisitions are also in the past.
Because they have previously been bound, they are said to be "already bound.
There are fetters that are already bound, yet those fetters are not past;
that is to say, future and present fetters that are already bound.
Since those fetters exist in the future and present, they must have existed in the past as that which was once bound;
for these fetters follow after their acquisition, like a calf following its mother. Therefore, regarding those fetters in the future, will those fetters bind [the object] when they arise?
It should be answered with four alternatives,
because the meaning is not fixed:
there are fetters of the future that are not bound by those same fetters in the present.
This refers to those fetters of the future that have been abandoned, fully understood, ceased, and vomited out, such that one will certainly not regress from them.
Herein, "abandoned" means that the thorough knowledge of abandonment has already been attained.
"Thoroughly known" means that one has already attained thorough knowledge through wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*).
"Already ceased" means that one has already attained cessation through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
"Already vomited up" refers to having already severed the acquisition of fetters and having already realized the acquisition of dissociation.
Some say as follows:
"Already severed, already fully known, already extinguished, and already vomited out" all equally manifest the meaning of relinquishment (*prahāṇa*).
"One who certainly shall not fall back" refers to an Arhat of the non-retrogressive type (*anāgāmin-dharman*).
For such a person, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the future will certainly never be lost.
For an Arhat of the "subject to regression" (parihāṇadharman) type, it is certain that they shall not regress from the fetters to be abandoned through seeing in the three realms in the future.
This also applies to an Arhat of the "not subject to regression" (aparihāṇadharman) type who is a Non-returner (anāgāmin),
provided they have already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
One will certainly not fall away from the fetters to be abandoned by insight within the three realms of the future, nor from the fetters to be abandoned by cultivation in the lower eight stages;
this remains the case even so long as one has not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
Regarding the fetters of the three realms to be abandoned by seeing in the future,
as well as the fetters of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation, one will certainly not regress;
this applies to those of the "regressive" type who are non-returners, as well as stream-enterers and once-returners.
Those with future [attainments] will certainly not fall away from the fetters abandoned through vision within the three realms.
This applies to those of the "non-falling" (aparihāṇadharman) type and to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Furthermore, those such as Bodhisattvas who have already become free from the defilement of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) will certainly not fall away from the fetters abandoned through vision and cultivation belonging to the eight lower stages in the future.

Furthermore, if one has already become free from the defilements of the desire realm but has not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna, there are fetters to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation belonging to that single future stage which will certainly not be subject to retrogression; these are called "fetters that exist in the future, but those fetters will not bind [the individual] in the future."

There are fetters that are destined to bind him, yet those fetters are not of the future; rather, they are past, already abandoned, already fully understood, already ceased, and already vomited out, such that he will certainly fall away from them.
The meaning of these various phrases is as explained previously.

"Those certain to fall back" refers to Arhats of the *parihāṇadharman* type who are certain to fall back from the fetters abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) belonging to the three realms that they have previously severed.
This also includes non-returners (*anāgāmin*) of the *parihāṇadharman* type who have already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Regarding the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the lower eight stages of the past, there is certain to be falling away;
this continues down to the point where, if one has not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
there is certain to be falling away regarding the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in one stage of the past.
If an ordinary person of the nature of falling away has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness,
there are certain fetters— abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the eight lower stages— that they will inevitably fall back upon;
this continues up to the case where they have already become detached from the defilements of the desire realm but have not yet become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
Regarding the fetters to be abandoned through vision and cultivation on a past stage, there are those that will certainly be subject to falling away;
these are called "fetters that will bind, but whose binding is not in the future.
There are also fetters in the future for which those same fetters will likewise bind.
This refers to one who has bound future [defilements], which have already been abandoned, fully understood, ceased, and vomited out, yet will certainly fall away.
Herein, "already abandoned" and so forth are explained as in the first phrase;
"will certainly fall away" is explained as in the second phrase.
However, what was previously discussed concerned the past; what is now discussed concerns the future.

There are fetters that are not of the future, and those fetters will likewise not be bound in the future—namely, those fetters that are past, already abandoned, already fully known, already ceased, and already vomited out.
It certainly does not include the fetters or the present bonds.
The various phrases herein are explained as in the first phrase.
However, while previously the future was discussed, here the past and present bonds are discussed.
This means that present fetters are neither future, because they are present;
nor are they "to-be-bound," because they are currently bound.
Are all fetters that are present also currently binding?
Answer: Those fetters that are present are those fetters by which one is currently bound.
This means that present fetters necessarily possess a present acquisition (*prāpti*), because they are like a physical form and its shadow, which must exist simultaneously.

There are fetters that currently bind, yet those fetters are not present; this refers to past and future fetters that currently bind, which possess a present acquisition (*prāpti*). As for past fetters: [they are those that have been acquired and have not yet been abandoned].
Just as a bull leader leads the way, those fetters yet to come follow behind like calves.
Because those [fetters] are present, they are called "presently bound"; one uses this path to sever the fetters of the desire realm.
"When one falls back from this path, does one again become bound by those fetters?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting other schools and clarifying the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that it is absolutely impossible for afflictions to arise through regression.
As for the Vibhajyavādins,
they cite worldly examples as proof,
making this statement:
Just as when a jar is broken, there remain only the shards and it can no longer function as a jar,
so too should it be with the Arhats:
once the afflictions have been destroyed by the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi), the afflictions should not arise again, nor should they fall back from their state.
Just as when wood has been burned, only the remaining ashes exist and it no longer becomes wood again,
so too should it be for the Arhats:
once the fire of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) has burned away the afflictions (*kleśa*), they should not arise again, nor should there be any falling back (*parihāṇi*) into those afflictions.
He cites these worldly examples to prove the point that there is no arising of afflictions through regression;
to refute his position, it is shown that there is indeed such arising.
If there were no such thing as falling away, it would contradict the sūtra.
As the sūtra says:
"There are two kinds of arhats."
First, those subject to regression;
second, those not subject to regression.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says:
There are five causes and conditions by which a time-liberated arhat may fall away, become obscured, or lose [their attainment].
What are these five?
First, engaging extensively in worldly affairs.
Second, they delight in various frivolous discourses;
third, they take pleasure in inciting strife and contention;
fourth, they enjoy traveling long distances.
The five aggregates are constantly subject to many ailments.
Furthermore, a sutra states that there was an Arhat named Ghoṭika.
At that time, having regressed from liberation six times,
he feared further loss at the seventh instance and took his own life with a blade to enter parinirvāṇa. Thus,
it is known that there is indeed regression due to the arising of afflictions.
Question: If there is the sense of falling back, how should one explain the present examples cited by the Vibhajyavādins?
Answer: It is not necessary to explain them. Why is that?
That is neither Sūtra, nor Vinaya, nor Abhidharma.
However, these are merely coarse and superficial worldly analogies;
worldly phenomena differ from the phenomena of the noble ones (ārya).
One should not use worldly phenomena to challenge the phenomena of the noble ones.
If it must be explained away, one should point out the fault in the analogy;
since the analogy is faulty, it fails to serve as proof.
For example, once a jar is broken, there will necessarily remain shards.
Once one has attained arhatship, are there still remaining afflictions?
If there were afflictions, one would not be an arhat.
If there are no afflictions, then the meaning and the metaphor differ, and thus it cannot serve as proof.
Just as when wood has been burned, there certainly remains residual ash,
does one who has attained arhatship still have residual afflictions?
If there were afflictions remaining, one would not be an arhat.
If there were no afflictions, then the distinction between the meaning and the metaphor would not serve as proof.
However, in the world, wood has no sense of being burned;
rather, it is simply that the atoms of wood, having acted as causes for the atoms of fire, have already ceased.
Since these fire-atoms have already ceased after having served as the cause for the ash-atoms,
it should be stated thus:
wood is the cause of fire, and fire is the cause of ash.
However, the worldly notion holds that fire burns wood and turns it into ash;
since the wood has perished, there remains residual ash.
Because it is not the case that the substance is entirely non-existent, this analogy does not correspond to the meaning of the Dharma.
Furthermore, although an Arhat has severed all afflictions, this does not mean they are entirely non-existent, because the nature and characteristics of past and future afflictions still truly exist.
This is so as long as the path that opposes the afflictions has not yet manifested within the continuum.
At that time, it is said that the afflictions have not yet been abandoned.
However, when the path that opposes the afflictions has manifested within the continuum,
one abandons the acquisition of the fetters and realizes the acquisition of disjunction from them.
The non-attainment of afflictions is called the "abandonment of afflictions.
One should speak thus:
the cultivation of the Noble Path is a marvelous thing.
Now, although an Arhat has severed the afflictions, he does not cause them to be non-existent.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"The severance of afflictions refers to their no longer functioning within one's own continuum; it does not mean they have been rendered entirely non-existent."
As it is said, when one says "Devadatta is not in his house," this does not mean that Devadatta is also not in other places.
One should know that the same applies to the abandonment of afflictions;
for they exist in the past.
If one encounters conditions for regression as a cause that draws forth future afflictions, then there must necessarily be the sense of regressing by giving rise to afflictions.
Question: How do the Vibhajyavādins explain away the sūtra cited by the Sautrāntikas?
The reply is that when one falls away, it is the path that is lost, not the fruit;
for the fruits of śrāmaṇya are unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Question: Since you admit that there is falling away, [how can this be so?]
What is the difference between falling away from the path and falling away from the fruit,
such that it is said there is no falling away?
Furthermore, they admit that one falls away from the stage of an Arhat (aśaikṣamārga).
If one were to attain the fruit of the path of training,
one would also necessarily fall away from it, because the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣaphala) does not constitute the path of training. If, on the other hand,
one were to attain nothing at all, there would be a great logical error.
One who falls away from the path of no-more-learning does not obtain the path of learning;
if that were so, one would necessarily abide in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
If, however, one is neither an ordinary person nor one on the paths of learning or no-more-learning...
If one were to admit that there are sentient beings distinct from both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*), it would follow that they are not disciples of the Blessed One.
Furthermore, one must admit that there is falling away (*parihāṇi*) due to the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Vibhajyavādins further state that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are the seeds of the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
The intrinsic nature of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is dissociated from the mind;
the intrinsic nature of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) is associated with the mind.
The outbursts arise from the latent dispositions.
Arhats fall away because the *paryavasthānas* (active outbursts) manifest;
since those who have already abandoned the *anuśayas* (latent tendencies) no longer give rise to these *paryavasthānas*, how could they fall away?
Therefore, it is correct to maintain that there is no falling away from the state of an Arhat.
He thus describes this as the fruit of ignorance,
the fruit of darkness,
and the fruit of nescience.
This is the result of a lack of diligent application of skillful means.
Nevertheless, there is indeed the sense that afflictions arise.
This treatise was composed in order to refute that position and to demonstrate the correct reasoning associated with the nature of those who are subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*).
Question: By what dharma is falling away (parihāṇi) characterized as its intrinsic nature? Some say:
"If such afflictions (kleśa) and entanglements (paryavasthāna) arise and become manifest, one falls away."
Thus, this very dharma is the intrinsic nature of falling away (*parihāṇi*).
If one were to say that falling away has the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) as its intrinsic nature,
other masters state:
If, at the time of falling back, that which conforms to the falling back is the nature of falling back,
then one may say that all phenomena constitute the nature of falling back;
for at the time of falling back, all phenomena possess the sense of conforming to falling back.
For example, the Venerable One spoke thus:
"Regressing has no intrinsic nature; it is merely a conventional designation. Why is this so?
Within one's body there were previously various wholesome merits;
now, encountering conditions for decline, one falls away from these dharmas—what inherent nature could such a thing have?
It is like a person possessing wealth who is robbed by a thief.
Someone asked,
"What is the nature of this loss of wealth that you have now suffered?
The owner of the wealth replied:
I originally possessed wealth, which has now been seized by thieves; since I have no material goods, what essence can there be?
It is like a person whose clothes have been taken away by another, remaining there naked.
Someone asked,
"Now that you have no clothes, what do you take as your body?
The owner of the clothes replied:
I previously possessed a garment which has now been taken away; what essence could there be [to it]?
It is like when a person's garment is torn and someone asks:
"Your garment is now torn; what does it take as its nature?"
The one whose robe was torn said:
"My robe was previously intact; now that it is torn, what nature does it possess?
Likewise, within this body there were formerly excellent qualities, yet now they have only declined and been lost—what self-nature does it possess?"
The commentary states:
That which has regressed from its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*);
it is precisely this non-acquisition that is subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāraskandha*).
That is to say, they are included among the remaining such factors that are dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*).
One should know that "decline" (*parihāṇi*) differs from the "dharma conducive to decline" (*parihāṇadharman*);
decline has non-possession (*aprāpti*), specifically non-accomplishment (*asamanvāgama*), as its intrinsic nature.
It is comprised within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind that are unobscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) have all unwholesome (*akuśala*) and obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) states as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Just as the schism of the Saṃgha differs from the offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha,
the schism of the Saṃgha has non-concord as its intrinsic nature;
it is comprised within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha) and is unobscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
The offense of schism has false speech as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The Saṃgha incurs the schism, while the schismatic person incurs the offense.
This is because such a falling away is distinct from the dharma of falling away (*parihāṇadharma*).
That the nature of retrogression is definitively and substantially existent,
and is subsumed within the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*),
is logically untenable and not established. *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Volume 60.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Sixty-one,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Two: The Single Path of Practice (*Ekāvacārādhikāra*), Part Six of the Second Chapter: The Aggregate of Fetters (*Saṃyojanaskandha*). Question: Does one fall away because afflictions manifest?
If it were the case that the defilements already abandoned manifest once again,
what fault would there be?
There would be faults in both scenarios.
Why is this so? If one were to fall away because afflictions manifest in the present,
how would one explain the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
As it is said, there are three conditions for the arising of the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*):
first, the latent tendency of sensual desire has not been abandoned and has not been fully understood;
second, phenomena conducive to the entanglement of sensual desire (*kāmarāgaparyavasthāna*) are present before one.
Third, there is improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) regarding that existence;
it should be understood that this applies extensively up to the arising of the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).
How, then, should one reconcile this with what is stated in the sūtras?
For example, it is said that there are five causes and conditions by which an arhat liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) may fall away:
namely, engaging in many worldly activities; [and so forth].
Furthermore, how is the statement in the *Samāhitā-skandha* to be reconciled?
For it says that through a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), one regresses and gives rise to the acquisition (*prāpti*) of learner-dharmas (*śaikṣadharma*).
How can it be that an Arhat gives rise to afflictions that manifest?
Furthermore, what kind of mind immediately precedes the manifestation of afflictions?
If it is the case that afflictions manifest after one has fallen away [from the state of an Arhat], [how does this occur]?
How should the *Prajñapti-śāstra* be reconciled when it says:
"When the mind is distant and rigid, the three envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) of the formless realm—
namely, greed, pride, and ignorance— manifest?"
Yet, they frequently give rise to pride.
When any one of those three envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) manifests,
it should be said that they fall away from the exhaustion of greed for the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*).
How is the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* to be reconciled with this,
which states that for a certain class of persons (*pudgala*), an afflicted mind of the formless realm manifests because they abide in the exhaustion of desire for form?

When one abandons the roots of wholesome merit of an arhat (aśaikṣa) and the roots of wholesome merit of a trainee (śaikṣa) continue, and when one falls away from the mind of an arhat and abides in the mind of a trainee—how then is the statement in the *Prakaraṇapāda* to be reconciled?
As it says: "What is the nature of one subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*)?"
That is to say, [the minds] that are unwholesome and obscured-unspecified.
Regarding which state of mind one abides in before an affliction manifests,
it should be answered as follows:
Because afflictions manifest before one, there is regression.
Question: This has already successfully resolved the subsequent difficulties;
how, then, should the preceding difficulties be resolved?
Answer: None of these constitute a contradiction or a valid objection. Why is this?
Because the *Prakaraṇapāda* states that the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) arise due to three conditions.
This is said with reference to one who has not yet completely abandoned the afflictions;
that is, when an affliction arises and manifests before them.
Alternatively, there may be one who has already completely abandoned the afflictions of their own stage.
Or, it refers to those who have not yet completely abandoned the afflictions of their own level;
it is said that they give rise to afflictions that manifest based on those unabandoned afflictions of their own level.
Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of afflictions:
Whether there is regression or non-regression,
it is taught that one who relies on non-regression gives rise to afflictions that manifest before them.
Furthermore, regarding those who give rise to afflictions that manifest before them:
Whether immediately following a defiled mind or immediately following a non-defiled mind,
it is taught that when one relies on a defiled mind, afflictions arise and manifest immediately thereafter.
Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of arisen afflictions,
there are those that possess the requisite causes and conditions and those that lack them;
here, it refers to the manifestation of arisen afflictions based on those that possess the requisite causes and conditions.
This means that sentient beings give rise to various afflictions due to three causes and conditions, which is termed "being endowed with causes and conditions":
first, by the power of the cause;
second, by the power of the object.
Third, by the power of application (*prayoga*):
when the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) has not been abandoned or fully understood, this is called the power of the cause (*hetubala*).
When phenomena conducive to the outburst of sensual desire (*kāmarāgaparyavasthāna-anukūladharma*) manifest before one, this is called the power of the object (*ālambanabala*).
Regarding those who possess improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), it is said that this is due to the power of application (*prayoga-bala*).
Furthermore, this statement was made to refute the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) asserted by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*):
that the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) arise by way of three conditions.
That is to say, the non-Buddhists claim that all afflictions arise solely from objects:
if an object is present, afflictions arise;
if the object is destroyed, afflictions do not arise.
To refute that intention,
it is said that the arising of the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) is also caused by the non-abandonment of their own corresponding latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and furthermore,
it occurs through improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) based on those [latent dispositions].
The Sūtra states that there are five causes and conditions by which a time-liberated (samaya-vimukta) Arhat may fall away;
it explains these causes and conditions for falling away within the context of the factors of decline.
As stated in other sūtras,
that which is fully described there is what is taught in the *Samādhiskandha*.
This refers to the attainment of the dharmas of a learner (*śaikṣa*) arising through the retrogression of a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
That [text] speaks of the falling away from the faculties (*indriya*) but does not speak of the falling away from the fruits (*phala*).
Furthermore, since the mind associated with afflictions (*kleśa*) is also termed "neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee" (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*),
the statement that there is falling away from the fruits does not contradict reason.
How can it be that one who is an arhat gives rise to afflictions that manifest before them?
First, such a person was an arhat, and subsequently afflictions arose and manifested.
If afflictions arise and manifest, then at that moment one is no longer an arhat.
Just as one who was previously an ordinary person later enters the noble path,
and having entered the noble path, is no longer an ordinary person;
or just as one who was previously a learner later gives rise to the qualities of one beyond learning.
Once one has arisen in the state of a non-learner (aśaikṣa), one is no longer a learner (śaikṣa).
This case is likewise; what contradiction is there in principle?
What kind of mind arises immediately before such that afflictions manifest?
If one has completely abandoned the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
yet falls away because the fetters of that stage manifest before them,
then immediately after a wholesome mind of that same stage, afflictions will manifest.
If one has not yet completely abandoned the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
because the fetters of that stage arise and become manifest,
for one who falls away, either a wholesome mind or a defiled mind of that same stage arises immediately prior to the manifestation of the afflictions.
It should be understood that the same applies up to the first dhyāna.
If one who has become completely detached from the defilements of the desire realm falls away due to the arising of a fetter (paryavasthāna) of the desire realm,
then immediately after a wholesome mind or an unobscured-neutral mind of the desire realm, an active affliction (kleśa) manifests.
If one has not yet completely abandoned the defilements of the desire realm, because the fetters of the desire realm arise,
one who falls back immediately gives rise to afflictions that manifest, following upon either a wholesome mind, a defiled mind, or an unobscured-neutral mind of the desire realm.
In this context, if one has not yet attained the fundamental wholesome meditative absorptions (dhyāna) or formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), and these are not present before them,
they cannot fall away because they are unable to bring forth the active entanglements (paryavasthāna) of the form or formless realms.
However, one falls away only because the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the desire realm can arise and become manifest.
If one has attained the fundamental wholesome dhyānas and they are manifest, but not the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*),
one cannot fall away because the fetters of the formless realm cannot arise and become manifest.
One falls away only when the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the desire realm or the form realm manifest;
however, if one attains the fundamental wholesome dhyānas or the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*),
one falls away because those enable the fetters of all three realms to manifest.
Other masters say that after falling away, the afflictions manifest.
This [explanation] has already satisfactorily resolved all the aforementioned difficulties.
Regarding the various objections that may arise hereafter, how should they be resolved?
The answer is: none of them constitute valid objections. Why is this so?
As explained in the *Prakaraṇapāda* and the *Vijñānakāya*,
this refers to the state of conscious awareness and does not refer to the time of retrogression;
that is, although one has previously regressed, it was not consciously perceived.
Because one only becomes aware [of them] when the afflictions manifest before one.
It is like someone who previously recited the four Āgamas,
but having been entangled by other affairs, subsequently forgot them.
Even until they have recited it, they do not yet realize [the loss];
only when they later attempt to recite it do they know they have forgotten it.
Although they had previously forgotten it, they only now become aware of it.
This case is likewise: one first falls away and later realizes [the truth].
Because this is stated in reference to the time of realization, it does not contradict reason.
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
The unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified are called "states conducive to decline" because they function to impair the category of wholesome qualities and cause one to move further away from them;
thus it is said that as each affliction manifests, [the wholesome qualities recede].
In this way and that way, because they cause one to distance oneself from wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*), they are said to be "conducive to decline" (*hānabhāgīya*).
This does not mean that decline occurs only when afflictions (*kleśa*) manifest;
rather, it is because wholesome factors have already been lost previously.
Abiding in what kind of mind do the afflictions subsequently manifest?
They manifest after abiding in an unobscured-neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
That is to say, they follow the minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), because those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are of a weak and inferior nature.
Question: Is it not the case that one who is weak and inferior is more prone to retrogression?

Answer: If, regarding the pure factors (*śukladharma*), one’s nature is indeed weak, yet regarding the defiled factors (*kliṣṭadharma*) one’s power is strong and superior, then while abiding in those [pure factors], one will retrogress.
Once one has regressed, the afflictions immediately manifest.
Because the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is inherently weak in both its pure and defiled aspects, while abiding in that mind, one neither progresses nor regresses.
Some say that among the three types of indeterminate minds (*avyākṛta-citta*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), each possesses the possibility of retrogression (*parihāṇi*) while abiding in them;
immediately following these minds, afflictions (*kleśa*) manifest.
However, this refers to the unobscured-indeterminate mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the desire realm.
There is that which is contrary to the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) of the three realms;
when one abides in this mind, one will certainly not regress or give rise to the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms.
There is also that which is contrary to the entanglements of the desire and form realms, but not contrary to the entanglements of the formless realm.
While dwelling in this state of mind, although one does not regress and give rise to the afflictions of the desire or form realms,
it is possible to regress and give rise to the afflictions of the formless realm.
There are [afflictions] that are contrary to the fetters of the desire realm but not contrary to the fetters of the form or formless realms.
While dwelling in this state of mind, although one does not regress and give rise to the afflictions of the desire realm,
it is possible to regress and give rise to the afflictions of the form and formless realms;
there are those that are not in contradiction with the entanglements of all three realms.
When abiding in this state of mind, it is possible for the afflictions of the three realms to arise through regression.
The critique states:
between these two explanations, the former is superior.
It is said that one falls away from superior qualities only when afflictions actually manifest; therefore, this refers to the state of falling away.

One who possesses the nature of falling away does not necessarily have afflictions manifesting before them, for there are those with the nature of falling away who do not fall away even while in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Question: At the time of falling away, does one abide in the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) or abide in the fivefold body of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*)?
Answer: It should be stated as follows:
one falls away while abiding in the mental ground, not while abiding in the fivefold body of consciousness.
Question: If that is so, how do you explain the account of King Udrāyaṇa?
Formerly, there was a king named Udrāyaṇa who, taking his consorts and retinue to Mount Udakavāna, removed all men and provided exclusively for women with the performance of the five kinds of music.
They indulged in playful diversions; the music was exquisite and the fragrances were most aromatic.
They commanded their women to dance naked before them.
At that time, five hundred rishis who had transcended desire, possessing the power of supernatural travel, passed over this place on their way.
Upon seeing exquisite forms, hearing exquisite sounds, or smelling exquisite fragrances, they all lose their supernormal powers;
falling upon this mountain like birds with broken wings, they can no longer fly.
When the king saw them, he asked,
"Who are you? The sages replied, "We are seers."
The King asked again,
"Have you attained the fundamental concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
The seer replied:
"We have not yet attained it.
The king then asked, "Have you attained the first dhyāna?
The sages replied, "We once attained it, but we have now regressed from it."
At that time, the king, filled with anger and resentment, spoke these words:
"How can one who has not yet abandoned desire gaze upon my palace women and maidens?
This is utterly improper."
He then drew his sharp sword and severed the hands and feet of five hundred seers.
Among those seers, some fell back relying on visual consciousness, some fell back relying on auditory consciousness, and some fell back relying on olfactory consciousness.
How can it be said that one who dwells in the stage of mind (*manobhūmi*) falls back?
Furthermore, how is the case of the seer Mṛgāra to be reconciled?
Formerly, there was a seer named Mṛgāra.
At mealtime, he was constantly invited by King Śatānīka.
Whenever it was time for the meal, he would travel by the power of his supernatural faculties, flying like a king of geese, to the top of the royal palace.

The king himself would receive him, embrace him, and place him upon a golden couch; then, burning incense and scattering flowers, he would pay him respectful homage and provide him with offerings of exquisite food and drink.
When the seer had finished eating, he set aside his utensils, rinsed his mouth, and offered a blessing for the king; then he flew through the air and departed.
Later, on account of affairs of state, the king wished to travel elsewhere and thought to himself:
"After I have departed, who will serve the seer as I do?
Should he not act according to the Dharma, the seer’s nature is impetuous;
he might perhaps cast a curse upon me and cause me to lose my royal throne."
Thinking, "He might take my life or harm the people of the country," he asked the young woman,
"After I have gone away, will you be able to serve the rishi as I do?"
The girl replied, "I can.
The king then earnestly instructed the young woman to provide offerings to the seer according to the customary rites.
Thereafter, he went forth to manage the affairs of state.
On a later day, when it was time for the meal, the rishi flew through the air and arrived at the royal palace.
The princess received him in her arms and placed him upon a golden couch.
Because the power of the seer’s detachment was weak and inferior, he lost his supernormal powers upon touching a soft and delicate surface;
thus, after receiving his usual offerings, finishing his meal, rinsing his mouth, and reciting the benediction, he wished to travel through the air but was unable to fly.
He entered the royal garden intending to practice his former path;
however, despite making the utmost effort of attention, he was unable to do so because of the various clamorous sounds of elephants, horses, and other creatures.
At that time, the seer knew that the men and women of Śrāvastī were constantly thinking as follows: [text continues]
"If this great seer walks upon the earth, we shall receive him by prostrating at his feet and making offerings.
At that time, the seer conceived a deceptive cleverness and said to the princess, "Tell the people in the city:"
"Today the seer has stepped upon the earth;
whatever you wish to do, you should do it.
Thereupon, the princess immediately followed these instructions.
Having heard this, the people removed the rubble, filth, and excrement from within the city, sweeping and sprinkling it until it was pure and clean.
They arrayed banners and streamers, burned incense, scattered flowers, and performed various musical performances, adorning the city with such magnificent beauty that it resembled a celestial city.
At that time, the seer departed on foot from the city; not far away, he entered among the trees of a forest.
Desiring to cultivate the ancient path, he heard the cries of various birds, which agitated his mind and prevented him from attaining it.
He then abandoned that place and went to the riverbank.
There, he again heard the sound of dragons and fish leaping and frolicking in the water;
his mind being thus agitated, he was unable to practice.
He then ascended the mountain and formed this thought:
"My retreat from the wholesome qualities is entirely due to sentient beings;
even if I were to practice the austerities of precepts and prohibitions, I would only result in the form of a winged cat or a wildcat."
Neither those who travel by water, land, or air could escape me.
Having made this evil vow, his poisonous mind subsided slightly;
after a short while, he was again able to leave the defilements of the eighth stage behind and was reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The field of the gate of ambrosial tranquility at the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) yields the enjoyment of secluded peace for eighty thousand kalpas; yet,
once their karma and lifespan are exhausted, they are reborn here in this world within the forest of the dharma of suffering.
He assumed the body of a cat-like beast with two wings, each fifty yojanas in width.
With this massive body, he harmed sentient beings; none among those traveling through the air, on water, or on land could escape him.
From this point, when their life ends, they fall into the Avīci Hell,
where they undergo intense sufferings from which there is little hope of escape.
Thus do these sages abide until their body-consciousness declines.
How can it be said that he dwelt in the stage of the mind (manobhūmi) and then regressed?
Furthermore, how does he understand the affairs of Śakra, Lord of the Devas?
It is said that before Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world, there was a seer named Dvīpaṃkara.
The Heavenly Lord frequently went to consult him and receive the meaning of the Dharma.
Later, on one occasion, as the Heavenly Lord was about to go to the seer’s abode in his carriage,
the Apsaras lady Śrīmatī secretly thought to herself:
Today Śakra, Lord of the Devas, will likely abandon me and go to the other beautiful women;
therefore, I shall first ascend the palanquin, conceal my form, and go along with him without Śakra knowing it.
Upon arriving at the seer’s dwelling, she looked back and saw him;
she then addressed him, saying, "Whence have you come?
This seer does not wish to see women."
"You ought to return to the palace immediately; you should not remain here.
Although Seshi made excuses and was unwilling to return to the palace, the Heavenly Emperor, being enraged, struck the lady with the stem of a flower.
He then offered his thanks with flattery and sycophancy.
Upon hearing this, the seer immediately conceived sensual desire; because he withdrew from his superior meditative concentration, his spiral-topknot (śikhā) fell away.
This was the seer’s falling away while abiding in the consciousness of the ear.
How can it be said that there is a regression from the stage of mental abiding (*manobhūmi*)?

It should be understood that these regressions from the stage of mental abiding occur because they are induced to arise by the visual and other sensory consciousnesses; thus, such a statement is made without contradicting the principle.
The Venerable Saṃghavasu said:
"What contradiction is there in principle for one abiding in the five consciousnesses to fall back?
For afflictions also arise at the time when the five consciousnesses apprehend their objects."
This is because it is possible for one whose power of the counteractive force (*pratipakṣa*) is extremely weak to fall back even upon seeing forms and so forth with the eye.
The critique states: one should say that falling back occurs while abiding in the mental stage (*manobhūmi*), not from the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*).
Because afflictions arise discriminatively in response to favorable and unfavorable objects,
it is said for this reason that if one abides in the mental level (*manobhūmi*), there are six superior qualities not shared by the five consciousnesses.
There are six [occasions]: first, falling away; second, detachment from defilement; third, death; fourth, birth; fifth, severing the roots of goodness; and sixth, reconnecting the roots of goodness.
There are three types of falling away:
first, falling away from what has already been attained.
Second is retrogression from what has not yet been attained;
third is retrogression from enjoyment.
Retrogression from what has already been attained refers to the case where one who has previously attained various superior virtues regresses due to encountering certain conditions.
Regarding those who have not yet attained [the fruit] and then fall back, as it is said in a gāthā:
"I observe the world of devas: They fall away from the noble eye of wisdom Because they are addicted to name-and-form, And do not see the Four Noble Truths."
The meaning of this verse is as follows:
all sentient beings, if they apply themselves with diligent skillful means, should all obtain the noble eye of wisdom;
however, because they are addicted to and attached to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), they are unable to exert themselves in cultivating the correct skillful means.
One has not yet attained direct realization (abhisamaya) regarding the Four Noble Truths;
thus, there is a falling away from that which has not yet been attained with respect to the noble eye of wisdom (āryaprajñācakṣus).
As it is said in a verse:
"He who is honored by the multitude of fools—this is his ruin;
he falls from the summit and is severed from all roots of virtue.
This verse was spoken by the Buddha concerning Devadatta.
This means that once those who have already produced the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) roots of goodness will, before long, produce the "summit" (*mūrdhan*) roots of goodness;
however, because they become attached to superior fame and profit in the interim, they may suffer a retrogression from the summit roots of goodness before they have attained them.
From this point on, they successively sever their roots of goodness;
such cases as these are termed "retrogression from what has not yet been attained.
As for "retrogression from enjoyment":
This refers to the non-manifestation of various superior qualities already attained;
for example, as the Buddha does not manifest the qualities already attained by other Buddhas,
nor does a Pratyekabuddha manifest the qualities already attained by other Pratyekabuddhas.
For a śrāvaka, the qualities already attained as a śrāvaka do not manifest;
the same should apply to the others as well.
Question: Regarding these three types of decline, how many kinds are there for each—Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas?
Answer: The Buddha has one kind of retrogression, namely, retrogression from enjoyment (*parihāṇi-vihāra*), because although he has already attained all virtues, they may not be manifest.
He has no retrogression from what has not yet been attained (*aprāpta-parihāṇi*).
Because they abide in the most excellent faculties among all sentient beings;
because there is no regression from what has already been attained, as all Buddhas are of the nature of non-regression;
and because Pratyekabuddhas are of two kinds.
This refers to the regression of non-attainment and the regression of enjoyment.
Regression of non-attainment occurs because one has not yet attained the supreme faculties of all Buddhas.
Regression of enjoyment occurs because, although there are already attained qualities, they do not manifest before one.
Because all Pratyekabuddhas who have already attained [the fruit] are of the nature of non-retrogression;

within the Śrāvaka vehicle, there are two types of "not-timely-liberation" (asamayavimukti), namely, those subject to retrogression from what has not yet been attained and those subject to retrogression from enjoyment.
Those who have not yet attained [the state of non-retrogression] do so because they have not yet obtained the faculties of the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Those who experience retrogression from enjoyment do so because the qualities already attained do not manifest before them.
There is no retrogression from what has been attained for those who are liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*), as they are not of a nature subject to retrogression (*aparihāṇadharman*).
The one liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) possesses three types [of retrogression]:
because for one who has already attained [the fruit],
there is the possibility of falling away from the qualities already acquired.
"Those who have not yet attained and then regress" refers to those who have not yet attained the non-regressive faculties of the three vehicles.
"Those who regress from enjoyment" refers to...
Because there are those who have already attained meritorious qualities that do not manifest before them. Some say:
"The Buddha has no retrogression whatsoever."
There is no falling away from what has already been attained, because all Buddhas possess the quality of non-retrogression.
There is no falling away from what has not yet been attained, because they abide in the most supreme faculties among all sentient beings.
There is no falling away from enjoyment, for throughout the three incalculable eons of the past, the Buddha...
One practices and accumulates hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful austerities solely for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

Having attained Buddhahood, one observes the realm of sentient beings throughout the six periods of day and night; yet, if there were no one capable of being transformed, one would not provide them with benefit.
Therefore, the Buddhas have no decline in enjoyment;
although their merits may not manifest before them, this is not called a "decline" because it was not what they originally intended.
Pratyekabuddhas possess only one kind of decline: that of enjoyment.
This is because there are those who have already attained qualities that do not manifest before them;

and because there are no instances of falling away from what has not yet been attained, as those whose faculties and lineage are fixed in the Pratyekabuddha vehicle no longer seek the superior faculties of a Buddha.
There are no Pratyekabuddhas who have fallen away from what they have attained, because all Pratyekabuddhas are of the nature of non-retrogression (*aparihāṇadharman*).
Within the Śrāvaka vehicle, even those who are liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*) possess only the retrogression from enjoyment (*upabhoga-parihāṇi*),
because there are cases where attained qualities do not manifest.
There is no falling away from what has not yet been attained,
because those whose faculties and dispositions are already fixed in the Śrāvaka vehicle do not further seek the vehicles of the Buddha or the Pratyekabuddha.
There is no falling away from what has already been attained.
Because they are of the nature of non-retrogression and are not liberated at an improper time.
There are two types of those liberated at a proper time (*samayavimukta*):
first, those who have already fallen away from what they had attained; [second, those who have not].
Because there is the possibility of falling away from already attained qualities;
second, because there is falling away from enjoyment when already attained qualities do not manifest.
There is no falling away from what has not yet been attained, because for those who are liberated by time (*samayavimukta*), their faculties and disposition are already fixed.
Because they do not seek the superior faculties of the three vehicles.
The critique states:
between these two explanations, the first is the better one.
Since all Buddhas certainly possess the retrogression from enjoyment (*parihāṇi-vihāra*),
and since Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas feel admiration for superior faculties,

and since those liberated by occasion (*samaya-vimukta*) can be transformed into those liberated at any time (*asamaya-vimukta*), how can it be said that they do not experience retrogression from what has been attained?
Question: How is it known that the Buddha undergoes a decline in enjoyment?
Answer: Because it is stated in the sūtras. As the sūtra says:
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Regarding the four higher states of mind (catvāraḥ ṛddhipādāḥ) through which the Tathāgata dwells in happiness in this very life,
I say that there is a possibility of falling away from them one after another."
For example, when I am gathered together with my disciples,
if one has personally realized the liberation of mind through immovability and dwells therein fully,
I say that there is no falling away from it whatsoever.
From this, it is known that the Buddha undergoes a decline in enjoyment (*bhoga-parihāṇi*).
Question: Does this sūtra speak of a decline from what has already been attained (*prāpta-parihāṇi*), or does it speak of a decline in enjoyment?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
Both positions possess errors. Why is this?
If this sutra states that one who has already attained [the fruits] may fall away,
then one should not fall away from the four higher mental states (adhicitta) that dwell in happiness in the present life,
for all Buddhas are of the nature of non-retrogression.

If this sūtra states that there is a decline in enjoyment (*parihāṇi*), then the immovable liberation of mind (*akopya-cetovimukti*) should also be subject to decline, because it does not manifest at all times.
Answer: In this context, it is stated that the Buddha possesses a decline in enjoyment.
Question: This has already successfully resolved the objection previously raised.
How, then, should the subsequent objection be resolved?
Namely, that there should also be regression from the immovable liberation of mind (*akopya-cetovimukti*).
Because it does not manifest at all times.
Answer: The immovable liberation of mind (akopya-cetovimukti) is superior by way of its accomplishment, for once that state is attained, there is nothing further to be done.
Although it is not manifest, it is not said to be a regression.
Regarding the fourth, the dwelling in happiness in the present life through the higher mind (*adhicitta*), since manifestation is paramount,
its non-manifestation is indeed said to be a regression.
Some say that in this sutra,
the "unshakable liberation of mind" (āniñjya-cetovimukti) refers to the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi).
The fundamental dhyānas are described as the "higher mind" (adhicitta) and "abiding in happiness in the present life" (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra). However,
the Blessed One frequently brings the threshold concentration (anāgamya) into manifestation,
rather than the fundamental dhyānas.
That is to say: before eating, after eating, when about to preach the Dharma,
when the preaching of the Dharma has concluded, and when, having finished preaching the Dharma, he enters his quiet chamber—
although the Buddha is able to enter all meditative concentrations with great swiftness.
Furthermore, it is because he enters [the meditative attainments] most frequently that the Buddha repeatedly enters the *anāgamya* concentration;
just as a valiant warrior, though able to travel swiftly between all locations, does so most often to his nearest destination.
Furthermore, because they frequent nearby places repeatedly rather than distant ones, this statement was made.
Other masters say: [text continues].

In this sutra, it is stated that the activity of benefiting others is called the "unshakable liberation of mind," while the activity of benefiting oneself is called "dwelling in happiness in the present life through the higher mind."
The Blessed One frequently manifests activities for the benefit of others;
he did not speak these words because of his own self-interest. Some say this.

In this sutra, it is stated that loving-kindness and compassion are called the "unshakable liberation of mind," while joy and equanimity are called the "superior mind dwelling in happiness in the present life.
The Blessed One frequently brings these states of loving-kindness and compassion into manifestation.
This statement was made because [the Buddha] had recently arisen from a state of joy and equanimity. Furthermore,
there are those who say that in this sutra, "great compassion" is designated as the "unshakable liberation of the mind."

The teaching that "great equanimity (mahopekṣā) is the dwelling in happiness in the present life through the higher mind" was stated because the Blessed One frequently brings great compassion (mahākaruṇā) to presence and only rarely brings great equanimity.
The Venerable Ghosaka has stated this: in this sutra,
it is said that the permanent abandonment of all fetters, known as universal knowledge, is the immovable liberation of mind.
The possession of all types of conditioned qualities is called the "higher mind" (*adhicitta*) and the "abiding in happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Because the Buddha is eternally accomplished in all unconditioned qualities (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), he is said to be "non-retrogressive."
Because there are certain conditioned meritorious qualities that the Buddha does not manifest, it is said that he has "regression" (parihāṇi).
This is because conditioned meritorious qualities take their manifestation as their primary function.
The Venerable Buddhadeva speaks as follows:

In this sutra, that which is capable of being attained is called "unshakable liberation of mind," and that which is attained is called "abiding in happiness in the present life through the higher mind."
Because the Buddha does not have all the merits he has attained manifest before him, it is said that there is "retrogression" (parihāṇi);
because the acquisitions (prāpti) that enable these attainments are always present before him, it is said that there is no "retrogression."
Question: If even a Buddha can experience a decline in enjoyment (*parihāṇi*), among these declines in enjoyment, which is most frequent—is it that of a Buddha, a Pratyekabuddha, or a Śrāvaka?
Answer: Among these declines in enjoyment, that of a Buddha is the most frequent.
This is not because the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas have few merits;
rather, it is because in a single kṣaṇa, the Buddha’s merits do not manifest before him, nor does he experience a decline in their enjoyment.

In contrast, the two vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) frequently experience a decline in the enjoyment of their various merits throughout the entirety of their *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous life-span).
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s merits are immeasurable, innumerable, subtle, radiant, most excellent, and utterly pure;
surpassing the number of atoms in all worlds, each and every merit should manifest before one.
