Because there is no falling away from enjoyment while [the Buddha] is present before others, the Buddha is most frequently subject to falling away from enjoyment (*parihāṇi*).
This is like a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) who rules over the four continents;
even for a single day and night, if he relinquishes his own realm, he undergoes such falling away from enjoyment.
All other minor kings, at the end of their respective life-span (*nikāya-sabhāga*), abandon their own kingdoms and experience a decline regarding their enjoyments.
Thus far, we have briefly discussed whether those in the three vehicles who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) possess or lack these three kinds of decline.
The same should be stated accordingly for those in the stages of training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana),
as explained in the *Samādhiskandha*.
For what reason do the [other] three fruits involve falling away (*parihāṇi*), whereas the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) does not?
Furthermore, that text states that the afflictions abandoned through seeing arise with respect to non-existent objects; therefore, once abandoned, they do not recur.
How, then, can it be said that they arise with respect to non-existent objects?
This means that because it does not function with respect to any locus, how is it that it does not function with respect to any locus?
It means that it functions with respect to a self; since, in the ultimate sense, a self is absolutely non-existent, once those afflictions have been severed, there is no falling back.
Since the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation arise with respect to existing entities (*savastuka*), there is falling away once they have been abandoned.
How is it said that they arise with respect to existing entities?
It is because they function with respect to a location (*sthāna*).
What is meant by "operating with respect to a limited portion"?
It refers to operating with respect to a limited portion of pure signs (*śubhanimitta*).
What is called a "limited portion of pure signs"?
This refers to the presence of some subtle signs of purity within the shape and color of the hair, nails, lips, teeth, face, eyes, hands, feet, fingers, and so forth;
yet, within these, there are also various signs of impurity, which one contemplates through appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
First, one contemplates those pure signs while free from afflictions.
One falls away due to the arising of afflictions through improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
There is not the slightest dharma characterized by "I" or "mine" that could cause one to fall away from the contemplation of non-self.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"All phenomena are without self, without a sentient being, without a life-principle, without a nourisher, and without a person (pudgala).
Within this body, there is no agent, no creator, no one who dispatches the creator, no experiencer, and no one who dispatches the experiencer; it is empty."
This is a collection of practices consisting of pure emptiness.
Therefore, once all fetters to be abandoned through vision have been severed by noble wisdom, they never regress.
Consequently, there is no regression from the fruit of stream-entry.
Furthermore, the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phala) is established by the permanent abandonment of the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya) within the three realms,
because there is no retrogression from that permanent abandonment of the fetters to be abandoned through seeing in the three realms.

Furthermore, the fruit of stream-entry is established by the permanent abandonment of the fetters to be abandoned through seeing at the level of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).

Because there is no falling away from the permanent abandonment of the fetters to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya-saṃyojana*) pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Question: How is it that there is no falling away from that permanent abandonment?
Answer: Because those fetters to be abandoned by insight pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
It is difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend;
therefore, once severed, it cannot be reconnected.
Furthermore, by means of patience (*kṣānti*) as the antidote to the afflictions that lack a real objective basis (*avastuka-kleśa*), the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) is established.
Because one who has attained patience (*kṣānti*) necessarily does not give rise to the fetters of the "baseless" (*anavasthāna*), they do not regress.

Furthermore, by the power of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*); since there is no regression for those who have attained the path of seeing, [the stream-enterer] is likewise certain not to regress.
Question: From this discussion, another question arises:
for what reason is it certain that there is no falling back from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)?
Answer: Because the path of seeing is an extremely swift path, a path upon which no volition for future duration arises.
Because there is no possibility of falling away from such a path.
Furthermore, once the various practitioners of yoga have entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
they are said to have "entered the river of Dharma," "entered the great stream of Dharma," "entered the waves of Dharma," and "entered the whirlpools of Dharma."
They do not even have the leisure to give rise to a wholesome mind associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) or an unobscured-neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*),
much less the capacity to give rise to a defiled mind and fall away.
It is like a person who has fallen into a mountain valley and is being swept away and drowned by the waves of a torrential flood.
One cannot even maintain one's position on either bank, let alone emerge from it.
Furthermore, the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is able to counteract all fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms that are to be abandoned by seeing;
for there is no regression from the path that serves as the antidote to those fetters of the three realms to be abandoned by seeing.
Furthermore, the path of seeing is able to counteract all fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception that are to be abandoned by insight;
this is because there is no path of insight that abandons those fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception from which one could fall away.
Furthermore, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is able to counteract the object-to-be-counteracted (*pratipakṣya*) afflictions regarding non-entities (*avastuka*),
because there is no retrogression from that path of counteraction.
Furthermore, the path of seeing first perceives the principles of the Four Noble Truths with decisive clarity.
Because there is no one who would again fall into delusion regarding this principle, they will certainly not regress.

Question: Just as there is regression from the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) while remaining in the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), why is it that there is no regression from the stage of cultivation while remaining in the path of seeing (darśanamārga)?
Answer: It is observed that within the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), there is the principle of the manifestation of active afflictions (kleśa);
however, within the stage of the path of seeing (darśanamārga), there is no such principle of the manifestation of active afflictions.
Therefore, these two cases cannot be used as analogies for one another.

Furthermore, because there may be those who regress during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one remains in the path of cultivation until reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

Because there are no instances of regression during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one does not remain in the path of seeing once the stage of the path of cultivation has been reached.
Question: When one falls away from the fruit of arhatship and abides in the fruit of stream-entry, is this called falling away from the fruits of non-returner or once-returner?
Answer: It is also called falling away from those.
Why is this? Because they abide in those lower states, it is like a person falling from the third story of a house to the ground;
that person might also be said to have fallen from the first or second stories, and this case is likewise.
Question: Since he originally did not possess the two intermediate fruits, why is it now said that he has regressed?
Answer: Because he does not possess them again after having already failed to possess them, this is also called "regression.

Question: How can it be said that he does not possess them again after having already failed to possess them? Answer: Because he was already distant from them previously, and is now even more distant.
Furthermore, because he had previously severed and exhausted those specific afflictions, the two fruits were established;
now, because he regresses and gives rise to those same afflictions again, it is said that he has fallen away.
Furthermore, because he had previously attained the abandonment of the objects to be countered by the two fruits, and now regresses from that attainment, it is said that he has fallen away.
Furthermore, regarding those who first employ such paths of uninterrupted transition and liberation to sever all afflictions and attain two fruits,
they now regress and give rise to the very afflictions they had severed, causing those two paths to become increasingly distant; therefore, their regression is spoken of.
Furthermore, because the fruits of Non-returner and Once-returner are causes for the fruit of Arhatship, when one falls away from that fruit, the cause is also said to have fallen away.
Question: Is the fruit of Stream-enterer not also a cause for the fruit of Arhatship?
If an Arhat were subject to falling away, then a Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) should also fall away.
The answer is: this fruit of stream-entry is the lowest stage of the noble ones;
when one falls away from a higher fruit, one remains at most within this [lower] fruit.
If one were to fall away from the fruit of stream-entry,
it would mean that a fruit previously attained is now no longer obtained;
for within the stage of the path of seeing (darśanamārga), there is no possibility of abiding [in a fruit].
That which should have originally seen the truths now no longer sees them;
that which should have originally been clear realization (abhisamaya) is now not clear realization;
that which should have originally been an noble one (ārya) has now become an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
In order to ensure that such faults do not exist, there is no possibility of falling away from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).

Furthermore, since the fruit of stream-entry is realized through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and it has already been stated that there is necessarily no falling away from the path of seeing, [there is no retrogression].
Therefore, there is no falling back from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
This statement refers to falling back from the stage (*avasthā*), not to falling back from the faculty-nature (*indriya-gotra*).
Since there are those who fall back even when transforming their faculties while in the fruit of stream-entry, one may thus fall back from the fundamental fruit of śramaṇaship.
If one has not yet regained [the state], there is no possibility of death.
Even if one has regressed toward that state, although one has not yet regained it, death is still possible. Why is this so?
The fundamental fruit-states are easy to perceive and easy to designate;
that is to say, "this is the fruit of stream-entry" up to "this is the fruit of arhatship.
Therefore, once one has fallen away from them, if they have not yet been regained, one will certainly not die.
The stage of the candidate (mukha-avasthā) is difficult to perceive and difficult to designate;
therefore, even after falling away from it, there is the possibility of death before one has yet regained it.
Furthermore, yogins at the level of the fundamental fruit (phala-avasthā) give rise to a sense of superior joy regarding that fruit.
It is just as a farmer who, after tending his crops during the six months of cultivation, gathers the grain and stores it in the threshing floor, experiencing great joy and celebration;
this case is also like that.
Therefore, when one falls away from the fruit, great distress arises;
if the fruit has not yet been regained, one will certainly not relinquish life.
In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), this is not the case; thus, although one has not yet regained [the fruit] upon falling away from it, there is the possibility of passing away.
Furthermore, the fundamental stage of fruition possesses three causes and conditions:
first, the relinquishing of previously attained paths;
second, the attainment of paths never before attained.
Because the three proofs of the severance of fetters are attained as a single taste, when one falls back from a fruit, if it has not yet been regained, one will certainly not pass away.
In the case of the candidate for a fruit, this is not so; therefore, although one has fallen back from that stage and has not yet regained it, it is possible that one may pass away.
Furthermore, the fundamental stage of fruition possesses five causal conditions:
first, relinquishing the path previously attained;
second, attaining the path never before attained.
Third, the realization of the severance of fetters through the attainment of the single flavor;
fourth, the simultaneous acquisition of the eight knowledges;
fifth, the simultaneous cultivation of the sixteen aspects.
Therefore, when one falls away from a fruit, if one has not yet regained it, there is no principle for death to occur;
in the case mentioned above, this is not so, and thus when falling away from that [fruit], although one has not yet regained it, there is the possibility of death.
Furthermore, the fundamental state of fruition (*mūla-phala-avasthā*) is the most supreme place of peace and rest for the yogācāra;
therefore, when one falls from that fruition, if it has not yet been regained, there is no possibility of death.
Since it was not so previously, one regresses; at that time, although one has not yet returned [to the fruit], there is the possibility of death.
Furthermore, the abandonment of the fetters belonging to the fundamental stage of fruition is both what is to be done and the completion of what was to be done.
All noble paths consist of effort and the culmination of effort;
therefore, when one falls away from a fruit, there is no principle by which they would not regain it before death.
In the state of "entering" (pratipannaka), the fetters are severed; this is the culmination of what was to be done, as opposed to what has not yet been done.
All noble paths are ultimate, whether they involve effort or are effortless;
therefore, even when one is regressing toward [a lower state], there is the possibility of death before one has regained them.

Furthermore, because practitioners at the level of the fundamental fruit are permitted to extensively cultivate the noble path, there is no logical possibility of death while one is regressing from that fruit before it has been regained.
Because one cannot extensively cultivate the noble path while facing toward [the lower realms], there is the possibility of death even after having already regressed.
Furthermore, yogins at the stage of the fundamental fruit are able to thoroughly discern virtues and faults.
Merit refers to the Path and its fruit;
fault refers to the causes and effects of birth and death.
Therefore, when one falls back from the fruit, there is no principle by which one would not die before regaining it.
Since it is not so in the intermediate state, one may undergo death even at that time before returning [to the womb].
Furthermore, it is only yogins at the stage of the fundamental fruit who are able to correctly apprehend the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths.
In the former case, it is not so, because the task has not yet been accomplished;
just as when one walks about on all four sides of a person, one cannot yet grasp their features well, but only when sitting in one place can one grasp them well.
Since the same applies to the fruits and the paths leading toward them, when one falls from a fruit, there is no principle that death would occur before it is regained.
However, when one falls from a path leading toward a fruit, although it has not yet been regained, there is the possibility of death occurring.
Furthermore, when there is one who possesses realization at the time of falling back from the fundamental fruit-stage, that person will certainly not die until they have regained it.
When there is no such realization at the time of falling back from the stage of approach, there is the possibility of death before one has regained it.
If one is robbed within a village or town where there are witnesses, the stolen goods can be swiftly recovered;
however, if one is robbed between two villages or towns where there are no witnesses, it is difficult to recover them.
Furthermore, when yogins at the fundamental stage of fruition have previously established themselves firmly through extensive preparatory application,
they will not die as long as they have not regained [their state] even if they regress from it.
Because it is not so in the intermediate state, there is the possibility of death at that time if one has not yet returned [to the lower realm].
As for those who have previously practiced extensively for the sake of the fruit of stream-entry,
this is because they first sought the fruit of liberation.
Diligently practicing the purification of generosity and ethical discipline,
abiding in mindfulness through the contemplation of impurity, the retention of the breath,
and the wisdom derived from hearing.
The wisdom derived from reflection,
the wisdom derived from cultivation,
as well as the stages of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas.
Furthermore, during the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
this is collectively termed "firmly established stability.
Some say as follows:
From the beginning up to the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is called the extensive preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The fifteen moments of mind in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are called the firm establishment.
For one who has previously engaged in the extensive preparatory application, [the attainment of] the fruit of the Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*)...

This refers to what was previously described, as well as the various paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the six paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the five paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for those free from the defilements of desire; these are termed "firmly established.
Some say: [the rest of the path].
The fruit of stream-entry is called "firmly established.
Regarding the fruit of non-returning, its prior extensive preparatory practices consist of the aforementioned paths,
as well as the various preparatory paths, three uninterrupted paths, and two paths of liberation for those who have abandoned the defilements of desire.
This very state is called "firmly established.
Some say that the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala) is what is meant by "firmly established."
Regarding the fruit of arhatship for one who has previously engaged extensively in preparatory practice:
this refers to what was explained above, as well as the abandonment of the defilements of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness.
For each respective stage, there are the various paths of preparation, nine paths of uninterrupted transition, and nine paths of liberation.
Together with the preparatory paths, the nine uninterrupted paths, and the eight paths of liberation for becoming detached from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
these are collectively termed "firmly established."
Some say that the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) is called "firmly established and stable.
Furthermore, regarding the fundamental stage of fruition, there are various yoga practitioners.
Because all factors of rebirth have been severed and stilled, there is no possibility of death during the period when one has fallen from a fruit, provided that fruit has not yet been regained.
This is not the case for those who are still training (śaikṣa); therefore, while falling from their state, there is the logical possibility of death even before the fruit has been regained.
This refers to the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala), wherein,
with the exception of seven births in the desire realm and one birth in each of the various locations of the form and formless realms,
all other births attain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).

The fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala) attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) regarding all other births, excluding two births in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and one birth in each location within the form and formless realms (rūpadhātu and ārūpyadhātu).
For the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), with the exception of one birth in each of the various locations within the form and formless realms,
all other births attain cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
This is because for the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), there is no further arising in any birth whatsoever, as it has attained cessation not through deliberation.

Furthermore, because the yogins at the fundamental stage of fruition have collectively attained the abandonment of all afflictions to be eliminated through the paths of seeing and meditation within the three realms,
they will never die before they have regained [their state] should they fall away from that fruition.
Since it is not so in the intermediate state, one may pass away at that time even before returning [to the desire realm].
This refers to the stage of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna), who has collectively attained the abandonment of all afflictions to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) belonging to the three realms.

The stage of the Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) consists of the abandonment of all defilements to be abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya) across the three realms, as well as the abandonment of the six grades of defilements to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the desire realm; the stage of the Non-returner (anāgāmin) consists of the abandonment of all defilements to be abandoned through seeing across the three realms.
Furthermore, there is the acquisition of the abandonment of the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm;
and at the stage of the fruit of arhatship, there is the collective acquisition of the abandonment of all afflictions to be abandoned through both seeing and cultivation across the three realms.
Furthermore, the fundamental fruit-stage (*mūla-phala-avasthā*) is the very state sought by the yogācāra;
therefore, once one has fallen from that fruit, if it has not yet been regained, one will certainly not die.
This is not the case for the stage of approach (*pratipannaka-avasthā*); thus, when falling from that stage, there is the possibility of death before it is regained.
If one is free from the defilements of the desire realm, or free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
or even up to being free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness,
one may thereafter enter into rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).

If one later regresses, it is certain that regression occurs only through the arising of the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of a lower stage, and not through the arising of the fetters of a higher stage. Why is this?

Because the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower stages have been destroyed by both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths of counteraction; thus, they lack the power to arise and cause such a regression.

Furthermore, after those fetters (*paryavasthāna*) have been severed, the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) arises and suppresses them from above; therefore, one cannot give rise to the fetters of the lower stages and fall away.
It is, for example, like a person falling from a mountain who, after having fallen, is further crushed by a collapsing mountain falling upon him.
Since they cannot even cause [the afflictions] to move, how much less can they give rise to their active manifestation?
Furthermore, because after severing those envelopments (paryavasthāna), there arises the patience and knowledge (kṣānti-jñāna) that is non-retrogressive,
one cannot give rise to the envelopments of a lower stage through retrogression.
Furthermore, after abandoning those fetters, one gives rise to the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge of categories (anvayajñāna);
since there is no complete regression from these knowledges, one cannot regress by giving rise to the fetters of the lower stages.

Furthermore, after abandoning those fetters, one gives rise to superior patience (adhimātra-kṣānti) and the supreme mundane dharmas (laukikāgra-dharma); since there is no regression from superior patience or the supreme mundane dharmas, [one does not regress].
Therefore, they cannot fall back by giving rise to the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the lower stages.
Furthermore, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the detachment from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation in each stage are collectively grouped into a single bundle and abandoned in nine grades.
Afterward, having entered the path of seeing and attained the fruit of a noble one,
even if one should fall away by giving rise to afflictions of a lower stage,
does one only obtain those fetters abandoned through cultivation?
If one also attains those fetters abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*),
or if one attains only those fetters abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
how can both types of fetters be abandoned by the same path?
When one falls away from that path, one obtains only one [defilement].
If one were also to obtain those fetters abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),
how could one obtain the fruit of an ārya while possessing fetters abandoned by insight?

Therefore, once an ordinary person has become free from the defilements of any particular stage or category and subsequently enters the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) to attain the fruit of an noble one,
there is absolutely no possibility of regressing by giving rise again to those afflictions previously abandoned.

Question: When one is about to attain the fruit of arhatship and abides in the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi), one still possesses the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
If one then falls away from the fruit of arhatship and again gives rise to the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, [what occurs]?
"Can they also achieve the diamond-like samādhi?
He replied, "They cannot achieve the diamond-like samādhi. Why is this?"
The diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) is attained through cultivation by means of the application of great effort and preparatory attention;
however, those lower-lower grade fetters (saṃyojana) are not attained through cultivation by means of the application of effort and preparatory attention.
Therefore, at the time of retrogression, one attains only those fetters and not this concentration.
Furthermore, it is attained at the time of superior progress toward the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi),
whereas it is attained at the time of falling away from the lowest-of-the-low grade of those fetters.
Therefore, at the time of falling back, one only loses those fetters and does not lose this meditative concentration.
Furthermore, when the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) manifests,
it opposes the actual manifestation of those fetters, but it does not oppose their possession.
Therefore, when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is present,
one still possesses those fetters; likewise,
when the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is present.
To contradict the manifestation of the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) is also to contradict its attainment;
therefore, when one regresses and gives rise to the fetters belonging to that category, one necessarily does not attain the diamond-like concentration.
Furthermore, the diamond-like concentration is the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga).
There are those who fall back from the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) without abiding;
there are also those who do not fall back and abide in the uninterrupted path;
and there are those who fall back while abiding in the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
There are also those who, having already fallen back, abide in the path of liberation.
Some say that there are also those who fall back while abiding in the path of superior progress.
Furthermore, there are those who, having already regressed, abide in the path of superior progress;
therefore, at the time of abiding in the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), they accomplish the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
When they regress and give rise to the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters of the Peak of Existence, [they do so].
One will certainly not again attain the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 60; *Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 61.
Composed by the Five Hundred Great Arhats and others;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Two: The Aggregate of Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha), Sub-section Two: The Chapter on Single Practices (Ekottara-nikāya), Part Seven. Question: In what places does falling away (parihāṇi) occur?
Answer: There is falling back (*parihāṇi*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), but not in the other realms;
there is falling back among the human destiny (*manuṣyagati*), but not in the other destinies.
Question: Why is there no falling back among the gods of the desire realm?
Answer: Because they lack the conditions for falling away (*parihāṇi*).
Question: Is it not the case that those gods possess the five types of exquisite sensual pleasures (*pañca kāmaguṇa*) superior to those of the human realm?
Why, then, do you say they lack them? Answer: Because the sūtras state that the five conditions for falling away do not exist among the gods, it is said that they lack them.

Furthermore, among the six heavens of the desire realm, those who first enter the noble path and attain the fruits of sainthood are all of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), and because all those of sharp faculties do not fall back.
Question: Among those of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*), once they have entered the noble path and are subsequently reborn in the heavens, is there any falling back?
The answer is that they also do not fall back. Why is this?
Because noble ones who have taken rebirth are certain not to fall back.
Nor does one undergo a transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), nor can one be reborn in the form or formless realms;
for the Noble Path, having resided within that continuum for a long time, has become exceedingly firm and stable.
Question: Why do they not fall back from within the three evil destinies?
Answer: Because there is no principle for them to become free from defilement and enter the Noble Path;
since they lack such superior qualities, they do not fall back.
Regarding where it is said that there is falling away:
if one asks why there is no falling away in the form and formless realms despite their possessing superior qualities,
the answer is that they lack the conditions for falling away, as their meritorious qualities are firm and stable.
Therefore, one does not regress. As for the question of what kind of person may regress and what kind of person cannot regress:
the answer is that there are those who enter the Noble Path by relying on others and following their inclinations.
There are those who, relying on their own confidence and entering the Noble Path according to their own inclinations:
the former may fall back,
while the latter cannot fall back.
Furthermore, there are those who enter the noble path without deliberating or examining gain and loss,
and there are those who enter the noble path through extreme deliberation and examination of gain and loss.
The former type of person is subject to regression.
Those who come later must not regress.
Furthermore, there are some whose power of causes, power of application, and power of heedfulness are all not extensive;
there are others for whom all three powers are entirely extensive.
The former person may fall back, while the latter person cannot fall back.
Furthermore, there are those who enter the noble path preceded by faith,
and there are those who enter the noble path preceded by wisdom.
The former person may fall back,
while the latter person cannot fall back.
Furthermore, there is one who enters the Noble Path preceded by śamatha.
There are those who enter the noble path preceded by vipaśyanā;
the former may fall away,
while the latter cannot fall away.
Furthermore, there is one who practices the cultivation of tranquility (śamatha) and one who practices the cultivation of insight (vipaśyanā).
The former may fall back.
Later practitioners must not regress.
Furthermore, there are many who take delight in and aspire to śamatha,
and many who take delight in and aspire to vipaśyanā.
The former person may regress;
the latter person cannot regress.
Furthermore, there is the predominance of tranquility.
There is a superior state of contemplation;
the former person may regress,
while the latter person cannot regress.
Furthermore, there are those whose minds are permeated by tranquility (*śamatha*) and who attain liberation by relying on insight (*vipaśyanā*);
and there are those whose minds are permeated by insight and who attain liberation by relying on tranquility.
The former may fall back, while the latter cannot fall back.

Furthermore, there are those who attain internal mental tranquility (śamatha) but do not attain the higher wisdom of the contemplation of phenomena (vipaśyanā), and those who attain the higher wisdom of the contemplation of phenomena but do not attain internal mental tranquility.
Of these, the former person may fall away.
Later generations must not regress.
Furthermore, there are those who delight in practicing meditative concentration but do not delight in extensive learning;
and there are those who delight in extensive learning but do not delight in practicing meditative concentration.
The former person may fall back,
while the latter cannot fall back.
Furthermore, there is one who delights in self-benefit but does not delight in benefiting others.
There are those who delight in benefiting others rather than benefiting themselves;
the former type may regress,
while the latter cannot regress.
Furthermore, there is the lineage of those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and the lineage of those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).
The former may fall away.
Those who come later must not regress.
Furthermore, there are those of dull faculties and those of sharp faculties.
The former person may regress;
the latter person cannot regress.
Furthermore, there is the power of conditions for entering the Path.
There are those who enter the Path by the power of causes;
the former may fall back,
while the latter cannot fall back.
Furthermore, there are those who enter the Path through the power of external friends and those who enter the Path through the power of internal friends;
the former may fall back.
Later generations must not regress.
Furthermore, there are those who enter the Path through the power of hearing the Dharma from others,
and there are those who enter the Path through the power of internal right reflection.
The former person is subject to regression, while the latter person is not subject to regression.
Furthermore, there is that which is dominated by non-attachment,
and there is that which is dominated by non-delusion.
The former person may fall back,
while the latter person cannot fall back.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra:
There are four qualities by which a person can accomplish much:
first, associating with virtuous persons;
second, hearing the true Dharma.
Third, appropriate mental attention;
fourth, practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Of these four, those who rely primarily on the first two factors may regress.
Regarding the latter two factors, when they are predominant, one cannot fall away.
Furthermore, there is a case where the mind is well-liberated but wisdom is not well-liberated;
and there is a case where wisdom is well-liberated but the mind is not well-liberated.
The former person may fall back,
while the latter person cannot fall back.
Some have made this statement.
There is one whose mind is well-liberated but whose wisdom is not well-liberated;
there is another whose wisdom is well-liberated but whose mind is not well-liberated.
These two types of persons are subject to regression.
There is one who is well-liberated in mind and well-liberated through wisdom;
such a person cannot fall away.
Question: How long do those who have already fallen away remain in that state?

Answer: He dwells for a short time in the meditative attainment until he is no longer aware of those discursive thoughts; once he has become aware of them, he swiftly cultivates superior progress. Furthermore, when afflictions arise and manifest such that he regresses, he feels deep shame and remorse, and immediately brings them to an end.
It is like a person with clear vision who suddenly stumbles on level ground during the day;
they quickly rise and look around, wondering, "Is there no one else who has seen me?
In this way, when a practitioner gives rise to afflictions, they feel deep shame and remorse.
One should think, "May no Buddha, nor a disciple of the Buddha, nor any other virtuous person know me.
Therefore, one should quickly cause [the affliction] to cease and return to its original state.
Furthermore, when those afflictions arise and manifest, they burn the body and mind; therefore, one should quickly cause them to be extinguished.
Just as when sparks fly from a soft substance and strike the body, one cannot endure them and they are immediately extinguished;
furthermore, when those afflictions arise and manifest and then recede, because one loathes their foul stench, they are quickly severed and eliminated.
Just as when a person who cherishes cleanliness has a small amount of excrement fall upon their body, they immediately wash it away;
furthermore, when those afflictions arise and manifest such that one regresses, because the body and mind are heavy, one quickly abandons them.
Just as a weak person who suddenly receives a heavy burden beyond his strength will immediately cast it aside;
some say that falling back is not certain.

Because they lack mastery, they give rise to various afflictions; yet, either they can swiftly sever them and return to their original state, or it takes a long time before they attain the original fruit.

This means that by means of the power of the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*) within the desire realm, they bring forth the noble path of the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) so that it manifests before them.
Having transformed their faith and resolve into the faculty of "attainment through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
they subsequently proceed toward the fruit of arhatship; therefore, once they have regressed,
the duration of that regression is not fixed, being either slow or swift.
Question: If one falls back from the fruit of a non-returner or an arhat, does one again perform those actions that ought not to be performed?
Answer: One is no longer able to do so.
Why is this? Because the activities of one who has fallen back from a higher fruit differ from the activities of a noble one who has not yet attained that fruit.
There are six types of arhats.
1. The one of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharman); 2. the one of the nature of reflecting (cetayitṛdharman);
3. the one of the nature of guarding (anurakṣaṇādharman).
4. Those who abide in the dharma;
5. those capable of penetration;
6. those of immovable nature.

Among these, one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) is one who is liable to fall away; one of the nature of reflection (*cetana-dharman*) is one who, having reflected, takes up a blade and commits suicide;
one of the nature of guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*) is one who earnestly guards liberation.
One who abides in the dharma is one who neither regresses nor advances.
One capable of reaching [the goal] is one capable of attaining the immovable state.
One of immovable nature is one who has originally attained the immovable lineage.
Or, one may attain the "unshakable" state through the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
Question: Does an Arhat of the "subject to regression" (*parihāṇadharman*) necessarily regress?
And so on, up to: does an Arhat of the "capable of reaching" (*prativedhanādharman*) necessarily refine the faculties to reach the unshakable state?
Some say this: among Arhats, one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman) will necessarily fall away;
one of the "nature of reflecting" (cetana-dharman) will necessarily reflect [upon death] and take his own life with a blade.
One who possesses the dharma of protection will certainly be able to guard liberation;
one who dwells securely in the dharma will certainly neither fall back nor advance further;
and one who possesses the dharma of capability for penetration will certainly be able to refine the faculties until they reach the immovable stage.
For this reason, they are called those of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*),
up to and including those of the nature of being capable of reaching [the highest state] (*prativedhanādharman*).
If one were to say that the six types of arhat are established based on six modes of activity,
it would be asserted that all six types exist within the desire realm.
In the form and formless realms, there are only two types:
namely, those who abide in peace and those of immovable dharma. Thus it is said.
An Arhat of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman) does not necessarily fall away;

likewise, up to an Arhat of the "nature of being capable of reaching" (prativedhanādharman) does not necessarily refine their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to reach the "immovable nature" (akopyadharman).
Question: If this is so, for what reason is he called one of the "nature of falling away"?
Up to the point of asking: "Is one who is called 'capable of attaining' (kandha-dhamma) necessarily one who can transform their faculties?

The answer is: Among Arhats, those of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇa-dharma) do not necessarily fall away; even if they do, it is from this specific lineage and not from another. Up to the point of one "capable of attaining," they do not necessarily need to train their faculties to reach the "immovable nature" (akopya-dharma).
If one is able to refine the faculties until they reach the immovable stage,
it is certain that this occurs from this very lineage and no other.
If one were to speak thus:
The names of the six types of arhats are established based on six types of spiritual lineages (*gotra*).
This teaching holds that all three realms possess these six types,
because the sixfold lineage is pervasive throughout the three realms.
Question: How are these six types of arhats established?
Answer: They are established based on their faculties (indriya).
Question: There are nine grades of faculties.
That is to say: the lowest-of-the-low, the intermediate-of-the-low, and the highest-of-the-low;
the lowest-of-the-middling, the intermediate-of-the-middling, and the highest-of-the-middling;
and the lowest-of-the-high, the intermediate-of-the-high, and the highest-of-the-high.
Why are six types established based on the faculties (*indriya*), rather than nine?
Some explain it thus:
among these six types, those of the "regressive nature" (*parihāṇadharman*) possess two grades of faculties.
That is to say, the lowest-of-the-low and the middle-of-the-low [faculties] constitute the accomplishment of one type of faculty,
namely, the lowest-of-the-high.
One who protects the Dharma accomplishes one faculty,
namely, the medium or inferior.
One who dwells securely in the Dharma accomplishes one faculty.
That is to say, the middling-of-the-middling;
one who is capable of reaching [the goal] accomplishes one type of faculty,
namely, the middling-of-the-superior.
An Arhat of immovable dharma accomplishes one type of faculty,
namely both the higher and the lower.
A Pratyekabuddha accomplishes one type of faculty.
That is to say, the superior and the intermediate.
The Buddha has perfected one type of faculty,
namely, the supreme-superior (adhimātra-adhimātra).
The critique states:
He should not make such a statement,
because there is no one who accomplishes both types of faculties simultaneously.
Even among those of sharp faculties, there are none who possess both types of faculties;
how much less could those of dull faculties possess both?
One should state it thus.
Among the arhats, those of the nature of falling back (parihāṇadharman) possess the lowest-of-the-low grade of faculties;
those of the nature of reflecting (cetana-dharman) possess the low-middle grade of faculties;
and those of the nature of guarding (anurakṣaṇā-dharman) possess the low-high grade of faculties.
One who abides in the dharma of accomplishment possesses faculties of middling-inferior grade;
one who is capable of reaching [the goal] through the dharma possesses faculties of middling-middling grade;
and from the stage of liberation through time, by refining the faculties, one reaches the dharma of immovability.
Those who have accomplished the superior-middle grade of the fundamental lineage possess immovable dharmas with superior-inferior grades of faculties;
Pratyekabuddhas possess superior-middle grades of faculties.
The Tathāgata has accomplished the highest grade of faculties (*indriya*).
Some say that among the six types of arhats, [he is the foremost].
The one of the nature of falling back (parihāṇadharman) performs one function,
namely, falling back.
The one of the nature of reflection (cetana-dharman) performs two functions.
That is to say: falling away and reflection;
the one who protects the Dharma performs three tasks:
namely, falling away, reflection, and protection.
One who abides in the state of "abiding in the dharma" performs four tasks:
namely, falling back, reflecting, guarding, and abiding.
One who abides in the state of "capable of penetration" performs five tasks.
That is to say: falling away, guarding through reflection, abiding securely, and refining the faculties until reaching the immovable state.
According to this explanation, one of the "dharma subject to falling away" performs three functions.
First, one remains in the stage of training with the faculties of a learner;
second, one refines the faculties up to the level of reflection;
third, one attains parinirvāṇa while remaining in that very state.
The practitioner who contemplates the Dharma performs four tasks:
first, they may regress and abide in the faculties of a learner;
second, they may regress and abide in the faculties of one subject to regression.
Third, they refine their faculties up to the stage of protection (*anurakṣaṇā*).
Fourth, they enter parinirvāṇa while remaining in that very state.
One who protects the Dharma performs five tasks.
1. Those who abide in the faculty of training (śaikṣa-indriya) while subject to falling back;
2. those who abide in the faculty of the nature of falling back (parihāṇadharmin);
3. those who abide in the faculty of the nature of reflecting (cetayitṛdharmin).
Fourth, refining the faculties until one reaches abiding;
fifth, attaining parinirvāṇa while remaining in that state.
Abiding in the Dharma performs six tasks.
First, those who abide in the faculty of training while subject to falling back;
second, those who abide in the faculty of the nature of falling back;
third, those who abide in the faculty of the nature of reflecting.
Fourth, falling back and abiding in the faculties for protecting the Dharma;
fifth, refining the faculties until reaching the stage of "capable of penetration";
sixth, attaining parinirvāṇa while remaining in that very state.
There are seven matters concerning those capable of attaining the state of *dharmakṣānti*:
first, they may regress and abide in the faculties of one in training (*śaikṣa*);
second, they may regress and abide in the faculties of the "dharma-of-regression" (*parihāṇadharman*).
Third, those who fall back and abide in the faculty of one who contemplates the Dharma;
fourth, those who fall back and abide in the faculty of one who protects the Dharma;
fifth, those who fall back and abide in the faculty of one who is firmly established in the Dharma.
Sixth, refining the faculties until reaching the state of an immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*).
Seventh, attaining parinirvāṇa while remaining in that very state.
Question: When an Arhat of the "thought-dharma" (*cetana-dharman*) type regresses and dwells in the faculties of a trainee (*śaikṣa*), what trainee faculties does he obtain?
Is it for the sake of attaining the faculties of a learner of the *parihāṇadharman* lineage?
Or is it for the sake of attaining the faculties of a learner of the *cetayitadharman* lineage?
Answer: It is for the sake of attaining the faculties of a learner of the *parihāṇadharman* lineage.
It is not the faculty of one of the "thought-dharma" lineage (cetanā-dharman-gotra). Why is this?
Because such a person, while previously in the stage of training (śaikṣa), had not yet attained the faculty of one of the thought-dharma lineage.
If one were now to fall back and obtain the faculty of a learner who contemplates the dharma,
this would be an advancement rather than a regression, which is contrary to correct principle.
As it is stated in the Sūtra:
There was an arhat named Godhika.
At that time, having six times fallen away from the fruit of arhatship due to his liberation through affection (*sneha-vimukti*),
he regained the fruit of arhatship for the seventh time.
Fearing that he might again fall away from his attainment and thus harm himself with a blade, one asks:
Is this person of the nature to fall away (*parihāṇadharman*), or is he of the nature to reflect (*cetayitadharman*)?
If it were so, what would be the fault?
Both positions entail faults.
Why is this? If he were of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), for what reason would he take his own life?
If one is a "thought-dweller" (cetanādharman), why would they fall away?
One should answer: such a person is actually a "one liable to fall away" (parihāṇadharman).
Question: If that is so, why does he harm himself with a blade?
Answer: He harms himself with a blade because he is weary and regressed.
If one harms oneself before having regressed, such a person is a *cetana-dharmin* (one who intends).
There are those who say:
having refined their faculties from the stage of "one liable to fall away" (parihāṇadharman) up to the stage of "contemplation" (cintāmayī),
they still fear falling back, and thus take their own lives with a blade.
Therefore, this does not contradict reason.
If one’s innate nature (*prakṛti*) is such that one has reached the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), there is certainly no possibility of falling back to the state of a learner (*śaikṣa*).
All those who employ this path to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm [do so with such a nature].
When one falls back from this path, does one again become bound by those fetters?
Answer: One again becomes bound by those fetters.
This applies to all who use this path to abandon the fetters of the form and formless realms.
When one retreats from this path, does one again become bound by those fetters?
Answer: One again becomes bound by those fetters.
Regarding this, some say:
The function of binding is called "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).
This means that when one was previously free from defilement, the function of those fetters was severed;
yet at the time of falling away [from that state], one regains the function of those fetters.
Some say that the fetters (saṃyojana) are called "bonds" (bandhana),
meaning that at the time one becomes free from defilement, one abandons all the fetters and attains [the state of being bound].
Now, at the time of withdrawing from the Path, one regains the fetters;
these fetters arise through mutual assistance.
However, this occurs only for a single moment.
There must necessarily be a second [factor].
That which binds and is not relinquished is termed the function of a fetter (*saṃyojana*); it need not be present.
Once the acquisition of a fetter (*saṃyojanaprāpti*) has occurred, that is the function of the acquisition of a fetter.
This [path] exists only in the present, because the past and future lack functional efficacy.

Question: If the path is able to sever the fetters while one abides in this path and does not fall away from it, yet if one falls away from this path while abiding in it, the fetters are not severed. How is this so?
This means that while the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is capable of severing all fetters (*saṃyojana*),
there is no one who, abiding in this path, can fall back. However,
for one abiding in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), falling back is possible.
The meaning of "this path severs all fetters" is that it is useless;
why then do you now say that this path severs all fetters of the three realms,
yet when one falls back from this path, one again becomes bound by those fetters?
Answer: This does not contradict reason.
Why is that? Because the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is the cause of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The path of liberation is the fruit of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
When one falls away from this fruit, it is also said that one falls away from its cause.
Furthermore, all uninterrupted paths are the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to the acquisition of afflictions (*kleśa-prāpti*).
When one falls back and gives rise to afflictions, it is also said that one has fallen back from those [attainments].
Furthermore, the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is established for the purpose of severing afflictions;
when one falls back and gives rise to afflictions, it is also said that one has fallen back from that [path].
Furthermore, there are two types of "abandonment":
one general and one specific.
The specific type pertains exclusively to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
All are paths of liberation;
now, because they rely on the general meaning [of the term], there is no contradiction.
The Venerable Saṃghavasu said:
There is the sense of falling away (parihāṇi) associated with both the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) and the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
For example, a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) who has already abandoned the first five grades of afflictions may give rise to the highest degree of the highest grade of fetters (paryavasthāna).
The stage of retrogression is defined as the five uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and five liberation paths (*vimukti-mārga*) of the preceding [five] categories.
The critique states:
One should not make such a statement.
Why is this? It is because there is certainly no falling back from the path of uninterrupted realization while one is abiding in it,
nor is there any abiding in the path of uninterrupted realization after having already fallen back.
Therefore, what was stated previously is logically sound: namely,
that when one falls away from a fruit, it is called "falling away" (parihāṇi),
and so forth regarding the causes and other factors.
There are nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*).
Namely: the first thorough knowledge is the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin in the desire realm;
the second thorough knowledge is the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin in the form and formless realms.
The third complete knowledge (*parijñā*) is the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation in the desire realm.
The fourth complete knowledge is the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of cessation in the form and formless realms.
The fifth complete knowledge is the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the path in the desire realm.
The sixth thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the form and formless realms.
The seventh thorough knowledge is the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*).
The eighth thorough knowledge is the exhaustion of the fetter of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga-saṃyojana*).
The ninth thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarva-saṃyojana-kṣaya*).
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To refute the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.

That is to say, there are some who claim that because all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), they are not objects of the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇaparijñā*).
In order to refute that position and demonstrate that unconditioned phenomena do indeed possess an intrinsic nature, [this treatise is composed].
The thorough knowledges of abandonment (prahāṇaparijñā) definitely exist as real entities. Alternatively,
some say that these thorough knowledges of abandonment are not merely nine.
Since all analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) could be termed "abandonment full-knowledge" (*prahāṇa-parijñā*),
this [statement] is made to exclude that view and demonstrate that abandonment full-knowledge consists of only nine types.
The nine causal conditions for establishing these will be explained later.
Some say that there is only one kind of abandonment through full knowledge (*prahāṇa-parijñā*),
because the essence of all analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is one and the same.
This treatise is composed to refute that intention and to demonstrate that the essence of the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) is not merely one.
Question: Since abandonment is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it cannot take objects as its cognitive focus and thus lacks the function of definitive discernment (*pariccheda*).
What is meant by "thorough knowledge" (parijñā)?
Answer: Although this [state] cannot take an object as its cognitive focus or engage in definitive discernment, it is nonetheless called "thorough knowledge" because it is the fruit of wisdom.
Just as an arhat is called "liberated" because they are the fruit of liberation;
just as the six spheres of contact are called "past karma" because they are the fruit of karma;
and just as the divine eye and ear are called "supernormal powers" because they are the fruit of supernormal powers.
This abandonment is likewise so.

Because it is the fruit of knowledge (*jñāna*), it is also called "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*). [Question: Since abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is the fruit of knowledge, it may be termed "thorough knowledge.
However, since abandonment through seeing (*darśana-heya*) is the fruit of receptivity (*kṣānti*), why is it called "thorough knowledge"?
Answer: That abandonment is also the fruit of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
This refers to the abandonment of the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) by means of the conventional path.

Because the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) within those eight stages is the fruit of conventional knowledge, it is also termed "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
Question: If the mundane path possesses the capacity for function, then because the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by insight is the fruit of knowledge, it may be termed "thorough knowledge.
However, this [mundane path] lacks the capacity for abandonment regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding how that which is abandoned through seeing is termed "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*),
the Venerable Saṃgharakṣita said:
"Because it is the fruit of wisdom, it is called thorough knowledge."
There are two kinds of abandonment:
first, that which is the fruit of knowledge;
second, that which is the fruit of wisdom.
In this context, the fruit of wisdom is termed "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
The critique states:
one should not speak in that manner.
Why is this? Because the sūtras state that there are only two types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*):
first, thorough knowledge by wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*).
Second, regarding the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*):
the Buddha never stated that there is such a thing as "thorough knowledge of wisdom" (*prajñā-parijñā*).
Furthermore, since wisdom is not itself knowledge, it would have to be called "thorough wisdom" (*pari-prajñā*) instead.
What is meant by "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*)?
Since this is a form of wisdom (*jñāna*), it should be explained as follows:

it is that which is attained through the receptivities (*kṣānti*), and which manifests at the time of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*). At that moment, what has been abandoned [by those receptivities] is thoroughly known.
Furthermore, because it can be realized, it is also called the fruit of knowledge (*jñānaphala*).
That is to say, the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) is the ultimate;
the cessation realized by that ascetic (*śramaṇa*) is called the fruit of the ascetic (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).

Because it is definitively proven that at the moment one attains the fruit of arhatship, one simultaneously realizes the abandonment of all defilements to be eliminated through both vision and cultivation within the three realms;
therefore, this abandonment is also termed "complete knowledge" (parijñā).
Furthermore, because patience (*kṣānti*) is an attendant of wisdom (*jñāna*), it is also called wisdom.
The cessation (*nirodha*) obtained through this patience is also called thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
Furthermore, since this abandonment (*prahāṇa*) is attained by means of the lineage of wisdom, it is therefore called thorough knowledge.
Just as one born of the Gautama clan is called a Gautama,
so too this abandonment is called "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) because it possesses the characteristic of thorough knowledge; furthermore,
it is so named because it is realized by wisdom.
Just as the eye of the past and the future does not see forms, yet because it does not abandon the characteristic of the eye, it is also called "eye.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka has made this statement.
This abandonment should be established as "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*),
because it is attained through the thorough knowledge of the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the principle of the final truth (*niṣṭhā-satya*).
As the Venerable Pārśva said:
This abandonment should be established as "thorough knowledge through relinquishment" (*prahāṇa-parijñā*),
because one thoroughly understands the defects of saṃsāra and thereby attains the permanent relinquishing of saṃsāra.
Although these two explanations do not contradict reason, the Sūtra speaks only of "abandoning through thorough knowledge" (*parijñā-prahāṇa*).
Therefore, among the three explanations, the first is the best.
Nevertheless, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of abandonment is also termed "abandonment."
It is also called detachment,
it is also called cessation,
and it is also called truth.
It is also called "thorough knowledge" (parijñā),
it is also called "the fruit of the ascetic life" (śrāmaṇyaphala),
and it is also called "the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder" (sopadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu).
It is also called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Among these eight types, some are present and others are absent at various stages;

specifically, this refers to the time when the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) has ceased and the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) has arisen.
That which has been abandoned by him is called abandonment, called detachment, called cessation, and called truth;
it is not yet called full knowledge.
It has not yet been called the fruit of śrāmaṇya;
it has not yet been called the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder;
it has not yet been called the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
When the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti) ceases and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) arises,
that which is abandoned thereby is termed abandonment, detachment, cessation, and truth.
It is not yet called "thorough knowledge";
it is not yet called the "fruit of the śramaṇa";
it is not yet called the "nirvāṇa realm with remainder."
It is not yet called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
At the time when the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises and the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*) is produced,
that which was previously abandoned is attained [as cessation].
It is called abandonment, detachment, cessation, truth, and full comprehension.
This refers to the full comprehension of the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin within the desire realm;
it is not yet termed a fruit of the śramaṇa.
It is not yet called the nirvāṇa-realm with remainder,
nor is it yet called the nirvāṇa-realm without remainder.
At the moment when the acceptance of the subsequent knowledge of origin arises and the subsequent knowledge of origin has been produced:
That which has been abandoned by him is called abandonment,
called detachment, called cessation, called truth, and called full comprehension;
that is to say, the full comprehension of the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin within the realms of form and formlessness.
It has not yet been called the fruit of śrāmaṇya;
it has not yet been called the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder;
it has not yet been called the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
When the receptivity to the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) arises,
that which is abandoned thereby is called abandonment, detachment, cessation, truth, and full comprehension.

That is to say, the full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the desire realm is not yet called a fruit of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*),
nor is it called the realm of nirvana with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
It has not yet been designated as the realm of nirvana without remainder.
At the moment when the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises,
that which was to be abandoned is eliminated.
It is called abandonment, detachment, cessation, truth, and full comprehension;
that is, the full comprehension of the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the form and formless realms is not yet termed a fruit of the śramaṇa.
It is not yet called the *nirvāṇa-dhātu* with remainder,
nor is it yet called the *nirvāṇa-dhātu* without remainder.
This is at the time when the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) ceases and the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) arises.
That which has been abandoned by him is called abandonment, detachment, cessation, truth, and full comprehension;
that is to say, the full comprehension of the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the path of seeing within the desire realm.
It is not yet called the fruit of śrāmaṇya;
it is not yet called the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder;
it is not yet called the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
When the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti) ceases and the subsequent knowledge of the path arises,
that which has been abandoned is called abandonment, detachment, cessation, truth, and full comprehension.

The complete knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness is called the fruit of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), namely,
the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).
It is not yet called the *nirvāṇa-element with remainder*,
nor is it yet called the *nirvāṇa-element without remainder*.

At that time, there is this abandonment, as well as the abandonment of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) belonging to the three realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation.
Together with the abandonment of the fetters to be eliminated through the path of seeing in the desire realm,
one collectively realizes the attainment of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) of a single flavor.
At that time, such abandonment is termed "abandonment," "disjunction," "cessation," "truth," and "complete knowledge."
That which was previously attained is called the fruit of śrāmaṇya;
namely, the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala).
It is not yet termed the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder (sopadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu).
It is not yet called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
When a stream-enterer seeks to realize the fruit of a once-returner and abandons from one to five grades of fetters of the desire realm;
That which has been abandoned by him is called abandonment, called detachment, called cessation, and called truth;
yet it is not yet called thorough knowledge,
nor is it yet called the fruit of the śramaṇa.
It is not yet called the nirvāṇa-realm with remainder,
nor is it called the nirvāṇa-realm without remainder;
it is the cessation through the path of immediate succession that abandons the sixth category of fetters.
When the path of liberation arises,
that which has been abandoned thereby is termed abandonment, termed detachment, termed cessation, and termed truth.
It is not yet called "thorough knowledge," but is termed a "fruit of śramaṇaship," namely,
the fruit of once-returning.
It is not yet called the nirvāṇa-realm with remainder,
nor is it yet called the nirvāṇa-realm without remainder.
At that time, this abandonment as well as the abandonment of the fetters to be abandoned by insight within the three realms [is accomplished].
Furthermore, upon the abandonment of the first five categories of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
one collectively realizes the attainment of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) of a single flavor.
At that time, their abandonment is termed "abandonment," "disjunction," "cessation," and "truth."
It is not yet called "thorough knowledge.
That which was previously attained is termed the fruit of the śramaṇa, namely,
the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala).
He has not yet been designated as having attained the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder,
nor has he been designated as having attained the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder;
he is one who seeks once more to realize the fruit of non-returning.
When one abandons the seventh and eighth categories of fetters,
that abandonment is termed "abandonment," "separation," "cessation," and "truth," but it is not yet termed "thorough knowledge."
It is not yet called the fruit of śrāmaṇya;
it is not yet called the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder;
it is not yet called the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
When the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the ninth category of fetters ceases and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises,
that which was abandoned by it [is attained].
It is called abandonment, detachment, cessation, truth, and full comprehension;
namely, the full comprehension of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters is called the fruit of śrāmaṇya.
That is to say, the fruit of non-returning is not yet called the realm of nirvana with remainder,
nor is it yet called the realm of nirvana without remainder.

At that time, there is the attainment of the single flavor of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) for both this abandonment and the abandonment of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) throughout the three realms,
as well as the abandonment of the first eight categories of fetters to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm.
At that time of abandonment, it is called abandonment, detachment, cessation, truth, and full comprehension.
Specifically, the exhaustion of the five lower fetters is called the fruit of śrāmaṇya through full comprehension.
That is to say, the fruit of non-returning is not yet called the realm of nirvana with remainder,
nor is it yet called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
When one is detached from each of the nine grades of fetters of the first dhyāna up to the third dhyāna,
as well as when one is detached from the first eight grades of fetters of the fourth dhyāna,
that which is attained is abandonment.
It is called abandonment, detachment, cessation, and truth;
yet it is not yet called full comprehension,
nor is it yet called the fruit of the śramaṇa.
It is not yet called the *nirvāṇa-dhātu* with remainder,
nor is it yet called the *nirvāṇa-dhātu* without remainder.
It is the cessation through the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the ninth category of fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the fourth dhyāna.
When the path of liberation arises,
that which was abandoned is termed abandonment, detachment, cessation, truth, and full comprehension; specifically,
this refers to the full comprehension of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm.
It is not yet called the fruit of śrāmaṇya;
it is not yet called the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder;
it is not yet called the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
Question: How is this full comprehension of the exhaustion of craving for form established?

Is it the exhaustion of all fetters to be abandoned through cultivation within the entire realm of form, or is it the exhaustion of all fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the fourth dhyāna?
Is it for the sake of exhausting the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters abandoned through cultivation in the fourth dhyāna?
Some say that it is solely for the sake of exhausting the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters abandoned through cultivation in the fourth dhyāna.
Other masters say that it is only in the fourth dhyāna that all fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through cultivation are exhausted.
[The author] critiques:
It should be stated thus:

the exhaustion of all fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) pertaining to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) constitutes the full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm.
However, when one abandons the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters, one attains the designation "one who has transcended the sphere of infinite space";
this continues up until the abandonment of each of the nine grades of fetters in the sphere of nothingness,
as well as the first eight grades of fetters in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
That which has been abandoned by him is called abandonment, called detachment, called cessation, and called truth;
it is not yet called thorough knowledge.
It has not yet been called the fruit of śrāmaṇya;
it has not yet been called the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder;
it has not yet been called the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) extinguishes that ninth category of fetters,
the abandonment attained at the moment the first knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises is [the abandonment of those fetters].
It is called abandonment, detachment, cessation, truth, and full comprehension.
That is to say, the complete exhaustion of all fetters is called the fruit of śrāmaṇya;
namely, the fruit of arhatship.
This is called the realm of nirvana with remainder;
it is not yet called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
At that time, these abandonments as well as the fetters to be abandoned through insight into the three realms are severed.
Furthermore, upon the abandonment of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the lower eight stages,
and the abandonment of the first eight categories of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
one collectively realizes the attainment of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) as a single taste.
At that time of abandonment, it is called abandonment, detachment, cessation, truth, and full comprehension. That is to say,
the exhaustion of all fetters is called the fruit of asceticism (śrāmaṇyaphala),
namely, the fruit of arhatship.
This is called the realm of nirvana with remainder;
it is not yet called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
It is when the aggregates, elements, and sense bases of an arhat are extinguished.
Thereafter, it is no longer continued.
Once one has entered the realm of nirvana without remainder,
at that time, that abandonment is called abandonment, called detachment, called cessation, called truth, and called full comprehension.
That which was previously attained is called the fruit of śrāmaṇya;
namely, the fruit of arhatship.
It is not termed the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder.
And it is called the realm of nirvana without remainder.

Question: Since all analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are termed "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*), and abandonment is the fruit of knowledge, they should all be termed "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
Why is this name applied only to these nine stages?
Why cannot it be known as "pervasive" (*parijñā*) in other stages?
Answer: Only within these nine stages...
One attains the designation "thoroughly knowing" (parijñā) when either four conditions or five conditions are fulfilled;
this is not the case in other stages, and therefore only nine are established.
