That is to say, the first six stages are exclusively the fruit of the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
One attains the designation "universal knowledge" (parijñā) by virtue of four conditions:
first, the cessation of both causes;
second, the separation from both fetters.
Third, the attainment of the untainted dissociation;
fourth, the deficiency of the universal [defilements] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
These latter three stages are the fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
One attains the designation "omniscient" (sarvajña) by virtue of five conditions:
namely, the four aforementioned conditions plus the permanent transcendence of the realms.
This occurs at the moment when the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) ceases and the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) arises.
The two causes have not yet been extinguished;
for although the cause to be abandoned through the vision of suffering has been extinguished,
the cause to be abandoned through the vision of the origin has not yet been extinguished.
One has not yet abandoned both types of fetters;
for although one has abandoned the fetters to be abandoned by seeing suffering,
one has not yet abandoned the fetters to be abandoned by seeing the origin.
Although one has attained the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) and lacks none of the universal [defilements] pertaining to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
because three conditions are missing despite the presence of one condition,
that which has been abandoned is not yet termed "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
When the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti) ceases and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna) arises,
the dual cause has not yet been eliminated,
even though the cause to be abandoned by the vision of suffering has been eliminated.
Because the causes to be abandoned by the vision of the origin have not yet been extinguished,
one has not yet become free from both fetters,
even though one has become free from the fetters to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
Because one has not yet abandoned the fetters to be severed by the vision of the origin [of suffering],
one nevertheless attains the untainted acquisition of dissociation (anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti) and the various universal [defilements] that lack the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
Although there are two conditions, because two conditions are lacking,
that which has been abandoned is not yet called "thorough knowledge" (parijñā).

At the moment when the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of origin (samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti) arises and the dharma-knowledge of origin (samudaya-dharmajñāna) is produced, it is said that "the dual causes have been extinguished."
Previously, the causes to be abandoned through the vision of suffering were extinguished;
now, because the causes to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] are extinguished,
one is also freed from both fetters.
Having previously abandoned the fetters to be severed by the vision of suffering,
one now abandons the fetters to be severed by the vision of the origin;
thus, one attains the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*).
And when the universal [defilements] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are eliminated,
because the four conditions are complete,
that which is attained and the aforementioned abandonment are called the first thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).

When the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises and the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) is produced, it is called the "extinction of the dual causes.

This is because the cause to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya-hetu*) was previously extinguished, and now the cause to be abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya-hetu*) is extinguished; thus, one is also liberated from both fetters (*ubhaya-bandhana-vigama*).
Having previously abandoned the fetters to be eliminated through the vision of suffering,
one now abandons the fetters to be eliminated through the vision of origination;
thus, one attains the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*).
And when the universal [defilements] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are eliminated,
because they possess four conditions,
that which is attained and the aforementioned abandonment are called the second thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
When the patience of the dharma-knowledge of cessation (nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) arises,
it is called the "extinction of the dual causes," because it first extinguishes the causes to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin,
and now extinguishes the causes to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
It is also free from both types of fetters:
first, it was freed from the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin;
now, it is freed from the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
Having already attained the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) and the various universal [defilements] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
[the path of liberation arises] because it possesses four conditions.
The abandonment attained therein is called the third thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).

At the moment when the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) is produced, it is termed "the destruction of the dual causes.
This refers to the prior destruction of the causes abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Now, because one abandons the cause that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation,
one also becomes free from the simultaneous fetters;
previously, one had already become free from the fetters to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin.
Now, because one is freed from the fetters to be abandoned by seeing and cessation,
and because one has attained the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*),
as well as the deficiency of the universal [defilements] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) due to the presence of the four conditions.
The abandonment thus attained is called the fourth thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).

At the moment when the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) ceases and the dharma-knowledge of the path arises, it is termed "the destruction of the dual causes.
This refers to the prior destruction of the causes abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin.
Now, because the causes to be abandoned by the path of seeing are extinguished,
one is also freed from simultaneous fetters;
previously, one was already freed from the fetters to be abandoned by the paths of seeing suffering and its origin.
Now, because one is freed from the fetters to be abandoned through the path of seeing,
one has already attained the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) and the deficiency of all universal [defilements] pertaining to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Because it possesses four conditions,
that abandonment attained is called the fifth thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).

At the moment when the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) ceases and the subsequent knowledge of the path arises, it is termed "the destruction of the dual causes."
Previously, one extinguished the causes abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin;
now, because one extinguishes the causes abandoned through the vision of the path,
one is also liberated from both fetters.
Having previously abandoned the fetters to be severed through the vision of suffering and its origin,
one now abandons the fetters to be severed through the vision of the path;
thus, one attains the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*).
And because they possess the four conditions, including the universal [defilements] that lack the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
the abandonment attained therein is called the sixth thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
These six types are exclusively the fruits of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

When one possesses the four conditions and establishes the abandonment of the first through the eighth category of afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) of the desire realm, the two causes have not yet been extinguished.
Although one has extinguished from one grade up to eight grades of causes,
because one has not yet extinguished from eight grades down to one grade of causes,
one has likewise not yet become free from both fetters.
Although one has abandoned from one grade up to eight grades of fetters,
because one has not yet abandoned from eight grades down to one grade of fetters,
even though one has attained the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) and the various universal [defilements] that lack the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Yet they have not permanently crossed over the realm;
although two conditions are present, because three conditions are lacking,
that abandonment which has been attained is not yet termed "thorough knowledge."
When the path of liberation arises immediately after the uninterrupted path that abandons the ninth grade of defilement,
it is called "the extinction of both causes," because the eight grades of causes were previously extinguished and the ninth grade of cause is now extinguished.
It is also free from both bonds;
for while one was previously freed from eight grades of bondage,
one is now freed from the ninth grade of bondage.
Having attained the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) and the various universal [factors] that lack the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
and having forever transcended the desire realm— because these five conditions are fulfilled—
the acquisitions thus obtained and the aforementioned abandonments are designated as the seventh thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
This refers to the full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*).

When one is free from one up to eight categories of defilements abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within each of the four dhyānas, although the dual causes have not yet been extinguished, even if one category up to eight categories of causes have been extinguished.
Because the causes from the eighth grade down to the first grade have not yet been extinguished,
one has not yet abandoned the simultaneous fetters.
Although one may have abandoned the fetters from the first grade up to the eighth grade, one has not yet abandoned the fetters from the eighth grade down to the first grade.
Although one has attained the acquisition of outflow-free dissociation and possesses the various universal [defilements] that lack the Peak of Existence,
one has not yet permanently crossed over the realms;
for although two conditions are present, three conditions are lacking.
The abandonment attained by that [path] is not yet termed "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
Except for the ninth category of defilements to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within each of the first three dhyānas,
when the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises at the moment the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) destroys [the defilements], it is called "the destruction of the dual causes."
Previously, the causes of the eight categories were extinguished;
now, because the cause of the ninth category is extinguished,
one is also freed from both types of fetters.
Previously, one was separated from the bonds of eight grades;
now, because one is separated from the bonds of the ninth grade,
although one attains the untainted acquisition of disconnection (anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti), [the path is still considered mundane].
Furthermore, although one may have abandoned the universal [defilements] of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) but has not yet permanently transcended that realm,
because one of the four conditions is lacking,

the abandonment attained therein is not yet termed "complete knowledge" (parijñā). This remains the case until the ninth category of defilement to be abandoned through cultivation in the fourth dhyāna has been severed.
When the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) ceases and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises, it is called "the cessation of the dual causes.
This is because the eight grades of causes were previously eliminated,
and now the ninth grade of cause is eliminated.
It is also free from both types of fetters;
for it has previously abandoned the eight grades of fetters and now abandons the ninth grade of fetters.
Having attained the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*),
as well as the deficiency of the universal [defilements] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and having permanently transcended the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*),
it is due to the presence of these five conditions.
The attainment of that [fruit] and the aforementioned abandonment are termed the eighth thorough knowledge (*parijñā*),
namely, the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā-kṣaya-parijñā*).

This occurs when one is free from even one up to eight categories of defilements abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within each of the four formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*), provided that the dual causes have not yet been extinguished.
Although one has extinguished from one grade up to eight grades of causes,
because one has not yet extinguished from eight grades down to one grade of causes,
one has likewise not yet abandoned the simultaneous fetters.
Although one has abandoned from one grade up to eight grades of fetters,
because one has not yet abandoned from eight grades down to one grade of fetters,
one does not obtain the untainted acquisition of dissociation (anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti).
Furthermore, although those who have abandoned the universal [defilements] of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) have not yet permanently transcended that realm,
because they lack three conditions despite possessing two,
the abandonment they have attained is not yet termed "complete knowledge" (parijñā).
When the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) that eliminates the ninth grade of defilement of each of the first three formless attainments— which are to be abandoned by cultivation—
arises as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is called "the destruction of the dual causes.
This is because the eight preceding grades of causes have already been eliminated.
Now, because the cause of the ninth category has been extinguished,
one is also freed from both types of fetters;
previously, one was freed from the fetters of the eight categories.
Now, because one is separated from the ninth category of fetters,

although one attains the untainted acquisition of disconnection (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) and the various universal [defilements] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are deficient, [the path of liberation arises].
Yet they have not permanently crossed over the realm;
although there are four conditions, because one condition is lacking,
that which has been abandoned by them is not yet called "thorough knowledge" (parijñā).
When the ninth grade of defilements to be abandoned through cultivation in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is abandoned,
and the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) ceases while the first knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) arises, this is called the "extinction of the dual causes."
Previously, the causes of eight grades were extinguished;
now, because the cause of the ninth grade is extinguished,
one is likewise freed from both fetters.
Because one has previously abandoned the bonds of eight categories and now abandons the bonds of the ninth category,
one attains the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*),
as well as the deficiency of the universal [defilements] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the permanent transcendence of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because five conditions are fulfilled,
that which is attained and the previous abandonment are termed the ninth thorough knowledge (*parijñā*),
namely, the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana-kṣaya-parijñā*).
These latter three are the fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), established by way of five conditions.
Question: The four fruits of the śramaṇa are places of rest;
regarding all abandonments (*prahāṇa*), one realizes a single taste (*ekarasa*) of the attainment of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
For what reason is the fruit of Arhatship established as a single "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*) by aggregating all the abandonments,
whereas for the Stream-enterer and Once-returner, a single "complete knowledge" is not established by aggregating all the abandonments?
Answer: Although the abandonments are collectively gathered across all four fruit-attainments, it is at the time of the latter two fruits that both conditions are fulfilled;
therefore, the collective gathering of all abandonments is established as a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
What are these two meanings?
First, the attainment of a fruit; second, the transcendence of a realm.
When one attains the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of once-returning, although this is the attainment of a fruit, it is not the transcendence of a realm.
When one is abandoning the ninth grade of defilement of the fourth dhyāna,
although this constitutes transcending a realm, it is not yet the attainment of a fruit.
At the time of attaining the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala), both criteria are fulfilled.
First, the attainment of the fruit,
which refers to the attainment of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
Second, the transcending of realms.
This means that when one transcends the desire realm and attains the fruit of arhatship, two meanings are simultaneously fulfilled.
The first is the attainment of the fruit.
The first is the attainment of the fruit of arhatship;
the second is the transcending of realms,
which refers to transcending the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
The term "collectively" (saṃgraha) means "unified.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), one attains the fruit of stream-entry by abandoning defilements partially,
and attains the fruit of arhatship by abandoning them entirely.
In the desire realm, one attains the fruit of once-returner by becoming detached from defilements partially,
and the fruit of non-returner by becoming detached from them completely.
In the form realm, one does not attain either fruit through partial or complete detachment from defilements.
Only in two cases are both meanings complete,
namely, because at the time of attaining the fruit, one simultaneously transcends a realm. Thus,
the abandonments of the Arhat and the Non-returner are collectively established as a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
Furthermore, one must possess two conditions for the complete and universal realization [of the knowledges] to be fully assembled:
first, transcending at least one of the three realms;
second, exhausting at least one type of the fetters conducive to the lower or higher realms.
When attaining the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of once-returning, both meanings are absent.
When one is free from the ninth grade of defilement of the fourth dhyāna,
although one has transcended the realm of form, one meaning is still lacking.
When attaining the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), two conditions are fulfilled without deficiency:
first, transcending the desire realm (kāmadhātu);
second, the exhaustion of the lower fetters (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana) that lead downward.
Upon attaining the fruit of arhatship, two meanings are likewise fulfilled:
first, transcending the formless realm;
second, because the higher fetters are exhausted.
The latter two fruits of realization only involve the total integration of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
Furthermore, they require the presence of two conditions for such total integration:
first, one must have transcended at least one of the three realms (*dhātu*).
Second, when one has exhausted even a single type among the unwholesome, neutral, or afflictive [states],
both meanings are absent at the time of attaining the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of once-returning;
this is also the case when one is free from the ninth grade of defilement of the fourth dhyāna.
Although one transcends the realm of form (rūpadhātu), one lacks a single factor.
At the time of attaining the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala), two factors are complete:
first, transcending the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).
Second, when the two unwholesome afflictions are exhausted and one attains the fruit of arhatship, it likewise possesses two meanings:
first, transcending the formless realm.
Because the two types of neutral afflictions (*avyākṛta-kleśa*) have been exhausted,
it is only at the stage of the latter two fruits that the thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) are collectively gathered.
Furthermore, they must possess two specific conditions before the thorough knowledges can be collectively gathered.
First, one transcends at least one realm within the three realms;
second, one exhausts at least one type of affliction, whether it be subject to maturation or not subject to maturation.
At the time of attaining the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of once-returning, both of these conditions are absent.
When one is free from the ninth grade of defilement of the fourth dhyāna,
although one has transcended the realm of form (rūpadhātu), one lacks one of the two required conditions;
when one attains the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala), both conditions are complete.
First, one transcends the desire realm;
second, the afflictions with karmic maturation are exhausted.
At the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship, both of these meanings are likewise present.
First, one transcends the formless realm;
second, because the afflictions that result in maturation have been exhausted,
it is only at the stage of the latter two fruits that the universal knowledges (*parijñā*) are collectively gathered.
Furthermore, two conditions must be fulfilled for the complete accumulation of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*):
first, one must transcend at least one realm within the three realms;
second, one must exhaust at least one type of affliction among those that produce either two or one fruit.
When attaining the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of once-returning, both meanings are absent.
When one is free from the ninth grade of defilement of the fourth dhyāna,
although one has transcended the realm of form, one meaning is still lacking.
When the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) is attained, two meanings are complete:
first, the transcendence of the desire realm;
second, the exhaustion of the afflictions that produce both the outflowing (niṣyanda) and the ripening (vipāka) fruits.
Upon attaining the fruit of Arhatship, one likewise possesses two meanings:
first, transcending the formless realm; second, having exhausted all afflictions, one experiences only the single fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
It is only in the latter two stages of fruition that the comprehensive knowledges (*parijñā*) are fully assembled.
Furthermore, two conditions must be fulfilled for the complete collection of universal knowledge (*parijñā*):
first, one must transcend at least one of the three realms;
second, one must exhaust at least one type of affliction associated with either a lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) or a lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*).
When attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) or the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), both meanings are absent.
When one is free from the ninth grade of defilement of the fourth dhyāna,
although one has transcended the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), one meaning is still lacking.
At the time of attaining the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), two conditions are fulfilled without deficiency:
first, the transcendence of the desire realm;
second, the exhaustion of those afflictions associated with a lack of shame (āhrīkya) and a lack of dread of blame (anapatrāpya).
Upon attaining the fruit of arhatship, one also possesses two meanings:
first, transcending the formless realm;
second, because the afflictions dissociated from shamelessness and lack of dread have been exhausted.
The latter two fruits of realization only involve the total collection of thorough knowledges (*parijñā*).
Furthermore, they require the presence of two conditions for this total collection to occur:
first, one must have transcended at least one of the three realms (*dhātu*).
Second, among the five destinies and four modes of birth, one exhausts one type accordingly;
when attaining the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of once-returning, both meanings are absent;
and when one is free from the ninth grade of defilement of the fourth dhyāna.
Although one who has transcended the realm of form lacks one of these two meanings,
at the time of attaining the fruit of non-returning, both meanings are complete:
first, transcending the realm of desire.
Second, those who exhaust the human realm and the womb-born mode of birth also possess two meanings when they attain the fruit of arhatship:
first, they transcend the formless realm.
Second, because those in the celestial realms who are born by transformation have been exhausted;
it is only at the stage of the latter two fruits that one fully assembles and attains complete knowledge (*parijñā*).
*Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle sixty-two.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Sixty-three,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Two: The Chapter on the Aggregates of the Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha), Part Two of the First Chapter on Single Practices (Ekādhika-nikāya), Section Eight. Thus, regarding the nine thorough knowledges (parijñā): who abandons how many, and who attains how many?
Answer: There are sentient beings who neither relinquish nor acquire, namely, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Question: This question and answer does not concern ordinary worldlings.
They exist only in reliance upon the Noble Ones (*ārya*).
Do the Noble Ones have any relinquishing or acquisition regarding the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*)?
Answer: Yes, they do.
This means that even when one abides in the fundamental nature and attains superior progress, there is neither relinquishing nor acquiring. Specifically,
this refers to the moment when the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) ceases and the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) arises,
as well as the moment when the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) ceases and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) arises.
In all nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*), there is neither abandonment nor acquisition.

At the moment when the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti*) ceases and the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*) arises, there is no abandonment and one acquisition.

At the moment when the subsequent receptivity to the knowledge of origin (*samudayānvayajñānakṣānti*) ceases and the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvayajñāna*) arises, there is no abandonment and one acquisition.

At the moment when the receptivity to the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) ceases and the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) arises, there is no abandonment and one attainment.

At the moment when the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*anvayajñānakṣānti*) ceases and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*anvayajñāna*) arises, there is no abandonment and one attainment.

At the moment when the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path (mārga-dharmajñāna-kṣānti) ceases and the dharma-knowledge of the path arises, there is neither abandonment nor acquisition of one [dharma].
At the moment when the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvayajñāna-kṣānti) ceases and the subsequent knowledge of the path arises,
if one has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire and enters into right nature (samyaktva-niyāma), there is likewise neither abandonment nor acquisition of one.
If one who has already become free from the defilement of desire enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they relinquish five and acquire one;
that is, they relinquish the aforementioned five and acquire the full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Regarding this, some say that in the path of seeing of the six stages, both the relinquishing and the acquisition are likewise.
Others say:
Regarding the latter five [categories], one does not attain full knowledge (*parijñā*) at the stage of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
When a noble one (*ārya*) becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) ranging from one to eight categories,
there is neither abandonment nor attainment.

When the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the ninth grade of defilement and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arise, one relinquishes six [knowledges] and acquires one.
That is to say, one relinquishes the previous six and acquires the full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca-avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
When one is free from even a single grade of defilement of the first dhyāna,
up until being free from eight grades of defilement of the fourth dhyāna,
there is neither abandonment nor acquisition.

When one abandons the ninth grade of defilement of the fourth dhyāna, at the moment the path of uninterrupted transition ceases and the path of liberation arises, there is neither abandonment nor acquisition; that is to say, the full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm.
When one is free from the defilements of a single category of the Sphere of Infinite Space,
up until being free from the eight categories of defilements of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception,
there is neither abandonment nor acquisition.
When one abandons the ninth grade of defilement of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
at the moment the diamond-like concentration ceases and the first knowledge of exhaustion arises, one abandons two and acquires one;
that is, one abandons the full-knowledge of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters and the full-knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm.
One attains the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana*).
This explains the abandonment and acquisition of thorough knowledge at the time of spiritual progress;
it also implies that there is abandonment and acquisition [of thorough knowledge] at the time of regression.
That is to say, when an Arhat falls away due to the arising of the fetters of the formless realm,
they relinquish one and acquire two;
namely, they relinquish the ninth and acquire the eighth and the seventh.
That is to say, when one falls away from the meditative absorption of the form realm due to the arising of its fetters, one abandons one and acquires another;
specifically, one abandons the ninth [acquisition] and acquires the seventh.
This also applies when one falls away from it due to the arising of the fetters of the desire realm.
One abandons one and acquires six;
that is, one abandons the ninth [category of defilement] and acquires the preceding six.
This refers to a non-returner who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm.
When one falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the form realm,
one abandons one and does not acquire it;
that is, one abandons the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm.
That is to say, when one regresses by giving rise to the fetters of the desire realm,
one abandons two and acquires six;
namely, one abandons the eighth and the seventh.
One who has attained the first six [liberations] but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm— the non-returner—
when falling away due to the arising of the fetters of the desire realm.
One abandons one and attains six;
that is to say, by exhausting the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana),
one attains the former six [liberations].
When a noble one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm falls away due to the arising of the fetters of the desire realm,
there is neither relinquishment nor acquisition regarding the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*).
Thus, regarding the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*), how many are the fruits of dhyāna?
Answer: Nine are the fruits of dhyāna and its attendants (*sānucara*).
Question: How many are the fruits of the formless realm (*ārūpya*)?
Answer: Two are the fruits of the formless [attainments] and their attendants;
that is, the exhaustion of craving for the form realm and the exhaustion of all fetters.
Question: How many are the fruits of the fundamental dhyānas?
The answer is five:
namely, the second, fourth, sixth, and the final two. Some say:
The second, the fourth, and the last three constitute five;
thus there are eight, according to the Venerable Ghosaka.
That is to say, excluding the seventh.
Question: How many are the fruits that are attendants of dhyāna?
Answer: Nine.
That is to say, it refers to the *anāgamya* concentration and not others;
the intermediate dhyāna is as explained for the fundamental dhyānas.
Question: How many are the fruits of the fundamental formless attainments?
Answer: One.
That is to say, the ninth.
Question: How many are the fruits that are the retinue of the formless realm?
Answer: One.
That is to say, the eighth [liberation] is the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), and not the others.
Question: How many are the fruits of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*)?
The answer is six;
that is, the aforementioned six.
Some say there are seven.
That is to say, the first seven.
Question: How many are the fruits of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga)?
Answer: Three.
This refers to the final three.
Question: How many are the fruits of patience (*kṣānti*)?
Answer: It should be stated that they are like the fruits of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Question: How many are the fruits of knowledge (*jñāna*)?
Answer: One should say they are like the fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Question: How many are the fruits of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
Answer: Three;
namely, the last three.
Question: How many are the results of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)?
Answer: Two;
namely, the latter two.
Question: How many are the fruits of the category of dharma-knowledge?
Answer: Six; namely, the first, the third, the fifth, and the last three.
Question: How many are the fruits of the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
Answer: Five.
This refers to the second, fourth, sixth, and the final two [of the ten stages].
Some say there are six:
namely, the second, fourth, sixth, and the final three.
Question: How many are the fruits of the mundane path?
Answer: Two;
namely, the seventh and the eighth.
Question: How many are the fruits of the untainted path?
Answer: Nine, because all are obtained through the power of the untainted path.

Question: If one who has already become free from passion for the form realm enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), at what time does that person attain the full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm?
The Venerable Saṃghavasu replied:
It is attained at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
This is because at that time, one is said to both abide in the fruit and abide in the path of progress (*pratipannaka*).
The critique states:
One should not make such a statement,
for one who abides in the fruit is not said to be abiding in the path of approach (*pratipannaka*).
This is because at the time of attaining the fruit, not even a single thought-moment of the path of approach has yet arisen before one.
What is meant by "directed toward"?
Other masters say:
it is when one subsequently becomes free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space.
At that time, one attains the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of attachment to form (*rūparāga*).
This is because, at that time, one cultivates the future untainted (*anāsrava*) stages of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) for their abandonment.
One should not, however, state it in such a manner.

At that time, he cultivates only the future uncontaminated meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya), which serve as antidotes to the formless realm but not as antidotes to the realm of form.
Furthermore, some say that he will subsequently attain the fruit of arhatship.
When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests,
one attains this thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of desire for the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*).
This means that at that time, one has abandoned all afflictions (*kleśa*) to be eliminated through seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*) throughout the three realms.
Because they equally realize the attainment of disjunction from the single flavor,
they too should not speak in such a manner;
at that time, all abandonments are collectively gathered as one.
This is called the full knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana-kṣaya-parijñā*).
How, then, can one speak of attaining the full knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for form (*rūparāga-kṣaya-parijñā*)?
One should explain it as follows:

It is only when that [practitioner] definitely emerges from the fruit and the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) manifests that they obtain this thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm.
If it were not admitted that they definitely emerge from the fruit and the path of superior fruit manifests, [then this would not be possible].

When those who have already become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna enter the path of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on a lower stage during the knowledge of the types of the path (mārga-jñāna-anvaya-jñāna),
they attain the third fruit.
Since the path of the superior fruit does not arise and manifest before them,
if they were to die and be reborn in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
they would not possess the untainted faculty of pleasure (anāsrava-sukhendriya).
If that were so, it would contradict the "Ten Gates" section (*daśamukha-uddeśa*),
which asks:
"Who possesses the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?"
Answer: If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven],
or if one is born below the Śubhakṛtsna,
or if an Ārya is born above the Śubhakṛtsna.
To avoid this error,
one must necessarily admit that once the fruit has been attained, one definitely arises from that fruit to produce the path of superior fruit;
only at that time is one said to have attained the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*).
According to this principle, if one has already abandoned three or four grades of defilement of the desire realm prior to entering the path of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
then at the moment of attaining the knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), one obtains the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
If such a person undergoes further rebirths, they are necessarily a "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) practitioner.

If one has already abandoned seven or eight grades of defilement of the desire realm and enters the path of the subsequent knowledge of the category of the noble ones (mārgānvaya-jñāna) at the stage of entering the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), one attains the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
If such a person undergoes rebirth, they are necessarily an "interval-one" (ekavicika).
If it is not admitted that one who has already attained a noble fruit necessarily arises from that fruit into a path of superior fruit,
then how could such a person, were they to undergo rebirth, possess the three, four, seven, or eight categories of untainted antidotal faculties?
Are all types of thorough knowledge (parijñā) subsumed within the nine types of thorough knowledge?
Or are the nine types of thorough knowledge subsumed within all types of thorough knowledge?
Answer: All are subsumed within the nine.
The nine do not encompass all.
Here, "nine" refers to those previously mentioned;
"all" refers to these as well as other abandonments.
Because its substance is all-encompassing, it can include the nine;
because the substance of these nine is narrow, they cannot include everything.
It is like a large vessel that can cover small vessels.
A small vessel cannot cover a large vessel.
What is not included?
This refers to when the knowledge of suffering has already arisen, but the knowledge of the origin [of suffering] has not yet arisen.
The exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering within the three realms is not comprised of nine [categories].

Specifically, it refers to the abandonment of all phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm that is attained at the moment when the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) ceases and the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) arises.
Furthermore, at the moment when the acceptance of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) ceases and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna*) arises,
all those factors belonging to the form and formless realms that were to be abandoned through the vision of suffering are severed.
Such abandonments are not included within the nine [categories of abandonment].
The first two universal knowledges (*parijñā*) of the fruit of the path of seeing are established [as such],
because the conditions for their completion have not yet been met.
This applies to a disciple who has attained vision but has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire.
The exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm is not comprised within the nine [categories of abandonment].
This refers to those noble ones who have abandoned from one up to eight categories of defilements to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
The various abandonments attained are not subsumed within the nine [knowledges];
they are established as the first thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the fruit of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
because the necessary conditions have not yet been fulfilled.

One who is already free from the defilements of desire but not yet free from the defilements of the form realm has exhausted the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the form realm, which are not included within the nine [categories].
This refers to noble ones who have abandoned even a single grade of the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation in the first dhyāna.
Up to the point of abandoning the eight categories of defilements to be eliminated through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the fourth dhyāna,
the various abandonments attained are not subsumed under the ninth [complete knowledge].
This is because the conditions for establishing the second complete knowledge as a fruit of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-phala*) have not yet been fulfilled.
One who is already free from the defilements of the form realm but not yet free from the defilements of the formless realm has,
regarding the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm, that which is not comprised within the nine [categories].
This refers to noble ones who have abandoned one grade of the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the sphere of infinite space.
Up to the abandonment of the eight categories of defilements to be eliminated through cultivation belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
the resulting abandonments are not included within the nine [complete knowledges],
because the third complete knowledge of the fruit of the path of cultivation is established only when its conditions are fully met.

Question: Regarding ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), from those who have abandoned one grade of the defilements to be eliminated through seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), up to those who have abandoned nine grades of the defilements to be eliminated through seeing and cultivation in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The various abandonments attained are likewise not subsumed within the nine [categories].
Why, then, are they not mentioned here? One should respond that when something ought to be stated but is not, [it is because it is]... [omitted].
One should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, in this context, the discussion is based solely upon noble ones (ārya) and not upon ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Because the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) are established as existing only within the continuum of a noble one (*ārya*).

Question: Regarding those who have already become free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and have entered into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*):
Regarding those various abandonments previously attained,

now that he has reached the stage of an ārya, they are appropriately designated by their respective names for the fruits of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, up until they are fully known.
That abandonment is also not included within these nine;
for what reason is it not mentioned here? One should respond that although it ought to be stated, it was not stated.
One should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, because this section briefly clarifies the initial entrance [to the path],
it describes the coarse characteristics but does not describe the subtle ones.
Furthermore, herein it is only those ordinary beings bound by all fetters who enter the noble path that are discussed.
Since they do not enter the noble path while remaining bound by all fetters,
they are not mentioned.
There are eight types of persons:
first, those entering the stream;
second, those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry.
1. The candidate for the first fruit;
4. the fruit of once-returning;
5. the candidate for non-returning.
Sixth, the fruit of non-returning;
seventh, the stage of the candidate for arhatship;
eighth, the fruit of arhatship.
Question: Regarding these eight types of *pudgala*, if there are eight names, how many are there in terms of substantial entities?
The masters of the Abhidharma say:
These names are eight, but their substantial entities are only five;
namely, the candidate for stream-entry and the fruit of arhatship.
These two names have two kinds of substantial entities, which are likewise two.
The candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of once-returning have two names but a single substantial entity; likewise,
the fruit of once-returning and the candidate for the fruit of non-returning [have two names but a single substantial entity].
Although there are two names, the substance is one:
the fruit of non-returning and the candidate for arhatship.
Although there are two names, the substance is one.
Because they carry the fruit while proceeding toward sentient beings as one,
the Venerable Ghosaka has stated that the eight types of persons (pudgala) exist both nominally and substantially as eight.
He asserts this:
"All those who are stream-enterers (srotāpanna), until they have yet produced the path superior to that fruit,
are called 'stream-enterers' because they possess the fruit of stream-entry."
If one gives rise to a path that is superior to that fruit, one then abandons the fruit of stream-entry;
therefore, such a person is called a candidate for the fruit of once-returning and is no longer a stream-enterer.
This remains true for all once-returners until they give rise to a path superior to that fruit.
One is called a "once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin) because they have attained the fruit of once-returning.
However, if they give rise to a path superior to that fruit, they abandon the fruit of once-returning;
thus, they are called a "candidate for non-returning" (anāgāmi-pratipannaka) rather than a once-returner.
All those who are non-returners (anāgāmin) are called "non-returners" because they have attained the fruit of non-returning so long as they have not yet generated a path superior to that fruit;
for once they generate a path superior to that fruit, they abandon the fruit of non-returning.
One is designated as a candidate for arhatship (arhattva-pṛthagjana) and not as a non-returner (anāgāmin),
because a person (pudgala) is established based on their faculties (indriya);
it is impossible for a single individual to possess two such designations simultaneously.
In the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* composed by him, it is asked:
"Does one who is a candidate for the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin) possess the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna)?
It is answered: "He does not possess it."
Question: Does one who is a candidate for the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmipratipannaka) possess the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala)?
Answer: No, they do not possess it.
Question: Does one who is a candidate for arhatship (arhattvapratipannaka) possess the fruit of non-returning?
Answer: It is not accomplished.
The critique says:
One should state it thus.
Regarding those who gradually attain the four fruits,
although they are designated by eight names, their actual entities are only five;
this is as it is with names and entities.
It is the designation of names and the designation of entities;
it is the difference in characteristics of names and the difference in characteristics of entities;
it is the difference in nature of names and the difference in nature of entities.
Naming is the establishment of the substance;
differentiation of names is the differentiation of the substance; and conceptualization is the conceptualization of the substance.
It should be understood that the same applies to the name "awakening" (bodhi) and the essence of awakening (bodhy-ātman).
Question: If there are eight real entities, yet only five [factors] exist, [how is this so]?
How are these eight types established?
Answer: They are established based on the manifestation of the path.
That is to say, from the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up until one has not yet generated the superior path leading to that fruit.
That fruit of stream-entry has been attained, and it is both accomplished within the person and manifested in the present.
However, regarding the path of the once-returner, it has not yet been attained;
it is neither accomplished within the person nor manifested in the present.
It is called the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) and not the path of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin-pratipannaka).
If the superior path to that fruit arises and becomes manifest,
that path of the once-returner is attained, and it is both possessed within the person and becomes manifest.
When one has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) but it is neither established within the body nor manifested in the present,
this is called being a candidate for once-returning (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka) rather than possessing the fruit of stream-entry.
This applies to all once-returners until they have yet to give rise to the path superior to that fruit.
That fruit of the once-returner has been attained, is present in the body, is accomplished, and is manifest; however,
regarding the stage of the candidate for non-returning,
it has not yet been attained, is not present in the body, is not accomplished, and is not manifest.
One is called a fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala) and not one heading toward the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmipratipannaka).
If the superior path to that fruit arises and manifests, one attains the state of heading toward the fruit of non-returning; it is both accomplished within the person and manifests in the present.

One who has attained the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala) but does not possess it as an actualized attainment within their own continuum is called one "proceeding toward non-returning" (anāgāmin-patipanna), not a once-returner.
This applies to all those who have not yet given rise to the superior path leading to that fruit.
That fruit of non-returning has been attained, is present in his person, is accomplished, and is manifest; however,
regarding the stage of the candidate for arhatship,
it has not yet been attained, is not present in his person, is not accomplished, and is not manifest.
This is called the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), not the path toward arhatship (arhattvapratipannaka).
If a superior path to that fruit arises and becomes manifest, one attains the state of being a candidate for arhatship; it is both achieved within one's person and is also present before one.
When one has attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) but it is not yet fully established within the body and does not manifest before one,
this is called "one heading toward arhatship" (arhattvapratipannaka) rather than "the fruit of non-returning. Therefore,
although there are five entities, there are eight designations.
If one attains the four fruits through both sequential and leap-over attainment,
there are eight entities in total, comprising seven types.

This means that within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is one who is a candidate for the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*) who has not yet attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).

There is one who is heading toward the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmiphala) but has not yet attained the fruit of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala); however, there is definitely no one who is heading toward Arhatship (arhattvaphalapratipannaka) without having attained the fruit of Non-returner.
Thus, in substance, there are seven [types]. Regarding these eight persons (pudgala), how many of the nine thorough knowledges (parijñā) do they possess?
"How many are not accomplished?
and so forth, as explained at length.
In this context, the *pudgala* (person) serves as the chapter and thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) serves as the gateway.
The eight types of persons have already been explained.
Now it shall be explained that among these eight, there are those who do not achieve and those who do achieve the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*).
Among those who achieve them, some achieve only a few, while others achieve many.
This refers to those entering the stream (srotāpanna-pratipannaka), who either do not possess or do possess one, two, three, four, or five [moments].

Those who do not possess them are in the stages from the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) up to the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti).
During these five moments of mind, none of the nine types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) pertaining to the paths of seeing and cultivation have been accomplished,
because neither four nor five conditions have been fulfilled.
As for the accomplishment of one:

This refers to the stages of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-akṣānti*) and the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-akṣānti*).

During these two moments of mind, one simultaneously accomplishes the single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the abandonment of those factors of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination.

The accomplishment of two [parijñās] occurs at the stage of the *samudaya-anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge of origin) and the *nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* (receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of cessation).

This is because during these two moments of mind, one accomplishes two universal knowledges (*parijñā*) regarding the abandonment of those dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin within the three realms.
Regarding the accomplishment of the three [types of abandonment]:
this refers to the stage of the receptivity to the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (dharmajñānakṣānti) and the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (anvayajñānakṣānti).
During these two moments of mind, one accomplishes the abandonment of the factors of the three realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin.
And because of the abandonment of the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, there are three universal knowledges (*parijñā*).
As for the accomplishment of four:
this refers to the stage of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) within the category-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*).
During these two moments of mind, one achieves four universal knowledges (*parijñā*) through the abandonment of the dharmas of the three realms to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origin,
and cessation. One achieves five [universal knowledges] at the stage of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).
During these two moments of mind, one accomplishes the abandonment of the dharmas of the three realms to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation,
as well as the abandonment of the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of the path;
this is because of the five universal knowledges (*parijñā*).
The stream-enterer (srotāpanna) accomplishes six [knowledges of abandonment].
That is to say, from the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) until before the arising of a superior path to that fruit,
they accomplish the six universal knowledges of abandonment (parijñā) of the dharmas to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) within the three realms.

If one who is a candidate for the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka) enters the state of right determination (samyaktvaniyāma) while having already abandoned double the defilements of desire, they are like a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattipratipannaka).
That is to say, they may not yet possess [the factors] during the first five moments of the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Alternatively, one may achieve one, two, three, four, or five [moments] during the ten moments of mind following the path of seeing;
these correspond respectively to two moments each.
This applies if one is proceeding from the fruit of stream-entry toward the fruit of once-returning.
Furthermore, one who has attained the fruit of once-returning accomplishes six [paths],
namely: from the arising of the superior path of the fruit of stream-entry,
up to the sixth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of detachment from the defilements of desire.

All those who are called "candidates for the fruit of once-returning" range from the stage of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) or the sixth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) regarding freedom from the defilements of desire,
up until they have not yet generated the superior path to that fruit.
The one named "Fruit of Once-returner" is endowed with six [knowledges].
That is, the six universal knowledges (*parijñā*) regarding the abandonment of the dharmas to be abandoned by insight within the three realms.

As for the candidate for the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmipratipannaka*), if they have already become free from the defilement of desire and enter into the state of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*), they are like the candidate for the fruit of Stream-enterer.
That is to say, one is either not yet accomplished during the initial five moments of the path of seeing,
or one is accomplished during one, two, three, four, or five moments— namely, during the ten subsequent moments of the path of seeing—
in pairs of moments according to their respective order.
Regarding this, some say:

those who have already abandoned the defilements of desire and enter into the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) based on any of the six stages are all described as being like those in the stage of a candidate for stream-entry (srotāpatti-pratipannaka).

Some say: if one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire enters the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on the threshold concentration (anāgamya), they are described as being like those in the stage of entering the stream (srotāpatti-pratipannaka).
However, if one enters the state of right determination by relying on the five higher stages, they are not like those in the stage of entering the stream.

That is to say, from the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) up until the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvayajñānakṣānti*), full comprehension (*parijñā*) is not yet accomplished.
From the subsequent knowledge of origin up until the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvayajñānakṣānti*), one [full comprehension] is accomplished.
This refers to the full comprehension of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) regarding the dharmas of the form and formless realms to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin;
these two are accomplished from the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) up to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).
This refers to the full comprehension of abandonment regarding the dharmas of the form and formless realms to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, its origin, and its cessation.
Because the aforementioned five paths of cultivation are not the antidotes for abandoning the factors of the desire realm,

one does not attain the three universal knowledges (*parijñā*) regarding the abandonment of factors abandoned through vision during the moments of the three *dharmajñānas* concerning origin, cessation, and the path.
If one proceeds from the fruit of once-returner toward the fruit of non-returner, one accomplishes six [paths],
namely, from the arising of the superior path of the once-returner up to the ninth uninterrupted path of detachment from desire.
All are called those who have entered the path toward the fruit of non-returning.
They accomplish six [knowledges],
namely, the six universal knowledges (*parijñā*) consisting of the abandonment of the dharmas to be abandoned through seeing in the three realms.
The fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) accomplishes one [category],
namely, the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (pañcāvara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana).
This occurs either from the path of subsequent knowledge (mārgānvaya-jñāna) or from the ninth path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) regarding the detachment from desire.
As long as one has not yet given rise to the path that results in a superior fruit, it is called the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
Such a person achieves the single full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*),
which comprises the total abandonment of all factors to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) throughout the three realms.
Furthermore, because its intrinsic nature consists of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
one who is a candidate for arhatship (arhattvaphalapratipannaka) either accomplishes one or two [of these].
That is to say, one who has not yet become free from the defilements of the form realm accomplishes one.
One who has already become free from the defilements of the form realm accomplishes two [stages]:
that is, from the arising of the superior path toward the fruit of non-returner,
up until the diamond-like concentration, one is called a candidate for arhatship (arhattvaphalapratipannaka).
If one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm, one accomplishes one [complete knowledge],
namely, the complete knowledge of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca-avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana-kṣaya-parijñā*).
If one has already abandoned the defilements of the form realm, one accomplishes two.
That is to say, it consists of the aforementioned preceding one and the full knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*).
The fruit of Arhatship accomplishes one:
namely, the full knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojanakṣayaparijñā*).
Because their intrinsic nature consists in the total cessation of all phenomena within the three realms,
both Pratyekabuddhas and Mahābuddhas— just like Arhats—
accomplish only the ninth thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
Question: How many [factors] does one in the stage of training (śaikṣa) of a pratyekabuddha accomplish?
Answer: For those who travel in groups (vargacārin), it is as explained for the śrāvakas;
for those who are like a rhinoceros horn (khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa), it is as explained for the bodhisattvas.
Question: How many [factors] are accomplished in the noble stages of a bodhisattva?
Answer: Regarding the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) for now, there is this explanation.
Just as in the case of one entering the stream, during the first five moments of mind,
none of the latter ten types are fully accomplished; subsequently, during the ten moments of mind,
two, two, one, one, three, four, and five types are accomplished respectively, in each successive moment.
Furthermore, there are those who say that during the first seven moments of mind, nothing at all is accomplished;
from the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*) up to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñānakṣānti*), one [factor] is accomplished.
This refers to the full comprehension of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) regarding the dharmas of the form and formless realms abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin;
from the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) up to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), one accomplishes two:
namely, the full comprehension of abandonment regarding the dharmas of the form and formless realms abandoned through the vision of suffering, its origin, and its cessation.
Because the fourth dhyāna is not the antidote for abandoning the phenomena of the desire realm,

one does not attain the three pervasive knowledges (parijñā) regarding the abandonment of phenomena abandoned through vision during the moments of the three knowledges of origin, cessation, and the path.

From the initial knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) up until the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi), one always accomplishes one [complete knowledge], namely, the complete knowledge of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (pañca-avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana-kṣaya-parijñā).
Question: At what time does a bodhisattva attain the complete knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (rūpa-rāga-kṣaya-parijñā)?
The Venerable Saṃghavasu said:
"One attains this thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) at the stage of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
The critique states:
One should not make such a statement,
because there is no attainment of the fruit or the path for even a single moment.
However, some do make this statement.

One attains this thorough knowledge at the moment of the first uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) when becoming detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
It should not be asserted that at that time one is cultivating only the antidote path (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) of the formless realm.
Because it is not an antidote to form.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one attains this thorough knowledge when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests.
He also should not speak in such a manner.
At that time, because one has abandoned all dharmas of the three realms to be abandoned through both seeing and cultivation,
attaining a single flavor of dissociation, it is termed the "complete knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters."
How is it that one attains the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga-kṣaya*) at this time? One should say:

a Bodhisattva in the noble stage (*āryāvasthā*) definitely does not attain the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) regarding those factors to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*) within the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpyadhātu*).

Furthermore, because there is the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*) and the collective thorough knowledge (*saṃgraha-parijñā*), there is no possibility of cultivating the antidote for their abandonment.

III. The Section on Sentient Beings (*sattva-nikāya*). II. The Aggregate of Bonds (*saṃyojana-skandha*). III. The First Part of the Third Section on Sentient Beings: In each of the three realms, there are two categories of bonds (*saṃyojana*), namely those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Having thus understood these chapters and the meaning of the explanations within them, one should next provide a detailed exposition.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to reveal that the two categories of fetters (*saṃyojana*) in each of the three realms cause sentient beings to undergo various kinds of suffering;
that is to say, these fetters [act] upon sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death.
It constitutes a great bondage, a great lack of benefit, and a great peril;
because of its existence, it causes all sentient beings to undergo various sufferings and afflictions within the three realms, cycling through birth and death.
Numerous times they enter the mother’s womb and dwell between the receptacle for undigested food and the receptacle for digested food,
oppressed by various impurities in a place of profound darkness;
yet once born, they do not recognize the faults and afflictions of this bondage.
Furthermore, they return to defilement and practice it, suffering without end.
Desiring to cause sentient beings to know, see, and awaken to these fetters,
they diligently cultivate the remedies to sever these fetters and attain eternal nirvāṇa.
One will no longer transmigrate through the cycle of birth and death and undergo its sufferings.
Just as one who fails to perceive an enemy’s binding, meaningless ambushes, and perilous traps cannot avoid them,
whereas one who perceives them is able to avoid them.
Therefore, one should contemplate, deliberate, and examine various wholesome teachings that censure and revile the fetters, so that they are not forgotten even throughout successive births.
It is just as when a mother speaks thus at the very moment her newborn child is born out of her deep maternal love.
In each of the three realms, there are two categories of fetters—
those to be abandoned through seeing and those to be abandoned through cultivation. Because sentient beings are bound by these,
they repeatedly enter the mother’s womb and undergo various sufferings and afflictions.
"In the cycle of birth and death, there is no easy time of escape.
He was asked, "Venerable One, for what reason did you speak such words at the moment of your birth?
He replied, "Because while that Venerable One was in his mother's womb, he was oppressed by manifold sufferings and then thought thus:"
"For what reason do sentient beings enter the mother's womb and undergo such suffering?
Having reflected thus,
through the power of his past aspiration for extensive learning and his delight therein, he was able to understand it immediately.
This is entirely because the two types of fetters within each of the three realms have not yet been permanently severed;
therefore, from birth, they are able to censure and revile the various faults and afflictions of these two types of fetters.
For this reason, this treatise is composed.
Question: What meaning does the word "section" (varga) intend to clarify here?
Answer: It intends to clarify the sense of a "group" (saṃgha).
Just as the class of bhikṣus is called the "bhikṣu-saṃgha" and the class of brahmins is called the "brahmin-saṃgha," so it is with the others as well.
The various groups gathered here differ in name but are identical in meaning.
Question: What meaning does the word "sudden" (頓) intend to reveal here?
Answer: It reveals the meaning of "simultaneous" (一時).
How is this known?
Because it is stated in the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra concerning Mahāsena, the Great King and Lord of Kosala:
He approached the place where the Buddha was,
and having arrived, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and withdrew to sit to one side.
He greeted the World-Honored One with words of reverence and affection.
The Buddha, in turn, comforted and exhorted him according to what was appropriate.
Having finished his inquiry and the exchange of metaphors, he addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
In the past, I heard the Buddha speak these words: "In the worlds of the past,
future, and present, there has never been a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who possesses true knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena."
"If one says that such a thing exists, it is impossible.
Does the Venerable Gautama remember these words?
The Buddha said:
"I do not remember.
He spoke again to the Buddha, saying,
"In this world, there may be people who..."
"It would be inconsistent for the Venerable Gautama to receive different texts and meanings and to give different explanations.
I pray that you will carefully recall and explain this to me."
The Buddha said,
"Great King,
I recall that in the past I once spoke these words."
In the past, future, and present worlds, there has never been, nor will there ever be,
any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who can suddenly attain knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena;
if one says such a person exists, it is impossible.
Having definitively practiced hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful asceticisms throughout three incalculable eons,
and having gradually perfected the six pāramitās,
one is then able to possess the realization and vision of true wisdom regarding all phenomena.
Therefore, it is known that "sudden" (tun) is intended to signify "at one time.

Is there any instance where the two classes of fetters (saṃyojana)—those to be abandoned through vision and those to be abandoned through cultivation—within the desire realm are acquired simultaneously?
Answer: There is.
This refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has already become free from the defilement of desire (*kāmarāga*).
It occurs at the time of falling away from that freedom from desire, as well as when passing away from the form or formless realms and being reborn in the desire realm.
That is to say, it refers to those ordinary persons who have already become free from the defilement of desire.
If one falls away due to the arising of the lowest-of-the-low fetters of the desire realm,
one simultaneously acquires the lowest-of-the-low fetters abandoned through both vision and cultivation of the desire realm.
If one falls away due to the arising of the middle-of-the-low fetters of the desire realm...
One suddenly acquires the two grades of fetters—namely the lowest-of-the-low and the middle-of-the-low—to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the desire realm;

and even if one falls away by giving rise to the highest-of-the-high entanglements of the desire realm, one suddenly acquires all nine grades of fetters to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the desire realm.
Because they were previously severed all at once, they are now regained all at once.
Furthermore, when one passes away from the two upper realms and is reborn in the desire realm,
whichever of the nine grades of fetters arises to cause the continuity of birth, all [the corresponding faculties] are regained all at once.
Because there are nine grades of fetters (*saṃyojana*) in the desire realm to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation, one may suddenly attain this bondage.
Is it possible to suddenly become detached from them?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to the time when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) becomes free from the defilements of desire;
it describes the stage at which an ordinary person is freed from the defilements of desire,
wherein all the fetters of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through seeing and meditation in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are collectively grouped into nine grades.
It is like the method of cutting grass, where each stalk is severed all at once;
that is to say, by means of the lowest-lowest grade of the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one simultaneously severs the highest-highest grade of fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through both insight and cultivation within the desire realm.
Up to and including the superior uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one suddenly severs the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the desire realm; therefore,
there is a sudden liberation from these bonds.
Is there any case where one is bound gradually? Answer:

No. That is to say, it is certainly impossible to first obtain the fetters abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) of the desire realm, and subsequently obtain the fetters abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) of the desire realm.

Furthermore, it is certain that one cannot first attain the fetters of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation and subsequently attain the fetters of the desire realm to be abandoned by vision; therefore,
while there is no gradual attainment of these bonds, is there not some gradual disentanglement from them?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, a disciple of the Blessed One first abandons those fetters to be abandoned by seeing, and subsequently abandons those fetters to be abandoned by cultivation.
This means that the noble ones first sever the fetters of the desire realm to be abandoned by seeing through the path of seeing,
and subsequently sever the fetters of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation through the path of cultivation; therefore,
