there is a gradual departure from these bonds.
Is there any case where one simultaneously becomes bound by the two categories of fetters—those to be abandoned through vision and those to be abandoned through cultivation—within the form realm?
Answer: Yes.
That is, when an ordinary person who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm falls away from that detachment.
And when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire or form realms—
specifically, when an ordinary person who has already become free from attachment to the form realm falls away due to the arising of the lowest-of-the-low fetters of the form realm.
If one falls away by giving rise to the lowest-middle grade of fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the form realm,
one simultaneously acquires the two grades of fetters— lowest-lowest and lowest-middle— of the form realm abandoned through both vision and cultivation.
Furthermore, if one falls away due to the arising of increasingly intense fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
one simultaneously acquires all nine grades of fetters to be abandoned through vision and cultivation belonging to that form realm;
this refers to the [fetters] of its own level.
Whenever one regresses from each of the nine grades of fetters belonging to those lower stages,
one simultaneously acquires all nine grades of fetters to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation belonging to the higher stage.
This is likewise the case whenever one regresses from each of the nine grades of fetters belonging to the desire realm.
They also all simultaneously attain [the abandonment of] the nine grades of fetters to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the form realm.
Regarding this, some say that one should state as follows:
When an ordinary person who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm falls away due to the arising of the fetters of the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
they simultaneously acquire both categories of fetters— those abandoned through vision and those abandoned through cultivation— belonging to the form realm.
The critique states:
One should not make such a statement. Why is this?
Because here it is stated in general that the realms of attachment (*dhātu*) are acquired simultaneously; the specific stages (*bhūmi*) are not mentioned.
Whether one falls away due to the arising of the fetters of the fourth dhyāna,
or even falls away due to the arising of the fetters of the desire realm,
in all such cases, one simultaneously acquires the fetters of the form realm to be abandoned by both vision and cultivation.
Since its meaning is no different from the previous case of sudden severance, it is now likewise attained all at once.
Furthermore, when one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the desire or form realms,
whichever of the nine grades of fetters arises causes the continuity of birth to proceed.
All [of them] suddenly attain the abandonment of the nine grades of fetters (saṃyojana) to be eliminated through both insight and cultivation within the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Regarding this, some say that one should state as follows:
When one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
one simultaneously acquires the two categories of fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through vision and cultivation belonging to the form realm.
The critique says:
He should not speak in this way. Why?
Because here it is stated in general that one attains [the faculties] belonging to the realms simultaneously; it does not specify the stages (*bhūmi*).
This applies whether one is born in the fourth dhyāna or even born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

In all cases, one simultaneously attains the abandonment of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) pertaining to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); thus, their meaning is no different.
Therefore, is there one who simultaneously attains this bondage (*bandhana*), and is there one who simultaneously becomes disjoined from it?
Answer: There is.
This refers to when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) become detached from the defilements of the form realm;

it describes the stage where ordinary beings, having become detached from the defilements of the form realm, collectively group the afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through both vision (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) within each meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of the form realm into nine grades.
Just as in the method of mowing grass, where each stalk is cut off all at once,

so too does the lowest-of-the-low path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) suddenly sever the highest-of-the-high fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through both seeing and cultivation within each meditative absorption (dhyāna) of the form realm.

Up to this point, by means of the supreme uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga), one suddenly severs the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through both seeing and cultivation within each meditative absorption (dhyāna) of the form realm;
therefore, there is a sudden liberation from these bonds.
Is it possible to be bound gradually?
Answer: No. That is to say, it is certain that one cannot first attain the fetters (saṃyojana) of the form realm that are to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya).
Furthermore, it is certain that one does not first attain the fetters abandoned through cultivation in the form realm and subsequently attain the fetters abandoned through vision in the form realm.
Therefore, there is no gradual attainment of this bondage.
Is there, however, a gradual dissociation from it?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to the disciples of the Blessed One who first abandon those fetters to be abandoned by seeing,
and subsequently abandon those fetters to be abandoned by cultivation;
that is, the noble ones who first abandon the fetters of the form realm to be abandoned by seeing through the path of seeing.
Subsequently, by means of the path of cultivation, one abandons the fetters of the form realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation;
thus, there is a gradual separation from these bonds.
Regarding the two categories of fetters in the formless realm—those to be abandoned through seeing and those to be abandoned through cultivation—[the same applies].
Is it possible to be bound [to the formless realm] all at once?
Answer: No. That is to say, there are no ordinary beings who are entirely free from the defilements of the formless realm.

Furthermore, there is no such principle that one who has fallen from their state due to the subsequent arising of lower fetters would suddenly acquire the fetters of the formless realm to be abandoned by vision and cultivation;
nor is there any case of an ordinary being dying in the upper realms of the three worlds and being reborn within those same three worlds.
Since it is impossible to simultaneously attain the state of being free from the fetters abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the formless realm,
there is no such thing as the simultaneous attainment of this disconnection. Is there,
however, any case of simultaneous disconnection from these bonds?
Answer: No.

This is because there is no sense in which an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) can be entirely free from defilement within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); therefore, it is certain that there is no simultaneous abandonment of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through both insight (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in the formless realm.
This is explained in terms of the *dhātus* (realms) and not in terms of the *bhūmis* (stages).
Although there is the sense of "sudden detachment" when explained in terms of the *bhūmis*,
this is not what is intended to be demonstrated here.
Therefore, there is no sudden liberation from these fetters.
One should understand that the absence of sudden attainment follows the same principle.
Is it possible to have gradual attainment of fetters?

Answer: No. That is to say, it is definitively impossible that one first attains the fetters of the formless realm to be abandoned by seeing, and subsequently attains the fetters of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation.
Furthermore, it is certain that one cannot first obtain the fetters of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation and subsequently obtain those to be abandoned by insight; therefore,
there is no gradual acquisition of these bonds.
Is there such a thing as being gradually freed from the fetters?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, a disciple of the Blessed One first becomes free from those fetters abandoned through seeing, and subsequently becomes free from those fetters abandoned through cultivation.
This refers to the noble ones who first abandon the fetters of the formless realm to be abandoned by seeing through the path of seeing,
and subsequently abandon the fetters of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation through the path of cultivation.
Therefore, there is gradual separation from these fetters.

Question: When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or a noble one (*ārya*) becomes separated from the nine grades of defilement of any given stage, how many paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and how many paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are required to achieve that separation?

Some say that an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) abandons the nine grades of defilement solely through three paths of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) and three paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga); that is,
they abandon the upper three grades of defilement by means of the lower grade path of immediate succession and path of liberation.
By means of the middle-grade uninterrupted path and path of liberation, one abandons the three middle grades of defilement;
by means of the superior-grade uninterrupted path and path of liberation, one abandons the three lower grades of defilement.
It is the same for noble ones (*ārya*).
Other masters say that ordinary beings abandon the nine grades of defilement all at once through a single grade of the path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation,
whereas noble ones gradually abandon the nine grades of defilement through nine grades of the path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation.
Why is this? Because the path of ordinary beings is dull regarding the abandonment of the objects of knowledge;
it cannot be differentiated into nine grades.
Therefore, a single category of the path eliminates it all at once.
For the noble ones, the benefit of the path lies in its capacity to eliminate what is to be known;
it is able to skillfully analyze [the afflictions] into the distinctions of nine categories.
Therefore, one gradually abandons them through the nine grades of the path.
The critique states:
He should not have made such a statement.
If one were to say this in order to show that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are inferior to noble ones (*ārya*),
it would conversely imply that noble ones are inferior to ordinary beings.
[Furthermore,] if ordinary beings were to abandon the nine grades of defilement by means of a single grade of the path...
The noble ones abandon the nine grades of defilement by means of the nine grades of the path;
is it not then the case that the noble ones are inferior to ordinary beings?
It is like when one who has consumed much poison is able to expel it all at once by drinking a small amount of medicine—who would not praise such a thing as excellent?
One should say this:

there are no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) or noble ones (*ārya*) who do not abandon the nine grades of defilement by means of the nine paths of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Question: If that is so, then...
What is the distinction between ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*)?

Answer: Ordinary beings, by means of nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), collectively categorize the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the paths of seeing and cultivation into nine grades.
Just as in the method of mowing grass, where it is cut off all at once in distinct sections,
so too do the noble ones, by means of a single path of uninterrupted realization and a single path of liberation,
suddenly sever the nine grades of fetters to be abandoned through seeing.

By means of nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one gradually abandons the nine grades of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
This is called the distinction between ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
Question: When an ordinary person or a noble one becomes detached from the defilements of a particular stage (*bhūmi*) in their nine grades, [how does this occur]?
By how many preparatory applications (*prayoga*) and by how many meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) is detachment attained? Some say:
through three preparatory applications and three meditative attainments, one becomes detached from the nine grades of defilement.
That is to say: by means of the first preparatory application and the first entry into meditative absorption, one abandons the three superior grades;
by means of the second preparatory application and the second entry into meditative absorption, one abandons the three intermediate grades;
and by means of the third preparatory application and the third entry into meditative absorption, one abandons the three inferior grades.
The critique states:
One should say this:
the matter is not fixed.
There may be one who, through a single preparatory effort and a single entry into meditative absorption, becomes free from the nine grades of defilement;
or there may be one who, through as many as nine preparatory efforts and nine entries into meditative absorption, becomes free from the nine grades of defilement.
Question: When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or a noble one (*ārya*) becomes detached from the nine grades of defilement of any given stage, is this for the sake of cessation or not?
Some say as follows:
Ordinary beings do not cease [from afflictions];
noble ones may either cease or not cease.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
The Noble One does not cease;
ordinary persons may either cease or not cease.
The critique says:
It should be stated as follows:
this matter is not fixed;
that is to say, both ordinary persons and noble ones may either cease or not cease their separation from the nine grades of defilement.
Other masters say that while one does not cease [the outflows] by being free from the defilements of the desire realm,
one may or may not cease them by being free from the defilements of the form and formless realms.
Some say that the cessation [of defilements] does not occur apart from the defilements of the form and formless realms;
it may or may not occur apart from the defilements of the desire realm.
The critique says:
One should say this:
this matter is not fixed;

for those who are free from the defilements of the three realms, there are both those for whom [the defilements] have ceased and those for whom they have not ceased, yet all are free from the nine grades.

Question: When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or a noble one (*ārya*) falls away due to the arising of the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments), which grade of *paryavasthāna* arises and which grade of *saṃyojana* (fetters) is acquired?
Regarding this, some say:
when an ordinary person falls away due to the arising of any one of the three lower grades of *paryavasthāna*, they acquire the fetters of the three lower grades.
Among these, when one falls away due to the arising of any one of the three grades [of defilements], one acquires six grades of fetters from the lower and middle categories;
when one falls away due to the arising of any one of the three grades [of defilements] from the upper category, one acquires nine grades of fetters.

When a noble one falls away due to the arising of the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters, they acquire the lowest-of-the-low grade of bonds; when they fall away due to the arising of the middle-of-the-low grade of fetters, they acquire two grades of bonds:
the lowest-of-the-low and the middle-of-the-low.
Up until the point where one falls away due to the arising of the highest-grade (adhimātra-adhimātra) fetters, one acquires all nine grades of fetters.
Furthermore, there are those who say that for an ordinary person (pṛthagjana),
whenever they fall away due to the arising of even a single grade of fetter among the nine grades, they acquire all nine grades of fetters.
The meaning of the noble ones' falling back is as previously explained.
Why is this? Because ordinary beings merely sustain their mental continuum through the power of worldly meditative concentration (*laukika-samādhi*).
Because the power of worldly meditative concentration is weak and inferior, the pure state is not firm and defiled phenomena are easily obtained;
even the noble ones maintain their continuity through the power of untainted meditative concentration.

Because the power of the various untainted concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*) is exceptionally strong, pure phenomena (*śukla-dharma*) are firm and stable, making it difficult for defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) to arise.
[The author] critiques:
"That person should not speak in this manner."
Why is this? Because neither ordinary beings nor noble ones have ever seen anyone die from taking poison without [the poison] being ingested.
One should speak thus.
When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) falls away due to the arising of the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters (*paryavasthāna*), they acquire the lowest-of-the-low grade of bonds (*saṃyojana*).
When they fall away due to the arising of the middle-of-the-low grade of fetters, they acquire two grades of bonds: the lowest-of-the-low and the middle-of-the-low.
Even up to the point where, when one falls away due to the arising of the highest-of-the-high grades of fetters (*paryavasthāna*), one acquires the nine grades of fetters;
it is the same for the noble ones (*ārya*).
Question: If that is so, then...
What is the distinction between an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and a noble one (*ārya*)?

Answer: When an ordinary person falls away due to the arising of the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters (*paryavasthāna*), they simultaneously acquire the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters to be abandoned through both vision and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*).
When one falls away due to the arising of inferior or medium-grade fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
one simultaneously acquires two grades of fetters to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation— namely, the inferior-inferior and the inferior-medium;
this continues until, when one falls away due to the arising of superior-superior-grade fetters.
One suddenly attains the nine grades of fetters to be abandoned through both vision and cultivation;
however, when a noble one falls away due to the arising of the lowest-of-the-low grade of entanglements,
they attain only the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation.
When one falls away due to the arising of inferior or medium-grade fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
one acquires only the two grades of fetters to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), namely the lowest-of-the-low and the low-of-the-medium;
this continues until, when one falls away due to the arising of the highest-of-the-high grade of fetters.
Only the nine grades of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) can be acquired through falling away;
there is no possibility of acquiring through falling away those fetters to be abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya).
This is what constitutes the distinction between ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) and noble ones (ārya).
Other masters say:
when one falls away from any one of the three lower grades of the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) of the desire realm,
one acquires the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three lower grades of the desire realm.
When one falls away from the abandonment of any one of the three grades of fetters of the desire realm,
one acquires the six grades of fetters of the lower and middle [levels] of the desire realm;
likewise when one falls away from the abandonment of any one of the three grades of fetters of the upper [level] of the desire realm.
When one falls away from the nine grades of fetters of the desire realm due to the arising of the lowest-low grade of entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) of the form or formless realms,
one acquires those lowest-low grade fetters.
When one falls away due to the arising of the lower-middle grade of entanglements of the form or formless realms, [one likewise acquires those].
When one falls away due to the arising of the two grades of fetters— the lowest-of-the-low and the low-of-the-middle— up to the highest-of-the-high fetters of the form and formless realms,
one acquires those nine grades of fetters.
Some say that when one falls away from any one of the nine grades of fetters belonging to the desire realm,
one simultaneously acquires all nine grades of fetters of the desire realm.
If one falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the form or formless realms,
the meaning is as previously explained. Why is this so?
In the desire realm, defiled states that lack meditative concentration are easily obtained;
whereas in the form and formless realms, defiled states that possess meditative concentration are difficult to obtain.
The critique says:
He should not speak in this way;
for when afflictions are abandoned, it is always by means of meditative concentration.
He should speak in this way:
Among the afflictions of the nine stages within the three realms,
when one falls back due to the arising of the lowest-of-the-low grade of fetters (paryavasthāna),
one acquires only the lowest-of-the-low grade of bonds (saṃyojana); likewise, when one falls back due to the arising of the middle-of-the-low grade of fetters...
In all cases, one acquires the two grades of fetters— the lowest-of-the-low and the low-of-the-middle—
and so on, up until the time when one regresses due to the arising of the highest-of-the-high entanglements,
at which point one acquires all nine grades of fetters.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume Sixty-three;
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Sixty-four.

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Two: The Aggregate of Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha). Sub-section Three: The Chapter on Sentient Beings (Sattva-nikāya), Part Two. There are three circumstances in which a noble one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) passes away.
1. One who dies having completely abandoned all defilements;
2. one who dies having completely fallen away from them;
3. one who dies having partially abandoned them.
Ordinary beings die only under two circumstances:
first, they die having completely detached from defilements;
second, they die having completely fallen away [from detachment].
There is no one who passes away without being free from defilement.
For a noble one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are two ways of passing away:
first, passing away while completely free from defilement; [second, passing away while still possessing defilements].
Those who pass away having become detached from two categories [of defilements] do not undergo retrogression,
because there is no possibility of retrogression in the form and formless realms.
Ordinary beings die with only one circumstance:
namely, that they have completely abandoned defilement, because there is no retrogression from it,
and because there is no death while still separated from defilement.
It should be understood that the same applies to noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Question: Why do noble ones die having separated from defilements (*kleśa*), whereas ordinary beings do not?
Answer: Because noble ones possess untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*).
It sustains the continuity [of the mind] and renders it extremely firm.
Ordinary beings possess only mundane meditative absorptions;
these sustain the continuity but do not render it extremely firm.
Furthermore, noble ones achieve superior śamatha and vipaśyanā, whereas ordinary beings do not.
Furthermore, noble ones possess the power of the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga), whereby they act according to their will.
Ordinary beings are not like this;
therefore, while it is possible for noble ones to die having separated from defilements,
this is not the case for ordinary beings.
Some say that all noble ones possess three kinds of power:
first, the power of the noble path; [and so forth].
Second is the power of afflictions;
third is the power of determinate karma.

Due to the power of determinate karma, there is the possibility of passing away while completely free from defilements; due to the power of afflictions, there is the possibility of passing away after having completely fallen back [from the state of non-defilement].
By the power of the Noble Path, there is the possibility of passing away while still separated from defilements; ordinary worldlings, however, possess only two kinds of power:
namely, the power of afflictions and the power of determinate karma.
Due to the absence of the power of the Noble Path,
yet by the power of determinate karma (*niyata-karma*), there is the possibility of passing away while entirely free from defilement (*vairāgya*).
Due to the power of the afflictions (*kleśa*), there is the possibility of passing away after having completely fallen away [from that state].
Because they lack the power of the Noble Path, there is no possibility of passing away while still possessed of defilements.
Other masters state that noble ones possess three powers.
First, the power of karma;
second, the power of afflictions;
third, the power of determinate karma.
Due to the power of the path, there are those who pass away having completely abandoned all defilements;
due to the power of afflictions, there are those who pass away having completely regressed;
and due to the power of determinate karma.
Therefore, there are those who die having completely abandoned defilements;
because they have attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of birth in that stage,
their determinate karma (*niyata-vedanīya-karman*) no longer yields its fruit.
Because this determinate karma acts as an obstacle,
there are those who die while still separated from defilement,
such as those who go from family to family (*kulaṃkula*).
Ordinary beings possess only two powers,
namely the power of the path and the power of afflictions;
they lack the power of determinate karma.
Due to the power of the path, there are those who die having completely abandoned defilement;
due to the power of afflictions, there are those who die having completely fallen away [from their attainment];
because there is no power of determinate karma, there are none who die having partially abandoned defilement.
Since it is possible for one who has completely abandoned defilement to be reborn again in this very stage,
karma that is definitely to be experienced (niyata-vedanīya) cannot be obstructed.
Alternatively, some say:
Regarding the separation from the defiled states, there is the distinct establishment of noble individuals (*ārya-pudgala*):
namely, by being separated from three or four categories of defilement of the desire realm, one is established as a "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) practitioner;
by being separated from six categories of defilement, one is established as a "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*).

Because one who has abandoned seven or eight categories [of afflictions] is established separately as an "ekavīcika" (one-interval practitioner), it follows that noble ones (ārya) can pass away while still possessing a partial separation from defilements (*kleśa-viveka*).

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), however, certainly do not possess such a state of partial separation from defilements; thus, they are not established as a distinct type of person (*pudgala*) in the manner of the noble ones.
Therefore, there is no sense in which one could pass away after having become free from defilement without being separated [from that state]. Furthermore,

some say that because noble ones possess mastery over meditative concentration, there are those who pass away while separated from only a small portion of their defilements at the time of becoming free from them.
Ordinary beings lack mastery over meditative concentration;
therefore, when they become free from passion, there is no one who dies while still possessing even a small portion [of defilements].
Thus said the Venerable Saṃghavasu:
Ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) may also die while in a state of being separated from defilements;
however, once they have died and at the moment of linking to a new birth (*pratisaṃdhi-citta*), the fetters previously severed necessarily reappear as accomplished.
The critique says:
He should not make such a statement,
for the power of his mind at the moment of death was weak.
Since the fetters previously abandoned have already been accomplished, what was stated previously is logically sound.
Question: When one becomes detached from all defilements by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), [what occurs]?
How many aspects do the paths of uninterrupted liberation possess?
Answer: The various paths of uninterrupted liberation possess three aspects.
First, the aspect of coarseness (*audārikākāra*).
Second, the aspect of ascetic practices;
third, the aspect of the obstacles;
and the various paths of liberation have three aspects.
First, the aspect of tranquility;
second, the aspect of excellence;
third, the aspect of detachment.
Question: Among the aspects (ākāra) within the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), which aspect arises subsequently, and what aspect arises in the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga)?
Regarding this, some say:
Following the coarse aspect,
after the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga),
one gives rise to the calm aspect as the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
Immediately following the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) characterized by the aspect of suffering,
there arises the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) characterized by the aspect of excellence.
Immediately following the uninterrupted path characterized by the aspect of the obstacle...
The path of liberation has the aspect of "arising and departing" (*niḥsaraṇa*).
Other masters say that it follows immediately after the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) which has the aspect of "coarseness" (*audārika*).
The aspect of "arising" (*udaya*) serves as the path of liberation;
following the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) characterized by the aspect of "suffering" (*duḥkha*),
the aspect of "stasis" (*sthiti*) arises as the path of liberation.
Following the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) characterized by the aspect of "hindrance," there arises the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) characterized by the aspect of "separation.
This is because they are respectively opposed to the aspects of coarseness and subtlety, suffering and tranquility, and hindrance and separation.
The commentary states:
This matter is not fixed;
it occurs after the path of uninterrupted transition from coarse characteristics.

The three types of mental aspects— peaceful (*śānta*), etc.— may arise as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) following the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that possesses the aspect of suffering (*duḥkha*). Subsequently, the three types of mental aspects—
sublime (*praṇīta*), etc.— may arise as the path of liberation following [the path of uninterrupted transition] that possesses the aspect of suffering.
Following the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) characterized by the aspect of obstructing [the defilements],
one may give rise to the three types of aspects— such as "separation" (*visamyoga*)— as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
This is because these six kinds of contaminated (*sāsrava*) aspects arise according to the inclinations of those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*).

Question: When one becomes detached from various defilements by means of the mundane path, what stage does each uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation path (*vimukti-mārga*) take as its object?
Answer: At the time of becoming detached from the defilements of the desire realm, the nine uninterrupted paths take only the desire realm as their object.
The nine paths of liberation take the first dhyāna as their object.
Question: If this is so, it is well consistent with what is taught in the Indriya-skandha.
As it is said:
"Is it possible that by contemplating the dharmas of the form realm (rūpadhātu),
one can fully comprehend the desire realm (kāmadhātu)?"
Answer: Yes.
His intention is to explain the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
How is it that the objects and aspects of the two paths do not become confused?
If the objects and modes of activity (*ālambana-ākāra*) of these two paths were confused, how could they not constitute an obstacle or hindrance to the state of freedom from defilement?
Answer: Although the objects and modes of activity of these two paths are indeed confused, [they do not obstruct it].
Regarding the state of freedom from passion (*vairāgya*), they are nonetheless unable to create obstacles or hindrances. Why is this?
Because they have already thoroughly cultivated the preparatory application (*prayoga*) along the paths leading to freedom from passion, and thus it has been perfected.
Just as in the Path of Seeing,
after the patience and knowledge that take the desire realm as their object, the patience and knowledge that take the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) as their object manifest;
and after the patience and knowledge that take the peak of existence as their object, the patience and knowledge that take the desire realm as their object manifest.
Although the objects of focus and the mental aspects may be confused during the process of clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
they cannot act as obstacles or hindrances.
Why is this? Because they have already perfected their preparatory practice (*prayoga*) through thorough cultivation within the various paths of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
This case is likewise.
Therefore, there is no error.

Some say that at the time of becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm, both the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation take the desire realm as their object.
The final liberation takes the first dhyāna as its object.
For example, when one becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception through the knowledge of cessation or the knowledge of the path,
both the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation take cessation or the path as their object.

The final path of liberation takes as its object the four contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); this case is likewise.
Other masters say that at the time of becoming free from the defilement of desire, there may be no cessation (*nirodha*), or there may be cessation.
Regarding those that are without cessation:
the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and eight paths of liberation all take the desire realm as their object;
the final path of liberation takes the first dhyāna as its object.
There is cessation:
either one ceases upon being separated from a single grade,
or one ceases upon being separated from two grades.
In this manner, it continues until, having abandoned up to eight categories [of afflictions],
one finally attains cessation. If cessation occurs upon abandoning only a single category,
that path of uninterrupted transition takes the desire realm as its object.
If the path of liberation takes the first dhyāna as its object and ceases upon the abandonment of two categories [of afflictions],
those two are the paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The first path of liberation takes the desire realm as its object;
the second path of liberation takes the first dhyāna as its object.
In this manner, it continues until, if one ceases [the defilements] only after abandoning eight categories, [the final path of liberation takes the ninth category as its object].
Those eight paths of uninterrupted transition and seven paths of liberation all take the desire realm as their object;
the eighth path of liberation takes the first dhyāna as its object.
Some teachers say:
When one becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm, both the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the nine paths of liberation take the desire realm as their object.
This is just as when one becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm through the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination;
in those cases, both the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the nine paths of liberation all take the desire realm as their object.
This case is also like that. Question:

If this is so, although there is no fault of confusion between the objects and aspects of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), [how is it resolved]?
How should one interpret what is stated in the *Indriya-skandha*?
For example, it asks:
"Is it possible that by contemplating the dharmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one can fully comprehend (*parijñā*) the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?"
Answer: There is.
That intention refers to the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
The answer was stated in reliance on the application proximate to the aggregate of faculties (*indriya-skandha*).
That is to say, when a practitioner is about to become free from the defilement of desire,
they first give rise to such analytical reflection:
"The suffering, coarseness, and hindrances of the desire realm are contrasted with the tranquility, subtlety, and seclusion of the first dhyāna."
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret what is stated later in the *Indriya-skandha*, such as:
"Is there anyone who, while contemplating dharmas of the formless realm, can fully comprehend [the dharmas] of the desire realm?"
Answer: No. His intention was to speak of the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇaparijñā*).
How could it be that a practitioner is about to become free from the defilement of desire?
Does one not first give rise to this discriminative reflection:
"Is the suffering of the desire realm coarse and obstructive, while the formless realm is tranquil, sublime, and detached?
Answer: Although one does indeed give rise to such discriminative reflection.
The distant is not the proximate.
It is not the case that by contemplating the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one can immediately induce the path that brings about freedom from desire;

rather, it is by contemplating the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as the proximate preparatory application (*sāmantaka-prayoga*) that one can immediately induce the path that brings about freedom from desire.
Therefore, those two explanations do not contradict one another.

Furthermore, there are those who say that at the time of becoming free from the defilements of desire, both the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) take the first dhyāna as their object.
Question: If that is so,
it is well explained by what is stated in the Indriya-skandha, as it says:
Is it possible that by contemplating the dharmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one can fully comprehend (*parijñā*) the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to the full comprehension through abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
Furthermore, there is no fault of confusion between the objects and modes of apprehension of two distinct paths.
How can one abandon the defilements of another stage by taking that other stage as an object?
Answer: There is no such fault here either.
Just as when the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path are free from all defilements,
they sever suffering and its origin even while taking cessation and the path as their objects;
this case is likewise.
The commentary states:
Although each of these various explanations can generate the wisdom of the disciples,
the first explanation is superior in terms of principle.
This means that all nine paths of uninterrupted transition take the desire realm as their object,
while all nine paths of liberation take the first dhyāna as their object. Why is this so?
When one becomes free from the defilements of desire through the mundane path,
it is by means of revulsion toward the lower realm and aspiration for the upper realm that detachment is achieved;
this is as when one becomes free from the defilements of the seven higher stages after being free from the defilements of the desire realm.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Question: Within each of the mundane paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), how many types of aspects (*ākāra*) can be cultivated?
Answer: When ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are free from the defilements of desire (*kāma-rāga*).
In the nine paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), one cultivates three aspects (*ākāra*):
namely, suffering (*duḥkha*), coarseness (*audārika*), and obstruction (*ādīnava*). In the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one cultivates six aspects:
namely, suffering, coarseness, obstruction, as well as tranquility (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).
Within the final path of liberation, one cultivates these six aspects;
one also cultivates the infinite aspects of the first dhyāna stage in the future.
In this manner, it continues until one is free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness.
It should be understood that the same applies according to the specific case.
When noble beings become detached from the defilements of desire,
they cultivate nineteen aspects within the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
This refers to the three aspects such as "coarse" (audārika) and so forth, as well as the sixteen noble aspects (ākāra) of the contaminated and uncontaminated.
Within the eight paths of liberation, twenty-two aspects are cultivated;
namely, the three such as "coarse" and the three such as "calm" (śānta).
As well as the sixteen noble aspects, both contaminated and uncontaminated;
within the final path of liberation, one cultivates these twenty-two aspects,
and also cultivates the infinite aspects of the stage of the first dhyāna in the future.
That is to say, when the noble ones become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
they cultivate nineteen aspects during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*):
namely, the three aspects such as "coarse" (*audārika*) and so forth, together with the sixteen pure (*anāsrava*) noble aspects.
Within the eight paths of liberation, twenty-two aspects (*ākāra*) are cultivated;
namely, the three aspects such as "coarse" (*audārika*), the three such as "calm" (*śānta*),
and the sixteen noble aspects (*āryākāra*) which are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
In the final path of liberation, one cultivates these twenty-two aspects;
likewise, one also cultivates the infinite aspects of the second dhyāna stage in the future.
This should be understood to apply accordingly up to the point of becoming free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Question: Why is it that the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna cultivates both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) sixteen aspects of the noble ones (*āryākāra*)?
Question: Do the access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) of the higher stages cultivate only the untainted (*anāsrava*)?

Answer: Since the access concentration of the first dhyāna possesses the aspects of the noble ones (*ārya*), it is able to cultivate both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted sixteen aspects of the noble ones.
The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher levels lack the aspects of the noble path;
therefore, they can cultivate only uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) aspects.
Some state this as follows:
When ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) become free from the defilement of desire,
they cultivate nine aspects during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*);
namely, the three beginning with "coarse" (*audārika*), as well as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
In the contemplation of impurity and the mindfulness of breathing,
one cultivates twelve aspects within the eight paths of liberation; that is,
the aforementioned nine together with the three aspects of tranquility and so forth.
In the final path of liberation, one cultivates these twelve aspects;
one also cultivates the infinite aspects of the first dhyāna stage in the future.
This is when the noble ones become free from the defilements of desire.
Within the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), twenty-five aspects of cultivation are practiced; namely,
the three aspects such as coarseness (*audārika*) and so forth, loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*),
the contemplation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*).
Furthermore, there are the sixteen noble aspects (ākāra) of both the contaminated and the uncontaminated.
Within the eight paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga), twenty-eight aspects are cultivated;
that is to say, the aforementioned twenty-five together with the three aspects of tranquility (śamatha) and so forth.
In the final path of liberation, one cultivates these twenty-eight aspects;
one also cultivates the infinite aspects of the future first dhyāna stage.
The meaning of cultivating the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher stages is as previously explained.
Question: Why is it that the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna can cultivate such various modes of activity (*ākāra*), whereas the preparatory stages of the higher levels cannot?
Answer: Because the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna possesses various roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Therefore, one is able to cultivate these various modes of activity; however,
because the wholesome roots in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher levels are slight,
one cannot cultivate such various modes of activity there.
Furthermore, the afflictions of the desire realm possess various characteristics and thus require the cultivation of various roots of goodness as their antidotes;
however, because the afflictions of the higher realms lack such various characteristics,
they do not cultivate various antidotes.
Question: It has already been explained previously that the present simultaneous carrying of a burden is functional,
and that its modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) pertain to the mundane path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
What is the object of those [mental applications] cultivated for the future?

Answer: At the time of becoming free from the defilements of desire, the three modes of activity—coarseness and so forth—that are cultivated during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition have only the desire realm as their object.
Within the eight paths of liberation,
the three modes of activity— coarseness and so forth— which are cultivated in the future,
take the desire realm and the first dhyāna as their objects.
The three aspects of tranquility and so forth pertain exclusively to the first dhyāna;
they occur within the final path of liberation.
The three modes of activity— coarse and so forth— which are cultivated in the future, have all three realms as their common object.
The three modes of activity— calm and so forth— have the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their objects.
When becoming detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
during the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*),
the future cultivation of the three aspects— coarseness (*audārika*) and so forth— takes as its object only the first dhyāna.
Within the eight paths of liberation,
the three modes of activity— coarseness and so forth— which are cultivated for the future, take the first and second dhyānas as their objects;
the three modes of activity— calmness and so forth— take only the second dhyāna as their object.
In the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
the three aspects of practice— coarseness (*audārika*) and so forth— which are cultivated for the future, have all three realms as their object;
the three aspects of practice— tranquility (*śānta*) and so forth— have the second dhyāna as their object.
Up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
at the time of becoming detached from the defilements of the second dhyāna,
during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition.

The three types of coarse and so forth (*audārikādika*) mental aspects cultivated for the future are cultivated exclusively within the eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), taking only the second dhyāna as their object.
The three aspects of "coarse" (*audārika*) and so forth take the second and third dhyānas as their objects;
the three aspects of "calm" (*śānta*) and so forth take only the third dhyāna as their object.
This occurs within the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The three modes of activity—coarse and so forth—which are cultivated in the future, have all three realms as their common objects.
The three modes of activity—calm and so forth—have the third dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their objects.
When one is free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition,
the future cultivation of the three aspects— coarseness and so forth— takes only the third dhyāna as its object.
Within the eight paths of liberation,
the three aspects of coarseness (*audārikatā*) and so forth that are cultivated for the future take the third and fourth dhyānas as their objects;
the three aspects of calmness (*śāntatā*) and so forth [take the lower stages as their objects].
In the final path of liberation that takes the fourth dhyāna as its object,
the three modes of activity— coarseness and so forth— which are cultivated for the future, have all three realms as their common objects.
The three aspects of tranquility (*śānta*) and so forth take the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as their object.
At the time of becoming detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,

the three aspects of coarseness (*audārika*) and so forth— which are cultivated for the future during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*)— take only the fourth dhyāna as their object.
Within the eight paths of liberation,
the three modes of activity— coarseness and so forth— which are cultivated for the future, take the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space as their objects;
the three modes of activity— calmness and so forth— take only the sphere of infinite space as their object.
In the final path of liberation,
one cultivates the future three modes of activity— coarseness and so forth—
as well as the three modes of activity— calmness and so forth.
[This refers to] the stages from the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Question: If one is free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, what are the three modes of activity—coarseness and so forth—that are cultivated in the future during the eight paths of liberation?
Regarding those who take the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space as objects, how is the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* to be reconciled?
As it asks: "Is there a wholesome mind of the formless realm that can discern dharmas of the form and formless realms?"
Answer: No. That [statement] negates the momentary, but does not negate the continuous.
That is to say, during the duration of a single moment, there is no wholesome mind of the formless realm.
It is impossible for one who can discern material and immaterial phenomena not to cultivate the three aspects—
coarseness and so forth— in the future, within the eight paths of liberation that are free from those defilements.
Whether it takes the fourth dhyāna of the form realm as its object,
or the sphere of infinite space of the formless realm as its object— since such cases exist, this refutes the momentary [nature] but does not refute the continuum.
Both this and that explanation are equally valid.
When one is free from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Space,
during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga),...
The three future modes of activity, such as "coarseness" (audārika) and so forth, which are cultivated,
take only the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana) as their object.
This refers to the three future modes of activity, such as "coarseness" and so forth, cultivated during the eight paths of liberation (vimuktimārga).
Taking the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness as objects,
the three aspects of "calm" and so forth take only the sphere of infinite consciousness as their object.
Within the final path of liberation, the three future aspects of "coarse" and so forth, as well as the three aspects of "calm" and so forth, are cultivated.
Regarding the spheres from the base of infinite consciousness up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
when one is detached from the defilements of the base of infinite consciousness,
the three aspects— coarseness and so forth— cultivated in the nine paths of uninterrupted transition take only the base of infinite consciousness as their object.
The three aspects— coarseness and so forth— cultivated in the future during the eight paths of liberation take the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and the Sphere of Nothingness as their objects.
The three aspects— tranquility and so forth— take only the Sphere of Nothingness as their object.
In the final path of liberation,
the future cultivated aspects of the three types— coarse and so forth— and the three types— calm and so forth—
which take the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their objects.
When one is detaching from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),

the three modes of activity— coarseness (*audārikatā*) and so forth— cultivated in the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) of the future exclusively take the sphere of nothingness as their object;
likewise, the three modes of activity— coarseness and so forth— cultivated in the eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) of the future [take the same object].
The three aspects of "calm" and so forth take the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their objects; however, these three aspects—
coarseness and so forth— which are cultivated in the future during the final path of liberation, take only the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their object.
And as for the three aspects of tranquility (*śānta*) and so forth, they take only the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as their object.

Question: Why is it that the aspects of coarseness (*audārika*) and so forth, which are cultivated in the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and are included within the future dhyānas, take all three realms as their objects?
Do the aspects such as "coarseness" (audārikatā) subsumed under the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu) exclusively take the formless realm as their object?
Answer: Within the stages of dhyāna, there is pervasive knowledge (sarvatraga-jñāna) that is able to take its own stage, the lower stages, and the higher stages as objects.
In the formless realms (*ārūpyabhūmi*), there is no knowledge that takes everything as its object;
it takes only its own level or higher levels as objects, but not lower levels.
Furthermore, in the dhyāna realms, spiritual qualities (*guṇa*) are coarse and manifest, making them easy [to perceive].
This is easy to understand.
It is not a formless stage (*ārūpyabhūmi*).
Furthermore, within the dhyāna stages, there are many virtues and many benefits.
The formless realms are not so.
Furthermore, within the stages of dhyāna, the wholesome states possess various different characteristics and natures;
the formless realms are not so.
Furthermore, within the stages of dhyāna, there are roots with distinct characteristics, sensations with distinct characteristics, and mental states and mental factors with distinct characteristics;
this is not the case for the formless realms.
Therefore, at that time, the practice of future [states] subsumed under dhyāna possesses the common characteristics of coarseness and so forth.
Those [aspects] such as "coarseness" that take the three realms as their object, and those subsumed under the formless [realms] which take only the formless realm as their object;
and the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned by vision in the desire realm— within what fruit are these included?
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Previously, it was explained how the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms and two categories are abandoned, both instantaneously and gradually.
It has not yet been stated under which fruit that abandonment is subsumed;
wishing now to explain this, the following treatise is composed.
Under which fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through insight in the desire realm subsumed?
Answer: It is included within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or it is not included in any.

That which is subsumed under the four fruits of śrāmaṇya refers to the time when one realizes the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) through the exhaustion of those fetters; at that moment, it is subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry.
When one realizes the fruit of once-returner, it is subsumed within the fruit of once-returner;
when one realizes the fruit of non-returner, it is subsumed within the fruit of non-returner;
and when one realizes the fruit of arhatship, it is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship.
Alternatively, "without a locus" refers to ordinary persons who have already abandoned the defilements of desire; their exhaustion of fetters is not subsumed under the fruits [of the path].
This also applies to those who, having already abandoned the defilements of desire, enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
During the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), those fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted but are not included within the fruit (*phala*).

Regarding the sequential practitioner (*anupūrvaka*), during the two moments of the clear realization of the path (*mārgābhisamaya*), those fetters are exhausted but are not included within the fruit.
Within which fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) included?
Answer: It refers to the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) or the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala).
Alternatively, regarding those not subsumed under the fruit of non-returning:
when one realizes the fruit of non-returning through the exhaustion of those fetters (saṃyojana), at that very moment they are subsumed under the fruit of non-returning.
Regarding that which is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship:
when one realizes the fruit of arhatship through the exhaustion of those fetters, it is then subsumed under the fruit of arhatship.
Alternatively, regarding "no location": this refers to ordinary persons who have already abandoned the defilement of desire; for them, the exhaustion of those fetters is not subsumed under any fruit.
For one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire and entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
the exhaustion of those fetters (*saṃyojana*) during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is not included within the [supramundane] fruits.
This is because that which lacks sequential progression is not included within the fruits.
Why is this? It is because those [defilements] are severed only when the ninth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the taints of desire ceases;
at the moment the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises, one realizes the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Since the exhaustion of those fetters is subsumed under the fruit of non-returning,
to which fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through vision in the form realm subsumed?
Answer: It is either among the four fruits of śrāmaṇya or there is no such place.
Regarding that which is subsumed within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya:
when one realizes the exhaustion of those fetters and attains the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), it is then subsumed within the fruit of stream-entry.
Up until the time one realizes the fruit of arhatship, it is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship.

Alternatively, regarding "no location," this refers to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*); their exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana-kṣaya*) is not subsumed under any [noble] fruit.
For one who has already become free from the defilement of form and has entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
the exhaustion of those fetters (*saṃyojana*) during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is not comprised within the fruit.
This is because that which lacks sequential progression does not have the sense of being comprised within a fruit.

Why is this? It is because it is precisely at the moment when the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) ceases that those [fetters] are abandoned; and at the moment when the subsequent knowledge of the path arises, one realizes the first three fruits as appropriate.
This is because the exhaustion of those fetters is subsumed within the first three fruits.
In what fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through cultivation in the form realm included?
Answer: It is included in the fruit of arhatship;
or, there is no specific location.
That which is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship refers to the exhaustion of those fetters at the moment one realizes the fruit of arhatship; it is thus subsumed under the fruit of arhatship.

Alternatively, "no location" refers to ordinary worldlings who have already become free from attachment to the realm of form; for them, the exhaustion of those fetters is not subsumed under any [noble] fruit.
For one who has already abandoned attachment to form (*rūparāga*) and entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
such as during the fifteen moments of mind in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) or at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) and so forth—
while still in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*)— the exhaustion of those fetters (*saṃyojana*) is not included within the [specific] fruits [of the spiritual path].

Regarding the sequence: from the ninth path of liberation that follows the detachment from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, up until the time when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, those fetters are exhausted but are not yet comprised within the fruit.
To which fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through vision in the formless realm subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
That is to say, when the exhaustion of those fetters is realized at the time of attaining the fruit of stream-entry, it is subsumed within the fruit of stream-entry.
Up until the time one realizes the fruit of arhatship, it is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship.
There is no sense in which an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is not subsumed within a fruit. Why is this so?

Because there is no ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) capable of abandoning the fetters to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Furthermore, the meaning of "not being included within the fruit" does not apply to those who follow the gradual path (*anupūrvika*). Why is this so?
It is only when the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) ceases that those [fetters] are abandoned;
at the moment the subsequent knowledge of the path arises, one realizes the first three fruits as appropriate,
because the exhaustion of those fetters is subsumed within those very three fruits.
To what fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm subsumed?
Answer: It is the fruit of arhatship.
That is to say, when the exhaustion of those fetters is realized at the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship, it is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship itself.
It is not the case that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are not included within the category of "fruits. Why is this?

Because there is no ordinary being capable of abandoning the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Furthermore, there is no sense in which that which lacks sequential order is not subsumed under the category of "result. Why is this?
Because it is only when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) manifests that those [defilements] are finally severed and exhausted.
When the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) first arises, one realizes the fruit of arhatship;
for that exhaustion of fetters is itself subsumed within the fruit of arhatship.
There are five classes of fetters.
This refers to the fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering, up to and including those abandoned through cultivation.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: Although it was previously stated that the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) of the three realms and two categories is subsumed within the various fruits [of the path], it was not yet stated which fruits subsume the exhaustion of the fetters of the five categories.
This treatise is now composed in order to explain this.
To which fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering subsumed?
The answer is: it is subsumed within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or there is no [specific] location.
As for being subsumed within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya: [it is so].
This means that when those fetters are exhausted and the fruit of stream-entry is realized, it is subsumed within the fruit of stream-entry;
and so on, up until when the fruit of arhatship is realized, it is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship.
Alternatively, "having no locus" means that there is no ordinary being (pṛthagjana);
it does not mean the sense of not being included within the fruits [of the path]. Why is this so?
There is no ordinary person capable of abandoning the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding the sequence: the clear realization of suffering lasts for the duration of a single moment of mind;
the clear realizations of origin and cessation each last for the duration of four moments of mind.
During the three moments of the path of clear realization (*mārgābhisamaya*),
the exhaustion of those fetters (*saṃyojana*) is not included within the fruit [of the path].
To which fruit does the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*) belong?
The answer is: either they are included within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, as previously explained;
or, regarding those not so included, there is no sense in which an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not subsumed under a fruit.

Why is this so? Because there is no ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) capable of abandoning the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

As for the sequence: the clear realization of the origin (*samudaya-abhisamaya*) lasts for one moment of mind, while the clear realization of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya*) lasts for four moments of mind.
During the three moments of mind of the path of clear realization (*mārgābhisamaya*),
that exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*) is not included within a fruit.
Within which fruit is the exhaustion of fetters abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) included?
Answer: It is comprised within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or it has no location.
That which is subsumed under the four fruits of śrāmaṇya is as previously explained.
Alternatively, "having no place" means that there are no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who are not included within the fruit [of the path]. Why is this so?

Because there are no ordinary beings capable of abandoning the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Regarding the sequence: the clear realization of cessation lasts for the duration of one moment of mind;
the clear realization of the path lasts for the duration of three moments of mind.
The exhaustion of those fetters is not included within the fruit.
To which fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through the path of seeing subsumed?
The answer is: the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
That is to say, when the exhaustion of those fetters is realized at the time of attaining the fruit of stream-entry, it is subsumed within the fruit of stream-entry.
Up until the time one realizes the fruit of arhatship, it is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship itself;
there is no sense in which an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is not subsumed within a fruit. Why is this so?

There is no ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who can abandon the fetters to be severed by the path of vision (darśanamārga-prahātavya-saṃyojana) pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Furthermore, there is no one who attains them successively; this is because [the fruit] is not comprised within the meaning of a result (phala). Why is that?
It is only when the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) ceases that those [fetters] are completely abandoned.
When the subsequent knowledge of the path arises, one realizes the first three fruits as appropriate,
because the exhaustion of those fetters is subsumed within those same three fruits.
By what fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) subsumed?
Answer: The fruit of arhatship (arhattva-phala).
That is to say, when the exhaustion of those fetters is realized at the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship, it is subsumed within that very fruit of arhatship.
There is no ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is not included within the category of the fruit. Why is this?

Because there is no ordinary person capable of abandoning the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Furthermore, there is no sense in which that which lacks sequential order is not subsumed under the category of "fruit. Why is this so?
Because it is only when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests that those [defilements] are finally severed and exhausted.
When the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) first arises, one realizes the fruit of arhatship; since that very exhaustion of fetters is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship,
there are nine classes of fetters,
namely, those fetters to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*).
Up to the fetters to be abandoned by cultivation.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Although it was previously stated that the exhaustion of the fetters of the five categories is subsumed within the various fruits [of the path], [this is further elaborated here].
However, it has not yet been stated how the exhaustion of the ninefold fetters (*navavidha-saṃyojana*) is subsumed within the various fruits (*phala*).
Desiring to explain this now, this treatise is composed.
That is to say, the aforementioned five classes of fetters are explained as ninefold based on the distinctions among their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
That is to say, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be countered by each of the categories of Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and Subsequent Knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are divided into eight groups;
when those to be countered by both combined are taken as one group, there are nine groups.
To which fruit does the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned by the Dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) belong?
Answer: There are four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Alternatively, there are cases where [the attainment] is not subsumed under the four fruits of śrāmaṇya;
that is to say, when one realizes the exhaustion of those fetters and attains the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), it is subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry itself.
Up until the time one realizes the fruit of arhatship, it is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship.
Alternatively, "without a locus" refers to ordinary beings who have already become free from the defilement of desire; their exhaustion of fetters is not subsumed within any [noble] fruit.
For one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire and entered the state of rightness (samyaktva-niyāma),
those fetters that are exhausted during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing are not included within the fruit.
As for the gradualist, this occurs during the three moments of the clear realization of suffering (duḥkha-abhisamaya).
The clear realization of the cessation of the aggregates lasts for four moments of mind,
and the clear realization of the path lasts for three moments of mind;
the exhaustion of those fetters is not included within the fruit.

To which fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) up to the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed under the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or it is not included in any [fruit]. Regarding its inclusion in the four fruits of śrāmaṇya: [it is as follows].
As previously stated: "Or,
regarding 'no location,' if the fetters to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*) are exhausted,
there is no sense in which an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not included within the fruits [of the path]."
Why is this so? Because there is no ordinary being capable of abandoning the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

As for the sequence: the clear realization of suffering occupies the duration of one moment of mind, while the clear realizations of origin and cessation each occupy the duration of four moments of mind.
During the three moments of the path of clear observation (*mārgābhisamaya*),
the exhaustion of those fetters (*saṃyojana*) is not included within the fruit;
this applies if it is the exhaustion of fetters to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (*samudayadharmajñāna*).
This refers to the exhaustion of those fetters in ordinary beings who have already become free from the defilement of desire, which is not comprised within the fruits [of the path].

It also refers to the exhaustion of those fetters during the fifteen moments of mind in the path of seeing for one who has become free from the defilement of desire and has entered into the state of correctness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), which is likewise not comprised within the fruits.
Regarding the sequence: the clear realization of accumulation lasts for three moments of mind;
the clear realization of cessation lasts for four moments of mind;
and the clear realization of the path lasts for three moments of mind.
The exhaustion of those fetters is not subsumed under the fruit.
If it is the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*),
there is no sense in which it is not subsumed under the fruit for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Why is this? Because no ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is able to abandon the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*) belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
As for the sequence: it occurs within the duration of a single moment of mind during the clear realization of the origin (*samudaya-abhisamaya*).
During the four moments of the clear realization of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya*) and the three moments of the clear realization of the path (*mārga-abhisamaya*),
those fetters are exhausted but are not yet comprised within the fruit (*phala*).
If the fetters to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma (dharmajñāna) are extinguished—
meaning that for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already become free from the defilement of desire, those fetters are extinguished but are not comprised within the fruits [of the path]—
yet they have already become free from the defilement of desire and entered into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
During the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), those fetters (*saṃyojana*) that are exhausted are not included within the fruit (*phala*).

Regarding the sequential [attainment], during the three moments of mind for each of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), those fetters that are exhausted are not included within the fruit.

If there were no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) whose fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted by the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), they would not be included within the fruits [of the path]. Why is this?

Because there is no ordinary being capable of abandoning the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the cessation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
