Regarding the sequence: the clear realization of cessation lasts for the duration of one moment of mind, while the clear realization of the path lasts for three moments of mind;
the exhaustion of those fetters is not included within the fruit.
If one considers the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through the knowledge of the path (mārga-dharma-jñāna)—
namely, that for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already become free from the defilement of desire, that exhaustion of fetters is not included within the fruits [of the path]—
yet for those who, having already become free from the defilement of desire, enter into the state of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
During the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), those fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted, yet they are not included within the fruit (*phala*).

As for the sequential [attainment], during the two moments of the clear realization of the path (*mārgābhisamaya*), those fetters are exhausted, yet they are not included within the fruit; therefore, it is said that there is no such place [where exhaustion occurs].
To which fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
That is to say, when the exhaustion of those fetters is realized at the time of attaining the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala), it is subsumed within the fruit of stream-entry.
Up to the realization of the fruit of arhatship, it is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship itself;
there is no sense in which an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not subsumed within a fruit. Why is this so?

There are no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who can abandon the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be severed by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Furthermore, there is no one who attains them in successive stages, as this would not entail the meaning of being included within the fruits [of the religious life]. Why is this so?
It is only when the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) ceases that those [fetters] are completely abandoned.
When the subsequent knowledge of the path arises, one realizes the first three fruits as appropriate;
for the exhaustion of those fetters is subsumed within the first three fruits.
To which fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through cultivation subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship.
That is to say, when the exhaustion of those fetters is realized at the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship, it is then subsumed under the fruit of arhatship.
There is no ordinary being (pṛthagjana) who is not included within the category of "fruition" (phala). Why is this?

Because there is no ordinary being capable of abandoning the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Furthermore, there is no sense of "succession" in that which is not subsumed under the category of results. Why is this so?
Because it is only when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests that those [defilements] are finally severed and exhausted.
At the initial arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), one realizes the fruit of arhatship;
for that exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship itself.
Question: Is it the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) that is able to sever the various fetters?
If it were the path of liberation that is able to sever all fetters,
what fault would there be in that?
There are faults in both cases.
Why is this so? If it is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that can sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*),
how is the statement in this text to be reconciled?
As it is said regarding the fetters to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*),
up to the fetters to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*):
if the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) can abandon these various fetters.
How should one interpret what is stated in the *Jñānakāya*? For example, it says:

"Those fetters (*saṃyojana*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) are not abandoned by the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), but are abandoned by the receptivity to suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*). This continues up to:

those fetters that are to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*) are not abandoned by the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), but are abandoned by the receptivity to the path (*mārga-kṣānti*)."
It is agreed that this is what was said:
only the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) is able to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Question: If this is so, it is well explained by what is stated in the *Jñānaskandha*.
How should this statement in the text be interpreted?
The answer is: this passage should be explained as follows:
there are nine categories of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
This refers to what is abandoned by the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*),

up to and including what is abandoned by the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*); however, there is a specific underlying intention for not stating it in that way.
This means that patience (kṣānti) belongs to wisdom (jñāna) and is its auxiliary;
therefore, that which is abandoned by various patiences is said to be "abandoned by wisdom.
It is just as the deeds performed by a minister are attributed to the king.
Furthermore, the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is that which truly severs the fetters,
while the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) maintains them so that they do not arise again.
This means that although the path of uninterrupted transition truly severs the fetters, [the path of liberation ensures their non-arising].
If there were no path of liberation to sustain [the mind] and prevent [defilements] from arising,
those fetters would arise again and become a source of affliction;
thus, it is shown that the path of liberation is efficacious for abandonment.
This passage explains that the dharma-knowledge of subsequent realization (dharma-anvaya-jñāna) effects abandonment.
Furthermore, the immediate [path] and the path of liberation perform the same function;
they both possess the power to effect the abandonment of the fetters.
It is like two strong men together harming a single enemy:
one throws him to the ground while the other ensures he does not rise;
otherwise, if he were to rise again, he would be able to cause further harm.
Furthermore, it is like two people pursuing the same thief:
one drives him out and firmly closes the door,
for otherwise he would re-enter and cause harm.
Furthermore, it is like two men who together seize a single snake;
one places it inside a jar and securely seals its mouth,
whereas the other does not and thus allows it to escape, which can cause harm.

The same applies to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) regarding the severance of fetters (*saṃyojana*). This is because it is shown that the path of liberation is effective for the severance [of fetters].
This passage explains that the subsequent knowledge of phenomena (*dharmānvaya-jñāna*) effects the severance.
Furthermore, to demonstrate that the path of liberation has multiple functions regarding the fetters abandoned by the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*),
these multiple functions are as explained in the *Indriya-skandha*. Therefore,
this passage states that they are abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma-similarity (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Furthermore, the various paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) correctly sever the fetters.
The various paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arise simultaneously with the acquisition of the severance of those fetters;
once that severance is attained, it possesses the functional capacity to effect that severance.
Therefore, this text states that it is abandoned by the dharma-subsequent knowledge (*dharmānvaya-jñāna*).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of abandonment:
first, specific; second, general.
The others are exclusively uninterrupted [paths], while those that lead to liberation are both.
This is not contrary to reason, as it is stated according to general usage.
Furthermore, in this context, the various "patiences" (*kṣānti*) are designated by the name "wisdom" (*jñāna*) because they induce wisdom; thus, the name of the effect is applied to the cause.
Just as hunger and thirst are named after their causes, so too is contact the cause of them;
therefore, it is only the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that can sever the fetters.
There are fifteen classes of fetters.
This means that each of the three realms has five [types of fetters]:
namely, the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering,
up to the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: Although it was previously stated that the exhaustion of the ninefold fetters is subsumed within the various fruits [of the path], it had not yet been stated that the exhaustion of the fifteenfold fetters is subsumed within the various fruits.
Now, wishing to explain this, I have composed this treatise; that is to say,
by means of the two gateways of the elements (*dhātu*) and the classes (*nikāya*),
the distinctions among the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) are analyzed as being of fifteen kinds.
To which fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path in the desire realm included?
Answer: It is included in the four fruits of śrāmaṇya;
or there is no fixed location.
Regarding what is subsumed under the four fruits of śrāmaṇya:
when one realizes the exhaustion of those fetters and attains the fruit of stream-entry, it is subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry;
and so on, until when one attains the fruit of arhatship, it is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship.
Alternatively, there are cases where there is no [attainment of] fruition: for example, when the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm are exhausted.
This refers to ordinary persons who have already become free from the defilement of desire; their exhaustion of those fetters is not included within the fruits [of the path].
It also refers to those who, having already become free from the defilement of desire, enter into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
During the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), those fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted but are not yet included within the fruits (*phala*).

As for the sequential order: it consists of three moments during the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*), and four moments each during the clear realizations of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
During the three moments of mind of the clear realization of the Path,
that exhaustion of fetters is not included within the fruit.
This applies if it is the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the desire realm.
This refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already abandoned the defilements of desire; their exhaustion of those fetters (*saṃyojana*) is not included within the fruits [of the path].

For those who, having abandoned the defilements of desire, enter into the state of rightness and departure from error (*samyaktva-niyāma*), during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
The exhaustion of those fetters is not subsumed under the fruit.

Regarding the sequence: it occurs during three moments of mind in the clear realization of origination (*samudaya-abhisamaya*), and during four moments of mind in the clear realization of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya*).
During the three moments of the path of clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
the exhaustion of those fetters (*saṃyojana*) is not included within the fruit;
this applies if it is the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) in the desire realm.
This refers to the exhaustion of those fetters by ordinary beings who have already become free from the defilement of desire, which is not subsumed under the fruit;

and the exhaustion of those fetters during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing by one who has become free from the defilement of desire and entered into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), which is also not subsumed under the fruit.
Regarding the sequence: the clear realization of cessation and the path each lasts for three moments of mind;
the exhaustion of those fetters is not included within the fruit.
This applies if it is the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm.
This refers to ordinary beings who have already abandoned the defilements of desire; their exhaustion of those fetters is not subsumed under the fruits [of the path].
It also refers to those who, having abandoned the defilements of desire, enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*);
during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), their exhaustion of those fetters is likewise not subsumed under the fruits.
Regarding the sequence: during the two moments of the path of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), those fetters are exhausted but are not included within the fruits [of the path].
Within which fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) included?
Answer: There is either no such place, or it is subsumed under the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).

That which is subsumed under the fruit of non-returning refers to the fact that at the moment one realizes the fruit of non-returning through the exhaustion of those fetters (*saṃyojana*), it is then subsumed under the fruit of non-returning.

That which is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship refers to the fact that at the moment one realizes the exhaustion of those fetters and attains the fruit of arhatship, it is then subsumed under the fruit of arhatship; or,
alternatively, there is no location [for it].
This refers to the exhaustion of those fetters in ordinary persons who have already abandoned the defilements of desire, which is not comprised within the fruits [of the path].

It also refers to the exhaustion of those fetters during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing for one who, having already abandoned the defilements of desire, enters into the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), which is likewise not comprised within the fruits.
That which lacks sequential order is not included within the category of results.

Why is this so? Because it is only at the moment the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) that eliminates desire-taint (*vairāgya-rāga*) ceases that those [defilements] are finally severed and exhausted.
Since the ninth path of liberation arises at the time one realizes the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), it is subsumed within that very fruit.
As for the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path within the realm of form (rūpadhātu), in which fruit is it subsumed?
Answer: There are four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or else there is no location for them.
As for the four fruits of śrāmaṇya:
As previously stated.
Alternatively, regarding "no location": this refers to the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

That is to say, for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm, that exhaustion of those fetters is not comprised within the [noble] fruits.
For one who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm and entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
those fetters (*saṃyojana*) that are exhausted during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are not included within the [resultant] fruits.
As for the gradualist (*ānupūrvika*), this occurs during the single moment of the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*).
The clear realization of the cessation of the aggregates lasts for four moments of mind,
and the clear realization of the path lasts for three moments of mind;
the exhaustion of those fetters is not included within the fruit.
If the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the form realm are exhausted—
meaning that for ordinary beings who have already become free from the defilements of the form realm, those exhausted fetters are not included within the fruits [of the path]—
yet they have already become free from the defilements of the form realm and entered into the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
During the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), those fetters are exhausted but are not yet comprised within the fruit.

As for the sequence: the clear realization of origin (*samudayasatyābhisamaya*) occurs during one moment of mind, while the clear realization of cessation (*nirodhasatyābhisamaya*) occurs during four moments of mind.
During the three moments of the path of clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
the exhaustion of those fetters is not included within the fruit.
This applies if it is the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
This refers to ordinary beings who have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm; their exhaustion of those fetters is not comprised within the fruits [of the path].
It also refers to those who, having become detached from the defilements of the form realm, enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*);
during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), their exhaustion of those fetters is likewise not comprised within the fruits.
Regarding the sequence: the clear realization of cessation lasts for the duration of one moment of mind;
the clear realization of the path lasts for three moments of mind.
The exhaustion of those fetters is not included within the fruit.
If the fetters to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the form realm are exhausted—
meaning that for those ordinary persons who have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm, those exhausted fetters are not included within the fruits [of the path]—
yet they have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm and entered into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
During the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), those fetters that are exhausted are not included within the fruit (*phala*).
This is because there is no sequential [attainment] for what is not included within the fruit. Why is this so?
It is only when the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) ceases that those [fetters] are completely abandoned.

When the subsequent knowledge of the path arises, one realizes the first three fruits as appropriate; since the exhaustion of those fetters is subsumed within the first three fruits, they are included therein.
In what fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the form realm included?
Answer: It is included in the fruit of arhatship, or it is not included in any [fruit]. Regarding its inclusion in the fruit of arhatship:
This means that when those fetters are exhausted upon realizing the fruit of arhatship, they are subsumed within the fruit of arhatship.
Alternatively, regarding "no location":
this refers to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have already become free from the defilements of the form realm; their exhaustion of those fetters is not subsumed within any [noble] fruit.
For one who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm and has entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),

the exhaustion of those fetters during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and during the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) and other stages of training (*śaikṣa-avasthā*) is not included within the [four] fruits.

Regarding the sequence: from the ninth path of liberation that follows the detachment from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, up until the time when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, those fetters are exhausted but are not yet comprised within the fruit.
To what fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation in the formless realm subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed under four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or there is no fixed location.
As for the four fruits of śrāmaṇya: [they are]... (as previously detailed).
As previously stated:
"Or 'no location' refers to the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the formless realm;
there is no sense in which an ordinary person is not subsumed under the [noble] fruits."
Why is this so? Because there is no ordinary being capable of abandoning the fetters to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
As for the sequence: it occurs in a single moment of mental concentration during the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*).
The clear realization of the cessation of the aggregates lasts for four moments of mind,
and the clear realization of the path lasts for three moments of mind;
the exhaustion of those fetters is not included within the fruit.
If the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the formless realm are exhausted,
there is no sense in which an ordinary person is not subsumed under a fruit;
the meaning is as previously explained.
Regarding the sequence: the clear realization of accumulation occurs in the duration of one moment of mind;
the clear realization of cessation occurs in the duration of four moments of mind;
and the clear realization of the path occurs in the duration of three moments of mind.
The exhaustion of those fetters is not included within the fruits [of the path].

If there were no exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there would be no sense in which an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not included within the fruits;
the meaning is as previously explained.
Regarding the sequence: the clear realization of cessation lasts for the duration of one moment of mind;
the clear realization of the path lasts for the duration of three moments of mind.
The exhaustion of those fetters is not included within the fruit.
If the fetters to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the formless realm are exhausted, by which fruit are they subsumed?
Answer: They are subsumed under the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
That is to say, when those fetters are exhausted and the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) is realized, they are subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry.
Up until the time one realizes the fruit of arhatship, it is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship itself;
there is no sense in which an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is not subsumed within a fruit.
The meaning is as previously explained.
Furthermore, there is no sense in which that which lacks sequential order is not subsumed under the category of "fruit.
Why is this? Because it is only at the moment when the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) ceases that those [defilements] are completely abandoned.
When the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) arises, one realizes the first three fruits as appropriate;
since the exhaustion of those fetters is subsumed within the first three fruits,
in which fruit is the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) included?
Answer: It refers to the fruit of arhatship.
That is to say, when one realizes the fruit of arhatship through the exhaustion of those fetters, it is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship itself;
there is no sense in which an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is not subsumed under a fruit.
The meaning is as previously explained.
Furthermore, that which lacks sequential order is not subsumed under the category of "result. Why is this so?
They are completely severed only when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests;
at the moment the first knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises, one realizes the fruit of arhatship, because that exhaustion of the fetters is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship.
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda, Volume Sixty-four;
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Sixty-five.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang in accordance with the Imperial Edict. Section Two: The Aggregate of Fetters (Saṃyojana-kāya). Sub-section Three: The Summary of Sentient Beings (Sattva-nikāya). Part Three. Regarding each of the three fetters up to the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), in what fruit is their total exhaustion subsumed?
Question: For what reason was this treatise composed?

Answer: Although it was previously stated that the exhaustion of the fetters of the fifteen chapters is subsumed within the various fruits [of the path], it had not yet been stated that the exhaustion of the afflictions of the sixteen chapters is likewise subsumed within the various fruits.
Now, wishing to explain this, I have composed this treatise.
Answer: Among the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), the exhaustion of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is subsumed within four of the fruits of śrāmaṇya;
or it is not so included.
Regarding what is subsumed under the four fruits of śrāmaṇya:
when one fully realizes the fruit of stream-entry, it is subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry;
and so on, until when one realizes the fruit of arhatship, it is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship.
"Or 'having no location' means that there is no sense of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) not subsumed under the fruit [of the path]. Why is this?
Because an ordinary person is able to abandon the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) regarding existence in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)."
Regarding the sequence: the clear realization of suffering lasts for the duration of one moment of mind;
the clear realizations of origin and cessation each last for four moments of mind;
and the clear realization of the path lasts for three moments of mind.
The exhaustion of the view of a self-identity is not included within the fruits [of the path],
just as the exhaustion of the view of a self-identity among the three fetters;
one should know that this applies likewise to the view of a self-identity among the five lower fetters.
Among the five views, the exhaustion of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is likewise [the same as the exhaustion of ignorance],
because their intrinsic natures are identical and they share the same antidote.
The exhaustion of the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) is subsumed within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The meaning of being subsumed within the four fruits should be understood as previously explained.
This [state] is not a case of being subsumed within the fruits because it is not an ordinary person (pṛthagjana). Why is that?

There are no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who can abandon the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Furthermore, there is no one who attains it through the successive stages (*anupūrvika*), for it does not fall within the category of the fruits [of the path]. Why is this so?
It is only when the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) ceases that those [fetters] are completely abandoned.
When the subsequent knowledge of the path arises, one realizes the first three fruits as appropriate;
this is because the exhaustion of the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) is subsumed within those first three fruits.
Just as among the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are exhausted,
so too should it be understood that among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*), the flood and yoke of views (*dṛṣṭy-ogha-yoga*) are exhausted;
and among the four graspings (*upādāna*), the grasping for views (*dṛṣṭy-upādāna*) and the grasping for precepts and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*) are exhausted.
Among the four bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*), the fetter of grasping at precepts and observances as supreme (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-satyagrāha*) is included;
among the five lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), grasping at precepts and observances and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are included;
and among the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and grasping at precepts and observances are included.
Among the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
the latent tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are likewise exhausted among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) as the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and doubt;
this is because their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are identical.
Because they share the same antidote,
the exhaustion of the three unwholesome roots is subsumed within the fruit of a non-returner or an arhat;
or else, there is no such place [for them].
Regarding those subsumed under the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*):
this means that when one fully realizes that fruit, they are then subsumed under the fruit of non-returning.
Regarding those subsumed under the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*): [the same applies].
This means that when one fully realizes the fruit of arhatship, it is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship.
Alternatively, regarding "no location":
this refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already become free from the defilement of desire; their cessation is not subsumed within any fruit.
For one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire and entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
those [defilements] are exhausted during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and are not included within the fruit.
This means that for one who lacks sequential realization, they are not included within the fruit.
Why is this? Because it is only when the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the defilement of desire ceases that those [defilements] are completely severed.
When the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises, one realizes the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), as this is precisely what is subsumed under the fruit of non-returning.
Just as with the exhaustion of the three unwholesome roots,
one should know that among the three outflows (*āsrava*), it is the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*);
and among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*), it is the flood and yoke of desire (*kāma-ogha* and *kāma-yoga*).
Among the four graspings (*upādāna*), it is the grasping for sensual pleasures (*kāmopādāna*).
Among the four bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*), it is sensual desire and ill will (*abhidhyāvyāpāda*).
Among the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), it is the first four hindrances.
Among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), there are the fetters of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*).
Among the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), there are sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
Among the six groups of craving for the body (*ṣaḍ-ātmabhāvābhiniveśa*), there is the group of craving born of nose-contact and tongue-contact.
Among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the same applies to sensual desire (*rāga*) and ill-will (*pratigha*);
among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the same applies to the fetters of malice (*pratigha*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*).
This is because their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are identical.
Because they share the same antidote,
the outflows of the taints (*āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) are subsumed within the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*).
That is to say, when one realizes their exhaustion, it is precisely at that time that they are subsumed within the fruit of arhatship.
There is no ordinary being who is not included within the category of "fruition. Why is this?
Because there is no ordinary being capable of abandoning the outflows of existence and the outflow of ignorance pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, there is no sense in which that which lacks sequential order is not subsumed under the category of "fruit. Why is this so?
Because it is only when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests that those [defilements] are finally severed and exhausted.
When the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) first arises, one realizes the fruit of arhatship; since that very exhaustion is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship,

it should be understood that among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*), the flood and yoke of ignorance (*avidya-ogha-yoga*) are included therein, just as when the outflows of the taints (*āsrava*)— namely, the outflow of ignorance— are exhausted.
Among the four graspings (*upādāna*), it is the grasping at a theory of self (*ātma-vāda-upādāna*).
Among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), it is the fetter of greed and the fetter of pride (*māna*).
Among the five higher fetters (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), it consists of the remaining four, excluding the greed for the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*).
Among the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*), it is the group of craving born of mental contact (*mano-saṃsparśaja-tṛṣṇā-kāya*).
Among the seven latent tendencies (*sapta-anuśaya*), they are greed, ignorance, and pride.
It is the same for the exhaustion of the fetters of craving, pride, and ignorance among the nine fetters (*nava-saṃyojana*).
Because of their intrinsic nature,
because they share the same antidote,
and because the hindrance of doubt is exhausted within them, the four fruits of śrāmaṇya are subsumed [within these stages].
Or there is no such place.
That which is subsumed within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya has been explained as before.
Or there is no such place.
This refers to ordinary beings who have already abandoned the defilement of desire; their exhaustion of the hindrance of doubt is not comprised within the fruits [of the path].
It also refers to those who, having abandoned the defilement of desire, enter into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*);
during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), their exhaustion of the hindrance of doubt is likewise not comprised within the fruits.
Regarding the sequence: during the two moments of mind in the clear realization of the path, the exhaustion of the hindrance of doubt is not included among the fruits.
The exhaustion of the fetter of desire for the form realm (*rūparāga-anuśaya*) is included in the fruit of Arhatship, or there is no specific location [for it].
That which is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship refers to the moment one fully realizes the fruit of arhatship; it is then subsumed under the fruit of arhatship.
Alternatively, there is no [other] location.
That is to say, for ordinary beings who have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm, that exhaustion is not included within the category of "fruit. Furthermore,
for those who have become detached from the defilements of the form realm and have entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),

during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) as well as the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) and other stages of training (*śaikṣa*), that exhaustion is not included within the category of "fruit."

Regarding the sequence: from the ninth path of liberation that follows the detachment from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, up until the time when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, those [defilements] are exhausted and are not included within the category of results.
Just as the craving for form is the exhaustion of the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*),
it should be known that the exhaustion of the group of cravings born from eye, ear, and body contact is likewise so,
because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is identical.
Because they share the same antidote,
yet there is a distinction;
herein it should be stated that "or there is no location."
This refers to ordinary beings who have already become detached from the defilements of the Brahma-world; their exhaustion is not included within the category of "fruit.

Furthermore, for those who have entered the state of right determination after becoming detached from the defilements of the Brahma-world—during the fifteen moments of mind in the path of seeing, as well as during the subsequent knowledge of the path and other stages of training (śaikṣa)—their exhaustion is likewise not included within the category of "fruit."

Regarding the sequence: from the ninth path of liberation that follows the detachment from the defilements of the first dhyāna, up until the time when the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) manifests, those [defilements] are exhausted and are not included within the category of results.

Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), those abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path in the desire realm are entirely subsumed within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or there is no such place [where they are not].
This is as explained regarding the exhaustion of the first four categories among the fifteen types of fetters (*saṃyojana*) in the desire realm.
The exhaustion of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm is subsumed within the fruit of non-returner or the fruit of arhatship;
or else there is no such place. This is as explained regarding the exhaustion of the fifth category among the fifteen categories of fetters (saṃyojana) in the desire realm.

The exhaustion of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is subsumed under four of the fruits of śramaṇaship, or there is no such place.
This is as explained regarding the exhaustion of the first four of the fifteen classes of fetters (*saṃyojana*) within the realm of form.

The exhaustion of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship, or there is no such place [for their abandonment].
This is as explained regarding the exhaustion of the fifth category among the fifteen categories of fetters (*saṃyojana*) in the realm of form.

The exhaustion of the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is comprised within four of the fruits of śramaṇaship, or there is no such place [for a fifth].
This is as explained regarding the exhaustion of the first three categories among the fifteen classes of fetters (saṃyojana) in the formless realm.
The exhaustion of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the formless realm is included within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya;
this is as explained regarding the exhaustion of the fourth category of the fifteen classes of fetters (saṃyojana) in the formless realm.
The exhaustion of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship;
this is as explained regarding the exhaustion of the fifth category of the fifteen categories of fetters (saṃyojana) in the formless realm.
Among those in the stage of entering the stream (srotāpatti-pratipannaka), by what fruit are the various fetters (saṃyojana) that have been exhausted subsumed?
Answer: There is no such place. Why is this so?
Because there is no fruit of the śramaṇa prior to the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), and because that [fruit] encompasses them all.
Within the fruit of stream-entry, by what fruit are the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) that have been exhausted subsumed?
Answer: By the fruit of stream-entry.
This means that within this fruit, all fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through seeing in the three realms are collectively subsumed.
As for the exhaustion of the fetters during the stage of the candidate for the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka), which fruit does it comprise?
The answer is: the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala), or there is no specific location [for its inclusion].
That which is subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry refers to the total inclusion within that fruit of the exhaustion of all fetters abandoned through vision across the three realms;
alternatively, it is "without location."
This refers to one who enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) while having already doubled the abandonment of desire-taints;
during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing, the exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) is not included within the fruit.
For one who proceeds by stages, the exhaustion of the first five categories of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm is also not included within the fruit.
Why is this? Because it is that which is realized through the path of the superior fruit;
just as the path of the superior fruit is not itself subsumed under the category of the fruit.
The principle regarding the exhaustion of fetters attained therein should also be understood in this way.
As for the exhaustion of various fetters within the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), by which fruit is it subsumed?
Answer: By the fruit of once-returning.
This means that within this fruit, there is the total inclusion of the exhaustion of all fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya) in the three realms,
as well as the inclusion of the exhaustion of the first six categories of fetters abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the desire realm.
Within the stage of the candidate for non-returning (anāgāmin-patipannaka), which category of fruit does the exhaustion of those fetters belong?
Answer: It is either the fruit of once-returning or it is not included therein.
Regarding that which is subsumed under the fruit of once-returning:
this refers to within that fruit.
This comprehensively subsumes the exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms,
as well as the exhaustion of the first six categories of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm; or,
it refers to those for whom there is no [remaining] locus.
This refers to one who, having already abandoned the defilements from the realm of desire up to the sphere of nothingness and has entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
has exhausted all fetters during the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), yet these are not yet subsumed under the fruit (*phala*).
Regarding the sequence:
the exhaustion of the seventh and eighth categories of fetters abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm is not included within the fruit [of the once-returner].
Within the fruit of the non-returner, to which fruit does the exhaustion of those various fetters belong?
Answer: It is the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).

This means that within this fruit, there is the total inclusion of the exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) across the three realms, as well as the inclusion of the exhaustion of all fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the desire realm.
Regarding the exhaustion of all fetters within the stage of the candidate for arhatship (arhattvaphalapratipannaka), by which fruit is it subsumed?

The answer is: it is either subsumed under the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) or there is no such place [for its inclusion]. As for its being subsumed under the fruit of non-returning: [it is so because]...
This means that within this fruit, there is the total inclusion of the exhaustion of all fetters abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) across the three realms,
as well as the inclusion of the exhaustion of all fetters abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm; or,
alternatively, it refers to those who have no [remaining] locus.

This refers to the exhaustion of the various fetters (saṃyojana) associated with the defilements of eight grades, from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana),
which are not included within the [four] fruits. Why is this so?
Because this is realized through the path of the superior fruit (*viśeṣamārga*),

just as the path of the superior fruit is not subsumed under the category of "fruit," so too should the principle regarding the exhaustion of the fetters (*kṣayaprāpti*) be understood. Within the fruit of Arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), under which fruit is the exhaustion of all fetters subsumed?
Answer: It refers to the fruit of arhatship.
This means that within this fruit, the exhaustion of all fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation across the three realms is comprehensively subsumed.
Question: Does this refer to the exhaustion of fetters accomplished by those in the stages of progress (pratipannaka) as well as those in the fruits?
If one were to say that it refers to the exhaustion of all fetters newly realized within the various paths and fruits,
what would be the fault?
There would be faults in both cases.
Why is this? If one were to speak of the exhaustion of all fetters (saṃyojana) accomplished within the states of those progressing toward and abiding in the fruits,
then the exhaustion of fetters within the first three fruits should not be described as being comprised solely by their respective fruits.

For example, one who has abandoned the first five grades of defilement of the desire realm and entered the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) realizes the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) at the moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna). At that time,
the five grades of fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm are exhausted.
It is not subsumed under this fruit.
Why is it not mentioned, or why is there no place for it?
Furthermore, regarding one who has already abandoned the defilements of the first eight stages and enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*):

When one realizes the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) at the time of the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) regarding the path, the seventh and eighth grades of fetters abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm have been exhausted; why then are these not included within this fruit, or why is it not mentioned? Or is there no such case?

Furthermore, for one who has already abandoned desire up to the level of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and enters into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they realize the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).

Since the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the seven stages of the two upper realms is not included within this fruit, why is it not mentioned? Or is there no such case?
If one were to say that the exhaustion of all fetters newly realized within the various paths and fruits is what constitutes them,
then the exhaustion of fetters within the latter three paths would not properly be said to be included within the preceding fruits.
Because the concentration of the exhaustion of fetters (āsravakṣaya-samādhi) realized by those currently training (śaikṣa) is not subsumed under the previous fruits.
The answer is: this passage speaks collectively of all the exhaustions of fetters accomplished by those both in the states of training and in the fruits.
Question: If that is so, the difficulty regarding the latter three candidates (*pratipannaka*) has been well resolved;
however, how should the difficulty regarding the first three fruits (*phala*) be resolved?
Answer: This is because it refers to those who enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) while still bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*).
The exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) accomplished through the first three fruits is said to be comprised solely by their respective fruits.
Some say that this is because,
within the state of fruition (*phalāvasthā*), it refers to what has been newly realized and the fulfillment of what was sought.
Because the stage of the candidate has not yet fulfilled the objective sought, it is described collectively as "accomplishment";
thus, both explanations apply well to the stage of the candidate for the fruit.
This refers to a disciple of the World-Honored One who possesses right view but has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire.
In what fruit are the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) included?

Answer: They are included in either the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala) or they are not included in any [fruit]. Regarding their inclusion in the fruit of once-returning: [it refers to those who have abandoned up to five categories of fetters].
This refers to the exhaustion of the first six categories of fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm;
or, in the case of "no location," it refers to the exhaustion of the seventh and eighth categories of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.

For one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm, in what fruit are the exhaustion of all fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the form realm included?
Answer: There is no such place.
This refers to one who has abandoned from one grade of the first dhyāna up to eight grades of the fourth dhyāna;
the exhaustion of those fetters to be abandoned by cultivation is not included within the fruit.
Such a person has already abandoned the defilements of the form realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm.
To which fruit is the exhaustion of all fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm attributed?
Answer: To none.
That is to say, it refers to the abandonment of the defilements of one category of the Sphere of Infinite Space up to eight categories of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
The exhaustion of those fetters abandoned through cultivation is not included within the fruits;
herein it is said that there are four fruits of śrāmaṇya:
namely, the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.
Question: For what reason are these four fruits of śrāmaṇya taught?
Answer: It is in order to refute the doctrines of others and to clarify one's own position.
That is to say, there are some who claim:
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are exclusively unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), according to the Vibhajyavādins.
Question: For what reason do they make this statement?
Answer: Because it is based upon the sūtras.
As it is said in a sutra:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus,
"I shall now explain to you the nature of a śramaṇa, as well as the fruits of a śramaṇa."
What is the nature of a śramaṇa?
It is the Noble Eightfold Path.
What is meant by a "śramaṇa"? It refers to one who has accomplished these dharmas.
What are the fruits of śrāmaṇya?
They are the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship.
What is the fruit of stream-entry? It is the permanent abandonment of the three fetters.
What is the fruit of once-returning? It is the permanent abandonment of the three fetters and the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion.
What is the fruit of non-returning? It is the permanent abandonment of the five lower fetters.
What is the fruit of arhatship?
This refers to the permanent abandonment of greed, hatred, delusion, and all afflictions.
Based on this sūtra, it was stated that the fruits of śrāmaṇya are exclusively unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
To refute that intention and demonstrate that the fruits of śrāmaṇya are both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned, [the following is said].
If the fruits of śrāmaṇya were exclusively unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), it would contradict the sūtras.
As the sūtra says:
"There are those who practice the four paths and those who abide in the four fruits."
In this context, "abiding" refers to abiding in conditioned fruits, not unconditioned fruits,
because it is impossible to abide in an unconditioned fruit.
This is what they say.
Because it can also be said that one abides within the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*), the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states:
"He abides in abandonment and does not seek further progress."
For the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained,
for the sake of acquiring what has not yet been acquired,
and for the sake of contacting what has not yet been contacted.
If it were for the purpose of proving what has not yet been proven,
that treatise would not be a proof. Why is this so?
The intended meaning of that treatise is that one abides in the path; that is to say,
one who abides in abandonment does not abide in abandonment in the manner that one riding an elephant or horse abides upon the elephant or horse.
However, abiding is defined as neither progressing nor regressing on the path of realization and abandonment.
Furthermore, there are other sūtras that state only conditioned phenomena constitute the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
As it is said: when the five faculties are superior, intense, swift, and fully perfected, one is called an Arhat of "liberation through both";
when they are subsequently diminished and inferior, one is called an Arhat of "liberation through wisdom."
Next, those who have diminished inferiority are called those with the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Next, those who have further diminished inferiority are called those with the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).
Those who have most thoroughly diminished inferiority are called those with the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).
In this context,
because it is taught that the distinctions between the superiority and inferiority of the five faculties— faith and the others— are what constitute the fruits of śrāmaṇya,
one knows the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
It is not only that [the fruits] are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Question: If the fruits of śramaṇaship are also conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), how do you reconcile this with the sūtra cited there?
Answer: The fruits of the four stages of śrāmaṇya encompass both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
As for why that sūtra speaks of them as being exclusively unconditioned, it is for the following reason:
Because that sutra speaks only of the fruit.
If a dharma were a fruit of śramaṇaship but not the nature of a śramaṇa, that sutra would have spoken of it as the path;
since it is both a fruit of śramaṇaship and the nature of a śramaṇa, it does not mention it [separately].
Furthermore, if there were dharmas that were the fruit of a brāhmaṇa but not of the nature of a brāhmaṇa, those would have been taught as the path in that sutra;
however, since these are both the fruit of a brāhmaṇa and of the nature of a brāhmaṇa, they were not so mentioned.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon were a fruit of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) but not itself of the nature of the holy life, it would have been mentioned as the "path" in that sutra;
however, because it is both a fruit of the holy life and of the nature of the holy life, it was not so stated.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is a fruit but not one that possesses a fruit, it is the "path" spoken of in that sutra;
since it is both a fruit and one that possesses a fruit, it is not so described there.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is detachment but not one that possesses detachment, it is the "path" spoken of in that sutra.
Because that [state] is both free from [craving] and yet possesses freedom from craving, it was not mentioned in that sutra.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon were something to be sought after but not something to be loathed, it would be the "path" spoken of in that sutra;
however, because it is both something to be sought after and something to be loathed, it was not mentioned.
The four fruits are taught in order to refute the assertions of other schools and to reveal the meaning of one's own school.
Furthermore, it is not merely for the sake of refuting others and displaying one's own position;
rather, they are taught so as to elucidate the correct principles of the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) and enable others to understand them.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya?
Answer: The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states as follows:
"The fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) is of two kinds."
It refers to the conditioned and the unconditioned.
What is the conditioned fruit of stream-entry?
It refers to one who has realized the fruit of stream-entry having already, or currently, or about to attain the various factors of training (*śaikṣadharma*).
That which has already been attained refers to the past;
that which is being attained refers to the present;
and that which is to be attained refers to the future.
What is the unconditioned fruit of stream-entry?
It refers to that which is currently being attained or has already been attained by one who has realized the fruit of stream-entry, consisting in the abandonment of all fetters.
That which has already been attained refers to the past;
that which is being attained refers to the present;
and that which is to be attained refers to the future.
It is asked: Since the path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and falls within the three periods of time, it can be said that one has attained, is attaining, or will attain it.
But since cessation (*nirodha*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall within the three periods of time, how can it be said that one has attained, is attaining, or will attain it?
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* should state it as follows:
regarding the attainment, acquisition, contact, and realization of the abandonment of all fetters (*saṃyojana*), one should not say that they have been, are being, or will be attained.
To speak in such a manner has a specific underlying intention.
To clarify the acquisition of that abandonment (*prahāṇa-prāpti*) and its continuous acquisition (*anubandha-prāpti*):
the acquisition of that abandonment is termed "already acquired" when it is in the past,
and "presently acquired" when it is in the present.
In the future, it is called "to be attained.
Regarding the continuity, this refers to the continuity of the realization of abandonment.
In the past, it is called "already attained."
When it exists in the present, it is called "attained correctly";
when it exists in the future, it is called "to be attained.
Furthermore, that treatise states that there are two types of the fruit of once-returning.
It refers to the conditioned and the unconditioned.
What is the conditioned fruit of once-returning?
It refers to one who has realized the fruit of once-returning.
Regarding the factors of training (*śaikṣadharma*), they have already been correctly attained;
the remainder is as previously explained.
What is the unconditioned fruit of once-returning (*anāsrava sakṛdāgāmiphala*)?
This refers to one who has realized the fruit of once-returning;
having already abandoned the fetters, they are currently attaining the remainder as previously described.
There are two types of non-returners.
It refers to the conditioned and the unconditioned.
What is the conditioned fruit of non-returning?
It refers to one who has realized the fruit of non-returning.
Regarding the various trainings (*śikṣā-dharma*), one has already correctly attained them, as further explained previously.
What is the unconditioned fruit of non-returning (*asaṃskṛta-anāgāmiphala*)?
It refers to one who has realized the fruit of non-returning.
When all fetters have been severed, one shall rightly attain [the fruit];
the remainder is as previously explained.
There are two kinds of Arhatship.
It refers to the conditioned and the unconditioned.
What is the conditioned fruit of arhatship?
It refers to one who has realized the fruit of arhatship.
Regarding the dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they have already attained, are currently attaining, or will attain them;
the rest is as previously explained.
What is the unconditioned fruit of arhatship (*asaṃskṛtam arhattvaphalam*)?
This refers to one who has realized the fruit of arhatship;
having already attained, or is currently attaining, the severance of all fetters.
The remainder is as previously explained.
The *Prakaraṇapāda* also states this:
"There are two kinds of the fruit of stream-entry:
namely, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
What is the conditioned fruit of stream-entry?
It refers to the acquisition of this fruit and the acquisition of that acquisition.
Regarding "the acquisition of this fruit":
This refers to the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the conditioned and unconditioned fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).
Regarding this "acquisition of the acquisition," it refers to the acquisition of that very fruit; by virtue of this acquisition of the fruit, one is established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Because one acquires this acquisition (*prāpti*), one accomplishes the acquisition of this fruit.

These include the faculties of training (*śaikṣendriya*), the powers of training (*śaikṣabala*), the morality of training (*śaikṣa-śīla*), the roots of goodness of training (*śaikṣakuśalamūla*), and the eight factors of training (*śaikṣadharma*),
as well as other dharmas of training belonging to this same category.
This is called the conditioned fruit of stream-entry.
What is the unconditioned fruit of stream-entry?
It refers to the permanent abandonment of the three fetters.
The permanent abandonment of these types of fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the dharmas associated with them;
the permanent abandonment of the eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the dharmas associated with these underlying tendencies.
This is called the unconditioned fruit of stream-entry.
The fruit of once-returning is of two kinds:
namely, the conditioned and the unconditioned.
What is the conditioned fruit of once-returning?
It refers to the attainment of this fruit and the attainment of that attainment.
The rest is as previously explained.
The faculties of training, the powers of training, the training in morality, the wholesome roots of training, and the eight factors of training,
as well as other such factors of training—
these are called the conditioned fruit of once-returning.
What is the unconditioned fruit of once-returning?
It refers to the permanent abandonment of the three fetters and the permanent abandonment of those dharmas of the same category as these fetters.
The eighty-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are forever abandoned,
as well as those types of phenomena associated with latent dispositions; greed, hatred, and delusion are twice abandoned,
as well as those types of afflictive phenomena associated with them.
This is called the unconditioned fruit of once-returning.
There are two kinds of fruits of non-returning:
namely, the conditioned and the unconditioned.
What is the conditioned fruit of non-returning?
It refers to the acquisition of this fruit and the acquisition of that acquisition.
The rest is as previously explained.
If there are the faculties of training, the powers of training, the training in morality, the roots of goodness of training, and the eight factors of training,
as well as other such factors of training,
these are called the conditioned fruit of non-returning.
What is the unconditioned fruit of non-returning?
It refers to the permanent abandonment of the five lower fetters and the permanent abandonment of all other dharmas of the same class.
The permanent abandonment of the ninety-two latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
as well as the permanent abandonment of those phenomena belonging to the same category of latent dispositions,
is called the unconditioned fruit of non-return (*anāgāmiphala*).
The fruit of arhatship is of two kinds:
namely, conditioned and unconditioned.
What is the conditioned fruit of arhatship?
This refers to the acquisition of this fruit and the acquisition of that acquisition.
The rest is as previously explained.

Furthermore, there are the faculties of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the powers of those beyond training, the morality of those beyond training, the roots of goodness of those beyond training, and the ten dharmas of those beyond training.
And these types of dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are called the conditioned fruit of arhatship.
What is the unconditioned fruit of arhatship?
It refers to the permanent abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion;
the permanent abandonment of all afflictions;
the transcending of all realms of existence; and the severing of all paths.
He extinguishes the three fires, crosses the four torrents,
crushes all arrogance, abandons all craving,
and destroys the ālayavijñāna.
The unsurpassed ultimate, the unsurpassed tranquility, the unsurpassed bliss,
as well as the extinction through the exhaustion of all craving and detachment from it—
this is called the unconditioned fruit of arhatship.
This is called the intrinsic nature, the personal entity, the characteristic, the division, and the fundamental nature of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Having already explained their intrinsic nature,
that which is the reason for this shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason is it called the fruit of the śramaṇa?
What is the meaning of "fruit of the śramaṇa"?
Answer: All noble paths constitute the nature of a śramaṇa.
The conditioned, the unconditioned, and analytical cessation—because these are its fruits, they are called the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Question: If that is so, then...
This fruit should not consist of only four [factors].
That is to say, within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the category of the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) constitutes the nature of the śramaṇa,
while the category of the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) constitutes the conditioned fruits of the śramaṇa (*saṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala*).
The severance of the eight classes of defilements is the unconditioned fruit of śrāmaṇya.
At the time of becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm, the nine paths of uninterrupted transition constitute the nature of śrāmaṇya,
and the nine paths of liberation constitute the conditioned fruit of śrāmaṇya.
The abandonment of the nine grades of dharmas is the unconditioned fruit of śrāmaṇya.
In this manner, it should be understood that the same applies up until the time of becoming free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Thus, there are eighty-nine conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya.
There are eighty-nine unconditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya.
According to this explanation,
these fruits of śrāmaṇya number two hundred and sixty-seven.
That is to say, eighty-nine [dharmas] exist in the past;
eighty-nine exist in the present;
and eighty-nine exist in the future.
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states as follows:
"What are resultant phenomena (*phala-dharma*)?
They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
For as many moments as there are in the various noble paths,
there are that many conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya;
and for as much as there is of impure phenomena, there is that much [of their cessation].
The unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is likewise of that same extent.
To the extent that there are instances of the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation,
there are likewise that many unconditioned fruits of the śramaṇa.
If one were to distinguish the fruits of śrāmaṇya according to each moment within the body,
there would be immeasurable essences of the fruits of śrāmaṇya;
why, then, are only four fruits of śrāmaṇya taught?
Some say that this was a concise and incomplete teaching given by the Blessed One because it was what was appropriate for his disciples to hear.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to fully comprehend the intrinsic nature, characteristics, functional efficacy, and limits of all phenomena through his perfect wisdom;
others cannot know them.
If something is capable of being established as a fruit of the śramaṇa, he then establishes it.
If it is not capable [of being established], then it is simply not established;
therefore, one should not raise an objection.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this.
This was spoken by the Blessed One in brief for the sake of those with wisdom;
therefore, it should not be challenged.
Furthermore, these four stages of fruition are easy to perceive and easy to designate.
That is to say, these are the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship;
the remaining stages are difficult to perceive and difficult to designate.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke only of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, regarding these four stages of fruition,
practitioners of yoga give rise to a sense of superior joy toward the fruition itself,
whereas they do not do so for other stages.
It is just as a farmer who, having cultivated his crops during the six months of summer,
experiences great joy when he subsequently gathers the grain and stores it in the threshing floor;
this case is exactly like that.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke only of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, these four stages of fruition possess three causes and conditions:
first, the relinquishing of previously attained paths.
Second, one attains the path never before attained;
third, one realizes the single taste of the severance of fetters.
Other stages are not like this.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke only of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, these four fruit-attainments possess five causal conditions.
First, they involve relinquishing the path previously attained.
Second, attaining the path never before attained;
third, realizing the single flavor of the severance of fetters;
fourth, attaining the eight knowledges instantaneously.
At one time, one cultivates all sixteen aspects;
this is not the case in other stages.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke only of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, these four stages of fruition are the most supreme places of peace and rest for the yogācāra;
since other stages are not so, the Buddha taught only the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, the noble paths belonging to these four stages of fruition constitute the application of effort;
the abandonment of the fetters resulting from the culmination of that effort constitutes the task to be accomplished;
and this constitutes the culmination of the task.
In other stages, the noble path is the culmination of effort rather than non-effort;
in other stages, the severance of fetters is the culmination of what is to be done rather than non-action.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke only of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, it is within these four stages of fruition that practitioners are able to extensively cultivate the Noble Path;
this is not the case in other stages.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke only of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, regarding these four stages of fruition,
the various practitioners of yoga are able to thoroughly discern their virtues and faults.
"Virtues" refers to the path and the fruit of the path.
Faults refer to the causes and effects of birth and death;
other stages are not so.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke only of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, it is only at these four stages of fruition that practitioners of yoga are able to correctly apprehend the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths;
this is not the case in other stages.
Just as when a person walks about in the four directions, they cannot properly discern their features,
but only when sitting in one place can they properly discern them.
This case is also like that;
therefore, the Buddha spoke only of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, regarding these four stages of fruition:
If there is a witness when [an object] is lost or stolen,
it is not so in other circumstances;
just as in a village or town, if a robbery occurs and there is a witness, it is not the case that there is none in the space between.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, regarding these four stages of fruition,
the practitioners of yoga first establish themselves firmly through extensive preparatory application (*prayoga*).
It is not so for the other stages.
Regarding the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), one who previously engaged in extensive preparatory practice does so because they first sought the fruit of liberation.
One diligently cultivates generosity and pure ethical discipline;
the meditation on impurity, mindfulness of breathing, and the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
as well as the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas.
Furthermore, during the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
this is collectively termed "firmly established stability. Some say:
From the beginning up to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is called the extensive preparatory application (*prāyogika*).
The fifteen moments of mind in the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) are called the firm establishment.
For one who has previously engaged in the extensive preparatory application and attains the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*):
This refers to what was previously explained, as well as all paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) for those free from the defilements of desire;
the six paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and five paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are precisely what is called "firmly established."
Some say that the fruit of stream-entry is called "firmly established," while the fruit of non-returning belongs to those who have previously engaged in extensive preparatory practice.
This refers to what was previously described, as well as all paths of preparation for those free from the defilements of desire,
the three paths of immediate succession, and the two paths of liberation;
these are termed "firmly established."
Some say that the fruit of once-returner is called "firmly established," while for the fruit of arhatship,
one must first perform extensive preparatory practice.
This refers to what was previously described, as well as all preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*) that have abandoned even a single category of defilement of the first dhyāna,
up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
This is collectively termed "firmly established."
Some say that because the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) is called "firmly established and stable," the Buddha taught only four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, in these four stages of fruition,
the practitioners of yoga sever and bring to rest all factors of rebirth;
this is not the case in other stages.
This means that for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), with the exception of seven births in the desire realm and one birth in each location of the form and formless realms,
all other births attain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).

For the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin), with the exception of two births in the desire realm and one birth in each location of the form and formless realms [all other births attain non-analytical cessation].
All other births obtain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), with the exception of one birth in each of the various places within the form and formless realms,
all other births obtain non-analytical cessation.
Because the fruit of arhatship attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding all future births,
the Buddha taught only four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, regarding these four stages of fruition,
all yogācāras collectively attain the abandonment of the afflictions to be eliminated through seeing and cultivation within the three realms;
this is not the case for other stages.

This refers to the attainment of the abandonment of all afflictions to be eliminated through seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms, which is collectively gathered at the stage of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*);

and the attainment of the abandonment of all afflictions to be eliminated through seeing within the three realms, as well as the first six categories of afflictions to be eliminated through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm, which are collectively gathered at the stage of the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*).
The stage of the Non-returner (anāgāmiphala) comprises the attainment of the abandonment of all defilements to be abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*) across the three realms,
as well as the nine grades of defilements to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm.
The stage of the Arhat (arhattvaphala) comprises the attainment of the abandonment of all defilements to be abandoned through both vision and cultivation across the three realms.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, these four stages of fruition are the very goals sought by practitioners of yoga.
Since this is not the case for other stages, the Buddha spoke only of four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, regarding these four fruit-stages,
the various yogācāras state that although there may be retrogression, one will certainly not die until the stage has been regained.
Other stages are not like this;
therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
