Furthermore, these four fruit-stages attain the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the acquisitions (prāpti) of the five destinies (gati).
The other stages are not so.
That is to say, one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts;
one who has attained the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) attains non-analytical cessation regarding a portion of the human realm.
The fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) attains the analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the human realm in its entirety as its antidote;
the fruit of arhatship attains the analytical cessation of the celestial realms as its antidote.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, these four stages of fruition counteract the acquisition of the four modes of birth, thereby attaining non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
other stages do not.
Specifically, the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) counteracts the acquisition of birth from eggs and moisture-born birth, thereby attaining non-analytical cessation.
The fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala) attains the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding one portion of womb-birth (jarāyu-ja).
The fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) attains the non-analytical cessation regarding the entirety of womb-birth.
The fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala) attains the non-analytical cessation regarding apparitional birth (upapāduka).
Therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, these four fruit-stages counteract the two extremes,
whereas other stages do not.
Regarding the "two extremes":
this refers to the desire realm and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). Because one counteracts the extreme of the desire realm, one attains the fruits of once-returner and non-returner;
because one counteracts the extreme of the peak of existence, one attains the fruits of stream-enterer and arhat.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, these four stages of fruition counteract the root of the two types of existence (*bhava*);
other stages do not do so. As for the root of the two types of existence:
That is to say, because one counteracts the fundamental existence of the desire realm, one attains the fruits of once-returner and non-returner;
because one counteracts the fundamental existence of the peak of existence (bhavāgra), one attains the fruits of stream-enterer and arhat.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, these four fruit-attainments can eternally counteract two kinds of unwholesome volitions,
as well as the aggregates that serve as the basis for their maturation.
The other stages are not like this.
The two kinds of evil volitions refer to the volition that severs the roots of goodness and the volition that gives rise to an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karman*).
The fruit of stream-entry can eternally counteract and sever the volition that cuts off the roots of goodness;
the fruit of once-returning can eternally counteract the volition that gives rise to the immediate karmic offenses;
and the fruit of non-returning can eternally counteract their resultant maturation.
The fruit of arhatship can eternally counteract those aggregates (skandhas) that serve as its basis;
therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, these four stages of fruition counteract three types of phenomena.
The other stages are not so;
that is to say, the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) counteracts the three fetters (saṃyojana),
while the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin) counteracts the three unwholesome roots (akuśalamūla) and a portion of the outflows of desire (kāma-āsrava).
The fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) counteracts the three unwholesome roots and the entirety of the outflow of desire (kāma-āsrava);
the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala) counteracts the outflows of existence (bhava-āsrava) and ignorance (avidyā-āsrava).
Therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, these four stages of fruition counteract four specific categories of phenomena,
whereas other stages do not. Specifically,
the stage of the Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) counteracts the flood and yoke of views, the grasping at views and the grasping at precepts and observances, as well as the last two fetters of the body.
The fruit of once-returning counteracts a portion of the flood, yoke, and grasping of desire, as well as a portion of the first two fetters.
The fruit of non-returning counteracts the flood, yoke, and grasping of desire, as well as the entirety of the preceding two fetters.
The fruit of arhatship counteracts the flood and yoke of ignorance as well as the grasping for self-identity;
therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, these four stages of fruition counteract five factors.
The other stages are not like this.
That is to say, the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) counteracts the hindrance of doubt, the latter three fetters conducive to the lower realms, and the five views.
The fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) counteracts the first four hindrances and the fetters of ill-will, envy, and stinginess.
And [it is the antidote] to one portion of the two aforementioned fetters conducive to the lower realms;
to the four hindrances—anger, envy, and stinginess—which are the objects countered by the fruit of non-returning;
and to the entirety of the two aforementioned fetters conducive to the lower realms.
The fruit of Arhatship counteracts the fetters of greed and pride,
as well as the five higher-tier fetters;
therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, these four fruits counteract the six bases of craving (*ṣaḍ-āyatanāni tṛṣṇāyāḥ*);
other stages do not do so.

Specifically, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) counteracts the basis of craving born of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja-tṛṣṇā-āyatana*) that is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
The fruit of once-returning counteracts a portion of the body of craving born of nose-contact and tongue-contact;
the fruit of non-returning counteracts the entirety of the body of craving born of nose-contact and tongue-contact.
The fruit of arhatship counteracts the group of cravings born of eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact,
as well as the group of cravings born of mind-contact that is to be abandoned through cultivation;
therefore, the Buddha spoke only of the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, these four fruits counteract the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*);
other stages do not.
Specifically, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) counteracts the underlying tendencies of views and doubt.
The fruit of once-returning counteracts a portion of the latent tendencies of sensual desire and ill-will;
the fruit of non-returning counteracts the entirety of the latent tendencies of sensual desire and ill-will;
and the fruit of arhatship counteracts the latent tendencies of attachment to existence, pride, and ignorance.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, these four fruit-stages counteract the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*),
whereas other stages do not.
That is to say: the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) counteracts the fetters of views, grasping at views, and doubt;
the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin) counteracts a portion of the fetters of ill-will, envy, and avarice;
and the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin) counteracts the full extent of the fetters of ill-will, envy, and avarice.
The fruit of arhatship counteracts the fetters of craving, conceit, and ignorance;
therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, these four stages of fruition counteract the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
The other stages are not so.
That is to say, the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) counteracts the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the three realms that are abandoned through seeing;
the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) counteracts a portion of the latent dispositions of the desire realm that are abandoned through cultivation.
The fruit of non-returning counteracts the entirety of the latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the desire realm;
the fruit of arhatship counteracts the latent tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the form and formless realms.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, each of these four fruit-attainments marks the transcendence of a specific category of heavy afflictions;
other stages do not do so.
This means that the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) transcends the limit of heavy afflictions to be abandoned through insight;
the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala) transcends the limit of heavy afflictions capable of giving rise to the five deeds of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma).
That is to say, these are the first six grades of afflictions of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) which are capable of giving rise to the five deeds of immediate retribution.
The latter three categories are not like this,
because their power is inferior.
The fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) emerges from the limit of all unwholesome and heavy afflictions.
The fruit of arhatship emerges from the realm of all neutral states and the limit of heavy afflictions;
therefore, the Buddha taught only four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Question: For what reason are two fruits of śrāmaṇya established for those who have become detached from the defilements of the desire realm?
Does this mean that the fruits of once-returning and non-returning are established as one śrāmaṇaphala by way of being free from the defilements of the form and formless realms,
namely, the fruit of arhatship?
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to fully know the nature, characteristics, functions, and limits of all dharmas; others cannot know them.
If one is free from these defilements and is capable of establishing two fruits, then one establishes those two immediately."
If one is capable of establishing a single fruit upon being free from these defilements, then one indeed establishes one;
therefore, this objection should not be raised.
Furthermore, there is no fruit among the four fruits of śrāmaṇya that is not established by reason of being free from the defilements of the three realms.

That is to say, the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phala) is established by being free from the defilements abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya) within the three realms. The fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmi-phala) is established by being free from those same defilements abandoned through seeing within the three realms,
as well as being free from the first six categories of defilements abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) within the desire realm.
If one is freed from the defilements abandoned through insight within the three realms,
as well as the defilements abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm, the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) is established.
If one is freed from the defilements abandoned through both insight and cultivation within the three realms, the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*) is established.
Furthermore, because the desire realm is an indeterminate realm, not a stage of cultivation, and not a stage of freedom from defilement,
two fruits of the śramaṇa are established based on being free from its defilements.
The form and formless realms, however, are determinate realms, stages of cultivation, and stages of freedom from defilement.
Therefore, when one is detached from those defilements, only a single fruit of śrāmaṇya is established.
Furthermore, because the desire realm is difficult to sever, difficult to destroy, and difficult to transcend,
two fruits of śrāmaṇya are established upon detachment from its defilements.
The form and formless realms are easy to sever, easy to shatter, and easy to transcend;
therefore, one establishes only a single fruit of śrāmaṇya for the abandonment of their defilements.
Furthermore, it is because the faults of the desire realm are so intense, its faults are so solid, and its faults are so numerous.
The two fruits of śrāmaṇya are established based on detachment from those [desire-realm] defilements;
since the form and formless realms are contrary to this,
only one fruit of śrāmaṇya is established for detachment from them.

Furthermore, because the afflictions of the desire realm are like a torrential flood that is difficult to cross, two fruits of śrāmaṇya are established for those who have become free from their defilements.
It is like a person crossing a river: its waters are deep and wide, and the waves are so swift that one must repeatedly rest before being able to reach the other side.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Householder, you should know that the term 'flood' is a metaphor for the five objects of sensual pleasure."
The form and formless realms are the opposite of this;
therefore, only one fruit of śrāmaṇya is established for those who are free from the defilements of those realms.
Furthermore, because the desire realm is a realm of peril and difficulty.
When afflictions increase in weight and karma increases in weight,
it is like a heavy burden that is difficult to cross over; therefore,
two fruits of śrāmaṇya are established based on being free from those defilements.
The realms of form and formlessness are not realms of peril and difficulty;
although the afflictions and karmic actions therein may be heavy, they are easily transcended.
Therefore, being free from those defilements, only one fruit of śrāmaṇya is established for them.
It is like a person carrying a heavy load up a steep and difficult mountain; only by resting repeatedly can they cross over.
Once they reach level ground, although they still carry the heavy load, it is easy for them to travel far.
This is also like that.
Furthermore, because the desire realm is a defiled realm—
just as a mire mixed with various excrement and filth is difficult to escape from.
Therefore, two fruits of śrāmaṇya are established for the abandonment of those defilements [of the desire realm].
Since the form and formless realms are contrary to this,
only one fruit of śrāmaṇya is established for the abandonment of their defilements.
It is like building a palace upon a heap of excrement;
though it may be exquisite and beautiful, no person would wish to dwell there.
The realms of form and formlessness are likewise thus.
Because it dwells above the defiled dharmas of the desire realm,
although it is exquisite, the noble ones do not delight in it;
for this reason, the Venerable Saṃgharakṣa spoke thus.
Within this realm of desire, there are many faults:
namely, the loss of parents, brothers, sisters, wives, children, and kinsmen; the forfeiture of wealth and status;
or being maimed by having one's ears, nose, hands, feet, and various limbs severed.
Or again, one may encounter the four hundred and four diseases;
through such various causes and conditions, one undergoes manifold intense sufferings.
Thus, the desire realm abounds in many faults.
If one were to establish all four fruits of śrāmaṇya apart from that detachment, they would still be too few, let alone two.
Furthermore, because the male and female bodies in the desire realm are difficult to transcend, [the fruits are established accordingly].
Therefore, two fruits of śrāmaṇya are established for those who have abandoned the defilements of the desire realm.
Because in the form and formless realms there is only the male body, which is easily transcended,
only one fruit of śrāmaṇya is established for those who have abandoned the defilements of those realms.
Furthermore, because the male and female faculties exist in the desire realm and are difficult to transcend,
two fruits of śrāmaṇya are established there for those who have detached from those defilements.
In the form and formless realms, however, the male and female faculties do not exist and are thus easy to transcend.
Therefore, only one fruit of śrāmaṇya is established for the abandonment of those defilements.
Furthermore, because the desire realm contains two kinds of afflictions—the unwholesome and the neutral—which are difficult to transcend.
Therefore, two fruits of śrāmaṇya are established based on being free from those defilements.
In the form and formless realms, there is only one kind of neutral affliction that is easily transcended;
thus, freedom from those defilements establishes only one fruit of śrāmaṇya, unlike the case of the two kinds of afflictions—the unwholesome and the neutral.
In this way, there are two types of arising—those with maturation and those without maturation—and two types of fruit—the arising of two fruits and the arising of one fruit.
It should be understood that the same applies to the afflictions associated with or dissociated from lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).

Furthermore, because the desire realm possesses the faculty of suffering, the faculty of grief, lack of shame and lack of dread, envy and avarice, the nutriment of physical food, as well as sensual desire, the five hindrances, the five objects of desire, the various evil destinies, and other such manifold afflictions that are difficult to escape from; [the desire realm is thus inferior].
Therefore, two fruits of śrāmaṇya are established for those who have abandoned the defilements of the desire realm.
Because the form and formless realms are the opposite of this, only one fruit of śrāmaṇya is established for those who have abandoned the defilements of those realms.
Furthermore, the desire realm possesses eighteen elements, twelve bases, and many other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) that are difficult to transcend.
Therefore, two fruits of śrāmaṇya are established for the abandonment of those defilements [of the desire realm].
Because the impure dharmas (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the form and formless realms are few,
only one fruit of śrāmaṇya is established for the abandonment of those [defilements].

Question: Why is the first fruit of śrāmaṇya established by being free from defilements abandoned through seeing (darśana-prahātavya), while the latter three fruits of śrāmaṇya are established by being free from defilements abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya)?
Answer: Defilements abandoned through seeing are easily removed.
Therefore, the first fruit of śramaṇaship is established at the time of abandoning those [defilements];
because the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation are difficult to distance oneself from,
the latter three fruits of śramaṇaship are established at the time of abandoning them.

Question: It was previously stated that the Noble Path is the nature of a śramaṇa, being conditioned and untainted (anāsrava).
And because various analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are the fruits of this [path], they are called "fruits of śramaṇaship" (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
That which is realized through the power of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) may properly be designated by this name;
however, that which is realized through the power of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), such as the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) or non-returner (*anāgāmin*), is not so designated.
What is called the fruit of śrāmaṇya?

The answer is: just as the limit of the fruit is established when one is freed from the defilements of the desire realm through the untainted path—whether partially or entirely—in the same way, a noble one may be freed from the defilements of the desire realm by means of the mundane path.
Whether doubled or complete, they are also established as the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning;
therefore, both also receive the name of "fruit of śramaṇaship.
The Venerable Saṃghavasu said:
When one becomes detached from the defilements of desire by means of the mundane path, one also cultivates [the fruits] in the future;
because the two fruits obtained through the various untainted paths are the fruits of that [detachment],
they may likewise be established under the name of "fruits of śramaṇa-ship."
He should not speak thus. Why is that?
Because the future noble path has not yet performed its function.
How do these two obtain the designation of "attainment of the fruit"?

Other masters say that when one becomes free from the defilements of desire by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) attains a state of constant, continuous activity.
Because the two fruits obtained are indeed their fruits,
they may also be established as having the name "fruits of śrāmaṇya. They should not, however, say this.
Why is this? Because one attains the realization of the function of severing the fetters through their non-interruption;
how then could there be the designation of "attaining the fruit" with respect to either of these?
Furthermore, there are those who say that for one who attains the two fruits by means of the mundane path,
when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, [the fruit is attained].
One realizes, all at once, the attainment of the single-flavored abandonment of what is to be abandoned through both the paths of seeing and cultivation within the three realms.
Because the previously attained abandonments are the fruits of this [realization], they are called the fruits of śramaṇa-hood;
for this concentration is the true nature of a śramaṇa.
They, too, should not speak in this way.
Why is that? Because at the time of attaining the two fruits, one has not yet attained this concentration.
If one attains this meditative absorption and loses that name for its fruit,
how can those two be called fruits of the śramaṇa?
One should explain it as follows:
The name is established primarily because it is for the most part the fruit obtained through the noble path.
That is to say, when the mundane path attains two fruits,
there is the abandonment of all defilements to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) belonging to the three realms.
Because these are all obtained through the power of the Noble Path (āryamārga), they are called the fruits of śramaṇaship (śrāmaṇyaphala).

Although there are cases where the abandonment of the six grades or nine grades of afflictions in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) is not obtained through the Noble Path, [the fruits of śramaṇaship are defined by what is obtained through that path].
Nevertheless, for the most part, the designation "fruit of śrāmaṇya" can also be established, because the single untainted acquisition (anāsrava-prāpti) encompasses all that is attained.
Question: Among the four fruits of śrāmaṇya thus described, how many are nominal designations (prajñapti)?
How many are of ultimate meaning?
Answer: Two are conventional designations, namely, the fruits of once-returner and non-returner.
The second is the fruit of actual reality, namely the fruits of stream-entry and arhatship.
Question: Why are the fruits of once-returning and non-returning called "provisional fruits"?
Are the fruits of stream-entry and arhatship called "fruits of ultimate meaning"?
Answer: All mundane paths are paths of conventional designation;
the two intermediate fruits obtain only a small portion of what those [mundane paths] attain.
Because many [factors] arise from few, they are designated as "fruits" by way of conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
The various untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) are the paths in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
The first and last fruits are obtained in their entirety through those [paths].
Therefore, the results of the beginning and the end are called results in the ultimate sense (*bhūtārtha-phala*).

Furthermore, the two intermediate results are called results in a conventional sense (*prajñapti-phala*), as they are attained by both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths.
"Conventional" here means that which is attained in common.
That which is shared is called a conventional entity (*prajñapti-dharma*).
The first and last fruits are obtained solely through the power of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) and are thus called fruits in the sense of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-phala*).
Ultimate reality is precisely that which is attained individually.
That which exists as a solitary entity is called a real object (*dravyārtha-vastu*).
Furthermore, because the two intermediate fruits are attained through the conventional designation of names and phrases by means of the noble path (*āryamārga*),
they are called "fruits of designation" (*prajñaptiphala*).
This means that when those two paths exist in the future, they provisionally employ conventional expressions;
since they pertain to the same matter, they vow to perform one and the same deed and should rejoice in one and the same [deed].
The first and last fruits are attained solely through the noble path.
Because it is not attained through the provisional designation of names and terms by means of two paths,
it is called the "actual fruit of the object.
Other masters say:
The provisional fruit refers to the first two fruits, because they are realized only by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
As for the fruit in its ultimate sense:
This means that the latter two fruits are realized by all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and mahābuddhas;
thus, they are for the most part the actual meaning and only rarely mere designations.
The critique states:
He should not make such a statement,
because "few" and "many" do not correspond to the meanings of the provisional (prajñapti) and the real (dravya).
In this context, the former explanation is logically sound.
Why is this? Because the fruits of the śramaṇa are obtained through the power of the nature of the śramaṇa.
Only the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) constitutes the nature of a śramaṇa;
one who accomplishes it is called a true śramaṇa.
Therefore, the two fruits obtained by him are termed the fruits of a śramaṇa in the ultimate sense.
The various mundane paths are not the nature of a śramaṇa;
those who accomplish them are called "nominal śramaṇas.
Therefore, the two fruits obtained through them are called "nominal fruits of the śramaṇa."
It is asked: The Path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), possesses the grades of inferior, middling, and superior, and arises according to the power of its causes; thus it may be called a fruit.
But cessation (*nirodha*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), lacks the grades of inferior, middling, and superior, and is not produced by causes; how can it be called a fruit?
Answer: Although abandonment does not arise [as a new entity], it is nonetheless called a "fruit" because it is attained through preparatory application (*prayoga*).
That is to say, the practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*) dwells either on the peak of a high mountain or in a secluded chamber.
Moderate one's food and drink, reduce sleep, and economize on requisites for the body.
Uphold the seven minor dhāraṇīs and the seven-day rite; stabilize the head with the *vīrakṣepa* (subduing) practice and carry the ritual staff.
From the setting of the sun today until the rising of the sun tomorrow,
one shall arouse exceptionally sublime and courageous diligence,
successively inducing the untainted noble path.
By this, he realized the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
At that time, the Guide praised and comforted him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

Because you were able to apply yourself with diligence to correct practice, you have now attained this fruit; it is like a farmer who, during the six months of summer, tends the furrows, weeds the crops, and subsequently harvests the grain to store it in the granary.
The former farmers consoled them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You have exerted much toil during these six months, and now you have obtained this fruit."
Therefore, both the Path and its abandonment receive the name of "fruit.
Regarding these four fruits of the śramaṇa thus described, [it is asked:
how many are the fruits of dhyāna?
Answer: Four are the fruits of the dhyānas and their attendants.
Question: How many are the fruits of the formless attainments?
Answer: One.
It refers to the fruit of arhatship.
Question: How many are the fruits of the fundamental dhyānas?
Answer: Two.
That is to say, the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of arhatship.
Question: How many are the fruits of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of dhyāna?
Answer: Four; namely, those of the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna, and not those of the other dhyānas.
The intermediate [stages] are as explained in the root [text].
Question: How many are the fruits of the fundamental formless [attainments]?
Answer: One.
This refers to the fruit of arhatship.
Question: How many are the fruits of the formless-sphere access concentrations?
Answer: None.
Question: How many are the fruits of the path of seeing?
Answer: Three;
that is, excluding the fruit of arhatship.
Question: How many are the fruits of the path of cultivation?
Answer: Three;
that is, excluding the fruit of stream-entry.
Question: How many are the fruits of patience?
Answer: Three;
that is, excluding the fruit of arhatship.
Question: How many are the fruits of knowledge (*jñāna*)?
Answer: Three; that is, excluding the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
Question: How many are the fruits of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)?
Answer: Three;
that is, excluding the fruit of stream-entry.
Question: How many are the fruits of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
Answer: One.
That is to say, regarding the question of how many are the fruits of the category of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna-pakṣa), the answer is three.
That is to say, excluding the fruit of stream-entry.
Question: How many are the fruits of the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
Answer: Four.
Question: How many are the fruits of the mundane path?
Answer: Two;
namely, the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning.
Question: How many are the fruits of the untainted path?
Answer: Four.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The King Ajātaśatru, son of the Videha princess and lord of Magadha, approached the place where the Buddha was;
having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there any visible fruit of the ascetic life?
The Buddha replied, "There is.
The King asked, "In what way?"
The World-Honored One said:
"I shall now question the King;
you should answer as you see fit."
If the king’s attendants or various servants are not at ease,
they may sometimes see the king ascend a high terrace or palace, where he provides the five kinds of musical entertainment and frolics and plays joyfully with his retinue.
Having seen this, he thought to himself:
"I too am a human being; why should I not do the same?
Yet, the King has cultivated many meritorious deeds in his past lives."
Therefore, in this present life, he has received such an excellent retribution.
"I, too, should now cultivate superior deeds so that I may likewise be admired and envied by the multitude like the King.
Having formed this thought, he immediately renounced the ways of the household.
Having shaved off their hair and beard and donned the saffron robes,
they received and maintained the three refuges and the pure precepts,
and were able to sever and cultivate the ten paths of karmic action.
The king’s remaining attendants saw him outside;
they immediately returned to report the matter in full detail,
requesting that the king pursue and reclaim him to employ him as he was before.
The king asked, "Did he speak as you requested?
The king replied, "No.
If such a person exists, I ought to go to see him, pay him homage, and make offerings to him."
Just as he served me in the past,
I shall now serve him for the remainder of his life,
providing him with clothing, food and drink, medicine, dwellings, and bedding.
He also provided all necessary provisions so that there was no lack whatsoever.
The Buddha said to the king,
"Is this matter not a visible manifestation of the fruits of the śramaṇa's life?"
The king said to the Buddha, "It is truly as the Holy Teaching declares.
I ask: are the fruits of the śramaṇa's realization only four?"
Why does this sutra further mention a fifth [fruit]?
Answer: There are only four actual fruits of true śrāmaṇya;
this [fifth] refers to one who currently manifests the fruit of śrāmaṇya.
However, renunciation is proximate to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Question: Since renunciation is not the true nature of a śramaṇa, how can it be said that there are fruits of a śramaṇa?
Answer: Although going forth is not the true nature of a śramaṇa, it is conventionally designated by the world as having the name "śramaṇa-nature.
Therefore, when people of the world see one who has gone forth...
One might then say: "I see such a śramaṇa;
therefore, one who has gone forth attains the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala), which is also conventionally designated by the name 'fruit of a śramaṇa'."
This term "manifest" (*vijñapti*) refers to appearance and does not denote a substantial reality.
Furthermore, the *Siṃhanāda-sūtra* states:
"Only within my Dharma are there four types of śramaṇas."
This refers to the first through the fourth types of śramaṇas.
Within the teachings of the non-Buddhists, there are no true śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas;
there are only empty titles.
Regarding such matters, he utters the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly without any fear.
It should be understood that, herein, the "first śramaṇa" refers to those who have attained the stage of stream-entry (srotāpanna).
The second śramaṇa refers to those who are once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin).
The third śramaṇa refers to those who are non-returners (anāgāmin).
The fourth śramaṇa refers to those who are arhats.
The Venerable Pārśva said:

"It should be understood that herein the Buddha spoke according to preeminence; he mentioned the first śramaṇa first, which refers to the arhats, and the second śramaṇa, which refers to the non-returners (anāgāmins)."
The third śramaṇa refers to those who are once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin).
The fourth śramaṇa refers to those who are stream-enterers (srotāpanna). Furthermore, it is stated in the *Sudharmasūtra*:
"If the Noble Eightfold Path exists in a place, one should know that there are four types of śramaṇas in that place."
This refers to the first śramaṇa up to the fourth.
Regarding this, some say that those who are directed toward the four fruits are called the four śramaṇas.
The first śramaṇa refers to one who is a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-pratipannaka).
The second śramaṇa refers to one who is a candidate for the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka).
The third śramaṇa refers to one who is a candidate for the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-pratipannaka).
The fourth ascetic refers to one who is a candidate for arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*).
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"In this sūtra, four types of candidates and four fruits are taught."
If this place possesses the Noble Eightfold Path, it is said to have the four candidates for the fruits;
one should know that where there are four śramaṇas, it is said to have the four fruits.
This is also stated in the Cunda Sūtra.
There are four types of śramaṇas and no fifth.
The four śramaṇas are:
first, the śramaṇa who has won the path (mārgajina).
Second, the śramaṇa who shows the path;
third, the śramaṇa who lives by the path;
fourth, the śramaṇa who defiles the path.
It should be understood that among these, the śramaṇa of the supreme path refers to the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, because he has awakened by himself;
it should be known that all pratyekabuddhas are likewise so.
The "Śramaṇa who shows the Way" refers to the Venerable Śāriputra,
because he is peerless and without equal.
Because they are the generals of the Great Dharma,
they are always able to follow the Buddha in turning the wheel of the Dharma;
it should be known that all Arhats who have nothing further to learn (aśaikṣa) are likewise so.
The śramaṇa who was commanded was the Venerable Ānanda;

although he remained in the stage of training (śaikṣa), he was like one beyond training (aśaikṣa) in his great learning, his retention of what he had heard, and his possession of pure ethical discipline.
It should be understood that all those in training (śaikṣa) are likewise so.
As for the "monk who defiles the path," this refers to,
for example, the bhikṣu Mokhalaka, who delighted in stealing the property of others and so forth.
Question: What is the distinction between the types of śramaṇas described in the three sūtras cited above?
Some say that the *Siṃhanāda-sūtra* defines a śramaṇa as one who abides in the four fruits [of the path].

In the *Sukhavihāra-sūtra*, it is said that a śramaṇa refers to one who practices the four paths; in the *Cunda-sūtra*, it is said that a śramaṇa refers to one who abides in the four fruits and practices the various paths.
Other masters say:
The *Siṃhanāda-sūtra* states that "śramaṇas" refers to those who abide in the four fruits [of the path].
The *Sudharmasūtra* states that "śramaṇas" refers to those who practice the four paths and abide in the four fruits.
In the *Cunda-sūtra*, it is stated that a "śramaṇa" refers to one who is fully endowed with all the qualities of a śramaṇa.
Some say that while the *Siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Bhadrika-sūtra* state that a śramaṇa is one who dwells in the four fruits, the *Cunda-sūtra* states that a śramaṇa is... [as above].
This refers to all śramaṇas who abide in the fruits or are progressing toward them.
Furthermore, some say that the *Siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Bhadraśrī-sūtra* state that "śramaṇa" refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
In the Cunda Sūtra, it is said that "śramaṇas" refers to those in training (śaikṣa),
those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
Some have stated as follows:
The *Siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Subhadda-sūtra* state that "śramaṇas" refers to the noble ones (*ārya*).
In the *Cunda-sūtra*, it is stated that "śramaṇas" refers to both the noble ones and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, some say that the *Siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Bhadraśrī-sūtra* state that a śramaṇa refers to one who upholds the precepts;
whereas the *Cunda-sūtra* states that a śramaṇa refers to both those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them.
Alternatively, some say that the meaning of "śramaṇa" taught in these three sūtras is without distinction. [Objection:
The first two sūtras state that there are four types of śramaṇas.
Are śramaṇas who defile the path included within the four [categories of noble persons]?
Answer: They are also included within the four;
namely, those who are candidates for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-pratipannaka).
However, those who are stream-enterers-in-training (srotāpanna-pratipannaka) are of two types: those who are near and those who are distant.
"Near" refers to those on the path of seeing (darśana-mārga).

"Distant" refers to those prior to that, including those in the stages conducive to penetration (nirvedha-bhāgīya), those in the stages conducive to liberation (mokṣa-bhāgīya), and even those who have left the household life out of right faith.
As stated in the sūtras,
there are four factors conducive to stream-entry (srotāpatti-aṅga),
namely: associating with virtuous persons (satpuruṣasaṃsevā).
Hearing the true Dharma, attending to it correctly,
and practicing in accordance with the Dharma are the causal factors for the branches [of the path].
Regarding the non-differentiation between name and meaning:
it is asked, the *Sukhavihāri-sūtra* states,
"If this place possesses the Noble Eightfold Path, one should know that there are four types of śramaṇas in this place."
Question: Are those śramaṇas who defile the path included herein?
Answer: They too are included herein, because the factors of the noble path exist both substantially and as designations.
The real refers to the eight [limbs] beginning with untainted right view;
the conventional refers to the eight beginning with tainted right view.
A śramaṇa who defiles the path may also achieve tainted right view.
Therefore, that too is included within the first type of śramaṇa.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the four types of śramaṇas mentioned in the two preceding sūtras are identical to this third type.
The four [categories] taught in the sūtra, such as the "superior path" (viśeṣamārga) and so forth, do not refer to those who are stream-enterers (srotāpanna) and the like.
Therefore, there is no discrepancy between what is taught in these three sūtras.
[Question: How then should one interpret what is stated in the first sūtra?
"Only within my Dharma are there four types of śramaṇas.
The Buddha makes this true lion's roar amidst the assembly.
Does the World-Honored One not say that this applies only within my Dharma?
There is no fault in answering that one may roar the lion’s roar even while violating the precepts. Why is this?
A defiled śramaṇa, although he has violated the precepts, has not violated his views;
although he has violated his application, he has not violated his intention.
Suppose someone were to ask:
"Is the evil of your transgression of the precepts good or is it unwholesome?
He replied, "It is unwholesome.
"Is it something that should be done or something that should not be done?"
He said that it should not be performed.
"Does it have a maturation, or does it lack a maturation?
He replied, "It has a maturation."
Is it for the sake of obtaining a desirable fruit or for the sake of obtaining an undesirable fruit?
He says it is for the sake of obtaining an undesirable fruit.
Is it for the sake of experiencing it in the miserable realms or for the sake of experiencing it in the happy realms?
He asks: "Regarding those who experience the miserable realms,
do they experience it for themselves,
or do they experience it for others?"
He said, "I myself experienced it.
"Is this the fault of the teacher, the fault of the teaching, or your own fault?
He replied, "It is not the fault of the teacher."
Nor is it a fault of the teaching; rather, it is my own fault.
He possesses such a form of tainted right view and believes in cause and effect.
Not being deluded regarding cause and effect—
such right view is something that does not exist among the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders.
Therefore, the Buddha utters the true lion’s roar in the midst of the assembly.
To speak based on that is likewise without fault, as stated in the sūtra:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
I truly know and see that there are three kinds of persons who perform much for sentient beings and whose kindness is difficult to repay,
even if one were to offer them the finest clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine for as long as one lives.
Even if one were to provide them with all other necessary resources and conditions for their support,
one still could not repay them.
What are these three?
First, there are those who preach the Dharma for others,
causing them to renounce the household life and enter the homeless state,
shaving off their hair and beards and donning the saffron robes.
First, one upholds the pure precepts with right faith.
Second, there is the person who expounds the Dharma for others,
causing them to know that all phenomena of origination are phenomena of cessation.
Third, there are those who teach the Dharma to others, causing them to exhaust all outflows and realize the liberation of mind and wisdom that is untainted. In this regard,
they give rise to the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, which is free from dust and free from defilement.
In this present life, he is able to personally realize for himself that birth has been exhausted and so forth, and dwells in its full possession.
Furthermore, one who exhorts others to receive the upāsaka (lay follower) vows is also called one who has done much and whose kindness is difficult to repay.
Why is this not stated in this sutra?
One should know that when something ought to be stated but is not,
the meaning therein is incomplete.
Furthermore, because the monastic discipline (*pravrajita-śīla*) is both cause and effect, the Sūtra speaks of it specifically;
that is to say, this is the fruit of the lay practitioner’s discipline (*upāsaka-śīla*),
and it is the cause of the bhikṣu’s discipline.
Furthermore, the exhortation to leave the household life is specifically taught in the sūtras because it exhorts people to enter the noble Dharma (āryadharma).
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of entry into the noble Dharma.
First is the conventional;
second is the ultimate.
Regarding the conventional:
That is to say, having abandoned the ways of the household life and gone forth into the homeless state,
shaving off hair and beard and donning the saffron robes,
one receives and upholds the pure precepts with right faith.
The ultimate meaning refers to entering the patience for the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) from the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukika-agra-dharma*).
Furthermore, the exhortation to leave the household life is specifically taught in the sūtras as an exhortation for people to escape from base and lowly affairs.
This means that householders are mostly oppressed by various kinds of common, base, and evil affairs;
those who have left the household life are liberated from these.
Furthermore, this is an exhortation for those who would leave the household life.
This is specifically taught in the sūtra because it encourages people to liberate themselves from all suffering;
that is to say, those who have left the household life are liberated from the various afflictions and sufferings of their present existence.
By means of this, they successively liberate themselves from the phenomena of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and distress throughout the cycle of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, exhorting one to leave the household life is equivalent to exhorting a person to experience happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha*).
Because this leads, through successive stages, to the attainment of ultimate sovereignty and peace, the Sūtra speaks specifically of it.
Furthermore, the exhortation to leave the household life is specifically taught in the sūtras as an exhortation for people to manifest the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Briefly, there are two kinds of manifesting the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
First is the conventional;
second is the ultimate.
As for the conventional:
That is to say, having abandoned the life of a householder and gone forth into homelessness,
shaving off beard and hair and donning the saffron robes,
one receives and upholds the pure precepts with right faith.
The ultimate truth refers to attaining true and pure awakening regarding the Four Noble Truths at the time of first going forth into homelessness.
Having already manifested as a conventional Buddha appearing in the world,
and having gone forth into homelessness, practicing the path through successive stages,
he further manifests as an ultimate Buddha appearing in the world.
Furthermore, the exhortation to leave the household life is specifically taught in the sutras as an exhortation for people to train in the bodies of all Buddhas;
that is to say, the bodies of all Buddhas are briefly of two kinds.
First is the birth-body;
second is the dharma-body.
If one abandons the household life and proceeds to the homeless state.
Having shaved off their hair and beard and donned the kashaya robes,
they receive and uphold the pure precepts with right faith;
one should know that this is precisely training in the Buddha’s birth-body (janmakāya).
If one can successively cultivate right practice and give rise to true and pure awakening regarding the Four Noble Truths,
it should be known that this is precisely training in the Buddha’s Dharma-body.
Furthermore, the exhortation to leave the household life is specifically taught in the sūtras because it is an exhortation for people to train in the practices of all Buddhas.
Briefly stated, these practices of the Buddhas are of two kinds.
First is the conventional;
second is the ultimate.
Regarding the conventional:
That is to say, having abandoned the ways of the household life and gone forth into the homeless state,
shaving off beard and hair and donning the saffron robes,
one receives and upholds the pure precepts with right faith.
The ultimate truth refers to the ability to correctly understand the Four Noble Truths;
from the time of first leaving the household life, one has already been able to train in accordance with the worldly conduct of the Buddha.
Having already left the household life,
he practices with diligence and is further able to train in accordance with the supreme conduct of the Buddha.
Furthermore, he exhorts others to leave the household life.
This is because the sutra speaks specifically of this in order to encourage people to enter the ocean of the Buddha-dharma;
that is to say, if anyone abandons the ways of household life and leaves home with pure faith,
they are said to have for the first time entered the ocean of the Buddhas' dharma.
If one exhausts all outflows and realizes parinirvāṇa,
this is called ultimately entering the ocean of the Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, there is the exhortation for those who have left the household life.
This is because the sutra speaks specifically of this in order to exhort people to resolutely enter the path of true liberation;
as it is said in the Sūtra:
"O all you who have gone forth..."
One attains the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the four noble truths through the certainty of knowing and seeing them as they truly are.
Furthermore, "encouraging one to go forth" means encouraging a person to definitely attain the three types of restraint (*saṃvara*).
The prātimokṣa restraint,
the dhyāna restraint, and the untainted (anāsrava) restraint.
Therefore, the sutra speaks of this specifically.
Furthermore, exhorting those who have left the household life is equivalent to exhorting people that they will certainly attain the three kinds of aggregates of virtue.
That is to say, the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of meditative concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom; therefore, the Sūtra speaks of them specifically.
Just as with these three aggregates of wholesomeness, it should be understood that the same applies to the three trainings, the three cultivations, and the three purities.

Furthermore, the exhortation to renounce the household life is specifically taught in the sūtras as an exhortation for people to certainly attain the threefold right path— namely, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
As it is with the three right paths, so it is with the three stages.
Furthermore, to exhort one to leave the household life is to exhort a person that they shall certainly attain the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).

This means that because of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*),
the Sūtra speaks of them specifically. Furthermore,
exhorting those who have left the household life is equivalent to exhorting people to attain the three kinds of enlightenment (*bodhi*) as they appropriately should.
This refers to the enlightenment of śrāvakas, the enlightenment of pratyekabuddhas, and unsurpassed enlightenment;
therefore, the sūtra speaks specifically of these.
Furthermore, it is intended to encourage those who have left the household life.
This is an exhortation that one will certainly attain the three types of *muni*:
namely, the *muni* of body, the *muni* of speech, and the *muni* of mind; thus the sutra speaks of them specifically.
This is also the case for the three kinds of tranquility (*śānti*) and the three kinds of purity (*viśuddhi*).
Furthermore, the exhortation to leave the household life is specifically taught in the sutras because it exhorts one to distance both body and mind from worldly attachments;
that is to say, at the time of leaving home, the body is freed from many affairs.
Because the body has few concerns, the mind also has few concerns;
by means of this, one remains far removed from afflictions and evil karma.
Furthermore, exhorting those who have left the household life is equivalent to exhorting people to free their bodies and minds from defilement; therefore, the sutra speaks specifically of this.
This means that at the time of renouncing the household life, the body becomes pure;
because the body is pure, the mind also becomes pure.
Because both body and mind are pure, the defilements of afflictions and karma are swiftly eliminated.
Furthermore, the exhortation to leave the household life refers specifically to the excellence of one’s body and mind; thus, the sutra speaks of it exclusively.
This means that at the time of leaving the household life, the body immediately becomes excellent.
Because the body is sublime and excellent, the mind is also sublime and excellent.
Furthermore, encouraging one to leave the household life is equivalent to encouraging the physical and mental dignity of a person; therefore, the sutra speaks of it specifically.
It means that at the time of going forth, the body becomes dignified;
because the body is dignified, the mind also becomes dignified.
Furthermore, to exhort one to go forth is to exhort a person that they shall certainly attain ultimate tranquility, which is nirvana; therefore, the sutra speaks of this specifically.
Furthermore, the exhortation to leave the household life is specifically taught in the sūtras because it encourages people to attain the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).
This refers to the deportment, attire, and activities undertaken at the time of leaving the household life.
It is not shared with any householders.
Furthermore, the exhortation to those who have left the home life is specifically taught in the sutra because it exhorts people to abandon the karma of afflictions.
This means that at the time of renouncing the household life, one shaves off hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and undertakes the pure precepts; thus,
afflictions and evil karma are gradually abandoned and left behind,
for the outward appearance of a layperson is not a fit vessel for them.
Just as foul odors do not abide upon a person who is fragrant and pure,
furthermore, to exhort one to leave the household life is to exhort that person to perform inexhaustible karma and thereby obtain inexhaustible wealth.
By performing blameless karma, one obtains blameless wealth;
by performing non-harming karma, one obtains non-harming wealth;
by performing karma not shared with outsiders, one obtains wealth not shared with outsiders.
Because they perform actions not shared with ordinary beings and acquire wealth not shared with ordinary beings,
the sūtra speaks of them specifically.

Furthermore, to exhort those who have left the household life is to exhort people to practice exclusively the conduct of the "conch-and-painting," which means practicing the pure and white brahmacarya for as long as life lasts.
Householders are unable to do so;
therefore, the Sūtra speaks specifically [of this].
Question: What is the meaning of the "conch-like" and "painted" modes of conduct?
The Venerable Vasumitra stated this:
"In the past, within this continent, there were two rishis;
one was named Śaṅkha."
The second was named Lixi (Rikṣa).
He was fully endowed with the foremost rules of conduct and the holy life (*brahmacarya*),
such that no householders could equal him.
To exhort others to leave the household life is to exhort them to become like that.
Some say it is like the engraved patterns on a conch shell, which are firm and difficult to destroy.
It cannot be easily destroyed by wind, sun, or other external conditions;
the practice of those who have gone forth is likewise so.
Those living at home are unable to cultivate such a practice.
Although they may temporarily uphold it, they soon destroy it.
Other masters say that it is like the engraved patterns on a conch shell, which are clean, clear, and free from all impurities.
The conduct of those who have left the household life is likewise so;
those remaining at home cannot cultivate such conduct,
for even if they uphold it to the utmost, it remains defiled and impure.
It is observed that there are householders who have attained the fruit of non-returning;
although they are free from the defilement of desire,
they remain at home and accept and keep things belonging to the category of animals rather than the category of living beings.
Their undertakings have not yet become particularly pure;
how much less so for those living at home who, having attained the first or second fruits, are no different from ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Even for those who have gone forth, though they may have violated the prohibitions, [they are superior].
This is superior even to those who maintain the precepts while remaining in the secular world; therefore,
the sutras specifically teach this,
exhorting people to leave the household life, for the kindness [of such an act] is difficult to repay.
Furthermore, to exhort one to leave the household life is to exhort a person to cultivate a noble and honorable practice;
the resulting retribution surpasses that of King Yama, a Wheel-Turning King, or Śakra.
Therefore, the sutras specifically state that the kindness of one who encourages another to leave the household life is difficult to repay;
this also applies to those who encourage others to receive and uphold the precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and so forth.
Because such a matter does not exist, the sūtra does not mention it.

Question: For what reason does this sūtra state only that the kindness of causing one to attain the first and last fruits is difficult to repay, and does not state that the kindness of causing one to attain the two intermediate fruits is so?
Regarding that which was promised but not yet explained:
one should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, herein the four fruits of śrāmaṇya are fully encompassed.

Why is this? It is because those who have distanced themselves from dust and departed from defilement, thereby generating the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, are said to have attained the first three fruits—
namely, those who are still bound by all fetters and those who have already abandoned five grades of defilement in the desire realm.
Entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
If, having abandoned six or seven grades of defilement of the desire realm,
one enters the state of right determination and gives rise to the pure Dharma-eye, one attains the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
If, having become detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness,
one enters into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), gives birth to the pure Dharma-eye, and attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*),
thereby exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*) and obtaining the state of being without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Liberation through both mind and wisdom is precisely the attainment of the fruit of arhatship.
Therefore, this sutra fully encompasses all four fruits.
Furthermore, when this sutra speaks of attaining the first and last two fruits, it is speaking of the attainment of all four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Because it manifests the beginning and the end.
"Beginning" refers to the fruit of stream-entry;
"end" refers to the fruit of arhatship.
Just as it is with the beginning and end of the present [process], so too should one understand that the initial entry and the culmination of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) are likewise.

Furthermore, when this sutra speaks of attaining the first and last fruits, it has already implied the attainment of the two intermediate fruits; that is to say, one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) will certainly attain the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*) immediately thereafter.
This is because one who attains the fruit of Arhatship necessarily preceded it by attaining the fruit of Anāgāmin.
Furthermore, the first and last fruits are specifically mentioned because they are both definitively obtained through the power of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
The two intermediate fruits may be obtained through the power of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*); therefore, they are not mentioned here.

It should be understood that this applies likewise to those obtained through the power of both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths, as well as those obtained through the power of the path of bondage and the path of liberation.
Furthermore, the first and last fruits are specifically mentioned because both transcend the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) upon their attainment.

That is to say, the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) transcends the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception through the abandonment of what is to be eliminated by insight (darśana-heya).
The fruit of arhatship transcends that which is to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, because this sutra briefly demonstrates the initial gateway [to the path],
it mentions only the first and the last fruits.
That is to say, among the fruits of śrāmaṇya, some are attained through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) as their cause,
and some are attained through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) as their cause.
If it is said that the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) is attained through the path of seeing, this should be understood as a general statement.
If it is said that the fruit of arhatship is attained through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), one should know that this is stated in general terms.
Just as [the fruits] are attained through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) and the path of cultivation,

so too should it be understood that they are attained through the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) on the stage of seeing (darśanabhūmi) and through the faculty of "having known" (ājñendriya) on the stage of cultivation (bhāvanābhūmi).
Furthermore, the various fruits of śrāmaṇya are established based on the exhaustion of afflictions abandoned through vision (*darśana-prahātavya*),
and they are established based on the exhaustion of afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

If it is said that the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) is established based on the exhaustion of afflictions abandoned through vision, this should be understood as a general statement regarding the cause of its establishment.
If it is said that the fruit of arhatship should be understood as being established by way of a general statement regarding the exhaustion of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation,
it is like how [the fruits] are established by way of the exhaustion of the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
In this way, because the afflictions— both those with an object and those without an object— are exhausted due to the cause,

it should be understood that the same applies to their establishment through the exhaustion of the afflictions that are the objects countered by patience (*kṣānti*) and the objects countered by knowledge (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, the various fruits of asceticism (śrāmaṇyaphala) are established because they serve as antidotes to the proliferation of views (dṛṣṭi-prapañca),
and they are established because they serve as antidotes to the proliferation of craving (tṛṣṇā-prapañca).
If it is said that the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phala) is established by way of summarizing the causes as the antidote to the conceptual proliferation of views (dṛṣṭi-prapañca),

one should know that if it is said that the fruit of arhatship (arhat-phala) is established by way of summarizing the causes as the antidote to the conceptual proliferation of craving (tṛṣṇā-prapañca).
Just as it is established because of the antidote to the two kinds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*),
one should know that it is likewise established because of the antidotes to the two extremes, the two arrows, and the two roots of contention.
Furthermore, the various fruits of the śramaṇa are attained either through the sudden abandonment of afflictions or through the gradual abandonment of afflictions.
If one speaks of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*),
it should be understood that this is stated generally because it is attained by the sudden abandonment of afflictions;
this includes those who attain the fruits of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and non-returner (*anāgāmin*) by means of leaping over stages.
If one speaks of the fruit of arhatship,
it should be understood that this is said generally because the afflictions are attained through gradual abandonment;
this refers to those who also attain the fruits of once-returner and non-returner in succession.
For these and various other reasons,
this sutra speaks only of how the kindness of causing others to realize the first and last fruits is difficult to repay;
such is the case for the trainee-dharmas (*śaikṣa-dharma*) accomplished by those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
"Is this dharma included within the fruit of stream-entry?
and so forth, as explained at length.
[Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Previously, only the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) fruits of śrāmaṇya were explained;
now, because one wishes to explain both the conditioned and unconditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya, this treatise is composed.
Within this, that which was asked previously is presented first in brief and subsequently in detail.
That is to say, first one asks about the dharmas of training and those beyond training that have been accomplished;
next, one asks about the untainted dharmas that have been accomplished;
and finally, one asks about all dharmas that have been accomplished.
Regarding the factors of training (śaikṣadharma) accomplished by those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna):
are these factors included within the fruit of stream-entry?
Answer: They are either included or not included.
Because the meaning is not fixed, how is it included?
Answer: It is the conditioned state of the fruit of stream-entry that has been attained and not lost.

"Those who have already attained" refers to those with faith and conviction (*śraddhādhimukta*) who have already attained the faculties of the lineage included within the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*),
and those who have reached vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) who have already attained the faculties of the lineage included within the fruit of stream-entry.
"Not losing" refers to one who,
being resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), does not change their faculties to become one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*); thus,
they do not lose the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) as a one resolved through faith.
Regarding those faculties included within the lineage that are not lost or regressed:
what is not so included?
Answer: It refers to the conditioned phenomena, such as the superior and progressive untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), attained by those who have entered the stream (srotāpanna).
This refers to the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),

the six paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), the five paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and the paths of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) that abandon the first six categories of afflictions of the desire realm through cultivation.
Such factors of training (*śaikṣadharma*) are accomplished by a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), yet they are not included within the fruit of stream-entry itself.
Because the path of the superior fruit is not subsumed under the category of "fruit.
If a dharma is subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry, is it a dharma of training (*śaikṣa*)?
Answer: It is either a dharma of training, or it is neither-training-nor-non-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Because the meaning is not fixed.
What is training?
Answer: It is the conditioned fruit of stream-entry.
This refers to the knowledge of the path of types (*mārgānvayajñāna*) and its attendants.
Why is it neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: It is the unconditioned fruit of stream-entry (*asaṃskṛta-srotāpattiphala*).
It refers to the abandonment of the factors of the three realms that are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
Are the factors of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*) accomplished by those who are once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*) subsumed under the fruit of once-returning?
Answer: It is sometimes included and sometimes not included, because the meaning is not fixed.
How is it included?
Answer: There is the conditioned fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), which has been attained and not lost.
Regarding "attained," this refers to those of the lineage of faith-resolve (śraddhādhimukta) who have attained the faculties subsumed within the fruit of once-returner of the faith-resolve type.
Regarding the faculties of one who has attained the stage of "seeing-attained" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) and is included within the lineage of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin),
"not losing" refers to the case where one resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta) does not transform their faculties to become seeing-attained.
The faculties of those belonging to the lineage subsumed within the fruit of a once-returner who possesses resolute conviction that does not fail,
or who does not fall away—
how are they not subsumed?
Answer: It refers to the conditioned phenomena, such as the superior, transcendent faculties (anāsrava-indriya) obtained by those who are once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*).

Specifically, these include the abandonment of the final three categories of defilements to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) regarding the desire realm, as well as the various paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the three paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the two paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The dharmas thus studied in the various paths of superior progress,
although accomplished by a once-returner,
are not subsumed within the fruit of once-returning.
Because the path of the superior fruit is not subsumed under the category of "fruit.
Suppose a dharma is subsumed under the fruit of the once-returner; is this a dharma of training (śaikṣa)?
Answer: It is either a dharma of training, or it is neither-training-nor-non-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
Because the meaning is not fixed, how is it "training"?
Answer: It is the conditioned fruit of the once-returner.
This refers to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) and so forth,
or the sixth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) from the defilements of desire and their associated factors.
Why is it neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
Answer: It is the unconditioned fruit of the once-returner (anāgāmiphala).

This refers to the abandonment of the dharmas to be abandoned by insight within the three realms, as well as the abandonment of the first six categories of dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation within the desire realm.
Regarding the factors of training accomplished by those who are non-returners:
are these factors subsumed within the fruit of non-returning?
Answer: They may be subsumed or they may not; the meaning is not fixed.
What is its inclusion?
The answer is: it is the conditioned fruit of non-returning that has been attained and not lost.
Regarding "that which has been attained":
This refers to the faculties belonging to the lineage comprised within the fruit of a non-returner who has attained liberation through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*),
and the faculties belonging to the lineage comprised within the fruit of a non-returner who has attained the state of "one who has seen" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
"Not losing" means that one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) does not transform their faculties (*indriya*) to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*). Thus,
they do not lose the faculties belonging to the lineage (*gotra*) subsumed under the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) within the state of being liberated through faith.
Or, they do not fall away from it.
What is not included?
Answer: The conditioned dharmas, such as the supreme, progressive untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) obtained by those who are non-returners (anāgāmin).

This refers to the paths of preparation, the uninterrupted paths, the paths of liberation, and the paths of advancement for those in training (*śaikṣa*), which effect the separation from the defilements of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
One who trains in these dharmas may achieve them even while not yet being a non-returner,
yet they are not subsumed within the fruit of non-returning.
Because the path of the superior fruit is not subsumed under the fruit itself.
Suppose a dharma is subsumed under the fruit of non-returning; is this a dharma of training (*śaikṣa*)?
Answer: It is either a dharma of training, or it is neither-training-nor-non-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Because the meaning is not fixed, what is training?
Answer: It is the conditioned fruit of non-returning.

That is to say, why are the path of subsequent knowledge (*mārgānvayajñāna*) and so forth, as well as the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) from the defilements of detachment and their attendants, neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
Answer: Because they are the unconditioned fruit of non-returner (*asaṃskṛtānāgāmiphala*).
This refers to the abandonment of the factors to be abandoned through seeing within the three realms,
as well as the abandonment of the factors to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm;
it also refers to the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) accomplished by all Arhats.
Is this dharma subsumed within the fruit of arhatship?
Answer: It is so.

That is to say, all the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and paths of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*) accomplished by an arhat are subsumed within the fruit of arhatship.
Because there is no path to a superior fruit,
and because there is no superior fruit to be sought after;
even if it were included within the state of an Arhat, it would be so designated.
"Are these the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
Answer: "Either they are the dharmas of one beyond training, or they are neither-of-training-nor-beyond-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa), because their meaning is not fixed."
What is the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
The answer is: the conditioned fruit of arhatship;
that is to say, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi), and their associated factors.
What is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: It is the unconditioned fruit of arhatship;
that is to say, the abandonment of all dharmas of the three realms to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
Regarding the untainted dharmas accomplished by those who are stream-enterers:
are these dharmas included within the fruit of stream-entry?
Answer: They are either included or not included.
Because its meaning is not fixed, how is it subsumed?
Answer: It consists of the conditioned and unconditioned states of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) that have been attained and not lost.
The conditioned fruit of stream-entry refers to the knowledge of the subsequent path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) and its attendants;
the unconditioned fruit of stream-entry refers to...
This refers to the abandonment of those dharmas of the three realms that are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).

"Already attained" means that one who is resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) has already attained the seeds subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) belonging to one resolved through faith.
The faculties of one of the nature of a *dṛṣṭiprāpta*;
the seeds comprised within the fruit of stream-entry attained by one who has become a *dṛṣṭiprāpta*;
and the faculties of one of the nature of [the same].
Furthermore, regarding the non-loss of the abandonment of those dharmas of the three realms that are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*):
this refers to one who possesses liberation through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) not transforming their faculties (*indriya*) into the state of one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Thus, they do not lose the seeds comprised within the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) associated with liberation through faith.
Regarding the faculties of one's nature:
why are they not included among those that are non-retrogressive?

Answer: It refers to the conditioned phenomena, such as the superior and progressive untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) obtained by those who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna),
as well as the exhaustion of the fetters (saṃyojana) realized by them,
together with the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) accomplished by those Stream-enterers.
The supramundane faculties and so forth acquired by those who have entered the stream (*srotāpanna*) as their further progress (*viśeṣa-gamana*),
which are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*),
refer to being free from the first six categories of defilements to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the desire realm.
Although a stream-enterer accomplishes these untainted dharmas— the various paths of preparation, the six paths of uninterrupted transition, the five paths of liberation,
and the various paths of superior progress— ...
However, it is not included within the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*),
because the path to a superior fruit is not itself subsumed under that fruit;
and as for the exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) realized therein—
This refers to the abandonment of the first five categories of dharmas in the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Because this abandonment is realized by the path of superior fruit (*viśeṣa-mārga*),
it is like the path of superior fruit itself.
It is not included within these fruits;
furthermore, it includes the non-analytical cessations (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) achieved by a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
That is to say, a stream-enterer attains non-analytical cessation with respect to the three realms and untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma).
Although he has attained this non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
