this non-analytical cessation is not included within the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*). Why is that?
Non-analytical cessation is indeterminate,
whereas the fruit of stream-entry is wholesome; therefore,
whatever dharma is subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry [must be wholesome].
"Is this an outflow-free (*anāsrava*) dharma?
Answer: "It is so.
This is because both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) fruits of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) are outflow-free.
Regarding the untainted dharmas accomplished by those who are once-returners:
are these dharmas subsumed within the fruit of once-returning?
Answer: They are sometimes subsumed and sometimes not.
Because the meaning is not fixed, how is it included?
Answer: It includes both conditioned and unconditioned states, specifically the fruit of once-returning that has already been attained and not lost.
The conditioned fruit of once-returner refers to the path of subsequent knowledge (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) and so forth,
or the sixth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) from the defilements of desire and its associated factors.
The unconditioned fruit of once-returner refers to the abandonment of the factors abandoned through seeing in the three realms,
as well as the abandonment of the first six categories of factors abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.

"Those who have already attained" refers to those resolved through faith who have already attained the seeds and faculties subsumed within the fruit of a once-returner belonging to the lineage of those resolved through faith.
Having attained the stage of "one who has attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta), they are comprised within the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin);
they possess the lineage and the faculties [of that stage],
and have already attained the abandonment of the dharmas to be abandoned by vision within the three realms.
Furthermore, regarding the abandonment of the first six categories of factors to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm,
"not losing" refers to those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) who do not transform their faculties to become those attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
One who has not lost their resolute confidence (*adhimukti*), is included among those who have attained the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*),
possesses the seeds and faculties [of that stage],
or has not fallen away from this as well as the abandonment of the first six categories of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm.
What is not included?

The answer is: the conditioned phenomena such as the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) acquired by those who have attained the stage of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) through further progress, as well as the destruction of the fetters (saṃyojana-kṣaya) realized by them.
Furthermore, there is the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) achieved by a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin),
as well as those conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) such as the superior, untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) attained by once-returners through their further progress;
that is to say, [the abandonment of] the final three categories of defilements to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) regarding the desire realm.

Although those who have attained the stage of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) possess such untainted dharmas as all paths of preparation (prayoga-mārga), the two paths of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga), the two paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga),
and the paths of further advancement (viśeṣa-mārga).
It is not, however, included within the fruit of the once-returner,
because the path to a superior fruit is not itself categorized as a fruit;
and as for the exhaustion of the fetters realized therein—
This refers to the abandonment of the seventh and eighth categories of dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm;
because this abandonment is realized by the path of superior fruit,
it is not included within the fruit of that [path], just as the path of superior fruit itself is not included within its own fruit.
Furthermore, regarding the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) achieved by a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin):
it means that a once-returner attains non-analytical cessation with respect to the three realms and untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma).
Although he achieves this non-analytical cessation, [it is not yet complete].
Furthermore, this non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is not included within the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin). Why is this so?
Because non-analytical cessation is indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Since the fruit of once-returning is wholesome,
if a dharma is subsumed under the fruit of once-returning,
is this an untainted (anāsrava) dharma?
Answer: It is so.
This is because both the conditioned and unconditioned once-returner fruits are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume Sixty-six;
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Sixty-seven.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others, translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Section Two: The Aggregate of Fetters; Sub-section Three: The Chapter on Sentient Beings; Part Five. The untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) accomplished by those who are Non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
Is this dharma subsumed under the fruit of non-returning?
Answer: It is sometimes subsumed and sometimes not, because its meaning is not fixed.
What is its inclusion?
The answer is: the conditioned and unconditioned fruits of non-returning that have been attained and not lost.
Regarding the conditioned fruit of non-returning:
This refers to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) and so forth;
or the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) and its attendants when one is free from the defilements of desire;
as well as the unconditioned fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
This refers to the abandonment of the factors of the three realms to be abandoned by insight,
as well as the abandonment of the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation,
which has already been attained.
This refers to the faculties belonging to the lineage comprised within the fruit of non-returning attained by those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta),
and the faculties belonging to the lineage comprised within the fruit of non-returning attained by those who have reached vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Furthermore, having attained the abandonment of the factors abandoned through seeing in the three realms,
as well as the abandonment of the factors abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
one does not lose them.
This means that because one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) does not transform their faculties to become one who has attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
they do not lose the faculties belonging to the lineage subsumed under the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) as one liberated through faith;
nor do they fall away from this, or from what is to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanāheya) in the desire realm.
The dharmas that are abandoned.
What are those not included?
Answer: The conditioned dharmas, such as the superior and progressive untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) obtained by non-returners (anāgāmin).
Furthermore, there are the various fetters that have been extinguished through his realization,
as well as the non-analytical cessations (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) accomplished by those who are Non-returners (anāgāmin),
and the conditioned dharmas such as the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) attained by those Non-returners as they progress toward higher excellence.

This refers to the paths of preparation, the uninterrupted paths, the paths of liberation, and the paths of special progress for those who have abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
as well as for those on the path of learning (śaikṣa).
Such untainted dharmas,
although accomplished by one who is a non-returner,
are not subsumed within the fruit of non-returning.
Because the path of superior fruit is not subsumed under the fruit itself;
and as for "the exhaustion of all fetters realized by that," this refers to the stages from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness.
The abandonment of each of the nine grades of dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation,
as well as the abandonment of the first eight grades of dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
constitute abandonments realized by the path of superior fruit.
For example, the path of superior fruit is not included within this fruit;
likewise, there is the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) achieved by a non-returner (anāgāmin).
That is to say, a non-returner attains non-analytical cessation with respect to the three realms and untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma).
Although he has attained this non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
this non-analytical cessation is not included within the fruit of a Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*). Why is that?
Non-analytical cessation is indeterminate,
whereas the fruit of non-returning is wholesome; therefore,
even if a dharma were included within the fruit of non-returning, [it would not be indeterminate].
"Is this an untainted (anāsrava) dharma?
"Yes," he replied.
"That is to say, it refers to the conditioned (saṃskṛta) and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) fruits of non-returning (anāgāmiphala)."
Since both are untainted (*anāsrava*),
are the untainted dharmas accomplished by all Arhats subsumed within the fruit of Arhatship?
Answer: It is sometimes included and sometimes not included, because the meaning is not fixed.
How is it included?
Answer: The conditioned and unconditioned fruits of arhatship, once attained, are not lost.

The conditioned fruit of arhatship refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*), and their associated factors.

The unconditioned fruit of arhatship refers to that which has already been attained through the abandonment of all phenomena to be eliminated by the paths of vision and cultivation within the three realms.

That is to say: the faculties belonging to the lineage subsumed under the fruit of arhatship attained through occasional liberation (samayavimukta), and the faculties belonging to the lineage subsumed under the fruit of arhatship attained through non-occasional liberation (asamayavimukta).
Furthermore, regarding the non-loss of the abandonment of those dharmas of the three realms to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation that have already been attained:
this refers to one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) who does not transform their faculties to become one liberated at all times (*asamayavimukta*).
Regarding the lineages, faculties, and so forth subsumed under the fruit of arhatship of one liberated at the proper time (*asamayavimukta*), why are these,
as well as the abandonment of the dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation within the three realms, not included [in the state of non-retrogression]?
Why are they not subsumed?
Answer: It refers to the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) accomplished by an arhat.
That is to say, an arhat attains non-analytical cessation regarding the three realms and untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma).
Although he accomplishes this non-analytical cessation, [it is not considered a conditioned dharma].
Furthermore, this non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is not included within the fruit of arhatship.
Why is this? Because non-analytical cessation is indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Since the fruit of arhatship is wholesome,
if a dharma is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship,
is this dharma necessarily untainted?
Answer: It is so.
This is because both the conditioned and unconditioned fruits of arhatship are untainted (anāsrava), and thus all such dharmas are accomplished by one who has entered the stream (srotāpanna).
Is this dharma subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry?
One should respond that there are four possible cases (catuṣkoṭi),
because the mutual inclusion of the attainment of these fruits varies in its breadth and narrowness.
There are dharmas that a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) possesses which are not included within the fruit of stream-entry itself.
These are the conditioned dharmas, such as the superior, untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), acquired by the stream-enterer upon further progress,
as well as the extinction of the fetters (saṃyojana-kṣaya) realized by him.
Furthermore, there are the contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) characterized by non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) that are accomplished by a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
Among these, there are four types of phenomena;
the first three are as previously explained.
The contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) accomplished by them are, in total, of three kinds:
namely, the wholesome (*kuśala*), the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), and the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Furthermore, the wholesome are of two types.
These refer to the wholesome states acquired through application (*prāyogika-kuśala*) and those acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*).
The defiled refers to the defiled phenomena of the three realms that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The non-obscured neutral refers to the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*), the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and those born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Thus, these dharmas accomplished by a stream-enterer are not subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry.
This is because that fruit is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*),
whereas these are tainted (*sāsrava*).
There are dharmas subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) that are not possessed by one who is a stream-enterer.
These refer to the fruit of stream-entry that has not yet been attained or has already been lost. Regarding "not yet attained": [it refers to those who have not yet realized it].

This refers to the faculties belonging to the lineage included within the fruit of stream-entry for those resolved through faith who have not yet attained the stage of "vision-attainment," as well as the faculties belonging to the lineage included within the fruit of stream-entry for those who have attained vision but have not yet attained the stage of being resolved through faith.
"Those already lost" refers to those who,

through the transformation of their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), transition from the lineage of one liberated by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*); thus,
they lose the faculties belonging to the lineage subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) that were characterized by liberation through faith.
There may be cases of retrogression.
There are dharmas that are accomplished by a stream-enterer and are also subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry;
namely, the fruit of stream-entry already attained and not lost.
It should be understood that the meaning herein is as previously explained.
There are dharmas which are neither accomplished by one who is not a stream-enterer nor included within the fruit of stream-entry;
namely, those other than the characteristics mentioned above.
In this context, the term "characteristic" (*nimitta*) refers to that which is expressed by a name.
That is to say, regarding those phenomena (*dharma*) that have already been designated or spoken of as being expressed by a name, one applies the first three propositions.
Excluding these, regarding those phenomena that have not yet been designated or spoken of as being expressed by a name, one applies the fourth proposition.
What, then, are these? They are the wholesome, the defiled, and the non-obscured neutral.
The wholesome is of two kinds.
That is to say, there are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Regarding contaminated wholesome states:

these refer to the wholesome states acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*), through detachment from passion (*vairāgya-labdha*), and those acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*), which are not possessed by a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
Regarding untainted wholesomeness (*anāsrava-kuśala*):
it refers to all noble paths (*ārya-mārga*) of lower or higher stages that have not yet been attained by a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*),
as well as the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of higher stages that has not yet been attained.
Defiled refers to the defiled dharmas abandoned through the vision [of the truths] within the three realms,
as well as the defiled dharmas abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm that have already been abandoned by a stream-enterer.
Regarding the non-obscured and neutral [states]:
these refer to the deportment, the arts and crafts, and those born of maturation that are not possessed by a stream-enterer,
as well as all transformative minds and so forth.
Such dharmas constitute the fourth alternative.
Regarding those dharmas attained by a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), are they subsumed within the fruit of a once-returner?
One should respond that there are four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).
Because these factors subsumed under the fruit of attainment vary in their mutual breadth and narrowness,
there are dharmas that are accomplished by a once-returner but are not subsumed under the fruit of a once-returner;
namely, the conditioned dharmas such as the superior, further-advanced untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) acquired by a once-returner.
Furthermore, there are the various fetters that have been exhausted through realization by him,
as well as the contaminated phenomena for which non-analytical cessation has been achieved by a once-returner;
herein, there are four dharmas.
The first three are as previously explained.
Those conditioned phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava*) that he accomplishes are, in total, of three kinds:
namely, the wholesome, the defiled, and the non-obscured neutral.
Wholesome [phenomena] are further of two kinds:
namely, wholesome through application (*prāyogika-kuśala*) and wholesome by birthright (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*).
Defiled [phenomena] refer to the defiled factors of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), belonging to the latter three categories.
And the defiled dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms;
as for the unobscured-neutral, they refer to those produced by deportment, those pertaining to the arts and crafts, and those born of maturation.
Such are these various dharmas.
The once-returner achieves [this],
though it is not subsumed under the fruit of once-returning;
for the fruit is exclusively untainted (anāsrava).
Because this is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
There are dharmas comprised within the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*) that are not accomplished by one who is a once-returner;
namely, those [dharmas] of the fruit of once-returning which have not yet been attained or have already been lost.

"Those who have not yet attained" refers to those whose faculties are comprised within the lineage of the fruit of once-returning as one liberated by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), but who have not yet attained the state of one who has reached vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*);
and those whose faculties are comprised within the lineage of the fruit of once-returning as one who has reached vision, but who have not yet attained the state of one liberated by faith.
"Already lost" refers to one who,
through the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), becomes a "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) from being "resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*); thus,
they lose the faculties belonging to the lineage (*gotra*) subsumed under the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) characterized by resolution through faith.
There may be some who fall away.
There are dharmas that are accomplished by a once-returner and are also subsumed under the fruit of once-returning;
namely, those dharmas of the fruit of once-returning already attained and not lost.
It should be understood that the meaning herein is as previously explained.
There are dharmas that are neither accomplished by a once-returner nor subsumed under the fruit of once-returning;
namely, those excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
In this context, the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to that which is signified by a name.
That is to say, if a phenomenon has already been designated or spoken of as being signified by a name, it constitutes the first three propositions;
however, it is excluded here.
If a phenomenon has not yet been designated or spoken of as being expressed by a name, it constitutes the fourth alternative.
What, then, is this? It refers to that which is wholesome, defiled, or non-obscured-neutral.
There are two kinds of wholesome [states]:
namely, those with outflows (sāsrava) and those without outflows (anāsrava).
As for wholesome states with outflows:
This refers to the wholesome states acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*), those acquired through detachment from passion (*vairāgya-labdha*),

and the untainted wholesome states (*anāsrava-kuśala*) that a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) has not yet attained; specifically, it refers to all the noble paths (*āryamārga*) of both lower and higher stages that a once-returner has not yet realized.
And the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of higher stages not yet attained.
As for the defiled, this refers to the defiled phenomena (*dharma*) of the three realms that are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
Furthermore, regarding the once-returner who has already abandoned the defiled dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm,
as well as the non-obscured and non-defined [dharmas]:

this refers to those [non-defined dharmas] such as the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*), the skills of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), which are not yet fully accomplished by the once-returner.
And all transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) and so forth—
such dharmas as these constitute the fourth case:
those dharmas which are accomplished by one who is not a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Is this dharma subsumed under the fruit of non-returning?
One should respond that it involves four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*),
because there is mutual variation in breadth and narrowness between the possession of these fruits.
There are dharmas that belong to a non-returner but are not subsumed under the fruit of non-returning;
namely, the conditioned dharmas such as the superior, untainted faculties obtained by a non-returner,
as well as the exhaustion of all fetters realized by them.
Furthermore, there are the non-analytical cessations (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the outflow-tainted dharmas (sāsrava-dharma) accomplished by one who is not a Non-returner (anāgāmin).
Within this, there are four types of dharmas;
the first three are as previously explained.
The contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) accomplished by that [being] are, in total, of three kinds:
namely, the wholesome (*kuśala*), the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), and the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Furthermore, the wholesome are of three types.
This refers to the wholesome states acquired through application, those born of detachment, and those acquired at birth;
as well as the defiled states,
namely the defiled dharmas of the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned through cultivation.
Unobscured-neutral [phenomena],
namely: those of deportment, those of the arts and crafts, those born of maturation, and the mind of transformation,
and so forth— such are these dharmas.
The non-returner (anāgāmin) achieves [this],
yet it is not subsumed under the fruit of non-returning.
This is because the fruit is exclusively untainted (anāsrava).
Because this is with outflows (sāsrava),
there are dharmas included within the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) that are not accomplished by one who is not a non-returner.
This refers to the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) that has not yet been attained or has already been lost.

Regarding "not yet attained," it refers to the faculties belonging to the lineage included within the fruit of non-returner that have been attained through resolute faith (śraddhādhimukta) but have not yet been attained through the state of one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).

Furthermore, regarding the faculties included within the lineage of those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) and not those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta), who have not yet attained the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala):
"those who have already lost them" refers to those who,
having been resolved through faith, have transformed their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) to become those who have attained vision.
Regarding the faculties of the lineage included within the fruit of non-returning that has lost its resolute conviction,
there may be some regression;
however, there are certain dharmas belonging to those who are non-returners which, though accomplished, are also included within the fruit of non-returning.
This refers to the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) which has been attained and not lost;
it should be understood that the meaning herein is as previously explained.
There are dharmas that are neither accomplished by one who is a non-returner, nor are they subsumed within the fruit of non-returning.
This means excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Herein, the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to that which is signified.
That is to say, if a phenomenon has already been designated or spoken of as being signified, it constitutes the first three propositions.
This is excluded here.
If a phenomenon has not yet been designated or spoken of as that which is "expressed" (*vyañjita*), it constitutes the fourth alternative. What, then, is this?
That is to say: wholesome, afflicted, and non-obscured neutral.
The wholesome is of two kinds:
namely, with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
As for contaminated wholesome [states],

this refers to the wholesome states— whether acquired through application, through detachment from passion, or as innate— that are not yet accomplished by one who has attained the fruit of non-returning.
As for uncontaminated wholesome [states]...
This refers to all noble paths of lower and higher stages not yet accomplished by a non-returner,
as well as the cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the higher stages not yet attained;
[this is] the defiled [state].
This refers to the defiled dharmas abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms,
as well as the non-obscured, non-defined (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) defiled dharmas abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the desire realm.

This refers to those states not accomplished by a non-returner, such as the minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*), of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), of maturation (*vipākaja*), and of transformation (*nairmāṇika*).
Such dharmas constitute the fourth category.
Regarding those dharmas accomplished by an Arhat:
are these dharmas subsumed within the fruit of Arhatship?
One should respond that this constitutes four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
Because these categories of "attainment" (*prāpti*) and "fruition" (*phala*) encompass one another with varying degrees of breadth and narrowness,
there are factors accomplished by an Arhat that are not subsumed under the fruition of Arhatship;
namely, the non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and contaminated factors (*sāsrava-dharma*) accomplished by an Arhat.
Regarding that which he has accomplished as non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
it is as explained extensively before.
Regarding those contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) he has accomplished, there are generally two kinds.
That is to say, they are wholesome and unobscured-neutral.
There are three types of the wholesome:
namely, that which is acquired through application (*prāyogika*), that which is acquired through the removal of defilements (*vairāgyaja*), and that which is acquired by birth (*upapattilābhika*).
Unobscured-indeterminate [states] refer to those such as the minds of deportment, craftsmanship, maturation, and transformation;
such are these various dharmas.
The Arhat is accomplished [by these],
yet they are not subsumed under the fruit of arhatship;
for the fruit is exclusively untainted (anāsrava).
Because these are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
There are dharmas subsumed under the fruit of arhatship that are not possessed by an arhat;
namely, those [dharmas] of the fruit of arhatship which have not yet been attained or have already been lost.

"Those who have not yet attained" refers to those of the lineage included within the fruit of arhatship of occasional liberation (samaya-vimukta) who have not yet attained the faculties included within the fruit of arhatship of non-occasional liberation (asamaya-vimukta),

as well as those of the lineage included within the fruit of arhatship of non-occasional liberation who have not yet attained the faculties included within the fruit of arhatship of occasional liberation.
"Already lost" means that because one who is liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) transforms their faculties to become one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*),
they lose the faculties associated with the lineage of the fruit of arhatship that was comprised within liberation by occasion.
There may be cases of falling away.
There are dharmas that an Arhat accomplishes and which are also subsumed under the fruit of Arhatship;
namely, those fruits of Arhatship already attained and not lost.
It should be understood that the meaning herein is as previously explained:
there are dharmas that are neither accomplished by an Arhat nor subsumed within the fruit of Arhatship;
namely, those other than the aforementioned characteristics.
In this context, the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to that which is expressed by a name.
That is to say, if a phenomenon has already been designated or spoken of as being "expressed," it is included in the first three propositions;
however, in this [present] case, such instances are excluded.
If a phenomenon has not yet been designated or explained by a name that expresses it, it constitutes the fourth alternative.
What, then, is this? It refers to that which is wholesome, afflicted, or non-obscured-neutral.
There are two kinds of wholesome [states]:
namely, those with outflows (sāsrava) and those without outflows (anāsrava).
As for wholesome states with outflows:

This refers to the wholesome states acquired through effort (*prāyogika*), those arising from detachment (*vairāgyaja*), and those acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*) which an Arhat does not possess;
as for the untainted wholesome states (*anāsrava-kuśala*),
these refer to all the qualities of those in training (*śaikṣadharma*).
"Defiled" refers to the defiled dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation within the three realms.
"Unobscured-neutral" refers to...

This refers to those minds not accomplished by an Arhat, such as the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*), the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*), and the mind of transformation (*nairmāṇika*).
Such dharmas constitute the fourth category.
Question: Does one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) transform their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta)?
If so, what is the fault?
There are faults in both cases.
Why is this? If one who possesses faith and liberation transforms their faculties to become one who has attained vision,
why is this not mentioned later in the *Indriya-skandha* (The Aggregate of Faculties)?
As it was said: "If one abandons uncontaminated faculties and acquires uncontaminated faculties, do they all proceed from fruit to fruit?
Answer: "If they proceed from fruit to fruit."
In all those cases, one abandons untainted faculties and acquires untainted faculties.

There are instances where one abandons untainted faculties and acquires untainted faculties without passing from one fruit to another, namely when the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) at the conclusion of clear observation (abhisamaya) is present before one.
When one who is liberated by time (samayavimukta) refines their faculties to become unshakable (akopya),
why does this Master of the Treatise not mention it?
[Why does he] not mention it when one who is resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta)?
If one who possesses faith and liberation does not transform their faculties to become one who has attained through vision,
how should the statement made here be interpreted? It is explained as follows:
There are dharmas included within the fruit of stream-entry that are not possessed by one who is a stream-enterer.
These refer to those who have not yet attained or have already lost the fruit of stream-entry;
or, in the case of one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) who does not transform their faculties to become one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
How could one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) lose it?
Furthermore, how is the subsequent statement in the *Jñānaskandha* to be reconciled, as it says:
[as stated there]?
For a stream-enterer, all three types of samādhi are accomplished in the future;
if they have already ceased but have not been lost, they are accomplished in the present;
and if they are currently manifest, they are accomplished.
If one who possesses faith and liberation does not transform their faculties to become one who has attained through vision,
how could a stream-enterer lose a meditative absorption that has already ceased?
Is it to distinguish such a case that it is said there exists [an absorption] that has ceased but is not lost?
How, then, is the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* to be reconciled? As it says:
"There exists a past mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that has already been realized, is not being realized now, and will not be realized in the future;
namely, when a time-liberated (*samayavimukta*) Arhat falls from the fruit of Arhatship and becomes one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*)."
Having refined his faculties to become a *dṛṣṭiprāpta*, he subsequently attains the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) subsumed under the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) has already been accomplished;
it is neither being accomplished now nor will it be accomplished in the future.
Regarding that which is designated as "the sound is cognized":
that which has already been cognized is what has already been accomplished, not what is being cognized now, nor what is being accomplished now;
it is not what will be cognized in the future, nor what will be accomplished in the future.
If one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) does not undergo a transformation of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
how can it be said that a time-liberated (samayavimukta) arhat falls from the fruit of arhatship and becomes one liberated through faith?
Having refined the faculties to become one who has attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), does one subsequently regain the fruit of arhatship?
One should answer thus:
there is the case where one who was previously liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines the faculties and becomes one who has attained through vision.
Question: If that is so, the difficulty raised later has been successfully resolved.
Why, then, is it not mentioned in the subsequent *Indriya-skandha*?
The answer should be stated later in the *Indriya-skandha*:

"There is the abandonment of uncontaminated faculties and the acquisition of uncontaminated faculties that does not involve passing from one fruit to another; this refers to when the *mārga-anvaya-jñāna* at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) manifests."
When one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*);
when one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) refines their faculties to become one of the nature of mental cultivation (*cetovimuktidharman*);
and when one who is liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) refines their faculties to become one who is immovable (*akopyadharman*).
The reason he does not state it in this way is that there is a specific underlying intention; namely,
he mentions both the beginning and the end.
It is said "because it is manifested within the shadows" (i.e., the subsequent knowledge).
When the path-knowledge of the category [of the truths] at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) is present, this refers to the time when one begins the explanation;
it refers to the time when one who is liberated through training refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become immovable (*akopya*).
This refers to mentioning the end;
by mentioning the beginning and the end,
the middle is implied.
When one who possesses faith and liberation (śraddhādhimukta) transforms their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
if there is no principle of transforming faculties within the stage of training (śaikṣa), then it should likewise be so in the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Just as in the stage of training there is no protection and no power, [so it would be here].
The same should apply to those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*);

thus, it is also shown that there are those who fall away from their state, and those who transform their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become those with the nature of reflection (*cetanādharman*), and so forth.
This is just as was illustrated by citing the beginning and the end.
It should be understood that the same applies to those who have already entered and completed the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
The Venerable Saṃghavasu said: "One who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) refines their faculties and becomes one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*)."
This is subsumed within what is explained in the *Indriya-skandha* (The Aggregate of Faculties),
because it is comprised of the transition from one fruit to another.

That is to say, once a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) has completed the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) for the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), they proceed toward the fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
If one attains the fruit of once-returner, it is immediately termed the transformation of the faculties;
there is no distinction between the time of attaining the fruit and the time of transforming the faculties.
If a once-returner, having cultivated the path of preparation for the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra-mārga*), proceeds toward the fruit of non-returning,
the moment they attain the fruit of non-returning is itself termed the "transformation of faculties" (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).
There is no distinction between the time of attaining the fruit and the time of transforming the faculties.
Question: Why is it that attaining the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) or the fruit of an arhat (*arhat*) is not itself called "refining the faculties" (*indriya-pariśodhana*)? Answer:
Transcending the desire realm is a practice that has been repeatedly performed since beginningless time.
Because there is not a single sentient being who has never been free from the defilements of the desire realm;
for this reason, those who seek to transform their faculties are able to do so because they have either partially or completely abandoned the defilements of the desire realm.
When one attains the second fruit, one simultaneously transforms the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) and transcends the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);
this is not a habitual, long-standing method from time immemorial.
Because there is not a single sentient being who has ever previously become detached from the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
for this reason, there is no one who seeks the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) by means of becoming partially or fully detached from the defilements of the Peak of Existence.
When one attains the two fruits, one also transforms the faculties (*indriya*).

Question: As you have stated, when one refines the faculties during the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) and advances to attain the two fruits, these are already included within the transition from one fruit to another; therefore, they are not mentioned separately.

Within the stage of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there are six types of dispositions (*gotra*): from the one liable to fall away (*parihāṇadharman*) transforming into the one who acts with reflection (*cetayitadharman*), up to the one who abides securely (*sthitākampya*) transforming into the one capable of penetration (*prativedhanādharman*).
Why, then, are these not mentioned later in the *Indriya-skandha*?
"But is it only when one who is liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) that they become immovable (akopya)? He replied:
"This too is included within the exposition in the Indriya-skandhaka."

Why is this? When one transforms the *parihāṇadharman* (one liable to fall away) into the *cetanādharman* (one capable of volition), one does not discard the *parihāṇadharman* faculty but acquires the *cetanādharman* faculty.

This continues until, when one transforms the *sthitākampya* (one stable in attainment) into the *prativedhanādharman* (one capable of penetration), one does not discard the preceding four faculties but acquires the *prativedhanādharman* faculty.
When one transforms from the "capable-of-attaining" (kandha) stage into the "immovable" (akopya) stage, one suddenly abandons the previous five faculties and acquires the immovable faculty;
therefore, he speaks only of the case when one who is liberated-by-time (samayavimukta) refines their faculties to become immovable.
The relinquishing of untainted faculties and the acquisition of untainted faculties does not occur by proceeding from one fruit to another.
It is not said that this involves the transformation of the retrogressive dharma or the performance of the meditative dharma.
The critique states:
One should not make such a statement.
Why is this? Because there is not even a single person who possesses both sexual organs simultaneously.
How much more so for one who has perfected the faculties of the five stages;
furthermore, although a non-returner who has cultivated the path of preparation for the refinement of faculties may not yet attain the fruit of arhatship, [they still possess such potential].
Why is it that one cannot transform [the faculties] to become a *dṛṣṭiprāpta*?
Although ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet attained the fruit can transform their faculties,
for what reason is there no possibility of transforming the faculties for a noble one (*ārya*) except at the time of attaining the fruit?
The preparatory practices for becoming free from passion (*vairāgya*) and for the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) are each distinct.
How then can one who attains two fruits while becoming free from passion simultaneously transform their faculties?
Therefore, in the subsequent *Indriyaskandhaka*, by mentioning the beginning and the end, the middle is implied.
It is not said that those resolved through faith refine their faculties to become those who have attained vision;
nor is it said that those subject to falling away refine their faculties to become those of the thought-type, and so forth.
Other masters say:
One who lacks faith transforms their faculty through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Question: If that is so, it is well-explained in accordance with what is stated in the *Indriyaskandha*; however, how should this statement here be explained?
Thus, it is said that there is the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) which has not been attained or has already been lost.
If one who is resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta) does not transform their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
how could the fruit of stream-entry be something that, having been attained, is then lost?
Regarding this, some say that one does not achieve the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the past or the future;
others say that one does.
There is the accomplishment of the past and future acquisitions.
If one were to say that there is no accomplishment of the past and future acquisitions:
He explains that the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry is termed "not yet attained" when it exists in the future;
"already lost" when it exists in the past;
and "accomplished" when it exists in the present.
If one were to say that there is the attainment of the past and the future,
they would be saying that the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) is of three kinds.
That is to say, there are the inferior,

the intermediate, and the superior. When one first dwells in the inferior stage of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), it is said that the intermediate and superior fruits of stream-entry have not yet been attained,
while the inferior grade of the fruit of stream-entry has been accomplished (*pariniṣpanna*).
One should not say that it has been lost, because there is nothing that has been lost. If,
during the first dwelling at the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), one has not yet attained the higher fruit of stream-entry,
then with respect to the lower fruit of stream-entry, it is said to have been "already lost."
Among these, the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) is designated as "attained.

When one first abides in the higher stage of the fruit of stream-entry, the lower stage of the fruit of stream-entry is designated as "already lost," while the higher stage of the fruit of stream-entry is designated as "attained."
One should not say that it has not been attained because it was previously unattained.

Question: If one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) while in the first dwelling has not yet attained [the fruit] at a lower level, and if one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry while in a higher first dwelling has not yet attained both the middle and lower levels, [how is this to be understood]?
"How is it said that they have been lost?
He replied: "Because one has transcended them, they are said to be 'lost'."
This means that what was previously attainable has now been surpassed upon reaching this superior stage and can no longer be attained; therefore, it is said to have been "lost.
By this principle, although there is faith and resolve, there is no one who transforms their faculties (*indriya*) to become one who has reached the stage of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).

If it is thus established that the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) can be said to have the sense of being "not yet obtained" or "already lost," how then is the subsequent statement in the *Jñānaskandha* to be reconciled?
As it says there: "A stream-enterer possesses all three samādhis in the future and [some] in the past."
If that which has already been extinguished is not lost, one then accomplishes it as present;
if it manifests before one, one accomplishes it.
This applies to one who possesses faith and resolve (*śraddhādhimukta*) and does not transform their faculties to become one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
How is it that for a stream-enterer, three types of samādhi have ceased and yet been lost?
Is it to distinguish them from such cases that it is said there are those that have ceased but are not lost?
He answers as follows:
This should be stated later in the section on the aggregate of wisdom (*jñānaskandha*):
"A stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) possesses all three samādhis in their future state; as for those that have already ceased in the past, he possesses them."
One should not say that there is no "non-loss" (avipraṇāśa); rather, those who speak of such non-loss are reciters who have committed an error.
How, then, is the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* to be reconciled?
As it says therein: "A time-liberated (*samayavimukta*) arhat may fall away from the fruit of arhatship and become one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*)."
Having refined his faculties to become a *dṛṣṭiprāpta* and subsequently attained the fruit of arhatship, he replied:
"I am unable to provide a comprehensive explanation of the *Śarīra-pada-śāstra*, for it is extremely profound."
The critique states: Since one cannot understand the *Kāyavādopadeśa*,
and furthermore, since the preceding passage from the *Jñānaskandhopadeśa* was subject to deprecation,
even if one were to understand this present text, it would still not be reasonable.
Therefore, one should accept that those with faith-resolve (śraddhādhimukta) can transform their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) to become those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
If those in the stage of training (śaikṣa) cannot transform their faculties,
then those in the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa) should likewise not be able to transform them, just as in the case of those in the stage of training.
There is no protection and no power;
it should be the same in the stage of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Therefore, the Venerable Buddhapālita spoke thus.
Regarding the transformation of the faculties from one liberated by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) to one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), there are six unique characteristics:
first, it occurs within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and not in the form or formless realms;
second, it relies upon the dhyānas and not upon the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
Third, they employ the untainted path and not the mundane path.
Fourth, they employ dharma-knowledge and not subsequent knowledge.
Fifth, they have already regressed and have not yet [attained] non-regression.
Sixth, one abides in the fruit but does not abide in the path of superior fruit.
Question: For what reason is this in the desire realm and not in the form or formless realms?
He answers as follows:
It is only through the power of preaching the Dharma that one can transform the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti), because such preaching exists only within the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
Question: Why does he rely on the dhyānas rather than the formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti)?
He answered thus: "The training of the faculties by one in the stage of training (śaikṣa) must depend on the stage of having attained the fruit;
there is no case where one attains the fruit of training by relying on a formless absorption (ārūpyasamāpatti)."
Therefore, one who trains in the transformation of the faculties does not rely on the formless realms.
Question: For what reason does he employ the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) rather than the mundane path (laukika-mārga)?
He answers as follows:
Only through a sharp and intense path can one transform the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*);
because the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) is dull, it is not employed for this purpose.
Question: Why does that [path] employ only the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and not the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)?
He answered thus: "One must be born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) in order to be able to transform the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti).
Only in the desire realm does one attain mastery over the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)."
Therefore, they do not transform their faculties by means of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Question: Why is it that these are those who have already fallen away, and not those who have not yet fallen away?
He replied as follows:
"Those who have become weary and desist are the ones who seek the refinement of their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra).
It is only after one has already experienced a regression that such weariness arises."
Therefore, for one who has not yet fallen away, there is no possibility of a transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
Question: For what reason does such a person abide in the fruit and not in the path of superior fruit?
He answers as follows:
If one who dwells in the path of the superior fruit were to refine their faculties,
they would, at the time of refining the faculties, abandon many paths and acquire few paths;
that should be called "retrogression" rather than "progress."
Therefore, the transformation of the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) occurs only while abiding in the fruit,
because at the time of refining the faculties, one attains only the fruit.
Thus say the masters of the Abhidharma treatises.
Regarding those six matters at the time of training for the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*),
three are reasonable and three are not.
That which was stated— that the training for the transformation of the faculties occurs in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and not in the form or formless realms— is reasonable.
This is because the transformation of faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) occurs only in the desire realm.
Furthermore, their statement that this relies on dhyāna and not on the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) is also logical,
for one attains the fruit of training (śaikṣa-phala) only by relying on dhyāna.
Furthermore, his statement that one employs the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) and not the conventional path (*saṃvṛti-mārga*) is also reasonable,
because the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) during the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) is like the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
However, his claim that one employs the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and not the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is untenable.
Why is this? Because the meaning is not fixed.
That is to say, one born in the desire realm may attain mastery over the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) but not the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Alternatively, it might be argued that this refers to one who has attained mastery over subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) but not yet to dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna).
Furthermore, their claim that this applies to those who have already regressed and not to those who have not yet regressed is also untenable.
Why is this? Because the meaning is not fixed.

That is to say, some have already fallen away while others have not yet fallen away; nevertheless, they either fear falling away or seek superior faculties and thus practice the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃvara).
Furthermore, that which you stated—that one who abides in the fruit does not abide in the path of superior fruit—is also untenable. Why?
Because the meaning is not definitive.

This refers to those training in the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), whether abiding in the stage of fruition (*phala-stha*) or abiding in the path of superior fruition (*viśeṣa-mārga*), seeking sharp faculties or fearing retrogression.
Question: If one refines their faculties while abiding in the path of superior fruition, they abandon many paths and acquire few; is this not retrogression?
Answer: There is no fault, because that person seeks the faculty of sharpness rather than seeking many paths;
it is like trading a large amount of copper or iron for a small amount of gold or silver—how could this be called a loss?
Question: Within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), at which location does the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) occur?
Is it only among humans, or also in the heavens?
Answer: It occurs only among humans, because their reception of the teaching is superior and because they fear falling back.
Question: Within the four continents, in which location does the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) occur?
The Venerable Kuṣāvatama replied:
"Only in Jambudvīpa is there the possibility of the transformation of faculties."
Because the faculties of the people of Jambudvīpa are sharp and keen,
the commentary states: one should explain that within the three continents of humans, all are capable of transforming their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti).
Excluding those of Uttarakuru because they lack superior qualities.
Question: Does the possibility of changing one's sexual organ (indriya-parāvṛtti) apply based on a male body, or does it also apply based on a female body?
Some have stated as follows:
The transformation of the faculties occurs only based on a male body,
because the qualities of the male body are superior to those of a woman.
The critique states that one should speak thus.
Those who undergo the transformation of faculties do so based on both the male body and the female body, for it is possible to generate superior qualities even by relying on the female body.
Question: Does one transform the faculties immediately upon the same stage (bhūmi) where one first attained the fruit of training?
Some say that this refers to the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) by one who is still a trainee (*śaikṣa*).
Furthermore, it may also rely on other stages (*bhūmi*), provided they are superior and not inferior.
That is to say, the first two fruits are attained through the fruit-transformation based on the *anāgamya* concentration, and do not rely on any other stage.
If the fruit of non-returning is attained based on a particular stage, one subsequently transforms the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) based on that same stage;
or it may be based on another stage, provided it is superior and not inferior.
At the very minimum, all non-returners accomplish the fruit of three stages.
At most, one achieves the fruits of six stages.
That is to say, for one who proceeds by gradual stages, at the moment of the ninth path of liberation when abandoning the defilements of the desire realm,
they achieve the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) of three stages.
That is, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the first dhyāna, and the intermediate dhyāna;
if one has already become free from the defilements of desire, one enters into rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on these three stages.
At the time of that subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*), one also simultaneously achieves the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) of these three stages.
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the second dhyāna,
at the time of that subsequent knowledge of the path, one achieves the fruit of non-returner of four stages.
This refers to the first three stages and the second dhyāna.
If one enters the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on the third dhyāna,
at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna), they achieve the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) across five stages.
This refers to the first four stages and the third dhyāna.
If one enters the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the fourth dhyāna,
at the moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna), they achieve the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin) across six stages.
This refers to those who, having attained the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) based on the first three stages and the fourth dhyāna among the aforementioned five stages,
subsequently transform their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) while relying on these same three stages.
He abandons the fruit of non-returner of the three stages and attains the fruit of non-returner of the three stages; that is,
if he transforms his faculties while relying on the second dhyāna.
He abandons the fruit of non-returner of the third stage and attains the fruit of non-returner of the fourth stage.
If he transforms his faculties while relying on the third dhyāna,
he abandons the fruit of non-returner of the third stage.
One who has attained the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmiphala) at the fifth stage—
if that person transforms their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) by relying on the fourth dhyāna—
abandons the fruit of a non-returner belonging to those three stages.
One attains the fruit of non-returner in the sixth stage.
If one attains the fruit of non-returner based on the second dhyāna and subsequently transforms the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) while remaining based on that same second dhyāna,
they relinquish the fruit of non-returner of four stages and attain the fruit of non-returner of those same four stages.
If that person transforms their faculties based on the third dhyāna,
they relinquish the fruit of non-returner belonging to four stages and attains the fruit of non-returner belonging to five stages.
If that person transforms their faculties based on the fourth dhyāna,
they relinquish the fruit of non-returner belonging to four stages and attains the fruit of non-returner belonging to six stages.
If one attains the fruit of non-returner based on the third dhyāna and subsequently transforms the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) while remaining based on that same third dhyāna,
they relinquish the fruit of non-returner belonging to five stages.
One who has attained the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmiphala) of the five stages,
if they subsequently transform their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) by relying on the fourth dhyāna,
relinquishes that fruit of a non-returner of the five stages.
One attains the fruit of a non-returner at the sixth stage.
If, having attained the fruit of a non-returner based on the fourth dhyāna,
one then transforms the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) while remaining based on that same fourth dhyāna.
He abandons the fruit of non-returner of the six stages and attains the fruit of non-returner of the six stages. One who,
having attained the fruit of non-returner based on a higher stage without dependence, subsequently transforms their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) based on a lower stage.
Why is this? Because one would not abandon the many paths to obtain only a few paths;
it should be called "diminution" rather than "augmentation."
Some say that there are those who,
having attained the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) based on a higher stage, subsequently transform their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) based on a lower stage;
they speak as follows.
If, having attained the fruit of non-returner based on the fourth dhyāna, one transforms the faculties based on the third dhyāna,
one abandons the fruit of non-returner belonging to six stages and acquires the fruit of non-returner belonging to five stages.
If one transforms the faculties based on the second dhyāna,
they relinquish the fruit of non-returner belonging to six stages and attain the fruit of non-returner belonging to four stages.
If that person transforms their faculties based on the first dhyāna or any of the other three stages,
they relinquish the fruit of non-returner belonging to six stages and attain the fruit of non-returner belonging to three stages.
Having attained the fruit of non-returner based on the third dhyāna,
if one transforms the faculties based on the second dhyāna,
they relinquish the fruit of non-returner belonging to five stages.
One who has attained the fruit of non-returner at the fourth dhyāna level,
if they subsequently transform their faculties while relying on any of the three lower levels such as the first dhyāna,
relinquishes the fruit of non-returner belonging to those five levels.
One attains the fruit of non-returner at the third stage.
Having attained the fruit of non-returner based on the second dhyāna,
if one transforms the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) based on the first dhyāna or any of the [other] three stages, [one does so].
He abandons the fruit of non-returner of the four stages and attains the fruit of non-returner of the three stages; herein,
only that which differs from the former is stated.
Regarding the relinquishment and acquisition [of faculties] by one who transforms their faculties while relying on a higher or lower stage, it should be understood as previously explained.
Question: If one attains the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) while relying on a higher stage and subsequently transforms their faculties while relying on a lower stage, [what occurs]?
Since one abandons many paths and attains few paths, it should be called "diminution";
how could it be "augmentation"? The answer is:
for one who seeks sharp faculties rather than many paths, there is no fault in abandoning what is much and attaining what is little.
It is like trading many items of little value for a few precious gems;
this is called an increase, not a decrease.
Having explained this according to the fruit (*phala*), if one explains it according to the path (*mārga*), regarding those who are non-returners (*anāgāmin*):
If one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna transforms their faculties while relying on any of the three stages beginning with the first dhyāna,
they abandon the noble paths of those three stages and acquire the noble paths of those three stages.

If one who has already abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna transforms their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) while relying on any of the three stages beginning with the first dhyāna,
they relinquish the noble paths (āryamārga) of four stages.
Having attained the noble path of the third dhyāna,
and being already free from the defilements of the second dhyāna but not yet free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
if one transforms the faculties while relying on any of the three stages beginning with the first dhyāna.
He abandons the noble path of five stages and attains the noble path of three stages.
Having already abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna but not yet having abandoned the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
he transforms his faculties while relying on any of the first three dhyānas.
He abandons the noble path of the six stages and attains the noble path of the three stages.
Having already become free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna but not yet free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space,
if he transforms his faculties while relying on any of the first three dhyānas, etc., [he proceeds as follows].
He abandons the noble path of the seventh stage and attains the noble path of the third stage;
he has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space, but has not yet become detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
If one transforms the faculties based on the three stages beginning with the first dhyāna,
they relinquish the noble paths of eight stages and attain the noble paths of three stages,
having already become free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
If one transforms the faculties based on the three stages beginning with the first dhyāna,
they relinquish the noble paths of nine stages and attain the noble paths of three stages.
If one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna transforms their faculties while relying on the second dhyāna,
they relinquish the noble paths of the four stages and acquire the noble paths of the four stages.
One who has already abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna,
if they transform their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) based on the second dhyāna, abandons the noble path of five stages and acquires the noble path of four stages.
Up to the point where one has already become free from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*),
if one transforms the faculties (*indriya*) based on the second dhyāna,
one abandons the noble path (*āryamārga*) of nine stages and attains the noble path of four stages.
If one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna transforms their faculties based on the third dhyāna,
they relinquish the noble path of five stages and acquire the noble path of five stages.
One who has already abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna but has not yet abandoned those of the fourth dhyāna,
if they transform their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) by relying on the third dhyāna,
abandons the noble path of six stages and acquires the noble path of five stages.
Up to the point where one has already become free from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*),
if one transforms the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) while relying on the third dhyāna,
one abandons the noble path (*āryamārga*) of nine stages and acquires the noble path of five stages.
If one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the fourth dhyāna transforms their faculties while relying on the fourth dhyāna,
they relinquish the noble paths of six stages and acquire the noble paths of six stages.

If one who has already abandoned the defilements of the fourth dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the sphere of infinite space transforms their faculties while relying on the fourth dhyāna,
they abandon the noble paths of seven stages and acquire the noble paths of six stages.
Up to the point where one has already become free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*),
if one transforms the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) by relying on the fourth dhyāna,
one abandons the noble path (*āryamārga*) of nine stages and acquires the noble path of six stages.
If one who has already become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna and so forth transforms their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) by relying on the second dhyāna and so forth,
one should reflect accordingly upon the extent of what is abandoned and what is acquired.
Regarding those who transform their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) without relying on the formless realm:
since the fruit of training does not rely upon the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti),
it should be stated as follows.
If one has already attained mastery over a higher stage and relies upon a lower stage to train in the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) and so forth,
one may still attain the untainted path of the fruit of the higher stage;
however, at the time of transforming the faculties, one cannot attain the formless realm, because that realm necessarily lacks the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
In this regard, one should pose the following question and answer:
Is it possible for a noble one (*ārya*) to abandon the noble path of nine stages and attain the noble path of six stages, such that this is called "progress" and not "retrogression"?

Answer: There is. It refers to one who has already abandoned the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) and, being one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), transforms their faculties while relying on the fourth dhyāna.
Is there any noble one (*ārya*) who, having already abandoned the defilements of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), possesses the Noble Path of only a single stage?
Answer: There is.

That is to say, one who has already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) enters into the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on the preparatory concentration (anāgamya).
During the fifteen moments of mind within that path of seeing,
is there any non-returner who has already abandoned the defilements of the sphere of nothingness and possesses only the untainted fruit-path of the three stages?
Answer: There is.

That is to say, one who has already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), yet possesses conviction through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and does not attain mastery over the higher stages.

When one transforms the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) by means of the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the first dhyāna, or the intermediate dhyāna, and thereby becomes a "one who has attained vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
is it possible that such a person who is a "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin) would not possess the untainted formless attainments (anāsrava-ārūpyasamāpatti)?
Answer: Yes.

This refers to the time when one who is a body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*), or one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), transforms their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) and becomes one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Sixty-seven.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Sixty-Eight,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Two: The Aggregate of Fetters; Sub-section Three: The Section on Sentient Beings; Part Six. Question: When one who has already become detached from the defilements of the Sphere of Nothingness transforms their faculties through resolute faith (śraddhādhimukta) into becoming one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), [at that time...]
Once one has abandoned the untainted paths of counteraction for the three formless realms, are the abandonments of the three stages also abandoned?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
There are faults in both cases.
Why is this? If one abandons that abandonment, how could one not be established in the afflictions of those three stages?
If one does not abandon it, how could one abandon that path while not abandoning the abandonment?
It is agreed that this is what was said.
[One] does not abandon those abandonments.
Question: Since one has already abandoned those paths, why does one not abandon the abandonments of the three stages?
Answer: In the three lower formless stages, there are two types of remedial paths:
first, the conventional;
second, the untainted.
When a trainee undergoes the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), although they relinquish those untainted [attainments], they do not relinquish the mundane ones;
for it is by means of the mundane that the abandonment of those [defilements] is maintained.
Thus, when a trainee undergoes the transformation of the faculties, they do not lose that abandonment.

Question: If, when one in training transforms their faculties while the mundane path is active, it is possible not to abandon what has been severed, how much more so when one in training transforms their faculties while the mundane path is not active? Why would one not abandon it in that case?

When one who has abandoned from one grade up to eight grades of defilement of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception transforms their faculties through faith and resolve to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*),
are the abandonments of the factors to be eliminated by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of that sphere considered relinquished or not relinquished?
If one abandons that abandonment, why would one not be non-possessed of the afflictions of that stage?
If one does not abandon it, why would one abandon its antidote yet not abandon the abandonment itself?
Regarding this, some say:
There is certainly no one who, while remaining defiled by the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).
If such a person were to transform their faculties, they would either be entirely free from defilement or else entirely fallen away.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
There are also those who, having separated from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), transform their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).
Although they abandon that path, they do not abandon the abandonment [of the defilements].
The critique states: one should speak thus.
Although he has abandoned the path and also abandoned the abandonment [attained therein], he does not accomplish the afflictions of that stage.

This is like ordinary beings who, having already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), pass away and are reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Just as one who has abandoned the path or the abandonment [of defilements] from the desire realm up to the sphere of infinite consciousness does not achieve the afflictions of those levels even though they have been relinquished,
so it is here as well; therefore, this objection should not be raised.
Question: While afflictions of a lower stage do not depend on the body of a higher stage and are abandoned through the path of relinquishment, one does not yet possess those lower-stage afflictions;

likewise, when one who is in training (śaikṣa) transforms their faculties, afflictions of a higher stage that depend on the body of a lower stage are also abandoned through the path of relinquishment. [In both cases, why is there no possession?]
How is it that one does not fail to achieve the abandonment of the afflictions already severed?

Answer: Having separated from one to eight grades of defilement of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one who transforms their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*)—after being free from those defilements—arises with a continuity maintained by the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) similar to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), ensuring that they do not fall back again.
For example, when an ordinary person, having already abandoned the defilements of the sphere of nothingness,
enters the state of right determination and attains the fruit of non-returner, they will certainly never again fall back and give rise to the fetters previously abandoned.
This case is also like this, so it should not be questioned.

Question: When one who is liberated through faith transforms their faculties to become one who has attained vision, by means of how many paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), how many paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), and how many paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) does one transform the faculties?

Some say that one transforms the faculties by means of one path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The critique states: they should not speak in this way.
Because the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) studied here are not long-cultivated and are easily transformable,
it should be stated as follows:

they transform their faculties by employing only one path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), one path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), just as in the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Question: When a time-liberated (samaya-vimukta) arhat transforms their faculties to become immovable (akopya), through how many paths of preparation (prayoga-mārga), how many paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), and how many paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) does he effect this transformation of the faculties?
