Some say that one transforms the faculties by means of a single path of preparation, a single path of immediate succession, and a single path of liberation.
The critique states: One should not speak in this manner.
Because the faculties of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have been cultivated for a long time and are difficult to relinquish;
furthermore, because it requires great effort to relinquish a heavy fruit and then attain another heavy fruit,
just as when a person demolishes a house and then builds another.
It involves much effort and is not like a creative act; rather,

one should say that he transforms his faculties by means of one path of preparation, nine paths of uninterrupted transition, and nine paths of liberation, because it is similar to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Question: When one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) transforms their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), are the preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*) and so forth contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: Those preparatory paths are either contaminated or uncontaminated.
The supernormal powers to be cultivated in the future are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Their uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) are exclusively uncontaminated;
those to be cultivated in the future are likewise only uncontaminated. Their paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are also exclusively uncontaminated.
Regarding that which is cultivated in the future,
some say it is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*). Others, however, say:
At that time, one cultivates both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Question: When a *samayavimukta* arhat transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) to become an *akopyadharman*, are the preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*) and so forth contaminated or uncontaminated?
Answer: That path of preparation may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Those cultivated in the future are both contaminated and uncontaminated.
The nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are exclusively uncontaminated.
That which is cultivated in the future is also exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
The ninth path of liberation is invariably untainted;
that which is cultivated in the future therein pertains to both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted.
At that time, because he concurrently cultivates all the roots of goodness belonging to the three realms according to what is appropriate for him,
it is asked: when one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) transforms their faculties to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*),
are the paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*) and so forth already previously obtained, or are they not yet obtained?
Answer: That path of preparation may be either previously attained or not yet attained;
however, both the path of immediate succession and the path of liberation are exclusively not yet attained.
Question: When an Arhat liberated by occasion transforms their faculties to become one who is immovable, [what is the case]?
Are the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and so forth previously attained or not yet attained?
Answer: Those paths of preparation may be either previously attained or not yet attained;
however, the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are exclusively not yet attained.
When one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) transforms their faculties to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*),
the preparatory path and the uninterrupted path are subsumed under the path of one liberated through faith,
while the path of liberation is subsumed under the path of one who has attained vision.
When an Arhat of occasional liberation transforms their faculties to become one of immovable liberation,
the nine paths of preparation, the eight paths of uninterrupted transition, and the path of liberation are subsumed within the category of the path of occasional liberation.
The ninth path of liberation is subsumed under the path of occasional liberation.
When one who is liberated through faith transforms their faculties to become one who has attained vision, or when one who abides in the fruit transforms their faculties;
[in these cases, it is the path of non-occasional liberation].
The preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are all subsumed under the path of fruition (*phala-mārga*).
However, if one transforms the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) while abiding in the path of superior fruition (*viśeṣa-mārga*),
then that preparatory path and uninterrupted path are subsumed under the path of superior fruition.
The path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) is subsumed under the path of fruition (phala-mārga).
When a temporarily liberated (samaya-vimukta) Arhat transforms his faculties to become immovable (akopya),
all of his paths of preparation (prayoga-mārga), uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga), and paths of liberation are subsumed under the path of fruition.
Because they lack the path of superior fruit,
when one who has attained liberation through faith transforms their faculties to become one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*),
if they transform their faculties while abiding in a fruit:
He abandons the path of the fruit and the path toward attaining the fruit.
If one transforms the faculties while abiding in the path of superior fruit,
he abandons both the path of the fruit and the path of superior fruit, and acquires only the path of the fruit.
When a *samayavimukta* arhat transforms their faculties to become an *akopyadharman*,
they abandon only the path of the fruit and acquire the path of the fruit;
this is because in the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there is no path of superior fruit.
There are six types of arhats:

namely, those of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharman), those of the nature of reflecting (cetayitadharman), those of the nature of guarding (anurakṣaṇādharman), those of the nature of abiding (sthitākampya), those of the nature of being capable of penetration (prativedhanādharman), and those of the nature of immovability (akopyadharman).
When an arhat of the nature of falling away transforms their faculties to become one of the nature of reflecting...
He abandons the faculty of one subject to falling away and acquires the faculty of one intent on reflection.
When an Arhat of the type intent on reflection transforms his faculties to become one who guards the dharma,
he abandons the faculty of one intent on reflection and acquires the faculty of one who guards the dharma.
When an Arhat who is a *dharmapāla* transforms his faculties to become one who abides in the dharma (*anusthita-dharman*),
he abandons the faculty of a *dharmapāla* and acquires the faculty of one who abides in the dharma.

When an Arhat who abides in the dharma transforms his faculties to become one capable of penetration (*prativedhanādharman*), [he abandons the faculty of one who abides in the dharma and acquires the faculty of one capable of penetration].
When one who abides in the faculty of the "one who attains through effort" (prativedhanādharman) attains the faculty of the "unshakable" (akopyadharman),
at the moment that Arhat of the "one who attains through effort" transforms his faculties to become unshakable,
he abandons the faculty of the "one who attains through effort" and acquires the faculty of the "unshakable."

In this way, each of the five stages achieves the transformation of the faculties through one path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
When those paths of preparation, the nine paths of uninterrupted transition, and eight paths of liberation arise, there is acquisition [of new qualities] but no relinquishing [of previous ones].
When the ninth path of liberation arises, there is both acquisition and relinquishment;
that is, one relinquishes the faculties such as the dharma of regression and acquires the faculties such as the dharma of reflection.
This refers to the paths of preparation, uninterruptedness, and liberation within the preceding four stages.
Furthermore, the preparatory, uninterrupted, and eight liberation paths of the fifth stage are all subsumed under the path of occasional liberation (*samaya-vimukta-mārga*).
The ninth liberation path is subsumed under the path of non-occasional liberation (*asamaya-vimukta-mārga*).
Just as there are six types of lineage in the path of no-more-learning,
so too are there these six types of lineage in the path of cultivation;
that is, from the lineage of the learner who is subject to falling away, up to the lineage of the learner who is immovable.
Question: When one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) transforms their faculties to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
if they abide in the lineage of those subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman),
do they transform the faculties of the lineage subject to falling away and thereby immediately obtain the faculties of the unshakable lineage (akopyadharman)?
One who possesses the faculties of the *parihāṇadharman* lineage transforms them so as to obtain only the faculties of the *cetanādharman* lineage;
through gradual and progressive advancement, one finally attains the faculties of the *akopyadharman* lineage.
Furthermore, for one who abides in the lineage of the dharma of stability,
if they transform the faculty of the lineage of the dharma of stability, they immediately obtain the faculty of the lineage of the immovable dharma;
or, by transforming the faculty of the lineage of the dharma of stability, they obtain only the faculty of the lineage of the penetrable dharma.
Furthermore, does one who possesses the faculty of the lineage capable of turning toward progress (prativedhanā-dharman) subsequently obtain the faculty of the immovable lineage (akopya-dharman)?
Regarding this, some say:
"If one abides in the lineage of those subject to falling away (parihāṇa-dharman)..."
One who possesses the faculties of the lineage of the retrogressive dharma immediately attains the faculties of the lineage of the immovable dharma;
it is not attained through gradual progression.
This applies even to one who abides in the lineage of the stable dharma.
By transforming the root of the lineage of the dharma of abiding, one immediately attains the root of the lineage of the immovable dharma;
it is not attained through gradual progression. Why is this so?
The transformation of the faculties at the stage of training differs from that at the stage of no-more-training.
This is because at the stage of no-more-training, it is difficult to relinquish and difficult to attain; it requires extensive effort and is accomplished only gradually.
It is not so for the stage of training, and therefore it is attained instantaneously.
The critique states: One should not make such a claim.

The ease or difficulty of relinquishing and attaining [the fruits] depends solely on the number of uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and does not differ based on whether the process is gradual or sudden.
It should be stated as follows:
if one who abides in the lineage of the nature of regression transforms the faculties of the lineage of regression, they obtain only the faculties of the lineage of reflection.
Advancing gradually and superiorly, one eventually reaches the immovable stage.
Furthermore, if one who abides in the lineage of the dharma of stability transforms the faculty of the lineage of the dharma of stability,
they obtain only the faculty of the lineage of the dharma of being capable of penetration.

Furthermore, one who possesses the faculties of the lineage capable of transformation attains the faculties of the immovable lineage; thus, in each of these five stages, the transformation of the faculties is achieved through one path of preparation, one path of immediate succession, and one path of liberation.
When that path of preparation (prayoga-mārga) and the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) arise, there is acquisition but no relinquishment.
When the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) arises, there is both acquisition and relinquishment;
that is to say, one relinquishes the faculties of the lineage of regression (parihāṇadharma-gotra) and acquires the faculties of the lineage of reflection (cetana-dharma-gotra).
The paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the first four stages,
as well as the paths of preparation and uninterrupted paths of the fifth stage, are all subsumed under the path of those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).
The path of liberation of the fifth stage is subsumed under the path of those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Just as there are six types of lineage in the stage of the path of cultivation,
there are likewise these six types of lineage in the stage of the path of seeing;
namely, the lineage of the learner who is subject to falling away, up to the lineage of the learner who is immovable.
However, there is no transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) at the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Why is this?

Because the path of seeing is so rapid that it does not give rise to a deliberate intention (*āśaya*); once it has arisen, its continuity must persist until the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), where further application (*prayoga*) can then be undertaken.
Just as there are six types of lineage in the stage of the path of seeing,
there are likewise these six types of lineage in the stage of practice through application (*prayogabhūmi*).
That is to say, in the stage of practice through application, there is the lineage of those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).
Up to the stage of the lineage of immovable dharma through corresponding practice,
there are six types of lineages within this stage;
namely, those of *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgradharma*.
This is because it is the proximate preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) for the Noble Path;
because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) toward the Truths (*satya*) resembles that of the Noble Path;
and because its basis (*āśraya*), body, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are identical to those of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Because the preceding stage is not so, six types of lineage are not established there.
This stage of the practice of application (*prayogabhūmi*) also possesses the meaning of the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*);

that is, one may transform the faculty of the lineage of "one who falls back" (*parihāṇadharman*) of the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and give rise to the faculty of the lineage of "one who reflects" (*cetayitṛdharman*) of the stage of "heat."

The faculty of the lineage of warmth regarding the turning toward the Dharma arises; from the faculty of the lineage of warmth regarding the turning toward the Dharma, the faculty of the lineage of warmth regarding the protection of the Dharma arises; and from the faculty of the lineage of warmth regarding the protection of the Dharma, the faculty of the lineage of warmth regarding abiding in the Dharma arises.

One transforms the lineage-root of the "mild" stage of warmth belonging to the *parihāṇadharman* into the lineage-root of the "mild" stage of warmth belonging to the *anurakṣaṇadharman*; one transforms the lineage-root of the "mild" stage of warmth belonging to the *anurakṣaṇadharman* into the lineage-root of the "mild" stage of warmth belonging to the *sthitākampya*.

One transforms the lineage-root of the "mild" stage of warmth belonging to the *sthitākampya* into the lineage-root of the "mild" stage of warmth belonging to the *prativedhanādharman*. One transforms the lineage-root of the "mild" stage of warmth belonging to the *prativedhanādharman* into the lineage-root of the "mild" stage of warmth belonging to the *akopyadharman*.
One transforms the roots of the śrāvaka’s stage of warmth (*uṣmagata*) into the roots of the pratyekabuddha’s stage of warmth;
one transforms the roots of the śrāvaka’s or pratyekabuddha’s stage of warmth into the roots of the Buddha’s stage of warmth.
As it is said regarding the stage of warmth (*uṣmagata*), so it is for the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*).
However, there is a distinction in the stage of patience (*kṣānti*):

namely, one transforms the faculties of the lineage of the "patience of falling back" (*parihāṇadharman*) and gives rise to the faculties of the lineage of the "patience of reflecting" (*cetana-dharman*).

Gradually, up to the point where the faculties of the lineage of the patience of the *kāmada* (attainable) dharma are transformed and the faculties of the lineage of the patience of the *akopya* (immovable) dharma arise;
and where the faculties of the lineage of the patience of the *śrāvaka* are transformed and the faculties of the lineage of the patience of the *pratyekabuddha* arise.

There is no sense in which the faculty of the lineage of patience belonging to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas can be transformed into the faculty of the lineage of patience belonging to Buddhas. Why is this?

Because patience is incompatible with the miserable realms; for one who has attained the nature of patience, non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is obtained regarding those miserable realms.
At times, Bodhisattvas, by the power of their great vows, take birth in the various evil realms for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;
however, there is no principle by which those in the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) of the Two Vehicles could aspire to the Buddha Vehicle.
Other masters say:
For Śrāvakas in the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, there is the possibility of turning toward the path of a Pratyekabuddha or a Buddha;
for Pratyekabuddhas in the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, there is no possibility of turning toward the path of a Buddha. Why is this so?
Just as the Buddha attained spontaneous awakening without a teacher, so too did the Pratyekabuddha.
Just as the Buddha resolved his mind and, through a single paryanka posture, brought forth the entire mass of all virtuous qualities.

From the contemplation of impurity up until the arising of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, the solitary realizer likewise maintains a continuous succession of mind without giving rise to any other thought.
The critique states: one should not make such a statement.
For the rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddha, it is possible that there is no possibility of turning toward the Buddha-vehicle during the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*.
However, for those who are like the herd-walkers (*vargacārin*), it is not contrary to reason that they may turn toward the Buddha-vehicle during the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*.
Therefore, what was stated previously is logically sound.

Question: For those who undergo the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) at the stage of the practice of application (*prayoga-bhūmi*), are there paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)?
Some say that there are also [distinct paths], namely,
when one transforms from a lineage such as the *parihāṇadharman* (one liable to fall away) and so forth to arise in a lineage such as the *cetanādharman* (one capable of volition) and so forth;
for each such case, there is separately one path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), and nine paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
Because the nature of the out-flowing (sāsrava) seeds has been cultivated for a long time, it is difficult to abandon and acquire;
this is like the transformation of the uncontaminated faculties (anāsravendriya) in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa). Other masters say:
In each case, there is only one path of application, one path of immediate succession, and one path of liberation for the cultivation of the "heat" stage and the others;
because these do not endure for long, they are easy to relinquish and easy to attain.
Just as there is the transformation of the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) for those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*),
so too, according to some teachers,
there is the transformation of faculties among all those within the associated stages (*saṃprayukta-bhūmi*).
However, by repeatedly applying effort and cultivating a sense of weariness toward the inferior while aspiring for the superior,
one eventually attains a superior state of lineage; yet, in this process,
there is neither a path of uninterrupted transition nor a path of liberation.
Because one does not abandon the inferior when attaining the superior, this is not like the state of the noble ones (*ārya*).
This is because those who transform their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) do not possess the two types of untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*),
and because upon attaining the superior grade, they necessarily abandon the inferior grade.
It requires both the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). The commentary states:

For those who transform their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) within the corresponding stages (*sabhāga-bhūmi*), although they do not abandon inferior faculties to acquire superior ones, at the time they attain the superior, the lineage (*gotra*) of the inferior faculties no longer manifests; therefore, it is also termed "abandoning."

Therefore, when one transforms from the lineage of the *parihāṇadharman* (one liable to fall away) and so forth, and arises in the lineage of the *cetanādharman* (one capable of volition) and so forth,

it is not contrary to reason that one attains this transformation of the faculties by employing extensive preparatory effort to induce a single path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and a single path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Because the cultivation of the levels of heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth does not take a long time, whereas the accomplishment of the contaminated preparatory practices (*sāsrava-prayoga*) is difficult;
and because if one turns toward another vehicle, there will be no time of immediate liberation, but rather accomplishment will only be achieved after a long duration.
Although there are six types of lineage in the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), because one does not transform the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) during that single moment,
the preceding stage of the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna-phala*) likewise possesses six types of lineage.
Since there are both those who undergo a change of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) and those who regress,
it is therefore said in response to a question regarding this:
"Is it possible for one to regress from the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna-phala*) without still possessing the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*)?"
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, at the time of falling away from a superior lineage.
Do all those who die and are reborn within the desire realm undergo a birth in the desire realm?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed? Answer:
To refute the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.
This means that some may claim there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for death and birth in any of the three realms;
in order to refute that position, it is shown that while the intermediate state definitely exists in the desire and form realms, it does not exist in the formless realm.

Alternatively, there are those who claim that because there is form within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is also an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) there, just as in the desire and form realms.
To refute that position and demonstrate that the formless realm lacks all forms, it is said that there is no intermediate state there either.
Alternatively, there are those who hold the view that within the desire and form realms, those whose karma is sharp and intense lack an intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
whereas those whose karma is dull and sluggish possess an intermediate state.

This treatise is composed to refute that school’s position and to demonstrate that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) exists in both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The term "existence" (*bhava*) used here signifies multiple meanings,
as has already been explained at length in the first section on "Existence" (*Bhava-nirdeśa*).

In this context, the term "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) belonging to the category of sentient beings (*sattvākhya*) within a particular homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Do all those who die and are reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) undergo existence in the desire realm?
One should answer by means of four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Because there is a mutual difference in breadth between death and birth in the desire realm and the acquisition of a desire-realm existence (*kāmadhātu-bhava*),
there are cases of death and birth in the desire realm that do not involve the acquisition of a desire-realm existence.
This refers to one who passes away from the desire realm and arises as an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) of the form realm.
This [intermediate state] belongs to both ordinary beings and noble ones.
The intermediate state of the form realm arises within the desire realm. Why is this so?
Such is the nature of phenomena:
wherever the aggregates of the death-existence cease,
right there the aggregates of the intermediate existence arise.
This is because it is the nature of phenomena that where a seed perishes, there a sprout arises.
In this context, one who dies in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) refers to one whose death-existence (maraṇabhava) in the desire realm ceases within the desire realm itself.
Regarding those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):
this refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) arising within the desire realm;
it does not mean that they have received a birth in the desire realm (*kāmabhava*).
This means that when one undergoes existence in the realm of form (*rūpabhava*), one undergoes the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the realm of form.
There is also the case of undergoing existence in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-bhava*) without dying and being reborn within the realm of desire;
that is, passing away from the realm of form and arising as an intermediate state being in the realm of desire.
This applies only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
An intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm arises within the form realm. Why is this so?
The Dharma should be thus.
As explained in detail previously,
herein, those who experience existence in the realm of desire—
This refers to the appropriation of the aggregates within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm;
it does not refer to one who dies in the desire realm,
because the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) of the form realm ceases within the form realm itself.
"Those not born in the desire realm" refers to those who,
while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm, arise in the form realm; and those who,
having died in the desire realm, are likewise reborn within the existence of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This refers to the death-existence in the desire realm and the arising of the intermediate existence (antarābhava) and birth-existence (upapattibhava) within the desire realm.
This applies to both ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) and noble ones (ārya).
Ordinary worldlings may take birth in any of the five destinies (gati).
The Noble One takes rebirth only among humans and devas. In this context,
when passing from the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), if one dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
it means that the death-existence of the desire realm ceases within the desire realm itself.
"Those born in the desire realm" refers to those who arise within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm.
"Those who experience existence in the desire realm" refers to...
This refers to the appropriation of the aggregates within the intermediate state (antarābhava) of the desire realm;
specifically, when one passes from that intermediate state into birth,
having died in the desire realm.
This means that the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm ceases within the desire realm;
as for those born in the desire realm,
it means their birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) arises within the desire realm.
"Experiencing the existence of desire" refers to experiencing the aggregates of the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) within the desire realm.
There are cases where one is neither in the process of dying or being born in the desire realm, nor is one experiencing the existence of desire.
That is to say: passing away from the form realm to be born in the form or formless realms;
passing away from the formless realm to be born in the formless or form realms;
and passing away from the form realm to be born in the form realm.
This refers to the arising of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and the arising of the birth existence (*upapattibhava*).
This applies to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
In this context, when one passes from the death existence to the intermediate existence, it does not occur for those who die within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This means that because the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) of the form realm ceases within the form realm,
it does not arise in the desire realm;
and because the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the form realm arises within the form realm.

"Not receiving existence in the desire realm" means that one receives existence in the form realm— that is, one receives the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm— if,
from that intermediate state, one proceeds toward birth in a [new] existence at a time when one has not died in the desire realm.
This means that the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) ceases within the form realm;
it does not arise in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This means that the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) of the form realm arises within the form realm.
"Not experiencing the existence of desire" means experiencing the existence of form—
that is, experiencing the aggregates of the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) within the realm of form.
This refers to one who passes away from the realm of form and is born into the formless realm.
This refers to "arising from birth" (upapattibhava), because there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This applies to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
Among these, it does not pertain to those who die in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This means that because the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) of the form realm ceases within the form realm,
it does not arise in the desire realm;
and because the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) of the formless realm arises within the formless realm.

"Not experiencing the existence of desire" means experiencing the existence of formlessness— that is, experiencing the aggregates of the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) in the formless realm. It refers to one who,
passing away from the formless realm, is born into the formless realm.
This refers to the existence of birth (jāti-bhava).
It applies to both ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) and all noble ones (ārya).
Among these, it does not pertain to those who die in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
This means that the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) of the formless realm ceases within the formless realm;
it does not belong to those being born in the desire realm.
This means that the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) of the formless realm arises within the formless realm.

"Not experiencing the existence of desire" refers to experiencing the existence of the formless realm— that is, experiencing the aggregates of the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) in the formless realm.
This applies to one who passes away from the formless realm and is born into the form realm.
This refers to birth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which belongs exclusively to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Among these, it does not refer to one who dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
that is to say, because the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) ceases within the formless realm itself.

"Not being born in the desire realm" means that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm arises within the form realm. "Not experiencing existence in the desire realm" means experiencing existence in the form realm— that is,
experiencing the aggregates (*skandha*) of the intermediate state of the form realm.
Do all those who die and are reborn in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) necessarily undergo existence with form (rūpabhava)?
One should answer that this involves four permutations (catuṣkoṭika),
because there is a mutual difference in scope between dying and being reborn in the realm of form and undergoing existence with form.
There are those who die in the form realm and are reborn without receiving a form existence;
that is, those who pass away from the form realm and arise as intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*) in the desire realm—these are exclusively ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
There are also those in the desire realm who arise as intermediate state beings in the form realm.
Among these, one who dies in the form realm refers to one for whom the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) of the form realm ceases within the form realm.
One who is born in the form realm refers to...
This means that the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm arises within the form realm.

"Not receiving the form existence" means that one who receives the existence of desire— that is, receives the aggregates (*skandha*) of the intermediate existence of the desire realm— does not receive the form existence.
There are those who possess form but do not die or take birth within the realm of form;
that is, those who pass away from the desire realm and arise as an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) of the realm of form.
This includes both ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and all noble ones (*ārya*).
The intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the form realm arises within the desire realm.
In this context, "experiencing the existence of form" refers to experiencing the aggregates (*skandha*) of the intermediate existence of the form realm.
It is not one who dies in the form realm;
that is to say, because the death-existence (cyuti-bhava) in the desire realm ceases within the desire realm itself.
It is not one who is born in the form realm.
This means that because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm arises within the desire realm,
there is also the case where one dies and is born in the form realm, thereby undergoing the existence of form (*rūpabhava*).
That is to say, having passed away from the form realm, one gives rise to the intermediate state and the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) of the form realm.
This [attainment] is common to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
When an ordinary being is born in a higher realm, they may also be reborn in a lower realm, and in each location they can undergo multiple births.
When a noble one is born in a higher realm, they are not reborn in a lower realm, and in each location they undergo only a single birth.
In this context, when one passes from the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), if one dies in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*),
it means that the death-existence in the realm of form ceases within the realm of form;
and if one is born in the realm of form, it means that the intermediate existence in the realm of form arises within the realm of form.
"Experiencing the existence of form" refers to experiencing the aggregates (*skandha*) of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
If one passes from the intermediate state into birth, and dies while in the form realm,
this means that the intermediate state of the form realm ceases within the form realm itself.
"Those born in the realm of form" refers to those whose existence in the realm of form arises within the realm of form.
"Experiencing existence in the realm of form" [refers to this].
This refers to receiving the aggregates of the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) in the form realm.
There are cases where one does not die or take birth in the form realm, nor receive a form-realm existence;
namely, those who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the desire realm or the formless realm.
Regarding those who die in the formless realm and are born in the formless realm or the desire realm,
and those who die in the desire realm and are born in the desire realm:
this refers to birth in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and birth in the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*).
This [intermediate state] is common to both ordinary beings and noble ones.
Among these, when one passes from the death-existence to the intermediate existence,
it does not occur for those who die in the form realm.
This means that those who die in the desire realm may have their cessation in the desire realm,
but not those who are born in the form realm.
This means that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of those in the desire realm arises within the desire realm.

"Those who do not undergo rebirth in the form realm" refers to those who undergo rebirth in the desire realm— that is, they undergo the aggregates (*skandha*) of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm— if,
from that intermediate state, they proceed to birth in a [new] existence and do not die while in the form realm.
This means that the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm ceases within the desire realm;
it does not arise in the form realm.
This means that the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) of the desire realm arises within the desire realm.

"Those who do not undergo existence in the realm of form" refers to those who undergo existence in the realm of desire— that is, they undergo the aggregates of the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) within the desire realm— and those who,
passing away from the desire realm, are born into the formless realm.
This refers to the existence of birth-and-birth (*jāti-jāti-bhava*).
It applies to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and all noble ones (*ārya*).
Among these, it does not pertain to those who die in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
This means that the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) of the desire realm ceases within the desire realm;
it does not arise in the form realm.
Furthermore, the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) of the formless realm arises within the formless realm.
"Experiencing existence in the formless realm" means experiencing existence as the aggregates of birth in the formless realm; that is,
for one who dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the formless realm.
This refers to the existence of birth (jāti-bhava).
It applies to both ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) and all noble ones (ārya).
Among these, it does not pertain to those who die in the form realm (rūpadhātu).
This means that the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) of the formless realm ceases within the formless realm;
it does not belong to one born in the form realm. This means that the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) of the formless realm arises within the formless realm.
"Not experiencing the existence of form" refers to experiencing the existence of the formless, that is, experiencing the aggregates of the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) in the formless realm.
This applies to one who passes away from the formless realm and is born into the desire realm.
This means that birth exists only for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Among these, it does not pertain to those who die in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
because the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) of the formless realm ceases within the formless realm itself.
"Not being born in the form realm" means that the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm arises within the desire realm.
"Not receiving a form existence" means receiving a desire existence— that is, receiving the aggregates (*skandha*) of the intermediate existence of the desire realm.
Do all those who die and are reborn in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) undergo existence in the formless realm?
Answer: All those who die and are reborn in the formless realm undergo existence in the formless realm.
This means that because there are no material forms (*rūpa*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
there is no possibility for an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) from a lower realm to arise there;
therefore, it cannot be said that one dies or is born there without undergoing that specific mode of existence (*bhava*).
This [attainment] is common to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).

While ordinary beings may be born in higher realms and also take birth in lower realms—being capable of undergoing multiple births in each location—noble ones, once born in a higher realm, are not born in lower realms; they undergo only a single birth in each location.
There is the acquisition of existence in the formless realm that does not involve dying in the formless realm and being reborn in the formless realm;
this refers to passing away from the desire or form realms and being born in the formless realm, wherein there is only the acquisition of the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*).
This applies to both ordinary beings and noble ones.
In this context, "experiencing existence in the formless realm" refers to experiencing the aggregates of the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) within the formless realm;
it does not refer to those who are dying in the formless realm.
This means that because the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) of the desire and form realms ceases within the desire and form realms,
one is born in the formless realm;
that is to say, the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) of the formless realm arises within the formless realm.
How many are there who die and are reborn within the desire realm?
Answer: Four;
namely, ordinary beings and noble ones of both the desire and form realms.
Among these, for ordinary beings and noble ones in the desire realm, both the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and the birth existence (*upapattibhava*) are present;
for ordinary beings and noble ones in the form realm, there is only the intermediate existence,
because the birth existence does not arise in the desire realm.
For one who dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the formless realm,
the birth-existence (upapattibhava) in the formless realm does not exist at the location where death occurred in the desire realm. Therefore,
there are only these four [types of existence].
One must not say there are six [realms],
because birth in the formless realm does not depend on a location of form;
therefore, it cannot be said that [the formless] arises within the desire realm.
How many are there who die and are reborn within the form realm?
Answer: Three;
namely, ordinary beings of the desire realm, ordinary beings of the form realm, and noble ones.
Among these, for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is only the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
For ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), both the intermediate existence and the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) are present.
This applies to those who, passing away from the form realm, are born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because the existence at birth in the formless realm does not depend on form, it cannot be said that it arises within the form realm; therefore,
there are only these three [realms],
and one cannot speak of five.
How many are there who die and are reborn within the formless realm?
Answer: Two.
That is to say, ordinary beings and noble ones of the formless realm; for their intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) necessarily arises based upon the sphere of form.

For those who die in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and are reborn in the desire or form realms (*kāmadhātu* or *rūpadhātu*), the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) does not arise within the formless realm;
therefore, these two [realms] alone cannot be said to possess all four [types of existence].
Are all those who do not die or take birth in the desire realm necessarily not subject to a desire-existence (*kāmabhava*)?
It is promised that there shall be four lines, and so forth, explained in detail;
that is to say, the first line of the previous four lines of the desire realm becomes this second line,
and the second line becomes this first line.
The third phrase becomes this fourth phrase;
the fourth phrase becomes this third phrase.
Herein, all meanings should be understood as previously explained.
Are all those who do not die or take birth in the form realm necessarily not experiencing existence in the form realm?
One should respond by establishing four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), and so forth in detail;
that is, the first permutation of the previous four permutations concerning the form realm is made here the second permutation.
The second line becomes the first line here;
the third line becomes the fourth line here;
and the fourth line becomes the third line here.
The meanings herein should be understood as previously explained.
Are all those who do not die or take birth in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) necessarily not experiencing existence in the formless realm?
Answer: All those who do not die or take birth in the formless realm are necessarily not experiencing existence in the formless realm.
This means that one who undergoes existence in the formless realm (*ārūpya-bhava*) necessarily takes birth in the formless realm;
however, there are those who undergo existence who do not take birth in the formless realm, yet do not die elsewhere and fail to be born in the formless realm.
This refers to one who dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire or form realms;
such a person is exclusively an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*).
The aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) belonging to one who dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire or form realms [are what is meant].
In this context, "not experiencing existence in the formless realm" means that one experiences existence in the desire and form realms;
it does not mean that one does not die in the formless realm.
This refers to dying in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
yet not being born in the formless realm; that is,
it refers to being born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or the form realm (rūpadhātu).
How many are those who do not die or take birth in the desire realm?
Answer: Five;
namely, ordinary beings of the desire realm, ordinary beings of the form realm, ordinary beings of the formless realm, and noble ones.
Question: There ought to be eight [cases]; why are only five mentioned?
Namely: (1) an ordinary person or an noble one who dies in the form realm and is reborn in the form realm;
(2) an ordinary person or a noble one who dies in the form realm and is reborn in the formless realm.
An ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) passing away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and being reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
an ordinary being or a noble one (*ārya*) passing away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and being reborn in the formless realm;
and an ordinary being passing away from the formless realm and being reborn in the form realm.
If there are eight such types, why speak of only five?
Answer: Because they belong to the same category, only five are mentioned.
That is to say, an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who dies in the form realm and is reborn in the form realm.
And those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who die in the formless realm and are born in the form realm:
although these two cases are distinct, they are explained together as one because the category of ordinary beings born in the form realm is the same.
[Likewise for] those ordinary beings who die in the form realm and are born in the formless realm.
And those who die in the formless realm and are reborn in the formless realm as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Although these two are distinct, because they are of the same category of formless-realm ordinary beings, they are combined and spoken of as one.
Noble ones who pass away from the form realm and are reborn in the formless realm,
as well as noble ones who pass away from the formless realm and are reborn in the formless realm—
although these two are distinct, they are spoken of as one because the category of noble ones in the formless realm is the same.

Since the remaining ordinary beings of the desire realm and the noble ones of the form realm each constitute one category, these added to the previous total make five. How many are there who do not die or take birth within the form realm?
Answer: Six.
That is to say, the ordinary beings and noble ones of the three realms.
Question: Since there should be nine, why are six mentioned?
That is to say: ordinary persons and noble ones who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the desire realm;
ordinary persons and noble ones who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the form realm;
and ordinary persons and noble ones who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the formless realm.
Ordinary beings and noble ones who pass away from the formless realm and are reborn in the formless realm;
and ordinary beings who pass away from the formless realm and are reborn in the desire realm—
there being thus nine [types], why are only six mentioned?
Answer: Because they are of the same category, only six are mentioned.
These are: ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who die in the desire realm and are reborn in the desire realm, and ordinary beings who die in the formless realm and are reborn in the desire realm.
Although these two are distinct, they are combined and explained as one because they share the same category of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the desire realm.
This refers to those ordinary beings who die in the desire realm and are reborn in the formless realm,
as well as those ordinary beings who die in the formless realm and are reborn in the formless realm.
Although these two are distinct, they are combined and spoken of as one because the category of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the formless realm is the same.
This includes noble ones (*ārya*) who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the formless realm,
as well as noble ones who pass away from the formless realm and are reborn in the formless realm.
Although these two are distinct, they are combined and spoken of as one because the types of noble ones (*ārya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are identical.

The remaining noble ones of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones of the form realm each constitute one category; thus, added to the previous, there are six.
How many are those who die and are born in states other than the formless realm?
Answer: Four;
namely, ordinary beings and noble ones of the desire and form realms.
Question: There should be seven such cases; why then are only four mentioned?
Namely: ordinary beings and noble ones who die in the desire realm and are reborn in the desire realm;
and ordinary beings and noble ones who die in the desire realm and are reborn in the form realm.
There are those who die in the form realm and are reborn in the form realm—both ordinary beings and noble ones—and those who die in the form realm and are reborn in the desire realm—ordinary beings.
Thus, there are seven such cases; why then do you say there are only four?
Answer: Because they are of the same category, only four are mentioned. These are:
(1) an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) who dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the desire realm; and (2) an ordinary being who dies in the form realm and is reborn in the desire realm.
Although these two are distinct, they are combined and spoken of as one because they share the same category of being an ordinary being in the desire realm.
Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who die in the desire realm and are reborn in the form realm,
as well as ordinary beings who die in the form realm and are reborn in the form realm—
although these two are distinct, they are spoken of collectively as one because they belong to the same category of ordinary beings in the form realm.
The noble ones who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the form realm,
and those noble ones who pass away from the form realm and are reborn in the form realm—
although these two are distinct, because the category of noble ones in the form realm is the same, they are combined and spoken of as one.
Adding the noble ones (*ārya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to the previous [categories], there are four.
Is it possible for one to die in the desire realm and not be reborn in the desire realm? ... [and so on, as explained at length].
The difference between what is stated here and what preceded is as follows:
This means that it is called "non-arising" because it precludes birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*);
even if the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) were to arise, it would still be called non-arising.
Is there any case where one dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) but is not reborn in the desire realm?
Answer: There is.

That is to say, one who arises in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire or form realms may be born in the formless realm or attain parinirvāṇa. Regarding "one who arises in the intermediate state of the desire or form realms": [this refers to those who have already passed away from a previous birth].
This refers to one who dies in the desire realm and arises as an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the desire or form realms;
although they arise while still within the desire realm, because this is not a birth-existence (*upapattibhava*), it is said that they are not born in the desire realm.
As for those born in the formless realm:
This refers to one who passes away from the desire realm and is born into the existence of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-bhavopapatti*).
Since such a person does not remain in the desire realm, it is said that they are not reborn in the desire realm;
this is what is meant by "attaining parinirvāṇa."
This means that those who exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*) upon passing away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) attain parinirvāṇa;
because they will never again be born, it is said that they are not born in the desire realm.
The remaining text provides a detailed explanation which should be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Question: For one who dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire or form realms, which of those two intermediate states (*antarābhava*) manifests?
Regarding this, some say:
Regarding the fourth dhyāna,
the critique states that one should not make such a claim. Why is this?
If the formless realm possessed spatial location, one could speak in this way;
however, the formless realm has no spatial location.
For what reason, then, does it reach as far as the fourth dhyāna?
Other masters say:
"If one dies from that realm and is reborn in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), the intermediate state (antarābhava) manifests right there in that location.
This, too, should not be asserted in such a manner.
Why is this? If one were to say that one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the formless realm, how could that be possible?
One should rather say:
if one passes away from the desire or form realms and is reborn in the formless realm.
As for those who die in the formless realm and are reborn in the formless realm,
when they die in that formless realm and are reborn in the desire or form realms,
their two intermediate states (antarābhava) manifest immediately at the place where they are to be born.
How many are those who die in the desire realm but are not reborn in the desire realm?
Answer: Six.
That is to say, the ordinary beings and noble ones of the three realms, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: Why is it that one who has attained parinirvāṇa is not mentioned?
Answer: When something that ought to be stated is not stated, one should know that this meaning is incomplete (sāvaśeṣa).
Furthermore, what is being discussed here is death and the subsequent taking of birth.
One who has entered parinirvāṇa does not speak because, having died, they are no longer reborn.
Furthermore, within this section of the *Naihsargika*, questions and answers are raised based on sentient beings and *pudgalas*.

One who has attained parinirvāṇa abandons the category of sentient beings and falls into the category of dharmas; since it is impossible to designate such a person as a *pudgala*, this is not mentioned here.
The subsequent cases should be understood by analogy.
Is there anyone who dies in the desire realm and is not reborn within the three realms?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, those who arise as an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the desire or form realms, or those who attain parinirvāṇa, and so forth, as explained at length.
In this context, since the treatise also negates birth,
those who arise in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and those who attain parinirvāṇa are all termed "non-arising.
How many are there among those who die in the desire realm and are not reborn within the three realms?
Answer: There are four types, namely: ordinary beings and noble ones of the desire realm;
and those who, passing away from the desire realm, arise as intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*) within the desire or form realms.
How many are those who die in the various realms of form (rūpadhātu) and are not reborn in the three realms?
Answer: Three;
namely, ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) of the desire realm, ordinary beings of the form realm, and noble ones (ārya).
Regarding those who die in the form realm and are born within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire or form realms:
how many are there who die in the formless realm and are not reborn in the three realms?
Answer: There are two types, namely, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire and form realms.
That is, one who dies in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is born into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire or form realms (*kāmadhātu* or *rūpadhātu*).
Since noble ones (*ārya*) are not reborn in lower stages, this refers exclusively to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Is there anyone who, at the end of life, does not take birth in the desire realm while still being unseparated from the defilement of desire? ... [and so on, as extensively explained].
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of other schools and elucidating the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who claim that one may attain rebirth in the higher realms merely by subduing the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Just as the Dārṣṭāntikas, in order to refute that view,
demonstrate that one who has suppressed the afflictions cannot be reborn in a higher realm; rather,
it must be the case that all afflictions of the lower stage are completely severed before one can attain rebirth in a higher realm— therefore, this treatise was composed.
The Vibhajyavādins, who deny the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), become utterly confused by these questions;
they claim that one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of a particular stage does not, upon death, take birth in that stage or in a lower stage.
If one has faith, no confusion will arise regarding these questions, as they serve to prevent the arising of existence.
One may ask: how is it known that one who has not abandoned the defilements of a lower realm cannot be reborn in a higher realm?
Answer: Because the afflictions of the lower stages obstruct the various merits of the higher stages;
since the fundamental merits of the higher stages have not yet been attained, those [merits] do not arise there.
If one were to maintain that merely suppressing the afflictions of the lower stages constitutes attaining rebirth in the higher stages, [it would be incorrect].
Those who suppress the afflictions through the power of the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection within the desire realm should not be born in the nine stages of the three realms,
because the power of the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection is capable of suppressing the afflictions of the nine stages of the three realms so that they do not arise.
It is not by the power of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) that the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are suppressed so as not to manifest;

rather, it is because the wisdoms of hearing (*śrutamayī*) and reflection (*cintāmayī*)—which analyze all phenomena—are superior to cultivated wisdom, and thus suppress the afflictions more effectively.
How many are those who, at the time of death, do not take birth in the desire realm while still being subject to the defilements of desire?
Answer: Two.
That is to say, ordinary beings and noble ones of the desire realm who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire, because they do not ascend to higher realms.
Among those ordinary beings and noble ones dwelling in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm,
how many, having not yet abandoned attachment to the form realm, will not be reborn in either the desire or form realms at the end of their lives?
Answer: Four.
That is to say, ordinary beings and noble ones of the desire and form realms.
Question: Since there ought to be seven, why are four mentioned?
That is to say: ordinary beings and noble ones who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the desire realm;
ordinary beings and noble ones who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the form realm;
and ordinary beings and noble ones who pass away from the form realm and are reborn in the form realm.
When an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) dies in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are thus seven [types]; why then do you say there are only four?
Answer: Because they belong to the same category, only four are mentioned.
This refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who die in the desire realm and are reborn in the desire realm,
as well as those who die in the form realm and are reborn in the desire realm.
Although these two are distinct, they are spoken of collectively as one because they share the same category of being an ordinary being in the desire realm.
An ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) who dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the form realm,
and an ordinary being who dies in the form realm and is reborn in the form realm—
although these two are distinct, they are spoken of as one because they are of the same category of ordinary beings in the form realm.
The noble ones who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the form realm, and those noble ones who pass away from the form realm and are reborn in the form realm—
although these two are distinct, because they belong to the same category of noble ones in the form realm, they are explained together as one.
Including the noble ones of the desire realm who remain, there are four in total.
How many are those who, having not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm, do not take birth in the three realms at the end of their lives?
Answer: Four.
This refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Question: Since there should be nine [types], why are only four mentioned? Answer:
They are the ordinary beings and noble ones who, passing away from the desire realm, are reborn in the desire realm.
An ordinary person or a noble one who passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the form realm;
an ordinary person or a noble one who passes away from the form realm and is reborn in the form realm;
and an ordinary person who passes away from the form realm and is reborn in the desire realm.

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who pass away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and are reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and ordinary beings who pass away from the formless realm and are reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):
since there are thus nine such cases, why is it said that there are only four?
Answer: Because their categories are identical, only four are mentioned.
This refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who die in the desire realm and are reborn in the desire realm,
as well as ordinary beings who die in the form or formless realms and are reborn in the desire realm.
Although these three are distinct, they are spoken of collectively as one because they share the same category of being an ordinary being in the desire realm.
Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who pass away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and are reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
as well as ordinary beings who pass away from the form or formless realms and are reborn in the form realm—
although these three groups are distinct, they are of the same category of ordinary beings in the form realm.
Taken together as one:
noble ones who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the form realm,
and noble ones who pass away from the form realm and are reborn in the form realm.
Although these two are distinct, they are combined and explained as one because the types of noble ones (*ārya*) in the form realm are the same.
When the other noble ones of the desire realm are added, there are four in total.
The preceding mention of "birth" (*upapatti*) all refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), as the treatise is composed by way of excluding the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*).

Section Seven of the Third Sub-section on the Appropriation of Sentient Beings within the Second Chapter on the Aggregates of Fetters: Among these, for ordinary beings and noble ones in the desire realm, how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase, and by how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) are they bound?
Answer: For ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase and they are bound by nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
For noble ones (*ārya*), ten underlying tendencies increase and they are bound by six fetters.
Regarding "among these," it refers to the fact that among all sentient beings previously mentioned, there are in total only six types.
This means that within each of the three realms there are both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
Ordinary beings in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) possess the increase of ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and are bound by the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Noble ones in the desire realm possess only the increase of ten underlying tendencies, which are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Because those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing have all already been abandoned;

and because among the six fetters and bonds, these three—view-grasping (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and [the corresponding view]—have also already been abandoned by the noble ones (*ārya*).
Regarding ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase, and how many fetters and bonds do they possess?
Answer: In ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), sixty-two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase along with the bondage of the six fetters (*saṃyojana*).
In noble ones (*ārya*), six underlying tendencies increase along with the bondage of the three fetters.
Regarding the statement that in ordinary persons sixty-two underlying tendencies increase:
This refers to thirty-one [fetters] each in the form and formless realms;
as for the thirty-six in the desire realm, they have already been abandoned.
Regarding the six fetters of bondage (*saṃyojana*), anger, envy, and avarice are excluded because they do not exist in the higher realms.
Regarding the six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase in the Noble One (*ārya*):
these refer to the three [dispositions] each belonging to the categories abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the realms of form and formlessness,
because he has already abandoned the four [dispositions] abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
The three fetters that bind are craving,
conceit, and ignorance,
because the others have already been abandoned.
Regarding how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase and how many fetters (saṃyojana) bind ordinary beings and noble ones in the formless realm:
the answer is that for ordinary beings, thirty-one underlying tendencies increase and they are bound by six fetters.
The three latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the noble ones increase in conjunction with the three fetters (saṃyojana).
Regarding the thirty-one latent dispositions that increase in ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana),
this refers to the thirty-one types belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Because the others have already been abandoned.
Regarding the six fetters and bonds:
anger, envy, and avarice are excluded, as they do not exist in that realm.
Regarding the three latent dispositions that increase in the Noble One:
these refer to the three [latent dispositions] of the formless realm abandoned through cultivation,
because the others have already been abandoned.
The three fetters that bind are craving,
conceit, and ignorance,
because the others have already been abandoned.
Question: Sentient beings of the desire realm are not subject to the increase of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the two higher realms.
For what reason, then, is it said that ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) of the desire realm are subject to the increase of all ninety-eight latent dispositions?
In the noble ones of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase.
For sentient beings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), no latent dispositions of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) increase.
Why, then, is it said that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the form realm have sixty-two latent dispositions that increase?
The six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase in the noble ones (*ārya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
This answer is given because it is stated in reference to their non-liberation from those [dispositions].

That is to say, although an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is not subject to the increase of latent dispositions belonging to the form or formless realms, [the same principle applies here].
However, because they have not yet attained liberation from those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), it is said that [the defilements] increase in accordance with them.

Although for a noble one (*ārya*) of the desire realm, the latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) belonging to the form and formless realms do not increase in accordance with them.
However, because they have not yet attained liberation from those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), it is said that [the latent dispositions] increase in accordance with them.

For this reason, it is not contrary to logic to say that for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the latent dispositions of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) also increase in accordance with them.
Furthermore, this is stated with reference to their manifestation based upon them.
That is to say, although the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms do not increase within an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm,
they are nonetheless said to "increase" because those [dispositions] can manifest in the present for that person.
Although the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the form and formless realms do not increase (*anuśerate*) in noble ones (*ārya*) of the desire realm,
they are nevertheless said to increase because those [dispositions] can manifest in the present for them.
Therefore, it is not contrary to reason to say that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm increase in ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*) of the form realm.
Furthermore, since this is explained in terms of what has been attained, what has not yet been attained, and what is currently being attained, it is likewise not contrary to reason.
That which has already been attained is said to be past attainment;
that which has not yet been attained is said to be future attainment;
and that which is being attained is said to be present attainment.
This means that although the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the higher realms do not increase in ordinary beings and noble ones within the desire and form realms,
they are said to "increase" because the acquisitions (prāpti) of those latent dispositions of the three times continue to flow on and have not yet been severed.
Furthermore, this statement is made based on the possibility of their manifestation.
That is to say, although the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms do not increase within ordinary beings and noble ones of the desire realm,
they are said to "increase" there as well because it is possible for those latent dispositions to manifest.
This is because, having already abandoned the defilements of desire, those [defilements] can no longer manifest.
By this principle, it should be understood that for ordinary beings and noble ones in the form realm, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm likewise increase accordingly.
Although it is possible for the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the lower realms to manifest even after one has regressed from that [higher state],
because they have already been abandoned and there is the capacity to never regress again, it is not said that the latent dispositions of the lower realms increase.
Furthermore, it is not contrary to reason to state that these [defilements] manifest as their own outflows (*niṣyanda*), because they have arisen from time immemorial;
that is to say, sentient beings of the desire realm have existed since an unknowable beginning.
Because there is no being who has not previously given rise to the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms, it is said that they increase.
Sentient beings of the form realm have done so since the beginningless limit of existence.
Because there is no one who has not previously given rise to the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm, it is said that they increase in accordance with them.
Question: Since sentient beings of the form and formless realms have existed from an unknowable beginningless limit...
There is no one who has not previously given rise to the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire and form realms.
Why, then, is it not said that these also increase (*anuśerate*) as latent tendencies of the lower realm?
Answer: Although they have indeed arisen previously, because they have been abandoned, they are not said to increase.

Question: There are also noble ones who possess all ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), namely those who are bound by all fetters at the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Why, then, is it said here that for a noble one of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), only ten types of underlying tendencies increase?
Answer: Although this is indeed the case, because it occurs for such a brief duration, it is said that there are only ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that increase.
That is to say, at the first moment, all ninety-eight [underlying tendencies] are present;
yet immediately after this moment, these ten have already been abandoned, and in an instant one reaches the sixteenth moment of mind.
Because time is so brief,
it is stated that only the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase [in this context].
Furthermore, there are seventy-three who enter the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
During the first moment of the preceding nine types of sentient beings,
although they possess all ninety-eight types [of afflictions], these do not manifest;
for even a wholesome contaminated mind has not yet arisen at the stage of the Path of Seeing, let alone a defiled or non-obscured neutral mind.
In this context, the distinctions among the states of sentient beings are established solely based on the manifest afflictions;
therefore, it is said that for the most part, at most ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in association with the noble ones (ārya).
Since only these ten types are capable of manifesting,
other sources also establish the distinctions among the states of sentient beings based on the active afflictions (*saṃudācāra-kleśa*).
As it is said in a sūtra:
A certain brahmin came to where the Buddha was and asked,
"World-Honored One, are you a deva?
The Buddha replied, "No."
He asked again: "Are they nāgas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, or non-humans?"
The Buddha said, "No.
Why is this? O Brahmin, you should know."
If there are various outflows (*āsrava*) that have not been abandoned and have not been fully understood because they are currently active,
one will be born in the heavenly realms and may become a deva;
as explained at length, up to being born in the human realms and may become a human.
I have already abandoned and fully understood all outflows (*āsrava*).
Like cutting the root of a tree or severing the head of a *tāla* palm,
by this means these outflows shall never again manifest.
Because all future existences have attained the state of non-arising,
I am certain that I shall no longer be reborn as a deva,
and so on, up to: I shall no longer be reborn as a human.
In some instances, the distinctions among the states of sentient beings are also established based on the manifest activity of maturation (*vipāka*).
As stated in a verse within a sutra:
The Buddha is a true person; Self-disciplined and ever-steadfast, He constantly traverses the Brahma-path.
One whose mind delights in tranquility and who undergoes the continuity of maturation (*vipāka*) in this realm is called a sentient being born in this realm.
That is to say, one who undergoes the continuity of maturation in the desire realm is called a sentient being born in the desire realm.
