"As it is with the realm of form, so it is with the realms of sound, odor, taste, and tangibility."
Because fragrance, taste, and touch are objects that can be apprehended in common.
Question: What is the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)?
Answer: Eye-consciousness produced with the eye and visible forms as conditions is called the eye-consciousness element.
Question: When visual consciousness arises, all phenomena other than its own nature act as conditions (*pratyaya*).
Why, then, are only the eye and visible forms said to be its conditions?
Answer: This is stated here because we are referring specifically to the most predominant conditions.
That is to say, regarding those phenomena which are the basis and the object of visual consciousness:
herein, "eye" refers to the basis of visual consciousness, and "form" refers to the object of visual consciousness.
Therefore, it is explained selectively;
other dharmas are not so.
Furthermore, if a dharma serves as the immediate dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for visual consciousness, it is "the eye" that is spoken of herein.
Furthermore, visible form acts as the immediate dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for visual consciousness;
it excels [other conditions] in bringing about the arising, abiding, change, and cessation of visual consciousness.
For this reason, it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is the unique and predominant condition for visual consciousness, it is here termed "the eye.
Both form and the eye act as the unique and predominant conditions for visual consciousness,
bringing about its arising, abiding, alteration, and cessation.
Therefore, it is explained in this partial manner.
Question: Since visual consciousness also arises with visible form as its condition, why is it called "visual consciousness" and not "form-consciousness"?
Answer: There are also sūtras that speak of this as "form-consciousness" (rūpa-vijñāna).
As it is said:
"Conditioned by the form realm, form-consciousness arises."
Up to the point where consciousness arises with the dharma-realm as its object.
Question: Only one sutra speaks in this manner;
all other sutras speak only of eye-consciousness.
Why is it not called "consciousness of form" (*rūpa-vijñāna*)?
Answer: Because the eye is internal, it is called only "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣur-vijñāna*);
because form is external, it is not called "form-consciousness."
Furthermore, because the eye is the basis (*āśraya*), it is called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*);
because form is the object (*ālambana*), it is not called "form-consciousness.
Furthermore, because the eye is a faculty (*indriya*), it is called only "eye-consciousness."
Because form is the object of the sense faculty, it is not called "form-consciousness.
Furthermore, because the eye possesses an objective domain, it is called only "eye-consciousness";
because form is the objective domain, it is not called "form-consciousness."
Furthermore, because the eye is unique [to each individual], it is called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*);
because visible form is common [to all], it is not called "form-consciousness.
Moreover, those who establish designations do so by indicating the distinctions of the names established based upon their respective supports.
Because the eye is the sense faculty upon which consciousness relies, it is called simply "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*);
likewise, up to the mind, because it is the sense faculty upon which mental consciousness relies, it is called simply "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*).
This is just as sound is named solely in reference to its basis.
This is because it reveals that the names established for them are distinct;
for example, when sound arises based on a drum,
it is called "the sound of a drum," and when it arises based on a conch, it is called "the sound of a conch."
One should know that the same applies to the vīṇā and other instruments.
Question: Since all six consciousnesses, beginning with the visual consciousness, arise based on the mind (manas), for what reason are the first five not called "mental consciousness" (manovijñāna)?
Answer: If a phenomenon is the basis for consciousness—being unmixed, unique, and undisturbed—that consciousness is called "dependent.
Because that eye is the unmixed, unique, and undisturbed basis for visual consciousness, it is therefore called "visual consciousness."
To speak at length, up to this point: because the body is the unmixed, unique, and non-confused basis for body-consciousness, it is called "body-consciousness.
The mind, however, is the mixed, common, and confused basis for the five consciousnesses.
Therefore, the first five [consciousnesses] are not called "mental consciousness" (manovijñāna). Question:
If that is so, then mental consciousness itself should also not be designated as "mental consciousness," should it?
Answer: The mental consciousness has no basis that is unmixed, unique, and non-confused in the manner of the preceding five consciousnesses;
therefore, it is designated simply as "mental consciousness.
For this reason, one should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena that are the support (*āśraya*) of visual consciousness but not its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*);
namely, the co-nascent eye.
There are phenomena that are the immediately preceding condition of visual consciousness but not its support.
It refers to those mental factors that have ceased immediately prior.
There is a phenomenon which is both the support (*āśraya*) of visual consciousness and its equivalent-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*; *samanantara-pratyaya*);
namely, the mental element (*manodhātu*) that has ceased immediately prior.
There are phenomena that are neither the support (*āśraya*) of visual consciousness nor its equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This refers to all cases except those previously mentioned.
The same fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*) applies up to tactile consciousness.
If a dharma is both the support (*āśraya*) of the mental consciousness and its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
there are dharmas that are the immediately preceding condition of the mental consciousness but not its support;
namely, all mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*) that have ceased in immediate succession.
The Venerable Vasumitra also stated this:
"Visual consciousness also arises with visible form as its condition.
For what reason is visual consciousness not called 'consciousness of form'?"
Answer: The eye is the support (*āśraya*) for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), whereas visible form (*rūpa*) is not.
Furthermore, the eye is the predominant condition (*pratyaya*) for visual consciousness.
Visible form is not like that.
Furthermore, the eye belongs exclusively to one's own continuum,
whereas visible form is not so restricted.
Furthermore, the eye exists only at a near distance,
because visible forms are not fixed [in location].
Furthermore, the eye exists only internally.
Because form is not fixed;
furthermore, because the eye is unique [to each individual],
whereas form is not so.
Furthermore, the eye is exclusively appropriated because its objects,
the forms, are not fixed.
Furthermore, the eye is subject to impairment and benefit.
Consciousness follows increase or decrease; form is not like this.
Question: If form undergoes increase or decrease, consciousness likewise follows that increase or decrease.
If visual consciousness were not to arise when there is no form, it should likewise be called "consciousness of name.
For what reason is it only called "visual consciousness"?
Answer: This case is not analogous.
Why is this so? Because for one who possesses the eye-faculty,
even if a single visible form has ceased, visual consciousness can still arise by taking another visible form as its object.
If the eye faculty is absent,
although many forms may constantly appear before one, visual consciousness does not arise; therefore,
the benefit or harm of visual consciousness follows the faculty and does not follow the object.
Furthermore, the eye possesses inferior, middling, and superior consciousnesses that correspond to those [levels];
visual forms are not so.
Furthermore, the eye is unique (asādhāraṇa).
Because form is not fixed,
there are cases where visual consciousness belonging to two realms arises with respect to a single realm of form as its object;
this is because there is no case where an eye belonging to one realm gives rise to visual consciousness belonging to two realms.
There is the arising of eye-consciousness belonging to five destinies from a single-destiny form that possesses conditions;
there is the arising of eye-consciousness belonging to two destinies from a single-destiny eye that lacks its support—
how much more so when many such factors are present?
When there are conditions, one birth produces matter and four births produce eye-consciousness;
when there is no support, one birth produces the eye and two births produce eye-consciousness—
how much more so when there are many?
Furthermore, the eye is the predominant and superior condition for visual consciousness,
whereas visible form is not;
thus says the Venerable One.
If there is an obstruction to the eye, there is also an obstruction to consciousness;
if there is no obstruction to the eye, there is also no obstruction to consciousness.
Therefore, it is called "eye-consciousness" and not "form-consciousness."
Question: If there is an obstruction regarding form, there is also an obstruction regarding visual consciousness, because visual consciousness does not arise when there is no object-form.
Answer: Form is manifold.
The eye is singular;
it should not be used as an analogy.
That is to say, even if one eye is impaired, visual consciousness can still arise by taking the second eye as its basis.
If, due to a second cause of destruction, visual consciousness arises with respect to a third form, and if other causes of destruction give rise to other consciousnesses in the same manner;
or if, within a single body, the eye-faculty is destroyed.
Even if immeasurable nayutas of forms were to appear directly before one,
the visual consciousness would still be unable to arise with respect to them;
therefore, visual consciousness is not called "form-consciousness."
It should be understood that this applies likewise up to body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
Question: There is a sūtra which says, "Forms cognized by the eye (*cakṣurvijñeya-rūpa*). What is the meaning of this?
All forms are cognized solely by visual consciousness,
because the eye-faculty itself cannot discern forms.
The answer is that this [statement] indicates the nature of the dependent (the consciousness) by means of its basis (the faculty).
Therefore, it does not contradict reason.
That is to say, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, sometimes reveals the supported by means of the support,
or sometimes reveals the support by means of the supported.
Regarding the case where the basis reveals the dependent phenomenon, it is as that sutra says: "forms cognized by the eye.
Regarding the case where the dependent phenomenon reveals the basis, [it is as follows].
As it is said in a certain passage:
"That which is experienced by visual consciousness and discerned by visual consciousness is called 'the seen'.
Furthermore, that sutra should have stated: "forms cognized by visual consciousness."
Because the reciter was mistaken, that [text] merely says "forms cognized by the eye.
Furthermore, that sūtra should have said "forms cognized by visual consciousness";
however, because the intermediate term was omitted, it simply says "forms cognized by the eye."
As it is said, because [the sūtra] speaks of the ox-cart,
of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and so forth. Furthermore, since that sūtra speaks based on the preeminent factors,
it does not contradict reason.
Just as it is said that the performance of an artisan, a dyer, or a scribe depends upon superior implements, so too is this case.
It is like when one performs music.
Although there are musical instruments, children, and other companions,
it is the master of the performance who alone receives the credit,
for he is the preeminent factor.
Furthermore, it is like when dyeing clothes:
although there are no water, dye, or the dyer as assistants that do not exist,
the term "dyeing" is applied specifically to the cloth itself.
Because these are its superior requisites;
it is just as when writing,
there cannot be [writing] without ink, water, an inkwell for storing the ink, a person, leaves, and so forth.
Yet because the brush excels, it alone receives the credit;
this case is likewise.
Although when perceiving color there are many consciousnesses present—such as space, light, and so forth—it is [the visual consciousness] that is designated.
However, because the eye is preeminent, it alone receives that name;
thus, that sutra says "forms cognized by the eye.
Furthermore, the eye is the basis upon which the cognition of forms depends.
That sutra speaks of "forms cognizable by the eye.
This is like saying that a road is the place where merchants and their like should travel;
yet, that road is actually the place where only feet should travel.
Just as that caravan and so forth receive their name specifically because they are the basis for those feet,
this case is likewise; it is like the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).
The same applies to the elements of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousness;
for the reasons for establishing their names based on their conditions and the explanations that clarify the meaning of the sūtras are all similar.
Question: What is the element of mind (manodhātu)?
Answer: That which has already cognized, is currently cognizing, or will cognize dharmas, as well as its homogeneous part (sabhāga), is called the mind-element (manodhātu).
"That which has already cognized dharmas" refers to the past mind-element.
The "dharmas already cognized" refers to the present mental faculty (*manodhātu*).
The "dharmas to be cognized" refers to the future mental faculty and its corresponding homogeneous state (*tatsabhāga*),
which refers to the future mental faculty that will ultimately never arise.
There is no past or present mental faculty (*manodhātu*) that is of the same class (*sabhāga*),
because mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) must necessarily depend upon an object (*ālambana*) in order to arise. Consequently,
the future mental faculty that is about to arise must also necessarily be of the same class.
Question: If the mind-element (*manodhātu*) arises taking the seventeen elements as its object, is it likewise *sabhāga* (homogeneous)?
Answer: It is also *sabhāga*.
Just as the eye-element and others possess functions such as seeing, they must necessarily be *sabhāga*.
The mind-element (*manodhātu*) is also like this:
that which possesses functional activity is termed "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
Question: What is the case with the phenomenon-element (*dharmadhātu*)?
Answer: All phenomena (dharmas) that have already been, are currently being, or will be cognized by the mind—this is called the dharma-element (dharmadhātu).
"Already cognized by the mind" means that all dharma-elements have already been cognized by the past mind-element (manodhātu).
"Currently being cognized by the mind" refers to those dharma-spheres that are currently being cognized by the present mind-sphere.
"To be cognized by the mind [in the future]" refers to...
This means that the various dharma-spheres (dharmadhātu) are to be cognized by a future mental sphere (manodhātu).
Question: Does the dharma-sphere possess its "homogeneous counterpart" (sabhāga)? Answer: No.
Why is this? Because there is no phenomenon that is not cognized by the immeasurable mental consciousnesses of the past, future, and present.
There is a mental consciousness that arises within a single moment.
This is because it discerns all other phenomena, with the sole exception of its own nature, its associated factors, and its co-existent factors.
Question: The remaining seventeen elements are also objects discerned by the mental consciousness.
If all [dharmas] were necessarily of the same class (sabhāga),
then there would be no such thing as the "counterpart of the same class" (tatsabhāga). How, then, can it be said that the counterpart of the same class exists?
Answer: The remaining seventeen elements are not established as "homogeneous" (sabhāga) or "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) based on the mental consciousness;
rather, they are established based on the mutual correspondence of their respective faculties and objects—namely, the eye in relation to visible form, and visible form in relation to the eye.
...up to the point where the body encounters tangibles and tangibles encounter the body.

Question: If that is so, then the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) should only be established as having the status of "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) in relation to the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*).
In that case, those [consciousnesses] which take the remaining seventeen elements as their objects would not be of the same class (*sabhāga*).
The answer is: it should indeed be so according to logic;

however, because the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are capable of thoroughly cognizing and discerning all phenomena (*dharma*), they are so designated.
The term "homogeneous" (sabhāga) is established based on its own functional activity;
for instance, the sense organs such as the eye possess functions such as seeing,
and they are never established as "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga).
Other masters say:
"The dharma-element (dharmadhātu) subsumes all phenomena exhaustively;
since the seventeen elements are also called 'dharma,' there is no such fault."
He should not speak in this way, for although the names of the dharmas are common [to all], the dharma-spheres (dharmadhātu) are distinct.
Therefore, what was stated previously is logically sound.
Herein, one should formulate the following question and answer.
Is there any co-existent dharma that is both sabhāga (homogeneous) and tatsabhāga (non-homogeneous)?
Answer: There is.
This refers to the arising, abiding, change, and cessation (*jāti*, *sthiti*, *anyathātva*, *anityatā*) of the seventeen elements (*dhātu*) that constitute the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
Because they are subsumed within the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), they are always termed "homogeneous.
Is there any associated (*samprayukta*) or co-existent (*sahabhū*) dharma [that is not so]?
Are there instances that are "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and instances that are "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*)?
Answer: There are.
That is to say, those future mental elements (*manodhātu*) and mental consciousness elements (*manovijñānadhātu*) that do not arise are non-homogeneous.
The mental factors associated with that [mind] and the matter that evolves along with it are always termed "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*),
because they are subsumed within the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 71.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Seventy-two,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Two on the Aggregates of Bondage (Saṃyojana-skandha), Part Four of Ten Gates (Daśamukha-nirdeśa), Second: Question: What is the consciousness element (manovijñāna-dhātu)?
The answer is: that consciousness which arises with the mind (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharma*) as conditions is called the consciousness element (*vijñāna-dhātu*).
Regarding this, the analysis of questions and answers should be understood as being the same as for the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñāna-dhātu*).
Question: For what reason are the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) states not mentioned regarding the six consciousness elements?
Regarding that which was promised but not yet explained,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, the six consciousness-elements are characterized by their arising.
The mind of its own kind (sabhāga-citta) is established based on that which has arisen;
because this [unmanifested mind] does not arise, it is described only as "of its own kind" (sabhāga).
Furthermore, the six consciousness-elements (ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu) are manifested through their activity.
The mind that is "of similar type" (sabhāga) is established based on its functional activity;
since it lacks such activity, it is merely called "of the same type" (tatsabhāga).
Furthermore, all six consciousness-elements (ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu) are subsumed within the mind-element (mano-dhātu).
It has already been stated that the mind-element (manodhātu) possesses its "homogeneity" (sabhāga).
One should understand that this effectively explains the six consciousness-elements (ṣaḍvijñānadhātu);
therefore, they are not mentioned again.
Question: If that were so,
one should not establish the six consciousness-elements (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu*),
because these six are already subsumed within the mind-element (*mano-dhātu*).

Answer: Although it is established as being identical to the mind-element (*manodhātu*), because the triad of faculties, objects, and consciousnesses each consists of six, it is further explained separately as having the distinction of the six consciousnesses. Question: In various sūtras, "mind" (*citta*), "intellect" (*manas*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are mentioned.
Regarding these three types of distinctions,
how are they defined? Some say that there is no distinction between them.
Mind (*citta*) is identical to thought (*manas*), and thought is identical to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
These three terms differ in sound but not in meaning,
just as the word for fire does.
It is called Fire, and it is also called Flame-Pinnacle;
it is also called Blazing,
and it is also called Producing Illumination.
It is also called "receiving offerings," also called "that which can ripen," and also called the "black path."
It is also called Dran-zi (Dranksi),
also called Duṅ-dbaṅ (Dhūmāketa),
and also called Gser-gyi rnam-pa (Suvarṇalakṣaṇa).
In this way, a single fire has ten names;
although the sounds differ, their essence is not distinct.
It is like the Lord Śakra, who is also named Śakrara.
He is also named Puraṃdara;
he is also named Maheśvara;
he is also named Vāsava.
He is also named Kauśika;
he is also named Śakra;
he is also named Indra.
He is also called Thousand-Eyed and also called the Honored One of the Thirty-Three;
thus, this single lord has ten names.
Although there are differences in terminology, there is no distinction in their essence.
As it is said in the Abhidharma, that which is called "feeling" (vedanā) is also called "experiencing" (anubhava).
It is also called distinct feeling,
also called awakened feeling,
and also called the approach to feeling.
In this way, this single sensation has five names;
although the terms differ, their essence is not distinct.
Therefore, the Sūtra speaks of the triad of mind, mentation, and consciousness.
Although there are differences in their sounds, there is no distinction [in their meaning].
Furthermore, some say that the three—
citta, manas, and vijñāna— also have distinctions.
This means that the names themselves are differentiated,
because they are distinct as "mind" (*citta*), "intellect" (*manas*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Furthermore, their temporal periods are also differentiated.
This is because that which is past is called "mind" (manas),
that which is future is called "thought" (citta),
and that which is present is called "consciousness" (vijñāna).
Furthermore, there is also a distinction in their designation:
"mind" (citta) is designated within the context of the elements (dhātu),
while "intellect" (manas) is designated within the context of the bases (āyatana).
Because consciousness is designated within the aggregates.
Furthermore, there is also a distinction in meaning:
that is, "mind" (citta) has the sense of being a lineage (gotra).
The mind has the meaning of being a gateway for birth;
consciousness has the meaning of accumulation.
Furthermore, there are also distinctions among karmas.
This refers to the mental activity of traveling far. As a verse says:
"It travels far and wanders alone; bodiless, it dwells within the cave."
One who subdues this mind is liberated from great fear;
mental action (manas-karma) precedes this.
As it is said in a verse:
All phenomena are preceded by the mind, led by the mind, and drawn forth by the mind.
When the mind is defiled or purified, speech acts accordingly. Just as a shadow follows a form, suffering and pleasure arise in continuous succession;
this is the karma of consciousness.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If consciousness were absent at the time of entering the mother's womb,
the kalala and subsequent stages could not be established."
Thus, it is known that the continuity of rebirth is the functional activity of consciousness.
Furthermore, the painting of colors is the activity of the mind,
as stated in the Sūtra:
"O bhikṣus, you should know that the various realms of animals are painted by the mind and possess manifold colors."
This mental karma is the destination;
as it is said in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know."
Thus, while these five faculties each have their own distinct range and distinct objects,
the mental faculty (manas) universally receives those ranges and objects;
the mind takes refuge in them and performs all its various activities.
Discrimination is the function of consciousness.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know..."
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is able to discern various objects and phenomena.
Furthermore, proliferation is the function of mind (*citta*);
deliberation is the function of intellect (*manas*).
Discrimination is the function of consciousness.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"To nourish and to divide is the function of the mind."
Reflecting and deliberating are the activity of the mind (manas-karma);
discerning and understanding are the activity of consciousness (vijñāna-karma).
It should be understood that herein, "nourishing and increasing" refers to the mind associated with outflows (sāsrava-citta).
The divider is the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*);
the deliberator is the tainted intellect (*sāsrava-manas*);
the reflector is the untainted intellect (*anāsrava-manas*).
Discrimination refers to contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*);
thorough comprehension refers to uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*).
Mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—these three constitute their distinction.
Question: Regarding the eye, visible forms, and the eye-consciousness element,
are they necessarily bound by the same fetters,
or can they also be bound by different fetters?
Answer: These three types may be of the same bond (sambandha) or of different bonds.
What is meant by being of the same bond?
It refers to when one born in the desire realm sees forms of the desire realm with eyes of the desire realm.
When an eye of the desire realm perceives a form of the desire realm, producing an eye-consciousness of the desire realm—
specifically, when that very [person] sees a form of the first dhyāna with an eye of the first dhyāna—
then that eye of the first dhyāna and that form of the first dhyāna produce an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
If one is born in the first dhyāna and sees forms of the first dhyāna with the eye of the first dhyāna,
then that eye of the first dhyāna, those forms of the first dhyāna, and the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna all arise.
This is called "bound by the same. What is "bound by different"?
It refers to when one born in the desire realm sees objects of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna;
at that time, the eye of the first dhyāna, the objects of the desire realm, and the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna arise.
When that person sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the second dhyāna,
those forms of the desire realm give rise to an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
When seeing a form of the first dhyāna,
that eye of the second dhyāna gives rise to an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna directed toward the form of the first dhyāna.
When seeing a form of the second dhyāna...
When one in the second dhyāna gives rise to an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna directed toward forms of the second dhyāna,
and that same person then sees forms of the desire realm with an eye of the third dhyāna:
When one in the third dhyāna sees forms of the first dhyāna with an eye belonging to the desire realm that has produced an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna,
those forms of the first dhyāna arise for that eye of the third dhyāna.
When the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna sees a form of the second dhyāna,
that third-dhyāna eye and second-dhyāna form give rise to the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
When one sees forms of the third dhyāna with [an eye of] the third dhyāna,
that eye of the third dhyāna and those forms of the third dhyāna give rise to an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
Likewise, when one sees forms of the desire realm with an eye of the fourth dhyāna, [the same applies].
When one in the fourth dhyāna sees forms of the first dhyāna with an eye belonging to the desire realm that gives rise to an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna,
that eye of the fourth dhyāna and those forms of the first dhyāna give rise to an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the second dhyāna,
the eye of the fourth dhyāna and the forms of the second dhyāna give rise to the visual consciousness of the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the third dhyāna...
When that eye of the fourth dhyāna perceives forms of the fourth dhyāna by means of an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna produced by forms of the third dhyāna,
that eye of the fourth dhyāna—
The matter of the fourth dhyāna gives rise to eye-consciousness when one is born in the first dhyāna.
If one is born in the first dhyāna...
When one sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna,
that eye of the first dhyāna gives rise to an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna directed toward those forms of the desire realm.
The remaining details are explained at length as in the case of being born in the desire realm;
if one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna,
the details should be understood accordingly.
Is there a case where an eye belonging to one tie (*saṃyojana*) and a visible form belonging to another tie give rise to an eye-consciousness belonging to yet another tie? Answer: Yes.
That is to say, when one sees a visible form of the desire realm with an eye belonging to the second dhyāna.
When one in the second dhyāna gives rise to eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna directed toward forms of the desire realm,
or when one with the eye of the third dhyāna sees forms of the desire realm,
that eye of the third dhyāna and the forms of the desire realm give rise to eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the second dhyāna,
the eye of the third dhyāna, the forms of the second dhyāna, and the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna arise.
When seeing the forms of the desire realm with the eye of the fourth dhyāna...
When one in the fourth dhyāna sees forms of the second dhyāna with an eye belonging to the fourth dhyāna and an eye-consciousness arising from forms of the desire realm in the first dhyāna,
that eye of the fourth dhyāna and those forms of the second dhyāna give rise to an eye-consciousness in the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the third dhyāna with the eye of the fourth dhyāna, the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna arises;
thus, these three factors are each bound to different levels.
This is called the meaning of the eye, form, and visual consciousness being either bound by the same fetters or different fetters.
Question: Are the body, the eye, form, and the visual consciousness element necessarily bound by the same fetters, or can they also be bound by different fetters?
Answer: These four kinds may be of the same bond (*saṃyoga*) or of different bonds.
What is meant by being of the same bond?
It refers to when one born in the desire realm sees a form of the desire realm with an eye of the desire realm.
When one belonging to the desire realm has a body of the desire realm, eyes of the desire realm, and forms of the desire realm, and produces eye-consciousness of the desire realm;
or when one born in the first dhyāna sees forms of the first dhyāna with eyes of the first dhyāna.

When one belonging to the first dhyāna level possesses the body of the first dhyāna, the eye of the first dhyāna, and gives rise to forms of the first dhyāna, and produces the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna—
this is called being bound by the same ties. What is meant by being bound by different ties?
That is to say, when one born in the desire realm sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna,
there arises in that body of the desire realm, by means of the eye of the first dhyāna, toward those forms of the desire realm, an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
When one sees a form of the first dhyāna,
that body of the desire realm, the eye of the first dhyāna, and the form of the first dhyāna give rise to the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
That same person, when seeing a form of the desire realm with an eye of the second dhyāna—
When one whose body belongs to the desire realm and possesses the eye of the second dhyāna sees a form of the first dhyāna with an eye-consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna, that [eye] arises.
When one born with a body in the desire realm sees a form of the second dhyāna with an eye of the first dhyāna,
the visual consciousness arises in the first dhyāna;
when that same person sees a form of the second dhyāna with an eye of the second dhyāna, the visual consciousness arises in the first dhyāna.
When that person sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the third dhyāna,
the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna arises, having as its basis the body of the desire realm, the eye of the third dhyāna, and the forms of the desire realm.
When seeing the forms of the first dhyāna,
the body belonging to the desire realm, the eye belonging to the third dhyāna, and the forms of the first dhyāna give rise to the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the second dhyāna...
When one with a body in the desire realm sees forms of the third dhyāna by means of an eye of the second dhyāna and an eye-consciousness produced in the first dhyāna,
there is an eye of the third dhyāna and forms of the third dhyāna arising for that person with a body in the desire realm, while an eye-consciousness is produced in the first dhyāna.
When that person, by means of the eye of the fourth dhyāna, sees forms of the desire realm,
there arises in the body of the desire realm, by means of the eye of the fourth dhyāna and the forms of the desire realm, an eye-consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna.
When seeing a form of the first dhyāna,
that body of the desire realm, the eye of the fourth dhyāna, and the form of the first dhyāna give rise to the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
When seeing a form of the second dhyāna...
When one with a body in the desire realm, possessing an eye of the fourth dhyāna, produces an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna to see a form of the third dhyāna,
that body in the desire realm, that eye of the fourth dhyāna, and that form of the third dhyāna produce an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the fourth dhyāna,
the eye of the fourth dhyāna belonging to that [being] and the forms of the fourth dhyāna give rise to an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna within a body of the desire realm;
this occurs if one is born in the first dhyāna.
When one sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna,
that body of the first dhyāna, that eye of the first dhyāna, and the forms of the desire realm give rise to the visual consciousness of the first dhyāna.
When that person sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the second dhyāna,
the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna arises— taking as its basis the body of the first dhyāna, the eye of the second dhyāna, and the forms of the desire realm.
When seeing a form of the first dhyāna,
that body of the first dhyāna, with the eye of the second dhyāna, gives rise to an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna directed toward a form of the first dhyāna.
When seeing a form of the second dhyāna...
When one belonging to the body of the first dhyāna gives rise to an eye of the second dhyāna and objects of the second dhyāna, and a visual consciousness of the first dhyāna arises;
that is, when such a person sees objects of the desire realm with an eye of the third dhyāna.
When one with a body in the first dhyāna, an eye in the third dhyāna, and forms in the desire realm gives rise to an eye-consciousness in the first dhyāna and sees forms of the first dhyāna,
there is a body in the desire realm, an eye in the third dhyāna, forms of the first dhyāna, and an eye-consciousness arising in the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the second dhyāna,
the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna arises, with the body of the first dhyāna, the eye of the third dhyāna, and the forms of the second dhyāna as its conditions.
When seeing the forms of the third dhyāna,
the eye of the third dhyāna and the forms of the third dhyāna belonging to that [being] give rise to an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna within the body of the first dhyāna.
When that person sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the fourth dhyāna,
the body is in the first dhyāna, the eye is of the fourth dhyāna, the forms belong to the desire realm, and the visual consciousness arises in the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the first dhyāna,
the body belongs to the first dhyāna, the eye belongs to the fourth dhyāna, the forms belong to the first dhyāna, and the eye-consciousness arises in the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the second dhyāna...
When one born in the body of the first dhyāna, possessing eyes of the fourth dhyāna, produces eye-consciousness of the second dhyāna,
sees forms of the third dhyāna.
When one born in the body of the first dhyāna, possessing an eye of the fourth dhyāna, perceives a form of the third dhyāna with an eye of the first dhyāna,
seeing a form of the fourth dhyāna.
When one belonging to the body of the first dhyāna gives rise to an eye of the fourth dhyāna and objects of the fourth dhyāna, there arises an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
As it is when born in the first dhyāna,
so it is when born in the second, third, or fourth dhyānas.
The detailed exposition should be understood according to the corresponding [rules].
As for the distinction:
if one is born in the second dhyāna, one should always speak of the body of the second dhyāna.
If one is born in the third dhyāna, one should always be described as having a body of the third dhyāna;
if one is born in the fourth dhyāna, one should always be described as having a body of the fourth dhyāna.
Is there a case where the body belongs to one bond, the eye to another bond, the visible forms to another bond, and the visual consciousness to yet another bond?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, when one born in the desire realm sees visible forms of the third dhyāna with an eye belonging to the third dhyāna.
When one born with a body of the desire realm and eyes of the third dhyāna perceives forms of the second dhyāna with an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna,
and subsequently sees those same forms of the second dhyāna with eyes of the fourth dhyāna.
When one with a body in the desire realm, possessing eyes of the fourth dhyāna, gives rise to eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna to see forms of the third dhyāna,
that body in the desire realm, with eyes of the fourth dhyāna, gives rise to eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna to see forms of the third dhyāna.
If one is born in the second dhyāna and sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the third dhyāna, then—
with that body of the second dhyāna, that eye of the third dhyāna, and those forms of the desire realm— eye-consciousness arises in the first dhyāna.
When that person sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the fourth dhyāna,
the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna arises in relation to those forms of the desire realm, based on the body of the second dhyāna and the eye of the fourth dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the third dhyāna,
the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna arises, with the body in the second dhyāna, the eye in the fourth dhyāna, and the forms in the third dhyāna.
If one is born in the third dhyāna and sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the fourth dhyāna, then—
with that body of the third dhyāna and that eye of the fourth dhyāna— eye-consciousness arises in the first dhyāna directed toward those forms of the desire realm.
When seeing the forms of the second dhyāna,
the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna arises, with the body of the third dhyāna, the eye of the fourth dhyāna, and the forms of the second dhyāna as its objects.
Thus, these four types are each bound to different levels.
This is what is meant by the sense of the body, eye, visible forms, and visual consciousness being either bound to the same level or to different levels.
As it has been said regarding the eye-element, the form-element, and the visual-consciousness-element being bound to the same level as the body or to different levels.

In this same manner, the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element—along with their being bound by the same [fetters] as the body or bound by different ones—should be understood in detail according to their respective correspondences.
Now, regarding the nose, odor, and nose-consciousness elements:
Are they necessarily of the same tie (*saṃyoga*), or can they also be of different ties?
Answer: These three types are exclusively of the same tie.
This refers to the nose of the desire realm, the odors of the desire realm, and the nose-consciousness of the desire realm arising together.
Although there may be other bound instances of the nose where odors and nose-consciousness are absent,
they are not mentioned here for that reason.
Question: Are the body, nose, odors, and nose-consciousness element necessarily bound by the same fetter, or can they also be bound by different fetters?
Answer: These four types are exclusively bound by the same fetter.
This refers to a body of the desire realm, a nose of the desire realm, and an odor of the desire realm giving rise to a nose-consciousness of the desire realm.
Although there may be other bodies and nose-elements belonging to different realms, because they lack odors and nose-consciousness, they are not mentioned here.
Just as the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, and the body are bound by the same fetters,
so too are the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, and the body bound only by the same fetters.
The detailed explanation should be understood according to the appropriate application.
Question: Are the body, tangibles, and the body-consciousness element necessarily bound by the same fetters (*paryavasthāna*), or can they also be bound by different ones?
Answer: These three types are either of the same bond (*samāna-bandhana*) or of different bonds.
What is meant by "of the same bond"?
That is to say: for one born in the desire realm, there is a body of the desire realm, contact of the desire realm, and body-consciousness of the desire realm arising.
Or, for one born in the first dhyāna, there is a body of the first dhyāna, contact of the first dhyāna, and body-consciousness of the first dhyāna arising.
This is called being bound by the same fetter (*samanvāgata*). What is meant by being bound by different fetters?

It refers to one born in the second dhyāna whose body belongs to the second dhyāna and whose contact belongs to the second dhyāna, yet who gives rise to a body-consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna.
If one is born in the third dhyāna, the body of that third dhyāna and the contact of that third dhyāna give rise to a body-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
If one is born in the fourth dhyāna, the body of that fourth dhyāna and the contact of that fourth dhyāna give rise to a body-consciousness of the first dhyāna.
This means that contact within the body belonging to one specific realm (niṣyanda) can never have an object belonging to a different realm.
This is because consciousness arises only through the conjunction of the sense faculty and its object,
and because the faculty and the object must necessarily be similar in their degree of coarseness or subtlety.
In this context, there are no fourfold pairs of relative similarity or difference, because there is no distinct basis for the body and the elements.
Question: Are the mental faculty (*manas*), phenomena (*dharma*), and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) necessarily bound by the same fetters?
"Is it also the case that they have different bonds?
The answer is: "These three types may either have the same bond or different bonds."
What is "common bondage" (*samanvāgama*)?
It refers to when the mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) gives rise to dharmas of the desire realm and a mental consciousness of the desire realm, and so on,
up to the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The phenomena of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception give rise to the mental consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is called "being bound by the same fetter."
What is meant by "belonging to a different realm"?
Regarding this, some say:
immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm, only the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration manifests.
Immediately after the threshold concentration (anāgamya-samādhi), a wholesome mind of the desire realm manifests.
Alternatively, some say that immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm, either the threshold concentration or the first dhyāna manifests.
Immediately after those two, a wholesome mind of the desire realm manifests.
Furthermore, some say that immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm, either the *anāgamya* concentration, the first dhyāna, or the intermediate dhyāna manifests.
Immediately following those three [unwholesome minds], a wholesome mind of the desire realm manifests.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka has stated:
"Immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm, either the *anāgamya* concentration, the first dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna, or the second dhyāna may manifest."
When those four immediate [minds] are present, a wholesome mind of the desire realm manifests;

this is because, as in the case of the leap-concentration (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*), when one leaps from the first dhyāna to the second dhyāna and so forth, the third dhyāna and subsequent states manifest immediately thereafter.
The critique states:
He should not make such a statement,
because the characteristics of concentrated and non-concentrated minds arise differently.
It should be stated as follows:
immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm, either the *anāgamya* concentration or the first dhyāna manifests;
and immediately after those two, a wholesome mind of the desire realm manifests.
Because the power of that immediate succession can only reach this point;
that is to say, when a wholesome mind of the desire realm is immediately followed by the access concentration (anāgamya) or the first dhyāna becoming manifest.
The mental consciousness of that desire realm and the mental consciousness of the stage of the first dhyāna consist of dharmas that are either bound to the three realms or unbound.
When a wholesome mind of the desire realm manifests immediately after those two, [the following occurs].
The mental consciousness of that first dhyāna stage takes as its objects dharmas belonging to the desire realm,
or those bound to the three realms, or those that are unbound.
When one enters the second dhyāna immediately following the first dhyāna in regular succession, [the mental consciousness] likewise functions in this manner.
The mental faculty (*manas*) of that first dhyāna and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its objects (*dharma*) of the second dhyāna are either bound to the three realms or unbound.
When one enters the first dhyāna immediately after the second dhyāna in reverse order, [these factors are involved].
The mental faculty of that second dhyāna takes as its objects the dharmas of the first dhyāna consciousness;
these are either bound to the three realms or are unbound.
When one enters the third dhyāna immediately and in direct succession from the second dhyāna, [the same applies].
The mind of that second dhyāna and the mental consciousness of the third dhyāna are either bound to the three realms or unbound.
When one enters the second dhyāna immediately after the third dhyāna in reverse order, [these states arise].
The mental consciousness of that third dhyāna takes as its objects the phenomena of the second dhyāna mental consciousness,
which may be bound to the three realms or unbound.
When one enters the fourth dhyāna immediately and in direct succession from the third dhyāna, [the same applies].
The mental faculty (*manas*) of that third dhyāna and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the fourth dhyāna take as their objects dharmas that are either bound to the three realms or unbound.
This occurs when one enters the third dhyāna immediately after, in reverse order, from the fourth dhyāna.
The mental faculty of that fourth dhyāna takes as its object the consciousness and mental phenomena of the third dhyāna,
which may be bound to the three realms or unbound.
When one enters the sphere of infinite space immediately and in direct succession from the fourth dhyāna, [the same applies].
The mental consciousness of that fourth dhyāna, which takes as its object the dharmas of the sphere of infinite space,
is either bound to the formless realm or unbound.
When one enters the fourth dhyāna immediately after [emerging from] the sphere of infinite space in reverse order, [this occurs].
The mental consciousness of that fourth dhyāna belonging to the sphere of infinite space consists of dharmas that are either bound to the three realms or unbound.
When one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness immediately and in direct succession from the sphere of infinite space:
The consciousness of the sphere of infinite space, the consciousness of the sphere of infinite consciousness,
and the mental phenomena thereof are either bound to the sphere of infinite consciousness, bound to the sphere of nothingness,
or bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Or it is unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).
When one enters the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) immediately after the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) in reverse order,
that [consciousness] of the sphere of infinite consciousness consists of the mind (*manas*) of the sphere of infinite space and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its objects (*dharma*).
It is either bound to the formless realm or unbound.
When one enters the sphere of nothingness immediately after the sphere of infinite consciousness in regular succession,
there is the mind of the sphere of infinite consciousness and the mental consciousness and mental objects of the sphere of nothingness.
Either bound to the sphere of nothingness,
or bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or unbound.
When one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana) immediately after the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana),
the mental consciousness of that sphere of nothingness and the mental consciousness of the sphere of infinite consciousness, as well as their associated dharmas,
are either bound to the sphere of infinite consciousness or bound to the sphere of nothingness.
It is either bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
or it is unbound.
This occurs when one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception immediately following the sphere of nothingness in regular succession.
The mental consciousness of that sphere of nothingness, which has as its object the phenomena of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
is either bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception or is unbound.
When one enters the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) in immediate succession to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),

that mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the mental consciousness of the sphere of nothingness, and its objects are either bound to the sphere of nothingness or [belong to] the sphere of nothingness.
It is either bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
or it is unbound.
When one enters the third dhyāna by means of direct transcendence immediately after the first dhyāna, [the mind] is as described.
The mental faculty (*manas*) of that first dhyāna and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its objects (*dharma*) of the third dhyāna are either bound to the three realms or unbound.
This occurs when one enters the first dhyāna immediately after, by way of retrogression or transcendence, from the third dhyāna.
The mental consciousness of that third dhyāna takes as its objects the dharmas of the first dhyāna consciousness;
these are either bound to the three realms or unbound.
Even when one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception immediately after the sphere of infinite consciousness in a direct transcendence,
the mind of that sphere of infinite consciousness and the mental consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception [arise].
It is either bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
or it is unbound.
This occurs when one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness immediately after, without interval, or by skipping over, from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

The mental consciousness of that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the mental consciousness of the sphere of infinite consciousness are either bound to the sphere of infinite consciousness or bound to the sphere of nothingness.
Or they are bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
or they are unbound.
The remaining stages should be explained in detail according to their respective characteristics.
Thus it is.
Having already explained entering meditative absorption in both direct and reverse order,
one should next explain the entry into absorption and the fruits of that absorption.
Among these, the fruits of meditative concentration consist of fourteen transformational minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*):
namely, four for each of the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
There are three in the second dhyāna,
two in the third dhyāna, and one in the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, regarding the four types of transformation-minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) in the desire realm:
This refers to the fruits of the first dhyāna up to the fruits of the fourth dhyāna.
These four transformation-minds (nirmāṇacitta) arise immediately after the pure (śuddha) four dhyānas;
likewise, the pure four dhyānas arise immediately after these four transformation-minds.
Immediately after the transformation mind that is the fruit of the desire realm or the first dhyāna,
when the pure first dhyāna manifests,
there are the mental faculty of that desire realm and the mental consciousness and dharmas of the first dhyāna.
It is either bound to the three realms or unbound.
When the transformation mind (nirmāṇacitta) that is the fruit of the desire realm or the first dhyāna manifests immediately after the pure (śuddha) first dhyāna, [the transformation mind] is present.
The mental consciousness of that first dhyāna takes as its object the dharmas of the desire realm,
namely the emanated forms, which consist of either four bases or two bases.
This continues in the same manner up until the emanation-mind that is the fruit of the fourth dhyāna of the desire realm.
When the pure fourth dhyāna manifests,

its mental faculty belonging to the desire realm and its mental consciousness and mental objects belonging to the fourth dhyāna are either bound to the three realms or unbound; this occurs immediately after the pure fourth dhyāna.
When a transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) that is the fruit of the fourth dhyāna of the desire realm manifests,
its basis is the mental faculty of that fourth dhyāna, while its objects are the dharmas of the desire-realm consciousness—
namely, the transformed objects themselves, which consist of either four bases or two bases.
The transformation minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) that are the fruits of the remaining ten dhyānas should be understood in detail according to their respective correspondences with the pure dhyānas.
Thus has been explained the entry into meditative absorption and its fruits;
next, one must explain death and rebirth.
This refers to when one dies in the desire realm and is born in the first dhyāna; at that time,
the mind of that desire realm and the mental consciousness of the first dhyāna take as their objects dharmas either bound to the eight higher stages or to the desire realm itself.
Or it is unattached.
When one dies in the first dhyāna and is reborn in the desire realm,
that mind of the first dhyāna is the mental consciousness of the desire realm, having the dharmas of the desire realm as its object.
It may be bound to the three realms,
or it may be unbound.
This occurs when one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn as far as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Those mental phenomena of the desire realm that are consciousnesses of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are either bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception or are unbound.
This occurs from the time of death in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception until the time of birth in the desire realm.
The mind of that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception consists of the mental consciousness and its mental objects belonging to the desire realm;
these may be bound to the three realms,
or they may be unbound.
When one passes away from the sphere of nothingness and is reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
the mind of that sphere of nothingness and the mental consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception [arise] with respect to phenomena.
Or it is bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
or it is unbound.
When one dies in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and is reborn in the sphere of nothingness, [the fetters are abandoned].
The mental consciousness of that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception takes as its objects the phenomena of the sphere of nothingness;
these are either bound to the sphere of nothingness or bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Or it may be unconditioned;
this is called being of a different category.
Within this, there is no fourfold correlation of identity or difference.
Because the mental element (*manodhātu*) and so forth pervade the nine stages and do not necessarily arise in dependence upon a physical body.
Question: Among these six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍvijñānakāya*), how many possess discrimination (*vikalpa*)?
How many are non-conceptual?
Answer: The first five groups of consciousness are exclusively non-conceptual;
the sixth group of consciousness may be either conceptual or non-conceptual.
Alternatively, they may be without conceptual differentiation (*nirvikalpa*). Those who are currently in meditative concentration (*samāhita*) are all without conceptual differentiation,
whereas those not in meditative concentration may possess conceptual differentiation.

Because conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) is universally associated with the indeterminate mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), this discussion for now refers to the conceptualizing mental consciousness that arises subsequent to visual consciousness.
Question: When one sees objects of the desire realm with the eye of the desire realm...
Furthermore, when the eye of the form realm sees forms belonging to the desire realm and the form realm,
how many types of visual consciousness arise with respect to those forms?
Subsequently, how many types of conceptual mental consciousness arise with respect to them?
Answer: When one who has severed the roots of goodness sees forms with the eye, two kinds of visual consciousness arise toward those forms:
namely, the defiled and the unobscured-neutral.
Thereafter, three types of conceptualizing mental consciousness arise therein:
namely, the wholesome, the defiled, and the non-obscured neutral.
This applies to ordinary beings who have not yet severed their roots of goodness and have not yet become free from the defilements of the desire realm.
When the eye sees a form, three types of visual consciousness arise with respect to that form—
namely, the wholesome, the afflicted, and the unobscured-neutral.
Subsequently, three types of conceptualizing mental consciousness belonging to the desire realm arise in relation to those same objects.
That is to say: wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured neutral [states].
Specifically, if one has been born in the desire realm and has already abandoned the defilements of the desire realm, but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna.
When one sees various forms with the eye of the desire realm,
two kinds of visual consciousness arise in relation to those forms;
that is to say, excluding the defiled.
Thereafter, a further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein;
for one of the "nature of falling back" (parihāṇadharman),
it consists of three types within the desire realm.
There are two types in the first dhyāna.
For one who is of the non-retrogressive type,
there are two types each in the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
This means that, excluding the defiled,
when one sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises toward those forms.
Thereafter, a further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein;
in the first dhyāna, two types arise, excluding the defiled;
in the desire realm, three types arise for those subject to regression.
There are two types of those who do not regress.
When seeing the form of the first dhyāna,
they give rise to an eye-consciousness regarding that form which is non-obscured and indeterminate.
Thereafter, a further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein.
In the first dhyāna, there are three types;
for those in the desire realm who are subject to regression, there are two types.
Excluding the indeterminate,
those of non-retrogressive nature possess only wholesome [states].
That same person has already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
When one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises toward those forms, followed subsequently by a conceptual mental consciousness directed toward them.
For one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman),
there are three types in the desire realm and two types in the first dhyāna;
for one of the "nature of non-falling away" (aparihāṇadharman), there are two types in the desire realm.
The first dhyāna is exclusively wholesome.
When seeing the forms of the first dhyāna,
one gives rise to an eye-consciousness that is non-obscured and indeterminate with respect to those forms.
Thereafter, a further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein.
For one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman),
there are two types in the desire realm.
Regarding the three types of the first dhyāna:
for one of the non-retrogressive type,
those in the desire realm and the first dhyāna are exclusively wholesome.
When one in that state sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the second dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises toward those forms;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises toward them as well.
If one is of the nature to fall away (parihāṇadharman),
there are three types in the desire realm and two types each in the first two dhyānas.
Regarding those of non-retrogressive nature:
in the desire realm and the second dhyāna, there are two types each;
in the first dhyāna, there is only the wholesome.
When seeing the forms of the first dhyāna,
an eye-consciousness that is non-obscured and indeterminate arises with respect to those forms;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises with respect to them as well.
For one of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharman),
there are two types each in the desire realm and the second dhyāna,
and three types in the first dhyāna.
For those of the non-retrogressive type, [the faculty] in the desire realm and the first dhyāna is exclusively wholesome;
in the second dhyāna, it is of two kinds.
This is because when one perceives visible forms of the second dhyāna, [it is indeterminate].
Regarding those forms, there arises an unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises regarding them.
For one of the "regressive" type (*parihāṇadharman*), there are two types each in the desire realm and the first dhyāna, and three types in the second dhyāna.
Regarding the dharmas of non-retrogression:
in the desire realm and the first dhyāna, they are exclusively wholesome;
in the second dhyāna, there are three kinds.
That is to say, when one has already become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna but is not yet free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
and sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna.
Regarding that form, an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises regarding it again.
This is the case for one who is subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*).
There are three types in the desire realm and two types each in the first three dhyānas.
As for those of the non-retrogressive nature:
The desire realm and the third dhyāna each have two kinds;
the first two dhyānas each have only the wholesome.
When seeing the forms of the first dhyāna:
Regarding that form, an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises with respect to it.
This is the case for one who is subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*).
The second and third dhyānas of the desire realm each have two types;
the first dhyāna has three types.
As for those of the non-retrogressive nature (*aparihāṇadharman*):
The desire realm and the first two dhyānas each consist exclusively of the wholesome;
the third dhyāna consists of both types.
This is because when one uses the eye of the second dhyāna to see forms of the desire realm, [the visual consciousness is indeterminate].
Regarding that form, an unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness arises;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises with respect to it.
For one of the "nature of falling back" (parihāṇadharman), there are three types belonging to the desire realm.
Regarding the two types of non-retrogressive dharmas in each of the first two dhyānas, those of the desire realm are of two types,
while those of the first two dhyānas are exclusively wholesome.
When one sees the form of the first dhyāna...
In relation to that form, an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises in relation to it.
For one of the "receding" type (*parihāṇadharman*), there are two types each in the desire realm and the second dhyāna.
There are three types of the first dhyāna.
For one who is of the non-retrogressive type (*avivartika*), [the consciousness] in the desire realm and in the first two dhyānas is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).
When seeing the visible forms (*rūpa*) of the second dhyāna, [it is so].
Regarding that form, there arises an eye-consciousness that is non-obscured and indeterminate;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises with respect to it.
For one of the "receding" type (*parihāṇadharman*), there are two types each in the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
Regarding the three types within the second dhyāna:
for one who is not subject to falling back (*aparihāṇadharman*), [the faculties] of the desire realm and the first two dhyānas are exclusively wholesome.
That same person, when seeing forms of the desire realm with the eye of the third dhyāna, [possesses these].
Regarding that form, an unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness arises;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises with respect to it.
For one of the "nature of falling back" (parihāṇadharman), there are three types in the desire realm and two types each in the first three dhyānas.
For those of non-retrogressive dharma, there are two types each in the desire realm and the third dhyāna;
in the first two dhyānas, there is only the wholesome.
When seeing the form of the first dhyāna:
Regarding those forms, an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises regarding them.
For one of the "regressive" type (*parihāṇadharman*), there are two types each in the second and third dhyānas of the desire realm.
Regarding the three types of non-retrogressive dharmas of the first dhyāna: those of the desire realm and the first two dhyānas are exclusively wholesome;
those of the third dhyāna are of two kinds.
When seeing the forms of the second dhyāna, [the former arise].
Regarding those forms, an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises regarding them.
For one of the "nature of falling back" (*parihāṇadharman*), there are two types each in the desire realm and in the first and third dhyānas.
Regarding the three types within the second dhyāna:
for those of the non-retrogressive type, [the mental states] of the desire realm and the first two dhyānas are exclusively wholesome;
in the third dhyāna, there are two types.
When seeing the forms of the third dhyāna,
an eye-consciousness that is non-obscured and indeterminate arises with respect to those forms;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises with respect to them as well.
For one of the "nature of falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*), there are two types each in the desire realm and the first two dhyānas;
in the third dhyāna, there are three types.
For one of the "nature of non-falling away" (*aparihāṇadharman*), there is only the wholesome in the desire realm and the first two dhyānas.

Regarding the three types of the third dhyāna: when one who has already abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the fourth dhyāna sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna.
Regarding that form, an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises with respect to it.
For one of the "deterioration-prone" (parihāṇadharman) type, there are three kinds [of consciousness] in the desire realm.
The four dhyānas each have two types.
For those of the non-retrogressive type (*avinivartanīya*), there are two types each in the desire realm and the fourth dhyāna;
for the first three dhyānas, there is only the wholesome.
When seeing the forms of the first dhyāna,
an eye-consciousness that is non-obscured and neutral arises with respect to those forms;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises with respect to them as well.
For one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman), there are two types each in the desire realm and the latter three dhyānas,
and three types in the first dhyāna.
For one of the "nature of non-falling away" (aparihāṇadharman), there is only the wholesome (kuśala) in the desire realm and the first three dhyānas.
There are two types of the fourth dhyāna.
That is to say, when one with the eye of the second dhyāna sees forms of the desire realm,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises toward those forms.
Thereafter, a further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein:
for one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman), there are three types in the desire realm and two types in each of the four dhyānas.
Regarding those of non-retrogressive nature, there are two types each in the desire realm and the fourth dhyāna.
In the first three dhyānas, when one perceives only the forms of the first dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises toward those forms.
Subsequently, a further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein.
For one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman), there are two types each in the desire realm and the latter three dhyānas;
there are three types in the first dhyāna.
Regarding those of non-retrogressive nature, in the desire realm and the first three dhyānas, [the form] is exclusively wholesome;
in the fourth dhyāna, there are two kinds.
When seeing the forms of the second dhyāna, [it is as follows].
Regarding that form, there arises an unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises with respect to it.
For one who is subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*), there are two types each in the desire realm and in the first, third, and fourth dhyānas.
In the second dhyāna there are three types.
For one of the non-retrogressive type, [the mind] in the desire realm and in each of the first three dhyānas is exclusively wholesome;
in the fourth dhyāna it is of two types.
When one in that state sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the third dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises toward those forms;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises toward them as well.
For one of the "regressive" type (*parihāṇadharman*), there are three types in the desire realm and two types in each of the four dhyānas.
For one of the "non-regressive" type (*aparihāṇadharman*), there are two types in the desire realm and two types in the fourth dhyāna.
The first three dhyānas are exclusively wholesome.
When seeing the forms of the first dhyāna,
one gives rise to an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness toward those forms.
Thereafter, a further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein.
For one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman), there are two types each in the desire realm and the latter three dhyānas, and three types in the first dhyāna.
Regarding those of non-retrogressive nature (*avinipātadharman*), in the desire realm and the first three dhyānas, it is exclusively wholesome;
in the fourth dhyāna, there are two kinds.
When seeing the forms (*rūpa*) of the second dhyāna...
Regarding that form, an unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness arises;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises with respect to it.
This is the case for one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman).
In the desire realm and in each of the first, third, and fourth dhyānas, there are two types;
in the second dhyāna, there are three types.
For one of the non-retrogressive type (*aparihāṇadharman*), [the states] in the desire realm and the first three dhyānas are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).
Regarding the two types of the fourth dhyāna:
when seeing the forms of the third dhyāna,
one gives rise to an eye-consciousness that is non-obscured and indeterminate with respect to those forms.
Thereafter, a further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein.
For one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman), there are two types each in the desire realm, as well as in the first, second, and fourth dhyānas;
there are three types in the third dhyāna.
Regarding the dharmas that are non-retrogressive:
in the desire realm and each of the first three dhyānas, they are exclusively wholesome;
in the fourth dhyāna, they are of two kinds.

Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Seventy-three.
Translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, who was commissioned by imperial decree, by five hundred great Arhats and others.
Section Two: The Aggregate of Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha), Chapter Four: The Summary of the Ten Gates, Part Three. When one sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the fourth dhyāna:
Regarding that form, an unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness arises;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises with respect to it.
For one who is subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), there are three types [of consciousness] belonging to the desire realm.
The four dhyānas each have two types.
For one of non-retrogression, there are two types each in the desire realm and the fourth dhyāna;
for the first three dhyānas, there are only wholesome types.
When seeing the form of the first dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises with respect to that form;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises with respect to it as well.
For one of the "dharma of falling away" (parihāṇadharman), there are two types each in the desire realm and the latter three dhyānas;
there are three types in the first dhyāna.
For one of the "dharma of non-falling away" (aparihāṇadharman), there is only the wholesome (kuśala) in the desire realm and the first three dhyānas.
When one in the fourth dhyāna sees the forms of the second dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises toward those forms;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises toward them as well.
For one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman), there are two types each in the desire realm and in the first, third, and fourth dhyānas;
there are three types in the second dhyāna.
For one of the "nature of non-falling away" (aparihāṇadharman), there is only the wholesome in the desire realm and in the first three dhyānas.
When one in the fourth dhyāna sees the forms of the third dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises toward those forms;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises toward them as well.
For one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman), there are two types each in the desire realm and in the first, second, and fourth dhyānas;
there are three types in the third dhyāna.

There are two types of the fourth dhyāna.
When one sees the forms of the fourth dhyāna,

For one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman), there are two types each for the desire realm and the first three dhyānas;

Regarding those of non-retrogressive nature (*avinipātadharman*), in the desire realm and the first three dhyānas, it is exclusively wholesome;
