provided that they have already become free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna.
With the eye of the four dhyānas, one sees forms of five stages;

regarding those forms, there arises an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and a varying amount of conceptual mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) belonging to those five stages.
It should be understood accordingly that, when one who is already free from the defilements of the first dhyāna and so forth sees various forms with the eye of the desire realm,

As this is easily understood according to what preceded, it will not be explained again.
If various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are born in the first dhyāna but have not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna.
When seeing forms of the desire realm,
two kinds of eye-consciousness arise with respect to those forms,
excluding the defiled.
Thereafter, a further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein;
it is of three types in the desire realm and of two types in the first dhyāna when perceiving the forms of the first dhyāna.
Regarding those forms, three kinds of visual consciousness arise;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises regarding them as well—
of two types in the desire realm.
There are three types of the first dhyāna;
that is, one who has already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna but has not yet become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna.
When one sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna,
visual consciousness arises and discriminates those forms;
this is explained in detail as before.
When seeing the forms of the first dhyāna,
one should understand that the two kinds of conceptualization arising from the visual consciousness regarding those forms are as previously described.
That is to say, when one sees the forms of the desire realm with the eye of the second dhyāna.
Regarding those forms, there arises an unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises with respect to them.
In the desire realm there are three types [of consciousness], and in the first two dhyānas there are two types.
When seeing the form of the first dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises with respect to that form;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises with respect to it as well.
The desire realm and the second dhyāna each have two types;
the first dhyāna has three types.
When seeing the forms of the second dhyāna:
Regarding those forms, there arises an eye-consciousness that is unobscured and neutral;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises regarding them.
In both the desire realm and the first dhyāna, there are two such types [of consciousness].
The second dhyāna has three types:
namely, those who have already become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna but have not yet become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
With the eye of the third dhyāna, one sees the forms of the fourth dhyāna;
or, having already become detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna,

Or, having already become free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
one sees forms of five stages with an eye belonging to four stages,
and gives rise to visual consciousness and discrimination regarding those forms.
It should be understood as being analogous to the preceding case.
Just as it was explained regarding an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) being born in the first dhyāna,
so too should it be understood for their birth in the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
Each of these should be understood in detail according to their respective correspondences.
Thus has been explained the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
As for those noble ones (*ārya*) who have not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-vairāgya*), [the following applies]:

When seeing a form of the desire realm, three types of visual consciousness arise with respect to that form; subsequently, three types of conceptualization of the desire realm arise again with respect to it.
That is to say, if one who has already been born in the desire realm is free from the defilements of the desire realm...
When one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna sees various forms with the eye of the desire realm,
two kinds of visual consciousness arise with respect to those forms.
Thereafter, further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein:
for one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman), it consists of three types in the desire realm and two types in the first dhyāna.
Regarding those of the non-retrogressive type, there are two kinds each in the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
That is to say, when such a person sees objects of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna,
they give rise to an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness toward those objects.
Thereafter, a further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein:
two types in the first dhyāna,
and three types in the desire realm for those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).
Regarding those of non-retrogressive dharma, there are two types of vision.
When they see the forms of the first dhyāna, an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises toward those forms;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises toward them as well.
The first dhyāna has three types;
in the desire realm, it is exclusively wholesome.
This refers to one who has already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
When one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises toward those forms.
Thereafter, a further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein:
for one of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman), it consists of three types in the desire realm and two types in the first dhyāna.
Regarding the dharmas of non-retrogression, there are two types in the desire realm;
in the first dhyāna, they are exclusively wholesome.
When one sees the forms of the first dhyāna:
In relation to those forms, an unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness arises;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises in relation to them.
This occurs in the Desire Realm and only in the First Dhyāna of the wholesome [realm].
If one is of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), there are three types;
if one is of the nature of not falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*), it is exclusively wholesome.
That is to say, when such a person sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the second dhyāna:
Regarding that form, there arises an unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises with respect to it.
For one of the "regressive" type (*parihāṇadharman*), this occurs in three ways within the desire realm.
The first two dhyānas each have two types.
For one of the non-retrogressive type (*aparihāṇadharman*), there are two types each in the desire realm and the second dhyāna;
in the first dhyāna, it is exclusively wholesome.
When seeing the form of the first dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness arises toward that form;
subsequently, with regard to it—
Furthermore, the discriminating mental consciousness that arises is exclusively wholesome in the desire realm;
in the second dhyāna, it is of two kinds.
Regarding the first dhyāna, for one subject to regression (parihāṇadharman), there are three types;
for one not subject to regression (aparihāṇadharman), it is exclusively wholesome.
This occurs when seeing the form of the second dhyāna.
Regarding those forms, an unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness arises;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises with respect to them.
In the Desire Realm and the First Dhyāna, these are exclusively wholesome.
The second dhyāna has three types.

That is to say, one who has already become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna but has not yet become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna sees forms of the fourth stage with the eye of the third stage.
Either one who has already become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna but not yet free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
or one who has already become free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna.
With the eye of the fourth stage, one sees the forms of the fifth stage;
regarding those forms, one gives rise to visual consciousness and conceptualization,
which should be understood accordingly.
In this context, when one who is already free from the defilements of the first dhyāna and so forth sees various forms with the eye of the desire realm,
visual consciousness arises and discriminates those forms.
As this is easily understood according to what preceded, it will not be explained further.
Having already explained how a noble one is born in the desire realm,
we shall now discuss what occurs if that same person is born in the first dhyāna.
When one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna sees forms of the desire realm,
two kinds of visual consciousness arise with respect to those forms.
Thereafter, two kinds of conceptualization arise again regarding that [first dhyāna].
When seeing the forms of the first dhyāna,
three types of visual consciousness arise with respect to those forms.
Thereafter, three types of conceptualization regarding that first dhyāna arise again for him; that is,
he has already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
but has not yet become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna.
When one sees forms of the desire realm with the eye of the first dhyāna,
visual consciousness arises and discriminates those forms;
this should be understood by analogy with what preceded.
When seeing the forms of the first dhyāna,
two types of eye-consciousness arise with respect to those forms;
subsequently, two types of conceptualization from those same two dhyānas arise again with respect to them.
When that person, by means of the eye of the second dhyāna, sees forms of the desire realm or the first dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises toward those forms.
Subsequently, two kinds of discernment from each of those two dhyānas arise again toward them.
When seeing the forms of the second dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises toward those forms;
subsequently, a conceptualizing mental consciousness arises toward them as well.
The first dhyāna is exclusively wholesome.
The second dhyāna is of three kinds; that is, when one has already become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna but has not yet become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
When one sees forms of the desire realm and the first dhyāna with the eye of the first dhyāna,
it should be understood that the arising of visual consciousness and its conceptualization regarding those forms is analogous to what was previously explained.
That is to say, when one sees forms of the desire realm and the first dhyāna with the eye of the second dhyāna...
Regarding that form, there arises an unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises with respect to it.
In the first and third dhyānas, there are respectively two types [of consciousness].
The second dhyāna is exclusively wholesome.
When seeing the forms of the second dhyāna,
one gives rise to an unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness toward those forms.
Thereafter, a further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein.
The first two dhyānas are exclusively wholesome;
the third dhyāna is of two kinds.
When that person sees forms of the desire realm or the first dhyāna with the eye of the third dhyāna,
an unobscured-neutral visual consciousness arises toward those forms;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises toward them as well.
The first and third dhyānas each have two types;
the second dhyāna is exclusively wholesome.
When one sees the forms of the second dhyāna, [the visual consciousness belongs to the first dhyāna].
In that [realm], there arises an eye-consciousness that is non-obscured and indeterminate;
subsequently, a conceptual mental consciousness arises in relation to it.
In the first two dhyānas, each is exclusively wholesome.
Regarding the two types of the third dhyāna:
when seeing the forms of the third dhyāna,
an eye-consciousness that is unobscured and indeterminate arises with respect to those forms.
Thereafter, a further conceptualizing mental consciousness arises therein.
The first two dhyānas are exclusively wholesome;
the third dhyāna is of three kinds.
That is, one who has already become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna but has not yet become free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
or one who has already become free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna.
When the eye of the fourth stage sees forms of the fifth stage,
the visual consciousness arises and discriminates those forms;
this should be understood accordingly.
Just as it is said that a noble one is born in the first dhyāna,
so too should it be understood in detail, according to the corresponding application, for their birth in the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
In this context, visual consciousness relies on the eye of its own level;
when taking objects of a lower level as its domain, two types are possible,
namely, excluding those that are defiled.
Regarding the forms of one's own level, there may be three possibilities.
If the eye belongs to a higher level, it is exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
As for wholesome or defiled visual consciousness, it can only arise when belonging to its own level and manifest in the present.
Because this [consciousness] is necessarily bound to birth,
the wholesome discriminating mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to take as its objects all levels— its own, those below, and those above.
The defiled discriminating mental consciousness, however, can only take as its objects its own level and those above.
The non-obscured neutral conceptualizing mental consciousness can only take its own level or a lower level as its object;
however, wholesome and defiled conceptualizing mental consciousnesses of its own or a lower level may arise and manifest.
It does not arise in a higher stage;
rather, the non-obscured neutral conceptual mental consciousness arises only in its own stage,
as it is necessarily bound to that birth.
The conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises subsequent to visual consciousness does not arise only once;
for it can also arise even after many moments have passed from the time of perceiving the visible object.
Question: For what reason is it produced in the three higher dhyānas?
"And can one manifest eye-consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna?
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"Who says that one born in the last three dhyānas is able to manifest eye-consciousness and other consciousnesses belonging to the level of the first dhyāna?"
Subsequently, the visual and other consciousnesses belonging to the three dhyānas rely upon the faculties of their own level to cognize objects of their own and lower levels.
If this were not the case,
how could those born in the higher realms employ skillful means?
They claim that the eye-consciousness and other consciousnesses of the first dhyāna are induced to become manifest.
The critique states: they should not make such a statement.
One should state it thus:
the last three dhyānas lack the visual consciousness and the others. Why is this?
Because they are devoid of vitarka and vicāra, whereas the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, always arise in association with vitarka and vicāra.
Question: For what reason are [these] produced in the latter three dhyānas?
It does not induce the various consciousnesses of the desire realm, such as the eye-consciousness, to manifest;
rather, it only induces the consciousness of the first dhyāna. Some say this:
Because the desire realm is inferior, one is born in a superior plane;
thus, one does not wish to induce those visual and other consciousnesses to become manifest.
Other masters say:
Because those realms are distinct.
That is to say, the various consciousnesses such as the eye-consciousness associated with the desire realm are not bound to the same realm as the faculties of the higher stages.
Although the consciousness of the first dhyāna is not of the same stage as the faculties of the higher stages, [it is still bound to the same realm].
However, because their realms are identical, they also arise based upon those [faculties].
Some say that the eye-consciousness and other such consciousnesses of the desire realm are neither fruits of cultivation nor fruits of supernormal powers.
They cannot arise manifest based on the faculties of a higher stage,
because the eye-consciousness and other such cognitions of the first *dhyāna* are the fruits of cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*) and the fruits of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*). However,
they can also arise manifest based on the faculties of a higher stage.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the visual and other consciousnesses of the desire realm do not belong to a fixed realm, nor to a stage of cultivation,
because they are not stages of detachment from defilement.
One cannot manifest [the visual consciousness, etc.,] based on the faculties of a higher stage,

because the visual consciousness and so forth of the first dhyāna belong to the realm of meditative concentration (*samāpatti-dhātu*), the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*), and the stage of freedom from passion (*vairāgya-bhūmi*). However,
one can also manifest them based on the faculties of a higher stage.

Due to various causes and conditions such as these, when one gives rise to the three higher dhyānas, the visual consciousnesses and other cognitions associated with the first dhyāna arise, while those belonging to the desire realm do not.
As it is said: "Visual consciousness relies upon faculties of various stages to cognize forms of various stages."
How many types of the three kinds of conceptualization are there within the drawn-in mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?
The other consciousnesses, such as the auditory consciousness and so forth, should be understood accordingly.
Question: Does one who possesses the eye-element also necessarily possess the form-element (*rūpadhātu*)?
Answer: If one accomplishes the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*), one also accomplishes the form element (*rūpadhātu*).
However, there are cases where one accomplishes the form element but does not accomplish the eye element;
namely, those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who have not yet obtained the eye.
Or having attained it, they lose it.
Those who have not yet attained the eye refers to those in the stages of the *kalala* and so forth, as well as those born blind.
"Having obtained and then lost" refers to having obtained the eye, which subsequently becomes putrid,
is plucked out, or is eaten by insects.
Or it may be destroyed by other conditions.
Question: Does one who possesses the eye-element also possess the eye-consciousness-element?
Answer: One should respond with four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are cases where one possesses the eye element but does not possess the eye-consciousness element;
namely, those born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna whose eye-consciousness element is not present before them.
There are those who achieve the eye-consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu) but do not achieve the eye element (cakṣurdhātu);
namely, those born in the desire realm who have not yet obtained the eyes, or who have obtained them but subsequently lost them.
There are also those who achieve both the eye element and the eye-consciousness element.
That is to say: having been born in the desire realm, one has obtained the eye faculty and does not lose it;
or, having been born in the first dhyāna, or having been born in the second, third, or fourth dhyānas, the visual consciousness element manifests before one.
There are those who do not possess the eye element,
nor do they possess the eye-consciousness element;
namely, those born in the formless realm.
Question: Do all those who accomplish the element of form (rūpadhātu) also accomplish the element of visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñānadhātu)?
Answer: If one accomplishes the element of visual consciousness, one also accomplishes the element of form.
There are those who possess the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) but do not possess the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*),
namely, those born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna whose eye-consciousness element is not present before them.
Question: If one does not possess the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), does one also not possess the form-element (*rūpadhātu*)?
Answer: If one does not possess the form-element, one also does not possess the eye-element.
There are those who do not possess the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) but are not non-possessors of the form-element (*rūpadhātu*).
This refers to those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who have not yet obtained the eye, or who have obtained it but subsequently lost it.
Question: Regarding all those who do not possess the eye-element...
Is it also not accomplished as the eye-consciousness element?
One should respond by means of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is the case where one does not accomplish the eye-element, yet it is not that one does not accomplish the eye-consciousness element.
This refers to one born in the desire realm who has not yet obtained the eye faculty,
or who has obtained it but subsequently lost it;
such a person does not possess the eye-consciousness element, yet it is not the case that they do not possess the eye element.
That is to say, when one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, the eye-consciousness element does not manifest;
such a person neither possesses the eye element nor possesses the eye-consciousness element.
This refers to those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
There are cases where one neither fails to possess the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*) nor fails to possess the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*);
that is, those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who have already acquired the eye and do not lose it.
Or one is born in the first dhyāna, or one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, and the eye-consciousness element manifests before them.
Question: Regarding those who do not possess the form realm...
Is one also not accomplished in the eye-consciousness element?
Answer: If one is not accomplished in the form element, one is also not accomplished in the eye-consciousness element.
There are cases where one does not possess the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) but is not non-possessed of the form element (*rūpadhātu*).
This refers to those born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna whose eye-consciousness element is not currently present.
Question: If one does not possess the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), can one also acquire it while in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
Answer: If one does not possess the form realm.
The same applies to the attainment of the accomplishment of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*).
There are cases where one does not accomplish the eye-element but subsequently accomplishes it, yet does not accomplish the form-element (*rūpadhātu*);
this refers to one born in the desire realm who gradually attains the eye-element.
Question: If one who did not previously possess the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) now attains its possession, does that person also attain the visual consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu)?
Answer: This should be analyzed in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are cases where one attains the possession of the eye-element without attaining the visual consciousness element.
This refers to one who dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna,
or is reborn in the desire realm and gradually acquires the eye element;
such a person possesses the eye element but does not achieve the eye-consciousness element.
One attains accomplishment of the non-eye-element (an-akṣi-dhātu), namely:
when one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna and the eye-consciousness element (cakṣur-vijñāna-dhātu) manifests;
or when one dies from those states and is reborn in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or the first dhyāna.
There are cases where one does not possess the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*),
yet acquires it as well as the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).
This refers to those who die in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and are reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the first dhyāna.
There are cases where one who did not previously possess the eye-element attains its possession, yet does not likewise attain the visual-consciousness-element.
This refers to instances other than those previously described.
Question: Is it the case that when one who did not previously possess any of the form-elements attains their possession, they also attain the visual-consciousness-element?
It can be answered in four propositions:
there are cases where one does not possess the form element (*rūpadhātu*),
yet possesses the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).
This refers to passing away from the formless realm and being born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna.
There is the case where the eye-consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu) is not previously possessed but is now attained, while the form element (rūpadhātu) is not.
This refers to one born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna who brings the eye-consciousness element into manifestation.
Or, having passed away from there, one is born into the desire realm or the first dhyāna;
while the form element is not yet accomplished,
it is now attained and accomplished, as is the eye-consciousness element.
This refers to those who die in the formless realm and are reborn in the desire realm or the first dhyāna;
they do not fail to possess the element of form,
yet they also do not attain the accomplishment of the eye-consciousness element.
That is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Question: Is it also the case that when one achieves the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), one simultaneously achieves and does not achieve the form-element (*rūpadhātu*)?
It can be answered in four propositions:
there are cases where one achieves the eye-element but does not achieve the form-element of the form realm.
This refers to one born in the desire realm who has already acquired the eye faculty but subsequently loses it;

such a person possesses the form element (*rūpadhātu*) but does not possess the eye faculty (*cakṣurdhātu*). It is not that they fail to achieve the eye faculty while still achieving the form element.
This refers to one who dies in the desire realm without possessing the eye faculty and is reborn in the formless realm;
such a person achieves the eye faculty but does not maintain it. It also refers to the case of the form realm:
namely, one who dies in the desire realm possessing the eye faculty and is reborn in the formless realm.
Or, one may die in the form realm and be reborn in the formless realm; in such a case,
there is the eye-element which is not accomplished, nor is it non-accomplished, nor does it belong to the form realm—
namely, excluding the aforementioned cases.
Question: Is one who achieves or fails to achieve the eye-element also [one who achieves or fails to achieve] the eye-consciousness-element?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are cases where one achieves or fails to achieve the eye-element, but not the eye-consciousness-element.
This refers to one who, having been born in the desire realm, has acquired the eye faculty but subsequently loses it;
or one who dies in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna and is reborn in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
In such cases, there is the non-acquisition of the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) while there is no non-acquisition of the eye faculty (*cakṣurdhātu*).
This refers to one who dies in the desire realm without possessing the eye faculty and is reborn in the formless realm;

or one who dies in the desire realm or the first dhyāna and is reborn in the second, third, or fourth dhyānas; or one who, while remaining in those [lower realms], has the eye-consciousness element already present before it is severed.
There are those who achieve the eye-element but do not achieve the eye-consciousness-element:
namely, those with eyes in the desire realm who die and are reborn in the formless realm,
or those who die in the first dhyāna and are reborn in the formless realm.
There are cases where the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) is neither attained nor not attained, and likewise the visual-consciousness-element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu) is neither attained nor not attained;
this refers to instances other than those previously mentioned.
Question: Are all cases where the form-element (rūpadhātu) is attained or not attained also cases where the visual-consciousness-element is attained or not attained?
It can be answered in four propositions.
There are those who possess the element of form (*rūpadhātu*) but do not possess the element of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).
This refers to those who die in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna and are reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
There are cases where one achieves the eye-consciousness element but does not achieve the form element:
namely, when one dies in the desire realm or the first dhyāna and is reborn in the second, third, or fourth dhyānas.
Alternatively, one may sever [the connection] while that very eye-consciousness element is present before one;
there is also the case where the form element is accomplished but the eye-consciousness element is not.
This refers to one who dies in the desire realm or the first dhyāna and is reborn in the formless realm.
There are cases where the form element (*rūpadhātu*) is neither attained nor unattained, and likewise the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) is not;
this refers to instances other than those previously described.

Just as there are twelve propositions regarding the mutual relationship between the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element, so it is with the mutual relationship between the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element.
Up to the mutual correlation between the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the phenomenon-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*),
there should likewise be twelve treatises for each.
Thus, it is explained that the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) relates to the homogeneous.
If the non-homogeneous were to be paired with the non-homogeneous,
one should state that there are five types of threefold discussions regarding the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element.
The ear element, sound element, and ear-consciousness element each have four types of threefold treatises.
The nose element, odor element, and nose-consciousness element each have three types of threefold treatises.
The tongue element, taste element, and tongue-consciousness element each have two types of threefold treatises.
Regarding the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element, there is one set of threefold propositions.
In this same manner, each [element] should be understood according to its corresponding [category].
As for the twelve bases (*āyatana*):

That is to say: the sense base of the eye, the sense base of forms; the sense base of the ear, the sense base of sounds; the sense base of the nose, the sense base of odors; the sense base of the tongue, the sense base of tastes; the sense base of the body, the sense base of tangibles; the sense base of the mind, and the sense base of mental phenomena.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of providing a detailed analysis of the meaning of the sūtras.
That is to say, a sūtra states:
"There was a brahmin named Jātiśroṇa."
He approached the place where the Buddha was,
and having arrived, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.
With palms joined in reverence, he paid his respects to the Buddha and withdrew to sit at one side.
And he said to the Buddha:
"Venerable Gautama,
you always teach everything to the assembly."
"What is 'all'? To what extent is this term 'all' established?
The Buddha said to the brahmin Jātiśroṇa:
I say that "all" refers precisely to the twelve bases (āyatana),
namely, from the eye base up to the mental-object base (dharmāyatana).
It is to this extent that the Tathāgata designates "all."
If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who speak thus:
"I am able to abandon everything taught by the Buddha and establish elsewhere a separate 'all' discourse."
That consists of mere words without actual meaning;
if one were to question him further, he would be unable to explain it,
and later, upon reflecting on it himself, he would become even more confused and distressed.
Why is this? Because it is not within their domain.
Although the Sūtra makes this statement, it does not analyze its meaning.
The sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Since those [sūtras] do not explain certain matters, I now wish to explain them;
for this reason, I have composed this treatise.
Question: If one makes this statement, saying that "all" refers to the eighteen elements (dhātus);
or if one makes this other statement:
"Everything" refers to the five aggregates and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Alternatively, it is said that "everything" refers to the four truths, space (*ākāśa*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Some may say: "When it says 'all,' it refers to name-and-form (nāma-rūpa).
To such statements, one must ask: "Is there not merely the word, but no actual meaning? The answer is: here, the meaning is negated, but the phrasing is not negated.
This is merely a designation based on negation;
it is not a designation based on affirmation.
This is what the Buddha intended to say.
The nature of all phenomena is entirely subsumed within these twelve bases (*āyatana*).
If anyone were to say, "I can designate that there are further phenomena existing apart from these," [they would be speaking falsely].
It is not included within these twelve bases (āyatana).
That [position] consists of mere words and lacks actual meaning;
it is not the Buddha’s intention that there are no distinct doctrinal categories such as name-and-form (nāmarūpa) outside of the twelve bases.
However, the teaching on the twelve bases (āyatana) as spoken by the Buddha is the most supreme and sublime, more so than any other dharma-gate.
Question: For what reason is this teaching the most supreme and sublime?
Answer: Because this is taught as the "bases" (āyatana), it encompasses all dharmas.
Although the teaching of the eighteen elements encompasses all phenomena,
it is an extensive exposition that is difficult to master;
nor is the teaching of the five aggregates merely a concise summary that is difficult to comprehend.
Furthermore, these [aggregates] cannot encompass all phenomena (*dharma*),
because the aggregates do not include the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
Only the teaching of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as taught by the Buddha encompasses all phenomena without exception.
It is neither extensive nor concise;
therefore, it is said to be the most supreme and sublime.
Thus, these words were spoken.
If one wishes to examine the nature and characteristics of all phenomena,
one should rely upon this teaching of the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*).
If one examines the nature and characteristics of all phenomena by relying upon this teaching of the twelve sense bases, [one will understand them correctly].
Thereupon, the light of wisdom regarding the twelve objects of cognition arises,
and the images of the twelve true meanings manifest,
like a person polishing twelve bright mirrors and hanging them in all directions.
If one enters therein, the images of twelve of one's own bodies immediately appear.
Within the body of each and every sentient being, twelve locations can be found. [Question: If there are twelve locations within a single body...
How are the twelve bases (āyatana) established?
Answer: Because their intrinsic natures (svabhāva) and functions (kāritra) differ.
That is to say, although the twelve bases exist within a single body, [they are distinct].
However, because the twelve kinds of intrinsic natures and their functions differ, they do not intermingle with one another,
just as there might be twelve people in a single room, each possessing distinct skills.
Although they occupy the same chamber, there are twelve distinct intrinsic natures and functions.
Furthermore, the twelve bases (āyatana) are established for two reasons:
first, by way of their support; [and second, by way of their objects].
The first consists of the six [faculties],
namely the eye and so forth; the second consists of the six objects of perception, namely form and so forth.
Furthermore, the twelve bases (āyatana) are established for three reasons:
first, by way of their intrinsic nature (svabhāva);
second, by way of their basis (āśraya).
Third, regarding "by way of the object-condition and by way of intrinsic nature," this refers to the establishment of the sense bases from the eye-base up to the mental-object-base (*dharmāyatana*).
"By way of the basis" refers to the establishment of the sense bases from the eye base up to the mind base.
"By way of the object" refers to...
That is to say, the establishment of the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the sense-sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
This is called the intrinsic nature, the substantial entity, the self-essence, the specific characteristic, and the fundamental nature of the sense-spheres.
Thus, the intrinsic nature of the sense-spheres has been explained.
Therefore, it shall now be explained.
Question: Why is it called a "base" (āyatana)?
What is the meaning of "base"?

The answer is: one should understand that the meaning of "basis" (āyatana) is the meaning of "gate of arising," the meaning of "path of arising," the meaning of "storehouse," the meaning of "granary," the meaning of "sūtra," the meaning of "place of slaughter," the meaning of "field," the meaning of "pool," the meaning of "stream," the meaning of "ocean," the meaning of "white," and the meaning of "pure."
Regarding the meaning of "birth-gate" as the meaning of "location":
it is like a city or town from which various things are produced,
by means of which the bodies of sentient beings are nourished and sustained.
In this way, various mental states and mental factors arise internally based upon their support and their objects;
by means of these, the continuity of defilement and purity is nourished.
The meaning of "place" (*sthāna*) is the meaning of the path of arising.
Just as various things grow within a road,
thereby nourishing the bodies of sentient beings,
so too do various mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) arise internally from the basis and the object of cognition.
By means of this, the continuity of defilement and purity is nourished.
Regarding the meaning of "storehouse" (*ālaya*) as the meaning of "location":
it is like a treasury in which precious objects such as gold and silver are accumulated.
In this way, the bases (*āśraya*) and objects (*ālambana*) internally consist of the accumulation of various phenomena, namely mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Regarding the meaning of "granary" (*koṣṭhaka*) as the meaning of "place":
it is like a granary or storehouse where various grains such as rice and wheat are accumulated.
In this way, there is an accumulation of internal mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) based upon their support (āśraya) and their objects (ālambana).
Regarding the meaning of "sūtra" as "place" (sthāna):
it is like the warp threads upon which the various weft threads are woven.
In this way, upon the basis and the object,
various mental states and mental factors are distributed throughout.
The meaning of "place" (*sthāna*) is the sense of being a locus for killing.
Just as on a battlefield one might sever hundreds of thousands of heads and cause them to fall to the ground,
so too, within the basis and the object, there are immeasurable varieties of mind and mental factors.
It is destroyed by impermanence and decay.
Regarding the meaning of "field" as the meaning of "location":
it is like having immeasurable varieties of crops growing within a field.
In this way, various mental states and mental factors grow within the basis and the object;
as for the meaning of "pool" being the meaning of "place," it is as if someone were to ask:
From what pool does the water flow? Where is the path not obstructed?
What encompasses the world? And where do suffering and pleasure alike come to an end?
The World-Honored One replied:
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as all other bases—these comprise name-and-form.
They cause [the water] to flow out from this pool without remainder; herein, no path leads through.
This place encompasses the world; the meaning of "place" (*sthāna*) is the sense of the exhaustion of all flows such as suffering and pleasure.
As it is said in response to a question:
When the various sense-bases are about to flow out, by what can they be restrained?
Once they have already flowed out from them, who could possibly block them?
The World-Honored One replied:

When the [senses] are about to flow out through the various bases, right mindfulness can restrain and prevent them; if they have already flowed out from those, pure wisdom can dam them up. This is the meaning of "bases" (*āyatana*). "Bases" means the sense-faculties and their objects. "Flowing out" means the arising of the mind and mental factors. "Restrain and prevent" means not allowing them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the six internal and external bases. "Flowing out" refers to the six classes of consciousness. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). "Flowing out" refers to the eighteen elements. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination. "Flowing out" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the four nutriments (*āhāra*). "Flowing out" refers to the four nutriments. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*). "Flowing out" refers to the five aggregates. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the six elements (*dhātu*). "Flowing out" refers to the six elements. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the three realms (*dhātu*). "Flowing out" refers to the three realms. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the four truths (*satya*). "Flowing out" refers to the four truths. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). "Flowing out" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). "Flowing out" refers to the eightfold noble path. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*). "Flowing out" refers to the nine successive meditative attainments. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the ten powers (*bala*) of a Tathāgata. "Flowing out" refers to the ten powers of a Tathāgata. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). "Flowing out" refers to the four analytical knowledges. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*) of a Buddha. "Flowing out" refers to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*). "Flowing out" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). "Flowing out" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). "Flowing out" refers to the four right efforts. "Restrain and prevent" means to block the gates of the senses and not allow them to arise. "Already flowed out" means that which has already arisen. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again. This is called the meaning of "bases. Furthermore, "bases" refers to the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). "Flowing out" refers to the four bases of psychic power. "Pure wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the noble ones. "Dam up" means to suppress and obstruct it so that it does not arise again
As the Blessed One has said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that for all classes of sentient beings, the eye is a sea;
the various forms present before them are its waves."
One who exercises self-restraint over the waves of forms can cross the ocean of the eye and escape various perils such as whirlpools and rākṣasas;
this applies extensively to the mind and mental objects as well.
Regarding the statement that "the meaning of 'white' is the meaning of 'base' (āyatana)":
this refers to the fact that the bases such as the eye are coarse, manifest, and clear. Regarding the statement that "the meaning of 'pure' is the meaning of 'base':
[this refers to the fact that they are the basis for the arising of pure phenomena].
This refers to the sense bases, such as the eye, being solid, pure, and limpid;
this is what is meant by "gate of birth" up to "the meaning of purity.
External treatises refer to this as *brūḍana*.
As the renunciant non-Buddhist Mākaṇḍika said:
"Gautama has taught that all the *brāhmaṇas* have entered into my mantra-words."
The term *bhavana* contains two meanings: first,
the meaning of "root" (*mūla*),
and second, the meaning of "productive cause" (*kāraṇa*).
Because the twelve bases (āyatana) serve as the foundation for the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta), and because they are capable of activating the mind and mental factors,
the reasons for establishing the designation "base" have been explained in general.
Now, their characteristics shall be explained individually.
Question: What is the sense base of the eye (*cakṣurāyatana*)?
Answer: All eyes that have seen, are seeing, or will see forms, as well as those that are "participating in the same class" (*tatsabhāga*), are called the sense base of the eye.
The statement "having already seen visible forms, etc. has been explained as in the section on the elements (*dhātu*);
it should be understood that this applies likewise up to the sense base of the mind (*manāyatana*).
Question: What is the sense base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*)?
Answer: Those forms which have been seen, are being seen, or will be seen by the eye, as well as their "homogeneous counterparts" (sabhāga), are called the sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana).
The phrases "already seen" and so forth are as explained previously in the section on the elements (dhātu).
It should be understood that this applies likewise up to the sense-sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Question: If ten of the bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and a portion of the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) all have form as their essential nature, why is only this one called the "base of form"?
Answer: Because in this single base alone, the characteristic of form is coarse and manifest, making it easy to see and easy to understand.
Therefore, it is called the "base of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpāyatana*), whereas other bases are not;
thus, it is established as a distinct name.
Furthermore, this alone is the objective domain of both eyes.
That is to say, because it is the object of the fleshly eye, it is called the "base of form" (*rūpāyatana*);
other bases are not so, and therefore it is given this distinct name.
Furthermore, this base alone is the domain of all three eyes.
That which is perceived by the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the noble wisdom-eye is called the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*).
Other bases are not so; therefore, it is established as a distinct name. Furthermore, this alone is the objective domain of both eyes.
Because it is the objective referent of visual consciousness, it is called the "sphere of form" (rūpāyatana).
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"If that which is the object of both eyes and the objective referent of visual consciousness is established as the name 'sphere of form'."
It is not so in other cases.
Furthermore, if there are distinctions of coarse and subtle, long and short, or this and that location, one may establish the designation "sphere of form" (rūpāyatana);
since other cases lack these features, they are not the sphere of form.
Furthermore, if a thing possesses magnitude, is accumulative, and is easily cognizable, it is designated by the name "visible form base" (*rūpāyatana*).
Other bases are not so; therefore, they are not the visible form base.
Furthermore, if a thing can be planted, grows, and is easily cognizable, it is designated by the name "visible form base."
Since this is not the case in other locations, it is not the case that planting and growth occur in the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*) throughout both internal and external divisions.
Regarding the external division, "planting" refers to the time of sowing the seed,
and "growth" refers to the time of sprouting.
"Long" refers to the stages of stem, leaf, flower, and fruit.
"Internal division" refers to the stage of *kalala*.
"Increasing" refers to the stage of *arbuda*.

The Elder [Vasumitra] says: "The stages such as *peśī*, *ghana*, *arbuda*, and *praśākhā* are also included. Furthermore, if something can be designated as having the nature of spatial extension (*dig-deśatva*), it is established as being the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*);
since other bases do not possess this quality, they are not the sense-base of form."
It is only with respect to the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) that all spatial directions and intrinsic natures are designated,
and not with respect to any other base.
Furthermore, if the nature of a *yojana* could be designated, the name "form-base" would be established for it.
Since it is not so in other locations, it is not the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*).
It is only with respect to the sense-field of form that the nature of all *yojana*s is designated,
and not in any other location.
Furthermore, if it is able to cover other material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), like a cloth or a hat, it is established as having the designation "base of form" (*rūpāyatana*).
Other bases do not possess this quality; therefore, they are not "bases of form."
Only the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) is able to collectively cover all other types of form,
whereas the other bases are not;
furthermore, it is only where both shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) and manifest-color (*varṇa-rūpa*) are present that the name "form-base" is established.
Other locations are not so; therefore, they are not the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
Furthermore, if a location possesses twenty kinds of form, or twenty-one, it is established as having the name "sense-sphere of form.
Other locations are not so; therefore, they are not the sense-sphere of form.
Question: Why is it called the "sphere of tangibles" (spraṣṭavyāyatana)?
Is it called the sphere of tangibles because it is something that can be touched, or is it called the sphere of tangibles because its essence is tangibility?
It is called the "sphere of contact" (spraṣṭavyāyatana) because it is the objective condition for contact.
If that were so, what fault would there be?
There would be faults in all three cases.
Why is this so? If something were called the "sphere of tangibility" (spraṣṭavyāyatana) because it could be touched,
then since atoms do not touch one another at all, [it would follow that there is no sphere of tangibility].
In what sense is the "sphere of the tangible" (spraṣṭavyāyatana) considered tangible?
If it were called the sphere of the tangible because its substance is itself tangible,
then the primary elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādāyarūpa) would not have tangibility as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
In what sense is the essence of the "sphere of tangibles" (spraṣṭavyāyatana) itself tangibility?
If it is called the sphere of tangibles because it is the object-condition (ālambana) of tangibility,
then this would also be the object of other minds and mental factors.
Why is it said that only the object-condition (*ālambana*) is contact?
One should answer: "This is called the sense-field of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) because it is that which is touched.
Question: Since atoms (*paramāṇu*) do not touch one another...
How is it that the sphere of tangibles is "tangible"?
The answer is: this is stated according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), not according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
That is to say, what is commonly said by the world to be the object experienced by the eye is called "visible."
The objects perceived by the ear are called audible;
the objects perceived by the nose are called olfactory;
the objects perceived by the tongue are called gustatory.
The objects experienced by the body are called the tangible;
the objects experienced by the mind are called the cognizable.
Therefore, because they are tangible, they are termed the "tangible base" (spraṣṭavyāyatana).
Furthermore, it is called the sense-base of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) because it gives rise to body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) by way of conditions.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"With the body and contact as conditions, body-consciousness arises."
Because this is the mind that, in the ultimate sense, cognizes objects,
its object of focus is called the sphere of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
Furthermore, this is called the sphere of contact and is also called the sphere of nourishment (*puṣṭyāyatana*).
Because this causes other material phenomena to grow and flourish,
just as that which can increase joy is called a "basis of joy" (*nandī-sthāna*),
this is called a "basis of nourishment" (*puṣṭi-sthāna*) because it can cause growth.
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke thus:
"Do atoms touch one another?
Answer: They do not touch one another."
If they were to touch one another, they would necessarily persist until the second moment.
The Venerable One says:
"In reality, no atoms ever touch one another."
It is merely by way of conventional designation that the term "contact" is applied to what is immediately contiguous.
Some maintain the following view:
atoms do not actually touch one another, nor are they even contiguous.
It is merely because they abide in conjunction and are proximate to one another that the conventional designation "contact" (sparśa) is established.
Question: Since the essential nature of all twelve bases (āyatana) is nothing other than phenomena (dharma), why is only one designated by the name "base of phenomena" (dharmāyatana)?
Answer: Although the substance of all twelve bases (āyatana) is entirely dharma, there is no fault in designating the name "dharma-base" (dharmāyatana) for only one of them;
for there is an illustrative analogy.
Just as with the eighteen elements (*dhātu*),
although their substance is entirely dharma,
the designation "dharma-element" is applied to only one of them.
Furthermore, just as although the ten knowledges all take phenomena (dharma) as their object,
the name "knowledge of phenomena" (dharmajñāna) is applied to only one of them;
likewise with the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga).
Although all [of these] are capable of discerning phenomena (dharmapravicaya),
the name "discernment-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment" (dharmapravicaya-sambodhyaṅga) is established for only one among them.
It is also like the case of the six recollections (anusmṛti).
Although all take phenomena as their objects,
only one is designated by the name "recollection of phenomena" (*dharmānusmṛti*);
it is just like the case of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Although all [of these] take phenomena as their object,
the designation "application of mindfulness to phenomena" (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) is applied to only one of them. It is just as,
for example, although all four types of verified confidence (avetyaprasāda) take phenomena as their object...
However, among these, only one is designated by the name "verified confidence in the Dharma" (*dharmanidhyānābhisampratyaya*).
It is just as, although all four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) take phenomena as their object,
only one is designated by the name "analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, just as the Three Jewels and the three refuges, though all are in essence *dharma*,
are designated by the names "Dharma Jewel" and "Dharma Refuge" only for one of them,
so too it is here: although the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are all in essence *dharma*.
However, there is no fault in designating it by a single name only for the locus of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Furthermore, the locus of phenomena has one name,
while the other loci have two names.
The first type of name refers to a common name,
because all twelve bases (āyatana) are phenomena (dharma).
The second type of name refers to both common and uncommon names.
The shared names are as previously stated.
As for the unshared names, they refer to the sense bases such as the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*).
These unshared names are made explicit so that they may be easily understood.
Because the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) has no other name that is not shared [with other categories], it reveals only those names that are shared;
therefore, it is called the "sphere of phenomena.
Furthermore, it gives rise to the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Because it is subsumed under this [category] alone, it is uniquely called the "dharma-base" (dharmāyatana).
Furthermore, the four characteristics of the conditioned are the seal, stamp, and insignia of all conditioned phenomena,
as they distinguish the conditioned from the unconditioned.
Because those characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are subsumed exclusively within this [base], it alone is called the "base of phenomena" (dharmāyatana).

Furthermore, because the bodies of names (nāmakāya), phrases (padakāya), and phonemes (vyañjanakāya)—which express, reveal, and make easy to understand the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all phenomena—are subsumed exclusively within this [base], it alone is called the "base of phenomena."
Furthermore, just as windows and openings are called "air-paths" because air passes through them,
so too is the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana);
it is called the sphere of phenomena because it serves as the common source from which all phenomena arise.
Because all afflictions, karma, meditative concentrations, wisdom,
and so forth are able to produce all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*),
and because they are also able to universally realize unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Furthermore, there is the door of liberation that realizes all phenomena are empty and selfless;
because it is subsumed within this [sphere], it is called the "dharma-sphere" (*dharmāyatana*).
Question: How can one grasp at phenomena as a self or what belongs to a self?
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is also included here.
Why, then, is this place not called the "place of the self"?
Answer: The view of a self-identity is a false attachment.
It is not understood by way of designating the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;
therefore, the name "self" is not established here.
Since the gate of liberation of emptiness realizes the true nature of phenomena, this place is designated as "dharma" based upon that.
Furthermore, analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), which is nirvāṇa, is permanent, wholesome, immutable, and unchanging;
it cannot be destroyed by birth, old age, sickness, or death, and is thus the ultimate reality (paramārtha-dharma).
Because that dharma is subsumed exclusively within this [sphere], it alone is called the "dharma-sphere" (dharma-āyatana).
Furthermore, it is the wisdom that analyzes the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena,
establishes the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, and—
by dispelling delusion regarding intrinsic nature and delusion regarding objects of perception— understands all phenomena as they truly are, neither increasing nor decreasing them.
It is called the "dharma-base" (dharmāyatana) because it alone subsumes [all phenomena];
other bases do not do so, and therefore they are given distinct names.
Furthermore, this base is called the dharma-base because it subsumes many dharmas.
Regarding the inclusion of many phenomena:
this refers to the presence herein of both material and non-material phenomena,
as well as associated and dissociated phenomena.
There are phenomena that have a basis and phenomena that lack a basis;
phenomena that have an object of cognition and phenomena that lack an object of cognition;
phenomena that have mental aspects and phenomena that lack mental aspects.
There are phenomena that are with vigilance and those without vigilance;
there are conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena.
Because it is not so in other instances, these are established as distinct categories.
Furthermore, this sphere is called the "sphere of mental objects" (dharmāyatana) because it relates to the mind;
whereas the spheres of the eye and so forth relate only to visible forms and so forth,
only the sphere of the mind relates to all phenomena (dharmas).
Regarding the mind-base (*manāyatana*), it receives its general name individually.
Due to various causes and conditions such as these, one among the twelve bases is specifically called the "dharma-base" (*dharmāyatana*).
Having thus explained the individual characteristics of each of the bases, [the text continues].
Now, the sequence of the bases (*āyatana*) should be explained further.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One first teach the internal bases and subsequently the external bases?
Answer: Because they were taught according to the sequence of the supports (*āśraya*) and objects (*ālambana*) of the six consciousnesses.
Question: For what reason does the Blessed One first speak of the eye-base among the six internal bases, and so on up to lastly speaking of the mind-base;
and among the six external bases, first speak of the form-base?
Up to the point where it later states, "in the place of teaching the Dharma," the answer is:
because it accords with the characteristics expressed by the phrasing and terminology;
furthermore, because it accords with the sequence of the teacher, the recipient, and the upholder of the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is because they follow the sequence of the coarse and the subtle.
That is to say, among the six internal bases, the eye-base is the coarsest;
therefore, it is mentioned first.
Up to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), which is the most subtle;
therefore, it is mentioned last. Among the six external spheres, the sphere of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*) is the coarsest;
therefore, it is mentioned first.
Furthermore, they are mentioned last because the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is the most subtle.
Moreover, they are taught according to the sequence of the determinate and the indeterminate:
among the six internal spheres, the first five are determinate in apprehending present objects, and are therefore mentioned first.
The sphere of mind (manāyatana) is mentioned last because its apprehension of objects is not fixed;
that is to say, it takes as its objects either collectively or individually the dharmas of the three time periods as well as unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas.
Among the first five bases (*āyatana*), the first four are mentioned earlier because they invariably apprehend derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*);
the body base (*kāyāyatana*) is mentioned later because its apprehension of objects is not determinate.
This refers to both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derived matter.
Whether taken collectively or individually as objects of apprehension (*grāhya*),
among the first four bases (*āyatana*), those that are distant, rapid, or clear with respect to their objects of apprehension are mentioned first;
those contrary to these are mentioned later.
This is explained according to the sequential order of the six internal bases;
the sequence of the six external bases is likewise.
Furthermore, it is explained according to the sequential order of the bases from lower to higher.
That is to say, within a single body, the sense-base of the eye is the highest;
the sense-base of the ear is next lower; the sense-base of the nose is next lower; the sense-base of the tongue is next lower; and the body mostly resides in the lower part.
Because the mind has no fixed location, it is mentioned last.
This is explained according to the sequential order of the six internal bases;
it should be understood that the same applies to the six external bases.
Furthermore, this statement is made based on the sequence of etiquette when sentient beings encounter one another.
That is to say, when they meet,
they first look at one another,
and then engage in conversation.
Next, offer incense and flowers;
next, provide food and drink;
next, bestow fine bedding and other such necessities.
Because they thus attain mutual understanding at the very end,
the sequence of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) is as described above. *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 73.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Seventy-four,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Four of the Fourth Sub-section on the Ten Gates within the Second Aggregate of Bonds (Saṃyojana-skandha). Question: How are the internal bases (ādhyātmikāyatana) and external bases (bāhyāyatana) established?
Is it by relying on the Dharma or by relying on the self?
If so, what is the fault?
There is a fault in both cases.
Why is this so? Because if one relies upon phenomena, phenomena lack functional activity;
and within all phenomena that lack functional activity, [there is no agent].
How are the internal and external bases established?
If there is no real self upon which to rely,
how can the internal and external bases be established based on a self?
Answer: They are established solely based on the dharmas, yet not all are so designated.
That is to say, the six groups of consciousness are the locus upon which defiled and pure dharmas depend.
Those that serve as the support for these six consciousnesses are called internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
That which acts as an object of perception is called an external base (*bāhyāyatana*).
Thus, the names "internal" and "external" bases are established based on the phenomena themselves.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is a faculty (*indriya*), it is established as an internal base.
If a phenomenon is a faculty (*indriya*), it is established as an external base (*bāhyāyatana*).
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is a subject (*viṣayin*), it is established as an internal base (*adhyātmikāyatana*);
if a phenomenon is an object (*viṣaya*), it is established as an external base.
Some say that the internal and external bases (āyatana) are established in dependence upon a self (ātman),
and that this self is none other than the mind (citta).
Because it is the basis for the grasping of a self,
the designation "self" is conventionally established upon this mind,
as stated in the sūtra:
By well-taming oneself, the wise attain birth in heaven;
one should well-tame the mind, for a tamed mind can lead to happiness.
Once the mind is well-tamed, then one has truly tamed oneself.
Therefore, one should know that the designation "self" is provisionally established upon the mind;
that which serves as the basis for this "mine" is established as the internal sense base (*ādhyātmikāyatana*),
and that which is the object of this "mine" is established as the external sense base (*bāhyāyatana*).
However, the designations "internal" and "external" are not ultimately established (pariniṣpanna). This is because that which is internal to me is external to another,
and that which is external to me is internal to another.
Moreover, the designation of "internal" and "external" based on a single [basis] is not indeterminate;
as it is said in a sutra:
"O bhikṣus, you..."
One should know the six internal bases as they truly are.
Question: One should also know the six external bases as they truly are.
Why, then, did the Blessed One exhort [disciples] to know only the internal bases?
Answer: The World-Honored One intended to cause his disciples to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) primarily through the internal gate.
As it is said in a sutra:
"O bhikṣus, you..."
One should observe that the internal faculties should not take external objects as their conditions.
Furthermore, the Blessed One intended for his disciples to cultivate internal meditative concentration (dhyāna) without any augmentation.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"O bhikṣus, you should cultivate meditative concentration within and not falsely superimpose [the notions of] permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
O bhikṣus, you should cultivate meditative concentration within and observe things as they truly are."
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; they arise from causes, originate from conditions, and are produced through accumulation.
By means of these eight aspects of noble wisdom, one should at all times contemplate all states of existence.
Furthermore, the Blessed One desired to cause his disciples to cultivate the uncommon meditative concentration within themselves.
As the Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus, you..."

"You should cultivate internal concentration; you should not practice those common forms of meditative absorption, namely, the contemplations of coarseness, suffering, obstacles, tranquility, excellence, and detachment.
You, bhikṣus, should cultivate internal concentration."
It means that one should cultivate the uncommon meditative concentration (asādhāraṇa-dhyāna) to contemplate all states of existence as being like a disease,
like an abscess, like an arrow piercing the body,
harmful, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
By means of these eight kinds of superior investigative staffs,
one is able to thoroughly subdue all that is subject to birth.
Furthermore, in this sutra:
The reason why one is exhorted only to observe the six internal bases is that the internal is the basis upon which the external depends;
thus, one is also exhorted to observe the latter.
Why is this so? Because when there is a self, there arises what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*).
Because there is the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), there is the view of what belongs to a self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).
Because there are five views of a self, there are fifteen views of what belongs to a self.
Because there is attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*), there is attachment to what belongs to a self (*ātmīya-grāha*).
Because there is delusion regarding a self, there is delusion regarding what belongs to a self (*ātmīya-moha*).
Because there is craving for a self, there is craving for what belongs to a self.
To nourish the internal self, one seeks external requisites.
Furthermore, the Blessed One, wishing to cause his disciples to first cultivate the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding internal phenomena,
taught that the practitioner first cultivates the foundations of mindfulness by taking internal phenomena as their object.
Only after it has been fully accomplished does one then take external objects as an object.
Due to various causes and conditions such as these,
the Blessed One exhorted [practitioners] to know only the internal.
As it is said in the Sūtra that there are six internal bases (ādhyātmikāyatana),
and as the Sūtra further states that there are six bases of contact (sparśāyatana),
one asks: what is the distinction between these two sets of six bases?
Some may say that these two are not distinct. Why is this?
The six internal bases are the six bases of contact;
the six bases of contact are the six internal bases.
Although there is a difference in terminology, there is no distinction in meaning.
Furthermore, there are those who say that there is indeed a distinction;
namely, that "name" (nāma) itself is a specific designation, for the six internal bases are designated as the "six bases of contact" (ṣaṭ-spraṣṭavyāyatana).
Furthermore, those which are of the same class are called the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Those which are of the same class as them are called the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-adhyātma-āyatana*).
Furthermore, all phenomena that are subject to arising are called the six bases of contact.
Dharmas that cannot arise are called the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*).
Furthermore, those possessing functional activity are called the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśāyatana*),
while those lacking functional activity are called the six internal bases.
If one were to say this:
those that are present are called the six bases of contact (ṣaḍ-āyatana),
while those that are past and future are called the six internal bases (ṣaḍ-adhyātma-āyatana).
Furthermore, those that have already arisen are called the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśāyatana*);
those not yet arisen are called the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*).
If one were to speak in this way:
Those of the past and present are called the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Those of the future are called the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-adhyātma-āyatana*).
Furthermore, that upon which the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) correctly depend and abide is called the six bases of contact.
The mind and mental factors, which do not abide in a proper basis but merely revolve in emptiness,
are called the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*).
