until when the aggregate of consciousness arises, that very aggregate of consciousness ceases.
There is a causal condition for saying that one dharma arises and another dharma ceases;
namely, that which belongs to the future world arises and that which belongs to the present world ceases.
Question: When all conditioned dharmas arise in the future...
If it were produced from the world as its substance, or produced within the world,
what fault would there be in either case?
Both positions entail errors.
Why is this? If the essence of phenomena were to arise,
then when a single phenomenon arises, all phenomena of the future world should likewise arise.
Once this has already arisen, there should be no future;
once this has already ceased, there should be no present.
Thus, the doctrine that all exists throughout the three times would be destroyed if [existence] were to arise within the time periods.
How is it that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) do not belong to different worlds?
One should answer:
Because there are causes and conditions, one speaks of the arising of the substance of the world.
Because the very moment an action arises is its arising in the future,
it is said to arise within a time-period due to the presence of causes and conditions;
for an action in the future consists of many moments.
Because among these, only one arises at a single moment.
Question: When conditioned phenomena arise in the future, do they arise through their own nature (*svabhāva*) or through the nature of another (*parabhāva*)?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
Both positions possess errors. Why is this?
If they were produced by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
how could it be that what was originally without intrinsic nature now possesses intrinsic nature,
or that what was originally without a real entity now possesses a real entity?
If things were produced through other-nature (parabhāva),
how could they not abandon their own-nature (svabhāva) and thus come to possess the characteristic of being without nature?
One should answer as follows:
It is not produced from self-nature,
nor is it produced from other-nature;
rather, within self-nature, such phenomena arise and subsequently cease.
Question: If a dharma has the nature of form (*rūpa*), does that dharma have the nature of the past?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are phenomena that have the nature of form but not the nature of the past;
namely, future and present forms.
There are phenomena that have the nature of the past but not the nature of form.
This refers to the nature of the four past aggregates.
There are phenomena that are both of the nature of form and of the nature of the past;
this refers to the nature of past form.
There are phenomena that are neither of the nature of form (*rūpa*) nor of the nature of the past.
These refer to the nature of the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the future and present, as well as the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is analogous to the fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*) established by contrasting the nature of form with the nature of the past.
By correlating the nature of form with its future and present natures, there are likewise four sets of four propositions for each.
Just as the aggregate of form has three sets of four propositions when correlated with the three periods of time,
so it is for the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness when correlated with the three periods of time.
Thus, there are fifteen sets of four propositions.
Question: If a phenomenon has the nature of form (*rūpa*), does that phenomenon have the nature of spatial location (*deśa*)?
Answer: If a phenomenon has the nature of spatial location, it is necessarily of the nature of matter (*rūpa*).
However, there are phenomena that are of the nature of matter but do not have the nature of spatial location;
namely, past and future matter.
And as for the nature of present atoms and non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Question: If a phenomenon has the nature of feeling (*vedanā*), does that phenomenon not have the nature of spatial location?
Answer: If a dharma is of the nature of feeling (*vedanā*), it is certainly not of the nature of spatial location (*deśa*).
There are dharmas that are not of the nature of spatial location but are not of the nature of feeling;
these are the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
As well as atoms (*paramāṇu*), non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It should be understood that this applies likewise to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth, up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Question: If a phenomenon is material (*rūpa*), [how is it so]?
Does that phenomenon possess resistance?
Answer: If a phenomenon possesses resistance, it is necessarily form (*rūpa*).
However, there are phenomena that are form yet lack resistance.
That is to say: past and future form, as well as present atoms and unmanifest form.
Question: If a phenomenon is feeling...
"Can that dharma experience [an object]?
Answer: "If a dharma can experience [an object], it is necessarily feeling (*vedanā*).
However, there are dharmas that are feeling but are not capable of experiencing."
This refers to past and future feeling.
Question: If a dharma is perception (*saṃjñā*), does that dharma apprehend an image (*nimitta*)?
Answer: If a phenomenon is able to apprehend a characteristic, it is necessarily perception (*saṃjñā*).
However, there are phenomena that are perception yet are not able to apprehend a characteristic;
namely, past and future perceptions.
Question: If a phenomenon is a formation (*saṃskāra*), is that phenomenon capable of performing an action?
Answer: If a phenomenon is capable of performing an action, it is necessarily a formation.
There are phenomena that are formations but not volitional activities;
these refer to past and future formations.
Question: If a phenomenon is consciousness, does that phenomenon cognize?
Answer: If a phenomenon is capable of discerning an object, it is necessarily consciousness.
However, there are phenomena that are consciousness yet not capable of discerning;
these refer to past and future consciousnesses.
Question: Future dharmas have emergence but no entry;
past dharmas have entry but no emergence.
Why, then, is decrease not established for the future?
How is it that increase is not designated for the past?
The Venerable Vasumitra stated:
"Because they have already been counted, decrease is not designated for the future."
Furthermore, it is asked: "Is increase not established for the past?
Since [the past] has not yet been calculated as a number, how can one say that decrease cannot be established for the future or that increase cannot be established for the past?
However, because past and future phenomena are infinite in measure,
it is impossible to establish that they increase or decrease;
they are like the waters of the great ocean, which are immeasurable and boundless.
He took hundreds of thousands of jars and did not perceive their depletion;
he cast in hundreds of thousands of jars and did not perceive their increase.
He further spoke these words:
Because future phenomena have not yet arisen and have not yet ceased, one does not designate them as decreasing;
because past phenomena have already arisen and have already ceased, one does not designate them as increasing.
Furthermore, it is said:
because future phenomena have not yet arisen and have not yet ceased, one does not designate them as "decreasing";
because past phenomena have already arisen and have already ceased, one does not designate them as "increasing."
Furthermore, it is said:
because future phenomena have not yet arisen and have not yet departed, decrease is not predicated of them;
because past phenomena have already arisen and have already departed, increase is not predicated of them.
As it is with origination in relation to cessation,
destruction, and separation, so too is the detailed exposition for birth in relation to cessation, destruction,
and separation. The Venerable One said:
If there were obstructed things flowing through the world,
one could say that they are conventionally established as having decrease or increase;
however, conditioned phenomena arise because their conditions converge, and having arisen, they immediately perish.
"How is it that one establishes that the past increases and the future decreases?
The Venerable Pārśva replied,
"Past and future dharmas lack functional activity."
How can it be established that there is increase and decrease?
Question: Do the past and future exist as accumulated entities, like walls and other objects in the present world?
Is it because there is no accumulation and each [element] is dispersed?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
There is a fault in both cases.
Why is this? If there were accumulations such as walls and so forth in the present world,
how could the effort of a donor in creating the objects to be relinquished not be in vain?
Why is it that the past and future have no spatial location?
Why is it that walls and such things are not all eternal?
Why is it that the past and future cannot be perceived through direct observation?
If there were no accumulation and each [moment] were to disperse individually,
how could it be said that past events exist?
As it is stated in the Sūtra:
In the past, there was a king named Mahāsudarśana who resided in the city of Gandhamādana at the Palace of Good Dharma (Sudharmā).
Such matters as these were immeasurable and boundless.
How can it be said that future events exist?
As a sūtra states:
"In the future there will be a Buddha named Maitreya."
At that time, there was a king named Śaṅkha,
whose capital city was named Ketumatī.
Such matters as these were immeasurable and boundless.
How is it that the knowledge of recollecting past lives contemplates past events;
the knowledge of death and rebirth contemplates future events;
and the knowledge of the excellence of vows contemplates both past and future events?
When future phenomena gather in the present,
how could these aggregated entities not be something that was previously non-existent and now exists?
And when present phenomena disperse into the past...
How can it be that an accumulation of things does not exist before it ceases to exist?
Some offer this explanation:
past and future [dharmas] also possess accumulation.
It is like objects such as walls in the present world. Question:
If that is so, while the latter objection has been successfully resolved, how should the former objection be resolved?
Furthermore, would not the effort exerted by donors in creating the objects they intend to give be in vain?
Answer: No, because it is directly perceived.
This means that although the object already exists before it is fashioned, it is not yet perceptible;
only after the donor has fashioned it can it be perceived.
Therefore, it is not wasted.
How is it that the past and the future have no spatial location?
Answer: If one grants that they do have a spatial location, what fault would there be?
Why then are walls and such things not all eternal?
Answer: Because it is conjoined with momentary impermanence.
Why are the past and future not perceptible?
Answer: Because they are not objects of the five present consciousnesses, they are not perceptible.
It must serve as the object of the five present consciousnesses to be visible;
the critique states that past and future things do not exist as accumulated aggregates like present objects, but rather exist only as individual, scattered entities.
Question: If that is so, the previous objection has been successfully resolved;
however, how should the subsequent objection be resolved?
Furthermore, how can it be said that past phenomena exist?
Answer: As was explained regarding the past and present, there is likewise no fault.
How can it be said that future phenomena exist?
Answer: As will be explained regarding the future and the present, there is likewise no fault.
How does the knowledge of recollecting past abodes (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna) and so forth observe events of the past and future?
Answer: It observes the events of the past and future just as they were previously experienced and just as they will be experienced.
What fault is there in this that it cannot be explained? Furthermore, some say:
just as when various syllables are uttered in successive succession, they give rise to names and phrases which manifest the meaning to be expressed.
Although those letters cannot be accumulated,
they are able to induce the arising of names and phrases that manifest meaning;
likewise, although the dharmas of the past and future worlds lack any accumulation, [they function in the same way].
And it is able to generate wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding the objects of knowledge that should be known according to their respective natures,
there are those who say that one contemplates the past and future by means of present phenomena as analogies.
Just as a farmer knows the past and future by means of the crops currently being cultivated,
so too, when future dharmas assemble in the present,
how could these gathered things not have existed previously and only now come to be?
When present phenomena disperse into the past, how could a composite entity that was not already non-existent become non-existent again?
The answer is: all phenomena of the three periods of time possess the nature of cause and the nature of fruit.
They are established in their respective order according to what is appropriate;
in substance they are eternally present, neither increasing nor decreasing,
but are said to exist or not to exist based solely upon their functional activity.
All things that are aggregates exist as mere designations based upon substantially existent entities.
Sometimes it exists and sometimes it does not.
What fault or difficulty is there in this school’s acceptance of such existence and non-existence?
It is simply that they cannot account for the various states [of the object].
Because existence and non-existence are what is accepted [by us].
*Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle seventy-six;
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle seventy.
Compiled by seven hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Two: The Aggregate of Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha), Chapter Four: The Ten Gates of Summary (Daśamukha-saṃgraha), Part Seven. Within the Sarvāstivāda school, there were four great masters of the treatises.
Each establishes a distinction between the two time periods in a different way:
the Venerable Dharmatrāta asserts that there is a difference in their substantial nature (*bhāva*),
while the Venerable Ghoṣaka asserts that there is a difference in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The Venerable Vasumitra says there is a difference in state (*avasthā*).
The Venerable Buddhadeva says there is a difference in dependence (*apekṣā*).
As for those who say there is a difference in category (*jāti*):
He maintains that when phenomena evolve within the world, there is a difference in their mode (ākāra) but no difference in their substance (dravya).
This is like when gold vessels and the like are broken to be made into other objects; although their shape differs, their color remains unchanged.
Furthermore, just as when milk and the like transform into curd and the like, they relinquish their taste, potency, and so forth, but do not relinquish their visible color;
in this same way, when these dharmas pass from the future world into the present world.
Although one relinquishes the future category and acquires the present category,
the essence of that dharma is neither acquired nor relinquished.
Furthermore, when it proceeds from the present world to the past world, [the same applies].
Although one relinquishes the present category and acquires the past category,
the substance of that dharma itself is neither acquired nor relinquished.
This is what is meant by saying their characteristics differ.
He [the opponent] says that when phenomena proceed through the time periods,
there is a difference in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) but not a difference in their substance (*dravya*).
Each phenomenon of a single time period possesses the characteristics of all three time periods.
When one characteristic is correctly conjoined, the other two characteristics are not separated;
just as when a person is currently impassioned by the beauty of one woman,
they are not said to be free from passion for other women.
When these dharmas abide in the past,
they are precisely conjoined with the characteristics of the past;
they are not said to be separated from the characteristics of the other two time periods.
When abiding in the future time,
it is precisely conjoined with the characteristics of the future;
it is not said to be dissociated from the characteristics of the other two times.
When abiding in the present time,
it is correctly conjoined with the characteristics of the present;
regarding the characteristics of the other two times, it is not said to be dissociated from them.
Regarding the statement that there is a difference in states:
they claim that when phenomena evolve through time,
there is a difference in their states but not a difference in their essence.
It is like moving a single counting-stick:
when placed in the unit position, it is called one;
when placed in the tens position, it is called ten.
Placing one hundred units in the hundreds place is called "one hundred.
Although the positions differ as they pass through the places, the substance of the counting sticks remains unchanged.
In this same way, all phenomena pass through the positions of the three periods of time.
Although it receives three names, its essence is without distinction.
According to this master’s position, the time periods are not confused,
for he establishes the distinctions of the three times based on activity.
That is to say, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) that have not yet performed their function are called the future;
those currently performing their function are called the present;
and those whose function has already ceased are called the past.
Regarding the statement that [difference] depends on relativity:
this means that when phenomena evolve through time, they are established as having difference based on their mutual dependence of prior and posterior states.

For example, a single woman is designated "daughter" in relation to her mother and "mother" in relation to her own daughter; although there is no distinction in her actual substance, she receives the names "daughter" and "mother" due to the difference in her relations.
In this way, these phenomena are called "past" in dependence upon what follows;
they are called "future" in dependence upon what precedes;
and they are called "present" when both are depended upon.
The temporal periods established by that master are confused.
Why is this? Because each individual period contains all three periods through their mutual dependence on one another.
That is to say, the preceding and succeeding moments of the past are called "past" and "future," while the intermediate moment is called "present" and "future.
The same should apply to the categories of the three periods of time.

If dharmas of the present world, though existing for only a single moment, were to depend on what follows, what precedes, and what is simultaneous with them, they would consequently have to be established as belonging to all three time periods;
how could this possibly accord with correct reasoning?
This is because their characteristics are said to be distinct.
The three times established [by you] are also confused,
because you admit that the phenomena of each individual time possess the characteristics of all three times.
As for those who claim there is a difference in their categories:
To claim that it is explained as a "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*) because it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is also irrational;
for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), when they pass from the future into the present, their prior homogeneous state would have to perish.
If [an entity] were to arise later from the present into the past,
how could it be consistent with correct reasoning that there is arising in the past and cessation in the future? Therefore,
only the third [position], which establishes the time periods [as real entities], is sound.
Because conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) can possess functional activity,
there are furthermore three types of dharmas:
namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas.
Question: What are wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*)?
Answer: The five wholesome aggregates (*skandha*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: What are unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma*)?
Answer: The five aggregates of the unwholesome.
Question: What are the indeterminate phenomena?
Answer: The five aggregates of the indeterminate, as well as space and non-analytical cessation.
The remaining meanings are explained in detail as in the previous "Unwholesome" section.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
namely, dharmas bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
Question: What are the phenomena associated with the desire realm?
Answer: The five aggregates associated with the desire realm.
Question: What are the phenomena associated with the form realm?
Answer: The five aggregates associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Question: What are the phenomena associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Answer: The four aggregates associated with the formless realm.
The remaining meanings are explained in detail as in the preceding *Asubha-uddeśa* (Chapter on the Unwholesome).
Furthermore, there are three categories of phenomena:
namely, those of the learner (*śaikṣa*), those of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and those that are neither of the learner nor the non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Question: What are the dharmas of training?
Answer: They are the five aggregates of training.
Question: What are the dharmas beyond training?
Answer: The five aggregates of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Question: What are the dharmas that are neither of training nor beyond training?
Answer: The five contaminated aggregates (sāsrava-skandha) and the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta).
Question: What is the meaning of the three dharmas, such as training (śikṣā) and so forth?
Answer: Training means that by means of the path free from greed, hatred, and delusion, one trains to abandon greed, hatred, and delusion.
Non-training means that by means of the path free from greed, hatred, and delusion, one does not train to abandon greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because they have already trained in abandonment, this is the meaning of "beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
That which is contrary to both is the meaning of "neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
Furthermore, it is because there is no path of craving.
Training in the severance of pleasant and unpleasant phenomena is the meaning of training (*śikṣā*).
By stating that one trains in severing attachment through the path of non-attachment,
the path of no-more-training (*aśaikṣamārga*) is excluded.
Regarding "unpleasant things," this excludes the mundane path;
for there is no path of non-attachment, as one has already trained in the abandonment of attachment and has completed that training.
Furthermore, "not being a matter of craving" is the meaning of "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).
Because there is no path of craving for one who does not train in abandoning craving,
this excludes the path of training (*śaikṣa*).
That which is "not the desired object" excludes the mundane path;
being contrary to both [the mundane and supramundane], it is the meaning of being neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Furthermore, the meaning of "training" (śaikṣa) is the training in the abandonment of afflictions and the training in the clear realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya).
Because one has not yet trained in the abandonment of afflictions, nor has one already completed the training in their abandonment;
and because one has not yet trained in the clear realization of the truths, nor has one already completed the clear realization of the truths, this is the meaning of "beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
That which is contrary to these two is the meaning of being neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
Furthermore, a trainee abandons two types of seeking— namely, the seeking of sensual desire (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*) and the seeking of existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*)—
while a trainee fulfills one type of seeking.
That is to say, the seeking of the holy life (brahmacarya) is the meaning of "training" (śikṣā).
This is because one has not yet trained in the abandonment of the two seekings, whereas through training, one has already abandoned them.
Not training for the sake of fulfilling the one [goal] constitutes the meaning of "beyond training" (aśaikṣa), because that which has already been fulfilled is beyond training.
Being contrary to both [training and beyond training] constitutes the meaning of "neither training nor beyond training" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
Furthermore, if within a continuum there is both the acquisition of afflictions and the acquisition of the untainted path,
yet one trains in abandoning the afflictions, this is the meaning of "training" (śaikṣa).
If within the continuum there is no acquisition of afflictions (*kleśa-prāpti*),
but there is the acquisition of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga-prāpti*),
then because one has already trained in abandoning the afflictions and has completed that training, this constitutes the meaning of "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).
That which is contrary to these two is the meaning of being neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, if within a mental continuum (*saṃtāna*) that has not yet abandoned craving,
there is the attainment of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) by which one trains to abandon craving, this is the meaning of being a learner (*śaikṣa*).
If, within the continuum, one has already abandoned craving and possesses the attainment of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*),
it is the meaning of "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*) because one has already trained in abandoning craving.
That which is contrary to both [the states of being in training and beyond training] is the meaning of "neither in training nor beyond training" (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, that which is subsumed under the paths of seeing and cultivation has the meaning of "in training" (śaikṣa).

That which is subsumed under the path of no-more-learning has the meaning of "beyond training" (aśaikṣa). That which is contrary to both has the meaning of "neither in training nor beyond training" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
Furthermore, that which is comprised within the stages of seeing and cultivation has the meaning of "in training" (śaikṣa).
That which is comprised within the stage of no-more-learning has the meaning of "beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
That which is contrary to both has the meaning of "neither in training nor beyond training" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
Furthermore, the meaning of "learner" (*śaikṣa*) is subsumed under the faculty of "knowing the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*).
The meaning of "non-learner" (*aśaikṣa*) is subsumed under the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
That which is contrary to both is the meaning of "neither learner nor non-learner" (*naivaśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa*).

Furthermore, the various untainted paths within the bodies of the five noble individuals— the follower by faith (śraddhānusārin), the follower by dharma (dharmānusārin), the one resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta),
the one attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), and the body-witness (kāyasākṣin)— constitute the meaning of "training" (śaikṣa).
These include those liberated through wisdom (prajñāvimukta) and those liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).
The various untainted paths within the bodies of the two types of noble ones constitute the meaning of "beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
That which is contrary to these two constitutes the meaning of "neither in training nor beyond training" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
Furthermore, this refers to the four stages of approach (pratipannaka) and the first three fruits of realization (phala).
The various untainted paths within the bodies of the seven noble beings constitute the meaning of "training" (śaikṣa).
The various untainted paths within the body of the one noble being who has attained the fourth fruit constitute the meaning of "beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
That which is contrary to these two is the meaning of being neither-learner-nor-non-learner.

Furthermore, all untainted paths within the bodies of the eighteen types of learners are the meaning of "learner," and all untainted paths within the bodies of the nine types of non-learners are the meaning of "non-learner."
That which is contrary to these two is the meaning of being neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).

Question: For one who abides in the fruit of a learner (*śaikṣaphala*), as long as they have not yet given rise to the path of superior fruit (*viśeṣamārga*), why are their various untainted paths (*anāsravamārga*) called "learner"?
Answer: Because the intention (*āśaya*) of one in training has not yet ceased, that untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) is also called "in training.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas.
This refers to phenomena that are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and those that are not abandoned (*aheya*).
Question: What are phenomena abandoned through seeing?

Answer: Those abandoned by the patiences (*kṣānti*) at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamaya-anta*) for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
What, then, is this? It refers to the eighty-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through seeing, as well as the mind and mental factors associated with them,
and the non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra) originated by them.
These are called the factors to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*).
Question: What are the factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Answer: They are those abandoned through cultivation by the learner (*śaikṣa*) who has seen the tracks [of the path].
What, then, is this? It refers to the ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation,
as well as the two types of action— bodily and vocal— that are associated with them and arise in conjunction with them.
The formations dissociated from consciousness that arise together with them,
as well as all non-defiled impure phenomena,
are called the factors to be abandoned by cultivation.
Question: What are the dharmas that are not subject to abandonment?
Answer: The five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha) and the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta).
The remaining meanings are explained in detail as in the previous section on unwholesome factors (*akuśala-nikāya*).
As for the Four Truths (*catvāri satyāni*),
they are the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the sake of extensively analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
That is to say, the sūtras state that there are four noble truths.
Although this has been stated, it has not been extensively analyzed.
Since the Sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies,
that which was not previously explained therein shall now be set forth.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these Four Noble Truths?
The masters of the Abhidharma say:
The five aggregates of clinging are the truth of suffering.
The cause of outflows is the truth of origination.
Their analytical cessation is the truth of cessation. The factors of those in training and those beyond training are the truth of the path.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
all name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya);
karma and afflictions (kleśa) are the truth of origination (samudayasatya).
The exhaustion of karma and afflictions is the truth of cessation;
śamatha and vipaśyanā are the truth of the path.
Thus say the Vibhajyavādins.
If there are the eight characteristics of suffering, these are suffering and constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are suffering but are not the Truth of Suffering.
Craving that brings about renewed existence (*paunarbhavikī-tṛṣṇā*) is origination and constitutes the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Other forms of craving and other causes of outflows are the origin of suffering, but not the Truth of Origin.
The exhaustion of the craving that invites future existence is cessation, and it is the Truth of Cessation.
Other forms of craving and the exhaustion of other causes of outflows are cessation, but not the Truth of Cessation.
Training in the noble eightfold path is both the path and the truth of the path;
other factors of training and all factors of one beyond training are the path but not the truth of the path.
If one speaks thus:
All Arhats accomplish only the two truths of suffering and cessation;
they do not accomplish the two truths of origination and the path. Why is this so?
The Venerable Ghosaka stated: "Because craving for future existence has been completely severed by Arhats,
and because all [factors] have already been relinquished when one attains the fruit of Arhatship through the Noble Eightfold Path."
Whether they fall within the five aggregates of one's own continuum,
or within the five aggregates of another's continuum,
or within the aggregates categorized as sentient or non-sentient.
All such things as these are suffering; they constitute the Truth of Suffering.
When a practitioner of meditation gives rise to clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they perceive only the five aggregates belonging to their own continuum as suffering.
One does not regard the five aggregates that have fallen into another’s continuum,
nor the aggregates categorized as insentient matter, as suffering. Why is this so?
The mode of being oppressive is the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of suffering.
This is because the aggregates that fall within the continuum of another or are categorized as insentient matter are not oppressive to one's own continuum;
thus, the *Jñānaprasthāna* states this.
The aggregates within one's own continuum cause extreme personal distress;
the aggregates belonging to other continua or to the category of insentient things do not.
It is impossible for others or insentient things, apart from one's own [aggregates], to cause such distress.
Since there is no self, what could afflict others or insentient things?
Therefore, at the time of clear realization (abhisamaya), one contemplates only the five aggregates belonging to one's own continuum as suffering, and nothing else.
Whether it be the cause for the five aggregates within one's own continuum,
the cause for the five aggregates within the continuum of another,
or the cause for the aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings as well as those of non-sentient things.
All such things as these are "origination" and constitute the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
When a practitioner of cultivation gives rise to clear realization (*abhisamaya*),

they contemplate only the causes of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that fall within their own continuum as origination, and do not contemplate the causes of the five aggregates that fall within the continua of others.
Furthermore, the causes of the aggregates belonging to insentient things constitute the origin (*samudaya*).
Whether they pertain to the exhaustion of the five aggregates within one's own continuum or to the exhaustion of the five aggregates within the continua of others.
When all aggregates—whether categorized as sentient or insentient—are exhausted, all such things are cessation;
this is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
When a practitioner of meditation gives rise to clear realization (*abhisamaya*), [they realize this].
One contemplates only the exhaustion of the five aggregates belonging to one's own continuum as cessation;
one does not contemplate the exhaustion of the five aggregates belonging to the continua of others,
nor the exhaustion of the aggregates categorized as insentient matter as cessation.
Whether it be the antidote to the five aggregates within one's own continuum,
the antidote to the five aggregates within the continua of others,
or the antidote to the aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings and the category of non-sentient things.
All such things as these are the path; they constitute the Truth of the Path.

When a practitioner of meditation gives rise to clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they contemplate only that which serves as the antidote to the five aggregates belonging to their own continuum as being the path.
The path is not the antidote for those aggregates that fall within the continuum of another, or those included among insentient things.
According to this teaching,
[the path] refers to those five aggregates that fall within one's own continuum.
If they fall within the five aggregates of another's continuum,
or if they are aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings or the category of insentient things—
all such things are suffering and constitute the Truth of Suffering.
When practitioners of meditation give rise to clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they all perceive [all phenomena] as suffering.
Question: Is the mode of apprehension (*ākāra*) of oppression the clear realization of suffering?
Since the aggregates that have fallen into the continuum of another or into the category of insentient things do not exert any pressure upon one's own continuum,
why does the practitioner of meditation also contemplate them as suffering when arising in direct realization (*abhisamaya*)?
Answer: Even if something does not cause personal distress, it is nevertheless regarded as suffering. Why is this?
Because from beginningless time, ignorance has arisen regarding all forms of suffering.
To counteract those [defilements], one should give rise to wisdom in all cases.
Since beginningless time, one has harbored doubt regarding all forms of suffering;
to counteract that, one should give rise to certainty in all cases.
Since beginningless time, one has harbored denial toward all forms of suffering.
To counteract this, one should cultivate faith in them all;
therefore, one should contemplate everything as being suffering.
Moreover, they are even capable of inflicting such distress upon themselves. Why is this?
Because if one is struck or touched by another, [the pain is felt].
This also gives rise to great suffering;
how could it not be a pressing affliction?
Should wood, stone, tiles, or the like fall from the sky onto one's own body, [it would likewise cause great pain].
It also gives rise to great suffering;
is this not indeed a state of oppression?
Since there is the sense of being oppressed within one's own continuum, [it follows that there is no self].
Therefore, at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), one also contemplates [them] as suffering,
whether they fall within the cause of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of one's own continuum or within the cause of the five aggregates of another's continuum.
Whatever causes constitute the aggregates, whether they belong to the category of sentient beings or the category of insentient things—
all such things are "origination" and constitute the Truth of Origination.
When a practitioner of meditation gives rise to clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they contemplate all of these as origination.
Whether it be the exhaustion of the five aggregates within one's own continuum,
the exhaustion of the five aggregates within the continua of others,
or the exhaustion of all aggregates, whether they belong to the category of sentient beings or the category of insentient things.
All such things as these are cessation; they constitute the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
When practitioners of cultivation give rise to clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they perceive all of them as cessation.
This occurs when there arises the antidote to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) within one's own continuum.
If it is the antidote to the five aggregates within the continuum of another,
or the antidote to the aggregates categorized as sentient and non-sentient—
everything of this kind is the Path, and it is the Truth of the Path.
When practitioners of meditation give rise to clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they all perceive it as the Path.
Such is called the self-nature, the substantial entity, the essence, the characteristic, the constituent part, and the fundamental nature of the four truths.
The intrinsic nature of the truths has already been explained.
That which is their reason for being shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason are they called "truths" (*satya*)?
What is the meaning of *satya*?
The answer is: the meaning of reality (*bhūta*) is the meaning of *satya*.
The meanings of truth (*tathya*), suchness (*yathābhūta*), non-perversion (*aviparyāsa*), and non-deceptiveness (*amṛṣā*) are the meanings of *satya*.
Question: If "truth" (satya) has the meaning of "reality," and even the meaning of "absence of falsehood" constitutes the meaning of truth,
then space and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) also possess the meaning of reality and even the meaning of absence of falsehood.
Why did the Blessed One not establish these as truths?
Answer: Because those phenomena which are suffering, the cause of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the remedy for suffering [are already established].
The Blessed One established [the other three] as truths;
however, space and non-analytical cessation are neither suffering, nor the cause of suffering, nor the cessation of suffering, nor the remedy for suffering.
Therefore, the Blessed One did not establish them as truths.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is an aggregate (*skandha*), the cause of an aggregate, the cessation of an aggregate, or the antidote to an aggregate, it is established as a truth (*satya*).

Since space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are neither aggregates, nor the cause of aggregates, nor the cessation of aggregates, nor the antidote to aggregates, they are not established as truths.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is a disease, a cause of disease, the cessation of disease, or an antidote to disease, it is established as a Truth (*satya*).

Since space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are neither disease, nor a cause of disease, nor the cessation of disease, nor an antidote to disease, they are not established as Truths.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is an affliction, a thorn, a torment, and a danger;
if it is the cause of that affliction, thorn, torment, and danger;
and if it is the exhaustion of that affliction, thorn, torment, and danger.
That which serves as the remedy for the afflictions and harms of this abscess-like arrow is established as a Truth (*satya*).
Since space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are neither of these, they are not established as Truths.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is a burden (*bhāra*), [it is not a Truth].
That which can bear the heavy burden and that which constitutes the exhaustion of the heavy burden—
these, being the antidotes to the heavy burden, are established as truths.
Since space and non-analytical cessation are neither of these, they are not established as truths.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is this shore, that shore, the river, or the boat and raft, it is established as a truth (*satya*).
Since space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are none of these, they are not established as truths.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is suffering, a cause of suffering, the path,
or the fruit of the path, it is established as a truth (*satya*).
Space and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are neither suffering nor causes of suffering.
Because they are neither the path nor the fruit of the path, they are not established as truths (*satya*).
Furthermore, if a phenomenon possesses the nature of being a cause or the nature of being a fruit, it is established as a truth;
since space and non-analytical cessation lack the nature of being a cause or the nature of being a fruit, they are not established as truths.
Furthermore, because space and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) are untainted (anāsrava), they are not the truths of suffering or its origin;
because they are indeterminate (avyākṛta), they are not the truth of cessation;
and because they are unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), they are not the truth of the path.
Furthermore, because space and non-analytical cessation do not fall within the world (*saṃsāra*), they are not the [first] three truths.
Because they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they are not the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Furthermore, because space and non-analytical cessation do not have the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*), they are not the [first] three truths.
Because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is not the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Furthermore, because space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) do not conform to suffering (*duḥkha*), they are not [the other] three truths;
because they are indeterminate, they are not the truth of cessation.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is the object of either false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) or untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*), it is established as a truth (*satya*).
Since space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) are not objects of either false view or untainted wisdom, they are not established as truths.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is the object of both ignorance (*avidyā*) and knowledge (*vidyā*), it is established as a truth (*satya*).
Space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are not objects of either ignorance or knowledge;
therefore, they are not established as truths.
Furthermore, those phenomena that constitute matters of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and matters of purification (*vyavadāna*) are established as truths (*satya*).
Space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are neither matters of affliction nor matters of purification.
Therefore, they are not established as truths (*satya*).
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is something that can be either rejoiced in or loathed, it is established as a truth;
however, space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are neither things to be rejoiced in nor things to be loathed.
Therefore, they are not established as truths.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is an object of mental attention characterized by delight or an object of mental attention characterized by aversion, it is established as a truth.
Space and non-analytical cessation are neither objects of mental attention characterized by delight nor objects of mental attention characterized by aversion.
Therefore, they are not established as truths (*satya*).
Question: If the meaning of "truth" is that which is non-erroneous (*aviparīta*), then the four kinds of perversions (*viparyāsa*) should not be included within the category of truth.
Why is this? Because they function in a distorted manner (*viparyāsa*).
Answer: They are established as distortions by virtue of other conditions.
Due to other conditions, these are subsumed under the truths;
that is to say, they are established as inversions for three reasons:
first, because of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).
Second, because they involve superimposition;
third, because they are exclusively inverted;
and fourth, because they correspond to what exists, what is real, and the true nature of reality, they are subsumed under the category of truth (*satya*).
Furthermore, because they perceive the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, the impure as pure, and the non-self as self, these are established as perversions (*viparyāsa*).
Since they possess the nature of cause and the nature of effect, they are subsumed under the category of truth (*satya*).
Question: If the meaning of "truth" (*satya*) is the absence of falsehood and deception, then all false and deceptive speech should not be subsumed under the category of truth. Why is this so?
Because it proceeds through deception.
Answer: False speech is established by virtue of other conditions;
that is to say, because it contradicts one's own perception and deceives others.
Because of other conditions, it is subsumed under truth;
that is to say, it exists, it is real, and it is associated with the true nature of reality.
Furthermore, because of other conditions, false speech is established.
That is to say: claiming to have seen what was not seen, or claiming not to have seen what was seen;
claiming to have heard what was not heard, or claiming not to have heard what was heard;
claiming to have cognized what was not cognized, or claiming not to have cognized what was cognized.
To claim knowledge when one does not know, or to claim ignorance when one knows— because of such other conditions,
these are subsumed under the category of truth (*satya*).
That is to say, because they possess the nature of cause (*hetu*) and the nature of effect (*phala*), the meaning of reality (*tattva*) is the meaning of truth (*satya*).
Up to: "The meaning of being without falsehood is the meaning of truth. Question: On what basis are these Four Noble Truths established?
Answer: They are established on the basis of real entities, and they are established on the basis of cause and effect.
Is it established through clear realization (*abhisamaya*)?
If so, what is the fault?
There are faults in all three cases.
Why is this so? If they were established based on actual entities,
there would necessarily be three truths.
That is to say, because the truths of suffering and its origin have no separate essence, they should be combined into one;
cessation is the second, and the path is the third.
Therefore, there are three truths.
If they were established based on cause and effect,
there would have to be five truths.
That is to say, since contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are established as two because their causes and effects are distinct,
the various uncontaminated paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) should likewise be divided into two because they too possess causes and effects; thus,
with cessation (*nirodha*) as the fifth, there are five truths (*pañca-satya*).
If they were established according to the process of clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
there would be eight truths;
that is to say, when a practitioner of yoga enters the stage of clear realization.
First, one contemplates the suffering of the desire realm individually;
subsequently, one contemplates the suffering of the form and formless realms collectively.
First, one contemplates the causes of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the desire realm individually.
Subsequently, one contemplates the causes of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the form and formless realms collectively;
first, one contemplates the cessation of the conditioned phenomena of the desire realm individually;
subsequently, one contemplates the cessation of the conditioned phenomena of the form and formless realms collectively.
First, one contemplates the antidotes to the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm individually;
subsequently, one contemplates the antidotes to the conditioned phenomena of the form and formless realms collectively.
Therefore, there are eight truths.
It is agreed that this should be stated thus:
these four noble truths are established based on cause and effect.
Question: If that is so, then...
Question: There ought to be five truths rather than four.
Answer: Because the cause and fruit of the Noble Path are established as one, there are four truths and not five.

That is to say, both the causal nature and the fruitional nature of the untainted path are established as one because they are both practices that lead to the ultimate cessation of the worldly birth, aging, sickness, and death of suffering.
Question: If that is so,

then since the nature of being a cause and the nature of being a fruit of the outflows are both capable of leading to the world’s cycle of birth, aging, sickness, and death— the accumulation and progression of suffering—
they too should be combined into one.
The truths should indeed be only three.
Answer: Although this is so, their aspects (ākāra) are both specific and general;
therefore, the Noble Truths are established as being only four.
That is to say, regarding the nature of the contaminated fruit, there are four aspects:
first, suffering; second, impermanence; third, emptiness; and fourth, non-self.
Regarding the nature of the contaminated cause, there are likewise four aspects.
Regarding the first cause, second collection, third production, and fourth condition,
within the nature of cause and fruit of the untainted path,
there are in total only four aspects.
One path, two suchnesses, three practices, and four exits.
Some say that the Four Noble Truths are established by way of three conditions.
First, because it is a single reality;
second, because it is cause and effect;
third, because of slander and faith.
Regarding "actual entities," it means that these four truths as actual entities are of two kinds:
first, those with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Second, regarding "the untainted" and "because of cause and effect":
this means that tainted phenomena possess the nature of having both causes and effects.
The nature of the fruit establishes the Truth of Suffering;
the nature of the cause establishes the Truth of Origination.

Within the category of untainted phenomena, there are two types: first, those possessing both the nature of cause and the nature of fruit; second, those possessing the nature of fruit but lacking the nature of cause.
That which possesses the nature of cause and the nature of fruit establishes the Truth of the Path;
that which possesses the nature of fruit but lacks the nature of cause [establishes the Truth of Cessation].
The Truth of Cessation is established.

Question: For what reason are the causal and resultant natures of contaminated phenomena each established as separate truths, while the causal and resultant natures of uncontaminated paths are combined and established as a single truth?
Answer: Because there are both specific and general forms of denial regarding those [objects].
That is to say, one denies each of the causal and resultant natures of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas individually:
first, one denies that the resultant nature is truly suffering.
Second, one slanders the nature of the cause by denying that it is truly the origin (*samudaya*).
Furthermore, one develops distinct convictions regarding the causal and resultant natures of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*):
first, one believes that the resultant nature is truly suffering (*duḥkha*).
Second, regarding the causal nature [of suffering], one believes it is truly the origin;
yet regarding the untainted path, which possesses both causal and resultant natures,
one gives rise to a single denial in its entirety, namely, the denial that it is not the path.
In sum, one gives rise to a single faith, namely, the conviction that this is the Path.
For this reason, the Four Truths are established through three conditions.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
The Four Truths are established on the basis of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Question:
If that is so, then the Noble Truths should be eight, not four.
Answer: Because the mode of practice regarding the truths is identical, there are four and not eight.

That is to say, although the suffering of the desire realm and the suffering of the form and formless realms are realized through distinct contemplations, they are both the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Furthermore, because they are observed through the same aspect of suffering and so forth, they are established as one [truth].
Although the causes of the formations of the desire realm and the causes of the formations of the form and formless realms are realized separately,
they are both the same Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Furthermore, because they are observed through the same causes and identical aspects, they are established as one.
Although the cessation of all formations in the desire realm and the cessation of all formations in the form and formless realms are distinct realizations,
they are both the Truth of Cessation.
Furthermore, because they are observed through identical aspects such as cessation and so forth, they are combined and established as one: namely,
the antidote to all formations of the desire realm,
and the antidote to all formations of the form and formless realms.
Although the individual realizations are distinct, they are nonetheless the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Furthermore, because they are observed through the same aspects (*ākāra*) of the path and so forth, they are established as one collectively.
Therefore, the four truths are established based on realization (*abhisamaya*) without addition or subtraction.
Question: What are the respective characteristics of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path?
Venerable Pārśva replied:
"Oppression is the characteristic of suffering."
Arising is the characteristic of origination;
tranquility is the characteristic of cessation;
renunciation is the characteristic of the path.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated as follows:
"Cyclic existence (saṃsāra) is the characteristic of suffering;
that which is capable of causing it to proceed is the characteristic of origination."
Cessation is the characteristic of extinction;
returning to cessation is the characteristic of the path.
Furthermore, it is said as follows:
The basis of birth as it flows onward is the characteristic of suffering.
That which can turn back the basis of birth is the characteristic of the origin.
The cessation of the basis of birth is the characteristic of cessation.
The characteristic of the path is that which is able to extinguish the basis of arising.
The Venerable One says:
"The designation 'truth' (satya) is established upon things that exist as real entities."
That is to say, the five aggregates of clinging.
Like a mass of extremely hot iron emerging from a furnace, they are accompanied by the three types of suffering;
they flow along with the stream of suffering, submerged in the ocean of suffering, and abide amidst suffering.
Just as a mass of iron, when combined with fire,
follows after the power of the fire and becomes extremely hot like fire itself,
so too are these five aggregates of clinging.
Because it is conjoined with suffering, it is like the composition of suffering;
therefore, being conjoined with suffering is the characteristic of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Thus, this aggregate of suffering arises from afflictions (*kleśa*).
The transformation of karma causes the wandering through the various realms of existence;
because this succession is beginningless, it can produce and evolve, which is the characteristic of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
This is because one ultimately becomes free from these afflictions and karma.
One no longer transmigrates through the various realms of existence;
thus, the absence of transmigration is the characteristic of the Truth of Cessation.
One cultivates pure ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and the correct contemplation of arising and ceasing.
Because it can sever that which has causes and can realize the exhaustion of existence, the capacity to sever and realize is the characteristic of the Truth of the Path.
Question: If there are four truths, [what is the Truth of Cessation?]
For what reason did the Blessed One say that there is but one truth?
As a gāthā says:
"There is but one truth, not two; yet sentient beings harbor doubts regarding it."
"Various truths have been taught by others; I say there is no ascetic [who teaches otherwise].
The meaning of this verse is that there is only one truth, whereas non-Buddhists, being hesitant, teach that there are many.
The Buddha taught that within those [other] teachings there is no path of the śramaṇa nor its fruits;
for the path of the śramaṇa and its fruits depend upon the Single Truth.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
Regarding the statement "one truth":
it means that each of the four noble truths is singular;
there is only one truth of suffering, and no second suffering.
The truth of origination alone exists; there is no second origination.
The truth of cessation alone exists; there is no second cessation.
The truth of the path alone exists; there is no second path.
Therefore, it is said that there is one truth;
this does not contradict the teaching of four truths.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that there is one truth:
This means that the single Truth of Cessation is intended to exclude other notions of liberation;
for various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) speak of four types of liberation,
the first of which is the "liberation of the bodiless" (aśarīra-vimokṣa).
Namely, the sphere of infinite space;
second, the liberation through the mental resolve of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Third is the liberation of the pure aggregate,
which is the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Fourth is the liberation of the worldly stūpa.
That is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The Buddha has declared that it is not a true liberation or deliverance.
This formless realm possesses true liberation;
it is solely the ultimate nirvana of the Truth of Cessation.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "one truth":
This refers to the single Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
It is intended to exclude other [alleged] truths of the path,
for various non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) propound many such truths.
Such as holding self-starvation to be the path,
or holding lying in ashes to be the path,
or holding following the movement of the sun to be the path.
Some maintain that drinking wind, drinking water, eating fruit, or eating vegetables constitutes the Way;
some maintain that being naked constitutes the Way;
and some maintain that lying upon thorns and the like constitutes the Way.
Some maintain that not lying down constitutes the path;
some maintain that wearing tattered old clothes constitutes the path;
and some maintain that consuming various medicinal substances and abstaining from food constitutes the path.
The Buddha spoke thus:
"That is not the true path;
it is a deviant path, a false path, and a deceptive path."
Such paths as these are not to be practiced by virtuous persons;
they are the tracks to be traversed by evil people.
The "path of true purity" refers to the single truth of the path,
namely the Noble Eightfold Path consisting of right view and the other factors.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "one truth," it refers to the single truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*),
because it forever abandons all suffering of birth and death.
Furthermore, there is one truth,
namely the Truth of the Path,
because it is able to sever all causes of birth and death.
In other sūtras, it is taught that there are two truths:
first, the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
second, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Question: What are the two truths, the conventional and the ultimate?
Some say that among the four truths, the first two are conventional truths.
The walking and staying of men and women, as well as jars, garments, and so forth—
all such worldly, conventionally perceived phenomena—
are included within the two truths of suffering and its origin.
The latter two truths are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*),
because all supramundane, genuine qualities are subsumed within the two truths of cessation and the path.
Furthermore, there are those who say that among the Four Noble Truths, the first three truths are conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
because within the truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), there are conventional phenomena.
The meaning is as previously explained.
The Buddha taught that the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is like a city, like a palace, or like the further shore.
All such conventional designations exist within the truth of cessation.
Therefore, the truth of cessation is also called conventional;
only the truth of the path is the ultimate truth,
because conventional designations do not exist therein.
Some say that all four truths are subsumed under conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
because within the first three truths there are conventional phenomena.
The meaning is as previously explained.
The Truth of the Path also possesses various conventional phenomena,
because the Buddha spoke of the Truth of the Path using the names "śramaṇa" and "brāhmaṇa."
Only the principle that all phenomena are empty and non-self is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*),
because within emptiness and non-self, all conventional things are beyond designation.
[The author] comments:
One should speak thus:
all four truths possess both the conventional and the ultimate. Regarding the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), that which constitutes the conventional truth is as explained previously.
Within the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), there is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*),
namely the principle that suffering is impermanent, empty, and non-self.
Within the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), there is the ultimate truth...
This refers to the principle of causes, origins, arising, and conditions.
Regarding the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), there is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
the Buddha taught that the truth of cessation is like a garden, like a forest, like the further shore, and so forth.
Within the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), there is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*),
which refers to the principles of cessation, tranquility, excellence, and detachment.
Within the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*), there is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
This means that the Buddha taught the Path as being like a boat or raft, like a rocky mountain, like a ladder or staircase, like a tower or pavilion, like a flower, and like water.
Within the Truth of the Path, there is the Ultimate Truth (paramārthasatya).
This refers to the principle that the path proceeds by way of emergence,
because it is taught that all four truths possess both conventional and ultimate dimensions.
Both the conventional and the ultimate encompass the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
Since both space and non-analytical cessation are also subsumed within the two truths,
one asks: Is the conventional nature within the conventional truth existent from the perspective of the ultimate truth,
or nonexistent from the perspective of the ultimate truth?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
Both positions possess errors. Why is this?
If conventional phenomena were to exist as conventional realities by virtue of being ultimate realities,
then there would be only one truth,
namely, the ultimate truth.
If conventional phenomena were non-existent by virtue of being conventional in nature from the perspective of the ultimate,
then there would likewise be only one truth,
namely, the ultimate truth.
I agree that this should be said:
within the conventional, conventional nature exists from the perspective of the ultimate;
if, within the conventional, conventional nature did not exist from the perspective of the ultimate, [it would be non-existent].
The Buddha’s statement that there are two truths would not be true;
however, since the Buddha’s statement that there are two truths is indeed true,
it follows that conventional reality exists as conventional reality and exists as ultimate reality.
Question: If that is so,
there should be only one truth,
namely, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Answer: In reality, there is only one truth, namely, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Question: If that is so, then...
Why are two truths established?
Answer: The two truths are established based on differentiated conditions, not based on substantial entities.
If they were established based on substantial entities, there would be only one truth.
That is to say, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Based on the distinction of conditions, two types are established.
If one relies on these conditions to establish conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), [it is so called].
The ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) is not established based on these conditions;
if the ultimate truth were established based on these conditions,
then the conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) would not be established based on these conditions.
For example, a single sensation has four types of conditions.
If one establishes the nature of the causal condition based on this particular condition,
one does not, based on that same condition, establish even the nature of the dominant condition.
If one establishes the nature of the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) based on this object,
one does not establish the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) based on it.
Furthermore, for example, a single feeling possesses the nature of six causes.
If, based on this condition, one establishes the nature of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*),
one does not, based on that same condition, establish even the nature of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Conversely, if, based on this condition, one establishes even the nature of the efficient cause, one does not, based on that same condition, establish the nature of the associated cause.
The two truths are likewise so:
they are established based on distinct conditions and do not depend on real entities.
Question: Can it be designated that the conventional and the ultimate are each a separate entity, existing without being intermingled?
Answer: It can indeed be designated.
What is its nature?
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke as follows:
That which can manifest is the conventional;
that which is manifested is the ultimate.
Furthermore, it is said:
That which accords with what is spoken by worldly people is called the conventional;
that which accords with what is spoken by the noble ones (ārya) is called the ultimate (paramārtha).
Thus says the Venerable One.
The verbal expressions arising from a non-erroneous mind that teach conventional entities such as sentient beings,
jars, and clothing constitute the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The teachings that proclaim the principles of dependent nature and dependent origination [constitute the ultimate truth].
Speech arising from a mind that is not false is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The Venerable Dāra-datta said:
"The intrinsic nature of names is the conventional (*saṃvṛti*)."
This is a portion of the truth of the origin of suffering;
its meaning and intrinsic nature are the ultimate truth.
This is a portion of the truth of the origin of suffering.
And there are the other two truths and the two unconditioned phenomena.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There are, in total, three kinds of Brahmin truths for the renunciant brahmins."
What are the three?
They are as follows: there are certain renunciant brahmins who speak thus:
"No sentient being whatsoever should be harmed."
What has been thus spoken is the truth and not falsehood;
this is called the first truth of the brahmins.
Furthermore, there are renunciant brahmacārins.
He spoke thus:
"I do not belong to them;
they do not belong to me."
What has been thus spoken is the truth and not falsehood;
this is called the second Brahmin truth.
Furthermore, there are renunciant brahmins who speak as follows:
Whatever phenomena arise are all subject to cessation;
what has been thus spoken is the truth and not falsehood.
This is called the third Brahmin truth.
Question: Among these, who is a *brāhmaṇa* and what is the truth?
Answer: Here, the intention is to refer to those non-Buddhist renunciants as *brāhmaṇas*.
Regarding that which they have taught:
The first three are truths;
the rest are all false. "All sentient beings should not be harmed" means that no sentient beings whatsoever should be killed.
"I do not belong to them;
they do not belong to me" means that I am not subject to them.
That does not belong to me.
Regarding all phenomena that arise, they all possess the nature of cessation;
that is to say, all things that are born must eventually return to extinction.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the intended meaning here is that one who abides in the Buddha-dharma is called a *brāhmaṇa*;
this refers precisely to the three types of "truths" (*satya*) mentioned previously.
This sutra was spoken by the Buddha for the sake of those non-Buddhists who claim,
"I am a true Brahmin," yet perform sacrifices by slaughtering various oxen and sheep.
Furthermore, regarding those who gather many diverse classes of sentient beings and take their lives,
the Buddha spoke thus to them:
"One who harms others is not a true brāhmaṇa."
A true brahmin should not harm any sentient being.
Yet there are non-Buddhists who claim for themselves, "I am a true brahmin."
Yet they diligently practice the holy life for the sake of being born in heaven to enjoy various sensual pleasures.
It was with reference to such individuals that the Buddha spoke thus:
"One who practices the holy life for the sake of celestial desires is not a true brāhmaṇa."
A true Brahmin is one whose will is unattached to all that exists and who practices the holy life (brahmacarya).
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who claim of themselves, "I am a true Brahmin."
Yet, by clinging to annihilationism or eternalism, they deviate from the Middle Way.
It was for this reason that the Buddha spoke thus to them:
"Those who cling to annihilationism or eternalism are not true Brahmins."
A true brāhmaṇa knows that whatever phenomena arise have the nature of cessation; because they arise,
they are not annihilated, and because they cease, they are not eternal.
It is neither annihilation nor permanence, but accords with the Middle Way.
Furthermore, the intention of this sutra is to explain that all sentient beings are not to be harmed; this refers to the preparatory practices (prayoga) associated with the three gates of liberation.
This explains the preparatory application for the gate of liberation through emptiness:
"I do not belong to them;
they do not belong to me."
The preparatory practice for the door of liberation of wishlessness is explained as:
"Whatever phenomena arise, all have the nature of cessation.
The preparatory practice for the door of liberation of signlessness is explained [as follows].
Some say that the intention of this sutra is to explain the three gates of liberation in their respective order. Others say:
The intention of this sūtra is to explain the three samādhis—
namely, emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness— in their respective order.
Furthermore, there are those who say:

The intent of this sutra is to state that the three aggregates— the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), and the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*)— are to be understood respectively in the same manner as the aforementioned three aggregates;
likewise, the three trainings (*śikṣā*), the three cultivations (*bhāvanā*), and the three purities (*viśuddhi*) should be known to be so as well.
As stated in the Sūtra,
the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Those who contemplate the four directions" refers to contemplating the Four Noble Truths.
Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One speak of the Four Noble Truths using the term "direction" (dis)?
Answer: Because he considered that those to be converted were suitable to hear them explained in this way.
That is to say, there are those to be converted who, upon hearing [them] explained with the term "direction," [attain understanding].
When the Four Noble Truths are taught, they are easily understood and entered;
therefore, the Buddha spoke of the truths using the term "four directions," as in other sūtras.
For the sake of those to be converted, the Buddha spoke the sounds of the eight directions regarding the eight liberations;
upon hearing them, those to be converted easily attained realization and entry.
This sutra is likewise so.
Therefore, the term "four directions" is used in reference to the Four Noble Truths.
Question: In what way do the Four Noble Truths resemble the four directions, such that the term "four directions" is applied to them?
Answer: Because the Four Truths, the four directions, and the number four are equivalent.
Question: Regarding which truth did the Buddha speak with a voice from which direction?
Answer: The Buddha spoke of the eastern direction in reference to the Truth of Suffering.
Regarding that Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), the word "West" (*paścima*) is used;
for at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), one first contemplates the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and subsequently contemplates the Truth of Origination.
Some have stated this.
The East is like origination and the West is like suffering,
because they are explained in sequence as cause followed by effect.
Regarding the Truth of the Path, the Buddha spoke of the sound of the South.
The Truth of the Path corresponds to the south because both [the Buddha and the Path] are worthy of offerings.
The Buddha spoke of the sound of the north regarding the Truth of Cessation,
for the Truth of Cessation and the north are both supreme.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Regarding the Four Noble Truths, one should understand the faculty of wisdom.
Question: Is this based on inclusion (*saṃgraha*) or based on the object of observation (*ālambana*)?
If they are categorized according to inclusion,
the faculty of wisdom regarding the four truths does not mutually include one another;
how then can it be said that the faculty of wisdom should be understood in relation to the four truths?
If one were to rely on the objects of focus (*ālambana*), then all phenomena (*dharma*) would be objects of focus;
why then speak only of the Four Noble Truths? One should answer:
this statement was made not by relying on inclusion, nor by relying on objects of focus.
However, when establishing the Four Noble Truths,
wisdom is the most predominant factor;
therefore, this statement was made.
Regarding the four noble truths, one should understand the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
Just as when establishing the four types of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*),
this statement is made because faith and understanding are preeminent.
