Regarding the four objects of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*), one should understand that they correspond to the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
Just as when establishing the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*),
it was stated that diligence (*vīrya*) is preeminent, so too is this said here.
Regarding the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), one should know that the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*) is predominant;
just as when establishing the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
mindfulness is said to be supreme because it is the most excellent.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, one should know that it is the faculty of mindfulness [that is predominant].
Just as when establishing the four bases of psychic power, concentration is said to be supreme; therefore, this statement is made.
One should know that the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*) corresponds to the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*);
it is the same here as well. Some say this.
This is based on the objects of focus.
Question: Since the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is capable of taking all phenomena as its objects, why is this statement made specifically regarding the four noble truths?
Answer: This refers specifically to those phenomena that are objects of both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) wisdom.
Space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are not mentioned here because they are objects of contaminated wisdom alone.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Fascicle Seventy-seven;
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Seventy-eight.
Compiled by five hundred great arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, who received the imperial decree. Section Two: The Aggregate of Defilements (*Saṃyojana-skandha*), Sub-section Four: The Ten Gates of Summary (*Daśamukha-nikāya*), Part Eight. As it is stated in the Sūtra:
The Venerable Śāriputra spoke thus:
"All wholesome dharmas that arise are subsumed within the Four Noble Truths and lead toward the Four Noble Truths.
[Objection: It may be granted that for the three truths which are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is appropriate to speak of their arising.
Since the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) truth of cessation has no sense of arising, how can it be said that the arising of all wholesome dharmas is subsumed within the Four Noble Truths?
Answer: The intent of this sūtra is to state that there is no arising of wholesome dharmas that is not subsumed within the Four Noble Truths.
There is no contradiction in principle if one does not state that each of the Four Truths individually encompasses all the wholesome dharmas produced.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of production.
First, it is called "arising" because it possesses intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Second, it is called "arising" because it originates from conditions (*pratyaya*).
Regarding the statement that it is called "arising" because it possesses intrinsic nature:
The term "arising" (jāti) indicates that the essence is not subject to destruction;
it is called "arising" because it originates from conditions.
Thus, the term "arising" is intended to manifest the meaning of originating from conditions.
Among all wholesome dharmas, those that possess both [types of] arising are subsumed under the three truths;
those that possess arising solely by virtue of their own nature are subsumed under the truth of cessation.
Therefore, what is taught in the sūtras does not contradict reason.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of arising:
first, arising by way of function;
second, arising by way of acquisition.
Among all wholesome dharmas, those that possess both [the dharma itself and its acquisition] are subsumed under the three truths;
only those whose acquisition alone arises are subsumed under the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*),
because although analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) does not arise, its acquisition does arise.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"In this sūtra, the various forms of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are described as 'wholesome states that have arisen.
These various patiences and knowledges are included within the Four Noble Truths as appropriate; it is not stated that they are universally subsumed [by them]."
The term "approaching the truths" (satyābhisamaya) means taking the truths as objects.

That is to say, the patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-kṣānti) and the knowledge regarding suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), which are subsumed under the truth of the path (mārga-satya), take the truth of suffering as their object;
the patience regarding origin (samudaya-kṣānti) and the knowledge regarding origin (samudaya-jñāna), which are subsumed under the truth of the path, take the truth of origin as their object.

The patience regarding cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) are subsumed under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and take the Truth of Cessation as their object.
The patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) are subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) and take the Truth of the Path as their object,
as stated in the Sūtra.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas have taught the Dharma of deliverance,
namely, the Four Noble Truths."
He proclaimed and revealed the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for the sake of delivering sentient beings from birth and death.
Question: For what reason was this Dharma of deliverance taught?
Answer: It is intended to show that liberation is achieved through one’s own diligent cultivation of the path and not through the cultivation of another.
How is this known? Because it is stated in the sūtras. As the sūtra says:
There was a brahmin named Daòdégā who came to where the Buddha was;
having arrived, he prostrated at the World-Honored One’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and spoke these verses:
I bow my head to this person among humans, the courageous and true brahmin whose pure eye surveys all with universal illumination; may he be able to dispel my doubts.
What meaning does one wish to reveal through this verse?

The answer is that this brahmin was by nature indolent; believing that others could eliminate his own afflictions through the practice of the Path, he addressed the Buddha with these verses of endearing speech (*priyavāda-gāthā*).
He intended to demonstrate that the World-Honored One was a celestial brahmin who, out of courageous aspiration, had come to be born among humans.
"Having already cultivated the Noble Path for the sake of liberating sentient beings,
I only pray that you will take pity on me and dispel my doubts.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for him:
"I cannot liberate you from doubt by my own sovereign power;
only when you have seen the supreme Dharma can you cross over the torrent.
Regarding this verse:
The Blessed One intended to demonstrate that there is no other path of cultivation for abandoning one's own afflictions.
If this were the case, then while I sat beneath the tree cultivating the Noble Path,
the afflictions of all sentient beings should have been abandoned.
I possess great compassion for all beings;
yet, because the afflictions of sentient beings have not been suddenly severed,
there is no other path by which one's own afflictions could be severed.
Just as when another person takes medicine but one's own illness is not cured,
it is only by taking the medicine oneself that the illness is healed;
from this it is known that one must cultivate the Path for oneself to possess the power of deliverance, for it does not come about through the cultivation of another.
Therefore, the World-Honored One has taught the Dharma of deliverance;
this Dharma of deliverance is none other than the Four Noble Truths,
intended to lead sentient beings to rely upon them for the cultivation of the path.
Having seen the Four Noble Truths, he severed his own doubts and asked:
"What is the meaning of 'deliverance'? He replied:
"It is called deliverance because one leads sentient beings from dangerous and difficult places and establishes them in a level place."
"Perilous places" refers to the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), which is like deep ravines, mountain crags, and other such terrifying locations.
"Level ground" refers to...
That is to say, the nature of the noble ones is like the royal highway;
by means of the Buddha’s proclamation of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths,
one proceeds from the extremely perilous state of being an ordinary person.
It leads all sentient beings to place them in the state of the noble ones, a most level ground;
that is, it causes them to enter the Path and attain the fruits of the Path, and is therefore called "rescue.
Furthermore, it leads them from the state of equality into the state of rightness, and is therefore called "rescue."
The state of equality refers to the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
The state of correctness (*samyaktva*) refers to the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*).
These are proclaimed by the Buddha through the teaching of the Four Noble Truths.

It is called "rescue" because it leads sentient beings from the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) into the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Furthermore, it is called "rescue" because it leads sentient beings away from the state of great suffering and establishes them in the state of great bliss.
The place of great suffering refers to saṃsāra;
the place of great bliss refers to nirvāṇa.
Because the Buddha proclaims the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to lead all sentient beings to transcend saṃsāra and attain great nirvāṇa, it is called "deliverance."
Question: For what reason are the Four Noble Truths called the "Dharma of Deliverance" (uttāraṇadharma), whereas the elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and aggregates (skandha) are not?
Answer: Because by contemplating the Four Noble Truths, one enters the Path, attains the fruits, becomes free from defilement, and exhausts the outflows (āsrava);
contemplating the elements, bases, and aggregates does not result in such [attainments].
Furthermore, contemplating the Four Noble Truths causes those to be converted to enter the Noble Path and realize the Dharmakāya in the near term;
contemplating the elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and aggregates (skandha) constitutes the remote preparatory application (dūraprayoga).
That is to say, during the stage of initial training within the remote preparatory application, the practitioner contemplates the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśadhātu).
Having already practiced the stage of cultivation by observing the twelve bases (*āyatana*),
one proceeds to the stage of transcendence of mental attention (*manasikāra*) by observing the five aggregates (*skandha*).
This occurs during the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) proximate to the levels of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*).
By contemplating the Four Noble Truths, one is able to enter the noble path, realize the fruit, and attain the Dharma-body;
therefore, only the Four Noble Truths are called the "Dharma that delivers.
One asks: what is the meaning of the term "Noble Truth"?
Is it because they are wholesome that they are called Noble Truths?
Is it because they are untainted that they are called Noble Truths?
Or is it because they are accomplished by the noble ones that they are called Noble Truths?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
All three [positions] involve errors. Why is this?
If that which is wholesome is therefore called a "noble truth" (*āryasatya*),
then among the four [truths], only the latter two could be called noble truths because they are exclusively wholesome.
Since the former two pertain to all three types [wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral], how can they also be called noble truths?
If they are called "Noble Truths" (āryasatya) because they are untainted (anāsrava),
then only the latter two among the four could be called Noble Truths, as they are untainted.
Since the former two are tainted (sāsrava), how can they be called Noble Truths?
If they are called "Noble Truths" because they are accomplished by the Noble Ones, then since non-Noble Ones also accomplish them, why are they called exclusively "Noble Truths"?
As it is said: "Who accomplishes the truths of suffering and its origin?"
This refers to all sentient beings.
Who accomplishes the truth of cessation?
Those who are not bound by all fetters.
It is agreed that they are so called because they are realized by the noble ones; thus, they are named "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*).
Question: If this is the case, the first two types of objections are well resolved, but how is the third objection resolved?
Answer: Because the noble ones (ārya) fully possess all four, they are called Noble Truths (āryasatya).
Ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are not so.
Question: Are there not also noble ones who do not fully possess all four, such as those still bound by all fetters?
Because at the initial moment of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) has not yet been accomplished.
The answer is that because the duration [of that state] is brief, it is not like that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

That is to say, although one bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) has not yet accomplished the four [truths] at the initial moment of the path of seeing, [the duration is so short that it does not constitute a full realization].
Thereafter, one necessarily possesses all four;
whereas ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) do not possess all four at that time.
For this reason, suffering and the others are uniquely termed "Noble Truths" (āryasatya).
Furthermore, within the category of the noble ones (*ārya*), those who possess all four [aspects] are therefore called "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*).
Within the category of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), because there are none who possess all four, it is not their truth.

Furthermore, if one’s continuum is sealed by the seal of the Noble Dharma (*āryadharma-mudrā*), one receives the name "noble one"; since that which belongs to them is the truth, it is called the "Noble Truth."

Furthermore, those who have already attained the precepts beloved by the noble ones are called "noble ones" (*ārya*); because these possess the truths, they are therefore called "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*).
Furthermore, those who have already attained noble wisdom are called "noble ones."
They are called "Noble Truths" because they belong to those who are noble.
Furthermore, those who have attained noble śamatha and vipaśyanā are called "noble ones"; because these truths belong to them, they are called "Noble Truths."
Furthermore, those who have already attained the noble wealth are called "noble ones" (*ārya*);
because they possess the truths, these are called the "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*).
Furthermore, those who have already entered the noble womb are called "noble ones."
They are called "noble truths" because they belong to those who are noble.
Furthermore, those who have attained the factors of noble awakening and the factors of the noble path are called "noble ones";
because these truths belong to them, they are called "noble truths."
The Venerable Saṃghavasu said:
"When the Buddha was in the world, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) engaged in debate.

The ordinary beings asserted that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are permanent, blissful, pure, and possess a self; the noble ones asserted that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
Ordinary worldlings declare the statement "self" to be true;
the noble ones likewise declare the statement "self" to be true.
This is for the purpose of extinguishing disputes.
They went together to the place where the Buddha was and requested that he resolve their doubt.
The Buddha spoke these words:
"The words of the noble ones are true; all other words are not true."
Why is this so? Because the Noble Ones possess direct knowledge, vision, and realization regarding suffering and the other truths, such that they declare them to be truths; ordinary beings do not.
Therefore, the Four Truths belong exclusively to the Noble Ones and not to ordinary beings; thus, they are called the "Noble Truths" (āryasatyāni).
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated as follows:
"These four truths are called 'noble truths' (āryasatya) because they are thoroughly realized by the noble ones (ārya) through their noble wisdom (āryaprajñā).
Question: What is the noble truth of suffering?

Answer: As stated in the sūtras, the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of encountering what is unpleasant, the suffering of separation from what is pleasant, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks—in brief, all five aggregates of clinging are suffering;
this is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
It should be understood that herein, it is called the suffering of birth because it is conjoined with the characteristic of arising;
it is called the suffering of aging because it is conjoined with the characteristic of duration-and-change;
and it is called the suffering of illness because it is conjoined with the characteristic of affliction.
It is called the suffering of death because it is conjoined with the characteristic of cessation.
It is called the suffering of encountering the unloved because it is conjoined with meeting with what is disagreeable.
It is called the suffering of separation from the loved because it is conjoined with being parted from what is agreeable.
Because it is associated with the state of lacking mastery and not obtaining what one desires, it is called the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
Thus, all such sufferings are subsumed within the contaminated aggregates of grasping (*sāsrava-upādānaskandha*).
Therefore, it is briefly said that all five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
Furthermore, because birth is the locus where all suffering is established and the fertile field for suffering, it is called the suffering of birth.
Old age is called the suffering of old age because it causes the deterioration of beloved youth.
Illness is called the suffering of illness because it destroys beloved well-being.
Death is called the suffering of death because it cuts off beloved life.
When undesirable objects come into contact with the body, they give rise to manifold sufferings; therefore, this is called the suffering of encountering the unpleasant.
When desirable objects depart from the body, they give rise to manifold sufferings; therefore, this is called the suffering of separation from the beloved.
When one seeks what is desired but does not achieve it, this gives rise to various forms of suffering; therefore, it is called the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
All such sufferings are comprised within the contaminated aggregates of grasping (*sāsrava-upādānaskandha*).
Therefore, it is called a "brief exposition" of the suffering of all five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
Question: Since the magnitude of the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging is vast, why is it called "brief"?
Answer: Although the suffering is vast, because it is expounded in summary, it is called "brief."

This refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), which are characterized by suffering and affliction to such a great extent that they cannot be described in detail; yet, so as to cause those to be trained to develop a general sense of weary detachment, they are explained here in brief.
It is, for example, like a person who has many faults and evils that cannot be described in detail.
If one asks about those faults, they can be answered collectively by saying, "This is an extremely evil person. Although these words are brief, the faults they imply are very extensive.
This case is likewise; therefore, it is called the "brief exposition of the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging."
Question: Is there pleasure within the aggregates?
If so, what fault would there be? Answer:
There are faults in both cases.
Why is this? If there were also pleasure within the aggregates,
why would they be called the Truth of Suffering rather than the Truth of Pleasure?
If there were no pleasure whatsoever within the aggregates,
how would one reconcile what is stated in the sūtras?
As it is said in a sūtra:
Great Name, you should know this:
if form were exclusively suffering and devoid of pleasure,
and were not accompanied by pleasure such that it could give rise to joy and happiness, [beings would not be attached to it].
Those who delight in detachment should not give rise to craving or attachment toward form as a source of pleasure;
for within all forms there is both suffering and pleasure,
and they are accompanied by pleasure and give rise to joy.
Because they do not depart from pleasure, sentient beings give rise to craving and attachment toward various forms (*rūpa*);
this is explained in detail for each of the aggregates up to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Furthermore, it is taught that the three types of feeling (*vedanā*) are each established as distinct and do not intermingle.
That is to say: pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The path depends upon the provisions, and nirvana depends upon the path."
Because one attains the bliss of nirvāṇa through the bliss of the Path,
and since the Path itself is bliss, how could it be said that there is no bliss within the aggregates?
One should answer as follows:
Within the aggregates (*skandha*),
there is also a small amount of pleasure; however,
because suffering is abundant and pleasure is meager within the aggregates— and because the few follow upon the many— they are designated simply as "aggregates of suffering."
It is like a jar of poison into which a single drop of honey has been placed;
because the small is subsumed by the great, it is called simply a "jar of poison.
The aggregates (*skandhas*) are likewise.
Because pleasure is slight and suffering is abundant, it is called solely the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Some say that because there is no pleasure whatsoever within the aggregates (*skandha*), they are designated only as the Truth of Suffering.
Question: If this is so, how should one interpret the statements in the Sūtras?
Answer: Names are established through mutual dependence; it is a conventional designation that there is pleasure.
That is to say, when experiencing intense suffering, one conceives the notion of pleasure toward that moderate suffering.
When experiencing suffering within the realm of sensation, one conceives the notion of pleasure regarding the lesser suffering;
when experiencing the suffering of hell-beings, one conceives the notion of pleasure regarding the suffering of animals;
and when experiencing the suffering of animals, one conceives the notion of pleasure regarding the suffering of the hungry ghost realm.
When experiencing the suffering of the realm of ghosts, one conceives the notion of pleasure regarding the suffering of humans;
when experiencing the suffering of humans, one conceives the notion of pleasure regarding the suffering of devas;
and when experiencing the suffering of outflows (*āsrava*), one likewise gives rise to the notion of pleasure regarding the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Therefore, it is said that there is pleasure. Furthermore,
some say that if one relies on worldly convention, pleasure is also said to exist within the aggregates (*skandhas*).
That is to say, when people in the world obtain food when hungry,
drink when thirsty, warmth when cold, coolness when hot, and vehicles, horses, and so forth when fatigued from travel.
All say they have attained happiness.
However, according to the designation of the noble ones (ārya), one should state that there is no happiness within the aggregates (skandha).
This refers to how the noble ones [view it] even when compared to the Avīci Hell.
Even unto the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
one views them all equally as being like a mass of glowing iron.
The commentary says:
It should be understood that among these, the first explanation is correct:
when suffering is predominant and pleasure is minimal, it is designated as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Question: What is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering (*duḥkhasamudayasatya*)?
Answer: As stated in the Sūtra:
"All craving whatsoever, craving for renewed existence, craving accompanied by delight, and craving for this or that pleasant thing."
This is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.

Question: Since all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) that function as causes constitute the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), why did the Blessed One state that the Truth of Origination is craving (*tṛṣṇā*) alone and nothing else?
Answer: Among the noble truths, craving possesses a more powerful efficacy within the truth of the origin than other contaminated phenomena;
therefore, craving alone is specifically designated as the origin, and not others.
However, all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).
Just as it is said that among the formations aggregate (*saṃskāraskandha*), volition (*cetanā*) is the most preeminent and thus volition is mentioned rather than the others,
yet in reality, both associated and dissociated formations are the formations aggregate.
For this reason, craving alone is specifically taught as the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Furthermore, craving is the fundamental cause of the manifold sufferings of the three periods of time;
it is the path and the source that acts as the condition for birth.
Because it is preeminent in terms of accumulation and origination, the truth of origin (samudaya-satya) is specifically taught.
Furthermore, because craving is preeminent in its ability to repeatedly summon and accumulate the fruits of suffering, it is specifically taught.
As a verse says:
Just as when the roots of a tree have not been pulled out, it grows back again and again despite being cut;
so too, as long as the latent tendency of craving has not been severed, one repeatedly experiences manifold sufferings.
Furthermore, because craving can both burn and moisten sentient beings, it is specifically mentioned here.
At the time of its cause it can moisten,
and at the time of its fruit it can burn. Just as a drop of hot oil, when it falls upon the body,
can both burn and moisten, so too is craving toward sentient beings.
Furthermore, craving is able to give rise [to rebirth] just as a *vetāla* (reanimated corpse) is able to summon the karma that produces birth;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
It is like a place where there is water and a *vetāla* is able to raise up a dead body.
Within the body possessed of craving, there exists karma that draws forth rebirth and is capable of drawing forth death.
Furthermore, because craving can encompass all internal and external things—both sentient and insentient—it is specifically mentioned here.
Regarding the gathering of sentient beings:
by the power of craving, one gathers in one's wife, children, slaves, servants, and laborers,
as well as elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, camels, donkeys, and other such things.
Regarding the grasping of insentient things:
by the power of craving, one appropriates palaces, houses, precious wealth, grain, and so forth.
Furthermore, craving is able to nourish the male and female bodies; therefore, it is specifically mentioned here.
This means that all sentient beings, through the power of craving, are able to properly honor their parents, teachers, and elders;
and through the power of craving, they are able to support and nourish their wives, children, servants, friends, and kinsmen, even down to birds and beasts.
From one valley, having harmed living beings, he carries them to another valley to nourish his own offspring.
Furthermore, through the power of craving, desiring to obtain a self-body in a future state of existence, and because of this desire to obtain it, he gives rise to longing.
Because of hope, one seeks; because of seeking, one obtains the basis for rebirth in a realm of existence; therefore, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, craving moistens all forms of existence (*bhava*) and the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), preventing them from withering away; for this reason, it is specifically mentioned.
Just as water can moisten trees, medicinal herbs, and grasses so that they do not wither or dry up, so too does craving moisten consciousness to produce the sprout of future existence.

That is to say, by the power of craving, one enters the mother’s womb, moistening the semen and blood to cause them to abide within the fetal receptacle; for this reason, it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, if there are bases, objects,
and modes of activity that can give rise to craving, those same bases, objects, and modes of activity will give rise to other afflictions.
It is just as when the place where the king of fish dwells and roams is followed by all the small fish.
This is likewise so; for this reason, craving is called the king of afflictions and is therefore mentioned specifically.
Furthermore, if there is craving within the continuum, all other afflictions gather therein.
Just as dust and grime easily adhere to a damp garment,
for this reason craving alone is specifically taught as the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Furthermore, if there is the water of craving within the continuity of existence, [suffering arises].
All other afflictions find their pleasure in abiding;
just as fish, shrimp, frogs, and the like all delight in dwelling where there is water, they are mentioned specifically for this reason.
Furthermore, craving is like a blazing fire that can burn everything.
Furthermore, just as one can never have enough salt water to drink, it is for this reason that it is specifically mentioned;
it is like throwing various objects into a blazing fire,
where they are all completely consumed without ever reaching satiety.
Furthermore, just as a thirsty person drinking salt water becomes thirstier with every sip and never reaches a point of satisfaction, so too,
those whose bodies have not yet abandoned craving never reach a point of contentment as they become greedily attached to sensory objects.
Furthermore, craving has the power to unite distinct sentient beings so that they do not become separate; therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
It is like water, which unites distinct sands and the like so that they do not fall apart.
Furthermore, craving causes the wholesome qualities of sentient beings to become coarse and unworkable;
craving moistens sentient beings, causing them to dwell in attachment and be unable to achieve liberation. For this reason, it is specifically mentioned.
This means that by the power of craving, the wholesome dharmas practiced by sentient beings become coarse and ineffective;
furthermore, it moistens sentient beings, causing them to cling to whatever they encounter within saṃsāra and preventing them from transcending it.
Just as flies, bees, and the like, upon reaching clarified butter,
oil, honey, or moist hides, have their wings and feet stuck by the adhesive substance and are unable to fly through the air;
furthermore, craving [functions similarly] toward sentient beings in both their causal and resultant states.
Because their functions differ, they are explained separately.
That is to say, the craving that arises conforms to sentient beings during the causal stage like a virtuous friend,
yet harms and opposes them at the resultant stage like a wicked enemy.
It is like merchants who have entered the sea to gather treasures;
upon reaching a certain island,
they encounter rākṣasīs who first manifest pleasant countenances and speak words of endearment.
She served him with ritual propriety and requested that he become her husband.
Later, she learned that he was trustworthy and skillfully enticed him,
leading him into the Iron City where one is forbidden from consuming meat or blood.
Gradually it reaches the point where everything has been consumed and only the bones remain;
the rākṣasas act in the same manner,
first causing sentient beings to play and thereby commit evil deeds.
Subsequently, this causes one to fall into the evil destinies and undergo various intense sufferings.
Furthermore, craving is the cause of origination; therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
As stated in the Sūtra:
Karma is the cause of birth, and craving is the cause of its arising;
thus do beings circulate through the flow of saṃsāra. Furthermore, because craving is difficult to sever and abandon, it is specifically mentioned here.
It is like a person who suddenly encounters two rākṣasīs.
First, when appearing in the form of a mother, it is difficult to escape;
second, when appearing in the form of an enemy, it is easy to escape.
Such is the case for sentient beings who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire.
There are two afflictions that manifest repeatedly:
first, craving, which is difficult to sever and abandon;
second, aversion, which is easy to sever and abandon.
Furthermore, craving manifests frequently and is subtle and difficult to perceive; therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
It is like the sharp tool used by a skilled turner, which cuts away [material] so subtly that it is difficult to discern.
Furthermore, craving (tṛṣṇā) is established as three distinct types within the link of existence (bhava-aṅga); therefore, it is explained specifically.
That is to say, at the time of its initial arising, it is called craving;
at the subsequent stage of expansion, it is called grasping (upādāna).
That which results after death is termed ignorance (*avidyā*).
Furthermore, among the ten defiled factors, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the foremost; therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
As stated in the Sūtra:
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Conditioned by craving, there is seeking;
conditioned by seeking, there is acquisition."
Conditioned by acquisition, there is accumulation;
conditioned by accumulation, there is craving;
conditioned by craving, there is attachment.
Due to attachment, there is stinginess;
due to stinginess, there is grasping;
due to grasping, there is guarding.
Because of guarding [possessions], they take up swords and staves;
they engage in strife, deception, flattery, and arrogance,
giving rise to immeasurable kinds of evil and unwholesome states.
Furthermore, craving is specifically mentioned because its power is particularly strong within the eight defiled attainments (*samāpatti*).
This is as when it is said that the first dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādanasamprayukta*) constitutes "relishing" at the time of meditative absorption.
It should be said that it is the relishing after having emerged from meditative absorption,
not the relishing while in meditative absorption.
The detailed exposition for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception associated with taste is likewise.
Furthermore, the Buddha taught that craving binds ordinary worldlings like a rope binding a bird; therefore, he spoke specifically of this.
Furthermore, the Buddha taught that craving is like a net and like a creeping vine, binding and entangling one so that it is difficult to escape; for this reason, he spoke of it specifically.
Furthermore, the Buddha taught that craving is deep and vast, as difficult to cross as the great ocean; for this reason, he spoke of it specifically.
Furthermore, the Buddha taught that craving is long-lasting like a river and difficult to trace; therefore, he spoke of it specifically.
As stated in a sutra: "The 'long river' is a metaphor for the three types of craving."
This refers to craving for sense-desires, craving for form, and craving for the formless.
Furthermore, it is specifically mentioned because the Buddha taught that craving is difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend.
Moreover, it is specifically mentioned because the Buddha taught that craving possesses many faults and afflictions, being both intense and firm.

Furthermore, the Buddha taught that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) can cause distinctions between realms (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), and classes (*nikāya*), and can give rise to all afflictions (*kleśa*); therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
It is for such various reasons as these.
Among the contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*),
the Blessed One specifically taught craving alone as the noble truth of origination; yet,
the noble truth of origination is not comprised of craving alone.
Question: What is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? Answer:
As stated in the Sūtra, it is all craving, craving for renewed existence, craving accompanied by delight, and craving for this or that specific object.
The remainderless abandonment, relinquishment, vomiting out, exhaustion, detachment, cessation, calming, and disappearance—this is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.
Question: Since it has been stated that the remainderless abandonment of all craving and so forth is called the Noble Truth of Cessation, [how is this so?]
If origination is also cessation, why is it called only the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering?
Answer: This should also be called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Origination.
That it is not so stated is because the teaching is incomplete (*sāvasesa-vacana*).
Furthermore, it has already been stated that when the cessation of suffering is taught, one should know that the truth of the origin is also taught as ceasing,
because suffering and its origin are one and the same thing.
Furthermore, if the cessation of suffering is taught, one should know that the truth of the origin is thereby taught as ceasing as well.
Because it is by extinguishing its causes and effects that [suffering] is extinguished.
Furthermore, because those to be converted delight in cessation, only the extinction of suffering is taught;
this is because those to be converted have a stronger sense of revulsion toward suffering than they do toward the origin of suffering.
Because they have been oppressed by suffering since beginningless time,
upon now hearing the Buddha’s teaching on the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, they immediately experience joy and say:
"How truly refreshing it is that these wretched and evil sufferings are utterly extinguished!"
Because of this joyful mind, one swiftly seeks to realize cessation (*nirodha*).
For various reasons such as these, the Blessed One spoke only of the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering,
and did not speak of it as the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Origination (*samudaya-nirodha*).
Question: What is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering?
Answer: As stated in the sūtras, it is the eightfold noble path, namely, right view up to and including right concentration.
This is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Question: This should also be stated as the path leading to the cessation of the origin [of suffering];
why is it only stated as the path leading to the cessation of suffering?
Answer: This too should be stated as the path leading to the origin, cessation, and the way [of suffering].
That it is not so stated is because the teaching is incomplete (*śeṣavacana*).

Furthermore, since the path leading to the cessation of suffering has already been explained, it should be understood that this itself explains the paths leading to the origin and cessation [of suffering].
This is because suffering and its origin are not separate entities.
Furthermore, if one speaks of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, it should be understood that this already implies the path leading to the cessation of its origin;
for the fruit can only cease once its cause has been extinguished.
Furthermore, this is said because those to be converted take delight in the cessation and the path.
That is to say, when those to be converted feel a profound weariness toward suffering, they hear that this path can lead to the cessation of suffering and experience extreme joy.
By means of this, one is able to swiftly cultivate the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the path;
therefore, it is said that [the path] leads to the cessation of suffering.
Furthermore, it is stated thus to show that the Noble Path is capable only of obstructing suffering so that it never arises again.
That is to say, suppose one asks:
"Do you have the power to cause a factor that is neither a cause nor an effect to become so?
One answers that one cannot.
However, as for those causes and conditions that can produce suffering,
I am able to apply antidotes so that suffering does not arise;
therefore, I speak only of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Furthermore, it is in order to refute the slander against the path that it is said to be "only the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
This refers to those who, at a young age of seven or eight years and so forth, realize the fruit of arhatship.
Only when their lifespan reaches a full hundred years does it finally end;
in the interim, they undergo various kinds of suffering,
such as the suffering of the four hundred and four diseases.
When people see this, they immediately slander it,
saying, "This noble path cannot bring an end to suffering.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke thus.
The Noble Path is able to extinguish the manifold sufferings of future existence.
For these and various other reasons,
the Blessed One taught only the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Yet they are not described as the truth of the origin, cessation, or path.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One first teach the truth of suffering, and so on, until finally teaching the truth of the path?
Answer: This was said for the sake of conforming to the phrasing;
that is, it was said so as to conform to the phrasing.
Furthermore, if one speaks in this way, it conforms to the manner of speaking.
The recipient and the holder are not anything other than this sequence.
Furthermore, this statement is made based on the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*);
that is, the dharmas of the sequence are briefly of three kinds.
First, the sequence of origination;
second, the sequence of easy explanation;
third, the sequence of clear realization.
Regarding the generation stage (*utpattikrama*):
it refers to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and so forth.
Among these, practitioners of yoga first develop the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Therefore, it is taught first;
up until the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) which arises last,
it is therefore taught last.
The detailed exposition for the dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) is likewise.
As for those categories that are easy to explain in their sequence, they are:

the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold path (*mārgāṅga*).
Although the four right efforts exist simultaneously, because they are easier to explain,
the abandonment of evil is taught first and the cultivation of good is taught later.
Within the abandonment of evil, the abandonment of evil that has already arisen is taught first.
Regarding the subsequent teaching on the prevention of unarisen evil,
within the cultivation of the wholesome, it first teaches the arising of unarisen wholesome states and subsequently teaches the increase of already arisen wholesome states.
If one were to speak in this way,
the ease of expression regarding the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and so forth would also be explained at length in the same manner.
As for the sequence of clear realization (*abhisamaya*):
That is to say, the Four Noble Truths.
Because practitioners of yoga first realize suffering at the stage of clear observation (*abhisamaya*), the Buddha taught it first.
Because it is the subsequent clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of origination, the Buddha taught it next;
because it is the subsequent clear realization of cessation, the Buddha taught it next;
and because it is the clear realization of the path, the Buddha taught it last.
Question: From this discussion, another question arises:
For what reason does a practitioner, when entering into clear realization (*abhisamaya*), first realize suffering and so forth, until finally realizing the path?
Answer: It is according to their relative coarseness and subtlety.
That is to say, among the Four Noble Truths, the truth of suffering is the coarsest and thus is realized first;
proceeding in succession, the truth of the path is the subtlest and thus is realized last.
Just as when learning archery, one first shoots at coarse objects,
gradually progressing until one can hit the tip of a hair;
furthermore, the delusion regarding suffering can sustain the delusion regarding the origin [of suffering].
Furthermore, as long as one has not eliminated the delusion regarding cessation,
one cannot eliminate the delusion regarding the path; likewise, as long as one has not eliminated the delusion regarding suffering,

one can never eliminate the delusion regarding its origin, and so on, until finally, as long as one has not eliminated the delusion regarding cessation, one can never eliminate the delusion regarding the path.
Therefore, one first realizes suffering (*duḥkha*) and finally realizes the path (*mārga*).
Furthermore, delusion regarding suffering (*duḥkha-sammoha*) can induce delusion regarding the origin (*samudaya-sammoha*),
and so on, until delusion regarding cessation (*nirodha-sammoha*) can induce delusion regarding the path (*mārga-sammoha*).
If the delusion regarding suffering is not first obstructed,
the delusion regarding its origin cannot necessarily be obstructed;
likewise, if the delusion regarding cessation is not first obstructed, the delusion regarding the path cannot necessarily be obstructed.
Therefore, one first realizes suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth, up to finally realizing the path (*mārga*).
Furthermore, through the contemplation of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), one can induce the contemplation of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*);
and so on, until through the contemplation of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*), one can induce the contemplation of the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
If one has not yet given rise to the contemplation of the truth of suffering, one will certainly be unable to give rise to the contemplation of the truth of the origin;
likewise, if one has not yet given rise to the contemplation of the truth of cessation, one will certainly be unable to give rise to the contemplation of the truth of the path.
Therefore, one first realizes suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth, up to finally realizing the path (*mārga*).

Furthermore, by means of the contemplation of the truth of suffering, one contemplates the truth of origination (*samudaya*) as the cause, the root, the path, the preliminary, the producer, the condition, and that which brings about arising.
Up to the contemplation of the truth of cessation, this is the contemplation of the truth of the path.
Because it is based on the fundamental path and its continuity, it is able to act as the condition for the arising and accumulation [of suffering].
If one has not yet given rise to the contemplation of the truth of suffering, one will certainly be unable to give rise to the contemplation of the truth of accumulation.
Furthermore, as long as the contemplation of the truth of cessation has not arisen, one can certainly not give rise to the contemplation of the truth of the path;
therefore, one first realizes the truth of suffering and finally realizes the truth of the path.

Moreover, the contemplation of the truth of suffering is the gateway upon which the preparatory application for the contemplation of the truth of origination relies, and it is the foundation upon which it stands.

Even up to the contemplation of the truth of cessation, this is the gateway upon which the preparatory application for the contemplation of the truth of the path relies and the basis upon which it is established.
If one has not yet given rise to the contemplation of the truth of suffering, one will certainly be unable to give rise to the contemplation of the truth of origination.
Furthermore, as long as one has not yet given rise to the contemplation of the truth of cessation, one certainly cannot give rise to the contemplation of the truth of the path;
therefore, one first realizes suffering and finally realizes the path.
As the Venerable Pārśva said:
Once the practitioner of meditation has understood that the five aggregates of clinging are like a disease, like an abscess, and like an arrow,

they next seek their cause and thus know it to be the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*). Next, seeking the state where [the cause] no longer exists, they know it to be the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Subsequently, seeking an antidote, one knows this to be the Truth of the Path.
It is like a person of weak constitution who, when afflicted by illness and the like,
being oppressed by suffering, gives rise to the thought:
"From what cause do these illnesses of mine arise?
He knew they arose from wind, heat, phlegm, and so forth.
Then he further reflected:
When will it be healed? One knows it at the time of its cessation.
Again, one forms this thought:
"By what means will it be healed? One knows it through such things as taking medicine.
For this reason, one first realizes suffering,
and so on, until finally realizing the path.
Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation knows that the five aggregates of clinging are fraught with many faults and afflictions.
Next, one seeks its cause; next, one seeks its cessation; thereafter, one seeks the remedy.
It is like a man who has a son who specializes in robbery and banditry, and the father reflects as follows:
"Because of whom has my son committed this evil? I know it is because of evil friends.
He further thought:
"When will my son's evil conduct cease? I know it will be when he is disciplined and made virtuous. He further thought: [and so forth].
Who causes one to become well-trained? It is through a virtuous friend.
For this reason, one first realizes suffering, and so on, until finally realizing the path.
Question: Since cause precedes effect in accordance with the sequential order, why does the practitioner first realize suffering (*duḥkha*) and subsequently realize its origin (*samudaya*)?
Answer: Because the sequence of knowing suffering and abandoning its origin is the proper order.
Question: What is the sequence for knowing suffering and abandoning its origin?
Answer: This follows the worldly sequence for felling a tree;
that is, one who fells a tree first cuts the branches and so forth, and only then pulls out the root.
The sequence for felling the tree of birth and death is likewise:
first knowing suffering is like cutting the branches,
and subsequently severing the origin is like uprooting the tree.

Question: Since the sequence of the path first and cessation later follows the order of conformity, why does the practitioner first realize cessation (*nirodha*) and subsequently realize the path (*mārga*)?
Answer: Because the sequence for realizing cessation and cultivating the path is in accordance with the natural order.
Question: What is the sequential order for realizing cessation and cultivating the path?
Answer: This follows the sequence of that which is to be reached and the means by which it is reached.
If one were to first speak of the cultivation of the path and subsequently speak of the realization of cessation, [it would be inconsistent].
One does not know whose path this is.
If one first speaks of the realization of cessation and subsequently speaks of the cultivation of the path,
then one knows that this path is the path leading toward cessation.
It is like a person who asks another, "Please show me the way," and the other person counters by asking, "Which way do you ask for?
to which the first person replies, "I am asking for the way to such-and-such city."

He then replied, "This is that path. Just as one first speaks of the realization of cessation and subsequently speaks of the cultivation of the path, it should be understood that this is likewise the case;
cessation is mentioned first to indicate the path in accordance with the proper sequence.
Furthermore, practitioners of yoga first eliminate the delusion regarding the three truths by means of the path that takes those three truths as its object;
subsequently, they eliminate the delusion regarding the truth of the path by means of the path that takes the truth of the path as its object.
Therefore, one first realizes cessation and only afterwards realizes the path.
It is like a person who first observes another's face to know its beauty or ugliness,
and subsequently, wishing to know the beauty or ugliness of his own face, takes up a mirror and gazes into it.
For this reason, one first realizes cessation (*nirodha*) and subsequently realizes the path (*mārga*).
Question: When realizing the truths (*satya*), does one contemplate their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)?
If it were so, what would be the fault?
Both [positions] entail faults.
Why is this? If one contemplates their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the distinctions between the specific characteristics of all phenomena are infinite.
There may be those who attain the ultimate state without having fully contemplated the truths.
For instance, one might die before having exhausted their contemplation of the boundless distinctions of the specific characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*).
How much more so when one can further observe the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of other phenomena?

If one observes their common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), how is it that the Four Noble Truths are not realized all at once (*sakṛt-abhisamaya*)? Furthermore, at what time does one observe the specific characteristics of the truths with knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*)?
If one cannot contemplate the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the truths, how can one be called a "realizer of the truths" (*satyābhisamaya*)?
One should answer that such a person contemplates the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Question: Why do the Four Noble Truths not manifest through simultaneous realization (*ekābhisamaya*)?
Answer: Although one contemplates their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) at the time of realizing the truths, one does not realize all common characteristics.
That is to say, one realizes only a limited portion of the common characteristics; however, the distinctions between individual and common characteristics are infinite.
Furthermore, the great element of earth is called both its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and its common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
It is called its own characteristic in relation to the other three great elements;
it is called its common characteristic because all instances of the earth element possess the characteristic of solidity.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is composed of the primary elements (mahābhūta) and the derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
Thus, this aggregate of form is called both "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) and "common characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
It is termed "specific characteristic" in relation to the other four aggregates.
That which is called the "common characteristic" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) refers to the fact that all material forms possess the characteristic of being subject to change and obstruction.
Thus, the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) together constitute the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya).
In this way, the truth of suffering is termed both the "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) and the "common characteristic."
That which is called the "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) is so designated in contrast to the other three truths;
that which is called the "common characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) is so designated because all aggregates possess the characteristic of oppression.
One contemplates such a common characteristic of oppression.
This is precisely the contemplation of the characteristics of suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self;
it is also termed the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truth of suffering.
Such a clear realization, when applied to the various truths, is called the observation of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-darśana*).
If one contemplates the common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) with respect to the aggregates (skandha),
then because of this contemplation of the common characteristics of the aggregates,
it is called "contemplating the common characteristics" at the time of clear realization (abhisamaya).
Because it is a contemplation of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of each of the truths,
there is no simultaneous realization (*abhisamaya*) of the four truths.
Furthermore, one truth is not the four.
The Four Truths are not one;
therefore, they are not realized all at once.
Furthermore, a single mode of apprehension is not four.
Because the four aspects are not identical,
there is no simultaneous clear realization (abhisamaya) of the Four Truths.
Furthermore, the characteristics of the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava) are each distinct.
Therefore, one does not realize the four truths all at once.
Furthermore, because the characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned are each distinct,
one does not realize the four truths all at once.
Furthermore, because the fruit and its cause, as well as the realized and the realizer, are each distinct,
there is no simultaneous clear realization (abhisamaya) of the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, it is because the Four Noble Truths either differ in their characteristics or differ in their essential nature and characteristics.
Therefore, there is no sense in which they can be realized all at once.
Furthermore, the meanings of the cognizer and the cognized, the faculties and their characteristics,
the aspects of activity and the objects of perception, and the aspects of the subject and its object, each have their own distinct natures.
Therefore, one does not realize the Four Noble Truths instantaneously.
Furthermore, since one does not even observe each individual truth instantaneously,
how much less could one observe all four truths simultaneously?
This means that during the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), one first contemplates the suffering of the desire realm individually,
and subsequently contemplates the suffering of the form and formless realms collectively;
likewise, one first contemplates the origin (*samudaya*) of the desire realm individually.
Afterward, one contemplates the origination of the form and formless realms collectively;
first, one contemplates the cessation of the desire realm individually;
afterward, one contemplates the cessation of the form and formless realms collectively.
First, one contemplates the path of the desire realm separately;
subsequently, one contemplates the paths of the form and formless realms together.
Therefore, there is no principle of simultaneously contemplating the Four Noble Truths.
Question: Based on this discussion, a further question arises:
for what reason does the practitioner first contemplate the suffering of the desire realm individually, and subsequently contemplate the suffering of the form and formless realms collectively?
Answer: One gives rise to clear realization (abhisamaya) based on the characteristics of coarseness and subtlety.
Because the suffering of the desire realm is coarse, it is realized first;
because the suffering of the form and formless realms is subtle, it is realized later.

Question: If that were so, the suffering of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), being coarse, should be realized first, while the suffering of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), being subtle, should be realized later.
How then can one realize the suffering of both realms simultaneously?
Answer: Because they are both comprised within the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*), they are combined in the clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
That is to say, because the suffering of the desire realm is not comprised within the stages of meditative concentration, it is first observed individually;
whereas because the sufferings of the form and formless realms are both comprised within the stages of meditative concentration, they are subsequently observed in combination.
Furthermore, because the suffering of the desire realm coexists with the body and is currently apprehended, it is observed separately first;
because the suffering of the form and formless realms does not coexist with the body and is not currently apprehended, they are observed together later.

Furthermore, because the suffering of the desire realm involves the oppression of manifest pain—like bearing a heavy burden—it is first observed separately; whereas the suffering of the form and formless realms does not involve the oppression of manifest pain like bearing a heavy burden, it is therefore observed subsequently in combination.
Furthermore, the suffering of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is observed individually first because it afflicts practitioners with immediate distress, like an enemy appearing before one's eyes;

the suffering of the form and formless realms (rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu) is observed collectively later because it does not afflict practitioners with immediate distress, as it is not like an enemy appearing before one's eyes.
Furthermore, because the suffering of the desire realm is proximate, it is observed separately first;
because the suffering of the form and formless realms is remote, they are observed collectively later.
As with proximity and remoteness, so it is with contiguity.
It is neither through proximity nor through conjunction that this body’s homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga) [is perceived];
it should be understood that the same applies to other bodies’ homogeneous classes.
Furthermore, because the suffering of the desire realm is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), it is first observed individually;
because the suffering of the form and formless realms is not directly perceived, they are subsequently observed collectively.
Question: When one enters the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), if the suffering of the form and formless realms is not directly perceived, how can it be called "clear realization"?
Answer: There are two kinds of direct perception:
first, direct perception of appropriation;
second, direct perception free from defilement.

Regarding the stage of entering clear observation (*abhisamaya*): because one possesses both types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) with respect to suffering in the desire realm, it is called "clear observation.
Regarding suffering in the form and formless realms, because there is only the direct perception of detachment from defilement (*vairāgya*), it is called "clear observation."
It is like a merchant who has two loads of goods:
one he carries himself and another he causes another to carry.
Regarding that which he carries himself, he possesses both forms of direct perception.
First is the direct perception of knowing the weight;
second is the direct perception of knowing the wealth.
As for having another carry it, there is only the single direct perception.
This means that wealth is known through direct perception.
Furthermore, because the suffering of the desire realm consists of three types—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—it is observed separately first.
Because the suffering of the form and formless realms consists only of two types—wholesome and neutral—it is observed collectively later.

Furthermore, because the practitioner has achieved the state of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they first contemplate the suffering of the desire realm individually;
this is because they have not yet achieved the state of an ordinary being in the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*).
Subsequently, one should contemplate the suffering of the form and formless realms;
such is the nature of things.
If one is established in the state of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) belonging to these realms...
That is to say, one first contemplates the suffering of this realm.
Furthermore, because one first gives rise to revulsion toward the suffering of the desire realm, one first attains individual clear observation (*pratyekābhisamaya*) and thereby generates faith.
Because one subsequently gives rise to revulsion toward the suffering of the form and formless realms, one later attains collective clear observation (*sāmānyābhisamaya*) and thereby generates faith.
Through such various causes and conditions as these,
one first contemplates the suffering of the desire realm individually,
and subsequently contemplates the suffering of the form and formless realms collectively.
The clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the three truths should be understood according to this.

Question: If one clearly realizes the truths by means of their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), at what time does one then observe the specific characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of the truths with knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*)?
If one cannot contemplate the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the truths, how can one be called a "realizer of the truths" (*satyābhisamaya*)?

Answer: It is not by means of a wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūtajñāna*) contemplating various specific characteristics as specific characteristics that this is called the realization of the truths.

Furthermore, the knowledge of reality (yathābhūtajñāna) observes the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena through their common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa); this is called the clear realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya).
Moreover, there is ignorance regarding the specific and common characteristics of the truths.
When one realizes the truths through clear observation (*abhisamaya*), although all [afflictions] are abandoned simultaneously and one observes their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*),
it is nonetheless called "clear observation of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the truths as they truly are.
Furthermore, suffering, impermanence, and so forth are termed the specific characteristics of the truths.
This is precisely what is called the "common characteristic" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of the aggregates.
Therefore, when one contemplates suffering and so forth regarding the various truths,
it is called the "clear realization" (abhisamaya) of both their specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and common characteristics.
The specific characteristics of the aggregates and so forth are infinite;
one cannot sever all afflictions by contemplating them individually.
Therefore, during the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they are not contemplated separately.
Question: Since one contemplates the aggregates in their entirety at the time of entering into clear realization (*abhisamaya*), how is it that one does not contemplate the truths in their entirety?
Answer: At the time of entering into clear realization, one contemplates the principles of the Four Noble Truths.
One abandons the afflictions that are deluded regarding the specific characteristics of the four truths;
since there is not a single affliction that is collectively deluded regarding all four truths,
one does not attain a collective clear realization (abhisamaya) of the four truths.
Because there is a general delusion regarding the aggregates,
one attains a general clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the aggregates.
Furthermore, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the aggregates are not the principle of the Truths.
Because they have already been understood since beginningless time, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the Four Truths are no longer observed;
because they were not understood since beginningless time, they are now realized individually. *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 78.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Seventy-nine,
composed by five hundred great Arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Nine of the Fourth Sub-section on the Ten Gates within the Second Chapter, the Aggregate of Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha): As stated in the Sūtra, the Noble Truth of Suffering should be fully known through wisdom.
The Abhidharma states:
"That which is to be fully known by wisdom refers to all phenomena.
Question: If all phenomena are that which is to be fully known, as stated in the Abhidharma, [then...]
Why does the sutra state only that suffering should be fully known through wisdom?
Answer: The sutra states that the Noble Truth of Suffering is to be fully known solely with reference to supramundane wisdom.
The Abhidharma, based generally upon both mundane and supramundane wisdom,
states that all phenomena are to be fully known.

As it is with the mundane and supramundane, so too should one understand the distinction between those with outflows and those without outflows, as well as those that are bound and liberated, or fettered and unfettered.
Furthermore, the sūtras speak of the noble truth of suffering as that which is to be fully known (*parijñeya*) based solely on the wisdom of proximate thorough knowledge;
the Abhidharma, however, speaks of all phenomena as being that which is to be fully known based on both proximate and remote wisdom.
It should be understood that the same applies to proximity and distance, to being contiguous and non-contiguous, and to being conjoined and non-conjoined.

Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks only with reference to the wisdom that contemplates common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), stating that the Noble Truth of Suffering is that which is to be fully known; whereas the Abhidharma, generally speaking, states with reference to the wisdom that contemplates both specific (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics that all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*) are that which is to be fully known.

Just as it is with the wisdom of specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), so too should one understand the awakening to specific and general characteristics and the mental attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward specific and general characteristics.
Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks only in reliance upon non-common wisdom (*asādhāraṇaprajñā*) when stating that the Noble Truth of Suffering is to be fully known.
The Abhidharma generally states, based on both common and uncommon wisdom, that all phenomena are that which is to be fully known (*parijñeya*).
Furthermore, the Sūtra, based on the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), states that the Noble Truth of Suffering is that which should be fully known.
The Abhidharma, relying on the truth of practice (*pratipatti-satya*), states that all phenomena are to be fully known (*parijñeya*).
Furthermore, the Sūtra, relying on the awakening to designations (*prajñapti-bodha*), states that the noble truth of suffering (*duḥkha-āryasatya*) is to be fully known.
The Abhidharma, based on the cognition of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), states that all phenomena (*dharma*) are to be fully known (*parijñeya*).
Question: What is the meaning of "cognition of designation" (*prajñapti-buddhi*)?
Answer: It is because [designation] is coarse, manifest, and easy to perceive in terms of its results.
Through skillful means, it is said that suffering is fully known;
through skillful means, it is said that the origin is eternally abandoned so that the causes of birth and death do not continue.
Based on that which possesses the two qualities and does not reside in the body,
it is taught through skillful means as that which should realize cessation;
based on the path capable of permanently severing all afflictions.
It is taught through skillful means that one should cultivate the path;
this is what is called the "provisional designation of the meaning of awakening.
It is not because it exhausts the ultimate principle that the name "provisional designation" is established.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"The World-Honored One has taught only that suffering should be fully understood;
or it may be said that suffering alone is what should be fully understood."
Therefore, in the Abhidharma it is said that all phenomena (dharmas) are to be fully known;
yet the Blessed One has taught only that the origin [of suffering] is to be permanently abandoned.
Some might say this is because only the origin is to be permanently abandoned.
In the Abhidharma, it is stated that all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) should be permanently abandoned;
yet the Blessed One has taught only that cessation (*nirodha*) should be realized.
Or rather, it may be said that only cessation is what should be realized.
Therefore, in the Abhidharma, based on the attainment of realization (*prāptisākṣātkriyā*), it is said that all wholesome dharmas should be realized.
Yet, the Blessed One spoke only of the Path as that which should be cultivated;
some even claim that only the Path is to be cultivated.
Therefore, in the Abhidharma, it is stated in general that all conditioned wholesome dharmas should be cultivated;
this [statement] reveals that the meaning of the Sūtra was not fully understood.
The Abhidharma is an exposition of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Furthermore, in order to bring about the permanent severance of the path of birth and death, the Buddha taught only that suffering should be fully understood.
That is to say, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the root of the sixty-two types of speculative views.
The views (dṛṣṭi-gati) are the root of the remaining afflictions;
all other afflictions are the root of karma;
and karma, in turn, is the root of maturation (vipāka).
Depending upon the maturation (vipāka), all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena arise and grow;
by means of this, one revolves through birth and death without end.
When suffering is fully known, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is abandoned.
Because the view of a self-identity is abandoned, the path of birth and death is cut off;
therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should fully understand suffering.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of bringing about the permanent abandonment of the five views of self and the fifteen views of "mine."
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should thoroughly understand suffering.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of permanently severing the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*),
and for the sake of realizing the meditative concentrations of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should fully understand suffering.

Furthermore, since beginningless time, sentient beings have conceived the notions of "self," "sentient being," "life-force," "born being," "nourisher," and "person" (pudgala) with respect to the five aggregates of clinging.
Who can sever these various evil and inverted perceptions and cause one to attain the perception of the Dharma, namely, the thorough knowledge of suffering? Therefore,
the Buddha taught only that one should thoroughly know suffering.
Furthermore, since beginningless time, one has conceived notions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity regarding the aggregates—which are in fact suffering, impermanent, empty, and non-self.
Who is able to sever these various inverted conceptions?
To cause them to attain non-perverted cognition— namely, the full comprehension of suffering—
the Buddha taught only that one should fully comprehend suffering.
Furthermore, since beginningless time, all classes of sentient beings...
Although they are afflicted and oppressed by the aggregates as if bearing a heavy burden,
they still crave and cling to those very aggregates like infants.
Although she beat, scolded, and coerced him while serving as his wet nurse,
he remained devoted to her;
this was because he desired to cause sentient beings to sever their attachment to the aggregates.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should fully comprehend suffering.
Furthermore, since beginningless time, all classes of sentient beings have been subject to afflictions,
unwholesome conduct, and perversions.
This causes the mind and mental factors to be deviant and crooked toward their objects.
Who makes them upright? It is the thorough knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-parijñāna*).
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should thoroughly know suffering.
Furthermore, when yogins fully comprehend suffering, they are able to abide in unerring perception and mind.
Even if they have already realized the Noble Truth of Suffering,
they do not need to realize the remaining Noble Truths again.
Someone asked, "Are these five aggregates of clinging suffering or happiness?
He replied, "They are only suffering, like a ball of hot iron.
He asked again, "Are the aggregates of clinging permanent or impermanent?"
He replied, "It is impermanent; after a single moment, it certainly does not remain.
He asked again, "Are the aggregates of grasping pure or impure?
He replied, "They are impure, like a heap of excrement and filth."
He asked again whether the appropriated aggregates possess a self or are without a self.
He replied: "They are without a self; neither an agent nor an experiencer can be found, for they are merely an empty collection of formations.
This is non-erroneous because suffering has been fully understood."
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should fully understand suffering.
Furthermore, the aggregates of clinging are like a disease in their nature of being unwholesome;
the aggregates of clinging are like an abscess in their nature of being oppressive and painful.
The aggregates of clinging are like the nature of an arrow, capable of inflicting harm;
the aggregates of clinging are like the nature of a sword, capable of wounding and cutting;
the aggregates of clinging are like the nature of poison, capable of killing.
The aggregates of grasping are like fire in their nature to burn;
the aggregates of grasping are like enemies in their nature to cause no benefit;
the aggregates of grasping are like a frontier city constantly harassed by the various thieves of karma and afflictions.
To be able to know this is called the thorough knowledge of suffering.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should thoroughly know suffering.
Furthermore, for all practitioners of yoga:
If one fully understands suffering, it is called encountering the true Buddha appearing in the world;
it is called entering the sublime, ultimate, and correct Dharma;
and it is called true renunciation.
