It is called "truly enjoying the treasure of the true Dharma" because one attains non-obstruction;
therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should fully understand suffering.
Furthermore, for all practitioners of yoga:
If one fully understands suffering, it is called abandoning what was previously conditioned and attaining what was not previously conditioned;
it is called abandoning the common and attaining the uncommon;
it is called abandoning the mundane and attaining the supramundane.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should fully understand suffering.
Furthermore, for all practitioners of yoga,
if they fully understand suffering, they open the door to the noble path that was previously unopened.
Therefore, one is able to relinquish the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), which has never before been relinquished,
and is able to attain the state of a noble one (*āryatva*), which has never before been attained. For this reason,
the Buddha taught only that suffering should be fully understood (*parijñeya*).

Furthermore, when a practitioner of yoga thoroughly understands suffering, they abandon names and acquire names, abandon realms and acquire realms, and abandon natures and acquire natures. Regarding the abandonment of names and the acquisition of names:

this refers to abandoning the name of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and acquiring the name of a noble one (*ārya*). Regarding the abandonment of realms and the acquisition of realms: [it refers to...]
This refers to abandoning the portion belonging to the realm of ordinary beings and attaining the portion belonging to the realm of noble ones;
it is the relinquishing of one's nature and the acquiring of another nature.
This means that because one abandons the lineage of ordinary beings and attains the lineage of the noble ones, the Buddha taught only that suffering should be fully understood.
Furthermore, regarding all practitioners of yoga:
If one fully understands suffering, one attains the mind but not the cause of the mind;
one attains suffering but not the cause of suffering;
one attains clarity but not the cause of clarity.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should fully understand suffering (*duḥkha*).
Furthermore, when a practitioner of yoga fully understands suffering,
they abandon the five types of homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and attain the eight types of homogeneity.
The five "homogeneous classes" (*sabhāgatā*) refer to the homogeneous class of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*).
The eight "homogeneous classes" refer to the homogeneous class of the four stages of approach and the four fruits of realization.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should fully understand suffering (*duḥkha*).
Furthermore, when practitioners of yoga thoroughly understand suffering,
they abandon the nature of ordinary worldlings— which is like a tuft of willow down—
and abide in the buddha-nature, which is like the banner of Indra.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should fully understand suffering (*duḥkha*).
Furthermore, for all practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*),
if they fully understand suffering, it is called "the first attainment of verified clarity regarding the Dharma" (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should fully understand suffering (*duḥkha*).
Furthermore, it is impossible for any practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*) to attain [the path] for the first time by means of fully understanding suffering.
As stated in the Sūtra, it is impossible for one who has seen the Noble Truths to take the life of another or to transgress the precepts, and so forth, as explained at length. Therefore,
the Buddha taught only that one should fully comprehend suffering (*duḥkha*).
Furthermore, when all practitioners of yoga thoroughly understand suffering,
it is called their initial entry into the great ocean of Dharma and their ascent of the great mountain of Dharma.
Having vanquished the great enemy and ascended the great Dharma throne,
the Buddha taught only that one should fully comprehend suffering.
Furthermore, suffering should be fully understood, but it is not to be entirely abandoned;
the origin should be entirely abandoned, but it is not to be merely fully understood;
cessation should be realized, but it is not to be merely fully understood.
The Path should be cultivated and not merely fully understood;
therefore, the Buddha taught only that suffering should be fully understood.
Furthermore, all four Noble Truths should be fully understood.
Because suffering is primary, only suffering is mentioned.
As the Sūtra says:
"The Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering should be permanently abandoned by means of wisdom."
The Abhidharma states that what should be eternally abandoned refers to contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
If it were said that craving alone constitutes the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), [this would be inconsistent].
One should ask him: "All contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) ought to be abandoned forever, as stated in the Abhidharma.
Why, then, did the Blessed One say only that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) should be abandoned forever, and not all other contaminated phenomena?"
Regarding the statement that "craving is the origin" as before, the response is:
if it is said that the cause of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) is the Truth of Origin (*samudaya-satya*), then one should ask:
since the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) must also be permanently abandoned, why is it stated only that the Origin must be permanently abandoned?
The Buddha replied: "I have made this statement for the sake of abandoning suffering. If you wish to abandon all sufferings, you should forever sever the origin [of suffering].
Because the origin is forever severed, suffering does not arise; this is called the true abandonment of suffering."
Furthermore, the Buddha made this statement for the sake of abandoning the fruit:
"If you wish to abandon the fruit of suffering, you should eternally sever its cause.
Because the cause is eternally severed, the fruit of suffering does not arise; this is called the true abandonment of the fruit."
Furthermore, this statement is made in order to stop the flow of suffering.
Just as one who wishes to stop a current must dam the source of the water, so too,
one who wishes to stop the flow of suffering should permanently eradicate its origin (*samudaya*).
Furthermore, because of the permanent abandonment of the origin [of suffering],
one destroys both causes and becomes detached from both fetters,
thereby attaining the untainted acquisition of detachment (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*).
Because it eliminates the omnipresent causes of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
the Buddha taught that only the origin (*samudaya*) should be permanently abandoned.
Furthermore, if the cause is severed, the fruit follows suit and is severed as well.
If the cause is extinguished, the fruit is accordingly extinguished;
if the cause is abandoned, the fruit is accordingly abandoned;
if the cause is vomited out, the fruit is accordingly vomited out.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that the origin [of suffering] should be permanently abandoned.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One made this statement because he wished to cause all sentient beings to cast off the heavy burden of the aggregates (*skandha*).
This is like a person carrying a heavy load who must traverse a place of peril and difficulty.
Furthermore, he stumbles and falls, wishing to cast off the burden but having no means to do so.
Someone says to him, "If you wish to cast off this burden, you must cut the rope of the burden; only then can you be released from it."
In this way, sentient beings carry the heavy burden of the aggregates and pass through the various perils of birth and death.
Because they are oppressed by the heavy burden of the aggregates, the Buddha told them:
"If you wish to be liberated from the heavy burden of the aggregates, you must forever sever its origination."
Once accumulation has been severed, the burden of the aggregates is cast off.
Furthermore, this statement is made in order to address the non-Buddhists,
for those non-Buddhists are oppressed by the fruit of suffering.
Although they loathe the fruit of suffering, they do not sever its cause;
they are like foolish dogs who abandon the person and chase after the clod of earth.
Therefore, the Buddha told them: "You who loathe suffering should forever sever its accumulation."
Once the cause of accumulation has been severed, the fruit of suffering no longer arises, and one thereby attains liberation.
Furthermore, accumulation draws forth the fruits of the three realms—low, middling, and superior;
if accumulation is permanently severed, the fruit of suffering does not arise.
Therefore, the World-Honored One told the classes of sentient beings:
"You should grow weary of suffering and forever sever its origin.
Furthermore, the origin is able to produce and grow three kinds of fruits of suffering.
If origination is permanently severed, those [sufferings] will not arise;
therefore, the Blessed One told sentient beings:
"If you are weary of the three kinds of suffering, you should permanently sever origination."
Furthermore, the origin [of suffering] brings about the growth of the four kinds of suffering.
If that origin is permanently severed, they will not grow.
For this reason, the Blessed One spoke to sentient beings.
If one is weary of the four types of suffering, one should forever sever the origin [of suffering].
Furthermore, the origin can cause the five realms of existence to grow;
if the origin is forever severed, they will not grow.
Therefore, the World-Honored One told the classes of sentient beings:
"If you are weary of the five kinds of suffering, you should forever sever the accumulation [of karma].
Furthermore, suffering should only be relinquished; it should not be severed."
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that the origin (*samudaya*) should be permanently abandoned.
For various reasons such as these, the Blessed One taught only that the origin should be permanently abandoned.

As the Sūtra says: "The noble truth of the cessation of suffering (*duḥkha-nirodha-āryasatya*) should be realized through wisdom (*prajñā*). The Abhidharma explains that what is "realized" refers to the attainment (*prāpti*) of all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).
Question: If all wholesome dharmas should be realized as stated in the Abhidharma, why did the Blessed One say only that cessation should be realized?
Answer: Cessation has the characteristic of liberation and dissociation from fetters.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that cessation should be realized.
Furthermore, cessation has no location and no basis;
therefore, the Buddha taught only that cessation should be realized.
Furthermore, although cessation is a cause, it has no effect;
and although cessation is an effect, it has no cause.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that one should only realize cessation.
Furthermore, although cessation is a cause, it is without a cause;
although cessation is a fruit, it is without a fruit.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that cessation should be realized.
Furthermore, cessation is a productive cause but not a productive cause that exists;
it is a condition but not a condition that exists;
it is a departure but not a departure that exists.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that cessation should be realized.
Furthermore, because cessation causes the aggregates to cease and is an unchanging dharma,
the Buddha taught only that cessation should be realized.
Furthermore, because cessation can pacify the three falls, the four prohibitions, and the five [obstacles], the Buddha taught that one should realize only cessation.
Furthermore, cessation is the single-flavored, vast fruit of the path.
Because it can purify the four castes as well as all conventional designations, it is called the Unsurpassed Dharma.

Therefore, the Buddha taught that cessation alone should be realized. Furthermore, cessation is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), whereas attainment (*prāpti*) pertains to both types [tainted and untainted]. Cessation is exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa*), whereas attainment pertains to all three categories [learner, non-learner, and neither-learner-nor-non-learner].
The attainment of cessation is subsumed under one truth; it is also subsumed under three truths.
Cessation is exclusively non-bound (apratisaṃyukta), yet its attainment can be of three kinds.
Cessation is exclusively non-abandonable (aprahātavya), yet its attainment can be of two kinds.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that cessation should be realized.
Furthermore, cessation is both wholesome and eternal;
it is both wholesome and transcendent.
This goodness is also detached from the aggregates;
this goodness has no three grades;
this goodness has no before or after.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that cessation should be realized.
Furthermore, cessation is the fruit of the śramaṇa, not the śramaṇa itself;
it is the fruit of the brāhmaṇa, not the brāhmaṇa itself.
This is the fruit of the holy life (brahmacarya), not the holy life itself;
this is the fruit of the path (mārga), not the path itself.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that cessation (nirodha) should be realized.
Furthermore, because it is for the sake of realizing cessation that one realizes conditioned wholesomeness,
the Buddha taught only that cessation should be realized.
It is by means of such various causes and conditions as these [that he spoke thus].
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that cessation should be realized.
As the Sūtra says: "The noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering should be cultivated with wisdom.
The Abhidharma states that those dharmas which should be cultivated are the conditioned wholesome dharmas.
Question: Since all conditioned wholesome phenomena should be cultivated, as stated in the Abhidharma, why did the Blessed One say only that "the Noble Path should be cultivated"?
Answer: The Noble Path should be cultivated; it should not be permanently abandoned.
Unlike other wholesome states which are to be abandoned or cultivated,
the Buddha taught that one should cultivate only the Noble Path.
Furthermore, the Noble Path consists solely of the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*).
Unlike other virtues, which possess four kinds of cultivation—
namely, attainment, practice, counteraction, and elimination—
the Buddha taught that one should cultivate only the Noble Path.
Furthermore, the Noble Path possesses both the wholesome and the untainted,
whereas other wholesome states possess only the wholesome.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that one should cultivate only the Noble Path.
Furthermore, the noble path should be cultivated so as to sever those afflictions such as craving that take it as their object;
it is not like other virtues, which both cultivate and sever the afflictions that take them as their objects.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that the noble path should be cultivated.
Furthermore, the Noble Path should be cultivated; it is emergence and not subsidence.
It is not like other wholesome states which, though they too should be cultivated, involve both emergence and subsidence—namely, emerging from the desire realm and subsiding into the first dhyāna.
...up to emerging from the sphere of nothingness and passing away from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should cultivate the noble path.
Question: One who has attained the noble path, having become free from the defilement of desire, is born into the first dhyāna.
Up to the point where, having become detached from the sphere of nothingness, one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
how is it that the noble path is emergence and not submergence?
Answer: Although this occurs, the various noble paths do not summon a ripened result (*vipāka*).
Unlike other virtues which can only induce maturation (*vipāka*),
the noble paths are therefore designated solely as "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*).
Furthermore, the cultivation of the noble paths is able to diminish all forms of existence (*bhava*).
It is able to harm all forms of existence (*bhava*);
it is able to destroy those who cultivate other virtues that nourish all forms of existence;
and it is able to gather and benefit all forms of existence.

Because it sustains all states of existence, the Buddha taught that one should cultivate the Noble Path. Furthermore, by cultivating the Noble Path, one severs the flow of existence and the cycle of birth, aging, sickness, and death, so that they do not continue in succession.
Cultivating other virtues merely sustains the flow of existence, ensuring that birth, aging, sickness, and death continue without interruption;
therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should cultivate the Noble Path.
Furthermore, cultivating the Noble Path is the practice for proceeding toward the cessation of suffering, of existence, and of birth, aging, sickness, and death in the world.
The cultivation of other virtues is a formative activity that leads to the accumulation of existence in the world of suffering, characterized by birth, aging, sickness, and death;
therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should cultivate the Noble Path.
Furthermore, the cultivation of the Noble Path does not fall under the category of the truths of suffering and its origin, nor is it a matter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The cultivation of other virtues is a matter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
it even falls within the scope of the truths of suffering and its origin.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should cultivate the Noble Path.
Furthermore, the cultivation of the Noble Path is not the cause for wandering through the realms, destinies, births, aging, sickness, and death;
whereas the cultivation of other virtues is the cause for wandering through the realms, destinies, births, aging, sickness, and death.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should cultivate the Noble Path.
Furthermore, by cultivating the Noble Path, the flow of transmigration through realms, destinies, births, aging, sickness, and death is brought entirely to an end;
whereas by cultivating other forms of merit, the flow of transmigration through realms, destinies, births, aging, sickness, and death is not ended.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should cultivate the noble path.
Furthermore, the noble path is exclusively that which is desirable and has desirable fruits;
it is that which is pleasing and has pleasing fruits.
That which is agreeable and the fruit of what is agreeable;
that which is delightful and the fruit of what is delightful;
that which is pleasurable and the fruit of what is pleasurable.
Other virtues are not like this;
therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should cultivate the noble path (*āryamārga*).
Furthermore, the noble path is itself the śramaṇa and the fruit of the śramaṇa (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
This is the brahmin; this is the fruit of the brahmin.
This is the holy life; this is the fruit of the holy life.
This is the path; this is the fruit of the path.
Therefore, the Buddha taught only that one should cultivate the Noble Path.
Furthermore, the cultivation of the Noble Path leads definitively to Nirvana,
whereas the cultivation of other virtues does not lead to a fixed destination.
Therefore, for these and various other reasons, the Buddha taught only that one should cultivate the noble path.
Thus, for such manifold causes and conditions,
the Buddha taught only that one should cultivate the noble path.
There are sixteen aspects that arise taking the four noble truths as their objects.
That is to say, there are four aspects taking the truth of suffering as their object:
first, suffering; second, impermanence; third, emptiness; and fourth, non-self.
The Truth of Origination has four aspects: first, cause;
second, origination; third, production; and fourth, condition.
The Truth of Cessation has four aspects.
First, cessation; second, tranquility; third, excellence; fourth, renunciation.
There are four aspects regarding the Truth of the Path: first, the path;
second, the right method; third, practice; and fourth, deliverance.
Question: Regarding the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), how many are there in terms of names and how many are there in terms of substantial entities (*dravya*)? Some say:
there are sixteen in terms of names, but seven in terms of substantial entities.
That is to say, regarding the four modes of activity (*ākāra*) that take the Truth of Suffering as their object, there are four names and likewise four substantial entities.
Regarding the four modes of activity for each of the other three Truths, although there are four names, there is only one substantial entity for each.

Question: Why is it that the four aspects (*ākāra*) conditioned by suffering (*duḥkha*) have four names and also four substantial entities (*dravya*), whereas those conditioned by the other three truths do not?
Answer: Because the aspects conditioned by suffering are the direct antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to the four perversions (*viparyāsa*).
Just as the four perversions (catur-viparyāsa) each have four names and four essential natures,
the mental aspects (ākāra) arising from taking the other three truths as objects are not the direct antidotes to the four perversions; therefore,
although there are four names, their actual substance is only one.
The commentary states: It should be explained in this way.
There are sixteen aspects (ākāra) both in name and in substance;
as with the names, so it is with the entities.
It is the designation of names and the designation of entities;
it is the difference in characteristics of names and the difference in characteristics of entities;
it is the difference in nature of names and the difference in nature of entities.
The differentiation of names and the differentiation of entities;
the establishment of names and the establishment of entities;
the thorough comprehension of names and the thorough comprehension of entities.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the characteristic of conduct?
Answer: Its intrinsic nature is wisdom (*prajñā*).
It should be understood that herein, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the aspect of activity (*ākāra*);
it is both the agent of activity and the object of activity.
Although the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) associated with wisdom are not themselves aspects of activity, they are both the agents of activity and the objects of activity.
There are formations dissociated from wisdom that coexist with it,
as well as other existing phenomena which, though neither the aspect of activity nor the agent of activity, are nevertheless objects of activity.
Some state this as follows:
Regarding the aspect of mental formations (*saṃskāra-nimitta*), it has all mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If one were to state it thus,
all minds and mental factors would be aspects of mental formations.
It is both that which practices and that which is practiced.
All other dharmas, although they are neither the aspect of practice nor that which practices, are nonetheless that which is practiced.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
What is called "aspect" (*ākāra*) has all phenomena as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If one were to say this,
then all associated phenomena (*samprayuktadharma*) would also be aspects.
It is both that which performs the activity and that which is the object of the activity.
Although non-associated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*) are indeed aspects of activity (*ākāra*) and objects of activity, they are not that which performs the activity.
The critique states: one should speak thus.
The characteristic of the mode of activity (*ākāra*) has wisdom as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), just as was previously stated.
This is called the characteristic of the mode of activity’s intrinsic nature;
it is the self-nature, the entity, the essential characteristic, the constituent part, and the fundamental nature.
The reason for its intrinsic nature has already been explained; now it shall be explained.
Question: Why is it called "aspect" (*ākāra*)?
What is the meaning of "aspect"?
Answer: The meaning of "aspect" (*ākāra*) is that which functions by discerning the characteristics of various objects.
Question: Why is it called "suffering," and so forth, up to why is it called "emergence"?
Answer: Because it is painful and oppressive, like bearing a heavy burden.
It is called suffering because it is contrary to the Noble One's mind.
It is said to be impermanent for two reasons:
first, by way of its being produced.
Second, by way of dependence on conditions.
By way of what is performed:
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are capable of performing an action within a single moment.
In the second moment, it can no longer act.
Because they depend on conditions— meaning that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are bound to various conditions before they can perform an action—
and because this contradicts the view of "mine," it is called empty (*śūnya*).
It is called "non-self" because it contradicts the view of a self.
It is called a "cause" because it functions like a seed.
It is called "origination" because it causes things to appear equally and simultaneously.
Because it causes [phenomena] to arise in continuous succession, it is called "birth" (*jāti*).
Because it has the capacity to bring about accomplishment, it is called a "condition" (*pratyaya*).
For example, a jar and other such things are accomplished through the combination of various conditions, such as a lump of clay, a potter's wheel, a string, and water.
Because the aggregates of grasping are forever exhausted, it is called cessation (*nirodha*).
Because the characteristics of the conditioned have subsided, it is called tranquility (*śānta*).
Because it is wholesome and eternal, it is called sublime (*praṇīta*).
Because it is the ultimate peace and security, it is called "detachment" (niḥsaraṇa).
Since the essence of this detachment is not something that exists as a separate entity to be detached from, it is so named.
Because it opposes and subverts false paths, it is called the "path" (mārga).
It is called "suchness" (tathatā) because it is not contrary to or harmful to reality.
It is called "path" (mārga) because it leads to the palace of Nirvāṇa.
It is called "exit" (niḥsaraṇa) because it enables one to transcend [saṃsāra] forever.
This is because it is a nature that emerges rather than a nature that perishes.
Furthermore, it is called suffering because it is oppressed by the heavy residues (*dausthulya*);
it is called impermanent because its nature is not ultimate.
It is called "empty" because it is internally devoid of a person (*pudgala*), an agent (*kāraka*), or an experiencer (*vedaka*), having dispensed with such an agent or experiencer.
It is called "non-self" (*anātman*) because its nature is not independent.
It is called a "cause" (*hetu*) because it brings about the various states of existence (*bhava*).
It is called "origination" (samudaya) because it causes existence and so forth to manifest;
it is called "arising" (jāti) because it has the capacity to produce and bring forth;
it is called "condition" (pratyaya) because there is that which is constructed and produced.
Because its nature is non-continuous and it exhausts all continuities, it is called "cessation" (nirodha).
Because the three fires are forever stilled, it is called "tranquility" (śānta).
Because it is liberated from all calamities and misfortunes, it is called "sublime" (praṇīta).
It is called "detachment" (*viveka*) because it transcends all faults and afflictions;
it is called the "path" (*mārga*) because it is the way of definitive deliverance;
and it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*) because it accords with correct principle.
Because it proceeds correctly toward [the goal], it is called "practice" (*caryā*);
because it eternally transcends birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is called "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*).
Question: There are four aspects of practice by which one contemplates the fruit of birth and death.
Why is this fruit designated only as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and not as the Truths of Impermanence, Emptiness, or Non-self?
Answer: It should also be described as the Truths of Impermanence and so forth;
that it is not so described is because the teaching is presented incompletely (*śeṣa-vacana*).

Furthermore, since it has been stated that [the aggregates] constitute the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), one should know that they have already been stated to constitute the truths of impermanence (*anitya*), emptiness (*śūnya*), and non-self (*anātman*), because their characteristics are identical.

Furthermore, the characteristic of suffering is unique; only those phenomena associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) are suffering and not others, and for this reason they are called the truth of suffering.
The three characteristics, such as impermanence and so forth, are common characteristics shared by others;
that is to say, the characteristic of impermanence exists in all three truths,
while the characteristics of emptiness and non-self pervade all phenomena.
Therefore, these are not termed "truths" such as impermanence and so forth.
Furthermore, suffering opposes all forms of existence;
because sentient beings, upon hearing of it, are able to renounce birth and death, it is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
If one offers delicious food and drink to a small child,
the child will immediately cast it aside if told that it is suffering; yet,
when told that things are impermanent and so forth, the child has no thought of renunciation.
Therefore, it is not called the "Truth of Impermanence" and so forth.
Furthermore, that birth and death involve suffering is something both the ignorant and the wise believe;
even when non-Buddhists hear this, they do not slander it.
Because one does not develop faith in [the notion that] impermanence and so forth exist,
it is called the Truth of Suffering rather than impermanence and so forth.
Furthermore, because the knower and the known can be easily distinguished.
It is designated only as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), and not as impermanence (*anitya*) and so forth.
This means that because the Blessed One said there is "knowledge of suffering," that which is known by it is designated only as the Truth of Suffering,
just as it is known by that knowledge.
The subject that perceives and the object perceived;
the meaning of each faculty;
and the aspects of activity and their objects.
It should be understood that the same applies to the subject and the object.
Furthermore, this designation "Truth of Suffering" is an ancient tradition; it is an archaic expression.
All the Buddhas of the past, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, have designated this truth by the name "suffering.
Since the present Buddha does likewise, he should not be held accountable for this.
Furthermore, among the four characteristics of this truth, the characteristic of suffering comes first.
Therefore, the Blessed One designated it only as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Question: There are four aspects (*ākāra*) by which one contemplates the cause of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Why is this cause designated only as the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), and not as the three other types of truths such as "cause" (*hetu*) and so forth?
The answer is that it should likewise be stated as the truth of cause, origination, and condition; that it is not so stated is an incomplete explanation.

Furthermore, since it has already been stated as the truth of accumulation (*samudaya-satya*), one should know that the truths of cause, origination, and condition have already been stated, as their characteristics are identical.

Furthermore, because that which knows and that which is known are easily distinguished, it is designated merely as the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) and not as the causal condition for arising.
That is to say, because the Blessed Buddha taught the existence of the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*), this object of knowledge is designated merely as the truth of origination.

It should be understood that the same applies to knowledge (*jñāna*) and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), as well as to the subject of cognition (*boddhṛ*) and the object of cognition (*boddhavya*).
Furthermore, this designation "Truth of Origination" (*samudaya-satya*) is an ancient tradition;
it is an archaic expression. All past Buddhas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, have represented this truth by the name "Origination."
The Buddha is likewise in this regard, and thus he should not be held accountable.
Furthermore, the characteristic of accumulation exists only in impure (*sāsrava*) phenomena,
for it brings about the gathering of birth and death, whereas such is not the case for pure (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
The characteristic of being produced by causes also exists in the untainted (anāsrava),
for the Noble Path is likewise called "produced by causes.
Because it is not shared [with ordinary beings], it is established with the name of a Truth (satya).
Therefore, the Blessed One designated it only as the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Question: There are four aspects through which one contemplates *nirvāṇa*.
Why is *nirvāṇa* designated only as the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and not as the three other truths, such as Peace (*śānta*), etc.?
The answer is that it should also be described as the truths of tranquility (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).
That they are not so stated is because the explanation is incomplete.

Furthermore, since it has already been stated that this is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), one should know that the truths of tranquility, excellence, and renunciation have already been implied, as their characteristics are identical.

Furthermore, because the knowledge and the object of knowledge are easily distinguished, it is designated merely as the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), rather than as tranquility (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), or renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).
That is to say, since the Blessed One taught that there is "knowledge of cessation," this object of knowledge is designated merely as the truth of cessation.
It should be understood that the same applies to knowledge (*jñāna*), the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), the subject of cognition (*buddhi*), and the object of cognition (*boddhavya*).
Furthermore, the name "Cessation" (*nirodha*) is established as a Truth (*satya*) because it is unique;
the name "Cessation" reveals exclusively ultimate cessation (*atyanta-nirodha*).

The term "tranquility" (śānta) is applied indiscriminately to meditative concentration (samādhi); therefore, to avoid such confusion, it is not called "tranquil. The term "sublime" (praṇīta) is applied indiscriminately to the Path (mārga); therefore, it is not called "sublime.
Furthermore, this designation of the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) is that which has been handed down from antiquity; it is an ancient textual formulation.
All the Buddhas of the past, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, have all designated this truth by the name "cessation" (*nirodha*).
Since the present Buddha does likewise, he should not be held accountable for this.
Furthermore, among the four characteristics of this truth, the characteristic of cessation is primary; therefore, the Blessed One designates it simply as the "Truth of Cessation."
Question: There are four aspects through which one contemplates the Noble Path.
Why is the Noble Path called only the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) and not also the other three truths, such as the Truth of Suchness (*tathatā-satya*)?
Answer: It should also be described as the Truth of Suchness (*tathatā*), the Truth of Practice (*pratipad*), and the Truth of Emergence (*niḥsaraṇa*).
That it was not mentioned constitutes an incomplete teaching (*śeṣavāda*).

Furthermore, since it has already been stated that [the path] is the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), one should know that the Truths of Practice (*pratipad*) and Emergence (*niḥsaraṇa*) have also been explained, because their characteristics are identical.
Moreover, it is because the knower and the known are easily distinguished.
It is merely called the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya) and is not like the "path as practice" or the "path as emergence.
This is because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught that there is "knowledge of the path";
therefore, this object of knowledge is designated solely as the Truth of the Path.
It should be understood that the same applies to knowledge (*jñāna*), the known (*jñeya*), the cognizer (*boddhṛ*), and the cognized (*boddhavya*).

Furthermore, the name "Path" (*mārga*) is established solely to indicate the way leading to Nirvāṇa; thus, the name "Truth" (*satya*) is established [for the Path] to avoid confusion with the correct principle (*nyāya*).
Practice pertains to the outflows,
while emergence pertains to nirvāṇa;
therefore, these are not called the truths of practice and emergence.
Furthermore, this designation of the Truth of the Path is an ancient tradition and consists of ancient phrases;
all the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have expressed this truth by the name "Path."
The Buddha is likewise now; therefore, he should not be held accountable.

Furthermore, because the characteristic of the path is the first among the four characteristics of this truth, the World-Honored One designated it specifically as the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
This is stated in the *Vinaya*.

At one time, the Blessed One first taught the Four Noble Truths to the Four Great Kings using the noble language (ārya-bhāṣā). Of those Four Great Kings, two were able to comprehend it while two did not.
Out of compassion and for their benefit, the Blessed One [acted accordingly].
He spoke the Four Noble Truths using the vernacular of a borderland country in South India, namely:
*ciṇi miṇi ḍabuda ḍabba*.
Among the two heavenly kings, one was able to understand and comprehend them, while the other was not.
Out of compassion and for the benefit of those beings,
the Blessed One further taught the Four Noble Truths using a certain Mleccha dialect:
namely, *maśa*, *duśa*, *saṃkrama*, and *svatrapraticchādana*.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings all attained understanding.
They asked the Buddha: "Can the Four Noble Truths, when explained using the noble language (āryabhāṣā), cause those to be converted to attain understanding?
If this were so, what would be the fault?"
Both positions entail faults. Why is this so?
If you say [the gods] are capable, then why did the latter two heavenly kings not understand the holy words when they heard them being spoken?
If this were not the case, how would one explain the verses spoken in the *Gāthā*?
As it is said in a verse:
"The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind."
All say that the World-Honored One speaks the same words as they; yet for me alone, he expounds various meanings.
"Single voice" refers to the Brahma-voice.
If a person from the land of Cīna comes and sits in the assembly, [he likewise hears it].
This refers to the Buddha’s explanation of the phonology and meaning of Cina.
At that time, such people as Licchavis, Kāśyapas, Vatsas, Dravidas, Mālavakas, Śakas, Tukhāras, and Tukhārakas came and sat in the assembly.
Each individual thinks, "The Buddha has taught the meaning of the sounds of my own country's language to me alone.
Having heard this, they each attain understanding according to their own kind.
Furthermore, those who are of a greedy temperament come to sit in the assembly.

If one who practices through aversion comes to sit in the assembly, they hear the Buddha expound the meaning of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). If one who practices through hatred comes to sit in the assembly,
they hear the Buddha expound the meaning of the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*).
If one who acts out of delusion comes to sit in the assembly and hears the Buddha explain the meaning of the contemplation of dependent origination,
those of the class characterized by pride and conceit should be understood to be similar to this.
Since this verse states this very thing,
how can it be said that the Buddha spoke the Four Noble Truths in a sacred language such that all sentient beings to be converted could not understand them?
Some say: "The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths in the noble language (ārya-bhāṣā) so that all sentient beings to be converted might understand them.
Question: If this is so, why were the latter two heavenly kings unable to understand when they heard the teaching in the noble language?
The answer is that the intentions of those Four Great Kings differ;
in order to fulfill their intentions, the Buddha spoke differently.
That is to say, two of the kings conceived this thought:
"If the Buddha were to teach the Four Noble Truths to me in the sacred language (ārya-bhāṣā), I would be able to receive and practice them.
The third Heavenly King thought thus:
"If the Buddha were to teach the Four Truths to me in the vernacular of a frontier country in South India, I would be able to receive and practice them. The fourth Heavenly King thought thus.
"If the Buddha would explain the Four Truths to me using any one of the Mleccha dialects, I would be able to receive and practice them.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke according to his intention.
Furthermore, the Blessed One made this statement because he wished to demonstrate that he is fully capable of understanding all forms of speech and sound.
This was in response to those who might harbor the doubt that the Buddha is able to teach the Dharma only by means of the noble tongue (*ārya-bhāṣā*).
Since mastery over other forms of speech and sound is not necessarily guaranteed,
the Buddha teaches the Dharma through various types of speech and sound to resolve those doubts,
thereby manifesting his mastery over all regional dialects and sounds.
All who hear the essential teachings he proclaims receive and practice them.
Furthermore, there are those to be converted who attain conversion by relying on the Buddha’s unchanging form and speech;
there are also those to be converted who attain conversion by relying on the Buddha’s transformed form and speech.
Regarding the statement that those who can be transformed by the Buddha receive his teaching based on his unchanging form:
if he were to teach the Dharma by changing his form, they would not be able to understand it.

For example, it is said that when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Magadha, in order to cross the Dṛḍhavati Pond, he walked twelve *yojanas*, whereby seventy thousand sentient beings all attained the vision of the Truth (*dṛṣṭasatya*).
They all receive transformation through the Buddha’s speech of unchanging form.
If he were to transform his form and speech to preach the Dharma for them,
those sentient beings would not perceive the Truth.
Those who are to be converted can do so by relying on the Buddha’s transformation of form and speech;
if he were to preach the Dharma without transforming his form and speech, they would be unable to understand it.
For this reason, the World-Honored One employs three kinds of speech.
He preached the Four Noble Truths for the sake of the Four Heavenly Kings. Furthermore,
there are those who say that the Buddha preached the Four Noble Truths with a single voice.
It does not cause all sentient beings who are to be converted to be able to understand [it].
Although the Blessed One possesses sovereign supernormal powers,
he cannot transcend the limits of the objective realm.
Just as it is not possible for the ear to see various forms or for the eye to hear sounds and so forth.
Question: If that is so, how should the preceding verse be interpreted?
Answer: It need not necessarily be interpreted, as it is not part of the Tripiṭaka.
Many verses in praise of the Buddha contain exaggerations beyond the facts;
for example, the Vibhajyavādins praise the Blessed One by saying that his mind is always in meditative concentration.
Because he is well-established in mindfulness and clear comprehension;
and because it is praised that the Buddha never sleeps and is free from all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Just as those praises of the Buddha do not reach the reality of his words, the preceding verse is likewise [inapplicable], and thus requires no further explanation.
Furthermore, the vocal sounds of the Tathāgata pervade all realms of sound; whatever he wishes to say, he is able to produce it.
For instance, if the Buddha were to speak the language of China, it would be superior to being born in China as a native of the Middle Kingdom.
Even if one were to speak the Bhoṭa language, it would be superior to being born in the capital of that country,
because the Buddha’s vocal resonance pervades all spheres of sound; thus, a verse says:
Furthermore, the Buddha’s speech is light, agile, swift, and quick to turn;
though he speaks in various ways, it is as if he speaks all at once.
For instance, having spoken in the language of Cīna, the Buddha immediately thereafter speaks in the language of the kingdom of Lāṭa.
Furthermore, even when speaking in the Bhoṭa dialect,
because the speech turns so rapidly, it is perceived as occurring all at once;
it is like a whirling firebrand, which is not a wheel, yet gives rise to the perception of a wheel.
Because the preceding verse relies upon this principle, there is likewise no contradiction.
Furthermore, although the vocal sounds of the Tathāgata are manifold,
they are said to be "a single voice" because they equally benefit [sentient beings].
As it is said in the Sūtra, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This noble truth of suffering— this dharma that I had not heard before—
I applied correct attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) toward it."
From this, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, and awakening:
"This noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood through wisdom; this, indeed, was not heard by me before," and so on at length.
"This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood through wisdom; this, indeed, was not heard by me before," and so on at length.
The detailed exposition of the truths of origin, cessation, and the path is likewise.
The passage beginning with "This noble truth of suffering was not heard by me previously" reveals the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
"Regarding this noble truth of suffering, it should be fully known through wisdom," and so forth,
indicates the faculty of having already known (*ājñātendriya*).
"Regarding this noble truth of suffering, it has been fully known through wisdom," and so forth.
This reveals the faculty of having already known (*ājñātendriya*).
It should be understood that for the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, each likewise reveals three faculties;
this is the explanation given by the Venerable Dharmatrāta.
As I contemplate this sūtra, my hair stands on end.
Since that which is spoken by the Buddha must not contradict the meaning and certainly possesses a specific sequence,
this present sūtra now teaches the faculty of full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) out of its proper order.
Furthermore, because the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is subsequently mentioned,
it is not the case that only Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas,
and Śrāvakas possess such a sequence of contemplative practice.
How could the faculty of one who has perfect knowledge (ājñātāvīndriya) arise again after [the attainment of] the initial untainted faculties?
If this sūtra were abandoned, it would certainly be unreasonable,
for the Buddha first taught it with the five bhikṣus as his primary disciples.
Because eighty thousand devas who heard this teaching all realized the Dharma,
those who wish not to abandon it yet find themselves contradicting the sequence will experience their body hair standing on end upon reflecting on this sutra.
Subsequently, although the Venerable One spoke thus, he did not abandon the Sūtra;
rather, he rephrased the wording and stated:
"This Sūtra should say: 'This is the Noble Truth of Suffering.'"
"In the past, I had not heard this," and so forth, as explained at length.
The same applies to the detailed exposition of the truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
This noble truth of suffering should be fully understood through wisdom.
This noble truth of the origin [of suffering] should be permanently abandoned through wisdom;
this noble truth of cessation should be realized through wisdom;
this noble truth of the path should be cultivated through wisdom.
The detailed explanation of "formerly unheard" and so forth is as previously stated.
This Noble Truth of Suffering has been fully known through wisdom;
this Noble Truth of Origination has been permanently abandoned through wisdom.
"This noble truth of cessation has been realized through wisdom;
this noble truth of the path has been cultivated through wisdom.
The detailed exposition, beginning with "not heard before," is as previously described.
If one were to speak in this way, the sequence would not be lost;
however, it would not accord with the realization (*abhisamaya*) as it is taught in the Sūtras.
Thus say the masters of the Abhidharma treatises.
One should not arbitrarily alter the words and phrases of this sutra.
In the past, there were immeasurable great masters of treatises whose sharp faculties and vast learning surpassed those of the Venerable One.
I do not even dare to alter the words and phrases of this sūtra,
much less should a person of great virtue now arbitrarily change them;
one should simply seek the intended meaning of this sūtra.
That is to say, the teacher of the Dharma relies on two sequences:
first, the sequence of teaching the Dharma in accordance with the order [of the sūtras], as taught in this very sūtra;
second, the sequence in accordance with the order of realization (*abhisamaya*), as taught by the Venerable One.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"This sutra does not speak of the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*);

it merely speaks of the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Four Truths under the Bodhi tree through the power of the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*) belonging to the desire realm."

Question: Since the Blessed One has stated that "I have realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening through this contemplation," how can there be the sense of realizing awakening through hearing and reflection?
Answer: It is by means of the power of the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection that a bodhisattva [realizes it].
It subdues and eliminates all ignorance regarding the Four Noble Truths;
because one will thereby certainly realize unsurpassed enlightenment,
it is said that through this, one attains bodhi.
It is like a person who previously had a moist hide covering their face,
but later manages to remove it and covers themselves with a coarse cloth;
since the obstruction is slight, one may say they are unobstructed.
Therefore, this does not refer to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
As it is said in the Sūtra, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Regarding the four noble truths, through their three turnings and twelve aspects..."
The eye, knowledge, clarity, and awakening arise.
Question: This [wheel] should have twelve revolutions and forty-eight aspects;
why, then, is it said to have only three revolutions and twelve aspects?
Answer: Although each individual truth (satya) is observed through three turns and twelve aspects (ākāra), they do not exceed these three turns and twelve aspects; therefore, this statement was made.
It is like the case of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), who undergoes at most seven more existences.
As well as the seven points of proficiency and the two dharmas, etc.
Herein, "eye" refers to the patience of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñānakṣānti*).
"Wisdom" refers to the knowledge of all phenomena;
"clarity" refers to—
The "patiences" (kṣānti) refer to the various types of subsequent knowledge-patience (anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti).
"Awakening" (bodha) refers to the various types of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
Furthermore, "eye" has the meaning of observing and seeing;
"knowledge" has the meaning of decisive discernment;
and "clarity" has the meaning of illuminating and comprehending.
Awakening (*bodha*) has the meaning of "police" [in the sense of guarding against what is to be abandoned].
Question: If these Four Noble Truths are abandoned by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), are they also abandoned by way of their objects (*ālambana*)?
Answer: One should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

There are cases where there is abandonment by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*) but not abandonment by way of the object (*ālambana-prahāṇa*), namely: [the abandonment of] uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) suffering and its origin (*samudaya*), as well as the abandonment of all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena that lack an object.
There are also cases where there is abandonment by way of the object but not abandonment by way of intrinsic nature.
This refers to the noble path that takes the contaminated as its object;
it is both abandoned by way of its own nature and abandoned by way of its object.
That is to say, it refers to [the path] that takes the contaminated suffering and origin as its objects.
There are those that are neither abandoned by way of their intrinsic nature nor abandoned by way of their objects;
these refer to the uncontaminated noble paths and the truth of cessation, which is the noble path without an object.

Section Ten on the Aggregates of the Ties, Part Four of the Fourth Chapter on the Ten Gates: Regarding Dhyāna (Meditative Concentration).
That is to say: the first dhyāna,
the second dhyāna,
and the third dhyāna.
The Fourth Dhyāna.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"What is the first dhyāna?
It refers to the five aggregates of wholesome factors subsumed under the first dhyāna."
...up to: what is the fourth dhyāna?
It refers to the five aggregates of wholesome factors subsumed under the fourth dhyāna;
it speaks only of wholesome dhyāna.
Some may harbor the doubt that dhyāna is exclusively wholesome,
neither defiled nor unobscured-neutral.
To resolve those doubts and clarify the four dhyānas—which encompass both the wholesome, the defiled, and the non-obscured neutral—this treatise is composed.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these four dhyānas?
Answer: Each has as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of its own level.
This is called the intrinsic nature, the self-substance, the essence, the characteristic, the constituent part, and the fundamental nature of dhyāna.
The intrinsic nature has thus been explained.
Therefore, it shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason is it called "dhyāna" (meditative concentration)?
Is it called dhyāna because it is able to sever the fetters?
If it were called "dhyāna" (meditative concentration) simply because it enables correct contemplation,
or if it were called "dhyāna" simply because it can sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*),
then the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) would also be able to sever the fetters and should likewise be named "dhyāna."
If it were the case that something is called "dhyāna" (meditative concentration) simply because it is capable of correct contemplation,
then the samādhis of the desire realm would also be called dhyāna, as they too are capable of correct contemplation.
Some say that it is called *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) because it can sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Question: Since the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) can also sever the fetters, they too should be called *dhyāna*.
Answer: If a concentration can sever both the two types of fetters—the unwholesome and the neutral—it is called *dhyāna*.
Since the formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samādhi*) sever only the neutral fetters and not the unwholesome ones, they are not called *dhyāna*.
Question: If it is asserted that only the *anāgamya* concentration can be called *dhyāna*,
because in the higher stages the unwholesome fetters (*asamprayukta-saṃyojana*) are not abandoned.
Answer: Although those higher stages lack the antidote that abandons [defilements], they do possess the antidote of revulsion and destruction;
since that which can revile and destroy is also termed "able to abandon," [the higher stages are included].
Question: If this were asserted,
then the categories of dharma-knowledge regarding cessation and the path in the higher stages,
as well as all categories of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) therein, would not be meditative absorption (dhyāna).
This is because they are neither abandonments through the antidote of distaste nor abandonments through the antidote of destruction for the desire realm.

The answer is: although there is no antidote for the entire realm or the entire level within the desire realm, it is possible for that realm and level to possess the antidote of destruction for unwholesome states.
By virtue of this power, the others are also designated by that name.
Furthermore, among the four dhyānas, there are those capable of counteracting unwholesome fetters (*saṃyojana*),
whereas these are entirely absent in the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
Therefore, the name "dhyāna" does not extend to the formless realms.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka stated:
"In the six stages of the form realm, there are both the antidotes for abandonment and the antidotes for the destruction of the fetters belonging to the desire realm."
However, the non-attainment concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) has already severed those fetters;
as for the antidotes of the other stages, there are no such [fetters] to be severed.
Although there are no [fetters] to be severed, they still possess the function of being antidotes.
Just as the sun, with its three phases, is capable of dispelling darkness—
once the first phase has dispelled it, there remains nothing further to be dispelled—
or as when six people share a single enemy.
Once one person has been killed, there is no further one left to kill.
It is like six lamps, all of which are capable of dispelling darkness;
if one is brought into a room, the darkness is already eliminated.
In the other five [dhyānas], there is no darkness to be dispelled at the time of entry.
Thus, in these six stages, all possess the capacity to sever the fetters of the desire realm,
not merely the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage].
If it were not so, then when one enters the path of seeing based on the five higher stages,
one would not realize the dissociation from the fetters to be abandoned by insight pertaining to the desire realm; yet,
since such realization is indeed attained, [it must be otherwise].
Thus, one should know that the six stages possess the antidotes for abandoning the fetters of the desire realm.
Furthermore, if a meditative concentration can completely abandon both types of fetters—those abandoned through seeing and those abandoned through cultivation—it is called dhyāna.
The formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are not meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) because they can only exhaust the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, that which can abandon the fetters while arising together with the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and serving as a basis for generating manifold virtues is [a meditative absorption].
He is able to fully embrace the fourfold and fivefold branches;
he is able to give rise to the six supernormal powers and possess the four paths of practice;
he possesses the three kinds of transformations, the three knowledges, the three faculties, the three paths, the three stages, the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, and the ninefold knowledge of all ways.
The two paths of seeing and cultivation— the two knowledges of dharma and subsequent knowledge,
as well as the various patiences and knowledges— are called meditative concentration (dhyāna).
Although the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) are able to sever the fetters, [they are not so designated].
Furthermore, because it does not possess the aforementioned qualities, it is not meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Others, however, say that it is called meditative concentration because it is able to correctly contemplate.
Question: If that were so, since there are also samādhis in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that can correctly contemplate [the truths], they too should be called dhyāna.
Answer: Only those that can both correctly contemplate and sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are designated as dhyāna.
Although the samādhis of the desire realm possess the capacity for correct contemplation,
they cannot sever the fetters;
therefore, they are not termed dhyāna.
Furthermore, if one can correctly contemplate with a firm and indestructible continuity that endures for a long time,
and maintains focused attention upon the object of observation without relinquishing it, this is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Because the samādhis of the desire realm lack such qualities, they are not dhyānas.
Furthermore, if a samādhi possesses both the name "concentration" (samāhita) and the function of concentration,
and is capable of correct contemplation, it is called dhyāna.
Although the samādhis of the desire realm bear the name "concentration," they lack the function of concentration;
like a mud rafter or beam that has a name but no utility, they are not dhyāna.
Furthermore, if a samādhi is not shaken by the winds of distraction, like a lamp in a sealed room, it is dhyāna.
That which is capable of correct contemplation is called *dhyāna*.
The *samādhi* of the desire realm is subject to the agitation of the wind of distraction;
like a lamp at a crossroads, it is not *dhyāna*.
According to this explanation,
one must possess two qualities to be designated as "dhyāna":
namely, the ability to sever the fetters and the ability to engage in correct contemplation.
Although the samādhis of the desire realm can correctly contemplate, they cannot sever the fetters;
although the formless absorptions can sever the fetters, they cannot correctly contemplate; therefore, they are not dhyānas.
Furthermore, that which can universally observe and universally sever the fetters is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Although the *samādhi* of the desire realm can universally observe, it cannot universally sever the fetters.
Because both meanings are absent in the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*),
they are not meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). Furthermore,
that which can pacify all afflictions (*kleśa*) and can contemplate all objects of focus (*ālambana*) is called meditative concentration.
Although the samādhis of the desire realm can contemplate all objects of focus,
they cannot pacify all afflictions;
because both of these two meanings are entirely absent in the formless attainments, they are not dhyānas.
Furthermore, the various formless absorptions possess tranquility but lack discernment;
the samādhis of the desire realm possess discernment but lack tranquility;
because the absorptions of the form realm possess both, they are called "dhyāna" (meditative absorption).
"Tranquility" refers to meditative equipoise;
"reflection" refers to universal observation;
therefore, it is called "dhyāna" (meditative absorption).
The branches of the four dhyānas comprise eighteen in total.
That is to say, the first dhyāna has five branches:
(1) vitarka, (2) vicāra, (3) prīti, (4) sukha, and (5) cittaikāgratā.
The second dhyāna has four factors:
first, internal serenity; second, joy; third, bliss; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind.
The third dhyāna has five factors.

The first dhyāna has five factors: (1) initial application, (2) sustained application, (3) rapture, (4) pleasure, and (5) one-pointedness of mind. The second dhyāna has four factors: (1) internal serenity, (2) rapture, (3) pleasure, and (4) one-pointedness of mind. The third dhyāna has five factors:

(1) equanimity, (2) mindfulness, (3) clear comprehension, (4) pleasure, and (5) one-pointedness of mind. The fourth dhyāna has four factors: (1) neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, (2) purity of equanimity, (3) purity of mindfulness, and (4) one-pointedness of mind.
Question: Of the eighteen names for the factors of the four dhyānas, how many are there in terms of actual entities?
Answer: There are only eleven.
That is to say, the factors of the first dhyāna consist of five both in name and in actual entity.
Although the factors of the second dhyāna are four,
three are as previously described, with the addition of internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
Although the factors of the third dhyāna are five...
As for the fifth [dhyāna], it is as before, with only the addition of the first four;
although there are four factors in the fourth dhyāna,
the latter three are as before, with only the addition of the first.
Therefore, although the factors of dhyāna are said to be eighteen in name, they consist of eleven substantial entities.
Furthermore, there are those who say that there are only ten substantial entities.
That is to say, the pleasures of the three dhyānas are combined into one.
The critique states:
One should not make such a statement.
The first and second dhyānas consist of the bliss of pliancy (praśrabdhi-sukha);
the third dhyāna consists specifically of the bliss of feeling (vedanā-sukha).
The bliss of the first and second dhyānas is subsumed within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
Since the bliss of the third dhyāna is subsumed within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*),
what was previously stated is logically sound.
This is just as a name is the actual entity (*dravya*) and a designation (*prajñapti*) is the conventional entity (*prajñapti-dravya*).
It is called the difference of names and the difference of entities;
the difference of natures and the difference of essences;
the difference of distinctions and the difference of substances.
The establishment of names is the establishment of the substance;
the awakening to names is the awakening to the substance.
One should know that it is likewise so.
Question: Among these, what is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)?
What are the factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*)?
Answer: One-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) is meditative concentration.
Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is samādhi, this [samādhi] and the others are the factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*).
Question: If samādhi is itself dhyāna, [how can it be a factor of dhyāna?]
If the first and third dhyānas each had only four factors,
and the second and fourth dhyānas each had only three factors,
then there would be only fourteen dhyāna-factors in total.
Why, then, are eighteen factors taught?
The answer is: samādhi is both dhyāna and a factor of dhyāna;
the remaining factors are factors of dhyāna but not themselves dhyāna. Therefore, there are eighteen.
Just as the discernment of phenomena is both awakening and a factor of awakening,
while the others are factors of awakening but not awakening itself;
so too, right view is both the path and a factor of the path.
The others are factors of the path but not the path itself;
abstaining from eating at improper times is both the fast (upavāsa) and a factor of the fast;
the others are factors of the fast but not the fast itself.
This is also like that.
Thus, these are called the factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*):

their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their selfhood (*ātman*), their substance (*vastu*), their essential body (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), their constituent parts (*bhāga*), and their fundamental nature (*prakṛti*).
The essential nature has already been explained;
that which constitutes it shall now be discussed.
Question: For what reason are they called the factors of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*)?
What is the meaning of "dhyāna-factor" (dhyānāṅga)?
Answer: It is called dhyāna because it involves tranquil contemplation;
that which accords with this dhyāna is therefore called a dhyāna-factor.
In the sense of conformity,
in the sense of bearing a heavy burden,
and in the sense of accomplishing a great task.
It is the meaning of "firm," the meaning of "ultimate reality," and the meaning of "constituent part."
Regarding "conformity to the meaning":
if a factor conforms to the meditative absorption (dhyāna) of a particular stage,
it is called a limb of that stage's meditative absorption.
Regarding the meaning of "bearing a burden":
if a dharma can induce the meditative absorption (dhyāna) of this stage,
it is called a limb (aṅga) of the meditative absorption of this stage.
Regarding the accomplishment of the great purpose:
if a factor is able to perform the function of this stage’s meditative absorption,
it is called a limb of this stage’s meditative absorption.
Regarding "firm and superior meaning":
if a factor assists in the accomplishment of this stage of dhyāna,
causing it to become firm and superior, it is termed a branch (aṅga) of the dhyāna of this stage.
Regarding the meaning of "discrimination" (*vibhāga*):

just as the various distinct components of an army or a chariot are called the "parts of an army" or the "parts of a chariot," so too the various distinct components of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are called the "factors of meditative concentration" (*dhyānāṅga*).
Having thus explained the names of the factors of dhyāna, one should next distinguish between their mixed and unmixed characteristics.
Question: If something is a factor of the first dhyāna...
Is it also a factor of the second dhyāna?
One should respond by formulating four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
There are factors that belong to the first [dhyāna] but not to the second.
That is to say, vitarka and vicāra.
There is that which is the second factor but not the first factor;
namely, internal serenity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda).
There is that which is both the first factor and the second factor, namely:
joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
There is that which is neither the first factor nor the second factor.
That is to say, setting aside the aforementioned characteristics, if one asks whether that which is a factor of the first dhyāna is also a factor of the third dhyāna,
the answer is that four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) must be made.
There are cases where something is a factor of the first [dhyāna] but not a factor of the third.
That is to say: vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha.
There are those which are the third factor but not the first factor:
namely, upekṣā, smṛti, prajñā, and sukha.
There is that which is both the first factor and the third factor, namely, one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
There is that which is neither the first factor nor the third factor,
namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Question: If something is a factor of the first dhyāna, is it also a factor of the fourth dhyāna?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
There are factors that are of the first [dhyāna] but not of the fourth.
That is to say, vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha.
There are those which are the fourth factor but not the first factor:
namely, upekṣā, smṛti, and amala-vedanā (neither-pain-nor-pleasure).
There is that which is both the first factor and the fourth factor,
namely, one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
There is that which is neither the first factor nor the fourth factor.
That is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics. Question:
If it is a factor of the second dhyāna, is it also a factor of the third dhyāna?
It should be stated in four propositions:
there is that which is the second factor but not the third factor,
namely, internal serenity, joy, and bliss.
There are factors that are the third limb but not the second limb;
namely, equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, and bliss.
There are factors that are both the second limb and the third limb.
This refers to one-pointedness of mind.
There are cases where it is neither the second factor nor the third factor;
that is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Question: If it is a factor of the second dhyāna, is it also a factor of the fourth dhyāna?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold permutation (catuṣkoṭika).
There are factors that are the second limb but not the fourth limb, namely:
internal serenity, joy, and bliss.
There are factors that are the fourth limb but not the second limb.
That is to say, equanimity and mindfulness that are neither painful nor pleasant.
There is one factor which is both the second limb and the fourth limb;
namely, one-pointedness of mind.
There are factors that are neither the second limb nor the fourth limb;
that is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Question: If it is a limb of the third dhyāna...
Is it also a factor of the fourth dhyāna?
One should respond by formulating four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are factors that belong to the third [dhyāna] but not to the fourth.
That is to say, it is wisdom and pleasure.
There is that which is the fourth factor but not the third factor;
namely, neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
There is that which is both the third factor and the fourth factor, namely:
equanimity, mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind.
There is that which is neither the third factor nor the fourth factor.
That is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Question: Since pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) exist in all stages, why is pliancy established as a factor (*aṅga*) in the first and second dhyānas, but not equanimity?
Why is equanimity (*upekṣā*) established as a factor (*aṅga*) in the third and fourth dhyānas rather than pliancy (*praśrabdhi*)?
The answer is: because it was previously stated that "conduciveness" (*anuloma*) is the meaning of being a factor.
That is to say, pliancy is established as a factor only because it is conducive to the first and second dhyānas.
Equanimity is established as a factor [only] because it accords with the third and fourth dhyānas alone.
Furthermore, this is because they mutually conceal one another;
that is to say, in the first and second dhyānas, pliancy (praśrabdhi) is predominant in its function.
Equanimity is established as a factor because it can conceal [the underlying states];
in the third and fourth dhyānas, the function of equanimity is predominant, and it is established as a factor because it can conceal pliancy. Question: Why are these two able to conceal one another?
Answer: Because these two aspects are mutually contradictory;
that is to say, the aspect of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is buoyancy, while the aspect of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is tranquility.
To exist simultaneously while being mutually contradictory is like a person who,
at one and the same time, both walks and stands,
or both sleeps and wakes— these are entirely contradictory.
However, because their respective antidotes within the wholesome mind differ, they can arise simultaneously;
that is to say, pliancy serves as the antidote to lethargy,
and equanimity serves as the antidote to restlessness.
Furthermore, in order to counteract the fivefold body of sensory consciousnesses belonging to the desire realm,
as well as the associated physical heaviness (*dausthulya*),
the first dhyāna establishes pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) as a constituent factor.
In order to counteract the three bodies of consciousness and the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the body induced by them in the first dhyāna,
pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is established as a factor in the second dhyāna.
Because the second and third dhyānas lack a coarse body of consciousness and the bodily heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) induced by it— which are the factors to be countered—
the third and fourth dhyānas do not establish pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) as a constituent factor.
Since he does not establish pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) as a factor in those [stages],
he establishes equanimity (*upekṣā*) as a factor instead.
Furthermore, in the first two dhyānas, there is defiled joy (*saṃkliṣṭa-prīti*) that agitates both body and mind.
Therefore, the Blessed One said that one should cultivate pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and should not abide in equanimity (*upekṣā*).
For this reason, only pliancy is established as a factor in the first and second dhyānas.
Regarding the third and fourth dhyānas, the Blessed One said that because they are free from the defiled joy (*prīti*) that agitates body and mind—
One should simply abide in equanimity (*upekṣā*) and not cultivate pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Therefore, in the third and fourth dhyānas, only equanimity as a mental factor (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*) is established as a constituent.
Furthermore, in the first and second dhyānas, pliancy has its cause.
This refers to all forms of wholesome joy.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Because the mind possesses joy, the body becomes pliant."
Therefore, only pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is established as a factor in the first and second dhyānas.
In the third and fourth dhyānas, there is no cause for pliancy;
that is to say, since there is no wholesome joy (*prīti*), one should abide solely in equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Therefore, equanimity alone is established as a factor [of the third dhyāna].
Furthermore, in the third dhyāna, one abandons extreme joy;
in the fourth dhyāna, one abandons extreme bliss.
Therefore, equanimity of formation (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*) alone is established as a factor [in the third dhyāna].
Since equanimity of formation is not established as a factor in the first two dhyānas,
there is no contradiction in establishing pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) as the factor [there instead].
Question: Since internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is in fact faith (*śraddhā*), and this exists in all stages, why is it established as a factor (*aṅga*) only in the second dhyāna?
Answer: Because it was previously stated that the meaning of a "factor" is that which is conducive [to the stage].
That is to say, faith conforms exclusively to the second dhyāna;
therefore, faith alone is established as a factor [of that dhyāna].
Furthermore, within the first dhyāna...
Applied thought and sustained thought are like fire;
body-consciousness is like mud;
these cause the continuum of the mind to persist.
The turbidity and agitation of feverish affliction prevent faith from being clear and pure;
it is like a reflection not appearing in hot mud.
In the second dhyāna, there is the fire of vitarka and vicāra and the mud of the aggregate of consciousness.
Within the continuity of the mind, the characteristic of faith becomes clear and pure,
just as reflections appear upon the surface of clear, cool water;
therefore, "inner serenity" (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) is established as a factor therein.
