The third dhyāna possesses the sensation of extreme joy (*prīti*), while the fourth dhyāna possesses the superior sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Because the mental continuum is covered by this [equanimity], the characteristic of faith (*śraddhā*) does not manifest; therefore, neither that [fourth dhyāna] nor the first [dhyāna] establishes the factor of internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
Furthermore, for the practitioners of yoga in the second dhyāna,
faith arises as the most predominant factor at the initial stage of detachment; therefore,
only this is established as the factor of internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
This refers to when a yoga practitioner, having become free from the defilements of the desire realm,
brings the first dhyāna into manifestation and reflects:
"Although I have already become free from the defilements of the indeterminate realm..."
Is the defilement of the various meditative stages (*dhyānabhūmi*) to be abandoned?
When one subsequently abandons the defilement of the first *dhyāna* and the second *dhyāna* manifests,
among those defilements of the realms and stages that are both to be abandoned, [the latter is abandoned].
Having first conceived great faith, one thinks: "Just as I am able to abandon the defilements of the desire realm, I will certainly be able to abandon the defilements of the form and formless realms;
just as the defilements of the first dhyāna can be abandoned."
Up to the point where the defiled meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception can be abandoned:
when the first dhyāna manifests, confidence in the concentration has not yet arisen;
this remains the case when the latter two dhyānas manifest.
Although there is settled confidence, because it is not initial, the characteristic of confidence is not manifest;
therefore, the factor of "internal serenity" is not established in either case.
Furthermore, the arising of superior confidence necessarily depends upon great joy as its cause.
For one who possesses joy, faith will necessarily be firm.
Because there is an exceptionally superior joy in the second dhyāna, it is only in this stage that the factor of "internal serenity" (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) is established.
Question: Since wisdom (prajñā) is present in all stages, why is it established as a factor only in the third dhyāna?
Answer: Because, as previously stated, the meaning of a "limb" (aṅga) is that which is conducive [to the state].
That is to say, wisdom (prajñā) is conducive only to the third dhyāna;
therefore, the limb of right wisdom (samyak-prajñā) is established only therein.
Furthermore, in the third dhyāna there is the sensation of pliancy (praśrabdhi-vedanā);
among all sensations of pliancy, this is the most excellent.
Because they are attached to it, the practitioners of yoga (yogācāras) [fall away].
One does not desire to seek the superior dharmas of the higher stages;
this very attachment is an obstacle within one’s own stage.
To counteract this, the factor of right wisdom (*samyakprajñā*) is established. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus.
One should awaken to this bliss with right wisdom;
do not remain stubbornly attached to it and fail to seek the higher stages.
Among the lower and higher stages, there is no obstruction to the supreme bliss of one's own stage as great as that which exists in this stage.
Therefore, right wisdom is not established as a factor therein.
Furthermore, within the first dhyāna,
coarse vitarka and vicāra obscure and obstruct right wisdom.
In the second dhyāna,
there is extreme rapture that obscures and obstructs right wisdom.
In the fourth dhyāna...
There exists a superior equanimity that obscures and obstructs right wisdom;
for while superior equanimity is a part of ignorance (*avidyā*), right wisdom is clarity (*vidyā*).
Since clarity and ignorance are mutually contradictory and destructive, [the former obstructs the latter].
Therefore, in all cases, right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*) is not established as a factor (*aṅga*).
However, because the third dhyāna lacks any factor that obscures right wisdom as it does in other stages, it is established as a factor there.
Question: Since mindfulness (*smṛti*) is present throughout all stages, why is it established as a factor only in the latter two dhyānas?
Answer: Because it was previously stated that "conduciveness" is the meaning of being a factor (*aṅga*).
That is to say, mindfulness is conducive only to the latter two dhyānas;
therefore, mindfulness is established as a factor only in those two.
Furthermore, in the latter two dhyānas,
there are obstacles that increase at each successive stage;
mindfulness is established as a factor in order to counteract them.
The other stages are not like this;
that is to say, the second dhyāna possesses an extremely intense joy that is restless and causes one to drift and drown,
like a rākṣasa for yogins.
Because of this decline, one cannot remain firm;
as an antidote to the defilements of its own level,
mindfulness is established as a factor in the third dhyāna.
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus:
"One should abide in right mindfulness, lest one be swept away or submerged by the joy of the lower stages and thereby fall away from one's own stage;
for in the third dhyāna, there is an exceedingly sublime bliss."
Among the pleasures of birth and death, this is the most supreme; yet for those who practice with obstruction, it is like a deceitful enemy appearing as a friend.
Because of this, all yogins decline and are unable to remain firm in their detachment from the defilements of their own stage.
To counteract that [affliction], mindfulness is established as a factor of the fourth dhyāna.
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus:
"One should abide in right mindfulness so as not to be obstructed or caused to fall away from one's own stage by the pleasure of the lower stages."
Furthermore, in the first dhyāna there are coarse vitarka and vicāra, which are like a violent wind that obscures right mindfulness.
In the second dhyāna there is extreme joy and elation,
which are like turbulent waves that obscure right mindfulness.
Therefore, in both cases, right mindfulness is not established as a factor.
In the latter two dhyānas, this fault does not exist;
for this reason, right mindfulness is established as a factor in both.
Question: If something is a factor of dhyāna (dhyānāṅga), is it also a factor of enlightenment (bodhipakṣya)?
Answer: One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi). There are those that are factors of dhyāna but not factors of enlightenment;
namely, vicāra, pleasure-feeling (sukha-vedanā), and equanimity-feeling (upekṣā-vedanā). There are those that are factors of enlightenment but not factors of dhyāna.
That is to say: diligence, right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
There are those that are both factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*) and factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);
namely, the remaining factors of enlightenment.
There are factors that are neither dhyāna-limbs nor factors of enlightenment;
these are, namely, those cases excluded by the aforementioned characteristics.
Question: Why are *vitarka*, pleasure (*sukha*), feeling (*vedanā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) not established as factors of enlightenment?
Answer: Because they are obscured and impaired.
That is to say, investigation (*vicāra*) is obscured and impaired by right reflection (*samyak-manasikāra*);
the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) is obscured and impaired by the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*).
The sensation of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā) is obscured and impaired by the mental factor of equanimity (upekṣā-saṃskāra);
therefore, it is not established as a factor of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
Question: If that is so, why is it established as a branch of meditative concentration (dhyānāṅga)?
Answer: Within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is established as a factor of enlightenment in order to stimulate right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).

Since the mode of activity of investigation (*vicāra*) is subtle, it would obscure and impair the stimulation of right view; therefore, the factor of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*) is established [to counteract this].
In order to exclude the mutual obscuration and impairment found among the evil and unwholesome dharmas of the lower stages,

[it is said that] within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) coexist in a single moment yet mutually obscure and impair one another.
Within the factors of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*), the distinctions between levels are established based on the sense of being "unobscured" (*anivṛta*) and "non-deficient" (*ahīna*);

whereas among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), equanimity (*upekṣā*) as feeling and equanimity as mental formation are coexistent in a single moment yet possess the characteristics of being "obscured" (*nivṛta*) and "deficient" (*hīna*).
Among the factors of dhyāna, the antidotes and benefits function as distinct branches without mutually obstructing one another.
Question: Why is diligence (*vīrya*) not considered a factor of dhyāna?
Answer: The factors of the various dhyānas are superior in accordance with their own respective stages;
diligence is superior in accordance with other stages.
That is to say, the diligence of the first dhyāna is superior as it accords with the second dhyāna.
Up to the sphere of nothingness, there is diligence; however,
as it conforms to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its superior state,
it is not established as a factor of meditative absorption (dhyānāṅga).
Furthermore, diligence harms the causes of samādhi;
the cause of samādhi is supreme bliss,
as stated in the sūtra.
Because of bliss, the mind becomes concentrated.
For one who exerts diligent effort, body and mind experience much suffering;
for one who cultivates samādhi, body and mind experience much bliss.
Therefore, diligence is not a factor of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Question: Why are right speech, right action, and right livelihood not factors of meditative concentration?
Answer: As for the factors of meditative concentration...
That is to say, when one abides in a state associated with dhyāna,
there must necessarily be a basis, an object, and a mental aspect;
furthermore, it is only when there is alertness that it is termed "associated."
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood do not possess such characteristics;
therefore, they are not established as branches of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*).
This is due to these four characteristics, as well as [the fact that] acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth [do not apply].

Dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*) should all not be established as limbs of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*), because they do not assist the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in abiding on a single object.
Question: Why are shame (*hrī*), dread (*apatrāpya*), non-attachment (*alobha*), and non-hatred (*adveṣa*) [not included]?
Are non-negligence (*apramāda*), non-harming (*avihiṃsā*), and so forth not branches of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*)?
Answer: No, because they do not accord perfectly with the various meditative absorptions.
These wholesome factors (*kuśaladharma*) mostly exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In the stage of scattering (*vikṣepa-bhūmi*), unwholesome factors (*akuśala-dharma*) are the immediate antidotes (*pratipakṣa*);
because their power is enhanced there and not in the stage of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bhūmi*),
they are not established as branches of dhyāna.
Question: Why are mental application (*manasikāra*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth not established as factors of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*)?
Answer: Because they do not accord perfectly with the various meditative absorptions.
The mind tends toward the flow [of saṃsāra], whereas concentration tends toward cessation (*nivṛtti*).
Therefore, the mind is not established as a constituent of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*).
Furthermore, the mind is preeminent like a king,
while all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) are like ministers and aides.
Since concentration (*samādhi*) is a mental factor (*caitta*), it is not established as a constituent of dhyāna;
just as kings do not serve their ministers, so too perception (*saṃjñā*),
volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and desire (*chanda*) all conform to the process of transmigration.
Because their functions are partial and preeminent,
and because they accord with the process of cessation (nivṛtti), they are not established as factors of dhyāna.
Attention (manasikāra) exists only in the distracted stage of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Because its object is superior and it does not pertain to all meditative stages,
it is likewise not established as a constituent of dhyāna.
Resolute confidence (adhimokṣa) is superior only in the stage of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Because meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is superior throughout all stages,
it is not established as a limb of that [absorption].
Furthermore, herein one should [consider] the limbs of the various meditative absorptions.

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are mutually inclusive of one another.
Furthermore, they should be understood through the factors of the first dhyāna up to the factors of the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding the mutual inclusion of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*),
one should further apply the factors of the first dhyāna up to the factors of the fourth dhyāna to the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path, showing their mutual inclusion.
Each should be explained in detail according to its specific characteristics.
Question: Are the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) established as having constituent factors (*aṅga*)?
If they are so established, why are these not mentioned here?
If this were not established, how would one reconcile the *Prajñapti-śāstra*,
which asks: "Is there such a thing as the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space?"

Is it the case that in the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, the faculties are superior, the path is superior, and the absorption itself is superior, while the factors [of the absorption] are equal?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, immediately upon arising from the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space.
Furthermore, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space.
Some maintain that the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the dhyānas and the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are also established as having factors (*aṅga*).
Question: If that is so, it would accord well with the statement in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*.
Why, then, is this not stated here?
Answer: It is indeed logical that it should have been stated; as for its not being stated, [it is because...]
It should be understood that this is an incomplete statement; namely,
that the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna, like the fundamental stage (*maula*), also possesses five factors,
with the exception that it excludes the feeling of joy (*prīti*) and increases the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna, like the fundamental stage itself, also possesses four factors;
it likewise excludes the feeling of joy (*prīti*) and increases the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The preparatory stage of the third dhyāna, like the fundamental stage itself, also possesses five factors.
However, with the exception of the preliminary stage of the fourth dhyāna and the formless attainments, where the feeling of pleasure is eliminated and the feeling of equanimity increases.
Just as the fundamental fourth dhyāna also possesses four factors,
the critique states:
one should speak in this manner.

The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are not established as having constituent factors (*aṅga*), because their qualities are few and they are subsumed under the path of suffering.
Question: If that is so, it provides a thorough explanation for what is stated here.
How should the statement in the *Prajñapti-śāstra* be reconciled?
The answer is: it is said to be "superior" because it is nourished by its causes.
As for the mention of "limbs" (*aṅga*) and so forth:
This refers to the factors of enlightenment and the path.
Question: Why are five factors established for both the first and third dhyānas, while four factors are established for both the second and fourth dhyānas?
Answer: Because it was previously stated that "conduciveness" is the meaning of "limb.
That is to say, each of the four dhyānas possesses exactly that number of factors conducive [to their respective stages], neither more nor less.
Furthermore, the various evils of the desire realm are difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend;
therefore, the first dhyāna establishes five factors as a firm and powerful antidote.
The second dhyāna possesses a profound ground of extreme joy.
It is difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend.
The third dhyāna establishes five factors as a firm and powerful antidote;
neither the first nor the third dhyāna possesses such qualities that are difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, or difficult to transcend.
Therefore, only four factors are established for the second and fourth dhyānas,
because in both cases there is no need for a strenuous counteractive measure (*pratipakṣa*).
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of counteracting the greed directed toward the five objects of sensual desire that predominate in the desire realm.
The first dhyāna is established with five factors as an antidote to the five classes of heavy ground— namely, joy and pleasure— belonging to the second dhyāna;
the third dhyāna is likewise established with five factors.
Because neither the first nor the third dhyāna possesses such factors to be countered,
both the second and fourth dhyānas are established as having only four branches.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of conforming to the method of transcending meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
That is to say, one transcends from a five-limbed absorption to enter a five-limbed absorption,
and again, transcends from a four-limbed absorption to enter a four-limbed absorption.
Because the factors [of the meditative absorptions] and so forth are easily transcended.
Question: If one transcends from the third dhyāna into the sphere of infinite space, and again transcends from the fourth dhyāna into the sphere of infinite consciousness.
How do those that lack both [external and internal] factors accord with [the path]?
Answer: External and internal matters are difficult at the time they are first undertaken, but once accomplished, they no longer require such conformity.
Furthermore, as for external matters, for example, Caṇaka and his minister Candra-garbha studied the art of alchemy for twelve years;
when they first succeeded, they produced a single grain the size of a wild barley kernel.
Then he let out a lion’s roar:
"We are now able to create a mountain of gold.
As for what is called "internal matters":
Just as a practitioner of yoga cultivates the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi*),
at first they rise from the ground by half a mustard seed's height;
subsequently, they rise by the height of one full mustard seed.
In this manner, it gradually decreased by half a barley grain, one barley grain;
half a finger-breadth, one finger-breadth;
half a cubit, one cubit; half a fathom, one fathom.
When that [attainment] is subsequently accomplished, one can travel at will to the Akaniṣṭha heaven;
the same applies to the leap-concentration (*vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*). Because it is difficult to achieve at the initial stage, the factors (*aṅga*) are established as being equalized.
Because they are easy to practice at later stages, even if the factors were not established [for them], one would still be able to enter [the meditative attainments] by skipping over them.
Therefore, five factors are established for each of the first and third [dhyānas],
while four factors are established for each of the second and fourth.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are four paths to the heavens which enable sentient beings who are not yet purified to become purified, and those who are already purified to become further clarified."
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One speak thus?

Answer: It was because he wished to cause sentient beings to develop a profound sense of weary revulsion toward the heavenly realms of birth, and to aspire to abide in the supreme path of the heavenly realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
As for those born in the heavens,
this refers to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
There, they possess four gardens adorned with exquisite and wondrous splendor.
The first is named Saṃtāraṇī (Crossing Over);
the second is named Raudrākṣī (Fierce-Eyed);
the third is named Saṃtoṣaṇī (Gladdening).
The fourth is named the Grove of Miscellaneous Delights (*Miśrakāvana*).
These four groves have four crossroads where the celestial maidens gather and sport.
Exquisite beauties dwell and sport therein;
various musical instruments are constantly played,
and diverse delicacies and foods are set out.
Rows of jewel trees stand in succession, their branches casting interlacing shade;
their flowers and leaves are lush and flourishing, their fragrance is rich and pervasive;
their fruits are abundant, radiant and pure, and sweet in flavor.
According to their wishes, they transform into birds whose elegant tones harmonize in song;
therein, the devas enjoy various sensual pleasures.
Once their play is finished, they enter the garden together.
Within this True Dharma and Vinaya,
analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and nirvāṇa are like those celestial gardens;
the four sublime meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are like the four crossroads.
The courtesans of universal clarity gather and roam therein;
the beautiful women of unimpeded liberation dwell and rest there;
and the music of the Tripitaka is constantly performed upon instruments.
Pure and delightful delicacies and foods were set out;
rows of jewel-trees representing the factors of enlightenment stood in array;
and immeasurable liberations, spheres of mastery, and spheres of totality were present.
The branches and twigs provide shade for the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) and the path factors (mārgāṅga);
the flowers and leaves flourish as the various sublime and pure precepts;
and the fragrant atmosphere is the various fruits of the śramaṇa.
Radiant, pure, sweet, and beautiful, it is possessed by those in training and those beyond training;
at their will, it transforms into birds whose elegant melodies harmonize,
while the assembly of sages within it experiences the bliss of supreme meditative concentration.
When their play has ended, they all enter parinirvāṇa. What are called the four heavenly paths?

They are: having departed from sensual desires, evil, and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and possessing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, one dwells fully in the first dhyāna.
This is called the first heavenly path for those who have abandoned desire and unwholesome states.
Question: When one attains the first dhyāna, one abandons all phenomena of the desire realm in their entirety;
why, then, is it said only that one has abandoned "desire and unwholesome states"?
Answer: It is because unwholesome and evil dharmas are the primary factors that one completely abandons the desire realm; therefore, this statement is made.
Furthermore, unwholesome and evil dharmas oppose and harm the intrinsic nature of the Noble Path and ought to be abandoned.
Once these have been severed, they are no longer possessed;
therefore, only the contaminated wholesome states and the non-obscured neutral states are specifically mentioned.
It does not contradict the noble path, nor is it abandoned by its own nature;
even after it has been abandoned, it can still be accomplished.
For this reason, it is not mentioned.
However, when tainted wholesome states and non-obscured neutral states are abandoned at the time of abandoning evil and unwholesome states, they are likewise said to be abandoned;
for they share the same antidote and are abandoned simultaneously.
Just as a lamp opposes darkness— not the wick, the oil, or the vessel—
yet at the moment it dispels the darkness, it is also able to burn away the wick, exhaust the oil, and heat the vessel. Furthermore,
evil and unwholesome dharmas are difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend.
Therefore, they are spoken of specifically.
Furthermore, unwholesome and evil dharmas possess many faults and afflictions that are both intense and firm;
for this reason, they are spoken of specifically.
Furthermore, when one is detached from the defilement of desire regarding evil and unwholesome dharmas,
these act as extreme obstacles, hindrances, and fetters,
like violent jailers; therefore, they are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, because all practitioners of yoga cultivate the first dhyāna specifically for the purpose of abandoning those evil and unwholesome dharmas,
it is mentioned specifically.
Moreover, because all practitioners of yoga loathe them, they completely renounce the desire realm.
Therefore, it is taught specifically as being "separated from evil and unwholesome states.
Furthermore, because evil and unwholesome states do not exist in the higher realms, it is taught specifically as being "separated" [from them].
For various reasons such as these, it is taught exclusively as being "separated from desire and evil, unwholesome states."
Question: In this context, what is desire (*chanda*) and what are the evil, unwholesome states (*pāpakā akuśalā dharmāḥ*)?
Answer: The objects of desire constitute desire.
The desire for afflictions (*kleśa*) is an evil and unwholesome dharma.
Furthermore, there is desire,
namely the five objects of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
Evil and unwholesome states refer to the five hindrances.
Furthermore, they refer to sensual desire.
This refers to sensual craving and evil, unwholesome states—
namely, all other afflictions belonging to the desire realm.
Furthermore, desire refers to the thoughts of sensual desire,
which are evil and unwholesome states.
This refers to the discursive thoughts of ill will and harm.
Furthermore, it refers to desire,
namely the desire realm.
Evil and unwholesome states refer to the element of ill will and harm;
furthermore, they refer to sensual desire.
That is to say, perceptions of sensual desire and perceptions of ill will and unwholesome states;
that is to say, perceptions of malice and harm.
Furthermore, desire refers to sensual craving and unwholesome, evil states.
This refers specifically to sensual craving (*kāmarāga*).
Here, it is explained as being free from various forms of sensual craving.
Regarding "with vitarka and with vicāra" (*savitarka-savicāra*): those phenomena that are concomitant with vitarka are called "with vitarka."
Dharmas that coexist with *vicāra* are called "with *vicāra*.
Regarding "separation from birth":
a question arises concerning the higher stages, which are superior, sublime, and pure, transcending the first *dhyāna*.
Why is it that only this is called "separation from birth"?
Answer: Because herein the beginning is cited to reveal what follows;
thus it is so stated.
In some instances, the Blessed One indicates the beginning by mentioning the end,
as when he said:
"What is it that is neither self-inflicted nor inflicted by another?"
This refers to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Just as one should understand that at the beginning and the end of the process—namely, when first entering and having already transcended—the preparatory application (*prayoga*) reaches its culmination, so it is here as well.
Furthermore, upon first attaining freedom from birth, one conceives a sense of wonder.
Because it is not so at a later time, this statement was made.
Furthermore, while the first dhyāna arises solely from detachment (*vairāgya*),
the subsequent dhyānas also arise from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Because it arises from detachment, it is called "born of detachment.
Just as that which is born from water is called "water-born," and that which is born on land is called "land-born."
Furthermore, because the first dhyāna is accompanied by two types of untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) as its retinue,
it alone is designated as "born of seclusion" (*vivekaja*).
This refers to the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
Furthermore, regarding the first dhyāna, it is called "separation" (*viveka*) by virtue of being the basis,
the preparatory application (*prayoga*), the cause, the fundamental path,
and the place of establishment for the subsequent separation. It alone receives the name "separation."
Furthermore, in the first dhyāna, one is free from both attraction and maintenance;
subsequently, being free from nourishment, it alone receives the name "separation.
Furthermore, in the first dhyāna, this freedom serves as the causal condition for the arising of all subsequent states of separation; thus, it alone receives the name "separation."
Furthermore, because the various detachments of the higher stages depend upon the first *dhyāna* for their attainment and initial arising,
the first *dhyāna* alone receives the designation "detachment. Moreover, when yogins,
having become detached from the defilements of the desire realm, give rise to the first *dhyāna* so that it manifests before them, [it is called detachment].
Because the joy and exultation are superior to those at later times,
it alone is called "detachment" (*viveka*),
like a person suffering from hunger and thirst who has first obtained food and drink.
Even though it is coarse and unpleasant, he gives rise to joy,
which is superior to obtaining fine food and drink at a later time.
Furthermore, practitioners of the three types of conduct rely on the first dhyāna to enter the state of being free from birth.
Because they attain the fruits, refine their faculties, and exhaust all outflows, they alone are called "detached" (vītarāga).
As for the three types of practitioners,
they refer to those who are bound by all fetters (sakalabandhana).
Regarding those who have partially abandoned desire and those who have completely abandoned desire;
furthermore, it is for the sake of enabling those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
It stands independently and is free from names.
It is like the desire realm, which possesses both vitarka and vicāra,
and wherein the various groups of consciousness exist as a hierarchy of master and retinue.
This same situation also occurs within the first dhyāna.
Some may harbor doubts, thinking that just as there is no [detachment] in the desire realm,
it is likewise absent in the first dhyāna.
To resolve this doubt, it is taught that the first dhyāna possesses detachment (*vairāgya*) rather than mere freedom from desire.
Furthermore, because the desire realm lacks the immediate antidote (*sāmantaka-pratipakṣa*) for such detachment,
the first dhyāna alone is designated by the name "detachment."
Furthermore, only the first dhyāna is capable of abandoning all afflictions of the three realms and thus independently receives the name "detachment" (*viveka*).
Moreover, only the first dhyāna possesses the paths for the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.

The path that is the fruit of the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) is uniquely termed "detachment" (*vairāgya*) because it possesses the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Furthermore, only the first dhyāna is capable of bringing about detachment from all [defilements].
Because of the faculty of suffering, the faculty of grief, the male faculty, the female faculty, shamelessness, lack of dread, craving for food, and craving for sexual intercourse;
because of the five hindrances, the five desires, stinginess, greed, envy, and anger;
and because of the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth, it alone is called "separation."
For these and various other reasons,
only the first dhyāna is uniquely designated as "born of seclusion" (vivekaja) bliss and joy.
Joy refers to the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*); pleasure refers to the pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhisukha*).
Furthermore, joy is subsumed under the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), while pleasure is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
"One who fully dwells in the first dhyāna" refers to one who has attained,
acquired, and accomplished the five aggregates of the wholesome first dhyāna; "attaining,
acquiring, and accomplishing" is what is meant by "fully dwelling."
Furthermore, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, his mind becomes internally purified and focused on a single point; free from applied and sustained thought,
he dwells having attained the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss.
This is called the second heavenly path where vitarka and vicāra are extinguished.
Question: When one attains the second dhyāna, does one completely extinguish all phenomena of the first dhyāna?
Why is it said that only vitarka and vicāra are extinguished?
Answer: Because vitarka and vicāra are the primary factors, this statement is made because they are extinguished in their entirety upon entering the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, vitarka and vicāra are difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend;
for this reason, they are specifically mentioned.
Moreover, vitarka and vicāra possess many faults and afflictions.
It is blazing and firm;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, when vitarka and vicāra are separated from the defilements of the first dhyāna, [they are abandoned].
Because they constitute extreme obstacles, hindrances, and fetters—
much like violent jailers— they are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, all practitioners of yoga are solely intent upon the abandonment of vitarka and vicāra.
One cultivates the second dhyāna;
therefore, it is mentioned specifically.
Furthermore, because all practitioners of yoga loathe vitarka and vicāra.
It is mentioned specifically because it involves the complete relinquishing of the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, it is mentioned specifically because vitarka and vicāra do not exist in the higher stages.
For these and various other reasons, it is said that when vitarka and vicāra have ceased, there is "inner serenity. Here,
"inner" refers to the mind and its associates,
while "serenity" refers to faith.
Because the inner mind is purified by the equality of faith, it is called "inner serenity" (adhyātmasaṃprasāda).
The Venerable Vasumitra stated:
"Vitarka and vicāra are restless and agitate the concentrated mind."
Faith is able to eliminate those [defilements] and cause the mind to be equally pure,
just as when waves subside, the water becomes clear and transparent;
therefore, faith is called internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
Furthermore, it is said:
"Defiled joy causes agitation and turbidity of the concentrated mind;
faith can eliminate that, causing the mind to become equanimous and pure."
Just as muddy water becomes clear when separated from its turbidity,
it is for this reason that faith is called "internal serenity.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta has stated this.
As the practitioner is about to enter the second dhyāna,
the mind inclines with faith toward the object of concentration and dwells in joy;
it no longer flows or scatters, but abides for a long time on a single object.
It is possible to attain the second dhyāna;
this is due to the power of faith.
Therefore, faith is called "internal serenity" (adhyātmasaṃprasāda).
"Single-pointedness of mind" means that it functions through a single door, unlike the mind of the desire realm which functions through six doors;
in the first dhyāna, the mind functions through four doors.
Because the mind of the second dhyāna functions through a single gateway, it is called "one-pointed" (*ekāgra*);
this means that the mental activity engages with a single object.
It is "without applied thought and sustained thought" (*avitarko 'vicāraḥ*).
Regarding the statement, "that which arises from concentration when vitarka and vicāra have ceased":
Question— since there is also concentration in the first dhyāna,
why is it that only the second dhyāna is called "born of concentration"?
Answer: In the second dhyāna, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is more abundant, superior, and exceptionally pure;
it transcends the first dhyāna.
Therefore, it is specifically mentioned. Furthermore, the second dhyāna is induced by concentration and nourished by concentration.
Because it manifests after the first dhyāna,
it is called "born of concentration" (samādhija),
unlike the first dhyāna itself.
It is not induced by meditative concentration,
nor is it nurtured by meditative concentration,
because it manifests immediately after a mind of the desire realm.
It is not called "born of concentration.
Furthermore, the mind of the first dhyāna is both concentrated and unconcentrated;
it functions either with internal orientation or with external orientation.
There are [states] conditioned by internal objects and conditioned by external objects.
In the second dhyāna, the mind mostly remains in meditative absorption;
it mostly functions through the internal door.
It is called "born of concentration" because it takes only internal objects as its condition.
Furthermore, in the second dhyāna, the basis of speech is extinguished.
As for this "basis of speech":
This refers to vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought).
As stated in the sūtra:
"Only after vitarka and vicāra have occurred can speech be produced."
It is not that there is no applied thought (*vitarka*) or sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Because applied and sustained thought have already ceased in the second *dhyāna*, and because it is the basis for the absence of speech, it is said to be "born of concentration.
Furthermore, the second *dhyāna* is called the "noble silence" (*ārya-tūṣṇīmbhāva*).
Therefore, it is called "born of concentration.
As stated in the Sūtra,
the Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"You all must not disparage the second dhyāna,
for this is the dharma of the noble ones' silence.
From such various causes and conditions, meditative concentration arises.
It exists only in the second dhyāna.
Regarding "joy and bliss":
joy refers to the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya).
Pleasure refers to the pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Furthermore, it is subsumed under the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) and subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Regarding one who dwells having attained the second dhyāna:
the attainment and accomplishment of the five aggregates of the wholesome second dhyāna is called "dwelling having attained.
From the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā* of the Sarvāstivāda school, Fascicle Eighty.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Eighty-one,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Eleven of the Fourth Sub-section on the Ten Gates within the Second Chapter on the Aggregates of the Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha): Furthermore, "abiding in equanimity, detached from joy."
With right mindfulness and right wisdom, one experiences pleasure with the body;
this is what the noble ones describe as abiding in the fulfillment of the third dhyāna through equanimity.
This is called the third path to heaven for those who have transcended joy.
Question: When one attains the third dhyāna, one is entirely detached from all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the second dhyāna;
why, then, is it said that one is detached only from joy (*prīti*)?

The answer is that joy (*prīti*) is mentioned as the primary factor because it is specifically singled out for its total departure from all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the second dhyāna.
Furthermore, it is mentioned specifically because joy is difficult to sever, difficult to destroy, and difficult to transcend.
Furthermore, because joy has many faults that are both intense and persistent,
it is specifically mentioned here.
Furthermore, when one is detached from the defilements of the second dhyāna by means of joy (*prīti*),
[that joy] acts as an extreme obstacle, a bond, and a hindrance,
like a violent jailer; therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, because practitioners of yoga cultivate the third dhyāna specifically as an antidote to joy (prīti),
it is mentioned here with particular emphasis.

Furthermore, because the practitioners of yoga (yogācāra) loathe and feel aversion toward joy (prīti), they abandon the second dhyāna as a whole; therefore, it is specifically mentioned [as being abandoned].
Furthermore, because there is no other factor remaining in the higher stages that can contain joy, joy is specifically mentioned.
For these and various other reasons,
it is taught that one dwells in equanimity, having abandoned joy.
Regarding "right mindfulness and right wisdom":
equanimity refers to the equanimity of mental formation;
right mindfulness refers to preeminent, wholesome mindfulness.
"Right wisdom" refers to superior, wholesome wisdom.
Regarding "the body experiences pleasure," "body" here refers to the mental body (*manomaya-kāya*).
Some say that when the mind experiences pleasure,
it also causes the physical body— composed of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)— to experience a sense of well-being and joy;
this is precisely what is called "bodily feeling of pleasure" (*kāyikī sukha-vedanā*), which corresponds to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
"An Arya should speak of relinquishment.
"Arya" refers to the Buddhas and their noble disciples;
they should explain it to others.
One should abide in equanimity oneself.
Question: It should be stated that the Noble One abides in equanimity across all stages;
why then is it mentioned only in the context of the third dhyāna?
Answer: The third dhyāna is specifically mentioned because it possesses two kinds of obstacles—those belonging to its own stage and those belonging to other stages.
The obstacle belonging to another stage refers to the joy (*prīti*) of the second dhyāna.
It is as fickle and unstable as a rākṣasa,
capable of causing the practitioner of yoga to fall away from detachment in the second dhyāna; therefore,
it is said that one should abandon it.
Do not be hindered by this joy.
What constitutes an internal hindrance is the bliss of the third dhyāna.
Among the pleasures of birth and death, this pleasure is the most supreme.
Various practitioners of yoga become attached to this pleasure and do not seek the superior and wondrous merits of the higher stages.
Therefore, it is said that for beginner practitioners (*yogācāra*),
this pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is a source of hindrance and should not be clung to.
Furthermore, the Buddha and his disciples should explain to others the third dhyāna in terms of its own stage (*svabhūmi*) and other stages (*parabhūmi*).
One should exhort others to abandon the faults of obstacles; therefore,
this is called "the noble one’s teaching on relinquishment," namely,
explaining the third dhyāna to others.
There is a superior pleasant sensation that causes sentient beings to become attached and deluded,
such that they do not seek the sublime and wondrous merits of higher stages.
"You all should abide in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension;
do not be obstructed by this pleasure,
and likewise teach the second dhyāna to others."
There is a superior feeling of joy that can cause sentient beings to drift, become restless, and fall away from the second dhyāna through its freedom from passion.
You should abide in right mindfulness and equanimity.
Do not let yourself be hindered by this joy,
just as an experienced caravan leader describes to new merchants all the dangers and calamities found in various kingdoms and towns.
This means that in such countries and such towns,
there are many courtesans, gambling dens, deceivers, taverns, and dangers from bandits; you should keep yourselves far away from these and guard against them,
lest you lose your wealth and goods.
To "dwell having fully attained the third dhyāna" means to obtain,
acquire, and accomplish the five aggregates of the wholesome third dhyāna; the state of obtaining,
acquiring, and accomplishing these is termed "dwelling having fully attained."
Furthermore, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow,
one enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
This is called the fourth heavenly path for those who have severed pleasure.
Question: When attaining the fourth dhyāna, one completely abandons all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the third dhyāna.
Why is it said that only pleasure (*sukha*) is abandoned?

Answer: Because pleasure is the foremost [of the factors to be abandoned], and because one completely abandons all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) of the third dhyāna, pleasure alone is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, pleasure is specifically discussed because it is difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend.
Moreover, pleasure possesses many afflictions that are both intense and firm.
Therefore, it is explained selectively.
Furthermore, when one seeks to abandon the defilements of the third dhyāna through the attainment of pleasure,
this [pleasure] constitutes an extreme obstacle, bondage, and hindrance.
It is spoken of specifically because it is like a violent jailer.
Furthermore, yogins cultivate the fourth dhyāna specifically as an antidote to pleasure;
therefore, it is mentioned specifically.
Furthermore, because the practitioners of yoga (yogācāra) loathe and detest pleasure, they abandon the third dhyāna in its entirety;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned [as being free from pleasure].
Furthermore, because there is no other factor that can exist in the higher stages than pleasure, pleasure is specifically mentioned.
For these and various other reasons, it is said that only the abandonment of pleasure and the abandonment of suffering [are taught].
Question: At the time of becoming free from the defilement of desire, the practitioner of meditation has already abandoned the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
Why is it that suffering (*duḥkha*) is said to be abandoned only at the time of becoming free from the defilements of the third dhyāna?
Answer: This refers to what has already been abandoned being designated as "abandoned"; that is, speaking of something distant using a term for proximity.
Just as one who has already come is said to be "coming now," so it is said:
"Great King, from where have you come?"
It is like using the term "liberation" for one who has already been liberated.
As it is said:
"By means of this knowledge and vision, the mind is liberated from the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance."
When one is free from the defilement of sensual desire, the mind is already liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
When one is free from the defilement of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
the mind is liberated from the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
It is like using the term "entering" with respect to one who has already entered;
as it is said:
"The bodhisattva enters the state of rightness and departure from birth."
One attains conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
This is like using the term "feeling" (*vedanā*) with respect to what has already been felt;
as it is said:
When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is that one is experiencing a pleasant feeling; there is no self-knower who experiences the present feeling.
Therefore, although the feeling has already been experienced, the word "feeling" (vedanā) is used.
Herein, it is likewise: although [the defilements] have already been abandoned, they are said to be "abandoned."
This refers to using a term for proximity to describe something distant.
Furthermore, regarding the simultaneous utterance of the term "abandonment" based on the exhaustion of paired phenomena (*dvaya-dharma*),
"paired phenomena" refers to suffering and pleasure.
At the time of becoming free from the defilements of desire, although suffering has already been exhausted, bliss has not yet been exhausted.
Now, having become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna, both suffering and bliss are exhausted;
thus, the word "cessation" is spoken for both.
Furthermore, "abandoning pleasure" refers to abandoning the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) of the third dhyāna;
"abandoning suffering" refers to...
This means the abandonment of the mind and mental factors associated with them.
Furthermore, "abandoning pleasure" refers to the abandonment of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in the third dhyāna.
"Severing suffering" refers to severing the inhalation and exhalation of the third dhyāna.
For noble ones, the perception of suffering regarding inhalation and exhalation is like the perception of suffering that ordinary beings experience in the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, "abandoning pleasure" refers to abandoning the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) of the third dhyāna.
"Abandoning suffering" refers to...
This means that one cuts off that faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
As it is said:
"Because it is impermanent, it is suffering."
Regarding the phrase "first, joy and sorrow subside":
when one becomes free from the defilement of desire, the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) has already subsided;
when one becomes free from the defilement of the second dhyāna, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) further subsides.
Therefore, it is said that now joy and sorrow have first subsided;
"neither-painful-nor-pleasant" refers to the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant.
"Purity of equanimity" refers to the practice of equanimity.
"Purity of mindfulness" refers to...
This refers to wholesome mindfulness (*smṛti*).

Question: Since the lower stages also possess untainted equanimity and mindfulness (*anāsrava-upekṣā-smṛti*), why is it said that only in the fourth dhyāna are equanimity and mindfulness "pure" (*pariśuddha*)?
The answer is: In the fourth dhyāna, equanimity and mindfulness are called "pure" because they are free from the eight disturbances.
Suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, inhalation, exhalation, vitarka, and vicāra are named the eight disturbances.
In this context, none of these are exclusively termed "pure.
Furthermore, the fourth dhyāna is called pure because it is free from internal and external calamities;
the three lower dhyānas are not called pure because they possess both internal and external calamities.
This means that because the first dhyāna contains the fire of vitarka and vicāra within, it is externally consumed by the calamity of fire;
because the second dhyāna contains the water of extreme joy (prīti) within, it is externally dissolved by the calamity of water.
Because the third dhyāna contains the winds of inhalation and exhalation within, it is swept away by the external calamity of wind;
because the fourth dhyāna lacks these three calamities, it is said to be pure.
Furthermore, the physical basis and the vessel-world of the fourth dhyāna are not reached by the three calamities;
mindfulness is free from forgetfulness and equanimity is free from distraction.
Because it is not like the lower stages, it is called "pure."
Furthermore, because the fourth dhyāna is free from all afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),
it is said that equanimity and mindfulness are purified there and not elsewhere.
That is to say, there exists equanimity and mindfulness that are free from all afflictions but not from secondary afflictions.

This refers to the untainted equanimity and mindfulness of the three lower dhyānas, which may involve equanimity and mindfulness that are free from secondary afflictions but not from primary afflictions;
as well as the tainted equanimity and mindfulness of the fourth dhyāna.
There may be equanimity and mindfulness that are free from all afflictions and secondary afflictions—
namely, the untainted equanimity and mindfulness of the fourth dhyāna—
or there may be equanimity and mindfulness that are not free from afflictions and secondary afflictions.
This refers to the contaminated equanimity and mindfulness of the three lower dhyānas, as well as all equanimity and mindfulness in the desire realm.
It should be understood that, within this context,
the secondary afflictions are precisely the eight disturbing matters mentioned above.
Furthermore, the physical body that serves as the basis for the fourth dhyāna is translucent, pure, and luminous.
Just as a lamp’s light is clear when its wick and oil are refined, so too is it pure because it relies upon equanimity and mindfulness.
Moreover, the fourth dhyāna is a perfect basis, the most excellent among all bases.
This is the ultimate stage, the most honored among all stages;
therefore, its equanimity and mindfulness are also called "pure.
Furthermore, the power of the concentration of the fourth dhyāna, known as the "unshakable concentration," pervades the entire body that serves as its basis.
Therefore, that equanimity and mindfulness are also called "pure.

Furthermore, the fourth dhyāna is the basis for the seven meditative concentrations because, from the lower to the upper levels, there are three types of untainted concentration (anāsrava-samādhi) in each.
By virtue of this, equanimity and mindfulness are also called "purified.
Furthermore, the fourth dhyāna has two aspects of vastness:
first, the vastness of its location.
Because these two roots of goodness are vast,
their equanimity and mindfulness are also called "pure.
Furthermore, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges rely upon this fourth dhyāna to enter the state of right determination and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Because they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
their equanimity and mindfulness are also called "pure.
Furthermore, yogins of the fourth dhyāna rely upon it to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth, to attain the fruits [of the path], and to exhaust all outflows.
This refers to the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas;
therefore, their equanimity and mindfulness are also called "pure.
Furthermore, [this applies to] the primary elements and derived matter of the fourth dhyāna.
Because both primary colors and shapes are extremely sublime and excellent,
that equanimity and mindfulness are also called "pure.
Furthermore, based on the fourth dhyāna, there is the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
Because it is able to take as its object the various past lives within the desire realm and the four dhyānas,
that equanimity and mindfulness are also called "pure.
It is by means of such various causes and conditions [that this is so].
In the fourth dhyāna, equanimity and mindfulness alone are termed "pure.
One who dwells fully endowed with the fourth dhyāna refers to one who has attained,
acquired, and accomplished the five wholesome aggregates of the fourth dhyāna.
To attain and achieve this is called "dwelling in fulfillment.
As stated in the Sūtra,
there are four kinds of higher mental states (*adhicitta*) for dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Question: For what reason are they called "predominant mental factors" (adhipati-citta-dharma)?
Answer: Among these, the mental factor is precisely samādhi;
without samādhi, no [mental factor] possesses great power.
Because it possesses great effort and is capable of accomplishing great matters,
and because it can function like the four fundamental dhyānas,
it alone is designated as the "higher mental faculty" (adhicitta).
Furthermore, within the four dhyānas there are immeasurable kinds of superior mental factors and sublime qualities,
such as the immeasurables (apramāṇa), the liberations (vimokṣa), the bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), the bases of totality (kṛtsnāyatana), and the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
Because [these include] the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), the meditative absorption of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*), and so forth,
they alone are designated as "higher mental states" (*adhicitta*).
Furthermore, based on the four dhyānas, there are various practitioners of yoga.
One experiences the mind’s delight through immeasurable doors,
namely, the previously mentioned doors of various merits as well as the three samādhis such as emptiness-of-emptiness;
for this reason, it alone is designated as "higher mental faculty" (adhicitta).
Furthermore, these four dhyānas are subsumed under the "pleasant practice" (sukha-pratipad).
For this reason, they alone are designated as the "higher mental states" (adhicitta).
Question: Within the four dhyānas, there are also qualities capable of inducing future happiness.
Why is it that only dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) is mentioned?
The answer is: it should also be stated as dwelling in happiness in future lives (*sāmparāyikasukhavihāra*).
That it is not so stated should be understood as this sutra being an incomplete teaching (*sāvadeśika*).
Furthermore, if it is said that this is "dwelling in happiness in the present life," one should know that "dwelling in happiness in future lives" has already been implied;
for dwelling in happiness in future lives is attained by taking dwelling in happiness in the present life as its cause.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"First one cultivates those attainments (samāpatti) in this world, and only afterwards is one born there.
Furthermore, dwelling in happiness in a future life is dependent upon and connected to dwelling in happiness in the present life.
The dwelling in happiness in the present life does not depend upon or belong to the dwelling in happiness in future lives;
therefore, by merely mentioning the dwelling in happiness in the present life, that [future dwelling] is already implied.
Furthermore, the dwelling in happiness in the present life serves as the gateway for the practice (*prayoga*) toward the dwelling in happiness in future lives.
If this has already been explained, then that has also been explained.
Furthermore, dwelling in happiness in the present life is the cause, while dwelling in happiness in future lives is the fruit;
if the cause has already been explained, then the fruit has also been explained.
As it is with cause and effect,
so it is with the agent and the acted upon,
and the producer and the produced.
The agent of accomplishment and that which is accomplished;
the agent of continuity and that which continues;
the agent of projection and that which is projected.
It should be understood that the same applies to the transformer and the transformed, as well as to the characteristic and the characterized.
Furthermore, the happiness of the present life is near, while the happiness of future lives is distant.
If that which is near has been explained, then that which is distant has already been explained as well.
It is just as with the near and the distant.
Adjacent and non-adjacent;
conjoined and non-conjoined;
this body and its homogeneous class.
It should be understood that the same applies to other bodies and their respective group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Furthermore, regarding dwelling in happiness in the present life, whether one is ignorant or wise, [the result is the same].
Because both those within our own school and those of external schools alike believe that right and wrong contemplation exist, these are specifically mentioned.
As for the subsequent dwelling in the joy of the Dharma, because there are those who do not believe in it— such as the various followers of external paths— it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, most foolish persons crave present pleasure and do not seek future happiness.
Within the realm of present pleasure, they crave minor sensual delights and do not seek the vast, sublime bliss of freedom from desire.
The Blessed One, wishing to cause them to abandon minor desires and pleasures and to attain the vast and sublime bliss of the four dhyānas,
spoke as follows.
If you seek vast happiness,
you should abandon sensual pleasures and cultivate the four dhyānas;
therefore, I have spoken only of dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Furthermore, when the four dhyānas are manifested, one necessarily experiences happiness in the present;
therefore, they are specifically mentioned.
As for future happiness, it is not fixed, as one may either fall back and be reborn in a lower realm or advance and be reborn in a higher realm.
Or because [the latter] is parinirvāṇa, it is not mentioned.
For such various reasons as these,
the Blessed One spoke only of the four dhyānas as the happiness of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukha*).

Although the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) also possess the sense of bliss, they are not mentioned here because they are subsumed under the practice of painful progress (*duḥkhā pratipad*).
As the Sūtra says: "These four kinds of abidings in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) are superior states of mind (*adhicitta*)."
Those who practice meditative concentration enter and emerge from it repeatedly;
they should correctly understand the peaceful liberation that transcends all forms.
One should correctly proclaim that those who practice meditative concentration enter and emerge repeatedly from the four formless absorptions.
Question: For what reason does the Blessed One exhort one to thoroughly understand the four dhyānas, yet exhort one to proclaim the four formless attainments?
Answer: Because the dhyānas are coarse, manifest, clear, and easy to perceive.
Because those who practice meditative concentration, having emerged from it, again desire to enter it, the Buddha told them:
"If you wish to re-enter, you should correctly discern the signs of entering and emerging from concentration, ensuring there is no error."
The formless realms possess subtle characteristics that are hidden and difficult to perceive;
because those who practice meditative concentration do not wish to re-enter them after emerging from them,
the Buddha said:
If one does not delight in re-entering [the meditative state], one should correctly explain it to others;
furthermore, one must not cause the signs of entering and emerging from concentration to be forgotten.
Moreover, within the four dhyānas, there are many various distinct signs and qualities.
Because those who practice meditative concentration, having emerged from it, again desire to enter it, the Buddha told them:
"If you wish to re-enter, you should correctly discern the characteristics of entering and emerging from concentration, so that no error occurs."
Within the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), there are no manifold qualities of diverse characteristics;
for those who practice meditative concentration, having emerged from them, do not delight in entering them again.
Thus the Buddha said.
If one does not delight in re-entering [the meditative state], one should correctly demonstrate it to others;
furthermore, one must not allow the signs of entering and emerging from concentration to be forgotten.
Moreover, within the four dhyānas, there are many diverse characteristics regarding the faculties, feelings, mind, and mental factors.
Because those who practice meditative concentration, having emerged from it, again desire to enter it, the Buddha told them:
"If you wish to re-enter, you should correctly understand the signs of entering and emerging from concentration, so as not to fall into error."
Within the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), there are no many distinct characteristics among the faculties, feelings,
or mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Because those who practice meditative concentration do not wish to re-enter them after emerging from them,
the Buddha declared:
If one does not delight in re-entering [the meditative state], one should correctly teach it to others;
furthermore, one must not allow the signs of entering and emerging from concentration to be forgotten.
Moreover, within the four dhyānas, there are immeasurable kinds of meritorious benefits.
Because those who practice meditative concentration, having emerged from it, again desire to enter it, the Buddha told them:
"If you wish to re-enter, you should correctly understand the signs of entering and emerging from concentration, so that no error occurs."
Within the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), there are no immeasurable kinds of meritorious benefits;
for those who practice concentration do not wish to re-enter them after having emerged from them.
Thus the Buddha declared.
If one does not delight in re-entering [the meditative absorption], one should correctly instruct others;
furthermore, one must not allow the signs of entering and emerging from concentration to be forgotten.
Moreover, within the four dhyānas, there is all-illuminating wisdom that takes as its object both what is above and below oneself.
When those who practice meditative concentration have emerged from that state,
because they again desire to enter it,
the Buddha said:
If one wishes to enter again, one should correctly understand the signs of entering and emerging from meditative absorption so as not to err;
within the formless absorptions, there is no pervasive wisdom capable of taking its own higher level as an object, nor can it take lower levels as objects.
Because those who practice meditative concentration do not wish to re-enter [the state] after emerging from it,
the Buddha told them:
"If you do not wish to re-enter, you should correctly teach and demonstrate it to others."
One should not allow the signs of entering and emerging from meditative absorption to be forgotten.
For these and various other such reasons,
the Buddha exhorted that one should thoroughly understand meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Regarding the four formless attainments, one should encourage their proclamation,
as stated in the Sūtra:
"The four dhyānas have four benefits."
The formless absorptions have one specific benefit.
Question: Why are there four benefits for the dhyānas, whereas there is only one benefit among the formless absorptions?
Answer: It is precisely due to the various causes and conditions previously explained that the benefits of the dhyānas and the formless attainments differ.
Furthermore, there are two unique responses to this point.
That is to say, within the dhyānas there are three types of concentration:
first, that with both vitarka and vicāra;
second, that without vitarka and with vicāra alone.
Among the three formless absorptions that are without applied thought and sustained thought, there is only one type: that which is without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Furthermore, within the four dhyānas, there are three types of feeling, namely:
joy, pleasure, and equanimity.
In the formless attainments, there is only the feeling of equanimity;
therefore, the benefits of the four dhyānas are fourfold,
whereas the benefit in the formless attainments is single.
Question: What is the distinction between the benefits of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)?
Answer: The very names constitute the distinction;
that is, they are called "meditative concentration" and "benefits."
Furthermore, there are three types of dhyāna:
namely, the wholesome, the defiled, and the non-obscured neutral.
Their excellence consists solely in being wholesome.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of dhyāna: namely, with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Its superior benefits (*anuśaṃsa*) pertain exclusively to that which is without outflows.
Furthermore, dhyāna is either bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Or it may be non-bound;
its excellence is exclusively non-bound.
Furthermore, meditative absorption may be either of the learner (śaikṣa) or of the adept (aśaikṣa).
Or it is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Its excellence consists solely in being learner and non-learner. Furthermore, meditative concentration (dhyāna) is either to be abandoned by vision or to be abandoned by cultivation.
Or it may not be subject to abandonment;
its superior benefit is exclusively not subject to abandonment.
Furthermore, dhyāna is both defiled and undefiled.
Victory is exclusively undefiled.
Furthermore, while meditative absorption (dhyāna) may be either with or without karmic maturation (vipāka),
victory is exclusively without karmic maturation.
Furthermore, meditative concentration (dhyāna) is subsumed under three of the truths,
excluding the truth of cessation;
its benefits are subsumed solely under the truth of the path.
This is called the distinction of the benefits of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
"In the first meditative concentration, the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) ceases."

Regarding the question of why the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) ceases in the second dhyāna: since sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*) are abandoned at the time of becoming free from the defilements of desire, for what reason does the Sūtra state this?
Answer: It is stated thus because it refers to that which has already been overcome by its antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
This means that although the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is abandoned at the stage of detachment from desire,
it is not yet called "transcending the remedy for suffering.
This occurs when one attains detachment from the first dhyāna.
It is called the cessation of suffering because it is the antidote to the suffering of the lower realms.
The antidote to suffering refers to the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, this statement is made based on the fact that one has not yet transcended the lineage that serves as the basis for suffering;
that is to say, although the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) is abandoned at the stage of detachment from desire,
one has not yet transcended the lineage that is the basis for suffering.
When one attains detachment from the first dhyāna,
because one has transcended the basis of suffering and the lineage of suffering, it is said that the basis and lineage for the cessation of suffering have been attained;
this refers to the various groups of consciousness.

Question: Although the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is abandoned at the stage of detachment from sensual desire, one has not yet transcended its basis of opposition (*pratipakṣa-āśraya*) nor its lineage (*gotra*);
therefore, it should not be said that sorrow ceases in the first dhyāna.
Answer: The antidotes to the faculty of sorrow (daurmanasyendriya) and their respective bases and lineages all reside in the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
Since they share the same locus as the faculty of sorrow within the mental consciousness, it is said that they are extinguished precisely at the time of right abandonment.
Because the basis of the faculty of suffering and the lineage of suffering do not coexist in the same consciousness with their antidote,
the cessation of suffering is said to occur only when one has transcended the basis and lineage of that antidote.
Some maintain this explanation:
that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) ceases in the second dhyāna means that vitarka and vicāra cease,
because the noble ones (*ārya*) conceive the notion of suffering regarding vitarka and vicāra.
Transcending all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), one feels aversion toward the suffering of hell;
because it can give rise to the perception of suffering, it is called the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*). In a certain *sūtra*, it is said that the four dhyānas are like a bed or seat.
Question: Why does the World-Honored One say that the four dhyānas are like a bed or seat?
Answer: Because they possess the nature of loftiness and excellence, and because they are characterized by being embraced [by these qualities].
As for "the nature of loftiness and excellence":
This is said with reference to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
because one departs from the desire realm by means of the four dhyānas.
As for "the nature of embracing" (*parigrahakatva*):
This is said with reference to wholesome dharmas,
because meditative concentration encompasses many wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, O noble ones:
Because one has become utterly weary of the long road of saṃsāra that has no beginning,
one rests for a time in meditative concentration (dhyāna),
just as one who is exhausted from a long journey pauses briefly upon a seat.
Therefore, the term "seat" is used in reference to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
A sūtra states:
"The four types of meditative concentration are like a cool breeze."
Question: Why does the Blessed One say that the four dhyānas are like a cool breeze?
Answer: Because they can suppress the heat of karma and afflictions.

That is to say, the first dhyāna can suppress the heat of various unwholesome karmas and afflictions of the desire realm; the second dhyāna can suppress the heat of karma and afflictions associated with vitarka and vicāra of the first dhyāna.
The third dhyāna can arrest the heat of the karmic afflictions associated with extreme joy belonging to the second dhyāna;
the fourth dhyāna can arrest the heat of the karmic afflictions associated with extreme bliss belonging to the third dhyāna.
Therefore, it is said that dhyāna is like a cool breeze.
In another sūtra, it is stated that the four dhyānas are like exquisite food and drink.
Question: World-Honored One, for what reason do you say that the four dhyānas are like food and drink?
Answer: Because they possess the sense of being able to sustain the dharmakāya, just as there are various excellent foods and drinks within a village or town.
All these are sent to the royal city to be nurtured and made most excellent.
In this way, all such various, supreme,
and wondrous roots of goodness are gathered in meditative concentration to nurture the Dharma-body.
Therefore, dhyāna is said to be like exquisite food and drink.
In a certain sūtra, the Buddha spoke to a brahmin,
describing the fourth dhyāna as the "ultimate track."
Question: Why, O Bhagavān, did you omit the first three dhyānas for the sake of the brahmin and declare the fourth dhyāna to be the "ultimate path"?
Answer: There was a brahmin who heard that the Buddha possessed all-encompassing knowledge and vision (*sarvajñajñānadarśana*).
Furthermore, I have heard that there are no Buddhas who do not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by relying upon the fourth dhyāna;
for all establishments, the fourth dhyāna is designated as the ultimate path.
He thought to himself: "If the Buddha has designated the fourth dhyāna as the ultimate path, he must certainly possess all-encompassing knowledge and vision.
Having formed this thought, he came to question the World-Honored One.
Knowing his intention, the Buddha spoke only of the fourth dhyāna as the ultimate path.
Upon hearing this, he gained resolute faith that the Buddha possesses all-encompassing wisdom and vision.
The Buddha further addressed that brahmin, saying:
"The fourth dhyāna is the track of the Tathāgata;
it is where the Buddha has traveled and where the Buddha has cultivated."
It is like a wild elephant in the summer season,
emerging from a dense forest and seeing a place where the ground is fertile and moist,
and flowers and fruits flourish in abundance.
The flowing springs and bathing pools have water that is clear and delicious;
various flowers bloom in reflection, making them exceedingly delightful.
Having seen this, he rejoices and digs into the earth with his tusks to plant his feet.
The World-Honored One is likewise.
Having brought forth equanimity through the fourth dhyāna, he digs into the ground of *jñeyadhātu* (the realm of the knowable) and establishes the feet of wisdom.
It should be understood that herein, "the tracks of the Tathāgata" refers to this.
The Buddha’s practice is said to be the ultimate śamatha of the fourth dhyāna;
it is said to be the ultimate vipaśyanā of the fourth dhyāna.
That which the Buddha practiced and cultivated is,
in summary, said to be the ultimate śamatha and vipaśyanā of the fourth dhyāna;
this is stated in a sūtra.
The four dhyānas are all abidings in happiness.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One say that the four dhyānas are abidings in happiness?
Answer: Because the fundamental dhyānas are easily brought into manifestation.
Therefore, it is called an abiding in happiness, unlike the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*),
which are difficult to manifest. Why is this so?
Sentient beings, bound by the karma and afflictions of the desire realm,
find it extremely difficult to bring the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) into manifestation,
just as one who is tightly bound from behind finds it very difficult to free themselves.
Sentient beings are likewise;
having been bound by the karma and afflictions of the desire realm,
they find it extremely difficult to induce the threshold concentration (anāgamya-samādhi) in order to release their own bonds.
By practicing the contemplation of impurity or mindfulness of breathing for ten or twelve years,
one may be able to induce the threshold concentration (anāgamya-samādhi).
Because it cannot be induced [by the lower stages], it is extremely difficult.
If one has abandoned the defilements of desire, the first dhyāna arises without effort and thus manifests easily.
From the first dhyāna, one further desires to induce the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
It requires much effort;
it is extinguished by one mental factor and produced by another mental factor;
it is extinguished by a coarse mental factor and produced by a subtle mental factor.
Since that which is accompanied by vitarka ceases and that which is accompanied by vicāra arises,
it is likewise difficult for the intermediate dhyāna to manifest.
For example, it is like a person who splits wood with wood; much effort must be exerted before it is finally split.
In the same way, when the mind belonging to the level of the first dhyāna ceases and arises within its own sphere, it is also like this.
