It should be understood that the access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) of the final three dhyānas are difficult to arise, whereas their fundamental states (*maula*) are easy to arise, just as in the case of the first dhyāna.
Question: Having already become detached from the defilements of the lower realms, one gives rise to the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
"Is it not also a peaceful dwelling because it is not difficult?
Answer: Although one is free from the defilements of the lower realms, because the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are extremely subtle, their arising is also difficult;
for when entering the dhyānas, it is easier than that.
Furthermore, since there are no forms whatsoever in the formless realm, it is not universally believed to exist;
thus, it is extremely difficult for a practitioner to give rise to that meditative absorption.
For instance, the Elder Nakhaka came and said to the Venerable Ānanda:
We householders have long been greedily attached to the five sensory objects, such as form;
hearing of the formless realm, we are struck with extreme terror as if standing at the edge of a deep pit.
How could sentient beings be entirely without form? Thus it is difficult to believe in its existence, and because it is difficult to believe, one gives rise to extreme hardship.
Furthermore, because it is easy to become free from defilement by relying on the four dhyānas—
and not so with the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and others— they are called "abodes of bliss" (*sukhavihāra*).
It is, for example, like two people traveling together to the same destination.
One travels by land and the other by boat;
although both arrive at the same destination, the one who traveled by boat does not encounter the hardships that the one on land does.
In this way, there are sentient beings who, relying upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), become free from defilement.
There are those who become free from defilement by relying on a preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) or the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
Although both cases involve freedom from defilement, for one relying on a dhyāna, it is not difficult, whereas for one relying on a preparatory stage and so forth, it is.
Therefore, only the dhyānas receive the name "abiding in happiness.
Furthermore, it is only within the dhyānas that both types of happiness are present, and thus they are called "abiding in happiness":
first, the happiness of pleasant feeling, and second, the happiness of pliancy (praśrabdhi).
The first three dhyānas all possess both types of pleasure.
Although the fourth dhyāna lacks the pleasure of sensation (*vedanā-sukha*),
its pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*) is so vast and powerful that it surpasses the two preceding pleasures.
Although the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) possess pliancy (*praśrabdhi*),
it is not called "bliss" because it is not extensive.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of bliss.
First is the primary pleasure;
second is the adventitious pleasure.
As for the primary pleasure:
This refers to arising in meditative absorption (dhyāna) based on meditative absorption.
"Guest-like pleasure" refers to abiding in the formless realm (ārūpya) based on meditative absorption.
Because one dwelling in the dhyāna stages fully possesses both types of bliss, it is called "abiding in bliss.
Because one dwelling in the formless (ārūpya) stages does not fully possess these two types of bliss, it is not "abiding in bliss.
Since the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) are not superior, they cannot be so named.
Furthermore, among the four dhyānas, there is no suffering or harm, and the power and function of bliss are vast;
because they are not merely access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) and so forth, they are called "abodes of bliss" (*sukhavihāra*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
If, in a certain state, there is an absence of all affliction and harm, it is called "happiness" (*sukha*).

Furthermore, when the fundamental dhyānas manifest, they nourish the primary elements within the entire body, causing the body to become full and refreshed; therefore, it is called "dwelling in happiness."
When the preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*) and so forth manifest,
the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that nourish [the body] arise solely from the limits of the mind;
because they do not bring about extreme satisfaction, they do not constitute a state of blissful abiding (*sukhavihāra*).
Some say that when the preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*) and so forth manifest,
the nourishing great elements (*aupacayika-mahābhūta*) arise throughout the entire body.

Furthermore, its nourishment is not equal to that when meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is present, because [in absorption] it nourishes the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); therefore, it is not a state of abiding in bliss.
It is, for example, like two people bathing in the same pool.
One person enters the water,
while the other uses his hand to pour [water] over him.
Although both are bathing, the one who enters the water receives greater benefit through moistening than the one whose body is merely poured upon by hand.
Furthermore, within the four dhyānas, because the powers of śamatha and vipaśyanā are equal, they are called "abodes of happiness.
In the preparatory stages (sāmantaka), vipaśyanā is strong and śamatha is weak;
in the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti), śamatha is strong and vipaśyanā is weak; in both cases, they are not abodes of happiness.
Furthermore, within the four dhyānas, diligence proceeds in equilibrium with tranquility (śamatha); therefore, they are called "abodes of bliss.
Although the power of diligence is strong in all stages, within the dhyānas it proceeds in equilibrium because it is regulated by tranquility.
The other stages are not so, and therefore they are not abodes of bliss.

Furthermore, within the four dhyānas, they are called abodes of bliss because an increase in equanimity (*upekṣā*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and detachment from defilements (*vairāgya*) can be found there.
That is to say, at the time of becoming detached from defilements, there are two kinds of abandonment.
First, abandonment through superior equanimity;
second, abandonment with effort.
These occur when one relies on the access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) of the formless realms (*ārūpya*) to become free from all defilements.
It is called "abandonment with effort" because it is extremely difficult;
when one abandons all defilements by relying on the fundamental dhyānas,
it is called "abandonment through superior equanimity" because it proceeds spontaneously.
It is like two people traveling together toward the same destination;
one rides a fine horse,
while the other rides a vicious horse.
One riding a fine horse reaches the destination with very little difficulty,
whereas one riding a poor horse reaches it only after great hardship.
Furthermore, within the four dhyānas, the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*) is called an "abiding in bliss" because it is attained through the abandonment of defilements.

Because the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) involve the path of effortful application (*sābhisaṃskāra-mārga*), they do not constitute a state of abiding in bliss;
it is like a great multitude of people crossing a large river together.
Some rely on bundles of grass;
some rely on hollow gourds;
some rely on rafts made of planks.
There are those who rely on a boat;
those who rely on a boat reach the other shore with effortless ease and comfort.
Those who rely on other means reach the other shore through fear and hardship.
Sentient beings are likewise; they cross the river of afflictions,
some relying on meditative concentration (dhyāna) and others relying on other stages (bhūmi).
Although both involve crossing from this shore of saṃsāra to the far shore of nirvāṇa, those who rely on the dhyānas reach it with ease and bliss;
therefore, these are called "abodes of bliss," whereas those who rely on the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) or the formless realms (ārūpya) are not.
Due to such various causes and conditions as these,
only the four dhyānas are called "abodes of happiness.
Just as they are called "abodes of happiness," they are likewise called "abodes of contact."
They abide together.
The four immeasurables are:
first, loving-kindness; second, compassion; third, sympathetic joy; and fourth, equanimity.
Question: Why are the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) taught immediately after the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)?
Answer: Because the meditative absorptions give rise to the four immeasurables.
Furthermore, because the meditative absorptions and the immeasurables mutually induce one another.
Furthermore, because the four immeasurables are the supreme qualities within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is asked:
what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these four immeasurables?
It is answered: both loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) have non-hatred (*avyāpāda*) as their wholesome root.
Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the antidote to hatred;
if associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta*) and concomitant factors (*anuvartin*) are also included,
then its intrinsic nature consists of four or five aggregates (*skandha*).
In the desire realm, there are four aggregates;
in the form realm, there are five aggregates.
Question: If both loving-kindness and compassion are based on the wholesome root of non-hatred, [how do they differ]?
Regarding those whose nature is to counteract hatred:
what kind of hatred does loving-kindness (*maitrī*) counteract?
What kind of hatred does compassion (*karuṇā*) counteract?
Answer: Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) counteracts the hatred that leads to taking life;
compassion (*karuṇā*) counteracts the hatred that leads to striking others.
Furthermore, loving-kindness counteracts hatred toward those who are objects of one's anger.
Compassion is the antidote to anger toward those who do not deserve it.
Some say that the immeasurable of loving-kindness consists of the wholesome root of non-anger.
Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the antidote to hatred,
the immeasurable of compassion (*karuṇā-apramāṇa*) has non-harming as its intrinsic nature, serving as the antidote to harming.
The immeasurable of sympathetic joy (*muditā-apramāṇa*) has the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) as its intrinsic nature.
If one takes both the associated [mental factors] and the co-arising [factors] together,
then those in the desire realm have the four aggregates as their intrinsic nature,
while those in the form realm have the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature.
Question: If immeasurable joy (*muditā-apramāṇa*) has the faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how should one interpret the statement in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
As it says:
What is the immeasurable of sympathetic joy (*muditā*)?
It refers to joy and the associated aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness,
as well as the two types of action— bodily and vocal— that arise from them.
If all those formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) that arise are called "joy" (*prīti*),
how could there be a feeling of joy (*prītivedanā*) that is associated with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*)?
The answer is that the text should have stated this.
This refers to joy (*prīti*) and the perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) associated with joy.
One should not say "feeling" (*vedanā*) where it says "feeling," for that is an error of the reciter.
Furthermore, that treatise states in general that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) constitute the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the immeasurable of joy.
Although the sensation of pleasure is not associated with [the aggregate of] sensation itself,
other mental states and mental factors are associated with sensation; therefore,
this statement does not contradict reason.
Other masters say that this immeasurable joy has gladness (*abhipramodana*) as its intrinsic nature;
the essence of gladness is not a feeling (*vedanā*), but is a distinct mental factor (*caitta*) associated with the mind.
Some say that *abhirati* (delight) is to be found within the group of mental factors associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
Others have said this:
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) arises subsequently because it is induced by the power of joy;
thus, if one were to say that this immeasurable joy is associated with feeling (*vedanā*), it would not contradict reason.
Equanimity has non-attachment as its intrinsic nature because it serves as the antidote to attachment.
If one includes its associated and concomitant factors,
then in the desire realm, its intrinsic nature consists of the four aggregates.
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) has the five aggregates as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
This is what is called the immeasurable intrinsic nature.
Question: What are the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) of these four immeasurables?
Answer: Self-nature is itself the characteristic;
the characteristic is itself self-nature.
This is because self-nature and the characteristic are not mutually separated.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated:
"Bestowing benefit is the characteristic of loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
removing misfortune is the characteristic of compassion (*karuṇā*)."
Rejoicing and attaining equanimity are the characteristics of sympathetic joy (*muditā*);
forgetting the self and abiding in impartiality are the characteristics of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Thus, the essential nature and the characteristics of the immeasurables have been explained.
Therefore, it shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason is it called "immeasurable" (apramāṇa)?
What is the meaning of "immeasurable"?
Answer: They are called "immeasurable" because they universally take sentient beings as their object and serve as antidotes to immeasurable conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and afflictions.
Question: There are two kinds of conceptual proliferation:
first, the proliferation of craving (*tṛṣṇā-prapañca*).
Second is the conceptual proliferation of views.
What are the immeasurables?
What conceptual proliferations do they counteract? Answer: The immeasurables cannot sever the various afflictions.
They can merely suppress it or cause it to recede;
at times, all four serve as antidotes to craving.
Sometimes all four serve as antidotes to views.
If one speaks according to their proximate antidotes,
it should be said that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) are the proximate antidotes to the proliferation of views (*dṛṣṭi-prapañca*).
Because those whose conduct is dominated by hatred have much anger,
joy and equanimity serve as their direct antidotes to the craving for conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Because those whose conduct is dominated by craving are prone to attachment, [joy and equanimity are prescribed].
Some say that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) are the direct antidotes to the conceptual proliferation of craving (*tṛṣṇā*),
while sympathetic joy (*muditā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are the direct antidotes to the conceptual proliferation of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, they are called "immeasurable" because they serve as antidotes for the immeasurable afflictions of heedlessness by universally taking sentient beings as their object.
This means that the four immeasurables can closely counteract the various afflictions of heedlessness belonging to the desire realm.
Furthermore, these four kinds are the vast playgrounds of the noble ones (ārya),
and thus they are called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).
This is just as a wealthy and noble person has immeasurable kinds of vast playgrounds.
This refers to various gardens, groves, palaces, towers, pavilions, and places for hunting and recreation.
Furthermore, these four types [of merit] are called "immeasurable" because they take immeasurable sentient beings as their objects,
generating immeasurable merit and leading to immeasurable results.
These four immeasurables exist within the desire realm and the form realm.
As for their levels, the three—compassion, loving-kindness, and equanimity—reside in seven levels, namely:
the desire realm and the four dhyānas.
Including the preparatory concentration (anāgamya) and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara),
some say it exists in ten stages.
That is to say, the four dhyānas, the four preparatory stages (sāmantaka),
the intermediate dhyāna, and the desire realm.
The immeasurable joy (muditā) exists in these three levels.
Regarding the desire realm and the first two dhyānas,
some other masters say that the first two dhyānas lack the immeasurable of compassion (*karuṇā*). Why is this?
In the first and second dhyānas, there is the superior feeling of joy (*prīti*), which functions with a mode of activity characterized by gladness;
the immeasurable of compassion (*karuṇā*) functions with a mode of activity characterized by sorrow.
If there were [the feeling of] compassion in the first and second dhyānas, [it would be so].
In that case, for there to be both joy (*prīti*) and sorrow (*daurmanasya*) within a single moment of mind would contradict correct principle.
Question: If this is so, how can there be untainted (*anāsrava*) disenchantment (*nirveda*) in the first and second dhyānas?
Answer: Untainted disenchantment is associated with correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) and is not incompatible with joy.
To the extent that one awakens to the true nature of an object,
to that same extent one gives rise to profound joy and consolation; and to the extent that one gives rise to profound joy and consolation regarding the object,
to that same extent one further delights in that awakening.
It is like a person seeking treasure who digs into the earth;
as they dig the earth, so do they obtain various treasures,
and as they obtain the treasures, so do they further rejoice in digging the earth.
Because immeasurable compassion is associated with attention characterized by resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*), it is incompatible with sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
The critique states:
one should speak as follows.
The first and second dhyānas possess the immeasurable state of compassion (*karuṇā-apramāṇa*).
How is this known? Because there is authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*) to that effect.
As stated in the *Samādhiskandha*,
because the first two dhyānas include the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) such as the first two dhyānas, it is known that compassion (*karuṇā*) exists.
This is the basis for these four immeasurables.
It arises only in dependence upon a body belonging to the desire realm.
As for its mode of activity (*ākāra*):
loving-kindness has the mode of activity of bestowing happiness.
Compassion has the characteristic of uprooting suffering;
sympathetic joy has the characteristic of rejoicing and consoling;
equanimity has the characteristic of setting aside.
As for its object of focus:
it takes only the desire realm as its object;
it takes only a collection [of phenomena] as its object.
It has only the combination of conditions as its object;
it has only sentient beings as its object.
That is to say, it takes as its objective sphere sentient beings consisting of the five aggregates or two aggregates within the desire realm.
If sentient beings abide in a mind belonging to their own level, they take those five aggregates as their object;
if sentient beings abide in a mind belonging to another level,
or are without mind, they take those two aggregates as their object.
Some say that the immeasurables of the first dhyāna take sentient beings of the desire realm as their object,
while the immeasurables of the second dhyāna [take those of the form realm as their object].
The immeasurables of the third dhyāna take as their objects sentient beings of the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
[The immeasurables] take as their objects sentient beings of the desire realm and the first two dhyānas.
The immeasurables of the fourth dhyāna take as their objects sentient beings of the desire realm and the three lower dhyānas.
Furthermore, some say that the immeasurables of the first dhyāna [take these same objects].
They take as their objects sentient beings of the desire realm and the first dhyāna;
the immeasurables of the second dhyāna take as their objects sentient beings of the desire realm and the first two dhyānas.

The immeasurables of the third dhyāna take as their objects sentient beings of the desire realm and the three lower dhyānas; the immeasurables of the fourth dhyāna [take as their objects sentient beings of all realms].
It takes as its object sentient beings of the desire realm and the four dhyānas.
Other masters say that the immeasurable of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) takes as its object sentient beings of the desire realm and the lower three dhyānas.
Why is this? Because the immeasurable loving-kindness functions with the characteristic of bestowing happiness,
and it is only in the four stages [of dhyāna] that there is the experience of pleasant feeling.
The immeasurable compassion takes only the desire realm as its object.
Why is this? Because the mode of activity of immeasurable compassion proceeds by way of extracting beings from suffering.
Because there is only the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhā vedanā*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
the immeasurable joy (*muditā-apramāṇa*) takes as its object the desire realm as well as the first and second dhyānas. Why is this so?
The immeasurable joy (*muditā*) functions with the aspect of comforting and rejoicing;
this is because the feeling of joy exists only in the [first] three dhyānas.
The immeasurable equanimity (*upekṣā*) takes the four dhyānas of the desire realm as its object.
Why is this? Because it functions by way of the aspect of relinquishing immeasurable things and setting them aside;
for there is the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) in all stages.
The commentary states:
Among these various explanations, the first is correct;
that is to say, the four [foundations of mindfulness] take only the realm of desire as their object.
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna): these four are associated exclusively with the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
Regarding wisdom (jñāna): these four are associated exclusively with conventional wisdom (saṃvṛtijñāna).
Regarding samādhi:
these four do not coexist with samādhi,
because they are exclusively tainted (sāsrava).
Regarding association with the faculties (*indriya*):
the three—compassion (*karuṇā*), loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—are associated with the three faculties of joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Joy (*prīti*) is entirely not associated with the faculty of feeling (*vedanendriya*).
If one speaks of it together with its associated and concomitant factors,
then joy is also associated with the faculty of joy (*somanasyendriya*).
Regarding those that are past, future, and present:
These four immeasurables all pertain to the three periods of time:
those of the past take the past as their object;
those of the present take the present as their object.
Future dharmas that are subject to arising take as their object future dharmas that are not subject to arising.
As for those that take as their object wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral dharmas of the three time periods,
these four immeasurables are exclusively wholesome and take all three types as their objects.
Regarding those bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm:
these four immeasurables bound to the desire and form realms take only that which is bound to the desire realm as their object.
As for those that are trainee, non-trainee, or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee: [the former two are as described above].
Regarding these four immeasurables, which are exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner and take as their objects only that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner:
among those factors abandoned by seeing, those abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned,
these four immeasurables are abandoned only by cultivation.
Regarding "having as their object that which is abandoned by seeing and cultivation":
these four immeasurables universally take both types [of objects] as their objects— namely, names and meanings.
Regarding those that take one’s own continuum as their object and those that take another’s continuum as their object:

these four immeasurables take only the continuum of others as their object. As for those acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*) and those acquired through the removal of defilements (*vairāgya-labdha*), these four immeasurables encompass both types.

It should be understood that herein, "attainment through detachment from defilement" refers to the attainment of the immeasurables of the first dhyāna by virtue of becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm,
and [likewise] for the immeasurables of the second dhyāna.
The third dhyāna and the immeasurables are attained by becoming free from the defilements of the first dhyāna;
they are attained by becoming free from the defilements of the second dhyāna.
The immeasurables of the fourth dhyāna are attained by becoming free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
or at the time of becoming free from the defilements of one’s own level or a higher level.
Regarding those attained through cultivation and attained through application:
the four immeasurables mostly manifest through application,
whereas the Buddha manifests without application.
Pratyekabuddhas manifest through inferior preparatory application;
Śrāvakas manifest through middling or superior preparatory application;
this is because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are mostly of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*).
Regarding that which has been attained and that which has never been attained before:
these four immeasurables (apramāṇa) both pertain to two types.
They pertain to both types for all noble ones (ārya) as well as for ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) who abide in subsequent existence.
All other ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have only previously obtained [the faculties].
Some say that all noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings who abide within the Dharma (*adhyātma-dharmastha*) possess both types.
External dharmas for ordinary beings are only those previously acquired.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll 81 (from the *Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll 80).
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Two: The Aggregate of Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha), Sub-section Four: The Ten Gates of Summary, Part Twelve. Question: What is the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for these four immeasurables?
Answer: One initiates the preparatory application (prayoga) by taking seven types of sentient beings as the object.
These seven types of sentient beings refer to the categorization of all sentient beings within the desire realm (kāmadhātu) into those who are enemies and those who are kin.
There are three grades within the middle category;
furthermore, the two categories of enemies and kin are each divided into three— namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
Because middle-grade sentient beings are collectively of one kind without distinction,
when practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*) within these seven categories of sentient beings,
one first takes as an object those who are close.
Within the category of relatives, one first takes as an object those of superior degree.
Those who are relatives of superior degree refer to one's own parents, preceptors, and teachers.
Or, toward any other person worthy of respect—
such as a fellow practitioner of the holy life who is wise and learned—
one reflects thus upon a sentient being who is a superior relative.
"How might I cause these classes of sentient beings to obtain such happiness?
Yet their minds are rigid and difficult to subdue,
for they have been habituated to this state since beginningless time.
Toward sentient beings who have been extremely kind, a malicious intention (āśaya) arises spontaneously and grows,
while a virtuous intention, even when intentionally cultivated, cannot remain.
Furthermore, one should exert oneself with vigor to contemplate their profound kindness and restrain the mind so that it remains fixed;
it is like throwing a mustard seed onto the point of an awl—
though it may momentarily adhere, it is difficult for it to stay.
Through long and uninterrupted practice, the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is perfected;
by the power of skillfulness, one is able to direct it and cause it to abide.
Thus, the practitioner [proceeds] with the superior grade.
One should diligently cultivate the intention to bring happiness to one's relatives;
after a long period of time, this becomes firmly established.
Once the intention to bring happiness to superior relatives has become firmly established, [one proceeds further].
Next, one again cultivates such an intention to bestow happiness toward neutral persons.
Once this is accomplished, one next cultivates such an intention to bestow happiness toward inferior friends.
Once this has been accomplished, one next [directs it] toward a person of middling quality,
then toward a minor enemy,
and then toward a middling enemy.
Thereafter, regarding those who were previously enemies,
each cultivates such an intentionality of bestowing happiness;
through gradual cultivation, this reaches the stage of full perfection.
One maintains a continuous flow of the intention to bestow happiness equally upon all sentient beings throughout the desire realm,
just as one would toward a superior relative.
The same applies to the highest level of enmity.
Reaching this point is called the perfection of the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
The sequence for cultivating compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is likewise.
The altruistic intentions of uprooting suffering and of providing consolation are distinct.
What is the altruistic intention of compassion? It is the thought: "How might I cause these sentient beings to be free from such suffering?"
That these classes of sentient beings obtain happiness and are free from suffering—how joyful!
This is the mental attitude of sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
When wishing to cultivate equanimity (*upekṣā*), one first takes the neutral state as the object.
This refers to giving rise to the intention of equanimity toward them,
because it is easiest to abandon those of middling capacity;
one feels affection for those who are close by taking them as an object.
Because anger arises toward enemies,
one first cultivates equanimity toward neutral persons.
Having abandoned the middling resentment,
one next abandons the minor resentment,
and then abandons the middling resentment.
Next, abandon superior enemies;
next, abandon inferior friends;
next, abandon neutral relatives.
Next, one abandons superior relatives. One first abandons one's enemies and subsequently abandons one's relatives,
because it is easier to abandon hatred toward them than the affection one feels for them.
When one has gradually cultivated this until it reaches fulfillment,
one establishes a continuous flow of equanimity toward all sentient beings throughout the desire realm, setting aside all partiality.
Free from discursive discrimination, it is like holding a scale;
regarding sentient beings as one contemplates a forest as a whole—
this is called the culmination of the cultivation of equanimity.
Question: What kind of sentient beings are able to cultivate the immeasurables?
Answer: There are, in brief, two types of sentient beings.
The first are those who seek out the faults of other sentient beings.
Second, one seeks out the virtues of sentient beings;
if one were to seek out their faults,
one would be largely unable to cultivate the four immeasurables.
Why is this? Because even Arhats and others can find faults in them,
for they too had flaws and lapses in the past.
Therefore, we now despise and revile them.
Who could possibly perform acts of benefit for such beings?
If one seeks to find virtue in sentient beings, [one would find none here].
One is largely able to cultivate the four immeasurables. Why is this?
Because even for one who has severed their roots of goodness, it is still possible to seek and attain these virtues.
Because he had extensively cultivated wholesome karma in previous times,
he has now obtained birth in a noble family, possesses a handsome appearance that all delight to behold,
and his speech is majestic and authoritative such that all who hear it receive it with respect.
People who possess wisdom and extensive learning all revere and look up to him;
I should perform deeds of benefit for them.
[The interlocutor] asks: What is the sequence of these four immeasurables?
Is it produced exactly as described, or is there a different sequence?
Some say that it is produced exactly as described.
This means that the yoga practitioner first desires to bring benefit to all sentient beings of the desire realm;
this "desire to bring benefit" is precisely the characteristic of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Therefore, the Buddha taught loving-kindness as the foremost.
Next, regarding the classes of sentient beings in the desire realm, there is the wish to eliminate their decline and suffering;
this elimination of decline and suffering is the very characteristic of compassion (*karuṇā*).
Therefore, the Buddha taught compassion as the second [immeasurable].
Once those sentient beings have obtained benefit and are further freed from decline,
one should next feel joy and consolation toward them;
this feeling of joy and consolation is the characteristic of sympathetic joy (*muditā*).
Therefore, the Buddha taught joy as the third [immeasurable].
Having already produced a sense of celebration and consolation toward sentient beings,
one should next maintain equanimity toward them.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is precisely the characteristic of relinquishment;
therefore, the Buddha taught relinquishment as the fourth.
Thus, the four immeasurables arise as described.

Furthermore, there are those who say that these four immeasurables proceed first with compassion (*karuṇā*), then loving-kindness (*maitrī*), then sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and finally equanimity (*upekṣā*).
This means that the practitioner of yoga first desires to eliminate the misfortunes and afflictions of sentient beings within the desire realm.
Next, one further desires to benefit them;
next, one feels deep joy and consolation toward them;
and finally, one maintains equanimity toward them.
The Venerable Saṅgharakṣita said:
"Compassion and sympathetic joy are mutually restrictive;
if compassion arises first, sympathetic joy will necessarily follow."
Because compassion causes the mind to sink, it must be stimulated by joy;
if joy arises first, compassion will necessarily follow.
Because joy causes the mind to become uplifted, it must be restrained by compassion.
The commentary states:
One should say this:
the four immeasurables do not arise in the manner described.
Why is this? Because practitioners of meditation are born according to their inclinations.
There are practitioners of meditation who first give rise to loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Next, one arouses compassion, then sympathetic joy,
and finally equanimity; to speak at length, there are even practitioners of contemplation who first arouse equanimity,
then sympathetic joy, then compassion, and finally arouse loving-kindness.

There may be those who are indeterminate; among practitioners of meditation, some attain loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and not the others, and so on in detail until some attain equanimity (*upekṣā*) and not the others.
Or there may be those who are indeterminate regarding the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), yet enter them in successive order.
Either entering in reverse order,
or entering in direct order by skipping stages,
or entering in reverse order by skipping stages.

Regarding the supernormal powers, liberations, spheres of mastery, and spheres of totality: if one has not yet produced the immeasurables of the first dhyāna, can one produce the immeasurables of the second dhyāna?
And so on, until: if one has not yet produced the immeasurables of the third dhyāna...
Can one give rise to the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) of the fourth dhyāna?
Some say that one cannot; [others say] the immeasurables of the first dhyāna and the immeasurables of the second dhyāna [cannot arise].
Because they serve as the preparatory gates and the rungs of the ladder for [the immeasurables of] the third dhyāna;
and so on, up to the fact that the immeasurables of the third dhyāna serve as the preparatory gates and the rungs of the ladder for the immeasurables of the fourth dhyāna.
Some say that the practitioner who is capable [of this] may,
if they have attained mastery over a particular stage, first give rise to the immeasurables based on that very stage.
If one can even give rise to the untainted noble path of a higher stage before having given rise to the untainted noble path of a lower stage,
how much more so could one not give rise to the four immeasurables?

Question: Is it faster for the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) of a higher stage to arise after those of a lower stage, or is it faster for the immeasurables of a lower stage to arise after those of a higher stage?
Answer: It is swift for an immeasurable state of a higher level to arise after an immeasurable state of a lower level;
it is not swift for an immeasurable state of a higher level to arise after an immeasurable state of a lower level.
This is like how it is swift to learn the Khaḷuṣṭa script after having learned the Brāhmī script.
One who has not previously studied the Khaḷuṣṭha script but later studies the Brāhmī script quickly becomes proficient.
[The interlocutor] asks: Can one immediately give rise to the immeasurables of the second dhyāna after the immeasurables of the first dhyāna?
Up to the third dhyāna, there are immeasurable moments of uninterrupted transition;
can one immediately give rise to the fourth dhyāna from those immeasurables?
The same question applies when asked according to the reverse order.
Some say that it cannot manifest because one must necessarily cultivate the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of its own level to induce its arising.
Others say that those who have already cultivated it to maturity can also give rise to it through a single application.
Alternatively, there may be no preparatory application (prayoga) capable of traversing the various stages (bhūmi), because immeasurable states arise either above or below.
Question: Can immeasurable compassion (karuṇā-apramāṇa) and so forth arise immediately after immeasurable loving-kindness (maitrī-apramāṇa) and so forth?
The answer is as explained in the *Samādhiskandha*:
"What does one contemplate when entering the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of loving-kindness?
That is to say, contemplating 'may sentient beings be happy,' and so forth, up to: what does one contemplate when entering the meditative attainment of equanimity?"
This refers to the relinquishing of sentient beings.
Some say that this explains the co-emergent aspects of the immeasurables.
Furthermore, there are those who say that he [the Blessed One] taught the immeasurables as immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*);
if one were to say this, they would be saying that he taught the immeasurables as co-arising mental aspects (*sahaja-ākāra*).
The immeasurables such as loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) can immediately give rise to the immeasurables such as compassion (*karuṇā-apramāṇa*).
If one were to say that those [immeasurables] constitute an immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
then the four types of preparatory applications (*prayoga*) of the immeasurables such as loving-kindness could not immediately give rise to the immeasurables such as compassion.
Because each arises subsequently to its own specific preparatory application (*prayoga*),
one should know that attention (*manasikāra*) is, in brief, of three types.
The first is attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*).
Second, attention to common characteristics;
third, attention to resolute conviction.
Regarding attention to specific characteristics:
For example, one may contemplate that earth has the characteristic of solidity,
water has the characteristic of moisture,
and fire has the characteristic of warmth.
Wind has motion as its characteristic.
All such [characteristics] are what is meant by "attention to common characteristics."

For example, there is the attention that arises concomitantly with the sixteen aspects of the noble ones (*ārya*). As for attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika-manasikāra*), it is, for example,

the attention that arises concomitantly with the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Question: Among the three types of attention, with which one do these four immeasurables arise simultaneously?
Answer: They arise only with the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), because they are produced as conceptual constructions (*parikalpita*).

Question: Furthermore, regarding the immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) which intends to bestow happiness upon others—what kind of happiness does it take as its object when bestowing it upon sentient beings?
Regarding this, some say:
Taking as their object the desire for the bliss within the third dhyāna and the bliss of birth and death among sentient beings—
since this [bliss] is the most excellent among them— if one were to say:
"All those who have not yet attained the third dhyāna..."
He would be unable to give rise to the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*).
Some say that he had previously experienced the bliss of the third dhyāna during other lifetimes.
Now, furthermore, relying upon the third dhyāna, one gives rise to the knowledge of recollecting past abodes,
taking as its object sentient beings and their previously experienced desires and pleasures.
If one were to speak thus:

Furthermore, those who have not yet attained the knowledge of past lives (pūrvanivāsajñāna) associated with the third dhyāna would be unable to give rise to the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (maitrī-apramāṇa).
Moreover, there are those who say:
Conditioned by that, he desires to bestow upon sentient beings all the pleasures he has just experienced,
namely: the pleasure of food and drink, or the pleasure of vehicles,
or the pleasure of clothing, or the pleasure of bedding.
Or there are various other kinds of pleasure experienced in the present;
based on these pleasures, one desires to give them to sentient beings.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this as follows:
It takes as its object the aspect of the pleasure experienced by sentient beings,
with the desire that those beings may constantly experience such pleasure.
If one were to say this, then loving-kindness (*maitrī*) would be unable to universally take all sentient beings as its object.
Why is this? It is because not all sentient beings possess happiness.
Furthermore, it is said:
Taking sentient beings as its object, it gives rise to the aspect of the faculty of pleasure,
desiring that sentient beings may constantly experience this pleasure.
If one were to speak thus:
Compassion would then be unable to universally take sentient beings as its object. Why is this?
It is because sentient beings do not exist in all states at all times.
Because the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is constantly present before them,
it is further stated:
they take as their object the food, drink, vehicles, and clothing enjoyed by sentient beings.
And regarding various pleasant conditions such as bedding and requisites,
if one were to say that one wishes for sentient beings to constantly experience such happiness:
Compassion would then be unable to universally take sentient beings as its object. Why is this?
Because not all sentient beings possess such instruments of happiness.
The Venerable One said:
"At the time of the preliminary application, one takes as an object the happiness previously seen in various sentient beings and,
with a mind of compassion, gives rise to the perception of resolute conviction."
He wishes that all sentient beings in the desire realm may equally obtain such articles of pleasure,
and by this cause and condition, may they all experience supreme bliss.
The meaning here is as follows:
various practitioners of yoga, dwelling in forest hermitages near villages or cities,
put on their robes and take up their alms bowls during the first part of the day.
Entering nearby villages and cities to beg for food in accordance with the Dharma,
he saw along his route that all sentient beings were experiencing nothing but supreme happiness,
traveling by means such as elephants, horses, palanquins, and carriages.
Adorned with various jewels, attended by servants and guards, and accompanied by music and hymns of praise,
they enjoy supreme happiness while arraying themselves with incense and flowers;
yet, like the sons of gods, they behold sentient beings undergoing only the most intense suffering.
That is to say, they were without clothing, their hair was disheveled, and their bodies were foul-smelling and filthy;
their hands and feet were cracked and split, and they wandered about begging with broken shards for bowls,
oppressed by the suffering of hunger and poverty like hungry ghosts.
Having seen this, he quickly returned to his dwelling,
gathered his robes, washed his feet, and sat cross-legged,
making his body and mind supple and well-adjusted.
Being free from all hindrances and obscurations,
one possesses the capacity to recollect the suffering and happiness previously experienced; thus,
one gives rise to universal compassion toward all classes of sentient beings.
If one wishes for all sentient beings to experience the supreme happiness that one perceives,
one might ask: since not all sentient beings who are the objects of focus actually attain such happiness,
how is it that the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is not a misconception (*viparyāsa*)?
Answer: Because it is originated from the intention of benefit;
because it is originated from the intention of happiness;
because it is originated from the intention of discipline; and because it is originated from the intention of compassion.
Because it is originated by appropriate attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
because it is associated with roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*),
and because it is associated with shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
Because its intrinsic nature is wholesome;
because it subdues all afflictions;
and because it is far removed from afflictions.
It is not called a perversion.
Furthermore, there are those who say that even if it were called a perversion, there would be no fault.
Question: If it were termed "inverted," it would follow that it is unwholesome.
Answer: There are two kinds of inversion: first, inversion by intrinsic nature; [second, inversion by association].
Second, regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*):
only when both [the subject and the object] possess perversion is it termed unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Although the immeasurable meditation on loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) possesses perversions regarding its object of focus, [it is not unwholesome].
Because it is not a perversion of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viparyāsa*), it is not unwholesome.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this:
although the immeasurable meditation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) cannot cause all sentient beings who are its objects to attain supreme happiness, [it is nevertheless wholesome].
Furthermore, because it takes as its object the various articles of pleasure belonging to those sentient beings, it is not erroneous.
It is further stated:
because it takes as its object the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) of all sentient beings, it is not erroneous.
Furthermore, it is said that because practicing this preparatory application (prayoga) can subdue the entanglement of aversion (dveṣa-paryavasthāna), it is not a perversion (viparyāsa).
The Venerable (Bhadanta) says:
Since this contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is able to counteract the mind of hatred (*dveṣa*), it is not a misconception (*viparyāsa*).

Question: Does this immeasurable loving-kindness take a single sentient being as its object and desire to bestow happiness upon them, or does it take many sentient beings as its object and desire to bestow happiness upon them?
Answer: When first practicing this immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one takes many sentient beings as the object, desiring to grant them happiness;
for one cultivates the mind of loving-kindness by taking sentient beings collectively as the object.
Once it has been fully perfected, it takes as its object either a single being or many beings,
and one is able to bestow happiness upon them with sovereign ease according to one's wish.
Just as this was explained in the analysis of the question-and-answer regarding the immeasurable *maitrī* (loving-kindness), the same should be understood for *karuṇā* (compassion).

As stated in the Sūtra: "Because one has extensively cultivated a mind associated with loving-kindness— free from enmity, free from opposition, free from affliction, and free from harm— that is vast, immeasurable, and well-developed—
one directs the resolute conviction of bestowing happiness, pervasively taking as an object one direction, two directions, three directions, four directions, the zenith, and the nadir."
Whether upright or horizontal, one directs a mind accompanied by loving-kindness toward all sentient beings throughout this world, pervading every part and every place.
"One dwells pervasively, having attained the resolute conviction of bestowing happiness," and so forth, as extensively explained.
Question: This immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) takes all sentient beings as its object.
Why does the Sūtra say "conditioned by one direction" and so forth?
Answer: This Sūtra should have said, "conditioned by sentient beings in the eastern direction and so forth."
As for the statement that [the mind] universally takes one direction as its object and so forth,
this refers to sentient beings by using the term "direction," just as one might point to a vessel to indicate the objects contained within it.
This sutra further states:
"Taking this world as an object, throughout all its parts and in all places,
one directs a mind accompanied by loving-kindness toward all sentient beings."
Regarding "dwelling fully endowed with the resolute conviction of bestowing happiness":
Question— when this immeasurable loving-kindness takes all sentient beings as its object,
does one contemplate them by means of spatial boundaries?
If one observes by way of the limit of sentient beings,
what fault would there be in that?
There are faults in both cases.
Why is this so? If one were to view it through the limits of specific regions,
why does the Sūtra state that this world is conditioned by [the elements] throughout all its parts?
Regarding all sentient beings throughout all places:
if one observes by way of the limit of sentient beings,
why is it that one does not separately perceive a limit to the ocean of sentient beings?
Some say this is observed by way of the boundaries of a region.
Question: If that is so, [what follows]?
If [the opponent] skillfully resolves the objection raised subsequently,
how should one resolve the objection raised previously?
It should be understood that this is what is being stated in response.
"Partial universality.
Regarding the term "all," there are briefly two types:
first, partial universality.
Regarding "all of all," this sutra speaks only of a partial "all"; therefore,
it does not contradict reason.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this is observed from the perspective of the limit of sentient beings.
Question: If that is so, [what follows]?
The previous objection has been successfully resolved;
how, then, should the subsequent objection be resolved?
Answer: Although there is no separate attainment of the limit of sentient beings, [the objection is resolved as follows].
Yet there is a comprehensive attainment of the limit of sentient beings,
just as the four modes of birth encompass all sentient beings;
there is not a single sentient being who is not included within these four modes of birth.
Some say that the Buddha observes by way of the limits of sentient beings,
while others observe by way of the limits of geographical regions.
Other masters say that both Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas observe the limit of sentient beings,
whereas Śrāvakas and ordinary worldlings observe only the limit of geographical regions.
The commentary states:
It should be said that this is not fixed,
because all four immeasurables are conceptual constructs.
All are associated with attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*).
Some observe everything by way of the limit of sentient beings (*sattvānta*),
while others observe everything by way of the limit of the spatial region (*deśānta*).
As the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that for seven years I cultivated a mind of loving-kindness."
During seven cycles of destruction and formation, they do not take birth here.
When the world is being destroyed, they are born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
once the world has been formed, they are born in the Brahma Palace of Emptiness.
He acted as the Great Brahmā King, possessing sovereign majesty and power,
being the sole honored one within a thousand worlds;
yet at a later time, he was reborn in the realm of desire.
Thirty-six times he became Śakra, Lord of the Devas;
for immeasurable eons he was a wheel-turning monarch,
possessing the fourfold army and accomplishing the seven treasures.
Because he governs the world through the Dharma, he is also called the Dharma King.
Regarding the "seven years" mentioned in this sutra,
the Buddha’s intended meaning is precisely seven rainy seasons.
It is said that in a former, superior age, there was a bodhisattva named Mahātejas who reigned as a great king in Central India;
with great majesty and benevolence, he governed and encompassed all.
However, that land was frequently plagued by heat.
Not far from the city there was a great forest;
its ground was high and cool, and its flowers and fruits were lush and abundant.
The trees and grasses are verdant, and the springs and ponds are cool and clear.
During the four months of the rainy season,
the people of that country mostly abandon their cities and towns to come here to escape the heat.
Each performed various activities according to their own inclinations.
At that time, the Bodhisattva King entrusted the affairs of state and the various cities and towns to his great ministers,
and he himself went to this forest to dwell in a high and quiet place.
Free from the defilements of the desire realm,
he cultivated the four immeasurables throughout the four months of the rainy season without ever becoming lax or negligent.
Once the rainy period had passed and the seasonal air gradually turned cool,
The people in the forest each returned to their respective cities and towns to attend to their various affairs.
At that time, the Bodhisattva also emerged from the forest and proceeded to the royal capital to establish a great Dharma sacrifice.
He extensively cultivated the merit of giving through various foods and drinks,
clothing, incense and flowers, elephants, horses, carriages and litters,
houses, servants, lamps, and bedding.
And he offered medicine and other necessities to śramaṇas,
as well as to brahmins, the poor, the sick, the solitary,
travelers, guests, and all who came seeking alms.
Having practiced giving, he maintained the pure precepts;
thus he traveled back and forth six times.
On his seventh journey, it was past the end of the rainy season.
Some say that at the end of their life they are reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; others say this.
When the time for the kalpa of destruction arrives, the Bodhisattva passes away and is reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; therefore,
we know that "seven years" refers to seven periods of the rainy season.
Question: The four immeasurable concentrations (apramāṇa-samādhi) cultivated by Bodhisattvas belong to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
On this basis, they may be reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven or among the Brahmā deities.
How, then, can they also become Śakra or a Universal Monarch (cakravartin)?
How could karma of the form realm (rūpadhātu) bring about a fruit in the desire realm (kāmadhātu)?
Answer: At that time, the Bodhisattva gives rise to the three immeasurables (traya-apramāṇa), one of which is bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
By this, one becomes Śakra or a Universal Monarch (cakravartin).
Second, those bound to the first dhyāna:
by this, one becomes Mahābrahmā.
Third, it is bound to the second dhyāna;
by means of this, one is born among the Ābhāsvara devas.
Furthermore, although the fundamental immeasurables do not exist in the desire realm, [they are present here].
There are, however, immeasurable states of mind involved in entering and emerging from meditative absorption;
these bring about the karmic maturation of a Wheel-Turning King or Śakra.
The fundamental immeasurables, on the other hand, induce rebirth in the Ābhāsvara Heaven or as a Great Brahmā King.
Furthermore, although the desire realm lacks ultimate immeasurability,
it possesses preparatory application; by means of this,
one may become Śakra or a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Ultimately, the immeasurable [roots] can lead to rebirth as a Brahmā king or in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Furthermore, the desire realm possesses all the seeds that resemble wholesome roots;
even the semblance of the meditative attainment of cessation exists there due to the presence of immeasurable similar wholesome roots.
One may become a wheel-turning monarch or Śakra, Lord of the Devas;
by virtue of possessing immeasurable and genuine roots of goodness,
one may be born in the Brahma Heaven or the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Furthermore, because the bodhisattva cultivates the immeasurables within the groves,
he is reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven or becomes a Brahmā King.
Returning to his royal capital, he establishes a great assembly for giving and becomes a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
By upholding the precepts, one becomes Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
Furthermore, this sutra speaks of three bases of meritorious action:
namely, generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation.
As it is said in that sutra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know:
I recall having performed three kinds of karma in the past, which resulted in three kinds of fruits."
By means of these, we now possess great majesty and virtue—
namely, generosity, self-discipline, and tranquility.
Generosity is precisely the meritorious action of giving.
Subduing is the meritorious action of ethical discipline;
tranquility is the meritorious action of cultivation;
the meritorious action of giving can bring about the state of a wheel-turning monarch.
The meritorious deed of observing the precepts brings about rebirth as Śakra,
Lord of the Devas; the meritorious deed of cultivating merit brings about rebirth as Mahābrahmā or in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
As stated in the Sūtra,
there are three kinds of meritorious actions:
first, meritorious action consisting of giving (*dāna-maya-puṇyakriyāvastu*).
That is to say, one offers food, drink, clothing, incense, flowers—
and as extensively explained, even including medicine and so forth—
to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others.
Second, the category of meritorious action consisting of the nature of the precepts,
namely: abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given,
and abstaining from sexual misconduct.
Abstaining from false speech,
abstaining from drinking intoxicants, and so forth—
these are the three types of meritorious actions consisting of cultivation.
That is to say, a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—
free from enmity, free from hostility, free from malice, and free from harm—
as explained in detail previously.
The detailed explanation for the minds associated with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity is likewise.
Question: Since there are many roots of goodness in the form and formless realms, why are only these four immeasurables mentioned?
Is it for the sake of cultivating meritorious actions of the nature of cultivation?
Answer: In the world, the notion of "meritorious action" arises only with respect to deeds that benefit others;
[this is not the case] among the various wholesome roots of the form and formless realms.
Because there is no desire to benefit others as there is in the four immeasurables,
this is specifically taught as the practice for cultivating meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, the world conceives the notion of "merit" regarding the fruits of merit.
Among all roots of goodness, there is none that can produce such vast and abundant beneficial results as these immeasurables;
therefore, they are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, regarding these four immeasurables and the fruits they attain:
Because it is firm and difficult to destroy, it alone is called "merit.
As a gāthā says:
"Merit cannot be burned by fire, Nor can it be shattered by the wind."
Merit cannot be rotted by water; it can purify and sustain the world.
Merit can courageously resist kings and thieves, and cannot be plundered by humans or non-humans.
Merit never suffers loss; like a firm and secure treasure-trove, it will certainly bring about happiness in this life and in future lives.
One might ask: does non-merit likewise not burn away like fire? [The answer follows: No, it does not.
Why is it that only merit (*puṇya*) is mentioned here?
The answer is: although non-merit (*apuṇya*) is not burned by fire and so forth, the fruit of non-merit is destroyed by fire and other such factors.
The four immeasurables of merit and their resulting fruits cannot be destroyed by fire or other elements in the past, future,
or present, as stated in the sūtras.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If among the disciples of Sunetra there were anyone who was completely and in every way perfected in all the training rules (śikṣāpada), [they would be such as this]."
Upon the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in the Brahma-world.
As for those who have fulfilled all aspects of every training rule (śikṣāpada) without exception,
upon the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn either in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Some are born in the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations;
some are born in the Tuṣita Heaven;
and some are born in the Yāma Heaven.
Some are born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
some are born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;
and some are born into great kṣatriya families.
They may be born into a great brahmin family,
or into a great householder family,
or into any other family of great wealth and nobility.
He is born into such noble and eminent families,
where wealth and treasures abound and storehouses overflow;
he possesses a great lineage and numerous kinsmen, servants, attendants, and laborers, as well as elephants, horses, carriages, and palanquins.
He constantly experiences happiness.
[The interlocutor] asks:
"If that is so, then Sunetra should be superior to the World-Honored One."
Why is this? Because disciples of Subhūti who have perfectly fulfilled the various points of training will be reborn in the Brahma world.
Those who have not perfected the unwholesome are reborn in the six heavens of the desire realm,
or are born among human beings to experience wealth, nobility, and happiness.
As for the disciples of the World-Honored One regarding the various precepts:
Is it not logical that those who fully cultivate what is wholesome are reborn in the heavens and attain liberation,
while those who fully cultivate what is unwholesome fall into the evil realms and undergo intense suffering?
Answer: One should not attempt to measure the Sublime Eye by means of the Buddha. Why is this?
Because even among the disciples of the Buddha, there are those who are most lowly and small.
This means that even the fruit of stream-entry possesses such sublime vision,
let alone other venerable ones;
furthermore, this was already so when the Blessed One was formerly in the stage of a bodhisattva.
He acted as a teacher of brahmins and was named Sunetra (Wonderful Eye).
One should not compare him with the Blessed One.
Question: Is it that the Bodhisattva was superior when he was still a seeker, and only became so after attaining Buddhahood?
The answer is that it is not because they surpass the Buddha, but rather due to a specific intention:
namely, that those with excellent eyes delight in cultivating the Brahma-abodes,
and their disciples seek rebirth in the Brahma-world.
Therefore, he reveals the method for cultivating the Brahma-abodes (brahmavihāra).
Among his disciples, those who delight in cultivating the Brahma-abodes and have already perfected the arising of these abodes—
When his body perishes at the end of life, he is reborn in the Brahma-world.
Among his disciples, those who delight in cultivating the Brahma-abodes (brahmavihāra),
if they have not yet perfected them, shall give rise to the Brahma-abodes.
At the dissolution of the body and the end of life, according to the extent of their merit,
they will be reborn among the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm,
or among the noble and eminent families of the human realm, where they will experience great happiness.

Furthermore, even those of superior time whose people are entirely virtuous and who do not cultivate immeasurable roots of goodness through applied practice are still born among gods and humans to experience happiness;
how much more so for those who do cultivate immeasurable roots of goodness through applied practice— would they not be born among gods and humans to experience happiness?
For the sake of his disciples attaining nirvāṇa,
the Buddha established the training rules of the Prātimokṣa discipline;
if there is a disciple who does not violate the discipline and does not break the training rules.
If one does not transgress the rules, one does not overstep the boundaries.

Such a person attains rebirth in heaven and realizes liberation. However, if a disciple violates the code of discipline (*vinaya*) and breaks the precepts (*śikṣāpada*), they transgress the rules and overstep the boundaries.
Having passed away, he fell into the various evil destinies.
Among the disciples of Sunetra, some had fully cultivated and others had not fully cultivated the trainings of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
Among the disciples of the Blessed One, [there were those who had likewise cultivated] the trainings of the Prātimokṣa vows.
There are those who hold [wrong views] and those who commit [transgressions]; therefore, they should not be compared with the Buddha.
Furthermore, that sutra states:
At that time, Sunetra had this thought:
"I should not now be born in the same place as my disciples;
I should cultivate the supreme loving-kindness and be reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven."
Having formed this thought,
he quickly cultivated the second dhyāna of the supreme immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*).
At the end of his life there, he was reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Question: Since the Bodhisattva Sublime Eye is already close to the stage of Buddhahood, he must certainly be free from the two forms of stinginess—regarding material wealth and the Dharma.
For what reason does he personally cultivate the second dhyāna and the supreme immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) to be born in that higher heaven?
He teaches only the first dhyāna and the four brahmavihāras to his disciples in order to cause them to be born in the Brahma world.
The answer is: because he observes what is appropriate to the faculties of those disciples, he teaches only the first dhyāna to them.
Furthermore, those disciples were brahmins who,
throughout the long night, had set their minds upon and aspired to the Brahma-world; therefore,
he taught them only the causes for rebirth in the Brahma-world.

Furthermore, when there is no Buddha in the world, there is no one capable of giving rise to the latter three dhyānas or the various immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas who are proximate to the stage of Buddhahood.
Question: The immeasurables of the higher stages are more luminous, pure, excellent, and sublime than those of the lower stages. Why is this?
Why is the second dhyāna called "superior loving-kindness" (*adhimātra-maitrī*)?
Answer: It is designated as superior in comparison to the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, it surpasses the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) cultivated by its disciples.
Therefore, it is called "supreme loving-kindness" (*maitrī*).
Furthermore, because that which is cultivated by Sublime Eye (*Sudarśana*) has never been attained before and surpasses what was previously attained, it is called "supreme loving-kindness.
Moreover, when there is no Buddha in the world, there is no one capable of giving rise to the latter three dhyānas or the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
Only those with excellent eyes can give rise to the immeasurables of the second dhyāna;
therefore, they are called "superior.
For this reason, the Venerable Ghosaka said:
Ordinary beings lack the capacity to give rise to the various immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) of the three higher stages;
however, by the power of the Buddha’s teaching, the disciples of the Blessed One are also able to give rise to them.
Question: For what reason are the immeasurables called "Brahma-abodes" (*brahmavihāra*)?
Answer: Because the Brahma-world is present at the beginning and possesses [all factors] there.
That is to say, although the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna) occurs at the very outset, it does not possess them all, because it lacks joy (prīti).
Although the second dhyāna possesses [these qualities], it is not the primary locus;
the higher stages lack them entirely.
Only the first dhyāna is the abode of the Brahmā gods.
They are called "Brahma-abodes" (brahmavihāra) because they possess [these qualities] from the very beginning.
Furthermore, they are called Brahma-abodes because they counteract that which is non-Brahma;
"non-Brahma" refers precisely to the afflictions of the desire realm.
In the first dhyāna, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy,
and equanimity are called the "Brahma-abodes" (brahmavihāra) because they serve as the direct antidotes to their opposites.
Furthermore, they are called Brahma-abodes because they counteract non-celibacy (abrahmacarya).
Non-Brahma-conduct refers to sexual activity.
Within the first dhyāna, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity serve as the immediate antidotes to that;
therefore, they are called the Brahma-abodes (brahmavihāra).
Furthermore, because they can be attained within the bodies of those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*),
they are called "Brahma-abodes" (*brahmavihāra*).
Furthermore, "Brahma" refers to the World-Honored One’s loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
They are called Brahma-abodes because they are established by the Buddha.
Furthermore, "Brahma" refers to the Brahma-voice—compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—as taught in the Brahma-voice;
therefore, they are called Brahma-abodes.
Furthermore, by practicing these four kinds [of immeasurables], one attains birth in the Brahma-heaven;
because one becomes a Great Brahma King, they are called the "Brahma-abodes" (*brahmavihāra*).
Moreover, among the merits of Brahma, the four immeasurables are the most excellent and most venerable.
Therefore, they are called the "Brahma Abodes.
Question: What is the distinction between these immeasurable Brahma Abodes?
Some offer this explanation:
There is no distinction;
that is to say, the four Brahmavihāras are themselves the four immeasurables (apramāṇa).
Furthermore, there are those who say:
There is also a distinction;
that is to say, the name itself constitutes the distinction.
This name refers to the "Brahma-abodes."
They are called "immeasurable" because of their name.
Furthermore, they are called "Brahma-abodes" (brahmavihāra) because they counteract what is non-Brahma-like;
they are called "immeasurable" because they counteract conceptual proliferation (prapañca).
Furthermore, that which counteracts non-celibacy is called the Brahma-abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
That which counteracts the practice of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is called the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
Furthermore, the body of one who practices celibacy may be designated as the Brahma-abode.
Within the body of one who has departed from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it may be termed "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).
Furthermore, that which counteracts lack of faith is called a "Brahma-abode" (*brahmavihāra*);
that which counteracts negligence is called "immeasurable."
Furthermore, those who abide in the Brahma-world are called "Brahma-abodes.
Those who abide in the higher stages are called "immeasurables.
Furthermore, those who abide in the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*) and the Brahma-world are called "Brahma-abodes."
Those on the higher stages are called "immeasurable.
Furthermore, those in the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*) and the Brahma-world are called "Brahma-abodes" (*brahmavihāra*),
and they are also called "immeasurable."
Those on the higher stages are designated merely as "immeasurables" (apramāṇa).
Furthermore, those previously attained are called "Brahma-abodes" (brahmavihāra),
while those not yet attained are called "immeasurables."
Furthermore, that which is attained by those within our own tradition is called both a "Brahma-abode" (*brahmavihāra*) and "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*);
whereas that which is attained by outsiders is called only a "Brahma-abode."
Furthermore, that which is acquired in common is called the "Brahma-abodes" (brahmavihāra);
that which is not acquired in common is called the "Immeasurables" (apramāṇa).
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
The Brahma-abodes are common,
for both ordinary worldlings and noble ones compete for these dharmas;
the immeasurables are uncommon.
Because noble ones and ordinary beings do not compete for this dharma,
the immeasurables of the Brahma-abodes are said to be their distinction.
The Buddha taught that there are four types of persons who can generate Brahma-merit.
What are the four? They are as follows:
there is a certain class of person who, at a place where a stūpa has never been established, [proceeds to establish one].
To erect a stūpa for the relics of a Buddha—
this is called the first type of person who can generate Brahma-merit.
Furthermore, there is another class of persons.
To establish a monastery for the disciples of the Buddha in a place where no monastery has previously been founded—
this is called the second type of person who can generate Brahma-merit.
Furthermore, there is another class of person who,
having seen the community of the Buddha’s disciples already divided, brings them back into harmony;
this is called the third kind of person capable of generating Brahma-merit.
Furthermore, there is another class of person who cultivates the four divine abodes;
this is called the fourth type of person capable of generating Brahma-merit.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"Not all such sūtras were spoken by the Buddha;
furthermore, among these, not all three [types of persons] produce Brahma-merit."
Because the fruits obtained by them are not similar;
that is to say, if there is a person who [is born] in the place where a Buddha was born or in the place where he attained enlightenment.
At the place where the Wheel of Dharma was turned and at the place of Parinirvāṇa,
he erected great stūpas adorned with various precious jewels.
Furthermore, there are others who, in various places,
gather sand, gravel, and other materials to construct small caityas.
How could the merit produced by those two possibly be similar?
Furthermore, suppose there is someone who,
as a disciple of the Buddha, constructs a monastery that is lofty, vast, and magnificently adorned.
Just as there are places such as the Jeta Grove, the Bamboo Grove, the Great Forest, and the Andhavana Monastery,
there are also other people who,
as disciples of the Buddha, have established small monasteries (saṃghārāma) according to their means.
How could the merit produced by those two possibly be similar?
Furthermore, suppose there is someone who causes the monastic community split by Devadatta to be reconciled once again.
Furthermore, there are others who are able to skillfully pacify the disputes and quarrels of the Saṃgha, such as those involving Kauśāmbī;
how could the merit produced by those two possibly be similar?
Therefore, one should know that not all those sūtras were spoken by the Buddha,
nor does everything therein produce Brahma-merit.
It is the *Catubrahmavihāra-sūtra* that was spoken by the Buddha.
These four divine abodes are all Brahma-merit.
The Abhidharma masters state that such sūtras were all spoken by the Buddha.
Among these, all four types generate Brahma-merit.
Question: Is the fruit obtained from them similar?
Answer: Because the purpose for which they are performed is equal, they all generate Brahma-merit.
That is to say, at a site where no stūpa has previously been established,
one erects a stūpa for the Blessed One, the True Great Brahmā;
whether large or small, such an act generates Brahma-merit.
In places where no monastery has previously been established,
to build a monastery for the disciples of the Buddha who practice the holy life—
whether large or small— generates the merit of Brahma.
Once the community of the Buddha’s disciples, whether large or small, has been divided,
they can no longer practice the pure holy life together;
if they are reconciled, they may once again practice the pure holy life together.
Therefore, those who engage in such harmonious association all generate Brahma-merit;
since their purpose is identical,
they are included within the first three [categories].
Although the specific actions differ, the merit is no different.
Furthermore, because they equally provide benefit and so forth, all produce Brahma-merit;
this is just as one cultivates the immeasurables with the desire to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
In this way, at places where a stūpa has not yet been established,
one should erect a stūpa for the relics of the Buddha;
this also brings benefit to immeasurable sentient beings.
This means that at this place,
immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings offer worship with various articles of offering, such as fragrant flowers, precious banners, flags, canopies, and musical performances.
From this, one gives rise to wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind;
or one is born into a noble family with abundant wealth and treasures,
possessing a handsome appearance that is beloved and respected by all.
Possessing the seeds of supreme excellence and great majestic power—
