whether they be the seeds of universal monarchs, Śakra the Lord of Devas, or Māra;
or the seeds of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhi of Buddhas.
In this way, he benefits immeasurable sentient beings;
just as he practices the immeasurables out of a desire to benefit immeasurable sentient beings, so too,
there was no place yet established for a saṃghārāma.
He establishes a monastery for the sake of the Buddha’s disciples and also for the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings;
that is to say, at this place there are countless hundreds of thousands of classes of sentient beings.
They offer and provide various requisites, such as food, drink, bedding, seats,
and medicinal supplies, for a period of one day, or seven days, or half a month, or a full month.
Whether for five years or continuously,
one thereby gives rise to wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind.
For this reason, the community of the Buddha’s disciples upholds,
recites, studies, contemplates, and explains the words and meanings of the Tripitaka;
they cultivate the contemplation of impurity, or maintain mindfulness of breathing, or practice the individual and general foundations of mindfulness.
Or, through the stages of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas, they enter into right determination,
attain the fruits [of the path], and reach the exhaustion of outflows.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, they cause their donors and others to be born into noble clans.
To speak at length, up to and including:
they may plant the seeds of the enlightenment of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or buddhas.
In this way, they bring benefit to immeasurable sentient beings.
Just as one cultivates the immeasurables out of a desire to benefit immeasurable sentient beings,
so too does this harmonious assembly of the Buddha’s disciples act for the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings.
That is to say, after the Sangha has been split,
one should enter the path of vision, attain the fruits, and exhaust the outflows;
one should uphold, recite, contemplate, and explain the words and meanings of the Tripitaka.
Dwelling in an araṇya, one will not achieve any of the wholesome qualities such as the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) or mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti). Furthermore,
one will be unable to plant the seeds of the enlightenment of the three vehicles (triyāna-bodhi).
Because of this, the Wheel of Dharma did not turn in this trichiliocosm;
even among the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, divergent thoughts arose.
It was only when the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples was restored to harmony that [the wheel turned].
They are able to accomplish everything, from entering the path of vision and attaining the fruits until the exhaustion of outflows, up to planting the seeds for the three vehicles.
By this means, the Wheel of Dharma was turned once again throughout this trichiliocosm;
even among the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, no divergent thoughts arose.
In this way, immeasurable sentient beings were benefited.
Because they bring benefit and so forth, all such acts generate Brahma-merit.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this:
"If it is a site where a stūpa has never before been established..."
One erects a stūpa for the relics of the Buddha.
Through four causes and conditions, one can generate Brahma-merit.
First, because one relinquishes great wealth through vast intentions and vows.
Second, it causes immeasurable sentient beings to plant roots of goodness;
third, it brings all undertakings of virtue to ultimate completion;
fourth, it establishes the treasury of the Tathāgata’s body-relics.
If a monastery has never been established at a site before,
and one builds a monastery for the disciples of the Buddha,
it can generate brahma-merit through four causes and conditions.
First, because they renounce abundant wealth through vast thoughts and vows;
second, because they cause immeasurable sentient beings to plant roots of goodness;
and third, because all the virtuous undertakings they have initiated reach ultimate completion.
Fourth, he causes the community of the Buddha’s disciples, who lack a basis for reliance,
to obtain a basis for relying upon as they cultivate wholesome deeds;
furthermore, he reconciles the Sangha once it has been divided.
Brahma-merit can be generated through four causes and conditions:
first, by abandoning the four types of verbal misconduct;
second, by undertaking the four types of verbal excellence.
Third, because it destroys what is contrary to the Dharma;
fourth, because it establishes the True Dharma.
If there are those who cultivate the four immeasurables...
Brahma-merit can be generated through four causes and conditions:
first, by being free from both aversion and attachment;
second, by abandoning all hindrances.
Third, because one attains the fruit of Brahma;
fourth, because one is bound to Brahma.
By these four kinds, all produce Brahma-merit.
Question: What is the measure of these four merits of Brahmā?
Some say: it is the karma that can bring about the fruit of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).
This is defined as the measure of one Brahma-merit.
Other masters say that it is the karma capable of bringing about the fruit of Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
This is defined as the measure of a single Brahma-merit (*brahmapuṇya*).
Some say that it is the karma capable of bringing about the superior fruit of the king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods.
This is defined as the measure of a single Brahma-merit.
Furthermore, some say that it is any karma capable of bringing about the fruit of a Brahmā King.
This is defined as the measure of a single Brahma-merit (*brahmapuṇya*).
Alternatively, some say that when the world is forming, all sentient beings—
The karma capable of producing a world as its dominant fruit (adhipatiphala)—
up to this point, it is called a single measure of Brahma-merit (brahmapuṇya).
Others further state:
Excluding the wholesome karma of bodhisattvas who are close to the stage of Buddhahood,
the karma of all other sentient beings capable of summoning the sovereign fruit of wealth—
this is defined as the measure of one Brahma-merit (*brahmapuṇya*).
There is another explanation:
it is the Brahma-merit obtained when Mahābrahmā first requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma.
This is defined as the measure of a single Brahma-merit (*brahmapuṇya*).
Question: At what time does the Brahmā King obtain this Brahma-merit?
Regarding this, some say:
When he first resolves to go and invite the Buddha,
at that very moment he attains the merit of Brahmā.
His teacher should not speak in such a manner.
If one were to speak in this way,
one would obtain merit even without having performed the action.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
When one formally invites the Buddha, this Brahma-merit is obtained;
yet that person should not speak in such a manner,
for at the time of formally inviting the Buddha, the mind is of the desire realm and is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
If the unobscured-neutral [karma] lacks a ripening fruit, how can it be called "Brahma-merit"?
One should explain it thus:
after the Great Brahma King had invited the Buddha, he returned to his Brahma palace.
Thereafter, the World-Honored One turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma;
the assembly of five bhikṣus and eighty thousand devas all attained the vision of the Truths.
The proclamation of the gods resounded throughout, reaching as far as the Brahma Palace.
Upon hearing this, Brahmā King rejoiced and leaped for joy,
thinking to himself:
"It is because I requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma."
"Having brought benefit to infinite classes of sentient beings,
I have completed what was to be done by me; only then,
O Brahmā King, does one obtain the merit of Brahmā."
The commentary states:
These various explanations regarding the measure of a "Brahma-merit" (brahma-puṇya) are all intended as praises of this Brahma-merit.
Although this has not been described according to its actual reality,
the merit of Brahmā is in fact immeasurable and boundless, for it is produced by a vast volition.
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-mahāvibhāṣā*, Fascicle Eighty-two.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Eighty-three,
composed by five hundred great Arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section Four of the Thirteen Sub-sections of the Second Chapter on the Aggregates of the Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha), according to the Sūtras.
One who dwells in the meditative concentration of loving-kindness cannot be harmed by swords, poisons, water, or fire;
they will certainly meet their end without encountering calamities or misfortunes.
Question: Why is this so?
Venerable Vasumitra explains it thus:
because the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) is a dharma that is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*).
Furthermore, it is said:
because the power of the samādhi of loving-kindness is great,
it is further stated as follows.
The samādhi of loving-kindness benefits others,
for all devas and benevolent spirits provide protection;
thus it is further said:
The sphere of those who cultivate meditative concentration is the realm of meditative concentration;
the sphere of those endowed with supernormal powers is the realm of supernormal powers,
for their majestic power is inconceivable.
Furthermore, it is said:
one who dwells in the meditative concentration of loving-kindness gives rise to a mind of superior grade,
for death and birth do not occur with a mind of non-superior grade.
The Venerable One said:
"If one dwells in the concentration of loving-kindness,
the primary elements of the form realm arise pervading the entire body."
It causes the body that serves as its basis to become as firm and dense as stone;
therefore, it cannot be harmed.
Question: Can the meditative absorptions of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) be harmed?
If it were subject to harm,
why is it that while the meditative concentrations of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) are included among the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) together with compassion (*karuṇā*),
sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), only the concentration of loving-kindness is said to be indestructible?
If they cannot be harmed, why does the sutra not state this?
One should respond by saying:
the meditative absorptions of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are likewise incapable of being harmed.
Question: If that is so, why does this sutra not state it?
Answer: That which ought to be stated but is not stated—[is as follows].
One should know that this meaning is incomplete. Furthermore,
since the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) has been explained,
it should be understood that the concentrations of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are likewise explained, as their categories are identical.
Furthermore, the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) comes first.

If one speaks of the concentration of loving-kindness, it should be understood that the concentrations of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) have already been spoken of.
Moreover, although one who dwells in the concentrations of compassion and the others cannot be harmed, [the following applies].
When emerging from concentration, the body experiences slight suffering;
this is not the case for the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), and therefore it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, although one dwelling in concentrations such as compassion (*karuṇā*) cannot be harmed, the skin may still be damaged.
The meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) is not like this;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned. Furthermore, although the roots of compassion and the others cannot be harmed, they can be injured during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is not like this; therefore, it is mentioned specifically.

It is heard that there was once a person who, although he had attained the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the loving-kindness concentration (*samādhi*) of the desire realm, violated the royal law and was seized by the judicial officials and brought before the king.
He addressed the king, saying,
"This man has committed a crime deserving of death.
At that time, the king was riding an elephant, intending to go out of the city for a stroll.
Having seen this, he dispatched men to examine the king’s laws.
They learned that according to the law, the king ought to kill the offender with his own hand.
The king then became greatly enraged and struck him with a spear.
Upon seeing this, the man immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness;
he caused the spear he was hurling to turn back toward the king and,
before it had gone far from him, it fell to the ground.
The king, seeing this, was struck with fear and asked the culprit,
"What sorcery do you possess that enables you to perform such a deed?
The man replied, "I have no special sorcery."
Seeing that the king was angry, he gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*),
whereby the man with the evil intent was unable to cause him harm.
Consequently, the king apologized and released him.
From this, it is known that the application of the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is likewise indestructible;
this is not the case for compassion (*karuṇā*) and the others, as stated in the Sūtra:
"The cultivation of loving-kindness eliminates hatred."
Cultivating compassion eliminates harm;
cultivating sympathetic joy eliminates discontent;
cultivating equanimity eliminates attachment and aversion.
Question: Since it has been stated that both loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) counteract hatred (*vyāpāda*), what is the distinction between the forms of hatred they counteract?
Answer: Loving-kindness counteracts the hatred that involves taking life.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the antidote to anger toward those who strike one;
furthermore, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the antidote to anger toward those for whom it is appropriate,
while equanimity is the antidote to anger toward those for whom it is inappropriate.
Question: Do the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) have the power to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*)?
If they can sever them, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Samādhiskandha*?
As it is said that loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity cannot sever the fetters—
if they cannot sever them,
how is this sūtra to be reconciled?
It is agreed that one should speak thus:
"The immeasurable cannot sever all afflictions.
Question: If that is so, [what then...]
It is well-established by what is taught in the *Samādhiskandha*.
How, then, should one interpret what is taught in this sutra?
The answer is: there are two kinds of abandonment.
First, temporary abandonment;
second, ultimate abandonment.
Based on temporary abandonment, this sutra speaks of "being able to abandon."
Based on the definitive abandonment of the aggregates, it is said that they are not abandoned;
thus, both the scriptural and treatise-based explanations are well-reconciled,
just as there are [the concepts of] temporary abandonment and ultimate abandonment.
In this way, there is that which has fragments and that which is fragmentless;
that which has shadow-fragments and that which is shadowless-fragmented;
that which has remnants and that which is without remnants.
There is abandonment with residual bondage and abandonment without residual bondage;
there is abandonment by severing parts and abandonment without severing parts;
there is abandonment through suppression and abandonment by uprooting.

It should be understood that the same applies to the abandonment of the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) through their suppression, and the abandonment of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) through their destruction.
Question: If the four immeasurables do not sever the afflictions, how then should one reconcile what is said in other sūtras?
For example, it says: "O Bhikṣus..."
One cultivates the concentration of loving-kindness;
if one does not progress further and abides in the fruit of non-returning, and so on,
as explained at length, up until the cultivation of the concentration of equanimity.
It should be understood that this is likewise the case.
The answer is that in those sūtras, the Noble Path is designated by names such as "the meditative concentration of loving-kindness" (*maitrī-citta-samādhi*),
just as the Buddha [designates] the Noble Path in various sūtras.
Some describe it as perception (saṃjñā), some as feeling (vedanā),
and some as volition (cetanā).
Some describe it as the mind;
some describe it as a lamp;
and some describe it as faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Some describe it as a boat or raft;
some describe it as mountain rocks;
others describe it as water lilies.
Each point is supported by scriptural citations as explained elsewhere;
that sūtra is likewise,
for it employs terms such as "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*) with reference to the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Nor does this contradict reason.
Furthermore, for those seeking the four Brahma-abodes such as loving-kindness who have abandoned the defilement of desire—
whether they be ordinary worldlings or noble ones— [this applies].
If an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) has previously attained the meditative absorptions of loving-kindness and so forth by becoming detached from the defilements of desire,
and later enters into the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) to realize the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmin);
yet, if at that earlier time they had not completely become detached from the defilements of the desire realm.
At a later time, they enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
realizing the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) or the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*).
That they subsequently realize the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*) is due to the power of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].
If an noble one, when becoming free from the defilement of desire,
attains the meditative absorptions of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth, as well as the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*),
it is on this basis that it is said that by cultivating the meditative absorptions of loving-kindness and so forth, one attains the fruit of non-returner.
Nor does this contradict reason,
as it is said in the Sūtra:
"The cultivation of the contemplation of impurity can sever sensual desire."
The cultivation of the immeasurable equanimity also severs sensual desire and greed.
What is the distinction between these two?
Answer: The cultivation of the meditation on impurity serves as the antidote to sensual desire and greed.
One cultivates the immeasurable equanimity as the antidote for attachment to objects.
Furthermore, one cultivates the contemplation of impurity as the antidote for attachment to color,
and cultivates the immeasurable equanimity as the antidote for attachment to shape.
Furthermore, one cultivates the contemplation of impurity as an antidote to craving for subtle touch;
one cultivates the immeasurable equanimity as an antidote to craving for physical demeanor.
Furthermore, one cultivates the contemplation of impurity as an antidote to craving for physical form.
Cultivating the immeasurable equanimity serves as the antidote to attachment toward sentient beings;
this is what constitutes the distinction.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
One cultivates the enlightenment factor of mindfulness together with loving-kindness,
based on seclusion and based on dispassion.
It relies on cessation and is dedicated toward equanimity.
The same threefold explanation applies to compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity as well.
Question: The immeasurables are with outflows (sāsrava), while the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are without outflows (anāsrava).
How can that which is with outflows and that which is without outflows coexist?
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated:
"By means of the four immeasurables, one subdues the mind,
making it upright and pliable."
Immediately following this, the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are induced;
immediately following the factors of enlightenment, the immeasurables (apramāṇa) are induced;
and the immeasurables and the factors of enlightenment arise in mutual intermingling.
Therefore, they are said to be "conjoined," yet in reality they do not coexist simultaneously.
Question: Among the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), which is the most excellent?
Some offer this explanation:
Loving-kindness is the most supreme. Why is this?
Because it cannot be harmed.
Other masters say that compassion (*karuṇā*) is the most excellent. Why is this?
Because the Buddha, out of great compassion,
has taught the True Dharma,
some say that joy is the most supreme.
Why is this? Because it severs non-delight.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Equanimity is supreme.
Why is this? Because it severs both greed and hatred.
The Venerable One said:
"Renunciation is most excellent due to two causes and conditions:
first, by what is performed."
That is to say, if one cultivates equanimity (*upekṣā*), one can sever both greed and hatred.
Second, it is by way of tranquility (*śānti*),
meaning that [the mind] proceeds without conceptual differentiation (*avikalpa*) toward sentient beings.
Therefore, he abandons the most excellent [of the four immeasurables].

Question: Why does the World-Honored One speak only of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and not of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), great sympathetic joy (*mahāmuditā*), or great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*)?
Answer: All should be described as "great," because all the merits within the Buddha’s body are great,
and because they arise from a mind that desires to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
It arises from the mind’s aspiration to rescue and deliver immeasurable sentient beings;
it arises from the mind’s desire to have compassion for immeasurable sentient beings;
and it proceeds as a continuous stream of virtuous equanimity toward all sentient beings.
However, one should not pose a question regarding this.
Why is that? Because if it is the intrinsic nature of compassion itself...
It is indeed compassion that may be the subject of this question;
however, since ordinary compassion (*karuṇā*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) differ in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*),
such a question should not be asked.

Furthermore, there are places in various sūtras where the terms "great loving-kindness" (*mahāmaitrī*), "great sympathetic joy" (*mahāmuditā*), and "great equanimity" (*mahopekṣā*) are also mentioned.
Question: What is the difference between compassion (*karuṇā*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)?
Answer: Their very names constitute the difference.
This is called "compassion" (karuṇā) because it is designated as "great compassion" (mahākaruṇā).
Furthermore, compassion has non-hatred (adveṣa) as its essential nature (svabhāva).
Great compassion has the root of goodness that is non-delusion as its intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, ordinary compassion counteracts the unwholesome root of hatred,
whereas great compassion counteracts the unwholesome root of delusion.
Furthermore, ordinary compassion (karuṇā) exists within the four dhyānas,
whereas great compassion (mahākaruṇā) exists only in the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, ordinary compassion is subsumed under the immeasurables (apramāṇa).
Great compassion is not subsumed within the category of the immeasurables.
Furthermore, ordinary compassion is accomplished within the bodies of both ordinary beings and noble ones,
whereas great compassion is accomplished only within the bodies of noble ones.
Furthermore, ordinary compassion (*karuṇā*) is present and perfected within the bodies of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas;
however, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is perfected only within the body of a Buddha.
Furthermore, while ordinary compassion is merely able to feel pity, it cannot provide salvation.
Great compassion is able both to feel pity and also to provide rescue.
It is like two people standing on the bank of a great river who see one person being swept away by the water;
one merely clasps his hand in sorrowful lamentation but cannot save him—their compassion is just like this.
Second, out of compassion, one casts oneself into the water to rescue them;
great compassion is likewise.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this.
Compassion takes as its object only those sentient beings suffering from the suffering of the desire realm;
great compassion takes as its object sentient beings suffering from the suffering of all three realms.
Furthermore, it is said:
Compassion takes as its object only sentient beings who are afflicted by coarse suffering,
whereas great compassion takes as its object sentient beings who are afflicted by both coarse and subtle suffering.
Furthermore, it is said:
Compassion takes as its object only those sentient beings who are afflicted by the suffering of suffering;
great compassion takes as its object sentient beings who are afflicted by all three types of suffering.
Furthermore, it is said:
Compassion takes as its object sentient beings who suffer from physical pain alone;
great compassion takes as its object sentient beings who suffer from both physical and mental pain.
Furthermore, it is said:
Compassion (*karuṇā*) takes as its object only those sentient beings currently afflicted by suffering in the present life;
great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) takes as its object sentient beings currently afflicted by suffering in both the present and future lives.
Furthermore, it is said that compassion takes as its object only those sentient beings afflicted by proximate suffering.
Great Compassion takes as its object sentient beings who are currently suffering from both proximate and remote forms of suffering;
furthermore, it is said that Compassion takes as its object only those sentient beings currently suffering from present suffering.
Great compassion takes as its object sentient beings who are afflicted by the sufferings of the three periods of time.
The Venerable One says:
"Great compassion is a unique quality of the Buddha’s fourth dhyāna."
It is able to follow along for a great distance, able to follow along with subtlety,
and able to follow along universally; it operates with equanimity toward all sentient beings— whether enemies, friends, or those of neutral character.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is equally accomplished by ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas;
it simply cannot take the form and formless realms as its object.
This is the distinction between compassion and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Question: For what reason is it called "great compassion" (mahākaruṇā)?
Answer: Because it rescues and delivers sentient beings from great suffering, it is called "great compassion."
"Great suffering" refers to the sufferings within the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, it refers to the deliverance of those sentient beings submerged in the mire of the three poisons,
establishing them upon the Noble Path and the fruits of the Noble Path.
Therefore it is called "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*).
Furthermore, because it gathers in classes of sentient beings through great benefit and the matter of great happiness,
it is called "great compassion."
That is to say, it causes sentient beings to cultivate the three types of sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind, thereby bringing about great nobility,
abundant wealth and treasures, a handsome and dignified appearance, and being loved and respected by all.
The fruits of being a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), Śakra, or Māra,
as well as the planting of the seeds of the enlightenment of the three vehicles—
all such matters arise from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Furthermore, it is called "great compassion" because it is obtained at a great price;
it is not like the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas,
which [is attained] by means of a single morsel of food on a single fast day.
If one gives a gift to a single person while generating a superior resolve and aspiration,
it is called planting the seed of that bodhi;
through this process of successive transmission, one attains that bodhi.
Great compassion necessarily requires a long period of time,
during which one bestows all kinds of supreme and exquisite articles of pleasure upon all sentient beings in every situation,
without any stinginess even regarding one’s own body or life.
Only when one generates the supreme thought and aspiration can it be called planting the seed of that great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Through this successive process, one then attains great compassion.
Furthermore, it is called "great compassion" because it is attained through great application (*mahāprayoga*).
It is not like the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, which is attained through the cultivation of preparatory practices for only sixty kalpas,
nor like the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, which is attained through the cultivation of preparatory practices for only one hundred kalpas;
rather, it is the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata, cultivated over three incalculable eons.
It is called "Great Compassion" because it is attained only after practicing hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful austerities.

When he gives rise to the sphere of infinite consciousness, his mind then takes pleasure in remaining there.
One who delights in cultivating equanimity becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of infinite space,
yet does not take pleasure in abiding in the mind of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Seeking further progress, one becomes free from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness;
when the mind arises in the Sphere of Nothingness, it dwells with delight.
Therefore, the term "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) is used in reference to this dwelling in delight.
Furthermore, this statement is made based on their mutual conformity of characteristics:
that is to say, the outflow of the desire realm produced by loving-kindness conforms to the third dhyāna,
and the outflow of the desire realm produced by the third dhyāna conforms to loving-kindness.
To speak at length, this extends even to the desire-realm outflow that is concordant with the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) arising from equanimity,
and the desire-realm outflow concordant with equanimity arising from the sphere of nothingness.
Therefore, in accordance with their characteristics, immeasurable sounds are taught.
Furthermore, to counteract the non-Buddhists' conception of liberation within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
immeasurable sounds are taught regarding the formless realm.
This demonstrates that all [realms] of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) are like the immeasurable [states], yet they are not true liberation.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"The various non-Buddhists (tīrthika), being ignorant, grasp the formless realm as liberation."
Therefore, the Buddha spoke of "immeasurable sounds" therein to indicate that which resembles the immeasurable but is not true liberation.
The four formless states refer to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
The sphere of infinite consciousness,
the sphere of nothingness,
and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of other schools and revealing the correct meaning.
That is to say, there are some who claim:
The Formless Realm possesses form,
as the Vibhajyavādins maintain;
or again, there are those who say so.
The formless realm is without form, as is stated in the *Yuktiśāstra*. One might ask:
according to what teaching and reasoning do the Vibhajyavādins claim that the formless realm also possesses form?
Answer: It is based on the sūtras.
That is to say, the sūtras state:
"Name-and-form conditions consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form."
Since there is consciousness in the formless realm, there should likewise be name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) there.
Furthermore, another sutra states that life-force (*āyus*),
warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are always in a state of union and are never dissociated from one another.
It cannot be established that there is a distinction or difference [between them].
Since vitality (*āyuṣ*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) already exist within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), warmth (*uṣman*) should also exist there.
Furthermore, another sutra states:
Apart from form, feeling, perception, and formations,
one should not say that consciousness has coming, going, staying, death, or birth.
Since consciousness is indeed present within the formless realm, [it cannot be said to perish].

Furthermore, there would be the following logical fallacy: the four stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) would also have to be complete [in the formless realm], yet this leads to further difficulties.
If there were no matter whatsoever in the formless realm, [the four stations of consciousness could not exist there].
When dying in the desire realm or the form realm and being reborn in the formless realm,
it is either twenty thousand kalpas or forty thousand kalpas.
Whether it be sixty thousand kalpas or eighty thousand kalpas,
once all form has been severed and one dies, how does form arise again when one is reborn in the desire realm or the form realm?
If form, once severed, could arise again,
then since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have been severed upon parinirvāṇa,
those conditioned phenomena would likewise have to arise again at a later time.
Do not fall into this error;
therefore, it is certain that there is form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Question: Upon what scriptural authority and reasoning do the proponents of the *Abhidharmasamayapradīpikā* (or *Śāstravādins*) maintain that there is no form whatsoever in the formless realm?
Answer: It is based on the sūtras.
That is to say, the sūtras state:
"The realm of form is the renunciation of desire."
The formless realm is the departure from form;
nirvana, which is tranquility, is the departure from the conditioned.
Since it has been stated that the formless realm is the departure from form...
Therefore, in the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), there are no forms whatsoever.

Furthermore, another sutra states that when entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one contemplates all form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as a disease, as an abscess.
...and so on, as extensively explained.
When entering the formless attainments,
one contemplates all feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
"It is like a disease, like an abscess," and so forth,
as explained at length. From this,
it is known that there are certainly no forms within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Other sūtras further state:
"The formless attainments are peaceful liberations that transcend all forms.
From this, it is known that there are certainly no forms within the formless realm.
Other sūtras further state that by transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance,
and not attending to perceptions of diversity,
one enters and dwells fully in the sphere of infinite space, having realized it.
Furthermore, there is a further fault regarding the meditative attainments of the formless realm (ārūpya-dhyāna) being devoid of all matter:
if matter still existed in the formless realm,
there would be no gradual cessation of phenomena.
If there were no gradual cessation of phenomena, there would be no ultimate cessation;
if there were no ultimate cessation, there would be no liberation, renunciation, or nirvāṇa. To avoid such an error, [this must be accepted].
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is definitely no form.
Question: Of these two explanations, which is the correct one?
Answer: That which was stated by the Sautrāntika masters is the correct one.
Question: How does the Proponent of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (or the Proponent of Reason) explain through and resolve the sūtra cited by the Proponent of the *Vibhāṣā*?
Answer: The sūtra cited by him is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*);
it is a conventional designation established with a specific underlying intention (*abhiprāya*).
Why is this? Because when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma,
he may do so based upon the desire realm.
Either depending on the form realm,
or depending on the formless realm,
or depending on both the desire and form realms.
Either based on the form realm or the formless realm,
or based on the three realms,
or based on being free from the three realms.
Regarding those based on the desire realm, it is as described for the three realms, the three searches, and the three perceptions—
namely, desire, ill-will, and harmfulness.
Regarding those based on the form realm:
As it was explained regarding the four dhyānas,
so it is for those based on the formless realm as explained for the four formless attainments,
and for those based on the desire and form realms.
Regarding the sūtra cited by him which relies on the form and formless realms, it is as stated:
"cultivating meditative concentration, that which is produced by the mind," and so forth;
this relies upon the three realms.
As it is said regarding the three realms (*tridhātu*) and the three states of existence (*tribhava*), etc.,
these depend on that which is free from the three realms;
as it is said regarding *nirvāṇa* and the noble path (*āryamārga*), etc.
Furthermore, regarding the *Ekottarika-āgama* sūtra cited by him which states that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) serve as mutual conditions for one another:
this is spoken with reference to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), however, only name and consciousness serve as mutual conditions for one another.
If one were to grasp the meaning according to the literal text,
then since that sutra states that the six sense bases condition contact,
would it not follow that the formless realm possesses all six sense bases?
Furthermore, that second sūtra cited by him, which states that life-force (*āyus*),
warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are inseparable,
also refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
If, in the formless realm, there were only life-force and consciousness remaining, mutually inseparable;
and if one were to grasp the meaning according to the literal text:
That very sutra states that life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) cannot be designated as distinct or separate from one another.
How could these three types not be designated as distinct or separate by way of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)?
Furthermore, the third sūtra cited by him—
which states that one should not say that consciousness exists apart from form, feeling, perception, and formations,
and that it has going and coming, etc.— also refers to the desire realm and the form realm.
If it were the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), one should say that it is free from feeling, perception, and formations;
one should not say that consciousness has coming and going, etc.
If one were to take the meaning according to the literal text, it would be as stated in other sūtras.
All sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment.
How could those in the two higher realms also rely on edible food?
[The opponent asks: How do you resolve the aforementioned objection regarding that point?
Answer: This does not require an explanation, as it is not part of the Tripiṭaka.
If it must necessarily be explained, its meaning and intent should be shown as follows:
regarding the death, birth, and coming and going within the three realms.
Either form continues from form;
or form continues from the formless;
or the formless continues from the formless.
Alternatively, because form arises from the continuity of the formless,
one should not say that all forms have been severed; for otherwise,
there would be no sense in which they arise again without being severed.
Question: If form arises again after having been separated from it, then once parinirvāṇa has been attained, conditioned formations (saṃskāra) should arise again.
Answer: There are two kinds of separation.
First, temporary separation;
second, ultimate separation.
Regarding temporary separation:
Furthermore, it may arise again; however,
for one who has attained ultimate detachment,
it will certainly not arise again, and thus this objection should not be raised.
Question: How does the Vibhajyavādin explain away the sūtra cited by the Sautrāntika? He replies:
This cited sūtra is of provisional meaning (neyārtha).
This is a provisional designation with a specific underlying intention. Why is this so?
Because that sutra speaks of "those who have emerged from form" in reference to the formless realm.
Departing from coarse form does not mean that subtle form is absent;
it is like how it is said that the realm of form departs from all desires,
yet form is still admitted to exist within the realm of form.
To say that the formless realm is the departure from all forms implies that one must admit the existence of form within the formless realm;
such a statement should not be made.
It cannot be said that form still exists in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) simply because it is taught as the departure from form;

for since it is taught as the departure from form, there must certainly be no form there. Furthermore, just as it is taught that the form realm is the departure from desire, yet subtle desire is not thereby absent, so too [the absence of form does not imply the absence of all things].
Since it is taught that the formless realm is the departure from form, there is likewise no subtle form therein.
Furthermore, since the formless realm lacks coarse feeling and so forth,
it should also be described as a realm without feeling and so forth.
Furthermore, since the matter of the form realm is subtler than that of the desire realm, one should say that the form realm is also called "formless.
Likewise, since the three lower formless realms are coarser than the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), one should say that those three lower levels are called the "form-possessing realm" (rūpadhātu).
Therefore, what he has stated is certainly unreasonable;
he is unable to resolve the contradictions with other sūtras or the logical difficulties raised against him.
Thus, it should be understood.
The one who engages in conceptual proliferation is the fruit of ignorance;
he is the fruit of darkness.
The fruit of ignorance;
not the fruit of constrained preparatory effort.
It is taught that even in the formless realm there still exists subtle matter.
However, since all forms are absent in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
this is stated in order to refute the assertions of other schools and to demonstrate the correct meaning of our own school.
It is not merely that we refute others to reveal what we ourselves have said.
Furthermore, this treatise was composed to reveal the correct principles of all phenomena and to enable others to understand them.
*Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Eighty-three.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Eighty-four,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Fourteen of the Fourth Sub-section on the Ten Gates within the Second Aggregate of the Fetters: What is the Sphere of Infinite Space?
The *Prakaraṇapāda* states:
"The sphere of infinite space is of two kinds:
namely, meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and birth (*upapatti*)."
If one is born in that place, the unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) feeling, perception, formations,
and consciousness are collectively termed the Sphere of Infinite Space;
the same explanation applies up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
In this context, "meditative absorption" refers to the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
"Birth" refers to birth in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
If one is born there, it consists of the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*) aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
This statement refers to the maturation (*vipāka*) of those four aggregates.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Transcending all perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), one extinguishes perceptions of resistance (*pratigha-saṃjñā*)."
Not attending to various perceptions, one enters and dwells,
having fully attained the sphere of infinite space, which is boundless space.
This is called the sphere of infinite space.
Regarding the phrase "transcending all perceptions of form" herein,
it means transcending the perceptions associated with visual consciousness.
Question: When one is free from the defilements of the first dhyāna, one has already transcended these perceptions;
why, then, is it said here that one transcends "all perceptions of form"?
Answer: Because it transcends its basis.
There are two kinds of transcendence:
first, the transcendence of intrinsic nature.
Second, the basis for the faults:
when one is free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
the transcendence of their intrinsic nature is called "leaping over."
When one becomes detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, it is called "transcending" that basis;
furthermore, it is because one transcends their active manifestation.
There are two kinds of transcendence.
First is the fault of abandonment;
second is the fault of non-manifestation. When one becomes free from the defilements of the first dhyāna, the abandonment of all perceptions of form is called "transcending."
When one is free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, that [state] does not manifest; this is called "transcending it.
Furthermore, it is because one has passed beyond that dwelling place.
There are two kinds of faults:
first, the fault of sensual desire;
second, the fault of the dwelling place.
When one becomes free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
the transcendence of desire for that [realm] is called "surpassing.
When one becomes free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna...
Because one speaks of "surpassing" that dwelling place, it is called "transcending it.
Furthermore, if one is born in the fourth dhyāna,
eye-consciousness brings about the manifestation of craving for those forms.
When one becomes detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
it is also said that one transcends all perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*),
because one no longer gives rise to craving for form as an object of cognition.
"The cessation of perceptions of resistance" refers to the cessation of perceptions associated with the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
Question: At what time does one become free from the defilements of the desire realm?
The perceptions associated with nose-consciousness and tongue-consciousness have already ceased;
at the time of becoming detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
the perceptions associated with ear-consciousness and body-consciousness have already been abandoned.
Why is it said here that "the perception of resistance (*pratigha-saṃjñā*) is ceased"?
Answer: Among the previous answers, each according to its application, also addresses this question.
Other masters state that perception associated with hatred (*dveṣa*) is called the perception of resistance.
Question: When one becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm, all perceptions associated with aversion have already been extinguished.
Why, then, is it said here that "perceptions of resistance" (pratigha-saṃjñā) are extinguished?
Answer: Because it transcends its basis.
That is to say, while various bases can give rise to perceptions of anger, at this time one is free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna.
Because they have all transcended those [notions], they are called "cessation.
Question: Why are they not called "the cessation of all perceptions of form" and "the transcendence of perceptions of resistance"?
Answer: They should also be stated reciprocally; this is intended to produce variety in the phrasing so as to inspire delight.
Furthermore, there is the desire to manifest two gateways,
and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding "not reflecting upon various perceptions":
This refers to the non-manifestation of various distracted perceptions associated with the mental consciousness of the fourth dhyāna.
Question: What is the meaning of "various perceptions"?
Answer: Because these perceptions take as their objects the distinct characteristics of various locations.
That is to say, the defiled [perception] takes the differentiated characteristics of the ten bases as its object,
while the non-defiled [perception] takes the differentiated characteristics of the twelve bases as its object;
therefore, this perception is called "various perceptions."
Question: For what reason is it said that one does not contemplate various perceptions?
Answer: Because when one is detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, various perceptions create extreme hindrances, fetters, and obstructions, like violent prison guards.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
when one is detaching from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
one should not give rise to various perceptions through mental reflection.
In this way, one is able to swiftly leave behind this defilement and enter the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Regarding the Sphere of Infinite Space:
why is it called the Sphere of Infinite Space?
Is it by way of intrinsic nature,
or by way of the object? If so,
what fault would there be?
Both positions entail faults.
Why is this? If [it is argued that it exists] by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),...
The sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) has the four aggregates as its intrinsic nature and thus should not be called "space.
If it takes as its object the sphere of infinite space, the four noble truths, or the non-analytical cessation of space, [it would still not be called "space"].
Why is it called merely the "base of infinite space"?
It should be answered thus:
it is not so by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor is it so by way of its object (*ālambana*).
It is designated as the "sphere of infinite space" solely on account of its preparatory application (*prayoga*).
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*: "By what preparatory application does one cultivate the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space?
By what preparatory application does one enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space?"
This means that a beginner should first contemplate the various characteristics of empty space, such as those found on walls, trees, cliffs, and rooftops.
Having grasped these characteristics, they should apply imaginative resolve (*adhimukti*).
One observes and clearly realizes the sign of infinite space,
having previously contemplated the sign of infinite space while practicing the preparatory application.
Because it successively induces the first formless absorption,
it is called the Sphere of Infinite Space.
Furthermore, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), the initial state of being far removed from the realm of form is designated as the Sphere of Infinite Space.
Furthermore, it is the nature of things that the first liberation from the realm of form is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
That is to say, the yoga practitioner first takes hold of a higher level of the form realm and becomes detached from the defilements of the lower levels of the form realm.
When one becomes detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
one does so by taking as an object the four aggregates of the sphere of infinite space;
first, one forms the perception of space directed toward the higher plane.
Subsequently, one gives rise to the path that leads away from the defilements of the lower realm.
This is like a person climbing a tree who first grasps an upper branch and then lets go of the lower branch;
once he reaches the top of the tree, since there are no further branches above to grasp, he simply gives rise to the perception of space.
Furthermore, this meditative absorption is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) on account of its outflow (*niṣyanda*).
That is to say, when a practitioner of yoga emerges from this absorption, a corresponding perception of space necessarily arises before them.
I have heard that once, after emerging from this meditative absorption,
a bhikṣu raised both hands and felt about in the air;
someone who saw him asked:
"What are you seeking?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I am seeking my own self."
He said, "Your body is right here upon this bed;
how can you seek for yourself elsewhere?"
Therefore, from this, one gives rise to the perception of space.
This perception is the outflow (niṣyanda) of the preceding meditative absorption.
As for "abiding fully": [it refers to]...
This refers to having attained, acquired, and accomplished the four aggregates of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Regarding the attainment, acquisition, and accomplishment, the term "abiding fully" (*paripūrṇavihāra*) is used;
therefore, it is called the sphere of infinite space.
What is the sphere of infinite consciousness?
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness."
Abiding fully in the sphere of infinite consciousness—
this is called the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Question: Why is this called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness?
Is it by way of its intrinsic nature, or by way of its object?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
Both positions possess errors. Why is this?
If the intrinsic nature of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) consists of the four aggregates,
it should not be named merely "Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.

Furthermore, if the object of focus for the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness includes the Four Noble Truths as well as space and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), it likewise should not be named merely "Sphere of Infinite Consciousness."
I agree to speak thus:
this is neither by way of intrinsic nature,
nor by way of an object of perception.
It is merely by way of its preparatory application (*prayoga*) that it is called the "sphere of infinite consciousness" (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*:
"By what preparatory application does one cultivate the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness?"
By what application does one enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness?
For a beginner, one should first contemplate the characteristics of the six types of consciousness, such as the pure visual consciousness;
having grasped these characteristics, one should apply imaginative resolve (*adhimukti*).
One observes and clearly realizes the signs of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantya*),
having previously contemplated the signs of infinite consciousness as the preparatory practice (*prayoga*).
This is because it successively induces the second formless attainment (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
This is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Furthermore, this meditative absorption is named the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness because it is based on its natural outflow (*niṣyanda*);
that is to say, when a practitioner of yoga emerges from this concentration, a corresponding image of consciousness necessarily arises before them.
This means dwelling with joy in the perception of consciousness.
As for "dwelling fully," it refers to having attained, acquired, and perfected the four virtuous aggregates of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Because one speaks of "dwelling fully" in the attainment and accomplishment [of this state],
it is therefore called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
What is the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)?
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness,
one enters and dwells, having fully attained, the sphere of nothingness."
This is called the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Question: Why is this called the sphere of nothingness?
Answer: Because within it there is neither self nor what belongs to a self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*).
Question: Since there is no "self" or "what belongs to self" in all stages (*bhūmi*), why is this one alone called the "Stage of Nothingness" (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)?
Answer: Because there is no other stage that can cause the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*) or the grasping of what belongs to a self (*ātmīya-grāha*).
Because this stage is weak, thin, and diminished in power,
it is uniquely called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Furthermore, in this stage, there exists no dharma that is real, permanent, constant, or unchanging.
Because it suppresses and overcomes the notion of permanence more effectively than all other stages,
this alone is named the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Furthermore, in this stage, there is no destination, no refuge, no house, nor any dwelling that can provide protection.
Because it overcomes pride, indolence, and negligence, surpassing all other stages, this stage alone is named the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Furthermore, within this stage, the aspect of "boundlessness" no longer exists; one first abandons that aspect.
Therefore, this alone is called the Sphere of Nothingness.
The Venerable Vasumitra stated:
"In this meditative absorption, no mental formations function as either subject or object."
As it is said: "There is no place, time, or object that belongs to a self, nor is there any place, time, or object belonging to a self.
Therefore, this alone is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
"Abiding in possession" means having attained,
acquired, and accomplished the four aggregates of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The term "abiding in possession" is used in reference to such attainment, acquisition, and accomplishment.
Therefore, it is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Question: For what reason does the Buddha say that the Sphere of Nothingness alone is called "equanimity" (*upekṣā*)?
Answer: Equanimity refers to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), for it is capable of completely relinquishing [all defilements].
Because this stage of the Noble Path (āryamārga-bhūmi) is the very last, the name "equanimity" (upekṣā) is established independently for this stage.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated:
"This stage is proximate to the relinquishing of conceptual constructions (saṃjñā), resolute conviction (adhimokṣa), and infinite modes of activity (ananta-ākāra)."
Because it is a coarse observation and understanding, it is established as having the name "equanimity" (*upekṣā*) alone.
The Venerable One says:
"In this stage, one abandons the mental application (*manasikāra*), effort (*prayoga*), and the infinite aspects of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*)."
Because it abides without effort, it alone is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
What is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Transcending the sphere of nothingness,
one enters and dwells in the fulfillment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Question: Why is this called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Answer: Because within this stage there is no characteristic of clear perception, nor is there the characteristic of non-perception;
therefore, it is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There is no characteristic of clear perception,
because it is not like the meditative absorption of perception found in the seventh stage;
nor is there any characteristic of non-perception.
It is not like the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*) or the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Because the perception (*saṃjñā*) in this stage is dull, feeble, and weak—
being neither clear nor determinate— it is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
"Abiding in possession" means that one has attained,
acquired, and accomplished the four wholesome aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
the term "abiding in possession" is used with respect to such attainment, acquisition, and accomplishment.
Therefore, it is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).

Question: For what reason is there no untainted path (anāsravamārga) in the Desire Realm or in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception? Answer: It is not because they are unsuitable vessels.
This means that those two stages are not the basis for the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Because they serve as its vessel, the untainted path does not exist within those two stages.
Furthermore, it is because the roots of existence (*bhavarāga*) have been severed.
This means that those two stages are the root of existence (*bhava*).
Since all untainted paths (*anāsravamārga*) sever the root of existence,
untainted paths do not exist within those two stages.
Furthermore, it is because of the abandonment of the two extremes.
That is to say, those two stages constitute the lower and upper extremes;
since the various untainted paths (anāsrava-mārga) are able to abandon these two extremes and abide in the Middle Way, they do not exist in those stages.
Furthermore, the desire realm lacks meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and is neither a stage of cultivation nor a stage of detachment from defilements.
The Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is dark, dull, and indecisive, resembling doubt.

Since all untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) necessarily rely on a stage of concentration and a stage of detachment from defilements—being luminous, sharp, and decisive—they do not exist in these two stages.
Furthermore, within the stages of the desire realm, restlessness (*auddhatya*) predominates;
within the stage of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), tranquility (*śamatha*) predominates.
Neither is a locus for the support of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Question: For what reason does the Blessed One employ the term "transcending" (*samatikrama*) with respect to all the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), but not so for the dhyānas?
Answer: The Buddha also employs the term "transcending" with respect to the dhyānas.
As the Blessed One told Udāyin: "Monks,
detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation,
and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, one enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, having attained its full perfection."
I say that this fire is both to be abandoned and to be transcended;
this applies likewise up to the fourth dhyāna.
Question: Why does a single sūtra state only that the dhyānas are to be transcended?
Other sūtras all state that the formless [attainments] are transcendent.
What is the meaning of this?
The answer is: within the dhyānas there are various distinct characteristics and dissimilar dharmas.
Therefore, "leaping over" is not mentioned [in the case of the formless realms]. It is not so for the formless realms;
hence, "leaping over" is mentioned specifically [for them].
Furthermore, within the dhyānas there exist various types of sense faculties, various types of sensations, and various types of mental states and mental factors;
therefore, they are not said to be "transcended.
This is not the case for the formless realms.
Therefore, only the "transcending" [of the dhyānas] is mentioned.
Furthermore, because there are many kinds of qualities and many kinds of benefits within the dhyānas,
they are not mentioned here.
The transcendence of the formless realms is not so;
therefore, it is specifically called "transcendence.
Furthermore, the dhyānas are coarse, manifest, clear, and perceptible to direct vision.
Therefore, "leaping over" is not mentioned [in relation to the form realm].
Because the formless [realms] are subtle, hidden, indistinct, and not directly perceptible,
"leaping over" is mentioned only in reference to them.
Furthermore, because dhyāna takes as its object all levels— both those above and below itself—
it is not said to "leap over" them.
The formless attainments (ārūpya), however, can only take as their objects the levels equal to or above themselves.
Therefore, it is specifically said that they "transcend.
Furthermore, although one does not die or take birth in the various dhyānas and their respective upper or lower stages, there is still movement back and forth between them;
that is to say, by means of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), one ascends from a lower stage to an upper one, or descends from an upper stage to a lower one.
Therefore, it is not said that there is no such principle regarding the transcendence of the formless realms;
thus, only [the transcendence of the dhyānas] is mentioned.
Furthermore, this is because the various dhyānas intermingle with the stages above and below them.
The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a lower stage manifests within a higher stage,
and the intermediate state of a higher stage manifests within a lower stage; since there is thus mutual intermingling,
[the intermediate state] is not distinct from the realms of existence.
Therefore, "leaping over" is not mentioned [in the context of the form realm].
Within the formless realms, such a principle does not exist;
thus, "leaping over" is mentioned exclusively [there].
Furthermore, when one born in a higher dhyāna gives rise to dharmas of a lower stage—
such as the various groups of consciousness, the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*), and so forth—
it is therefore not said that there is "leaping over" (*vyutkrāntaka*).
One born in the higher formless realms (*ārūpya*) necessarily does not give rise to any lower tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*);
therefore, it alone is described as "transcending.
Furthermore, for one born in the higher dhyānas, the dharmas of the lower stages continue to follow them constantly.
As in the case of the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) and so forth,
it is therefore not said that there is "leaping over.

When one is born in a higher formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is necessarily no sense in which the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the various contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas of lower stages can follow along.
Therefore, it is specifically said that there is "leaping over.
Due to various causes and conditions such as these,
the Buddha speaks of the existence of "leaping over" with respect to the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
The meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are not like this; as the Sūtra says:
"The lifespan in the Sphere of Infinite Space is twenty thousand kalpas."
The lifespan in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness is forty thousand kalpas;
in the Sphere of Nothingness, sixty thousand kalpas;
and in the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, eighty thousand kalpas.
Question: For what reason do the lifespans in the formless realms increase by doubling,
increase by half,
or increase by a small fraction?
Answer: It is because the retributive cause possesses as much power as there is, and thus one receives a corresponding amount of retributive fruit.
Furthermore, while the spheres of Infinite Space and Infinite Consciousness possess the aspect of boundlessness, they also possess other aspects.
That is to say, the infinite aspect of the sphere of infinite space brings about a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas;
other aspects also bring about a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas.
The infinite aspect of the sphere of infinite consciousness brings about a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas.
Other modes of conduct also bring about a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas.
Beyond this, there are no further infinite modes of conduct;
there are only these remaining modes of conduct.
Therefore, their lifespan does not increase twofold [as it does in the lower levels].
However, in the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), there exists a distinct, superior,
and virtuous contemplative practice that subdues the notions of "I" and "mine," which differs from those of other stages.
Because that [wholesome karma] well-attracts a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas,
the lifespans attracted by other modes of practice likewise increase twofold.
Furthermore, in the spheres of Infinite Space and Infinite Consciousness, there are both śamatha and vipaśyanā.
That is to say, the śamatha of the sphere of infinite space brings about a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas;
the vipaśyanā also brings about a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas.
The śamatha of the sphere of infinite consciousness brings about a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas.
Vipaśyanā also brings about a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas;
beyond this, there is no superior vipaśyanā,
for there is only śamatha.
Therefore, their lifespan does not increase twofold;
the remainder is as previously explained.
Furthermore, because none of the four formless stages possess various manifold qualities (guṇadharma).
Each of these realms has a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas.

As for the three higher formless realms, because they are free from the defilements of the lower stages and because their [attainments] increase in degree, their lifespans double at each successive level.

This means that having already abandoned the defilements of the lower single formless stage, one attains a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness; together with the original twenty thousand, this constitutes forty thousand kalpas.
Having already abandoned the defilements of the two lower formless stages, [one attains a lifespan of forty thousand kalpas] in the Sphere of Nothingness.
It draws forth a lifespan of forty thousand kalpas; together with the original twenty thousand, this makes sixty thousand kalpas.
Having already abandoned the defilements of the three lower formless stages, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception draws forth a lifespan of sixty thousand kalpas;
together with the original twenty thousand, this makes eighty thousand kalpas.
Regarding the eight liberations:
first, the liberation of one possessing form who perceives forms;
second, the liberation of one who, being internally without the perception of form, perceives external forms.
Third, one realizes the liberation of purity with the body and dwells in its full attainment.
Fourth, transcending all perceptions of form and extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance,
one no longer attends to diverse perceptions and enters the sphere of infinite space.
He dwells, having fully attained the liberation that transcends all of the sphere of infinite space.
He enters the sphere of infinite consciousness, transcending all of the sphere of infinite space,
and dwells, having fully attained the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Sixth, transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness,
one enters and dwells in the full possession of the sphere of nothingness, which is liberation.
Seventh, transcending the sphere of nothingness.
Entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
he dwells fully established in liberation.
This is the eighth [liberation], which transcends all of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
[The practitioner] enters the cessation of perception and feeling, realizes it with the body, and dwells fully in this liberation.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these eight liberations?
Answer: The first three liberations have the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*) as their intrinsic nature.
All of these serve as antidotes to greed;
therefore, if one includes both the associated and the co-arising factors,
those belonging to the desire realm have the four aggregates as their intrinsic nature.
The realm of form has the five aggregates as its intrinsic nature.
The four formless liberations all have the four aggregates as their intrinsic nature.
The liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling—
It has the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This is what is called the intrinsic nature of liberation:
its own-being (*ātman*), substance (*vastu*), essence (*ātmatva*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), part (*bhāga*), and fundamental nature (*prakṛti*).
The intrinsic nature has already been explained.
Now, therefore, the question shall be addressed: for what reason is it called "liberation"?
What is the meaning of liberation?
Answer: The meaning of relinquishing and turning away is the meaning of liberation.
Question: If it is called liberation because of relinquishing and turning away, what kind of liberation relinquishes and turns away from what kind of mind?
Answer: The first two liberations involve turning away from the mind that craves form;
the third liberation involves turning away from the mind of the contemplation of impurity;
and the liberations of the four formless realms each involve turning away from the mind of the stage immediately below it.
The liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-vimokṣa) turns its back on all minds that possess an object of cognition;
therefore, the meaning of "turning away" is the meaning of "liberation.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this.
The mind is liberated from afflictions and becomes pure;
therefore, it is called "liberation.
The Venerable One said:
Because one attains liberation through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*),
it is called "liberation.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
Because there is something that is relinquished, they are called "liberations.
Regarding the realms of these eight liberations:
the first three liberations belong to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Regarding the first three formless-sphere liberations:
those that are with outflows belong to the formless realm;
those that are without outflows are unconditioned by any realm.
The latter two liberations belong to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
As for their stages: the first two liberations exist in the first and second dhyānas, as well as in the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
Similar wholesome roots also exist in other stages.
Yet they are not established as the first and second liberations.
Why is this? Because the power of the distracted and averse states of the desire realm is weak.
Therefore, the first two liberations are not established [in this context].
Because they turn their backs on the mind that, led by the body-consciousness of the desire realm and the first dhyāna, craves for objects of form,
the first two impure liberations are established in the first and second dhyānas.

Because the second and third dhyānas lack a consciousness-body that induces a mind of craving for form, the first two impure liberations (aśubha-vimokṣas) are not established there; rather, the third liberation is established in the fourth dhyāna.
The lower stages also possess similar roots of goodness,
yet they are not established as the third liberation. Why is this so?
The pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*) is established in order to abandon and turn away from the mind of the impurity meditation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
If it were in a lower stage, it would be overcome by the power of the impurity meditation;
because it would not be extensive or clear, it is not established there.
Although the third dhyāna lacks the first two impure liberations,
it is not established [as such] because it is deluded by superior pleasure and is neither extensive nor clear.
The fourth liberation resides in the sphere of infinite space.
Question: Within this stage, which phenomena are liberations and which phenomena are not liberations?
Answer: The preparatory paths for detaching from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
the nine uninterrupted paths, the eight paths of liberation,
and the innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) are not [the path of] liberation.
Other conditioned wholesome states are liberation.
The fifth liberation is in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Question: Within this stage, which phenomena constitute liberation?
Which dharmas are not liberation?
Answer: The preparatory paths for becoming free from attachment to the sphere of infinite space;
the nine uninterrupted paths; and the eight paths of liberation.
Furthermore, the innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) and so forth are not liberation;
other conditioned wholesome states are liberation.
The sixth liberation resides in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Question: Within this stage, which phenomena constitute liberation and which do not?
Answer: The preparatory paths that abandon the defilements of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
as well as the wholesome states acquired by birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*) and so forth,
are not liberation; all other conditioned wholesome states are liberation.
The seventh liberation resides in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Question: Within this stage, what phenomena constitute liberation, and what phenomena do not?
Answer: The preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*) for detaching from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
and the innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) and so forth are not [the path of] liberation.
Other conditioned wholesome states are liberation.
The liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling exists in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
As for its basis:
The first three liberations arise based on a body belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling arises based on a body belonging to either the desire or form realms (*rūpadhātu*).
The remaining four liberations arise based on bodies belonging to all three realms.
Regarding their modes of activity (*ākāra*):
the first two liberations (*vimokṣa*) function with the mode of impurity,
while the third liberation functions with the mode of purity.
The four formless-sphere liberations (ārūpya-vimokṣa) perform sixteen aspects (ākāra),
or other aspects;
the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa) does not perform any aspects.
Regarding the objects of focus:
the first three liberations take the form-sphere (*rūpāyatana*) of the desire realm as their object;
the fourth liberation takes the four formless spheres as its object.
Furthermore, there are all categories of the knowledge of types (*jñāna*) pertaining to those causes and their cessation;
