as well as the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the category of the knowledge of types,
non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and space (*ākāśa*).
Whether it be considered as a single entity or as multiple entities, all are objects of focus;
the fifth liberation takes the final three formless realms as its object.
And those causes of that [cessation], the entire category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-pakṣa*),
as well as the final three formless attainments, the category of subsequent knowledge,
analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and space (*ākāśa*).
Whether one considers it as a single entity or as multiple entities,
all are conditioned by causes.
The sixth liberation takes as its object the latter two formless attainments (*ārūpya*),
their causes, their cessation, and all categories of the knowledge of classes (*anvaya-jñāna-pakṣa*).
If it concerns the latter two formless attainments and the categories of the knowledge of classes:
Regarding non-analytical cessation and space:
whether one considers them to be a single entity or multiple entities.
All are conditioned by objects.
The seventh liberation is conditioned by the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
as well as its cause, its cessation, and all categories of the knowledge of classes (*jñāna*).
If one considers the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the category of subsequent knowledge,
non-analytical cessation, and space as being a single entity;
[this would be a fallacy].
If it is claimed that there are many objects,
[then] all [of them] would be the objectless liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*). Some have stated this.
The liberation of the sphere of infinite space also takes the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the fourth dhyāna as its object;
the remaining objects are as previously described,
up to the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It also takes the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the sphere of nothingness as its object;
other objects are as previously described.
As for the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*):
The first three liberations are associated with the application of mindfulness of the body;
the four formless-sphere liberations are associated with all four applications of mindfulness;
and the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling is associated with either the application of mindfulness of its own nature or the mixed application of mindfulness.
It should be said that it does not coexist with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
If one considers it in terms of its object (*ālambana*), it should be said to be the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The first three liberations (*vimokṣa*) of the wise are associated with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The first three formless-sphere liberations are associated with six types of knowledge:
namely, the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; conventional knowledge; and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is associated with conventional knowledge.
The liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling is not accompanied by wisdom.
Regarding meditative absorption (samādhi),
the first three liberations and the latter two liberations are not concomitant with meditative absorption.
The first three formless-sphere liberations are associated with the three samādhis,
or they may not be associated with samādhi.
As for their association with the faculties:

The first two liberations are associated with the faculties of joy (*prīti*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*); the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*) is not associated with any faculty.
The remaining five liberations are all associated with the faculty of equanimity.
Regarding the three time periods:
All of them take the three periods of time as their objects.
Regarding the three periods of time:
the first three liberations take the past as their object.
The present takes the present as its object.
As for the future, if it is a dharma that is subject to arising, it takes the future as its object;
if it is a dharma not subject to arising, it takes the three periods of time as its object.
The four formless-sphere liberations have as their objects the three periods of time and that which is beyond time;
the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling has no object.
Regarding those that are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral:
all are exclusively wholesome.
As for those that take as their object the wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral: [they are likewise exclusively wholesome].
The first three liberations take the three types [of objects] as their conditions.
The four formless-sphere liberations take only the wholesome and the neutral as their conditions.
The liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling has no object-condition.
Regarding those bound to the three realms and those unbound:
the first three liberations are bound only to the realm of form;
the latter two liberations are bound only to the formless realm.
The first three formless-sphere liberations that are with-outflows are bound to the formless realm.
That which is untainted (anāsrava) is unbound.
It takes as its object both that which is bound to the three realms and that which is unbound.
The first three liberations take only that which is bound to the desire realm as their object.
The four formless-sphere liberations take that which is bound to the formless realm and that which is unbound as their objects.
The liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling has no object.
Regarding those that are neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee:
the first three and the last two liberations are exclusively neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
The first three formless-sphere liberations (ārūpya-vimokṣa) are associated with three types of objects:
those of the learner (śaikṣa), the non-learner (aśaikṣa), and neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa).
The first three liberations take as their objects only that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
The four formless-sphere liberations have three types of objects;
the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling has no object.
[Regarding] those abandoned by seeing, those abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned:
The first three and the last two liberations (vimokṣa) are abandoned solely through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
As for the first three formless-sphere liberations,
those that are with outflows (sāsrava) [are abandoned through cultivation].
Those abandoned through cultivation are with outflows; those that are without outflows are not to be abandoned.
Regarding those [objects] to be abandoned by seeing, those to be abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned:
the first three liberations take only those to be abandoned by cultivation as their objects;
the four formless-sphere liberations take all three types as their objects.
The liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling has no object.
Regarding those who hold that [the liberations] take names as their objects or meanings as their objects:
the first three liberations take only meanings as their objects.
Regarding the four formless-sphere liberations:
if it is claimed that the formless realm also possesses "name," that statement refers to [the fact that] they universally take both name and meaning as their objects.
If it is claimed that there is no "name" (nāma) in the formless realm,
then that refers only to the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling which takes only the object as its condition;
it does not take as its object one's own continuum, another's continuum, or what is not a continuum.
The first liberation takes as its object the mental continuums of both oneself and others.
Regarding the second and third liberations, some say:
They pertain only to the mental continuums of others;
some say they also pertain to both one's own and others' continuums.
The liberations of the four formless spheres take three types as their objects.

Regarding the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*), which is without an object of focus and is obtained either through application (*prayoga*) or through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*):
the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling is obtained solely through application.
The remaining seven liberations are also obtained through application (*prayoga*) and obtained through the removal of defilements (*vairāgya*).
Regarding those obtained through the removal of defilements:
The liberation of the first dhyāna stage is attained when one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm;
likewise, up to the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
it is attained when one becomes free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness.
Later, that [attainment] manifests through application (*prayoga*).
That which is acquired through application is obtained by means of application,
and it also manifests by means of application.
Śrāvakas [attain it] either through middling application or through superior application;
pratyekabuddhas do so through inferior application.
The Buddha does not attain [the cessation of perception and feeling] through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), nor does he bring it to manifestation;
as for what has been previously attained and what has never been attained,
the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*) is exclusively what has never been attained before.
The remaining seven liberations pertain to both those previously attained and those not yet attained.
That is to say, for all noble ones (*ārya*) and for those born within the Dharma (*adhyātma-dharmika-pṛthagjana*), they pertain to both the previously attained and the not yet attained;
for those born outside the Dharma (*bāhya-dharmika-pṛthagjana*), they pertain only to what has been previously attained. Thus has the general characteristic of liberation been explained.
Each individual characteristic should now be explained in detail.
"Possessing form, one perceives forms" refers to the first liberation.
Regarding "possessing form":
This refers to one who has not yet detached from, abandoned, or eliminated internal, individual perceptions of form,
yet contemplates various forms; that is,
for the purpose of detaching from, abandoning, and eliminating internal, individual perceptions of form.
By means of attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*),
one contemplates external forms as either livid, or festering, or bloated, or a skeleton;
this is the first liberation (*prathama-vimokṣa*).
"Initial" means that its name and numerical position are at the beginning.
Alternatively, it refers to the fact that this meditative absorption occurs first in the sequence of the liberations (*vimokṣa*).
That is to say, when one enters this absorption, all wholesome form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are collectively termed "liberation."
The second liberation is: perceiving external forms while having no perception of internal form.
"Having no perception of internal form" means that one has already become detached from, abandoned, and eliminated the individual perceptions of internal form.
Regarding the observation of external forms:

this refers to observing various external forms through the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*), without having abandoned or removed internal, individual perceptions of form.
If the details regarding the livid corpse and so forth are as explained previously,
and the second [liberation] and the deliverances are also as explained previously,
one asks: when contemplating external forms, is there the perception of internal formlessness?
When observing external forms, is there no perception of internal form?
If that were so, what would be the fault? There would be defects in both cases. Why is this?
If, when observing external forms, there is the perception of internal formlessness,
how can one mind not produce two distinct understandings?
If it were to produce two understandings, there would necessarily be two minds.
The substance of the one mind and the two substances are inconsistent with principle.
If, when observing external forms, there is no perception of internal form,
how should the statement made here be reconciled— that "observing external forms while having no perception of internal form" constitutes the second liberation?
It is agreed that one should speak thus.
When observing external forms while lacking the internal perception of form, the question is: if this is so, then...
How should one explain what is stated here, given that it has been successfully answered by the previous resolution of the objection?
The answer is: because it is spoken in accordance with the aspirational resolve (*praṇidhāna*) of the practitioner.
That is to say, the practitioner first forms an aspirational resolve.
"When I am without the perception of internal form, I should contemplate external forms.
It was with reference to this that the Blessed One said:
"Being without the perception of internal form, one contemplates external forms."
Furthermore, this is because it is taught according to the preliminary conceptual practice undertaken by the practitioner.
That is to say, the practitioner first performs such conceptual practice as follows:
"When I am without the perception of internal form, I should contemplate external forms."
Therefore, this statement was made.
Furthermore, the phrasing here is explained by inference from its meaning;
that is to say, when one has no perception of internal forms, it follows by implication that one must necessarily contemplate external forms.
When observing external forms, by implication it must necessarily be that one lacks the perception of internal form.
Furthermore, the phrasing in this passage includes both the preparatory application (*prayoga*) and the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*);
"lacking the perception of internal form" refers to the roots of virtue of the preparatory application.
One who contemplates external forms is said to possess ultimate roots of goodness.
Furthermore, "one who has no perception of internal form" is described in terms of the basis (*āśraya*), while "one who contemplates external forms" is described in terms of the object (*ālambana*).
The third liberation is the attainment of the liberation of the beautiful, having realized it with one’s own body and dwelling therein.

Question: Is this liberation of the beautiful identical to "perceiving forms while possessing form," or is it identical to "possessing the internal perception of formlessness while perceiving external forms"?
If one who possesses internal form perceives external forms,
what difference is there between this and the first liberation?
If one who lacks the perception of internal form perceives external forms...
What is the difference between this and the second liberation?
It should be said in response:
this pure liberation is precisely the contemplation of external forms while possessing the internal perception of no-form.
Question: If that is so, what is the difference between this and the second liberation?
Answer: The difference lies in their names.
That is called the second,
and this is called the third;
furthermore, there are also distinctions among the stages (bhūmi).
That is to say, the former exists in the first and second dhyānas,
while this exists in the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, there is also a distinction in their continuity.
That is to say, the second liberation applies to the mental continuities of both non-Buddhists and Buddhists,
whereas the pure liberation applies only to the mental continuities of Buddhists.
Furthermore, the second liberation functions by way of the aspect of impurity.
The pure liberation (śubha-vimokṣa) functions with the aspect of a pure practice.
Furthermore, the second liberation counteracts craving for form (rūpa-rāga),
while the pure liberation counteracts the meditation on the foul (aśubha-bhāvanā).
Furthermore, the second liberation is attained with little preparatory effort and little exertion,
whereas the pure liberation is attained with great preparatory effort and great exertion.
Furthermore, the second liberation is luminous and pure by nature, while its object of focus is not luminous and pure.
The pure liberation has a nature that is sublime, but its object is not sublime;
the liberation of the beautiful has both a nature and an object that are clear, pure, and sublime.
This is called the second and third distinction.
Question: For what reason does the practitioner of meditation cultivate this pure liberation?
Answer: It is because they wish to test whether their roots of goodness are fulfilled or not.
That is to say, the practitioner of meditation reflects thus:
"Although I contemplate the sign of impurity and do not give rise to afflictions,
I do not yet know whether my roots of goodness have been brought to fulfillment."

If afflictions do not arise when one contemplates the aspect of purity, one knows that the roots of goodness have already reached fulfillment; thus, one contemplates the aspect of purity to cultivate the liberation of purity.
Furthermore, for a practitioner of meditation, if the mind becomes depressed and dejected when contemplating the aspect of impurity, wholesome qualities will not increase.
In order to cause wholesome qualities to further increase,
one again contemplates pure signs and cultivates the liberation of purity,
just as when wandering among burial grounds, one repeatedly observes the impurity of corpses.
Because the mind is depressed and dejected, wholesome qualities do not increase.
In order to cause wholesome qualities to further progress,
one contemplates exquisite gardens, flowing springs, and lotus ponds.
Alternatively, one may travel through cities and towns to observe various wonderful sights that gladden the mind and enable the cultivation of superior virtues;
this too should be done, and thus one contemplates the aspect of purity.
Furthermore, a practitioner of meditation has long contemplated impurity.
If the mind becomes attached to and delights in wholesome qualities such that they do not increase,
one should abandon the contemplation of the impure and cultivate the liberation of the pure, in order to bring about the further advancement of those wholesome qualities.
Furthermore, the practitioner of contemplation, wishing to demonstrate that his own mind is firm and non-retrogressive—
meaning that even when taking a pure object as its condition, afflictions do not arise, much less when taking other objects—
therefore contemplates the sign of purity and cultivates the liberation of purity.
Furthermore, the practitioner of contemplation demonstrates that their own roots of goodness possess great power;
that is to say, if afflictions do not arise even when taking a pure object as their condition, how much less so when taking other objects?
Therefore, they contemplate the sign of purity and cultivate the liberation of purity.
Furthermore, it is revealed that the pure liberation is not something that all sentient beings are capable of cultivating and realizing;
rather, it is only those who have died among the gods of the Sublime Resolve (Abhirati) and Pure Joy (Śubhakṛtsna) realms and are reborn among human beings who are able to cultivate and realize it.
Therefore, the practitioner cultivates the liberation of purity.
It was heard that once, during the afternoon, a bhikṣu came to the Buddha’s dwelling and requested a fine room; the Buddha commanded Ānanda to grant him a fine room.
Ānanda received the command and handed it over to him.
That bhikṣu said, "It would be well to sweep and sprinkle the ground,
hang silk streamers and canopies, burn incense, and scatter flowers."
"Spread soft bedding and arrange a comfortable pillow;
I shall accept it, otherwise I will not.
Ānanda then reported this matter in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "You should give him whatever he requests.
At that time, Ānanda prepared everything and presented it to him.
Having received it, the bhikṣu arose during the first watch of the night and attained the pure liberation.
Following this sequence, other liberations arise;
with the permanent exhaustion of all outflows, he becomes an Arhat and further cultivates preparatory application to induce supernormal powers.
At dawn, he departs by means of these powers.
Later, Ānanda went to that room but did not see the bhikṣu;
seeing only the bed and seat, he immediately went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Do not underestimate him."
Last night, he gave rise to the liberation of purity and other liberations, attained arhatship, and manifested supernormal powers;
since the morning has passed, that bhikṣu has proceeded from that sublime resolution.
When one dies in the Heaven of Delight in Purity and is reborn among humans,
if they do not obtain a pure and exquisite dwelling, they will be unable to cultivate the third liberation,
and so on, up to the supernormal powers of the ultimate fruit.
From this, it is known that this pure liberation is not something that all sentient beings are able to cultivate and realize;
only those who delight in the pure can bring it forth.
The third [liberation] and its deliverance are also as previously explained.

The four formless liberations (ārūpya-vimokṣa) are as explained for the four formless [attainments]. The liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa) shall be analyzed in detail later in the Indriya-skandha.
The enumeration and the liberations should be understood according to what precedes. Question: For what reason are only a portion of the wholesome roots of the dhyānas established as liberations?
Are all stages of the formless realm established as liberations?
Answer: Because the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are coarse, manifest, and clearly perceived, only a small portion of the wholesome roots therein are established as liberations.
Because the formless [attainments] are subtle, hidden, indistinct, and not directly perceptible, liberation is established for all the fundamental stages.
Furthermore, within the dhyānas, there are various dissimilar phenomena with differing characteristics.
Therefore, those with few roots of virtue are established as being liberated;
this is not the case for those in the formless realm, and thus they are established collectively.
Furthermore, within the dhyānas, there exist distinct characteristics such as faculties, feelings, mind, and mental factors.
Therefore, those with few roots of virtue are established as being liberated;
this is not the case for those in the formless realms, and thus they are established collectively.
Furthermore, the dhyānas possess many meritorious benefits.
Therefore, those with few roots of virtue are established as being liberated;
this is not the case for those in the formless realms, and thus they are established collectively.
Furthermore, dhyāna universally takes as its object its own level, as well as the levels above and below.
Therefore, those with few roots of goodness are established as being [in the stage of] liberation.
Because the formless attainments take only their own or higher levels as objects, not lower ones, they are established collectively.
Furthermore, the dhyānas and liberations are established separately because they are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).
The formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*) also include the untainted (*anāsrava*); therefore, they are established collectively.
A question arises from this discussion:
for what reason are the dhyāna-liberations exclusively tainted?
Do the formless liberations (ārūpya-vimokṣa) pertain to both the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) and the outflow-free (anāsrava)?
Answer: As previously stated, they also pertain to both according to the five gates.
Furthermore, there is one unique [distinction] herein.

The answer is: because the liberations within the dhyānas are associated exclusively with attention consisting of resolute conviction (adhimokṣa-manasikāra), whereas the liberations within the formless realms are for the most part associated with attention consisting of reality (tattva-manasikāra), they are not similar.
Question: For what reason does the Blessed One describe the eight liberations using the term "directions"?
Answer: Because he considers those to be trained; it is like describing the four truths using the term "four directions.
Question: What similarity exists between liberation and direction?
Answer: Because liberation and direction both possess eight [aspects].
Question: Since directions are ten, how can they be similar?
Answer: It is like the method for training elephants, which relies solely upon the eight directions.
Because there is no above or below, they are thus similar.
Furthermore, just as a person on a flat surface perceives only the eight directions,
so too does one with a rectified mind cultivate the eight liberations.
Furthermore, just as one can tame dragon-elephants by relying on the eight directions,
so too is liberation:
by relying on the eight applications, it manifests and removes the obstacles to liberation.
The Venerable Ghosaka spoke thus:
"Regarding the three points of similarity and the three points of difference between liberation and [the other two],
as for the three points of similarity:"
Just as an elephant trainer can only tame an elephant by directing it toward a specific goal,
so too is the Blessed One:
he can only train those to be converted by directing them toward liberation.
Second, like an elephant trainer who at one time approaches from only one direction to train a single elephant,
so too is the Blessed One.
At one time, relying solely on a single type of liberation, he tames those to be trained;
this is like a trainer of elephants who,
when causing the elephant to move toward one direction, makes it travel far from other directions.
The Blessed One is likewise;
when he causes a being to be converted to give rise to one liberation so that it manifests before them, the other liberations remain distant and do not manifest.
Thus, they are said to be different in three ways.
It is like an elephant trainer:
one must lead the elephant toward a specific direction in order to train it.
The World-Honored One is not like this.
Sitting upright in one place, he also enables those being transformed to give rise to liberation.
Second, he is like an elephant trainer who,
at one time, approaches from only one direction to train a single elephant.
The World-Honored One is not so;
at one time, he causes many who are to be transformed to give rise to many liberations.
This is like a trainer of elephants.
When a trained elephant is directed toward one direction, it remains far from other directions;
the Blessed One is not so.
When he causes a transformed being to give rise to one liberation such that it manifests before them, the other liberations remain near because they are already accomplished.
Furthermore, the Buddha, wishing to manifest himself as the supreme tamer,
spoke of liberation using directional terminology.
It was heard that the great King Prasenajit, the lord of Kośala, once said:
The king issued an edict for elephant catchers to capture large wild elephants and commanded the elephant trainers to tame them skillfully according to the methods of elephant training.
Once the elephants were tamed, the king would ride out together with the elephant masters to hunt.
At that time, the elephant he was riding upon saw a herd of female elephants;
his lustful desire flared up, and he immediately bolted in pursuit.
Although the mahout exhausted all his skills, he could not turn the elephant back.
The king and the elephant trainer were both wounded.
By chance, [the trainer] climbed a tree and escaped with his life back to the palace.
The king reprimanded the elephant trainer and subjected him to legal punishment.
Then the elephant trainer said to the Great King, "That elephant is truly tamed;
I pray that Your Majesty will permit me to verify this.
At that time, the elephant, desiring rest, quickly returned to the palace.
Seeing this, the elephant trainer was about to go to the king’s presence;
he then placed a red-hot iron ball upon the elephant’s head and spoke slowly to it, saying:
"This is the final method for taming you."
"You should endure it.
If you do not endure it, they will certainly subject you to the same sequence of painful training that was previously used to tame you.
Upon hearing this, the elephant endured it and remained as immovable as a mountain.
At that time, a glowing red-hot iron ball scorched the elephant’s head like burning birch bark.
When the king saw this, he marveled at it and ordered the iron ball to be removed.
He then asked the elephant trainer, "Since this elephant has already been tamed, why did you act in such a manner before?"
The elephant trainer knelt and said,
"I am able to train the body, but I cannot train the mind.
The King asked, "Is there anyone who can train the mind?"
The elephant trainer said, "There is one called the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
who can cure the various ailments of the body and mind of sentient beings.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and immediately granted his permission to the elephant trainer.
Mounting a well-trained elephant, he proceeded to where the Buddha was;
there he saw the World-Honored One surrounded by a multitude of many hundreds of thousands preaching the Dharma.
He went forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha then expounded the profound Dharma for the king—
teaching that is not within the knowledge of solitary realizers or śrāvakas—
and addressed the bhikṣus as one who tames an elephant.
When training an elephant, one trains it by directing it toward only one of the eight directions;
the same applies to training horses, oxen, and so forth.
When the Unsurpassed Tamer trains those to be converted, he does so simultaneously by means of the eight directions. These "eight directions" are a metaphor for the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
Thus, it is revealed that the World-Honored One is the supreme tamer.
Regarding the eight liberations, he spoke using the term "direction.
*Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Eighty-four.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Eighty-five,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section Two: The Aggregate of Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha), Part Four: The Chapter on the Ten Gates (Daśamukha-nirdeśa), Fifteenth Subsection. As stated in the Sūtra:
A certain bhikṣu approached the Buddha,
prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
you speak of the element of light, the element of purity,
and the element of the base of infinite space.
The sphere of infinite consciousness,
the sphere of nothingness,
and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*). Regarding these seven elements, by what conditions are they established?
The Blessed One replied:
The element of light is designated in dependence upon darkness;
the element of purity is designated in dependence upon impurity;
and the element of the sphere of infinite space is designated in dependence upon the realm of form.
The sphere of infinite consciousness is designated by taking the limit of conditions as its object;
the sphere of nothingness is designated by taking all that exists as its object;
and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is designated by taking the presence of a body as its object.
Because the body has ceased due to conditions, the element of cessation is designated.
Question: Upon what matter does the bhikṣu here base his question?
And upon what matter does the Blessed One respond?
Answer: Herein, the bhikṣu asks by way of concealed characteristics based on the eight liberations, and the Buddha also answers by way of these same concealed characteristics.
As for "clarifying the elements":
This refers to the first two liberations.
The "pure realm" refers to the third liberation.
The four formless bases and elements refer to the four formless liberations.
The element of cessation refers to—
This refers to the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-vimokṣa*).
Question: For what reason do the bhikṣus rely on the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) to frame their questions and answers?
Answer: Because those bhikṣus have few desires and are content, concealing their own virtues.
He asked this question because he did not wish others to know that he himself possessed such virtue.
Why did the Blessed One answer by concealing the characteristics with the eight liberations?
He replied: it was because he wished to fulfill the inclinations of the bhikṣus.
That is to say, that bhikṣu thinks to himself:
"If the Buddha were to answer me by concealing his true intent,
would it not be excellent regarding the eight liberations?"
For this reason, the Blessed One answered by way of a concealed formulation (*paryāya*).
In this context, the establishment of the element of light (*ālokadhātu*) based on darkness (*andhakāra*) refers to the following:
"darkness" denotes the craving for the sense-object of form (*rūpāyatana*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The first two liberations are established as being based upon those [objects] because they serve as their antidotes.
Regarding the designation of a "pure realm" based on the impure:
"impurity" refers to the first two liberations and the third liberation.
Because it is the antidote to that, it is established by taking that as its object.
Regarding the designation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-dhātu*) as having the realm of form (*rūpāyatana*) as its object:
the "realm of form" refers to the fourth dhyāna and the fourth liberation (*vimokṣa*).
Because it serves as the antidote to that [preceding level], it is established by taking that as its object.
As for the designation of the "sphere of infinite consciousness" (vijñānānantyāyatana-dhātu) based on the limit of the object:
the "limit" refers to the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana).
Because that [attainment] abides at the limit of form, the fifth liberation is established by taking that as its object, as it serves as its antidote.
As for the designation of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) based on the object "there is nothing": [it is so called because one perceives that there is nothing whatsoever].
"All" refers to the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), because therein the aspect of infinity operates.
Since the sixth liberation is its antidote, it is established by taking that as its object.

As for the designation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) based on the "existence of body": [it is so called] because of the presence of the physical body.
The "existence-body" refers to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
This is because there is still a body of birth and death, and it is not entirely non-existent;
therefore, the seventh liberation is established as having that [sphere] as its object, since it serves as its antidote.
Regarding the statement that "the element of cessation is designated based on the cessation of the basis-of-existence (ātmabhāva)":
the cessation of the basis-of-existence refers to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
because it is capable of ceasing the phenomena of the basis-of-existence belonging to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The eighth liberation is established by taking that [previous state] as its object, because it serves as its antidote. Some say:
herein, the bhikṣu asks based on the characteristics of the brief and extensive separation from the defilements and obscurations of the three realms.
The World-Honored One also answered by means of this indirect indication (*paryāya*).
Regarding the "clear realm" (*vidyā-dhātu*),
it briefly reveals the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) for detachment from the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Regarding this designation based on darkness:
"darkness" refers to the craving for the five objects of desire in the desire realm.
Since the preparatory stage of the form realm is its antidote, it is established by taking that [craving] as its object.
The "pure realm" briefly indicates freedom from the defilements of the desire realm.
The "realm of infinite space" briefly indicates freedom from the defilements of the form realm.

The "sphere of infinite consciousness," the "sphere of nothingness," and the "sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" extensively reveal the abandonment of defilements pertaining to the formless realm;
the "sphere of cessation" briefly reveals the abandonment of defilements pertaining to the formless realm.
Regarding this, some say that the "element of light" (*āloka-dhātu*) briefly indicates freedom from the defilements of the desire realm,
because it is only through the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration that the darkness of desire is severed.
The "pure realm" (*śuddhadhātu*) extensively reveals the freedom from the defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
because the four dhyānas and so forth are all termed "pure.
As for the "realm of infinite space" (*ākāśānantyāyatana*):
The latter three formless bases and elements briefly illustrate the abandonment of defilements pertaining to the form realm;
the element of cessation extensively illustrates the abandonment of defilements pertaining to the formless realm.
This briefly indicates the detachment from the defilements of the formless realm;
for in the desire realm, there is defilement in only one stage.
It also briefly indicates the antidotes to the defilements of the four stages each in the form and formless realms.
The extensive and concise [teachings] reveal their respective antidotes.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
herein, a bhikṣu asks by means of a concealed formulation based on the eight attainments (*samāpatti*).
The Buddha also answered by means of this indirect method (*paryāya*).
However, there are variations in the recitation of this sūtra text;
that is to say, some increase the number of elements (*dhātu*) while others decrease the "vast elements" (*vistara-dhātu*).
Regarding the "element of light":

this refers to the first and second dhyānas. As for the statement that these are "designated by way of darkness as their object," "darkness" refers to external conditions consisting of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
The first and second dhyānas are established as having those [defilements] as their objects because they serve as their antidotes.
The "pure realm" refers to the third dhyāna.
The "vast realm" refers to the fourth dhyāna.
The realms of the four formless states are, that is, the four formless states themselves.
As this sutra states:
At that time, those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, received it with joy and reverence,
and further addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what concentration are the element of light up to the element of cessation attained?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
Thus, these various elements are attained through their own respective practices or through other meditative concentrations.
Having heard this, the bhikṣu rejoiced, respectfully accepted it, prostrated to the Buddha, and departed.
Regarding this, some say:
He asked about the attainment of the elements (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, there are those who say he asked about the attainment of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
If one asks how those elements (dhātus) are attained, the intention of that question is as follows:
"By what meditative concentration (samādhi) is the essence of these various elements attained?
The Buddha’s answer is intended to mean: [as follows].
The element of light up to the element of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are attained through one's own meditative concentration.
"One's own meditative concentration" refers to one's own preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*).
Through the separation from the defilements of a lower stage by means of the threshold concentration (*sāmantaka*) of one's own stage, one attains the liberations of that stage.
That is to say, through the separation from the defilements of the desire realm by means of the threshold concentration of the first *dhyāna*, one attains the first and second liberations.
By means of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the fourth dhyāna, one becomes free from the defilements of the third dhyāna and attains the pure liberation (*śuddhavimokṣa*).

By means of the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one becomes free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna and attains the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.
Up to the attainment of the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of its preparatory stage (sāmantaka),
one becomes free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness; however,
the realm of cessation (nirodhadhātu) is attained solely through other meditative concentrations.
The remaining concentrations refer to those concentrations that have a basis,
namely the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
This is because it is the fundamental concentration for all states of existence (*bhava*).
Some say that this is called "possessing superior concentration" because it is the most excellent among all states of existence.
Some call this the "attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*),
because it is the entry into and emergence from the cessation of perception and feeling.
By means of this attainment, one obtains the eighth liberation.
If one asks how those questions are to be severed, the intention of that question is as follows:
by which meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are these various elements (*dhātu*) severed? The Buddha’s response is intended to mean: [by the meditative absorption of cessation].
The element of light up to the element of nothingness is attained by means of one’s own practice and other meditative concentrations.
Regarding "attainment through one’s own practice": [it refers to] meditative concentration achieved through one's own cultivation.
This refers to the contaminated concentrations (*sāsrava-samādhi*) belonging to their respective preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
"Other concentrations" refers to all uncontaminated concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*),
ranging from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
In all cases, detachment from defilement and the abandonment of those [defilements] are attained through these two meditative absorptions;
however, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is attained solely by means of other meditative absorptions.
Only untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) can abandon the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and thereby attain their cessation;
therefore, the element of cessation (*nirodha-dhātu*) is attained solely by means of that which remains.
"That which remains" refers to the cessation of the personal existence (*satkāya-nirodha*), which is precisely nirvāṇa.
At the time of parinirvāṇa, the abandonment of the attainment of cessation is called "cessation.
Because that cessation is attained through the remainder of nirvāṇa, it is said to be "attained by means of the remainder.
As for the eight bases of mastery (aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni):
First, perceiving internal forms while observing external forms that are limited;
second, perceiving internal forms while observing external forms that are manifold;
third, having no perception of internal forms while observing external forms that are limited.
Fourth, having no perception of internal forms, one contemplates external forms that are manifold.
Having no perception of internal forms, one contemplates various external forms— blue, yellow, red, and white—
which are further divided into four types.
These eight kinds are called the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these eight bases of mastery?
Answer: Their intrinsic nature is the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*), because they serve as the antidote to attachment.
If one takes both the associated [mental factors] and the concomitant [factors] together,
then those in the desire realm have the four aggregates as their intrinsic nature,
while those in the form realm have the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature.
This is called the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*):
its own-being, substance, essence, characteristic, constituent part, and fundamental nature.
Having already explained its essential nature, I shall now explain its purpose.
Question: Why are they called "bases of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana)?
What is the meaning of "base of mastery"?
Answer: They are called bases of mastery because they master the objects of perception.
Furthermore, they are called "mastery objects" (*abhibhvāyatana*) because they overcome all afflictions.
Although a practitioner may not be able to master every object of focus,
the fact that they do not give rise to afflictions toward those objects is also termed "mastery."
As stated in the sūtras:
they are called "bases of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana) because one attains mastery therein.
These eight bases of mastery belong entirely to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Regarding the stages: the first four spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are located in the first and second dhyānas, as well as in the preparatory stage (anāgamya) and the intermediate dhyāna;
the latter four spheres of mastery are located in the fourth dhyāna.
As for their basis, they all arise based on a body belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As for their mode of activity (*ākāra*), none of them possess a clear or distinct mode of activity.
As for their object (*ālambana*), they all take as their object all forms (*rūpāyatana*) within the desire realm.
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret the sūtra?
It says that the Venerable Aniruddha was staying in a monastery in Śrāvastī, at which time there were four celestial maidens of delightful appearance.
They approached the Venerable One’s seat and stood before him, saying:
"We possess mastery over the transformation of the four types of physical forms."
They are able to manifest whatever forms they desire;
they enjoy themselves with these manifestations, playing according to their hearts' delight,
and they can manifest all kinds of clothing and ornaments.
"I pray that you will graciously accept this to serve as my offerings.
The Venerable Aniruddha thought to himself,
"I should take him as the object for the cultivation of the meditation on impurity."
Having formed this thought, he entered the first dhyāna;
yet, even taking that as his object, he was unable to give rise to the perception of impurity.
This continued until he later entered the fourth dhyāna, where likewise, even taking that as his object, he was unable to give rise to the perception of impurity.
Again, he thought:
"The bodies of these goddesses possess various colors that delude the minds of men;
if they were made of only a single color,"
I am able to give rise to the contemplation of impurity regarding them.
Having brought this to mind, I spoke before my sisters and others, saying: "I have attained mastery over the transformation of the four bases of form;
I pray that you may all manifest the color blue for me."
The goddess followed the instruction and immediately manifested the color blue;
however, he was still unable to give rise to the perception of impurity.
He then thought again:
He possesses mastery over the transformation of the four primary colors;
if he produces another color or brings to mind an object of perception to give rise to the contemplation of impurity, having reflected, he utters the words: "May the yellow appear."
The celestial maidens immediately manifested themselves all as yellow;
yet he was still unable to give rise to the perception of impurity.
He spoke again to the celestial maidens, and they all manifested themselves as red.
Even with such conditions, one is still unable to give rise to the perception of impurity.
Furthermore, one reflects:
"Among all forms, white is most conducive to the contemplation of impurity."
"I shall cause them all to appear white.
Having thought this, she spoke, saying, "May they appear white.
The celestial maidens then all appeared white.
Even with such conditions, he was unable to give rise to the perception of impurity.
The Venerable Anuruddha thought to himself:
"The celestial form is so exquisite and marvelous that it cannot be overcome."
Thereupon, he closed his eyes and sat in silence.
The devas, knowing that the Venerable One was entirely free from any defiled mind,
felt ashamed at their mutual gaze and suddenly vanished.
At that time, the Venerable One’s meditative concentration could not overcome that object,
nor could the object overcome the Venerable One’s concentration;
it was like two strong men whose strength is equal, such that neither can overcome the other.
This case is also like that.
How should one interpret what is said in this sutra?
The answer is: although the Venerable Aniruddha was unable to master the objective sphere of the celestial form realm, [he could still perceive it].
Śāriputra and others, possessing sharp faculties and superior meditative concentration, are all able to surpass it.
Question: Is it possible for one to give rise to the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-saṃjñā) by taking the physical form of the Buddha as the object?
Some say: [it is possible].
It is impossible.
Because the Buddha’s body, its color, and its radiance are brilliant, pure, and stainless,
no one can give rise to the perception of impurity toward it.
Some say that all ordinary beings,
śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are unable to give rise to the perception of impurity regarding the physical form of the Buddhas.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to give rise to the perception of impurity regarding the physical form and appearance of a Buddha’s body.
Some say that there are two kinds of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
First, contemplating the defects of form;
second, contemplating the dependent origination of form.
Regarding the contemplation of the defects of form:
One cannot give rise to the perception of impurity toward the Buddha.
However, one who contemplates the dependent origination of form can also give rise to the perception of impurity toward the Buddha.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
There are two types of contemplation on impurity:
first, that which operates with respect to specific characteristics;
second, that which operates with respect to general characteristics.
Regarding that which functions with respect to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
one cannot give rise to an impure perception toward the Buddha.
Regarding that which functions with respect to general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*),...
One can also take the Buddha as an object and give rise to the perception of impurity.
Question: Do these various contemplations on impurity belong to the mental ground (manobhūmi) or to the five sensory consciousnesses?
Answer: They belong to the mental ground, not to the five sensory consciousnesses.
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret the sūtra?
For example, it says: "Having seen forms with the eye, one contemplates them as impure and reflects in accordance with reality," and so on at length, up to:
"Having felt tangibles with the body, one contemplates them as impure and reflects in accordance with reality."
Answer: Because the various contemplations on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) are induced through the application of the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), this statement was made.

Just as the mental applications (*manopavicāra*) actually belong only to the mental level (*manobhūmi*), so too should it be understood that these [contemplations] are likewise induced by the five consciousnesses.
Question: Since all contemplations of impurity take only the sense-sphere of form as their object,
one should simply say that after having seen a form with the eye,
one contemplates it as impure and engages in appropriate reflection.
Why is it also said that after hearing a sound with the ear—and so on, in detail, until—after feeling a tangible object with the body, one reflects according to the principle?
Answer: Just as the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) can suppress greed for visible forms, it can also suppress greed for the other four objects.
To speak in this way is not contrary to reason. Some say:
"Having seen forms with the eye," and so on at length, "until having felt tangibles with the body."
Each and every one of these is capable of inducing the contemplation of the impurity of form; therefore, it is said thus.
Alternatively, some say that the contemplation of impurity does not arise by taking sound and so forth as its object.
There is another distinct aspect of the impure that is preeminent,
which arises as an object-condition for the aspect of impurity such as sound and so forth.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
The various yoga practitioners first take the sense-sphere of form as their object and cultivate the meditation on impurity;
once this has reached maturity, they subsequently take sound and the other [sense-objects] as their objects.
One should give rise to the perception of revulsion to overcome that object;
it is well if one can thus overcome it.
If one cannot overcome it, one should again take the sense-sphere of form as an object and practice the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
It is like those who make their living by practicing combat;
when they emerge from the wooden chest and defeat others in battle, it is well.
If they do not achieve victory, they return to the wooden chest.
This case is likewise, and therefore there is no contradiction.
Other masters say that this sūtra does not state that the contemplation of impurity arises with form as its object.
It merely speaks of generating the perception of revulsion toward form and so forth;
having observed this to completion, one is eventually able to feel revulsion even for the mind and mental factors themselves.
Therefore, that sutra says: "Having cognized phenomena with the mind..."
Because one contemplates impurity through appropriate reflection (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
the term "impure" indicates the perception of revulsion (*pratikūla-saṃjñā*) rather than the actual meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Therefore, the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*) take all visible forms (*rūpa-āyatana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as their objects of focus.
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), these eight are associated exclusively with the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding wisdom (*jñāna*), all are associated exclusively with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*):
None of these are associated with samādhi.
Regarding those associated with the faculties, it is stated in general that they are associated only with joy (prīti) and equanimity (upekṣā).
As for the three time periods, they all pertain to all three time periods.
Regarding the objects of the three periods of time:
these eight bases of mastery take the past as their object when they are past,
and the present as their object when they are present.
Regarding future [dharmas]: if they are dharmas that will arise, they take the future as their object;
if they are dharmas that will not arise, they take the three periods of time as their objects, whether they are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
All [of these] are exclusively wholesome; those that take wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral [factors] as their objects all take these three kinds as their objects.
Those that are bound to the three realms and those that are unbound are all exclusively bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Those that take factors bound to the three realms and those that are unbound as their objects [are likewise so].
All [of these] take only those bound to the desire realm as their objects;
those that are trainee, non-trainee, or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee are all exclusively neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
Regarding those conditioned by what is in training, what is beyond training, and what is neither in training nor beyond training:
all of these take only that which is neither in training nor beyond training as their object.
As for those [factors] to be abandoned by seeing, those to be abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned: [the same applies].
All are abandoned solely by cultivation.
Those that take as their objects what is abandoned by seeing, what is abandoned by cultivation, and what is not abandoned,
all take as their objects only what is abandoned by cultivation.
Regarding those that take names as conditions and those that take meanings as conditions: all of them take only meanings as conditions.
As for those that take their own continuum, another's continuum, or what is not a continuum as conditions: [they likewise take only meanings as conditions].
The first two take as their objects both one's own and others' mental continuums;
regarding the latter six,
some say they take only others' continuums as their objects.
Some say that it takes both one's own and others' continuums as its object,
and is acquired through preparatory effort or through the abandonment of defilements.
Both types are common to all.
That which is obtained through the abandonment of defilements is acquired when one attains the first dhyāna by becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm.
Those in the second dhyāna attain it when they become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna;
those in the fourth dhyāna attain it when they become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
As for those who attain it through application (*prayoga-pratilambhika*), they attain it by means of application, as it manifests through application.
It also manifests through application;
the śrāvaka does so either by means of middling application or by means of superior application.
The Pratyekabuddha attains it through inferior preparatory effort,
whereas the Buddha attains it and brings it to manifestation without preparatory effort;
this refers to what has been previously attained and what has not yet been attained.
All [of these] pertain to both what has been previously attained and what has not yet been attained;

that is to say, both noble beings (*ārya*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) within the Buddhist tradition (*adhyātma-dharma*) pertain to both types, whereas ordinary persons outside the Buddhist tradition (*bāhya-dharma*) pertain only to what has been previously attained.
Thus has the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) been explained.
Each individual characteristic should now be explained in detail.
Having the perception of internal forms, one observes external forms that are few, whether beautiful or ugly;
having superior knowledge and superior vision regarding those forms, this is the first sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
In this context, "possessing internal perception of form" means that one has not yet become detached from, has not yet abandoned, and has not yet eliminated the various internal perceptions of form.
"Contemplating external forms" means that one has become detached from, abandoned, and eliminated those various internal perceptions of form.
By means of attention consisting of resolute conviction, one contemplates external forms.
"Small" refers to two kinds of smallness:
first, smallness of the object of focus.
Second, it has little self-mastery.
As for its excellence,
it means that the colors— blue, yellow, red, and white— are not marred or degraded.
As for "the foul," it refers to bluish,
yellowish, reddish, or whiteish colors that are decayed and ruined;
regarding those various colors, one possesses superior knowledge and superior vision.
That is to say, for the sake of subduing sensual desire,
for the sake of severing and destroying sensual desire,
and for the sake of transcending sensual desire.
Regarding those various forms, one gives rise to superior knowledge and vision and gains mastery over them;
that is to say, one masters them by means of grasping them and subduing them,
just as a great lord or his son masters his own servants by means of gathering them and disciplining them.
Therefore, it is called "superior knowledge and superior vision.
Regarding "this is the first base of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*):
"first" refers to its position as the initial one in the numerical sequence.
Regarding "or entering that meditative absorption in the sequence of the first base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)," this refers to all wholesome form,
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness present at the time of entering that absorption;
these collectively are termed the "base of mastery."
As with the first base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), it should be understood that the second base of mastery is likewise;
the difference is that here,
in the second, one contemplates external forms as "many" (*bahudhā*).
There are two kinds of "abundance": first, abundance of the object of focus;
second, abundance of mastery.
The rest is as previously explained.
Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are few, whether beautiful or ugly;
one gains mastery over those forms through superior knowledge and vision.
This is the third base of mastery.
In this context, "having no perception of internal forms" means that one has already detached from, relinquished, and eliminated the individual perceptions of internal forms.
"Contemplating external forms" refers to [the subsequent stage].
That is to say, without having abandoned or removed internal, individual forms,
one contemplates external forms through the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
The rest is as previously explained.
As with the third sphere of mastery, it should be understood that the fourth sphere of mastery is likewise;
the difference is that in the fourth sphere of mastery, one contemplates external forms as manifold.
Without internal perception of form,
one perceives external forms that are blue— blue in color, blue in appearance, and emitting blue light—
infinite, pure, sublime, lovely, delightful, and not disagreeable.
Just as with the umāka flower,
or like the indigo-dyed garments of Vārāṇasī,
one has such a perception regarding those various colors, knowing them clearly and seeing them clearly.
This is the fifth base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Herein, the meaning of "internally perceiving no form while externally perceiving forms" is as previously explained.
"Blue" refers to all blue-colored things.
Whether large or small, they are collectively described as blue.
As for "blue manifestation," it means that this blue color is illuminated by the eye and is the objective domain traversed by the eye; therefore, it is called blue manifestation.
Regarding "the manifestation of blue":

this means that once that blue color has been cognized by the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), it subsequently induces the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to also conceptualize it; therefore, it is called the "manifestation of blue."
"Blue light" means that it is called blue light because the radiance of that blue color shines forth.
"Immeasurable" means...
That is to say, because that blue color is vast and without limit, it is called "immeasurable.
Regarding "immeasurably pure and sublime":
this means that, just as the blue color is vast and without limit, [so too is its purity].
Those pure and wondrous marks are likewise without limit; therefore,
they are called "immeasurable purity and wonder," which is to say,
"delightful."
That is to say, because that blue color is delightful and pleasing, causing the mind to be joyful, it is called "delightful" (*abhirāma*).
As for "delightful to behold" (*abhipreta*), it means that the blue color is lovely and worthy of being played with.
If one takes this as an object and no longer longs for anything else, it is therefore called "delightful.
That which cannot be opposed means that the blue color causes the mind to become patient, compliant, and inclined toward it.
Therefore, it is called "irreversible.
It is like the *umaka* flower or the indigo-dyed robes of Vārāṇasī;
because that [color] is an extreme blue, it is cited as a metaphor.
Regarding those forms, one possesses superior knowledge and superior vision;
the meaning is as previously explained.
"One who has such a perception" means:
That is to say, when the perception of blue appears before one regarding those blue objects as previously described,
this is the fifth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*);
its meaning is also as explained before.
As it was stated regarding the blue superior sphere (*kṛtsnāyatana*), one should know that the same applies to the yellow, red, and white superior spheres.
The distinction is that for the yellow superior sphere, one should speak of it as being like the *karṇikāra* flower.
The red *kṛtsnāyatana* should be described as being like the *pāṇḍubhūtika* flower;
the white *kṛtsnāyatana* should be described as being like the *uśanastārā* [Venus] in Vārāṇasī.
The yellow, red, and white garments should be described according to their respective types.
Question: Among the four primary colors, which is the most excellent?
Venerable Vasumitra stated: "White is the most excellent, for it is commonly said by the world to be auspicious."
Just as the eastern direction is the most excellent among the four directions because it is auspicious, so too is the white color.
The Venerable One said:
When focusing on the color white, it causes the mind to become clear and pure;
because it does not conform to dullness and sleep,
it is most excellent for being able to sustain the body.
The ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana) refer to the totalities of blue, yellow, red, white, earth, water, fire, wind, infinite space, and infinite consciousness.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of these ten totalities?
Answer: The first eight spheres of mastery (*kṛtsnāyatana*) have non-attachment as their wholesome root for their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because they serve as the antidote to attachment.
If one includes their associated and concomitant factors, those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have the four aggregates (*skandha*) as their intrinsic nature.
The form realm has the five aggregates as its intrinsic nature.
The latter two universal bases both have the four aggregates as their intrinsic nature.
This is what is called the intrinsic nature of the universal bases.

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of my own entities, their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and their fundamental essence (*prakṛti*) have already been explained; now, the reason for their designation shall be explained.
Question: Why are they called "totality-spheres" (*kṛtsnāyatana*)?
What is the meaning of "totality" (kṛtsnāyatana)?
Answer: It is called a totality for two reasons:
first, by way of continuity.
Second, by way of vastness.
Regarding "uninterrupted":
it is called uninterrupted because the mental engagement of resolute conviction—such as that which perceives [the earth] as purely blue and so forth—is not interspersed with anything else.
Regarding "vast": this refers to the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*) directed toward objects such as blue.
It is called "vast" because the characteristics of its object are boundless.
The Venerable One said:
"They are called 'totalities' (kṛtsnāyatana) because their objects of focus are vast and without interval.
These ten totalities are [as follows]:..."
The first eight universal bases belong to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
the latter two universal bases belong to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
As for their level, the first eight universal bases are situated in the fourth dhyāna.
The ninth universal base (kṛtsnāyatana) is situated in the sphere of infinite space;
the tenth universal base is situated in the sphere of infinite consciousness. Why is this so?
Because the pure liberation resides in the fourth dhyāna,
one is thereby able to enter the latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
These latter four spheres of mastery, in turn, enable one to enter the former eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Among these, liberation grasps only the general aspect of purity regarding the object of focus,
yet is unable to differentiate between blue, yellow, red, and white.
The latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), however, are able to differentiate between blue, yellow, red, and white.
Yet they have not yet been able to produce the aspect of "boundlessness.
The first four *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totalities) are not merely conceptualizations of blue, yellow, red, and white;
they are also capable of producing the aspect of boundlessness.
This means that one contemplates each [color], such as blue, as being boundless; then,
one further reflects upon what these colors, such as blue, depend upon,
and realizes that they depend upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Next, one contemplates that each element, such as earth, is individually infinite.
Then, one reflects on what causes this perceived form to be so vast, and realizes it is due to space.
Subsequently, one gives rise to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and further reflects on what serves as the basis for this perceiving consciousness.
Knowing that it depends upon the consciousness of infinite space,
one next gives rise to the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
This consciousness which serves as its basis has no further distinct basis.
Therefore, the higher [realms] are not established as *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality bases).

Regarding their basis: the first eight *kṛtsnāyatanas* arise based solely on a body in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whereas the latter two *kṛtsnāyatanas* arise based on bodies belonging to all three realms (*tridhātu*).
As for the aspects (*ākāra*):
these ten all function with infinite aspects.
As for the objects of focus (*ālambana*):
The first eight universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) take only the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) within the desire realm as their object;
the latter two universal bases each take the four aggregates (skandha) of their own respective level as their object.
As for the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna):
The first eight spheres of mastery (kṛtsnāyatana) are associated with the application of mindfulness to the body;
the latter two are associated with the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
All of these are associated with conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna); none of them are associated with meditative absorption (samādhi).
Regarding association with the faculties (*indriya*):
all are associated exclusively with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Regarding the three time periods (*adhvan*): [all are associated].
All of them pertain to the three periods of time.
Regarding those that take the three periods as their objects:
among the first eight universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), those in the past take the past as their object.

The present [totality] takes the present and future as its object; if it is a dharma that arises, it takes the future as its object, whereas if it is a dharma that does not arise, it takes the three time periods as its object.
The latter two totalities both take the three time periods as their objects.
Regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral:

all [of these] take only the wholesome as their object; the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral [objects] take the preceding eight universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) as their objects of the three types.
Regarding the fact that the latter two universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) take as their objects the wholesome and the indeterminate,
as well as those bound to the three realms and those that are unbound:
the first eight universal bases are bound only to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
The latter two universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) are associated exclusively with the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Regarding those that take as their objects both what is associated with the three realms and what is unassociated:
the first eight universal bases take as their objects only what is associated with the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The latter two spheres of mastery take only those things bound to the formless realm as their objects.
As for those that are associated with training, those beyond training, and those that are neither associated with training nor beyond training,
they are all exclusively associated with neither-training-nor-beyond-training.
Regarding those conditioned by that which is in training (śaikṣa), that which is beyond training (aśaikṣa), and that which is neither in training nor beyond training:
all of these take as their object only that which is neither in training nor beyond training.
As for those [factors] to be abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya), those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), and those not to be abandoned (aheya): [the same applies].
All are abandoned solely by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Regarding those that take as their objects what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), what is abandoned by cultivation, and what is not abandoned:
the first eight *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totalities) take only what is abandoned by cultivation as their object.
The latter two universal bases take as their objects those [defilements] abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
Regarding that which takes names as its object and that which takes meanings as its object:
both take meanings as their object.
Regarding those that depend on one’s own continuum, another’s continuum,
or neither: some say that this refers to the first eight universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
They take only the mental continuums of others as their object.
Some say they take both one's own and others' continuums as objects.
The latter two *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totality bases) both take both one's own and others' continuums as objects.
Regarding those acquired through application and those acquired through detachment from defilement,
both are comprised of acquisition through application and acquisition through detachment from defilement.
As for those acquired through detachment from defilement:
The first eight spheres of mastery (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are attained when one becomes free from the defilements of the third dhyāna;
the ninth sphere of mastery is attained when one becomes free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna;
and the tenth sphere of mastery is attained when one becomes free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Later, that [attainment] manifests through application;
for one who attains it by means of application,
it is acquired through application and also manifests through application.
Śrāvakas [attain it] either through middling application or superior application;
pratyekabuddhas through inferior application.
The Buddha attains and manifests [these qualities] without relying on preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Regarding those already attained and those never before attained,
both categories are comprised within the "already attained" and the "never before attained."
This means that for noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the Buddhist teaching, these [attainments] are both previously obtained and not yet obtained;
for ordinary beings outside the Buddhist teaching, they are only previously obtained.
Question: What is the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for these ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*)?
Answer: The first four universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) take visual consciousness as their preparatory application;
at the time of fulfillment, they take the four colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—as their objective spheres.
The middle four universal bases take tactile consciousness as their preparatory application.
At the time of their full accomplishment, they take the four tangible objects— earth, water, fire, and wind— as their objective spheres.
Some maintain that the first seven universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) employ visual consciousness as their preparatory application (prayoga).
In one instance, the sphere of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) takes tactile consciousness as its preparatory application.
Why is this? Because [the spheres of totality] of earth, water, fire, and...
Because it takes color manifested by shape as its object;
because the wind-kasiṇa takes the tactile quality of motion as its object.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
The first eight bases of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) all take visual consciousness as their preparatory application (prayoga). Why is this?
Because even the base of totality of wind takes visible form (rūpa) as its object (ālambana).
As it is said in the world:
there are east winds, south winds, west winds, and north winds;
there are winds with dust and winds without dust.
The Vixnava wind, the Vairambha wind,
the wind-circle wind, and so forth.
Therefore, the sphere of infinite wind also takes the sphere of form as its object.
The sphere of infinite space takes space as its preliminary application (*prayoga*),
and the sphere of infinite consciousness takes consciousness as its preliminary application.
Thus, the general characteristics of the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) have been explained.
Now, their individual specific characteristics shall be briefly described.
Regarding all that is blue—whether above, below, or across—
Non-dual and immeasurable;
the arising of the single perception of blue is the first *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality sphere).
As for "all that is blue":
That is to say, all blue colors, whether small or large, are collectively termed "blue.
"Above" refers to the upper direction;
"below" refers to the lower direction.
"Surrounding" means the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions.
"Without duality" means that it is purely blue in appearance, without any other intermingling.
"Immeasurable" means...
This refers to being boundless.
Regarding "giving rise to the perception of a single blue":
this means that through the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), one gives rise to the perception of a single blue in all places.
Regarding "this is the first universal base" (*kṛtsnāyatana*):
"first" means that it stands at the beginning in terms of numerical sequence;
or, it refers to the fact that this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) occurs first in the sequence of the universal bases.
