This refers to the wholesome form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness present at the time of entering this meditative absorption; these collectively are termed "totalities" (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
As explained in detail for the totality of blue, so it is for all others, up to and including the totality of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Regarding the distinction:
the latter two universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) should not be described as "form" (rūpa);
they should be described only as the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Question: Regarding the first eight universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), it is possible for them to have "above" and "below," because their objects of focus possess spatial location.
As for the final two universal bases, they take space and consciousness as their objects.
Since the objects of focus have no spatial location, nor superiority or inferiority, how can one say that there is superiority or inferiority? Answer:
Although the objects of the latter two universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) have no spatial location, nor superiority or inferiority, [they are so designated].
However, since the meditative concentrations upon which they rely are of three grades,
one may speak of "higher" and "lower.
"Higher" refers to relying on a superior grade of concentration.
"Lower" refers to relying on a state of concentration of inferior grade;
"sideways," as mentioned again, refers to relying on a state of concentration of middling grade.
Furthermore, for the practitioner of contemplation:
Because the places where bodies reside have upper and lower levels, one may speak of "above," "below," and "sideways.
Regarding these locations and so forth, what are their specific characteristics? "Below" refers to those dwelling among human beings;
"middle" refers to those dwelling in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).
Those at the highest level dwell in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
In this manner, extending even to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, they are distinguished as lower, middling, and superior in relation to one another;
those at the highest level are called "superior."
The inferior is called "downward," and the middling is called "sideways.
Question: Why is it that in the third dhyāna there are no liberations (vimokṣa), spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), or spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana)?
The answer is: "Because it is not a field or an implement," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, it serves as an antidote to the craving for form induced by the group of consciousnesses within the first dhyāna of the desire realm.
The first and second dhyānas establish the liberations, the bases of mastery, and the bases of totality as having impurity as their object;
this is because in the second and third dhyānas there is no craving for forms induced by the body of consciousness.
As for the third and fourth dhyānas...
The impure liberations (*aśubha-vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are not established [in the higher levels].

This is because the first three dhyānas possess vitarka, vicāra, joy, and bliss, and because they are disturbed by the activity of inhalation and exhalation; therefore, there are no pure liberations (*śubha-vimokṣa*) therein.

The latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the first eight totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) take pure and sublime objects as their cognitive focus and are able to subdue the afflictions; this matter is extremely difficult.
Therefore, they can only be accomplished by relying on a stage that is free from disturbance.
Furthermore, the third dhyāna is distant from the desire realm and is not the most excellent among the dhyānas;
therefore, it lacks the liberations, the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality. Moreover, the third dhyāna is like the third formless attainment.
Because they lack manifold merits, there is no liberation and so forth.
That is to say, the Sphere of Infinite Space and the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness possess the merit of infinite mental modes (*ākāra*),
while the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception possesses the merit of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
In the sphere of nothingness, there is no aspect of infinite conduct, nor is there the meditative attainment of cessation;

therefore, the merits of this stage are diminished compared to the third dhyāna. Just as in that [third dhyāna], it likewise lacks the merits of the liberations, the bases of mastery, and the totalities.
Furthermore, because the third dhyāna contains the most excellent experience of pleasure within the cycle of birth and death—
which causes the practitioner to become attached and deluded— it lacks the liberating bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Question: If that were so, there would be no immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), higher knowledges (*abhijñā*), or other such remaining qualities.
Answer: It is said that while the qualities are few, they are not entirely non-existent.
If the immeasurables and so forth were absent from this stage, this dhyāna would be empty and devoid of all qualities.

Furthermore, while those who possess the superknowledge of universal focus on the immeasurables sport in this stage, they do not attain the qualities of liberation, the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), or the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
This is because the suppression of afflictions through the specific focus on form and so forth is difficult to accomplish; therefore, these are absent in this stage.
As stated in the sutras:
one who has attained the meditative concentration on the earth-totality (*pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana*) forms this thought:
The earth is myself, and I am the earth;
the earth and I are non-dual and without distinction.
This is attained by one who has mastered the remaining universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
The detailed explanation regarding one's own respective objects of focus is likewise.
Question: One who attains the meditative absorption of the totalities (kṛtsnāyatana) must necessarily have already become detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
The view of self that arises therein must belong to the fourth dhyāna.
If it is a view of self belonging to the fourth dhyāna,
it must take as its object only the eight universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) of the fourth dhyāna stage and those preceding it.
It takes only the visible form (*rūpāyatana*) of the desire realm as its object.
How, then, can it be said that it shares the same objective basis (*ālambana*) as the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), which takes earth and so forth as its objects?
Regarding this, some say:
In this context, the term "one who has attained that concentration" is used for one who has not yet attained it;
just as one who is not a śramaṇa is called a śramaṇa,
and one who is not a brāhmaṇa is called a brāhmaṇa.
This means that by means of the preliminary stages of cultivation consisting of hearing and reflection regarding the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) within the desire realm,
one is still unable to abandon the afflictions of the desire realm and has not yet attained the fundamental stages of the spheres of totality.
Therefore, it is possible for the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) to arise with reference to the earth and so forth. Alternatively,
some say that it is not contradictory even to describe it using its former name.
It is like a king who,
although he has lost his royal throne,
is still conventionally designated by the name "king" and continues to be addressed as such.
Thus, although one has previously attained the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and so forth,
and now regresses from them, one is still said to have "attained" them;
such a person gives rise to the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) belonging to the desire realm.
It is not logically contradictory to conceive of a self based on the levels of the desire realm and so forth.
Furthermore, some say that this is based on the view of self associated with the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), which enter and emerge rapidly.
This statement is also not contradictory;
it means that although one has previously attained the earth-kasiṇa and other spheres,
one later quickly regresses and gives rise to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) belonging to the desire realm.
Taking the levels of the desire realm and so forth as a self,
one quickly regains the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) of the fourth dhyāna level, which likewise take those levels of the desire realm and so forth as their objects.
For example, Devadatta first attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
By means of the supernormal power of the base of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*), he transformed himself into a small child,
wearing a lay robe of gold thread and fashioning his hair into five topknots.
He played gracefully upon the lap of Prince Ajātaśatru,
causing the prince to realize that this was the Venerable Devadatta.
At that time, Ajātaśatru, out of affection and love, took him up and fondled him.
He blew upon it and placed it back into his mouth;
because Devadatta was greedy for gain and offerings, he swallowed the saliva.
Therefore, the Buddha rebuked him, saying:
"You are a corpse who eats human saliva.
As soon as he swallowed his saliva, he withdrew from his meditative absorption;
he quickly regained it, causing his transformed body to remain upon the prince's knee as before and play.
It should be understood that the view of self regarding the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) is likewise so.
Other masters say that among these,
the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) grasps the level of the fourth dhyāna and so forth as the self.
The first eight universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) also take the level of the fourth dhyāna and so forth as their objects.
Question: Is it not the case that the first eight universal bases take the forms of the desire realm as their objects?
Answer: They take both the forms of the desire realm and the forms of the fourth dhyāna as their objects.
Question: Since the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are purely and uniformly white in color, how can they be perceived as blue and so forth?
Answer: The sentient beings of the form realm are indeed purely and uniformly white in color.
"Those that are categorized as non-sentient also possess blue and other colors.
[The critique says:
"One should not make such a statement regarding them."
If there were a view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) that was associated with and co-existent with the eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
one might raise the objection: "How can a dharma that is associated and co-existent [with them] take either the fourth dhyāna or the desire realm as its object?"

However, one should not raise an objection on the grounds that the first eight universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are neither associated with nor co-existent with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
for a single sentient being may be called both "one who conceives of a self" and "one who has attained meditative concentration."
One is called a "proponent of self" because of the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
One is called an "attainer of meditative concentration" because of its universal presence.
The view of a personal identity grasps the level of the fourth dhyāna and so forth as being the self.

Since the first eight *kṛtsnāyatanas* (totalities) take as their objects the forms (*rūpa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and do not exist simultaneously with them, this [explanation] well accounts for this sūtra.
Furthermore, this view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) shares the same physical basis (*āśraya*) as the eight totalities, yet its objective referent (*ālambana*) is different.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"There are the meditative concentrations on earth and so forth, and there are the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) on earth and so forth.
Question: What is the difference between these meditative concentrations on earth and so forth and the universal bases on earth and so forth?

Answer: The meditative absorptions (samāpatti) such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth exist in the desire realm; the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth exist only in the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, they are termed "meditative absorptions such as the earth" during the stage of preparatory application (prayoga).
When they are fully accomplished, they are called the "totalities" (kṛtsnāyatana) of earth and so forth.
Furthermore, at the stage of the cause, they are called the "concentrations" (samādhi) of earth and so forth;
at the stage of the fruit, they are called the "totalities" of earth and so forth.
Furthermore, when one practices the meditative realization of a limited portion, it is called the "earth-kasiṇa" and so forth;
when one practices the meditative realization of its totality, it is called the "earth-kasiṇa universal base" (pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana) and so forth.
This is the distinction between them.
Question: What is the distinction between the liberations (vimokṣa), the bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana)?
Answer: Their very names constitute the distinction; that is to say, these are called "liberations," these are called "bases of mastery," and these are called "spheres of totality."
Furthermore, inferior roots of goodness are called "liberations" (vimokṣa);
middling roots of goodness are called "bases of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana);
and superior roots of goodness are called "totalities" (kṛtsnāyatana).
Furthermore, minor roots of goodness are called "liberations" (vimokṣa);
great roots of goodness are called "bases of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana);
and immeasurable roots of goodness are called "totalities" (kṛtsnāyatana).
Furthermore, the cause alone is called "liberation" (vimokṣa);
the fruit alone is called "totality" (kṛtsnāyatana);
and that which encompasses both cause and fruit is called "sphere of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana).
Furthermore, that which is capable of renouncing and turning away [from defilements] is called liberation (*vimokṣa*);
that which is capable of overcoming and subduing objects is called the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*);
and that which is capable of expanding the object of focus is called the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Furthermore, the mere exercise of resolute conviction is called liberation (*vimokṣa*);
that which can subdue the afflictions is called the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*);
and that which is non-dual and immeasurable with respect to its objective referent is called the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Furthermore, if one has attained liberation, it does not necessarily mean that one has already attained the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
If one has attained the spheres of mastery, one has necessarily already attained liberation,
though it does not necessarily mean that one has already attained the spheres of totality.
If one attains the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana), one has necessarily already attained the liberations (vimokṣa) and the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).
Why is this? Because one enters the spheres of mastery from the liberations.
Because one enters the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) from the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana),
these are called the distinctions between the liberations (vimokṣa), the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality.
Within this, there are eight knowledges (jñāna) and three samādhis.
The threefold samādhis will be analyzed in detail later in the Section on Knowledge (Jñānaskandha).
[This includes] the three fetters (saṃyojana) up to the ninety-eight proclivities (anuśaya).
Thus has the first aggregate been extensively analyzed.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll 85 (of the Sarvāstivāda Jñānaprasthāna Mahāvibhāṣā Śāstra), Scroll 80.
Composed by the Six Hundred Great Arhats and others;
translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section Four of the Ten Gates on the Aggregates of Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha), Part Sixteen: The Eye Faculty (cakṣur-indriya).
Up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—
among these ninety-eight latent tendencies,
how many latent tendencies increase in each one?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the "gates" (dvāra) based on the preceding chapter;
that is, it clarifies the meanings of the ten types of gates, such as the latent dispositions (anuśaya), by relying on the previously explained forty-two chapters.
Furthermore, this is for the purpose of refuting other schools and clarifying the correct principle.
That is to say, some may hold the view that even dharmas such as the eye-faculty within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are likewise untainted (anāsrava).

This is to refute that attachment by showing that the eye-faculty and so forth are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), because they are the objects upon which the various underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase.
Alternatively, there are those who hold the view that afflictions (*kleśa*) and inversions (*viparyāsa*) lack a real objective referent (*ālambana*).
This is to refute that attachment and demonstrate that the various afflictions possess real objects of perception;
or else, there may be those who hold the view that there is no sense of "bondage through association" with an object of perception.
If there were the sense of bondage with respect to the object of cognition (*ālambana*),
then there would have to be the sense of bondage in relation to untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
If there were the sense of bondage with respect to association (*samprayoga*), [then...]
If that were the case, then even one who has already severed [the bonds] would still possess bondage.
To refute such a position and to clarify the meaning of bondage as being associated with an object of perception (*ālambana*), it is said:
"Bondage by way of the object of perception" means...
This is because, among the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take contaminated objects as their conditions, they necessarily increase [in strength] with respect to them;
whereas although they may take uncontaminated objects as their conditions, they do not increase [in strength], and thus lack the sense of "bondage.
As for the bondage of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*):
It is required that the associated afflictions have not yet been abandoned;
for once the afflictions have been abandoned, although the association remains, there is no sense of bondage.
Furthermore, it is to preclude the occurrence of overweening pride regarding one's own person, whereby one might claim to be liberated while still being bound.
This means that although they have temporarily suppressed their afflictions and claim for themselves that they have already attained liberation,
[the Buddha] wishes to make them know that within their own eyes and other faculties, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) such as attachment still persist and increase.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of extensively analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.

That is to say, although the sūtras state that the eye-faculty and so forth are accompanied by the increase of various greed-afflictions (*anuśaya*), they do not provide an extensive analysis of this point.
Now, wishing to provide a detailed analysis, this treatise is composed.
It should be understood that within this there are five categories of phenomena,
which are respectively increased by the five categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
The five categories of phenomena refer to those abandoned through the vision of suffering, up to those abandoned through cultivation.
It should be understood that the five categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are likewise.
Among these, the factors abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) are increased by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Dharmas abandoned by the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) are increased by all latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned by the vision of the origin,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya).
Dharmas abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya) are increased by all latent dispositions abandoned by the vision of cessation.
Furthermore, they are augmented by the pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
Phenomena abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*) are augmented by all latent dispositions abandoned by the path of seeing,
as well as by the pervasive latent dispositions.
The factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-dharma*) are increased by all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation,
as well as by the universal latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of factors.
Furthermore, they are increased by nine kinds of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
As for the ten kinds of phenomena,
this refers to two kinds of phenomena each for those abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
First, those associated [with the mind];
second, those dissociated [from the mind].
Those to be abandoned by cultivation also consist of two kinds of phenomena.
First, the defiled;
second, the non-defiled.
Regarding the nine kinds of latent tendencies (anuśaya):
That is to say, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin each have two types:
first, those that are universal (*sarvatraga*),
and second, those that are non-universal (*asarvatraga*).
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path each have two types:
first, those with outflow as their object (sāsravālambana); second, those without outflow as their object (anāsravālambana).
Together with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation,
there are nine types in total.
Among these, the factors associated with what is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*)—
It is increased by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering, as well as by the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin.
Regarding its own category (*sva-nikāya*),
it is bound by objects and association according to what is appropriate.
As for those belonging to other categories,
they possess only the bondage of the object;
these are the dissociated factors abandoned through the vision of suffering.
They are all increased by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering,
as well as by the universal underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of the origin; in all cases,
they are bound solely by way of the object-condition (ālambana-bandhana).
The associated factors abandoned by the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) are increased by all latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned by the vision of the origin,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya).
"One's own category" refers to that which is bound by association with its respective object of cognition as appropriate.
"Another category" refers to...
There is only the bondage of the object-condition (ālambana-bandhana).

The dissociated factors (viprayukta-dharma) abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) are [the objects] for all latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin.

Furthermore, those factors abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) which are increased by the universal underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) are bound solely by the bondage of the object (*ālambana-bandhana*).
As for the associated factors abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*),
they are [bound] by all underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of cessation.

Furthermore, regarding those [defilements] that are increased by the universal latent tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) and those belonging to their own category that have outflowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana),
they are bound by objects and association according to what is appropriate for each case.
Regarding those with untainted objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*),
there is only the bond of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*).
Regarding those of other categories (*parakīya*):
There is only the bondage of the object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*):

the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*) abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) serve as the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) with outflows (*sāsrava*) directed toward cessation, which are themselves to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.

Furthermore, those factors associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) that increase through their influence are all bound solely by the bondage of the object (*ālambana-bandhana*).
This applies to the factors associated with [the afflictions] abandoned by the path of vision (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*).
It is increased by all latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned by the path of seeing,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions; and for those [factors] belonging to its own category that take contaminated objects as their conditions.
According to what is appropriate, there is bondage through association with an object; however,
for that which has uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*),
there is only bondage through association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*).
As for other categories,
they possess only the bondage of the object (ālambana-bandhana),
namely, those dissociated factors (viprayukta-dharma) abandoned by the path of vision (darśana-mārga).
They are increased by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the path of seeing that take contaminated objects as their condition,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions; in all such cases,
there is only bondage by way of the object-condition (ālambana-bandhana).
Defiled dharmas abandoned through cultivation are increased by all latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through cultivation,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions.
Regarding those belonging to one's own category (*svabhāga*), there is bondage through both the object-condition (*ālambana*) and association (*samprayoga*) as appropriate;
regarding those belonging to another category (*parabhāga*), there is only bondage through the object-condition.
This applies to non-defiled phenomena (*akliṣṭadharma*) that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
They are all increased by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation and by the universal latent dispositions; in all cases,
they are bound solely by the bondage of the object (ālambana-bandhana).

It should be understood that herein, the universal underlying tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) act as objects and as associated bonds, as appropriate,
toward those factors associated with the universal underlying tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Regarding other contaminated phenomena within one's own level and both one's own and other categories,
they are bound only by way of being objects;
this refers to the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Regarding those phenomena associated with the non-pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering,
they constitute objects of perception (*ālambana*) and bonds of association (*samprayoga*) as appropriate; furthermore,
regarding other contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of their own level, whether belonging to their own category (*sva-nikāya*) or another category (*para-nikāya*).
However, they are bound by their objects of perception: namely,
the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin,
which [bind] those factors associated with the universal proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of the origin.
They are bound to their objects through association as appropriate;

however, with respect to other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the same stage (*svabhūmi*) but belonging to different categories (*nikāya*), they are bound solely by way of being objects (*ālambana-bandhana*).
This applies to the non-universal (*asarvatraga*) proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding those phenomena associated with the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*),
they constitute objects of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*) and mental association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) as appropriate;
furthermore, regarding other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of their own level (*svabhūmi*) and their own category (*svanikāya*).
However, they are bound by their objects of perception (*ālambana*).

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) with outflow (*sāsrava*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) [are bound] to those factors associated with the latent dispositions with outflow that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
According to what is appropriate, they are bound to them by way of both being an object (*ālambana*) and by association (*samprayoga*);
however, with respect to other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of their own level (*svabhūmi*) and their own category (*svanikāya*),
they are bound solely by way of being an object.
The untainted-object (anāsrava-ālambana) proclivities to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-heya) act,
as appropriate, solely as the bondage of association (saṃprayoga-bandhana) toward those factors associated with the untainted-object proclivities to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) with outflows (sāsrava) that take [objects] as their conditions (ālambana),
which are to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśanamārga-prahātavya), bind—
either by way of object (ālambana-bandhana) or by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana)— those factors associated with such latent dispositions, as the case may be.
Regarding other contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) of its own level and its own category,

it is bound by them only as an object-condition (ālambana-bandhana); however, regarding phenomena associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya) and have uncontaminated objects (anāsrava-ālambana), [it is bound] by those very latent dispositions.
However, they are bound by association;
the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation [are associated] with those phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation that are associated with them.
According to what is appropriate, they constitute bondage through association with their objects;
regarding other contaminated phenomena of the same level and the same category,
they constitute bondage solely through being objects.
Furthermore, there are forty-one kinds of phenomena,
upon which thirty-six kinds of latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase.
As for these forty-one kinds of phenomena:
This refers to the eleven factors abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*):
namely, the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and their associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*).
These are not associated.
There are eleven factors;
among them, eight factors are abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
That is to say, the seven latent dispositions (anuśaya) together with their associated factors (saṃprayukta-dharma) and their non-associated factors (asaṃprayukta-dharma) constitute eight.
The same applies to those abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya).
There are nine factors to be abandoned by the path of seeing:
namely, the eight factors associated with the underlying tendencies (anuśaya),
together with the dissociated factor, making nine.
There are five factors to be abandoned through cultivation:
namely, the four afflictive tendencies (*anuśaya*) in their associated states,
together with the dissociated factors, making five.
The thirty-six types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are as follows:
there are ten to be abandoned through the vision of suffering;
seven each to be abandoned through the vision of the origin and the cessation [of suffering].
There are eight [afflictions] to be abandoned by the path of seeing and four to be abandoned by the path of cultivation;
this is stated solely in terms of the categories (*nikāya*), and not in terms of the realms (*dhātu*).
Among these, the phenomena associated with the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) are increased by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the view of a self-entity and its associated ignorance;
they are bound by them through their respective objects (*ālambana*) and associations (*saṃprayoga*), as the case may be.
This is the general explanation; to explain it specifically:

if something is a bondage by way of being an object-condition (ālambana-bandhana) with respect to that [mind], it is not a bondage by way of association (saṃprayoga-bandhana) with respect to that same [mind].
If something constitutes a bond by way of association with respect to a certain object,
it does not constitute a bond by way of being an object-condition with respect to that same object;
the other cases should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, this is increased by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering,
as well as by the pervasive latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin;
it is bound only by way of being an object (*ālambana*).
For example, there are phenomena associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*),
and the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*).
The same applies accordingly to all phenomena associated with pride.

Phenomena associated with the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering are increased by the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) of the unique ignorance to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
It is bound to its corresponding object (ālambana) according to what is appropriate;
furthermore, it is increased by all other latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
However, they are bound by their objects of perception;
the factors dissociated from [the afflictions] abandoned through the vision of suffering are bound by all latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Furthermore, they are increased by the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*),
but are bound only by way of being objects (*ālambana-bandhana*),
just like the eleven factors abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
The eight factors abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) are likewise,

as appropriate. Factors associated with false view abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) constitute the object for the false view abandoned through the vision of cessation.
It is also increased by the underlying tendency of ignorance associated with it,
which acts merely as an associated fetter;
furthermore, it is [increased] by other underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of cessation that take contaminated objects as their conditions.
Furthermore, they are increased by the universal underlying tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) and are bound only by way of the object (ālambana-bandhana),
such as the factors associated with false view that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-heya).
The same applies accordingly to the factors associated with doubt that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
As for the factors associated with the grasping at views that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation,
they are [the objects] of the grasping at views to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
It is also increased by the underlying tendency of ignorance associated with it;
as appropriate, it serves as the object-condition and the associated bond for these.
Furthermore, it is [the object] for other underlying tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of cessation that take contaminated phenomena as their object.
Furthermore, those factors increased by the pervasive latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) are bound only by way of being objects of perception (ālambana-bandhana),
such as the factors associated with the view of grasping at views (dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa) abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya).
The same applies accordingly to the factors associated with greed, hatred, and pride abandoned through the vision of cessation.

Dharmas associated with the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation are the locus for the increase of the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of that same unique ignorance to be abandoned by the vision of cessation; they are, however,
bound only by association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*).
Furthermore, this is also augmented by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation which take contaminated objects as their conditions,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions; however,
it is bound only by way of being an object-condition (ālambana).
Dissociated dharmas abandoned through the vision of cessation are increased by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have outflow-conditions and are abandoned through the vision of cessation,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions.
They are merely bound by their objects of perception,
such as the eight dharmas abandoned through the vision of cessation and the nine dharmas abandoned through the vision of the path.
The same applies accordingly:
phenomena associated with greed abandoned by cultivation are increased by the latent tendencies of greed abandoned by cultivation and the ignorance associated with them.
It is bound to its corresponding objects (ālambana) as appropriate;
furthermore, it is increased by other latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) as well as by the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya).
They are merely bound by their objects of perception (*ālambana*),
such as the factors associated with greed abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
and the factors associated with hatred and pride abandoned through cultivation.
The same applies accordingly:

dharmas associated with the non-common ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*) to be abandoned by cultivation are increased by the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) of the non-common ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation.
It is bound to its object through association according to what is appropriate;
furthermore, it is increased by other latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation,
as well as by universal latent dispositions.
However, those dissociated factors abandoned by cultivation are objects of all latent dispositions abandoned by cultivation.
Furthermore, they are increased by the universal underlying tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya),
yet they are bound only as objects (ālambana-bandhana).
If one speaks of the inclusion of phenomena (dharma-saṃgraha), it should be based on the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśa-dhātu).
If one speaks of the various consciousnesses, they should be based on the twelve bases (āyatana).
If one speaks of the various knowledges (jñāna), they should be based on the four noble truths (āryasatya).
If one speaks of the various latent dispositions (anuśaya), they should be based on the five categories (pañca-varga).
Now, in order to explain the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
the distinctions regarding their differentiation and their increase are analyzed according to five parts.
The eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is pervasive (*sarvatraga*).
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
because the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) pertains to both the desire and form realms and is exclusively abandoned through cultivation,
there are as many such latent dispositions that increase [in relation to it].
However, this eye-faculty extends across five stages,
namely the desire realm and the four dhyānas;
each of these five serves as the universal [mental factor] for its own respective stage.
As for the statement that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation increase [in these faculties],
the same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body;
they likewise pertain to the five stages of the desire realm and the form realm.
Because it is exclusively abandoned through cultivation, like the eye faculty,
the female faculty is subject to the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are omnipresent in the desire realm as well as those abandoned through cultivation.
Because the female faculty (*strīndriya*) is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
there are that many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) which increase therein.
The same applies to the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) and the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*).
Furthermore, because it is like the female faculty (*strīndriya*), it is also abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

As for the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase in accordance with it are those that are omnipresent (*sarvatraga*) throughout the three realms as well as those abandoned through cultivation.

Because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) pertains to all three realms and is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), it is accompanied by as many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) as there are; furthermore, this life-faculty exists throughout nine stages, namely:
the desire realm, the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
These nine [faculties] each serve as the pervasive [conditions] for their own respective stages,
and the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation increase in relation to them.
The same applies to the five faculties beginning with faith.
The five faculties, beginning with faith, are common to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Those that are contaminated also pertain to all three realms and nine stages,
because they are exclusively abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), just like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
The untainted (anāsrava) is not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya).
Regarding the statement that "all latent dispositions increase in the faculty of mind (manas)":
the faculty of mind encompasses both the tainted (sāsrava) and the untainted (anāsrava).
Because the tainted (*sāsrava*) factors pertain to all three realms and five categories (*pañca-varga*),
there are that many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) which increase in association with them.
Furthermore, this mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) exists in nine stages (*bhūmi*).
That is to say, the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments of the desire realm—
these nine each serve as the basis for the increase of all latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to their own respective levels.
Those that are untainted (anāsrava) do not serve as the basis for the increase of latent dispositions.
The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is likewise:
it also encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
As for the contaminated, it also encompasses the three realms, the nine stages, and the five categories (*pañca-varga*), because it is like the faculty of mind (*manendriya*).

Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in association with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya)— namely, all those of the form realm (rūpadhātu), the universal [dispositions] of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), and those to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya)—
the faculty of pleasure pertains to both the desire and form realms and exists only in three stages.
This refers to the desire realm and the first and third dhyānas.
Those in the desire realm exist within the five consciousnesses;
those in the first dhyāna exist within three consciousnesses.
Since both of these are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
each serves as the basis for the increase of its own level’s universal (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned (*bhāvanā-heya*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Regarding the third dhyāna, it exists within the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) as both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
As for the contaminated, it is associated with all five categories (*pañca-varga*) and with all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of its own level increase [in relation to it];
those that are untainted (*anāsrava*) do not increase as latent dispositions.
As for the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), all [dispositions] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) [increase].
Excluding doubt that takes the untainted as its object and the ignorance associated with it,
all other latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase [in relation to] the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya).
This faculty of joy extends throughout the desire realm and the form realm, existing only in three stages.
This refers to the desire realm and the first two dhyānas. Within the desire realm,
[the mind] pertains to all five categories [of afflictions],
yet it is not associated with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of aversion or doubt.
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) functions with a mode of activity characterized by gladness,
whereas hatred and doubt function with a mode of activity characterized by dejection;
this is because gladness and dejection are mutually contradictory and cannot coexist.

In the desire realm, with the exception of the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) associated with doubt to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated therewith,
all other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm increase in association with it.
This applies to the doubt to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, as well as the ignorance associated therewith.
Regarding the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), it is not bound by the object-condition (*ālambanabandhana*) because it takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object;
nor is it bound by the association-condition (*samprayogabandhana*) because it is dissociated from [those afflictions].
Although other doubts and hatred are also dissociated [from this faculty], [they are not bound to it in the same way].
However, regarding the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), there is the sense of being bound by objects;
therefore, it is said that the faculty of joy in the desire realm excludes doubt (*vicikitsā*) that takes the untainted as its object,
as well as the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with it.
All other latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in association with it.
In the first two dhyānas, the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) is associated with both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava).
That which is contaminated is associated with all five categories (pañca-varga) and is concomitant with all latent dispositions.
Because doubt on the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*) is also associated with joy and bliss,
and because all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of their respective stages increase therein,
it is said that all latent dispositions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) increase in relation to the faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*).

The untainted [root] is not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya). As for the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), all latent dispositions of the desire realm increase in relation to it;
this is because the faculty of grief belongs exclusively to the desire realm, pervades all five categories (*pañca-varga*), and is associated with a portion of the latent dispositions.
There are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase [in those states].
Regarding the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), no underlying tendencies increase therein,
because no underlying tendencies can increase with respect to any untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma).
Why is this? Because if a phenomenon is an object of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
it is an object of perversion (*viparyāsa*).
This is the locus of the latent tendencies;
this is the place where greed, hatred, and delusion are established.
It is that which is stained, defiled, and turbid.
They are subject to the increase of the underlying tendencies (anuśaya),
whereas uncontaminated phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) are not;
therefore, they are not subject to the increase of the underlying tendencies.
Furthermore, wherever there is craving, there the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase accordingly.
It is like a damp and oily place where dust and filth easily adhere;
the untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) are not so.
Therefore, it is not that which is increased by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is grasped as "self" or "mine" by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
in that case, the underlying tendencies increase.
The untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*) are not like that.
Furthermore, if a dharma is both an object of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and an object in which they increase,
[it is subject to outflow].
It is thus that [the object] is increased by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Although untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) are objects of perception for the underlying tendencies, they are not objects of their increase;
therefore, they are not increased by the underlying tendencies.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is both the objective basis (*ālambana*) of a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) and the locus where it increases,
then that phenomenon is indeed subject to increase by that latent tendency.

Although untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are objects of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are not places where [the tendencies] increase; therefore, the underlying tendencies do not increase therein.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
The untainted, smooth, and pure [state] does not allow the various proclivities (anuśaya) to plant their feet;
therefore, the proclivities do not increase therein.
It is like beryl (vaiḍūrya), which is extremely smooth and pure.
Mosquitoes, horseflies, and flies cannot find a stable footing there.
The Venerable One said:
"The heat of the outflow-free flames is such that no latent dispositions (anuśaya) can find a footing within it."
Therefore, the latent dispositions do not increase therein,
just as one cannot place one's foot upon burning ground.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka spoke thus.
The untainted (anāsrava) and formidable latent dispositions (anuśaya), though taking that [object] as their condition, do not increase therein;
it is like the son of a caṇḍāla who, upon beholding the face of a formidable king, feels extreme trepidation in his heart.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this.
When latent dispositions (anuśaya) arise in relation to tainted phenomena (sāsravadharma), the latent dispositions gradually increase,
just as the faculty of the eye grows when a person gazes at the moon;
therefore, latent dispositions increase in accordance with tainted phenomena.
When latent dispositions (anuśaya) arise in relation to untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma), those dispositions gradually diminish.
This is like a person whose visual faculty is impaired when looking at the sun;
therefore, untainted phenomena are not subject to the increase of latent dispositions.
Regarding the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, tangibles, and the elements of eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and body-consciousness:
as for the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal in the desire and form realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation,
these eleven elements pertain to both the desire and form realms.

Because they are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there are that many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) which increase in association with them; this is stated with reference to the realms (*dhātu*).
However, there are differences in terms of the levels (*bhūmi*):
namely, the eight [faculties] beginning with the eye pertain to all five levels.
They are subject to the increase of the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the fifth stage.
Since eye-, ear-, and body-consciousness exist only in two stages—
namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna— they are therefore pervasive only within those two stages.
Furthermore, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation increase therein.

This applies to the sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, and tangibles; to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); and to the aggregate of appropriation of form (*rūpopādānaskandha*).
The same also applies to the first five elements (*dhātu*), which are material, visible, and possess resistance (*sapratigha*).
These various dharmas likewise pertain to the five stages of the desire and form realms;
they are exclusively abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), just like the eye-element and so forth.
The elements of odor, taste, and nose-consciousness and tongue-consciousness are pervasive throughout the desire realm.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
since these four elements are abandoned only through cultivation in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
they are accompanied by as many such latent dispositions as there are.
The same applies to the spheres of odor and taste,
as they are likewise abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, just like the sphere of fragrance and so forth.
As for the mind, mental objects, and the mental consciousness element, all latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.
Thus, all three realms (tridhātu) encompass both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava).
The contaminated encompasses the nine stages (navabhūmi), the five categories (pañcavarga), and is associated with all latent dispositions (anuśaya).
This is because it is associated with all [defilements].
All [factors] are increased by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Those that are untainted (*anāsrava*) are not increased by the underlying tendencies.

These include the sense-sphere of mind (*manāyatana*), the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), the last four aggregates (*skandha*), the last four graspable aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), and the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*).
"Formless, invisible, and non-obstructive;
past, future, and present conditioned phenomena with outflows;
and likewise, phenomena that are neither of the learner nor of the adept."
Among these dharmas, some are exclusively contaminated (sāsrava),
while others are both contaminated and uncontaminated (anāsrava).
All contaminated dharmas pertain to the three realms, the nine stages, and the five categories.
Furthermore, because they are associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
they are subject to the increase of all latent dispositions; however,
those that are untainted (*anāsrava*) are not subject to the increase of latent dispositions.
Regarding the statement that "outflow-free (anāsrava) unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas are not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya),
and the same applies to dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and those not to be abandoned (aprahātavya)":
because these are all outflow-free, their meaning is as previously explained.

Regarding the wholesome factors and those factors abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the three realms, the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.
Among these, wholesome factors encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Dharmas abandoned through cultivation are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).
All contaminated dharmas pertain to all three realms and nine stages,
because they are abandoned solely through cultivation.
There are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase;
those that are untainted (anāsrava) do not have underlying tendencies increasing within them.
This applies to unwholesome factors and those factors bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
Regarding the fact that all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to everything in the desire realm:
since these two factors pertain exclusively to the desire realm and encompass all five categories (*pañca-varga*),
there are as many latent dispositions as there are that increase in relation to them.

Regarding indeterminate dharmas: they are those in which the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin increase, including all [dharmas] of the form and formless realms, as well as two categories of the desire realm.
These are the indeterminate dharmas.
This refers to all defiled dharmas of the form and formless realms,
as well as non-obscured neutral dharmas,
and those defiled dharmas belonging to the categories of the view of a self-identity and the view of extreme adherence within the desire realm.
As well as unobscured-neutral dharmas,
along with space and non-analytical cessation,
and the neutral dharmas of the form and formless realms.
Because they pertain to both realms, eight stages, and five categories,
they are the objects of increase for all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms.
As for the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas of the desire realm that are defiled:
Because it is abandoned only through the vision of suffering,
all universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering and those abandoned through the vision of the origin of suffering increase in relation to it.
Because that which is undefiled is abandoned only through cultivation,
it is subject to the increase of all defilements abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
as well as the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
In space and in cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not increase.
Regarding the statement that "all underlying tendencies bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) increase with respect to phenomena bound to the form realm":
this is because these [phenomena] pertain exclusively to the form realm and encompass all four stages and five categories (*pañca-nikāya*).
There are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase;
as for the factors associated with the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma),
all underlying tendencies of the formless realm increase therein.
Because this [category] pertains only to the formless realm and encompasses four stages and five classes,
there are that many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) which increase in association.
Regarding those phenomena abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), all underlying tendencies abandoned by insight increase in association with them.
Because this [defilement] pervades the three realms, the nine stages, and the first four categories,
there are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase in association with it. These are the underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).

Because it cannot take as its object the dharmas abandoned through seeing, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through cultivation do not increase therein. As for the statement that "all latent dispositions increase in the Truths of Suffering and Origin":
[this refers to the fact that] all latent dispositions increase in relation to these two truths.
Because the two truths of suffering and its origin encompass all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) across the three realms, the nine stages, and the five categories,
they are the basis for the increase of all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). In contrast,
the truths of cessation and the path are not subject to the increase of latent dispositions.
The same applies to the three samādhis of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path:
because they are all untainted (*anāsrava*), none of them provide a basis for the increase of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
These three samādhis are exclusively untainted.
In this context, only the concentrations subsumed under the three gates of liberation are discussed.

As for the statement that "the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the entire form realm increase in relation to the four dhyānas," these four dhyānas encompass both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava).
The outflowing [factors] belong exclusively to the form realm and pertain to all five categories, being both defiled and non-defiled.
Whether they are states of meditative concentration or states of rebirth, they are all subsumed within these four dhyānas.
Therefore, all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the entire form realm increase in relation to them.
The untainted (anāsrava) is not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya).
As for the four immeasurables (apramāṇa), the pervasive [defilements] of the form realm (rūpadhātu-viṣkambha),
and those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), they are subject to the increase of latent dispositions.
Among these, it is taught that only the accomplishment of the immeasurables occurs exclusively in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
However, the immeasurable of sympathetic joy (*muditā*) occurs only in the first and second dhyānas.
The remaining three immeasurables pertain to all four dhyānas, and all are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Therefore, it is stated in summary that the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned (*bhāvanā-heya*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase [in relation to these objects].

Regarding the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the first eight bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and likewise the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): [the same applies].
Since this also explains the accomplishment of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
they are comprised solely within the abandonments through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Their distinctions according to the levels (*bhūmi*) should be understood as previously described.
The supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
As for the contaminated variety, it exists only in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), is associated with all four dhyānas, and is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
This and the [other] three preceding types of contaminated [supernormal powers] are as explained in the section on the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
Regarding the statement that "the four formless [attainments] are the basis for the increase of all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm":
among the four formless states, the first three are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
while the fourth is exclusively contaminated.
All contaminated states belonging to the formless realm pertain to all five categories and are both defiled and non-defiled;
whether they are attained through meditative concentration or arise through birth, they are all subsumed within these four formless attainments.
Therefore, they are collectively subject to the increase of all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm;
however, they are not subject to the increase of latent dispositions that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
This applies to the last five liberations (*vimokṣa*) and the last two spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Regarding the increase of the pervasive and cultivation-abandoned latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) within the formless realm:
among these, those that are tainted (*sāsrava*) vary according to the distinctions of their respective stages;
however, because they belong exclusively to the formless realm and are abandoned solely through cultivation, [the analysis is as follows].
There are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase;
those that are untainted (anāsrava) do not have underlying tendencies increasing within them.
This excludes worldly knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) that takes the untainted as its object, as well as the [tainted] views.
Regarding the remaining all-pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase [in association with it]:
this conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) pervades the three realms, the nine stages, and the five categories,
because it is a defiled or non-defiled outflowing wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) of all kinds.
There are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase [in association];
excluding those that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object—
that is, excluding the false views (mithyādṛṣṭi) abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path.
That [wisdom] is not bound to its object by way of the conventional wisdom,
because it takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object; nor is it bound through association,
because a nature is not associated with itself.
Because false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is itself conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

However, regarding the objects (*ālambana*) and associations (*samprayoga*) of conventional knowledge, one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) concerning the distinctions among the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
There are some latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that, with respect to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*),
are bound by way of being an object (*ālambanabandhana*) but not bound by way of association (*samprayogabandhana*);
namely, those views (*dṛṣṭi*) which have outflowing objects (*sāsravālambana*).
There are some underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that, with respect to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*),
constitute a bond of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) but not a bond of object (*ālambana-bandhana*);
namely, those excluding the views (*dṛṣṭi*) that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
Regarding other latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take uncontaminated phenomena as their object,
there are some latent dispositions that are bound to conventional knowledge both by way of being its object and by way of association.
This refers to all other latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have outflowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana), excluding those views (dṛṣṭi) that take outflowing things as their objects;
this is the general statement.
If explained individually:
that which constitutes a bondage by way of being an object (ālambana-bandhana) with respect to something is not,
with respect to that same thing, a bondage by way of association (saṃprayoga-bandhana).
If there is an associated bondage with respect to a certain [object],
there is no object-condition bondage with respect to that same [object]. Or,
there may be latent dispositions (anuśaya) with respect to conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
It is neither bound by the object of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
Regarding this point— that [afflictions] which take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object—
Venerable Ghosaka states that there are four distinct positions.
There may be latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are bound to conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) by way of being its object (ālambana-bandhana),
but not by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana).
This refers to those latent dispositions of views (dṛṣṭyanuśaya) belonging to their own level, which take conventional knowledge as their object and have not yet been abandoned.
There may be latent dispositions (anuśaya) that, with respect to conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna),
constitute a bondage through association (saṃprayoga-bandhana) but not a bondage through object (ālambana-bandhana);
this refers to those [dispositions] excluding those that take their own level or other realms as their objects.
Either taking another stage as an object,
or taking both one's own realm and other realms as objects,
or taking other phenomena of one's own stage as objects.
Or there are latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with views that take the untainted as their object;
others take their own level or another realm as their object,
or take other levels as their object, or take both their own realm and other realms as their objects.
Either they take other dharmas of their own level as objects,
or the latent dispositions (anuśaya) taking uncontaminated objects have not yet been abandoned,
or there are latent dispositions regarding conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
It is bound by both the object-condition (ālambana) and by association (saṃprayoga).
That is to say, with the exception of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) that take their own level as an object,
all other latent dispositions of conventional knowledge belonging to one's own level that have not yet been abandoned [are bound].
This is the general explanation.
To explain it specifically:
if one is bound by that [object] as an object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*).
That which is not an associated bond with respect to a certain [object] is not an object-condition bond with respect to that same [object]. Alternatively,
there are underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that exist with respect to conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
It is neither bound by the object of cognition (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*);
that is to say, all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of other stages,
as well as those of one's own stage that have already been abandoned.
If it has not been abandoned,
it takes another realm as its object,
or another stage as its object, or both one's own realm and another realm as its object.
Or [there are] latent tendencies of views that take other dharmas of their own level as objects, or that take untainted dharmas as objects;
these are the threefold samādhis and the universal [tendencies] of the three realms.
Regarding those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) that increase in association with it:
the "repeated" (*guru*) samādhi pervades the nine stages of the three realms,
because it is abandoned solely through cultivation.
There are as many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that increase [therein] as there are:
the fetter of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana),
which consists of all those abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya).
Furthermore, regarding those universal underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) that increase [in association]:
among the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) pertains to all three realms and nine stages,
as it is exclusively abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase;
the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), which is a fetter conducive to the lower realms (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana),
and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) are likewise so.

This refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) among the five fetters that bind one to the lower realms (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), as well as the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) among the five views;
these are also found throughout the three realms and nine stages, and are abandoned solely through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Just as among the three fetters, because of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
all fetters of attachment to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) are abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya),
as well as those that are universal (sarvatraga) and are abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudayadarśana-prahātavya).
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take contaminated objects as their focus and increase through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*):
these refer to the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśasaṃyojana*) among the three fetters.
It pertains to all three realms and nine stages, and is abandoned exclusively by the path of seeing suffering (*duḥkhadarśana*).
Only because they have outflowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) do so many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase;
the underlying tendencies to be abandoned by the path of seeing that have non-outflowing objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) are not bound to the view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*),
because they do not take non-outflowing phenomena as their object.
Because they are not bound by association, as they are dissociated [from consciousness].
The same applies to the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the fetter of clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśasaṃyojana*),
and the clinging to rules and observances among the fetters conducive to the lower realm (*avarabhāgīyasaṃyojana*).
That is to say: among the four graspings, it is the grasping at precepts and observances;
among the four bodily fetters, it is the fetter of precepts and observances;
and among the five lower fetters, it is the fetter of precepts and observances.

Among the five views, the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) also pertains to all three realms and nine stages; it is abandoned solely by the path of seeing suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya).
It has only impure objects as its cognitive domain (sāsrava-ālambana), because it is like the clinging to rules and observances among the three fetters (saṃyojana).
Regarding the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*), which is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and has outflowing objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*),
as well as the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) associated with that doubt which has non-outflowing objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*)—
that is to say, among the three fetters, the fetter of doubt pervades the nine stages (*bhūmi*) of the three realms (*dhātu*).
Because the first four categories universally take both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as their objects,
there are that many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) which increase in association with them.
As for those abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) that take the contaminated as their object:

This refers to all latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, as well as those with outflow-objects (sāsrava-ālambana) abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path,
and those without outflow-objects (anāsrava-ālambana) abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path.
Regarding the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*):
it is not a bondage by way of object (*ālambana-bandhana*), because its objects are the untainted (*anāsrava*);
nor is it a bondage by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*), because it belongs to a different category (*nikāya*).
Alternatively, because a self-nature does not correspond with itself,
the doubt that is a fetter conducive to the lower realms, the latent tendency of doubt,
and the fetter of doubt are likewise so designated.
This refers to the fetter of doubt among the five lower-tier fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni),
the latent tendency of doubt among the seven latent tendencies (sapta anuśayāḥ),
and the fetter of doubt among the nine fetters (nava saṃyojanāni).
They also pertain to the three realms and nine stages.
The first four categories have both contaminated and uncontaminated objects,
just as with the fetter of doubt among the three fetters.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in association with the unwholesome roots of greed and hatred which have the outflows of the desire realm as their object:
among the three unwholesome roots, greed and hatred pertain exclusively to the desire realm and encompass all five categories [of afflictions].
Only because they have contaminated objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) do so many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase;

as for those underlying tendencies that have uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*), they do not bind through the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) with respect to greed or hatred, because they take the uncontaminated as their object.
They are not bound by association because they belong to different aggregates;
the others should be understood accordingly.

This applies to the first two bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*), the first two hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the fetter of aversion (*pratighasaṃyojana*), the first two fetters conducive to the lower realms (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), and the first two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
"The fetter of ill will (*vyāpāda-saṃyojana*) is also like this" means that among the four bodily ties (*kāyagrantha*), there are greed and hatred;
and among the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), there are greed and hatred.
Among the five fetters (saṃyojana), it is the fetter of aversion;
among the five lower-tier fetters (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana), it is greed and aversion;
and among the seven latent tendencies (anuśaya), it is sensual desire and ill will.
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*),
the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) likewise exists only in the desire realm, pervades all five categories, and has only impure objects as its condition;
