this is because it is like the unwholesome roots of greed and hatred.
Regarding the unwholesome root of delusion (*moha-akuśalamūla*) in the desire realm— excluding that ignorance which takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object—
all other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase therein.
That is to say, among the three unwholesome roots:
Because delusion exists only in the desire realm, pervades all five categories, and takes both the contaminated and the uncontaminated as its objects,
that many latent dispositions increase accordingly;
this excludes ignorance that takes the uncontaminated as its object.
The non-associated ignorance that is associated with the untainted objects and is abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path is not bound to the unwholesome root of delusion,
because it does not take the untainted as its object-condition.
It is not bound by association, because a self-nature does not associate with itself.
Regarding the statement that the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) increases along with all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm:
among the three outflows, the outflow of desire belongs exclusively to the desire realm and pervades all five categories (*pañca-varga*).
Because they take both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as their objects,
there are that many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) which increase [in them].

The same applies to the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the yoke of desire (*kāma-yoga*), the grasping of desire (*kāma-upādāna*), and the hindrance of sloth-torpor and restlessness (*styāna-middha-auddhatya-nivaraṇa*).
That is to say: among the four floods, it is the flood of sensual desire;
among the four yokes, it is the yoke of sensual desire;
and among the four clingings, it is the clinging to sensual desire.

Among the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of lethargy-and-drowsiness (*styāna-middha*) and restlessness-and-agitation (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) belong exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and pervade all five categories (*pañca-varga*).
This is because they take both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as their objects, just like the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
Regarding the fact that all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the realm of form and the formless realm increase with respect to contaminated form:
this refers to the contaminated [outflows] among the three outflows, which pertain to the five categories across the eight stages of the realms of form and the formless.
Because they take both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as their objects,
there are that many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) which increase [in relation to them].
The same applies to the floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and the grasping of self-identity (*ātmavādopādāna*).
That is to say: among the four floods, there is the flood of existence;
among the four yokes, there is the yoke of existence;
and among the four clingings, there is the clinging to the doctrine of self.
They also pertain to the five categories across the eight stages of the form and formless realms;
because they have outflow (sāsrava) as their object, they are like the outflowing [factors].
Regarding the outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava), one excludes that which has the outflow-free (anāsrava) as its object.
Regarding all other latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) that increase [in association]:
among the three outflows (*āsrava*), the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) pervades the nine stages and five categories across the three realms,
because it takes both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) objects as its conditions.
There are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase;
excluding those [tendencies] that take the untainted as their object,
they [increase] with respect to the outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava).
It is not bound by the object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*), because it takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object;
nor is it bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*), because a nature does not associate with itself.
The same applies to the flood (*ogha*) and yoke (*yoga*) of ignorance, as well as the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) and fetter (*saṃyojana*) of ignorance.
That is to say: among the four floods, it is the flood of ignorance;
among the four yokes, it is the yoke of ignorance;
and among the seven latent tendencies, it is the latent tendency of ignorance.
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) also pervades all three realms, nine stages, and five categories;
this is because its objects include both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), just as in the case of the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
The floods and yokes of views;
those conditioned by outflows abandoned through the vision [of the truths],
as well as those associated with views that are conditioned by the outflow-free.

Regarding the latent tendency of ignorance that increases: this refers to the flood of views among the four floods, and the yoke of views among the four yokes, which pervade the nine stages of the three realms and consist of the first four categories [of afflictions].
Because they take both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as their objects,
that many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase therein,
with the exception of the wrong view and doubt that take the uncontaminated as their object.
And that ignorance associated with doubt,
as well as the non-shared ignorance that takes the untainted as its object,
because they [constitute] the flood and the yoke of views.
It is not bound by the object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*), because it takes uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena as its object;
nor is it bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*), because a self-nature does not associate with itself,
or because it belongs to a different aggregate (*skandha*).

Regarding the statement that "the latent tendency of views (dṛṣṭy-anuśaya) and the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) are likewise [treated as] the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) and wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi)":
this refers to the grasping at views among the four graspings (catvāra upādānāḥ),
and wrong view among the five views (pañca dṛṣṭayaḥ).
Among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the underlying tendency of views;
among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of views—
both also pertain to the four preceding categories across the three realms and nine stages.
It has both contaminated and uncontaminated objects as its conditions,
because it is like the flood and the yoke of views;
this is the fetter of clinging to a real body.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) with outflows that have objects as their condition and which increase through being abandoned by insight:
these refer to the "body-tie of dogmatic adherence to a real self" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-kāyagrantha*) among the four body ties;
it pervades the first four categories across the nine stages of the three realms.
Because they have only outflowing objects as their conditions,
there are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase accordingly.
The same applies to the fetter of grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa-saṃyojana).
This refers to the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) among the five views,
and the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśasaṃyojana*) among the nine fetters;
it also pervades the first four categories across the three realms and nine stages.
It has only impure objects as its conditions.
Because it is a fetter consisting of the adherence to reality (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*),

the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal in the desire realm— namely, the hindrance of regret (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*)— as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase and adhere to it.
This means that among the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of remorse (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*) is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
therefore, there are as many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that increase [in association] with it.

Regarding the fetters of envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*), the "body of craving" (*tṛṣṇākāya*) born of nose-contact and tongue-contact, and the fetters of envy and avarice themselves, are also like this.
That is to say: among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetters of envy and avarice;
among the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ tṛṣṇākāyāḥ*), the group of craving born of nose-contact and tongue-contact;
and among the nine fetters (*nava saṃyojanāni*), the fetters of envy and avarice.
Furthermore, it is exclusively [the defilements] of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation, because they are like the hindrance of regret (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*).

As for the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*), it consists of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of doubt that are abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) in the desire realm and have outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*),
as well as the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) associated with doubt that have non-outflow-objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*), which increase [in strength].
This refers to the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*) among the five hindrances;
it pertains only to the Desire Realm and encompasses all four categories [of afflictions],
because its objects include both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*).
There are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase [in association],
excluding the doubt and wrong view that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object in the desire realm,
as well as the ignorance associated with those wrong views.
And it includes untainted objects and the unshared ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*),
because those are not bound to the hindrance of doubt by way of being its object, as they take untainted phenomena as their object.
It is not a bound state through association, because a self-nature does not associate with itself,
or because it belongs to a different aggregate.
As for the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the fetters of greed (*rāga*) and pride (*māna*), which increase in accordance with the outflow-bound objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) of the three realms:
This refers to the fetters of attachment and pride among the five fetters;
they pertain to all three realms, nine stages, and five categories,
because they take only contaminated objects as their conditions.
There are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase [in association]:
the underlying tendencies of the group of craving born of mental contact and of pride;
the fetters of craving and pride are likewise.
This refers to the aggregate of craving born from mental contact among the six aggregates of craving;
the latent tendency of pride among the seven latent tendencies;
and the fetters of craving and pride among the nine fetters.
It also extends across the three realms, the nine stages, and the five classes;
it has only impure objects as its conditions,
because it is like the fetters of greed and pride among the five fetters.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase through the pervasive [afflictions] of the form realm regarding desire for form, as well as those abandoned through cultivation,
refer to the desire for form among the five fetters of the higher realms (pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni).
Only those [defilements] abandoned through cultivation belonging to the four stages of the form realm [are present],
because they manifest within the body of a non-returner;
thus, that many latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.
In the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), because the universal [defilements] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) already possess the bondage of an object of attachment toward that [form realm],

the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)— both the universal ones and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)— increase in relation to the craving for the formless realm.
That is to say, among the five fetters binding one to the higher realms (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*),
attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*) is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the four stages of the formless realm,
because it manifests within the body of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
There are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase [in association with them].
The rest is as previously explained.
The latter three fetters conducive to the higher realms (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana) are pervasive throughout the form and formless realms.
Regarding those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
these refer to restlessness (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) among the five fetters pertaining to the higher realms (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
These pertain exclusively to the eight stages of the form and formless realms and are abandoned solely through cultivation.
Because these manifest within the body of a non-returner (anāgāmin),
there are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase;
the rest is as previously explained.
The group of cravings born from eye-, ear-, and body-contact,
which are pervasive throughout the desire and form realms and in which the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation increase.
This refers to the craving-bodies (*tṛṣṇākāya*) arising from eye-, ear-, and body-contact among the six craving-bodies.
Because these pertain to the desire realm and the first dhyāna and are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
that many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase therein.
Regarding the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) in the form and formless realms that increases in association with outflowing objects (*sāsravālambana*):
this refers to the latent tendency of sensual desire among the seven latent tendencies.
Pervading the eight stages of the realms of form and formlessness across five categories,
because they have only the outflow-bound as their object,
there are that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) which increase in association.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm:
all such dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm,
as well as the universal (sarvatraga) latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of origination (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya), increase [in association with them].

That is to say, among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), each of the ten underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) serves as [the cause] for all underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) increase [in association with them].
Specifically, all latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) increase.
Furthermore, regarding those universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering that increase [in association]:
this refers to the seven latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of origin among the ninety-eight latent dispositions within the desire realm.
Each and every one of these is increased by all the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*),
as well as by the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),
and by the proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Regarding those [defilements] in the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, with the exception of the untainted-object (anāsravālambana) and the unshared ignorance (āveṇikī avidyā),
all other [defilements] and the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [therein].
That is to say, among the ninety-eight proclivities, there are seven proclivities to be abandoned by the vision of cessation in the desire realm.
Each one is increased by that many underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
Regarding the underlying tendencies to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya) in the desire realm:

this includes all those to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm, with the exception of those that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object and the unshared ignorance (āveṇikī avidyā).
Regarding "all others and the pervasive underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase [in association with them]":

this means that among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies, each of the eight underlying tendencies of the desire realm to be abandoned by the path of seeing is increased in association by as many of those same underlying tendencies.
Regarding those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path,
it is stated in both cases that the untainted-object (anāsravālambana) and the unique ignorance (āveṇikī avidyā) are excluded;
this refers to their status among the latent tendencies (anuśaya).
They are not bound by the object-condition because they take uncontaminated phenomena as their objects;
they are not bound by association because they do not associate with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
[This refers to] the underlying tendencies of the desire realm that are abandoned through cultivation.
All [defilements] of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation,
as well as those pervasive latent tendencies (anuśaya) that increase [in association with them],
refer to those among the ninety-eight latent tendencies.
Regarding the statement: "The four latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm—each one is augmented by that many latent dispositions;
the detailed explanation for the five categories of latent dispositions in the form and formless realms is likewise."
That is to say, among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya),
there are thirty-one belonging to the five categories of the form realm (rūpadhātu) and thirty-one belonging to the five categories of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Each one is increased by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of its own realm and its own category,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions;
this is explained in detail as in the case of the desire realm, because their characteristics are the same.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School,
Volume 86; The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume 87.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, who received the Imperial Decree. Section 17: The Second Chapter on the Aggregates of Fetters (*Saṃyojana-skandha*), Sub-section Four: The Ten Gates of Summary, Part Seventeen. Herein, regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in relation to the various latent dispositions:
Regarding the bondage of the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) and the bondage of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*),
one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) based on their differing scopes.
There may be some underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Among the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), there are those that are bound by way of being an object (*ālambana-bandhana*) but not bound by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
These are the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and the non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*),
as well as certain other latent dispositions.

Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), they constitute a bond of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) rather than a bond of object (*ālambana-bandhana*), with the exception of those that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object and the unique ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*).
This refers to all other latent dispositions that take the untainted as their object.
There are some underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that,
with respect to other underlying tendencies, constitute both an object-condition bondage (*ālambana-bandhana*) and an associated bondage (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
This refers to all [underlying tendencies] except for those with outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
This is a general statement regarding all other latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that have outflow (*sāsrava*) as their object.

To speak of them specifically: if a [latent tendency] is bound to something by way of being its object (*ālambana-bandhana*), it is not bound to that same thing by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If a latent disposition (anuśaya) is bound to something by way of association, it is not bound to that same thing by way of being an object-condition (ālambana). Alternatively,
there may be latent dispositions that are neither bound to other latent dispositions by way of being an object-condition nor by way of association.
This refers to the unique ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) that takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object. Regarding this point,
the Venerable Ghosaka states:
There are four distinct cases.
There may be an underlying tendency (anuśaya) that,
with respect to other underlying tendencies, constitutes a bondage by way of being an object (ālambana-bandhana) but not a bondage by way of association (saṃprayoga-bandhana).
This refers to the fact that when the unique ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) of one's own level has not been abandoned,
it serves as a condition for those [defilements];

or, there may be latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that constitute a binding through association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) with other latent dispositions, rather than a binding through their object (*ālambana-bandhana*).
That is to say, excluding those conditioned by their own stage,
by another realm, by another stage,
or by both their own and another realm.
Either it has other dharmas of its own stage as its object;
or it has as its object the untainted (anāsrava), the non-common ignorance (āveṇikāvidyā), or other [dharmas] belonging to its own stage or to another realm;
or it has a different stage as its object.
Either with objects belonging to one's own realm or another realm,
or with phenomena belonging to one's own stage or other stages,
or with untainted objects— such latent dispositions (anuśaya) remain unabandoned.
There are some underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that,
with respect to other underlying tendencies, constitute both an object-binding (ālambana-bandhana) and an association-binding (samprayoga-bandhana);
namely, those excluding the unique ignorance (asādhāraṇa-avidyā) belonging to their own stage that takes them as its object.
This is a general statement regarding all other underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of one's own level that have not yet been abandoned and which take those [factors] as their objects.
To explain it specifically:

If there is a bondage by way of being an object-condition (ālambana-bandhana) with respect to something, there is no bondage by way of association (saṃprayoga-bandhana) with respect to that same thing;
if there is a bondage by way of association with respect to something,
there is no bondage by way of being an object-condition with respect to that same thing.
There are some latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are neither bound to other latent dispositions by way of an object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*);
namely, those latent dispositions that have already been abandoned.
If they have not been abandoned:
whether they are latent dispositions (anuśaya) of another stage,
or those belonging to one's own stage that take another realm as their object.
Either taking another stage as its object,
or taking both its own realm and other realms as its object,
or taking other phenomena within its own stage as its object.
Or [there is] untainted-object (anāsrava-ālambana) non-specific ignorance (āveṇika-avidyā).
Question: If the various underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, are they bound to objects that are themselves accompanied by vitarka and vicāra?
It may be answered in four propositions:
there are underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that possess both vitarka and vicāra, yet are not bound by way of an object (ālambana-bandhana) toward phenomena possessing both vitarka and vicāra.
This refers to those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra which have already been abandoned,
even if others remain unabandoned that take other realms as their object or other stages as their object.
Either having their own realm or another realm as an object-condition;
or having dharmas of their own stage or other stages as an object-condition;
or having the untainted (anāsrava) as an object-condition.
There are certain underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are bound to phenomena characterized by both vitarka and vicāra as their objects, yet are themselves not characterized by vitarka and vicāra;
namely, those underlying tendencies that are without vitarka and possess only vicāra.
These are outflow-tainted objects; as long as they have not been abandoned, there are underlying tendencies (anuśaya) present.
Furthermore, those accompanied by vitarka and vicāra are also bound by the objects of those dharmas accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
This refers to those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are accompanied by vitarka and vicāra,
which have as their object the outflows (sāsrava) of their own stage and have not yet been abandoned;
there are also certain latent dispositions that are not accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
Furthermore, they are not bound by objects consisting of phenomena with both vitarka and vicāra;
that is to say, those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that possess vitarka but only vicāra have already been abandoned,
even if they have not yet been abandoned when they take other realms as their objects.
Either taking another stage as its object,
or taking its own realm and other realms as its object,
or taking other phenomena of its own stage as its object.

Or, there are those that have untainted objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) and the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*). Question:

If certain latent dispositions are without applied thought and possess only sustained thought (*avitarko vicāramātraḥ*), are they bound by way of being an object (*ālambana-bandhana*) toward phenomena that are without applied thought and possess only sustained thought?
It can be answered in four propositions:
there are underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are without vitarka and with vicāra alone,
yet they are not bound by object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*) to those phenomena that are without vitarka and with vicāra alone.
This refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have been abandoned such that they are without vitarka and possess only vicāra;
even if not yet abandoned, they take other realms as their object or other stages as their object.
Either taking their own realm or another realm as an object;
or taking dharmas of their own stage or other stages as an object;
or taking the untainted (anāsrava) as an object.
There are certain latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are bound to objects consisting of states with no vitarka but only vicāra,
yet they themselves are not without vitarka and only with vicāra;
namely, those latent dispositions that possess both vitarka and vicāra.
These are the outflow-tainted conditions belonging to their own stage that have not yet been abandoned;
there are also underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that involve no vitarka but only vicāra,
which likewise constitute an object-binding (ālambana-bandhana) with respect to phenomena that involve no vitarka but only vicāra.
This refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are without vitarka and with only vicāra,
which have impure objects (*sāsravālambana*) and for which those objects have not yet been abandoned;
there are also certain latent dispositions that are neither without vitarka nor with only vicāra.
Furthermore, they are not bound by objects that are without vitarka and with only vicāra;
that is to say, the various latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with both vitarka and vicāra have already been abandoned,
even if those [dispositions] that take other realms as their object have not yet been abandoned.
Either taking another stage as an object,
or taking both its own realm and other realms as objects,
or taking other phenomena within its own stage as objects.
Or they have uncontaminated objects.
Furthermore, those latent dispositions that possess vitarka and vicāra yet belong to another stage,
as well as those latent dispositions that are without vitarka and vicāra.
Question: If the various latent dispositions (anuśaya) are without vitarka and without vicāra, are they bound to objects (ālambana-bandhana) that are without vitarka and without vicāra?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭi).
There are certain latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are without applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*),
yet they are not bound by being objects of focus (*ālambana-bandhana*) with respect to phenomena that are without applied and sustained thought;
that is to say, these latent dispositions are themselves without applied and sustained thought and have already been abandoned.
Suppose it has not been abandoned, yet it has another realm as its object,
or another stage as its object,
or both its own realm and another realm as its object.
Or there are those that have uncontaminated objects.
There are certain underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that are bound to phenomena devoid of vitarka and vicāra as their objects,
yet they themselves are not devoid of vitarka and vicāra.
That is to say, among the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), there are those with vitarka and vicāra,
or those without vitarka and with only vicāra, which take the contaminated (*sāsrava*) objects of their own level as their conditions and have not yet been abandoned;
there are also various latent tendencies that are without vitarka and without vicāra.
It is also bound by objects that are without vitarka and without vicāra;
that is to say, the various latent dispositions (anuśaya) which are themselves without vitarka and without vicāra have not yet been abandoned,
taking as their object those [states] belonging to their own stage that are associated with outflows (sāsrava).
There are certain latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are not without applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*),
and yet they are not bound by being objects of focus (*ālambana-bandhana*) with respect to states that are without applied and sustained thought;
namely, those latent dispositions that possess applied and sustained thought.
Or, while vitarka is absent and only vicāra remains,
it may be either abandoned or, if not yet abandoned,
have its object in another realm or another stage.
Either taking their own realm or another realm as an object;
or taking dharmas of their own stage or other stages as an object;
or taking the untainted (anāsrava) as an object.
Question: If the various latent dispositions (anuśaya) possess both vitarka and vicāra, are they bound by association (saṃprayoga-bandhana) with those dharmas that possess both vitarka and vicāra?
Answer: If the various latent dispositions are bound by association with dharmas that possess both vitarka and vicāra, they necessarily possess both vitarka and vicāra.
There may be latent dispositions (anuśaya) that possess both vitarka and vicāra,
yet are not bound by association with phenomena possessing vitarka and vicāra;
this refers to those latent dispositions that possess vitarka and vicāra but have already been abandoned.

Question: If certain latent dispositions (anuśaya) are without vitarka and possess only vicāra, are they bound by association (saṃprayoga-bandhana) with those phenomena that are without vitarka and possess only vicāra?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭi).
There are certain underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are without vitarka and with only vicāra,
yet they do not constitute an associated bondage (*saṃprayukta-bandhana*) toward phenomena that are without vitarka and with only vicāra;
namely, those underlying tendencies that are without vitarka and with only vicāra and have already been abandoned.
There are certain underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are bound by association with phenomena that are without vitarka and possess only vicāra,
yet they themselves are not without vitarka and possess only vicāra;
namely, those underlying tendencies that possess both vitarka and vicāra.
Regarding dharmas that are without vitarka and with only vicāra, they are bound by association;
there are also certain underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that are without vitarka and with only vicāra,
which likewise bind those dharmas without vitarka and with only vicāra through association.
This refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are without vitarka and possess only vicāra but have not yet been abandoned;
there are also latent dispositions that are neither without vitarka and possessing only vicāra,
nor are they bound by association with phenomena that are without vitarka and possess only vicāra.

This refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra which have already been abandoned, as well as those latent dispositions that are without vitarka and without vicāra.
Question: If there are latent dispositions that are without vitarka and without vicāra...
Are those [latent dispositions] bound by association with states that are without vitarka and without vicāra?
One should answer by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
There are latent dispositions that are without vitarka and without vicāra.
Furthermore, there is no binding through association with dharmas that are without vitarka and without vicāra;
that is to say, those latent dispositions (anuśaya) which are themselves without vitarka and without vicāra have already been abandoned.
Yet, there are certain latent dispositions that [pertain] to dharmas without vitarka and without vicāra.
There are those that are bound by association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) yet are neither without vitarka nor without vicāra;
namely, those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are without vitarka and possess only vicāra,
which act as a bond of association with respect to dharmas that are without vitarka and without vicāra.
There are certain latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are without applied thought and sustained thought (avitarkāvicārāḥ),
which also constitute an associated bondage (saṃprayoga-bandhana) with respect to phenomena that are without applied thought and sustained thought;
namely, those latent dispositions that are without applied thought and sustained thought and have not yet been abandoned.
There are certain latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are neither without vitarka nor without vicāra,
yet they do not constitute an associated bondage with respect to dharmas that are without vitarka and vicāra;
this refers to those latent dispositions that have been abandoned while being without vitarka and possessing only vicāra.
Furthermore, regarding the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra:
is there any phenomenon that is contaminated (*sāsrava*), is a mental factor (*caitasika*),
and is without vitarka but with only vicāra, which has neither been abandoned nor fully understood?
Is it not the case that the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of "without vitarka and with vicāra only" increase therein?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, the vitarka of the desire realm.
Is there any phenomenon that is with-outflows (*sāsrava*), is a mental factor (*caitta*),
and for which the *vitarka* is absent and only *vicāra* remains— yet, being neither abandoned nor fully understood,
it is subject to the increase of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with both *vitarka* and *vicāra*?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, the *vitarka* (applied thought) of the desire realm and the first *dhyāna*.
Is there any phenomenon that is with-outflows (*sāsrava*), is a mental factor (*caitasika*), and is without *vitarka* and *vicāra* (without applied and sustained thought)?
Is it not the case that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with [states] that are without vitarka and without vicāra?
Answer: Yes, there is.
Namely, the vicāra of the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
Is there any aggregate that arises at one time and abides at one time?
Simultaneously extinguished;
having a single basis;
having a single object.
The characteristic of co-arising:
they arise together at the time of arising and perish together at the time of perishing.
Furthermore, regarding those [defilements], are there latent dispositions (anuśaya) that constitute both associated bondage (saṃprayukta-bandhana) and non-associated bondage?
Answer: There are;
namely, the cluster of unshared ignorance (āveṇikī-avidyā).
Ignorance has the bond of association with respect to those [factors];
that is to say, there is the bond of non-association with respect to factors associated with ignorance;
that is to say, with respect to the intrinsic nature of ignorance itself.
Regarding the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—

among these ninety-eight latent tendencies, how many latent tendencies increase in each of the consciousnesses that take them as objects and the consciousnesses that take those objects as their objects?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of other schools and elucidating the correct meaning.
Specifically, the Dārṣṭāntikas (Exemplifiers) have asserted as follows:
The objects of the six groups of consciousness, beginning with the eye-consciousness, are each distinct.
They maintain that the mental consciousness has its own distinct objects of perception and does not take as its objects those perceived by the five consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness.
Furthermore, it is said that the six consciousnesses only take external objects as their conditions,
not internal faculties nor other consciousnesses.
This is intended to refute that view and to clarify that each of the first five consciousnesses has its own distinct object of perception.
It takes only external objects as its object, not the sense organs or consciousnesses.

The objects of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) may be the same as or different from the objects of the five sensory consciousnesses; it also takes internal organs as its objects and takes all consciousnesses as its objects.
Furthermore, this treatise is composed in order to reveal the correct principles of all phenomena so that others may understand them.
It should be known that the phenomena which serve as objects of focus herein are of sixteen kinds.
That is to say, the various consciousnesses that take as their objects the five categories of each of the three realms,
as well as untainted dharmas, likewise possess these sixteen kinds of distinctions.
Question: Among these, which phenomena are the objects of how many consciousnesses?
Answer: The phenomena of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering are the objects of five consciousnesses:
first, all consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
1. Consciousness associated with the universal latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm; 2.
Wholesome and unobscured-neutral consciousness to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the desire realm; 3.
Wholesome and unobscured-neutral consciousness to be abandoned through cultivation in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The five types of untainted consciousness belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge,
as well as the objects of the five consciousnesses that are dharmas abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the desire realm, are likewise [untainted].
As for the distinctions:
this refers to all consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*),
and consciousnesses associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
The dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of cessation are the objects of six consciousnesses:
first, the consciousness associated with the universal proclivities to be abandoned by the vision of suffering in the desire realm;
second, the consciousness associated with the universal proclivities to be abandoned by the vision of origin in the desire realm.

Third, the consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm that have outflow (sāsrava) and take cessation as their object, which are to be abandoned through seeing;
fourth, the wholesome and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation.
The wholesome consciousnesses and the non-obscured neutral consciousnesses of the five material realms that are abandoned through cultivation;
the six types of untainted consciousness belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge;
and likewise, the objects of the six consciousnesses that are abandoned through the path of vision regarding the desire realm—all these are as previously described.
As for the distinctions:
this refers to the consciousness associated with the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that have outflow-conditions (*sāsrava*) and are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*),
as well as the objects of the five consciousnesses among the phenomena abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) in the desire realm.
First, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm;
second, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the desire realm.
Third, the wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
as well as the defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses;
fourth, the wholesome and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the form realm.

The untainted consciousness belonging to the category of the five dharma-knowledges is the object of eight types of consciousness regarding the factors abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form realm:
first, the consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.

1. Consciousness associated with universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take other realms as their object, which are abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm; 2.
wholesome consciousness abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the desire realm; 3.
all consciousness associated with latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the form realm.

1. Consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the fivefold realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*).
2. Wholesome (*kuśala*) and non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) consciousnesses in the realm of form abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
3. Wholesome consciousness in the realm of formlessness (*ārūpya-dhātu*) abandoned through cultivation.

The same applies to the eight consciousnesses that take as their objects the phenomena of the form realm abandoned through the vision of the origin of suffering within the category of subsequent knowledge (kṣayajñāna).
The difference is as follows:
This refers to all consciousnesses associated with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the form realm;
consciousnesses associated with the universal latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*);
and the nine consciousnesses that take as their objects the phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the form realm.
First, consciousness associated with universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm;
second, consciousness associated with universal latent dispositions that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the desire realm.
1. Wholesome consciousness in the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation;
2. Consciousness associated with the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form realm;
3. Consciousness associated with the pervasive latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the form realm.
Six: consciousnesses associated with the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the form realm;
seven: wholesome and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses to be abandoned through cultivation within the form realm.
The eighth is the wholesome consciousness of the formless realm abandoned through cultivation;
the ninth is the untainted consciousness belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
It is the same for the objects of the nine consciousnesses regarding the factors abandoned through the path of seeing in the form realm.
As for the distinctions:
the consciousness associated with the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that have outflows and take [the factors] to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the form realm as their object;
and the eight consciousnesses that take the phenomena to be abandoned by the path of cultivation in the form realm as their objects.

1. Consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm;

2. consciousness associated with the universal proclivities that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm.
1. Wholesome consciousness in the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation;
2. Consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form realm;
3. Consciousness associated with the universal proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the form realm.
1. The wholesome, afflicted, and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses of the form realm that are abandoned through cultivation; 2.
The wholesome consciousnesses of the formless realm that are abandoned through cultivation;
3. The untainted consciousnesses belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
The dharmas of the formless realm abandoned through the vision of suffering are the objects of ten consciousnesses:
first, the consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.

1. Consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm; 2. consciousness associated with the universal proclivities that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of the origin in the desire realm;
3. wholesome consciousness (*kuśala-vijñāna*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the desire realm; 4.
consciousness associated with the universal proclivities that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the form realm.

1. Consciousness associated with the universal underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) that take other realms as their object, which are abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the five form realms;
2. Wholesome consciousness in the six form realms that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*);
3. All consciousness associated with the underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realms.
Eighth, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realm;
ninth, wholesome and non-obscured neutral consciousness (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-vijñāna*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the formless realm.

The ten types of untainted consciousness belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) likewise have the phenomena of the formless realm abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] as their objects.
The difference is as follows:
This refers to all consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realm;
consciousnesses associated with the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*);
and the eleven consciousnesses that take as their objects the phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realm.

1. Consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm;

2. consciousness associated with the universal proclivities that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm.
1. Wholesome consciousness abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm;

2. Consciousness associated with pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) in the form realm;
3. Consciousness associated with pervasive latent dispositions that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*) in the form realm.
Sixth, the wholesome consciousness of the form realm that is abandoned through cultivation;
seventh, the consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering in the formless realm;
eighth, the consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the formless realm.

Ninth, the consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have outflows and take cessation as their object, which are to be abandoned by the vision [of the truth] regarding the formless realm;
tenth, the wholesome and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses of the formless realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation.
The untainted consciousness belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is the object of eleven types of consciousness;
the same applies to the factors abandoned through the path of vision (darśana-mārga) in the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu).
The difference is as follows:
This refers to the consciousness associated with the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) proclivities (anuśaya) abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) that take the formless realm as their object.
It is the object of ten types of consciousness regarding the phenomena abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) in the formless realm:

first, the consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatragānuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha) in the desire realm.

1. Consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms as their object, which are abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm; 2.

Consciousness associated with the universal proclivities that take other realms as their object, which are abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the form realm. 3. Wholesome consciousness in the desire realm abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya); 4. Consciousness associated with the universal proclivities that take other realms as their object, which are abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the form realm.

1. Consciousness associated with universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take other realms as their object, which are abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the fivefold realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
2. Wholesome consciousness in the realm of form that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
3. Consciousness associated with universal latent dispositions that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Eighth, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realm;
ninth, wholesome, afflicted, and non-obscured neutral consciousness in the formless realm to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The ten types of untainted consciousness belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) take the ten types of untainted phenomena as their objects:

first, the consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have the untainted as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya) within the desire realm.

1. Consciousness associated with the untainted-object (anāsrava-ālambana) proclivities abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) in the desire realm; 2. Consciousness associated with the untainted-object proclivities abandoned through the path of seeing in the form realm;
3. Wholesome consciousness abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) in the desire realm; 4.
Consciousness associated with the untainted-object proclivities abandoned through the path of seeing the cessation [of suffering] (nirodha-darśana-heya) in the form realm.
1. Consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take the untainted as their object, which are abandoned through the path of seeing in the five form realms;
2. wholesome consciousness in the six form realms abandoned through cultivation;
3. consciousness associated with the latent dispositions that take the untainted as their object, which are abandoned through the vision of cessation in the formless realm.

1. The consciousness associated with the untainted objects (anāsrava-ālambana) of the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) in the formless realm; 2–8. [The seven types of consciousness associated with the latent tendencies to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) in the formless realm];
9. The wholesome consciousness (kuśala-vijñāna) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the formless realm; 10.
The untainted consciousness belonging to the category of the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna-pakṣya) and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna-pakṣya).
Question: For each of these sixteen consciousnesses, how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in association?
Answer: For the consciousness of the desire realm abandoned through the vision of suffering, all [underlying tendencies] abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm [increase].

Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) increase [in relation to] the consciousnesses of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of the origin; that is,
all [consciousnesses] of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of the origin.

Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering increase [in relation to] the consciousness of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of cessation,
as well as all [factors] of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
And the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase therein.
Regarding consciousness abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm,
all [factors] abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm [increase].
And the pervasive latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase therein.
Regarding the consciousnesses of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya),
all [factors] of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation [increase].
And the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [therein].
It is the same for the fivefold classes of consciousness in the form and formless realms;
the difference is as follows:
That is to say, one should explain for each [category] its own realm’s untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*).
The meaning of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increasing through association is as previously stated.
Furthermore, the objects (*ālambana*) of this [consciousness] consist of thirty-two kinds of phenomena.
This means that each of the aforementioned sixteen dharmas has two types.
Regarding the two types of the first four categories:
the first is association (*samprayoga*).
The two types not associated [with the mind] that are abandoned through cultivation are:
first, the defiled; and second, the non-defiled.
The second is the non-defiled.
Regarding the two kinds of untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena:
the first is the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The two unconditioned [factors] and the conditioned untainted [factors],
namely the categories of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
The unconditioned and untainted [factors] refer to the three unconditioned phenomena.
The consciousnesses that take these as objects likewise consist of thirty-two types.
This means that each of the aforementioned sixteen consciousnesses is of two kinds.
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin,
the first is consciousness associated with pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
Second, consciousness associated with non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), there are two types:
first, consciousness associated with latent dispositions that take conditioned phenomena as their object (*saṃskṛtālambana-anuśaya*).
The two types of consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) as their object;
the two types [of consciousness] to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśanamārga), namely:
first, consciousness associated with the latent dispositions that take the contaminated (sāsrava) as their object.
The two types of consciousness associated with latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have the untainted as their object;
the two types to be abandoned by cultivation:
first, defiled consciousness.
Second, non-defiled consciousness.
Regarding the two types of untainted [consciousness]:
first, the untainted consciousness belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna).
Regarding the second category, the untainted consciousnesses of the class of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*):
herein, for each individual dharma, there are as many objects of consciousness as there are;
and for each individual consciousness, there are as many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that increase in association as there are.
Each should be explained according to its respective case, following the previous pattern.
Furthermore, the dharmas that serve as objects of focus herein number one hundred and twenty;
specifically, there are ninety-eight defiled dharmas belonging to the five categories within the three realms.
That is to say, the category of the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Within this, there are both their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) and their associated factors (*samprayukta*).
If they arise from those [defilements],
they are all designated as belonging to that category.
There are seventeen non-defiled dharmas within the three realms that are abandoned through cultivation.
That is to say: seven in the desire realm,
six in the form realm,
and four in the formless realm.
Regarding the seven [types] in the desire realm:
there are two kinds of wholesome [dharmas].
First, those wholesome dharmas acquired at birth.
Second are the wholesome dharmas of application (*prayoga-kuśala*).
There are five types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas:
first, those born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Second, the dharmas of the modes of deportment;
third, the dharmas of the spheres of craftsmanship;
fourth, the indeterminate dharmas resulting from liberation.
The five intrinsic natures are indeterminate dharmas.
Regarding the six [dharmas] of the form realm,
there are two types of wholesome [dharmas].
As explained for the desire realm,
there are four types of neutral [states],
excluding those pertaining to the sphere of craftsmanship.
The rest is as explained for the desire realm.
Regarding the four [categories] of the formless realm:
that is, the wholesome has two [types].
As explained regarding the desire realm,
there are two types of neutral [states]:
first, those born of maturation (vipākaja).
The two intrinsic natures are indeterminate.
There are five types of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*):
namely, the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) and the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Including the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*),
there are one hundred and fourteen cognitions that can take them as objects.
That is to say, there are ninety-eight defiled cognitions belonging to the five categories within the three realms.
That is to say, the consciousnesses associated with the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
There are fourteen non-defiled consciousnesses to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) across the three realms;
specifically, there are six in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
First, the consciousness acquired at birth;
second, the consciousness resulting from application;
third, the consciousness born of maturation.
1. Consciousness pertaining to the four modes of deportment;
2. consciousness pertaining to the arts and crafts; 3.
indeterminate consciousness that is the fruit of supernormal powers.
In the realm of form, there are five;
excluding the consciousness of the sphere of craftsmanship,
the rest are as described for the desire realm.
The formless realm has three types:
first, innate wholesome consciousness;
second, acquired through application wholesome consciousness.
Third, the consciousness produced by maturation (*vipākaja*).
There are two types of untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*):
first, the untainted consciousness belonging to the category of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*).
Regarding the second category, the untainted consciousnesses belonging to the class of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*): herein,
each individual dharma is the object of apprehension for a corresponding number of such consciousnesses,
and each such consciousness has a corresponding number of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase in association with it.
Each should be explained according to its respective case, following the previous [explanation].
Question: What dharmas can the wholesome consciousness acquired at birth (upapattilābhika-kuśala-vijñāna) take as its object?
Answer: Those belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu).
It can take as its objects all phenomena of the three realms as well as the untainted (anāsrava).
Regarding the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
it can take as its objects all tainted and untainted phenomena of its own level and the levels above it, as well as space.
Question: What dharmas can the wholesome consciousness of application (prayoga-kuśala-vijñāna) take as its object? Answer:
That which belongs to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu) can take all dharmas of the three realms as well as the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas as its objects.
That which belongs to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)—

It can take as its objects all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena of its own level and higher levels, as well as space, and furthermore, the contaminated phenomena of the immediately lower level.
Question: What kind of phenomena can the indeterminate consciousness born of maturation (*vipākaja-avyākṛta-vijñāna*) take as its objects?
Answer: The unwholesome fruits of the desire realm take only those dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation as their object.
As for the wholesome fruits:
It takes as its object only the five categories of phenomena belonging to the desire realm.
As for the form realm,
it takes as its objects all contaminated phenomena of its own level and those of lower levels.
Some say that it takes as its object only the five categories of phenomena belonging to its own level;
those in the formless realm take as their objects only the five categories of phenomena belonging to their own level.
Question: What dharmas can the consciousness of the modes of deportment take as its object?
Answer: For those in the desire realm, it takes only the five categories of dharmas of the desire realm as its object.
Regarding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*):
it takes as its object only the five categories of phenomena within the desire and form realms.
Question: What phenomena can consciousness pertaining to the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) take as its object?
Answer: It takes as its object only the five categories of phenomena belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Question: What kind of phenomena can the neutral consciousness of supernormal power (*abhijñā*) take as its object?
Answer: Those belonging to the desire realm.
Those belonging to the form realm take only those dharmas abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm as their object;
those belonging to the formless realm take only those dharmas abandoned through cultivation in both the desire and form realms as their object.
Question: By which consciousnesses are space and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) taken as objects?
Answer: They are objects of the wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) within the three realms.
Regarding the eye faculty, the consciousness that takes it as an object belongs to the three categories (prakāra) of the desire and form realms.
The universal [defilements] of the formless realm and the objects of consciousness to be abandoned through cultivation—
these four categories across the three realms— and the eye faculty, which pertains to the five stages of the desire and form realms and is exclusively to be abandoned through cultivation.
Among the sixteen types of consciousness, those that take the eight consciousnesses as their objects are:
first, the consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm;
this [consciousness] takes as its object everything that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) increase in association [with these].
Second, there are the consciousnesses associated with the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned by the vision of the origin in the desire realm;
these consciousnesses include all [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of the origin in the desire realm.
Furthermore, the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering increase therein.
Third, there are the wholesome, afflicted, and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation;
these consciousnesses comprise all those of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation.
as well as the pervasive latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that increase [in association with it].
Fourth, the consciousness associated with the pervasive latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form realm;
this consciousness is associated with all [factors] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form realm.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) increase [in these].
In the five form realms (*rūpa-dhātu*), there is consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin;
this consciousness [is associated with] all [factors] abandoned through the vision of the origin in the form realm.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering increase therein.
There are six types of consciousness belonging to the form realm that are abandoned through cultivation: wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses.
All of these consciousnesses are abandoned through cultivation in the form realm.
And the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase therein.
The seven wholesome consciousnesses of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation are the wholesome minds of the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of the Sphere of Infinite Space.
This consciousness is accompanied by the increase of all latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
as well as the universal latent dispositions; it is also associated with the eight untainted (anāsrava) consciousnesses.
This refers to the categories of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge regarding suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-dharmānvaya-jñāna-pakṣa*).
Since these consciousnesses are not increased by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
it is said that the eye-faculty has as its object the three categories of the desire and form realms.
The pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase [in relation to it].
As for the eye faculty,
it is the object of thirteen out of the sixteen types of consciousness within the category of consciousness that takes it as its object.

First, all consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are consciousnesses that take the eye faculty as their object-of-object (*ālambanālambana*),
and they take the eye faculty as their object.

The consciousnesses and so forth associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm; therefore,
this consciousness is subject to the increase (*anuśayana*) of all [defilements] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm,
as well as the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

Second, all consciousnesses associated with the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) within the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are consciousnesses that take the eye faculty as their object-of-the-object (ālambanālambana),
while taking the eye faculty itself as their object.

The consciousnesses and so forth associated with the universal underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm; therefore,
this consciousness is subject to the increase (*anuśerate*) of all [tendencies] to be abandoned by the vision of the origin in the desire realm,
as well as those universal underlying tendencies to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
The third is the consciousness associated with the untainted-object (anāsrava-ālambana) latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) within the desire realm;
this is the consciousness that takes the eye faculty as its object-of-the-object (ālambana-ālambana), and which itself has the eye faculty as its object.
This consciousness is associated with the category of the dharma-knowledge of the origin of suffering;
therefore, all pervasive and non-pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of vision in the desire realm increase in relation to this consciousness.
The fourth [category] consists of the wholesome, afflicted, and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation;
these are the consciousnesses that take the eye faculty as their object-of-the-object (ālambanālambana) and take the eye faculty as their object.
Since this consciousness consists of the consciousnesses and so forth that are abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned (*bhāvanā-heya*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in association with it.

The consciousness associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering within the realm of the five colors is the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object-of-object;
it takes the eye-faculty as its object-of-object.
The consciousnesses and so forth associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the form realm; therefore,
this consciousness is increased by all [dispositions] abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form realm,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

The consciousness associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the six spheres of form is the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object-of-the-object;
it takes the eye-faculty as its object.

The consciousnesses associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the form realm, and so forth; therefore,
this consciousness is subject to the increase (*anuśerate*) of all [dispositions] abandoned through the vision of the origin in the form realm,
as well as those universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

The consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) in the seven form realms (rūpadhātu) and which take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object is a consciousness that takes the eye-faculty (cakṣurindriya) as its object-of-the-object;
it takes the eye-faculty as its object-of-the-object.
Because this consciousness is associated with the category of the subsequent knowledge of the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudayānvayajñāna*),
all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and [non-pervasive] latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) in the form realm increase (*anuśerate*) within it.

The virtuous consciousnesses, as well as the afflicted and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses, of the eight form-realms that are to be abandoned by cultivation are the consciousnesses that take the eye-faculty as their object-of-object;
they take the eye-faculty as their object-of-object.
Since these are consciousnesses and so forth abandoned through cultivation in the form realm,
all pervasive and non-pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation in the form realm increase in relation to this consciousness.

The consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the nine formless realms is a consciousness that takes the eye faculty as its object-of-the-object;
it takes the eye faculty as its object.
This wholesome consciousness of the formless realm is abandoned through cultivation;

therefore, all pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and those abandoned through the vision of the origin increase in association with this consciousness.

The consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the ten formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) is a consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object-of-the-object;
it takes the eye-faculty as its object-of-the-object.
Because this wholesome consciousness of the formless realm is abandoned through cultivation,
all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm that are abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering],
as well as those abandoned through the vision of suffering that are universal, increase in association with this consciousness.

The eleventh is the consciousness associated with the untainted-object (anāsrava-ālambana) latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu);
this is the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object-of-the-object (ālambanālambana), and which itself has the eye-faculty as its object.
Because this consciousness is associated with the category of the subsequent knowledge of the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudayānvayajñānapakṣa*),
