all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and omnipresent (*anuvartin*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) increase (*anuśerate*) therein.
The twelve types of consciousness belonging to the formless realm that are abandoned through cultivation which are wholesome,
as well as those that are defiled or non-obscured-neutral,
are the consciousnesses that take the eye faculty as their object-condition.
With the eye faculty as its object-condition,
there are the wholesome consciousnesses and so forth of the formless realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation;
therefore, this consciousness consists of all those [factors] of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase therein.
The thirteen types of untainted consciousness (anāsrava-vijñāna) belonging to the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin,
and the path are the consciousnesses that take the eye-faculty as their object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Because the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for the eye-faculty consists of both contaminated and uncontaminated consciousness,
this consciousness is not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya).
Therefore, it is said that for the eye faculty as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for consciousness,
the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms and four categories increase;
the same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
That is to say, the ear and other faculties also pertain to the five stages of the desire and form realms;
they are abandoned solely through cultivation, just like the eye faculty.
The consciousness that takes the female faculty as its object belongs to the three categories of the desire realm.
The universal [afflictions] of the form realm,
as well as the objects of consciousness to be abandoned through cultivation,
and the four categories of the desire realm.
The three categories of the form realm,
the universal [afflictions] of the formless realm,
and those to be abandoned through cultivation.
The female faculty is the object of five consciousnesses among the sixteen consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm:
first, the consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.

This consciousness is associated with all pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm, as well as those abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, it is associated with two types of consciousness: those abandoned through the vision of origin in the desire realm that are themselves associated with pervasive latent dispositions.
This consciousness is increased by all the proclivities (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-heya) in the desire realm,
as well as the universal proclivities abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-heya).
It is also increased by the three wholesome [states] abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the desire realm.
Furthermore, regarding the defiled and the non-obscured-neutral consciousnesses,
all pervasive and universal proclivities (anuśaya) increase in association with these consciousnesses throughout the desire realm, as well as all [proclivities] to be abandoned through cultivation.
The wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the form realm,
as well as the non-obscured neutral consciousnesses—
all such consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the form realm.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase therein.
As for the five untainted consciousnesses (anāsrava-vijñāna)—
namely, those belonging to the categories of the dharma-knowledge of suffering and origin— these consciousnesses are not subject to the increase of latent dispositions.
Therefore, it is said that the female faculty conditions consciousness;
the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three categories of the desire realm, the universal [dispositions] of the form realm,
and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in association with it.
Regarding consciousness conditioned by the female faculty as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
among the sixteen types of consciousness, it is the object of nine consciousnesses.

First, all consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm are consciousnesses conditioned by the female faculty as their object-condition.
With the female faculty as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),

there are consciousnesses and so forth associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) in the desire realm; therefore,
this consciousness consists of all [factors] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.
Furthermore, it is associated with the increase of the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

Second, all consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are the consciousness that takes the female faculty (*strīndriya*) as its object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for the female faculty consists of consciousness and so forth associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-heya) in the desire realm; therefore,
this consciousness comprises all [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of the origin in the desire realm.
Furthermore, the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering increase [in relation to it].
Third, there are the consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions to be abandoned through the path of vision that take the untainted as their object;
these consciousnesses take the female faculty as their object, and they take the consciousness that takes the female faculty as its object as their own object.
This consciousness is associated with the category of the dharma-knowledge of the origin of suffering;
therefore, all pervasive and non-pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of vision in the desire realm increase within this consciousness.
The wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
as well as defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses,
are the consciousnesses that take the female faculty as their object-condition.
Taking the female faculty as its object-condition,
it consists of consciousnesses and so forth that are abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm;
therefore, this consciousness comprises all those factors abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
And the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [therein].

The consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) within the five form realms (rūpa-dhātu) is the consciousness that takes the female faculty (strī-indriya) as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
The female faculty serves as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for consciousness that is wholesome and abandoned through cultivation in the form realm,
as well as for unobscured-neutral consciousness.
Therefore, in this consciousness, all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the form realm abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),
as well as the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), increase;
and [there are] six consciousnesses associated with the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin in the form realm.
This is the consciousness that takes the female faculty as its object-condition;
it takes the female faculty as its object-condition,
being the wholesome [state] abandoned by cultivation in the form realm.
And because it is also an unobscured-neutral consciousness,
this consciousness is increased by all the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the realm of form that are abandoned through the vision of origin,
as well as those abandoned through the vision of suffering that are universal.
The wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the seven realms of form,
as well as defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses,
take the female faculty as their object-condition; these consciousnesses take the female faculty as their object-condition.
Because it consists of the wholesome [states] abandoned through cultivation in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
as well as non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) consciousnesses and so forth,
this consciousness is entirely abandoned through cultivation in the form realm.
And the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase therein.
The wholesome consciousness of the formless realm abandoned through cultivation is the object-conditioned consciousness for the female faculty.
Taking the female faculty as its object-condition,
there are the wholesome and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses of the form realm that are abandoned through cultivation; therefore,
this consciousness [takes] all [consciousnesses] of the formless realm abandoned through cultivation [as its object].
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase therein.
The nine types of untainted consciousness (anāsrava-vijñāna) belonging to the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin,
and the path are the objects of the consciousness that takes the female faculty (strīndriya) as its object-condition.
With the female faculty as its object-condition,
there are both tainted and untainted consciousnesses;
therefore, latent dispositions do not increase in accordance with this consciousness.
Therefore, it is said that the female faculty conditions consciousness through its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya):
four categories of the desire realm and three categories of the form realm.
The universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation increase [therein].
It is the same for the male faculty and the faculty of suffering.
That is to say, the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) are also exclusively abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
just like the female faculty (*strīndriya*).

As for the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*), its objects-of-consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) belong to the three realms and the three categories [of afflictions], while its objects-of-objects-of-consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*) likewise belong to the three realms and the three categories.
Regarding the four categories within the three realms:
the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) pervades the three realms and nine stages, is abandoned solely through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya),
and is the object of ten of the sixteen consciousnesses.

First, there is the consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This consciousness is permeated by all [latent dispositions] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Second, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm:
this consciousness is augmented by all [dispositions] to be abandoned through the vision of the origin in the desire realm,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
The third [category] consists of the wholesome, afflicted, and non-obscured-neutral consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
These consciousnesses are all increased by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions.
Just as there are three categories of consciousness in the desire realm,
so too are there three categories each in the form and formless realms;
together, these constitute nine types of consciousness.
The ten untainted consciousnesses refer to the categories of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge regarding suffering and its origin;
because these consciousnesses are not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

It is taught that the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), when taken as a condition for consciousness, is associated with the increase of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms and the three categories.
Regarding the life-faculty as a condition for consciousness,
among the sixteen types of consciousness, it is the object of thirteen types of consciousness.

All consciousnesses associated with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are consciousnesses that have the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as their object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
They take the life-faculty as their object-condition,
such as consciousnesses associated with the universal latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.
Therefore, in this consciousness, all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm,
as well as the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), increase. Furthermore,
it is associated with all latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin in the desire realm.
This life-faculty is the object-condition for consciousness;
it is the object-condition for the life-faculty,
namely, consciousnesses associated with the universal underlying tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin of suffering, and so forth.
Therefore, this consciousness is accompanied by all latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm,
as well as those universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya). Furthermore,
it is associated with the latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object.
This life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is consciousness conditioned by an object-condition;
it is consciousness associated with the category of dharma-knowledge regarding suffering and its origin that conditions the object-condition of the life-faculty.
Therefore, this consciousness is pervaded by all the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the path of seeing in the desire realm,
as well as by the wholesome [states] abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
Furthermore, defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses are the object-conditioned consciousness (ālambanapratyaya-vijñāna) of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya),
and they take the life-faculty as their object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Because this consciousness consists of those factors of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and non-pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation in the desire realm increase within it.
Just as there are four categories of consciousness in the desire realm,
so it is for each of the four categories of consciousness in the form and formless realms.
The difference is as follows:
This refers to the consciousness associated with the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that are abandoned by the path of seeing and which take the outflow-free (anāsrava) as their object;
it takes the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) as its objective support,
and it is the consciousness associated with the category of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin (duḥkha- and samudaya-anvaya-jñāna).
The subsequent [categories] should be understood accordingly as constituting twelve consciousnesses.
The thirteenth is the untainted consciousness belonging to the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path.
This life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for consciousness;
consciousness that takes the life-faculty as its object-condition may be either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
Therefore, latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase in accordance with this consciousness.
Therefore, it is said that for the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),

which serves as an object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for consciousness, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the three realms and four categories increase. *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle Eighty-seven.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Eighty-eight,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Four of the Ten Gates on the Aggregates of the Second Chapter, "The Aggregate of Fetters," Part Eighteen: Regarding the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), consciousness as its object, consciousness as the object-of-the-object (*ālambanālambana*), and conditioned phenomena as conditions.

Because the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) pervades the three realms, nine stages, and five categories of both contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena— specifically the category of the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)—
it is the object of sixteen types of consciousness: first,
all consciousnesses associated with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm.
This consciousness is associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm,
as well as those universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, it is associated with all latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin in the desire realm.
This consciousness is associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm,
as well as the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). Furthermore,
it is associated with the conditioned-object (*saṃskṛtālambana*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm.

This consciousness is associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation within the desire realm and which have conditioned phenomena as their object,
as well as with the universal latent dispositions. Furthermore,
it is associated with all latent dispositions abandoned through the path of vision within the desire realm.
This consciousness is subject to the increase of all pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the desire realm,
as well as the wholesome, afflicted, and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the five [realms] of the desire realm.
This consciousness is subject to the increase of all latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, as well as the universal ones,
just like the five categories of consciousness in the desire realm that take conditioned phenomena as their objects.
In the realms of form and formlessness, there are likewise five categories each of consciousness conditioned by the conditioned;
these together constitute fifteen types of consciousness,
along with sixteen untainted (anāsrava) types of consciousness.
This refers to the categories of the receptivities and knowledges of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge regarding suffering, origin, and the path.
In these states, this consciousness is not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

Therefore, it is said that the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), when taking consciousness as its object, is subject to the increase of latent dispositions that have conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as their objects.
The mind-faculty that takes consciousness as its object-condition is also the object of sixteen consciousnesses.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in relation to this mind-faculty that takes consciousness as its object-condition,
just as it was explained regarding the mind-faculty that takes consciousness as its object.

Therefore, it is said that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with the mind-faculty (manas-indriya) when it has consciousness as its object-condition and conditioned phenomena as its objective condition;

the same applies to the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya). This is because the faculty of equanimity, like the mind-faculty, also extends across the three realms, the nine stages, the five categories, and both contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena belonging to the category of the knowledge of classes (anvaya-jñāna-pakṣa).
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) has as its object the four categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It has as its object the conditioned factors (*saṃskṛta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and two categories of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
as well as the universal objects (*sarvatraga*) and the four categories of the desire and formless realms that take consciousness as their object.
Regarding those conditioned by the form realm:
the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) extends through the desire realm, the first dhyāna, and the third dhyāna.
As for the desire realm:
In the first dhyāna, there is association with the five groups of consciousness; in [the higher stages],
there is association with three groups of consciousness.
These two exist only as contaminated (*sāsrava*) and are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
As for the third dhyāna,
that which is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-samprayukta*) is both contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The contaminated (*sāsrava*) [factors] pertain to all five categories (*pañca-varga*).
The uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [factors] pertain to the categories of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Therefore, among the sixteen consciousnesses, this faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is the object of twelve consciousnesses.
First, regarding the consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm:
this consciousness is accompanied by the increase of all [proclivities] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm,
as well as the universal proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Second, the consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm:
this consciousness is accompanied by all [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of the origin in the desire realm,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

Third, regarding the consciousness associated with the untainted-object (anāsrava-ālambana) latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya) in the desire realm:
this consciousness is increased by all [latent dispositions] to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm,
as well as by the universal (sarvatraga) latent dispositions.
The fourth consists of the wholesome [states] abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
as well as the defiled and the non-obscured-neutral consciousnesses;
this consciousness includes all [factors] abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
And the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [in relation to] it.
In the five form-realm consciousnesses associated with all latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering,
this consciousness is associated with all [latent dispositions] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form realm.
Furthermore, there is the increase of the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
There are six consciousnesses associated with all latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin in the form realm;
these consciousnesses are associated with all [latent dispositions] abandoned through the vision of the origin in the form realm.
Furthermore, it is accompanied by the increase of the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Regarding the consciousness associated with the latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation that take conditioned phenomena as their object within the seven realms of form:

this consciousness is accompanied by the increase of the latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation that take conditioned phenomena as their object, as well as the universal latent dispositions.

The consciousness associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) within the eight form realms is increased by all those [dispositions] to be abandoned through the path of vision in the form realm,
as well as by the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions.
The wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation and the defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses of the nine levels of the form realm—
this consciousness is increased by all the latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through cultivation in the form realm,
as well as by the universal latent dispositions.

10. The consciousness associated with the untainted objects (anāsrava-ālambana) of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya) in the formless realm; all such [dispositions] to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the formless realm, as well as the universal (sarvatraga) latent dispositions, increase in association with this consciousness.
11. The wholesome consciousness (kuśala-vijñāna) to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the formless realm.
This consciousness is accompanied by the increase of all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions;
it consists of twelve untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses.
This refers to the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin, path, and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Because latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase in accordance with this consciousness,
it is said that the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) takes this consciousness as its object.

The four categories of the desire realm, the conditioned objects of the form realm, and the two categories of the formless realm—along with their pervasive and specific latent dispositions (anuśaya)—increase [in association].
Regarding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), sixteen consciousnesses take it as their object; among these, fourteen consciousnesses are its objective supports (*ālambana*).

First, all consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm are consciousnesses that take the faculty of pleasure as their object-of-object;
they take the faculty of pleasure as their object.
The consciousnesses and so forth associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) in the desire realm; therefore,
all [factors] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm,
as well as the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), increase (*anuśerate*) in this consciousness.

Second, all consciousnesses associated with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm are consciousnesses that take the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as their object-of-the-object;
these include consciousnesses associated with the universal latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin, and so forth.
Therefore, this consciousness is associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm,
as well as those universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Thirdly, it is associated with all latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm.
This is the consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya),

and which itself is associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm abandoned by the path of vision (darśana-mārga) that have the outflow-free (anāsrava) as their object, taking the faculty of pleasure as its object-condition.
Furthermore, it is associated with the categories of knowledge regarding suffering, origin, and the path (*duḥkha-samudaya-mārga-dharma-jñāna-pakṣya*).

Therefore, all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*) in the desire realm increase (*anuśerate*) within this consciousness, as do the wholesome [states] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the four desire realms.
As well as defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses,
these are the consciousnesses that take the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as their object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), and which in turn take the faculty of pleasure as their object.
Since this consciousness consists of the consciousnesses and so forth abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
all pervasive and non-pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm increase in association with it.

The consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering in the five formless realms is a consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object;
it takes the faculty of pleasure as its object-of-the-object.

This refers to the consciousnesses and so forth associated with the untainted-object (anāsrava-ālambana) latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśanamārga) within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Therefore, this consciousness comprises all [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya) in the formless realm.
Furthermore, there is the increase of the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are six consciousnesses associated with the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
these are the consciousnesses that take the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as their object.
With the faculty of pleasure as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya),

there are the consciousnesses and so forth associated with the outflow-free object (anāsrava-ālambana) proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). Therefore,
this consciousness [is associated with] all [proclivities] to be abandoned by the path of seeing the origin (samudaya) in the formless realm.
Furthermore, it includes the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) which increase therein.

The seven consciousnesses associated with all latent dispositions abandoned through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are consciousnesses that take the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as their object-of-object (*ālambanālambana*).
The object-condition for the faculty of pleasure consists of:
the untainted-object-corresponding consciousnesses abandoned through the path of seeing in the formless realm,
as well as the untainted consciousnesses belonging to the category of the subsequent knowledge of the path.
Therefore, all [defilements] abandoned through the path of seeing in the formless realm,

as well as the pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), increase within this consciousness; furthermore, they increase within the wholesome, afflicted, and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses that are abandoned through cultivation in the eight formless realms.
This refers to the consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), and which in turn has the faculty of pleasure as its object-condition;
namely, the wholesome consciousnesses of the formless realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Therefore, this consciousness is accompanied by the increase of all latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
as well as the universal latent dispositions,
and the five classes of conditioned-object consciousnesses in the form realm.
This is the consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), and which in turn takes the faculty of pleasure as its object;
it consists of both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava) consciousnesses, as appropriate.
Therefore, in this consciousness, the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that have conditioned phenomena of the form realm as their object increase accordingly.
These five, together with the previous eight, constitute thirteen types of consciousness.
The fourteenth is the untainted consciousness belonging to the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path.
This consciousness has the faculty of pleasure as its object-condition;
it is a consciousness—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object-condition.
Therefore, latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not increase in accordance with this consciousness.
Therefore, it is said that the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness;
the four categories [of latent dispositions] belonging to the desire realm and the formless realm,
as well as those with conditioned objects (*saṃskṛtālambana*) belonging to the form realm, increase in accordance with these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
The consciousness conditioned by the faculty of joy (somanasyendriya) has as its objects the conditioned factors of the desire and form realms,
the two categories [of afflictions] and the universal [afflictions] of the formless realm;
the consciousness conditioned by the object-condition (ālambanapratyaya) likewise has as its objects the conditioned factors of the desire and form realms.
Regarding the four categories of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*):
the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) extends through the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first two dhyānas;
it is associated exclusively with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Regarding the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
it consists exclusively of the outflowing (*sāsrava*) states and pervades all five categories (*pañca-varga*).
Regarding the first and second dhyānas:
They encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The contaminated ones encompass all five categories (*pañca-varga*),
while the uncontaminated ones encompass the categories of the forbearances and knowledges (*kṣānti-jñāna*) of the Dharma and Subsequent [Dharmas] (*dharma-anvaya*).
This faculty of joy (*somanasyendriya*) is the object of thirteen consciousnesses among the sixteen.
First, it is associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm;
this consciousness [is associated with] all [such dispositions] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.
Furthermore, the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) increase [in relation to] them.
Second, there is the consciousness associated with all latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin in the desire realm;
this consciousness [is associated with] all [latent dispositions] to be abandoned through the vision of the origin in the desire realm.
Furthermore, the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering increase [in relation to this].
Third, there is the consciousness associated with the latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of cessation that take conditioned phenomena as their object;
this consciousness takes conditioned phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of cessation as its object.
And the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase therein.
Fourth, all consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya) in the desire realm;
these consciousnesses [are associated] with all [the latent dispositions] to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase therein;
as do the wholesome [states] abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the desire realm,
as well as the defiled and non-obscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) consciousnesses.
In this consciousness, all pervasive and universal proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm increase;
as it is with the five categories of conditioned-object consciousness in the desire realm, so it is with the five categories of conditioned-object consciousness in the form realm.
These combined constitute ten consciousnesses.
The eleventh is the consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take the untainted as their object and are to be abandoned through the path of vision in the formless realm;
this consciousness comprises all [factors] to be abandoned through the path of vision in the formless realm.
And the universal proclivities increase therein.
There are twelve wholesome consciousnesses of the formless realm abandoned through cultivation;
these consciousnesses comprise all those of the formless realm abandoned through cultivation.
And the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [in relation to them].

The thirteen untainted consciousnesses (anāsrava-vijñāna)—namely, those belonging to the categories of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (dharma-anvaya-jñāna) regarding suffering, origin, and the path—are not subject to the increase of latent dispositions;
therefore, it is said that the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) takes these consciousnesses as its objects.
In the desire and form realms, the two categories of latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take conditioned phenomena of the formless realm as their object,
as well as the universal latent dispositions, increase in association.
Within the sixteen consciousnesses that take the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) as their object, fifteen of those consciousnesses serve as the objects [of the faculty of joy].

First, all consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are consciousnesses that take the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) as their object-of-object;
they take the faculty of joy as their object-of-object.
Because it is a contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) belonging either to its own category or another category as appropriate,
this consciousness is subject to the increase of all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm,
as well as those universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

Consciousness associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] is consciousness that takes the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) as its object-condition;
it takes the faculty of joy as its object-condition.
Because this consciousness is a contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) belonging either to its own category or another category as appropriate,

all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) increase in association with it.

The consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation in the desire realm and which have conditioned phenomena as their object is a consciousness that takes the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) as its object;
it takes the faculty of joy as its object-of-the-object (ālambanālambana).
This consciousness is associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have conditioned phenomena of its own category as their object;

therefore, this consciousness is subject to the increase of both the latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of cessation that take conditioned phenomena of the desire realm as their object,
as well as the universal latent dispositions.

All consciousnesses associated with the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the desire realm are consciousnesses that take the faculty of joy as their object-of-the-object;
they take the faculty of joy as their object-of-the-object.
This consciousness is associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of its own category,
as well as those associated with the categories of the dharma-knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path; therefore,

all latent dispositions to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) in the desire realm, as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions, increase in association with this consciousness.
The wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the five desire realms,
as well as defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses,
are the consciousnesses that take the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) as their object-condition.

The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) consists of consciousnesses and so forth that are to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the desire realm (kāmadhātu). Therefore,
this consciousness comprises all [factors] to be abandoned by cultivation in the desire realm.
And the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [therein].
Just as it is with the five classes of consciousness conditioned by the conditioned in the desire realm,
so it is also with the five classes of consciousness conditioned by the conditioned in the form realm.
Taken together, these constitute ten consciousnesses.

The eleventh is the consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
this is the consciousness that takes the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) as its object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
With the faculty of joy as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),

there are the consciousnesses and so forth associated with the untainted-object (*anāsrava-ālambana*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Therefore,
this consciousness [is associated with] all [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realm.
Furthermore, there is the increase of the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
There are twelve consciousnesses associated with the universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
these are the consciousnesses that take the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) as their object, which in turn take the consciousness that takes the faculty of joy as its object.

Because this consciousness is associated with the untainted-object (anāsrava-ālambana) latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the formless realm, all [dispositions] to be abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*) in the formless realm,
as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*), increase in association with it.
The consciousness associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the formless realm is a consciousness that takes the faculty of joy as its object;
it takes the faculty of joy as its object-of-the-object.

This consciousness consists of the consciousness associated with the untainted objects (anāsravālambana) of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
as well as the consciousness associated with the categories of the subsequent knowledges (anvayajñāna) regarding suffering, origin, and the path;
therefore, this consciousness comprises all [factors] to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the formless realm.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase therein.

The fourteen types of consciousness belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)— namely, those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), the wholesome, the afflicted, and the non-obscured neutral—
are the consciousnesses that take the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) as their object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Taking the faculty of joy as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
it consists of the wholesome consciousnesses of the formless realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Therefore, this consciousness comprises all [factors] of the formless realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation.

Furthermore, the fifteen untainted consciousnesses belonging to the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path are increased by the universal underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
These are the consciousnesses that take the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) as their object; they take the faculty of joy as their object-of-the-object (*ālambanālambana*).
Because it is a consciousness that is both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava), this consciousness is not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya). Therefore,
it is said that the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) takes consciousness as its object-of-the-object (ālambanālambana).
The four categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm, which have conditioned phenomena of the desire and form realms as their objects, increase [in association] with it.
The consciousness that takes the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) as its object has the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena of the desire realm as its objects.
The objects of the universal [defilements] and those to be abandoned by cultivation within the form realm that take consciousness as their object;
and those in the desire realm that take conditioned phenomena of the form realm as their objects— namely, the three categories [of defilements] belonging to the form realm,
as well as the universal [defilements] and those to be abandoned by cultivation belonging to the formless realm.

The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) exists only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), is associated with the outflow-tainted mental consciousness (*sāsrava-manovijñāna*), and pertains to all five categories (*pañca-varga*).
Among the sixteen types of consciousness, it is the object of seven types of consciousness:
first, all consciousnesses associated with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm.
This consciousness is associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm,
as well as those universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, it is associated with all latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin in the desire realm.
This consciousness is associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm,
as well as those universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). Furthermore,

it is associated with the conditioned-object (*saṃskṛtālambana*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the three [realms] of the desire realm.

This consciousness is associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm and which have conditioned phenomena as their object,
as well as with the universal (sarvatraga) latent dispositions;

it is also associated with the four types of consciousness in the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya) and have outflowing (sāsrava) phenomena as their objects.

This consciousness is increased by the outflows-based (sāsrava) objects and the universal (sarvatraga) underlying tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through the path of vision (darśanamārga) within the desire realm;
as well as by the five wholesome and afflicted non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) within the desire realm.
In this consciousness, all latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
as well as the universal [latent dispositions], increase;
and in the six [consciousnesses] of the form realm, the wholesome [dispositions] to be abandoned through cultivation [increase].
And with respect to the unobscured-neutral consciousness,
all pervasive and omnipresent latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in association with this consciousness throughout the form realm, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation.
The seven untainted consciousnesses refer to the categories of the dharma-knowledge of suffering and the origin;
because these consciousnesses are not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

It is taught that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)— which take as their object consciousness conditioned by the outflows (*sāsrava*) of the desire realm and which are universal (*sarvatraga*) throughout the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)— increase [in relation to it].
Regarding the consciousness conditioned by the faculty of grief, among the sixteen types of consciousness, it is the object of ten types of consciousness.
First, there is all consciousness associated with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

This refers to consciousness that takes the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) as its object, and which, in turn, takes as its object the faculty of mental grief that belongs to its own category or another category, as appropriate, and which is tainted (*sāsrava*).

Therefore, in this consciousness, all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), increase; and it is associated with all latent dispositions of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of the origin.
This is the consciousness that takes the faculty of sorrow as its object-condition; it is the consciousness—
whether belonging to its own category, another category, or as appropriate—
that takes the faculty of sorrow as its object-condition and is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Therefore, this consciousness is associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm,
as well as those universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Thirdly, it is associated with the conditioned-object (*saṃskṛtālambana*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm.

This is a consciousness that takes the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) as its object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*). It is a consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) of its own category as their object-condition, which take the faculty of sorrow as their object-condition.
Therefore, this consciousness belongs to the desire realm and is to be abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering], having the conditioned as its object-condition.
And the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase therein.

Fourth, the consciousness associated with the proclivities that have outflow-objects (sāsrava-ālambana) and are abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya) in the desire realm is the consciousness that takes the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya) as its object-of-object (ālambanālambana).

Because it is a consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have the outflow-conditions (sāsrava-ālambana) belonging to its own category as their object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
this consciousness is subject to the increase of the latent dispositions to be abandoned by the path of vision (darśana-mārga-heya) within the desire realm that have outflow-conditions,
as well as the universal (sarvatraga) latent dispositions.
The wholesome consciousness of the five desire realms abandoned through cultivation,
as well as defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousness,
are the consciousnesses that take the faculty of mental grief as their object-condition.
Because [this consciousness] takes as its object the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
this consciousness is thus increased by all the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
as well as by the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions.

The consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the six form realms (*rūpadhātu*) is the consciousness that takes the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) as its object;
it takes as its object the wholesome states abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) within the form realm that have the faculty of mental grief as their object.
And because it is also an unobscured-neutral consciousness,

all pervasive and non-pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) increase in this consciousness within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the seven form realms (*rūpadhātu*) is the consciousness that takes the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) as its object-of-object;
it takes the faculty of mental grief as its object.
The wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the form realm,
as well as the non-obscured neutral consciousnesses; therefore,
this consciousness [is associated with] all [defilements] of the form realm abandoned through the vision of origin.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering increase therein;
as do the eight types of consciousness belonging to the realm of form that are abandoned through cultivation,
whether they be wholesome, defiled, or non-obscured neutral.
This is the consciousness that takes the faculty of sorrow as its object-condition;
it takes the faculty of sorrow as its object-condition,
specifically the wholesome [states] of the form realm abandoned through cultivation.
As well as non-obscured neutral consciousnesses and so forth;
therefore, all pervasive and universal proclivities increase in association with this consciousness in the realm of form.
The wholesome consciousness of the nine formless realms abandoned through cultivation is a consciousness that takes the faculty of mental grief as its object;
it takes the faculty of mental grief as its object-of-the-object.
The wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the form realm,
as well as the non-obscured neutral consciousnesses;
therefore, this consciousness includes all [factors] abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
Furthermore, the universal underlying tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase therein.
The ten types of untainted consciousness (anāsrava-vijñāna) belonging to the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin,
and the path are the objects of the object-condition for the consciousness associated with the faculty of mental grief (daurmanasyendriya).
With the faculty of mental distress as its object-condition,
there are both tainted and untainted consciousnesses;
therefore, latent dispositions do not increase in accordance with this consciousness.
Therefore, it is said that the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) has as its object-condition consciousness that takes conditioned phenomena of the desire realm as its object,
and the three categories [of the path] of the form realm.

The pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase in association with the five faculties, such as faith, which take consciousness as their object;
and those that take the object of that object-consciousness, which pertain to four categories across the three realms.
The five faculties, such as faith and the rest, are common to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Those that are contaminated pertain to all three realms and nine stages (*bhūmi*), and are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Those that are uncontaminated pertain to the categories of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) across the nine stages.
Therefore, these five faculties, beginning with faith,
are the objects of thirteen consciousnesses among the sixteen types of consciousness:
first, the consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering within the desire realm.
In this consciousness, all pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm,
as well as those abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), increase in association. Furthermore,
there are two types of consciousness associated with the pervasive latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin in the desire realm.
This consciousness is associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm,
as well as those universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). Furthermore,
it is associated with the latent dispositions abandoned through the path of vision (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm that take the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as their object.
This consciousness is subject to the increase of all pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm,
as well as the four wholesome [states] abandoned by cultivation in the desire realm.
Furthermore, in defiled and unobscured-unspecified consciousnesses, all [defilements] to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
as well as the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), increase;
this is just as in the four categories of consciousness in the desire realm.
The consciousnesses of the form and formless realms each likewise consist of four categories;
together these constitute twelve types of consciousness,
plus thirteen untainted (anāsrava) consciousnesses.
This refers to the categories of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) regarding suffering, origin, and the path.
Since latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not increase in accordance with this consciousness,
it is said that the five faculties, such as faith, take this consciousness as their object.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms and four categories increase [in association] with them.

Among the sixteen types of consciousness that take the five faculties—faith and so forth—as their objects, thirteen types of consciousness also have them as their objective supports (*ālambana*). These are:
all consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm.

These five faculties, beginning with faith, are consciousnesses that take objects as their objects (ālambanālambana-vijñāna). This is because they are tainted consciousnesses that, as appropriate, take as their objects the five faculties— faith and the rest—
belonging either to their own category (sva-bhūmi) or another category (para-bhūmi).

This consciousness is associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm, as well as all latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) that are universal (*sarvatraga*), and it is further increased by these two types of latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin in the desire realm. It is also associated with the consciousness itself.
These five faculties, beginning with faith, are consciousnesses that take objects as their objects (ālambanālambana-vijñāna), because they are consciousnesses—
whether tainted (sāsrava) or otherwise— as appropriate— that take as their objects the five faculties beginning with faith,
whether belonging to their own category (sva-nikāya) or another category (para-nikāya).
This consciousness is associated with all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm,
as well as those universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). Furthermore,
it is associated with all latent dispositions abandoned through the path of vision (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) in the three [realms] of the desire realm.
These are the consciousnesses that take as their object the five faculties beginning with faith;

the consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to one's own category that take as their object the five faculties beginning with faith when those faculties are untainted (anāsrava);
and the consciousnesses associated with the categories of the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) regarding suffering, origin, and the path.

Therefore, all pervasive (sarvatraga) and associated (anuvartaka) latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśanamārga) in the desire realm increase in this consciousness;
as do the four wholesome [dharmas] to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) in the desire realm.
Furthermore, defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses are the consciousnesses that take as their object the five faculties beginning with faith;
these include the consciousnesses of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation, which take as their objects the five faculties beginning with faith.

Therefore, all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and universal (*sarvaga*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm increase (*anuśerate*) in this consciousness,
just as they do in the four categories of consciousness in the desire realm.
The consciousnesses of the form and formless realms each likewise consist of four categories;
together these constitute twelve consciousnesses.
The thirteenth is the untainted consciousness belonging to the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path.
These five faculties, such as faith, are consciousnesses that take objects as their objects;
they are consciousnesses—both with and without outflows—that take the five faculties, such as faith, as their objects.
Therefore, latent dispositions do not increase in accordance with this consciousness.
Therefore, it is said that for the five faculties beginning with faith, which take objects as their objects,
the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the three realms and four categories increase.
For the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), the latent dispositions of the two categories within the three realms increase in relation to their objective consciousness.
Regarding the universal mental factors and the consciousnesses that take them as objects,

those belonging to the four categories of the three realms are the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), which pertain to the categories of the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) concerning suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Among the sixteen types of consciousness, seven types of consciousness have this as their object:

first, the consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object and are to be abandoned by the path of vision (darśanamārga) within the desire realm;
this [consciousness] consists of all those factors to be abandoned by the path of vision within the desire realm.
And the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [therein].
Second, there is the wholesome consciousness of the desire realm abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
This consciousness [is associated with] all [proclivities] abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
And the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [therein].
As it is with the two classes of consciousness in the desire realm,
so it is with the two classes of consciousness in each of the form and formless realms.
These constitute the six consciousnesses.
The seventh is the untainted consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*),
which refers to the category of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
This consciousness is not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Therefore, it is said that the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) take this consciousness as their object;
[in this case], the latent dispositions of the two categories and the universal (*sarvatraga*) dispositions of the three realms increase therein.
The three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) have consciousness as their object;
among the sixteen types of consciousness, they are the objects of thirteen types of consciousness:
[1] consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.
These three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) are consciousnesses that have objects as their objects (ālambana-ālambana-vijñāna).

They consist of consciousnesses associated with the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) toward the untainted that are to be abandoned by the path of vision (darśana-mārga) in the desire realm, which take the three untainted faculties as their objects.
Therefore, all [consciousnesses] in the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),
as well as those associated with the pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*),
are accompanied by these [tendencies]. Second, there is consciousness associated with the pervasive latent tendencies to be abandoned by the vision of the origin in the desire realm.
These three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) are consciousnesses that take objects as their objects.
They are associated with the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the desire realm abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya),
which have the untainted faculties as their objects, and so forth.
Therefore, this consciousness is accompanied by all the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*),
as well as those universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Thirdly, it is associated with all latent dispositions of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).

This consciousness that takes the three untainted faculties as its object-condition is the consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm to be abandoned by the path of seeing, which have the untainted as their object and are associated with the three untainted faculties as their object-condition.
And because it is associated with the category of the knowledge of the dharma of the path,
this consciousness is subject to the increase of all pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) as well as those to be abandoned through the path of vision in the desire realm.
The fourth consists of the wholesome consciousnesses to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
as well as defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses;
these are the consciousnesses that take the three untainted faculties as their objects.

Because [this consciousness] takes as its object-conditions the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and the wholesome consciousnesses (*kuśala-vijñāna*) of the desire realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
this consciousness is increased by all pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm.
Just as there are four categories of consciousness in the desire realm,
so too are there four categories each in the form and formless realms;
together these constitute twelve types of consciousness.
The untainted consciousnesses of the thirteenth category, the Knowledge of the Path regarding Suffering and its Origin,
are the consciousnesses that take the three untainted faculties as their object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
They are the tainted and untainted consciousnesses that take the three untainted faculties as their object-condition.
Therefore, this consciousness is not subject to the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Thus, it is said that the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) take as their object a consciousness upon which the latent dispositions of the three realms and four categories increase.
The consciousness conditioned by the elements of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds,
and tangibles belongs to the three categories of the desire and form realms,
as well as the universal category of the formless realm.
And the objects of consciousness to be abandoned by cultivation;
the four categories within the three realms of the bases of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible form, sound, and tangibility;
and the aggregate of grasping at form—these are likewise the first five elements, which are both visible and resistant.
In this way, all these dharmas pertain to the five stages of both the desire and form realms,
as they are exclusively abandoned through cultivation;
their characteristics should be understood in the same manner as those of the eye-faculty and so forth.
The objects of the fragrance, odor, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness elements consist of the three categories of the desire realm,
the universal [defilements] of the form realm,
and those to be abandoned through cultivation that take consciousness as their object.
The four categories of the desire realm,
the three categories of the form realm,
and the universal [defilements] of the formless realm.
Regarding the statement "and those abandoned through cultivation;
the same applies to the spheres of odor and taste":
this is because all such dharmas are exclusively abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm.
Their characteristics should be understood as being like those of the female faculty (*strīndriya*) and so forth.
As for the eye, ear, and body consciousness elements (*vijñānadhātu*),
they take as their objects the three categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The object-conditioned consciousness consists of the four categories of the desire and form realms,
the two categories of the formless realm,
and the universal factors.
These phenomena pertain to the desire realm and the first dhyāna;
they are abandoned solely through cultivation and are the objects of seven among the sixteen consciousnesses.
First, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm;
second, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the desire realm.
Third, the wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
as well as the afflicted and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses,
are like the three categories of consciousness in the desire realm.
The consciousnesses of the three categories within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are likewise;
together they constitute six types of consciousness,
plus seven untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses.

That is to say, because it belongs to the category of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge regarding suffering and its origin, the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and body consciousness-elements take this consciousness as their object;
thus, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the three categories belonging to the desire and form realms increase in relation to this consciousness.
Such is the consciousness that takes [this] as its object.
Among the sixteen types of consciousness, eleven types of consciousness have [the following] as their objects:
first, all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm;
second, the consciousness associated with [them]; and third, [those to be abandoned] through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*) in the desire realm.
1. All consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned; 2.

Consciousness associated with the outflow-free objects (anāsrava-ālambana) of the latent dispositions to be abandoned by the path of vision (darśana-mārga) in the desire realm; 3. [Consciousness associated with] the latent dispositions to be abandoned by the path of vision in the desire realm;
4. Wholesome [consciousness] to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the desire realm.
As well as defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses.
Just as there are four classes of consciousness in the desire realm,
so too are there four classes of consciousness in the form realm.
These constitute the eight consciousnesses.

Ninth is the consciousness associated with the untainted-object (*anāsrava-ālambana*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
Tenth is the wholesome consciousness (*kuśala-vijñāna*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm.
Because it is the untainted consciousness of the category of the subsequent knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path;
the eye, ear, and body-consciousness elements have as their object-condition the four categories of the desire and form realms.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
the two categories [of afflictions] and the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in association.

Regarding the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), there is consciousness as the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) and consciousness as the object-of-object-condition (*ālambanālambanapratyaya*), which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Regarding the statement that "the four aggregates following the sense-base of mind (manāyatana), as well as conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) of the past, future, and present,
are also thus," such phenomena all pertain to the three realms (tridhātu) and the nine stages (navabhūmi).

The five categories of contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna-pakṣa) should be understood in their characteristics as being like the faculty of mind (manas-indriya) and so forth.
The consciousness that takes the dharma-dhātu as its object consists of all [consciousness] of the three realms.
