Regarding the statement, "The object-condition consciousness has conditioned phenomena as its objects;
the same applies to formless, invisible, non-obstructive,
and wholesome phenomena," among these various phenomena:
Excluding the wholesome factors, all other dharmas pertain to the three realms and nine stages.

This is because they include the five categories of contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas, the category of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), the category of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), and the three unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) phenomena;
thus, they are the objects of sixteen types of consciousness.
These objects of consciousness that take conditions as their object are also the objects of sixteen types of consciousness,
with the exception of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The wholesome phenomena that serve as objects for consciousness taking conditions as its object encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The outflowing (sāsrava) factors pertain to all three realms and nine stages;
they are to be abandoned solely through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
As for the untainted (*anāsrava*),
because it comprises the categories of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), as well as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*),
these wholesome dharmas are also the objects of sixteen consciousnesses.
However, among those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin,
one takes only the consciousness associated with the universal latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*);
and among those abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path...
One takes only those consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have untainted objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*).
These consciousnesses that take wholesome phenomena as their objects are also the objects of sixteen consciousnesses,
excluding only those consciousnesses that take unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) as their objects.
Therefore, regarding these dharmas as objects, all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms increase in relation to the consciousness that takes them as its object.
Regarding the consciousness that takes those [objects] as its object, the latent dispositions with conditioned objects increase.
Regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as an object, the four categories of the desire and form realms [increase].
The two categories of the formless realm,
as well as the pervasive and object-conditioning consciousnesses—
these four categories of the three realms— and likewise the material phenomena [of the same four categories], are also thus.
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and all phenomena possessing form (*rūpin-dharma*) are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
As for the contaminated,
they pertain to the five stages (*bhūmi*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
It is abandoned only through cultivation;
as for the untainted [path],
it pertains to the six stages because it belongs to the categories of dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge.
Among the sixteen types of consciousness, eleven types of consciousness have [the aforementioned] as their object:
first, consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm;
second, consciousness associated with the universal proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm.

Third, the consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) in the desire realm and which have the outflow-free (anāsrava) as their object;
fourth, the wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses that are abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) in the desire realm.
Just as there are four categories of consciousness in the desire realm,
so it is with the four categories of consciousness in the form realm;
together they constitute eight consciousnesses.
9. Consciousness associated with the untainted objects (anāsrava-ālambana) of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) in the formless realm;
10. wholesome consciousness (kuśala-vijñāna) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) in the formless realm;
11. untainted consciousness (anāsrava-vijñāna).
This refers to the categories of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) regarding suffering, origin, and the path.
Therefore, the consciousnesses that take the aggregate of form and so forth as their objects consist of four categories in the desire realm and the form realm,
and two categories in the formless realm.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [in relation to it].
This aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) and so forth is the object of thirteen of the sixteen consciousnesses that take it as their condition;
namely, four classes of consciousness from each of the three realms.
Excluding the consciousnesses abandoned through the vision of cessation,
however, among those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the formless realm,
one takes only the consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
Taken together, these constitute twelve types of consciousness.
Thirteenth is the untainted consciousness pertaining to the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path.

Therefore, regarding the aggregates such as form (*rūpaskandha*), the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the three realms and four categories increase in relation to the consciousness that takes them as objects.
The latter four aggregates of clinging;
consciousness conditioned by outflows; consciousness conditioned by the object-conditioned; consciousness conditioned by the conditioned; the consciousness-element; outflowing phenomena;
and likewise, phenomena abandoned through vision.
Among these dharmas, with the exception of those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*),
all remaining dharmas pertain to the three realms, the nine stages, and the five categories (*pañca-varga*).
Only those dharmas abandoned by seeing that are *sāsrava* (with outflows) [are excluded].
They pervade the three realms and nine stages.
Since the first four categories are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*),
they are all objects of perception for the sixteen types of consciousness.
However, excluding those consciousnesses that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object and are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path,
these various consciousnesses that take [the aforementioned objects] as their objects are also the objects of sixteen consciousnesses; yet,
one must exclude those consciousnesses that take unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) as their objects and are abandoned through the vision of cessation.

Therefore, regarding these phenomena, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the outflowing (sāsrava) objects of consciousness increase in relation to that consciousness; the latent dispositions associated with conditioned (saṃskṛta) objects of consciousness increase in relation to that consciousness;

and regarding untainted (anāsrava) phenomena, the latent dispositions belonging to the three realms, the three categories, and the universal (sarvatraga) increase in relation to the object-consciousness.
The same applies to conditioned phenomena that have uninterrupted [dharmas] as their objects.

This is because "uncontaminated" (*anāsrava*) and "uninterrupted" (*aprahātavya*) dharmas refer to the truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the path (*mārga-satya*), as well as space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
thus, they are the objects of ten of the sixteen types of consciousness.

First, consciousness associated with the proclivities (anuśaya) that take the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the desire realm;
second, consciousness associated with the proclivities that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of the path within the desire realm.
The wholesome consciousnesses to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm are like the three categories of consciousness in the desire realm;
the three categories of consciousness in each of the form and formless realms are likewise.
Combined, these constitute nine consciousnesses.

The ten untainted consciousnesses refer to the categories of the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Therefore, these two dharmas serve as objects for the consciousnesses of the three realms and the three categories,
and the universal and specific latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in relation to them.
These two dharmas serve as objects for sixteen consciousnesses.
Among these, excluding only those consciousnesses that take the unconditioned as their object,
these two factors— the conditioned objects and the latent dispositions— increase through the consciousness that takes them as its object.
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are the objects of the consciousnesses belonging to two categories within the three realms,
as well as the universal [mental factors]. Regarding those that take conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as their objects,
the three unconditioned phenomena are the objects of seven of the sixteen types of consciousness.
First, consciousness associated with the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that take unconditioned phenomena as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the desire realm;
second, wholesome consciousness in the desire realm that is to be abandoned through cultivation.
As with these two categories of consciousness in the desire realm, so it is for the others.
The consciousnesses of the form and formless realms, each consisting of two categories, are likewise;
these together constitute six types of consciousness,
along with seven untainted (anāsrava) consciousnesses.
This means that because they belong to the categories of the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path,
the unconditioned phenomena serve as objects for consciousnesses belonging to two classes within the three realms,
and the universal underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in relation to them.
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are the objects of sixteen consciousnesses that take them as their objective conditions (*ālambana*).
Among these, one must exclude only those consciousnesses that take unconditioned phenomena as their objective conditions;

therefore, latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take conditioned phenomena as their objective conditions increase (*anuśerate*) with respect to unconditioned phenomena as their object-condition (*ālambanālambana*).
The consciousness that takes unwholesome dharmas as its object consists of those conditioned by the outflows of the desire realm,
those that are universal in the form realm,
and those that take as their objects the factors to be abandoned through cultivation.
The conditioned factors of the desire realm that take the three categories of the form realm as their object,
as well as the universal [factors] of the formless realm and those abandoned through cultivation, [are so classified].
The same applies to the factors bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-saṃprayukta-dharma*).
Because unwholesome (*akuśala*) and other such factors pertain only to the desire realm and span all five categories (*pañca-varga*),
their characteristics should be understood as being like those of the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) mentioned previously.
The consciousness conditioned by indeterminate dharmas consists of the three categories of the desire realm.
The consciousness conditioned by the outflow-tainted objects of the form and formless realms, and the consciousness conditioned by the objects of the four categories of the desire realm,
as well as those with conditioned objects from the form and formless realms— [these are the objects].
The indeterminate dharmas pervade the three realms.
Those belonging to the desire realm are abandoned through cultivation.
Furthermore, regarding the category of the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) among those things to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*):
as for those belonging to the form and formless realms,
because they pertain to all five categories (*pañca-nikāya*) as well as the two unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*), [they are included].
Among the sixteen consciousnesses, indeterminate dharmas are the objects of fourteen consciousnesses:
(1) all consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm;

and (2) consciousnesses associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm.
These are: the wholesome consciousnesses of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation;
the defiled and the non-obscured neutral consciousnesses;
and the consciousnesses of each of the five categories of the form and formless realms.
Among these, excluding only those consciousnesses that take uncontaminated phenomena as their objects,
there are thirteen consciousnesses combined;
the uncontaminated consciousnesses number fourteen.
This refers to the categories of the knowledge of suffering and its origin (duḥkha-samudaya-dharma-jñāna and anvaya-jñāna).
Therefore, the consciousness that takes neutral phenomena as its object consists of the three categories of the desire realm.
The outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) proclivities (*anuśaya*) that take the form and formless realms as their objects increase [in association] with it.
Regarding consciousnesses that take indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena as their objects,
among the sixteen types of consciousness, they are the objects of fifteen consciousnesses.
Excluding the consciousnesses to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the desire realm,
and excluding the consciousnesses that take the unconditioned as their object from among the five classes of consciousness in each of the form and formless realms,
there are thus four classes of consciousness in the desire realm that have indeterminate dharmas as their objects.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take conditioned phenomena of the form and formless realms as their object increase [in relation to them].
Regarding consciousness that takes phenomena bound to the form realm as its object:
it consists of the three categories of the desire realm.
The objects of consciousness consisting of the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) factors of the form realm,
the universal (sarvatraga) factors of the formless realm,
and those factors of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
The three categories of the desire realm have the conditioned factors of the form realm as their object;
the four categories of the formless realm [have them as objects] because the factors bound to the form realm encompass all five categories.
Among the sixteen types of consciousness, ten types of consciousness have [these] as their objects:

first, consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm;

second, consciousness associated with the universal proclivities that take other realms as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm.
The three wholesome consciousnesses of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation,
together with the five categories of tainted-object consciousnesses of the form realm,
constitute eight consciousnesses in total.
Ninth, the wholesome consciousnesses of the formless realm to be abandoned through cultivation;
tenth, the untainted consciousnesses,
namely those belonging to the category of the subsequent knowledges of suffering and origin.
Therefore, the consciousness that takes as its object the dharmas associated with the form realm consists of the three categories of the desire realm and the outflowing objects of the form realm.

The pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation increase [in relation to] the consciousness that takes as its object the factors associated with the form realm.
Among the sixteen types of consciousness, thirteen are objects of cognition.
First, all consciousnesses associated with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Second, all consciousnesses associated with the underlying tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm.
Third, the wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
as well as defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses,
and the five categories of conditioned-object consciousnesses in the form realm.
These constitute the eight consciousnesses.

Ninth is the consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Tenth is the consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realm.

11. Consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and have uncontaminated objects (anāsravālambana).
12. Wholesome consciousness, as well as defiled and non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) consciousness, which are abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) in the formless realm.
In the thirteenth chapter on the Knowledge of Suffering, Origin, and Path,
it is stated that because they are untainted consciousnesses, the consciousnesses that take as their objects the factors bound to the form realm consist of the three categories of the desire realm.
Regarding the conditioned objects of the form realm,
the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the four categories belonging to the formless realm increase.
This refers to the consciousness that takes as its object the phenomena associated with the formless realm.
The three categories of the desire and form realms;
the consciousness that takes as its object the outflow-tainted objects of the formless realm;
and the three categories of the desire realm.
The four categories of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding those conditioned by the formative factors of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*):
because the phenomena bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātupratisaṃyukta-dharma*) pertain to all five categories (*pañca-nikāya*).
Among the sixteen types of consciousness, twelve have objects [belonging to other realms]:
first, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm;
second, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the desire realm.
The wholesome consciousnesses to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm are like the three categories of consciousness in the desire realm;
the three categories of consciousness in the form realm are likewise.
These together constitute six consciousnesses.
Furthermore, including the five categories of contaminated consciousness with outflow directed toward the formless realm,
they together constitute eleven consciousnesses.

The twelve types of untainted consciousness refer to those belonging to the category of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin; these are the consciousnesses that take phenomena associated with the formless realm as their object.

Regarding the consciousnesses that take phenomena associated with the formless realm as their object, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the three categories belonging to the desire and form realms, as well as those with outflow (sāsrava) belonging to the formless realm, increase in accordance with them. These are the consciousnesses that take phenomena associated with the formless realm as their object.
Among the sixteen types of consciousness, thirteen are objects of perception.
These consist of the three groups of consciousness in the desire realm— namely, those abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origination, and through cultivation—
and the four groups of consciousness in the form realm.
Excluding the consciousnesses abandoned through the vision of cessation,
among the consciousnesses abandoned through the vision of the path,
one takes only those consciousnesses associated with latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have the untainted as their object.
The five categories of conditioned-object consciousnesses belonging to the formless realm constitute twelve consciousnesses;
together with the untainted consciousnesses of the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path, they total thirteen.
Therefore, for the consciousness that takes as its object the factors associated with the formless realm,
there are three categories from the desire realm and four categories from the form realm.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) conditioned by the conditioned (saṃskṛta) of the formless realm increase [in relation to them].
The consciousness that takes the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) as its object belongs to two categories within the three realms.
Regarding the universal, object-condition, and object-consciousness [factors] belonging to the four categories of the three realms:

the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are exclusively untainted (anāsrava), as they pertain to the categories of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) across the four noble truths.

As with the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), one should know that the consciousness which takes as its object dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*) consists of four categories of the three realms (*dhātu*) and those [defiled states] to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*) that take tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*).
Regarding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for consciousness that has conditioned phenomena as its condition:
these dharmas pertain to all three realms and all five categories,
because they are exclusively with outflows (sāsrava).
Sixteen consciousnesses take this as their object;
this excludes only those consciousnesses that are supramundane and abandoned through the Path of Seeing.
Therefore, it is the object of consciousnesses that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the outflows that are to be abandoned through the path of seeing, pertaining to the four categories within the three realms, increase in accordance with this dharma.
Furthermore, the consciousness that takes this dharma as its object is also the object of sixteen types of consciousness.
However, excluding the consciousness that takes the unconditioned as its object,
this consciousness that takes phenomena as its object is thus increased by latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take conditioned phenomena as their objects.
The consciousness that takes phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation as its object belongs to the three realms and the three categories.
Regarding the consciousness that takes objects as its conditions (ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna) belonging to the three realms and four categories:
because the dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) pertain to all nine stages across the three realms,
their characteristics should be understood as being like those of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume Eighty-Eight;
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Eighty-Nine.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section 19: The Ten Gates on the Aggregates of Grasping, Part 4 of 2, Chapter 2: The Truths of Suffering and its Origin. The Consciousness Conditioned by the Truths of Suffering and its Origin.
Regarding the statement that "the consciousness conditioned by outflows (sāsrava) has conditioned objects as its object-condition (ālambanapratyaya),
and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is likewise":
this is because the Truths of Suffering and Origination, and so forth, all pertain to the three realms and nine stages.
Because the five aggregates are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*),
their characteristics should be understood as being like those of the latter four aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) and so forth.
The consciousness that takes the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) as its object belongs to two categories within the three realms.
Regarding those [factors] that have universal application as their object-condition and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as their objective condition,
their characteristics should be understood in the same manner as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
The consciousness that takes the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) as its object belongs to two categories within the three realms.

Furthermore, regarding the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), the object-conditioned consciousnesses (*ālambanapratyayavijñāna*), and the four categories of knowledge— suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—
pertaining to the three realms, as well as the three samādhis,
their characteristics should be understood in the same manner as those of the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*).
The consciousnesses that take the four dhyānas as their objects consist of the four categories of the desire realm and the conditioned objects of the form realm.
The objects of the two categories and the universal [defilements] of the formless realm are the four categories of the desire and form realms.
Regarding those in the form realm that have conditioned phenomena as their object,
they pertain to all four dhyānas, both contaminated and uncontaminated.
As for those with outflows (sāsrava),
they pertain exclusively to the five categories within the form realm (rūpadhātu).
As for those without outflows (anāsrava):
Because it penetrates the categories of the Dharma-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) regarding the Four Noble Truths,
among the sixteen consciousnesses of the four dhyānas, it is the object of twelve consciousnesses:

first, the consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) within the desire realm.

2. Consciousness associated with universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms as their object, which are abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm;
3. Consciousness associated with proclivities that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object, which are abandoned through the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm.
Fourth, the wholesome consciousnesses of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation;
these, together with the five categories of conditioned-object consciousnesses of the form realm, constitute nine consciousnesses.
Tenth, the consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm to be abandoned by the path of seeing that take the untainted as their object.
Eleventh, the wholesome consciousness of the formless realm abandoned through cultivation;
twelfth, untainted consciousness— namely,
those belonging to the category of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origination, and the category of the subsequent knowledge of the path and phenomena.
The consciousnesses that take the four dhyānas as their object are increased by the four categories of the desire realm, the conditioned factors of the form realm,
the two categories of the formless realm,
and the universal proclivities.
The objects of the four dhyānas consist of fourteen of the sixteen consciousnesses;
these exclude the consciousnesses abandoned through the vision of suffering and cessation within the desire and formless realms,
as well as the consciousnesses that take the unconditioned of the form realm as their object.
Because within untainted consciousness one apprehends the categories of knowledge regarding suffering, origin, and the path,
the four dhyānas take as their objects the consciousnesses that have those as objects,
as well as the four classes [of afflictions] belonging to the desire realm and the formless realms.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) conditioned by the conditioned (saṃskṛta) in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) increase [therein].
The consciousnesses conditioned by the immeasurables (apramāṇa) of loving-kindness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā),
and equanimity (upekṣā) belong to the three categories (prakāra) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the realm of form.
The universal [defilements] of the formless realm,
the objects of the path of cultivation that take consciousness as their object-condition,
and the three categories of the desire realm.
The four categories of the form and formless realms,
the pure liberation,
and the latter four spheres of mastery.
The same applies to the first eight bases of mastery (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

This is because the three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) pertain to all four levels of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), whereas the pure liberations (*śuddhavimokṣa*) and so forth belong exclusively to the fourth dhyāna; furthermore, all of these are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) and are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Among the sixteen types of consciousness, there are eight types of consciousness that take [the objects of] the eight consciousnesses as their focal objects (*ālambana*):

first, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm;

second, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm.
1. Wholesome consciousness abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm;
2. Consciousness associated with the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form realm;
3. Consciousness associated with the pervasive latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the form realm.
Sixth, the wholesome consciousness of the form realm abandoned through cultivation,
as well as the defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousness;
seventh, the wholesome consciousness of the formless realm abandoned through cultivation.
The eight untainted consciousnesses refer to those belonging to the category of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origination (*duḥkha-samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*).
The consciousnesses that take the three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth as their objects [are also included].
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three categories of the desire and form realms,
those that are universal in the formless realm,
and those to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) increase [in association with this].
The three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth take consciousness as their object;
among the sixteen types of consciousness, they are the objects of twelve types of consciousness, namely:

those belonging to the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*), the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
And the fourfold consciousnesses of the form and formless realms,
excluding the consciousness abandoned by the vision of cessation;
among those abandoned by the vision of the path:
One takes only those consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have untainted objects;
among those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the formless realm,
one takes only those consciousnesses associated with the universal latent dispositions.
Taken together, these constitute eleven consciousnesses.
This is because the twelve types of untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*)—namely, the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path—do not include them.
Furthermore, the three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth take as their objects the three categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The four categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms increase [in relation to this].
The consciousness that takes the immeasurable joy as its object is the consciousness that takes [the objects] of the three categories of the desire and form realms as its objective condition.
The three categories of the desire realm,
the four categories of the form realm,
and the two categories of the formless realm.
As for the statement,
"The two initial liberations and the first four bases of mastery are likewise," it means that they are similar [to the preceding cases].

Because the immeasurables such as *muditā* (altruistic joy) exist only in the first two *dhyānas* and are abandoned through the cultivation of contaminated (*sāsrava*) states, they are the objects of seven among the sixteen types of consciousness. These seven are:

first, the consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) that take other realms as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm.

1. Consciousness associated with universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm; 2.

consciousness associated with universal latent dispositions that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the form realm. 3. wholesome consciousness in the desire realm abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*); 4. consciousness associated with universal latent dispositions that are abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form realm.

The consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the fivefold realm of form;
and the wholesome, afflicted, and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses of the sixfold realm of form to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The seven untainted consciousnesses—
namely, those belonging to the category of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge of origin—

are such that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the three categories [of defilements] within the desire and form realms increase in association with the consciousnesses that take the immeasurables of joy and so forth as their objects.
The immeasurable states such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) take consciousness as their object;
among the sixteen types of consciousness, they are the objects of ten types of consciousness.

That is to say, they are the objects of the consciousnesses of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*), the vision of origination (*samudaya*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
And the four categories of consciousness belonging to the form realm,
excluding the consciousness abandoned through the vision of cessation;
among those abandoned through the vision of the path:
Taking only the consciousness associated with the untainted-object (anāsrava-ālambana) latent dispositions (anuśaya),
these are combined to form seven consciousnesses;
the eighth is the consciousness associated with the untainted-object latent dispositions to be abandoned by the path of vision (darśana-mārga-prahātavya) in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Because there are the nine wholesome consciousnesses of the formless realm abandoned through cultivation,
and the ten untainted consciousnesses belonging to the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path;
and because the immeasurables such as sympathetic joy take these consciousnesses as their objects.
The three categories of the desire realm,
the four categories of the form realm,
and the two categories of the formless realm.
And the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [therein].
The first three formless attainments have consciousness as their object and have the object-of-consciousness as their object.
The three categories of the desire realm,
the four categories of the form realm,
and those in the formless realm that have conditioned phenomena as their object.
The first three formless attainments (ārūpya) are both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava).
As for the contaminated ones,
they belong exclusively to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and encompass all five categories (pañca-varga).
Regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*):
because it encompasses the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) across the four truths,
among the sixteen types of consciousness—
Thirteen consciousnesses have objects of perception:

first, consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm;
second, consciousness associated with the universal proclivities that take other realms as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the desire realm.
The wholesome consciousnesses of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation are like the three categories of consciousness of the desire realm;
the three categories of consciousness of the form realm are likewise.
Furthermore, there are the consciousnesses associated with the outflow-free (anāsrava) object-afflicted latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the path of vision in the form realm,
together with the consciousnesses of the five categories that take conditioned phenomena as their objects in the formless realm;
these combined constitute twelve types of consciousness.
The thirteen untainted consciousnesses refer to the categories of the subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering, origin, and the path,
as well as the first three formless-sphere consciousnesses that take [the lower realms] as their objects.
It is also the object of thirteen consciousnesses among the sixteen consciousnesses;
namely, the consciousnesses of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin and through cultivation,
as well as the four categories of consciousness of the form realm.
Excluding the consciousnesses to be abandoned by the vision of cessation,
as well as the five classes of consciousness conditioned by the conditioned in the formless realm,
these together constitute twelve types of consciousness.
Because the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path (duḥkha-samudaya-mārga-jñāna) in the thirteenth category is untainted (anāsrava),
the consciousnesses that take the first three formless realms as their objects, as well as the consciousnesses that take those objects as their objects,
both belong to the three categories of the desire realm.

The four categories of the form realm and the conditioned-object latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm increase [in association] with the consciousness that takes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its object.
The three categories of the desire and form realms;
the consciousness that takes as its object the outflow-tainted [factors] of the formless realm;
and the three categories of the desire realm.
The four categories of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and those conditioned by the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that take the conditioned as their object—

specifically the non-percipient and non-non-percipient sphere (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which consists exclusively of the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and permeates all five categories— are the objects of twelve consciousnesses among the sixteen consciousnesses.

First, consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm;

second, consciousness associated with the universal proclivities that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm.
The wholesome consciousnesses of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation are like the three categories of consciousness of the desire realm;
the three categories of consciousness of the form realm are likewise.
Together with the five categories of contaminated consciousness conditioned by the objects of the formless realm,
these constitute eleven types of consciousness.
The twelve uncontaminated consciousnesses consist of the categories of the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin within the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
Regarding the consciousness that takes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its object,

the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) associated with the three categories of the desire and form realms, as well as those associated with the outflow-tainted objects of the formless realm, increase in association.
This applies to the consciousness that takes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its object.
Among the sixteen consciousnesses, thirteen are objects of cognition:
namely, the consciousnesses of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin and through cultivation,
as well as the four categories of consciousness in the form realm.
Excluding the consciousnesses abandoned through the vision of cessation,
among those abandoned through the vision of the path,
one takes only the consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have the untainted as their object.
Together with the five categories of conditioned-object consciousnesses belonging to the formless realm,
these constitute twelve types of consciousness;
this is because the thirteen [types] include the untainted consciousnesses of the categories of knowledge regarding suffering, origin, and the path.
The object-condition consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception consists of three categories of the desire realm and four categories of the form realm.
In the formless realm, the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that take conditioned phenomena as their object increase;
namely, those of the spheres of Infinite Space, Infinite Consciousness, and Nothingness.
The consciousness that takes liberation as its object; the consciousness that takes the object-of-object as its object;
and the three categories of the desire realm.
Regarding the four categories of the form and formless realms:
these three liberations are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
As for the contaminated:
Only those [factors] of the formless realm that are included within the wholesome states acquired through application (*prāyogika-kuśala*) and are untainted (*anāsrava*) are [included],
because the untainted ones belong exclusively to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Among the sixteen types of consciousness, twelve have objects that are external realms:

first, consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm;
second, consciousness associated with the universal proclivities that take other realms as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the desire realm.
The wholesome consciousnesses to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm are like the three categories of consciousness in the desire realm;
the three categories of consciousness in the form realm are likewise.
Together with the consciousness associated with the untainted-object (anāsrava-ālambana) proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the path of vision (darśanamārga) in the form realm,
these constitute seven types of consciousness.
Eighth is the consciousness associated with the universal (sarvatraga) proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the formless realm.

Ninth, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Tenth, consciousness associated with the latent dispositions having the outflow-free as their object (*anāsrava-ālambana-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realm.
11. The wholesome [consciousness] abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm, as well as the defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses.
12. Untainted consciousness, namely those belonging to the category of the subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering, origin, and the path.
These three liberations take consciousness as their object;
they are also the objects of twelve types of consciousness, namely:
the consciousnesses of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origination, and through cultivation.
The consciousnesses of the form and formless realms each consist of four categories;
excluding the consciousness abandoned through the vision of cessation,
these together constitute eleven types of consciousness.
Because the twelve knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path are untainted consciousnesses (*anāsravavijñāna*),
these three liberations take consciousness as their object and take the object-of-object consciousness as their object.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with the three categories of the desire realm and the four categories of the form and formless realms.
The last two liberations and the objects of the last two spheres of totality consist of the three categories of the three realms.
Regarding the objects of the object-condition consciousness (*ālambanapratyaya-vijñāna*),
there are three categories in the desire realm and four categories in the form and formless realms.
These four factors are comprised solely of the wholesome states acquired through application (*prāyogika-kuśala*) that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the formless realm.
Among the sixteen types of consciousness, ten types of consciousness have [these] as their objects:

(1) consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) that take other realms as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm;

and (2) consciousness associated with the universal proclivities that take other realms as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm.
The wholesome consciousnesses to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm are like the three categories of consciousness in the desire realm;
the three categories of consciousness in the form realm are likewise.
These constitute the six consciousnesses.
Seventh, the consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the formless realm.
Eighth, the consciousness associated with the universal proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the formless realm.
The nine wholesome consciousnesses of the formless realm abandoned through cultivation,
as well as the ten defiled and non-obscured-neutral consciousnesses and the ten untainted consciousnesses—
namely, those belonging to the category of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge of origination.
These four factors are objects of consciousness;
the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the three realms and three categories increase in relation to them.
These four factors are objects of consciousness.
Among the sixteen types of consciousness, twelve types of consciousness have [the aforementioned] objects as their cognitive objects (*ālambana*).

These are: the consciousnesses of the three realms that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*);

and the consciousnesses associated with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) directed toward the untainted (*anāsrava*) that are abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) within the realms of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
Furthermore, because they consist of untainted consciousnesses belonging to the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin,
and the path, these four types of consciousness take as their objects the three categories of the desire realm.
The four categories [of afflictions] of the form and formless realms increase as latent tendencies (anuśaya) with respect to the consciousness that takes the dharma-knowledge as its object.
The two categories of the desire realm and the universal [factors],
the universal [factors] of the form realm and those abandoned through cultivation which take consciousness as their object-condition,
and the four categories of the desire realm.
The three categories of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
the universal [defilements] of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) [are objects of dharma-knowledge],
because dharma-knowledge exists in six stages (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*).
Among the sixteen consciousnesses, there are four objects of cognition:

first, the consciousness associated with the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that have the outflow-free (anāsrava) as their object and are to be abandoned through the path of vision (darśanamārga) within the desire realm;
second, the wholesome consciousness to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) within the desire realm.
The wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation in the three realms,
and the four untainted consciousnesses—
namely, those belonging to the category of the Dharma-knowledge of the Path.
The dharma-knowledge has as its object consciousness associated with the two categories [of afflictions] of the desire realm and the universal [afflictions],
as well as the universal [afflictions] of the form realm and the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation, which increase therein.
Dharma-knowledge takes consciousness as its object;
among the sixteen types of consciousness, it is the object of nine types of consciousness:
first, the consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.
Second, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm;
third, all consciousness associated with the latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm.
Fourth, the wholesome consciousnesses of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation,
as well as defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses; and fifth,
the consciousnesses associated with the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form realm.
Six are the consciousnesses associated with the universal latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the form realm;
seven are the wholesome, afflicted, and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the form realm.
Because there are the eight wholesome consciousnesses of the formless realm abandoned through cultivation,
and the nine untainted consciousnesses belonging to the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path; thus,
the dharma-knowledge takes these as its objects of cognition.
The four categories of the desire realm,
the three categories of the form realm,
and the universal [defilements] of the formless realm.
Furthermore, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation increase [in relation to this consciousness].
Regarding the consciousness that takes subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) as its object,
there are the two categories of the form and formless realms, as well as the universal [dispositions].
The objects of the consciousness that takes them as its objective condition are the three categories of the desire realm: those universal to the desire realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation.
Regarding the four categories of the form and formless realms:
because subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) exists in nine stages,
it is the object of six consciousnesses among the sixteen consciousnesses.

This refers to the consciousnesses associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) and take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object within both the form and formless realms,
as well as the wholesome consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) in the three realms;
these combined constitute five types of consciousness.
The six untainted consciousnesses (anāsravavijñāna) are so called because they belong to the category of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānapakṣa). Thus,
subsequent knowledge takes consciousness as its object.

The two categories [of afflictions] of the form and formless realms, as well as the universal [afflictions], and the universal [afflictions] and those to be abandoned by cultivation of the desire realm, increase in accordance with these latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This knowledge of categories (*dharmajñāna*) takes sixteen consciousnesses as its objects; among these, it is the object of twelve consciousnesses.
This refers to the consciousnesses associated with the universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin within each of the three realms,
as well as the wholesome consciousnesses and the defiled and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation.
Together with all the consciousnesses associated with the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the form and formless realms,
these constitute eleven consciousnesses;
this is because the twelve [consciousnesses] include the untainted consciousnesses belonging to the categories of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path.
The subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) takes as its object the consciousnesses of the three categories of the desire realm and the four categories of the form and formless realms.
The latent dispositions increase accordingly.
Question: Regarding which realm, which stage, and which category of the noble path do the false views abandoned by the path of vision take as their object?
Which realm and which stage [of the path] do they take as their object?
Some say that this wrong view takes as its object only the Noble Path, which is the antidote to cessation.
If one were to say this:
In the desire realm, wrong view takes as its object only the noble path subsumed under the preparatory concentration (anāgamya).
In the first dhyāna, wrong view takes as its object only the noble path subsumed under the three stages.
The wrong view of the second dhyāna takes as its object only the noble path subsumed under four stages;
the wrong view of the third dhyāna takes as its object only the noble path subsumed under five stages.
The fourth dhyāna and wrong views pertaining to the formless realm both take as their object only the noble path comprised within the six stages.
Furthermore, there are those who say that those wrong views also take as their object the Noble Path which is the antidote through subduing and destruction.
If this is asserted, then the wrong views of the desire and form realms would all take as their objects the Noble Path comprised within the six stages.
The wrong view regarding the sphere of infinite space takes as its object the noble path comprised within seven stages;
the wrong view regarding the sphere of infinite consciousness takes as its object the noble path comprised within eight stages.

The wrong views regarding the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) both take as their object the noble path (*āryamārga*) subsumed within nine stages.
The critique states:
It should be stated as follows:
the false view to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm takes as its object the noble path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge across all six stages.

The false views abandoned through the path of seeing in the form and formless realms all take as their object the noble paths of the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) across all nine stages,
because they are of the same type.
The knowledge of others' minds takes as its object the consciousnesses of the four categories of the desire realm, the four categories of the form realm,
the two categories of the formless realm, and the universal [defilements].
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*),

that which pertains to the three realms and four categories consists of the supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna-abhijñā*), both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
As for the outflowing [states],
they pertain to the four stages of the form realm;
they are exclusively to be abandoned through cultivation and are subsumed under the category of preparatory wholesome states.
The untainted [path] pervades the four levels of dhyāna,
because it belongs to the category of the knowledge of the path and the subsequent knowledge.
The knowledge of others' minds has eleven of the sixteen types of consciousness as its objects:

first, consciousness associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm.

Second, consciousness associated with universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms as their object and are abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm;
third, consciousness associated with proclivities that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object and are abandoned through the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm.
1. Wholesome consciousness in the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation;
2. Consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the form realm;
3. Consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering] in the form realm.

1. Consciousness associated with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) in the form realm and have the outflow-free (anāsrava) as their object;

2–7. The eight types of consciousness in the form realm that are wholesome (kuśala), as well as those that are defiled (kliṣṭa) or non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta), which are abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).

1. Consciousness associated with the untainted objects (anāsrava-ālambana) of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) in the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu); 2–9. [The remaining types of consciousness associated with those latent dispositions]; 10.
Wholesome consciousness (kuśala-vijñāna) to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) in the formless realm;
11. Untainted consciousness (anāsrava-vijñāna).
This refers to the category of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and its origin,
as well as the category of the subsequent knowledge of the path; thus,
the knowledge of others' minds takes consciousness as its object.
The four categories of the desire and form realms,
the two categories of the formless realm,
and the universal latent dispositions increase [in these objects].
The knowledge of others' minds takes as its object thirteen of the sixteen types of consciousness;
that is to say, the four categories of consciousness belonging to each of the three realms,
excluding those abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering].
Among the consciousnesses in the formless realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin,
one takes only those associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) and combines them to form twelve consciousnesses.
Because the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path (duḥkha-samudaya-mārga-jñāna) in the thirteenth category is untainted (anāsrava),
the knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna) takes that [untainted] consciousness as its object; thus,
the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the four categories of the three realms increase therein.
The triple samādhis take as their objects the consciousnesses of the three realms and three categories.
As for the consciousness that takes those objects as its own object, it takes as its objects the consciousnesses of the three realms and four categories.
This is because the triple samādhis pervade the nine stages of the three realms.
Because it is comprised solely of the wholesome states acquired through application (*prayoga-kuśala*) that are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
it is the object of ten of the sixteen consciousnesses:
first, the consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the desire realm.
Second, consciousness associated with the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm;
third, wholesome, afflicted, and non-obscured neutral consciousnesses to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the desire realm.
Just as there are three categories of consciousness in the desire realm,
so too are there three categories each in the form and formless realms;
together, these constitute nine types of consciousness.
The ten untainted consciousnesses refer to those belonging to the categories of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge regarding suffering and its origin;
these are the consciousnesses that take the threefold samādhi as their object.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the three realms and three categories increase [in relation to it].
It takes the consciousnesses of the three types of samādhi as its object;
among the sixteen consciousnesses, it is the object of thirteen consciousnesses.
This refers to the twelve consciousnesses comprising the four categories of each of the three realms, excluding those abandoned through the vision of the cessation of suffering;
this is because there are no untainted consciousnesses within the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path that would constitute a thirteenth.

Regarding the consciousness that takes the threefold samādhi as its object, the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the four categories belonging to the three realms increase therein. As for the consciousness that takes the fetter of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) as its object, it pertains to the three categories of the three realms;
that is to say, this consciousness takes the fetter as its object.

In each of the three realms, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three categories—those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, and through cultivation—increase in accordance with their respective objects.
Regarding the consciousness that takes these as its object, the latent dispositions of the four categories within the three realms increase;
that is to say, for this consciousness which takes them as its object, the latent dispositions of the four categories in each of the three realms increase.
"Excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of cessation;
the same applies to the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) among the fetters conducive to the lower realms (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
This refers to the view of a self-identity among the five fetters conducive to the lower realms.

Among the five views, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) have their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase with respect to consciousness and the objects of consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*).
This is also as explained regarding the fetter of the view of a self-identity among the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*).
The fetter of adherence to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana) takes as its object the consciousness associated with the three realms and the three categories [of afflictions],
as well as those factors with outflows (sāsrava) to be abandoned by the path of seeing;
that is to say, this fetter takes such consciousness as its object.
In each of the three realms, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),

through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)— these three categories— as well as those with outflow (*sāsrava*) that take [the objects of] the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) as their object,
increase in association. Regarding the consciousness that takes these as its objects, it belongs to four categories within the three realms.
This means that for this object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of four categories from each of the three realms increase,
with the exception of those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) and the view of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
As for the fetter of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*),
the lower-tier fetter of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-aṇuśaya*),
and likewise attachment to precepts and observances itself: [these are all one and the same].
That is to say: among the four graspings, it is the grasping at precepts and observances;
among the four bodily fetters, it is the fetter of precepts and observances;
and among the five lower fetters, it is the fetter of precepts and observances.
Among the five views, the grasping at precepts and observances is the object-condition for the consciousness that takes objects as its objects;
the latent tendencies increase in accordance with that consciousness which takes objects as its objects.
This is also as explained regarding the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) among the three fetters.
Regarding the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*), its objects are consciousnesses with outflows (*sāsrava*).

This means that for this fetter, the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the five categories (*pañca-varga*) of each of the three realms, which have outflows as their object, increase in accordance with those objects.
Regarding the conditioned objects of the object-condition consciousness (*ālambanapratyaya-vijñāna*):

it means that for this consciousness which takes conditioned objects as its object, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the five categories within each of the three realms increase in accordance with those objects.
These include the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), the flood (*ogha*), the yoke (*yoga*), and the view of grasping (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*).
These are the fetters of clinging to a real body,
the knots of greed, pride, and doubt,
and the lower-tier fetters.
The underlying tendencies of wrong view, adherence to views,
craving born of mental contact,
pride, ignorance, views, and doubt.
The same applies to the fetters of craving, conceit, ignorance, views, and doubt.
This refers to ignorance among the three outflows (*āsrava*),
and ignorance among the four floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*).
Among the four graspings, it is the grasping at views;
among the four bodily fetters, it is the adherence to this as real;
and among the five fetters, it is greed and pride.
Among the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*), it is doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Among the five views (*pañca dṛṣṭayaḥ*), it is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Among the six classes of craving for the body (*ṣaḍ ātmabhāvānuśayāḥ*), it is the craving born of mental contact (*manosaṃsparśajā tṛṣṇā*).
Among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), there are pride, ignorance, views, and doubt;
among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), there are craving, pride, ignorance,
views, and grasping, as well as doubt.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in relation to the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes the condition of that condition as its object;
this is also as explained regarding the fetter of doubt among the three fetters.
This applies likewise to the three unwholesome roots and the outflow of desire (kāma-āsrava) in relation to the consciousness that takes [them] as its condition.
Regarding those [factors] of the desire realm that have outflow (sāsrava) as their object and are universal (sarvatraga) in the form realm,
as well as those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya):
these refer to the consciousnesses that take these four factors as their objects.
The five categories of the desire realm that have outflowing objects,
as well as the universal proclivities of the form realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation, increase in association with these [defilements].
The object-condition consciousness has as its objects the conditioned factors of the desire realm,
the three categories of the form realm,
and the universal [defilements] of the formless realm.
As for those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
these four dharmas take as their object the consciousness that takes objects;
they pertain to the five categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and have conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as their objects.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the three categories— those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and those abandoned through cultivation—
in the form realm, as well as the universal [dispositions] and those abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm, increase [in association with it].
The floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and grasps (*upādāna*) consist of the first two [floods, yokes, and grasps] along with the first two bonds (*saṃyojana*).
With the exception of regret (*kaukṛtya*), the remaining hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*),
there are the first two fetters conducive to the lower realm (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Regarding the statement that "the latent tendencies of sensual desire and ill will, as well as the fetter of ill will,
are likewise," this refers to sensual desire within the four floods, yokes, and graspings,
and to the first two among the four bodily ties.
Among the five hindrances, it excludes remorse;
among the five fetters, it is ill-will;
and among the five lower fetters, it consists of the first two.
Among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), desire-greed (*kāmarāga*) and hostility (*pratigha*);
and among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the fetter of hostility—
these underlie and increase in association with consciousness that takes them as its object.
It is also as explained regarding the three unwholesome roots and the outflow of desire;
[the same applies to] consciousness conditioned by the outflows of existence.
Regarding the three categories of the desire realm and those with outflow-conditions (*sāsrava-ālambana*) of the form and formless realms:
this refers to the three categories of consciousness with outflow-conditions that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and through cultivation, within the desire realm.
In the form and formless realms, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take the contaminated as their object increase in each of the five categories.
As for the consciousness that takes those [objects] as its object-of-object (ālambanālambana), it consists of three categories in the desire realm,
and those in the form and formless realms that have conditioned things as their objects.
This refers to the outflow-tainted object-conditioned consciousness.

It is increased by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with conditioned objects belonging to the three categories— those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, and through cultivation— of the desire realm,
as well as those belonging to the five categories of each of the form and formless realms.
Regarding the statement that "the floods (ogha), yokes (yoga),

and the grasping of self-theory (ātmavādopādāna) are likewise [associated with] the latent tendency of craving for existence (bhavarāgānuśaya)," this refers to the floods and yokes within the four [categories].
Among the four graspings, there is the grasping of self-theory (*ātmavāda*);
among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), there is the underlying tendency of lust (*rāga*).
These underlie and increase in relation to both the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and the object-conditioned object-consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*).
It is also as with the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) among the three outflows, which is said to have the hindrance of remorse (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*) as its object-consciousness;
it consists of the three categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the universal [defilements] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
As for those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
this refers to the consciousness that takes the hindrances as its object;

it consists of the three categories [of afflictions] belonging to the desire realm that are abandoned through seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and accumulation (*samudaya*), as well as through cultivation.
The pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the form realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation increase [in this consciousness];
as for the object-conditioning consciousness, it consists of the four categories of the desire realm.
The three categories of the form realm,
the universal [defilements] of the formless realm,
and those abandoned through cultivation.
This means that this hindrance takes as its object the consciousnesses belonging to the four categories of the desire realm,
excluding those abandoned through the vision of cessation.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the three categories— those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, and those to be abandoned through cultivation—
in the form realm, as well as the universal [dispositions] and those to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm, increase in association with it.
Regarding "the fetters of envy and avarice are likewise the body of craving born from nose-contact and tongue-contact":
this refers to envy and avarice among the five fetters.
Among the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*), the craving born of nose-contact and tongue-contact;
and among the nine fetters (*nava-saṃyojana*), envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*):

these have their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to both the object-consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and the consciousness of the object-of-object (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*).
This is also as explained regarding the hindrance of regret (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*).

The craving for form (*rūparāga*), which is a fetter conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), takes as its object the consciousness of the three categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
as well as the universal [defilements] of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
As for those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
this refers to the consciousness that takes these fetters as its object,
specifically the three categories abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-heya*) within the realms of desire and form.
The universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation increase [in this consciousness]. Regarding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
the consciousness [of this stage] takes as its objects the three categories of the desire realm.
Regarding the four categories of the form and formless realms:
these refer to the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*) associated with these fetters,

as well as the three categories of the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*), the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
In the form and formless realms, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of each of the four categories increase, excluding those abandoned through the vision of cessation.
Regarding the latter four fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*),
the consciousness that serves as their object belongs to three categories within the three realms.
