This means that for this consciousness which takes [the object] as its condition (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three categories— those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*), the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)— increase within each of the three realms.

For the consciousness which takes that [conditioned] consciousness as its object (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*), there are the three categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the four categories of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*).
That is to say, for this object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*),
there are the three categories [of afflictions] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin, as well as through cultivation, belonging to the desire realm;
and four categories each belonging to the form and formless realms.
Excluding those abandoned by the vision of cessation,
the latent dispositions increase accordingly.
This refers to the aggregate of craving born of eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact, which takes consciousness as its object.
Regarding the three categories of the desire and form realms:
this refers to the consciousness conditioned by this craving-body (*tṛṣṇā-kāya*).

In the desire and form realms respectively, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three categories—those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origination, and through cultivation—increase.
The objects of the object-condition for consciousness consist of the four categories of the desire and form realms,
as well as the universal [defilements] of the formless realm and those abandoned through cultivation.
This refers to the consciousness that takes this craving for the body as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);
it consists of four categories each from the desire realm and the form realm,
excluding those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*).
The pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm,

as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation, increase [in relation to this object]; likewise, the [latent dispositions] of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin [increase].

Furthermore, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation consist of the three categories of the desire realm and the universal [defilements] of the form realm, which take consciousness as their object.
Regarding those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):

these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) take as their object the consciousnesses belonging to the three categories abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*), the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the form realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation increase [in this consciousness].
As for the object-conditioned consciousness, it consists of the four categories of the desire realm.
The three categories of the form realm,
the universal [defilements] of the formless realm,
and those abandoned through cultivation.
That is to say, these latent dispositions (anuśaya) take as their object the consciousness that takes objects;
they consist of the four categories of the desire realm,
excluding those abandoned by the vision of cessation.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the three categories— those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and those to be abandoned through cultivation—
in the form realm, as well as the universal [dispositions] and those to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm, increase [in association with it].

The consciousnesses that serve as objects for the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm consist of the three categories [of the desire realm] and those with outflows (sāsrava) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
Regarding those [defilements] that are universal in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
this refers to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take consciousness as their object.
The three categories [of afflictions] in the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, and cultivation;
those with outflow-conditions to be abandoned through the vision of cessation;
and the universal [afflictions] of the form realm.
Furthermore, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation increase [in this consciousness].
Regarding the object-conditioned consciousness, it has conditioned factors of the desire realm as its objects,
and the three categories of the form realm.
Those that are universal in the formless realm and those abandoned through cultivation refer to these proclivities which take consciousness as their object-condition.
The five categories of the desire realm have conditioned objects;
those of the form realm are the three categories abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, and cultivation;
and those of the formless realm are the universal [defilements].
Furthermore, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation increase [in relation to it].
Regarding the consciousness conditioned by the latent dispositions to be abandoned by the path of vision in the desire realm,
there are the three categories of the desire realm.
As well as those abandoned by the path of seeing that take contaminated objects as their conditions,
those universal [defilements] of the form realm,
and those abandoned by the path of cultivation.

That is to say, these latent dispositions (anuśaya) take as their objects the three categories of consciousness in the desire realm— namely, those abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, and cultivation—
as well as those with outflows (sāsrava) abandoned through the path of vision that have [defiled] objects.
The pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the form realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation increase [in this consciousness],
which takes the object-conditioning consciousness as its object.
The four categories of the desire realm,
the three categories of the form realm,
and the universal [defilements] of the formless realm.
Regarding those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) take as their object the consciousness that takes objects (*ālambana-ālambana-vijñāna*),
specifically the four categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*).
The three categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, as well as through cultivation,

in the form realm; and the universal [dispositions] and those to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm, increase in relation to the form realm’s [categories] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin.
Furthermore, regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) that take consciousness as their object:
these consist of the three categories of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the universal [defilements] of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
and those to be abandoned by cultivation.

This means that these latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with the three categories— those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, and those to be abandoned through cultivation—
of both the desire and form realms, as well as the universal [dispositions] and those to be abandoned through cultivation of the formless realm.
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambanapratyaya-vijñāna*):
it consists of the three categories of the desire realm and the four categories of the form and formless realms.
That is to say, these latent dispositions (anuśaya) take as their object the consciousness that is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya):
the three categories [of defilements] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin and through cultivation in the desire realm,
and four categories each in the form and formless realms.
Excluding those abandoned through the vision of cessation,

the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that increase in accordance with the consciousness conditioned by the underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of cessation in the form realm consist of the three categories of the desire and form realms.
And those [factors] of the form realm that are associated with the outflows and are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation;
those that are universal in the formless realm;
and those that are to be abandoned by cultivation.

That is to say, these latent dispositions (anuśaya) take as their objects the three categories— namely, those abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, and through cultivation— of the consciousnesses belonging to the desire realm and the form realm,
as well as the contaminated objects of the form realm abandoned through the vision of cessation.
The universal proclivities of the formless realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation increase [in relation to] the consciousness that takes them as its object.
The three categories of the desire realm;
the conditioned objects of the form realm;
and the four categories of the formless realm.
That is to say, these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) take as their object the consciousness that is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
namely, the three categories [of afflictions] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and through cultivation, belonging to the desire realm;
and the five categories [of afflictions] belonging to the form realm that have conditioned phenomena as their object.
The four categories of the formless realm do not have the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation increase; rather,
it is the latent dispositions to be abandoned by the path of vision in the form realm that take this consciousness as their object.
The three categories of the desire and form realms,
the outflow-conditions (sāsrava-ālambana) abandoned through the path of vision in the form realm,
and the universal [defilements] of the formless realm.
Regarding those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
this refers to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take consciousness as their object;

these belong to the three categories—namely, those abandoned through seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*), those abandoned through seeing origination (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)—within both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, the outflow-tainted objects of the path of seeing in the form realm,
the universal [defilements] of the formless realm,
and the latent dispositions abandoned through cultivation increase in association with it.
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*):
it consists of the three categories of the desire realm and the four categories of the form and formless realms.
That is to say, these latent dispositions (anuśaya) take as their object the consciousness that is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya):
the three categories [of defilements] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin and through cultivation in the desire realm,
and four categories each in the form and formless realms.
Excluding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation that increase [in relation to it],
the latent dispositions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation, take consciousness as their object within the formless realm.
Regarding the three categories within the three realms:
this refers to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take consciousness as their object;

in each of the three realms, the latent dispositions of the three categories—those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origination, and through cultivation—respectively increase in association with them.
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*):
it consists of the three categories of the desire realm and the four categories of the form and formless realms.
That is to say, these latent dispositions (anuśaya) have as their object the consciousness that takes objects;
they consist of the three categories abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and through cultivation, within the desire realm,
and four categories each within the form and formless realms.
Excluding the increase of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation,
the consciousness that takes as its object the latent dispositions to be abandoned by the vision of cessation in the formless realm consists of the three categories of the three realms.
And as for those [defilements] of the formless realm that are abandoned through the vision of cessation and have outflowing objects:
these latent dispositions take consciousness as their object;
they belong to each of the three realms and consist of the three categories abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origination, and through cultivation.

Furthermore, the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya) within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), which take [the object] as their condition, increase [in association with] the consciousness that takes them as its object;
these consist of the three categories (trika) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The four categories of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding those [defilements] in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that have conditioned phenomena as their object:
these refer to the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take consciousness as their objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The three categories [of afflictions] in the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and accumulation and through cultivation;
and the four categories in the form realm,
excluding those to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
The five classes [of afflictions] of the formless realm increase through the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that have conditioned phenomena as their object.
The latent tendencies of the formless realm to be abandoned by the path of seeing take consciousness as their object.
Regarding the three realms and three categories,
as well as those with outflows (sāsrava) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) within the formless realm that take [other] outflows as their object:
these refer to the consciousnesses upon which these underlying tendencies (anuśaya) depend.
In each of the three realms, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the three categories abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin,

as well as those abandoned through the path of cultivation, increase in relation to [their objects]. Furthermore, the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) latent dispositions abandoned through the path of vision that take the object-conditioned consciousness as their object increase in relation to that object-conditioned consciousness.

The three categories of the desire realm and the four categories of the form and formless realms refer to these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take consciousness as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The three categories [of defilements] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and through cultivation, in the desire realm;
and four categories each in the form and formless realms—
excluding the latent tendencies to be abandoned through the vision of cessation— increase in accordance with their respective objects.

Question: Why is it that here only the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*) are mentioned, while the object-of-object-of-object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanālambanālambana-vijñāna*) and so forth are not?
Answer: It is in order to avoid the fault of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
That is to say, if one were to further explain a third consciousness as a condition,
one would have to further explain a fourth consciousness as a condition;
in this manner, it would proceed indefinitely until there is no end.
Furthermore, just as with the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
one should contemplate only up to the second turn and not the third turn and beyond;
the same should apply to the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, regarding the objects of consciousness (ālambana-vijñāna) and the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that increase in accordance with the objects of object-consciousness (ālambanālambana-vijñāna),
for the most part there is a difference between them.
Therefore, it must certainly be stated that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with the third turning and so forth; however,
because for the most part there is no difference, they are not stated again.
Furthermore, the Abhidharma briefly indicates the general direction so that those of wisdom may successively enter into realization; therefore,
it does not further discuss a third turning and so forth.
From the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—
within the fifteen categories of mind across the three realms—
how many minds arise as their immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for each one?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.
That is to say, some may claim that the mind serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the mind, but not for mental factors (*caitta*).
Mental factors serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for other mental factors, but not for the mind itself—
as the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain.
This is stated in order to refute their view and to demonstrate that both the mind and mental factors can mutually serve as equal-and-immediate conditions for one another.
This treatise is not composed merely because of their similarity;
rather, it is intended here to clarify the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Therefore, the inquiry concerns only mind and mental factors (*cittacaittadharma*).
Question: Why, in this context, is there a question only regarding the arising of a mind with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*), and not regarding the arising of a mind without outflows (*anāsrava-citta*)?
Answer: This is the *Saṃyojana-skandha* (Aggregate of Fetters).
Only the mind with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*) can increase the fetters (*saṃyojana*); therefore,
it is mentioned specifically.
Question: The analysis of the various fetters (saṃyojana) relies solely upon the five categories (pañca-varga).
Why, then, is there now a question regarding fifteen moments of mind?
Answer: In this present aggregate, it is not only the fetters that are being revealed.
This also clarifies the objects of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), as these pertain to all three realms.
Question: Regarding the fifteen classes of mind within the three realms...
Among the mind and mental factors, the mind is the most preeminent;
therefore, this question concerns the mind alone and not the mental factors.
Herein, "arising" refers to the moment of actual arising.
Because they function as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
all minds are said to total sixteen:
namely, the aforementioned fifteen plus the untainted mind (*anāsravacitta*).
Question: Regarding these sixteen moments of mind, how many do they each arise from when viewed in relation to one another, and how many do they each produce?
Answer: The first four categories of mind in the desire realm.
Each arises from fifteen types of mind;
excluding the untainted mind,
it can only give rise to the five categories of mind belonging to the desire realm.
This is because a defiled mind of a lower stage cannot produce a mind of a higher stage,
nor can a defiled mind produce an untainted (anāsrava) mind.
A mind of the desire realm that is abandoned through cultivation arises from sixteen types of minds.
Furthermore, it can give rise to sixteen minds.
The first four classes of minds in the form realm arise from eleven types of minds, excluding the first four classes of minds in the desire realm and the untainted (anāsrava) minds.
It can produce only the ten minds of the desire and form realms.
The mind abandoned through cultivation in the form realm arises from twelve minds,
excluding the first four categories of minds in the desire realm.
Furthermore, it can produce sixteen minds.
The first four categories of mind in the formless realm arise from seven types of mind:
namely, the five categories of mind within its own realm.
Furthermore, the minds of the desire and form realms that are abandoned through cultivation can also produce fifteen types of mind,
excluding the untainted (anāsrava) mind.
The mind of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation arises from eight types of minds:
namely, the five categories of mind within its own realm, the minds of the desire and form realms to be abandoned by cultivation,
and the untainted (anāsrava) mind.
Furthermore, it can produce sixteen minds.
The untainted mind arises from four minds,
and it in turn can produce four minds.
This refers to the minds abandoned through cultivation within each of the three realms, as well as untainted minds.
This is because untainted minds do not enter into or emerge from defiled minds.
Here, the reference is made generally to all sentient beings.
Alternatively, it may be stated that such things can exist at all times;
it does not mean that such a thing occurs for a single *pudgala* within a single moment.
Regarding the statement that fifteen minds arise immediately after the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*):
among the sixteen types of mind, the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is excluded,
as it is not what is being discussed here.
This is the general explanation.
As for the specific distinctions:
if one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm, six types of mind may arise immediately following the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) and so forth of the desire realm.
This refers to the five [types of] mind of the desire realm and the mind abandoned through cultivation in the form realm—
namely, the wholesome preparatory mind of the *anāgamya* concentration—
if one has already become free from the defilements of the desire realm but has not yet become free from the defilements of the form realm.
Immediately following the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) and so forth of the desire realm, ten types of mind may arise:
namely, the five minds of the desire realm at times such as during a retrogression (*parihāṇi*),
and the five minds of the form realm at times such as during rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*).
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm, eleven types of mind may arise immediately following the mental faculty (*manas*) of the desire realm:
namely, the five minds of the desire realm as in the case of falling away (*parihāṇi*), and so forth,
and the one mind of the form realm as in the case of entering meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
In the formless realm, it is as during the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*).
If one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm, eleven types of mind may arise immediately following the mental faculty (*manas*) and so forth;
that is to say, the five minds of the desire realm may arise, as during the moment of rebirth-linking or at the time of falling away (*parihāṇi*), and so on.
Regarding the five minds of the form realm and the mind abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—
specifically, the preparatory wholesome mind of the threshold stage (*sāmantaka*) of the Sphere of Infinite Space and so forth, as when entering meditative absorption—
if one has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm, eleven minds may arise immediately after the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) of the form realm.
This refers to the mind of the desire realm abandoned through cultivation, namely the mind resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) and so forth;
the five [minds] of the form realm during times such as falling away (*parihāṇi*);
and the five [minds] of the formless realm during times such as rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*).
Immediately following the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) and so forth of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), fifteen types of minds may arise:
namely, the five of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as when one is reborn [into it];
and the five of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as when one is reborn [into it] or falls away from it, and so forth.
And as for the five [faculties] of the formless realm,
the faculty of equanimity, and likewise the five faculties beginning with faith:
this is because fifteen moments of mind arise, just as with the faculty of mind.
Regarding the eleven minds that arise immediately after the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*):
these consist of five each from the desire realm and the form realm,
as well as the mind abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm.

This is because one immediately follows the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and so forth of the third dhyāna to enter the contaminated concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); furthermore, it is impossible to pass away while in the four types of feeling, such as pleasure, or within the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*).
The four preceding classes of mind do not arise immediately after [the formless mind].
Regarding the five minds that arise immediately after the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*):
this refers to the five [minds] of the desire realm; the same applies to the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Furthermore, five mental states arise because they are like the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
One cannot enter a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) from sorrow or suffering,
for those states are utterly incompatible with a concentrated mind.
Regarding the ten minds that arise immediately after the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*):
these refer to the five classes of mind from each of the desire and form realms.
Specifically, the faculty of joy belonging to the desire realm gives rise to the five [classes] of the desire realm.
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) of the form realm gives rise to five [minds] of the form realm;
it does not arise immediately after the faculty of joy of the desire realm.

Furthermore, a defiled mind of the form realm accompanied by joy does not arise immediately after the faculty of joy of the form realm, nor does a defiled mind of the desire realm accompanied by joy arise immediately after the faculty of joy of the form realm.
Because the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) can only induce afflictions (*kleśa*) of its own level,
some say herein that the wholesome or neutral mind of the desire realm arises immediately after the faculty of joy of the form realm.
The wholesome or indeterminate minds of the form realm do not arise immediately after the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and so forth of the desire realm; rather,

it is because the mind of the form realm and its associates can only arise immediately after the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) and so forth of the desire realm that the mind does not arise immediately after the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and so forth.
Because the fifteen moments of mind within the three realms do not arise;
for this very reason, the Sūtra designates the Path of Seeing as "signless" (*animitta*),
since no contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind arises immediately thereafter.
It has already been established that the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) arises immediately after three types of minds:
namely, the wholesome minds of the three realms that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

In this context, having attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) or once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), one may emerge [from meditative absorption] with a mind belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Alternatively, one may emerge from meditative absorption with a mind of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
Having attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), if one relies upon the threshold concentration,
one likewise emerges from it with these two types of minds.
If one relies on any of the other five stages,
one emerges from them all by means of their own respective stage.
Once the fruit of Arhatship has been attained, if one relies on the threshold concentration (anāgamya), [one emerges from it].
One may emerge with a mind of the desire realm,
or with a mind of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
If one relies on the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one emerges with a mind of the sphere of nothingness.
Or one may emerge with a mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
If one relies on any other stage,
one emerges entirely with a mind belonging to that specific stage.
Regarding the arising of ten minds from the visual, auditory, and tactile consciousness elements:
these refer to the five categories of each of the desire and form realms.
Only those belonging to their own respective realms arise from the olfactory and gustatory consciousness elements.
The arising of five minds refers to the five categories of the desire realm.
The arising of three minds of untainted dharmas refers to those abandoned through cultivation in the three realms.
Regarding the past dharmas that give rise to two types of mind:
these refer to those abandoned through cultivation in the realms of form and formlessness,
specifically upon emerging from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) or the maturation of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya*).
When the mind of the non-ideational absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) reaches the time of its arising,
the past minds and mental factors that were able to enter [that state] then possess the function of the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) in taking and giving their fruit.

Question: Does the mind emerging from the maturation of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñi-vedayita-vipāka*) pertain to all five categories of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or is it only that which is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
If so, what would be the fault [in either case]?
Both positions entail faults.
Why is this so? If it were to pertain to all five categories of the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Why is this not stated here?
That is to say, one should state that six minds arise in the past;
why then is it said that only two arise in the past?
If it were only the faculties abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) that are spoken of in the aggregate of faculties,
how would one reconcile [this] with what is said: "Once those perceptions have arisen, those sentient beings pass away from that place"?
That perception should be described as either wholesome or indeterminate.
Regarding that perception, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the outflows and having the form realm as their object increase.
It should be stated that the mind which is the fruition of non-perception (āsaṃjñika-vipāka) belongs to all five categories of the form realm.
Question: If that is so, why is this not stated here?
Answer: That which ought to be stated but is not stated [is as follows].
One should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, in this context, only the emergence from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is mentioned because it is induced by the power of preparatory effort;
the emergence from the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*) of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñin*) is not induced by the power of preparatory effort.
Therefore, this is not mentioned.
Furthermore, in this context, it is stated that only a wholesome mind emerges;
the resultant mind of non-conception may be wholesome, defiled, or neutral.
Therefore, this is not mentioned.
Some say that the mind which emerges from the maturation of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-vipāka-citta*) is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Question: How should one interpret what is stated in the *Indriya-skandha*?
Answer: That text should be explained as follows:
"The pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of that [realm] increase in relation to the ideation and form of the Form Realm."
However, because it excludes those with uncontaminated objects, it is said that latent dispositions (anuśaya) with contaminated objects increase [in relation to their objects].
The critique states:
"Between these two explanations, the former is superior."
Question: Why do those perceptions not have the outflow-free (anāsrava) as their object, such that the latent tendencies (anuśaya) increase therein?
Answer: Because they grasp non-perception (asaṃjñi) as nirvāṇa and grasp the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñisamāpatti) as the noble path (āryamārga).
Therefore, at that time, one does not give rise to the wrong view of repudiating cessation and the path;
from this point onward, it is possible for such wrong views to arise.
This is because a future dharma that has not yet arisen is not an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Regarding the four immeasurables giving rise to six types of mind:
these refer to the five categories of the form realm and those abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
because they take the desire realm as their object.
Because they take sentient beings as their object,
one cannot give rise to the first two liberations or the first four spheres of mastery within the formless realm.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Because they take the desire realm as their object,
the fourth and fifth liberations produce six types of consciousness.
That is to say, the five categories of the formless realm and those abandoned through cultivation in the form realm;
as for the arising of the knowledge of others' minds, it arises in six moments of mind.
That is to say, the five categories of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—
the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth— cannot induce a mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as their immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This refers to the third liberation (*vimokṣa*).
Regarding the four latter spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the eight former spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
they give rise to five types of consciousness.
This means that all five categories of the form realm involve distinct objects of observation and cannot induce the mind of the formless realm.
As for the latter two universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) producing five types of mind:
This means that the five categories of the formless realm are conceptual contemplations;
they cannot induce the meditative mind of the form realm.
Regarding the "non-arising mind" of the eighth liberation:
Although these are immediate antecedents of mind, they are not the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) for mind;
thus, when the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) arises, two types of mind are produced, namely:
the minds to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the desire realm and the form realm.
Because they take the Four Truths of the desire realm as their object,
they cannot give rise to a mind of the formless realm.
Regarding the two minds produced by the fetter of attachment to the form realm that leads upward (*rūparāga-ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*):
This means that because the defiled minds of lower stages belonging to the desire and form realms do not arise in the higher [stages],
the latter four fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) give rise to three types of mind; that is,
the minds abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the three realms.
Because these five fetters manifest only while one is in the body of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*),
the remaining text is easy to understand and thus not analyzed here.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School,
Volume Eighty-nine (and Volume Ninety-five),
composed by the One Hundred Great Arhats and others.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Section Four of the Ten Gates on the Aggregates of the Second [Chapter], "The Aggregate of Fetters," Part Twenty: From the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
Regarding each of the increased latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), should they be said to be with vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka and with vicāra only, or without vitarka and without vicāra?
Why was this treatise composed? It is answered:
in order to refute the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.
That is to say, some say that because vitarka and vicāra are the coarse and subtle characteristics of the mind, they exist up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
and all defiled minds possess both vitarka and vicāra.
Therefore, vitarka and vicāra exist throughout all three realms,
as the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain;
[this passage] refutes that position to demonstrate that they exist only in the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
In the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), there is both vitarka and vicāra;
in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), there is no vitarka and only vicāra;
from the second dhyāna up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there is neither vitarka nor vicāra.
For this reason, this treatise is composed.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in relation to the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya), they possess all three [characteristics].
That is to say, they refer to those latent dispositions that increase in relation to the eye-faculty as their object.
They pertain to the four dhyānas of the desire realm across the five stages, as well as to those abandoned through cultivation.
Thus, these underlying tendencies exist in the desire realm and the first dhyāna where there is both vitarka and vicāra.
If one is in the intermediate dhyāna, there is no vitarka and only vicāra;
if one is in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, there is neither vitarka nor vicāra; therefore, it is said that [the first dhyāna] possesses all three.
It should be understood that for all subsequent mentions of possessing these three, the same principle applies.
However, in the stages devoid of vitarka and vicāra,
they may be present either partially or in their entirety.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the female faculty (strī-indriya):
those that are accompanied by vitarka and vicāra are so called because the latent dispositions increased by it exist only in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase within the spheres of visual, auditory, and tactile consciousness:
they are either accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra alone.
Although the five consciousnesses, such as the visual, are indeed accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra...
Furthermore, for those in the first dhyāna,
these also serve as the objective fetters (*ālambana-bandhana*) for the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the intermediate dhyāna; thus,
the underlying tendencies that increase therein also pertain to the state of being without vitarka and with only vicāra.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase in the first dhyāna,
they are either with both vitarka and vicāra, or without vitarka and with vicāra alone;

this is because the term "first dhyāna" collectively indicates the three stages— the preliminary (*anāgamya*), the fundamental (*maula*), and the intermediate (*dhyānāntara*)— and thus it is said that there are two types.
Even if one were to speak only of the fundamental [dhyānas], there must necessarily be two [categories of latent dispositions],
because the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the intermediate dhyāna and the first dhyāna, etc., take all three stages as their objects.
The remaining text is easy to understand and thus is not analyzed here.

Regarding each of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) from the eye-faculty up to the ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), with which [faculties] should they be said to be associated:

the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of other schools and elucidating the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who hold [the following] view:
The two sensations of pleasure and pain exist in dependence upon the body throughout all levels from the desire realm up to the fourth dhyāna.
The two sensations of joy and sorrow exist in dependence upon the mind.
These exist from the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
To exclude that notion, it is intended to show that pleasant feeling exists only in the first and third dhyānas of the desire realm.
The two sensations of suffering (*duḥkha*) and mental grief (*daurmanasya*) exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The sensation of joy (*saumanasya*) exists only in the desire realm and the first two dhyānas.
Only the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is present throughout all stages.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that the mind and mental factors arise in succession and do not correspond with one another,
such as the Dārṣṭāntikas.
To refute that intention and to demonstrate that the mind and mental factors arise simultaneously and possess the characteristic of association (*samprayoga*),
this treatise was composed for these reasons:
the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) predominant in the eye faculty are associated with four faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) predominant in the eye faculty pertain to the five stages of the desire and form realms, including those that are universal, those to be abandoned by cultivation,
and those associated with the faculties of joy, sorrow, and equanimity when located in the desire realm.
If it occurs in the first or second dhyāna, it is associated with the faculties of joy and equanimity;
if it occurs in the third dhyāna, it is associated with the faculties of pleasure and equanimity;
if it occurs in the fourth dhyāna, it is associated solely with the faculty of equanimity.
Therefore, it is said in general that [the afflictions] correspond with the four faculties.
The faculty of suffering corresponds only with the five consciousnesses.

Since within the five consciousnesses there are no underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take the eye-faculty and so forth as their objects, they certainly do not correspond with the faculty of suffering.

Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) predominant in the female faculty (*strī-indriya*), they are associated with three faculties, excluding the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*) and pain (*duḥkha*).
The latent dispositions predominant in the female faculty exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
because in the desire realm, both pleasure and pain are present in the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
That [defilement] is not associated with pleasure or pain.
Regarding the latent tendencies (anuśaya) increased by the mental faculty (manas-indriya) that are associated with the five faculties:
because the mental faculty is universally associated with the five feelings (vedanā), these associated fetters are thus associated with the five faculties.
If there are four objects of cognition (ālambana) that bind, excluding suffering;
three types of latent tendencies (anuśaya) increased by the threefold samādhi;
and four faculties (indriya) associated with them, excluding the faculty of suffering.
The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) takes only the five objects such as form (*rūpa*) as its conditions and not the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth;
the three types of samādhi are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not increase [in these cases]. This is what is being discussed here; other passages are easy to understand and will not be further analyzed.
Lest those of wisdom become weary, [the author asks]:
Who possesses the faculties from the eye-faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm?
Who does not achieve [this]?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To refute the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.

That is to say, there are some who hold the view that the natures of attainment (*prāpti*) and non-attainment (*aprāpti*) do not exist substantially, but are merely established as conventional designations;
they maintain that the natures of attainment and non-attainment are intended to be revealed as substantially real entities.
If it were not so, it would contradict the sūtra;
as the sūtra says:
It should be understood that such a person (*pudgala*) is endowed with both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"I am endowed with the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and so forth."
If there were no nature of accomplishment or non-accomplishment,

then the definitive establishment of ordinary beings and noble ones, those in training and those beyond training, and those who have severed the roots of virtue and those who have not, would all be impossible.
Because a determinate cause and condition cannot be found.
Nevertheless, that which is accomplished and that which is not accomplished exist conventionally;
whereas the nature of accomplishment and the nature of non-accomplishment exist ultimately.
That which is like birth and death exists conventionally;
the phenomena of birth and death exist ultimately.
That which enters and emerges from meditative absorption exists conventionally.
The entering and emerging from meditative absorption exist as ultimate reality;
the agent and the experiencer exist as conventional reality;
and the karma and its ripened fruit exist as ultimate reality.
Thus, the nature of accomplishment and non-accomplishment exists as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-sat*),
whereas the designation of "accomplished" and "unaccomplished" exists as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-sat*).
That is to say, when there is the nature of accomplishment within a body, one is called "accomplished."
If that which possesses the nature of non-attainment within the body is called "non-attainment," then it is like trees and so forth,
where the [derived] forms and so on are provisional,
while the four primary elements are real.
In this way, the *pudgala* is a designation,
whereas the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, are real.
Within this continuum of the body of that designated being, [the aggregates persist].
Based on acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), it is said that there is the possession (*samanvāgama*) or non-possession (*asamanvāgama*) of dharmas.
For this reason, this treatise is composed.
Regarding the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), when it has been acquired and not lost in the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) and the desire realm (*kāma-dhātu*).
Regarding "accomplishment":
because the various devas of the form realm possess all sense faculties,
they are definitively accomplished with the five faculties, beginning with the eye.
This statement regarding "possessing faculties" is made with reference to those who are manifest.
Even those who are not manifest—namely, those lacking the female or male faculties—are said to possess the faculties.
Furthermore, because they are capable of possessing them and all such beings are endowed with them, they are described as possessing the faculties.
It is not the case that everything exists, for sorrow, suffering, and so forth also exist [in those states]. Furthermore,
regarding those who have already attained [the state] in the desire realm—
namely, at the stage of *praśākhā* (the stage of limbs)— it is because they do not lose it.
This means not being decomposed, not having fallen away, not being eaten by insects, and not being harmed.
Regarding those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who have not yet acquired or have already lost [the faculties] and thus do not possess them:
because there is no form in the formless realm, they do not possess the eye and other sense faculties.
And those who have not yet attained [the state] in the desire realm;
that is, during the stages of kalala, arbuda, peśī, and ghana.
As for those who have already lost it:

Regarding the statement that "the faculties of the ear, nose, and tongue are likewise [subject to] decay, falling away, being consumed by insects, or being harmed," this is as explained for the eye faculty;
as for the body faculty, it is accomplished in the desire realm and the form realm.
Because those born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) necessarily possess the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
Those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) do not possess it because they lack physical form.
As for the female and male faculties, those in the desire realm who have already obtained them and have not lost them possess them.
As explained regarding the eye faculty:
those in the form realm, the formless realm,
and the desire realm who have not yet acquired it or have already lost it do not possess it.
In the realms of form and formlessness, there are no female or male faculties because of the absence of sensual desire;
one abandons these faculties out of aversion when reborn in those realms.
Furthermore, in the realms of form and formlessness, there is no solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
Because these faculties exist only by reason of solid food;
because these faculties exist by reason of a lack of shame and a lack of dread;
and furthermore, because those [deities] have no use for the female and male faculties.
Question: If that were so,
then the nose and tongue would also not exist there,
because those two lack the functions of smelling odors and tasting flavors.
Answer: The two faculties of nose and tongue are functional there, namely for the adornment of the body and for the production of speech.
The two faculties of female and male, however, cause the body to appear unattractive.
Those who possess a sense of shame and modesty will certainly conceal it.
The Venerable Ghosaka stated this because there is no karma that brings about rebirth in the two upper realms.
Question: Since the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) does not exist in the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*), they should not be considered "men" (*puruṣa*).
Answer: They are called "men" because they possess the function of a man in the form and formless realms.
As for this "function of a man": [text continues]
It is said that one who is able to abandon desire and accomplish wholesome deeds is called a "great man" (*puruṣa*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
those on the four paths and those who have attained the four fruits are all called great men.
It is not that all women lack the attainment of the fruits of spiritual realization;
as the Sūtra says regarding this Mahāprajāpatī:
Although she was a woman, she entered the noble path;
having attained the fruit and exhausted the outflows, she is also called a "great man" (*puruṣa*).
Regarding this meaning, one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There may be a man who does not possess the male organ,
such as those born in the form realm or the formless realm;
or there may be one who possesses the male organ but is not designated as a "man."
This includes those such as *śaṇḍhas* and *paṇḍakas*,
or even certain males who possess the male organ,
namely those who possess the male organ and are free from the defilement of desire.
There are some who are neither males nor endowed with the male organ;
that is to say, excluding those previously mentioned,
there are those born from a womb, an egg, or moisture who die gradually.
One gradually abandons the six types of material sense-faculties,
such as the eye; among these, one also gradually abandons the body-faculty,
namely the hands, feet, and so forth.
If one were to abandon all the atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), one would immediately die;
yet even when the limbs and joints are severed in hell,
or even when the body is decomposed and putrefied, the body-faculty still exists.
Some say that at that time there are also the eyes and so forth; for if they were entirely non-existent,
[the following would not hold].
Thereafter, it should not arise again,
because once the maturation has been severed, it does not continue.
Some have said this:
In the various hells, the six faculties, such as the eye, though severed, are restored;
this is because they are drawn forth by karma and because it is the inherent nature of the destinies.
Just as the limbs and joints of humans and others, once severed or destroyed, cannot be rejoined, those of beings in the hells and other realms, having been severed, immediately regenerate.
Such is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the various destinies; they cannot be compared to one another.
Therefore, while the eyes and other [faculties] may be severed and then regenerated,
the body-faculty (kāyendriya) can never be entirely severed;
for if it were entirely severed, there would be no possibility of its continuity.
Because these are the bases for the various material sense-faculties (*rūpindriya*),
they possess a small number of corporeal sense-faculty atoms (*kāyendriya-paramāṇu*);
depending upon these, the limbs and joints are subsequently regenerated.
The body-faculty (kāyendriya) within all the joints, once severed, grows back again just like the eye-faculty and other such faculties.
Other masters say that although the bodies of those in the various hells are dismembered into hundreds or thousands of pieces, [the faculty remains].
Furthermore, within each of its parts there exists the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*),
because there is continuity between the various parts,
just as in the case of broken pieces of *douzhong* (Eucommia) or lotus roots and stalks.
It is also like the seeds and the stalk of a split gourd,
which are not separate from one another; for if they were separate, the body-faculty would not exist,
as it is impossible for a single sentient being to possess two bodies.
Yet, we observe in the world that when the bodies of various insects are severed,
they often continue to move; this is driven by the force of the wind and does not imply the presence of a body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
Regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the mind-faculty (*manendriya*), and the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣendriya*):
all sentient beings possess these, because they are constantly accomplished throughout all stages of the three realms and nine levels.
As for the pleasure-faculty (*sukhendriya*), it is accomplished by those from the Śubhakṛtsna heaven downward, as well as by noble ones (*ārya*) born in higher realms.

Regarding those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who do not achieve [the higher stages], the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) exists only in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and in the first and third dhyānas.
It is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
However, that which belongs to the Desire Realm and the first dhyāna is exclusively contaminated.
The third dhyāna pertains to both types.
Those that are contaminated (sāsrava) are not accomplished when one is born in a higher stage, because they produce equanimity (upekṣā) in the lower stages.
Those that are uncontaminated (anāsrava), however, do not abandon the lower stages when one is born in a higher stage.
The untainted [faculties] are abandoned only at the time of attaining a fruit, transforming the faculties, or falling away.
Question: If one is born in the second dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna, which level’s faculty of pleasure does that person possess?
Answer: He possesses the defiled faculty of pleasure of the third dhyāna;
if he has already become detached from the defilements of the second dhyāna, he further acquires the undefiled faculty of pleasure of the third dhyāna.
Therefore, those born from the Śubhakṛtsna heaven downward all possess the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
This term "Śubhakṛtsna" generally indicates its own level; by mentioning the latter, the former is implied.
The same principle applies to all other cases.
Question: Is there any noble one born in the fourth dhyāna or above who does not possess the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?
Some say there is; namely, one who has already become detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
Relying on the second dhyāna and the three lower stages, one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Having attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), one does not arise again toward the higher paths;
at the end of life, one is reborn in the fourth dhyāna or in the stages above it.
"He does not possess the faculty of pleasure.
The critique says:
He should not have made such a statement.
If one who has already become detached from the defilements of a higher stage enters the state of rightness and departure (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on a lower stage,
once they have attained that fruit, they will necessarily give rise to the path of superior fruit.
Having cultivated the untainted (anāsrava) states of the higher stages and attained the cessation (nirodha) of those higher stages, they subsequently pass away.
For example, one who has already abandoned three or four grades,
or seven or eight grades, of the defilements of the desire realm enters into rightness and the state beyond birth.
Having attained that fruit, he will necessarily give rise to the path of superior fruit.
By cultivating the superior grade of the untainted (*anāsrava*), he attains the superior grade of cessation (*nirodha*) and then passes away.
Question: If one has already become detached from the defilements of the third *dhyāna*, [what occurs]?
Relying on the second dhyāna and the three lower stages,
those who possess liberation through faith refine their faculties to become "attainers by vision.
They do not arise in the subsequent stage of "progression toward," nor do they pass away from there to be reborn in the fourth dhyāna or any higher stages.
What faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) does he accomplish?

Answer: When he attains mastery over the higher stages and undergoes the refinement of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*), he is also able to cultivate the untainted (*anāsrava*) faculty of pleasure of the higher stages.

Even if one does not attain mastery over the higher stages, once that fruit has been attained, one must necessarily give rise to the path of superior fruit and cultivate the untainted states of the higher realms before passing away; therefore, noble ones are born above the Śubhakṛtsna heaven.
It is certain that they accomplish the untainted faculty of pleasure (*anāsrava-sukhendriya*).
The accomplishment of the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) should be explained accordingly.
The faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) is accomplished in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Those who do not possess [the faculties] of the form and formless realms—
even sentient beings of the desire realm, up to and including the Buddhas, possess the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
This is because suffering arises when one is oppressed by an adverse object, occurring without depending on conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
In the realms of form and formlessness,
there is no faculty of suffering because they are nourished by the power of meditative concentration and because there are no disagreeable objects.
Because there are no unwholesome karmas or afflictions [therein].
Furthermore, because the realms of form and formlessness are superior realms;
that is to say, even in these inferior realms, superior bodies may still experience painful sensations.
Just as in the desire realm, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas,
and mahābodhisattvas do not experience painful sensations even when possessing inferior bodies within superior realms,
so it is with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the form and formless realms.
Just as in a year afflicted by calamities,
even excellent crops may suffer from insect damage and the like,
whereas in a year free from calamities, even weeds do not suffer from insect damage and the like.
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is possessed by one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire,
but is not possessed by one who has already abandoned it;
this is because the faculty of sorrow necessarily arises from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Those who have not yet abandoned desire give rise to sorrow through conceptualization;
those who have already abandoned desire do not give rise to sorrow or distress when conceptualization arises.
Therefore, the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), even if it were of a wholesome nature, would not be possessed by one who has abandoned the defilement of desire.
Because they are induced by the afflictions of the desire realm,
the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) that have already been obtained are not lost;
those not yet obtained are brought to fulfillment.
Regarding "already lost" and "not accomplished":
this refers to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), which is termed "already obtained" once one has entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It is termed "not lost" as long as the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has not yet become manifest.
When the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) has not yet manifested, it is called "not yet obtained.
After the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) has manifested, it is called "already lost.

When the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*) has already arisen, or when one has regressed from the fruit of arhatship after having attained the subsequent knowledge of the path, it is called "already obtained."
When the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) has not yet manifested, it is called "not lost.
When the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has not yet manifested, or when one has not yet fallen away from the fruit of arhatship, it is called "not yet attained.
After the knowledge of exhaustion has manifested, it is called "already lost."
When the faculty of one who has full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) are present before one, it is called "already attained.
Not falling back from the fruit of arhatship is called "not lost.
When the knowledge of exhaustion has not yet become present before one, it is called "not yet attained."
Falling away from the fruit of arhatship is termed "already lost.
The elements of body, visible form, sound,
and tangibility are accomplished in the desire realm and the form realm.
Regarding those who do not possess [the elements] of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*):
it may be granted that this applies to the elements of body, visible form, and tangibility;
but how is it that the element of sound (*śabdadhātu*) is always possessed?
Some maintain this view:
the sound element necessarily arises from the conjunction and disjunction of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
This applies whether sentient beings reside within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
"Because the primary elements (mahābhūta) exist perpetually, they constantly produce sound.
[The author] critiques this, saying: "That person should not speak thus.
If the four primary elements necessarily and perpetually produced sound," [it would lead to absurd consequences].
By which primary elements (mahābhūta) is this produced sound created?
If it were created by those very same [elements], it would follow that it is a single instance of derived matter (upādāyarūpa) produced from the four primary elements;
yet if one says it is created by others, then other four primary elements must likewise produce sound.
In this way, there would be the fault of an infinite regress.
One should state it thus:
[it exists] within the bodies of sentient beings born in the desire and form realms.
The four great elements (mahābhūta) exist in abundance within a single body;
when they strike against one another, sound is produced, but when they do not strike, no sound arises.
Although the sound-element (śabdadhātu) must necessarily exist within a single body,
it is not the case that all parts of the body produce sound everywhere;
thus says the Venerable Buddhadeva.
The realms of eye, ear, and body consciousness are not always present in the desire and form realms;
this statement in the root treatise is made based on the majority of cases.
Below the Brahma-world and for those born in the upper three dhyānas,
it is accomplished both when manifest and when not manifest.
Regarding those who do not possess [the formless realm],
this refers to those born in the desire realm or the first dhyāna,
who possess [the factors] as appropriate to their respective states.
Among the defiled, the wholesome, and the neutral [states] of the three consciousnesses,
those that have been habitually practiced are also constantly accomplished,
such as superior deportment, craftsmanship, and the fruition of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*).
If one is born in the second dhyāna or above,
when it is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta), it is possessed if it is manifest;
if it is not manifest, it is not possessed.
Because the nature of the five groups of consciousness is weak and inferior,
their manifestation in other stages lacks firm power.
This is also the case for the transformative minds and so forth within the mental consciousness.
Even if one is born in another stage, because its power remains firm and strong, it is accomplished even though it does not manifest before one.
As for the untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) [dharmas], such as the sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth, they are always accomplished.
This refers to non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because there is no sentient being who does not possess it.
The subsequent "dharmas that are never severed" should be understood accordingly.
The threefold *samādhi* is like the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) and so forth.
Regarding those already attained and those not yet attained:
because that which has been attained will never again be lost or relinquished,
and because it is only at the point of entering parinirvāṇa that one cultivates its attainment.
Having entered parinirvāṇa, one no longer belongs to the category of sentient beings;
therefore, it cannot be said that [the factors] are not accomplished.
The remainder of the text is easy to understand and thus is not analyzed.
When one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of each of the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation— from the eye faculty up to the formless realm—
among the ninety-eight latent tendencies:
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully understood (*parijñāta*)?
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are exhausted?
Why was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting other schools and revealing the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that even among material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), there are those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
This is to refute that intention and to demonstrate that all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
Alternatively, there are those who hold the view that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are unable to abandon the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by insight.
Others again maintain that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are unable to abandon the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), being able only to suppress them.

To refute this view and to demonstrate that ordinary beings are indeed able to abandon the latent dispositions abandoned through seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*) from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), [the author] states:
This treatise is composed specifically to exclude the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Furthermore,
there are briefly two kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
There are two types of thorough knowledge: first, thorough knowledge as cognition;
second, thorough knowledge as abandonment. Herein, the discussion is based solely upon thorough knowledge as abandonment.
This abandonment is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); although it is not itself full knowledge (*parijñā*), it is called "full knowledge" because it is the fruit of full knowledge.
This is like how the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśāyatana*) are referred to as "past karma," where the name of the cause is applied to the effect.
Full knowledge (*parijñā*) is likewise. Furthermore, it is said here that one who attains full knowledge does so by means of the exhaustion of those [defilements].
That is to say, when whatever phenomena are abandoned reach ultimate exhaustion, it is called the attainment of full knowledge.
It is not necessary that this must be explained solely in terms of the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*).
Regarding the statement, "When the eye-faculty attains thorough knowledge, craving for visible forms is exhausted," this refers to the eye-faculty existing in five stages (*bhūmi*).
At the moment when desire for the four dhyānas of the desire realm is exhausted,
the eye-faculty of the desire realm attains full knowledge (*parijñā*).
This continues until, at the moment when desire for the fourth dhyāna is exhausted, the eye-faculty of the fourth dhyāna attains full knowledge.
This is now explained according to the attainment of complete knowledge (*parijñā*) at its ultimate stage.
Therefore, the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā-kṣaya*) is termed the attainment of complete knowledge;
all other cases should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the ordinary person who attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of thirty-one latent dispositions (*anuśaya*):
at that time, the ordinary person has completely abandoned all thirty-one latent dispositions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to be abandoned through seeing and meditation.
Therefore, regarding "one for whom no fetters are exhausted":
this means that among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), at that time not even one has been ultimately exhausted.
Although all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are also termed "fetters," [the specific context here refers to the nine].
Within this context, the distinct categories of dharmas are explained;
that is to say, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are said to rely upon ninety-eight [categories],
and the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are said to rely upon nine.
Other examples should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the noble one’s attainment of full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the three latent dispositions (*anuśaya*):
it is because at that time, the noble one attains full knowledge solely of the three latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
"One for whom no fetters are exhausted" means that among the nine fetters, not even one has been exhausted.
"One for whom sensual desire is exhausted at the time of attaining full knowledge of the female and male faculties" refers to...
This means that because the female and male faculties exist only in the desire realm,
the exhaustion of craving for the desire realm is termed "attainment of full knowledge" (*parijñā*).
Regarding the thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), their attainment of full knowledge is as follows:
At that time, because the ordinary person has completely abandoned the thirty-six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) to be eliminated through seeing and cultivation within the desire realm,
the three fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted;
that is to say, among the nine fetters, the fetters of malice (pratigha), envy (īrṣyā), and avarice (mātsarya) have reached their ultimate exhaustion at that time.
Regarding the noble one who has attained full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
at that time, the noble one has attained full knowledge solely of the four underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm.
As for the exhaustion of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), it is as explained in the case of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

However, among the fetters of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), it is only at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)— which is abandoned through cultivation—
that the craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*) is exhausted.
This means that when the craving for the desire realm is exhausted while the life-faculty remains in the nine stages, [the craving for the formless realm is exhausted].
When the craving for the desire realm is exhausted, the life-faculty of the desire realm is fully known;
this continues until, when the craving for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is exhausted,
the life-faculty of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is fully known.
This is now explained according to the attainment of final thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
Therefore, the exhaustion of craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya-tṛṣṇā*) is called the attainment of thorough knowledge.
Regarding the attainment of thorough knowledge of the three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
At that time, because the three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm have been completely severed,
the "three fetters" (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted;
that is to say, among the nine fetters, the three fetters of craving, pride, and ignorance have been exhausted.
Regarding the time when the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) attains full knowledge (*parijñā*):
at the moment when craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm is exhausted and the faculty of pleasure thus attains full knowledge,
one does not yet attain the ultimate exhaustion of even a single underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies.
Therefore, this statement was made;
other examples should be understood accordingly.
However, there are seventeen stages of full knowledge (*parijñā*).
This refers to the time of the four patiences and knowledges regarding the dharmas, and the four subsequent patiences and knowledges; at these times,
one attains only the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of those dharmas to be abandoned by seeing,
from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness.
At the time when craving for the eighth stage is exhausted, one simultaneously attains the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of all phenomena abandoned through both seeing and cultivation.
At the time when craving for the single stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is exhausted,
one attains only the thorough knowledge of phenomena abandoned through cultivation.
All dharmas within these seventeen stages are termed "thoroughly known" (*parijñāta*).
I shall explain them according to their respective correspondences; fearing that the text would become overly prolix, I do not set them forth individually here.
This includes the faculty of the eye, up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
When each [defilement] is abandoned and realized,
among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
how many underlying tendencies are abandoned and realized?
Regarding the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are exhausted?
Why was this treatise composed? It is answered:
in order to refute the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.
That is to say, some maintain that when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests,
one simultaneously abandons all afflictions of the three realms to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
Prior to this, those [practitioners] were only able to suppress the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) but had not yet severed the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
They are like śramaṇas who sever [defilements] all at once;
it is said that they attain the fruit of arhatship through sudden awakening.
Just as one suddenly abandons drowsiness upon waking from a dream,
this [text] refutes that view and clarifies the abandonment of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*);
there are eighty-nine distinct categories of these states.
Because cessation is realized within all these stages.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that only the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) abandons the acquisition of the latent dispositions (anuśaya).
Only the path of liberation can realize that cessation.
As the śramaṇas of the West say:
"The uninterrupted path does not sever the afflictions."
One does not realize that cessation through the path of liberation; rather,
this is to refute such a view and demonstrate that it is the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) that is able to sever the afflictions,
thereby creating an interval between the acquisition of the afflictions so that they do not continue.
Furthermore, because they can realize cessation and induce the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) so that it correctly arises,
all paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are termed "realizing cessation," as they manifest simultaneously with the acquisition of dissociation.
Furthermore, this treatise is composed to demonstrate the principle of realizing cessation so that the wise may understand it.
There are, in brief, two kinds of realization regarding phenomena:
first, realization through knowledge (*jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*).
Second is the realization of attainment.
Regarding the realization through wisdom,
this refers to the knowledge of all phenomena.
"Capable of realizing and attaining realization" means that among all wholesome dharmas,
