those that are resultant (vipāka) or acquired through effort (prāpti) are capable of being realized and attained.
In this context, it is spoken of solely in terms of attainment (*prāpti*) and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).
Within that, it is spoken of solely in terms of the realization of cessation (*nirodha-sākṣātkriyā*).
"Cessation" refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The arising of the attainment of cessation within the various stages is termed "the realization of cessation.
This realization of cessation has eighty-nine varieties according to the distinctions of the stages;
that is to say, at the times of the four dharmakṣāntis, the four dharmajñānas, the four anvayakṣāntis, and the four anvayajñānas.

Furthermore, at the time of each of the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for each of the [lower] nine stages, and at the time of the four patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding the phenomena and their subsequent categories (*dharma-anvaya-kṣānti-jñāna*), one realizes only the cessation of the phenomena abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
This also applies during the first eight paths of uninterrupted transition and paths of liberation prior to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Only the cessation of those dharmas abandoned through cultivation is realized;
for the remaining seventy-three [dharmas], the cessation of those abandoned through both seeing and cultivation is realized throughout all stages.
Furthermore, there are five stages in total for the realization of cessation.
That is to say, at the time when the path that serves as the specific antidote for each respective category arises;
at the time of realizing the four fruits of śrāmaṇya;
and at the time of refining the faculties (indriya).

It should be stated that there are six [stages], yet because one necessarily attains the fruit at the time of refining the faculties (indriya), and because these are subsumed within the four fruits, five stages are taught.
Within these five positions, the afflictions (kleśa) abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the three realms [are eliminated].
At the time of realizing cessation, there are those who possess [the factors] and those who do not.
Alternatively, some afflictions exist for only a single moment;
namely, the ninth category of those to be abandoned by cultivation in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
At the very moment one realizes the fruit of arhatship,
there may be certain afflictions that exist only at two specific times:
namely, the first eight categories of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
And for the nine grades of each of the seven lower stages to be abandoned through cultivation,
[abandonment occurs] at the time when their respective counteractive paths arise,
as well as at the time of realizing the fruit of arhatship.
The ninth category of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm also occurs at two times,
namely, when attaining the latter two fruits.
Alternatively, there are afflictions that occur at only three times.
This refers to the time when the seventh and eighth categories of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm are being countered by their respective antidotes,
as well as the time of realizing the latter two fruits of śrāmaṇya;
the sixth category of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm likewise involves three such times.
That is to say, at the time of realizing the latter three fruits of śrāmaṇya,
there are certain afflictions that exist for only four periods;
namely, those abandoned by the path of vision (darśana-mārga) within the realms of form and formlessness.
At the very moment one realizes the four fruits of śrāmaṇya,
the first five categories of afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation are also realized at four moments;
that is, at the time when the respective antidote for each category arises.
Furthermore, when one realizes the latter three fruits of śrāmaṇya,
there are certain afflictions that possess five periods;
namely, those abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation within the three realms.
And when the [afflictions] of the desire realm to be abandoned by the path of seeing are respectively countered by their own specific antidotes,
as well as at the time of realizing the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
This is explained with reference to the realization of cessation by noble beings (*ārya*).

If, however, one considers ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the realization of cessation regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through seeing and meditation across the eight stages occurs only at the time when the specific antidote (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) for each respective category arises.
When realizing the cessation of other contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, one should understand this according to the preceding [explanation of] afflictions.
The realization of cessation through the various stages, as it proceeds through the forty-two sections beginning with the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), is explained as set forth in the treatise.
Question: What is the difference between the preceding door of full comprehension (*parijñā*) and this present door of the realization of cessation (*nirodha-sākṣātkriyā*)?
Answer: The preceding door of full comprehension reveals the distinction of abandonment attained when the eye-faculty and so forth reach ultimate exhaustion.
The gateway of realizing cessation reveals that when the eye-faculty and so forth reach their ultimate exhaustion,
as well as the distinctions in the realization of cessation in subsequent stages;
that is to say, in those subsequent stages, one repeatedly realizes the cessation of the eye-faculty and so forth through the attainment of a single-flavored realization (*ekarasa-prāpti*).
The masters of the West explain it thus:
the preceding section on "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) reveals the attainment of the severance of afflictions through the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*);
the section on "extinction and realization" (*nirodha-sākṣātkriyā*) reveals the attainment of dissociation from bondage through the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The masters of this country explain it as follows:
the preceding "gate of thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) reveals only the attainment of the abandonment of afflictions through the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*);

the "gate of cessation and realization" (*nirodha-sākṣātkriyā*) reveals both the attainment of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) realized through the path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Furthermore, the preceding "gate of thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) reveals only the attainment of the thorough knowledge of abandonment at the initial stage;
the "gate of the realization of cessation" (*nirodha-sākṣātkriyā*) universally reveals the realization of cessation both at the initial and subsequent stages.
This is the distinction between the two gates of thorough knowledge and the realization of cessation.
Within these ten gates, there are five distinct stages throughout the forty-two chapters previously explained.
That is to say, the forty-two chapters previously explained comprise three general categories.
This refers to the twenty-two faculties,
up to those factors to be abandoned by vision, by cultivation,
and those that are not to be abandoned; these are termed the "categories of objects."
The four noble truths up to the threefold triple samādhis are categorized as the class of virtues.
The three fetters up to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies are categorized as the class of faults.
Within the class of objects, there are the twenty-two faculties.
Because they are numerous at the beginning, they are established as a separate category;
because they are numerous at the end, the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) among the categories of faults are established as a separate category.
Since the remaining three categories of phenomena each constitute a single position, there are five positions in total.
Among these five positions, those that are similar are each briefly categorized by their commonalities,
while those that are dissimilar are each analyzed in detail.
The wise should thoroughly understand this.
Herein, the Venerable One briefly summarizes the preceding forty-two chapters by means of ten categories.
Within this, there are further many varieties, namely:
from the eye faculty up to the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm;
as well as the consciousness that takes these as its object and the consciousness that takes that object-consciousness as its object.

Among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many underlying tendencies increase (*anuśerate*) in each? Regarding the consciousness that takes as its object the path of abandonment for the eye-faculty, up to the ignorance-underlying-tendency to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm: [The answer: In the case of the eye-faculty, there are four underlying tendencies that increase: the underlying tendency of attachment to sensual desire, the underlying tendency of aversion, the underlying tendency of pride, and the underlying tendency of ignorance. These increase in relation to the consciousness associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

In the same manner, for each of the faculties from the ear-faculty up to the mind-faculty, and for the objects from visible forms up to mental phenomena, one should understand the number of underlying tendencies that increase according to their respective categories. Regarding the ignorance-underlying-tendency to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm, in the consciousness that takes it as its object during the path of abandonment, there are seven underlying tendencies that increase: the underlying tendencies of attachment to sensual desire, attachment to existence, aversion, pride, views, doubt, and ignorance. This is because such a consciousness is associated with the underlying tendencies of attachment to existence, pride, and ignorance, and is also associated with the underlying tendencies of views and doubt, which are to be abandoned through cultivation. Thus, these seven increase in relation to that consciousness.
Furthermore, regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase in each instance?
From the eye faculty up to the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—
[this refers to] the underlying tendencies that increase in relation to the consciousness that takes [them] as its object and the consciousness that takes [those objects] as its object-conditions.
How many are bound by the object-condition (ālambana-bandhana) but not by the association-condition (samprayoga-bandhana)?
How many are bound by the association-condition but not by the object-condition?
How many are bound both by the object-condition and by the association-condition?
How many are neither bound by the object (*ālambana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga*)?
They are the cessation of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
as well as the latent tendencies augmented by the consciousness that takes them as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
How many are bound by the object of perception (ālambana-bandhana) but not by association (saṃprayoga-bandhana)?
How many are bound by association but not by the object of perception?
How many are bound both by the object of perception and by association?
How many are neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*)?
They are the path of abandonment for the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm, from the eye-faculty up to that point,
as well as the latent tendencies augmented in the consciousness that takes those [factors] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
How many are bound by the object of perception (ālambana-bandhana) but not bound by association (samprayoga-bandhana)?
How many are bound by association but not bound by the object of perception?
How many are bound both by the object of perception and by association?
Some are neither bound by the object-of-perception (ālambana-bandhana) nor by association (saṃprayoga-bandhana).
These include the eye-faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
as well as the consciousness that takes these as its objects and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
Within the fifteen categories of mind belonging to the three realms,
how many minds arise immediately after each one?
This applies from the eye-faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by consciousness as a condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and by consciousness as an object-condition (*ālambanālambana-pratyaya*),
how many minds arise in immediate succession (*samanantara*) for each?

[This continues] from the eye faculty up until the cessation of the latent disposition of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
How many minds arise in immediate succession from each of the consciousnesses that take [the eye] as their object and the consciousnesses that take those objects as their objects?
This applies from the eye-faculty up to the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.

Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by consciousness conditioned by objects (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and consciousness conditioned by the objects of objects (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*),
how many minds arise in immediate succession (*samanantara*) for each?

This applies from the eye faculty up to the path of abandonment of the latent disposition of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes [that] condition as its condition:
how many minds arise in immediate succession from each?
This applies from the eye-faculty up to the path of abandoning the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) augmented by consciousness as an object (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and consciousness as an object of an object (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*),
how many minds arise immediately one after another (*samanantara*) for each?

This applies from the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) up to the latent disposition of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
The consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes [that condition] as its object-condition should be said to be with vitarka and vicāra,
or without vitarka and with vicāra only.
Are they without vitarka and without vicāra?
From the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
as well as the latent tendencies increased by the consciousness that takes them as objects and the consciousness that takes that object-consciousness as its object.
Should it be said that they possess both vitarka and vicāra,
or that they are without vitarka and possess only vicāra,
or that they are without both vitarka and vicāra?
Regarding the cessation of the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
as well as the consciousness that takes this as its object and the consciousness that takes that object as its object,
it should be said that these are accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
Is it without vitarka and with only vicāra,
or without both vitarka and vicāra?
It is the cessation of the eye faculty, up to and including the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in relation to consciousness as object and consciousness as object-of-object should be said to be "with vitarka and vicāra" or "without vitarka and with vicāra only."
Is it without vitarka and without vicāra?
It is the path of abandonment for the eye faculty, up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm;
it consists of the consciousness that takes [these] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
Should it be said that they possess vitarka and vicāra,
or that they are without vitarka and possess only vicāra,
or that they are without both vitarka and vicāra?
Regarding the path that abandons the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—

the proclivities increased by the consciousness that takes this as its object, as well as the consciousness that takes that object as its own object, should be said to be "with vitarka and with vicāra."
Are they without vitarka and with vicāra only,
or without both vitarka and vicāra?
[They range] from the eye-faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.

Should it be said that the consciousness conditioned by [the object] and the consciousness conditioned by the object-conditioned are associated with the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, grief, or equanimity?
[This applies] from the eye-faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase through the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the object-object-condition (ālambanālambana-pratyaya),
should they be said to be associated with the faculties of pleasure up to equanimity?

[This concerns] the cessation of the latent disposition of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm, from the eye-faculty up to [the cessation of] that very same [disposition].

Should it be said that the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and the object-condition-of-object-condition consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*) are associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) up to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
[This applies] from the eye-faculty up to the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase through the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the object-object-condition (ālambanālambana-pratyaya),
should they be said to be associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) up to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?

[This concerns] the path of abandonment for the latent disposition of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), ranging from the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) up to that point.

Should it be said that the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and the object-of-object-condition consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*) are associated with the faculties ranging from pleasure (*sukha*) to equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?

[This applies to] the path of abandoning the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), ranging from the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) up to that point.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase through the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the object-of-object-condition (ālambanālambana-pratyaya),
should they be said to be associated with the faculty of pleasure up to the faculty of equanimity?
[This applies to] the eye-faculty up to the latent disposition of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm.
Regarding the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*):
who possesses which, and who does not possess which?
[This applies to] the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by objects of consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and objects-of-objects-of-consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*):
who possesses them and who does not?
[This extends] from the eye faculty up to the cessation of the latent disposition of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and the object-of-object-condition consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*),
who accomplishes which and who does not accomplish which?
[This concerns] the cessation of the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the object-object-condition (*ālambanālambana-pratyaya*):

who possesses them and who does not possess them? This concerns the path of abandonment for the latent disposition of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), extending from the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) up to that point.
Regarding the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*),
who accomplishes which and who does not accomplish which?
[This concerns] the path of abandonment for the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) augmented by the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*):
who possesses which, and who does not possess which?

[This includes] from the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) up to the latent disposition of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
At the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes the condition of that object as its condition,
among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known?
Among the nine fetters (saṃyojana), how many are exhausted?
[This includes] from the eye faculty up to the underlying tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.

When the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) associated with the object-conditioned consciousness (ālambana-vijñāna) and the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness (ālambanālambana-vijñāna) are fully understood (parijñā),
how many underlying tendencies are fully understood,
and how many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?
When one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the cessation of the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
as well as the consciousness that takes these as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known?
How many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?
[This extends] from the eye faculty up to the extinction of the underlying tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
When the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that increase through the object-conditioned consciousness and the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness are fully understood (parijñā),
how many underlying tendencies are fully understood?
When the path that abandons the fetters—
ranging from the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—

is attained, and when full comprehension (parijñā) of both the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes that [conditioned consciousness] as its condition is achieved.
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known?
How many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?
[This concerns] the path of abandonment for the eye faculty up to the ignorance underlying tendency (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
When the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that increase through the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the object-of-object-condition (ālambanālambana-pratyaya) are fully understood (parijñā),
how many underlying tendencies are fully understood?
How many fetters are exhausted?
From the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm:
the consciousness that takes [them] as its object, and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
When realizing cessation,
among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya),
how many underlying tendencies are realized as ceased?
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are exhausted?
From the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—
the latent tendencies increased by the consciousness that takes [the aggregates] as its object, as well as the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
When cessation is realized,
how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are realized as ceased,
and how many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?
When one realizes the cessation of the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
as well as the consciousness that takes these as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object.
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are realized as extinguished?
How many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?
From the eye faculty up to the extinction of the underlying tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.

When one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase through the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*),
how many latent dispositions are realized as ceased?
Regarding the exhaustion of several fetters:
it is the path that abandons the eye faculty, up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm;
this includes both the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes that [conditioned] consciousness as its condition.
When one realizes the cessation [of suffering],
how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are realized as ceased,
and how many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?
When one realizes the cessation [of the outflows] through the path that abandons the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm—
along with the consciousnesses that take these as objects and the latent tendencies increased by the consciousnesses that take those objects as their objects.
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are realized as extinguished?
How many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?
From the eye faculty up to the underlying tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm.
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), by how many fetters are they bound?
Among the three bonds (*bandhana*), by how many bonds are they bound?
Among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), by how many underlying tendencies do they increase (*anuśerate*)?
Among the six stains (*mala*), by how many stains is it defiled?
Among the ten fetters (*paryavasthāna*), by how many fetters is it bound?
[This applies to] the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
Regarding the consciousness that takes [an object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes the object-condition as its condition:
by how many fetters (saṃyojana) are they bound,
and so on, up to by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) are they enveloped?
Regarding the cessation of the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm:
by how many fetters (saṃyojana) is the consciousness that takes this as its object, as well as the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object, bound?
And by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is it enveloped?
Regarding the path that abandons the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm:
how many fetters (saṃyojana) bind the consciousness that takes [these] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object?
Up to: how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) do they accomplish and become bound by?
Regarding the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm:
by how many fetters is one bound,
and so on, up to by how many envelopments is one possessed?
Regarding the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm:
how many fetters (saṃyojana) bind the consciousness that takes these as its object, as well as the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object?
Up to how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) does one possess when the eye faculty,
up to the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned by cultivation in the formless realm, is extinguished?
By how many fetters (saṃyojana) is one bound?
Up to how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) must be present for the cessation of the eye faculty,
up to the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
as well as the consciousness that takes these as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object?
By how many fetters (saṃyojana) is one bound,
up to being possessed by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna)? Furthermore,
regarding the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm, [how many fetters, etc., apply]?
By how many fetters (saṃyojana) is one bound,
and so forth, up to by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is one possessed?
[This concerns] the path that abandons the latent tendencies of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm, beginning with the eye-faculty.
Regarding the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes the condition of that condition as its object:
by how many fetters (saṃyojana) is it bound,
and so forth, up to by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is it not accomplished?
Regarding the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm:
by how many fetters is one bound,
and up to by how many envelopments is one not endowed with?
Regarding the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm:
as for the consciousness that takes these as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object,
by how many fetters are they bound?
Up to the point where one is not yet accomplished due to being bound by certain envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
and regarding the cessation of the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) bind such a person?
Up to the point where one is not yet accomplished due to being bound by certain fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
there is the cessation of the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This refers to the consciousness that takes [the aggregates] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
By how many fetters (saṃyojana) is one bound,
and so forth, up to by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is one not endowed with them?
This concerns the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), starting from the eye faculty.
By how many fetters (saṃyojana) is one bound,
and so forth, up to by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is one not endowed with being enveloped?
This concerns the path of abandonment for the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm, ranging from the eye-faculty up to that point.
Regarding the consciousness that takes [an object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes that [conditioned object] as its condition:
by how many fetters (saṃyojana) is it bound,
and so on, up to by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is it enveloped?
There are immeasurable gateways of this kind;
together with the forty-two chapters previously explained,
those who possess wisdom should investigate and determine them accordingly.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume Ninety;
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Ninety-one.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, who received the Imperial Decree. Section Twenty of the Fourth Sub-section on the Ten Gates within the Second Aggregate of Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha): From the Eye Faculty up to the Formless Realm.
Regarding the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation,
there are the consciousnesses that take [the aggregates] as their object and the consciousnesses that take those objects as their object;
among the ninety-eight latent tendencies, [these are as follows].
Regarding how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in each case:
the answer is that for the consciousness whose object is the cessation of the eye-faculty,
there are two categories [of defilements] belonging to the desire realm and the form realm.
And the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [therein].
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna), it has conditioned phenomena of the desire and form realms as its objects.

The two categories [of defilements] of the formless realm and the universal latent dispositions increase [in relation to] the consciousnesses that take the cessation of the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, pleasure, and joy as their object.
The same applies to the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*).
Regarding the cessation of the female faculty (*strī-indriya*), the consciousness conditioned by it belongs to two categories within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
And the universal [defilements],
the universal [defilements] of the form realm,
and the proclivities to be abandoned by cultivation increase [therein].
The object-condition consciousness consists of the conditioned objects of the desire realm and the three categories of the form realm.
The universal proclivities of the formless realm and those proclivities to be abandoned by cultivation increase [in relation to it].
It is the consciousness that conditions the cessation of the male faculty, the faculty of suffering, and the faculty of mental grief.
The same applies to the object-condition consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*).
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has as its condition the consciousnesses belonging to two categories within the three realms (*tridhātu*).
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase in accordance with them.
Regarding the object-condition consciousness (ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna), the latent dispositions that take conditioned phenomena of the three realms as their objects increase in accordance with it.

The mental faculty (*manas*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) take as their objects both consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the object of that consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*).
This same principle applies to the remaining chapters; it should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the path that abandons the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—
both for the consciousness that takes this as its object and for the consciousness that takes the object of that consciousness as its object—
how many latent tendencies increase in each case?
Answer: In the path of abandoning the eye faculty,

the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms and four categories increase with respect to both the consciousness that takes [the eye faculty] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
The paths of abandonment for the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, equanimity, and the five [spiritual] faculties (*śraddhā*, etc.
are likewise [both] consciousnesses that take [the path] as their object and consciousnesses that take the object of that consciousness as their object.
The path of abandonment for the female faculty is a consciousness that takes [the path] as its object.
The four categories of the desire realm and the three categories of the form realm latent dispositions increase [in association].
The objects of the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for these consciousnesses are the four categories of both the desire and form realms.
In the formless realm, the two categories [of defilements] and the pervasive latent dispositions increase;
this is the path for severing the male faculty and the faculties of suffering and mental grief.
The same applies to the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes the object of that condition as its condition.
Regarding the path of abandoning the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
the consciousnesses that take it as their condition consist of the four categories belonging to the desire realm and the form realm.
The two categories [of afflictions] of the formless realm and the pervasive latent dispositions increase in association with the consciousness that takes them as its object.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the four categories within the three realms increase in accordance with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) during the path of abandonment.
This applies equally to the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes that [conditioned] consciousness as its condition.
One should understand that the principles for the remaining chapters are to be inferred accordingly.
From the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—
regarding the consciousness that takes these as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object—
how many of these augmented latent tendencies are bound by way of the object (ālambana-bandhana) but not by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana)?
How many are bound by association but not by object?
How many are bound both by object and by association?
How many are neither bound by object nor by association?

Answer: Regarding the latent tendencies (anuśaya) increased by consciousness conditioned by the eye-faculty, there is bondage through the object (ālambana-bandhana) but not bondage through association (saṃprayoga-bandhana).
This refers to those non-universal [tendencies] of the desire and form realms that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin.
The universal proclivities of the formless realm and those proclivities abandoned through cultivation are fetters associated with conditioned phenomena,
but not fetters by way of being objects of perception.
That is to say, regarding the eye faculty as an object, the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) belonging to the desire realm, the form realm,
or other realms and stages constitute both an objective fetter (ālambana-bandhana) and a concomitant fetter (samprayoga-bandhana).
This refers to the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire and form realms,
as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation,
which increase in relation to the consciousness that takes the eye faculty as its object.
There is nothing that is neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If it were not an underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) increased therein,
yet were neither bound by the object nor bound by association with respect to that [object], [it would be impossible].
This refers to the two categories [of defilements] within the three realms,
as well as the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the formless realm;
these are the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the eye faculty as its object.
There are those bound by the object-condition (ālambana-bandhana) of conditioned phenomena, but not by the association-condition (saṃprayoga-bandhana).

These are: the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) objects abandoned by the path of seeing (darśanamārga) within the three realms, as well as those abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin (duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
The non-universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) are bound to conditioned phenomena by association, not by way of being their objects;
that is to say, those which are abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) in the three realms and have the outflow-free (anāsrava) as their object.
Furthermore, regarding the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take other realms and stages within the desire and form realms as their objects,
they are bound both by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) and by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
That is to say, these refer to the three categories [of afflictions] within the desire and form realms.
The pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm,
as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation,
are the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the eye faculty as its object-of-object.
There is nothing that is neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If it is not an underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) increased therein,
yet is bound to it by way of the object, [that is impossible].
Nor are they bound by association.

This refers to all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the three realms, as well as the consciousnesses that take the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties as their objects,
and likewise the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes those objects as its own object.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by consciousness conditioned by the female faculty:
they are bound to their objects (ālambana-bandhana) but not bound through association (saṃprayoga-bandhana).
This refers to those non-universal [dispositions] abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin in the desire realm.
Among the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
there are none that constitute a binding by association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) with conditioned phenomena but do not constitute a binding by object (*ālambana-bandhana*).
Conditioned objects are bound both by the bondage of the object and by the bondage of association;
namely, the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by consciousness conditioned by the female faculty (strīndriya):
there are none that are neither bound by the object (ālambana-bandhana) nor bound by association (samprayoga-bandhana).
If they are not the latent dispositions increased by this [faculty], [they are likewise absent].
Regarding that which is neither bound by the object of focus nor bound by association,
this refers to the two categories [of afflictions] within the desire and form realms.
The non-universal proclivities abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the form realm,
as well as all proclivities in the formless realm,
and the proclivities increased by the consciousness that takes the female faculty as its object-condition.
There are those that are bound by their objects (ālambana-bandhana) but not bound by association (saṃprayoga-bandhana);
namely, the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) factors abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) in the desire realm,
and the non-universal (avyāpaka) factors abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the form realm.
The universal proclivities of the formless realm and those proclivities abandoned through cultivation are bonds associated with conditioned phenomena,
but not bonds by way of being objects of perception.
This refers to the untainted objects (anāsrava-ālambana) abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) in the desire realm,
as well as the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms or stages as their objects within the desire and form realms;
these are bound both by way of the object (ālambana-bandhana) and by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana).
This refers to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three categories of the desire realm, the universal [dispositions] of the form realm,
and those to be abandoned through cultivation; specifically,
it refers to the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the female faculty as its object-condition.
There is nothing that is neither bound by the object (*ālambana*) nor bound by association (*saṃprayoga*).
If it were not an underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) increased therein,
it could not be bound by the object therein.
Nor are they bound by association;
that is to say, those abandoned through the vision of cessation in the desire realm,
and all [factors] belonging to the two categories in the form and formless realms.
Furthermore, the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin within the formless realm,

as well as the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the male faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) as its object, and by the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object, are likewise [to be understood].

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in dependence on the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and consciousness (vijñāna) are bound to conditioned objects (saṃskṛtālambana) but not bound through association (saṃprayoga).
These are the non-universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin within the three realms.
There are those that are bound by association with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) but not bound by their objects (*ālambana*).
These refer to the pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), other realms within the three realms, or other stages as their objects.
There are also those that are both bound by their objects and bound by association with conditioned phenomena.
This refers to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are universal throughout the three realms and those to be abandoned through cultivation;
specifically, the latent dispositions augmented by the consciousness conditioned by the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
These are not bound by way of being an object-condition (ālambana-bandhana).
Nor is it the case that there is no binding through association;
for if it were not an underlying tendency increased therein,
it would not be a binding by way of being an object (*ālambana-bandhana*) therein either.
Furthermore, it is not bound by association;
this refers to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms and three categories,
as well as the latent dispositions augmented by the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), the object-condition (ālambanapratyaya), and the consciousness that takes it as its object.
There are latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are bonds by way of their object (ālambana-bandhana) but not bonds by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana);
these are the outflowing (sāsrava) objects of the latent dispositions abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) within the three realms.
There are also those that are bonds by way of association but not bonds by way of their object.
This refers to the untainted objects (anāsrava-ālambana) abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) within the three realms,
as well as the universal latent tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms and stages as their objects.
These are bound both by way of the object (ālambana-bandhana) and by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana).
This refers to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms and the three categories.
Regarding the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the life-faculty as its object-condition,
there are none that are neither bound by the object-condition nor bound by association.
If it is not an underlying tendency (anuśaya) increased by this [object],
yet is neither bound to it by way of being its object (ālambana-bandhana) nor bound to it by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana), [then it does not exist there].
This refers to all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering] within the three realms,

as well as the underlying tendencies increased by the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*), its object-consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*), and the consciousness that takes that object-consciousness as its object.
There is nothing that is bound by the object-condition (ālambana-bandhana) of conditioned phenomena but not bound by association (saṃprayoga-bandhana).
There are, however, cases where there is binding by association but not by the object-condition;
namely, those [defilements] of the three realms abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object.
Furthermore, regarding the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take the mind-faculty (*manas*), the three realms, other realms, or various stages as their objects:
these are bound both by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) and by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
This refers to the latent dispositions that have the contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of the three realms as their objects.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the mental faculty (manas-indriya) with respect to its objects:
there are none that are neither bound by way of the object (ālambana-bandhana) nor bound by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana).
If they are not the latent dispositions increased by this [faculty], [then they are bound by both].
Regarding that which is neither bound by the object of focus (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*):
this refers to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of the three realms as their object.
The same applies to the latent tendencies increased by the equanimity faculty (upekṣendriya) with respect to consciousness as its object and consciousness as the object-of-object.
Regarding the latent tendencies increased by the pleasure faculty (sukhendriya) with respect to consciousness as its object,
they are bound by conditioned objects (saṃskṛtālambana).
It is not a bound [affliction] through association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*).
This refers to those with outflows (*sāsrava*) conditioned by the objects of vision (*darśana-heya*) in the realms of desire and formlessness;
and those non-universal [afflictions] in the realm of desire that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
The universal proclivities of the formless realm and those proclivities abandoned through cultivation are fetters associated with conditioned phenomena,
but not fetters by way of being objects of perception.
This refers to the untainted objects of the abandonments through the path of vision within the three realms,
as well as the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as their object across the desire and form realms and across different levels.
These are bound both by the object of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and by association (*saṃprayoga*).
This refers to the pervasive proclivities of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation,
as well as the proclivities with outflow directed toward the form realm that increase in association with the faculty of pleasure.
There is nothing that is neither bound by the object of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*),
unless it is an underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) increased by these two.
That which is neither bound by the bondage of the object of focus nor by the bondage of association refers to the desire realm and the formless realm.
All [defilements] of the form realm to be abandoned by the vision of cessation that take the unconditioned as their object,
and the non-universal underlying tendencies of the formless realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of origination.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as its object-condition:
they are bound to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) by way of the object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*), not by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
These refer to the non-universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
There are fetters associated with the conditioned that are not fetters by way of being objects of perception;
these refer to the untainted-objects (anāsrava-ālambana) universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) abandoned through the path of seeing within the three realms,
as well as the universal proclivities that take other realms or stages as their objects.
Conditioned objects are bound both by the bondage of the object and by the bondage of association;
that is to say, the outflow-tainted objects of the three categories of the desire realm abandoned through the path of vision,
and all outflow-tainted objects of the form realm.
The universal proclivities of the formless realm,
those to be abandoned through cultivation, and those to be abandoned through the path of vision,
which have outflowing objects as their conditions.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as its object-condition:
there are none that are neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
Furthermore, if they are not the latent dispositions increased by this [consciousness], [they do not exist].
Regarding those that are neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*):

these refer to all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) in the desire and formless realms to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as the latent tendencies in the form realm to be abandoned through the vision of cessation that take unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) as their object.

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in dependence on consciousness associated with the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) are bound to their objects (ālambanabandhana) by conditioned phenomena, but not bound through association (samprayogabandhana);
namely, the universal [dispositions] of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have outflows (sāsrava) as their object, which are to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) and those to be abandoned through the path of vision (darśana-mārga-heya),
constitute bonds associated with conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-saṃprayukta-bandha), but not bonds by way of being objects (ālambana-bandha).
This refers to the untainted objects (anāsrava-ālambana) abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) within the three realms,
as well as the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) and the objects of other realms within the desire and form realms as their conditions;
these constitute the bondage of conditioned objects (saṃskṛta-ālambana-bandhana).
There are also those bound by association (*saṃprayukta-bandhana*), namely:
all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) with outflows (*sāsrava*) that take [objects] of the desire and form realms as their objective support;
and the latent dispositions increased by consciousness that takes the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) as its objective support.
There is no such thing as being bound neither by the object of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*),
unless it is an underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) increased by these two.
Regarding that which is neither bound by the object-of-cognition (ālambana-bandhana) nor bound by association (samprayoga-bandhana):
this refers to the [afflictions] of the desire and form realms that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya) and have the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) as their object.

All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as well as the non-pervasive (*asarvatraga*) latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*),
are the latent dispositions that increase in the consciousness that takes the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) as its object-of-object (*ālambanālambana*).
There are those that are bonds by way of being an object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*) but not bonds by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*);
namely, the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
There are those that are bonds by way of association but not bonds by way of being an object-condition.
This refers to the untainted objects of the abandonments through the path of seeing within the three realms,
as well as the universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take other realms and stages as their objects;
these constitute both bondage by way of the object of focus and bondage by way of association with the conditioned.
This refers to all outflow-tainted (sāsrava) objects of the desire and form realms;
the universal (sarvatraga) [defilements] of the formless realm;
and the outflow-tainted objects of the latent tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) and those to be abandoned through the path of vision (darśana-mārga).
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in the consciousness conditioned by the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*),
there are none that are neither bound by way of the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If it is not an underlying tendency (anuśaya) that increases therein,
yet is neither bound to it by way of being an object (ālambana-bandhana) nor by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana), [then what is it?].
This refers to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the consciousness conditioned by the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), namely:
those in the desire and form realms abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) that take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their object,
as well as all such latent dispositions in the formless realm abandoned through the vision of cessation.
There are those that are bound by the object of perception (ālambana-bandhana) but not by association (saṃprayoga-bandhana);
namely, the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) of the form realm and the proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
There are no conditioned phenomena that are bound by association but not by object.
There are conditioned phenomena that are bound both by object and by association;
namely, all latent dispositions (anuśaya) in the desire realm that take contaminated objects as their focus.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by consciousness conditioned by the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*):
there are none that are neither bound by way of the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
Furthermore, if they are not the latent dispositions increased by this [consciousness], [they do not exist].
Regarding that which is neither bound by the object-condition nor bound by association:
this refers to all uncontaminated objects within the desire realm.
The two categories [of afflictions] in the form realm;
the non-universal [afflictions] abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin;
and all latent tendencies in the formless realm.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by consciousness that takes the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) as its object-condition:
they are bound to conditioned phenomena by way of the object-condition (*ālambanabandhana*), not by way of association (*samprayogabandhana*).
That is to say, the non-universal [dispositions] abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The universal proclivities of the formless realm and the proclivities abandoned through cultivation are fetters associated with conditioned phenomena by way of association, not by way of being objects of cognition.
This refers to the untainted objects of the defilements to be abandoned through the path of vision in the desire realm,
as well as the universal underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take other realms or levels as their objects within the desire and form realms;
these are bound both by the object of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*) and by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
This refers to all the outflow-tainted objects of the desire realm,
as well as the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in relation to consciousness conditioned by the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*),
there are none that are not bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) and are also not bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If it is not an underlying tendency (anuśaya) increased by this [object],
and is neither bound to it by way of being an object (ālambana-bandhana) nor by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana), [then it does not exist there].
This refers to the non-conditioned object (asaṃskṛtālambana) abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodhadarśana-prahātavya) in the desire realm;
the two categories [of afflictions] in the form and formless realms;
and the non-universal (asarvatraga) proclivities (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the formless realm.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) augmented by consciousness that take the five faculties, such as faith, as their objects,
are bound to conditioned phenomena by way of objective association (ālambana-bandhana), not by way of concomitant association (samprayoga-bandhana).
This refers to the non-universal [dispositions] abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin within the three realms.
Furthermore, regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) that are abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*),
those bound through association with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-saṃprayukta-bandhana*) are not bound by way of their objects (*ālambana-bandhana*).
This refers to those [dispositions] abandoned by the path of vision in the three realms that have the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as their object.
Furthermore, regarding the five faculties such as faith and so forth,
as well as the universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take other realms and stages as their objects within the three realms,
these constitute both an object-binding (ālambana-bandhana) and an associated-binding (saṃprayoga-bandhana) for conditioned phenomena.
This refers to the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms,
as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation,
and the latent dispositions augmented by the consciousness that takes the five faculties— faith and the rest— as its objects.
There is nothing that is neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*),
unless it is a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) increased by this [object].
Regarding those that are neither bound by the object nor bound by association:
these refer to all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the consciousness that takes the five faculties, such as faith, as its objects:

there are none that are bound to conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) by way of the object (ālambana-bandhana) but not by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana). However, there are those that are bound to conditioned phenomena by way of association but not by way of the object.
This refers to the untainted objects (anāsrava-ālambana) abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) within the three realms,
as well as the pervasive latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms and stages as their objects;
these constitute both the bondage of the object (ālambana-bandhana) and the bondage of association (samprayoga-bandhana).
This refers to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms and the three categories,
as well as those with outflow (sāsrava) that take objects of perception and are abandoned through the path of vision (darśanamārga),
and the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the five faculties— faith and the rest— as its objects.
There is nothing that is neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If it is not an underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) increased by this [object],
it is not bound by the object.

Furthermore, those that are not bound by association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) refer to all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms,
as well as the latent dispositions increased by the consciousnesses that take the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) as their objects.
They are bound by the object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*) of conditioned phenomena,
but not by the association-condition (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
That is to say, they are the universal [defilements] of the three realms that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, regarding the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) that take [the conditioned] as their object,
they constitute bonds through association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) but not bonds through being an object (*ālambana-bandhana*).
This refers to the proclivities to be abandoned by the path of vision in the three realms that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
There is nothing that is both bound by the object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*) and bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the consciousness that takes the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) as its object,
these are not bound by the object-condition.
Nor is it the case that there is no binding through association;
for if a latent disposition (anuśaya) does not increase with respect to something,
yet is not bound to it by way of being an object (ālambana), [it would follow that it is not bound at all].
Nor are they bound by association;
this refers to all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of cessation within the three realms,
as well as the non-universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase through the consciousness which takes the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) as its object-condition:
they are bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) but not by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
These refer to the non-universal latent dispositions (*asarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the three realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin.
There are bonds associated with the conditioned, but not bonds by way of being objects of perception;
these refer to the outflow-free objects of the universal proclivities abandoned by the path of vision within the three realms,
as well as the universal proclivities that take other realms and stages as their objects.
There are those that are bound by both the object-condition (*ālambana*) and by association (*saṃprayoga*).
These are the universal proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the three realms that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
as well as the contaminated object-conditions abandoned through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the consciousness that takes the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) as its object-condition:
there are none that are not bound by the object-condition (ālambana-bandhana), nor are there any that are not bound by association (samprayoga-bandhana).
If it is not an underlying tendency (anuśaya) increased by this [object],
yet is neither bound to it by way of being an object (ālambana-bandhana) nor by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana).
This refers to all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering] within the three realms.

By analogy with the meaning of the other chapters, one should understand that this extends from the eye-faculty up to the cessation of the latent disposition of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation within the formless realm.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase through the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the object-of-object-condition (ālambanālambana-pratyaya),
how many are bound by way of the object (ālambana-bandhana) and not bound by way of association (saṃprayoga-bandhana)?
How many are bound by association (saṃprayoga-bandhana) but not bound by object (ālambana-bandhana)?
How many are bound by object?
They are also bound by association.
How many are neither bound by the object of perception nor bound by association?

Answer: Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in dependence on the consciousness associated with the cessation of the eye-faculty, they are bound to conditioned objects (ālambana-bandhana) but not bound by association (saṃprayoga-bandhana).
That is to say, these are the universal [dispositions] of the desire and form realms.

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) and those abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-heya) which have conditioned objects (saṃskṛta-ālambana):
these are fetters by association (saṃprayoga-bandhana) but not fetters by object (ālambana-bandhana).

This refers to the latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation that have unconditioned objects (asaṃskṛta-ālambana) within the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu).
There is nothing that is bound by both the object and by association with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

There is nothing that is neither bound by the object nor bound by association with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increased by consciousness whose conditions are the cessation of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
If it is not an underlying tendency (anuśaya) increased by this [level], nor bound to this [level] by way of being an object (ālambana-bandhana),
nor bound by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana),
it refers to all those abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya) within the desire and form realms.
The non-universal proclivities abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin,
as well as all proclivities of the formless realm,
are the proclivities increased by the object-conditioned consciousness.
There are those that are bound by their objects (ālambana-bandhana) but not bound by association (saṃprayoga-bandhana);
namely, the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) factors abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) within the three realms,
as well as the non-universal (asarvatraga) factors abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the desire and form realms.

Furthermore, the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) constitute bonds associated with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-saṃprayukta-bandhana*), but not bonds by way of being objects (*ālambana-bandhana*).
This refers to the untainted objects of the abandonments through the path of vision within the three realms,
as well as the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take other realms or stages as their objects within the desire and form realms;
these are bound both by the object of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*) and by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
This refers to the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire and form realms,
those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and those to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*), which have conditioned phenomena as their objects;
as well as the latent dispositions augmented by the consciousness that takes the cessation of the eye faculty as its object-condition.
There is nothing that is neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If it is not an underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) increased therein,
yet it is not bound to it by way of the object.
Nor are they bound by association;
this refers to those [defilements] in the desire and form realms that are abandoned through the vision of cessation and have the unconditioned as their object,
as well as all those in the formless realm abandoned through the vision of cessation.
Furthermore, the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin,
as well as the consciousness that takes the cessation of the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity of the ear, nose, tongue, and body as its object,
and the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object, are likewise [abandoned].
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by consciousness that has the cessation of the female faculty as its object:
they are bound to their objects (*ālambana-bandhana*) but not bound through association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
That is to say, they are the universal [dispositions] of the desire and form realms.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) that take conditioned phenomena as their object are fetters by way of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*),
but not fetters by way of object (*ālambana-bandhana*).

That is to say, among the latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation that take unconditioned phenomena as their object, there are none that are both fetters by way of object and fetters by way of association with conditioned phenomena.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by consciousness conditioned by the cessation of the female faculty (*strīndriya*):
there are none that are neither bound by way of the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If they are not the latent dispositions increased by this [consciousness], [they do not exist].
Regarding those that are neither bound by the object of perception nor bound by association,
these refer to all [defilements] of the desire realm to be abandoned by the path of seeing.
The non-universal [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin;
the non-universal [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin belonging to the two categories of the form realm;
and all latent tendencies of the formless realm.

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase through the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) of consciousness are bound to conditioned objects (saṃskṛta-ālambana), not bound by association (saṃprayoga).
This refers to those [dispositions] of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) which have outflowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana).
The non-universal proclivities (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the desire and form realms,
as well as the universal proclivities and those abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
constitute bonds associated with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-saṃprayukta-bandhana*), but not bonds by way of being objects of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*).
This refers to the untainted objects of the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the desire realm,
