as well as the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take other realms or stages as their objects within the desire and form realms;
these are bound both by way of the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) and by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).

This refers to the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-eliminated (*bhāvanā-heya*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire and form realms, as well as the conditioned-object (*saṃskṛtālambana*) latent dispositions eliminated by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-heya*) in the desire realm;
and the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the cessation of the female faculty (*strīndriya-nirodha*) as its object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
There is nothing that is neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If it is not an underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) increased by this [object],
yet is not bound by the object with respect to this [object].
Nor is it bound by association (*saṃprayoga*),
namely: the [afflictions] of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) that take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their object,
and those of the two classes [of afflictions] in the form and formless realms.
The same applies to the non-universal underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),

as well as to the underlying tendencies increased by the consciousness that takes the male faculty, the faculty of pain, and the faculty of mental grief as its object, and by the consciousness that takes those objects as its object.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase based on consciousness as the condition for the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*):
they are bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) but not by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
That is to say, these are the universal [dispositions] of the three realms (*tridhātu-sarvatraga*) that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the cessation of suffering that take conditioned phenomena as their object:
these are fetters by way of association, not fetters by way of being an object.
This refers to the latent dispositions associated with the cessation of suffering in the three realms that take unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) as their object.
There is nothing that is bound both by the object of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*) and by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).

There is nothing that is not bound by the object of perception and not bound by association, yet where the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase in dependence upon the consciousness at the moment of the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya-nirodha*).
If it is not an underlying tendency (anuśaya) that increases therein,
and it is neither bound to it as an object (ālambana-bandhana) nor bound to it through association (samprayoga-bandhana), [then what is it?]
This refers to all [defilements] abandoned through the path of seeing in the three realms,
as well as the non-universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin,
and the latent dispositions augmented by the object-conditioning consciousness.
There are those that are bound by their objects (*ālambana-bandhana*) but not bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*);

namely, the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) objects abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) within the three realms, as well as the non-universal (*avyāpaka*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned by the paths of seeing suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).
There are bonds associated with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) that are not bonds by way of being objects (*ālambana-bandhana*);
namely, those universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the three realms that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object,
as well as those universal [dispositions] taking other realms or stages as their objects.
There are those that are both bound by their objects (*ālambana*) and bound by association (*samprayoga*).

These are the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-abandoned (*bhāvanā-heya*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) pertaining to the three realms that take conditioned phenomena as their objects, as well as those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) which take conditioned phenomena as their objects;
and the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya-nirodha*) as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
There is nothing that is neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If it were not an underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) increased by this [object],
yet were bound to it by way of the object, [it would be impossible].

Furthermore, those that are not bound by association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) refer to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their object and are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms.

This also applies to the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the mind-faculty (*manas*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) as its objects, as well as by the consciousness that takes that [consciousness] as its object.
The principles of the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this:
regarding the path that abandons the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation, from the eye-faculty up to those belonging to the formless realm,
[one should consider] the latent tendencies increased by the consciousness that takes them as its object and the consciousness that takes that object-consciousness as its object.
How many are bound by the object-condition (ālambana-bandhana),
but not by association (saṃprayoga-bandhana)?
How many are bound by association?
It is not bound by the object of cognition (*ālambana-bandhana*).
How many are bound by the object of cognition and also bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*)?
How many are neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*)? Answer:
Those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that increase in a consciousness which takes as its object the path that severs the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
There are those that are bound by the object of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*) but not bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*);
namely, the outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) within the three realms,
as well as the non-universal (*avyāpaka*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).
There are bonds associated with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) that are not bonds by way of being objects of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*).

These are: the untainted objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) within the three realms, as well as the pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) that take other levels of the desire and form realms as their objects.
Conditioned phenomena are bound both by the bondage of the object and by the bondage of association;
that is to say, the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the three realms,
as well as the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes as its object the path of abandonment for the faculty of the eye, which are to be abandoned through cultivation.
There is nothing that is neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If it were not an underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) increased by this [object],
yet were bound to it by way of the object, [it would be impossible].
Furthermore, those that are not bound by association refer to all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation within the three realms,
as well as the latent dispositions augmented by the object-conditioned consciousness.
There is nothing that is bound by the object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*) of conditioned phenomena but not bound by association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*).
There are, however, cases where there is binding by association but not by the object-condition;
namely, those [defilements] of the three realms abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.

Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take other realms and stages as their objects are bound both by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) and by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*); that is,
those belonging to the three categories within the three realms.
Furthermore, regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the outflows that are abandoned by the path of seeing and which take the outflows as their object:
among those latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object through the path of abandonment,
there are none that are neither bound by the object nor bound by association.
If it is not an underlying tendency (anuśaya) that increases with respect to this [object],
and it is neither bound by the bond of the object (ālambana-bandhana) nor by the bond of association (saṃprayoga-bandhana) with respect to this, [then it does not exist there].
This refers to all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the cessation of suffering within the three realms.

It is likewise for the latent dispositions increased by those [faculties] that take the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties as their objects, as well as the consciousnesses and the objects of those consciousnesses that serve as the path of abandonment.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the consciousness that takes the female faculty (*strī-indriya*), the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*), and objects as its conditions:
they are bound to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) by way of the object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*), not by way of the association-condition (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
This refers to those [dispositions] of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) which take contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) as their objects.

Furthermore, the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin within the desire and form realms constitute bonds associated with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-saṃprayukta-bandha*),
but not bonds by way of being objects (*ālambana-bandha*).
This refers to those [dispositions] in the desire realm abandoned through the vision of the path that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.

Furthermore, the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) that take other realms or levels as their objects within the desire and form realms are bound both by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) and by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
That is to say, the universal [proclivities] of the desire and form realms [are so bound].
Furthermore, regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
and those latent dispositions increased by consciousness that takes the faculty of femininity (*strī-indriya*) as its object during the path of abandonment—
there are none that are bound neither by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If it is not an underlying tendency (anuśaya) that increases in this [state],
yet is neither bound to it by way of being an object (ālambana-bandhana) nor bound to it by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana), [then it does not exist there].
This refers to all [defilements] in the desire and form realms to be abandoned by the vision of cessation,
all [defilements] in the form realm to be abandoned by the vision of the path,
and all underlying tendencies (anuśaya) in the formless realm.

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by consciousness that takes objects as its conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) are bound to conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) by way of the object-condition (ālambana-bandhana), not by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana).

This refers to those [dispositions] belonging to the realms of form and formlessness that are to be abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) and have outflowing objects (sāsrava-ālambana).

The pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and cultivation-eliminated (*bhāvanā-heya*) latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) constitute bonds through association with conditioned phenomena (*saṃprayukta-bandhana*), but not bonds through being an object (*ālambana-bandhana*).
This refers to those [tendencies] of the three realms that are eliminated by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.

Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take other realms and levels of the desire and form realms as their objects are bound both by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) and by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
That is to say, these belong to the three categories within the desire and form realms.
Furthermore, regarding the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the desire realm that take objects as their conditions:

there are none among those proclivities increased by the consciousness that takes the faculty of femininity (*strīndriya*) as its object of cognition which are neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If it is not an underlying tendency (anuśaya) that increases in this [state],
and is neither bound to it by way of the object (ālambana-bandhana) nor by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana), [then what is it?]
This refers to all [latent dispositions] abandoned through the vision of cessation within the three realms,
as well as the non-universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the formless realm.

The same applies to the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the male faculty, the faculty of pain, and the faculty of grief as its objects, as well as by the consciousness that takes those objects as its objects.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by consciousness conditioned by the path that severs the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) are bound to conditioned objects (saṃskṛtālambana),
not bound through association (saṃprayoga).
That is to say, they are the outflowing (sāsrava) factors abandoned by the path of seeing (darśanamārga) within the three realms that take [conditioned] objects as their condition.
Furthermore, regarding the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin:
these constitute bonds associated with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-saṃprayukta-bandha*), but not bonds by way of being objects (*ālambana-bandha*).
That is to say, they refer to those [dispositions] abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) within the three realms that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.

Furthermore, the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take other realms and stages as their objects are bound both by the object of focus (ālambana-bandhana) and by association (samprayoga-bandhana);
that is to say, those which are pervasive throughout the three realms.
Furthermore, regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
there are none that are increased by the consciousness which takes the path of severing the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as its object,
such that they would neither be bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If it is not an underlying tendency (anuśaya) that increases with respect to this [object],
and is neither bound to it by way of being an object (ālambana-bandhana) nor by way of association (samprayoga-bandhana), [then what is its connection?]

This refers to all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the cessation [of suffering] within the three realms, which increase by means of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the consciousness that takes them as its object.
Among these, there are none that are bound to conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-ālambana-bandha*) but not bound through association (*saṃprayoga-bandha*).
There are those that are bound by association with conditioned phenomena but not by being their objects;

these are the outflow-free (anāsrava) objects of the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) within the three realms, as well as those universal proclivities that take other realms or stages as their objects.
Furthermore, there are those that are both bound by being objects of conditioned phenomena and bound by association.
This refers to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the three realms and the three categories, as well as those with outflow that are objects of the path of seeing,
and those latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the path which severs the life-faculty as its object-condition.
There is nothing that is neither bound by the object of perception (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*),
unless it is a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) increased by these.
Regarding those that are neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*):
these refer to all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).

The same applies to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the consciousness that takes the path of abandonment as its object and the consciousness that takes that [path] as its object-condition, in relation to the faculty of equanimity and the five faculties beginning with faith.
Regarding the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the path of abandonment as its object in relation to the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya):
There are those that are bound by their objects (*ālambana-bandhana*) but not bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*);
namely, the outflowing factors (*sāsrava*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) within the three realms,
as well as the non-universal [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire and form realms.

The pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation are fetters associated with conditioned phenomena, but not fetters by way of being their objects.
This refers to the untainted objects (anāsrava-ālambana) abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) within the three realms,
as well as the pervasive latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) that take other realms or levels as their objects within the desire and form realms;
these are bound both to their conditioned objects (saṃskṛta-ālambana-bandha) and through association (saṃprayoga-bandha).
This refers to the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire and form realms,
as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
which increase in relation to the consciousness that takes the path of abandonment as its object while associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
There is nothing that is neither bound by the object of perception (ālambana-bandhana) nor bound by association (samprayoga-bandhana),
unless it is a latent tendency (anuśaya) increased by these [factors].
As for that which is neither bound by the object-condition nor bound by association,
it refers to all [defilements] of the three realms to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
Furthermore, regarding the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),

the latent dispositions increased by the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanapratyayavijñāna*) constitute a bondage to conditioned objects (*saṃskṛtālambanabandhana*), not a bondage by association (*saṃprayogabandhana*).
This refers to the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin within the formless realm;
these constitute bonds associated with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-saṃprayukta-bandhana*), but not bonds by way of being objects of cognition (*ālambana-bandhana*).
This refers to those [dispositions] belonging to the three realms that are abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
Furthermore, the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take other realms and stages as their objects are bound both by the object (ālambana-bandhana) and by association (samprayoga-bandhana);
these refer to the three categories [of defilements] belonging to the desire and form realms.
The universal proclivities of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation,
as well as the contaminated object-conditioned proclivities of the three realms to be abandoned by the path of seeing,
and the proclivities increased by the consciousness that takes the path of abandonment as its object-condition for the faculty of pleasure.
There is nothing that is neither bound by the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) nor bound by association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).
If it is not an underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) increased therein,
yet is bound to it by way of the object, [it does not exist].
Nor are they bound by association (*samprayoga*).
This refers to all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms.

The same applies to the latent dispositions increased by consciousness that takes the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) as its object or takes the object of that consciousness as its object, which are abandoned by the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*).
The principles of the other chapters should be understood accordingly.
This applies from the eye-faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
including both the consciousness that takes [an object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes that [conditioned] consciousness as its condition.
Regarding the fifteen classes of mind within the three realms, how many minds arise immediately following each one?
Answer: The eye-faculty, the consciousness that takes it as its object, and the consciousness that takes that [object-consciousness] as its object.
Each one arises in immediate succession as fifteen minds.

This applies equally to the ear and so forth, up to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), regarding both the consciousness that takes them as objects and the consciousness that takes those objects as its own objects.
One should understand that the principles explained in other chapters are to be applied accordingly.
From the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—
regarding the consciousness that takes these as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object—
how many minds arise in immediate succession from each one?

Answer: Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the cognition of the eye-faculty and the cognition of the object of that cognition, fifteen moments of mind arise one after another in immediate succession.

The same applies to the latent dispositions increased by the cognition of the ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, pleasure, joy, equanimity, and the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the consciousness conditioned by the female faculty arise as the equal-and-immediate condition for ten minds;
the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness conditioned by the object-conditioned consciousness arise as the equal-and-immediate condition for fifteen minds.

The same applies to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in relation to the male faculty, the faculty of suffering, the faculty of grief, the consciousness that takes them as objects, and the consciousness that takes those objects as its own objects.
One should understand that the principles governing the remaining chapters follow this same pattern.
This extends from the eye faculty up to the cessation of the latent disposition of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
Regarding the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*):
how many minds arise immediately and successively (*samanantara*) from each?
Answer: When the eye-faculty ceases, there arise the object-conditioned consciousness and the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness.
Each one arises in immediate succession as fifteen moments of mind.

This applies likewise to the cessation of the ear and so forth, up to the five faculties such as faith, as well as to consciousnesses that take them as objects and consciousnesses that take those objects as their objects.
One should understand that the principles for the other chapters are to be inferred accordingly.
From the cessation of the eye-faculty up to the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,

how many minds arise in immediate succession for each of the latent tendencies increased by the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes that [conditioned] consciousness as its condition?
Answer: With the eye faculty as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), ten minds arise in immediate succession (*samanantara*) that are increased by underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
With the consciousness that takes that [eye] as its object-condition as the object-condition, fifteen minds arise in immediate succession that are increased by underlying tendencies.
The same applies to the cessation of the five faculties from the ear up to faith,
as well as to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase based on the object-consciousness (ālambana-vijñāna) and the consciousness of the object-of-object (ālambanālambana-vijñāna).
One should understand that the principles explained in other chapters are to be applied accordingly.
Regarding the path that abandons the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—
how many minds arise as its immediate antecedent conditions (samanantara-pratyaya), both those taking it as their object and those taking the object of that object?

Answer: Regarding the path of abandonment of the eye faculty, there are fifteen moments of mind produced one after another as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the object-of-object-condition (*ālambanālambana-pratyaya*).
This is likewise true for the paths of abandonment of the ear faculty up to the five faculties beginning with faith.
The principles of the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this:
[it refers to] the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation, from the eye faculty up to the formless realm.

Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) augmented by consciousness conditioned by objects (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and consciousness conditioned by objects of objects (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*), how many minds arise immediately one after another (*samanantara*) for each?

Answer: For the faculty of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*) at the moment of the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*), there are the consciousness conditioned by objects and the consciousness conditioned by objects of objects, along with the latent dispositions augmented therein.
Each one arises in immediate succession as fifteen minds.
This applies equally to the paths of abandonment for the ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, joy, pleasure, equanimity, and the five faculties such as faith,
as well as to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes that [conditioned] object as its condition.

The ten minds that arise in immediate succession (*samanantara*) from the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the consciousness conditioned by the female faculty (*strīndriya*) and its object arise [from them].
The fifteen minds that arise in immediate succession from the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness conditioned by the object of that object arise [from them].

The same applies to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the consciousness that takes the male faculty, the faculty of suffering, the faculty of grief, the path, and its object as its objects.
This principle should be understood by analogy for the other chapters,
from the eye faculty up to the formless realm.
The latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation,
whether it takes consciousness as its object or takes the object of consciousness as its object,
should be said to be accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
Is it without vitarka and with vicāra only, or without both vitarka and vicāra? Answer:
It is the eye faculty, as well as the consciousness that takes it as its object and the consciousness that takes that [consciousness] as its object.
Each possesses three [types of consciousness].

This applies likewise to the ear and so forth, up to the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), regarding both the consciousness that takes them as objects and the consciousness that takes those objects as its own objects.
The principles for other chapters should be understood by analogy with this.
From the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
[this includes] the latent tendencies increased by the consciousness that takes [these] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
Should it be said that they are with vitarka and vicāra,
without vitarka and with vicāra only,
or without both vitarka and vicāra?
Answer: Regarding the eye faculty, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by both consciousness as an object and consciousness as an object-of-object each possess three types.
This is likewise true for the ear faculty up to the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), regarding consciousness as an object and consciousness as an object-of-object.
The meaning of the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this:
it is the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation, from the eye faculty up to the formless realm.
Regarding the consciousness that takes [objects] as its condition and the consciousness that takes those conditions as its object,
it should be said that they are either with vitarka and vicāra,
or without vitarka and with vicāra only.
Are they without vitarka and without vicāra?
Answer: For the eye-faculty, the consciousness conditioned by its cessation, and the consciousness conditioned by that object-condition, each possesses three [types].
The same applies to the ear and the other four faculties up to faith; the consciousness that takes them as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object are likewise so.
This principle should be understood by analogy for the meanings of the remaining chapters.
This extends from the eye faculty up to the formless realm.
Regarding the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),

it should be said that the latent tendencies augmented by the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*) are either with vitarka and vicāra,
or without vitarka and with vicāra only.
Are there [states] without vitarka and without vicāra?

Answer: For the eye-faculty, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the consciousness that takes cessation as its object and the consciousness that takes the object of that object as its support each possess three types.

The same applies to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by objects and object-objects of consciousness that take the ear and so forth, up to the five faculties such as faith, as their conditions.
One should understand that the principles explained in other chapters are to be applied accordingly.
The eye faculty, up to the formless realm,
the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation,
the consciousness that takes [these] as its object, and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
Should it be said that they possess both vitarka and vicāra,
or that they are without vitarka and possess only vicāra,
or that they are without both vitarka and vicāra?

Answer: Regarding the eye faculty, the consciousnesses that take the path of abandonment as their object and the consciousnesses that take the objects of those objects as their objects each possess three [types].

This is likewise true for the ear faculty up to the five faculties beginning with faith, regarding the consciousnesses that take the path of abandonment as their object and the consciousnesses that take the objects of those objects as their objects.
The principles of the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this:
from the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
it is the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation.
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in relation to consciousness as object and consciousness as objective-condition should be said to be either with vitarka and vicāra,
or without vitarka and with vicāra only.
Are they without vitarka and vicāra?

Answer: Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the consciousness that takes the path of abandonment of the eye-faculty as its object and the consciousness that takes that [path] as its object-condition, each possesses three [types].

The same applies to the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the path of abandonment of the ear-faculty up to the five faculties beginning with faith as its object and the consciousness that takes that [path] as its object-condition.
The principles of the other chapters should be understood accordingly.
From the eye faculty up to the formless realm,

there are the latent tendencies of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which consist of consciousness as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and consciousness as an object-condition of an object-condition (*ālambanālambana-pratyaya*).
Should it be said that [the eye faculty] is associated with the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, sorrow, or equanimity?

Answer: The eye faculty is associated with four faculties—namely, the consciousness that takes the object as its condition and the consciousness that takes that [conditioned] consciousness as its condition—with the exception of the faculty of pain.

The same applies to the ear faculty up to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), as well as to the consciousness that takes them as objects and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
The principles for the remaining chapters should be understood by analogy with this.
This extends from the eye faculty up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding the latent tendencies of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which increase in relation to the consciousness that takes [the faculties] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object—should these be said to be associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) up to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)? Answer:

The latent tendencies that increase in relation to the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object—[these should be said to be associated with the faculty of equanimity].
It is associated with four faculties,
excluding the faculty of suffering;
these are the ear faculty up to the three untainted faculties.

The same applies to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase in relation to consciousness as its object (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and consciousness as the object of an object (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*).
This principle should be understood by analogy for the other chapters,
from the eye faculty up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Should it be said that the consciousness which is the condition for the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as well as the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), are associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) up to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)? Answer:
The consciousness which is the condition for the cessation of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), as well as the object-conditioned consciousness, [are so associated].
It is associated with four faculties,
excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).

The same applies to the ear and so forth, as well as to the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), regarding both the consciousness that takes [them] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object.
The principles for the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this.
From the eye faculty up to the formless realm,

there are the latent dispositions (anuśaya) augmented by the consciousness that takes as its object the cessation of the ignorance-latent disposition abandoned through cultivation, as well as the consciousness that takes as its object that which takes such cessation as its object.
Should it be said that [these] are associated with the faculty of pleasure up to the faculty of equanimity?
Answer: The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the eye-faculty’s cessation-conditioning consciousness and its object-conditioning consciousness are associated with four faculties.
Excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).

The same applies to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase in relation to the consciousness that takes the ear and so forth up to the five faculties beginning with faith as its object, as well as the consciousness that takes those objects as its object.
The principles for the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the eye faculty up to the formless realm,

should the consciousness that takes as its object the path of abandoning the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation, as well as the consciousness that takes that [path] as its object-condition, be said to be associated with the faculty of pleasure up to the faculty of equanimity?
Answer: The eye faculty, as the path that severs [defilements], takes consciousness and the object-of-consciousness as its objects;
it is associated with four faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering.

The same applies to the ear and so forth, up to the five faculties beginning with faith, regarding consciousness that takes the path of abandonment as its object and consciousness that takes that [path] as its object-of-object.
The principles for other chapters should be understood by analogy with this.
This holds from the eye faculty up to the formless realm.
Regarding the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
which increases the latent tendencies associated with the consciousness that takes [the path] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object—
should it be said to be associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) up to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?

Answer: Regarding the eye faculty, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the consciousness that takes the path of abandonment as its object and the consciousness that takes the object of that object as its object are associated with four faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya).

The same applies to the ear faculty and so forth, up to the five faculties beginning with faith, regarding the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes the path of abandonment as its object and the consciousness that takes the object of that object as its object.
The principles of the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this:
from the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
there are the latent tendencies of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation, which take consciousness as their object and take the object-of-consciousness as their object.
Who accomplishes it and who does not?
Answer: The visual faculty is accomplished by those from the Sphere of Infinite Space downward, for whom consciousness takes it as an object.
Furthermore, when an Ārya is born in a higher realm, they possess [the faculties]; when an ordinary being (pṛthagjana) is born in a higher realm, they do not possess them.
Regarding the consciousness that takes [these] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-consciousness] as its object, all sentient beings possess them.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties, regarding both the consciousness that takes them as objects and the consciousness that takes that [object-consciousness] as its object.
The consciousness conditioned by the female faculty exists in the desire and form realms;
it is also accomplished by noble ones born in the formless realm,
but it is not accomplished by ordinary beings born in the formless realm.
The object-condition consciousness (ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna) exists from the Sphere of Infinite Space downward;
it is accomplished by noble ones (ārya) born in the higher realms,
but is not accomplished by ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) born in the higher realms.
The same applies to the male faculty, the faculty of suffering, and the faculty of grief, as well as to the consciousness conditioned by them and the consciousness conditioned by that condition.
All sentient beings possess the life-faculty, both as the consciousness conditioned by it and as the consciousness conditioned by that condition.
The five faculties of mental volition, joy, equanimity, and faith, as well as the three untainted faculties,
are likewise [both] object-conditioning consciousness and object-of-object-conditioning consciousness.
One should understand that the principles for other chapters are to be applied accordingly.
From the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
there are the latent tendencies of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation;
these include the latent tendencies increased by the object-conditioned consciousness and the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness.
Who accomplishes it and who does not?

Answer: Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object, one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Space accomplishes them;
one who has already abandoned the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Space does not accomplish them.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) augmented by the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*):
those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) possess them;
those who have already abandoned the defilements of the formless realm do not possess them.

The same applies to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the consciousness that takes the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body as its object, as well as by the consciousness that takes that [object-]consciousness as its object.
Regarding the female faculty, the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes it as its object are possessed [by one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm].
One who has already abandoned the defilements of the form realm does not possess [them];
one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the sphere of infinite space possesses the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes that as its object;
one who has already abandoned the defilements of the sphere of infinite space does not possess [them].

The same applies to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the male faculty, the faculty of suffering, and the faculty of grief, with respect to consciousness as object and consciousness as object-of-object.
The same also applies to the latent dispositions increased by the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), with respect to consciousness as object and consciousness as object-of-object.
For one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm, [these] are accomplished;
for one who has already abandoned the defilements of the formless realm, they are not accomplished.

The same applies to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that increase in relation to the consciousnesses and the object-of-consciousness consciousnesses associated with the mental faculty, pleasure, joy, equanimity, and the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
The principles of the other chapters should be understood accordingly:
from the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
there is the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding the consciousness that takes [the eye] as its object and the consciousness that takes [that consciousness] as its object:
who accomplishes which, and who does not accomplish which?
Answer: When the eye-faculty has ceased, the consciousness that takes it as its object belongs to the desire realm and the form realm.
Furthermore, noble beings born in the formless realm possess it, while ordinary beings born in the formless realm do not.
As for the object-condition consciousness (*ālambanapratyayavijñāna*), all sentient beings possess it.
The faculties of pleasure, joy, ear, nose, tongue, and body cease.
The same applies to the consciousness that takes them as objects and the consciousness that takes that consciousness as its object.
As for the female faculty, it ceases; the consciousness that takes it as its object is accomplished by those born in the desire realm, the form realm, or by noble ones born in the formless realm.
Ordinary beings born in the formless realm do not possess [the consciousnesses] that take the sphere of infinite space and those below it as objects; however,
noble ones born in the higher realms do possess them.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) born in a higher realm, the male faculty is not established;

the same applies to the cessation of the faculties of pain and mental grief (*daurmanasya*), as well as to the consciousness conditioned by their cessation and the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*).
The same applies to the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), as well as to the consciousness conditioned by its cessation and the object-conditioned consciousness.
All sentient beings possess these.

The same applies to the cessation of the five faculties—mind, equanimity, faith, and so forth—as well as to consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and consciousness that takes [that condition] as its condition.
One should understand that the principles explained in other chapters follow this same pattern.
From the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
there is the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation,
as well as the latent tendencies augmented by the consciousness that takes [the aggregates] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
Who accomplishes it and who does not accomplish it?

Answer: Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the consciousness conditioned by the cessation of the eye-faculty, one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm (rūpadhātu) accomplishes them.
Those who have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm do not possess [the latent dispositions] increased by the object-conditioned consciousness; however,
those who have not yet become detached from the defilements of the formless realm do possess them.
For one who has already become free from the defilements of the formless realm, these are not accomplished.

The same applies to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increased by the consciousness that takes as its object the ear, nose, tongue, body, pleasure, joy, and the consciousness that takes as its object that [consciousness] which takes those as its object.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by consciousness that conditions the cessation of the female faculty:
those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm possess them;
those who have already abandoned the defilements of the form realm do not possess them.
Regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-vijñāna*):
one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) possesses them;
one who has already abandoned the defilements of the sphere of infinite space does not possess them.

The same applies to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by consciousness conditioned by the cessation of the male faculty and the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), as well as by object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanapratyayavijñāna*).
The same applies to the latent dispositions increased by consciousness conditioned by the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and by object-conditioned consciousness.
It is accomplished when one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm,
and unaccomplished once those defilements have been abandoned.

The same applies to the latent tendencies (anuśaya) augmented by the cessation-conditioned consciousness and the object-of-cessation-conditioned consciousness regarding the faculty of equanimity of the mind and the five faculties beginning with faith.
The principles for the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Ninety-one. [From] the *Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Ninety.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Twenty-two of the Fourth Sub-section on the Ten Gates within the Second Aggregate of Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha): From the eye faculty up to the formless realm.
Regarding the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
which consciousnesses take it as their object and which take the objects of those consciousnesses as their objects—
who possesses them and who does not?
Answer: All sentient beings accomplish the path that severs the eye-faculty,
as well as the consciousness that takes it as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object.
The paths of abandonment for the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, pleasure, joy, equanimity,
and faith are likewise [the same] regarding the consciousness that takes them as objects and the consciousness that takes that consciousness as its object.
The path of abandonment for the female faculty has as its object the consciousnesses of the desire realm and the form realm.
Furthermore, noble ones born in the formless realm possess [this consciousness],
whereas ordinary beings born in the formless realm do not. However,
all sentient beings possess this consciousness that takes [the aforementioned] as its object-condition.
The male faculty, the faculty of suffering, and the faculty of mental distress are abandoned by the path;
the same applies to their object-consciousness and their object-of-object-consciousness.
This principle should be understood as applying analogously to the meanings of the remaining chapters.
Regarding the path that abandons the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
as well as the consciousnesses that take these as objects and the latent tendencies increased by those consciousnesses that take them as objects:
who possesses which, and who does not possess which?

Answer: It refers to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in relation to the eye-faculty, the path of abandonment, the consciousness that takes it as its object, and the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object.
It is accomplished when one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm,
and it is not accomplished when one has already abandoned the defilements of the formless realm.
This applies to the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, pleasure, joy, equanimity, and the five beginning with faith, at the moment of the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*).
The same applies to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by consciousness having [the object] as its condition and consciousness having that [conditioned object] as its condition.
Regarding the latent dispositions increased by consciousness conditioned by the path of abandoning the female faculty (*strī-indriya*),
those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) possess them.
It is not possessed by one who has already abandoned the defilements of the form realm.
It is the latent disposition (anuśaya) augmented by the consciousness that takes this as its object.
It is possessed by one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the sphere of infinite space.
Having already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space, one does not possess [the male faculty].
This refers to the path that severs the male faculty, the faculty of suffering, and the faculty of mental grief,
as well as the consciousnesses that take these as objects and the consciousnesses that take those [objects] as their objects.
The same applies to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase therein.
This principle should be understood by analogy for the other chapters,
from the eye faculty up to the formless realm.

Regarding the ignorance (*avidyā*) proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which consist of consciousness conditioned by objects (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and consciousness conditioned by the conditions of objects (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*):
at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*), among the ninety-eight proclivities,
how many proclivities attain full knowledge?
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are exhausted?

Answer: At the time when one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object, craving for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is exhausted.
That is, when one attains full knowledge of the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object, there is no exhaustion of fetters;
at the time one attains full knowledge of the consciousness that takes that [eye-faculty] as its object,
there is the exhaustion of craving for the formless realm.
The three underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known;
the three fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.
It is the same when the consciousness that takes the ear, nose, tongue, or body faculties as its object, as well as the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object, are fully known.
When consciousness conditioned by the female faculty is fully known, craving for form is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known,
yet there is no exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
For the Noble One, when there is full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), there is the exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
At the time of attaining full comprehension of the consciousness that takes this as its object,
craving for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is exhausted.

That is, when the consciousness conditioned by the female faculty (*strīndriya*) and the consciousness conditioned by that [consciousness] attain full knowledge (*parijñā*), there is no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).

It is the same when the consciousness conditioned by the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) and the suffering faculty (*duḥkhendriya*), as well as the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), and the consciousness conditioned by those [faculties] attain full knowledge.
When one attains full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which conditions consciousness and the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambanapratyaya-vijñāna*),
there is the exhaustion of craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).

At that time, three latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully comprehended, the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted, and there is the mental application of equanimity, joy, and the five faculties— faith and the others— as well as the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*).

The same applies when one attains full comprehension (*parijñā*) regarding the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes that [conditioning] consciousness as its condition.
One should understand that the principles for other chapters are to be applied accordingly based on this.

When one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)— ranging from the eye faculty up to the ignorance (*avidyā*) latent disposition to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm—
that increase in relation to the consciousness that takes [those objects] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known (parijñāta), and how many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?
Answer: At the time when the underlying tendencies increased by the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object are fully known.
With the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of infinite space,
one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object; however,
there is no exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding these latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in the object-condition consciousness (ālambana-vijñāna),
at the time of attaining full comprehension (parijñā), craving for the formless realm (ārūpya-rāga) is exhausted;
thus, three latent dispositions attain full comprehension.

It is the same when one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the consciousness that takes the ear, nose, tongue, or body faculty as its object, as well as the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object, at the moment the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by consciousness conditioned by the female faculty (*strī-indriya*):
at the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*), there is the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*).
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), thirty-one latent dispositions are fully known, yet no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
For the Noble One, when there is the full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), there is the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
At the time of attaining full comprehension of those underlying tendencies that increase by taking consciousness as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), [the fetters are exhausted].
With the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of infinite space,

one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) and the cessation of fetters (*saṃyojana*) regarding those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase in dependence upon the consciousness that takes the female faculty as its object-condition.

The same applies to the time when one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that increase in relation to the male faculty, the faculty of suffering, the faculty of grief, the consciousness that takes them as objects, and the consciousness that takes those objects as its own object.

Regarding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the time when one attains full knowledge of the underlying tendencies that increase in relation to the consciousness that takes it as an object and the consciousness that takes that object as its own object is when craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*) is exhausted.
When the three latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are fully known (*parijñāta*), the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
This is likewise the case when the five faculties— namely, mental pleasure (*saumanasya*), joy (*prīti*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and faith (*śraddhā*)—
as well as the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), and the latent dispositions increased by consciousness and its objects of cognition, are fully known.
The principles of the other chapters should be understood accordingly:
from the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
there is the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation.

When one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the consciousness that takes [the eye] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object, how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are fully known, and how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted?
Answer: When the eye-faculty ceases and the consciousness that takes it as its object is fully known, craving for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) is exhausted.
Ordinary persons attain full knowledge (*parijñā*) of thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), yet there is no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Noble ones (*ārya*) attain full knowledge of three underlying tendencies, yet there is no exhaustion of fetters.
At the time when they attain full knowledge of the consciousness that takes this as its object, craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*) is exhausted.
The two underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully understood; the three fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted;

and the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity pertaining to the ear, nose, tongue, and body, as well as the consciousness that takes them as objects and the consciousness that takes that consciousness as its object, cease.
It is the same when one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*).
At the moment of attaining full knowledge through the cessation-conditioned consciousness of the female faculty (*strī-indriya*), craving for the form realm (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there is the attainment of full knowledge regarding thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), yet there is no exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
For the Noble One, when there is full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), there is the exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
At the time of attaining full comprehension of the consciousness that takes this as its object,
craving for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is exhausted.

That is to say, when the female faculty (*strī-indriya*) ceases, both the consciousness that takes it as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object attain full knowledge (*parijñā*), yet there is no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).

The same applies when the male faculty (*puruṣa-indriya*) and the faculties of suffering (*duḥkha-indriya*) and mental distress (*daurmanasya-indriya*) cease; at the time they cease, both the consciousness that takes them as objects and the consciousness that takes those [objects] as objects attain full knowledge.
When one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as conditioned by consciousness (*vijñāna*) and its object-condition (*ālambana-vijñāna*),
craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*) is exhausted;
three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known and three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned.
When the mental faculty, equanimity, and the five faculties such as faith cease—

and likewise when one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding the consciousness that takes [them] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-consciousness] as its object— it is also thus.
The meaning of the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this:
from the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
there is the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation.

When the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes the conditions for that object as its condition are fully understood (parijñā),
how many latent dispositions are fully understood and how many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?

Answer: When one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase in dependence on the consciousness associated with the cessation of the eye-faculty, craving for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) is exhausted;
this applies to the thirty-one latent dispositions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
One attains full knowledge (parijñā) and the exhaustion of fetters (saṃyojana-kṣaya).
For the noble ones (ārya), there is the attainment of full knowledge and the exhaustion of fetters regarding the three underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
These are the underlying tendencies that increase based on the consciousness that takes them as its object (ālambana-viṣaya-vijñāna).
At the time of attaining full knowledge, craving for the formless realm is exhausted;
three latent tendencies are fully known,
and three fetters are extinguished.

The same applies when one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increased by the consciousness that takes as its object the cessation of the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, pleasure, and joy, as well as by the consciousness that takes as its object that [consciousness].
It is also the case for the female faculty (*strīndriya*) when it ceases, regarding the latent tendencies increased by the consciousness that takes it as its object.
At the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*), there is the exhaustion of craving for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*).
For ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there are thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*);
at the time of attaining full knowledge, there is the exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) without exception.
For the Noble One, when the three underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known (parijñāta), there is the exhaustion of fetters (saṃyojana). At the time these underlying tendencies,
which increase by taking that object as their condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
are fully known, craving for the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana-tṛṣṇā) is exhausted.
That is, when the female faculty (*strī-indriya*) ceases, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*) are fully understood,
and there is the exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
When the male faculty (*puruṣa-indriya*) and the faculties of suffering and mental grief (*duḥkha* and *daurmanasya*) cease.

The same applies when one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by consciousness conditioned by objects (*ālambana-vijñāna*) and consciousness conditioned by the objects of objects (*ālambanālambana-vijñāna*).
This also holds for the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which is increased by consciousness conditioned by objects and consciousness conditioned by the objects of objects.
At the time of attaining full knowledge, craving for the formless realm is exhausted;
three underlying tendencies are fully known,
and three fetters are abandoned.

The same applies when one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase through the object-consciousness and the consciousness of the object, at the time when the mental equanimity and the five faculties such as faith cease.
One should understand that the principles of the other chapters are to be applied accordingly.
When one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
as well as the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
along with the consciousness that takes these as objects and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known (parijñāta), and how many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?

Answer: On the path of abandonment of the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya), there is the consciousness that takes it as its object (ālambana-vijñāna) and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object (ālambanālambana-vijñāna).
At the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*), craving for the formless realms (*ārūpya-tṛṣṇā*) is exhausted;
three latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully known and three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
This occurs through the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*) regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, pleasure, joy, equanimity, and the five faculties such as faith.

The same applies when one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes the condition of that condition as its object. Regarding the female faculty (*strīndriya*),
it is the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*) that takes consciousness as its condition.
At the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*), there is the exhaustion of craving for form (*rūparāga*).
For ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there are thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*);
at the attainment of full knowledge, there is the exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) without exception.
When the noble one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), there is no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
When full knowledge of the consciousness that takes these as its object is attained, there is the exhaustion of craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).
When full knowledge of the three underlying tendencies is attained, there is the exhaustion of the three fetters.
The same applies when one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding the male faculty, the faculty of suffering,
and the faculty of grief, as well as the consciousness that takes these as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-consciousness] as its object.
The principles for other chapters should be understood by analogy with this:
from the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
it is the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) associated with the object-conditioned consciousness (ālambana-vijñāna) and the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness (ālambanālambana-vijñāna) are fully understood (parijñā),
how many underlying tendencies are fully understood,
and how many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?

Answer: When one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the consciousness that takes the eye-faculty as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object— [which occurs] during the path of abandonment of the eye-faculty—
the craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*) is exhausted.
There is the full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
the exhaustion of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*),
and the path of abandonment for the ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, pleasure, joy, equanimity, and the five faculties beginning with faith.

The same applies when one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and by consciousness that takes the conditions for that object as its condition.
Regarding the path that severs the female faculty (*strīndriya*),
it concerns the latent dispositions increased by consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition.
When full knowledge is attained, the craving for form is exhausted.
For ordinary persons, thirty-one underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are fully known, yet no fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.
For noble ones (ārya), three underlying tendencies are fully known, and no fetters are exhausted.
When the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with this object-conditioned consciousness are fully understood,
craving for the formless realm is exhausted,
and three latent dispositions are fully understood.

The same applies when one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the acquisition of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase through consciousness and object-consciousness, at the time when the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted and the male faculty of suffering and the faculty of mental grief are severed by the path.
The principles of the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this.
This includes the eye faculty up to the ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).

When one realizes the cessation of the consciousness that takes [phenomena] as its object and the consciousness that takes the object of that object as its object, among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
how many underlying tendencies are realized as ceased?
Regarding the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are exhausted?
Answer: When one realizes the cessation of consciousness conditioned by the eye-faculty, craving for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is exhausted.
That is, one realizes the cessation of consciousness conditioned by the eye-faculty;
there is no exhaustion of fetters until,
reaching the stage of Arhatship, one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
When the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted,
at the moment one realizes the cessation of this object-conditioned consciousness (*ālambana-pratyaya-vijñāna*), one attains the fruit of Arhatship;
this constitutes the realization of the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

It is the same when one realizes the extinction of the nine fetters, as well as the cognition that takes the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties as its object, and the cognition that takes that [object-cognition] as its object.
When one realizes the cessation of consciousness conditioned by the female faculty, craving for the form realm is exhausted;
for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are realized as ceased,
but no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
The Noble One realizes the cessation of the three underlying tendencies;
there is no further exhaustion of fetters.
Up to the stage of Arhat, one realizes the cessation of ninety-eight underlying tendencies.
When the nine fetters are exhausted and one realizes the cessation of the consciousness that takes this as its object-condition,
the craving for the sphere of infinite space is exhausted; at that moment, one realizes the cessation of the consciousness that takes the female faculty as its object-condition.
There is no further exhaustion of fetters;
up to the Arhat, one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the nine fetters.

It is the same when one realizes the cessation of the male faculty, the faculty of suffering, and the faculty of grief, as well as the consciousness conditioned by them and the consciousness conditioned by that object;
at the time of realizing the cessation of the life-faculty, the consciousness conditioned by it, and the consciousness conditioned by that object, one attains the fruit of Arhatship.
When one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya), the nine fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted.

This is likewise the case when one realizes the cessation of consciousness and its objects, as well as the consciousness that takes those objects as its objects— namely, the mental faculty, pleasure, joy, equanimity, and the five faculties beginning with faith, along with the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
The principles of the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this:
from the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation within the formless realm.
When one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by consciousness as an object and by consciousness as an object-of-object,
how many latent dispositions are realized as ceased,
and how many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?

Answer: When one realizes the cessation of the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increased by the consciousness conditioned by the eye-faculty, the craving for the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana) is exhausted;
that is the realization of the cessation of the underlying tendencies increased by the consciousness conditioned by the eye-faculty.
There is no exhaustion of fetters.
Up to the Arhat, one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the nine fetters.
When one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) augmented by this object-conditioned consciousness,
one attains the fruit of arhatship; that is,
one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight latent dispositions.

It is the same when one realizes the extinction of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increased by the consciousness that takes the nine fetters as its object and the consciousness that takes those objects as its object.

It is also the same when one realizes the extinction of the latent tendencies increased by the consciousness that takes the female faculty (*strīndriya*) as its object; at that time, craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*) is exhausted.
An ordinary person realizes the cessation of thirty-one underlying tendencies,
yet does not exhaust all fetters.
A noble one realizes the cessation of three underlying tendencies and exhausts all fetters.
