Upon reaching arhatship, one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
At the time of realizing the cessation of those underlying tendencies augmented by the consciousness that takes this as its object, [the same occurs].
With the exhaustion of craving for the base of infinite space,
one realizes the cessation of the latent tendencies increased by the object-conditioned consciousness associated with the female faculty;
yet there is no exhaustion of fetters.

When one reaches the stage of an Arhat, there is the realization of the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), and likewise,

at the time of realizing the cessation of the underlying tendencies increased by the consciousness that takes the male faculty, the faculties of suffering and mental grief, and their respective objects and object-conditions as its conditions.

When one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in dependence on the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), the consciousness (vijñāna), and the object-conditioned consciousness (ālambanapratyayavijñāna), one attains the fruit of Arhatship;
this constitutes the realization of the cessation of ninety-eight latent dispositions.

It is the same when one realizes the cessation of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the mental faculty (*manas*), pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*);
as well as when one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase in relation to consciousness and its objects.
The meaning of the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this:
from the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
there is the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
When one realizes the cessation of consciousness as a condition and consciousness as a condition for conditions,
how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are realized as ceased, and how many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?
Answer: When one realizes the cessation of the eye-faculty through the condition of the cessation of consciousness, craving for forms (*rūparāga*) is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there is the realization of the cessation of thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) but no exhaustion of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
For a noble one (*ārya*), there is the realization of the cessation of three underlying tendencies but no exhaustion of fetters.
Upon reaching arhatship, one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
At the moment of realizing the cessation of the consciousness that takes these as its objects, one attains the fruit of arhatship.
When one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana),
it is likewise when one realizes the cessation of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-faculties, as well as the pleasure and joy faculties,
along with their corresponding consciousnesses and the consciousnesses that take those as objects.
When one realizes the cessation of consciousness conditioned by the cessation of the female faculty (*strī-indriya*), craving for the form realm (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) is exhausted.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), this realization constitutes the cessation of thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*).
For a noble one (*ārya*), it constitutes the cessation of three underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of all fetters.
Upon reaching arhatship, one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
When one realizes the cessation of the consciousness that takes these as its objects, craving for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is exhausted.
That is, by realizing the cessation of the female faculty as its condition, one realizes the cessation of consciousness conditioned by that faculty, yet there is no exhaustion of fetters.
Up to the stage of Arhat, one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the nine fetters.
The same applies when one realizes the cessation of the male faculty, the faculty of suffering, and the faculty of grief,
as well as the consciousness that takes them as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-consciousness] as its object.
This also applies to the cessation of the life-faculty, the consciousness that takes it as its object, and the consciousness that takes that [object-consciousness] as its object.
When one realizes the cessation [of these defilements], one attains the fruit of arhatship.
One realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya), the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana),
and the cessation of mental equanimity and the five faculties beginning with faith.
It is the same when one realizes the cessation of consciousness conditioned by objects and consciousness conditioned by those objects.
This principle should be understood to apply to the remaining chapters as well,
from the eye faculty up to the formless realm.
When one realizes the cessation of the latent tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned by cultivation—
namely, the latent tendencies of ignorance (avidyā), the consciousness that takes them as its object, and the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object—
how many latent tendencies are realized as being ceased?
Question: How many fetters are exhausted?
Answer: When one realizes the cessation of the latent tendencies (anuśaya) increased by consciousness conditioned by the extinction of the eye-faculty, craving for form (rūpa-tṛṣṇā) is exhausted.
An ordinary person realizes the cessation of thirty-one underlying tendencies,
yet does not exhaust all fetters.
A noble one realizes the cessation of three underlying tendencies.
There is no exhaustion of fetters.
Up to the stage of Arhat, one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
These are the underlying tendencies increased by the consciousness that takes them as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
When one realizes the cessation [of these], one attains the fruit of arhatship;
one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and brings the nine fetters (saṃyojana) to an end.

It is likewise when one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increased by the consciousness that takes as its object the cessation of the pleasure and joy faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body, as well as by the consciousness that takes that [cessation] as its object.
Regarding the female faculty, it is the latent dispositions increased by the consciousness that takes as its object its cessation.
When the cessation [of the desire for form] is realized, there is the exhaustion of the thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
yet no fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
For a noble one (*ārya*), three underlying tendencies are realized as ceased.
There is no exhaustion of fetters.
Up to the stage of Arhat, one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
At the time of realizing the cessation of the underlying tendencies increased by the consciousness that takes this as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), [the same applies].
With the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of infinite space,
one realizes the cessation of the latent tendencies increased by the object-condition of consciousness that conditions the extinction of the female faculty.
There is no exhaustion of fetters.
Up until the stage of Arhat, one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies and the exhaustion of the nine fetters;
for a male, the faculties of pain and mental grief cease.
It is likewise when one realizes the cessation of the latent tendencies increased by consciousness as a condition and consciousness as a condition for conditions;

at the time of realizing the cessation of the latent tendencies increased by consciousness as a condition and consciousness as a condition for conditions, one attains the fruit of Arhatship, which is the cessation of the life-faculty.
When one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana),

it is likewise when one realizes the cessation of the underlying tendencies increased by consciousness that takes [the mind] as its object and consciousness that takes that [object] as its object, occurring at the time of the cessation of mental equanimity and the five faculties such as faith.
The principles of the other chapters should be understood accordingly:
from the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
this refers to the path for abandoning the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation.

When one realizes the cessation of consciousness conditioned by the eye-faculty and consciousness conditioned by that [eye-faculty], how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are realized as ceased, and how many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?
Answer: It is the path of abandonment for the eye-faculty, which takes as its object consciousness conditioned by the eye-faculty and consciousness conditioned by that [eye-faculty].
When the cessation [of these] is realized, one attains the fruit of Arhatship.
There is the realization of the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
This occurs through the path of abandonment for the ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, equanimity, joy, pleasure, and the five faculties beginning with faith.
It is the same when one realizes the cessation of the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes that [conditioned] object as its condition.
When the path that severs the female faculty is realized as the cessation of the consciousness that takes it as its condition, craving for the form realm is exhausted.
Ordinary persons realize the cessation of thirty-one latent dispositions (anuśaya), yet there is no exhaustion of fetters (saṃyojana).
Noble ones realize the cessation of three latent dispositions,
yet there is no exhaustion of fetters.
Upon reaching arhatship, one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
At the moment one realizes the cessation of the consciousness that takes these as its objects, one attains the fruit of arhatship.
When one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*),

it is likewise when one realizes the cessation of the consciousness that takes the male faculty as its object, the consciousness that takes the faculties of suffering and mental grief as its objects, and the consciousness that takes those [objects] as its further objects.
The principles of the other chapters should be understood accordingly.
This applies from the eye faculty up to the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
When one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) augmented by consciousness as a condition and by consciousness as a condition for conditions,
how many latent dispositions are realized as ceased,
and how many fetters (saṃyojana) are exhausted?
Answer: When one realizes the cessation of the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that increase through the eye-faculty, the path of abandonment, the consciousness that takes it as an object,
and the consciousness that takes that [object] as its object, one attains the fruit of arhatship.
The realization of the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The exhaustion of the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The path of abandonment for the ear, nose, tongue, body, life-force, mind, pleasure, joy, equanimity, and the five faculties such as faith.

It is the same when one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the object-conditioned consciousness (ālambana-vijñāna) and the object-of-object-conditioned consciousness (ālambanālambana-vijñāna).
When one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions increased by the object-conditioned consciousness associated with the path that severs the female faculty (strī-indriya),
the craving for the form realm (rūpa-rāga) is exhausted.
An ordinary person realizes the cessation of thirty-one underlying tendencies (anuśaya), but does not bring about the exhaustion of all fetters (saṃyojana).
A noble one (ārya) realizes the cessation of three underlying tendencies.
There is no exhaustion of fetters.
Up until the stage of Arhat, one realizes the cessation of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the exhaustion of the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
When one realizes the cessation of these latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in dependence upon consciousness as an object-condition, one attains the fruit of arhatship;
this constitutes the realization of the cessation of the ninety-eight latent dispositions.
When the nine fetters are exhausted,

it is likewise when one realizes the cessation of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increased by the consciousness that takes as its object the male faculty of suffering and mental grief, as well as the consciousness that takes those objects as its objects, at the time of the path that severs them.
The principles of the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this:
from the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation within the formless realm.
Among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), by how many are they bound?
Among the three bonds (*bandhana*), by how many are they bound?
Among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), by how many do they increase through latent proliferation?
Among the six stains (*mala*), by how many stains is it defiled?
Among the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), by how many envelopments is it enveloped?
Answer: The eye-faculty is bound by nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the ten underlying tendencies,
and defiled by the six stains.
Enveloped by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
The same applies to the five faculties from the ear up to faith.
The meaning of the other chapters should be understood accordingly based on this principle.
From the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
there are the latent tendencies of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation;
these consist of the consciousness that takes [the faculties] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
By how many fetters (saṃyojana) is it bound, and so on, up to by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is it enveloped?
Answer: The eye-faculty is associated with consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition, as well as with consciousness that takes that [consciousness] as its condition.
Bound by the nine fetters,
bound by the three bonds,
with the ten latent tendencies increasing, and defiled by the six stains.
Bound by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
the same applies to the five faculties beginning with the ear and ending with faith,
as well as to the consciousness that takes them as objects and the consciousness that takes that consciousness as its object.
The principles of the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this:
from the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
there is the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Regarding the consciousness that takes [an object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes [that] condition as its object:
by how many fetters (saṃyojana) is it bound,
and so on, up to by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is it enveloped?
Answer: When the eye faculty ceases, it conditions consciousness and the object-conditioned consciousness;
these are bound by the nine fetters and bound by the three bonds.
The ten underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by the six stains and enveloped by the ten fetters.

The same applies to the ear and so forth, up to the five faculties such as faith, regarding the consciousness that takes [them] as its object and the consciousness that takes that object as its object.
This principle should be understood by analogy for the meanings of the other chapters.
This extends from the eye faculty up to the formless realm.
Regarding the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) bind the consciousness that takes [this path] as its object, as well as the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object?
Up to: by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is it enveloped?
Answer: It is the consciousness that takes the path of abandonment of the eye-faculty as its object (ālambana), and the consciousness that takes that [path] as its object (ālambanālambana).
It is bound by nine fetters (saṃyojana).
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the ten latent tendencies,
and defiled by the six stains.
Bound by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
the same applies to the ear and so forth, up to the five faculties such as faith,
as well as to the consciousness that takes the path of abandonment as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-taking] consciousness as its object.
The principles of the other chapters should be understood accordingly.
This refers to one who possesses the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation within the formless realm.
By how many fetters (saṃyojana) is one bound, and so on, up to by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is one enveloped?
Answer: One who possesses the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya).
If an ordinary person has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire, they are bound by the nine fetters,
constrained by the three bonds,
and subject to the increase of the ten underlying tendencies.
Tainted by the six impurities and bound by the ten envelopments,
he has already abandoned the defilement of desire but has not yet abandoned the defilement of the first dhyāna.
It is bound by the six fetters,
constrained by the two bonds,
and increased by the nine underlying tendencies.
Tainted by the three impurities and bound by the two fetters,
he has already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
Bound by the six fetters,
bound by the two bonds,
and increased by the nine underlying tendencies.
First, they are defiled by stains;
second, they are bound by fetters.
This refers to noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire and have entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
As long as the subsequent knowledge of suffering has not yet arisen,
one is bound by the nine fetters and constrained by the three bonds.
The ten latent dispositions increase and are defiled by the six stains,
and are bound by the ten fetters.
The knowledge of the category of suffering has already arisen, but the knowledge of the category of the path has not yet arisen.
Bound by the nine fetters,
bound by the three bonds,
and increased by the eight underlying tendencies.
Tainted by the six stains and bound by the ten fetters;
one for whom the subsequent knowledge of the path has arisen but who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire.
Bound by the six fetters,
bound by the three bonds,
and increased by the four underlying tendencies.
Tainted by the six stains and bound by the ten fetters,
one who has already abandoned the defilement of desire but not yet abandoned the defilement of the first dhyāna enters into the state of right determination and departure from birth.
As long as the subsequent knowledge of suffering has not yet arisen,
one is bound by six fetters and constrained by two bonds.
The nine underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by the three stains and bound by the two envelopments.
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,
one is bound by six fetters and bound by two bonds.
The seven underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by the three stains and ensnared by the two fetters.
When the subsequent knowledge of the path has arisen but one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna,
one is bound by the three fetters and constrained by the two bonds.
The three underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by the three stains and enveloped by the two fetters.

Having already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna and having entered the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), but before the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has yet arisen,
one is bound by six fetters (saṃyojana) and bound by two bonds (bandhana).
The nine underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by one stain and ensnared by the secondary fetters.
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,
one is bound by six fetters and bound by two bonds.
The seven latent dispositions increase [in strength];
it is defiled by one stain and bound by the fetters.
When the subsequent knowledge of the path has arisen but one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm,
one is bound by the three fetters and constrained by the two bonds.
The three underlying tendencies increase [in strength];
it is defiled by one stain and bound by the fetters.
Having already become free from the defilements of the formless realm, one is without fetters or bonds, and so forth,
up to being without the envelopments;
one is endowed with the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, female, male, life, and mind.
The same applies to the five faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, equanimity, and faith.
One who possesses the faculty of grief, if they are an ordinary person (pṛthagjana),
is bound by nine fetters (saṃyojana).
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the ten latent tendencies,
and defiled by the six stains.
Bound by the ten envelopments (paryavasthāna),
if an noble one has not yet produced the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna),
they are fettered by the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the ten latent tendencies,
and defiled by the six stains.
Bound by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
with the knowledge of the category of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) already arisen but the knowledge of the category of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) not yet arisen,
one is fettered by the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the eight underlying tendencies,
and defiled by the six stains.
Bound by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
with the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) already arisen,
one is fettered by the six fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the four latent tendencies,
and defiled by the six stains.
One who is bound by the ten fetters and possesses the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire.
For one who has entered the state of right determination but for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen,
there are the fetters of nine bonds and the bondage of three ties.
The ten underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by the six stains and enveloped by the ten fetters.
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering has arisen,
one is bound by nine fetters and constrained by three bonds.
The eight underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by the six stains and ensnared by the ten fetters.
Having already become free from the defilement of sensual desire but not yet free from the defilement of the first dhyāna,
and while the knowledge of the category of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) within the entry into the state of rightness (samyaktva-niyāma) has not yet arisen,
one is bound by six fetters.
Bound by the two fetters,
the nine underlying tendencies increase therein,
and it is defiled by the three impurities.
Bound by two envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
with the knowledge of the subsequent category of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*) already arisen,
he is fettered by six fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Bound by the two fetters,
the seven latent tendencies increase,
and it is defiled by the three stains.
Bound by the two envelopments (paryavasthāna),

having already abandoned the defilement of the first dhyāna and entered the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), but with the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) not yet arisen,
one is bound by the six fetters (saṃyojana).
Bound by two fetters,
increased by nine underlying tendencies,
and defiled by one stain.
Bound by the two envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
with the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna*) already arisen,
he is fettered by the six fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Bound by the two fetters,
increased by the seven latent tendencies,
and defiled by the single stain.
One who is bound by the two envelopments and has attained the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya), if they have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire,
is fettered by the six fetters.
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the four latent tendencies,
and defiled by the six stains.
Bound by the ten envelopments;
if one has already become free from the defilement of desire but is not yet free from the defilement of the first dhyāna,
one is fettered by the three fetters.
Bound by the two fetters,
increased by the three latent tendencies,
and defiled by the three impurities.
Bound by the two envelopments; or,
having already become free from the defilement of the first dhyāna,
being fettered by the three fetters.
Bound by the two fetters,
increased by the three latent tendencies,
and defiled by the single stain.
Bound by the two envelopments,
one who has accomplished the faculty of perfect knowledge (ājñātendriya) is without fetters or bonds, and so on,
up to being without the envelopments that envelop.
The principles for other chapters should be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the possession of the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm:
how many fetters (saṃyojana) bind the consciousness that takes [the object] as its condition, as well as the consciousness that takes that [conditioned] consciousness as its condition?
Up to: "By how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is one enveloped?
Answer: One is endowed with [the faculties] from the eye up to the faculty of one who has fully known (ājñātāvīndriya).
Regarding the consciousness that takes [these] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-consciousness] as its object:
Regarding being bound by the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) up to being entangled by the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
it is as explained previously concerning the accomplishment of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
One should understand that the principles for the remaining chapters are to be applied accordingly.
For one who has accomplished the destruction of the eye-faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm,
how many fetters bind them, and so on, up to how many envelopments enshroud them?
Answer: Regarding the accomplishment of the cessation of the eye-faculty:
it is when an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna and is bound by the six fetters and constrained by the two bonds.
The nine underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by the three stains and bound by the two envelopments.
Having already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
one is bound by six fetters and constrained by two bonds.
The nine underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by one stain and ensnared by the fetters.

If a noble one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna and has not yet produced the knowledge of the category of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) upon entering the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma),
they are bound by six fetters (saṃyojana) and bound by two bonds (bandhana).
The nine latent dispositions increase therein;
it is defiled by the three impurities and bound by the two envelopments.
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,
one is bound by six fetters and bound by two bonds.
The seven latent tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by the three impurities and ensnared by the two fetters.
When the subsequent knowledge of the path has arisen but one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna,
one is bound by the three fetters and constrained by the two bonds.
The three underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by the three stains and bound by the two envelopments.

Having already become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna and having entered the state of rightness (samyaktva-niyāma), but before the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has yet arisen,
one is bound by six fetters (saṃyojana) and bound by two bonds (bandhana).
The nine underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase therein;
it is defiled by one stain (mala) and enveloped by the envelopments (paryavasthāna).
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering has arisen but the subsequent knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,
one is bound by six fetters and bound by two bonds.
The seven latent tendencies increase [in strength];
it is defiled by one stain and bound by the secondary fetters.
When the subsequent knowledge of the path has arisen but one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm,
one is bound by the three fetters and bound by the two bonds.
The three underlying tendencies increase [therein];
it is defiled by one stain and bound by the fetters.
Having already become free from the defilements of the formless realm, one is without fetters or bonds, and so on,
up to being without the envelopments.
The same applies to the cessation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, female, male, life, and the five faculties such as faith.
Regarding the accomplishment of the cessation of the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*):
if an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire,
they are bound by the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the ten underlying tendencies,
and defiled by the six stains.
Bound by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
one who is already free from the defilement of desire but not yet free from the defilement of the first dhyāna is fettered by the six fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Bound by the two fetters,
increased by the nine underlying tendencies,
and defiled by the three stains.
Bound by the two envelopments,
already free from the defilement of the first dhyāna,
and fettered by the six knots.
Bound by the two fetters,
the nine underlying tendencies increase,
and it is defiled by the single stain.
Bound by the two envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),

if an noble one (*ārya*) has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire and has entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), such that the knowledge of the category of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) has not yet arisen,
they are bound by the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Bound by the three fetters,
the ten latent tendencies increase therein,
and it is defiled by the six stains.
Bound by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
with the knowledge of the category of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) already arisen but the knowledge of the category of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) not yet arisen,
one is fettered by the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the eight underlying tendencies,
and defiled by the six stains.
Bound by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
with the knowledge of the path-category (*mārgānvayajñāna*) already arisen but not yet free from the defilement of desire,
one is fettered by the six knots (*grantha*).
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the four latent tendencies,
and defiled by the six stains.
Bound by the ten envelopments,
having already abandoned the defilement of desire but not yet abandoned the defilement of the first dhyāna,
one has entered into the state of rightness and departure from birth, though the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen.
Bound by the six fetters,
bound by the two bonds,
and increased by the nine underlying tendencies.
Tainted by the three impurities and bound by the two fetters;
the knowledge of the category of suffering has already arisen, but the knowledge of the category of the path has not yet arisen.
Bound by the six fetters,
bound by the two bonds,
and increased by the seven latent tendencies.
Tainted by the three stains and bound by the two envelopments,
with the knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) having already arisen but not yet being free from the defilement of the first dhyāna.
Bound by the three fetters,
bound by the two bonds,
and with the three latent tendencies increasing.
Tainted by the three stains and bound by the two envelopments,

one has already abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna but has not yet given rise to the knowledge of the category of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) within the entry into the state of rightness (samyaktva-niyāma).
Bound by the six fetters,
bound by the two bonds,
and increased by the nine underlying tendencies.
First, being defiled by the outflows (*āsrava*);
second, being bound by the fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
This occurs when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen.
Bound by the six fetters,
bound by the two bonds,
and increased by the seven latent tendencies.
First, those defiled by the stains (*mala*);
second, those entangled by the fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
These refer to those for whom the knowledge of the path-category (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) has already arisen, yet who have not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*).
Bound by the three fetters,
bound by the two bonds,
and with the latent dispositions increasing therein.
First, stained by the defilements;
second, bound by the fetters;
[and third,] having already abandoned the stains of the formless realm and being free from the bonds of the fetters.
This applies even up to the cessation of the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, grief, and equanimity when they are not bound by the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The meaning of the other chapters should be understood accordingly based on this principle.
When the eye faculty is accomplished up to the formless realm,
there is the cessation of the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation;
this refers to the consciousness that takes [the aggregates] as its object and the consciousness that takes that object-consciousness as its object.
By how many fetters (saṃyojana) is one bound, and so on, up to by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is one enveloped?
Answer: One achieves [the state where] the eye-faculty, up to the five faculties such as faith, has ceased.

Those who are bound by the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and even entangled by the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) based on consciousness and the object-conditioned consciousness are as previously explained regarding the cessation of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
The principles for the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this.
One who has attained the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation, from the eye faculty up to the formless realm.
By how many fetters (saṃyojana) is one bound, and so on, up to by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is one enveloped?
Answer: One who has accomplished the faculty of the eye, and so on, up to the five faculties beginning with faith, is one for whom the path of abandonment has been realized.
Regarding those bound by the various fetters (saṃyojana) up to those entangled by the various envelopments (paryavasthāna),
it is as previously explained concerning the possession of the faculty of mind (manas-indriya) at the moment of its cessation;
this applies likewise to the possession of the faculty of eye (cakṣur-indriya) up to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Regarding the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation:
for those who are bound by the fetters and even entangled by the envelopments, [this applies] to consciousness as an object and to consciousness as the object of an object.
As previously explained regarding the accomplishment of the cessation of the mind-faculty (*manas*),
this applies to what was said concerning the consciousness that takes [the mind] as its object and the consciousness that takes that [object-consciousness] as its object.
One should understand that the principles for the remaining chapters are to be applied accordingly.
Regarding one who is not possessed of the eye-faculty up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
and who possesses the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) bind them, and up to how many envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) enshroud them?
Answer: For one who does not possess the eye, ear, nose, tongue, female, or male faculties,
they are bound by all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and even enveloped by all envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
as was explained previously regarding one who possesses the eye faculty.
One who does not possess the body-faculty is either an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) bound by the six fetters (*saṃyojana*) and bound by the two bonds (*bandhana*).
The nine underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by one stain and enveloped by the fetters.
If a noble one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm,
they are bound by the three fetters and constrained by the two bonds.
The three underlying tendencies increase [in strength];
it is defiled by one stain and bound by the secondary fetters.
Having already become free from the defilements of the formless realm and being without fetters or bonds,
up to and including being without the envelopments,
one does not possess the faculties of pleasure or joy.
Bound by six fetters,
bound by two bonds,
and increased by nine underlying tendencies.
First, being defiled by the stains;
second, being bound by the fetters;
and those who do not possess the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
If an ordinary person has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna,
they are bound by the six fetters and constrained by the two bonds.
The nine underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by the three stains and ensnared by the two fetters.
Having already become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
one is bound by six fetters and constrained by two bonds.
The nine underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by one stain and bound by the envelopments.
If a noble one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna,
they are bound by the three fetters and constrained by the two bonds.
The three latent dispositions increase therein;
it is defiled by the three stains and bound by the two envelopments.
Having already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna but not yet free from the defilements of the formless realm,
one is bound by the three fetters and bound by the two bonds.
The three underlying tendencies increase [in strength];
it is defiled by one stain and bound by the fetters.
Having already become free from the defilements of the formless realm, one is without fetters or bonds,
and so on, up to being without the entanglements;
such a person does not possess the faculty of grief.
Bound by all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and even entangled by all envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
as previously explained regarding the one who has attained the cessation of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*);
this refers to one who does not possess the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
Bound by the nine fetters,
bound by the three bonds,
and increased by the ten underlying tendencies.
Tainted by the six impurities,
bound by the ten fetters,
and not possessing the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is bound by the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) and even entangled by the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
it is as previously explained regarding the accomplishment of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) by an ordinary person.
If a noble one has not yet become free from the defilement of desire,
they are bound by the six fetters and constrained by the three bonds.
The four latent proclivities increase therein;
it is defiled by the six stains and ensnared by the ten fetters.
Having already become free from the defilement of sensual desire but not yet free from the defilement of the first dhyāna,
one is bound by the three fetters and constrained by the two bonds.
Three latent dispositions increase therein;
it is defiled by the three stains and bound by the two fetters.
Having already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna, but not yet free from the defilements of the formless realm,
one is bound by the three fetters and constrained by the two bonds.
The three underlying tendencies increase [therein];
it is defiled by one stain and bound by the fetters.
Having already become free from the defilements of the formless realm, one is without fetters or bonds,
and so forth, up to being without the envelopments;
yet, one does not possess the faculty of "I-have-known."
If they are ordinary persons (pṛthagjana),
bound by various fetters (saṃyojana) and even entangled by various envelopments (paryavasthāna),
it is as previously explained regarding ordinary persons who do not possess the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātām-ājñāsyāmīndriya).
If an noble one is on the path of seeing and has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire, and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen,
they are bound by nine fetters.
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the ten latent tendencies,
and defiled by the six stains.
Bound by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
with the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*) already arisen,
he is fettered by the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the eight underlying tendencies,
and defiled by the six stains.
Bound by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),

one who is already free from the defilement of desire but not yet free from the defilement of the first dhyāna, for whom the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen,
is bound by the six fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Bound by the two fetters,
the nine underlying tendencies increase therein,
and it is defiled by the three impurities.
Bound by the two envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) already arisen, one is fettered by six fetters (*saṃyojana*) and bound by the two bonds (*bandhana*).
The seven latent tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by the three stains and enveloped by the two fetters.
Having already become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna, but before the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has arisen,
one is bound by six fetters and bound by two bonds.
The nine underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by one stain and ensnared by the fetters.
When the subsequent knowledge of suffering has arisen,
one is bound by six fetters and constrained by two bonds.
The seven latent tendencies increase [in strength];
it is defiled by one stain and enveloped by the secondary afflictions (paryavasthāna).
In the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga), there is no fettering by the knots (saṃyojana),
nor even by the envelopments (paryavasthāna);
one does not possess the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya).
If an ordinary person is bound by the various fetters,
and even entangled by the various envelopments.
As previously stated regarding those who have not yet attained the faculty of "already known" (ājñātāvīndriya), namely ordinary beings;
so too for noble ones on the path of seeing (darśanamārga) who are bound by various fetters (saṃyojana) and even entangled by various envelopments (paryavasthāna).
As previously stated regarding those who have not yet attained the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya) during the path of seeing,
so too during the path of cultivation, they remain bound by all fetters (saṃyojana) and even ensnared by all envelopments (paryavasthāna).
As previously stated regarding those who have not yet attained the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
this same principle should be understood to apply to other chapters by analogy.
This includes the non-possession of the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) bind that consciousness which takes [the object] as its condition and that consciousness which takes [that] conditioned consciousness as its condition?
Up to: "Bound by how many envelopments (*paryavasthāna*)?
Answer: "Those who do not possess the eye-faculty and whose consciousness does not take it as an object are bound by six fetters (*saṃyojana*)."
Bound by the two fetters,
the nine underlying tendencies increase,
and it is defiled by the single stain.
One who is bound by the two envelopments (paryavasthāna) does not possess the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, female, male, suffering, or mental grief.
As for the consciousness that takes these as its object:
The same applies to those who have not attained the female or male faculties, as well as the faculties of suffering and mental grief;
the same is true for the consciousness that takes these as its object.
The principles for the remaining chapters should be understood by analogy with this.
For one who has not yet attained the eye faculty up to the formless realm,
and for whom the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation has been extinguished:
by how many fetters is such a person bound?
Up to: "How many envelopments (paryavasthāna) does one possess?
Answer: One who has not attained the cessation of the eye-faculty—if they are an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) in the desire realm."
Bound by the nine fetters,
bound by the three bonds,
and increased by the ten underlying tendencies.
Tainted by the six impurities and bound by the ten envelopments,
it exists above the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.
Bound by six fetters,
bound by two bonds,
and increased by nine underlying tendencies.
First, being stained by the outflows (*āsrava*);
second, being bound by the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).
If a noble one (*ārya*) is still bound by the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and even entangled by the various entanglements during the paths of seeing and cultivation.
As previously stated regarding noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire while on the paths of seeing and cultivation,
the same applies to those who do not possess the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, female, male, pleasure, or pain, as well as the faculty of cessation.
Regarding the distinction:
one who has not yet attained the cessation of the female or male faculties and the faculty of suffering should be said to exist in the second dhyāna or above.
Regarding those who have not yet accomplished the cessation of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
one should say they are either bound by all fetters in the third dhyāna or are situated above the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Regarding those who have not achieved the extinction of the faculty of joy:
if an ordinary person in the desire realm is bound by all fetters,
they are bound by the nine fetters.
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the ten latent tendencies,
and defiled by the six stains.
Bound by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
situated above the fourth dhyāna,
and fettered by the six knots (*grantha*).
Bound by the two fetters,
the nine underlying tendencies increase,
and it is defiled by the single stain.
Bound by the two envelopments,
when a noble one who is still fully fettered enters the first moment of the state of rightness and departure from corruption,
they are bound by the nine fetters.
Bound by the three fetters,
increased by the ten latent tendencies,
and defiled by the six impurities.
The same applies to one who is bound by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and has not accomplished the cessation of the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
The difference is as follows:
It should be said that this occurs from the second dhyāna upward.
Regarding those who have not yet attained the life-faculty and the five faculties such as faith,
and whose cessation [of these] occurs while they are bound by the various fetters (saṃyojana) and even entangled by the various envelopments (paryavasthāna).
If they are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), they are as described for ordinary persons who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire (*kāmarāga*).
If they are noble ones (*ārya*) on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) or the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
they are as described for noble ones on the path of seeing or the path of cultivation who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire.
Those who do not possess the faculty of equanimity of the mind at the moment of its cessation are:
ordinary persons bound by all fetters,
and noble ones bound by all fetters.
At the very first moment of entering the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma),
one is bound by all nine fetters (saṃyojana) and constrained by the three bonds (bandhana).
The ten underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by the six stains and ensnared by the ten fetters.
The principles for other chapters should be understood by analogy with this:
one does not achieve the cessation of the eye faculty, nor even the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation, up to the formless realm.
Regarding the consciousness that takes [an object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes the conditions for that object as its condition:
by how many fetters (saṃyojana) is it bound,
and so forth, up to by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is it enveloped?
Answer: One who does not achieve the cessation of consciousness conditioned by the eye-faculty is bound by the six fetters and constrained by the two bonds.
The nine underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase therein;
it is defiled by one stain (mala) and bound by the envelopments (paryavasthāna).
One does not possess the consciousness that has the cessation of the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, pleasure, or joy as its object; likewise,
one does not possess the consciousness that has the cessation of the female, male, pain, or grief faculties as its object,
nor the consciousness that takes that [cessation] as its object-condition.
The meaning of the other chapters should be understood by analogy with this:
one does not possess the eye faculty,
and so on, up to the formless realm.
Regarding the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) bind it,
and so on, up to how many envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) enshroud it?
Answer: One who has not accomplished the path that severs the eye-faculty is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) in the desire realm,
bound by the nine fetters (saṃyojana).
Bound by the three bonds,
with the ten latent tendencies increasing,
and defiled by the six impurities.
Bound by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
situated above the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*),
and fettered by the six knots (*grantha*).
Bound by the two fetters,
the nine underlying tendencies increase,
and it is defiled by the single stain.
Bound by the two envelopments;
if a noble one is bound by the fetters of the paths of seeing and cultivation,
up to being enveloped by the various envelopments.
As it is stated regarding those noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire while on the paths of seeing and cultivation,
so it is also for those who have not yet accomplished the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, female, male, pleasure, or pain, and who are on the path of abandonment.
Regarding the distinctions:
one who has not accomplished the path for abandoning the female or male faculties should be said to be in the second dhyāna or above;
one who has not accomplished the path for abandoning the faculty of pleasure should be said to be in the third dhyāna or above.
One should say that it exists in the third dhyāna prior to the arising of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*),
as well as in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and above, for those who have not yet accomplished the path of abandoning joy (*prīti-indriya*).
If an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is in the desire realm (kāmadhātu),
they are bound by the nine fetters (saṃyojana) and bound by the three bonds (bandhana).
The ten latent dispositions increase therein;
it is defiled by the six stains and ensnared by the ten fetters.
Above the fourth dhyāna,
one is bound by six fetters and constrained by two bonds.
The nine underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by one stain and bound by the envelopments.
If a noble one is bound by the fetters of the paths of seeing and cultivation,
or even enveloped by the envelopments,
it is as described for those noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire while on the paths of seeing and cultivation.
The same applies to those who have not accomplished the path of abandonment regarding the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
The difference is that one should state that they exist from the second dhyāna upwards.
Those who have not accomplished the severance of the path of the five faculties, such as the life-faculty and faith,
whether they be ordinary worldlings or noble ones,
remain bound by various fetters and even ensnared by various envelopments.
As previously stated regarding those in the desire realm who do not possess the faculty of the eye,

it was explained that both ordinary beings and noble ones [do not possess] the path of abandonment for the faculty of mind and the faculty of equanimity. Regarding those who do not possess the path of abandonment for these:
Whether they be ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) or noble ones (*ārya*),
those bound by the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and even those entangled by the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*)—

as previously explained regarding ordinary persons and noble ones in the desire realm who have not yet attained the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and have not yet severed the path— [the same applies here].
The principles of the other chapters should be understood accordingly:
one does not possess the eye faculty, nor the path that abandons the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned by cultivation, up to and including the formless realm.
Regarding the consciousness that takes [an object] as its condition and the consciousness that takes the conditions for that object as its condition:
by how many fetters (saṃyojana) is it bound,
and so on, up to by how many envelopments (paryavasthāna) is it ensnared?
Answer: One who has not accomplished the consciousness conditioned by the female faculty, the path of abandonment,
and the object-condition is bound by six fetters and bound by two bonds.
The nine underlying tendencies increase therein;
it is defiled by one stain and bound by the envelopments.
The same applies to those who do not possess the male faculty, the faculty of suffering, or the faculty of grief, regarding the consciousness that takes the path of abandonment as its object.
The principles for other chapters should be understood by analogy with this.
The remaining sections of the *Viniścaya* should be explained according to the preceding method.

Section Three: The Aggregate of Wisdom (Jñānaskandha). Chapter One: The Sub-section on the Factors of Training (Śaikṣāṅga-nirdeśa). Part One of One. As the Blessed One has said:
One who is training in the path of practice achieves the eight factors of training.
How many of these does he achieve in the past?
Having already grasped the meaning of such chapters as "How many are future?
and "How many are present," one should next provide a detailed explanation.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra:
The learner (śaikṣa) who has accomplished the tracks of practice accomplishes the eight branches of the learner;
the Arhat whose outflows are exhausted (kṣīṇāsrava) accomplishes the ten branches of the non-learner (aśaikṣa).
Although the sūtra states this, [it does not mean that these factors exist simultaneously].
Yet it does not state how many of those are accomplished in the past or how many in the future.
Regarding the present section on "Number":
the Sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Those points not yet explained therein shall now be set forth.
Furthermore, it is in order to refute the tenets of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that the past and the future lack a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Although it exists in the present, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is to refute that [opponent's] intention and to demonstrate that the past and future truly exist so that they may be established;
for if they did not exist, they could not be established.
Just as with a second head,
since the sixth aggregate and so forth can be established, we know they truly exist.
Furthermore, it is to demonstrate that dharmas of the present age are necessarily conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and subject to arising and ceasing.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that there is no real nature of attainment or non-attainment,
such as the Dārṣṭāntikas.
They explain that when sentient beings are not separated from phenomena, they are said to be "endowed" with them;
when separated from phenomena, they are said to be "not endowed.
Both are merely conventional designations.
Just as when five fingers are joined they are conventionally designated as a "fist," yet it is not a fist when they are separated, so too is this case.
Question: For what reason do they hold such a view?
The answer is that he holds this view based on a sūtra.
Specifically, the sūtra states:
"There is a wheel-turning monarch who possesses the seven jewels."
If the nature of possession were substantially existent,
then because of possessing the wheel-treasure and the divine jewel-treasure,
the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) would be destroyed.
Why is this? Because they are both sentient beings and non-sentient beings,
as they comprise the precious elephant and the precious horse.
Furthermore, they should also be included among those subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because they are both animals and humans.
Because he has attained the jewel of a woman, his body must again perish. Why is this?
Because it is both a male body and a female body.
Because he has achieved the status of a lord of the army and a minister of the treasury, his karma must again be destroyed.
Why is this? Because of the confusion between ruler and minister.
To avoid such an error, it must be established that the nature of possession (*prāpti*) is not substantially real.
To refute that intention and demonstrate that the nature of possession is indeed substantially real, [the author] states:
"If it were otherwise, it would contradict the sūtra."
As it is said:
"The learner who has accomplished the path of practice accomplishes the eight factors of the learner;
the Arhat whose outflows are exhausted accomplishes the ten factors of the non-learner."
When a noble one manifests a contaminated mind,
they should not possess past and future uncontaminated dharmas;
how then could they possess the eightfold or tenfold path?
Furthermore, it contradicts other sūtras,
such as when it says:
"Such a person (pudgala)..."
One accomplishes both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
When those wholesome dharmas are present before one,
one should not accomplish unwholesome dharmas.
If unwholesome dharmas manifest,
one should not be endowed with wholesome dharmas;
likewise, when indeterminate dharmas manifest.
One would then fail to accomplish wholesome and unwholesome dharmas;
how then can it be said that one accomplishes wholesome and unwholesome dharmas?
Furthermore, this contradicts other sūtras.
As it is said:

"One who accomplishes the seven wholesome qualities dwells much in joy and happiness in this very life; by practicing with proper diligence, they will surely be able to exhaust the outflows. The seven wholesome qualities consist in knowing the Dharma, knowing the meaning, and so forth, as explained at length."
Among these seven, when one is present, one would not possess the other six wholesome dharmas;
and when another dharma arises and becomes present,
one would not possess all seven.
How is it that one accomplishes the seven wholesome dharmas?
Furthermore, this contradicts other sūtras,
as it is said:
The Tathāgata has accomplished the ten powers.
When one power arises and is present before him,
he should not be endowed with the other nine.
If other dharmas were to manifest before him,
he would not possess these ten;
how then does the Tathāgata possess the ten powers?
Furthermore, there is another fault:
it would follow that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), when an undefiled mind is present before them,
would become those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Because they have not yet abandoned all afflictions of the three realms,
those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) who give rise to a contaminated mind (*sāsrava-citta*) in the present moment would consequently become ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Because one does not accomplish all the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training,
let there be no such error;
therefore, the nature of accomplishment is definitely and truly existent.
Question: If the nature of possession (*prāpti*) were a real entity (*dravyasat*), how would one interpret the sūtra cited by the preceding Dārṣṭāntika?
Answer: Because a wheel-turning monarch possesses sovereign power over those [objects] and enjoys them according to his will, as if they were already possessed.
The name "accomplishment" is established [based on this].
If one were to entirely deny the existence of a real nature of accomplishment,
how could the name "accomplishment" be established with respect to that?
Furthermore, there are other masters who maintain that there is the possession [of dharmas] and the non-possession [of them].
They argue as follows:
"The nature of possession must be substantially existent because it possesses functional activity."
Since the nature of non-accomplishment possesses no functional activity,
how can it be substantially real?
To refute that attachment, it is shown that non-accomplishment is likewise substantially real.
If that which is not established were not substantially existent,
then it would likewise not exist as a substantially established nature dependent upon its counterpart;

therefore, like the cases of shadow and light, darkness and day, cold and heat, and so forth, these things are established through mutual dependence, and if one is missing, the other cannot be established.
This is also the case here.
Furthermore, because the nature of non-accomplishment and the nature of accomplishment are closely opposed to one another, both are truly existent;
just as greed and non-greed, hatred and non-hatred, and delusion and non-delusion are closely opposed to one another, they are all truly existent.
Furthermore, if that which is not accomplished were not of a truly existent nature, one could not designate it as a dharma through which afflictions are abandoned. Why is this?
It is not the case that the arising of the Noble Path abandons the various afflictions.
Just as a knife cuts an object,
or as a stone grinds incense,
so it is when the various noble paths manifest before one.
It causes the afflictions that have already been established to be extinguished,
and it causes those afflictions that have not yet been established to arise;
at that time, this is called the severance of all afflictions.
Others again maintain that the path is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
such as the Vibhajyavādins.
They state this as follows:
The unique, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is eternally abiding and indestructible;
as various Buddhas appear in the world, although those who realize it differ, that which is realized is without distinction.
It is like a magnificent and exquisitely adorned elephant-king;
although many people may ride it one after another in succession,
that elephant-king remains the same from beginning to end.
Question: For what reason do they hold this position?
Answer: They rely upon the sūtras;
as it is said in a sūtra:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Because I have realized the ancient path, I know that the Noble Path is certainly unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This was said to refute their attachment and to reveal that the Noble Path falls within the three periods of time."
Concentration is necessarily a conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomenon and not an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) one,
because it falls within the three periods of time.
Furthermore, [some] maintain that the essence of the Noble Path is unconditioned.
This would contradict the sūtra.
As the sūtra says:
"There was a lay follower named Viśākhā."
He went to where the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā was and asked her,
"Is the Noble Path conditioned?"
[The opponent asks: "Is this conditioned or unconditioned?
The bhikṣuṇī replied:
"The Noble Path is conditioned, because it falls within the three periods of time."
Question: If the noble path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), how should one interpret the sūtra cited by the Vibhajyavādins?
Answer: It is called the "ancient path" because of five points of similarity.
First, they are similar in terms of the stage (*bhūmi*),
because all Buddhas attain enlightenment (*bodhi*) by relying upon the fourth dhyāna.
Second, they are similar in terms of their preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Because all Buddhas have practiced the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) throughout three incalculable eons (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa) until they attained perfection,
their three objects of focus are similar;
because all Buddhas realize enlightenment by taking the principles of the Four Noble Truths as their object of focus.
Fourth, similarity of aspect (*ākāra*):
because all Buddhas cultivate the Noble Path by means of the sixteen aspects, such as suffering (*duḥkha*) and impermanence (*anitya*).
Fifth, similarity of activity (*kārya*).
All Buddhas, by means of the power of the untainted path,
sever all afflictions within their own bodies and also cause immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
If one does not rely on this interpretation of the term "old path" but instead insists that it refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*),
then according to that same sutra, when it speaks of an "old city" or an "old capital," would those old cities and capitals also be unconditioned phenomena?
Furthermore, if a sutra states that one realizes the former noble path, one would then hold that the noble path is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Yet, the *Sūtra* also says:
When a snake sheds its old skin, is that old skin of the snake an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)?
As a verse in the Gāthās says:
"If one cuts off craving without remainder, Like a lotus flower in the water..."
"A bhikṣu abandons this and that, like a snake shedding its old skin.
Just as with the "old city" and other such examples, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are likewise [transient].

The principle regarding the "ancient noble path" (*paurāṇamārga*) should also be understood in this way. This treatise is composed in order to refute the assertions of other schools and to reveal the correct reasoning regarding all phenomena.
As the Blessed One has said:
"The practitioner on the path of training accomplishes the eight factors of training.
In this context, what are the eight factors of training?
This refers to those who have accomplished the training in right view up to right concentration.
Question: Who accomplishes this—is it the accomplishment of the dharma, or the accomplishment of the person (pudgala)?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
Both positions possess errors. Why is this?
If phenomena were established,
then since all phenomena are devoid of activity,
among these phenomena that lack activity, what phenomenon could establish what phenomenon, and by what phenomenon would anything be established?
If a person were established,
then in truth and in the ultimate sense,
a person would be entirely unfindable.
Since there is no truly existent *pudgala*,
how can it be said that such a person accomplishes phenomena?
One should answer as follows:
There is neither the accomplishment of non-dharmas nor the accomplishment of a *pudgala*.
However, there is the reality of the nature of accomplishment and the nature of non-accomplishment,
yet there is no real accomplisher or non-accomplisher.

Just as there truly exist the causes and effects of affliction and purification, bondage and liberation, saṃsāra and cessation, birth and death, the various karmas and their maturation, as well as the paths and the fruits of the paths;
yet there is no one who truly undergoes affliction and purification, up to and including those who cultivate the path and realize the fruits of the path.
There is one who says:
"Phenomena are established.
Question: If that is so, since phenomena lack functional activity, how can they be established?
Answer: Although all phenomena lack functional activity (*kāritra*), they do possess efficacy (*śakti*).
Question: If that were so, the sense base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) would entail the other eleven bases, and the eleven bases would likewise entail the sense base of the eye.
Answer: Even if explained according to this principle, there is no fault, because all possess the functional capacity to mutually induce one another.
Evaluation:
It should be stated thus:
that which is capable of accomplishment is neither the dharma nor the person (pudgala).
Because there is no truly existent activity,
and because the *pudgala* is not substantially real;
nevertheless, when the four or five aggregates arise, [the designation "person" occurs].
To be accompanied by such types of acquisitions (*prāpti*) is called "possession" (*samanvāgama*);
to be accompanied by such types of non-acquisitions (*aprāpti*) is called "non-possession.
Question: If this is so, how should one interpret the sūtra?
As it is said:
"Such a person accomplishes wholesome dharmas as well as unwholesome dharmas.
This answer was given by the Blessed One regarding the aggregates (skandhas) from the perspective of conventional truth (saṃvṛti).
It is not said that a person (pudgala) truly exists as the one who accomplishes (samanvāgata) various dharmas.
[Question: What is the meaning of "accomplishment" in this context?
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke as follows:
The meaning of "non-interruption" is the meaning of "accomplishment.
Question: If that is so, then a person who is bound by all fetters would be said to have accomplished all phenomena.
"They should all be accomplished.
Answer: "They are not all accomplished, because there are those who have not yet attained them.
He further says this:
"Already obtained" has the meaning of "accomplished.
Question: If that were so, one who is beyond training (aśaikṣa) would have already obtained the dharmas of one in training (śaikṣa) and should therefore accomplish them.
Answer: No, because one does not accomplish those [dharmas] since they have already been abandoned.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The meaning of non-abandonment is the meaning of accomplishment.
Question: If that were so, then one in training (śaikṣa) would also accomplish those dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), since they do not abandon them.
The answer is: one does not possess it because one has not yet attained it.
Furthermore, it is stated that the meaning of "possession" (samanvāgama) is the state of having already attained something and not yet having relinquished it.
This statement is logical,
because when a dharma has already been acquired and has not yet been relinquished, one necessarily possesses it.
The Venerable [Vasumitra] says:

Sentient beings in the conventional world do not exist apart from the accomplishment of provisional designations regarding all phenomena, because in the ultimate sense there is no nature of accomplishment.
Question: For what reason is "training" (śikṣā) called training, and why is that which is to be trained in called the "dharma of training" (śikṣitavyadharma)?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
Both positions entail errors. Why is this?
If one is called a "learner" (śaikṣa) because they are training in what is to be learned,
how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the Section on Concentration (samādhiskandha)?
As it is said:
There is that which is training and not what is trained by training;
this refers to one who is in training abiding in their own nature,
or who is called a "trainee" because they have attained the dharmas of training.
How should the statement in the Sūtra be reconciled?
As it is said:
The Buddha addressed Śivaka, saying:
Because one trains in what is to be trained in, it is called "training" (*śaikṣa*).
One should answer thus:
because one trains in what is to be trained in, it is called "training."
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret what is stated in the *Samādhiskandha*?
Answer: That passage refers to what is conventionally designated by those in training (*śaikṣa*);
it means that when one is training or not training in what is to be learned.
The world collectively regards him as a scholar;
therefore, the masters of the fundamental treatise say that he is a scholar while in fact he is not.
Furthermore, his aspiration for what is to be learned does not cease.
Based on that mental resolve, it is called "training" (*śaikṣa*).
Some say: because one has attained the dharmas of training, it is termed "training."
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret what is stated in the sūtras?
Answer: The sūtra makes this statement based on the fact that he did not cease his resolve nor abandon his application of effort.
That is to say, although a learner (śaikṣa) may give rise to either a wholesome mind or an unwholesome mind.
Even when they give rise to a neutral state of mind,
because they never abandon the mind directed toward nirvāṇa and its preparatory application,
they are at all times said to be "training in what is to be trained."
However, there are also times when one does not study what ought to be studied,
such as when a person on the road pauses briefly to rest. At that time,
someone might ask:
"Where do you wish to go?
The man replied,
"I wish to go to such-and-such a direction."
Because the mind does not abandon the state of "entering," it is called "entering" even while one is abiding;
since this is the path of practice for those in training (*śaikṣa*), it is called the "path of practice of one in training.
Question: The path of practice of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is more luminous, pure, excellent, and sublime than that of those in training.
For what reason is it said that there is only the path of training (*śaikṣa-mārga*)?
Answer: One should also say that there is a path of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa-mārga*); its non-mention here is because the explanation is incomplete (*sāvasesa-vacana*).
Furthermore, since the beginning has already been explained, the end is likewise explained;
thus, when the path of training (*śaikṣa*) has been explained, the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is also explained.
Moreover, it is intended to manifest that each possesses its own distinct excellence.
This means that in the stage of training (śaikṣa), the path of practice (pratipad) is preeminent;
in the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa), liberation (vimukti) is preeminent.
It is like a king and his minister, each having their own distinctive excellence.
That is to say, the king’s majesty and nobility are preeminent in subduing others;
the minister’s prowess in affairs and warfare is preeminent.
Furthermore, the path of training (*śaikṣa-mārga*) is capable of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Arhat (aśaikṣa), having conquered the enemies that are the afflictions,
is not like this. Furthermore, the śaikṣa practices the path in order to abandon the afflictions,
diligently cultivating the preparatory application.
It is not so for those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, the meaning of "repeated practice" is the meaning of "path" (pratipad);
those in training (śaikṣa) practice repeatedly.
The one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is not like this;
therefore, the path of practice for one beyond training is not mentioned.
How many past, how many future, and how many present [factors] does he possess?
Answer: If, based on the concentration with vitarka and vicāra, the vision of a beginner manifests, there are none from the past;
eight are present and future.
Regarding "the concentration with vitarka and vicāra":
this refers to the preparatory stage (anāgamya) and the first dhyāna. As for the "basis":
[it refers to the physical body].
Some say that co-arising is the basis.
Others say that the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) is the meaning of "basis" in this context.
The commentary states:
It should be explained in this way:
those two stages together are designated as the basis.
Initially, there are four kinds.
First is the initial entry into the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma-avakrānti*);
this refers to entering the state of rightness and separation from birth for the first time by relying on that particular stage (*bhūmi*).
Second, the first attainment of the fruit,
meaning that one first attains the fruit of training (śaikṣa-phala) based on that stage. Third,
the first transformation of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra).
