This refers to the initial refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) for one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) based on that stage, thereby becoming one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Fourth is the initial separation from defilements;
this refers to having already separated from all defilements by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
This is because, at the very beginning, the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) arises and becomes manifest based on those stages.
Here, the treatise is composed generally with reference to the four initial [stages],
yet throughout the various positions, there are instances where these are complete and instances where they are incomplete.
One should carefully examine and discern according to what is appropriate.
Regarding the statement "the vision of one in training manifests before him," it is asked:
does the vision of one who is neither in training nor beyond training (naśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa) also manifest before such a person?
That is also the vision of one in training (*śaikṣa*),
because it is the vision arising in those who are in training. Why,
then, is it not stated here that the vision of one in training manifests for those in training?
Although one has promised to speak in this way,
if one does not speak,
it should be understood that within this context there is an intentional, incomplete statement (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*).
Furthermore, in this context, the "view of one in training" (śaikṣadṛṣṭi) refers precisely to the view of one who is still training;
it does not refer to the view of one who is no longer in training (aśaikṣa). Therefore, one should not find fault with this.
As for the claim that [the past] does not exist:
This means as previously stated:
when the first moment manifests, there is no past at all,
because not even a single thought-moment has yet arisen and ceased.
If one has already produced and extinguished [the paths], obtained the fruit, or undergone a transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*),
or because of falling back and relinquishing them,
there are eight future [paths].
This means that at the very first moment, one fully cultivates the eight branches of training for the future;
as for the eight present ones,
it is because at that time the eight branches are manifested in the present.
Once that has ceased, it is not lost.
If one again relies on the concentration with directed thought and evaluation (*savitarka-savicāra*) and trains so that the vision of the present manifests,
there are eight [factors] belonging to the past, future, and present.
In this context,
"that" refers to those eight factors.
"Having ceased" means:
This refers to impermanence.
Regarding "that which is not lost after cessation," it means that the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) is lost due to three causes and conditions.
First, because of attaining the fruit;
second, because of the transformation of the faculties;
third, because of falling away and relinquishing.
Because these three conditions are absent, it is said that [the action] is not lost.
"If, moreover, based on...
and so forth refers to the second moment and subsequent moments.
Furthermore, based on the meditative concentration with applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), the training and vision (*śikṣā-darśana*) manifest before one.
Question: For what reason does one again give rise to the training and vision of this stage?
Answer: Because of the mindfulness of repaying kindness.
This means that because one has relied upon this stage to destroy the enemy of the afflictions,
one again arises [in it] out of mindfulness of repaying that kindness;
it is like how, after subduing an enemy with armor and weapons, one does so once more.
Furthermore, one repeatedly cultivates, cherishes, conceals, and guards it.
Moreover, for four reasons, one again gives rise to it with renewed emphasis:
first, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Second, for the sake of sporting in merit;
third, for the sake of contemplating one's original deeds;
fourth, for the sake of enjoying the noble wealth.
Regarding the eight past [factors]:
this refers to those that have already arisen and ceased at the moment of the first instant, which are accomplished from the second instant onward.
Regarding the eight future and present [factors] each: they are as previously described.
It should be understood that once those have ceased, they are not lost. If one,
relying on a meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without vitarka and vicāra, brings forth the training in view,
there are eight [factors] in the past and future, and seven in the present.
Regarding "the meditative absorption without vitarka and vicāra" herein, this refers to the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
Question: Why is the intermediate dhyāna not mentioned?
Regarding what was promised but not yet explained:
one should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, in the intermediate dhyāna and the three subsequent stages, there is neither increase nor decrease in their constituent factors (aṅga).
Therefore, they are not mentioned.
That there are eight each for the past and the future should be understood as previously explained.
As for the seven of the present:
With the exception of right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), because that [state] is without applied thought (*avitarka*),
once it has ceased, it is not lost.
If, relying on the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), one brings the training in vision (dṛṣṭi-śikṣā) to presence,
there are eight [factors] in the past and future,
and four in the present.
Regarding the immaterial attainments herein, they refer to the first three immaterial attainments.
Question: Why is the fourth immaterial attainment not mentioned?
Answer: Because that stage lacks the noble path (āryamārga), and because it will be explained later that one gives rise to a conventional mind (saṃvṛtijñāna).
Regarding the fact that there are eight [minds] each for the past and future, this should be understood as previously stated.
Regarding the four present [factors]:
excluding right thought, right speech, and right livelihood, because these do not exist in that stage, they are not lost once they have ceased;
thus, whether one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) or brings a mundane mind (*laukika-citta*) into presence, they remain.
There are eight in the past and future, but none in the present.
Herein, one who enters the meditative attainment of cessation refers to one who is correctly abiding in the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
The mundane mind refers to the tainted (sāsrava) meditative mind that emerges from the attainment of cessation or from other tainted meditative attainments,
or the arising of other tainted meditative minds.
Regarding the fact that there are eight [factors] each for the past and the future:
this refers to the eight branches of the first-attained concentration with vitarka and vicāra in the past,
as well as those cultivated in the future.
The present non-existent [factors] are absent because the noble path is absent during the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
and because the eight untainted path-factors (*anāsrava-mārgāṅga*) do not arise during the time of a conventional mind (*saṃvṛti-citta*). If,
relying on a meditative concentration without applied or sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra-samādhi*), the beginner brings the vision (*darśana*) into manifestation.
In the past, there are none;
in the future, eight;
in the present, seven.
In this context, the meaning should be understood as previously explained.
The meditative absorption without vitarka and without vicāra consists of the latter three dhyānas.
The first [dhyāna] possesses all four factors, as described in detail above.
The explanation regarding the observation of the meaning is also as previously stated.
As for the non-existence of the past:
at the initial moment, not even a single thought has yet arisen and ceased.
Because the three conditions for that which has already arisen and ceased have been relinquished.
Regarding the eight of the future:
this means that at that very first moment, one fully cultivates the eight branches of training pertaining to the future.
Regarding the seventh [factor] of the present:
because that stage lacks right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*),
once it has ceased, it is not lost.
If, moreover, one relies on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra and brings the training in view to manifestation,
there are seven [factors] in the past and present,
and eight in the future.
Regarding this, the phrase "once it has ceased, it is not lost" and so forth is explained as previously stated.
As for the "seven past [dharmas]," they are said to be accomplished from the second moment onward.
At the very first moment, seven [moments] have already arisen and ceased;
once they have ceased, they are not lost.
This is the case when relying on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
When the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) manifests before one,
seven [factors] are past and eight are future.
There are four in the present.
Among these, the seven past ones refer to those that have arisen and ceased in the first moment.
The rest is as explained previously.
Once that [attainment] has ceased, it is not lost;
whether one enters the attainment of cessation or brings a mundane mind (*laukika-citta*) into manifestation, [the seeds remain].
Seven in the past,
eight in the future,
and none in the present.
In this regard, everything is as previously stated;
it should be understood that once those [states] have ceased, they are not lost,
provided one relies on a meditative concentration accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
When the vision of training manifests,
there are seven past [factors],
and eight future and present [factors].
Among these, the seven past factors refer to the seven limbs of the concentration without vitarka and vicāra that first arose previously;
the eight future factors refer to...

That which is cultivated in the future at the very first stage is explained as occurring after the conventional mind that follows entry into the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
As for the arising of the concentration with vitarka and vicāra:
This shall be analyzed later. If,
based on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one first practices so that insight (*darśana*) manifests,
there is no past [insight].
There are eight in the future and four in the present; herein,
these refer to the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
Regarding the first of the formless attainments among the aforementioned three,
this treatise explains it solely in terms of detachment from defilement.
Because, having become free from all defilements by means of the mundane path, one first gives rise to the untainted [path] as the three formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti) manifest;
for there is no sense of entering the path of seeing (darśanamārga) while relying on the formless [realms].
There is no entry into the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by means of the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, there is no sense in attaining the fruits of training (*śaikṣa-phala*) based on the formless attainments (*ārūpya*),
nor is there any sense in refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) during the stage of training while relying on the formless realm.
Therefore, there is no initial attainment of the fruit or the transformation of faculties;
the rest is as explained previously.
Question: Do the impure formless attainments necessarily arise with pure dhyāna as their preparatory practice?
The untainted formless attainments (*anāsrava-ārūpya-samāpatti*) should likewise necessarily arise by taking untainted dhyāna as their preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Why, then, is it said here that for one who is first learning, the vision [of reality] manifests based on the formless attainments?
"Is it not the case that one has already accomplished the eight limbs in the past?
Answer: "The untainted path-limbs belong both to the dhyānas and to the formless attainments.
Those belonging to the dhyānas, although accomplished in the past,"
However, for those belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they do not possess the past [factors].
Therefore, it is said that there are no eight branches in the past. Some say this:
There is one who, having attained the fruit of non-returner by means of the mundane path,
does not give rise to the untainted path,
but again uses the mundane path to become detached from the defilements of the four dhyānas.
Alternatively, when one has already become free from the defilements of the three formless realms and first gives rise to an untainted (anāsrava) formless absorption,
that past [state] does not possess the eight branches of the noble path.
Therefore, this statement was made:
in the past, there is absolutely none; that which has been extinguished is not lost.
Furthermore, when one relies on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and the training in vision (*dṛṣṭi-śikṣā*) manifests before one, there are four [factors] in the past and present.
There are eight future [factors].
Among these, the four past ones refer to the first four factors of the initial moment previously mentioned.
Regarding the "eight future [factors]":
this refers to the eight branches previously cultivated in the future.
The remainder is as explained before.
Once those have ceased, they are not lost; if one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti),
or if a mundane mind (laukikacitta) manifests,
there are four past [dharmas].
There are eight in the future and none in the present;
all matters herein are as previously stated.
It should be understood that once those have ceased, they are not lost.
If one practices the training in the concentration with vitarka and vicāra, and the vision of the present manifests,
there are four past [factors].
There are eight in the future and present.
Among these, the four past ones refer to the four factors that first arise in the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
Regarding the "eight future [factors]":
this refers to cultivating the eight factors of the future at that time.
Question: Is it not the case that immediately after a formless absorption (ārūpya-samāpatti), one is necessarily unable to give rise to a meditative absorption accompanied by vitarka and vicāra?
Why is it stated in this context in such a manner?
The answer is: one should know that what is taught here is the sequential order;
it is not a fixed sequence, but rather an exposition given in accordance with the logical progression of the teaching.
If one does not rely on meditative concentration but teaches in accordance with it, having already attained its cessation, one does not lose it.
If one relies on a concentration free from applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra-samādhi*) and the vision of training manifests before one,
there are four past [factors].
There are eight in the future and seven in the present.
Among these, there are four in the past.
This refers to the four factors first arising based on the formless attainments;
as for the "eight future ones," these are the eight factors cultivated in the future by means of those same attainments.
Question: Regarding the eight factors of the concentration with vitarka and vicāra that arose immediately prior, they should all remain undissipated upon entering the past.
Why, then, is it said that only four [factors] remain in the past?
Answer: What is stated here regarding the past and future refers to their initial arising and cultivation;
it does not refer to what arises or is cultivated in subsequent stages, and therefore there is no fault.
Because they manifest at all times in the present, they are explained according to their arising.
Question: What kind of trainee (*śaikṣa*) is being described here?
Answer: It refers to those trainees who enter into all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) in their proper sequence.
This refers to ascending the steps in successive order, as follows:
first, the practitioner in training enters the concentration with vitarka and vicāra;
next, they enter the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra.
Next, one enters the formless attainments;
next, one enters the attainment of cessation;
finally, one gives rise to a conventional mind.
This is what is meant by "one who trains in this way.
If such a trainee first enters the concentration with directed thought and evaluation,
and subsequently enters the concentration without directed thought and evaluation.
Next, one enters the formless attainments;
next, one enters the attainment of cessation;
finally, one gives rise to an untainted mind.
These scholars are not what is being discussed here;
as stated in the *Saṃgītiparyāya*:
"If there is a certain class of person (*pudgala*)."
That which possesses the twelve links of dependent origination is what is here taught;
that which does not possess them is not what is here taught.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
First, one sees the physical form of a woman, dignified and beautiful, a sight that all delight in;
next, one sees her in old age;
and next, one sees her afflicted by illness.
Next, one sees her passing away;
next, one sees the various stages of her decomposition after death.
Such is the woman described in this sutra.
If it were not so, it would not be as taught in the Sūtras;
those who study this should know that it is likewise here.
The critique says:
It should be stated thus: herein,
all those in training are collectively referred to,
according to each respective practitioner in training.
Since all the factors of training (śikṣā-aṅga) arising within the various stages are fully subsumed therein,
one should know that there are four distinctions in the paths of practice (pratipad):
first, the path of difficult progress with slow intuition (duḥkhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā).
2. The practice that is difficult and quick;
3. The practice that is easy and slow;
4. The practice that is easy and quick.
However, the tracks of practice should be described as being of one kind:
namely, the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,
which is the practice leading to the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, and death within the world of existence.
Alternatively, one should speak of two:
namely, the practice leading to the cessation of name-and-form,
and the practice leading to the cessation of form.
Alternatively, one should speak of three,
namely, the practices for the cessation of the three realms;
or one should speak of five.
This refers to the practice leading to the cessation of the five aggregates;
alternatively, it should be said that there are twelve,
referring to the practice leading to the cessation of the twelve-linked dependent origination.
Alternatively, one should say they are immeasurable, because their distinctions in terms of continuity and moments are without limit.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One explain them extensively as one, two, or three?
Why are these four modes of practice established by summarizing the twelve [factors] and so forth?
Answer: Because of three reasons.
First, by way of the stage;
second, by way of the faculty;
third, by way of the person (pudgala).
This is the general explanation.
To explain it specifically, however,
it is based on only two matters.
This refers to [classification] by way of stage (*bhūmi*), by way of faculty (*indriya*), or by way of stage and person (*pudgala*).
Regarding "by way of stage and faculty," this refers to the *anāgamya* (preparatory) concentration.
The noble path belonging to those of dull faculties within the intermediate dhyāna and the three formless absorptions is called the "difficult practice with slow progress."
The noble paths belonging to those of sharp faculties on these various stages are called the "path of swift progress with ease";
the noble paths belonging to those of dull faculties on the four fundamental dhyānas are called the "path of slow progress with ease."
In these very stages, the noble paths belonging to those of sharp faculties are called the "path of easy and swift progress," both by reason of the stage and by reason of the individual (pudgala).
That is to say: the preparatory concentration (anāgamya),
the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara),
and the three formless concentrations (ārūpyasamāpatti).
The noble path of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those liberated through conviction (*śraddhādhimukta*),
and those liberated with delay (*samayavimukta*) is called the "path of difficult progress" (*duḥkhā pratipad*).

This same [path], when belonging to those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), those attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and those liberated without delay (*asamayavimukta*), [is called the path of easy progress].
All noble paths are called the "difficult progress with quick realization.

For those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those whose conviction is based on faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), and those who are liberated through time (*samayavimukta*) within the four fundamental dhyānas,
all their noble paths are called the "easy progress with slow realization."

The noble paths belonging to those on these various stages who are practitioners by dharma-following (dharmānusārin), vision-attainers (dṛṣṭiprāpta), or those liberated at any time (asamayavimukta) are called the "path of easy and swift progress.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of these four paths of progress?
The answer is that they have five aggregates or four aggregates as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Specifically, those situated in the dhyānas and their preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) have five aggregates as their intrinsic nature,
while those situated in the formless realms (*ārūpya*) have four aggregates as their intrinsic nature.
This is called the intrinsic nature of the path of practice (*pratipad-svabhāva*).
Having already explained its intrinsic nature— its substance, essence, characteristics, divisions,
and fundamental nature— I shall now explain the reason for it.
Question: For what reason is it called "the path of practice" (pratipad)?
What is the meaning of "path of practice"? Answer: "Path" (pratipad) means thorough penetration (prativedha), and "practice" (padā) means the track (mārga).
To be able to correctly penetrate and proceed toward nirvāṇa is the meaning of "path of practice.
As for the path of practice that is painful and slow:
Question: Since the Noble Path is neither of the nature of painful feeling nor associated with painful feeling,
why is it called "suffering"?
Answer: Because the formless attainments of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are difficult to accomplish, the noble path (*āryamārga*) arising therein is termed "suffering.
Because the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*) are easy to accomplish, the noble path arising therein is termed "pleasure."
This detailed analysis is as previously set forth in the section on the four dhyānas within the *Saṃyukta-skandha*.
Question: For what reason is the noble path described as "slow"?
Answer: Because it is the noble path generated by those of dull faculties.
Because they cannot swiftly proceed toward ultimate nirvana, they are said to be "slow.
Because the noble paths generated by those of sharp faculties swiftly proceed toward nirvana, they are said to be "quick."
Question: Is one who possesses faith-resolve (śraddhādhimukta) and swiftly attains nirvāṇa superior to one who has attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta)?
For instance, while one with faith-resolve who practices with diligence quickly realizes nirvāṇa, one who has attained through vision who is indolent cannot realize it quickly.
As it is said in a verse:
"Non-negligence and negligence, Awakening and sleep—
Like riding swift and slow horses, The diligent practitioner arrives first."
It is as if two people were traveling toward the same destination;
one rides a swift horse,
while the other rides a sluggish horse.
One who rides a swift horse does not reach the destination quickly because they do not travel with diligence;
one who rides a slow horse reaches it quickly because they travel with diligence.
In the same way, those who have attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and those who are liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) both proceed toward nirvāṇa.
If those with faith and resolution who practice with diligence quickly realize nirvāṇa,
whereas those who have attained vision but are indolent cannot quickly realize it,
why is it said that the noble path of dull faculties cannot proceed swiftly and is therefore called "slow"?
The answer is: the intention here is to say that for one who practices with equal diligence, if they are a "vision-attainer" (dṛṣṭiprāpta), they quickly realize [the goal];
because they are not a "one liberated by faith" (śraddhādhimukta), it is said that [the latter] is slow.
Question: Since these four types of practice take the five aggregates or the four aggregates as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), why are they called "universal" (*sāmānya*)? Answer:
Because "universal" refers exclusively to wisdom (*prajñā*) and not to the other aggregates.
The answer is: because wisdom is predominant, they are called only "supernormal powers" (abhijñā).
This is just as, although all five aggregates are present within the path of seeing (darśanamārga), it is designated simply by the name "seeing" because wisdom is predominant.
Just as the conventional wisdoms at the conclusion of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*),
although they have the four or five aggregates as their nature,
are designated simply by the name "wisdom" because wisdom is predominant.
Although the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) has the four or five aggregates as its nature,
it is designated simply by the name "concentration" because meditative absorption (samādhi) is predominant;
the same applies to the path of practice (pratipad).
Therefore, one should not find fault [with this].
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"What is the path of practice that is difficult and slow?"
That is to say, the bhikṣus revile, disparage, and feel aversion toward the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

Question: Since the path of sluggish progress with difficulty (*duḥkhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā*) takes the objects of the four noble truths as its domain, why did the Blessed One speak only of it taking suffering (*duḥkha*) as its object?
The answer is that one should also state that this [conditioning] takes the other three truths as its object;
that it is not so stated is because the explanation is incomplete.
Furthermore, since the Truth of Suffering comes first, it has already been stated that [the cause] takes suffering as its object.
It should be understood that this also refers to taking the other three truths as objects.
Furthermore, in that sutra, only the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) is revealed, not the fundamental stage (*maula*).
That is to say, at the time of the preparatory stage, one gives rise to the aspect of revulsion (*nirveda*) by taking the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as the object.
When reaching the fundamental stage, one takes the Four Noble Truths as objects.
The *Saṃgītiparyāya* states as follows:
"What is the path of practice with sluggish progress?"
This refers to the five faculties, such as faith and so forth, that are dull and not included within the dhyānas.
What is the path of swift progress with suffering?
This refers to the five faculties, such as faith and so forth, that are sharp and not included within the dhyānas.
What is the practice with ease and slow progress?
It refers to the five faculties, such as faith, which are dull and subsumed under meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
What is the practice with ease and quick progress?
This refers to the five faculties—such as faith and so forth—that are subsumed under meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Question: Since these four paths of practice (*pratipad*) have the five aggregates or four aggregates as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), why does that treatise speak only of the sharp and dull [faculties] consisting of the five faculties such as faith?
Answer: This is said in terms of preeminence.
That is to say, among the formations of the five aggregates or four aggregates, the five faculties are the most preeminent.
Furthermore, the five faculties, such as faith and so forth, possess skillful means regarding the tasks to be accomplished.
Because they are able to accomplish [the goal] swiftly and are superior to those with other aggregates, they are specifically mentioned.
Question: Do there exist among the classes of sentient beings those of middling faculties?
If such do exist, why does that treatise not mention them?
If it did not exist, how would one reconcile this with the sūtra?
As the sūtra says:
"There are sentient beings who are born in the world and dwell in the world."
There are those with sharp faculties,
those with middling faculties,
and those with dull faculties.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that there is no such thing as a person of middling faculties.
Why is this? Because there are two types of those who see the path:
first, those who follow the path by faith.
Second is the path of practice in accordance with the Dharma.
The path of cultivation also has two types:
first, the path of liberation through resolute faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).
Second is the path attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta-mārga*).
The path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) also has two types:
first, the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Second, the path of non-periodic liberation;
because there is no third path,
there is no intermediate faculty.
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret the sūtra?
Answer: Those who have received the Buddha’s transformation may have already seen the truths previously.
There are those who realize the truths while still living,
and there are those who realize the truths after death.
Those who realize the truths first are said to possess sharp faculties.
Those who realize the truths in the middle [period] are said to have middling faculties;
those who realize the truths later are said to have dull faculties.
Furthermore, among those who receive the Buddha’s transformation, there are some who realize the truths quickly.
There are those who perceive the truths from afar,
and those who perceive the truths neither near nor far.
Those who perceive the truths nearby are said to possess sharp faculties.
Those who have long since seen the truths, such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others,
are said to be of dull faculties; those such as Subhadra and others are likewise [described].
Those who perceive the truths neither too closely nor too distantly are said to possess medium faculties,
such as Rāṣṭrapāla and others.
Furthermore, there are those who say that there are also those of middling faculties.
[The opponent] asks: "If that is so, why does that treatise not mention them? [The respondent] replies: "It should have mentioned them, yet it did not."
One should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, those of medium faculties are subsumed within both the sharp and the dull. Why is this so?
When describing those of dull faculties, those of middling faculties are called "superior" because they are superior to the dull;
when describing those of sharp faculties, those of middling faculties are called "dull and inferior" because they are inferior to the sharp.
For this reason, the Venerable Vasumitra said:
It should be said that those of medium faculties are included within the category of sharp faculties,
because they are superior to those of dull faculties;
yet, it may also be said that they are included within the category of dull faculties.
Because they possess inferior and sharp faculties,
the Venerable One said:
"Those of middling faculties may be said to be included within either the sharp or the dull."
Yet it cannot be said that they are subsumed under superior or inferior faculties. Why is this?
Because those with sharp and dull faculties each have three grades.
How is this known to be so?
Because the Greatly Awakened One (Mahābuddha), the Solitary Realizers (Pratyekabuddhas), Śāriputra,
and others are all included within the lineage of those who practice in accordance with the Dharma (Dharmānusārin-gotra).
How could these three types of faculties be similar? Since there are already three grades within the nature of sharp faculties,
we know that the nature of dull faculties likewise possesses three grades.
The two paths—the sharp and the dull—each consist of three grades;
therefore, the sūtras state that there are three grades of faculties (*indriya*).
This is because a third path cannot be found.
The Abhidharma states that there are no intermediate faculties (*madhyendriya*).
In this way, both the Sūtras and the Śāstras are properly reconciled.
Furthermore, the Saṃgītiparyāya makes this statement:
If the practice of the path with difficulty and slow progress is cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced,
it can fulfill the path with difficulty and quick progress.
If the practice of the path with ease and slow progress is cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced, [it can fulfill the path with ease and quick progress].
It is able to fulfill the path of swift practice that brings happiness.
Question: What is it that is fulfilled? Is it the fulfillment of the faculties (*indriya*), or the fulfillment of the separation from defilements (*vairāgya*)?
If it is the fulfillment of the faculties...
If one practices, cultivates, and frequently performs the practice of painful progress with slow superknowledge,
it is logically fitting that it should fulfill both the path of pleasant progress with fast superknowledge and the path of painful progress with slow superknowledge.
If one practices, cultivates, or frequently performs [these],
one should likewise be able to fulfill the two types of swift progress;
if fulfilled, one will be free from defilement.
If it is to be fulfilled slowly, it should be fulfilled slowly;
if it is to be fulfilled quickly, it should be fulfilled quickly.
For what reason does that treatise make such a statement?
It is agreed that such a statement refers to the fulfillment of the faculties and speaks of similarity rather than dissimilarity;
for suffering is similar to suffering and not to pleasure,
and pleasure is similar to pleasure and not to suffering.
Question:
Who accomplishes how many modes of practice (pratipad)?
Answer: Some accomplish one.
This refers to those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire;
some may possess two [factors],
namely those who have already abandoned the defilement of desire.
The Venerable Saṃghavasu said:
There are those who possess the accomplishment of the four paths of practice;
that is, when one who is refining their faculties based on the fundamental dhyānas abides in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Without having abandoned the two sluggish modes of practice,
one attains the two swift modes of practice.
The critique says:
He should not make such a statement;
if he were to make such a statement,
he would be undermining the person who has destroyed the faculties (indriya).
At that time, one who has destroyed the faculties would be both dull-facultied and sharp-facultied;
one who has destroyed the person (pudgala) would likewise be both one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and one attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Do not fall into this error.
Therefore, what was stated previously is logically sound:
there are those who possess one or two [of these].
There is no accomplishment of three or four [faculties].
There is no accomplishment of one, because of the distinction between sharp and dull faculties.
Question: Who employs how many modes of progress (*pratipad*) to perform their respective tasks?
Answer: There are those that employ only one,
some that employ two,
and some that employ three.
There are those who possess all four functions,
yet not simultaneously;
there are also those who possess only one.
That is to say, one performs the task to be accomplished using only the path of difficult progress with sluggish intuition,
such as a person of dull faculties relying on the *anāgamya* concentration.
In the intermediate dhyāna and the three formless absorptions,
one enters into rightness and the state beyond corruption as appropriate to each case.
Having attained the fruit and become free from passion, they cultivate further meritorious qualities and enter parinirvāṇa;
or alternatively, they accomplish their task using only the path of swift suffering,
as those of sharp faculties do by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the three formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
According to their respective capacities, they enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
attain the fruits [of the path], become free from defilement, cultivate further meritorious qualities,
and enter parinirvāṇa.
Alternatively, one may perform the task at hand using only the path of difficult progress with ease;
for example, as one of dull faculties who, having become free from the defilement of desire,
relies on the four fundamental dhyānas as appropriate.
Entering into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one attains the fruits, becomes free from defilements,
cultivates further meritorious qualities, and enters parinirvāṇa; or else,
by means of the path of pleasant and swift progress (*sukha-āśu-pratipad*) alone, one accomplishes what is to be done.
Just as one of sharp faculties, having already become free from the defilement of desire,
enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the four fundamental dhyānas as appropriate,
thereby attaining the fruits and becoming free from defilement.
They attain parinirvāṇa by cultivating other meritorious qualities.
There are two types of those who possess application:
namely, some possess the path of difficult progress with sluggish realization.
Furthermore, regarding the practice of slow progress with ease,
it refers to those of dull faculties who rely on the access concentration (*anāgamya*) and so forth,
as well as the first dhyāna and so forth, to accomplish their tasks.
According to what is appropriate for them, they enter the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
attain the fruits, become free from defilement, cultivate further meritorious qualities, and enter parinirvāṇa;
or else they employ the path of practice that is difficult and slow (*duḥkhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā*).
Furthermore, regarding the practice of the path of swift progress,
it performs its respective functions just as those with dull faculties do when relying solely on the *anāgamya* concentration and so forth;
accordingly, they enter into the state of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*), attain the fruits, refine their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), and become free from defilements.
Having cultivated other meritorious qualities, they enter parinirvāṇa;
or again, there are those who perform their tasks by means of either the pleasant-slow path of practice or the painful-fast path of practice.
Just as one of dull faculties, depending on the first dhyāna and so forth,
as well as the preparatory concentration (anāgamya) and so forth,
enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma), attains the fruits, refines their faculties, and becomes free from defilement according to what is appropriate.
They cultivate other meritorious qualities and enter parinirvāṇa;
or again, they employ either the path of difficult progress with ease or the path of easy progress with speed to accomplish their tasks,
such as those of dull faculties who rely solely on the first dhyāna and so forth.
According to what is appropriate for them, they enter the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), attain the fruits, refine their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*),
become free from defilement, cultivate further merits, and enter parinirvāṇa; or alternatively,
some employ the path of swift progress through suffering (*duḥkhā pratipat kṣiprābhijñā*).
And there is the practice of the path of swift progress for performing one's tasks,
such as when those of sharp faculties rely on the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and so forth,
as well as on the first dhyāna and so forth.
According to their respective capacities, they enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma), attain the fruits [of the path], become free from defilement,
cultivate further meritorious qualities,
and enter parinirvāṇa.
There are three types of utility:
namely, the path of difficult progress with slow intuition,
and the paths of pleasant progress with either slow or quick intuition, which perform their respective functions.
Just as one of dull faculties, relying on the *anāgamya* concentration and so forth,
as well as on the first *dhyāna* and so forth,
enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) as appropriate, attains the fruits, refines the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), and becomes free from defilement.
They cultivate other meritorious qualities and attain parinirvāṇa;
or again, they employ the difficult-slow path of practice,
as well as the difficult-fast and easy-fast paths of practice, to accomplish their tasks.
Just as one of dull faculties, relying on the *anāgamya* concentration and so forth, as well as the first *dhyāna* and so forth,
enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) as appropriate, attains the fruits, refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), and becomes free from defilement.
They cultivate other meritorious qualities and attain parinirvāṇa;
or again, they employ the path of painful practice with slow progress,
as well as the paths of pleasant practice with slow progress and pleasant practice with quick progress.
Just as one of dull faculties, relying on the *anāgamya* concentration and so forth,
as well as on the first *dhyāna* and so forth,
enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) as appropriate, attains the fruits, refines the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), and becomes free from defilement.
Having cultivated other meritorious qualities, they enter parinirvāṇa;
or else, there are those who perform their tasks by means of the pleasant-slow path of practice,
as well as the painful-fast and pleasant-fast paths of practice.
Just as those of dull faculties, relying on the first dhyāna and so forth, as well as the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*) and so forth,

enter into the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), attain the fruits, refine their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), and become free from defilements according to their respective capacities.
One attains parinirvāṇa by cultivating other meritorious qualities.
There are four types of practitioners who employ these:
namely, those of dull faculties who rely on the *anāgamya* concentration and so forth.
Furthermore, relying on the first dhyāna and so forth,
as appropriate, they enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma), attain the fruits, refine their faculties, become free from defilement,
cultivate other meritorious qualities, and enter parinirvāṇa.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume Ninety-three;
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Ninety-four.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang in accordance with the Imperial Edict. *Jñānaskandha*, Chapter Three: Section on the Factors of Training (*śikṣāṅga*), Part One, Section Two. Question: Who, among these four types of practice (*pratipad*), attains how many and abandons how many?
Answer: For all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there is neither attainment nor abandonment [of these paths], because these four modes of practice (*pratipad*) are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
When the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are present before one, [this is the case].
One may attain one or two [paths] without yet having relinquished anything.
Question: In this context, the treatise is not composed based on ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), but only based on noble ones (*ārya*).
Answer: There are indeed noble ones who, regarding the four paths of practice (*pratipad*), neither attain nor relinquish anything.
This means that within the stages of progress and regression of one abiding in the natural state, there is the sense of acquisition and abandonment.

Furthermore, regarding the stage of progress: if one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), then from the moment of abiding in the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) up until the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), there is neither abandonment nor acquisition of any [attainments].
At the moment of the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*), one abandons one [acquisition] and acquires one.
If one has already abandoned the defilements of desire and enters the state of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the *anāgamya* concentration,

then from the time one abides in the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) up until the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*), there is likewise no abandoning and no acquiring.
At the time of the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti), one abandons one and acquires two.
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on a higher stage,

there is neither abandonment nor acquisition of either during the abidance in the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) up until the dharma-knowledge of the path (mārga-dharma-jñāna).
At the time of the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti), one abandons two [factors] and acquires two.
If a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) is proceeding toward the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin),
this occurs during the five paths of preparation (prayogamārga), the five uninterrupted paths (ānantaryamārga), and the five paths of liberation (vimuktimārga).
In all these cases, there is neither abandonment nor acquisition of one [acquisition].
At the time of the sixth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), however, there is the abandonment of one and the acquisition of one.
This applies when a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) is proceeding toward the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
During the various paths of preparation, the two paths of immediate succession, and the two paths of liberation, there is no relinquishing, but one obtains [the fruit].
At the time of the ninth path of immediate succession, one relinquishes one and obtains two.
This applies when a non-returner proceeds toward the fruit of arhatship.
From the separation from the defilements of the first dhyāna up to those of the sphere of nothingness,
during all the preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths, there is neither abandonment nor acquisition.
When one is free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
during the eight paths of preparation, the eight paths of uninterrupted transition, and the eight paths of liberation,
there is likewise neither abandonment nor acquisition in either case.
At the time of the ninth uninterrupted path, one abandons two and acquires two;
this is called the stage of being free from defilement.
If one has not yet become free from the defilements of desire, one is a person resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).
When refining the faculties to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
during the stage of the preparatory path (prayoga-mārga), there is neither relinquishing nor acquiring;
during the stage of the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga), one relinquishes one [faculty] and acquires one.

If one who has already become free from the defilements of desire and possesses liberation through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
there is neither abandonment nor acquisition during the various stages of the preparatory path (prayoga-mārga).
At the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), one abandons two [factors] and acquires two.
When an Arhat liberated by resolution (*samayavimukta*) refines their faculties to become unshakable (*akopya*),

during all the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the eight paths of uninterrupted transition, and the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), there is neither abandonment nor acquisition of these two.
At the time of the ninth path of immediate succession, one abandons two [factors] and acquires two;
this is described as the stage of transforming the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti).
This applies to a noble one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire.
When one gives rise to various similar qualities— such as the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*),
and the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)— at all such times, there is no single moment of acquisition or abandonment.
If an noble one who has already become detached from the defilements of desire gives rise to the immeasurables,
the liberations, the spheres of mastery, the spheres of totality,
the meditation on impurity, mindfulness of breathing, and the various foundations of mindfulness.
The analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā-jñāna*), the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*),

the meditative absorption of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*), the three types of samādhi, the triple samādhi, the cultivation of the dhyānas through intermingling, the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*),
and at the times of the various paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the five paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the three paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
In all these cases, there is neither abandonment nor acquisition.
When entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), even during the subtle thought of perception, there is likewise neither abandonment nor acquisition.
During the state of the extremely subtle mind (*sūkṣmasūkṣmacitta*), there is neither abandonment nor acquisition.
All such cases as these describe the stage of cultivating merit.
This includes those Arhats who have regressed from their stage,
as well as those in training (śaikṣa) who have already become free from the defilement of desire.
When one regresses from superior faculties and abides in inferior faculties, in all such cases, one abandons two and acquires two.
This applies to those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire when they regress from superior faculties and abide in inferior faculties.
In all cases, one relinquishes one [quality] and acquires another;
this is called the stage of regression from the faculties.
This applies to an arhat as well.
When one falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the form or formless realms, one abandons two and acquires two.
When one falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm, one abandons two and acquires one.
This applies to one who is a non-returner.
When one who has already abandoned the defilements of the form realm and so forth regresses by giving rise to the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) of the form realm and so forth,

they abandon two attainments but do not acquire any new ones. That is, when a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) regresses by giving rise to the envelopments of the desire realm, they abandon two attainments and acquire one.
If a once-returner falls away from the path of superior fruition,
at that time they relinquish one attainment and do not acquire another.
When falling back from the fruit of Once-returner, one abandons one and acquires one;
if it is a Stream-enterer,
when falling back from the path of superior fruit, one abandons one and acquires none.
This explains the stage of falling away from the state of freedom from defilement;
the meaning of falling away from other meritorious qualities should be understood by analogy,
as stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*.
There are four types of persons (*pudgala*).
That is to say, there is the person who is slow in this present life but quick after the destruction of the body;
or there is the person who is quick in this present life but slow after the destruction of the body.

There may be a person who is slow both in the present life and slow after the destruction of the body; or there may be a person who is quick both in the present life and quick after the destruction of the body.
Question: It may be so for the latter two;
but as for the former two, how is it?
Answer: For the Noble Ones (*ārya*), rebirth is determined, such that they neither fall back nor transform their faculties (*indriya*).
Having undergone rebirth in the desire realm,
one will certainly not enter the form or formless realms; how, then,
can it be said that the present [result] is delayed while the subsequent [result] is swift?
Furthermore, how can it be said that one is swift in the present but delayed in the future?
Could there be one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) and, after passing through a birth,
falls back to become one resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta)?
The answer is that the treatise does not mention the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) or falling away (*parihāṇi*),
but speaks only of diligence (*vīrya*) and laziness (*kausīdya*).
If one is lazy in the present life but diligent in a future life, [the former state is not lost].
It is called "slow in the present life but quick after the destruction of the body" if one is diligent in the present life but becomes lax in a future life.
It is called "quick in the present life but slow after the destruction of the body" if one is diligent in the present life but becomes lax in a future life.
If one is indolent in this present life and will also be indolent in future lives,
it is called being slow in this present life and also slow after the destruction of the body.
If one is diligent in this present life and will also be diligent in future lives...
It is called "swift in the present life" and also "swift after the destruction of the body.
Such is the intended meaning of that treatise,
as stated in the Sūtra.
There are four kinds of conduct:
first, conduct of intolerance;
second, conduct of tolerance.
Third, the practice of subduing;
fourth, the practice of tranquility.
What is the practice of intolerance?
That is to say, being unable to endure cold and heat,
hunger and thirst, mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, sun, snakes, scorpions, and harmful touch;
as well as the harassment of evil people and irrational speech.
The various pains that arise within the body,
which one is unable to endure regarding such matters—
this is called "unbearable conduct."
What is the practice of endurance?
It refers to being able to endure such things as cold and heat as previously described;
this is called the practice of endurance.
What is the practice of subduing?
It refers to the restraint of the sense faculties;
this is called the practice of subduing.
What is the practice of tranquility?
It refers to the untainted path;
this is called the practice of tranquility.
Question: Do the four modes of practice subsume those four types of conduct, or do those four types of conduct subsume the four modes of practice?
Answer: Those four types of conduct subsume the four modes of practice.
The four modes of progress do not subsume those four practices.
Which ones are not subsumed?
Namely, the first three.
As stated in the Sūtra,
there are four kinds of abandonment:
first, abandonment through painful and slow penetration.
Second, suffering that is quickly and easily abandoned;
third, pleasure that is slowly and with difficulty abandoned;
fourth, pleasure that is quickly and easily abandoned.
Among these, "painful with slow penetration" is called inferior because it is both painful and slow to penetrate and sever [the afflictions].
"Painful with quick penetration" is called inferior solely because it is painful.
The path of liberation that delights in slow penetration and abandonment is called inferior simply because it is slow.
The path that delights in swift penetration and abandonment is also called inferior because it cannot properly manifest vast benefit for the multitudes of devas and humans, as it is not extensive.
The Blessed One alone is called "Sublime" because he possesses the thorough abandonment [of the outflows] and can correctly manifest vast benefit for the multitudes of devas and humans.
Question: Are the four types of thorough abandonment subsumed within the four paths of practice?
Do the four types of penetration subsume the four modes of progress?
Answer: They subsume one another reciprocally, each according to its respective case.
That is to say, the abandonment through the path of sluggish progress with regard to suffering is itself the mode of progress of sluggish progress with regard to suffering.
Up to "the path of swift and easy abandonment is the path of swift and easy progress";
thus, according to their respective functions, they mutually encompass one another.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are exclusively for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);
the four paths of practice (*pratipad*) pertain to both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training.
If one explains it in this way:
The four paths of practice encompass the four abandonments through the four paths;
however, the four abandonments through the four paths do not encompass the four paths of practice.
What is it that they do not encompass?
This refers to the four paths of practice for those in training (*śaikṣa*).
Question: The noble path (*āryamārga*) is sublime and should not be called inferior, as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
What are inferior phenomena (*hīna-dharma*)?
They refer to unwholesome (*akuśala*) and obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena.
For what reason does the Sūtra state that the four kinds of abandonment are called "inferior"?
Answer: Inferiority is of two kinds:
first, defiled inferiority;
second, diminished inferiority.
Although the four types of supernormal powers (abhijñā) are not defiled or inferior,
they possess the inferiority of being limited; some say this.
The path of liberation that is slow and with effort pertains to the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the three formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*);
it is subsumed under the noble path of those who are liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*).
It is swiftly and thoroughly severed;
that is, it is comprised within the noble path of the śrāvaka vehicle of that stage,
which is characterized by non-periodic liberation (*asamayavimukta*).
The path of liberation characterized by delight and slow penetration is comprised within the four fundamental dhyānas and the path of those liberated by occasion (samayavimukta).
Those which are pleasant, characterized by swift penetration and abandonment, yet cannot perfectly manifest vast benefit for the multitudes of devas and humans, are the four fundamental dhyānas.
These are comprised within the noble paths of the Śrāvaka vehicle for those who are not liberated at all times (asamayavimukta).

Among those that are pleasant, swift, and lead to the abandonment [of afflictions], that which can correctly manifest vast benefit for the multitudes of devas and humans is subsumed within the Noble Path of the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*).
Question: Under which category is the Noble Path of the Pratyekabuddhas subsumed?
Some say it is included within the category of the Śrāvakas; others, however, say:
It is subsumed within the Chapter on the Buddha. Why is this?
Because, like the Buddha, he was able to awaken by himself without a teacher.
Other masters say:

It should be understood as previously stated that among the three types of swift and easy abandonment (*kṣipra-sukha-prativedha*), those included within the noble path of the Pratyekabuddhas cannot correctly manifest vast benefit for the multitudes of devas and humans; whereas those included within the noble path of the Bhagavān can correctly manifest vast benefit for the multitudes of devas and humans.
Question: To which category does the noble path of the śrāvaka who is liberated at an improper time (akāla-vimukta) when abiding in the fundamental dhyānas belong?
Some say it belongs to the category of the pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is subsumed under the category of the Buddha. Why is this so?
Because those untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) are obtained by relying on the Buddha,
some say that the first three superknowledges (abhijñā) are for outsiders who are ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Among those who delight in swift penetration and abandonment,
that which cannot correctly manifest vast benefit for the multitudes of devas and humans is subsumed under the noble path of the Pratyekabuddhas.
Among those who delight in swift penetration and abandonment, that which can correctly manifest vast benefit for the multitudes of devas and humans is subsumed under the noble path of the Bhagavān.
Question: To which category does the noble path of the śrāvaka belong?
Some say it is included within the category of the pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is subsumed under the category of the Buddha. Why is this so?
Because those untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) are obtained by relying upon the Buddha,
some say that the first three [supernormal powers] are common to all non-Buddhists (tīrthika).

Among those who delight in swift penetration and abandonment, that which cannot correctly manifest vast benefit for the multitudes of devas and humans is subsumed under the noble path of the śrāvakas.
Among those who delight in swift penetration and abandonment...
That which can correctly manifest the vast benefit for the multitudes of devas and humans is subsumed within the Noble Path of the Blessed One.
Question: To which category does the Noble Path of the Pratyekabuddhas belong?
Some say: [it belongs to the same category].
It is included in the Chapter on Śrāvakas.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is included in the Chapter on the Buddha.
Why is this so? Because, like the Buddha, he was able to awaken by himself without a teacher.
The commentary says:
Although these various explanations each give rise to the realization of their respective disciples,
in terms of the actual meaning, the fourfold universal abandonment constitutes the four paths of practice (*pratipad*).
The second and fourth [categories] comprehensively encompass the noble paths of the three vehicles;
however, that which cannot fully manifest the vast benefit for the multitudes of devas and humans within the fourth is subsumed under the two noble paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
That which can correctly manifest vast benefit for the multitudes of devas and humans is subsumed within the Noble Path of the Buddha;
this penetrates both types of abandonment and is not restricted solely to the fourth [dhyāna].
In that sutra, it is not stated that this [path] is exclusively the pleasant path of quick penetration because it is abandoned;
rather, whatever exists within the Buddha’s body is entirely sublime.
Question: Among the four paths of practice (*pratipad*), by which path of practice does the Blessed One rely?
Regarding those who enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), attain the fruits [of the path], become free from defilement, and exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*):
by which type of practice (*pratipad*) does a Pratyekabuddha rely?
And by which type of practice does a Śrāvaka rely?

Answer: The Blessed One, relying on the path of swift progress characterized by ease, enters into rightness and departure from birth, attains the fruits, becomes free from defilement, and exhausts the outflows.
How is this known to be so?
Because the sūtras are authoritative,
as it is said in a sūtra:
at one time, Māluṅkyamātā came to where the Buddha was.
He asked this question:
"By means of which practice did the World-Honored One realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
The Buddha told Māluṅkyamātā:
"All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, have realized unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment by relying upon the practice of the path of swift progress with ease."
At that time, Māluṅkyamātṛ put forth two challenges:
"The World-Honored One formerly practiced asceticism for six years before attaining unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
"How is it that you speak of the path of swift progress through ease?
The Buddha said,
"Foolish man, I did not realize great enlightenment by means of those six years of ascetic practice."
Having relinquished that [practice], he accepted the milk-rice offering;
thereafter, relying upon the path of swift progress characterized by ease,
he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
From this it is known that the Blessed One,
relying on the path of swift progress characterized by ease, entered the path of seeing and so forth;
he entered rightness and the state beyond corruption (samyaktva-nyāma) by relying upon the fourth dhyāna.
This continues until the attainment of bodhi.
A solitary realizer (pratyekabuddha) who emerges alone is like the Buddha, the World-Honored One;
however, a solitary realizer who emerges from a group has an indeterminate basis of reliance, similar to that of the śrāvakas.

Within the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Venerable Śāriputra entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and attained the fruit through the path of swift progress with difficulty (*duḥkhā pratipad kṣiprābhijñā*),
whereas he exhausted all outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) by means of the path of swift progress with ease (*sukhā pratipad kṣiprābhijñā*).
Why is this? Because they enter into rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the *anāgamya* concentration to attain the fruits and become free from defilements,
and they exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*) based on the fourth dhyāna.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, relying on the path of swift progress through suffering,
entered into the state of right determination, attained the fruit, became free from defilement,
and exhausted the outflows. Why was this so?

Because he entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the *anāgamya* concentration to attain the fruits and become free from defilement, and because he exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) based on the formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samādhi*).
Question: For what reason were Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana [sent]?
While both rely on the *anāgamya* concentration to enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), attain the fruits,
and become free from defilements, Śāriputra attained the fruit of Arhatship based on the fourth *dhyāna*.
Did Mahāmaudgalyāyana attain the fruit of arhatship by relying on the formless absorptions?
Answer: Both of these venerable ones were śrāvakas who had reached the ultimate goal.
They will certainly attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya in gradual succession;
therefore, both rely upon the *anāgamya* concentration to enter into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
As for the Venerable Śāriputra:
This is because the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana attained the fruit of Arhatship by relying on the fourth dhyāna through the practice of vipaśyanā;
whereas [the other] did so through the practice of śamatha.
One attains the fruit of arhatship by relying on the formless absorptions.
Question: Are all śrāvakas who have reached the ultimate necessarily destined to attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa in a gradual sequence?
Answer: All of them will certainly attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya in gradual succession.
Why is this? Because all śrāvakas who have reached the ultimate limit [of their path].
All of them are those who turn the wheel of Dharma following the Buddha.
If they had not attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya through gradual stages,
how could they skillfully explain the states of mind involved in entering, abiding in, and emerging from [meditative absorption]?
Question: Regarding the ability to skillfully explain the entry, abiding, and emergence of the minds associated with the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, there is no one like the Buddha.
Does the Buddha, then, attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya gradually?
Answer: One should not raise such an objection regarding this matter against the Buddha.
Because when the Buddha was formerly a bodhisattva,
he was already able to skillfully explain the excellence of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya;
Śāriputra dwells in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
Therefore, one should not challenge the Buddha by citing the Śrāvakas;
for the Śrāvakas have not personally realized this state,
and thus they are unable to explain it to others with mastery.
Some maintain this view:
not all śrāvakas who have reached the ultimate necessarily attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa through a gradual process.
Why is this? If one were already free from the defilement of desire while still in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
would they not have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) even before encountering the Buddha’s teaching of the essential Dharma, rather than only attaining it after falling away?
Question: If that is so, how can one skillfully explain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya?
Answer: This should not be questioned.
For example, although Ānanda was of dull faculties, he remained in the stage of training (śaikṣa).
Yet he was able to skillfully explain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya and enable immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to become arhats;
how much more so could he not have explained [the stages] for those of sharp faculties who, by transcending [the lower stages], proceed toward realization and abide in the stage of no-more-learning?
The commentary states:
It should be said that all śrāvakas who have reached the ultimate stage will, without exception,
definitely attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa in gradual succession.
It is not because of their ability to speak, but simply because it is the nature of things (*dharmatā*),
that all the śrāvaka disciples who have reached the ultimate goal among the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, numbering more than the sands of the Ganges, [possess this].
All of them gradually realized the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; therefore,
it is not reasonable to raise an objection against this natural law (dharmatā),
as the Blessed One has said.
The Arhat whose outflows are exhausted accomplishes the ten factors of one beyond training (*daśa-aśaikṣāṅgāni*).
Among these, what are the ten factors of one beyond training?
They are the right view of one beyond training, up to and including the right concentration.
And [there are] the right liberation and right knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Question: Does the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) possess right liberation and right knowledge?
If it does, why are they not mentioned here?
If it were non-existent, how would one reconcile what is stated in the sūtras?
For example, as the sūtra states,
the Venerable Śāriputra consoled the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, saying:
Do not fear, do not fear, you ordinary worldlings who lack learning!
Because you have accomplished a lack of faith, immoral conduct, little learning, stinginess, and poor wisdom;
because of your wrong views, wrong intention, wrong resolve, wrong liberation, and wrong knowledge.
Fearing falling into the realms of hell beings, animals, or hungry ghosts,
you have already forever severed lack of faith, immoral conduct,
and even wrong liberation and wrong knowledge.
Because one has accomplished faith, ethical discipline, learning, relinquishment, and wisdom,
and possesses right view, right intention, right resolve, right liberation, and right knowledge, one should not be afraid.
One should answer by saying this.
The stages of training (*śaikṣa*) also possess right liberation and right knowledge.
Question: If this is so, why are they not mentioned here?
Answer: There are two kinds of "existence" (*bhava*).
First, there is the essence;
second, there are the factors.
Although the stage of training possesses the essence of right liberation and right knowledge, [it lacks the factors].
Yet they are not established as factors of right liberation and right knowledge.
Question: Why are right liberation and right knowledge established as factors in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), but not in the stage of learning (*śaikṣa*)?
Answer: Because it is established based on superiority.
That is to say, among all phenomena, the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are superior to the dharmas of one in training (śaikṣa).
Among persons (*pudgala*),
the person beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is superior,
not the person in training (*śaikṣa*).
Therefore, although these two exist within the stage of training (śaikṣa), they are not established as factors [of the noble path].
Furthermore, it is only in the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa) that right liberation and right knowledge possess such great power and efficacy.
Because its intrinsic nature is preeminent and because it is free from faults,
it is established as a constituent member.
Furthermore, only the right liberation and right knowledge of the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) are established as factors,
because they have already severed the root of all existence.
Furthermore, only the mind of one beyond training possesses both types of liberation.
First is the intrinsic nature;
second is the continuity.
Therefore, the corresponding resolute conviction and wisdom are established as branches.
Regarding the distinction between the two types of liberated mind,
one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There may be a mind that is liberated by its own nature.
It is not a liberation of the mental continuum;
that is to say, it refers to the untainted mind of one in training (śaikṣa),
or there is a liberation of the mental continuum.
It is not liberation by nature;
that is, the contaminated mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Alternatively, there is a mind that is liberated by nature.
There is also liberation through continuity,
namely the untainted mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Alternatively, there is a mind that is not liberated by its own nature.
Nor is it the liberation of the continuum;
that is to say, the tainted minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and all the minds of ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Furthermore, the right liberation and right knowledge of one in training are not established as factors because they are obscured and impaired by wrong liberation and wrong knowledge.
Question: Since the right view, right intention,
and so forth of those in training are also obscured and impaired by wrong view, wrong intention, and so forth,
why are they established as factors [of the path]?
Answer: The right view, right thought, and so forth of one in training directly sever wrong view, wrong thought, and so forth;
they destroy all afflictions and act as armor against the enemies that are the afflictions, just like weapons and shields.
Therefore, they are established as factors [of the path].
Question: Do not the right liberation and right knowledge of one in training (śaikṣa) also have the power to destroy all afflictions?
Answer: Liberation does not directly destroy the afflictions, because one attains liberation after having destroyed the afflictions.
Although right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) can indeed destroy all afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), [it does so indirectly].
Furthermore, because these cannot harm those factors to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), they are not established as limbs.
Moreover, only right liberation and right knowledge in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) are established as limbs,
as there are no factors contrary to them.
Factors that are diametrically opposed refer to false liberation and false knowledge.
Furthermore, because only the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) possesses complete and analytical liberation, it is associated with the mind.
Adhimokṣa (resolute confidence) and jñāna (knowledge) are established as factors;
it is not like the mind of one in training (śaikṣa), which is only partially liberated,
meaning that it is not partially liberated from all the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya).
This refers to all afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, it is associated with the mind because of the liberation and dissociation from all [afflictions] of the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Resolve and wisdom are established as the factors.
"All liberations" refers to [the liberation from] the afflictions of the five classes.
"Those who are entirely dissociated" refers to those who,
regarding the objects of the five categories,
furthermore possess the liberation of mind of an Aśaikṣa alone from all obstructions.
Because it is free from all hindrances, it is associated with the mind;
resolve and wisdom are established as its factors.
That which is liberated from all hindrances—
That is to say, regarding the five classes of hindrances,
one who is far removed from all hindrances refers to the objects of focus within those five classes.
Furthermore, only in the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is there the severance of craving for the "vine" (*vīraṇa*), thereby becoming free from all fetters;
therefore, those two factors are established as limbs.

Furthermore, only in the stage of one beyond training is there the severance of the heavy topknot of afflictions based on the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); therefore, those two factors are established as limbs.

Furthermore, it is only in the stage of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) that those two factors are established as branches, because they have already shaved off the hair and beard of the afflictions of the three realms.
Furthermore, because liberation is perfected only in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*),
those two factors are established as its branches.
Furthermore, because in the stage of no-more-learning alone is pliancy and bliss supreme, being unharmed by the fever of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Only those in the stage of no-more-learning experience the vast and sublime bliss of pliancy, for they have already accomplished their task;
they are like a king who has already destroyed all his enemies.
The happiness experienced is vast and sublime;
it belongs solely to those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa),
who have already extinguished all afflictions.
It is said that the Sage’s intention is fulfilled because,
