in the stage of no-more-learning alone, one casts off the burden of the defiled aggregates and attains the burden of the purely pure aggregates.
Only those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) abandon the realms and locations of feverish affliction,
because they attain the realms and locations of coolness;
only those in the stage of no-more-learning abandon the basis for the unwholesome roots.
Because it serves as the basis for the acquisition of wholesome roots;
and because, in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) alone, one abandons the very substance of the afflictions and attains a pure substance.
Only those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) are fields of merit for all the world;
as the Blessed One said:
"If one possesses greed and so forth, it is like a field infested with weeds."
Therefore, by giving to a field that is free from greed and other [defilements], the donor obtains a great fruit;
yet, because one who is in the state of training (śaikṣa) incurs an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) through mere harm,
it is only in the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that one destroys all attachments.
Because they have severed all fetters and abandoned all hindrances,
those in the stage of no-more-learning alone fully comprehend the four nutriments and the four stations of consciousness.
Because it transcends the nine abodes of sentient beings,
and because only the qualities of those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) manifest without any admixture of defilement—
meaning that there is only sublime conduct and no unwholesome conduct.
There are only roots of goodness and no unwholesome roots.
Due to such various causes and conditions,
only in the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are right liberation and right knowledge established as factors [of enlightenment].
Question: If there is a stage of training (śaikṣa),
is there also false liberation and false knowledge?
How should one interpret what is stated in the sūtras?
For example, it says:
"Householder, do not fear, do not fear."
“Have you already forever severed lack of faith and bad precepts,
up to and including wrong liberation and wrong knowledge?
He replied, “Wrong liberation and wrong knowledge are of two kinds.”
The first is that which causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil destinies;
this has been permanently severed by those who have abandoned it through the path of seeing.
The second is that which does not cause sentient beings to fall into the three evil destinies.
They are still possessed of those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation.
As it is said in a sutra,
the Buddha told Ānanda:
Śāriputra is a wise bhikṣu who was able to skillfully analyze the ten meanings of the four factors of stream-entry for the sake of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Question: How are the four factors of stream-entry analyzed according to ten meanings?
The Venerable Pārśva replied:
Regarding each individual factor of stream-entry...
All are analyzed by means of ten points;
that is to say, from the analysis of approaching virtuous persons by means of ten points,
up to the analysis of practicing in accordance with the Dharma by means of ten points.
The Venerable Vaṅgīsa spoke thus:
"One distinguishes through faith by associating with virtuous persons;
one distinguishes through learning by hearing the true Dharma."
The Venerable Ghoṣaka has stated that one practices *yoniśo-manasikāra* (appropriate attention) through right view,
and practices the "conformity to the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*) through the remaining forms of discrimination.
One distinguishes through faith and ethical discipline by drawing near to virtuous persons;
one distinguishes through learning by hearing the true Dharma;
and one distinguishes through right view by applying attention in accordance with reality.
Regarding the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma through other forms of discernment,
the masters of the Abhidharma say:
"Through discernment of faith and ethical discipline, one draws near to virtuous persons."
One discriminates the hearing of the sublime Dharma through learning and wisdom;
one discriminates appropriate mental attention through right view;
and one discriminates the practice in accordance with the Dharma through the remaining [faculties].
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this:
one approaches virtuous persons by means of the distinctions of faith, ethical discipline, and relinquishment;
and one listens to the true Dharma by means of the distinctions of learning and wisdom.
One practices *yoniśomanasikāra* (appropriate attention) by means of right view;
one practices the "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*) by means of the other forms of discrimination.
Thus says the Venerable One.
Venerable Śāriputra,
for the sake of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada,
has skillfully distinguished the four factors of stream-entry.
Regarding the four forms of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*):
the four factors conducive to stream-entry (*srotaāpattyaṅga*) are the detailed analysis of the four factors conducive to stream-entry,
while the ten types of meaning are the detailed analysis of the four forms of verified confidence.
This means that the four forms of verified confidence (avetyaprasāda) are analyzed by way of three factors:
first, by way of their intrinsic nature (svabhāva);
second, by way of their origination (samutthāna).
Regarding "because they are of three grades" and "because of their intrinsic nature":
this refers to faith and ethical discipline.
Regarding "by way of origination":
this refers to hearing, renunciation, wisdom, right view, and right reflection.
Through the wisdom arising from hearing, one gives rise to faith.
"By means of right reflection, one gives rise to ethical discipline;
by means of relinquishing [wrong] views, faith and discipline increase as a natural outflow" refers to right resolve,
right liberation, and right knowledge.
Question: What is the difference between right resolute confidence (*samyag-adhimokṣa*) and right liberation (*samyag-vimukti*)?
Answer: The cause is called right resolute confidence;
the fruit is called right liberation.

Furthermore, that which exists at the time of application is called right resolve (*samyag-adhimokṣa*), while that which exists at the time of culmination is called right liberation (*samyag-vimukti*).
Question: What is the distinction between right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) and right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) as they pertain to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*)?
Answer: "Hearing" refers to the wisdom consisting of what is heard;
"reflection" refers to the wisdom consisting of reflection;
[these constitute] right view and right knowledge.
That is to say, the wisdom produced through cultivation is called "right view" when it is the cause,
and "right knowledge" when it is the result.
The Venerable Zuo-shou (Vāmana) has explained that the four factors of stream-entry and their concordant fruits are analyzed by way of ten meanings.
That is to say: through faith, ethical discipline, and relinquishment, one distinguishes and draws near to virtuous persons;
through learning, one distinguishes and listens to the true Dharma;
and through right reflection and right resolve.
One discriminates through appropriate mental attention;
with wisdom, one correctly views and discriminates the practice in accordance with the Dharma;
and by means of right liberation and right knowledge.
Regarding the analysis of their outflowing fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*),
the Venerable Ghosaka stated:
"In this context, ten meanings constitute five categories."
The four types of verified confidence (avetyaprasāda) are distinguished:
first, by way of their intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
namely faith and ethical discipline (śīla).
Second, because it resembles [the former],
namely, by abandoning correct resolve;
third, because of its application.
This refers to hearing and wisdom,
because they accord with the four [right efforts]:
namely, right view and right intention.
Because there are five fruits;
namely, right liberation and right knowledge.
The Venerable Buddhadeva has stated this.
In this context, the four factors conducive to stream-entry (*srotāpatti-aṅga*) are distinguished by means of ten meanings.
That is to say, faith, ethical discipline, and relinquishment distinguish "approaching a virtuous friend" (*satpuruṣasaṃsevā*);
while learning and wisdom distinguish "hearing the true Dharma" (*saddharmaśravaṇa*).
Through right reflection, one discriminates through appropriate mental attention;
through other forms of discrimination, one practices in accordance with the Dharma.
Question: For what reason is one called an Arhat?
Because he has consented to receive the supreme offerings of the world,
he is called an Arhat;
that is to say, there is nothing among the conditions for a pure livelihood in the world that an Arhat ought not to accept.
Furthermore, "A-ra" refers to all afflictions;
in the Han language, it is called "that which can harm."
Because one uses the sharp sword of wisdom to destroy the thieves of the afflictions,
leaving none remaining, one is called an arhat.
Furthermore, "arhat" is a name for birth.
"Ā" means "non-existence.
Because they are without birth, they are called Arhats;
for within all realms, all destinies, and all modes of birth—the phenomena of saṃsāra—they are no longer born again.
Furthermore, in the Chinese language, "all evil and unwholesome dharmas" is the meaning of *āra*.
The term *āra* signifies "distancing" or "abandoning."
Because they have distanced themselves from all evil and unwholesome dharmas,
they are called arhats.
In this context, "evil" refers to unwholesome karma.
The unwholesome refers to all afflictions (*kleśa*).
They are called unwholesome because they obstruct wholesome phenomena;
thus, they are contrary to the meaning of the wholesome.
As it is said in a verse:
"Having distanced oneself from evil and unwholesome states, Abiding in the ultimate truth, one should receive the offerings of the world; Therefore, one is named an Arhat."
"Exhaustion of outflows" (āsravakṣaya) refers to the permanent exhaustion of all outflows.
Question: Since the phenomena conducive to the outflows can also be permanently exhausted, why is it stated only that "those outflows are exhausted"?
The answer is that he takes the exhaustion of the outflows (āsrava-kṣaya) as the foremost;
it should be understood that this also refers to the exhaustion of those phenomena conducive to the outflows.
Furthermore, the various outflows are difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend.
They are mentioned specifically because they are not factors conducive to the outflows (*āsrava*).
Furthermore, the faults of the outflows are numerous, predominant, and firm;
they are mentioned specifically because they are not factors conducive to the outflows.
Furthermore, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the outflows (*āsrava*) is severed; once severed, they are no longer established.
Because they are diametrically opposed to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), their exhaustion is specifically taught.
When the Noble Path arises, it is directly opposed to all afflictions (*kleśa*).
They are neither contaminated wholesome states nor unobscured neutral states;
nevertheless, when the various noble paths sever the afflictions, they also simultaneously sever those [states].
This is like a bright lamp arising: it is opposed to darkness, yet it does not oppose the oil, the wick, or the vessel.
However, when dispelling darkness, it also causes the oil to be exhausted, the wick to burn out, and the vessel to become hot.
Question: Why is it that only the "exhaustion of outflows" (āsravakṣaya) is mentioned, and not the "floods" (ogha) or "yokes" (yoga)?
Answer: Because the three outflows (traya-āsrava) mentioned previously encompass all afflictions (kleśa).
Therefore, they are explained selectively.
Although the floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), and so forth exhaustively include all afflictions (*kleśa*), they do not appear at the beginning.
[Instead,] the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*) are presented first.
Although they are placed at the beginning, they do not encompass all afflictions;
therefore, it is said that Arhats have only "exhausted the outflows" (*āsravakṣaya*),
and not [exhausted] the floods (*ogha*) and so forth.
How many [knowledges] does he accomplish in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?
Answer: If, relying on the concentration with vitarka and vicāra, the first knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) manifests in the present.
Regarding the past, there are ten; regarding the future, ten; regarding the present, nine.
Among these, "concentration with vitarka and vicāra" refers to the preparatory stage (anāgamya) and the first dhyāna as its bases.
Some say that co-arising is the basis;
others further say:
The meaning of "basis" (*āśraya*) here refers to the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
The critique states: it should be explained in this way.
These two stages are collectively designated as the basis.
Although there are four types of the first [stage] as explained extensively above,
the present treatise relies only on the first two.
First, the initial attainment of the fruit,
which refers to the first attainment of the fruit of Arhatship based on that stage.
Second, the initial transformation of the faculties.
This refers to when one who is liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*), relying on that stage, first refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) to become immovable (*akopya*).
When the knowledge of an adept (*aśaikṣajñāna*) manifests before them, it is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Question: Does an adept also have the manifestation of knowledge and vision that is neither of a learner nor of an adept (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣajñānadarśana*)?
That is also the knowledge and vision of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
because it is the knowledge and vision produced by those who are beyond training.
Why, then, is it not stated here that the knowledge and vision of one beyond training is present?
One should know that although it was promised to speak thus,
the fact that it is not spoken indicates that this is an incomplete explanation.
Furthermore, in this context, the "knowledge and vision of one beyond training" refers precisely to the knowledge and vision of one beyond training;
it does not refer to the knowledge and vision of those who are not yet beyond training, and thus it should not be criticized.
As for the statement that they do not exist in the past:
This means that, as previously stated, when the two [paths] first manifest at the initial moment, they are entirely non-existent in the past,
because not even a single thought-moment has yet arisen and ceased. Even if [a thought-moment] had already arisen and ceased,
it would have attained its fruit or undergone a transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).
Or because of retrogression and relinquishment.
Regarding the ten future [factors]:
this means that at the very first moment, one fully cultivates those ten factors of the future.
Because there are ten factors for one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
As for "nine in the present," it is because at that time nine factors are manifested before one.
This means that, with the exception of right view,
there is no possibility for [other afflictions] to arise within this moment; therefore, once they have ceased, they are not lost.
Furthermore, if one relies on the concentration with vitarka and vicāra,
when the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) manifests,
there are nine [knowledges] in the past and present.
There are ten future [factors]. Among these,
"those" refers to those nine branches.
"Having ceased" means having ceased through impermanence.
"Not lost" means that there is no loss of that noble path due to the three causes and conditions.
As previously stated.
"If, moreover, based on [the first moment], etc.
refers to from the second moment onward.
Furthermore, based on the meditative concentration with vitarka and vicāra, either the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) manifests.
Question: For what reason does one again give rise to the knowledge of this stage?
Answer: Because of the mindfulness of repaying kindness.
Due to four conditions,
as explained extensively before.
Regarding the nine past [factors]:
This refers to the period from the second moment onward;
it consists of that which was already produced and ceased at the time of the first moment, having been accomplished in the past.
The remainder is as previously explained.
Once that has ceased, it is not lost. If,
based on a meditative concentration without vitarka or vicāra, the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) manifests,
there are nine past [moments].
There are ten in the future and eight in the present; herein,
there is the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra.
This refers to the final three dhyānas.
The meaning of the intermediate dhyāna is not explained here, as it was previously stated.
Regarding the eight present factors, correct reflection (samyak-saṃkalpa) is excluded.
Because that [state] is without vitarka,
the rest is as previously explained.
Once it has ceased, it is not lost.
If, based on the formless attainments, the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) is present,
there are nine past [knowledges] and ten future [knowledges].
There are five in the present.
Among these, "formless attainments" refers to the first three formless attainments.
The fourth is not mentioned;
its meaning is as previously explained.
As for the five of the present:
Excluding right thought, right speech, and right livelihood,
these are absent in that stage;
the rest is as previously explained.
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If one enters the attainment of cessation or brings a mundane mind (*laukikacitta*) into presence,
there are nine past [dharmas].
There are ten in the future and none in the present. Among these,
one who enters the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) [is as follows].
This refers to abiding in the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
"Worldly mind" (*laukikacitta*) refers to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) meditative mind that emerges from the attainment of cessation.
Alternatively, one may give rise to other contaminated (*sāsrava*) meditative states.
Regarding "the past nine":
this refers to the nine factors (*aṅga*) of the initial state of concentration characterized by both applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*) that were previously arisen.
Regarding the ten factors of the future:
these are the very same ten branches cultivated at the initial stage;
they are absent in the present because, at that time, the Noble Path has not yet manifested.
Once that has ceased, it is not lost.
If one relies on a meditative concentration with vitarka and vicāra,
the first fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) manifests in the present.
There are nine in the past and present,
and ten in the future.
Among these, the first refers to those who have attained the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This refers to the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding "the nine [factors] of the past":

this refers to the nine factors of the aggregate that arises simultaneously with the first-attained concentration accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), which is conjoined with the wisdom of one beyond training.
The ninth [category] of the present consists of those factors excluding right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*),
because vision (*darśana*) and knowledge do not arise simultaneously.
Regarding the ten factors of the future:
these are the ten branches cultivated through both the aforementioned initial wisdom and the present initial vision.
The remainder is as previously explained.
Once that has ceased, it is not lost.
Furthermore, if one relies on a meditative concentration with applied thought and sustained thought (savitarka-savicāra),
then for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), either knowledge (jñāna) or vision (darśana) manifests in the present.
There are ten in the past and future,
and nine in the present;
herein, if one is wise...
Any one of the knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising;
if it is vision, it is the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The ten of the past are as follows:
This refers to the ten factors of the aggregate that arise simultaneously with the initial wisdom and initial vision mentioned previously;
the ten of the future are those very same factors being cultivated,
while the nine of the present are as follows.
At the time of wisdom (*jñāna*), vision (*darśana*) is excluded; at the time of vision, wisdom is excluded;
the remaining nine factors are as previously described.
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If, based on a concentration without vitarka and without vicāra,
either knowledge or vision manifests,
there are ten [factors] in the past and future.
"Present eight": herein,
"present eight" refers to the remaining eight factors,
excluding either right intention or wisdom-and-vision.
The rest is as previously explained.
Once that has ceased, it is not lost.
This applies if one relies on the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
When the knowledge or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is present,
ten [factors] are past and future,
and five are present.
Among these, the five present factors consist of the five limbs excluding one from among right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right knowledge-and-vision;
the rest are as previously explained.
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If one enters the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) or brings a mundane mind (laukikacitta) into presence,
there are ten [factors] belonging to the past and future.
There is nothing present here.
Among these, the ten factors of the past and future are the ten branches that arose and were cultivated at the time of the initial wisdom and initial vision mentioned previously.
The rest is as previously explained.
If one relies on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra,
the first knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) manifests before him.
In the past, there are none;
in the future, ten;
in the present, eight.
Among these, the first knowledge of one beyond training that is present is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
That which is past does not exist.
At the initial moment, not even a single thought has yet arisen and ceased;
even if it had already arisen and ceased, the three conditions would have been relinquished.
As for the ten future [factors]:
This means that at the very first moment, one fully cultivates the ten factors of a future Arhat;
as for the eight present factors, these exclude right intention and right view,
while the remainder are as previously described.
Once that has ceased, it is not lost.
Furthermore, if one relies on a meditative concentration free from applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra-samādhi*),
the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*) manifests before them.
There are eight in the past and present,
and ten in the future.
Among these, that which is the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) is present.
This refers to either the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
The rest is as previously explained.
Once that has been extinguished, it is not lost.
If, relying on the formless attainments,
the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) manifests,
there are eight past [moments].
There are ten in the future and five in the present.
Among these, there are eight in the past.

This refers to the eight factors arising together with the first supramundane knowledge (*aśaikṣajñāna*) of the previously mentioned concentration free from applied and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra-samādhi*).
The rest is as explained before;
once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) or brings a mundane mind (*laukikacitta*) into manifestation, there are eight [minds] in the past,
ten in the future,
and none in the present.
Among these, the eight factors of the past refer to the eight branches of the initial group that arises simultaneously with wisdom; the remainder are as previously explained.
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If, based on a meditative concentration with applied and sustained thought (savitarka-savicāra),
the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) manifests,
there are eight past [moments].
There are ten in the future and nine in the present.
Among these, the nine in the present are as follows:
That is to say, with the exception of right view,
the rest are as previously described;
once they have been extinguished, they are not lost.
If, based on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra,
the first fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-darśana) manifests,
there are eight [dharmas] of the past and present.
There are ten future [factors].
Among these, the first, "the vision of one beyond training appearing in the present," refers to the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
The eight factors of the past refer to the eight branches of the aggregate that arises simultaneously with the initial wisdom.
The ten factors of the future refer to...
This refers to the ten factors cultivated through both the previous initial wisdom and the present initial vision;
the remainder is as previously explained.
Once they have been extinguished, they are not lost.
Furthermore, whether it be based on the concentration without vitarka and without vicāra,
or proceeding successively down to the concentration with vitarka and with vicāra,
when the knowledge or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) manifests before them, and so forth.
All should be explained accordingly based on what is appropriate as before.
If one relies on the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*),
the first knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*) manifests.
In the past, there are none;
in the future, ten;
in the present, five.
Among these, that which first manifests as the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
That which was previously absent is...
At the initial moment, not even a single thought-moment has arisen and ceased;
even if it had arisen and ceased, the three conditions would have been relinquished.
As for the ten future [factors]:
This means that at the very first moment, one fully cultivates the ten branches of future non-learner (aśaikṣa) qualities;
as for the five present ones,
these exclude right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right view.
The rest is as previously explained.
Once that has ceased, it is not lost.
If one further relies upon the formless absorptions...
When the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) is present,
there are five [knowledges] in the past and present,
and ten in the future.
Among these, the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*) that is present consists of either the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Those that are future are ten.
This refers to the ten factors cultivated at the time of the initial wisdom.
The remainder is as previously explained;
once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If one enters the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) or brings a conventional mind (laukikacitta) into presence,
there are five past [dharmas] and ten future [dharmas].
There is none in the present.
Herein, the five of the past refer to the five factors of the first cluster that arises simultaneously with wisdom.
The rest is as previously explained.
Once that has ceased, it is not lost.
This applies if one relies on a meditative concentration accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
This continues up to: when one relies on a meditative concentration without applied thought or sustained thought (*avitarkāvicārā samādhiḥ*),
and the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*) manifests before them,
all such cases should be explained accordingly, following the previous pattern as appropriate.
If one relies on the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti),
when the first type of non-learner's vision (aśaikṣadṛṣṭi) manifests,
there are five [factors] belonging to the past and present.
There are ten future [factors].
Among these, the first, which has the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) as its present manifestation,
refers to the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi).
The five of the past refer to the five factors of the aggregate that arises simultaneously with the aforementioned initial wisdom.
The ten of the future are as follows:
This refers to the ten future factors cultivated through both the former initial knowledge and the present initial vision;
once they have ceased, they are not lost.
Furthermore, this applies if one relies on the formless absorptions.
When the knowledge or vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is present,
six [factors] are past and ten are future.
There are five in the present.
Among these, the six in the past refer to the five factors of the aforementioned first group of wisdom that arises simultaneously.
Together with the five factors that arose simultaneously when first seen previously, these are combined to make six.
The rest is as explained before.
Once they have ceased, they are not lost.
If one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) or brings a conventional mind (*laukikacitta*) into manifestation;
or proceeding further, if one relies on a meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without applied or sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra*),
such that either the knowledge (*jñāna*) or the vision (*darśana*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is brought into manifestation, and so forth.
All [points] should be explained according to what is appropriate, following the previous [explanation].
Here, all past and future [factors] are said to be those that first arise and are cultivated;
those that arise and are cultivated in subsequent stages are not mentioned.
This is explained according to what arises and manifests at present.
What has been stated regarding those beyond training (aśaikṣa) applies to all cases as well;
it does not refer exclusively to those who enter meditative absorption through the sequential order.
Question: Why is it that when attaining the fruits of training (*śaikṣa-phala*),
vision (*darśana*) serves as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and vision serves as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)?

When attaining the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), does insight (*darśana*) serve as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)?
Answer: In the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning, all that was to be accomplished has been fully completed.
Because the preparatory application has ceased and one no longer seeks further,
it is not called "vision" (*darśana*);
the fruit of training (*śaikṣaphala*) is not like this, and therefore it receives the name "vision."

Question: Why is it that for those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), knowledge (*jñāna*) is mentioned first and vision (*darśana*) is mentioned later, whereas for those in the stage of learning (*śaikṣa*), vision is mentioned both at the beginning and at the end?
Answer: Because at the very beginning of the stage of no-more-learning, one necessarily gives rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Therefore, wisdom is explained first;
subsequently, when superior qualities arise,
there is also a process of inferential deliberation, and thus "view" is explained later.
The stage of realization first gives rise to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Because it is exclusively vision (*darśana*) and not yet knowledge (*jñāna*), it is initially termed "vision.
Subsequently, the function of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) remains incomplete.
Because one also attains the designation "seeing" through uninterrupted investigation,
"seeing" is mentioned last.

The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Ninety-Fifth,

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Three: The Aggregate of Wisdom (Jñānaskandha), Chapter One: The Sub-section on the Factors of Enlightenment (Śaikṣāṅga-nirdeśa), Part Three.
What is "view" (dṛṣṭi)? [The text continues] at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the tenets of other schools and revealing the correct principle.
That is to say, some may assert:
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) possess the nature of seeing (darśana). Why is this?
Because that which has a sharp and intense mode of activity (ākāra) is designated as "seeing."
All conditioned phenomena possess activity and have a sharp, intense mode of operation;
therefore, some hold that all conditioned phenomena are of the nature of vision (*darśana*).
To refute this view and demonstrate that only the eye faculty and the wisdom of discernment (*adhimokṣa*) constitute vision, and nothing else, [the author] states:
Alternatively, some say that even the receptivities at the edge of clear realization (abhisamayāntika-kṣānti) possess the nature of knowledge (jñāna),
as the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain.
He asserts this:
when the eye of untainted wisdom first encounters its object, it is called "patience" (kṣānti);
subsequently, when it abides securely within that object, it is called "knowledge" (jñāna).
It is like a traveler on a road who, upon reaching level ground,
first pauses and then comes to rest.
The Venerable One has also said:
Inferior wisdom is called "patience" (kṣānti) and superior wisdom is called "knowledge" (jñāna).
To refute that view and demonstrate that untainted patience is vision (darśana) rather than knowledge,
others further state:
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are also vision (*darśana*) of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
To refute that [opposing] view and to demonstrate that such inquiry has ceased,
it is no longer inferred that this knowledge is not vision.

Furthermore, within this aggregate of wisdom (*jñāna-skandha*), one should thoroughly distinguish the differences between the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) of vision (*darśana*), wisdom (*jñāna*), and insight (*prajñā*); therefore, this treatise is composed.
What is meant by "vision"?
Answer: The eye faculty consists of the five views,
mundane right view, and the views of those in training and those beyond training.
Question: For what reason is the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya) said to be "seeing" (darśana)?
Answer: Because of four reasons.
First, because it is so stated by the noble ones (ārya).
Second, because it is spoken of according to worldly convention;
third, because it is spoken of in the sūtras;
fourth, because it is perceived by the world through direct observation.
Regarding the phrase "because it is spoken by both the noble ones and worldly people":
this means that both the noble ones and worldly people alike say,
"I saw with my own eyes his coming and going, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, and so forth."
Furthermore, if one sees a person stumble or fall into confusion,
both [the observer and the person] say:
"Since you have seen this with your own eyes, why do you act thus?"
Regarding the phrase "because it is stated in the sūtras":
this refers to what is stated in the sūtras that after the eye has seen a form,
one should not grasp at its signs (*nimitta*) nor grasp at its secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).
Furthermore, it says this:
"Having seen forms with the eye, one should contemplate them as impure and reflect in accordance with reality.
It further says this:
Having seen a form with the eye, one should not be attached to what is pleasant nor should one be repelled by what is unpleasant.
Furthermore, it is said:
having seen a form with the eye, one gives rise to the three mental applications (manopavicāra) of joy, sorrow, and equanimity.
Furthermore, it is said:
having seen forms with the eye, one should neither rejoice nor be grieved;
rather, one should abide in equanimity with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
Regarding "because it is seen in the world":
this means that what is seen in the world by those with clear and pure vision is free from error.
Those who lack clear understanding perceive erroneously.
Furthermore, it is observed in the world that those possessing the visual faculty can see various forms,
whereas those lacking the visual faculty cannot see forms.
Furthermore, it is observed in the world that the eye can see a visible form only when it is directed toward it;
it cannot see it when not so directed.
Moreover, it is observed in the world that many cannot see obscured forms because the eye is obstructed.
The Venerable Vasumitra stated as follows:
"For what reason is the eye-faculty called 'seeing'?
It is because it is observed in the world that those with pure eyes say, 'I see purity.'"
One who possesses impure eyes says, "I see what is impure.
The Venerable One said:
For what reason is the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya) called "seeing" (darśana)?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"That which is apprehended by the eye-faculty and cognized by the visual consciousness is called 'the seen' (dṛṣṭa).
This is likewise the case in conventional usage.
Therefore, the eye faculty is said to be "seeing.
As for the five views, they are:
the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Extreme views,
false views,
and the grasping of views.
The clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Question: For what reason are these five called "views" (*dṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: Because of four reasons.
Because it is a form of viewing.
That is to say, it is able to view the objects that are to be grasped.
Question: How are these five types of deviant, perverse, and inverted viewing designated as "view" (*dṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: Although this is a perverse and inverted observation,
it is called "view" because its nature is wisdom,
just like the visual faculty of a person.
Although it is not clear, one is still able to observe and view;
therefore, it is also called "seeing" (*darśana*).
Second, because it involves decisive judgment.
This refers to the ability to determine the object that is to be grasped.
Question: Since this occurs in a single moment, how can there be such determination?
Answer: Because its nature is sharp and intense, it is designated by the term "determination."
Third, because of stubborn adherence;
that is, a firm and perverse attachment to one's own objects which cannot be relinquished even by the sword of the Noble Path.
Because the Buddha and his disciples sever those "fangs of views" with the sword of the Noble Path before casting them aside,
it is like the sea creature named Śiśumāra.
Whatever object it holds in its mouth, it clutches firmly and will not let go;
only by using a sharp sword to sever its tusks can one cause it to finally release.
The five views are likewise so because they penetrate deeply;
that is to say, they are sharp and penetrate their objects with such intensity as a needle sinking into mud.
Furthermore, for two reasons these five are called "views":
first, because they illuminate;
second, because they investigate.
Furthermore, for three reasons these five are called "views" (*dṛṣṭi*):
first, because they are associated with the characteristics of a view;
second, because they are capable of accomplishing the function of a view.
Third, because they are unimpeded regarding their objects.
Furthermore, for three reasons these five are called "views":
first, because of their underlying intention (*āśaya*).
Second, because of attachment;
third, because of seeking.
Furthermore, it is called "view" (dṛṣṭi) on account of three factors.
First, due to intention;
second, due to application;
third, due to ignorance.
"By way of intention" refers to what is seen by one who has attained meditative concentration;
"by way of application" refers to...
"Those who investigate by means of seeking see" refers to the perspective of those who seek through investigation.
"Because of ignorance" refers to the perspective of those who merely follow what they have heard.
Furthermore, regarding "by way of intention," this refers to the view of one whose intention is corrupted.
Regarding "by way of application":
The view of those whose preparatory effort has failed refers to the view of those who see [the self] through ignorance;
the view of those who have failed in both respects refers to the view of those who see [the self] through both [ignorance and the failure of preparatory effort].
Therefore, these five are also said to be "views.
Worldly right view refers to wisdom associated with a wholesome mental consciousness.
Because it is the nature of seeing, it is called "seeing.
"Training in seeing" refers to training in untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
The vision of one beyond training refers to the right view of one beyond training;
since both of these are also of the nature of vision, they are termed "vision."
It should be understood that herein, the five views regarding their objects are like seeing forms on a cloudy night;
mundane right view regarding its object is like seeing forms on a clear night;
and the vision of those in training regarding its object is like seeing forms on a cloudy day.
The vision of one beyond training perceives objects as clearly as seeing forms on a clear day.
What is meant by "knowledge" (jñāna)?
Answer: It is the wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses, excluding the untainted forbearances (anāsrava-kṣānti).
The remaining wisdom associated with the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is as follows:
herein, the wisdom associated with the five sensory consciousnesses is of three kinds;
first, the wholesome (kuśala).
The second is defiled;
the third is unobscured-neutral.
As for the wholesome, it refers exclusively to that which is innate wholesome.
Regarding the defiled:

it refers exclusively to that which is associated with greed, hatred, and delusion abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Regarding the non-obscured neutral: [it refers to that which is associated with]...
That is to say, it arises as a result of maturation (*vipākaja*);

there is also a small portion that arises simultaneously with the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*), the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and the mind of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*).
Furthermore, the wisdom associated with the remaining mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is also of three types.
There are three types: first, the wholesome; second, the defiled; and third, the non-obscured neutral.
The wholesome is of two kinds:
first, that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The second is the untainted (anāsrava).
The tainted wholesome (sāsrava-kuśala) has three types:
first, that acquired through application (prāyogika-labdha).
Second, that acquired through the removal of defilements;
third, that acquired by birth.
That which is acquired through application refers to the wisdom consisting of hearing.
Wisdom derived from reflection,
wisdom derived from cultivation,
and wisdom derived from hearing.
That is to say, it is the reasoned discernment of the words and their meaning.
As for the wisdom consisting in reflection,
it refers to the meditation on impurity and the mindfulness of breathing.
As for the wisdom produced by cultivation, such as the applications of mindfulness and so forth,
it refers to the stages of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas.
The conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamaya*),

as well as the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) that are acquired through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgyalābhika*).

This refers to the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and so forth.
As for those acquired by birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*), these refer to the wholesome states naturally obtained upon being born in those respective realms.
The untainted (anāsrava) is of two kinds:
first, that of training (śaikṣa), and second, that of no-more-training (aśaikṣa).
"Training" refers to the eight knowledges of one in training.
The state of no-more-learning consists of the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising,
as well as the wisdom of right view of one beyond training.
As for that which is defiled:
This refers to those indeterminate states that are associated with the afflictions and secondary afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation;
specifically, it refers to those arising simultaneously with the mind of maturation, the mind of deportment, the mind of craftsmanship, and the mind of supernormal powers.
What is wisdom? The answer is: wisdom associated with the six consciousnesses.
This is of three kinds.
That is to say: wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured neutral [states], as explained in detail previously.
The distinction is as follows:
The eight untainted patiences (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) are likewise subsumed under wisdom (*prajñā*),
because they are common to the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). Wisdom is present in association with all states of mind.
The three natures of vision and wisdom have already been explained.
Furthermore, one should distinguish between the characteristics of these three as being either mixed or unmixed.
Are all views considered wisdom?
It should be stated in four propositions.
Because the intrinsic natures of seeing (*darśana*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) differ in their respective breadth and narrowness,
there is that which is seeing but not wisdom.
This refers to the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and untainted receptivity (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
Question: Why is the eye faculty not called "knowledge" (*jñāna*)?
Answer: Because the eye faculty is material form (*rūpa*).
Because wisdom is not form.
Furthermore, the eye-faculty is non-associated and lacks a basis.
It has no object of focus,
no mental aspect,
and no alertness.
Because wisdom is not thus.
Question: For what reason is untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) not considered wisdom?
Answer: Because untainted patience, with respect to the truths being contemplated...
Although they have attained patience, they have not yet reached a definitive resolution;
although they have practiced contemplation, they have not yet attained thorough discernment;
although they have engaged in seeking, they have not yet reached the ultimate conclusion.
Although he investigates, he does not yet fully comprehend;
although he attains clear realization, he does not yet scrutinize it repeatedly;
he merely exerts effort in his preparatory application without ceasing.
Therefore, it is not called "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, the meaning of certainty is the meaning of knowledge.
Patience (*kṣānti*) arises simultaneously with the doubt that is to be abandoned.
Because it is not yet definitively certain regarding the object perceived,
it is not termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this as follows.
Although patience (*kṣānti*) toward the Noble Truths is indeed correct endurance,
it is not called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because it does not involve definitive discernment.
The Venerable One said:
The designation "knowledge" (jñāna) is established only when the object is seen to its ultimate conclusion.
This does not occur at the stage of the initial patience (kṣānti).
Therefore, although untainted patience is not called knowledge, it is in fact knowledge.
The Venerable Vimalamitra said:
"To contemplate again is called wisdom;
[this concerns] the Four Noble Truths from time immemorial."
There has never been a single moment of noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*) that has observed [the object] repeatedly;
because patience (*kṣānti*) arises as the initial observation, it is not yet called "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
Although the wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses cannot observe its object repeatedly, [it is still not considered wisdom].
Furthermore, since beginningless time, infinite observations of contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) have already arisen regarding objects such as form;
because these belong to the same category, they are described as "repeated observation."
Therefore, it is also called "knowledge.
Other contaminated knowledges that do not take [the same object] as a repeated object should be understood accordingly.
One should not raise an objection.
There is wisdom that is not vision;
namely, the wisdom associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness, as well as the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
Excluding the five views and mundane right view, it is the remaining defiled wisdom associated with the mental consciousness.
Question: Why is the wisdom associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness not considered a "view"?
Answer: That which has a sharp and intense mode of activity (*ākāra*) and penetrates deeply into its object (*ālambana*) is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).

The wisdom associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya-saṃprayukta-prajñā*) does not have a sharp and intense mode of activity, and it cannot penetrate deeply into its object.
Therefore, it is not called "view.
Furthermore, view is capable of discrimination,
whereas that wisdom is not capable of discrimination.
Views can take both specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) as their objects;
for while that wisdom (prajñā) can only take specific characteristics as its object,
views can take the three times as well as the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) as their objects.
Because that wisdom can only take the present as its object,
whereas vision (*darśana*) can repeatedly apprehend objects;
because that wisdom can only apprehend an object for a single moment.
When one perceives an object and deliberates upon it through investigation,
that wisdom is not like this;
such are the various causes and conditions.
The wisdom associated with the five groups of consciousness is not called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
Question: Why are the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) not views?
Answer: Because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of these two knowledges are not sharp or intense.
Because it does not penetrate deeply into the object of focus (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, one observes that the application of effort (*prayoga*) in its cultivation is uninterrupted;
the two types of knowledge (*jñāna*) are not so.
Because it is like a bird perched at ease, it is not called "seeing.
Furthermore, seeking and investigating are designated as "seeing," whereas these two types of knowledge are not so.
Therefore, it is not called "vision.
For this reason, the Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"The knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising signify that what was to be done has been accomplished."
There is nothing further superior to be sought;
therefore, it is not called "seeing.
Some say this: [text continues].
All untainted wisdoms (anāsravaprajñā) are, in brief, of two kinds:
first, that which can counteract wrong views;
second, that which can counteract ignorance.
That which can counteract wrong views is called "vision" (dṛṣṭi).
Since the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (kṣayānutpādajñāna) can only counteract ignorance,
it is not called vision.
Furthermore, there are those who say that all untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is comprised of three types in total:
first, that which can exclusively counteract wrong views.
Second, it can only counteract ignorance;
third, it can counteract both wrong views and ignorance.
Regarding that which can only counteract wrong views:
This is a vision, not a knowledge;
it refers to the untainted receptivities at the conclusion of clear realization,
which are capable only of counteracting ignorance.
This knowledge is not vision;
it refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
These are capable of acting as antidotes to both.
This knowledge is also vision;
that is to say, it refers to other untainted wisdoms.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this.
Investigation is termed "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).

Since the tasks of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) have reached their culmination, one no longer investigates; therefore, they are not termed "view."
Furthermore, it is said that seeking is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*);
because the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising has accomplished what was to be done,
there is no further seeking, and thus it is not called a "view."
Furthermore, it is said:
if the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising were of the nature of vision (*darśana*),
then all Arhats would possess only nine factors of one beyond training (*aśaikṣāṅga*).
Excluding the factor of right knowledge;
however, the Blessed One stated that all Arhats are endowed with the ten factors of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-aṅga).
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are not views (*dṛṣṭi*).

Question: Just as mundane right view (*laukikī samyagdṛṣṭi*), the view of those in training (*śaikṣadṛṣṭi*), and the view of those beyond training (*aśaikṣadṛṣṭi*) are also forms of knowledge yet are designated as "views. Why is this not the case here?
If the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising,
although they are also "views," are nevertheless called "knowledge," what fault is there in this?
Answer: As when first practicing the preparatory cultivation (*prayoga*),
although conventional right view (*sāṃvṛtikasamyagdṛṣṭi*) possesses the nature of both knowledge (*jñāna*) and vision (*darśana*),
it is established as the limb of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭyaṅga*) rather than the limb of right knowledge (*samyagjñānāṅga*).
Although the eight knowledges of those who have entered the stage of training possess the nature of both knowledge and vision,
they are established as the factor of right view and not as the factor of right knowledge.
Having already reached the stage of no-more-learning, one possesses the nature of both knowledge and vision;
yet, while being established as the factor of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), it is not established as the factor of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

This is because even if the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) also possess the nature of both knowledge and vision, [they are categorized differently].
Furthermore, one should establish that it is the factor of right view and not the factor of right knowledge; in that case,
all Arhats would possess only nine factors of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
In this way, it would contradict what the Blessed One said:
that all Arhats are endowed with ten factors.
The Venerable One says:

Because the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are definitively of the nature of vision (*darśana*) and the nature of decisive penetration (*niścaya*). Question:
If that is so, then an Arhat should possess only nine factors (*aṅga*).
Answer: Two factors exist only on the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*), namely right liberation (*samyag-vimukti*) and right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
Eight factors exist on both the stages of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This refers to the remaining eight limbs.
Although the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are also forms of vision,
their specific functions have already reached ultimate completion.
Since this differs from the previous stage of training,
it should not be difficult to establish it as a separate factor.
The critique states:
It should be stated thus:
the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are knowledge, not vision;
for that which was to be done has been accomplished.
Because one no longer seeks after the four noble truths and the application of effort has ceased;
this refers to all tainted wisdom associated with the mental consciousness, excluding the five views and mundane right view.
This is of two kinds:
first, defiled;
second, non-obscured neutral.
Defiled [wisdom] refers to wisdom associated with greed, hatred, pride, doubt,
and the unique ignorance (āveṇikī avidyā).
Regarding those that are non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*):
these refer to the wisdom co-arising with the minds of maturation (*vipākaja*), deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Question: For what reason is the wisdom associated with greed and other afflictions on the level of the mind (*manobhūmi*) not considered a view (*dṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: Because the aspect of that wisdom is not sharp and intense, it cannot penetrate deeply into the object of focus.
Furthermore, because those two are obscured and impaired by afflictions.
The two afflictions refer to any one of greed, hatred, pride, or doubt,
along with the ignorance associated with them.
Question: If that were so,
then the wisdom associated with the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) should be a view (*dṛṣṭi*),
because it arises in association with only a single affliction.
The answer is: that ignorance is of two kinds.
First is the non-common ignorance abandoned through seeing, which is more heavily obscuring than the other two afflictions.
Second, the non-common ignorance abandoned through cultivation is associated with the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and impurities (*mala*) that arise by their own power,
because it functions independently.
Because it can obscure and impair wisdom, just like greed, hatred, and so forth;
thus, the wisdom associated with those [afflictions]—just as wisdom associated with greed and the like—is also not called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
Question: Why is unobscured-neutral wisdom (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-prajñā*) not a view?
The answer is: because the aspect of that wisdom is not sharp, it cannot penetrate deeply into the object of focus;
furthermore, because the power of that wisdom is extremely weak and inferior, it is not termed "view" (dṛṣṭi).
Because it must possess power over its object and be firm to be designated as "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
Question: It is logically acceptable that the wisdom (*prajñā*) arising from maturation (*vipākaja*) and that belonging to the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*) have weak power.
The wisdom pertaining to the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) and the wisdom associated with the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) possess a very powerful force;
why then are they not considered "views" (*dṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: Although the wisdom pertaining to the spheres of craftsmanship possesses the most powerful force, [it is not a view].

Just as the knowledge arising according to one's wishes produced by Viśvakarman and other such beings is not called "vision" because it is obscured and impaired by wrong livelihood; so too is this case.
This means that all crafts arise with the desire for livelihood as their cause;
thus, although the mind and mental factors present during the practice of a craft are not defiled.
Because they are produced by the power of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*),
it is said that being obscured and impaired by wrong livelihood is equivalent to being obscured and impaired by greed (*lobha*).
Even if one were not obscured and impaired by greed, [it would still be so].
Because its power is superficial and its mode of activity is weak and dull,
it cannot penetrate deeply into the object of focus; therefore,
it is not called "view" (*darśana*).
Furthermore, the wisdom pertaining to the arts and crafts operates like doubt;
it cannot reach a definitive conclusion regarding its object. Why is this so?
Even though an extremely skillful person performs a work of artistry,
they become hesitant when it is criticized by others; likewise,
the wisdom resulting from supernormal powers (abhijñā-phala-prajñā) is not sharp or intense with respect to its object of focus.
Because it cannot penetrate deeply into the object of focus,
but rather functions spontaneously, being drawn forth by the power of a preceding meditative concentration,
and because it does not investigate the object of focus, it is not termed "view."
Furthermore, the wisdom that is the fruit of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) is produced by being drawn forth from the transformed objects (*nirmāṇa*) as its cause through prior habituation;
because it is like practicing a craft, it is not termed "seeing" (*darśana*).
Furthermore, the four types of indeterminate wisdom, such as that born of maturation (*vipākaja*), are all weak in power.
Just as they do not constitute the wholesome nor the defiled,
they likewise do not constitute "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
There are those that are both views and cognitions;
namely, the five views and conventional right view,
excluding the untainted patiences (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) and the cognitions of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*).
The remaining untainted wisdom consists of the eight knowledges of the learner (*śaikṣa*),
as well as the untainted wisdom of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) which is right view;
furthermore, it includes the five [supramundane] views and mundane right view.
Because all [factors] possess both the characteristics of view (*darśana*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), they are subsumed under the third category.
There are those that are neither view nor knowledge, namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics;
"characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) here refers to that which is designated by a name.
If a phenomenon is that which is expressed by the first three phrases, it is termed a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).
Any phenomenon other than these constitutes the fourth phrase;
such is the phenomenon expressed by the fourth phrase.
What, then, is this? It refers to the remaining forms within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), excluding the eye;
and the remaining formations within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), excluding wisdom (*prajñā*).
Together with the three aggregates in their entirety and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), these constitute the fourth alternative.
Are all views (*dṛṣṭi*) wisdom (*prajñā*)?
One should answer that there are four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).
Because the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of vision (*darśana*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) differ in their breadth and narrowness,
there are instances of vision that are not wisdom: namely, the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), because it is capable of seeing and because its intrinsic nature is form (*rūpa*).
There is wisdom that is not vision;
this refers to the wisdom associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness, as well as the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising,
excluding the five views and mundane right view.
The remaining contaminated wisdom associated with the mental consciousness is [prajñā] because it has the nature of discerning phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*),
but it is not [vitarka] because it does not involve discursive investigation.
As explained in detail previously, "view" also includes wisdom (*prajñā*);
that is, all untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*),
as well as the five views and mundane right view (*laukika-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
That is to say, the untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*), the eight knowledges of the learner (*śaikṣa*), and the right view of the adept (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*) and so forth;
for they are capable of inferential deliberation and possess the nature of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
It possesses two characteristics.
There are those that are neither views nor wisdom,
namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to that which is named;
this has been explained in detail previously.
Are all cognitions (jñāna) wisdom (prajñā)?
Answer: All forms of knowledge (*jñāna*) are wisdom (*prajñā*), because that which is capable of definitive discernment is the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*).
However, there is wisdom that is not knowledge.
This refers to the fact that untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) has not yet reached definitive certainty when first contemplating the objects of the truths. [The text continues:
"Is knowledge subsumed by vision, or is vision subsumed by knowledge?
and so forth, as explained at length.
In this context, there are two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding one type of two-proposition set, its characteristics should be understood by analogy with the preceding inquiry into determination:
"Does one who possesses vision also possess that knowledge? and so forth, as explained at length.
In this context, there are three: vision, wisdom, and knowledge.
If one is accomplished, the other two must necessarily be present as well;
therefore, the response is given for each in this manner.
Question: Who accomplishes the wisdom of vision?
Answer: All sentient beings.
This is a general statement, yet there are variations in degree.
This refers to one who has severed the roots of goodness,
who possesses the wisdom of views to be abandoned through insight pertaining to the three realms,
and who possesses the defiled wisdom to be abandoned through cultivation pertaining to the three realms.
One who has achieved non-obscured, indeterminate wisdom of the desire realm,
whose roots of goodness are not severed, and who has not yet attained wholesome states of mind of the form realm,
achieves the wisdom of views to be abandoned by insight pertaining to all three realms.
One achieves the defiled wisdom abandoned through cultivation within the three realms;
one achieves the wholesome wisdom of right view within the desire realm;
and one achieves the non-obscured neutral wisdom within the desire realm.

One who has already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire accomplishes the wisdom of insight that abandons what is to be abandoned by vision in all three realms,
and accomplishes the afflicted wisdom that abandons what is to be abandoned by cultivation in all three realms.
One who has accomplished wholesome wisdom pertaining to the desire and form realms;
one who has accomplished non-obscured, indeterminate wisdom pertaining to the desire realm;
and one who is already free from the defilements of desire but has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm.
If one is born in the desire realm, one possesses the wisdom of views to be abandoned by insight pertaining to the form and formless realms,
as well as the defiled wisdom to be abandoned by cultivation pertaining to the form and formless realms.
One achieves the wholesome, discerning wisdom of the desire and form realms;
one achieves the non-obscured, neutral wisdom of the desire and form realms.
However, if one is born in the form realm, one does not achieve the wholesome, discerning wisdom of the desire realm.
The accomplishment of the others is as explained regarding birth in the desire realm.
One who has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm but has not yet abandoned attachment to the form realm—
If one is born in the desire realm, one possesses the wisdom of the views to be abandoned through seeing pertaining to the form and formless realms;
one also possesses the defiled wisdom to be abandoned through cultivation pertaining to the form and formless realms.
One achieves the wisdom of good vision pertaining to the three realms.
One achieves the wisdom that is non-obscured and indeterminate pertaining to the desire and form realms.
If one is born in the form realm, one does not achieve the wisdom of good vision pertaining to the desire realm.
The accomplishment of the remaining [factors] is as explained regarding those born in the desire realm.

One who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm and is born in the desire realm accomplishes the wisdom of the view that is abandoned by insight belonging to the formless realm.
He achieves the defiled wisdom abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm;
he achieves the wholesome wisdom of vision pertaining to the three realms;
and he achieves the non-obscured, neutral wisdom of the desire and form realms.
If one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu), one does not possess the wholesome vision and wisdom of the desire realm (kāmadhātu);

one possesses the remainder as described for those born in the desire realm. If one is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), one does not possess the wholesome vision and wisdom of either the desire or form realms.
Furthermore, when one does not possess the wisdom that is non-obscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta) of the desire or form realms,
and if a mind born of maturation (vipākaja) manifests before one,
then one possesses the wisdom that is non-obscured and indeterminate of the formless realm.
If the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) does not manifest,
then one also does not possess the non-obscured, neutral wisdom (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-prajñā*) of the formless realm;
the possession of other [factors] is as explained for birth in the desire realm.
It is thus for ordinary beings.
As for noble ones,
as long as the knowledge of suffering has not yet arisen for those who practice through faith or through dharma, [they are likewise].
One who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire accomplishes the wisdom of the views to be abandoned by insight within the three realms,
and accomplishes the defiled wisdom to be abandoned by cultivation within the three realms.
They achieve wholesome vision and wisdom pertaining to the desire and form realms;
they achieve non-obscured, neutral vision and wisdom pertaining to the desire realm;
and they achieve untainted vision and wisdom.

That is to say, one who is already free from the defilement of desire but not yet free from the defilement of form possesses the vision-wisdom to be abandoned by insight regarding the realms of form and formlessness,
and possesses the afflicted wisdom to be abandoned by cultivation regarding the realms of form and formlessness.
One who has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm possesses the wholesome vision and wisdom of the desire and form realms;
one who has already attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm [possesses that as well].
They achieve the wisdom of right view regarding the three realms;
they achieve the wisdom that is non-obscured and indeterminate within the desire and form realms;
and they achieve untainted vision and wisdom.
That is to say, one who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm possesses the wisdom of insight that abandons [defilements] through vision belonging to the formless realm,
and possesses the afflicted wisdom that abandons [defilements] through cultivation belonging to the formless realm.
They achieve the wisdom of correct vision regarding the three realms;
they achieve the wisdom that is non-obscured and indeterminate within the desire and form realms;
and they achieve untainted vision and wisdom.
When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen,
one who is not yet free from the defilement of desire possesses the wisdom of the vision of origin, cessation, and the path regarding the three realms,
as well as the defiled wisdom of the three realms that is to be abandoned through cultivation.
He achieves the wholesome wisdom of the desire and form realms;
he achieves the non-obscured, neutral wisdom of the desire realm;
and he achieves untainted (anāsrava) wisdom of vision.

That is to say, one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm possesses the wisdom of views to be abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path pertaining to the form and formless realms;
they also possess the afflicted wisdom to be abandoned through cultivation pertaining to the form and formless realms.
One who has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm possesses the wholesome vision and wisdom of the desire and form realms;
one who has already attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm [possesses those of all three realms].
They achieve the wisdom of right view regarding the three realms;
they achieve the wisdom that is non-obscured and indeterminate within the desire and form realms;
and they achieve the wisdom of untainted vision.

That is to say, one who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm possesses the wisdom of vision that abandons [the afflictions] of the formless realm through the seeing of origin, cessation, and the path;
and they possess the afflicted wisdom of the formless realm that is abandoned through cultivation.
They achieve the wisdom of right view regarding the three realms;
they achieve the wisdom that is non-obscured and indeterminate within the desire and form realms;
and they achieve the wisdom of untainted vision.
For one in whom the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, and who is not yet free from the defilements of desire,
there is the possession of the wisdom of insight that abandons [defilements] through the vision of the cessation and path of the three realms,
as well as the possession of the defiled wisdom that is abandoned through cultivation in the three realms.
They achieve wholesome vision and wisdom pertaining to the desire and form realms;
they achieve non-obscured, neutral vision and wisdom pertaining to the desire realm;
and they achieve untainted vision and wisdom.
That person has already become free from the defilement of desire,
but is not yet free from the defilement of form;
they possess the wisdom of vision that abandons the [defilements] to be abandoned through the vision of the cessation and the path within the realms of form and formlessness.
One who has accomplished the defiled wisdom abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms,
but has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm,
accomplishes the wholesome view-wisdom of the desire and form realms.
One who has already attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm accomplishes the wholesome wisdom of vision belonging to the three realms,
and accomplishes the non-obscured, neutral wisdom of the desire and form realms.
One who has accomplished untainted insight and wisdom,
for whom the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, and who is not yet free from the defilement of desire,
accomplishes the insight and wisdom regarding the factors to be abandoned through the path of seeing within the three realms.
One achieves the defiled wisdom abandoned through cultivation within the three realms;
one achieves the wholesome wisdom of seeing within the desire and form realms;
and one achieves the non-obscured neutral wisdom of the desire realm.
One achieves untainted vision and wisdom. Specifically,

one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm achieves the vision and wisdom that abandon what is to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the form and formless realms, as well as the defiled wisdom that abandons what is to be abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms.
One who has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm possesses the wholesome vision and wisdom of the desire and form realms;
one who has already attained the wholesome mind of the formless realm...
They achieve the wisdom of right view regarding the three realms;
they achieve the wisdom that is non-obscured and indeterminate within the desire and form realms;
and they achieve the wisdom of untainted vision.
That is to say, having already become free from the defilement of form,
one achieves the wisdom of insight that abandons what is to be abandoned through the path of seeing in the formless realm,
and achieves the afflicted wisdom that is to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
They achieve the wisdom of right view regarding the three realms;
they achieve the wisdom that is non-obscured and indeterminate within the desire and form realms;
and they achieve the wisdom of untainted vision.
Those who possess faith-resolve (śraddhādhimukta) or have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), but have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire,
possess the defiled wisdom to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the three realms,
as well as the wholesome wisdom of seeing belonging to the desire and form realms.
He achieves wisdom that is non-obscured and indeterminate within the desire realm;
he achieves untainted vision and wisdom;
and he has thereby already become free from the defilement of desire.
One who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm, if born in the desire realm,
possesses the defiled wisdom to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the form and formless realms,
and possesses the wholesome wisdom of seeing belonging to the desire and form realms.
One achieves the non-obscured, neutral wisdom of the desire and form realms,
and achieves the untainted wisdom of vision. However,
if one is born in the form realm, one does not achieve the wholesome wisdom of vision pertaining to the desire realm.
The accomplishment of the remaining [factors] is as explained regarding birth in the desire realm.
That same person who has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm,
but has not yet abandoned attachment to the form realm, if born in the desire realm—
He achieves the defiled wisdom abandoned through cultivation in the realms of form and formlessness;
he achieves the wholesome wisdom of vision belonging to the three realms;
and he achieves the non-obscured neutral wisdom of the desire and form realms.
One who has attained untainted vision and wisdom, if born in the form realm, does not possess the wholesome vision and wisdom of the desire realm;
the possession of the remainder is as explained for one born in the desire realm.
That very person, having already become free from the defilement of form,
if born in the desire realm,
accomplishes the defiled wisdom of the formless realm that is to be abandoned through cultivation.
He achieves the wisdom of right view regarding the three realms;
he achieves the wisdom that is non-obscured and indeterminate within the desire and form realms;
and he achieves the wisdom of untainted vision.
If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one does not possess the wholesome wisdom of vision pertaining to the desire realm;
