the possession of other [wisdoms] is as explained for those born in the desire realm.

If one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one does not possess the wholesome wisdom of vision pertaining to either the desire or form realms, nor does one possess the non-obscured, neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) wisdom pertaining to the desire or form realms.
If a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is present before one,
then one possesses the non-obscured neutral wisdom (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-prajñā*) of the formless realm;
if a mind born of maturation is not present before one, [one does not].
Furthermore, they do not achieve the non-obscured, indeterminate wisdom of the formless realm;
their achievement of other [types of wisdom] is as explained regarding those born in the desire realm.
This applies to an Arhat who is born in the desire realm.
He achieves the wisdom of right view regarding the three realms;
he achieves the wisdom that is non-obscured and indeterminate within the desire and form realms;
and he achieves the wisdom of untainted vision.
If one is born in the form realm, one accomplishes wholesome vision and wisdom of the form and formless realms;
one accomplishes non-obscured neutral vision and wisdom of the desire and form realms;
and one accomplishes untainted vision and wisdom.
If one is born in the formless realm and the mind born of maturation does not manifest,
one accomplishes the wholesome vision and wisdom of the formless realm,
and accomplishes untainted vision and wisdom.
If a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is present before one,
and one also possesses the unobscured-neutral wisdom (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-prajñā*) of the formless realm,
has that wisdom already been abandoned and fully understood (*parijñāta*) by means of the various views?
Question: Is it the case that when wisdom has been abandoned and fully known, those views are also [abandoned and fully known]?
Answer: It is so. Question:
When all views have been abandoned and fully known, is that wisdom also [abandoned and fully known]? Answer: It is so.
Answer: It is so stated.
Does wisdom, having already abandoned and already fully understood that view?
Answer: It is so.
If various cognitions (*jñāna*) have already been abandoned and fully understood, has that wisdom (*prajñā*) also [been abandoned and fully understood]?
Answer: It is so.
If wisdom has already been abandoned and fully understood, have those cognitions also [been abandoned and fully understood]?
Answer: It is so.
Why is this? Because the stages of the three types of complete knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding vision, wisdom, and abandonment are all similar.
Question: Who has already abandoned and fully understood [the defilements] through vision and wisdom?
Answer: All Arhats; these are said to be those who have attained ultimate abandonment and full understanding.
For those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana), the degree of abandonment is indefinite.
That is to say, for Arhats of the three realms,
all views and wisdom have already been abandoned and fully known;
as for those who are Non-returners (Anāgāmins):
If one has already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness,
the vision and wisdom that abandon what is to be abandoned by insight regarding the three realms,
as well as the vision and wisdom that abandon what is to be abandoned by cultivation across the eight stages, have been severed and fully known.
...up to: if one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna,
there is the wisdom of insight that abandons the views of the three realms through seeing,
as well as the wisdom of insight that abandons the views of the desire realm through cultivation.
Having been abandoned and fully understood:
for all Once-returners and Stream-enterers,
the views to be abandoned through insight within the three realms have already been abandoned and fully understood by means of the wisdom of insight.
For those practicing in accordance with faith or in accordance with the Dharma, if the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen,
the wisdom of insight regarding the views to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin,
and cessation within the three realms has already been abandoned and fully understood.
If the knowledge of origination has already arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen,
then the knowledge and vision regarding the views to be abandoned through the seeing of suffering and origination within the three realms have already been abandoned and fully understood.
If the knowledge of suffering has already arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen,
then the insight-knowledge that abandons what is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering within the three realms has already been abandoned and fully understood.
It is so for the Noble Ones.
As for ordinary persons who have already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness,
their knowledge and vision regarding what is to be abandoned through insight and cultivation across the eight stages [is as follows].
Having already abandoned and fully understood [them],
up to having already become free from the defilements of the desire realm but not yet free from the defilements of the first dhyāna:
this is the wisdom of insight that abandons [defilements] through seeing and cultivation belonging to one stage.
"Already abandoned and already fully understood"—this is called the third [category] among the three: views, wisdom, and knowledge.
Now follows the analysis of the five gates concerning the attainment of abandonment through the inclusion of meditative concentration.
"Are all right views the factor of enlightenment consisting in the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is that the preceding treatise is the fundamental basis for this;
namely, it was previously stated:
"What is meant by 'view'?"
"What is knowledge? What is wisdom?
Although this was said, right view and right knowledge were not yet distinguished.
The [factors] associated with the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) have varying degrees of breadth and narrowness;
it is for the purpose of distinguishing them that this treatise is composed.
Now, within this Abhidharma Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra, there exists a definitive characteristic.
If the factors of the path are analyzed after the factors of enlightenment, then the factors of the path are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*),
because the seven factors of enlightenment are exclusively untainted. If, however,
the factors of the path are analyzed prior to the factors of enlightenment...
Thus, the factors of the path (mārgāṅga) pertain to both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava).
Since the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) were previously analyzed within this context as being the factors of the path,
one should understand that the factors of the path likewise pertain to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated.
This is called the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point;
those who possess wisdom should analyze it accordingly.
Are all right views the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena?
It should be answered with four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
This is because right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmavicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) have different scopes of inclusion.

There is right view that is not the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena; namely, conventional right view (*saṃvṛti-samyagdṛṣṭi*), because all awakening factors assist in awakening to reality as it is (*yathābhūtam*) and are therefore exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
There is the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) that is not right view;
this refers to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (kṣayānutpāda-jñāna), because it is not of the nature of seeing (darśana).
There is also that which is both right view and the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena.
This refers to the remaining untainted wisdom (anāsravaprajñā) other than the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), namely:
the eight patiences (kṣānti) at the limit of clear observation (abhisamayāntika), the eight knowledges of those in training (śaikṣa), and the right view of those beyond training (aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi).
These three types possess both characteristics.
There is that which is neither right view nor the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena;
this refers to everything except the aforementioned characteristics.
"Characteristics" refers to what is designated by those names, as explained extensively above.
What, then, is this? It refers to all other factors within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)— excluding the wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness—
as well as the entirety of the other four aggregates and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), which constitute the fourth alternative.
Are all right knowledges (*samyagjñāna*) factors of the awakening consisting in the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
One should respond that there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*),
because right knowledge and the factor of the awakening consisting in the investigation of phenomena also have mutual differences in their scope.
There is right knowledge that is not the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena; this refers to conventional right knowledge, because it lacks the characteristics of an awakening factor.
There is the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena that is not right knowledge;
this refers to untainted forbearance (*anāsrava-kṣānti*), because it lacks the characteristics of knowledge.
There is that which is both right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
This refers to all untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) other than the untainted patiences (*kṣānti*), namely:

the eight knowledges of those in training (*śaikṣa*), as well as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the right view of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because these possess both characteristics.
There is that which is neither right knowledge nor the factor-of-enlightenment of investigation of phenomena;
this refers to everything except the aforementioned characteristics.
"Characteristics" refers to what has been designated as such, as explained extensively above.
What, then, is this? It refers to all other formations within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), excluding the wholesome wisdom associated with the six consciousnesses.
And the entirety of the four aggregates, together with unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), constitute the fourth alternative.

Question: Why is it stated here that only right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) have a relationship of mutual breadth and narrowness with the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Is it not the case that the other members of the path (*mārgāṅga*) and the other factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) have varying degrees of breadth and narrowness?
Answer: This is because the intention of the author of the treatise was such;
and so on, as explained at length.
Furthermore, it should also be asked here: Are all those that are right efforts (*samyak-vyāyāma*) also factors of enlightenment consisting of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
The answer is: Those that are factors of enlightenment consisting of energy are also right efforts; however, there are right efforts that are not factors of enlightenment consisting of energy.
That is to say: Are all those that are mundane right effort, and so forth, up to those that are right concentration, also factors of enlightenment consisting of concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: All those that are factors of enlightenment consisting of concentration are also right concentration.
There is right concentration that is not a factor of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga);
namely, mundane right concentration.
This should have been stated [in the sūtra], yet it was not.
One should know that this is an incomplete statement (*sāvadeśanā*).
Furthermore, what is stated here— showing only the beginning and the end while omitting the middle—
is spoken thus for the sake of brevity.
That which begins with right view and ends with right knowledge is like the beginning and end of a manifestation: just as one first enters and then crosses over,
it should be understood that the same applies to the ultimate perfection of skillful means.
Furthermore, if a pair of dharmas fulfills all four permutations (catuṣkoṭi), they are explained herein;
if a pair of dharmas possesses only the "consequent permutation" (anuloma-paścāt-koti), they are not explained herein.
Furthermore, within this aggregate of wisdom (*jñāna-skandha*), those phenomena that are of the nature of insight (*darśana*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are analyzed as being of the category of wisdom;
since diligence (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*),
and concentration (*samādhi*) are not of the category of wisdom, they are not mentioned here.
When each of the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and the eight factors of the path (mārgāṅga) manifests, how many factors of enlightenment and how many factors of the path manifest?
Why was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting other schools and revealing the correct principle.
That is to say, some may claim that the various mental factors (caitta-dharma) arise sequentially.
They do not arise simultaneously,
as the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain;
the Bhadanta also says this.
The various mental factors arise in succession;
they do not arise simultaneously,
just as a large caravan of merchants passes through a narrow path one after another.
Each must pass through [the stages] one by one, being neither two nor many.
It is the same for all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*);
each arises individually as a produced characteristic from its own cause.
There is certainly no sense in which they arise through simultaneous conjunction.
Question: On the basis of what authority (*pramāṇa*) do they make such a statement?
Answer: On the basis of the authority of the authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If at that time the mind is sunken or in danger of sinking,
to cultivate three factors of enlightenment is called untimely cultivation."
This refers to lightness, tranquility, and equanimity;
these are called the three factors of enlightenment cultivated at this time, namely:
investigation of phenomena, energy, and joy.
If at that time the mind is agitated or feared to become agitated,
cultivating three factors of enlightenment is called untimely cultivation;
namely, the investigation of phenomena, energy, and joy.
The cultivation of the three factors of enlightenment is called "cultivation at this time," namely:
lightness, tranquility, and equanimity.
They explain it in this way.
Since the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are cultivated both at the proper time and at improper times,
it is known that mental factors arise in succession and do not arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, another sutra states: Śāriputra said,
"I am certainly able to dwell at will and with mastery in the seven factors of enlightenment."
That is to say, if I wish to dwell in this awakening-factor concentration during the first watch of the day,
I am immediately able to dwell therein;
if I wish to dwell in this awakening-factor concentration during the middle watch of the day, [I am immediately able to dwell therein].
Even if I am able to abide [in them],
if I wish to abide in this factor-of-enlightenment concentration during the latter part of the day,
I am immediately able to abide therein.
He spoke thus:
"Since the Venerable Śāriputra was able to abide as he wished within the seven factors of enlightenment,
one knows that mental factors arise in a sequential order."
The principle that they do not arise simultaneously is established;
this treatise is composed to refute that view and to demonstrate that all mental factors (caitta) arise at one and the same time.
Question: If all mental factors arise simultaneously, [how is this so?]
How does this accord with the sūtra cited by him?
The answer is: the aforementioned sūtra states that one cultivates the three factors of enlightenment at the proper time and not at the improper time.
It is thus proven that mental factors do not necessarily arise one after another in succession,
because it is taught that the three factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are cultivated simultaneously;
this proves that all mental factors arise at the same time.
Question: If the factors of enlightenment arise—
either six or seven— at one time according to the level upon which they depend,
why does the Sūtra state that there are only three types each for cultivation at the proper time and at the improper time?

Answer: This is stated because the power and function of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) increase or decrease depending on their respective categories of calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā).
That is to say, three factors of enlightenment belong to the category of calm abiding, while three factors of enlightenment belong to the category of insight.
If the factors of enlightenment belonging to the category of śamatha increase such that the mind becomes sunken,
one should at that time cultivate the factors of enlightenment belonging to the category of vipaśyanā to rouse and uplift the mind;
because one is instead cultivating the category of śamatha, it is said to be "untimely."
If, when the factors of enlightenment belonging to the category of vipaśyanā increase, they cause the mind to become agitated,
one should at that time cultivate the factors of enlightenment belonging to the category of śamatha to suppress the mind and bring it down;
because one is instead cultivating the category of vipaśyanā, this is called "untimely."
Although the factors of enlightenment arise simultaneously,
only three are mentioned because their functions vary in degree.
Furthermore, at the time of entering the Noble Path, one relies upon the categories of serenity (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā).
Because there is a distinction [between the two], it is stated as follows: that is to say,
if one enters the Noble Path by means of the factors of enlightenment belonging to the category of *śamatha*,
one should cultivate the factors of enlightenment belonging to the category of tranquility (*śamatha*) to suppress the mind and cause it to descend.
Because one is practicing the factors of insight (*vipaśyanā*), it is said that this is not the proper time [for such application].
If, however, one enters the Noble Path by means of the factors of enlightenment belonging to the category of insight (*vipaśyanā-pakṣya*),
one should cultivate the factors of enlightenment belonging to the category of insight to stimulate and uplift the mind.
Because one practices the category of tranquility (śamatha), it is said to be "untimely.
Other masters say that it is the opposite of the above.
That is to say, if one enters the noble path by relying on the factors of enlightenment belonging to the category of śamatha,
and the mind becomes excessively sunken,
one should cultivate the factors of enlightenment belonging to the category of vipaśyanā to rouse and uplift the mind.
Because they cultivate the category of tranquility (*śamatha*), it is said that [the factors] are untimely;
if one enters the noble path through the awakening factors (*bodhyaṅga*) based on the category of insight (*vipaśyanā*),
the mind becomes excessively agitated.
When one should cultivate the factors of enlightenment belonging to the category of tranquility (*śamatha*) to suppress and lower the mind,
yet instead cultivates those belonging to the category of insight (*vipaśyanā*), it is said that this is "untimely.
Although the essential natures of all the factors of enlightenment arise simultaneously, [they are designated as such based on their specific application].
Since those functions undergo increase and decrease,
what is stated in the Sūtra does not contradict simultaneous arising;
it only contradicts the notion that they arise one after another in succession.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Fascicle Ninety-five;
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Ninety-six.

The *Śāriputra-sūtra*, cited later by the five hundred great arhats and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree, also does not definitively exclude the possibility of simultaneous arising.
Śāriputra, it means that he well knows the mind entering and emerging from the meditative concentration of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga),
and [remains] within that meditative concentration of the factors of enlightenment.
One can abide with mastery according to one's will;
this refers to abiding in the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) with voluntary mastery according to the occasion,
not to the separate arising of each individual factor of enlightenment.
Therefore, it does not constitute a valid proof.
Furthermore, since that sutra speaks in reliance upon the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) as they abide on the three stages,
this statement also does not contradict reason.
That is to say, in the first part of the day, when one wishes to abide in the factors of enlightenment belonging to the stage with both vitarka and vicāra,
one is immediately able to so abide;
in the middle part of the day, when one wishes to abide in the factors of enlightenment belonging to the stage with no vitarka and only vicāra, [one is immediately able to so abide].
Even if he is able to abide [in that state],
when it is the latter part of the day and he wishes to abide in the stage of the awakening factors that are without applied thought and sustained thought,
he is immediately able to abide therein.
Therefore, this statement does not contradict [the fact that they] arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, that sutra speaks in reliance upon the awakening factors associated with abiding in the three faculties, which is likewise not contrary to reason;
that is to say, during the first part of the day, one desires to abide in the awakening factor associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Even if he is able to abide,
during the middle part of the day, if he wishes to abide in a factor of enlightenment associated with the faculty of joy,
he is immediately able to abide therein.
In the latter part of the day, when one wishes to abide in the awakening factor associated with the faculty of equanimity,
one is indeed able to so abide; therefore,
this statement does not contradict their simultaneous arising.
Furthermore, that sutra’s teaching based on the awakening factors (*bodhyaṅga*) co-arising with the three samādhis is also not contrary to reason.
That is to say, during the first part of the day, one desires to abide in the awakening factor co-arising with the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Even if he is able to abide,
during the middle part of the day, he desires to abide in the awakening factor co-arising with the wishless samādhi,
and he is indeed able to abide therein.
In the latter part of the day, when one wishes to abide in the awakening factor of equanimity associated with the signless samādhi,
one is indeed able to so abide; therefore,
this statement does not contradict their simultaneous arising.
Furthermore, that sutra’s teaching based on abiding in the awakening factors (*bodhyaṅga*) co-arising with the three types of knowledge is also not contrary to reason.
That is to say, at the first part of the day, one desires to abide in the awakening factor co-arising with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Even if he is able to abide,
during the middle part of the day, he desires to abide in the awakening factor that arises together with the knowledge of non-arising;
even then, he is able to abide.
In the latter part of the day, when one wishes to abide in the awakening factor of discernment that arises together with the knowledge of the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
one is indeed able to so abide; therefore,
this statement does not contradict their simultaneous arising.
Furthermore, it is also not unreasonable that the aforementioned sutra speaks in reliance upon the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) abiding in the nine stages;
that is to say, during the first part of the day, one wishes to abide in the factors of enlightenment of the three stages, such as the *anāgamya* concentration and so forth.
Even if he is able to abide [in them],
should he wish to abide in the factors of enlightenment belonging to the three higher dhyāna stages during the middle part of the day,
he is immediately able to abide [in them].
In the latter part of the day, when one wishes to abide in the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā) belonging to the three lower formless attainments,
one is indeed able to so abide; therefore,
this statement does not contradict their simultaneous arising.
Alternatively, some maintain that in the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of the dhyānas there is joy but no morality;
or again, others maintain [the same].
From the intermediate dhyāna upward, there is right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
Alternatively, some maintain that ethical discipline (*śīla*) can also be present within the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This treatise is composed in order to refute these various divergent attachments and to reveal the correct principle.
When the mindfulness factor of enlightenment manifests based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna), [the following occurs].
In the case of a learner (*śaikṣa*), six factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are present.
In the case of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), six factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path are present.
Among these, the six factors of enlightenment exclude the factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*).
Regarding the nine path factors, with the exception of either right view or right knowledge,
all others are fully present.
This statement serves to exclude the presence of joy and the absence of ethical discipline in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of dhyāna.
There is also a recitation which says:
"If, relying on the access concentration (anāgamya) accompanied by applied and sustained thought (savitarka-savicāra),
the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) manifests before one..."
Although this does not add to the meaning, it is stated for the purpose of dispelling doubt,
as explained elsewhere:
the term "unattained" (anāgamya) refers to both the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).

Furthermore, because the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher levels have not yet reached those fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*), they are designated by the name "not-yet-reached" (*anāgamya*).
Now, in order to exclude the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) and the preparatory stages of the higher levels, [the term *anāgamya* is used].
Therefore, it is said that if one relies on the "not-yet-attained concentration" (anāgamya-samādhi) which is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra,
this indicates that the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) manifests only when relying on the "not-yet-attained concentration" prior to the first dhyāna.
If the awakening factor of mindfulness is present based on the first dhyāna,
for one in training (śaikṣa), seven awakening factors and eight path factors are present;
for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), seven awakening factors and nine path factors are present.
Among these, the nine path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) are as previously explained;
all others are fully present.
If, based on the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*) manifests, [the remaining factors are likewise present].
In the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), six factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and seven factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are present.
In the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), six factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path are present.
The same applies when relying on the third and fourth dhyānas.
Among these, the six factors of enlightenment exclude the factor of joy;
the seven factors of the path for those in training exclude right intention;
and the eight factors of the path for those beyond training exclude both right intention and either right view or right knowledge.
This explanation concludes the [objection] that the higher stages also possess the factor of right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
When the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) manifests based on the second dhyāna,
seven awakening factors and seven path factors manifest for one in training (*śaikṣa*).
The seven factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are manifested.
In that stage, there is joy (*prīti*), but no right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
The rest is as previously explained.
When the awakening factor of mindfulness manifests based on the formless attainments,
for one in training (*śaikṣa*), six awakening factors and four path factors manifest;
for one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), six awakening factors and five path factors manifest.
Among these, the six factors of enlightenment exclude the factor of joy;
the four factors of the path for those in training exclude right intention,
right speech, right action, and right livelihood.

Regarding the five factors of the path of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), these consist of the aforementioned [factors] excluding the first four, as well as either right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) or right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

This explanation concludes that within the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), there are likewise the factors of mindfulness of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), diligence (*vīrya*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The path factors of right view, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration are likewise;
they all pertain to all stages just as the awakening factor of mindfulness does, and this is the general statement.
As for the distinctions:
When the path factor of right view is present, right knowledge is necessarily excluded.
When the enlightenment factor of joy is present based on the first dhyāna, for one in training (śaikṣa),
seven enlightenment factors and eight path factors are present.
The seven factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are present.
Among these, as for the nine factors of the path, with the exception of either right view or right knowledge— whichever one is excluded—
all others are fully possessed.
If, based on the second dhyāna, the awakening factor of joy manifests, for one in training (śaikṣa),
seven awakening factors and seven path factors manifest;
for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), seven awakening factors and eight path factors manifest.
Among these, for those in training (*śaikṣa*), seven members of the path are included, excluding right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
For those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), eight members of the path are included,
excluding both right intention and either right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) or right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
Question: Why is there no factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*)?
Answer: Because they are not suitable vessels for it.

Furthermore, in all preparatory stages, both those who have already abandoned the defilements of the lower level and those who have not yet abandoned them can bring [the factor of joy] into manifestation.
Because it is not particularly extraordinary, joy does not arise;
it is like when a person who has been bound experiences the superior state upon being liberated—
the mind does not regard this matter as something marvelous.
Therefore, joy does not arise.
Furthermore, if there were also joy in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*),
they would be no different from the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*).
Furthermore, if the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) also possess joy (*prīti*),
one would become attached to this joy and fail to seek the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*).
If that were the case, it would obstruct the abandonment of the defilements of the lower stage.
Just as a person who is attached to something along the way cannot reach their destination quickly,
so too the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) lack the factor of joy (prīti).
When right reflection based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya-samādhi) is present, for one in training (śaikṣa),
six factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and eight factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present;
for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), six factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path are present.
Among these, regarding the six factors of enlightenment,
the factor of joy is excluded;
regarding the nine factors of the path:
When right view and right knowledge are present, one type is excluded accordingly,
while the others are all possessed.
This is the case when right thought belonging to the first dhyāna is manifested.
For one in training (*śaikṣa*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are manifested.
For one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the seven factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path are manifested.
Among these, the nine factors of the path for one beyond training should be understood as previously explained.
Question: Why is there no right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) in the higher stages?
Answer: Because they are not suitable fields or vessels.
Furthermore, [right thought] serves as the antidote for the seeking of higher stages that arises from discursive thought (*vitarka*).
If there were also vitarka within the higher stages,
one would not aspire to initiate superior application.
Furthermore, if the dharmas of the lower stages were present in all the higher stages, [the distinction between them would be lost].
In that case, there would be no such thing as gradual cessation.
If there were no gradual cessation, there would be no ultimate cessation.
If there were no ultimate cessation...
There would otherwise be no liberation, renunciation, or nirvāṇa;
lest such an error occur,
it is therefore held that there is no right thought in the higher stages.
Furthermore, one correctly contemplates that the higher stages are subtle compared to the coarse [lower stages].
Furthermore, correct contemplation is the characteristic of seeking.
Because there is no seeking above [the level], it does not exist there.
Furthermore, if there were bodily or vocal informative action within the earth element,
or if any one of the five consciousnesses were present therein, [it would exist].
Right attention can exist in this stage;
however, it does not exist in the higher stages because they lack bodily and vocal informative karma as well as the five bodies of consciousness.

If, based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya-samādhi), right speech is present, then for one in training (śaikṣa), six factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and eight factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present;
for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), six factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path are present.
Among these, regarding the six factors of enlightenment,
with the exception of the factor of joy,
the rest are as previously explained.
If, based on the first dhyāna, right speech manifests, then for one in training (śaikṣa),
seven factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path manifest;
for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), seven factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path manifest.
Among these, the nine path factors of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) should be understood as previously described.
If, based on the intermediate dhyāna, right speech (samyagvāk) is present, then for one in training (śaikṣa),
six awakening factors (bodhyaṅga) and seven path factors (mārgāṅga) are present.
For one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), six factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are present.
The same applies when relying on the third and fourth dhyānas;
among these, the factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*) is excluded from the six factors of enlightenment.
The seven factors of the path of training exclude right intention;
the eight factors of the path of no-more-learning exclude right intention and either right view or right knowledge.
If, based on the second dhyāna, right speech manifests, then for one in training,
seven factors of enlightenment and seven factors of the path manifest;
for one beyond training, seven factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path manifest.
Among these, the seven factors of the path of training (*śaikṣa-mārga*) and the eight factors of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) are both as previously explained.
It is the same for right action (*samyak-karmānta*) and right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*),
because both exist only in six stages.
Question: For what reason are there no three types of precepts, such as right speech, in the formless realm?
Answer: Because it is not a field or a vessel [for them].
Furthermore, the precepts are a portion of form (*rūpa*).
Because the formless realm is formless, it lacks precepts.
Furthermore, precepts are derived from the great elements;
since the formless realm lacks the great elements, it also lacks precepts.
Question: Since there are no untainted (anāsrava) primary elements (mahābhūta), should there also be no untainted precepts?
Answer: Precepts are established by means of the primary elements.
Form is not produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Because the untainted (*anāsrava*) is produced solely through the power of the mind, it is untainted.
Furthermore, having become weary of all forms, one enters the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
Since morality is material form (*rūpa*), it does not exist within those stages.
Furthermore, if there were still material form within the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*),
then there would be no gradual cessation of phenomena.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, they possess no morality.
Furthermore, it is because it serves as the antidote to immoral conduct that there exists virtuous morality.
The formless meditative absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti) cannot counteract unwholesome ethical conduct;
therefore, there is no wholesome ethical conduct therein. Why is this so?
All unwholesome precepts exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) possesses the four types of remoteness from the desire realm, it cannot serve as their antidote.
What are these four types of remoteness?
First, remoteness of basis;
second, remoteness of object;
third, remoteness of aspect.
Fourth, because they are distant due to being counteragents,
the formless absorptions lack the three types of ethical factors, namely right speech and so forth.
There are thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
That is to say: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path.
Although the Blessed One has taught the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), he did not state that there are thirty-seven types.
However, only the seven factors of enlightenment are designated as the "factors conducive to awakening" (bodhipakṣadharma). How is this known?
Because the sūtras are the authoritative source (pramāṇa).
It refers to what is stated in a sutra: a certain bhikṣu approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Blessed One has said..."
"What are the seven factors of enlightenment? What is meant by the seven factors of enlightenment?
The Blessed One replied:
"The seven types of factors conducive to enlightenment are called the seven factors of enlightenment."
Question: There are thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
For what reason did the Blessed One speak of only the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*) as the factors of enlightenment?
Answer: The Buddha answered according to the question posed by the bhikṣu.
Because that bhikṣu asked only about the seven factors of enlightenment,
the Buddha spoke only of the seven limbs of awakening.
Had that bhikṣu asked about the four foundations of mindfulness, or even up to the eightfold path, [the Buddha would have taught accordingly].
The Buddha should also answer each question according to what was asked.
Furthermore, that sūtra speaks only of the untainted factors conducive to enlightenment (*anāsrava-bodhipakṣadharma*).
Only the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are exclusively untainted.
Therefore, it is explained partially;
the others are not mentioned because they are generally associated with outflows (*sāsrava*). Some say this:
Other sūtras also fully explain that there are thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
Since a great deal of time has passed, those sūtras have disappeared.
How do we know this to be so?
As that venerable Dārudatta has said:
"The Blessed One at times speaks of one factor of the path,
and at times he speaks of two."
At times, thirty-seven are taught;
these are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*),
as illustrated by the simile of the axe-handle.
The Sūtra states that among the thirty-seven factors of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-dharma*), if one were to take only those that are definitive,
then one should speak of seven factors of the path of cultivation; that is,
the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), because they are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
If one were to take only that which is indeterminate,
then one should speak of the remaining six stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
namely, from the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold path.
Because it encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
If one were to include both the determinate and the indeterminate,
then one should speak of thirty-seven kinds of factors for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-dharma*).
That is to say, it consists of the preceding six stages and the seven factors of enlightenment;
thus, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are also taught by the Blessed One in the sūtras.
Question: It is said that there are thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) by name;
how many are there in terms of their actual substance (dravya)?
Answer: As for these actual substances:
There are eleven or twelve factors.
If all are subsumed within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), there are seven factors of enlightenment;

although the names are seven, the actual entities (*dravya*) are also seven, as right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) consists of only one type, while right speech (*samyag-vāc*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*) each constitute a single entity.
Some say there are two,
because right livelihood is identical to right speech and right action.
Others say there are three.
Since right livelihood exists apart from right speech and right action,
if one speaks of two [factors], there are only eleven;
if one speaks of three, there are twelve.
Why is this? It is because the four foundations of mindfulness,
the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, and right view are subsumed within the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

The four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the power of energy (*vīryabala*), and right exertion (*samyagvyāyāma*) are subsumed within the factor of enlightenment of energy (*vīryasambodhyaṅga*). The four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*),

the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*), the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) [are subsumed within the factor of enlightenment of concentration].
The factor of enlightenment of concentration is subsumed [under the awakening factor of concentration].
The faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness,
and right mindfulness are subsumed under the awakening factor of mindfulness.

Because the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the power of faith (*śraddhābala*) are combined as a single "faith," if all [factors] are subsumed within the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), there are eight path-factors; however,
although their names are eight, their substantial entities (*dravya*) are not fixed.
If it is said that right mindfulness is identical to right speech and right action,
then in substance there are only seven [factors].
If it is said that right livelihood is not identical to right speech and right action, [then there are eight].
There are eight substantial entities;
furthermore, there are four— faith, joy, pliancy, and equanimity—
thus making eleven in total.
Or there may be twelve.
Why is this? It refers to the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, and the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena.
They are subsumed under right view.
The four right strivings, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, and the factor of enlightenment of energy are subsumed under right effort.
The four bases of psychic power, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of concentration are subsumed within right concentration.
The faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness [are subsumed within right mindfulness].
It is subsumed under right mindfulness,
because the faculty of faith and the power of faith are combined into a single faith. Some say this.
Since right speech, action, and livelihood have the nature of ethical discipline (*śīla*), they ought to be combined into one.
If this is asserted,
there would be thirty-seven names for the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
There are only ten substantial entities (*dravya*).
Just as there are substantial entities, so too are there nominal designations (*prajñapti*).
The designation of the entity;
the difference in names;
the difference in entities.
The difference in name;
the difference in essence;
the differentiation of names.
The differentiation of essence is called the differentiation of essence; this differentiation is called awakening.
The realization of the essence should be understood in the same way.
These are called the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).
The intrinsic nature of phenomena— their own-being, substance, characteristics, and fundamental nature—
has already been explained as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, it shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason are they called the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma)?
What is the meaning of "factors of enlightenment"?
Answer: The knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are designated as bodhi, because one has already attained the ultimate awakening to the four noble truths.
Any dharma that accords with this ultimate awakening and possesses predominant power is [also so designated].
Among these, they are called the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Having already explained their general name,
their individual reasons for being so designated shall now be explained separately.
Question: Why are they called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*)?

Answer: Because the self-substance (*svabhāva*) is broken and eliminated through the power of mindfulness, they are called foundations of mindfulness; this self-substance is precisely the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca sāsravaskandhāḥ*).
Since they must be eliminated by means of the foundations of mindfulness,
these [foundations] are the most excellent among the correct exertions (*samyakpradhāna*) for properly restraining body, speech, and mind;
therefore, they are called "right efforts" (*samyakprahāṇa*) or "right abandonments."
When one is correctly practicing the cultivation of the factors for abandonment,
they are called "right abandonments" (*samyakprahāṇa*) because they are able to eliminate laziness and because they serve as the basis for sublime and wondrous qualities.

It is called the "basis of supernormal power" (*ṛddhipāda*). Because its efficacy is preeminent, it is called a "faculty" (*indriya*); because it is difficult to suppress or restrain, it is called a "power" (*bala*.
It is called a "limb of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*) because it assists in the realization of reality as it is.
They are called "limbs of the path" (*mārgāṅga*) because they assist in seeking the correct goal.
Question: What is the meaning of "limbs of awakening" (*bodhyaṅga*)? Answer:
They are called "limbs of awakening" because they are capable of bringing about awakening.
They are called factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) because they are branches of enlightenment;

if they were called factors of enlightenment simply because they can bring about awakening, then one [factor] would be [an enlightenment factor] while the other six would not. If, however, they are called factors of enlightenment because they are branches of enlightenment, [then all six are so].
Then it would follow that six [of these factors] are correct and one is not.
Some offer this explanation:
"Because these can awaken, they are called factors of awakening (bodhyaṅga)."
Question: If that were so, then one would be a factor [of enlightenment] while the other six would not be.
Answer: The six are factors of enlightenment because they are able to accord with enlightenment.
Speaking from the perspective of their excellence, they are also called factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). Furthermore,
others say that because they are branches of enlightenment, they are called factors of enlightenment.
Question: If that were so, then among the six [factors], one would be awakening (bodhi) and the others would not be.
Answer: The investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya) is both awakening and a factor of awakening;
the other six are factors of awakening but are not awakening itself.
Just as right view is both the path and a limb of the path,
while the other seven are limbs of the path but not the path itself;
so too, one-pointedness of mind is both meditative absorption (dhyāna) and a limb of meditative absorption.
The others are factors of meditative absorption (dhyānāṅga) but are not meditative absorption itself.
Abstaining from eating at improper times is both the fast (upavāsa) and a factor of the fast;
the others are factors of the fast but are not the fast itself.
This is also like that.

It is asked: what is the meaning of "factors of the path" (*mārgāṅga*)? Is it called a factor of the path because it is capable of seeking and proceeding toward [nirvāṇa], or is it called a factor of the path because it is a limb of the path?
If they were called "limbs of the path" (*mārgāṅga*) because they themselves seek and proceed toward [nirvāṇa],
then only one would be a limb of the path and the other seven would not.
However, if they are called "limbs of the path" because they are limbs *of* the path, [then all eight are indeed limbs].
Thus, seven [of these factors] would be correct and one would be incorrect. Some say:
"Because this is able to seek and proceed toward [the goal], it is called a branch of the path (*mārgāṅga*)."

Question: If that were so, then one would be a path-factor and seven would not be. Answer: All seven are path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) because they are able to accord with the path; they are called "limbs of the path" (*mārgāṅga*) from the perspective of their predominance.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Because these are branches of the path, they are called "path-factors" (mārgāṅga).
Question: If that is so, then seven [of them] should be factors and one should not be.
Answer: Right view is both the path and a branch of the path;
the remaining seven are branches of the path but are not the path itself.
This is just as the discernment of phenomena is both awakening and a branch of awakening.
The remaining six are factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) but are not enlightenment itself.
The rest is as previously explained.
The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) have now been discussed.
Therefore, the sequence shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason are the four foundations of mindfulness taught first, and so on, up to the eight factors of the path taught last?
Answer: Because it follows the sequence of the skillful arrangement of the phrasing of the text.
Furthermore, it is because [this] teaching accords with the ease and sequential order of both the speaker and the listener.
Furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness extend from the stage of a beginner up to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.
Because their power and function are always superior, they are explained first.
The four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) range from the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) up to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*);
because their power and function are always superior, they are explained next.
The four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) range from the summit (mūrdhan) up to the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna);
because their functional power is constantly superior, they are explained next.
The five faculties (indriya) range from patience (kṣānti) up to the knowledge of non-arising.
Because their power and function are always superior, they are explained next.
The five powers (*pañca-balāni*) extend from the state of supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) up to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*);
because their power and function are always superior, they are explained next.

The eight factors of the path (aṣṭāṅgamārga) are preeminent within the path of vision (darśanamārga), while the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga) are preeminent within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Question: For what reason are the eight factors of the path preeminent within the path of vision, and the seven factors of enlightenment preeminent within the path of cultivation?
Answer: The meaning of "seeking to proceed" (*yāna*) is the meaning of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).

Because the vision of the path (*darśanamārga*) is swift and does not exceed its intended purpose, and because it accords with the meaning of seeking to proceed, the eight factors of the path are preeminent within the vision of the path.
The meaning of awakening (*bodha*) is the meaning of the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*).

Because they accord with the meaning of awakening through repeated awakening during the nine grades of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the seven factors of awakening are preeminent within the path of cultivation.
Question: If that is so,
why were the seven factors of enlightenment taught first,
and the eightfold path taught afterwards?
Answer: Because it accords with the skillful sequence of words and phrases;
furthermore, because it accords with the easy and convenient sequence for both the speaker and the listener;
and furthermore, because it accords with the sequence of increasing numerical categories.
This means that they are taught first as four, then as five, then as seven, and finally as eight.
Furthermore, it is to manifest how the dharmas of purification gradually increase;
that is, one first cultivates four, then five, then seven, and finally eight.
Other masters say that practitioners first,
by means of the foundations of mindfulness, [attend] to objects such as the body.
One understands the specific and general characteristics as they truly are;
by removing delusion regarding specific characteristics and delusion regarding the object of focus, one leads others to give rise to various virtues,
just as one with sight guides a group of blind people.
Therefore, the four foundations of mindfulness are taught first.
Having understood the objects through the power of mindfulness,
one is able to exert right effort in the tasks of abandonment and cultivation.
Therefore, the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are taught in the second [foundation of mindfulness].
By the power of these right efforts, faults are diminished and virtuous qualities are made to flourish within the mental continuum.
Because one is able to correctly cultivate the sublime concentrations,
the four bases of power (ṛddhipāda) are taught in the third [chapter].
By the power of these bases of power, the five faculties beginning with faith serve as the dominant conditions (adhipatipratyaya) for supramundane dharmas.
Therefore, having established the meaning of the "faculties" (*indriya*) in the fourth [chapter],
it is taught that in the fifth [chapter] there are the five powers (*bala*), which are capable of summoning one away from the miserable destinies and cannot be overcome by afflictions or evil karma.

Since the meaning of the powers has already been established as being able to realize the objects of the four noble truths exactly as they are without hesitation, the seven factors of enlightenment are taught in the sixth [chapter];
for once the four noble truths have been realized exactly as they are, [the factors of enlightenment arise].
Because one grows weary of and relinquishes saṃsāra while joyfully aspiring toward nirvāṇa,
the eight factors of the path are taught in the seventh [chapter].
The critique states:
It should be understood that among these, the former explanation is superior;
because the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is proximate to enlightenment and possesses the excellence of being conducive to awakening,
it is called the "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*).
Furthermore, because one can repeatedly awaken to the excellence of the factors of awakening (bodhyaṅga) throughout the nine stages and nine grades of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
the sequence of the seven stages of the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣadharma) has thus been explained in general.
Now, the sequential order of the two stages—the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*)—will be explained separately.
Question: For what reason are the factors of enlightenment taught beginning with the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-bodhyaṅga*) and ending with the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-bodhyaṅga*)?
The answer is: because it accords with the skillful sequence of words and phrases;
furthermore, because it accords with the convenient sequence for both the speaker and the listener.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka has stated this.
One who has already seen the truths takes as the primary focus the objects previously realized through direct observation,
and cultivates the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā) so that they gradually reach fulfillment.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Regarding these dharmas, he binds his mindfulness to them and reflects upon them so as not to fall into confusion;
he arouses the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) and cultivates it until it is perfected."
Having fulfilled mindfulness, one investigates, weighs, and examines phenomena, thereby giving rise to the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena and cultivating it to fulfillment.
Once the discrimination of phenomena is fulfilled, one arouses diligent effort so that the mind does not retreat or become discouraged.
He arouses the factor of enlightenment of energy and cultivates it to fulfillment.
Once energy is fulfilled, he gives rise to sublime joy and remains undefiled by attachment;
he arouses the factor of enlightenment of joy and cultivates it to fulfillment.
Once joy is fulfilled, the body and mind become pliant and comfortable because of the departure from lethargy;
thus, one arouses the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and cultivates it to fulfillment.
Once tranquility is fulfilled, the body and mind experience bliss, and one attains samādhi.
He cultivates the awakening factor of concentration until it is perfected.
Once concentration is perfected, he becomes free from sensual desire and grief, and his mind abides in equanimity.
He cultivates the awakening factor of equanimity until it is perfected.
Therefore, the seven factors of enlightenment follow this sequence.
Question: Why, among the eight factors of the path, is right view taught first, and so on, until right concentration is taught last?
The answer is: because it accords with the skillful sequence of the words and phrases;
furthermore, because it accords with the convenient sequence for both the speaker and the listener.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka has stated this.

One who seeks to realize the truths first takes right view as the precursor to the process of clear observation (*abhisamaya*), cultivating the factors of the path until they gradually reach fulfillment.
As the Sūtra says:
"By means of right view, one gives rise to right intention."
Through right reflection, one attains right speech;
through right speech, one further attains right action;
and through right action, one further attains right livelihood.
From right livelihood, one initiates right effort;
from right effort, right mindfulness arises;
and from right mindfulness, one is able to give rise to right concentration.
Therefore, the eight factors of the path follow this sequence.
Having explained the sequence,
the stages upon which they rely shall now be discussed.
Question: How many factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) are present in which stages?
Answer: There are thirty-six in the preparatory concentration (anāgamya), excluding the factor of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga).
In the first dhyāna, all thirty-seven factors are present.
In the intermediate dhyāna, as well as in the third and fourth dhyānas, there are only thirty-five each;
the factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) and right thought (samyak-saṃkalpa) are excluded.
The second dhyāna has thirty-six [factors],
excluding right thought (samyak-saṃkalpa).
The first three formless attainments (ārūpyas) have thirty-two.

Excluding the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and [the factors of] right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), right speech (*samyag-vāc*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*),
there are twenty-two [factors] each in the desire realm and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Excluding the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*).
Because the factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are exclusively untainted (anāsrava).
If one were to speak of the factors of the path prior to the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga),
it would be because the factors of the path exist even in the desire realm and the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), as they also pertain to the tainted (sāsrava).
The bases have already been explained;
their manifestation shall now be discussed.
Question: On which bases do how many factors of enlightenment manifest simultaneously?
Answer: Within the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi), there are thirty-six factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).
However, only thirty-three manifest simultaneously, excluding the three applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Why is this? Because the objects of the four foundations of mindfulness are distinct;
even two of them cannot manifest simultaneously.
How much more so for three or four?
Within the first dhyāna, although thirty-seven factors are complete,
only thirty-four manifest simultaneously.
Excluding the three applications of mindfulness,
there are thirty-five in each of the intermediate dhyāna and the third and fourth dhyānas; in these cases,
only thirty-two manifest simultaneously, excluding the three applications of mindfulness.
In the second dhyāna there are thirty-six [factors],
but only thirty-three manifest simultaneously,
excluding the three applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
In the first three formless attainments, there are thirty-two [factors],
yet only twenty-nine manifest simultaneously,
excluding the three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
In the Desire Realm and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are twenty-two [factors], yet only nineteen manifest simultaneously.
With the exception of the three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the others are explained according to their respective meanings; they are not necessarily distinct entities.
The manifestation [of these factors] has already been explained.
Now, their mixed and unmixed characteristics shall be discussed.
Question: Among these thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), [which are mixed and which are unmixed?]
Are all those that are factors of enlightenment also factors of the path?
One should respond by establishing four permutations.
There are those that are factors of enlightenment but not factors of the path.
That is to say: joy, pliancy, and equanimity.
There are factors that are limbs of the path but not limbs of awakening;
namely, right intention, right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
There are factors that are both factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*);
namely, all other factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) with the exception of faith (*śraddhā*).
There are also factors that are neither factors of enlightenment nor factors of the path.
It refers to faith.
Question: For what reason is joy established as a factor of enlightenment?
Answer: The meaning of being conducive to awakening is the meaning of a factor of enlightenment.
Joy is established as a factor of enlightenment because it accords with that excellence.
Question: In what way does joy accord with that excellence?
Answer: Because within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one repeatedly cultivates excellent awakening through the nine stages and nine grades.
To the extent that one awakens to the truths as they truly are,
to that same extent one gives rise to superior joy;
and to the extent that joy arises, [one proceeds further].
It is so, it is so. Furthermore, one delights in the truths and gives rise to realization in accordance with reality,
just as a person digging the earth might discover various precious treasures.
Just as one digs the earth, so too does one find treasure and give rise to joy;
and just as one finds treasure and gives rise to joy,
so too does one further delight in digging the earth.
This is also the case here.
Question: Why is joy (*prīti*) not established as a factor of the path (*mārgāṅga*)?
Answer: The meaning of "factor of the path" is that which accords with the sense of seeking and proceeding toward [the goal].
Joy (*prīti*) is not established as a factor of the path because it does not accord with that which is supreme.
Question: In what way does joy not accord with that which is supreme?
Answer: To the extent that one gives rise to supreme joy regarding the Truths (*satya*), [joy increases].
Thus, thus dwelling in delight, one does not depart;
therefore, the joy of seeking a destination is not conducive [to liberation].
It is like a person on a road who becomes attached to something they find pleasant.
Just as one cannot travel quickly toward a destination, so it is in this case as well.
Question: For what reason are both pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: The meaning of "factor of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*) is that which accords with the sense of awakening.
Since pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) accord exceptionally well with that [awakening], both are established as factors of enlightenment.
Question: In what way do pliancy and equanimity both accord exceptionally well with that [awakening]?

Answer: Because through the power of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), one quiets all activities and abides in equanimity (*upekṣā*), thereby being able to give rise to realization of the truths as they truly are; thus, it is conducive to that excellence.
Question: For what reason are pliancy and equanimity not established as limbs of the path (*mārgāṅga*)?
Answer: The meaning of a branch of the path (*mārgāṅga*) is that which accords with the sense of proceeding toward [liberation].
Since pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are not superior in accordance with that, they are not established as branches of the path.
Question: In what way are these two not superior in accordance with that?
Answer: Seeking tranquility is contrary in every respect to seeking [sensual] objects;
the former involves relinquishing and not delighting [in them], whereas the latter involves seeking and pursuing their meaning.
Just as going and staying, or sleeping and waking, are mutually exclusive, so it is in this case as well.
Question: For what reason is right intention established as a factor of the path (*mārgāṅga*) rather than a factor of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: The meaning of "limb of the path" (mārgāṅga) is the sense of conforming to the pursuit of the goal.
By exerting right view (samyagdṛṣṭi), one seeks to transcend birth and death and swiftly proceed toward nirvāṇa;
thus, it is established as a limb of the path, just as a cow is driven to its destination quickly by the striking of a staff.
The factor of enlightenment of right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) consists in the unceasing pursuit [of the goal].

Since the meaning of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) is not concordant with this, those who are tranquil are able to awaken to reality as it is; therefore, that [tranquility] is not established as a factor of enlightenment.
Question: For what reason are right speech, right action, and right livelihood established as branches of the path (*mārgāṅga*) but not as branches of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: The meaning of a branch of the path is that which accords with the sense of proceeding toward [the goal].
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood are like the hub [of a wheel], for they are able to bring about the wheel of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
They are established as branches of the path (*mārgāṅga*) in the sense of conforming to the goal;
they are branches of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) in the sense of conforming to awakening.
Awakening is non-material (*arūpa*), and thus it is associated (*saṃprayukta*).
It has a basis,
it has an object,
and it has mental aspects.
There is alertness (*samprajanya*).
Right speech, action, and livelihood are not established as factors of enlightenment because they are contrary to that [alertness].
Question: Why is faith (*śraddhā*) not established as either a factor of enlightenment or a factor of the path?
Answer: At the time of first setting out, faith is predominant;
once one has entered the stage of the noble ones and cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the time periods differ, and therefore neither is established [as predominant].
Furthermore, among the various pure phenomena within the category of purity,
there are those whose characteristics are complete and those whose characteristics are incomplete.
As for those that are complete:
That is to say, it possesses the characteristics of the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), and factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*);
that which is contrary to these is called "incomplete.
Within this state of incompleteness, there are still the characteristics of the factors of enlightenment.

Those factors possessing the characteristics of the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) but lacking the characteristics of the awakening-factors (*bodhyaṅga*) are established as path-factors rather than awakening-factors;
such are joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Those possessing the characteristics of the path-factors but lacking the characteristics of the awakening-factors [are likewise established as such].
They are established as factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) but not as factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*),
such as right intention, right speech, and right action and livelihood.
Those whose characteristics are complete are established as factors of enlightenment and factors of the path.

Just as with mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and so forth, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are not established for those that lack the characteristics of awakening, such as faith.
Question: Why is the mind (*citta*) not established as a factor of enlightenment?
Answer: Because the mind lacks the characteristics of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

Furthermore, the mind’s functional capacity is equal toward both the categories of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*), whereas the factors conducive to enlightenment pertain only to the category of purification.
Because their functional power increases disproportionately, they are not established [as such].

Furthermore, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) mostly take common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) as their objects, whereas the mind mostly takes specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) as its object; therefore, they are not established [as such].
Furthermore, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) serve as antidotes to the afflictions (kleśa).
Since all afflictions are mental concomitants (caitta),
their antidotes likewise cannot be the mind (citta) itself.
Furthermore, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) assist toward awakening;
the mind-king (citta-rāja), however, should not be assisted by them,
for it would be like a king who lacks the function of assisting ministers.
Furthermore, the mind causes the cycle of birth and death to revolve without end.

Since the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are capable of severing birth and death, their meaning is incompatible [with that of the mind]; therefore, they are not established [as being the mind].
Furthermore, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are able to subdue the mind;
that which is to be subdued cannot itself be the agent of subduing.
For those who wish to equate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) with the mind, [this would be untenable].
It is taught that the mind (*citta*) is also a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);
however, because that contradicts reason, it is not the subject under discussion here.

Question: Among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmikadharma*), why are only mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and feeling (*vedanā*) established as factors of enlightenment?
Answer: Mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom possess a predominant power and function that accord with the category of purification;
the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are likewise so.
Therefore, these three are included.
Because sensation possesses superior power and function within both the defiled and purified categories,
it is also established as a factor of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
Other masters say:
Although the power and function of the defiled [state] it receives are superior, it performs beneficial work for the pure category;
it is like the Caṇḍāla caste, which, though lowly and inferior, performs beneficial work for noble lineages.
Therefore, these are also established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
However, because perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and desire (*chanda*) exert a predominant influence within the category of defilement (*saṃkleśapakṣa*),
they are not established as factors of enlightenment.
In conceptual contemplation (*parikalpita-bhāvanā*), resolute confidence (*adhimukti*) predominates;
since the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) accord with authentic contemplation (*tattvārtha-bhāvanā*),
resolute confidence is not subsumed under them.
Other masters say that while the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) predominate during the stage of training (śaikṣa),
it is only upon reaching the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa) that resolute conviction (adhimukti) becomes superior.
Therefore, it is not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Mental attention (*manasikāra*) causes the mind to become alert toward its object, but it is easily abandoned and lacks stability.
The factors of enlightenment cause the mind to abide upon its object.
It is also not established because it would be inconsistent with the meaning.
Other masters say that at the initial moment of apprehending an object, the power of attention (*manasikāra*) is predominant.
When the continuity of the object reaches its end, the power of that [object] gradually diminishes;
since the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) only arise after the object has been apprehended for a long duration,
this interpretation is inconsistent with the meaning and is therefore not established.
Question: Why is it that while all three feelings (vedanā) are equally accessible to the untainted (anāsrava), only joy (prīti) is established as a factor of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma)?
Answer: Because the two feelings of pleasure (sukha) and equanimity (upekṣā) lack those characteristics.
Furthermore, because the aspects of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) are sharp and intense,
while the feeling of pleasure is dull and sluggish, they are not established together.
Furthermore, because uncontaminated pleasant feeling is obscured and diminished by the pleasure of pliancy (praśrabdhi).
Because equanimity (*upekṣā*) is obscured and impaired by the equanimity of practice (*prayoga-upekṣā*), its characteristic is not clearly manifest;
therefore, it is not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Question: Why are both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) equally accessible to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state?
[Vitarka] alone is established as a factor of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma). [The opponent asks:
Why is vicāra not so established? [The response: Because it lacks those characteristics.
Furthermore, the factors of enlightenment possess a sharp and intense mode of activity (ākāra).
Vicāra is not established [as a separate factor] because its function is weak;
furthermore, because the function of vicāra is obscured and impaired by vitarka,
the function of vitarka predominates when exerting right view.
Therefore, investigation (*vicāra*) is not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Question: Among the great wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), why are only these four—faith, diligence, pliancy, and equanimity—established as factors of enlightenment?
