Answer: Because these four types are preeminent for conforming to enlightenment (*bodhi*), they are specifically established as the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
That is to say, faith is the foremost [factor] for proceeding toward enlightenment.
As one is about to initiate the various practices, faith serves as the primary foundation;
therefore, faith is established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Diligence universally exerts and impels one toward the practice leading to enlightenment.
Because it causes one to swiftly advance toward the bodhi of the three vehicles,
it is also established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and adaptability counteract lethargy (*styāna*) and are preeminent within the category of factors conducive to insight (*vipaśyanā-pakṣya*).
The practice of equanimity (*upekṣā*) serves as the antidote to restlessness (*auddhatya*) and is superior within the category of factors that assist calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Since both calm abiding and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are predominant among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*),
they are established together as factors conducive to enlightenment.
Although the six wholesome factors such as shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) possess superior power within the category of miscellaneous wholesome states (*pṛthag-kuśala*),
their power is weak and inferior in relation to the wholesome states of meditative concentration (*samādhi-kuśala*); therefore,
they are not established as factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Because they are well-subsumed within the concentrations of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), other masters state that among the great wholesome dharmas,
those whose objects of opposition are powerful and whose intrinsic natures are superior are established as factors of enlightenment.
The others are not so; that which is strong by way of being the object of counteraction refers to those associated with all defiled minds.
That which is strong by way of its intrinsic nature—
That is to say, among the factors fundamental to all practices, those that incite all practices and assist in the excellence of śamatha and vipaśyanā—
namely faith, diligence, pliancy, and equanimity— all possess both meanings [of being both a root and a branch].
Among the six qualities such as shame and dread, none possess both.
That is to say, in the case of the five factors such as shame (*hrī*), both [the meanings of] "two" and "meaning" are absent;
in the single factor of heedfulness (*apramāda*), only the excellence of its own nature (*svabhāva*) is lacking.
Therefore, they are not established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Question: Why are *abhirati* (delight) and *vidūṣaṇā* (revulsion), which are also essentially wholesome, not established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)?
Answer: Because these two dharmas cannot take all things as their objects.
In the "Chapter on the Single Mind," it is impossible for [mental factors] to arise simultaneously;
since they do not assist awakening as superior factors, they are not established [as such].
Question: For what reason, among all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), is it only non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) [that is so categorized]?
Is it that only certain factors are established as limbs of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and not other dharmas?
Answer: Right speech, right action, and right livelihood are established as limbs of enlightenment because their functional efficacy is particularly predominant in accordance with the Noble Path.
Other dharmas are not like this; therefore, they are not established [as such].
Question: Why are the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) not established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Because they pertain to both the householders and the monastic community.
The two factors that are superior are established as the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*):
first, the superiority of the mind at a single moment;
second, the superiority of practice and reception.
Those four noble lineages possess two superior qualities for those in the homeless life,
and one superior quality for those in the household life;
that is to say, while there is the aspiration for them, there is no sense of their being received or practiced [by the laity].
Just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, sits upon a jeweled flower throne,
surrounded at all times by twelve nayutas of celestial maidens,
and always accompanied by sixty thousand musical instruments.
They engage in such diversions for their amusement;
although they may harbor aspirations toward the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), they lack the sense of actually practicing them.
This was the case with King Śakrāditya and other great kings.
The same applies to the great householders such as Anāthapiṇḍada and others.
Therefore, the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are not established as factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
Some say this: [text continues].
The first three noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) have non-attachment as their wholesome root for their intrinsic nature.
The fourth noble lineage is diligence itself,
because it is subsumed under diligence— the delight in abandoning and the delight in cultivation.
If one were to say that the fourth noble lineage (āryavaṃśa) is also a factor of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga),
then the Vibhajyavādins would establish forty-one factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).

That is to say, because it would be illogical for the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) to be included within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*), they are not discussed here in this *Prakaraṇapāda*. What, then,
is the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
It refers to the noble disciple who,
regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path, contemplates suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, thereby giving rise to mindfulness that aids enlightenment.
...and so on, as explained at length.
This is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
Or, it refers to those in training who perceive the defects of saṃsāra and the excellence of nirvāṇa.
It gives rise to the mindfulness that assists awakening,
and so forth, as explained at length;
this is the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*).
Or an arhat, contemplating the liberation of the mind, gives rise to mindfulness that can assist toward awakening;
and so forth, as explained at length.
This is the faculty of final knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
These are called the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*) up to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣāsambodhyaṅga*).
The detailed explanation is likewise.
What is right view?
It refers to a noble disciple who, regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, contemplates suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path,
thereby giving rise to the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
...and so on, up to the detailed explanation of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Alternatively, for those trainees (*śaikṣa*) who perceive the defects of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the excellence of nirvāṇa,
there arises the discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*), and so on, as detailed at length.
This is the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya). Or, an Arhat,
contemplating the liberation of the mind, gives rise to the discernment of dharmas (dharmapravicaya).
...and so on, as explained at length.
This faculty of one who has already attained knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is called right view;
the same applies, as explained at length, up to right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).

Question: Why is it that among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), there is mention of "arousing the mindfulness that assists awakening" and so forth, whereas among the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), there is no mention of "arousing the discernment of phenomena that assists awakening"?

Should this not have been stated? Answer: It should indeed have been stated, yet it was not. This is because [the factors of the path] are already included within the factors of enlightenment. Specifically, the factor of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is itself the discernment of phenomena that assists awakening; therefore, it is not mentioned separately. Furthermore, since the other factors of the path—such as right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) and right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*)—are subsumed under the factors of enlightenment, they do not need to be mentioned again. Thus, although it should have been stated, it was not.
One should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to manifest different explanations and different phrasings;
it is by means of these different explanations and different phrasings [that the meaning is clarified].
Both the speaker and the listener give rise to joy and delight.
Furthermore, wishing to manifest two gates, two summaries, two staircases, two steps, two torches, two illuminations, two radiances, and two shadows, he makes this statement.
Furthermore, it was previously stated that the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are called bodhi.
Within the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), the meaning of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) becomes manifest.
Because it is proximate to enlightenment, it is called an "aid to enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*).
In the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the meaning of the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) is manifest;
because [the path of cultivation] is distant from enlightenment, they are not mentioned there.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"One cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness together with the contemplation of impurity,
relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, and turning toward equanimity."
The detailed exposition for the others, up to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity, is likewise.
Question: The contemplation of impurity is with outflows (*sāsrava*), whereas the seven factors of enlightenment are without outflows (*anāsrava*).
How do tainted phenomena coexist with untainted phenomena?
The Venerable Vasumitra stated:
"By means of the contemplation of impurity, one subdues the mind."
Once they have been made extremely pliant and serviceable, the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) can immediately arise and become manifest;
from this, one is further able to give rise to the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā).
It is with reference to this meaning that the word "together" (saha) is spoken.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If the noble disciples listen to the Dharma with a single-minded focus and attentive ears."
One is able to sever the five hindrances and swiftly bring the seven factors of enlightenment to fulfillment through their cultivation.

Question: It is essential that the wisdom produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can sever the afflictions, and not within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).

Question: Since one can sever the afflictions through the wisdom born of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*), why is it said that if one listens to the Dharma with a single-minded ear, one can sever the five hindrances (*pañca nīvaraṇāni*)?
Answer: This statement is made by way of an indirect cause (*pāramparyahetu*).
That is to say, a wholesome ear-consciousness immediately induces a wholesome mental consciousness;
this wholesome mental consciousness immediately induces the wisdom derived from hearing;
and this wisdom derived from hearing immediately induces the wisdom derived from reflection.
This wisdom consisting of reflection immediately induces the wisdom consisting of cultivation;
once this wisdom consisting of cultivation has been practiced to maturity,
it is able to sever the five hindrances, and thus it does not contradict reason.
Question: At the time of abandoning the five hindrances (*pañca nīvaraṇāni*), one has not yet been able to fully cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅgāni*).
Why, then, does the Sūtra state that by abandoning the five hindrances, one cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment and causes them to be swiftly perfected?
Answer: When one is free from the defilements of the desire realm, it is called "able to sever the five hindrances";

when one is free from the defilements of the form realm, it is called "cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment"; and when one is free from the defilements of the formless realm, it is called "quickly bringing them to fulfillment. Therefore, there is no error.
Some say: when one is free from the defilement of desire, it is called "able to sever the five hindrances";
when one is free from the defilement of the formless realm, it is called "cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment so that they are swiftly brought to fulfillment."
This explanation involves omitting the middle portion for the sake of brevity at the beginning and end, and thus there is no fault.
Furthermore, others say that it is during the time of the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*) that one is said to be able to sever the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
At the time of the path of liberation, one is said to cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment so as to bring them quickly to fulfillment.
Because they are closely proximate, it is said that they are "quick.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section Three: The Aggregate of Wisdom (Jñānaskandha). Sub-section One: The Chapter on the Factors of Training (Śikṣāṅga-nirdeśa). Part Five. All phenomena associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga).
"Is that dharma associated with the awakening factor of the investigation of dharmas?
and so forth, as explained at length.
[Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This is for the purpose of refuting other schools and revealing the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that because there is no real association (*samyoga*), the various minds and mental factors do not arise simultaneously.
In order to refute that intention and to demonstrate that the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are substantially existent entities (*dravyasat*), this treatise is composed.
It should be answered by means of four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Among these, [the first two] are the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*) and the investigation-of-dharmas factor of enlightenment (*dharmapravicayasambodhyaṅga*).
Because it accompanies all stages and all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*),
one should formulate four minor permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*).
There are factors associated with mindfulness that are not [associated with] the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
Regarding the "factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena" (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*):
it refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena that arises simultaneously with mindfulness (*smṛti*).
That [nature] is associated with mindfulness, not [any other] factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena.
Due to three reasons, intrinsic nature does not associate with intrinsic nature:
first, because two entities do not arise simultaneously;
second, because [they exist] as prior and posterior.
Because they do not coalesce;
thirdly, because all phenomena do not observe their own essence,
as they necessarily arise with the essence of another as their condition.
There are factors that are associated with the investigation of phenomena but are not mindfulness.
This refers to the intrinsic nature of the awakening factor of mindfulness that arises simultaneously with the investigation of phenomena.
That which is associated with the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*) is not the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*).
The principle that a nature (*svabhāva*) is not associated with itself has been explained previously.
There are, however, factors that are both associated with mindfulness and associated with the investigation of dharmas.
Regarding "the factors associated with those two":
this refers to the factors associated [with them], excluding the intrinsic natures of those two, which arise simultaneously with the mindfulness and investigation-of-dharmas factors of enlightenment.
That is to say, the eight universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), the ten wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*),
as well as vitarka, vicāra, and so forth, which exist according to the respective stages, along with the mind itself.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with mindfulness nor are they the investigation of phenomena;
namely, all other mental states and mental factors, as well as matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind—
excluding the uncontaminated mental states and mental factors.
All other contaminated mental states and mental factors,
as well as all matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind, constitute the fourth alternative,
just as in the case of the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of dharmas.
Regarding the application of the fourfold formula to the enlightenment factors of energy, tranquility, and equanimity,
as well as to right effort and right concentration—

it should be understood that just as the fourfold minor formula was applied to the enlightenment factor of mindfulness in relation to the enlightenment factor of discrimination of phenomena, it applies likewise to the enlightenment factor of energy up to right concentration.
Are those factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness also associated with the awakening factor of joy?
One should respond by formulating four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Among these, the awakening factor of mindfulness pervades all stages and all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*).
The factor of enlightenment of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) pervades all untainted minds (anāsrava-citta),
but not all stages (bhūmi). Therefore,
one should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) regarding this.
There are factors associated with mindfulness but not with joy;
namely, those factors associated with the enlightenment factor of mindfulness that are either the enlightenment factor of joy itself or are dissociated from joy.
This refers to the intrinsic nature of the enlightenment factor of joy that arises simultaneously with mindfulness.
That [mindfulness] is associated with it, but it is not itself the enlightenment factor of joy;
the principle that an intrinsic nature is not associated with itself is as explained previously.
And those factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness that are dissociated from joy:
namely, the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna,
the latter two dhyānas, and the first three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Regarding the factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness:
these are associated with mindfulness but not with the awakening factor of joy,
because joy is entirely absent in those stages.
There is a state associated with joy but not with mindfulness;
that is, mindfulness associated with the factor of awakening called joy,
which refers to the intrinsic nature of the mindfulness factor of awakening co-arising with joy.
That [factor] is associated with joy (*prīti*), but it is not the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The principle that a self-nature is not associated with itself has been explained previously.
There are factors that are associated with both mindfulness and joy.
Regarding "associated factors":
this refers to the associated factors other than the two intrinsic natures that arise simultaneously with the mindfulness and joy factors of enlightenment.
That is to say: the eight universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), the ten universal wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*),
as well as vitarka, vicāra, and other mental factors associated with the respective stages, which are neither associated with mindfulness nor with joy.
This refers to the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness dissociated from joy,
as well as other mental states and mental factors, material phenomena, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind;
specifically, it refers to the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).

The intrinsic nature of the factors of enlightenment— mindfulness and investigation of phenomena— in the latter two dhyānas and the first three formless attainments is not associated with those [factors],
because an intrinsic nature is not associated with itself.
Nor is it associated with the factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga),
because joy is entirely absent in those stages,
except for untainted (anāsrava) mind and mental factors.
All other contaminated mental states and mental factors,
as well as all matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind, constitute the fourth alternative,
just as in the case of the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Regarding the same fourfold analysis for right view and right intention:
just as the awakening factor of mindfulness was analyzed in relation to the awakening factor of joy through the middle four propositions,
it should be understood that the same applies to right view and right intention.
If various phenomena are associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness, are those phenomena associated with right mindfulness?
Answer: It is so.
If a dharma is associated with right mindfulness, is that dharma also associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness?
Answer: It is so; this is because the awakening factor of mindfulness is itself right mindfulness.
One should formulate the statement in this manner.
Regarding those factors associated with the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*),
are they also associated with the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
One should respond by formulating four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

In this context, since the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) and the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya*) both pervade all stages and all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*),
one should formulate four minor propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are factors that are associated with the investigation of phenomena but not with energy.
Regarding the "enlightenment factor of diligence":
this refers to the intrinsic nature of the enlightenment factor of diligence that arises simultaneously with the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
That [diligence] which is associated with the investigation of phenomena is not itself the enlightenment factor of diligence.
Because a nature does not associate with itself.
There is a factor associated with diligence that is not associated with the investigation of phenomena;
namely, the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
This refers to the essential nature of the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that arises together with diligence (*vīrya*).
That [awakening factor] is associated with diligence, but it is not the essential nature of the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena,
because an essential nature is not associated with itself.
There are factors that are both associated with the investigation of phenomena and associated with diligence;
these refer to those factors associated with both,
namely, those arising together with the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena and the awakening factor of diligence.
Excluding the two intrinsic natures, the remaining associated factors consist of the nine universal mental factors (*mahābhūmikadharma*),
the nine wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmikadharma*),
as well as vitarka, vicāra, and so forth, according to their respective stages, along with the mind itself.

There are phenomena that are neither associated with the investigation of dharmas nor associated with diligence; these are the remaining mental states and mental factors, as well as matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
This refers to all mental states and mental factors except for those that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
All other contaminated (*sāsrava*) mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*),
as well as all matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), constitute the fourth alternative.

Just as this applies to the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) in relation to the awakening factors of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), as well as to right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), so it is likewise here.
Just as the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅga) forms four minor permutations with the factor of enlightenment of energy (viriya-sambojjhaṅga),

it should be understood that the same applies to its relationship with the factors of enlightenment of tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā), as well as to right effort (sammāvāyāma), right mindfulness (sammāsati), and right concentration (sammāsamādhi).
Are those phenomena that are associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena also associated with the awakening factor of joy?
One should respond by establishing four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Among these, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena pervades all stages and all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*).
The factor of enlightenment of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) is present in all untainted minds (anāsrava-citta), but not in all stages (bhūmi).
Therefore, one should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are factors associated with the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya) that are not associated with joy.
This refers to the factor associated with the awakening-factor of investigation-of-dharmas that is not associated with the awakening-factor of joy.
It refers to the intrinsic nature of the awakening-factor of joy that arises simultaneously with the investigation-of-dharmas.
That which is associated with the investigation of phenomena (dharmavicaya) but not with the awakening factor of joy (prītisambodhyaṅga),
because a nature is not associated with itself;
and those factors associated with the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena that are not associated with joy.
Namely, the factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of dharma-discernment (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) in the preparatory concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna,
the latter two dhyānas, and the first three formless attainments (ārūpya).
That which is associated with the investigation of dharmas (dharmapravicaya) is not associated with the factor of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga), because joy is entirely absent in those stages.
There are factors associated with joy that are not associated with the investigation of dharmas;
namely, those instances of the investigation of dharmas that are associated with the factor of joy.
This refers to the intrinsic nature of the factor-of-enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) that arises together with joy.
That [joy] is associated with it, but it is not the intrinsic nature of the factor-of-enlightenment of investigation of phenomena;
for an intrinsic nature is not associated with itself.
There are factors that are associated with both investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) and joy (*prīti*).
These refer to the factors associated with both;
that is, those factors that arise simultaneously with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena and the awakening factor of joy.
Excluding the two intrinsic natures, the remaining associated dharmas consist of the eight universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*),
the ten wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*),
as well as vitarka, vicāra, and so forth, according to their respective stages, along with the mind itself.
There are factors that are neither associated with the factor of investigation (*dharmapravicaya*) nor associated with joy (*prīti*);
namely, the factor of investigation-enlightenment-factor (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) when it is not associated with joy,
as well as other mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitasika-dharma*).

Matter that is unconditioned and dissociated from mind refers to the intrinsic nature of the *dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga* (the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena) within the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*),
the intermediate dhyāna, the latter two dhyānas, and the first three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
It is not associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*),
because a nature is not associated with itself.
Nor is it associated with the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Because joy is entirely absent in those stages,
all other contaminated (*sāsrava*) mental states and mental factors— excluding uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors—
as well as all matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), constitute the fourth category.
"Just as it is with regard to the factor of enlightenment of joy,
so it is with regard to right intention":

this means that just as four intermediate permutations were established for the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena in relation to the factor of enlightenment of joy, [so they are here].
It should be understood that the same applies to right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
Are those factors associated with the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) also associated with right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: Those factors associated with right view are also associated with discrimination of phenomena.
There are phenomena that are associated with the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) but not associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
These refer to those factors associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena that are not included within right view;
namely, those factors associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
That [knowledge] is associated with the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga), but it is not right view (samyagdṛṣṭi),
because the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) do not have the nature of view.
Since the scope of the investigation of phenomena is broad while that of right view is narrow, this is formulated as a "concordant subsequent phrase" (anuloma-paścādvākya).
Are those phenomena associated with the awakening factor of energy also associated with the awakening factor of joy?
One should respond by establishing four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Among these, the awakening factor of energy pervades all stages and all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*).
The factor of enlightenment of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) pervades all untainted minds (anāsrava-citta),
but not all stages (bhūmi). Therefore,
one should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) regarding this.
The detailed explanation of the four alternatives should be understood according to the preceding [analysis].
As it is with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), so it is likewise:
just as the factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) forms the middle four alternatives in relation to the factor of joy.
It should be understood that the same applies to right view and right intention.
Regarding those phenomena associated with the enlightenment factor of energy,
are those phenomena also associated with the enlightenment factor of tranquility?
It is stated that there are four lines [of verse].
Herein, the factors of enlightenment of diligence (*vīrya*) and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) both pervade all stages and all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*).
One should construct four minor tetrads; it should be understood that the detailed explanation of these four tetrads follows the same principle as before.

As it is with the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), so it is with the factors of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*), as well as with right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Just as the enlightenment factor of energy (vīrya-sambodhyaṅga) forms four minor permutations with the enlightenment factor of tranquility (praśrabdhi-sambodhyaṅga),

it should be understood that the same applies to its relationship with the enlightenment factors of concentration (samādhi), equanimity (upekṣā), right mindfulness (samyak-smṛti), and right concentration (samyak-samādhi).
All dharmas associated with the enlightenment factor of energy [are likewise to be understood].
Are those dharmas associated with right effort?
Answer: Yes. If dharmas are associated with right effort, [are they those dharmas]? Answer: Yes.
Is that dharma associated with the awakening factor of energy? Answer:
It is so, because the awakening factor of energy is itself right effort.
One should formulate the proposition as follows:
"Are those factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy also associated with the factor of enlightenment of pliancy?"
It should be stated that there are four alternatives.
Among these, the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is present in all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*), but not in all stages (*bhūmi*).
This is because the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is present in all untainted minds and also in all stages.
One should formulate four middle propositions.
The detailed explanation of these four propositions should be understood by analogy with what was previously stated regarding the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Regarding the concentration factor of equanimity (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), it is likewise:
just as the joy factor of enlightenment (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) forms four middle tetralemmas (*catuṣkoṭi*) in relation to the tranquility factor of enlightenment (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*),
one should know that it is the same for the concentration factor of equanimity, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Regarding those phenomena associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*),
are they also associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)?
One should respond by formulating four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).
In this context, the factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) pervades all untainted minds (anāsrava-citta) but not all stages (bhūmi),
because right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) pervades all stages but not all untainted minds.
One should formulate four great propositions.
There are factors associated with joy that are not right view;
namely, right view associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Regarding phenomena associated with the awakening factor of joy that are not associated with right view:
this refers to the intrinsic nature of right view that arises simultaneously with the awakening factor of joy; it is associated with the awakening factor of joy, but is not itself right view.
Because intrinsic nature is not associated with intrinsic nature,
and because it is not associated with right view,
[it is] a dharma associated with the factor of joy in enlightenment.

That is to say, it consists of the factors associated with the enlightenment factor of joy that arise simultaneously with the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising in the first and second dhyānas.
These are associated with the enlightenment factor of joy,
but not with right view, because the latter belongs to a different aggregate.
There are phenomena associated with right view but not with joy,
namely: the factor of enlightenment of joy that is associated with right view,
and those factors dissociated from the factor of enlightenment of joy.
Regarding phenomena associated with right view:
this refers to the intrinsic nature of the factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) that is associated with right view;
it is that which is associated with right view but is not itself the factor of joy.
Because intrinsic nature is not associated with itself,
and because it is not associated with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*),
the factors associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) are precisely the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the dhyāna-intermediate (*dhyānāntara*), and [the first dhyāna].
The factors associated with right view in the latter two dhyānas and the first three formless attainments are not associated with the awakening factor of joy,
because joy is entirely absent in those stages.
There are factors associated with joy and also accompanied by right view;

that is to say, those factors associated with both [joy and right view] refer to the factors associated with the awakening factor of joy and co-arising with right view, excluding the two intrinsic natures themselves.
These consist of the eight universal mental factors (*mahābhūmikadharma*), the ten wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmikadharma*),
as well as vitarka, vicāra, and the mind itself, according to their respective stages.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with joy nor with right view;
namely, right view that is not associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy,
and the factor of enlightenment of joy that is not associated with right view.
As well as other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma),
material phenomena (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra)—
namely, right view (samyag-dṛṣṭi) that is dissociated from the factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga).
That is to say, the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*),
the intermediate dhyāna, the last two dhyānas, and the first three formless attainments;
these, being of the nature of right view, are not associated with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Because joy is entirely absent within those stages,
it is also not associated with right view;
for a nature cannot be associated with itself.

The factor of enlightenment of joy dissociated from right view is the intrinsic nature of the factor of enlightenment of joy that arises simultaneously with the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising in the first two dhyānas;
for it is not associated with right view, as it belongs to a different aggregate.
Nor is it associated with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*),
because a nature is not associated with itself,
nor with other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*).

Namely, the mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) that arise simultaneously with the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) within the preparatory concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), the latter two dhyānas, and the first three formless attainments (ārūpya).
Furthermore, all contaminated mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*),
as well as all matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), constitute the fourth alternative.
As it is with respect to right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), so it is also with respect to right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).
Just as the factor of enlightenment of joy forms four great propositions in relation to right view,
it should be understood that the same applies in relation to right thought.
All dharmas associated with the factor of enlightenment of pliancy [should be understood in the same way].
Is that dharma associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
It should be answered by means of four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).

In this context, because lightness (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena are all pervasive throughout all stages and all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*).
One should formulate four short propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The detailed explanation of these four propositions should be understood as corresponding to what was stated previously.

As it is with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) in relation to the factor of concentration (*samādhi-bodhyaṅga*), so it is also in relation to the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-bodhyaṅga*), right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Just as the factor of enlightenment of pliancy forms four minor permutations with respect to the factor of enlightenment of concentration,
it should be understood that the same applies to its relationship with the factor of enlightenment of equanimity, up to right concentration.
Are those phenomena associated with the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) also associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)?
One should respond by formulating four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).
Among these, the factor of enlightenment of pliancy pervades all stages and all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*).
Because right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) pervades all stages but is not present in all untainted minds (anāsrava-citta),
one should formulate four middle alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
The detailed explanation of these four alternatives should be understood according to the preceding [analysis].
Regarding the statement "as it is for right view, so it is for right intention":

just as the lightness factor of enlightenment (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga) forms four intermediate propositions in relation to right view, one should know that it is likewise in relation to right intention.
If various dharmas are associated with the factor of enlightenment of investigation (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga),
are those dharmas also associated with the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga)?
One should answer by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
Among these, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) should be analyzed in terms of four minor permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*),
because it is present in all stages and in all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*).
The detailed explanation of the four alternatives should be understood according to the preceding [analysis].
As it was with the equanimity factor of enlightenment (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and the factors of right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) and right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), so it is here:
just as a "small" tetralemma was constructed for the concentration factor of enlightenment (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) in relation to the equanimity factor of enlightenment.
It should be understood that the same applies to right effort and right mindfulness.
Regarding those factors that are associated with the awakening factor of dharma-discernment,
are those factors also associated with right view?
It should be stated in four propositions:
herein, the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is present in all stages and in all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*);
however, right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is present in all stages but not in all untainted minds.
One should formulate four middle propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
It should be understood that the detailed explanation of these four propositions follows the previous pattern.
As it is with respect to right view, so it is also with respect to right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).

Just as with the concentration enlightenment factor (*samādhi-sambojjhaṅga*) in relation to right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*), one should know that the same fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*) applies to its relation to right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*).
Regarding all phenomena associated with the concentration enlightenment factor:
are those phenomena also associated with right concentration (*sammā-samādhi*)?
Answer: It is so.
If a dharma is associated with right concentration, is that dharma necessarily associated with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness?
The answer "it is so" means that since the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is itself right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), one should formulate the statement thus:
"All phenomena are associated with the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*)."
"Is that dharma associated with right view?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Herein, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity forms four middle permutations in relation to right view and right intention.
Regarding right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, there is a "small" tetralemma.
Regarding right view in relation to right thought, there is a "large" tetralemma;
in relation to right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, there is a "medium" tetralemma.
Right intention forms four intermediate sets of four propositions in relation to right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Right effort forms a minor set of four propositions in relation to right mindfulness and right concentration.
Right mindfulness forms a minor set of four propositions in relation to right concentration.
All such cases should be understood according to the preceding [explanation].
What is mundane right view?
And so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the profound and hidden meanings within the various sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra:
If one achieves superior mundane right view,
even after passing through hundreds of thousands of births, one will never fall into the evil destinies.
Although such sūtras speak of various kinds of mundane right view, they do not provide an extensive explanation thereof.
The Sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies;
those portions not yet explained shall now be analyzed.
Furthermore, although it was previously stated in general terms that there are three—view, wisdom, and knowledge—[they shall now be distinguished].
However, it has not yet been explained separately what constitutes mundane right view and what constitutes mundane right knowledge.
The preceding treatise serves as the fundamental basis for this.
That which has not yet been stated shall now be explained.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of refuting the positions of others and demonstrating correct reasoning;
that is to say, some may assert:
Not all wholesome, contaminated wisdom associated with the mental consciousness is "view" (dṛṣṭi).
For example, the Dārṣṭāntikas assert that it is the karma of manifest action induced by the five sensory consciousnesses.
Furthermore, at the time of death, the wholesome wisdom of the mental level (manobhūmi) is not of the nature of vision (*darśana*). Why is this?
Because vision involves conceptual discrimination, whereas the wholesome wisdom of the mental level is induced by the five sensory consciousnesses.
Just as the five groups of consciousness (pañca-vijñāna-kāya) are not of the nature of vision because they lack the capacity for discrimination,
so too the wholesome wisdom of the mental level (manobhūmi) is not of the nature of vision;
for while vision arises by operating through the internal gate and can manifest outwardly as physical and vocal action, the wisdom of the mental level operates by turning toward external objects.
Because its activity is forceful and fierce, it is "good wisdom" (*sādhumati*) at the end of life;
because its power and activity are weak and inferior, it is not of the nature of vision (*darśana-svabhāva*).
Question: How is this reconciled with what is taught in the *Sūtra*?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"At the time of his death, his wholesome mind and mental factors proceed together with right view," and he gave this answer.
The Blessed One said that when one is about to die,
a continuous stream of wholesome mind arises together with right view;
it is not the case that right view functions at the actual moment of death.
To refute that attachment and to demonstrate that all wholesome wisdom coexists with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and is subsumed under the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*),
this treatise is composed based on such various causes and conditions.
What is mundane right view?
The answer is: it is contaminated, wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness.
This is of three kinds.
First, obtained through application;
second, obtained through the removal of defilements;
third, obtained through birth.
That which is acquired through application refers to the wisdom consisting of hearing and the wisdom consisting of reflection.
The wisdom produced through cultivation includes,
within this context, specific distinctions such as the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*),
and the various applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Furthermore, it includes the wisdom that arises simultaneously with the heat, summits, patience, and the highest mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Regarding those obtained through the separation from defilements (*vairāgya-prāpta*),
these refer to the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and the liberations (*vimokṣa*).
The wisdom co-arising with the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
as well as that acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*),
refers to the wholesome wisdom obtained upon being born in those respective stages.
Such worldly right views as these are of infinite variety,
like the countless drops in the waters of the four great oceans; here,
I shall briefly describe only those worldly right views that are coarse and manifest.
What is conventional right knowledge?
Answer: wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as contaminated wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness.
Wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses refers to wholesome wisdom associated with visual consciousness,
up to and including wholesome wisdom associated with tactile consciousness.
Wholesome wisdom associated with visual consciousness refers to the contemplation of one’s parents, the Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, preceptors,
instructors, and other venerable ones who share the holy life.
The wholesome wisdom associated with the visual consciousness that arises,
and the wholesome wisdom associated with the auditory consciousness,
refers to listening to one's parents, teachers, and preceptors.
And all wholesome speech from other respected ones, fellow practitioners of the holy life,
and so forth; as well as the wholesome wisdom associated with the auditory consciousness that arises from hearing the Dharma teachings of the Tripitaka from the Buddhas and their noble disciples.
Wholesome wisdom associated with the consciousnesses of nose, tongue,
and body refers to the wholesome wisdom arising in association with these three consciousnesses at the time of consuming edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
This is not something that can be produced by everyone.
It should be understood that this arises only when a practitioner,
while observing the nature of edible food, partakes of it; it is a tainted,
wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness, as described extensively above.
The intrinsic nature of mundane right view and right knowledge has already been explained.
Their characteristics of being mixed or unmixed shall now be discussed.
Regarding all mundane right views:
Is this mundane right knowledge?
Answer: All mundane right views are also mundane right knowledge;
however, there is mundane right knowledge that is not mundane right view.
This refers to the wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses.
Within this context, because conventional right view must involve repeated and thorough deliberation regarding its object,
the wisdom concomitant with the five consciousnesses is not termed "view," as has already been explained previously.
Does mundane right view include mundane right knowledge?
Or does mundane right knowledge include mundane right view?
Answer: Mundane right knowledge includes mundane right view.
Worldly right view does not encompass worldly right knowledge.
What does it not encompass?
It refers to the wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses.
In this context, because the essence of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is broad while right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is narrow,
the former subsumes the latter but the latter does not subsume the former.
This applies to all those who have accomplished mundane right view.
Is that mundane right knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
If one possesses mundane right knowledge...
Is that mundane right view?
Answer: It is so.
Question: Who possesses mundane right view and right knowledge?
Answer: Regarding those who have not severed their roots of goodness, this is a general statement.
If explained in detail, there are many and there are few.
That is to say, there may be those who possess only the mundane right view and right knowledge of the desire realm;
or those who possess only those of the form realm;
or those who possess only those of the formless realm.
Some achieve [the mundane right view and right knowledge] of the desire and form realms;
some achieve those of the form and formless realms;
and some achieve the mundane right view and right knowledge of all three realms.
As it has been stated regarding the three realms, so it is for the nine stages;
whether fewer or more, they should be explained according to reason.
All mundane right view has already been abandoned and fully understood.
Is that mundane right knowledge? Answer:
It is so. Furthermore, if mundane right knowledge has been abandoned and fully understood, [is it so? Answer: It is so.
Is that mundane right view?
Answer: It is so.
Question: Who possesses mundane right view and right knowledge?
"Are they already abandoned and already fully understood?
The answer is: "All Arhats.
This is the general statement.
If explained separately, there are cases where [the factors] are many and cases where they are few.
That is to say, for ordinary beings and noble ones who have already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
the mundane right view and right knowledge of the eight stages have already been abandoned and fully understood.
Up to and including ordinary beings and noble ones who are already free from the defilement of sensual desire but not yet free from the defilement of the first dhyāna,
their mundane right view and right knowledge of a single stage have been abandoned and fully understood.
Because this mundane right view and right knowledge are with-outflows (*sāsrava*), they are analyzed according to five categories:
the inquiry, the inclusion within meditative concentration, the accomplishment, and the abandonment.
Question: For what reason is it called "mundane" (*saṃvṛti*)?
It is called "conventional" because it is subject to transformation and decay;
it is called "conventional" because it serves as a basis for craving.
If it is called "conventional" because it is subject to transformation and decay, then...
The Noble Path is also subject to change and decay; it should therefore be called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).
If it is called "conventional" because it is the basis for attachment (*rāga*), then it is also the basis for hatred (*dveṣa*) and delusion (*moha*); why then do you speak of attachment alone?
It is agreed that it is so called because it is subject to transformation and disintegration; therefore, it is termed "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).
Question: If that were the case, then the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) would also be subject to transformation and disintegration, and should thus be termed conventional.
Answer: That which is subject to transformation and decay, and which can continue the various states of existence (*bhava*) and increase them, is called the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Although the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) is subject to transformation and decay, it cannot continue the various states of existence.
Furthermore, because it causes all things to diminish, it is not the conventional. Moreover,
that which is subject to transformation and decay, which causes the cycle of birth and death to flow on without end,
and wherein birth, aging, sickness, and death constantly continue, is called the conventional.
Although the Noble Path is subject to change and decay, it does not cause the cycle of birth and death to flow on endlessly;
rather, because it severs birth, aging, sickness, and death so that they do not continue, it is not mundane.
Furthermore, that which is subject to transformation and decay is the practice leading to the accumulation of suffering;
likewise, that which is the practice leading to the accumulation of birth, aging, sickness, and death within the world of existence is called the conventional.
Although the Noble Path is subject to change and decay, it does not proceed toward the origin of suffering;
nor does it proceed toward the origin of existence, birth, old age, sickness, and death in the world. Therefore, it is not mundane.
Furthermore, if that which is subject to transformation and decay were the basis for the view of a self-identity,
the basis for perversion, or the basis for craving, [it would not be the case that the Tathāgata is free from these].
The locus of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*):
this is the foundation upon which greed, hatred, and delusion stand.
It is defiled, poisonous, faulty, thorny, turbid, and stained.
That which conforms to the world and conforms to the truths of suffering and its origin is called the conventional (saṃvṛti).
Although the noble path is subject to change and destruction, because it is contrary to those [truths], it is not conventional.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"It is called 'conventional' (saṃvṛti) because it is the basis for craving.
Question: If that is so, since it is also the basis for hatred and delusion, why speak of craving alone?
Answer: Although that [object] is likewise a basis for hatred and delusion, greed is preeminent at the outset; therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
However, the Sūtra states that it is called "conventional" (saṃvṛti) because it is subject to transformation and disintegration.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The Venerable Āḍhya approached the Buddha,
prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘the conventional’ and ‘the meaning of the conventional’ that you have spoken?
The Buddha told Puṇyavanta:
"Because it is subject to transformation and decay, it is called 'conventional' (saṃvṛti)," said the Venerable Āḍhya,
and further addressed the Buddha.
"What is meant by 'subject to transformation and decay'?
The Buddha told Puṇyavanta:
"The sense base of the eye is subject to transformation and decay."
The sense-base of form is subject to transformation and decay;
likewise, up to the sense-base of mind, and the sense-base of phenomena,
are subject to transformation and decay.
It is called "conventional" (saṃvṛti) because it is subject to transformation and decay.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One state that only the twelve bases (āyatana) are conventional because they are subject to transformation and decay, and not other phenomena?
Answer: It is observed that those who are to be converted should hear that the "bases" (āyatana) are conventional designations;
because they thereby attain awakening and understanding, the bases are taught specifically.
Just as in other sūtras the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*) and so forth are designated as conventional (*saṃvṛti*), this sūtra is likewise.
Furthermore, while the teaching on the twelve bases (*āyatana*) is a middle-way exposition,
it is taught here specifically because it encompasses all phenomena exhaustively.
Question: Are all things that undergo transformation and disintegration merely conventional?
Answer: One should respond by means of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are things that are conventional but not subject to transformation and disintegration.
This refers to the two truths of suffering and its origin in the past and future;
there are also those that are subject to transformation and disintegration yet are not conventional,
namely, the truth of the path in the present.
There are those that are both conventional and subject to transformation;
namely, the two truths of present suffering and its origin.
There are those that are neither conventional nor subject to transformation.
This refers to the Noble Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) in its past and future states, as well as all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta).
Question: What is the difference between transformation (vipariṇāma) and destruction (bhaṅga)?
Answer: "Transformation" (vipariṇāma) indicates subtle impermanence;
"destruction" (bhaṅga) indicates coarse impermanence.
Furthermore, "transformation" indicates momentary impermanence.
"Destruction" (bhaṅga) indicates the impermanence of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Furthermore, "transformation" (*vipariṇāma*) indicates the impermanence of internal constituents,
while "destruction" indicates the impermanence of external constituents.
Furthermore, "transformation" (vipariṇāma) indicates the impermanence of sentient beings,
while "destruction" (bhaṅga) indicates the impermanence of non-sentient things,
as when it is said that a house is destroyed or a granary is destroyed.
"What is untainted vision (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*)? and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Although the three—vision, wisdom, and knowledge—were previously mentioned in general terms, [this treatise is composed] to provide a detailed analysis.
However, it has not yet been explained separately what constitutes untainted vision (*anāsravadṛṣṭi*) and what constitutes untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*).
The preceding treatise serves as the fundamental basis for this;
that which was not stated therein shall now be explained.
Furthermore, although conventional views and knowledges have already been explained previously,
this treatise is now composed to reveal their direct antidotes.
What is untainted view?
Answer: It is untainted wisdom (anāsravaprajñā) other than the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Furthermore, what is this?
It refers to the eight untainted patiences (anāsravakṣānti) at the conclusion of clear realization (abhisamaya).
And regarding the eight knowledges of one in training and the right view of one beyond training:
what is untainted knowledge?
Answer: It is all untainted wisdom (prajñā) excluding the untainted patiences (kṣānti).
What, then, is this? It refers to the eight knowledges of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Thus has been explained the intrinsic nature of untainted vision and knowledge.
Now, the characteristics of the mixed and the unmixed shall be demonstrated.
Are all untainted views untainted knowledge?
One should respond that this involves four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is untainted vision that is not untainted knowledge;
namely, untainted receptivity (*anāsravakṣānti*).
This possesses the characteristic of vision but lacks the characteristic of knowledge.
There is untainted knowledge that is not untainted vision;
namely, the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
This is because it possesses the characteristic of knowledge but lacks the characteristic of vision.
There is untainted view that is also untainted knowledge;
this refers to all other untainted wisdoms, excluding the untainted patiences (*kṣānti*) and the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*). Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to the eight knowledges of one in training (*śaikṣa*) and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Because these possess both the characteristic of vision (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of knowledge (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*),
there are those that are neither untainted vision (*anāsrava-darśana*) nor untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
This refers to the exclusion of the aforementioned characteristics.
"Characteristics" refers to that which is designated by names, as explained extensively above.
Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to all other formations within the aggregate of formations— excluding untainted wisdom—
as well as the four remaining aggregates in their entirety,
together with unconditioned phenomena.
This constitutes the fourth proposition.
One should know that the four propositions regarding the mutual inclusion of untainted vision (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*) and untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) are established accordingly.
For those who possess untainted vision, do they also possess untainted knowledge?
Answer: Those who possess untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) also possess untainted vision (anāsrava-dṛṣṭi).
However, there are those who possess untainted vision but do not possess untainted knowledge;
this refers to the time when the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) is present.
At that time, because untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) had not yet been cultivated,
this Master of the Treatise thoroughly understood the distinctions between the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena;
whatever was to be explained, he would explain it individually, even down to a single moment of thought.
That which should not be spoken is not spoken even if it were to exceed the measure of the great oceans of the four elements.
Whether what is spoken is extensive or concise, it must be observed for its utility.
Question: Why is it that herein only the four—asking, determining, gathering, and accomplishing—are mentioned, while abandoning is not?
Answer: That which is defiled is abandoned;
because the untainted (anāsrava) is undefiled, it is not said to be abandoned.
It is like clothing or vessels: only that which has stains must be cleansed.
It must be washed and cleansed; it is not that which is already free from defilement.
Therefore, the untainted (*anāsrava*) should not be said to be abandoned.
Question: If untainted phenomena are not to be abandoned, [how can they be so described]?
How should one reconcile what is stated in the sūtras?
For example, as it says regarding a bhikṣu:
If you understand this Dharma teaching of the raft analogy as I have explained it,
then even the Dharma should be relinquished,
let alone what is not the Dharma.
This dharma should be understood as the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
The answer is that there are two kinds of abandonment:
first, the abandonment of craving (*tṛṣṇā-prahāṇa*).

Second, there is the abandonment through relinquishment (*prahāṇa-parityāga*). Although there is no abandonment through the cutting off of craving, there is abandonment through relinquishment because one relinquishes this at the time of parinirvāṇa.
That is to say, the bhikṣus first attained the exhaustion of all outflows by relying on the noble path; therefore, out of mindfulness of their debt of gratitude, they relinquish it.
He repeatedly cultivated and brought forth the Noble Path so that it would manifest before him.
Later, because he was tormented by the various sufferings of the four hundred and four worldly diseases,
the Buddha told him:
"O bhikṣus, you have already performed what was to be done by relying on the Noble Path;
you should now cast it aside and enter the nirvana without remainder."
It is like a person who, having relied upon a raft to cross a river, continues to carry it on their head out of gratitude for its kindness;
yet another person says to them: "You have already crossed the river by relying on this."
"Now you may depart, casting aside your sovereignty; the bhikṣu is likewise.
Question: "In this context, what is the Dharma and what is non-Dharma?
Answer: "The teachings of our own school are the Dharma."
The teachings of the non-Buddhists are not the Dharma;
the teachings of our own school reveal emptiness and non-self, accord with nirvana,
and enable the permanent severance of birth, old age, sickness, and death— one should abandon even these [teachings].
How much more so regarding the teachings of the non-Buddhists,
which turn their backs on emptiness and non-self, oppose nirvāṇa,
and cause the cycle of birth, old age, sickness, and death in the world to increase and continue without end?
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"That which consists of the well-retained sets of names, phrases, and syllables is the Dharma;
that which consists of the poorly-retained sets of names, phrases, and syllables is not the Dharma."
Even those who have properly received and maintained [the teachings] should abandon them;
how much more so should those who are unwholesome be abandoned.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka spoke thus.
That which is well-accepted and upheld in the Āgamas is the Dharma;
that which is not well-accepted and upheld in the Āgamas is not the Dharma.
Even that which is well-accepted and upheld should be abandoned.
"How much more so for that which is unwholesome, which ought not to be abandoned?
Venerable Pārśva said:
"Appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) is the Dharma."
Improper mental attention is contrary to the Dharma;
even proper mental attention should be abandoned,
so how much more so improper mental attention, which certainly should not be unabandoned?
Furthermore, shame and remorse are Dharma;
lack of shame and lack of remorse are non-Dharma.
The three roots of goodness are Dharma.
The three unwholesome roots are non-Dharma;
the four foundations of mindfulness are Dharma;
the four perversions are non-Dharma.
The five faculties are the Dharma;
the five hindrances are non-Dharma;
the six recollections are the Dharma.
The six bases of craving are non-Dharma;
the seven factors of enlightenment are Dharma;
the seven underlying tendencies are non-Dharma.
The eightfold noble path is the Dharma;
the eightfold wrong path is non-Dharma.
The nine successive attainments are the Dharma.
The nine fetters are non-Dharma;
the ten paths of wholesome action are Dharma;
the ten paths of unwholesome action are non-Dharma.
If even these pure phenomena (*śukla-dharma*) should be abandoned, how much more so those defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), which ought not to be abandoned? 2.

The Fifth Section on the Fivefold Compendium (*pañca-vidha-nikāya*). Part One of the Second Section of the Third Chapter on the Aggregate of Knowledge (*jñāna-skandha*): What is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)? [This includes] such chapters and the explanation of their meaning.

Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing and clarifying the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"O Bhikṣus,
you should know that those who hold false views..."
The bodily and vocal actions that arise according to what is seen,
as well as the volitions, aspirations, and practices—
all such phenomena are of this same nature; they are all capable of bringing about that which is undesirable.
It is not to be rejoiced in;
it does not accord with one's desires;
its fruit is contrary to one's wishes.
Why is this so? Because this wrong view is a violent and malevolent view.
Although there is such a statement in the Sūtra, [it refers to something else].
Yet its meaning has not been analyzed.
This sutra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies;
that which was not previously explained therein shall now be explained here.
Furthermore, although it was previously stated in general terms that there are three— view, wisdom, and knowledge—
it has not yet been explained specifically:
what is wrong view, and what is wrong knowledge?
The preceding treatise is the fundamental basis upon which this work relies.
Since that [treatise] did not yet explain certain matters, they shall now be explained; therefore, this treatise is composed.
What is wrong view?
Answer: If they are not established [as distinct], then all five views are termed false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
That is to say, if one does not establish the specific names and the distinctions of the characteristics of the five views, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth.
All five of those views are termed false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*),
because they all involve erroneous conceptualization regarding their objects.
If one were to establish them [as distinct], they would consist solely of the denial of giving and the denial of the pleasant.
There are no sacrifices;
there is no wholesome conduct;
there is no unwholesome conduct.
The view that there are no sublime or evil karmic actions,
nor their fruits and maturations, is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This refers to the establishment of the names and the distinctions of the characteristics of the five views, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth.
As for that which functions solely as the aspect of non-action,
it alone is termed "wrong view," because it is the extreme within the wrong;
as it is said in the case of "smelling ghee" and "the wicked caṇḍāla," and so forth.
What is wrong wisdom?
The answer is: defiled discernment associated with the six consciousnesses.
Among these, defiled discernment associated with the five [sensory] consciousnesses is as follows:
This refers to wisdom associated with greed and hatred.
Wisdom associated with the mental consciousness that is defiled refers to the five views,
as well as greed, hatred, pride, doubt, and non-specific ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
Furthermore, all wisdom associated with the remaining fetters and stains is termed false wisdom (*mithyājñāna*). Thus,
the intrinsic nature of false view and false wisdom has been explained.
The characteristics of the mixed and the unmixed shall now be explained.
Are all wrong views wrong knowledge?
Answer: All wrong views are wrong knowledge.
This means that because one who engages in wrong investigation necessarily makes wrong determinations,
there is defiled wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses that is not wrong view.
It is the wisdom associated with greed and hatred;
the defiled wisdom associated with the mental consciousness, excluding the five views;
and the wisdom associated with greed, hatred, pride, doubt, the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*), as well as other envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and stains (*upakleśa*).
Does wrong view encompass wrong knowledge, or does wrong knowledge encompass wrong view?
Answer: Wrong knowledge encompasses wrong view;
it is not that wrong view encompasses wrong knowledge. What, then, is not encompassed?
This refers to the afflicted wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as the afflicted wisdom associated with the mental consciousness— excluding the five views—
because it possesses the characteristic of definitive discernment but lacks the characteristic of investigative deliberation.
Question: Are those who possess wrong view also possessed of wrong knowledge?
Answer: Those who possess wrong view are also possessed of wrong knowledge;
for wrong knowledge is predominant, and because a view is also a form of knowledge.
This refers to the stage when the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) has not yet arisen;
there are those who possess false knowledge (mithyājñāna) but do not possess false view (mithyādṛṣṭi),
namely, those in training (śaikṣa) who have seen the tracks [of the truths] once the subsequent knowledge of the path has already arisen.
All those in the stage of training (śaikṣa) are called "those who have seen the tracks" (dṛṣṭapada),
because they have already fully perceived the tracks of the Four Noble Truths;
this is the general description.
If explained individually, there are many and few;
that is to say, some may possess the false knowledge of nine stages,
and so on, up to some who possess the false knowledge of a single stage.
In each of the stages (*bhūmi*), there may be those who have accomplished nine grades of false knowledge,
or even those who have accomplished only one grade of false knowledge.
Are all such false views already abandoned and fully understood by them, and is that false knowledge likewise [abandoned and fully understood]?
Answer: That which is wrong cognition (*mithyājñāna*) is both abandoned and fully understood, and it is also wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
However, there is wrong view that has been abandoned and fully understood by an Arhat which is not wrong cognition.
This refers, for example, to the "learner who has seen the path" (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta*); this is the general explanation.
If explained individually, there may be many or few; that is to say,
there may be cases where the false knowledge of nine stages has not been abandoned or fully understood,
up to and including cases where the false knowledge of even a single stage has not been abandoned or fully understood.
Within each stage, there may be nine grades of false knowledge that have not yet been abandoned or fully understood,
up to and including the possibility that even a single grade of false knowledge has not yet been abandoned or fully understood.
Because the nine grades of defiled wrong knowledge are abandoned.
