Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra:
"Those who possess right view [perceive] according to how they see."
The volitions that initiate bodily and vocal actions, as well as the seeking, aspiring, and practicing, are all of this same category.
All such things are capable of summoning results that are desirable, pleasant, delightful, and joyous, occurring exactly as one wishes and according to one's intent.
Why is this? It is because this right view is a noble and virtuous vision.
Although the sūtra contains this statement, it does not analyze its meaning.
The Sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies;
those points not yet explained therein shall now be set forth.
Furthermore, although the three—view (*dṛṣṭi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and knowledge (*jñāna*)—were previously mentioned in general terms, [they require further elaboration].
However, it has not yet been explained separately what right view is and what right knowledge is.
The preceding treatise serves as the fundamental basis for this;
that which was not stated therein shall now be explained.
Furthermore, although wrong view and wrong knowledge have already been explained previously,
this treatise is now composed in order to explain their direct antidotes.
What is right view?
Answer: It is wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness that is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) or the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
This is of two kinds: first, the contaminated (sāsrava); [second, the uncontaminated].
There are two types:
the untainted and the tainted.
As for the tainted, it is mundane right view, as explained in detail previously.
The untainted (anāsrava) refers to the untainted patiences (kṣānti), the eight knowledges of those in training (śaikṣa), and the right view of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What is right knowledge (samyagjñāna)?

Answer: It refers to wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness that is not subsumed under the untainted patiences (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
This is of two kinds.
First, the contaminated [right view], which is mundane right view;
second, the uncontaminated [right view], which consists of the eight knowledges of those in training and those beyond training.
Thus has been explained the intrinsic nature of right view and right knowledge.
The characteristics of the mixed and the unmixed shall now be explained.
Are all right views right knowledge?
One should respond by formulating four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is right view that is not right knowledge;

this refers to the untainted forbearances (*anāsrava-kṣānti*), because these possess the characteristic of view but lack the characteristic of knowledge. There is right knowledge that is not right view;
this refers to the wholesome wisdom associated with the five sensory consciousnesses.
And up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Because these possess the characteristic of knowledge (*jñānalakṣaṇa*) and lack the characteristic of vision (*darśanalakṣaṇa*),
they are right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and also right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
This refers to untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*),
which is wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness that is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
This is of two kinds.
The first is the mundane right view, which is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The second is the supramundane [right view], which consists of the eight knowledges of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and the right view of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Both of these possess the characteristics of both view (*darśana*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
There is that which is neither right view nor right knowledge;
this refers to what has been excluded from the aforementioned characteristics.
It is explained in detail as previously stated.
This refers to all other formations within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) excluding wholesome wisdom,
the entirety of the other four aggregates,
and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma), which constitute the fourth category.
This summary of the four propositions should be understood as established by analogy.
Is it the case that all who possess right view also possess right knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
If one is established in right knowledge, is one also established in right view?
Answer: It is so.
Question: Who is established in both right view and right knowledge?
Answer: The statement "one who has not severed the roots of goodness" is a general description.
If explained in detail, there are cases where it is many and cases where it is few;
that is to say, some may possess only two [factors] of the desire realm.
Some possess only the two [faculties] of the form realm;
some possess only the two of the formless realm;
and some possess only the two untainted [faculties] of the form realm.
Some possess only the two untainted [attainments] of the formless realm;
some possess only the two of the desire and form realms;
and some possess only the two of the form and formless realms.
Some possess all three [attainments] of the desire, form, and formless realms;
some possess two—the desire and form realms and the untainted;
and some possess two—the form and formless realms and the untainted.
Or, is there one who has accomplished the two types of untainted [knowledge] regarding the three realms?
As for those with right view who have already abandoned and fully understood [the defilements], do they possess that right knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
If right knowledge has already been abandoned and fully understood, has that right view also been abandoned and fully understood?
Answer: It is so.
Question: Who has abandoned and fully understood both right view and right knowledge?
The answer regarding the arhat is stated in general terms.
If explained specifically, there are many and few;
namely, those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) who have already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
In the eighth stage, right view and right knowledge have already been abandoned and fully understood.

This extends even to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already become free from the defilement of desire but have not yet become free from the defilement of the first dhyāna;
for them, all right view and right knowledge have already been abandoned and fully understood.
According to the ultimate teaching, this refers exclusively to the Arhat.

Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of other schools and revealing the correct principle.
That is to say, some may claim that defiled wisdom (kliṣṭā prajñā) is not of the nature of a fetter (saṃyojana).
They assert this:
"How can wisdom have the sense of being bound?
To refute that attachment, it is shown that defiled wisdom, which has the nature of views, is comprised within the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
Are all instances of wrong wisdom (mithyā-prajñā) fetters (saṃyojana)?
One should respond that there are four possible cases (catuṣkoṭi).
Because wrong wisdom (*mithyāprajñā*) and the fetters (*saṃyojana*) differ in their breadth and narrowness,
there is wrong wisdom that is not a fetter;
namely, all defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭaprajñā*) other than the two fetters.
"Having abandoned two fetters" refers to having abandoned the fetter of views and the fetter of grasping;
"other afflicted wisdom" refers to the remaining types of afflicted discernment.
This refers to the wisdom associated with greed, hatred, pride, doubt, and the unique ignorance (āveṇika-avidyā),
as well as other entanglements (paryavasthāna) and impurities (mala).
This possesses the characteristic of "crooked wisdom" (kuṭila-prajñā) but lacks the characteristic of a "fetter" (saṃyojana).
There are fetters that do not possess the characteristic of wrong wisdom;
namely, the seven fetters, which are the seven beginning with craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
This is because these fetters possess the characteristics of fetters but lack the characteristics of wrong wisdom.
There are those that are both wrong wisdom and fetters;
namely, the two fetters—the view-fetter and the grasping-fetter—because they possess both characteristics.
There are also those that are neither wrong wisdom nor fetters.
This means excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
"Characteristics" refers to that which is designated by names, as explained extensively above.
Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to the formations aggregate (saṃskāra-skandha) excluding defiled wisdom (kliṣṭa-prajñā) and the other seven fetters (saṃyojana),
as well as all remaining formations aggregates and the entirety of the other four aggregates.

Question: Why is it called "left" (*vāma*)?
What is the meaning of "left"?
The answer is: because its intention is leftward and because it falls into the category of the left, it is called "left.
This means that its application is biased and not expedient.
Furthermore, because they transgress against liberation, the correct principles, and the categories of wholesome qualities,
they are called "left" (vāma). Furthermore, because they are inauspicious, they are called "left."
For instance, when one does not circumambulate to the right before the stūpas of Buddhas and noble ones,
or at the shrines of celestial spirits, it is called "left" because it is inauspicious.
Furthermore, it is called "left" because it is not a skillful means (*upāya*).
Just as people in the world who act in a left-handed manner are all said to be unskillful,
furthermore, because their conduct is improper, it is called "left."
As it is said, those of external paths are "left-handed people" because their speech and conduct are entirely incorrect.
Question: If defiled wisdom is called "left-handed wisdom," [what then is right-handed wisdom?]
Why is it said that the Buddha’s body has "left light"?
Answer: The reasons for establishing the designation "left" differ in their meanings.
Specifically, because defiled wisdom violates the correct principle of liberation and opposes the category of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-pakṣa*), it is designated as "left."
The Buddha possesses a constant radiance that arises from his body.
Because it abides eternally, it is designated as "left," for it differs from other lights,
which arise and cease without constancy.
Because the Buddha’s body possesses a constant radiance extending one fathom,
even minute particles and tiny insects are scorched by the majesty of this light and do not approach his body.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the Buddha possesses three radiances that outshine all other lights, causing them to appear as leftward (inauspicious);
for this reason, it is said that the Buddha’s body has "leftward light."
Regarding the three lights of the Buddha:
first, the light of the Buddha’s body is of true golden color.
When this light touches the various mountains of gold, it causes their own majestic radiance to vanish and become unmanifest.
Second, the light from the Buddha’s teeth is an extremely brilliant white;
when this light touches the King of Snow Mountains, it causes that mountain's majestic radiance to vanish and become invisible.
Third, the light of the Buddha’s wisdom is pure and shines everywhere.
This light shines upon and touches the heterodox treatises of non-Buddhists, causing them all to be crushed, subdued, and made to vanish from sight.
Thus, these three lights cause others to recede and disappear;
because they all become left-handed (vāma), they are called "left" (vāma).
Some say that when the golden light of the Buddha’s body illuminates the brilliant white light emitted by his teeth,
it reveals the extreme majesty and splendor of the Buddha’s countenance.
It is like the brilliant autumn sun shining upon the Snowy Mountains, causing the majesty of that king of mountains to become even more magnificent.
[The Buddha] asked: "Do all Buddhas possess such light on their left side?"
Question: Do all Buddhas constantly emit light for a fathom around their entire bodies?
Answer: All Buddhas possess such left-hand light, which constantly emits illumination for a fathom around their entire bodies.
Question: If that is so, how is the account of the former life of Dīpaṃkara Buddha to be reconciled? As it is said in a sūtra:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara’s bodily radiance was so brilliant that it illuminated the city of Dīpavatī."
It encircles [the tree] for a distance of one *yojana*.
For twelve years, there was no distinction between day and night; one could know the day and night only by observing the opening and closing of the flowers.
This being so, how is it that all Buddhas possess a constant radiance extending one fathom?
Answer: That sūtra does not state this.
It merely says that the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara emitted a constant light from his entire body, one fathom in length, for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Manifesting great supernormal transformations and emitting emanated light,
he performed Buddha-activities for twelve years.
Some have said this:
It is not the case that the bodies of all Buddhas possess such a constant light extending one fathom.
This is because the radiance of a Buddha’s body is not comprised within the primary or secondary marks (lakṣaṇa and anuvyañjana);
it may be great or small, and its arising and ceasing are not fixed.
The commentary states: It should be explained in this way.
All Buddhas possess such a light on the left side that radiates a fathom-wide halo around their bodies, constantly emitting illumination.
Although it is not included among the primary or secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana), it exists eternally as a natural law (dharmatā).
Because the bodies of all Buddhas always possess supreme and wondrous majestic radiance.

Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: Although it was previously stated in general terms that there are three—view (*dṛṣṭi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—it has not yet been explained specifically what constitutes training in view, what constitutes training in knowledge, and what constitutes training in wisdom.
The preceding treatise is the fundamental basis upon which this work relies.
Since certain matters therein were not yet explained, they shall now be set forth;
for this reason, this treatise is composed.
What is the vision of one in training?
Answer: It is the wisdom of one in training, namely, the untainted forbearances (*kṣānti*) and the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) of one in training.

From the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), all untainted wisdoms (*anāsrava-prajñā*) are termed "the vision of one in training" (*śaikṣa-darśana*).
What is "the knowledge of one in training" (*śaikṣa-jñāna*)?
Answer: One trains in the eight knowledges, namely, the four dharma-knowledges and the four subsequent knowledges.
What is the wisdom of one in training?

This means that the "vision of one in training" (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭi*) and the "knowledge of one in training" (*śaikṣa-jñāna*) are collectively termed "wisdom of one in training" (*śaikṣī prajñā*), because both vision and knowledge possess the characteristic of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
Having already explained the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the vision, wisdom,
and knowledge of one in training, the characteristics of their being mixed or unmixed shall now be explained.
Are all those that are trainee-views also trainee-knowledges?
Answer: All trainee-knowledges are also trainee-views, because trainee-knowledge necessarily possesses the characteristic of investigative deliberation (*abhyūhanā*).
There are views of those in training that are not knowledges of those in training;
namely, the untainted patiences (*anāsrava-kṣānti*), because these patiences do not yet possess the characteristic of definitive certainty.
Are all views of those in training also wisdoms of those in training?
Answer: It is so.
Furthermore, if there is wisdom that is training, is it also vision that is training?
Answer: It is so.
Because the trainee’s vision and wisdom are pervasive throughout the untainted mind, are all trainee knowledges (*jñāna*) trainee wisdoms (*prajñā*)?
Answer: All trainee knowledges are also trainee wisdoms.
There is that which is trainee wisdom (*śaikṣī prajñā*) but not trainee knowledge (*śaikṣaṃ jñānam*).
This refers to the meaning of untainted receptivities (*anāsravakṣānti*), as explained previously.
The inclusion of these three [categories] should be understood according to their established definitions.
Question: Do those who possess the vision of training (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭi) also possess the knowledge of training (śaikṣa-jñāna)?
Answer: Those who possess the knowledge of training also possess the vision of training, because that very knowledge is itself vision.
However, there are those who possess the vision of training but do not possess the knowledge of training.
That is to say, when the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) is present,
at that time there is as yet no untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Therefore,
do all those who have attained the vision of a learner (*śaikṣa-dṛṣṭi*) also possess the wisdom of a learner (*śaikṣa-prajñā*)?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes the wisdom of training, does one also possess the vision of training?
Answer: It is so.
Because the wisdom of one in training (śaikṣa-jñāna) and the insight of one in training (śaikṣa-prajñā) are necessarily co-existent.
If someone possesses the wisdom of one in training, does that person also possess the insight of one in training?
Answer: Whoever possesses the wisdom of one in training also possesses the insight of one in training.
There are cases where one possesses the wisdom of training (śaikṣa-prajñā) but not the knowledge of training (śaikṣa-jñāna).
This refers to when the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti) is present;
for while receptivity has the characteristic of wisdom, it lacks the characteristic of knowledge.

Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: Although it was previously stated in general terms that there are three—view, knowledge, and wisdom—it has not yet been explained specifically what constitutes the view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), what constitutes the knowledge of one beyond training, and what constitutes the wisdom of one beyond training.
The preceding treatise is the fundamental basis upon which this one relies.
Since certain matters therein were not yet explained, they shall now be set forth;
for this reason, this treatise is composed.
What is the vision of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadṛṣṭi*)?

Answer: It is the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣaprajñā*) that is not included within the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*; it is called the right view of one beyond training).
What is the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*)?
Answer: It consists of the eight knowledges of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), namely, the four knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the four subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*).
What is the wisdom of one beyond training?

Answer: The vision of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-darśana*) and the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-jñāna*) are collectively termed "wisdom of one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa-prajñā*), because they necessarily possess the characteristic of the discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*).
Having already explained the characteristics of the intrinsic natures of these three—whether they are mixed or unmixed—we shall now explain them.
Are all views of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) also knowledges (jñāna) of those beyond training?
Answer: All views of those beyond training are also knowledges of those beyond training;
for within the stage of one beyond training, that which is capable of inferential deliberation (abhyūhana) must necessarily be definitive discernment (niścaya).
There is knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna) that is not vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣadṛṣṭi);
namely, the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna). This is because this knowledge has ceased seeking and does not involve inferential deliberation.
Are all visions of one beyond training wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣaprajñā)?
Answer: All vision of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) is also wisdom of those beyond training.
However, there is wisdom of those beyond training that is not vision of those beyond training; namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).

Because this knowledge possesses only two characteristics—discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) and definitive resolution—it follows that all knowledges of those beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*) are wisdoms of those beyond training (*aśaikṣaprajñā*).
Answer: It is so.
If it is asked: Is the wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-prajñā) necessarily the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-jñāna)?
The answer is: It is so.
This is because both wisdom and knowledge of one beyond training pervade all minds that are beyond training and untainted (anāsrava).

What is knowledge that is neither of training nor beyond training?
Answer: Wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses.
Furthermore, the tainted wisdom associated with the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is common to all three types—

What is wisdom that is neither of training nor beyond training?
The answer is: wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses, as well as contaminated wisdom associated with the mental consciousness.
The contaminated wisdoms are all pervasive across all categories of contaminated mental states,
because they all possess the characteristic of discerning and determining the nature of phenomena.
Having already explained the characteristics of these three as being either mixed or unmixed in their intrinsic natures, I shall now explain them further.
Regarding all views that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner:
are they wisdom that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
One should respond by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
Because this view and wisdom differ in their mutual breadth and narrowness:
here, the first phrase refers to the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*),

The second phrase refers to wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth associated with the five consciousnesses;

and the entirety of the other three aggregates.
The unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are also treated as the fourth alternative.
The same fourfold analysis applies to the relationship between vision (*dṛṣṭi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*),

All replied in this manner.
These three categories of meaning should be understood according to their established definitions.
The detailed explanation of accomplishment (*siddhi*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*) should be understood as being analogous to what was taught in the first chapter (*āhnikam*).
If one possesses one certainty, one necessarily possesses the other two;
once any one has been abandoned and full knowledge attained, the same applies to the other two.
Therefore, they inquire of one another.
They all replied in this manner:
"Just as the Great Brahmā has spoken thus:
'I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the All-Powerful One.'"
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Because various wrong views cause sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to give rise to great defiled attachment and lead them to great lack of benefit.
It serves as the great basis for the suffering of birth and death;
that is to say, whoever possesses this will certainly wander through the cycle of rebirth within the three realms,
undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.
Time and again they enter the foul and dark womb,
dwelling between the stomach and the intestines,
constantly oppressed by various impurities.
When emerging from the birth canal, one undergoes intense suffering;
upon being born and falling onto grass and such, it is as if being cut by sharp blades.
Such painful experiences are immeasurable and boundless.
All this arises from not knowing and not seeing the faults of one's inclinations;
wishing to cause them to know these faults so that they may develop revulsion for them, bring them to an end, and extinguish them, I have composed this treatise.
As the Great Brahmā has said:
"I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Sovereign.
I am able to create and produce this world; I am its father.
To which of the five views does this belong?
By seeing which truth is this view abandoned?
In this context, one investigates the various types of views through two matters:
first, by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Second, by way of the antidote.
Regarding the essential nature:
what constitutes the essential nature of these various views?
Regarding the antidotes:
by what are these various views countered?
This is explained in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* within the *Kṣudraka-skandha* and the *Dṛṣṭi-skandha*.
All of these also investigate the various tendencies of views by means of two things:
namely, by way of their intrinsic nature and by way of their antidotes.
As stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*: [insert citation].

To slander this path is subsumed under wrong view.
This is their intrinsic nature, abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It is abandoned when the counteractive wisdom (*pratipakṣajñāna*) arises.

That slander of this path is subsumed under wrong view;
it is of the nature of that [wrong view] and is abandoned by the path of seeing.
It is at the time when the wisdom of the remedial path arises.
One is able to sever such unreal seeking,
and so forth, as explained at length in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
One also investigates views through two matters:
first, by way of their intrinsic nature;
second, by way of their origination.
In the *Brahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, the pursuit of views is investigated through a single factor,
namely, the motivation (*samutthāna*).
In this manner, across these various locations, the pursuit of views should be investigated by means of three factors.
First, by way of intrinsic nature;
second, by way of origination;
third, by way of antidote.
The Venerable Pakṣika said:
"One should not seek to investigate various evil views. Why is this so?"
"Who among the wise would weary themselves by interrogating one who is ignorant, blind with darkness, and fallen into a pit?
The commentary states:
"One should investigate their philosophical view (dṛṣṭi-gati) by means of three matters."
Why is this? Because if one investigates their views through these three matters,
even though they are ordinary beings possessed by the fetters of affliction, [they do not fall into those views].
Yet, for those who have attained the state of a sage (*ārya*), various evil views never manifest again.
Regarding this, the causes and conditions for being a true Dharma-preacher should be explained,
as has already been set forth in detail within the *Saṃyukta-skandha*.
Answer: "I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Sovereign.
To grasp an inferior dharma as superior is subsumed under the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
In this regard, the King Brahmā is not actually the true Brahmā.
He is not the true Mahābrahmā;
he does not possess sovereign mastery over all things,
yet he claims that his own self is truly Brahmā, truly Mahābrahmā.
They have attained mastery over all things;
yet, they regard inferior phenomena as supreme.
Therefore, the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) constitutes their essential nature.
Why is this? Because among all phenomena, Nirvāṇa alone is the most supreme;
and among all sentient beings, only the Noble Buddha is the most supreme.
One who has attained mastery over the mind also attains mastery over phenomena.
Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have not yet attained mastery over all phenomena,
they have already attained mastery over their own minds.
The Brahmā King has not yet attained mastery over these two kinds [of power],
yet he claims to have attained it; because he conceives what is inferior to be superior,
this is subsumed under the view of clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
When the knowledge of suffering arises, it is able to sever such unreal seeking and unreal conceptualization;
because it causes perverted and evil views to be extinguished forever,
it is called "abandoned through the vision of suffering," as it is their antidote.
Because this grasping at views arises in relation to the state of suffering,
it is permanently extinguished when suffering is seen—
just as light frost is immediately dispelled as soon as the sun rises.
"Just as dew on the tip of a blade of grass falls when shaken by the wind,
so too, my claim that 'I am the creator and progenitor of the world'—
that I am their father— is a false cause attributed to what is not the cause."
The adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is subsumed under that which is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
The intent here is to state that all sentient beings experience their internal bodies and external objects as the result of their own respective karma.
Yet that Brahmā king claims he himself can emanate and bring forth [beings],
taking what is not the cause to be the cause.
The grasping at rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) comprises its intrinsic nature;
it is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya), as its antidote, as should be understood from what preceded.
As the Brahmakāyika gods have said:
"This is Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, who has attained mastery.
He is the one who can create and give birth to this world;
he is our father."
To which of the five views does this belong?
By the vision of which truth is this view abandoned?

Answer: This is the view that "this is Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the one who has attained mastery," which takes an inferior phenomenon to be superior; it is categorized as the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Among these, the Brahmakāyika gods hold that Mahābrahmā is Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, who has attained universal mastery;
this is comprised within the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which conceives what is inferior to be superior.
This is their intrinsic nature; it is abandoned through the vision of suffering and is their antidote, as explained in detail previously.
This is capable of creating and producing within the world.

"To be our father" is a grasping at rules and observances that takes what is not a cause to be a cause; it is subsumed under the view of grasping at rules and observances and is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Herein, [it refers to] the Brahmakāyika gods.
The Great Brahmā King clings to the notion that he is the universal creator of the world,
its progenitor, and its father;
this grasping at what is not a cause as a cause is subsumed under the view of adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and it constitutes his inherent nature.
That which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) is its antidote;
this is explained in detail as previously stated.
Question: What is the distinction between this "Brahmā" and the "Great Brahmā" (*mahābrahmā*) who has attained mastery?
The answer regarding this "Brahman" refers to the grasping of the five aggregates of clinging as the fruit of Brahmā,
which one regards as true purity, tranquility, and bliss.
This "Great Brahmā" refers to one who clings to the fruit of the five aggregates of grasping as a Brahmā king,
and who is held to be the most venerable among all that is truly pure, serene, and blissful.
"One who has attained mastery" refers to one who grasps the fruit of the five aggregates of clinging as the Brahmā King;
possessing the most eminent function, they exercise sovereign control over all things.
All such cases are termed "taking the inferior for the superior," meaning that one clings to what is foul and suffering as being truly pure and pleasant,
and because there exists [a notion] of purity, pleasure, and supreme utility.
The "true, blissful, and pure" refers to the truths of cessation and the path.
Both the truths of cessation and the path are truly supreme;
among all phenomena, nirvana is the most excellent.
This is wholesome and eternal because it transcends all other phenomena;
among conditioned phenomena, the Noble Path is supreme because it can eternally transcend the phenomena of birth and death.
Because all latent tendencies (anuśaya) do not increase therein.
As it is said in a verse:
"Nirvāṇa is supreme among all phenomena; The Path is supreme among conditioned things."
Among all sentient beings, the Tathāgata is the most supreme;
among those in the Brahma world, the Brahmā King is the most supreme.
To regard him as supreme would be right view.
How can it be said that this is a wrong view?

Answer: If one were to claim that [the assertion] "supremacy exists only within the Brahma-world" is not a wrong view, it would still be subsumed under wrong views because he claims it to be supreme over all.
Because he considers himself inferior to the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and the higher devas;
furthermore, because he falsely clings to the fruit of the five aggregates of clinging as being identical to true cessation and the Path, it is subsumed under wrong view.
Question: In this context, regarding that which is capable of creating and producing the world, what is the distinction between it and those who are its fathers and so forth?
Answer: Regarding "in the world": [the text continues].
This refers to that which is capable of creating the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world;
that is to say, it is capable of fashioning the receptacle world.
Furthermore, it refers to that which is capable of manifesting through transformation the world of sentient beings as their progenitor;
that is to say, it is capable of producing material things categorized as non-sentient, thereby further clarifying the meaning of "creation.
As for the phrase "he is their father and so forth":
This refers to the meaning of manifesting as the father of all sentient beings.
These attachments are all instances of regarding what is not a cause as a cause;
that is, they cling to the Brahmā King as the result of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
He is able to create and transform all worlds;
yet those sentient beings who constitute the various worlds each arise from their own karma and afflictions.
Regarding those categorized as non-sentient:
they are collectively produced by the dominant power of the karma of all sentient beings.
They are grasped as superior causes for inferior effects.
Since it does not regard what is not a cause as a cause, it is subsumed under the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Both this [clinging] and the aforementioned clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) are deluded regarding the fruit;
because they arise from the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), both are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, because they are drawn forth by the force of the persistent grasping at a self,
they are all established as being abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Thus has the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these wrong views been explained.
And regarding their antidotes and their origination:
how does the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* describe that origination?
As that sūtra states concerning the time when the previous kalpa was destroyed:
Most classes of sentient beings pass away from here and are reborn within the homogeneous group (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
When this kalpa is being formed, a Brahmā palace first arises in space.
At that time, there was a sentient being in the Ābhāsvara Heaven whose lifespan,
karma, and merit were exhausted; he passed away from that celestial realm and was reborn in the Brahma Palace,
where he remained alone for a long time in solemn stillness.
Thereafter, he gives rise to craving and thoughts of companionship, thinking:
"How might other sentient beings be born into my own group to become my companions? One asks:
By what conditions does he give rise to such craving and thoughts?
The Venerable Pakṣika said:
"One should not interrogate those who are ignorant, blind, and stumbling.
Some have made this statement.
For one who goes to that place,
at that time, by the very nature of things (dharmatā), this affection arises;
that is to say, the power of dharmatā is the condition for that birth.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
since beginningless time, sentient beings have delighted in mutual association;
because the power of such habitual practice induces the arising of craving, that craving and recollection arise through the force of causes.
Some say that because he had not yet eliminated his affection for gathering a following—
having previously served as a leader of a community and later being born in that heaven— he still possessed residual habits; by the power of this, that affection was aroused.
Other masters say that beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven come to the Brahma-world and manifest various transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the first dhyāna.
He enjoyed himself together with the Great Brahmā King.
Later, having ceased his emanations, he returned to his own celestial palace.
Thereupon, the Brahmā King yearned for and missed his companion.
Out of such affectionate thoughts, some say:
"The Brahmā King himself arose from the first dhyāna, manifested the bodies of the Brahma-multitude, and took his pleasure among them.
Later, becoming weary, he withdrew his supernormal powers; once the manifested multitude had vanished, [he remained alone]."
He formed this thought:
"Who is able to constantly manifest various emanated bodies?
How may I cause other sentient beings to be born into the same class as myself so that they become my companions?"
Others further say:
"The Brahmā King first arises with the divine eye of his own level and looks sideways at other realms.

Seeing himself surrounded by the Brahma-Purohitas and Brahma-Kāyikas in respectful attendance, he thinks to himself: 'Their physical form, appearance, and majestic radiance are not superior to mine.'"
"He has a retinue, whereas I have none alone;
how can I cause other sentient beings to come to be born in my presence to become my retinue?
That sutra further states:
When the Brahma King gave rise to this thought,
there were other sentient beings among the Ābhāsvara devas whose life-span, karma, and merit had all been exhausted.
They all passed away from that realm and were reborn in the Brahma-world.
Upon seeing them, the Brahmā King thought to himself:
"These sentient beings have been created by me."
Question: For what reason did the Brahmā King give rise to this thought?
Answer: Because that Brahmā King had previously formed a volitional aspiration that those classes of sentient beings should be born through mere recollection.
Therefore, that Brahmā King gave rise to such a thought.
Others say: after Brahmā had manifested the various Brahmā assemblies by means of transformation, [he gave rise to this thought].
Having entered the intermediate meditative absorption and having attained that state, the manifested assembly vanished;
at that time, sentient beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven passed away and were reborn in the Brahma-world.
Later, after the Great Brahmā King arose from his concentration, seeing the Brahma-hosts, he thought to himself:
The assembly previously emanated should have already vanished;
as for these sentient beings now appearing before me,
they must have been produced through the power of my emanation.
Alternatively, it may be that this was produced by a prior thought or aspiration;
thus, Mahābrahmā formed this thought:
"These sentient beings were created by me."
That sutra further states:
"The Brahmā-beings have already formed this thought:
'We have previously seen such sentient beings who were long-lived and remained for a long time.'"
Question: Where did he dwell when he previously saw the Brahmā King? Answer: He dwelt in the Brahma-world when he previously saw the Brahmā King;
however, he does not recall knowing exactly where he saw him.
It is like seeing a certain person at a gathering, yet not remembering the specific location.
After a long period of time, they met again;
although they were awake when they had previously seen one another, they did not remember the location.
Some have said this:
While dwelling in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), he once saw Brahmā.
If that is so, how could he have seen Mahābrahmā as long-lived and long-abiding?
This is because the body in the intermediate state, desiring quickly to seek a place of birth, does not remain for long.
Furthermore, there are those who say that he came from the Ābhāsvara Heaven to the Brahmā Palace for recreation,
and that the Brahmā King had previously seen him at that time.
Question: Since they have already lost the second dhyāna, how can they remember past lives in higher realms?
Answer: Those Brahmā assemblies have become detached from the defilements of their own level.

Furthermore, relying on the second dhyāna, one gives rise to the supernormal power of the knowledge of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānābhijñā*), which enables one to remember events previously witnessed in higher realms.
Question: If this is so, why did he give rise to such a wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) by taking Mahābrahmā as its object?
Answer: Because one falls away from the state of freedom from passion (*vairāgya*), evil views arise once again directed toward the Brahmā King.
Question: Is it not the case that there is no falling away in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
Answer: At the time of the formation of a kalpa, even there, there is falling away.
Other masters say that he recollects past events previously seen by means of innate recollective knowledge (*patisandhi-ñāṇa*). [Objection:
Is it not the case that innate recollective knowledge does not exist in the form realm?
Answer: At the time of the formation of the eon, those in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) also possess the innate knowledge born of recollection (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
Some say that the Brahmā King first entered the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) and remained there for a long period of time.
Those Brahmā hosts, having passed away from the higher realms and been reborn in the Brahma-world,
saw that Mahābrahmā was long-lived, had resided there for a long time, and possessed brilliant majesty;
thus they did not dare to approach him until he had later emerged from meditative concentration.
He commanded the assembly of Brahmās to offer mutual greetings.
Then the assembly of Brahmās said to one another,
"We have previously seen sentient beings such as these who were long-lived and remained for a great length of time."
That sutra further states:
At that time, the assembly of Brahmās had this thought:
"We have all been created by the King of Brahmā."
"He who was born from that is our father.
[Question: For what reason did he give rise to such a thought?
[Answer: He heard the Brahmā King frequently making this statement.
"I am the creator; I am the progenitor;
I am your father. Having heard this, they believed it with deep conviction.
Furthermore, they had previously seen the Brahmā King, who was long-lived and remained for a great duration.
Because he has developed such deep faith and reverence, he gives rise to this thought:
"It is like a king who, though actually devoid of skill or utility,
yet boasts of himself before his ministers and subjects."
"In the past, I possessed great majesty and valor;
personally leading my troops, I subdued powerful enemies.
When my ministers heard of this, there was none among them who did not believe and accept it."
They all said, "We are fortunate to have encountered the Great King;
our friends and the people of the land have all attained peace and happiness.
Furthermore, some spoke thus:
Having heard the Brahmā King speak as previously described,
in order to reach a definitive conclusion, he gave rise to the supernormal power of the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānābhijñā*).
He observed the continuity of his own and others' aggregates (*skandha-saṃtati*) in successive stages, down to the very first moment of consciousness at conception (*pratisaṃdhi-citta*).
Yet they cannot observe the state of their own death that preceded it,
because those of a lower level cannot perceive the objects of a higher realm;
they know that the Great Brahmā, Lord of Men, has long resided there by means of his supernormal power.
Later, when we reflected on this, the thought arose within us:
"From this we know for certain that we have all been emanated by the Brahmā King;
he has arisen from that state, and he is our father."
Therefore, by means of supernormal power, he gave rise to this thought:
"At the time of the formation of the world at the beginning of a kalpa,
how many classes of sentient beings simultaneously give rise to the perverted perceptions and views as previously described?"
Some say that within a small chiliocosm there is one Mahābrahmā, ten individual Brahmās, and a thousand retinues of Brahmās;
within a medium chiliocosm there are a thousand Mahābrahmās, ten thousand individual Brahmās, and a hundred thousand retinues of Brahmās.
Within a trichiliocosm, there are one thousand great Brahmās, ten billion solitary Brahmās, and one hundred billion Brahmā assemblies.
Furthermore, some say that within a small chiliocosm,
there is one great Brahmā, one thousand solitary Brahmās, and ten thousand Brahmā assemblies.
Within a medium chiliocosm, there are one thousand Great Brahmas, ten thousand solitary Brahmas, and one hundred million Brahma-pariṣadyas.
Within a great trichiliocosm, there are ten thousand Great Brahmas, one hundred million solitary Brahmas, and one billion Brahma-pariṣadyas.
There is a discourse on various matters:
within a great trichiliocosm, there are ten million Great Brahmas, one hundred billion Solitary Brahmas, and one hundred thousand billion Brahma-assembly deities.
The commentary states:
It should be stated as follows:
Within a great trichiliocosm, there are ten million Great Brahmās, one hundred billion Solitary Brahmās, and ten billion nayutas of Brahma-assembly deities.
At the time of the kalpa’s initial formation, they simultaneously give rise [to these thoughts], as previously described.
With perverted perceptions and views, they asked:
"In what place does the Great Brahmā King reside?
Where do the Brahma-purohitas and the Brahma-pārṣadyas dwell?"
The masters of the West (Paścātyas) speak as follows:
there are three distinct locations within the stage of the first dhyāna.
First, the abode of the Brahmakāyika devas;
second, the abode of the Brahmapurohita devas;
third, the abode of the Mahābrahmā devas.
This very place is the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
The masters of Kaśmīra state that the stage of the first dhyāna consists of only two locations.
Within the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita), there is a lofty,
superior, and tranquil place, like an excellent grove near a village where the Great Brahmā King constantly resides;
this place is precisely the Intermediate Dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
Question: What is the body size of the Great Brahmā and the others?
Answer: The body size of the Great Brahmā King is one and a half *yojana*;
the body size of the gods of the Brahma-purohita heaven is one *yojana*.
The body size of the gods of the Brahmakāyika heaven is half a yojana.
Question: What is the lifespan of the Mahābrahmā gods and others?
Answer: The lifespan of the Great Brahmā King is one and a half kalpas.
The lifespan of the Brahmā-purohita devas is one kalpa;
the lifespan of the Brahmakāyika devas is half a kalpa.
It should be understood that in this context, forty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpas) are combined to constitute one [great] kalpa.
Question: For what duration does the Great Brahmā Heavenly King dwell alone?
For what duration does he dwell together with the assembly?
And for what duration does he again dwell apart from the assembly?
Some say that he dwells alone for five intermediate kalpas and dwells together with a multitude for five intermediate kalpas.
After five intermediate kalpas, he again parts from the assembly.
Others say that he dwells alone for ten intermediate kalpas.
He dwelt together with the assembly for ten intermediate kalpas;
then, for another ten intermediate kalpas, he lived apart from the assembly.
The commentary states:
It should be stated thus:
he dwelt alone for half an eon,
and he dwelt together with the assembly for half an eon.
After half a kalpa had passed, he again parted from the assembly.
Twenty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa) constitute the measure of a half-kalpa.
The Brahmapurohitas and the Brahmakāyikas pass away and take rebirth by means of a mind belonging to the stage of the Threshold (anāgamya).
The Great Brahmā passes away and takes rebirth by means of a mind of the intermediate dhyāna.
Why is this? The minds at the moment of death and rebirth are associated exclusively with equanimity (*upekṣā*), and equanimity exists only in the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna.
Because it is not a fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*).
Regarding this view that "I accept all things," among the five views (*pañcadṛṣṭi*), under which view is it subsumed?

Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
That is to say, the sūtra states:
The brahmin Dīrghanakha came to where the Buddha was and addressed the Buddha,
saying: "Gautama."
"One should know that I do not tolerate anything," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Although the sūtra makes this statement, [it does not contradict the Abhidharma].
Yet it is not stated which of the five views this [view] is subsumed under,
nor by the vision of which truth (*satya*) this view is abandoned.
The Sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which has not yet been explained shall now be explained;
therefore, this treatise is composed.
Question: For what reason is he called the Brahmin Dīrghanakha?
Answer: Because that brahmin’s body and nails were both long, he was called the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail).
Question: For what reason did he keep his nails so long?
The answer is that their habituation to greed makes it impossible for their karma to be severed.
Some say that because they constantly dwell in the mountains,
although their nails and hair grow long, there is no one to clip or shave them.
Furthermore, there are those who say that while he was a householder, he delighted in practicing stringed and wind instruments;
even after he had left the home life, he still cherished his long nails and therefore did not clip them.
Other masters say that he went forth within the teachings of the non-Buddhists; among the non-Buddhist teachings,
there were those who left their fingernails untrimmed.
Therefore, he is called the brahmin Dīrghanakha.
Herein, his philosophical view is investigated through two matters:
first, by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Second, by means of the antidote;
this should be understood according to the text.
Question: How do these evil views and their origins arise?
The answer is: the venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s going forth under the Buddha is the origin of this [account].
This refers to the brahmin Dīrghanakha,
who was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra and had previously taught the venerable one the scriptures and treatises of the non-Buddhists.
Hearing that Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana had returned to the Buddha and left the household life, he felt deep regret and sorrow, thinking to himself:
"The realm of wisdom is infinite; even if one understands it profoundly and far-reaching, there will ultimately be a point of turning back."

Question: For what reason did the Venerable [Vasubandhu] compose this treatise based on the first two types of knowledge?
Answer: It is because that Venerable One intended it so.
That is to say, the master of the treatise composes his work according to his own intent without contravening the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, one should not find fault with this;
thus the Venerable One composed this treatise in the *Indriyaskandhaka* based on both the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Within the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), the treatise is composed based on the two knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

Furthermore, within the aggregate of faculties (*indriya-skandha*), the treatise is composed based on the four knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path (*duḥkha-samudaya-nirodha-mārga-jñāna*).

Regarding the aggregates of fetters (*saṃyojana-khandha*) and the aggregates of meditative attainments (*samāpatti-khandha*), as well as this present aggregate, the discourse is composed based on eight knowledges (*ñāṇa*).
Regarding the cultivation of knowledge and so forth, the discourse is composed based on ten knowledges.

Likewise, in this aggregate, the Venerable One initially composes the discourse based on two knowledges: the knowledge of others' minds (*parassa-citta-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of past lives (*pubbe-nivāsānussati-ñāṇa*).
Just as a skilled potter first thoroughly prepares a lump of clay and places it upon the wheel,
then fashions vessels and other objects according to his own intention,
so too is the Venerable One.
By means of the wisdoms arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one observes the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*),
thereby severing delusion regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-moha*) and delusion regarding objects of perception (*ālambana-moha*),
and composes treatises according to one's inclination.
Therefore, one should not hold them accountable.

Furthermore, because the first two types of knowledge both pertain to what is acquired through application (*prayoga*) as well as what is acquired through the separation from defilements (*vairāgya-lābhika*),
they are both comprised within that which is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*).
Since both are of a pervasive nature and are both the fruits of the fourfold and fivefold dhyānas,
this treatise is composed specifically based upon them.
Furthermore, the first two types of knowledge both have wisdom and vision as their intrinsic nature,
and both apprehend their objects according to specific limits.
That is to say, the knowledge of others' minds takes only the present as its object.
The knowledge of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna) takes only the past as its object;
therefore, this treatise is composed specifically based upon it.
