Having already attained it and not lost it,
one is able to know the present mental states and mental factors of the desire and form realms within the continuums of others,
or their untainted (anāsrava) mental states and mental factors.
This is called the knowledge of others' minds.
In this context, if it is a wisdom produced through cultivation,
it means that its intrinsic nature consists of the wisdom produced through cultivation.
"Being the fruit of cultivation" means that it is the fruit of the fourfold and fivefold dhyānas.
"Relying on cultivation" refers to...
This means that it is accomplished through repeated cultivation;
"having attained and not lost" means that what has been realized has not been abandoned.
Question: Why are those [factors] that have not yet been attained or have already been lost not mentioned?
Answer: When something that ought to be stated is not stated, one should know that the meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, if it is by means of this knowledge that one is said to be accomplished in the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others,
it is explained here that those who have not yet attained or have already lost the knowledge of others' minds do not possess such a quality.
Therefore, it is not stated that one can know the present mind and mental factors of others' continua within the desire or form realms, or their untainted (anāsrava) mind and mental factors.
This means being able to know, as they truly are, the present-time [states] within the bodies of other sentient beings belonging to the desire or form realms.
Alternatively, it consists of untainted mind and mental factors;
this explains the characteristics of the objects of the knowledge of others' minds.
There is another recension which states:
If wisdom manifests such that one knows, in accordance with reality, that other sentient beings have something they seek,
something they investigate,
and something they grasp.
The mind and its mental concomitants that arise from various conditions—
this is called the knowledge of others' minds.
Regarding this, if such knowledge is currently manifesting:
The phrase "knowing as it truly is" refers to the knowledge of others' minds as they manifest;
this distinguishes it from the knowledge of signs and omens, and so forth.
"Other sentient beings" refers to those who distinguish and know their own minds and mental factors.
"Those who have something to seek" refers to...
This refers to the mind and mental factors of the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
That which possesses investigation (*vicāra*) refers to the mind and mental factors of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
That which is "appropriated" refers to the mind and mental factors of the latter three dhyānas.
Furthermore, some say:
"Having something to seek" indicates the desire realm and the first dhyāna;
"having something to examine" indicates from the desire realm up to the intermediate dhyāna.
The phrase "that which is grasped" indicates [the range] from the desire realm up to the fourth dhyāna; herein,
it demonstrates the capacity for seeking and so forth.
Therefore, dharmas such as form are not the objects of this cognition.
As for that which arises from multiple conditions:
just as the cognizing wisdom itself arises from four conditions.
The objects of knowledge also arise from four conditions.
Regarding "the mind and its mental concomitants," the mind is simply the citta.
All mental factors (caitta-dharma) are called "belonging to the mind" (manas-svaka).
Thus, these are all said to be the objects of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
This knowledge of others' minds should perhaps be described as being of one kind.
That is to say, the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds and the demonstration;
or it should be stated as two:
namely, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
There is bondage and liberation;
there is being fettered and not being fettered.
Alternatively, one should speak of three.
That is to say, there are inferior, middling, and superior grades; or rather,
one should speak of four,
namely, the fruits of the four dhyānas.
Alternatively, one should say there are six,
meaning that both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) each have three categories.
Or, one should say there are eight.
That is to say, each of the four dhyānas has both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) fruits;
alternatively, one should speak of nine,
namely from the lowest-of-the-low grade up to the highest-of-the-high grade.
Alternatively, one should say there are twelve,
meaning that each of the four dhyānas has three grades of fruit.
Or, one should say there are eighteen.
That is to say, there are nine grades each for both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Alternatively, one should speak of twenty-four,
meaning that the fruits of each of the four dhyānas are each either contaminated or uncontaminated.
Each of these, moreover, has three grades;
thus, one might say there are thirty-six,
meaning that each of the four dhyānas has nine grades as its fruit.
Alternatively, one should say there are seventy-two;
that is, each of the four dhyānas has both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) fruits,
and each of these further has nine grades.
If one were to analyze it according to each moment in which it exists, it should be said to be immeasurable and boundless.
Here, however, it is described in general as a single "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*).
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this knowledge of others' minds?
The answer is that its intrinsic nature is wisdom (*prajñā*).
This refers to the intrinsic nature, the self-entity, the substantial body, the specific characteristic, the constituent part, and the fundamental nature of the knowledge of others' minds.
Thus, the intrinsic nature has been explained.
Therefore, it shall now be explained.
Question: Why is it called "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*)?
What is the meaning of "knowledge of others' minds"?
Answer: It is called "knowledge of others' minds" because it knows the minds of others.
Question: Since this also knows the various mental factors (*caitta*) of others, why is it called only "knowledge of others' minds"?
Answer: The intention and application of the various yoga practitioners is to know the minds of others, not their mental factors;
therefore, it is designated only by the name "knowledge of others' minds" (paracittajñāna).
With the mind as the precursor, one also knows the mental factors (caitta).
For example, when a person intends and applies effort solely with the desire to see a king,
upon seeing the king, they also see his ministers and so forth.
Furthermore, the designation of all phenomena (dharmas) relies upon multiple conditions;
that is to say, it may rely upon their intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
or it may rely upon their antidote (pratipakṣa).
Either by way of preparatory application,
or by way of association,
or by way of the basis.
Either by way of the object of focus,
or by way of the mode of activity,
or by way of both the object of focus and the mode of activity.
Regarding those established by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*):
these refer to the five aggregates, the four truths, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and so forth.
Regarding those established by way of antidote (*pratipakṣa*):
This means that dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) serve as the antidotes for the desire realm and the two higher realms, respectively.
As for those established by name according to their preparatory application (prayoga),
these are the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness.
The five types of direct perception, such as the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*),
are established by name based on their association (*saṃprayoga*), as explained in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
What are the factors conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanīya*) and so forth?
This refers to association with pleasant feelings and so forth.
All such cases where a name is established based on its support refer to eye-consciousness and the rest.
Regarding those established by way of their object of observation (*ālambana*),
these refer to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the concentration on signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*), and so forth.
Regarding those established by way of their aspect (*ākāra*):
This refers to the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of its origin.
Because these two have unmixed aspects (*ākāra*) but mixed objects (*ālambana*),
they are designated by name based upon their objects and their aspects.
This refers to the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path.
Because the objects and aspects of these two are entirely unmixed,
there are immeasurable such causes and conditions for establishing their names.
Now, the knowledge of others' minds is designated by its name solely on the basis of its preparatory application (*prayoga*) and not otherwise.
Furthermore, because the mind is preeminent among the factors associated with it (*samprayukta-dharma*),
this knowledge is named after that preeminent factor which it cognizes.
As it is said: "When it is said that the king arrives, it does not mean he is without his ministers.
Furthermore, they are called mental factors (caitta-dharma) because they depend upon the mind;
the mind is the universal ground (mahābhūmika).
Therefore, all mental factors (caitta-dharma) are called "great grounds" (mahābhūmika).
Because they exist [in every state of mind], one speaks only of the mind.
Furthermore, this refers to the stage of the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) when cultivating the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (paracittajñāna-abhijñā).
Because it takes only the mind as its object, it is said that one "knows the mind.
Regarding this knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*),
the contaminated (*sāsrava*) knowledge of others' minds belongs to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The untainted knowledge of others' minds is unconditioned by any realm.
Question: Why is there no knowledge of others' minds in the formless realm?
Answer: Because it is not a suitable field or vessel.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Furthermore, because the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds arises in dependence upon form (*rūpa*),
its stage (*bhūmi*) is restricted solely to the four fundamental dhyānas and not to the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
Because in the formless realms, one cannot manifest the five supernormal powers in those stages.
Question: By the wisdom of which stage can the minds and mental factors of the intermediate dhyāna be known?
Some offer this explanation:
The superior wisdom of the first dhyāna can know it;
furthermore, some say that the inferior wisdom of the second dhyāna can also know it.
The commentary states:
One should say that the three grades of knowledge in the first dhyāna are all capable of knowing. Why is this so?
Because it is subsumed under the first stage (*bhūmi*),
its basis arises solely in dependence upon the bodies of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
As for its mode of activity (*ākāra*):
The untainted knowledge of others' minds operates by taking the four aspects of the Truth of the Path as its object.
As for the tainted knowledge of others' minds:
It functions with an unclear mode of activity.
As for its object:
the knowledge of others' minds in the first dhyāna takes as its object the mind and mental factors belonging to the desire realm and the level of the first dhyāna.
The knowledge of others' minds in the second dhyāna takes as its object the mental states and mental factors of the desire realm and the first two dhyānas.
The knowledge of others' minds in the third dhyāna takes as its object the mental states and mental factors of the desire realm and the first three dhyānas.
The knowledge of others' minds in the fourth dhyāna takes as its object the mind and mental factors of the desire realm and the four dhyāna stages;
there is no knowledge of others' minds capable of knowing the mind and mental factors of the formless realms.
Because that stage is superior,
just as the knowledge of others' minds belonging to the first dhyāna and so forth does not know the mind and mental factors of the second dhyāna and so forth.
Question: Are the mind and mental factors arising in the formless realm that are produced by those born in the desire or form realms objects of the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: They are not objects of that knowledge.
Just as it is with the fruit, so it is with the cause.
As for the applications of mindfulness,
these are the three applications of mindfulness, excluding the application of mindfulness to the body.
The knowledge of others' minds consists of four types of knowledge:

namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). These are collectively designated as the knowledge of others' minds.
That which is associated with samādhi:
untainted knowledge of others' minds is associated with the path of wishlessness;
tainted knowledge of others' minds is not associated with samādhi.
Regarding association with the faculties (*indriya*):
in general, it is said that this is associated with three faculties,
namely, pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The three times refer to the conditions of the three times;
the three times refer to...
The past takes the past as its object;
the present takes the present as its object;
and regarding the future, if it is a dharma that has arisen, it takes the future as its object.
If non-arising dharmas take the three periods of time as their objects—
whether they be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—
they are exclusively wholesome.
Regarding those conditioned by the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral, they take all three as their objects.
As for those that are bound and those that are unbound:
the knowledge of others' minds that is with outflows is bound only to the realm of form.
The untainted knowledge of others' minds is exclusively unbound.
Regarding that which takes as its object both the bound and the unbound:
it takes as its object that which is bound to the desire realm and the form realm, as well as that which is unbound.
Those that are trainee, non-trainee, and neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee pertain to all three types.
Those that take as their object the trainee, the non-trainee, and the neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee [pertain to all three types].
It has three types of objects:
those abandoned by seeing, those abandoned by cultivation, and those not abandoned.
The knowledge of others' minds that is contaminated is abandoned only by cultivation.
The untainted knowledge of others' minds is uninterrupted;
that which takes as its object what is abandoned by seeing, what is abandoned by cultivation, and what is uninterrupted,
takes all three types as its objects.
Regarding "conditioned by names and conditioned by meanings":
it is conditioned only by meanings.
Regarding "conditioned by those within one's own or another's continuum, or by those not in a continuum": [it refers to the objects of cognition].
Those acquired through application and through detachment from defilements, taking only the mental continuums of others as their object,
are those acquired through both application and detachment from defilements.
Regarding those acquired through detachment from defilement:
this refers to what is acquired by one in the first dhyāna at the time of becoming detached from the defilements of the desire realm,
and so on, up to what is acquired by one in the fourth dhyāna at the time of becoming detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
Alternatively, it may also be acquired through cultivation when one is free from the defilements of one's own stage or a higher stage.
That which is acquired through preparatory effort refers to what is obtained at the time of practicing superior preparatory application.
And they bring it forth by initiating the preparatory application (*prayoga*):
that is to say, the śrāvakas do so through middling or superior application,
while the pratyekabuddhas do so only through inferior application.
The Buddha does not bring [these] into manifestation through applied effort (*prayoga*).
As for those who have already attained or those who have never before attained them:
these include all noble ones (*ārya*) as well as ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) within the internal Dharma.
All [these] are categorized as both previously acquired and not yet acquired.
External dharmas and those of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are exclusively previously acquired.
Question: What is the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for cultivating the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?
Answer: The *Prajñapti-śāstra* states that a beginner who has already attained mastery over worldly concentration repeatedly brings it forth into manifestation.
Having caused [the mind] to become increasingly clear and sharp, one first carefully observes the characteristics of one's own body and mind;
when such signs appear in the body, [one should recognize them].
At that time, such a mental image arises;
whenever one gives rise to such a mental image within oneself,
at that time such a physical manifestation appears in the body.
Having personally examined and observed the characteristics of one's own body and mind,
one next examines and observes the characteristics of the bodies and minds of others.
At whatever time such characteristics appear in the body, [one observes them].
At that time, one gives rise to such a mental state characterized by these signs;
and when another person gives rise to such a mental state,
then such signs appear upon one's own body.
Having carefully observed the characteristics of another’s body and mind,
one next contemplates exclusively their mental states and mental factors,
reflecting as follows:
I should observe those mental states and mental factors: what do they seek,
and what do they examine?
What is it that is grasped?
Having reflected thus, one contemplates exclusively the distinctions in the characteristics of the preceding and succeeding moments of that mental continuum.
One contemplates those mental characteristics until they become thoroughly proficient.
This is called the fulfillment of the preparatory application for the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
The *Saṃgītiparyāya* states as follows:
"What is the preparatory application for the knowledge of others' minds?"
This refers to the discerning observation of the five aggregates of clinging as being characterized by suffering,
impermanence, emptiness, and non-self; through such distinct modes of wisdom and practice,
one is gradually able to induce the arising of untainted (anāsrava) knowledge.
Skillfully knowing the minds of others is called the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Question: Since the untainted knowledge of others' minds can take the Four Noble Truths as its object, why is it said here that it only takes the truth of suffering as its object?
The answer is that one should also state that it takes the other three truths as its object;
however, because they are not mentioned, one should know that there is an omission.
Furthermore, in this context, only the initial entry into the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) is being discussed.
It is only said that the knowledge of suffering takes [suffering] as its object, and not that it takes others as its object;
yet, at a later stage in the continuity [of consciousness], it also takes other knowledges as its objects.
Question: What is the difference between the preparatory application (*prayoga*) described in the earlier *Prajñapti-śāstra* and that described in the later *Saṃgīti-paryāya*?

The answer is: the former refers to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the knowledge of others' minds with outflows (*sāsrava*), while the latter refers to the preparatory stage for the knowledge of others' minds without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, the former refers to the preparatory stage for the knowledge of others' minds [in general].
It is not supreme, excellent, luminous, or pure. Later,
the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the knowledge of others' minds is said to be supreme,
excellent, luminous, and pure.
However, although the knowledge of others' minds arises by taking form as its object during the stage of preparatory application,
it no longer takes form as its object at the time of its full accomplishment. Why is this so?
First, one contemplates coarse phenomena in order to enter into the subtle.
Furthermore, although the knowledge of others' minds takes one's own continuum as its object during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*),
at the time of its full accomplishment, it takes only the continuum of another as its object.
Why is this so? Because that which takes itself as its object is not called "knowledge of others' minds.
Furthermore, knowledge of others' minds takes only the minds of others as its object.
It does not take as its object the focal point or mode of activity of another's mind.
If it were to take as its object the focal point or mode of activity of another's mind,
it would instead be taking its own mind as its object and would therefore not be the "knowledge of others' minds."
Because one's own mind is both the object of cognition (*ālambana*) and the subjective aspect (*ākāra*) of that [cognition].
Question: If the eye does not see form, can it know another’s mind?
Answer: It can know it.
Because one hears sounds with the ear.
Question: If one does not see forms but hears sounds, can one know the minds of others?
Answer: One can know them.
Because of the odors of fragrance and stench in the nose.
Question: If one does not see forms, hear sounds, or smell odors, can one still know the minds of others?
Answer: It can know, because the tongue tastes flavors.
Question: If one does not see forms, hear sounds, smell odors, or taste flavors, [how can it know]?
"Is it possible to know the minds of others?
"Yes, it is possible to know them,
because one perceives contact through the body."
Question: If one does not see forms, hear sounds, smell odors, taste flavors, or feel tangibles, can one still know the minds of others?
Regarding this, some say as follows:
They cannot know it. Why is this?
Because the knowledge of others' minds arises dependent upon form as its causal condition.
The commentary states:
One should say that at the time of initial arousal, it cannot be known.
Those who have already attained perfection can know [the minds of others] even without taking form as an object.
There are fifteen types of previously acquired tainted mental states and mental factors that constitute the objects to be apprehended by the knowledge of others' minds.
That is to say, in the desire realm and the four dhyānas,
there are respectively three grades— lower, middle, and upper— of mind and mental factors.
There are twelve types of previously acquired knowledge of others' minds that are with outflows (sāsrava).
This means that each of the four dhyānas possesses three grades—lower, middle, and upper—of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
Among these, there is the lower grade of the impure (sāsrava) knowledge of others' minds previously obtained in the first dhyāna.
One who has previously experienced middling defiled mental states and their associated mental factors within the three grades of the desire realm and the lower grade of the first dhyāna,

is able to know the three grades of the desire realm and both the lower and middling grades of the first dhyāna among those previously experienced defiled mental states and their associated mental factors.
Regarding the superior grade:
one is able to know the previously acquired contaminated mental states and mental factors of the desire realm and the first dhyāna, each in their three grades.
In this manner, proceeding successively, one knows up to the previously acquired superior-grade contaminated knowledge of others' minds of the fourth dhyāna.
One can know the previously acquired contaminated mental states and mental factors of three grades each within the desire realm and the four dhyānas;
just as the previously acquired twelve types of knowledge of others' minds know fifteen types of previously acquired contaminated mental states and mental factors.

The previously unattained twelve types of knowledge of others' minds with outflows (sāsrava) know fifteen types; the same applies to the previously unattained outflow-possessing mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma).
As for the outflow-free (anāsrava) mind and mental factors, there are twelve types.
This is the object to be apprehended by the knowledge of others' minds.
The untainted knowledge of others' minds also consists of twelve types;
that is, there are three grades for each of the four dhyānas.

Among these, the inferior grade of untainted knowledge of others' minds belonging to the second dhyāna can know only the inferior grades of untainted mind and mental factors of the first and second dhyānas respectively.
The middling type is able to know the two grades— lower and middling— of untainted mind and mental factors in both the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna.
The superior type...
One is able to know the three grades of untainted (anāsrava) minds and mental factors of the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna respectively;
thus proceeding successively until one knows the superior grade of untainted knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) up to the fourth dhyāna.
One is able to know the three grades of untainted mind and mental factors of each of the four dhyānas.

Question: Why is it that the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), when it is tainted and belongs to a higher stage, lower stage, or middle grade, is simultaneously able to know the three grades of tainted mind and mental factors belonging to a lower stage?
Does the superior-inferior and middle-grade untainted knowledge of others' minds not know the middle-superior grade of untainted mind and mental factors belonging to a lower stage?
Answer: Tainted and untainted mind and mental factors are established as distinct categories.
This means that contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are established based on the continuity (*saṃtāna*).
Within the continuity of a single body, one accomplishes the three categories of contaminated minds and mental factors.
The untainted (anāsrava) mind and mental factors are established according to their respective categories (pakṣa) based on the faculties.
Within a single continuum of existence, one does not accomplish two categories of untainted mind and mental factors, much less three.
Since their establishments are distinct, we know they are different.
There are fourteen types of resultant minds and mental factors that are all objects to be apprehended by the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
That is to say, the desire realm and the first dhyāna each have the fruits of all four dhyānas;
the second dhyāna has the fruits of the latter three dhyānas;
and the third dhyāna has the fruits of the latter two dhyānas.
The fourth dhyāna possesses only the result of the fourth dhyāna.

Question: Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) of the first dhyāna, [what is its relationship] to the mind and mental factors of the desire realm and the results of the four dhyānas?
How many kinds can it know?
Some say that it can know four kinds.
Why is this? Because all of them are subsumed within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, there are those who say:
One can only know the fruit of the first dhyāna and not the other three.
Why is this? Because it is just as one does not know the cause; the same applies to the fruit.
All knowledges of others' minds [differ] according to the distinctions of stages and faculties.
Regarding the stage of the *pudgala*,
one cannot know the mental states and mental factors;
as for the stage of the earth, one cannot know the mental states and mental factors therein.
That is to say, the knowledge of others' minds belonging to the first dhyāna cannot know the mental states and mental factors of the second dhyāna and above;
this applies likewise up to the knowledge of others' minds belonging to the third dhyāna.
One cannot know the mental states and mental factors of the fourth dhyāna and above;
regarding the inability to know the mental states and mental factors across different levels of faculties,
this refers to the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) in those of dull faculties.
One cannot know the mental states and mental factors of those with sharp faculties;
regarding the inability to know the mental states and mental factors of a person who has transcended them,
this refers to the knowledge of others' minds belonging to those still in training (śaikṣa).
One cannot know the mind and mental factors of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Question: Do all instances of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) belonging to those beyond training know all the mind and mental factors of those still in training (śaikṣa)?
Answer: No. That is to say, the knowledge of others' minds belonging to one liberated by occasion cannot know the mind and mental factors of one who has attained through vision.
Even the knowledge of others' minds attained through vision cannot know the mind and mental factors of one liberated by occasion. Why is this so?

The knowledge of others' minds belonging to one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) does not know the minds and mental factors of one attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), because it transcends them in terms of faculties (*indriya*). Furthermore, it does not know [the minds of] those attained through vision,
because it transcends them in terms of the person (*pudgala*) relative to the minds and mental factors of one liberated by occasion.
Question: Regarding the knowledge of others' minds belonging to a higher stage by one in training (śaikṣa),
and the knowledge of others' minds belonging to a lower stage by one beyond training (aśaikṣa)—
do these two enable mutual cognition?
Answer: No. Why is this?
Because there is the knowledge of others' minds belonging to a higher stage for those in training (śaikṣa).
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds belonging to a lower stage within the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa),
it does not know [the minds of those] higher because of the distinction of the person (pudgala).
This refers to the knowledge of others' minds belonging to a lower stage within the state of no-more-learning.
Because it transcends the stage of the knowledge of others' minds belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and the higher stages, [the latter] does not know [the former].
Question: Regarding the knowledge of others' minds on the higher stages of a Śrāvaka and the knowledge of others' minds on the lower stages of a Tathāgata...
Do these two know each other?
Answer: No. Why is this so?

The knowledge of others' minds belonging to a higher stage of a śrāvaka does not know the knowledge of others' minds belonging to a lower stage of a Tathāgata, because it is surpassed by the faculty [of the Tathāgata].
The knowledge of others' minds belonging to a lower stage of a Tathāgata...
Because they have transcended the stage of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) belonging to the higher stages of the Śrāvakas, [the Śrāvakas] do not know [it].
Regarding Pratyekabuddhas in relation to other vehicles, it should be explained according to the same principle as above.
As for the Tathāgata’s untainted (*anāsrava*) mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), [they are not known by others].

Furthermore, never-before-attained contaminated mental states and their associated mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) are not objects currently apprehended by the knowledge of others' minds; rather,
they are previously attained contaminated mental states and their associated mental factors.
If the Buddha wishes for others to know something, they shall know it immediately.
That is to say, if the Buddha wishes for those of dull faculties to know his mind,
yet not those of sharp faculties, then even Sarpadāsa and others will know the Buddha’s mind.
Śāriputra and the others were all unable to know it.
If one wishes to cause those in the animal realm and so forth to know my mind,
then even those in the animal realm and so forth— rather than those in the realms of humans or devas— will likewise know the Buddha’s mind.
Neither humans nor those in the heavenly realms can know it.
How is this known to be so?
Because it is stated in the sūtras.
It is said in a sutra:
At one time the Buddha was staying at the Kalandakanivāpa, on the side of the Monkey Pond, in the Multi-storied Hall near Vaiśālī.
At that time, the bhikṣus placed both the World-Honored One’s bowl and their own bowls in an exposed location.
A monkey descended from a śāla tree and approached the place where the bowls were kept.
At that time, the community of bhikṣus, fearing it would damage the bowls, vied with one another to drive it away.
The Buddha said, "You should not drive it away."
He had a specific intention which shall be understood momentarily.
Then that monkey took the World-Honored One’s bowl,
slowly climbed back up the tree, and filled it with flowing honey.
He descended slowly and respectfully offered it to the World-Honored One;
however, because there were insects within it, the World-Honored One did not accept it.
The Buddha then gave rise to a state of mind associated with outflows (*sāsrava-cittavarga*) that caused those insects to depart.
The monkey immediately understood and withdrew to a single spot;
having selected and removed the insects, he returned to offer them to the World-Honored One.
Because they had not yet been purified, the Buddha again did not accept them.
The Buddha arose from his state with previously attained outflow-tainted mental states and had him sprinkle water everywhere to purify the area;
the monkey immediately understood and withdrew to stand at one side.
Having purified it with water, he offered it back to the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, out of compassion, the World-Honored One accepted it;
the monkey was filled with immeasurable joy and leaped for delight.
While dancing, he stumbled backward and fell into a pit where he died;
by virtue of this meritorious karma, he was reborn among human beings.
Upon reaching adulthood, he left the household life and diligently cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Before long, he attained the fruit of arhatship.
The world collectively named him the Elder Honey-Offerer (Madhupindika).
As for the Venerable One’s power of debate, it arose from those very causes and conditions.
He praised the Buddha with these sublime verses:
"O Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Gods and Men, you are able to cause even those in the evil realms to know the mind.
When the mind abides in the profound and subtle meditative concentration, even gods and humans cannot comprehend it."
The Buddha’s knowledge of others’ minds can know three paths;
the Pratyekabuddha’s knowledge of others’ minds can know two paths;
and the Śrāvaka’s knowledge of others’ minds can know one path.
Question: Does a Buddha obtain the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) that takes a Buddha as its object? Some say he does not. Why is this so?
Because two Tathāgatas do not appear in the world simultaneously.
Furthermore, there is another explanation that [the Buddha] attains it;
this refers to the capacity for objective cognition, not its actual manifestation.
Question: Does a solitary realizer (pratyekabuddha) who has attained awakening alone possess the knowledge of the minds of other solitary realizers?
Answer: One who is like a rhinoceros horn can only be known by a Buddha.
A group-dwelling solitary realizer definitely possesses the knowledge of the minds of other solitary realizers.
This explains both the capacity to take [an object] as its cognitive focus (*ālambana*) and the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*).
Śrāvakas also certainly attain the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) directed toward other Śrāvakas;
this likewise explains both the capacity to take [an object] as its cognitive focus and the actual manifestation.
An ordinary person (pṛthagjana) definitely attains the knowledge of others' minds directed toward an ordinary person,
as stated by the multitude, the pratyekabuddhas,
and the śrāvakas. Some, however, say this:
The rhinoceros-horn-like pratyekabuddha also definitely attains the knowledge of the minds of others that takes a rhinoceros-horn-like pratyekabuddha as its object;
it is said to be able to take such an object and is said to be manifest.
This is because there is no logical reason to preclude the appearance of rhinoceros-horn-like pratyekabuddhas in other worlds.
Only the uncontaminated mind and mental factors of a Buddha,
as well as contaminated mind and mental factors never previously attained,
certainly cannot be taken as objects by the knowledge of others' minds when they are currently arising.
All mind and mental factors of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are certainly not objects of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*),
because they do not fall within its domain.
