Section Three of the Third Chapter on the Aggregate of Wisdom (*Jñānaskandha*), Sub-section Three of the Third Part on the Knowledge of Others' Minds (*Paracittajñāna-nirdeśa*): Among the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*) there are also birthplaces where beings possess the wisdom acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-jñāna*) capable of knowing the minds of others and so forth.
How is this known to be so?
Once, there was a woman who left her child in one place while she attended to other affairs;
at that time, a wolf seized the child and carried him away.
Those standing nearby pursued him, speaking these words to the wolf:
"For what reason are you now taking another's child away?
The wolf then replied:
Throughout five hundred past lifetimes, her mother constantly harmed my son;
likewise, throughout five hundred past lifetimes, I also constantly harmed her son.
This cycle of mutual enmity has not ceased even until now.
"If he can renounce it, I shall likewise renounce it.
A bystander then said to the child's mother,
"If you cherish your son, you should renounce your heart of enmity."
The woman replied, "I have already abandoned him.
The wolf observed her intention and saw that she did not truly abandon her resentment;
she merely spoke falsely of having abandoned him out of fear that he would harm her child.
He then killed his son, abandoned him, and departed.
[The interlocutor] asks: "At what time do animals come to know the minds of others?
[The respondent] answers: "They are able to know them throughout all stages—beginning, middle, and end."
Question: With what kind of mind does one who abides therein know the minds of others and so forth—
is it wholesome or defiled?
Is it unobscured-neutral?
Answer: All three types can know it.
Question: Does one abide in the mental consciousness (manovijñāna)?
Question: Is it while abiding in the five consciousnesses that one knows the minds of others and so forth?
Answer: Only while abiding in the mental consciousness.
Question: Is it by means of a mind abiding in the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*),
or a mind abiding in the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*),
or a mind arisen from maturation (*vipākaja*) that one knows the minds of others and so forth?
Answer: All three types can know it,
because that [state] also involves the manifestation of a mind pertaining to the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*),
and because the mind, mental faculty, and consciousness born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are also present therein.
It is not as in the hells, where one definitely does not experience the ripening of virtuous karma;
for among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), there are also those born in places who possess knowledge gained through birth, such as the knowledge of others' minds.
How is this known to be so?
In the past, there was a woman who had been possessed by a ghost; she became so emaciated that she was on the verge of death.
A mantra-master asked the ghost, "Why are you now tormenting this woman?"
The ghost then replied,
"In five hundred past lives, this woman constantly took my life;
I, too, in five hundred past lives, constantly took her life."
"Enmity begets enmity; even now it has not ceased.
If he can relinquish it, I too shall relinquish it.
The incantation master then replied to that woman:
"If you cherish your life, you must abandon your heart of enmity.
The woman replied, "I have already abandoned it.
The ghost observed her intention and saw that she did not abandon her enmity at all.
Fearing that his life might not be spared, [the man] falsely claimed he had already renounced [the world].
Consequently, [the ghost] took his life and departed. [The interlocutor] asks:
At what point in the realm of ghosts does one come to know the minds of others and so forth?
Answer: One is able to know [the minds of others] throughout all stages—the initial, middle, and final.
Question: Abiding in what state of mind does one know the minds of others and so forth?
Is it a wholesome state?
Is it defiled?
Or is it unobscured-neutral?
Answer: It can know all three types.
Question: Does one know the minds of others and so forth while abiding in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), or while abiding in the five sensory consciousnesses?
Answer: Only while abiding in the mental consciousness.
Question: Is it by means of a mind abiding in the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*),
a mind abiding in the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*),
or a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) that one knows the minds of others and so forth?
Answer: All three types are capable of knowing.
As explained regarding the animal realm, there are also those in the heavenly realm who possess knowledge acquired at birth, such as the knowledge of others' minds.
However, because they are subtle, they are not explained separately.
The rest is as extensively explained in the realms of animals and hungry ghosts.
Within the human realm, there is no acquisition of knowledge at birth, nor the knowledge of others' minds, and so forth.
Why is this? Because they are not vessels for the field.
There is a superior perception of their marks.

Because it is obscured and impaired by the knowledge derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) and so forth, and because it is eclipsed by the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (paracittajñāna-abhijñā), the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna), and so forth.
Question: Who, through the knowledge acquired at birth (upapattipratilambhika-jñāna), knows the minds of how many realms of existence (gati)?
Some say that each knows only for themselves. Others say:
Those in hell know only hell;
those in the animal realm know two;
those in the hungry ghost realm know three.
The gods' realm knows five [types of knowledge].
As the *Prajñapti-śāstra* states regarding the nāga king Elāpattra Suvastu’s knowledge of the minds of the gods:
this is knowledge through the cognition of signs (*nimitta-jñāna*), not knowledge acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-jñāna*).
The commentary states:
It should be said that one attains knowledge of birth-places within the four realms of existence.
Each knows the five destinies;
this does not contradict the principle.
Question: Is there also a type of innate knowledge (*patisandhiñāṇa*) within the human destiny?
One should be able to know the minds of others and so forth;
why, then, is this not mentioned?
The answer is: when something ought to be stated but is not, [it is because it is unnecessary].
One should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, it is not mentioned because it is rare;
that is to say, because those who attain this wisdom within the human realm are extremely few, it is not spoken of.

Some say that because the category of knowledge arising from the nature of mindfulness (*prakṛti-smṛtyutpāda-jñāna*) cannot directly know the minds and mental factors of others, it is not said to possess the knowledge of others' minds; yet, it does indeed directly know the minds and mental factors of others.
That is to say, it is wisdom produced through cultivation,
which is the basis for the fruit of cultivation, and which,
once attained through cultivation, is not lost.
One is able to directly know the present mental states and mental factors of others belonging to the desire realm or the form realm,
or their untainted (anāsrava) mental states and mental factors.
This is the supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds in the present, as explained in detail previously.
There is that which is neither the knowledge of others' minds nor the direct knowledge of the minds and mental factors of others;
this refers to all cases except those previously mentioned.
"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to what is designated by such names, and so forth, as explained at length.
This refers to all [knowledges] within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), with the exception of the supernormal knowledge of others' minds regarding the three times,
and the exception of the knowledge acquired through birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-jñāna*)— which arises from observing signs or hearing speech—
that is capable of directly knowing the minds and mental factors of others.
All other factors of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the entirety of the other four aggregates, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) constitute the fourth alternative.
Do all knowledges of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) necessarily involve the present recollection and knowledge of all past-life events?
It is agreed that there are four lines [of verse].
Herein, the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) pertains to the three periods of time;
however, when one currently recollects and knows various events of past lives, it refers only to the present.
However, since this encompasses both the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) and that which is not the knowledge of recollecting past lives,
there are four logical possibilities (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*),
which does not involve the direct recollection of past events;
that is to say, it is the knowledge of recollecting past lives regarding the past and the future.
This possesses the characteristic of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*),
yet it lacks the function of presently recollecting and knowing those past events,
because the activities of all that is past have already ceased.
Because that which is future has not yet performed its function,
there is the present recollection and knowledge of various past lives,
yet this is not the "knowledge of recollecting past lives" (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
That is to say, there is one who has attained the knowledge born of the recollection of one's original nature,
or has attained such knowledge acquired at birth,
and is thus able to clearly recollect and know the events of various former existences.
The knowledge of recollecting past lives through the arising of innate mindfulness exists only among the human realm;
it does not exist in the other four realms because they lack this specific knowledge.
As for the knowledge acquired at birth that enables one to recollect various past lives:
This refers to their existence in the hells and so forth.
What is the nature of these matters?
First, regarding the hells, it is as stated in the Sūtras.
The sentient beings in hell say to one another, "How strange that we have deceived ourselves!
In the past, we heard śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas speak of the faults and afflictions of sensual desires."
"You should sever that which leads to terrifying events in the future;
yet though we heard this, we did not believe or act upon it.
Now, because of our desires, we undergo this intense suffering."
Question: At what time does he recollect his past lives?
Answer: Initially, when born in hell, before he has yet experienced suffering.
Once he has begun to experience suffering, he is no longer able to recollect even the events that ceased immediately prior.
How much more so for an event long extinguished—how can it be recollected?
Question: Abiding in what state of mind does one recollect past lives?
Answer: One is able to recollect while abiding in a wholesome, afflicted, or non-obscured neutral state of mind.
Among the six consciousnesses, he dwells solely in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
among the three types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*), he dwells solely in the deportment (*airyāpathika*).
Question: Regarding the knowledge acquired at birth (*upapattilābhajñāna*) in that realm, how many lifetimes can he recollect and know? Answer: He is able to recollect and know one lifetime.
This refers to those who have passed away from that state and are born here.
Some say that they can even know up to five hundred lifetimes.
Regarding those in the animal realm who possess the knowledge acquired at birth and are able to recollect and know their past lives,
as it is said in the Sūtra:
There was a dog with a conch-like voice who had formerly been a brahmin named Dātika.
Remembering his past lives, he caused his son to ascend the seat, eat rice, and display treasures.
They all followed his words.
When asked at what time they remembered their past lives,
they replied that they were able to recollect and know them during the initial, middle, and final stages.
Question: Abiding in what state of mind does one recollect past lives?

Answer: One is able to recollect and know them while abiding in states that are wholesome, defiled, or non-obscured-neutral; among the six consciousnesses, this occurs only while abiding in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Among the three types of neutral states, the state of abiding (sthiti) encompasses all three.
Question: Regarding the knowledge acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-jñāna*), how many lifetimes can one recollect and know?
Some offer this explanation:
One remembers only a single lifetime—
that is, one who has passed away from that [previous] life and been reborn here.
The critique states:
One should say that it is capable of recollecting many lifetimes,
just as a wolf remembers the events of five hundred births. Furthermore,
in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), there is also the acquisition of knowledge pertaining to one's place of birth.
Regarding the ability to manifest the recollection of past lives,
as stated in a gāthā:
"In the past, I accumulated treasures, both by means of the Dharma and by unrighteous means."
"He now enjoys wealth and happiness, while I alone suffer poverty and misery.
When asked at what time he remembered his past lives,
he replied that he was able to recollect and know them throughout the initial, middle, and final stages.
Question: Abiding in what kind of mind does one recollect past lives?
Answer: One is able to recollect and know them while abiding in any of the wholesome, afflicted, or non-obscured neutral states.
Among the six consciousnesses, this occurs only while abiding in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Among the three types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*), the state of abiding (*sthiti*) pertains to all three.
Question: Regarding the knowledge acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-jñāna*), how many lifetimes can one recollect and know?
Some say as follows:
They remember only one lifetime—that is, they recall passing away from that place and being reborn here. Regarding this, the evaluation states:
one should speak thus.
One can remember many lifetimes;
for example, a hungry ghost remembers the events of five hundred lifetimes.
Among the celestial realms (*deva-gati*), there is likewise the attainment of knowledge (*jñāna*) upon birth.
Regarding the ability to manifest and recollect past lives,
as stated in a gāthā:
"I offered the Jeta Grove, and thus received the dwelling of the Great Dharma King."
Because the noble Sangha partakes [of these offerings], my heart rejoices.
He was asked: "At what time do you recollect past lives?
He replied: "I am able to recollect and know them at all stages—the beginning, the middle, and the end."
Question: Abiding in what kind of mind does one recollect past lives?
Answer: One is able to recollect and know them while abiding in wholesome, defiled, or non-obscured neutral states.
Among the six consciousnesses, this occurs only while abiding in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Among the three types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*), the state of abiding (*sthiti*) encompasses all three.
Question: Regarding the knowledge acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-jñāna*), how many lifetimes can one recollect and know?
Some offer this explanation:
One remembers only a single lifetime—
that is, one who has passed away from that [previous] life and been reborn here.
The critique states:
It should be stated thus:
one is able to recollect many lifetimes;
among the realms of human beings, there is no place where one does not attain the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
Because it is not a vessel for the [wholesome] fields;
because it is impaired and obscured by innate mindfulness, the knowledge of others' minds, and so forth;
and because of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives.
Furthermore, because it is eclipsed by the knowledge of aspirations (*praṇidhijñāna*) and so forth,
there is also the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), which likewise directly recollects and knows various events of former existences;
that is to say, such knowledge is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
This is the basis for the fruit of cultivation.
Having cultivated it, one attains it and does not lose it;
one is able to manifest recollection and knowledge of various past lives, including their diverse characteristics, appearances, and spoken words.
This is the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives in the present;
it is explained in detail as previously stated.
There are, however, those who possess neither the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives nor the present recollection of various past events.
This means excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
"Characteristics" refers to that which is named, and so forth, as explained at length;

specifically, it excludes from within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānābhijñā*) throughout the three periods of time.
And excluding the innate wisdom born of mindfulness (*prakṛtijāti-smṛtijñāna*) and the wisdom acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhikajñāna*),
which are capable of recollecting and knowing past lives.

The remaining factors of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the entirety of the other four aggregates, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) constitute the fourth alternative.
Does all knowledge of the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) know the mental continuum of others' past aggregates, bases, and elements?
It shall be explained in four statements.
Herein, the first statement refers to the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) directed toward one's own continuum.
The second statement refers to the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) directed toward the continua of others.
And the preparatory application for the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
The third phrase refers to the knowledge of recollecting past lives that takes the mental continuum of others as its object.
The fourth phrase refers to the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) that takes one’s own mental continuum as its object.
And the preparatory application for the knowledge of past lives;
this is the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
There is the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
It is not the knowledge of the mental continuum of another’s past aggregates, bases,
and elements; rather, it is that wisdom which is produced by cultivation and serves as the basis for the fruit of cultivation.
Having cultivated it, one attains it and does not lose it.
One knows the mental continuity of one's own past aggregates, bases, and elements in previous lives;
this is precisely the knowledge of recollecting former abodes with respect to one's own continuity.
Because it takes as its object the events of one's own past lives,
there exists a knowledge of the mental continuum of others' past aggregates, bases, and elements; however,
this is not the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
That is to say, it is wisdom produced through cultivation,
which is the basis for the fruit of cultivation, and which,
once attained through cultivation, is not lost.
To know the mental continuum of another’s past aggregates,
bases, and elements is the preparatory stage for the knowledge of aspirations regarding the mental continua of others and the knowledge of past lives.
Because one takes as an object the present arising of another's past events,
there is the knowledge of recollecting former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), which also knows the mental continuum of another's past aggregates, bases, and elements;
that is to say, this knowledge is produced through cultivation.
This is the basis for the fruit of cultivation;
having cultivated it, one attains it and does not lose it.
One knows the mental continuum of others' past aggregates, bases, and elements from previous lives.
This is precisely the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) that takes the mental continuum of another as its object,
because it takes the events of the past lives of others as its object. There is, however,
a knowledge of recollecting past lives that does not take [the continuum of another] as its object.
Nor does it know the mental continuum of another’s past aggregates, bases, and elements;
rather, if this knowledge is produced by cultivation,
it is the result of that cultivation and its basis.
Having cultivated it, one attains it and does not lose it.
One knows that from this point onward, the mind-continuum of the past aggregates, bases, and elements arises;
this is precisely the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) taking one's own continuum as its object.
Furthermore, because the preparatory application for the knowledge of recollecting past lives takes as its object events from previous births that occurred since this [present] life,
among these, the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) takes only this life as its object.
Regarding past conditioned phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*),
the knowledge of recollecting former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) takes as its object only those past conditioned phenomena belonging to previous births.
This is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the knowledge of recollecting former abodes.
Furthermore, it is only by taking this as an object that past conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) arise;
however, while the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) universally takes all three periods of time as its objects,
here we take only that which takes this as an object for the arising of past conditioned phenomena.
Question: Regarding the previously mentioned "innate wisdom born of recollection" (prakṛti-smṛtyupasthāna-jñāna), what constitutes its intrinsic nature (svabhāva)?
Answer: Wisdom (prajñā) constitutes its intrinsic nature.
This is called the nature of the wisdom born of mindfulness (*dharmasthitijñāna*). Its self-nature, substance, essence, characteristics, and constituent parts have already been explained;
its cause shall now be discussed.
Question: Why is it called "the wisdom born of innate mindfulness" (*prakṛti-smṛtyutpādajñāna*)?
What is the meaning of "the wisdom born of innate mindfulness"?
Answer: "Born" refers to the various contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) of previous lives.
"Knowledge" refers to the cognition that arises capable of knowing that [object].
"Mindfulness" refers to the superior mindfulness that arises simultaneously with this knowledge.
The term "intrinsic nature" (prakṛti) serves to distinguish it from that which is acquired through cultivation.
That is to say, because the wisdom of the original nature (prakṛti-jñāna) knows all contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) of past lives through the power of superior mindfulness,
it is called the wisdom of the arising of mindfulness of the original nature (prakṛti-smṛtyutpāda-jñāna).
Furthermore, by abiding in the mind of the original nature, one gives rise to this wisdom through the power of superior mindfulness.
Because one knows all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of past lives,
it is called the "knowledge of the recollection of innate nature" (*prakṛti-smṛtyutpāda-jñāna*).
As for the "mind of innate nature":
That is to say, it is wholesome, afflicted, or non-obscured neutral;
it is called "innate" because it is not acquired through cultivation.
Furthermore, as for "innate":
It refers to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, which is the very nature of the various contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena produced in past lives.
Because wisdom knows this innate nature through the power of mindfulness,
it is called "knowledge of the arising of innate mindfulness" (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
Furthermore, regarding "original nature" (*prakṛti*):
it refers to the *dharmatā* of the prior limit, that is, the *dharmatā* of the contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) of past births.

Because wisdom knows the arising of this original nature through the power of mindfulness, it is called "knowledge of the arising of the original nature through mindfulness" (*prakṛtisthānusmṛtijñāna*).
Question: Since there are many types of phenomena that arise simultaneously with this wisdom, why is mindfulness alone mentioned?
Answer: Because the power of mindfulness is predominant, as in the case of the four foundations of mindfulness, mindfulness of breathing, and the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
Although they have wisdom as their essence,
they are called "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth because the power of mindfulness is predominant;
this is just as the suppression and removal of the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), although its essence is wisdom.
However, because the power of conceptualization increases, it is called "suppressing and removing the perception of form.
This [state] is likewise;
although its essence is wisdom (*prajñā*), [it is designated differently].
Because the power of mindfulness increases therein, it is called "innate wisdom born of mindfulness" (*prakṛti-smṛtyutpāda-jñāna*).
Question: In which realm does this innate wisdom born of mindfulness exist?
Answer: It exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Question: In which realms of existence does this innate wisdom born of mindfulness exist?
Answer: It exists only in the human realm. Why is that?
Only those in the human realm of the desire world (*kāmadhātu*) can perform the distinguished karma that induces this knowledge.
Furthermore, within the human realm, wisdom is sharp and acute, surpassing that of other realms.
[Question: Regarding this innate knowledge born of mindfulness (*prakṛti-smṛtyutpanna-jñāna*):
By what karmic power is this brought about?
Some say: if sentient beings take pleasure in speaking words of endearment that cause others to rejoice, [they will experience such results].
The power of that karma is able to induce this wisdom.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
if sentient beings delight in recounting pleasant news so as to gladden the minds of others and cause their bodies to attain peace and happiness.
The power of that karma is able to induce this knowledge.
Other masters say:
"If sentient beings see others in a state of panic and fear..."
Through skillful means, he consoles and encourages them, acting as their refuge to bring them fearlessness;
by the power of that karma, he is able to induce this wisdom. Some say:
If sentient beings see others in distress and, through the Dharma, provide them with instruction and analogy so that they may become free from sorrow,
the power of that karma can induce this wisdom.
Others further say:
If sentient beings see narrow and treacherous places and cultivate them until they are wide and spacious,
so that those who pass to and fro encounter no hardship,
through the power of that karma they will experience no suffering from confinement while in their mother’s womb; thus they obtain this knowledge.
Or there is another explanation:
if sentient beings give various kinds of exquisite food and drink to others,
by the power of that karma they are able to induce this knowledge.
The commentary states:
One should speak thus:
"If there are sentient beings..."
He did not perform any karma that would cause affliction or harm to others,
but constantly engaged in deeds that benefited them;
by virtue of this karma, he remained within his mother’s womb.
They are not oppressed by diseases such as wind, heat, phlegm, or mucus;
when they later emerge from the womb, they experience no pain of constriction.
For this reason, they are able to remember their various past lives.
Therefore, there is this teaching:
if sentient beings, while dwelling in their mother’s womb or at the time of emerging from the womb,
were not afflicted by the suffering of being oppressed by various diseases.
All should be able to recollect the events of their past lives; however, due to the mother’s illness and the suffering of confinement, they all forget them.
Question: Among this innate wisdom of recollecting births (*prakṛti-jāti-smara-jñāna*), which is superior—at the beginning, the middle, or the end?
The answer is that this is not fixed;
that is to say, there are some who are superior at the time of their initial birth,
such as Śvetaketu and others at the time of their first birth.
He then spoke thus:
"Is there perhaps some wealth in this household that would allow me to practice giving as I please?"
Some are superior during middle age, such as the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla and others;
some are superior in old age,
such as Āmrapālī and others.
As explained at length in the sūtras, if one asks how many lifetimes this innate wisdom of recollection can remember,
some say that it can only remember the events of a single lifetime.
This refers to those who have passed away from that realm and are born here.
Some teachers say that such a person can remember two lifetimes.
Or even as far as seven births: for example, there was a butcher in Rājagṛha named Kaṭa,
who had been a childhood friend of King Ajātaśatru.
He once said to the Crown Prince:
"When you ascend the throne, what boon would you grant me?
The Crown Prince replied: "I shall grant you whatever you may request."
Later, when Ajātaśatru had killed his father and established himself as king,
Ghaṭa then requested a boon from the king.
The king replied, "I shall grant you whatever you desire."
Kāṭha said, "I pray that Your Majesty will grant me permission to slaughter [beings] alone within the city of Rājagṛha.
The King then replied:
"Why do you now seek such an evil vow?
Are you not afraid of the suffering that will come in the future?
The butcher replied to the king:
"If all virtuous and non-virtuous karmas were without fruit, what would there be to fear?
The king then asked, "How do you know this? Kāṭhaka replied to the king:
I recall six past lives in which I constantly practiced slaughter within this city of Rājagṛha;
in my final life, I was born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and experienced great happiness.
Having passed away from that heaven and been reborn here in this world,
he became a close friend to the king from his youth; therefore,
one knows that the fruits of good and evil are certainly non-existent.
Upon hearing this, the king gave rise to doubt and went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha told the king,
"This matter is not false."
However, that butcher once gave a single meal to a pratyekabuddha and made a perverted vow, saying:
"May I always carry out slaughter alone within the city of Rājagṛha, and afterwards be reborn in heaven."
Through the power of his superior karma, he has fulfilled his vow;
however, that prior superior karma which granted the fruit has now been exhausted.
Seven days hence, he will certainly meet his end and be reborn in the Raurava Hell.
He experiences the bitter fruits of his former occupation as a butcher in successive order.
For this reason, this wisdom knows up to seven births at most.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
This person is exceptionally capable of recollecting the events of five hundred lifetimes.
That is to say, there was a bhikṣu who recollected that during five hundred past lives he had fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts;
as he recalled the suffering of hunger and thirst he endured there, [he felt great compassion].
His entire body broke into a sweat as his heart was filled with deep fear and distress;
he ceased all worldly activities and applied himself with blazing diligence,
after which, after a long time, he attained the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
He thought to himself:
"From the past until now,
I have relied upon the bhikṣus for the provision of all my necessities."
"May my fears be forever extinguished.
Now I must seek out various requisites for sustaining the body to repay his prior kindness.
Having formed this thought, he searched everywhere for such requisites.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they said to him, "Previously you had few affairs; why do you have so many now?
He then related his past history in detail to them.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who recalled his own past five hundred births in the realm of hell.
When he recollected the suffering he had endured in those hells,
blood flowed from every one of his pores.
His body and clothing were constantly foul-smelling and filthy;
every day he would go to the water to bathe and wash his clothes.
The people called him one who reckoned water to be purity.
Having exerted himself with intense diligence in his work for a long time, he realized arhatship.
Thereafter, he did not frequently bathe or wash his robes.
When the people saw this, they marveled and asked about it.
He also recounted this past life in detail for others;
from this, it is known that this wisdom recollects up to five hundred births.
Other masters say: [it is more].
This wisdom can know the events of past kalpas of destruction and formation;
that is to say, when the Buddha was formerly a bodhisattva,
he made great vows for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
At one time, he was once a Caṇḍāla king named Triśaṅku,
who was thoroughly proficient in all scripts, treatises, and incantations.
At that time, Ānanda was his prince, named Siṃhakarṇa.
His countenance was so upright and handsome that he was peerless in the world.
At that time, Śāriputra was a brahmin named Kūṭadanta,
who was thoroughly proficient in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, along with his retinue.
He had a daughter named Chastity (Brahmacāriṇī),
whose appearance was so dignified and beautiful that all delighted in beholding her.
At that time, the king went to the brahmin’s residence to seek a marriage alliance for his son.
Cīra, filled with great indignation, said to that king:
"Among all castes, you are the most base and lowly;
I am a brahmin, the most honored among all castes."
"For what reason have you come here to treat me with such contempt and insult?
At that time, the king addressed the brahmin, saying,
"The nobility or lowliness of one's lineage is likewise not fixed."
"Why do you look upon this with such disregard and yet pride yourself so highly?
Have you ever heard from whom the letters of the various Brahmanical scriptures were created?
Puṣkarasārin replied:
"I have heard that in ancient times there was a brahmin named Govinda;
this was composed by him.
The king said:
"At that time, Gopīta was none other than myself.
Furthermore, have you heard who created the Kharoṣṭhī script?
The brāhmaṇa replied, "I have heard that in ancient times there was a great ṛṣi named Kharoṣṭha."
"This was created by him.
The King said,
"The great seer of that time was none other than myself."
The king asked again, "Have you ever heard who composed the various Vedic treatises, their auxiliary branches, and secular texts?
The Brahmin replied, "It is so, it is so; [these are] the books and treatises of the various schools."
He then replied to those various brahmins and ṛṣis who had composed the treatises on kingship:
"Do you perhaps know that all of them were my names in former times?"
"How is it that you now boast of yourself while looking down upon me?
At this, Lake-Firm (Poṣadha) investigated each point one by one and found that what the king had said was true and not erroneous.
With a heart of deep reverence and admiration, he then consented to the marriage with the king.
From this, it is known that this wisdom can recollect the events of the formation and destruction of world-systems throughout the most remote past eons.
As stated in the Sūtra,
the Buddha told the village headman:
As I recall back through ninety-one eons of the past,
I have never failed to provide food, drink, and other necessities to the field of pure precepts;
nor do I recall ever having harmed or violated the precepts for the sake of food, drink, or similar things.

Question: Does the Blessed One recollect this matter by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), or does he recollect it by means of the knowledge of mindfulness of the arising of [past] existences (*prakṛtismṛtyutpādajñāna*)?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If this matter is known by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*),
why does he recollect only ninety-one *kalpas* and no more?
If it is known by means of the knowledge of recollecting births by natural disposition (*prakṛtismṛtijñāna*).
Why was it previously stated that some say this wisdom recalls only one lifetime,
some say it recalls two up to a maximum of seven lifetimes,
and others say it recalls five hundred lifetimes?
Some say that one can remember the formation and destruction of kalpas,
yet they do not say that one can remember nine or eleven kalpas.
Having agreed to speak thus, the Blessed One recalled this matter by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
[The interlocutor] asks:
"If that is so, why does he recall only ninety-one *kalpas* and not more?"
Answer: It is indeed capable of remembering much, yet it is spoken of as only this much.
Question: If that is so, why is it not said that it remembers much?
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"When all beings harbor doubts, whether one says that mindfulness is much or that mindfulness is little, they both give rise to questions.
Therefore, as long as it accords with the facts, there is no contradiction in principle; one should not raise objections."
Furthermore, it is because the seven World-Honored Buddhas were established starting from him that he is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, it is because from his time onward the karma for the primary and secondary marks was cultivated that he is specifically mentioned.

Furthermore, from that time onward, his paths of action have been pure, he has not fallen into the evil destinies, he has always received a male body, and he constantly remembers his past lives; for these reasons, he is specifically mentioned.
Others say: [text continues].
The Blessed One, by means of the knowledge born of the recollection of his own original nature, recalled this matter. [An objection:
If that is so, why was it previously stated that some recall only a single lifetime?
Even if it is said that one can remember the formation and destruction of kalpas, why is it not said that one can remember ninety-one kalpas?
The answer is: the previous statement concerned how much other people can remember, but did not refer to the Buddha.
If one speaks of the Buddha, he is likewise able to recollect much.
Question: Is the innate knowledge of mindfulness (*prakṛti-smṛtyutpāda-jñāna*) capable of recollecting and knowing the events of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
There is this explanation given:
One cannot recollect or know it.
Why is this? Because the matter of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is extremely subtle, and thus it is not within the scope of this cognition.
The commentary states:

One should say that the innate wisdom born of mindfulness (*prakṛtijā smṛtijā prajñā*) is also capable of recollecting and knowing the events within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Why is this so?
If one does not recollect and know this, then the object known by this cognition would become confused;
that is to say, because it would be partially cognized and partially not cognized.
Question: Since a Bodhisattva in previous lives already possesses innate wisdom born of recollection (*pūrvajanma-jāti-smṛti-jñāna*), does he also possess it in his final birth?
If so, what would be the fault?
If it exists, why is the power of conditions superior and not the power of causes? If it does not exist,
why does the bodhisattva not undergo decline or regression?
It is agreed that this is how it should be stated:
even for a bodhisattva in their final existence, there is the innate knowledge of recollecting births (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
Question: If that is so, [what follows]?
What is meant by "the power of conditions rather than the power of a superior cause"?
The answer is: it is not that there is no power of conditions;
rather, this is called having internal causal power.
Furthermore, because their faculties are sharp, they are said to possess internal causal power;
that is to say, this bodhisattva possesses causal power because their spiritual faculties are the most excellent among all sentient beings.
Moreover, who says that a bodhisattva lacks the power of conditions?
When the Śuddhāvāsa devas manifested old age, sickness, and death,
awakening in the Bodhisattva a mind of weary detachment from birth and death— was this not the power of conditions?
Furthermore, the Śākya maiden Mṛgajā recited verses in praise of Nirvāṇa for the Bodhisattva.
The arousal of a bodhisattva’s aspiration for nirvāṇa is also due to the power of conditions,
as it is said:
Before long you shall obtain: Taking peace as your mother, Taking freedom from sorrow as your father, And taking nirvāṇa as your wife.
Having seen and heard of these matters, the Bodhisattva [reflected].
Having thus increased his sense of renunciation and aspiration, he left the city to become a renunciant.
Furthermore, in past lives, there were immeasurable Buddhas who,
for him as a bodhisattva, taught the provisions for awakening.
All such instances as these are termed the power of conditions (*pratyaya-bala*).
Some say that in his final existence,
a bodhisattva does not possess the innate knowledge of recollecting births (*jāti-smara-jñāna*).
Question: If that is so, why does it not degenerate?
Answer: Although this wisdom is absent, [it does not degenerate].
However, because they possess the superior knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*),
the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*),
and so forth, they do not undergo decline.
The commentary states:
It should be understood that the former explanation is the correct one,
because this wisdom has existed continuously throughout ninety-one kalpas.
It asks: "What is the liberation through loving-kindness (*maitrī-vimokṣa*), and so forth, as explained at length?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"A bhikṣu should not delight in gathering with the multitude or indulge in various frivolous discourses."
If one delights in assemblies and is addicted to conceptual proliferation,
they can realize the liberation of mind through love associated with time,
as well as the unshakable liberation of mind.
This is impossible.
If bhikṣus do not delight in congregating and do not indulge in frivolous discourse,
they will be able to realize the two kinds of liberation.
There is indeed such a case.
Although the sūtra makes this statement,
it does not provide an extensive explanation of its meaning.
The intrinsic nature of these two liberations and the causes and conditions for their attainment are not explained here;
although the *Indriya-skandha* does explain the two causes and conditions for their attainment.
Its intrinsic nature has not yet been revealed;
it is now intended to be revealed.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of refuting the tenets of other schools and manifesting the correct principle.
That is to say, some say that liberation through a mind accompanied by affection is for those in training (śaikṣa) who still have work to do,
whereas immovable liberation of the mind is for those beyond training (aśaikṣa) who have no further work to do.
This is to refute their view and demonstrate that both types of liberation are *aśaikṣa* (beyond training) and have nothing further to be done.
Alternatively, some say that liberation through love and affection (*sāmayikī-kāntā-vimukti*) is contaminated (*sāsrava*).
The liberation of the immovable mind (*akopya-cetovimukti*) is untainted (*anāsrava*).
This is stated to preclude the notion that [only one] is so; rather, it reveals that both liberations are untainted.

Furthermore, there are those who maintain that the liberation through love and affection (*sāmayikī-kāntā-vimukti*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), whereas the liberation of the immovable mind is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
In order to refute that intention and to demonstrate that both types of liberation are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), for these reasons the treatise states: "When is there liberation through love?
Answer: At the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) of an Arhat who is liberated by occasion (*samaya-vimukta*)."
Or, it is the resolve associated with the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
which has already resolved or will resolve.
What is the immovable liberation of mind (*āniñjya-cetovimukti*)?
Answer: It is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) of an Arhat of immovable dharma,
or the mental resolve associated with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
which has already resolved, or will resolve.

Among these, the mind associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*) excludes that which belongs to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*).
"Resolve" (*adhimokṣa*) refers to the present.
Those who have already attained resolute conviction refer to the past;
those who are about to attain resolute conviction refer to the future.
This serves to distinguish [this liberation] from unconditioned liberation.
This demonstrates that the two types of liberation have as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) only the resolve (adhimokṣa) associated with the untainted mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Nevertheless, among all phenomena (dharmas), only these two factors constitute the intrinsic nature of liberation.
That is to say, among unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of liberation;
among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), the resolute confidence (*adhimokṣa*) subsumed under the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmikadharma*) is the intrinsic nature of liberation.
This resolve is of two kinds.
First is the defiled,
which refers to that associated with greed and so forth, termed "wrong resolve."
The second is non-defiled,
which refers to right resolve associated with non-attachment and so forth.
This right resolve is further of two kinds.
First, there is that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*),
namely: the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*),
and the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) associated with the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
The second is the untainted (anāsrava).
This refers to the resolve of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The "resolve of those in training" refers to the resolve comprised within the four stages of approach (pratipannaka) and the three fruits of realization (phala).
It refers to the resolute conviction associated with the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering up to the diamond-like concentration.
Resolute conviction of one beyond training refers to the resolute conviction comprised within the fruit of arhatship.
This is the resolute confidence associated with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi) that arises from the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.
Furthermore, this resolute confidence of one beyond training is of two kinds:
first, liberation through loving-kindness (sneha-vimukti).
That is to say, the liberation through resolute confidence (adhimokṣa) included within the five types of arhatship is also called "liberation by occasion" (samayavimukti).
Second, the immovable liberation of mind (akopya-cetovimukti);
that is, the liberation through resolute confidence included within the fruit of an arhat of the immovable nature (akopyadharman) is also called "liberation not by occasion" (asamayavimukti).
These two liberations each have two types.
The first is called liberation of mind,
because it is free from craving and attachment.
The second is called liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
This is because it is free from ignorance (*avidyā*).

Question: If the liberation of mind (*citta-vimukti*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is so named because their resolute confidence (*adhimokṣa*) is free from craving and attachment, [how does this differ from liberation through wisdom]?
Regarding the statement that one is "liberated through wisdom" (prajñā-vimukta) because of being free from ignorance (avidyā),
how should this be reconciled with the *Saṃgītiparyāya*,
which asks: "What is liberation of the mind (citta-vimukti)?"
That is to say, if the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*) counteracts craving (*tṛṣṇā*), how is it that one is liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*)?
And if the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha*) counteracts ignorance (*avidyā*)?
The answer is that the *Saṃgītiparyāya* should state it as follows:
What is liberation of mind?
It is the resolute conviction associated with the wholesome root of non-attachment.
What is liberation by wisdom?
This refers to the resolute conviction associated with the wholesome root of non-delusion.
Although it should have been stated thus, the fact that it was not stated is due to a specific underlying intention:
namely, to demonstrate the resolute conviction by way of its basis in the wholesome roots.
If, by relying on non-attachment, the mind is liberated from craving,
the corresponding resolve is called "liberation of the mind.
If, by relying on non-delusion, wisdom is liberated from ignorance, [the corresponding resolve is called "liberation through wisdom"].
This associated resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) is called liberation through wisdom (prajñā-vimukti).
Therefore, in this context, both types of mental liberation have the resolute conviction of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-adhimokṣa) as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
This is called the essential nature, the substance, the self-entity, the characteristic-part, and the fundamental nature of liberation.
Having already explained its essential nature,
that which follows shall now be explained.
Question: Why is it called "liberation by time" (*samaya-vimukta*)? What is the meaning of "liberation by time"?
Answer: Because that liberation is attained in dependence upon time.
Although there are many [occasions], in brief there are six types:
first, the time when one obtains fine clothing;
second, the time when one obtains fine food.
Third, when one obtains excellent bedding;
fourth, when one obtains an excellent location;
fifth, when one obtains excellent teaching of the Dharma.
Sixth, regarding the occasion when one encounters a person of good character:
"waiting for the occasion of obtaining fine robes" means that such a person attains liberation only upon obtaining clothing that is fine, soft, fresh, pure, and excellent.
If it were not so, one would not attain liberation.
"Waiting for the time when excellent food is obtained" means that one must obtain exquisite food and drink, such as ghee and honey, at which time one then attains liberation.
If it were not so, one would not attain liberation.
"Waiting for the time when good bedding is obtained" means that one must obtain thick, soft bedding, mattresses, and the like before one can attain liberation.
If it were not so, one would not attain liberation.
"Waiting for a favorable location" means that one must wait until obtaining a place of tranquility and an excellent dwelling before one can attain liberation.
If it were not so, one would not attain liberation.
"Waiting for a time when the Dharma is well-expounded" means that one attains liberation only when one receives instruction and counsel that is appropriate to the occasion and accordant with reality.
If it were not so, one would not attain liberation.
"Waiting for the time when a worthy person (pudgala) is found" means that one must find someone who possesses excellent virtuous conduct, a gentle nature, and is easy to dwell with.
One attains liberation only when dwelling together with others;
if it were otherwise, one would not attain liberation.
Question: For what reason is this called "liberation at an improper time" (asamaya-vimukti)?
What is the meaning of "liberation not dependent on time" (*asamayavimukti*)?
The answer is: because that liberation is attained without depending on time.
"Time" refers to the six types previously mentioned.
"Those who do not wait for the time when fine robes are obtained" means that even when they obtain coarse rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*),
they are able to swiftly attain liberation.
Regarding those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*):
when they obtain a garment worth hundreds of thousands of gold pieces,
they do not wait for the time when excellent food is available.
This means that although they obtain coarse and inferior food and drink,
they are able to attain liberation quickly;
they are those who possess "liberation at superior times."
Regarding "when obtaining food and drink of a hundred flavors" and "without waiting for the time of obtaining good bedding":
this means that even when one obtains inferior bedding such as stone slabs or beds, [one remains content].
And one is able to swiftly attain liberation.
As for those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*),
it is when they obtain excellent bedding and seats.
"Without waiting for a favorable location" means that even when one encounters a noisy place or an inferior dwelling,
one is still able to swiftly attain liberation.
Regarding those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*):
because they attain a state of tranquility and excellence, they quickly enter meditative concentration upon becoming weary of worldly clamor;
thus, they do not wait for the occurrence of a favorable time for hearing the well-expounded Dharma.
This means that although they receive instructions and teachings that are contrary to reason or miss the mark regarding the occasion,
they are able to attain liberation quickly; thus,
they are superior to those liberated by time.
When one receives reasoned instructions and counsel that are appropriate to the occasion,
because one becomes weary of what was previously said and quickly enters meditative concentration,
one does not have to wait for the time when a person of superior qualities (pudgala) is found.
This means that even when living together with those who, by nature, have acquired a lack of virtuous conduct and are stubborn and difficult to dwell with,
one is still able to swiftly attain liberation.
Regarding those liberated by occasion (samayavimukta):
when they dwell together with those who possess virtuous conduct and other such qualities,
they become weary of the latter's coarseness and evil, and thus quickly enter meditative concentration.
Furthermore, because one attains liberation by relying on a narrow and minor path, it is called "liberation by time.
As for the "narrow and minor path," this refers to planting roots of goodness at the very fastest in one's first birth.
In the second birth, they are brought to maturity;
in the third birth, they attain liberation.
For others, it is not fixed.
One who attains liberation by means of the extensive path is called one liberated at an indefinite time (*asamayavimukta*).
As for the "extensive path," it refers to those who are extremely slow in the Śrāvaka vehicle.
One attains liberation after sixty kalpas,
as did Śāriputra in his vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas;
one attains liberation after one hundred kalpas.
Like the rhinoceros-horn simile of the Buddha-vehicle,
one attains liberation after three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Furthermore, because one attains liberation by relying on a weak and inferior path, it is called "liberation through time" (*samaya-vimukti*).
The "weak and inferior path" refers to being unable to constantly and earnestly cultivate the application of wholesome qualities for the sake of liberation.
If one practices during the first watch of the day,
one will not be able to practice during the middle or later watches;
likewise, if one practices during the first watch of the night.
In the latter part [of the day], one is unable to practice;
even if one can practice for a time, it is not done with earnestness, nor is liberation attained by relying on a powerful and superior path.
Therefore, this is called "liberation at an improper time" (asamayavimukti).
The path of those who are powerful and victorious is the opposite of the above.
Furthermore, because one attains liberation by relying on a path characterized by the predominance of serenity (*śamatha*), it is called "liberation at a specific time" (*samaya-vimukta*).
Because one attains liberation by relying on a path characterized by the predominance of insight (*vipaśyanā*), it is called "non-timed liberation" (*asamaya-vimukta*).
Furthermore, one attains liberation by relying on a path that can be diverted; therefore, it is called "liberation through time" (*samayavimukti*).
A path that can be diverted refers to the cultivated path that may be either agreeable or disagreeable.
Beneficial and non-beneficial things,
and the acquisition or loss of the requisites for pleasure and pain—
relying on the path that cannot be led astray by these.
Because they attain liberation [at will],
they are called "those liberated at any time" (asamaya-vimukta).
Those who possess a path that cannot be led astray or taken away are the opposite of the aforementioned.
Furthermore, one attains liberation by relying on the fivefold paths of spiritual lineage; therefore,
it is called "liberation by time" (samayavimukti).
The five paths of the various spiritual lineages (gotra) refer to the path of the lineage of those subject to regression (parihāṇadharman),
up to the path of the lineage of those capable of reaching the ultimate (prativedhanādharman).
Because one attains liberation by means of a single type of lineage-path (gotra-mārga), it is called "liberation not dependent on time" (asamaya-vimukti).
A single type of lineage-path refers to the lineage-path of the immovable dharma (akopyadharman).
This explains that the Arhats of the five lineages (*gotra*) are termed "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*),
while the Arhats of the immovable lineage (*akopyadharman-gotra*) are termed "not liberated by occasion" (*asamayavimukta*).
From this discussion, another question arises.
For what reason are the first five types of arhats collectively established as those liberated at all times (samayavimukta),
while the sixth type of arhat is separately established as one liberated not at all times (asamayavimukta)?
Answer: Because there are distinct conditions,
those liberated by time are many,
while those not liberated by time are few.
That is to say, based on their spiritual lineage (*gotra*),
the first five types of lineage are designated as "Arhats liberated by time" (*samayavimukta*).
The sixth type of person is called "not liberated at all times" because they possess specific conditions [for liberation] and because those liberated at all times are few.
Those who are "not occasionally liberated" (asamayavimukta) are numerous.
This is because, while according to the designation of vehicles there are only Śrāvaka-vehicle Arhats who are "occasionally liberated" (samayavimukta),
Arhats who are "not occasionally liberated" exist within all three vehicles.
There is a distinct reason for the two types of liberation being equal;
namely, both liberations are equally free from afflictions,
and both are comprised within the noble path within the pure body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, because those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) are inferior, five types are established;
because those liberated regardless of occasion (*asamayavimukta*) are superior, one type is instituted.
This is just as there are kings, ministers, elders, and householders in the world today.
Those who are wealthy and noble are extremely few in number,
while those who are poor and lowly are exceedingly numerous.
Furthermore, it is like how in the world the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas who have reached the ultimate goal are extremely few in number.
The other śrāvakas are exceedingly numerous.
It is like how in the world the wise are few while the ignorant are many;
it is like how in the world those who do good are few while those who commit evil are many.
Furthermore, it is like how in the world those with right view are few while those with wrong view are many;
or like how in the world those who are handsome are few while those who are ugly are many;
or like how in the world those who are gentle and flexible are few while those who are stubborn and rigid are many.
Thus, because the first five arhats are inferior, they are collectively termed "liberated by time" (samayavimukta).
Because the sixth arhat is superior, he is individually termed "not liberated by time" (asamayavimukta).
Furthermore, the first five arhats are easily attained in the world.
Therefore, those who are established collectively as "liberated by occasion" (samaya-vimukta) are rare in the world even among the sixth type of Arhat;
thus, they are established separately under the name "not liberated by occasion" (asamaya-vimukta).
Nowadays, among the people of this world, those who travel to that country and return from Siṃhala are extremely few,
while those who travel to nearby villages and return are very many.
This case is also like that.
Furthermore, the first five types of arhats attain their state without expending much effort,
without applying much preparatory practice,
and without much mental attention.
Therefore, those who are established as having a single name are called "liberated by timely means" (samayavimukta).
The sixth type of Arhat is the opposite of the aforementioned;
therefore, he is separately established with the name "liberated not by timely means" (asamayavimukta).
Furthermore, the first five types of arhats undergo increase and decrease;
therefore, they are collectively designated by the single name "one liberated by occasion" (samaya-vimukta).
The sixth type of arhat neither increases nor decreases.
Therefore, a separate category is established called "one liberated at any time" (asamayavimukta).
In this context, "increase" refers to progress,
and "decrease" refers to regression.
