Section Three of the *Jñānaskandha* (The Aggregate of Wisdom), Part Four of the Sub-section on the Knowledge of Others' Minds (*paracittajñāna*). For what reason is the liberation of mind at that time called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*)?
The Arhat of occasional liberation (samayavimukta) constantly and earnestly guards,
cherishes, and treasures this dharma.
May I not encounter conditions that cause me to fall away from this Dharma.

Just as a person with only one eye, together with their own friends and relatives, diligently guards, cherishes, and treasures [their eye], lest it encounter conditions such as cold, heat, dust, or cataracts.
It causes this one eye to be further ruined;
because it is likewise [destructive] for the other, it is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).
That is to say, for those of dull faculties, craving for their own qualities—which they regard as precious jewels—is more excessive than that of those with sharp faculties.
Just as women, by their very nature,
possess a loving affection for their own sons and daughters that exceeds that of men,
so too does an Arhat liberated at times (samayavimukta) lack mastery over his own liberation.
It must be manifested through the application of great effort;
once it has been manifested, because one regards it with joy and profound esteem, it is called "love" (preman).
This refers to the Arhat who is liberated at specific times (samayavimukta).

Having attained mastery over one's own liberation, one is able to manifest it before oneself with little exertion; yet, because although it is manifested, it is not intensely craved, it is not termed "craving" (tṛṣṇā).
Furthermore, the qualities of an Arhat liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) are subject to decline;
because such an Arhat fears decline and repeatedly brings [the antidotes] into manifestation, this is termed "craving" (tṛṣṇā).
The qualities of an Arhat not liberated by occasion (asamaya-vimukta) do not decline.
Because they do not fear falling back and because [the attainment] does not manifest frequently, it is not called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).

Furthermore, an Arhat liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) is called "one who craves" (*tṛṣṇāvat*) because they realize the path through the increase of faith; an Arhat not liberated by time (*asamayavimukta*) is not so called.
Because they realize the path through the increase of wisdom, they are not called "craving.
Furthermore, because time-liberated arhats are by nature well-disciplined and much loved by others, they are called "craving."
An Arhat who is liberated at an inappropriate time (asamayavimukta) is not called "loved" because their nature is mostly rigid and harsh, and thus they are not loved by others,
just like people of the present day.
Those whose nature is not sharp are for the most part gentle and virtuous people whom others like to associate with;
those whose nature is not dull are for the most part fierce and violent people whom others do not associate with.
Furthermore, there are Arhats liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*).
Because they lack the roots of goodness that involve aversion toward the Noble Path, they are called "those who love" (tṛṣṇā).
Arhats who are not liberated at all times possess the roots of goodness that involve aversion toward the Noble Path; therefore, they are not called "those who love."

The roots of goodness that turn away from the Noble Path refer to the roots of goodness associated with the samādhis of emptiness-of-emptiness, wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and signlessness-of-signlessness.
Although this is not explicitly addressed in the questions and answers of the main body of this treatise.
Since there is a specific meaning [to this], it should now be explained.
Question: For what reason is one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*) called "immovable" (*akopya*)?
Answer: It is called immovable because its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is preeminent.
Nowadays, in this world, excellent food, drink, clothing, and ornaments are called "immovable," because they are not subject to fluctuation through comparison with inferior objects.
Furthermore, afflictions such as greed cause the bodies and minds of sentient beings to become light and restless.
Because it causes the various roots of goodness to sprout, scatter, and disperse, it is called "shaking.
Because an Arhat who is liberated at an improper time is not shaken by such afflictions, he is called "unshakable."
Furthermore, because afflictions such as greed cause sentient beings to fluctuate不定 (indeterminately) between superior and inferior states across various conditions, they are called "movement.

An Arhat who is not liberated at all times is called "immovable" because he is not moved by such afflictions; he is like a valiant man who cannot be shaken by an opponent and is thus termed "immovable."
Furthermore, an Arhat who is liberated at any time (asamayavimukta) is called "immovable" because they never fall away from their various meritorious qualities.
This is like a skilled archer who is called "immovable" because his arrows invariably hit the mark.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra,
"If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and so forth..."
Regarding one who has accomplished the jewel-like liberation of the immovable mind:
they are able to sever unwholesome dharmas and are able to cultivate wholesome dharmas. Question: For what reason is it called "the immovable liberation of the mind"?
It is called the maṇi-jewel because it is firm through the liberation of the immovable mind.
Because it is supreme and wondrous;
because it is faultless; because it is luminous and penetrating;
and because it is stainless.
Because it is pure;
because it is difficult to obtain;
and because it is lovely and delightful.
It is called a maṇi jewel.
Furthermore, because it can shatter the darkness of ignorance through the liberation of the immovable mind, it is called a maṇi jewel.
Just as placing a luminous maṇi jewel within a dark room can dispel that darkness and perform the function of illumination,
so too is it with the maṇi jewel of the liberation of the immovable mind.
It is established that within the continuum [of consciousness], it performs the function of illuminating by destroying the darkness of ignorance.
Furthermore, because the liberation of the immovable mind (*akopya-citta-vimukti*) can eliminate the dust and stains of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
It is called the maṇi-jewel.
Just as when a water-clearing maṇi is placed in turbid water, the water immediately becomes clear and pure,
so too does one place the maṇi-jewel of immovable liberation within the continuum of one's being.
It is able to remove all the dust and defilements of affliction.
Furthermore, because it is well-established through the liberation of the immovable mind, it is called a maṇi-jewel.
Just as a maṇi from the Vaipulya sūtras remains well-established wherever it is placed.
In this way, by placing the mani-jewel of immovable liberation within the continuum,
one dwells well-established in meditative concentration without any decline.
Furthermore, because the liberation of the immovable mind can eliminate the poverty of the noble riches, it is called a *maṇi* jewel.
Just as an invaluable *maṇi* placed within a house can attract wealth and treasures, thereby removing all forms of destitution.
Thus, by placing the jewel of immovable mental liberation within one’s continuum,
one is able to attract the wealth of the noble ones and eliminate the merit of deprivation.
Furthermore, because the immovable mental liberation is able to benefit all sentient beings, it is called a "jewel."

Just as a wish-fulfilling gem placed atop a high banner rains down all manner of precious objects according to one's desires, thereby providing relief to hundreds of thousands of destitute sentient beings;
so too does the World-Honored One, by means of the mani-jewel of the liberation of the immovable mind.
It is placed atop the immeasurable banner of heedfulness,
raining down the jewels of the true Dharma according to the diverse inclinations of sentient beings.
It enables immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to leave behind the suffering of birth and death and to fulfill their roots of goodness.
Through such various causes and conditions as these,
it is called the "unshakable liberation of mind."
It is called the "jewel-treasure.
Question: If the immovable liberation of mind possesses such superior qualities, why did the Blessed One say that the immovable liberation of mind is a dharma without decrease and without increase?
Answer: This is because it is taught from the perspective of the equality of practitioners.
That is to say, suppose there were immeasurable sons of the kṣatriya caste in the eastern direction, and immeasurable sons of the brāhmaṇa caste in the southern direction.
In the west there are immeasurable Vaiśya sons,
and in the north there are immeasurable Śūdra sons;
they all come to take refuge in me, shave their hair and beards, don the saffron robes, and with right faith leave the household life to enter the homeless state.
Whether one dwells having personally realized and fully attained the liberation of mind through immovability, or otherwise,
this liberation of mind through immovability neither diminishes nor increases.
Furthermore, this is because it is taught that the qualities of the Noble Teaching (ārya-śāsana) are infinite.
That is to say, within the Noble Teaching there are infinite qualities;
it is not the case that there is only the immovable liberation of mind (akopyā cetovimuktiḥ).

Furthermore, because this immovable liberation of mind neither decreases when departing nor increases when coming; moreover, it is spoken of in reliance upon the boundlessness of the Buddha’s qualities, meaning that within the Buddha’s body there are infinite qualities.

It is not that there is only the liberation of mind through immovability; for even if the liberation of mind through immovability departs, it does not decrease, and even if it comes, it does not increase.
Furthermore, this statement was made in order to eliminate the doubts of the multitude.
That is to say,
on the night of the *poṣadha*,
Mahāmaudgalyāyana expelled the bhikṣu of Campā.
He ordered him to be expelled from the assembly.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu conceived a doubt in his mind, thinking:
"May the community of bhikṣus not suffer a reduction in numbers."
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"Even if one who possesses liberation through an immovable mind were expelled from a community that is like a grove of preeminent virtues."
My community of bhikṣus does not diminish;
even if he were to come, the assembly would not increase—
how much less so when that bhikṣu has broken the precepts and transgressed the prohibitions?
Since they destroy all dignified deportment and distance themselves from pure qualities (*śukladharma*),
how could they cause the pure assembly to decrease or increase?
Furthermore, because the liberation through the immovable mind (*āniñjya-cetovimukti*) cannot be lost, it is said to be "without decrease."
Because there is no further progress, it is said to be "without increase.
Therefore, although the immovable liberation of mind possesses superior qualities,
the Buddha taught that it is neither diminished nor increased.
"Are all instances of the liberation through loving-kindness at various times associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
and so forth, as explained in detail.
[Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is in order to bring certainty to those who are doubtful.

That is to say, there are those who, upon hearing it said that a *samayavimukta* arhat cultivates only the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*), then doubt that an *asamayavimukta* arhat likewise cultivates only these two.

Furthermore, there are those who, upon hearing it said that an Arhat of non-timely liberation (asamaya-vimukta) cultivates the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), and the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi),
immediately suspect that an Arhat of timely liberation (samaya-vimukta) likewise cultivates these three.

To remove that doubt, it is shown that those who are liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) cultivate only two types [of faculties], whereas those who are not liberated by occasion (asamaya-vimukta) cultivate all three.
Furthermore, although the intrinsic nature of the two types of liberation was previously explained, [it shall now be further detailed].
However, the characteristics of their being mixed or unmixed have not yet been explained;
since I now wish to explain them, I compose this treatise.
In this context, there are four propositions regarding the liberation through love and time (*sāmayikī-kānta-vimukti*) in relation to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
The immovable liberation of mind is associated with the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
All subsequent formulations should be understood as they appear in the original text.
Question: Which Arhat cultivates only the two untainted wisdoms (*anāsrava-prajñā*) of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*)?

What kind of arhat is one who possesses the fully cultivated knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the three types of untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) of right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: There are arhats whose minds are well-liberated but whose wisdom is not well-liberated.
There are Arhats whose minds and wisdom are both well-liberated;
the former cultivate only two [faculties],
while the latter cultivate all three.
Furthermore, there are Arhats for whom the power of their causes, the power of their application, and the power of their heedfulness are all limited;
there are also Arhats for whom the power of their causes, the power of their application, and the power of their heedfulness are all vast.
In the former case, one cultivates only two;
in the latter, one cultivates all three.
Furthermore, there are arhats who are practitioners of śamatha.
There are Arhats who practice vipaśyanā. Those mentioned previously cultivated only two [of the three trainings],
while those mentioned later fully cultivate all three.
It is the same for the two types of practice, the two types of delight, the two types of desire,
and the two types of craving. Furthermore, there are arhats who enter the noble path preceded by the cultivation of tranquility (śamatha),
and there are arhats who enter the noble path preceded by the cultivation of insight (vipaśyanā).
In the former case, one cultivates only two;
in the latter, one cultivates all three.

Furthermore, there are Arhats who cultivate the mind through *śamatha* (calm abiding) and attain liberation by relying on *vipaśyanā* (insight), and there are Arhats who cultivate the mind through *vipaśyanā* and attain liberation by relying on *śamatha*.
In the former case, one cultivates only two;
in the latter, one cultivates all three.
Furthermore, there are arhats who have attained internal śamatha.
One cannot attain the contemplation of the Dharma through higher wisdom.
There are Arhats who have attained internal śamatha and also attained the contemplation of the Dharma through higher wisdom.
In the former case, one cultivates only two;
in the latter, one fully cultivates all three.
Furthermore, as it is said in the Sūtra:
There are two causes and two conditions that can give rise to right view:
first, hearing the voices of others externally;
second, applying correct attention internally.
If one is dominated by hearing external sounds from others, one cultivates only two;
if one is dominated by internal right attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), one fully cultivates all three.
Furthermore, as it is said in the Sūtra:
There are four dharmas by which one accomplishes much:
first, associating with virtuous persons;
second, hearing the true Dharma.
Third is appropriate mental attention;
fourth is practice in accordance with the Dharma.
For those in whom the former two have increased, they cultivate only these two.
Regarding the increase in the latter two, those who cultivate all three are complete practitioners.
Furthermore, those of dull faculties cultivate only two,
while those of sharp faculties cultivate all three.
As with dull faculties and sharp faculties, the power of conditions and the power of causes,
external factors and internal factors, so too are there the knowledge of what has been taught and the knowledge of what has been heard.
It should be known that it is likewise so. Furthermore, if the wholesome root of non-attachment predominates, one cultivates only two;
if the wholesome root of non-delusion predominates, one fully cultivates all three.
Furthermore, if one exhausts the fetters of the three realms through the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path, one cultivates only two.
If one exhausts the fetters of the three realms through the knowledge of suffering and its origin, one fully cultivates all three.

Furthermore, if one exhausts the fetters of the three realms through the signless path and the wishless samādhi, one cultivates only two. If one exhausts the fetters of the three realms through the emptiness, the knowledge of suffering and its origin, and the wishless samādhi, one fully cultivates all three.
Among these, for an arhat with liberation through occasional love,
the diamond-like concentration lasts for only a single moment,
whereas the flow of the knowledge of exhaustion continues in succession for a long duration.
Emerging from the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna),
one either gives rise to the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi) or gives rise to a conventional mind;
this refers to an Arhat who has attained the unshakable liberation of mind (akopyacittavimukti).
The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) each last for only a single moment.
The knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) flows in a continuous stream for a long duration.
One emerges from this knowledge of non-arising.
Either the right view of one beyond training arises, or a conventional mind arises.
While all Arhats cultivate the perfection of the right view of one beyond training,
it is not the case that it is present in all of them at all times.

Question: What is the distinction between the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)? Answer: First, their names themselves constitute the distinction;
that is to say, this is called the knowledge of exhaustion, and this is called the knowledge of non-arising.
Furthermore, [the former] is the knowledge of exhaustion because it is based on this [exhaustion].
The fruit is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Furthermore, that which has already been accomplished is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*);
it is through the nourishment of this [exhaustion] that there is the knowledge of non-arising.
Furthermore, it is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that consists in either attaining what has not yet been attained, or attaining again what has already been attained;
it is exclusively the attainment of what has not yet been attained.
This is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Furthermore, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) is comprised either by the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) or the path of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*);
the knowledge of non-arising is comprised solely by the path of advancement.
Furthermore, based upon this, five types of arhats are established; this is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Based upon this, one type of arhat is established; this is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Furthermore, both those of sharp and dull faculties who attain it obtain this knowledge of exhaustion.
Only those of sharp faculties attain this knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*);
this is what constitutes the distinction.
Question: What kind of knowledge is the initial knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)?
Some say this is the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna). Why is that?
The various practitioners of yoga contemplate the fruits of birth and death and thereby enter the noble path;
for by contemplating the fruits of birth and death, the noble path is fulfilled.
It is like shooting various birds and beasts with a poisoned arrow.
That poison first enters through the wound;
having gradually pervaded the entire body and performed its toxic effects,
at the time of death it exits once again through the wound.
The Noble Path is also like this.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"This is the subsequent knowledge of origin (samudaya-anvaya-jñāna). Why is that?"
All yogācāras contemplate the effects of birth and death in order to enter the noble path, and they contemplate the causes of birth and death because the noble path is fulfilled thereby;
thus, all birth and death are subsumed within effects and causes.
First one thoroughly knows the fruit,
and subsequently one thoroughly knows the cause;
thus, the path of birth and death is severed and no longer continues, which is called the "end of suffering."
The commentary states:

if one gives rise to the subsequent knowledge of origination, at that time one does not give rise to the subsequent knowledge of suffering, as stated in the Sūtra.

However, the term "birth" (jāti) manifests various meanings;
that is to say, some instances of the term "birth" manifest entry into the mother's womb,
while others manifest emergence from the mother's womb.
There are some births designated by names that manifest the five aggregates in their specific stages;

some births designated by names that manifest a portion of the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*); some births designated by names that manifest the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); and some births designated by names that manifest the process of entering the mother’s womb.
As it is said: "What is birth?
It refers to the birth and so forth of various sentient beings within their respective homogeneous classes (*nikāya-sabhāga*)."
"Birth" refers to entering, arising, and appearing.
Alternatively, "birth" may be defined as emerging from the mother's womb,
as it is said that when the Bodhisattva was first born, he immediately took seven steps.
There is a birth named "manifesting the five aggregates of the various states," as when it is said that there is birth with conditions.
There is also a name for birth.
To illustrate a portion of the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*):
as it is said, "What is birth?
It is the arising of the aggregates."
There are those whose birth is designated as the manifestation of the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
As it is said here, "My births have been exhausted. Now, one asks: what kind of birth is this exhaustion of?
Is it in the past, the future, or the present? If it exhausts past births, since past births have already ceased, what further remains to be exhausted?
If it exhausts future births...
If future birth has not yet arrived, what is there to be exhausted?
If it is present birth that is being exhausted,
since present birth does not abide, why would it need to be exhausted?
It is agreed that this statement is made because it exhausts births throughout the three periods of time. Why is this?
Because here, the term "birth" clearly refers to the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The yogācāras collectively contemplate the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
because the four aggregates of the three times are free from defilement therein,
the causes and effects of birth are rendered unable to be established.
The Venerable One said:
"Regarding the statement 'my births have been exhausted,' it is as the Blessed One has said: 'The Muni contemplates the exhaustion of birth.'"
This too should be questioned separately in the same manner,
and one should answer: "Until the end of future births," because the practitioner upholds the precepts and diligently cultivates the holy life.
All are for the purpose of obstructing and preventing the arising of birth in future lives.
For example, suppose there is a person who faces three calamities:
the first has already been experienced.
Second is what has been correctly received;
third is what is to be received.
As for those things already received, because they have already been received, they are no longer obstructed.
Those who have already received [the gift] cannot be turned back because they have already received it;
those who are about to receive it should be provided for with wealth or through the influence of friends.
Or by other skillful means,
one restrains it;
the practitioner does likewise.
Past births need not be prevented because they have already ceased;
present births cannot be prevented because they are currently being experienced;
future births are prevented by practicing correct application so that they never arise again.
Therefore, it is said that [craving] is exhausted.
"The holy life has been established" means that the untainted (anāsrava) practice has been established.
Question: Is it one who has established the holy life as a learner (*śaikṣa*), or is it one who has established the holy life as one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*)?
Answer: It is one who has established the holy life as a learner.
It is not the brahmacarya of one beyond training (aśaikṣa). Why is this?
Because the brahmacarya of one beyond training is only now being established.
"One who has accomplished what was to be done" means that all afflictions have been severed and all tasks to be performed have been brought to ultimate completion.
Because all paths have been blocked,
and furthermore, because the birth, aging, sickness, and death within all realms and destinies have been utterly exhausted,
it is called "having accomplished what was to be done."
"Not subject to further existence" (*anupādisesa*) reveals the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Question: Not all arhats attain the knowledge of non-arising.
For what reason do all the sūtras state at their outset that arhats will not undergo further existence?
Some offer this explanation:
The Buddha spoke according to what existed within the sūtras;
however, the compilers (saṃgītikāra) universally prefixed the title to the beginning of the sūtras.
Furthermore, those who compiled the Dharma all attained sublime qualities such as the knowledge resulting from vows (praṇidhijñāna) and the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
When observing the World-Honored One as he preached various sūtras,
if among the assembly of arhats there were those possessing the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna),
he would state that they would not undergo further existence; if there were none possessing the knowledge of non-arising, he would not so state.
Thus, it is not said that he will not undergo further existence.
Because those who recite it later do not properly distinguish this,
it is recited universally at the beginning of all sūtras.
The Venerable Ghosaka has stated this:
since all Arhats are free from further existence, they are collectively described as "not subject to future birth.
It is not, however, said that the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) itself is "not subject to future birth."
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"If the various afflictions have not been abandoned and have not been fully understood..."
None of them declared: "Birth has been exhausted for me;
the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished;
there will be no further existence."
If all afflictions have been abandoned and fully understood,
these are collectively described as: "My births are exhausted," up to "there will be no further existence."
Question: Regarding the statement "My births are exhausted...
[and] I shall not undergo further existence," one should ask for each instance: what kind of knowledge is this? Some say:
"My births are exhausted" is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
"The holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence"— this is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Some, however,
say that "birth has been exhausted and the holy life has been established" is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
"Having done what was to be done, there is no further existence"—this is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Furthermore, others say:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished"—this is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
The knowledge that there will be no further existence is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Question: For an Arhat liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*), when first giving rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), it lasts for only a single moment without interruption.
One will necessarily give rise to the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
Since there is not even the principle that the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) gives rise to the knowledge of non-arising immediately after two moments,
how much less could it be that the knowledge of non-arising arises only after three moments of the knowledge of exhaustion?
How is it that what is now said— "my births are exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished"— is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*),
while "there is no further existence" is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)?

Answer: Regarding the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) in a single moment, it is explained as threefold for the sake of its meaning; since this does not involve three moments, it does not contradict reason.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
In this context, the fourfold formula does not mention the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*,
nor does it mention the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*).

Rather, it provides a general praise, stating that for all Arhats, "all births are exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
These four kinds have no distinct intrinsic nature.
Some say that among these,
"my births are exhausted" is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
"The holy life has been established" is the knowledge of the path;
"what was to be done has been accomplished" is the knowledge of cessation;
"there is no further existence" is the knowledge of non-arising.
Some say that herein,
"my births are exhausted" is the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna),
and "the holy life has been established" is the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
That "what was to be done has been accomplished" is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
That "there will be no further existence" is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*). Some say:
In this context, "my births are exhausted" is the full knowledge of suffering;
"the holy life has been established" is the full knowledge of the path;
and "what was to be done has been accomplished" is the full knowledge of cessation.
"Not being subject to further existence" is the full comprehension of suffering.
Some say that herein,
"my births have been exhausted" is the contemplation of the origin [of suffering].
"The holy life has been established" is the contemplation of the path;
"what was to be done has been accomplished" is the contemplation of cessation;
"there will be no further existence" is the contemplation of suffering.
Some say that herein,
"my births have been exhausted" is the realization of the cessation [of suffering],
and "the holy life has been established" is the realization of the path.
"Having done what was to be done" is the realization of cessation;
"no further existence is to be undergone" is the realization of suffering. Some say:

In this context, "my births are exhausted" refers to the abandonment of the origin [of suffering]; "the holy life has been established" refers to the cultivation of the path; "what was to be done has been accomplished" refers to the realization of cessation;
and "there is no further existence hereafter" refers to the knowledge of suffering.
Some say that herein,
"my births have been exhausted" is the cause for relinquishment,
and "the holy life has been established" is the attainment of the Path.
"Having done what was to be done" is the realization of the fruit;
"no further existence hereafter" is the knowledge of the task accomplished. Some say:
In this context, "my births are exhausted" is the wishlessness regarding origination;
"the holy life has been established" is the wishlessness regarding the path;
and "what was to be done has been accomplished" is the signlessness regarding cessation.
"Not subject to further existence" refers to suffering, wishlessness, and emptiness.
Question: For what reason is it called "knowledge of exhaustion"?
Is it called "knowledge of exhaustion" because it takes exhaustion as its object?
Is it called "knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣayajñāna) because it arises within the body when the afflictions have been exhausted?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If it is called "knowledge of exhaustion" because it takes exhaustion as its object, [then...]
The knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) should take only the noble truth of cessation as its object;
it should not be said to take all four noble truths as its object.
If it is called the knowledge of exhaustion because it arises within the body when the afflictions have been exhausted, [then it takes only cessation as its object].
Then the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*) should also be called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*),
because they too arise within the body when the afflictions have been exhausted.
One should answer as follows:
Because it arises within the body only when afflictions have been exhausted, it is called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣayajñāna).
Question: If that were so, then the "knowledge of non-arising" (anutpādajñāna) and the "right view of one beyond training" (aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi) should also be called the knowledge of exhaustion.
Answer: If afflictions have been exhausted and [the knowledge] first arises and pervades the body, it is then called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣayajñāna).
Although the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi) is likewise pervasive, it is not its initial arising.
The knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) is not universally present,
because it is not attained by those who are liberated by occasion (samayavimukta).
Nor does it arise at the very beginning.
This is because it necessarily manifests only after the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). Some say:
"Because this takes exhaustion as its object, it is called the knowledge of exhaustion."
Question: Since this [knowledge] takes the Four Noble Truths as its object, why is it designated solely by the name "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*)?
Answer: Because exhaustion is preeminent, it alone is designated by that name.
That is to say, among the Four Noble Truths, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is the most excellent.
Because it has the nature of *nirvāṇa* and is virtuous and eternal, the wisdom that takes this as its object is established by name as "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*).
Question: Is there untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) that is apart from the sixteen aspects of the noble path?
If that were the case, what would be the fault? If it did exist,
why is it not mentioned in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*?
If [the knowledge of exhaustion] does not exist, how should one reconcile this with the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, which asks:
"What is the knowledge of exhaustion? It is: 'I have already known suffering;
I have already abandoned the origin.'"
Having realized cessation and having cultivated the path—
among those sixteen aspects, which ones are subsumed?
Furthermore, it is asked: what is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)?
It refers to the realization: "I have already known suffering and shall no longer know it," and so on, up to:
"I have already cultivated the path and shall no longer cultivate it."
Among those sixteen aspects, which ones are subsumed?
Furthermore, how is the *Saṃgītiparyāya* to be reconciled when it says:
"I have exhausted the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance; this is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)"?
He shall no longer give rise to this knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Among those sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), by which is it subsumed?
Furthermore, how is this reconciled with the *Dṛṣṭi-skandha* (Treatise on Views)?
As it is said: "When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is that one is experiencing a pleasant feeling.
Among these sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), by which are they subsumed?
Furthermore, how are the statements in the *Sūtra* to be reconciled?
Regarding the statement, "My births are exhausted...
[and so forth]... I shall not undergo further existence," among those sixteen aspects, by which aspect is it subsumed?
It is agreed that one should speak thus.
Apart from the sixteen aspects (ākāra), there is no separate untainted wisdom (anāsravaprajñā).
Question: If this is so, then...
[Question: One is well-versed in the *Śarīrapada-śāstra*;
how then should one interpret the *Prakaraṇapada-śāstra*?
[Answer: "I have already known suffering; I shall not know it again."
These are the four aspects of suffering.
That which has already abandoned the origin and will not abandon it again—
these are the four aspects of the origin.
"I have already realized cessation and shall not realize it again"—
this refers to the four aspects of cessation.
"I have already cultivated the path and shall not cultivate it again."
This path consists of four aspects.
Question: How is the *Saṃgītiparyāya* to be reconciled?
Answer: Knowing the exhaustion of the three outflows and that they will not arise again constitutes six aspects.
That is to say, there are four [aspects]: suffering, impermanence, and the two regarding origination from conditions.
Question: How is this further reconciled with the *Dṛṣṭiparyāya-varga* (Chapter on Views) of this treatise?
Answer: The intention of that [text] is not to state that one cognizes a pleasant feeling as pleasant.
It merely speaks of the four aspects of practice, such as "knowing that which is the path is itself the path.
[Question: How should one interpret what is stated in the sūtras?
[Answer: This statement is made on account of five kinds of conditions.
First, by way of application;
second, by way of counteractive;
third, by way of performing the task.
Fourth, because of continuity;
fifth, because of the *pudgala*.
Regarding "because of application":
It means that when the yoga practitioner first engages in the preliminary application, he forms this thought:
"I shall exhaust all births," up to and including, "I shall not undergo further existence."
Regarding "by way of the antidote":
this means that the yoga practitioner cultivates such an antidote so as to bring all births to an end.
"Even to the point of ensuring there is no further existence" refers to the yogācāra performing such an act.
"Exhausting all births up to not undergoing further existence through continuity" means that the yogācāra attains such a continuity whereby all births are brought to an end.
"Up to and including not being subject to further existence.
Regarding the "person" (pudgala):
it means that such a person is easy to perceive and easy to designate.
This refers to the exhaustion of all births up to the point of no further existence.
Based on these five conditions, the Sūtra states:
"My births have been exhausted... up to no further existence."
Such modes of activity do not exist within untainted contemplation;
rather, this conceptualization must arise subsequent to two types of knowledge.
Some have stated as follows:
There is also untainted wisdom that is free from the sixteen aspects.
Question: If this is so, it is well-reconciled with the *Prakaraṇapāda* and other treatises.
Why is it not mentioned in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*?
The answer is: that treatise explains those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) whose characteristics are presently functional and capable of performing superior activities.
If it were not so, that treatise would not have stated it. Furthermore,
if those characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) can lead one into the Noble Path,
attain the fruits, become free from defilement, and exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*), then that treatise explains them.
If it were not so, that treatise would not have stated it. Furthermore,

if the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are present in all four paths— namely, the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga), the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga), the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), and the path of excellence (viśeṣa-mārga)— then [the following applies].
That treatise explains it thus:

because the other aspects of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) can only be found in the distant path of preparation (*dūre prayoga-mārga*) and the distant path of further progress (*dūre viśeṣa-mārga*).
That treatise does not state this.
The critique says:
one should state it as follows.

If there were no untainted wisdom (anāsravaprajñā) apart from the sixteen aspects of the noble path, how could there be "the training in clear knowledge" (*vidyā-śikṣā*), and so forth, as explained at length?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra, the Buddha told a householder:
Just as you previously observed the Four Noble Truths with the wisdom of one in training, the vision of one in training, and the clarity of one in training,
so too does this youth Yaśas now observe the Four Noble Truths with the wisdom of one beyond training, the vision of one beyond training, and the clarity of one beyond training.
Therefore, this youth will certainly no longer take pleasure in dwelling at home,
accumulating assets, or enjoying the pleasures of the five senses;
although the sūtras speak thus.
Yet its meaning has not been analyzed.
This sutra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies;
that which was not previously explained therein shall now be explained here.
Furthermore, people in the world falsely cling to various incantations and treatises as true illumination (*vidyā*).

These include the *aṅga-vidyā*, *vastu-vidyā*, *mṛga-vidyā*, *pakṣi-vidyā*, *gauravī-vidyā*, *kṣaṇika-vidyā*, *gaṇḍarī-vidyā*, *tāraka-vidyā*, *kāka-vidyā*, *mayūra-vidyā*, *hastāṅkuśa-vidyā*, *nāga-bhujaṅga-vidyā*, *agni-vidyā*, *jala-vidyā*, and *mohana-vidyā*.
Furthermore, regarding various non-Buddhist treatises,
the world conceives of them as true illumination;
in order to refute that notion and to demonstrate that there exists a distinct, superior, ultimate true illumination, this treatise was composed.
What is the training in clear knowledge?
Answer: It is the training in wisdom;
that is, the untainted wisdom of one in the stage of training.
What is the knowledge of those in training?
Answer: It consists of the eight knowledges of those in training;
that is, the four dharma-knowledges and the four subsequent knowledges belonging to the stage of training.
What is the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-vidyā*)?
Answer: It is the wisdom of one beyond training;
that is, all untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) belonging to those at the stage of one beyond training.
What is the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*)?
Answer: It consists of the eight knowledges of one beyond training;
that is, the four knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the four subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*) belonging to the stage of one beyond training.
Question: For what reason is it called "clarity" (*vidyā*)?
Answer: It is called "clarity" because it penetrates and fully understands.
Question: If that is so, [then...]
If it is asked whether all wholesome, outflow-tainted wisdom that penetrates and understands should also be called "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*), the answer is:
only that which can penetrate and understand while also constituting a definitive discernment and direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the Four Noble Truths is termed "clear knowledge."

Although various wholesome, contaminated forms of wisdom can penetrate and comprehend [their objects], they are not called "clear knowledge" (vidyā) because they lack the definitive discernment and direct realization (abhisamaya) regarding the Four Noble Truths,
such as the wisdom comprised within the levels conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya).
Although it is extremely intense and sharp,
one has not yet been able to achieve decisive discernment or direct realization regarding the Four Noble Truths.
Because they have not yet attained the ultimate, true, decisive realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truths.
Furthermore, if one is able to penetrate and understand [the truths] so as not to be confused by ignorance,
doubt, or wrong views, and having severed views and doubt, does not allow them to arise again.
It does not increase the various states of existence characterized by birth, aging, sickness, and death;
it is not a matter of the view of a self-identity,
nor does it fall within the accumulation of suffering.
It does not increase ignorance;
that which is eternally free from the demons and spirits of the afflictions is called "clarity" (*vidyā*).
Although various wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) forms of wisdom can penetrate and comprehend [objects], they do not constitute this clarity.
Because it lacks other virtues, it is not called "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, all wholesome mundane wisdom (*prajñā*) pertains to both categories.
Therefore, it is not called "clarity" (*vidyā*).
This is because it functions as three conditions for both clarity and ignorance;
just as when a person interacts with both an enemy and a relative, they cannot be definitively termed a "relative."

Furthermore, all wholesome, outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) that coexists with the denial of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) is not called "clear knowledge" because it is subsumed under the categories of suffering, its origin, and the world.
Question: If wholesome, outflow-tainted wisdom is not called "clear knowledge," [why is this so?]
How should one interpret what is stated in the sūtras?
For example, it is said that there are three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*):
first, the realization through wisdom of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyāvidyā*).
Second is the clear realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth;
third is the clear realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
While the latter may be so, how can it be said of the former two?
Answer: Because the former two also possess a slight degree of clear manifestation, they are metaphorically termed "clarity" (*āloka*).
This is because they oppose the afflictions and are not intermingled with the afflictions.
Because it accords with the light of ultimate truth and because it induces the outflow-free light,
the Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
Among the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*), only the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) is ultimate clear knowledge;
the other two are designated as "clear knowledge" only figuratively because they lead to the attainment of ultimate clear knowledge.
Furthermore, the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) constitutes clear knowledge.
Because he has thoroughly penetrated and understood the phenomena of the past limit,
the knowledge and vision of death and rebirth is realized.
Because he has thoroughly penetrated and understood the phenomena of the future limit, [the knowledge and vision of the exhaustion of birth is realized].
The realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows is called "clarity," because it penetrates and fully understands the nature of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the first clear knowledge is so called because it knows the phenomena of forward progression regarding the past limit;
the second clear knowledge is so called because it knows the phenomena of forward progression regarding the future limit;
and the third clear knowledge is so called because it knows the phenomena of cessation.
All are said to be "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, the first clear knowledge removes ignorance regarding the past limit (*pūrvānta*),
while the second clear knowledge removes ignorance regarding the future limit (*aparānta*).
The third [type of] clarity (*vidyā*) is called clarity because it removes ignorance regarding *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, the first clarity is so called because it removes delusion regarding the aggregates (*skandha*).
The second clarifies the removal of delusion regarding sentient beings;
the third clarifies the removal of delusion regarding phenomena.
Both are described as "clarity" (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, the first knowledge clearly understands the prior limit of all sentient beings,
wherein they die there and are born here through the continuity of cause and effect based on such karma;
the second knowledge clearly understands the subsequent limit of all sentient beings.
By means of such karma, there is the continuity of cause and effect as one dies here and is born there;
thirdly, it clearly knows that by such a path, all sentient beings are able to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*) and sever the continuity of cause and effect.
Only this one type is the ultimate science (*paramārtha-vidyā*);
the former two types are conventional sciences (*saṃvṛti-vidyā*).
Furthermore, all three of these sciences are able to accord with the wearying rejection of saṃsāra.
Because they are all able to bring forth sublime qualities and all lead toward ultimate nirvāṇa,
they are called "clear insights" (vidyā).
In reality, however, clarity consists solely of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
Question: Why, among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), are three established as "clarity" (*vidyā*) while the other three are not?
Answer: The supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the divine realm functions like the spheres of craftsmanship;
the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the divine ear can only apprehend sound;

and the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of others' minds apprehends only specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and lacks superior utility; therefore, they are not established as "clear knowledges" (vidyā).
The latter three concentrations all possess superior utility, and are therefore established as "clear insights" (vidyā).
This superior utility means that they are all capable of conforming to and inducing weary detachment from birth and death.
All are able to induce sublime qualities;
all are able to lead toward ultimate nirvāṇa.
Question: Why do the latter three [concentrations] all possess this superior function?

The answer is: the fourth is the supernormal knowledge of the realization of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*), through which one deeply generates weary detachment upon seeing the events of the past;
the fifth is the supernormal knowledge of the realization of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*).
Seeing the phenomena of the future limit, he develops deep revulsion and detachment.
This is the sixth supernormal power, the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
Having developed revulsion and detachment, he takes joy in Nirvana.
By means of this, they are all able to accord with the renunciation of birth and death,
and even all are able to proceed toward ultimate nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, through the fourth supernormal knowledge, one perceives the events of one's own decline in the past and gives rise to profound weary detachment.
Through the fifth supernormal knowledge, one deeply generates weary detachment upon seeing the decline and loss of others in the future;
through the sixth supernormal knowledge, having already generated weary detachment, one takes delight in nirvāṇa.
For these reasons, all [of these] possess the three aforementioned superior functions.
Furthermore, through the fourth superknowledge, one deeply generates weary detachment by seeing the various successions of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases throughout the past;
through the fifth superknowledge, one deeply generates weary detachment by seeing the various disintegration and destruction of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases throughout the future.
Having already become weary of and detached from existence through the sixth supernormal power, one takes joy in nirvāṇa;
consequently, all [the powers] possess the three aforementioned superior functions.
Furthermore, the fourth supernormal power is able to eliminate the view of eternalism.
The fifth supernormal power is able to eliminate the view of annihilationism;
the sixth supernormal power, having already departed from the two extremes, abides in the Middle Way.
Consequently, both possess the three aforementioned superior functions.
Furthermore, the fourth supernormal power can induce the gate of liberation of emptiness;
the fifth supernormal power can induce the gate of liberation of wishlessness;
and the sixth supernormal power can induce the gate of liberation of signlessness.
Consequently, each of these possesses the three aforementioned superior functions.
Through such various causes and conditions,
all three subsequent supernormal powers possess superior functions.
Therefore, among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), they are specifically established as "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*). The *Saṃgītiparyāya* states:
"There are three kinds of clear knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣavidyā*)."
First, the realization through direct knowledge of the recollection of past lives of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
which is the knowledge beyond training that knows the continuity of the existences and conduct of all sentient beings.
Second, the realization through direct knowledge of death and rebirth of one beyond training.
This refers to the knowledge of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣajñāna*) that knows the superiority and inferiority of the karma of all sentient beings.
Third is the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyā*),
which refers to the knowledge of no-more-learning that knows the exhaustion of the outflows.

Question: Regarding the clear realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyā*), since it is a dharma of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*), it may be called the knowledge of one beyond training.
As for the preceding two clear realizations, they are dharmas that are neither of training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣadharma*).
How can it be said that this is the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*)?
The answer is: that treatise should state that there are three kinds of illumination of one beyond training (*aśaikṣavidyā*).
Furthermore, it should be described as the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*);
however, because it does not state this explicitly,
one should understand that it arises within the continuum of one beyond training.
The first two are also called "those beyond training" (aśaikṣa);
the intermediate terms have been omitted, as in the case of "ox-cart" and so forth.
This is as stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*.
There are two kinds of samādhi:
first, the noble (ārya), and second, the non-noble (anārya).
The noble [samādhi] further has three types: first, the wholesome with outflows (sāsrava-kuśala).
There are two types of untainted (*anāsrava*) and three types of non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Among these,
wholesome tainted (*sāsrava*) meditative absorptions are called "noble" (*ārya*) by virtue of being wholesome.
It is not because they are untainted (*anāsrava*) that they are called "noble" (*ārya*).
Rather, if an untainted concentration is both wholesome (*kuśala*) and untainted, it is called noble.
Although an unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) concentration is untainted, it is not called noble because it is not wholesome.
Furthermore, because it arises within the body of an Ārya, it is also called "Ārya.
This [knowledge] is likewise called "Aśaikṣa" because it arises within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
as well as being the knowledge of one beyond training.

Question: Since the two preceding types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) also exist in those at the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), why are they established as belonging exclusively to the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Answer: Because the meaning of "clarity" is preeminent in the stage beyond training.
That is to say, if one speaks of the superiority of the dharmas, it is the dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) that are superior, not those of those in training (śaikṣa).
If one speaks of the superiority of the person (pudgala),
it is the person beyond training who is superior, not the person in training.
Furthermore, because the knowledge of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is superior and unmixed with ignorance (*avidyā*),
whereas the knowledge of those in training (*śaikṣa*) is inferior and mixed with ignorance,
it is not established as "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*).
There are four kinds of sublime qualities:
first, penetration; second, clarity; third, power; and fourth, guidance.
Within the body of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna) is endowed with these four meanings.
That is to say: the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows,
the clear vision of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, and the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows.
Regarding the instruction and guidance for Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats who have attained the state beyond training,
the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows possesses three meanings.
This means that, with the exception of the meaning of "power," the other three are as previously described.
Within the body of a Tathāgata, the knowledge of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) and the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*) possess three kinds of meanings;
that is, with the exception of the demonstration (*prātihārya*), they possess the powers of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) and clear vision (*vidyā*).
The two types of knowledge belonging to the Pratyekabuddhas, the Aśaikṣa Śrāvakas, and those mentioned previously possess two meanings:
namely, they are supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and clarifications (*vidyā*), but not powers (*bala*) or demonstrations (*prātihārya*).
Furthermore, these exist within the bodies of those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
That is to say, the first two types of knowledge possess only the meaning of "pervasion" (abhijñā) and lack the other three types.
Some state that within the body of an Arhat liberated by occasion (samayavimukta), the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna) possesses only two meanings.
This refers to the path that provides guidance;
it is neither a power nor an illumination.
As for the other two knowledges, they possess only a single meaning each.
This means that it is common to all [three vehicles] and not otherwise.
Regarding the supernormal power of the knowledge of psychic travel and the knowledge of others' minds, within all bodies there are only two meanings:
namely, they are both supernormal powers and demonstrations.
Regarding the wisdom of the divine ear, within all bodies there is only one meaning, namely that it is pervasive and nothing else.

Question: For what reason is the wisdom within the body of a Tathāgata established as a power (*bala*), while the various wisdoms within the bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not so established?
Answer: The meaning of "power" (*bala*) is the sense of being invincible and unobstructed.
The various forms of knowledge within the bodies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are still subject to subjugation by ignorance.
Furthermore, because they possess obstructions, they are not called "powers.
It was once heard that while the Buddha and the Venerable Śāriputra were walking together in a certain place,
a sentient being approached them.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"You should observe where these sentient beings previously served as your close friends.
At that time, Śāriputra—
Whether by means of the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna,
one observes with the knowledge of recollecting past lives,
yet in all cases, nothing can be seen.
He then arose from concentration and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"By the power of my meditative concentration, I am unable to see it through observation.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
Such sentient beings were once your close friends many eons ago; because that time is so remote,
it is not within the sphere of experience of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and thus you do not know them.
On another occasion, the Buddha was walking for exercise together with Śāriputra.
At that time, a certain person died due to some circumstance.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"You should observe where he will be reborn.
Then, Śāriputra, by means of the first dhyāna, [observed].
Even when he observed with the divine eye of the fourth dhyāna,
he could not see them at all.
He then arose from his meditative absorption and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I cannot see this with my divine eye.
The Buddha told Śāriputra,
"When this person's life ends, they will be reborn in such-and-such a world."
Since that place is so remote, it is not within the sphere of experience of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; therefore, you do not know it.

Question: Since there is no difference between the three vehicles regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), why is the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows not considered a "power" (*bala*) for the two vehicles?
Answer: The Buddha’s knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows is supreme, wondrous, and sharp;
it is not to be equaled by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Although both have exhausted their outflows, there is a difference in the speed [of their attainment].
Suppose there are two people, each felling a tree.
One is courageous and strong, using a sharp axe;
the other is weak in strength, using a blunt axe.
Although both cut down trees, there is a difference between being swift and slow;
therefore, the Buddha’s knowledge of the destruction of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna) is established as a power (*bala*) that the two vehicles do not possess.
Furthermore, although the knowledge of the two vehicles can exhaust the outflows, [it does not constitute this power].
Because residual habits remain, it is not called a "power.
Furthermore, the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna) is established as a power not because it depends on being able to exhaust the outflows within one's own person.
It is solely based on the ability to cause the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya) in others;

that is to say, the Buddha thoroughly understands that such sentient beings should attain the exhaustion of outflows by relying on the path of difficult progress with sluggish intuition (duḥkhā pratipad dhandhābhijñā).
"Up to this point, such sentient beings should attain the exhaustion of outflows by relying on the path of swift progress characterized by ease;
for this purpose, he teaches the True Dharma through these skillful means."
Because they cause all outflows to be exhausted, they are designated as "powers" (*bala*);
the followers of the Two Vehicles do not do so, and therefore these are not called powers.
*Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 102.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 135,
composed by the Great Arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section Three of the *Jñānaskandha*, Part Five of the Sub-section on the Knowledge of Others' Minds within the Six Supernormal Powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Question: Regarding the six supernormal powers...
How many are insight but not guidance?
How many are guidance but not insight?
How many are both insight and guidance?
How many are neither *vidyā* (clear knowledge) nor *nairyāṇika* (leading to liberation)?
Answer: Two are both *vidyā* and not *nairyāṇika*;
namely, the supernormal power of the realization of the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*).
And the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth.
These two supernormal powers are demonstrations and guides, but they are not clear insights (*vidyā*);
namely, the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of miraculous feats (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*).
And the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of others' minds—
these one supernormal power is both a clear knowledge (*vidyā*) and a guide (*nairyāṇika*).
That is to say, the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*).
One supernormal power is neither illumination nor guidance;
this refers to the supernormal power of the divine ear-knowledge.
Question: For what reason are three of the six supernormal powers guidance, while the other three are not?
Answer: It is called "guidance" (nidarśana) because it displays rare and marvelous phenomena to cause others to believe and submit, thereby leading them into the True Dharma.
This meaning applies to the third [of the four reliances], whereas the other three do not.
That is to say, if one says of oneself: "I can hear from afar;
I can see from afar;
I can recollect various past lives."
They all gave rise to doubt as to whether it was false or true,
and did not immediately submit with faith; therefore,
this was not a demonstration or guidance.
I have heard that there was once a lay devotee who believed in the teachings of non-Buddhist outsiders.
He invited the son of the Nirgrantha and his followers to his home,
where he provided them with food and drink.
As soon as the Venerable Vatsīputra entered the house, he smiled.
The householder, wondering at this, asked, "Master, you have abandoned all agitation; why do you smile?"
He then replied, "I possess sublime virtues; how could you, who remain a householder, know them all?
Thereupon, the layman questioned him with great earnestness.
He then said, "On the banks of the Narmadā River, two monkeys were fighting incessantly;
they both fell into the river and were swept away by the current.
It was for this reason that I smiled out of compassion."
The householder praised him, saying,
"How truly rare!
The Great Master’s divine eye is so pure."
When the time for the meal arrived, the householder thought to himself,
"I shall test his truthfulness by means of the food.
He then covered the rice with the soup and first presented it to the teacher.
He poured broth over the rice and gave it to his disciple.
When the disciple had received it, he ate immediately, but the teacher did not eat.
The householder asked:
"For what reason, Great Master, do you alone not eat?
He replied, "Without broth, how can one eat it?
The householder then said:
"How marvelous is this divine eye!
It can see from afar yet cannot observe what is near.
At that time, the teachers and disciples of the non-Buddhist paths felt profound shame.
Therefore, the three [powers] beginning with the divine eye are not "guidances by demonstration" (ādeśanā-prātihārya),
because they consist of self-proclamation, distant hearing, and the ability to recollect the distant; furthermore,
they do not cause others to immediately gain faith and submission.
Since they do not have faith or submission, how can they be led to enter the True Dharma?

Therefore, these three are all not [proper] guidance. If, however, one were to manifest the supernormal power of the knowledge of psychic transformations (ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā), [they might be guided].
Transforming the one into many and the many into one, and so forth,
possessing sovereign mastery of supernatural power even up to the Brahma-world,
he causes many sentient beings to develop deep faith and submission, leading them into the True Dharma; therefore, this is called "guidance by demonstration."
If, for the purpose of manifesting the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds,
one were to explain the specific distinctions of another's thoughts and intentions,
and if what was thus explained were entirely true and not false, it would cause many sentient beings [to gain faith].
Because they lead those who have deep faith and submission into the True Dharma, it is called "guidance.
If one manifests the supernormal power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows,
one provides instruction and counsel according to what is appropriate for each.
May they swiftly realize the truths, becoming free from dust and defilement;
may the pure Dharma-eye arise regarding all phenomena,
continuing in succession until all outflows are forever exhausted.
It causes many sentient beings to develop deep faith and submission, leading them into the True Dharma;
therefore, it is called "instruction. One should ask: for what kind of *pudgala* should one manifest miraculous feats (*ṛddhiprātihārya*)?
Answer: It should not be manifested to those who have firm faith in the Buddha’s Dharma or to those who lack faith;
however, it should be manifested to those who are uncertain, thereby leading them into the True Dharma.
Because there is no other expedient means apart from this.
How is this known to be so?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
At one time, the Buddha was staying near the city of Nata-khaṇḍa,
in a grove of mango trees (āmra-vana) that surrounded it.
There was a son of a householder named Kevaddha.
He approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side, addressing the Buddha:
"In this city, all is peaceful, prosperous, and joyful;
many people possess deep faith and reverence for the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will allow one disciple to remain constantly in this place,
so as to manifest supernormal powers and demonstrate superhuman feats before the śramaṇas, brahmins, and others."
He caused those within this city who believed in the Buddha-dharma to redouble their firm faith,
and he caused even those non-believers who merely passed through to have faith in and accept the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the son of the householder, saying:
I have never, at any time, commanded my assembly of disciples to manifest supernatural transformations or display superhuman feats before other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
"However, I always instruct my assembly of disciples to conceal their own virtues and disclose their own faults.
At that time, the householder’s son spoke again to the Buddha:
If a disciple of the Buddha were to manifest miraculous feats before various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas to demonstrate superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*),
what fault or disadvantage would there be such that the Buddha did not permit it?
"If a disciple of the Buddha conceals his own virtues and discloses his own faults,
what merit is there for which the Buddha permits this?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the son of the householder:
I now ask you; answer as you see fit.
If my disciples, in the presence of various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, manifest supernormal feats—transforming one into many and many into one.
Even up to the Brahma world, they possess mastery through supernormal power.
Those who have faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, having witnessed this event,
speak these words to those who do not believe:
"How marvelous! The noble disciples of the World-Honored One are able to manifest such exceedingly rare phenomena.
At that time, those without faith said to those with faith:
What is so extraordinary about this?
There is a vidyā-mantra in the world called Gandharī;
one who properly upholds it can likewise manifest such illusions and deceptions.
"Who among those possessed of wisdom would perform such a base act?
The Buddha said to the son of the householder,
"What do you think?"
There were those who lacked faith and spoke thus to mock those who did have faith.
The son of a householder said:
"This is indeed true."
The World-Honored One further addressed the son of a householder, saying:
"If my disciples provide a declaration regarding the distinctions in the thoughts and intentions of others,
all that they declare shall be true and not false."
Those who have faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, having understood this matter,
speak these words to those who do not yet believe:
"How marvelous are the World-Honored One and his noble disciples!"
Thereupon, such a most rare occurrence took place.
At that time, those who lacked faith said to those who had faith, "What is so rare about this?
There is a world-renowned incantation called Kṣaṇika."
One who has properly mastered [these teachings] can likewise create such illusions and delusions.
What wise person would perform such a base act? The Buddha said to the householder’s son, "What do you think?"
There were those who lacked faith and spoke thus to deride the believers,
saying, "Householder's son,
such a thing truly exists."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the son of a householder:
"If my disciples, in the presence of various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
manifest miraculous feats and display superhuman dharmas..."
Because there are such faults and afflictions, I do not permit it.
If my disciples conceal their own virtues and disclose their own evils,
they will accord with the Dharma of the noble ones and be praised by the world.
Because he possesses such merit, I grant him permission.
For this reason, it should be known that one who possesses resolute faith and one who lacks faith should not be shown various miraculous feats.
If they are not yet settled [in the path], one should manifest them for them,
employing skillful means to lead them into the Buddha’s True Dharma.
In this sūtra, the Buddha explains three kinds of guidance for the son of a householder.
First, the demonstration through miraculous powers;
second, the demonstration through knowledge of others' minds;
third, the demonstration through instruction and admonition.
Question: For what reason is it called "guidance" (*nidarśana*)?
Answer: "Guiding" (*ni*) means manifesting;
"leading" (*darśana*) means leading forth.
It is called "guidance" (*nidarśana*) because it introduces beings into the True Dharma by manifesting rare and wondrous events;
it is like the title "gatekeeper" given to one who stands at the gate,
for a gatekeeper manifests what is within and leads outsiders inside.
To manifest external matters in order to guide internal people,
and to manifest internal matters in order to guide external people means that when the king is not bathing,
sleeping, eating, or viewing treasures, [the attendants] immediately lead him to see them.
"Manifesting external affairs to guide internal persons" means that when others observe the offering of rare treasures and exotic gifts from distant lands, they are led to accept them;
in this way, the subtle and wondrous merits within the Buddha’s True Dharma are manifested.
Because he guides and leads the sentient beings to be converted,
causing them to enter [the path], it is called "instruction" (*nidarśana*). Furthermore, this sutra states that the bodhisattva,
during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, respectively gives rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
Having aroused the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and the clear insights (*vidyā*), he attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment at the time when the stars appeared.
Question: For what reason does the Bodhisattva arouse the supernormal knowledges and clear insights during each of the first, middle, and last watches of the night?
Answer: Because for Bodhisattvas who have passed beyond [the number of] Ganges sands and are about to realize great enlightenment, the Dharma-nature is such that it must be so.
Furthermore, during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, they each give rise to supernormal knowledge and clear vision.
It is because he wishes to make his own person a fit vessel for the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is because he wishes to manifest supernormal transformations (*ṛddhi*) and thoroughly comprehend all phenomena.
Through these powers, he is able to manifest supernormal transformations.
Because clear insight can thoroughly comprehend phenomena,
one gives rise to supernormal knowledge (abhijñā).
Furthermore, it is because one desires to manifest and establish distant activities.
Because they universally manifest and firmly establish themselves,
and clearly illuminate distant activities,
they give rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and clear knowledge (*vidyā*).

Furthermore, just as there are the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), [the former] is like the path of uninterrupted transition, and [the latter] is like the path of liberation.
*Vidyā* (clear knowledge) is like the path of liberation.
Therefore, the supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) and clear insights (vidyā) arise.
Furthermore, just as there are the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga),
the supernormal knowledges are like the path of seeing.
Clarity is like the cultivation of the path;
therefore, supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) arises.
Furthermore, it is intended to reveal that which is wholesome, tainted (sāsrava), and non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
Because tainted, untainted, and pure dharmas are currently functional,
one gives rise to supernormal powers and clear knowledge.
As for wholesome tainted dharmas:
That is to say: the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the divine realm, and the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of recollecting past lives;
these are dharmas that are non-obscured and indeterminate.

The two supernormal powers consisting of the realization through the knowledge of the divine eye and the realization through the knowledge of the divine ear are both contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena.
The supernormal power consisting of the realization through the knowledge of others' minds refers to both contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena.
As for the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*),
they refer to the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*).
