Furthermore, it is for the purpose of successively subduing the enmity of Māra.
During the first, middle, and last watches of the night, he repeatedly rose to practice intense illumination.
Having previously heard that the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of practicing asceticism was not the true path,
he then accepted the sixteen-virtue-perfected honey-milk gruel offered by the sisters Nandā and Nandabalā.
Having eaten, his body and mind were peaceful and secure,
and he possessed strength. From the auspicious person, he received the auspicious grass (kuśa),
went to the Bodhi tree, and personally spread it out with his own hands.
Just as the Naga King Vasuki coils his body and sits in the full lotus posture,
having sat down, he makes this firm vow:
"If I do not exhaust all outflows here and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I vow never to rise."
At that time, the great earth, the vast oceans, and all the mountains shook in six ways;
like a light boat upon the sea rising and falling with the waves,
even the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven were shaken throughout.
Just as a fierce wind blows upon the leaves of a plantain tree,
the King of Māras was struck with alarm and watched for the cause of its trembling;
he then beheld the Bodhisattva sitting beneath the Bodhi tree.
Holding his body upright and remaining motionless, he vowed to attain bodhi.
He quickly departed from his palace and went to where the Bodhisattva was, saying to him:
"Son of a Kṣatriya, you may rise from this seat.
In this present age of defilement and evil, sentient beings are stubborn and fierce;
they will certainly not be able to realize unexcelled bodhi."
"Furthermore, you should now accept the position of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin);
I shall offer you the seven treasures.
The Bodhisattva replied:
What you have just said is like trying to lure a child;
one might as well cause the sun, moon, planets, and stars to fall,
or make the mountains, forests, and great earth ascend into the void.
"It is absolutely impossible that I would not attain great awakening and rise from this seat.
At that time, the Māra King said to the Bodhisattva:
"If you will not accept my gentle and sweet words,"
"In a mere moment, I shall cause you to witness a most terrifying sight.
Having spoken these words, he caused flowers to rain down and returned to his palace, where he issued a proclamation throughout the six heavens:
"All of you, quickly prepare bows, crossbows, swords, blades, battle-wheels, lassos, spears, javelins, halberds, and all other implements for combat!"
"I have a great enemy at the Bodhi tree;
I shall go with you all immediately to strike him down.
At that time, the Bodhisattva had this thought:
One should not treat even a fight with an ordinary person lightly,
let alone against Maheśvara, the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. Having reflected thus,
one should swiftly cultivate the path that is free from the defilement of desire.
Having become free from the defilements of the desire realm, he gives rise to the supernormal power of the divine ear and the knowledge of the movement of others' minds within the first dhyāna;
he then manifests various weapons for overcoming his adversaries.
If the demonic armies approach in the form of birds, [he manifests other forms to counter them].
If I should manifest in the form of a cat or a wildcat to oppose him,
and the Māra army manifests in the form of a cat or a wildcat,
I shall manifest in the form of a dog or a wolf to oppose them.
If the demonic armies take the form of dogs and wolves,
I shall manifest as a jackal or leopard to oppose them.
If the demonic armies take the form of jackals and leopards, [I shall manifest as their equal].
I should manifest in the form of a tiger to oppose them.
If the demonic armies come in the form of tigers,
I should manifest as a lion to oppose them.
If the demonic armies take the form of lions,
I shall manifest as dragon-unicorn warriors to oppose them;
if the demonic armies come as dragon-unicorns, [I shall manifest as their adversaries].
I should manifest fierce fire as an adversary against them.
If the Māra army should come forth with fierce fire,
I should manifest torrential rain as an adversary against it.
If the armies of Māra should come as a torrential rain,
I shall manifest as a great parasol to oppose them.
Such opposing forces are of immeasurable varieties.
He further manifested a firm platform of vaidūrya;
although his body was situated within it, he was able to see far off beneath the ground before his seat.
He then manifested the great elements capable of emitting the roar of thunder.
Having performed this transformation, he further thought to himself:
"May it not be that in my previous lives I obstructed others from practicing virtue.
Thereupon, he gave rise to the clear knowledge of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
He sees for himself that in his previous lives he never obstructed those practicing various forms of virtue,
but rather assisted them by providing all manner of requisites for such practice.
Furthermore, he reflects to himself:
He thought, "May my own wholesome karma not be inferior to that of the Māra.
Having reflected thus, he saw that in a previous life,
the Māra King had performed only a single unobstructed sacrificial assembly (*iṣṭi*).
In that assembly, there was a pratyekabuddha who,
by virtue of this wholesome karma, had now attained birth in the heavens;
he himself saw that in his previous life, he had established an unobstructed assembly.
Their number, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, is difficult to know;
likewise, the numbers of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others within those various assemblies are also difficult to know.
He then reflected further upon this.
Even the merit of my giving does not compare with theirs,
let alone their immeasurable wholesome karmas such as morality and meditative concentration, from which I am entirely excluded.
Having formed this thought:
With body upright and mind composed, he sat in solemn stillness.
Thereafter, the Māra King led thirty-six koṭis of māra armies,
each manifesting various terrifying forms.
Wielding an infinite variety of weapons,
they all rushed simultaneously toward the foot of the Bodhi tree over a distance of thirty-six yojanas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva addressed the Māra, saying:
"In the past, when you held but a single great assembly of offerings, such was its divine efficacy;
yet in ages gone by, I held an unrestricted assembly (an-avārīka-maṇḍala)."
Their number is hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, difficult to know;
as for the remaining merits, you have no share in them at all.
For what reason have you come here wishing to trouble us?
Then the Evil Māra said to the Bodhisattva,
"My merits have you as their witness; who,
in turn, can bear witness to your merits?"
The Bodhisattva then extended his hands, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, and struck the ground before his seat.
At that moment, the earth beneath him thundered like a roar and shook in six ways with a great sound.
Upon hearing this, Māra’s army was struck with terror and retreated in dispersal.
Realizing they were not enemies, each returned to their own palace.
Because of the karmic power accomplished by the Bodhisattva, his eyes and ears could perceive and hear from as far as one *yojana*; thus, the māra army was already at a great distance.
Desiring to hear what their voices had to say,
he then activated his divine ear; having heard their voices,
he desired to observe their forms to see what they were doing.
Having further aroused the divine eye and seen their forms,
he wished to know their thoughts; thus,
he aroused the knowledge of others' minds and perceived that the assembly of Śakra-devānām-indra had conceived a heart of joy.
The followers of the Māra King conceived feelings of jealousy and vexation.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva again reflected deeply:
"For what reason have these factions of Māra initiated such evil deeds?"
He realized that the arising of evil deeds is entirely conditioned by the five desires,
and that attachment to the five desires stems from the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Having come to loathe the afflictions, he subsequently exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).
Having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
he wished to successively subdue the enemies that are the Māras;
therefore, during each of the first, middle, and last watches of the night, he gave rise to supernormal powers and clear vision.
At the time of the clear realization of the truths, with respect to what does one first attain *avetyaprasāda*—
the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha?
Why was this treatise composed?
The answer is: it is for the purpose of refuting other schools and revealing the correct principle.
That is to say, there may be those who claim that the four noble truths are realized all at once, such as the Vibhajyavādins.
Question: For what reason does he make this statement?
Answer: He bases it on the sūtra, as the Blessed One has said:
If one has no doubt regarding the truth of suffering,
one likewise has no doubt regarding the truths of the origin, cessation, and the path;
thus, one is suddenly free from doubt concerning all four truths.
Therefore, one should know that clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is necessarily sudden and not gradual.
To refute that view and clarify the timing of clear realization,
it is established that with respect to the Four Noble Truths, it is necessarily gradual and not sudden.
If it were not so, it would contradict the sūtra.
As the sūtra says:
"The householder Anāthapiṇḍada came to where the Buddha was."
Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
regarding all practitioners of yoga..."
Regarding the four noble truths, is there sudden realization or gradual realization?
The Buddha told the householder:
"O practitioners of yoga..."
One realizes the four noble truths through a gradual meditative penetration, like the method of gradually ascending a ladder with four rungs.
Question: If one realizes the four truths gradually, [how is this so?]
How should one explain and resolve the sūtra cited by the Vibhajyavādins?
The answer is that the sūtra they cite should be stated as follows:
"If one has no doubt regarding the Truth of the Path."
Furthermore, one has no doubt regarding the truths of suffering, its origin, and its cessation;
however, one should understand that the reason this was not explicitly stated is due to a specific underlying intention.
That is to say, the sutra speaks of those who have already attained the fruit.
If one has no doubt regarding the truth of suffering,
one likewise has no doubt regarding the other three truths,
because all doubts concerning the four truths have been severed.
The Venerable Vasumitra stated as follows:
"The intention of that sutra is to say that doubt does not manifest."
That is to say, when a yoga practitioner has entered into the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truth of suffering and is free from doubt,
any doubts regarding the remaining three truths, even if not yet abandoned, will never again arise.
Because non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) has already been attained therein,
the Venerable One says:
"If one first attains entry into the state of correct nature and transcendence of birth (samyaktva-niyāma)."
Regarding all the jewels of the truths, these are called "present faith.
Question: That Venerable One also stated that when one attains the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the four noble truths, it is gradual rather than instantaneous;
why then do you now make this statement?

The answer to that is: if one abides in the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), and if one does not attain faith in all four truths, there is necessarily no sense of "abiding.
It is like carrying an earthen vessel up to the top of a multi-storied pavilion and then throwing it to the ground.
Just as when a vessel has not yet reached the ground, although it has not yet broken, it is nonetheless designated by the name "broken" because it is certain to break;
this case is likewise so.
Therefore, this treatise is composed in order to refute the assertions of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.
In this context, "Buddha" refers to all the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) within the Buddha's body.
The untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) directed toward them is called "purity of conviction regarding the Buddha" (*buddha-saṃpratyaya-viśuddhi*).
In this context, "dharmas" refers to the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training— such as the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*)— within the bodies of pratyekabuddhas;
and the various dharmas of training, such as the two untainted faculties, within the bodies of bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the untainted faith directed toward the three truths of suffering, origin, and cessation is called the "verified purity regarding the Dharma.
In this context, the "Saṅgha" refers to the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training within the community of Śrāvakas.
Because that untainted faith is called the "clarity of conviction regarding the Saṅgha.
All untainted precepts are called the "clarity of conviction regarding the precepts.
Because they are pure by nature and because they arise based on realization, they are also termed "clarities of conviction" (saddhā-vimokkha).
When one realizes the suffering, its origin, and its cessation, one first attains verified clarity regarding the Dharma.
When one realizes the Path, one first attains verified clarity regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
In this context, when one realizes suffering, one first attains verified clarity regarding the Dharma.
This refers to attaining untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) precisely regarding the phenomena of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma*).
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"At that time, one perceives the defects (*ādīnava*) within faith regarding suffering."
One also has faith that there is excellence in the cessation of suffering;
that is to say, this cessation of suffering is utterly pure and sublime.
How wonderful it is that such a lowly, base, and defiled cessation of suffering is so exceedingly blissful!
Regarding those who first attain verified clarity (avetyaprasāda) toward the dharmas at the time of the clear realization of the origin (samudaya-abhisamaya),
this refers to attaining untainted faith (anāsrava-śraddhā) specifically toward the dharma of the origin.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
At that time, there is a fault in faith regarding origination,
and there is also a benefit in faith regarding the cessation of origination;
that is to say, this cessation of origination is extremely pure and sublime.
Thus, it is truly a matter of great joy that this base, lowly, and defiled accumulation has been extinguished.
At the moment of the clear observation of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya*), one first attains verified clarity regarding the Dharma;
that is to say, one attains untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) precisely regarding the dharma of cessation.
Faith in the excellence of cessation is exceedingly pure and sublime;
that is to say, it is truly a matter of great joy that the conditioned phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are ultimately stilled.
Question: At the time of attaining the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the three Noble Truths...
Each and every one attains two kinds of verified purity (*avetyaprasāda*), namely faith (*śraddhā*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*). Why, then, is it said here that they attain only faith?
It should be said that they attain both; however, although they are not mentioned, [they are indeed attained].
It should be understood that this is an incomplete statement.
Furthermore, herein it is not merely asked who attains how many forms of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*),
but rather it is asked who attains how many verified clarities based upon which jewels.
Although it is not stated that the precepts have no object of focus when they are attained,
some say that regarding the Dharma,
one first attains verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*).
It is not said that one attains verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) only with respect to the dharma as an object;
rather, it is said that one attains verified clarity regarding the dharma.
This is because both faith and ethical discipline are obtained by reason of the Jewel of the Dharma.
All are termed "verified clarity regarding the Dharma" (dharmābhisampratyaya).
Regarding those who first attain verified clarity toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha at the time of the clear realization of the Path (mārgābhisamaya),
the masters of foreign lands (bahirdeśaka) speak as follows.
At the time of the clear realization of the Path,
during three moments, one possesses present faith and the concordant precepts;
it should be understood that these fully embody the meaning of the four types of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*).
That is to say, this very faith, because it takes as its object the dharmas of one beyond training within the body of a Buddha, is called "purification through faith in the Buddha.

Furthermore, this faith, because it takes as its objects the dharmas of both training and beyond training within the body of a Pratyekabuddha, as well as all the dharmas of training within the body of a Bodhisattva, is called "purification through faith in the Dharma."
This faith, furthermore, takes as its object the untainted dharmas within the person of a śrāvaka; therefore, it is called "verified clarity regarding the Saṃgha.
The morality that accords with this is called "verified clarity regarding morality.
[The author] critiques: one should not speak in that manner.
At that time, because faith currently takes as its object the untainted dharmas of all three vehicles in their totality,
it is comprised solely within the "pure confidence in the dharma" (*dharmābhisampratyaya*) that takes mixed objects; yet,
when this very faith manifests in the present, [it is so].
One also cultivates faith for many future moments.
Within these immeasurable moments of faith,
that which takes as its object only the Buddha’s dharmas beyond training is called "purity of conviction regarding the Buddha."
If there is that which takes as its object only the untainted dharmas of Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas,
it is subsumed under the "pure confidence in the Dharma" (*dharma-prasāda*) with unmixed objects.
If there is that which takes as its object only the śrāvaka’s dharmas of training and beyond-training within the Saṅgha, it is called "pure confidence in the Saṅgha."
If there are those who take as their object of focus the untainted dharmas within the bodies of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas;
or if there are those who take as their object of focus the untainted dharmas of Buddhas and Śrāvakas.
If there are those who take as their object of focus the untainted dharmas within the bodies of pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas;
or if there are those who take as their object of focus the untainted dharmas of Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas.
All of these are subsumed under the clear confidence in the Dharma as a mixed object.
The present and future faith that follows along with the precepts constitutes the clear confidence in the precepts.
This occurs, for example, during the three moments of the path-insight (*mārgābhisamaya*) within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It should be understood that the same applies at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
The difference is that it occurs in three moments.
One cultivates only the various forms of faith and morality that take the path as their object;
at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna),
one cultivates the various forms of faith and morality that take all four truths as their objects.
Question: The two truths of cessation and the path are matters of purification and are objects of trust;
at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), one can attain the purity of conviction (*avetyaprasāda*) regarding them.
The two truths of suffering and its origin are matters of defilement and are not objects of trust.
Because these afflictions are the basis for perverted and unwholesome conduct, how can one attain verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) at the time of direct realization (*abhisamaya*)?
Answer: One attains verified clarity by means of two conditions.
First, by way of being trustworthy;
second, by way of being worthy of pursuit.
Regarding the truths of cessation and the path, one attains verified clarity through both conditions.
Regarding the truths of suffering and its origin, one attains verified clarity through a single condition alone:
namely, that they are to be trusted rather than sought after,
just as when a person digs and excavates a place where treasure is known to exist.
In that case, there is faith but no seeking,
as when a person digs or excavates a place where there is no treasure.
In that case, there is faith but no seeking.
Although there are no such things as precious waters at this location,
one digs and excavates it for a specific purpose;
since this case is likewise so, there is no fault.
The Venerable Ghosaka spoke thus:
"All practitioners of yoga first perceive that suffering and its origin are fraught with defects."
Subsequently, one perceives the excellence of cessation and the path,
thinking: "This cessation and this path are exceedingly pure and sublime,
for they eternally stifle and eliminate such foul and evil truths of suffering and its origin."
By this means, although the practitioner has no further seeking regarding the truths of suffering and its origin, they nonetheless attain verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*).
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"All practitioners of yoga..."
Being oppressed by the truth of the origin of suffering,
one perceives excellence in cessation and the path; it is,
for example, like a person oppressed by wind and rain.
Thus, seeing that the chamber’s canopy is worthy of taking refuge,
even though there is nothing sought regarding suffering or its origin, one attains verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*).
This is the case for all practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*).
In all cases, one attains verified clarity regarding the truth of cessation through two conditions:
first, by virtue of its being trustworthy;
second, by virtue of its being worthy of pursuit.
It is not the case that the conviction of certainty regarding the Truth of the Path is attained through both conditions in all instances.
That is to say, for one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin), the conviction of certainty regarding the path of following by faith is attained through both conditions;
likewise, for one who follows by dharma (dharmānusārin), the conviction of certainty regarding the path of following by dharma is attained through both conditions.
One who practices in accordance with the Dharma attains verified clarity through two conditions on the path of practicing in accordance with the Dharma;
one who practices in accordance with faith attains verified clarity through only one condition on the path of practicing in accordance with faith.
This means that because it is trustworthy, it is not something to be sought after.
Regarding those with faith-resolve (śraddhādhimukta),
they [abide] in the path of faith-resolve and the path of one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Both are attained through two conditions.
For one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
the attainment of verified clarity (avetyaprasāda) regarding the factors of one who has attained vision is accomplished entirely through these two conditions.
For those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) on the path, they attain verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) by means of a single object alone;
that is to say, because it is something to be trusted rather than something to be sought after.
As for those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*):
At that time, both the path of occasional liberation and the path of non-occasional liberation attain verified clarity through two conditions.
As for those of non-occasional liberation:
On the path of non-periodic liberation (asamayavimukti),
one attains verified clarity (avetyaprasāda) by means of two conditions;
on the path of periodic liberation (samayavimukti), [one does so] by means of three.
However, one attains verified clarity through a single condition:
namely, that it is trustworthy and not something to be sought after.
This refers to those of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
In all three vehicles, one attains verified clarity through two conditions.

For those of the Pratyekabuddhayāna, they attain verified clarity regarding both their own vehicle and the vehicle above them through these two conditions; as for the Śrāvakayāna path, it is likewise.
However, one attains verified clarity through a single condition:
namely, that it is trustworthy and not something to be sought after.
This refers to those of the Buddha-vehicle.
Certainty of faith (avetyaprasāda) regarding the vehicle of the Buddhas is attained through two conditions,
whereas certainty of faith regarding the vehicles of the two [lesser] vehicles is attained through only one condition;
that is to say, because they are objects of trust rather than objects of personal seeking.
Question: If one gives rise to untainted faith (anāsrava-śraddhā) by taking as an object the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-dharma) within the body of Śāriputra,
is this the "verified clarity regarding the Dharma" (dharma-saṃpratyaya) or the "verified clarity regarding the Saṅgha" (saṅgha-saṃpratyaya)?
If that were the case, what would be the fault?
If it were the "verified confidence in the Dharma," how could it be called verified confidence in the Dharma when it arises taking the unlearned dharmas of the Śrāvakas as its object?
If it were the "verified confidence in the Saṃgha," [how could it be so when directed toward those same dharmas?]
How can a single *pudgala* be called a "community"?
It should be answered thus:
it is because of the "clarity of faith in the Saṃgha."
Question: Since he is solitary and alone, how can he be called a *saṃgha*?

Answer: Because that Śāriputra is the most honored and supreme among the followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle, although he is a single individual (*pudgala*), there is "pure confidence in the *saṃgha*" (*saṃgha-prasāda*) toward him.
Based on the Dharma, one establishes that there is no "non-person" (pudgala),
because untainted faith arises by taking the unlearned dharmas of the Śrāvaka vehicle as its object;
untainted faith does not take a conventionally designated sentient being as its object.
If, based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the previously unattained purity of conviction in the Buddha manifests,
one cultivates two purities of conviction in the present and four purities of conviction in the future.
When the verified confidence in the Buddha has previously been attained and is now present before one,
two verified confidences are cultivated in the present,
but none in the future.
It should be understood that this is likewise for those relying on the fourth dhyāna.
When one relies on a formless attainment (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and the previously unobtained faith in the Buddha (*buddha-prasāda*) manifests before them,
they cultivate one faith in the present.
In the future, one cultivates the four forms of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*).
When the verified confidence in the Buddha, previously attained, manifests in the present,
one cultivates one verified confidence in the present.
There is no future [existence].
Just as it is with the verified confidence in the Buddha,
one should know that the same applies to the other three verified confidences.
Regarding the distinctions:
within the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), there is no verified clarity regarding the precepts (*śīla-prasāda*).
Question: How are the four types of verified clarity established?
Is it by way of its own substance,
or by way of its object?
If it were by way of its own substance, there would be only two [types].
That is to say, faith and morality.
If categorized by their objects alone, there should be only three:
namely, the verified clarity regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Because morality has no objective referent,
it should be stated that it also exists by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, the four forms of verified confidence (śraddhā) are established by way of their objects;
that is to say, verified confidence in the precepts (śīla-prasāda) is established by way of its own essence.
Because ethical discipline has no object of focus (*ālambana*), the remaining three forms of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) are established by means of their objects of focus.
Since faith takes the Three Jewels as its object, it is established by means of its object just as it is established by means of its own essence (*svabhāva*).
It should be understood that the same applies to the establishment [of these] by way of their own essence, by way of the Three Jewels, by way of their own essence, and by way of recollection.
This is called the nature, the entity, the essence, the characteristic, the portion, and the fundamental nature of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*).
The intrinsic nature has already been explained; now its reason for being so named shall be discussed.
Question: Why is it called "verified purity" (*avetyaprasāda*)?
What is the meaning of "verified purity"?
The answer is: "Purity" refers to faith and ethical discipline because they are free from defilement.
One observes each of the four noble truths individually and deliberates upon them individually.
One realizes and attains this purity through distinct and individual awakening; therefore, it is called "verified purity" (*avetyaprasāda*).
The Venerable Pārśva said:
This should be called "indestructible.
Regarding the term "pure and indestructible":
it is so called because it cannot be destroyed by lack of faith or by various forms of immoral conduct.
"Purity" refers to pure faith, because it is the characteristic of the mind's purity;
"precepts" refer to the characteristic of the purity of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Thus did the Venerable Vasumitra speak.
This should be called "uninterrupted purity.
This means that once this has been attained, no śramaṇas, brahmins, or others have the power to draw it away, cause its severance, or bring about its destruction.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
This is called faith associated with vision as its root, with realization and wisdom;
it cannot be led away, stolen, severed, or destroyed by worldly śramaṇas, brahmins, and the like.
The Venerable One said:
If one is unable to observe, deliberate, realize, and awaken to the Buddha-dharma,
the faith and precepts obtained will be easily moved and shifted, like a boat upon the water.
If one is able to carefully observe, deliberate, realize, and awaken to the Buddha-dharma...
Because the faith and precepts thus obtained are immovable, like the banner of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*),
they should properly be called "immovable purity" (*akampya-śuddhi*).
The Venerable Ghosaka has stated this.
These four kinds should be called "purity of vision" (*dṛṣṭi-viśuddhi*), as they involve seeing the Four Noble Truths.
Because one attains this purity, or because it functions in conjunction with noble wisdom (*ārya-prajñā*), it should also be called "purity of wisdom.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One first speak of "purity of conviction regarding the Buddha"?
"Up until the later explanation regarding the purification through confidence in the precepts?
Answer: "If one were to speak thus, it would be because it accords with the sequence of the textual phrasing."
Furthermore, it is because they accord with the sequence of the speaker, the listener, and the upholder of the Dharma. Furthermore, since the Buddha is the speaker, he should come first;
since the Dharma is that which is spoken, it should follow next.
Faith in the Sangha should come next because it is that which is to be accomplished;
faith in the precepts is taught last because it is that upon which the Sangha abides.
Furthermore, the Buddha is like a skilled physician, and thus he should be mentioned first.
Faith in the Dharma is like being free from illness, and thus it should come next;
faith in the Saṃgha is like the caregiver, and thus it should come next;
faith in the precepts is like excellent medicine, and thus it is taught last.
Furthermore, the Buddha is like a caravan leader who can show the way; therefore, he should come first.
Faith in the Dharma is like a jewel island, for it is the true destination; therefore, it should come next.
Faith in the Sangha is like fellow travelers who can act as companions; therefore, it should come next.
Faith and precepts are mentioned last because they are like provisions that can properly sustain one.
Furthermore, since the Buddha is like a boatman, he should come first;
and since the Dharma is like the further shore, it should follow next.
Faith in the Saṃgha is like a vehicle, and thus it should follow [faith in the Dharma];
faith in the Śīla is like a boat or raft, and thus it is taught last.
For these reasons, these four forms of verified clarity (śraddhā-prasāda) follow this sequence.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"The morality cherished by the noble ones is unbroken, unperforated, unmixed, and untainted;
it is that which is practiced by the noble ones and not adopted by the ordinary."
It is praised by the wise, capable of being brought to ultimate perfection, and capable of being successfully induced.
Question: Why is it called "the morality beloved by the noble ones" (*āryakānta-śīla*)?
Answer: Because it is the locus upon which all these virtues depend.
It means that because the noble ones delight in meritorious qualities, they cherish this precept.
Just as a person who loves jewels also loves a jewel casket,
so too do the noble ones cherish this precept because they delight in the jewel-like merit of the pure factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

Furthermore, they cherish such a vessel of the precepts as their basis; moreover, noble ones loathe all forms of broken and evil precepts, for these precepts are able to counteract the breaking of precepts and evil conduct, and thus the noble ones cherish them.
Furthermore, noble ones loathe the precepts that lead to various perilous and evil destinies;
because these precepts enable one to transcend such perilous and evil destinies, noble ones cherish them.

Furthermore, noble ones loathe the precepts [associated with] the cyclic flow of birth and death; because these precepts enable one to transcend the cyclic flow of birth and death, noble ones cherish them.
Furthermore, noble ones cherish nirvāṇa;
because ethical discipline leads to nirvāṇa, the noble ones cherish it.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Ethical discipline can lead progressively toward nirvāṇa;
it is cherished by the noble ones.
Question: It is unbroken, unpierced, unmixed, and unsullied.
What is the distinction between these four propositions?
Some say there is no distinction;
these four types are as follows.
Although there are differences in expression, there is no distinction in meaning; as stated in the *Saṃgītiparyāya*,
one should constantly practice and constantly apply these various precepts.
Exhorting others to practice and exhorting them to turn [the wheel of Dharma] is also called "unbroken" and also called "unpierced."
It is also called "unmixed" and also called "untainted. Thus,
one should know that these four terms differ in sound but are identical in meaning.
Some say that these four also have distinctions;
namely, that the names themselves constitute the distinctions:
this name is not broken, this name is not pierced, this name is not mixed, and this name is not defiled.
Furthermore, because one does not transgress the first category of offenses, it is called "unbroken";
because one does not transgress the second category of offenses, it is called "unpierced";
and because one does not transgress the third and fourth categories of offenses, it is called "unmixed."
It is called "unstained" because one does not transgress the fifth category of offenses.
Furthermore, it is called "unbroken" because one does not transgress them,
and "uncorrupted" because one does not rely on craving.
It is called "unmixed" because it does not rely on hatred;
it is called "unstained" because it does not rely on delusion.
Furthermore, it is called "unbroken" because it does not transgress [the truth].
It is called "unpierced" because it relies on non-attachment;
it is called "unmixed" because it relies on non-hatred;
and it is called "unstained" because it relies on non-delusion.
Furthermore, it is called "unbroken" because it does not transgress;
it is called "unpierced" because it relies upon *śamatha*;
and it is called "unmixed" because it relies upon *vipaśyanā*.
It is called "unstained" because it is able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, it is called "unbroken" because it does not transgress [the precepts].
It is called "unpierced" because it is not damaged or destroyed by unwholesome thoughts (*akuśalavitarka*).
It is called "unmixed" because its own essence remains firm and stable;
it is called "unstained" because it is utterly pure.
Furthermore, it is called "indestructible" because its intrinsic nature is solid and strong.
It is called "unpierced" because it is far removed from what is not its proper sphere;
it is called "unmixed" because it is not interspersed with the evils of transgressing the precepts;
it is called "uncorrupted" because it does not abandon the noble intention.
Furthermore, it is stated herein:
that which is utilized by the noble ones is the basis upon which all such merits depend.
"It is not grasped by the non-superior" means that ordinary worldlings do not grasp this pure ethical discipline as the true path.
"It is praised by the wise."
Because it is praised by the Buddha and his disciples;
because those who can bring it to perfect completion achieve full fulfillment simultaneously.
"Capable of effectively inducing" means being able to bring about desirable fruits,
as stated in the Sūtra.
There is a great dragon-elephant who takes faith as its trunk,
relinquishment as its tusks,
and wisdom as its head.
With mindfulness as its neck, it carries upon its two shoulders the accumulation of wholesome qualities.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One say that faith is the hand?
Answer: Because they grasp wholesome dharmas.
Just as an elephant has a trunk with which it can grasp various objects, both sentient and insentient, so too the noble one possesses the hand of faith.
One is able to grasp various subtle and excellent dharmas;
for this reason, the World-Honored One has said that faith is the hand,
as stated in the Sūtra.
"O bhikṣus, you should know that from time to time four sounds arise among the devas.
What are these four?"
That is to say, if in this world there is a noble disciple who has achieved and frequently dwells in verified confidence in the Buddha,
at that time, because he has achieved verified confidence in the Buddha,
the devas rejoice, leap for joy, and cry out in a loud voice:
"Because I previously accomplished the verified clarity regarding the Buddha, I have come to be born here.
Now, because these noble disciples have accomplished and frequently dwell in the verified clarity regarding the Buddha,
they too shall be born within my own class of beings."
"It is truly a great joy to have you as my companion.
The detailed explanation regarding the accomplishment of and abiding in the other three forms of verified clarity (*śraddhā*) is likewise.
[The Buddha] asked: "Regarding these noble disciples and those devas..."
All are fully endowed with and have accomplished the four kinds of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*).
For what reason is it said that there are those who accomplish and frequently abide in the verified confidence in the Buddha, and so on,
up to those who accomplish and frequently abide in the verified confidence in the Dharma, the Sangha, and the precepts?
Answer: This is said with reference to entering the Dharma by means of practicing preparatory application (*prayoga*).

That is to say, there may be a practitioner who, seeking verified clarity regarding the Buddha (*buddha-prasāda*), diligently practices preparatory application and thereby enters the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).
Furthermore, there may be practitioners who,
seeking purity through the realization of the precepts and diligently applying themselves to spiritual cultivation,
enter the Noble Path; it is for this reason that such a statement is made.
Furthermore, this is explained in reliance upon the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of predominant delight.
That is to say, there may be a practitioner who predominantly delights in mental attention directed toward the Buddha as its object,
and so on, until there may be a practitioner who predominantly delights [in other objects].
This statement is made with reference to the mental attention directed toward ethical discipline (*śīla-manasikāra*).
As it is said in the Sūtra,
the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
If there are those who have faith and delight in what you have said,
you should, out of compassion, skillfully explain for them the four kinds of verified purity (*avetyaprasāda*),
exhorting them to abide therein and thereby achieve self-discipline.
Why is this? While the four great elements may be made to undergo change,
those who have accomplished these four kinds of verified clarity (avetyaprasāda) never undergo change.
Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One speak this sutra?
Answer: To demonstrate the proper procedure for a Dharma-preacher when preaching the Dharma;
that is to say, there are those who preach.
Not knowing whether the recipient is a worthy vessel or not,
one speaks to them with such levity that the recipient may either develop contempt or become timid and fearful, resulting in nothing being gained.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"If there are those who have faith and delight in what you say,
you should compassionately employ skillful means to explain it for them."
Do not treat this lightly.
Furthermore, it is shown that this is the true repayment of kindness,
as stated in other sutras.
"O bhikṣus, you should know that if there were a filial son who carried his father on one shoulder and his mother on the other,"
Even after wandering from place to place for a hundred years,
one still has not truly repaid the kindness of one's parents.
If there is a filial son who can exhort his parents...
Regarding the dharmas such as the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, cause, and effect,
he causes those who have not yet developed faith to believe, and those who already believe to increase in their faith;
and he exhorts those who lack pure ethical discipline to receive and uphold the precepts.
To those who possess stinginess and greed, they exhort the practice of giving;
to those who lack superior wisdom, they exhort the cultivation of superior wisdom,
causing them to dwell securely in virtue and thereby achieve self-subjugation.
This is what is called truly repaying the kindness of one's parents.
Therefore, this sutra teaches them by means of the Dharma.
[The interlocutor] asks: Among the teachings of all Buddhas, there are immeasurable kinds of precious jewels of merit and dharma.
All [of these] should be expounded to others through skillful means.
Why, then, is it that one is specifically instructed here to expound only the four forms of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*)?
It should be understood that among these, verified confidence is primary.
He generally caused him to explain all the treasures of merit.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"In this regard, O Blessed One..."
The noble paths are described by means of the term "verified purity" (avetyaprasāda);
that is to say, the noble paths are either associated with it or co-existent with it.
If "faith" is mentioned, it should be understood as referring collectively to the noble path associated with it;
if "precept" is mentioned, it should be understood as referring collectively to the noble path co-existent with it.
Furthermore, this briefly elucidates the initial entry into the gateway of the Dharma.
This refers to the various jewels of merit within the Buddha-dharma,
which may be either material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) or non-material phenomena (*arūpadharma*).
If one speaks of the precepts (*śīla*), it should be understood that these are collectively described as material jewel-like phenomena.
If one speaks of faith, it should be understood that this is a general statement concerning non-material dharmas (arūpadharma).
O Jewel,
as with the material and the non-material, so it is with the associated and the dissociated, and with those having a basis and those lacking a basis.
Having an object of focus or being without an object of focus;
having a mental aspect or being without a mental aspect;
being alert or being non-alert.
It should be understood that the same applies to the faculties (*indriya*) and non-faculties (*anindriya*), and so forth.
Furthermore, these four forms of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*) are specifically mentioned because they possess the characteristics of being indestructible and pure.
Moreover, they are based on the outflow (*niṣyanda*) induced by the four forms of verified confidence.
They are specifically mentioned because they represent the excellence of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, they are specifically mentioned because these four forms of verified clarity (avetyaprasāda) can bring an end to the fear of rebirth in evil destinies and the fear of poverty.
Because ethical discipline (*śīla*) can stop the fear of the miserable realms (*apāya*),
and faith (*śraddhā*) can stop the fear of poverty; thus,
although untainted (*anāsrava*) faith and discipline do not bring about karmic maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, because untainted faith and precepts necessarily induce and are induced by tainted faith and precepts,
they are able to ward off two kinds of fear.
Moreover, it is for the purpose of skillfully guiding and leading those externalist sentient beings who are capable of being transformed so that they may enter the Buddha-dharma.
This refers to cases where certain bhikṣus have relatives who,
out of affection, come to offer greetings while they are still followers of external paths;
at such times, the bhikṣus do not protect their feelings.
By praising the Buddha’s Dharma and disparaging non-Buddhist paths,
one causes those [non-believers] to harbor resentment and become further estranged from the Buddha’s Dharma;
therefore, the World-Honored One said to you bhikṣus:
One who lacks such qualities as power, fearlessness, and great compassion,
and who does not know the faculties, inclinations, dispositions, and conduct of sentient beings,
should not rashly preach the Dharma to others.
If there are those who have faith and delight in what you have said,
you should out of compassion skillfully explain for them the four kinds of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*),
exhorting them to abide therein and thereby achieve self-discipline.
Why is this? While the four great elements may be made to undergo change,
those who have accomplished these four kinds of verified clarity will never undergo change.
Question: Since the nature of all phenomena is entirely without change, why are only the four great elements mentioned?
Answer: It is because one wishes to manifest four phenomena by means of four phenomena.
Furthermore, the practitioners of yoga first contemplate that the primary elements possess no characteristic of transformation,
and subsequently contemplate that the nature of all phenomena is unchanging.
The mind becomes joyful, and for this reason they are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, because the four great elements are able to sustain all phenomena—both sentient and non-sentient—they are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, because the four great elements are able to sustain the entire cycle of birth and death, they are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, because the four great elements (mahābhūta) can sustain the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), preventing them from being severed, they are specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, various non-Buddhists (tīrthika) claim that there are five great elements whose nature is eternally abiding.
To counter that [view], the Buddha taught that there are only four [elements] and that they are impermanent.
Even if you were to maintain that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are permanent, they could still undergo transformation;
however, for one who has attained pure faith (*avetyaprasāda*), there is ultimately no transformation.
As stated in the sutra:
King Ajātaśatru was able to achieve rootless faith and questioned the Blessed One regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
There is nothing that does not possess roots.
Why, then, is it said that this faith is rootless?
Answer: Because this faith lacks the roots of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
"This is called faith associated with the root of vision, with realization, and with knowledge.
That is to say, the faith accomplished by Ajātaśatru does not rely on the path of vision; therefore, it is called "rootless."
Nevertheless, his faith is firm and difficult to destroy,
just like that which relies upon the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, the faith achieved by King Ajātaśatru is unalterable.
Just as there is untainted faith that lacks [ordinary] faculties,
all untainted faiths rely upon untainted faculties,
because they take untainted wisdom and untainted wholesome roots as their foundation.
Furthermore, this faith is said to be "rootless" because it lacks a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
This means that from time immemorial, one has not yet attained such firm and powerful faith.
It is like a tree that grows dependent on another's trunk; since it possesses no roots of its own, it is called a "rootless tree."
Furthermore, the faith accomplished by King Ajātaśatru is firm by its very nature;
because it is able to arise without depending on proximity to the Buddha or his disciples, it is called "rootless."
By the power of this faith, whether riding an elephant or a horse, or atop a high tower,
upon seeing the World-Honored One from afar, they immediately cast themselves down to prostrate at his two feet;
by the power of their firm faith or the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, they suffered no injury.
Furthermore, because the faith achieved by King Ajātaśatru has not yet escaped the miserable destinies, it is called "rootless.
This is because after his death, he will temporarily fall into hell, and only after experiencing a small amount of suffering there will he be reborn in heaven.
