translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Three: The Aggregate of Wisdom (Jñānaskandha); Sub-section Four: The Chapter on the Cultivation of Wisdom (Bhāvanājñāna), Part Two. There is a single wisdom that encompasses all wisdoms.
That is to say, dharma-knowledge is not [merely] "like" dharma-knowledge, because the essence of knowledge itself is dharma.
Alternatively, there are two types of knowledge that encompass all knowledge:
namely, contaminated knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*) and uncontaminated knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Alternatively, there are three types of knowledge that encompass all knowledge:
namely, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and conventional knowledge.
Alternatively, there are four types of knowledge that encompass all knowledge.
This refers to the addition of the knowledge of others' minds to the previous three knowledges.
Alternatively, there are five knowledges that encompass all knowledges:
namely, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Alternatively, there are six knowledges that encompass all knowledge,
namely the aforementioned five knowledges plus the knowledge of others' minds.
Alternatively, there are seven knowledges that encompass all knowledge.
This means that among the eight knowledges, with the exception of the knowledge of others' minds, there are instances where the eight knowledges encompass all knowledges;

namely, those mentioned here: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of origin, knowledge of cessation, and knowledge of the path.
Question: If these eight knowledges encompass all knowledge,
there are furthermore another eight knowledges,
namely, the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna).
The knowledge of nirvana,
the knowledge of death and rebirth,
and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
The knowledge of recollecting past abodes,
the sublime knowledge resulting from vows,
and the knowledge of exhaustion.
The knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Regarding these eight knowledges, by which [categories] of knowledge are they subsumed?
Answer: They are all subsumed within these [eight], as appropriate.
That is to say, the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna) is the knowledge of causes.
This is because it correctly knows the causes upon which the phenomena of the lower, middle, and superior fruits within the three realms depend.
That knowledge is subsumed within these four knowledges.
That is to say, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna).

Knowledge of nirvāṇa is the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna); that knowledge is subsumed within these four knowledges—namely, the knowledge of phenomena, the subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of cessation.
The knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*) is subsumed under this conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The Venerable Ghosaka states that the knowledge of death and rebirth is subsumed under four knowledges.

That is to say: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of subsequent types (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
The critique states: one should know that among these, the former explanation is the correct principle.
Regarding those who maintain that the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna) is so called because it takes the dharma of the destruction of the outflows as its object:

it is subsumed under four knowledges, namely, the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), and the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna).
For those who maintain that the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) is so called because the body has attained [this state],
it is subsumed under the eight knowledges.
The knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) is subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The Venerable Ghosaka states that the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) is comprised of six knowledges; that is,
among the eight knowledges, it excludes the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Because they take past phenomena as their object,
and because the knowledge of cessation takes conditioned phenomena as its object.
The commentary states:
It should be understood that among these, the former explanation is logical;
the knowledge of excellent vows (*praṇidhijñāna*) is subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The Venerable Ghosaka states that the knowledge of the excellence of vows (praṇidhijñāna) is subsumed under eight knowledges; that is,
among the ten knowledges, it excludes the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Because this is the nature of seeing.
The critique states:
It should be understood that among these, the former explanation is the one that accords with reason.
The knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) are both subsumed under six knowledges;
this excludes the knowledge of others' minds because it is not of the nature of vision,
and excludes conventional knowledge because it is untainted (anāsrava).
All knowledge is subsumed within these eight knowledges.
The Venerable Saṃghavasu said:
"One should speak of only a single knowledge."
This means that definitive knowledge is so called because the meaning of "definitive" is the meaning of "knowledge.
This definitive knowledge has two distinctions.
First, those with outflows;
second, those without outflows.
As for those with outflows:
It is called conventional knowledge by virtue of its intrinsic nature;
if it is untainted,
it is so called by virtue of its specific antidote.
Furthermore, two types are established:
that which counteracts the desire realm is called dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna),
and that which counteracts the form and formless realms is called subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
That is to say, if the aforementioned three knowledges can cognize the minds and mental factors of others, they are termed the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Furthermore, based on the distinctions among their aspects (*ākāra*), the untainted knowledges (*anāsravajñāna*) are further established as four knowledges.
If one proceeds by way of the four aspects regarding the truth of suffering, it is called the knowledge of suffering;
likewise, up to if one proceeds by way of the four aspects regarding the truth of the path, it is called the knowledge of the path.
Question: If decisive knowledge consists of only one, two, or three types, why are eight knowledges established herein?
Answer: Eight knowledges are established on account of five factors.
1. The knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge (dharmajñāna and anvayajñāna) are established by way of their respective antidotes;
2. conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is established by way of its intrinsic nature;
3. the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) is established by way of its preparatory application (prayoga).
The knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination are established by way of four aspects;
the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path are established by way of five aspects and their objects.
Thus spoke the Venerable Vātsīputra.
Eight types of knowledge are established in order to counteract four kinds of delusion.
These four kinds of delusion are:
first, delusion regarding the realms (*dhātu*).
1. Delusion regarding the mind; 2.
delusion regarding phenomena; 3.
delusion regarding the truths.
The knowledge of dharma and subsequent knowledge are established to counteract delusion regarding the [conditioned] realms;
the knowledge of others' minds is established to counteract delusion regarding the mind;
and conventional knowledge is established to counteract delusion regarding phenomena.
The knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path are established because they serve as antidotes to delusion regarding the truths.

This is called the essential nature of the eight knowledges. Having already explained their nature as self, substance, essence, characteristic, part, and fundamental nature, I shall now explain the reason for the essential nature of these knowledges.
Question: For what reason is it called "knowledge" (jñāna)?
What is the meaning of "knowledge"?
Answer: The meaning of certainty is the meaning of knowledge.
Question: If that were so, then wisdom associated with doubt should not be called "knowledge" (*jñāna*), because it is not determinate regarding its object of focus.
Answer: That too is knowledge, because even for a single moment, it is determinate regarding its object of focus.
However, within this aggregate, the force and function of doubt are predominant;
because they cause the mind to waver and fail to reach a decision regarding its object for many moments,
it is called the aggregate of doubt.
Just as samādhi remains constantly upon its object within a single moment,
if at times it becomes associated with restlessness (auddhatya),
causing it to shift from the object for many moments, this is called distraction (vikṣepa).
Furthermore, if a sentient being has much greed, they are said to be "greed-dominant" (rāga-carita);
if they have much anger, they are said to be "anger-dominant" (dveṣa-carita);
if they have much delusion, they are said to be "delusion-dominant" (moha-carita).
Each one does not lack other afflictions;
since this case is also like that, there is no fault.
Thus say the Dārṣṭāntikas.
If the mind possesses wisdom, there is no ignorance;
if the mind possesses doubt, there is no certainty;
if the mind possesses coarseness, there is no subtlety.
However, the dharma-characteristics taught by the Abhidharmikas are like a noisy thicket:
they claim that within a single moment of mind,
there is both cognition and non-cognition.
There is that which is neither knowledge nor ignorance;
there is doubt and there is certainty;
there is that which is neither doubt nor certainty.
There are those that are coarse,
those that are subtle, and those that are neither coarse nor subtle.
Thus say the masters of the Abhidharma treatises.
What fault is there in allowing that mental factors arise simultaneously?
It means that all mental factors arise through their mutual power within a single moment of mind, while their characteristics and functions are each distinct.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is called "non-cognition" (*ajñāna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) is neither cognition nor non-cognition.
This refers to other mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is indecision;
certainty (*niścaya*) is wisdom (*jñāna*).
Neither doubt nor certainty refers to the other mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
"Coarse" refers to *vitarka* (applied thought).
"Subtle" refers to investigation (*vicāra*).
That which is neither coarse nor subtle refers to the remaining mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
Just as various material phenomena arise simultaneously despite being of different categories,
so it is with mental factors;
therefore, there is no fault.
Some say that the meaning of "knowledge" (jñāna) is the sense of repeated definitive discernment regarding its object.
Because all contaminated wisdom (sāsravā prajñā) has repeatedly and repeatedly discerned its objects since beginningless time, it is all termed "knowledge."
All untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) that involves repeated discernment is termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Only untainted patience (*anāsravakṣānti*) regarding the four noble truths is not termed "knowledge," because it has not yet reached the stage of repeated discernment.
Furthermore, there are those who say that it is called "knowledge" (jñāna) for two reasons:
namely, the sense of realization and the sense of knowing.
And as for "thoroughly knowing the meaning":
"realizing the meaning" refers to realizing suffering up to realizing the path; therefore, it is called knowledge (*jñāna*).
To "thoroughly know the meaning" means that because one thoroughly knows one's own continuum and thoroughly knows the continua of others, it is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
Having already explained the general reasons for the various types of wisdom, the specific reasons for each shall now be discussed.
Question: For what reason is it called "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna)?
Answer: Because the essence of this knowledge is the dharma, it is called dharma-knowledge.
Question: If that is so, then the other knowledges are also essentially the dharma.
Why is it not called "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna)?
Answer: Although the essence of all knowledge is indeed dharma, the name "dharma-knowledge" is applied to only one of them, just as in the case of the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśadhātu).
The twelve bases,
the seven factors of enlightenment,
and the six recollections.
The four foundations of mindfulness,
the four types of verified confidence,
and the four analytical knowledges.
The Three Jewels and the Three Refuges all have the Dharma as their essence, yet the name "Dharma" is established specifically for one of them.
This case is likewise, and thus one should not find fault with it.
Furthermore, the term "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna) is merely a single name;
that is to say, it is a common designation.
The remaining wisdoms have two names,
namely, the common and the uncommon.
To distinguish them, the name "uncommon" is specified.
Furthermore, because one first cognizes the phenomena (dharma), it is called dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna);
because one subsequently cognizes the phenomena, it is called subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
Furthermore, if one attains the knowledge associated with the pure confidence (avetyaprasāda) regarding the phenomena for the first time, it is called dharma-knowledge.
Because it is obtained subsequent to this, it is called "subsequent knowledge" (anvaya-jñāna).
Furthermore, because one attains direct perceptual knowledge regarding phenomena that are directly perceived, it is called "dharma-knowledge" (dharma-jñāna).
Because it is obtained subsequent to this, it is called "subsequent knowledge" (anvaya-jñāna).
Furthermore, the desire realm contains many unrighteous afflictions,
namely the associated afflictions such as anger, enmity, concealment, resentment, jealousy, and stinginess.
If a wisdom is the direct antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to those [defilements], it is called "dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna*).

Since there are no such non-dharmic afflictions in the form and formless realms, the wisdom that arises subsequent to the antidote for them is called "subsequent knowledge" (*anvayajñāna*). Furthermore, if a wisdom is comprised within the six stages...
The knowledge that takes one stage as its object is called dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna).
If a knowledge is comprised within nine stages and takes eight stages as its object,
it is called subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
This is explained with reference to the contaminated stages (*sāsrava-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, if a cognition is comprised within six stages and is able to take those six stages as its object,
it is called "dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna*).
If wisdom is comprised within the nine stages and is able to take those nine stages as its object,
it is called "subsequent knowledge" (anvaya-jñāna).
This is explained with reference to the untainted (anāsrava) stages.
Furthermore, if a wisdom that serves as the antidote to the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas) is called dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna);
if a wisdom that serves as the antidote to fourteen elements, ten bases, and five aggregates is called subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
Furthermore, if wisdom serves as the antidote to the five aggregates that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, it is called dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna).
If wisdom serves as the antidote to the five aggregates that are wholesome or indeterminate, it is called subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
Furthermore, if wisdom serves as the antidote for those who practice meritorious, non-meritorious, or immovable deeds, it is called dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).
If wisdom serves as the antidote for those who practice both meritorious and immovable deeds, it is called subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

Furthermore, if knowledge that serves as the antidote to craving for food and sensual desire is called "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna), and if knowledge that serves as the antidote to craving for meditative absorptions is called "subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna).
Question: For what reason is it called "knowledge of others' minds" (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: It is called "knowledge of others' minds" (paracittajñāna) because it knows the minds of others.
Question: Since this also knows the various mental factors (caitta-dharma) of others, why is it called only "knowledge of others' minds"?
The answer is that it is because of the intention to know [the mind]. That is to say, a practitioner first gives rise to the aspiration (āśaya) desiring to know another's mind;
by virtue of this aspiration, when they subsequently know the mind, they also know the mental factors (caitta).
Just as when a person’s initial intention is to see the king,
upon later seeing the king they also see his ministers;
furthermore, phenomena receive their names due to the multiplicity of conditions.
That is to say, it may derive its name from its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
such as the truths (*satya*), the aggregates (*skandha*), or conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*);
or it may derive its name from its counteragent (*pratipakṣa*).

Just as with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), some are designated by their preparatory application (prayoga), such as the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna),
while others are designated by their associated mental factors (samprayukta).
As it is said:
"Phenomena associated with pleasant feeling and so forth are called phenomena conducive to pleasant feeling and so forth."
Alternatively, they may be designated by way of their basis,
as in the case of visual consciousness and so forth;
or they may be designated by way of their mode of activity.
Just as with the knowledge of suffering and its origin,
some are named after their objects,
such as the foundations of mindfulness and so forth.

Alternatively, it is named according to its mode of activity (*ākāra*) or its object (*ālambana*), as in the case of the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path. Furthermore, it is called "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*) by virtue of its preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Moreover, because the mind (*citta*) is predominant, although mental factors (*caitasika*) are also known, [the name is derived from the mind].
It is simply called "knowledge of others' minds," as in the expression "the king has arrived" and so forth.
Furthermore, it is because the mind is a universal mental factor (mahābhūmika).
Mental factors are called "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmika*).
Furthermore, because at the time of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the supernormal power of knowing others' minds, one takes only the mind as its object;
and furthermore, because it is said that the mind travels far and wanders alone, and so forth.
Furthermore, it is said that the mind is the precursor and so forth;
furthermore, it is said that the mind is the sovereign king;
furthermore, it is said that the mind is the lord of the city.
Furthermore, it is said that the mind is the basis of reliance;
furthermore, it is said that the mind can give rise to wholesome and unwholesome precepts;
furthermore, it is said that the mind can lead one to wholesome and unwholesome realms of existence.
Furthermore, mind is an internal sense-base (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) because it pervades all realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*) and possesses an object of perception (*sālambana*).
Furthermore, mind is the basis (*āśraya*) and not a mental factor (*caitta*).
Furthermore, wherever the mind operates, the mental factors follow it.
Furthermore, when the mind is disciplined or undisciplined,
all mental factors (caitta-dharma) are likewise so.
Furthermore, when the mind is distracted or not distracted...
Since all mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) are likewise [known] in this manner,
for these reasons, although this knowledge of others' minds also knows their mental factors, [it does not know them as objects].
It is called "knowledge of others' minds. Question: Why is it called "conventional knowledge" (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?
Answer: Because it knows the conventional, it is called conventional knowledge.
Question: Does it not also know the ultimate (*paramārtha*)?
Why is it called merely "conventional knowledge" (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)?

The answer is: although it also knows, to a small extent, various ultimate phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and the Four Noble Truths, it mostly knows [mundane things] such as men and women, coming and going, jars, clothing, vehicles, houses, forests, and mountains.
It is called conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) because it pertains to conventional phenomena.
Furthermore, although this conventional knowledge lacks the actual characteristic of knowledge,
worldly convention collectively establishes the name "knowledge" for it.
Just as among those who are not of royal lineage but are merely common people,
they collectively designate and establish the title "king" through conventional conceptualization;
furthermore, this conventional wisdom is universally accepted by all sentient beings without dispute.
Just as the *sthavira* of the Saṃgha is so called because he is pleasing to the multitude and is approved by the multitude,

it is for this reason termed "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*). Furthermore, this conventional knowledge is termed "conventional" because it pervades all sentient beings and takes all objects as its cognitive domain.
Furthermore, this conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is the basis for delusion;
it is bound to delusion and is the ground upon which those who are deluded stand. Therefore, it is called "conventional.
Etymologists state that this conventional knowledge is shrouded by various forms of ignorance.
It is called "conventional" (saṃvṛti) because it is like objects within a vessel that are covered and obscured by the vessel.
Furthermore, this conventional wisdom is called "conventional" because it is subverted by the path of its antidote, and because it is cherished by the ignorant.
Question: Why is it called the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), and so on up to the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)?
Answer: It is called the knowledge of suffering because it functions with respect to the four aspects (*ākāra*) of the noble truth of suffering.
It is called "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*) because it functions with respect to the noble truth of the path through its four aspects.

Question: Since conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is also able to take the four truths as its objects and function through each set of four aspects, would it not then also be called the [other] four knowledges?
Answer: If it takes only the Truth of Suffering as its object and proceeds by means of only four aspects, it is called the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
This continues up to: if it takes only the Truth of the Path as its object and proceeds by means of only four aspects, it is called the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
The various conventional knowledges take the four noble truths as their objects either by perceiving them individually one by one,
or by combining them two by two,
or by combining them three by three.
Either they take all four as their object collectively,
or they take other dharmas as their object,
or they take the mental aspects (ākāra) arising from those collective objects as their object.
Furthermore, because it is not determinate, it is not termed the knowledge of suffering, up to the knowledge of the path;
this is due to its being disordered.
Moreover, if one were to separately take the four truths as objects, each turning according to its four aspects.
Knowledge of the four truths is that which is not bound by the same fetters as suffering and its origin.
Although conventional knowledge also functions by taking each of the four truths as its distinct object and proceeding through their respective four aspects, [it is not so designated].
Yet, because it is bound by the same fetter as suffering and its origin, it is not called the knowledge of the Four Truths.
Question: This [knowledge] is not bound by the same fetter as cessation and the path.
Why are the knowledges of cessation and the path not established?
Answer: Because they were not established at the beginning, they are likewise not established later.
Furthermore, if [the knowledges] were to arise separately by taking each of the four truths as their objects with their respective four aspects, [they would be so established].
That which can counteract the afflictions is called the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths.

Although various conventional knowledges also arise by taking each of the Four Noble Truths as their respective objects and proceeding through their four respective aspects, [they do not constitute the knowledge of the truths].
Because it cannot counteract the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is not called the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths (*catur-āryasatya-jñāna*).
Furthermore, if one contemplates each of the Four Noble Truths individually through their respective four aspects (*ākāra*),
one will clearly realize and see the Four Noble Truths.
Not being deluded by the doubts and ignorance of views,
not increasing afflictions, and not summoning rebirth in the three realms of existence,
but resolutely proceeding toward nirvana— this is called the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths.
Because conventional knowledges do not possess such a meaning, they are not termed "knowledges of the four truths.
Furthermore, if one were to separately take the four truths as objects, each would proceed by way of its own four aspects.
This noble nature is termed the knowledge of the four truths.
Because various conventional knowledges are not subsumed under the noble nature, they are not termed the knowledge of the four truths.
Regarding these eight knowledges:
as for the knowledge of others' minds, if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it belongs to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) pervades the three realms.
The remaining six knowledges are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).
As for their stages (*bhūmi*), the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) resides in six stages.
Subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) exists in nine stages;
knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna) exists in four stages;
conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) exists in eighteen stages.
This refers to the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the dhyānas, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As for the remaining four knowledges (*jñāna*),
those subsumed under the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) reside in six stages.
That which is subsumed under subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) exists in the nine stages.
As for its basis:
dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) arises based solely on the desire realm.
The knowledge of others' minds arises only in dependence on the desire realm and the form realm.
Inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) both arise in dependence on all three realms.
As for the remaining knowledges, those subsumed under the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)...
That which arises based solely on the desire realm is subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*);
that which is subsumed under subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) arises based on all three realms.
Regarding the aspects (*ākāra*): both dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) perform the sixteen aspects.
As for uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) knowledge of others' minds, it performs the four aspects of the Path (*mārga*).
The tainted [knowledge] functions with indistinct modes of activity;
conventional knowledge functions with the sixteen modes of activity,
and also with other modes of activity.
The knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path each perform four aspects of mental application (*ākāra*).
Question: Do all instances of the knowledge of suffering function by performing the aspect of "suffering"?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold logical alternative (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There may be knowledge of suffering that does not function by way of the aspect of practicing suffering— that is,
knowledge of suffering that functions by way of the aspects of impermanence, emptiness, and non-self.
Or there may be that which functions by way of the aspect of practicing suffering but is not knowledge of suffering.
This refers to the factors associated with the knowledge of suffering that function by taking the aspect of suffering.
Alternatively, there is the knowledge of suffering itself which also functions by taking the aspect of suffering;
that is, the knowledge of suffering functioning by taking the aspect of suffering.
There are instances that are neither the knowledge of suffering nor do they function by way of the aspect of practicing the cultivation of suffering.
If one were to take only this category,
it refers to those factors associated with the knowledge of suffering that function by way of the aspects of impermanence (*anitya*), emptiness (*śūnya*), and non-self (*anātman*).
If one does not take only this specific category— that is, excluding the aforementioned characteristics—
one should know that there are likewise four propositions regarding what has already been transformed and what is yet to be transformed, just as there were for the turning [of the wheel].
Just as there are three sets of four propositions concerning the knowledge of suffering in relation to the aspect of the practice of suffering.
The same should be understood for the applications of mindfulness associated with impermanence, emptiness, and non-self.
Just as there are twelve phrases for the knowledge of suffering,
it should be known that the same applies to the knowledges of origination, cessation, and the path.
Thus, there are forty-eight four-line sets in total.
Regarding the objects of focus:
both dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge take the Four Truths as their objects.
The knowledge of others' minds takes as its object the mind and mental factors of others;
conventional knowledge takes all phenomena as its object;
and the knowledge of suffering takes the truth of suffering as its object.
The knowledge of origination takes the truth of origination as its object;
the knowledge of cessation takes the truth of cessation as its object;
and the knowledge of the path takes the truth of the path as its object.
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness:
the knowledge of others' minds consists of three foundations of mindfulness, excluding the foundation of mindfulness of the body;
the knowledge of cessation is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
The remaining knowledges pertain to all four foundations of mindfulness.
As for "knowledges," these eight knowledges are precisely the eight knowledges.
Regarding samādhi: dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) are associated with the three samādhis [emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness].
As for uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds, it is associated with the path-samādhi and the wishlessness-samādhi.
That which is with outflows is not associated with samādhi;
conventional knowledge is not associated with samādhi;
the knowledge of suffering is associated with the samādhis of emptiness and wishlessness.
The knowledge of origination is associated with the samādhi of the wishless regarding origination;
the knowledge of cessation is associated with the signless samādhi;
and the knowledge of the path is associated with the path and the wishless samādhi.
Regarding association with the faculties:
conventional knowledge is associated with five faculties;
the remaining knowledges are associated with three faculties.
These are pleasure, joy, and equanimity.
Regarding the three time periods:
these eight knowledges all pertain to the three time periods.
Regarding those that take the three periods of time as their object:
dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and conventional knowledge all take the three periods of time and that which is beyond time as their objects.
Knowledge of others' minds takes the past as its object when it is itself past.
The present takes the present as its object.
Future phenomena that are subject to arising take future phenomena not subject to arising as their object;
they take the three time periods as their objects.
The knowledge of cessation takes that which is transcendent as its object;
the remaining knowledges take the three periods of time as their objects.
As for what is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate:
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is of three types;
the remaining knowledges are exclusively wholesome.
They take as their objects the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
Subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) takes the wholesome and the indeterminate as its objects;
the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) take only the wholesome as their objects;
the remaining knowledges take all three types as their objects.
Regarding those bound to the three realms and those that are unbound:
the knowledge of others' minds, if it is with outflows, is bound to the form realm;
if it is without outflows, it is unbound.
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is bound to all three realms;
the remaining knowledges are unbound (anibaddha).

Regarding those that take as their object what is bound to the three realms and what is unbound: dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) takes as its object what is bound to the desire realm and what is unbound.
Subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) takes as its object that which is bound to the form and formless realms, as well as that which is unbound.
Knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna) takes as its object that which is bound to the desire and form realms, as well as that which is unbound.
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) takes as its object that which is bound to the three realms, as well as that which is unbound.
The knowledge of suffering and its origin takes as its object that which is bound to the three realms;
the knowledge of cessation and the path takes as its object that which is unbound.
These pertain to those in training, those beyond training, and those who are neither in training nor beyond training.
The supernormal knowledge of others' minds consists of three types of wisdom.
Conventional wisdom is exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
the remaining wisdoms are both learner and non-learner.
Regarding those conditioned by the trained (*śaikṣa*), the untrained (*aśaikṣa*), and that which is neither trained nor untrained:

the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) all take all three types as their objects.

The knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) take only that which is neither trained nor untrained as their object.

The knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) takes as its object that which is to be cultivated (śaikṣa), that which is beyond cultivation (aśaikṣa), that which is to be abandoned by vision (darśana-heya), that which is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), and that which is not to be abandoned (aheya).
As for the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), if it is with outflows (sāsrava), it is to be abandoned by cultivation.
If it is untainted (anāsrava), it is not to be abandoned;
conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is to be abandoned by both seeing and cultivation;
the remaining knowledges are not to be abandoned.
Regarding those [knowledges] that take as their objects what is abandoned by seeing and cultivation, or what is not abandoned:

the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), and the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) take all three types as their objects.
The knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna) and the knowledge of origin (samudayajñāna) take as their objects what is abandoned by seeing and cultivation.
The cessation and the path have non-interruption as their object.
Regarding the term "object" (ālambana), its meaning refers to the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna),
subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledges of suffering and origination (duḥkha-jñāna and samudaya-jñāna).
The [knowledge of] penetration takes both names and meanings as its objects;
other types of knowledge take only meanings as their objects.
As for that which takes as its objects those within one's own or another's continuum, or those not belonging to a continuum:
The dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and conventional knowledge take three types [of objects].

The knowledge of others' minds takes the mental continua of others as its object; the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path take the mental continua of both oneself and others as their objects;
and the knowledge of cessation takes that which is not a mental continuum as its object.
Regarding those obtained through application, obtained through detachment from defilement, and obtained by birth:
conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) pertains to all three types;
the remaining knowledges pertain to both application and detachment from defilement.
Regarding "that which was previously attained and that which was never before attained":
the supernormal power of the conventional knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna-saṃvṛtijñāna) involves both what was previously attained and what was never before attained;
the remaining knowledges involve only what was never before attained.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).
First, it is called dharma-knowledge because it knows the dharmas for the first time.
Second, it is called dharma-knowledge because it knows the dharmas directly in the present.
Third, it is called dharma-knowledge because it truly knows the dharmas;
fourth, it is called dharma-knowledge because it knows the renunciation from the dharmas.
Inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) likewise has four types.
First, one knows the effect by analogy with the cause;
second, one knows the cause by analogy with the effect;
third, one knows the mind by analogy with the actions of body and speech.
Fourth, one knows the Buddha by analogy with the Dharma he has taught.
The knowledge of others' minds also has four types;
that is, it arises from four conditions and can also serve as four conditions.
The objects known by this wisdom are likewise so.
Conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) also has four types.
The first is the conventional knowledge of names (*nāma-saṃvṛti*).
Second, knowing the conventional of bondage;
third, knowing the conventional of provisional designation;
fourth, knowing the conventional of attachment.
The knowledge of suffering also has four aspects: first, knowing the suffering of birth;
second, knowing the suffering of saṃsāra;
third, knowing the suffering of burning affliction.
Fourth is the knowledge of the harmony [of conditions] that constitutes suffering.
The knowledge of origination also has four kinds.
The first is the knowledge of karma.
Second, knowing the afflictions;
third, knowing craving;
fourth, knowing phenomena.
The knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) also has four aspects: first, knowing that the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) have been permanently severed;
second, knowing that greed, hatred, and delusion have been attenuated;
third, knowing that the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) have been exhausted.
Fourth, knowing that all fetters are exhausted.
Path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*) also has four types.
First, knowing all that is performed by the eighth type of person (*pudgala*) and all those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).
Second, knowing how to subdue enemies;
third, observing one's original actions;
fourth, observing the immediate exhaustion of outflows.
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) also has four types:
first, that which is not subsumed under [the category of] views;
second, that which is dissociated from the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatāsamādhi*).
Third, it is not the knowledge of others' minds.
Fourth, the preparatory application is sluggish.
The knowledge of non-arising also has four types.
First, because of the cause;
second, because of the fruit;
third, because of the continuity.
Regarding the four types of persons (*pudgala*):
the four knowledges (*jñāna*) such as the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) mentioned herein provide a general explanation of the various distinctions among the knowledges taught in the sūtras.
They are not all subsumed within the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and so forth.
Furthermore, one should explain that the ten knowledges collectively constitute a single knowledge;
that is, because all knowledge of phenomena has "phenomena" as its essential nature.
One should state that the ten knowledges collectively constitute a single knowledge;
namely, because all subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) belong to the category of the noble ones (*ārya*), one should state that the ten knowledges collectively constitute a single knowledge,
namely, definitive knowledge (*niścaya-jñāna*).
Since the meaning of "ascertainment" (*niścaya*) is the meaning of "knowledge" (*jñāna*),
one should speak of the ten knowledges collectively as a single knowledge; that is,
because the knowledge of the knowable (*jñeya-jñāna*) knows the knowable and because it is a repeated, critical ascertainment.
One should say that the ten knowledges collectively constitute a single knowledge;
that is to say, because the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) is subsumed within the truth of the path (mārgasatya).
One should say that the ten knowledges collectively constitute a single knowledge.
This means that because the knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) fulfills one's aspirations,
it should be stated that the ten knowledges collectively constitute a single knowledge; namely,
the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), because it is attained within the body of one whose afflictions have been exhausted.
One should explain that the ten knowledges collectively constitute a single knowledge,
namely, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), because it is non-retrogressive.
What is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)?

Answer: It is the untainted wisdom regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the desire realm, the causes of those conditioned phenomena, the cessation of those conditioned phenomena, and the path capable of severing those conditioned phenomena.
Herein, "conditioned phenomena" refers to the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
The cause of all conditioned phenomena refers to the truth of origination;
the cessation of all conditioned phenomena refers to...
The truth of cessation refers to the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). The path that is able to sever them is the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
The untainted wisdom that comprehends these four truths of the desire realm is collectively termed "dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna*).
Furthermore, the untainted wisdom pertaining to dharma-knowledge and the stage of dharma-knowledge is what is called dharma-knowledge.
Question: Why is this stated again?

Answer: Although it was previously stated that the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) can sever the various formations (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm, the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*), the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*) were not yet mentioned.
I shall now explain it.
Herein, "knowledge of phenomena" (dharmajñāna) refers to the knowledge of phenomena regarding the three paths.
The stage of dharma-knowledge refers to those dharmas that are associated with and co-existent with the dharma-knowledge of the three paths.
Furthermore, it is that which is capable of severing the path.
This refers to the dharma-knowledge of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
As for "dharma-knowledge," it refers to the dharma-knowledge of the remaining three paths.
The stage of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-bhūmi*) refers to the dharmas associated with and co-existent with the four paths of dharma-knowledge,
as well as the category of the four dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*).
Furthermore, regarding the path capable of abandonment:
this refers to the four untainted paths that are capable of abandoning the afflictions of the desire realm.
As for the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna):
This refers to the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) that arises and is cultivated at other times.
As for the "stage of dharma-knowledge" (dharma-jñāna-bhūmi),
it refers to those factors associated with and coexistent with it.
Subsequently, subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) should be understood by analogy with this.
The knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) and so forth are explained at length in the text;
their characteristics should be understood accordingly.
Regarding how many of the eight knowledges each of the knowledges—from dharma-knowledge up to path-knowledge—subsumes:
Why was this treatise composed? It is answered:
To refute the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.
This refers to those who hold the view that all phenomena are subsumed [by categories],
such that they subsume the nature of others but do not subsume their own nature;
for example, the Vibhajyavādins.
This treatise was composed in order to refute that attachment and to demonstrate that all phenomena are comprised of their own nature (*svabhāva*) and not comprised of the nature of others.
The underlying principle herein has already been analyzed at length in the *Saṃgītiparyāya* (The Compendium of Aggregates).

Answer: Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) subsumes dharma-knowledge and a portion of five other knowledges—namely, the knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
In this context, it is stated in general that dharma-knowledge subsumes dharma-knowledge.
However, the dharma-knowledge exists in six stages:
that which pertains to the threshold concentration (anāgamya) includes the threshold concentration,
up to that which pertains to the fourth dhyāna includes the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*):
namely, the knowledge of the truths, wherein the knowledge of suffering subsumes the knowledge of suffering, up to the knowledge of the path subsuming the knowledge of the path.
Moreover, dharma-knowledge exists throughout the three periods of time.
The past is subsumed by the past;
the future is subsumed by the future;
the present is subsumed by the present.
The past and future [moments] each consist of many kṣaṇas, each of which is self-contained.
As for the statement that this dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) includes a portion of the knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna),
it means that the knowledge of others' minds can be both with outflows (sāsrava) and without outflows (anāsrava).
There is that which is untainted (*anāsrava*). This [category] comprises only the untainted;
furthermore, within that untainted, there is the category of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*).
There is the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). This [category] comprises only the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*).
Therefore, it is said that it comprises a portion of the latter; that is, this dharma-knowledge comprises a portion of the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
That is to say, each of those four knowledges has its own category of dharma-knowledge and its own category of subsequent knowledge.
This refers exclusively to the category of dharma-knowledge;
therefore, it is said to subsume a small portion of that [knowledge].
Inferential knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) subsumes inferential knowledge itself and a small portion of five other knowledges.
This refers to the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Herein, it is stated in general that conventional knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) subsumes conventional knowledge;
however, conventional knowledge exists in nine stages.
Those who possess the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi) are included among those who possess the preparatory concentration;
likewise, up to those who possess the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), they are included among those who possess the sphere of nothingness.
The rest is explained in detail as in the case of the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna).
The knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) subsumes a portion of four knowledges:

namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). These are stated here in general terms.
Within this context, the knowledge of others' minds is itself subsumed by the knowledge of others' minds.
However, the knowledge of others' minds within the four fundamental dhyānas is comprised by those belonging to the first dhyāna up to those belonging to the fourth dhyāna,
which is comprised by those belonging to the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
That which is contaminated is subsumed under the contaminated;
that which is uncontaminated is subsumed under the uncontaminated. Regarding this contaminated [knowledge]:
There is that which has been previously attained and that which has not been previously attained.
That which has been previously attained is subsumed under "previously attained," and that which has not been previously attained is subsumed under "not previously attained."
This untainted [knowledge] consists of the category of dharma-knowledge and the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
The category of dharma-knowledge subsumes the category of dharma-knowledge;
the category of subsequent knowledge subsumes the category of subsequent knowledge.
Furthermore, this supernormal knowledge of others' minds spans the three periods of time:
that which pertains to the past encompasses the past,
and that which pertains to the future encompasses the future.
The present [knowledge] subsumes the present;
the past and future each subsume their own respective many moments.
Thus, this knowledge of others' minds subsumes a small portion of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
That is to say, dharma-knowledge exists in six stages;
however, this [text] includes it only as being present in the four fundamental dhyānas.
Furthermore, dharma-knowledge is of four kinds.
This refers to the knowledge of the four truths.
This [knowledge] comprises only that knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Furthermore, regarding that knowledge of the path:
There are those that have specific objects of focus,
those that have general objects of focus,
and those that have the present as their object.
There are those that have the past and future as their object;
there are those that have one's own continuum as their object;
and there are those that have another's continuum as their object.
Regarding those mental states and mental factors that have an object (*sālambana*),
some have the other aggregates as their object.
Since these [factors] exclusively comprise those distinct present mental states and mental factors belonging to another continuum, it is said that they comprise a small portion of them.
As it is said:
"This describes a small portion of the knowledge of inclusion (*saṃgraha-jñāna*);
the description of a small portion of the knowledge of inclusion of categories (*anvaya-jñāna*) is likewise."
Regarding the distinction:
one should state that subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) exists in nine stages;
this [text], however, includes it only within the four fundamental dhyānas.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that this knowledge of others' minds encompasses a portion of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*):
conventional knowledge exists in eighteen stages (*bhūmi*),
whereas this [knowledge of others' minds] encompasses only that which resides in the four fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*).
Furthermore, conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) is of three types: wholesome, afflicted, and non-obscured neutral.
This [knowledge] here comprises only its wholesome variety;
moreover, among those wholesome varieties, it includes only that which has a distinct object.
Regarding those that take [objects] collectively, the detailed explanation is as previously stated.
Since these only include those that take as their objects the mind and mental factors of other continua in the present,
it is said that they include only a small portion of those.
Furthermore, regarding the fact that this knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) subsumes a small portion of the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna):
the knowledge of the path exists in nine stages,
whereas this [knowledge of others' minds] subsumes only that which resides in the four fundamental dhyānas.
Furthermore, regarding that knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), there is that which has specific objects and that which has general objects;
this is explained in detail as previously stated.

Because this [category] only includes those mental states and mental factors belonging to other continua that are presently perceived through specific conditions, it is said to include only a small portion of them.
As for conventional knowledge including conventional knowledge and a small portion of the knowledge of others' minds: [it is because] it includes those very same [states].
In this context, it is stated in general that conventional knowledge subsumes conventional knowledge;
however, conventional knowledge exists in eighteen stages,
wherein that which belongs to the desire realm subsumes that which belongs to the desire realm.
"Up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" includes that which belongs to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) is wholesome, defiled, or non-obscured neutral.
The wholesome includes the wholesome;
the defiled includes the defiled;
and the non-obscured neutral includes the non-obscured neutral.
Furthermore, conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) extends across the three periods of time:
that which belongs to the past encompasses the past,
and that which belongs to the future encompasses the future.
The present is subsumed by the present;
the past and future each subsume their own respective moments in great number.
Furthermore, regarding how conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) subsumes a small portion of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*):
That is to say, the knowledge of others' minds is both with outflows (sāsrava) and without outflows (anāsrava).
Because this [knowledge] subsumes only those [knowledges] that are with outflows (sāsrava), it is said to subsume only a small portion of them.
The knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) subsumes a small portion of two knowledges: the knowledge of suffering itself and [the knowledge of origination].
Regarding the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna):
herein it is stated in general that the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna) subsumes the knowledge of suffering;
however, the knowledge of suffering exists in nine stages.
Those who have attained the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi) are included among those who have attained the preparatory concentration;
likewise, up to those who have attained the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), they are included among those who have attained the sphere of nothingness.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that this knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) subsumes a portion of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*):
since the knowledge of phenomena comprises the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path,
it is said to subsume a portion of those because it subsumes only the knowledge of suffering among them.
As it has been said:
"This explains a portion of the knowledge of inclusion (*saṃgraha-jñāna*);
the explanation of a portion of the knowledge of inclusion of categories (*anvaya-jñāna*) is likewise."
Just as the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) subsumes one knowledge and a portion of two knowledges,
it should be understood that the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) are likewise.
The knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) subsumes the knowledge of the path and a portion of three knowledges.
This refers to those who possess the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Herein, it is stated in general that the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) subsumes the knowledge of the path;
however, this knowledge of the path resides in nine stages (*bhūmi*).
Those who have attained the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna) include those who have attained the preparatory concentration; likewise,
up to those who have attained the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana),
they include those who have attained the sphere of nothingness.
The rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, regarding how this knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) subsumes a portion of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*),
it is to be understood in the same manner as the previous explanation of how the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) subsumes a portion of the knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that this knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) subsumes a portion of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna):
the knowledge of others' minds is both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava);
this [knowledge of the path] subsumes only its uncontaminated aspect.
Therefore, it is said that they encompass a small portion of those [dharmas].
Herein, "encompassing" means encompassing their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The intrinsic nature is truly obtainable within the intrinsic nature;
being neither separate nor detached, it is eternally present and not empty.
Because it constantly acts as an obstruction, it is said to be "encompassing."
"If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was in order to refute the doctrines of other schools and to manifest the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that there is no real nature of accomplishment or non-accomplishment,
such as the Dārṣṭāntikas.

This treatise is composed to refute that attachment and to demonstrate that the nature of possession (*prāpti*) and the nature of non-possession (*aprāpti*) are definitively and substantially existent.
Regarding the knowledge of the factors of possession among these eight knowledges:
How many are accomplished and how many are not accomplished?

Answer: It may be three, four, five, six, seven, or eight. That is to say, at the time of the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* (knowledge of the dharma of suffering) and the *duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti* (receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering), when there is no *para-citta-jñāna* (knowledge of others' minds), one accomplishes three.
One who possesses the knowledge of others' minds accomplishes four [knowledges].
Among these, three are the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna),
the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna), and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
The fourth consists of the aforementioned three plus the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
If one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire enters into the state of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*), [these four are cultivated].
At that time, one possesses three.
If one has already become free from the defilement of desire and has entered the state of rightness and departure from birth,
at that time one possesses four.
All subsequent explanations should be understood according to this principle.
At the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna), one accomplishes both dharma-knowledge and the knowledge of suffering in the present and future.
That is to say, the single essence of wisdom is called "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna) by virtue of its function as an antidote;
it is called "knowledge of suffering" (duḥkhajñāna) by virtue of its cognitive aspect (ākāra).
Conventional knowledge and knowledge of others' minds are established with respect to the past and the future.
At the time of the patience of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti),
there is an increase in vision, an increase in wisdom, and an increase in the path;
it is neither knowledge nor a designation.
At that time, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna),
or the knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna) all exclusively accomplish [the past and future],
because they do not exist in the present.
Subsequent explanations should be understood according to this principle.
At the moment of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the dharma-knowledge-receptivity regarding origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*),
one who possesses the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) accomplishes four knowledges.
There are five [knowledges] accomplished by the knowledge of others' minds.
Among these, four are the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Fifth: this refers to the four aforementioned [knowledges] plus the knowledge of others' minds.

At the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), there is an increase in vision, an increase in wisdom, an increase in the path, and an increase in knowledge; thus it receives its name.
This means that when the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is designated as "knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-jñāna*),
it is because it has already been obtained at the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*).
At the stage of the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the path of insight-wisdom (*darśana-prajñā-mārga*) is augmented.
It is neither knowledge nor designation.

At the time of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origination up to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation, there is no knowledge of others' minds; one accomplishes five.
One who possesses the knowledge of others' minds accomplishes six [knowledges].

Among these, five are: the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna), and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
Sixth: this refers to the aforementioned five [knowledges] plus the knowledge of others' minds.
At the time of the arising of the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*), the designation "vision" (*darśana*) and "wisdom" (*prajñā*) are added to the path and its name.
This means that the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) is called the dharma-knowledge of this [truth],
because it has already been attained at the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna).

This is also the case at the time of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of origin (samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti), the subsequent knowledge of origin (samudaya-anvaya-jñāna), and the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation (nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti).
The path of increased vision and wisdom is neither knowledge nor a designation.
Why is this? It is because the name "knowledge of origin" is applied at the time when one attains the "subsequent knowledge of origin."

This is because the name "subsequent knowledge of origin" obtained at that time is not different from the name "subsequent knowledge of origin" obtained at the time of the knowledge of origin regarding suffering;
and the name "subsequent knowledge" obtained at that time is not different from the name "subsequent knowledge" obtained at the time of the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering.
At the time of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of cessation up to the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of the path,
one who lacks the knowledge of others' minds possesses six;
one who possesses the knowledge of others' minds possesses seven.
Among these, the six are the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna),

inferential knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna). The seventh is...
This means that to the previous six [knowledges], the knowledge of others' minds is added.
At the moment of the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*), the designation "vision" (*darśana*) and "wisdom" (*prajñā*) are added to the name "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
That is to say, the name "knowledge of cessation" (*nirodhajñāna*) refers to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñānakṣānti*).

At the moment of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path (mārga-dharmajñānakṣānti) within the category of cessation (nirodha-anvayajñāna), one increases the vision-wisdom of the path (darśana-prajñā-mārga).
It is neither knowledge (jñāna) nor a designation (nāman). Why is this so?

The name "subsequent knowledge of cessation" (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna) obtained at the time of [attaining] the subsequent knowledge of cessation is not different from the name "knowledge of cessation" (nirodha-jñāna) obtained at the time of the knowledge of cessation regarding phenomena (dharma-jñāna); therefore,
it is designated by the name "subsequent knowledge" at that time.
Because there is no difference in the designation of "subsequent knowledge" (anvaya-jñāna) obtained at the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering.
From the time of the dharma-knowledge of the path up until the subsequent knowledge of the path,
when one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, one accomplishes seven knowledges.
There are eight [knowledges] accomplished by one who possesses the knowledge of others' minds.
Among these, seven are comprised of the eight knowledges with the exception of the knowledge of others' minds.
Eighth: this refers to the addition of the knowledge of others' minds to the preceding seven;
at the time of the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), the designation "vision," "wisdom," and "knowledge" is added to the path.
That is to say, the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) is termed the acceptance of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti).
At the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path, the wisdom of vision (darśanaprajñā) increases within the path;
it is neither [ordinary] knowledge nor a name.

Why is this? Because the designation "path-knowledge" (mārgajñāna) obtained at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) is not different from the designation "path-knowledge" obtained at the time of the dharma-knowledge of the path (mārgadharmajñāna).

The designation "subsequent knowledge" (anvaya-jñāna) obtained at that time is not different from the designation "subsequent knowledge of suffering" (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) obtained at the time [of realizing] suffering; thus,
whether one has attained subsequent knowledge or even up to the attainment of the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
Regarding the degree to which these eight knowledges are accomplished— whether few or many—
one should understand their characteristics as explained at length in the text.
This includes the increase of the path of vision and wisdom, as well as the designation of "knowledge."
Its characteristics should be understood as they are in the case of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
However, one accomplishes both the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of suffering;
it is at the moment of the knowledge of the phenomenon of suffering that this is first accomplished.
Subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is first accomplished at the moment of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna).
Knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna) is first accomplished by the ninth path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) when one becomes free from the defilements of desire,

as well as by the mind of rebirth-linking (pratisandhi-citta) during the intermediate existence (antarābhava) when passing away from the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu) to be born in the form realm (rūpa-dhātu).
Conventional knowledge has no beginning, as it is fundamentally accomplished by all sentient beings from the outset.
The accomplishment of the knowledge of origination takes the moment of the dharma-knowledge of origination as its initial point of accomplishment;
the accomplishment of the knowledge of cessation takes the moment of the dharma-knowledge of cessation as its initial point of accomplishment.
The knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) takes the moment of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) as its beginning;
it consists of the knowledges of phenomena, subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path,
following their initial attainment.
Up until their final parinirvāṇa, they are constantly endowed with it.
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is constantly accomplished from the unknowable beginningless limit up until their final parinirvāṇa.
The knowledge of others' minds is always accomplished by one who is already free from the defilements of desire, has not yet been born into the formless realm, and has not yet attained parinirvāṇa.
This is the brief *Vibhāṣā* on this point.
"If one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also cultivate the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)? ...
[and so forth, as extensively explained].
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This is in order to refute the positions of other schools and to clarify the correct principle.
That is to say, some may claim that wholesome, defiled, and indeterminate dharmas all possess the meaning of being cultivated (*bhāvanā*).
To refute that attachment and to demonstrate that only conditioned wholesome phenomena possess the meaning of "cultivation" (bhāvanā),
how is this known?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Wholesome conditioned phenomena are what should be cultivated, and no others.
Why is this? Because when a wise person regards any phenomenon as an object of knowledge, it is for the sake of its desirable fruit.
To cultivate with diligence so that [wholesome qualities] gradually increase is called "cultivation" (bhāvanā).
Only conditioned phenomena that are wholesome can yield desirable fruits.
This means that because one attains the dominant fruit of desirable worldly maturation,
and also attains the supramundane fruit of dissociation,
those who possess wisdom should practice with diligent effort.
By proceeding from the lower to the middle, and from the middle to the upper, one swiftly attains the desired and beloved fruits;
because defiled indeterminate dharmas, as well as wholesome unconditioned dharmas, do not function in this manner, they are not termed "cultivation" (bhāvanā).
There are some who deny the reality of cultivation in the future,
asserting that both the past and the future lack substantial existence.
To refute this attachment and demonstrate that the past and the future definitely exist as real entities, [the text states]:
One can now cultivate future wholesome dharmas;
that is to say, with the superior wholesome states of the present life as the cause,
one brings about the acquisition (*prāpti*) of various wholesome dharmas in the future.
Because one attains those dharmas, they are said to be "cultivated.
If there were no one capable of cultivating future wholesome states,
then the principle of attaining fruits and so forth would not exist.
That is to say, at the time of attaining the fruits and so forth, there is only one present knowledge and eight future knowledges are cultivated;
there is only one present aspect (*ākāra*) and sixteen future aspects are cultivated.
At present, there is only a single moment; in the future, one cultivates immeasurable moments.
At present, there may be only contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors;
in the future, one cultivates both contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors.
Alternatively, there would be cases where only uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors exist in the present,
while uncontaminated and contaminated minds and mental factors are cultivated in the future;
such matters as these would all fail to be established.
Furthermore, when the Buddhas realize great enlightenment,
there exists at present only the merit of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
If there were no sense of cultivating wholesome qualities in the future, [this would not be possible].
Otherwise, it would follow that the Buddhas lack omniscience;
since such great faults must not be allowed,
one must certainly admit the cultivation of future wholesome dharmas.
This treatise is composed to refute these various divergent attachments and to reveal the correct principle.
There are four types of cultivation, as explained extensively above.
In this context, the treatise is composed based solely upon two types of cultivation:
namely, the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*). *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 106.

Within all the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),

Question: Why is it that within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one cultivates only those [knowledges] of the same category?
In the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), can one cultivate both the similar-type (*sabhāga*) and the dissimilar-type (*tatsabhāga*)?
Answer: Because the locus and the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) are fixed in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one cultivates only the similar-type;
however, in the path of cultivation, both the locus and the antidote are not fixed.
Therefore, one is able to cultivate both the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and the heterogeneous (*visabhāga*).
Furthermore, because the objects of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are fixed and their antidotes are fixed, one cultivates only the homogeneous;
whereas the objects of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are not fixed and their antidotes are not fixed.
Therefore, one is able to cultivate both the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and the heterogeneous (*tatsabhāga*).

Furthermore, because one first attains the noble lineage (*āryagotra*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and initially cultivates the aspects of the noble practice (*āryākāra*) regarding the four noble truths, one cultivates only the homogeneous.
Having already attained the lineage of the noble ones during the path of cultivation and having already cultivated the noble aspects regarding the Four Noble Truths,
one is thus able to cultivate both the homogeneous and the heterogeneous.
Furthermore, because one first attains the vision of the truths and first attains clear realization (*abhisamaya*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
one cultivates only those [factors] that are of a similar class (*sabhāga*).
Because one has already attained the vision of the truths and already attained clear realization within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), [one cultivates both].
Therefore, one is able to cultivate both homogeneous and heterogeneous [paths].
