in the future, six knowledges are cultivated.
Excluding the conventional knowledge of others' minds,
during the eight paths of liberation, two dharmas and four subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) are cultivated in the present according to the two [types of path];
seven knowledges are cultivated for the future.
Excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*),
within the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), two types of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are cultivated as present,
and eight knowledges are cultivated for the future.
Furthermore, noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire cultivate the four immeasurables, thereby developing immeasurable roots of goodness within the three realms.
The first two liberations,
the first four bases of mastery,
and the meditation on impurity.
When practicing mindfulness of breathing and when abiding in mundane applications of mindfulness,
one cultivates only mundane knowledge in the present.
In the future, one cultivates seven knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of others' minds,
at the time of practicing the mixed cultivation of dhyāna.
During the first moment, four dharmas and four types of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) are cultivated as present;
seven knowledges are cultivated for the future,
excluding the knowledge of others' minds.
In the second moment, one presently cultivates only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*),
and in the future, one cultivates seven knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
In the third moment, four dharmas and four types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) are cultivated as present in accordance with two [moments];
eight knowledges are cultivated for the future.
When inducing the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), [the same applies].
During the five paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one cultivates only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) in the present,
and seven knowledges in the future.
Excluding the knowledge of others' minds,
during the various paths of preparation and the two paths of liberation,
one cultivates only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) in the present.
In the future, one cultivates eight knowledges.
Within a single path of liberation, one cultivates eight knowledges in the future;
in the present, one cultivates only conventional knowledge and the knowledge of others' minds.
Some say that one also cultivates the dharma-knowledge-path and the subsequent knowledge-path; however,
one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds during the two paths of liberation, because such knowledge is indeterminate (avyākṛta).
When a noble one who has already become free from the defilement of desire gives rise to the four immeasurables,

the mundane liberations, the spheres of mastery, the spheres of totality, the meditation on the foul, mindfulness of breathing, mundane applications of mindfulness, mundane analytical knowledges, the knowledge of non-contention, the knowledge resulting from prayer, the meditative attainment of the limit of existence, and the samādhis of emptiness-of-emptiness, wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and signlessness-of-signlessness, or enters the attainment of cessation, at that time there is a subtle mind characterized by perception.
At present, one cultivates only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*);
in the future, one cultivates eight knowledges.
This occurs when the untainted knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñāna*) arises.
In the present, one cultivates two types of knowledge—either the dharma-knowledge or the subsequent-knowledge of the path, along with the knowledge of others' minds;
in the future, one cultivates eight knowledges.
This is based on the stages of meditative concentration (dhyāna).
When one gives rise to the untainted foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and the untainted analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid),
four dharmajñānas and four anvayajñānas are cultivated in the present according to two [foundations],
and eight knowledges are cultivated in the future.
When one gives rise to the analytical knowledge of unimpeded eloquence regarding the untainted,
one cultivates two knowledges— the dharma-knowledge and the subsequent knowledge— concerning the Path in the present,
and cultivates eight knowledges in the future.
When one gives rise to the untainted foundations of mindfulness, the untainted analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), or the untainted liberations based on the formless attainments,
four types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) are cultivated as present in accordance with two [categories].
In the future, one cultivates eight knowledges.
When, based on the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), one gives rise to the untainted analytical knowledge of eloquence (*apratighapratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), there are currently two knowledges:
the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
When one cultivates the eight knowledges in the future and gives rise to the extremely subtle mind that enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
one cultivates only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) in the present.
In the future as well, one cultivates only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
This is the brief *Vibhāṣā* on this point.
If one cultivates dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), does one also cultivate subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)?
It can be answered in four propositions.
Because the meaning is not fixed, there are cases where one cultivates dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) but not subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
This refers to the time when one enters the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the dharma-knowledges regarding suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
When the learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) has attained the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) that is present before him— specifically,
at the time of entering into the clear realization (abhisamaya) of the dharma-knowledges regarding suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
This refers to the four moments of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
At these times, one cultivates only dharma-knowledge and does not cultivate subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*). Why is this so?
If, within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one thus cultivates such qualities in the present for the sake of the future,
then at the moment when the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) of such cultivated qualities manifests in the present,
one cultivates only the category of future dharma-knowledge.
When subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is present,
one cultivates only the category of future subsequent knowledge; thus, for those who have seen the tracks [of the path]— the learners (śaikṣas)— and for Arhats,
when dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has already been attained and is present.
"Those in training" (*śaikṣa*) refers to the individuals who are stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners;
"tracks" (*pada*) refers to the four noble truths.
Because they have already fully perceived the tracks of the four truths by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), they are called "those in training who have seen the tracks."
An Arhat refers to one who is liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta) or one who is doubly liberated (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta).

When these trainees (śaikṣas) or those beyond training (aśaikṣas) bring the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) that has already been attained into manifestation, they cultivate only the dharma-knowledge.
Because this is a matter of cultivation through practice, one does not cultivate subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna). Why is this?
Because when a dharma previously attained manifests in the present, [one does not cultivate it further].
Being weak in power, they cannot even reach the second moment,
let alone cultivate other future distant factors.
There are those who cultivate anvaya-jñāna but not dharma-jñāna.
This refers to when one enters the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) regarding suffering, its origin, and its cessation;

that is, when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat brings this subsequent knowledge into manifestation. Regarding the phrase "when entering the clear realization of the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering, its origin, and its cessation": [it means] at the time of entering the clear realization of the subsequent knowledge of suffering, its origin, and its cessation.
This refers to the time of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
At that time, one cultivates only subsequent knowledge and does not cultivate dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*).
The meaning is as previously explained.
Regarding those in training who have seen the tracks and arhats at the time when their subsequently attained knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is manifest:
this refers to the time when the subsequently attained knowledge, previously acquired by those in training or those beyond training, is manifest.
One cultivates only the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) and does not cultivate the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna);
the meaning is as previously explained.
There are cases where both are cultivated.
This refers to when one enters the path of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) at the stage of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*);
or when a learner who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭapada*) or an arhat has not yet brought an untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) into manifestation.
When one has not yet attained mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) such that it is present before them,
and is able to cultivate both simultaneously—
specifically, at this point when entering the path of the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) within the clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
This means that at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) following the path of seeing (darśana-mārga),
one is able to cultivate both the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
In this stage, one abandons the paths previously attained and attains paths never before attained,
realizing the single flavor of the attainment of the severance of the fetters.
One suddenly attains the eight knowledges,
because one simultaneously cultivates the sixteen aspects [of the four truths].
This applies to those in training who have seen the tracks, as well as Arhats.
Regarding the phrase "when untainted knowledge (anāsravajñāna) has not yet arisen before one":
this refers to those in the stage of training (śaikṣa) who, by means of the untainted path, become free from the defilement of desire;
that is, when they apply themselves to the practice of the untainted [path].
It is the same during the nine paths of preparation, the nine uninterrupted paths, and the nine paths of liberation,
up until the time one becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness.
When one is free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and applies oneself to the untainted [path],
during the nine paths of preparation, the eight paths of uninterrupted transition, and the path of liberation,
one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties and becomes one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
If one performs the preparatory application (prayoga) by means of the untainted (anāsrava),
then at the time of the path of preparation, the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga), and the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) thereof;
and at the time of the initial and final moments of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna.
When the untainted knowledge of others' minds, the untainted foundations of mindfulness, and the untainted liberations arise;
that is to say, at such times during the stage of training when the untainted knowledges have not yet been attained but are now manifesting before one.
One is able to cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and also cultivates subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

This occurs at the time of the ninth path of liberation when, in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
When one who is liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) refines their faculties to become immovable (akopya),
if they perform the preparatory application (prayoga-mārga) by means of the untainted (anāsrava),

then at the time of the nine paths of preparation (prayoga-mārga), the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), the nine paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga), and at the time of the first and final moments of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna (dhyāna-vyavakiraṇa).
When the untainted knowledge of others' minds arises, when the untainted foundations of mindfulness arise, when the untainted analytical knowledges arise, and when the untainted liberations arise;
likewise, at such times during the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) when untainted knowledge that has not yet been attained manifests before one.
One who is able to cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) also cultivates the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
This refers to one who, when the conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) has not yet been attained, is able to cultivate both simultaneously as it becomes present.
This refers to a trainee who, by means of the mundane path, becomes detached from the defilements of desire.
If they employ the mundane path as their preparatory application,
then during the nine paths of preparation, the nine paths of uninterrupted transition, and the nine paths of liberation, [they remain in that state].
The same applies even up to the time of becoming free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
When one becomes free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
if one employs worldly preparatory effort (*laukika-prayoga*), [the attainment is worldly].
At the time of that path of preparation,
one who has attained liberation through faith refines their faculties to become one who has attained vision;
this occurs if they perform the preparatory effort by means of the mundane path.
At the time of the path of preparation;
at the time of the intermediate mind during the mixed cultivation of dhyāna;
and at the times of the paths of preparation, the five paths of uninterrupted transition, and the three paths of liberation for the elicitation of the five supernormal powers.

When one gives rise to the four immeasurables, the mundane liberations, the spheres of mastery, the spheres of totality, the meditation on the foul, mindfulness of breathing, the mundane foundations of mindfulness, and the subtle mind that enters the attainment of cessation.
If one who is in the stage of no-more-learning refines their faculties to achieve unshakability through liberation,
and performs a worldly preparatory application,
then at the time of that path of preparation:
At the time of practicing the mixed cultivation of dhyāna during the intermediate state of mind;

at the time of the preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*), the five uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the three paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for inducing the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

at the time of giving rise to the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), mundane liberations (*vimoṣa*), spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), mundane applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), mundane analytical knowledges (*pratisamvid*), the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā-jñāna*), the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), the concentration of the limit of existence (*bhavāgra-samādhi*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), the wishlessness of wishlessness (*apranihitā-praṇihita*), the signlessness of signlessness (*animittā-animitta*), and the concentration of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)—during these moments of subtle thought.
In such cases, when those in the stages of training (śaikṣa) or beyond training (aśaikṣa) have not yet brought conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) into manifestation,
they are able to cultivate future dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
There is the case where neither is cultivated:
namely, when a learner who has seen the tracks (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭiprāpta) or an arhat brings worldly knowledge (lokasaṃvṛtijñāna) into manifestation.
When mundane knowledge has not yet been attained and is not present before one,

and neither [of the two knowledges] is being cultivated— namely, at all times when an ordinary person possesses a defiled or neutral mind, during the attainment of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), the state of non-conceptual beings (asaṃjñika), or during the moments of uncontaminated receptivity (anāsrava-kṣānti).
Regarding those among these who have attained the fruit of the path of seeing and are Arhats, when conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) has already been acquired and is present before them:
this refers to those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) and the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) when conventional knowledge, having already been acquired, is present before them.
Those whose faculties are weak and inferior cannot even cultivate future, homogeneous, contaminated merits;
how much less can they cultivate heterogeneous dharmas belonging to the categories of dharma-knowledge and class-knowledge?
As for those who have not yet attained mundane knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) and do not cultivate it when it is present before them:
This refers to those in the stages of training (śaikṣa) and beyond-training (aśaikṣa) who have not yet attained the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection;
as well as when the extremely subtle mind of the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is present,
they are all unable to cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
"All ordinary beings" refers to those at the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) who,
during all moments of consciousness, are unable to cultivate the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*),
because these are not the dharmas to be cultivated by ordinary beings.
Regarding "defiled minds":
this refers to the fact that when any defiled minds of the noble ones (ārya) manifest,
they are all unable to cultivate dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) or subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
Because a defiled mind belongs to the category conducive to decline, its nature is heavy and associated with indolence;
it is not even capable of cultivating for oneself, much less can it cultivate the untainted merits of others.
Because one can cultivate wholesome states only when the mind is compliant with the superior portion, light, subtle,
and associated with diligence;
"neutral mind" refers to the moments when neutral minds are present before the various noble ones (*ārya*).
None of them are able to cultivate dharma-knowledge or subsequent knowledge,
because their indeterminate minds are lowly, weak, and inferior— like rotten seeds—
and thus not even fit for cultivation themselves.
How much more so for being able to cultivate the untainted merits of others?
It requires a firm and superior mind to be able to cultivate such merits.
As for the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation:
This means that when one abides in the attainment of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) or the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti),
one is unable to cultivate either dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) or subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
It is only in states where the mind is present that there can be cultivation.
Because one cannot cultivate [the path] within the state of non-mentation.
Regarding the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva), some say:
Because those born there do not give rise to wholesome thoughts at any time,
they are unable to cultivate dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna). Some say:
Although those born there may give rise to wholesome states of mind,
they are unable to cultivate the wholesome dharmas of applied practice,
because they give rise only to that which is wholesome by birth.
If one cannot yet cultivate even the contaminated preparatory practices (*prayoga*),
how much less could one cultivate the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*);
for how could one do so during the moments of uncontaminated patience (*anāsravakṣānti*)?
This means that during the eight untainted patiences (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one cannot cultivate wisdom;
at that time, one cultivates only those merits of the same category,
and not those of other categories.
Question: Why is it that when wholesome dharmas already acquired manifest before one, one cannot cultivate other future wholesome merits?
Answer: Because their functional activity is inferior.
Because it has already been experienced;
because the task has already been accomplished;
and because the fruit has already been bestowed.
Furthermore, because that which has already been cultivated and stilled lacks power and function;
furthermore, when a previously attained dharma manifests in the present,
one practices it again through cultivation, having already cultivated it previously.
In the second case, throughout successive lifetimes there is only diminution and no increase;
how could one further cultivate wholesome states never before attained?
It is like a person consuming wealth previously accumulated.
There is only diminution and no increase;
how could this be called further accumulating wealth never before accumulated?
Furthermore, regarding those wholesome dharmas produced through great exertion:
One is able to cultivate other future wholesome dharmas because,
once they have arisen and attained, when wholesome states manifest in the present, they do not require much effort;
however, one cannot cultivate future wholesome dharmas [at that time].
Furthermore, if one who has already attained wholesome states can cultivate various future wholesome dharmas when they manifest in the present,
then at the time when the Blessed One was about to enter parinirvāṇa—
One who enters the various dhyānas and samāpattis in successive order should also be able to cultivate future merits;
this was when the Blessed One manifested the initial arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
If one has already fully acquired and cultivated all merits,
yet now cultivates again that which was previously unattained,
then the merits of the preceding stage would not have been perfected.
It would follow that at the time of first attaining Buddhahood, one has not reached the ultimate state;
therefore, to avoid this error, it must be admitted that one realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment [only then].
When wholesome states already acquired are present before one,
it is certainly impossible to cultivate future wholesome dharmas.
The meaning of the remaining cultivation of knowledge is explained at length in the text.
One should understand their characteristics according to the preceding [explanation].
Regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) up to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*),
among these eight knowledges, how many knowledges does each one take as its object?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of other schools and elucidating the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who claim:
The various objects of cognition (ālambana-pratyaya) do not possess a real substantial entity.
To refute that attachment and to demonstrate that the object-condition does indeed possess a real intrinsic nature, this treatise is composed.
Answer: Dharma-knowledge takes seven knowledges as its objects.
Excluding conventional knowledge,
conventional knowledge takes seven knowledges as its object. Excluding dharma-knowledge, [dharma-knowledge takes seven knowledges as its object].
Why is this so? Because dharma-knowledge takes the lower realms as its object, while conventional knowledge takes the upper realms as its object;
therefore, they do not take one another as objects.
It is like two people living in the same place, where one person observes the ground.
One person contemplates emptiness;
thus, these two do not see one another.
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge, both take the eight knowledges as their objects.
Because these two can collectively take both mind and mental factors as their objects,
the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin both take these two knowledges as their objects;
that is to say, the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge [take them as objects].
These two [knowledges] can only take contaminated mental states as their objects;
the knowledge of cessation does not take knowledges as its object because it takes the unconditioned as its object;
and the knowledge of the path takes seven knowledges as its objects, excluding conventional knowledge.
Because it takes the truth of the path as its object,
others pose a further question regarding this:
from dharma-knowledge up to path-knowledge.
Regarding the eight knowledges, how many knowledges does each one take as its object?
He answers this himself:
the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) takes four knowledges as its object.
Excluding the subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering, origin, and cessation,
the subsequent knowledges take four knowledges as their objects.
Excluding the dharma-knowledges (*dharma-jñāna*) regarding suffering, origin, and cessation.
The knowledge of others' minds is the object of seven knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of cessation.
Conventional knowledge is the object of six knowledges.
Excluding the knowledge of the path,
the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path take five knowledges as their objects;
excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation.
Regarding the dharma-knowledge up to the path-knowledge, how many conditions do they serve when compared to one another?
Why was this treatise composed? It is answered:
in order to refute the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that conditions have no real substance.
To refute their view and to demonstrate that the four conditions possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this treatise is composed.
The answer is: dharma-knowledge is related to dharma-knowledge by way of the four conditions.
...and so forth, as explained at length.

Question: Why is there a difference between what is stated here and what was said in the previous section on the "Unwholesome" chapter of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, namely that here it is taught that dharma-knowledge serves as four conditions for dharma-knowledge?

Regarding the section on the unwholesome (*akuśala-nikāya-saṃgraha*), it is asked: Are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and [other afflictions] related to one another as four, three, two, or one object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
The answer is: As it is explained here, so it should also be understood there.
It should be understood that this is also as previously stated;
however, it is done merely to reveal different characteristics and different phrasings so that those who uphold [the teaching] may give rise to joy.

Furthermore, it is intended to manifest two gates, two summaries, two reflections, two ladders, two steps, two lights, and two torches, so that they may know how what has been taught mutually illuminates one another.
Furthermore, that [teaching] is said to be of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*),
while this [teaching] is said to be of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
That [teaching] is said to have no underlying intention (*abhiprāya*).
This statement has a specific intention.
That [previous] statement asserts that there is no distinct condition;
this statement asserts that there is a distinct condition.
That [previous] statement was made in reliance upon the ultimate truth (paramārtha), while this statement is made in reliance upon conventional truth (saṃvṛti).
Furthermore, that was stated by way of fourfold distinctions.
That is to say: the differentiation of elements,
the differentiation of time periods,
and the differentiation of moments.
Regarding the distinctions among the equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
this is explained solely based on one particular distinction;
namely, the distinction among the equal-and-immediate conditions.
Regarding how dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) acts as four conditions for dharma-knowledge:
namely, as the causal (hetu), the immediately preceding (samanantara), the object-conditioned (ālambana), and the dominant (adhipati) conditions.
Among these, the causal condition is like the nature of a seed.
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is like the act of clearing the way;
the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is like a pillar or a staff;
and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is like the act of not obstructing.
Regarding the fact that dharma-knowledge serves as the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) for dharma-knowledge:
this means it acts as one cause, namely the similar cause (sabhāga-hetu).
Regarding its serving as the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya): [it means that]...
That is to say, when dharma-knowledge arises in the present immediately after [a preceding] dharma-knowledge,
acting as an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
it means that dharma-knowledge arises taking dharma-knowledge as its object.
Regarding its function as a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*):
it means that dharma-knowledge does not obstruct the arising of dharma-knowledge;
and with respect to subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), it serves as three conditions, excluding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
That is to say, dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) serve as three conditions [for each other],
excluding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
As for their serving as causal conditions (hetu-pratyaya):
That is to say, dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) constitute a single cause,
namely the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu);
as for their functioning as the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya):
This means that when subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) manifests immediately after the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna),
it serves as a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
That is to say, the knowledge of phenomena does not obstruct the arising of subsequent knowledge.
Regarding "excluding those that take it as an object":
this means that dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge do not take each other as objects.
Regarding their serving as four conditions for the knowledge of others' minds, and so forth: [the text continues].
That is to say, dharma-knowledge serves as the cause and the equal-and-immediate condition for the knowledge of others' minds within one's own continuum,
but it is not its object-condition.
The knowledge of another's mind takes the mental continuum of another as its object;
it is not [conditioned by] causes or immediate antecedents.
The rest is as previously stated.
Regarding its being three conditions for mundane knowledge— excluding the causal condition:
this means that the causal condition is like the nature of a seed,
whereas the untainted and the tainted are not of the nature of a seed.
Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) do not function as causal conditions (hetu-pratyaya);
they serve as only three conditions.
With respect to the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation, they serve as three conditions, excluding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
That is to say, the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination take contaminated phenomena as their objects;
because the dharma-knowledge is uncontaminated, it does not take those as its objects.
The knowledge of cessation takes unconditioned phenomena as its object.
Because dharma-knowledge is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for that [subsequent knowledge].
It serves as four conditions for path-knowledge, as previously explained.
Similarly, subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) serves as four conditions for subsequent knowledge, and so forth.
Its characteristics should be understood according to the preceding explanation of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).
Regarding the statement that "knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) serves as four conditions for knowledge of others' minds," herein,
it is the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*).
That is to say, it is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
The rest is as previously explained.
Regarding its functioning as four conditions for conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*):
In this context, "causes and conditions" refers to the two causes: the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
The rest is as previously explained.
Regarding the statement that [the knowledge of others' minds] serves as four conditions for the knowledge of suffering and its origin:
this means that untainted knowledge of others' minds serves as a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for the knowledge of suffering and its origin.
Concentration is certainly not its object, because that [concentration] takes the contaminated as its object.
If there were a contaminated knowledge of others' minds that took the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination as its objects, [it would follow that concentration is their object].
Concentration is not a causal condition (hetu-pratyaya),
because that which is with outflows (sāsrava) does not serve as a causal condition for that which is without outflows (anāsrava).
It serves as three conditions for the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), excluding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Because it takes the unconditioned as its object,
its function as four conditions for the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) is as explained previously.
Regarding mundane knowledge acting as four conditions for mundane knowledge, among these,
it is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
This refers to the three causes—homogeneous, pervasive, and retributive.
The rest is as previously explained.
Regarding their serving as three conditions for the knowledge of suffering and the origin, they exclude the causal condition.
Because contaminated phenomena do not serve as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) for uncontaminated phenomena; however,

they serve as two conditions— namely, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)— for the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path,
because those [knowledges] take the uncontaminated as their object.
The rest is as previously explained.
Regarding its serving as three conditions for the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), with the exception of being a cause-condition:
this is because that which is contaminated (sāsrava) and that which is uncontaminated (anāsrava) are not related to one another like seeds.
Regarding the statement that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) serves as four conditions for the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*):

this means that conventional knowledge acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the contaminated knowledge of others' minds within one's own continuum.
It serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds within one's own continuum,
but it is not its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
It serves as the object-condition for the contaminated knowledge of others' minds within the continua of others.

It is not a cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) nor an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Regarding how the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) serves as three conditions— namely, for the knowledge of suffering itself and for the knowledges of origin and cessation— excluding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
it is explained at length in the text.
Among these, one should understand that, as previously established, those fetters bound to the desire realm are abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
[This applies] up to the full exposition.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is in order to enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.

That is to say, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) can sever the fetters of the form and formless realms, whereas the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) cannot sever the fetters of the desire realm.
Some may raise a doubt:
"If dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) is able to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the form and formless realms,
can subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) likewise sever the fetters of the desire realm?"
Just as subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) cannot sever the fetters of the desire realm,
does dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) likewise fail to sever the fetters of the form and formless realms?
This [passage] is intended to provide a definitive resolution to this doubt.
This treatise is composed because it is demonstrated that the concentration of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-samādhi*) is capable of severing the fetters of the form and formless realms,
whereas the concentration of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna-samādhi*) cannot sever the fetters of the desire realm.

Question: Why is it that dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) can sever the fetters of the form and formless realms, whereas subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) cannot sever the fetters of the desire realm?
Answer: Because dharma-knowledge first severs the fetters of the desire realm.
It can also sever the fetters of the form and formless realms.
Since subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) does not first sever the fetters of the form and formless realms,
it cannot sever the fetters of the desire realm.
Furthermore, because subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the form and formless realms,
dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) severs them;
whereas because dharma-knowledge has already severed the fetters of the desire realm, subsequent knowledge does not sever them.
Furthermore, if the faculty of knowledge through analogy (anvaya-jñāna) can sever the fetters of the desire realm, how does it do so?
Does it first sever the fetters of the form and formless realms?
Does one first sever the fetters of the desire realm and subsequently sever the fetters of the form and formless realms,
or does one first sever the fetters of the form and formless realms and subsequently sever the fetters of the desire realm?
If one were to first sever the fetters of the form and formless realms and subsequently sever the fetters of the desire realm,
it would be because the fetters of the desire realm are coarse and have already been severed [previously].
Furthermore, what is it that is abandoned?
If one were to first abandon the fetters of the desire realm and subsequently abandon the fetters of the form and formless realms,
then subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) would be subject to the reproach of others.
If one has not yet been able to abandon the fetters within one's own realm, how can one wish to sever the fetters of other realms?
It is like a king who, before having subdued the enemies within his own country, desires to conquer another nation; he would be censured by others.
Furthermore, all subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) necessarily has dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) as its cause;
thus, dharma-knowledge can assist in the abandonment of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) belonging to the form and formless realms.
However, it is not the case that all dharma-knowledge necessarily has subsequent knowledge as its cause.
Therefore, subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) cannot assist dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) in abandoning the fetters of the desire realm.
Furthermore, after the path-subsequent knowledge (mārga-anvaya-jñāna), subsequent knowledge for the most part does not manifest;
even if it were to manifest, its power and function would be weak and inferior.

Because it is only after one has definitively abandoned the fetters of the desire realm that the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) can manifest; therefore, it cannot sever the fetters of the desire realm.
Furthermore, the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) must likewise have already abandoned the fetters of the desire realm.
Because it is sharp and intense;
by virtue of its intensity, it is able to sever the higher fetters.
Subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) requires that one has already become detached from the fetters of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
The application is both skillful and sharp. When it is sharp,
since the lower fetters have already been severed, what further remains to be severed?
Furthermore, the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) is extremely sharp and powerful;
it does not even require effort to sever unwholesome fetters (saṃyojana),
much less fail to sever those that are indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Just as even an extremely sharp blade can cut through iron,
let alone grass, wood, and the like;
so too, subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is not extremely fierce or sharp.
If one must still exert great effort to sever even the indeterminate fetters,
how much more so for the unwholesome fetters?
It is like using a dull blade to cut through grass, wood, and the like.
If [the cutting of wood] still requires great effort,
how much more so for the cutting of iron?
Furthermore, the dharma-knowledge is fully capable of severing the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
Just as there is a strong man whose strength rivals a thousand men and can sever the higher fetters,
so too subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is able to sever fourteen elements (dhātu), ten bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha).
Because its power and function are inferior, it does not sever the lower fetters.
Furthermore, wrong view within the desire realm first severs the suffering and origin of the three realms as its objects;
once that has been severed, one then desires to sever those very objects themselves.
Therefore, the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) can sever the fetters of the two upper realms;
however, wrong views belonging to the form and formless realms cannot take the suffering or origin of the desire realm as their object.
Therefore, subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) cannot sever the fetters of the desire realm.
Furthermore, regarding the universal fetters of the desire realm that take other realms as their objects,
those which take the suffering and origin of the form and formless realms as their objects are severed first.
Since he further desires to sever those objects of perception (*ālambana*),
the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is able to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the two upper realms,
as well as the pervasive fetters (*sarvatragasaṃyojana*) that take other realms as their objects.
It does not take the suffering or the origin of the desire realm as its object;
therefore, subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) cannot sever the fetters of the desire realm.
It is like a king who first slays his enemies and thieves.
Later, he likewise destroys those places of play.
Furthermore, the aggregates of the desire realm oppress sentient beings more than a heavy burden;
having severed them, he repeatedly praises their antidotes and their cessation.
At that time, one is further able to sever the higher aggregates;
therefore, the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) can sever the fetters of the upper realms,
whereas the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) cannot sever the fetters of the desire realm.
However, as for the dharma-knowledge that can sever the fetters of the form and formless realms,
it is the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path, not the dharma-knowledge of suffering and its origin. Why is this so?
Because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
That is to say, when a practitioner is oppressed by the aggregates (*skandha*) of the desire realm as if by a burden too heavy to bear, once he has abandoned them,
he brings forth their antidote (*pratipakṣa*) as a retribution for that abandonment.
Furthermore, because they eliminate evil,
they repeatedly observe;
when they observe repeatedly, they are naturally able to sever the fetters of the realms of form and formlessness.
Furthermore, the desire realm is the realm of instability; it is not the stage of cultivation, nor is it the stage of freedom from passion.
The form and formless realms are the realm of stability, the stage of cultivation, and the stage of freedom from passion, yet they are not characterized by revulsion.
Because the dharmas of the indeterminate realm can sever the fetters of the determinate realms.
Furthermore, the desire realm is coarse,
while the form and formless realms are subtle.
This is because one cannot sever the fetters of the subtle realms by means of revulsion toward the coarse realm.
Furthermore, the desire realm is inferior,
whereas the form and formless realms are superior and sublime, and thus not objects of revulsion.
Because the dharmas of the inferior realm can sever the fetters of the superior and sublime realms.
Furthermore, the desire realm is inferior,
while the form realm is middling.
The formless realm is superior and not subject to revulsion;
however, dharmas of the lower realms can sever the fetters of the middle and upper realms.
Furthermore, if the wisdom that understands the dharmas of suffering and its origin were able to sever the fetters of the form and formless realms, [it would follow that such wisdom is unnecessary].
Thus, one cultivates disenchantment in one place and attains liberation in another;
it is like cutting the hand that binds the hand to achieve liberation,
or cutting the foot that binds the foot to achieve liberation.
One cannot attain liberation by severing the hand while binding the feet,
nor can one attain liberation by severing the feet while binding the hands.
Therefore, it is the wisdom of the Dharma that is able to sever the fetters of the realms of form and formlessness.
This is the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path, not the dharma-knowledge of suffering and origin.

However, as for this dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path being able to sever the fetters of the form and formless realms, it occurs only when one is born in the desire realm, not when one is born in the form or formless realms. Why is this so?
The mind that employs the skillful means of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding entering and emerging belongs exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This is because those in the two higher realms have already abandoned this mind, and it necessarily does not arise there.
Furthermore, there is the morality that follows from the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānānuvartaka-śīla*).
It arises solely from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
because those born in the two higher realms necessarily abandon these primary elements and do not give rise to them.
Furthermore, one born in the two higher realms has necessarily already accomplished what was to be done regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
The preparatory application has ceased and no longer manifests,
just as for an Arhat, the path that serves as the antidote for severing the fetters of the three realms no longer manifests once what was to be done has been accomplished.
Question: If that is so, for what reason do the Arhats give rise to untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*)?
Answer: It is because they wish to contemplate the faults and afflictions (*ādīnava*) of the aggregates (*skandha*) that have been relinquished.
Furthermore, because he contemplates the excellence of the cessation and the path that have been attained,
he gives rise to various untainted knowledges (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Moreover, he gives rise to untainted knowledge by means of four conditions.
First, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life;
second, for the sake of sporting with meritorious qualities;
third, for the sake of contemplating what was originally undertaken.
Fourth, it is for the sake of enjoying the noble wealth.
The Venerable Ghosaka spoke thus:
"The disciples of the Blessed One are born in the formless realm."
Regarding the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the virtues produced therein:
those born in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) are also able to produce them.
What is the meaning of that statement?
He says that if one is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
one does not give rise to the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) that abandons the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the higher realms. However,

one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), if they have not yet abandoned the defilements (*kleśa*) of the form and formless realms, is also able to give rise to the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*) and the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) that abandons the fetters of the form and formless realms.
The critique states:
He should not make such a statement. Why is this?
If this were the case, it would not be determinate;
that is to say, one born in the form realm would be able to give rise to a portion of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and unable to give rise to another portion.
That which can partially give rise [to it] refers to a portion of the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path;
that which cannot give rise [to it] refers to the remainder.
That is to say, regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering and its origin,
there are those that can arise and those that cannot arise.
There may be those who are able to give rise [to it],
meaning they have not yet abandoned defilement regarding that;
there may also be those who are unable to give rise [to it].
This refers to one who has already become detached from those defilements;
at times they are able to give rise [to them], and at times they are unable to give rise [to them].
As for "at times they are able to give rise":
This refers to when one gives rise to the path of detachment;
or, when at times one is unable to give it rise,
it refers to the time of drawing forth the roots of goodness.
Therefore, what was stated previously is logically sound.
Regarding those fetters bound to the desire realm, are they abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
One should respond that this involves four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Because their nature is not fixed,
there are fetters bound to the desire realm that are not abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñāna*).
That is to say, the fetters of the desire realm.
Some are abandoned by patience (*kṣānti*),
some are abandoned by other types of knowledge (*jñāna*), and some are not abandoned at all.
Among these, those abandoned by patience are as follows:
This refers to abandonment through the four patiences of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñānakṣānti*), or abandonment through other knowledges;
that is to say, abandonment through conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Or, "not abandoned" refers to that which has already been abandoned,
or to that for which the application of abandonment has not yet arisen.
There are fetters abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) that are not bound to the desire realm;
namely, the fetters of the form and formless realms abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena,
which are the cessation of the fetters abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms and are abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path.
There are fetters bound to the desire realm that are also abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
That is to say, the fetters of the desire realm abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena;
specifically, the four types of fetters of the desire realm abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) are abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena.
There are fetters that are neither bound to the desire realm nor abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna);
namely, the fetters of the form and formless realms,
or those abandoned by patience (kṣānti).
Some are abandoned by subsequent knowledge,
some are not abandoned;
herein, those abandoned by receptivity (kṣānti) are as follows.
This refers to abandonment by the four types of subsequent-knowledge patience (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), or abandonment by other knowledges; that is,
abandonment by subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) or conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Regarding "or not abandoned":
this refers to that which has already been abandoned,
or to that for which the application of abandonment has not yet arisen.
Regarding those fetters bound to the form and formless realms:
are those fetters abandoned by the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)?
Answer: Those fetters are abandoned by the subsequent knowledge.
Those fetters bound to the form and formless realms refer to the four types of fetters abandoned through cultivation that are severed by the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
There are also fetters bound to the form and formless realms that are not severed by the subsequent knowledge.
That is to say, the fetters of the form and formless realms are abandoned either by patience (*kṣānti*) or by other forms of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Or it is not abandoned.
Herein, "abandoned by patience" refers to abandonment by the patiences associated with the four types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).
"Or that which is abandoned by other types of knowledge" refers to the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) or that which is abandoned by conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Regarding "or not abandoned":
this refers to that which has already been abandoned,
or to that for which the application of abandonment has not yet arisen.
Regarding those fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering:
are those fetters abandoned by the knowledge of suffering?
Answer: Those fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering...
Those fetters are not abandoned by the knowledge of suffering;
they may be abandoned by patience,
or by other knowledges, or they are not abandoned at all.

Among these, that which is abandoned by receptivity refers to abandonment by the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*); that which is abandoned by other knowledges refers to [abandonment] by the remaining knowledges.
This refers to that which is abandoned by conventional knowledge,
or that which is not abandoned;
the latter being so called because it has already been abandoned.
Alternatively, because the preparatory application for their abandonment has not yet arisen,
there can certainly be no knowledge of suffering that can sever those fetters,
since untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is capable only of severing what is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
If a fetter is abandoned by the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), is that fetter abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*)?
Answer: All fetters abandoned by the knowledge of suffering [are so abandoned].

Those fetters which are not abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) but are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) cannot be severed by untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*),
because untainted knowledge cannot sever those [fetters] abandoned by vision.
This refers to the fetters abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*).
The abandonment of the fetters through the knowledge of origin, cessation, and the path should be understood according to the above principle.
Only the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) is capable of abandoning the various fetters;
this is because it is stated therein that the knowledge of suffering and the others cannot abandon the fetters to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*).
