Section Three: The Aggregate of Wisdom (Jñānaskandha), Sub-section Four of the Fourth Chapter on the Cultivation of Wisdom (Bhāvanājñāna-nirdeśa). Regarding the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) abandoned through the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*): is that cessation of the fetters realized through the knowledge of phenomena?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To refute the doctrines of other schools and to manifest the correct principle.
That is to say, some maintain that the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) abandons the acquisitions of the fetters (saṃyojana),
while the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) realizes the acquisition of their cessation (nirodha).
Just as the various masters of foreign treatises,

in order to refute that intention, demonstrate that the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) can sever the acquisitions of the fetters (*saṃyojana-prāpti*) and also realize the acquisition of their cessation;
for if the path of uninterrupted transition were to sever only the fetters themselves, [it would not realize their cessation].
If one were to claim that the path of liberation alone can realize the attainment of that cessation, it would contradict this teaching:
"The fetters abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) are realized as ceased by the knowledge of phenomena," and so forth.
If one attains ultimate detachment from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception through the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path,
that person takes dharma-knowledge as the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
How can it be said that those fetters are abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
and that the cessation of those fetters is realized through the knowledge of phenomena?
Therefore, this should be understood.

It is logically impossible to deny that the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) can sever the acquisitions of the fetters (saṃyojana-prāpti) and also realize the acquisition of their cessation (nirodha-prāpti).
For this reason, this treatise is composed:
Are those fetters that are abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) also realized as their cessation through the knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: Those fetters are abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), and the cessation of those fetters is realized through the knowledge of phenomena;
that is to say, the knowledge of phenomena serves as the uninterrupted path (ānantaryamārga).
One abandons that many fetters;
because this path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is precisely what realizes the cessation (*nirodha*) of those [fetters],
there are cases where the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) acts as the realization of the cessation of a certain fetter, yet that fetter is not abandoned by that dharma-knowledge.
That is to say, whether it is abandoned through patience or abandoned through other forms of knowledge,
the dharma-knowledge realizes the cessation of those fetters.
Just as a stream-enterer,
having abandoned from one to five grades of fetters of the desire realm by means of the mundane path,
further employs the dharma-knowledge as the path of immediate succession.
Upon abandoning the sixth category [of afflictions], one attains the fruit of a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).

At that time, the Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) realizes the cessation of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms, which were previously abandoned by the [preliminary] patiences (*kṣānti*).

Furthermore, having realized the cessation of the first five categories of fetters belonging to the desire realm that are abandoned through cultivation— which were previously abandoned by conventional wisdom—
the Once-returner, by means of the conventional path, has already abandoned the seventh and eighth categories of fetters of the desire realm.
Furthermore, taking the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) as the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*),
one abandons the ninth category [of afflictions] and attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
At that time, the knowledge of phenomena serves as the path of immediate succession.
He realizes the cessation of the fetters abandoned through the prior patience regarding the views to be abandoned within the three realms,
as well as the cessation of the first eight categories of fetters abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm by means of the previously attained conventional knowledge.
The Non-returner, by means of the mundane path or through subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
becomes detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Having abandoned the eight grades of fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) by means of subsequent knowledge, [he attains the fruit].
Furthermore, taking the dharma-knowledge as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one abandons the ninth category [of afflictions] and attains the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*).
At that time, the dharma-knowledge of the path of uninterrupted transition—
One realizes the cessation of the fetters abandoned through seeing in the three realms, which were previously abandoned by patience;
one realizes the cessation of the fetters abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, which were previously abandoned by conventional knowledge;
and one realizes the cessation of the fetters abandoned through cultivation in the seven stages, which were abandoned by both subsequent knowledge and conventional knowledge.

The cessation of the eight grades of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception— which are abandoned by subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)—
is realized through the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*). Yet,
those fetters are not abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena.
Regarding those fetters abandoned by subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*):
is the cessation of those fetters realized through subsequent knowledge?
Answer: Those fetters abandoned by subsequent knowledge...
That cessation of the fetters is realized through subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*);
that is to say, as each subsequent knowledge serves as the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
it abandons a corresponding number of fetters.

Because this path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is precisely that which realizes the extinction of those respective fetters (*saṃyojana*), there is a subsequent knowledge of extinction (*kṣaya-jñāna*) that bears witness to it.
Those fetters are not abandoned by subsequent knowledge; rather, they are abandoned either by receptivity (*kṣānti*) or by other forms of knowledge.

He realizes the cessation of those fetters through subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), just as the noble ones, by means of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) or the mundane path, become free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Having abandoned the eight grades of fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) by means of dharma-knowledge, [he proceeds].
Furthermore, by means of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), one abandons the ninth category [of afflictions] and attains the fruit of arhatship (aśaikṣa-phala).

At that time, the subsequent knowledge of the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) realizes the cessation of the fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through vision (darśana-heya) within the three realms, which were previously abandoned by the [previously attained] patiences (kṣānti).

Furthermore, upon realizing the previously mentioned dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), one attains the cessation of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) belonging to the eight stages as severed by conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*);

and through dharma-knowledge, one attains the cessation of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the first eight categories of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
In this way, the various fetters are realized through the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) as being extinguished;
yet those fetters are not abandoned by subsequent knowledge.
Are the various fetters abandoned by the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), and is their extinction realized through the knowledge of suffering?
Answer: All fetters are abandoned by the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), and that cessation of those fetters is realized through the knowledge of suffering.
That is to say, according to the knowledge of suffering acting as the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), one abandons a corresponding number of fetters.
Because this path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is precisely what realizes the cessation of those respective fetters (*saṃyojana*),
there are cases where the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) serves as the realization of the cessation of a fetter, yet that fetter is not abandoned by the knowledge of suffering;
rather, it is abandoned by patience (*kṣānti*).
Or, when other knowledges abandon [the fetters],
he realizes the cessation of those fetters through the knowledge of suffering,
as is the case with a stream-enterer.
Having abandoned one to five grades of fetters of the desire realm by means of the mundane path, or through the knowledge of origin, cessation, or the path,
one then uses the knowledge of suffering as the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) to abandon the sixth grade.

At that time, the path of uninterrupted transition consisting of the knowledge of suffering realizes the cessation of the fetters to be abandoned through seeing in the three realms— which were previously abandoned by the [preceding] patiences—

as well as the cessation of the first five categories of fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, which were previously abandoned by the conventional knowledges of origin, cessation, and the path.
The Once-returner, having abandoned the seventh and eighth grades of fetters of the desire realm by means of the mundane path and the knowledge of the origin, cessation, and path,
further employs the knowledge of suffering as the path of immediate succession.
Upon abandoning the ninth grade [of afflictions], one attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).

At that time, the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) within the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) realizes the cessation of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) across the three realms, which were previously abandoned by means of patience (*kṣānti*).

Furthermore, upon realization, one abandons those fetters of the desire realm belonging to the first eight categories that are to be abandoned through cultivation— which were previously abandoned by conventional knowledge of origin,
cessation, and the path. An Anāgāmin, by means of either the conventional path or the knowledge of origin, cessation, and the path, [abandons these].
Having become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness,
and having abandoned the eight grades of fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of the knowledge of origin, cessation, and the path;
Furthermore, taking the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) as the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one abandons the ninth category [of afflictions] and attains the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*).
At that time, it is the path of immediate succession.
The knowledge of suffering realizes the cessation of the fetters to be abandoned through seeing within the three realms that were previously abandoned by patience,
as well as the cessation of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation across the eight stages that were previously abandoned by conventional knowledge of origin, cessation, and the path.

The cessation of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation— the first eight categories— pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which are not abandoned by the [path of] seeing the truths of suffering, origin, or cessation;
such is the cessation of these various fetters.
One realizes the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*),
yet those fetters (*saṃyojana*) are not abandoned by the knowledge of suffering.
As it is said regarding the knowledge of suffering, so it is for the knowledges of origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*).
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Question: What is the difference between the preceding section and this section?
Answer: There are those who maintain that the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) severs the acquisitions of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding the statement that the path of liberation realizes the attainment of that cessation:
it is said that the preceding section reveals the function of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
while this section reveals the function of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

As for those who maintain that the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) can both sever the acquisitions of the fetters (*saṃyojana-prāpti*) and realize the acquisition of their cessation (*nirodha-prāpti*),
they state that the preceding section clarifies how the path of uninterrupted transition severs the acquisitions of the fetters and realizes the acquisition of their cessation.
This section reveals exclusively that the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) realizes the attainment of the extinction of all fetters (saṃyojana).
Just as one realizes the attainment of their extinction upon severing the fetters,
one abandons faults and cultivates virtues.
Abandoning the meaningless, one attains the meaningful;
abandoning the inferior, one attains the sublime;
and free from the suffering of craving and defilement.
It should be understood that the realization of the bliss of tranquility is likewise so.
Furthermore, the preceding section reveals the abandonment of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This section reveals the realization of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, while the preceding section revealed instantaneous abandonment (*sakṛt-prahāṇa*),
this section reveals gradual abandonment (*anupūrva-prahāṇa*).
Furthermore, while the preceding section reveals that realization occurs at the very moment of abandonment, this section reveals that realization follows after abandonment.

This is the distinction between the preceding section and this section. [This applies to] the eye faculty up to the latent tendency of ignorance to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm.
Among the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), how many know [this]?
Thus it is explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of others and revealing the correct principle.
That is to say, there may be those who maintain that there are certain cognitions which lack an objective referent (*ālambana*).
Just as in the case of perceiving illusions, gandharva cities, reflections,
the moon in water, shadows, light, mirages, whirling firebrands, and so forth,
all such various cognitions lack any real objective referent.
To refute that attachment, it is shown that all cognitions and wisdoms possess real objects.
Alternatively, there may be those who hold the view that there exists a knowing cognition that does not know its object of knowledge.
There may be an object of cognition that is not known by a cognition;
this [text] refutes such a tenet by demonstrating that there is no cognizing cognition that does not know its object of cognition,
and likewise, there is no object of cognition that is not known by a cognition.
For these reasons, this treatise is composed.
If one asks concerning inclusion, one should answer after careful consideration based on the eighteen elements (*dhātus*).
If one asks concerning consciousness, one should answer after careful consideration based on the twelve bases (*āyatanas*).
If one asks about the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), one should answer after careful reflection based on the five categories (*pañca-varga*).
If one asks about knowledge (*jñāna*), one should answer after careful reflection based on the four noble truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*).
In this way, these phenomena are easily demonstrated.
It is easy to establish.
Since this inquiry concerns knowledge, one should answer by reflecting carefully upon the Four Noble Truths.
However, all phenomena can be summarized into five types.
This refers to those factors included within the Four Noble Truths and those not so included.
Among these, the factors comprised within the truths of suffering,
origin, and the path each have two types.
That is to say, there is only one kind each for dharmas subsumed under the truth of cessation that are associated, those that are dissociated,
and those not subsumed under any of the [other] truths.
That is to say, it is dissociated [from mind],
subsumed under the truths of suffering and origin within the desire realm,
and is known by seven knowledges regarding associated phenomena.

Excluding the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), the dissociated factors (*viprayuktadharma*) are known by six knowledges. Excluding the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of destruction, and the knowledge of the path, [the remaining six knowledges cognize them].
Those factors associated with the truths of suffering and origin pertaining to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are known by seven knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-dharma*) are known by six types of knowledge—
excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
They are comprised within the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and origin (*samudaya-satya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
Associated and dissociated phenomena are both known by six knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.
Phenomena subsumed under the truth of cessation are known by six knowledges.
Excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path,
the associated factors subsumed under the truth of the path are known by seven knowledges;
excluding the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation.
Dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-dharma*) are known by six knowledges (*jñāna*),
excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin,
and the knowledge of cessation. Phenomena not subsumed under the [Four] Truths are known by one knowledge.
That is to say, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). This is the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
Herein, the eye-faculty is known by seven knowledges, and so forth.
Its characteristics should be understood as previously explained.
Question: Why is it called "knowledge" (jñāna)?
Answer: It is called knowledge because it is able to know that which is to be known.
Question: For what reason is it called "the knowable" (*jñeya*)?
Answer: It is called "the knowable" because it is that which is known by wisdom (*jñāna*).
The Venerable Ghosaka spoke thus.
That which measures is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*);
that which is measured is called the "object of knowledge" (*jñeya*).
It should be understood that the same applies to the measurer and the measured, as well as the one who evaluates and the evaluated, and the one who crosses over and the one crossed over.
The Venerable Pārśva said: "It is called 'knowledge' (jñāna) because it is capable of knowing.
If a phenomenon is that which is traversed, taken as an object, or grasped by knowledge, it is termed 'the knowable' (jñeya)."
Wisdom is established in relation to the object of knowledge; therefore,
there is no wisdom that does not know its object of knowledge,
nor is there any object of knowledge that is not known by wisdom.
There is no wisdom and nothing to be known;
there is no object of knowledge and no wisdom, as it is said regarding the perception of impermanence:
whether practiced or cultivated.
If practiced extensively,
it can eliminate all sensual desire and desire for form.
Lack of desire for the formless realm,
restlessness,
and the conceit "I am."
Ignorance, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of providing a detailed analysis of the meaning of the sūtra.
That is to say, the sūtra states:
"If the perception of impermanence is practiced, cultivated, and frequently performed..."
The detailed explanation is as previously stated.
Although the sūtra contains this teaching, it does not analyze its meaning;
yet the sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which has not yet been explained should now be explained;
therefore, this treatise is composed.
Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One speak this sutra?
Answer: There are sentient beings whose minds are largely characterized by indolence, who do not exert diligent effort, and who abandon the yoke of all wholesome qualities.
This sutra was spoken in order to exhort and spur them on.
Furthermore, this sutra was spoken in order to encourage practitioners to abandon craving for future existence.
That is to say, when the World-Honored One spoke of the time when Maitreya would attain Buddhahood in the future,
certain practitioners had this thought:
"I vow that I shall see the event of his attaining Buddhahood before entering parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, the Buddha said to them:
"You all, at this time..."
Because various requisites are pleasing for a short time, one craves future existence;
however, if one lacks the conditions for sustenance and is oppressed by suffering, one will have no desire or delight for any form of existence whatsoever.
At that time, one should cultivate this perception of impermanence to exhaust all outflows and attain parinirvāṇa;
therefore, one should not crave for future existence.
Therefore, for the sake of those who study, I have explained this sutra.
Now, as for the perception of impermanence:
if it is practiced, cultivated, or frequently performed—
That which is able to eliminate all desire and greed should be described as being associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), namely,
the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna).
This perception should be described as having both vitarka and vicāra,
because it arises together with vitarka and vicāra in the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna).
This perception should be described as associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
This refers to that which arises together with the faculty of equanimity in the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*).
This perception should be said to be associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*),
meaning it is associated with the wishless directed toward suffering.
This perception should be said to have as its object that which is bound to the desire realm;
that is to say, it takes the five aggregates of the desire realm as its object and is able to eliminate all craving for form.
This perception should be said to be associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
namely, the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).
This perception should be so described.
There are states with both vitarka and vicāra,
namely those in the *anāgamya* concentration and the first *dhyāna*, where vitarka and vicāra arise together;
or there are states without vitarka and with vicāra alone.
That is to say, in the intermediate dhyāna there is only co-arising with vicāra;
or it is without vitarka and without vicāra,
namely, in the latter three dhyānas.
This perception should be said to be associated with either the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
namely when one is in the third dhyāna.
It may be associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*),
as in the first and second dhyānas;
or it may be associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
That is to say, in the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna,
this perception should be said to be accompanied by the wishless (*apraṇihita*); that is,
it is associated with the wishless regarding suffering.
This perception should be said to have as its object that which is bound to the form realm;
that is, it takes the five aggregates of the form realm as its object and is able to eliminate all craving for the formless.
This perception should be said to be associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
namely, the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).
It may be accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
It may be with vitarka and without vicāra,
or without both vitarka and vicāra;
it is associated with the faculties of pleasure, joy, or equanimity, and is conjoined with the wishless (apraṇihita).
Conditioned by that which is bound to the formless realm,
as previously explained regarding the perception capable of removing desire for form, there is a distinction:
this perception may be without vitarka and without vicāra.
That is to say, it exists in the final three dhyānas and the first three formless attainments,
and is associated with the faculty of equanimity.
This refers to the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the fourth dhyāna, and the first three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
It takes as its object that which is bound to the formless realm;
specifically, it takes as its object the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the formless realm.
That which is able to eliminate all restlessness, conceit,

and ignorance should be described as being associated with the knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge (*dharmajñāna* and *anvayajñāna*), namely, the knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna* and *anvayajñāna*).
Regarding this perception,
it should be said that it is either with vitarka and vicāra,
or without vitarka and with vicāra alone.
Alternatively, those [attainments] that are without vitarka and without vicāra,
associated with the faculties of pleasure, joy, or equanimity, and conjoined with the wishless (apraṇihita),
are all as previously explained regarding the ability to eliminate the perception of greed for the formless realm.
This perception should be said to be either conditioned by the desire realm; that is,
it takes the five aggregates of the desire realm as its object.
Or it takes as its object that which is bound to the form realm,
namely, the five aggregates of the form realm;
or it takes as its object that which is bound to the formless realm.
That is to say, it takes the four aggregates of the formless realm as its object.
Question: Since all noble paths are capable of severing the fetters, why is it that only the perception of impermanence is mentioned?
Answer: Herein, the term "perception" (*saṃjñā*) indicates the various noble paths (*āryamārga*).

That is to say, the Buddha sometimes uses the terms "feeling" (*vedanā*), "perception," "volition" (*cetanā*), "mind" (*manas*), "lamp," "faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom," "raft," "mountains and stones," "water," "flowers," or "loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity."
This reveals the various noble paths;
as explained extensively before,
it is the same here as well, so there should be no objection.
Question: The perception of impermanence can only counteract two categories of afflictions, namely those abandoned through the vision of suffering and those abandoned through cultivation.
Why, then, is it said here that it can eliminate all greed and other afflictions of the three realms?
Answer: In this context, one should speak only of that which can eliminate craving for the three realms and so forth;
one should not speak of "all.
Yet, it is spoken of as "all" because—
"All" is of two kinds: namely, "partial all" and "all-all."
In this context, "all" refers only to a partial portion;
that is, all [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering and through cultivation, and nothing else.
Furthermore, the Buddha spoke this sūtra for the sake of the noble ones.
Since he has already permanently severed the fetters to be abandoned through vision,
there is no fault in exhorting him to cultivate this perception of impermanence so that he may sever all fetters to be abandoned through cultivation within the three realms.
Question: The perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*) can counteract the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Why, then, is it said here that it specifically severs only greed (*rāga*), conceit (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*)?
Answer: Because these three types [of defilements] pervade all three realms and all five categories (*pañcavarga*).
Therefore, they are explained selectively:
although the five views and doubt pervade all three realms, they do not extend across all five categories;
and although hatred extends across all five categories, it does not pervade all three realms.
Therefore, they are not mentioned.
Furthermore, because these three types can all be manifested by both ordinary beings and noble ones throughout the three realms.
Therefore, they are explained selectively;
although the five views and doubt pertain to all three realms,
they never manifest in the minds of the noble ones.
Although hatred can manifest in both ordinary beings and noble ones,
it does not pertain to all three realms;
therefore, it is not mentioned here.
Question: For what reason are the factors of greed divided according to the distinctions of the three realms, while restlessness and so forth are not?
Answer: They too should be divided according to the distinctions of the three realms;
however, that they are not so divided should be understood as being due to ellipsis.
Furthermore, it is because he wishes to manifest diverse explanations and diverse phrasings to adorn the meaning,
so that those who uphold it may give rise to joy;
furthermore, it is because he wishes to manifest two gateways and two summaries.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, craving is heavy, difficult to sever, and difficult to destroy;
it possesses many faults and afflictions.
Therefore, it is partial.
Furthermore, because of craving and attachment, there are distinctions among the various realms, stages, and divisions;
therefore, it is partial.
Question: It is said that cultivating the perception of impermanence can eliminate the seven types of pride;
why then is it stated here that it eliminates only the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*)?
Answer: This is because, in this context, only its immediate antidote is being discussed.
That is to say, the perception of impermanence is the direct antidote to the conceit of "I am.
As it is said in a sutra:
"If, O bhikṣus..."
One who cultivates the perception of impermanence can induce the perception of non-self.
If one dwells in the perceptions of impermanence and non-self,
one can sever the conceit of "I am" and swiftly exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).
Question: Why is it that among all the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), only restlessness (*auddhatya*) is mentioned?
Answer: Among the secondary afflictions, restlessness alone possesses an increased degree of fault;
that is to say, it pervades the three realms and is subsumed under the category of the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments).
Although *styāna* (sloth) possesses these two characteristics,
because it is conducive to meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in the higher realms,
its defects do not increase there.
Therefore, among these, restlessness (uddhacca) is specifically mentioned;
as it is said regarding the seven points of proficiency and the contemplation of the three meanings,
one is able to quickly exhaust all taints (āsrava) within this Dharma-Vinaya.
What are the seven? They are:
knowing, as it truly is, form, the origin of form, the cessation of form, the practice leading to the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form.
It is the same for the seven [aspects] regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Should this wisdom be called dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) up to path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*)?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of extensively analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
That is to say, a sūtra states:
"Bhikṣus, you should know."
There are the seven points of proficiency and the contemplation of the three meanings;
these have been explained in detail as previously stated.
Although the sutra makes this statement, it does not analyze their meaning.
The Sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Since those [points] have not yet been explained therein, they shall now be set forth;
for this reason, this treatise is composed.
Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One speak this sutra?

Answer: There are those among the learners (*śaikṣa*) who have already entered the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and abide in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), yet are afflicted by the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The World-Honored One, wishing to cause them to cultivate that remedy,
said: "You have already attained the Noble Path."
Why do you not rely upon this to sever the remaining afflictions?
It is like a valiant man who is being tormented by an enemy;
another person tells him, "Since you are already valiant..."
It would be better not to harm the enemy and instead suffer affliction for his sake.
Furthermore, there are those among the trainees who have already attained the first fruit but fail to apply themselves toward the subsequent, superior fruits.
If they were to apply themselves to practice without knowing it as it truly is,
the Blessed One, wishing to inspire them to superior application, said:
"If you are able not to abandon the previously attained applications for the fruit of stream-entry..."
Before long, they will surely attain the ultimate exhaustion of the outflows (āsravakṣaya).
For their sake, the Buddha spoke this sūtra:
"To know form as it truly is constitutes four kinds of knowledge."
That is to say, regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*),
conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*): herein, the knowledge of phenomena knows the form-fruit of the desire realm,
while subsequent knowledge knows the form-fruit of the form realm.
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) knows all material fruits (*rūpaphala*).
Knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) knows that tainted material fruits are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Although there are four such knowledges, they are established as one wholesome [knowledge].
Because they all equally observe the single fruit that is form (*rūpa*),
one knows the arising of form as it truly is through four knowledges; namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*),
the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of arising (*samudaya-jñāna*).
In this context, dharma-knowledge cognizes the causes of form in the desire realm;
subsequent knowledge cognizes the causes of form in the form realm;
and conventional knowledge cognizes all causes of form.
The knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) knows that the cause of contaminated form arises from origination and conditions;
although this consists of four [aspects], they are established as one wholesome [knowledge],
because they all equally observe the single cause of form.
To know the cessation of form as it truly is constitutes four types of knowledge:
namely, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of cessation.
Among these, dharma-knowledge cognizes the cessation of form belonging to the desire realm.
Subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) knows the cessation of form within the form realm;
conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) knows the cessation of all forms;
and the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) knows the cessation of tainted form as peaceful, sublime, and detached.
Although there are four [of these], they are established as one wholesome [category] because they all equally observe the cessation of a single form.
To know, in accordance with reality, the practice that leads to the cessation of form— these are the four knowledges.

This refers to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). Among these, the knowledge of phenomena knows the path that serves as the antidote to the form of the desire realm;
subsequent knowledge knows the path that serves as the antidote to the form of the form realm.
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) knows all paths that serve as antidotes to form (*rūpa*).
Knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) knows the paths that serve as antidotes to contaminated form (*sāsravarūpa*) according to their mode of practice and emergence.
Although there are four [types of such knowledge], they are established as one wholesome [category].
Because they all equally observe the path of a single form,
one knows the flavor of form as it truly is through four knowledges; namely, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna),
subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna).
Among these, the four knowledges all understand the gratification of form (*rūpa-rasa*) as previously explained; this should be understood accordingly.
Although there are four, they are established as one wholesome [knowledge], because they all equally observe the single accumulation of form.
To know the peril of form as it truly is consists of four knowledges:
namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
Among these, all four knowledges know the peril of form; this should be understood as previously explained.
Although these consist of four [knowledges], they are established as one wholesome [knowledge],
because they all equally observe the suffering of a single form (*rūpa*).
One knows the emergence of form as it truly is through these four knowledges.
This refers to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
Among these, it should be understood that all four knowledges know the emergence from form (*rūpa-niḥsaraṇa*) as previously described.
Although there are four, they are established as one wholesome [knowledge].
Because they all equally observe the cessation of a single form (*rūpa*),
one knows feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are; these seven are also like this,
just as it was explained regarding the observation of form.
Question: If that is so, one should speak of wholesomeness in thirty-five bases or in immeasurable bases; why then do you speak of seven?
Answer: When one contemplates each individual aggregate (*skandha*), there are seven in each;
because they do not exceed the number seven, it is said that there are seven, as stated in other sūtras.
Stream-enterers have at most seven more existences.
If one were to speak of them separately according to the two realms and two types of existence, there would be twenty-eight:
namely, seven existences in the human realm and seven in the heavenly realm.
Among humans there are seven [days], and among intermediate states (*antarābhava*) there are seven.
However, because they do not exceed seven, they are designated by the name "seven.
Furthermore, as other sūtras state, there are two dharmas.
This refers to the eye and forms, up to the mind and mental phenomena.
Furthermore, as stated in other sūtras, the turning of the wheel of Dharma has twelve aspects through three revolutions;
since these do not exceed two and twelve, they are said to be twenty-two.
This case is also like that.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"In this sutra, it should have been stated: 'one knows form as it really is, up to consciousness.'"
One knows, as they truly are, the arising of form up to the arising of consciousness;
one knows, as they truly are, the cessation of form up to the cessation of consciousness;
and one knows, as they truly are, the practice leading to the cessation of form up to the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness.
One knows, as it truly is, the gratification of form up to the gratification of consciousness;
one knows, as it truly is, the danger of form up to the danger of consciousness;
one knows, as it truly is, the escape from form up to the escape from consciousness.
If one were to say that there are only seven points of proficiency,
rather than thirty-five or an immeasurable variety;
furthermore, if one were to speak of them briefly, there are seven points of proficiency.
If explained extensively, there are thirty-five or even immeasurable kinds;
however, because the sūtra provides a brief exposition, there are only seven. This is like the relationship between the concise and the extensive, or the general and the specific.
One should know that the same applies to non-conceptualization, conceptualization, sudden teaching, and gradual teaching.
Furthermore, for those of sharp faculties, the seven points of excellence (*saptasthāna-kauśalya*) are taught;
for those of dull faculties, thirty-five or even immeasurable varieties are taught.
As with sharp faculties and dull faculties, there are the power of causes and the power of conditions; the internal factor and the external factor;
and the power of internal reflection and the power of external hearing.
It should be understood that the same applies to the exposition of wisdom through the opening of wisdom.
Furthermore, based on observation of what is proximate, one speaks of proficiency in the seven points;
based on observation of what is remote, one speaks of thirty-five or immeasurable kinds.
Just as there are those that are proximate or remote, contiguous or non-contiguous, manifest or non-manifest,
so too should it be understood for this *nikāya-sabhāga* and other *nikāya-sabhāgas*.
Furthermore, the "skill in the seven bases" (*saptasthāna-kauśalya*) is taught in reliance upon untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*).
Based on the contemplation of that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), thirty-five or immeasurable varieties are taught,
just as there are distinctions between the contaminated and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
and between worldly and supramundane bondage and liberation.
It should be understood that the same applies to the bound and the unbound.
Furthermore, based on the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), one speaks of proficiency in seven points;
based on the time of investigation, one speaks of thirty-five or immeasurable varieties.
Furthermore, based on the contemplation of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), the seven points of proficiency (*saptasthānakauśalya*) are taught;
based on the contemplation of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), thirty-five or immeasurable varieties are taught.
This is as in the case of the contemplations of general and specific characteristics.
One should know that the observation of specific and general characteristics,
the awakening to specific and general characteristics,
and the mental attention toward specific and general characteristics are likewise to be understood in this way.

Question: In this context, is it the attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) that is being described, or is it the attention to general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*)?
If so, what would be the fault [in either case]?
If one speaks of attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*),
how should the following statements be reconciled?
For example, there is the teaching on proficiency in the seven points (*saptasthānakauśalya*) and the contemplation of the three meanings (*trividhārthapratyavekṣā*).
Within this *viniścaya* on the Dharma, one can swiftly exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*);
these outflows cannot be exhausted through attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*).
If one speaks of attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*), [it is through this that they are exhausted].
How, then, should one reconcile what is stated here?

As it is said, "knowing form as it truly is," up to "knowing consciousness as it truly is," one should respond by saying this: [it refers to knowing] the arising and passing away of form, and so on, up to the arising and passing away of consciousness.
Herein, the attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) is being explained.
Question: If that is so, how can one quickly exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*)?
Answer: This attention to specific characteristics is able to induce the attention to general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*).
That attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) can swiftly exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*).
This statement is made because they function as successive causes (*pāramparyahetu*).
Furthermore, there are those who say:
In this context, the mental engagement with common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) is being discussed. Question:
If that is so, how is it that this sūtra says, "one knows form as it really is, up to knowing consciousness as it really is"?
Answer: This sūtra should have stated it thus:

"One knows, as they truly are, the aggregates, the arising of the aggregates, the cessation of the aggregates, the path leading to the cessation of the aggregates, the gratification of the aggregates, the danger of the aggregates, and the escape from the aggregates.
Yet, it speaks of them separately.
One should know that there is a difference in the time of the teaching and a difference in the time of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
For example, when the Buddha first taught the Four Noble Truths to the Four Great Kings, he used the noble language (*ārya-bhāṣā*).
The two cases of understanding and the two cases of not understanding have already been explained above;
therefore, it is known that the time of the teaching is distinct from the time of realization.
That is to say, they are taught as being distinct in terms of their timing.
Because at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), there is a comprehensive clear realization.
Question: What is the difference between the "skill in the seven bases" (*saptasthānakauśalya*) and the "contemplation of the three meanings"?
Answer: Their names themselves constitute the difference.
This is called "skill in the seven bases," because it is the contemplation of the three meanings.
Some have said this.
The sevenfold proficiency (*saptasthānakauśalya*) is untainted (*anāsrava*);
the threefold contemplation of meaning (*trividhārthaparyeṣaṇā*) is tainted (*sāsrava*).
Question: If this is so, how should the following statement be reconciled?
To know form as it truly is constitutes four types of knowledge, namely:
dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of suffering.
Answer: Although this conventional knowledge may also be present, it does not manifest [at that time].
Furthermore, these seven points of proficiency (*saptasthāna-kauśalya*) are the characteristics of noble practice (*ārya-caryā*).
While they are described as being untainted (*anāsrava*), they also truly pertain to the tainted (*sāsrava*).
When viewed in contrast to the three meanings [of the noble path], they are not the characteristics of noble practice.
It is called "untainted" (anāsrava) precisely because it is otherwise tainted (sāsrava).
Question: Can one enter the contemplation of the three meanings by means of the seven points of excellence (saptasthāna-kauśalya)?
Answer: No; for the seven points of excellence are untainted modes of activity (anāsrava-prakāra).
Because the contemplation of the three meanings consists of outflow-tainted (sāsrava) modes of activity.
Furthermore, some say that proficiency in the seven points (saptasthāna-kauśalya) encompasses both the outflow-tainted and the outflow-free (anāsrava).
The contemplation of the three meanings pertains exclusively to that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Question: Is it possible to enter the contemplation of the three meanings by means of the seven points of excellence (*saptasthāna-kauśalya*)?
Answer: It is possible.
However, it requires much exertion of effort,
much application of mental attention,
and much performance of preparatory practice.
That is to say, one knows form as it truly is, up to and including consciousness;
one knows the danger of form as it truly is, up to and including the danger of consciousness, and thereby enters the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*).
One knows the origin of form as it truly is, up to and including the origin of consciousness.
One knows the gratification of form, up to the gratification of consciousness, as it truly is, and enters into the contemplation of the sense bases (*āyatana*).
One knows the cessation of form, up to the cessation of consciousness, as it truly is.
One knows the escape from form, up to the escape from consciousness, as it truly is, and enters into the contemplation of the elements (*dhātu*).
Although one can thus enter the contemplation of the three meanings through proficiency in the seven points,
it requires great effort and the frequent application of mental attention.
One performs many preparatory practices (*prayoga*).

Question: Since the contemplation of the three meanings (*trividha-artha-vipaśyanā*) comes first and the seven points of proficiency (*saptasthāna-kauśalya*) come later, for what reason did the Blessed One first teach the seven points of proficiency?
Question: Is it not the case that the contemplation of the three meanings (*trividhārthapratyavekṣā*) was taught later?

Answer: Although the contemplation of the three meanings precedes the excellence of the seven stations (*saptasthānasuvidhi*), the reason the excellence of the seven stations is taught first and the contemplation of the three meanings is taught later is as follows:
Because it accords with both the meaning and the phrasing;
furthermore, because such a sequential explanation accords with both the speaker and the listener;
furthermore, if one were to speak in this manner:
Because it is complete in both the letter and the meaning.
If one were to first explain the contemplation of the three meanings and subsequently explain the seven points of proficiency:
Thus, while it is complete in meaning, it is not complete in its phrasing.
The Venerable Ghosaka stated: "That which should have been said previously was indeed said previously."
If one follows the latter explanation, then both subsequent explanations are free from fault.
When examining the distinctions between stages through three meanings, there are two [positions]:
first, that which exists prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The second [category] exists prior to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
That which exists prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) is not discussed here;
that which exists prior to the path of cultivation is what is discussed here.
Just as it is with the path of seeing and the path of cultivation,

so too should the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the faculty of "having known" (ājñendriya) regarding the stage of seeing and the stage of cultivation be understood.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
In this context, four stages are taught:
namely, the stage of practice (*prayoga-bhūmi*), the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*), the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*), and the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*).
As it is said, those who are skilled in the seven points and who contemplate the three meanings are described as being on the stage of practice.

To know form as it truly is—its arising, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation—and likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness up to consciousness itself, is called the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*).

To know form as it truly is—its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it—and likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness up to consciousness itself, is called the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*).
The stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣabhūmi*) is taught for those who swiftly exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).

Question: For what reason are four bases of wholesomeness (*kuśalamūla*) taught within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), whereas only three bases of wholesomeness are taught within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
The answer is: because the path of seeing has a fixed locus and a fixed antidote, whereas the path of cultivation does not;
furthermore, because the path of seeing has a fixed object of focus and a fixed antidote, whereas the path of cultivation does not.
Furthermore, it is because through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one first attains the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) and first attains clear realization (*abhisamaya*);
whereas through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one has already attained the vision of the truths and already attained clear realization.
Furthermore, it is because through the path of seeing, one first attains the noble lineage (*āryagotra*) and first attains the characteristics of the noble conduct (*āryacaryā*).
Because one has already attained the noble lineage and the noble modes of conduct through the cultivation of the path.
Question: For what reason are the first three truths stated again within these seven points of skill?
First, regarding the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Answer: Because it is distinguished here by way of the enumeration of the Truth of the Path;
that is to say, knowing form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*) as they truly are.
This knowledge of things as they truly are is the Truth of the Path.
It is the knowledge of the arising of form, up to the arising of consciousness;
and the knowledge of the cessation of form, up to the cessation of consciousness, and the way leading thereto.
The practice of the cessation of form, up to the practice of the cessation of consciousness;
the gratification of form, up to the gratification of consciousness;
the danger of form, up to the danger of consciousness.
The emergence of form up to the emergence of consciousness—
knowing these as they truly are is also entirely the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya).
Since it has already been categorized and analyzed within the Truth of the Path, it is not mentioned again here.
Furthermore, there is suffering that has already arisen and suffering that has not yet arisen;
there is a cause of suffering that has already arisen and a cause of suffering that has not yet arisen;
there is the cessation of suffering that has already arisen and the cessation of suffering that has not yet arisen.
Thus, regarding these phenomena, only the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) is able to know, abandon, and realize them;
therefore, by speaking of the [other] three truths, one has already explained the Path.
Furthermore, there is suffering that is proximate and suffering that is remote.
There are proximate causes of suffering and remote causes of suffering;
there is the proximate cessation of suffering and the remote cessation of suffering.
Regarding these phenomena, only the Truth of the Path is able to know, abandon, and realize them.
Therefore, by speaking of the three truths, one has already spoken of the path.
Furthermore, because the three truths are finite, they are stated twice;
because the truth of the path is infinite, it is stated only once.
Question: Following from this discussion, one asks:
for what reason are the three truths said to have limits, while the truth of the path is said to be limitless?
Answer: Suffering can be fully known.
The accumulation [of suffering] can be completely severed;
its cessation can be completely realized;
but the path cannot be completely exhausted through cultivation.
The remaining meanings are explained in detail as in the section on conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Furthermore, the first four sections have excellently explained the stage of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Because the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) necessarily involves the investigation of the four truths, all four are fully explained there.
The latter three locations excellently explain the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The noble path cultivated during the stage of the path of cultivation is precisely the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
It is not necessarily the case that one contemplates all four noble truths simultaneously; therefore, only three types are mentioned.
Furthermore, while all noble ones (ārya) weary of suffering and its origin and rejoice in nirvāṇa, the noble path (āryamārga) is not like this.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke of the three truths twice and spoke of the truth of the path once.

Question: For what reason is the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya) mentioned first and the truth of origination (samudaya-satya) mentioned later within the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), whereas within the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), the truth of origination is mentioned first and the truth of suffering is mentioned later?

Answer: This is stated because, in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one relies on the sequence of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), whereas in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one relies on the sequence of cause and effect.
Furthermore, in the path of seeing, it relies on the sequence of vision.
This statement is made because it follows the sequence of exposition within the path of cultivation;
for while the sequence of realization presents the result first and the cause later,
the sequence of exposition presents the cause first and the result later.
Furthermore, the Buddha, based on the path of cultivation for those who act out of craving,
taught the method for abandoning craving, saying:
"You should first examine the gratification within the aggregates."
Having examined flavors, one perceives their defects;
having perceived their defects, one is able to swiftly emerge from them.
Furthermore, because one has already established a limit regarding cyclic existence during the stage of the path of cultivation, one does not feel excessive loathing for suffering.
However, because the mind is disturbed and turbid by the afflictions (*kleśa*), one generally feels aversion toward the afflictions.
Among all the afflictions, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is most frequently active; therefore, one is mostly averse to craving.
Consequently, within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one first contemplates the gratification (*āsvāda*) of craving.
Next, one contemplates the affliction of craving;
subsequently, one contemplates the transcendence of craving.
Furthermore, in the present, craving is most capable of drawing the mind to rush and flow toward various objects.
Craving is most capable of moistening existence in the future and ensuring its non-interruption;
therefore, the noble ones increase their revulsion toward craving.
Within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they first contemplate the gratification (*āsvāda*) of craving.
Next, one contemplates the affliction of craving, and subsequently, one contemplates the transcendence of craving.
Question: For what reason does the Blessed One cause those to be trained to repeatedly observe the objects of knowledge?
Answer: Since beginningless time, they have been deluded regarding the objects of knowledge and have lost the right path.
Sunk in saṃsāra, they undergo various sufferings.
The World-Honored One desires to cause them to awaken to the objects of knowledge and proceed upon the right path.
To transcend birth and death and leave behind all manner of suffering,
one must repeatedly contemplate the objects of knowledge.
The essential point herein is as follows:
This refers to proficiency in the seven bases and the contemplation of the three meanings.
Question: What is the difference between "prior accumulation" and "subsequent enjoyment"?
Answer: The distinction lies in their names themselves.
This refers to the accumulation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth,
due to the gratification (*āsvāda*) of name-and-form and so forth.
Furthermore, while accumulation pertains to all six consciousnesses, gratification belongs only to the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
Furthermore, accumulation (*upādāna*) pertains to both the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and the non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*),
whereas attachment (*āsvāda*) is exclusively defiled.
Furthermore, accumulation pertains to all three realms (*dhātu*), whereas attachment pertains only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, while the accumulation (*ācaya*) common to both karma and afflictions has the flavor (*rasa*) of only afflictions,
the accumulation common to all afflictions has as its flavor only craving (*tṛṣṇā*); this is the distinction.
Question: Are the various aggregates (skandhas) identical or distinct?
If so, what would be the fault?
If they were identical, how would one reconcile this with what is taught in the sūtras?
As it is said: "Because of the accumulation of delight, there is the accumulation of form; because of the accumulation of contact, there is the accumulation of the three aggregates;
because of the accumulation of name-and-form, there is the accumulation of consciousness.
If these were different [from one another], [this would not be so].
How, then, is the statement in the *Prajñapti-śāstra* to be reconciled?
For it says: "Whether this craving is past, future, or present, it is in all cases the cause of suffering."
The root of suffering, the path of suffering,
the source of suffering,
and that which produces suffering.
Suffering arises; suffering has its conditions;
suffering has its accumulation;
and suffering co-arises.
It is granted that this may be said:
due to specific conditions, the collection of the aggregates is one;
due to specific conditions, the collection of the aggregates is distinct.
That is to say, based on the remote cause, the collection of the aggregates is one;
based on the proximate cause, the collection of the aggregates is distinct.
This is like how, based on being remote or proximate, [a thing] is not present there or is present here.
It should be understood that the same applies to this body’s homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) as it does to the homogeneous classes of other bodies.
Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks of three types of accumulation of diversity: first, the accumulation of afflictions (*kleśa*);
second, the accumulation of suffering (*duḥkha*).
"Accumulation" refers to the three types of karma.
Regarding "accumulation": because of the accumulation of delight, there is the accumulation of form; this refers to the accumulation of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because of the accumulation of contact, there is the accumulation of the three aggregates (*skandha*); this refers to the accumulation of suffering (*duḥkha*).
Regarding the statement that "with the arising of name-and-form, there is the arising of consciousness," this refers to the arising of karma;
for in this sutra, karma is designated as "name-and-form.
This is just as it is said that the arising of afflictions, suffering, and karma is due to afflictions.
Suffering karma possesses afflictions;
suffering karma gives rise to afflictions.
One should know that the path of suffering karma is likewise.
Furthermore, it is stated in the sūtras that there are three distinct times:
first, the time of accumulation;
second, the time of enjoyment.
Third is the time of protection.
This means that because of the accumulation of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), there is the accumulation of form; this is called the time of accumulation.
Because of the accumulation of contact (*sparśa*), there is the accumulation of the three aggregates (*skandha*); this is called the time of enjoyment.
When it is said that "with the arising of name-and-form, there is the arising of consciousness," this refers to the time of protection.
Furthermore, within this context, three distinct times are specified as being different:
first, the time immediately preceding union.
Second, the time of actual conjunction;
third, the time of non-separation.
This means that because they delight in gathering together, it is said that when there is the arising of form, it is the time immediately preceding their conjunction.
The statement that "due to the arising of contact, there is the arising of the three aggregates" refers to the time of their perfect conjunction;
the statement that "due to the arising of name-and-form, there is the arising of consciousness" refers to the time when they are not yet separated.
Furthermore, in this sutra, three distinct aspects are taught.
First, the intermediate existence;
second, the existence at birth;
third, the existence as a living being.
That is to say, because of the accumulation of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), there is the accumulation of form (*rūpa*); this refers to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Because of the accumulation of contact (*sparśa*), there is the accumulation of the three aggregates (*skandha*); this refers to the prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*).
Because of the accumulation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), there is the accumulation of consciousness (*vijñāna*); this refers to the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
Furthermore, when it is said that "because of the accumulation of pleasure (*nandī*), there is the accumulation of form (*rūpa*)," this is called "conditioned by form" (*rūpapratyaya*).
When it is said that "because of the accumulation of contact (*sparśa*), there is the accumulation of the three aggregates (*skandha*)," this is called "conditioned by name" (*nāmapratyaya*).

When it is said that "because of the accumulation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), there is the accumulation of consciousness (*vijñāna*)," this is called "name conditioned by form" (*rūpapratyayo nāma*).
Furthermore, because craving seeks after the self-identity of the various future existences (*bhava*), the Blessed One said:
"Because of the accumulation of delight, there is the accumulation of form.
Contact (*sparśa*) is able to nourish and develop the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Because it sustains and draws [the object] so as to bring it into manifestation, the Blessed One said: "Due to the arising of contact, there is the arising of the three aggregates.
Consciousness, depending upon name-and-form, increases and expands.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Because of the arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), there is the arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Question: What is the distinction between suffering (*duḥkha*) mentioned first and the origin of suffering (*samudaya*) mentioned later?
Answer: The very names constitute the distinction.
This refers to the suffering of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth,
because name-and-form and so forth are afflictions.
Furthermore, suffering pervades all three types of feeling (*vedanā*).
Suffering consists solely of painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*).
Furthermore, while suffering applies to both the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and the undefiled (*akliṣṭa*), affliction (*ādīnava*) applies only to the defiled.
Furthermore, while suffering applies to all three realms (*dhātu*), affliction applies only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, suffering (duḥkha) pertains to all afflictions (kleśa), whereas calamity (ābādha) pertains only to afflictions.
Furthermore, suffering pertains to all afflictions,
whereas calamity exists only in craving (tṛṣṇā).
This is called the distinction:
the cessation of form up to consciousness,
and the emergence of form up to consciousness.
What is the distinction?
The answer is: if, by means of this craving, various forms arise, the abandonment of that [craving] is called the cessation of form.
If other forms of craving increase by taking form as their object, the abandonment of that [craving] is called "exit from form," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: Why is it that here the cessation of form and so forth is questioned, while the cessation of craving and so forth is answered?
Answer: Because the cause is severed, the fruit follows in being severed;
because the cause ceases, the fruit follows in ceasing; because the cause subsides, the fruit follows in subsiding.
Because one abandons the cause, one also abandons the fruit;
because one vomits out the cause, the fruit is also vomited out.
If the path is severed, the various states of existence will not continue.
Because the permanent cessation of form and so forth leads to the end of suffering.
Question: Form and so forth are said to cease, yet craving and so forth are said to cease;
why is it that here the abandonment of craving and so forth that have already arisen is called "cessation"?
Is the abandonment of unarisen craving and so forth called "emergence"?
Answer: Once afflictions and karma have already arisen, once they have already performed their functions, and once they have already obstructed the Noble Path.
Having already produced their fruit and having already bestowed their fruit,
they have already functioned as homogeneous causes, pervasive causes, and retributive causes.
Having already taken up the results of outflow and maturation,
one has already rendered one's own continuum defiled and already subjected it to bondage.
Since the work of suffering has already been done,
it can only be brought to cessation;
because there is no further escape from it, it is called "cessation."
The karma of afflictions that have not yet arisen is the opposite of the aforementioned;
because it can be transcended, it is described as "transcendence" (*niḥsaraṇa*),
just like the three types of suffering.
First, that which has already been received;
second, that which is currently being received;
third, that which is yet to be received.
Those who have already attained right reception cannot escape it;
as for those who are about to receive it, they may do so either by their own power or by the power of others.
Or [it may be that] one can achieve liberation through wealth and power.
Question: Why is craving mentioned three times here, while the other afflictions and karma are mentioned only once?
The answer is that because craving is difficult to sever and difficult to destroy,
difficult to transcend and fraught with many faults and afflictions,
and is utterly worthy of censure, it is stated three times.
Just as one first censures and detests women and other evil dharmas collectively,
and then censures and detests them individually;
furthermore, by the power of craving, there arise distinctions of realm (*dhātu*), stage (*bhūmi*), and group (*nikāya*).
All afflictions arise from craving;
because they increase due to craving, it is stated three times.
Question: For what reason are various questions posed in different places?
Question: Why is it that the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) alone—and no other—is repeatedly analyzed?

Answer: Because this Truth of Cessation is the most excellent and sublime among all phenomena, and because it is also the most excellent and sublime among the Four Noble Truths, it is therefore analyzed extensively.

Question: Why is it that in this context only the distinctions regarding cessation are questioned and explained through analysis, rather than the distinctions regarding origin, gratification, suffering, and danger?
Answer: Those two types of distinctions should also have been explained.
That which is not stated here is an incomplete teaching.
Furthermore, in this context, the subsequent [explanation] serves to clarify what precedes it;
that is to say, the distinctions regarding cessation are elucidated through the analysis of questions and answers.
It should be understood that the first two [truths] should also be explained in this manner.

Furthermore, because the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is preeminent, it is analyzed in detail, whereas the truths of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*) are not so explained as they are not preeminent.
