Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Five: The Chapter on the Seven Noble Persons (Saptāryapudgala-nirdeśa). Part One of Five: Within the Third Aggregate of Knowledge (Jñānaskandha), the Fifth Sub-section: From the Follower by Faith (Śraddhānusārin) up to the One Liberated in Both Ways (Ubhayatobhāga-vimukta).
Regarding the eight knowledges (*jñāna*),
how many are accomplished and how many are not accomplished?
Such are the chapters and the explanations of the meaning of these chapters.
Having already grasped the essential meaning, one should now provide a detailed exposition.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was composed in order to refute the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who hold the view that the natures of accomplishment and non-accomplishment do not exist as real entities.
To refute that attachment and to demonstrate that the essences of both accomplishment and non-accomplishment are substantially existent, this treatise was composed.

Question: Why is it that both this section and the subsequent Section on the Aggregates (Skandha-skandha) base their exposition upon the seven types of individuals (pudgala), whereas the preceding Section on the Unwholesome (Akuśala-nikāya) within the Section on the Fetters (Saṃyojana-skandha) did not?
"Is it only on the basis of these five types of *pudgalas* that the treatise is composed?
Answer: "It is because the intention of the author of the treatise was such," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, because the preceding discussion on the aggregates of fetters (*saṃyojana-skandha*) was composed based on individuals who possess fetters,
the latter two types of persons were not mentioned there.
This [present section] and the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), however, are based on individuals who possess both knowledge and concentration.
However, because this is a formal treatise (*śāstra*), the latter two are also mentioned.
Furthermore, in the preceding section on the aggregate of grasping (*upādānaskandha*), the person (*pudgala*) was treated as the primary topic;
since that section was structured around the gateway of the afflictions (*kleśa*), the latter two were not mentioned there.
This and the *Samādhiskandha* take the *pudgala* as their subject matter;
because they have wisdom (*jñāna*) and concentration (*samādhi*) as their gateways, the latter two are also mentioned.

This is because those who are liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*) and those who are doubly liberated (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), though free from afflictions (*kleśa*), [are distinguished by these factors].
However, because there exist those with wisdom and meditative concentration, seven types of *pudgalas* are fully explained.

A detailed analysis of these seven types of *pudgalas* is as previously presented in the *Saṃyojana-skandha*, in the section on the unwholesome, in response to the question regarding the faith-follower (*śraddhānusārin*) in relation to the eight knowledges (*jñāna*).
Alternatively, because the accomplishment of one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight [knowledges] is not fixed:
that is to say, at the moment of the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*, there is one [knowledge] if there is no knowledge of others' minds;
there are two if there is knowledge of others' minds.
If one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
they do not possess the knowledge of others' minds and are therefore said to lack the knowledge of others' minds;
such a person possesses only one type of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
If one has already become free from the defilement of desire and entered into the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma),
they are said to possess the knowledge of others' minds because they have attained that knowledge;
such a person possesses both the conventional knowledge of others' minds and [the supramundane] knowledge.
At the moment of the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*),
there are three [knowledges] when there is no knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and four when there is knowledge of others' minds.
During these two moments of mind, if one does not possess the knowledge of others' minds, one possesses only three.
That is to say, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), then one possesses four;
that is, the aforementioned three plus the knowledge of others' minds.
The increase in knowledge in the subsequent stage should be understood by analogy with what precedes it.
The same applies to those who follow the Dharma (dharmanusārin),
as they may likewise accomplish one up to eight [knowledges], just like those who follow through faith (śraddhānusārin).
Because these two noble stages are equal in terms of the path and the basis of support, they are also equal in their freedom from defilement;
they differ only in their faculties.
That is to say, those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) are comprised within those of dull faculties.
If one follows the practice according to the Dharma (dharmānusārin), they are included among those of sharp faculties.
As for those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta), they either possess eight knowledges or seven or eight;
that is to say, if they lack the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), they possess seven.
Regarding the statement "there are eight when there is knowledge of others' minds":
this means that one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire does not possess the knowledge of others' minds and thus possesses only seven;
if, however, one has already abandoned the defilements of desire and also possesses the knowledge of others' minds, they fully possess all eight.
The same applies to those who have attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta): like those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta),
they either possess seven [limbs] or are endowed with all eight.
Because these two noble stages are equal in terms of the path,
the basis of that path, and the detachment from defilements, they are identical; one should understand,
according to the preceding principle, that they differ only in their faculties (*indriya*).
Regarding the body-witness, the one liberated through wisdom,
and the one liberated in both ways—

those who have accomplished all eight knowledges among these [categories] do so because these three types of noble ones have already abandoned the defilement of desire and fully accomplished the eight knowledges.
Regarding those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) up to those who are liberated through both parts (ubhayatobhāgavimukta),
how many of the eight knowledges (jñāna) do they possess in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?
Why was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the tenets of others and revealing the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that neither the past nor the future exists as real entities;
in order to refute that position and demonstrate that they do indeed exist as real entities, [this treatise was composed].
Furthermore, although it was previously stated in general that one accomplishes the eight knowledges,
their specific quantities have not yet been distinguished according to the three periods of time.
Now, wishing to explain this, I compose this treatise.

Answer: For one who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), regarding the eight knowledges (*jñāna*): at the time of the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), there is one past and future knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and none in the present. At the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), there are two past and future knowledges of others' minds, and none in the present. At the time of the subsequent patience of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), there is one past and future knowledge of others' minds, and none in the present. At the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna*), there are two past and future knowledges of others' minds, and none in the present. Regarding the remaining [patiences and knowledges], it is as with the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering. For one who follows by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), it is as for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of one who follows by faith. For one who has attained through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), it is as for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of one who follows by faith. For one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who follows by dharma. For one who is liberated by both parts (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who is liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*). For one who is liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who is liberated by both parts. For one who is liberated through the power of concentration (*samayavimukta*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who is liberated by wisdom. For one who is liberated through the power of non-concentration (*asamayavimukta*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who is liberated through the power of concentration. For one who is a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who is subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who is liberated through the power of non-concentration. For one who is a non-returner who is not subject to falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who is subject to falling away. For one who is a non-returner who is immovable (*akopyadharman*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who is not subject to falling away. For one who is a non-returner who is destined to attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who is immovable. For one who is a non-returner who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who is destined to attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state. For one who is a non-returner who attains parinirvāṇa with effort (*sābhisamskāraparinirvāyin*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth. For one who is a non-returner who attains parinirvāṇa without effort (*anabhisamskāraparinirvāyin*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort. For one who is a non-returner who goes upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort. For one who is a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who is an upstream-goer. For one who is a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who is a once-returner. For one who is a worldling (*pṛthagjana*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who is a stream-enterer. For one who has entered the stage of certainty (*nyāmāvakrānta*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who is a worldling. For one who has not yet entered the stage of certainty, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has entered the stage of certainty. For one who has fallen away from the fruit, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has not yet entered the stage of certainty. For one who has not fallen away from the fruit, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has fallen away from the fruit. For one who has fallen away from the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has not fallen away from the fruit. For one who has not fallen away from the roots of goodness, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has fallen away from the roots of goodness. For one who has fallen away from the noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has not fallen away from the roots of goodness. For one who has not fallen away from the noble lineage, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has fallen away from the noble lineage. For one who has fallen away from the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has not fallen away from the noble lineage. For one who has not fallen away from the supernormal powers, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has fallen away from the supernormal powers. For one who has fallen away from the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has not fallen away from the supernormal powers. For one who has not fallen away from the meditative concentrations, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has fallen away from the meditative concentrations. For one who has fallen away from the analytical knowledges (*pratisamvid*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has not fallen away from the meditative concentrations. For one who has not fallen away from the analytical knowledges, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has fallen away from the analytical knowledges. For one who has fallen away from the dhāraṇīs (*dhāraṇī*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has not fallen away from the analytical knowledges.

For one who has not fallen away from the dhāraṇīs, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has fallen away from the dhāraṇīs. For one who has fallen away from the eloquence (*pratibhāna*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has not fallen away from the dhāraṇīs. For one who has not fallen away from the eloquence, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has fallen away from the eloquence. For one who has fallen away from the dharmas conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has not fallen away from the eloquence. For one who has not fallen away from the dharmas conducive to penetration, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has fallen away from the dharmas conducive to penetration. For one who has fallen away from the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has not fallen away from the dharmas conducive to penetration. For one who has not fallen away from the roots of goodness conducive to liberation, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has fallen away from the roots of goodness conducive to liberation. For one who has fallen away from the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has not fallen away from the roots of goodness conducive to liberation. For one who has not fallen away from the roots of goodness conducive to penetration, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has fallen away from the roots of goodness conducive to penetration. For one who has fallen away from the roots of goodness conducive to the fruit (*phalabhāgīya*), it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has not fallen away from the roots of goodness conducive to penetration. For one who has not fallen away from the roots of goodness conducive to the fruit, it is as for the path of cultivation of one who has fallen away from the roots of goodness conducive to the fruit.
