Regarding those who currently lack [the knowledge of others' minds], they do not possess the knowledge of others' minds; the meaning of possessing the knowledge of others' minds is as explained previously.
The first refers to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*);
the second refers to conventional knowledge of others' minds (*saṃvṛtiparacittajñāna*).
Because patience (*kṣānti*) is not knowledge (*jñāna*), it is entirely absent in the present.
At the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*),
there is one past [knowledge], namely the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*).
That is to say, regarding the three future knowledges,
they are the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Regarding the two present knowledges, they are the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of suffering.
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), there are two in the past and four in the future.
As for the two in the present, these consist of the past and future [knowledges] with the addition of the knowledge of others' minds; the present [knowledge] itself is not added.
This is because, during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is certain that the knowledge of others' minds cannot manifest, nor can it be cultivated.
Regarding the subsequent stage, the increase in wisdom should be understood by analogy with what preceded.
The same applies to those who practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*);
the detailed explanation of these two stages and so forth is as previously stated.
For one with conviction and resolution, regarding the eight knowledges:
if they lack the knowledge of others' minds, seven are future;
if they possess the knowledge of others' minds, eight are future.
If that which has passed away has already ceased but is not lost, and if that which is present is currently manifest, then regarding the past:

if it has already ceased, one achieves its possession [again] through the attainment of a fruit, the refinement of faculties, or through falling away from a higher state. If it is lost, then one does not possess it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or even if it has already been extinguished,
it is lost— and thus no longer accomplished— due to three conditions.
This refers to untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Alternatively, the knowledge of others' minds is not conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Since conventional knowledge is necessarily possessed in both the past and future, it may consist of one, two, or three types in the present.
If one is without mind, none are accomplished at all;
the same applies to those who have attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), which should be understood according to the preceding [explanation].
The three [attainments], such as the body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*), are explained in detail in the text.

"Already extinguished but not lost" means that if something has been extinguished, it is not lost due to the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) or through falling away (*parihāṇi*); thus, it is possessed.

This applies when the stage of one who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) up to the stage of one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), and when the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) up to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) is manifest.
How many knowledges (*jñāna*) manifest?
Why was this treatise composed? It is answered:
in order to refute the doctrines of other schools and to reveal the correct principle.
That is to say,
there may be those who hold the view that although various types of knowledge can manifest one by one, two cannot manifest simultaneously.
To refute that position, it is shown that when knowledge manifests, it may do so as one, as two, or even as three kinds.
Others further maintain that when entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), one contemplates the four truths collectively and the four knowledges arise instantaneously;
in order to refute that position, [the text] clarifies the nature of the clear realization.
Since the wisdom that perceives each truth individually and the wisdom that perceives them as non-dual arise simultaneously, how much more so could multiple [wisdoms] arise?
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that multiple consciousnesses arise together and multiple wisdoms arise concurrently.
This treatise was composed to refute that attachment and to demonstrate that within a single sentient being, at a single moment, only one consciousness arises;
the same applies to the essence of wisdom.
The answer is: when the dharma-knowledge of the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārī*) manifests.
Two knowledges are present before one: namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
To speak at length, up until the time when the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) is present before one, two knowledges are present before one.
This refers to the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*).
Second, it refers to the time when the seven knowledges manifest during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
although the essence of each momentary knowledge is one, they are described as two from a functional perspective.
That is to say, they are called "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna) or "subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna) by way of their antidotes;
or they are called "knowledge of suffering" (duḥkhajñāna), up to "knowledge of the path" (mārgajñāna), by way of their aspects (ākāra).
The same applies to those who follow the Dharma by faith (śraddhānusārin).
These two stages and so forth are explained in detail as previously stated.
When the dharma-knowledge of those resolved through faith manifests,
either two or three knowledges manifest simultaneously.

This refers to when the two types of knowledge regarding the suffering of phenomena (*dharmaduḥkhajñāna*) are extensively explained, up to the point when the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) manifests;
at that time, either two or three knowledges manifest, namely:
the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). These are the two.
There are three cases where it is the knowledge of others' minds;
there are two cases where it is the subsequent knowledge of the path but not the knowledge of others' minds;
and there are three cases where it is the knowledge of others' minds.
This means that when various knowledges manifest during the stage of the path of cultivation,
although the essence of each momentary knowledge is one,
it is explained as being twofold or threefold in terms of its meaning.
This means that when untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is present,
the knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation, as well as the knowledge of others' minds— excluding the knowledge of the path— are metaphorically designated as two types.
That is to say, because they are antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), they are called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharma-jñāna*).
It is called "subsequent knowledge" (anvaya-jñāna) by way of its mode of activity; it is called "knowledge of suffering" (duḥkha-jñāna), and so on,
up to being called "knowledge of the path" (mārga-jñāna).
If the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) is subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), it is explained according to its meaning as threefold:
it is called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñāna*) or "subsequent knowledge" (*anvayajñāna*) by virtue of being an antidote,
and it is called "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*) by virtue of its aspect (*ākāra*).
It is called "knowledge of others' minds" by virtue of its preparatory application (*prayoga*).
When a contaminated knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*) manifests,
if it is not the knowledge of others' minds, then there is only one single knowledge present.
This refers to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
If it is the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*), it is explained in two senses:
first, by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is called conventional knowledge.
It is called "knowledge of others' minds" because it is a preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The same applies to those who have attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and those who have realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*);
this is because their stages are equivalent and the sense of the various knowledges manifesting before them is similar.
When the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) is present for one liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta),
two or three knowledges are present;
namely, the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are two; the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising are three.
This is explained in detail up until the point when the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) is present before one.
Or two or three knowledges may be present before one,
namely: the knowledge of the path (mārga-dharma-jñāna),
and not the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), or the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna).
This [knowledge] is either the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), or the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)—these three.
The subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is either the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of others' minds—these two.
This [knowledge] is either the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, or the knowledge of others' minds—these three.
This means that when the various knowledges of one in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) manifest,
although the essence of each momentary knowledge is one, it is explained as two or three from the perspective of its meaning.

This refers to when untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) is present: specifically, the knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) or the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), as well as the knowledge of the path not subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna); these are merely designated as "two" in terms of their meaning.
That is to say, by way of antidote, it is called "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna) or "subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna);
by way of its aspect (ākāra), it is called "knowledge of suffering" (duḥkhajñāna).
Up to and including what is called "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*).
Furthermore, the knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation that is subsumed under either the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*),
as well as exhaustion or non-arising itself.
Alternatively, when the knowledge of the path is subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds, it is explained according to its meaning as being threefold;
that is to say, by way of its antidote, it is called either dharma-knowledge or subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
It is called the knowledge of suffering because it takes [the aspects of] suffering as its mode of activity;
likewise, it is called up to the knowledge of the path.
It is called the knowledge of exhaustion because the task has been accomplished.
It is called the "knowledge of non-arising" because its causes are perfected;
it is called the "knowledge of others' minds" because it is a result of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
This occurs when a contaminated knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*) manifests before one.

If it is not the knowledge of others' minds, then there is only one knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). If it is the knowledge of others' minds, then in terms of its meaning, two are spoken of:
it is called conventional knowledge by virtue of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It is called "knowledge of others' minds" (paracittajñāna) because it is a preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Question: Why are the essential natures of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds not mutually intermingled?
Answer: The knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising do not have the nature of vision (*darśana*).
The knowledge of others' minds does not intermingle because it perceives their intrinsic nature;
the activities initiated by the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising also do not intermingle because their respective modes of operation differ.
This means that "suffering has been known by me" and so forth are the aspects (ākāra) arising from the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna);
"it shall not be known again" and so forth are the aspects arising from the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
It is the same for those liberated in both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).
This refers to the equality of their stages and so forth.

Regarding those ranging from the faith-follower (*śraddhānusārin*) to the one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), how many of the three samādhis do they accomplish and how many do they not accomplish? Why was this treatise composed?
Answer: This is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of others and revealing the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that the essence of the three samādhis is actually one, and that they are spoken of as three only in terms of their meaning.
This treatise is composed to refute that attachment and to demonstrate that these three natures are each distinct.

Answer: For one who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārī*), regarding the three samādhis, two are accomplished as long as the dharma-knowledge-patience (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) of cessation has not yet arisen.
Regarding the three factors already produced that are accomplished:
this refers to when the *dharmajñānakṣānti* of cessation has not yet manifested, one accomplishes only two—emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
This is because at the time of the *duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*, one cultivates both pairs [of the four noble truths].
From the moment the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) has arisen,
up until the time when the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) is present, one accomplishes all three;
furthermore, one additionally accomplishes the signless (*animitta*).
The same applies to those who practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
These two stages and so forth are explained in detail as previously stated.
This is because those from the stage of "resolute confidence through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) up to "both-liberated" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) have already fully attained all three types of samādhi.
Regarding the three samādhis, how many are accomplished by one who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) up to one who is liberated through both parts (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*),
in terms of the past, the future, and the present?
Answer: For one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin), regarding the three samādhis,
at the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) upon entering rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on emptiness,
there is none in the past.
In the future there are two, and in the present there is one.
This is explained in detail up to the stage of the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*).
Up to the moment of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*), there are two in the past.
Three in the future and one in the present;
that is to say, if one relies on emptiness to enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth.
At the initial moment of seeing suffering, there is nothing past.
During the four moments of seeing suffering, there is one present [knowledge], namely the knowledge of emptiness.
During the three subsequent moments of seeing suffering, there is likewise one present [knowledge].
Furthermore, during the initial moment of seeing and comprehending (*abhisamaya*) the origin (*samudaya*), one [moment] from the past is [attained],
namely the three moments following the mind that sees the origin as empty.
During the initial moment of seeing and comprehending cessation (*nirodha*), two [moments] from the past are [attained].
That is to say: during four moments of mind when seeing suffering and origination through the gateways of emptiness and wishlessness, two future [moments] arise;
during four moments of mind when seeing cessation through the gateways of emptiness and wishlessness, one present [moment] arises;
and during four moments of mind when seeing origination and three moments of mind when seeing the path through the gateway of signlessness, one present [moment] arises.
This means that during the three moments of mind immediately following the vision of cessation,
and during the three moments of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), all three [knowledges] are present in the past.
During the four moments of the vision of cessation and the three moments of the path of vision, all three are likewise present in the future.
It should be understood that the same applies to entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
The difference is this:
there is no past [concentration].

Emptiness has only one or two [aspects]. During the four moments of mind that see suffering and the four that see origin, as well as during the three moments of the path of seeing, it is always present as one:
namely, the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
Question: What kind of person (*pudgala*) enters into rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on emptiness?
What kind of person enters into rightness and departure from birth by relying on wishlessness?
Answer: If one is a practitioner who follows through vision, they enter into rightness and departure from birth by relying on emptiness;
if one is a practitioner who follows through craving, they enter into rightness and departure from birth by relying on wishlessness.
Except for Bodhisattvas, who,
although they practice through attachment, enter the state of right determination by relying on emptiness;
furthermore, there are two kinds of those who practice through vision.
Those who cling to the view of a self enter the state of rightness and transcendence by means of the aspect of non-self;
those who cling to the view of "mine" enter the state of rightness and transcendence by means of the aspect of emptiness.
Those who follow the practice of craving also have two types:
those in whom the conceit of "I am" predominates enter the state of rightness and departure from birth by relying on the aspect of impermanence;
those in whom indolence predominates enter the state of rightness and departure from birth by relying on the aspect of suffering.
Furthermore, those with sharp faculties mostly enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
those with dull faculties mostly enter the state of right determination by relying on wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
As it is for those with sharp and dull faculties, so it should be understood for those who speak of the knowledge of opening (*āvajjana-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of speaking (*bhāsana-ñāṇa*).
If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth by relying on the wishless (*apraṇihita*),

then for such a person, while relying on the wishless and the signless (*animitta*), the defilements of the three realms may be exhausted, yet the emptiness of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) does not manifest.
The same applies to those who practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmanusārin*).
These two stages and so forth are explained in detail as previously described,
from those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) up to those liberated through both parts (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
Regarding the three samādhis, there are three [factors] that are all future;
as for the past, if they have already ceased and have not been lost;
and as for the present, if they are currently manifest.
All of these should be understood according to the preceding [explanation].

This applies from the stage of one who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) up to the stage of one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), when the samādhis of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*) manifest before them.
How many knowledges are present?
Answer: When the emptiness samādhi of a follower by faith (śraddhānusārin) is present, either two or none are present.

The detailed explanation up to "the same applies to those liberated through both [wisdom and concentration]" means that during the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is no wisdom;
at the time of wisdom (*jñāna*), there are two types of wisdom.
During the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), when there is knowledge of suffering, origin, or cessation, there are two knowledges;
at the time of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), there are either two or three knowledges.
During the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), there is knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation.
Those comprised by the right view of one beyond training each consist of two knowledges;
those not comprised by the right view of one beyond training each consist of three knowledges.
If path-knowledge is not subsumed under the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), it consists of three knowledges;
if it is subsumed under the right view of one beyond training as the knowledge of others' minds, it likewise consists of three knowledges.
If these are not the knowledge of others' minds, there are only two knowledges.
Question: Why do the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising not correspond with the emptiness samādhi?
Answer: Because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ.
That is to say, the mode of activity of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is not that of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*);
nor is the mode of activity of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising that of emptiness.
Furthermore, the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) is associated with vision (*darśana*),
whereas the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) are not of the nature of vision.
Furthermore, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the concentration on emptiness is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The aspect of the activity that arises is also the ultimate truth;
although the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising is the ultimate truth,
the aspect of the activity that arises is not the ultimate truth.
That is to say, following this knowledge, one forms the thought:

"Birth for me has been exhausted," and so forth; because these modes of activity (*ākāra*) pertain to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and not the ultimate (*paramārtha*), they apply to those ranging from the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) up to the one liberated through both parts (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).

When the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and the eight factors of the path (mārgāṅga) manifest in accordance with their respective conditions, how many knowledges (jñāna) manifest?
Answer: When the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñātavya-indriya) manifests for one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin).
"Either two or none;
as explained at length, it is the same even for those liberated through both [wisdom and concentration].
This means that during the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is no wisdom whatsoever.
At the time of each of the seven knowledges, there are two knowledges respectively.
During the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), at the time of the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation, there are two knowledges respectively.
At the time of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), there are either two knowledges or three knowledges.

Within the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path should be understood according to the preceding [explanation] as being either two knowledges or three knowledges.
Question: Why is it stated here repeatedly that one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) gives rise to the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?
This [attainment] must necessarily depend upon the fundamental dhyānas.
If one liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) is also able to manifest the fundamental dhyānas,
does this not contradict the Suśīma Sūtra?
That sutra states:
"One liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) cannot manifest the fundamental dhyānas.
The answer is: there are two kinds of those liberated by wisdom.
First is the partial [attainment],
and second is the complete [attainment].
Those with partial liberation through wisdom can give rise to one, two, or three of the four dhyānas.
Those who are liberated by wisdom in its entirety (sakalābhijñā-vimukta) are unable to produce [the knowledge of others' minds] within any of the four dhyānas.
This treatise, however, speaks of those liberated by wisdom in part (prādeśika-prajñā-vimukta);
therefore, they are able to produce the knowledge of others' minds.
The *Sūśma-sūtra* speaks of complete liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*),
which cannot arise within any of the four dhyānas;
thus, both of these explanations are well-justified.

For this reason, those liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*) may even be able to attain the meditative absorptions up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), yet they do not attain the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
If they do attain the attainment of cessation, they are called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).
If various phenomena are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
are those phenomena also associated with the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)?
[The same applies] up to the full exposition.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of other schools and revealing the correct principle.
That is to say, there are some who hold the following view:
Mental states and their concomitants do not arise one by one; there is no sense of association [in such a case].
To refute that attachment, it is shown that mental states and their concomitants necessarily arise simultaneously and possess the characteristic of association.
Furthermore, some maintain that the mind and mental factors correspond sequentially; others,
again, maintain [the following].
The intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is associated with itself.
To refute that attachment, it is shown that what is associated must necessarily arise simultaneously;
because they possess distinct substantial entities (svabhāva), this treatise was composed.
In this context, all phenomena interact with and correspond to one another through three conditions;
that is to say, some phenomena do so by virtue of their mutual inclusion.
There are phenomena that interact with one another like wisdom with wisdom;
or again, there are phenomena that interact through association, such as wisdom with meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

or again, there are phenomena that interact through both inclusion and association, such as wisdom with the faculties (*indriya*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
This is the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point:
Are those phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) also associated with the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)?
Answer: Not so. Even if it is associated with the knowledge of dharma-classes (dharma-anvaya-jñāna), is it necessarily associated with the knowledge of dharmas (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: It is not so.
Why is this? Because it is not a single mind.
Because their objects of focus differ.
The same applies to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). Why is this so?
It is not because they are a single mind;
for the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) aggregates are each distinct.
All phenomena are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
Are those dharmas associated with the knowledge of others' minds?
One should respond that there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*),
because the meaning is not fixed.
There are dharmas that are associated with dharma-knowledge but not with knowledge of others' minds.
These are the dharmas associated with dharma-knowledge that are not subsumed under knowledge of others' minds. What are these dharmas?
This refers to the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) regarding the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation;
as well as those factors associated with the dharma-knowledge of the path that are not subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna).
There are also factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not dharma-knowledge.
This refers to those mental factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not subsumed under the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
What are these factors?
They are the mental factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are subsumed under the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
There are phenomena that are associated with both dharma-knowledge and knowledge of others' minds.
These are the phenomena associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are subsumed under dharma-knowledge.
What are these phenomena?
That is to say, this [state] is associated with the nine universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*),
the ten wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*),
vitarka, vicāra, and the mind itself.
There are factors associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) that are not also the knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna);
namely, the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of others' minds.
Furthermore, there are all other mental states and mental factors not included within dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) or knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*),
as well as matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
Among these, regarding dharma-knowledge and knowledge of others' minds:
Because intrinsic nature does not associate with intrinsic nature;
because the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) do not include it and are not associated with it;
and because it is not included among any other mental states or mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Excluding that which is dissociated from its own nature,
and excluding that which is associated with it,
one takes up all other mental states and mental factors.

What is this dharma? It refers to the collection of factors associated with the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna), which is not subsumed under the subsequent knowledge of suffering, origin,
or cessation, nor under the knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna).
The aggregate associated with untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*);
all tainted (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors dissociated from the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*);
and form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and those factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*).
This means that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta), as well as unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta),
are neither associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) nor with the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), because they lack an object of cognition (ālambana).
The same applies to the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as to right view.
Just as with the knowledge of others' minds, four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) are established for the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
This is likewise the case for its relation to the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as to right view among the eight factors of the path.
Are those phenomena associated with the knowledge of phenomena also associated with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*)?
It should be stated in four propositions:
herein, the dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) is associated with three samādhis;
the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi) is associated with two knowledges and two patiences.
The two knowledges refer to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna).
The two patiences refer to...
That is to say, the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) and the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti).
Therefore, within this context, four great propositions are established:
there are dharmas that are associated with dharma-knowledge but are not empty.
This refers to the emptiness associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
as well as those factors associated with the knowledge of phenomena that are not themselves associated with emptiness.
Among these, "the emptiness associated with the knowledge of phenomena" refers to:
This refers to the emptiness samādhi that arises simultaneously with the dharma-knowledge.
This [samādhi] is not associated with the dharma-knowledge itself,
because a self-nature cannot be associated with itself.
Regarding those factors that are associated with emptiness but not with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
these refer to the factors co-arising with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and signless (*animitta*) [samādhis] that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena;
there are also factors associated with emptiness that are not associated with the knowledge of phenomena.
That is to say: the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) associated with emptiness,
as well as the phenomena associated with emptiness that are not associated with the knowledge of phenomena.
Regarding the "knowledge of phenomena associated with emptiness" herein:
this refers to the knowledge of phenomena that arises simultaneously with emptiness;
it is not the knowledge of phenomena itself that is associated with emptiness.
Because intrinsic nature does not associate with intrinsic nature;
and as for those factors associated with emptiness that do not associate with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna),

these refer to the factors associated with the samādhi of emptiness that arise simultaneously with the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkhānvayajñāna) and the receptivity to the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe kṣānti).
There are phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and are also empty;
namely, those phenomena associated with both.
Herein, "those phenomena associated with both" refers to:
That is to say, within the collection of factors co-arising with the dharma-knowledge of emptiness,
excluding its two intrinsic natures,
all other remaining mental states and mental factors.
What is this dharma?
It consists of two types of association: the eight universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharmas) and the ten wholesome universal mental factors (kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharmas).
Vitarka, vicāra, and the mind—
these factors are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and are not empty;
that is to say, they are the emptiness that is dissociated from the knowledge of phenomena.
The knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) that is dissociated from emptiness,
as well as that which is not subsumed under the emptiness of the knowledge of phenomena,
are dissociated.
Regarding all other mental states, mental factors, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind:

herein, that which is associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and is empty refers to the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) arising simultaneously with the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the receptivity to the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*).
This is because it is associated with the knowledge of the non-dharmas (*adharma-jñāna*) and belongs to another category;
nor is it associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*),
because a self-nature (*svabhāva*) is not associated with itself.
Regarding the knowledge of dharmas dissociated from emptiness:
this refers to the dharma-knowledge that arises simultaneously with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and signless (*animitta*).
This is not associated with emptiness because it belongs to a different aggregate (*skandha*).
Nor is it associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
A nature is not associated with itself;
furthermore, it is not associated with that which is not subsumed within the emptiness of the knowledge of phenomena.
Other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) are not included;
this excludes the two types of dissociation from their own nature and excludes the two types of association.
It takes up the remaining minds and mental factors.
What are these dharmas?
They are the clusters associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), as well as those associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and signless (*animitta*).

And all contaminated (*sāsrava*) mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), as well as matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
That is to say: all matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
All of these are not associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
nor do they have emptiness as their object.
The same applies to the factors of joy, awakening, and right reflection associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and signless (*animitta*).
Just as the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) forms four great propositions in relation to emptiness (śūnyatā),
so it is also in relation to wishlessness (apraṇihita), signlessness (animitta), the factor of awakening of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga), and right thought (samyak-saṃkalpa).
All these factors are associated with the dharma-knowledge of phenomena.
Are those dharmas associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?
One should respond that this involves four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), as the meaning is not fixed.
There are dharmas that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) but are not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."

This refers to those factors associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) that are not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*). What are these factors?
They are the factors associated with the knowledge of phenomena that are subsumed under the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
This is associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), but it is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*),
because it belongs to a different aggregate.
There are factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are not associated with the knowledge of phenomena.
This refers to the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya),
as well as those dharmas not included in dharma-knowledge that are dissociated from it but associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
Among these, the dharma-knowledge included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" is as follows:
This refers to the dharma-knowledge within the collection of factors that arise simultaneously with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
This [dharma-knowledge] is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," but it is not the dharma-knowledge itself,
because a factor cannot be associated with its own self-nature.
As for those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that are neither included in nor associated with dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*):
these refer to all categories of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and the clusters of factors arising simultaneously with the untainted patiences (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
Regarding the factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya):
these are not the knowledge of the dharma (dharmajñāna) when associated with that faculty,
because they belong to a different aggregate.
There are phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and also associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*).
These are the phenomena associated with the knowledge of phenomena that are subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
What are these phenomena?
This refers to the other eight faculties and their associated [factors],
as well as other non-faculty mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).

There are also factors that are associated with the knowledge of what has already been known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), yet are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
This refers to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*),

as well as all other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) that are neither subsumed under nor associated with the knowledge of phenomena and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
Form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind—

among these, "knowledge of dharmas not included within the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" refers to the knowledge of dharmas that arises together with the assembly [of factors] associated with the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
This is not associated with the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñāna*),
because a nature is not associated with itself.
Nor is it associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Because they belong to a different category (*nikāya*),

as well as because they are not included in and are dissociated from the faculty of knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*),
all other minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) [are excluded].

This refers to those mental states and mental factors that arise together with the faculty of "already known" (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*), which are not included in or associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*);
as well as all contaminated (*sāsrava*) mental states and mental factors.
None of these are associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
nor are they the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*),
because they belong to a different aggregate.
Regarding form as non-associated with the mind and non-conditioned:
this means that all forms, non-associates, and non-conditioned phenomena are entirely non-associated with one another,
because they lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Regarding the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), it is also thus:
just as there are four propositions concerning the faculty of one who knows what is yet to be known (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) in relation to the faculty of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*),
so too are there four propositions in relation to the faculty of having already known (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Are all phenomena associated with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) also associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛtisambodhyaṅga)?
One should answer that this involves four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), as the relationship is not fixed.

There are phenomena associated with the knowledge of phenomena that are not associated with mindfulness; namely, the awakening factor of mindfulness itself when it is associated with the knowledge of phenomena.
This [dharma-knowledge] is associated with the awakening factor of dharma,
but not with mindfulness, because a nature is not associated with itself.
There are factors that are associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness but not with dharma-knowledge.
This refers to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and those factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness that are not themselves associated with the knowledge of phenomena.
Herein, "knowledge of phenomena" refers to the knowledge of phenomena that arises simultaneously with the awakening factor of mindfulness.
This is associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), but it is not the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).
This is because a nature (*svabhāva*) is not associated with itself, and furthermore,
it is not associated with the knowledge of phenomena.
Regarding the factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness:

these refer to the factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness within the collection of mental states that arise simultaneously with untainted receptivity (*kṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
These are associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness, but are not [themselves] the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).
Because it belongs to that same collection (*nikāya*),
there are factors (*dharma*) that are associated with both dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*).
That is to say, within the collection co-arising with dharma-knowledge, one excludes dharma-knowledge itself and mindfulness.
All other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) are associated with these two.
What, then, are they? They are the eight universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma) that are associated with these two.
The ten great wholesome mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*), as well as the mind itself,
are associated with knowledge of what is dharma and what is non-dharma, yet they are not mindfulness (*smṛti*).
That is to say: the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness dissociated from dharma-knowledge,
as well as other mental states and mental factors,
form, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.

Among these, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness dissociated from the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) refers to the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness within the collection of factors that arise simultaneously with the untainted patiences (anāsrava-kṣānti) and subsequent knowledges (anvaya-jñāna).
This is not associated with the knowledge of phenomena, because it belongs to a different collection of factors.
Nor is it associated with mindfulness,
because a self-nature is not associated with itself,
and [it is likewise dissociated] from other mental states and mental factors.
These are not untainted (anāsrava) mental states and mental factors;
rather, they are tainted (sāsrava) mental states and mental factors,
as well as matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra).

This means that all material form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) are all equally non-associated because they lack an object of cognition (*anālambana*).

The same applies to the factors of enlightenment of energy (*vīrya*), lightness (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), as well as to right effort (*samyag-vīrya*), right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Regarding the relationship between dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) and the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga), there are four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
This same analysis applies to its relationship with the awakening factors from diligence (vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga) up to right concentration (samyak-samādhi).
All phenomena associated with dharma-knowledge [are to be understood in this manner].
Are those phenomena associated with the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: All phenomena associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) are also the knowledge of phenomena within the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena.
This is because all [such factors] are subsumed under the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
There are factors that are associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena but are not the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*);
namely, those factors associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena that are not themselves subsumed under the knowledge of phenomena.
What is this dharma?

It refers to the dharmas associated with the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) within the collection of factors that arise simultaneously with untainted receptivity (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
This is associated with the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of dharmas, but it is not the knowledge of dharmas (*dharma-jñāna*).
Because it belongs to that same category.
Just as the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) relates to what follows,
so too does the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) relate to what follows.

Just as dharma-knowledge relates to subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), so it is for all stages up to right concentration; likewise, subsequent knowledge relates to the knowledge of others' minds and so on up to right concentration.
All these factors are associated with the knowledge of others' minds.
Are those dharmas associated with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?
One should answer that this involves four possibilities (*catuṣkoṭi*), as the meaning is not fixed.
There are dharmas associated with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) that are not associated with conventional knowledge.
This refers to those factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not subsumed under conventional knowledge.
What are these factors?
They are the factors associated with untainted knowledge of others' minds.
There are phenomena associated with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that are not associated with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
That is to say, these are the phenomena associated with conventional knowledge that are not subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds.
What are these phenomena?

This refers to those phenomena associated with mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) that are wholesome, afflicted, or non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), and which are not subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
There are also phenomena that are associated both with the knowledge of others' minds and with mundane knowledge.
It refers to those phenomena associated with conventional knowledge that are subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds.
What are these phenomena?
They are those associated with it.
The nine universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*),
the ten wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*), vitarka, vicāra, and the mind itself—
there are phenomena that are not associated with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Nor is it conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

That is to say, it refers to those other mental states and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) that are not included in, and are dissociated from, the conventional knowledge of others' minds (*paracittasaṃvṛtijñāna*).
Form and the unconditioned are formations dissociated from mind.
Among these, conventional knowledge of others' minds is not associated with itself,
because a nature is not associated with itself.
Furthermore, those other mental states and mental factors not subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds or conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)— and which are not associated with them—
are the untainted patiences (*anāsravakṣānti*) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation (*duḥkha-samudaya-nirodhajñāna*).
Furthermore, the collection of mind and mental factors that arise simultaneously with the knowledge of the path— which is not subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds—
are mutually non-associated because they belong to different aggregates.
This also applies to matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
That is to say, all form, the unconditioned, and the formations dissociated from mind are likewise non-associated because they lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
The same applies to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Just as there are four permutations regarding the knowledge of others' minds in relation to conventional knowledge,
so it is also in relation to the knowledge of the path, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena, and right view.
All these factors are associated with the knowledge of others' minds.
Is that dharma associated with the knowledge of suffering?
Answer: No. Furthermore, if a dharma is associated with the knowledge of suffering, is that dharma associated with the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: It is not so.

As for the statement that "the same applies to the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (ājñāsyāmīndriya) in relation to the knowledge of origination and cessation, and to the samādhis of emptiness and signlessness," this is because they do not constitute a single moment of mind.
Either because their modes of activity differ,
or because their objects differ,
various dharmas are associated with the knowledge of others' minds.
Is that dharma associated with the *samādhi* of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)?
One should respond by formulating four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), because the meaning is not fixed.
There are dharmas associated with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) but not with wishlessness.
This refers to the wishlessness associated with the knowledge of others' minds, as well as those factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not associated with wishlessness.
Among these, "wishlessness associated with the knowledge of others' minds" is as follows:
This refers to the wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) that arises simultaneously with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
This [wishlessness] is associated with the knowledge of others' minds,
but it is not itself wishlessness, because a factor cannot be associated with its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding those factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are not associated with the wishless [samādhi]:
these refer to the factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are tainted (*sāsrava*).
These are associated with the knowledge of others' minds but not with the wishless, because they belong to a different category (*skandha*).
There are phenomena associated with the wishless that are not the knowledge of others' minds.
This refers to the knowledge of others' minds associated with the wishless,
as well as phenomena associated with the wishless that are not associated with the knowledge of others' minds.
Among these, "knowledge of others' minds associated with the wishless" refers to the knowledge of others' minds that arises simultaneously with the wishless;
it is not the case that this [knowledge] is associated with the wishless while being something other than the knowledge of others' minds.
Because a nature does not associate with itself,
and because the knowledge of others' minds does not associate with those dharmas associated with the wishless—
namely, the wishless [aspect] regarding suffering and its origin.
Furthermore, it is not associated with the knowledge of others' minds.
It is associated with the path and with the wishless (apraṇihita).
This is because this wishless association is not the knowledge of others' minds, as it belongs to a different category (skandha).
There are dharmas that are associated with both the knowledge of others' minds and the wishless concentration;
namely, those dharmas associated with both,
which are the co-arising aggregates within the untainted knowledge of others' minds.
Excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the wishless samādhi,
what are these remaining mental states and mental factors?
That is to say: the eight universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), vitarka, vicāra, and the mind itself.
There are phenomena that are not associated with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Nor is it non-wishful (apranihita).
That is to say: wishlessness dissociated from the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge of others' minds dissociated from wishlessness.
As well as all other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma),
matter (rūpa), the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra).
Among these, the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) is dissociated from the wishless (apraṇihita).

This refers to the path associated with the wishless (apranihita) that is dissociated from both the knowledge of suffering and its origin (duḥkha-samudaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna).
This is because it is not associated with the knowledge of others' minds, as it belongs to a different category;
nor is it associated with the wishless.
Because a self-nature does not correspond with itself.
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds that is not associated with wishlessness (*apraṇihita*):
this refers to the knowledge of others' minds that is tainted (*sāsrava*); it is not associated with wishlessness because it belongs to a different category (*skandha*).
Nor is it associated with the knowledge of others' minds,
because a nature is not associated with itself;
and as for all other mental states and mental factors.

This refers to the associated and dissociated contaminated mental states and mental factors that are not included within the aggregate of mind and mental factors arising together with emptiness and signlessness, nor are they included within the knowledge of others' minds;
these are dissociated from them because they belong to a different aggregate.
Matter that is unconditioned and dissociated from mind refers to all matter that is unconditioned and dissociated from mind.
Because these [factors] are dissociated and lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
The same applies to the factors of mindfulness, diligence, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, as well as to right thought, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Just as there are four propositions regarding the knowledge of others' minds in relation to the wishless (*apraṇihita*),
so it is also in relation to the six factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the four factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
All these dharmas are associated with the knowledge of others' minds.
Are those dharmas associated with the faculty of known (ājñendriya)?
One should respond that this involves four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭika), as the meaning is not fixed.
There are dharmas associated with the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
It is not the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*).
This refers to those factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) that are not subsumed under the faculty of one who has already known. What are these factors?
This refers to the mental states and mental factors associated with the knowledge of others' minds that are subsumed under the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*),
as well as those associated with the tainted (*sāsrava*) knowledge of others' minds.
These dharmas are associated with the knowledge of others' minds but do not constitute the faculty of one who has already known, because they belong to a different aggregate (*skandha*).
There are phenomena associated with the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya) that are not the knowledge of others' minds;
namely, the knowledge of others' minds subsumed under the faculty of "already known."
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) does not include those factors that are dissociated from it,

nor those associated with the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*). Among these, the knowledge of others' minds included within the faculty of "already known" refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledge of others' minds during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This is associated with the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya) but is not the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna),
because a factor cannot be associated with itself by its own nature,
and because the knowledge of others' minds does not include those factors associated with the faculty of "already known" that are themselves dissociated from it.
This refers to the collection of mental states and mental factors that arise simultaneously with the knowledge of suffering, origin,
and cessation during the path of cultivation, as well as those that arise simultaneously with the knowledge of the path not subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds.
This [dharma] is associated with the faculty of having already known (*ājñātendriya*), but it is not the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), because the latter belongs to another category.
There are dharmas that are both associated with the knowledge of others' minds and associated with the faculty of having already known;
namely, those dharmas included within the faculty of having already known that are associated with the knowledge of others' minds.
What is this dharma?
It refers to the dharmas associated with the untainted knowledge of others' minds within the path of cultivation;
that is, the eight untainted faculties associated therewith.
And those other mental factors associated with it that are not faculties.
There are phenomena that are neither associated with the knowledge of others' minds nor associated with the faculty of "I-have-known."
This refers to the knowledge of others' minds not subsumed under the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya),

as well as that which is incompatible with the knowledge of others' minds not subsumed under the faculty of "already known," and all other remaining mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma).
Form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind—

among these, that which is known as "knowledge of others' minds not subsumed under the faculty of one who has already known" refers to the knowledge of others' minds subsumed under the faculty of one who has already fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
And there is the outflow-tainted knowledge of others' minds.
This is not associated with the knowledge of others' minds,
because a nature is not associated with itself.
Nor is it associated with the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya), because it belongs to a different group;
furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds is not subsumed under the faculty of "already known" and is not associated with it.
As for all other mental states and mental factors:
This refers to the collection of mind and mental factors arising simultaneously with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*),
excluding those not subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and those that are dissociated (*viprayukta*).
It also refers to the collection of mind and mental factors arising simultaneously with the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñendriya*).
The knowledge of others' minds does not include the dissociated factors associated with contaminated minds and mental states,
because these dissociated factors belong to a different aggregate.
Form that is unconditioned and dissociated from mind refers to all unconditioned forms;
it is dissociated from both [mind and] mental factors dissociated from mind because it lacks an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Regarding the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), it is likewise:
just as there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) when the knowledge of others' minds is related to the faculty of one who has already known,
so too is it when related to the faculty of one who has already known.
Are those phenomena associated with conventional knowledge also associated with the knowledge of suffering, up to and including right concentration?
Answer: No. Even if phenomena are associated with the knowledge of suffering, up to and including right concentration, [they are not necessarily associated with conventional knowledge].
Is that dharma associated with conventional knowledge? Answer: No. Why is this so?
Because it is not a single mind;
for from the knowledge of suffering up to right concentration, all are untainted (*anāsrava*).
All dharmas are associated with the knowledge of suffering.
Are those factors associated with the knowledge of the collection of phenomena (*dharmasamgraha-jñāna*)? Answer: No.
Even if they were associated with the knowledge of the collection of phenomena...
Is that dharma associated with the knowledge of suffering?
Answer: No. The same applies to the signless samādhi in relation to the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path.
Why is this? Because they are not a single mind;
because their modes of activity differ.
Alternatively, because their objects of focus differ:
are those phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of suffering also associated with the concentration on emptiness?
Because it is admitted that the fourfold definition of meaning is indeterminate:
there are phenomena associated with the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) that are not associated with emptiness (śūnyatā);
namely, the emptiness associated with the knowledge of suffering.
Regarding "emptiness that is not associated with emptiness":
this refers to the emptiness samādhi associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
This is associated with the knowledge of suffering, but it is not itself emptiness.
Because intrinsic nature does not associate with intrinsic nature;
and as for those factors associated with the knowledge of suffering that do not associate with emptiness,
these refer to the factors associated with the knowledge of suffering that arise simultaneously with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) concentration.
This [dharma] is associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) but not with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because it belongs to a different category (*anya-skandha*).
There are dharmas associated with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) but not with the knowledge of suffering;
namely, the knowledge of suffering that is associated with emptiness.
And those phenomena associated with emptiness that are dissociated from the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
Among these, the knowledge of suffering associated with emptiness refers to the knowledge of suffering that arises simultaneously with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
This is associated with emptiness but is not the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*),
because a nature is not associated with itself,
and because it is a phenomenon associated with emptiness that is not associated with the knowledge of suffering.
This refers to those factors associated with emptiness that arise simultaneously with the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*).
These are associated with emptiness but are not the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), because they belong to a different aggregate (*skandha*).
There are also factors that are both associated with the knowledge of suffering and associated with emptiness.
It refers to the dharmas associated with the two [factors].
What are these dharmas?
They are emptiness associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
Within the co-emergent collection, excluding the knowledge of suffering and emptiness,
all other mental states and mental factors are the eight universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma).
Among the ten great wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*), as well as applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*),
and the mind itself, there are factors that are neither associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) nor are they empty (*śūnya*).
This refers to emptiness dissociated from the knowledge of suffering,
and so forth, as explained at length.
In this context, "emptiness dissociated from the knowledge of suffering" means:
This refers to the emptiness that arises simultaneously with the receptivity to suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*).
It is not associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), because it belongs to a different category;
nor is it associated with emptiness itself.
Because self-nature does not correspond with self-nature,
the knowledge of suffering that is non-corresponding with emptiness refers to the knowledge of suffering that arises simultaneously with the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
This is not associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*),
because a nature is not associated with itself.
Nor is it associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because it belongs to a different aggregate (*skandha*).
"And as for the other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma):
this refers to the collection of mental states and mental factors arising together with the wishless (apraṇihita) that are dissociated from the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna),
as well as those arising together with the signless (animitta)."
All contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*),
as well as those dissociated from them (*viprayukta*) that belong to a different aggregate (*anya-skandha*),
and material form (*rūpa*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This refers to all form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind;
these are likewise non-associated because they lack an object of cognition.
The same applies to the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
Just as there are four propositions regarding the knowledge of suffering in relation to emptiness,
so it is also in relation to the wishless.

As for its relation to the three untainted faculties, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight factors of the path, it is as explained in the case of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
Just as the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) corresponds to the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) and so forth,
so too does this knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) correspond to the three untainted faculties and so forth;
the detailed explanation is likewise.
