translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Three: The Aggregate of Wisdom (Jñānaskandha), Part Five: The Sub-section on the Seven Noble Persons (Saptāryapudgalanirdeśa), Part Two. All dharmas are associated with the knowledge of accumulation (saṃbhārajñāna).
Is that dharma associated with the knowledge of cessation?
Answer: No. Even if a dharma were associated with the knowledge of cessation...
Is that dharma associated with the knowledge of the collection (*dharmajñāna*)?
Answer: No. The same applies to the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) and the signless (*animitta-samādhi*) in relation to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Why is this? Because they are not a single mind;
because their modes of activity differ.
Alternatively, because their objects of focus differ:
are those phenomena associated with the knowledge of the collection of phenomena (dharmajñāna) also associated with the concentration of wishlessness (apraṇihitasamādhi)?
Because it is admitted that the fourfold formulation of meaning is indeterminate:

there are factors associated with the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) that are not associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*). That is to say, those factors associated with the knowledge of origination that are associated with the wishless.
This refers to the wishless samādhi (apraṇihita-samādhi) that arises simultaneously with the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna).
This [samādhi] is associated with the knowledge of origin,
yet it is not itself wishless, because a nature cannot be associated with itself.
There are phenomena associated with the wishless that are not associated with the knowledge of origination;
namely, the knowledge of origination itself and those phenomena associated with the wishless that are not associated with the knowledge of origination.
Among these, as for the knowledge of origination:
This refers to the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) that arises simultaneously with the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
This [knowledge] is associated with the wishless, but it is not itself the knowledge of origination,
because a nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be associated with itself.
Regarding those factors associated with the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) but dissociated from the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*) and associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*):

this refers to the wishless-associated factors within the mental complex (*kalāpa*) that arises simultaneously with the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhakṣānti*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the patience regarding origin (*samudayakṣānti*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), the patience regarding the path (*mārgakṣānti*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
This [knowledge] associated with wishlessness is not the knowledge of origin because it belongs to another category (*nikāya*).
There are, however, factors associated with both the knowledge of origin and wishlessness;
that is to say, those factors associated with both. What are these factors?

This refers to all other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) arising simultaneously with the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna), excluding the knowledge of origination itself and the wishless concentration (apraṇihita-samādhi); that is,
the eight universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma).
Regarding the ten great wholesome mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), vitarka, vicāra, and the mind:
there are factors that are neither associated with the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*) nor are they the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
This refers to those factors that are not associated with the knowledge of origination and are wishless.
...and so on, as explained at length. Herein,

the wishless (apraṇihita) that is dissociated from the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) refers to the wishless within the collection of mental factors arising simultaneously with the receptivities to suffering (duḥkha-kṣānti), the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), the receptivity to origin (samudaya-kṣānti), the receptivity to the path (mārga-kṣānti), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
This is not associated with the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*), because it belongs to a different category;
nor is it associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*),
because a nature cannot be associated with itself.
Regarding "and all other mental states and mental factors":
this refers to the mental states and mental factors arising together with emptiness and signlessness,
as well as all contaminated (sāsrava) mental states and mental factors.
These are all non-associated because they belong to a different aggregate.
"Matter and unconditioned phenomena are formations dissociated from mind" refers to all matter.

The unconditioned factors dissociated from mind are likewise dissociated because they lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*). Regarding their correspondence with the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*),
the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), it is as explained for the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
That is to say, just as the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) corresponds to the three untainted faculties (anāsravendriya) and so forth,
so too does this knowledge of origination (samudayajñāna) correspond to the three untainted faculties and so forth;
the detailed explanation is likewise.
If various dharmas are associated with the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), are those dharmas also associated with the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)? Answer: No.
If a dharma is associated with the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), is that dharma also associated with the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna)? Answer: No.
The same applies to the samādhis of emptiness and wishlessness. Why is this?
Because they are not a single mind.
Because their modes of activity differ and their objects of focus differ,
they are associated with the knowledge of the cessation of all phenomena.
Is that dharma associated with the samādhi of signlessness (*animitta*)?
One should respond by establishing four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), as the meaning is not fixed.
There are dharmas associated with the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) that are not associated with signlessness.
This refers to the signless (animitta) associated with the knowledge of cessation;
that is, the signless samādhi co-arising with the knowledge of cessation.
This is associated with the knowledge of cessation, yet it is not itself signless.
Because a nature does not associate with itself.
There are phenomena that are associated with the signless but not with the knowledge of cessation;
namely, the knowledge of cessation itself and those phenomena associated with the signless that are dissociated from the knowledge of cessation.
In this context, "knowledge of cessation" refers to the knowledge of cessation that arises concomitantly with the signless;
it is not the knowledge of cessation that is associated with the signless.
Because intrinsic nature does not associate with itself;
and as for those phenomena that do not associate with the knowledge of cessation but do associate with the signless,
these refer to the phenomena associated with the signless that arise simultaneously with the acceptance of cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*).
This [wisdom of cessation] is associated with signlessness but not with the wisdom of cessation, because it belongs to a different category.
There are also phenomena that are associated with both the wisdom of cessation and signlessness;
namely, those phenomena associated with both.
What is this dharma?
It refers to that which arises together with the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) within the complex [of mental factors],
excluding the knowledge of cessation itself and the signless (animitta).
All other mental states and mental factors consist of the eight universal ground-factors (mahābhūmika),
the ten wholesome ground-factors (kuśalamahābhūmika), vitarka, vicāra, and the mind itself.
There are phenomena that are not associated with the knowledge of cessation,
nor are they signless;
that is to say, those which are not associated with the knowledge of cessation and are signless.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Herein, that which is signless and dissociated from the knowledge of cessation refers to the signlessness co-arising with the acceptance of cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*).
This is not associated with the knowledge of cessation, because it belongs to a different category;
nor is it associated with the signless,
because a nature cannot be associated with itself.
"Furthermore, as for the other mind and mental factors":
this refers to the mind and mental factors arising together with emptiness and the wishless,
as well as all contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind and mental factors.
These are all non-associated because they belong to a different aggregate.
Matter and the unconditioned are the formations dissociated from mind;
that is to say, all matter.
The unconditioned factors and the formations dissociated from mind are both dissociated from this [mind],
because they lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*).

Regarding the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) as explained in relation to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*):
that is to say, just as the knowledge of phenomena relates to the three untainted faculties and so forth,
so too does this knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) relate to the three untainted faculties and so forth.
The detailed exposition is likewise:
Are those phenomena that are associated with the knowledge of the path also associated with the concentration on emptiness?

Answer: Not so. Even if a phenomenon is associated with the concentration on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā-samādhi*), is that phenomenon necessarily associated with the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
Answer: It is not so.
The same applies to the signless samādhi (animitta-samādhi). Why is this?
Because they are not a single mind;
because their modes of activity differ;
and because their objects differ.
Regarding those phenomena associated with the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*),
are they also associated with the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihitasamādhi*)?
One should respond by establishing four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), because their relationship is not fixed.
There are dharmas associated with the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) but not with the wishless (apranihita).
This refers to the wishless associated with the knowledge of the path—
that is, the wishless co-arising simultaneously with the knowledge of the path.
This is associated with the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*),
but not with the wishless (*apraṇihita*), because a nature is not associated with itself.
There are factors that are associated with the wishless, but not with the knowledge of the path.
This refers to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and those factors associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) that are not associated with the knowledge of the path.
Herein, "knowledge of the path" refers to the knowledge of the path that arises simultaneously with the wishless.
This is not the knowledge of the path associated with wishlessness,
because a nature does not associate with itself,
and because it is a phenomenon associated with wishlessness that is dissociated from the knowledge of the path.

This refers to the factors associated with the wishless (apraṇihita) within the collection of mental states that arise simultaneously with the patience toward suffering (duḥkha-kṣānti), the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), the patience toward the origin [of suffering] (samudaya-kṣānti), the knowledge of the origin (samudaya-jñāna), and the patience toward the path (mārga-kṣānti).
These are associated with the wishless because the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) is not part of this same collection.
There are dharmas that are associated with both the knowledge of the path and the wishless [concentration].
These refer to the dharmas associated with those two.
What are these dharmas?

This refers to all other mental states and mental factors within the collection of phenomena arising simultaneously with the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), excluding the knowledge of the path itself and the wishless concentration (apraṇihita).
These consist of the eight universal mental factors (mahābhūmikadharma).

The ten great wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), vitarka, vicāra, and the mind—there are factors that are neither associated with the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) nor with the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
That is to say: those not associated with the knowledge of the path and [not associated with] the wishless.
...and so forth, as explained at length. Herein,

"the wishless dissociated from the knowledge of the path" refers to the wishless [aspiration] that arises simultaneously with the group of factors associated with the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the patience regarding origin (*samudaya-kṣānti*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), and the patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*).
This is not associated with the knowledge of the path, because it belongs to a different category;
nor is it associated with the wishless,
because a nature cannot be associated with itself.
As for "and all other mental states and mental factors," this refers to the mental states and mental factors arising together with emptiness and signlessness,
as well as all contaminated (sāsrava) mental states and mental factors.
These are all non-associated because they belong to a different aggregate.
Regarding "matter, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind":
this refers to all matter, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind.
These are both non-associated because they lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*).

Regarding the statement that [the factors] correspond to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) as explained for the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*):
this means that just as the knowledge of phenomena corresponds to the three untainted faculties and so forth, so too do these.
The detailed explanation regarding this path-knowledge in relation to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and so forth is likewise.
All phenomena are associated with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Are those dharmas associated with the wishless samādhi?
Answer: No. Even if dharmas are associated with the wishless samādhi...
Is that dharma associated with the samādhi of emptiness?
Answer: No. The same applies to the signless [samādhi].
Why is this? Because they are not a single mind;
because their modes of activity (ākāra) differ.
Alternatively, because their objects of focus differ:
are those phenomena associated with the concentration on emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi) also associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñātāvīndriya)?
Because it is admitted that the fourfold logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) are indeterminate,
there are factors associated with emptiness that are not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya).
That is to say, those factors associated with emptiness which are not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is this dharma?
It refers to the dharmas associated with emptiness that arise together with the faculty of one who has known (*ājñātendriya*) and the faculty of one who has fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
These are associated with emptiness because the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) belongs to a different category (*skandha*).
There are phenomena associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are not empty;
namely, those emptinesses included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," as well as those not included in emptiness and not associated with it.
Regarding the factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*):

herein, that which is empty as subsumed within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" refers to the emptiness within the collection of factors arising simultaneously with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
This is not dissociated from the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*),
because a nature is not dissociated from itself,
and because that which is not included within emptiness is dissociated [from it].
Regarding the factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*):

these refer to the factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" within the collection of co-arising [factors] that are both wishless (*apraṇihita*) and signless (*animitta*).
These are associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" because they are not empty of being a collection other than themselves.
There are phenomena that are both associated with emptiness and constitute the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
These are the phenomena associated with emptiness that are subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
What are these phenomena?
This refers to the eight faculties within this aggregate, as well as those associated mental factors that are not faculties;
these are phenomena that are neither associated with emptiness nor associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
This refers to the emptiness not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," and so forth,
as explained at length. Herein,
"the emptiness not subsumed under the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" means:
This refers to the emptiness within the collection of factors that arise simultaneously with the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya) and the faculty of "having fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
This is not associated with emptiness,
because a self-nature cannot be associated with itself.
Nor is it associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," because that belongs to another category;
furthermore, it is not included within nor associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and other remaining mental states and mental factors.
This refers to the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*), which is subsumed under the faculty of one who has fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*);
the mental states and mental factors arising together with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and signless (*animitta*) concentrations;
and all contaminated (*sāsrava*) mental states and mental factors.
These are all non-associated because they belong to a different aggregate.
"Matter, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind" refers to all matter, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind.
These are both non-associated because they lack an object of cognition (*anālambana*).
Regarding the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) in relation to the faculty of one who knows (*ājñendriya*), it is likewise:
just as there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) in relation to the faculty of one who will come to know the unknown (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
The same applies to the faculty of one who has already known and the faculty of one who has fully known.
If various phenomena are associated with the concentration of emptiness,
are those phenomena also associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness?
Because it is admitted that the fourfold definition of meaning is indeterminate:
there is mindfulness associated with the emptiness of phenomena (dharmas) which is not [simply] mindfulness;
that is to say, mindfulness associated with emptiness.
This refers to the awakening factor of mindfulness co-arising with the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
This is not mindfulness associated with emptiness,
because a nature cannot be associated with itself.
There are phenomena associated with mindfulness that are not empty;
namely, emptiness itself and those phenomena associated with mindfulness that are not associated with emptiness.
Regarding these, "emptiness" refers to:
This refers to the emptiness samādhi that arises simultaneously with the awakening factor of mindfulness.
This [samādhi] is associated with mindfulness but is not itself empty,
because a nature cannot be associated with itself.
Regarding the factors associated with mindfulness that are not associated with emptiness:
these refer to the factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness that arise simultaneously with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and signless (*animitta*) [samādhis].
These are associated with mindfulness but not with emptiness, because they belong to a different aggregate (*skandha*).
There are phenomena that are associated with emptiness and also associated with mindfulness;
namely, those phenomena associated with both,
excluding emptiness and mindfulness themselves from the collection of factors co-arising with emptiness.
As for the other mental states and mental factors, what are these factors?
They are the eight universal mental factors (mahābhūmikadharma).
The ten great wholesome mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and the mind itself—
there are factors that are neither associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*) nor associated with mindfulness (*smṛti*),
namely, mindfulness that is not associated with emptiness.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Herein, "mindfulness dissociated from emptiness" refers to the awakening factor of mindfulness that arises concomitantly with the wishless (*apranihita*) and signless (*animitta*) [samādhis].
This is not associated with emptiness, because it belongs to a different category;
nor is it associated with mindfulness,
because a self-nature cannot be associated with itself.
"And as for the other mind and mental factors," this refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind and mental factors;
these are not associated with it because they belong to a different aggregate (*skandha*).
Matter that is non-associated with the mind and a non-conditioned formation refers to all matter that is non-associated with the mind and a non-conditioned formation;
these are both non-associated because they lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
The same applies to the factors of enlightenment consisting of investigation of phenomena, diligence, pliancy, and equanimity, as well as to right view, right diligence, and right mindfulness.
That is to say, just as there are four permutations regarding the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness in relation to the emptiness samādhi, so it is here.
The same applies to this [analysis] regarding the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*) and so forth.
Are those dharmas associated with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) also associated with the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Because it is admitted that there are four possibilities regarding the indeterminate nature of their association:
there are phenomena associated with emptiness that are not associated with joy,
namely, joy associated with emptiness and those phenomena associated with emptiness that are not associated with joy.
Regarding "joy associated with emptiness" (*śūnyatā-saṃprayukta-prīti*) here:
this refers to the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) within the collection co-arising with emptiness;
it is not that the joy itself is associated with emptiness.
Because intrinsic nature is not associated with itself;
and as for those phenomena associated with emptiness that are dissociated from joy,
these refer to the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
In the latter two dhyānas and the first three formless stages,
there are factors associated with the emptiness samādhi;
these are associated with emptiness but not with joy, because they belong to other stages.
There are phenomena associated with joy that are not empty;
namely, emptiness associated with joy, and phenomena associated with joy that are not associated with emptiness.
Among these, regarding "emptiness associated with joy":
This refers to the emptiness samādhi within the collection of factors co-arising with the awakening factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*).
This [samādhi] is associated with joy,
but it is not itself emptiness, because a nature cannot be associated with itself.
Regarding "dharmas associated with joy that are not associated with emptiness":
this refers to the dharmas associated with joy within the collection of factors co-arising with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and signless (*animitta*).
These are associated with joy but not with emptiness, because they belong to a different collection.
There are phenomena that are associated with emptiness and also accompanied by joy;
namely, those phenomena associated with both [factors],
which exist within the co-arising complex of emptiness in the first two dhyānas.
Excluding emptiness and joy,
what are these remaining mental states and mental factors? What dharma is this?
That is to say: the eight universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma), the ten wholesome universal mental factors (kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma), vitarka and vicāra, and the mind itself.
There are factors that are neither associated with emptiness nor associated with joy.
This refers to joy that is dissociated from emptiness,
and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding this "joy dissociated from emptiness":
This refers to the joy that arises together with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and signless (*animitta*) [concentrations].
Since this belongs to a different aggregate (*skandha*) than that which is associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is not associated with emptiness;
nor is it associated with joy itself.
Because self-nature does not associate with self-nature,
"emptiness dissociated from joy" refers to the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
In the latter two dhyānas and the first three formless stages, there is the emptiness samādhi; however,
this is not associated with emptiness,
because a nature cannot be associated with itself.
Nor is it associated with joy, because it belongs to another stage;
this also includes all other mental states and mental factors,
namely those of the *anāgamya* (preliminary concentration) and the *dhyānāntara* (intermediate dhyāna).
In the latter two dhyānas and the first three formless stages (ārūpya-bhūmi),
there are the mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) arising together with the wishless (apraṇihita) and signless (animitta) [samādhis],
as well as all contaminated (sāsrava) mental states and mental factors.
These are all non-associated because they belong to a different aggregate.
Regarding "matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind":
this refers to all matter, all unconditioned phenomena, and all formations dissociated from mind.
Because these are both dissociated [from consciousness] and lack an object of perception (*ālambana*).
The same applies to right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*):
just as with the threefold concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) in relation to the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established.
The same applies to right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
If various phenomena are associated with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*),
are those phenomena necessarily associated with the factor of enlightenment of investigation (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

Answer: Those phenomena that correspond to emptiness also necessarily correspond to concentration (*samādhi*), because all emptiness-trance-samādhis (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) are subsumed under the awakening-factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
However, there are phenomena that correspond to concentration but do not correspond to emptiness.
This refers to the factors associated with meditative concentration that are not subsumed under emptiness.
What are these factors?
They are the factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of concentration within the co-arising clusters of the wishless and the signless.
This is because it is associated with the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and is not empty, as it belongs to a different aggregate.
The same applies to right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*);
just as the emptiness-trance (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) forms a "concordant antecedent" (*pūrvapadaka*) in relation to the factor of enlightenment of concentration.
The same applies to its relation with right concentration.
Just as emptiness relates to the subsequent wishlessness and signlessness,
so it is also in relation to what follows.
As with the emptiness samādhi in relation to the subsequent wishlessness and signlessness,
the detailed explanation regarding the subsequent [samādhis] is likewise.
The difference is as follows:
As with the emptiness [samādhi] in relation to the enlightenment factor of joy, right thought, the wishless, and the signless,
so it is with the emptiness in relation to the enlightenment factor of joy, right view, and right thought.
All these dharmas are associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
Are those dharmas associated with the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātendriya)?
Answer: No. Even if dharmas are associated with the faculty of one who has already known...
Are those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?
Answer: No. The same applies to the faculty of one who has already known.
Why is this? Because they are not a single mind and because their states are each distinct.
All phenomena are associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Is that dharma associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness?
One should respond by establishing four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), because the meaning is not fixed.
There are dharmas associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that are not associated with mindfulness.
This refers to mindfulness subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*);
that is, the mindfulness within the aggregate of factors co-arising with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
This is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," but it is not the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Because a nature does not associate with itself.
There are factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness that are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
These refer to factors associated with mindfulness that are not subsumed within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."

What is this dharma? It refers to the mental factors associated with mindfulness within the collection [of dharmas] that arise together with the faculty of one who has known (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of one who has fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
This is because it is associated with mindfulness, whereas the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) belongs to a different collection.
There are dharmas that are associated with both the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*).
These are the dharmas associated with the mindfulness included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
What are these dharmas?
This refers to the other eight faculties, their associated mental factors,
and all non-faculty mental factors;
there are phenomena that are neither associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" nor are they mindfulness.
This refers to mindfulness not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," and so forth,
as explained at length. Regarding this,
"mindfulness not subsumed under the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" means:
This refers to mindfulness within the collection of factors that arise together with the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of one who has fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*);
this is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*),
because it belongs to a different collection.
Nor is it associated with mindfulness,
because a self-nature does not associate with itself,
and [it is dissociated] from other mental states and mental factors.
This refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
It is not concomitant with them because it belongs to a different aggregate (*anya-skandha*).
Form that is unconditioned and dissociated from mind refers to all form that is unconditioned and dissociated from mind;
these are mutually dissociated.
"Because there is no object of focus;

the same applies to the application of energy for the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-vīrya*), the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).

This means that, just as there are four permutations regarding the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) in relation to the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The same applies to the factors such as the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
If various phenomena are associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*),
are those phenomena also associated with the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
It should be answered with four alternatives,
because the meaning is not fixed.
There are factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) that are not associated with joy (prīti).
This refers to the joy included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya),
as well as those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are not included within joy and are dissociated from it.
Among these, regarding the joy included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown":
This refers to the joy (prīti) within the complex of mental factors co-arising with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
This [joy] is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," but it is not [the faculty of] joy itself.
Because intrinsic nature does not associate with itself;

and because those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that are neither included in nor associated with joy (*prīti*) are those belonging to the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*),
the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and so forth.
The factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) within the stages of the third and fourth dhyānas are not associated with joy (*prīti*),
because they belong to other stages.
There are factors associated with the awakening factor of joy that are not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
These refer to factors associated with joy that are not included within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is this dharma?

It refers to those dharmas associated with joy within the collection of factors that arise together with the faculty of "already known" (ājñendriya) and the faculty of "one who has already fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
These are associated with joy, but they are not the faculty of "yet to be known" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
Because it belongs to that category,
there are factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that are also associated with joy (*prīti*);
namely, those factors associated with joy that are subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is this dharma?
It refers to the other eight faculties and their associated mental factors that are not faculties.
There are dharmas that are neither associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" nor are they joy.
This refers to joy not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Within this context, "joy not subsumed under the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" means:
This refers to the joy within the collection of factors co-arising with the faculty of having known (ājñātendriya) and the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātavindriya);
this is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya),
because it belongs to a different collection.
Nor is it associated with joy (*prīti*),
because a nature is not associated with itself. Furthermore,

it refers to all other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are neither included within nor associated with joy or the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

This refers to the mental states and mental factors within the aggregate of co-arising [factors] of the faculty of one who has known (ājñendriya) and the faculty of one who has fully known (ājñātāvindriya), occurring in the preparatory concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna, the latter two dhyānas, and the first three formless stages.
And all contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*):
these are not concomitant with it,
because they belong to a different aggregate (*anya-skandha*).
Matter that is unconditioned and dissociated from mind refers to all matter that is unconditioned and dissociated from mind;
these are mutually dissociated.
Because they lack an object of perception (*anālambana*).
Are those phenomena associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) also associated with the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
It should be answered with four alternatives,
because the meaning is not fixed.
There are factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that are not pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
This refers to the pliancy associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
It is not the case that this [faculty] is associated with pliancy,
because a factor cannot be associated with itself.
There are phenomena associated with pliancy that are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
These are the phenomena associated with pliancy that are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
What are these phenomena?
This means that within the collection of factors co-arising with the faculty of "already-known" (ājñātāvīndriya) and the faculty of "one who has already known" (ājñātendriya),
those factors associated with pliancy (praśrabdhi) are associated with pliancy; they are not, however,
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya).
Because it belongs to that category,
there are dharmas associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that are also associated with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*);
namely, those dharmas associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that are also associated with pliancy.
What is this dharma?
It refers to the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharmas) and the nine wholesome universal mental factors (kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharmas).
Regarding vitarka, vicāra, and the mind:
there are factors that are neither associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) nor are they pliancy (praśrabdhi).

These refer to the pliancy that is dissociated from the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," as well as the pliancy within the collection of factors co-arising with the faculty of "having known" (ājñendriya) and the faculty of "one who has fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
This is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," because it belongs to a different category;
nor is it associated with pliancy.
Because intrinsic nature does not associate with itself,
and as for "other mental states and mental factors," this refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) mental states and mental factors.
These are all non-associated, because they belong to a different aggregate.
As for matter, unconditioned phenomena, and mental factors dissociated from mind: [they are likewise non-associated].
This refers to all form, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind;
these are all dissociated from it because they lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
"The same applies to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity" means that,
just as there are four permutations regarding the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) in relation to the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga),
it is likewise so in relation to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga).
Regarding those phenomena associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*),
are they also associated with right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*)?
One should answer by means of four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Because the meaning is not fixed:
there are factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that are not right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
That is to say, [there are] those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" which are right reflection.
And those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) that are dissociated from right reflection (samyak-saṃkalpa).
Among these, as for the right reflection associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown":
This refers to right reflection within the collection of factors arising simultaneously with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
This right reflection is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," because a factor cannot be associated with itself.
Regarding the factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that are dissociated from correct attention (*samyak-manasikāra*):
these refer to the factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" within the intermediate dhyāna and the three higher dhyāna stages.
This [factor] is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), but it is not right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*),
because it belongs to a different aggregate.
There are factors that are associated with right thought but are not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
It refers to those factors associated with right attention that are dissociated from the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
What are these factors?

They are the factors associated with right attention within the collection of mental states co-arising with the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya) and the faculty of "having fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
This dharma is associated with right reflection;
it is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," because it belongs to a different category.
There are phenomena that are associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and are also associated with right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
That is to say, those phenomena associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" which are also associated with right reflection.
What are these phenomena?
That is to say: the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma),
the ten wholesome universal mental factors (kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma),
vitarka, vicāra, and the mind (citta).
There are phenomena that are neither associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) nor with right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
That is to say, right reflection that is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," and so forth,
as explained in detail.

Among these, right thought that is dissociated from the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" refers to right thought within the collection of factors co-arising with the faculty of "one who knows" and the faculty of "one who has fully known."
This is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," because it belongs to a different aggregate;
nor is it associated with right intention.
Because intrinsic nature does not associate with itself,
as well as with other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*),

this refers to the collection of mental states and mental factors that arise simultaneously with the faculty of one who has known (*ājñātendriya*) and the faculty of one who has fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) within the intermediate dhyāna, the latter three dhyānas, and the first three formless stages (*ārūpya-bhūmi*).
And with all contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*),
it is not concomitant (*asamprayukta*),
because they belong to a different aggregate (*anya-skandha*).
Matter that is unconditioned and dissociated from mind refers to all matter that is unconditioned and dissociated from mind;
these are mutually dissociated.
Because there is no object of focus.

As it is with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) in relation to the subsequent faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*), so it is also with the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) in relation to what follows.
The difference is as follows:
Regarding the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) in relation to right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*) should be formulated;
it differs from what preceded.
There are factors associated with the faculty of one who has already known that are not right view.
This refers to the right view comprised within the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya),
as well as those factors associated with the faculty of one who has already known that are not comprised within right view and are dissociated from it.
Among these, [first] the right view comprised within the faculty of one who has already known:
This refers to the right view that arises simultaneously with the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
This [right view] is not associated with the faculty of one who has already known,
because a factor cannot be associated with itself.
As for those factors associated with the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) that are not subsumed under and are not associated with right view:

these refer to the factors associated with the faculty of one who has already known within the complex of mental states co-arising with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
This [factor] is associated with the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya), but it is not right view (samyagdṛṣṭi),
because it belongs to a different aggregate.
There are factors that are associated with right view but are not associated with the faculty of one who has already known.
It refers to those factors associated with right view that are not subsumed under the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*). What are these factors?

They are the factors associated with right view within the collection of mental states co-arising with both the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñendriya*).
This is associated with right view but is not the faculty of one who has already fully known,
because it belongs to a different category.
There are, however, factors that are both associated with the faculty of one who has already fully known and associated with right view.
It refers to those phenomena associated with right view that are subsumed under the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*). What are these phenomena?
They are the remaining eight faculties, as well as the non-faculty mental factors (*caitta*) associated with them.
There are dharmas that are neither associated with the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya) nor are they right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).
This refers to right view not included within the faculty of one who has already known,
and so forth, as explained at length.

Among these, that which is right view not included within the faculty of one who has already attained full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) refers to the right view within the collection of factors co-arising with both the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñendriya*).
This is not associated with the faculty of one who has already attained full knowledge.
Because it belongs to a different category (*nikāya*),
it is also not associated with right view;
for a self-nature (*svabhāva*) is not associated with itself.
"And as for all other mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma)," this refers to all contaminated (sāsrava) mental states and mental factors;
these are not associated with it.
Because they belong to the category of others (*parasaṃtānika*).
"Matter, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind" refers to all matter, the unconditioned, and formations dissociated from mind.
These are not associated with one another because they lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
The factors from the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) up to right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) will be explained in detail later.
Regarding the *Bodhyaṅga-varga*,
it has already been explained in detail in the first *varga* of this *skandha*,
as it was said:
"O Bhikṣus, I shall now explain to you forty-four matters of knowledge.
You should listen attentively and apply your minds with great care," and so forth,
as extensively taught.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the sake of providing a detailed analysis of the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain for you forty-four matters concerning knowledge.
You should listen attentively."
...and so on, as explained at length.
Although the sūtra makes this statement, it does not analyze its meaning.
The sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which has not yet been explained should now be explained;
therefore, this treatise is composed.
Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One speak this sutra?
The answer is: In the past, the Blessed One realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of this preparatory practice as his gateway and path;
now he again teaches this to his disciples.
If you are able not to abandon such a path of application,
before long you shall attain the permanent exhaustion of all outflows.
It is, for example, like a householder who, by means of this skillful method, [achieves his goal].
Having accumulated precious wealth, he enjoys prosperity and happiness.
Furthermore, by means of this very method, he instructs his sons and grandsons, saying:
"If you are able not to abandon such a method..."
One will certainly obtain precious wealth and likewise enjoy prosperity and happiness.
The World-Honored One is also like this.
What are the forty-four matters of knowledge?
That is to say: knowledge of aging and death,
knowledge of the origin of aging and death,
and knowledge of the cessation of aging and death.
He possesses the knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of old age and death.
Likewise, he possesses the knowledge of birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations.
He possesses the knowledge of the origin of volitional formations.
Knowledge of the cessation of formations;
knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of formations—
these are called the forty-four matters of knowledge.
Question: Why is it that the knowledge of the wisdom of non-existence (*anupalambhajñāna*) and so forth are not mentioned here?
Answer: When something should be stated but is not, one should know that this meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is subsumed under the members of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda),
has the members of dependent origination as its cause,
and is the fruit of the members of dependent origination.
This is explained here:

although ignorance is also subsumed under the links [of dependent origination], it is not caused by the link of existence (*bhava*), nor is it the fruit of the link of existence; therefore, it is not mentioned in this context.
Furthermore, if one relies on this dharma, all four knowledges arise;
this is what is explained herein.
However, relying on ignorance, only three knowledges arise.
This is not mentioned because there is no knowledge of the arising of the link of existence (*bhava-aṅga*).

In this context, should the forty-four cognitive objects, such as the knowledge of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa-jñāna*), be described as ranging from the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) up to the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)?
It is stated that the knowledge of aging and death consists of four knowledges;

namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), and so forth, as explained at length.
In this context, the knowledge of aging and death comprises these four knowledges.
That is to say, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) knows old age and death in the desire realm;
the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) knows old age and death in the form and formless realms;
and so too do conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) and the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).
One knows old age and death in all three realms.
Just as one knows suffering through four types of knowledge, one should know that it is likewise for the origin, cessation, and the path.
As sixteen cognitive objects arise based on old age and death, so it is here.
One should know that it is likewise for the basis of conduct (*caryā*).
Thus, there are one hundred and seventy-six cognitive objects (*jñeya-vastu*) in total.
If distinguished according to the moments of the continuum (*saṃtati-kṣaṇa*), however, there are immeasurable and boundless cognitive objects.
In this context, because the Blessed One gives rise to four types of knowledge for each of the eleven branches of the four noble truths,
it is said that there are forty-four instances of knowledge.
These forty-four instances of knowledge—
How many are with outflows (sāsrava) and how many are without outflows (anāsrava)?
Answer: All of them pertain to both the with-outflow and the without-outflow.
How many have with-outflow objects and how many have without-outflow objects?
Answer: Twenty-two conditions pertain to the contaminated (*sāsrava*);
twenty-two conditions pertain to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
How many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)?
How many are unconditioned?
Answer: All are conditioned.
How many have conditioned objects as their conditions?
How many conditions are for the unconditioned?
Answer: Thirty-three conditions are for the conditioned;
eleven conditions are for the unconditioned.
How many are past, how many are future, and how many are present?
Answer: All of them pertain to all three periods of time.
How many take the past as their object?
How many conditions pertain to the future?
How many pertain to the present?
Answer: Thirty-three conditions pertain to the three periods of time.
The eleventh condition is non-temporal.
If it were like the temporal divisions of the *Saṃyuktāgama*,
one should say that three conditions are past.
That is to say, the knowledge of suffering,
the knowledge of the origin of suffering,
and the knowledge of the cessation of the origin of suffering take three conditions as their future objects.
That is to say: knowledge of aging and death;
knowledge of the origin of aging and death;
and knowledge of birth.
Sixteen take the present as their object;
that is to say, the knowledge of the origin of birth and the knowledge of existence.
One knows the knowledge of the origin of existence;
one knows the knowledge of grasping and the knowledge of the origin of grasping;
one knows the knowledge of craving.
He knows the knowledge of the origin of craving, he knows the knowledge of feeling,
he knows the knowledge of the origin of feeling,
and he knows the knowledge of contact.
The knowledge of the arising of contact;
the knowledge of the six sense bases;
and the knowledge of the arising of the six sense bases.
Knowledge of name-and-form;
knowledge of the arising of name-and-form;
knowledge of cessation.
Eleven [factors] have the three time periods as their object;
eleven have that which is non-temporal as their object.
Question: Since such knowledge and its objects cannot enter the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), [how can they lead to the fruit of stream-entry?]
Regarding the attainment of the fruits, the departure from defilement, and the exhaustion of all outflows:
for what reason do the noble ones cultivate them so that they become manifest?
Answer: It is due to four conditions.
First, for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life;
second, for the sake of sporting with meritorious qualities;
third, for the sake of contemplating one's original deeds.
Fourth, it is for the sake of receiving the noble wealth.
As it is said:
"Bhikṣus, I shall now explain to you seventy-seven matters of knowledge."
"You should listen attentively and apply your minds well," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the sake of extensively analyzing the meaning of the sūtra.
The detailed explanation is as given previously.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One speak this sūtra?
Answer: World-Honored One, in the past,
by means of this preparatory practice as a gateway and a path,
it was explained at length as previously described.
What are the seventy-seven matters of knowledge? They are:
the knowledge that aging and death have birth as their condition;
the knowledge that aging and death do not arise without birth as their condition.
The knowledge that past birth is the condition for aging and death;
the knowledge that it is not the case that aging and death do not have that as their condition;
and the knowledge that future birth is the condition for aging and death.
Knowing that there is no non-arising of conditions for old age and death,
as well as the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*),
one thoroughly understands that these are impermanent and conditioned.
It is produced through volition,
arises from conditions,
is subject to exhaustion, subject to diminution, subject to detachment, and subject to cessation.
Just as seven knowledges arise based on the condition of birth giving rise to old age and death,
so it is for everything down to ignorance being the condition for volitional formations;
thus, there are seventy-seven bases of knowledge.
Question: Why is it that the knowledge of the conditions from which ignorance arises is not mentioned here?
Answer: When something should be stated but is not, one should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, regarding those phenomena that are subsumed under the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*),
and which, having the factors of existence as their cause, are the fruits of the factors of existence—
it is these that are explained herein.
Although ignorance is also subsumed under the members [of dependent origination],
it does not have the member of existence as its cause,
nor is it the fruit of the member of existence.
Therefore, it is not mentioned here.
Furthermore, if one gives rise to the seven types of knowledge regarding the branches of dependent origination based on this dharma,
they are explained herein.
Because the seven knowledges that do not arise from the conditions of ignorance— the conditions for the link of existence—
are not mentioned here; rather,
it refers to the knowledge within this context that birth is the condition for aging and death, and so forth.
Regarding the seventy-seven matters of knowledge (*jñānavastu*),
should they be described as ranging from dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) up to path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*)?
One should answer that they consist of knowing that old age and death have birth as their condition, and so forth.

The first six knowledges are all four knowledges: namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).
The seventh is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*).
This is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Just as there are seven knowledges for knowing that birth conditions aging and death,
so too it is for the seven knowledges up to knowing that ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

In this context, "knowledge of phenomena" (dharma-jñāna) is the knowledge that birth in the desire realm is the condition for old age, death, and so forth; "subsequent knowledge" (anvaya-jñāna) is... [the knowledge of these same factors in the form and formless realms].
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) both know the birth, old age, death, and so forth,
conditioned by the realms of form and formlessness within the three realms.
Question: It has already been stated that birth is the condition for aging and death, and so forth.
Why, then, is it further stated that aging and death do not arise without birth as their condition?
Answer: There are two types of treatises.
First, establishing one's own school;
second, refuting the schools of others.
Regarding the establishment of one's own school:
Just as those who speak the Dharma well establish the thesis of speaking the Dharma well,
those who speak the Dharma poorly establish the thesis of speaking the Dharma poorly,
and those who argue according to reason establish the thesis of arguing according to reason.
The Vibhajyavādins establish the tenets of the Vibhajyavāda school;
they refute the systems of others just as those who preach the Dharma well refute the systems of those who preach the Dharma poorly.
Those who propound false doctrines refute the tenets of those who propound true doctrines;
those who rely on reasoning refute the tenets of the Analysts;
and the Analysts refute the tenets of those who rely on reasoning.
If one were to speak only of birth as the condition for old age and death and so forth,
some might harbor doubts and engage in debate,
making such a statement:
The principle is not necessarily so.
To resolve that doubt and demonstrate that this principle is certain,
it is further stated that aging, death, and so forth do not arise without conditions.
In this context, knowing that old age and death arise conditioned by birth constitutes four types of knowledge:
dharma-knowledge, subsequent-knowledge, conventional-knowledge, and knowledge of origination.
Knowing that old age and death do not arise when there is no birth likewise constitutes these same four types of knowledge.
In total there are eight knowledges.
Knowing old age and death as conditioned by birth in the past and future also each involves eight knowledges.
In total, there are twenty-four knowledges;
since the seventh, the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna), is exclusively conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna),
when added to the preceding, there are twenty-five knowledges.
Just as one knows that old age and death have birth as their condition,
so it is for everything down to knowing that formations have ignorance as their condition;
thus, there are two hundred and seventy-five knowledges in total.
If analyzed according to the moments of the continuum,
there are immeasurable and boundless cognitive objects;
herein, the Blessed One relies upon eleven factors.
Since seven knowledges arise for each of the distinctions of the three periods of time, it is said that there are seventy-seven instances of knowledge.
Question: Why is it not stated that one knows the present?
Some say that among the seven [knowledges], the first two know the present. Others say:
Among the seven [knowledges], the first two are designated as "knowledge of the three time periods";
because the past and future are difficult to comprehend,
they are further explained separately as "knowing."
It is not so now;
therefore, they are not explained separately.
These are the seventy-seven matters of knowledge.
How many are with outflows (sāsrava)?
How many are without outflows (anāsrava)?
Answer: Eleven dharmas; the knowledge abiding in phenomena (dharmasthiti-jñāna) is exclusively with outflows.
Because it is comprised solely within the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*),
the remaining sixty-six knowledges pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
as they are subsumed under four knowledges.
Some say that all [these] pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
How many conditions are contaminated?
How many take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object?
Answer: All take the tainted (*sāsrava*) as their object.
How many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)?
Question: How many are unconditioned?
Answer: All are conditioned;
there is certainly no essence of wisdom that is unconditioned.
Because this is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
How many conditions are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
and how many conditions are unconditioned?
Answer: All have conditioned phenomena as their object.
How many are past?
How many are future?
How many are present?
Answer: All of them pertain to the three periods of time.
How many take the past as their object?
How many take the future as their object?
How many take the present as their object?
Answer: For those who maintain that, among the seven [types of craving], the first two take only the present as their object.
He explains that twenty-two conditions pertain to the past,
twenty-two conditions pertain to the future,
and twenty-two conditions pertain to the present.
The eleven conditions take the three time periods as their objects.
Regarding those who maintain that the first two among the seven [conditions] universally take the three time periods as their objects,
they state that twenty-two [conditions] take the past as their object.
Twenty-two take the future as their object;
thirty-three take the three periods of time as their object.
This knowledge cannot enter into the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) and so forth.
Cultivation brings [the path] to manifestation by way of four conditions, as explained previously. Question:
For what reason is the seventh called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*)?
Answer: "Dharma" refers to the fruit;
"abiding" refers to the cause.
This is because one knows the cause in which the dharma of the fruit abides.

This is called the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*). That is to say, knowing the causes upon which the fruits—low, middling, and superior—of the three realms depend is termed the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
This knowledge knows only the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of those causes.
Because it does not possess the characteristics of noble conduct,
it is subsumed solely under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Some, however, maintain that this [knowledge] is common to all four knowledges.
That is to say, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna). Question:
If that is so, why is it said to be "one" conventional knowledge?
Answer: In reality, it also encompasses the untainted (*anāsrava*).
However, what is discussed here is for the most part the tainted (*sāsrava*), because this [knowledge] primarily cognizes the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of causes.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
because the first six knowledges are knowledges that understand causes, they are called "dharma-abiding" (dharmasthiti);
the knowledge that arises taking them as its object is called "knowledge of dharma-abiding" (dharmasthitijñāna).
This knowledge that knows the path—though it does not know the cause of origination—is also comprised within four knowledges;
namely, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
Question: If this is so, [then...]
For what reason is it said thus:
"One thoroughly knows that this is impermanent, conditioned,
and produced through volitional effort"?
They arise from conditions;
they are phenomena that are subject to exhaustion, diminution, detachment, and cessation.
How could those that are untainted (anāsrava) be called "phenomena of detachment"?
Answer: In this context, one should simply state as follows:
"One thoroughly understands that this is impermanent, conditioned, and so forth, up to being subject to cessation."
One should not say that there is a "separation from phenomena.

However, when one speaks of "separation from phenomena," it is intended to show that even noble ones feel weary of the untainted (*anāsrava*) and do not take delight in it; thus, they speak of "separation from phenomena."
Others further state:
the aforementioned knowledge of causes is of the nature of four knowledges;
the knowledge that now knows those [four] is called the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna).
Therefore, this knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna) also knows that conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) as the knowledge of the transcendence of phenomena.
The critique states:
It should be understood that among these, the first explanation is the correct one,
as the Blessed One said:
"Suśama, you should know this."
First there is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna), and subsequently there is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.
Question: Among these, what is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena?
What is the knowledge of nirvāṇa?
Some say that the knowledge of the origin [of suffering] is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna).
The knowledge of cessation is the knowledge of nirvana.
Others further state that the knowledge of suffering and its origin is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammatthitiñāṇa).
The knowledge of the cessation and the path is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.
Some say that the knowledge of suffering,
its origin, and the path is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa).
The knowledge of cessation is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.
Question: If that is so, why is it said that there is first the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna)?
Is there knowledge of nirvāṇa after [knowledge of the stability of phenomena]?
Answer: Although there is knowledge of the stability of phenomena that follows knowledge of nirvāṇa, there is also knowledge of the stability of phenomena that precedes knowledge of nirvāṇa.
Therefore, this statement was made.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the knowledge of the process of saṃsāra is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna).
Knowledge of cessation and returning is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, knowledge of dependent origination is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna);
knowledge of the cessation of dependent origination is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the knowledge that understands birth and death is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*).
The knowledge that understands the cessation of birth and death is the knowledge of *nirvāṇa*.
Other masters say:
Knowledge of the preparatory stages is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna);
knowledge of the fundamental stages is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.
How is this known to be so?
Because the sūtras are the authoritative standard.
As it is said in a sūtra:
"There were certain non-Buddhists who gathered together and deliberated, saying:"

Before the Buddha appeared in the world, we received much fame and material gain; now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, such fame and gain have suddenly ceased, just as when the sun rises, the light of a torch fades away.
By what means can one restore one's reputation to its former state?
However, Gautama excels in two respects:
namely, his mastery of the sūtras and śāstras.
His physical appearance was dignified and majestic;
yet while his form was difficult to alter, the sūtras and śāstras were easy to plagiarize.
Within our assembly, there is one named Suśīma.
With mindfulness and wisdom firm and strong, he was capable of stealing that dharma;
having obtained that dharma, his fame and profit were as they were before.
Once they had deliberated together, he informed Suśīma.
Due to two conditions, he accepted the invitation:
first, his affection for his kinsmen and friends; second, the ripening of his roots of virtue.
He then departed from Rājagṛha and proceeded to the Bamboo Grove Monastery.
He said to the bhikṣus,
"I wish to go forth.
Then the bhikṣus took him with them and went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha, knowing their faculties and dispositions,
dispatched various bhikṣus to ordain them as renunciants and confer upon them full ordination (upasampadā). Not long thereafter, they had memorized the texts of the Tripiṭaka.
Having also gained some slight understanding of the meaning,
he thought to himself:
"Now is the very time to benefit my kinsmen and friends."
He then departed from the Bamboo Grove, intending to return to Rājagṛha.
However, the Buddha possesses the divine eye that universally surveys and protects the Dharma,
constantly observing the world to see who might attempt to steal it.
At that time, there were five hundred arhat bhikṣus who,
in the presence of Suśīma, praised their own virtues,
saying: "Birth has been exhausted for us."
The holy life has been established;
what was to be done has been accomplished;
there will be no further existence.
Suśīma asked: "Upon what meditative concentration do you rely for your realization?
Is it the first dhyāna, or does it extend even to the sphere of nothingness?"
The bhikṣus said,
"What we have realized is entirely independent of him. Suśīma said:
"If we do not rely upon that, how can we attain realization?
The bhikṣus replied,
"We are all those liberated through wisdom."
At that time, having heard this, Suśīma was bewildered and did not understand what was meant;
he then thought to himself:
"If my dear friend were to ask about the meaning of this..."
"What shall I do? I shall return to the place where the Buddha is and inquire about this matter.
The World-Honored One replied:
Suśīma, you should know that first there is the knowledge of the abiding of phenomena (dharmasthitijñāna),
and subsequently there is the knowledge of nirvāṇa (nirvāṇajñāna).
Susīma said:
"I do not now know which is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) and which is the knowledge of Nirvana (nibbānañāṇa)."
The Buddha said,
"Whether you know it or not, such is the nature of phenomena.
At that time, Suśīma did not achieve his prior wish.
However, after those five hundred arhat bhikṣus had attained the exhaustion of outflows by relying on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration,
they were only then able to give rise to the fundamental attainments (*mauladhyāna*).
From this, it is known that the knowledge of the stage of access (*sāmantaka*) is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*).
The fundamental stage wisdom is the wisdom of nirvāṇa.
