Section Three of the *Jñānaskandha* (The Aggregate of Knowledge), Chapter Five of the Seven Noble Persons (*Saptāryapudgala*), Part Three: "If one is accomplished in the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)."
Is that the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)?
Answer: If it is attained.
Herein, "attained" means:
It is already designated as "attainment" (*prāpti*).
That is to say, after the present manifestation of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*),
all subsequent mentions of "attainment" are to be explained according to this principle.
If one has attained the knowledge of categories (anvaya-jñāna), has one also attained that dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: Yes. That is to say, after the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) has become manifest.
Because the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna) are always accomplished.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena, does one also accomplish the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: If it has been attained and not lost.
In this context, "attainment" refers to having already become free from the defilement of desire;
"non-loss" refers to...
This refers to one who does not regress and does not give rise to afflictions of the desire realm.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess that dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has been attained—that is, after the dharma-knowledge of suffering has manifested.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
Answer: It is so;
for there is no sentient being who does not accomplish conventional knowledge.
If one possesses conventional knowledge, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: If it has been attained;
that is to say, after the knowledge of the phenomenon of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) has become manifest.
The remaining knowledges (*jñāna*) follow a single mode as explained at length in the text.
However, regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledges of the four truths (*catur-āryasatyajñāna*),
once they have been attained, one always possesses the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Regarding those with outflows who have already abandoned the defilement of desire:
if they do not regress and give rise to afflictions of the desire realm,
they constantly accomplish [the attainment] of the formless realm without being reborn there.
Those who are untainted (anāsrava) have already abandoned the defilements of desire;
if they do not regress, they always possess the afflictions of the desire realm.
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is always possessed by all sentient beings.
This is called the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
If one has attained the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding the past,
has one also attained it regarding the future?
The answer is: "It is so.
This is because one who has accomplished the past necessarily accomplishes the future.
In what stage does this occur?
It occurs for one who has already entered the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma),
during the interval of the latter two moments following the clear observation of suffering (duḥkha-abhisamaya).
One attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya during the four moments of mind for the clear realization of the origin and cessation [of suffering],
and during the three moments of mind for the clear realization of the path.
Furthermore, once those in training and those beyond training have refined their faculties (indriya),
if the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has already been extinguished but not lost,
and they have attained it in the future; [then...]
Is it past? Answer:
If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it;
that is to say, the various stages previously described.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished and lost, then it is not accomplished.
In what stage does this occur? It refers to one who has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
In the duration of a single moment of the clear observation of suffering—
that is, at the time of the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering— one attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya;
this also applies after one has trained the faculties (indriya) as a learner (śaikṣa) or a non-learner (aśaikṣa).
The knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has not yet been extinguished, or even if it has been extinguished, it has been lost—
meaning it is lost due to attaining a fruit, refining the faculties (indriya), or through falling away.
This applies if one has accomplished past dharmajñāna.
"Is it present? Answer: "If it is manifested before one;
that is, if the various patiences (kṣānti) of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) have not yet arisen."
Alternatively, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) does not exist in the state of mindlessness.
At that time, the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) must necessarily be present before one.
In what stage does this occur?
This refers to one who has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
During the single moment of mind for each of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of the origin, cessation,
and path, that is, at the time of the three dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*), one attains the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, once those in training and those beyond training have refined their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra),
if the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has already ceased but is not lost and is present before them,
even if it is currently accomplished.
Is that [possession] past?
The answer is: if it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
This refers to the various stages previously described in sequence.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then it is not accomplished.
At what stage does this occur?
It refers to the single moment of mind during the present observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*) when one has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
This refers to attaining the four fruits of śrāmaṇya at the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*),
as well as after the faculties have been refined through training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*).
This applies even if the dharma-knowledge has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has subsequently been lost.
When the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) is present before one, if one possesses the future knowledge of phenomena, does one also possess it in the present?
Answer: If it is present before one.
In what stage does this occur?
It is said to be when one has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
during the single moment of mental focus for each of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
This refers to when one attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya at the time of the four dharma-knowledges;
and after the faculties have been refined by those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa),
if dharma-knowledge is present before them.
If one achieves it in the present, does one also achieve it in the future?
Answer: It is so.
For if one achieves the knowledge of dharmas in the present, one necessarily achieves it in the future.
If one has attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) regarding the past, does one necessarily possess it regarding the future and the present?
Answer: One certainly possesses it regarding the future;
regarding the present, it depends on whether it is currently manifest.
This is as previously explained regarding the accomplishment of the past and present.
If one accomplishes the future and the present, does one also accomplish the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one accomplishes it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished and lost, then it is not accomplished;
this is as previously stated.
If one accomplishes the present, does one also accomplish the past?
If one has attained the future knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), has one also attained it in the past and present?
Answer: There is [attainment] in the future, but not in the past or present.
This means that they have already been acquired;
even if not yet extinguished, or having been extinguished, they have been lost and do not manifest before one.
Herein, "already acquired" indicates their existence in the future.
"Those not yet extinguished, or those already extinguished but lost," indicates that there is no past;
"not manifesting in the present" [indicates that there is no future].
This reveals the absence of the present.
At what stage does this occur?
It refers to the attainment of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, once those in training and those beyond training have refined their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra),
if the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has not yet arisen and ceased,
or if that which previously arose and ceased has already been lost.
And there are those that do not manifest before one.
There are future and past [dharmas] that are not present;
that is to say, they have already ceased, yet are not lost, and do not manifest before one.
In this context, "that which has already ceased but is not lost" indicates that the past exists;
"not manifesting in the present" indicates that the present does not exist.
Wherever there is a past, there must necessarily be a future. At what stage does this occur?
It refers to one who has already entered the state of right determination and transcendence of birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
During the two moments of mind following the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*),
and during the three moments of mind for each of the clear realizations of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*),
with the exception of the moment of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).
During the moments of mind associated with the two patiences of the clear realization of the path,
one attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya;
furthermore, this occurs after the faculties have been refined through training and beyond-training.
If a dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is neither lost nor present before one,
there may be instances where it exists in the future and the present but not in the past;
that is to say, when it is currently manifesting but has not yet ceased, or if it has already ceased but been lost.
In this context, "presently manifest" indicates that it exists in the present and has not yet ceased;
"even if it has ceased and is lost" refers to [the case where it has already perished].
It is shown that there is no past;
however, where there is the present, there must necessarily be the future.
In what state does this occur?
This refers to one who has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
During the single moment of the present observation of suffering—
that is, at the time of the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering— one attains the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, once those in training and those beyond training have refined their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*),
if a dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) has not yet been extinguished— or having previously been extinguished and lost—
now manifests before them, it exists in the future, as well as in the past and present.
This means that it has already ceased but is not lost,
and it is also present before one. Herein, "already ceased but not lost" indicates the existence of the past.
The phrase "also appearing before one" indicates the existence of the present.
If there is a past and a present, there must necessarily be a future.
This is as previously established regarding the past and present.
If one possesses [the attainment] of the past and present, does one also possess it of the future?
Answer: Yes.
However, because one who achieves the past and present necessarily achieves the future,
if one achieves the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) in the present, [one necessarily achieves it in the future].
Is that [attainment] past or future?
Answer: It is certainly accomplished in the future.
Regarding the past, if it has already ceased but has not been lost, then it is accomplished.
As previously explained regarding the accomplishment of the three time-periods:
if [the dharma] has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished and lost, then one does not accomplish it.
This is as previously explained regarding the accomplishment of the future and present, but not the past.
If one achieves [the attainment] of the past and future,
does one also achieve it in the present?
If it is manifested before one, it is as previously explained regarding the achievement of the three time-periods.
Regarding the statement that "just as the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) traverses six [objects], so too do the subsequent knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path":
this means that just as there are six sets of questions and answers concerning the three time periods based on the knowledge of phenomena, the same applies to the subsequent knowledges.
The same applies to the knowledge of suffering, origin,
cessation, and the path.
The difference is that each is referred to by its own name as appropriate.
If one has attained the knowledge of others' minds in the past, has one attained it in the future? Answer: Yes.
However, because one who has accomplished the past necessarily accomplishes the future,
in what state does this occur? It refers to one born in the desire realm who is already free from the defilement of desire,
or one born in the form realm, or a learner (*śaikṣa*).
In the desire and form realms, once the untainted knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñāna*) has arisen, it is not lost.
If one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and has not yet attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*),
even if they possess that [knowledge] in the future, do they also possess it in the past?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already been extinguished but not lost, then one possesses it;
this refers to the various stages previously described in succession.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it.
In what stage does this occur?
It refers to a trainee (śaikṣa) in the desire realm or the form realm who has not yet produced the untainted knowledge of others' minds (anāsrava-paracittajñāna).
If it arises, it is lost.
If one is born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and it arises, it is not lost.
Being born into the formless realm, one attains the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣaphala).
If one has attained the knowledge of others' minds in the past, does one possess it in the present?
Answer: If it is manifest before one.
That is to say, when other knowledges and various patiences do not arise,
it is not a state of mindlessness;
at that time, this knowledge is necessarily present before one.
In what stage does this reside?
It resides in those who are noble ones (ārya) or in ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
When this knowledge of others' minds manifests for one born in the desire realm or the form realm,
if it is accomplished in the present,
is it also accomplished in the past?
Answer: It is so.
This refers to the various stages previously described in sequence;
[it applies] when the knowledge of others' minds is present before one.
One necessarily accomplishes the past *sāsrava* knowledge of others' minds;
as for the *anāsrava*, it is not fixed.
If one accomplishes the future knowledge of others' minds, [the same applies].
Is it present? Answer: If it is manifested before one.
This is as previously explained regarding the possession of the past and the present.
If one achieves [the attainment] in the present, does one achieve it in the future? Answer: Yes.
However, because one who possesses [the knowledge] of the present necessarily possesses that of the future,
if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) of the past,
does one also possess it of the future and the present?
Answer: One definitely accomplishes it in the future.
As for the present, if it is manifested before one, in what state does this occur?
This refers to when the knowledge of others' minds is present; at that time,
ordinary beings and noble ones of the desire and form realms may,
if they have attained it, possess it both in the future and the present.
"Is that past? "Answer: Yes.
These refer, in their respective order, to the various stages previously described.
If one accomplishes the future knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess it in the past and present?
Answer: One possesses it in the future.
It is neither past nor present;
that is to say, it has already been attained and not lost,
yet it has not ceased, or even if it has ceased, it has been lost and does not manifest before one.
In this context, "that which has been obtained and not lost" indicates that it exists in the future;
"that which has not yet ceased, or having ceased, has already been lost" [indicates its non-existence].
To manifest that there is no past means to manifest that there is no present.
In what stage does this occur?
It refers to when a trainee (śaikṣa) abiding in the desire realm or the form realm has not yet produced uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds (anāsrava-paracittajñāna).
If it arises and is subsequently lost;
or if it arises and is not lost when one is born into the formless realm;
or if one attains the fruit of no-more-learning while born in the formless realm.
There are those belonging to the future and the past, but not the present;
that is to say, they have already ceased, have not been lost, and do not manifest before one.
In what state does this occur?
It refers to one who has been born in the desire realm and is already free from the defilements of desire,
yet the knowledge of others' minds is not present before them.
If one is born in the form realm, the knowledge of others' minds does not manifest.
If a trainee (śaikṣa) resides in either the desire or form realms,
once they have produced untainted knowledge of others' minds, it is not lost.
For one born in the formless realm who has not yet attained the fruit of arhatship, there are future, past, and present [knowledges];
that is to say, when they are manifested.
This refers to ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire or form realms.
When the knowledge of others' minds is present,
if one is endowed with it in the past and the present,
is one also endowed with it in the future?
The answer is: it is so.
This refers, in sequence, to the various stages previously described;
if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds in the present.
"Are they past or future?
"The answer is: yes;
they are likewise as described in the preceding stages."
If one accomplishes [the attainment] of the past and future, does one also accomplish it in the present?
Answer: If it is manifest before one.
This is also as previously explained regarding the various stages:
if one has attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the past,
does one also possess it in the future?
Question: Is it the case that if one accomplishes the future [conventional knowledge], one also accomplishes the past?
Answer: It is so.
For there is no sentient being who does not accomplish both the past and the future conventional knowledge.
If one has accomplished conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the past, does one possess it in the present?
Answer: If it is manifest before one—that is, provided that no untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) has arisen and one is not in a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*).
If this conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is certainly present before one, and it is established that one possesses it in the present, does one also possess it in the past?
Answer: It is so.
These cases should be understood according to their characteristics as previously explained.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one also possess past subsequent knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one possesses it.
In what stage does this occur? It refers to one who has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
It lasts for four moments of mind during the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of the origin and cessation [of suffering], and three moments of mind during the clear realization of the path.
Having attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya,
and having refined the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) as both learners (śaikṣa) and non-learners (aśaikṣa),
the dharmajñāna and anvayajñāna that have arisen and ceased are not lost.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then it is not accomplished.
In what stage does this occur?
It refers to one who has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
During the final two moments of the clear realization of suffering,
one attains the fruit of once-returner or non-returner; likewise,
this occurs after a learner has refined their faculties.
If the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost,
while the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased but is lost;
and if one possesses past subsequent knowledge.
Is that past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
This is as previously explained regarding the stage of possessing past dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished and lost, then it is not accomplished.
In what stage does this occur?
It refers to the attainment of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, once those in training and those beyond training have refined their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra),
the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) that has already been extinguished is not lost;
whereas the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) that has not yet been extinguished, or even if it has been extinguished, is lost.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one also have future subsequent knowledge?
Answer: If it has been attained.
This refers to the stage when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has already arisen.
In what position does this occur?
It occurs when one has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
Following the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*), it lasts for one moment of mind;
the clear realizations of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*) each last for four moments of mind;
and the clear realization of the path (*mārga*) lasts for three moments of mind.
Having attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya,
and having refined the faculties (indriya-pariśodhana) as both learners (śaikṣa) and non-learners (aśaikṣa),
if the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has already been extinguished and is not lost.
If one has attained future anvaya-jñāna (subsequent knowledge), has one also attained past dharma-jñāna (knowledge of phenomena)?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one has attained it.
These refer, in order, to the various stages previously described.
If [the factors] have not yet been extinguished, or if they were already extinguished but have since been lost, then one does not possess them.
At which stage does this occur?
This refers to having attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya,
and having already refined one's faculties (indriyasaṃcāra) as a learner (śaikṣa) or one beyond learning (aśaikṣa),
such that the dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) has not yet been extinguished, or even if it has been extinguished, it has been lost.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one also possess present anvaya-knowledge?
Answer: If it is present before one.
That is to say, if other knowledges and various patiences do not arise,
this concentration does not manifest in a state of mindlessness.
In what stage does this occur? It occurs when one has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
during the single moment of mind for each of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, origin, and cessation.
This refers to the time of anvaya-jñāna (subsequent knowledge),
when one attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya,
as well as having trained the faculties (*indriya*) through both the paths of learning (*śaikṣa*) and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
If the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost,
and conventional knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is present before one,
even if one possesses the present conventional knowledge;
Is that past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
This refers to the various stages previously described in succession.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it.
In what state does this occur?
It refers to the attainment of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, when those in training and those beyond training have refined their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*),
even if the dharma-knowledge has not yet been extinguished, or has been extinguished but subsequently lost,
the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) manifests.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one also have past and present anvaya-knowledge?
Answer: There are cases where one has past dharma-knowledge, but not past and present anvaya-knowledge.
That is to say, the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but has not been lost;
the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased, it has been lost and does not manifest before one.
In what stage does this occur?
This refers to one who has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
during the single moment of the present observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*),
specifically at the time of the receptivity to subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Having attained the fruit of once-returner or non-returner,
and having already trained the faculties,
if the dharma-knowledge has been extinguished but not lost.
When subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) has not yet been extinguished, or has already been extinguished and lost, it does not manifest in the present.
There are cases where past dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) and past subsequent knowledge exist but are not present;
that is to say, when dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge have already been extinguished but have not been lost.
In which stage does subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) not manifest?
It refers to one who has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
during the three moments of each of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of origin, cessation, and the path.
Excluding the time of the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna),
one attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya;
as well as after having trained the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) while still in training (śaikṣa) or beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) and its subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) have already ceased but are not lost;
yet, the subsequent knowledge does not manifest in the present.
There is past dharma-knowledge and present subsequent knowledge that is not past.
That is to say, the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost;
the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is present and has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased, it has already been lost.
In what stage does this occur?

This refers to the moment of a single mental instant when one has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and is engaged in the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of suffering;
that is, at the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).
At this point, one attains the fruit of either a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) or a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Furthermore, once one has trained in the faculties,
if the dharma-knowledge has already been extinguished but not lost,
while the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has not yet been extinguished— having previously been extinguished and then lost— it now manifests before one.
There is past dharma-knowledge,
as well as past and present inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*);
that is to say, the dharma-knowledge and inferential knowledge have already ceased but have not been lost.
When subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is present, in what stage does this occur?
It is said: when one has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
The clear realizations of the cessation of the aggregates each last for the duration of a single moment of mind;
that is to say, one attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya at the time of anvaya-jñāna,
as well as after the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) by those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge have already ceased but are not lost,
and the subsequent knowledge is now present before one.
Even if one has attained past and present subsequent knowledge, [it is so].
Is that past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
This refers to the various stages previously described in succession.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished but lost, then it is not accomplished.
In what stage does this occur?
It refers to one who has attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, once those in training and those beyond training have refined their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*),
if the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) has already been extinguished and not lost,
or if the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) has not yet been extinguished— or even if it has been extinguished but was subsequently lost— and the subsequent knowledge is now present before them.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one also have future and present category-knowledge?
Answer: There are cases where one has past dharma-knowledge but not future and present category-knowledge.
This refers to the state where dharma-knowledge has already ceased but subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has not yet been attained.
In what stage does this occur? It occurs when one has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
During the momentary concentration of the clear realization of suffering— that is,
at the time of the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti)—
there is past dharma-knowledge and future subsequent knowledge, but no present [knowledge].
This refers to the state where the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost,
and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has already been attained but is not currently manifest.
In what stage does this occur?

This refers to one who has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and attains the four fruits of the śramaṇa during the first three moments of each of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of origin, cessation, and the path.
Furthermore, once those in training and those beyond training have refined their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*),
if the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) has already ceased but is not lost,
and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) does not manifest before them.
There is past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*),
as well as future and present subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*);
that is to say, dharma-knowledge has already ceased but has not been lost.
When subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) manifests, in what stage does this occur?
It is said: it occurs when one has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Immediately following each of the clear realizations (abhisamaya) of suffering, origin, and cessation,
one attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya;
this also applies after the training and post-training refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) for those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
If the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost,
and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is present before one,
then one would possess both the future and the present subsequent knowledge.
Is that past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
This refers to the various stages previously described in sequence.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished and subsequently lost, then one does not possess it.
At what stage does this occur?
It refers to the attainment of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, when those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) have refined their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra),
even if the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has not yet been extinguished, or has been extinguished but subsequently lost,
the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) manifests before them.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one also have past and future subsequent knowledge?
Answer: There are cases where one has past dharma-knowledge but not past and future subsequent knowledge.
This refers to when the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has not yet been attained.

At what stage does this occur? It occurs at the moment of a single mind-instant during the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*), having already entered the state of right determination and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
This refers to the time of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*).
At that time, there is past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and future subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), but not [subsequent knowledge] that is past.
This means that the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but has not been lost.
If the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) has already been attained but not yet abandoned,
or if it was previously abandoned after having been attained—
what stage does this refer to?
This refers to one who has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma),
and within a single moment of mind following the clear observation of suffering (duḥkha-abhisamaya),
attains the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) or non-returner (anāgāmin).
Furthermore, once one has trained the faculties (*indriya*),
if the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) has already been extinguished but not lost,
while the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but has already been lost.
There is past dharma-knowledge as well as past and future subsequent knowledge;
that is to say, when dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge have already ceased but have not been lost.
In what state does this occur?
This refers to those who have already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*):

for the clear realization of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya*), it lasts for four moments of mind; for the clear realization of the path (*mārga-abhisamaya*), it lasts for three moments of mind. Each of these constitutes a period of four mental instants.
Having attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya and having refined the faculties (indriya-pariśodhana) as both learners (śaikṣa) and non-learners (aśaikṣa),
the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) that have already ceased are not lost.
If one has attained the future knowledge of categories (anvaya-jñāna) regarding the past, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) regarding the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one possesses it.
These correspond, in order, to the stages previously described.
If [the defilements] have not been extinguished, or if they have been extinguished but subsequently lost, then one does not possess them. In which stage does this occur?
It refers to the attainment of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, once those in training and those beyond training have refined their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*),

the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) that has already been extinguished is not lost; whereas the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) that has not yet been extinguished, or which has been extinguished and then lost, [is not retained].
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one also possess past, future, and present category-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
Answer: There are those who have past dharma-knowledge.
It is not the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) of the past, future, or present;
that is, the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has already ceased and the subsequent knowledge has not yet been attained.
In what stage does this occur?
This refers to one who has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
It occurs during the momentary duration of a single mind in the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*),
specifically at the time of the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).
There is past dharma-knowledge and future subsequent knowledge,
but not past or present [subsequent knowledge].
This refers to the case where dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost, and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has already been attained;
yet, [dharma-knowledge] has not ceased, or even if it has ceased, it has been lost and does not manifest before one.
In what stage does this occur?
This refers to one who has attained the fruit of a Once-returner or a Non-returner,
and having already trained the faculties (indriya), if the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has been extinguished and not lost,
while the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has not yet been extinguished; or if it has been extinguished but was subsequently lost and does not manifest before them.
There is dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) that is past,
as well as subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) that is future or present but not past;
that is to say, the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but has not been lost.
When subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is present before one,
it has not yet been extinguished, or even if it has been extinguished, it has already been lost.
In what stage does this occur?
This refers to one who has already entered the state of rightness and transcendence (samyaktva-niyāma),
and within a single moment of mind following the clear observation of suffering (duḥkha-abhisamaya),
attains the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) or non-returner (anāgāmin).
Furthermore, once the faculties have been trained through cultivation,
if the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost,
and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) has not yet ceased— or even if it has ceased and been lost— is now present before one.
There is past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*),
as well as past and future subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) that is not present;
that is to say, dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge have already ceased but have not been lost.
When does subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) not manifest?
It refers to the stage when one has already entered the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma).
One attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya during the first three moments of each of the clear realizations (abhisamaya) of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
as well as after the training and refinement of the faculties (indriyasaṃcāra) by those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) have already ceased but are not lost.
Subsequent knowledge is not present before one.
There is past dharma-knowledge, as well as past, future, and present subsequent knowledge.

This refers to the case where the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge have already ceased but have not been lost, and the subsequent knowledge is now present before one. In what stage does this occur?
It occurs when one has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
In each of the subsequent moments of the clear realizations of the origin and cessation [of suffering],
one attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya;
this also applies after the training and non-training faculties have been refined.
The dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) have already ceased but are not lost,
and yet the subsequent knowledge is present before one.
Even if one possesses past, future, and present subsequent knowledge, [it is so].
Is that past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
This refers to the various stages previously described in succession.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but subsequently lost, then it is not accomplished.
At what stage does this occur?
It refers to the attainment of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, once those in training and those beyond training have refined their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*),
if subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) has already ceased but is not lost and is also present before them,
while dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but is already lost; [then such a person is one who possesses both].
Regarding the statement "as with the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) forming the 'small seven' [set],
so it is also for the knowledges of origin, cessation, and the path":
this means that just as the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) forms the "small seven" set in relation to the subsequent knowledge, so it is for the other three knowledges.
The same applies to the seven small sets regarding the knowledge of origin,
cessation, and the path.
The difference is that each is stated by its own name as appropriate.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one possess past knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
In what stage does this occur?
It occurs when one has already become free from the defilements of desire and has entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
during the interval of the latter two moments of the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*).
The clear realization of the cessation of the aggregates lasts for four moments of mind;
the clear realization of the path lasts for three moments of mind.

One attains the latter two fruits of śrāmaṇya, and having already abandoned the defilements of desire, the dharma-knowledge that has been cultivated through the refinement of the faculties of those in training and those beyond training is not lost once it has ceased.
If a learner’s untainted knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and knowledge of others’ minds (*paracittajñāna*) have already ceased but have not been lost,
and they are born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) without yet having attained the fruit of arhatship (*aśaikṣaphala*),
then [these knowledges] are not possessed. Alternatively, if they have not yet ceased, or if they have ceased but have been lost, then they are likewise not possessed.
In what stage does this occur?

It refers to the two moments of mind following the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, when one has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire and has entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The clear realization of the cessation of the aggregates lasts for four moments of mind,
and the clear realization of the path lasts for three moments of mind;
during these, one attains the first two fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, after one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire has trained the faculties (*indriya*),
if the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) has already ceased but is not lost;
or if, for a trainee (*śaikṣa*), the dharma-knowledge has already ceased and is not lost.
If untainted knowledge of others' minds has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has already been lost;
or if one is born in the formless realm and has not yet attained the fruit of no-more-learning—
even if such a person were to possess past knowledge of others' minds.
Is that past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one possesses it.
This is as previously explained regarding simultaneous possession.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished and lost, then one does not possess it.
In what state does this occur?
It refers to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Having been born in the desire realm and become free from the defilement of desire,
or having been born in the form realm,
if one has become free from the defilement of desire and entered the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma).
During the first two moments of the clear realization of suffering,
one attains the latter two fruits of śrāmaṇya,
as well as [the state of] being already free from the defilement of desire.
After the faculties have been refined by those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa),
if the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has not yet been extinguished, or even if it has been extinguished but subsequently lost—
if it is one in training, the untainted knowledge of others' minds (anāsrava-paracitta-jñāna) that has already been extinguished is not lost.
If the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but subsequently lost,
and one is born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) without having attained the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣaphala),
then one does not possess past dharmajñāna.
Is that [knowledge] the knowledge of others' minds regarding the future?
Answer: If it has already been attained and not lost.
Herein, "already attained" means:
This means that one has already become free from the defilement of desire;
"not losing" it means not regressing to the arousal of desire.
In what stage does this occur?

It refers to the period of two moments of mind following the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*), when one has already abandoned the defilements of desire and entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The clear realizations of the cessation and the origin each last for four moments of mind;
the clear realization of the path lasts for three moments of mind.
During these, one attains the latter two fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, once one has abandoned the defilements of desire and refined the faculties as a learner (śaikṣa) or one beyond learning (aśaikṣa),
the dharma-knowledge that has already been extinguished is not lost.
This applies whether the learner is in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The dharma-knowledge has already been extinguished but not lost;
having been born in the form or formless realms, one has not yet attained the fruit of no-more-learning.
Even if one possesses the future knowledge of others' minds, [it is not so].
Is that past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
These correspond respectively to the various stages previously described.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished and lost, then one does not possess it.
In what stage does this occur?
It refers to ordinary beings who have already attained the knowledge of others' minds and have not lost it.
If one has already abandoned the defilements of desire and entered the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma),
one attains the latter two fruits of śramaṇa during the first two moments of the clear observation (abhisamaya) of suffering.
Furthermore, for one who has already become free from the defilement of desire and has refined their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) as a learner (śaikṣa) or one beyond learning (aśaikṣa),
if the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has not yet been extinguished,

or even if it was extinguished and subsequently lost; or if a learner in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) has not yet extinguished the dharma-knowledge, or even if it was extinguished and subsequently lost.
If one is born into the form or formless realms and, even after [the knowledge] has ceased, does not lose it,
one will attain the fruit of arhatship there.
This applies if one possesses past dharma-knowledge.
Is that the knowledge of others' minds in the present?
Answer: If it is present before one.
In what state does this occur?
This refers to having attained either of the latter two fruits of śrāmaṇya,
as well as having already become free from the defilement of desire, and having refined one's faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) whether as a learner (śaikṣa) or a non-learner (aśaikṣa);
such that the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has already ceased but is not lost.
When the knowledge of others' minds is present,
if one possesses the present knowledge of others' minds,
does one also possess the past knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: If [the defilement] has already been extinguished and not lost, then one possesses it;
this refers to the various stages previously described.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it; in which stage does this occur?
That is to say, when ordinary beings bring the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) into manifestation,
or when those who have attained the latter two fruits of the śramaṇa,
as well as those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) who have already abandoned the defilements of desire, have refined their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra).
When the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) is present, even if the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished but lost,
one nevertheless possesses the past knowledge of phenomena.
Does that [knowledge] consist of knowledge of others' minds regarding the past or the present?
Answer: There is knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding the past that is not knowledge of others' minds regarding the past or the present;
namely, when the knowledge of phenomena has already ceased but has not been lost.

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), even if it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost and is not presently manifest, in what stage does this occur?

It refers to the period of two moments of mind following the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkhābhisamaya*), when one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire enters the state of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*).
The clear realizations of the cessation and the origin each take four moments of mind,
while the clear realization of the path takes three moments of mind;
during these, one attains the first two fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, once one who is still in training (*śaikṣa*) has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire and has already refined their faculties (*indriya*),
the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) that has already ceased is not lost.
If it is a trainee whose dharma-knowledge has already ceased, it is likewise not lost.
If uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but been lost,
and one is born into the formless realm without having attained the fruit of no-more-learning,
there exists past dharma-knowledge and past knowledge of others' minds, but none that are present.
This refers to the case where the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) have already ceased but have not been lost,
while the knowledge of others' minds is not currently manifest.
In what state does this occur?
This refers to one who, having already become free from the defilement of sensual desire, enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
It consists of two moments of mind during the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of suffering,
and four moments of mind each during the clear observation of origin and cessation.
In the duration of three moments of the path of clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
one attains the latter two fruits of śrāmaṇya; likewise,
this occurs once one has already become free from the defilement of desire and has refined the faculties (*indriya*) as a learner (*śaikṣa*) or a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
The dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost;
the knowledge of others' minds is not present before him.
If it is a learner (śaikṣa), the untainted knowledge of others' minds has already ceased but is not lost.
For one born in the formless realm who has not yet attained the fruit of arhatship,
there exists past dharma-knowledge as well as past and present knowledge of others' minds;
that is to say, the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but has not been lost.
When the knowledge of others' minds manifests,
in what state does this occur?

It occurs when one has attained the latter two fruits of the śramaṇa, as well as when one who is still in training (śaikṣa) or already beyond training (aśaikṣa) has become free from the defilement of desire and has refined their faculties (indriya).

If, after the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already ceased without being lost, the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) manifests in the present, and one possesses both past and present knowledge of others' minds,
does that person also possess the past knowledge of phenomena?
The answer is: if [the defilement] has already been extinguished and not lost, then one possesses it;
this refers to the various stages previously described in succession.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but subsequently lost, then one does not possess it.
In what stage does this occur?
It refers to when ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) bring the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) into manifestation,
provided they have attained either of the latter two fruits of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, when one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire— whether a trainee (śaikṣa) or one beyond training (aśaikṣa)—

has refined their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra), and at the time when the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) is present, even though the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has not yet been extinguished,
or having been extinguished, has been lost, if one possesses past dharmajñāna.
Does that [knowledge] consist of future or present knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: There is past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), but it is not future or present knowledge of others' minds.
This means that the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already ceased but has not been lost,
while the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) has not yet been attained; or,
even if it was attained, it has already been lost.
In what stage does this occur?

It occurs during the two moments of mind following the present observation (*abhisamaya*) of suffering for one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire; during the four moments of mind each for the present observations of origin and cessation;
and during the three moments of mind for the present observation of the path.
Having attained the first two fruits of śrāmaṇya and having already trained the faculties while still a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire,
the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) that has already ceased is not lost;
there is past dharma-knowledge and future knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*), but none is present.
This refers to the case where the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already ceased but is not lost,
and the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) has already been attained but is not lost and is not currently manifest.
In what state does this occur?
This refers to one who, having already become free from the defilement of desire, enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
It consists of two moments of mind during the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*),
and four moments of mind each during the clear observations of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
In the duration of three moments of the path of clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
one attains the latter two fruits of the śramaṇa; likewise,
this occurs once one has already become free from the defilements of desire and has refined the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) as a learner (*śaikṣa*) or a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).

The dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost, while the knowledge of others' minds is not present before one; there is past dharma-knowledge as well as future and present knowledge of others' minds.
That is to say, the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost.
When the knowledge of others' minds is present,
this is explained as previously stated regarding the accomplishment of past dharma-knowledge and the present knowledge of others' minds.
Even if one accomplishes future and present knowledge of others' minds, [the same principle applies].
Is that past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
This refers to the various stages previously described in succession.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it was extinguished but has already been lost, then one does not possess it;
this is as previously explained regarding the possession of present knowledge of others' minds and the non-possession of past dharma-knowledge.
If one has accomplished past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also possess past and future knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: There is [the case of] having past knowledge of phenomena.
The knowledge of others' minds regarding the past or future refers to when the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but has not been lost,
while the knowledge of others' minds has not yet been attained,
or even if attained, has already been lost.
This is as previously stated regarding the case where there is past dharma-knowledge but no future or present knowledge of others' minds;
there is also the case where there is past dharma-knowledge and future knowledge of others' minds, but no past [knowledge of others' minds].
That is to say: the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already ceased but is not lost;
the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) has already been attained and is not lost;
[the former] has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased, it has already been lost.
In what stage does this occur?
It refers to a learner (*śaikṣa*) for whom the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) has already ceased but is not lost;

who has not yet ceased, or has ceased but lost, the untainted knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñāna*); and who, having been born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), has not yet attained the fruit of arhatship (*aśaikṣaphala*).
There are past dharma-knowledge as well as past and future knowledge of others' minds;
that is to say, the dharma-knowledge and the knowledge of others' minds have already ceased but have not been lost.
This is as previously explained regarding the possession of past dharma-knowledge and knowledge of others' minds.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds regarding the past and future, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) regarding the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it; if it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
This is as before.
If one has attained past knowledge of others' minds,
has one also attained past dharma-knowledge?
If one possesses past dharma-knowledge, does that person possess past, future, or present knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: There is [a case of] possessing past dharma-knowledge.
It is not the knowledge of others' minds pertaining to the past, future, or present; that is to say,
the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost,
while the knowledge of others' minds has not yet been attained, or if attained, has already been lost.
This is as previously stated regarding the case where there is knowledge of dharmas of the past but not of the future or present, nor of the knowledge of others' minds;
there are cases where there is knowledge of dharmas of the past and knowledge of others' minds of the future, but not of the past or present.
That is to say: the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already ceased but is not lost;
the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) has already been attained and is not lost;
and [the knowledge of others' minds] has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased, it has been lost and does not manifest before one.
This is as previously stated: there is the past dharma-knowledge and the future knowledge of others' minds, but not the past [knowledge of others' minds].
There is the past dharma-knowledge and the past and future knowledge of others' minds, but not the present [knowledge of others' minds].
This refers to the case where the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) have already ceased but have not been lost,
and the knowledge of others' minds is not currently present.
This is as previously explained regarding the past knowledge of phenomena and the past knowledge of others' minds, which are described as being non-present.
There is past dharma-knowledge as well as past, future, and present knowledge of others' minds;
that is to say, the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost,
while the knowledge of others' minds is presently manifest.
This is as previously explained regarding the past dharma-knowledge and the past and present knowledge of others' minds.
Suppose one possesses the past, future, and present knowledge of others' minds.
Is that past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then it is possessed;
if it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then it is not possessed.
This is as before. Suppose one possesses the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) belonging to the past and the present;
does that person possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) belonging to the past?
If one is endowed with past dharma-knowledge, is one also endowed with past conventional knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
Because all sentient beings possess conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) regarding the past and future, in what stage does this [knowledge] reside?
It is said: it belongs to one who has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
During the two moments of mind following the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*),
there are four moments of mind each for the clear realizations of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*),
and three moments of mind for the clear realization of the path (*mārga*).
Having attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya,
and having refined the faculties through the paths of training and beyond-training,
if the dharma-knowledge has already been extinguished but not lost.
If one has accomplished conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the past, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) of the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one possesses it.
These refer, in order, to the various stages previously described.
If [the qualities] have not yet been extinguished, or if they were extinguished but have since been lost, then one does not possess them.
In which stage does this occur?
This refers to all ordinary beings (pṛthagjana),
as well as those who have already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma),
during the first two moments of the direct realization of suffering (duḥkha-abhisamaya).
Having attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya and having refined the faculties (indriya) as both learners (śaikṣa) and non-learners (aśaikṣa),
the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has either not yet been extinguished, or, even if it has been extinguished, has already been lost.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, has one also accomplished future conventional knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
This is as explained previously.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge,
has one also accomplished conventional knowledge of the past?
Conversely, if it is said that one has accomplished future conventional knowledge, has one also accomplished past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it;
if it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
This is as explained previously.
If one has attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the past,
does one possess the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) of the past?
It is said that if one possesses the knowledge of phenomena of the past...
Is that [concentration] conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the present?
Answer: If it is present before one;
that is to say, if no untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) arises, and it is not a state of non-consciousness (*acittaka*), then this concentration is present before one.
In what stage does this occur?
It occurs when one has attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya and has already refined the faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) as both a learner (śaikṣa) and one beyond learning (aśaikṣa).
If, when the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) has arisen and is present— having already ceased and not been lost—
the practitioner possesses that present conventional knowledge,
does he also possess that past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)?
Answer: If [the defilements] have already been extinguished and have not been lost, then one possesses them.
These correspond to the various stages previously described.
If they have not yet been extinguished, or if they have been extinguished but subsequently lost, then one does not possess them. In which stage does this occur?
This refers to all ordinary beings (pṛthagjana),
as well as those who have attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya,
and those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) who have already refined their faculties (indriya).

When conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) arises and is present before one, even if the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished but lost,
the characteristics of the remaining [knowledges] should be understood according to the preceding text.
If one has accomplished past dharma-knowledge, does one also possess past knowledge of suffering?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one possesses it.
In what stage does this occur? It refers to one who has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

It lasts for two moments of mind following the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*), and four moments of mind each during the clear observations of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
Within the duration of three moments of mind during the clear realization of the Path,
one attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; furthermore,
this occurs after having refined the faculties (indriya-pariśodhana) as both a learner (śaikṣa) and one beyond learning (aśaikṣa).
If the dharma-knowledge and the knowledge of suffering have already ceased but have not been lost, [one possesses them].
If they have not yet ceased, or if they have ceased but have been lost, then one does not possess them.
In what stage does this occur?
That is to say, having attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya,
and having refined the faculties (*indriya*) as both learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-learners (*aśaikṣa*),
if the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) has not yet ceased or has not been lost.

If the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has not yet been extinguished, or even if it has been extinguished but has been lost—if one possesses past knowledge of suffering, does one possess past knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)? Answer: If it has already been extinguished and has not been lost, then one possesses it.
This is as previously explained regarding the non-accomplishment of the knowledge of past phenomena and the knowledge of suffering.
If [the defilements] have not been extinguished, or if they have been extinguished but subsequently lost, then one does not accomplish them.
At what stage does this occur?
That is to say, having attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya and having refined one's faculties (indriya-pariśodhana) as both a learner (śaikṣa) and one beyond learning (aśaikṣa),
if the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) has already ceased but is not lost.
If the dharma-knowledge has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished but lost,
and one possesses past dharma-knowledge,
does one also possess future knowledge of suffering?
Answer: It is so.
If one possesses the knowledge of past phenomena, one necessarily possesses the knowledge of future suffering.
In what stage does this occur?

It is said: it occurs during the two moments of mind immediately following the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*), once one has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

One attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya during four moments of mind each for the clear realizations of the cessation of the origin and the cessation [of suffering], and during three moments of mind for the clear realization of the path;
this occurs after one has trained the faculties (indriya) as a learner (śaikṣa) or a non-learner (aśaikṣa).
If the dharma-knowledge has already ceased but is not lost,
and one possesses the future knowledge of suffering,
does that person also possess the past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If [the defilements] have already been extinguished but not lost, then one possesses them;
these correspond to the various stages previously described.
If they have not yet been extinguished, or if they have been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess them.
In what stage does this occur?
It occurs when one has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) during the single moment of mind of the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of suffering.
This refers to the time of the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna),
when one attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya,
as well as after having refined the faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) through both the paths of training (śaikṣa) and beyond training (aśaikṣa).
If the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost,
and one possesses past dharmajñāna,
does one also possess present knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)?
Answer: It manifests when it is present before one.
That is to say, it manifests when no other cognitions or patiences arise;
it does not manifest during states of mindlessness.
In what stage does this occur?
It is said: when one has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and dwells for a single moment of mind during the direct realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*).
This refers to attaining the four fruits of śrāmaṇya at the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna),
as well as after the faculties have been refined through training (śaikṣa) and beyond-training (aśaikṣa),
provided that the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) has already ceased but is not lost.
And when the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) is present before one,
if that person possesses the present knowledge of suffering,
does he also possess the past knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: If [the dharma] has already been extinguished but not lost, then one possesses it;
these cases correspond to the various stages previously described.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it.
In what stage does this occur?

It is said: it occurs when one has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), during the single moment of the present contemplation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*).
This refers to attaining the four fruits of śrāmaṇya at the time of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna),
as well as after the refinement of faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) by those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa). [In these cases],
even if the dharma-knowledge has not yet ceased, or has ceased but been subsequently lost, [the fruit is still attained].
When the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) manifests,
the characteristics of the remaining [knowledges] should be understood by analogy with what precedes;
just as the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) forms seven small groups when compared with the subsequent [knowledges].
"Up to the point where the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) is paired with the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna),
the 'small sevenfold' [analysis] should be applied accordingly in the same manner"—
that is to say, just as the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) is paired with subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) and so forth to form the small sevenfold analysis.
In this manner, it should be understood that subsequent knowledge of others' minds and so forth are related to subsequent conventional knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
and likewise up to the point where the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) is related to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
As it is with the seven small [categories], so it is with the seven large [categories].
That is to say, just as the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) form seven small sets when preceding ones are paired with succeeding ones,
it should be understood that the same applies to the formation of seven large sets when these eight knowledges precede and follow one another.
The difference is as follows:
Regarding the application of two or more [factors] to one, or one to two or more:
it is said that within the aforementioned "small sevenfold" [arrangement], there is necessarily a one-to-one correspondence.
Now, within the "Great Seven," there are cases where two or more correspond to one, or where one corresponds to two or more;
this is called the distinction between the "Small Seven" and the "Great Seven."
Just as there are seven [categories] beginning with the past,
so too there are seven each beginning with the future, and even those beginning with the past, future, and present;
this is how they should be understood.
That is to say, just as when taking past *dharmajñāna* and so forth as the primary subject, one asks about the three periods of time regarding *anvayajñāna* and the like—
distinguished by the seven categories of small and great—
in the same way, one takes future *dharmajñāna* and so forth as the primary subject.
Question: Beginning with the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the three times, up to the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) of the past, future, and present, and so forth—
each of these instances of subsequent knowledge of the three times also possesses seven distinctions, categorized as minor and major.
One should understand their characteristics according to what is appropriate for each case.
Within this, the meaning of the distinctions such as the single category, the six small sets, and the seven large sets,
should be understood as they were explained at length in the previous section on the Aggregate of Formations (Saṃskāra-skandha).

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, in accordance with the Imperial Edict. Chapter Four: The Aggregate of Karma (Karmaskandha). Section One: The Sub-section on Evil Conduct (Duścarita-nirdeśa). The first part of the first sub-section of the fourth aggregate of karma: The three types of evil conduct and the three unwholesome roots.
Does the former include the latter, or does the latter include the former?
Having thus mastered these chapters and the meaning of their exegesis,
[one should proceed].
Next, it should be explained in detail.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing and clarifying the meaning of the sūtras.
As stated in the sūtras,
there are three types of unwholesome conduct and three unwholesome roots.
Although the sūtras speak thus, they do not provide a detailed exposition.
Furthermore, it has not yet been stated that the three types of unwholesome conduct subsume the three unwholesome roots,
nor that the three unwholesome roots subsume the three types of unwholesome conduct.
The Sūtra is the foundation of this treatise.
That which has not yet been explained shall now be explained;
for this reason, this treatise is composed.
Regarding the three types of unwholesome conduct:
That is to say: misconduct of body,
misconduct of speech,
and misconduct of mind.
What are bodily and other unwholesome actions?
As the Blessed One said:
"What is bodily unwholesome action?"
Namely: taking life,
taking what is not given,
and sexual misconduct.
What is verbal misconduct?
It refers to false speech and divisive speech.
Harsh speech and frivolous speech.
What are the unwholesome actions of the mind?
That is to say: covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view.

It should be understood that herein the Blessed One spoke only of unwholesome conduct subsumed under the fundamental courses of action (*maula-karmapatha*), and not of unwholesome conduct subsumed under the preliminary application (*prayoga*) or the subsequent conclusion (*pṛṣṭha*) of those courses of action.
This *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* explains all unwholesome bodily actions,
whether they are subsumed under the paths of action (*karmapatha*) or not subsumed under the paths of action.
All such things are called bodily misconduct;
this collectively refers to all unwholesome vocal karma that is subsumed under the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
Whatever is not subsumed under the paths of action—
all such verbal misconduct and, generally speaking,
all unwholesome mental karma— are likewise [included].
Whether they are subsumed under the paths of action or not subsumed under the paths of action—
all such cases are termed mental misconduct.
In this treatise, all unwholesome courses of action are subsumed;
the *Saṃgītiparyāya* also states this, saying: [as follows].
What is bodily misconduct?
It refers to taking life and taking what is not given.
Sexual misconduct.
These aforementioned points accord with the sūtras.
Furthermore, it says: "Next, taking life."
Taking what is not given and unchaste conduct;
in this way, they further include those previously mentioned that were not included.
Regarding the performance of sexual acts with one's own wife,
it is further stated that there are other unwholesome bodily actions.
In this way, all preparatory and consecutive stages of the paths of action are further subsumed. It is further stated:
"There are other bodily actions that are induced by what is unreasonable.
Question: What is a bodily action induced by what is unreasonable?
