Question: If one takes a hidden treasure located between two countries with the intention of stealing it, from whom does one incur the fundamental path of action?
Answer: If a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, it is obtained from the place where the Wheel-Turning King resides;
if there is no Wheel-Turning King, it is not obtained from any place at all.
Question: If one steals property belonging to a Tathāgata’s stūpa...
Regarding from whom one acquires the fundamental path of action (maula-karmapatha),
some say it is also acquired from a king.
Some say it is obtained from the donor; others say: [it is obtained from the field of merit].
It is obtained from those who guard it.
Some say it is obtained from those capable of protecting it— such as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or non-humans.
Those who speak thus have attained it in the presence of the Buddha. Why is this so?
As the Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, you should know that if I were to remain in this world, those who would offer me respect and make offerings to me..."
And for up to a thousand years after my parinirvāṇa,
if one reverently makes offerings to my *dhātu* even as small as a mustard seed,
I say that such a person abides in a mind of equanimity.
The maturation of the fruit of retribution is perfectly equal.
By virtue of this statement,
even though a thousand years have passed since the Blessed One’s parinirvāṇa, [the fruit remains].
The Buddha, who is honored and venerated by all the world, accepts everyone.

Question: If one commits an impure act with a woman who has undertaken the training of the precepts—namely, a bhikṣuṇī or an upāsikā who is diligently practicing the holy life (brahmacarya)—[what is the consequence?]
Furthermore, regarding those who engage in the arduous ascetic practices of non-Buddhists with fervor,
from whom does one incur the fundamental path of action when violating them?
Some say that it was obtained from their respective individual teachers;
others say that it was obtained from [the Buddha].
Regarding the statement that it is obtained among fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*),
some say it is obtained at the court of a king.
Since she is protected by the king, one asks:
if one commits an act of sexual misconduct with a woman who has been entrusted to him as a guest,
against whom does he incur the fundamental path of action?
Some say that it is obtained from the person to whom one has entrusted [the goods].
Such is their explanation.
It is obtained from the king, because she is protected by the king. Question:
What if one commits an act of sexual misconduct with a woman who is his own property?
From whom does one obtain the fundamental path of action?
Answer: If the price has been paid, it is obtained from no one at all;
if the price has not been paid, it is obtained from the king.
Question: Regarding one who commits an impure act with an unmarried girl, against whom is the fundamental path of action (maula-karmapatha) incurred?
Answer: If she has already been betrothed to another, it is incurred against the husband.
If it has not yet been permitted by her parents or various relatives, one asks:
"Suppose there is a woman who is protected by her parents, brothers, sisters, kinsmen, and so forth?"
There are those who are subject to punishment and restraint, such as the wives or concubines of others,
or those protected by another; even if one were to offer them a single flower garland,
if one engages in unwholesome sexual conduct with them, [it constitutes an offense].
From whom does one obtain the fundamental path of action?
Answer: One obtains it from one who provides protection, up to and including the gift of a single flower garland.
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, the people of Jambudvīpa engage in sexual intercourse through physical union;
those of Pūrvavideha [do so]... [through embracing].
Aparagoyānī, Uttarakuru,
and the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
The Trāyastriṃśa gods are likewise.
In the Yāma heaven, sexual union is accomplished by embracing;
in the Tuṣita heaven, it is accomplished by holding hands.
In the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, sexual union is accomplished through laughter;
in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, it is accomplished through mutual glances.
[The text] asks about the preparatory stages of sexual acts arising from the various terrestrial abodes.
This refers to the fundamental paths of action for those dwelling in the sky-dwellers' realms.
Are there preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for these paths of action for the sky-dwellers?
The answer is: all of them possess preparatory stages.
That is to say, among the Yāma devas, [the act of love] consists of holding hands,
laughing together,
and gazing at one another.
For the preparatory practice, one should cultivate the visualization of the Tuṣita Heaven by means of joyful laughter and glancing looks.
The gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations take a mere glance as their preliminary effort (*prayoga*).
Question: Is there a preliminary effort even in those cases where the path of action (*karmapatha*) is completed by a simple mutual glance?
Answer: There is indeed such a preliminary effort in those cases as well.
First, while gazing at one woman, one turns one's gaze toward another direction;
the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) is not yet seen, but once it is seen,
the fundamental act (*maula*) is established.
First, while seated in one palace, he rises for the sake of looking at another woman and proceeds to a different palace;
the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) has not yet been seen,
but the fundamental stage (*maula*) is now perceived.
Question: For what reason do those dwelling on earth engage in sexual intercourse to fulfill their lust, while those dwelling in the air do not?
Answer: Because this affliction is coarse [among those on earth].
Those afflictions are subtle;
these afflictions are heavy;
those afflictions are light.
These afflictions are persistent,
while those afflictions are sharp;
furthermore, the sensory realms of those devas are intensely flourishing.
The objective sphere is luminous and pure;
the objective sphere is sublime and wondrous.
It is because one is led and drawn forth by such an objective sphere.
As soon as they encounter it, they are immediately made intoxicated and bewildered;
therefore, the fire of desire for them is easily extinguished.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
The aforementioned devas have recently departed from the path of desire;
therefore, the fire of desire within them gradually diminishes.
Thus it is said.
In all matters of sexual intercourse, the fire of desire is only extinguished when two forms unite.
Question: If this is so, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*?
The answer explains the differences in the duration and speed of their time:
for example, in the Yāma Heaven, the fire of desire is extinguished as soon as they embrace one another;
this continues up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Just as when one glances [at them], the fire of desire is extinguished;
the *Prajñapti-śāstra* makes this statement based solely on the duration of time.
[This refers to] the three types of wholesome conduct and the ten paths of wholesome action.
"Do the three subsume the ten, or do the ten subsume the three?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As the sūtra says:
"There are three types of sublime conduct and ten paths of wholesome action."
Although the sūtra makes this statement,
it does not provide an extensive analysis;
the detailed explanation is as previously set forth.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"The three kinds of sublime conduct have already been analyzed,
but the ten paths of wholesome action have not yet been analyzed."
Now, wishing to provide a detailed analysis, this treatise is composed.
Herein, the three types of sublime conduct (*sucarita*) are concise in terminology but extensive in substance;
the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*) are extensive in terminology but concise in substance.
Therefore, the three types of wholesome conduct subsume the ten paths of wholesome action,
but the ten paths of wholesome action do not subsume the three types of wholesome conduct;
the illustration is as stated previously.
What is not included?
It refers to all other wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, excluding those instances of wholesome conduct of body,
speech, and mind that are subsumed under the courses of action (*karmapatha*).
Among these, which bodily and vocal sublime actions are not subsumed under the paths of action?
They are the preliminary and concluding stages of the bodily and vocal paths of action,
as well as the various actions described in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
Furthermore, it excludes all actions subsumed under the obstructive offenses (*āvaraṇa-sāvadya*).
What constitutes excellent mental conduct that is not included within the paths of action?
It refers to wholesome volition (*kuśala-cetanā*).
Now, one should demonstrate the threefold distinctions of the ten paths of wholesome action:
the root, the preliminary application, and the subsequent conclusion;
that is to say, the abstention from the roots of the ten unwholesome paths of action.
This is the very basis of the ten paths of wholesome action;
it is the abandonment of the preliminary and concluding phases of unwholesome paths of action,
and constitutes the preliminary and concluding phases of the wholesome paths of action themselves.
Furthermore, how is this so?
It is just as when a śrāmaṇera receives full ordination:
first, he arranges his robes and enters the ordination enclosure.
He prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha and requested a preceptor;
having received the robes and bowl, he went to inquire whether there were any obstacles [to ordination].
He then returned to the midst of the assembly.
When one again asks about the obstacles and hindrances,
from the single motion (*jñapti*) up until the third motion has not yet been completed,
this is called the preliminary application (*prayoga*) of the wholesome paths of action.
When the third *karmavācanā* reaches its conclusion,
at that moment the manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) and the non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) of that same instant are called the fundamental path of wholesome karma (*kuśala-karmapatha-mūla*).
From this point onward, he explains matters such as the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*) and the four grave offenses (*caturmahāśrāmaṇya*).
This is called the subsequent action (*pṛṣṭha*) following the paths of wholesome karma.
Among these, the seven fundamental paths of wholesome karma are [as follows].
If both the manifest [action] and the non-manifest [action] of this moment each possess seven meanings,
the first is *śīla* (ethical discipline).
Second, right conduct;
third, restraint;
fourth, individual liberation.
5. The prātimokṣa restraint;
6. karma; 7. paths of action.
From this point onward, each of the various types of non-informative karma (*avijñapti-karman*) possesses only five meanings;
that is to say, with the exception of the prātimokṣa vows and the paths of action (*karmapatha*),
because for those who have already attained ultimate liberation from evil, these [vows] are neither initial nor primary.
Furthermore, it is only at the moment when volition reaches its culmination that it is designated as a course of action (*karmapatha*).
Question: Through how many wholesome courses of action does volition arise and reach its culmination simultaneously?
Answer: At the time of receiving the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*) and the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*).
If one abides in a wholesome mind associated with the five consciousnesses,
the volition arising simultaneously with the six wholesome courses of action reaches completion;
if one abides in a wholesome mind associated with the mental consciousness.
The volition that arises simultaneously with the seven paths of wholesome action reaches its culmination;
this occurs even when one abides in a defiled or neutral state of mind.
The volition arising simultaneously with the four wholesome courses of action reaches its culmination;
it is the same when receiving the ten precepts.
When receiving full ordination, if one abides in a wholesome mind within the five sensory consciousnesses, [the same applies].
The volition that arises simultaneously with the nine wholesome courses of action reaches its culmination;
if one abides in a wholesome mental consciousness,
the volition that arises simultaneously with ten or nine wholesome courses of action reaches its culmination.
If one abides in a defiled mind,
or an indeterminate mind,
or in a state of non-cognition.
When volition arises together with the seven paths of wholesome karma and reaches completion while one is in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
there are the seven paths of wholesome karma of body and speech.
The duration is indefinite, depending on the intended period;
as for the three wholesome courses of action of the mind,
they may or may not exist.
They may be absent;
they may be many;
or they may be few.
For one born in the desire realm, if they give rise to a wholesome mind of the five sensory consciousnesses of the desire realm,
it proceeds to completion through volition (cetanā) arising simultaneously with two wholesome courses of action (karmapatha).
If they give rise to a wholesome mind of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) of the desire realm...
The volition that arises simultaneously with the three paths of wholesome action reaches completion;
this occurs when one gives rise to a wholesome mind of the form realm,
or a mind arising simultaneously with the untainted right view of that stage.
When the mind conjoined with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) of that stage arises,
it reaches completion through volition (*cetanā*) conjoined with nine paths of wholesome action.
If one gives rise to a wholesome mind of the formless realm,
or a mind co-arising with the untainted right view of that stage,
it reaches completion through the volition co-arising with the three wholesome paths of action.
If one gives rise to a mind co-arising with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) belonging to that stage,
the volition (*cetanā*) co-arising with these two wholesome paths of action reaches its culmination;
this applies to one who is born in the first dhyāna.
If one gives rise to a wholesome mind of the three consciousnesses,
it reaches completion through the volition (cetanā) that arises simultaneously with two wholesome courses of action (karmapatha).
If one gives rise to an indeterminate wholesome mind of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) belonging to its own level, [it likewise reaches completion].
The volition (*cetanā*) that arises simultaneously with the three paths of wholesome action reaches completion when it arises together with a contaminated meditative mind of one's own stage,
or with a mind arising simultaneously with the untainted right view (*anāsrava-samyagdṛṣṭi*) of one's own stage.
When the thought co-arising with the ten paths of wholesome action reaches its culmination, it proceeds by means of that thought;
if one gives rise to a mind co-arising with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) belonging to one's own level,
it proceeds by means of the thought co-arising with nine paths of wholesome action.
If one gives rise to a wholesome mind of the second, third, or fourth dhyāna,
as well as a mind co-arising with the untainted right view of those stages,
it reaches completion through the volition co-arising with the ten paths of wholesome action.
If one gives rise to a mind co-arising with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) belonging to that stage,
it proceeds to completion through volition (*cetanā*) co-arising with the nine wholesome courses of action (*kuśalakarmapatha*).
If one gives rise to a wholesome mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), [the same applies].
And by means of the volition that arises simultaneously with the uncontaminated right view of that stage,
one brings to completion the transformation [of the path] through the three wholesome paths of action; or,
if one gives rise to the mind that arises simultaneously with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) of that stage.
By means of the volition that arises simultaneously with two wholesome courses of action, one brings them to completion;
as it is for birth in the first dhyāna,
so it is for birth in the second dhyāna.
This should be explained in detail up to birth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The distinction is that the three groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) are excluded.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one likewise excludes the first seven courses of action (*karmapatha*).
Question: In which realm and in which destiny (*gati*) are how many wholesome courses of action obtainable?
Answer: In the desire realm, all ten are present;
they are either comprised within restraint, or comprised within neither restraint nor non-restraint.
The form realm (*rūpadhātu*) also possesses all ten,
which are entirely subsumed under ethical discipline (*saṃvara*).
Within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are ten that are accomplished.
There are only three present [faculties].
Among the various realms of existence,
in the hells (naraka), there are the latter three.
In the realms of animals and hungry ghosts,
all ten [unwholesome paths] are present.
None of these are comprised within either restraint or non-restraint.
They are fully present in all ten [faculties] among those in the human realm of the three continents and among the gods of the desire realm.
Some are comprised within restraint; some are comprised within neither restraint nor non-restraint.
In Uttarakuru, there is only the latter three.
None of these are comprised within either restraint (*saṃvara*) or non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Regarding the gods of the form and formless realms, it has already been explained as before.
As for the three types of action and the ten paths of action, the three comprise the ten.
"The ten [factors] subsume the three [realms]," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As the sūtra says:
"There are three types of action and ten paths of action."
Although the sūtra makes this statement,
it does not provide an extensive analysis;
the detailed explanation is as previously set forth.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is because they wish to reveal that the course of karma is most profound, most subtle, difficult to see,
and difficult to realize. Why is this so?
Among all the sūtras spoken by all Tathāgatas,
none is more profound than the *Karma-sūtra*.
Among the twelvefold wheel [of the Dharma], none is more profound than the *Karma-vartman*.
Among the ten powers of the Buddha, none is more profound than the power of karma.
Among the eight aggregates, none is more profound than the aggregate of karma.
Among the four inconceivables, none is more profound than the inconceivability of karma.
For this reason, at one time the Blessed One, dwelling with great skill in diligent attention,
withdrew his mind, reflected, entered a secluded place,
and sat in silent meditation, observing with profound discernment.
As for the various ministers and assistants of the kingdom of Magadha,
in which realm do they dwell,
and what kind of rebirth have they received?
"Where have they gone?
It was only through this reflection that he was able to understand that those ministers had departed.
In such a destiny,
undergoing such a birth,
and going to such a place.
Question: Since it is the nature of all Buddhas that as soon as they raise their minds,
their superior wisdom and vision operate without obstruction regarding all phenomena,
for what purpose do they dwell so perfectly and apply themselves with such diligent attention?
The full explanation continues until he sits in silence.
Some say this is to reveal that the course of karma is most profound.
Because it is most subtle;
because it is most difficult to see;
because it is most difficult to awaken to.
Furthermore, there are those who say that [the Blessed One] did so in order to carefully examine the various causal natures of the ministers and officials of the kingdom of Magadha.
The nature of various fruits,
the nature of various continuities,
and the nature of various antidotes.
This includes the mind at the moment of death and the mind that continues into rebirth;
by means of this investigation, one should come to know all such cases as they apply.
Furthermore, the Blessed One, wishing to thoroughly know the differences in the birthplaces of those ministers,
focused his attention intensely; alternatively,
it is said that he did so in order to wait for those to be converted in the future.
There are those who have been born through transformation who ought to hear the Dharma and perform beneficial deeds;
they have not yet assembled among this multitude.
Furthermore, there is another speaker.
Because he was waiting for Cāṇakya and Lālityāyana,
they— who were formerly King Bimbisāra—
had not yet assembled among this multitude.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this was intended to cause Ānanda to give rise to a sense of reverence,
so that he might receive, uphold, contemplate, and examine [the teaching] with diligent respect and without error.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this is for the purpose of eliminating the arrogant and haughty minds of those with various false conceits; namely, those who,
having gained only a slight understanding of the Dharma, [become overweening].
Consequently, they give rise to arrogance and fail to practice and study.
To eliminate that mindset, it is shown that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, through no deliberate effort,
possesses unimpeded and supreme wisdom and vision regarding all phenomena.
Since he still applies diligent observation even when answering all manner of questions,
how much more so should you, with your limited wisdom, not fail to train yourself in the absence of pride?
Furthermore, there is another who says:
In order to manifest the qualities of a true noble being (*satpuruṣa*),
all who are true noble beings should, by the very nature of things, properly contemplate what is to be contemplated and properly speak what is to be spoken.
He has performed what was to be done well.
Furthermore, there is one who says:
at one time the Blessed One entered a secluded place and sat in silent meditation.
The Venerable Ānanda inquired about this matter;
before the World-Honored One had replied, he entered a state of meditative absorption.
Upon arising from that concentration, he then gave his formal explanation.
For these reasons, this treatise was composed.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the treatise was composed due to three causes and conditions.
First, for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras;
second, for the purpose of refuting the assertions of others;
third, for the purpose of clarifying the phenomena perceived through worldly direct observation.
Regarding the analysis of the meaning of the sūtras:
the sūtras state that there are two kinds of karma— first,
volitional karma (*cetanā-karma*), and second, karma produced by volition (*cetayitvā-karma*).
The karma described therein shall now be explained in detail;
this is called the "Analysis of the Meaning of the Sūtras.
It is intended to refute what has been asserted by others.
For example, the Vaiśeṣika non-Buddhists speak of five types of action:
namely, taking up, putting down, contracting, extending, and movement as the fifth action.
The Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists speak of nine types of action.
That is to say, the actions of grasping, releasing, contracting, extending, lifting, lowering, opening, and closing constitute the ninth type of karma.
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who claim that all twelve bases (*āyatana*) are of the nature of karma;
they speak as follows:
What is the function of the eye?
It is the seeing of forms.
What is the function of form?
That is to say, the range of the eye;
and so on, in detail, up to:
what action does the mind perform?
It refers to that which is able to cognize phenomena (*dharma*).
What is the activity of phenomena?
It refers to the range of the mind (*manas*).
In order to refute such false tenets established by others and to reveal the unerring nature of karma,
the Dārṣṭāntikas say:
The actions of body, speech, and mind are all one volition (*cetanā*).
This [statement] is intended to preclude that view and to clarify that, apart from the essence of volition,
there exist two distinct natures for the actions of body and speech.
Furthermore, the Vibhajyavādins establish that sensual desire, ill will, and wrong view are the intrinsic nature of karma.
Why do they make this assertion?
It is because it is based on the sūtras.
As stated in the sūtra:
"The three types of bodily karma created through intentional volition—
having been performed and accumulated— are evil and unwholesome."
The four types of verbal karma and the three types of mental karma intentionally committed produce manifold suffering and experience the maturation of that suffering.
These evil and unwholesome deeds have already been performed and accumulated;
they give rise to manifold suffering and result in the maturation of suffering.
These are the three types of mental action.
This refers to greed, malice, and wrong view.
Based on this sūtra, it is said that these three—greed and the others—are the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of karma;
however, in order to refute that intention and clarify that covetousness and the rest are not the intrinsic nature of karma, [the following is stated].
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
Question: If covetousness and the like are not of the nature of karma, how is the sūtra cited by the Vibhajyavādins to be reconciled?
Answer: Because it is the equipment (*sambhāra*) for karma, it is called "karma.
As the Blessed One has stated in various sūtras, that which serves as the equipment for a given phenomenon is designated by the name of that phenomenon.
This was explained at length previously, such as when the equipment for pleasure and so forth is called "pleasure" and so on.
It is the same here as well;
that which serves as the equipment for karma is designated as "karma.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta has stated this.
In this context, the Blessed One has merely subsumed their karma;
he speaks thus in order to demonstrate the nature of that karma by way of its basis.
That is to say, when the culmination of superior reflection proceeds by relying upon these stages,
the name "karma" is proclaimed in this context;
all such cases are termed as refutations of what others have asserted.
To clarify the activities commonly observed in the world:
it refers to how people in the world apply the designation and concept of "action" (*karman*) to its results,
just as they perceive objects such as painted images or brocades.
To say that such marvelous craftsmanship is actually not karma but rather the fruit of karma is called "clarifying the matters of worldly experience as they are perceived."
For these three reasons, this treatise is composed.
The three types of action (karma) are:
namely, bodily action, vocal action, and mental action.
Question: How are these three types of action established?
Is it by way of their intrinsic nature, or by way of their basis?
This is because they are the motivating factors (*samutthāna*).
If it were by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there would be only a single type of karma,
namely, vocal karma (*vāk-karman*).
Since speech is itself an action,
if it were the basis [of action],
then all actions would have to be called bodily action.
Since all three types of action depend upon the body,
if it were the motivating cause (*samutthāna*),
then all actions would have to be designated as mental action (*manas-karman*).
Because all three are originated by the mind (*manas*), the answer is:
the three types of action are established by means of three conditions.
First, verbal action is established by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Kāya-karma (bodily action) is established because it is the basis for the two [other actions];
mānasa-karma (mental action) is established because it is the motivator.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
The three types of karma are established based on three conditions:
first, by way of one's own sphere;
second, by way of another's sphere.
Third, because they rely on the locus of association:
vocal action is established by relying on one's own locus,
while bodily action is established by relying on another's locus.
Mental action is established by way of its association with the [mental] basis.
Such is called the intrinsic nature of the three types of action.
The intrinsic nature has thus been explained.
Therefore, it shall now be explained.
Question: Why is it called "karma"?
What is the meaning of karma?
Answer: It is called "karma" (action) for three reasons:
first, because of its functional activity;
second, because it maintains formal rules; and third, because it differentiates results.
Regarding "by way of activity":
this means that activity itself is designated as karma.
Regarding "upholding the formal rules": [it refers to]...
This means being able to maintain the disciplinary codes of the seven classes of followers.
As for "discriminating results," it means being able to discriminate between desirable and undesirable results.
Question: If that is so, are those co-existent and associated dharmas—which are also capable of differentiating between desirable and undesirable fruits—all designated as "karma"?
Answer: In this context, only the predominant factor is designated as "karma."
Because these three types of karma are the most preeminent among all co-existent and associated phenomena,
they receive their respective names, just as various things in the world receive various names based on their most distinguished features.
This is also like this.
It is as when people in the world say, "The musician performs music.
In this case, it is not that there are no musical instruments, musical equipment, or musicians.
However, because the musician is the most excellent among them, he receives that name.

It is also like the case of a scribe: it is not without various kinds of paper, ink, pens, and so forth, nor without diligent effort and the combination [of these factors], that characters are formed.
However, it receives its name according to the most prominent person;
the analogies of the dyer and the smith are likewise so.
Now, this case is also the same.
Although all various types of co-existent and associated dharmas with intrinsic nature are capable of producing maturation results (*vipākaphala*),
among them, karma that differentiates the result is the most preeminent.
Therefore, it is explained selectively. Furthermore,
there are those who say that it is called "karma" (action) because of three meanings.
First, because it possesses functional activity;
second, because it possesses movement;
third, because it possesses volitional construction.
That which possesses activity is vocal action (*vākkarman*).
It is that by which one deliberates, "I shall perform such and such an act."
There is that which possesses motion;
that is, although bodily action (kāyakarman) is in reality devoid of movement, it appears as if going to another location.
There is that which performs an act.
That is to say, it refers to the mental karma that constructs the preceding two [types of karma].
For this reason, it is called "karma.
As for the ten courses of action (daśa-karmapatha):
That is to say: the three courses of action of the body,
the four courses of action of speech,
and the three courses of action of the mind.
Question: Since there are ten paths of wholesome action and ten paths of unwholesome action, should they not be said to total twenty?
Why, then, are only ten mentioned here?
Answer: Because they do not exceed ten.
That is to say, based on the locus that serves as the support for misconduct,
one initiates the ten unwholesome courses of action;
it is precisely by means of distancing oneself from this very locus that [one achieves purification].
One is then able to initiate the ten paths of wholesome action.
Furthermore, some teachers say that while they are briefly stated as ten, they are extensively explained as twenty.
As with the concise and the detailed,
so too are there the undifferentiated and the differentiated,
and the general and the particular.
Pervasive and non-pervasive;
without difference and with difference;
it should be understood that the same applies to simultaneity and succession.
Furthermore, there are those who say that ten [stages] are taught according to those of sharp faculties,
while twenty are taught according to those of dull faculties.
As it is with those of sharp faculties and dull faculties,
so it is with the power of causes and the power of conditions, the internal power and the external power.
Internal power is the sustaining force of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
It should be understood that the same applies to the power of extensive cultivation regarding the sounds and speech of others,
as well as the power of concise analytical knowledge and the power of expansive analytical knowledge.
This is called the intrinsic nature of the ten paths of action.
Having already explained their intrinsic nature,
that which is their cause shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason is it called a "path of action" (karmapatha)?
What is the meaning of "path of action"?
Answer: Volition (cetanā) is what is termed "action."
When volition (*cetanā*) reaches its culmination through the process of engagement, it is termed a path of action (*karmapatha*).
Question: If volition is called "action," and that which is engaged by volition reaches its culmination and is termed a path of action, [how is this so?]
All other wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral states—
none of which fail to be traversed and ultimately manifested by volition—
all should be designated as paths of action (*karmapatha*).
What are the distinguished and uncommon causes and conditions for which only these ten are taught as courses of action (*karmapatha*)?
Answer: This is the Blessed One’s teaching with intentional omission (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*).
The Great Master taught in brief, observing the mental activities, dispositions, and inclinations of those beings to be converted.
The Venerable Pārśva said: "Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has ultimately and thoroughly realized the nature and characteristics of all phenomena."
One also knows its functional power,
which is not known by others;
this applies to any phenomenon that possesses the characteristics of a karmic path.
Even if one were to establish [them],
that which does not exist cannot be established.
The Venerable Ghosaka also spoke thus.
The Great Master knew that these ten paths of action possess such power and efficacy,
and are so formidable.
Approaching it in this way enables the volition of karma to proceed along its path and bring it to completion;
apart from these paths of action, no other phenomena possess such a capacity.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the paths of action are established by two causes and conditions:
first, being censured and reviled by the world.
That which is praised by the world in both [this and future] lives consists of the ten types of unwholesome paths of action and the wholesome paths of action.
Question: If that which is censured and reviled by the world is called a path of action, [then how are the wholesome ones so designated]?
This [act] of drawing blood from the body of a Buddha with an evil mind is something that all the world collectively censures and reviles; why, then,
is it not declared to be a course of action (karmapatha)?
Answer: If something is censured and reviled by the world,
and exists at all times whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or not,
it is established as a course of action (karmapatha).
Shedding the blood of a Buddha occurs only when a Buddha exists in the world and not when no Buddha exists; therefore,
it is not established as a course of action (karmapatha).
It should be understood that the same applies to all questions and answers concerning the avoidance of shedding blood during acts of praise.
Furthermore, some teachers state that the paths of action are established by way of three causes and conditions.
First, by way of the basis;
second, by way of designation;
third, by way of discriminating between pleasant and unpleasant results.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"If, by means of this, internal and external things undergo occasional decay and loss."
At times they increase and establish the paths of action;
one should know that what resides therein is external.
Longevity and so forth constitute the internal [factors].
How does external matter suffer decline because of these?
It refers to the time when the karmic path of taking life increases.
All external objects possess little luster and do not remain stable for long.
When the karmic path of taking what is not given increases,
all external objects become subject to calamities and afflictions.
They will frequently encounter obstacles such as frost, hail, dust,
and filth. When the path of sexual misconduct increases,
all external things will be subject to much strife and contention.
When the path of action of false speech increases,
all external objects become largely foul and impure.
When the path of action of divisive speech increases, [all external objects become largely discordant].
All external objects are for the most part uneven and irregular;
there are hills, mounds, pits, chasms, precipices, and vast distances.
This occurs when the path of karma consisting of harsh and evil speech increases.
All external things become coarse, shabby, base, and evil, like poisonous thorns, grit, and pebbles.
Even if there are treasures such as gold and silver, they are scarce, lack luster, are unrefined, and difficult to use.
This occurs when the karmic path of frivolous speech increases.
All external things undergo seasonal changes and aberrations;
they quickly perish and for the most part do not reach fruition.
This is especially so when the karmic path of covetous desire increases.
Most external objects undergo significant deterioration, becoming minute and scarce;
when the path of action of malice increases,
most external objects become withered and their fruits become bitter and astringent.
When the path of action of wrong view increases,
most external objects wither and fall away;
they become deficient in flowers and fruits, or are entirely without fruit.
This is called "causing external things to diminish by means of this. How, moreover, is it known that by means of these paths of action, internal things such as the lifespan are diminished?
It is said that when the ten unwholesome paths of action fully increase, [the lifespan and so forth are diminished].
In this Jambudvīpa, four types of decline appear in the world:
namely, the decline of lifespan and the decline of sentient beings.
The decay of requisites,
the decay of wholesome qualities,
and the decay of lifespan.
This refers to the time at the beginning of a kalpa,
when the lifespan of the people of this Jambudvīpa was immeasurable years,
until the end of the kalpa, when the human lifespan reaches ten years.
Regarding the decline of sentient beings:
at the beginning of the kalpa,
this Jambudvīpa was vast, magnificent, and pure.
There were many sentient beings who were pure, virtuous, and meritorious;
the towns and cities were filled with people in succession,
yet by the end of the kalpa, only ten thousand people remained.
Regarding the decline of requisites:
this refers to the time at the beginning of the eon,
when this Jambudvīpa was peaceful, prosperous, and joyful.
Various kinds of earth-essence, bamboo shoots,
and rice were considered the most excellent food;
yet at the end of the kalpa, when the people suffer from famine, only weeds such as *tī* and *pái* will be regarded as the most excellent food.
Regarding the decline of wholesome qualities:
this refers to the time at the beginning of the eon,
when the ten paths of wholesome action flourished and were perfectly fulfilled in this Jambudvīpa.
During the period of the kalpa’s decline, the ten paths of unwholesome action increase and reach their full extent.
How is it that because of these, external objects sometimes increase?
It is said: when the path of action consisting of taking life is absent, [external objects increase].
All external objects possess abundant luster and remain stable for a long duration.
During times when the karmic path of taking what is not given is absent,
all external objects are free from calamities and afflictions.
When they are no longer afflicted by obstacles such as frost and hail,
and when the path of action free from sensual desire and misconduct increases,
all external things will be devoid of enmity and contention.
When the path of action of abstaining from false speech increases,
all external objects become largely fragrant and pure.
When the path of action of abstaining from divisive speech increases...
All external objects are magnificent and easy to obtain;
the earth is as level as the palm of a hand, vast, and pure.
This occurs when the path of action consisting of coarse and evil speech has been abandoned.
All external objects are subtle, exquisite, and abundant;
they are free from ruggedness, thorns, and gravel.
Precious substances such as gold and silver are supple, luminous, pure, and highly functional.
When the path of action of abstaining from frivolous speech increases, all external objects do not undergo seasonal aberrations at their respective times; they become stable and substantial.
When the path of action of non-covetousness increases, [the same occurs].
When external objects are abundant, complete, and flourishing,
and when the path of non-hatred increases,
external objects become lustrous and their fruits become sweet.
When the path of action of right view increases,
external objects become abundant and flowers and fruits flourish;
this is called "causing external objects to increase by means of this."
How, moreover, is it known that by means of this karma the internal factors such as the lifespan are increased?
It is said: when the ten paths of wholesome action are fully cultivated and increased.
In this Jambudvīpa, four types of flourishing appear in the world:
namely, the flourishing of lifespan and the flourishing of sentient beings.
The abundance of requisites,
the abundance of wholesome qualities,
and the abundance of lifespan.
This refers to the time at the end of a kalpa,
when the lifespan of the people of this Jambudvīpa is ten years,
until the time of the kalpa's increase, when the lifespan reaches eighty thousand years.
Regarding the increase of sentient beings:
this refers to the time at the end of a kalpa,
when only ten thousand people remain in this Jambudvīpa.
When the kalpa increases, it becomes vast, extensive, and pure;
there are many sentient beings who are sincere, virtuous, and possessed of merit,
and cities and towns stand side by side, filled with people.
Regarding the abundance of requisites:
this refers to the time at the end of the kalpa in this Jambudvīpa.
The people suffer from famine,
taking weeds such as tǐ and pài as their finest and most excellent food.
When the kalpa increases, there will be peace, security, abundance, and joy.
Various kinds of earth-essence, wild bamboo,
and rice served as their exquisite food for those whose virtuous qualities were flourishing.
This refers to the time at the end of a kalpa,
when the ten unwholesome paths of action in the world increase and flourish until the period of the kalpa's expansion.
The ten paths of wholesome action flourish in the world.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the ten courses of action are established by way of three fruits.
First, the fruit of maturation;
second, the fruit of outflow;
third, the dominant fruit.
That is to say, taking life—
if one practices it, cultivates it, or frequently cultivates it—
one will be born in the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts.
This is the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
Having passed away from that place, they are reborn among human beings;
they are frequently ill and short-lived.
This is the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Because of that predominance (*adhipati*), the external objects experienced all lack luster and do not remain stable for long.
This is the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala):
all acts of taking what is not given,
whether practiced, cultivated, or frequently cultivated.
Birth in the realms of hell-beings, animals,
or hungry ghosts is the fruit of maturation;
from those places, one passes away and is reborn among human beings.
The depletion of wealth and treasures is its flow-on result (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Because of that predominance, the external objects experienced as results are beset by calamities and afflictions;
they frequently encounter obstacles such as frost, hail, dust, and filth.
This is the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala):
the various forms of sexual misconduct,
whether practiced, cultivated, or frequently cultivated.
Birth in the realms of hell-beings, animals,
or hungry ghosts is the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
Having passed away from those places, one is born among human beings.
The wife is unchaste;
this is the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Because that [karma] was predominant, the external objects experienced as a result are characterized by much strife and contention.
This is the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala):
all instances of false speech,
whether practiced, cultivated, or frequently cultivated.
Birth in the realms of hell-beings, animals,
or hungry ghosts is the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Having passed away from those places and being reborn among humans, one frequently encounters slander.
These are the flow-on results (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Because of that predominance (*adhipati*), the external objects experienced are largely foul and impure;
these are the dominant results (*adhipati-phala*).
If one practices, cultivates, or frequently habituates oneself to various forms of divisive speech,
one will be reborn in the realms of hell beings, animals, or hungry ghosts.
This is the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Passing away from that place and being reborn among humans is the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*),
characterized by the alienation of kinsmen and friends.
Because of that predominance, the external objects experienced as results are for the most part uneven and irregular—
consisting of hills, mounds, pits, ravines, precipices, and vast chasms;
these are the environmental results (*adhipatiphala*).
If one habituates oneself to,
cultivates, or frequently practices various harsh words,
one will be reborn in the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts.
This is the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
Having passed away from that place and been reborn among humans,
they constantly hear various kinds of unpleasant sounds.
This is the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Because that [karma] is predominant, the external objects experienced are coarse, inferior, base, and evil, consisting of thorns, gravel, and pebbles;
although there may be a small amount of gold and the like, it lacks luster, is unrefined, and difficult to use.
This is the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala):
all instances of frivolous speech (sambhinna-pralāpa),
whether practiced, cultivated, or frequently habituated, lead to rebirth in the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts.
This is the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
Having passed away from that place, one is reborn among human beings;
it is said that one lacks majesty and authority.
This is the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Because those [causes] are predominant, the external objects they induce undergo seasonal abnormalities;
they perish rapidly and for the most part do not reach fruition.
This is the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala):
whenever one has desire and greed,
whether through habituation, cultivation, or frequent practice thereof.
Birth in the realms of hell-beings, animals,
or hungry ghosts is the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
Having passed away from those places, one is born among human beings.
Intense and sharp covetousness is its outflow fruit; because that [covetousness] is predominant,
the external objects it brings about are for the most part diminished, subtle, and meager.
This is the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala):
for all those who harbor ill will,
whether they practice it, cultivate it, or frequently habituate themselves to it.
Birth in the realms of hell-beings, animals,
or hungry ghosts is the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*);
from those places, one passes away and is reborn among human beings.
Intense hatred is its flow-on result (*niṣyanda-phala*). Because of its predominance,
the external objects experienced as its effect are for the most part withered and parched, and their fruits are bitter and astringent.
This is the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala).
For those who possess wrong views,
whether they practice them, cultivate them, or habitually cultivate them extensively.
Birth in the realms of hell-beings, animals,
or hungry ghosts is the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Having passed away from those places, one is born among human beings.
Intense ignorance is the flow-on result (*niṣyanda-phala*). Because that [ignorance] is predominant,
the external objects experienced as its result are for the most part withered and sparse in flowers and fruits, or even entirely devoid of fruit.
This is the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala):
having abstained from taking life,
if one practices it, cultivates it, or repeatedly cultivates it.
Birth in the realms of humans or devas is the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
Passing away from those places and being reborn here, one is free from illness and possesses a long life.
These are the results of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Because of that predominance (*adhipati*), the external objects experienced are all highly lustrous and remain firm for a long duration;
these are the results of predominance (*adhipati-phala*).
By this principle, the remaining nine wholesome courses of action belonging to the white category should all be explained in detail as being the opposite of those mentioned above. Therefore,
the ten courses of action are established by way of three results.
Question: Why is volition (*cetanā*) not said to be a path of action (*karmapatha*)?
Answer: Volition is itself karma;
because it proceeds by means of volition, it is called a "path of action."
One should know that the paths of action are not identical to volition (cetanā);
therefore, they are not so designated.
It is like when the path traveled by a king is called the "king's road."
Yet, the royal road is not the king;
this case is likewise.
Because they are what is practiced through volition, they are called paths of action (*karmapatha*).
Furthermore, the paths of action are not volition itself;
the analogies of the royal throne and so forth are likewise so.
Moreover, there are those who say:
If a phenomenon arises from the conjunction of three factors, like volition (*cetanā*),
and functions with an active operation, it is established as a path of action (*karmapatha*).
Volition does not arise from the conjunction of three factors, such as volition itself.
Because it functions through an active operation, it is not a path of action (*karmapatha*).
Furthermore, some say:
"If a phenomenon arises simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*," [it is not a path of action]."
When there is an active operation, it is established as a course of action (*karmapatha*);
when volition (*cetanā*) does not arise simultaneously with [the action],
and there is no active operation, it is not established as a course of action.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
if a phenomenon exists simultaneously with volition in the present,
it serves as the path for that volition and is established as a course of action (karmapatha).
Volition does not coexist with volition in the present;
that which serves as a path for volition does not constitute a course of action (*karmapatha*).
Question: If one dispatches another to take a life...
Even when engaging in frivolous speech,
if the messenger takes many days before acting upon it,
the intention of the one who dispatched him has long since ceased.

How is it that intention (*cetanā*) and [the action] existing simultaneously in the present are established as the path (*mārga*), such that intention reaches its culmination and is designated as a course of action (*karmapatha*)?
Answer: A course of action is established on the basis of the sense of "attainability" (*upalabdhi*).
That is to say, other dharmas can be established as courses of action (karmapatha) because they can coexist with volition (cetanā) at the same time;
however, it is not possible for two volitions to exist simultaneously in a single moment as a present course of action.
For this reason, volition (cetanā) is not established as a course of action (karmapatha).
Question: Volition is also present at the same time as another volition in the mental continuum of another.
That is to say, it refers to the volition within the continuum of another.
Why is this not stated?
The answer is: the paths of action (karmapatha) are established based on one's own continuum, not based on another.
The intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the three types of action and the ten paths of action has already been explained.
Now, the characteristics of the mixed and the unmixed shall be demonstrated.
Regarding the three types of action and the ten paths of action:
do the three encompass the ten?
Regarding the ten [paths of action] subsuming the three [categories],
one should respond by formulating four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are actions that are not paths of action (*karmapatha*).
This refers to bodily and vocal karma not subsumed under the paths of action, as well as the entirety of mental karma.
There are also paths of action that are not themselves karma,
namely the last three paths of action.
There are actions that are also paths of action,
namely the first seven paths of action.
There are those that are neither actions nor paths of action.
This means excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
"Characteristics" refers to that which is named,
as explained extensively above.
This refers to the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) excluding karmic appropriation,
and within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha), excluding unwholesome greed, hatred, and wrong view, as well as non-greed, non-hatred, right view, and all volitions (cetanā).
One takes the remaining formations (saṃskāra-skandha) that are associated or dissociated, as well as the three aggregates in their entirety and the unconditioned dharmas (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
Since all such cases constitute the fourth alternative, it is said: "namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics."

Question: Among the ten paths of action (*karmapatha*), why are the first seven established as both karma and paths of action, while the latter three are established only as paths of action and not as karma?
Answer: As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
All instances of taking life are karma and activity;
they serve as the cause, the path, the track, and the road for the volition that initiates the taking of life.
To speak extensively, up to all forms of frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*) are karma and activity;
they serve as the cause, the path, the track, and the road for the volition that initiates frivolous speech.
All unwholesome covetousness, ill-will,
and wrong view are neither karma nor karmic action;
they are solely associated with the volition (cetanā) that arises simultaneously with them.
It is the cause, the path, the track, and the way.
Abstinence from taking life is its karma and its function;
it is associated with the volition that initiates abstinence from taking life.
It is the cause, the path, the track, and the way.
To speak at length, up to the point that abstaining from frivolous speech is the action and the function;
it is associated with the volition that initiates the abstention from frivolous speech.
It is the cause, the path, the track, and the way;
it consists of all non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view,
which are neither karma nor karmic action.
It is only with the volition (*cetanā*) that arises simultaneously with it that [the action] constitutes the cause, the path, the track,
and the way; by this it is proven that such must be the meaning.
