translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section Four: The Aggregate of Karma (Karmaskandha), Part One of Three: The Sub-section on Evil Conduct (Duṣcarita-nikāya-saṃgraha). The Three Kinds of Action (Tri-karma).
This refers to the actions of body, speech, and mind.
There are four types of action, namely: black action with black maturation.
Wholly white karma with wholly white ripening;
black-and-white karma with black-and-white ripening;
and non-black, non-white karma without ripening.
Can one exhaust all karmas?
Are the three [factors] subsumed by the four,
or are the four subsumed by the three?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As the sūtras speak of three types of karma and four types of karma.
Although the sūtras speak in this way,
they do not provide an extensive analysis,
nor have they ever stated that the three categories subsume the four.
"The four [means of attraction] subsume the three," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Although the three types of karma were previously distinguished,
the four types of karma have not yet been distinguished;
since I now wish to distinguish them, I compose this treatise.
In this context, what is "karma that is black with black maturation"?
It refers to unwholesome karma that brings about maturation in the miserable realms.
Question: Maturation should not be called "black. Why is that?
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"What are black phenomena?
They are unwholesome phenomena and obscured-unspecified phenomena."
What are the white dharmas?
They are the wholesome dharmas and the non-obscured neutral dharmas.
All maturation fruits are non-obscured neutral.
Why is it called "black"?
The answer is: herein one should simply explain what constitutes black karma;
that is, unwholesome karma which brings about rebirth in the miserable realms.
The term "black maturation" (kṛṣṇavipāka) should not be stated again.
What is the intention behind stating it as one does instead of saying it should be stated thus?
This means that what has been stated establishes that "black" is the cause and not the effect.
It is as when it is said:
"Thief-child! These words you have uttered are an insult to your father; you are no son."
It is the same here as well. Furthermore,
there are those who say that this statement is made in reliance upon what is disagreeable and black.
There are two kinds of black:
first, defiled black;
second, disagreeable black.
In this context, karma is called "black" because it possesses two types of blackness;
its maturation (vipāka) is also called "black" solely because it is black in the sense of being disagreeable.
Question: Does black karma also produce maturation among gods and humans?
Why is it said that [this karma] only brings about maturation in the miserable realms?
The answer is: although it should also have been stated, its non-mention indicates that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this is not definitive;
namely, that within the realms of humans and devas, wherever there is the maturation (*vipāka*) of black karma, [that place is considered a lower realm].
In this place there must necessarily be the maturation of white karma;
there is no place where there is only the maturation of black karma,
nor any place where there is no maturation of white karma.
In any of the evil destinies where there is the maturation of white karma,
there must also be the maturation of black karma; however,
there are places where there is only the maturation of black karma.
Regarding the absence of the maturation of white karma:
because the intermediate states (*antarābhava*) of the miserable realms (*apāya*) are exclusively places for the maturation of black karma,
it is mentioned specifically in that regard.
The *Saṃgītiparyāya* further states:
"What is black karma with black ripening?
It refers to unwholesome karma that brings about rebirth in the hell realms (*naraka-gati*)."
Question: Since non-virtuous karmas also induce maturation in the realms of animals and hungry ghosts, why is it stated that they induce only the hells (*naraka*) and not the others?
Answer: That which should have been stated but was not stated [is as follows].
One should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, there are those who say that it is not definitive.
That is to say, the realms of animals and hungry ghosts experience both the maturation of unwholesome karma and the maturation of wholesome karma;
whereas the realm of hell-beings experiences exclusively the maturation of unwholesome karma.
Therefore, it is taught selectively.
Furthermore, there are those who say that in the sūtras,
the Blessed One used grave evil karma to terrify sentient beings.
In order to conform to that sūtra, it is stated that only those unwholesome karmas which bring about rebirth in hell are called "black karma with black ripening.
To clarify this meaning, one should cite that sūtra.
There were two non-Buddhist practitioners:
one named Pūraṇa Kāśyapa,
who observed the cow-vow.
The second was named Acelakṣapaṇaka,
who observed the dog-vow.
At one time, these two non-Buddhist practitioners gathered together and sat in assembly.
They spoke these words:
"We two have completed our training in all the difficult ascetic practices and prohibitions found in the world."
"Who can truly prophesy the karmic maturation we have experienced?
We have heard that a prince has been born in the Śākya clan, whose countenance is upright and handsome,
and whose body is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs."
Beholding him never brings satiety;
his body is of true golden color,
his constant radiance extends one fathom, and his speech is clear, resonant, harmonious, and pleasing to the mind.
Surpassing the kalaviṅka bird in its wondrous voice,
his wisdom and vision were unimpeded and his eloquence was unhindered;
he grew weary of and renounced the ways of the household, departing for the homeless life and diligently practicing austerities.
Furthermore, having again become weary of and detached from the practice of the middle way,
they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
endowed with all-knowledge, they realize and see the nature and characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are.
Severing all nets of doubt,
bestowing all certainty,
and thoroughly penetrating the fundamental source of all questions and treatises.
"The two of us should go now to ask him.
If we receive a prophetic declaration regarding the karmic maturation resulting from our observance of the precepts,
it would be most wonderful if we were then to rely upon that training."
Thereupon, the two men came to where the Buddha was;
having exchanged various words of affection and offered mutual greetings, they sat down.
Having withdrawn to sit on one side,
at that time Pūraṇa was questioned by another.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This Kṣairika has completed his training by observing the dog-vow;
where will he go, and where will he be reborn?"
The World-Honored One said:
"Pūraṇa, stop; there is no need to ask further.
Do not let this matter cause you all to be unable to endure it, to lose faith, or to harbor shame and resentment."
Thus he asked a second and a third time.
As he continued to inquire with persistent earnestness,
the Buddha, out of compassion, addressed him, saying:
Listen attentively; I shall give you a true prediction according to reality.
If you uphold the dog-precepts without any transgression, you shall be reborn among dogs.
If there are transgressions, you shall fall into hell.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, Pūraṇa was filled with anxiety and fear;
he wept and choked with sobs, unable to restrain himself.
The World-Honored One said to him:
Did I not previously warn you many times, saying:
"Cease; there is no need to ask; do not concern yourselves with this matter"?
Yet you all could not restrain yourselves and, lacking faith, harbored feelings of shame and resentment.
Now the result was indeed thus.
At that time, Pūraṇa restrained himself and said to the Buddha:
"It is not because the World-Honored One has predicted for Cīraka..."
"I weep out of compassion because I am destined for rebirth in the realm of dogs.
Furthermore, having long practiced and perfected the observance of the cow-vow, I fear that I too shall likewise come to such a state; this is why I am filled with anxiety and dread."
“I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will explain for me the observance of the cow-vow:
where shall one go, and where shall one be reborn?
The World-Honored One replied:
If one observes the cow-vow without any transgressions, one shall be reborn among cattle;
if there are transgressions, one shall fall into hell.
Such matters are explained at length in the sūtras.
Question: How is it that upholding the dog-vow or the ox-vow is called being without deficiency or transgression?
Answer: If one upholds the dog-vow exactly according to the laws of a dog, it is called being without deficiency or transgression;
if one upholds the ox-vow exactly according to the laws of an ox, it is called being without deficiency or transgression.
If it were otherwise, it would be called a deficient transgression.
Therefore, the Blessed One, in order to terrify sentient beings with the gravity of evil karma,
spoke of those unwholesome karmas that bring about rebirth in the *naraka* realms.
In order to accord with that sūtra, the *Saṃgītiparyāya* states as follows:
"The unwholesome karmas that bring about rebirth in the hells are called 'black-with-black-ripening' karmas.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
The unwholesome karmas to be abandoned by the path of seeing are called "black-with-black-ripening" karma,
because within their own category there is no admixture of white.
This is what is said.
All unwholesome karmas are termed "black-with-black-ripening" karma.
This is because within the desire realm, unwholesome states are so powerful that they are not overwhelmed or interspersed by wholesome dharmas.
Because unwholesome dharmas can suppress and sever the wholesome dharmas of their own level,
wholesome karma becomes weak and inferior, being overwhelmed and intermingled with the unwholesome;
for the wholesome of the desire realm cannot sever the unwholesome.
What is white karma with white maturation?
It refers to wholesome karma bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Question: Does not wholesome karma bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) also produce a white maturation?
For what reason is it said that only wholesome karma bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśala-karma*) is called "white-with-white maturation" (*śukla-śuklavipāka-karma*),
while wholesome karma bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśala-karma*) is not so called?
It should have been stated, yet it was not.
One should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
if one speaks of wholesome karma bound to the form realm as "white-with-white-ripening" karma, [it is because it produces both a pleasant ripening and the purity of the form realm].
It should be understood that when [the wholesome karma] bound to the formless realm has been explained, that [karma] is also included;
for both are dharmas cultivated in the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*).
Thus, when this is stated, it should be known that the other is also stated.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
if various wholesome karmas can induce two kinds of ripened fruits—
namely, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and birth (*upapatti*)— then these wholesome karmas are called "whitish-white ripening karma" (*śukla-śuklavipāka-karma*).
Karma of the formless realm produces only rebirth-existence (upapatti-bhava) and does not produce intermediate existence (antarābhava); therefore,
it is not mentioned.
Just as it is with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of existence (*upapattibhava*),
so too does one give rise to the experience of birth and the experience of sensation;
one gives rise to the arising of maturation (*vipāka*) and the maturation itself.
The same should be understood for arising fruits and produced fruits,
as well as for subtle fruits and coarse fruits.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
if karma can induce two kinds of maturation—
namely, that which is material and that which is non-material— these wholesome karmas are called "white-with-white-maturation" karma.
Karma of the formless realm produces only that which is non-material and does not produce matter; therefore,
it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if one possesses two types of karma capable of inducing maturation—
namely, material and non-material karma— then [the result follows].
Among these, wholesome karma is called "white-with-white-ripening" karma.
In the formless realm, there is only non-material karma;
there is no material karma.
Therefore, it is not spoken of.
As with form and non-form,
so it is with the associated and the unassociated.
Having a basis or being without a basis;
having a mode of activity or being without a mode of activity;
having an object of cognition or being without an object of cognition.
There is that with attention and that without attention;
it should be known that the two types of karma are likewise so.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
If one possesses the three types of karma capable of producing maturation—
namely, those of body, speech, and mind—
this pure, wholesome karma is called "white-with-white-maturation" karma.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), only mental karma (manaskarman) can produce maturation (vipāka);
therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
If all five aggregates are capable of producing maturation,
this pure wholesome karma is called "white-with-white-maturation" karma.
In the formless realm, only four aggregates are capable of producing maturation.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if one is fully endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action, they can bring about karmic maturation.
This pure, wholesome karma is called "white-with-white maturation" karma.
Within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are only three wholesome paths of action that can induce maturation.
For this reason, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if within this realm there are two types of purity, [it is not mentioned].
There are two kinds of clarity:
first, the cause;
second, the fruit.
In this realm, wholesome karma is called "white-with-white maturation" (śukla-śukla-vipāka-karma).
Within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is one kind that is exceptionally pure and white;
this refers to the cause.
Therefore, it is not so stated.
For these and various other reasons,
only wholesome karma bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is called "white-with-white-ripening" (*śukla-śuklavipāka*) karma.
It is not a wholesome karma bound to the formless realm.
What is black-and-white karma with black-and-white ripening?
It refers to wholesome karma bound to the desire realm.
It is the karma that can induce the maturation (*vipāka*) in the realms of humans and gods.
Question: Since there is no single karma that is both black and white, why is it called "karma that is black-and-white with black-and-white maturation"?
Answer: It is in order to demonstrate that within a single basis and within a single continuum,
one experiences the two kinds of maturation induced by karma.
First, black;
second, white.
Therefore, they are called "black-and-white karma with black-and-white maturation."
Question: Since the maturation of both black and white karma is also experienced within the various evil realms,
why is it stated that only the karma capable of producing maturation in the human and celestial realms is called "karma with black-and-white maturation"?
Is it not said that there are actions which bring about maturation in the miserable realms?
One should understand this point: that which ought to have been stated but was not stated.
Furthermore, there are others who say:

if one speaks of karma that produces the wholesome karma of humans and devas as "black-and-white karma with black-and-white maturation," it should be understood that this already includes the wholesome karma that produces the miserable realms, which is also that same type of karma.
Because there is no distinction between the various and the variegated characteristics;
if one speaks of this, it should be understood that one has already spoken of that.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
That is not fixed;
therefore, it is not mentioned.
That is to say, it refers to those within the human and celestial realms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
There is not a single place where the maturation of black and white karma is not experienced in a mixed manner.
Although among the various evil destinies there are places where the maturation of black and white karma is experienced in a mixed manner.
Furthermore, there are places where one experiences exclusively the maturation of black karma:
namely, a portion of the animals and hungry ghosts,
as well as all the hells.
Because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the miserable realms (*apāya*) is not fixed,
it is therefore not mentioned.
Furthermore, there are those who say:

Wholesome and unwholesome karma belonging to the desire realm that is to be abandoned through cultivation is called "karma that is both black and white with black-and-white maturation," because two types of karma are mixed within a single category.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
if wholesome or unwholesome karma can induce the maturation (vipāka) of the realms of humans, devas, animals, or hungry ghosts within the desire realm;
This is called "black-and-white karma with black-and-white maturation," because within a single realm of existence one experiences the maturation of both types of karma.
Thus it is said.

All wholesome karma of the desire realm is called "karma that is both black and white with both black and white maturation," because although the essence of that wholesome karma is white, [it is mixed with unwholesome elements].
However, it is defiled by being intermingled with the unwholesome black [factors],
because the unwholesome can sever the wholesome of its own level,
whereas the unwholesome [in this context] does not do so.
It is not overwhelmed or intermingled with the wholesome karma of its own level,
because wholesome karma of its own level cannot abandon unwholesome karma of its own level. For this reason,
wholesome karma of the desire realm is called the third type of karma.
What is non-black, non-white karma without maturation that can exhaust all karma?
It refers to the volition of training (*śaikṣa-cetanā*) that is capable of permanently severing all karma.
Question: Since all untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) is ultimately white (*paramārtha-śukla*), why is it called "non-black, non-white"?
Answer: The *Saṃgītiparyāya-śāstra* and the *Prajñapti-śāstra* both state that this karma is not uniform:
it is unwholesome, defiled, and black.
Furthermore, it is called "non-black" because its maturation is disagreeable and black;
nor is it the same as the white of wholesome contaminated [dharmas],
for it is called "non-white" because its maturation is agreeable and white.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
because this fruit is white by virtue of its basis, it is said to be "non-white.
There are two kinds of white.
First, white in terms of cause;
second, white in terms of fruit.
Wholesome contaminated karma is called "white" because it possesses both forms of whiteness.
All untainted (anāsrava) karmas have only white causes but no white fruits; therefore,
they are not called "white."
Furthermore, there are those who say it is called "non-white" because its maturation (*vipāka*) is white.
There are two kinds of white.
First, white by its own nature;
second, white by way of maturation (*vipāka*).
Wholesome contaminated karma (*sāsrava-kuśala-karman*) is called "white" because it possesses both forms of whiteness.
Untainted karma (anāsrava-karma) is not called "white" because it possesses only the whiteness of its own nature and lacks white maturation (vipāka). Furthermore,
some say that this untainted karma is able to sever the maturation cherished by the world.
It is not loved by the world and lacks white characteristics;
therefore, it is not called "white.
For this reason, it is termed "neither black nor white."
This untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) does not produce a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) as do the three preceding types;
therefore, it is called "karma without ripening" (*avipāka-karman*).
This untainted karma brings about the ultimate cessation, the exhaustion, and the universal exhaustion of the three preceding types of karma.
It is eternally severed, eternally destroyed, abandoned, vomited out, detached from desire, and extinguished;
therefore, it is called that which can exhaust all karma.
Thus are the seventeen types of volition of training described.

This refers to the twelve types of volition (*cetanā*) associated with the Śaikṣa: namely, the volitions associated with the four *dharmajñānakṣāntis* during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and the volitions associated with the eight uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) that abandon the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
These twelve volitions are capable of exhausting karma that is black and has black maturation (*kṛṣṇakṛṣṇavipāka-karma*).

The volition associated with the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the defilements of the desire realm is capable of exhausting both purely black karma with purely black maturation and karma that is both black and white with both black and white maturation.
The volition associated with the ninth path of uninterrupted transition for abandoning the defilements of the first dhyāna,
up to the volition associated with the ninth path of uninterrupted transition for abandoning the defilements of the fourth dhyāna— this is the volition of one in training (śaikṣa).
These seventeen types of untainted volition (*anāsrava-cetanā*) are capable of exhausting white karma that has white maturation;
they are called the "volitions of training that sever all karma."
Furthermore, there are those who say that all uncontaminated volitions (*cetanā*) within the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) are called "volitions of training capable of severing all karma."
Because all paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) are capable of severing all karmas.
Furthermore, there are those who say that all volitions of one in training (*śaikṣa-cetanā*) are called "volitions of one in training that are capable of severing all karmas."
Because all thoughts associated with the trainings (*śaikṣa*) are capable of counteracting outflow-tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*),
those who speak thus maintain that,
according to the initial teaching, there are only seventeen types of untainted thought (*anāsrava-cetanā*).
Because it is precisely able to counteract the three preceding types of karma.
Question: Are all untainted wisdoms (*anāsrava-prajñā*), together with their associated and co-existent factors, capable of correctly severing the three preceding types of karma?
Why is it that only the untainted (anāsrava) volition of training is mentioned?
The answer is: because volition is able to initiate all phenomena so that they may be abandoned, it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Although all [mental factors] are capable of abandoning [defilements], "volition" (cetanā) alone is mentioned here because it is specifically distinguished as being karma.
Question: If that is so, one should also mention the bodily and vocal actions that follow [the volition].
Why is it said that it is only volition (*cetanā*)?
Answer: Because this training volition proceeds in association with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), sharing the same object of focus (*ālambana*) and the same mode of activity (*ākāra*).
Sharing a single basis,
they possess the power to assist one another in severing all karma;
such a thing cannot occur in the case of bodily or vocal karma.
Therefore, it was not mentioned.
Having already explained the intrinsic nature of the three and four types of karma,
we shall now demonstrate their characteristics of being mixed or unmixed.
Regarding the three karmas and the four karmas: do the three encompass the four, or do the four encompass the three?
Answer: The three encompass the four, but the four do not encompass the three.
What is not included? This refers to all other untainted (anāsrava) karma, excluding the volition of training that is capable of severing all karma;
as well as all wholesome karma associated with the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) and all indeterminate (avyākṛta) karma.

In this context, excluding the uncontaminated karma consisting of volition (*cetanā*) belonging to the training (*śaikṣa*) that is capable of severing all karmas, there are those who assert that the fourth type of karma consists of seventeen uncontaminated volitions;
they maintain that these seventeen volitions are excluded [from the category of the third karma].
Furthermore, it includes the volition associated with the remaining untainted paths of preparation, uninterrupted transition, liberation, and special progress,
as well as the karma that follows along with the state of training (śaikṣa),
and all karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This is called "other untainted karma.
As for those who assert that the volition associated with all paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) constitutes the fourth type of karma,
they exclude all paths of uninterrupted transition from their definition.
Furthermore, there are the volitions associated with the paths of preparation, liberation, and special progress that are untainted,
as well as the karma that follows these [volitions] belonging to those in training (śaikṣa),
along with all karma belonging to those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This is called other untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
As for those who assert that all volitions (*cetanā*) of one in training (*śaikṣa*) constitute the fourth type of karma,
they are referring to the karma that accompanies the state of training (*śaikṣānuparivartin-karma*).
All karma of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) is called "other untainted karma" (anāsrava-karma).
This is what is meant by that statement.
This refers to what was stated first: excluding wholesome karma bound to the formless realm;
that is, all wholesome karma bound to the formless realm, with the exception of indeterminate karma.
This refers to all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) karma bound to the three realms.

By this principle, the three types of karma fully encompass the karma of those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
The four types of karma encompass only the karma of those in training and those who are neither in training nor beyond training.
The three types of karma fully encompass the karma bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
The four types of karma encompass only the karma bound to the desire realm and the form realm.
The three types of karma fully encompass wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral karma.
The four types of karma encompass only wholesome and unwholesome karma.
The three types of karma fully encompass karma to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), karma to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and karma that is not to be abandoned (*aheya*).
The four types of karma encompass only a portion of these three kinds.
The three types of action fully encompass all actions that are with outflows and without outflows,
defiled and undefiled actions,
and actions that have maturation and those that do not have maturation.
Karma that is associated and dissociated;
karma that has a concomitant and karma that lacks a concomitant;
manifest and non-manifest karma.
The four types of karma encompass only a small portion of the two types of karma.
Such categories should all be explained in detail.
Therefore, it is said that "the three encompass the four."
It does not include three of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). What is not included?
It refers to the volition (*cetanā*) of training that is capable of severing all karma, with the exception of that [volition].
Other untainted karma;
wholesome karma bound to the formless realm;
and all indeterminate karma.
The three types of action refer to the actions of body, speech, and mind; furthermore, there are another three types of action, namely:
karma to be experienced in the present life, karma to be experienced in the next birth, and [karma to be experienced in subsequent lives].
Regarding "karma to be experienced in subsequent births":
Why was this treatise composed?
It is answered: because it is intended to analyze the meaning of the sūtras.
As stated in the Sūtras,
there are three types of karma— such as that to be experienced in the present life and so forth—
but they are not explained in detail here.
The detailed explanation is as before.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
although the three types of action—body and so forth—were previously distinguished, [they are not yet fully established].
However, the three types of karma—such as that to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and so forth—have not yet been analyzed.
Desiring to analyze them now, this treatise is composed.
What is karma to be experienced in the present life?
That is to say, if karma is performed and accumulated in this very life,
and its ripened fruit is experienced in this very life,
it is called "karma to be experienced in the present life" (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma).
Question: If karma is both performed and accumulated at this time, is its maturation fruit experienced at this same time? Answer: No.
Why is this? All wholesome and unwholesome karmas must depend upon a continuum,
or else cross over that continuum, before their maturation (vipāka) is experienced.
That is to say, if this karma is performed and accumulated,
either within this same continuum or at this same moment.
Alternatively, one may experience the ripening fruit within this very same homogeneous life-stream (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Such is called karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*).
There is certainly no karma that is created in this very moment [and yet not experienced].
Thus, this and the subsequent moment have the sense of "ripening" because they belong to a different category and because they directly induce it.
Among these, regarding those karmas seen by the world that are to be experienced in the present life,
it has been heard that there was once a woodcutter.
Entering the mountains, he encountered snow and lost his way.
As evening fell, the snow grew deep and the cold became freezing;
on the verge of death, he soon entered a dense forest.
He then saw a bear already within the forest;
its form and color were deep blue-black, and its eyes were like twin torches.
The man was struck with terror, feeling that his life was surely forfeit.
This was in fact a bodhisattva manifesting in the body of a bear.
Seeing his fear and anxiety, he immediately comforted him, saying:
"Do not be afraid now."
"Parents may sometimes harbor divergent thoughts toward their children,
but I now have no ill intent whatsoever toward you. Having said this,
he immediately went forward, took him up in his arms, and entered the cave.
Having warmed his body and restored him to breath,
he gathered various roots and fruits and urged him to eat as much as he desired;
fearing that the food might not digest due to the cold, he held him in his arms and lay down.
Thus nourished with such kindness,
after six days had passed and on the seventh day,
the sky cleared, the path appeared, and people returned with hearts of devotion.
Once the bear had learned this, he again took sweet fruits and fed them to him until he was full as a parting gift.
He escorted him outside the forest and bid him farewell with great earnestness.
The man knelt in gratitude and said:
"How can I repay your kindness?
the bear asked.
"I do not require any other repayment at this time."
"However, on this day, I shall protect your body;
you, too, must likewise pledge to protect my life.
The man respectfully agreed and carried the firewood down the mountain.
He encountered two hunters and asked them,
"What beasts or birds have you seen in the mountains?"
The woodcutter replied,
"I saw no other beasts;
I saw only a single bear."
The hunter requested,
"Could you please show me [the way]?
The woodcutter replied:
"If you can give me two-thirds [of the meat],
I shall show it to you.
The hunter agreed to this, and they went together.
Having finally killed the bear, he divided the meat into three portions.
As the woodcutter reached out with both hands to take the bear's flesh,
his two arms fell off simultaneously due to the power of his evil karma.
It was like a string of pearls being severed,
or like cutting through the root of a lotus;
the hunter, frantic with alarm, asked in wonder what had happened.
The woodcutter, filled with shame and remorse, recounted the details of the matter.
The two hunters then rebuked the woodcutter, saying,
"Since he has bestowed such great kindness upon you..."
"How can you now endure committing such an evil and rebellious act?
How strange that your body does not rot away!
Thereupon, the hunter took the meat together with them and offered it to the saṃghārāma.
At that time, the Elder of the Sangha attained the wondrous knowledge of vows (praṇidhijñāna).
He then entered meditative concentration to observe what kind of meat it was,
and he knew it was the flesh of a Great Bodhisattva who brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
He immediately emerged from meditative absorption and reported this matter to the assembly.
The assembly was filled with wonder and admiration;
together they gathered fragrant wood, cremated his flesh, and collected his remaining bones.
They erected a stūpa to pay homage and make offerings.
Such evil karma must wait for the continuity [of its conditions].
Or, one may receive its fruit only after the continuity [of the karmic stream] has been transmuted.
Furthermore, in the past, there was a butcher who traded in cattle.
Driving the oxen across the road, many people ran out of provisions and were exhausted by hunger, thirst, and heat;
they paused to deliberate, saying,
"These herds of oxen will certainly never become our own property."
"It would be appropriate to cut off my tongue to relieve his hunger and weakness.
Thereupon, he smeared salt upon the mouths of several oxen;
the oxen, craving the salty flavor, extended their tongues and licked it.
Then, using sharp knives, they cut off [the flesh] all at once;
they roasted it over a fire in the dark and ate it together.
Having finished eating, they went together to the water to wash and rinse their mouths.
Having finished chewing the *yāshchi* (tooth-sticks) and brushing their teeth,
they split them to scrape their tongues; yet,
due to the power of their evil karma, [the sticks do not break].
The tongue-faculties of all these people will fall off simultaneously like rotten fruit;
such evil karma must wait for the continuity [of the stream of existence] to take effect.
Alternatively, one may experience its fruit only after the continuity [of the karmic stream] has been crossed.
Furthermore, it is heard that in the past there was a person of violent and evil character.
He had his mother hold a vessel while he himself milked the cow;
having milked it excessively,
his mother stopped him, saying:
The remainder could be kept to feed the calf; however,
upon hearing this, the man suddenly gave rise to anger and resentment,
cupping his hands to scoop up the milk and scatter it over the mother's face.
According to the amount of milk drops from the mother’s body,
that person’s body will likewise develop an equal number of white leprosy spots due to the power of their evil karma.
Such is the nature of this evil karma.
One must wait for the continuity [of the stream of consciousness] to be completed, or for it to pass beyond,
before one receives its fruit.
This is a brief citation of the three types of evil karma that yield results in the present life.
Formerly, in the kingdom of Kośala, there was a king named Jayasena who begot a daughter endowed with eighteen physical deformities.
The poor and lowly do not give;
the wealthy and noble do not seek.
There was once the son of an elder whose wealth and status were lost.
When the king heard this, he dispatched a messenger to summon him and said,
"I have a young daughter who lacks beauty; if you do not disdain her,
I shall provide you with generous stipends and precious wealth."
The man agreed to this.
Upon hearing it, the king was filled with joy and bestowed upon him abundant wealth, treasures, fields, houses, and servants, granting him whatever he desired.
She was received as a bride with due ceremony and secretly sent back to her residence;
the man, filled with shame, locked the doors whenever he went out,
so that no relatives or acquaintances could see her.
There were some close friends who reproached him, saying,
"Why do you not show your wife to us?"
The son of the elder said,
"Why such haste?
The crowd marveled at his procrastination and consequently made a collective agreement.
"Seven days from now, each of you shall bring your family to meet at such-and-such a garden for merriment and feasting.
Any who fail shall be fined five hundred pieces of gold.
On the seventh day, all acted according to their agreement.
Only the son of the elder did not bring his wife;
relying on his own wealth, he left the matter of the fine's amount to fate.
His wife remained alone at home, reproaching and resenting herself.
"What sin did I commit in my past lives to receive such a wretched body?
While all others find joy, I alone suffer.
It would be better for me to die early."
With single-minded devotion recollecting the Buddha, he was about to take his own life.
The Buddha, knowing that the time had come,
vanished from that place and reappeared before him.
Upon seeing the Tathāgata, the woman gave rise to profound feelings of compassion and joy;
with a fervent and pure mind, she contemplated the Buddha’s physical marks and signs,
owing to the power of her wholesome karma.
In an instant, her body transformed until she resembled a celestial maiden;
her joy redoubled as the Buddha preached the Dharma for her.
Having distanced herself from dust and left behind defilement, she attained the fruit of stream-entry.
When the World-Honored One had returned, the woman sat alone;
she was incomparably beautiful and dwelt in peace and happiness.
At that time, his companions, seeing that he had not brought his wife with him,
intoxicated him with wine and secretly took his house keys to go to his home together.
From afar, they beheld his wife, whose exquisite beauty was peerless, like that of Śakra’s consort.
Thereupon, the multitude felt profound admiration and respect,
and said to one another,
"The reason he has not revealed himself to others until now is surely because of this."
She then hurried to the garden to offer her apologies to her husband and to congratulate him on his success.
The man felt abashed, thinking she was mocking him;
yet when he returned and saw her, he was deeply struck with suspicion and wonder.
He asked,
"Noble lady, are you a master of illusion,
or are you a malevolent spirit?"
"Where is my wife? His wife answered him by relating all that had occurred.
Thereupon, her husband experienced what he had never known before and took refuge in the Three Jewels.
Such wholesome karma must await the continuity [of the stream of being],
or transcend that continuity.
Only then will they receive their retribution.
Formerly, in the kingdom of Gandhāra,
King Kaniṣka had an eunuch who constantly supervised the affairs of the inner palace.
Having briefly gone outside the city, he saw a herd of cattle numbering more than five hundred entering the city.
He asked the cowherd,
"What kind of cattle are these?"
He replied,
"This bull has been taken away along with its seed.
Thereupon, the eunuch reflected to himself:
"Because of my evil karma from past lives, I have received this body of a eunuch.
Now, I ought to use my wealth to rescue these oxen from their peril.
He then paid their price and caused them all to be set free.
By the power of his wholesome karma,
this eunuch was restored to a male body;
filled with profound joy, he immediately returned to the city.
Standing at the palace gate, he sent an attendant to inform the king,
requesting entry to have an audience.
The king ordered him to be summoned inside and questioned him with surprise regarding his reason for coming.
Thereupon, the eunuch reported the matter in full to the King.
Upon hearing it, the King was both surprised and delighted;
he bestowed upon him abundant treasures and wealth, and promoted him to a high office, charging him with the supervision of external affairs.
Such wholesome karma must either await the continuity [of the stream of being] or transcend that continuity.
Only then will they receive their fruit.
Formerly, in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā,
there was a woman who went to the site where King Candraprabha had sacrificed his thousand heads and paid homage at the spirit temple built for King Aśoka.
Seeing that there was dog excrement in front of the Buddha’s seat,
he immediately thought:
"This place is pure."
"How can dog excrement defile this place?
Thinking thus, he removed it with his hands and smeared fragrant mud as an ornament.
This was due to the power of his wholesome karma.
This causes the woman’s entire body to emit a fragrance like that of the sandalwood tree,
and her mouth to constantly exude the scent of the blue lotus.
Such is the result of these wholesome karmas.
One must await the continuity of the stream,
or transcend the continuity,
before receiving its fruit.
This is a brief citation of the three types of wholesome karma that yield results in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
What is karma that yields results in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*)?
It refers to karma that is performed and accumulated in this very life.
That which experiences its ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) in the second birth is called karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karma*).
What is karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karma*)?
That is to say, if karma is performed and accumulated in this life,
it may follow along with the third birth or the fourth.
Or, it may even exceed this; when one experiences the ripening fruit [in a subsequent life],
this is called karma to be experienced in a later successive birth (aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karma).
Question: Are all karmas that are to be experienced in the present life necessarily experienced in the present life?
The same question applies to those to be experienced in the next life and those to be experienced in subsequent lives.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say that this is not definitive,
because all karma can be transformed.
Even karma of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*) can be transformed. Question:
If that is so, why are they called "karma to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*) and so forth? They answer as follows:
Karmas that are to be experienced in the present life are indefinite;
they may or may not yield their ripened fruit within the present life.
If they are to be experienced, it is certain that they will be experienced in the present life and not in another.
Therefore, it is called "karma to be experienced in the present life.
The descriptions for "karma to be experienced in the next life" and "karma to be experienced in subsequent lives" are likewise the same.
It is taught that all such karma can be transformed.
Even the karma of immediate retribution can be transformed;
if the karma of immediate retribution could not be transformed,
there would be no one capable of transcending the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Nevertheless, since there are those who can transcend even the "summit of existence" (bhavāgra),
it follows that even the karma of immediate retribution (ānantarya) should be capable of being transformed.
Thus say the masters of the Abhidharma treatises.
All karma to be experienced in the present life is definitively experienced as its ripened fruit within the present life; therefore,
it is called "karma to be experienced in the present life."
The same applies to what has been said regarding karma to be experienced in the next life and in subsequent lives.
Therefore, if one asks why it is called "karma to be experienced in the present life," up to and including "karma to be experienced in subsequent lives":
One should answer in this way.
Furthermore, there are other masters who speak of four kinds of karma.
That is to say: karma to be experienced in the present life,
karma to be experienced in the next life,
and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Karma that is to be experienced indeterminately,
karma to be experienced in the present life,
and even karma to be experienced in subsequent lives— this karma cannot be altered.
All karma conducive to indeterminate feeling can be transformed;
it is solely for the sake of transforming this fourth type of karma that one observes the prohibitions and precepts and diligently practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
He thinks thus:
"By means of this, may I transform this karma.
Furthermore, there are other teachers who say:
Five kinds of karma are taught:
namely, karma to be experienced in the present life (dr̥ṣṭadharmavedanīya),
and karma to be experienced in the next birth (upapadyavedanīya).
Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Each of these consists of only one type. Furthermore, among the types of karma to be experienced at indefinite times, there are two kinds:
first, that which is determined regarding its maturation (*vipāka-niyata*).
Second, the indeterminacy of maturation:
this refers to those karmas conducive to experience in the present life and those conducive to experience in the next life.
Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives and karma to be experienced at indefinite times whose maturation is fixed are both unalterable.
Among the karmas of indefinite experience, those whose maturation is not fixed can be transformed;
it is solely for the sake of transforming this fifth type of karma [that this teaching is given].
They uphold the prohibitive precepts and diligently cultivate the holy life, thinking:
"By means of this, I shall transform this karma.
Furthermore, there are other teachers who hold this view.
Eight types of karma are taught.
Regarding karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*), there are two kinds:
first, that which is determinate in its maturation (*niyata-vipāka*).
Second, the indeterminacy of maturation:
karma to be experienced in the next life,
and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Karma that is to be experienced at an indefinite time likewise has two types:
first, that which is determinate in its maturation;
second, that which is indeterminate in its maturation.
These are called the eight types of karma.
Among them, all karmas with fixed maturation (*niyata-vipāka*) are irreversible;
all karmas with indefinite maturation (*aniyata-vipāka*) are reversible.
In order to turn this away, one undertakes the prohibitive precepts and diligently cultivates the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Therefore, in this context, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be formulated:
namely, there may be karma whose timing is determined but whose maturation (*vipāka*) is indeterminate; [and so forth].
There is karma whose maturation is determined but whose timing is undetermined;
there is karma whose timing is determined and whose maturation is also determined;
and there is karma whose timing is undetermined and whose maturation is also undetermined.
What is the determination of the timing of karma while its maturation is indeterminate?
It refers to karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and karma to be experienced in the next birth (*upapadyavedanīya*).
Among the karmas to be experienced in subsequent lives,
there are those with indeterminate maturation.
What is meant by karma with determinate maturation?
The indeterminate timing refers to those karmas among the category of karma with indeterminate ripening whose maturation is fixed.
What is karma that is both determinate in its timing and determinate in its ripening?
It refers to karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).
Regarding karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*) and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*),
what is karma whose timing is indefinite and whose maturation (*vipāka*) is also indefinite?
This refers to karma whose maturation is indefinite among those karmas that are to be experienced indeterminately.
These are called the eight karmas in four categories.
Question: Is it possible for one to produce three types of karma simultaneously within a single moment?
That is to say: karma to be experienced in the present life,
karma to be experienced in the next birth,
and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, one first dispatches two messengers to take a life.
Having committed taking what is not given,
he subsequently engages in sexual misconduct himself;
because this is brought to completion by his own action and not by another.
If such a kind of dharma arises,
the three types of karma all reach their culmination simultaneously;
among them, the first type of karma receives its ripened fruit (vipāka-phala) within the present life.
The second type of karma receives its maturation fruit in the immediately following birth.
The third type of karma receives its maturation fruit in subsequent births from the third birth onward.
The same distinction applies to the remaining courses of action regarding whether they are performed by oneself or incited in others.
Question: Among these types of karma, such as karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*),
how many are able to project the fruit of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*),
and how many are able to fulfill the fruit of the homogeneous class?
Some say that both [types of karma] can project the fruit of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*),
and they can also fulfill the fruit of the homogeneous class.
That is to say: karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karma*) and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karma*).
These two are capable of fulfilling the fruit of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
They cannot produce fruits that are of the same category as the individual existence (*nikāyasabhāga*),
namely: karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*) and karma to be experienced at an indefinite time (*aniyatavedanīya-karman*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that three [karmas] can project the fruit of a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*),
and they can also fulfill the fruit of a homogeneous class of beings.
That is to say, excluding those [karmas] to be experienced in the present life,
one [type of karma] can fulfill the fruit of the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga) but cannot project the fruit of the homogeneous class.
This refers to karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
Furthermore, there are those who maintain that karma to be experienced in the present life can also project the fruit of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
If one were to say this:
that all four types of karma are capable of projecting the fruit of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
And [it brings about] the fulfillment of the fruit of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Question: Among these various types of karma, which is the most excellent? Some say:
Karma to be experienced in the present life is the most excellent. Why is this?
Because its fruit is attained proximately.
Furthermore, there are those who say that karma to be experienced in subsequent lives is the most preeminent. Why is this so?
The karma of all bodhisattvas is the most supreme;
yet, because it is all to be experienced in subsequent lives, [one might ask:
how can karma to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma) obtain its fruit so quickly?
Among all types of karma, it can be said to be superior; yet,
since the fruit of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives is remote in time,
how is it the most excellent?
Answer: Although karma to be experienced in the present life attains its fruit quickly, that fruit is inferior and thus not called supreme;
whereas although karma to be experienced in subsequent lives is distant from its fruit, [it is superior].
Because its fruit is so exceptionally sublime that it cannot be fully described, it is called "supreme.
For example, among external seeds, some attain their fruit quickly yet the fruit is inferior,
while others take a long time to reach their fruit yet the fruit is most sublime.
Just as autumn seedlings bear fruit after three and a half months,
these fruits are most recent and inferior;
whereas rice, wheat, and the like take six months for their fruit to ripen.
The further the fruit is from its cause, the more excellent it becomes.
For example, the *Kharjūra* tree bears fruit only after five or six years, or even twelve;
such fruit is more excellent.
Just as the tāla tree bears its fruit only after a hundred years—
and that fruit is most excellent—
so too, external seeds are closest to their fruit, yet that fruit is most inferior.
The further removed from the fruit, the more excellent that fruit becomes;
the most distant from the fruit yields the most excellent fruit.
Thus, the seed conforms to the distinctions of excellence or inferiority found in its fruit.
Internal karma is likewise:
karma to be experienced in the present life has the most immediate result, yet its fruit is the most inferior.
Karma to be experienced in the next life has its fruition further removed [in time] than the former, yet its fruition is superior.
Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives has its fruition most remote, yet its fruition is most excellent.
Karma is distinguished by the superiority or inferiority of its respective fruits;
therefore, karma to be experienced in subsequent lives is the most preeminent, and not others.
Question: In which realm can how many types of karma be produced?
Some say that in the desire realm one can create four kinds of karma— wholesome and unwholesome—
while in the form and formless realms one can create three kinds of wholesome karma.
Excluding those [karmas] to be experienced in the present life. Why is this?
Because within the desire realm, one acts toward Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, parents, teachers, elders, and those possessed of virtue.
Because they initiate superior wholesome and unwholesome karma,
this karma swiftly brings about its ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
In the form and formless realms, such dominant conditions do not exist.
Therefore, one cannot produce such karma to be experienced in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*) with respect to them.
Question: If that is so, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
As it is said:
"Karma to be experienced in the present life;
karma to be experienced in the next birth."
Regarding karma to be experienced in subsequent lives,
it is increased by all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
The answer is that this should be stated in that treatise as follows:
Karma to be experienced in the present life is augmented by all underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the desire realm.
Karma to be experienced in the next life...
Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives consists of all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm,
as well as the universal latent dispositions of the form and formless realms.
Furthermore, it should be stated that [the object] is also increased by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation;
yet, this is not stated.
What is the underlying intention?
One should know that the aforementioned passage is a general and concise statement.
Question: If that is so, then...
How, then, is the statement in the *Saṃgītiparyāya* to be reconciled? As it says there:
"Karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*)."
Karma to be experienced in the next life,
karma to be experienced in subsequent lives,
and all latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the desire realm.
It is increased by the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms,
as well as by the latent dispositions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The answer should be stated in that text as follows:
Karma to be experienced in the present life is increased by all the latent proclivities (anuśaya) of the desire realm.
Karma to be experienced in the next life...
Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives consists of all latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm,
as well as the pervasive latent dispositions of the form and formless realms.
Furthermore, it should be stated that [this] is also augmented by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation;
what is the intention behind not stating this?
It should be understood that within this context, the statement is made because it is led by the force of the expression;
such is the meaning of this teaching.
The form and formless realms can also give rise to karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*).
Question: It was previously stated that in the desire realm, one can give rise to karma to be experienced in the present life through superior conditions such as Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
In the two higher realms, these superior conditions do not exist;
how, then, can [the afflictions] arise there?
Answer: In those places, they are merely sustained by the power of their causes.
It can also give rise to karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are also cases where such karma arises solely through the power of the cause;
that is to say, for instance, when a certain person opens their doors and practices great giving as an offering to the noble ones (*ārya*).
Yet it cannot induce karma to be experienced in the present life;
whereas there may be someone who, by giving a single mouthful of food to a single animal,
is able to induce karma to be experienced in the present life.
From these and other such points, we know that this karma does not necessarily arise based on superior conditions.
Rather, it is essential that it be sustained by the power of its cause (*hetu-bala*) before it can be induced.
For this reason, the great masters of the Abhidharma of Kaśmīra all made this statement: [text follows].

If one, with a sincere and pure mind, offers a handful of grass as food for another’s cow, it should be known that this can induce karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).
Question: In which realms of existence (*gati*) can how many types of karma be created?
Answer: In the hells, one can perform four types of unwholesome karma and three types of wholesome karma, excluding those to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
This applies to animals (*tiryagyoni*) and hungry ghosts (*preta*) as well.
Furthermore, among the inhabitants of the three continents and the gods of the desire realm,
one is able to create four kinds of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
In Uttarakuru, one can perform four types of wholesome karma and three types of unwholesome karma,
excluding those to be experienced in the next life.
This also applies to the gods of the form and formless realms.
The extent to which they can be produced is as previously explained.
Question: In which birth can how many types of karma be produced?
Answer: Within the four modes of birth, all four types of wholesome and unwholesome karma can be produced.
Question: Who, in which realm, is able to create how many types of karma?

Answer: If ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and have not yet abandoned the defilements (*kleśa*) of the desire realm, they are able to create the four types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—belonging to the desire realm.
If one has already become free from the defilements of the desire realm but has not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
and is of the nature to fall away (parihāṇadharman),
such a person is capable of creating the four types of karma belonging to the desire realm.
One can create three types of karma pertaining to the first dhyāna,
excluding that which is to be experienced in the present life (dr̥ṣṭadharmavedanīya). Some say:
He can perform two kinds of karma pertaining to the first dhyāna:
namely, karma to be experienced in a subsequent life and indeterminate karma.
This applies to one who is of a nature not to fall away.
He is able to perform three kinds of wholesome karma of the desire realm,
excluding that which is to be experienced in the next life;
he is also able to perform three kinds of karma of the first dhyāna.
Excluding those [karmas] to be experienced in the present life:
if one has already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
but has not yet become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna.
If one is of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharman),
they can create four kinds of karma of the desire realm and three kinds of karma of the first two dhyānas.
Excluding karma to be experienced in the present life,
some say that it can produce two kinds of karma for the second dhyāna, namely, karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
And regarding indeterminate karma:
if one is of the non-retrogressive type (aparihāṇadharman),
they are capable of creating three kinds of wholesome karma pertaining to the desire realm.
Excluding karma to be experienced in the next life,
one can create two types of karma for the first dhyāna,
namely: karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Furthermore, one can perform three types of karma pertaining to the second dhyāna that are of indeterminate timing for their fruition,
excluding those to be experienced in the present life;
this is explained in detail up to [the third dhyāna].
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness,
yet is of a nature subject to regression,
such a person can create four kinds of karma belonging to the desire realm.
One can perform three types of karma regarding the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments,
excluding that which is to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya). Some say:
They are able to perform two kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
namely, that to be experienced in a subsequent life,
and that of indefinite experience.
If one is of the non-retrogressive type (aparihāna-dharman),
they are able to perform the three kinds of wholesome karma of the desire realm,
with the exception of that which is to be experienced in the next life (upapadyavedanīya).
One can perform two kinds of karma regarding the four dhyānas and three formless attainments—
namely, karma to be experienced in subsequent lives and indeterminate karma—
and three kinds of karma regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Excluding those [karmas] to be experienced in the present life.
Thus has been explained the birth and existence of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the desire realm.
Now, as for those ordinary beings born in the first dhyāna who have not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna:
He can perform the four kinds of karma pertaining to the first dhyāna.
If he has already become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna but is not yet detached from the defilements of the second dhyāna,
he can perform three kinds of karma pertaining to the first dhyāna.
Excluding karma to be experienced in the next life,
one can perform three types of karma pertaining to the second dhyāna;
excluding karma to be experienced in the present life.
To speak at length, up to:
if one has already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness,
they can perform the three kinds of karma pertaining to the first dhyāna.
Excluding karma to be experienced in the next life,
one can create two types of karma for the three dhyānas and the three formless attainments:
namely, karma to be experienced in subsequent lives and indeterminate karma.
One can perform three types of karma pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
excluding that which is to be experienced in the present life;
this is as explained regarding birth in the first dhyāna.
In this manner, it should be explained in detail up to birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Thus has been explained the ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) of the various stages.
As for the noble ones (*ārya*), if they are born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and have not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm:
He is capable of performing the four types of wholesome and unwholesome karma of the desire realm.
Having already become detached from the defilements of the desire realm but not yet detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
he is capable of performing two types of karma of the desire realm.
That is to say, with the exception of karma to be experienced in the present life,
one performs the three types of karma pertaining to the first dhyāna that are either to be experienced in the present life or of indefinite experience.
Having already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
but not yet having become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna,
if one is of the nature to fall away (parihāṇadharman).
He is able to perform two kinds of karma in the desire realm,
namely, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and karma of indefinite timing (*aniyatavedanīya*).
He is able to perform three kinds of karma in the first and second dhyānas.
Excluding karma to be experienced in the present life,
some say that he can create two kinds of karma pertaining to the second dhyāna.
That is to say, [karma] to be experienced in subsequent lives and karma of indefinite experience.
If one is of the nature not to fall away (anapāyī),
they are capable of creating two kinds of wholesome karma in the desire realm.
That is to say, karma to be experienced in the present life and karma of indefinite experience can produce a single type of karma for the first dhyāna;
namely, karma of indefinite experience.
One can perform three types of karma pertaining to the second dhyāna,
excluding that which is to be experienced in the present life,
up until the point where one has become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness.
One who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
if they are of the nature of falling back (parihāṇadharman),
is capable of creating two kinds of karma pertaining to the desire realm.

That is to say, one can perform the three types of karma of the four dhyānas, excluding that which is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), as well as that which is of indefinite experience (*aniyatavedanīya*).
One can perform three types of karma regarding the four formless realms,
excluding that which is to be experienced in the present life;
this is the general statement.
If explained individually,
among the four formless attainments,
if one performs karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karma*).
Then one does not create karma to be experienced in subsequent lives;
if one creates karma to be experienced in subsequent lives,
then one does not create karma to be experienced in the next life.
Some say that he creates two kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
namely, karma to be experienced in a subsequent life and indeterminate karma.
If one is of a nature not to fall back,
they are capable of performing two kinds of wholesome karma in the desire realm:
namely, that to be experienced in the present life and that of indefinite experience.
One can create karma of four kinds in the four dhyānas and one kind in the three formless attainments—
namely, karma of indefinite timing—
and two kinds of karma in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This refers to karma to be experienced in the next life and karma of indefinite timing.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
they can create two kinds of karma pertaining to the desire realm.
This refers to karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and that of indefinite experience (*aniyatavedanīya*).
It is capable of producing karma of a single type within the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*):
namely, that of indefinite experience.
Thus it has been explained that noble ones are born in the desire realm.
Now, as for those noble ones who are born in the first dhyāna but have not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna:
He is capable of performing the three types of karma pertaining to the first dhyāna,
with the exception of that which is to be experienced in subsequent lives,
provided he has already become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
Not yet free from the defilements of the second dhyāna,
he performs two kinds of karma pertaining to the first dhyāna:
namely, karma to be experienced in the present life (dr̥ṣṭadharmavedanīya) and karma of indefinite experience (aniyatavedanīya).
One can perform three types of karma pertaining to the second dhyāna,
excluding that which is to be experienced in the present life,
provided one has already become detached from the defilements of the second dhyāna.
One who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna can perform two kinds of karma pertaining to the first dhyāna: namely,
karma to be experienced in the present life (dr̥ṣṭadharmavedanīya) and karma of indefinite experience (aniyatavedanīya).
One can create one type of karma for the second dhyāna,
namely that of indefinite experience;
one can create three types of karma for the third dhyāna.
Excluding those [karmas] to be experienced in the present life,
and so forth in detail, up until:
if one has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness.
Not yet free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
one can perform two kinds of karma pertaining to the first dhyāna:
namely, karma to be experienced in the present life and indeterminate karma.
One can create karma of three kinds in the three dhyānas and one kind in the four formless attainments—
namely, that of indefinite timing—
and two kinds of karma in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
That is to say, [these are] karma to be experienced in the next life and karma of indefinite timing.
If one has already become free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
one can create two kinds of karma pertaining to the first dhyāna.
This refers to karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and that which is indeterminate (*aniyata-vedanīya*).
It can produce one type of karma for each of the three dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*),
namely, karma that is indeterminate.
As it is said regarding the noble one being born in the first dhyāna,
so too is the detailed explanation for being born in the second, third, and fourth dhyānas;
this applies except in the case of those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of their own level.
The four types of karma they can produce in their own stage differ from the previous case.
This applies to those noble ones who are born in the Sphere of Infinite Space but have not yet abandoned the defilements of that sphere.
He can perform two kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*):
namely, that to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and that of indefinite experience (*aniyata-vedanīya*).
This applies if he has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space.
Not yet free from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness,
one performs two kinds of karma pertaining to the Sphere of Infinite Space:
namely, karma to be experienced in the present life and karma of indefinite experience.
One can perform two kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of infinite consciousness:
namely, karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*) and karma of indefinite experience (*aniyatavedanīya*).
This applies provided one has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Not yet free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness,
one performs two kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of infinite space:
namely, karma to be experienced in the present life and karma of indefinite experience.
One type of karma capable of producing the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) is that of indefinite maturation (*aniyata-vedanīya*).
Two types of karma are capable of producing the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
This refers to karma to be experienced in the next life and indeterminate karma,

[in the case of one] who has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness but has not yet become detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
One can perform two kinds of karma regarding the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*):
namely, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) and karma of indefinite experience (*aniyata-vedanīya*).
Regarding the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one performs only one kind of karma.
That is to say, [beings] create two kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
namely, karma to be experienced in the next life and karma of indefinite experience.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
they can perform two types of karma pertaining to the sphere of infinite space:
namely, karma to be experienced in the present life and karma of indefinite experience.
It can produce one type of karma for the three formless realms, namely, karma of indefinite timing (aniyata-vedanīya).
As it is said: "When a noble one is born in the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana)..."
In this manner, the detailed exposition up to birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is likewise.
While abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm,
one is capable of creating twenty-two kinds of karma.
This refers to the karmic maturation of both determinate and indeterminate actions during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
as well as that of the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages.
Peśī, ghana, and praśākhā.
The newborn,
the infant,
and the child.
In the stages of youth and vigor, as well as old age and decline,
there are respectively determinate and indeterminate karmas of maturation.
These are called the twenty-two karmas.
Abiding in the stage of the kalala,
one is able to produce twenty kinds of karma.
This means that, with the exception of the two types of karma pertaining to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
one can likewise create two types of karma while remaining in the stage of old age— that is,
determinate and indeterminate karma belonging to that stage of old age.
Question: If various karmas created during the intermediate state (antarābhava) result in maturation (vipāka) upon reaching the state of existence in the womb (pratisandhi),
should these karmas be described as "to be experienced in the present life" (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya)?
"Is it karma to be experienced in the next life?
Answer: "This is karma to be experienced in the present life;

Karma conducive to painful feeling,

Among these, the first three types of karma are exclusively determinate (*vyākṛta*).
The latter three [categories] include both the determinate (*vyākṛta*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Therefore, it is said that the latter subsumes the former, but the former does not subsume the latter.
What is it that is not subsumed?
That is, neutral karma (*avyākṛta-karman*).
The three types of karma refer to past karma and so forth.
Furthermore, there are another three types of karma.
That is to say, there are wholesome and other types of karma;
furthermore, there are three types of karma,
namely, those of the learner (śaikṣa) and so forth.
Furthermore, there are three types of karma,
namely karma to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) and so forth;
the former subsumes the latter.
Does the latter subsume the former?
Answer: They mutually subsume one another according to their respective functions, because while their meanings differ, their essence does not.
The three types of karma refer to past and so forth karma.
There are also three types of karma referring to those bound to the desire realm and so forth.
Does the former subsume the latter, or does the latter subsume the former?
Answer: The former includes the latter, but the latter does not include the former.
What is it that is not included?
That is, it refers to uncontaminated (anāsrava) karma.
Among these, the first three types of karma pertain to both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated,
while the latter three are exclusively contaminated.
Therefore, it is said that the former includes the latter, but the latter does not include the former.
What is not included? It refers to uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma.
The three types of karma refer to wholesome and so forth;
furthermore, there are three types of karma,
namely those bound to the desire realm and so forth.
Does the former include the latter, or does the latter include the former?
Answer: The former includes the latter, but the latter does not include the former.
What is not included? It refers to untainted (anāsrava) karma.
Among these, the first three types of karma pertain to both the tainted (sāsrava) and the untainted.
The latter three types of karma are exclusively with outflows (sāsrava).
Therefore, it is said that the former includes the latter, but the latter does not include the former.
What is it that is not included?
That is, untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
There are three types of karma, namely wholesome and so forth.
Furthermore, there are another three types of karma.
