That is to say, there are the actions of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth.
Furthermore, there are three types of action:
namely, actions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth.
Does the former include the latter, or does the latter include the former?
Answer: They include one another reciprocally according to their respective functions.
Because their meanings differ while their substance does not.
The three types of karma refer to karma bound to the desire realm and so forth.
Furthermore, there are another three types of karma.
That is to say, there are the actions of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth.
Furthermore, there are three types of action:
namely, the actions to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and so forth.
Does the former include the latter, or does the latter include the former?
Answer: The latter includes the former, but the former does not include the latter.
What is not included?
It refers to untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
Among these, the first three types of karma are exclusively tainted (*sāsrava*).
The latter three types of karma encompass both the out-flowing (sāsrava) and the non-out-flowing (anāsrava).
Therefore, it is said that the latter subsumes the former, but the former does not subsume the latter.
What is it that is not subsumed?
This refers to untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
There are three types of karma, namely the karma of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth.
Furthermore, there are another three types of karma.
That is to say, regarding karma to be abandoned by seeing and so forth:
does the former subsume the latter,
or does the latter subsume the former?
Answer: They are mutually inclusive according to their respective functions, as explained previously.
Is there any karma that results in bodily sensation but not mental sensation?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to unwholesome karma;
that is to say, because unwholesome karma results exclusively in the maturation of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
Question: Why does unwholesome karma not result in mental feeling (*cittavedanā*)?

The answer is that such a type of mind experiences feeling, namely the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*); however, because the faculty of grief is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*), it does not induce mental feeling.
Question: For what reason is the faculty of grief not a result of maturation?
Answer: Because it arises from attention associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*),
because its conceptualization is strong,
and because it is free from the equanimity of one who has abandoned desire.
Retribution is not like that.
Is there any karma that produces mental feeling but not bodily feeling?
Answer: There is.
This refers to wholesome karma that is without vitarka.
Regarding this, for those who maintain that the lower stages lack the ripening fruit of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,
the mental feeling ripened by such wholesome karma without vitarka [is what is meant].
That is to say: the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) in the second dhyāna;
the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in the third dhyāna;
and [the faculty of equanimity] in the fourth dhyāna.
And the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Some say that it also brings about the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) of the first dhyāna, because they belong to the same level (*ekabhūmika*).
However, it does not induce the maturation associated with the three consciousnesses,
because this karma is subtle.
As for those who maintain that even the lower realms possess the maturation fruit of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*), [they argue as follows].

The mental feeling that is the maturation resulting from this wholesome karma free from vitarka consists of the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) in the second dhyāna,
and the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity in the third dhyāna.
The faculty of equanimity in the fourth dhyāna and in the formless realm;
some say this.
It also brings about the faculty of equanimity of the intermediate dhyāna.
Some say that it also brings about the faculties of joy and pleasure of the first dhyāna, but because these are coarse, they are not brought about by this karma.
Is there any karma that results in feelings of body and mind?
Answer: There is;
namely, wholesome karma accompanied by vitarka.
For those who maintain that there is no fruit of ripening consisting of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling in the lower realms,
this wholesome karma accompanied by vitarka,
if it exists in the desire realm, brings about a result associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness.
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is the maturation of bodily sensation (*kāyika-vedanā*),
as well as that which induces maturation associated with mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is the maturation of mental sensation (*caitasika-vedanā*).
If one is in the first dhyāna, it results in the maturation of the faculty of pleasure associated with the three bodies of consciousness as bodily sensation,
as well as that associated with the mental consciousness.
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is the maturation (*vipāka*) of mental feeling.
For those who maintain that there is also the maturation fruit of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*) in the lower stages,
this refers to wholesome karma accompanied by vitarka (*savitarka*).

If one is in the desire realm, there is the maturation of bodily sensation associated with the five groups of consciousness corresponding to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*),
as well as that which corresponds to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The faculties of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) are the mental feelings that constitute maturation (*vipāka*).

If [this occurs] in the first dhyāna, it constitutes the maturation of bodily feeling as the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity, associated with the three groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*).
And it includes the maturation of the mental feelings associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Question: Why is the faculty of joy a fruit of maturation, whereas the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not?
Answer: The modes of activity (*ākāra*) of pleasant feeling have both coarse and subtle aspects;
they do not necessarily arise through constant mental attention (*manasikāra*), nor are they necessarily constant strong conceptualizations (*vikalpa*).
Because it is also present within the subtle meditative absorptions (*sūkṣma-samādhi*).
Furthermore, this faculty of joy (*prīti-indriya*) is not a relinquishment (*upekṣā*) free from desire;
since it is not incompatible with the nature of maturation (*vipāka-dharma*), it is indeed a maturation.
The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not like this, and therefore it is not a maturation (*vipāka*).
Question: Why is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) induced only by wholesome karma and not by unwholesome karma?
Answer: Because the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the faculty of equanimity is subtle and tranquil.
Because it is what the wise delight in, it is produced by wholesome karma.
Since the nature of unwholesome karma is coarse and agitated,
it cannot produce the maturation of equanimity.
Is there any karma that does not produce feelings of body or mind, yet produces a ripened result (*vipāka*)?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, there are various karmas that produce the ripened results of form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The maturation of form refers to the nine bases, excluding the sound base.
The maturation of formations dissociated from mind refers to...
This refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character of a group (*nikāyasabhāga*), and birth, subsistence, aging,
and impermanence. Some say it also includes the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*).
Question: Among these, what is called bodily feeling (kāyikī vedanā) and what is called mental feeling (caitasikī vedanā)?
Answer: If a feeling occurs within the five groups of sensory consciousness (pañcavijñānakāya), it is called bodily feeling.
That which is in the mind is called mental feeling (*cittika-vedanā*). Furthermore,
there are those who say that among all feelings, those that are non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) are called bodily feeling (*kāyika-vedanā*).
That which involves conceptual discrimination is called mental feeling (*caitasika-vedanā*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that if a feeling takes an object characterized by its own specific mark (*svalakṣaṇa-viṣaya*) as its condition, it is called bodily feeling (*kāyikī vedanā*).
That which takes as its object the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is called mental feeling (*cittavedanā*). Furthermore,
some say that if feeling takes a present object as its condition, it is called bodily feeling (*kāyavedanā*).
That which takes as its object the three periods of time and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is called mental feeling (*cittavedanā*).
Furthermore, some say that if a feeling takes a substantially existent object as its condition, it is called bodily feeling (*kāyavedanā*).
The mind and feelings are so named because they take as their objects that which exists substantially and that which exists nominally. Furthermore,
some say that if a feeling grasps an object in a general or superficial manner, it is called bodily feeling (*kāyikī vedanā*).
That which is apprehended repeatedly is called mental feeling (*cittavedanā*). Furthermore,
some say that if a feeling cognizes an object upon a single momentary engagement, it is called bodily feeling (*kāyavedanā*).
That which is understood through investigation is called mental feeling (*cittavedanā*).
Furthermore, some say that among the various feelings,
those that depend on form and take form as their object are called bodily feeling (*kāyikavedanā*).
If one relies on that which is non-material to condition both material and non-material [phenomena], this is called "mental feeling.
As with material and non-material, so too with the resistant and the non-resistant,
and the accumulated and the non-accumulated.
The same applies to the explanations regarding the harmonious and the non-harmonious.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"The Buddha taught two types of sensation."
That is to say: bodily feeling and mental feeling.
What is called bodily feeling?
What is called mental feeling?
In this state, there is no bodily sensation;
all sensations whatsoever are mental sensations. Why is this?
Because it is associated with the mind;
however, whatever feeling arises in dependence upon the five sense faculties is called "bodily feeling" (*kāyikī vedanā*),
because the body always serves as its predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
If it arises based on the mental faculty (manas), it is called mental feeling (citta-vedanā),
because the mind always serves as its predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
Some have stated this as follows:
There is no bodily sensation;
all sensations whatsoever are mental sensations. Why is this?
Because it is associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*).
However, whatever sensation (*vedanā*) arises in dependence upon the three faculties (*indriya*),
taking a composite object, is called bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*).
Because it constantly forms conceptualizations.
If it arises based on the three faculties and apprehends a non-concordant object, it is called mental feeling (*caitasika-vedanā*),
because it does not constantly form conceptualizations.
The Venerable One said:
"There are two kinds of sensation:
first, bodily sensation."
The second is mental feeling.
That which is bodily feeling is also mental feeling.
There is mental feeling that is not bodily feeling;
that is to say, all such feelings do not apprehend external objects but give rise to conceptualization,
and instead rely solely on internal objects to grasp their signs and give rise to conceptualization.
That is to say, taking all *pudgalas* as objects,
as well as the form included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)— these are called mental feelings (*caitasikavedanā*).
Venerable sir, you wish to cause such mental perception [to arise].
There is no real objective realm; it is merely conceptual construction that evolves.
This is as stated regarding the three obstacles.
These are the affliction-obstructions, the karma-obstructions, and the maturation-obstructions.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"If sentient beings possess six qualities,
even though they hear the Dharma and Vinaya realized and taught by the Tathāgata..."
Yet they were unable to transcend the dust and leave behind defilement,
nor did they develop the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
What are these six?
First, the obstacle of afflictions;
second, the obstacle of karma;
third, the obstacle of maturation.
Fourth, lack of faith;
fifth, lack of joy;
sixth, unwholesome wisdom.
Although it has been stated that one accomplishes these six dharmas,
they have not yet been extensively analyzed, nor has it been explained what is meant by the "afflictive obstruction" (kleśāvaraṇa).
What is the obstacle of karma?
What is the obstacle of maturation?
That sūtra is the fundamental source for the origin of this treatise.
That which was not previously explained shall now be explained; for this reason, this treatise is composed.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
although various karmas were previously analyzed, [they have not yet been fully categorized].
However, those obstacles such as karma have not yet been analyzed;
wishing now to analyze them, this treatise is composed.
Such are the three obstacles.

In brief, its essential nature consists of the various maturations such as the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) and the hells (*naraka*), which are characterized by intensely burning and acute afflictions (*kleśa*).
Having already explained its essential nature, I shall now explain the reason for it.
Question: Why are they called "obstructions"?
Answer: Because these three kinds [of factors] are able to obstruct the noble path and the roots of goodness that constitute the preparatory application for the noble path.
For this reason, it is called an "obstruction.
What is the obstruction of afflictions?
It refers to someone who, by their very nature, is fully possessed of the blazing afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because of this, it is difficult for them to develop revulsion [for cyclic existence] and difficult to instruct.
It is difficult to awaken to;
it is difficult to escape from;
it is difficult to attain liberation from.
Among these, those who are naturally endowed with intense and fierce afflictions of desire are such as Nanda and others;
those who are endowed with intense and fierce afflictions of hatred are...
Those such as Aṅgulimāla,
who were fully possessed of the blazing and intense affliction of delusion;
and those such as Kāśyapa, who were otherwise.
Question: If that is so, as it has been said, they are difficult to inspire with world-weariness,
difficult to instruct,
and difficult to awaken.
It is difficult to escape from it;
it is difficult to attain liberation from it.
These words are well-founded.
Since they were all taught through diligent skillful means and thereby perceived the Truths,
how can this be reconciled with the statement that [certain factors] obstruct the Noble Path and the roots of goodness conducive to the practice of the Noble Path?

The answer is: although he is able to obstruct the Noble Path and the roots of goodness that serve as its preliminary practice, by means of the Buddha’s power and skillful transformative expedients, he is enabled to realize the Truths (satyadarśana).
This is not within the scope of those who can be transformed by the great Śrāvakas such as Śāriputra and others.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one who is fully possessed of the blazing and intense affliction of greed is like a eunuch and the like.
Those who possess the intense and fierce affliction of hatred are like those who exhale breath and so forth;
those who possess the intense and fierce affliction of delusion are likewise.
Like the six masters and others.
Question: If that is so, then the statement that they can obstruct the noble path and the roots of goodness that serve as the preparatory application for the noble path is well-justified.
Since they ultimately do not perceive the Truths,
how can one reconcile this with such statements as that they are difficult to inspire with world-weariness and difficult to instruct?
Since it is not called "difficult" because they ultimately do not attain the vision of the truths,
one should answer by saying:
"They do not produce weariness [with saṃsāra] and cannot be instructed," and so forth.
What is the intended meaning of not making such a statement?
It means that the very failure to produce revulsion is called "the difficulty of producing revulsion," and so on,
up to the point that one does not attain liberation.
It is called "liberation difficult to attain.
Question: How is this obstacle of afflictions established?
Is it based on their actual possession?
Is it based on manifest activity?
Answer: It is based on manifest activity, not on possession.
If one relies on their possession [of afflictions], then all sentient beings are without distinction,
as they equally possess all afflictions.
It is by relying on their actual manifestation that the distinctions among afflictions are established.
This constitutes four permutations:
there are afflictions that are blazing but not intense;
and there are afflictions that are intense but not blazing.
There are afflictions that are both blazing and sharp;
there are afflictions that are neither blazing nor sharp.
Regarding those afflictions that are blazing but not sharp:
This refers to those who frequently practice with weak-grade afflictions.
Those who possess intense but not burning [afflictions] refers to those who do not frequently practice with strong-grade afflictions.
That which is both blazing and intense refers to those who frequently practice with superior-grade afflictions.
That which is neither blazing nor intense refers to others.
This refers to those who do not frequently engage in inferior-grade afflictions.
Among these, even those afflictions that are burning but not intense constitute an afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Consequently, although these afflictions are of a low grade, because they occur frequently,
they give rise to the middling grade based on the low, and the high grade based on the middling.
Gradually, this even leads to the severing of the roots of goodness.
Those [afflictions] are neither intense nor blazing afflictions,
nor are they the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Because these afflictions, although they are of a superior grade,
are not frequently practiced, they can gradually be diminished until one is able to enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and achieve ultimate eradication.
Those afflictions that are both blazing and intense constitute the entirety of what is heavy regarding the hindrance of afflictions;
those afflictions that are neither blazing nor intense do not.
The afflictive hindrances are not all light;
likewise, there are four permutations regarding these roots of goodness.
There may be roots of goodness that are blazing but not intense.
There are roots of goodness that are sharp but not blazing;
there are roots of goodness that are both blazing and sharp;
and there are roots of goodness that are neither blazing nor sharp.
That which is "blazing but not intense" refers to those who practice with inferior roots of goodness.
That which is "intense but not blazing" refers to... [as above].
This refers to those who possess superior roots of goodness but do not practice them frequently.
"Blazing and also intense" refers to those who possess superior roots of goodness and practice them frequently.
That which is neither blazing nor intense refers to those with inferior roots of goodness who do not practice frequently.
Among these, there are roots of goodness that are blazing but not intense.
It is not obstructed by the hindrance of afflictions;
therefore, although these are roots of goodness of an inferior grade, because they are practiced frequently,
they develop from the inferior to the middling level.
Based on the intermediate [level], one gives rise to the superior;
gradually increasing, one is able to swiftly attain the realization of the severance of all fetters.
Those roots of goodness are both intense and not yet blazing.
Thus, one is obstructed by the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Consequently, although these are superior roots of virtue, because they are not practiced frequently,
it is possible that the afflictions will manifest repeatedly.
Gradually increasing, they are able to sever the roots of goodness.
Among them, those that are blazing and intense are all superior;
those that are not blazing and not intense are all inferior.
What is the obstacle of karma?
It refers to the five deeds of immediate retribution. What are these five?
First, killing one's mother;
second, killing one's father;
third, killing an arhat.
Fourth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha;
fifth, with an evil mind, drawing blood from the body of a Buddha.
Question: As previously stated, these are able to obstruct the Noble Path and the roots of goodness that are the preparatory practices for the Noble Path.
Therefore, they are called obstructions.
Apart from the five deeds of immediate retribution,
there are furthermore other forms of sublime conduct and evil conduct.
This refers to karma that determines an eighth existence,
as well as the intense obsession with malice that leads to the harming of *kuṇapa* ants and the like;
because of these obstacles, one is unable to enter the Noble Path in the present life.
Why is it not said to be an obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*)?
Answer: It should indeed be stated that this is also an obstacle of karma;
however, that it is not so stated should be understood as meaning that the explanation is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Regarding these three obstacles, there are various explanations.
Furthermore, some teachers maintain that because the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) are certain to act as obstacles, they are specifically mentioned here.
Other forms of skillful conduct and unskillful conduct may either act as obstacles or not act as obstacles.
For this reason, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the five deeds of immediate retribution (pañcānantarya-karma) must possess five causal conditions.
Because it is easy to see and easy to know, it is explained selectively.
What are the five? First, by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Second, because of the two destinies;
third, because of the three births;
fourth, because of the fruits.
Regarding the five types of persons:
as for their intrinsic nature,
it means that these five natures are determinate and extremely grave evil karma.
Regarding "because of the destiny":
these five are definitely experienced in the hells and not in any other destiny.
Regarding "because of birth":...
These five are definitely to be experienced in successive births;
they are not to be experienced in the present life,
nor are they to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Regarding the phrase "because they do not accord with [karma] whose fruit is experienced indeterminately":
this means that these five types definitely bring about extremely undesirable fruits in the world for the person (*pudgala*). Regarding the phrase "because of the person":
[it refers to the fact that] they are experienced by the person.
This means that these five types of persons who commit such acts are easy to see and easy to recognize:
namely, this one who can kill his mother,
and this one who can kill his father.
Up to and including this shedding of the Buddha’s blood—
apart from these five types, all other sublime conduct and unwholesome conduct lack such fivefold causal conditions.
Because it is easy to see and easy to understand, it is not discussed here.

Question: Regarding the preparatory actions (*prayoga*) for the various immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) that can fulfill their respective results—do these lead to those results with certainty or without certainty?
If it were fixed, why is it not stated here?
Furthermore, how could the Venerable Aṅgulimāla Śrīgupta have been able to turn back [the Buddha]?
If it were not fixed, [why did he not turn him back?]
How is what is stated in the *Nāmarūpapariccheda* to be reconciled?
For it asks: "Is there a case where one has not yet killed a living being, yet the killing has not ceased, and the maturation (*vipāka*) of this karma is certain to arise in hell?"
Answer: It is as when one dies while engaged in the preliminary application (*prayoga*) for an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*).
Some say that this karma is certain regarding its fruit.
Question: It would have been well-explained if the section on "taking life" had been included;
why is it not mentioned here?
Answer: This section should have discussed the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) as well as their preliminary preparations (*prayoga*).
What is the intention behind not mentioning it?

The answer is: this has already been explained as being included within the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), because the five deeds of immediate retribution take this as their preliminary application (*prayoga*).
If one speaks of the fruit, it should be understood that the preparatory application (*prayoga*) has already been explained.
Question: How was the Venerable Aṅgulimāla able to turn back?
Answer: He had not yet performed the immediate preparatory application (*ānantarya-prayoga*).
Therefore, he said: "I shall not kill my mother for now; first, I must eat. Question:
Does this not mean he intends to harm the Omniscient One?
Answer: At that time, he was applying the preparatory effort of harm toward one who was not the Omniscient One.
It is not because of omniscience;
for this reason, the World-Honored One manifested as an ordinary bhikṣu and entered the Tāpa Grove,
lest that venerable one [be disturbed].
The preparatory act of killing toward omniscience is incurable.
If sentient beings were to commit the preparatory act of killing toward omniscience,
even if there were Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, [it could not be remedied].
Nor can they rescue him so as to liberate him from hell.
Therefore, it is known that he initiated the act of killing with respect to one who is not omniscient,
and not with respect to an omniscient one.
Question: How is it that Śrīgupta was able to turn [the king] away?
Answer: He did not perform the preparatory application for an immediate transgression;
therefore, although he secretly laid out a fire-pit and food mixed with poison, [the king did not fall into them].
He thought to himself:
"If the Tathāgata is indeed omniscient, he shall naturally avoid it;
if he is not omniscient, then I shall utterly destroy him."
This is so that they may not be deluded and devoured by the world.
Furthermore, because that preparatory effort for killing directed toward an Omniscient One cannot be turned back, others have said:
This karma is not fixed with respect to its fruit.
Question: If it is not mentioned here, then it would be well-explained.
Venerable Śrīgupta of Aṅgulimāla held that karma can also be transformed.
How should one interpret the section on the taking of life?

The answer is: regarding those actions whose preparatory stages (*prayoga*) are uninterrupted and which can bring their respective fruits to completion, these may be either determinate or indeterminate with respect to that fruit.
Regarding the section on taking life,
it is said that the specific practitioner referred to there was the Venerable Śrīgupta, also known as Aṅgulimāla, who underwent a transformation.
Regarding this indeterminacy,
both of these explanations are equally valid. What, then,
is the obstacle of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*)?
That is to say, the various sentient beings dwelling in the hells and the animal realm.
The realm of hungry ghosts,
the northern continent of Uttarakuru,
and the station of the non-percipient devas.
Question: On other continents as well, there are those for whom maturation (vipāka) acts as an obstacle, such as the śaṇḍha, the paṇḍaka, the sexless, and the hermaphrodite.
Why are these not mentioned here?
Answer: One should know that when something is not stated here despite being something that ought to be stated, it is because the teaching is incomplete (*śeṣavāda*).
For this reason, it was previously stated that all three obstacles mentioned herein are also taught incompletely.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"In this context, only that which is definitely an obstacle is mentioned;
that [other factor] is not definite."
Because the maturation (*vipāka*) experienced by those sentient beings may either constitute an obstruction or not, it is not mentioned here.
Question: Of these three obstructions, how many can be established within a single continuum?
Answer: Sometimes only one is accomplished—
meaning that among the three types, one or another is accomplished— or sometimes two are accomplished,
namely the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the karmic hindrance (*karmāvaraṇa*).
There are either the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) or the ripening hindrance (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
There is no one who possesses the karmic hindrance (*karmāvaraṇa*) and the ripening hindrance without also possessing the afflictive hindrance;
for this reason, there is likewise no one who possesses all three.
Question: Among these three obstructions, which is the most serious?
Some say that the obstruction of maturation (vipāka-āvaraṇa) is the most serious.
Why is this? Because at the time of the cause it can be transformed,
whereas at the time of the fruit it cannot be transformed.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the karmic obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*) is the most heavy. Why is this?
Because the karmic obstruction can induce the ripening obstruction (*vipākāvaraṇa*); thus it is said.
The afflictive hindrances are heavy;
for the afflictive hindrances can induce karmic hindrances,
and karmic hindrances in turn can induce maturational hindrances.
Thus, because all [unwholesome states] have afflictions as their root, they are the most grave.
Among the three types of unwholesome conduct, which constitutes the greatest offense?
It is the false speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha.
This karma can bring about the ripening fruit of suffering with a lifespan of one kalpa in the Avīci Hell;
other karmas are not fixed in this way.
Question: This teaching states that the false speech of causing a schism in the Saṃgha is the greatest of all sins.
In another place it is further said that mental action is the greatest offense;
in yet another place it is further said.
"Wrong view is the greatest of all sins.
What is the distinction between these three great sins? Some say:
There are three kinds of offenses:
first, karma;
second, afflictions.
Among the three types of unwholesome conduct,
mental action is the greatest offense;
among the afflictions, false view is the greatest offense.
Among the unwholesome actions, the false speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha is the gravest offense.
Furthermore, others say that intentional karma which disturbs and agitates the great assembly is the gravest offense.
Wrong view is a great sin because it destroys all roots of virtue;
the deceptive speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha is a great sin because it can bring about the maturation of great suffering as its result.
Furthermore, there are those who say that among the three types of karma, mental karma is the greatest offense;
and among the five views, false view is the greatest offense.
Among the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), the false speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha is the greatest offense.
Furthermore, some say that among the paths of action (*karmapatha*) to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is the greatest offense.
Among the paths of action to be abandoned through cultivation,
the false speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha is the greatest offense;
among the actions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation, mental action is the greatest offense.
Furthermore, there are those who say that mental action (manas-karma) is declared to be a great transgression because it is based on volitional action (cetanā-karma),
and because it is based on the action performed through volition.
It is taught that the false speech of causing a schism in the Saṃgha is a great transgression because it is based on non-action;
furthermore, it is taught that wrong view is a great transgression because it is based on action.
Moreover, there are those who say:
Based on that which initiates action, mental karma is said to be a great offense;
based on that which is produced by action, the false speech of schism is said to be a great offense;
and based on that which is non-action, wrong view is said to be a great offense.
Furthermore, there are those who say that mental action is declared to be a great transgression based on the karma that initiates [the act],
whereas it is based on the karma that is initiated [by it].
Speaking false speech to cause a schism in the Saṃgha is declared a great sin because it is based on non-action;
holding wrong view is declared a great sin because it is based on action.
These are called the three distinctions among great sins.
Question: At the time of that schism in the Saṃgha, there were also bodily actions such as coming and going, preparatory effort, and reflection, as well as other vocal actions.
Why, then, is it said that only false speech can cause a schism in the Saṃgha?
Answer: This refers to cases where the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) for schisming the Saṃgha reaches its completion (*niṣṭhā*) at all times;
among all karmas, it is only in the case of false speech that the preparatory effort reaches completion [at all times].
Because these [actions] are capable of causing a schism in the Saṃgha at all times, they are specifically mentioned;
other karmas are not so, and therefore they are not mentioned.
Question: As it is said that they can bring about the fruit of the Avīci Hell, [how is this so?]
Why is it called the Avīci Hell?
Answer: This is a conventional designation and a conventional conceptualization;
it is not necessarily the case that every meaning is fully present within the name.
Furthermore, this hell is also called "Uninterrupted" (Avīci);
it is also called "The Blazing Intense Flames of Hot Iron Piercing the Limbs";
and it is also called "Constantly Experiencing All Manner of Suffering and Distress through the Six Bases of Contact."
It is also called "suffering summoned by karma experienced by oneself.
Furthermore, some say it is called "uninterrupted" because within it there is no interval or gap that would allow a pleasant sensation to manifest even for a moment.
Question: In the other hells, are there such things as singing, dancing, food, drink, and other sources of pleasure?
Answer: Although there is no ripened (*vipāka*) pleasure in the other hells, [there are still other forms of enjoyment].
Yet there is a joy and bliss that is a result of maturation (*niṣyanda*),
as stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
"In the Saṃjīva hell, at times and for a duration, a cool breeze blows briefly."
Or, upon hearing such a voice crying out,
"Revive! Revive!",
those sentient beings suddenly come back to life.
The joints, flesh, and blood are restored to their original state,
and for a brief moment, joy and pleasure arise;
because such things do not occur in the Avīci Hell, it is named "Uninterrupted" (Avīci).
Furthermore, there are those who say that because the number of sentient beings born there is so vast that there is no interval or gap between them,
it is therefore called "Avīci" (the Uninterrupted).
This statement is incorrect.
Why is this so? Because it is those who have committed superior grades of evil conduct that are born in that hell.
Not all sentient beings in the world are able to give rise to superior unwholesome conduct;
just as one must cultivate superior wholesome conduct to be born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
not all sentient beings in the world are able to give rise to superior wholesome conduct.
Therefore, those born at the Peak of Existence are few;
likewise, those born in the Avīci Hell are also few.
For this reason, they are not mentioned.
Question: If that is so, why is it called "uninterrupted" (ānantarya)?
Answer: It is designated as "uninterrupted" with reference to its maturation fruit (vipākaphala), because sentient beings who commit great evil deeds are born in those hells.
Having attained a vast body, each and every bodily form is entirely expansive;
because it pervades those many locations without any intervening gaps, it is called "uninterrupted" (*nirantara*).
From the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-mahāvibhāṣā* of the Sarvāstivāda school, scroll number one hundred and fifteen.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 116,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Four: The Aggregate of Karma (Karmaskandha), First Sub-section: The Chapter on Evil Conduct (Duścarita-nirdeśa), Part Five. Question: Regarding this karma that can take the fruit of a lifespan for one kalpa, what kind of kalpa is it?
Some say this is the kalpa of formation;
others say it is the kalpa of destruction.
This is the kalpa of destruction.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is a great kalpa (mahākalpa).
This refers to an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
This is because, as stated in the Vinaya, there are those who attain liberation even before that intermediate kalpa has fully elapsed.
Devadatta shall be reborn among humans when the human lifespan is forty thousand years;
he will certainly realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
This is beyond the reach of Śāriputra and others.
One must explain how the following verse is to be understood:
"Those who break the Saṃgha / Destroy the harmonious Saṃgha."
Regarding those born in the Avīci Hell, the *Āyuṣpramāṇa-sūtra* states that they remain for a full kalpa.
The Venerable Vasumitra says:
"Even dwelling for less than a kalpa is termed 'one kalpa'."
Just as people in the world refer to one who performs their duties for even a day less than the full term as being "on duty" (zhirì),
so it is in this case as well.
Question: This offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha can also bring about the maturation of the five aggregates in hell;
why, then, is it said only that it brings about a lifespan of one kalpa? Some say:
With life as the foremost,
the World-Honored One spoke in general terms of the fruit of grasping at the five aggregates.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
In this context, the Blessed One taught the most preeminent dharma;
that is to say, among the five aggregates, vitality (*āyus*) is the most preeminent, and for this reason it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Life-span (*āyus*) is specifically mentioned because it can sustain all five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*),
preventing them from disintegrating.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Life-force proceeds from birth until the exhaustion of the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga) without interruption,
thereby ensuring that the homogeneous class also remains uninterrupted;
other dharmas are not like this, and for that reason they are not mentioned.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the world is known to be either increasing or decreasing by virtue of its lifespan.
There may be progress or retreat, or rise or decline;
for this reason, it is explained in part by asking: "Why does causing a schism in the Saṃgha result in the offense of being barred from dwelling for an eon?"
Is it not by giving rise to an evil mind that one sheds the blood of a Buddha?
Answer: If one gives rise to an evil mind and sheds the blood of a Buddha, thereby destroying the Buddha’s physical body;
or if one destroys the Saṃgha, thereby destroying the Buddha’s Dharma-body.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
revere the Dharma-body and do not value the birth-body.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
If one gives rise to an evil mind and draws blood from the body of a Buddha, one merely insults the Honored One;
if one causes a schism in the Saṃgha, it is called insulting that which is cherished by the Honored One;
if one gives rise to an evil mind and draws blood from the body of a Buddha, one merely harms the Great Teacher.
If one causes a schism in the Saṃgha, it is called injuring that which the Great Teacher himself teaches.
Just as it is with the Great Teacher,
so too is it with the Dharma-king, the refuge, the support, and the resort.
Some say that when one gives rise to the intent to kill and sheds the blood of a Buddha,
this constitutes only an offense of preliminary application (*prayoga*).
Because the nature of the Buddha-dharma is such that it cannot be harmed;

whereas the schism of the Saṃgha is not so, and is thus a fundamental offense (mūlāpatti), just as there is a distinction between the preliminary application (prayoga) and the fundamental act (maula).
The culmination of such preparatory effort is likewise so.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if one gives rise to an evil mind and draws blood from the body of a Buddha, [it constitutes an immediate offense].
One does not initiate extensive preparatory efforts,
but rather causes injury through sudden and violent impulsiveness;
the schism of the Saṃgha is not like this.
One must initiate extensive preparatory applications for a period ranging from one month to four months,
employing skillful means to entice and deceive newly ordained bhikṣus so that they comply with oneself.
Only then can it be destroyed; therefore, the offense is grave.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if one gives rise to an evil mind and draws blood from the Buddha’s body, yet does not disturb or trouble the great assembly, [the offense is different].
Although they wound the Buddha’s body, they cannot cause the Buddha to give rise to a mind of affliction or agitation,
nor do they disturb him;
for by performing this act, they [benefit] the sentient beings of the world.
Because some may hear it while others do not;
and because if the Saṃgha were split, there would be extreme clamor and great disturbance, causing vexation to the great assembly.
This is because those who, at the time of the schism, ought to enter the state of right nature and transcendence (samyaktva-niyāma) [would be hindered].
One cannot enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Those who ought to realize the fruits of the path do not realize them;
those who ought to become free from desire do not become free from desire.
Those who ought to exhaust their outflows will not be able to exhaust them;
they will not be able to recite, uphold, or contemplate the Tripiṭaka;
nor will they be able to contemplate all phenomena in a place of stillness.
Although they cultivate the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti),
they are unable to plant the seeds of the Three Vehicles;
thus, the Wheel of Dharma does not turn within this trichiliocosm.
The sound spreads from one to another until it reaches the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens,
causing their awakened wisdom to be unable to remain in a state of tranquil clarity and manifest its activity.
This occurs when the schismatic Saṃgha is about to be reconciled.
Those who were to enter the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) entered that very state;
those who were to realize the fruits of the path realized those very fruits.
Those who were to become free from desire attained freedom from desire;
those who were to exhaust their outflows attained the exhaustion of outflows.
Thereupon, there arose those who recited, upheld, and contemplated the Tripiṭaka.
In secluded places, they contemplate all phenomena,
cultivate the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti),
and are likewise able to plant the seeds of the three vehicles.
The wheel of Dharma was turned once again throughout the trichiliocosm.
The sound spread from one to another until it reached the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens,
causing their awakening wisdom to become tranquil, clear, and manifest in its activity.
For this reason,
even if one gives rise to an evil mind and sheds the blood of a Buddha,
one cannot produce a transgression that persists for the duration of an eon.
If one causes a schism in the Saṃgha, one is able to give rise to a transgression that persists for an eon.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a schism in the Saṃgha?
Answer: Its intrinsic nature consists of non-concordance (*asaṃprayoga*), which is an unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) dissociated formation (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*).
This is subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
That is to say, as stated elsewhere, there are other such types of formations dissociated from mind;
therefore, the schism of the Saṅgha is distinct from the offense of causing a schism in the Saṅgha.
The schism of the Saṃgha is a state of non-concordance that is unobscured and indeterminate;
it is subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
The offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha is false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).
Unwholesome vocal karma is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Just as the essence of retrogression differs from the dharma of retrogression,
the essence of retrogression is the state of non-possession (*aprāpti*), which is unobscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*),
and is subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayuktasaṃskāraskandha*).
The dharma of retrogression is unwholesome and is comprised within the five aggregates of the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
This is likewise distinct from the schism of the Saṃgha and distinct from the offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
By this, the schism of the Saṃgha is accomplished;
the offense of schism is accomplished by the person who causes the schism.
Question: In what place does the schism of the Saṃgha occur?
Answer: It occurs among humans in the desire realm.
If it is a schism of the formal community (*karmasamgha*), it occurs throughout the three continents;
if it is a schism of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-samgha*), it occurs only in Jambudvīpa.
Why is this? For wherever a Great Teacher can be found and where the Path can be found,
it is precisely in such a place that there is a schism in the Wheel of Dharma.
In other continents, there is neither a Great Teacher nor the Path;
therefore, there is likewise no one who can destroy the Wheel of Dharma.
For example, in this world, wherever there is a king, it is only there that a false king may arise.
Just as wherever there is a strongman, there arises one who engages in wrestling,
so it is here: wherever there is a Great Teacher, [there arise those who engage in debate].
In this place, false teachers arise;
where there is the True Path, there the false path arises. It is the nature of things that the false and the true are in opposition when occupying the same location.
Question: What is the difference between a schism in the Saṃgha through formal legal action (*karmabheda*) and a schism in the Wheel of Dharma (*cakrabheda*)?
Answer: Regarding the "breaking of the *karmavācanā*," this refers to a case where within a single boundary (*sīmā*),
two groups of the Saṃgha reside separately and perform the *poṣadha-karmavācanā* and the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*) individually.
One who breaks the wheel of the Dharma refers to one who establishes a different teacher and a different path,
such as Devadatta.
He says, "I am the Great Teacher;
I am not the śramaṇa Gautama.
These five dharmas are the Path."
This is not the Noble Eightfold Path taught by Gautama. Why is this?
Because if one can cultivate these five dharmas...
To quickly realize nirvāṇa, it is not by means of the Eightfold Path.
What are the five dharmas?
First, wearing rag-robes for as long as one lives.
Second, to subsist on almsfood for as long as life lasts;
third, to eat while seated in one posture for as long as life lasts;
fourth, to always dwell in the open air for as long as life lasts.
Fifth, for as long as one lives, one does not consume any fish, meat, blood-flavored foods, salt, clarified butter, milk, and so forth.

This is called the distinction between breaking the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) Saṃgha and breaking the Dharma-wheel Saṃgha. Regarding the time of breaking the Saṃgha, what is the absolute minimum number of persons required to constitute the act of breaking the Saṃgha?
Answer: To split the *saṃgha* by means of a formal act (*karmabhedaka*) requires at least eight persons;
only when there are four or more is it designated as a "Saṃgha," whereas three persons do not constitute such.
Within a single boundary (*sīmā*), there are two divisions of the Saṃgha, each residing separately.
When one performs the *poṣadha* *karmavācanā* and recites the precepts,
it is called a "destruction of the *karman*"; thus,
the minimum number required for a schism of the Wheel (*cakrabheda*) is nine persons.
Within a single boundary (sīmā), there are two divisions of the Saṃgha residing separately;
among those who lack a sense of shame (ahrikya-apatrāpya),
there is certainly one person who is respected by the assembly and capable of providing instruction.
You should know that this was Devadatta;
in the assembly of the righteous, there were at least four people,
and in the assembly of the heterodox, there were at least five.
In this way, when there are at most nine persons down to a minimum of nine, the Saṃgha of the Wheel of Dharma is destroyed.
Question: To what extent can it be said that the Saṃgha of the Wheel of Dharma is destroyed?
Answer: The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states:
Devadatta himself took the fifth tally;
at this point, it should be said that the Saṃgha of the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra-saṃgha) was split.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Having performed the formal declaration (jñapti),
there are others who say that one should depart from the place where the teaching was heard.
Furthermore, some say it is apart from the place where one sees;
others say it is apart from the places where one sees and hears.
Regarding this statement: if,
out of intention, one vows to accept another teacher,
that refers to those deluded bhikṣus.
Due to a resolute intention (*āśaya*), one gives rise to such a thought and utters such words as:
"Devadatta is my great teacher, not the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Up to this point, it should be said that the Wheel of Dharma and the Saṃgha have been destroyed.
Question: What kind of person (pudgala) causes a schism in the Saṃgha that disrupts the Wheel of Dharma?
Answer: There are two kinds of persons:
first, those whose conduct is dominated by craving (tṛṣṇā-carita).
The second is the schism caused by those who act out of views.
Those who act out of views destroy the Saṃgha of the Wheel of Dharma, not those who act out of non-affection.
This is because the underlying intentions of those who act out of views are firm and intense.
Regarding the tasks pertaining to the categories of affliction and purification, they possess a certainty from which there is no regression;
because those who act out of craving lack such qualities, they cannot cause a schism.
Furthermore, only a male can cause a schism in the Saṃgha that turns the Wheel of Dharma.
It is not women, nor is it *śaṇḍhas* or *paṇḍakas*, and so forth.
Why is this? Because at the time the Wheel of Dharma is broken, it is the natural law that [the one who breaks it] establishes themselves as the Great Teacher.
However, women are not superior vessels;
because they are unsuitable for the Great Teacher, they cannot cause a schism.
Nevertheless, they can extensively employ the means to bring about a schism in the Saṃgha.
Just as in the case of the bhikṣuṇī Audārikī and others, all *śaṇḍhas*,
*paṇḍakas*, those without sexual organs, and those with both sets of organs are characterized by craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*).
The inclinations (*āśaya*) of those characterized by craving are neither firm nor intense.
Because they are not fixed in either the defiled or the purified categories, such persons are unable to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
Question: At what time does one split the Dharma-wheel Saṃgha?
Answer: Among the six periods, one cannot cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
at other times, one can. That is to say, it is not during the initial period, nor during the final period, nor when the two types of boils have not yet appeared.
It is not at a time when [the community] has not yet come together to establish a boundary;
it is not at a time when the first pair [of disciples] has not yet been established;
nor is it at a time after the Great Teacher has entered parinirvāṇa.
Regarding "neither at the beginning nor at the end":
it is because during these two periods,
the community of bhikṣus remains unified in a single flavor within the holy teaching and cannot be divided.
"Not when the two blisters have not yet emerged" means that within the Noble Teaching,
it is not at a time when the two kinds of blisters— namely, those of precept and view— have not yet arisen.
"Not when [the community] has not yet come together to formally establish the boundary" means...
Since it is only when there are two assemblies of monks within a single boundary (*sīmā*),
dwelling separately and holding different views, that it is termed "schism" (*saṃghabheda*),
this does not apply before the first pair [of disciples] has been established.
This means that as long as the first pair [of disciples] has not yet been established, there is certainly no one capable of breaking the Wheel of Dharma within the Saṃgha;
it is the natural law of all Buddhas that they always possess this first pair of noble disciples.
If there are those who have disrupted the Wheel of Dharma and the Sangha,
he reunites this first pair before even a day and night has passed—
not after the Great Teacher has entered parinirvāṇa.
If, after the Great Teacher has entered parinirvāṇa,
someone were to say, "I am the Great Teacher, not the Tathāgata," everyone would collectively rebuke him, saying:
"While the Great Master was in the world, why did you not say, 'I am the Great Master'?
Only now, after his parinirvāṇa, do you speak these words.
Therefore, it is certain that the Wheel of Dharma shall not be destroyed during these six periods."
During other times, the Wheel of Dharma may be destroyed.
Question: In what state of mind does the Saṃgha become split? Some say:
Some say it abides in visual consciousness;
others say it abides in auditory consciousness.
Furthermore, there are those who say that it abides in the mental consciousness;
such is their explanation.
Within the six groups of consciousness, it is possible for a saṃgha to be split while abiding in any one of them.
Question: Abiding in what kind of feeling does a saṃgha become split?
Some say: [it occurs] in neutral feeling (*upekṣā*).
Some say he dwells in the faculty of pleasure;
others say he dwells in the faculty of pain.
Furthermore, some say that one abides in the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*). Others say: [one abides in the faculty of equanimity].
Some say they abide in the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*);
others say they abide in the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
According to this explanation, among the five types of feeling, the schism of the Saṃgha can occur while abiding in any one of them.
Question: Of what kind of mental state is the schism of the Saṃgha the fruit?
Some may say that this is the fruit of the mind of renunciation. Why is this so?
Because there is no destruction of the Saṃgha among householders.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the fruit of the mind is received through full ordination (upasaṃpadā).
Why is this? Because for the *śrāmaṇera*, there is no schism in the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
If one takes the result of the mind of receiving full ordination as proximate,
or takes the result of the mind of going forth as remote,
such is the explanation.
If the Saṃgha is split while abiding in this mind, it is the fruit of that very mind.
Question: What kind of *pudgala* can be split?
Answer: Only ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), not any of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Why is this? Because the Blessed One has declared that it is impossible and out of the question for any noble being (ārya) to be destroyed.
Question: Is it possible for those who have already attained the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) to be destroyed?
Some say that, apart from these,
all else is subject to destruction; others say:
This too may be refuted.
Why? Because the Blessed One has declared that there is no possibility or occasion for any noble being to be destroyed, whereas he did not make such a declaration regarding others.
Question: Since Devadatta was able to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, why is it said that the World-Honored One’s retinue is indestructible?
The Venerable Vasumitra replied:
In this context, those who have entered the four paths and attained the four fruits are called the retinue of the World-Honored One;
they are the true disciples and the genuine Saṃgha.
It is indestructible.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of the Buddha’s retinue:
first, those who are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The second is an *ārya*.
Devadatta only split [the community] among ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
For this reason, it is said that he was able to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
All noble ones (ārya) are indestructible.
For this reason, it is said that the retinue of the Blessed One is indivisible.
The Venerable One said:
The Buddha’s retinue is twofold:
first, the inner; second, the outer.
The inner refers to the noble ones, who are immovable and indestructible.
"External" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), who are movable and destructible.
Because ordinary worldlings therein are subject to movement and destruction,
Devadatta was able to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
Because the Noble One is immovable and indestructible, it is said that the Blessed One’s retinue is indestructible.
Question: At the time of the schism of the Saṃgha, was the Buddha present within the assembly?
Answer: At that time, the Buddha resided within the boundaries of that realm, but he was not among the assembly.
How is this known?
It was heard that when Devadatta intended to cause a schism in the Saṃgha,
the Buddha, out of compassion, rebuked and restrained him, saying:
Devadatta, do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
do not give rise to such extremely grave, evil, and unwholesome karma;
do not head toward a state of undesirable and great suffering as its fruit.
Although the Buddha thus earnestly rebuked and restrained him,
the man had no intention at all of desisting. At that time,
the World-Honored One gave rise to right knowledge and vision and examined the past.
"May it not be that in the past I destroyed the retinue of another.
He then observed for himself: "In the past, immeasurable and incalculable eons ago, I once destroyed the retinue of a rishi."
The maturation of that karma now manifested before him;
observing this, he knew that the Saṅgha would certainly be split.
He then entered his private chamber and sat in silent meditation.
Devadatta then brought about a schism in the Saṃgha.
Thus we know that the World-Honored One was within the boundary (sīmā) but not among the assembly.
Question: Do all Buddhas encounter such an event of a schism in their Saṃgha?
Some say: "It is not so. Why is that?"
If there is such an act of destroying another's karma,
and it is performed and increased, then there is a schism in the Saṃgha;
if such karma does not exist, then there is no schism in the Saṃgha— this applies except for the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni.
Because such karma was previously created and increased,
the present schism in the Saṃgha occurs, whereas it is not so for other Buddhas. Some say:
Other Buddhas also had their Saṃghas split.
It was heard that during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
there was a bhikṣu named Puṣpa, who was the son of Yaśottara.
One who commits the five deeds of immediate retribution severs the roots of goodness.
Question: Did Devadatta first cause a schism in the Saṃgha and subsequently sever the roots of goodness, or did he first sever the roots of goodness and subsequently cause a schism in the Saṃgha?
Some say that he first split the Saṃgha and subsequently severed his roots of goodness. Why is this so?
One must possess ethical discipline (*śīla*), extensive learning,
physical excellence, noble lineage, dignified authority, and skill in speech in order to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
If one severs the roots of goodness, one loses the pure precepts;
because it is not predominant, it cannot cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
The Venerable Vasumitra also spoke thus.
Devadatta first caused a schism in the Saṃgha and subsequently severed his roots of goodness.
Had he first severed his roots of goodness and only later caused a schism,
he would not have been able to incur the offense of dwelling for an eon at the time of the schism.
Why is this? It is not that a person who has severed their roots of virtue gives rise to the perception of what is non-Dharma within that which is non-Dharma.
One conceives the notion that there is an offense regarding the schism of the Saṃgha;
or, regarding what is non-Dharma, one conceives the notion that it is Dharma;
or, regarding the schism of the Saṃgha, one conceives the notion that there is no offense.
Furthermore, one who causes a schism in the Saṃgha can never produce the offense that lasts for an eon;
this requires that one perceive what is not the Dharma as not the Dharma,
and that one perceive the act of causing a schism as being sinful.
If it is only through such schisming of the Saṃgha that one can give rise to the offense of dwelling for an eon (*kalpa-sthāyin*),
does it follow by this principle that all who cause a schism in the Saṃgha necessarily give rise to the offense of dwelling for an eon?
If there are those who can generate the offense that causes one to remain for a kalpa, does it follow that all such persons can cause a schism in the Saṃgha?
One should formulate four propositions: there may be cases where one causes a schism in the Saṃgha but does not generate the offense that lasts for a kalpa.
That is to say, conceiving the notion that what is not Dharma is Dharma,
and conceiving the notion that the schism of the Saṃgha is not an offense,
one then causes a schism in the Saṃgha.
There may be cases where one generates a karma that results in dwelling for an eon, yet does not constitute a schism in the Sangha;
this refers, for example, to the severing of the roots of goodness.
There may also be cases where one both effects a schism in the Sangha and generates a karma that results in dwelling for an eon.
That is to say, one conceives of what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma,
and within the context of schisming the Saṃgha, one conceives of it as being blameworthy,
and thereby causes a schism in the Saṃgha.
There may be those who are unable to cause a schism in the Saṃgha,
nor can they incur the offense of dwelling for an eon;
this refers to excluding the aforementioned thoughts.
The Venerable One said:
"When he initiates the preparatory effort for schism in the Saṃgha,
he also initiates the preparatory effort for severing the roots of goodness."
When one initiates the preparatory effort to sever the roots of goodness,
one also initiates the preparatory effort to cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
therefore, at the time of that schism, the roots of goodness are severed.
When the roots of goodness are severed, the Saṃgha is split;
because he simultaneously commits these two offenses,
he incurs the most grievous and unwholesome karma.
Yet, they do not have even a single thought of regret or shame.
[The Buddha] asked: "Regarding those who commit the deeds of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karman), do they sever their roots of goodness?
Or, if they sever their roots of goodness, do they necessarily commit the deeds of immediate retribution?"
It can be answered in four propositions.
There are those who commit an act of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma) but do not sever the roots of goodness,
such as King Ajātaśatru and others.
There are those who sever the roots of goodness but do not commit an immediate transgression (ānantarya-karma),
such as the six heretical teachers;
there are also those who both commit an immediate transgression and sever the roots of goodness.
For example, Devadatta, Śakti, and others;
or there are those who neither commit an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*) nor sever their roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*),
which refers to all cases except those previously mentioned.
Among the three types of wholesome conduct (*sucarita*), which yields the greatest fruit?
It is the volition (*cetanā*) within the meditative attainment of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
This karma can secure the fruit of an eighty-thousand-eon lifespan in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
It should be understood that this answer is given based on the question concerning the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
If the question were based on the five fruits,
or if it were based solely on the fruit of disconnection (*visamyogaphala*), the answer should be formulated as follows.
This refers to the volition associated with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
This volition is capable of realizing the fruit of the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) that all fetters (*saṃyojana*) have been completely abandoned.
It is because the intention here is to inquire about the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) that this answer is given.
Question: Is it a single volition that brings about a lifespan of eighty thousand kalpas, or are there many volitions?
If it is a single volition, [how can this be so]?
How can a small amount of karma produce such a vast result?
If it were the case that there are many volitions (*cetanā*),
why is it not called a distinct result of a single homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*)?
Some say that a single volition (*cetanā*) is capable of producing [the result].
Question: How can a small amount of karma produce such a vast fruit?
Answer: First, a single volition brings about the general result; subsequently, many volitions bring it to completion.
It is like a painter who first uses a single color to create the outline, and later fills it in with various colors.
This is also like that.
Furthermore, there are those who say that it is volition (cetanā) that is capable of producing [karmic results].
Question: Why is it not called "the fruition of a single homogeneous group" (*eka-sabhāgatā-phala*)?
Answer: Because within that meditative absorption, one takes a single object and a single type of mental aspect (*ākāra*).
There are many volitions that arise in succession;
some are capable of bringing about a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas,
while others are capable of bringing about twenty thousand kalpas.
Some are able to bring about a lifespan of thirty thousand kalpas;
some are able to bring about a lifespan of forty thousand kalpas, and so forth.
In this way, various portions of volitional thought produce their respective results through differentiation.
However, based on a single type of preparatory application for a meditative concentration,
one gives rise to a corresponding state of concentration that takes a single object and a single mode of activity;
because many such thoughts arise in succession and manifest before the mind, they are termed "a single body."
Regarding this teaching:
a single volition initiates the process,
while multiple volitions bring it to completion.
Question: Is this volition included within the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka-bhūmi*), or is it included within the fundamental stage (*maula-bhūmi*)?
Some teachers say:
This is the preparatory stage (sāmantaka-bhūmi).
Furthermore, there are those who say it is the fundamental stage (maula-bhūmi).
To speak in this manner is not definitive;
it may refer either to the preparatory stage (sāmantaka-bhūmi) or to the fundamental stage (maula-bhūmi).
Why is this? Because all volitions belong to the same stage (*bhūmi*).
Question: What kind of eon (*kalpa*) is the "eighty thousand eons"?
Some say that this refers to an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*); others say:
[it refers to a great kalpa].
This is the kalpa of formation.
Furthermore, there are those who say this is the kalpa of destruction.
According to this explanation, this refers to a great eon (*mahākalpa*).
Question: Since this karma can take the maturation (*vipāka*) of the four aggregates, why is it said that it takes only the fruit of life-span?
Some say that with life as the precursor,
the Blessed One spoke in general of the four aggregates as the fruit of grasping.
Furthermore, there are those who say that herein the Blessed One taught the most preeminent dharma;
namely, that among the four aggregates, vitality is the most preeminent, and for this reason it is specifically mentioned.
Some say that it is life-force alone that can sustain the four aggregates so that they do not disintegrate; therefore, it is mentioned specifically. Others say:
Life-force remains uninterrupted throughout its single period,
causing the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) to likewise remain without interruption;
other dharmas are not so, and for this reason it is mentioned specifically.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the world is known to be either increasing or decreasing by virtue of its lifespan.
Whether advancing or retreating,
whether flourishing or declining—
it is for these reasons that "life span" is specifically mentioned.
Just as it was stated that misconduct and virtuous conduct bring about the greatest fruits of the agreeable and the disagreeable,
so too should the wholesome and unwholesome roots, along with the ten paths of action, be explained in detail.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots:
What is the greatest sin?
It is the false speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha.
This unwholesome root brings about the fruit of a lifespan of one kalpa in the Avīci Hell.
Among the ten unwholesome courses of action,
which constitutes the greatest offense?
It is the false speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha.
This karma can bring about the fruit of a lifespan of one eon in the Avīci Hell.
Among the three roots of goodness,
which one yields the greatest fruit?
This refers to the volition that can give rise to the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
This root of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) is capable of securing the fruit of eighty thousand *kalpas* of lifespan in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Among the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa kuśalakarmapatha*), [this is the foremost].
What is the greatest fruit?
It is that which is conjoined with volition within the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);
this path of action can induce the fruit of an eighty-thousand-aeon lifespan in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
It should be understood that because this is a brief exposition, only the greatest fruits of misconduct and sublime conduct are mentioned, and not others.

**The Section on Wrong Speech (Mithyāvāda-nirdeśa)** The first part of the second section of the fourth aggregate of action (*karmaskandha*), the Section on Wrong Speech: Are all those who engage in wrong speech also engaged in wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*)?
If one possesses wrong livelihood, does one also possess wrong speech?
Having thus mastered these sections and their respective commentaries,
one should next provide a detailed explanation.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was in order to refute the tenets of other schools and to clarify one's own doctrine.
That is to say, the Dārṣṭāntikas assert that right livelihood and wrong livelihood have distinct essential natures apart from speech and action.
For what reason do they make this assertion?
On account of the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra regarding the Noble Eightfold Path, they say this:
Regarding the eight factors taught by the Buddha,
each has its own essential nature and they do not intermingle;
it is on this basis that right livelihood and wrong livelihood are distinguished.
This treatise is composed to refute the view that there exists a substantial entity apart from vocal action,
and to clarify that right livelihood and so forth are themselves vocal action;
this is as in the case of the unwholesome paths of vocal action.
If that which arises from greed is called wrong speech,
it is also called wrong livelihood,
because it is undertaken for the sake of livelihood.
That which arises from hatred and delusion is called only wrong speech,
not wrong livelihood,
because it does not arise for the sake of one's livelihood.
Among the unwholesome courses of bodily action,
that which arises from greed is called wrong action and is also called wrong livelihood.
Those actions arising from hatred and delusion are called merely "wrong action" (mithyākarmānta),
but are not called "wrong livelihood" (mithyājīva).
The reason is as stated previously.
Among the wholesome paths of verbal action,
that which arises from non-attachment is called right speech and is also termed right livelihood.
Because it serves as an antidote to wrong livelihood,
that which arises from the absence of hatred and delusion is called right speech, not right livelihood.
Therefore, as previously stated,
within the wholesome courses of bodily action,
that which is originated by non-greed is called right action (samyak-karmānta).
It is also called right livelihood.
That which arises from the absence of hatred and delusion is called right action,
but it is not called right livelihood.
Therefore, as previously stated,
this demonstrates that right livelihood and wrong livelihood both have verbal action as their essential nature.
This is called the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
Are all instances of wrong speech also wrong livelihood?
Or, if there is wrong livelihood, is that necessarily wrong speech?
It can be answered in four propositions.
There is wrong speech that is not wrong livelihood;
this refers to the four types of evil conduct of speech, excluding those instances of speech that constitute wrong livelihood.
All other verbal misconduct consists of vocal karma arising from hatred and delusion;
because it is of the nature of vocal karma and does not arise for the sake of livelihood, it is not included [in the separate category].
There is that which is wrong livelihood but not wrong speech;
this refers to the three types of bodily misconduct arising from wrong livelihood,
specifically those bodily actions born of greed that are undertaken for the sake of one's livelihood.
Because it does not have the nature of vocal action (*vākkarman*).
This explanation should be applied accordingly to the subsequent section on speech.
There are cases where there is both wrong speech (*mithyāvāc*) and wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
This refers to the arising of speech that constitutes wrong livelihood and the four types of misconduct.
There are cases that are neither wrong speech nor wrong livelihood;
these refer to the three bodily misdeeds, excluding those that lead to wrong livelihood.
Regarding other bodily misconducts and various wrong actions,
are they all wrong livelihood? Conversely,
is whatever is wrong livelihood necessarily a wrong action?
It can be answered in four propositions.
There is unwholesome action that is not wrong livelihood;
this refers to the three types of bodily misconduct, excluding those that constitute wrong livelihood.
All other bodily misconduct is physical action (kāyakarman) arising from hatred and delusion;
because it is of the nature of physical action,
it is not undertaken for the sake of one's livelihood.
There is that which is wrong livelihood but not wrong action;
namely, the four types of verbal misconduct that constitute wrong livelihood,
which are vocal actions arising from greed because they are undertaken for the sake of livelihood.
Because it is not of the nature of bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
The latter two phrases are to be explained accordingly.
There is that which is both wrong action (*mithyākarma*) and wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
This refers to the three unwholesome bodily actions that lead to wrong livelihood.
There are also those which are neither wrong action nor wrong livelihood,
namely, excluding the four unwholesome verbal actions that lead to wrong livelihood.
Regarding the other verbal misconducts,
those among them that arise from greed are called wrong livelihood because they tend toward a wrong way of life.
Are all those who possess right speech also possessed of right livelihood?
If one possesses right livelihood, does one also possess right speech?
One should respond by setting forth four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is that which is right speech but not right livelihood.
This refers to all other forms of verbal good conduct (vāksucarita), excluding the four types of right speech that constitute the path to right livelihood;
these are vocal actions arising from non-hatred and non-delusion.
Because this is of the nature of vocal action (*vākkarman*),
and because it is not the antidote to wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*),
there is right livelihood that is not right speech.
This refers to the three types of excellent bodily conduct that constitute the pursuit of right livelihood;
specifically, it is the bodily action arising from non-greed,
as it serves as the antidote to wrong livelihood.
Because they do not have the nature of vocal action.

The latter two phrases are explained accordingly: there is also right speech that constitutes right livelihood, namely, those vocal fourfold wholesome paths of action that lead toward right livelihood.
There is that which is neither right speech nor right livelihood;
namely, with the exception of the three types of bodily wholesome conduct that lead to right livelihood,
