all other remaining types of bodily wholesome conduct.
Is that which is right action also right livelihood?
And is that which is right livelihood also right action?
One should answer by means of four propositions (catuṣkoṭika).
There is right action that is not right livelihood;
this refers to all other bodily wholesome courses of action, excluding those three bodily wholesome courses of action that constitute right livelihood.
It is the bodily action arising from non-hatred and non-delusion;
because it is of the nature of bodily action,
it is not the antidote to wrong livelihood.
There is right livelihood that is not right action;
this refers to the speech of one who has entered right livelihood and the four sublime courses of action,
which are vocal actions arising from non-greed.
Because it is the antidote to wrong livelihood and because it does not have the nature of bodily action;
the latter two phrases are explained accordingly.
There is that which is both right action and right livelihood;
namely, the three types of sublime conduct of body that lead toward right livelihood.
There is that which is neither right action nor right livelihood.
This refers to all other forms of verbal good conduct (vāksucarita), excluding the four types of right livelihood and speech,
which among these are originated from non-attachment (alobha).
Because they all tend toward right livelihood, they are called "right livelihood.
Having briefly demonstrated the characteristics of the mixed and the unmixed,
I shall now explain their specific distinctions in detail.
That is to say, if one engages in various unwholesome actions for the sake of profit and livelihood,
this is called wrong speech, wrong action,
and also wrong livelihood.
Because this is of the nature of vocal action,
because it is produced for the sake of livelihood,
and if there are other various causes and conditions.
Engaging in various evil deeds is termed wrong speech and wrong action,
but it is not termed wrong livelihood,
because these are by nature vocal and physical karma.
It is not for the sake of initiating life.
The other categories should be explained accordingly.
Furthermore, if there are various incantations for animals that correspond to their respective types.
Based on wrong livelihood,
the arising of various evil actions is called wrong verbal karma;
it is also termed wrong livelihood.
If one engages in various evil deeds for other diverse reasons,
it is termed wrong verbal action (*mithyāvākkarman*),
but it is not termed wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Furthermore, if one engages in various unwholesome actions due to the four causes and conditions of craving,
this is called wrong speech-action and is also called wrong livelihood.
If one engages in various unwholesome actions due to other conditions, it is termed wrong speech (*mithyāvākkarman*), but not wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Furthermore, if there is the practice of hypocrisy, hinting, or seeking profit through profit by means of the five conditions of wrong livelihood; [these constitute wrong livelihood].
Engaging in various unwholesome actions is called wrong verbal karma,
and it is also termed wrong livelihood.
If one engages in various unwholesome actions for other reasons, it is called wrong speech (*mithyāvāg-karman*),
but not wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Furthermore, if one initiates the preliminary application (*prayoga*) for an unwholesome action...
It is called wrong speech-action and is also called wrong livelihood.
If one initiates the fundamental paths of action that constitute unwholesome conduct, it is termed wrong speech-action.
This is not called wrong livelihood.
Why is this? Because it is difficult to eliminate through preparatory effort, as it pertains to the fundamental [state].
Furthermore, if one commits various prohibited offenses (pratikṣepaṇasāvadya),
it is called wrong verbal action (mithyāvākkarman) and is also called wrong livelihood (mithyājīva).
If one commits a natural transgression (prakṛti-sāvadya),
it is called wrong verbal action (mithyā-vāk-karman),
but it is not called wrong livelihood (mithyājīva).
Why is this so? Because prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*) are difficult to guard against, whereas they are not intrinsic transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
This is according to the principles explained through these six or seven categories.
It is certain that there is no "wrong livelihood" (mithyājīva) established separately outside of vocal karma.
Question: If this is so, why are the three types beginning with wrong speech mentioned, and why is the Eightfold Noble Path taught in the sūtras?
Is right livelihood explained separately from right speech and right action?

Answer: Because the Buddha taught that wrong livelihood deludes and deceives people, and because it is subtle and difficult to perceive, he manifested it simultaneously with right speech and right action, yet also manifested it separately.
It is like a commander of a bandit army who, after having his subordinates executed en masse,
has them further beheaded individually.
Others say it is because various forms of wrong livelihood are difficult to purify completely.
Therefore, he censures them simultaneously with their verbal karma;
furthermore, he censures them separately, just as one censures women for both their desire for various activities and their desire for afflictions,
censuring them for their faults both simultaneously and separately.
What is wrong livelihood that is difficult to purify?
It refers to two things that are difficult to eliminate and difficult to abandon:
namely, wrong view in those who live as householders.
Furthermore, those who have left the household life may maintain a wrong livelihood.
Although laypeople may be extremely intelligent and uphold the five precepts,
when oppressed by suffering, they resort to various incense, flowers, food, and drink to offer sacrifices and prayers to celestial deities.
Although those who have left the household life may be extremely wise and maintain the full precepts,
because the conditions for sustaining their physical lives are dependent upon others,
when they see a donor, they immediately adjust their deportment and manifest an appearance of intimacy and friendliness.
For this reason, wrong livelihood and right livelihood are explained separately;
both the Sūtras and the Prajñapti-śāstra state that everything from taking life up to wrong view is of three kinds.
First, those arising from greed;
second, those arising from hatred;
and third, those arising from delusion.
How is taking life born of greed?
It refers to a case where someone, out of desire for skin, flesh, sinews, bones, and so forth,
harms another sentient being.
Or one might commit the act of killing someone who is beloved,
pleasing, or a friend who has previously or will in the future provide benefit to oneself.
Or another may seek to kill oneself by means of wealth and various benefits;
for example, kings and others recruit the brave and valiant with wealth and positions to subdue those who have not yet been conquered.
Such killings as these are said to arise from greed.
How do they arise from hatred?
It is when, for example, there is someone who, toward another sentient being...
There is a mind of harm and affliction,
a mind of resentment and aversion,
and a mind of malicious intent.
To take their life,
or to harm their relatives and friends in order to sever the path of enmity—
killing of this kind is said to arise from hatred.
How does [wrong view] arise from delusion? There is a certain class of people who give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine:
"Camels, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, deer, and so forth..."
They are all for the purpose of sacrificial offerings and for human consumption;
therefore, there is no sin in killing them.
Furthermore, there is another class who gives rise to such a view.
He establishes this argument:
"Tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, centipedes, snakes, and the like cause harm to humans;
therefore, to eliminate such a calamity for the sake of others, killing them incurs no sin."
Furthermore, in this western region, there is a mleccha named Mūka who holds such a view and propounds such a doctrine:
"When one's parents have grown old and infirm..."
Furthermore, if one encounters a chronic illness,
if one is able to kill [the patient], one will obtain merit and incur no guilt. Why is this so?
Now, those who are aged and infirm have their faculties decayed and are unable to eat or drink;
if they were to die, they would obtain new and superior faculties and could drink fresh, warm milk.
If one encounters a chronic illness and undergoes much suffering and affliction,
killing them so that they may be liberated upon death is without fault.
Such killings as these are said to arise from delusion.
Because one gives rise to false slander due to delusion regarding the fruits of karma,
how is taking what is not given born of greed?
It is as when someone, desiring another's property, takes it without it being given.
Or one commits theft against those who are beloved,
pleasing, or dear friends, or those who have previously or will in the future bestow benefit upon oneself.
Or when another seeks to take from oneself through wealth or various benefits by committing theft—
such as enlisting soldiers to plunder the treasures of others—
this kind of theft is said to arise from greed.
How does it arise from hatred?
It refers to when someone possesses toward sentient beings a mental disposition characterized by malice, resentment, enmity, and aversion.
Furthermore, stealing those objects to cause them distress,
or stealing the wealth of their friends and relatives out of hatred for them—
such acts of stealing are said to arise from anger.
How does it arise from delusion?
For example, there is a certain class of brahmins who give rise to such a view:
They establish this doctrine:
that all that exists upon the great earth was originally created by the supernatural power of the Brahmā King and bestowed upon the brahmins.
Now, the power of the Brahmins is weak;
as the Kṣatriyas and others encroach upon and seize their enjoyments,
when a Brahmin takes such enjoyments, he is taking his own property and incurs no guilt for theft.
However, when one takes such things while perceiving them as belonging to another,
theft of this kind is said to arise from delusion (*moha*),
because one is confused regarding karmic cause and effect and gives rise to false denial.
How is sexual misconduct born of greed?
It refers to that which is for the most part performed with a mind of attachment and defilement,
or for the sake of wealth, profit, and various beneficial matters.
Engaging in sexual misconduct toward various objects is called that which arises from greed.
What is that which arises from hatred?
That is to say, there is someone who, toward another sentient being,
possesses a mind characterized by malice, resentment, and ill will,
desiring to humiliate them and cause them to undergo various forms of decline and loss.
One then engages in sexual misconduct with that person;
this is called arising from hatred.
What arises from delusion?
It refers to the Brahmins who give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine:
"All Brahmins should maintain four wives."
Three for a kṣatriya,
two for a vaiśya,
and one for a śūdra.
If the number [of Brahmins] has not yet been completed,
there is no offense even in having sexual relations with another's wife;
however, at the time of that sexual act, the thought arises that it belongs to another.
Furthermore, in this western region there is a mleccha named Muka,
who holds such a view and maintains such a doctrine.
Regarding mothers, daughters, sisters, sons' wives, and so forth,
there is no offense whatsoever in engaging in sexual desire with them. Why is this?
All women are like ripe fruits, prepared food and drink, roads, bridges, boats, staircases, and mortars;
it is the nature of things that they are to be enjoyed in common by sentient beings.
Therefore, there is no fault in engaging in sexual desire with them.
These types of misconduct are said to arise from delusion,
for the reasons previously stated.
How is false speech born of greed?
It is as when someone, for the sake of fame or profit,
speaks while concealing their true perception regarding another sentient being.
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others—
just as kings and others recruit eloquent debaters to travel and engage in persuasion in order to entice those who have not yet submitted.
At that time, for the sake of wealth and status,
that person may deceive others based on what is internal,
or deceive themselves based on what is external.
Or, based on two [factors], one deceives two;
such false speech is called "arising from greed.
How does it arise from hatred?
That is to say, for instance, when one possesses a mind intent on harming others,
a mind of resentment and malice, and,
desiring to bring them down, utters false and deceptive speech.
Alternatively, when one utters false speech toward those who are beloved and dear friends out of hatred for them,
such false speech is said to arise from hatred.
How is it produced from delusion?
It refers to when someone gives rise to such a view and establishes such a doctrine.
Those who speak falsely when their own lives or the lives of others are at risk do not incur the offense of lying; for example,
as when a hunter asks where a deer is located.
Furthermore, when the enemy army asks where the king's army is located,
even if one has actually seen it and actually knows its position,
there is no fault in not answering truthfully if one fears that doing so would harm them.
One should know that such persons are not without fault.
Because they claim there is nothing at all, they repeatedly engage in such actions;
these instances of false speech are said to arise from delusion.
Therefore, it is as stated previously.
How is divisive speech born of greed?
It is said that there is someone who, for the sake of fame and profit, [engages in such speech].
One engages in divisive speech toward those sentient beings or their friends,
whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others,
such as when kings and others recruit eloquent debaters.
They cause divisive conduct to be practiced in order to bring others into submission;
at that time, those people, for the sake of wealth and status,
either turn inward or alienate themselves from others.
Either based on the external being separated from the internal,
or based on both being separated from both;
furthermore, there are two types of donors among the Brahmins.
First, the gift of clothing;
second, the gift of food.
The brahmin thought to himself:
If two donors are in harmony with one another,
I receive one item from each of them;
if they are at odds, I receive two items from each location.
Due to these causes and conditions, one engages in divisive speech;
this is said to arise from greed.
How does it arise from hatred?
If one possesses a mind that seeks to harm or afflict others, a sense of resentment, or a malicious intention,
and thereby causes a schism between them or between them and their friends in order to destroy them,
this is said to arise from hatred.
How does it arise from delusion?
For example, there is a certain class of Brahmins and others who give rise to such a view.
He established this argument:
"In households where there is no restraint,
if they seek to reconcile with one another, their evil deeds will only increase."
If they were to become estranged, their commission of evil would be diminished.
Therefore, if one speaks words of division among such classes of beings,
there is ultimately no fault.
This is called arising from delusion;
the reason is as stated before.
How does harsh speech arise from greed?
For example, using fame and profit to revile and humiliate other sentient beings—
whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others—
is like a king or similar authority entrusting cruel enforcers of the law to preside over the prisons.
Furthermore, when one commands military subordinates to compose proclamations and edicts,
and by means of such causes and conditions utters coarse and wicked speech,
this is said to arise from greed.
What is born from hatred?
It refers to when one possesses a mind intent on harming others, a mind of resentment and malice,
and then reviles them or their friends, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another.
This is called arising from hatred.
What is meant by arising from delusion?
It refers, for example, to the non-Buddhist practitioner known as Śikhin, who was called "Fire-Worshipper."
His nature was extremely impetuous and he frequently spoke coarse and evil words;
his disciples, considering this to be excellent, all practiced such coarse speech.
This is called arising from delusion.
Therefore, it is as stated previously.
How does frivolous speech arise from greed?
It refers, for example, to when someone engages in frivolous speech for the sake of their own or others' fame, profit, and so forth.
It is like an actor who, for the sake of profit,
engages in various songs, verses, jests, and miscellaneous talk in a great assembly;
or like men and women who, with minds stained by passion, engage in various forms of impure speech.
Furthermore, there are those who compose worldly writings and receive, maintain, and recite them; this is called arising from greed.
What is it that arises from hatred?
That is to say, as when one possesses a mind intent on harming others,
a mind of resentment, hatred, or ill will,
and speaks frivolous speech by means of belittling or mocking them.
Or, one may mock or deride those who are dear and beloved to another out of hatred for that person;
this is said to arise from hatred.
How does it arise from delusion?
For instance, there is a certain class of brahmins who give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine.
There are those who kindle sacrificial fires,
or worship other deities,
or recite the various mantras and incantations of the Vedas.
All attain pure liberation;
this is called arising from delusion,
for the reasons previously stated.
How is it that greed arises from greed?
It means that immediately after the entanglement of greed, the entanglement of greed manifests before one;
this is called greed arising from greed.
How is it that greed arises from anger?
It means that immediately after the obsession of anger (*dveṣa-paryavasthāna*), the obsession of greed (*rāga-paryavasthāna*) manifests before one.
This is called greed arising from anger.
How does it arise from delusion?
It means that immediately following the envelopment of delusion (*moha-paryavasthāna*), the envelopment of craving (*rāga-paryavasthāna*) manifests before one.
This is called craving arising from delusion.
How is it that hatred arises from greed?
It means that immediately after the obsession with greed (*lobha-paryavasthāna*), the obsession with hatred (*dveṣa-paryavasthāna*) manifests before one;
this is called hatred arising from greed.
What is that which arises from hatred?
It refers to the manifestation of the obsession of hatred immediately following the obsession of hatred;
this is called that which arises from hatred.
How does it arise from delusion?
It means that immediately after the envelopment of delusion (*moha-paryavasthāna*), the envelopment of hatred (*dveṣa-paryavasthāna*) manifests before one.
This is called hatred arising from delusion.
How is it that wrong view arises from greed?
It means that immediately after the obsession of greed, the obsession of wrong view manifests before one;
this is called wrong view arising from greed.
How does it arise from hatred?
It means that immediately after the obsession of hatred (*dveṣa-paryavasthāna*), the obsession of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-paryavasthāna*) manifests.
This is called wrong view arising from hatred.
How does it arise from delusion?
It refers to the manifestation of the fetter of wrong view immediately following the fetter of delusion;
this is called wrong view arising from delusion.
Question: It has already been understood that all ten unwholesome courses of action arise from greed, hatred, and delusion.
Among these, how many constitute the preliminary application (*prayoga*) for each one?
To what extent can it be said that [the mind] is ultimately capable of arising?
Some teachers have said:
The three [karmas] of taking life, harsh speech, and malice have their preparatory stage through greed,
while their completion is through hatred.
So too for taking what is not given and sexual misconduct.
And there are three [paths of action] involving covetousness,
which are preparatory acts completed through covetousness.
The remaining paths of vocal action are three.
The three [types of misconduct] have wrong view as their preparatory stage and ignorance as their consummation;
the one type [of sexual misconduct] has ignorance as its preparatory stage and ignorance as its consummation.
Furthermore, there are those who say that sexual misconduct is not fixed; that is to say,
if one maintains that it only constitutes a path of action when it results in the emission of semen.
Thus, three [actions] constitute the preliminary effort (*prayoga*), while [the act] is completed through greed (*lobha*).
If one were to maintain that the path of action (*karmapatha*) is established as soon as one enters the "foul gateway" (*durgatidvāra*),
then three [actions] would constitute the preliminary effort, and [the act] would be completed by all three.
All remaining courses of action are entirely characterized by three [factors]:
they have three as their preliminary application (*prayoga*) and are completed by means of the three. *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 116.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 117,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section 2 of the Second Sub-section on Wrong Speech within the Fourth Aggregate of Action (Karmaskandha):
There is restraint; there is non-restraint.
There are those who abide in restraint and those who abide in non-restraint.
What is restraint?
It consists of seven types, namely:
abstaining from taking life,
up to and including abstaining from frivolous speech.
What is non-restraint?
It also consists of seven types, namely:
taking life, up to and including frivolous speech.
What is meant by "abiding in the vows"?
It refers to the seven classes of practitioners:
first, the bhikṣu.
1. Bhikṣuṇīs; 2. Śikṣamāṇās; 3.
Śrāmaṇeras. 4. Śrāmaṇeras.
5. Female śrāmaṇerikās; 6. Upāsakas; 7. Upāsikās.
What is meant by "dwelling in non-restraint"? It refers to twelve kinds of families of non-restraint:
first, sheep-slaughterers;
second, poultry-slaughterers.
Third, pig slaughterers;
fourth, bird catchers;
fifth, fishers.
Sixth, hunting;
seventh, committing robbery;
eighth, serving as an executioner.
9. Binding dragons;
10. Guarding hell;
11. Boiling dogs.
Twelfth, the *pāguḷika*. Herein,
a sheep-slaughterer,
for the sake of making a living, harbors a mind of killing.
Whether buying or selling, or raising livestock for slaughter,
all such acts are termed "butchering sheep.
Butchering chickens and butchering pigs are likewise so called.
Bird-catchers,
for the sake of making a living, capture various birds;
those who catch fish and so forth do likewise.
As for those who bind dragons,
they practice incantations against dragons and snakes for the sake of their livelihood;
some say they bind elephants.
"Dog-cookers" refers to those such as the Caṇḍālas and other defiled and wicked people.
"Bakula" refers to...
There is a class of animals called *bakuḷa*,
which are a species of python;
they constantly devour traveling merchants in the wilderness.
There was a man who specialized in killing them,
taking the price of the merchant caravans to sustain his own life;
for this reason, he was named Bāhulika.
Some say that a snare or trap is called *vāgurā*. There are those who,
for the sake of making a living, constantly set such snares and traps.
He is called Bāhulika because he seizes sentient beings;
some say he is called Bāhulika because he is a master hunter.
As it is said in a verse:
"As a deer that has emerged from the *bāhulika* forest of suffering never again returns to the *bāhula* grove,
so the wise who have abandoned the mundane world and gone forth into homelessness never again return to the oppression of suffering."
The Venerable Ghosaka spoke thus:
"If one receives a superior command to interrogate a prisoner and,
following one's own whims, inflicts cruel and violent suffering upon them."
Whether it be adjudicating matters unjustly or imposing taxes with a malicious mind—
all such as these are called those who abide in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Question: These various forms of restraint (*saṃvara*) must be received in order to be obtained.
Is it the same for this non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)? Some say: [it is].
It is also acquired through formal undertaking;
that is, holding a weapon in one's hand and vowing from this day until the end of life to constantly perform this action as a means of livelihood.
At that moment, one then acquires this non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that even if one takes up the instruments of killing and makes a personal vow, [one acquires it].
However, one does not obtain this non-restraint [merely by birth].
It is obtained through two conditions:
first, through the performance of an action; [the second being the undertaking of a vow].
Second, by way of undertaking the activity;
that is, by way of the agent,
it refers to one born into a family of non-restraint who first performs those actions such as killing.
At that time, one acquires this non-restraint by undertaking the activity; that is,
being born into another family, one conceives a mind of killing for the sake of making a living.
He goes to those who practice the non-restraint of sheep-slaughterers and the like,
and makes this vow: "From this day forth until the end of my life,
I shall constantly perform the work you do for my livelihood."
At that time, one then acquires this non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that this also occurs at the very first moment of performing that action.
Only then does one obtain this non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
He asserts that non-restraint is obtained through a single condition:
if one undertakes the various restraints (*saṃvara*) by means of a weak mind (*mṛdu-citta*) while performing informative action (*vijñapti-karman*).
Throughout the entirety of that homogeneous life-span (*nikāya-sabhāga*), those various restraints continue to function at a low level;
even though at a later time one exerts effort to initiate bodily, vocal, and mental conduct comprised of either unwholesome or wholesome deeds.
However, that restraint always functions at a low level and does not further increase.
If one undertakes various restraints by means of a mind of medium intensity and performs informative action (*vijñapti-karman*),
those restraints will persist at a medium level for as long as the life-span (*nikāya-sabhāga*) lasts.
Although at a later time they exert effort to initiate the restraint of misconduct and the practice of sublime conduct through body, speech,
and mind, their discipline nevertheless continues to function constantly at a middling level, neither increasing nor decreasing.
If one generates manifest karma and receives the various vows with a superior mind,
those vows will continue to function at a superior level for as long as that homogeneous life-stream persists.
Even if, at a later time, one exerts effort to produce bodily, vocal, or mental misconduct or virtuous conduct, [the vows remain superior].
However, that restraint always functions at a superior level and does not diminish further; therefore, it is so.
Question: Is it possible for a newly ordained bhikṣu to achieve a superior level of restraint?
"And does an Arhat achieve a lower grade of restraint?
Answer: "Yes.
That is to say, there is a newly ordained bhikṣu who, with a superior mind,"
There are those who, having given rise to informative action (vijñapti-karman), receive various vows (saṃvara).
There are Arhats who, with a mind of inferior grade,
give rise to informative action and receive various vows.
In this way, a newly ordained bhikṣu may possess the highest grade of restraint,
whereas an arhat may possess only the lowest grade of restraint.
Suppose there were one who, initially, with a mind bound by the lowest grade of fetters, were to take the life of a living being.
In this regard, with respect to these sentient beings, one incurs the manifest and unmanifest karma comprised by the minor grade of taking life,
as well as that comprised by non-restraint (*asaṃvara*),
with respect to all other sentient beings.
One acquires only an unmanifest action (avijñapti) subsumed under an inferior grade of non-restraint; however,
if at a later time one takes the life of a sentient being while bound by fetters (paryavasthāna) of inferior, medium, or superior grades,
one acquires [unmanifest action] of inferior, medium, or superior grades respectively with respect to that sentient being.
The manifest and unmanifest karma subsumed under the taking of life does not further entail manifest and unmanifest karma subsumed under non-restraint,
because it has already been acquired; thus, at the very beginning, by means of a medium-grade or superior-grade fetter (*paryavasthāna*).
The same applies to the detailed exposition.
This is because, regarding acts such as taking life and so forth,
one may acquire non-restraint either gradually according to specific instances or all at once in its entirety.
Question: If one who slaughters sheep does not wish to kill other sentient beings, why is it that this person incurs non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) toward all sentient beings?
Answer: Although the non-restraint arises specifically with respect to sheep, [it extends to all].
However, all sentient beings possess the aggregates, elements, and bases [of a sheep];
furthermore, because the object of that evil mind is vast and pervasive,
one incurs non-restraint with respect to all of them.
It is impossible for this to occur because of conceptual differentiation;
even if all sentient beings were to take the form of sheep and come to stand before one, toward them all—
All give rise to malicious intent and all desire to kill;
therefore, they incur non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) toward all sentient beings.
One who abides in non-restraint—
There is the acquisition of non-restraint toward all sentient beings,
which does not arise from all factors (aṅga) nor from all causes (hetu).
There is one who acquires non-restraint with respect to all sentient beings by means of all its constituent parts,
but not by means of all its causes.
There is the case where one incurs non-restraint with respect to all sentient beings by means of all causes,
but not by means of all factors.
There is the acquisition of non-restraint toward all sentient beings by means of all factors and by means of all causes.
If, by means of all factors and all causes,
one acquires non-restraint (asaṃvara) but not toward all sentient beings;
This category of "not being any single sentient being" is precisely the category of all sentient beings.
As for "all branches":
This refers to taking life up to and including speaking frivolous and corrupt speech.
"All causes" refers to the lower,
middling, and superior fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
Alternatively, through greed, hatred, or delusion,
one may incur non-restraint with respect to all sentient beings,
but not by means of all its constituent factors.

"Not by all causes" means that one takes the life of a sentient being through either a medium or superior degree of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*), and not otherwise; nor does it arise from other factors.
Furthermore, there are those who incur non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) with respect to all sentient beings.
"By all factors, but not by all causes" refers to cases such as taking the life of a living being through the lower fetters,
up to and including the utterance of frivolous speech.
Or it may be of medium or superior grade, but not otherwise.
There are those who acquire non-restraint toward all sentient beings through all causes, but not through all factors.
This refers to one who, by means of weak, medium, or strong fetters (*paryavasthāna*), takes the life of a living being and does not give rise to the other factors;
such a person incurs non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) toward all sentient beings,
by way of all factors and by way of all causes.
This refers to taking the lives of sentient beings through weak, medium, or intense fetters,
up to and including the utterance of frivolous speech;
[this applies] to one who abides in the restraint.
There is the attainment of restraint with respect to all sentient beings,
but not by means of all branches,
nor by means of all causes.
There is the attainment of restraint with respect to all sentient beings by means of all branches,
but not by means of all causes.
There is the attainment of restraint toward all sentient beings,
by way of all factors and by way of all causes.
If one were to obtain restraint toward all sentient beings through all causes but not through all branches,
such a case does not exist.
If one were to obtain restraint through all its branches and through all its causes,
yet not with respect to all sentient beings,
then there would likewise be no such thing as "all sentient beings."
This refers to all classes of sentient beings.
"All factors" refers to abstaining from taking life up to and including abstaining from frivolous speech.
The "all causes" refers to the minds of inferior, middling, and superior grades,
or [the roots] of non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
There is the case where one obtains restraint with respect to all sentient beings,
yet not through all branches and not through all causes;
this refers to receiving the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) with an inferior mind.
Whether medium or superior, or both [medium and superior], but not otherwise.
There are those who obtain the restraint with respect to all sentient beings,
yet possess all branches but not all causes.
That is to say, one receives the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) up to those of a monk (*bhikṣu*) with either an inferior, middling, or superior mind;
or with two [of these], but not otherwise.
There are those who obtain the restraint (*saṃvara*) with respect to all sentient beings.
Regarding that which consists of all branches and all causes:
this refers to receiving the lay follower (*upāsaka*), novice (*śrāmaṇera*), and full monk (*bhikṣu*) precepts respectively by means of inferior, middling, and superior minds.
Question: If one receives the vows of the upavāsa,
the upāsaka, or the śrāmaṇera through inferior, middling, or superior states of mind, respectively,
is it then said that one obtains the restraint (saṃvara) with respect to all sentient beings?
Furthermore, while it is the case that all [vows] have causes, they do not all possess every branch.
Why, then, is it said that [the one-day vow] has none?
The answer is: this discussion is based solely upon the lifelong restraint (*yāvajjīva-saṃvara*), and does not apply to the day-and-night restraint (*rātri-divasa*).
Why is this? Because that which is called "fasting" (upoṣadha) is not definitive within the context of the vows of restraint (saṃvara).
Question: Just as one who has received the vows of restraint may subsequently attain the medium grade after the inferior grade,
and the superior grade after the medium grade,
is it the same for those who possess non-restraint?
Some say that as it is with the acquisition of restraint (*saṃvara*), so it is with non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). Why is this?
Even those who practice various wholesome restraints with great effort and great application obtain them only intermittently;
how much more so, then, the case of non-restraint?
Regarding this statement that discipline is acquired gradually and not non-discipline: why is this so?
Because restraint is difficult to obtain, it is received and acquired gradually;
because non-restraint is easy to obtain, it is received and acquired all at once.
Question: Just as with virtuous restraint, there may be cases where its branches are incomplete.
Is it the same for all forms of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)?
The masters of the Gandhāra country reply:
"The karma of non-restraint does not possess all its constituent parts (*aṅga*)."
If sentient beings are born into various families of non-restraint and are born mute and unable to speak for the duration of their entire lifespan,
they can only possess the nature of non-restraint regarding the three types of bodily action.
One must not say there are four [types].
All the great masters of Kaśmīra unanimously maintain this view:
that those who lack the vows of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) do not possess all its constituent parts.
Just as one who gradually undertakes a virtuous discipline may lack some of its constituent factors,
such is not the case for non-discipline (*asaṃvara*),
because it is not undertaken gradually and is easily acquired.
Question: When one who dwells in non-restraint receives the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), they relinquish non-restraint and acquire restraint.
Upon reaching the following morning, do they relinquish that restraint and return to non-restraint?
The masters of the Gandhāra country reply:
"When one who abides in non-restraint receives the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa),
they relinquish non-restraint and acquire restraint."
When morning comes, by relinquishing the restraint, one returns to non-restraint.
Because one has obtained the restraint, non-restraint was severed;
because one has relinquished the restraint, non-restraint continues.
The great masters of Kaśmīra all maintain this position:
when one who abides in non-restraint receives the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa),
they relinquish non-restraint and acquire restraint.
When morning arrives, one abandons the non-restraint and does not obtain it;
because one obtains restraint, one abandons the non-restraint.
Furthermore, one abandons the restraint because its duration has reached its limit.
Therefore, at that time, it is called neither restraint nor non-restraint.
If those sentient beings exhaust their commonality of kind (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and no longer perform [the action],
they do not fail to acquire non-restraint.
If one who has undertaken [the vows] again commits an act that results in non-restraint,
the lifelong restraint is relinquished through four conditions.
First, by abandoning what has been studied.
Second, being born with both sexual organs;
third, severing the roots of goodness;
fourth, relinquishing the homogeneous character of one's class.
The masters of the Vinaya say that the disappearance of the Dharma constitutes the fifth condition;
that is to say, at the time when the Dharma disappears.
All that is to be studied:
the going forth, the reception of full ordination,
the demarcation of boundaries, and the formal acts of the Saṃgha.
All [afflictions] are completely extinguished;
therefore, at that time, the restraint is also relinquished.
Thus it is said.
At that time, one who has previously obtained the vows does not forfeit them;

those who have already left the household life are still called "those who have left the household life," and those who have already received full ordination are still called "those who have received full ordination."
Those who have not yet left the household life shall no longer leave it;
those who have not yet received full ordination shall no longer receive it.
It is on this basis that it is said that "all things have ceased."
The various forms of non-restraint are abandoned through four conditions:
first, by undertaking the prātimokṣa restraint;
second, by attaining the dhyāna restraint.
Third, the arising of both genders;
fourth, the relinquishing of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Question: Just as one who possesses the virtuous restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*) relinquishes the training (*śikṣā*), [how does one relinquish it]?
Is the relinquishing of this non-restraint also like this?
Answer: Some say that if one can definitively renounce all instruments of killing, [the non-restraint is relinquished].
Regarding the statement that "at that time, one abandons the non-restraint":
although one has indeed definitely discarded all the instruments of killing, [the non-restraint is not thereby abandoned].
If one does not receive the precepts, one may obtain the discipline of goodness,
but one can never be said to have abandoned non-discipline or the three types of evil conduct.
The three types of defilement and turbidity;
this is explained at length.
Question: For what reason was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As the sūtra states:
"There are three types of unwholesome conduct."
Third is the corruption of defilement.
Although the sūtras state this,
they do not provide an extensive analysis or detailed exposition as was done previously.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"In the preceding section (*naṣika*), the three types of unwholesome conduct (*akuśala-karman*) have already been analyzed,
but the three types of crookedness, corruption, and turbidity (*vaṅka-doṣa-kaṣāya*) have not yet been analyzed."
Now, wishing to provide a detailed analysis, I have composed this treatise.
There are three types of crookedness, defilement, and turbidity:
namely, crookedness of body, defilement of body, and turbidity of body.
What are the three crookednesses: crookedness of speech, impurity of speech, and turbidity of speech;
crookedness of mind, impurity of mind, and turbidity of mind?
What are these three crookednesses?
This refers to the actions of body, speech, and mind arising from guile (*śāṭhya*). Why is this so?
Guile is defined as crookedness (*vaṅka*).
The three types of action arising from phenomena characterized by crookedness are called "crooked" because they are the fruit thereof.
Question: For what further reason is guile (śāṭhya) called "crooked"?
Answer: Because they are directly contrary [to the path]. As a verse says:
"All that is winding and crooked, Uneven, not straight, and not upright."
"Steep pits, ravines, and dense forests"— these all serve as metaphors for their deceit.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because all sentient beings are defiled and corrupted by deceit.
It is difficult to emerge from birth and death and difficult to enter nirvana,
just as it is difficult for a crooked tree to exit a dense forest or enter a village;
because this is also like that, it is called "crooked."
Furthermore, there are those who say that because sentient beings are defiled by deceit,
when their various undertakings are about to manifest before them, [they falter].
Furthermore, having turned away and being about to speak, one again withdraws and restrains oneself;
because one's nature is treacherous and evil,
making it difficult to grasp one's intent and hard with whom to associate, it is called "crookedness."
Furthermore, there are those who say that because sentient beings are defiled by deceit,
all the wise should keep them at a distance.
Just as a person who delights in purity flees from the stench and filth of corpses in a cemetery because they find it loathsome,
that [state] is called "crooked.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Because sentient beings are defiled by deceit,
the Buddhas likewise abandon great compassion toward them,
just as a skilled physician abandons a patient who is deceitful.
It is called "crookedness" because it obstructs correct transformation.
Question: Where does guile reside?
Answer: It resides in the desire realm and the first dhyāna, but not in the higher stages.
Question: For what reason is there no guile (*śāṭhya*) in the higher realms? Answer:
In the higher realms, guile is not a field, not a vessel, not a ground, and not a basis.
Because they are not fields, not vessels, and not bases,
these do not exist therein.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
In order to eliminate such flattery and proceed to the higher stages,
if one were to encounter flattery again within those higher stages,
one should not apply effort to seek further advancement to them.
If the dharmas of a lower stage were also present in a higher stage,
one could not establish the gradual cessation of dharmas;
and if one does not establish the gradual cessation of dharmas, [the stages cannot be differentiated].
Then there would be no such thing as a dharma that is ultimately extinguished.
If there were no dharma that is ultimately extinguished,
there would be no liberation.
If there were neither liberation nor birth-and-death, then all phenomena would not exist.
To avoid such an error, it is said that the higher stages are free from guile (*māyā*).
Furthermore, others say:
If, in this regard, one establishes kings and ministers,
or establishes the distinctions of high and low among sentient beings,
then there is guile.
Because such matters do not exist in the higher realms, there is no guile (*śāṭhya*).
Wherever there are kings, ministers, leaders, or distinctions of high and low status,
guile and crookedness (*anṛjutā*) must necessarily be harbored in their mutual interactions.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"In whatever place there are various groups of consciousness,
there is both vitarka and vicāra."
Furthermore, where there is the karma of bodily and vocal intimation possessing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is also deceit (*śāṭhya*).
Since such phenomena are entirely absent in the higher stages, there is no deceit there.
What are the three corruptions (*dausthulya*)?
This refers to the bodily, vocal, and mental karma arising from hatred. Why is this so?
Hatred is called "impurity."
The three types of action (karman) arising from phenomena characterized by impurity are called "impure" because they are the fruit thereof.
Question: Are all afflictions (kleśa) impure? As a verse says:
Just as the various weeds of the world can defile a fertile field,
so too do these weeds of greed defile all sentient beings.
The various weeds of the world can defile a fertile field.
In this way, these various defilements— the defilements that pollute all sentient beings,
namely conceit, craving, and ignorance—
as well as the remaining afflictions, are explained in the verses in the same manner.
Why is it that among these, only hatred (*dveṣa*) is called "corruption" (*kaṣāya*)?
Answer: Although all afflictions (*kleśa*) are indeed called corruptions, only hatred is uniquely designated as such because it alone possesses the name of both types of corruption.
As stated in the verse above: "In this way, all sentient beings are defiled by these various impurities.
Furthermore, some say that through this anger, one's own continuum is defiled.
It defiles the continuum of others;
because it is superior to other afflictions, it is called "corruption.
How does it corrupt one's own continuum?
That is to say, when hatred manifests,
the entire body becomes coarse and rigid, distressed and withered, contorted and trembling, and lacks composure;
one is as unpleasant to behold as a person possessed by a ghost.
What is meant by defiling the mental continuum of another?
It refers to when, through anger and malice, one disturbs another, causing them to become defiled and stained,
or even subjecting them to flogging, beating, or even the loss of life.
Question: Where does anger reside?
Answer: It resides in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), not in the two higher realms.
Question: Why is there no aversion (*dveṣa*) in the two upper realms?
Answer: Because they are not a field (*kṣetra*) nor a vessel (*bhājana*), and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, there are those who say: [text continues].
In order to eliminate hatred, one seeks to proceed to the higher realms, as explained in detail previously. Furthermore,
some say that wherever there is the fetter of stinginess and envy, there is also hatred.
Why is this? Because sentient beings, relying on the fetters of stinginess and envy,
give rise to hatred toward the mental continuums of others.
The higher realms are not like this, and therefore there is no ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
Furthermore, wherever there is a lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and a lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), there is ill-will; the higher realms are not like this.
Furthermore, wherever there are the faculties of suffering and grief, there is also the faculty of aversion;
this is not the case in the higher realms.
Furthermore, wherever there are the male and female faculties...
Thus, there is ill-will [in the desire realm], but it is not so in the higher realms.
Furthermore, wherever there is craving for edible food and craving for sexual desire, there is ill-will;
it is not so in the higher realms.
The explanations are all as before.
Therefore, there is no ill-will (dveṣa) in the higher realms.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
If there is a cause for resentment or harm in a given place, then there is anger.
A cause for resentment or harm refers to the nine grounds for malice (*navāghātavastūni*).
Because the realms of form and formlessness lack causes for resentment or harm, anger does not exist there.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghosaka said:
"The conditions of enmity and harm cause hatred to increase.
Or, as some say:
If the body that serves as the basis is dry, coarse, and rigid, then there is ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
Because the bodies that serve as the basis in the higher realms are moist and supple, there is no ill-will.
Furthermore, some say:
In the form and formless realms, there is an antidote to hatred, namely, the equanimity of meditative concentration; therefore, hatred does not exist there.
It is just as, for example, if there were a Vairambha wind in such a place.
In this place, the field of clouds can never abide; it is the same for the higher realms.
Because there is compassion—which is a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*) that serves as the antidote to anger—the field of clouds of anger does not abide there due to the *vairambha* winds.
What are the three turbidities?
They refer to the bodily, vocal, and mental actions arising from greed. Why is this so?
Greed is called turbidity.
The three types of karma arising from phenomena characterized by turbidity are also called turbidity,
because they are its results.
Question: For what reason is greed called "turbidity"?
Answer: Because it can defile and cloud.
In the world, that which colors things is called turbidity.
As it is said in the world: "the turbidity of roots, the turbidity of stems, the turbidity of branches, the turbidity of leaves, the turbidity of flowers, and the turbidity of fruits.
These are all called "turbidities" because they are capable of defiling.
Furthermore, "turbidity" (kaṣāya) carries the meaning of being base and inferior.
The world generally refers to those with much desire as base and turbid.
Furthermore, "turbid" (*kaṣāya*) has the meaning of being impure;
for by greed, the mind is obscured, leading one to associate with defiled phenomena and abandon pure phenomena.
Question: In what locations does greed reside?
Answer: It resides from the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having explained its intrinsic nature, I shall now demonstrate its characteristics of being associated and dissociated.
Do the three types of misconduct encompass the three crookednesses, corruptions, and turbidities?
Or do the three crookednesses, corruptions, and turbidities encompass the three types of misconduct?
One should respond that this involves four permutations.
There are unwholesome actions that are neither crooked,
nor corrupt, nor turbid; namely, all other unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, excluding those arising from the crookedness, malice, and greed of the desire realm.
There are crooked, defiled, and turbid actions that are not unwholesome:
namely, the bodily, vocal, and mental karma arising from guile and greed in the first dhyāna,
as well as the mental karma arising from greed in the remaining realms of form and formlessness.
There are unwholesome actions that are also crooked, corrupt, and turbid;
these refer to the unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind arising from deceit, hatred, and greed within the desire realm.
There are also those that are neither unwholesome actions nor crooked, corrupt, and turbid.
This refers to excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
"Characteristics" refers to that which is designated by a name, as previously explained;
specifically, it means excluding unwholesome form (*akuśala-rūpa*) from within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Furthermore, it includes the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) matter arising from flattery and greed;
it takes up the remaining aggregates of form;
and within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha), it excludes unwholesome volition (cetanā).
The volition that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and arises from greed, hatred, false views, and deceit;
the remaining factors of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), whether associated or dissociated [with mind];
the three aggregates in their entirety; and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Since all such cases constitute the fourth alternative, it is said: "namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Within this, there are two kinds of motivation (*samutthāna*):
namely, causal motivation (*hetu-samutthāna*).
Furthermore, there is the simultaneous arising at each moment (*kṣaṇa-samutthāna*).
That which arises as a cause is called the "transforming mind" (*pravartaka-citta*),
while that which arises simultaneously at each moment is called the "concomitant mind" (*anuvartaka-citta*).
Question: Can the five consciousnesses also initiate the two types of co-arising bodily and vocal karma?
Some say that the five consciousnesses cannot initiate bodily and vocal karma.
Why is this? It is because only the mental consciousness acts as the primary mover and the secondary follower regarding bodily and vocal actions, causing those actions to manifest.
The five consciousnesses cannot act as the initiator,
nor can they act as the follower;
they cannot cause that karma to manifest.
Question: If that is so, then as it is said, one's own bodily informative action (kāyavijñapti) and one's own vocal informative action (vāgvijñapti) are cognized by three consciousnesses.
How is this to be reconciled?
The answer is: one does not perceive the bodily intimation, but perceives other signs;
one does not hear the vocal intimation, but hears other sounds.
It is precisely by virtue of this meaning that they are called "seeing" and "hearing.
Regarding the cognition by the three consciousnesses:
it takes the bodily karma of another as its object, not one's own bodily karma.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the five consciousnesses can also initiate bodily and vocal karma,
because the mental consciousness acts as both the initiator (*pravartaka*) and the follower (*anuvartaka*).
Although the five consciousnesses do not act as the primary movers,
they do act as the secondary movers because they initiate those karmic activities;
if one were to speak in this way:

This effectively resolves the view that one’s own body manifests through bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and that one’s own speech is manifested through vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*). Why is this so?
Because it is by means of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that [the body] acts as the primary mover (*pravartaka*) and the follower (*anuvartaka*).
Furthermore, if one acts as a concomitant (anuvartaka) by means of visual consciousness, one perceives bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti).
If one acts as both the initiator (pravartaka) and the concomitant by means of mental consciousness,
and also acts as a concomitant by means of auditory consciousness, one hears vocal intimation (vāgvijñapti).
Regarding the three consciousnesses that cognize:
they take both one's own karma as an object and the karma of others as an object.
The Venerable Saṃghavasu said:
The five consciousnesses can also initiate bodily and verbal karma as both the causal motivation (*kāraṇa-samutthāna*) and the momentary motivation (*tatkṣaṇa-samutthāna*). Why is this so?
Suppose, for example, there is a man who, having previously formed no intention,
suddenly strikes another when struck by him;
at that moment, he does not give rise to the thought, "I shall strike him."
It should be understood that this is precisely the bodily consciousness abiding [in its object] and striking it.
Therefore, the five consciousnesses are also capable of giving rise to both bodily and vocal karma,
acting as the causal motivation (*kāraṇa-samutthāna*) and the momentary motivation (*kṣaṇa-samutthāna*).
Regarding this statement:
the five consciousnesses cannot act as the causal motivation (*hetu-samutthāna*) for bodily and vocal actions.
Why is this? Because it is the mental consciousness that acts as the initiator (*pravartaka*) and the follower (*anuvartaka*) with respect to bodily and vocal actions.
Because the five consciousnesses function only as concomitants (*anuvartaka*) and do not function as initiators (*pravartaka*),
if a wholesome mind acts as the initiator here,
then that same wholesome mind acts as the concomitant.
If a defiled mind acts as the initiator (*pravartaka*),
then a defiled mind acts as the follower (*anuvartaka*).
If a mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) acts as the initiator, [then a mind of deportment acts as the follower].
That is, the mind of deportment acts as the concomitant (anuvartaka) to that which acts as the initiator (pravartaka);
if it is the mind of craftsmanship, then the mind of craftsmanship acts as the initiator,
and the mind of craftsmanship acts as the concomitant.
It initiates bodily and vocal karma.
Question: If the mind of the path of deportment acts as the initiator (*ākṣepaka*), then that same mind acts as the follower (*anuvartaka*).
For example, when walking along a road, one might encounter a Buddha image and give rise to a wholesome visual consciousness,
or see a courtesan and give rise to a defiled visual consciousness. In such cases,
would it not be the case that karma is produced in accordance with those wholesome or defiled mental states?
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this:
"This arises from the rapid movement of discerning wisdom, giving rise to overweening pride;
that is to say, one gives rise to this visual consciousness while still in the stage of mental formations."
However, when actually practicing, neither wholesome states of mind nor defiled states of mind manifest.
When wholesome or defiled states of mind do manifest, one immediately ceases [the practice] and does not proceed;
such are these wholesome and defiled states of mind.
However, that which merely accompanies [the action] is not called its "co-arising" (samutthāna).
Furthermore, there are those who say:
when an action is initiated by a mind belonging to the sphere of deportment (airyāpathika-citta), [it is not co-arising].
Since wholesome and defiled minds arise through mutual assistance,
when a mind of deportment (airyāpathika) occurs,
its corresponding subsequent minds (anuvartaka-citta) may be of three types.
That is to say: wholesome, defiled, and indeterminate.
Question: If a mind of the artisan’s domain acts as the initiator (*pravartaka*), does that same mind act as the follower (*anuvartaka*)?
For example, when a painter paints a Buddha, a wholesome visual consciousness arises;
when he paints a woman, a defiled visual consciousness arises.
In this way, is it not the case that wholesome and defiled [minds] arise in accordance with the object and trigger those respective karmas?
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated this:
"One's cognitive wisdom arises with such rapidity that it gives rise to overweening pride,
leading one to claim that this visual consciousness arises at the very moment of painting."
In reality, at the time of painting, neither a wholesome mind nor a defiled mind is present.
If a wholesome mind or a defiled mind were present, one would stop painting immediately.
These [states of] wholesome and defiled minds...
However, that which is merely an associate is not termed "co-arising.
Furthermore, there are those who say that when a mind of craftsmanship initiates karma, [it is not co-arising].
A wholesome mind and a defiled mind assist one another in their arising; therefore,
when a mind pertaining to the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika-citta*) acts as the primary motivating mind (*pravartaka*),
its corresponding secondary minds (*anuvartaka*) may be of three types.
That is to say: wholesome, defiled, and neutral.
Question: Why is it that a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) cannot initiate the two types of bodily and verbal karma?
Answer: It is because powerful minds initiate bodily and verbal karma.
Because the nature of the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is weak and inferior, it cannot produce [karma].
Furthermore, some say:
if bodily and vocal karma were produced by a mind born of maturation...
Regarding those [actions] initiated by the two types of motivation:
what should these bodily and vocal actions be called?
Are they the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*)?
It is either a skillful art,
a result of maturation,
or a mode of deportment.
Alternatively, how can a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) produce [action] belonging to the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*)?
If this bodily or vocal action were born of maturation, it would itself have to be a result of maturation.
However, bodily and vocal actions are certainly not maturation (vipāka),
because they arise from preparatory effort (prayoga).
Furthermore, they cannot be said to be either wholesome or defiled.
Because it is produced by a mind that arises from maturation (*vipākaja*),
this mind of maturation cannot initiate bodily or vocal karma.
Furthermore, if a mind abandoned through seeing acts as the primary mover (*pravartaka*),
a mind abandoned through cultivation acts as the follower (*anuvartaka*);
or, a mind abandoned through cultivation acts as the primary mover.
It is possible for a mind abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) to act as a concomitant (*anuvartaka*),
thereby initiating bodily and vocal actions; however,
it is not possible for a mind abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) to act as such an initiator.
That is to say, it is impossible for a mind abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) to act as the conforming factor (*anuvartaka*),
or for a mind abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) to act as the instigating factor (*pravartaka*),
such that a bodily or vocal action is produced with a mind abandoned by seeing acting as the conforming factor. This has no basis in reality.
Why is this? Because the mind abandoned through seeing cannot produce bodily or vocal karma as its momentary origination (*kṣaṇasamutthāna*).
Now, in this context:
From this discussion, another question arises:
Why is it that while abiding in a mind to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),
one cannot produce bodily or vocal karma through momentary origination (*kṣaṇa-samutthāna*)?
Answer: It is required that a coarse and distracted mind can produce bodily and vocal karma through momentary origination (*kṣaṇasamutthāna*);
because this [subsequent] mind is subtle, it cannot produce them.
Furthermore, a mind that operates through the external doors can produce bodily and vocal actions through momentary origination (*kṣaṇasamutthāna*); however,
because this [specific] mind operates through the internal door, it cannot produce them.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
if a mind abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) can produce bodily and vocal actions through momentary origination (kṣaṇa-samutthāna).
Regarding this karma, it should be asked:
is it to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),
or is it to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
They would both be abandoned by seeing.
If they were abandoned by seeing,
then these bodily and vocal actions would not have the factors abandoned by cultivation as their basis for preparation.
This refers to that which is derived from the four great elements and is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). If it is to be abandoned by cultivation,
it should not be apprehended by a mind to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*).
If it were the momentary motivation (kṣaṇasamutthāna),
then whichever karma arose simultaneously with what was to be abandoned would necessarily become twofold.
If this were so, a single dharma would possess two intrinsic natures;
however, since this is not the case, the mind abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) does not function as an instantaneous origination (*kṣaṇa-samutthāna*).
Question: If the mind abandoned by insight cannot act as an instantaneous origination, [how can it arise]?
Regarding the undertaking of physical and vocal actions,
how should one reconcile this with what is taught in the sūtras?
As it is said in a sūtra:
Whatever physical, verbal, or mental karma performed by those with wrong views—
whether through volition, seeking, or actual execution—
all results in fruits that are undesirable, unpleasant, and disagreeable.
Why is this so? Because this view is violent and evil, namely, wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
[The interlocutor] replies: "This was said in reliance upon its causes, conditions, and origination."
There is no fault, because it does not depend on a momentary origination (*kṣaṇa-samutthāna*).
Furthermore, if this mind of the same category (*nikāya-sabhāga*) acts as the primary mover (*pravartaka*),
then this very mind of the same category acts as the follower (*anuvartaka*).
It is possible that a mind belonging to one homogeneous class of beings acts as the initiator,
while another mind belonging to the same homogeneous class of beings acts as the follower,
thereby giving rise to bodily and vocal karma. This is indeed the case.
If the mind of one homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga) acts as the initiator (pravartaka),
while the mind of another homogeneous class acts as the follower (anuvartaka),
it is impossible for bodily and vocal actions to be produced.
Furthermore, there are those who say that such a case is possible:
namely, as when someone makes a vow to hold a five-year great assembly, yet passes away in the interim.
By the power of this vow, one is born into a wealthy and noble family and remembers one's past lives;
thus, everything is accomplished exactly as previously vowed.
This is called the mind of this particular class of beings (nikāya-sabhāga) acting as the agent of transformation.
The remaining minds of the same homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga) act as the concomitants that initiate bodily and vocal karma.
These are the three types of wholesome conduct (sucarita) and the three purities (pariśuddhi), namely: purity of body, speech, and mind.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing and elucidating the meaning of the sūtras.
As stated in the sūtras, there are three types of sublime conduct and three types of purity;
although this has been said, it was not explained in detail.
The detailed exposition is as previously described.
Furthermore, there are those who say:

"In the preceding section (*naṣika*), the three types of wholesome conduct (*sucarita*) have already been analyzed, but the three types of purity (*pariśuddhi*) have not yet been analyzed; it is for the purpose of analyzing these that this treatise is composed."
Do the three types of pure conduct subsume the three types of wholesome conduct?
Or do the three types of pure conduct subsume the three types of wholesome conduct?
Answer: They mutually subsume one another according to their respective functions.
Why is this? All forms of excellent conduct of body are themselves purity of body;
all forms of excellent conduct of speech are themselves purity of speech.
All excellent mental conduct is itself mental purity.
Question: Untainted excellent conduct may be called "purity" because it is forever free from defilement, impurity, and turbidity;
however, since tainted excellent conduct possesses defilement, impurity, and turbidity, how can it be so designated?
What is meant by "purity"?
Answer: It is called purity because tainted sublime conduct (*sāsrava-praṇīta-caryā*) is distinguished as pure. Why is this so?
Furthermore, there are those who say that even tainted sublime conduct (*sāsrava-kuśala-caryā*) can abandon the defilements of the afflictions up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*);
therefore, it is termed "pure.
Moreover, there are others who state:
The contaminated sublime conduct (*sucarita*) can induce it;
because it accords with the ultimate purity, it is also called "pure.
There are three types of sublime conduct and three types of silence (*mauna*).
That is to say, the body, speech, and mind are in a state of silence;
this is explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra:
"There are three types of sublime conduct and three types of silence."
Although this has been stated, it is not explained in detail;
the full exposition is as previously described.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
In the preceding section on the *nirdeśa*, the three types of sublime conduct (*sucarita*) have already been analyzed,
but the three types of silence (*mauna*) have not yet been analyzed.
Now, wishing to analyze them, this treatise is composed.
Regarding the three types of good conduct and the three types of silence:
are the three types of silence subsumed by the three types of good conduct?
Or are the three types of good conduct subsumed by the three types of silence?
It can be expressed in four propositions:
there are wholesome courses of action that are not silent [restraint],
namely, wholesome courses of bodily and vocal action excluding those of the Aśaikṣa.
There are other instances of excellent conduct of body and speech,
as well as all excellent conduct of mind,
that are characterized by silence rather than being [explicitly] excellent conduct.
That is to say, there is the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-citta),
which is both sublime conduct and silence;
that is to say, the sublime conduct of body and speech of one beyond training.
There is that which is neither sublime conduct nor silence;
this refers to cases other than those previously mentioned.
"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to what is designated by those names, as explained in detail above.
That is to say, within the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), wholesome form is excluded;
within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), non-attachment, non-hatred, right view,
and all wholesome volitions (cetanā) are excluded.
Within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), excluding the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-citta*),
one takes the remaining form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) aggregates, as well as the two complete aggregates [feeling and perception] and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
All such cases constitute the fourth category.
Therefore, it is said that, excluding the aforementioned characteristics,
the three purities and the three silences are subsumed within the three purities.
Are the three types of silence subsumed by the three types of purity?
One should respond that this involves four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is that which is pure but not silent.
This refers to all other purities of body and speech,
as well as all purities of mind, excluding the purity of body and speech belonging to those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

What, then, is this? It refers to the purity of body and speech of those in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa),
as well as the three kinds of purity of mind.
Because mental silence pertains exclusively to the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
there may be silence that is not purity;
that is to say, the mind of one beyond training is not of the nature of karma.
There is that which is both pure and silent,
namely the purity of the body and speech of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
There is that which is neither pure nor silent.
This means excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
"Characteristics" refers to that which is designated by names, as explained extensively above.
Question: For what reason [is this said] regarding the five aggregates?
Is it that the two aggregates of form and consciousness alone establish the state of silence, and not the other aggregates?
One should know that if they were to be established in their entirety yet are not so established,
this meaning must be understood as being incomplete.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this statement is made to indicate the first and the last [aggregates] therein;
"first" refers to the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), and "last" refers to the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha).
Just as it was stated regarding the beginning and the end, so too should one understand the entering, exiting, proceeding, crossing over,
the application of means, and the culmination; furthermore, there are those who say:
This demonstrates the coarsest and the subtlest among them.
Within the five aggregates (*skandha*),
the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is the coarsest.
The aggregate of consciousness is the most subtle.
Furthermore, some say that true silence consists solely of the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
By what is this mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) inferred?
It is by means of bodily and vocal actions;
therefore, it is only the bodily and vocal actions that constitute the mind of one beyond training.
He establishes silence.
Question: Why is silence found only in those beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
Answer: Silence is obtainable only within the body of one beyond training.
It cannot be found within the bodies of those in training (*śaikṣa*), nor within those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa*).
Following this line of inquiry, one might ask: for what reason is it that silence can only be found within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Is it not otherwise?
Answer: Because this silence is the most supreme dharma;
a supreme dharma cannot be found within an inferior body.
Why is this? If one speaks of "superior dharmas," these refer to the dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣadharma);
they are superior to the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣadharma), and so forth.
If one speaks of the most excellent *pudgala*, it refers to the *aśaikṣa* (one beyond training) *pudgala*,
for they are more excellent than those who are not yet beyond training (*na-śaikṣa*), and so forth.
Furthermore, there are others who say:
Within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the mental verbalization of afflictions has reached ultimate cessation;
because it is perfectly tranquil and silent, it is established as "the silent one.
Other bodies are not so, and therefore it is not so established.
Question: What is the distinction between sublime conduct (*sucarita*), purity (*viśuddhi*), and silence (*tūṣṇīmbhāva*)?
Some say that their names themselves constitute the distinction.
That is to say, it is called sublime conduct;
it is called purity;
it is called silence.
Furthermore, there are those who explain that the meanings are also distinct:
the meaning of skillful action is the meaning of sublime conduct;
the meaning of a pure essence is the meaning of purification.
The meaning of being free from delusion and confusion is the meaning of silence.
Furthermore, there are those who say that it is called "sublime conduct" because it can bring about desirable fruits.
It is called "pure" because it is unmixed with afflictions;
it is called "silent" because it is ultimately stilled.
These are the three distinctions of sublime conduct: purity and silence.
Are all bodily misdeeds instances of bodily action that are prompted by what is irrational? Conversely,
are all instances of bodily action prompted by what is irrational necessarily bodily misdeeds?
