Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As a sūtra states:
"There are bodily, vocal, and mental actions that are induced by what is unreasonable."
Although the sūtra makes this statement, it does not explain it in detail;
the detailed exposition is as previously set forth.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Although the three types of unwholesome conduct were already distinguished in the preceding section,
the bodily, vocal, and mental actions induced by irrationality (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) have not yet been distinguished.
Now, wishing to distinguish them, this treatise is composed.
Are all bodily misdeeds instances of bodily action that are improperly motivated? Conversely,
are all instances of bodily action that are improperly motivated [necessarily] bodily misdeeds?
Does that exhaust all bodily misconduct?
Answer: All bodily misconduct is exhausted by that which is unreasonably induced bodily karma. Why is this so?
Because all unwholesome actions contradict reason and are originated by improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*),
there exists bodily action that is induced by what is unreasonable.
It is not bodily misconduct;
that is to say, it refers to obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) bodily karma,
as well as unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) [bodily karma].
Bodily action induced by improper reasoning that is obscured-neutral refers to bodily action arising from afflictions such as guile and attachment belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna.
Bodily action induced by improper reasoning that is unobscured-neutral refers to...
That is to say, one should go and come in such a manner,
yet one goes and comes in a manner that is not so;
this is explained in detail as previously stated.
Are all verbal misconducts instances of vocal karma that are improperly motivated? Conversely,
are all instances of vocal karma that are improperly motivated instances of verbal misconduct?
Is that which is exhausted all verbal misconduct?
Answer: All verbal misconduct is exhausted;
it is all verbal action induced by what is unreasonable.
Why is this? Because all unwholesome actions contradict reason and are originated by improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
There is vocal karma induced by improper reasoning that is not vocal misconduct;
namely, vocal karma that is obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
And there is vocal action induced by improper reasoning that is non-obscured and neutral.
As for vocal action that is obscured and neutral,
it refers to vocal action arising from such states as guile and craving within the level of the first dhyāna.
Vocal action that is unobscured-neutral and induced by improper reasoning refers, for example,
to failing to speak a word that ought to be spoken;
the full explanation is as previously stated.
Are all unwholesome mental actions necessarily mental karma induced by irrationality? Conversely,
is all mental karma induced by irrationality necessarily unwholesome?
Does that exhaust all mental misconduct?
One should respond by formulating four propositions (catuṣkoṭi):
there is mental misconduct that is not induced by irrationality (ayoniśomanasikāra).
This refers to the three types of mental misconduct: covetousness, malice, and wrong view.
There are also mental actions induced by improper reasoning that are not considered mental misconduct;
these refer to mental actions that are obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Furthermore, there is unobscured-neutral mental karma induced by improper reasoning,
as well as obscured-neutral mental karma;
the latter refers to the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) bound to the desire realm.
Volition associated with the view of extremes;
volition associated with all afflictions of the form and formless realms;
and non-obscured neutral mental action induced by improper reasoning.
This refers to the volition that can give rise to it,
as previously described:
namely, non-obscured neutral bodily and vocal actions induced by what is not in accordance with reason.
There is mental action that is both an unwholesome mental conduct and induced by improper reasoning;
this refers to unwholesome mental action.
There is also mental action that is neither an unwholesome mental conduct nor induced by improper reasoning.
This means excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
"Characteristics" refers to that which is designated by a name, as explained extensively above.
That is to say, one should formulate four propositions regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Within this, one excludes greed, hatred, and false views,
as well as afflicted volition (cetanā),
and unobscured-unspecified volition that is induced by what is unreasonable.
Taking the remaining formations of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)— both those associated with and dissociated from mind—
as well as the four aggregates in their entirety and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*),
all such cases constitute the fourth alternative.
Therefore, it is asked: "Excluding the aforementioned characteristics,
are all bodily virtuous actions (kāya-sucarita) necessarily bodily karma (kāyakarman) induced by correct reasoning (yoniśomanasikāra)?"
If one asks: "Is all bodily action that is induced by correct reasoning necessarily wholesome bodily conduct? The answer is:
All wholesome bodily conduct is necessarily bodily action induced by correct reasoning.
Why is this? Because all sublime conduct does not contradict reason,
and because it is originated by appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
There is bodily action induced by correct reasoning that is not a sublime bodily action;
namely, unobscured-neutral bodily action induced by correct reasoning. What, then, is this?
That is to say, one should go and come in such a manner,
and is indeed able to go and come in such a manner;
this is explained in detail as previously stated.
Are all instances of verbal good conduct (vāksucarita) necessarily verbal actions (vākkarman) induced by correct reasoning?
Conversely, are all verbal actions induced by correct reasoning necessarily instances of verbal good conduct?
Answer: All verbal virtuous conduct (*vāksucarita*) is entirely speech-action (*vākkarman*) induced by reason.
Why? Because all virtuous conduct does not contradict reason.
Because it is originated by appropriate attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
there is vocal action induced by what is appropriate,
yet which is not a sublime vocal conduct (*vāksucarita*).
This refers to unobscured-neutral verbal action induced by correct reasoning.
What, furthermore, is this?
It refers to speaking one word when one word ought to be spoken, and so forth.
As explained extensively above:
Are all those mental wholesome courses of action necessarily mental karma induced by correct reasoning?
If one performs mental karma that is induced by correct reasoning,
is that the entirety of excellent mental conduct?
One should respond by establishing four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are wholesome mental actions that are not induced by correct reasoning;
these refer to the three types of wholesome mental action: non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view.
There is mental action induced by correct reasoning that is not a sublime mental action;
namely, a portion of unobscured-neutral mental action induced by correct reasoning.
It is thought that these are able to initiate [action],
as previously described:
namely, the two types of bodily and vocal karma that are non-obscured and neutral, and which are induced by correct reasoning.
There is mental wholesome conduct,
which is also mental action induced by correct reasoning;
that is, wholesome mental action.
There is mental misconduct that is also not mental action induced by correct reasoning;
this refers to cases other than those previously described.
"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to that which is designated [as such], as explained extensively above. That is to say,
one should formulate four propositions regarding the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha),
from which non-attachment, non-hatred, right view, and wholesome volition (kuśala-cetanā) are excluded.
It also includes the unobscured-neutral [states],
such as volition induced by correct reasoning,
as well as the remaining associated and dissociated factors of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
Together with the four aggregates in their entirety and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), all such cases constitute the fourth alternative;
therefore, it is said: "except for the aforementioned characteristics."

Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of others and clarifying one’s own position.
That is to say, [it concerns] the Vātsīputrīyas and the Vibhajyavādins.
If one wishes to maintain that vocal sound is a maturation result (*vipākaphala*), the question arises:
by what authority is such a statement made?
The answer is: it is by virtue of the words of the Noble One (*āryavacana*).
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*:
"For what reason does a bodhisattva obtain the mark of a Great Man that is the Brahma-like voice?
Because in other previous lives..."
By abandoning harsh speech, one attains the voice of Brahmā upon the completion of that karma.
Because of this statement, some might conclude that sound is a maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*).
To refute this intention and to demonstrate that not all sounds are maturation fruits, this treatise was composed.
If various phenomena are acquired through karma, should those phenomena be described as wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral? Answer:
With respect to the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), those phenomena acquired through karma are neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Question: For what reason is this said?
Answer: There are certain dharmas that, although acquired through karma, are not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), such as the various forms of restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
This statement is made in order to distinguish those dharmas;

that is, those dharmas which, as maturation fruits, are acquired by karma through those [causes] are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Herein, the Vibhajyavādins among the Vātsīputrīyas [assert as follows].
He asks the proponent of the *Nyāyānusāra* (The Treatise on Reasoning):
"Is it definitively asserted that those dharmas which serve as the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) are obtained by karma only if those dharmas are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
This is a statement intended to definitively establish the position of the opposing school.
If one were to raise an objection against another without first ascertaining the position they have established, one would be unable to find fault with them;
furthermore, such an objection would merely be questioning what was not stated by the other party. Therefore, it is said that [one must] "ascertain."
Do you now accept and definitively maintain this statement:
that those dharmas which arise from karma as its maturation fruit (vipākaphala) are themselves neutral (avyākṛta)?
The proponent of the *yuktivādin* replies, "It is so.
He asks again, "What do you mean? [The opponent replies:
"The Tathāgata speaks words with a virtuous mind."
"Exquisite sound, beautiful sound, harmonious and elegant sound, and pleasing sound—
is this speech wholesome?
The one who speaks according to reason replies, "It is so."
He then raised an objection, saying:
"Listen as I point out your position of defeat, your position of loss, and your position of contradicting your own statement.
If you speak thus..."
If, according to the view that all phenomena which are maturation fruits are neutral because they are obtained through karma,
then one should not say that when the Tathāgata speaks with a virtuous mind— uttering sublime sounds, beautiful sounds, harmonious and elegant sounds, and pleasing sounds— these words are virtuous.
To speak in this manner is not reasonable.
If one were to say that the Tathāgata, with a virtuous mind, utters various sublime sounds, beautiful sounds, harmonious and elegant sounds, and pleasing sounds.
If this statement were correct, one should not have said that "the dharmas which are the maturation fruit are obtained by karma through those dharmas being neutral";
therefore, to make such a statement is unreasonable.
The proponents of the *Yukti* (Reasoning School) explain that objection as follows:
"It should be stated that in other previous lives, the Bodhisattva..."
Through the performance and accumulation of great karmic actions that bring about the ripening fruit,
and by reason of these causes and conditions, there successively arise the subtle primary elements of the Tathāgata’s throat.
From this, one is able to produce sublime speech and sounds, yet these sounds are not the result of karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
Question: If all sounds are not the fruit of karmic maturation, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*?
Answer: This is stated based on indirect causes (*pāramparyahetu*).
However, not all sounds are the result of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Question: For what reason are all sounds not the result of maturation?
Some say that sound belongs to the third transmission:
namely, the initial karma produces the primary elements (mahābhūta).
Sound is produced from the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Because sound belongs to the third category, it is not a result of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Sound belongs to the fifth transmission.
That is to say: the primary karma produces the great elements of maturation (*vipāka-mahābhūta*);
these great elements of maturation, in turn, produce the great elements of nourishment (*aupacayika-mahābhūta*).
The great elements that produce growth give rise to great elements of outflow;
from these great elements of outflow, sound is produced.
Because sound belongs to the fifth category, it is not a result of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, some say that sound functions according to one's will, whereas non-maturation phenomena cannot function according to one's will. Others say:
Sound produces sound; it is not the case that a result of maturation (vipāka) is produced from another result of maturation.
Some say that sound is produced by present effort (prayoga).
The ripening fruit (vipākaphala) arises from prior karma.
Furthermore, some say that when one becomes free from the defilements of the first dhyāna, vocal intimation (vāgvijñapti) is severed.
If it were a maturation (vipāka), it should only be severed at the time one becomes free from the defilements of the three realms.
Furthermore, some say that sound is of three kinds.
That is to say, [karma] is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
The ripened fruit (vipākaphala) is exclusively neutral. Some say:
If sound were a result of karmic maturation (*vipāka*),
then those born in desirable realms would always produce sounds that accord with their wishes,
while those born in undesirable realms [would produce the opposite].
Sound ought to produce unpleasant sounds at all times;
however, we observe that there are times when the opposite occurs.
Therefore, sound is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, there are those who say:
sound is intermittent, whereas resultant form (vipākaja-rūpa) is non-intermittent;
therefore, sound is not resultant.
However, bodhisattvas, by means of two causes and conditions, make a vow to seek the Buddha’s marks of a great man and his subtle, sublime Brahma-voice: first, because they have previously seen them;
second, because they have heard of them from others.
Second, by what has been heard;
and by what has been seen,
which refers to that bodhisattva.
I have seen him in great assemblies where he has encountered various Buddhas,
proclaiming the True Dharma with a Brahma-voice for the sake of all sentient beings and subduing opposing arguments.
Subtle, profound, and far-reaching, and endowed with the marks of a great man—
this refers to those bodhisattvas who have previously heard [the teaching].
Having heard the Tathāgata proclaiming the True Dharma with the Brahma-voice,
and so forth, up until possessing the marks of a Great Man,
the Bodhisattva, upon seeing and hearing this, rejoiced and took deep delight in his heart.
Thereupon, I vow to accept and accord with those primary causes;
all my prohibitions, pure conduct (*brahmacarya*),
and diligent efforts shall be dedicated toward the aspiration for the future.
Having attained such a state of conduct befitting a great being,
through this intention, they further offer various kinds of exquisite incense, flowers, ritual implements,
and music as offerings to the Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and the images of caityas.
While serving, making offerings to, and attending upon one's parents, teachers, elders, and fellow practitioners of the holy life,
and while cultivating such sublime merits,
one should dedicate each and every one of them toward the attainment of this mark of the Brahma-voice.
Furthermore, one diligently purifies two types of paths of action:
namely, harsh speech and frivolous speech.
By diligently purifying harsh speech,
one attains the sublime Brahma-voice of a Great Being;
by means of this Brahma-voice, one subdues all the heterodox arguments of outsiders.
By diligently purifying frivolous speech,
one attains a voice that is majestic, solemn, and clear;
by means of this voice, one outshines all worldly disputations.
It is, for example, as if someone were to see another person staying in a magnificent hall adorned with flowers,
where five kinds of music are arrayed and they enjoy themselves at will;
and that person hears the sounds of those five musical instruments being played.
He reflected thus:
"When shall I obtain such a sublime hall and pavilion,
where I may arrange the five kinds of music and enjoy myself in delight?"
Having reflected thus, he applies diligent effort;
he accumulates wealth and treasures, accomplishing everything according to his wishes.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: through seeing and hearing, [he acts accordingly].

Question: For what reason was this treatise composed?
Answer: Those who disregard the past and future and are deluded regarding the three periods of time desire to establish that the past and future are non-existent,
asserting only that the present and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) are existent.
This treatise is composed in order to refute that attachment and to demonstrate that the past and future are substantially existent dharmas.
Furthermore, the reason for composing this treatise is the desire to stop the assertions of the non-Buddhists.
He says that all phenomena take what follows as the cause for what precedes it.
It is just as when a spring of water presses from behind upon what is in front, causing it to surge and flow;
in this way, the subsequent water acts as the cause for the preceding water.
All phenomena are likewise; because they are impelled by subsequent moments of phenomena,
they arise from the future and enter the present, and then,
passing away from the present, they enter the past.
Therefore, the future is the cause of the present,
and the present is the cause of the past.
To refute that attachment, it is explained that all phenomena [are devoid of intrinsic nature].
The preceding serves as the cause for the succeeding, but the succeeding does not serve as the cause for the preceding.
If one were to claim that a subsequent phenomenon is the cause of a preceding one,
it would contradict the dependent origination of all internal and external phenomena.
Regarding the contradiction with the internal dependent origination:
this refers to [the claim that] ignorance conditions formations,
and so on, up to birth conditioning old age and death.
It is because of children that there are parents;
conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises;
and so on, up to: conditioned by the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises.
From the *arbuda* arises the *kalala*,
and so on, until from old age arises middle age.
This is the dependent origination that contradicts external phenomena.
That is to say, one would have to claim that the sprout is the cause of the seed,
and so on, up to the fruit being the cause of the flower; if this were the case, there would be a great fault, namely,
that what has not yet been produced would already be obtained.
One should first experience the maturation of good and evil karma,
and only afterwards perform good and evil deeds;
[otherwise] one would first fall into the Avīci Hell.
One may first receive the rank of a Wheel-Turning King and later commit the five heinous crimes;
or one may first perform the deeds of a Wheel-Turning King and later commit those same crimes.
One first realizes unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and only thereafter practices the bodhisattva path;
if it were obtained without having performed these [practices], [it would be impossible].
Furthermore, that which has already been performed would also be lost;
in such a case, there would be neither bondage nor liberation.
Let there be no such fault.
Therefore, among all phenomena, the preceding serves as the cause for the succeeding,
but the succeeding is not the cause for the preceding. For this reason, this treatise is composed.
If various karmas are past, are their fruits also past?
Answer: Their fruits may be past, or they may be future.
Or there is the present fruit;
that is, the ripening fruit (vipākaphala) is established as threefold based on distinctions such as having already ceased and so forth.
Are those various karmas future, and their fruits also future?
Answer: It is so.
This is because the cause does not precede the fruit.
If various karmas are present, is their fruit also present?
Answer: Its fruit is either present or future;
the explanation is as before.
Regarding this, some say:
the treatise is composed based on the present moment;
according to what is stated here, all such karmas are past.
Regardless of which time period that fruit belongs to,
those karmas are all of four types; namely, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
Up to and including karma conducive to indeterminate experience,
all karmas— whether future or present—
possess four types of results according to their respective fruits.
Furthermore, one should not say that when various karmas are present, their fruits are also present;
for it is not the case that one experiences the ripened fruit (vipāka-phala) in the very same moment that the karma is performed.
Some say: herein the discussion is based on the present state;
according to this explanation, when the various karmas are past, their fruits are also past.
Regarding future and present [actions]:
for all future actions and present actions, their results are future;
all of these are as previously explained.
Regarding those actions whose results are manifest in the present,
such actions are of two kinds;
that is to say, they are those to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
This refers to karma to be experienced at an indefinite time. Furthermore,
some say that this discussion is based on a single homogeneous life-stream (*nikāya-sabhāga*) in the present.
Regarding the various karmas mentioned here, if they are past,
their fruits may be past as previously explained,
or they may be future; in the latter case, that karma has two aspects.
That is to say, there are three types of such karma: those to be experienced in a subsequent life,
those to be experienced at an indefinite time, and those to be experienced in the present life.
Excluding those [karmas] to be experienced in the present life,
all other karmas in the future are also as previously described.
Regarding those karmas in the present life whose fruits may also be in the present:
That karma is of two kinds:
namely, that to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya) and that to be experienced at an indefinite time (aniyatavedanīya).
Regarding those [karmas] that ripen in the future, there are three types;
those to be experienced in the present life are excluded.
Question: Is there any karma to be experienced in the present life?
Is it the case that the cause exists in the past while the fruit exists in the future?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to the present [moment] as distinguished by its temporal state (*avasthā*) within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
It is not spoken based on a single present *nikāya-sabhāga*. Furthermore,
there are those who say it is also spoken based on a single present *nikāya-sabhāga*.
That is to say, for example, there is a person who,
having performed and accumulated karma to be experienced in the present life,
dies suddenly before that karma has yet yielded its fruit.
At that time, it is said that the cause is in the past and the fruit is in the future.
Is there any karma to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya) whose cause is in the past and whose fruit is in the present?
Or is it that the cause exists in the present while the fruit exists in the future?
If the question is asked based on a single *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class of beings) existing in the present, one should answer: "No."
The Venerable Ghosaka says that there is such a thing, as previously stated:
"Is there any bodily karma that brings about a ripened fruit?"
Is it not the same for vocal and mental karma?
This is explained at length.
Herein, by means of this method, the desirable and undesirable fruits produced by the three types of karma are demonstrated.
Later, within the section on the "Expedient Display of the Differentiation of States" among the aggregates,
that which was asked here is answered first regarding the dark category (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*),

This is a brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
Is it possible that bodily action (*kāyakarman*) produces a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*),
while vocal and mental actions do not?
Answer: There is.
For example, when one does not guard the body but guards speech, at that time one possesses either a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind.
This refers to the arising of unwholesome bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti-karman*) at the present time,
by which non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*) is initiated and subsequently proceeds;
as well as the arising of wholesome vocal informative action (*vāg-vijñapti-karman*) either at the present time or previously.
From this, the non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*) arises and continues;
at that very moment, either a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind manifests.
Among these, bodily action brings about an undesirable maturation (*vipāka*).
Vocal karma produces a desirable maturation;
as for mental karma, if it arises from a wholesome state of mind, it produces a desirable maturation,
whereas if it arises from a neutral state of mind, [it produces a neutral maturation].
They do not experience the maturation of either the agreeable or the disagreeable.

Answer: There is.
For example, when one guards the body but does not guard speech, at that time one possesses either a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind.

Vocal karma brings about an unpleasant ripening;

If an indeterminate state of mind arises,
it does not bring about a desirable or undesirable maturation;

At that time, he gives rise to an unwholesome mind or an indeterminate mind;

These contradictions and so forth should be explained by analogy with what was previously stated. In this context, if mental karma produces an undesirable maturation, then bodily and vocal karma produce a desirable maturation;

Answer: This, too, is without fault.

Answer: It brings about the maturation of the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

this karma can induce the four types of ripening in the miserable realms.
That is to say, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous group-characteristic (*nikāyasabhāga*), and birth, subsistence, aging, and impermanence;
these are able to induce the two types of maturation (*vipāka*) of humans and devas—
that is, they bring about birth, subsistence, aging, and impermanence.
Furthermore, regarding karma to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) that consists of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*):
this karma can induce the ripening (*vipāka*) of painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*) and its associated [factors].
As for those [factors] dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*): [the same applies].
This karma can induce four types of maturation in the miserable realms, namely:
the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*), birth (*jāti*), subsistence (*sthiti*), aging (*jarā*), and impermanence (*anityatā*).
It can also induce two types of maturation in the human and celestial realms.
That is to say, it refers to the acquisition of birth, duration, aging, and impermanence.
Regarding the matter of karma to be abandoned through cultivation,
this karma is of two kinds.
That is to say, they are wholesome and unwholesome.
Regarding wholesome karma as form:
this karma can induce the maturation of rebirth in nine locations within the realms of humans and devas.
That is to say, with the exception of the sphere of sound,
there are four spheres that can induce maturation in the miserable destinies:
namely, visible form, odor, flavor, and tangible objects.
Regarding unwholesome karmic matter:
this karma can induce retribution in nine locations within the miserable realms,
namely, excluding the location of sound.
It is capable of producing the matured result (*vipāka*) in four locations within the realms of humans and gods—
namely, visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects.
The causal relationship of such maturation has already been explained in detail in the *Jñānaprasthāna* (Chapter on Knowledge), within the section on the *Saṃgītiparyāya*.

3. The Section on Taking Life (Prāṇātipātādhikaraṇa). Within the fourth aggregate of action (Karmaskandha), the first part of the third section on taking life: Is there a case where one has already taken life, yet the act of killing has not yet ceased?
Having thus understood these chapters and the meaning of the explanations within them,
one should next provide a detailed exposition.
In this context, there are cases where non-killing is expressed by the term "killing."
There are cases where that which is not preparatory is designated by the term "preparatory.
That is to say, the preparatory stage of killing is also called "killing," and what arises subsequent to the act of killing is also called "preparatory."
This is called the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
Is there a case where one has already killed a living being, yet the act of killing has not yet ceased?
Answer: There is.
For example, when one has already taken another's life but the preparatory effort has not yet ceased;
that is to say, as when a person, for the purpose of harming another's life,
inflicts injury with a sword, a staff, or other such means.
The preparatory effort has not yet ceased, yet that life has already been cut off.
The same applies in detail to the dispatching of messengers, incantations, and medicines.
Is it possible for the act of killing to have already ceased while the living being has not yet been harmed?
Answer: There is.
For example, when one has not yet taken another's life, but the preparatory effort for it has already ceased.
This refers, for example, to a person who, in order to take another's life,
inflicts injury with a sword, staff, or other weapons;
although that life has not yet been severed, he believes it has already been severed.
They no longer inflict further harm.
The same applies to the detailed explanation regarding the dispatch of messengers and the use of incantations and medicines.
Is it possible that once a living being has been harmed, the act of killing has already ceased?
Answer: Yes.
For example, when one has already taken another's life and that preparatory effort has ceased;
that is to say, as when someone acts for the purpose of harming another's life.
When one inflicts harm with weapons, staves, and the like,
the preparatory effort ceases at the very moment life is cut off;
the same applies in detail to the dispatching of messengers, the use of mantras, and medicinal drugs.
Is there perhaps the case where living beings have not yet been harmed and the act of killing has not yet ceased?
Answer: There is.
For example, when one has not yet terminated another's life.
That preparatory effort has not yet ceased;
that is to say, for example, there is someone who, in order to take another's life,
inflicts injury with a sword, a staff, or other such means.
While its life-force has not yet been severed and its preparatory effort has not yet ceased—
the same applies to the detailed explanations regarding the dispatching of messengers, incantations, and medicinal substances—
is it possible for a living being to have been killed while the act of killing has not yet ceased?
Is it certain that the maturation (*vipāka*) of this karma will be rebirth in hell?
Answer: Yes.
For example, one who dies while still engaged in the preliminary application (*prayoga*) of an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*).
What is this matter? It is as follows:
suppose there is a person who, desiring to kill his mother, has just begun the preparatory action when he is captured by the authorities.
Or there may be a mother who, possessing great power, instead harms her own son;
or there may be a mother whose merit causes a deity to kill her son and cast him into hell while she herself remains alive;
or there may be one who initiates an action that results in the certain death of her mother.
If one then feels regret and brings about one's own death, one will likewise be reborn in hell.
Just as with killing one’s mother, it should be understood that the same applies to committing the other *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses.
Question: Since there are only phenomena (*dharma*) and no sentient beings (*sattva*), how can there be the transgression of killing?
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"Just as there may be the notion of a sentient being even though no sentient being exists."
Thus, although there is no sentient being,
there is still the transgression of killing.
Furthermore, regarding these aggregates, elements, and sense-bases:
One is able to give rise to the notion of a self,
the notion of a sentient being,
and [the notion of] a life-principle.
The notion of a person (pudgala) regarding that which is born and that which nourishes.
Therefore, if one cuts or destroys that [basis], one incurs the offense of killing.
Furthermore, regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases,
they give rise to the notion of a self and the notions of permanence, bliss, and purity.
Therefore, if one cuts or destroys it,
one incurs the offense of taking life.
Thus spoke the Venerable One.
These aggregates, elements,
and sense bases are possessed of appropriation and give rise to cognitions of the three times,
namely: "I shall kill," "I am killing," and "I have killed."
Therefore, if one cuts or destroys it, one incurs the offense of taking life.
However, while sentient beings exist as conventional reality,
this offense of taking life exists as ultimate reality.
It is attained through two conditions:
first, the initiation of the preparatory application;
second, the final completion of the result.
If one initiates the preparatory effort but the result is not finalized,
or if the result is finalized without having initiated the preparatory effort,
in neither case is the sin of killing incurred.
If one initiates the preparatory effort and the result is also brought to completion, only then does one incur the offense of killing.
Question: Is there a case where one initiates the preparatory effort and the result is also brought to completion, yet one does not incur the offense of killing?
Answer: Yes.
For example, when both the killer and the killed die at the same time, or when the killer dies first.
Question: Regarding the killing of which aggregate is it called "killing"?
Is it the past or the future?
It is present;
the past has already ceased,
and the future has not yet arrived.
Since the present does not abide and is entirely devoid of the meaning of killing, how can it be called "killing"?
Answer: It is the killing of future aggregates (*skandha*).
It is not the past or the present.
Question: Since the future has not yet arrived, how can it be killed?
Answer: One dwells in the present and obstructs the conjunction of the aggregates (skandhas) in the future; this is what is called "killing."
One incurs the offense of killing by obstructing the conditions for the arising of the aggregates through their combination with others.
Some say that one kills present and future aggregates, but not past ones.
[The opponent] asks: "The future may be so; however, the present does not endure, for even if one does not kill it, it would perish naturally."
What is killing?
It is answered: the severance of its functional power is called killing. Why is this so?
Although the present aggregates do not persist and perish,
they are nonetheless unable to prevent the subsequent aggregates from continuing;
likewise, the present aggregates now perish without persisting.
Because it prevents the subsequent aggregates from continuing, one incurs the sin of killing even with respect to the present aggregates.
Question: Among the various aggregates, which aggregate can be killed?
Regarding that, one incurs the sin of killing.
Some say it is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha). Why is this so?
Because only form (*rūpa*) can be contacted by weapons, staves, and so forth.
Some say that all five aggregates (*skandha*) are [the object of killing].
Question: Since the other four aggregates lack tangibility, how can they be killed?
The answer is: because that [consciousness] depends upon form for its activity, when the aggregate of form perishes, it no longer functions; therefore, it is also called "killing.
It is like when a jar is broken, the milk and other contents are also lost.
Furthermore, because he gives rise to an evil mind toward those aggregates and kills them, he incurs the offense of killing.
Question: Is the act of killing indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Regarding the offense incurred therein, is it of three kinds?
Some say it is indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Why is this? Because only that which is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) can be touched by swords, clubs, and the like.
Some say there are three types.
Question: Since wholesome and defiled phenomena lack contact (*spraṣṭavya*), how can they be killed?
Answer: Wholesome and defiled phenomena proceed in dependence upon the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because it does not proceed when there is neutral (avyākṛta) destruction, it is also called "killing.
The rest is explained in detail as before.
Question: Suppose one, through a single application of effort (prayoga), simultaneously kills both one's mother and another woman.
In that case, one incurs both the offense of killing and the unmanifest (avijñapti) karma of an immediate transgression (ānantarya) with respect to one's mother;
however, with respect to other women, one incurs only the unmanifest karma of killing.
Now, does this manifest karma (vijñapti-karman) result in only one [offense], or does it result in two?
Some say that one obtains only a single informative act (*vijñapti*). Why is this so?
Because there is no distinction in the simultaneous killing through a single application of effort,
the Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
"He obtains two manifest actions."
Why is this so? Because this bodily manifest karma is composed of atoms;
the atoms of harming one's mother and those of other [actions] are each distinct.
As it is with the acquisition of non-manifest [action], so it should be for the two types of manifest [action].
Question: Just as when one performs a single application of effort to kill many sentient beings, one incurs as many instances of non-manifest transgression as there are sentient beings killed.
Furthermore, does this manifest karma (vijñapti-karman) result in only one [atom] or many?
Some say it results in only one. Why is this so?
Because there is no distinction in the simultaneous killing through a single application of effort,
the Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
"He acquires many manifest actions."
The detailed explanation is as before.
Question: Does one incur the offense of killing when killing someone whose life-span is destined to end?
Answer: If, at that very moment, the life-span is destined to end.
At that very moment, the perpetrator does not incur the sin of killing.
However, if by means of such harm one causes even a single moment of life to persist without arising,
then all such dharmas constitute the sin of killing.
How much more so in the case of many moments?
Question: Does one who kills by severing the *marmaccheda* (vital points) incur the offense of killing?
Answer: If at this very moment one is about to pass away, then at that time the perpetrator does not incur the offense of killing.
If, by means of the assault, one causes even a single moment of life to persist and not cease, [then there is no offense].
In every case, one incurs the sin of killing;
how much more so when it involves many moments [of consciousness].
Question: If one harms another such that they are certain to die, [does one incur this sin?]
"Does one who thus takes their own life incur the offense of killing? Answer: No. Why is this so?"
Because that fruit has not yet reached its culmination,
one loses one's life and lacks a subsequent homogeneous existence (nikāya-sabhāga) in which to accomplish that offense.
Question: If, during a battle, they inflict mutual harm upon one another and both die at the same time, does each incur the offense of killing?
Answer: No, they do not.
Why is this? Because both have results that are not yet ultimate;
they would both lose their lives and lack the subsequent homogeneous life-continuum (*nikāyasabhāga*).
This is because one can indeed accomplish that transgression.
Question: If one is coerced by a king or others to commit murder, does one incur the sin of killing?
Some say it cannot be obtained.
Why is this? Because it is constrained by external forces and is not due to one's own intention.
One who speaks in this manner also incurs the sin of killing,
except in the case where one has made a personal vow: "I would rather give up my own life than ever harm another."
In this way, there is no offense.
Question: If one follows the laws established by former kings and inflicts punishment such that an excess occurs, does one incur the sin of killing?
Answer: If one obtains a king or a judicial official and dispatches them to kill, one incurs the non-informative offense (*avijñapti*) of killing;
this applies to the person dispatched as well.
Furthermore, if one commits suicide, one incurs both the manifest and unmanifest offenses of killing.
If a multitude of sentient beings conspire to harm a single life,
the offense belongs to that person who initiates the preparatory action and personally severs the life-force.
One who commits the act of killing incurs the offense of both the manifest (vijñapti) and the unmanifest (avijñapti) forms of taking life; those who conspire with others or provide support, however,
incur only the unmanifest form of taking life.
If many people together apply effort to take the life of a single individual,
it should be known that they all incur the offense of both manifest and unmanifest [action].
Is there any case where this occurs without physical action?
"And does one incur the offense of killing?
Answer: "Yes.
That is to say, by commanding another to kill."
Is it possible to incur the offense of false speech without uttering a word?
Answer: Yes; namely, through bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
Is it possible to incur two offenses without acting with the body or uttering speech?
Answer: Yes;
namely, when a rishi is provoked by mental anger.
And at the time of the *poṣadha*, one expresses purity by remaining silent.
*Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 118;
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 100.

Section Four: The Aggregate of Karma; Sub-section Three: On Harmful Acts; Part Two. Is there karma that is unwholesome, which conforms to a ripening of painful feeling, yet has not yet matured? [The full exposition continues as follows.]
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the positions of others and clarifying one's own position.
That is to say, there are some who claim:
There is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Alternatively,
some say that although an intermediate state exists, there is none for those who are born in the evil destinies.
Alternatively, some say that although those born in the evil destinies possess an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), those who are to be born in hell do not;
or again, others say:
Although those who are to be born in hell possess an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there are none among them who have previously committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karman*).
Alternatively, some say that those who have previously committed an immediate transgression [do not possess it].
Although there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one does not experience the retribution of immediate maturation (*ānantarya-vipāka*) within that intermediate state;
or again, some say that even while dwelling in the intermediate state, one does experience the retribution of immediate maturation.
However, [some] maintain that one receives only the four aggregates and not the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
To refute these various erroneous attachments and to demonstrate the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
it is shown that it exists in all places of birth within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Within that [realm], one also experiences the maturation (*vipāka*) of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
For this reason, this treatise was composed:
Is there any unwholesome karma conducive to the maturation of painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanīya*) that has not yet matured?
Is it not the case that one may give rise to a defiled mind even while not yet experiencing the first fruition of karmic maturation?
Answer: Yes, there is.

Just as when one performs and accumulates an immediate (ānantarya) karma, the first retributive fruit of maturation (vipākaphala) arises for that karma in the intermediate state (antarābhava) of hell.
Question: What is the difference between performing (kṛta) and accumulating (upacita)?
Some say there is no distinction;
others say there is.
Names are differentiated:
this name is formative,
and this name is accumulative.
Some say that there is also a distinction in meaning:
namely, some fall into the evil destinies due to a single unwholesome action,
while others do so due to three.
If one falls into an evil rebirth due to a single unwholesome action,
that action is termed "committed" (*kṛta*) during its preliminary stage,
but not "accumulated" (*upacita*). If it reaches completion, it is termed both "committed" and "accumulated."
If one falls into the evil destinies by means of all three [factors],
then when one or two [of these factors] are present at a given time, it is called "commission" (karaṇa) but not "accumulation" (upacaya);
if all three are present, it is called both "commission" and "accumulation."
As it is with the three types of unwholesome conduct, so it is with the three types of wholesome conduct.
The difference is that one is born in a happy destination.
Furthermore, there are cases where one falls into hell due to a single immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).
Or it may be complete through all five.
If it occurs through only one, that is the stage of preliminary application (*prayoga*);
it is called "performance" (*karaṇa*) but not "increase" (*upacaya*).
If it reaches its ultimate limit, it is called "karmic formation" (*abhisamskāra*) and also called "increase" (*upacaya*).
If it possesses all five [conditions] yet forms only one through four [of the results],
it is called only "karmic formation" and not "increase."
If one fully commits all five, it is called both "performance" and "augmentation.
Furthermore, some fall into the evil destinies by means of a single unwholesome path of action,
while others do so by means of all ten.
If it is by means of a single [action], then in its stage of preliminary application (*prayoga*),
it is called "performance" (*abhisamskāra*) but not "accumulation" (*upacaya*);
if it reaches completion, it is called both "performance" and "accumulation."
If one commits from one to nine [unwholesome actions] while possessing all ten [causes],
it is called "commission" (kṛta) but not "accumulation" (upacita).
If one commits all ten, it is called both "commission" and "accumulation."
As it is with the ten unwholesome courses of action,
so it is with the ten wholesome courses of action;
the difference is that they lead to rebirth in the happy realms.
Furthermore, there are cases where many sublime deeds (*sucarita*) bring about a single homogeneous life-state (*nikāyasabhāga*),
such as the final homogeneous life-state of the Bodhisattvas,
which is brought about by three hundred and twenty merits (*puṇya*).
If one creates from one hundred merits up to three thousand one hundred merits,
it is merely called "creation" and not "increase.
It is only when one fully creates three thousand two hundred merits that [it is called increase].
It is called "karma performed" and also called "karma accumulated.
Furthermore, some karma is produced through intentional volition,
while other karma is not produced through intentional volition.
If that which is created through intentional reflection is called "karma performed" (abhisamskāra), it is also called "increased" (upacita).
If it is not created through intentional reflection,
it is only called "performed" and not "increased."
Constructed through deliberate reflection;
constructed impulsively.
The same applies to verbal expression.
Furthermore, there is karma that is to be experienced in three periods of time,
and there is karma that is to be experienced indeterminately.
That which is to be experienced in three periods of time is called "performed" (*kṛta*) and is also called "accumulated" (*upacita*).
Karma conducive to indeterminate experience is merely termed "created" (abhisamskrta) and not "accumulated" (upacita).
[This applies to] karma conducive to determinate experience and karma conducive to indeterminate experience.
The same applies to what is taught.
Furthermore, there are some karmas that accord with determinate experience in a specific life,
and there are some karmas that accord with indeterminate experience.
Karma that is to be experienced in a specific subsequent life is called both "created" (*kṛta*) and "accumulated" (*upacita*);
karma that is not to be experienced in a specific subsequent life is called only "created," not "accumulated."
Furthermore, there are some karmas for which both the timing and the maturation are fixed;
there are others for which the maturation is fixed but the timing is not.
When both [the intention and the action] are determinate, it is called both "committed" (*kṛta*) and "increased" (*upacita*).
When only one is determinate, it is called only "committed," not "increased.
Furthermore, there is unwholesome karma that results in retribution within the evil destinies.
There are unwholesome karmas that result in experiences within the favorable realms of rebirth.
The former is called both "committed" (*kṛta*) and "accumulated" (*upacita*);
the latter is called "committed" but not "accumulated."
Wholesome karma is the opposite of this;
the explanation is likewise.
Furthermore, there is unwholesome karma.
Unwholesome [karma] has unwholesome karma as its concomitant,
while wholesome karma has wholesome karma as its concomitant;
the former is termed both "formative" (*abhisamskāra*) and "accumulative" (*upacaya*).
The latter is called "formative" (abhisamskāra) but not "increasing" (upacaya).
The same applies to the explanation of wholesome karma (*kuśala-karman*), which is the opposite of this.
Furthermore, there is unwholesome karma associated with the view of non-action and wrong view,
which arises within the continuity of cause and effect;
there is also unwholesome karma associated with the view of action and right view.
One is not deluded regarding birth within the continuity of cause and effect.
The former is called "formative action" (*abhisamskāra*) and is also called "accumulation" (*upacaya*);
the latter is called "formative action" but is not called "accumulation."
Wholesome karma is the opposite of this;
the explanation is likewise.
Furthermore, there is unwholesome karma that destroys ethical discipline and destroys right view.
There are unwholesome karmas that destroy the precepts but do not destroy the views.
The former is called both "committed" and "increased";
the latter is called "committed" but not "increased."
Wholesome karma is the opposite of this;
the explanation is likewise.
Furthermore, there is unwholesome karma that is both impaired in its preliminary application and impaired in its underlying intention.
There are unwholesome karmas where the preparatory application is destroyed while the intention is not;
the former is called both "committed" (*kṛta*) and "increased" (*upacita*),
whereas the latter is called "committed" but not "increased."
Wholesome karma is the opposite of this;
the explanation is likewise.
Furthermore, there is karma which, once performed, is not abandoned, does not change, is not disgorged, and does not rely upon an antidote.
There is karma that, once performed, is abandoned, transformed, and rejected through its antidote;
the former is called both "created" (*kṛta*) and "accumulated" (*upacita*),
while the latter is called "created" but not "accumulated."
In this way, there is karma that is perceived at three times,
karma that is not perceived at three times,
and karma for which there is no regret after it has been performed.
Having acted, one regrets it; having acted, one reflects upon it;
having acted, one does not reflect upon it;
and one repeatedly recollects it.
It is not repeatedly recollected;
the same applies to its exposition.
Furthermore, if an action is capable of both grasping and yielding its fruit.
It is called "formative" (*abhisamskāra*) and also called "accumulative" (*upacaya*).
If karma takes up a fruit but cannot grant it,
it is merely called "formative" and not "accumulative."
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"If the intention regarding the action performed is manifested through the intention of dedication,
and it is praised and proclaimed for those of a similar kind."
This is called "formative action" (abhisamskāra) and is also called "accumulation" (upacaya).
If the karma performed is contrary to these characteristics,
it is merely called "formative action" and not "accumulation."
Some say: "If the karma that has been performed is complete in every respect and consummated in every respect."
Just as when the construction and decoration of a caitya are fully completed,
this is called "construction" and also called "growth.
If the action performed is contrary to this, [it is otherwise].
It is merely called "formative activity" (abhisamskāra) and not "growth" (upacaya).
The Venerable One says:
"If the karma that has been performed meets with the convergence of various conditions, it will necessarily..."
That which definitely brings about its fruit is called "karma performed" (abhisamskāra) and also called "increased" (upacita).
If the karma performed is contrary to this,
it is called only "performed," not "increased."
There are immeasurable such categories;
these are called the distinctions of formation and increase.
There are five types of immediate karmas (*ānantarya-karma*).
First, killing one's mother;
second, killing one's father;
third, killing an arhat.
Fourth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha;
fifth, with a malicious mind, drawing blood from the body of a Buddha.
Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature of these five deeds of immediate retribution?
Answer: They have bodily and vocal actions as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Of these, the first three have bodily action as their intrinsic nature, while the fourth has vocal action as its intrinsic nature.
Therefore, these five are subsumed within three realms, three bases, and one aggregate.
The three realms are the realm of form, the realm of sound, and the realm of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
The three bases are the base of form, the base of sound, and the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
The single aggregate is the aggregate of form;
this is called the intrinsic nature of immediate karma (*ānantarya-karma*).
The intrinsic nature has thus been explained.
Therefore, it shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason is it called "uninterrupted" (ānantarya)?
Answer: It is designated as "uninterrupted" due to two conditions.
First, it precludes the present and the future;
second, it precludes other realms of existence.
Regarding the preclusion of the present and the future:
These five are exclusively karma to be experienced upon rebirth (upapadyavedanīya);
they are not karma to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya) nor karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparaparyāyavedanīya).
Therefore, they are called "uninterrupted" (ānantarya).
"Excluding other destinies" means that this [retribution] is determined to be experienced in hell,
and is not interspersed with other destinies.
Therefore, it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*).
It is established as uninterrupted by two causes and conditions:
first, the ingratitude of failing to repay kindness.
Second, the destruction of the field of merit.
Those who turn their backs on kindness and nurturance refer to those who harm their mother or harm their father.
Regarding those who destroy the field of merit,
this refers to the other three types;
they incur the immediate offense (ānantarya-karma) due to two causes and conditions.
When both the preparatory effort and the two fruits are completed,
although the preparatory effort has been undertaken, if the fruit is not finalized,
one does not incur the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
Even if one does not initiate the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) once the result is finalized, one still incurs the immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*).
Regarding those who do initiate the preparatory effort but do not finalize the result: this refers, for example, to someone who intends to kill their mother.
When the mother realized this, she hid [the child] among the grain.
Another woman was in the mother's sleeping quarters;
when that person arrived, thinking it was her own mother, she killed her with a knife.
Having already caused harm, he then went further into a heap of grain to wipe his blade; as the blade touched his mother’s body, she lost her life.
At the time the preparatory effort was initiated, the result had not yet been finalized.
When the fruit is finalized, there is no longer any preparatory effort (*prayoga*);
therefore, the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) is not established.
This is because when the fruit is finalized, one does not initiate further preparatory effort.
It is, for example, like someone supporting their parents as they cross a perilous path;
fearing that bandits might come,
they urge them forward by pushing and pressing them along.
The parents fell and died as a result;
although the fruit was ultimately accomplished, it did not arise from an intentional application (*prayoga*).
Therefore, both the initiation of the application and the ultimate completion of the fruit must occur for the immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) to be established.
Question: Is there a case where one initiates the preparatory effort and brings it to completion, yet does not incur the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*)?
Answer: There is.
This refers to dying at the same time as the victim;
since there is no subsequent *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous class of beings) through which that offense could be established, [the killer] would not incur it.
However, if an elder brother sends his younger brother to kill their mother, the younger brother incurs the immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) by following his elder brother's instruction.
If a younger brother dispatches another person or harms [the mother] together with another,
only the younger brother incurs the immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
There is a case where an elder brother dispatches his younger brother to cause another person to harm their mother.
If both brothers follow their elder brother’s instruction, both incur the immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).
If the younger brother harms himself or is harmed by another, only the younger brother incurs the immediate transgression.
There is also the case where an elder brother dispatches his younger brother to harm their mother together with another.
If the younger brother follows the elder brother’s instruction and both commit the act, they both incur the immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).
However, if the younger brother kills on his own initiative or causes another to kill him alone,
only the younger brother incurs the immediate transgression.
Suppose there is an elder brother who sends his younger brother’s mother to be killed.
If the younger brother follows his brother’s instructions and both commit the act, they both incur the immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
However, if the mother departs and he only kills her later, then only the younger brother incurs the immediate retribution.
Just as an elder brother dispatches a younger brother, so too does he dispatch a younger sister; as the younger brother dispatches the elder brother, so too does he dispatch his elder sister.
Just as he dispatches one who comes to harm, so too does he dispatch one who goes, stands, sits, or lies down.
As it is with killing one's mother or father,
so too is it with killing an arhat or shedding the blood of a Buddha.
The distinctions regarding the dispatching of messengers should be understood as being analogous to this.
If a non-human kills the parents of another non-human, one does not incur the immediate retribution (ānantarya) offense.
It should be understood that the same applies when a non-human kills a human, or when a human kills a non-human.
Only humans who kill their own parents incur the immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
Question: If one who is a *śaṇḍha*, a *pandaka*, or one who is sexless or possesses both sexual organs kills their parents, does one incur the immediate retribution? Answer: One does not.
Why is this? Because by the very nature of that body,
its mental power is so feeble and inferior that it is incapable of performing either restraint (*saṃvara*) or non-restraint (*asaṃvara*),
as it is of such a physical constitution.
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke thus:
"Those such as the *śaṇḍhaka* (eunuchs) who kill their father or mother do not incur the immediate retribution (*ānantarya*). Why is this so?"
They lack love and respect for their parents,
because that which was previously manifest has now been destroyed.
Furthermore, they lack a sense of superior shame and dread of blame toward their parents.
Because they can first manifest and are now subject to destruction.
The Venerable One stated:
"Because their afflictions are increased, those such as *ṣaṇḍhaka* are certainly included within the evil destinies (*durgati*)."
Because they are comprised within the miserable destinies (*apāya*), there is no immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).
Question: If one kills one's father or mother among the various classes of animals (*tiryagyoni*), does one incur an immediate transgression?
Answer: One does not.
Why is this? Because that body is by its very nature such that its willpower is weak and inferior;
it is incapable of being the basis for either restraint or non-restraint.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"Among the various classes of animals, killing one's father or mother does not constitute an immediate transgression (ānantarya). Why is this so?"
They lack love and reverence for their parents,
because that which was previously manifest has now been destroyed.
Furthermore, they lack superior shame and dread of wrongdoing toward their parents.
Because that which was previously manifest has now been destroyed;
as the Venerable One said:
"Among the various classes of animals, there are those who kill their own parents."
Regarding the ānantarya offenses, there are those that can be obtained and those that cannot.
That is to say, the wise obtain them, while the unwise do not.
It is said that there once was a wise dragon-horse.
Out of greed for its lineage, humans caused it to mate with its mother.
Later, the horse realized this and died after castrating itself.
Question: Suppose one, through a single application of effort, simultaneously kills one’s mother and another woman.
As has been explained previously regarding the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) associated with that, from whom does the informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) derive?
Answer: It is obtained from the mother.
Why is this? Because among those [five heinous crimes], the immediate transgression (ānantarya-karma) is the most grave.
The Venerable Ghosaka stated:
"All informative actions (vijñapti-karma) are composed of atoms (paramāṇu)."
Because the mother and the other [victim] are distinct entities, each consisting of unique atoms, the offense of manifest action (vijñapti) is incurred in relation to both persons.
Question: Suppose there is a woman whose *kalala* has fallen out.
If another woman receives [the embryo] within her body, and a son is later born, who is considered the mother, and by killing whom does one incur the immediate retribution (*ānantarya*)?
Answer: The former is the biological mother (*jananī*).
If one later becomes the foster mother,
it is only by harming the biological mother that one incurs the immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma);
this is because the kalala depends upon the former [the biological mother] for its birth.
In all matters to be done, one should consult the foster mother.
To kill one who is not one's mother while perceiving her as one's mother,
or to kill one who is one's mother while perceiving her as someone who is not, [constitutes matricide].
Neither incurs the offense of immediate retribution (ānantarya).
It is only when one kills a mother while perceiving her as a mother that one incurs the offense of immediate retribution.
It should be understood that the same applies to the father and others as well.
Is there any woman who is neither one's mother nor an Arhat?
"Is it possible to commit an ānantarya offense by killing one's father who has undergone a change of gender to become female?
Answer: "Yes;
that is, if one kills one's father who has changed his faculties to become a woman."
Is there any man who, though he is neither his father nor an Arhat,
incurs the offense of immediate retribution by killing him?
Answer: Yes;
that is, when one harms a mother who has undergone a change of faculties to become a male.
Question: What if the mother is an Arhat?
Suppose one's father is an Arhat;
when that person kills him, does he incur only one ānantarya offense,
or does he incur two?
If one says that he has obtained only one [of these],
he repays the kindness of his upbringing and destroys the field of merit.
How is it that one [attainment] is established?
How, furthermore, is the Sūtra to be reconciled?
For example, as the Buddha told Śrīkṣānti:
You have now committed two immediate offenses (ānantarya-karma):
namely, killing your father and killing an Arhat.
If you say that you have committed both—
How can one who takes a single life incur two offenses?
One should answer that they incur but one;
for such a person both betrays the kindness of their nurturer and destroys a field of merit.
Since both [factors] operate within a single body,
the Sūtra should have stated:
"You incur the offense of immediate retribution (ānantarya) due to two conditions."
Regarding the statement that one who harms his father and an arhat incurs two offenses:
this is intended to reprove such a person by means of these two offenses.
Other masters say:
although the substance of the offense is one, the suffering it induces is twofold;
therefore, two are mentioned.
Question: Just as killing an arhat incurs an immediate transgression (ānantarya-karma), does killing those who are still in training (śaikṣa) also incur this same offense?
Answer: It does not.
Why is this? It was previously stated that the immediate [offense] is acquired through two conditions:
first, being ungrateful for the kindness of one's nurturer.
The second is the destruction of the field of merit.
This harms those in training (śaikṣa), but it does not destroy the field of merit itself,
because they possess both virtues and faults.
There are both sublime conduct and evil conduct;
there are both roots of goodness and roots of unwholesomeness.
Therefore, it is asked: what causes one to fall away from the fruit of arhatship?
"Would one who harms them incur the Avīci hell? The answer is:
"No, because they are still in the stage of training (śaikṣa)."
As previously stated.
Question: At the final moment when life is about to cease, must one necessarily abide in the state of an Aśaikṣa?
Why is it that one does not incur an immediate retribution (*ānantarya*)?
The answer is: because there is no malicious intent toward the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
That is to say, he only gives rise to the intention to kill and the preparatory action (*prayoga*) toward the body of one still in training (*śaikṣa*).
It does not apply to those beyond training (aśaikṣa),
because since they lack the cause of immediate succession (ānantarya-hetu), they cannot incur an immediate offense (ānantarya-āpatti).
This is stated in the Vinaya.
In the Śāla grove, there were many bhikṣus who were killed by a band of thieves and robbed of their clothing and belongings;
those nearby officials all captured them.
They were escorted to the king’s presence, and the king commanded that they be dealt with according to the law.
Among them, one thief fled to Jetavana Forest seeking to go forth as a monk;
at that time, the community of bhikṣus did not conduct a thorough investigation.
He ordained him so that he might receive full precepts.
At that time, the executioners led the remaining bandits to a cemetery,
intending to butcher and dismember them.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus, in order to understand the things of the world that are to be loathed,
all went together to see it;
those who had gone forth were also among them.
Seeing the various sinners with their limbs and joints dismembered and scattered in different places,
that newly ordained monk was immediately struck with terror.
He fainted and fell prostrate upon the ground, regaining consciousness only after a long time.
When the assembly asked him the reason for this,
he replied:
"The deceased was my companion.
Yesterday, I engaged in this very same act together with him.
Had I not gone forth into homelessness, I too would have met with such suffering."
Having heard this, the bhikṣus said to one another,
"How shall we deal with this evil man?
and they went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"This person has killed a community of bhikṣus;
he has committed an ānantarya offense and is unfit for ordination."
If they have already gone forth as members of the community, they should be expelled and not allowed to dwell together with us. Why is this?
Because those who commit an act of immediate retribution (ānantarya) [cannot abide] within my True Dharma and Vinaya.
Because they are unable to cause various wholesome dharmas to grow.
Question: Since that person does not realize they are an arhat, for what reason do they incur the immediate transgression (ānantarya-karma)?
Answer: One does not incur an offense by virtue of knowing;
rather, one incurs an offense because of destroying a field of merit.
This refers to [the case] among the community of bhikṣus.
One gives rise to a murderous intention that lacks discernment;
by means of such an extremely evil mind, one harms and kills an Arhat.
Therefore, one incurs the immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma).
Question: If one first commits another immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) and subsequently causes a schism in the Saṃgha,
which result will that person experience first upon being born in hell?
If one were to first experience the fruit of another immediate transgression,
then the schism of the Saṃgha would have to be categorized as a subsequent transgression; if,
however, one were to first experience the fruit of the schism of the Saṃgha...
The other immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) would consequently have to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Answer: If one has previously committed another immediate transgression, one will be unable to cause a schism in the Saṃgha later on.
If one first causes a schism in the Saṃgha and subsequently commits other deeds of immediate retribution (ānantarya),
all those later actions are due to the predominant power of that initial schism.
They equally invite the fruit of the Avīci Hell;
other misdeeds that result in retribution upon rebirth should be understood accordingly,
following the analogy of the immediate karmas (*ānantarya-karma*).
Furthermore, if one first causes a schism in the Sangha and subsequently commits other deeds of immediate retribution (ānantarya),
all those later deeds are due to the predominant power of that initial schism.
They are likewise summoned to the Avīci hell;
even when they experience the full lifespan of one kalpa as their fruit, there is no further increase in that lifespan.
This refers to other unwholesome actions whose results are to be experienced in subsequent births.
The length of the lifespan for those who commit the immediate karmas (ānantarya-karma) should also be understood accordingly.
Question: If one is born into the Avīci Hell due to causing a schism in the Sangha, and the world-system were to undergo destruction before their lifespan there has expired?
Do they die prematurely?
If they were to die prematurely, how could their lifespan—drawn forth by extremely heavy karma—be cut short?
If they do not die prematurely, why do they not create an obstacle to the destruction of the world-system?
As stated in the Sūtra:
"In whatever place even a single sentient being remains, that place is not destroyed by the calamities.
Answer: If their lifespan is fixed, they do not suffer premature death.
Question: If that is so, why does one not encounter obstacles during the destruction of the world-system?
Answer: By the power of karma, they are drawn and placed into the hells of other world-systems to undergo [retribution].
It is like when a royal capital intends to grant a general amnesty:
first, the heavy criminals are moved to prisons on the outskirts,
and only then is the amnesty proclaimed.
It is the same for that [wind] as well.
Some say that when this world is about to undergo destruction:
If there are sentient beings who commit deeds of immediate retribution,
it is the natural law that upon the end of their lives they will not be reborn in this world,
but will necessarily be born in the hells of other worlds to undergo the karmic fruit of these deeds.
Some say that when the world is about to undergo destruction,
there are certainly no sentient beings who commit extremely evil karmas.
Question: Is it possible for one to commit all five ānantarya [karmas]? Some say no. Why is that?
Because this karma is so extremely heavy that no vessel is capable of withstanding it or containing it.
Other masters say that there are those who commit all five.
For example, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
there was a bhikṣu named Puṣpadanta,
the son of Yaśodatta, who committed the five deeds of immediate retribution.
And the severance of the roots of goodness.
Question: Is it by means of one uninterrupted [karma], or even up to five?
What is the distinction regarding those who fall into hell?
The answer is: for one who falls into hell due to a single *ānantarya* (immediate) offense, their body is narrow and small, and the instruments of torture are not numerous.
The painful sensations that manifest are not extremely intense;
however, for those who fall into hell due to the five deeds of immediate retribution,
their bodies become vast and the instruments of suffering increase.
The experience of suffering that manifests is extremely intense and sharp.
Question: Among the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), which is the most grave?
Answer: It is the schism of the Saṃgha, for it destroys the Dharma-body.
Next, one sheds the blood of a Buddha;
next, one harms an Arhat;
next, one harms one's mother.
Later, he harmed his father.
This is because the mother’s kindness and nurturing are more significant toward the father,
and the power of the field of merit (guṇakṣetra) is superior to that of the field of gratitude (upakārikṣetra).
Question: The Blessed One has stated that all the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are called the Buddha, and these cannot be harmed.
How then can one incur an immediate transgression (ānantarya-karma) by shedding blood with an evil mind?
The Venerable Vasumitra says:
It is because one gives rise to an evil intention with the desire to destroy the factors that can bring about great enlightenment.
Although one harms the physical body, one incurs the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) with respect to that [body].
Furthermore, the unlearned qualities (*aśaikṣadharma*) of all Buddhas depend upon the physical body for their manifestation;
therefore, one should know that if the support (*āśraya*) is destroyed, that which is supported (*āśrita*) is likewise destroyed.
Just as milk is lost when a jar is broken, one thereby incurs the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
Question: What of the case where one gives rise to an evil mind and draws blood from the body of a Buddha?
One incurs the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
Is it possible that by giving rise to an evil mind, even without drawing blood,
one also incurs this offense of immediate retribution?
Answer: There is.
Therefore, one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is the case where one gives rise to an evil mind and draws blood from the body of a Buddha, yet does not incur the immediate offense (*ānantarya-karma*).
This refers to cases where one gives rise to the intent to strike and blood flows;
or where one gives rise to an evil mind but does not cause blood to flow,
yet still incurs the immediate transgression (ānantarya).
That is to say, from the arising of the intent to kill up until causing the blood to flow from its place—
there are those who, having given rise to an evil mind, shed the blood of a Buddha,
and they too incur the immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*).
This refers to cases where one gives rise to the intent to kill and blood is shed; however,
if one gives rise to a malicious mind but does not reach the point of shedding blood,
one does not incur the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
