likewise, for a long night, the Bodhisattva’s parents have also cultivated the karma that brings about a noble son.
If one were to undergo transformational birth (upapāduka), then the cultivation of both [the male and female organs] would be empty and fruitless;
therefore, it is not accepted. Some say:
To manifest that the Bodhisattva is in every way supreme—
namely, in terms of wisdom, vision, lineage, and rank—
for this reason, he does not undergo transformational birth (*upapāduka*).
Some say that in order to sever the pride of sentient beings regarding their lineage,
[the Buddha] did not undergo transformation-birth (upapāduka) based on a superior lineage.
Some say that because he wished to attract those who delight in the household life and lead them into the Dharma, he did not undergo transformational birth (*upapāduka*).
If he had undergone transformational birth, they would have said: [he was born from such-and-such].
Since the Buddha has no relatives, he abandoned his family life; how could he be compared to us?

If a bodhisattva is born into a kṣatriya family with powerful kinsmen, yet is able to renounce them as if discarding nasal mucus or saliva, opening the gate of ambrosia and attaining equal and perfect enlightenment.
Then they all conceived a sense of wonder and received what was said with reverence;
so it is said.
Because Bodhisattvas wish to serve as internal and external protectors for the Dharma banner, they do not undergo transformational birth (*upapāduka*).
All Buddhas possess both internal and external protection;
"internal" refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
"External" refers to relatives.
If there were no external protection, they would be ruined by the evil factions of non-Buddhists;
therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, delivered the Śākyas in order to protect the True Dharma.
Because of this, even the group of six bhikṣus said:
"If any non-Buddhists come to harass the Buddha,
and if the Buddha does not restrain them, we too shall be able to subdue them by force."
Some say that he did not accept birth by transformation (*upapāduka*) in order to stop the slanders of non-Buddhists;
that is to say, the Buddha personally passed away from the Tuṣita heaven.
His bodily radiance was brilliant, illuminating the great trichiliocosm.
Having entered his mother’s womb and completed ten full months,
he emerged from the womb and immediately took seven steps, proclaiming himself the sole Honored One.
Having left the household life, practiced austerities, and attained perfect enlightenment at the Bodhi tree, he was still slandered with these words:
"After more than a hundred kalpas, a great illusionist shall appear who has neither father nor mother and will devour the world."
If he were to undergo transformational birth (upapāduka), it would increase slander;
therefore, the Bodhisattva does not undergo transformational birth. Some say:
In order to benefit sentient beings of the future, he does not undergo birth by transformation.
Why is this? If he were to undergo birth from a womb, there would be a physical remains;
even after a thousand years have passed since his parinirvāṇa, [the Dharma would still be preserved].
There are immeasurable sentient beings who, even if they can give rise to a sincere and pure mind toward a portion of the relics of the body as small as a mustard seed,
and offer respectful worship, will obtain boundless merit.
One is born in heaven to experience bliss and attain parinirvāṇa;
if one were born by transformation, these matters would not occur. Why is this so?
Because the life of a transformation being ends like the extinguishing of a lamp’s light, leaving nothing behind.
Here, a further inquiry arises from the discussion:
Why does the life of a transformation being end without any remainder?
Answer: Because when they are born, the sense faculties arise all at once,
so when they pass away, they likewise perish all at once,
just as a person playing in water suddenly emerges and suddenly submerges.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the transformation body is light and subtle like a cloud or lightning;
it is also like a flame of wind that, once extinguished, leaves no remainder and its location can no longer be known.
Furthermore, in the case of beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*), derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) increases;
in the other three modes of birth, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) increase.
Because derived matter increases [in the case of transformation], when it ceases, it ceases all at once.
Furthermore, in the case of the transformation-born (nirmāṇa), the faculties (indriya) increase;
in the other three [births], non-faculty dharmas (anindriya-dharma) increase.
Because the faculties increase, when they cease, they cease all at once.
This refers to those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), whose physical forms, hair, nails, and so forth lack sense organs and consist of minimal material substance.

Question: If there is no residue remaining for those born by transformation, why does the Sūtra state that the *garuḍa* (wondrous-winged bird) born by transformation takes the *nāga* (serpent) born by transformation as its food?
He replied, "Because I did not know [what it was], I took it as food;
however, it did not satisfy my hunger. Some say:
While that dragon was not yet dead, he was able to satisfy his hunger for a time;
once it had died, he became hungry again.
Hungry once more, he went forth to seize food without fail or hindrance.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the bodies of nāgas born by transformation are so refined and subtle that,
like clarified butter or oil, they become food as soon as they are swallowed into the belly.
Some say that the magically born garuḍas possess many skillful means by which they obtain magically born nāgas;
pressing them with their feet at the neck, they swallow them from the tail.
As long as life has not been severed, one is able to take food;
once dead, it is not so.
Other masters say:
When that garuḍa eats a spontaneously born nāga,
his saliva first flows out, dissolving the brain as it descends;
he swallows it together with the nāga, and the act of eating is thus completed.
It is not the case that only spontaneously born (*upapāduka*) nāgas alone constitute the object of this meal.
One may ask: how then are other statements in the sūtras to be reconciled?
For example, as it is said:
Within the great hells,
there are black-spotted dogs, robust and fierce,
which seize sentient beings and throw them down upon the ground of iron.
They tear open their bellies and devour their entrails and stomachs.
It is said that they "eat" because, as long as those entrails and stomachs have not yet left the body,
they are able to temporarily satisfy their hunger.
Some say that because of the power of the evil karma of those sentient beings undergoing retribution,
it merely causes them to experience suffering and does not function as food.
If one accomplishes the body, does one also accomplish verbal action?
One should answer that this involves four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are cases where one accomplishes the body but not verbal action.
There are those who accomplish verbal karma but not bodily karma;
there are those who accomplish both bodily and verbal karma;
and there are those who accomplish neither bodily nor verbal karma.
All of this is as previously explained in the section on bodily action (*kāyakarman*) regarding the body;
the difference here is that it speaks of vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*),
because there can certainly be no distinction in the presence or absence of the levels (*bhūmi*) to which bodily and vocal actions are bound.
If one accomplishes the body, does one also accomplish mental karma?
Answer: All those who accomplish the body necessarily accomplish mental karma.
There are those who accomplish mental action but not bodily action;
namely, those born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes the body, does one also accomplish bodily and verbal actions?
Answer: There are those who possess the body but not bodily or verbal karma;
namely, those dwelling within an eggshell, or various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) abiding in the womb, or those born in the desire realm who abide in neither restraint nor non-restraint.
There is no bodily or vocal intimation, or if it exists, it has been lost.
There is one who possesses the body and bodily action,
but not vocal action.
This refers to one born in the desire realm who dwells in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline,
currently possessing bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
or having previously possessed it without losing it, while lacking verbal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) even if it were present but has been lost.
There is one who accomplishes both bodily and vocal karma,
but not bodily karma; that is,
one born in the desire realm who dwells in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint and currently possesses vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
Or, there are those who previously possessed it and have not lost the non-manifest (avijñapti), even if they should lose the manifest (vijñapti).
There are those who possess both the body and bodily and vocal actions;
namely, the noble ones (ārya) dwelling within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and abides in restraint,
or abides in non-restraint,
or abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint.
There is currently a bodily or vocal intimation,
or one previously possessed that has not been lost;
this applies even if one is born in the form realm and possesses bodily or vocal karma.
Does he possess that body?
Answer: He may possess it, or he may not possess it.
What is accomplishment?
It is as previously described.
What is non-accomplishment?
This refers to noble ones born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If they possess the body, do they also possess bodily action (*kāyakarman*) and mental action (*manaskarman*)?
Answer: There are those who possess both the body and mental action.
It is not bodily action;
that is to say, when one is within an eggshell,
or when ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) abide within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and dwells in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, and lacks bodily intimation—
or even if such exists, it has been lost—
there is the possession of the body and of mental action, as well as bodily action.
This refers to noble ones dwelling within the womb,
whether they are born in the desire realm and abide in restraint or abide in non-restraint.
If one abides in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and there currently exists a bodily intimation,
or one previously possessed of it has not been lost.
If one is born in the form realm and possesses both bodily and mental karma, does that person possess the body?
Answer: They may or may not possess it.
Or it may not be accomplished.
How is it accomplished?
It is as previously described.
What is non-possession?
It refers to noble ones born in the formless realm who possess the body.
Does he accomplish verbal and mental karma?
Answer: There are those who accomplish bodily and mental karma, but not verbal karma.
There is the accomplishment of bodily action, vocal action, and mental action.
These are all as previously explained regarding the body in relation to bodily and mental actions;
the difference is as follows:
This explains the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
Suppose one accomplishes both vocal and mental karma;
does that person also accomplish bodily [karma]?
Answer: One may be endowed with it, or not endowed with it;
this is also as stated therein.
If one is endowed with the body, is one also endowed with bodily action, vocal action, and mental action?
Answer: There are those who are endowed with the body and mental action.
It is not bodily action or vocal action.
There is the accomplishment of body, bodily action, and mental action,
but not vocal action.
There is one who accomplishes bodily action, vocal action, and mental action,
but not bodily action;
there is one who accomplishes the body.
As for the bodily, vocal, and mental actions,
these are all explained in the same manner as the bodily and vocal actions discussed previously regarding the body;
this is because mental action is accomplished at all times.
If one accomplishes bodily action, vocal action, and mental action, does that person accomplish the body?
Answer: They may accomplish it.
Or it may not be accomplished,
as it was explained there.
If one accomplishes bodily action (kāyakarman), [the same applies].
Does he also accomplish verbal action?
One should respond that there are four possible cases (catuṣkoṭika).
There is one who accomplishes bodily action but not verbal action.
This refers to one born in the desire realm who dwells in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, currently possessing bodily intimation—
or having previously possessed it without losing it—
and lacking vocal intimation.
There is the case where something exists but is lost.
There is one who accomplishes vocal karma but not bodily karma;
namely, one born in the desire realm who dwells in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint.
There is currently a vocal intimation,
or one previously possessed that has not been lost;
there is no bodily intimation.
There are cases where [the action] exists but is lost.
There are those who accomplish both bodily and vocal karma,
namely, the noble ones dwelling within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm, whether abiding in restraint,
abiding in non-restraint,
or abiding in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint.
There is currently a manifestation of body or speech,
or one previously possessed that has not been lost;
this is the case if one is born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
If noble ones are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
there are cases where they do not possess bodily action (kāyakarman) nor vocal action (vākkarman).
That is to say: those dwelling within an eggshell;
or various ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) dwelling within the womb;
or those born in the desire realm who abide in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline.
There is no bodily or vocal intimation;
even if it existed, it would have been lost.
This is the case for those ordinary beings born in the formless realm.
If one accomplishes bodily action, does one also accomplish mental action?
Answer: Those who accomplish bodily action also accomplish mental action.
There are cases where one accomplishes mental action but not bodily action;
namely, those dwelling within an eggshell,
or ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) who abide within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and dwells in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
there is no bodily intimation;
even if it existed previously, it has been lost.
If ordinary beings are born in the formless realm and possess bodily action,
do they also possess vocal action and mental action?
Answer: There are those who possess bodily action (*kāyakarman*) and mental action (*manaskarman*), but not vocal action (*vākkarman*).
This refers to those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who abide in a state that is neither discipline (*saṃvara*) nor non-discipline (*asaṃvara*).
There is currently a bodily intimation,
or one previously possessed that has not been lost;
there is no vocal intimation.
There is the case where something exists but is lost:
there are those who have accomplished bodily, vocal, and mental karma,
namely, the noble ones dwelling within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm, whether abiding in restraint,
abiding in non-restraint,
or abiding in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint.
There currently exists a bodily or vocal intimation,
or one previously possessed that has not been lost;
this is the case if one is born in the form realm.
If noble ones are born in the formless realm,
and they possess vocal and mental karma,
do they also possess bodily karma?
Answer: One may possess it, or one may not possess it.
How does one possess it?
This is as previously stated.
What constitutes non-possession?
It refers to one born in the desire realm who dwells in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline.
There is currently a vocal intimation,
or one previously possessed that has not been lost;
there is no bodily intimation.
Suppose there is possession and then loss.
If one accomplishes verbal action,
does one also accomplish mental action?
Answer: Those who accomplish verbal action also accomplish mental action;
however, there are those who accomplish mental action [but not verbal action].
It is not vocal action.
This is as previously explained regarding bodily action in contrast to mental action;
the difference is as follows:
This explains the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
The general summary of what has been stated above is as follows:
namely, if that body is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is not accomplished [in those states].
Those born in the desire realm or the form realm definitely possess those bodily and vocal actions. However,
if one is an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) within an eggshell or in the womb,
or if one is an ordinary being born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they definitely do not possess them.
All noble ones,
ordinary beings of the form realm,
and ordinary beings of the desire realm.
Those who abide in either wholesome or unwholesome precepts definitely accomplish them;
others may or may not accomplish them.
All mental karma is invariably accomplished.
*Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 120.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 100.
Compiled by the twenty-one [scholars] and five hundred Great Arhats, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Section Four of the Third Sub-section on Taking Life within the Fourth Aggregate of Karma: If karma has not yet abandoned defilement...
"Is the maturation of that karma not free from defilement?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This is in order to refute the positions of other schools and to clarify our own doctrine.
Specifically, the Vātsīputrīyas assert that the five classes of karma and the resulting maturations (vipāka) likewise pertain to all five classes.

Desiring to stop that misconception, [the author] composed this treatise to show that although karma generally pertains to all five categories, its maturation (*vipāka*) is exclusively abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
If karma has not been freed from defilement,
has its maturation also not been freed from defilement?
Answer: Regarding those actions that have not yet abandoned defilement, the maturation of those actions is necessarily not yet free from defilement;
or there may be actions whose maturation is not yet free from defilement.
That karma has already been freed from defilement;
that is to say, for a stream-enterer, the karma to be abandoned by seeing has already been freed from defilement,
yet the maturation of that karma has not yet been freed from defilement.
It should be understood that among these, there are some karmas whose defilement is first abandoned,
while their maturation is abandoned only later;
and there are some karmas whose defilement and their maturation are abandoned simultaneously.
It is necessarily impossible that one first attains freedom from defilement regarding the ripening [of karma],
and only later does that karma itself become free from defilement;
this refers to the time of the four dharmakṣāntis.
This causes all unwholesome karma subsumed under the fourfold assembly to first become free from defilement,
yet it is not their maturation (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, this occurs during the eight uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) prior to becoming detached from the defilements of the desire realm.
One first attains detachment from the unwholesome karma to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the first eight categories;
these are not its maturation.
As for those various maturations, one attains detachment from them only upon reaching the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
This is called the prior detachment from defilement regarding karma;
subsequently, its maturation (vipāka) also attains detachment.
This occurs at the time of the ninth uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) when one becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm.
It causes the ninth grade of all unwholesome karma,
all unwholesome bodily and vocal karma,
and wholesome karma of the desire realm [to cease].
Furthermore, when one simultaneously becomes free from passion regarding those various karmic maturations and the first dhyāna—
specifically at the time of the ninth uninterrupted path that abandons passion for the first dhyāna—
one causes both the karma of the first dhyāna and its maturation to simultaneously become free from passion.

In this manner, up until the moment of the ninth uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) when one becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana),
it causes the karma of that sphere [to be transformed].
And when that [action] and its maturation are simultaneously freed from defilement,
this is called the simultaneous freedom from defilement of the action and its maturation;
for it is by means of non-material unwholesome action.
Those comprised within the five classes are also severed by the nine grades of the path;
these include all unwholesome material karma and contaminated wholesome karma.
All results of maturation (*vipāka*) are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
because they are severed only by the path of the highest degree of intensity.
This is called a brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
Furthermore, the discussion herein is based upon two types of karma;
that is to say, it is stated thus with reference to those [karmas] to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
If one were to compose a treatise based on the five types of karma,
then one should not say, "The karma of a stream-enterer to be abandoned by vision," and so forth,
as explained at length.
It should be stated as follows:
for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire,
the knowledge of suffering has already arisen, but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen.
One has already become detached from the karma to be abandoned through the vision of suffering,
yet one is not yet detached from the maturation of that karma;
the knowledge of origin has arisen, but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen.
Regarding karma to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin that has already been freed from defilement,
the maturation of that karma is not yet freed from defilement;
this is the case when the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen.
Regarding karma to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, its origin, and its cessation, one who has already become detached from it,
yet whose maturation of that karma has not yet been abandoned;
and one for whom the knowledge of the path has arisen, but who has not yet become detached from the defilements of the desire realm.
Having already become detached from the karma to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path,
one has not yet become detached from the maturation (*vipāka*) of that karma.
One is detached from even a single grade of the defilements of the desire realm.
Up until the stage of the eighth category [of defilements],
that karma of the eighth category has already been freed from defilement,
yet the maturation (vipāka) of that karma has not yet been freed from defilement.
At the time of the ninth uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) for the abandonment of attachment to the desire realm,
that karma of the ninth grade and all unwholesome bodily and vocal actions [are abandoned].
Wholesome karma of the desire realm,
as well as its various maturations, simultaneously become free from defilement—
becoming free from the defilements of the first dhyāna up to those of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
At the time of the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
the wholesome karma of all stages and its maturation (*vipāka*) are simultaneously freed from defilement;
yet, this is not explicitly stated.
Since this treatise is composed based on two types of karma:
if an action is already free from defilement,
is the maturation (vipāka) of that action also free from defilement?
Answer: Regarding those karmas whose maturation has already been abandoned through detachment, those karmas are necessarily already abandoned through detachment;
however, there may also be karmas that have already been abandoned through detachment [but whose maturation has not yet occurred].
The maturation of that karma has not yet been freed from defilement;
that is to say, for a stream-enterer, although the karma to be abandoned by seeing has already been freed from defilement,
the maturation of that karma has not yet been freed from defilement.
The detailed analysis herein is as previously explained.
If an action has a fruit,
does that action necessarily have a ripening (*vipāka*)?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To refute heterodox doctrines and to manifest the correct meaning.
This refers to certain non-Buddhists who maintain that all wholesome and unwholesome karmas have no ripening fruit (*vipāka*).
To refute their view and to demonstrate that there is no karma that does not have a fruit, this treatise was composed;
for it is held that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome and unwholesome karmas possess ripening fruits.
However, it is stated in the sūtras that there are five kinds of fruits: first,
the fruit of uniform outflow (niṣyanda-phala).
Second, the fruit of maturation;
third, the fruit of dissociation;
fourth, the fruit of human effort.
Fifth is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Regarding the flow-on fruit (*niṣyandaphala*):
it refers to the arising of the wholesome from the wholesome.
The unwholesome gives rise to the unwholesome;
the indeterminate gives rise to the indeterminate.
As for the fruit of maturation:
This refers to the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) produced by all unwholesome dharmas and wholesome dharmas associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Its results, whether wholesome or unwholesome, are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
It is designated as "maturation" because it ripens as something of a different nature [from its cause].
As for the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*):
it refers to the severance of all afflictions by means of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
This path of uninterrupted transition...
The abandonment of afflictions and so forth constitutes the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) constitutes the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
And as for the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*):
subsequent paths that are equal or superior to their own kind are the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
This applies if they are uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Because one is able to realize the abandonment and cessation of all previously arisen afflictions,
this uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) takes that abandonment of those afflictions as its sole result of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala).
This is the general explanation.
To explain it specifically:
it is the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).

The abandonment of the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and so forth in the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) constitutes both the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The category of the dharma-knowledge of suffering constitutes its outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and its fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*);
furthermore, subsequent superior untainted paths constitute its outflow fruit.
In this manner, up to the *mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*,

the abandonment of the fourteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and so forth to be abandoned through the path of seeing within the realms of form and formlessness constitutes its fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).
And with respect to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*):
the category of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is its outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) and its fruit of human effort.
Subsequent superior untainted paths constitute the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

By means of these, one realizes the abandonment of the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, as well as those to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the three realms, and those to be abandoned through the vision of the path within the desire realm. One thus realizes the attainment of their abandonment and their cessation.
This path-category-forbearance (mārga-anvaya-kṣānti) takes those various abandonments as its fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala).
This applies to all stream-enterers (srotāpanna).
When seeking to realize the fruit of once-returner,
the first five paths of immediate succession abandon the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of those five categories.
It is the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
By means of the five paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
it is the fruit of natural outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of human effort.
Subsequent paths that are equal or superior within their own category constitute its outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

The sixth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) has the abandonment of the sixth grade of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) as its disjunction fruit (*visamyoga-phala*) and its fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The sixth path of liberation is taken as both a result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and a result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Subsequent paths that are equal or superior within their own category are taken as results of outflow.
Furthermore, [the paths of abandonment] of the three realms abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those of the desire realm abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are [taken as results].
The abandonment of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and so forth in the first five categories is realized through the attainment of their cessation;
this sixth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) takes those various abandonments as its fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
When those who are once-returners seek to realize the fruit of non-returning, the path of uninterrupted realization arises,
capable of severing the four underlying tendencies of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation.
If the seventh and eighth categories [of afflictions] are abandoned,
this uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) abandons the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and so forth of those two categories.
They are the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The two paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are the fruit of uniform outflow (*niḥṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of human effort.
Subsequent paths that are equal or superior within their own category are likewise [the fruit of uniform outflow].
It is the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
When the ninth grade of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) severs [the defilements],
it is because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the ninth grade and so forth are abandoned.
It is the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
By means of the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
it is the fruit of natural outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of human effort.
Subsequent paths that are equal or superior within their own category serve as the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

This is because [the abandonment] consists of the abandonment of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms to be abandoned by seeing, as well as the first eight categories of those to be abandoned by cultivation in the desire realm, which constitute the accumulation [of defilements].
This ninth path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) attains realization;
it takes those various abandonments as its fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala).
When those who are non-returners seek to realize the fruit of no-more-learning, the path of immediate succession arises,
which is capable of abandoning the six underlying tendencies to be abandoned through cultivation within the realms of form and formlessness.
If one abandons the first dhyāna’s defilements,
whether it be from one grade up to nine grades,
these constitute the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The abandonment of those nine grades of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) constitutes both the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) constitute the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of human effort.
Subsequent paths that are equal or superior to their own kind constitute the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

This continues in this manner until the eight preceding uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) for the abandonment of the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The abandonment of those eight categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) constitutes both the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) constitute both the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of human effort.
Subsequently, the various untainted paths (anāsrava-mārga) that are equal or superior serve as the outflow fruit (niṣyanda-phala).
The diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) effects the abandonment of the ninth grade of latent dispositions (anuśaya).
It is the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The first category of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is its outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and its fruit of human effort;
subsequent superior and more excellent untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) are likewise [its fruits].
It is the result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
This is because it consists of those [defilements] abandoned through seeing in the three realms, as well as those abandoned through cultivation in the lower eight stages,
but not those abandoned through cultivation in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The first eight chapters concern the abandonment and realization of the accumulation [of defilements] such as the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
This diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) takes those various abandonments as its virile fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
If ordinary beings, having become detached from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness,
[attain] the various uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandon defilements through both seeing and cultivation,
as well as their various paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Furthermore, subsequent paths of the same category that are equal or superior serve as its fruits;
one should reflect upon their relative quantities according to reason.
Regarding the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*):
if a phenomenon is established by virtue of that [other] human effort,
it is said to be the fruit of that human effort.
Regarding the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*):
if a phenomenon arises through the dominance of another,
one should know that this phenomenon is both that [other phenomenon's] dominant condition and its dominant fruit.
These others are dominant conditions but not dominant fruits;
that is to say, all dharmas produced later are the dominant condition and the dominant fruit of preceding dharmas.
The dharmas of previous births are the dominant condition for subsequent dharmas, but they are not their dominant fruit.
This applies to all future dharmas as well.
These are the past and present phenomena that serve as the dominant condition and the dominant fruit;
[they refer to] all past and present phenomena.
Future dharmas are the dominant fruits, but not the dominant results,
of past dharmas; future and present dharmas are the dominant fruits of past dharmas.
And as for the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*):
past dharmas are the dominant conditions for future and present dharmas.
It is not an adhipatiphala (dominant fruit).
Question: What is the distinction between the puruṣakāraphala (fruit of human effort) and the adhipatiphala?
Answer: It refers to all things that are produced through action.
With respect to the agent, it is both the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*);
with respect to the experiencer, it is only the dominant fruit.
For example, the various tasks performed in agriculture and so forth are the fruit of human effort for the farmer and others.
And as for the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*):
with respect to the experiencer, it is solely the dominant fruit.
That which arises through the power of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
That which arises through the power of predominance is called the predominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
The power of predominance is broad because it consists of non-obstruction;
the power of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is narrow because it is able to induce realization.
This is called the distinction between the two fruits.
The masters of the West maintain that there are nine kinds of fruits;
that is, to the aforementioned five, they add four more kinds.
First, the fruit of establishment;
second, the fruit of application;
third, the fruit of conjunction.
Fourth is the fruit of cultivation.
Regarding the fruit of establishment:
this refers to the establishment of the water mandala upon the wind mandala.
Furthermore, based upon the water wheel, the gold wheel is established;
based upon the gold wheel, the great earth is established;
and based upon the great earth, all categories of sentient and insentient beings are established.
In this context, each subsequent [stage] is the fruit of each preceding one.
Other types of established fruits should be understood in the same way.
As for the fruit of application (*prayoga-phala*):
That is to say, the contemplation of impurity or mindfulness of breathing serves as the preliminary application.
Therefore, it gradually induces the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Other fruits of preparatory application (*prayoga-phala*) should be understood in the same manner.
As for the fruit of combination (*sāmagrī-phala*):
That is to say, the conjunction of the eye and visible forms gives rise to visual consciousness;
likewise, up to the conjunction of the mind and mental phenomena gives rise to mental consciousness.
Other types of results arising from such conjunctions should be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the fruit of cultivation:
it refers to the manifestation of transformations and the production of speech in the desire realm by means of the path of the form realm.
This transformation and this speech are the fruits of cultivation;
other fruits of cultivation are likewise.
The masters of the Kaśmīra country say that among these,
the latter four are subsumed within the former five,
because they are respectively the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
One should know that the activity of the mundane path of counteraction is said to possess a fruit by virtue of five fruits;
this refers to the activities of its preparatory, liberation, and special progress paths.
Furthermore, other unwholesome and wholesome contaminated karmas are said to possess fruits by virtue of four fruits,
excluding the fruit of disconnection (visamyoga-phala).
If the activities of the various untainted paths of counteraction are also said to possess fruits by way of four fruits— excluding the ripening fruit (vipākaphala)—
this refers to the activities of the preparatory path (prayoga-mārga), the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), and the path of excellence (viśeṣa-mārga).
And neutral karma is said to possess fruit by virtue of three fruits,
excluding the fruit of disconnection and the ripening fruit.
This is called a brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
If an action has a fruit, does that action necessarily have a maturation (*vipāka*)?
Answer: All actions that have a maturation [have a fruit].
All those karmas have results;
one should know that these karmas [yield results] either by way of five fruits.
Alternatively, it is called "having fruit" by virtue of the four fruits;
or there is karma that possesses fruit.
That karma has no maturation;
namely, indeterminate karma and untainted karma.
It should be understood that this karma is said to possess fruit either by way of four fruits or by way of three fruits.
However, because it is not solid and lacks the moisture of craving, it does not have maturation (vipāka).
If an action has no fruit, does that action necessarily lack maturation?
Answer: There is no karma that is without fruit;
that is to say, every karma has either five fruits or four fruits.
Alternatively, it is because they possess fruits that three [types of karma] are said to have fruits; thus,
there may be karma that lacks maturation (vipāka).
That is to say, indeterminate karma and untainted karma,
as previously explained.
Question: If all karma possesses a fruit, how should one interpret the verse spoken by the Buddha?
As it says:
Just as a flower may be lovely, possessing color but lacking fragrance,
so too may there be exquisite speech that bears no fruit and accomplishes nothing.
This verse was spoken by the Buddha, the Teacher of Dharma, in response to a questioner.
This means that when the Dharma is being taught,
if those listeners are unable to accept it with faith and practice it according to the instructions,
it is called "fruitless."
Alternatively, although a teacher of the Dharma may speak skillfully, they cannot put it into practice; therefore, it is said that there is no fruit.
Or, having previously made a statement promising to give something to another, [they fail to do so].
Because it cannot bestow benefit later, it is said to be "without fruit.
[The opponent] asks: How then are other statements in the sūtras to be reconciled?
For example, as it is said:
There is a life of pleasure characterized by dullness and sleep;
it is empty, fruitless, meaningless, tasteless, and without benefit.
It is utterly devoid of any arising that could lead to the attainment of superior virtues upon awakening.
Because they delight in sleep, they waste this time in vain.
The Blessed One, referring to them, spoke these verses.
Question: If delighting in sleep is empty and fruitless, [why does one do so?]
How, then, are other sūtras to be reconciled?
For example, it is said:
"It would be better to sleep than to engage in other discursive thoughts."
Answer: There are those who, while awake, give rise to evil thoughts and investigations, engaging in strife and causing distress to immeasurable sentient beings.
It was for the sake of admonishing them that the Buddha made this statement.
For this reason, the sūtra has a specific underlying intention;
it does not mean that all karmas are entirely without fruit.
If an action is unwholesome, is that action necessarily inverted?
It can be answered in four propositions.
There is karma that is unwholesome, yet that karma is not inverted;
namely, there is someone who perceives the existence of cause and effect.
Holding such a view and maintaining such a doctrine, one performs misconduct of body,
speech, and mind while there is karma and the ripening of the fruit of karma.
Question: For what causes and conditions does one engage in unwholesome conduct?
Answer: Due to three causes and conditions.
First, due to the time.
Second, by way of location;
third, by way of the person (pudgala).
Regarding "by way of time":
This refers to the fact that when the five corruptions increase,
sentient beings find their majesty and virtue diminished, take pleasure in committing various evils,
and because they exist at such a time, they also engage in unwholesome conduct.
Regarding "by way of location":
this refers to those classes of sentient beings born among the *ḍomba* and *mleccha* peoples,
whose natures are foolish and base, and who frequently commit evil deeds.
Because they are born in that place, they also engage in unwholesome conduct.
Regarding "by way of the individual" (pudgala):
this refers to a certain class of beings who have obtained a homogeneous group (nikāya-sabhāga) characterized by unwholesome conduct.
Their nature is fierce and violent, and they frequently commit evil deeds,
such as the various non-virtuous occupations like butchering sheep.
Because they associate with such people, they also engage in evil conduct.
It should be understood that this karma is called unwholesome by virtue of its intrinsic nature,
because it is comprised within the misconduct of body, speech, and mind;
and it is called non-perverted by virtue of its basis.
This is the view of volitional action (kriyā-dṛṣṭi), which is not deluded regarding cause and effect,
because it arises with right view within the body;
it is like various excrement and filth being contained within a precious vessel.
There is karma that is inverted, yet that karma is not unwholesome;
namely, as when someone who views cause and effect as non-existent gives rise to such a view.
They establish such a doctrine:
"There is no karma and no ripening of the fruit of karma," yet they nevertheless practice sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind.
Question: For what causes and conditions does that person practice sublime conduct?
Answer: Due to three causes and conditions.
First, by way of time.
Second, by way of location;
third, by way of the person (pudgala);
and by way of time. Regarding "by way of time":
This refers to a time when the five corruptions have not yet increased;
at that time, sentient beings possess great majestic power and delight in practicing various virtues.
Even though they do not delight in doing so, they nevertheless practice sublime conduct.
Regarding "by way of location," this refers to those classes of sentient beings born in the Central Land.
Their nature is intelligent and their will is harmonious and gentle;
because they have cultivated many wholesome karmas to be born in that place,
they practice sublime conduct even though they do not take pleasure in doing so.
Regarding "by way of the person":
this refers to a certain class of beings who have attained a homogeneous group characterized by sublime conduct;
their nature is gentle and refined, and they frequently cultivate wholesome deeds.
Just as one who abides in restraint acts with sublime conduct even though they do not delight in doing so because they associate with those [who practice it],
one should know that this karma is called "perverted" by virtue of its basis.
This view of non-action is ignorant regarding cause and effect;
because it arises equally within a body characterized by wrong views,
it is not unwholesome by its very nature.
Because these are subsumed under the sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind,
they are like precious jewels contained within a defiled vessel.
There is also karma that is both unwholesome and perverted.
That is to say, there is one who views cause and effect as non-existent,
giving rise to such a view and establishing such a doctrine:
"There is no action, and no ripening of the fruit of action."
Furthermore, they engage in misconduct of body, speech, and mind.
Question: For what causes and conditions do they engage in such misconduct?
Answer: Due to three causes and conditions, as previously explained.
It should be understood that this karma is called unwholesome by virtue of its intrinsic nature,
as it is comprised of the misconduct of body, speech, and mind;
furthermore, it is called inverted by virtue of its basis.
This view of non-action is a delusion regarding cause and effect,
for it arises within the body as a form of false view;
it is like filthy excrement being contained within a defiled vessel.
There is karma that is neither unwholesome nor perverted;
namely, as when someone perceives that there is cause and effect,
and gives rise to such a view.
Having established such a doctrine—
that there is karma and the ripening of the fruit of karma—
they further practice sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind.
Question: For what causes and conditions does that person practice sublime conduct?
Answer: Due to three causes and conditions, as previously explained.
It should be understood that this karma is called "non-unwholesome" by virtue of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because they are embraced by the sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind,
they are non-erroneous by virtue of their basis;
they possess the view of purposeful action and are not deluded regarding cause and effect.
Because it arises within the body of right view,
it is like precious jewels contained within a jeweled vessel.
If an action is wholesome, is that action not inverted?
It is agreed that there shall be four propositions:
namely, the former second proposition becomes the first of these,
and the former first proposition becomes the second of these.
The former fourth phrase becomes this third phrase;
the former third phrase becomes this fourth phrase.
The details are as previously explained.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation regarding this:
"If an action is unwholesome, is that action necessarily inverted?
One should respond by formulating four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is unwholesome karma that is not based on a cognitive distortion.
For example, suppose someone perceives what exists as non-existent;
when another asks them, "Did you see it? [they respond falsely].
He may act for his own sake, or for the sake of others,
or for the sake of fame and profit.
He then conceals this perception, this acceptance, this view, and this desire,
and replies:
"I have seen it."
It should be understood that this karma is called unwholesome by virtue of the power of perception (*saṃjñā*),
because it is spoken of with a concealed perception.
However, the matter as it was spoken is not erroneous.
Because one speaks of seeing when one has seen,
there is an inverted action that is not unwholesome;
that is to say, as when someone perceives what exists as if it were non-existent.
He asked, "Do you see?
He does not act for himself."
Not for the sake of others;
not for the sake of fame or profit;
and not concealing this thought, this patience, this view, or this desire.
He replied,
"I did not see it.
It should be understood that this action is termed "perverted" (viparyāsa) on account of the matter thus described.
Because one says "I did not see" regarding what was seen,
it is called "not unwholesome" due to the power of perception;
for it is spoken without concealing one's perception.
There is karma that is both unwholesome and inverted;
for example, there is someone who perceives existence while having the perception of existence,
and another asks him:
Do you see this?
He may act either for himself or for others.
Or, for the sake of fame and profit,
one conceals this perception, this acceptance, this view, and this desire,
and replies:
It should be understood that this karma is called unwholesome by virtue of the power of perception (*saṃjñā*).
Because it is spoken with a concealed perception, and because of the matter thus spoken, it is further termed "perverted" (*viparyāsa*).
Because one says "I do not see" regarding what has been seen,
there is karma that is neither unwholesome nor perverted;
namely, as when someone who sees has the perception of seeing.
He asked: "Do you see that which is neither self-made nor made by another?"
Not for the sake of fame or profit,
he does not conceal this thought, this patience, this view, or this desire,
and answers, saying:
I see it.
It should be understood that this karma is not unwholesome by virtue of the power of perception (*saṃjñā*),
because it was spoken with a perception that was not concealed.
The names of the objects thus described are not erroneous, because one speaks of "seeing" with respect to what is seen.
Just as four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) are formulated regarding what is seen,
so too are four alternatives formulated respectively for what is heard, sensed, and known.
Just as one constructs four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) for each of what is seen, heard, sensed,
and known, so too does one construct four propositions for each of what is not seen, heard, sensed, or known.
Just as one applies eight sets of four propositions by contrasting the unwholesome with the inverted.
In this way, it should be understood that the same applies to the wholesome in contrast to the non-perverted;
thus, these constitute sixteen fourfold sets, which,
together with the previous two fourfold sets, make eighteen fourfold sets.
Furthermore, the nine minor fourfold sets of unwholesome [factors] and the nine minor fourfold sets of wholesome [factors] are each combined to form one major fourfold set.
Therefore, there are twenty-four phrases in total and specific categories.
Among these, that which is apprehended by visual consciousness is called "seen";
that which is apprehended by auditory consciousness is called "heard."
That which is experienced by the three consciousnesses is called "perception" (saṃjñā);
that which is experienced by the mental consciousness is called "cognition" (vijñapti).
It is in reference to these four objects that one speaks of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing.

These are faculties (indriya) and not consciousness (vijñāna); however, the mention of "consciousness" indicates that the eye and other faculties must be assisted by consciousness in order to apprehend their objects.
This is because only the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) faculties possess functional activity, whereas those that are *tatsabhāga* (non-homogeneous) do not.
Question: For what reason are the objects experienced by the three consciousnesses of the eye and so forth each established as a distinct type,
whereas the objects experienced by the three consciousnesses of the nose, tongue,
and body are combined and established as one type called "apperception" (*vitarka*)?
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"The objects of the three consciousnesses are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because their objects are indeterminate, the faculty is designated by the name 'perception' (*buddhi*)."
Furthermore, because the three faculties perceive only objects that reach them and because they are in contact with those objects,
they are designated by the term "cognition" (*buddhi*).
As the Venerable One said:
Only these three faculties have dull and obscure objects, like a corpse;
therefore, when consciousness arises, it is designated as "awakening.
Other masters say:
The two consciousnesses of the eye and ear rely on their own realm while taking both their own and other realms as objects;
the mental consciousness relies on both its own and other realms.
Because they take both their own and other realms as objects, each of those experiences is established as a distinct type.
The three consciousnesses of the nose and so forth rely exclusively on their own realm and perceive exclusively their own realm;
therefore, what they experience is established as a single type.
This is also explained in the same way regarding the homogeneous and heterogeneous [realms] of one's own realm and other realms.
Other masters state:
"The two consciousnesses of the eye and ear depend upon the homogeneous (sabhāga),
and take as their objects both the homogeneous and the non-homogeneous (tatsabhāga)."
Because the mental consciousness relies on both homogeneous and heterogeneous bases and takes both homogeneous and heterogeneous objects as its conditions,
each of its respective experiences is established as a distinct type.
Because the three consciousnesses of the nose and so forth rely exclusively on the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and take exclusively the *sabhāga* as their object,
that which they experience is established as a single type.
This explains the homogeneity of the elements (*dhātu-sabhāga*).
Some say that the visual and auditory consciousnesses rely on the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and take the three types as their objects.
Because the mental consciousness relies on three types of objects,
each of those experienced by it is established as a distinct type.
The three consciousnesses of the nose and so forth rely exclusively on the indeterminate and take exclusively the indeterminate as their objects.
Therefore, what they experience is established as a single category.
Some say that the two consciousnesses of the eye and ear depend on proximate and remote conditions respectively.
Because the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) relies on both proximate and remote objects,
that which it perceives is established as a distinct category.
The three consciousnesses of the nose and so forth rely only on proximate objects and perceive only what is proximate.
Therefore, those objects of experience are established as a single category.
These three faculties and their objects must abide contiguously in order to be able to give rise to consciousness.
This is called "proximate.
Some say that for the two consciousnesses of the eye and ear, the great elements upon which they rely may be large while their objects of perception are small.
Either the object of perception is large while the basis is small,
or the basis and the object of perception are equal.
Regarding the case where the basis of visual consciousness is large while the object of perception is small:
For example, seeing the tip of a hair and so forth;
that which has a large object of perception (*ālambana*) but a small basis (*āśraya*) is like seeing a mountain and so forth;
and that where the basis and the object of perception are equal [is as follows].
Just as one perceives grapes and the like,
so too should the ear-consciousness be understood according to its measure.
Although the size— whether large or small— of the basis of the mental consciousness cannot be specified, [it should be understood in the same way].
However, because their objects of cognition are either small or large,
what they experience is established as being of two distinct types.
This is because for the three consciousnesses— nose, tongue, and body— the dimensions of their bases and their objects are equal.
That which is perceived by them is established as a single type;
it corresponds to the number of atoms of the sense-faculties upon which it depends,
and it coincides with that same number of atoms of the object when they come together.
Only then can the consciousnesses of the nose and so forth arise.
Some say that the three consciousnesses of the eye and so forth take both karma and non-karma as their objects.
Therefore, what is experienced by those [first three consciousnesses] is established as one type.
Since the three consciousnesses of the nose and so forth take only non-karmic objects as their conditions,
what is experienced by them is collectively established as one type.
Some say that the three consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness and the others,
take the observance of precepts, the violation of precepts, and other dharmas as their objects.
Therefore, those objects experienced by each [of the first five consciousnesses] are established as distinct types.
Since the three consciousnesses of the nose and so forth perceive only other phenomena (*dharmas*),
the objects experienced by them are collectively established as a single type.
Other masters state that the three consciousnesses,
such as the visual consciousness and so forth,
take as their objects both restraint (*saṃvara*), non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), and other phenomena.
Therefore, what is experienced by those [three] is each established as a distinct category.
Since the three consciousnesses of the nose and so forth take only other phenomena as their objects,
what is experienced by them is combined and established as a single category.
Some say that because the three consciousnesses of the eye and so forth take as their objects both the manifest and other dharmas,
each of those experienced is established as a distinct type.
The three consciousnesses of the nose and so forth take only other dharmas as their objects;
therefore, what they experience is established as a single type. Some say:
The three consciousnesses beginning with the eye-consciousness take both defiled and non-defiled phenomena as their objects;
therefore, each of those experiences is established as a distinct type.
The three consciousnesses beginning with the nose-consciousness take only non-defiled phenomena as their objects.
Therefore, that which is experienced by them is established as a single type.
Some say: "The three consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness..."
Because they universally take as their objects both sublime conduct and unwholesome conduct, as well as other phenomena,
each of those experienced [sensations] is established as a distinct type.
The three consciousnesses, beginning with the nose, take only other phenomena as their objects.
Therefore, those objects experienced are established as a single category.
Based on what has been explained regarding seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing,
there are both specific and general distinctions according to the consciousness, its support, and its object.
If one accomplishes unwholesome karma, does that person also accomplish karma bound to the realms of form and formlessness?
Answer: All those who accomplish unwholesome karma [also accomplish such karma].
That person certainly possesses karma bound to the realms of form and formlessness;
that is to say, if one born in the desire realm has severed the roots of goodness,
they certainly possess unwholesome karma.
And there is one type of karma bound to the form and formless realms,
namely, defiled karma.
The same applies to those who have not severed their roots of goodness but have not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm.
If one has already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm,
that person accomplishes unwholesome karma.
And two types of karma bound to the form realm—
namely, the wholesome and the defiled—
and one type of karma bound to the formless realm.
This refers to those who are defiled.
There are those who possess karma bound to the form and formless realms but do not possess unwholesome karma;
namely, those born in the desire realm who have already become detached from the defilements of the desire realm.
If one is born in the form realm—
meaning one who has been born in the desire realm and has already become free from the defilements of the desire realm,
yet has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm.
He accomplishes three types of karma associated with the form realm—
namely, wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured neutral—
and one type of karma associated with the formless realm.
That is to say, it is defiled;
or, if one has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm.
He accomplishes three types of karma bound to the form realm—
namely, the wholesome, the defiled, and the non-obscured neutral—
and two types of karma bound to the formless realm.
That is to say, it is both wholesome and defiled;
[it occurs] when one has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm but has not yet become detached from the defilements of the formless realm.
He accomplishes two types of karma bound to the form realm—
namely, the wholesome and the non-obscured neutral—
and two types of karma bound to the formless realm.
That is to say, wholesome and defiled [actions].
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the formless realm,
they accomplish two types of karma bound to the form realm.
That is to say: wholesome and unobscured-neutral [karma].
There is one type of karma bound to the formless realm, which is to say: wholesome.
If one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu),
that is, if one has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
one accomplishes the three types of karma bound to the form realm.
This refers to karma that is wholesome, defiled, or non-obscured-neutral.
Regarding karma bound to the formless realm, there is one type,
namely, the defiled.
If one has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm,
that person accomplishes the three types of karma bound to the form realm.
That is to say: wholesome, defiled, and unobscured-neutral karma bound to the formless realm;
specifically, these are the two types of karma, namely the wholesome and the defiled.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm but has not yet become detached from the defilements of the formless realm,
that person accomplishes two types of karma bound to the form realm.
That is to say: wholesome and non-obscured neutral [karma].
There are two types of karma bound to the formless realm:
namely, wholesome and defiled [karma].
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the formless realm,
they possess two types of karma bound to the form realm:
namely, the wholesome and the non-obscured neutral.
There is one type of karma bound to the formless realm,
namely the wholesome.
If one possesses wholesome karma bound to the desire realm, [one also possesses this].
Does one who achieves [the state of] being bound to the form and formless realms necessarily achieve karma bound to the form and formless realms?
Answer: Those who achieve wholesome karma bound to the desire realm necessarily achieve karma bound to the form and formless realms.
There are those who possess karma bound to the realms of form and formlessness,
but not karma bound to the desire realm that is wholesome;
this refers to a person (pudgala) who has severed their roots of virtue.
If one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu),
it means that although one has accomplished wholesome karma of the desire realm (kāmadhātu),
one has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm.
He accomplishes one karma associated with the form and formless realms;
that is, if he has already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm.
He accomplishes two types of karma bound to the realm of form and one type of karma bound to the formless realm,
provided he has already become detached from the defilements of the desire realm.
One who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm possesses three types of karma bound to the form realm and one type of karma bound to the formless realm.
If one has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm,
that person accomplishes the three types of karma bound to the form realm.
There are two types of karma bound to the formless realm:
those belonging to one who has already become free from the defilements of the form realm but has not yet become free from the defilements of the formless realm.
He accomplishes two types of karma bound to the form realm and two types of karma bound to the formless realm,
provided he has already become detached from the defilements of the formless realm.
He accomplishes two types of karma bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and one type of karma bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
provided he has not severed his roots of goodness (kuśalamūla).
He accomplishes one karma associated with the form and formless realms.
If he is born in the form realm and has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm,
he accomplishes three karmas associated with the form realm.
One type of karma bound to the formless realm:
if one has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm.
He accomplishes three types of karma bound to the form realm and two types of karma bound to the formless realm,
provided he has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm.
Not yet being free from the defilements of the formless realm,
he accomplishes two types of karma bound to the form realm and two types of karma bound to the formless realm.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the formless realm,
they possess two types of karma bound to the form realm and one type of karma bound to the formless realm.
Regarding those who previously severed their roots of goodness,
they do not possess [the wholesome karma] of this life in the form realm,
because the wholesome karma bound to the desire realm has already been severed by the severing of the roots of goodness.
Because that wholesome [karma] has already been abandoned:
if one accomplishes wholesome karma bound to the desire realm,
does one also accomplish wholesome karma bound to the form and formless realms?
It can be answered in four propositions.
There is the accomplishment of wholesome karma bound to the desire realm,
but not of wholesome karma bound to the form or formless realms.
That is to say, one born in the desire realm who has not severed the roots of goodness,
yet has not attained a wholesome mind of the form realm,
may possess wholesome karma associated with the form and formless realms.
It is not the case that wholesome karma bound to the desire realm [is abandoned].
That is to say, one born in the form realm who attains a wholesome mind of the formless realm may still possess wholesome karma bound to the desire realm.
There are also wholesome karmas bound to the form and formless realms;
that is, one born in the desire realm who has attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm may not possess wholesome karma bound to the desire realm.
Nor is it wholesome karma bound to the form or formless realms;
that is to say, a person who has severed their roots of virtue (kuśalamūla) may still possess karma bound to the desire realm.
Does he accomplish karma bound to the realm of form?
Answer: Yes. If one accomplishes karma bound to the realm of form...
Does he accomplish karma bound to the desire realm?
Answer: Yes. That is to say, one born in the desire realm who has severed the roots of goodness.
He accomplishes two types of karma bound to the desire realm and one type of karma bound to the form realm,
provided that he has not severed his roots of goodness.
Yet, having not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm,
he accomplishes three types of karma bound to the desire realm and one type of karma bound to the form realm.
If one has already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm,
that person accomplishes the three types of karma bound to the desire realm.
There are two types of karma bound to the form realm:
those for one who has already become free from the defilements of the desire realm but has not yet become free from the defilements of the form realm.
He accomplishes two types of karma bound to the desire realm and three types of karma bound to the form realm;
if he has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm,
he accomplishes two types of karma bound to the desire realm.
Regarding the two types of karma bound to the form realm:
if one is born in the form realm and has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm,
they possess one type of karma bound to the desire realm.
Regarding the three types of karma bound to the form realm:
if one has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm,
they accomplish one type of karma bound to the desire realm.
Regarding the two types of karma bound to the form realm:
if one accomplishes karma bound to the desire realm,
does that person accomplish karma bound to the formless realm?
Answer: Those who possess karma bound to the desire realm also possess karma bound to the formless realm;
that is to say, one born in the desire realm who has severed their roots of goodness.
He accomplishes two types of karma bound to the desire realm and one type of karma bound to the formless realm,
provided he has not severed his roots of goodness.
One who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm accomplishes three types of karma bound to the desire realm and one type of karma bound to the formless realm.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the desire realm but has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm,
that person accomplishes two types of karma bound to the desire realm.
There is one type of karma bound to the formless realm:
that of one who has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm.
He accomplishes two types of karma bound to the desire realm and two types of karma bound to the formless realm;
this is so even if he has already become detached from the defilements of the formless realm.
He accomplishes two types of karma bound to the desire realm and one type of karma bound to the formless realm,
provided he is born in the form realm and has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm.
He accomplishes one karma bound to the desire realm and one karma bound to the formless realm,
provided he has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm.
Not yet free from the defilements of the formless realm,
he accomplishes one karma bound to the desire realm and two karmas bound to the formless realm.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the formless realm,
they accomplish one karma associated with the desire realm and one karma associated with the formless realm.
There are those who accomplish karma associated with the formless realm,
but not karma associated with the desire realm;
namely, individuals born in the formless realm.
This refers to one born in that realm who,
not yet being free from the defilements of that realm,
gives rise to a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja-citta*).
He accomplishes the three types of karma associated with the formless realm.
If he does not give rise to a mind born of maturation,
he accomplishes two types of karma associated with the formless realm.
If one who has already become detached from the defilements of the formless realm gives rise to a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
they accomplish two types of karma bound to the formless realm.
If one does not give rise to a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
that person accomplishes one karma associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and does not accomplish any karma associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Since those [karmas] have already been abandoned,
if one accomplishes karma bound to the desire realm,
does one also accomplish karma that is unbound?
It can be answered in four propositions:
there is the accomplishment of karma bound to the desire realm,
but not of unbound karma.
This refers to ordinary beings born in the desire or form realms who possess karma that is not bound [to any realm],
rather than karma bound to the desire realm.
This refers to noble ones born in the formless realm who possess both karma bound to the desire realm and karma that is unbound.
This refers to those noble ones born in the desire realm or the form realm who neither possess karma bound to the desire realm nor possess karma that is unbound.
That is to say, when ordinary beings are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
if they possess karma bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu),
do they also possess karma bound to the formless realm?
Answer: Those who have accomplished karma bound to the form realm necessarily accomplish karma bound to the formless realm;
that is to say, those born in the desire realm who have not yet attained wholesome minds of the form realm.
He accomplishes one karma bound to the form realm and one karma bound to the formless realm,
provided that he has already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm.
Not yet free from the defilements of the desire realm,
he accomplishes two types of karma bound to the form realm and one type of karma bound to the formless realm.
If one has already become free from the defilements of the desire realm but has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm,
that person accomplishes the three types of karma bound to the form realm.
There is one type of karma bound to the formless realm:
that of one who has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm.
He accomplishes the three types of karma associated with the form realm and the two types of karma associated with the formless realm,
provided he has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm.
Not yet free from the defilements of the formless realm,
he accomplishes two types of karma bound to the form realm and two types of karma bound to the formless realm.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the formless realm,
they possess two types of karma bound to the form realm and one type of karma bound to the formless realm.
If one is born in the form realm and has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm,
they possess three types of karma bound to the form realm and one type of karma bound to the formless realm.
If one has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm,
that person accomplishes the three types of karma bound to the form realm.
There are two types of karma bound to the formless realm:
[the first is] when one has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm,
but has not yet become detached from the defilements of the formless realm.
He accomplishes two types of karma bound to the form realm and two types of karma bound to the formless realm;
this is the case if he has already become detached from the defilements of the formless realm.
He accomplishes two types of karma bound to the form realm and one type of karma bound to the formless realm.
There are those who accomplish karma bound to the formless realm.
It is not karma bound to the form realm;
that is to say, when sentient beings are born in the formless realm—
meaning, having been born in that realm, they have not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm.
If they give rise to a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja-citta*),
they accomplish the three types of karma bound to the formless realm;
if they do not give rise to a mind born of maturation, [they do not].
