He accomplishes two types of karma associated with the formless realm;
if he has already become detached from the defilements of the formless realm,
he gives rise to a mind born of maturation.
He accomplishes two types of karma associated with the formless realm;
if he does not give rise to a mind born of maturation,
he accomplishes one type of karma associated with the formless realm.
If one accomplishes karma bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-karma),
does that person accomplish karma that is unbound (apratisaṃyukta-karma)?
One should respond by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
There are those who possess karma bound to the form realm,
but not karma that is unbound;
this refers to various beings born in the desire or form realms.
There are those who accomplish karma that is non-bound,
which is not karma bound to the realm of form;
this refers to the various noble ones (āryas).
One born in the formless realm may possess karma bound to the realm of form as well as karma that is unbound.
This refers to those noble ones born in the desire realm or the form realm who do not possess karma bound to the form realm.
Nor is it non-bound karma;
that is to say, when various ordinary beings born in the formless realm possess karma bound to the formless realm.
Does one who accomplishes non-bound karma necessarily accomplish karma bound to the formless realm? Answer:
All those who accomplish non-bound karma necessarily accomplish karma bound to the formless realm.
This refers to noble ones born in the desire or form realms who have not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm;
they possess the unconditioned karma of training.
There is one type of karma bound to the formless realm:
that of one who has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the formless realm.
He accomplishes the untied training karma and the two types of karma bound to the formless realm;
this is the case if he has already become detached from the defilements of the formless realm.
He accomplishes the non-bound karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) and the karma bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
This is the case when noble ones (āryas) are born in the formless realm.
Not yet free from the defilements of the formless realm,
he gives rise to a mind born of maturation;
he accomplishes the unconditioned karma of one in training.
Regarding the three types of karma bound to the formless realm:
if one does not give rise to a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
one accomplishes the unbound karma of training (*śaikṣa*).
There are two types of karma bound to the formless realm;
if one has already become detached from the defilements of the formless realm and gives rise to a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja-citta*).
He accomplishes the non-bound karma of one beyond training,
as well as the two types of karma bound to the formless realm,
provided that he does not give rise to a mind born of maturation.
He accomplishes the unconditioned karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) and the karma bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
There are those who accomplish karma bound to the formless realm.
It is not non-bound karma;
that is to say, when ordinary beings born in the desire realm or the form realm have not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm.
He accomplishes one karma associated with the formless realm.
If he has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm,
he accomplishes two karmas associated with the formless realm.
If ordinary beings are born in the formless realm and give rise to a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
they possess the three types of karma associated with the formless realm.
If one does not give rise to a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja-citta*),
one accomplishes two types of karma bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
If one accomplishes karma bound to the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, or that which is unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Where is he reborn after his life ends?
Answer: Either in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or in the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Or [it may be] the formless realm,
or a place where there is no rebirth;
that is, when noble ones are born in the desire realm.
One who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm accomplishes three types of karma bound to the desire realm and two types of karma bound to the form realm.
There is one type of karma bound to the formless realm and one type of unbound karma of training;
having died there, he is reborn in the desire realm.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the desire realm but has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm,
that person accomplishes two types of karma bound to the desire realm.
Three types of karma are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu);
one type of karma is bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu);
and there is the unbound karma of training (śaikṣa).
Having passed away from there, he is reborn in the form realm.
If he has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm.
He accomplishes two types of karma bound to the desire realm,
three types of karma bound to the form realm,
and two types of karma bound to the formless realm.
Not bound by their studies,
they are reborn in the form realm at the end of their lives,
provided they have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm.
Not yet having abandoned the defilements of the formless realm,
he possesses two types of karma bound to the desire realm and two types of karma bound to the form realm.
There are two types of karma bound to the formless realm and unbound karma of training;
having died, one is reborn in the formless realm.
If one has already become free from the defilements of the formless realm,
they possess two types of karma bound to the desire realm and two types of karma bound to the form realm.
There is one type of karma bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and the unbound karma of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Upon their death, there is no place of rebirth for those noble ones (*ārya*) who are born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
One who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm possesses one karma bound to the desire realm and three karmas bound to the form realm.
There is one type of karma bound to the formless realm,
and unbound learned karma;
having passed away from there, he is reborn in the form realm.
If one has already attained a wholesome mind of the formless realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm,
they possess one karma bound to the desire realm and three karmas bound to the form realm.
There are two types of karma bound to the formless realm and unbound karma of training;
having died there, one is also reborn in the form realm.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm but has not yet become detached from the defilements of the formless realm,
that person accomplishes one type of karma bound to the desire realm.
Two types of karma are bound to the realm of form;
one type of karma is bound to the formless realm;
and there is the unbound karma of training.
Having passed away from there, he is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If he has already become detached from the defilements of the formless realm,
he accomplishes one type of karma associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
One type of karma bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta),
one type of karma bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta),
and the unbound karma of one beyond training (asaikṣa-karma).
Upon the end of his life, he has no place of rebirth.
For this reason, it is said that one who accomplishes the four karmas, at the end of his life,
is either reborn in the desire realm.
Some are born in the realm of form;
some are born in the formless realm;
or there is no place of birth.

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang in accordance with the Imperial Edict. Chapter Four: The Aggregate of Karma. Section Four: The Sub-section on Manifest and Non-manifest [Karma]. One who possesses manifest bodily karma (*kāyavijñapti*).
Does he accomplish this non-informative [matter]?
Such are the chapters and the explanations of their meanings.
Having already grasped the meaning, one should next provide a detailed explanation.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of other schools and clarifying our own position.
Specifically, the Dārṣṭāntikas assert that manifest and unmanifest karma lack substantial reality. Why is this so?
If manifest karma were a real entity, one could rely upon it to cause unmanifest karma to exist;
however, manifest karma lacks reality.
How, then, can it produce unmanifest karma so that it exists?
Furthermore, since even manifest karma lacks non-manifest [karma], how could it exist?
To say that it exists is merely the deceptive and false claim of the masters of the Abhidharma,
like a man who, upon encountering a beautiful woman, speaks out of the influence of his defiled attachment.
He spoke thus:
"You may now discard your human garments;
I shall clothe you in celestial robes."
Hearing this, the woman was delighted and acted as she had been told.
That man then approached her and touched her in various ways;
having indulged his mind and desires at will, he spoke these words:
"The celestial robe has already been put on you.
The woman said,
"My body is now exposed in this way."
"It would be better to die than to expose one's undergarment;
where is it? He replied, "The celestial robes are so subtle and exquisite that only I can see them; you are not able to see them."
In this way, such a fool originally possesses no celestial robes,
much less would he wear them for another.
The explanation given by the Abhidharmikas is likewise.
Since there is no such thing as manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), how much less could there be non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) arising based upon it? Therefore,
the Abhidharmikas have raised this argument in vain.
Furthermore, if both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) were material form (*rūpa*),
what would blue, yellow, red, and white be? Moreover,
how could they constitute the nature of the wholesome (*kuśala*) or the unwholesome (*akuśala*)?
If it were the case that the nature of good or evil is established through movement,
why would flowers, swords, and so forth not be likewise?
This is stated in order to refute the views of those who employ such analogies.
To manifest his own tenet—
that both manifest and unmanifest karma are substantially existent—
he composed this treatise.
If all manifest karmas lacked substantial reality,
they would contradict the sūtras.
As a sūtra says:
The craving of foolish people is called "thirst" (tṛṣṇā).
That which is manifested by thirst is called "karma.
Furthermore, a sūtra says:
Seeking and examining at night is like smoke arising;
moving body and speech at dawn is like flames breaking out.
If non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*) lacked substantial reality, [these would not occur].
This would also contradict the sūtras;
for as the sūtras state:
"Form is comprised of three categories that encompass all form."
There is that which is material, visible, and resistant;
there is that which is material, invisible, and resistant;
and there is that which is material, invisible, and non-resistant.
If non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) did not exist,
then there would be no establishment of the three types [of restraint],
because the third would be absent.
Furthermore, regarding the denial of manifest and unmanifest form:
[this refers to] King Ajātaśatru and the syllable *vaitihī*.
One should not commit the immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) of harming one's father;
that is to say, at the moment the manifest action (*vijñapti*) is performed, the father’s life still persists,
whereas by the time the father’s life has ended, the manifest karma has already ceased.
Because one obtains subsequent non-informative action (*avijñapti*) through the power of prior informative action (*vijñapti*),
Ajātaśatru committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*).
Furthermore, that ascetic heretic Daṇḍakin [did so as well].
Furthermore, there would also have to be no harm caused by contact and no immediate retribution;
that is to say, Maudgalyāyana’s life would still have endured during the stage of manifesting [the action],
yet at the time of Maudgalyāyana’s parinirvāṇa, the manifest karma had already ceased, because he attained subsequent non-manifest karma through the power of the prior manifest karma.
Those non-Buddhists commit the immediate karmic offenses;
furthermore, if they deny the existence of manifest and unmanifest karma,
there should be no establishment of the three distinct categories [of persons].
That is to say: those who abide in the category of restraint,
those who abide in the category of non-restraint,
and those who abide in the category of neither restraint nor non-restraint.
However, as for what he said— that if the essence of these informative and non-informative [karmas] were form (rūpa),
then what would they be, given that form consists only of blue,
yellow, red, and white?— this objection is not valid, because there is no distinct form apart from the primary colors (varṇa-rūpa).
One should know that bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) is shape (*saṃsthāna*) and not color (*varṇa*);
vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) is sound (*śabda*) and likewise not the two kinds of visible form (*rūpa*).

Since non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is subsumed under the category of "matter included in the sphere of mental objects" (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), it cannot be criticized on the grounds of being identical to blue and so forth.
However, there are generally four types of the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
First, there are forms where only the color (*varṇa*) is discernible, not the shape (*saṃsthāna*).
Second, there are forms where only the shape is discernible, not the color.
Three of the material sense bases (rūpāyatana) can be discerned both by their color-appearance (varṇa) and their shape (saṃsthāna).
Four of the material sense bases cannot be discerned either by their color-appearance or their shape.
Regarding those that can be discerned by color-appearance but not by shape:
That is to say: blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, light, brightness, and darkness.
Regarding shape (*saṃsthāna*) as being discernible rather than color (*varṇa*), this refers to bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).

That which is discernible both as color and shape refers to all remaining forms where both color and shape can be discerned. That which is indiscernible both as color and shape refers to the form of the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
Furthermore, as it has been said:
"If bodily movement constitutes the nature of good or evil,
why is it that the movement of flowers, swords, and the like does not do so?"
This is also not the case;
there is a difference between phenomena that possess faculties and those that lack faculties.
The body is included within the category of sentient beings;
because it is moved by the mind, it can manifest virtuous or non-virtuous mental states and mental factors.
Flowers, swords, and the like are not so.
Manifest and unmanifest [karma] are definitely substantially existent.
However, manifest and unmanifest karma arise based on the body; some are dependent on a single part [of the body], such as snapping one's fingers or lifting one's foot.
A portion of movement that performs wholesome or unwholesome karma with a basis is "partial" (ekadeśa),
such as prostrating to a Buddha or chasing away an enemy;
this involves moving the entire body to perform wholesome or unwholesome karma.
In this context, the number of atoms of the informative action corresponds to the number of atoms of the body upon which it depends;
as is the number of atoms of the informative action, so too is that of the non-informative action.
Question: In each and every case of karma, if there is informative intimation (*vijñapti*), is there necessarily non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*)?
And if there is non-informative intimation, is there necessarily informative intimation?
Regarding this, some say:
The seven fundamental courses of action (karmapatha) definitely possess both informative (vijñapti) and non-informative (avijñapti) karma.
Regarding preparatory (prayoga) and consecutive (pṛṣṭha) actions, informative karma certainly exists, while non-informative karma is not necessarily present;
it occurs only when the underlying afflictions (paryavasthāna) are intense.
And through intense faith,
that which is performed gives rise to non-informative matter (*avijñapti*),
and not otherwise. Some say:
Regarding the seven fundamental courses of action (*karmapatha*), the non-informative (*avijñapti*) is necessarily present, while the informative (*vijñapti*) is not fixed.
If one performs the act oneself, there is informative [action]; if one dispatches another to perform it, one obtains only the non-informative.
The preliminary application (*prayoga*) and the subsequent conclusion (*pṛṣṭha*) are as previously explained.
The commentary says:
One should state it thus:
with the exception of sexual misconduct, the remaining fundamental paths of action [are what is meant].
Non-informative action (avijñapti) necessarily exists, whereas informative action (vijñapti) is not certain.
If one performs the act oneself and it reaches completion at that very moment, there is informative karma;
however, if one dispatches another to perform it, it exists only at the time of completion.
When the manifest [action] has already ceased, there is only the unmanifest.
If there is manifest action in sexual misconduct, it is also certain that there is a manifest action during the stage of preparation;
however, the unmanifest is not necessarily present, as previously stated.
In the subsequent stage, there is certainly non-informative action (avijñapti);
as for informative action (vijñapti), it is not certain: if one performs it, it exists;
if one does not perform it, it does not exist.
It should be understood that this explains what is produced by a distracted mind.
As for the distinction between meditative concentration and distraction regarding the branches [of the path],
one should reflect accordingly upon the existence or non-existence of informative and non-informative action.
It is neither comprised within discipline nor non-discipline.
Non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is not severed due to three causes for virtuous or non-virtuous conduct:
first, because the underlying intention (*āśaya*) does not cease.
Second, by not relinquishing through application;
third, by the limit of the force not having passed.
Regarding "not relinquishing through application due to the non-cessation of the intention": [it refers to] not abandoning the application because the underlying intention has not ceased.
Just as when one gives rise to a pure and sincere mind to pay respectful homage and make offerings to an image of the Buddha, a stūpa, or the like,
the unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*) produced thereby persists from the first moment until the underlying intention has ceased.
Alternatively, [the non-informative action] continues in an uninterrupted succession as long as the preparatory effort has not been abandoned.
If the intention ceases and the preparatory effort is relinquished, the non-informative action is then severed,
provided that the momentum has not yet expired.
This refers to the wholesome or unwholesome actions performed with a pure mind or through intense obsession (*paryavasthāna*);
according to their respective force, the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) continues without interruption.
For example, as when one kills many ants due to intense obsession.
The unmanifest [action] thus produced continues in succession for as long as one lives;
the same applies to that performed with a pure and sincere mind.
That is to say, it is like a person who gives rise to profound and reverent faith.
One should prepare ritual implements and offer them to the Saṃgha,
making various offerings such as burning incense and scattering flowers;
or [one may do so] on occasions such as the festivals of the sun, the moon, or every five years as taught by the Buddha.
He makes various offerings to the assembly of monks,
giving rise to a pure and sincere mind and engaging in the activities of body and speech,
until his aspiration has not yet ceased.
Alternatively, the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) is not severed as long as the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) has not been relinquished;
however, if the intention (*āśaya*) ceases and the preparatory effort is abandoned, the non-informative [action] is then severed.
The same is explained at length regarding those who abide in the intermediate state (*madhyama*) in other passages.

Furthermore, there are intermediate courses of wholesome and unwholesome conduct wherein the non-informative matter (avijñapti) persists throughout the entire duration of one's homogeneous life-span (nikāyasabhāga) without being interrupted.
Regarding these wholesome courses of conduct:
Suppose one makes a vow such as:
"I shall never eat before first making offerings to the images of the Buddhas, stūpas, and so forth.
Then, day after day, according to their capacity and means, they [perform this].
Down to making an offering of even a single flower or a single incense stick,
the non-manifest (avijñapti) remains uninterrupted throughout the entirety of one's homogeneous life-span (nikāya-sabhāga).
Alternatively, there are those who establish a formal vow.
If there are no life-sustaining requisites to give to others,
he never eats first; rather,
day by day, according to his capacity, he [provides for them].
Down to the point of giving another person even a single morsel of food or a piece of cloth the size of half a cubit,
the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) remains uninterrupted throughout the entire duration of one's homogeneous life-span (*nikāyasabhāga*). Or,
there may be those who have made a formal vow.
If one has not first made offerings to the Triple Gem,
one shall never eat first;
such a person, day by day, according to their capacity, [should do so].
Down to the point of giving a single vessel of food to the Sangha,
or even sweeping and cleaning a space the size of one foot,
the non-informative karma (avijñapti) remains uninterrupted throughout the entirety of that homogeneous life-span (nikāya-sabhāga).
Some may establish a vow to give to the poor on a certain day each year,
or to make offerings to the Sangha;
they then take a small amount of their own goods to provide for those needs.
One sets aside remaining wealth for future provision;
as long as one's *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous life-span) endures, the *avijñapti* (non-informative action) is never severed.
Such instances as these are termed "sublime conduct" (*sucarita*).
Regarding the practitioner of evil deeds:
suppose one makes a vow,
"I shall daily inflict all manner of misfortunes and harms upon that enemy."
If one does not do so, one shall never eat first. Thus, day after day,
down to even a single blow or a single harsh word of scolding, reviling, or humiliation,
the non-informative [karma] (avijñapti) remains uninterrupted throughout the entirety of that life-constituent (nikāya-sabhāga).
Such acts as these are called evil deeds.
Alternatively, there are those who fashion images of the Buddhas, stūpas, and other articles for making offerings,
or who transcribe the True Dharma contained within the Tripiṭaka.
They fashion images of the noble Saṃgha and establish monasteries;
they provide robes, medicine, and all requisites for sustaining the body;
they establish houses of merit and plant groves of trees.
Regarding the construction of wells, bridges, boats, stairways,
and the like— the unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*) produced by these various manifest actions (*vijñapti*) continues in an uninterrupted succession due to three conditions.
First, by way of intention;
second, by way of the basis;
third, by way of the object.
By way of intention (*āśaya*),
it means that one generates a deep sense of joy regarding that object, and this intention does not cease.
By way of basis (*āśraya*), it means...
This refers to the state when the continuity of the homogeneous life-stream of the supporting body has not yet come to an end.
Regarding "by way of things," it refers to when the objects constructed, such as Buddha images and the like, have not yet completely perished.
If any one of these three conditions is lacking,
the previously generated non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is thereby severed.
This is called "sublime conduct" (*sucarita*).
"Evil conduct" refers to such acts as setting snares, nets, knives, arrows, and the like;
this should be understood according to what was previously explained.
This concludes the brief *vibhāṣā* on the explained manifest and unmanifest karma.
If one accomplishes bodily manifest action,
does one also accomplish its unmanifest [action]?
It can be answered in four propositions.
There are cases where one accomplishes bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti*) but not its corresponding non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
This refers to those born in the desire realm who abide in a state that is neither discipline (*saṃvara*) nor non-discipline (*asaṃvara*).
One who currently possesses bodily intimation does not acquire this non-intimation;
or, one who previously possessed bodily intimation and has not lost it does not acquire this non-intimation.
Regarding "one who currently possesses bodily intimation":
This refers to not sleeping, not being intoxicated, not being dazed, and not abandoning the preparatory effort while seeking to produce a bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*).
One who does not obtain this non-intimation (*avijñapti*) is one who lacks earnest faith.
It is not due to intense entanglement (*paryavasthāna*);
even if one produces a bodily informative act (*kāyavijñapti*), one does not obtain this non-informative act (*avijñapti*),
unless one previously possessed a bodily informative act that has not been lost.
That is to say, one does not abandon manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) due to three conditions:
first, because the underlying intention (*āśaya*) does not cease;
second, because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is not relinquished.
Because the three time-limits have not yet passed,
one does not acquire this non-informative [action];
the meaning is as previously explained.
There are those who possess the non-informative (avijñapti) of the body but not this informative (vijñapti).
This refers to noble beings dwelling within the womb,
or those born in the desire realm who abide in restraint but have not obtained the prātimokṣa restraint and lack bodily informative action.
If it exists, it is lost.
If one is born in the form realm, bodily intimation does not exist;
even if it existed, it would be lost.
If noble beings are born into the formless realm,
those noble beings, while dwelling in the womb, are unable to produce manifest action; furthermore,
the manifest karma from previous lives has already been lost.
However, one who abides in restraint accomplishes only the meditative and untainted non-informative [matter].
"Abiding in restraint" refers to abiding in the meditative and untainted restraints.
Regarding those who lack bodily intimation:
this refers to one who, being asleep, intoxicated, or unconscious,
relinquishes all preparatory effort and does not seek to initiate bodily intimation.
Therefore, regarding that which exists but is lost:
it refers to the abandonment of bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*) due to three conditions.
First, because the underlying intention (*āśaya*) has ceased.
Second, because of the relinquishing of the preparatory effort;
third, because of the exhaustion of its momentum.
If one is born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and lacks bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), [it would follow that there is no unmanifest karma].
This means that because they have abandoned preparatory effort and do not seek to initiate manifest action (*vijñapti*),
even if such action were present, it would be lost as previously explained.
This applies to those noble ones (*ārya*) who are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Those in training (śaikṣa) accomplish the unmanifest (avijñapti) of one in training;
those beyond training (aśaikṣa) accomplish the unmanifest of one beyond training.
There are those who accomplish bodily manifest action (kāyavijñapti) and also this same unmanifest.
This refers to one born in the desire realm who abides in restraint,
yet does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint;
such a person currently possesses bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) and also obtains this non-intimation (avijñapti).
Alternatively, one may first possess this manifest action without losing it,
and also acquire this non-manifest action,
if one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint.
If one abides in non-restraint,
or if one abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and currently possesses bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), one also acquires this non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
Either one previously possessed bodily intimation that has not been lost and also acquires this non-intimation;
or, if born in the form realm, one currently possesses bodily intimation;
or, one previously possessed bodily intimation that has not been lost.

Regarding the statement, "In this context, there is also the present bodily intimation that acquires this non-intimation (avijñapti)," it means by means of earnest faith or through intense obsession (paryavasthāna).
One may also possess non-informative action (avijñapti) alongside informative action (vijñapti).
Whether one abides in the prātimokṣa vows or abides in non-restraint,
such a person certainly accomplishes both bodily informative and non-informative actions.
If one is born in the form realm and currently possesses bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
it means that they have not relinquished their preparatory application (*prayoga*) in seeking to give rise to an act of intimation.
The rest is as previously explained.
There are cases where one neither possesses bodily intimation nor its corresponding non-intimation; this refers, for example,
to those dwelling within an eggshell.
If ordinary beings dwell within the womb,
or if they are born in the desire realm and abide in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline,
there is no bodily intimation; even if it were present, it would be lost.
If ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),

or if those classes of ordinary beings dwelling within the womb or egg have already lost the manifest and unmanifest karma (*vijñapti-avijñapti-karman*) of their previous lives and are currently unable to produce it; [then they lack these].
It should be understood as previously explained:
having been born in the formless realm, one has already abandoned the contaminated [states] but has not yet attained the uncontaminated;
because there is no form in that stage, the rest is as stated before.
If one accomplishes a wholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
does one also accomplish its non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
One should answer that this involves four permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*).
There are those who possess wholesome bodily intimation but not its corresponding non-intimation;
namely, those born in the desire realm who abide in a state of non-restraint.
Furthermore, one who abides in neither discipline nor non-discipline may currently possess a virtuous bodily intimation,
yet does not acquire this corresponding non-intimation.
Alternatively, one may previously have possessed this informative [action] without losing it;
one does not possess this non-informative [action], yet possesses a virtuous bodily informative action,
meaning that one is not sleeping and so forth.
"One who does not obtain this non-informative [action] (avijñapti)" refers to one for whom it has not arisen from a state of profound faith; or,
"one who previously possessed this informative [action] (vijñapti) and has not lost it."
This means that, due to the three conditions previously mentioned,
one does not obtain this non-informative [action].
That is to say, it is also because it is not produced by a sincere and profound faith.
Question: What kind of wholesome bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) does one who dwells in non-restraint possess?
Answer: He also possesses it toward his parents, teachers, elders, the Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddhas.
Because making offerings and showing respect gives rise to wholesome manifest [action],
there are cases where one possesses wholesome bodily non-manifest [action] but not this manifest [action].
This refers to noble ones (ārya) dwelling within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and abides in restraint, yet does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint,
there is no virtuous bodily intimation;
even if it were present, it would have been lost.
If one is born in the form realm, there is no wholesome bodily intimation;
even if it existed, it would have been lost.
This is also the case for all noble ones born in the formless realm.
In this context, one who abides in restraint refers to one who abides in the restraint of meditative concentration (dhyāna-saṃvara) or the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara),
but does not obtain the restraint of individual liberation (prātimokṣa-saṃvara).
This means that one who abides in this restraint necessarily accomplishes the non-informative (avijñapti) matter of a wholesome body;
the rest is as previously explained.
There are those who accomplish both the informative (vijñapti) matter of a wholesome body and this non-informative matter.
This refers to one born in the desire realm who abides in restraint,
yet does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint;
such a person currently possesses a virtuous bodily intimation and also obtains this non-intimation (avijñapti).
Or, one may first possess this manifest action (vijñapti) without losing it and also acquire this non-manifest action (avijñapti),
whether abiding in the prātimokṣa vows or abiding in non-restraint (asaṃvara).
Furthermore, one who abides in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline may currently possess a virtuous bodily intimation and also acquire this non-intimation,
or may have previously possessed such an intimation without losing it.
One also obtains this non-informative [action] if one is born in the form realm and presently possesses a virtuous bodily informative action,
or if one previously possessed such an action and has not lost it.
In this regard, all points are as previously explained.
There are cases where one does not possess a virtuous bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
nor does one possess its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
That is to say: those dwelling within an eggshell;
or various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) dwelling within the womb;
or those born in the desire realm who abide in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
And for one who abides in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
there is no wholesome bodily intimation;
even if it existed, it has been lost.
If ordinary beings are born in the formless realm and possess unwholesome bodily intimation,
do they also possess that non-intimation?
Answer: Those who have accomplished unwholesome bodily non-informative action (avijñapti) necessarily accomplish this informative action (vijñapti).
There are also those who accomplish unwholesome bodily informative action.
This is not non-informative [matter].
That is to say, it refers to those born in the desire realm who abide in restraint,
as well as those who abide in neither restraint nor non-restraint.
There is currently an unwholesome bodily intimation,
yet one does not acquire this non-intimation;
or, such an intimation existed previously and has not been lost.
One does not obtain this non-informative [matter] when there is currently present an unwholesome bodily informative [action],
such as when one is not sleeping and so forth.
"One who does not obtain this non-informative [action] (avijñapti)" means that it is not produced by intense fetters (paryavasthāna).
"One who previously possessed this informative [action] (vijñapti) and has not lost it" refers to...
This refers to the three conditions previously mentioned;
the rest is as explained before.
Question: Abiding in which restraint does one possess unwholesome bodily intimation?
Answer: It is possible for all three types of restraint to exist [in such a person].

Question: For one who abides in the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) or the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), what kind of unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) could there be?
Answer: Yes.

When one gives rise to unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), such as striking sentient beings, one should also be said to possess unwholesome bodily non-intimation (*kāyāvijñapti*) even when there is no bodily intimation.
This refers to such acts as inciting another to kill and so forth.
In this context, one should formulate four logical permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Why, then, is the "conformity with the subsequent clause" (*anuloma-paścāt-kotika*) employed here?
Some say that there should be four permutations (catuṣkoṭi):
there is one who possesses unwholesome bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti).
This is not the case for non-informative action (avijñapti);
that is to say, it refers to one born in the desire realm who abides in restraint (saṃvara),
or who abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint (asaṃvara).
There is currently an unwholesome bodily intimation,
yet one does not acquire this non-intimation;
or, such an intimation existed previously and has not been lost.
One does not obtain this non-informative [action],
yet there is the possession of unwholesome bodily non-informative [action],
but not of this informative [action].
This refers to one born in the desire realm who abides in either a state of restraint,
or in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and then dispatches another to commit acts such as killing.
There is the accomplishment of unwholesome bodily intimation as well as its non-intimation;
that is to say, one born in the desire realm who dwells in a state of non-restraint.
If one abides in restraint,
or abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and currently possesses unwholesome bodily intimation.
One also acquires this non-informative [action] (avijñapti);
or, having previously possessed this informative [action] (vijñapti) without losing it,
one also acquires this non-informative [action].
There are those who neither possess unwholesome bodily intimation nor its corresponding non-intimation;
that is to say, those dwelling within an eggshell.
If ordinary beings dwell within the womb,
or if they are born in the desire realm and abide in either restraint,
or in neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint.
There is no unwholesome bodily intimation;
even if it existed, it would have been lost,
and one cannot obtain this non-intimation.
If one were born in the form or formless realms, one should have made such a statement;
since it was not stated, one should know that this text speaks only with reference to the informative and non-informative [karma] of those belonging to the same category.
It does not depend on a different category;
that is to say, when bodily non-informative action (*kāyavijñapti*) arises from bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*),
this is called "of the same category."
If the non-informative [action] of the body is produced by the informative [action] of speech,
this is called "of a different kind.
It should be stated thus.
There is no one who accomplishes only unwholesome bodily non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
Therefore, this should be formulated as a "consequent clause" (*uttarapada*). Why is that?
If one can utter words that incite another to kill or the like,
thereby giving rise to an unmanifest bodily action (*kāyavijñapti-avijñapti*),
one necessarily also accomplishes an unwholesome manifest bodily action (*kāyavijñapti*).
Because it is necessarily capable of moving the body, hands, and so forth.

If this were not the case, then regarding the previously mentioned accomplishment of wholesome bodily non-informative matter (*kāyavijñapti*), one would likewise have to say that it is not included within this [category of] informative matter (*vijñapti*).
If one abides in non-restraint,
or abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and by means of virtuous speech prompts another to perform acts such as giving;
From this, one produces and attains wholesome unmanifest bodily action (*kāyavijñapti*).
Since this was not previously mentioned among the wholesome [actions],
we know that the expression "speech" refers to the instigation of others to perform acts such as giving.
Because one who has produced and attained bodily non-informative action (*kāyavijñapti*) must also be able to move their hands, body, and so forth,
they thereby accomplish wholesome bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti-karman*).
Therefore, neither of these two locations contains this statement:
"If one accomplishes a concealed-neutral bodily intimation,
does one also accomplish its non-intimation?"
Answer: There is no one who possesses the unmanifest (avijñapti) of the body that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
However, there are those who possess its manifest (vijñapti), namely, those born in the form realm (rūpadhātu) who currently possess the manifest of the body that is obscured-unspecified.
Question: Why is there no obscured-unspecified bodily intimation (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-kāya-vijñapti*) in the desire realm?

Answer: Because the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm that act as the motivating cause (*samutthāpaka*) for the production of bodily and vocal actions are all exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Only the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes,
and the ignorance associated with them.
Although these are obscured-neutral,
they are all abandoned by insight;
a mind that is not abandoned by insight cannot give rise to bodily or vocal karma.
Because it arises through the internal door and is extremely subtle.

Question: If one who has been born in the desire realm and has already become free from the defilements of the desire realm gives rise to the afflictions of the first dhyāna as manifesting before them?
Why does one not produce obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) bodily or vocal informative action (vijñapti-karma)?
Answer: Those born within the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are only able to give rise to the afflictions of meditative attainment (samāpatti-kleśa), not the afflictions of birth (upapatti-kleśa).
Among the various afflictions (*kleśa*), those that give rise to bodily and vocal actions produce only further afflictions.
Other masters say:
"The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) must be thus."
If the afflictions of this level arise and become manifest,
they can still cause the continuity of the maturation (vipāka) of this level to fluctuate and give rise to the manifest karma (vijñapti-karma) belonging to this level.
All defiled karma necessarily takes the continuity of its own level’s maturation as its basis;
it is not possible for one born in the desire realm to possess the continuity of maturation belonging to the form realm.
Therefore, it is only within the first dhyāna of the Form Realm that one can produce this obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) bodily and vocal informative action (vijñapti-karman).
If one possesses unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) bodily informative action, [it is likewise produced there].
Does one who possesses this non-informative [matter] (avijñapti) necessarily possess it?
Answer: There is no one who possesses non-obscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) bodily non-informative matter; however, there is one who possesses its informative matter (vijñapti).
That is to say, one born in the desire realm or the form realm who currently manifests non-obscured-neutral bodily informative matter.
The distinctions therein should be understood according to reason.
If one accomplishes past bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*),
does that person also accomplish its non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
It shall be answered in four propositions:
there is that which accomplishes past bodily intimation,
but not its corresponding non-intimation.
This refers to one born in the desire realm who dwells in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline,
who previously possessed a bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) which has not been lost,
yet has not acquired this non-intimation (avijñapti).
Regarding the fact that a prior bodily intimation is not lost:
this is due to the three conditions as previously explained.
One who does not obtain this non-intimation [is as follows].
This refers to that which is not originated by earnest faith or by intense fetters; thus,
there are those who possess past bodily non-informative action (*avijñapti*) but not this informative action (*vijñapti*).
This refers to those noble ones who dwell within the womb,
or those born in the desire realm who abide in restraint but do not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint.
Previously there was no bodily intimation, or even if it existed, it has been lost;
or if born in the form realm, previously there was no bodily intimation,
or even if it existed, it has been lost.
If those who are still in training (śaikṣa) are born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), they lack bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) and so forth;
this should be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Question: If those who are still in training attain the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) by means of the mundane path (laukikamārga)?
Since one has never previously manifested the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) when being born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
how could such a person possess past non-informative karma (*avijñapti-karma*) of the body?
If they do not possess it, [how is this explained]?
For what reason is this passage stated thus?
If those who are trainees (śaikṣa) are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
some say as follows:
Furthermore, there are also learners born in the formless realm who do not possess past bodily non-informative karma;
however, this passage speaks only with reference to those who do possess it.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Other masters say that once the fruit of an ārya has been attained, one must necessarily bring the supramundane path of the higher fruit into manifestation.
Those in training who are born into the formless realm necessarily possess past bodily non-informative karma (*kāyavijñapti-avijñapti*).
Some also possess past bodily informative karma (*kāyavijñapti*) as well as this non-informative karma.
This refers to one born in the desire realm who abides in restraint,
yet has not obtained the prātimokṣa restraint;
such a person possesses prior bodily intimation that has not been lost and also obtains this non-informative [action].
Whether one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint,
or abides in non-restraint,
or abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint.
One who previously possessed a bodily informative act (*kāyavijñapti*) and has not lost it also acquires this non-informative act (*avijñapti*).
If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and has not lost a previous bodily informative act, and if,
within this state, one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint (*saṃvara*), [one likewise acquires it].
Regarding those who abide in non-restraint,
some say that this text refers only to the moments from the second instant onward;
it does not apply to the first instant.
Because past manifest and non-manifest [karma] do not yet exist.
Some say that even in the first moment, one accomplishes past manifest and non-manifest karma.
Because the prior formative action (karmasamutthāna) has been accomplished,
there are cases where one does not possess past bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti),
nor does one possess its corresponding non-intimation (avijñapti).
That is to say: those dwelling within an eggshell;
or various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) dwelling within the womb;
or those born in the desire realm who abide in a state that is neither discipline (*saṃvara*) nor non-discipline (*asaṃvara*).
Previously there was no bodily intimation, or even if it existed,
it has been lost. This applies to Arhats and ordinary beings born in the formless realm who have acquired past wholesome bodily intimation.
Does one who possesses this non-informative [matter] (avijñapti) necessarily possess it?
It should be answered by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
There is the case where one possesses past wholesome bodily informative matter (kāya-vijñapti), but does not possess this non-informative matter.
This refers to one born in the desire realm who dwells in non-restraint,
or who dwells in neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and who previously possessed a virtuous bodily intimation that has not been lost.
One does not obtain this non-informative [action].
There are those who possess past virtuous bodily non-informative action but not this informative [action],
namely, those noble ones (ārya) dwelling within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and abides in restraint,
yet does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint,
there is no prior wholesome bodily intimation; even if it existed, it has been lost.
If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) where previously there was no wholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), or if such existed but has been lost;
or if those who are trainees (*śaikṣa*) are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
they possess both past wholesome bodily intimations and their corresponding non-intimations (*avijñapti*).
This refers to one born in the desire realm who abides in restraint but has not obtained the prātimokṣa restraint;
such a person possesses prior wholesome bodily informative action (*vijñapti*) which is not lost,
and also obtains this non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
Whether one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint,
or abides in non-restraint,
or abides in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint.
If one previously possessed a wholesome bodily intimation that has not been lost,
one also acquires this non-intimation.
If one is born into the Form Realm and previously possessed a wholesome bodily intimation that has not been lost, [one likewise acquires this].
Regarding those who abide in the prātimokṣa restraint, the two explanations herein should be understood as previously stated.
Question: What about those born in the form realm (rūpadhātu)?
How does one accomplish past virtuous bodily intimation?
Answer: For example, at one time the Buddha went to the Brahma world, where the gods of the Brahma assembly prostrated to him and circumambulated him.
Until that preparatory effort has been relinquished,
one accomplishes past virtuous bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti*); however,
there are cases where one neither accomplishes past virtuous bodily informative action nor its corresponding non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
That is to say: those dwelling within the shell of an egg;
or various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) dwelling within the womb;
or those born in the desire realm who abide in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
And for those abiding in neither restraint nor non-restraint, there was previously no virtuous bodily intimation; even if it existed, it has been lost.
This applies to arhats as well as ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding those born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu):
if they possess past unwholesome bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti),
do they also possess its non-intimation (avijñapti)?
Answer: Those who have accomplished past unwholesome bodily non-informative action (avijñapti) also accomplish this informative action (vijñapti).
However, there are those who have accomplished past unwholesome bodily informative action but do not accomplish this non-informative action.
This refers to one born in the desire realm who abides in restraint,
or who abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and who has not lost a previously existing unwholesome bodily intimation.
One does not obtain this non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*).
In this regard, two explanations should be understood as previously stated.
If one possesses past obscured-unspecified bodily informative [matter] (*kāya-vijñapti*), [one also possesses its non-informative counterpart].
Does one who possesses this non-informative [matter] (avijñapti) also possess it?
Answer: No one possesses past obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) bodily informative matter (kāyavijñapti) and this non-informative matter.
If one possesses past unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) bodily informative matter, does that person also possess this non-informative matter?
Answer: No one accomplishes past non-obscured-neutral bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
If one accomplishes future bodily intimation, does that person also accomplish its non-intimation?
Answer: There is no one who possesses future bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), but there are those who possess its non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
This refers to all noble ones (*ārya*) dwelling within the womb.
Having been born in the desire realm and having attained a wholesome mind of the form realm,
or being born in the form realm, or being an noble one (ārya) born in the formless realm—
why is it that there is no possession of future bodily or vocal informative action (vijñapti-karma)?
Answer: There is no such thing as pre-fabricating future manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*), because it has not yet arisen.
If one were to possess future manifest karma of body and speech, it would follow that one could experience the results of karma even before it has been performed.
For what reason does one accomplish future non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)?
Because it arises simultaneously with the mind and is cultivated in accordance with the mind.
This applies if one accomplishes future wholesome bodily informative matter (*vijñapti*).
Does one who possesses this unmanifest (avijñapti) also possess it?
Answer: There is no one who possesses future wholesome bodily manifest (kāya-vijñapti), yet there is one who possesses this unmanifest.
This refers to noble beings who, while dwelling within the womb,
have either been born into the desire realm and have already attained a wholesome mind of the form realm,
or have been born into the form realm itself.
If noble ones are born in the formless realm,
and they possess future unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
do they also possess this non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: No one accomplishes both future unwholesome bodily intimation and its corresponding non-intimation.
If one accomplishes future obscured-unspecified bodily intimation, does that person accomplish its corresponding non-intimation?
Answer: No one achieves future obscured-unspecified bodily intimation, nor its corresponding non-intimation.
If one achieves future unobscured-unspecified bodily intimation, does that person achieve its corresponding non-intimation?
Answer: There is no one who possesses future non-obscured-neutral bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) or its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
Question: For what reason is there no one who possesses past or future obscured or non-obscured neutral informative action (*vijñaptikarma*)?
Answer: That which is accomplished possesses only such power;
it can only accomplish karma of the same moment, but lacks the power to accomplish that which has already ceased or that which has not yet arrived.
If that karma is past, its acquisition is also past;
if that karma is future, its acquisition is also future;
if that karma is present, its acquisition is also present.
Some say that because the latencies (*vāsanā*) of those actions are not firm,
there is no one who achieves [the possession of] past or future [dharmas].
Just as the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of wholesome and unwholesome karma are firm and stable,
they are able to bring about results in both the past and future lives;
the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is not so.
If one accomplishes present bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
does one also accomplish its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?
One should respond by setting up four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).
There are those who possess present bodily intimation but not its corresponding non-intimation;
namely, those born in the desire realm who abide in restraint.
One cannot obtain the prātimokṣa restraint;
even if there currently exists a bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), one does not obtain this non-intimation (avijñapti).
Even if a prior bodily intimation existed and was not lost, [one still does not obtain it].
Yet one does not obtain this non-informative [matter] (avijñapti).
If one abides in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint and currently possesses bodily informative [matter] (vijñapti), one does not obtain this non-informative matter;
even if one previously possessed bodily informative matter, it is not lost.
Yet one does not obtain this non-informative [matter].
If one is born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) and currently possesses bodily informative [matter],
among these, there is the case of one who abides in the restraint (saṃvara) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
This refers to one who abides in the meditative concentration (dhyāna) and the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara),
and currently possesses bodily intimation (kāya-vijñapti);
this indicates that at such a time, the mind is not in meditative absorption and is not asleep, and so forth.
The statement that "this non-informative [matter] is not obtained" indicates that the past and present informative [acts] were not motivated by earnest faith nor by intense fetters.
Because there is no production of non-informative [matter],
one does not possess present bodily non-informative matter that is not this informative [matter].
That is to say, one born in the desire realm who abides in restraint.
One cannot obtain the prātimokṣa restraint;
whether one is currently in meditative concentration or not,
there is at present no bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti).
First, there is the case where one possesses a prior bodily intimation and has not lost the acquisition of this non-intimation;
second, the case where one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint or abides in non-restraint (asaṃvara) and currently lacks bodily intimation;
and third, the case where one abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint and currently lacks bodily intimation.
First, there is the non-forfeiture of a previously existing bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*), by which this non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is acquired.
If one is born in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is currently in meditative absorption (*samāpanna*),
herein "currently in meditative absorption" refers to:
The mention of the existence of the unmanifest (avijñapti) also excludes the existence of the manifest (vijñapti).
By stating that one "attains" this unmanifest,
it indicates the existence of past bodily manifest action.
The unmanifest bodily karma that has been produced continues to function in the present for one who abides in either the prātimokṣa vows or in non-restraint.
Regarding those who currently lack bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
some say that this refers to the period from the second moment onward.
Because that [action] necessarily possesses informative expression (*vijñapti*) at its initial moment. Some say:
"That initial moment is also what is referred to by the term 'existent'."
There is currently no manifest bodily intimation,
because one has undertaken non-restraint,
and because one has acquired full ordination while in meditative absorption.
There are those who possess both present bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
This refers to those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who abide in restraint (*saṃvara*),
yet have not obtained the prātimokṣa restraint.
One who currently possesses bodily intimation also acquires this non-intimation;
or, one who previously possessed bodily intimation and has not lost it acquires this non-intimation.
If one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint or in non-restraint,
and there is currently a bodily intimation present.
If one abides in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline,
and currently possesses bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), one also acquires this non-intimation (*avijñapti*);
or, if one previously possessed bodily intimation, it has not been lost.
One acquires this non-informative [matter].
In this context, it refers to one who abides in the prātimokṣa vows or abides in non-restraint.
Regarding those who currently possess bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
some say that it is taken only from the moment after the first instant onward.
Because there is no bodily intimation in any single moment,
some say that other moments are also included.
Furthermore, because bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) can also arise in the subsequent stage,
there are cases where one neither possesses present bodily intimation nor this non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
This refers to those dwelling within the eggshell or residing inside the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and abides in restraint,
yet does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint,
and is neither in meditative concentration nor currently manifesting bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti).
Even if one previously possessed bodily intimation that has not been lost, one does not obtain this non-intimation (avijñapti).
Or, if one abides in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline and currently lacks bodily intimation,
even if one previously possessed bodily intimation that has not been lost.

Yet one does not obtain this non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) if one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is not currently in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), nor if one has no bodily informative [matter] (*kāyavijñapti*),
or if one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
In this context, "not being in meditative concentration" indicates the non-accomplishment of present non-informative matter (*avijñapti*);
the rest is as previously explained.
If one accomplishes a present virtuous bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti),
does one also accomplish its non-intimation (avijñapti)?
One should answer by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
There are those who possess present virtuous bodily intimation but not its corresponding non-intimation;
namely, those born in the desire realm who abide in restraint but have not obtained the prātimokṣa restraint.
There is currently a virtuous bodily intimation,
yet this non-intimation is not obtained;
even if a previously existing virtuous bodily intimation has not been lost.
Yet one does not acquire this non-informative [action] if one abides in non-restraint,
or if one abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint.
There is currently a virtuous bodily intimation,
yet this non-intimation is not acquired;
even if a prior virtuous bodily intimation existed and has not been lost.
Yet one does not obtain this non-informative [matter].

If one is born in the form realm and currently possesses a wholesome bodily informative [action], in that case—should one be born in the form realm and currently possess a wholesome bodily informative [action]— [The text continues:
...if one is born in the form realm and currently possesses a wholesome bodily informative [action].
One will certainly not accomplish present non-informative matter (*avijñapti*),
because one is necessarily not in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The rest is as previously explained.
There is one who possesses present unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) of a wholesome body but not its manifest form (*vijñapti*; i.e., bodily action).
This refers to one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who abides in a restraint (*saṃvara*), yet has not obtained the prātimokṣa restraint.
While in meditative concentration (*samāhita*), one does not currently manifest a virtuous bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*).
One acquires this non-intimation (*avijñapti*) while a previously existing virtuous bodily intimation has not been lost.
Alternatively, while abiding in the prātimokṣa restraint (*saṃvara*), one does not currently manifest a virtuous bodily intimation.
If one abides in non-restraint,
or abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and currently lacks wholesome bodily intimation.
First, one possesses an unlost virtuous bodily intimation and acquires this non-intimation;
or, if born in the form realm, one is currently in meditative absorption;
or, one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint.
Regarding those who do not currently manifest a virtuous bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
some say that this refers to the period from the second moment onward.
Some say that because it applies to the first moment as previously explained,
there is one who possesses both the present virtuous bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
This refers to one born in the desire realm who abides in restraint,
yet does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint;
such a person currently possesses a virtuous bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) and also obtains this non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
First, there is the non-loss of a prior virtuous bodily intimation,
through which one obtains this non-intimation;
this occurs if one abides in the prātimokṣa vows.
There currently exists a virtuous bodily intimation for one who abides in non-restraint,
as well as for one who abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint.
There is currently a virtuous bodily intimation,
and one also acquires this non-intimation; or,
having previously possessed a virtuous bodily intimation that has not been lost, one acquires this non-intimation.
There are those who do not possess the present virtuous bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
nor its non-intimation (*avijñapti*);
namely, those dwelling within the shell of an egg.
And while dwelling within the womb,
or if one is born in the desire realm and dwells in restraint,
one does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint if one is not in meditative concentration.
There is no present virtuous bodily intimation;
even if a previously existing virtuous bodily intimation has not been lost,
one does not obtain this non-intimation.
If one abides in non-restraint,
or abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and currently lacks virtuous bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti).
Suppose one previously possessed a virtuous bodily manifest action that has not been lost,
yet one does not obtain this non-manifest action;
this would be the case if one were born in the form realm and was not in meditative concentration.
There is no present virtuous bodily intimation.
Or, if one is born in the formless realm,
or if one possesses a present non-virtuous bodily intimation.
Does he accomplish this non-informative [action] (avijñapti)?
It should be answered by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
There is one who accomplishes a present unwholesome bodily informative [action] (kāyavijñapti) but not this non-informative [action].
This refers to one born in the desire realm who abides in either restraint,
or in neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint,
and currently possesses unwholesome bodily intimation.
One does not obtain this non-informative [matter].
Even if one previously possessed an unwholesome bodily informative [act] that has not been lost, one still does not obtain this non-informative [matter] while abiding in restraint.
This refers to those who abide in the three types of restraint but do not obtain this non-informative [matter],
because it is not produced by intense fetters.
The rest is as previously explained.
There are those who possess the present unwholesome bodily non-informative (avijñapti) but not this informative (vijñapti).
This refers to those born in the desire realm who abide in a state of non-restraint (asaṃvara).
There is currently no unwholesome bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti),
whether one abides in restraint (saṃvara) or abides in neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint (naivasaṃvaranāsaṃvara).
There is currently no unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*);
however, while the previously existing unwholesome bodily intimation has not been lost,
one acquires this non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
Regarding one who abides in non-restraint and currently lacks unwholesome bodily intimation, some say:
excluding the first moment.
Some say it applies to the first [moment].
Others say it is because non-restraint of body is produced solely by speech.
Some possess both the present unwholesome bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) and its corresponding non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
This refers to one born in the desire realm who abides in either restraint or in neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint,
and currently possesses unwholesome bodily intimation.
One also acquires this non-informative [action] (avijñapti).
One who previously possessed an unwholesome bodily informative action (kāya-vijñapti) and has not lost it acquires this non-informative action if they abide in a state of non-restraint (asaṃvara).
The existence of present unwholesome bodily intimation is in all respects as previously explained.
There are cases where one does not possess present unwholesome bodily intimation.
Nor is this non-informative [matter] present when one is within an eggshell or dwelling within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and abides in restraint,
or abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and currently lacks unwholesome bodily intimation.
Suppose one previously possessed an unwholesome bodily intimation that has not been lost, yet one does not acquire this [corresponding] non-intimation.
This is as explained previously for those born in the form realm or the formless realm.
If one accomplishes a presently existing obscured-neutral bodily intimation...
Does one who possesses this non-informative [matter] (avijñapti) necessarily possess it?
Answer: One does not possess present obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) bodily non-informative matter;
however, there are those who possess its informative matter (vijñapti).

That is to say: if one born in the form realm currently possesses a manifest bodily action (kāyavijñapti) that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta), or if one accomplishes a manifest bodily action that is unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta), does such a person also accomplish this non-manifest action (avijñapti)?
Answer: There is no one who possesses the present non-obscured-neutral bodily non-informative [matter] (kāya-avijñapti).

However, there are those who possess this informative [matter] (vijñapti), namely, those born in the desire realm or the form realm who currently possess non-obscured-neutral bodily informative matter.
As explained extensively above regarding bodily intimation and non-intimation,
so it is with verbal intimation and non-intimation.
The detailed explanation is likewise.
However, regarding the distinction between the vocal sounds mentioned here and those previously discussed, the definitive meaning stated herein is that in the desire realm,
there is necessarily no non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) that follows the mind (*cittānuparivartin*).
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there is certainly no arising of non-informative action (avijñapti) based upon informative action (vijñapti).
Question: Why is this so?
Answer: Because such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

Furthermore, there are those who say that in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), non-informative action (*avijñapti*) arises based on informative action (*vijñapti*). Therefore,
there is necessarily no non-informative action that follows the mind (*cittānuparivartin*).
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) that follows the mind;
therefore, it is certainly never the case that unmanifest action is produced based on manifest action (*vijñapti*).
Furthermore, some say:
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) can produce non-manifest action (*avijñapti*);
therefore, there is necessarily no non-manifest action that follows the mind (*cittānuparivartin*).
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), manifest action does not produce non-manifest action.
Therefore, there exists an unmanifest [action] that follows the mind.
Furthermore, some say that because the innate mind capable of initiating karma in the desire realm is both earnest and intense, it can produce such an unmanifest action.
The manifest action that can produce non-manifest action [exists] because the innate mind that produces karma in the Form Realm is neither earnest nor intense; therefore,
the manifest action cannot produce non-manifest action.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
because one born in the desire realm lacks a concentrated mind,
and because an unconcentrated mind is superior [in that context].
The manifest action that can produce non-manifest action exists in those born in the Form Realm because they possess a concentrated mind,
whereas their unconcentrated mind is inferior.
Because the manifest [action] cannot produce the unmanifest,
and for such reasons as these, there is necessarily no reliance on manifest or unmanifest action in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
In the realm of desire, there is no non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) that follows the mind.
Question: Is the sound of vocal resonance a verbal action (*vāk-karman*)?
Answer: It is not a verbal action; it is merely called "vocal sound" because it arises from speech.
Question: Are the sounds of the *xiao* flute, the *di* pipe, and so forth, vocal actions (*vāg-karman*)?
Answer: They are not vocal actions; they are merely called "vocal sounds" because they are produced by the movement of wind and breath.
Question: Are the sounds of various birds and beasts vocal karma?
Some maintain this view:
they are not vocal karma, but are merely called "vocal sounds."
Because they hear it but are unable to comprehend its meaning.
Other masters say that this refers to vocal action;
although a person does not understand the meaning of what is spoken, [the action still occurs].
Furthermore, those of the same class understand one another,
just as those who understand the language of birds and beasts know what is being said upon hearing their sounds.
Question: Are the words of emanations considered vocal karma?
Some say that they are indeed vocal karma because they are produced by the mind.
Other masters say that these are not vocal actions (vāg-karman) but are merely vocal sounds (vāk-śabda),
because the manifested bodies lack appropriation (anupātta). If an action is bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), is its fruit also bound to the desire realm?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
It should be understood that the discussion here is based on the four fruits, excluding the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*),
because the sovereign fruit is not determinate and is excessively broad and diffuse.
This means that for each individual realm into which one is born, there are the results of the three realms and the karma of the four realms.
Each of these takes the various phenomena of the four realms as its dominant result (*adhipatiphala*).
If the karma is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), [it likewise produces such results].
Are the fruits of those karmas bound to the desire realm?
Answer: All karmas bound to the desire realm have fruits that are likewise so;
namely, three fruits or two fruits.
There is karma whose fruit is bound to the desire realm, yet that karma itself is not [bound to the desire realm].
That is to say, when one employs the path of the form realm to produce a transformation-body (nirmāṇa) in the desire realm or to issue speech in the desire realm,
this transformation-body and speech are the fruits of the activity of a practitioner belonging to the form realm.
If an action is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), is its fruit also bound to the form realm?
Answer: All actions whose fruits are bound to the form realm are such that their actions are also so;
that is to say, they have three or two fruits. However, there are actions bound to the form realm whose fruits are not.
That is to say, by means of a path belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one produces emanations in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and utters speech in the desire realm;
these emanations and that speech are the fruits of the activity of a practitioner of the form realm.
Furthermore, by means of a path belonging to the form realm, one realizes the abandonment of the various fetters (*saṃyojana*).
That is to say, the mundane paths belonging to the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the various dhyānas constitute this path;
those abandonments are its fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and its fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The analysis according to the stages (bhūmi) should be understood as corresponding to what was stated previously.
If an action is bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
is its fruit also bound to the formless realm?
Answer: There are various karmas whose fruits are bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), and those karmas themselves are likewise so.
That is to say, there are three or two fruits; furthermore, there are karmas bound to the formless realm that do not have those [specific] fruits.
This refers to the realization of the abandonment of all fetters by means of the path of the formless realm;
that is, the various preparatory paths (*sāmantaka*) of the formless realm.
Those abandonments are the fruits of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and the fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of this path.
The distinctions according to the stages (*bhūmi*) should be understood as corresponding to what was previously explained.
If an action is not bound to a stage, is the fruit of that action also not bound?
Answer: All actions that are not bound likewise have fruits that are not bound.
This refers to those fruits—whether three or two—in which there is karmic fruit that is not bound [to the realms], yet is not the karma itself.
This refers to the abandonment of all fetters (saṃyojana) realized through the paths of the form and formless realms;
that is, the abandonment achieved through the mundane paths of the preparatory stages (sāmantaka).
This is the fruit of dissociation and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of this path.
The distinction according to the stages (*bhūmi*) should be understood by analogy with what preceded.
This applies if the karma is not bound to the desire realm.
Is the fruit of that karma not bound to the desire realm?
Answer: Whatever fruits of karma are not bound to the desire realm, that karma is likewise [not bound to the desire realm].
However, there is karma that is not bound to the desire realm, yet its fruit is not [necessarily] so.
