Section Four: The Aggregate of Karma (*Karmaskandha*), Sub-section Four: The Summary of Manifest and Unmanifest Action (*Vijñapti-avijñapti-nikāya*), Part Three. Question: Is there anyone who, by merely taking the three refuges, becomes a lay follower (*upāsaka*)?
Is it possible to become a lay follower (*upāsaka*) with a deficient set of vows?
If you say that it is possible,
would not the specific wording of the Sūtra then be rendered meaningless?
As it is said: "I, [name], take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
May the Venerable One remember me;
I am a lay follower (*upāsaka*). From this day forth until the end of my life..."
Regarding the protection of life and the return to purity,
one should also speak of those who possess deficient vows, such as śrāmaṇeras and bhikṣus; if there were none [who possessed them], [this would not be possible].
If the wording of the aforementioned sūtra is indeed differentiated, how could it be devoid of meaning?
For what reason are lay followers (*upāsaka*) established as being of one part, a small portion, a large portion, or the full portion?
The masters (*ācārya*) of the Gandhāra country say:
One becomes a lay follower (*upāsaka*) even if one receives only the three refuges and the vows are incomplete.
Question: If one becomes a lay follower by receiving only the three refuges, how is it that the wording of the *Sūtra* is not rendered meaningless?
The Sūtra states that when a lay follower (upāsaka) receives the vows of discipline,
he makes this declaration before the preceptor: "I, [name],
take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha."
May the Venerable One remember me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
From this day forth until the end of my life,
during that interval, I shall protect living beings and take refuge in purity.
The answer is: by means of that expression, one merely obtains the three refuges and is designated a lay follower (*upāsaka*), yet has not yet obtained the vows (*saṃvara*).
Only when the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) are subsequently recited does one obtain the vows.
However, those words are not without meaning,
because the subsequent self-vow serves to make the preceding three refuges firm;
for if one does not protect living beings, the refuge is not pure.
Question: If one who has deficient vows could still become a lay follower (*upāsaka*), it would accord well with statements such as "one part" and so forth. Why is that?
If one accepts one name, it is called "one part";
if one accepts two names, it is called "a small portion";
if one accepts three or four names, it is called "a large portion."
Because they have fully received all five names.
Why, then, would there not be śrāmaṇeras, bhikṣus, and so forth who possess deficient vows?
The answer is: the Buddha observed that the capacities and dispositions of those to be converted were diverse.
The bestowal of the vows is likewise not of a single kind; for instance,
in order to attract those lay followers (*upāsaka*) who do not wish to renounce the household life,
the Buddha allowed them to receive as many or as few of the five precepts as they desired according to their own inclinations.
Therefore, that restraint may be received with deficiencies;
however, for the sake of establishing the bhikṣu and śrāmaṇera who have the intention to renounce the household life, the complete restraint was prescribed.
Because it is obtained only through complete reception, that restraint is received without deficiency;
for this reason, he is an intimate retainer of the Blessed One.
Thus say the masters of the treatises in Kaśmīra.
There is no one who merely receives the three refuges and possesses deficient discipline who can be called an upāsaka.
Question: If this is so, how is it that the sūtra is not rendered meaningless when it says, "I, [name], take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha"?
...and so on, as explained at length.
The answer is: because he has obtained the three refuges through this very expression, he also obtains the restraint (*saṃvara*), and thus becomes a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
Question: This [vow] is merely a personal pledge to abstain from taking life.
How, then, does one fully acquire all five [precepts] by means of this?
Answer: By relying upon this personal pledge to abstain from killing as the basis.
The five types of restraint are also acquired simultaneously;
for among the five precepts, that [restraint] is preeminent,
since the one who receives the vows does so for the purpose of not harming living beings.
Among those things that cause harm to living beings, killing is the foremost;
therefore, abstaining from killing is established as the basis for the five precepts.
Furthermore, the expression "protecting life" does not refer solely to abstaining from killing.
This means not harming or afflicting any sentient being.
One makes a personal vow: "From this day forth until the end of my life, I shall not take the lives of any sentient beings."
One does not steal their property,
does not violate their wife,
and does not engage in false or deceptive speech.
In order to protect the [first] four precepts,
one also abstains from drinking alcohol;
therefore, the statement regarding the protection of life does not refer solely to the abstention from killing.
However, there is an alternative recitation that says "abandoning living beings" (*jīva*).
The intended meaning of this statement is "abandoning killing and so forth";
it omits "killing" and the like, mentioning only "abandoning living beings."
Furthermore, the term "abandoning birth" indicates the category of sentient beings;
"abandoning harmful acts" refers specifically to the fivefold restraint (*pañca-saṃvara*),
as these are all intended to prevent and guard against acts that harm living beings.
It is by means of this self-vow that one attains restraint;
therefore, that sūtra is not without meaning.
Question: If restraint is attained solely through self-vow, [how is this so?]
Why, then, are five types of training rules (śikṣāpada) further taught?
Answer: Although one has already obtained the restraint (saṃvara) through one's own vow, one has not yet fully understood their specific characteristics.
In order to make this known, the five precepts (śikṣāpada) were taught;
therefore, what he has said is not without purpose.
Question: If that is so, why is it said that there are lay followers (upāsaka) who possess only one part [of the precepts], and so forth?
The answer is: this explains the stage of maintaining [the precepts], not the stage of undertaking them.
That is to say, among the five [precepts], maintaining one while not maintaining four is called "one part";
maintaining two while not maintaining three is called "a small portion."
Holding three [precepts] is called "partial" (*bhūyaḥ*), while holding four is called "mostly partial.
Fully holding five is called "complete" (*paripūrṇa*).
The Venerable Saṃghavasu’s classification is the same as that of the two aforementioned masters.
They assert that there is no such thing as becoming a lay follower (*upāsaka*) by merely taking the three refuges;
rather, one also becomes a lay follower even if the fivefold restraint is incomplete.
This refers to when one is about to receive the lay precepts.
First, one should deliberate thoroughly with the preceptor:
"I am able to undertake such training rules;
I am not able to undertake such training rules."
Once the detailed deliberation is complete and one has returned to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha,
one makes a solemn vow and commitment to attain a certain number of precepts; according to the extent of what was previously deliberated and accepted—
whether few or many— one now attains the corresponding number of vows within the Vinaya discipline.
For this reason, it is said that the lay follower's discipline (upāsaka-saṃvara) is called the "precept of consultation" (sammatīya-śīla);
the precepts of the novices (śrāmaṇera) and others do not receive this name.
Thus it is said.
It is not the case that merely taking the three refuges constitutes becoming a lay follower (upāsaka),
nor is there a deficient lay discipline;
one who becomes a lay follower is as if without deficiency.

the basis, and the preliminary application for this discipline.

Some say it is indeterminate: if one does not know that one must first receive the three refuges before receiving the precepts, yet receives the restraint because of faith in the precept-master, that person obtains the restraint while the precept-master incurs a fault;

The answer is: precisely by means of vocal intimation, one makes a vow to oneself, "I now again become a śrāmaṇera or an upāsaka," and thereby obtains two types of restraint;

According to this explanation, one does not abandon the former precepts when obtaining the latter precepts, because what is subsequently received is not a factor that contradicts what was previously received.

Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing and clarifying the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The Buddha addressed the Māṇava:
"All sentient beings in the world are governed by their own karma."
All are portions of karma;
all arise from karma and take karma as their basis.
Karma is able to differentiate the various classes of sentient beings.
Although the sūtras state that various locations differ in terms of height, depth, excellence, and inferiority,
they do not yet extensively explain the meaning of "one's own karma."
The sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which was not explained therein shall now be explained;
for this reason, this treatise is composed.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"Sentient beings in the world are all governed by their own karma;
that is to say, they themselves perform actions and themselves experience their maturation."
"All are portions of karma" means that one experiences such a maturation (vipāka) exactly as the karma was performed.
"All arise from karma" means...
This means that karma acts as the cause of birth,
taking up the fruit of maturation and being born in various respective places where one is destined to be born;
thus, karma serves as the basis.
This means that karma serves as the basis and cause for experiencing various forms of existence;
it is karma that distinguishes among the classes of sentient beings in their respective locations,
whether they be high or low, superior or inferior.
This refers to what was stated previously:
that in various places of birth, one's status—whether high or low, superior or inferior—is determined by karma.
What, then, is "one's own karma"?
Answer: If karma has already obtained its maturation in the present existence, and if the maturation of that karma has already arisen and is currently being experienced;
if karma has already obtained its maturation in the present existence—then [it is so].
This phrase indicates karma to be experienced in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
as well as the one for whom the maturation of that karma has already arisen and is currently being experienced.
This phrase indicates karma to be experienced in the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
Just as there is karma conducive to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), so too there is karma conducive to the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*);
one should know that there is also karma conducive to the maturation (*vipāka*) of arising.

The fruition to be experienced in the next life (upapadyavedanīya) is the fruit to be experienced upon arising; the fruition to be experienced in the next life is the fruit to be experienced [in that subsequent birth].
The same applies to karma that results in subtle fruits and karma that results in coarse fruits.

Is it called "one's own karma" by virtue of its result?

The latter phrase states that "karma and its maturation have already arisen and are being experienced.

This means that karma has already obtained its maturation (*vipāka*) in the present existence. Some say:
it is called "one's own karma" simply by virtue of being the cause.
Based on the preceding phrase,
some say that one is said to "possess one's own karma" solely by virtue of the result; based on the subsequent phrase...
Regarding this explanation:
it is simply by virtue of the cause that it is called "one's own karma.

Some say that all these phrases reveal the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*),

In some instances, that which is a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda*) is spoken of using the term "maturation" (*vipāka*).

Answer: It is said that this agent performs and this same one experiences because of the presence of specific conditions.
On account of certain conditions, it is said that one creates and another experiences;
on account of certain conditions, it is said that there is no creator and no experiencer;

This means that although the aggregates, bases, and elements are distinct in each successive moment within their continuous succession, they may be spoken of as one.

There is no sentient being,

It is empty and devoid of an internal person;

Within one's own continuum,

Guarding and further guarding;

Therefore, it is called "one's own karma.

Question: While the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome karma can serve as nourishment and so forth for one's own continuum, how can the maturation of unwholesome karma do anything but cause harm to one's own continuum?
Just as in the hells, where thirteen fierce flames envelop and burn one's body,
how could there possibly be anything such as nourishment therein?
Answer: There are two kinds of nurturing and so forth:
first, causing growth;
second, preventing interruption.
The maturation of wholesome karma is said to "nourish" and so forth in one's own continuum due to two factors;
the maturation of unwholesome karma is said to "nourish" and so forth in one's own continuum simply because it prevents [the continuum] from being severed.
There is no fault because it does not cause [the karma] to increase.

This karma should be said to be past.

Answer: Because one does not first experience the fruit and subsequently create the cause.

it is a wholesome volition (cetanā) arising together with the faculty of regret (kaukṛtya) or the faculty of mental grief (daurmanasya), [it is different].
If there are various karmas of the dhyānas and formless attainments, such as those conducive to retrogression,
up to those conducive to penetration, and so forth.
Because that which has already been acquired in the future will certainly not arise, and because it certainly does not arise,
this karma will certainly not undergo maturation (vipāka).
This applies to karma that is neutral (avyākṛta) or untainted (anāsrava), provided it is possessed [by the practitioner].
This refers to neutral (avyākṛta) and untainted (anāsrava) karma;
although it is accomplished, its nature is not solid or stable,
and because it lacks the moisture of craving (tṛṣṇā).
This karma will certainly not undergo maturation;
there is karma that will certainly undergo maturation,
yet this karma is not established.
This refers to past karma—whether unwholesome, wholesome, or tainted—that has not yet ripened;
such karma has already been lost.
It also refers to future karma—whether unwholesome, wholesome, or tainted—that has not yet been acquired but is certain to arise.
In this context, it refers to past unwholesome or wholesome contaminated karma whose maturation has not yet ripened.
Regarding the phrase "this karma has already been lost," it is like the case of the karma of restraint (*saṃvara*).
Having already manifested and having already projected its maturation,
this is of three kinds;
namely, that which is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
Karma to be experienced in the next life, karma to be experienced in subsequent lives—
the fruit of which has not yet manifested— is already lost.
Due to the aforementioned causes for the various faults,
there may be non-restraint (asaṃvara-karma),
or that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint (naivasaṃvara-nāsaṃvara).
Other virtuous and non-virtuous actions of body and speech;
if they are wholesome or unwholesome volitions bound to the desire realm;
or if they are wholesome volitions arising together with remorse and the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasya*).
If there are various karmas of the dhyānas and formless attainments,
ranging from those conducive to retrogression up to those conducive to penetration.
Having already manifested and having already drawn forth its maturation (vipāka),
this is of three kinds;
namely, those to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya) and so forth, as previously explained.
If the fruit has not yet manifested,
this karma is already lost due to the aforementioned causes of loss.
Furthermore, if future karma— whether unwholesome, wholesome, or tainted— is not acquired, it will certainly not arise.
This means that although the various deeds of immediate retribution have not yet been acquired in the future,
they will certainly arise;
and because they will certainly arise, their maturation (vipāka) will certainly be experienced.
Whether it be karma of restraint,
karma of non-restraint,
or karma that is neither restraint nor non-restraint.
Other instances of excellent or unwholesome conduct of body and speech;
wholesome or unwholesome volitions (cetanā) bound to the desire realm;
and wholesome volitions arising together with regret (kaukṛtya) or the faculty of mental grief (daurmanasyendriya).
If there are various karmas of the dhyānas and formless attainments, such as those conducive to decline,
up to those conducive to penetration, and so forth.
That which has not yet been attained in the future will certainly arise;
because it will certainly arise, its maturation (vipāka) will certainly be experienced.
This is of three kinds.
This refers to karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth, as previously described;
there is karma which, once accomplished,
will certainly result in the experience of its maturation.
This refers to past karma—whether unwholesome or wholesome—that is tainted (*sāsrava*) and whose maturation (*vipāka*) has not yet ripened; such karma is not lost.
It also refers to future karma—whether unwholesome or wholesome—that is tainted and which, having already been acquired, is certain to arise.
If an action is currently unwholesome, wholesome, or with outflows;
and if, among these, an action is past—whether unwholesome, wholesome, or with outflows—and its maturation has not yet ripened, such that this action is not lost.
This refers to those actions of immediate retribution that have already manifested and have already drawn forth their maturation,
yet whose fruit has not yet manifested;
as well as those actions of restraint.
Whether it be non-restraint,
that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
or any other wholesome or unwholesome conduct of body and speech.
If it is wholesome or unwholesome volition bound to the desire realm;
if it is wholesome volition arising together with remorse or the faculty of grief;
or if it pertains to the meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
The karma of the formless realm,
from the stage conducive to decline up to the stage conducive to penetration,
having already manifested and already drawn forth its maturation.
This is of three kinds, namely:
those to be experienced in the present life and so forth, as previously explained.
Even when the fruit has not yet manifested, this karma is not lost.
Because the aforementioned conditions for those faults are absent,
if karma— whether unwholesome or wholesome with outflows— is yet to come, has already been acquired, and is certain to arise,
this refers to wholesome and unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*) bound to the desire realm.
That which has already been acquired in the future will also certainly arise;
because it will certainly arise, it will certainly undergo its maturation (vipāka).
This is of three kinds.
That is to say, as previously explained, [it refers to] karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth;
furthermore, it includes wholesome volition arising together with regret and the faculty of mental grief,
as well as the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
Karma belonging to the formless realm— ranging from the stage conducive to decline up to the stage conducive to penetration—
that has already been acquired in the future will certainly arise;
because it will certainly arise, its maturation will certainly be experienced.
This is of three kinds, namely:
those to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya) and so forth, as previously explained.
If karma is currently unwholesome or wholesome with outflows (sāsrava), [it is as follows].
That is to say, when various actions of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma) are present before one,
whether they be actions of restraint (saṃvara-karma) or actions of non-restraint (asaṃvara-karma).
That which is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
namely all other wholesome and unwholesome conduct of body and speech.
If it is wholesome or unwholesome volition bound to the desire realm;
or wholesome volition arising together with remorse and the faculty of mental grief;
or the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
The karma of the formless realm,
from the stage conducive to decline up to the stage conducive to penetration,
is now manifest before one.
This is of three kinds, namely:
karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth, as previously described.
There is also karma that is not accomplished, such that its maturation will certainly not be experienced.
This refers to karma that is past—whether unwholesome, wholesome, or contaminated—and whose maturation has already ripened such that this karma has already been lost;
or karma that is future—whether unwholesome, wholesome, or contaminated—which has not yet been acquired and is certain never to arise.
If an action is neutral (*avyākṛta*) or untainted (*anāsrava*), it is not accomplished.
In this context, it refers to past unwholesome or wholesome tainted actions whose maturation has already ripened and which have already been lost.
This refers to those who, within other homogeneous classes of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*), have already digested and experienced the various deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*);
the detailed explanation is as previously stated.
Whether it be karma of restraint,
karma of non-restraint,
or karma that is neither restraint nor non-restraint.
Other virtuous and non-virtuous actions of body and speech;
or wholesome and unwholesome volitions (cetanā) bound to the desire realm;
or wholesome volitions arising together with remorse (kaukṛtya) and the faculty of mental distress (daurmanasyendriya).
If there are various karmas of the dhyānas and formless attainments, such as those conducive to retrogression,
up to those conducive to penetration, and so forth.
It has already been exhausted and experienced in the past,
as explained in detail above;
this karma has already perished.
Because of the aforementioned conditions for those faults,
if karma that is future— whether unwholesome or wholesome with outflows— is not acquired, it will certainly not arise;
this refers to the fact that various immediate karmas (*ānantarya-karma*), being future and unacquired, will certainly not arise.
Because it will certainly not arise, it will certainly not undergo maturation.
This applies to the karma of restraint,
and so on, as explained at length, up to...
If there are various karmas of the dhyānas and formless attainments, such as those conducive to decline,
up to those conducive to penetration, and so forth.
That which has not yet been attained in the future will certainly not arise;
because it will certainly not arise, it will certainly not undergo maturation (*vipāka*).
This applies to karma that is neutral (*avyākṛta*) or untainted (*anāsrava*), as well as that which is not currently possessed (*asamanvāgata*).
This means that because it is neither stable nor moistened by affection,
or because it was not previously attained,
or because it was lost after being attained, it is not [a root].
There are also four propositions;
they should be understood as the reverse of these.
That is to say, the former second proposition becomes this first proposition.
The first clause of the preceding [verse] becomes this second clause;
the fourth clause of the preceding becomes this third clause;
and the third clause of the preceding becomes this fourth clause.
The detailed explanation is as before: "If one is a stream-enterer,
there may be unwholesome karma that conduces to painful feeling," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to bring about certainty for those who harbor doubts.
As it is said: "Two causes lead one to fall into the evil realms."
This refers to karma abandoned through seeing and karma abandoned through cultivation.
Although stream-enterers have already permanently abandoned all karma abandoned through seeing, [they still possess that abandoned through cultivation].
Yet, because they have not yet abandoned the karma to be abandoned through cultivation,
some may give rise to doubt,
thinking that those who have attained the stage of stream-entry (srotāpanna) might fall into the evil destinies.
Alternatively, there may arise doubt that he must have already abandoned the karma to be abandoned through cultivation;
it is in order to bring certainty to that doubt [that this is taught].
This demonstrates that although a stream-enterer has not yet permanently severed the karma to be abandoned through cultivation,
they are nonetheless certain not to fall into the miserable realms.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
If a stream-enterer possesses unwholesome karma that conduces to painful feeling, [how can they be said to have abandoned all unwholesome karma?]
If the maturation has not yet ripened and that [karma] is already accomplished, why does one not fall into an evil destiny? For what obstacle regarding which path does one not fall?
Answer: It is because the fetters of the two categories bind sentient beings and cause them to fall into evil destinies.
This refers to the fetters abandoned through seeing and the fetters abandoned through cultivation.
Although stream-enterers have not yet permanently severed the fetters abandoned through cultivation, they have already permanently severed the fetters abandoned through seeing.
If one lacks even a single provision of the accumulations, one will not fall into the evil destinies.
Just as a chariot equipped with two wheels can transport a load,
or a bird with two wings can fly through the sky— it is otherwise if either is missing.
This case is likewise.
Therefore, a stream-enterer does not fall into the miserable realms;
this is the explanation according to the original treatise.
However, some say:
"The foolish fall into the evil destinies, but the wise do not;
for all stream-enterers (srotāpanna) are wise."
Those who fall into the miserable realms are not so for the noble ones (*ārya*), because all stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) are noble ones.
Those with malicious dispositions and harmful intentions fall into the miserable realms;
those with virtuous dispositions and non-harming intentions do not, because all stream-enterers possess virtuous dispositions and non-harming intentions.
Those who violate the precepts fall into the evil destinies;
those who uphold the precepts do not. All stream-enterers are upholders of the precepts, because they have already obtained the firm ship of the precepts beloved by the Noble Ones.
Furthermore, there are those who say that all stream-enterers (srotāpanna) attain the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding the various evil destinies.
As for those dharmas regarding which one attains non-analytical cessation:
Those dharmas never manifest before him;
therefore, a stream-enterer does not fall into the evil destinies.
Other masters say:
If there are those who do not see the faults of unwholesome conduct and the merits of sublime conduct, they fall into the miserable realms;
whereas all stream-enterers know and see reality as it is regarding good and evil, gain and loss.
Because of the loss of mindfulness,
although one may momentarily give rise to unwholesome karma, one does not fall into the evil destinies.
Some have made this statement.
One who has not abandoned and not fully understood the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) may fall into the miserable destinies if they commit evil deeds; however,
all stream-enterers (srotāpanna) have already abandoned and fully understood the view of a personal identity.
Although one may temporarily give rise to unwholesome karma,
one does not fall into the evil destinies,
as the Blessed One has said.
If one has already abandoned and fully understood the view of a self-identity,
they possess five merits.
The first is that it obstructs rebirth in the three evil destinies.
Second, it prevents the five deeds of immediate retribution;
third, it liberates one from various erroneous views and tendencies;
fourth, it establishes a definitive limit for the boundless cycle of birth and death.
Fifth, at the time of death, the mind and spirit are clear and lucid.
Some say this is because the wisdom of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) purifies the interior of the abdomen.
Although they possess evil karma, they do not fall into the evil realms.
It is like two people who eat what should not be eaten:
one has weak internal heat, so the food is not digested and leads to great suffering.
First, when the internal fire is intense, what is consumed is easily digested and does not cause great suffering.

In this way, although both ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) experience objects and perform unwholesome deeds, the "stomach of wisdom" of ordinary worldlings is impure.
Because they lack the fire of the Noble Path, they fall into the evil destinies and undergo various intense sufferings.
Because the "wisdom-belly" of those who have attained the stream-entry (srotāpanna) is pure,
they undergo only slight suffering among humans and devas.
Some say that a stream-enterer is so called because they are born from the noble lineage of immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Although they possess evil karma, they do not fall into the evil realms.
It is like two people who have both violated the king’s law:
one is a commoner and thus receives a severe punishment, while the other does not.
First, the prince merely received a reprimand.

Likewise, although both ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) may commit evil deeds, because ordinary worldlings are not of the noble lineage (*āryagotra*), the evil karma they create brings about the suffering of the miserable realms.
Because all stream-enterers (srotāpanna) belong to the lineage of the noble ones (āryagotra),
evil karma merely invites slight suffering among gods and humans.
Some say:
Because the stream-enterer perceives the faults of sensory objects,
even though they possess evil karma, they do not fall into the evil realms;
it is like two fish that both greedily crave the bait on a hook.
One who lacks skill is swallowed by the hook as food and loses his life;
one who possesses skill strikes the bait with his tail, seizes it, and eats it without losing his life. Such is the case with the ordinary worldling and the stream-enterer respectively.
Although both [the noble ones and ordinary beings] experience objects and perform unwholesome deeds,
because ordinary beings lack noble wisdom, they do not perceive the faults in what they enjoy;
thus, they develop deep attachment and consequently incur heavy suffering.
Because all stream-enterers possess noble wisdom,
they perceive the faults in all that is experienced and enjoyed; thus,
they do not become deeply attached, but undergo only slight suffering.
Some say that because a stream-enterer possesses both serenity (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā), even though they may have evil karma, they do not fall into the miserable destinies.
This is like the story of Gauda and the crow who, together on the water, ate a corpse.
Someone shot him with an arrow;
being without wings, Gūḍa immediately sank into the water,
whereas the crow, having wings, flew away at once.
Thus, although both ordinary worldlings and stream-enterers may equally experience objects and perform unwholesome deeds,
when they are struck by the arrow of impermanence, [the latter are not so afflicted].
Because ordinary beings lack the wings of śamatha and vipaśyanā,
they immediately sink into the waters of the evil destinies;
because stream-enterers possess the wings of śamatha and vipaśyanā, [they do not].
They then ascend to the realm of emptiness of the nirvana of devas and humans.
Some say this applies to those who have attained the stage of stream-entry (srotāpanna) and once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin).
Because the mind is pliant and supple;
because it accords with nirvāṇa;
and because the seeds of faith are firm.
Because the roots of faith are deep,
although one may possess evil karma, one does not fall into the evil realms.
This is like the ocean, which by its nature governs all flowing streams.
"You may now immediately sweep away all the trees and bring them together at my location.
The various currents replied,
"We can sweep away everything else, with the sole exception of the willows."
The sea asked for the reason.
The various streams replied,
"Willow possesses two virtues that prevent it from being carried away."
First, its roots are deep and firm;
second, it is supple and flows with the current,
so that even if waves and billows surge, they cannot uproot or sweep it away.
"In this way, the flood of delusion (moha-ogha) that signifies the miserable destinies may now sweep you away.
Let all those who indulge in sensual desires gather at my abode.
The Flood of Delusion replied:
All others can be swept away,
with the sole exception of two fruits.
When asked the reason for this regarding the evil destinies, [it was said:]...
The Stream-enterer further states:
"One who possesses two qualities cannot be swept away:
first, the roots of faith are deep and firm; second, the mind and conduct are harmonious and supple."
The waves of karmic activity cannot sweep them away; therefore,
a stream-enterer does not fall into the evil destinies,
as the Blessed One has said.
"My noble disciples should personally recognize for themselves:
'I have exhausted the perilous pits of the miserable destinies— the hells, the animal realm, and the hungry ghosts,' and so forth,
as explained at length."
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to bring certainty to those who harbor doubts, as the Blessed One has said:
If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or others who,
through diligent contemplation, perceive within themselves the four forms of verified confidence (avetyaprasāda) manifesting before them.
One should personally and carefully record this:
"I have exhausted the perilous pits of the miserable destinies of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
If a learned noble disciple is able, through successive contemplation,
to see within themselves that the four forms of verified confidence are presently manifest, [he is one who has attained the fruit].
That noble disciple, having personally and thoroughly ascertained that he has exhausted the perilous pits of the miserable destinies of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts,
may still harbor doubts regarding those who are stream-enterers.
Is there a direct perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) capable of correctly knowing one's own past experiences in the hells, the animal realm, the hungry ghost realm, and so forth?
This is for the purpose of making those [who have not yet realized it] know that they are stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*).
Since the matters previously discussed are known through inference (*anumāna*) alone and not through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), this treatise is composed.
Do those who have attained the state of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) possess a direct cognitive capacity by which they can personally and critically know [this] for themselves?
"Have you already exhausted the perilous pits of the miserable destinies— the hells, the animal realm, and the hungry ghosts—
and do you thus declare this of yourself?
He replied, "I cannot."
If that is so, how is it known?
The answer is: because one has faith in the Buddha’s words.
That is to say, the Blessed One said:
If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and so forth—
as previously explained in detail—
the Blessed One further said:
If there is a learned noble disciple—
expanding the description up to—
the point that they have already exhausted the treacherous pits of the miserable destinies of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Question: Since the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts herein already encompass the evil destinies (*durgati*), why is it further stated that there are "precipices and pits of the evil destinies"?
Answer: The former is detailed while the latter is concise.
The former is specific while the latter is general;
the former is analytical while the latter is synthetic;
thus there is no fault of redundant repetition.
Some say that the term "hell" (naraka) indicates the hell beings,
and the term "animal" (tiryagyoni) indicates the animals.
The term "hungry ghosts" (preta) indicates the realm of hungry ghosts.
The phrase "precipitous and evil pit of rebirths" indicates the śaṇḍhas,
paṇḍakas, those lacking sexual organs, and those with dual sexual organs.
Because they are pits of dangerous and evil destinies among human beings;
furthermore, there are those who say that terms such as "hell" (niraya) indicate the hells and so forth.
The phrase "the pit of the perilous miserable destinies" indicates those who have committed the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*),
because they will necessarily fall into hell in their next birth.
Other masters say:
The mention of "hells" and so forth indicates the hells and other such realms;
the mention of "precipices of the perilous miserable destinies" indicates those who have severed their roots of virtue,
because if they do not reconnect them, they will inevitably fall into hell.
Other masters say that the terms "hell" and so forth indicate the hells and so forth,
while the term "precipice of the miserable destinies" indicates those who lack moral discipline (*asaṃvara*).
This is because they are destined to fall into the various evil destinies.
Some teachers say that terms such as "hell" indicate the fruits of the evil destinies.
The phrase "the precipices of the perilous miserable destinies" indicates the causes for going there.

As the Blessed One said: "O bhikṣus, if you see anyone practicing the three evil deeds, you should know that they have already seen the miserable destinies of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts."
Others further state that the mention of "hell" and so forth indicates the three evil destinies,
while the term "precipice" specifically emphasizes hell.
Because there is no ripening of wholesome karma in the hells and they are characterized by instability,
the term "unfortunate destinies" (*durgati*) indicates the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
This is because their resources are perpetually deficient and the places they frequent are entirely wretched.
The term "pit" (khaṭa) indicates the animal realm (tiryag-yoni),
because it is difficult for those born when the kalpa is forming to escape, and for those born when the kalpa is dissolving to perish [and thus leave].
Other masters say:
The term "perilous" generally indicates the three evil destinies,
because the three evil destinies are extremely perilous.
The term "evil destinies" likewise generally indicates the three evil destinies.
Because those realms to which they go are all foul and evil,
the term "pit" also generally indicates the three evil destinies;
for both their bodies and minds therein are extremely inferior.
Because one dwells amidst base and defiled phenomena as if in a pit of excrement.
Question: There are immeasurable varieties of instruments of suffering in places such as the hells;
how do they exist in the present?
It may be said that [the realms of] hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts have been exhausted.

The answer is: because all noble ones (*ārya*) are not reborn there, and because they will no longer undergo those aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), it is said that they have been "exhausted."
It is not that their instruments of suffering have entirely ceased before they can be said to have "exhausted" [the defilements].
Question: Are there not also ordinary beings who do not fall into the evil destinies?
Why is it said that only the noble ones have exhausted [the defilements]?
Answer: Because for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is not certain;
some do not fall [into the lower realms].
There are also those who fall;
because they are not fixed, it is not said that they have already exhausted [the possibility].
Since all noble ones (ārya) are certain not to fall, it is specifically stated [in their case].
Question: Since stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) also partially exhaust [the karma] of the human and celestial realms, why is it said that they only exhaust the hells and so forth?
Answer: For stream-enterers, there are cases where birth in the human and celestial realms occurs and cases where it does not.
Because it is certain that they will never again be born in the hells and other such realms, this is stated specifically.
Furthermore, a stream-enterer has already attained the four knowledges, namely:
the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.
Because they have not yet attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Question: For what reason is this treatise further composed?
Answer: It is intended so that those who harbor doubts may attain certainty.
It refers to the arising of doubt:
that since stream-enterers only infer what has already been exhausted,
they should likewise infer the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, there may arise doubt:
since those who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) have already abandoned the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) along with their fruits,
they should also have already attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
To eliminate that doubt, it is shown that the stream-enterer has already attained the four knowledges,
though he has not yet attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Because he has attained these four knowledges, he realizes and understands the Four Noble Truths through direct knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*).

Because they have not yet attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), they infer that [defilements] are already exhausted and thus compose this treatise.
Question: For what reason does a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) not yet possess the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising?
Answer: It exhausts all births,
cuts off all delusions,
and accomplishes all tasks.
Only then does one give rise to the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising;
it is not the case that a stream-enterer has exhausted all births or severed all afflictions.
One accomplishes all tasks;
therefore, one has not yet attained the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*).
Other masters say:
Only when one has eternally exhausted all realms of existence, destinies, places of birth, and the cycle of birth, aging, sickness,
and death can one realize the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*).
A stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) has not yet eternally exhausted all realms of existence, destinies, places of birth, and the cycle of birth, aging, sickness, and death.
Therefore, as long as one has not yet attained the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*),
it is as the World-Honored One said:
"By observing through the wisdom of a Nāga that [the king] intends to plot his destruction, [it was foretold] that after seven days the house of Kośala would surely perish."
"What is the training in plotting harm?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know."
By harming the vessel of moisture, he destroys the power of his ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because of his plot to cause harm, Nāgadatta observed through meditative insight that seven days hence the house of the Kośala king would surely be utterly destroyed.
What is meant by "one who harms wet vessels"?
It refers to Virūḍhaka, the lord of Kośala.
"Reckless and deranged, he has harmed the Śākyas;
these Śākyas are his own mother's kin,
with whom he has shared meals from the same vessel since childhood."
The world calls this a "moist vessel.
Because one kills by favoring that [other] and turning one's back on this [vessel], and because one harms the one who is the relative of the moist vessel,
it is said that "the moist vessel is harmed."
Some say: it should be stated that he did not kill out of contempt for those whose faces were wet with tears— that is, the Śākyas who wept and sought his mercy—
but rather because their faces were wet [with blood].
Some say it should be stated that he harmed his eyes by making them moist; that is to say,
the Śākyas, with tears filling their eyes out of grief, failed to give rise to compassion and instead took his life.
Due to this karma, one will certainly be utterly destroyed.
Why is it called "the destruction of the majesty of śīla"?
It is because it destroys both mundane and untainted (anāsrava) precepts.
Regarding those who train in malice:
"those who train" refers to stream-enterers and once-returners.
They practice malice because, through that malice, they cause that royal lineage to perish before long.
What is meant by "the nāga’s contemplation"?
Here, the term "nāga" refers to an arhat;
it is the arhats who contemplate that [object] with thorough discernment.
Alternatively, the Bhagavān is named Mahānāga.
This means that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, should observe with careful scrutiny:
"Seven days from now, the house of Kośala will surely perish."
Because he plotted his own destruction,
the entire clan of Vīrūḍhaka was exterminated seven days later;
thus say the masters of the West.
On the seventh day from now, the house of the Kosalas will surely be destroyed by those who plot its ruin.
Desiring now to analyze the meaning taught in that sutra, I have composed this treatise.
What is the training in malice?
Answer: It is as when a trainee has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire.
When he was being harmed, he thought to himself:
"May he be ruined and may his mother lose her beloved son.
[The Buddha] asked: "For what reason was the learner (śaikṣa) harmed by another?"
Answer: It is due to three conditions, namely:
walking at an improper time, at an improper place, and by an improper path.
Regarding walking at an improper time:
That is to say, while wandering through villages, hamlets,
and waystations during the night, one is seized, bound, and interrogated by those on patrol at the checkpoints, and subjected to various forms of harm.
One who engages in improper conduct refers to one who enters taverns, brothels, royal palaces, gambling dens,
and the like, and is subsequently apprehended by the authorities.
They were subjected to various forms of harsh and agonizing punishment, such as flogging and interrogation.
Regarding those who acted contrary to the Way:
this refers to those who, during the months for farming, would enter orchards and fields to trample upon the crops of others.
Having been seized by the guardians,
and being tormented by the infliction of various sufferings,
he then thinks to himself:
It shall cause the mother to suffer ruin and lose her beloved son.
"Ruin" refers to death and extinction;
because the mother and son are separated, it is called "the mother losing her beloved son."
Question: Since those who have studied have already attained the restraint of non-action (*akaraṇa-saṃvara*), for what reason do they nevertheless engage in such plots of harm?
Answer: Because they are oppressed by suffering, they give rise to such thoughts regarding their own bodies.
"It would be better for me to suffer decay and lose what I love than to be oppressed by such suffering; therefore,
there is no fault in this regarding the bodies of others."
Some say that one may also give rise to this thought toward others; however,
it is merely intended as a reprimand and not as a desire to inflict harm.
Why is this? Because if one understands that through such malice one could even kill a single ant egg, [one would refrain].
Even if it meant saving one's own life, one would not give rise to such a thought;
therefore, this reflection is intended solely for the purpose of self-reproach.
Question: Is this training in plotting harm performed merely through mental reflection?
Some also speak words;
others say that one merely recollects them without speaking.
Some say that even speaking such words is without fault,
as it is for the purpose of rebuking and not for the purpose of inflicting harm.
Why is this? Because if one understands that by such verbal action—
even down to the point of being able to harm a single ant’s egg— [it constitutes a transgression].
If one would not even give rise to the thought of saving one’s own life, how much less would one give rise to verbal karma?
Question: If a city or town is the residence of one’s parents, would a practitioner conceive of plotting harm against those within it?
Some say it does not arise;
others say it does.
It also arises; however,
it is for the purpose of censure,
as explained in detail previously.
Furthermore, it is like a trainee who has already abandoned the defilement of sensual desire;
when others inflict harm upon him, he regresses from that state of abandonment and thinks:
"I shall cause her ruin and destruction, and deprive her of her beloved son."
Question: Did he utter these words after having already regressed, or did he conceive this malicious intent before regressing?
If he uttered these words after having already regressed:
Then, how could the harmful schemes they devise ever succeed quickly?
If they were to initiate such harmful schemes before their faculties have declined,
they would lack both desire and malice.
How should one speak when giving rise to such thoughts of malice?
One should respond by saying:
"He will certainly retreat."
Question: Since there is no power [in such a person], how can they achieve success quickly?
Answer: When one has not yet abandoned desire, one's power is weak and inferior;
it is only through generating many mental states and devising schemes of harm that success is achieved.
At the time of falling away from the state of freedom from desire,
the residual force of the superior path provides support for that mental aspiration, causing the plot to harm [the preceptor] to be swiftly accomplished. Some say this.
While he has not yet fallen from his station, gods, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts revere his virtue and submit with sincerity;
yet when he encounters adverse conditions and regresses to plot harm,
these celestial beings provide assistance so that his undertaking is swiftly accomplished.
Question: Since one who has regressed from the state of a non-returner (anāgāmin) acts with intent to harm, does one who has regressed from the state of an arhat also act with intent to harm?
Answer: One who has regressed from the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) does not act with intent to harm.

Because of the excellence of the fruit, even when there is a temporary regression, the mode of activity and the performance of functions differ from those of one who has regressed from the state of training (*śaikṣa*).
Question: Since even after having regressed from the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) there is still no intent to harm, how much less could such intent exist before one has regressed?
If that is so, how are the sūtras to be reconciled? For example, it is said that when Krakucchanda Buddha uttered the command "Hoṭi!
Tāraya! to Māra, that Māra immediately fell into hell.
Answer: He did so only to rebuke him and had no desire to inflict harm.
However, when that person's karma was exhausted, he naturally fell into hell. It has been heard that this Buddha once took a single attendant named Zhiyuan (Extremely Far).
He entered the village of Śālā to beg for alms in sequence.
At that time, a messenger of Māra transformed himself into a youth and hurled a stone from afar to strike his attendant.
With his head split open and blood streaming down his face,
he followed behind the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha turned to the right like an elephant king.
Beholding these events,
he rebuked Māra, saying:
"Why do you, out of place, commit such evil deeds?"
When Māra’s karma is exhausted, he immediately falls into hell;
therefore, [the Buddha] merely rebukes him and does not intend to inflict harm.
Question: When those in training plot to cause harm, is it only for their own sake, or also for the sake of others?
Answer: There is also that which is for others.
For example, in the past, in this land of Kaśmīra, there was a royal capital named Śrāvastī.
Not far from the city was a saṃghārāma.
It is named Stone Cliff.
Within it dwells a bhikṣu who is an arhat;
by the side of the saṃghārāma, he personally dyes his own kashaya robes.
A man from the city had lost a calf and,
having searched for it until he arrived here,
asked the bhikṣu from afar, "Have you seen the calf?"
He replied, "I did not see him.
As he proceeded further along,
the power of the bhikṣu’s karma caused that person to appear before him.
The robes resembled cowhide and the dye was like blood;
the boiled wood-shavings looked like flesh and the vessels were like ox-heads.
Having seen this, they were struck with alarm and anger, and shouted, "Great thief!"
"How is it that this bhikṣu stole my calf and furthermore slaughtered it?
He has been subjected to flogging and bound, then sent to the King's presence.
The King handed him over to the legal authorities, who cast him into prison.
By the power of that karma,
his disciples did not remember [the events] for a long time;
once their evil karma was exhausted, those disciples all regained their recollection.
"Where is our teacher? they asked, and upon searching, they learned he was imprisoned in a jail.
They then went together to inform the king, "Our teacher is innocent, yet he has been unjustly confined for many years.
We pray that Your Majesty will investigate and grant our teacher his release."
The King issued an edict to the legal authorities, saying: "Release him immediately.
That Arhat has been imprisoned for a long time;
his robes are tattered and his hair is grown long, so he no longer bears the appearance of a śramaṇa."
The judicial officers went on patrol but did not see any bhikṣus;
they returned and informed the king that no such prisoners were present.
The disciples reported again, saying, "The Master is certainly among them."
Having been imprisoned for many years, I have lost the appearance of a śramaṇa.
I pray that you will proclaim within the prison:
"Whoever is a śramaṇa, let them be released by the King's grace."
The king, following those words, immediately ordered a proclamation to be made.
As soon as the Arhat heard the call, his evil karma having been exhausted,
he was awakened from it like one waking from a dream.
By means of his supernormal powers, he ascended into the void and remained suspended there,
like a king of geese soaring through the sky.
When the king saw this, he threw himself down in a swoon of despair.
Cold water was sprinkled on his face, and after a long while he revived.
He lamented his own ignorance for having unjustly detained a holy being,
and realized that he would surely fall into the evil realms with no hope of escape.
Thereupon, together with his ministers, he gazed into the sky and prostrated in gratitude,
praying only that the Holy One would compassionately forgive his transgression.
At that time, the Arhat looked down and said:
"I have never once given rise to anger toward you.
The king said, "If this is so,
I pray that you will accept me as your disciple."
The Venerable One, out of compassion, descended into the royal palace.
The king and his ministers rejoiced, praising and prostrating before him;
they shaved his hair and beard and offered him new robes.
Together with his disciples, they extensively prepared offerings;
escorted by incense and flowers, he was sent to the monastery.
Among those disciples were many noble beings.
Then the Arhat exhorted the assembly, saying,
"I have encountered this unjust confinement due to my own past misdeeds;
do not harbor ill will."
While he was observing that royal capital,
there was a śrāmaṇera who had attained the fruit of srotāpanna;
being far away, his body did not hear these words.
Later, while following the bhikṣu into the royal capital,
he saw his teacher imprisoned and secretly conceived a harmful intent, thinking:
"This city of lawlessness has unjustly incarcerated my preceptor."
Having endured the passage of many years and undergone manifold hardships,
alas, this bitter suffering is truly difficult to bear.
At that time, there was a non-human being who revered and placed faith in the Triple Gem.
Knowing that he was diligently applying mindfulness,
during this very night rain fell and filled the city until everything was completely buried.
Furthermore, in this same country there was once a royal capital.
Not far from the city named Sujanaka,
there was a monastery called Yajñavāha,
where there resided a bhikṣu who was an arhat.
He entered deep meditative concentration without closing the door or panels.
A man in the city whose wife had run away took refuge in the monastery;
seeing the monk absorbed in dhyāna, he hid beneath the bed.
Her husband subsequently entered the monastery and questioned the monks;
the monks did not investigate thoroughly and replied that they had not seen her.
The husband then searched everywhere under the bed and caught her; he then scolded and reviled him, saying, "Thief of a bhikṣu!
How can you, a śramaṇa, hide my wife and indulge your lusts?"
The Chu state bound him with thongs and sent him to the King’s location.
The King handed him over to the judicial authorities, as described in detail previously.
The point that differs from what was stated before is as follows:
There were those who, having entered the monastic order late in life and realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*),
nevertheless plotted harm against non-humans and set fire to the royal capital,
thereby destroying it; thus, one should know that there are also those who plot harm for the sake of others.
Question: What is the essential nature of malice (*vyāpāda*)?
Answer: Volition (*cetanā*) associated with hatred (*dveṣa*) is the essential nature of malice;
it is an internal dharma termed "malice."
External dharmas are called mental indignation.
When external sages experience mental indignation, they cause villages to become non-villages and cities to become non-cities.
It causes the country to become no country.
Because of this, one incurs the offense of harming living beings through physical contact.
Question: Why does it cause both villages and so forth to be utterly destroyed?
Question: External sages incur faults, whereas those within [the Buddhist path] do not. Answer: Without, there is no Noble Path;
within, there is the Noble Path. Without, samatha and vipaśyanā are lacking;
within, samatha and vipaśyanā are fully possessed.
Externally, there is physical harm; internally, there is verbal reproach.
In the former case, one also engages in actual action;
in the latter, one merely gives rise to the intention and speaks the words.
Therefore, external practitioners incur transgressions, not those within [the Buddhist fold].
Question: Do the schemes devised by those who train in malice necessarily succeed?
Answer: This is not certain.
If sentient beings have performed and accumulated karma of great power,
its maturation will manifest and prevent their [other] results from being realized.
For example, in the past there was a Brahmin king named Puṣyamitra who harbored hatred and jealousy toward the Buddha-dharma.
He burned the scriptures,
destroyed stūpas, demolished monasteries, and harmed the community of bhikṣus.
In a certain border region of the kingdom of Kaśmīra, he committed these acts.
He destroyed five hundred monasteries, let alone other places;
the evil Māra employed skillful means to cause the yakṣa and ghost Kūpaṇḍa to secretly provide assistance and power,
so that wherever he went, no one was able to resist him.
As the Buddha-dharma gradually declined until it reached the Bodhi tree,
the deity of the Bodhi tree, named Satyavādin (Truth-speaker), had this thought:
This wicked king is now exceedingly foolish and tyrannical;
he intends to destroy as many Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
and to shatter the state of wondrous enlightenment attained by vanquishing the armies of Māra.
She immediately manifested herself in the form of an exceptionally beautiful woman and stood before him;
upon seeing her, the king was instantly overcome with lustful desire.
The protective deities who guard the Dharma then took advantage of this opportunity;
they killed the king, his army, and the host of evil spirits, leaving none to escape.
At that time, there were many scholars within the Buddha-dharma.
Although they plotted to cause harm, not a single one succeeded,
because the power of that king’s merit was so great.
It was just as in the past with King Dṛḍhārtha.
He entered the kingdom of Kaśmīra,
where he destroyed the Buddha-dharma,
killed the assembly of bhikṣus, and demolished stūpas.
They destroyed monasteries and burned the scriptures.
At that time, there were many worthy sages in that country;
although they attempted to plot their harm, none succeeded.
Because that evil king possessed such great power of merit,
it is for this reason it is said:
"If sentient beings perform and cultivate actions of great majestic power..."
When the maturation (vipāka) manifests, it does not then bring about its fruition. *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 125.
