Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As stated in the Sūtra:
At that time, the Bhagavat retained his life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) and relinquished his longevity-force (*jīvita-saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, in order to analyze the meaning of the Vinaya,
it is as stated in the Vinaya:
"With Mahāprajāpatī at their head..."
Although there is this statement in the Vinaya regarding five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who retained some of their life-force while relinquishing much of their lifespan,
the specific causes and conditions for such retention and relinquishment have not yet been analyzed.
Those sūtras and the Vinaya constitute the foundation of this treatise.
Since they have not yet been explained therein, they shall now be explained;
for this reason, this treatise is composed.
Furthermore, all treatises are composed for the purpose of analyzing the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena;
this present work is no exception.
Therefore, one should not pose such a question.
How does a bhikṣu retain his life-force?
Answer: It refers to an arhat who has attained supernormal powers and mastery over the mind, whether in the midst of the Saṃgha or before an individual.
Having given robes and alms bowls,
or having given any one of the requisites for a śramaṇa’s livelihood, he makes a vow and immediately enters the fourth dhyāna at its ultimate limit.
Having arisen from meditative absorption, he thinks and speaks:
"May all those karmas of mine that are capable of producing the maturation of wealth instead produce the maturation of longevity."
At that time, those karmas capable of summoning the maturation of wealth are instead transformed to summon the maturation of the fruit of longevity.
Question: For what reason does he retain his many formations of longevity?
Answer: Briefly stated, there are two conditions for the practice of prolonging life:
namely, to benefit others and to sustain the Buddha-dharma.
"Benefiting others" refers to instructing disciples in the cultivation of various contemplative practices,
such that they examine with precision [the nature of things] and abide for as long as one's own lifespan remains.
"Have these disciples attained the supreme Dharma?

Even if my life were to end, would there still be others capable of skillfully elucidating what is the path and what is not the path? If I see that they are incapable, I shall then sustain the formations of longevity."
To be one who sustains the Buddha-dharma means to undertake tasks such as constructing Buddha images and monastic dwellings;
he carefully observes that these shall endure for the duration of his own life.
"Will this undertaking be successfully accomplished?
Even if my life were to end, would there be any other skillful means by which it could still be accomplished?
If he sees that it cannot be done, he then sustains his life-force (*āyus-saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, he observes that there will be kings, ministers, elders, and others who wish to destroy the Buddha-dharma;
he then carefully examines whether, as long as his life remains, there will be any skillful means by which the dharma may not be destroyed.
"If my life were to end, would there be any other skillful means by which it could be sustained?
If he perceives that there is no such means, he then performs the action of sustaining his lifespan; having performed this action of sustaining his lifespan, he remains.
Regarding the giving of robes, alms bowls, and so forth to the Sangha or to individuals,
it is as stated in the sūtras;
that is to say, the Blessed One said:
If there is a donor who can bestow material things upon others, it is called the "giving of five things.
By means of this, one shall in turn obtain the fruit of five things:
first, longevity; second, beauty; third, strength; fourth, happiness; and fifth, eloquence.
He carefully examines whether giving to the community of monks will yield a great fruit,
or if giving to an individual will do so;
if he sees that giving to the community will yield a great fruit, he then gives it to the community.
If one knows that by giving to a specific individual one will obtain a great fruit, one should give to that individual.
For this reason, one may give robes or alms bowls to the Saṃgha or to an individual,
or give any of the requisites for the livelihood of a śramaṇa as a gift.
Having given the gift, he makes a vow and immediately enters the fourth dhyāna of the limit (*prāntakoṭika*).
Emerging from that concentration, he reflects in his mind and speaks with his voice:
"Whatever karma of mine is capable of producing the maturation of wealth,"
May this [karma] instead produce the ripening fruit of longevity.
At that time, the karma capable of producing the ripening fruit of wealth would instead be transformed to produce the ripening fruit of longevity.
Question: It is logically impossible for the ripening fruit of wealth to become the ripening fruit of longevity.
Why, then, is it said that karma with the maturation of wealth can also transform to bring about the maturation fruit of longevity?
Answer: There is no such thing as a transformed fruit-entity.
There is the power to transform karma;
that is to say, through the power of concentration at the limit of generosity,
one transforms karma that would otherwise result in a wealthy rebirth so that it instead brings about the fruit of a long life.
Although both can be transformed, at this time he disregards the fruit of wealth because he prays for the fruit of longevity;
thus say other masters.
There is karma that first brings about the maturation fruit of longevity;
however, when there are calamities and obstacles, through the power of the limit of present generosity and meditative concentration,
those calamities and obstacles are extinguished, and the maturation fruit of longevity arises.
Although both [types of karma] can be transformed, at this time he disregards the fruit of wealth because he prays for the fruit of longevity.
Some have made this statement:
There is karma that previously brought about the ripening fruit of longevity;
however, it was not certain [to manifest], but by means of the power of the limit of this present generosity and meditative concentration,
it causes the karma for longevity to become certain to yield its fruit.

Furthermore, there are those who maintain that through the power of meditative concentration (samādhi) associated with giving, one draws forth the residual maturation (vipāka) of lifespan from previous lives;
that is to say, an Arhat possesses the residual maturation of lifespan remaining from a subsequent birth.

By means of the power of concentration at the limit of this present generosity, he causes the power of concentration to manifest; through the inconceivable power of concentration, that which has been long severed is made to continue.
Question: By what precisely is the life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) that is retained brought forth?
Is it by the power of generosity or by the power of meditative concentration?
If it were by the power of generosity, one would not enter meditative absorption;
if it were by the power of meditative concentration, one would not practice generosity.
Some say it is by means of giving;
others say it is by means of meditative concentration. This is what is said.
Both depend on two factors:
although one may practice extensive giving, if one does not enter meditative absorption, it can ultimately not induce the fruit of longevity;
and although one may frequently enter meditative absorption, if one does not practice giving, it can ultimately not induce the fruit of longevity.
However, the power of generosity can induce the power of meditative concentration to become decisive.
For this reason, it is said that both are required.
How does a bhikṣu relinquish his long life-span?
The answer is: It refers to an Arhat who has accomplished the supernormal powers and attained mastery over the mind.
Having performed a gift as previously described, he makes a vow and immediately enters the fourth dhyāna of the limit (*prāntakoṭika*).
Having arisen from meditative absorption, one thinks and speaks:
"May all those karmas of mine that are capable of producing the maturation of longevity now instead produce the maturation of wealth."
At that time, the karma that was capable of summoning the maturation of a long life is then transformed so as to summon the maturation of wealth.
Question: For what reason does he relinquish the extensive formations of longevity?
Answer: Because both self-benefit and benefit for others have been brought to ultimate completion.
One has attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and thus self-benefit is complete;
as for the matter of benefiting others—
If there is one capable of accomplishing this task, they shall enter parinirvāṇa immediately upon its completion;
if there is no such capability, it is nonetheless called "ultimate.
Some have said this.
He loathes his own body as if it were a vessel of poison;
therefore, he wishes to renounce it.
As a verse says:
Having perfectly established the holy life and well cultivated the noble path,
one rejoices at the time when life comes to an end, just as one would rejoice at discarding a vessel of poison.
Having relinquished the activities of life, one gives robes, alms bowls, and other requisites to the Sangha and to individuals.
According to the sūtras,
the Blessed One stated that there are, in brief, three kinds of meritorious actions:
first, meritorious actions consisting of giving (*dāna-maya-puṇyakriyāvastu*).
Second, the meritorious action consisting of the nature of morality;
third, the meritorious action consisting of the nature of cultivation.
Regarding the meritorious action consisting of giving:
If one practices, cultivates,
or frequently performs [this],
it brings about the fruit of great wealth.
...and so on, as explained at length.
He carefully examines whether giving to the Saṃgha will yield a great fruit or giving to an individual will.
If he sees that giving to the Saṃgha will yield a great fruit, he then gives it to the Saṃgha.
If one knows that by giving to a specific individual one will obtain a great fruit, then one gives to that individual.
Therefore, whether toward the Saṃgha or a specific individual,
one gives with robes or alms bowls.
Alternatively, one may give any requisite for the sustenance of a śramaṇa’s life;
having given it, one makes an aspiration and immediately enters the fourth dhyāna of the limit (prāntakoṭika).
Upon arising from that meditative absorption, one reflects in the mind and speaks with the voice:
"May all my karma capable of producing the maturation of longevity now instead produce the maturation of wealth.
At that time, that karma capable of producing the maturation of longevity—
It can then be transformed so as to attract the ripening fruit of wealth.
Question: Logically, it is impossible for the ripening fruit of longevity to become the ripening fruit of wealth.
For what reason, then, is it said that [such karma] is the ripening karma of longevity?
Thus, it can further bring about the ripening fruit of wealth.
Answer: There is no transformation of the substance of the fruit;
there is only the transformation of the power of karma.
This means that by the power of the limit of giving (*dānaparyanta*),
one transforms karma that would otherwise result in longevity (*āyur-vipāka*) so as to bring about the fruit of wealth (*bhoga-vipāka*).
Although both [types of karma] can be transformed, at this time [the practitioner] disregards the fruit of longevity.
For the sake of praying for the fruit of wealth,
other masters say that there is karma which first brings about the ripening fruit of wealth.
However, there are obstacles and hindrances.
Through the power of the meditative concentration at the limit of this current giving, those obstacles and hindrances are extinguished and the karmic maturation of wealth arises.
Although both [the life-span and wealth] can be transformed, at this present time he disregards the fruit of longevity.
For the sake of praying for the fruit of wealth, some say:
there is karma that first brings about the ripening fruit of wealth.
However, it is not certain;
by the power of the present limit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) regarding giving,
the karma for wealth is made to definitely yield its fruit.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
there is karma that previously brought about a ripening fruit of wealth that was coarse rather than sublime;
now, by the power of the limit of this present generosity, [it becomes sublime].
It causes coarse karma to instead produce an excellent result;
that is to say, whereas that [karma] previously projected a long-lasting coarse fruit,
it now— by the power of the aspiration made through giving and meditative concentration— [produces a superior one].
This causes them to subsequently attract a sublime fruit in the present life.
Furthermore, there are those who maintain that through the power of giving and meditative concentration, one draws forth the remaining maturation of wealth from past lives—
namely, the maturation of residual wealth remaining from other births belonging to an Arhat.
This is brought forth into manifestation by the power of concentration at the limit of present generosity;
through the inconceivable power of concentration, that which has been severed for a long time is made to continue again.
Question: By what is this maturation of wealth specifically induced?
Is it by the power of generosity or by the power of meditative concentration?
If it were by the power of generosity, one would not enter meditative absorption;
if it were by the power of meditative concentration, one would not practice generosity.
Some say it is by means of giving;
some say it is by means of meditative concentration.
Those who speak thus maintain that it is by means of both.
Although one may practice much giving, if one does not enter meditative absorption, it will ultimately fail to bring about the fruit of wealth.
Although one may frequently enter meditative absorption, if one does not practice giving,
it will ultimately fail to bring about the fruit of wealth.
However, the power of generosity can induce the power of meditative concentration to become decisive.
For this reason, it is said that both are required.
Question: If the fruits of longevity and wealth for sentient beings were not fixed, it would be possible to retain or relinquish them.
If both are determined, how can there be retention or relinquishment?
The answer is: it is merely a matter of establishing a limit; there is no actual act of retaining or relinquishing.
It is, for example, like a limit prescribed by a skilled physician, which cannot be exceeded.
This should also be understood in the same way.
The Venerable Ghosaka has stated that those Arhats do so by means of generating a limit.
The fourth concentration draws forth the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) so that they manifest within the body;
yet those primary elements may be either conducive to the life-process (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) or contrary to the life-process.
Due to these causes and conditions, one may either retain or relinquish [the life-force].
Some say that those Arhats,
by means of this power of mastery over samādhi, [retain their life-force].
It transforms away the momentum for the duration of the sense faculties and primary elements produced by past karma,
and draws forth the momentum for the duration of the sense faculties and primary elements produced by the power of unprecedented meditative concentration.
That assertion is incorrect, because the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) has as its intrinsic nature a distinct great element (mahābhūta) that is not itself a faculty.
As the Sūtra states: "The Blessed One retained his life-force for a long time."
What is the meaning of "renouncing a portion of the life-span"?
Some say that the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, renounce one-third of their lifespan.
Some say that the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, relinquish one-fifth of their lifespan;
others say that the Buddhas relinquish one-third of their lifespan.
They say that the lifespan of the Blessed One Śākyamuni should have remained at one hundred and twenty years, but he relinquished the final forty and accepted only eighty.
Question: At the time when the Buddha appeared in the world, the lifespan of the people of this continent did not exceed one hundred years.
Why is it that the Blessed One Śākyamuni’s lifespan is one hundred and twenty years?
Answer: Because the Buddha’s physical form, strength, lineage, wealth and status, retinue, and wisdom and vision surpass those of other sentient beings.

His lifespan should likewise exceed that of ordinary people; therefore, if it is said that the Buddhas relinquish a fifth portion of their lifespan, it implies that the lifespan experienced by the Blessed One Śākyamuni should have remained at one hundred years.
Having relinquished the latter twenty years, they receive only eighty.

Question: Since the Buddhas possess physical strength, lineage, wealth, retinues, and wisdom that surpass those of other sentient beings, for what reason is their lifespan equal to that of ordinary people?
Answer: Because they are born at such a duration of lifespan.

This is based on the statement in the Sūtra regarding those who relinquish the practice of longevity, meaning they relinquish forty or twenty years of life while retaining the practice of sustaining their life-force.
This refers to his remaining for three months.
Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One remain, relinquishing those life-formations (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) while not increasing or decreasing the life-span formations (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*)?
Answer: Because the Buddha’s activities were perfectly accomplished.
Because the buddha-activities of all Buddhas reach perfect completion within that specific duration of time, they neither increase nor decrease.
Some say: it is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, relinquish or retain only such a lifespan.
Some say: This is intended to show that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not crave their own life-span and are thus able to relinquish it early,
whereas other sentient beings, because they crave their life-span, are unable to relinquish it.
Diligently seek parinirvāṇa without harboring any doubt;
the Buddha is likewise,
and thus he relinquished the life-force.
To manifest his distinction from other sentient beings and because his work of conversion was not yet finished, he remained for another three months.
Some say that he relinquished the life-force (*āyus-saṃskāra*) in order to demonstrate that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, dwell well within the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
This means that just as the Blessed One was deeply content with existence (*bhava*) and the requisites for existence (*bhavopakaraṇa*), he was likewise so regarding his lifespan (*āyus*).
Some say that the Blessed One relinquished the formations of life (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*) in order to avoid the stage of senescence.
Because the work of converting sentient beings was not yet complete, he remained for another three months.
For instance, on one occasion, Udāyin massaged the Buddha’s limbs and observed extraordinary signs.
Then he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
your limbs are now relaxed and your faculties have undergone transformation."
His appearance has changed from its usual state;
if it is already so now while he still holds his position,
how much more so when he passes eighty?
Therefore, they avoid decay and old age and relinquish the life-formations that sustain longevity.
Some say this is because they wish to manifest mastery over meditative concentration.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has relinquished his life-span.
As the World-Honored One has said:
"Because I have well cultivated the four bases of psychic power, I could remain for an eon or even longer than an eon."
They are able to abide at will.
Some say this is to manifest that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are able to subdue all Māras and retain or relinquish their life-span as they please.
This means that at the time of realizing unsurpassed, sublime bodhi, one has already subdued two māras,
namely the celestial māra and the affliction-māra;
now, as one is about to realize entry into the realm of nirvāṇa, one again subdues two māras.
This refers to the aggregates and death.
Because he has subdued the māra of the aggregates, he relinquishes the formations of longevity;
because he has subdued the māra of death, he retains the formations of life.
Question: What is the difference between the life-force (*jīvita*) and the formations of vitality (*āyus-saṃskāra*)?
Some say there is no difference, as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
What is the life-faculty?
It refers to the lifespan of the three realms. Some say: [it is the continuity of the aggregates].
There is also a distinction between these two;
namely, their names themselves constitute the distinction,
for they are called "vital formations" (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) and "life-formations" (*jīvita-saṃskāra*).
Some say: "Because of this, that by which one lives is called the formations of vitality (jīvitasaṃskāra);
because of this, that by which one dies is called the formations of life (āyuḥsaṃskāra). Others say: [the same].
That which is retained is called the formations of vitality (*jīvitasaṃskāra*);
that which is relinquished is called the formations of life-span (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*). Some say:
Dharmas that are subject to arising are called the formations of vitality (*jīvitasaṃskāra*);
dharmas that are not subject to arising are called the formations of life-span (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*). Some say:
Momentary duration is called the life-force (*jīvitasaṃskāra*);
duration for the span of a single lifetime is called the life-span (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*).
Some say that the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) is what is called the life-force.
The term "sabhāgatā" (homogeneity) refers to the formations of vitality (*jīvitasaṃskāra*).
Some say that the fruit of cultivation is called the formations of life (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*).
The fruit of karma is called the formations of life (*āyusaṃskāra*).
Some say that the fruit of untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) is called the formations of vitality (*jīvita-saṃskāra*).
The fruit of tainted karma is called the formations of vitality (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*).
Some say that the fruit of clarity (*vidyā*) is called the formations of life (*jīvita-saṃskāra*).
The fruit of ignorance is called the formations of longevity (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*).
Some say that the fruit of new karma is called the formations of life (*jīvita-saṃskāra*).
Therefore, the fruit of past karma is called the "formations of life" (*āyusaṃskāra*).
Some say that the karma which yields that fruit is called the "formations of vitality" (*jīvitasaṃskāra*).
The karma that does not yet yield its fruit is called the "life-force" (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*);
some say that the karma which is proximate to yielding its fruit is called the "vitality-force" (*jīvita-saṃskāra*).
The fruition of distant karma is called the formations of longevity (*āyus-saṃskāra*);
this is the explanation given by the Venerable Ghoṣaka.
The fruition of karma to be experienced in the present life is called the formations of life (*jīvita-saṃskāra*).
The fruits of karma to be experienced in the next life, in subsequent lives,
or at indefinite times are called the formations of lifespan (*āyus-saṃskāra*).

The formations of life (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) and the formations of vitality (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*): this is what constitutes their distinction. Question: What is the meaning of the term "many" (*bahu*) in the expression "many formations"?
Answer: The word "many" indicates that what is retained or relinquished is not a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
The term "activity" (saṃskāra) indicates that what is retained and what is relinquished are impermanent phenomena.
Question: Where are the activity of life (jīvitasaṃskāra) and the activity of vitality (āyuḥsaṃskāra) retained or relinquished?
Answer: In the desire realm (kāmadhātu), not in other realms.
It occurs among human beings and not in other realms;
it occurs in the three continents and not in the northern continent.
Question: Who is able to suspend the process of dying and prolong the life-force?
Answer: These are noble ones, not ordinary beings;
they are those beyond training, not those still in training;
they are those liberated at any time, not those liberated only at specific times.
"Is he both male and female?
How does his mind become deranged?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the sake of explaining the sūtras and the vinaya.
As it is said in a sūtra:
The Brahmin woman Vāsiṣṭhī, having lost six sons,
became deranged in mind and wandered about naked;
upon seeing the World-Honored One, she regained her original sanity.
The Vinaya states:
Because Śrīvatsa’s mind was deranged,
he engaged in countless kinds of non-śramaṇa practices that were contrary to the Dharma.
In the Vinaya, it is further stated:
"If one is oppressed by painful sensations and the mind becomes deranged,
or if one is at the stage of a beginner, there is no offense."
Although this has been stated in the Sūtras and the Vinaya,
it was not explained in detail;
now, in order to provide a detailed explanation, this treatise is composed.
What is mental derangement?
The answer is: it refers to the state where the mind is driven to derangement by the force of four conditions.
First, by non-humans manifesting hideous forms and appearances.
Upon encountering them, they become terrified, causing their minds to go mad.
That is to say, non-human beings manifest before them in terrifying forms such as elephants, horses, camels, oxen, or sheep;
when these appear, the mind immediately becomes deranged.
Question: Has he not seen elephants, horses, and so forth before?
Why is it that upon seeing them now, he is struck with terror?
Answer: Although he has seen them before, on this occasion he sees them at an improper time, in an improper place, and by an improper path, and thus it is sudden and unexpected.
Regarding the term "inopportune time":
it refers to seeing elephants, horses, and so forth during the night, and then thinking,
"For what reason have elephants, horses, and the like come to my place at this time?"
It is certain that a non-human being has come to oppress and harm him;
due to this terror, his mind becomes deranged.
Regarding the phrase "in an improper place":
That is to say, when seeing elephants, horses, and so forth in places such as halls, pavilions, rooms, or chambers, one thinks:
"For what reason are there elephants, horses, and so forth in this place?
Surely it is a non-human being who has come to harass and harm me."
Due to this terror, the mind becomes deranged.
That which is called "a non-path" refers to a place such as a cemetery that is not a path commonly traveled by elephants, horses, and the like.
Upon seeing elephants, horses, and the like, he immediately thinks:
"For what reason are there elephants, horses, and so forth here?
Surely it is non-human beings who have come to oppress and harm me."
First, due to this terror, the mind becomes deranged.
Second, because non-humans strike their limbs in anger,
they are oppressed by painful sensations that cause the mind to become deranged.
That is to say, in places where a great assembly dwells or frequents,
one discards excrement and urine with a mind of contempt;
or within the monasteries of the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
If one engages in impure conduct, the benevolent deities become enraged and strike the joints of one's limbs.
Since a person possesses joints as numerous as mustard seeds,
when they are struck, the mind immediately becomes deranged.
Third, the mind becomes deranged due to the disharmony of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
That is to say, when one consumes large quantities of walnuts, sesame seeds, *tila* seeds, and so forth,
the primary elements such as heat and wind become disturbed, and the mind consequently falls into derangement.
Fourth, the mind becomes deranged due to the maturation (*vipāka*) of prior karma;
that is to say, having previously experienced joy and exultation,
one subsequently spreads news of terrifying events, causing others to fall into grief and distress.
Some dig pits and traps to cause sentient beings to fall into them;
some release fierce fires to burn mountains and marshes;
or they use force to compel others to drink alcohol.
Or one might explain the sūtras through distorted perceptions;
such karmas cause the mind to become deranged.
However, this derangement is not a result of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
It arises solely from the maturation (*vipāka*) of unwholesome karma;
for unwholesome karma does not induce maturation in the mental level (*manobhūmi*). Some say:
Insanity arises from five conditions.
The first four are as previously stated;
the fifth is grief and anxiety.
That is to say, due to the loss of a beloved child or similar circumstances, the mind becomes entangled in the poison of grief and subsequently gives rise to madness.
Question: In what place does this mental madness occur?
Answer: It exists in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), but not in the form or formless realms (rūpadhātu and ārūpyadhātu).
However, it does not exist in the hells.
Because the mind is constantly disturbed.
Regarding "a mind that is deranged":
this refers to humans, non-humans, ghosts, and animals whose minds are occasionally deranged.
They also exist among humans and devas,
with the exception of those in Uttarakuru;
for there, the predominant fruit of unwholesome karma does not exist.
Question: Regarding this mental derangement, who possesses it and who does not?
Answer: It may occur in both noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Among noble ones, it applies to all except for the Buddhas.
The Buddha has no mental distraction, no impaired vocal sound,
no cessation of the *manas*,
and no gradual relinquishing of life.
The distracted mind of an ordinary person arises due to all five conditions,
whereas for a noble one it arises solely from the disharmony of the primary elements;
the noble one is free from alarm and fear.
Because he has transcended the five fears,
there is no assault by non-human beings and no occurrence of impure matters.
Furthermore, there is no maturation of evil karma from previous lives,
because one who possesses determinate karma must first experience its results before entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*);
this refers to indeterminate karma.
Because it has already been overturned and extinguished by the power of the Noble Path,
there is no sorrow;
for one has realized the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Some say that the mental derangement of noble ones arises from two conditions:
namely, the disharmony of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
And as for being struck by non-human beings:
one asks, "Since the Noble One has already attained the restraint of non-action (*akaraṇa-saṃvara*), there is certainly no impure conduct; why would non-human beings be angry?"
Answer: Those who have faith in the Buddha’s Dharma revere and honor the various sages and never cause them offense or distress.
Those who lack faith harbor hatred and jealousy toward the sages, watching for opportunities to offend or distress them.
Therefore, even the Sage was struck by non-humans.
Question: Abiding in what kind of mind does one experience derangement?
Answer: One abides in that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), not in that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
It abides in the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), not in the five sensory consciousnesses. Question:
If that is so, for what reason does one see two moons and the like?
Answer: All of these are conceptual constructions of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); such confused interpretations do not exist within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*).
Question: Is this confusion said to exist in an unmadened mind, or is it said to exist in a mad mind?
Answer: It is not that one speaks of derangement with a mind that is not yet deranged, nor is it that one speaks of derangement with a mind that is already deranged;
rather, there exists a state of deranged mind.
There is no deranged mind abiding in the future;
if one encounters conditions for derangement, then the absence of a deranged mind ceases.
When a deranged mind arises,
if it encounters conditions that are not deranging,
then the deranged mind ceases.
No deranged mind arises.
Question: If the mind is deranged, is it also distracted?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold permutation (catuṣkoṭi).
There is a state of mind that is deranged but not distracted;
this refers to the case where a person who is insane possesses a mind free from defilement.
There is a state of mind that is distracted but not deranged.
That is to say, one who is not insane possesses a defiled mind;
there is also a mind that is both deranged and distracted—
that is, one who is insane possesses a defiled mind.
There is a state of mind that is neither deranged nor distracted;
namely, when one who is not deranged manifests an undefiled mind.
Which associated factors of the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are exclusively unwholesome?
Answer: It refers to lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).
Question: There are ten kinds of entanglements (*paryavasthāna*);
why are only lack of shame and lack of dread mentioned?
The answer is: because it is the intention of the author of this treatise to be thus, and so forth, as explained at length. Some say:
These two are exclusively unwholesome and are also concomitant with all unwholesome minds.
Although anger (*krodha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*),
avarice (*mātsarya*), and envy (*īrṣyā*) are unwholesome, they are not concomitant with all unwholesome minds.
Although lethargy and restlessness accompany all unwholesome states of mind,
they are not exclusively unwholesome,
because they also pertain to both the unwholesome and the neutral (avyākṛta) natures.
Drowsiness and regret are not exclusively unwholesome;
nor do they accompany every unwholesome state of mind.
Drowsiness permeates all three moral natures.
Because regret (kaukṛtya) pertains to both natures,
and because neither vigilance (apramāda) nor remorse (kaukṛtya) as a defiled state of mind can function therein.
In all unwholesome states of mind, there are always lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).
All instances of lack of shame and lack of dread are concomitant with unwholesome minds and are mutually inseparable;
therefore, they are mentioned specifically.
In this regard, one should also ask: which factors associated with the wholesome are themselves wholesome?
The answer is: shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
This is because shame and dread of blame accompany the wholesome mind, following it and never being separated from it.
As for why these two are not mentioned [separately]:
it is because they are not only subsumed under the nature of the wholesome;
rather, they pervade all wholesome states of mind.
What is Buddhism?
[The text continues] with a detailed exposition. As for the question of why this treatise was composed, the answer is:
to stop the misconception that what is not Buddhism is Buddhism.
Nowadays there are those who say:
"I speak the Buddha's teaching;
I have heard the Buddha's teaching."
They conceive the notion that what is not the Buddha's teaching is the Buddha's teaching.
To prevent such a notion and to demonstrate that what was spoken by the Buddha is the true Buddha's teaching, [this was said].
What has been stated by others is not the true teaching of the Buddha;
therefore, this treatise is composed.
Question: Why, at this time, do some people speak in such a manner?
"I speak of the Buddha's teaching;
I have heard the Buddha's teaching.
His answer was made based on the fundamental [principle].
This refers to the teachings on defilement and purity, bondage and liberation, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, cause and effect, and so forth,
which are all fundamentally the words of the Buddha. Some say:
He speaks based on similarity; that is to say,
because the Buddha previously expounded for others by means of such a sequence of names, phrases, and phonemes,
and now likewise proclaims by means of such a sequence of names, phrases, and phonemes, some say [this].
He speaks in accordance with conformity; that is to say,
the Buddha previously expounded for others based on such a conforming collection of names, phrases, and syllables,
and now he likewise proclaims it based on such a conforming collection of names, phrases, and syllables.
Some say: because they share the same basis for accomplishing the task, such a statement is made;
that is to say, it is as if one had personally heard the essential points of the Dharma from the Buddha himself.
Entering the noble state, attaining the fruits, becoming free from defilement, and exhausting the outflows—
by hearing what has been said now, one may likewise accomplish these matters.
What is the Buddha’s teaching?
Answer: It refers to the Buddha’s speech, utterances, discourses, vocal sounds, vocal paths, vocal karma, and vocal intimation;
this is called the Buddha’s teaching.
Question: For what reason is the Buddha’s teaching exclusively vocal?
Is it that the manifest [action] is not the non-manifest?
Answer: It is called the Buddha’s teaching because it produces correct understanding in others.
Correct understanding arises in others solely through manifest action, and not through non-manifest action.

Some say that because the Buddhist teaching is apprehended by the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), while non-informative action (*avijñapti-karma*) cannot be apprehended by the auditory consciousness,
it is not the Buddhist teaching. Others say:
According to Buddhism, while non-informative karma (*avijñapti-karman*) apprehended by two consciousnesses is apprehended by only one consciousness,
[the opponent's position] is therefore not Buddhist. Some say:
The World-Honored One, through diligent and arduous practice over three incalculable eons, sought the expression of the Buddha’s words;
now they have been fully realized,
for it is not by means of the unmanifest (avijñapti).
This means that in the past, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, diligently practiced asceticism under immeasurable Perfectly Enlightened Ones in order to seek unsurpassed wisdom.
He taught the Dharma for the sake of others,
and based upon the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, he sought out the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Through successive transmission and continuity, they have now attained Buddhahood and expound the essential teachings of the Dharma for all sentient beings,
causing them to abandon birth and death and attain parinirvāṇa.
All these matters arise from the Buddha’s informative action (*vijñapti-karman*).
Therefore, the Buddha’s teaching consists solely of the Buddha’s informative action.
Question: What constitutes the essence (*svabhāva*) of such a Buddha-teaching?
Is this vocal action?
Or is it names and so forth?
If it is vocal action, [then...]
How should one interpret what was stated subsequently?
For example, when it is asked, "What dharma is called 'the Buddha's teaching'?
the answer is: "It refers to the collection of names (nāmakāya), the collection of phrases (padakāya), and the collection of phonemes (vyañjanakāya)."
Arranged in successive order.
Deployed in successive order.
Connected in successive order.
Furthermore, how is the statement in the gāthā to be reconciled?
As it says: "Desire is the cause of verses; the text consists of syllables;
and verses proceed based on names."
The creator serves as the basis.
If this is so, how should one interpret what is stated here regarding names and so forth?
For example, how should one understand the statement concerning the Buddha’s teaching?
It refers to the Buddha’s speech, up to and including vocal intimation;
this is called the Buddha's teaching.
One should answer by saying this.
Its essence is vocal action.
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret what is stated immediately following?
As it is said: "What dharma is called 'Buddha-teaching'?
The answer is: "It refers to the collection of names (nāmakāya), the collection of phrases (padakāya), and so forth," as explained at length.
The subsequent passage serves to clarify the function of the Buddha-teaching.
One does not intend to reveal the intrinsic nature of the Buddha’s teaching;
rather, it is said that its sequential arrangement, deployment, and conjunction— namely,
the bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes— constitute the functional application of the Buddha’s teaching.
Question: How then should one interpret what is stated in the gāthās?
Answer: Some [terms] apply to names, while others apply to meanings.
Regarding this, for the time being, we shall speak of that which functions with respect to names (*nāman*).
Some say that the Buddha’s teaching has names and so forth as its essence.
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret this passage?
For example, it says: "What is the Buddha’s teaching?"
This refers to the Buddha’s words,
and so forth, as explained at length.
The answer is that this statement is made based on successive causes.
Just as descendants are produced through successive generations, so too do phenomena arise in succession:
that is to say, speech gives rise to names,
and names are able to manifest meanings.
According to this explanation, the Buddha’s teaching has vocal action as its essence,
because it is what the Buddha intends to say and what others hear.
Should the Buddha’s teaching be said to be wholesome?
"Is it indeterminate?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is this treatise further composed?
Answer: Although the preceding [section] has revealed the intrinsic nature of the Buddha’s teaching, it has not yet revealed its origination.
Now, desiring to reveal this, I compose this treatise.
Should Buddhism be said to be wholesome or indeterminate?
Answer: It may be wholesome.
Or it is indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
It refers to the speech taught by the Buddha’s wholesome mind, up to and including vocal intimation.
What is the indeterminate?
It refers to the verbal expressions and even the vocal intimation produced by the Buddha’s indeterminate mind.
Question: Within the Buddha’s teaching, what is wholesome?
What is indeterminate?
Answer: The Abhidharma-piṭaka and the Sūtra-piṭaka.
For the most part, it is wholesome;
for the most part, the Vinaya Piṭaka is indeterminate,
as the Blessed One has said.
The door should be closed;
the robes and bowl should be placed on a bamboo rack or a dragon-toothed stand.
Since such statements as these are all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), [they do not constitute a formal rule].
Some say: "If the Buddha's teaching is spoken for the sake of those to be converted, it should be known as wholesome;
if it is spoken for other matters, it is then indeterminate."
As the Blessed One told Ānanda:
"Go and observe whether it is raining in the heavens or not;
why is there such loud and great clamor in the garden?"
Since such statements as these are all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
some say that if a teaching of the Buddha is spoken with deliberate effort, it should be known as wholesome (*kuśala*).
If it is spoken spontaneously, it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Some say that those things subsumed under the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) of the Buddha's teaching should be known as wholesome (*kuśala*).
That which is not subsumed under the powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth, is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
When Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas utter speech with a virtuous mind,
it reaches completion whether accompanied by a virtuous or an indeterminate mind.
When speech is initiated by an indeterminate mind, it reaches completion simultaneously with either an indeterminate or a wholesome mind.
When speech is initiated by the Buddha’s wholesome mind, it reaches completion with a wholesome mind.
When speech is initiated by an indeterminate mind, it reaches completion simultaneously with either an indeterminate or a wholesome mind.
It is certain that there is no instance where speech is initiated with a wholesome mind and brought to completion by an indeterminate mind;
for the Dharma taught by the Buddhas increases and never diminishes,

What phenomena are designated as "name" (*nāman*) in Buddhism?
The answer is: name-bodies (*nāmakāya*), phrase-bodies (*padakāya*), and phoneme-bodies (*vyañjanakāya*), arranged in successive order.
They are arranged in sequence and joined in sequence;

Question: What is the meaning of the term *sūtra*?
Answer: Briefly stated, there are two meanings.
The first is the sense of "compilation."
Second, the definition of the term "compilation" (*saṃgīti*).
The meaning of "compilation" refers to the Buddha’s speech being able to sustain and preserve the meaning.
It is like a flower garland;
just as one who binds a garland uses thread to fasten the flowers upon the heads of sentient beings so that they remain long without being scattered,
so too is the compilation of the doctrinal categories of the Buddha’s teaching.
The "crown" refers to the mind of sentient beings, which has long been free from forgetfulness.
The "editorial definition" means that the Buddha’s speech is able to definitively resolve meanings.
It is like a carpenter’s marking line;
just as a skilled craftsman uses a marking line on various pieces of timber to easily distinguish the correct from the erroneous,
removing what is crooked and retaining what is straight.
Thus, this published definitive gateway of the Buddha’s teachings makes it easy to discern right from wrong,
to abandon evil, and to preserve the good.
How should the verses of praise (*geya*) be understood?
This refers to those passages in the various sūtras where the prose text of the sūtra, previously explained in detail,

these include the *Saṃgīti-paryāya* and other such collections.
As the Blessed One told the assembly of bhikṣus:

If there were no knowledge and vision by which the outflows could be exhausted,"
This is impossible.
The World-Honored One has spoken these words in prose,
which have now been further condensed into verse.
Then he recited these words:
"One who possesses knowledge and vision has exhausted the outflows; one without knowledge and vision does not.
When one penetrates the arising and passing away of the aggregates, the mind is liberated from defilements."
What is the exposition of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*)?
It refers to instances within the sūtras where the disciples question the Tathāgata and he provides a prediction,
or where the Tathāgata questions the disciples and they provide a prediction.
Alternatively, there are questions asked by disciples and answers given by disciples;
the same applies to the questions and answers posed by various devas and others.
Thus, within the various sūtras, there are four types of questions and answers.

If one asks what a *gāthā* is when it records the realization attained, the place of birth, and so forth, it refers to the concluding verses and stanzas found within various sūtras; that is, those specific utterances such as the *gāthās*. As the *gāthā* says:
By associating with those one loves and those one hates, greed and hatred arise;
therefore, the wise all avoid them and dwell alone in walking meditation like the horn of a rhinoceros.
How is this described?
This refers to those discourses in which the Blessed One himself spoke concerning matters of sorrow or joy.
Regarding matters of joy,
for example, on one occasion the Buddha saw a wild elephant king.
Then he spoke in verse:
"The elephant king dwells in the wilderness, Free and unrestrained, his mind free from sorrow;
The wise man abides in the secluded forest, Wandering at ease, his will tranquil and still."
Regarding those who suffer due to grief:
once, the Buddha saw an elderly couple and spoke this verse:
Having failed to cultivate the holy life in youth, we have lost the treasure of the noble wealth;
now like two old cranes, we together guard a single dried-up pond.
What is the cause and condition for this?
This refers to that which is spoken in various sūtras in response to specific causes and conditions,
such as the diverse causes and conditions found in the *Arthavargīya* and other texts, or as stated in the *Vinaya*.
Because the son of Sudhana and others first committed an offense,
the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and established the training rule (śikṣāpada).
What is the analogy for this?
This refers to the various and numerous parables taught in the sūtras, such as the *Dīrgha-avadāna* and the *Mahāvadāna*, and so forth.
For example, in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the Vinaya-holder asks: "What is the *itivṛttaka*?"
This refers to those sūtras that proclaim matters seen and heard regarding the past,
such as the statement: "In the past, there was a great royal capital named Sugandhamāla."
The king was named Sudarśana.
In the past, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin.
For the sake of his disciples, he taught this Dharma: "In the past,

He taught such dharmas to his disciples.
What, then, are these [tales] such as the Jātakas?
This refers to those sūtras that proclaim the events of past births,
such as the Jātaka tales of the bear, the deer, and others,
or as when the Buddha recounted five hundred previous births on account of Devadatta.
What is Vaipulya?
It refers to those sūtras that extensively expound various profound meanings of the Dharma,
such as the Pañcatriṃśat-sūtra, the Brahmajāla, the Māyājāla, and [treatises on] the five aggregates, the six bases, and the great dependent origination.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"In this context, Prajñā is called Vaipulya because its function is vast.

This refers to the extremely rare events concerning the Three Jewels and so forth taught within the various sūtras.
Other masters state that these are the disciples' praises of the World-Honored One’s rare and marvelous qualities.
Just as Śāriputra praised the unsurpassed virtues of the Blessed One,
and the Venerable Ānanda praised the exceedingly rare qualities of the Blessed One—
what is the discussion regarding this?
This refers to the teachings in various sūtras that provide definitive judgments through silent discourse, spoken discourse, and so forth;
it is also like when the Buddha, having briefly expounded a sūtra on one occasion,
would then enter a quiet chamber and remain in meditative silence for a long time.

Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?"

Answer: It is in order to enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty. That is to say, within this treatise, the self-nature and its specific distinctions regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) are extensively analyzed, so that no one might give rise to the doubt:
"The author of this treatise understands only the ultimate truth and is unacquainted with the conventional (*saṃvṛti*)."
This treatise is composed to demonstrate that the proponent thoroughly understands both the ultimate and the conventional truths.
What phenomenon is designated by the term "writing"?
The answer is: it refers to bodily action transformed in accordance with reality, as well as the various skillful means of wisdom upon which it relies.
In this context, "writing" (lipi) does not refer to the characters themselves that are produced;
rather, it refers to the method capable of producing those characters.
Because it is that which brings characters into existence, it is called writing.
Regarding the activity of the body that transforms according to principle:
this reveals that the fruit which arises is the basis for the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) for those possessing skillful wisdom.
It is shown that the causes capable of producing [the written word] are precisely the four aggregates (*skandha*).
Thus, these five aggregates constitute the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of writing.
What dharma is designated by the name "number" (*saṃkhyā*)?
Answer: It is the mental action that transforms in accordance with reality, as well as the various skillful means of wisdom upon which it relies.
Regarding the term "repeatedly" (or "numerically") herein:
This does not refer to the objects being counted, such as rice, sesame, and so forth, in numbers such as hundreds or thousands;
rather, it refers to all things that possess the capacity to count.
Because these are the factors capable of counting, they are designated as "number."
Among the Buddha’s disciples, the Venerable Ānanda was preeminent in his mastery of numerical methods, such that none could surpass him.
On one occasion, for the purpose of begging for alms,
he took up his robes and bowl and set out for the city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist ascetic before the city gate who,
seeing Ānanda from afar, thought to himself:
"I have heard that this śramaṇa is foremost in his mastery of mathematics."
"I shall now test whether this is indeed so.
At that time, by the side of the city gate,
there was a great tree with luxuriant branches and leaves named Nyagrodha.
The non-Buddhist practitioner stepped forward, pointed to the tree, and asked,
"Do you know now how many leaves there are on this tree?
The Venerable One looked up at it and immediately replied:
"Now these tree leaves number several hundreds of thousands.
Having said this, he entered the city.
Later, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reflected thus:
By what reasoning and evidence can one know whether that statement is false or true?
He then took a few leaves and hid them away.
When Ānanda emerged from the city, the non-Buddhist asked him again.
"Venerable sir, how many have you enumerated as being fixed?
Ānanda replied,
"I have already stated this previously."
The non-Buddhist practitioner spoke again,
saying, "Please explain this once more.
The Venerable One looked at the tree and replied immediately.
"Previously there were so many, now there are only this few.
The non-Buddhist was delighted; he apologized and sighed in admiration, saying, "Your knowledge of numbers is supreme;
I truly believe you are the only one capable of such insight."
Furthermore, it is like Pāruṣyaka,
who as soon as he saw the Buddha’s chin, immediately remarked, "He certainly possesses forty exquisite teeth.
There are truly many of such types who interpret things in this manner.
"Skillful wisdom that serves as the basis for mental activity transformed according to reality" indicates the fruit that arises.
"Wisdom that is skillful means" refers to the basis upon which it relies.
It is revealed that the nature of this [calculation] consists of these four aggregates as its causal basis.
What dharma is designated by the term "calculation"?
The answer is: it is vocal action (*vākkarman*) that has undergone transformation in accordance with reality (*yathārtha*).
And the skillful wisdom that serves as the basis for this:
herein, "calculation" does not refer to the objects of calculation, such as the numbers one, ten, hundred, thousand, ten-thousand, hundred-thousand, million, and so forth.
However, all methods capable of calculation are called "calculation" because they are the means of calculating.
This refers to verbal action that is transformed according to reason.
The manifestation of the result that arises is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
The skillful wisdom regarding the basis manifests the cause that gives rise [to it], which consists of the other four aggregates.
If these five aggregates constitute the nature of calculation, what dharma is designated as "seal"?
The answer is: bodily action that is transformed in accordance with reality.
And the various skillful means and wisdoms that serve as the basis for this:
herein, "seal" does not refer to a seal that is produced,
but rather to all the dharmas that are capable of producing a seal.

Because this is capable of forming a seal, it is called a "seal" (*mudrā*); as for the phrase "the activity of the body transformed according to principle," this reveals that the resulting fruit is precisely the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
As for the phrase "the skillful means of wisdom which is the basis": [This refers to] the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya-jñāna*) which serves as the support.
It reveals that the causes capable of producing [the seal] are precisely the four aggregates (*skandha*).
Thus, what dharma is designated by the name "the verse on the self-nature of the seal" consisting of these five aggregates?
The answer is: it refers to vocal action (*vākkarman*) that has been transformed in accordance with reality (*yathābhūta*).
And the various skillful means and wisdoms that serve as the basis for this:
herein, "poetry" (kāvyam) does not refer to what is actually being chanted or recited,
but rather to all those factors capable of accomplishing the composition of verse.
Because this is capable of composing verses, it is called "poetry" (*kāvyam*).
The phrase "vocal action transformed in accordance with reality" indicates that the resulting fruit is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The wise one who possesses skillful means regarding the basis reveals that the cause of arising consists of the four aggregates;
thus, these five aggregates constitute the intrinsic nature of poetry.
Question: Among various prose and verse compositions, what constitutes poetry (*kāvyam*) and what does not?
Some say as follows:
The Buddha’s words are not poetry;
other words are poetry.
Some other masters say this.
The inner teaching is not poetry;
the outer teaching is poetry.
Thus it is said.
A composition that accords with its meaning and leads toward benefit and profit is not called poetry (*kāvyam*).
Poetry refers to worldly verses that are the opposite of this.
What dharma is designated by the term "various worldly crafts and occupations" (*śilpasthāna*)?
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is because one wishes to encompass many meanings within a concise text.
That is to say, if one were to explain this extensively according to each of the various fields of craft and industry, it would give rise to much discursive talk;
therefore, wishing to subsume those [topics] under a brief statement, this treatise is composed.
What is the dharma designated as the various worldly crafts and occupations?
Answer: It refers to those crafts and occupations performed with wisdom as the precursor.
And the various skillful means and wisdoms that serve as the basis for this;
herein, the specific actions performed are not analyzed,
but rather the methods by which those actions are performed are revealed.
"Engaging in various crafts and occupations" refers to the bodily,
vocal, and mental actions that arise as their respective fruits,
which depend upon skillful means and wisdom as appropriate.
This reveals the cause that brings about [the result].
Thus, its intrinsic nature consists either of the five aggregates or of the four aggregates.
In various places, the "path of deportment" (airyāpathika) and the "arising of the path of deportment" are taught.
As for the path of deportment:
This means that its substance consists of the four bases of visible form, odor, taste,
and tangibility. That which gives rise to the modes of deportment has as its substance the two bases of mind and mental phenomena.
The four consciousnesses of the eye, nose, tongue, and body are the preparatory applications (*prayoga*) for the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*),
but they do not themselves give rise to the modes of deportment.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the preparatory application for the modes of deportment.
It is also that which gives rise to the pathways of deportment (*airyāpathika*).
Furthermore, the four consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are able to take the pathways of deportment as their objects.
The mental consciousness cannot take the modes of deportment as its object;
however, it can take the modes of deportment as its object and can also give rise to the modes of deportment.
There are others who, by means of the mental consciousness induced by this [meditative state],
are fully capable of taking the twelve bases as objects;
it is in these various places that the "bases of craftsmanship" (śilpasthāna) are taught.
And there is the arising of the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthāna*). As for the spheres of craftsmanship,
they have as their essence the five spheres of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects.
That which arises from the sphere of craftsmanship (śailpasthānika) has as its essence the two spheres of mind and mental objects (manodharma-āyatana).
The five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness and so forth, are the preparatory application (prayoga) for the sphere of craftsmanship.
It does not arise as the actual state of craftsmanship;
rather, the mental consciousness is the preparatory application for the state of craftsmanship,
and it also arises as the state of craftsmanship itself.
Furthermore, the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, can take the bases of craftsmanship (*śailpasthāna*) as their objects,
but they cannot take the origination of the bases of craftsmanship as their objects. The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), however, can take the bases of craftsmanship as its object,
and it can also take the origination of the bases of craftsmanship as its object.
There are others who, by means of this consciousness induced [by that],
are fully capable of taking the twelve bases as their cognitive objects,
provided they have accomplished the training in the precepts.
Does he accomplish the morality that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
It should be answered with four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
There is one who accomplishes the morality of a learner (śaikṣa), but not the morality that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
This refers to a learner (śaikṣa) who has been reborn in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Because that person’s conventional morality (saṃvṛti-śīla) is abandoned upon transcending the level of the realm,
there is the case of one who possesses neither-learner-nor-non-learner morality (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-śīla) but does not possess learner morality (śaikṣa-śīla).
This refers to arhats and ordinary beings born in the desire realm and the form realm; specifically,
those arhats who reside in the desire and form realms.
One definitely achieves the precepts that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
one definitely does not achieve the learner’s precepts,
because they have already been relinquished.
If ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the desire realm or the form realm possess either non-learner-non-non-learner morality (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣaśīla*),
all ordinary beings certainly do not possess learner morality (*śaikṣaśīla*).
Because it has not yet been attained,
there are those who possess the precepts of training (śaikṣa-śīla) but do not possess the precepts that are neither of training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-śīla);
namely, those who are trainees born in the desire realm or the form realm.
All learners (śaikṣa) in the desire and form realms necessarily possess both the precepts that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa) and the learner's precepts (śaikṣa),
because they have not yet abandoned them.
There are those who neither possess the precepts of training nor the precepts that are neither of training nor beyond training;
namely, arhats and ordinary worldlings born in the formless realm.
Those born there as arhats certainly do not possess the precepts of a learner (śaikṣa),
because they have already relinquished them.
Those born there as ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) certainly do not possess the precepts of a learner.
Because they have not yet attained them,
those two types of conventional precepts are both unaccomplished;
this is because they are relinquished upon transcending the respective realms and stages.
If one is accomplished in the precepts of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
is that person also accomplished in the precepts that are neither of one in training nor of one beyond training?
One should respond by formulating four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is one who possesses the precepts of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) but not the precepts that are neither of training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
This refers to an Arhat born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu);
because his conventional precepts are abandoned upon transcending the level of that realm.
There are those who possess neither-learner-nor-non-learner morality, yet do not possess non-learner morality;
namely, all learners (śaikṣa) and ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) born in the desire realm or the form realm.
A learner (śaikṣa) in the desire realm or the form realm is necessarily endowed with conventional morality (saṃvṛti-śīla).
An ordinary person (pṛthagjana) in the desire realm or the form realm is likewise [endowed with it].
Or, one may accomplish mundane precepts,
yet fail to accomplish both types of precepts of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
because neither has been attained.
There are those who possess both the precepts of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-śīla) and the precepts that are neither of training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-śīla);
namely, Arhats born in the desire realm or the form realm.
There are also those who do not possess either the precepts of one beyond training or the precepts that are neither of training nor beyond training.
This refers to those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) who are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu); for them,
there is no unlearned morality (aśaikṣa-śīla).
Because neither has been attained, and because both have already been relinquished in that conventional morality (*saṃvṛti-śīla*).
Question: Is everything that is morality also karma?
Answer: All that is morality is indeed karma;
however, there is karma that is not morality, namely mental karma and so forth.
Question: Wherever there is ethical discipline (*śīla*), is there also karma?
Answer: Wherever there is ethical discipline, there is also karma.
There are places where there is karma but no precepts, such as the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and so forth.
Question: If one is endowed with precepts...
Does he accomplish karma?
Answer: If he accomplishes ethical discipline, he accomplishes karma.
There are those who accomplish karma but not morality, namely, ordinary beings born in the formless realm and so forth.
Question: If there is morality...
Does he possess karma?
Answer: If he possesses precepts, he possesses karma;
or he may possess karma without possessing precepts.
This refers to ordinary beings born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and so forth.
