Some say: [this is] to refute what was stated by other masters;
that is to say, within this school there were two masters.
First is Buddhadeva and second is Dharmatrāta. According to what Buddhadeva says,
matter consists solely of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Mental factors are identical to the mind.
They maintain that derived matter is simply a differentiation of the primary elements.
Mental factors (caitta) are simply distinctions within the mind itself.
Why did he state this?
Because it is based on the sūtras.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Within the fleshy mass of the eye,
whatever is internal, distinct, solid by nature, and of a solid kind..."
That which is appropriated and proximate is called the internal earth element;
likewise, up to the individual nature and category of motion,
that which is appropriated and proximate is called the internal wind element.
Based on this sūtra, he asserts that derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is identical to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Furthermore, a sūtra states: "What is meditative concentration (*samādhi*)?
It is the one-pointedness of a virtuous mind (*citta-ekāgratā*)."

For this reason, it is said that mental factors (*caitta*) are themselves the mind (*citta*). To the question, "How then are those [factors] established as elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and aggregates (*skandha*)?
the answer is given: "It is said that among the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), there is that which is capable of seeing."
There is that which is seen,
up to and including there is that which is able to touch and that which is touched.
All that can see is established as the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*);
all that is seen is established as the form-element (*rūpa-dhātu*).
This continues up to: all that can touch is established as the body-element (*kāya-dhātu*).
All that which is touched is established as the element of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*).
Within the mind, there is that which relies upon the eye-faculty,
up to and including that which relies upon the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*).
Based on the eye-faculty, the visual consciousness-element is established;
likewise, up to based on the mind-faculty, the mental consciousness-element is established.
That is to say, the six groups of consciousness that have just ceased without interval are established as the mind-element.
It is precisely the differentiation of the mind that is designated as feeling,
designated as perception,
and designated as volition.
Together with the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), these are established as the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*).
As it is with the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*), so it is with the aggregates (*skandha*). Regarding the aggregates:
The various primary elements (mahābhūta) are established as the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
The various distinctions of mind are termed feeling (vedanā) and termed perception (saṃjñā).
That which is called volition and that which is called consciousness are established as the four aggregates.
How does this accord with what is taught in the sūtras?
"All forms whatsoever are the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements.
To this, he replied as follows.
Sound that is not derived does not have a cause distinct from the four great elements; rather, sound that is derived is established based upon those very great elements.
How is this known?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Bhikṣus, you should know that contact arises from two conditions:
namely, the eye and visible forms, up to the mind and mental phenomena.
There are six bases of contact that were previously performed and previously created;
I declare these to be past karma.
It should be understood that by means of these, unlearned worldlings experience pleasure and experience pain when touched.
Whether it be produced by these [elements] or by any one of them,
there is no seventh sense-field of contact (spraṣṭavyāyatana) apart from the preceding six that could serve as the basis for establishing the term "produced" (bhautika).
Thus, the six [sensory objects] previously mentioned are said to be derived (upādāya-rūpa).
The same applies to the preceding sutra.
There are no derived forms that exist apart from the primary elements (mahābhūta).
Thus, sound is established as being derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta).
This does not pose a difficulty for me, for the Abhidharma masters state that the sūtra they cited possesses a specific underlying intention (abhiprāya).
The previously cited sūtra cannot be used as a scriptural proof;
for when that sūtra speaks of the "six bases of contact" earlier,
it is speaking with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) regarding the stage prior to full clarity.
The subsequent statement, "by this which is produced" or "by any one of these," refers to the state of being already manifest,
spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*),
just as [it was explained] for the state not yet manifest.
Thus there are the state of non-conceptualization and the state of conceptualization;
the state not yet manifest and the state already manifest;
the state not yet expressible and the state already expressible.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Furthermore, the "six bases of contact" (ṣaḍ-āyatana) refer to the intermediate state (antarābhava);
that which is produced by these refers to the state of existence at birth (upapattibhava).
The Venerable Ghosaka said:
"In that sutra, the 'six bases of contact' mentioned previously were spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) to refer to a state in which the sense faculties (*indriya*) are unimpaired."
Regarding the subsequent statement, "by this, that which is produced, etc.," it refers to an intentional teaching (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) concerning the state of having impaired faculties.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"The mention of 'six bases of contact' is an intentional teaching referring to the desire realm."
"Produced by this" refers to the form realm (rūpadhātu) as spoken with intentional meaning (saṃdhāya). Or,
"any one of these."
The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) was spoken of with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*). Such is the meaning of the sūtra.
How, then, can the statement regarding "derived matter" (*upādāya-rūpa*) found in the aforementioned sūtra be proven?
Furthermore, if what is produced were not distinct [from the producer],
how would one reconcile other statements made in the sūtras? As it is said in a sūtra:
The Venerable Pūrṇa said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Venerable friend,
you should know that whatever constitutes the grasping at a self is produced by form."
The self-clinging produced by feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is precisely the view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
If the term "produced" were devoid of any distinct meaning,
could the view of a personal identity then be identical to form and the other aggregates?

However, since there is a separate self-clinging apart from form and the other [aggregates], we know that what the sutras describe as "derived matter" (bhautika-rūpa) is not identical to the primary elements (mahābhūta).
Question: If derived matter exists separately from the primary elements, [how is this so?]
How should one interpret that cited sūtra which states, "Within the physical mass of the eye, there are the earth element and so forth"?
The answer is: that sūtra speaks of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) relies; it does not speak of the essence of the eye itself.
Furthermore, that sutra states that what is commonly known in the world as the "flesh-ball" is called the eye;
it does not refer to the visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya),
because worldly convention applies the designation "eye" to the flesh-ball.
The Venerable Ghosaka also stated this:
"The world designates the name 'eye-faculty' (cakṣur-indriya) for the primary elements (mahābhūta),
because it is that upon which the eye-faculty depends."
Other masters say that the sūtra cited by them does not contradict the meaning;
that sūtra merely states that within the physical mass of the eye there are the elements (dhātus) such as earth and so forth.
It does not say that the earth element and so forth are themselves the eye faculty;
what contradiction is there in this meaning?
The Venerable Dharmatrāta says:
They maintain that derived matter exists separately from the primary elements,
and that mental factors are not identical to the mind; yet,
they also assert that among the categories of matter, two [types] are not substantially real.
That is to say, derived tangible objects and the matter of the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*) are established as aggregates,
bases, and elements according to the Abhidharma school;
yet even that is not correct.
Furthermore, the various types of derived tangible objects (*upādāya-spraṣṭavya*) ought to exist as distinct entities, just like other derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Moreover, if there were no matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), then non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), such as the precepts, would not exist.
This treatise is composed in order to refute the assertions of these two teachers;
some say it is to refute the assertions of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
This refers to the claim of non-Buddhists that there are five great elements (mahābhūta),
namely the aforementioned four plus space (ākāśa). Here,
however, only four are mentioned, making it clear that space is not a great element.
Question: For what reason is space not established as having the great elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Venerable Vasumitra offers this explanation:
"Because space lacks the characteristics of the great elements."
That which possesses increase and decrease is the characteristic of the primary elements (mahābhūta);
that which is without increase or decrease is the characteristic of space (ākāśa).
Therein, there is both loss and gain.
These are the characteristics of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
To be without loss or gain is the characteristic of space (*ākāśa*); to have arising and decay is the characteristic of the great elements;
to be without arising or decay is the characteristic of space.
Therefore, space does not establish the great elements (mahābhūta).
The Venerable Ghoṣaka offers this explanation:
the characteristics of space and the great elements are each distinct.
That is to say, all the primary elements (mahābhūta) within the bodies of sentient beings are for the most part produced as the maturation (vipāka) of prior karma; however,
space (ākāśa), being devoid of intrinsic substance, lacks the quality of being produced through maturation.
For this reason, space is not established as a primary element (*mahābhūta*).
The Venerable One said:
"Although space is vast, its essence is not that of an element."
Because they cannot produce [them].
Although other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) can serve as seeds, their substance is not "great," because their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are not pervasive.
For this reason, the great elements are not established in space.
This treatise was composed in order to refute such attachments held by non-Buddhists and to reveal our own school’s tenets.
Other masters say:
This treatise was not composed merely to refute the tenets of others and establish one's own school;
rather, it was written so that the meanings corresponding to the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) might be clearly elucidated.
Question: Why is it that the great elements (mahābhūta) and their derivatives (bhautika) are distinguished first here?
Answer: It is because the author of the treatise intended it so.

That is to say, the original master of the treatise, following his own intention while not contravening the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), distinguished the great elements and their derivatives first.
Some say that sentient beings regard these two types as the true gateways to the ambrosia of the Buddha-dharma:
first, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Second, mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) observes derived matter (upādāyarūpa),
whereas mindfulness of breathing observes the primary elements (mahābhūta).
Some say:

If one contemplates the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) in their gradual sequence, one can realize the three types of enlightenment—those of a Buddha, a Pratyekabuddha, and a Śrāvaka.
That is to say, if one observes them with superior wisdom:
One gives rise to the superior stage of the application of mindfulness to the body;
from this, one subsequently gives rise to the superior stage of the application of mindfulness to feelings,
and then to the mind.
Next, the dharmas;
next, the arising of the stage of mixed objects;
next, the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas.
Next, from the arising of the path of vision up to the arising of the path of no-more-learning,
all are of the superior grade.
At that time, they are called superior virtuous persons who have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If one examines them with middling wisdom:
One gives rise to the middling degree of the application of mindfulness to the body;
this is explained in detail up until the arising of the path of no-more-learning, all of which is by means of the middling degree.
At that time, one is called a person of middling virtue.
He realizes the middling level of pratyekabuddha enlightenment.
If he observes that with inferior wisdom,
he gives rise to the inferior application of mindfulness on the body.
To speak extensively, up until the arising of the path of no-more-learning,
all [stages] are of the inferior grade;
at that time, one is called an "inferior virtuous person."
One realizes the inferior level of the śrāvaka’s enlightenment.
Some say that if one contemplates the primary elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādāyarūpa), [one attains this].
One is then able to subdue all forms of arrogance and negligence.
This refers to how sentient beings give rise to various forms of arrogance and negligence on account of their physical appearance, lineage, wealth, power, retinue, and so forth.
When the great elements and so forth have not yet been investigated,
whichever one appears becomes powerful and dominant;
once they have been investigated, it is then possible to subdue them.
Why is this? Just as the primary elements (mahābhūta) belonging to the body of a wheel-turning monarch are the same as those belonging to dogs and other such beings,
by observing this, one abandons arrogance and negligence.
Based on such causes and conditions as have been explained,
the primary elements (mahābhūta) and their derivatives (upādāyarūpa) are first distinguished within these aggregates;
this is because the Sūtra states that "all that is form" [is comprised of these].
All these are the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements.
All that is spoken of can be summarized into two kinds.
First, there is the sense of being incomplete;
second, there is the sense of being complete. Regarding the sense of being incomplete:
it is as when people in the world say, "I wish to eat every bit of food that exists."
This merely intends to consume whatever small portion may be obtained;
it has no further meaning,
just as when people in the world say, "I wish to know all phenomena whatsoever."
This is intended to provide a general understanding of the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma*).
The phrase "all that exists" used herein collectively indicates that all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are fully encompassed.
That is to say, all forms are comprised of two general types:
first, the four great elements; second, form derived from the four great elements.
Second, derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Apart from these, there is no third essence of matter.
Question: For what reason are the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) only four?
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"This should not be questioned. Why is that?"
Whether there is increase or decrease, doubt arises in both cases;
yet one does not violate the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) merely because of such doubt.
Rather, one follows the noble teaching, which speaks of only four types.
Other masters say:
"If there were fewer than four, the functional capacity would be deficient;
if there were more than four, they would likewise be useless."
Just as a square bed frame has only four legs.
Question: Why is it called "great element" (mahābhūta)?
Answer: Because it is great and it is an element.
Therefore, they are called "great elements" (mahābhūta),
just as one speaks of "the great earth" or "the great king."
The meanings are distinct while the substance is the same;
it should be analyzed as a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Question: What is the meaning of "great" (*mahat*)?
What is the meaning of "seed" (*bīja*)?
The answer is: that which can decrease and increase, can diminish and augment, whose essence undergoes arising and ceasing;
this is the meaning of "seed. Its essential characteristics, forms, and dimensions pervade all regions, accomplishing great undertakings.
This is the great purpose.
Question: How do these four constitute a great undertaking?
Answer: They serve as the basis for the formation of the great accumulation of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Causing destruction and causing formation are the great tasks;
for this reason, there are exactly four, neither fewer nor more.
That is to say, if they were fewer, the great task could not be accomplished; if they were more, they would be useless for the task.
Question: For what reason are other phenomena not called great elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Answer: Because others lack such characteristics of a great element.
That is to say, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are "great" but not "elements."
Because other conditioned elements are not "great," only these four are designated as the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Question: What is the meaning of "producing" (*abhinirvṛtti*)?
Does this mean it is the cause (hetu) and does it mean it is the condition (pratyaya)?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
Both positions are seen to have defects.
If it is in the sense of being a cause,
these four great elements lack all five types of causes with respect to derived matter;
how then can it be said that they are able to produce all forms?
If "condition" refers to the meaning of being a condition for all derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), then—
with the exception of its own self-nature— all other dharmas are indeed this predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Why, then,
is it stated that [derived matter] is produced only by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?
It is agreed that "to create" (*karoti*) has the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*).
Question: Since this [unmanifest form] lacks all five causes for derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), how can it have the sense of being a cause?
Answer: Although the five causes, such as the cause of similar type and so forth, are all absent, there are nevertheless five other distinct types of causal meanings:

namely, the generative cause (*janana-hetu*), the supporting cause (*āśraya-hetu*), the establishing cause (*pratisthā-hetu*), the sustaining cause (*dhṛti-hetu*), and the nourishing cause (*puṣṭi-hetu*).
By this, it is able to produce [them].
Other masters say that "producing" (kṛ) has the meaning of "conditioning" (pratyaya).

Question: Since all derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), with the exception of its own self-nature, has all other phenomena as its predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), why is it said only that [derived matter] is produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Answer: Regarding the meaning of the predominant condition:
There are those who are close and those who are distant; there are those who are near and those who are far;
there are those with whom one is in harmony and those with whom one is not.
Some exist in this life,
while others exist in future lives.
Those that are closely associated and belong to this life are designated as "causes."
That which is distant and does not coexist in other lifetimes is called a "condition" (*pratyaya*).
For this reason, it is said that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) act as the cause and the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Nor does this contradict reason.
Question: What are the characteristics and functions of earth, water, fire, and wind?
Answer: Solidity is the characteristic of earth.
Upholding is the function of earth;
moisture is the characteristic of water;
and cohesion is the function of water.
Heat is the characteristic of fire;
ripening is the function of fire;
motion is the characteristic of wind.
Length is the product of wind.
Question: Earth has the characteristic of solidity and also the characteristic of form (*rūpa*).
[This continues] at length, up to...
Wind has the characteristic of motion and also the characteristic of form.
How can one dharma possess two characteristics?
Answer: There is no fault in this.
By this principle, within a single dharma,
it is possible to designate many characteristics;
for example, as in the case of a single contaminated (sāsrava) dharma.
This includes being like a disease, like an abscess,
and so forth; as explained in detail,
it encompasses up to one hundred and forty phrases describing various forms of faults and afflictions, without any deficiency.
This is also like that.
Other masters say:
"Characteristics are of two kinds."
First, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
second, the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion are the specific characteristics.
The characteristic of form (*rūpa*) is a common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, these two characteristics do not contradict one another;
there is no fault in establishing them both within a single dharma.
Question: Are these four great elements inseparable at all times?
Answer: It is so.
How is this known to be so?
As stated in the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*,
the Buddha told Ānanda:
"At first, there is the kalala."
If there were an earth element without a water element,
it would simply crumble and disperse;
that it does not so disperse now is because it is held together by water.
If there were the water element without the earth element,
it would simply flow away;
that it does not flow now is because it is supported by the earth.
If there were the elements of earth and water but no element of fire, they would surely become putrid and rotten;
that they do not rot now is because they are matured by fire. Thus, all three elements must exist.
If there were no wind element, it would not increase;
yet since it does increase now, it is because it is moved by the wind. One might ask:
how then should the statements in other sūtras be reconciled?
The earth element becomes disturbed,
causing some to die or causing sentient beings to undergo the suffering of imminent death;
this applies likewise even to the wind element.
Answer: This explains that when any one of the great elements increases, it is capable of causing disturbance;
it does not mean that the four kinds are ever separated from one another.
Question: How many categories of these four great elements are there?
The answer is that there are four categories:
namely, maturation (vipāka), growth (aupacayika),
and outflow (naiṣyandika).
Regarding transformations,
other masters state that there are three categories.
That is to say: born of maturation,
nurtured growth,
and outflowing continuity.
That which undergoes transformation is subsumed under growth and nourishment.
Furthermore, there are those who say that there are two categories.
That is to say, the great elements born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and those through growth (*aupacayika*),
as well as the transformed (*nairmāṇika*) great elements, are included within the category of those through growth.
The outflowing [result] is subsumed within the ripening and the nourishing [results].
The critique states:
among the three preceding explanations, this one is the best.
Because there are four great elements that are not subsumed under either [of the two categories].
Question: Does one great element produce only one atom of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa-paramāṇu*), or can it produce many?
If only one [cause] were created,
how could it not constitute four fruits and one cause?
It is logically untenable for there to be many causes and few fruits.
If many [derived forms] can be produced,
then there would be many atoms (paramāṇu) of derived matter from a single set of the four great elements;
how then could they not be mutual simultaneous causes (sahabhū-hetu)?
The Abhidharmikas state that derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) characterized by resistance has no simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) when viewed in mutual relation;
to grant otherwise would contradict the tenets of the Abhidharma school.
It is agreed that this should be stated thus:
the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) can only produce a single atom (*paramāṇu*) of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Question: Why does it not follow that there are four causes and one fruit?
It is not logically tenable that there should be many causes and few results.
Response: There is no logical fault in having few results from many causes, for such a phenomenon is observed in the world.
There is no logical contradiction in [the view that] four [types of derived matter] arise from one [great element].
Some say many [derived matters] are produced.
Question: If that is so, then for a single set of the four great elements, there would be many atoms (*paramāṇu*) of derived matter.
Why are successive [factors] not simultaneous causes?
Answer: Because they do not share a single fruit, they are not simultaneous causes;
for dharmas that are simultaneous causes must necessarily have the same fruit.
This does not constitute a valid reason, as it is equivalent to doubt.
The critique states: what was said previously is correct.
Question: How do the primary elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādāyarūpa) abide?
Do the primary elements (mahābhūta) abide below and the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) above?
Or do the primary elements abide above and the derived matter below?
Or do the primary elements and the derived matter abide in mutual intermingling?
Are the primary elements (mahābhūta) outside while the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is within its locus? If that were so, what fault would there be?
There would be every fault.
If the primary elements were below and the derived matter were above, [it would contradict the nature of their support].
Thus, those derived forms that are proximate to the primary elements may take those primary elements as their productive causes; however,
among derived forms, there are those that are separated by distance.
How can the primary elements (mahābhūta) serve as causes?
If the primary elements were above and the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) were below,
then the derived matter would have to be the cause of the primary elements.
The primary elements (mahābhūta) should not be the cause of derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
If the primary elements and derived matter were to abide in mutual intermingling—
such that the primary elements are on the outside and the derived matter is within— [this would be untenable].
When it is being severed, one sees its internal cavities like those of a lotus stalk being cut.
Some say that because it is situated below, it must be so by virtue of being the supporting basis for the cause.
Question: If that is so, can it be said that [the primary elements] are the creators with respect to matter that is in close proximity?
How is it produced in relation to that which is distant?
Answer: It is not said that all the primary elements (mahābhūta) belonging to a single tree are located beneath it and produce all the derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
It is simply stated that for each part of a single tree, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are below and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is above.
Some maintain that they abide in a state of intermingling,
with the primary elements on the outside and the derived matter in the middle.
Question: If that were so, then when it is being cut or severed, one should see the pores and fissures as if it were a lotus root being severed.
Answer: Although there are pores and fissures, they cannot be seen;
this is because the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are not visible, whereas the pores that are seen are derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Question: The characteristics of internal and external phenomena are each distinct.
Regarding the distinction of internal phenomena:
it refers to when hundreds or thousands of sentient beings gather in one place, their deportment and physical appearances are each different.
External objects that are distinct refer to things such as fruits and stones,
which may be blue, yellow, red, or white.
The characteristics of fragrance, taste, and so forth are each distinct.
Such differentiation of characteristics—
does it arise from the diversity of karma?
Is it due to the difference in the primary elements (mahābhūta), or is it due to the difference in the derived matter (upādāyarūpa)?
Answer: It is due to all three kinds.
Based on the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it is said that [beings] differ due to karma;
based on the productive cause (*janana-hetu*) and the supporting cause (*niśraya-hetu*),
the [remaining] causes are established.
Because they possess the causes of maintenance and the causes of nourishment, it is said that [the primary elements] differ by way of the great elements (*mahābhūta*);
because they rely on the cause of homogeneous nature (*sabhāgahetu*),
it is said that [the derived matter] differs by way of the derivative form (*upādāyarūpa*).
Question: By what difference in karma do external objects differ?
Answer: If sentient beings perform various sublime deeds, they bring about external objects with forms and characteristics that are level and straight.
The colors, fragrances, tastes, and textures are all exquisite and sublime.
If sentient beings engage in various evil deeds,
they will experience external objects with forms and characteristics that are rugged and distorted.
Visible forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles are all coarse and inferior.
It is asked: the characteristics of various fruits, stones, and so forth are each distinct;
they differ in color—blue, yellow, red, white—and in shape and appearance.
Question: By what power does similarity occur?
Answer: It occurs by three powers, yet the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are predominant.
That is to say, when the primary elements are in a state of imbalance.
Thereupon, various differences arise, such as those of manifest form and so forth;
if they were equal, they would be similar.
Question: Regarding the sounds produced by the mouths of all classes of sentient beings...
It should be said that it is produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) located in the throat.
Some say it is produced by the primary elements at the side of the throat.
Some say it is derived from the primary elements at the periphery of the mind; others say: [it is derived from the primary elements of the body].
It is produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) located at the navel.
The critique states:
generally speaking, this sound is produced by the primary elements of all the limbs of the body.
If explained individually,
soft and small sounds should be said to be produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) located at the throat;
this includes sounds such as hissing, snorting, roaring, and screaming.
One should say that it is produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) pervading the entire body, for we observe that such [actions] cause the whole body to tremble.
Question: Is there any form (rūpa) that is not derived from the four great elements?
"Is it also not produced by the four great elements?
Answer: "It is.
That is to say, one, two, or three of the great elements."
Although this is form, it is not the four great elements (mahābhūta),
because it consists of only one, two, or three [of them].
Nor is it derived from the four great elements, because the great elements themselves are not derived.
Question: For what reason are the great elements (mahābhūta) not derived (upādāya)?
Answer: Because the natures of the producer and the produced are distinct, and because cause and effect are different.
Because the nature of the means of accomplishment and the object to be accomplished are each distinct;
as it is with the means of accomplishment and the object to be accomplished,
so it is with the inducer and the induced.
It can produce that which is produced;
it can perform that which is performed;
it can bring about the conjunction of that which is conjoined.
It should be understood that the same applies to the transformer and the transformed, as well as to the characteristic and the characterized.
Some say: if the primary elements (mahābhūta) were to produce derived matter (bhautika),
would three produce one?
If four [causes] produce one [result],
or if three produce one,
how can they produce it when their essence and function are deficient?
If the four [great elements] were to produce one [derived form],
then the earth element and so forth would have to produce the earth element and so forth;
this would entail the fallacy of a nature observing its own nature.
However, all phenomena take the nature of others as their conditions and are able to perform functions regardless of their own essence;
for this reason, the primary elements (mahābhūta) are not termed "derived" (bhautika).
The four great elements are of eleven kinds,
namely: that which is the basis for the sense-base of the eye,
up to that which is the basis for the sense-base of the body.
From the basis of the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the basis of the sense-field of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
there are likewise eleven kinds of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*):
namely, from the sense-field of the eye (*cakṣurāyatana*) up to the sense-field of the body (*kāyāyatana*).
From the sense base of form up to the sense base of mental objects.
Question: How many derived forms does the primary element that serves as the support for the sense base of the eye produce?
Up to the great elements that serve as the basis for the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
how many derived forms (bhautika-rūpa) can they produce?
One should answer as follows:
The primary elements that serve as the basis for the eye-base produce only the eye-base;
likewise, up to the primary elements that serve as the basis for the dharma-base produce only the dharma-base.
Some maintain this view.
The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) relies can produce three bases:
namely, the eye-base, the body-base (*kāyāyatana*), and the tangible-base (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
The same applies to the primary elements upon which the ear, nose, and tongue bases rely.
The great elements that serve as the basis for the body consist of two kinds:
namely, the sense-base of the body and the sense-bases of tangibles;
and the sense-bases of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and mental objects.
The same applies to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as their basis.
While the primary elements that serve as the basis for the sense-field of tangibles (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*) only produce tangibles,
there are others who maintain that all primary elements are capable of producing visible form, sound, and tangibles.
In the desire realm, the primary elements all produce odor and flavor.
It is said that the primary elements upon which the sense-base of the eye relies can produce seven kinds [of derived matter],
namely, the sense-base of the eye.
The bases of the body;
the bases of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
and likewise the primary elements that serve as the support for the bases of the ear, nose, and tongue.
The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the basis for the body-base (*kāyāyatana*) produce six kinds [of derived matter]:
namely, the primary elements that serve as the basis for the bases of visible form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are likewise.
The primary elements that serve as the basis for the base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) produce five kinds.
That is to say, the sense bases of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects;
and the primary elements that serve as the support for sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects are likewise so.
Other masters say:
The primary elements upon which the eye-base depends are capable of producing eleven kinds [of derived matter];
this applies likewise up to the primary elements upon which the dharma-base depends.
The critique states:
Among these various explanations, the first is correct.
That is to say, the primary elements (mahābhūta) upon which the sense-base of the eye relies produce only the sense-base of the eye;
and so on, up to the primary elements upon which the sense-base of mental objects (dharmāyatana) rely, which produce only the sense-base of mental objects.
Question: How can great elements (*mahābhūta*) of dissimilar characteristics produce derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) of similar characteristics?
Answer: There is no fault in saying so, because it is spoken of by considering a specific sense.
That is to say, it is by considering a specific sense that this is said.
It is said that primary elements (mahābhūta) of different characteristics produce derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) of identical characteristics;
this is stated from the perspective of a specific analytical meaning.
It is also said that primary elements of identical characteristics produce derived matter of different characteristics.
Because they are observed from a distinct perspective,
it is said that the primary elements (mahābhūta) with distinct characteristics produce derived matter (upādāyarūpa) with distinct characteristics;
this is because they are observed from a distinct perspective.
It is said that primary elements of similar characteristics produce derived matter of similar characteristics;
this is stated from the perspective of observing their distinct meanings.
It is also said that primary elements of dissimilar characteristics produce derived matter of similar characteristics.
That is to say, the primary elements (mahābhūta) characterized by solidity, moisture, heat, and motion;
and the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) characterized by the tangible. Some say:
Regarding these [elements] that produce the characteristics of visible form and so forth:
because they are observed from a specific perspective, it is said that the primary elements (mahābhūta) of identical characteristics produce derived matter (upādāyarūpa) of different characteristics;
that is to say, the primary elements characterized by tangibility.
They produce eleven kinds of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*). This is because,
when considering their specific characteristics,
it is said that primary elements (*mahābhūta*) with distinct characteristics produce derived matter with distinct characteristics.
That is to say, the primary elements characterized by solidity, moisture, heat,
and motion produce eleven kinds of derived matter when considered from the perspective of their distinct meanings.

Regarding the statement that "great elements of similar characteristics produce derived matter of similar characteristics," this refers to great elements characterized by tangibility producing derived matter characterized by tangibility.
Some say:
This refers to the primary elements (bhūta) that produce derived matter (bhautika-rūpa), such as visible form and so forth.
Question: What are the specific characteristics of the distinction between the primary elements and derived matter?
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke as follows:
The primary elements (mahābhūta) are the cause and the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is the fruit.
That which is capable of producing is the primary element;
that which is produced is the derived matter.
The primary elements (mahābhūta) are the support;
the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is that which depends upon them.
The primary elements are the defining characteristics; the derived matter is that which is defined by them.
The primary elements (mahābhūta) are the conjunction;
that which is produced by conjunction is derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
The primary elements are capable of establishing [matter].
That which is established [as derived matter] is the product of the primary elements (*bhautika*).
The Venerable One says:
"The characteristics of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion are the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)."
If form has the great elements as its cause,
yet lacks the characteristics of the great elements, it is derived matter (bhautika-rūpa).
Thus say some other masters.
The primary elements are like the Lord of Devas;
derived matter is like the celestial hosts.
The primary elements are like Maheśvara.
Derived matter is like attendants;
the primary elements are like kings,
and derived matter is like ministers.
The primary elements (mahābhūta) are like the orbs of the sun and moon;
derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is like the sunlight and moonlight.
The primary elements are like the trunk of a tree.
Derived matter is like branches and so forth;
the primary elements are like a wall;
derived matter is like a shadow.
The primary elements (mahābhūta) are like the flame of a lamp;
derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is like the light of the lamp.
The primary elements are like the lotus stalk.
Derived matter is like a flower;
the primary elements are like a mirror;
derived matter is like a reflection.
Therefore, the Venerable Vīra said:
The sense-faculties arise from the primary elements, Just as a lamp-flame produces light,
As a lotus grows from a lotus-root, And as a mirror produces various images.
The masters of the Abhidharma say:
the primary elements (mahābhūta) are invisible;
derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is both visible and invisible.
The primary elements (mahābhūta) are resistant;
derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is both resistant and non-resistant;
the primary elements are with outflows (sāsrava).
Derived matter may be with outflows or without outflows;
the primary elements are neutral;
derived matter may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
The primary elements (mahābhūta) are bound to the realms of desire and form;
derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is bound to the realms of desire and form, as well as being unbound.
The primary elements are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
Derived matter is of the categories of the learned, the unlearned, and neither-learned-nor-unlearned.
The great elements are to be abandoned by cultivation;
derived matter is both to be abandoned by cultivation and not to be abandoned.
The primary elements (mahābhūta) are subsumed under the truths of suffering and its origin; derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is subsumed under the truths of suffering, its origin, and the path.
The primary elements have no maturation (avipāka);
derived matter may have maturation or be without maturation.
The great elements (mahābhūta) are not defiled, nor do they cause derived matter (upādāyarūpa) to be defiled;
the great elements are not karma, while derived matter may be either karma or non-karma.
All such [instances] of the great elements and derived matter are thus.
There are immeasurable ways of distinguishing between the two characteristics; however, regarding the actual entities of the sense-field of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), there are eleven kinds:
namely, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the seven kinds of derived tangibles (*upādāyarūpa*).
Tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*) refer to smoothness, roughness, lightness, heaviness, cold, hunger, and thirst.
Smoothness means being fine and soft.
"Roughness" refers to being coarse and rigid;
"lightness" refers to being unweighable;
"heaviness" refers to being weighable.
Cold refers to that which, when one is oppressed by it, gives rise to a desire for warmth.
Hunger refers to that which, when one is oppressed by it, gives rise to a desire for food.
Thirst refers to that which, when one is oppressed by it, gives rise to a desire for drink.
Question: Through the predominance of which primary elements (*mahābhūta*) do smoothness and so forth, up to thirst, arise?
Regarding this, some say:
Smoothness, up to thirst, does not arise from a partial increase of the primary elements; rather,
it arises solely from a specific distinction in the nature and category of the primary elements.
There are those that produce the fruit of smoothness,
up to and including those that produce the fruit of thirst.
Other masters say:
Due to the increase of water and fire, there is smoothness;
due to the increase of earth and wind, there is roughness;
and due to the increase of fire and wind, there is lightness.
Because the elements of earth and water increase and because of their heaviness,
the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (or *Prakaraṇapāda*) poses this question:
"For what reason is the body light and well-adjusted while one is alive?"
"Does the body become heavy and lose its flexibility immediately upon death?
He replied, "While alive, because the fire and wind elements have not yet ceased, the body is light and flexible;
after death, because the fire and wind elements within the body have already ceased."
They are heavy and lack composure;
because water and wind increase, they feel cold;
because wind increases, they feel hunger.
This means that because wind increases, it strikes and agitates the digested food, inducing the sensation of hunger, which then gives rise to the desire for food.
Because fire increases, thirst arises;
that is to say, because fire increases, it parches and presses upon the digested drink.
When thirst-inducing contact arises, it immediately gives rise to the desire to drink.
Question: Among the eleven types of contact, how many at most serve as conditions for the arising of body-consciousness?
Some say that body-consciousness arises from each individual object separately,
because eleven kinds of characteristics and functions are augmented.
Other masters say that at most five factors serve as conditions for the arising of body-consciousness:
namely, the four great elements and any one of the [tangibles] such as smoothness.
Furthermore, there are those who say that body-consciousness also arises by taking all eleven [bases] as its object collectively.
Question: Is it not the case that the five consciousnesses take only their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objects?
Answer: There are two kinds of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa):
first, the specific characteristic of the thing (vastu-svalakṣaṇa); second, the specific characteristic of the location (sthāna-svalakṣaṇa).
Based on the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object, it is said that eleven kinds of contact serve as conditions for the arising of body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
Based on the specific characteristic of the sense-base (*āyatana*), it is said that the five groups of consciousness apprehend objects characterized by their own specific characteristics.
Therefore, there is no fault.
According to this explanation,
body-consciousness also arises conditioned by eleven objects,
just as it arises conditioned by twenty types of objects in the case of the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*).
The arising of visual consciousness should also be understood in this same way.
Therefore, while the five groups of consciousness can take both general and specific objects as their conditions,
there is no fault of the five consciousnesses apprehending a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
Although many phenomena possess their own specific characteristics, a single consciousness is able to take them as its object;
however, it does so without clarity. [Question: Does a body-consciousness arise based on the primary elements (mahābhūta) that serve as the support for the five sense-faculties?
[Answer: Some say: [it does].
It does not arise.
Just as the five material sense-faculties do not give rise to body-consciousness because they cannot be touched,
the same principle should apply to their supporting primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Question: If that is so, why is it said to be cognized by body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*)?
Answer: It is said to be cognized by body-consciousness in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), because it is the object of body-consciousness in a future lifetime.
However, there is no principle by which present [elements] could give rise to body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
Some say that,
with the exception of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) depends, all [other primary elements] are capable of giving rise to body-consciousness.
Because it is situated in immediate proximity to the basis of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), it cannot produce a body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
Nevertheless, because it is the objective sphere (*ālambana*) of another's body-consciousness,
it may also be designated as "cognized by body-consciousness."
Question: Of the eleven kinds of contact (*spraṣṭavya*), how many are in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and how many are in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
Answer: Two exist only in the desire realm.
That is to say, hunger and thirst.
Nine [types of touch] pertain to both the desire realm and the form realm.
Question: If there is heavy touch within the intermediate state (antarābhava) of the form realm, [how is this so]?
For what reason does the *Prajñapti-śāstra* state that the weight of clothing in Uttarakuru is one *liang*?
The garments of the Cāturmahārājakāyika devas weigh half a *liang*;
those of the Trāyastriṃśa devas weigh one *zhu*;
and the garments in the Yāma heaven weigh half a *zhu*.
The garments of the Tuṣita Heaven weigh one-fourth of a *liǎozhū*;
the garments of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven weigh one-eighth of a *liǎozhū*;
and the garments of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven weigh one-sixteenth of a *liǎozhū*.
"Are all these celestial garments of the higher realms indeed immeasurable? Some say:
"Although the garments of the form realm (rūpadhātu) are immeasurable, other objects therein are measurable."
Some say that although a single garment in that realm cannot be weighed, a collection of many garments can be weighed;
it is like how fine threads or light fur become heavy when accumulated.
Question: If there is the sensation of cold in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
why does the *Prajñapti-śāstra* further state that it is like the cold and warmth possessed by humans and the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
Is it the case that both [types] are absent in the higher realms?
Answer: Cold is of two kinds.
First, that which can provide benefit.
Second, they are capable of causing harm, yet there is nothing capable of harming them;
furthermore, they are capable of providing benefit.
Moreover, regarding what was said concerning cold and heat, these are entirely absent in the upper realms.
Does this statement mean that heat (uṣman) is also absent in that realm? If that were so,
then the primary elements (mahābhūta) there would consist of only three, yet they would still be capable of producing derived matter (upādāyarūpa) without lacking their functional efficacy.
Within the form realm (rūpadhātu), both cold and heat exist.
Question: Are the two tactile sensations of hunger and thirst of the nature of nourishment (aupacayika) or of uniform outflow (naiṣyandika)?
Regarding this [eye], it is a maturation (*vipāka*).
The Western Masters of the Gandhāra country state that it also includes the nurtured (*aupacayika*) and the outflowing (*naiṣyandika*).
It is not born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
because it can be interrupted by food and drink.
The Abhidharmikas do not admit that matter born of maturation, once interrupted, continues again.
Some say that hunger and thirst also pertain to that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
because their nature consists in the temporary cessation of food and drink rather than its permanent cessation.
There are two kinds of abandonment:
namely, permanent abandonment and temporary abandonment.
Permanent abandonment cannot be resumed; it is not temporary abandonment.
Just as in the hells, when a portion of the body is briefly severed,
the matter born of maturation (vipākaja-rūpa) is interrupted and then arises again;
so say the masters of the treatises from Kaśmīra.
When one is full, it cannot be perceived because it does not interrupt the obstruction of food and drink;
once the food and drink have been digested, it can again be perceived.
Question: If this is a result of maturation (*vipāka*),...
"Is it the fruit of wholesome karma or the fruit of unwholesome karma?
He replied, "It is the fruit of both kinds."
Therefore, hunger and thirst in the wealthy are the fruit of wholesome karma;
hunger and thirst in the poor are the fruit of unwholesome karma. Question: By which great elements (*mahābhūta*) are hunger and thirst produced?
Some say:
It is composed of the primary elements (mahābhūta) located at the side of the abdomen;
as stated in the *Garbha-vakrānti-sūtra*,
it exists within the mother's womb.
At times, around the navel of those sentient beings,
there arises through the maturation of karma a subtle wind;
from that very place, the primary elements (mahābhūta) capable of producing hunger and thirst come into being.
Other masters say that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) pervading all parts of the body produce hunger and thirst,
because at those times they cause agitation and affliction throughout the entire body.
