translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section Five: The Aggregate of the Great Elements (*Mahābhūta-skandha*). Part One of Two: The Sub-section on Derived Matter (*Upādāya-rūpa-nirdeśa*). The Bases of Derived Matter.
How many are with visibility?
How many are without visibility?
Question: Why is it not asked how many are with form and how many are without form?
The answer is that it is because the intention of the author of that treatise was such;
he composed the treatise according to his own intent.
However, as long as it does not contradict the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one should not criticize the fact that it was so stated.
Since there are no derived [phenomena] that are formless,
one cannot ask how many are with form and how many are formless;
likewise, there is no such question regarding the unconditioned.
Later, one should not ask how many are conditioned and how many are unconditioned;
nor should one answer such a question.
However, if one does so later, it should be understood that this is a statement made with further implications.
Some say: [The Buddha] intended to adorn the meaning with various phrases and various explanations so that it might be easily understood.
Furthermore, one wishes to mutually illustrate [the subject] through two gates, two steps, two summaries, two clarifications, two torches, two shadows, and two lights.
For instance, because that which is unconditioned is formless, it is not questioned.
In this way, because that which is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is without anything produced, it should not be questioned; yet,
just as one may question regarding that which is unconditioned and without anything produced,
so too should one question regarding that which is formless (arūpa), even though it is without anything produced.
In this way, these two approaches illustrate one another,
demonstrating that the logic of the preceding and succeeding questions and answers is consistent.
Other masters say:
Regarding this, among the various derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced by conceptualization (*vikalpa*), how many are visible (*sanidarśana*) and so forth?
Since the chapter has already raised "the various derived forms" as its subject matter,
why should one further ask how many possess form (*rūpin*) and so on?
The mention of "various forms" (rūpa) explicitly indicates that they possess form;
for the essence of form always carries the meaning of changeability and resistance.
Because they possess the characteristic of form, they are called "possessing form" (rūpin).
It is not like having clothes or having children.
Among the bases derived from the great elements, how many are visible?
Answer: One, namely the base of form (rūpāyatana).
Question: For what reason is the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) called "visible" (*sanidarśana*)?
Answer: Because the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) is called "seeing," it possesses the function of seeing;
since the form that is seen exists by virtue of the eye that can see it, the form-sphere is therefore called "visible."
If there is an owner or someone who sees it,
this can manifest the coarse characteristics of the sense base of form (*rūpāyatana*),
which can be manifested as having distinctions of appearance such as being "here" or "there."
Visible form (*sanidarśana*) is so called because it can be displayed;
it is like [the term] "name" (*nāman*), and so forth.
Alternatively, "visible" refers to those reflected images (*pratibimba*).
Only the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) can possess a reflected image and is therefore called "visible" (sanidarśana);
the others are not so. How many are invisible?
Answer: Eight [bases] and a portion of two.
The eight refer to the bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, sound, odor, and taste.
As for the portion of two:
That is to say, the sphere of tangibles and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Although all spheres of tangibles are included within the category of the invisible,
not all of them are derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
If derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) were also invisible, then this would be what is asked;
since it is not, it is said to be "partial. The same applies to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Among the bases derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), how many are resistant (*sapratigha*)?
Answer: Nine and a portion of one.
"Nine" refers to the five internal bases and the four external bases.
The "one part" refers to the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
Although all spheres of tangibles are included within the category of resistance (*sapratigha*),
not all of them are derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*).
If derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) were also characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*), this would be what is questioned;
since the rest are not what is questioned, it is said that "only a small portion" [is so].
How much is without resistance (*apratigha*)?
Answer: A small portion of one [base], namely the base of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Although all bases of mental phenomena are included within the non-resistant, not all of them are derived matter (bhautika-rūpa).
If derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) were also non-resistant (*apratigha*), it would be the subject of this inquiry while other things would not; therefore, only a portion is discussed.
However, there are three kinds of resistance (*pratigha*): first, resistance as obstruction (*āvaraṇa-pratigha*).
That is to say: first, the ten bases of form;
second, objective resistance, which refers to the five material sense faculties as well as the mind and mental factors;
third, resistance with respect to the object.
This refers to mind and mental factors.
Here, it is said that "obstructive resistance" (pratigha) pertains to these and not to others.
Among the great elements (mahābhūta) and their derivatives (upādāyarūpa), how many bases (āyatana) are with outflows (sāsrava)?
The answer is: a portion of nine and two.
"Nine" is as previously explained.
"A portion of two" refers to:

This refers to the sense base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) and the sense base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Although all instances of the sense base of tangibles are comprised within the category of being with outflows (*sāsrava*),
not all of them are derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*).
If derived matter were also with outflows (*sāsrava*),
it would be what is questioned here; since other things are not questioned, it is said to be "a small portion" rather than all bases of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
All are included within the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*).
Nor are all of them derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
If derived matter were also outflow-tainted, [then...]
Because this is what was asked and the rest was not, it is described in part.
How many are untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: One part, namely the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
It is not the case that all bases of phenomena (dharmāyatana) are comprised within the untainted (anāsrava),
nor is it the case that everything is derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
If derived matter were also untainted, [it would lead to logical fallacies].
Because this is what was asked and the rest was not, it is explained in brief. Question:
Among the great elements (mahābhūta) and the derived bases (upādāya-rūpa), how many are conditioned (saṃskṛta)?
Answer: Nine, and a portion of two.
The ninth is as previously explained.
Regarding the two partial portions:
these refer to the sense-base of tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana) and the sense-base of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Although all bases of tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana) are subsumed under the conditioned (saṃskṛta),
not all of them are derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
If derived matter were also conditioned, [then what?]
Because this is what was asked and other matters were not, I have spoken only in part.
Not all bases of phenomena (dharmāyatana) are comprised within the conditioned (saṃskṛta),
nor is everything therein derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
If derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is also conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), this is what is being asked;
since the rest are not being asked, it is said to be "a small portion.
How many are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
Answer: None.
Because they are all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Regarding the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*upādāyarūpa*), how many bases (*āyatana*) are past?
Answer: A portion of eleven, namely, excluding the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*).
Although all sense-bases of the eye (*cakṣurāyatana*) are comprised within derived matter (*bhautika*), [the others are not].
Yet not all [conditioned phenomena] exist in the past,
for some exist in the future and the present.
If that which is produced were also [exclusively] of the past, [it would follow that it does not exist].
Because this is what was asked and the rest was not, only a portion has been explained.
The same applies to the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, odors, and tastes.
Not all instances of the sense base of tangibles are comprised within derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Nor is it the case that all [factors] exist in the past.
If that which is produced were also [necessarily] of the past, then this would be what is asked;
since the remainder is not what is asked, only a partial portion is stated.
The same applies to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Just as it was stated for the past,
so too should it be stated for the future and the present.
Because there is equality in number and so forth.
Regarding the derived matter produced from the great elements, how many bases are wholesome?
Answer: Three partial portions.
This means that although the sense bases of form, sound, and mental objects are all subsumed under the category of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*),
not all of them are of a virtuous nature (*kuśala*).
If that which is derived were necessarily of a virtuous nature, [it would follow that all such things are virtuous].
Because this is what was asked and other matters were not, only a portion has been explained.
It is the same for the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*).
Not all spheres of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are comprised within the category of derived matter (*bhautika*).
Nor are all of them of a virtuous nature.
If that which is produced were exclusively of a virtuous nature, then this would be what is questioned;
since the remainder is not what is questioned, it is said to be "only a small portion."
How many are unwholesome?
Answer: Three partial aspects, as previously stated.
How many are indeterminate?
The answer is: a portion of seven and three.
"Seven" refers to the five internal bases (āyatana) and the bases of odor and taste.
"A portion of three" refers to...
This refers to the spheres of visible form, sound, and tangibles.
Although all spheres of visible form are subsumed under derived matter,
not all of them are indeterminate (avyākṛta).
If that which is produced is also unrecorded (avyākṛta), this is what is being questioned;
because other things are not being questioned, it is described as "a small portion.
The same applies to the sphere of sound (śabdāyatana).
Although all bases of tangibles are subsumed under the indeterminate,
not all of them are derived matter.
If that which is indeterminate were also derived matter, [then...]
Because this is what was asked and the rest was not, it is described in brief. Regarding the question:
"How many bases derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta) are bound to the desire realm?
The answer is: two and nine partial portions.
The second refers to the spheres of odor and taste.
The nine partial portions refer to the five internal spheres.
And as for the bases of visible form, sound, tangibles,
and mental phenomena: although all bases of the eye are comprised within derived matter,
not all of them are bound to the desire realm.
If that which is derived is also bound to the desire realm,
it is "a small portion" because this is what is being questioned while the rest is not.
The same applies to the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, and sounds.
Not all bases of tangibles are comprised within derived matter,
nor are all of them bound to the desire realm; however,
those that are derived matter and also bound to the desire realm [are as follows].
Because this is what was asked and the rest was not, it is described as "a small portion. The same applies to the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
How many are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta)?
Answer: A portion of nine is as previously stated.
How many are bound to the formless realm?
Answer: None.
Because they are formless.
Regarding the bases derived from the great elements, how many are trainee (śaikṣa)?
Answer: A small portion of one.
This refers to the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana). Not all spheres of phenomena are subsumed under what is to be learned (śaikṣa),
nor is everything therein derived (bhautika).
If that which is produced is also included within the *śaikṣa*,
then because this is what is being asked and the rest are not, it is said to be "only a small portion.
How many are *aśaikṣa*?
Answer: A small portion of one is as previously stated.
How many are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: Nine and a small portion of two.
The ninth refers to the five internal bases and a small portion of the four external bases.

That is to say, the sense-sphere of tangibles and the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Although all instances of the sense-sphere of tangibles are comprised within what is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*),
not all of them are derived matter (*bhautika*).
If it were both neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee and something produced,
then that which is asked here would be distinct from what is not asked, and thus only a partial portion would be stated.
This is because not all bases of phenomena (dharmāyatana) are subsumed under the category of being neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
Nor is it the case that everything is derived;
for if that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner were also derived,
[it would follow that it is conditioned].
Because this is what is being asked and the rest is not, it is stated in brief:
"Regarding the bases derived from the great elements, how many are abandoned by vision?
Answer: None.
Because there are certainly no material forms that are abandoned through seeing.
How many are abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: Nine and a small portion of two.
The ninth is as previously explained.
Regarding the "two partials," these refer to the sense base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) and the sense base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Although all bases of tangibles are included within what is abandoned by cultivation,
not all of them are derived matter.
If that which is abandoned by cultivation were also derived matter, [it would follow that]...
Because this is what was asked and other matters were not, only a partial explanation has been given.
Not all bases of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are subsumed under what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
nor is everything [therein] derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
If that which is abandoned by cultivation is also derived, this is what is being questioned;
since the remainder is not being questioned, it is said to be "a small portion.
How many are not abandoned?
Answer: A small portion of one, namely the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
It is not that all spheres of phenomena are subsumed under "non-interruption" (anupaccheda).
Nor is it the case that all [phenomena] are derived.
If one were to say that whatever is derived is also non-interruption, this would be what is questioned;
since the remainder is not what is questioned, only a partial portion is stated.
If one accomplishes the primary elements (mahābhūta), does one also accomplish the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) produced by them?
Answer: All who accomplish the primary elements also accomplish the derived matter.
There are those who possess derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) but not the primary elements (mahābhūta),
namely, the noble ones (ārya) born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Who possesses both the primary elements and derived matter?
This refers to all sentient beings of the desire and form realms;
this is the general statement.
To speak of them specifically:
There are some sentient beings who possess many primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and many derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*);
there are also some sentient beings who...
That which consists of few primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and few derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*),
and that which consists of many primary elements and many derived matter,
is like the physical forms obtained by various sentient beings within the great ocean.
Their bodies may measure one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, five, six, seven, or eight hundred *yojanas* in size,
as vast as the physical form obtained by the asura king Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Just as the physical form attained in Akaniṣṭha is sixteen thousand yojanas in measure,
so too are the few primary elements and the few derived matter therein established.
They are like mosquitoes, gnats, aquatic insects, and so forth, down to the most minute beings that are beyond the range of the human eye.
Question: For what reason are noble ones born in the formless realm?
Is it only that one achieves derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) but not the primary elements (mahābhūta)?
Answer: Because in that realm there is no form, and furthermore, one does not achieve the primary elements of another realm.
Because one abandons tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena by transcending stages, derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) is not like this;
since it also pertains to the untainted (*anāsrava*), it is accomplished across different stages.
There is no noble one (*ārya*) who does not accomplish untainted discipline (*anāsrava-śīla*).
Therefore, when a Noble One is born in that realm, they possess only derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Among these, one who is a trainee (*śaikṣa*) possesses the matter that evolves in accordance with the trainee state (*śaikṣānuparivartin-rūpa*),
while one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) possesses the matter that evolves in accordance with the state beyond training (*aśaikṣānuparivartin-rūpa*).
If one does not possess the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), does one also not possess the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)?
Answer: All those who do not possess derived matter [also do not possess the primary elements].
They do not possess the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
There are those who do not possess the great elements but do possess derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*);
namely, those noble ones (*ārya*) born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Who does not achieve derived matter and the primary elements?
It refers to all ordinary beings born in the formless realm,
because there is no matter whatsoever in that realm.

Furthermore, because one has not yet attained the form of the lower realms, and because all contaminated forms are lost when one is born in the higher [realms], and because one has not yet acquired uncontaminated forms there.
Question: What is not included within the preceding statement?
Furthermore, is it necessary to establish a "concordant subsequent phrase"?
The answer is: within the "concordant preceding phrase," there is included all sentient beings of the desire and form realms, as well as all noble ones (ārya) of the formless realm.
This does not yet include all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
In order to include them, a subsequent phrase is established:
"If one possesses the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), does one possess their wholesome matter (*kuśalarūpa*)?"
It can be answered with four propositions.
There are cases where one possesses the primary elements (mahābhūta) but not virtuous matter (kuśala-rūpa);
this refers to those dwelling within an eggshell.
If ordinary beings dwell within the womb,
or if they are born in the desire realm and abide in non-restraint,
or in neither restraint nor non-restraint.
There is no virtuous bodily or vocal intimation;
even if it existed, it would have been lost.
In that place, within the eggshell.
Regarding the informative and non-informative matter belonging to previous lives while dwelling in the womb,
all of it has already been relinquished due to the loss of its basis, namely the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*);
furthermore, at this stage, one is currently unable to produce informative matter.
Furthermore, because there is no entry into a fixed state of concentration, one does not accomplish any wholesome form (*rūpa*).
Question: Why is it that in this stage one is unable to give rise to informative action (*vijñapti*)?
The answer is: because the body upon which it relies is extremely weak;
for it is only when the body is robust that one can initiate manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*).
Furthermore, it is because the mind in this state is extremely feeble.
A mind that is coarse and predominant can produce manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*).
Furthermore, because the mind in this state operates internally,
whereas manifest karma is produced by a mind that operates externally.
Furthermore, in this stage, the embryo is so cramped within the womb that it cannot even move,
let alone produce informative action (*vijñapti*).
However, there are times when the fetus moves about.
This is due to the power of the wind and is not produced by the mind.
Manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) must necessarily arise through the power of the mind.
Question: For what reason is there no entry into the state of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) at this stage?
Answer: Because in this stage both body and mind are equally weak and inferior;
furthermore, because there is no causal condition for the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of entering meditative absorption;
and because one who has attained patience (*kṣānti*) relinquishes that patience at the end of life.
As was already extensively determined in the preceding *Karmaskandha*,
the detailed exposition of the four modes of birth (*yoni*) is likewise as in the *Karmaskandha*.

If one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and dwells in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), or in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint (*naivasaṃvara-nāsaṃvara*), and lacks wholesome bodily or vocal intimation (*vijñapti*):
This refers to those who, due to sleep, intoxication, or fainting,
as well as through the relinquishing of application, do not seek to initiate manifest action;
or even if such action exists, they lose it.
It is said that it is lost due to three conditions:
first, the cessation of the intention;
second, the relinquishing of the application.
The three limits of momentum have passed;
this is also explained in detail in the *Karmaskandha*.
There is the accomplishment of wholesome form (*rūpa*) without the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
This refers to noble beings born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Because they are noble beings, they possess wholesome form; because they are born in the formless realm, they do not possess the primary elements (mahābhūta).
Those noble ones consist of both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Those in training accomplish the wholesome form of one in training;
those beyond training accomplish the wholesome form of one beyond training.
There are those who possess both the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and wholesome form (*kuśalarūpa*),
namely: noble ones (*ārya*) dwelling within the womb,
or those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who abide in restraint (*saṃvara*).
If one abides in non-restraint,
or in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and currently possesses virtuous bodily and vocal intimation.
Alternatively, it may have existed previously and not been lost.
For instance, in the case of a noble one born in the form realm who remains in the womb,
they will certainly possess both contaminated and uncontaminated non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), because the power of the path is so strong.
If one is born in the desire realm and dwells in restraint, this refers to dwelling in whichever of the three types of restraint is appropriate;
or dwelling in non-restraint; or dwelling in neither restraint nor non-restraint.
Those who currently possess virtuous bodily and vocal intimation are those who are neither sleeping nor intoxicated.
Without becoming despondent and without abandoning their application,
they seek to give rise to manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*).
Alternatively, there may be those who previously possessed it and have not lost it;
this is due to the three conditions as explained before.
Furthermore, if one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they necessarily possess the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*).
There are instances where wholesome form exists but is not accomplished by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
This refers to ordinary beings born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
because they are born in the formless realm, they do not accomplish the primary elements.
Because tainted wholesome form is abandoned by transcending the realm, and untainted wholesome form has not yet been attained;
and if one possesses the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), does one possess unwholesome form?
Answer: All who possess unwholesome form [possess the primary elements].
That concentration necessarily accomplishes the primary elements (mahābhūta).
There are those who accomplish the primary elements but do not possess unwholesome matter (akuśala-rūpa).
This refers to those dwelling within an eggshell or residing in the womb,
as well as those born in the desire realm who abide in restraint,
or in neither restraint nor non-restraint.
There are no unwholesome bodily or vocal intimation;
even if they existed, they have been lost.
This is the case if one is born in the form realm.
That is to say, one who possesses unwholesome form necessarily exists in the desire realm;
for there is no one in the desire realm who does not possess the great elements, as they must necessarily have a body.
By this, it is established as a "concordant subsequent phrase" (anuloma-paścātpādaka).
The answer and explanation for the remaining phrases should be understood by analogy with what precedes.
If one accomplishes the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), does one also possess obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter?
Answer: All who accomplish obscured-unspecified matter necessarily accomplish the primary elements.
There are those who possess the great elements but do not possess obscured-unspecified matter;
namely, those born in the desire realm or those born in the form realm who currently lack obscured-unspecified bodily or vocal intimation.
That is to say, if one possesses obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) form, one necessarily resides in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
This is because there is no one in the realm of form who does not possess the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), as they must have a body.
For this reason, it constitutes a "consequent" (or "subsequent") phrase.
Answer: There is no arising of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) informative action (*vijñapti*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This is because wholesome and defiled informative actions depend upon the bodies of oneself or others.
If one possesses the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), does one also possess unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes unobscured-neutral matter, does one also accomplish its primary elements?
The answer is: "It is so.

This is because one who possesses the primary elements (mahābhūta) necessarily possesses the body-faculty (kāyendriya) and so forth, and one who possesses the body-faculty and so forth necessarily possesses the primary elements.
All sentient beings born in the desire and form realms possess both the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter;
those born in the formless realm possess neither of these two.
If one is endowed with the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), is one also endowed with wholesome or unwholesome form?
Answer: There are those who are endowed with the primary elements but not with wholesome or unwholesome form;
namely, those dwelling within an eggshell.
If ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) dwell within the womb,
or if they are born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and abide in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline (naivasaṃvara-nāsaṃvara),
and possess no virtuous or non-virtuous bodily or vocal intimation (vijñapti).
There is the case where something exists but is lost.
There are those who possess the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and also wholesome form (*kuśala-rūpa*), yet not unwholesome form (*akuśala-rūpa*);
namely, those noble ones (*ārya*) dwelling within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and abides in restraint,
there are no unwholesome bodily or vocal manifest actions;
even if they were present, they have been lost.
If one abides in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and currently possesses virtuous bodily or vocal intimation,
or previously possessed it and has not lost it.
There are no unwholesome bodily or vocal intimation;
even if they existed, they would have been lost.
If one is born in the form realm, one possesses the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
It is also neither unwholesome matter nor wholesome matter;
that is to say, one born in the desire realm who dwells in non-restraint and lacks wholesome bodily or vocal intimation.
Suppose there is possession [of non-restraint] which is lost;
that is, one who abides in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint currently possesses unwholesome bodily and vocal intimation.
Either there was previously [an unmanifest action] that has not been lost,
or there is no wholesome bodily or vocal manifest action; or,
even if it existed, it has been lost.
There are those who possess both the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and wholesome or unwholesome form.
This refers to one born in the desire realm who abides in restraint (*saṃvara*),
and who currently possesses unwholesome bodily or vocal intimation (*vijñapti*), or who previously possessed it and has not lost it.
If one abides in non-restraint,
there currently exists a virtuous bodily or vocal intimation,
or one previously possessed that has not been lost.
If one abides in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and there currently exists a virtuous or non-virtuous bodily or vocal intimation,
or such an intimation previously existed and has not been lost.
If one accomplishes wholesome or unwholesome matter, does one also accomplish its primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Answer: It is so.
That is to say, one who accomplishes wholesome or unwholesome matter necessarily resides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because those in the desire realm necessarily possess the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
If one possesses the primary elements, does one also possess wholesome or obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter?
Answer: There are cases where one possesses the primary elements but does not possess wholesome or obscured-unspecified matter.
This refers to those dwelling within an eggshell;
or various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) abiding in the womb;
or those born in the desire realm who abide in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), or in neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint (*naivasaṃvara-nāsaṃvara*).
There are no wholesome bodily or vocal informative intimation (*vijñapti*).
Even if they existed, they have been lost.
There is the possession of primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as well as wholesome matter, but not obscured-unspecified matter.
This refers to noble ones dwelling within the womb,
whether they are born in the desire realm and abide in restraint,
or abide in non-restraint, or abide in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint.
There currently exists a wholesome bodily or vocal intimation,
or one previously possessed that has not been lost;
or, if born in the form realm, there is currently no obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) bodily or vocal intimation.
There are those who possess both the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and wholesome or obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter;
namely, those born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) who currently manifest obscured-unspecified bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*).
If one possesses wholesome or obscured-unspecified matter, does one also possess its primary elements?
The answer is: so it is.
That is to say, one who possesses wholesome or obscured-unspecified matter necessarily exists in the form realm;
for those existing in the form realm invariably possess the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
If one accomplishes the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), does one also accomplish wholesome or non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) form?
Answer: There are those who accomplish the primary elements and also non-obscured-neutral form, but not wholesome form.
That is to say: those dwelling within an eggshell;
or various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) dwelling within the womb;
or those born in the desire realm who abide in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Furthermore, for those who possess neither restraint nor non-restraint,
there are no virtuous bodily or vocal intimation;
even if they existed, they have been lost.
There are those who possess both the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and wholesome or non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter;
namely, noble ones (*ārya*) dwelling within the womb,
or those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who abide in restraint (*saṃvara*).
If one abides in non-restraint,
or in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and currently possesses wholesome bodily or vocal intimation.
Or, it may have existed previously and not been lost;
for instance, if one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu),
even if one possesses wholesome and non-obscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) matter.
Are those great elements [also possessed]? Answer: Yes.
That is to say, one who possesses wholesome or non-obscured-neutral matter.
They must exist in the desire realm and the form realm.
This is because those who exist in the desire and form realms necessarily possess the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
If one accomplishes the great elements, does one also accomplish unwholesome or obscured-unneutral matter?
Answer: No.
This is because one who accomplishes unwholesome matter must necessarily reside in the desire realm.
One who possesses obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter necessarily exists in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
because no sentient being is born simultaneously in two realms.
If one possesses the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), does one also possess that [matter] which is unwholesome (*akuśala*) or unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)?
Answer: There are those who possess the primary elements (mahābhūta) and also unobscured-neutral matter (anivṛtāvyākṛtarūpa),
but not unwholesome matter (akuśalarūpa).
This refers to those dwelling within an eggshell,
those residing in the womb,
or those born in the desire realm who abide in restraint.
And for those who possess neither restraint nor non-restraint,
there are no unwholesome bodily or vocal intimation;
even if they existed, they have been lost.
If one is born in the form realm and possesses the primary elements (*mahābhūta*),
they also possess unwholesome and non-obscured-neutral matter;
that is to say, one who is born in the desire realm and abides in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
If one abides in restraint,
or in neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint,
and currently possesses unwholesome bodily or vocal intimation.
Or, if one previously possessed [them] without losing them, does one who has accomplished unwholesome or non-obscured-neutral matter also possess its primary elements?
Answer: It is so.
That is to say, one who accomplishes unwholesome or non-obscured-neutral matter [also possesses its primary elements].
It must exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This is because those in the desire realm necessarily possess the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
If one possesses the primary elements, does one also possess obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter?
Answer: There are those who possess the primary elements (mahābhūta) and also unobscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) matter,
but not obscured-neutral (nivṛtāvyākṛta) matter.
That is to say, one who is born in the desire realm,
or one who is born in the form realm,
currently lacks manifest obscured-unspecified bodily and vocal informative intimation.
There is one who possesses the primary elements (mahābhūta) as well as obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) and unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) matter; that is,
one born in the form realm who currently possesses obscured-unspecified bodily and vocal intimation (vijñapti).
If one achieves obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) or unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter, does one also achieve its primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Answer: It is so.
That is to say, whoever achieves these two types of unspecified matter [also achieves their primary elements].
It must exist in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

One who exists in the form realm necessarily possesses the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). If one possesses the primary elements, does one also possess wholesome, unwholesome, or obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter?
Answer: No. That is to say, one who possesses wholesome or unwholesome form necessarily exists in the desire realm;
whereas one who possesses wholesome or obscured-unspecified form [necessarily exists in the form realm].
It must exist in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
because no sentient being is born simultaneously in two realms.
If one possesses the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Does he possess wholesome, unwholesome, or non-obscured-neutral matter?
Answer: There is one who possesses the primary elements (mahābhūta) and also possesses non-obscured-neutral matter.
It refers to non-virtuous and non-non-virtuous form,
namely that which exists within an eggshell or when ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) dwell within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and dwells in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline,
and lacks wholesome or unwholesome bodily or vocal intimation— or even if such exists,
it has been lost— [one does not possess the restraint].
There are those who possess the great elements as well as wholesome and non-obscured-neutral matter,
but not unwholesome matter;
namely, those noble ones dwelling within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and abides in restraint,
there are no unwholesome bodily or vocal intimation;
even if they existed, they have been lost.
If one abides in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and there currently exists a virtuous bodily or vocal intimation,
or one previously possessed that has not been lost.
There are no unwholesome bodily or vocal intimation;
even if they existed, they would have been lost.
If one is born in the form realm, one possesses the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Furthermore, there is unwholesome and non-obscured-neutral form that is not wholesome form;
this refers to one born in the desire realm who dwells in non-restraint and lacks wholesome bodily and vocal intimation.
There is the case where it exists but has been lost:
if one abides in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline,
and currently possesses unwholesome bodily or vocal intimation.
Either there was previously [a state] that has not been lost,
or there is no wholesome bodily or vocal intimation; or,
even if it existed, it has been lost.
There is one who accomplishes both the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and wholesome, unwholesome, or non-obscured-neutral matter;
namely, one born in the desire realm who abides in restraint and currently possesses unwholesome bodily or vocal manifest action (*vijñapti*).
Or, there may be that which was previously acquired and not lost;
for example, one who dwells in non-restraint currently possesses virtuous bodily and vocal informative intimation (*vijñapti*).
Or, there may be that which was previously acquired and not lost;
namely, when one abides in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline,
and currently possesses wholesome or unwholesome bodily or vocal informative intimation (*vijñapti*).
Or perhaps they were previously possessed and have not been lost.
If one possesses wholesome, unwholesome, or non-obscured-neutral matter,
does one also possess its primary elements?
Answer: It is so.
That is to say, one who accomplishes these three types of form must necessarily reside in the desire realm.
Because those in the desire realm necessarily possess the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
If one possesses the primary elements, does one also possess wholesome, obscured-unspecified, or unobscured-unspecified matter?
