Sub-section One: The Chapter on Derived Matter (*Upādāya-rūpa-nirdeśa*). Part Four. Question: Regarding these four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*)...
How many [factors] draw forth that which is to be (bhaviṣyat) and cause it to manifest?
How many sustain the present existence (vartamāna-bhava) and cause it to continue?
Regarding this, some say:
First, it draws forth that which is to be (bhaviṣyat), causing it to manifest before one;
this refers to the nutriment of mental volition (manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra).
Third, it sustains the present existence, causing it to continue and abide.
This refers to the other three nutriments.
Some say that two of them draw forth future existence.
This refers to mental volition and consciousness.
The other two sustenances maintain present existence. Other masters say: [the remaining two sustenances maintain future existence].
The three that draw forth future existence are contact,
volition, and consciousness;
the one that sustains present existence is [craving].
Regarding what is called "edible food" (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra): according to this teaching,
all four types of nutriment draw forth future existence and cause it to manifest in the present.
All sustenance maintains what currently exists so that it continues to abide.
Question: Regarding all types of sustenance and existence (*bhava*), how many cause what has not yet arisen to arise, and how many nourish what has already arisen?
Some say: among the various nutriments that sustain existence,
one causes that which has not yet arisen to arise.
That is to say, the food of mental volition nourishes those who have already been born;
that is to say, the remaining three foods.
Furthermore, there are those who say that two [factors] cause what has not yet arisen to arise,
namely: mental volition and consciousness.
The two [nutriments] nourish what has already been born;
these refer to the other two nutriments.
Other masters say:
Third, causing that which has not yet arisen to arise—
namely, contact, volition, and consciousness—
and nourishing that which has already arisen.
Regarding what is called "edible food":
as it is thus taught, these four types of sustenance cause that which has not yet arisen to arise within existence,
and cause that which has already arisen to grow and flourish.
Question: Among the various foods, which food predominates in nourishing which phenomena?

Answer: Because edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) is superior in nourishing the sense faculties and the primary elements (mahābhūta), it predominates in nourishing the sense faculties and the primary elements.
Because the nutriment of contact nourishes the mind and mental factors more preeminently,
it is particularly predominant as a nutriment for the mind and mental factors.
Because the nutriment of volition nourishes future existence more preeminently, [it is particularly predominant as a nutriment for future existence].
Regarding all forms of nutriment for future existence (*punarbhava*), the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) is predominant, because it is superior in nourishing name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Regarding all name-and-form, the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) is predominant. As it is said: "The meaning of 'drawing forth' (*ākṣepa*) is the meaning of 'nutriment' (*āhāra*)," and so forth.
Does this statement mean "cause" (hetu) or does it mean "condition" (pratyaya)? If so,
what fault would there be?
Both positions entail faults.
If it means "cause," then external odors, tastes, and tangibles lack all five causes within the internal sense bases;
how, then, could they function as nutriment?
If it is in the sense of being an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), then with the exception of its own internal nature,
all other phenomena are equally this predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Why, then, are only four types designated as "nutriments" (*āhāra*)?
Some say that "having" (sa-) has the meaning of "cause.
Question: If that were so, then external odors, tastes, and tangibles would lack all five causes in relation to the internal sense bases.
What constitutes nutriment?
The answer is: external odors, tastes, and tangibles act as the causes for the arousal of cognition, enabling internal odors and so forth to function as the actual process of eating.
The internal [objects] of odor, flavor, and tangibility are called "nutriments" (āhāra) because they possess the sense of being causes for the internal bases;
that is to say, the eye has only the sphere of tangibility as its nutriment.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, and sounds.
Odor takes the odor-base and the tangible-base as its nutriment;
taste takes the taste-base and the tangible-base as its nutriment.
The sense-base of tangibles takes only the sense-base of tangibles as its nutriment;
the mind and mental factors take three nutriments as their nutriment.
Regarding this, the meaning of "cause" should be reflected upon according to reason.
Some say that this has the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*).
Question: If that is so, [then] excluding its own internal nature (*svabhāva*), [what remains]?
All other phenomena are likewise predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for these;
why, then, are only four types designated as "nutriments" (*āhāra*)?
Answer: Because they are the predominant conditions for the internal sense bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
There are those who are close and those who are distant; there are those who are near and those who are far;
there are those with whom one is in harmony and those with whom one is not.
There are those in this life and there are those in other lives;
all are brought together through intimacy.
That which arises in this life is said to be nutriment;
that which is remote and does not pertain to other lives is not said to be nutriment.
Therefore, there are only four kinds of nutriment.
All four of these can function as nutriment with respect to the twelve internal bases (*āyatana*).
Nevertheless, there are variations in their intensity and subtlety, as previously described.
Question: Why is the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) not established as nutriment?
Some say it is because it lacks the characteristic of nutriment.

Some say that when the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is grasped, if it is coarse and heavy at the time of grasping, it is not called "nutriment" (*āhāra*); rather, that which is subtle and light at the time of grasping is called nutriment,
because it must be subtle and light in order to nourish the body.
Some say that the sense-sphere of visible form is apprehended without reaching it,
whereas food is apprehended only by reaching it.
It is not the case that what is not the body constitutes the act of eating;
some say that the function of eating is only accomplished when the sense-sphere of form reaches the stage of transformation and decay.
That is to say: being rotted by immersion in water,
transformed by ripening through fire,
and shaken by wind.
Only then does it become food;
that which has been prepared but has not yet undergone transformation of its physical form cannot be designated as food.
Therefore, visible form is not nutriment, whereas odors and so forth are not like that.
Other masters say:
"If visible form were nutriment..."
"When seeing forms with the eye, one should eliminate hunger and thirst;
if this were so, the expenditure by the donor would be in vain.
Others further say:
If form were food,
then when those who have gone forth see forms with their eyes, they would be transgressing the rule of abstaining from eating at improper times.
Or, as some say:
If form were food, then the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) would have to consume edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), because they take up various forms.
One should know that what is said regarding the latter three [objects] contradicts reason;
for odors and tangibles would likewise incur such faults.
It should be understood that what was stated regarding the first four [nutriments] is correct.
Question: If form (*rūpa*) is not a nutriment, how is the sutra to be reconciled?
As the Blessed One said:
"Householder, the food you have offered is excellent,
possessing perfect color, fragrance, and flavor. He replied,
"Though it possesses color, it is not food."
It is in order to inspire the intention of the donor that the Buddha spoke thus;
that is to say, when the Buddha praised the food being offered,
the donor would then give rise to a sublime intention and aspiration.
"How wonderful that the Tathāgata has praised and accepted my food!
I shall surely obtain extraordinary merit and benefit.
[The Buddha] asked: "If you praise physical form, yet physical form is not food, what is it?"
Furthermore, it would follow that fragrances and so forth should also not be considered food;
since those are food, these should be as well. The answer is:
in this context, the Buddha did not intend to make a distinction between what is food and what is not food.
It is merely intended to inspire the donor’s intention and resolve that this sūtra be preached.
If this praise were itself the food, then that which is not praised would necessarily not be food.
Question: What is the meaning of "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*)?
Answer: It is called edible food because it is consumed in distinct morsels (*kavaḍa*).
Question: If that is so, are things such as drinks and suckles not edible food?
Answer: Since this is stated from the perspective of the majority, there is no fault.
Furthermore, some say that even during the acts of drinking and sucking, one forms distinct segments [of the food].
Other masters say that it is explained from the beginning: namely,
at the time of the first eon, human beings partook of the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa).
Because all [foods] are divided into portions and then swallowed and consumed, they are called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Question: The Buddha taught that edible food is both coarse and subtle;
how should one understand the distinction between the coarse and the subtle?
The *Saṃgītiparyāya* answers:
edible food is to be understood through the mutual relativity of its coarse and subtle aspects;
that is to say, among aquatic creatures, the small serve as food for the large.
The relative coarseness and subtlety established through mutual dependence is as follows:
for example, what is eaten by a *timitimiṅgila* is coarse,
while what is eaten by a *timitimiṅgila* is subtle.
What the *Ḍimbhaka* demons eat is coarse;
what the *Ḍimbas* eat is fine;
what the *Ḍimbhas* eat is coarse.
That which is eaten by large fish, turtles, tortoises, makaras, śiśumāras, and so forth is subtle;
that which is eaten by large fish, turtles, and the like is coarse.
That which is eaten by other aquatic insects is subtle.
Among the various terrestrial species, that which is eaten by elephants, horses, camels, and the like is coarse;
that which is eaten by sheep, deer, pigs, and the like is subtle.
For sheep, deer, pigs, and the like, what they eat is coarse.
That which is eaten by rabbits, cats, and wildcats is subtle;
that which is eaten by rabbits, cats, and wildcats is coarse.
That which is eaten by other land-dwelling insects is subtle.
Among the various garuḍas of the kṣatriya lineage, that which is consumed is coarse;
whereas that which is consumed by geese, swans, peacocks, parrots, śārikas, and jīvañjīvaka birds is fine.
That which is eaten by geese, swans, peacocks, and the like is coarse;
that which is eaten by other sky-dwelling creatures is subtle. Some say this.
If sentient beings take grass, wood, and the like as food, what they consume is coarse;
if they take cakes, rice, and the like as food, what they consume is subtle.
Other masters say that what is eaten by those who consume food such as cakes and rice is coarse,
while what is consumed by those who eat ghee, oil, and the like is subtle.
Others further state that the swallowing of food through the mouth is coarse,
while its entry through the pores of the navel is subtle.
That is to say, for all sentient beings within the womb, food enters through the navel;
however, for Bodhisattvas alone, food enters through all the pores of the skin.
Some have said this:
If, after having eaten it, there is a subsequent outflow (*niṣyanda*), this food is coarse;
if there is no subsequent outflow, this food is subtle,
such as the taste and fragrance of *sudhā* used as food.
Question: Do the nutriments of contact, volition, and consciousness have coarse and subtle aspects?
If they do, why does the Sūtra speak only of edible food as having coarse and subtle aspects?
If they do not, why is it that only edible food has coarse and subtle aspects, and not the others?
Answer: The nutriments of contact, volition, and consciousness also have coarse and subtle aspects, because they are mutually relative according to their realms and stages.
That is to say, the desire realm is coarse, while the form realm is subtle.
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) is coarse;
the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is subtle.
The first dhyāna is coarse.
The second dhyāna is subtle;
up to the sphere of nothingness, it is coarse;
and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is subtle.
Question: If that is so, why does the sūtra not state it?
Answer: When something should have been stated but is not, one should know that the meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*). Some say:
The sūtra mentions the first to indicate the subsequent;
it has already been stated that edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) has both coarse and subtle aspects, and one should know that the other types of food likewise have coarse and subtle aspects.
It is said that edible food [is categorized] by way of four causes and conditions.
Because [the former] exists in varying degrees, its coarseness or subtlety can be known;
the remaining food is not so,
because it is sought after in a single manner.
Second, because of accumulation;
third, because of enjoyment;
fourth, because of outflow.
Regarding "due to pursuit":
this refers to the fact that sentient beings pursue edible food,
whether in great or small measure.
That which is sought in great quantity is coarse; that which is sought in small quantity is subtle.

Regarding "due to accumulation," this means that among sentient beings, there is much or little accumulated in their consumption of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); that which is accumulated in great quantity is coarse, and that which is accumulated in small quantity is subtle.
Regarding "by way of enjoyment":
this refers to the fact that sentient beings enjoy solid food (kavaḍīkārāhāra) in varying degrees—some more and some less.
That which is enjoyed in greater measure is coarse; that which is enjoyed in lesser measure is subtle.

Regarding "because of being a result of uniform outflow" (*niṣyanda*): this means that among sentient beings, there are those for whom the uniform outflow of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is great and those for whom it is small.
For those whose uniform outflow is great, what they eat is coarse; for those whose uniform outflow is small, what they eat is subtle.
Some say: In relation to the various sense bases (*āyatana*), edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) can be described as coarse or subtle, whereas other foods cannot.
That is to say, in relation to visible form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*), odor (*gandha*), taste (*rasa*), and tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) can be described as subtle.

In relation to the mental objects (dharmas), they may be described as coarse; however, these three—contact, volition, and consciousness—are subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Among all the spheres, these are subtle and not coarse; since there is no other relative standard for comparison, they are not described as coarse or subtle.
Question: In which realms are there how many nutriments?
Answer: In the desire realm, all four types of nutriment are present, with the nutriment of physical food being predominant;
in the form realm, there are three.
The nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) predominates [in the first dhyāna].
In the formless realms (*ārūpya*), there are likewise three [nutriments];
however, in the lower three formless realms, the nutriment of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*) predominates.
In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) predominates.
Some say that in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*) also predominates.
Because a single volition can induce a lifespan as the fruit of eighty thousand kalpas.
Question: How many types of nutriment exist in which realms of existence?
Answer: All four are present in the hells.
The nutriment of consciousness (vijñānāhāra) is predominant there.
Question: What kind of edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra) exists within the hells?
Answer: They drink molten copper.
They swallow hot iron balls as their segmentary food (kavaḍīkārāhāra).
[The interlocutor] asks: "Now, that which serves as food must provide some nourishment and benefit."
When this substance enters the body, it burns the lips, tongue, palate, throat, chest, and abdomen;
having passed through from below, its flames increase in intensity until the entire body is scorched.
How can this be called food?
Answer: Although it is for the purpose of burning away afflictions, it possesses the characteristic of food because, when it first enters the body, it temporarily removes hunger and thirst.
Animals possess all four [types of nutriment].
Because there are distinctions in their types, locations, and dimensions, one or another [of these four] predominates; thus,
the realm of hungry ghosts (preta-gati) possesses all four.
The craving for food increases particularly.
It was once heard that when the Venerable Pūrṇa was about to enter the city of Puṣkaravatī for the sake of alms, he [encountered this].
Before the city gate, he suddenly saw an old female hungry ghost (preta).
He asked her, "Why are you standing here now? The female ghost replied in turn, "Does your reverence see me?"
The Honored One replied thus.
The female ghost then said,
"My husband has entered the city hoping that there might be some elder or other person in this city with a festering, ulcerated abscess."
"Previously, when we were squeezed together, we would take the pus and blood and eat it together;
for that reason, I am staying here now to wait.
Furthermore, I ask you: how long has it been since your husband entered?"
The ogress replied,
"Deluded by hunger and thirst, I do not remember how long it has been since my husband entered the city;
however, I do recall this great river on the outskirts of the city."
He moved seven times to the south of the city and seven times to the north of the city;
even now he has not returned.
The Venerable One, feeling pity and distress, departed.
Thus, this female ghost has maintained her bodily continuity for a long time through the hope of food; therefore,
one knows that the craving for food is particularly intense in the realm of ghosts.
Humans and the gods of the desire realm all possess the four types of nutriment;
however, among them, edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) is predominant.
As for the gods of the form and formless realms, it is as explained in their respective sections.
Question: In which mode of birth are there how many nutriments?
Answer: In the egg-born, all four are present, with the nutriment of contact being predominant.
Some say that the nutriment of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*) is predominant. How is this known?
As it is stated in the *Saṃgītiparyāya*.
There is a beast in the ocean that occasionally emerges onto the shore;
there it lays its eggs among the sandbars,
buries them with sand, and returns to the sea.
While remaining within the eggshell,
because he recollects his mother, his body does not decay;
that is to say, he recollects the tactile sensations she experienced when she first incubated him with warmth.
If she forgets her mother, her body will immediately rot and decay.
Other masters say that if the mother keeps the child within the egg in mind, the egg will not perish.
If the mother were to forget them, those eggs would perish;
this is not reasonable. Why is that?
Do not think that other types of food can sustain one's life;
therefore, what was stated previously is logically sound.
Those born from a womb possess all four [nutriments].
In the case of egg-born beings, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) predominates;
in moisture-born beings, all four types of nutriment are present;
and in mind-born beings, contact-nutriment (*sparśa-āhāra*) predominates.
Those born by transformation possess all four [nutriments],
yet one or another predominates due to differences in their species, location, and physical constitution.
Regarding the term "food" as it has been explained, there are two distinctions:
first, the conventional;
second, the ultimate.
The conventional is as it is spoken of in the world:
for example, "a vessel with leftover food" and "a vessel without leftover food," or as the world speaks of "the food of a city."
That is to say: "This food comes from the city of Śrāvastī; this food comes from the city of Takṣaśilā;
this food comes from the city of Sāketa;
this food comes from the palace of Śānti."
In this manner, as the praisers also speak of the names of various foods,
such as the *cātaka*-food and the *mudita*-food.
These are the foods praised by the Buddha,
such as the fourfold food and so forth,
as further explained in the sūtras.
Regarding "eating in accordance with" and "eating in opposition to": as for eating in accordance,
it is as the Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus, you should know that all things have nourishment.
For instance, when the heavens send down torrential rain with its drops pouring down in great torrents,
the mountain streams and valleys are the first to become completely filled."
When the mountain torrents and valleys are full, the small streams and brooks are filled;
when the small streams and brooks are full,
the large channels and ravines are filled.
When the great ravines and gullies are full,
the small rivers and streams are filled.
When the small rivers and streams are full, [the larger rivers are filled].
The great rivers become full;
once the great rivers are full,
the great ocean becomes filled.
Regarding the statement on "food that is contrary":
as the World-Honored One said,
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there are all kinds of food."
The great ocean has its nutriment,
namely the great rivers.
The great rivers have their nutriment.
That is to say, there are small rivers, and in those small rivers there is food;
there are large gullies,
and in those large gullies there is food.
This refers to small streams and rivulets.
Where there are small streams and rivulets, there is food;
namely, the mountain valleys.
There is food in the valleys and ravines,
namely the heavy rain sent by the heavens;
this is the food in the ultimate sense.
This means that these four nutriments truly sustain and benefit all sentient beings.
Question: Are all material objects (kavaḍīkāra) considered food?
Answer: One should respond by establishing four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is a portion that is not nutriment;
that is to say, there are portions which, acting as conditions,
are unable to nourish and increase the sense faculties and the primary elements.
There is nutriment that is not substantial (kavaḍīkāra), namely that which,
having contact, volition, and consciousness as conditions,
is able to nourish and increase the sense faculties and the primary elements.
There is also nutriment that consists of mouthfuls;
that is to say, by taking mouthfuls as a condition,
one is able to nourish and increase the sense faculties and the primary elements.
There are those that are neither edible food nor nutriment;
namely, those which have contact, volition, and consciousness as conditions,
and which cannot nourish or increase the sense faculties and the primary elements.
Just as there are four propositions regarding edible food,
so too there are four propositions for each of the nutriments of consciousness, volition, and contact;
all of these should be explained in detail.
Thus, through these distinctions, sixteen propositions are established.
Question: Is that which cannot nourish the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) not, then, nutriment?
Answer: It is so.
Why is this? Because it was previously stated that the characteristic of nutriment (*āhāra*) is to provide long-term benefit.
Question: But we currently observe that there are cases where pain is induced after having consumed food.
Up to and including causing one to lay down the burden of the body—what are the characteristics of this food that increase and benefit [the practitioner]?
Answer: Although what is consumed as food may be either detrimental or beneficial.
However, what is now being discussed regarding food refers to that which is beneficial rather than harmful.
There are two times when it is beneficial:
first, at the time of initial consumption.
Second, at the time of digestion.
There may be cases where it is harmful at the time of digestion but beneficial at the time of initial consumption.
Just as eating delicious poison is also called "eating," because it may cause harm at the time of first consumption but benefit during digestion;
or like taking bitter medicine, this too is called "eating."
Because these two types function as food at one and the same time,
both are designated as "food. Therefore,
it is said that the characteristic of food consists in providing long-term benefit and nourishment.
Some say that although such beings may experience discomfort immediately after eating,
it later proves beneficial when it is transformed and expelled; therefore,
what was previously stated regarding the specific characteristics of food is established.
The Sūtra states that these four kinds of nutriment enable beings who have already come into existence to remain,
and they provide benefit and support for beings who seek further existence.

Question: Regarding the bhūtas mentioned in this sūtra, what is the distinction between the two types of sentient beings called "those who abide in existence" (bhava-stha) and "those who seek existence" (bhava-aiṣin)?
Answer: Those who abide in the fundamental [state] are named bhūtas;
those who abide in the intermediate state are named bhava-aiṣins.
Because they seek future existence through the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*),
some say that the noble ones (*ārya*) are called *bhūta* (beings),
while ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are called "seekers of existence" (*bhavaiṣin*).
Because those types of beings mostly seek future existence (*bhava*),
some say that "many" (*bahu*) refers to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The name "learner" (śaikṣa) implies the seeking of existence, because they may still aspire to future existence.
Question: Can ordinary beings (pṛthagjana-sattva) also be included and benefited?
Sentient beings who seek existence can also abide [in this state].
Why, then, is it said only that it enables *bhūta* sentient beings to abide and benefits those sentient beings who seek existence?
Answer: This scriptural passage should, in both cases, be explained in two ways.
That it is not so stated should be understood as indicating that the meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*). Some say:
In this context, various expressions and various modes of exposition are employed to adorn the meaning so that it may be easily understood.
Some say that herein two gateways and two summaries are intended to be manifested.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Some say that the state of "original existence" (pūrvakālabhava) abides for the longest duration of time.
The Noble Ones and those beyond training seek a temporary dwelling;
it is with reference to this meaning that the term "dwelling" is explicitly taught.
Others are not like this, and thus the term "dwelling" is not applied to them.
The Sūtra states that these four kinds of nutriment for bhikṣus are the root of all diseases and the root of all abscesses and sores.
This is the root of the poisoned arrow;
this is the cause of old age and death;
this is the condition for old age and death.
Question: Food can also serve as the foundation for well-being, as the Blessed One said:
"The path depends on its provisions; nirvana depends on the path."
Because of the joy of the path, one attains the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Among the provisions for the path, food is the foremost.
Why, then, is it said to be the root of illness and so forth?
Answer: It is in order to stop sentient beings' desire for edible food.
Because of their craving for food, they give rise to various unwholesome actions that bring about intense suffering;
therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus.
Even if various types of edible food were causes for pleasure in the present life alone,
a wise person should still not give rise to craving or attachment toward them,
because doing so gives rise to unwholesome karma that invites suffering in the future.
How much more so for manifesting the body as the root of all illnesses and so forth;
therefore, the wise should not be stained by attachment.
For this reason, the Buddha spoke this sūtra.
The Sūtra states that a bhikṣu should contemplate edible food as being like the flesh of a child in the wilderness;
he should contemplate contact-food as being like a cow whose hide has been freshly flayed;
and he should contemplate volition-food as being like the glowing embers of a fiery pit.
One should contemplate the food of consciousness as being like three hundred sharp spears.
Question: How should a bhikṣu contemplate the food of edible morsels as being like the flesh of a wilderness child?
Answer: It is, for example, like a husband and wife who have only one son.
His countenance was upright and handsome, and his affection was deep.
Encountering a famine in his country, he intended to travel to another land;
however, having traveled into the wilderness, his provisions were completely exhausted.
The road ahead was still long, yet they had not eaten for several days;
all were exhausted and on the verge of death.
Her husband thought to himself in secret:
"The road is far and our provisions are exhausted; our lives hang by a thread.
It is only right that three of us cannot all survive together.
How could we endure watching one another perish?"
In this situation, if one person now provides food, then one will die and two will survive;
this is better than all perishing together.
However, if I offer myself as a gift, I fear my wife’s resolve will falter out of grief and resentment, leading her to commit suicide and thus fail to escape the calamity.
"If we offer our wife [to him], we fear that our son will lose his mother and likewise not survive;
thus, we would suffer a double loss.
Yet this beloved son is one born of us."
"If husband and wife survive, offspring may yet be obtained;
it would be better to sacrifice my son's life to cross this wilderness.
Having formed this thought, she was overcome with grief beyond measure.
The wife then found this strange and questioned him about the reason;
her husband then related his thoughts to her in detail.
Upon hearing this, the wife choked with sobs, fainted, and collapsed upon the ground.

After a long while, he revived and wailed aloud, crying out to Heaven and protesting his grievous and cruel suffering. His husband then slowly consoled him, and after a long time, granted his request.
Thereupon, husband and wife embraced their child and wept together.
Losing his voice, he cried out in grief, "How unexpected! What suffering!
After weeping and sobbing for a long time, he finally brought his son's life to an end;
he then cut the body into strips of meat to serve as provisions for the journey.
Every time they wished to eat, the husband and wife wept together;
calling out the name of their son, they ate while shedding tears.
Once they had finished eating, they sighed in lamentation, reproaching and blaming themselves.
Yet from the time that couple first deliberated,
until they had finished eating and were traveling along the road,
they never experienced any joy; they thought only of their beloved son.
Thus, the practitioner dwelling in a secluded place never becomes negligent,
but correctly contemplates his wife,
giving birth to a beloved, excellent, and virtuous son.
The mind constantly maintains mindfulness without ever abandoning it;
weary of the realm of birth and death, it proceeds toward the direction of nirvāṇa.
For a long time, one has cultivated this practice while lacking the necessary provisions and conditions.
For the sake of maintaining this body of suffering which serves as the basis for upholding the Noble Path,
he abandoned his dedicated practice and entered the city to beg for food,
accompanied by heedfulness and right reflection.
From the time he renounced his secluded dwelling until he had finished eating,
he never once harbored a mind of attachment or delight;
he thought only of the Dharma he had renounced and the practice he was now devotedly cultivating.
In this way, a bhikṣu should contemplate morsel food as being like the flesh of a child from the wilderness as previously described.
If one has completely understood and abandoned morsel food, [one attains liberation].
Craving for the five objects of desire is also abandoned and fully understood,
because they are equally suppressed and have a single antidote.
If craving for the five objects of desire has been abandoned and fully understood, [then so too is the view of self-identity].
Thus, there is not a single fetter that remains unsevered or unknown which could bind him to rebirth in the desire realm;
this is based on his attainment of the fruit of non-return through the abandonment of sensual craving.
This was spoken with the underlying intention (*saṃdhi*) of the exhaustion of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Question: How should a bhikṣu contemplate the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) as being like a cow whose hide has been freshly flayed?
Answer: It is as if that cow had committed an offense against its owner.
Because they desired to cause suffering, they were born with their skin stripped away.
At that time, because the oxen lacked skin,
wherever they stayed— whether on the ground or in the air— [they suffered].
All manner of worms come vying with one another to gnaw and devour him;
in order to remove these worms, he rubs himself against fences, grass, trees, walls, and so forth, which only increases his agony.
At that time, how could that ox possibly have even the slightest bit of pleasure?
Whether touched or untouched, all experience great suffering.
Thus, in these various states of existence, how could there be even the slightest happiness?
Whether already born or yet to be born, there is nothing that is not suffering.
In this way, a bhikṣu should contemplate the nutriment of contact (sparśāhāra),
just as it was described regarding a cow with its hide freshly flayed.
If one has already abandoned and fully understood the nutriment of contact, [one is liberated].
Consequently, one also achieves the abandonment and full knowledge of the three feelings,
because all feelings arise with contact as their condition,
as the Sūtra says: "Contact is the condition for feeling."
If one has already abandoned and fully understood the three types of feeling,
then because what was to be done has been accomplished, one should investigate and seek to abandon the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*).
This refers to attaining the fruit of Arhatship by transcending the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
This was spoken with the underlying intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) that all fetters (*saṃyojana*) have been exhausted.
How should a bhikṣu contemplate the nutriment of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*) as being like the flames and embers of a fiery pit?
The answer is: suppose there were a great fiery pit near a city or town.
It was without flame and without smoke, yet filled with glowing embers.
A person who was not foolish or immature, but possessed of wisdom, having seen it, thought to himself:
"This great pit of fire is filled with glowing embers."
"If I were to fall, I would certainly die; there is no doubt.
Having formed this thought, he immediately gave rise to a wish and, desiring to distance himself from it, departed at once.
When those who are foolish, childish, stubborn, and lacking wisdom see it, they think to themselves,
"This pit is glowing red and lovely," and they immediately rush toward it, only to suffer and meet their end.
Just as a wise person, seeing a great pit of fire, fears it and avoids it from afar,
so too do the noble ones feel deep revulsion toward and renounce the thought of future existence (*punarbhava*). Conversely,
just as an ignorant person throws himself into a great pit of fire and suffers the loss of life, [so do those who cling to existence].
In this way, ordinary beings give rise to the volition for future existence;
they undergo boundless suffering and lose their life-force of wisdom.
Monks, you should contemplate the food of volition in this manner.
Regarding the pit of glowing embers and fire as described above:
for one who has already abandoned and fully understood craving for food through reflection,
they have likewise abandoned and fully understood the three types of craving.
Because those three types of craving are the causes of origination;
as it is said in the Sūtra:
