while that condition is real?
The Venerable One has also said this.
These names provisionally established by the various masters do not exist as real entities in their essence;
they are also intended to refute the aforementioned claim that the entities of the conditions are substantially real.
If the nature of conditions were not truly existent,
then all phenomena would not be truly existent,
for dependent origination encompasses all conditioned phenomena.
The equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) comprises past and present mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta),
with the exception of the final mental complex of an Arhat.
Because the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) encompass all phenomena (*dharma*).
Furthermore, if the nature of being an object were not substantially real,
one would not be able to designate the profound nature of all phenomena.
That is to say, if one observes without relying on causes and conditions, the nature of all phenomena is coarse, shallow, and easy to understand. However,
if one observes by means of causes and conditions,
then the profound meaning exceeds the four great oceans.
Only a Buddha can know this; it is not to be fathomed by others.
Furthermore, if the nature of objects were not substantially existent, one would not be able to designate the three types of enlightenment.
That is to say, by observing causes and conditions with superior wisdom, one attains the Bodhi of a Buddha;
by observing them with middling wisdom, one attains the Bodhi of a Pratyekabuddha;
and by observing them with inferior wisdom, one attains the Bodhi of a Śrāvaka.
Furthermore, if the nature of causes and conditions were not substantially real,
one should not designate three grades of wisdom;
that is to say, inferior wisdom would always remain inferior.
That which is intermediate should always remain intermediate,
and that which is superior should always remain superior,
because there is no power of real conditions to cause them to increase or decrease.
If that were so, there would be no instruction or training between teacher and disciple;
furthermore, the nature of teacher and disciple would not undergo any change.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka also stated this.
If one relies on a teacher who is not genuine, they should not cause the disciple’s awakened wisdom to progress—
such as advancing from the inferior to the middling, or from the middling to the superior.
Because there would be no cultivation through conditions to cause growth,
the instruction between teacher and disciple could not be established;
the teacher would always remain a teacher, and the disciple likewise would remain a disciple.
Based on the principles thus explained, it is known that the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) exists as a determined reality by its own nature.
Question: If the object-condition exists as a reality, how do you reconcile this with the meaning of the sūtra cited by the Dārṣṭāntika masters?
Answer: Although ignorance is a single [factor], its functions are manifold.
Because it frequently serves as a condition, it gives rise to formations (*saṃskāra*) with diverse characteristics;
for conditioned phenomena arise in dependence upon various conditions.
Because there are immeasurable gateways of distinct functions;
for example, a single person may possess five capacities without contradiction, and this case is likewise.
Some say: This is to demonstrate that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are weak and inferior by nature;
they cannot arise of themselves but must depend upon external conditions.
This treatise was composed because there is no real activity and no sovereign power [in phenomena].
Here, "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the self-essence of a phenomenon (*dharma*).
Alternatively, it may be said that this reveals the inherent weakness of the intrinsic nature of all produced phenomena.
Because they are weak and inferior, they depend upon four conditions,
or three, or two, before they can arise;
since even dharmas do not exist that arise by depending on only a single condition, how much less could there be anything that arises without depending on any conditions at all?
Just as a weak and sick person must rely upon four, three,
or two supporting conditions in order to arise and move.
Since they do not even depend on a single [condition] in a figurative sense, how much less could they exist without depending on them at all?
Alternatively, it is said that this reveals the inherent weakness of the productive causes and conditions;
because they are weak, they must mutually support one another—whether by four, three, or two—to be able to produce a phenomenon.
It is like those who are weak and frail;
whether four, three, or two, they rely upon one another to accomplish a single task,
as stated in the Sūtra.
Form is impermanent, and the causes and conditions of form are also of an impermanent nature.
How could form, which arises from that which is impermanent, be permanent?
Because all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) are weak and feeble by nature, they cannot arise of themselves.
This means that they lack the power to arise by themselves;
because they do not arise autonomously, they depend on others for their emergence,
as they can only be produced through the power of conditions.
Because they rely on other conditions, phenomena lack agency;
that is to say, a phenomenon does not have the desire to form the thought,
"I should act," nor does it think, "Who shall cause me to act?"
Because there is no agency, there is no sovereignty;
that is to say, within the thought "may I not arise" or "may I not cease," all conditioned phenomena lack sovereignty.
Some say that this treatise was composed in order to dispel ignorance regarding dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
As for this ignorance regarding dependent origination:
That is to say, when they hear it said that "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations," and so on,

up to "conditioned by birth are aging and death," they assume that this alone is the dharma of dependent origination; [the Buddha] now wishes to definitively demonstrate that which is produced from conditions.
All internal and external phenomena are dependently originated.
It is on account of such conditions that this treatise is composed.
How many conditions do the primary elements (mahābhūta) serve as for one another?
Answer:
It is a cause-condition and a predominant condition.
As for causes, there are two types of causes:
namely, the co-existent cause and the homogeneous cause.
Co-arising [dharmas] are mutually *sahabhū-hetu* (simultaneous causes) for one another;
those that arise earlier are *sabhāga-hetu* (homogeneous causes) for those that arise later.
As for the *adhipati* (dominant condition), it refers to that which does not obstruct arising.
And "merely unobstructed.
This is stated according to their general characteristics by way of category.
However, the four great elements (mahābhūta) are of eleven kinds.
That is to say, the basis of the eye-base,
up to the basis of the dharma-base.
The basis of the eye-base serves as the cause for the basis of the eye-base.
The dominant condition [of a basis] with respect to other bases is merely a single dominant condition.
This continues until the basis of the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) acts as the cause for the basis of the sphere of mental objects;
its dominant condition with respect to other bases is merely a single dominant condition.
The primary elements (mahābhūta) upon which the eye-base depends are further of two kinds:
namely, the left and the right. The left [eye] and its own supporting elements act as causes for one another;
however, the right [eye] and its supporting elements act only as a single predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
The right [eye] acts as the cause for its own support;
the dominant [condition] acts as the sole dominant [condition] for the left support.
Furthermore, the primary elements (mahābhūta) that serve as the support for the left eye are of two kinds.
That is to say, there are those produced by nourishment (*aupacayika*) and those born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Nourished phenomena serve as causes for other nourished phenomena;
however, [nourished phenomena] and those born of maturation serve as only a single dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for one another.
The ripened [great elements] have ripened [elements] as their cause;
the dominant [elements] and those that are nurtured have only the single dominant [cause].
Furthermore, the ripened great elements are of two kinds.
That is to say, there is the maturation of wholesome karma and the maturation of unwholesome karma.
The maturation of wholesome karma serves as the cause for the maturation of wholesome karma;
it serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the maturation of unwholesome karma, but only as a single dominant condition.
The same applies to the explanation of unwholesome karma.
Furthermore, there are two types of great elements that are the maturation of wholesome karma:
namely, those of devas and those of humans.
The gods take the gods as their cause;
for the gods and humans, there is only a single dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
It is the same when speaking of humans.
The great elements of the heavens are further divided into two types:
those of the desire realm and those of the form realm.
Those of the desire realm serve as causes for the desire realm.
The predominance [of the great elements] over the form realm is only one type of predominance;
the same is said for the form realm itself.
Furthermore, there are four types of great elements within the form realm.
This refers to the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna.
The first dhyāna acts as a cause for the first dhyāna;
as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it relates to the other dhyānas, but only as a single dominant condition.
The same applies up to the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, there are three types of great elements that are the maturation of unwholesome karma:
those of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Hell realms take hell realms as their cause;
for the other two [realms], they are only the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The same explanation applies to the animal and hungry ghost realms.
As it is said regarding maturation (*vipāka*),
so it is regarding nourishment (*aupacayika*).
As it is said regarding the left and right, so it is likewise.
As it is said regarding the primary elements upon which the sense-base of the eye depends,
so it is for the primary elements upon which even the sense-base of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana) depends.
The difference here is as follows:
That is to say, one should reflect upon the distinctions among the five external bases, such as those belonging to one's own body or another's body, and those that are sentient or insentient.
Question: Regarding the distinctions of place within the same realm of rebirth and the same level (*bhūmi*).
If one asks whether these [factors] are mutually related as causes for one another,
the answer is that some say they have no cause.
This is not reasonable,
for there would have to be primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that are momentary;
namely, those belonging to the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Because birth and death have never arisen since beginningless time.

It should be understood that the eleven types of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) and so forth are to be explained in detail according to the preceding exposition of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
How many conditions do the primary elements serve as for the derived matter?
Answer: As for causes,
there are five types of causes, including the predominant cause (adhipati-hetu).
That is to say: the cause of arising,
the cause of dependence,
and the cause of establishment.
The sustaining cause,
the nurturing cause,
and the predominant cause refer to that which does not obstruct arising.
And it is merely unobstructed.
Some say that the primary elements (mahābhūta) serve as homogeneous causes for the derived tangible objects (upādāyarūpa).
This is not reasonable,
because the primary elements (mahābhūta) and the derived tangibles (upādāyarūpa) are not of the same kind.
As for how many conditions (pratyaya) a derived form serves as a condition for another derived form:
Answer: As for the causes, there are the dominant cause and the causal causes;
the causal causes consist of three types of causes.
That is to say: coexistent,
similar-type,
and maturation.
"Predominance" means that which does not obstruct arising and is merely non-obstructive;
this is the general definition.
Regarding the detailed explanation, one should reflect upon it according to reason as was done for the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
As for how many conditions derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) serves as a condition for the primary elements: the answer is, it is a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The dominant cause consists of one cause,
namely, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
"Predominant" means that which does not obstruct arising,
as well as that which is merely non-obstructive.
Some say that the derivative tangible (bhautika-spraṣṭavya) acts as a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for the primary elements (mahābhūta).
This is not reasonable.
Because the primary elements that constitute tangibility are not of the same class [as the derived matter].
How many conditions do the primary elements serve as for the mind and mental factors? Answer: They serve as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Regarding the predominant object:
it refers to the body-consciousness and its associated mental factors.
Furthermore, the mental consciousness and its associated mental factors take those [objects] as their cognitive objects;
the body-consciousness and its associated factors apprehend specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The mental consciousness and its associated factors apprehend specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
As for their predominance (ādhipatya), it is as previously explained.
How many conditions do mind and mental factors serve as for mind and mental factors?
Answer: They serve as the cause-condition and the equal-and-immediate condition.
The objects of focus,
the predominant conditions,
and the causes consist of five causes.
That is to say: association,
coexistence,
and homogeneity.
Universal, resultant,
and immediately antecedent [conditions].
That is to say, immediately following the mind and mental factors,
the mind and mental factors manifest;
as for the object of perception:
This means that mental states and their concomitants serve as the object-condition (*ālambana*) for other mental states and their concomitants;
as for their predominance-condition (*adhipati*), it is as previously explained.
How many conditions do the mind and mental factors have with respect to the primary elements?
Answer: They are causes and predominant conditions.
As for the cause,
there is one cause,
namely the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Regarding "predominance" (*adhipati*), it is as previously explained.
How many conditions do the great elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as for the sense-base of the eye? Answer: They serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Regarding the predominant cause (*adhipati-hetu*), there are five causes;
namely, the five beginning with the productive cause (*janana-hetu*).
Regarding the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously explained.
With how many conditions is the eye-base related to the eye-base? Answer: It is related by way of the cause-condition and the predominant condition.
The cause is the single cause,
namely the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
The predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is as previously explained.
With how many conditions is the eye-base related to the primary elements?
Answer: One, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The meaning of "dominant" is as explained previously.
As it is with the sense-base of the eye,
so it is with the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, odor,
and flavor. How many conditions do the primary elements serve as for the sense-base of form?
Answer: [There are] the cause and the predominant condition.
As for the cause, there are five causes.
That is to say, the five [factors] beginning with birth.
As for "predominance," it is as previously explained.
How many conditions does the sense-sphere of form serve as a condition for the sense-sphere of form?
Answer: The cause and the predominant condition.
As for the cause, there are two types of causes.
That is to say, the homogeneous,
the retributive,
and the dominant conditions are as previously explained.
How many conditions does the sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana) have with respect to the primary elements (mahābhūta)?
Answer: It is a causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) and a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
The cause is a single cause,
namely the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu).
The predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is as previously explained.
As it is with the sense-base of form,
so it is with the sense-bases of sound and tangibles;
although they are described collectively, their meanings differ.
This means that the primary elements (mahābhūta) act as the cause and the predominant condition for the sphere of sound. As for "cause":
[it refers to the efficient cause].
There are five causes,
namely the five beginning with arising (*jāti*).
As for the predominant cause (*adhipati*), it is as previously explained.
The sound-base is the cause and the dominant condition for the sound-base.
As for the cause, there is one cause.
This refers to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
As for the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously explained.
The sphere of sound (*śabda-āyatana*) acts as a cause for the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
The predominant cause consists of one cause,
namely, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
As for predominance (*adhipati*), it is as previously explained:
the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) act as the predominant cause for the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
The causes are seven causes;
namely, the five beginning with the cause of production,
as well as the co-existent cause.
Regarding the predominance of the similar class (*sabhāga-adhipati*), it is as previously explained:
the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) acts as the cause and the predominant condition for the sphere of tangibles.
The causes are seven:
namely, the five beginning with the cause of arising,
together with the co-existent cause.
Regarding the similar and dominant conditions, they are as previously explained.
The sense-base of tangibility serves as the cause for the primary elements.
The dominant cause consists of two causes,
namely: the co-existent cause.
Regarding similar [causes] and dominant [conditions], they are as previously explained.
How many conditions do the great elements serve as for the sphere of mind?
Answer: Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati*).
As for the object-condition, it means serving as the object-condition for body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

The body-consciousness apprehends its own specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). The mental consciousness apprehends both its own specific characteristic and the common characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
When the body-consciousness apprehends, whether it be one or many, it is as explained extensively above.
With how many conditions does the mind-base (manāyatana) act as a condition for the mind-base?
Answer: As a cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya) and as an immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
The object-condition,
the dominant-condition,
and the cause-condition constitute the three conditions.
That is to say: the similar-type,
the universal,
and the retributive [causes].
Regarding "immediately preceding" (samanantara):
it refers to the immediately preceding condition of the sense base of mind (manāyatana);
that is, when the sense base of mind manifests in the present.
As for the object-condition (*ālambana*):
it means that the sense-sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) takes the sense-sphere of mind as its object-condition.
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati*): it is as previously explained.
This is stated according to the general characteristics of the categories;
however, the sense base of mind (manāyatana) is of six kinds, namely:
visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna), and so forth.
This extends up to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Among these, eye-consciousness is the cause of eye-consciousness as its equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
It is a predominating condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), but not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
As for its causes (*hetu*), there are two causes.
This refers to the homogeneous,
the retributive,
and the immediately antecedent; that is, the immediately antecedent condition of visual consciousness and so forth.
Visual consciousness is present before one.
As for its predominance, it is as previously explained.
It is not an object-condition because visual consciousness takes only visible form as its object.
Because visual consciousness is not form (*rūpa*).
As it is with visual consciousness in relation to visual consciousness,
so it is with visual consciousness in relation to auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses.
Visual consciousness and mental consciousness are [related] as cause, equal-and-immediate,
object-condition,
and predominant condition.
As for causes,
there are two types of causes,
namely, the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
Regarding "the maturation immediate antecedent," this refers to the case where,
immediately following a visual consciousness or similar [sensory consciousness],
a mental consciousness manifests.
As for the object-condition (*ālambana*):
it refers to visual consciousness and mental consciousness taking [the object] as their object-condition.
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati*): it is as previously explained.
Just as visual consciousness relates to the other five consciousnesses,

so too do the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses relate to the six; likewise, mental consciousness serves as the cause for mental consciousness by way of being its equal-and-immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
The object-condition,
the dominant condition,
and the causal condition constitute the three conditions.
That is to say: the similar-type,
the pervasive,
and the retributive.
"Immediately preceding" refers to the immediately preceding condition of the mental consciousness; that is,
when the mental consciousness manifests in the present.
As for the object-condition (*ālambana*),
it means that mental consciousness takes mental consciousness as its object-condition.
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati*), it is as previously explained.
The mental consciousness (manovijñāna) and the visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) are its causes;
they are its immediate antecedent (samanantara) and predominant (adhipati) conditions,
but not its object-condition (ālambana).
As for causes, there are three causes:
namely, the similar-type cause (sabhāga-hetu) and the pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu).
Regarding "maturation" and "immediately preceding":

as for the immediately preceding condition of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it refers to that which acts as the dominant condition for the manifestation of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) in the present, as previously explained.
Regarding that which is not an object of perception:
visual consciousness perceives only form,
whereas mental consciousness does not perceive form.
Just as the mental consciousness relates to the visual consciousness, so it is with respect to the other consciousnesses.
Question: Do the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, arise in immediate succession (anantara) one after another?
The various yogācāras reply: The five consciousnesses,
such as the visual consciousness and so forth, do not manifest immediately after one another,
because they all arise immediately from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The masters of the Abhidharma say that the five consciousnesses,
such as the visual consciousness and so forth, can all arise immediately after one another.
If this were not the case, it would contradict the exposition in the *Indriya-skandha*.
As it has been said:
the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) is the cause of the faculty of suffering,
and its equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya).
It is an adhipati condition,
but not an ālambana condition.
How many conditions does the sphere of mind (manāyatana) serve as a condition for the great elements (mahābhūta)?
Answer: As for the causes, there is the dominant cause (*adhipati-hetu*).
Regarding the causes, there is one cause.
This refers to the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously explained.
How many conditions do the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as for the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?
Answer: The causes are the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant-condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
The causes consist of seven types:
namely, the five beginning with the cause of arising (jāti-hetu),
together with the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
Regarding the similar class:
as for the object-condition,
it refers to those phenomena associated with body-consciousness.
And the mental factors associated with the mental consciousness serve as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously explained.
How many conditions does the dharma-base serve as a condition for the dharma-base?
Answer: It serves as the cause-condition and the equal-and-immediate condition.
The objects of focus,
the predominant conditions,
and the causes consist of five types of causes.
That is, the five beginning with the associated [factors].
Regarding "immediately preceding" (samanantara): it refers to the immediately preceding condition of the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) and so forth.
The dharma-base manifests as present.
As for its object:
this means that the dharma-base takes the dharma-base as its object.
Regarding "predominance" (*adhipati*), it is as previously explained.
As for how many conditions the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) constitutes for the primary elements (*mahābhūta*): the answer is, it is a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The dominant cause consists of three causes,
namely: the co-existent cause.
The homogeneous,
the ripening,
and the dominant [conditions] are as previously explained.
How many conditions do the great elements serve as for the eye faculty?
Answer: They serve as the cause-condition and the predominant condition.
The causes are the five causes,
namely the five beginning with "arising.
The predominant condition is as previously explained.
How many conditions does the eye-faculty have with respect to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Answer: One, the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
The meaning of "dominant" is as explained previously.
As it is with the eye faculty,
so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, body, male, and female faculties.
How many conditions do the great elements serve as for the life faculty?
Answer: One is the predominance condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The meaning of "predominance" is as previously explained.
How many conditions does the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) serve as for the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Answer: One is the predominance condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The meaning of "predominance" is as previously explained.
How many conditions do the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as for the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*)?
Answer: Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati*).
The meanings of the object-condition and the dominant condition are all as previously explained.
How many conditions does the mind-faculty have with respect to the primary elements?
Answer: It has two conditions: the causal condition and the predominant condition. Regarding the causal condition, there is one cause.
That is to say, it refers to the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
As for the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously explained;
it is like the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*).
The same applies to the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, grief, equanimity, faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

As for the great elements (mahābhūta), how many conditions do they serve as for the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya)? Answer: They serve as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Regarding the predominance of the object (ālambana):
it refers to the primary elements (mahābhūta) in relation to the patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-kṣānti) and the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).
The accumulation of patience and the accumulation of knowledge,
along with their associated faculties, serve as the objects of focus;
their predominance is as previously explained.
How many conditions does the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) serve as for the great elements (mahābhūta)?
Answer: It serves as one condition, the predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
The meaning of the predominant condition is as explained previously.
As it is with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," so it is with the faculty of "having known" and the faculty of "one who has fully known.
There are three types of questions and answers regarding the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their corresponding bases.
Why are there only two questions and answers regarding the faculties?
The answer is: because that author of the treatise intended it so.
That is to say, the treatise was composed in accordance with his intention.
Provided that it does not contradict the characteristics of the Dharma,
one should not question its underlying reason. Some say:
This is an incomplete explanation.
Some say that herein various texts and various expositions are manifested.
It is for the purpose of adorning the meaning so that it may be easily understood.
Some say that herein two doors and two summaries are presented, and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that the faculties (indriya) are subsumed within the bases (āyatana);
if one speaks of the bases, it should be understood that the faculties have already been spoken of.
For this reason, it was not asked.
Some say that herein [the teaching] proceeds through a sequence of detailed and abbreviated expositions.
This refers to the first four questions, followed by three, and finally two;
since the latter can be understood by reference to the former detailed exposition,
the text is gradually abbreviated to avoid prolixity.
Question: Do material phenomena (rūpadharma) possess a homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) with respect to material phenomena?
Answer: The masters of the Western regions and the Venerable Dārṣṭāntika say so.
Regarding whether form is a homogeneous cause for form,
the masters of the Abhidharma state that form is indeed a homogeneous cause for form.
As was already extensively analyzed in the preceding section on the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) within the *Saṃgītiparyāya*,
why is it that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) share the same arising, abiding, and ceasing yet are not associated (*saṃprayukta*),
whereas the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) that share the same arising, abiding, and ceasing are said to be associated?
Answer: Just as the four great elements may decrease or increase, the mind and mental factors are not like this.
Among these, that which arises is...
That is to say: arising is that which arises;
abiding is that which abides;
and change is that which changes.
"Cessation" refers to the cessation of that which is to be ceased.
Question: Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) each possess arising, abiding, and cessation, why is it said that there is "one arising, one abiding, and one cessation"?
Answer: Because there are causes and conditions, it is said that each has its own arising, abiding, and ceasing;
that is to say, because each possesses its own distinct characteristics, they are not of a single characteristic.
Because there are causes and conditions, it is said that there is a single arising, a single abiding, and a single ceasing.
This means that they are all inseparable from a single moment of time and so forth, because they arise, abide, and perish simultaneously.
Question: Do the essential natures of the four great elements increase or decrease?
If that were the case, what fault would there be? Both positions would be erroneous.
If there were increase or decrease, how could they not be distinct? Why is this so?
If, within a solid object, the earth atoms are predominant while those of water,
fire, and wind are few,
then the earth atoms will intermingle with the water atoms in equal measure, while the others remain separate.
The same applies even to animals.
If there were no increase or decrease in substances such as water or stone,
distinctions such as hardness or softness could not be established.
It was stated that the essential nature of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) undergoes increase and decrease.
Question: If this is so, how can they be said to be inseparable?
Answer: Although there is increase and decrease, they remain inseparable.
This is because they mutually support one another to perform their respective functions.
For example, although within a solid object the atoms of earth are predominant while those of water, fire, and wind are few,
it cannot perform its functional activity apart from the atoms of water and the other elements.
The same applies even to animals. For example,
when several villages perform a single task together,
although the number of people differs, [the collective merit remains].
Yet they require one another and cannot be separated.
Question: Since the substance of the mind and mental factors also undergoes increase and decrease, how can you say that it is not so?
This refers to mental factors within the three realms,
the three natures, and those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Regarding the untainted [states], within the various mental aggregates, some are many and some are few.
Answer: Because they are equal in terms of their objective basis (vastu), they are not designated as increasing or decreasing.
If there were two perceptions, one feeling, and so forth within a single moment of mind, they could be called "increasing" or "decreasing.
However, since there is only one perception and one feeling within a single moment of mind, they differ from the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Some say:
The essential nature of the primary elements (mahābhūta) neither increases nor decreases.
Question: How can there be differences such as hardness or softness in stones and other objects?
Answer: Because the power of the primary elements varies, being either increased or diminished.
Just as within solid objects the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) have equal numbers of atoms (*paramāṇu*), yet the atoms of earth predominate in their power;
the same explanation applies even to sentient beings.
It is like placing one *liang* of salt and one *liang* of flour upon the tongue:
the consciousness produced by the salt is intense, while the consciousness produced by the flour is faint.
This case is also like that.
The analogy of water and vinegar blending together to produce gustatory consciousness;
the analogy of a needle point and a bird’s feather producing tactile consciousness—
the detailed explanation is likewise so.
Question: Do the mind and mental factors also possess degrees of intensity,
such that, for example, Angulimāla possessed sharp faculties while Āśvajit possessed dull faculties?
How can it be said that it is not so?
The answer is: because the power of the four great elements is coarse and manifest, and their increase or decrease is easy to discern, they are thus spoken of.
The mind and mental factors are not like this;
for this reason, the primary elements (mahābhūta) are said not to be associated.
Furthermore, all minds and mental factors possess an object of cognition (ālambana).
The four great elements have no object of perception.
It cannot be said that a dharma which lacks an object of perception can be associated [with others]. Why is this?
The mind and mental factors have a basis and possess objective aspects.
Because there is the arising of realization,
there must be an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Because there is an object of cognition, it is always associated and never dissociated.
The four great elements are the opposite of this; therefore,
they lack an object of cognition, and because they lack an object of cognition,
although they are not dissociated, they do not associate.
Non-separation is of two kinds:
first, because the primary elements (mahābhūta) are non-separate as they collectively produce a single derived form;
second, because the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) are non-separate as they collectively take a single object as their cognitive focus.
Although the five aggregates coexist within a single body,
there are no two things that do not exist in mutual inseparability;
therefore, the great elements are not said to be associated.
Question: How is it known that these four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are always inseparable?
Answer: Because their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and their functional activities (*karmakriyā*) are found within all aggregates.

That is to say, because the own-characteristic of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is perceptibly found within an aggregate of solidity, its existence is established as an ultimate reality (*paramārtha-siddha*).
If the water element were not present within this aggregate,
gold, silver, tin, and so forth would be unable to be melted;
furthermore, if water were absent, they would disperse.
If the fire element did not exist, fire would not arise from the striking together of stones and other materials.
Furthermore, if fire were absent, there would be nothing to bring things to maturity, and they would consequently rot.
If the wind element did not exist, there would be no movement or oscillation.
Furthermore, if there were no wind, there would be no growth;
since the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the water element (*abdhātu*) is perceptible within a moist mass, this principle is thoroughly established.
Within such a mass, if the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*) were absent, it could not become ice even when subjected to extreme cold.
Furthermore, if the earth element did not exist, things such as boats would sink;
if the fire element did not exist, there would be no time of warmth;
and if the fire element were absent, things would undergo putrefaction.
If the wind element did not exist, there would be no movement;
furthermore, if wind were absent, there would be no growth.
Since the specific characteristic of the fire element is perceptible within a mass of heat, the existence of this principle is thoroughly established.
Within this aggregate, if the earth element were absent, the flame of lamps and candles would not be able to turn back.
Furthermore, if earth were absent, it could not support objects.
If the water element were absent, there would be no flowing or generation.
Furthermore, if water were without heat (tejas), it would not coalesce;
if it were without the wind element (vāyu-dhātu), it would not move or vibrate;
and if there were no wind, there would be no growth.
The meaning that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the wind element is perceptible within the collection of moving matter is firmly established.
If the earth element were not present within this collection, it would not be obstructed by walls and the like, and thus it would not turn back.
Furthermore, if earth did not exist, it would not support material objects;
if the water element did not exist, there would be no cool winds.
Moreover, if water did not exist, those [objects] would disperse.
If the fire element did not exist, there would be no warm wind;
furthermore, if fire were absent, things would undergo putrefaction.
Question: These four great elements have distinct characteristics and are mutually contradictory.
How is it that they arise simultaneously and are not mutually separated?
The Venerable Vasumitra states:
"The causes and conditions for their distinct characteristics are each different."
It is not the case that all distinct characteristics are necessarily contradictory.
Those characteristics which are not contradictory yet remain distinct may arise simultaneously and exist without mutual separation.
Just as the four great elements, as well as odor, flavor, tangibility, blue, yellow, and so forth,
possess distinct characteristics that are mutually exclusive,
they necessarily never arise at one time without being inseparable from one another.
Like fuel and fire;
like hail and the harvest;
like a *rāhu* and the lunar disc.
Medicine, Disease, Light, and Darkness.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 131. *Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 100.
Compiled by three hundred and fifty great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Part Two of the Second Section on Conditions within the Fifth Aggregate of Great Elements (*Mahābhūta-skandha*). Question: If solid and non-solid things act as mutual conditions for one another, how is this so?
How is it that all phenomena do not abandon their own characteristics?
How do they manifest their characteristics?
It is like the nature of water, which is soft, yet congeals into ice when winter arrives.
Even if struck with an axe, gold and other such substances remain firm by nature;
yet if placed in a blazing furnace, they melt away like water.
Is this not, in such cases, the abandonment of their own intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) by all phenomena?
Answer: It is not that solid things transform into non-solid things, nor that non-solid things transform into solid things.
Rather, the dharmas of solidity and non-solidity abide in the future world.
If one encounters firm conditions,
then non-firm phenomena cease and firm phenomena continue to arise;
if one encounters non-firm conditions, then firm phenomena cease and non-firm phenomena continue to arise.
The same applies to the others.
Therefore, there is no fault of [the elements] abandoning their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Question: Is there an interval within the aggregate of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
Both positions would be flawed.
If there were an interval between them, how could they not be separated?
If there were no intervals, how could they not become one?
The answer is: some say that this is because the empty element (*ākāśadhātu*) exists within these intervals and dwells intermingled therein.
Question: If that is so, why is it called "inseparable"?
Answer: Because within it, the space element can conceal itself.
It causes one to perceive objects as being inseparable from one another,
like a woman in a thicket who conceals her own body. Some say:
Because these [atoms] abide without interval, being pressed against one another in immediate succession.
Question: If that is so, why do they not become a single entity?
Answer: Although there is no interval, they do not constitute a single unity.
For example, within the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and the three periods of time, although there is no interval, they do not constitute a single unity.
It is the same with that [case].
Furthermore, because the intrinsic natures and functions of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth are each distinct,
they cannot constitute a single unity.
Question: Do the various atoms (paramāṇu) touch one another?
If so, what fault would there be?
Answer: Both positions entail errors.
If they were to touch one another, would they not necessarily become a single entity,
or would they not possess parts?
If they did not touch, then at the moment of impact, they should either disperse or there should be no sound.
It is agreed that one should say this:
atoms do not touch one another;
if they did touch, it would have to be either entirely or partially.
If they were touched throughout their entirety, there would be the fallacy of them becoming a single entity;
if they were touched only in part, there would be the loss of their being partless.
Yet, atoms have no further subdivisions.
Question: When the forms of an aggregate strike one another, why do they not disperse?
Answer: Because they are held together by the wind element (*vāyudhātu*), they do not disperse.
Question: Does the wind element not have the power to blow things apart and scatter them?
Answer: There are those capable of dispersing it, as during the period of world-destruction;
there are also those capable of sustaining it.
As in the case of the kalpa of formation.
Question: If they do not touch one another, how is sound produced at the moment of their mutual impact?
Answer: It is precisely for this reason that sound is produced.
If [the atoms] were to touch one another, how could sound be produced?
If it were the case that atoms possess physical contact with one another,
then when hands and such things come together, their substances would necessarily intermingle.
Since there would be no intervening space between them, how could sound be produced?
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated as follows:
"If atoms were to touch one another,
they would necessarily persist into the subsequent moment."
The Venerable One said:
"In truth, they do not touch;
it is merely that within a continuous succession of aggregations, [the subsequent moment] arises."
According to conventional truth, they are designated as "contact" by way of a provisional name. Question:
Are all things that are contacts produced because contact is their cause?
They arise with non-contact as their cause;
all things that are non-contact arise with non-contact as their cause.
Is it produced with contact as its cause?
Answer: Sometimes that which is not contact is produced with contact as its cause;
namely, at the moment when objects in conjunction are precisely separating.
Sometimes contact arises with non-contact as its cause,
namely at the moment when separated objects are in the process of coming together.
Sometimes contact arises with contact as its cause.
This refers to when a conjoined entity further enters into conjunction; at times,
that which is non-contact arises with non-contact as its cause,
namely, the homogeneous continuity of motile dust particles.
Question: Should it be said that an atom (paramāṇu) is visible or invisible?
Answer: The Venerable Ghoṣaka states as follows:
An atom should be said to be visible.
Because it is the object of the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*),
the Abhidharma masters say that an atom (*paramāṇu*) should be described as invisible,
since it cannot be seen by either the physical eye or the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*).
In this context, the question is not asked from the perspective of the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*),
because there is no differentiation among all phenomena (*dharma*).
Is it possible for past primary elements (*mahābhūta*) to produce past derived matter (*rūpa*)?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was intended to refute the positions of others and to clarify one's own position.
This refers to certain other schools who deny the existence of the past and future and claim that the present world is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
To refute their view and demonstrate that the past and future do exist,
as well as to clarify that the present is a conditioned dharma (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), [the author] says:
As explained extensively above,
there are furthermore certain non-Buddhists who,
relying on worldly analogies, maintain that conditioned phenomena serve as the cause for what precedes them.
He says this: "We see with our own eyes that a spring, being pressed from behind by what precedes it, causes [the water] to surge forth;
in the same way, these dharmas are caused to enter the present by the pressure of future dharmas."
Furthermore, because the present forces the past to appear,
conditioned phenomena would have the later as the cause for the earlier;
we now wish to refute that which is asserted by those non-Buddhists.
This demonstrates that for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), the preceding can produce the succeeding, but the succeeding is not the cause of the preceding;
otherwise, it would contradict the principle of internal and external dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*),
implying that worldly parents must be born from their children.
The eye and visible forms should arise from visual consciousness;
ignorance and so forth should be produced from volitional formations and so forth;
and seeds and so forth should arise from sprouts and so forth.
If one first experiences the retribution of pleasure and pain and only afterwards creates wholesome or unwholesome karma;
or if one first attains bodhi and only afterwards practices cultivation—
then that which has not yet been done would already have been obtained, and that which ought to have been done would already have been lost.
If that were so, there would be no possibility of attaining liberation.
Furthermore, to refute the claim that the primary elements (mahābhūta) and their derived matter (upādāyarūpa) necessarily belong to the same time period,
it is shown that they can belong to different time periods.
For these reasons, this treatise is composed:
[concerning] all derived matter that is resistant,
as well as unmanifest matter that evolves in accordance with the mind.
In whichever world they exist, they are produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) of that very world;
that is to say, those of the past are produced by the past, those of the present by the present,
and those of the future by the future.
Furthermore, regarding the various non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) produced by informative matter (vijñapti),
there are three categories whose timing of formation is unequal;
that is to say, the first moment is like that of [matter] with resistance (sapratigha), and so forth.
Each is produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) belonging to its own respective time;
if it occurs in the second moment within the past or present,
both are produced by past primary elements.
If it is in the future, it is generally derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta) of both the present and the future;
for subsequent moments, those of the past and present are as previously described.
If it is in the future, it is generally derived from the primary elements of all three time periods.
Why is this so? Because for all those who, relying on manifest action, initiate restraint (*saṃvara*), non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), or that which is neither,
there is, during the first moment, both manifest and unmanifest form (*rūpa*).
Together with these and the other primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that produce them, they perish simultaneously in the present;
having perished, by the second moment thereafter, both the manifest action (*vijñapti*) and the primary elements exist in the past.
Various unmanifest forms (avijñaptirūpa) exist in the past,
exist in the future,
and exist in the present.
This is called the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point: Is there any past primary element (*mahābhūta*) that produces past derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)?
Answer: There is.
Namely, all past resistant derived matter.
The non-informative [matter] that follows the mind and the non-informative [matter] produced by informative [action] are created solely by past primary elements.
Is there any case where past primary elements produce future matter?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, there is the unmanifest (avijñapti) produced by a future manifest (vijñapti).
It is produced solely by past primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Is there any case where present matter (*rūpa*) is produced by past primary elements?
Answer: There is.
It is said that there is unmanifest form (avijñapti) produced by a present manifest form (vijñapti) which is created solely by past primary elements (mahābhūta).
Is it possible for future matter (rūpa) to be created by future primary elements?
Answer: There are.
Namely, all future derived matter that is resistant, as well as the non-informative matter that follows the mind.
Furthermore, there is the unmanifest (avijñapti) produced by a future manifest (vijñapti),
which is created solely by future primary elements (mahābhūta).
Is it possible for past or present matter (rūpa) to be created by future primary elements?
Answer: No. This is because it is illogical for the effect to exist prior to the cause.
Is there any instance where present primary elements (mahābhūta) produce present derived matter (rūpa)?
Answer: Yes.
It refers to all presently existing derived matter that is resistant, as well as the non-informative matter that follows the mind.
Furthermore, there is unmanifest form (avijñapti) produced by a present manifest form (vijñapti) that is created solely by present primary elements (mahābhūta).
Is it possible for past matter (rūpa) to be created by present primary elements?
Answer: No. This is because it is illogical for the effect to exist prior to the cause.
Is there any case where present primary elements (mahābhūta) produce future matter?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, there is future unmanifest (avijñapti) produced by manifest (vijñapti), which is created solely by present primary elements (mahābhūta).
All unmanifest forms (avijñapti) that follow the mind are outflows (niṣyanda),
are non-appropriated (anupātta),
and are comprised within the category of sentient beings (sattvasaṃkhyāta).
The great elements that constitute its basis are nurtured (aupacayika),
non-appropriated (anupātta), and included within the category of sentient beings (sattvasaṃkhyāta);
it is the unmanifest (avijñapti) arising from manifest action (vijñapti).
These are outflows (niṣyanda).
They are comprised within the category of sentient beings and are not appropriated (anupātta).
The primary elements (mahābhūta) that produce them are also outflows.
There are two kinds of unmanifest form (avijñapti) that are appropriated,
included within the category of sentient beings, and follow the mind.
First, those subsumed under the dhyāna restraint;
second, those subsumed under the untainted (anāsrava) restraint.
Each of these has seven types.
That is to say, from abstaining from taking life up to abstaining from frivolous speech;
these seven types are subsumed under the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*).
They are all produced from the same four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The seven types of untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) are likewise.
There are three kinds of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) that arise from informative action (*vijñapti*).
First, those comprised within ethical discipline (*saṃvara*);
second, those comprised within non-discipline (*asaṃvara*);
and third, those comprised within neither discipline nor non-discipline.
Furthermore, there are seven types subsumed under ethical discipline (*saṃvara*),
namely: abstaining from taking life,
up to abstaining from frivolous speech.
Thus, each of these seven types is produced by one of the four great elements.
Furthermore, there are two kinds that are distinct from taking life:
namely, informative and non-informative [action].
Each of these two is produced by its own set of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Other masters say that both this manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) karma are produced by a single common set of the four great elements.
Therefore, he asked: "Is there any case where the four great elements produce matter belonging to two bases?
He replied: "There is; namely, matter belonging to the base of visible form and the base of mental phenomena."
This also applies to the sense-sphere of sound and the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The Venerable Ghoṣaka also speaks thus.
The masters of the Abhidharma treatises say:
That explanation is irrational;
it is impossible for a single set of the four great elements to produce two effects, one coarse and one subtle.
Therefore, what was stated previously is correct.
Just as abstaining from taking life consists of both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), each being produced by its own set of four great elements (*mahābhūta*),
so it is likewise for all [the other precepts] up to abstaining from frivolous speech.
There are likewise seven types subsumed under non-restraint (asaṃvara), namely:
taking life up to frivolous speech.
There are two sets of seven types that are not subsumed under either [restraint or non-restraint].
That is to say: taking life and abstaining from taking life, up to frivolous speech and abstaining from frivolous speech.
Each of these seven types is produced by a single set of the four great elements.
Each of these seven categories further has two types,
namely, informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*).
Each of these is likewise produced by one set of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The explanation for other masters should be understood as being the same as before.
If one possesses past primary elements (*mahābhūta*),
does one also possess the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) of the past?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To refute the denial of the two time periods of the past and the future.
Furthermore, when it is stated that the entities of attainment (*prāpti*) and non-attainment (*aprāpti*) do not exist as real entities,
the intention is to clarify that the past and future worlds,
as well as attainment and so forth, are indeed real dharmas.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
If one is endowed with past primary elements (*mahābhūta*),
is one also endowed with the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) of the past?
Answer: There is no one who possesses past primary elements (*mahābhūta*), yet there are those who possess past derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
This refers to noble ones (*ārya*) dwelling within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and abides in restraint,
or abides in non-restraint,
or abides in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint.
First, there is the non-loss of previous bodily and vocal intimation;
this applies to those born in the form realm,
as well as to those learners (śaikṣa) born in the formless realm.
Question: There are also those in training (śaikṣa) who, having been born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), do not possess past created matter (rūpa).
This refers to those who previously existed in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Regarding those untainted paths that have neither arisen nor ceased,
one who dies and is reborn in the formless realm does not at all possess the past matter produced by them.
How then is it said:
"If those in training (śaikṣa) are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), do they possess the matter (rūpa) produced in the past?"
Answer: This is stated with reference to those who have attained [the path].
That is to say, for a learner (śaikṣa) previously in the desire or form realms, the various untainted paths (anāsravamārga) have already arisen and have already ceased.
Because he has accomplished the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) created in the past.
Some say that while he was in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), [he accomplished it].
One must have already produced and ceased the various untainted paths;
just as with the path of further progress, these must necessarily arise and manifest before one,
for there is no such thing as passing away while abiding in the fruit.
If one possesses past primary elements, does one also possess future primary elements?
Answer: There is no one who possesses both past and future primary elements.
Question: For what reason is there no accomplishment (*samanvāgama*) of past or future primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Answer: Because those primary elements possess only such a limited power of accomplishment; they are accomplished only when they manifest in the present moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Regarding those that have already ceased and have not yet manifested, there is no possession (*prāpti*).
This is because the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their possession must necessarily belong to the same time period;
since at this present moment that possession has not manifested, there is no possession.
Some say that because the latencies of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are not firm,
there is no one who possesses [the seeds of] the past and future.
Because these are weak, inferior, and indeterminate (avyākṛta) by nature;
that is to say, because the latencies (vāsanā) of the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth are firm,
there is the accomplishment of [dharmas] belonging to the past and future.
Inferior indeterminate dharmas are not like this;
they are like holding a highly fragrant flower or object for a brief moment—
the residual impression (vāsanā) still persists even after it has been washed and wiped clean.
It is not like holding other objects such as wood or stone,
which cease to exist as soon as one’s hand lets them go. Some say:
If one were to possess the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the past and future worlds,
then a single realm would possess the primary elements of all five realms;
thus, a single body would be a body of all five realms.
In that case, both the basis for proceeding would perish and the basis itself would perish.
To avoid such a fault, it is therefore established that the great elements do not exist in the past or future.
Question: Just as one is born into a single realm while accomplishing the karmas and afflictions of all five realms, yet that realm is not destroyed; [how is this so?]
This should also be understood in the same way.
It is answered that the distinctions between the various realms of existence (*gati*) are spoken of in terms of their maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*),
and not in terms of karma or afflictions (*kleśa*).
However, if any of the great elements were to be a result of maturation (vipākaphala),
there would be the fault of the destruction of the realms of existence (gati) and the destruction of their basis;
