one should know that this meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*). Some say:
When the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of that realm arise, there is no increase of form;
therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, others say:
It abides in three kinds of mind.
Question: This may be so for a wholesome mind, because it possesses a concordant fruit (*anuvartaka-phala*).
What fruit do the remaining two have that causes them to manifest?
Answer: When one born in the desire realm gives rise to a wholesome mind of the form realm, [they manifest].
Because it follows along with the evolving form,
it causes that [form] to manifest when a defiled mind arises.
Because the matter of the space-element belonging to that stage is present within this body, intermingled with it,
it causes that [matter] to manifest.
When an indeterminate mind arises,
because the transformed matter (*nirmāṇa-rūpa*) of that stage exists and causes it to manifest,
one can give rise to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of that stage while abiding in any of the three types of minds.
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School,
Volume 132; Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume 133.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others, translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.

Section Five: The Aggregate of the Great Elements; Part Three of the Second Sub-section on Conditions. How many conditions do the great elements bound to the desire realm serve as for the great elements bound to the desire realm?
Answer: [They are] the cause and the predominant condition.
As for the cause, there are two causes.
That is to say,
coexistent and homogeneous dharmas that arise simultaneously act as coexistent causes (sahabhū-hetu) in relation to one another.
A preceding birth serves as the homogeneous cause for a subsequent birth.
As for the predominant condition,
it means not obstructing the arising [of phenomena].
And as for mere non-obstruction:
how many conditions do the great elements bound to the desire realm serve as for the derived matter bound to the desire realm?
Answer: The causes are the dominant cause and the causal conditions.
As for the causal conditions, there are five types of causes.
That is to say: the cause of arising,
the cause of dependence,
and the cause of establishment.
The sustaining cause,
the nourishing cause,
and the predominant cause are as previously explained.
How many conditions do derived matter bound to the desire realm serve as for derived matter bound to the desire realm?
Answer: They serve as the cause-condition and the predominant condition.
As for causes, there are two types of causes:
namely, the similar-type cause (sabhāga-hetu) and the maturation cause (vipāka-hetu).
Regarding "predominance," it is as previously explained.

As for the conditioned matter bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-rūpa*), how many conditions does it have with respect to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the desire realm? Answer: It is the cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The dominant cause consists of a single cause,
namely the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
As for "predominance," it is as previously explained.
With how many conditions do the great elements (mahābhūta) bound to the desire realm serve as conditions for the great elements bound to the form realm?
Answer: One—predominance.
The meaning of "predominance" (adhipati) is as previously explained.

Regarding the question of how many conditions (pratyaya) the great elements (mahābhūta) bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu) serve as for other great elements bound to the form realm: they serve as the cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya) and the predominance-condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
As for causes, there are two types of causes:
namely, the coexistent cause and the similar-type cause.
The predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained.
With how many conditions do the great elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) serve as conditions for the great elements bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
Answer: One, the predominant condition.
The meaning of "predominance" (adhipati) is as previously explained.
How many conditions do the primary elements (mahābhūta) bound to the desire realm serve as for the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) bound to the form realm?
Answer: One, namely, predominance.
The meaning of "predominance" (adhipati) is as previously explained.
With how many conditions is derived matter bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) a condition for derived matter bound to the form realm?
Answer: It is a cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya).
The dominant cause consists of three causes,
namely: the co-existent cause.
The homogeneous,
the resultant,
and the dominant [conditions] are as previously explained.
How many conditions do derived matter bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu) have with respect to the primary elements (mahābhūta) bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu)?
Answer: One, the condition of predominance (adhipatipratyaya).
The meaning of "predominance" (*adhipati*) is as previously explained.

How many conditions do the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) have with respect to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
Answer: One, namely, predominance.
The meaning of "predominance" (adhipati) is as previously explained.
How many conditions do the primary elements (mahābhūta) bound to the form realm serve for derived matter (upādāyarūpa) bound to the desire realm?
Answer: One—predominance.
The meaning of "predominance" (adhipati) is as previously explained.
How many conditions do derived matter bound to the desire realm serve as for derived matter bound to the form realm?
Answer: One, namely, predominance.
The meaning of "predominance" (adhipati) is as previously explained.
How many conditions do derived matter bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) serve as for derived matter bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta)?
Answer: One, namely, predominance.
The meaning of "predominance" (adhipati) is as previously explained.

With how many conditions do the primary elements (mahābhūta) bound to the realm of form serve as conditions for the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) bound to the realm of form? Answer: They serve as the cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya).
The dominant cause consists of five causes; namely,
the five beginning with the productive cause (janaka-hetu).
As for "predominance," it is as previously explained.
Regarding the derived matter bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many conditions does it have with respect to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the form realm?
Answer: It is a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The predominant cause consists of one cause,
namely, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Regarding "predominance," it is as previously explained.
As for those forms that are bound to the desire realm,
are all those forms derived from the great elements (mahābhūta) that are bound to the desire realm?
It may be stated in four propositions:
there are [dharmas] that are bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) but are not derived from the great elements (mahābhūta) bound to the desire realm.
This refers to the primary elements (mahābhūta) bound to the desire realm;
for the primary elements are not themselves derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
There is also derived matter of the form realm that is bound to the desire realm.
It is not bound to the desire realm;
that is to say, it is derived from the great elements (mahābhūta) that are unbound or bound to the desire realm.
Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to matter that follows the category of knowledge regarding all phenomena,
as well as matter that follows the category of subsequent knowledge manifesting in dependence on a body belonging to the desire realm;
such matter is bound to the desire realm and is derived from the primary elements bound to the desire realm.
That is to say, it is matter bound to the desire realm,
produced by the primary elements bound to the desire realm.
Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to the resistant derived matter bound to the desire realm,
as well as the non-informative matter (avijñapti) produced by informative action (vijñapti).
There is also matter that is not bound to the desire realm.
It is not produced from the primary elements (mahābhūta) bound to the desire realm;
rather, it is produced from the primary elements bound to the form realm,
provided that the matter itself is bound to the form realm.
It is derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta) bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
If the matter is not bound [to any realm],
it is derived from the primary elements bound to the realm of form.
Are all those forms that are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are bound to the form realm?
One should answer by means of four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).
There are forms that are bound to the form realm...
It is not produced by the great elements (mahābhūta) bound to the form realm;
that is to say, it is produced by the great elements bound to the form realm,
just as previously stated regarding those with form that are produced by the great elements bound to the form realm.
It is not bound to the form realm;
that is to say, it is unbound to form.
It is produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) that are bound to the form realm.
What, then, is this? It refers to matter that arises in dependence on a body belonging to the form realm, which conforms to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*);
such matter is bound to the form realm.
It is derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta) bound to the realm of form;
that is to say, the matter is bound to the realm of form and is derived from the primary elements bound to the realm of form.
What, then, is this? It refers to the derived matter that is resistant and bound to the realm of form,
as well as the outflowing non-informative matter that arises in accordance with the mind.
There is matter that is not bound to the form realm,
yet is not derived from primary elements bound to the form realm;
namely, the primary elements bound to the desire realm.
If form is bound to the desire realm,
it is derived from the great elements bound to the desire realm; if form is unbound, [it is derived from the great elements that are unbound].
Regarding those material forms derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta) bound to the desire realm that are past:
are all those forms derived from past primary elements?
It can be answered in four propositions.
There is that which is matter of the past but not derived from past primary elements;
namely, past primary elements themselves.
Therefore, as previously stated,
there is matter that is derived from past primary elements,
yet is not itself past.
This refers to matter produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the future, present, and past.
What, then, is this? It refers to the non-informative (avijñapti) matter arising from informative (vijñapti) action of the future and present.
It is derived from past primary elements,
because it relies upon past manifest action (*vijñapti*).
It possesses form and is derived from past primary elements that are themselves past.
That is to say, form is past,
produced by past primary elements. What, then, is this?
This refers to all past derived matter that is resistant,
as well as the non-informative matter that follows the mind and the non-informative matter produced by informative action.
There is matter that is neither past nor derived from past primary elements;
namely, future and present primary elements,
as well as matter that is future or present.
If the matter is present, it is derived from present primary elements;
if the matter is future,
it is derived from future primary elements.
Regarding all forms that are future:
are all those forms derived from future primary elements?
Answer: All forms that are future are derived from primary elements.
Regarding that "all future form," what does this mean?
It refers to all derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) that is characterized by resistance (sapratigha) in the future.
The non-informative [action] that follows the mind:
if it is the non-informative [action] produced by informative [action],
it is constructed from future primary elements.
Because it relies on future manifest form (vijñapti),
there is matter that is future but not produced by future primary elements (mahābhūta);
namely, the future primary elements themselves.
If form is future,
or produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the past or present, how is this so?
This refers to the non-informative matter (avijñapti) produced by future informative matter (vijñapti),
which is derived from past and present primary elements (mahābhūta),
because it depends upon past and present informative matter.
Regarding all forms that are present:
are all those forms derived from present primary elements?
One should respond by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
There is matter that is present but not produced by present primary elements;
namely, matter that is present and produced by past primary elements.
What, then, is this? It refers to the non-informative (avijñapti) matter produced by present informative (vijñapti) action,
which is derived from past primary elements (mahābhūta).
Therefore, as previously stated,
it is asked: does this unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa) also have present primary elements (mahābhūta) as its support?
Why is it not so stated?
The answer is: because that is the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), and not a created basis.
This unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa) has two kinds of bases:
the first is the basis of transformation,
namely the present primary elements (mahābhūta).
Because it functions through that power,
the second is the basis for production,
namely, the past primary elements (mahābhūta).
Because it is produced by that power,
only the basis of production (*utpatti-āśraya*) is mentioned here,
not the basis of transformation (*parāvṛtty-āśraya*).
Therefore, it is not stated [as a cause],
because the five causes capable of producing [matter] are all past,
whereas matter exists in the present.
That which is derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) is not present;
that is to say, future matter (*rūpa*) is derived from present great elements.
Furthermore, what is this?
It refers to the unmanifest (avijñapti) produced by a future manifest (vijñapti),
which is derived from present primary elements (mahābhūta).
Therefore, as previously stated:
there is form that is present,
produced by present primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
It refers to matter that is present and produced by present primary elements.
Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to all present derived matter that is subject to resistance,
the non-informative matter that follows the mind,
and the non-informative matter produced by present informative matter.
It is produced by the great elements of the present,
because it depends upon present manifest action (*vijñapti*).
There is form that is not of the present.
It is not produced by present primary elements;
that is to say, it is produced by past or future primary elements.
If the matter is past...
Regarding matter derived from the primary elements of the future and the past:
if matter is of the future,
how is it derived from the primary elements of the future?
...and so on, as explained at length. Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to bring about certainty for those who harbor doubts;
that is to say, this treatise extensively expounds upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Or perhaps some may harbor doubts,
thinking that the author of this treatise is skilled only in the ultimate truth (paramārtha) and not skilled in the conventional truth (saṃvṛti).
In order to bring certainty to those who harbor doubts,
this treatise is composed to demonstrate the distinction between the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) and the earth (*pṛthivī*), and so forth.
What is earth? The answer is:

it is manifested color and shape; this is the conventional designation of "earth. That is to say, regarding manifested color and shape, worldly people establish the designation "earth" based on a common conceptual construction.
As it is said in the world regarding blue or yellow earth,
or long or short earth,
what is the earth element?
Answer: It is the tangible element of solidity (*khara-spraṣṭavya*). This is the ultimate, primary substance of earth.
What is water?
Answer: It is in reference to color and shape that this is conventionally designated as "water.
That is to say, in the world, based on common conventional designations, the name "water" is applied to color and shape.
As it is said in the world regarding blue, yellow, and so forth,
or long, short, and so forth as being "water," what is the water element (*ābdhātu*)?
Answer: It is the tactile quality of moisture.
This is the ultimate, primary substance of water.
What is fire?
Answer: It is manifested through color and shape; this is a conventional designation for "fire.
That is to say, in the world, based upon color and shape, people collectively establish the conventional designation "fire" by means of shared conceptualization.
It is as when people in the world speak of fire that is blue or yellow,
or fire that is long or short;
it is also like the way a brahmin contemplates fire.
The verse says:
Red flames bring many epidemics; Yellow armies arise from famine.
Variegated brings abundance; green brings decline. White and black preside over prosperity and destruction.
What is the fire element?
Answer: It is the tactile quality of heat.
This is the ultimate, primary substance that constitutes fire.
What is wind? The answer is: it is the wind element.
What is the wind element?
Answer: It is the element of mobility (*īraṇatva*) that is contact.
Question: Why is the conventional wind not mentioned?
Answer: Because worldly people do not form conceptual designations (*parikalpa*) regarding wind.
Other masters say that because the world also forms conceptual designations for wind only to a minor extent, it is not mentioned;
as when people in the world speak of "dusty wind."
These are the arajas wind,
the vaiśvānara wind,
and the vāyu wind.
Regarding small winds, great winds,
the dust-circle winds, and so forth—
by how many bases (āyatana) are earth, water, fire, and wind subsumed?
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to bring certainty to those who harbor doubts.
That is to say, upon hearing the teachings on the conventional levels (*saṃvṛti-bhūmi*) and so forth,
one then claims they have no substantial reality and are not included within the [proper] spheres of existence.
It is not that which is cognized by consciousness.
Or, it may be said that the provisional and the real are subsumed within the same locus and are cognized by the same consciousness.
To eliminate that doubt, it is shown that although earth and so forth are conventionally designated, they also possess a real substantial nature;
they are subsumed under one of the five bases and cognized by one of the five consciousnesses.
Furthermore, it is to reveal that the conventional and the real are not subsumed within the same locus and are not cognized by the same consciousness;
for these reasons, this treatise is composed.
By how many bases (āyatana) are earth, water, fire, and wind subsumed?
By how many consciousnesses (vijñāna) are they cognized?
Answer: Earth, water, and fire are subsumed by one base.
That is to say, the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is that which is seen by the eye;
it is cognized by two types of consciousness,
namely, visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) and mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
Visual consciousness apprehends its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); mental consciousness apprehends both its own specific characteristic and the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Wind is comprised within a single location.
This means it is obtained by the body through the sense-base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
It is cognized by two types of consciousness, namely, body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
One should understand that they grasp both specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), as previously explained.
Some say that this is also included within the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*),
but it is not mentioned because it is cognized by eye-consciousness only to a minor extent.
By how many bases (āyatana) are the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind subsumed, and by how many consciousnesses are they cognized?
Answer: They are subsumed under one base, namely the base of the tangible (spraṣṭavyāyatana), because they are acquired by the body;
they are cognized by two consciousnesses.
That is to say, body-consciousness and mental-consciousness;
they grasp their own and common characteristics as previously explained.
Question: How many bases (*āyatana*) must be combined to be described as "capable of drawing forth"?
In how many places is it said that there is a conjunction [of conditions] such that one is "drawn"?
Answer: If it is from one sentient being to another sentient being, then nine bases are capable of drawing one forth.
Nine bases are drawn [toward it].
If it pertains to the category of sentient beings and not the category of non-sentient things, then nine bases are able to draw it.
Four bases are drawn [toward it].
If it is not among the category of sentient beings but among that which is not sentient,
then the four bases can attract it,
and it is attracted by the four bases.
If one who does not belong to the category of sentient beings enters into the category of sentient beings,
then four bases can attract [the result],
and nine bases are attracted.
The same applies to what has been said regarding drawing, holding, transporting, and so forth.
Question: How many locations combined are designated as the "means of measurement" (pramāṇa), and how many locations combined are designated as the "object of measurement" (prameya)?
Answer: The four bases are the means of cognition, and the four bases are the objects of cognition;
this is because the five faculties are subtle and are not cognizable phenomena.
Question: How many bases (āyatana) combined are said to be the "weigher," and how many bases combined are said to be the "weighed"?
Regarding this, some say:
The four bases can weigh that which is weighed by those four bases.
Other masters say that the four bases can weigh, and heaviness is what is weighed.
Question: How many bases (āyatana) combined are said to be the burner, and how many bases combined are said to be the burned?
Regarding this, some say:
Four bases are capable of burning;
four bases are what is burned.
Other masters say:
Heat is that which burns;
the four [elements] are that which is burned.
Question: How many bases (āyatana) must be combined to be called "that which cuts"?
In how many places is it said that [the path] is combined as that which is to be abandoned?
Some say that four places are able to abandon it.
It is abandoned by the four spheres.
Other masters say that the nature of solidity is that which abandons it.
The four bases are that which is to be cleansed.
Question: How many bases combined are said to be the cleanser?
How many bases combined are said to be that which is cleansed?
Some say that four parts are able to wash,
and four parts are what is washed.
Other masters say that four bases are capable of washing;
it is the base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) that is washed.
As it is said, they are bright white after being washed,
or like the color of gold;
furthermore, there are those who say:
The four bases are that which can wash;
contact is that which is washed.
As it is said: "A cup filled with bathing powder is taken to the edge of a certain pond."
He rubs and washes his body to remove dust and impurities.
Some say that the four places [of the body] are what can be washed.
The twelve sense bases are that which is to be washed.
Through this bathing,
all twelve internal sense bases become completely clear and pure, free from all defilements and turbidity.
Question: Among these four great elements, how many are capable of acting as calamities?
Answer: Three;
excluding earth. Question: For what reason is earth incapable of acting as a calamity?
The answer is: "It is not their field;
it is not their vessel," and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that only that which is violent and sharp can cause calamity;
the nature of earth is dull and sluggish, and thus cannot cause calamity.
Some say: "If one can cause damage to internal phenomena,
they can also bring about calamity for external phenomena."
That which is called the "cutting of the vital points" (marmaccheda) is termed the destruction of internal phenomena;
this consists solely of the three great elements.
Therefore, earth is not a calamity.
Some say that calamities are established for the purpose of destroying the earth;
because the three great elements can burn, inundate, and strike the earth, they are called calamities.
The earth is not like that.
Some say: "If the earth were also subject to destruction by calamities..."
It should proceed from the wind-circle up to the fourth dhyāna, making them all firm and solid,
merging them into a single mass; this constitutes the kalpa of formation, not that which can destroy.
Some say: if a particular stage were capable of acting as a calamity,
it would necessarily destroy even the fourth dhyāna.
However, as for the fact that those [lower realms] are not subject to destruction by calamities,
this gives rise to a further inquiry:
For what reason do the calamities of those levels not reach it?
Some say it is because the earth itself is not subject to calamity;
others say:
If that stage were subject to calamity, then there would be no ultimate summit above all calamities;
for the three higher meditative absorptions (dhyānas) serve respectively as the summits of the three types of calamity.
If the fourth meditative absorption were destroyed by calamity, [there would be no such summit].
Consequently, there is no further location that could serve as the pinnacle of higher calamities,
because the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu) lack spatial location.
Some say this is because [the formless beings] wish to avoid the gods of the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa).
Because there is no further rebirth for them,
if those abodes were subject to the calamities [of destruction],
then the Śuddhāvāsa deities would not all attain parinirvāṇa at the end of their lifespans.
If that is so, how is their lifespan known?
If one were to say that there is also parinirvāṇa at the end of the lifespan,
then the calamities of that stage would have no cause to arise.
As it is said: "In whatever place there remains even a single ant's egg, that place is not destroyed by the calamities.
Others say: "Wherever there is an internal calamity, there is also an external calamity."
Because the fourth dhyāna is free from internal calamities, external calamities do not reach it.
This is because the first dhyāna possesses internal fires such as vitarka and vicāra,
and therefore has external fire calamities.
Because there is internal joy like water within the second dhyāna, there is an external calamity of water.
Because there is the wind of inhalation and exhalation within the third dhyāna, there is an external calamity of wind.
In the fourth dhyāna, there are no further internal calamities;
therefore, external calamities cannot reach it.
Question: When the calamity of fire arises, from where does the fire emerge?
Some maintain this view:
when the world is formed, seven sun-discs arise simultaneously and remain hidden behind Mount Yugandhara.
Thereafter, the sun-disk rises in that place and circumambulates Mount Sumeru, providing illumination,
until the time when the fire calamity arises at the end of the kalpa.
The remaining six suns emerge in succession;
by their power, the world is destroyed.
Some say:
When the world is about to be destroyed,
the single sun-disk divides into seven suns;
by their power, the world is then destroyed.
Some say that when the single sun-disk reaches the end of the kalpa,
it becomes sevenfold hotter and incinerates the world-system.
Others say:
Having first been hidden underground for seven days,
it subsequently gradually emerges and functions as previously described.
Thus it is said.
Through the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings,
the world is formed until the end of the kalpa.
Because the power of karma is exhausted,
a calamitous fire arises in the vicinity;
it burns and consumes everything as far as the Brahma palace.
Question: When the calamity of water arises, from where does the water emerge?
Some offer this explanation:
"From the periphery of the third dhyāna, hot ash-water rains down."
By this means, everything up to the Ābhāsvara Heaven is inundated.
Some say that it surges upward from the water-wheel below.
By the power of those [actions], the world is destroyed.
Thus it is said:
the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings causes the world to be formed.
At the end of the kalpa, because the power of karma is exhausted,
calamitous waters arise in nearby regions;
through those causes and conditions, the world is destroyed.
Question: When the calamity of wind arises, from where does the wind emerge?
Some offer this explanation:
At the boundary of the fourth dhyāna, there is a great wind called Pātāpa.
Suddenly, hundreds of koṭis of world-systems were upheaved;
Sumeru, the King of Mountains, the golden wheel, the surrounding mountains, and all else were uprooted and cast down,
causing them to strike one another and toss upward and downward.
It is like a ball of flour or dough that disperses and vanishes into the air.
Other masters say that a fierce wind arises from the lower wind-circle.
It scatters the world.
Thus it is said that the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings causes the world to be formed.
At the end of the kalpa, because the power of karma is exhausted,
destructive winds arise in their vicinity,
reaching as far as the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven and utterly destroying everything there.
Question: When the three calamities arise, do all external objects undergo transformation in accordance with those calamities?
Regarding this, some say:
All things undergo transformation and follow this sequence:
it is said that when the calamity of fire arises in this world,
all external objects become entirely light and dry.
It is just as when dry grass, cotton wool, or birch bark is touched by fire;
it is immediately burned away and consumed.
If a calamity of water should arise, all external objects [are likewise destroyed].
All will be melted away like granulated sugar;
as soon as they are touched by water, they immediately dissolve and perish.
If the calamity of wind arises, all external objects [will likewise be destroyed].
All things will be dispersed like a handful of sand;
as soon as the wind touches them, they immediately fall apart.
If this were so, all phenomena would have to abandon their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
According to this explanation,
when the three calamities arise, even solid and moist substances do not undergo transformation; rather,
it occurs solely through the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings.
These three calamities arise and are able to destroy that which is difficult to destroy;
thus, these three calamities and the objects they destroy must necessarily be comprised within the same homogeneous realm and level (*sabhāga-dhātu-bhūmi*).
This means that the calamities of the desire realm can destroy the desire realm;
the calamities of the first dhyāna destroy the first dhyāna,
and so on up to the third dhyāna, which is likewise.
Question: If that is so,
how should one interpret the sūtra when it says,
for example, that the great earth, Sumeru, and so forth are all completely ablaze?
The wind blew the extinguished embers along until they ascended and burned the Brahma palaces.
Among the Ābhāsvara devas, there were some who had been born there for only a short time and were not well-acquainted with the formation and destruction of the kalpa.
Having seen this, they were struck with fear and thought:
"Lest those flames consume the Brahma palace, they shall surely burn this as well.
The answer is: one should know that the sutra speaks in reliance upon the continuity [of the stream of consciousness].
This means that the fire of the form realm continues from the desire realm and burns the Brahma palaces;
one should understand that the same applies by analogy to the fire, water, and wind that continue from the desire realm.
Question: What is the sequence in which these three calamities arise?
Answer: Fire, water, and wind follow this order of succession;
however, these three do not arise immediately one after another.
This means that seven calamities of fire arise in succession first,
and only thereafter does one calamity of water arise;
in this manner, it passes through seven sets of seven fire-kalpas.
Following seven water kalpas and another seven fire calamities,
immediately thereafter, one wind calamity arises.
Therefore, the kalpas of wind and water both arise following the fire kalpa,
because the fire kalpa begins its count from three. By this,
the lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna devas as sixty-four kalpas is correctly explained.
What has been stated thus constitutes the measure of a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).
Each of these consists of eighty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*),
because the periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness each consist of twenty [intermediate kalpas].
Furthermore, when the initial fire kalpa was about to destroy the world,
the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa was eighty thousand years;
they lived in peace and abundance, and their numbers were exceedingly great.
In the kingdoms, cities, villages, and towns, chickens could fly from one to another;
many people practiced the ten paths of wholesome action.
From that time forward, sentient beings in the hells who passed away were no longer reborn there.
At that time, twenty *kalpas* of abiding have already passed;
this is the first of the twenty *kalpas* of destruction.
From this point on, sentient beings in the hells gradually diminish until finally not a single one remains.
This is called the destruction of the realm of sentient beings in hell;
next, the destruction of the animal realm;
and next, the destruction of the hungry ghost realm.
Each instance of destruction is as described for the hells.
Next, the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa are destroyed.
[Question: Regarding the animals and hungry ghosts, do they perish before the humans?
How could the flavors required by humans, such as milk and curd,
as well as activities such as plowing and driving,
possibly exist? Some say:
Through the predominant power of human karma,
there are insentient objects that appear like animals,
yielding milk and other flavors, and performing various functions.
Question: It is said that the human body currently contains eighty thousand types of parasites that act as supporting conditions to maintain the continuity of the body.
Since those [parasites] are absent at that time, how can the body persist?
Answer: At that time, the human body naturally remains stable.
Just as the bodies of bodhisattvas and wheel-turning kings remain stable by their very nature even though they lack various parasites, so too does this body remain stable by its own nature.
According to this teaching,
the great oceans are the original dwelling places of these various animals;
if there were not even a single animal remaining in them, [they would no longer be so].
This is called the destruction of the realm of sentient beings consisting of animals.
If the animal species dwell interspersed with humans,
they are destroyed only when those humans are destroyed.
One should understand that the destruction of the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) follows this same pattern.
However, when the human realm of Jambudvīpa is about to be destroyed,
it is by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) that at that time there remains a single sentient being.
Without a teacher, he reflected for himself and entered the first dhyāna.
Emerging from that concentration, he uttered these words:
"This first dhyāna is exceedingly blissful and exceedingly peaceful."
The news was proclaimed from one to another throughout Jambudvīpa;
those who heard it concentrated their minds and all entered the first dhyāna.
Thereafter, when they passed away, they were reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
When the sentient beings in Jambudvīpa gradually decrease until not even a single sentient being remains,
it is called "Jambudvīpa."
The realm of sentient beings perishes;
next, the continent of Videha perishes;
next, it perishes.
The destruction of each of the individual features of Aparagoyānī is as described for Jambudvīpa.
Uttarakuru is like the three evil destinies.
There are none who attain the meditative absorptions and are reborn in the Brahma world;
rather, when their lifespan there ends, they will necessarily be reborn among the gods of the desire realm,
until the realm of sentient beings in that place is exhausted.
This is called the destruction of the realm of sentient beings in Uttarakuru.
Once the human destiny has been destroyed, it is the natural law that one being among the gods of the Four Great Kings attains the first dhyāna.
Emerging from that meditative absorption, he proclaims as before,
until the realm of sentient beings in that place is exhausted;
this is called the destruction of the realm of sentient beings in that heaven.
Next, the Heaven of the Thirty-three is destroyed;
next, the Yāma Heaven is destroyed;
next, the Tuṣita Heaven is destroyed.
Next, the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations is destroyed;
next, the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations is destroyed.
The specific signs of destruction for each are as described for the first heaven.
When sentient beings of the desire realm have been destroyed in succession,
at that time, a single sentient being in the first dhyāna,
by the very nature of things (dharmatā), is able to enter the second dhyāna.
Emerging from that meditative absorption, he uttered these words:
"The second dhyāna is exceedingly blissful and exceedingly tranquil.
Thus, by successive transmission, the sound pervaded the Brahma palace.
Those who heard it focused their minds and entered the second dhyāna;
at the end of their lives, they were all reborn in that heaven.
Consequently, the sentient beings in the heavens of the first dhyāna gradually diminished.
When not even a single sentient being remains,
it is said that the realm of sentient beings of the Brahmā world has been destroyed.
Such is the destruction of the desire realm and the various palaces of the Brahmās.
For a long time, the world was empty and devoid of sentient beings;
then, after many eons had passed, the great earth, Jambudvīpa,
and its various mountains experienced a period when the heavens sent down no rain.
All grasses and trees become completely parched and withered;
they no longer sprout and eventually perish entirely.
After a long time, a second solar disc appears in the world.
The intense heat becomes even more fierce, thereby drying up the pits, streams, springs,
and ponds until not a single drop of moisture remains.
After a long time, a third sun disc appears in the world.
The blazing heat becomes doubly intense;
by this, all rivers and streams are dried up,
until not a single drop of moisture remains.
After a long time, a fourth sun appeared in the world,
its blazing heat doubling that of the previous ones;
by this, Lake Anavatapta was completely parched and dried up.
That is, from where the four great rivers originate—
the Gaṅgā, Sindhu, Vakṣu, and Sītā—
until they are completely deprived of moisture.
After a long time, a fifth solar disc appeared in the world,
its scorching heat twice as intense;
by this means, the great oceans were gradually dried up.
Eventually, it becomes completely devoid of moisture.
After a long time, a sixth sun disc appears in the world,
its blazing heat being twice as intense.
Consequently, this great earth, Sumeru,
and all else are completely parched and scorched, emitting thick clouds of smoke and blazing flames;
after a long time, a seventh solar disc appears in the world.
The heat is so intense and extreme that,
because of it, the great earth, Sumeru the king of mountains,
and all others simultaneously burst into flames, blazing fiercely from within and without.
Even the palaces of Brahmā were utterly consumed by fire;
from the world of Brahmā above down to the wind-circle below,
everything was completely incinerated, leaving not a single trace of ash or ember behind.
Just as when ghee or oil is completely consumed by fire,
nothing remains;
this case is also like that.
At that time, the desire realm and the first dhyāna were entirely empty and void;
there was nothing at all.
The twenty eons of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*) have now passed.
From this point begins the first of the twenty eons of emptiness (*śūnya-kalpa*).
Question: How many eons does it take for sentient beings to be destroyed?
For how many kalpas does the receptacle world perish?
Some say that it takes ten kalpas for sentient beings to perish.
The receptacle world is destroyed over ten kalpas;
some say that sentient beings are destroyed over fifteen kalpas.
Regarding the statement that the receptacle world is destroyed over five kalpas:
it is said that the sentient beings within it are destroyed over nineteen kalpas.
During one kalpa, the receptacle world is destroyed;
because it is not a collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*), individual karmas (*pratyeka-karman*) cannot be altered. Thus, this world remains in a state of destruction for a long period of time.
In the space below, a subtle wind arises;
at this moment, twenty eons of emptiness have already passed,
and twenty eons of formation begin from this point.
The subtle wind that arose gradually expanded and thickened;
after a vast period of time had passed, it coalesced into a wheel,
sixteen billion yojanas in thickness.
If expanded, they are innumerable;
their substance is firm and dense.
Suppose there were one great Nārāyaṇa.
He brandished the vajra-wheel with fierce power and struck it suspended above;
the vajra was shattered, yet the wind-circle remained unharmed.
Next, clouds arose and rained down upon the wind-circle.
Drops as large as chariot axles accumulate to form a wheel of water;
thus, while this water-wheel has not yet solidified,
it is eleven billion two hundred million yojanas deep.
Some say that the vast dimensions are expressed in terms of the wind-circle and so forth,
while the narrowest portion is one hundred koṭis.
There are one hundred koṭis of wheels,
all of which are equal in measurement;
that is, their diameter is twelve billion three hundred and four and a half [yojanas], and their circumference is three times that.
It measures thirty-six hundred million, ten thousand, three hundred and fifty yojanas.
This [ocean] does not flow sideways due to the karmic power of sentient beings.
Other masters say that,
impelled by the power of the wind,
[the earth] subsequently forms upon the water wheel.
A distinct wind arises,
which strikes this water so that it solidifies into gold;
this constitutes the Golden Wheel, three hundred and twenty million *yojanas* thick.
The water wheel subsequently diminished until its depth was only eight lakṣas.
Some say that the width of the golden wheel is equal to the measure of the water.
Other masters further state that,
following the relatively narrow water-circle,
clouds arise and rain down upon the gold-circle.
Drops as large as axle-trees fell for a long period of time;
the accumulated water became vast and its depth exceeded eighty thousand [yojanas],
whereupon fierce winds struck together, causing the jewels and other elements to transform and arise.
Furthermore, there are other winds that cause differentiation and distinction, namely: they divide the precious lands to form the various mountains and continents;
they separate the sweet and salty waters to form the inner and outer oceans;
and first, the four wonderful jewels form Mount Sumeru.
It emerges from the midst of the ocean and stands upon a golden wheel.
On its four sides, in order—north, east, south, and west—are the precious substances of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal;
according to the majestic power of these jewels, their colors manifest in the sky.
Therefore, Jambudvīpa appears empty and has the color of lapis lazuli.
This mountain rises eighty thousand yojanas above the water;
it is likewise [submerged] within the water for that same distance.
It is majestic and lovely.
Next, the seven golden mountains, formed of gold and jewels,
encircle Mount Sumeru and rest upon the golden wheel.
Within the waters, its measurements are equal to Mount Sumeru;
above the water, as they face one another, each is reduced by half and half again.
Subsequently, the four great continents are formed from earth and other elements.
At the bottom, it rests upon the Golden Wheel (kāñcanacakravāḍa) and encircles the outer edge of the Golden Mountains;
finally, it is formed by the Iron Rim-Mountain (cakkavāḷapabbata),
which stands outside the four continents like a wall surrounding them.
The seventh golden mountain, which emerges from the water, is half as high;
its height above the water is equal to that of Mount Sumeru,
and the breadth of all these mountains is equal to their respective heights above the water.
Between the seven golden mountains are seven inner seas,
filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
Outside the seven golden mountains lies the salt outer sea.
Each of these eight great oceans is eighty thousand [yojanas] deep.
The dimensions of the first seven are equal to the mountains that encircle them.
Regarding the eighth, some say:
Its width is three hundred and twenty-two thousand yojanas;
some say it is further increased by one thousand two hundred and eighty-seven and a half yojanas.
Mount Sumeru has four terraces.
The first terrace extends outwards by sixteen thousand [yojanas];
each of the three upper terraces is reduced by half successively.
The distance between each of the four tiers is ten thousand [yojanas].
Some say that the bottom of the first tier is level with the surface of the water.
The next two layers are each ten thousand [yojanas] below the one above;
the fourth layer is twenty thousand [yojanas] below the bottom.
The four sides of these four layers are like Mount Sumeru.
Adorned with the four precious substances, it is exquisitely beautiful;
its four tiers, in order,
are held by Vajrapāṇi and Mālādharī.
They are constantly arrogant.
The hosts of the Four Great Kings dwell upon the Yugandhara Mountains and the other seven golden mountains;
there are also villages and towns belonging to the retinues of the Four Great Kings.
Because the seven mountain ranges, the four terraces, the sun, the moon,
and the other celestial deities are all subsumed within the Heaven of the Four Great Kings,
this heaven is the most extensive among the heavens of the desire realm.
From the fourth level, there are another forty thousand yojanas to the summit of Mount Sumeru;
this is the abode of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Each of the four sides of the mountain summit measures twenty thousand [yojanas].
Calculated by its circumference, this totals eighty thousand.
Other masters say:
Each face measures eighty thousand [yojanas].
Its dimensions are exactly equal to those of its four sides at the base.
At each of the four corners of the mountain summit, there is a peak.
Its height and breadth are each five hundred [yojanas].
There dwells a yakṣa deity named Vajrapāṇi,
who resides therein to protect the devas.
In the center of the mountain summit is a city named Sudarśana.
Each side measures two thousand and five hundred yojanas, and its circumference is ten thousand yojanas.
The golden wall is half a yojana in height.
The ground is level and composed of pure gold,
adorned throughout with one hundred and one varieties of diverse jewels;
its surface is as soft to the touch as *tūla* cotton.
When one steps upon them, they reach up to the knees, rising and falling in accordance with the movement of the feet.
A gentle breeze arises, blowing away the withered flowers and drawing forth fresh,
wondrous blossoms that spread everywhere across the ground.
This is the great capital city where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, resides.
The city has a thousand gates, adorned with magnificent splendor.
At each gate stand five hundred yakṣas clad in blue garments.
Brave, heroic, and majestic, they were each a yojana in height;
clad in armor and bearing weapons, they stood guard at the city gates.
Within that city was a most excellent palace.
It is fully adorned with various kinds of exquisite jewels;
because it outshines all other celestial palaces, it is called "Excellence" (Viśeṣa).
Each side measures two hundred and fifty [yojanas].
It is one thousand yojanas in circumference.
At the four corners of the city are four terraced pavilions,
composed of the four jewels, such as gold and silver.
Adorned with various ornaments, it is exceedingly delightful.
Outside the city on its four sides are four gardens,
which serve as the places where those devas sport together.
First is the Garden of Various Vehicles (Citraratha),
meaning that within this garden, various kinds of vehicles appear according to the power of the gods' merit.
Second is the Garden of Coarse Evil (Pāruṣyaka).
When the devas wish to engage in battle, whatever armor, weapons, and the like they require appear before them.
Third is the Grove of Mixed Forests (Miśrakāvana);
when the devas enter it, all that they enjoy produces a simultaneously arising, supreme joy.
There are four pleasure groves where all varieties of most exquisite sensual objects are gathered; one may view them without ever growing weary.
These four groves are all square in shape.
Each one measures one thousand yojanas in extent;
in the center of each is a wish-fulfilling pond,
measuring fifty yojanas on each side.
Within it, the water of eight virtues flows in abundance;
there are exquisite flowers, jeweled boats, and beautiful birds according to one's desires,
each wondrous and lovely, adorned in every way.
On the four sides of the four groves are four exquisite grounds;
each is situated twenty yojanas from its respective grove,
and each side of these grounds measures two hundred [yojanas].
This is the place where the hosts of devas engage in their supreme pastimes;
there, the devas compete for victory and enjoy themselves in delight.
To the northeast outside the city is the Pārijāta tree.
This is the place where the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enjoy sensual pleasures;
its roots are coiled and its base is five yojanas in depth and breadth,
with its trunk rising upward and its branches spreading out to the sides.
Its height and breadth are each one hundred yojanas;
its petals unfurl and its flowers bloom with a wondrous fragrance that,
carried by the wind, perfumes the air for a full hundred yojanas.
Even when the wind blows against it, its fragrance still pervades fifty [yojanas].
Outside the city, at the southwest corner, there is the Great Hall of the True Dharma (Mahāsudharman).
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven regularly gather there on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of each half-month.
Gathering within this hall, they clearly distinguish between humans and devas,
and subdue the asuras and others;
matters concerning what is in accordance with the Dharma and what is not, and other such categories, are explained extensively in other places.
