Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was composed in order to refute the positions of others and to clarify one's own position.
As the Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"All things that are transformations are not substantially existent.
If they were substantially existent, how could they be called 'transformations'?"
The Venerable One also said:
"Transformations are not substantially existent;
they are manifested through cultivation."
Just as a corpse may rise through the power of a ghost-possessing spell,
so too, in order to clarify that the intended meaning of what has been said is that all manifested phenomena are substantially real,
this treatise was composed based on such reasons.
When one born in the desire realm creates a transformation-body of the form realm and utters speech of the form realm, by which primary elements (mahābhūta) are that bodily and vocal matter derived?
Answer: It is bound to the form realm.
When one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) creates a transformation (*nirmāṇa*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and utters speech of the desire realm,
by which primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are that bodily and vocal form produced?
Answer: They are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This is because all outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) derived matter is produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the same homogeneous realm and level.
Nevertheless, there are eight distinct types of emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
This means that for one born in the desire realm who creates a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) within the desire realm, there are two types:
first, resembling one's own body;
second, resembling the body of another.
There are also these two types for those who manifest emanations of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, there are two types of emanations of the form realm manifested by one born in the form realm:
first, those resembling one's own body; [and second, those resembling others].
Second is that which resembles another's body.
When manifesting transformations of the desire realm, there are likewise these two.
These are called the eight.
In this context, the treatise is composed based on only two types of cases:
namely, one born in the desire realm who creates a transformation-body in the form realm,
and one born in the form realm who creates a transformation-body in the desire realm that resembles the body of another.
Question: Why is it that in this treatise the discussion is based solely upon the two bodies?
Answer: It is because the author of the treatise intended it to be so;
he composed the treatise according to his own intention.
Provided that it does not contradict the characteristics of the Dharma,
one should not question its underlying reason. Some say:
Only these two bodies are subtle, difficult to see, and difficult to comprehend;
therefore, they are specifically mentioned. Some say:
Only these two bodies are most difficult to manifest,
for they can only be produced by relying upon extensive preparatory application (*prayoga*). Some say:
This is difficult for the world to believe and accept;
namely, who could create another realm or another body? Some say:
These two are the most extraordinary:
namely, the ability to manifest a different realm and a different body.
Therefore, they are specifically mentioned.
There are, in total, two kinds of transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*):
first, those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and second, those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Alternatively, they may be classified as five.
That is to say, they are bound to the desire realm and the four dhyānas;
alternatively, there are twelve,
namely the minds of the twelve types of emanators.
That is to say, those who have attained the fruit of the first dhyāna,
up to those who have attained the fruit of the fourth dhyāna,
each have three types.
What are the three?
First, ordinary beings;
second, those in training.
There are three types of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, there is another teaching of three:
first, external persons who are ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Second, ordinary beings of the internal dharma;
third, noble ones.
Furthermore, there is another explanation of three [categories].
This refers to attainment at three stages:

first, attainment at the time of becoming free from defilement, which means attaining the dhyānas when one becomes free from the defilements of a lower level; second, attainment at the time of realizing the fruit.
This means it is acquired at the time of attaining the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), and it is acquired at the time of refining the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra); that is,
when transforming the faculties to become "attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) or "immovable" (akopya).
Alternatively, they may be divided into fourteen;
that is to say, there are four belonging to the desire realm,
which are the fruits of the four dhyānas.
Those bound to the first dhyāna also consist of four types,
as explained for the desire realm.
Those bound to the second dhyāna consist of three types.
Then, the fruits of the three higher dhyānas are those connected to the third dhyāna;
there are two [types of] fruits of the two higher dhyānas.
There is one [resultant mind] bound to the fourth dhyāna;
that is, the fruit of the fourth dhyāna,
because the minds of the lower stages are weak and inferior.
One cannot manifest transformations in a higher stage;
alternatively, they may be divided into fifteen,
namely, the various transformative minds bound to the five stages.
Each has superior, middling, and inferior grades.
Some say that those who have attained the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the five stages each possess three categories.
This refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth, as previously described.
Alternatively, they may be divided into forty-two types,
meaning that each of the fourteen aforementioned categories is further distinguished by superior, middling, and inferior grades.
Some say that those who have attained the fourteen types of transformative minds each belong to three categories, namely:
ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth, as previously explained.
Those who manifest emanations of the desire realm have bodies that resemble sentient beings of the desire realm;
those who manifest emanations of the form realm likewise [resemble sentient beings of the form realm].
That body resembles that of a sentient being in the form realm.
Question: By how many bases (āyatana) is the emanated body produced therein subsumed?
Answer: If one born in the desire realm produces an emanation of the desire realm, [it is subsumed by all ten bases].
One's own body and the bodies of others are all subsumed within the four bases—
namely, visible form, odor, flavor, and tangibility—
when manifesting as transformations of the form realm.
One's own body and the bodies of others are both subsumed under two bases,
namely, visible form and tangibility.
This applies when one born in the form realm creates a transformation-body belonging to the form realm.
When manifesting transformations of the desire realm, both one's own body and the bodies of others are comprised of two bases (*āyatana*).
When manifesting transformations of the form realm,
both one's own body and the bodies of others are comprised of four bases.
As previously stated.
Some say that if it is produced as another's body, it is comprised within four bases (*āyatana*).
If one considers the self-body as being comprised of only two bases,
it is so that one does not establish the existence of the bases of odor and taste therein.
Thus it is said.
Although there is no fault in the transformation of odors and tastes, they are not "accomplished" [as inherent qualities],
just as the clothing, ornaments, and flower scents of a person,
though present upon the body, are not accomplished [as part of its essential nature].
Question: If one born in the desire realm produces a transformation-body (nirmāṇa) of the desire realm as the fruit of the first dhyāna,
and produces a transformation-body of the form realm as the fruit of the first dhyāna—
between these two types, which is inferior and which is superior?
Answer: These two modes of operation are equal and without distinction.
However, the form realm (rūpadhātu) is superior because its constituent elements (dhātu) are superior.
Question: If one born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) produces a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) of the desire realm that is the fruit of the second dhyāna...
Regarding the transformation of the form realm produced as the fruit of the first dhyāna—between these two types, which is inferior and which is superior?
Answer: That of the desire realm is superior in its activity.
Because they are able to travel back and forth from the desire realm up to the second dhyāna;
as for the "form realm," it is superior in terms of its realm because the dharmas of the form realm are superior to those of the desire realm.
Question: If one born in the desire realm produces a transformation-body (nirmāṇa) of the desire realm as the fruit of the first dhyāna,
and produces a transformation-body of the form realm as the fruit of the second dhyāna—
between these two types, which is inferior and which is superior?
Answer: Those of the form realm (rūpadhātu) excel in two respects:
first, excellence of realm;
second, excellence of movement.
As it is said:
one born in the desire realm produces emanations of the desire and form realms,
which are the fruits of the first and second dhyānas.
Distinguishing between superior and inferior in comparison:
thus, one born in the desire realm who produces emanations of the desire and form realms [produces] the fruits of the first and third dhyānas.
The fruit of the first and fourth dhyānas;
the fruit of the second and third dhyānas;
the fruit of the second and fourth dhyānas.
Regarding the fruits of the third and fourth dhyānas,
their relative superiority and inferiority should be understood through reasoning,
following the pattern of the preceding questions and answers.
Just as it is for those born in the desire realm,
so it is for those born in the first dhyāna and those born in the second dhyāna.
Regarding those born in the third dhyāna,
it should be understood that the detailed explanation should be expanded upon as appropriate;
this is because they possess the mind capable of giving rise to bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*), just as in the case of those born in the first dhyāna.
It causes the emanated body to perform various functions such as coming and going;
the aforementioned meditative absorptions (dhyānas) do not possess such a mind.
The master of the emanation produces the emanated being in those [higher realms].
How can there be functions such as coming and going?
Answer: It is like when one is born in the first dhyāna and initiates a mind of manifest action (vijñapti).
It causes the transformation body to perform functions such as coming and going.
Likewise, when one gives birth to the higher dhyānas,
one also initiates the mind of manifest action (vijñapti-citta) by means of the first dhyāna.
It causes the manifested bodies to perform functions such as coming and going,
just like visual consciousness and so forth;
thus say other masters.
The various emanated bodies possess no such functions as coming or going;
they merely abide in silence through the power of the emanator.
It causes those [beings] to appear as if there were activities such as coming and going;
it is like the play of Indra’s net, appearing as if existent though it is not.
Question: At the time when these transformative events arise...
"Does it necessarily manifest only by having something upon which to rely,
or is it otherwise?
Some say:
A transformative act must have a basis; that is,
it must rely upon wood, stone, clods of earth, or the like,
for the master of transformation to be able to perform the act of transformation.
Other masters say:
if one who first gives rise to supernormal powers (abhijñā) produces a transformation (nirmāṇa), it necessarily depends on something external;
however, this is not the case for one whose supernormal wisdom is perfected.
Without any basis, the provisional [mind] is able to initiate transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*).
Question: Is it one mind that produces one manifestation, or is it one mind that produces many manifestations?
If there is only one mind and one transformation,
how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the sutras and verses?
For example, it is said:
When the single master speaks, all those who are emanated speak;
when the single master is silent, all the emanations are silent.
If one mind produces many emanations, [the same applies].
How, then, is the statement in the *Prajñapti-śāstra* to be reconciled?
For it asks:
"What is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge regarding the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-sākṣātkriyābhijñā*)?"
By what means does one give rise to the supernormal knowledge of the realization of psychic power?
Answer: That beginner practices mundane concentration until it becomes extremely proficient;
once it is extremely proficient, he causes it to arise and manifest before him.
Because it is present before one, one is able to induce the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*).
From that, one is then able to produce a single transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
Even for the production of a single transformative act, such a number of moments of mind is required.
How much more so when there are many?
Some state that a single mind performs a single transformation.
If this is so, how should one interpret the scriptural verses cited?
Answer: First, by means of many minds, one prays for many emanated voices;
subsequently, by means of a single mind, one causes the voices to issue forth simultaneously.
The preceding state of many minds is the transformation.
Subsequently, it proceeds in accordance with a single mind.
Other masters say that a single mind produces many emanations.
Question: How should one interpret the *Prajñapti-śāstra* in this regard?
Answer: If one possesses the power of transformation at its initial stage, one can transform a single object with a single mind;
if one’s mastery of supernormal powers is perfected, one can transform many objects with a single mind.
Question: Regarding the transformative activities produced within a single moment of mind, are they necessarily of the same class or also of different classes?
Some say:
It must transform into something of the same class;
that is to say, when it becomes an elephant, it does not become a horse or the like. Some say:
It is also transformation into a different category;
that is to say, when one first gives rise to supernormal powers,
a single mind can only produce objects of a single category.
If one’s supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) is perfected, one can, with a single mind, manifest the fourfold army consisting of elephants and so forth.
Question: One already understands the transformative activities accomplished through cultivation (bhāvanā-maya).
Is there also transformation [attained] through birth?
Some say there is not,
because the power and function attained through birth are inferior.
It can merely be transformed so as to appear different from its original;
some say that it does indeed exist [in such a state].
However, it can only act as a cause for itself and not for anything else.
Question: If this is so, how does one reconcile this with what is stated in the sūtras? As a sūtra says:
There were three māra-maidens, each of whom manifested hundreds of female forms:
namely, girls who had not yet reached puberty, those who had recently given birth, those who had not yet given birth,
middle-aged women, and old women.
Each of these numbered one hundred.
Furthermore, they manifested various transformed bodies adorned with diverse ornaments and approached the Bodhisattva’s dwelling out of a desire to delude and entice him.
He said to the Bodhisattva, "Rise, Śramaṇa!
We have come now; we wish to attend to your needs."
The Bodhisattva did not accept it;
he immediately caused her body to take on the form of one who is aged and infirm, whereupon she withdrew in shame.
The answer is that [the transformation] occurred precisely upon the basis of the māra-maiden’s own karmic maturation (vipāka).
He manifests as the many hundreds of female bodies previously described;
just as a *kośika* caterpillar does not leave behind its cocoon, so it is said.
The mind acquired at birth is capable of manifesting transformations for both one's own body and the bodies of others.
How is this known?
It was once heard that the Venerable Upagupta...
While he sat in meditative concentration with his body upright, Māra came to harass him;
he placed a garland of flowers upon the Venerable One’s head.
Emerging from samādhi, the Venerable One was struck with wonder and thought to himself:
He thought, "Who has done this? and immediately realized it was the work of Māra.
To subdue him, he used his supernormal powers to manifest three corpses and fastened them around the neck of the Māra King.
It was said to be a dead snake, a dead dog, and a dead man. Thereupon,
the Māra King felt extreme shame and,
though he employed various skillful means, he was unable to depart.
Three corpses bound to him wound themselves around his neck;
as they tightened and grew increasingly foul-smelling, the demon became despondent and his terror redoubled.
In order to escape the corpses, he...
He then sank into the earth and emerged again, soaring into the air;
he further submerged himself in the great ocean waters and entered the interior of Mount Sumeru,
yet despite exerting all his strength to break through, he was ultimately unable to leave.
Māra, already exhausted and his own powers of deliverance at their end,
gradually passed through the six heavens seeking a way to escape; being unable to find one,
he went to the vicinity of the Brahma Palace and entreated Mahābrahmā, saying:
"I only pray that you will have compassion and remove this humiliation from the rishi upon my neck.
Brahmā replied:
"I cannot depart;
you may return to the one who originally bound you.
When Māra heard this, he descended to Jambudvīpa.
Prostrating with his five limbs in sincere devotion at the feet of the Venerable One,
he said: "O Great Virtue!"
"I only pray that you will, out of compassion,
forgive my former transgressions and depart from this place.
Then, the Venerable Upagupta slowly addressed the Māra, saying:
"I know the time.
Māra bowed his head repeatedly, apologized for his transgression, and sought mercy,
requesting to be shown when his humiliation would be removed.
The Venerable One said, "Will you,
from this day forth until the holy teaching of the Tathāgata has not yet perished, no longer harass or disturb the bhikṣus?
Māra replied:
"Indeed. We shall act according to your instructions.
Please grant us further instruction."
"It shall be as the Venerable One has ordained.
The Venerable One spoke again:
"I have indeed acted for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, yet I had a private aspiration."
"Now I wish to request you to do so.
Māra said,
"As you command."
The Venerable One replied:
"A hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, my body was born.
I have now beheld the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata."
That which has not yet been seen refers to the Buddha’s birth-body (janmakāya).
Could you now, O Benevolent One, manifest it for me?
Māra said, "This matter is very easy; I am capable of performing it.
I pray that when you see me, you do not immediately pay me homage."
"May I not incur sin.
The Venerable One said, "So be it," and immediately,
for the sake of the Māra, he caused the three corpses to dissolve and depart.
The Mara King, filled with joy, thanked the Venerable One and immediately entered the forest,
where he transformed his own body into the likeness of the Tathāgata,
complete with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs of excellence.
His majestic radiance was more brilliant than a thousand solar discs.
He further manifested a multitude of bhikṣus,
with Śāriputra on his right and Mahāmaudgalyāyana on his left.
The Venerable Ānanda followed behind holding his alms bowl,
together with Ājñātakauṇḍinya and twelve hundred and fifty other disciples,
emerging from the forest in the shape of a half-moon.
When the Venerable Upagupta saw this, he was filled with joy at such an unprecedented occurrence;
with a mind of pure sincerity, he was unable to contain himself, like a tree whose roots have been severed.
Unconsciously, he cast himself down to prostrate at the feet of the Māra.
The Māra was struck with terror and immediately caused his illusory manifestation to vanish.
From this, one knows that the wisdom obtained at birth is such.
He was also able to manifest transformations of his own body and the bodies of others.
When questioned, it was said that the venerable Upagupta possessed mastery over such transformative feats that surpassed that of Māra the Evil One by many millions of times.
"For what reason does the Venerable One not himself manifest [a form] by transformation,
but instead painfully entreats Māra to do so?
He replied, "The Venerable One possesses mastery over that which is produced through cultivation."
Since his birth-attained power of transformation was inferior to that of Māra,
and wishing to test Māra’s birth-attained power of transformation,
he requested that Māra transform himself into the body of a Buddha.
Some say:
A transformation produced through cultivation does not give rise to a sense of wonder in the Venerable who attained it himself;
however, a transformation produced by birth does give rise to a sense of wonder in the Venerable who did not attain it.
Desiring to entrust the King of Māras with the transformation of his perception of birth,
he therefore sought him to manifest as a Buddha-body. Some say:
The Venerable One’s profound mind reveres the Buddha;
had he manifested it himself, his reverential heart might not have been able to sustain it.
Therefore, he caused Māra to create it.
Some say: "The Venerable One has few desires;
if he were to manifest himself through transformation, he fears that devas, humans, and others might think he is already a Buddha and thus offer him the utmost veneration and support."
After his parinirvāṇa, the devas and people of the world made offerings to him with grief, as if he had entered extinction alongside the Buddha.
For this reason, they requested only Māra to act [as the messenger].
Question: What is the difference between the two kinds of transformations—those acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanā-labdha*) and those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*)?
Answer: There is no difference in those who are transformed;
however, for those who attain it through cultivation, it is pure, swift, perfect, and sublime, whereas this is not the case for those who obtain it by birth.
Some say that transformation obtained through birth relies solely on the body of one's own realm,
whereas transformation obtained through cultivation relies upon the bodies of both one's own realm and other realms.
Question: Is there such a thing as the retention of a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)?
If so, for what reason did the Buddha not retain a transformation body at the time of his parinirvāṇa, so that it might remain after his passing to sustain the teaching and benefit sentient beings?
If it were non-existent,
why did the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having already entered parinirvāṇa, leave his body to remain for a long time?
It has been heard that the Venerable Mahākāśyapa—
Having entered the city of Rājagṛha for his final almsround,
he ascended Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain not long after finishing his meal.
The mountain has three peaks that resemble the outstretched feet of a cock.
The Venerable One entered within and sat cross-legged,
making this solemn declaration:
"May this body of mine, along with my alms-bowl and staff, remain for a long time without decaying."
Until fifty-seven koṭis and six hundred thousand years have passed,
when the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maitreya appears in the world, he shall perform the buddha-work.
Having made this vow, he immediately entered parinirvāṇa;
at that moment, the three peaks merged into one,
covering the Venerable One as he remained in solemn stillness.
When the Buddha Maitreya appears in the world,
he will lead immeasurable humans and devas to this mountain and address the assembly, saying:
"Do you wish to see Kāśyapa, the foremost among the great disciples within the assembly of Śākyamuni Buddha’s followers who have perfected the ascetic virtues (dhūta-guṇa)?
The entire assembly replied in unison:
"We wish to see him.
Then Maitreya Tathāgata stroked the summit of Mount Kukkuṭapāda with his right hand;
immediately, the peak split open and became divided into three parts.
At that time, Kāśyapa took up his alms-bowl and staff,
emerged from the midst [of the assembly], and ascended into the air.
Immeasurable devas and humans beheld this miraculous transformation.
They marveled at this unprecedented event, for their minds had become pliant and supple.
When the World-Honored One Maitreya preached the Dharma according to their needs, they all attained the vision of the Truths.
If there were no such phenomena as the non-retaining emanations, how could this have occurred?
Some say that there is the preservation of emanated matters.
[An objection is raised: If this is so, why did the Blessed One not preserve an emanation body to remain and teach the Dharma after his parinirvāṇa?
The answer is that what ought to be done has been brought to completion;
that is to say, all those whom the Buddha was to deliver have already been delivered,
while those who remain undelivered are delivered by his noble disciples.
Some say that there is no prolonging of transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*).
Question: If that is so, how can the episode of Kāśyapa be accounted for?
Answer: Because it was sustained by those deities who possess faith and reverence.
Some say that at that time, Kāśyapa had not yet entered parinirvāṇa.
It would be unreasonable for him to attain final nirvāṇa only at the time of Maitreya Buddha; rather,
one might as well say that he does not exist, rather than saying that he remained silent for so long a time and dwelt in vain.
According to this teaching,
there remains the matter of manifested transformations;
therefore, Mahākāśyapa has already entered parinirvāṇa.
Question: The Sūtra states that at one time he performed a double demonstration,
namely, emitting fire from the lower part of his body and water from the upper part of his body.
Water flows from the lower part of the body and fire issues from the upper part.
Is this performed with one mind or two minds?
If it is performed with one mind:
How can a single mind have two contradictory results?
If they were produced by two minds,
how could two minds arise simultaneously at one time?
Some say that it is produced by a single mind.
Question: How can a single mind have two contradictory results?
Answer: First, one separately prays for water and fire with two distinct minds;
subsequently, one abides in a single mind to cause them both to issue forth together.
The former two minds are the preparatory stages (*parivarta*).
Subsequently, it proceeds in accordance with a single mind;
some say it is produced by two minds.
Question: How can two minds arise simultaneously?
Answer: Due to the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the two minds of water and fire revolve with such rapidity that they appear to arise at the same time.
It is like a man splitting wood:
his left hand emits light while his right hand follows his words to divide the bedding and requisites for the Saṃgha.
When it is time to manifest the formal motion (*jñapti*), there is no room for emitting light.
At the time when light is emitted, there is no possibility for the manifestation of bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
Due to the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the two minds that produce light and intimation revolve so rapidly that they appear to be emitted simultaneously.
It should be understood that the two minds of water and fire are likewise so; the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states:
"At one time, the Buddha manifested a transformation-buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), whose body was of true golden color and adorned with the primary and secondary marks."
When the World-Honored One speaks, the emanation also speaks;
when the emanation speaks, the World-Honored One also speaks.
When a disciple creates an emanated disciple, they both speak at the same time.
Having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the saṃghāṭī robe,
whenever the disciple spoke, the emanation remained silent;
whenever the emanation spoke, the disciple remained silent.
Why is this? Because the Buddha has attained mastery over both the mind and meditative concentration;
he enters and emerges from them with swiftness, without abandoning his object of focus.
Having uttered a natural utterance, one then utters a transformative utterance;
having uttered a transformative utterance, one again utters a natural utterance.
Because they occur with extreme rapidity, they appear as if they were uttered simultaneously.
The disciple’s mind is concentrated, yet not entirely sovereign;
his entry into and emergence from concentration are slow, and he repeatedly loses the object of focus.
Having produced speech from himself, he then produces emanated speech.
When the emanated speech arises, one's own speech has already ceased;
having emitted the emanated speech,
one then emits one's own speech once more.
When one's own speech arises, the emanated speech has already ceased;
because it is not extremely rapid, the sequence of before and after is perceived.
Question: Can all the great śrāvakas also do this?
What is unique about the Blessed One in this regard?
The answer is: the Buddha, with a single mind, can produce two utterances—namely, those of himself and those of his emanations.
When the self has spoken, the emanation then speaks;
when the emanation has spoken, the self then speaks.
Because it is extremely rapid, though they do not speak simultaneously, it is said that they speak together.
A śrāvaka, though single-minded, also utters two kinds of speech:
that of himself and that of his emanation.
Once his own speech has ceased, the emanation then speaks.
Once the emanated speech has ceased, the [Buddha’s] own speech then proceeds;
because it is not extremely rapid, they are not perceived simultaneously, nor do they occur together.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has attained mastery over all objects of knowledge.
This does not apply to the śrāvakas;
therefore, the Buddha also possesses what is uncommon (āveṇika) in this regard.
Furthermore, it is said in reverse that at one time the Buddha manifested a transformation-buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha).
His body was of the color of pure gold, adorned with the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
When the World-Honored One spoke, his emanation remained silent;
when the emanation spoke, the World-Honored One remained silent.
The disciple at one time manifested as a transformed disciple;
having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the saṃghāṭī robe,
whenever the disciple spoke, the transformed one also spoke.
When the Teacher speaks, the disciples also speak;
one might ask whether the great śrāvakas are also capable of this.
What, then, is the unique quality (āveṇika) of the Blessed One in this regard?
Answer: The Buddha has attained mastery over both the mind and meditative concentration;
he enters and emerges from them with swiftness without abandoning his object of focus, and is able to produce two utterances with a single mind.
This refers to oneself and to emanations.
Among them, those intended to speak do so,
while those not intended to speak remain silent.
The mental concentration of a śrāvaka is not supremely sovereign;
his entry into and emergence from it are sluggish, and he frequently loses the focal object.
Although he can produce two utterances with a single mind, [he lacks such mastery].
This refers to both oneself and one's emanation.
Within this context, one may desire that when the first speaks, the second also speaks;
or one may desire that when the first remains silent, the second also remains silent.
It cannot cause one to remain silent while the other speaks.
Furthermore, because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has attained mastery over all spheres of knowledge whereas the śrāvakas have not,
the Buddha also possesses this uncommon quality therein.
In a sutra it is said:
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"By means of my supernormal power, I can, with a mind-made body, arrive instantaneously in the Brahma world."
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"How inferior this is!
Even a śrāvaka is capable of this."
"World-Honored One, why should you praise yourself?
That which is created by transformation is called a 'mind-made body' (manomaya-kāya),
and even śrāvakas are able to reach the Brahma-world by means of this."
If the Buddha were such as that, what would be his unique quality?
Could the World-Honored One possibly be free from supernormal powers,
using a coarse, gross physical body born of parents composed of the great elements?
"In an instant, can one reach the Brahma-world?
The Blessed One replied,
"I am also capable of this."
Ānanda spoke again:
"This matter is truly difficult to understand.
I pray that you will provide a simile so that I may gain faith and comprehension."
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively.
It is like iron in the world."
Whether as a flat cake or a ball, it is placed within a glowing furnace;
gradually becoming light, soft, pliable, and pure,
it may be fashioned according to one's will.
In this way, the body of the Tathāgata follows the movement of the mind.
By fixing the mind upon the body and forming perceptions such as lightness and softness,
the body accomplishes matters such as lightness and softness through the power of the mind.
By the power of the mental continuum that is capable of binding,
the body which is bound is made to move according to one's will.
Regarding this, some say:

At the moment the Buddha attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), he acquires the previously unobtained mind and mental factors that are non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) within the desire realm.
By the power of this [attainment], he does not enter meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) nor give rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
At the very moment they resolve their minds, they are able to lift their entire bodies to the Akaniṣṭha heaven,
let alone to the Brahma-world. Some say this.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to a mind focused on the wind, causing his body to move and lift itself up.
Other masters say that a mind focused on emptiness can cause the Buddha’s body to proceed without obstruction.
Some say: The Buddha’s intention was to state that this body is called "mentally formed" (*manomaya*) because,
through the power of the mind, it accomplishes activities such as becoming light and supple.
Because they can transport this body to the Brahma-world through the power of concentration and supernormal abilities, they differ from the śrāvakas. Some say:
The Buddha taught that the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) is such that the emanated body does not require the attainment of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) to reach the Brahma world;
this distinguishes it from that of the śrāvakas. Some say:
The Buddha taught that through the supernormal power of mental mastery (*manojavitva-ṛddhi*), he causes his emanated bodies to reach the Brahma world with speed;
such swift power as this is not shared by those of the two vehicles and other classes.
Therefore, the Buddha relies upon this to manifest his own preeminence.
Question: Is there a case where a mind of transformation (nirmāṇacitta) is severed in a single moment and not obtained;
or is obtained and not severed; or neither?
Answer: There is.
This refers to the time of the final path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) when one is free from the defilements of desire;

regarding the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*), there are these four propositions. As for "having been abandoned but not attained": [it refers to] the case where the mind of transformation has been severed but not yet acquired.
This refers to the fruits of the three higher dhyānas belonging to the desire realm that have been attained but not yet abandoned; specifically,
it refers to the fruit of the first dhyāna belonging to the first dhyāna.
"Both abandoned and attained" refers to the fruit of the first dhyāna connected with the desire realm.
"Neither abandoned nor attained" refers to...
That is to say: the fruits of the three higher dhyānas connected with the first dhyāna;
the fruits of the three higher dhyānas connected with the second dhyāna;
and the fruits of the two higher dhyānas connected with the third dhyāna.
The fourth dhyāna is bound to the fourth dhyāna and has the fourth dhyāna as its fruit.
Just as four permutations were established regarding the final path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) for the abandonment of attachment to the desire realm,
so too [should they be established] for the final path of uninterrupted transition for the abandonment of attachment to the first dhyāna.
Up to and including the final uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) for the abandonment of the defilements of the third dhyāna,
there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) for each case as appropriate.
Regarding the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), should it be said that it possesses primary elements (*mahābhūta*) or does not possess primary elements?
Answer: It should be said that there are primary elements (mahābhūta), because no manifest form exists apart from the primary elements.
It should be said that the transformation possesses derived form (upādāyarūpa).
Is there no derived matter?
Answer: It should be said that there is derived matter.
There are two kinds of transformations.
First, those acquired through cultivation;
second, those acquired at birth.
The transformations acquired through cultivation, if they belong to the desire realm, are subsumed under four bases.
If they are bound to the form realm, they are subsumed under two bases;
if they are acquired at birth or are transformations, and are bound to the desire realm, they are subsumed under nine bases;
if they are bound to the form realm, they are subsumed under seven bases.
Since the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) is established by means of such dharmas,
should it be said that the emanation has a mind or is without a mind?
Answer: It should be said that they are without mind.
However, there are two kinds of emanations;
the first is that which is obtained through cultivation and is without mind.
Second, there is the mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*), which possesses this [mind].
Herein, it is taught that the mind produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*) is not the support for transformation (*nirmāṇa*), because it is not the basis of the mind.
Furthermore, there are two kinds.
First, when manifesting another's body, this [transformation] is without mind;
second, when manifesting one's own body, this has mind.
Herein, it is taught that the manifestation of another's body is not based on mind.
If one transforms the bodies of other sentient beings, it is as explained regarding one's own body.
Regarding such transformations, one should ask: by whose mind are they produced?
Answer: One should say it is the creator of the transformation.
This is because the manifest [action] exists due to the mind of the creator;
however, once the transformation has been produced through cultivation, it proceeds by the power of the creator’s mind.
If the transformation produced by birth proceeds from one's own mind,
this [treatise] speaks of the transformation acquired through cultivation.
Furthermore, the manifestation as another body proceeds from the mind of the master of the transformation.
If one creates a body for oneself through the transformation of one's own mind, this refers here to the transformation of another's body.
Question: Are all transformations extinguished?
Answer: Transformations acquired through cultivation are subject to cessation;
those acquired at birth may or may not be subject to cessation.
This refers to when beings such as devas, nāgas, and yakṣas manifest their own bodies through transformation.
There arises a distinct color-form and so forth;
at a later time, this distinct color-form and so forth ceases,
yet the self remains.
Furthermore, that which is created as another's body ceases.
That which is created as one's own body may either cease or not cease.
If one creates the body of another sentient being through transformation, it is explained in the same manner as one's own body.
Question: In whom’s stomach is the food consumed by those who are emanated digested?
Answer: If it is something required and suitable for the emanator, then it is digested within the emanator’s own stomach.
If it is not food required or suitable for the emanator,
such as grasses, trees, and so forth, gathered together in one place;
if he intends to cause other emanated sentient beings to eat and drink it, [he must first transform it].
Whether the intent of the transformation is fulfilled or not depends on the purpose of the transformation.
Question: From what does the emanation body produce smoke, flames, and so forth?
Answer: It arises from the power of the master of the transformation.
That is to say, when the master of emanations intends to produce smoke, flames,
peaks of smoke and flames,
or a house of smoke and flames at a particular location.
Then, smoke and flames arise from that place.
Question: By what means do some emanated bodies burn while others do not?
Furthermore, for what reason does the body burn while the robe does not?
The robes are burned, but the body is not.
Is it both or neither?
Answer: It is due to the power of the transformation-master (nirmāṇa-vaśitā).
This means that those who manifest emanations may, according to their will,
either burn or not burn them,
as stated in the Sūtra.
The Venerable Dārukarṇī, by means of his supernormal power,
ascended into the sky and consumed his body with the fire-element until not even a trace of ash remained.
When asked about that Venerable One as he was burning his body with fire:
Regarding the question of whether this occurs before or after nirvāṇa, in response to those who claim that a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) is retained,
they state that after nirvāṇa, fire arises to cremate the body.
This means that having attained mastery over mental concentration and being about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he ascended into the air by his supernormal power, and within the sky,
he manifested a couch and various kinds of firewood.
Thereupon, by the power of his vow, he entered the fire-samādhi;
as soon as the fire was kindled, he attained parinirvāṇa,
whereby his body was consumed so that no ashes or embers remained.
Regarding those who maintain that there is no transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) remaining,
they say that before his life-span is exhausted, fire arises and consumes his body;
this refers to one who has attained mastery over meditative concentration (samādhi).
Desiring to enter parinirvāṇa, he ascended into the air through his supernormal powers and entered the meditative absorption of fire.
He caused his body to gradually die, and as each part became rootless, fire arose to incinerate it;
until finally, there remained only the locus of mind and life.
Just as [the fire] enters nirvāṇa at the extent of an extremely fine hair-tip, it likewise ceases;
that which is not burned, being the measure of a remaining hair-tip, is difficult to perceive due to its subtlety.
That is to say, it is without ash or residue.
Regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), should it be said that it possesses the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) or does not possess the primary elements?
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: Why does the transformation [of consciousness] follow immediately after the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
Answer: Because it is the intention of the author of this treatise that it be so.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that both the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are subtle and difficult to discern.
Other masters say that both of these are bodies produced by the mind (*manomaya-kāya*). Some say:
These two [positions] are subject to much censure;
that is to say, the Dārṣṭāntikas assert that a transformation is not real.
The Vibhajyavādins deny the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Previously, it was clarified that emanations (*nirmāṇa*) are substantially existent;
now, it is clarified that the intermediate state is not non-existent.
For this reason, it is next transformed into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Regarding this intermediate state, one should ask: does it possess primary elements (*mahābhūta*) or not?
The answer is: one should say it possesses primary elements, because it lacks manifest form apart from those primary elements.
Regarding that which exists therein, should it be said that there is derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) or no derived matter?
Answer: It should be said that there is derived matter.
It is comprised within nine locations of the desire realm and seven locations of the form realm,
because by means of such dharmas that body is constituted.
Regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), should it be said that it possesses mind or is devoid of mind?
Answer: It should be said that it possesses mind.
Regarding the intermediate state, should it be said that it is transformed by whose mind?
Answer: It should be said that it is one's own mind, because the manifest karma arises through the power of one's own mind.
The meaning of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is explained at length in the *Saṃyuktāgama* (or *Saṃyukta-skandha*).
"What dharma is designated by the term 'world'?
Answer: "It is the formations (saṃskāra) manifested by this metaphorical designation (adhivacana).
Question: "For what purpose was this treatise composed? Answer: "To refute the doctrines of other schools and to clarify our own school."
That is to say, the Dārṣṭāntikas and the Vibhajyavādins maintain that the world and its formations are distinct in their essential natures.
The substance of conditioned formations is impermanent,
while the substance of the world is permanent;
all impermanent formations [are thus subsumed].
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) constantly shift through the times of the world, like fruits and other objects within various vessels,
or like people entering various houses;
this is to refute that [false] attachment and to reveal that the substance of the three times is precisely these conditioned phenomena.
Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, the world is also impermanent.
For these reasons, this treatise was composed.
The meaning of the three time periods (*adhvan*) is also explained at length as in the *Saṃyukta-skandha*.
What dharma is designated by the term "kalpa"?
Answer: It refers to the fortnight, month, season, and year as manifested through this metaphorical designation (*adhivacana*).
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of explaining the sūtra.
As it is said in a sūtra:
"There was a bhikṣu who came to where the Buddha was."
Having prostrated at his feet, he stood to one side and addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"The Buddha constantly speaks of kalpas."
"What is the measure of this?
The Buddha said,
"O Bhikṣus."
The duration of a kalpa is so vast that it cannot be known by means of hundreds or thousands of years.
The bhikṣu spoke again:
"Is there not a simile for this?"
The World-Honored One said, "It exists.
I shall now explain it for you:
suppose there were a solid rock mountain near a city or town."
Its length, breadth, and height each measure one *yojana*.
Even if it were brushed once every hundred years with a fine cloth from Kāśī,
the mountain would be completely worn away before this kalpa had ended.
Bhikṣus, you should know that for a long night, throughout these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas,
you have dwelt in the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, among humans and devas,
one undergoes various intense sufferings and revolves through the cycle of birth and death with no end in sight;
how can one remain at ease without seeking liberation?
That sūtra is the scriptural basis for this treatise.
Although it speaks of kalpas, it does not yet distinguish what the essence of a kalpa is; since we now wish to make such a distinction, this treatise is composed.
Question: Why are only the half-month, month, season, and year said to constitute a kalpa?
Is it not said that *kṣaṇas*, *lava-s*, *muhūrta-s*, days and nights constitute an *kalpa*?
One should know that where something ought to be stated but is not stated,
the meaning therein is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Some say that herein the coarse is cited to include the subtle; that is to say,
the subtle [moments] such as the *kṣaṇa* and so forth.
The fortnight, the month, and so forth are coarse.
If one speaks of the coarse, it should be understood that the subtle has already been spoken of as well;
for the accumulation of subtle moments constitutes a coarse duration of time.
Some say that here,
the near is cited to include the distant;
that is to say, the kalpa is proximate insofar as it is composed of [periods] such as half-months.
Since [periods such as] half-months are further established by means of [units such as] kṣaṇas,
the near time has already been explained, and the distant time is likewise explained.
What is the essential nature of a kalpa?
Some say it is the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana).
How is this known to be so?
As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*,
at the beginning of the kalpa, the bodies of human beings were constantly illuminated by their own radiance;
however, due to their craving for flavors, that radiance vanished and darkness arose.
Thereupon, a solar disc arose in the east;
its radiance was brilliant and clear, just like its former illumination.
Having seen this, he said with joy:
The light of heaven arrives;
because the light of heaven arrives, it is called day.
Before long, in a mere moment, the solar disk sets in the west.
Darkness arose as before.
Having seen this, he sighed and said,
"The light of heaven has vanished."
Because celestial light has subsided, it is called "night.
From this it is proven that the substance of a kalpa is matter (*rūpa*),
for the substance of a kalpa is entirely composed of accumulated days and nights.
According to this teaching,
throughout the states of day and night, there is nothing that is not the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates;
by this principle, the substance of the eon (*kalpa*) is likewise established.
Since a kalpa is a temporal unit that pervades the three realms,
it takes the five aggregates or four aggregates as its intrinsic nature.
The intrinsic nature has thus been explained.
Therefore, it shall now be explained.
Why is it called a *kalpa*?
What is the meaning of *kalpa*?
Answer: It is called a *kalpa* because it is a period of differentiation;
that is to say, it differentiates moments (*kṣaṇa*), *lava*s, and *muhūrta*s.
The division of *kṣaṇas* constitutes day and night;
the differentiation of the divisions of day and night constitutes the half-month;
and the differentiation of the half-month and other divisions of time constitutes the month, the season, the year, and the eon (*kalpa*).
Because the kalpa is the ultimate limit within the divisions of time, it receives this general name.
The etymologists say:
"It is called a kalpa because it is a period of conceptual differentiation."
Why is this so? Because an eon (*kalpa*) is the ultimate stage among the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) that are conceptually differentiated.
There are three kinds of eons.
1. An intermediate kalpa;
2. A kalpa of formation and destruction;
3. A great kalpa.
The intermediate kalpas are further of three kinds:
first, the kalpa of decrease;
second, the kalpa of increase.
The three kalpas of increase and decrease.
As for the decrease, it begins from a human lifespan of immeasurable years and decreases until it reaches ten years.
The period of increase refers to when the human lifespan increases from ten years up to eighty thousand years.
The periods of increase and decrease refer to when the human lifespan increases from ten years to eighty thousand years,
and then decreases again from eighty thousand years back down to ten years.
In this context, there are eighteen periods of increase and decrease, consisting of one decrease and one increase.
Twenty intermediate kalpas elapse; after twenty intermediate kalpas, the world is formed.
Having been formed for twenty intermediate kalpas, it remains stable.
This collectively is called the kalpa of formation.
The world remains in a state of destruction for twenty intermediate kalpas;
having been destroyed, it remains empty for twenty intermediate kalpas.
This combined period is called the kalpa of destruction.
Altogether, eighty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpas) are collectively termed a great kalpa (mahākalpa).
Within the period of abiding after formation, during the first twenty intermediate kalpas, there is only decrease at the beginning.
The last one increases only;
the eighteen intermediate ones both increase and decrease.
Question: Among these three, which endures the longest?
Some say that the kalpa of decrease is the longest,
while the kalpa of increase is of medium length.

The most rapid increase and decrease refers to the fact that the duration of time during which the body possesses radiance is long, whereas the duration of time until that bodily radiance ceases is not; likewise,
the duration of time from the present until the period when the taste of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) was consumed is long, whereas the duration of time until that taste of the earth ceased is not.
Thus, even until now, when we eat earth-cakes, the time that has elapsed is long, yet the earth-cakes are not exhausted;
even until now, when we eat forest creepers, the time that has elapsed is long, yet they are not exhausted from that source.
Even until the present time, when we eat the naturally grown rice,
the duration that has passed has not been exhausted from that [original store],
continuing even until now.
Therefore, this period of the kalpa of decrease is the longest.
According to this explanation,
there are eighteen intermediate periods between the initial decrease and the subsequent increase.
The duration of each of these twenty kalpas is equal.
Only during the period of decrease do Buddhas appear in the world;
only during the period of increase do wheel-turning monarchs appear in the world.
When [the lifespan] increases or decreases, Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world.
The Prajñapti-śāstra states:
"Among humans, day and night are distinguished across the four continents by means of the sun and moon."
How are the days and nights of the gods of the desire realm known?
Answer: They are known by means of signs.
That is to say, on those celestial realms, when the *padma* lotuses close.
The utpala flowers bloomed;
the various birds sang in rare harmony;
and a cool breeze arose with great force.
When delight in play is slight and pleasure in sleep is great,
you should know that at such a time it is called "night."
At that time, when the *utpala* flowers close and the *padma* flowers open,
the flocks of birds sing together in harmony.
A gentle breeze rises slowly;
many delight in play,
while few desire sleep.
It should be known that at that time it is called "day.
