It is like a person of wealth and status who, having grown weary of the pleasures of desire, delights in dwelling in the joy of the Dharma; and having grown weary of the joy of the Dharma, delights in dwelling in the pleasures of desire.
It is like the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
This indicates the gods of the second dhyāna:
sentient beings with form who are uniform in body and uniform in perception,
such as the Śubhakṛtsna gods.
This is the fourth station of consciousness.
It possesses form and so forth as previously described.
Regarding "a single perception":
This means that those sentient beings possess an unobscured-neutral perception that is undifferentiated,
such as that of the gods of the Universal Purity Heaven (*Śubhakṛtsna*).
This indicates the various heavens of the third dhyāna.
Because those sentient beings in the formless realm have completely transcended all perceptions of form,
because all perceptions of resistance have vanished,
and because they do not attend to perceptions of diversity.
Entering the sphere of infinite space,
he dwells having fully attained the base of infinite space,
just like the devas who dwell in the realm of infinite space.
This is the fifth station of consciousness.
Because all formless sentient beings have completely transcended the sphere of infinite space,
they enter the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Abiding fully in the sphere of infinite consciousness,
just like the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness—
this is the sixth station of consciousness.
Because those sentient beings of the formless realm have completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness,
they enter and dwell, having fully attained the sphere of nothingness where there is not even the slightest thing,
just like the gods of the sphere of nothingness.
This is the seventh station of consciousness.
Regarding those who are formless therein,
it means that those sentient beings have no form that can be perceived.
There is no material body;
because there is no establishment of form within the sphere of the formless realm, it is called "formless."
"Sentient beings," and so forth, are as previously explained.
"Transcending all the spheres of infinite space," and so forth, are as explained in other passages.
Regarding the "abodes of consciousness":
This refers to the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with that [realm].
Question: Why is there a diversity of bodies in the first dhyāna, but not in the higher stages?
Answer: Because in the first dhyāna, distinctions are established among kings, ministers, and the common populace.
This refers to the Great Brahmā King, who repeatedly assembles with the Brahmā-purohitas and the Brahmakāyikas;
therein, they manifest various forms and appearances,
and their clothing, speech, and manners each differ.
It is not so for the higher stages.
Some say that in the first dhyāna, there is no distinction between superior, middling, and inferior feelings.
Because of the maturation of karma, there are differences among bodies;
this is not the case for the higher stages. Some say:
The feeling of the first dhyāna is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra;
because it is the maturation (vipāka) of karma, there is a difference in the body.
This is not the case for the higher stages.
Some say that because the feeling associated with the first dhyāna consists of the maturation (vipāka) of manifest and unmanifest karma,
there is a difference in the body.
The higher stages are not like this.
Some say that in the first dhyāna, feeling is associated with the four groups of consciousness.
The body differs due to the maturation of karma;
this is not the case for the higher stages. Some say:
The feeling of the first dhyāna is associated with three types of feeling;
because it is the maturation of karma, there is diversity in the body.
This is not the case for the higher stages.
Due to such various causes and conditions as these,
the body of the first dhyāna is distinct from the bodies of the higher stages.
Furthermore, regarding the first dhyāna:
The second dhyāna is said to have "uniform ideation" (ekasaṃjñā) because its ideation is defiled;
it is said to have "diverse ideation" (nānātvasaṃjñā) because its ideation is wholesome.
In the third dhyāna, it is said that there is "singleness of perception" by virtue of the non-obscured, neutral perception of maturation (*vipāka*).
Question: Why is this not the case in the miserable destinies (*apāya*)?
Are the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception not both established as stations of consciousness?
Answer: Some say that they,
too, should be established among the stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti),
yet they are not so established.
This is an incomplete explanation.
The Venerable Vasumitra has stated that this was spoken by the Blessed One as a concise summary.
However, the miserable realms and so forth are included within these;
that is to say, one should know that the various miserable realms are included within the first station of consciousness,
while the fourth dhyāna is included within the [remaining] three.
The last three [liberations] are subsumed under the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Why is this?
Because their realms are identical.
Some say: if a location where two kinds of consciousness are predominantly found can be identified,
it is established as a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
First, consciousness appropriated by craving;
second, consciousness appropriated by views;
[and those in] the evil destinies and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
In the fourth dhyāna, consciousness that is grasped by craving is for the most part unobtainable;
consciousness that is grasped by views is for the most part unobtainable.
Therefore, it is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Some say:
"If a place where three types of consciousness are for the most part obtainable [is a station of consciousness]."
They are established as the stations of consciousness:
first, consciousness abandoned through seeing;
second, consciousness abandoned through cultivation.
Third, the consciousness that is not severed [exists] in the evil destinies and in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The consciousness associated with non-interruption cannot be found.
In the fourth dhyāna,
the consciousness to be abandoned by insight is for the most part not found.
Therefore, it is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Question: Is it not the case that in the fourth dhyāna, the consciousness of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) that is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) can still be found?
Answer: Although they exist, they are not found in abundance in those stages, because they are entirely absent in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Question: [Regarding] humans and the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):
The uninterrupted consciousness is also unapprehendable;
it should not be a station of consciousness.
Answer: There are two ways in which it is apprehendable.
First, the self-nature is obtainable;
second, the basis is obtainable:
humans and the gods of the desire realm.

Although the consciousness that is not interrupted cannot be apprehended by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is established as a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) because its support can be apprehended.
Question: Is it not the case that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) [is also such]?
Can the support for the uninterrupted consciousness also be found?
Because one may attain arhatship while being born there.
Answer: Although it exists, it is not the case for the majority.
Because, having been born therein, they briefly give rise to the noble path and attain the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣaphala),
yet until their parinirvāṇa, [the noble path] does not manifest again.
Some say: A location where the six types of consciousness are predominantly present may be established as a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*);
that is to say, the consciousness abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
...up to the consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation and the consciousnesses not to be abandoned,
as well as the miserable destinies.
In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
consciousness cannot be found as something that is not interrupted;
this is the case in the fourth dhyāna as well.
Because the consciousnesses to be abandoned by the first four [paths] are for the most part unobtainable, they are not stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
The analysis through question and answer should be understood as previously described.
Some say that a place where consciousness delights in dwelling is established as a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*);
because they are oppressed by suffering, consciousness does not delight in dwelling within the various miserable destinies (*apāya*).
Because the bliss of the fourth dhyāna is subject to movement and fluctuation, consciousness does not abide therein;
that is to say, ordinary beings may instead take pleasure in entering the formless realms.
Some delight in entering the state of non-perception;
some delight in causing consciousness to cease;
and if they are noble ones, some delight in entering the formless realms.
Some delight in entering the Pure Abodes;
some delight in entering the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, which is without remainder.
Because it is extremely tranquil and the mind is faint and weak, consciousness does not delight in abiding there.
Some say: "It is a place where no factor exists that could destroy consciousness."
That which can be attained is established as a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Among these, the miserable destinies (*apāya*) involve extremely painful sensations,
as does the fourth dhyāna.
There is the attainment of non-conception;
there is the ripening of non-conception, which is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
and there is the attainment of cessation.
Because they are dharmas capable of destroying consciousness, they are not stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Some say:
"If a place [is a station] by virtue of two factors..."
The arising of various distinct and superior consciousnesses and causing them to manifest is established as a station of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) for one reason:
by way of meditative concentration (samādhi).
Second, by way of birth:
[birth in] the miserable realms and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Both factors are absent in the fourth dhyāna;
for although it possesses meditative concentration, it lacks rebirth.
Some say: In the miserable realms, both [the meditative absorption and the birth] are absent; although the fourth dhyāna possesses the absorption, it lacks the birth;
and although the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception possesses the birth, it lacks the absorption.
Due to various causes and conditions such as these, the miserable destinies and so forth are not stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*).
Question: For what reason is consciousness itself not a station of consciousness among the four stations of consciousness?
Regarding the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), consciousness itself is a station of consciousness.
Answer: The four stations of consciousness are established based on a distinct cause, whereas the seven stations of consciousness are established based on a distinct cause.
That is to say, if there are phenomena which consciousness mounts and governs,
which proceed together with consciousness, and which are proximate and conjoined with it,
these are established as the four stations of consciousness.

Consciousness is not established as one of the four stations of consciousness because it does not stand in such a relationship to itself; for a phenomenon to be established as a station of consciousness,
it must serve as either a cause or an effect for that consciousness.
They are established as the seven stations of consciousness by mutually supporting one another;
since consciousness relates to consciousness in this manner,
they are thus established among the seven stations of consciousness.
Regarding the nine abodes of sentient beings,
as stated in the Sūtra:
there are material beings who differ in body and differ in perception.
Just as the Heaven of the Single Division (Ekadeva) is the first abode of sentient beings,
so too are there sentient beings with form who possess diversity of body but unity of perception.
As with the Brahmakāyika devas,
this is the second abode of sentient beings,
where there are sentient beings possessing form who are uniform in body but diverse in perception.
Like the Ābhāsvara devas,
this is the third abode of sentient beings:
there are sentient beings with form who are uniform in body and uniform in perception.
The Śubhakṛtsna devas constitute the fourth abode of sentient beings;
they possess form and so forth, as previously described.
The "abodes of sentient beings" refers to the form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness bound to those [realms],
as well as that which constitutes the dwelling place of sentient beings.
The place where one dwells,
the place where one rests,
and the place of birth.
Therefore, it is called an abode of sentient beings.
There are sentient beings with form who are without perception and without distinct perceptions.
The Heaven of Non-percipient Sentient Beings is the fifth abode of sentient beings;
it possesses form and so forth, as previously described.
Regarding "those without perception":
because perception and so forth have been extinguished for a long duration in that place,
they are called the gods of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) by virtue of this meaning.
The sentient beings of the formless realm have completely transcended all perceptions of form;
thus, all perceptions of resistance have vanished,
and they do not attend to perceptions of diversity.
Entering the sphere of infinite space, they dwell fully possessing the sphere of infinite space,
just like the gods of the Heaven of Infinite Space;
this is the sixth abode of sentient beings.
As for the sentient beings of the formless realm,
because they have completely transcended all the spheres of infinite space,
they enter the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Abiding fully in the sphere of infinite consciousness,
like the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness—
this is the seventh abode of sentient beings.
Because those beings of the formless realm have completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness,
they enter and dwell, having fully attained the sphere of nothingness, wherein there is not even the slightest thing that exists.
As with the gods of the Sphere of Nothingness,
this is the eighth abode of sentient beings;
for the formless sentient beings have completely transcended the sphere of nothingness.
Entering and abiding fully in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
just like the devas of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
this is the ninth abode of sentient beings.
The formless [attainments] and so forth are as previously explained.
That all [beings] transcend the sphere of nothingness and so forth is as explained in other passages.
Question: For what reason are the evil destinies and the state of non-perception not included?
The Bṛhatphala devas and others are not abodes of sentient beings.
In response, some say:
they too should be established as abodes of sentient beings.
As for the fact that it is not established [as a separate category],
this is a statement made with further intent. The Venerable Vasumitra has spoken thus.
This is what the Blessed One has taught in brief;
however, the miserable realms (*apāya*) and so forth are included herein.
That is to say, one should know that all the miserable realms are subsumed within the first abode of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*).
Those not included among the non-percipient beings,
such as the gods of the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala), should be known to be included in the fifth abode of sentient beings. Why is this so?
Because the ground is the same. Some say:
wherever other beings come to dwell in happiness.
Having already resided therein,
one does not delight in moving elsewhere;
such a place may be established as an abode for sentient beings.
In the various evil destinies, both [of these] are not the case;
rather, it is solely by the power of karma that one is made to go and remain there.
If it were according to one's own will, one would not remain for even a single moment; therefore, such a state is not established.
In the fourth dhyāna, with the exception of the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva),
although others may wish to come, they prefer to move on,
just as people from a frontier city do not enjoy residing there.
That is to say, those ordinary beings may delight in the formless realms or in the state of non-perception; or,
if they are noble ones, they may delight in the Pure Abodes.
Or they may proceed toward nirvāṇa;
just as when a border city of a kingdom is constantly invaded by thieves and neighboring enemies,
the nobility take their wealth and gladly transfer it elsewhere.
Although a small portion was left behind to serve as a garrison,
when various merchants came seeking goods for their trade,
the garrison guards said to them:
"This place is plagued by many calamities and cannot provide mutual protection," said the merchants and travelers in unison.
"This is no city."
Thus, as for those gods not included among the non-percipient beings,
they are driven by afflictions and karma and constantly delight in migration and movement;
therefore, they are not described as abodes of sentient beings.
The three natures have already been analyzed;
now the characteristics of the mixed and unmixed shall be explained.
[Next,] the four stations of consciousness and the seven stations of consciousness will be discussed.
Do the four encompass the seven?
Or do the seven encompass the four?
One should respond by means of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There are four that are not seven:
namely, the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts,
and the form, feeling, perception, and formations of the Bṛhatphala heaven.
And in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
there are seven [factors]— feeling, perception, and formations— and not four.
That is to say: humans,
the gods of the desire realm,
and the Brahmakāyika devas.
The Sphere of Utmost Purity,
the Sphere of Universal Purity,
and the Sphere of Infinite Space.
In the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness,
there are four and seven [types of] minds respectively.
That is to say: humans,
the gods of the desire realm,
and the Brahma-pāriṣadya devas.

The sphere of infinite light, the sphere of infinite purity, and the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception; as well as the form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness of these.
In the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness, there are feeling, perception, and formations;
there are those that are neither four nor seven.
That is to say: the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts,
the Heaven of Great Fruit,
and the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The reasons for this are as explained extensively before.
Question: Regarding the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and the nine abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*), do the four subsume the nine?
Are the nine [factors] subsumed by the four?
One should respond that this involves four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*):
there are those that are four but not nine.
This refers to the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts;
the gods of the Heaven of No-Thought; and those not included among the Broad Fruit (Bṛhatphala) gods—namely, form, feeling, perception, and formations.
There are nine [realms] that are not four;
namely, humans,
the gods of the desire realm, and the Brahmakāyika gods.
The Heaven of Utmost Purity,
the Heaven of Universal Purity,
and the Heaven of Non-conceptualization.
Regarding the four formless minds,
there are both four and nine;
that is, humans.
The gods of the desire realm,
the Brahmakāyika gods,
and the Ābhāsvara gods.
The Śubhakṛtsna [heaven],
the Āsaṃjñika heaven,
and form, feeling, perception, and formations.
And the four formless [aggregates].
Feeling, perception,
and formations are neither four nor nine.
This refers to the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts,
as well as the minds of the *bṛhatphala* deities that are not included among those of the *asaṃjñisattva* heaven.
The reason for this is also as previously explained.
Question: Regarding the seven stations of consciousness and the nine abodes of sentient beings,
do the seven subsume the nine,
or do the nine subsume the seven?
Answer: The nine encompass the seven;
the seven do not encompass the nine.
What is it that is not encompassed?
Answer: There are two places,
namely the realm of non-perception (asaṃjñisattva) and the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
The reason for this is also as previously explained.
Question: For what reason, World-Honored One, [is it so] regarding the Heaven of Non-conception?
Furthermore, the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is frequently described as a "station" (*sthāna*).
The answer is: there are certain non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who cling to these two stations as being liberation (*mokṣa*).
The Buddha spoke of these as "places of birth" (upapatti-sthāna) in order to refute them.
Some say that non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) cling to these two places as being the most tranquil.
The Buddha taught that these are "bases" (*āyatana*),
clarifying that they are agitated and not tranquil,
because they are the bases for the transmigration of realms, destinies, and births.
Some say that non-Buddhists cling to these two states,
asserting they are true liberation from which there is never again any falling back.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that those states are places of regression and not true liberation;
that is to say, one passes away from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
They are mostly reborn in the lower realms;
those who pass away from the Heaven of Non-conception will necessarily be reborn in the Desire Realm. Some say:
The lifespans of those two devas are exceedingly long; consequently,
many non-Buddhists falsely cling to them as true *nirvāṇa*,
specifically regarding the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) as belonging solely to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding the maximum lifespan among all places of birth,
the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) has the longest lifespan; therefore,
the Buddha taught that it is a place of impermanence.
Some say that the Blessed One has taught the nine abodes of sentient beings using two names for each.
Regarding those seven types, two names are given:
namely, "stations of consciousness" (vijñānasthiti) and "abodes of sentient beings" (sattvāvāsa).
For the remaining two types as well, two names are likewise given.
This refers to what are called the "bases" (*āyatana*) and the "abodes of sentient beings" (*sattvāvāsa*).
Other masters state that the Buddha taught that the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and the abodes of sentient beings mutually subsume one another.
As for the remaining items that are not exhausted, there are only two locations;
they should not be explained otherwise,
because the Sphere of Infinite Space and so forth are also called "locations" (*āyatana*).
Some say that because it occupies the final position among the fruits of diligent effort in the place of birth,
it is called a "place" (*sthāna*).
This refers to the fruits of diligent effort among all places of birth for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
with the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) as the ultimate limit.
Among all such fruits of diligent effort in every place of birth, [this is the highest].
The Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is the ultimate limit. 4.
Section on Appropriation (*upātta*), the Fourth Part of the Fifth Aggregate of Great Elements (*mahābhūta-skandha*). There are great elements that are appropriated (*upātta-mahābhūta*).
With how many conditions do the great elements that are appropriated (upātta) function?
Such are the sections [of the treatise].
Once the meaning of the chapters has been understood through this explanation, one should provide a detailed analysis.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is that it is because the author of that treatise intended it so;
the treatise was composed according to his intention.
As long as it does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one should not hold him accountable.
Furthermore, in order to refute those who claim that the law of dependent origination and the past and future worlds do not truly exist,
this treatise was composed to demonstrate that the past and future of all conditioned phenomena do indeed truly exist.
Among these, "appropriated primary elements" refers to those primary elements belonging to the category of sentient beings at the present moment,
which are appropriated by mind and mental factors.
"Non-appropriated primary elements" refers to those included within the category of sentient beings— namely, past, future, and a portion of present [elements]—
as well as all primary elements included within the category of non-sentient things throughout the three periods of time.
This is called the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point:
how many conditions do appropriated great elements serve as for other appropriated great elements?
Answer: As for causes, there is the dominant cause (*adhipati-hetu*).
Regarding causes, there is one cause.
This refers to the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati*), it means that which does not obstruct arising,
as well as that which is merely non-obstructive.
However, there is a distinction:
that which has a single fruit serves as a cause in relation to things of different categories.
Regarding "predominant" (adhipati):
that which is not a single fruit has only one predominant condition.
How many conditions do appropriated primary elements serve as for non-appropriated primary elements?
Answer: As for the causes, there is the dominant cause (*adhipati-hetu*).
Regarding the causes, there is one cause.
That is to say, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously explained;
however, there is a distinction.
That is to say, appropriated primary elements serve as the cause for future primary elements belonging to the category of sentient beings.
As for predominance:
it exercises only a single predominant influence over other non-appropriated great elements.
How many conditions do non-appropriated primary elements serve as conditions for non-appropriated primary elements?
Answer: The causes are the efficient cause and the causal cause.
As for the causal cause, there are two types of causes, namely, the co-existent cause and...
The homogeneous and dominant [conditions] are as previously explained;
however, there is a distinction.
That is to say, past primary elements belonging to the category of sentient beings act as causes for past primary elements belonging to the category of sentient beings.
The dominant cause consists of two causes.
That is to say, the co-existent,
the homogeneous,
and the predominant [conditions] are as previously explained.
It has as its cause and dominant condition the primary elements (mahābhūta) belonging to the category of future sentient beings,
as well as the non-appropriated primary elements belonging to the category of present sentient beings.
As for the cause, there is one cause,
namely the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
As for the predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya), it is as previously explained.
With other non-appropriated primary elements, there is only a single dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Past primary elements that do not belong to the category of sentient beings [are related] to past primary elements that do not belong to the category of sentient beings.
It acts as a cause and a predominance condition. As for the causes,
there are two types of causes.
That is to say, the co-existent,
the homogeneous,
and the predominant conditions are as previously explained.
It acts as the cause and the predominant condition for the primary elements (mahābhūta) that are not classified as sentient beings, belonging to the future and the present.
The cause is the single cause,
namely the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
The predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is as previously explained.
With respect to the primary elements (mahābhūta) belonging to the category of sentient beings in the past and future,
as well as the non-appropriated primary elements belonging to the category of sentient beings in the present,
there is only a single dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
The primary elements (mahābhūta) belonging to the category of sentient beings in the future serve as causes for the primary elements belonging to the category of sentient beings in the future.
The predominant cause consists of a single cause,
namely, the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
As for "predominance," it is as previously explained;
with other non-appropriated primary elements,
there is only a single predominant condition.
Future great elements that are not included among sentient beings act as causes for future great elements that are not included among sentient beings.
The dominant cause consists of one cause,
namely, the coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
The predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained.
It serves as the sole predominant condition for other non-appropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*),
namely, those non-appropriated great elements that currently belong to the category of sentient beings.
It takes as its cause and its dominant condition the great elements (mahābhūta) that are currently categorized as sentient beings and are non-appropriated (anupātta).
As for the cause, there is one cause,
namely the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
As for the predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya), it is as previously explained.
They act as the cause and the dominant condition for the primary elements that will constitute the number of sentient beings in the future.
The cause is the single cause,
namely the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
The predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is as previously explained.
With other non-appropriated great elements,
there is only a single predominance;
[this refers to] present great elements that do not belong to the category of sentient beings.
It acts as the cause and the predominant condition for the primary elements (mahābhūta) that are currently non-sentient.
As for the cause, there is one cause:
namely, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
As for the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously explained.
It acts as the cause and the dominant condition for the primary elements (mahābhūta) that are not sentient beings and belong to the future.
The cause is the single cause,
namely the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
The predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is as previously explained.
With other non-appropriated great elements,
there is only a single predominance;
[this applies to] non-appropriated great elements.
With respect to the appropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*), how many conditions (*pratyaya*) do they constitute?
Answer: They are the cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The cause is the single cause,
namely the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
The predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is as previously explained.
However, there is a distinction:
namely, that the primary elements belonging to the category of past sentient beings are appropriated primary elements.
As cause and as predominance.
Regarding "cause," there is one cause.
That is to say, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), as previously explained;
the others are the non-appropriated great elements (*anupātta-mahābhūta*).
With the appropriated primary elements (mahābhūta),
there is only a single predominance (adhipati).
Having explained the primary elements, the derived matter (bhautika) shall now be discussed.
The derived [matter] is also twofold:
namely, appropriated and non-appropriated;
it belongs to the category of sentient beings in the present moment.
That which is appropriated by mind and mental factors is "appropriated.
This includes all past, future, and present things categorized as sentient beings, as well as all things categorized as non-sentient throughout the three times.
This is without appropriation (*anupātta*).
This is called the brief *vibhāṣā* regarding this point:
there is derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) that is with appropriation (*sopātta*).
With respect to derived matter that is possessed of appropriation (sopādāna), how many conditions (pratyaya) are there?
Answer: One, the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya).
The meaning of "predominance" is as previously explained.
Regarding "absence of cause":
derived matter that possesses resistance does not stand in the relation of co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) with respect to one another.
How many conditions do derived matter that is appropriated and derived matter that is non-appropriated serve as one another?
Answer: The cause and the predominant condition.
As for the cause, there are two types of causes.
That is to say, the homogeneous,
the retributive,
and the dominant [conditions] are as previously explained.
However, there is a distinction:
namely, between derived matter that is appropriated and derived matter belonging to the category of future sentient beings.
It serves as the cause and the predominant condition for other non-appropriated derived matter.
There is only one predominance:
derived matter that is not appropriated [as a basis] acts as the predominant condition for derived matter that is not appropriated.
By how many conditions?
Answer: By the causal condition and the predominant condition.
As for causes, there are three causes:
namely, the co-existent cause and the homogeneous cause.
Regarding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*),
the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained;
however, there is a distinction.
That is to say, the derived matter belonging to sentient beings of the past serves as the cause for the derived matter belonging to sentient beings of the past.
The dominant cause consists of three causes,
namely: the co-existent cause.
The homogeneous cause,
the retributive cause,
and the dominant condition are as previously explained.
It acts as the cause and the predominant condition for the derived matter that constitutes the number of future sentient beings.
As for causes, there are two types:
namely, the similar-type cause (sabhāga-hetu) and the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu).
The predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained;
it serves as the causal predominant condition for the non-appropriated derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) currently existing within the category of sentient beings.
The cause is the single cause,
namely the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
The predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is as previously explained.
With other non-appropriated derived matter;
with only one dominant past derived matter not belonging to the category of sentient beings;
and with past, future, and present derived matter not belonging to the category of sentient beings.
It acts as a cause and a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
As for the cause, there is one single cause.
This refers to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously explained.
It also functions as the cause for other types of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) that are not appropriated (*anupātta*).
There is only one predominance:
future derived matter belonging to the category of sentient beings [acts as the predominant condition] for future derived matter belonging to the category of sentient beings.
It acts as a cause and as a dominant condition (*adhipati*).
As for the causes, there are two types of causes.
That is to say, the co-existent,
the retributive,
and the predominant [conditions] are as previously explained.
With other non-appropriated derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*),
it has only a single dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
As for future derived matter that does not belong to the category of sentient beings (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*), [it is likewise].
With all non-appropriated derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*),
there is only a single dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
This applies to present non-appropriated derived matter belonging to the category of sentient beings (*sattvagaṇa*).
It acts as the cause and the predominant condition for the currently existing, sentient-class, non-appropriated derived matter.
As for the cause, there is one cause,
namely the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
As for the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously explained.
It acts as the cause and the dominant condition for the derived matter that constitutes the number of future sentient beings.
As for causes, there are two types of causes:
namely, the similar-type cause (sabhāga-hetu) and the maturation cause (vipāka-hetu).
As for predominance (*adhipati*), it is as previously explained.
With other non-appropriated derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*),
there is only a single relationship of predominance.
Present derived matter that is not included within the category of sentient beings serves as the cause for future derived matter that is not included within the category of sentient beings.
The predominant cause consists of one type of cause,
namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
The predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained.
It serves as the sole predominant condition for other types of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) that are non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
How many conditions do derived matter that is non-appropriated serve as for derived matter that is appropriated?
Answer: The causes are the efficient cause and the dominant cause.
As for "causes," there are two types of causes.
That is to say, the homogeneous,
the retributive,
and the dominant conditions are as previously explained.
Nevertheless, there is a distinction:
namely, between derived matter consisting of past sentient beings and derived matter that is appropriated.
They serve as causes and as predominant conditions. Regarding the causes,
there are two types of causes.
That is to say, the homogeneous,
the retributive,
and the dominant [conditions] are as previously explained.
Other unappropriated derived matter and appropriated derived matter have only a single type of predominance.
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School,
Volume 137; Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume 138.
Compiled by the five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang in accordance with the Imperial Edict. Part Two of the Fourth Section on Appropriation within the Fifth Aggregate of Great Elements: Factors Corresponding to Causes.
With how many conditions are phenomena associated with causes related?
Answer: By way of cause.
The immediate,
the object-condition,
and the dominant condition.
As for "causes," there are five causes,
namely: association.
Co-existent,
homogeneous,
and pervasive.
Regarding "maturation" and "immediately antecedent":
this refers to the immediately antecedent condition of the factors associated with the cause.
Regarding "the factors associated with causes being present":
as for the object,
it refers to the factors associated with causes.
The dharmas associated with their causes serve as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
That is to say: non-obstruction of arising,
and being merely the absence of an obstacle,
as well as factors associated with causes.
How many conditions do factors dissociated from causes serve as?
Answer: They serve as the cause, equal-and-immediate, and predominant conditions.
Regarding "cause," there are four types of causes.
That is to say: coexistent,
homogeneous,
and pervasive.
Regarding "maturation" and "immediately preceding":
this refers to the immediately preceding condition of the factors associated with the cause.
When dissociated mental factors (viprayuktadharma) manifest,
there is the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
This is because it is a dharma that serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the mind and mental factors.
As for its being a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously explained.
It is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Because dissociated factors lack an object of cognition,
a dissociated factor [does not take] a dissociated factor as its cause.
By how many conditions?
Answer: By the causal condition and the predominant condition.
The causes are the four causes:
namely, the co-existent, the similar-type,
and the pervasive.
Regarding maturation and predominance, they are as previously explained.
As for factors that are not associated with causes:
As for dharmas associated with causes, how many conditions do they constitute?
Answer: Causes.
The object-condition,
the dominant condition,
and the causal condition.
There are four causes:
namely, the coexistent cause and the similar-type cause.
Regarding the universal,
the resultant,
and the object-condition:
That is to say, factors dissociated from causes take factors associated with causes as their objects of perception.
The predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained.
Regarding the non-equivalent-immediate condition (*na samanantara-pratyaya*):
it is because factors dissociated from causes (*hetu-viprayukta-dharma*) do not constitute an equivalent-immediate condition.
With respect to dharmas that possess an object,
how many conditions do they serve as conditions for other dharmas that possess an object?
Answer: [They arise] due to the causes of immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
As for "cause," there are five causes, namely: the associated cause (*samprayukta-hetu*).
Co-existent,
similar-type,
and universal.
Regarding "maturation" and "immediately preceding":
this refers to the immediately preceding condition of those dharmas that possess an object of cognition.
There is a dharma with an object that manifests before one.
As for "the object," it refers to a dharma that possesses an object.
With respect to those dharmas that possess an object,
they serve as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), as previously explained.
With how many conditions is a dharma that has an object related to a dharma that lacks an object?
Answer: [They are] the causal, immediate, and predominant conditions.
As for the causal condition, there are four causes, namely: the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Homogeneous,
pervasive,
and resultant.
Regarding "immediately preceding" (samanantara):
it refers to the case where, immediately following a dharma that has an object of cognition (sālambana),
a dharma without an object of cognition (anālambana) manifests.
That is, the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation;
for these are states that are the immediate antecedents (samanantara-pratyaya) of mind and mental factors.
The predominant condition is as previously explained.
As for that which is not an object-condition:
it is because there is no dharma that is not an object-condition, since all dharmas have objects.
How many conditions do non-objective phenomena serve as conditions for other non-objective phenomena?
Answer: [There are] the cause and the predominant condition.
As for the cause, there are four causes.
That is to say: co-existent,
homogeneous,
and universal.
Regarding maturation and predominance, they are as previously explained.
There are no dharmas that lack an object of cognition.
With respect to phenomena that possess an object, how many conditions are there?
Answer: They are the causal condition, the object condition, and the predominant condition.
As for causes, there are four causes:
namely, the co-existent cause and the similar-type cause.
Universal, resultant,
and objective-conditioned.
That is to say, that which is without an object serves as the object for those dharmas that possess an object.
The "predominant" [condition] is as previously explained.
Regarding those that are not "equal-and-immediate":
because there are no dharma-s without an object of cognition (ālambana) that function as equal-and-immediate conditions, they are material dharma-s (rūpa-dharma).

With respect to material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), how many conditions (*pratyaya*) are there? Answer: They are the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
As for causes, there are three types:
namely, the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) and the similar-type cause (sabhāga-hetu).
Regarding maturation and predominance, they are as previously explained.
As for material phenomena:

With respect to formless phenomena (*ārūpya-dharma*), how many conditions (*pratyaya*) are there? Answer: They are the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The causes are three causes:
namely, the co-existent cause and the similar-type cause.
Regarding maturation:
as for the object-condition,
it refers to material phenomena.
It takes formless phenomena as its object;
as for its predominance, it is as previously explained.
Regarding those that are not equal-and-immediate [conditions]:
because material phenomena (rūpadharma) do not function as equal-and-immediate conditions,
they are non-material phenomena (arūpadharma).
With respect to formless phenomena (*ārūpya-dharma*), how many conditions (*pratyaya*) are there?

Answer: They are the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The causes are the five causes,
namely the five beginning with the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*).
As for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*):
That is to say, immediately following formless states (ārūpya-dharma),
formless states manifest;
as for their objects of cognition (ālambana):
That is to say, formless phenomena serve as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for formless phenomena;
their role as the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is as previously explained.
How many conditions do formless phenomena serve as for material phenomena?
Answer: [There are] the cause and the predominant condition.
As for the cause, there are four causes.
Namely: coexistent, similar-type,
universal, and retributive [causes].
The "predominant" (adhipati) is as previously explained.
The same applies to the explanations of "with vision" and "without vision," and "with resistance" and "without resistance.
The distinction, however, is as follows:
Visible phenomena serve as two causes for visible phenomena.
That is to say: homogeneous, retributive;
all others are as previously explained.
With how many conditions do contaminated phenomena serve as conditions for contaminated phenomena?
Answer: [They arise] by way of the causal, immediately antecedent, objective, and predominant conditions.
As for the causal condition, there are five causes;
namely, the five beginning with the associated cause.
Regarding "immediately preceding" (samanantara):
it means that when impure dharmas arise in immediate succession,
impure dharmas manifest before one.
The object of focus refers to contaminated phenomena and their relation to contaminated phenomena.
They serve as objects of perception (*ālambana*).
As for their predominance (*adhipati*), it is as previously explained.
[This applies to] contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) and uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*).
By how many conditions?
Answer: By the conditions of equal-immediate, object, and predominant.
Regarding "equal-immediate":
That is to say, when an uncontaminated dharma manifests immediately after a contaminated dharma;
as for the object of focus:
This refers to contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) serving as the objects of focus (*ālambana*) for uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*),
namely those mental states and mental factors belonging to the categories of receptivity (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) regarding suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).
The "predominant" [condition] is as previously explained.
As for "not being a cause," this is because a cause is like a seed.
It is not a contaminated phenomenon (*sāsrava-dharma*),
because it serves as the seed for uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
Uncontaminated phenomena...
How many conditions do they serve as for untainted (anāsrava) dharmas?
Answer: They serve as the causal (hetu), equal-and-immediate (samanantara), object (ālambana), and predominant (adhipati) conditions.
Regarding the causal condition, there are three causes.
That is to say: association,
coexistence,
and homogeneity.
Regarding "immediately preceding" (samanantara):
it refers to when an untainted dharma manifests immediately after an untainted dharma.
The object of focus refers to untainted phenomena and their association with untainted phenomena.
The objects of focus (*ālambana*) are the mental states and mental factors belonging to the categories of patience and knowledge regarding cessation and the path.
The predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously explained.
How many conditions do untainted phenomena serve as for tainted phenomena?
Answer: Equal-immediate,
object-conditioned,
and predominant conditions.
"Immediately preceding" (samanantara) refers to when, immediately following an outflow-free dharma (anāsrava-dharma),
an outflowing dharma (sāsrava-dharma) manifests.
"Object-condition" (ālambana) refers to...
That is to say, uncontaminated phenomena serve as the objects of perception for contaminated phenomena.
The "predominant" [condition] is as previously explained.
As for "not being a cause," this is because a cause is like a seed.
It is not an untainted (anāsrava) dharma,
because it serves as the seed for tainted (sāsrava) dharmas;
it is a conditioned (saṃskṛta) dharma.

With respect to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), how many conditions (*pratyaya*) do they serve as? Answer: They serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
As for "causes," there are five causes,
namely the five beginning with association.
As for "immediately preceding condition" (samanantara):
This refers to when a conditioned phenomenon manifests immediately after another conditioned phenomenon;
as for the object of focus:
That is to say, conditioned phenomena serve as the object-condition for conditioned phenomena.
The "predominance" is as previously explained.
It concerns conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena.
By how many conditions?
Answer: None.
It is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
With regard to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), how many conditions (*pratyaya*) do they serve as?
Answer: None.
How many conditions do unconditioned phenomena serve as for conditioned phenomena?
Answer: Regarding the object-condition (ālambana) and the dominant condition (adhipati).
As for the object-condition:
That is to say, unconditioned phenomena serve as the object-condition for conditioned phenomena.
The "predominant" [condition] is as previously explained.
Question: For what reason do conditioned phenomena possess causes and possess conditions?
Are unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) without causes and without conditions?
Answer: Because the nature of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) is weak and inferior.
Conditioned phenomena depend upon various causes and conditions,
whereas unconditioned phenomena are powerful and do not depend upon causes and conditions;
they are like an inferior person who relies on others.
The powerful do not rely [on anything].
This is also like that.
Some say:
Because all conditioned phenomena possess functional activity, they depend upon causes and conditions;
because unconditioned phenomena lack functional activity, they do not depend upon causes and conditions.
It is like a reaper who requires a sickle.
One who digs requires a spade;
one who has nothing to do requires nothing.
This case is also like this.
Some say that because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) function within the world, grasp results,
and cognize objects, they require causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*);
whereas unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) do not have such functions and therefore do not require causes and conditions.
Just as a long-distance traveler requires provisions,
whereas one who does not travel does not,
so it is in this case as well.

Some say that conditioned phenomena are like a king and also like his retinue; therefore, they possess causes and conditions. Unconditioned phenomena are like a king but not like his retinue; therefore, they lack causes and conditions.
This is like the case of a king and his retinue.
As it is with those who are wealthy and noble and their retinues,
so too should one understand it to be with Śakra and the retinue of Śakra.
Question: When conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) sometimes do not arise, what creates this obstruction?
Is it conditioned phenomena or unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)?
Answer: All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) constitute obstacles;
unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) do not, because unconditioned phenomena always act as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for conditioned phenomena.
And as for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
it is because it poses no obstruction to either arising or non-arising,
such as the case of a lion’s mouth beside a spring or pond.
When water does not flow, there are other conditions present that act as obstructions; it is not this [lack of flow] itself that constitutes the obstruction.

Question: Do the unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) serve as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and object conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)?
Regarding that which is capable of being an object of cognition and that which is incapable of being an object of cognition, do they differ in terms of their predominance as *adhipati-pratyaya*?
Answer: In the sense of being a *adhipati-pratyaya*, there is no distinction between them.
Since there is no obstruction whether [the object] is taken as a condition or not,
the meaning of the "object-condition" (ālambanapratyaya) is thus differentiated:
it acts as an object-condition for that which takes it as an object.
Regarding those who are unable to take such objects as their cognitive focus,
they do not engage in the entanglements that lead to the continuity of existence in hell;
this is explained at length.
The meanings of the term "existence" (*bhava*) as explained here are manifold,
as described at length in the *Saṃyukta-skandha*.
Here, it refers to the continuity of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
The five aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings are called "existence" (bhava).
Furthermore, there are five types of continuity:
first, the continuity of the intermediate state (antarābhava).
Second, the continuity of birth;
third, the continuity of states;
fourth, the continuity of phenomena.
The five moments of continuity:
regarding the continuity of the intermediate state (antarābhava),
it refers to the cessation of the aggregates of the existence at death (maraṇabhava).

The arising of the intermediate state (antarābhava) constitutes the continuity of the intermediate state; the continuity of the birth-existence (upapattibhava) constitutes the continuity of the birth-existence.
This refers to the cessation of the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the arising of the aggregates of the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
The continuity of the birth-existence following the intermediate state is called the "continuity of birth-existence.
As for the continuity of states (*avasthā-santati*):
This means that when the aggregates of the *kalala* stage cease, the aggregates of the *arbuda* stage arise;
and so on, until the aggregates of the middle-aged stage cease and the aggregates of the old age stage arise.
In all these cases, the continuity from one stage to the next is termed "continuity by way of stages" (*avasthā-saṃtati*).
Regarding the continuity of phenomena (*dharmasaṃtati*):
it refers to when, immediately following wholesome phenomena and so forth,
defiled or neutral phenomena manifest.
Immediately after defiled dharmas,
wholesome or indeterminate dharmas manifest;
immediately after indeterminate dharmas, [wholesome or defiled] dharmas manifest.
Whether wholesome or defiled phenomena manifest,
the fact that subsequent phenomena follow preceding phenomena is called the continuity of phenomena (*dharma-saṃtati*).
As for momentary continuity (*kṣaṇa-saṃtati*):
Immediately following the aggregates of the first moment,
the aggregates of the second moment manifest;
this succession of subsequent moments following the preceding moments is called the continuity of moments (*kṣaṇasaṃtati*).
These five all enter into two continuities, namely,
the continuity of phenomena (*dharma-saṃtāna*) and the continuity of moments (*kṣaṇa-saṃtāna*),
because they are never apart from phenomena and moments.
Regarding the analysis by realm:
the desire realm possesses all five;
the form realm possesses four, excluding the state of abiding.
In the formless realm there are three, excluding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
As for the classification of destinies (*gati*),
there are four in the hells, excluding the states of transition (*avasthā*).
The other realms of existence possess all five.
Regarding the classification by birth,
all possess all five.
Among these five continuities,
the treatise is composed based on two continuities,
namely: the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*).
The primary sense faculties and primary elements first acquired by one who, bound by the various fetters, continues existence in hell—
those sense faculties and primary elements.
With how many conditions do those mental states and mental factors act as conditions for one another?
Answer: One, the predominance condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
That is to say, those very mental states and mental factors [act as such].
Answer: They serve as one condition, namely, the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

When one is bound by the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), the roots and great elements (*mahābhūta*) first acquired at the moment of continuing existence among animals, hungry ghosts, humans, or gods [are so related].
How many conditions do those sense faculties and great elements serve as for those mental states and mental factors?
Answer: One, the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Regarding those very minds and mental factors, how many conditions do they serve as for those sense faculties and primary elements?
Answer: One, the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Question: If those minds and mental factors do not take those sense faculties and primary elements as their objects when linking rebirth,
can it be said that those sense faculties and primary elements [exist]?
With those mental states and mental factors,
there is only a single predominance.
If those mental states and mental factors...
That which arises conditioned by those sense faculties and primary elements—
those very sense faculties and primary elements.
With respect to those mental states and mental factors, it serves as two conditions, namely,
the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
Why, then, is the definitive answer given that it is only one— namely, the dominant condition?
The answer should also state that there are two [types], yet because it does not do so, one should know that this meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Some say that what is stated here is definitive;
that is, the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) is fixed.
The objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is not fixed;
therefore, it is not mentioned here.
Some say that what is discussed in this context is mutual possession.
That is to say, the faculties and the great elements serve as mutual dominant conditions for the mind and mental factors;
therefore, it is said that the mind and mental factors do not serve as object-conditions for the faculties and the great elements.
For this reason, it is not mentioned.
Some say that what is discussed here is mutual support;
that is to say, those sense faculties and the primary elements (mahābhūta) mutually support the mind and mental factors, and their meaning as predominant conditions (adhipati-pratyaya) is superior.
The object-condition (*ālambana*) is not like this,
for [the mind] can arise in dependence upon any phenomenon whatsoever; therefore,
it is not mentioned [in that context].
Born in the desire realm, one enters the contaminated first dhyāna,
up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
thereby nourishing the sense faculties and augmenting the primary elements.
How many conditions do those sense faculties and great elements serve as for those mind and mental factors?
Answer: One, the predominance condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, how many conditions do those mind and mental factors serve as for those sense faculties and great elements?
Answer: There is one predominance (*adhipati*).
Question: Regarding those mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), if one enters meditative absorption by taking other phenomena as objects, it may be as you have described.
If one enters meditative absorption by taking those very sense faculties and primary elements as objects, there would then be two conditions.
Why, then, is it said that there is only one predominant condition?
One should understand that when it is appropriate to speak yet remains unsaid, this indicates that the meaning is incomplete.
Some say that among these, only those with fixed objects are mentioned;
because their objects are indeterminate, they are not mentioned here.
Some say: "In this context, although it is stated that they possess one another, the objects of perception (*ālambana*) are not so; therefore, they are not mentioned."

Some say that what is described here as "mutual assistance" (saṃbhāra) refers to the fact that the mind and mental factors mutually assist those sense organs and great elements, and that the meaning of their predominance (adhipatya) is superior.
The objects of focus (*ālambana*) are not like this;
regardless of what phenomenon they take as their object, they all arise. Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Question: What is the distinction between entering the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) to increase the faculties and the great elements, and entering the formless attainments (*ārūpya*)?
Answer: The nourishment provided by dhyāna is abundant but not exquisite;
it is like the food of the country of Bāhlika. The nourishment provided by the formless [attainments] is exquisite but not abundant;
it is like the food of Central India.
When one is born in the desire realm and enters the untainted first dhyāna,
up to the sphere of nothingness,
one nurtures the sense faculties and increases the primary elements.
How many conditions do those sense faculties and primary elements serve as for those mental states and mental factors?
Answer: One, namely the predominance condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, how many conditions do those same mental states and mental factors serve as for those sense faculties and primary elements?
Answer: There is one predominance (*adhipati*).

In this context, the meaning of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is not discussed, nor are the specific distinctions regarding the benefits of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
This should be understood as previously explained.
Question: When entering contaminated (*sāsrava*) dhyāna or formless (*ārūpya*) attainments, how do the faculties (*indriya*), the great elements (*mahābhūta*), and their derivatives increase?
What is the distinction between these and the entry into the outflow-free (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: The outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) provides much benefit but is not sublime;
the outflow-free provides sublime benefit but is not much. The two analogies are as previously stated.
Born in the form realm, one enters the contaminated first dhyāna,
up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
thereby nourishing the sense faculties.
Regarding the increase of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*):
as for those primary elements of the sense faculties, how many conditions do they serve as for those mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*)?
Answer: One, namely, the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Regarding those very minds and mental factors, how many conditions do they serve as for those sense faculties and primary elements?
Answer: One, the predominance condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
When one is born in the form realm and enters the first dhyāna of the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
Up to the sphere of nothingness,
they nourish the sense faculties and augment the great elements.
How many conditions do those sense faculties and primary elements serve as for those mental states and mental factors?
Answer: One, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
How many conditions do those same mental states and mental factors serve as for those sense faculties and primary elements?
Answer: One is predominant.
In this context, the objects of focus (ālambana), as well as the dhyānas and formless attainments (ārūpya), are not discussed.
The distinctions regarding the increase and benefit of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are all as previously explained. What is the meaning of "appropriated" (*upātta*)?
Answer: It refers to those phenomena included within one's own personal existence (*svabhāva*) that are revealed by this technical designation (*adhivacana*).
What is the meaning of "non-appropriated" (*anupātta*)?
Answer: This term denotes those phenomena that do not fall within the nature of the self-body (*svātmabhāva*).
Nevertheless, the expression "appropriated" (*upātta*) is frequently used in many places.
What is the meaning of "appropriated" as explained here?
It refers to those phenomena that fall within one's own personal continuum (*sva-ātmabhāva*). Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The appropriated aggregate of feeling gives rise to manifold sufferings."
It refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, and the suffering of death.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The unlearned person, throughout the long night, cultivates the grasping at a self. Another sutra further states: [the suffering of] conditioned existence.
How much more so for this body, which dwells temporarily within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as something appropriated (*upātta*).
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"A portion of nine bases (*āyatana*) is called appropriated."
The *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* states that the appropriated aggregates (*upātta-skandha*) are the object of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Question: What is the difference in meaning between these various explanations?
The answer is: herein, the five aggregates included within the internal body are called "appropriated" (*upātta*).
The first sutra states that the five aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings, which continue the commonality of the group (*nikāya-sabhāga*), are called "appropriated."
Next, a sutra states that the five aggregates, which are the objects of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) from beginningless time,
are called "appropriated" (upātta).
Later, another sutra states:
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) comprised within the internal body is called "appropriated" (upātta);
the Prakaraṇapāda states that this occurs for even a single moment.
A portion of nine bases is called "appropriated" (*upātta*).
The *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* states that a single moment of a portion of the five aggregates is called "appropriated."

Some say that the *Prakaraṇapāda* and the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* state that a portion of nine bases (*āyatana*) belonging to the category of sentient beings (*sattvākhya*) in a single moment is termed "appropriated" (*upātta*).
Some say that both treatises state that a portion of nine bases (āyatana), which are subsumed under the faculties (indriya) within a single moment,
are termed "appropriated" (sopādāna).
Some say that according to two treatises, a portion of nine bases (*āyatana*) comprised within a single moment of maturation (*vipāka*) is termed "appropriated" (*sopādāna*).
This is called the distinction.
Question: For what reason does loving-kindness take only form as its object?
Answer: At the time of initial cultivation, it takes form as its object.
At the time of its formation, it takes the five aggregates as its object.
The masters of the West say that there are four types of appropriated [matter].
First, there is possession by a single body;
second, there is possession by a continuity;
third, there is possession by a homogeneous class.
Fourth, there is the conventional designation of "appropriated.
Regarding the body being appropriated:
this refers to what is called "appropriated" in the first sutra mentioned above.
Regarding the continuity of the aggregate of suffering having appropriation:
it is as when it is said that "I have an appropriated continuity of the sense-faculty body.
Regarding the continuity of the homogeneous class having appropriation: [it is the same].
As it is said: "I possess the sense faculties, the body, and the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga) which are appropriated.
Just as there is a conventional designation of an "appropriator," so it is said: "I appropriate this heavy burden."
Regarding such activities:
herein, the five internal aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are said to be "appropriated" (*sopādāna*).
Those phenomena not included therein are "unappropriated" (*anupādāna*). This question is as previously stated.
What are the characteristics of that which is appropriated (*upātta*) and that which is non-appropriated (*anupātta*)? The answer is:
some say that if it dwells in conjunction with blood, flesh, sinews, and bones, it is called appropriated.
That which is contrary to this is called "non-appropriated.
Some say that when it is cut, pierced, or split, [it does not feel pain].
That which is associated with the sensation of pain and the laying down of the burden is called "appropriated" (sopādāna);
the opposite of this is called "non-appropriated" (anupādāna).
The Venerable Ghoṣaka has stated it in this way.
If a phenomenon has already arisen but not yet ceased,
belongs to the category of sentient beings, is resistant, and is not audible, it is called "appropriated.
The term "already arisen" excludes that which is future.
"Unextinguished" excludes those that are past.
"Included among sentient beings" excludes what is not included among sentient beings.
"With resistance" excludes the sense base of mind and the sense base of mental phenomena.
That which is not heard excludes the sense-sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*).
That which is contrary to this is called "non-appropriated" (*anupātta*).
The Venerable Dharmatrāta has stated as follows:
If a phenomenon possesses spatial parts,
belongs to the category of sentient beings, is connected to the body,
is resistant, and can be drawn or repelled, it is called "appropriated."
That which possesses spatial parts excludes the past and the future;
that which belongs to the category of sentient beings excludes that which does not belong to the category of sentient beings.
That which is bound to the body refers to what is excluded from the body,
namely hair, body hair, and so forth.
"Having resistance" excludes the sense base of mind and the sense base of mental phenomena;
it refers to that which can be drawn toward or repelled.
Excluding the sense base of sound, those contrary to this are called non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
Question: Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), [which are appropriated?]
How many are appropriated (upātta)?
How many are non-appropriated?
Answer: Those born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) consist of a portion of nine bases (āyatana).
This is possessed of appropriation (sopādāna):
it comprises three bases in their entirety and a portion of nine bases.
These are without appropriation (*anupātta*).
The three bases are the sound base (*śabdāyatana*), the mind base (*manāyatana*), and the phenomena base (*dharmāyatana*).
If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they comprise a portion of seven bases.
This is possessed of appropriation (upātta):
it comprises three bases in their entirety and a portion of seven bases.
This is without appropriation.
The three locations are as previously explained.
Question: Within this body...
Among the thirty-six kinds of impure substances,
how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and how many are non-appropriated (*anupātta*)?
Answer: The roots of the hair, body hair, nails, and teeth are appropriated;
the rest are non-appropriated.
Skin, bile, brain, and blood are born as appropriated.
The decaying [parts] are without appropriation (*anupātta*);

the bones, flesh, sinews, veins, heart, lungs, spleen, kidneys, liver, intestines, stomach, membranes, fat, marrow, brain, and the two receptacles—the raw and the cooked—all possess appropriation (*sopātta*).
