This dharma arises from grasping (*upādāna*);
because it can produce grasping, it is called "conducive to grasping" (*anupādāniya*). Some say:
This dharma proceeds from grasping;
because it can turn toward grasping, it is called "conducive to grasping" (*parāmarśānukūla*). Some say:
This dharma is called "conducive to grasping" (upādānīya) because it is drawn forth by grasping and can itself draw forth grasping;
some say that this dharma is nurtured by grasping.
It is called "conducive to grasping" (*upādānīya*) because it can nourish grasping.
Some say that these phenomena are further expanded by grasping.
They are called "conducive to grasping" (*upādānīya*) because they cause grasping to increase and expand.
The term "increase and expand" indicates the sense of spreading like creeping vines. Some say:
These phenomena are bound to grasping;
therefore, they are called "conducive to grasping" (*upādāniya*).
This is just as those who belong to a king are called "king's subjects."
Because there is no self within,
if someone were to ask,
"To whom do you belong? [one would have no answer].
The answer is: they belong to grasping (*upādāna*). Some say:
"All forms of grasping exist within this dharma."
That which is about to arise has already arisen;
that which is about to be grasped has already been grasped;
that which is about to abide has already abided.
Therefore, it is called "conducive to grasping" (*upādānīya*).
Some say that all forms of grasping exist within these phenomena.
Because they nourish what has already been nourished, they are called "conducive to grasping" (*upādānīya*).
Some say that the various forms of grasping exist within these phenomena.
Because they will increase what has already increased,
they are called "conducive to grasping" (*parigrahānukūla*). Some say:
The various types of grasping adhere firmly to this,
just as dust and grime adhere to a moist and oily object; therefore,
they are called "conducive to grasping" (upādānīya).
Some say that the various types of grasping find pleasure in this abiding,
just as fish and frogs delight in staying within water.
Therefore, it is called "conducive to grasping" (*upādānīya*).
Some say that because these phenomena serve as the basis for taking up [grasping] and for establishing a secure footing,
they are named "conducive to grasping."
This means that based upon this dharma,
all forms of craving, pride, views, doubt, hatred, delusion,
the various fetters (paryavasthāna), and impurities (mala) are produced and grow.
All contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are acquired through their respective homogeneous grasping (*sabhāga-upādāna*);
they are termed "conducive to grasping" (*upādānīya*) because they are not acquired through heterogeneous grasping.
That is to say, phenomena of the desire realm are acquired through the grasping of the desire realm.
Dharmas of the form realm are grasped by the grasping of the form realm;
dharmas of the formless realm are grasped by the grasping of the formless realm;
and so are the dharmas of the stage of the first dhyāna.
By means of the factors of the first dhyāna stage,
one grasps up to the factors of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
by means of the factors of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one grasps [those same factors].
Because the contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and its stages (*bhūmi*) are not intermingled;
however, if one relies on the continuity (*saṃtati*), there is the sense of intermingling.
That is to say, by means of one's own body taking up the dharmas of another's body, the designation "concordant" (*anulomika*) is obtained.
Because one grasps one's own phenomena by means of another's body, they receive the designation "appropriated" (*upādāna*).
If this were not the case, external phenomena would not be "appropriated," because there is no appropriation with respect to the external.
What is the meaning of "conducive to fetters" (*anuloma-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: It is that which is revealed by this designation (*adhivacana*).
What is the meaning of "outflowing phenomena not conducive to fetters"?
Answer: This refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas manifested by this designation.

A detailed explanation of the meanings of "conducive to bondage" (*saṃyojanīya*) and "not conducive to bondage" (*asaṃyojanīya*) is as previously stated in the discussion on "conducive to grasping" (*upādānīya*) and "not conducive to grasping" (*anupādānīya*).
What is the meaning of "locus of views"?
Answer: This is indicated by a metaphorical designation (*adhivacana*).
It refers to those contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) that are not loci of views.
What is the meaning of this?
The answer is: it refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas manifested by this designation (*adhivacana*).
However, regarding the term "basis of views" (*dṛṣṭisthāna*), it is said that there are many such bases; it is in this sense that it is spoken of here.
What is meant by "view-standpoints" (*diṭṭhiṭṭhāna*)? It refers to those things associated with the outflows (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, the Kāṇḍadvaya Sūtra states:
"Whatever views there are, and whatever view-standpoints there are..."
All fetters of views,
all origins of views,
and all afflictions caused by views.
The Blessed One knows and sees everything.
In this context, "view" refers to the five views;
"the locus of view" refers to the objective referent of those views.
The "entanglement of views" refers to the active manifestation of views;
the "origination of views" refers to the cause of views;
and the "harm caused by views" refers to the cessation of views.
The Blessed One’s “knowing all and seeing all” refers to the vision that serves as an antidote.
Some say that the vision of the locus of views and the entanglement of views constitute the Truth of Suffering.
"Seeing that which gives rise [to suffering] refers to the truth of origination (samudaya-satya).
Seeing that which harms [suffering] refers to the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya).
That the Blessed One knows and sees everything refers to the truth of the path (mārga-satya)."
The *Āḷavaka-sutta* further states that there are six bases for views,
namely: all forms whatsoever.
Whether past, future, or present— this is explained in detail—
up to: "O bhikṣus, one should,
with right wisdom, contemplate all of those as neither self nor belonging to a self."
"Do not give rise to the conceit 'I am.
Whatever sensations there may be...
and so forth, as extensively explained.
All perceptions whatsoever—
expounded at length— whatever is seen,
heard, sensed, or known, whether attained or sought.
The mind follows vitarka and vicāra,
and so forth, as explained at length.
Those who hold this view...
"There is a self, there are sentient beings, there is a world;
it is permanent, eternal, stable, and unchanging—a phenomenon that remains just as it is.
Thus it is said at length.
Those who hold such views as: "I should not exist; I should not be."
"I shall not exist; I shall not be. Monks, one should observe with right wisdom that all of this is neither self nor belongs to a self.
Do not give rise to the conceit of "I.
A bhikṣu should, regarding such bases for views and bases for grasping,
observe accordingly that there is neither self nor what belongs to a self.
If one can act in this way, then one will have no grasping or appropriation toward the world;
thus it is said at length.
Herein, all that exists as form, feeling, and perception—
Namely, the aggregates of form, feeling, and perception.
"All those who hold this view that there is a self, a sentient being," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Regarding the statement, "Those who hold the view that 'I should not exist,' and so forth,
in detail," this refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), including all seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
This refers to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Question: The meanings of "seeing," "hearing," "sensing," and "knowing" have already been fully explained.
What, then, are the meanings of "attaining," "seeking," and "the mind following discursive thought and investigation" (*vitarka* and *vicāra*)?
What further is being revealed?
The answer is: previously it was extensive, now it is concise;
previously it was specific, now it is general.
What was previously opened is now closed;
what was previously gradual is now sudden.
This is what is revealed by the *Āsravasaṃvara-sūtra*, which further states:
Through improper reflection upon the six bases for views, one gives rise to some form of attachment toward the internal body, thinking:
"In truth, because of its persistence, there is a self; in truth, there is what belongs to a self."
Because of abiding, there is "I" and "not-I.
One who sees "I" sees "I";
one who sees "not-I" sees "not-I," and one who sees "not-I" sees "I."
Or there may be a self here,
a sentient being,
or a life-principle.
There are those who are born,
there are those who nourish,
and there are persons (pudgala).
There is the arising of volition.
There is a certain Māṇava who is either past, future, or present.
In those various places, one experiences the maturation of the fruits of various wholesome and unwholesome karmas already performed or yet to be performed.
Question: What is the distinction between these four bases and what is expressed by the term "basis for views" (*diṭṭhi-ṭhāna*)?
Answer: Some say that the "bases of views" (*diṭṭhāyatana*) mentioned here reveal all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
This refers to the "bases of views" spoken of in the first sutra.
This collectively reveals the five views.
The "bases of views" (*diṭṭhi-ṭhāna*) taught in the second sutta reveal both the views themselves and the phenomena dissociated from views.
The "bases of views" (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna*) described in the third sutra reveal the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme adherence (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*). Some say:
The bases of views (*diṭṭhi-ṭhāna*) taught in this [sūtra] and in the first two sūtras collectively manifest the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānakkhandhā*).
The bases of views taught in the third sūtra...
This merely reveals a small portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Some say that this and the first two sūtras [are intended to show this].
The third sutra reveals both associated and dissociated phenomena;
it alone reveals associated phenomena.
As with the associated and the dissociated,
there are those with a basis and those without a basis,
and those with mental aspects and those without mental aspects.
The same applies to having an object of perception and being without an object of perception,
as well as being alert and being unalert.
Some say this refers to these [two] along with the first two sūtras.
The first [sūtra] generally reveals both material and immaterial phenomena;
the third sūtra reveals only immaterial phenomena.
As it is with the formless and the form-possessing,
so it is with the visible and the invisible,
and likewise with the resistant and the non-resistant.
Some say that this [sūtra] and the first two sūtras collectively reveal both defiled and undefiled dharmas,
while the third sūtra...
It reveals only defiled phenomena;
for example, as with the defiled and the non-defiled,
or the blameworthy and the blameless.
Obscured and unobscured;
black and white;

that is, these [six] include the six equanimity mental applications in their full extent.
As for "thirty-six in their entirety": [this refers to the following:]
There are six types of equanimity based on attachment and six types of equanimity based on renunciation;
each of these pertains to the three periods of time.
Therefore, it is said that according to their respective matters,
there are thirty-six feelings and one hundred and eight feelings.
Are the thirty-six [factors] subsumed by the one hundred and eight, or are the one hundred and eight subsumed by the thirty-six?
Answer: They mutually subsume one another according to their respective natures;
that is to say, each of the thirty-six subsumes three complete sets.
This itself comprises thirty-six [factors].
Regarding the three complete sets:
these are the thirty-six [factors] each distinguished by the three time periods.
Therefore, it is said that they correspond to their respective objects.
Question: How are the eighteen mental applications (manopavicāra) established?
Are they established by way of association (saṃprayoga)?
Is it by way of intrinsic nature,
or by way of the object of cognition?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If categorized by association, there is only one,
namely the mental application associated with the mental consciousness.
If categorized by intrinsic nature, there are only three.
That is to say: the mental application of joy,
the mental application of grief,
and the mental application of equanimity.
If categorized by way of their objects, there are only six—
namely, the mental applications to visible forms (*rūpa-upavicāra*) up to the mental applications to mental phenomena (*dharma-upavicāra*).
Why, then, are eighteen spoken of?
Answer: In total, eighteen are established based on three conditions.
That is to say, the first is that the mental concomitants (anuvicāra) associated with the single consciousness possess three types of intrinsic nature: joy, sorrow, and equanimity.
Because each arises by taking the six kinds of objects—form and so forth—as its respective objective condition, there are eighteen.
Having explained their essential nature, the reason for this shall now be stated.
For what cause and conditions?
They are called "mental applications" (*manopavicāra*).
Answer: These eighteen types of feeling take the mind as their proximate condition and operate upon objects.
They are called "mental applications" (*manopavicāra*).
Furthermore, they are called mental applications because they serve as proximate conditions that cause the mind to range repeatedly over its objects.
Moreover, by depending upon the mind, they proceed in proximity to their objects.
They are called "mental applications" (*manopavicāra*).
Because they rapidly and skillfully engage in frequent conceptualization regarding their objects,
they are termed "applications," just like a nimble woman.
She frequently counts her husband and gives rise to discriminative mental activities,
perhaps grasping at signs of delight.
Sometimes they grasp at the sign of distress,
and sometimes they grasp at the sign of renunciation;
in this way, they rapidly and skillfully experience the enumeration [of objects] within the six sense-fields.
They give rise to discursive formations;
they may proceed according to signs concordant with joy,
or they may proceed according to signs concordant with sorrow.
Or they proceed with the characteristic of equanimity;
for these reasons, they are called "mental applications" (*manopavicāra*).
Question: Regarding these eighteen mental applications—
Is it only on the level of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), or does it also exist in the five sensory consciousnesses?
Answer: It exists only on the level of the mental consciousness, not in the five sensory consciousnesses.
Question: If that is so, why does the Sūtra state that after the eye has seen a form,
one gives rise to an approach toward joy regarding a form conducive to joy,
and gives rise to an approach toward sorrow regarding a form conducive to sorrow?
Regarding forms that are conducive to equanimity, one gives rise to the mental application of equanimity;
this is explained in detail up until: having cognized mental phenomena with the mind, one gives rise to the mental application of joy regarding phenomena that are conducive to joy.
Do mental applications of grief arise toward phenomena conducive to grief, and do mental applications of equanimity arise toward phenomena conducive to equanimity?
Answer: Because they are induced by the five groups of sensory consciousness.
This was stated for the sake of providing a path of progression;
however, mental applications (*manopavicāra*) exist only on the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*),
just as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) exists only on the level of the mental consciousness.
However, when a sūtra states that "having seen a form with the eye,
one dwells fully established in the contemplation of its impurity," this is also because it is induced by visual consciousness.
This was said for the sake of providing a path.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Having seen forms with the eye," and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, it is known that the mental applications (*manopavicāra*) do not exist within the five consciousnesses.
Question: Since it is also said that "the mind knows phenomena (*dharma*)," how could they not also exist within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?
Answer: There is no fault, because this is stated according to what is predominant.
That is to say, although the initial states such as joy (*prīti*) are also near-approaches (*upavicāra*), they are not clear and sharp.
Subsequently, when the analysis becomes more intense regarding the object and more swift and sharp,
it is called "near-approach" (*sāmantaka*).
For this reason, it is said that "the mind, having known the phenomena..."

Furthermore, as previously stated, the sense-consciousnesses (pañca-vijñāna) lack the meaning of "mental application" (*upavicāra*). Question: Are the conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) regarding the past and future also mental applications?
Why does the Sūtra not mention them?
Answer: These mental applications (*manopavicāra*) are stated to be present only for the sake of clarity;
by this same principle, it is shown that those of the past and future are also included.
Question: Are there any who do not first perceive a form before mentally discriminating that form?
Up to: "Is that which is not contact, but having contacted [an object], is discriminated as contact—the joy and so forth arising from this—considered 'mental application' (*manopavicāra*)?
Answer: It is mental application.
However, in the sūtras, based on the explicit meaning,
it is said: "Having seen forms," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Question: After one has seen forms with the eye, conceptualizations of sounds and so forth arise;
and so on, until after one has cognized mental objects with the mind.
One gives rise to conceptualizations of form and so forth.
Are the joy and other states produced by these [conceptualizations] "mental applications" (*manopavicāra*)?
Answer: They are mental applications.
However, in the sūtras, based on the explicit meaning (*nītārtha*), it is said:
"Having seen forms," and so forth, at length.
If this were the case, then there would be the perceiver and the perceived.
Regarding the meaning of each faculty:
their modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) are all clearly discerned;
were it otherwise, they would not be distinct.
Question: Among these eighteen mental applications (*manopavicāra*),
how many have mixed objects (*miśrālambana*) and how many have unmixed objects (*amiśrālambana*)?
Answer: Fifteen are non-mixed objects,
namely the three mental applications (*manopavicāra*) regarding form,
and so on, up to the three mental applications regarding contact.
The remaining ones are those with mixed objects and those with unmixed objects;
that is, the three mental applications (manopavicāra) regarding phenomena (dharma), which have as their objects the six internal bases and the external base of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Whether taken collectively or individually, these are called "non-confused objects.
Whether one takes these seven collectively or individually,
or one or two from among the five external [objects], [these constitute the non-confused objects].
Alternatively, up to five [objects] are termed "mixed objects.
Among the five external [objects],
if two are combined as the object of focus.
Alternatively, even up to five may be called "mixed objects" (*miśrālambana*),
because the term "dharmas" is inclusive;
since they take a combined object, they are not among the previous fifteen.
Question: Is there any form, etc., that is definitively conducive to joy, up to being definitively conducive to equanimity?
Answer: It depends on the object of focus (*ālambana*).
Because there is a continuity that is without support,
it exists; that is to say, there are those who possess form and so forth.
At times it may be pleasing;
at times it may be displeasing;
or it may be pleasing with respect to that [object].
Regarding this, it is disagreeable;
regarding others, it is neither agreeable nor disagreeable.
Some say:
Visible forms and so forth are conducive to joy regarding those who are friendly,
conducive to grief regarding those who are hostile,
and conducive to equanimity regarding those who are neutral.
Question: Of these eighteen mental applications (*manopavicāra*), how many continue at birth and how many at death?
Answer: Six.
This refers to the six mental applications of equanimity. Why is this?
Because all mental applications of joy and sorrow proceed through a predominant mode of attention.
There is no superior mental attention (*manasikāra*) for the continuity of rebirth at the end of life.
Question: Within each stage, such as the *kalala* and so forth, how many mental applications (*manopavicāra*) are there?
Answer: All are capable of possessing eighteen.
Question: How many mental applications (*manopavicāra*) are able to abandon defilement?
Answer: One, namely that which has mixed objects (*miśrālambana*).
The mental application of equanimity regarding phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*) can serve as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*),
whereas the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) may also involve mixed objects.
The mental applications of joy (*saumanasya-saṃsparśa*) are predominant;
however, the preparatory and superior stages also extend to the remaining [mental applications].
Question: Regarding these eighteen mental applications (*aṣṭādaśa-manopavicāra*):
How many [factors] exist in which realms and stages?
Answer: In the desire realm (kāmadhātu), all are present.
Within the form realm (rūpadhātu), they exist in the first two dhyānas.
Each has twelve, excluding the six types of sorrow;
the third and fourth dhyānas each have six.
Furthermore, excluding the six types of joy,
regarding the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the Sphere of Infinite Space within the Formless Realm,
if one were to allow that there is a distinct [mental state] directed toward the lower realm, [then it would follow that it is not a preparatory stage].
There are four types of equanimous mental applications (upekṣā-manopavicāra), namely:
those directed toward visible forms, sounds, tangibles, and mental objects (dharmas).
If one were to allow only the general perception of the lower realms as the object, [the following would occur].
If it were said that there is only one mental application of equanimity (*upekṣā-manopavicāra*),
then according to this explanation,
it should be stated that there are four.
The four fundamental formless attainments (*ārūpya-maula*) and the three higher preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) each possess only one mental application of equanimity (*upekṣā-manopavicāra*).
Question: How many mental applications (*manopavicāra*) take phenomena belonging to which realms as their objects?
Answer: Among the eighteen [mental applications] bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), six take only phenomena bound to the desire realm as their objects.
That is to say, the mental applications (*manopavicāra*) of joy, sorrow,

and equanimity conditioned by odors and tastes pertain to both the desire realm and the form realm. The nine mental applications of joy, sorrow, and equanimity conditioned by visible forms, sounds, and tangibles pertain to both the desire realm and the form realm.
The three types of contact have as their objects those things bound to the three realms as well as those that are unbound;
that is to say, they have as their objects the mental applications of joy, sorrow, and equanimity toward phenomena (*dharmālambana*).
Among these, there are twelve each within the first two dhyānas.
Four [mental applications] take only those bound to the desire realm as their objects;
that is, the mental applications of odor, flavor, joy, and equanimity.
Six take both those bound to the desire realm and those bound to the form realm as their objects.
These refer to the mental applications (*manopavicāra*) of joy and equanimity that take form, sound, and touch as their objects.
Two of these— namely, the mental applications of joy and equanimity toward phenomena (*dharma*)— take as their objects both those things bound to the three realms and those that are unbound.
In each of the third and fourth dhyānas, there are six intermediate [mental applications].
Two of these take only objects bound to the desire realm as their conditions;
namely, the equanimity-based mental applications directed toward odors and tastes.
Three [mental applications] take as their objects those things bound to the desire and form realms—
namely, the applications of equanimity toward visible forms, sounds, and tangibles.
One takes as its object those things bound to all three realms as well as those that are unbound.
This refers to the mental application of equanimity directed toward phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*),
which constitutes the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
This is provided that one accepts the existence of four types of mental applications.
Three [mental applications] take only those bound to the form realm as their objects;
that is to say, the mental applications of equanimity directed toward visible forms, sounds, and tangibles.
One [mental application] takes as its object those bound to both the form and formless realms, as well as those that are unbound.
This refers to the mental application of equanimity having phenomena as its object.
If one were to allow that there is only a single mental application of equanimity— that is,

the mental application of equanimity toward phenomena— then that one would universally take as its objects both those things bound to the realms of form and formlessness, as well as those that are unbound.
The four fundamental formless attainments and the three higher preparatory stages each possess one mental application of equanimity toward phenomena.
All of them take as their objects both that which is bound to the formless realm and that which is unbound.
Question: Among these various mental applications (*manopavicāra*), who accomplishes how many?
Answer: One born in the desire realm who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm accomplishes all [factors] of the desire realm.
The first and second dhyānas each have eight;
the third and fourth dhyānas each have four;
and the formless realm has one.
If one attains a wholesome mind of the form realm but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm,
that person accomplishes all [factors] of the desire realm.
There are ten in the first dhyāna,
eight in the second dhyāna,
and four each in the third and fourth dhyānas.
One [type] belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This refers to one who has already become free from the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) but has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the second dhyāna.
He accomplishes twelve [factors] each for the first dhyāna of the desire realm;
eight for the second dhyāna;
and four each for the third and fourth dhyānas.
One [type] belongs to the formless realm.
If one attains a wholesome mind of the second dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna.
He accomplishes twelve for each of the first dhyāna of the desire realm;
ten for the second dhyāna;
and four for each of the third and fourth dhyānas.
One [type] belongs to the formless realm.
This refers to one who has already become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna but has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the third dhyāna.
He accomplishes twelve each in the desire realm and the first two dhyānas;
four each in the third and fourth dhyānas;
and one in the formless realm.
If one has attained the wholesome mind of the third dhyāna but has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the fourth dhyāna,
that person possesses twelve [mental factors] each from the desire realm and the first two dhyānas.
The third dhyāna has six;
the fourth dhyāna has four;
and the formless realm has one.
If one has attained a wholesome mind of the fourth dhyāna but has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the sphere of infinite space,
that person accomplishes twelve [mental factors] each for the desire realm and the first two dhyānas.
There are six each for the third and fourth dhyānas,
and one for the formless realm;
this refers to the acquisition of the wholesome mind of the sphere of infinite space.
According to those who maintain that there are four types of mental application (*manopavicāra*) in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of those dhyānas,
one who has attained them accomplishes twelve each in the desire realm and the first two dhyānas,
and six each in the third and fourth dhyānas.
There are four [mental applications] for the sphere of infinite space,
and one each for the three higher formless spheres.
According to those who maintain that the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of those levels possess only a single mental application (*manopavicāra*).
He accomplishes one of each of the four formless attainments;
the rest is as previously explained.
If he is born in the first dhyāna...
If one has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the second dhyāna,
one possesses twelve factors of the first dhyāna and eight factors of the second dhyāna.
There are four each for the third and fourth dhyānas,
one for the formless realm,
and one for the accomplishment of the desire realm.
This refers to the mental application of equanimity regarding phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*),
which is associated with the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*),
because it arises by taking form and so forth as its object in a collective manner.
Some say that he accomplishes three: namely,
the mental applications of equanimity toward visible forms, sounds, and mental phenomena.
This is concomitant with the mind of fruition (vipākaja-citta).
If this mind takes as its object the bodily intimation (kāya-vijñapti) that has arisen,
there is then the mental application of equanimity (upekṣā-manopavicāra) taking form (rūpa) as its object.
If this mind takes as its object the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) that has arisen,
it then possesses the mental application (*manopavicāra*) of abandoning sound;
if this mind takes as its object a manifested thing (*nirmāṇa*), it does so by way of a general apprehension (*saṃgraha*).
That is, there are mental applications (manopavicāra) that involve the relinquishing of conditioned phenomena (sappaccaya-dhamma).
Some say that he accomplishes six.
This refers to the six equanimity-based mental applications (*upekṣā-manopavicāra*),
which are associated with the result-of-attainment consciousness (*prāpti-phala-citta*). This is because such a mind can take both general and specific objects as its cognitive domain.
If one attains the wholesome mind of the second dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna,
that person accomplishes ten factors of the second dhyāna.
The rest is as previously explained.
If one has already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna but has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the third dhyāna.
He accomplishes twelve [factors] of the second dhyāna;
the rest are as previously explained.
If he attains the wholesome mind of the third dhyāna...
If one has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the fourth dhyāna,
one possesses six factors of the third dhyāna;
the rest is as previously explained.
If one has attained the wholesome mind of the fourth dhyāna but has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the sphere of infinite space,
that person accomplishes six [factors] of the fourth dhyāna.
The rest is as previously explained.
Regarding the attainment of the wholesome mind of the sphere of infinite space,
some say:
He accomplishes four [attainments] of the sphere of infinite space,
and one each for the three higher formless spheres;
so some say.
He accomplishes four;
for each of the formless [attainments], one each;
the rest is as previously explained.
One born in the second dhyāna who has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the third dhyāna possesses twelve [factors] of the second dhyāna.
There are four for each of the third and fourth dhyānas,
one for the formless realm,
and those of the desire realm are as previously explained.
In the first dhyāna, one is accomplished in one mental application (manopavicāra),
namely, the mental application of equanimity regarding phenomena (dharmopekṣā-manopavicāra),
because it takes [all objects] collectively as its object.
Some say that one accomplishes three: namely,
the mental applications of equanimity toward forms, sounds, and phenomena.
If one gives rise to bodily intimation conditioned by [an object],
there is the mental application of equanimity directed toward form; if one gives rise to vocal intimation conditioned by [an object], [there is likewise the mental application of equanimity].
There is, then, the mental application that takes sound as its object and abandons [other objects];
and if it takes a manifested phenomenon as its object,
this is because it takes it in a general way.
There are those who abandon the mental applications (manopavicāra) regarding conditioned phenomena.
Some say that they accomplish four [of them].
This refers to the mental applications of equanimity toward visible forms, sounds, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
When one is born in the second dhyāna and gives rise to the three groups of consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna, [these mental applications occur].
It is possible for those retinues to exist separately as objects of form, sound, and touch,
because an unobscured-neutral mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna is present.
Alternatively, it is because the result-of-attainment mind takes both general and specific objects;
for instance, when one has attained the wholesome mind of the third dhyāna but has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the fourth dhyāna.
He accomplishes six [factors] of the third dhyāna;
the remainder is as previously stated.
If he attains the wholesome mind of the fourth dhyāna...
If one has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the Sphere of Infinite Space,
they possess six factors of the fourth dhyāna;
the rest is as previously stated.
If one attains a wholesome mind of the sphere of infinite space,
some say that such a person accomplishes four [factors] of the sphere of infinite space.
Each of the three higher formless realms [possesses] one [attainment].
Some say that they possess four.
There is one for each of the formless realms.
The rest is as previously explained.
One is born in the third dhyāna.
If one has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the fourth dhyāna,
one possesses six factors of the third dhyāna and four factors of the fourth dhyāna.
One [attainment] belongs to the formless realm;
those of the desire realm and the first dhyāna are as previously explained;
one [attainment] accomplishes the second dhyāna.
That is to say, the mental application of equanimity regarding phenomena (dharmopavicāra) is associated with the mind of fruition (abhijñā-phala-citta),
because it arises by taking form and so forth as its object in a collective manner.
Some say that he accomplishes three, namely:
the mental applications of equanimity toward visible forms, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
It is associated with the mind of fruition (vimukti-phala-citta), for this mind can take both general and specific objects.
If one attains the wholesome mind of the fourth dhyāna and so forth, it is as previously described.
Regarding those born in the fourth dhyāna,
the extent of their attainments should be understood according to what was previously explained.
Those born in the formless realm do not possess the lower [attainments].
The accomplishment of the higher stages should also be explained in detail according to the preceding [passage].
Question: How are these various *manopavicāras* (mental explorations) acquired?

Answer: At the time of the eight paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) prior to becoming detached from the defilements of the desire realm.
Each obtains six preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna.
At the time of the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one obtains the first dhyāna together with its twelve attendant factors (*parivāra*).
One obtains one [mental application] of the desire realm,
namely, the mental application of equanimity regarding phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*). Some say:
Three are obtained;
namely, the applications of attention (*manopavicāra*) regarding visible forms, sounds, and mental phenomena (*dharma*). Some say:
One attains six,
namely the six equanimity-approaches (*upekṣā-upavicāra*),
upon becoming free from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
During the eight preceding paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
one respectively attains six [attainments] of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna.
During the ninth path of uninterrupted transition, one attains the third dhyāna and twelve [attainments] of its preparatory stage.
The desire realm is as previously explained.
One [mental application] of the first dhyāna is acquired,
namely, the mental application of equanimity regarding phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*).
Some say that three are acquired: namely,
the applications of attention (*manopavicāra*) regarding visible forms, sounds, and mental phenomena.
Some say that four are acquired: namely,
the applications of mindfulness regarding equanimity toward visible forms, sounds, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
When one is free from the defilements of the second dhyāna,
during each of the first eight paths of uninterrupted transition and paths of liberation,
one respectively attains six [attainments] of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the third dhyāna.
At the time of the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one attains the third dhyāna and its six preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*);
the desire realm and the first dhyāna are as previously explained.
In the second dhyāna, there is one:
namely, the mental application of equanimity regarding phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*). Some say:
One attains three:
namely, the applications of equanimity toward visible forms, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
One is free from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
During the eight preceding paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
one respectively attains the six [attainments] of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the fourth dhyāna.
During the ninth path of uninterrupted transition, one attains the fourth dhyāna itself and its six preparatory stages.
The first two dhyānas of the desire realm are as previously explained;
one obtains the third dhyāna.
Some say: [as follows].
Three are attained,
as explained in the case of the second dhyāna.
One becomes detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna.

At each moment of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one respectively attains four [factors] of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*);
some say one is attained.
From the time one becomes detached from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Space up to detachment from the defilements of the Sphere of Nothingness,
during all moments of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one attains only one [fruit] at a time.
At the time of realizing the fruit of arhatship, one acquires twelve [types of knowledge] each for the desire realm and the first two dhyānas;
six each for the third and fourth dhyānas;
and four for the sphere of infinite space.
Some say there is one [attainment].
Each of the three higher formless realms has one.
This concludes the explanation of attainment through the separation from defilement (*vairāgya-lābha*).
Regarding those obtained through rebirth:
this refers to when one dies from a higher plane and is born into a lower plane,
thereby obtaining all [dharmas] belonging to that own plane.
Furthermore, regarding the lower stages, the acquisition and relinquishment should be understood as previously explained according to what is appropriate;
the abandonment should also be explained in detail based on the preceding account.
These are the eighteen mental applications (*manopavicāra*).
Due to the distinction between reliance on worldly attachment (*gardha*) and reliance on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*),
the Blessed One has taught thirty-six "foundations of the Teacher" (*śāstṛpada*).
Among these, feelings that accord with defilement are termed "reliance on attachment."
Those that are concordant with the wholesome and associated with feeling are called the bases of renunciation (*naiṣkramyāśrita*).
Question: Why are the unobscured-neutral states not mentioned?
Answer: Because they are also included within these two categories.
That is to say, among the unobscured-neutral [states],
there are those that accord with the category of defilement and those that accord with the category of the wholesome.
Those that accord with the defiled category are subsumed under the basis of attachment;
those that accord with the wholesome category are subsumed under the basis of renunciation.
Question: Why are these called the "Teacher's Words"?
Answer: These distinctive phrases can represent the Great Teacher;
because they are the teacher's insignia, they are called "teacher-phrases.
By means of these phrases—
Only the Great Teacher, the Buddha, is able to know and speak without obstruction;
as it is said in a sutra:
"If at any time the assembly does not respectfully accept the Tathāgata with faith, [the Buddha] feels no joy."
If one does not respectfully accept [the teachings], yet remains free from anxiety,
dwelling in pure equanimity with right mindfulness and clear comprehension—
so it is said by some.
These are the words of non-Buddhist teachers;
for they harbor deluded attachments regarding this matter.
Some say:
This should be called the "trace of the Teacher," for it is the path traversed by all those who were false teachers. Some say:
This should be called the "path of the enemy.
Craving is the enemy;
it proceeds by depending upon this.
Alternatively, all afflictions are termed "enemies.
Because they arise based upon these [bases], they are called "paths of enmity.
Some say that these should be called "paths of swords."
Those who wander through this [world] are subject to injury and harm.
As it is said regarding the third "sword of the mind" of a brahmin:
when it is brandished, it gives rise to evil and invites suffering.
Question: Of these thirty-six [factors], how many exist in which realms and stages?
Answer: In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all are present.
Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are twenty each in the first and second dhyānas.
The third and fourth dhyānas each have ten [factors].
In the formless realm, the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space has five,
provided that one allows for the existence of distinct objects of focus.
If one says that they only take the aggregate as their object, then there would be only two;
however, according to this explanation, there should be five.
The four fundamental formless absorptions (*ārūpya-maula*) and the three higher access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) each possess only two [objects].
Question: Regarding these thirty-six [mental states], how many in which realms and stages take which realms and stages as their objects?
Answer: Among the thirty-six [factors] of the desire realm, twelve take only those bound to the desire realm as their object;
eighteen take as their objects both those bound to the desire realm and those bound to the form realm.
The six supernormal knowledges take as their objects those things bound to the three realms as well as those that are unbound.
Within each of the first two dhyānas, there are twenty [mental states];
four of these take only those things bound to the desire realm as their objects.
Six [factors] take only those bound to the form realm as their object;
six take as their objects both those bound to the desire realm and those bound to the form realm;
two take as their objects both those bound to the form and formless realms and those that are unbound.
Two [of these] take as their objects both that which is bound to the three realms and that which is unbound.
Among the ten [objects] of each of the third and fourth dhyānas,
two take only that which is bound to the desire realm as their object.
Three [factors] take only those bound to the form realm as their object;
three take those bound to both the desire and form realms as their objects;
one takes those bound to both the form and formless realms as its object.
And as for the unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*):
one type of [concentration] takes as its object both that which is conditioned by the three realms and that which is unconditioned;
this refers to the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
If one says there are five,
three take only that which is bound to the form realm as their object,
while one universally takes both that which is bound to the formless realm and that which is unbound as its object.
One [type of object] takes as its object that which is bound to the form and formless realms as well as that which is unbound.
If one speaks of two [types],
one takes as its object that which is bound to the formless realm as well as that which is unbound.
One [type of consciousness] takes as its object that which is bound to the form and formless realms as well as that which is unbound;
four [types] take as their objects the fundamental stages of the formless realm and the three higher access concentrations.
Each of these two pairs both takes as its object that which is bound to the formless realm and that which is unbound.
Question: Among these thirty-six [factors], who accomplishes how many?
Answer: One born in the desire realm who has severed the roots of goodness accomplishes eighteen [mental factors] of the desire realm and eight each of the first and second dhyānas.
The latter two dhyānas each have four [types],
and the four formless attainments each have one,
provided that the roots of goodness have not been severed.
One who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm possesses thirty-six [factors] of the desire realm;
those of the higher stages are as previously explained.
If one has attained the wholesome mind of the first dhyāna but has not yet become free from the defilements of the desire realm,
that person possesses thirty-six [factors] of the desire realm.
There are fourteen [mental applications] in the first dhyāna;
those of the higher stages are as previously described.
This applies if one has already become free from the defilements of the desire realm.
If one has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the second dhyāna,
that person possesses twelve [minds] of the desire realm and twenty [minds] of the first dhyāna.
The higher stages are as previously explained.
If one attains the wholesome mind of the second dhyāna but has not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
He accomplishes twelve [factors] of the desire realm,
twenty of the first dhyāna,
and fourteen of the second dhyāna.
The higher stages are as previously explained.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna but has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the third dhyāna.
He accomplishes twelve [factors] each for the first dhyāna of the desire realm and twenty for the second dhyāna;
for the higher stages, it is as previously explained.
If one has attained a wholesome mind of the third dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna,
that person possesses twelve factors each from the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
The second dhyāna has twenty;
the third dhyāna has ten;
the higher stages are as previously explained.
If one has already become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna but has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the fourth dhyāna,
they possess twelve [mental factors] each for the desire realm and the first two dhyānas.
The third dhyāna has ten [factors].
The higher stages are as previously explained.
If one attains the wholesome mind of the fourth dhyāna...
One who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna accomplishes twelve factors each for the desire realm and the first two dhyānas,
and fourteen factors each for the latter two dhyānas.
There is one for each of the formless [attainments].
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna but has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the sphere of infinite space.
He accomplishes twelve [factors] each in the first and second dhyānas of the desire realm;
six in the third dhyāna;
and fourteen in the fourth dhyāna.
There is one for each of the formless realms.
If one has attained the wholesome mind of the Sphere of Infinite Space but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the fourth dhyāna:
He accomplishes five [attainments] of the sphere of infinite space;
some say two;
and one each for the three higher formless spheres.
The lower stages are as previously explained.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna but has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
He accomplishes six [factors] in the fourth dhyāna;
five in the sphere of infinite space;
some say two.
Each of the three higher formless realms has one;
the lower stages are as previously explained.
If one attains the wholesome mind of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), [the following occurs].
Not yet free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space,
one accomplishes two [attainments] of the sphere of infinite consciousness and one each of the two higher formless spheres.
The lower stages are as previously explained.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Space but has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the Sphere of Nothingness.
He accomplishes four [attainments] of the sphere of infinite space;
some say one.
He accomplishes two of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The two higher formless realms each have one;
the lower stages are as previously explained.
If one attains the wholesome mind of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), [the following occurs].
One who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness accomplishes two [attainments] of the Sphere of Nothingness and one of the Peak of Existence.
The lower stages are as previously explained.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness but has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
He accomplishes the sphere of infinite consciousness as one,
the sphere of nothingness as two,
and the peak of existence as one.
The lower stages are as previously explained.
If one attains a wholesome mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), [the following applies].
He accomplishes two [attainments] of the Peak of Existence;
those of the lower stages are as previously explained.
This applies if he has already become detached from the defilements of the Sphere of Nothingness.
One who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) possesses one [attainment] of the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) and two of the Peak of Existence.
The lower stages are as previously explained.
If one has already become detached from the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
they possess one [defilement] of the Peak of Existence.
The lower stages are as previously explained.
One is born into the first dhyāna;
if one has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the second dhyāna.
He accomplishes twenty factors of the first dhyāna,
eight of the second dhyāna,
and four for each of the latter two dhyānas.
There is one for each of the four formless [attainments].
One is accomplished in the desire realm;
that is, the factor of renunciation based on equanimity.
Some say that three are accomplished:
namely, those based on form, sound, and phenomena, as well as renunciation and equanimity.
Others say that six are accomplished.
This refers to the six types of renunciation based on equanimity:
if one has attained the wholesome mind of the second dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna.
He accomplishes fourteen factors of the second dhyāna;
the rest is as previously explained.
This applies if he has already become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
If one has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the third dhyāna,
they possess twelve factors of the first dhyāna and twenty factors of the second dhyāna.
The rest is as previously explained.
Thus, it continues up to the abandonment of the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
as detailed extensively before.
Just as it is for being born in the first dhyāna, so it is for being born in the second dhyāna and so forth;
these should be understood in detail according to the preceding explanation. The three—attainment, relinquishment, and abandonment—should also be understood according to what was previously stated.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Because the six renunciations rely upon joy as their support, their basis, and their foundation."
Regarding the six types of attachment based on delight,
one is able to abandon them, relinquish them, and vomit them out;
in this way, they are severed.
By means of the six bases of renunciation,
which serve as a support, a reliance, and a foundation for sorrow,
one is able to abandon, relinquish, and vomit out the sorrow based on the six bases of attachment.
In this way, they are severed,
because the six modes of renunciation serve as their support, reliance, and foundation.
Regarding the six bases of attachment,
one is able to abandon, relinquish, and vomit them out;
in this way, they are severed.
It should be understood that this teaching refers to temporary abandonment as "abandonment.
Furthermore, it states that one relies upon the six bases of renunciation,
taking them as a support, a reliance, and a foundation.
Regarding the six kinds of renunciation from sorrow,
one is able to discard them, abandon them, and vomit them out;
in this way, they are severed.
It should be understood that this explains the departure from the defilements of the desire realm.
Furthermore, it states that one relies upon, depends upon,
and establishes oneself by means of the six bases of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).
By relying on joy toward the six forms of renunciation,
one is able to abandon, relinquish, and vomit them out;
in this way, they are severed.
It should be understood that this statement refers to the abandonment of the defilements of the second dhyāna;
furthermore, it says that one abandons them by means of a single type of basis (*gotra*),
for the sake of relying upon, depending upon, and establishing [the result].
Regarding the relinquishing of the basis for various natures,
one is able to cast off, abandon, and vomit them out;
in this way, they are severed.
It should be understood that this statement refers to being free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna;
furthermore, it says that because [the formless attainments] do not possess the nature of that [fourth dhyāna],
they serve as its support, its basis, and its foundation.
Regarding the basis of a single nature,
one is able to relinquish, abandon, and cast it out;
in this way, it is severed.
It should be understood that this teaching refers to the departure from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
it does not pertain to those of that same nature.
That is to say, the untainted path must necessarily proceed by means of this very path.
Because it is able to abandon the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
From the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda,
Volume 139 (also titled *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 100).
Compiled by four hundred and fifty great Arhats, translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Five:

The Aggregate of the Great Elements; Sub-section Four: The Chapter on Appropriation, Part Four. Realizing the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) by means of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
When cultivating that path, how many of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are cultivated in the present,
and how many are cultivated in the future?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To refute the doctrines of other schools and to clarify one's own position.
That is to say, some may claim that there is no cultivation of the future,
lest there be the attainment of what has not yet been performed.
To refute that attachment, it is shown that there is cultivation of the future;
for although [the specific instance] has not yet arisen, its type has already arisen.
Alternatively, some say that two minds proceed together.
Because seeing, hearing, and so forth occur simultaneously,
this [passage] refutes that attachment by demonstrating that two minds do not coexist; rather,
they arise in rapid succession within a single moment such that, though not simultaneous, they appear to be so.
Alternatively, some may say that the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) and so forth do not function simultaneously because their causes differ;
to refute that attachment, it is shown that these four types can exist simultaneously as a single entity without distinction.
Alternatively, some say that faith and the other [faculties] are exclusively untainted (anāsrava),
because the Sūtra states that ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) lack the faculties such as faith.
To refute their attachment that the faculty of faith and the others are common to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
the sūtra speaks only of the uncontaminated faculties.
Alternatively, there are those who say:
The faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) differ in substance because they are distinguished by their respective states of superiority and inferiority.
To refute that attachment, it is shown that although their states differ, the faculties and powers function as a single essence.
Alternatively, some say that the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) include those with outflows (sāsrava),
because it is taught that one cultivates the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (smṛti-bodhyaṅga) in conjunction with the meditation on impurity (aśubhā).
To refute that attachment and to demonstrate that the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*),
the Sūtra states that they exist together and simultaneously.
Alternatively, there is another explanation:
The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) possess joy (*prīti*).
Since the Sūtra states that one relies on joy to abandon and emerge from sorrow,
[the author] clarifies that the preparatory stages lack joy in order to refute that [erroneous] attachment.
Because the Sūtra states that what has already been abandoned and what is to be abandoned are both termed "abandoned.
Alternatively, some say that right speech,
right action, and right livelihood do not exist simultaneously.
Because within a single moment there are no two [distinct] bodies or speeches,
this is stated to refute that attachment and to demonstrate that the three types of restraint arise together from the three faculties.
Because they can be attained at one time.
Alternatively, some say that stream-enterers and once-returners also attain dhyāna.
This is to refute that attachment by showing that neither [the faculty of patience nor the faculty of knowledge] is attained as long as one has not yet abandoned desire.
Alternatively, some say that patience (*kṣānti*) is itself wisdom (*jñāna*).
To refute that position, it is shown that acceptance (*kṣānti*) is not wisdom (*jñāna*),
because it has not yet reached a definitive resolution regarding the objects of the truths (*satya*).
Alternatively, there are those who say:
Because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have not yet seen the truths, they do not abandon the afflictions;
this is stated in order to refute their attachment [to the view that they do], clarifying that ordinary beings also abandon the afflictions by seeing the coarse and so forth.
Alternatively, there are those who say:
Noble ones do not abandon afflictions by means of the mundane path;
this is to refute that misconception and to demonstrate that noble ones exercise mastery, employing whichever path they so choose.
Alternatively, some may claim that the higher stages also possess the factor of right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
To refute that attachment, it is shown that the higher stages lack this factor because they are devoid of applied thought (*vitarka*).
Alternatively, there may be those who hold the view that the formless realm also possesses the untainted (anāsrava) factors of morality;
in order to refute that position:
This reveals that they lack ethical discipline because they lack form.
Alternatively, some say that the three samādhis differ in meaning but are identical in essence.
To refute that attachment,
it is shown that the essence is also distinct because its aspects are different;
this is done to cease these various divergent tenets and to reveal what is correctly elucidated.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
When one realizes the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) by means of the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga),
and while cultivating that path, how many of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are cultivated in the present?
How many are cultivated in the future?
The four right efforts and the four bases of power.
The five faculties,
the five powers,
and the seven factors of enlightenment.
The eight factors of the path,
the four meditative absorptions,
and the four immeasurables.
The four formless attainments,
the eight liberations,
and the eight bases of mastery.
Regarding the ten bases of totality,
the eight knowledges, and the three types of meditative concentration:
how many are cultivated in the present?
How many are cultivated in the future?
Answer: One is cultivated in the present;
four are cultivated in the future.
The right abandonments and the bases of psychic power have four [factors] each in the present and future;
the faculties and powers have five each in the present and future;
and the factors of enlightenment have six each in the present and future.
Regarding the factors of the path, there are eight in both the present and the future.
There are no dhyānas and no immeasurables.
There are no formless realms,
no liberations,
and no bases of mastery.
There are no universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana).
There is no concentration of knowledge (jñānasamādhi).
In the present and future, there is one.
Regarding the statement that "one [foundation of mindfulness] is present and four are future," this excludes the simultaneous operation of two minds.
Furthermore, there would be no grasping at future cultivation.
If two minds were to function simultaneously,
then one would be cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness in the present.
However, the four foundations of mindfulness do not necessarily function simultaneously,
because there cannot be four types of wisdom associated with a single moment of mind.
Furthermore, these four cannot be established as a single entity, because their aspects (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) differ.
It is not the case that multiple minds arise simultaneously within a single continuum,
lest many sentient beings be established by virtue of them. Furthermore,
if there were no sense of cultivation regarding the future life, [the path would be fruitless].
In that case, the wholesome qualities one cultivates would have no sense of increase or expansion;
the exertion of great effort would be in vain,
because even with much application, the gain would be meager.
Furthermore, at the time of first attaining Buddhahood, one would not yet be fully endowed with all merits;
for fear of such faults as these,
there is cultivation in the future.
Because the future world is vast, one cultivates all four [foundations of mindfulness];
for the power of present cultivation can induce the corresponding dharmas of the future,
causing them to manifest before one.
The first "present" refers to the application of mindfulness to phenomena with mixed objects,
because it perceives the Truth of the Path.
Regarding the statement that "the right abandonments (samyak-prahāṇa) and the bases of psychic power (ṛddhi-pāda) exist in both the present and the future, yet there are four":
this is intended to preclude the claim that the right abandonments and the bases of psychic power do not exist simultaneously;
rather, the essence of right effort (samyak-vyāyāma) consists of four types.
Its function is like that of a lamp;
at one time, it performs four functions,
because samādhi arises from four causes.
The four designations are established based on their respective causes;
as for those cultivated in the future,
they are also one in essence but distinct in meaning.
Regarding the statement that one cultivates the four faculties and powers in both the present and the future:
the phrase "the five in the present and the future" serves to preclude the notion that the entities of the faculties and powers are distinct.
Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the five types of sequential arising of grasping:
although the stages of the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) differ, their essential nature (*svabhāva*) is not distinct.

Thus, the single entity of faith and the others arises, and there is no mutual contradiction between designating them as "faculties" when they overcome [defilements] and as "powers" when they establish [virtuous qualities].
Because they arise in mutual dependence,
these five do not arise sequentially.
Regarding the statement that "the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) exist in six ways in both the present and the future":
This, then, precludes the claim that there is joy (*prīti*) in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*);
for in these stages, one has not yet attained the fundamental levels (*maulabhūmi*) and has not yet abandoned fear of the lower realms.
Because joy has not yet arisen.
When the Sūtra states that one relies on joy to abandon and emerge from sorrow,
this refers to the stage of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
Because it is not the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), there is no contradiction.
This is based on the fact that the "unconcentrated" (*anāgamya*) stage lacks joy (*prīti*); thus, there are six [factors].
As for the statement that eight factors of the path are present and future: [this refers to the case when one is in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)].
This refers to the intention that speech, action, and livelihood are not simultaneous;
for the non-informative [matter] (avijñapti) produced by non-greed, non-hatred,
and non-delusion each arises simultaneously in seven types.
Regarding those "without dhyāna," this refers to the intention that stream-enterers and once-returners may also attain dhyāna;
for they have not yet abandoned desire when entering the path of seeing.
Because one who has already abandoned desire does not belong to either of the two paths;
as for "there is no immeasurable," this negation of the immeasurable also applies to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, within the path of seeing (darśanamārga), one cultivates immeasurability (apramāṇa) because it takes sentient beings as its object;
however, the untainted (anāsrava) path of seeing is rapid.
Furthermore, because it is newly attained, one cannot yet practice it concurrently;
moreover, because the fundamental stage (maulabhūmi) has not yet been attained,
one does not cultivate the immeasurables (apramāṇa).
"Those without the formless realm":
this negates the attachment that the path of seeing exists within the formless realm;
because there is no wisdom therein that takes [all objects] as its universal object, the path of seeing necessarily does not exist in the formless realm.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that because one has not yet attained the formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti),
there are no liberations (vimokṣa), spheres of mastery (abhibhv-āyatana), or spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana):
this excludes the three aforementioned liberations and so forth.
It is also held that this applies to the untainted (anāsrava).
However, because it is not subsumed under the sixteen aspects (ākāra), it is not called untainted;
furthermore, at that time, one has not yet attained the fundamental stage (maulabhūmi).
Those who do not cultivate that [patience] are "those lacking wisdom.
This serves to preclude the claim that patience is itself wisdom;
for since patience has not yet reached a definitive and realistic discernment regarding the objects of the truths, it is not designated as wisdom.
Furthermore, because one cultivates only those factors belonging to one's own stage at this point,
one does not cultivate the various knowledges of the future; therefore,
it is said that there is no meditative concentration (samādhi).
Regarding the first point concerning the present and future:
this refutes the claim that the three samādhis differ in meaning while being identical in substance,
because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the three types of concentration (*samādhi*) are distinct.
The essence also has distinctions.
The first occurs at the time of the patience associated with the path of the category of "wishless" meditative concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).
Because one cultivates only this,
although all eight patiences (*kṣānti*) are paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
it is the patience of the path of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-anvaya-kṣānti*) that is designated as such when based on the stage of realizing the fruit, and not the others.
One realizes the fruit of once-returner by means of the path of uninterrupted transition.
When cultivating that path, there are the four foundations of mindfulness,
up to and including the three types of meditative concentration.
How many are cultivated in the present?
How many are cultivated in the future?
Answer: If one has already doubly detached from the defilements of desire.
When entering the state of rightness and separation from birth and cultivating that path,
one mindfulness establishment is present and four are future.
The right abandonments and the bases of psychic power are fourfold in both the present and the future.
The faculties and the powers are fivefold in both the present and the future.
The factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are six in the present and future;
the factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are eight in the present and future.
There are no dhyānas.
There are no immeasurables.
There are no formless attainments.
There are no liberations.
There are no spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana),
no spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana),
and no meditative concentrations of knowledge (jñānasamādhi).
Regarding the one [category] of the present and future:
if one who has doubly abandoned the defilements of desire enters into rightness-in-detachment (samyaktva-niyāma),
this precludes the statement that an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) does not abandon the afflictions.

However, ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) can abandon the defilements of the desire realm up to those of the sphere of nothingness by means of six types of mental aspects, such as the coarse and so forth;
this applies even if they have already abandoned six categories of desire-realm defilements.
This is called "further free from desire," because it is further [removed] than the latter three.
All remaining phrases and sentences are explained as before.
If one realizes the fruit of once-returner from the fruit of stream-enterer by means of the mundane path,
when cultivating that path,
one mindfulness establishment is present.
The four [foundations of mindfulness] are present and future; the right exertions and the bases of psychic power are present and future as four;
the faculties and powers are present and future as five.
The factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are absent in the present;
six are in the future.
The factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are absent in the present.
In the future, there are eight;
there are no dhyānas and no immeasurables.
There are no formless attainments, no liberations,
and no bases of mastery.
Regarding the knowledge of the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana):
there is one in the present and seven in the future.
In the present, there is none;
in the future, there are three,
by means of the worldly path (*laukika-mārga*).
Regarding those who realize the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*):
this precludes the claim that noble ones (*ārya*) abandon afflictions by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
For noble ones, there are two paths.
Because both are fully accomplished,
they manifest according to one's wish;
thus, by means of that, [the afflictions] are severed.
The foundations of mindfulness are present.
The first is the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas with mixed objects.

Regarding "the two [types of] knowledge being present": [The answer is: It is the knowledge of the mind of another (*paracitta-jñāna*) and the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*). Why? Because the knowledge of the mind of another has the mental states of others as its object, while the knowledge of destruction has the cessation of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) as its object. Since these two knowledges do not have the same object, it is impossible for them to arise simultaneously. Therefore, when one knows the minds of others, one does not simultaneously know that their outflows are exhausted; thus, at that time, only the knowledge of the mind of another is present. When one knows that outflows are exhausted, one does not simultaneously know the minds of others; thus, at that time, only the knowledge of destruction is present. Consequently, there is no instance where both are present simultaneously. Furthermore, the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and so forth do not take the minds of others as their object, nor do they take the cessation of outflows as their object; therefore, they are not included here. As for the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), since they are not included among the six knowledges, they are also not mentioned here.
