Question: Just as there are no untainted great elements (*anāsrava-mahābhūta*), yet there is untainted discipline (*anāsrava-śīla*).
Thus, although the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of that stage do not exist,
there still exists the morality (*śīla*) of that stage;
what fault is there in this?
Answer: Untainted (anāsrava) precepts do not fall within the realms or stages;
they are derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the body upon which they rely.
For this reason, although untainted primary elements do not exist, [the precepts are nonetheless established].
As for the unconditioned (anāsrava) precepts that are produced,
they do not fall within the realms or stages;
they are produced solely by the primary elements (mahābhūta) of their own stage.
Because those [beings] lack the great elements (*mahābhūta*), their morality (*śīla*) also does not exist.

Question: If untainted morality (*anāsrava-śīla*) is produced by the great elements that serve as its basis, then when one born in the desire realm or the form realm enters the untainted formless absorption (*ārūpya-samādhi*), there should arise the untainted morality concomitant with that absorption, because there exists the great elements of the body that serves as its basis.

Answer: Although untainted (anāsrava) discipline is produced from the primary elements (mahābhūta) that serve as its basis, it must nonetheless be produced by the primary elements belonging to a specific level;
only then does tainted (sāsrava) discipline arise in accordance with that same category.
Because there are no great elements (*mahābhūta*) that produce [matter] within the formless realm (*ārūpya*),
and because the untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) are distinct from the tainted precepts (*sāsrava-śīla*),
the untainted precepts do not exist there either; for they are produced based on whatever exists therein.
Question: For what reason is the essence of the precepts (śīla-svabhāva) exclusively form (rūpa)?
Answer: Because it arises as the prevention of unwholesome forms;
furthermore, because its nature is that of bodily and vocal karma (kāya-vāk-karman).
Since the two types of action—bodily and vocal—are material in nature, a question is asked:
For what reason is mental action not considered ethical discipline (*śīla*)?
The answer is: Because it cannot directly obstruct unwholesome conduct.
Question: Why is it that immoral conduct (*duḥśīla*) is not mental action (*manaskarma*)?
Answer: Because those who have not yet abandoned desire all accomplish unwholesome mental action.
Could they all be called those who have violated the precepts or those who possess non-restraint?
Therefore, bad conduct is not mental karma.
Furthermore, if good mental karma were identical to virtuous restraint, [it would follow that one could never lose it].
Then it would follow that all those who have not severed their wholesome roots are called "abiding in restraint," because they all possess wholesome mental karma. If this were accepted,
[it would lead to further consequences].
If a single sentient being were both called one who abides in restraint and one who abides in non-restraint,
then there would be no distinction between the three types [of persons].
If this were so, it would contradict the sacred teachings,
for both virtuous and non-virtuous ethical discipline (*śīla*) are not mental actions (*manas-karman*).
Furthermore, it is universally acknowledged in the world that what prevents and restrains body and speech is designated as "ethical discipline."
Mental action is not itself morality;
one should know that mental action is the cause for the arising of morality.
That which is the cause of morality cannot be designated as morality itself.
One must not allow for the error of confusing cause and effect;
therefore, there are only four factors of the path in the formless realm,
because one universally cultivates the untainted [factors] of lower stages in the future.
There are eight formless liberations;
that which is present is one,
namely any one of the three stages previously mentioned as its basis.
The remainder is as explained previously.

Among the faculties, it is the faculty of wisdom;
among the powers, it is the power of wisdom;

Within the factors of the path,

Alternatively, they are divided into three, namely:
inferior, middling, and superior;

That is to say, those bound to the three realms and those unbound;
or alternatively, they are divided into five:
those bound to the three realms, and those who are in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Even if one were to differentiate them by their continuous succession and momentary distinctions, they would be immeasurable.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One, regarding this matter, open up the few and consolidate the many, teaching only these four types?
Answer: The Buddha established four types based on the differences in coarseness and subtlety regarding the aspects and objects of correct wisdom (*samyag-prajñā*).
Question: If that is so, why does the Sūtra speak of twelve distinct varieties by observing the internal, external, and both together?
Answer: Because they do not exceed four, only four types are mentioned.
Just as with the seven-leaf tree and the seven-times-born stream-enterer, it is the same in this case.
Question: Since this essence is wisdom (*prajñā*), for what reason did the Blessed One call it the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)?
Answer: Wisdom is called the foundations of mindfulness because it abides upon its object through the power of mindfulness;
or alternatively, it is called the foundations of mindfulness because the power of this wisdom causes mindfulness to abide upon its object.
Because these two mutually support one another regarding their objects more effectively than other dharmas, they are called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
A detailed exposition of the foundations of mindfulness is as explained elsewhere.

Question: The *Dharmaskandha-śāstra* and other treatises state that the abandonment of arisen evil and unwholesome dharmas consists of four types.
This refers to one who, for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen,
generates desire, exerts effort, and maintains the mind;
such a person abandons those evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen.
It can also cause those evil and unwholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen not to arise;
furthermore, it causes wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen to arise, and those already arisen to abide, and so forth.
Even when it is said that the cultivation of wholesome dharmas that have already arisen causes them to remain stable and so on, these likewise possess four aspects.
This refers to the state in which one who has generated desire, exerted effort, and applied mental focus in order to stabilize, prevent the forgetting of, repeatedly cultivate,
and further expand those wholesome dharmas already arisen,
practices those already arisen wholesome dharmas.
It can also cause those evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen to be abandoned,
and prevent those not yet arisen from arising;
furthermore, it causes wholesome states that have not yet arisen to arise.
In this way, there are thus sixteen right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Why, then, are only four mentioned here?
Answer: Because they are based on the differences in the aspirational intentions (*āśaya*) of the practitioners.
This statement is made with reference to the stage of application (*prayoga*).
That is to say, although he previously gave rise to a single intention (*āśaya*),

Thus, this statement is made because one reaches the stage of application (prayoga) by relying on those four types of intention;
however, at the time of application, there are only these four.
However, because there are no more than four, only four types are taught.
Just as they are taught by way of intention (*āśaya*) and application (*prayoga*),
so too are they taught by way of entry (*avatāra*) and application (*prayoga*).
This is spoken of by way of the basis and the application;

What of the latter two?
Answer: There is no fault, as they are designated by the first term.
Alternatively, all four of these possess the meaning of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
This means that the former two abandon the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
while the latter two abandon the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
because one abandons ignorance when cultivating wholesome dharmas.
Because both temporary abandonment and permanent abandonment are termed "abandonment," some sources refer to this as "right effort" (*samyakpradhāna*),
since it correctly exerts itself to accomplish superior tasks.
Question: What is the difference between "evil" (pāpa) and "unwholesome" (akuśala)?
Answer: "Evil" refers to the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta);
"unwholesome" refers to all that is unwholesome.
Some say that "evil" refers to the defiled dharmas of the form and formless realms,
as well as a portion of the desire realm.
The unwholesome refers to the majority of defiled phenomena within the desire realm.
Some say that "evil" refers to the categories of the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes within the desire realm.
The unwholesome refers to the remaining afflictions and so forth of the desire realm.
Question: For what reason is it said that unwholesome and unvirtuous dharmas that have already arisen should be abandoned, while those not yet arisen should be prevented from arising?
The answer is: that which has already arisen is said to be "cut off" because it has already performed its function within its own continuum;
that which has not yet arisen [is so called] with respect to its own continuum.
Because it has no activity, it is said to cause [the dharma] not to arise.
Some say that for that which has already arisen, [it acts] within its own continuum.
Because they have already obstructed the Noble Path, it is said that they must be abandoned;
because those not yet arisen do not obstruct the Noble Path within one's own continuum, it is said that they must not arise.
Some say that regarding those [defilements] already arisen within one's own continuum,
because they have already taken up their fruit and are currently giving forth their fruit, they are said to be "caused to be severed."
Regarding those [dharmas] that have not yet arisen within one's own continuum,
it is said that they are "prevented from arising" because they have neither yet taken nor produced their fruit. Some say:
Those that have already arisen are said to be "cut off" because they have already produced their own continuums' outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) and ripening fruits (*vipāka-phala*).
Those that have not yet arisen [are cut off] within their own continuums.
Because the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) have not yet been taken up, it is said that they are made not to arise. Some say:
"That which has already arisen [is made not to arise] within one's own continuum."
Because the homogeneous and pervasive causes have already been repaid, it is said that [the defilements] are to be abandoned;
because the [defilements] yet to arise have not yet repaid the homogeneous and pervasive causes within their own continuum, it is said that they are to be prevented from arising.
Some say that because that which has already arisen within one's own continuum has already been scorched and afflicted, it is said to be "caused to be severed."
Because that which has not yet arisen has not been burned or afflicted within one's own continuum, it is said that [the path] causes it not to arise.
Some say that [it applies] to that which has already arisen within one's own continuum.
They have already been subjected to reproach;
they have already been defiled;
they have already been mired in the mud.
Because they have already fallen into malicious intent, it is taught that they should be severed;
as for those who have not yet arisen, one does not yet reproach them within one's own continuum.
Because they have not yet produced defilement,
have not yet created a sticky mire,
and have not fallen into evil intentions, it is said that [the Buddha] causes them not to arise.
Question: Since all cultivated wholesome dharmas perish as soon as they arise,
and there is no possibility that once arisen they remain for even a single moment beyond that,
how can it be said that one should cause already arisen wholesome dharmas to abide, not be forgotten, and be further cultivated and expanded?
It should be understood that two categories of wholesome dharmas are taught herein:
namely, those conducive to maintenance (*sthity-anukūla*) and those conducive to progress (*viśeṣa-anukūla*).
That which causes one to abide securely without forgetting is called the factor conducive to stability (*sthity-anulomika-bhāgīya*).
That which causes one to cultivate further and expand is called the factor conducive to excellence (*viśeṣa-anulomika-bhāgīya*).
Both depend upon the mental continuum for its successive advancement.
Because it speaks of "abiding" and so forth,
there is no fault. Some say:
In this context, three grades of wholesome dharmas are taught—
namely, inferior, middling, and superior— which cause one to abide securely and not forget them;
it is said that by relying on inferior roots of goodness, one advances to the middling grade.
Regarding "causing them to cultivate and expand twofold":
this refers to the transition from medium-grade roots of goodness to superior grade;
although they arise for a single moment and then immediately perish.
However, this statement is made based on the continuity [of the series].
Here, there are four right abandonments for the desire realm;
it is the same for the form and formless realms.
Question: In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are unwholesome and non-virtuous states that can be said to be fourfold.
Why, then, are they also said to be fourfold in the higher realms?
Answer: Although those [higher realms] do not possess the full extent of such afflictions (*ādīnava*).
Yet it possesses those very qualities.
Some say that although it lacks an object to be remedied, it nonetheless possesses the capacity to remedy.
Question: While this may be the case for the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-bhūmi*), how is it for the higher stages?
Answer: There are many kinds of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), namely, the antidote of relinquishment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*).
The antidote of abandonment,
the antidote of maintenance,
and the antidote of distancing.
Regarding the antidote of repudiation (*vidūṣaṇapratipakṣa*):
although higher stages lack the antidotes of equanimity (*upekṣā*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*),
they do possess other antidotes.
Question: While it may be so for the dhyānas, how is it for the formless attainments (ārūpya)?
Answer: Although the formless attainments lack the antidote of destruction, they possess the antidotes of maintenance and remote separation.
These right abandonments each possess four types in both the stage of training (śaikṣa) and the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Question: It may be so for the stage of training, as there exist evil and unwholesome dharmas;
but how is it for the stage beyond training?
The answer is: although it lacks faults, it possesses merits.
Some say that although it lacks that which is to be remedied, it possesses the capacity for remedy.
This refers to the various types of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*) as previously explained.

Although they lack both abandonment (*prahāṇa*) and relinquishment (*tyāga*), there remains the question: to which right abandonment (*samyakprahāṇa*) does diligence directed toward the object-condition of nirvāṇa belong?
Some say that the first right abandonment (samyak-prahāṇa) subsumes [the others], because abandonment itself is nirvāṇa.
Others say:
The second right abandonment subsumes it because nirvāṇa is non-arising.
Some say it is subsumed by the third right abandonment.
Because wholesome dharmas arise at the time of attaining nirvāṇa,
some say it is subsumed under the fourth right abandonment (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Because wholesome dharmas increase at the time of attaining nirvāṇa,
those who speak thus maintain that [these qualities] are subsumed within the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa).
Because when taking nirvāṇa as an object, four things are accomplished.
That is to say, when taking the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of all phenomena as an object,
it causes all evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen to be abandoned.
The four bases of supernatural power (*ṛddhipāda*) are that which prevents what has not yet arisen from arising,
causes all mundane and supramundane virtues that have not yet arisen to arise, and causes those already arisen to increase and expand.
1. The basis for spiritual power consisting of concentration of desire and the accomplishment of the formative forces of abandonment;
2. The basis for spiritual power consisting of concentration of effort and the accomplishment of the formative forces of abandonment;
3. The basis for spiritual power consisting of concentration of mind and the accomplishment of the formative forces of abandonment.
The basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through the cultivation of the formations of abandonment accompanied by the four applications of mindfulness.
Question: What is called "psychic power" (*ṛddhi*) and what is called "basis" (*pāda*)?
Regarding this, some say:
Samādhi is called the "divine being" (deva),
while desire and the other three are the "feet.
This is because samādhi proceeds when it is sustained by these four factors.
Question: Since there are many factors associated with and co-existent with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), why are only these four specifically called "bases of spiritual power" (*ṛddhipāda*)?
Answer: Because they are preeminent in their conformity to meditative concentration.
That is to say, among the co-existent and associated dharmas,
these four are preeminent for sustaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Samādhi is both a faculty and a power;
the four beginning with desire are only faculties, not powers.
Just as the discernment of dharmas is both enlightenment and a factor of enlightenment.
The remaining six are only factors (*aṅga*) and not the awakening (*bodhi*).
Right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is both the path (*mārga*) and a factor.
The remaining seven are only factors and not the path.
Abstaining from eating at improper times is both the fast (upavāsa) and a constituent limb;
the remaining seven are only limbs and not the fast itself.
It is the same in that case as well.
Question: If samādhi is the divine power (ṛddhi) and also the basis (pāda), should one not establish only one, or should one not establish five?
Why, then, are four taught?
Answer: Only samādhi is established as the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda).
Because they arise from four causes, they are said to be four;
namely, in the stage of preparatory application (prayoga).
Alternatively, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) may be induced and brought into manifestation through the power of desire;
this is explained in detail up to its being induced and brought into manifestation through the power of insight (*vipaśyanā*).
In the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), four factors increase accordingly.
Because it causes meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to arise, one attains the state of stability.
Four types are established within this single meditative concentration.
Having already explained its essential nature (*svabhāva*), the reason for its establishment shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason are these four called "bases of spiritual power" (*ṛddhipāda*)?
Answer: Because everything that is thought of, sought after, desired, or wished for is accomplished according to one's will, they are called "spiritual" (*ṛddhi*).
Because they induce supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), they are called "bases of supernormal power" (*ṛddhipāda*).
Now, these functions of supernormal power are briefly of two kinds:
first, those esteemed by worldly people; [and second, those esteemed by the noble ones].
It is that which the two sages delight in:
dividing the one into many,
and combining the many into one.
These are called the things that worldly people delight in.
If one does not dwell on thoughts of compliance toward those things in the world that are agreeable,
nor dwell on thoughts of aversion toward those things in the world that are disagreeable.
Regarding all things that are agreeable or disagreeable,
one dwells in equanimity with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension;
these are called "that which is cherished by the noble ones."
Furthermore, there are three types of supernormal power (ṛddhi):
first, the movement of the body; second, resolution; and third, mental force.
Regarding the supernormal power of moving the body:
This refers to the entire body soaring through the air like a flying bird,
or like a celestial immortal depicted on a wall;
such is the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
This means that by perceiving what is distant as being near, through the power of this [meditative concentration],
one may either reach out with one's hand from this continent to touch the sun and moon,
or arrive at the Akaniṣṭha Heaven in the time it takes to bend or extend one’s arm.
As for the divine power of mental mastery (*ādhipateya-ṛddhi*),
it refers to the visual consciousness reaching up to the Peak of Form (*rūpāvacara-bhavana-agra*) or,
at most, to the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*akaniṣṭha*).
Or [one may] traverse boundless worlds in an instant.
Regarding these three supernormal powers, by what are they accomplished and how many does one possess? Some say:
Śrāvakas accomplish one [type of supernormal power],
namely, the transport of the body (ṛddhi-viṣaya-vaśitā).
Pratyekabuddhas accomplish two, excluding the power of the mind (manojavitva).
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is fully endowed with all three types.
Some say that other beings form a single [type].
This refers to the movement of the body (*kāya-vihāra*).
Of the two types achieved by those of the Two Vehicles, the power of mental speed (*manojavitva*) is excluded.
However, that which is manifested by the movement of the body belongs to the Śrāvakas.
The Pratyekabuddha is characterized by the manifestation of the mastery of mental resolve;
the Buddha is characterized by the manifestation of the three types of mastery of mental resolve,
or alternatively, by the five kinds of supernormal powers.
First, karma;
second, maturation;
third, manifestation.
Fourth, the possession of virtues;
fifth, the arousal of the mind.
As for the "spiritual efficacy of karma":
This refers to those such as beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Regarding the supernormal power of maturation (*vipākaja-rddhi*),
this refers to those such as birds.
The miraculous power of manifestation refers to the ability,
based on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
to divide one into many.
Combining many into one category:
that which possesses virtuous spiritual power refers to the four bases of supernormal power (ṛddhipāda).
Those who activate the mental faculty are the devas, nāgas, and so forth;
among these, "devas" refers to the devas of the desire realm.
Among the five types of divine activity that have been explained, this section describes the divine activity possessed of excellence.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Bhikṣus, you should know."
One cultivates the basis for psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) consisting in the concentration of desire and the accomplishment of the formations of abandonment;
this is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
[The same applies to] the concentration of exertion and the concentration of mind.
The explanation regarding the samādhi of contemplation is also like this.
In this context, what is meant by "separation" (viveka) and so forth?
Some say as follows:
This samādhi is what is being described.
If one cultivates the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) by taking samādhi as the object,
it is called "based on seclusion" and so forth due to two conditions.
This refers to the intention and the object of focus.
If one cultivates the bases of psychic power by taking other phenomena as objects,
they are designated as "relying on seclusion" and so forth based solely on that single condition.
This means it is by way of intention (*āśaya*),
not by way of the object (*ālambana*). Other masters say that it is the quiescent nirvāṇa.
He says that if one cultivates the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) by taking the quiescent nirvāṇa as an object,
it is called "separation" and so forth due to two conditions: namely,
the condition of intention (*āśaya*) and the condition of the object (*ālambana*).
If one cultivates the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) by taking other phenomena as objects,
they are designated as "relying on seclusion" and so forth based on a single condition;
that is, by way of intention (*āśaya*), not by way of the object (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that these are samādhi and the cessation of nirvāṇa;
they claim that if one takes these two as objects and cultivates the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) therein, [one attains them].
They are called "detached" and so forth for two reasons:
namely, by way of intention and by way of the object.
If one cultivates the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) by taking other phenomena as objects, [they are likewise so designated].
However, it is solely by virtue of a single condition that they are called "detached" and so forth;
that is, by way of intention (*āśaya*), not by way of the object (*ālambana*).
One should understand that herein, "based on detachment" refers to this.
That is, the first dhyāna;
that which relies on the undefiled is the second dhyāna.
That which relies on cessation refers to the third dhyāna.
That which is directed toward equanimity—
This refers to the fourth dhyāna.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Bhikṣus, you should know:
what is called 'life'?"
This refers to the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Question: For what reason are the bases of psychic power called "life" (*āyus*)?
Answer: Because life is not interrupted by taking these as its basis.
This means that while one is in the state of meditative equipoise, the life-force is necessarily uninterrupted.
Some say this is because,
by relying on this [state], one is free from the calamities that shorten life.
This means that while in the state of meditative equipoise, one is free from the calamities of life;
some say this is because one possesses mastery over this lifespan.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others,
who practice, cultivate, or repeatedly cultivate the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda)..."
If they should desire to abide for a kalpa or more than a kalpa,
they do so with sovereign ease according to their will;
for this reason, the supernormal power (ṛddhi) is called "life" (āyu).
As it is said in a sutra:
A certain brahmin came to where the Venerable Ānanda was staying.
Having exchanged various words of affection and inquiries after his well-being,
he withdrew to sit at one side and asked Ānanda:
"Why does he practice the holy life under the śramaṇa Gautama?"—
if one asks why the brahmin poses this question,
the answer is that he was Ānanda’s friend in a former life.
He understood thoroughly that the Venerable One was a practitioner of desire,
because he had previously and constantly been addicted to the five sensual pleasures; thus,
he came to test whether he was practicing the holy life for the sake of severing desire.
He asked this question because he wondered: "Is it for the sake of seeking superior sensual desires that you practice the holy life?
Ānanda replied, "It is for the sake of abandoning craving that I diligently practice the holy life in the presence of the Buddha."
Question: One diligently cultivates the holy life to sever the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Why, then, do you say only that "I am for the sake of severing craving" (*tṛṣṇā*)?
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
"I also know that this brahmin is one who acts out of craving and is deeply attached to various sensual desires;
it is for the purpose of drawing him in [toward the Dharma] that I have spoken thus."
The intention [of this] is as follows: "If you, being entangled by craving, desire to be free from it, you should abandon the ways of household life and come to the presence of the World-Honored One;
follow me and diligently cultivate the pure holy life."
Therefore, he answered me with a skillful means, saying, "I am one for whom craving has been severed. The brahmin asked,
"Does the śramaṇa Gautama truly possess the path and its traces that can sever craving?"
Ānanda said: "It is indeed so; do not doubt it.
If you come to practice meditative concentration, you will be able to sever craving."
The brahmin requested, saying, "I pray that you will explain this for me so that my mind may be opened; I shall certainly comply with your command.
The Venerable One replied:
"O World-Honored One,
you truly know and see, and have taught the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*);
by practicing in reliance upon them, one quickly becomes free from the entanglements of craving."
Question: If one is able to cultivate any one of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
such as the four foundations of mindfulness, one can sever craving.
Why is it said that one cultivates only the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*)?
The answer is: because these are the direct antidotes to the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*).
That is to say, those possessed by craving scatter their attention among various objects.
"Samādhi can serve as its direct antidote.
The brahmin spoke again:
"As you have said, the bases of spiritual power (ṛddhipāda) are boundless; how can one ever exhaust them through cultivation?"
Question: For what reason did the brahmin speak these words?

Answer: The brahmin’s intention was to say that the essence of these four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) is omnipresent throughout both the stages of training (śaikṣa) and the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Since that [object] is boundless, how could one ever finish cultivating it?
If one does not finish cultivating it, how could one sever craving?
Ānanda replied:
"This is not infinite.
The brahmin spoke again,
"Please explain this to me."
Ānanda said: "I now ask you; answer as you please.
What do you think?"
"Have you ever felt a desire to enter a garden for recreation?
The brahmin replied, "Yes.
He asked again, "Once you had entered the garden and finished your sightseeing, did you feel a desire to return?"
The brahmin said, "It is so.
He asked again, "Is there not a difference between the pleasure and desire arising at those two times?
The brahmin said, "It is so."
The Venerable One replied, "Just as there are two distinct moments in the arising of your desire:
first, when you wish to enter the garden; [and second, when you actually enter]."
Second, the desire to emerge again.
Likewise, the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) of those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) and those in the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are each distinct.
That which is cultivated by those in the stage of training is for the purpose of severing craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
That which is cultivated by one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is for the sake of happiness in the present life;
it varies according to what is cultivated and is not said to be infinite.
How could a brahmin claim that cultivation is inexhaustible?
Upon hearing this, he rejoiced and gave rise to a pure mind;
he took refuge in the Buddha, left the household life, and practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
As for the five faculties (*pañcendriya*):
These are the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
The five powers are likewise.
These five, according to their respective names, each have one of the mental factors as their intrinsic nature.
The intrinsic nature has already been explained; now the reason for it shall be explained.
Question: For what reason are these five called "faculties" (*indriya*) and called "powers" (*bala*)?
Answer: They are called "faculties" (*indriya*) because they are able to produce wholesome dharmas;
they are called "powers" (*bala*) because they are able to destroy unwholesome dharmas. Some say:
That which cannot be shaken is called "faculty" (*indriya*);
that which can subdue others is called "power" (*bala*). Some say:
The sense of having predominant power is "faculty" (indriya);
the sense of being invincible is "power" (bala).
If distinguished by their respective stages, those in the lower stage are called faculties.
The higher stage is called "power.
If one considers the actual meaning, each and every stage possesses both types.
These two are explained in detail elsewhere.
The seven factors of enlightenment are:
first, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness;
second, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena.
3. The awakening factor of energy;
4. The awakening factor of joy;
5. The awakening factor of tranquility.
The six factors of concentration-enlightenment;
the seventh is the factor of equanimity-enlightenment.
The investigation of dharmas is itself wisdom.
Joy (*prīti*) is the faculty of joy (*prītīndriya*).
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) refers to equanimity as a mental formation (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*).
The remaining four are, according to their names, each by nature one of the mental factors (*caitasika*) among those [already mentioned].
Having explained their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their reason for being so designated shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason are these seven called "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: "Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) refers to ultimate enlightenment (*atyanta-bodhi*).
It is the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*).
Alternatively, it is untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) through realization as it truly is.
Because the seven factors are constituent parts of that [wisdom], they are called "limbs" (*aṅga*).
The investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is both an awakening factor (*bodhyaṅga*) and a limb of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika*).
The remaining six are limbs of enlightenment but not awakening factors.
These seven are explained in detail elsewhere.
The eight factors of the path are:
right view and right intention.
Right speech,
right action,
and right livelihood.
Right effort,
right mindfulness,
and right concentration.
Right view is wisdom;
right thought is investigation;
and [right] speech, action, and livelihood [are the remaining factors].
These are the unmanifest forms of body and speech produced by the three faculties that follow the mind.
The remaining three are, as their names imply, of the nature of mental factors (*caitta*).
Having explained their intrinsic nature, their reason for being so shall now be stated.
Question: Why are these eight called "limbs of the path" (*mārgāṅga*)?
Answer: Because that which is traversed leads to thorough penetration, it is called the "path.
Since these eight are its constituent parts, they are called "limbs."
Right view is both the path and a factor of the path;
the remaining seven are factors of the path but not the path itself.
This is also as explained extensively in other passages.
The four dhyānas refer to the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna.
Some say:
The dhyānas associated with joy, bliss, and equanimity are, respectively, four in number.
These are of two kinds: first, those acquired through cultivation (bhāvanā-labdha).
The two types are those acquired by birth and those acquired through cultivation;
these refer to the one-pointedness of mind belonging to that respective stage.
If accompanied by its associates, it consists of the nature of the five aggregates.
As for that which is acquired at birth,
its nature consists of the remaining five aggregates as bound to their respective stages.
The intrinsic nature has already been explained; now its reason for being so designated shall be explained.
Question: For what reason are these four called "dhyānas" (meditative absorptions)?
Answer: "Dhyāna" means tranquility (*śamatha*).
"Dhyāna" (靜慮) refers to deliberation (*cintā*).
Because concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are in equilibrium within these four stages, they are called "dhyānas.
Any other states that lack one of these [factors] do not receive this name.
These four are analyzed in detail elsewhere.
As for the four immeasurables,
they are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) refers to that which is associated with the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of bestowing happiness;
its nature is the wholesome root of non-hatred (*avyāpāda*).
Compassion (*karuṇā*) refers to that which is associated with the mental attention of removing suffering.
Its nature is the wholesome root of non-hatred;
some say its nature is non-harming.
Joy (*prīti*) has the faculty of joy (*prītīndriya*) as its intrinsic nature, associated with the mental application of congratulation and consolation.
Some say that its intrinsic nature is *abhyutsāha* (exertion) among the wholesome mental factors (*kuśalacaitta*).
Equanimity (upekṣā) is associated with balanced attention (samatā-manasikāra) and has non-attachment (alobha) as its wholesome root (kuśala-mūla) for its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Its nature has already been explained; now its reason [for being so] shall be explained.
Question: For what reason is it called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*)?
Answer: Because by means of these four kinds of conditions, one takes immeasurable sentient beings as objects and gives rise to immeasurable wholesome dharmas.
Because they summon immeasurable superior fruits,
these four are explained in detail as in other passages.
As for the four formless [attainments]:
That is to say, the sphere of infinite space,
up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this also has two kinds.
First, that acquired through cultivation;
second, that acquired at birth.
Regarding that acquired through cultivation:
That is the one-pointedness of mind belonging to that stage;
together with its attendants, it consists of the nature of the four aggregates.
As for that which is acquired at birth:
These have as their nature the remaining four aggregates belonging to that same level.
Having explained their intrinsic nature, their reason for being so designated shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason are these four called "formless" (*ārūpya*)?
Answer: Because within these four stages one transcends all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*),
because one opposes and subverts all material phenomena,
and because material phenomena have no possibility of arising therein, they are called "formless" (*ārūpya*).
These four are also explained in detail elsewhere.
Regarding the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*):
the first is the liberation of one who possesses internal perception of forms while contemplating external forms.
2. The liberation consisting of perceiving external forms while having no internal perception of form;
3. the liberation of the pure, which one realizes bodily and dwells in its full perfection;
4. the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.
Up to the seventh liberation, which is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
and the eighth liberation, which is the cessation of sensation and perception, realized bodily and dwelt in fully.
Among these, the first three have the wholesome root of non-attachment as their intrinsic nature.
If the accompanying factors are included, their nature consists of the five aggregates.
The subsequent four [immeasurables] have as their nature the four aggregates of the preparatory wholesome states of that fundamental stage. Some say:
Furthermore, those [attainments] of the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) have the first eight paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) as their nature;
the final path of liberation has the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) as its nature.
The intrinsic nature has already been explained; now its reason shall be explained.
Question: For what reason is it called "liberation" (vimukti)?
Answer: Because it liberates one from whatever constitutes its obstacles.
The remaining meanings are explained extensively elsewhere.
Regarding the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*):
first, having the perception of internal forms, one contemplates external forms that are few.
...and so forth, up to the full exposition.
Second, having the perception of internal forms, one contemplates external forms as manifold;
and so forth, up to the full exposition.
Third, having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as limited;
this is explained at length up to...
Fourth, having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as vast.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Contemplating blue, yellow, red, and white further constitutes four types.
These eight all have non-attachment as their wholesome root for their intrinsic nature.
If taken together with their associated factors, they are of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Having already explained their essential nature (*svabhāva*), one should now explain the reason [for their name].
Question: For what reason are they called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*)?
Answer: They are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*) because they subdue their objects of focus and utterly destroy craving and attachment;
the detailed explanation of their meaning is as described in other sources.
As for the "ten bases of totality" (*kṛtsnāyatana*):
That is to say, observing blue, yellow, red, and white individually;
earth, water, fire, and wind constitute the first eight;
and the ninth is the sphere of infinite space.
The ten spheres of infinite consciousness:
among these, the first eight have non-attachment as their wholesome root for their intrinsic nature;
if including their associated factors, they have the five aggregates as their nature.

The latter two universal bases have as their intrinsic nature the four aggregates associated with the category of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), which are the contaminated preparatory wholesome states of those respective stages.
Having explained their intrinsic nature, their rationale shall now be explained.
Question: Why are they called "totalities" (kṛtsnāyatana)?
Answer: Because their objects of focus are vast and universal, and because the resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) regarding them is boundless, they are called totalities.
The remaining meanings are as explained elsewhere.
As for the "eight knowledges," they refer to the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).

Subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna), knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna), knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna),
and knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) do not include the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna),
because their status is restricted by their specific stages. These eight all have wisdom (prajñā) among the mental factors (caitta-dharma) as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
The intrinsic nature has already been explained; now its reason for being so designated shall be explained.
Question: For what reason is it called "knowledge" (*jñāna*)?
Answer: Because it involves the thorough investigation and definitive determination of the phenomena that serve as its objects.
Therefore, it is called "wisdom.
Other meanings are explained extensively elsewhere.
Regarding the three types of meditative concentration (samādhi):
First, emptiness; second, wishlessness; third, signlessness.
These three all have samādhi among the mental factors as their intrinsic nature, and they encompass both the contaminated and the uncontaminated.
In this context, because only the untainted doors of liberation are being discussed:
when both aspects of emptiness and selflessness are present together,
the untainted meditative concentration is called the emptiness samādhi.
If one contemplates impermanence, suffering, the cause, origination, arising, conditions,
the path, practice, and emergence— these ten aspects together with the outflow-free meditative concentration (samādhi) are called the wishless samādhi (apraṇihita-samādhi).
If an untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) is accompanied by the four aspects of cessation, tranquility, excellence,
and detachment, it is called the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*).
Having explained its essential nature, its reason for being so named shall now be stated.
Question: For what reason is it called *samādhi* (concentration)?

Answer: It is called *samādhi* because it holds the mind with equanimity, causing it to be one-pointed on a single object and thereby accomplishing what is to be achieved. These three [terms] are explained in detail elsewhere as they have been analyzed.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are:
first, the fruit of stream-entry;
second, the fruit of once-returning.
Third is the fruit of non-returning;
fourth is the fruit of arhatship.
Each of these four has two factors as its intrinsic nature.
There are two types: the unconditioned and the conditioned.
Regarding the unconditioned fruit, it refers to the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), which results from the abandonment of what is to be severed through the vision of the three realms.
It has the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of [the afflictions] as its nature.

The fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin-phala*) has as its nature the analytical cessation of the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) in the three realms, as well as the abandonment of the first six categories of those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm.

The fruit of non-returning has as its nature the analytical cessation resulting from the abandonment of the defilements to be abandoned through seeing in the three realms, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
The fruit of arhatship has as its nature the analytical cessation resulting from the abandonment of the defilements to be abandoned through both seeing and cultivation in the three realms.
As for conditioned fruits,
they all have the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) as their nature according to what is appropriate.
Having explained their essential nature, the reason why [they are so] shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason is it called the fruit of the śramaṇa?
Answer: One who exerts themselves correctly to pacify and eliminate defiled phenomena is called a śramaṇa.
That which is induced and realized by these śramaṇas is called the fruit of the śramaṇa.
This is also explained in detail elsewhere.
As for the five supernormal powers (abhijñā):
first is the supernormal power of the knowledge of miraculous feats (ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā).
Second, the supernormal power of the divine eye;
third, the supernormal power of the divine ear;
fourth, the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others.
Fifth is the supernormal knowledge of recollecting former abodes.
These five all have wisdom as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Having explained their intrinsic natures, their reasons shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason is it called "supernormal power" (abhijñā)?
Answer: Because it is a wondrous, unimpeded function that correctly and non-erroneously penetrates its own objects of focus, it is called "supernormal power."
Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): four are exclusively bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
The supernormal knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is bound to the realm of form or is unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*):
Within the fundamental stages of the four dhyānas,
it is neither in the preparatory stages nor in the formless realms. Why is this so?
If a stage possesses the sublime samādhis that serve as the basis for the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*),
then that stage possesses the five supernormal powers;
however, the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) do not possess the sublime samādhis that serve as the basis for the five supernormal powers.
Therefore, those [beings] do not possess these various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Some say:
"If, on a particular level, there is calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*..."
In that stage, there are five supernormal powers (abhijñā) through impartial grasping;
however, because any one of them is lacking in the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) and the formless realms (ārūpya), they do not possess the five supernormal powers.
As for the basis:
They all depend upon the desire realm and the form realm.
As for their modes of activity (*ākāra*),
these four are exclusively of an unclear mode of activity.
The supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds:
if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), its modes of activity (*ākāra*) are also not clear;
if it is without outflows (*anāsrava*), it functions as the four modes of activity of the Path (*mārga*).
As for the object of focus:
the supernormal power of the knowledge of psychic travel takes as its object either four bases or two bases within the desire realm and the form realm.
The supernormal power of the knowledge of the divine eye takes as its object the sphere of visible forms within the desire and form realms;
the supernormal power of the knowledge of the divine ear takes as its object the sphere of sounds within the desire and form realms;
and the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds—
It takes as its objects the mind and mental factors associated with the desire realm, the form realm, and those that are unconditioned.
The supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives takes as its objects the five aggregates of the desire and form realms.
As for the foundations of mindfulness:

The first three [supernormal powers] consist solely of the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). The supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds consists of three applications of mindfulness, excluding that of the body.
The supernormal power of the knowledge of past lives consists solely of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The four types of knowledge of the wise are exclusively conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
As for the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna-abhijñā*),
if it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is conventional knowledge.
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds:
if it is untainted, it is either knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), or knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
When this knowledge of others' minds is conjoined with meditative absorption (*samādhi*), [it is so].
The four types [of supernormal powers] are not associated with samādhi;
likewise, the supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds,
if it is contaminated (sāsrava), is also not associated with samādhi.
If it is untainted and associated with the path, the wishless samādhi,
and the faculties, then,
speaking in terms of its category, it is associated with three faculties.
That is to say, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Regarding their temporal status, all five types fall within the three periods of time.
Of these, the first four, when past, take the past as their object.
The present [condition] takes the present as its object.
The future, if it has arisen, takes the future as its object;
if it has not yet arisen, it takes the three periods of time as its object.
The supernormal power of knowledge of past lives:
that which pertains to the past takes the past as its object;
that which pertains to the future takes all three times as its object.
Regarding "wholesome and so forth":
the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear are indeterminate (avyākṛta) and take three types [of objects] as their conditions.
The supernormal power of the knowledge of the divine realm has wholesome objects and is indeterminate;
the others have wholesome objects and are of three kinds.
Regarding those bound to the desire realm and so forth:
four are bound to the form realm and take as their objects that which is bound to the desire and form realms.
The supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds belongs to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) and is also unconditioned (apratisaṃyukta).
It takes as its object that which belongs to the realms of desire and form, as well as that which is unconditioned.
Regarding "the trainee" (śaikṣa), etc.: [text continues].
The fourth is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
it takes as its object that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
This is the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds.
Regarding "these are the trainee, the non-trainee, and that which is neither trainee nor non-trainee;
those conditioned by the trainee, the non-trainee, and that which is neither trainee nor non-trainee,
and those abandoned by insight," three are abandoned by cultivation.
It takes as its object that which is abandoned by cultivation.
The supernormal knowledge of others' minds is both abandoned by cultivation and not abandoned;
it takes as its object that which is abandoned by seeing, that which is abandoned by cultivation, and that which is not abandoned.
The supernormal power of knowledge of past lives is abandoned through cultivation;
it takes as its object that which is abandoned through both seeing and cultivation.
Regarding "conditioned by names and conditioned by meanings":
the supernormal power of knowledge of past lives universally conditions both names and meanings.
The remaining four take only objects as their cognitive support (*ālambana*).
Regarding those that take one's own continuum and so forth as their support:
this refers to the supernormal knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*).
They take only the mental continuums of others as their objects.
The remaining four [knowledges] all take as their objects both one's own and others' continuums, as well as that which is not a continuum.
These are acquired through application or through the abandonment of defilements.
Question: Are these five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) obtained through preparatory effort (prayoga), or are they obtained through the abandonment of defilements (vairāgya)?
If they are obtained through preparatory effort, [then...]
How is what is stated in the *Jñānakāya* (The Compendium of Knowledge) to be reconciled?
For example, it asks: "If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds in the present, does one also possess it in the past and future?"
Answer: It is so.
If it is acquired through the separation from defilements (*vairāgya-lābhika*), how is this to be reconciled with what was previously stated regarding these aggregates?
As it is said, when one realizes the supernormal power of the knowledge of psychic travel (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*) by means of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one cultivates one application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) in the present and four in the future, and so forth.
It is not that there is prior cultivation of what has already arisen in the future.
Some say it is obtained solely through application (*prayoga*).
Question: How is what is stated in the *Jñānakāya* (The Aggregate of Knowledge) to be reconciled?
Answer: That text should be stated as follows:
"If one possesses present knowledge of others' minds..."
Regarding the future, one definitely accomplishes the past;
if it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one accomplishes it.
If it has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased but has been lost, then one does not accomplish it.
As for why it was not stated,
some say it is because the answer was given in a general and abbreviated manner, being drawn out by the force of the context. Others say:
It is obtained solely through the removal of defilements (*vairāgya*).
Question: How is what was previously stated to be reconciled with this?
Answer: It is taught that the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are subject to repeated refinement; it does not refer to their initial cultivation.
At that time, because it merely causes what was previously attained to become more luminous and superior,
such an explanation applies to both those acquired through preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and those acquired through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*).
This section on the aggregates (skandha) speaks only of those acquired through application (prāyogika),
while the section on knowledge (jñāna-skandha) speaks only of those acquired through the removal of defilements (vairāgyalābhika).
In this way, the two explanations are mutually consistent.
Some say that among those acquisitions through the abandonment of defilements,
there are some that have been previously practiced.
There are those who have not previously practiced;
the *Jñānakāya* speaks of those who have already practiced,
while this *Kāya* speaks of those who have not yet practiced.
In this way, the two explanations are also well-reconciled.
That which is acquired through the separation from defilement refers to that which is induced by the first dhyāna.
That which is induced by the fourth dhyāna is acquired at the time of becoming free from the defilements of the third dhyāna;
this applies down to that which is acquired at the time of becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm.
If it is the noble ones (*ārya*) or ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who will be reborn (*punarbhava*), they may attain both those previously practiced and those never before practiced;
others attain only those previously practiced.
Once it has been attained through the separation from passion (*vairāgya-lābha*), it manifests through application (*prayoga*).
For a Buddha, no application is required;
for a Pratyekabuddha, a minimal application is required.
Whether the śrāvakas are of middling or superior capacity,
furthermore, whatever they cultivate and attain at the time of the path of liberation through the abandonment of defilements is all attained through the abandonment of defilements.
If it is attained through cultivation at another time, it is all attained through application (*prayoga*).
As for where it arises: it can arise in both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Within the desire realm, it exists only among humans and devas;
among humans, it exists only in the three continents,
and it occurs in both male and female bodies.
Ordinary beings, noble ones, those in training (śaikṣa), and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) can all manifest [the supernormal powers].
Question: Are the various supernormal powers subsumed under the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), or are they subsumed under the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga)?
If it were subsumed under the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
how would one reconcile this with what is stated in the Sūtra:
"dividing the one into many, and combining the many into one"?
...and so on, as explained at length.
Such a thing does not occur within a single moment of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
If it were included within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), [then...]
How should one reconcile what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
As for how it is explained there:
it refers to the supernormal powers of wholesome wisdom, the divine eye, and the divine ear, as well as the path of liberation.
How is it that this indeterminate wisdom (avyākṛta-prajñā) is called "supernormal power" (abhijñā)?

Answer: All supernormal powers are subsumed under the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), just as the fruits of the ascetic life (śrāmaṇya-phala) are subsumed under the path of liberation and not under the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga).
This case is also like that.
If it is asked how the explanation in the *Prakaraṇapāda* is to be reconciled,
the answer is that the explanation given there differs from this one.
That [other] teaching states that all wholesome wisdom (*kuśala-prajñā*) is called "supernormal knowledge" (*abhijñā*),
because it teaches that all phenomena are what is to be thoroughly penetrated. In this context,
however, the term "supernormal knowledge" refers specifically to superior wisdom (*viśiṣṭa-prajñā*).
This supernormal power (abhijñā) is either wholesome (kuśala) or indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Regarding the relationship between supernormal power and wholesome wisdom (prajñā), four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) can be established.
There is supernormal power that is not wholesome wisdom.
That is to say, there are the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear.
There is also wholesome wisdom that is not a supernormal power;
this refers to all wholesome wisdom excluding those [two] supernormal powers.
There are cases where both are present,
namely the other four supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
There are cases where neither is present.
That is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Question: Do these five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) arise exactly as described, or not?
Regarding this, some have made the following statement:
They arise according to how they were taught.
That is to say, because the supernormal power of the knowledge of miraculous feats (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*) arises first, it is mentioned by the Buddha first;
and so on, until because the supernormal power of the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-abhijñā*) arises last, it is mentioned by the Buddha last.
This means that although they hear of the gods of the form realm (rūpadhātu), they are unable to go there;
and although they first give rise to the power of supernormal travel (ṛddhi-gati),
they are unable to see their forms.
Next, he arouses the supernormal power of the divine eye; although he sees [the beings], he cannot hear their speech.
Next, he arouses the supernormal power of the divine ear; although he hears [their speech], he cannot know their minds.
Next, he arouses the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others; having known their minds, he still does not yet know whether they have met him in previous lives.
The supernormal knowledge of past lives arises subsequently;
the Blessed One taught it according to this sequence.
Thus it is said.
The sequence is not fixed; that is,
one may first give rise to the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*),
or even first give rise to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
Some possess only the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*),
such as Devadatta and others;
some possess only the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
As in the case of Sunakṣatra and others,
therefore the various supernormal powers have neither progressive entry nor regressive entry,
nor do they involve skipping over stages.

Just as with the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), or as with the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Question: When cultivating and arising the supernormal powers of the base of psychic power (*ṛddhiviṣaya*) and the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*):
What is the difference between these two types of light that both possess radiance?
Answer: If it is the light produced by the cultivation of the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhi*), or that which is manifested through transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
Alternatively, it exists by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*).
If one cultivates the light induced by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*),
it is not produced through transformation (*nirmāṇa*) but exists solely by way of its own nature.

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang in accordance with the Imperial Decree. Section Six: The Aggregate of Faculties (Indriya-skandha). Chapter One: The Sub-section on the Inclusion of Faculties (Indriya-samgraha-varga). Part One of the First Sub-section of the Sixth Aggregate of Faculties: The Twenty-two Faculties.

The eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, female faculty, male faculty, life faculty, mind faculty, pleasure faculty, pain faculty, joy faculty, grief faculty, equanimity faculty, faith faculty, energy faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, wisdom faculty, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
Of these twenty-two faculties,
how many are of the learner (śaikṣa) and how many are of the non-learner (aśaikṣa)?
How many are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Such are the chapters and the explanations of their meanings.
Having already grasped this, one should now analyze it in detail.
Question: For what reason did the Venerable One compose this treatise using the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*)?
Answer: Because that Venerable One so desired.
This treatise is composed according to their inclinations without contradicting the characteristics of phenomena;
one should not question the reasons for this. Some say:
One should not ask this.
That Venerable One has taught the twenty-two faculties (indriya) based on the Sūtras;
those Sūtras concerning the faculties constitute the foundation of this treatise.
One cannot be faulted for the reasons behind composing this treatise based on that sutra;
for that Venerable One could not reduce the twenty-two faculties taught by the Buddha to fewer than twenty-one.
One cannot add even a little to speak of twenty-three;
because that which was spoken by the Buddha is without increase or decrease, it cannot be increased or decreased.
Just as it cannot be increased or decreased, [so too is the nature of reality].
It cannot be measured as more or less;
it cannot be diminished or increased.
One should know that the same applies to that which is immeasurable and boundless.
Because that which is spoken by the Buddha is immeasurable and boundless,
such that one cannot establish a measure or limit within it;
"immeasurable" means its meaning is difficult to fathom.
"Boundless" means that its textual expression is difficult to comprehend;
it is like the great ocean, which is immeasurable and boundless.
"Immeasurable" refers to its depth.
"Boundless" means vast.
It should be understood that what the Blessed One has spoken is likewise so,
even if it were to number hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas.
For instance, great masters of treatises such as Śāriputra composed hundreds of thousands of treatises to analyze and explain the meaning of even two lines of verse spoken by the Buddha.
The nature of his awakening is such that its limits cannot be reached;
therefore, one should not reproach that venerable one.
Setting aside that venerable one for now:
Why did the Blessed One speak this sūtra?
Answer: Because he observed that those to be converted would obtain great benefit by hearing this Dharma.
Furthermore, there is a specific causal origin (*nidāna*) for this sūtra.
There was a brahmin named Jātiśroṇa who came to where the Buddha was, and with joy,
he exchanged greetings with him.
Sitting to one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How many faculties (indriya) must be established to encompass all faculties?
The Buddha replied:
I have stated that the twenty-two faculties encompass all faculties exhaustively.
If anyone were to deny this and propose additional faculties,
it should be understood that their statement has words but no meaning.
If one were to question him in return, it would only give rise to further delusion and confusion. Why is this?
Because it is not within his domain; this is due to the question posed by the brahmin.
This sūtra was spoken for this reason;
therefore, one should not inquire into the Buddha’s intention in speaking it.
Setting aside the question of the Buddha’s intention:
Question: For what reason does the brahmin ask only about the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and not about the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or bases (*āyatana*)?
Answer: He asks in accordance with his own doubts.
One should not reproach him;
for perhaps that brahmin is of a naturally virtuous disposition,
and whenever he hears something, he joyfully inquires about it in detail.
Seeking to understand the full meaning of the faculties (*indriya*), he traveled extensively through ninety-six paths of existence to inquire about the measure of those faculties.
Just as the Nirgranthas posit a single faculty—the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)—which pervades all internal and external things.
Therefore, they established a rule not to drink cold water and not to cut living grass because it possesses life.
[The Buddha] asked the various non-Buddhists regarding external objects:
What roots does grasping possess that it is called "a phenomenon with roots"?
Answer: There is grasping for external objects that possesses the mental faculty (manas-indriya);
there is grasping for external objects that possesses the life-faculty (jīvita-indriya).
There are those who maintain that external objects possess two faculties:
by virtue of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), they are called "possessing-faculty phenomena" (*sendriya-dharma*);
and by virtue of the life-faculty (*jīvita-indriya*), they are called "possessing-life phenomena" (*sajīva-dharma*).
There are those who maintain that external objects possess two roots;
namely, karma and the mind, as should be explained according to the circumstances.
Furthermore, there is the non-Buddhist Pārasīya.
He spoke thus:
"The eye does not see forms;
the ear does not hear sounds."
This is called the "Noble Cultivation of the Faculties.
Question: For what reason is it called *pāraselī*?
Answer: This is a name that has been established; one should not question the reason for establishing a name.
Because names established by convention do not necessarily possess a corresponding real referent;
some say that this is his clan name.
That is to say, among the brahmins there are those of the Kaccāna clan,
those of the Vāseṭṭha clan,
and those of the Bhāradvāja clan.
There was one whose clan name was Kauṇḍinya;
there was one whose clan name was Bhāradvāja;
and there was one whose clan name was Vāśiṣṭha.
Some say that this is of mixed caste,
meaning it arises from a Kṣatriya and a Brāhmaṇa.
It is called *pārasīka*.
Just as that which is born from a donkey and a horse is called a mule, so it is said.
This was his clan name.
He had a disciple named Uddala who once came to the place where the Buddha was staying.
Joyfully exchanging greetings, he sat to one side.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying:
"Your teacher, Pārasīla..."
"Shall I teach you the method for cultivating the faculties?
Udāyin replied,
"My teacher has indeed spoken of it."
The Buddha asked, "How is it so? He replied,
"My teacher speaks thus."
The eye does not see forms,
and the ear does not hear sounds;
this is called the noble cultivation of the faculties because there is nothing to be grasped.
The Buddha then challenged him, saying:
"If that were so, then a blind person should be called one who has cultivated the faculties, because they do not see forms.
At that time, Ānanda was standing in attendance beside the Buddha.
While fanning the Buddha with a fan,
he immediately raised an objection: "If so,
then those who are deaf should also be called noble ones (ārya), for they have cultivated their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) and do not hear sounds."
Question: Suppose there were hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of non-Buddhists,
whose wisdom and eloquence were equal to that of Śāriputra.
The Buddha is able to subdue them all.
For what reason did the World-Honored One raise the first challenge,
and why did the Venerable Ānanda raise the second?
Why did the World-Honored One not prevent him?
The answer is: The Buddha observed that Ānanda had a certain mark upon his throat;
knowing that he intended to pose a difficult challenge, the Buddha then desisted of his own accord.
For when the Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path with diligent effort throughout the three incalculable eons in the past,
he did not even interrupt the eloquence of others.
Even his disciples do not obstruct him,
let alone the Buddha now having attained enlightenment and cutting off the eloquence of others.
Furthermore, the Buddha clearly knows that which he himself has spoken.
If Ānanda speaks of equality and non-differentiation,
it is not refuted because there is neither increase nor decrease;
furthermore, it demonstrates that both teacher and disciple are capable of subduing others.
If both teacher and disciple are capable of subduing [the opponent],
this is called "skillful subduing," and therefore it is not prohibited or restricted.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to ensure that they have no further words to say.
That is to say, if the Blessed One were to pose the first challenge and Ānanda did not pose the second challenge,
then those non-Buddhists would simply return to their own assembly.
Out of residual pride, they speak thus:
"Although we have been subdued by that teacher, we are not his disciples;
although he is able to subdue us, he is not our teacher."
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
were to pose the first challenge and Ānanda were to pose the second challenge,
then he would forever abandon his mind of pride.
"If even his disciples are able to subdue us, how much more so their teacher?
Even if our own teacher were to come, he would not be able to withstand him, let alone we.
Furthermore, desiring to fulfill the wishes of that brahmin, he thought thus:"
Among the Śākyas, the Venerable Gautama is unsurpassed;
he is capable of subduing and defeating all debaters without ever being cowed,
and he is the most exalted among all masters of discourse.
"In the past, even all those great masters of treatises were unable to respond to him, let alone we;
if his disciples were to engage in discussion with me,"
It would be most fitting for me to respond;
for the Buddha fulfills the intentions of those he transforms at all times,
drawing them forth in accordance with their thoughts.
Therefore, [the Buddha] did not refute what Ānanda had questioned.
Furthermore, the Buddha took Ānanda as a witness to the meaning;
thus, those followers of the non-Buddhist schools held Ānanda in high esteem.
Because that venerable one possessed a dignified and handsome appearance and was well-versed in the *Indra-śabda-vidyā* treatise,
the Buddha intended for him to question those who held his own faith.
Does the tradition of the self-attested masters accord with correct reasoning?
Because Ānanda spoke at that time, the Buddha did not stop him.
Furthermore, it was intended to demonstrate that the Blessed One had no apprehension of anyone superior to himself.
This means that because various non-Buddhists fear that among their disciples there might be some who surpass them,
they suppress their speech and eloquence; the Buddha has no such concern,
even if he were to have disciples numbering in the hundreds of thousands, koṭis, nayutas, or more.
His eloquence and wisdom were like those of Śāriputra;
moreover, there was no one who could equal the Buddha in posing difficult questions, let alone surpass him.
Furthermore, he wished to demonstrate that he had severed the defilement of stinginess regarding the Dharma.
This means that the various non-Buddhist teachers do not permit their disciples to engage in debate with others,
lest they gain excessive fame, honor, and material gain therefrom;
the Buddha, however, does not act in this way.
Even if everyone in the world were to obtain boundless fame and profit,
the Buddha would never harbor even a hair’s breadth of jealousy.
Therefore, it does not contradict what Ānanda has said.
Furthermore, it is intended to demonstrate that the disciples are also superior to others;
that is to say, the various non-Buddhists fear that their own followers might suffer defeat and humiliation when engaging in debate with others.
There are no disciples of the Blessed One who do not excel others.
When engaging in debate, they further illuminate and exalt the True Dharma of the Tathāgata; therefore, it is not prohibited.
Furthermore, it is because he wishes to demonstrate that within the well-spoken Dharma, the words and meanings are complete and free from divergent views.
That is to say, within the poorly taught doctrines of the various non-Buddhists,
the words and meanings are contradictory and the views of teachers and disciples differ;
thus, whatever they establish, whatever they proclaim, and whatever they interpret, [is all flawed].
The teacher and the disciple each contradict one another;
such a fault does not exist within the Buddha’s True Dharma.
In accordance with what is established, what is taught, and what is understood, [there is no contradiction].
The disciple and the teacher are of one and the same flavor.
For these reasons, the Buddha and Ānanda each posed a challenge to those non-Buddhists.
Question: If you, O non-Buddhist, admit that those who are blind or deaf are noble ones (*ārya*) who have cultivated their faculties (*indriya*), how can this be considered a difficulty?

Answer: This constitutes a great difficulty; it is also a general statement of the faults of the non-Buddhists for which no one can provide a rebuttal. That is to say, if you admit that those who are blind or deaf are [noble ones], [then...]
They may also be called "noble ones who have cultivated their faculties.
For what reason have you abandoned the household life to diligently practice the various holy conducts day and night?
One need only destroy the two faculties of eye and ear to be called a practitioner who has cultivated the faculties in the noble way; therefore,
what was stated previously constitutes a great difficulty.
This is also a general censure of all non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas assert that there are five sense faculties:
the olfactory, gustatory, visual, tactile, and auditory faculties constitute the five.
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas speak of eleven faculties:
namely, the five sensory faculties, the five faculties of action, and the mental faculty.
As for the five sensory faculties:
The so-called faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body;
the five faculties of action are those of speech,
hands, feet, and the organs of excretion and reproduction.
The mental faculty (*manas*) serves as the eleventh;
alternatively, there are those who say there are one hundred and twenty faculties.
That is to say, the eyes, ears, and nose each have two, making six;
together with the tongue, body, mind, life-faculty, and the five faculties of sensation,
and the five faculties beginning with faith, they total twenty.
The six destinies each have twenty [subdivisions], making one hundred and twenty.
They explain that the asuras constitute the sixth destiny.
Others say:
The "root" (mūla) refers to a sovereign lord.
Those non-Buddhists (tīrthika) speak of one hundred and twenty such lords,
