such as the Lord of the Devas, the Lord of the Nāgas, the Lord of the Asuras, and the Lord of Humans, and so forth.
"One must undergo such a body of one hundred and twenty superior and wondrous realms before attaining liberation.
Having heard these and other such words, the brahmin Śravaṇa [was moved].
Because the explanations regarding the faculties differ, confusion arises;
one does not know which among them is the true teaching.
One hears that a great son was born in the palace of the Śākyas.
He was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics;
his body was of a true golden color, and his halo extended one fathom.
Those who saw him were filled with joy, never wearying of gazing upon him.
Renouncing the rank of a universal monarch, he left the city to enter the homeless life;
through diligent cultivation of difficult and ascetic practices,
he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He is the all-knower and the all-seer;
he severs the entire web of doubt and bestows certain resolution upon all;
he is able to exhaust the very source and bottom of every difficult inquiry.
Having heard this, he immediately went to where the Buddha was, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Many śramaṇas speak of faculties; how many faculties do they say encompass all faculties?"
Question: Why did the brahmin, instead of explaining the distinctions among the faculties (indriya) according to what he had heard, ask the Buddha directly about this?
Answer: Because he possessed wrong wisdom (kuprajñā), fearing that the Buddha might [refute] the distinctions among the faculties as explained by others.
Because he wished to explain what is excellent by means of selection, he therefore posed a general question.
In response to that question, the Buddha said:
"I declare that the twenty-two faculties encompass all faculties exhaustively."
If there were an obstruction to this, one might further state other faculties;
as explained at length,
[this is not the case] because it is not their object.
Question: World-Honored One, for what reason do you again speak these words?
If someone were to obstruct this and instead explain other faculties, one should know that their speech has words but no meaning.
If one were to question them in return, they would instead become confused. Why is this?
Because it is not their domain.
Answer: It is intended to make them know that the previously mentioned single faculty, up to the one hundred and twenty faculties, are all not real; therefore, it is said by way of meaning:
"I am the all-knower and the all-seer."
Furthermore, among the twenty-two faculties (indriya),
one cannot reduce even a single faculty to speak of twenty-one,
nor can one increase even a single faculty to speak of twenty-three.
How much more so for the various non-Buddhists, who, possessed of biased views and ignorance, claim that among the sense faculties there can be an increase or decrease,
ranging from one up to one hundred and twenty?
For this reason, they came to the Buddha.

This inquiry concerns only the meaning of the faculties (*indriya*), not the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth. If one asks how many substantial entities there are among these twenty-two named faculties, the Abhidharmikas reply:
[The text continues: "The Abhidharmikas say..."
There are twenty-two by name,
but seventeen in actual substance;
this is because among them, the male and female faculties and the three untainted faculties do not possess distinct substantial entities.
Question: Why do the female and male faculties have no separate substance?
Answer: Because these two are subsumed within the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).
As it is said: "What is the female faculty?"
It refers to a portion of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).
What is the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*)?
It refers to a portion of the body faculty.
Question: For what reason do the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) also lack a distinct substantial entity?
Answer: Because these three are subsumed within nine faculties.
The "nine" refers to the mind faculty (manas-indriya).
The faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity,
along with the five faculties beginning with faith—
these nine faculties, when they exist in a particular state, are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
There is a stage called the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya);
there is a stage called the faculty of "having fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya),
which is precisely the stage of the path of vision (darśanamārga).
The stage of the path of cultivation and the stage of the path of no-more-learning should be understood respectively in this manner.
Furthermore, within the continuum of those practicing through faith or through dharma,
it is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.

Within the continua of those who have attained through faith, those who have attained through vision, and those who have realized through bodily witness, [it is called the faculty of one who has known].
It is called the faculty of "having known" (ājñendriya).
Within the mental continuum of those liberated through wisdom (prajñāvimukta) and those doubly liberated (ubhayatobhāgavimukta),
it is called the faculty of "one who has fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
Because the nine faculties are grouped together and described as three according to their respective stages, they have no separate entities.
For this reason, it is said that although there are twenty-two faculties, there are only seventeen substantial entities.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta has stated that there are twenty-two names,
but only fourteen substantial entities.
This means that the aforementioned five [faculties], along with the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), have no separate substantial entities.
Question: For what reason is it said that the life-faculty lacks a substantial entity?
Answer: The life-faculty is subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāraskandha*).
They assert that the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*) lacks substantial reality.
Question: For what reason do they further state that the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) has no separate substance?
Answer: They assert that apart from the feelings of suffering and pleasure, there is no separate feeling of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Why is this? Because whatever sensations there may be—
whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
What is meant by "feeling" (vedanā)?
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret the sūtra which speaks of the three feelings?
Answer: It is stated there as follows:
Pleasurable feeling, painful feeling,
and neither-pleasurable-nor-painful feeling are each superior or inferior,
sharp or dull, restless or calm.
Those who are superior, sharp, and restless are said to experience feelings of pleasure and pain;
those who are inferior, dull, and tranquil are said to experience neither-pain-nor-pleasure feelings.
The nature of these [latter] is indeterminate, shifting like doubt.
Question: For what reason is it said that the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*) likewise has no separate substance?
Answer: Because it is said that there is no substance of concentration apart from the mind.
As it is asked: "What is concentration?"
That is to say, it is one-pointedness of mind.
By virtue of this, the faculties are said to be twenty-two in number,
though they are fourteen in terms of substantial entities.
The Venerable Buddhadeva asserts that while there are twenty-two names,
in actual substance there is only one.
Regarding what is called the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), they say this:
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) possess two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
First, the great elements;
second, the mind.
Apart from the great elements, there is no derived matter.
Apart from the mind, there are no mental factors.
All material phenomena are merely distinctions of the primary elements;
all non-material phenomena are merely distinctions of the mind.
For this reason, in reality, the faculties are only one.
According to the true meaning,
they should be called twenty-two, as previously stated.
Just as the seventeen entities correspond to their names,
so too do the designation of names and the designation of entities.
It is called the difference in characteristics of names and the difference in characteristics of entities; it is called the difference in nature of names and the difference in nature of entities;
it is called the distinctness of names and the distinctness of entities.
Just as "name" is the essence of discrimination and "discrimination" is the essence of name,
one should know that "awakening" is likewise the essence of realization and "realization" is the essence of awakening.
This is called the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the faculties.
Having already explained their nature as entities, their characteristics, and their essence, we shall now explain the reason [for their designation].
Question: For what reason are they called "faculties" (*indriya*)?
What is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*)?
The answer is: the meaning of sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) is the meaning of faculty;
the meaning of illumination (*prakāśana*) is the meaning of faculty.
The meaning of manifestation is the meaning of faculty (*indriya*).
The meaning of delighting in contemplation is the meaning of faculty.
The meaning of being dignified and beautiful is the meaning of faculty.
The meaning of "ultimate" (*paramārtha*) is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*). The meaning of "supreme" (*agra*) is the meaning of "faculty.
The meaning of "predominant" (*adhipati*) is the meaning of "faculty."
Question: If the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) is the sense of "predominance," then all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) exercise mutual predominance over one another,
and all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) exercise predominance over conditioned phenomena.
If that were so, all phenomena (*dharma*) should be established as faculties (*indriya*).
Why, then, did the Blessed One establish twenty-two?
The Venerable Pārśva said:
The Buddha has attained ultimate and thorough mastery over all phenomena;
he well understands the essence, characteristics, and functional powers of all phenomena, which others cannot know.
If a phenomenon possesses the characteristic of being a faculty (*indriya*), it is established as a faculty.
That which does not exist cannot be established, and thus should not be subject to questioning.
Some say that among dominant conditions (adhipatipratyaya), there are those that are inferior and those that are superior, as well as those that are weak and those that are excellent.
The superior establish the faculties;
the inferior do not. Some say:
Although all phenomena possess the nature of being dominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*),
it is not the case that they all manifest as dominant conditions,
up to and including the sense of "predominance" (*ādhipatya*).
Regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*):
just as all sentient beings possess the sense of being a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for one another, yet some are superior.
Just as King Yama is supreme among the realm of hungry ghosts,
the lion king is supreme among the animal realm,
and the village headman is supreme within the village.
Among those within the kingdom, the king is supreme;
among the four great continents, the universal monarch (cakravartin) is supreme;
and within the desire realm, the Lord of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (Vaśavartin) is supreme.
Within a thousandfold world system, the Brahmā King is supreme;
within the three realms, the Buddha is most supreme.
Among all classes of sentient beings, the Buddha is supreme.
He alone is called the Dharma King because he is without peer;
thus, although all these phenomena are superior conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*),
not all of them possess the status of a superior condition.
Up to and including the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown. Just as there are twenty-two faculties,
for this reason the Buddha taught only these twenty-two faculties.
Question: If the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) is the sense of "predominance," then what predominates over what?
Answer: The eye-faculty predominates over four bases.
First, it adorns the self;
second, it guides and nourishes the self;
third, it serves as the basis for consciousness and so forth.
Fourth, performing uncommon deeds:
regarding the adornment of one's own body,
although one may possess a wondrous body with all its limbs complete, [it remains unadorned without these].
If the faculty of the eye is deficient, people do not delight in looking at one;
therefore, among the adornments of the body, this [the eye] is preeminent for those who guide and nourish themselves.
By means of the eye faculty, one perceives beautiful and ugly forms;
it abandons danger and seeks safety, enabling the body to endure for a long time,
and serves as the basis for consciousness and the other mental factors.
Visual consciousness and its associated mental factors arise in dependence upon this;
as for performing the unique function,
it is the eye-faculty alone that sees forms, and not the other faculties.
The faculty of hearing exercises sovereignty in four ways:
first, in the adornment of one's own body;
second, in the guidance and nourishment of one's own body.
Third, it serves as the basis for consciousness and so forth;
fourth, it performs its unique function.
As for "adorning one's own body":
Although one may possess a wondrous body with all its limbs complete,
if the faculty of hearing is deficient, people will not delight in beholding it;
therefore, in the context of adorning the body, this [hearing] is paramount.
Regarding the cultivation and maintenance of oneself:
by means of the faculty of hearing, one hears pleasant and unpleasant sounds;
by abandoning danger and seeking safety, one causes the body to endure for a long time.
Regarding its being the basis for consciousness and so forth:
auditory consciousness and its associated mental factors arise depending upon it. Regarding its performing a non-common function:
[it performs a function not shared by other bases].
Only the auditory faculty hears sound, not the other faculties.
Other masters say that the visual faculty is preeminent because it guides the production of the physical body.
The method of cultivating the faculty of hearing is supreme for attaining the Dharma-body.
As it is said:
"Just as a person with clear vision / Is able to avoid present dangers,"
In this world, there are those who are wise and able to avoid suffering;
the learned are able to know the Dharma. Through much learning one can avoid transgression;
through much learning one abandons what is meaningless; through much learning one attains Nirvana.
Furthermore, there are those who say that both the eye faculty and the ear faculty are capable of guiding and producing both the physical body and the Dharma-body.
The manner in which they guide and produce the physical body is as previously explained.
Regarding the method for cultivating the Dharma-body:
through the faculty of the eye, one draws near to virtuous friends;
through the faculty of the ear, one hears the true Dharma.
Because this can induce proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*),
practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*), and so forth, leading ultimately to the successive realization of *nirvāṇa*, the Sūtra says:
"Brahmin Brahmāyu, do not damage your two faculties—namely, the eye and the ear.
[The question: Why, among the collection of all the sense-faculties, [are only these two mentioned]?
Why is it said only that the two faculties [of sight and hearing] must not be impaired?
Answer: Because when a Buddha appears in the world, the faculties of eye and ear serve as the path and the gateway for entering the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, when the eyes and ears encounter a Buddha, one is able to infer through analogy that this is indeed the Buddha.
As it is said: "O Bhikṣus, if you are unable to know the mind of the Buddha, you should seek it in two places."
First, that which is heard;
second, that which is seen.
These are spoken of specifically so as not to subvert the two faculties.
The faculties of the nose, tongue, and body each exercise sovereignty over four matters:
first, the adornment of one's own person;
second, the guidance and nourishment of one's own person.
Third, it serves as the basis for consciousness and so forth;
fourth, it performs unique functions.
As for "adorned with one's own body":
Although one may possess a wondrous body with all its limbs complete,
if even one of the three faculties is deficient, people will not take pleasure in beholding it;
this is for the sake of guiding and nourishing oneself.
By means of these three faculties, one partakes of solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) so that the body may endure for a long time;
for solid food consists of odor, taste, and tangibility.
Furthermore, they serve as the basis for consciousness and the other [mental factors].
Olfactory consciousness and its associated mental factors arise dependent upon the olfactory faculty;
gustatory consciousness and its associated mental factors arise dependent upon the gustatory faculty;
tactile consciousness and its associated mental factors arise dependent upon the tactile faculty.
Regarding those functions that are unique:
only the nose can smell,
and only the tongue can taste.
The body alone perceives tangibles,
and each [sense faculty] is not the other;
the mental faculty (manas) exercises sovereignty over both locations.
First, it is able to continue subsequent existence;
second, it functions through sovereign control.
Regarding "being able to continue subsequent existence":
As it is said: "If consciousness were not to descend into the mother's womb, would name-and-form develop as the kalala?
No, World-Honored One.
This refers to that which functions according to sovereign power.
As it is said:
"That which is led by the worldly mind, and that for which the mind exerts itself—
if the mind arises toward these, they all proceed in accordance with its mastery."
Some say that the mental faculty (*manas*) exercises sovereignty over both the defiled and purified categories;
as it is said: "Because the mind is afflicted, sentient beings are afflicted."
Because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure.
The male and female faculties exercise sovereignty over two matters:
first, the differentiation of sentient beings.
Second, the distinction of differentiation.
Regarding the differentiation of sentient beings:
it is by means of these two faculties that all sentient beings are differentiated into the distinct categories of male and female.
Due to these two faculties, there arise distinctions such as physical form, speech, and breasts; that is to say,
at the beginning of the kalpa, there was no distinction between female and male, but later,
a small amount of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) arose in those locations.
There then arise distinctions in male and female forms, physical characteristics,
appearances, speech and sounds, clothing, food and drink, and modes of enjoyment. Some say:
These two are predominant with respect to the categories of defilement and purification.
Regarding their predominance in defilement,
it is not because of sexual desire, for there is no doubt in that regard.
However, if these two are either impaired or deficient,
[there is no transgression] regarding non-restraint or the five deeds of immediate retribution.
They are unable to undertake [the practice],
nor can they sever their roots of goodness toward those who are pure and superior.
If these male and female faculties are impaired or deficient,
one will be unable to give rise to any form of restraint (saṃvara),
nor will one be able to free oneself from the defilements of the three realms.
It cannot plant the seeds of the three vehicles.
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) exercises predominance in two respects:
first, it causes one to say that the faculties exist.
Second, it causes the faculties not to be severed;
for as long as the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) exists, one can be said to possess the faculties,
and because it causes the various faculties to continue in succession.
Some say that the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is preeminent in four respects:
first, it continues the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga).
Second, maintaining the homogeneous class;
third, protecting and nourishing the homogeneous class;
fourth, ensuring that the homogeneous class is not interrupted.
The five feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*) exercise sovereignty over the category of affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣa*); for by the power of feeling,
sentient beings pursue objects in all four directions, wandering like those bound by iron chains.
On perilous paths, they use hooks and ropes to climb mountains and cross valleys;
they crawl and prostrate themselves,
or enter the great ocean and encounter various terrors and hardships.
That is to say: the perils of waves, whirlpools, *śiṃśumāra* monsters, black winds, whirlwinds, submerged mountains, sandbanks, and shoals; falling into the palaces of evil *nāgas*;
and the dangers of *rākṣasa* islands, *kumbhīra* crocodiles, bandits, and thieves.
All such various [phenomena] are caused by the various feelings (*vedanā*).
Question: How does untainted feeling (*anāsrava-vedanā*) exercise sovereignty over the category of defilement (*saṃkleśapakṣa*)?
Answer: At the time of first initiating the preparatory application (*prayoga*) and entering [the path].
It also predominates over the category of affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣa*);
that is to say, when a practitioner seeks those sensations,
they must also seek out such things as food and clothing.
Because defilement also arises by the power of this [feeling],
some say that feeling is superior in both the defiled and the pure.
Regarding pleasant feeling,
for those who are predominant in defilement,
it is as said: "In pleasant feeling, craving increases accordingly."
Regarding those who are pure and superior:
as it is said, because of pleasure, the mind is concentrated; [this refers to] the sensation of suffering.
Regarding those who excel in defilement:
as it is said, hatred increases in accordance with painful feeling.
Regarding those who excel in purity:
As it is said that suffering is the basis for faith,
so too is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling predominant in regard to defilement.
As it is said that ignorance increases in relation to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
and as it is said regarding purity and excellence,
there are the six bases of renunciation associated with equanimity.
The five faculties, such as faith and the rest,
are predominant with respect to the category of purification,
as it is said:
Faith gives rise to the ability to take refuge;
diligence can cross the ocean of the flow of heedlessness and eliminate suffering; wisdom can attain purity.
Furthermore, it is said that my noble disciples are endowed with faith.
Iṣika was able to abandon unwholesome states and cultivate wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Diligence can attain bodhi."
Furthermore, it is said that my noble disciples possess the power of diligence;
they abandon unwholesome dharmas and cultivate wholesome dharmas.
Moreover, it is said that mindfulness can pervade all activities and provide protection for everything.
My noble disciples possess mindfulness as a protection;
they abandon unwholesome states and cultivate wholesome states.
Furthermore, it is said that concentration is the right path, while lack of concentration is the wrong path.
Liberation is attained through a concentrated mind, not through an unconcentrated mind;
furthermore, a concentrated mind is able to know the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (skandhas).
It is also said:
My noble disciples possess the garland of the three concentrations;
they are able to abandon what is unwholesome and cultivate wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, it is said:
Wisdom is supreme in the world; it is able to lead toward decisive discernment, to correctly know all phenomena, and to bring an end to the suffering of old age and death.
It is also said:
Among all phenomena, wisdom is supreme.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Sister," [it is as follows].
My noble disciples are able, by means of the sword of wisdom,
to sever all fetters, latent tendencies, obsessions, and impurities.
Furthermore, it is said:
My noble disciples possess the protective wall of wisdom;
they are able to obstruct unwholesome dharmas and increase wholesome dharmas.
This is the faculty of "knowing what is not yet known."
The faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) has predominance with respect to seeing the truths for those who have not yet seen them;
the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) has predominance with respect to the elimination of the faults of the afflictions for those who have already seen the truths.

The faculty of one who has already attained full knowledge (ājñātāvindriya) exercises predominance over the attainment of dwelling in happiness in the present life, once the faults of the afflictions have been eliminated.
Because each of these possesses a sense of predominance (*adhipatya*) in its respective domain,
they are called "faculties" (*indriya*).
The Venerable Kūṣāvatīya has stated this as follows:
Only the single faculty of mind (manas) is a supreme faculty (paramārthendriya),
because it is internal and universally possesses an object of cognition.
As for its being "internal":
Because it is comprised within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
As for its pervasiveness:
it extends from the Avīci Hell up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
That which possesses an object of perception does so because it takes all phenomena as its object;
other faculties, such as the eye and so forth, do not possess this characteristic.
Therefore, they are not established as supreme faculties (*paramārthendriya*).
This means that although the five [faculties] beginning with the eye are included among the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*),
they are neither all-pervasive nor possess objects of cognition.
Although the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is pervasive, it is not an internal sense-base (āyatana),
nor does it possess an object (sālambana).
[The same applies to] suffering, pleasure, grief, and joy.
Although they have objects of perception (*ālambana*), they are neither pervasive nor internal.
The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are pervasive and possess objects, yet they are not internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
The three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) are as explained in the section on the nine faculties.
Question: If only the mind (*manas*) is a faculty in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-indriya*), why are the other twenty-one called faculties?
Answer: Because they serve as the bases (*āśraya*) for the mental faculty.
It acts as a basis;
it brings about defilement;
it brings about purification.
Because they establish the state of purification,
they are also called faculties (*indriya*).
Who is it that acts as their support?
This refers to the five faculties, beginning with the eye.
What acts as their support?
It is the life-faculty.
Who brings about defilement?
It is the five faculties of feeling.
Who brings about purification?
This refers to the five faculties beginning with faith.
Who constitutes the state of purification? It refers to the three untainted (anāsrava) faculties.
That is, [the faculties of] the stage of seeing, the stage of cultivation, and the stage of no-more-learning.
Question: For what reason are male and female also designated as "faculties"?
Answer: Because they cause sentient beings to be born.
Because it gives rise to sensual pleasure,
because it restrains the afflictions,
and because it serves as the basis for defilement.
"Beings who are born" refers to beings born from a womb or born from an egg.
"Those who give rise to desire and pleasure" refers to...
This means that in this state, first there arises a desire for pleasure, which subsequently pervades the entire body;
just as when the noble bliss first arises between the eyebrows and subsequently pervades the entire body,
so it is here for one who has subdued the afflictions.
This means that this mental faculty (āśaya) is able to temporarily suppress the various afflictions (kleśa).
Regarding its being the basis for defilement:
it refers to the defiled consciousness (kliṣṭa-vijñāna) and its associated factors (saṃprayukta-dharma), which serve as its support (āśraya).
In other places, the body-faculty gives rise to three kinds of consciousness;
here, however, it gives rise only to defiled consciousness and no others.
When this consciousness arises, because it functions solely as an associated mental state (*manas*), it is necessarily accompanied by greed.
The Venerable Saṅghavasu spoke thus:
"Only the six beginning with life are ultimate faculties (paramārthendriya), namely:
eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and life, because they are the basis of sentient beings."
Question: If the six faculties, beginning with life, are ultimate faculties (*paramārtha-indriya*), why are the remaining sixteen called faculties?
Answer: Because they are associated with the six [faculties], beginning with life.
It acts as the seed;
it acts as defilement;
it acts as purification.
Because it constitutes the state of purification,
it is also called a faculty (*indriya*).
What constitutes the seed?
That is to say, the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*).
What performs the defilement?
That is to say, the five feeling-faculties (*pañca-vedanendriya*).
Who performs purification?
It is the five faculties, beginning with faith.
Who establishes the state of purification?
This refers to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), which correspond to the stages of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*), cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*).
Question: Why are male and female also designated as faculties?
Answer: Sentient beings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have desire as their seed.
Desire is like a crop;
upon what does it depend?
It depends on the male and female faculties.
Therefore, these two are also designated as faculties (*indriya*).
The Venerable Ghoṣaka stated that the eight types beginning with life-force (*jīvita*) are the ultimate faculties (*paramārthendriya*).
That is to say, because the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, male, female, and life-faculty are the bases of sentient beings.
Question: If these eight, such as the life-faculty, are the ultimate faculties (*paramārtha-indriya*), why are the remaining fourteen called faculties?
Answer: It acts as the seed for the eight factors beginning with life;
it effects defilement and it effects purification.
Because they constitute the state of purification,
they are also called faculties (*indriya*),
as explained in detail previously.
Question: Since the atoms of the body faculty (*kāyendriya-paramāṇu*) are equally present throughout the entire body and so forth,
why is this [faculty] alone designated as the female and male faculties (*strī-puruṣendriya*),
and further described as being "manifest"?
The Venerable Vasumitra stated this:
because these [faculties] can manifest whether one is male or female, they are called the male and female faculties;
furthermore, they are said to be "manifest" (*prabhāvita*).
Question: Can one who possesses both sexual organs also manifest [the gender]?
Answer: This cannot be manifested because it is indeterminate.
For this reason, it is said that such a person is neither female nor male.
Some say: because this place is where those who undergo the process of transmigration and those who undergo its cessation [abide],
the six heterodox teachers such as Pūraṇa and others are called "those who transmigrate."
Regarding those called Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas,
and Tathāgatas who have attained cessation (vyāvṛtti),
the Venerable One said:
This place is capable of giving birth to various sages,
munis, and those who are wise and well-disciplined.
Because they facilitate communal living,
they are called the male and female faculties;
they are also said to be termed "manifestations."
The general characteristics of the faculties have already been explained;
now their individual specific characteristics shall be demonstrated.
Question: What is the eye-faculty?
Answer: If one has already seen forms,
is now seeing forms,
or will see forms.
Together with what remains beyond this, these are called the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
That which has already seen visible forms is called the past eye;
that which is currently seeing visible forms is called the present eye.
When one sees a form, it is said that the eye is "future.
This refers to the *sabhāga* (homogeneous).
That which remains besides this is called the *tatsabhāga* (quasi-homogeneous).
The eye faculty is as explained in detail within its own element;
this applies likewise up to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
Question: What is the female faculty (*strī-indriya*)?
Answer: A portion of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).
What is the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*)?
Answer: A portion of the body faculty.
What is the life-faculty?
Answer: It is the lifespan of the three realms.
What is the pleasure-faculty?
Answer: Based on the mental and physical pleasure produced by contact conducive to pleasure,
that which is comprised within the feeling of equanimity is called the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
What is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*)?
Answer: It is the bodily pain produced by contact conducive to suffering;
it is that which is comprised within the category of unwholesome feeling (*vedanā*). This is called the faculty of suffering.
What is the faculty of joy (*somanasyendriya*)?
Answer: It is mental gladness produced by contact conducive to pleasure;
it is comprised within the category of feeling that is equanimous (*upekṣāvedanā*).
This is called the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
What is the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)?
Answer: It is the mental distress produced in dependence on contact conducive to suffering (*duḥkhānukūlaspraṣṭavya*).
That which is comprised by the feeling of unequanimity is called the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
What is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
Answer: It refers to the equanimity of body and mind produced by contact that is neither painful nor pleasant;
it is a feeling comprised within feeling that is neither even nor uneven.
This is called the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
What is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*)?
It is the state of mental purity consisting of faith, compliance,
approval, acceptance, and aspiration toward those wholesome dharmas born of renunciation and seclusion.
This is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
The faculties of energy (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are explained at length according to the text.
Question: What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*)?
Answer: For those who have not yet seen the truths and have not yet attained clear realization,
it refers to the wisdom of those in training and the faculty of wisdom.
As well as all their faculties;
those who practice through faith and those who practice through the Dharma,
who have not yet realized the Four Noble Truths but are capable of realizing them.
This is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
In this context, because one has not yet seen the Four Noble Truths,
one is termed a "seer of the truths-to-be-seen" (an-āśaikṣa).
One who has not yet attained clear realization is called "one who has not yet realized.
The wisdom of those in training and the faculty of wisdom—
this refers to the faculty of wisdom as well as all other faculties possessed by them.
For those practicing through faith (śraddhānusārin) and those practicing through dharma (dharmānusārin), who have not yet realized the four noble truths but are capable of realizing them,
the remaining eight faculties are taught;
these nine faculties taken together are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñātāvya-jñendriya).
Question: Among these nine faculties, why is the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) stated twice, while the other faculties are each mentioned only once as a general summary?
Answer: Because the name and meaning of "wisdom" are preeminent.
This means that within the aggregate of the faculties, wisdom is the most preeminent,
just as a king is preeminent among those in a country,
or a village headman is preeminent among those in a village.
The other faculties are not like this.
Some say it is because wisdom serves as the guide.
As it is said:
"O bhikṣus,
all wholesome dharmas arise."
Wisdom is the foremost guide;
wisdom is the preceding cause.
It is by means of this that all shame and remorse are induced.
Some say that wisdom possesses the three types of clear observation (*abhisamaya*); that is to say,
wisdom possesses the three types of clear observation.
First, the clear realization of direct vision;
second, the clear realization of the object;
third, the clear realization of the entity.
There are two types of clear realization (abhisamaya) for factors associated with wisdom (*prajñā*),
namely, excluding vision (*darśana*) because it does not have wisdom as its intrinsic nature.
For wisdom itself, there is one type of clear realization for all factors.
This means that the object is not anything else,
because it does not have the nature of wisdom and lacks an objective referent.
Some say that wisdom sees the afflictions so that they do not remain for long,
like creatures dwelling in holes.
If a person sees it, it immediately returns to its hole.
Some say that when the light of wisdom continues in succession, the afflictions cannot invade.
Just as thieves cannot steal what is in a room where a lamp is lit,
some say that wisdom is able to illuminate all phenomena.
External phenomena such as the sun and moon illuminate only a single realm, a single location, a single aggregate, and a small portion of a single time;
wisdom, however, can universally illuminate the eighteen realms and the twelve bases.
The five aggregates,
the three periods of time,
and unconditioned phenomena.
Some say:
those without wisdom are bound;
those with wisdom are liberated.
Some say that it is because wisdom enters the Buddha-dharma with great joy; that is to say,
within the Buddha-dharma, understanding is held to be supreme.
Therefore, those who possess wisdom behold the jewel-treasure of the sublime Dharma;
they rejoice therein like a person with clear vision entering an island of jewels.
If one lacks wisdom, even though they have entered the Buddha-dharma, they see nothing and thus constantly harbor grief and sorrow.
It is like a person born blind who, upon reaching a place where treasures are gathered, only increases their sorrow and distress.
Some say that the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) is like a guide.
Like a guide,
like an eye,
like a head.
This is the awakening factor of investigation;
this is the path factor of right view. Some say:
Wisdom guides the remaining factors of enlightenment so that they do not follow divergent paths,
just as one with clear vision leads a group of blind people along the correct road;
this case is likewise.
Some say that wisdom severs the fetters just as a sharp blade does,
as it is said:
Sisters, my noble disciples are able,
by means of the sword of wisdom, to sever all fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, obsessions, and impurities.
Some say that wisdom is like a terrace or palace,
as the Venerable Aniruddha stated:
Relying on the precepts and abiding in the precepts,
I have ascended to the terrace-palace of unsurpassed wisdom.
Thus it is said.
Wisdom can establish the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena,
can discern the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena,
and can destroy ignorance regarding intrinsic nature as well as ignorance regarding the objects of cognition.
It functions without increasing or decreasing among all phenomena.
Some say that wisdom is what all Buddhas cherish and revere.
The Buddha does not cherish or revere sentient beings’ physical form, strength, lineage, wealth, or sovereignty;
he cherishes and reveres only wisdom, for it is through wisdom that one can realize all meritorious qualities. Some say:
Wisdom alone can manifest the Buddha’s peerlessness;
that is to say, physical beauty, strength, lineage, wealth, prosperity, nobility,
and sovereign power cannot manifest the Buddha as the most supreme and honored.
Only wisdom can manifest it,
because omniscience belongs exclusively to the Buddha;
the other faculties are not so.
By means of such immeasurable causes and conditions,
the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is explained as being distinct from the other faculties.
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-mahāvibhāṣā*, Fascicle 142.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 143,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Six: The Aggregate of the Faculties (*Indriya-skandha*). Part One of Two: The Chapter on the Inclusion of the Faculties (*Indriya-saṃgraha*). Question: What is the faculty of having already known (*ājñātendriya*)?
The answer is: for one who has already seen the truths and has already attained clear realization,
it consists of the wisdom of those in training, the faculty of wisdom,
and all other faculties that they possess.
The faculty of "I-have-known" (ājñātendriya) refers to the state where one who is a faith-follower (śraddhādhimukta),
a dharma-follower-attainer (dṛṣṭiprāpta), or a body-witness (kāyasākṣin) has already attained clear realization and repeatedly practiced clear realization regarding the Four Noble Truths.
In this context, because one has already seen the Four Noble Truths,
one is called "one who has seen the truths" (*dṛṣṭasatya*).
Because one has already attained direct realization (*abhisamaya*), one is called "one who has attained direct realization" (*abhisamitavat*).
Regarding those who train in wisdom and the faculty of wisdom:
this refers to the faculty of wisdom and all its associated faculties,
including those of faith-resolved, vision-attained, and body-witnessed realization.
Regarding those who have already attained clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Noble Truths and are undergoing further clear realization,
it is said that they possess the remaining eight faculties.
The totality of these nine faculties is termed the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*).
Question: Do not all those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) also undergo repeated clear observation (*abhisamaya*) regarding the Four Noble Truths?
For example, as when one transitions from the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) to the nature of reflecting (*cetana-dharman*).
Up to the point where one transitions from the stage of being capable of penetration (*kṣānti-dharma*) to the immovable stage (*akopya*).
Why is it that only the "repeated clear realization" (*abhisamaya*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*) is mentioned, and not that of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Answer: It should also be stated for those beyond training.
As for that which is not mentioned,
one should know that there is more to be said. Some say:
In this context, by mentioning the first, the latter is implied.
If one speaks of the repeated clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*),
it should be understood that the repeated clear observation of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) has also been explained.
As when mentioning the beginning reveals what follows,
mentioning the initial entry reveals that one has already crossed over,
and mentioning the preparatory application reveals the final consummation.
It should be understood that it is likewise so. Some say:
"If one abandons afflictions never before abandoned."
Regarding those who attain the fruits of śramaṇaship never before attained,
this refers to the "repeated clear observation" (punarabhisamaya).
At that time, for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), there is no severing of afflictions not previously severed.
Furthermore, it is not that one has attained a fruit of śrāmaṇya never before attained;
for this reason, it is not mentioned. Some say:
If one severs a previously unsevered acquisition of fetters and attains a previously unattained acquisition of disjunction,
this is called "repeated clear observation" (punar-abhisamaya).

At that time, although the one beyond training (aśaikṣa) attains the acquisition of disjunction (visaṃyoga-prāpti) never before attained, they do not sever the acquisition of fetters (bandhana-prāpti) never before severed;
therefore, this is not mentioned,
just as in the case of severing the acquisition of fetters.
One attains the acquisition of dissociation;
one eliminates faults and cultivates virtues;
one abandons the inferior and realizes the sublime.
Abandoning the meaningless and grasping the meaningful,
exhausting thirst and craving, and ending suffering and painful sensation to attain the coolness of bliss—
this should be understood in the same way.
Some say: one abandons the ignorance never before abandoned and attains the wisdom never before attained.
This explains the "re-manifestation" (punarabhisamaya).
Although at that time one who has no more to learn (aśaikṣa) attains wisdom never before attained,
they do not abandon ignorance never before abandoned.
Therefore, it is not mentioned. One should understand that this is stated in reliance upon defiled non-knowledge.
It is by means of such various causes and conditions [that this is so].
The faculty of one in training (śaikṣa) emphasizes direct realization, not that of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Question: What is the faculty of one who has full knowledge (ājñātāvīndriya)?
Answer: It is the Arhat whose outflows are exhausted (kṣīṇāsrava).
The wisdom of all those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*),

and all other faculties by which one attains liberation through wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*) or both-fold liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukti*) and dwells in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Among these, the faculty of wisdom belonging to the Arhats who have exhausted the outflows and are beyond training refers here to the faculty of wisdom and all the faculties associated with it.
This includes those liberated by wisdom,
those liberated both ways, and those capable of attaining dwelling in happiness in the present life.
The remaining eight faculties are spoken of;
these nine faculties taken together are called the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya).
Question: Does the learner (śaikṣa) also possess dwelling in happiness in the present life?
Why is it that only those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are mentioned?
Answer: Those still in training (śaikṣa) should also be mentioned;
however, they are not mentioned because—
One should know that there is more to it.
Some say that here,
by mentioning the end, the beginning is revealed.
If it is said that those beyond training (aśaikṣa) attain dwelling in happiness in the present life,
one should know that this already implies that those in training (śaikṣa) also attain dwelling in happiness in the present life;
for by mentioning the end, the beginning is revealed.
Just as the mention of "having already crossed" reveals the initial entry,
one should know that the mention of "ultimate completion" likewise reveals the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, regarding this statement that the meaning is superior:
in terms of the dharmas,
the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) are superior.
In terms of *pudgalas*,
the *aśaikṣa* (one beyond training) *pudgala* is superior.
Some say:
Regarding the statement here that one attains the bliss of pliancy (praśrabdhi) which is not impaired by the heat of the afflictions (kleśa):
although a practitioner in training (śaikṣa) may attain the bliss of pliancy,
they are still impaired by the heat of the afflictions.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, in this context, the mention of "the mastery over the vast bliss of pliancy" refers to one who is training because there is still work to be done.
Although one experiences the bliss of pliancy,
it is neither autonomous nor vast.
Just as a king who has not yet eliminated all his enemies may enjoy royal pleasures,
yet lacks sovereignty and finds them neither vast nor extensive.
That case is also like this;
therefore, it is not mentioned. Some say:

Regarding the statement here that "the intention of one who has already stilled the afflictions is fulfilled, and thus possesses the marks of a Muni," this does not apply to those in training; therefore,
it is not mentioned in their case.
Some say that what is taught here is that there is dwelling in happiness in the present life,
but no dwelling in happiness in future lives.
Since both types of learners abide happily in both [realms],
they are not mentioned.
It is for such reasons as these that [they are excluded].
It is said that the state of abiding in happiness belongs to those beyond training (aśaikṣa), not to those still in training (śaikṣa).
Question: Are there Arhats who possess the three types of higher knowledge (traividyā)? If there are, [what of them]?
Why is it not stated here?
If [the self] does not exist,
how can one explain the various scriptural passages that speak of it freely?
As it is said:
the Venerable Śāriputra, with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One,
these five hundred bhikṣus..."
How many are those possessing the three knowledges (trividyā)?
How many are those liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta)?
How many are those liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta)?
In this context, a further question arises from the preceding discussion:
Does the Venerable Śāriputra know this matter?
If he knows it, why does he ask?
If one does not know this,
how can they be called a Śrāvaka who has attained the pāramitās?
One should speak thus:
That venerable one knows.
If so, why does he ask?
There are indeed those who ask even though they know.
As stated in the Vinaya:
at that time, the Blessed One, though already knowing [the answer], asked the question intentionally.
For this reason, one should not withhold answering a question merely because one already knows it.
Some say that the Venerable One [asked this] for the sake of benefiting others; that is to say,
although Śāriputra already understood it himself, [he asked].
Yet he knows that among the assembly there are those who do not understand;
because they lack fearlessness, they are unable to question the Buddha.
Śāriputra, however, is free from such faults.
He asked the question for the sake of benefiting others.
Some say it was because the Venerable One wished to reveal the specific distinctions within the general category.
This means that the Buddha taught the Dharma appropriately to five hundred bhikṣus;
upon hearing it, they all attained the fruit of arhatship,
forever severing future existence and bringing joy to the Buddha's heart.
"All sentient beings who truly meet the Buddha’s heart" refers to those who have attained the fruit of arhatship and have forever severed further existence.
The Venerable Śāriputra then thought to himself: "Those bhikṣus..."
Although all have attained the fruit of arhatship and forever severed future existence,
it is not yet known which among them first applied themselves with diligent exertion and which did not; thus,
one wishes to reveal the distinctions within that general category.
Therefore, he asked this question.
Some say that the Blessed One had previously taught the Dharma to five hundred bhikṣus, causing them to abide equally in the fruits [of the path].
The Venerable Śāriputra asked this question because he wished to demonstrate that there are distinctions within that path. Some say:
The World-Honored One had previously taught the Dharma to five hundred bhikṣus,
causing them to abide in the liberation of equanimity and the unconditioned.
Venerable Śāriputra—
This question was posed in order to demonstrate that there is indeed a distinction between those [beings] and liberation;
thus it is said.
The Venerable One, wishing to manifest this treasury of merit so that it may be known by the world, acted as follows:
just as a worldly treasure is covered over by earth such that people do not see it, yet once it is uncovered they are able to see it and conceive a sense of wonder; so too is this case.
This treasury of merit, which was covered by the soil of fewness-of-wishes and remained unknown to the world,
became known to all people and inspired thoughts of wonder because it was revealed by Śāriputra.
Some say that the Venerable One intended to inspire a superior resolve in the donors; for there were certain donors who,
during the four months of the rainy season, [gave alms].
By providing robes and other necessities to the community of monks,
they may give rise to this thought:
"Is the field to which I have made this offering excellent and beautiful?"
Desiring to cause them to give rise to the certain knowledge that "we have planted merit in a fertile field; how joyful is what we have done!
Our effort has not been in vain," the Venerable One therefore posed this question.
Some say that the Venerable One intended to manifest the ritual protocol between teacher and disciple, for it is the proper method:
namely, that a disciple ought to question his teacher.
The Master’s duty is to instruct his disciples.
Some say that the Venerable One manifested this to show that his pursuit of the Dharma was insatiable and that he was free from all indolence and pride.
It is the same for others as well;
therefore, this question is asked. Some say:
The Venerable One, wishing to cut off the worldlings' sense of being slightly knowledgeable—
which leads them to become conceited and satisfied, and thus not to inquire of others—
thought to himself: "The wisdom of these worldlings..."
"It does not equal even one-sixteenth part of what I possess;
yet I still question others.
How much more so should you, who have but little knowledge and little insight, not ask?"
Some say that the Venerable One wished to demonstrate his freedom from the defilement of stinginess regarding the Dharma;
for one who is stingy with the Dharma does not even give rise to joy when seeing others inquire about it.
How much more so when asking oneself.
Some say that the Venerable One [asked this] in order to stop the slanders of the non-Buddhists.
It refers to how various non-Buddhists constantly slander the Buddha, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama, because he has taken Upatiṣya and Kolita under his care,
receives the Dharma from them at night and preaches it to others during the day."
If Śāriputra were to join his palms in reverent salutation before the great assembly and inquire about this,
such slander would then cease.
Some say that the Venerable One asked this question because he wished to demonstrate that all well-spoken words of the Blessed One’s disciples must be sealed with the seal of the Buddha.
Just as all official warrants and documents issued by a king are not accepted by anyone without the royal seal,
and are obstructed at all passes and checkpoints; so it is with this.
If a person possesses a royal seal, all will trust and believe them, and they will encounter no obstacles wherever they go. Likewise,
whatever well-spoken teachings a disciple of the Buddha possesses,
if they lack the seal of the Buddha, others will not trust or accept them.
After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, the fourfold assembly will likewise not respectfully accept [the teachings].
However, those which are sealed with the seal of the Buddha,
upon hearing them, they shall practice accordingly.
The fourfold assembly of the remaining Dharma also gave rise to deep respect.
For these reasons, Śāriputra posed this question:
"If there were no Arhats possessing the three types of supernormal knowledge (traividyā)..."
How is what is stated in that sutra to be reconciled?
One should reply that there are Arhats who possess the three types of higher knowledge (trividyā).
[The opponent] asks: If that is so, then...
That sutra explains it well;
why is this not stated here?
The answer is: it should indeed be stated here as follows.
Furthermore, regarding all those who possess the faculties, the liberation through wisdom, the twofold liberation, and the three knowledges (trividyā),
and who are able to attain dwelling in happiness in the present life—
yet [the Buddha] does not speak of them.
One should know that there is more to be said.
Furthermore, it has already been stated among the previous explanations,
namely, the arhat of the three clear knowledges (traividya).
Either one liberated by wisdom,
or one liberated both ways.
If it is said that they are liberated by wisdom:

It should be understood that by speaking of the wisdom-liberated one (prajñāvimukta), one has already spoken of the three knowledges (trividyā) of the wisdom-liberated one; if one speaks of the doubly-liberated one (ubhayatobhāgavimukta),
it should be understood that one has already spoken of the three knowledges of the doubly-liberated one.
Therefore, it is not explained separately.
Formerly, regarding this meaning, there were two masters:
one was named Kālavīra.
The second was named Kauṣṭhila.
The Venerable Śāriputra particularly praised wisdom,
while the Venerable Kauṣṭhila particularly praised the meditative attainment of cessation.
At that time, Vīra spoke as follows:
"Superior wisdom is not the attainment of cessation;
wisdom possesses an object of perception."
Because the attainment of cessation has no object of cognition, Rāśīvarman stated as follows: "The attainment of cessation is superior;
it is not an extinction through wisdom, and it exists only for noble ones."
Because wisdom is present even in ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those who praise wisdom have said this:
"If one possesses the three types of higher knowledge (*traividya*) but does not possess the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*),
this is called 'one who possesses the three types of higher knowledge'."
If one possesses both the three knowledges (trividyā) and the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa),
they are also called "one who possesses the three knowledges. If one possesses the eight liberations but not the three knowledges, [they are not so called].
This is called liberation through both [tranquility and insight].
If one possesses either one clear knowledge or two clear knowledges,
this is called liberation through wisdom.
Why is this? Because wisdom excels the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
Those who praise the meditative attainment of cessation speak as follows:
If one possesses the eight liberations but is not one of the three knowledges,
this is called "liberated through both.
If one possesses the eight liberations and also the three knowledges, [this is called "liberated through wisdom"].
They are also called "liberated through both.
If one possesses the three knowledges (*traividya*) but does not possess the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*),
this is termed "one with the three knowledges."
If one possesses either one clear knowledge or two clear knowledges,
they are called "liberated by wisdom. Why is this so?
Because of the superior wisdom of the meditative absorption of cessation,
the efforts made by both of these [positions] are rendered futile;
they are of no benefit to the letter and no benefit to the meaning.
However, among those who possess the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā), some attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and some do not.
Those who attain it are called "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) and possess the three types of supernormal knowledge.
If one does not attain [the higher fruits], they are called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñā-vimukta) and possess the three types of clear knowledge (trividyā).
Now, I shall further explain the reasons for the distinct designations of each of the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
Question: Why is it called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñātāvya-indriya)?
Answer: It is that which knows what was not yet known and realizes what was not yet realized.
Because it abandons ignorance, it is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Question: If this is so, when the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises,
one attains direct realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the suffering of the five aggregates within the desire realm.
When the dharma-knowledge of suffering arises, one again attains clear observation (*abhisamaya*) therein;
this would then be a clear observation after having already attained clear observation.
Why, then, is it still called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?
Is it not called the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya)?

Answer: The patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is termed "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*) with respect to the suffering of the five aggregates in the desire realm;
however, it is not yet "already realized."
When the dharma-knowledge of suffering arises, it is then called "already having realized" (abhisamita);
however, because it is not a case of realizing what has already been realized,
it is not termed the faculty of "having known" (ājñātendriya).

Some say that although the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*) with respect to the suffering of the five aggregates in the desire realm,
it is not called "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Because it is not yet of the nature of wisdom (*jñāna*),
it is only when the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) arises that it can be called "knowing.
At that time, although it is termed "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*), [it is still not the full knowledge].
However, this is a direct realization (*abhisamaya*) rather than knowing what was already known;
therefore, it is not called the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātendriya*).
Furthermore, the discussion here is based on the direct realization through wisdom (*jñānābhisamaya*).
Because it is not patience (*kṣānti*),
it is neither called "already having realized" nor "realizing"; how, then,
could it be called the faculty of having known (*ājñātendriya*)?
Some say that after the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna), there still arises a path that has not yet been fully realized (anabhisamita).
This knowledge, being unmanifested, is overwhelmed and covered by what is to be awakened; it looks downward from the higher [level] to the lower.
Because it is under the dominant influence of that [subsequent cognition], this [previous stage] lacks sovereignty;
for this reason, the dharma-knowledge of suffering is not termed the faculty of "already known.
The same applies to the remaining patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*).
Question: Why is it called the faculty of "one who has already known"?
Answer: Because one knows what has already been known, and realizes through direct insight what has already been realized.
It is called the faculty of "I have known" (ājñātendriya) because it is the abandonment of ignorance.
Question: If that is the case, when the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti) arises...
Excluding its own nature, its associated factors, and its co-existent factors,
one attains clear realization (abhisamaya) regarding all other paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
Following this, the subsequent path-knowledge (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) arises.
One attains clear realization (abhisamaya) regarding the factors that are of the same nature as, associated with,

and co-existent with the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti). At that time, one realizes those factors— the nature of that patience and so forth— which had not yet been clearly realized.
Why is it called the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya) and not the faculty of "yet to be known" (ājñāsyāmīndriya)?
Answer: The masters of foreign lands (bahirdeśaka-ācārya) say that all sixteen moments of mind constitute the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Question: We are not currently asking about them.
However, it is asked: why are fifteen moments of mind designated as the path of seeing?
Regarding this, the Venerable Saṃghavasu said:
When the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti) manifests in the present,
one is able to cultivate, in the future, the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path in immeasurable world-systems.
That which is cultivated by them has already attained clear realization (abhisamaya) with respect to the present patience and so forth.
"Therefore, there is no fault.
This is not reasonable,
because a future path lacks functional activity.
One should answer thus:
"In terms of the majority, they are said to have already attained clear realization (abhisamaya).
That is to say, those who have already attained clear realization are immeasurable and boundless."
Those who have not yet attained clear realization are but few;
those who have already attained clear realization and continue to realize it are like the great earth.
Those who have not yet realized what is to be realized are like a single mote of dust on Mount Sumeru,
or a single drop of water in the great ocean.
The analogy of the mosquito in empty space is likewise.
Therefore, from the perspective of the majority of cases, it is called the faculty of "having already known" (ājñātendriya).
Question: At the moment of the sixteenth mind, it should be like the seven knowledges (jñāna).
Why is it specifically called the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātendriya*), rather than "one who knows what was not yet known"?
Answer: This too is stated from the perspective of the majority.
This means that although the first moment resembles the seven knowledges,
all subsequent moments differ from them; yet,
speaking in terms of the majority, they are all designated as the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya).
Because it is of a single nature.
Some say that after this,
there is nothing further that has not yet been known.
That which is overwhelmed and covered by the Path does not allow the lower to adhere to the upper,
thereby depriving one of self-mastery;
for it must necessarily be so.
Regarding the statement "one who knows says they know":
it is just as one who is in the process of going is called "one who has gone";
that case is also like this.
Question: Why is it called the faculty of one who has already known?
Answer: Because one knows what is already known, and realizes what has already been realized.
Because ignorance has already been severed and will not arise again, it is called the faculty of one who has perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*). Question:
If this is so, then all those in the three vehicles who have attained the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) would possess this faculty of perfect knowledge.
For what reason is the Blessed One alone named Buddha?
Answer: Because he is able to awaken first, and because he is able to awaken universally.
Because he is able to awaken to [the truth] that others cannot,
he is called a Buddha; the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to awaken to it initially,
nor are they able to awaken to it universally.
Because they cannot discern and awaken [to this],
they are not called Buddhas. Some say:
If one has personally awakened to, universally awakened to,
and awakened without error regarding all that can be known (*jñeya*),
one is called a Buddha.
Although the pratyekabuddhas are able to awaken by themselves,
they lack the other two types [of awakening];
the śrāvakas lack both.
Therefore, they are not called Buddhas. Some say:
"If one is able to awaken spontaneously to all conditions..."
One who possesses the awakening to all aspects is called a Buddha.
Although a Pratyekabuddha possesses spontaneous awakening,
they lack the awakening to all aspects.
Śrāvakas lack both;
therefore, they are not called Buddhas. Some say:
If wisdom, with respect to the subject and object of cognition,
the modes of activity and the objects of focus,
and the faculties and their respective objects—
One who possesses the capacity for objects and,
within the sphere of the knowable (*jñeya*),
is able to illuminate and awaken universally, is called a Buddha.
The two vehicles are not like this.
Some say: "If one hears [the teaching] and does not abandon it..."
This is what is called a Buddha;
the two vehicles are not so. Some say:
If, within the continuum [of consciousness],
all irrational habitual tendencies are forever suppressed,
one is called a Buddha.
The followers of the two vehicles are not like this.
Some say that if one can exhaust the source and bottom of the river of profound dependent origination, [one attains liberation].
They are designated as Buddhas;
the followers of the two vehicles are not so.
Therefore, the sutra uses the metaphor of three animals crossing a river.
These refer to the rabbit, the horse, and the elephant.
The rabbit crosses by merely floating upon the water; the horse either treads on the ground or floats while crossing;
and the fragrant elephant always treads upon the bottom as it crosses.
The śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas cross the river of dependent origination in that same sequence, respectively;
so it is said by some.
If one eliminates two kinds of ignorance—
namely, the defiled and the non-defiled—
one is called a Buddha.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are able only to sever defilement,
but they do not sever non-defilement;
therefore, they are not called Buddhas.
Some say: if one abandons two kinds of doubt, namely,
doubt regarding the object (*vastu*) and latent proclivity (*anuśaya*).
One is designated as a Buddha because of this;
although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have eliminated the latent tendencies (anuśaya), they have not eliminated the objective phenomena (vastu),
and therefore they are not called Buddhas.

Some say that at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), both obstacles are severed— the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstacle to liberation (*vimokṣāvaraṇa*)— and the mind attains liberation;
this one is called a Buddha.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas may first be liberated from the afflictive obscurations and later from the cognitive obscurations;
or they may first sever the cognitive obscurations.
Subsequently, regarding the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
there are none who are liberated from both [obstacles];
therefore, they are not called Buddhas.
Some say that one who possesses both perfections is designated as a Buddha.
This refers to other sentient beings who possess both the basis and that which depends upon it;
or those who possess the perfection of the basis but not that which depends upon it,
such as a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
Alternatively, there may be perfection of the basis but not of the supported;
this refers to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Only the Buddha possesses both, and thus receives the name "Buddha."
It should be understood that the same applies to the basis and the based, as well as to the vessel and everything within that vessel,
including light and formations (*saṃskāra*). Some say:
If these three factors are perfected, one is called a Buddha— namely,
physical form (*rūpa*), lineage (*jāti*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
The followers of the two vehicles do not possess these.
Some say that if three factors are perfected, one is called a Buddha: namely,
the making of a vow, the accomplishment of its fruit, and the answering of questions at will.
The followers of the two vehicles are not like this.
Some say that one who possesses the three forms of non-protection and the three uncommon applications of mindfulness is called a Buddha.
The two vehicles are not like this.
Some say that if what is spoken of is non-dual, [then it is so].
With inexhaustible eloquence and infallible prophecy,
he is called a Buddha.
The followers of the two vehicles are not like this.
Some say that if one possesses the four knowledges, they are called a Buddha.
That is to say, it refers to knowledge of causes, knowledge of time, knowledge of characteristics, and knowledge of exposition;
the followers of the two vehicles do not possess these. Some say:
If one possesses four types of wisdom, one is called a Buddha;
namely, unattached wisdom and unimpeded wisdom.
It is unerring wisdom and non-retrogressive wisdom;
the two vehicles are not thus.
Some say: if one possesses various causal cognitions and various resultant cognitions.
The various successive awakenings and the various counteractive awakenings are designated as "Buddha."
The two vehicles are not like this. Some say:
"If one cannot be defiled by the eight worldly dharmas," [one is a bodhisattva].
One who has reached the further shore of merit such that no one can equal them,
and who is capable of rescuing all those in peril and distress,
is called a Buddha.
The two vehicles are not so.
Some say that if one possesses the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma), [one is a Buddha].
The ten powers,
the four fearlessnesses,
and great compassion.
The three unique applications of mindfulness are designated as belonging to the Buddha alone;
the two vehicles do not possess them in this way.
Some say: If one possesses a profound, subtle,
and universal great compassionate mind that is impartial, [one may enter this state].

He is called a Buddha because he has accumulated [merit and wisdom] over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). As for "profound and far-reaching," it is because it has been amassed over those three incalculable eons.
It is subtle because it perceives the three types of suffering; it is pervasive because it accompanies all states of existence.
Because it takes the three realms as its object.
It is "equal" because it functions without distinction toward enemies and friends.
Due to such various causes and conditions, among the three types of those possessing complete knowledge (*trividyā*), only one is designated as a Buddha.
Question: For what reason, O Bhagavān, [is this so] regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)?
Why are only the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and so forth established as faculties (*indriya*), and not the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*) and so forth?
Answer: Because the form-base and so forth lack the characteristics of a faculty.
Some say that those subsumed under the internal bases (ādhyātmikāyatana) are established as faculties (indriya),
while those subsumed under the external bases (bāhyāyatana) are not.
Some say: if something functions as a basis (*āśraya*), it is established as a faculty (*indriya*);
however, that which functions solely as an object (*ālambana*) is not so established.
The same applies to the statement regarding the possessor of an object and the object itself.
Some say that only those things included within the category of sentient beings are established as faculties (*indriya*).
If it were indeterminate, it would not be established as such.
Some say that only those which are appropriated (*upātta*) are established as faculties (*indriya*).
Those that are non-existent or indeterminate are not established [as faculties]. Some say:
"Only those subsumed within the continuum are established as faculties."
Those that are indeterminate are not established [as faculties]. Some say:
"If something is experienced solely within one's own continuum, it is established as a faculty."
Those that are indeterminate are not established [as faculties].
Some say that only those which are unique (unshared) are established as faculties.
If they were common [to both], they would not be established as distinct.
Question: For what reason, World-Honored One, do you establish two separate faculties for painful feeling and pleasant feeling within the aggregate of sensation?
Is the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant established as only one?
Answer: The sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant should also be established as two;
yet it is not so established.
One should know that this is an incomplete teaching.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to adorn the meaning with various phrases and various explanations so that it may be easily understood.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to manifest two gateways and two summaries.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Furthermore, the two feelings of suffering and pleasure may be sharp and clear,
or they may not be sharp and clear.
There is restlessness;
there is non-restlessness;
there is stability.
There are those who do not abide securely;
for those who are intelligent, fickle, and lack stability,
the feelings of sorrow and joy are established.
For those who are not dull-witted, not fickle, and who abide in stability,
there arise feelings of pleasure,
pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Because they are merely not clear-sharp and not light-fickle, but abide [in their respective states],
they are established as one combined category.
Furthermore, because the transformation of painful feeling and pleasant feeling differs, [they are distinguished].
Each is divided into two:
namely, the transformation of the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) and the transformation of the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya);
and the transformation of the faculty of pain (duḥkhendriya).
The faculty of grief undergoes transformation,
whereas neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling does not undergo such transformation; therefore,
they are combined and established as one.
Furthermore, because painful feeling and pleasant feeling are mutually contradictory,
each is divided into two;
that is to say, they are distinguished by their mutual opposition as suffering and pleasure.
Sorrow and joy are mutually contradictory;
however, the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant lacks such contradiction.
Therefore, it is only said: "Why is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) not established as a faculty (*indriya*)?"
Answer: Non-faculty dharmas (*anindriya-dharma*) are numerous;
why ask specifically about perception (*saṃjñā*)? [Objection:
Just as within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), few are established as faculties (*indriya*).
The aggregates of feeling and consciousness are both established as faculties,
yet only perception (saṃjñā) is not so established;
for what reason is this asked?
The answer is: because perception lacks the characteristic of being a faculty (*indriya*).
Furthermore, a faculty functions by its own power, whereas perception is induced by another.
Just as a hired laborer acts immediately when instructed by another and does not act when not so instructed,
so too does perception (saṃjñā) operate toward its object.
It is likewise in this way:
