translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Six: The Aggregate of the Faculties (*Indriya-skandha*). Chapter One: The Summary of the Faculties (*Indriya-saṃgraha*). Part Four. Of these twenty-two faculties, how many are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and so forth, as explained at length?
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed once again?

Answer: While the preceding section refuted the intention of those who claim that [the afflictions] are abandoned all at once (*sakṛt-prahāṇa*), it has not yet refuted the claim that there is a simultaneous realization (*sakṛt-abhisamaya*).
Furthermore, the gradual realization (anupūrvābhisamaya) has not yet been clarified;
now, wishing to exclude misconceptions and reveal the truth, this treatise is composed. Some say:
The preceding section also refuted sudden realization (*sakṛt-abhisamaya*) and indicated gradual realization (*anupūrva-abhisamaya*),
though not with full clarity.
Now, wishing to make this clear, this treatise is composed.
Some say that the reason for composing this treatise is the desire to analyze the five classes of afflictions and their five corresponding antidotes.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
The five categories of afflictions refer to those abandoned through the vision of suffering,
up to and including those abandoned through cultivation.
The fivefold antidotes refer to the patience regarding suffering and the knowledge regarding suffering,
up to the patience regarding the path and the knowledge regarding the path.
Of these twenty-two faculties,
how many are abandoned through the vision of suffering,
and how many are abandoned through the vision of the origin?
How many are abandoned through the vision of cessation?
How many are abandoned through the vision of the path?
How many are abandoned through cultivation?
How many are not to be abandoned?
Answer: Nine are to be abandoned by cultivation;
three are not to be abandoned.
Ten [factors] should be distinguished.
Nine are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
namely, the seven material faculties, the life-faculty, and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
The three that are non-abandonable refer to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Regarding the ten that should be analyzed:
That is to say, the mental faculty (manas) and the five faculties beginning with sensation (vedanā).
That is to say, the mental faculty is either abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya),
or abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, or the path (samudaya-nirodha-mārga-darśana-prahātavya).
Some are abandoned through cultivation;
some are not abandoned.
What is abandoned through the vision of suffering?

This refers to the mental faculty (*manendriya*) abandoned by the patience at the limit of the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya-antika-kṣānti*), which follows either faith or the Dharma.
Furthermore, what is this?
It refers to the mental faculty associated with the twenty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned through the vision of the origin?
It refers to the faculty of mind belonging to those who practice in accordance with faith or in accordance with the Dharma,
which is abandoned by the patience at the conclusion of the clear realization of the origin.
Furthermore, what is this?
It refers to the mental faculty (*manas*) associated with the nineteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*)?
This refers to the mental faculty (manas-indriya) of those who practice through faith (śraddhānusārin) or through the Dharma (dharmānusārin),
which is to be abandoned by the patience (kṣānti) at the conclusion of the clear realization of cessation (nirodha-abhisamaya). Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to the mental faculty (*manas*) associated with the nineteen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*)?
It refers to the mental faculty belonging to those who practice the path by following faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or by following the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
It is abandoned by the patience at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, what is this?
It refers to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) associated with the twenty-two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
What is abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to the faculty of mind that belongs to those in training who have seen the path and is abandoned through cultivation.
What, again, is this?
This refers to the mental faculty (*manas*) associated with the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the non-defiled, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) mental faculty.
What is not to be abandoned?
It refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) mental faculty.
As with the faculty of mind,
so it is with the faculty of equanimity.
The faculty of pleasure may be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Some are abandoned by the vision of suffering, some by the vision of origin, some by the vision of cessation, and some by the vision of the path;
some are abandoned by cultivation;
and some are not abandoned.
What is abandoned through the vision of suffering?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure belonging to those who practice in accordance with faith or in accordance with the Dharma,
which is abandoned by the patience at the edge of the clear observation of suffering.
What, furthermore, is this?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with the nine underlying tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
What is [the faculty of pleasure] to be abandoned through the vision of the origin?
This refers to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) belonging to those who practice through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or through the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*),
which is to be abandoned by the patience at the limit of the clear realization of origination (*samudayābhisamayāntika-kṣānti*). Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with the six underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
What is abandoned through the vision of cessation?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure belonging to those who practice in accordance with faith or in accordance with the Dharma.
It is abandoned by the patience at the stage of the clear observation of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya-antya-kṣānti*). What, then, is this?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) associated with the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
What is abandoned by the path of seeing?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure belonging to those who follow by faith or follow by dharma,
which is abandoned by the receptivities at the limit of the clear realization of the path.
What, then, is this? It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with the seven underlying tendencies abandoned through the path of seeing.
What is abandoned through cultivation?

This refers to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have seen the tracks [of the path] and is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). What, then, is this?
It is the faculty of pleasure associated with the five latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are to be abandoned by cultivation.
And the undefiled, outflow-tainted faculty of pleasure (*anāsrava-sāsrava-sukhendriya*).
As for the five latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are:
craving and ignorance belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Regarding the greed, pride, and ignorance of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), how are they not abandoned? It is said:
by means of the untainted faculty of pleasure (*anāsrava-sukhendriya*).
The faculty of joy (sukhendriya) is either abandoned through the vision of suffering,
or abandoned through the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, or the vision of the path,
or it is abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Or it is not abandoned.
What is abandoned through the vision of suffering?
It refers to the faculty of joy belonging to those who practice in accordance with faith or in accordance with the Dharma.
It is abandoned by the patience at the conclusion of the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya-antya-kṣānti*). What, then, is this?
It refers to the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) associated with the seventeen underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
The seventeen latent dispositions (anuśaya) consist of all those of the form realm, excluding anger and doubt from the desire realm.
What is abandoned through the vision of the origin?

It refers to the faculty of joy (*somanasyendriya*) that is abandoned by the patiences (*kṣānti*) at the conclusion of the clear realization of the origin for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to the faculty of joy associated with the eleven underlying tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
What is abandoned through the vision of cessation?
It refers to the faculty of joy belonging to those who practice in accordance with faith or in accordance with the Dharma.
It is abandoned by the patience at the conclusion of the clear realization of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya-antya-kṣānti*). What, then, is this?
It refers to the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) associated with the eleven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
What is abandoned by the path of seeing?
It refers to the faculty of joy belonging to those who follow by faith or follow by dharma,
which is abandoned by the patiences at the conclusion of the clear realization of the path.
What, furthermore, is this?
It refers to the faculty of joy associated with the twelve latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of seeing.
What is that which is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya)?
This refers to the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have seen the tracks [of the path] and is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, what is this?
It refers to the faculty of joy associated with the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are to be abandoned through cultivation.
And the non-defiled, out-flowing faculty of joy (*anāsrava-saṃkliṣṭa-prīti-indriya*).
As for the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
they consist of those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) with the exception of hatred (*dveṣa*).
All [factors] of the form realm.
How is it that they are not to be abandoned?
It refers to the untainted faculty of joy (*anāsrava-prīti-indriya*).
The faculty of sorrow (daurmanasyendriya) is either abandoned through the vision of suffering,
or abandoned through the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, or the vision of the path,
or it is abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
What is abandoned through the vision of suffering?
It refers to the faculty of mental grief (daurmanasyendriya) belonging to those who practice in accordance with faith (śraddhānusārin) or in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusārin),
which is abandoned by the patience (kṣānti) at the conclusion of the clear observation of suffering (duḥkhābhisamaya).
What, then, is this? It refers to the faculty of grief associated with the four proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
As for these four proclivities:
This refers to the false view, hatred, doubt, and ignorance of the desire realm.
How are these abandoned through the vision of the origin?
This refers to the faculty of mental grief for those who practice according to faith or according to the Dharma.
It is abandoned by the forbearance at the limit of the full comprehension of the origin (*samudaya-abhisamaya-antya-kṣānti*). Furthermore, what is this?
It refers to the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) associated with the four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin.
What is abandoned through the vision of cessation?

It refers to the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) that is abandoned by the patience at the limit of the clear realization of cessation for those who practice in accordance with faith or in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to the faculty of mental grief associated with the four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
What is abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*)?

It refers to the faculty of mental grief abandoned by the patiences (*kṣānti*) at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamaya-anta*) for those who practice according to faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or according to the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
What, then, is this? It refers to the faculty of grief associated with the four underlying tendencies (anuśaya) abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga).
What is abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga)?
This refers to the faculty of grief that is abandoned through cultivation by those on the path of training who have seen the tracks [of the truths].
Furthermore, what is this?
It refers to the faculty of grief associated with the two types of latent dispositions abandoned through cultivation, as well as the non-defiled faculty of grief.
The two underlying tendencies refer to aversion and ignorance within the desire realm;
the five faculties, such as faith and so forth, are either to be abandoned through cultivation.
Or they are not abandoned.
What is abandoned through cultivation?
It refers to the five faculties, such as faith, that are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
What is "not to be abandoned"?
It refers to the five untainted faculties (indriya), such as faith and so forth.
The various faculties have already been analyzed according to whether they are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and so on.
The meaning of "abandoned through the vision of suffering" (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) and so forth shall now be explained.
Question: What is meant by "abandoned through the vision of suffering," up to and including "abandoned through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Answer: If a phenomenon is an antidote, it is a definitive antidote;
its object of focus is also definitive.
These are termed "to be abandoned by the vision of suffering," up to "to be abandoned by the vision of the path.
This applies to those dharmas whose antidotes are not fixed.
Those whose objects of counteraction are not fixed are called "to be abandoned by cultivation. Some say:
If a dharma is determined by its locus and determined by its object,
it is called "to be abandoned through the vision of suffering" up to "to be abandoned through the vision of the path."
If a dharma is not determined by its locus and its antidote,
and its object is not determined,
it is called "to be abandoned by cultivation."
Some say: if a phenomenon has the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) as its antidote,
it is called "to be abandoned by seeing suffering" (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, if a phenomenon has path-acceptance (*mārga-kṣānti*) or path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*) as its antidote, it is called abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*).
If a phenomenon has the various knowledges (*jñāna*) as its antidote,
it is called abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Some say: if a phenomenon is abandoned by the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*),
it is called "abandoned through the vision of suffering" (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, those phenomena that are abandoned by the patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*) are called "abandoned by the path of seeing" (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*);
those phenomena that are abandoned by the various knowledges (*jñāna*) are [called "abandoned by the path of cultivation"].
It is called "to be abandoned by cultivation. Some say:
if a dharma is abandoned by the contemplation of the Truth of Suffering.
Those [dharmas] abandoned through the vision of suffering are called "abandoned by the vision of suffering," and so on,
up to: those dharmas abandoned through the contemplation of the truth of the path are called "abandoned by the vision of the path."
If a phenomenon is either contemplated as the truth of suffering,
or contemplated as the truths of origin, cessation, or the path,
or is not abandoned through the contemplation of the truths.
These are called "to be abandoned by cultivation. Some say:
if a dharma is contrary to the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya), [it is to be abandoned by cultivation].
Those [factors] are called abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Likewise, up to those factors that are contrary to the vision of the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) are called abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
If a phenomenon contradicts the vision of the four truths,
it is called "to be abandoned by cultivation.
These [refer to] the twenty-two faculties.
How many are views?
How many are not views?
And so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to refute the view of those who claim that all phenomena (dharmas) are of the nature of seeing (*darśana*).
They assert as follows:
That which is characterized by intensity is called a "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).

Since there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not intense with respect to its own function, all things would [otherwise] be called views; it is for the sake of precluding such an attachment that [the definition is restricted].

This treatise is composed to clarify that, among all phenomena, only the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and a small portion of wisdom (*prajñā*) are designated as "vision" (*darśana*), and nothing else.
These are the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).
How many are views?
How many are not views?
Answer: One is a view.
Seventeen are not views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Four should be analyzed.
One is a view.
That is to say, the eye faculty.
Seventeen are not seeing:
namely, the six faculties of visible form, the life faculty, the mind faculty, the five faculties of feeling, and the four faculties beginning with faith.
Regarding the four that should be analyzed:
this refers to the three untainted faculties of wisdom.
The faculty of wisdom is either vision (*darśana*).
Or it is not vision. What is vision?
It refers to the faculty of wisdom associated with the mental consciousness that is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
What is that which is not view?
It refers to other faculties of wisdom, namely the faculty of wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses,
as well as the faculty of wisdom subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" is either seeing or not seeing.
In what way is it seeing?
This refers to the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
Why is it not [simply] "view" (dṛṣṭi)?
It refers to the other faculties subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
That is, the remaining eight faculties.
As it is with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," so it is also with the faculty of "having known."
The faculty of one who has already attained full knowledge (ājñātāvīndriya) is either vision or not vision. What is vision?

It refers to the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) included within the faculty of one who has already attained full knowledge, but which is not subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) or the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
What is that which is not vision?
It refers to the remaining faculties subsumed under the faculty of one who has perfect knowledge (ājñātāvīndriya),
namely, the other eight faculties.
Furthermore, regarding the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*),
the faculties such as vision (*darśana*) have already been analyzed;
their meanings shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason is it called "view" (*darśana*), and what is the meaning of this term?
Answer: It is called "view" by virtue of four conditions.
First, because it is capable of observation;
second, because it is investigative and decisive;
third, because it is firm and persistent.
Regarding "because of penetrating deeply into the object of focus" and "because of being able to observe":
this refers to seeing the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Question: Regarding wrong view and inverted view, what is their object of observation?
Answer: Therefore, it is said that they have the intrinsic nature [of phenomena] as their object.
This means that although it is a false and inverted view,
its intrinsic nature is that of vision and wisdom; therefore,
it is said to be "capable of observing."
Just as a person is called a "capable observer" whenever they perceive something,
unlike one who is blind;
so too is it for one who has reached certainty through inference.
This refers to the ability to investigate and determine.
Question: How can one investigate within the span of a single moment?
Answer: Because its nature is sharp and acute, it is called "investigation."
Regarding "due to stubborn adherence":
this refers to various views and biased attachments that are so firm and tenacious that they cannot be relinquished except through the power of the Noble Path.
"Deeply entering the object of focus" means penetrating the objective field with intensity,
like a needle falling into soft mud.
Some say that it is called "view" (dṛṣṭi) due to two conditions:
first, because its nature is that of illuminating and discerning.
Second, because it is of a nature that involves inferential judgment (*tarka*).
Some say that it is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) by virtue of three conditions.
First, because it possesses the characteristic of being visible;
second, because it constitutes the object of seeing;
third, because it is unimpeded with respect to its object.
Some say that it is called "view" (dṛṣṭi) due to three conditions:
first, because of intentionality (āśaya).
Second, because of attachment;
third, because of determination. Some say:
It is called "view" (dṛṣṭi) by virtue of three conditions:
first, due to intention;
second, due to application; and third, due to ignorance.
"By way of intention" means one whose intention is corrupted;
"by way of application" means...
This refers to those whose preparatory application has been destroyed;
"due to lack of wisdom" refers to those whose [application] is destroyed in both respects.
Furthermore, "by way of intention" refers to the practitioner of meditative concentration;
"by way of application" refers to the preparatory effort.
"Those who investigate" refers to those who lack wisdom;
"those who follow what they have heard" refers to those who merely repeat what they have been taught.
Of these twenty-two faculties,
how many are with vitarka and with vicāra?
[The answer continues] at length as follows.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to refute the assertions of the Dārṣṭāntikas (Analogists).
They claim that [the process of rebirth] extends from the Desire Realm up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
All [of these] possess vitarka and vicāra. Why is this?
Because it is so stated in the sūtras.
As stated in the sūtra:
"The coarse nature of the mind is vitarka;
the subtle nature of the mind is vicāra."
Regarding the nature of the coarseness and subtlety of the mind up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
that Venerable One stated:
"The masters of Abhidharma say..."
Vitarka and vicāra are the coarse and subtle natures of the mind.
These natures of coarseness and subtlety are established in mutual dependence;
they are found manifest even up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
To say that vitarka and vicāra exist only in the desire realm and in the Brahma-world is a poor explanation, not a good one.
The masters of the Abhidharma say:
"Our exposition is well-stated and not poorly stated,
for the nature of the coarse and the subtle is explained through many different approaches and is not of a single kind."
As it is said:
"The outbursts (paryavasthāna) are coarse, while the latent dispositions (anuśaya) are subtle;
herein, vitarka and vicāra are neither coarse nor subtle."
Because they are both of the nature of active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
As it is said:
"The aggregate of form is coarse; the four aggregates are subtle."
In this context, both vitarka and vicāra are subtle,
because both are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
As it is said:
The desire realm is coarse and the first dhyāna is subtle;
herein, both vitarka and vicāra are categorized as both coarse and subtle, because both are included within two levels.
As it is said:
The first dhyāna is coarse and the second dhyāna is subtle;
herein, both vitarka and vicāra are coarse.
This is because coarseness and subtlety are explained by way of multiple criteria.
Therefore, vitarka and vicāra do not extend up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
If it were said that vitarka and vicāra extend to the Peak of Existence,
one should not speak of the distinction between three stages.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
from the desire realm up to the peak of existence,
all possess the three natures— wholesome, afflicted, and indeterminate.
All defiled dharmas of every stage are termed "with vitarka and with vicāra.
Only the wholesome and the neutral have distinctions among the three stages. If that is so, then...
Why is it said that with the cessation of vitarka and vicāra,
one enters the second dhyāna, which is without vitarka and vicāra and possesses the joy and bliss born of concentration? He says:
This is stated with reference to wholesome vitarka and vicāra;
it does not refer to those that are defiled.
This explanation is incorrect.
For what reason do you say that it is the wholesome vitarka and vicāra that are extinguished, rather than the defiled ones?
One ought to first extinguish the defiled vitarka and vicāra,
because they must necessarily be severed at the time of becoming free from defilement.
Because they abandon the wholesome by crossing over the boundaries of the stages,
the Dārṣṭāntikas have indeed spoken erroneously;
[the author] wishes to refute their view and demonstrate that vitarka and vicāra exist only in two stages.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
Among these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are with vitarka and vicāra?
How many are without vitarka and with vicāra only?
How many are without vitarka and without vicāra?
Answer: Two have vitarka and vicāra;
eight are without vitarka and without vicāra.
The twelve [faculties] should be analyzed.
Two possess vitarka and vicāra:
namely, the faculties of suffering and mental grief.
The eight that are without vitarka and without vicāra refer to the seven material faculties and the life-faculty.
The twelve that should be analyzed are as follows:
That is to say: the mind-faculty,
the three feelings,
and the five faculties beginning with faith.
The three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
The mind faculty (manas-indriya) is either with vitarka and vicāra,
or without vitarka and with vicāra only.
Or [it is] without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is with vitarka and with vicāra?
It refers to the faculty of mind associated with attention (manasikāra) that possesses vitarka and vicāra.
What, then, is this? It refers to the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) of the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
How is it that there is no vitarka and only vicāra?
This refers to the mental faculty (manas-indriya) associated with attention that is without vitarka and possesses only vicāra.
Furthermore, what is this?
It is the mental faculty of the intermediate dhyāna.
What is "without vitarka and without vicāra"?
It refers to the mental faculty (manas-indriya) associated with attention that is without vitarka and without vicāra.
Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) from the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
As with the faculty of mind,
the same applies to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhādi-pañcendriya*), and the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*).
The faculty of pleasure is either with vitarka and vicāra,
or without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is meant by "with vitarka and vicāra"?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with mental attention that is accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra. What, then, is this?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure in the desire realm and in the first dhyāna.
What is that which is without vitarka and without vicāra?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with mental attention that is without vitarka and without vicāra.
Furthermore, what is this?
This refers to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in the third dhyāna.
As it is with the faculty of pleasure,
so it is with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
However, there is a distinction:
namely, that the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) in the second dhyāna is termed "without vitarka and without vicāra.
The various faculties, such as those with vitarka and vicāra, have already been analyzed.
The meaning of "with vitarka and vicāra" and so forth shall now be explained.
Question: What is meant by "with vitarka and vicāra," and "without vitarka and with only vicāra"?
"Are they without vitarka and without vicāra?
Answer: "If a dharma coexists with vitarka and vicāra, it is associated with vitarka and vicāra."
When vitarka and vicāra arise and both operate together,
it is called "with vitarka and with vicāra."
If a dharma is not associated with vitarka,
but is associated solely with vicāra,
it is dissociated from vitarka.
It is associated only with vicāra;
it does not arise from vitarka,
but arises only from vicāra.
When vitarka has already ceased and only vicāra continues to operate,
it is called "without vitarka and with only vicāra."
If a phenomenon does not coexist with vitarka and vicāra,
is not associated with vitarka and vicāra,
and does not arise from vitarka and vicāra.
When vitarka and vicāra have ceased, it is called "without vitarka and without vicāra.
Some say: if a dharma possesses seeking (paryeṣaṇā), [it is with vitarka].
That which possesses investigation is called "with vitarka and with vicāra.
If a dharma lacks seeking (vitarka), [it is without vitarka].
There is that which possesses investigation (vicāra) but is called "without initial inquiry (vitarka) and with investigation only.
If a dharma lacks both initial inquiry and investigation, [it is called "without initial inquiry and without investigation"].
It is called "without vitarka and without vicāra.
Among these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*),
how many are associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was composed in order to refute the doctrines of other schools and to clarify one's own position.
Just as the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain that the mind and mental factors arise sequentially,
that Venerable One says that the mind and mental factors arise one by one.
As the sutra says: "On a narrow path,
there is not even space for two to pass side by side,
let alone for many."
Alternatively, some say:
if a phenomenon arises through the power of another, it is said to be associated with that [other], and not otherwise;
this is because the mind is able to produce both mind and mental factors.
The mind and mental factors are associated with the mind,
because mental factors can only produce other mental factors. Furthermore,
all mental factors are also mutually associated with one another.
Because mental factors cannot produce the mind,
it is not said that the mind and mental factors are associated.
Alternatively, there are those who hold the following view:
All phenomena are associated only with their own essence.
They state that the meaning of "universal conjunction" (samprayoga) is the meaning of "association" (saṃprayukta).
There is no other universal conjunction [of factors] such as that which exists of a self-entity with respect to itself; therefore,
it is said that association is with one's own nature and not with another.
There is an assertion:
the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is neither associated (*saṃprayukta*) nor dissociated (*viprayukta*) with itself.
It is not associated because it does not observe itself.
It is not that they are non-associated, because they are universally conjoined.
This is to cease such various divergent explanations and to reveal that the mind and mental factors arise simultaneously and are mutually associated.
This treatise is composed not merely with reference to the self-entity, but for the sake of others;

therefore, it asks: among these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), and how many are associated with the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*)?
How many are associated with the faculty of joy?
How many are associated with the faculty of grief?
How many are associated with the faculty of equanimity?
Answer: The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) are associated with portions of nine faculties.
The faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) are associated with portions of six faculties.
Regarding the statement that the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity are associated with portions of nine faculties: [the details follow].
This refers to the mental faculty (*manas*), the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Question: How do pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) correspond with a portion of these nine?
Answer: The mental faculty and the five faculties beginning with faith are all associated with the five types of feeling (*vedanā*).
In this context, it is called "a small portion" because it is taken only as that which is associated with the three feelings (*vedanā*).
Since the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) have multiple dharmas as their nature,
they are now called "a small portion" because the substance of feeling itself is excluded and only what is associated with the others is taken.
Regarding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*), which are associated with a portion of six faculties—
namely, the mind faculty (*manas*) and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*)—
the question is: how do suffering and mental distress correspond with this portion of those six?
Answer: These six faculties are associated with the five feelings (*vedanā*).
Here, however, because we are taking only those associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and physical pain (*duḥkha*), it is said to be "a small portion.
Question: Why is there a question only regarding association with feeling?
Is it not the case that other minds and mental factors are not being questioned?
The answer is: because this is the intention of the author of the treatise;
the treatise is composed according to his intention.
However, if it does not contradict the characteristics of the Dharma,
one should not hold them accountable. Some say:
"All phenomena ultimately converge upon sensation; it is for this reason that I ask.
Some say: "A single sensation possesses the characteristics of multiple faculties."
That is to say, among the various factors, sensation alone is divided into five faculties, whereas other phenomena are not;
therefore, the question concerns sensation alone. Some say:
The various feelings (vedanā) are established without mutual contradiction;
however, their manifestation (samudācāra) is contradictory.
Therefore, he asks specifically about this.
Regarding the accomplishment of non-contradiction:
this refers to a single sentient being accomplishing five types of feeling.
Regarding contradiction in manifestation: [this refers to their simultaneous occurrence].
That is to say, within a single moment,
a single sentient being cannot give rise to two [minds], let alone many.
Some say that because feeling is the hub of the wheel of dependent origination,
it is questioned specifically.
Some say: "Apart from sensation, what else do you wish to ask?
If you ask about the five faculties such as faith and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*)."
That [state] is exclusively wholesome;
it does not have the sense of being associated with all that exists.
This refers to the question regarding the eight faculties, such as the life-faculty and so forth.
That [mind] is exclusively indeterminate and moreover dissociated.
Question: If that is so, why is the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) not questioned?
Answer: Since associated phenomena are originally established by means of the mental faculty (*manas*), it is improper to ask in return whether they are associated with the mind.
Therefore, in this context, the inquiry concerns only the sense of being associated with feeling (*vedanā*).
Because the five feelings do not correspond with themselves by their own nature,
one further inquires about feeling solely through other dharmas; thus,
the various faculties and their correspondence with feeling have already been analyzed.
The meaning of that association shall now be explained.
Question: Why is it called "association" (*samprayoga*)?
What is the meaning of "association"?
Answer: The meaning of "equal" (sama) is the meaning of "associated" (samprayukta).
Question: Within the various mental complexes (citta-kalāpa), the mental factors (caitasika-dharma) are sometimes many and sometimes few; how can they be called "equal"?
That is to say, [the objects] of the desire realm are many, those of the form realm are few;
those of the form realm are many, those of the formless realm are few;
wholesome [objects] are many, unwholesome [objects] are few.
The unwholesome is predominant and the indeterminate is slight;
the obscured-indeterminate is predominant and the unobscured-indeterminate is slight.
In what sense is "equality" (samatā) the meaning of "conjunction" (saṃprayoga)?
The answer is: they are called "equal" because their factors are equal.
That is to say, within a single mental state (*citta-kalāpa*), if there are two feelings (*vedanā*).
One might say that while perception (*saṃjñā*) and the others are not equal [to feeling],
within a single mental complex (*citta-kalāpa*), just as there is one feeling,
so too are there [one] perception and the others.
Therefore, it is called "equality" (*samatā*).
Some say that the five kinds of equality constitute the meaning of "association" (*samprayoga*).
That is to say: the basis and so forth,
the object and so forth,
and the mode of activity and so forth.
Regarding the equality of time,
the equality of matter,
and so forth, the rest is explained in detail as in the first section of the *Saṃgītiparyāya*; these are the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).
"How many are bound to the desire realm?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is in order to refute the positions of others and to clarify one's own doctrine.
That is to say, some maintain that the male and female faculties exist in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and they speak as follows:
In all places where there is a physical body (*rūpakāya*), both the female and male faculties (*indriya*) can be found.
To refute that notion and to demonstrate that the female and male faculties exist only in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*),
this treatise was composed.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of pain are obtainable in five stages,
namely: the desire realm and the four dhyānas.
They claim that wherever there is a body, there is always both suffering and pleasure.
To refute this attachment,
it is shown that the faculty of suffering exists only in the Desire Realm.
The faculty of pleasure exists only in three stages;
therefore, this treatise was composed.
Alternatively, there are those who say:
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) are obtainable in nine stages,
namely from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
They maintain that wherever there is mind, there are both grief and joy.
Because there is mind in all nine stages of the three realms.
Furthermore, even though the body in the desire realm is impure and loathsome,
one still gives rise to joy at the time of union.
When separated from it, one gives rise to sorrow;
how much more so when, in the higher realms, the body is exceedingly pure and subtle like the flame of a lamp,
and the mind is free from turbidity like a cool, clear pool.
Yet, regarding separation and union, one attains freedom from both sorrow and joy.
To refute that attachment,
it is shown that sorrow exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Joy exists up to the second dhyāna;
it is absent in all higher stages.
Therefore, this treatise was composed.
Among these twenty-two faculties,
how many are bound to the desire realm,
and how many are bound to the form realm?
How many are bound to the formless realm?
How many are unbound?
Answer: Four are bound to the desire realm.
Three are non-bound;
fifteen should be analyzed;
four are bound to the desire realm.
The female and male faculties, as well as the faculties of suffering and mental grief;
the three that are unconditioned (unbound) refer to the three untainted faculties.
Regarding the fifteen that should be analyzed:
these refer to the five faculties of form, the life faculty, the mind faculty, the three faculties of feeling, and the five faculties beginning with faith.
The eye faculty is either bound to the desire realm.
Or it is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
It refers to the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) bound to the desire realm.
What is that which is bound to the realm of form?
It refers to the eye-faculty produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) bound to the realm of form.
As it is with the eye-faculty, so it is with the others.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue,
and body. The life-faculty is either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm.
Or it is associated with the formless realm.
What is associated with the desire realm?
It refers to the life-force associated with the desire realm.
What is that which is bound to the realm of form?
It refers to the life-force bound to the realm of form.
What is that which is bound to the formless realm?
That is to say, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
while the mind-faculty (manas-indriya) is either bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Either bound to the formless realm or unbound.
What is bound to the desire realm?
This refers to the mind-faculty associated with attention bound to the desire realm.
What is that which is bound to the form realm?
It refers to the mind-faculty associated with attention bound to the form realm.
What is that which is bound to the formless realm?
It refers to the faculty of mind associated with attention bound to the formless realm.
What is that which is unbound?
This refers to the faculty of mind associated with untainted attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*).
As it is with the faculty of mind,
so it is with the faculty of equanimity and the five faculties beginning with faith.
The faculty of pleasure is either bound to the desire realm,
or bound to the form realm, or unbound.
What is bound to the desire realm?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with attention bound to the desire realm.
What is bound to the form realm?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with attention bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
What is it that is not bound?
It refers to the faculty of pleasure associated with untainted (*anāsrava*) attention.
As it is with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), so it is with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
Question: Why are there no male or female faculties (*strīpuruṣendriya*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
The answer is: "It is not their field;
it is not their vessel," and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say: [as follows].
In order to discard the male and female faculties,
they cultivate the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and are reborn in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
If those [beings] were also to possess male and female faculties, [this would not be the case].
Then there should be no seeking of birth in those higher realms. Furthermore,
if a phenomenon belonging to a lower stage were also present in a higher stage,
one could not establish the existence of phenomena that are extinguished through gradual stages.
If there were no dharma of gradual cessation,
there would likewise be no dharma of ultimate cessation,
because the dharma of gradual cessation can induce the dharma of ultimate cessation.
If there were no dharma of ultimate cessation, there would be no liberation;
if there were no liberation,
there would be no transcendence.
Because there would otherwise be many such faults,
there are no male or female faculties in the form realm. Some say:
The two faculties of female and male are induced by edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
"At the beginning of the kalpa, human beings lacked the female and male faculties, and their physical forms were indistinguishable."
After they consumed the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*), male and female sexual organs arose;
from this, the distinction between male and female characteristics came into being.
Because the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is free from solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), these two organs do not exist there.
Some say that the two faculties of male and female are functional in the desire realm,
but not in the form realm.
Therefore, those two do not exist there.
Question: Since the two faculties of nose and tongue have no function there, how can they possibly exist?
Answer: The two faculties of nose and tongue are functional in that realm because they contribute to physical beauty;
however, the female and male faculties do not possess the quality of contributing to beauty.
Because they are objects of shame and loathing.
Question: Are the celestial hosts of the form realm female or male?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
If it were female, it should possess the female faculty;
if it were male, it should possess the male faculty.
If it were neither, it would contradict the scriptural teaching.
As it is said:
"A female body cannot become a Brahmā king and so forth, yet this does not preclude the male.
One should respond by saying this.
They are all males.
Question: Is it not the case that such beings do not possess the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*)?
Answer: Although they lack the male faculty, they still possess other characteristics of a man.
Furthermore, because one is able to be free from defilement,
one is called "male," as it is said in the Sūtra:
All those in the fruits and the paths of approach are called "great beings" (puruṣa).
It is not that women do not practice the paths or abide in the fruits;
rather, it should be understood that they too are called "great beings" because they are likewise able to abandon defilement.
In the Vinaya, it is also stated thus:
The Buddha took up the great bone of Mahāprajāpatī with both hands and addressed the assembly of bhikṣus.
Listen attentively:
the nature of all women is fickle and unstable;
they are prone to much jealousy, flattery, and avarice.
Although Mahāprajāpatī was a woman,
she was free from all the faults of women and performed the deeds of a man.
They have attained what is attained by true men;
I declare that such as these are called "true men.
The principle should likewise apply to the various devas of the form realm.
Because he is able to be free from defilement, he is called a "great man" (puruṣa).
Based on this, one should establish a fourfold classification (catuṣkoṭi):
there are those who are males but do not possess the male organ (purisindriya).
This refers to those such as the gods of the form and formless realms and Mahā-Māyā;
there are those who possess the male faculty but are not men,
namely those who are hermaphrodites (*ubhayavyañjana*).
There are those who are males and also possess the male faculty;
that is to say, all men who possess the male faculty.
There are also those who are neither males nor possess the male faculty.
That is to say, with the exception of the aforementioned cases,
all who are women necessarily possess the female faculty (*strīndriya*). However,
there are those who possess the female faculty but are not women.
Regarding those with both sexual organs:
according to the meaning of the Vinaya as cited here,
the case of women should also be explained by extending the fourfold formulation.
Question: For what reason are there no faculties of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) or suffering (*duḥkha*) in the higher realms?
Answer: Because they are not a field (*kṣetra*), nor are they a vessel (*bhājana*);
and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that one cultivates the various dhyānas and is reborn in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) for the purpose of abandoning the faculties of sorrow (daurmanasya) and suffering (duḥkha).
If those realms also possessed the faculty of sorrow and the faculty of suffering,
then there would be no desire to seek birth in those realms.
If a dharma exists in a lower stage and also exists in a higher stage, [it follows that it must exist in all stages].
One should not posit the existence of dharmas that undergo gradual cessation;
the detailed explanation is as before,
so that such an error does not occur.
Therefore, the upper realms lack the faculties of sorrow and suffering.
Some say: for what reason do the faculties of sorrow and suffering not exist in the form realm?
Because this is a unique fault of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
each realm and stage (*bhūmi*) possesses its own unique merits and faults.
Regarding the faults of the desire realm:
This refers to the faculty of suffering and so forth.
As for "virtues," it refers to being able to enter the path of seeing and so forth.
The virtues and faults of the higher realms should be explained in detail according to each respective stage. Some say:
The desire realm is a realm of defects.
Because it is a realm of defects, even those with superior bodies still experience suffering,
such as Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and universal monarchs.
The higher realms are realms of merit.
Because they are realms of merit,
even those with inferior bodies experience no suffering.
Just as in a bad year, even if there is fine grain, one cannot avoid disaster;
whereas if one encounters a good year, even the various weeds are not affected by calamity—
so it should be understood for the Desire Realm and the Higher Realms.
As for why there is also no sorrow in the higher realms:
it is because all faculties of sorrow have been abandoned through the relinquishing of desire;
furthermore, it is because [sorrow] is the outflowing fruit of heavy ignorance.
Those born in the higher realms are free from heavy ignorance;
therefore, the faculty of grief does not exist there.
Having thus analyzed the faculties according to their connection with the desire realm and so forth.
The meaning of their being bound to the desire realm and so forth shall now be explained.
Question: What is meant by "bound to the desire realm" (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) and "bound to the form realm" (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta)?
"Are they bound to the formless realm?
Answer: "If a dharma is bound to the desire realm, it is called 'bound to the desire realm';
if it is bound to the form realm, it is called 'bound to the form realm'."
That which is bound to the formless realm is called "bound to the formless realm," just as a cow tied to a post and so forth is called "tied to a post" and so forth.
Alternatively, some say:
If a phenomenon is bound to the desire realm, it is termed "bound to the desire realm.
If it is bound to the form or formless realms, it is termed "bound to the form or formless realms.
The term "bound" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
As it is said:
"The Buddha’s range of activity is boundless and without limit.
Who could lead him away? It is like a person with feet who can travel in the four directions."
If one lacks feet, one cannot travel; likewise,
if one possesses the "feet" of afflictions,
one is able to travel through the various realms, destinies, and births within the cycle of birth and death.
If one lacks the feet that are free from afflictions, one cannot go. Or, as some say:
if a phenomenon is bound by the fetters of birth and death in the desire realm.

That which is bound by the cycle of birth and death in the desire realm is called "bound to the desire realm. That which is bound by the bonds of the cycle of birth and death in the form and formless realms is called "bound to the form and formless realms."
Some say: if a phenomenon is stored within the ālayavijñāna of the desire realm and grasped by the mamakāra (the sense of "mine"), [it is called a dharma].
It is called "bound to the desire realm" (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
It is stored within the ālayavijñāna of the form and formless realms,
and is grasped by the mamakāra (the sense of "mine").
Name-and-form belongs to the form and formless realms;
*ālaya* refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*),
and *mamakāra* refers to views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Some say: if a phenomenon is moistened by craving of the desire realm and is grasped as "I" or "mine" through views,
[it is called "associated with outflows"].
It is called "bound to the desire realm" (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
It is moistened by craving for the form and formless realms,
and is grasped through views as "self" and "mine."
Name-and-form belongs to the realm of form and the formless realm.
Some say that if a phenomenon is conjoined with the desires for pleasure in the desire realm, [it is so classified].

That which is conjoined with the desire for the realm of desire is called "bound to the realm of desire. That which is conjoined with the pleasure and desire of the realms of form and formlessness is called "bound to the realms of form and formlessness."
Pleasure is called craving;
desire is called views.
Or, as some say:
If a phenomenon is defiled by the stains of the desire realm,
poisoned by its poisons,
and sullied by its impurities.
It is called "bound to the desire realm," being defiled by the impurities of the form and formless realms and poisoned by their toxins.
That which is defiled by impurities refers to the factors bound to the realms of form and formlessness;
herein, all afflictions are termed "impurities."

"How many causes are associated?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is intended to stop those who claim that dependently originated phenomena (pratītyasamutpāda) are not substantially real,
thereby demonstrating that dependently originated phenomena are definitively and truly existent;
it is also intended to refute the minds of those ignorant of association (saṃprayoga) who cling to the notion that associated phenomena are not substantially real.
This treatise was composed in order to demonstrate that associated [factors] (saṃprayukta) are substantially existent (dravyasat).
Regarding this point:
Some say that the treatise is composed based on a single cause,
namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
Because the term "associated" (saṃprayukta) is used here,
those who interpret this passage according to that underlying intention [state]:
these twenty-two faculties...
How many factors are associated?
Answer: Fourteen;
namely, the mind faculty, the five feelings, the five faculties beginning with faith, and the three untainted faculties.
This is the intrinsic nature of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
Because the faculties (*indriya*) are associated with phenomena that have the intrinsic nature of the associated cause,
they are termed "associated causes."
How many causes are dissociated?
Answer: Eight, namely the seven material faculties and the life-faculty.
Question: Since these eight are not the substance of the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*), how can it be said that they are "causes dissociated [from mind]"?
Answer: Although these eight are not the substance of the associated cause, [they are so called because they are dissociated from mind].
Since its essence as a corresponding cause is dissociated [from the mind],
it is described as a "cause that is dissociated.
What fault is there in this?
How many causes are associated and how many are dissociated?
Answer: Of the aforementioned fourteen [causes], a portion are associated with causes, and a portion are dissociated from causes.
That which is partially associated with causes refers to when one nature is partially a cause for another nature.
That which is not associated with causes refers to when a nature is [not a cause] for itself.
How many are not associated with causes, and how many are not dissociated from causes?
Answer: A portion of the aforementioned fourteen.
It is not associated with non-causes.
Regarding that which is partially dissociated from non-causes and partially associated with non-causes:
this refers to a nature [being related] to itself.
Regarding the partial non-correspondence with causes:
this refers to an intrinsic nature [not corresponding] with another nature. Some say:
In this context, the treatise is composed based on two causes:
namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
This is because, by virtue of these two causes, [the mind and mental factors] are never dissociated from those phenomena.
Interpreting this passage according to that intended meaning:
among these twenty-two faculties,
how many are associated with causes?
Answer: Fourteen.
These are the intrinsic natures of the two causes, because the faculties are associated with the dharmas that constitute the intrinsic natures of those two causes.
This is called "correspondence with causes.
It should be understood that the questions and answers for the latter three are as previously explained.
Some say that in this context, the treatise is composed based on three causes.
That is to say: the associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu),
the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu),
and the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
Because these three causes apply to all three natures (trividha-svabhāva),
some say that the treatise here is composed based on four causes.
This means that the two causes— the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)— are excluded, because these four causes pertain to all three time periods.
Some say:
In this context, the treatise is composed based on five causes; that is,
with the exception of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
because it is common to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and is not a direct or predominant factor.
Some say that this treatise is composed based on the six causes,
because the term "cause" used here is general in its application.
However, associated dharmas may constitute six causes as their own essence,
or five causes as their own essence,
or four causes as their own essence.
As explained at length in the Mahābhūta-skandha,
if one interprets this passage according to that underlying intention,
these twenty-two faculties [are as follows].
How many causes are associated?
Answer: Fourteen;
namely, the intrinsic natures of the six causes.
The faculty is associated with six causes as its own-nature phenomena;
it is associated with five causes as the own-nature of the five causes. The faculty is associated with five causes as their own-nature phenomena.
The four causes constitute its own essence.
Because the faculties are associated with these four causes and their essential natures, they are termed "associated with causes.
The latter three questions and answers should be understood as before.
Of these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many have an object (*sālambana*)? ...
[and so on] up to the full exposition.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was intended to refute those who claim that the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is not real, and to demonstrate that the object-condition is indeed a real existent.
Thus he composed this treatise:
Of these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*),
how many have an object (*sālambana*)?
Answer: A portion of thirteen [factors].

That is to say, a portion of the mental faculty (*manas*), the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and a portion of the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
These have objective referents (*sālambana-dharma*) as their objects of perception (*ālambana*).
Therefore, this is called the "phrase of the condition for that which has a condition.

How many conditions are unconditioned?
Answer: Thirteen [of the eighteen elements] and a portion of one.
The first refers to the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya).
"A portion of thirteen" is as previously explained.
Since dharmas that lack an object serve as the object for this [consciousness],

It is like a person with clear vision looking at one who is blind from birth.
That person born blind sees nothing at all;
one should know that it is the same regarding the phrase "conditioned by the unconditioned.
How many conditions are conditioned, and how many are unconditioned?
Answer: It consists of a portion of the aforementioned thirteen [categories],
namely those phenomena that possess an object and those that do not,
which serve as the objects of this [consciousness].
Therefore, this is called the statement regarding that which has an object-condition and that which lacks an object-condition.
It is like a person with clear vision seeing another person with clear vision as well as one who is born blind;
that person with clear vision further perceives what is seen [by the other].

It should be understood that the same applies to the statements regarding the blind man who has no further objects of sight, whether they have an object-condition (*ālambana*) or lack an object-condition. Others say:

Because it contradicts the root treatise,

"With respect to conditioned phenomena that have objects, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase by taking those very conditioned phenomena as their objects."
All underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in relation to both objects that have conditions and objects that lack conditions.
Regarding objects that have conditions and objects that lack conditions,
the underlying tendencies increase in relation to conditioned objects.
Neither with respect to dharmas that have objects nor with respect to dharmas that lack objects do the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take tainted objects increase;
yet there exists mental consciousness along with its associated factors.
In a single kṣaṇa, one takes as objects both conditioned (sālambana) and unconditioned (anālambana) dharmas in their totality.
Therefore, what was stated previously is correct.
How many [dharmas] are neither conditioned by objects nor unconditioned by objects?
Answer: Eight, namely the seven material faculties and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Therefore, this is called the phrase "neither conditioned by conditions nor unconditioned by conditions.

The aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness constitute the first three phrases;
the aggregate of formations constitutes all four phrases.
As it is with the aggregates, so it is with the bases of grasping (*upādānaskandha*).

To explain the faculties in detail: is this dharma produced by those same faculties, or by different faculties?
If the faculties belong to a worldling (*pṛthagjana*), do those faculties belong to this dharma?
Answer: There are faculties that belong to this dharma, yet those faculties do not belong to a worldling.
There are faculties that belong to a worldling, yet those faculties do not belong to this dharma.
Question: What is meant by "this dharma"?
What is meant by "an ordinary person" (pṛthagjana)?
Answer: "This dharma" refers to the noble ones (ārya).
Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are indeed ordinary beings.
As for those faculties by which one is not an ordinary being:
this refers to the fact that the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are possessed exclusively by noble ones (*ārya*).
It does not belong to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
Those faculties belonging to ordinary persons are not this dharma;
that is to say, the faculties to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
It is possessed only by ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) and not by any noble ones (ārya).

This refers to an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) abiding in the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti). An ordinary person abiding in the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) is also referred to as such.
Regarding the statement that "the faculties associated with this dharma and those faculties are not of a different nature from those of an ordinary person":
this refers to the faculties that arise simultaneously with the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
It means that only for one who abides in the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering do these faculties manifest.

It is not the case that one who abides in the supreme mundane dharma has faculties different from those of an ordinary person; rather, the faculties of such a person are not [the same as] those of this dharma,
namely, the faculties that arise simultaneously with the supreme mundane dharma.
It manifests only for one abiding in the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*),
not for one abiding in the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Some say this.

This refers to the five faculties of sensation (vedanendriya).
Regarding "a portion of three," this refers to a portion of the three untainted faculties (anāsravendriya).

How many faculties are subsumed within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)?
Answer: None; because non-perception (*asaṃjñi*) is not a faculty.
How many faculties are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?

As for the six elements:
That is to say: the eye-consciousness element, the ear-consciousness element, the body-consciousness element, the mind element, the mind-consciousness element, and the mental-object element.
As for the two bases:
they are the mind base and the mental-object base.

Answer: None.

Answer: Thirteen elements, seven bases, and four aggregates.
As for the thirteen elements:
This refers to the twelve internal elements and the dharma-element.
As for the seven bases:
That is to say, the six internal bases and the base of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana).
As for the four aggregates:
That is to say, excluding the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha),
it comprises only the non-obscured neutral roots (anivṛtāvyākṛta-mūla).
How many elements (dhātu), how many bases (āyatana), and how many aggregates (skandha) does it consist of?

As for the five elements:
The five elements of the five material sense faculties,
such as the eye and so forth; the five bases refer to the five locations of the material sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth.

they refer to the twelve internal elements.
