Can a faculty serve as a condition for the arising of a faculty?
...and so on, as explained at length.
Some say that herein there is one heading, one brief explanation, and one detailed explanation.
As it is said:
"Is there a faculty that, being a condition, gives rise to another faculty? and so forth;
this is the thesis statement.
"Does the eye-faculty arise with the eye-faculty as its condition? and so forth—this is the explanation. [It asks:
"In how many ways does the eye-faculty serve as a condition for the eye-faculty? and so forth.
This is the extensive explanation.
Some say that within this there are three headings, three explanations, and three extensive explanations.
As it is said:
"Is there a faculty that, being a condition, gives rise to another faculty? This is the proposition.
The answer is: "It does."
"This is the brief explanation.
"Is birth not a faculty? and so forth;
this is the detailed explanation.
"Can the eye-faculty arise with the eye-faculty as its condition?
This is the proposition.
The answer is: "It can."
"This is the concise explanation.
"From the arising of the ear-faculty up to the arising of the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge," and so forth,
is the detailed explanation.
"How many conditions does the eye-faculty have with respect to the eye-faculty?
This is the proposition.
The answer is: "It has two: the cause-condition and the predominance-condition."
This is the concise explanation.

The passage from "up to serving as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the faculty of perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*)" is the detailed explanation.
Some say that herein there are three headings and three explanations,
as it is said:
"Can a faculty (indriya) serve as a condition for the arising of a faculty?
and so forth—this is the thesis.
The answer is "it can arise," and so forth.
"Does the eye-faculty arise with the eye-faculty as its condition? and so forth—this is the proposition.
"It arises," and so forth, is the answer.
"This is the explanation" refers to the statement:
"How many conditions does the eye-faculty serve as a condition for the eye-faculty? and so forth;
this is the heading.
The answer, beginning with "Due to the increase of causes, etc.," is the explanation.
Is it the case that a faculty serves as a condition for the arising of a faculty?
Question: What is arising?
Answer: It is as when the eye serves as the basis for the arising of the three faculties of feeling—pleasure, pain, and equanimity—and the five faculties beginning with faith.
Or, taking the eye as an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
there arise the four mental faculties (indriya)— namely, the faculty of mind, the faculty of equanimity, and so forth— and the five [faculties] beginning with faith,
as well as the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya). Is it possible for a faculty to serve as a condition for the arising of that which is not a faculty?
Answer: Arising.
What is arising?
Answer: It is like the eye serving as the basis.
Perception, volition, contact, attention, and so forth arise; or,
with the eye as the object-condition,
perception, volition, contact, and attention arise.
And [factors] such as regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*).
Is there any faculty that, serving as a condition, gives rise to both a faculty and a non-faculty?
Answer: Yes, it does.
What is its arising?
Answer: Just as the eye serves as the basis, there arise mental factors such as the three feelings, faith and the other four faculties, perception, volition, contact, and attention.
Alternatively, with the eye as the object-condition (ālambana),

there arise mental factors such as the four feelings, the five beginning with faith, the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manaskāra), and so forth,
as well as regret (kaukṛtya), sleep (middha), and the like.
Is there that which is not a faculty (anindriya) which arises conditioned by what is not a faculty?
Answer: It does arise.
How does it arise?
Answer: Just as when form serves as an object-condition (*ālambana*),
it gives rise to perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), and so forth,
as well as regret (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), and the like.
Is it possible for that which is not a faculty (*indriya*) to serve as a condition for the arising of a faculty?
Answer: It does arise.
How does it arise?

Answer: Just as with form serving as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), there arise the five faculties of feeling associated with the mind, the five beginning with faith, and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Is it possible for that which is not a faculty to serve as a condition?
Is it "arising" (jāti) or "non-arising"?
Answer: It is arising.
What is arising?
Answer: Just as when form serves as the object-condition (ālambana),

there arise the five faculties of feeling associated with the mental consciousness, the five [faculties] beginning with faith, the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manasikāra), and so forth,
as well as regret (kaukṛtya), sleep (middha), and the like.
Question: Can faculties and non-faculties, acting as conditions, give rise to both faculties and non-faculties?
Answer: Yes, they can.
What is "arising"?
The answer is: it is like the eye serving as the basis and visible form serving as the object-condition.
Regarding the five faculties such as faith (śraddhā) among the mental factors, as well as perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manaskāra), and so forth:
can any faculty or non-faculty serve as a condition to produce a faculty?
Answer: It can.
How does it arise?
The answer is: as when the eye serves as the basis and visible form serves as the object.
Regarding the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) among the faculties of the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*):
can there be a case where a faculty that is not itself a faculty arises conditioned by a faculty?
Answer: Arising.
What is arising?
Answer: It is as the eye serves as the basis.
Form is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
There arise perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), and so forth; others formulate this as a second textual passage.
Is it possible that when a faculty (*indriya*) serves as a condition, only a faculty is produced?
Answer: It does not arise.
This is because from this faculty (*indriya*), that which is not a faculty (*anindriya*) also arises.
Is there a case where a faculty serves as a condition for the arising of only that which is not a faculty?
Answer: It does not arise.
This is because this faculty also gives rise to faculties.
Is there any case where a faculty serves as a condition for that which arises solely as a faculty and not as a non-faculty?
Answer: Arising.
What is arising?
Answer: It is, for example, as the eye serves as the basis.
Regarding the five faculties such as faith and so forth, which are associated with the three feelings, as well as perception, volition, contact,
attention, and so on— is it possible for that which is not a faculty to serve as a condition and give rise solely to that which is not a faculty?
Answer: It does not arise.
This is because that which is not a faculty (*indriya*) also arises as a faculty.
Is there anything that is not a faculty yet serves as a condition?
Is it only the sense-faculties that arise?
Answer: No, they do not.
Because non-faculties also arise from non-faculties.
Is it possible for that which is not a faculty (*indriya*) to serve as a condition, such that only a faculty arises while the non-faculty does not?
Answer: It is possible.
How does it arise?

Answer: Just as form serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*), there arise the mental factors of feeling, perception, and so forth—namely, the five feelings, the five faculties beginning with faith, the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), as well as volition, contact, attention, and so on.
Furthermore, regarding [mental states] such as regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*),
can there be cases where faculties and non-faculties serve as conditions,
yet only faculties arise, while non-faculties do not?
Answer: Arising.
What is arising?
Answer: It is like the eye serving as the basis.
Taking form as an object-condition,
there arise the mental factors of the three feelings, the five faculties beginning with faith, perception, volition, contact, attention, and so forth.
Is it possible for these faculties or non-faculties to serve as conditions?
"Is it only produced from the faculties?
Answer: "It is not produced.
Because this faculty is neither a faculty nor is it produced from a non-faculty."
Is it the case that when faculties and non-faculties serve as conditions, they produce only non-faculties?
Answer: They do not.
Because these faculties are both non-faculties and yet give rise to faculties,
others have formulated a third proposition regarding this:
"Is it possible that only a faculty serves as the condition for the arising of a faculty?"
Answer: It does not arise.
This is because this faculty also arises with non-faculties as its conditions.
Is there any case where only a faculty serves as the condition for the arising of a non-faculty?
Answer: It does not arise.
This is because it arises from that which is neither a faculty (*indriya*) nor an object-condition (*ālambana*).
Is there any case where only a faculty serves as the condition for the arising of something that is both a faculty and not a faculty?
Answer: It does not arise.
This is because this faculty arises from both a faculty and a non-faculty as its conditions.
Is there any case where only a non-faculty serves as a condition for the arising of a non-faculty?
Answer: It does not arise.
This is because it arises both from that which is not a faculty (*anindriya*) and with a faculty as its condition (*pratyaya*).
Is there any case where that which is exclusively non-faculty serves as a condition for the arising of a faculty?
Answer: It does not arise.
This is because this faculty also arises with a faculty as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Is there any case where only that which is not a faculty serves as the condition for the arising of both a faculty and that which is not a faculty?
Answer: It does not arise.
This is because this faculty arises both from what is not a faculty and by taking a faculty as its condition.
Is there anything that arises solely by taking what is neither a faculty nor a non-faculty as its condition?
"Is it a faculty of birth or not a faculty?
Answer: "It is birth.
Explained at length as above.
Is it the case that only those which are both faculties (*indriya*) and non-faculties serve as conditions to produce a faculty?
Answer: They do.
The detailed explanation is as above.
Is it the case that only that which is neither a faculty (indriya) nor a non-faculty arises conditioned by [something] that is neither a faculty nor a non-faculty?
Answer: It does so arise.
The detailed explanation is as above.
Can it be said that the eye-faculty arises conditioned by the eye-faculty?
Answer: It does arise.
How does it arise?
Answer: It means that which does not obstruct arising, as well as that which is merely non-obstructive.
Is it possible for the eye-faculty to serve as a condition for the arising of the ear-faculty, up to and including the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge?
Answer: Arising.
What is arising?
Answer: It is as the eye serves as the basis.

Some, by slandering the eye-faculty, fall into the various evil destinies and undergo the maturation of the faculties of form, life, mind, and suffering; others,
by having faith in the eye-faculty, are born into the various auspicious destinies.
The maturation of the various faculties— the faculty of form, the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of joy,
and the faculty of equanimity— is called the arising of the ear-faculty, up to the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge, with the eye-faculty as its condition.
As it is with the eye faculty,
so it is with the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, female, male, and life; however,
there is a distinction.
That is to say, the female and male faculties are not the bases for the faculty of suffering or the five faculties beginning with faith;
the life-faculty is not the basis for all the faculties.
Could it be that, with the mind-faculty as a condition, there arises the mind-faculty,
or the eye-faculty, and so on,
up to the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge?
Answer: Birth. What is birth? Answer:
It is that which has the faculty of mind as its basis.
The five faculties of faith and so forth, the three untainted faculties,
or the mental faculty serve as objects of perception,
giving rise to the four mental faculties, the five faculties of faith and so forth, and the three untainted faculties.

Or, by slandering the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*), one falls into the various evil destinies and undergoes the maturation (*vipāka*) of the faculties of form, life, mind, and suffering; or else,
one has faith in the faculty of mind.
They are born into the various happy realms and experience the maturation (*vipāka*) of the physical faculties, the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of joy,
and the faculty of equanimity. Furthermore, the mind-faculty is both wholesome and unwholesome.
Wholesome [karma] results in the maturation of the various faculties of form, life, mind, pleasure, joy, and equanimity within the happy realms.
Unwholesome [karma] results in the maturation of the various faculties of form, life, mind, and suffering within the miserable realms.
As it is with the faculty of mind,
so it is with the five faculties of feeling and the five faculties beginning with faith;
however, there is a distinction.
That is to say, none of them are the basis [for others];
the faculty of suffering is not its own object;
and the five faculties beginning with faith are not unwholesome.
Is it the case that, with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) as a condition,
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" arises?
Or do the faculty of the eye (*cakṣurindriya*) up to the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) arise?
Answer: It is birth. What is birth? Answer:
It is as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) serves as its basis.
The three faculties of "the mind that has not yet known but will know," "that which has already known," and "faith" (along with the other four faculties) arise; or,
taking the faculty of "the mind that has not yet known but will know" as its object,
there arise the four faculties of "the mind that has already known," "faith" (and the others), and the three untainted faculties.
Or, by slandering the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," one falls into the various miserable realms and undergoes the maturation of the physical faculties,
the life-faculty, the mental faculty, and the faculty of suffering.
Or, through the faculty of faith and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," one is born into the various happy realms and experiences the maturation of the various material faculties,
the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of joy, and the faculty of equanimity.
As it is with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," so it is with the faculty of "one who has known" and the faculty of "one who has fully known";
however, there is a distinction.
That is to say, with the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) as its basis,
there arise the faculty of "having fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*), the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), the three faculties of feeling, and the five faculties beginning with faith.
With the faculty of "having fully known" as its basis...

[One] is endowed with the faculty of final knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*), the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), the three faculties of feeling (*vedanā*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
Question: Of how many conditions is the eye-faculty a condition for the eye-faculty?
Of how many conditions is it a condition for the ear-faculty, and so on, up to the faculty of final knowledge?
Up to: how many conditions does the faculty of one who has known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) serve as a condition for the faculty of one who has known?
And how many conditions does it serve as a condition for the eye faculty, up to the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñendriya*)?
Answer: The eye faculty [serves as a condition] for the eye faculty.
It acts as a cause and a dominant condition.
As for the cause, there is one cause:
namely, the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Regarding "predominance" (*adhipati*):
it refers to that which does not obstruct arising and is merely non-obstructive.
The subsequent meanings of predominance are all explained in this same way.
It has a single predominance with respect to the other material faculties, the life-faculty, and the suffering-faculty;
it has the predominance of being an object with respect to the remaining faculties.
As for "the remaining faculties":
That is to say: the mind faculty, the four faculties of feeling, the five beginning with faith, and the three untainted faculties.
As it is with the eye faculty, so it is with the ear, nose, and tongue faculties.
The body-faculty is the cause and the dominant condition for the body-faculty, the female-faculty, and the male-faculty.
As for the cause, it is a single cause.

That is to say, the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) serves as a single predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) for the other material faculties, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), and the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya).
It serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant-condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the other faculties.
As for the "other faculties," they are as previously described.
The female faculty (strī-indriya) and the female body faculty (kāyendriya) act as cause (hetu) and predominance (adhipati).
As for the cause, it is a single cause.

That is to say, the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) serves as a single dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) for the other sense organs, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), and the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya).
It serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the other faculties.
As for the "other faculties," they are as previously described.
As it is with the female faculty,
so it is with the male faculty.
The life faculty is the cause and the predominant condition for the life faculty.
As for the cause, there is one cause:
namely, the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu),
which serves as the cause for the seven material faculties and the faculty of suffering (duḥkha-indriya).
It serves as a single predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
It acts as an object-predominant condition for the other faculties.
As for "the other faculties":
As previously stated,
the mental faculty (manas-indriya) acts as the cause,
the equal-and-immediate condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition for the mental faculty.
As for causes, there are three causes:
namely, the homogeneous cause, the pervasive cause, and the retributive cause.
As for the immediately preceding condition:
This refers to the mental faculty (manas) being present immediately after the mental faculty [of the preceding moment],
with respect to its object.
That is to say, the mind-faculty takes the mind-faculty as its object;
this refers to the sense of "immediate succession" (samanantara) and "object-condition" (ālambana).
All are to be understood according to this explanation:
they serve as the cause and the predominant condition for the seven material faculties and the life-faculty.
As for the cause, there is one cause:
namely, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
It serves as the cause, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the faculty of suffering.
It is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
As for causes (*hetu*), there are five:

namely, the associated cause (*samprayukta-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Regarding "immediately preceding" (samanantara):

it refers to the faculty of the mind (manas-indriya) being immediately followed by the manifestation of the faculty of suffering (duḥkha-indriya). Regarding "not being the object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya): [it refers to the faculty of suffering not having the faculty of the mind as its objective support].
The faculty of suffering has form as its object;
because the mental faculty is non-material,
it serves as the cause, equal-and-immediate, objective, and predominant condition for the other faculties.
As for the remaining faculties,
they refer to the faculties of pleasure, joy, equanimity, sorrow, and the five beginning with faith, as well as the three untainted faculties;
these are spoken of collectively because they depend upon the presence of all necessary conditions.
However, there is a difference in their causes;
that is to say, they serve as five causes for the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity— namely,
the five [causes] beginning with association (samprayoga).
It acts as four causes for the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*),
excluding the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*).
It acts as three causes for the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhādīndriya*) and the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*).
These are the associated, coexistent, and homogeneous causes.
As it is with the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*),
so it is with the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
It should be understood that this is stated in general terms because the objects, conditions, numbers, and so forth are equal;
however, since there are distinctions among the causal conditions,

Now, they are fully analyzed as follows:

the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) acts as the cause (hetu), the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), the object-condition (ālambanapratyaya), and the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya) for the faculty of pleasure.
The causes are three causes—
namely, the homogeneous cause, the pervasive cause, and the retributive cause—
which [act as causes] for the seven material faculties and the life-faculty.
It serves as both a cause and a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
As for the cause, there is one single cause,
namely the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
It serves as the cause, equal-and-immediate, object-condition, and dominant condition for the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
Regarding the "cause," there are five causes,
namely the five beginning with association (*samprayoga*).

With respect to the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), it is its cause, equal-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), and dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), but not its object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
As for "cause," there are two types of causes.
That is, it is a cause of similar type and a ripening cause,
but not an object-condition; for instance,
the faculty of suffering takes form as its object.
Because the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is not material,
it serves as the cause, equal-and-immediate, object, and predominant condition for the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
Regarding the "cause," there are two types of causes.
That is, it is a homogeneous and retributive cause (*sabhāga-vipāka-hetu*).
As for its being a cause, an equal-and-immediate cause, an object-condition, and a dominant condition for the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), there is one cause:
namely, the homogeneous cause.
It functions as the cause, equal-and-immediate, object, and dominant conditions for the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Regarding the cause, there are three causes: namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
The five faculties beginning with faith and the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) function as causes,
equal-and-immediate conditions (samanantara-pratyaya), object conditions (ālambana-pratyaya), and dominant conditions (adhipati-pratyaya).
Regarding "causes," there are three types of causes.
That is to say, they are associated, co-existent, and homogeneous causes.
The faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) acts as the cause,
the equal-and-immediate, the object-condition (ālambana), and the predominant condition (adhipati) for the faculty of joy.
As for the causes, there are three:
namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
These serve as the causes for the seven material faculties and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
It acts as a cause and a dominant condition.
As for the cause, there is one cause,
namely the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
With respect to the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*),
[the dharmas] serve as its cause, equal-and-immediate, object, and predominant conditions.
As for "cause," there are five types of causes.
That is, the five [factors] beginning with association act as the cause, equal-and-immediate,
object, and predominant conditions for the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
As for the causes, there are three: namely, the homogeneous cause, the pervasive cause, and the ripening cause,
which [function] in relation to the faculty of suffering.
It acts as the cause, the equal-and-immediate condition, and the predominant condition,
but not as the object-condition.
As for "cause," it refers to three causes.
That is, the similar-type cause, the pervasive cause,
and the retributive cause act as the causal, immediately antecedent, objective, and dominant conditions for the faculty of grief.
As for causes, there are two causes:
namely, the similar-type cause (sabhāga-hetu) and the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu),
which are associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
They function as causes, equal-and-immediate conditions, objective conditions, and dominant conditions.
Regarding "cause," there are three types of causes:
namely, the homogeneous cause, the pervasive cause, and the retributive cause.
The five faculties beginning with faith and the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) act as causes,
equal-immediate conditions (samanantara-pratyaya), objective conditions (ālambana-pratyaya), and dominant conditions (adhipati-pratyaya).
Regarding the "causes," there are three types of causes.
That is, they are associated causes, co-existent causes, and homogeneous causes.
The faculty of equanimity acts as the cause,
equal-immediate antecedent condition, object condition, and dominant condition for the faculty of equanimity.
As for the causes, there are three causes—
namely, the homogeneous cause, the pervasive cause, and the retributive cause—
which [serve as the basis] for the seven material faculties and the life-faculty.
It functions as both cause and predominant condition.
As for "cause," there is one cause:
namely, the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu).
With respect to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*),
[the object] acts as its cause, equal-immediate, objective, and dominant condition.
As for "cause," there are five types of causes.
That is, the five [factors] beginning with association act as the cause, equal-and-immediate,
object-condition, and predominant condition for the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy.
As for the causes, there are three:
namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
These serve as the causes for the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha-indriya*).
It functions as the cause, the equal-and-immediate, and the predominant conditions,
but not as the object condition.
Regarding "cause," there are three types of causes.
That is to say, the homogeneous, pervasive, and retributive causes,
as well as the cause, equal-and-immediate, objective, and dominant conditions, act as causes for the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
As for the causes, there are two causes:
namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
These are associated with the five faculties beginning with faith and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
It functions as the cause, equal-and-immediate, object, and dominant conditions.
Regarding the "cause," there are three causes—
namely, the associated, co-existent, and homogeneous causes— by which the faculty of faith [acts] upon the faculty of faith.
They function as causes, equal-and-immediate conditions, objective conditions, and dominant conditions.
As for the cause, there is one cause:
namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Together with the seven material faculties and the life-faculty,
they act as cause and predominance conditions.
As for the cause condition, it is a single cause.

It is the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*). With respect to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), the faculty of pleasure (*sukha-indriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasya-indriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā-indriya*), it serves as the cause,
the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
As for causes, there are four causes—
excluding the pervasive cause—
that serve as the cause, equal-and-immediate condition, and dominant condition for the faculty of suffering.
It is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
As for its causes (*hetu*), there are three causes:
namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
With the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*),
it acts as cause, equal-and-immediate, object, and predominant condition.
As for "cause," there are three types of causes.
That is to say, it is the associated, co-existent, and homogeneous causes.
With respect to the four faculties such as diligence and the three untainted faculties, it acts as the cause, the immediate antecedent, the object-condition, and the dominant condition.
As for "cause," it refers to these three types of causes.
That is to say, they are associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*),
and homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*). As it is with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), so it is with the four faculties beginning with diligence (*vīrya*).
The faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) is the cause,
the equal-and-immediate condition, and the predominant condition for the faculty of suffering;
it is not its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
As for "causes," there are two causes:
namely, the homogeneous cause and the ripening cause.
They are not objective conditions.
Because the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) has form as its object while the faculty of suffering itself is not form,
it acts as the cause and the predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) for the seven material faculties and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
The cause is a single cause,
namely the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*),
which [is associated] with the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
It functions as the dominant condition by way of being an object of focus (*ālambana*).

As for the "object of focus," it refers to taking as its object the categories of the receptivity to suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the receptivity to the origin [of suffering] (*samudaya-kṣānti*), and the knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-jñāna*).
It serves as the cause, equal-and-immediate, object, and predominant condition for the other faculties.
As for the "other faculties," these refer to the mental faculty, the faculties of pleasure, joy, equanimity, sorrow, and the five beginning with faith.
This is also stated collectively because it possesses the same conditions and so forth;
however, there is a difference in its causes,
namely, that it acts as four causes for the mental faculty (manas-indriya).
Excluding the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*),
it acts as two causes for the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*);
namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
It shares one cause with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*),
namely the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
It shares three causes with the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhādi-pañcendriya*).
That is to say, they are associated, co-existent, and homogeneous causes.
The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) serves as the cause,
equal-immediate, object-condition, and dominant condition for the faculty of grief.
As for causes, there are two causes:
namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
These serve as the dominant causes (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the seven material faculties and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
As for the cause, there is one cause:
namely, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
It serves as the cause, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha-indriya*).
It is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
As for the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), there are three causes:
namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
With respect to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*),
it serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati*).
As for the object-condition:

That is to say, it takes as its object the categories of the receptivity to suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the receptivity to origin (*samudaya-kṣānti*), and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*).

It serves as the cause, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the other faculties. As for "the other faculties": [they refer to]...
This refers to the five faculties of desire, resolve, joy, equanimity, and faith.
These are also spoken of collectively because they possess [the same] objects and other such characteristics;
however, there are differences in their causes.
That is to say, it acts as five causes for the mind-faculty (manas-indriya),
namely the five beginning with association (samprayukta).
It acts as three causes for the faculties of pleasure (sukha), joy (saumanasya), and equanimity (upekṣā).
That is, the homogeneous, pervasive,
and retributive causes act as three causes for the five faculties beginning with faith;
namely, the associated, co-existent, and homogeneous causes.

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) acts as the cause (hetu), equal-immediate (samanantara), object (ālambana), and predominant (adhipati) conditions for itself.
As for the cause, there are three causes:
namely, the associated (samprayukta), co-existent (sahabhū), and homogeneous (sabhāga) causes.
As for the object-condition (*ālambana*):
it refers to that which serves as the object-condition for the categories of patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*) and knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*),
and which serves as the causal, object, and dominant condition for the faculty of one who has attained full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
That which is not an equal-and-immediate cause has one cause,
namely, the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
As for the object-condition (*ālambana*):
it refers to taking the categories of patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*) and knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) as its object.
It is not the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Because the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya) does not manifest immediately after the faculty of one who knows the unknown (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya),
it is associated with the seven material faculties, the life-faculty, and the faculty of suffering.
It serves as a single predominant condition (*adhipati*);
it serves as an object-predominant condition (*ālambanādhipati*) for the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), and as [a predominant condition] for the remaining faculties.
They serve as causes, equal-and-immediate conditions, objective conditions, and predominant conditions.

As for the remaining faculties, these refer to the mental faculty (*manas*), the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), as well as the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*).
This is also stated collectively because it possesses the same conditions and so forth;
however, there is a distinction in its causes,
namely that it acts as three types of causes for the nine faculties beginning with the mental faculty (*manas*).
That is to say, the associated, co-existent,
and homogeneous causes act as a single cause for the faculty of one who has already known;
that is, they are the homogeneous cause.

The faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) and the faculty of one who has already known take [the faculty of one who has already known] as their cause, equal-immediate, object, and predominant conditions.
As for the cause, there are three causes.
That is to say, the associated, coexistent,
and homogeneous causes [of the mental factors] serve as a single dominant condition for the seven material faculties, the life faculty, and the faculty of suffering.

It serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*). For the other faculties,
it serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition, and the predominant condition.
As for the remaining faculties, they refer to the mental faculty (*manas*), the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*),
and the faculty of one who possesses full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*). These are also spoken of collectively because they likewise possess [the same] conditions and so forth.
However, there is a difference in terms of causes; that is to say, [the mental factors] act as three types of causes for the nine faculties beginning with the mind-faculty:
namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
It shares a single cause with the faculty of one who has already known;
that is, they are mutually similar causes (sabhāga-hetu).
The faculty of one who has already known likewise [shares a single cause] with the faculty of one who has already known.
They function as causes, equal-and-immediate conditions, object conditions, and dominant conditions.
Regarding the causes, there are three types:
namely, the associated cause, the co-existent cause, and the homogeneous cause.
Together with the seven faculties, the life-faculty, and the faculty of suffering,
they constitute one predominance.
Together with the faculty of grief, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," and the faculty of "having known," [they constitute another].
It serves as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
It also serves as the cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya), the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), the object-condition, and the dominant condition for the other faculties.
As for "the other faculties":
This refers to the five faculties of intention, joy, pleasure, equanimity, and faith.
As for their causes, there are three:
namely, the associated cause, the co-existent cause, and the homogeneous cause.
Regarding "immediately preceding" (samanantara):
it refers to the manifestation of the nine faculties, beginning with the mental faculty (manas), immediately following the faculty of perfect knowledge (ājñendriya).
As for the object-condition (*ālambana*):
it refers to the faculty of full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) taking the nine faculties, such as the mental faculty (*manas*), as its objects.
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati*): [it refers to...]
That is to say, it is that which does not obstruct arising and is merely non-obstructive.
