Chapter Six: The Aggregate of the Faculties (Indriya-skandha), Section Two of the Second Sub-section on Intermediate Existence (Antarābhava). All faculties that have the untainted (anāsrava) as their object and are bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
Is this faculty associated with dharma-knowledge? Furthermore,
if this faculty is associated with untainted dharma-knowledge,
does this faculty take that which is bound to the desire realm as its object?
It can be answered in four propositions:
there are faculties that are untainted (*anāsrava*), take the desire realm as their object (*ālambana*),
yet are not associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
This refers to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) and its associated faculties (indriya),
as well as the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) and the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origination (samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti).
And as for the associated faculties:
herein, the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*).
This faculty takes as its object that which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
It is not associated with the knowledge of the non-phenomenal (adharma-jñāna), because patience (kṣānti) is not associated with knowledge,
and also because it is associated with the faculties (indriya).
This refers to the eight untainted faculties associated with the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
These faculties also take the factors bound to the desire realm as their object,
yet they are not associated with dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*).
Because it is associated with patience (*kṣānti*),
the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is also an untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*).
This faculty likewise takes that which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) as its object.
It is not associated with non-dharma-knowledge (*adharma-jñāna*),
because a self-entity is not associated with itself.
That is to say, for three reasons, a self-entity is not associated with itself.
First, because the two natures are simultaneously co-emergent;
second, because preceding and succeeding moments do not exist concurrently;
and third, because all phenomena do not depend upon their own intrinsic nature to serve as conditions for others.
The patience of the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti*) and its associated faculties;
the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*) is also like this.
There are faculties that are untainted (*anāsrava*) and associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
These faculties do not take the objects of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) as their cognitive objects;
namely, those faculties associated with the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*) and the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*).
These are the eight untainted faculties associated with the dharma-knowledge of the path of cessation.
These faculties do not take the factors bound to the desire realm as their object,
because they take as their objects those factors that are unbound.
There are faculties that are untainted (*anāsrava*) and take the desire realm as their object;
these faculties are also associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
namely, those faculties associated with the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering and its origin.
These are the eight untainted faculties associated with the dharma-knowledge of the origin of suffering.
These faculties take as their object that which is bound to the desire realm,
because they take as their object the suffering and the origin within the desire realm.
There are faculties that are untainted (*anāsrava*) and do not take the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as their object;
these faculties are also not associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
That is to say, they are the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*).
And the faculties associated with these two:
the acceptance of the knowledge of the category of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the category of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*),
as well as the faculties associated with these two.
The patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) and its associated faculties;

the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*); the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*), together with their two associated faculties.
The patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*),
as well as its associated faculties;

the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*).
And there are the two faculties associated with them.

Among these, both the acceptance of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*) are the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsravaprajñendriya*).
This faculty does not take as its object that which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Because it is associated with the form and formless realms,
it is also not associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*);
for patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are not mutually associated.
Regarding the eight faculties associated with the two types of receptivity and knowledge:

these refer to the eight untainted faculties associated with the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*).
These faculties do not take as their object that which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
Because it is associated with the form and formless realms,
it is also not associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*); rather,
it is associated with the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*).
The same applies to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origin (samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti) and the subsequent knowledge of origin (samudaya-anvaya-jñāna),
as well as the faculties associated with these two.
The patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) is the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*).
This faculty does not take that which is bound to the desire realm as its object,
because it takes that which is unbound (*asaṃyukta*) as its object.
Nor is it associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
because patience (*kṣānti*) is not associated with knowledge,
and [it is] associated with the faculties (*indriya*).
This refers to the eight untainted faculties associated with the receptivity to the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*).
These faculties do not take the desire realm as their object,
because they take unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃbaddhadharma*) as their object.
Nor is it associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
because it is associated with receptivity (*kṣānti*).
Furthermore, the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*nirodhadharmajñāna*) is also an untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsravaprajñendriya*).
This faculty does not take the factors bound to the desire realm as its object,
because it takes unbound phenomena as its object;
nor is it associated with dharma-knowledge.
Because a self-entity does not associate with itself,
the path-dharma-knowledge-acceptance (mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) and its associated faculties [do not associate with themselves].
The same applies to the path-dharma-knowledge (mārga-dharma-jñāna).

Both the acceptance of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*) are the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsravaprajñendriya*).
This faculty does not take objects bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*),
because it takes as its object phenomena that are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta-dharma*).
Nor is it associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),
because patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are not mutually associated,
and because [it is] a faculty associated with both.
This refers to the eight untainted faculties associated with the patience of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of cessation itself.
These faculties do not take the desire realm as their object,
because they take unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃyukta-dharma*) as their object.
Nor is it associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*),

because it is associated with the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*). [The same applies to] the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
The same applies to the faculties associated with those two [knowledges].
Regarding those faculties that have the untainted as their object and are bound to the form and formless realms:
are these faculties associated with the knowledge of categories (*anvaya-jñāna*)?
If a faculty is associated with the untainted subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna),
does that faculty take as its object that which is bound to the form realm (rūpa-dhātu) or the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu)?
One should respond by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are faculties that have untainted objects and are bound to the form and formless realms;
these faculties are not associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
namely, the receptivity to subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñānakṣānti*).
And the faculties associated with them;
the receptivities to the subsequent knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge of origin,
and the faculties associated with them.

Regarding the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaye ’nvayajñāna*): herein, the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) is the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsravaprajñendriya*).

This faculty takes as its object that which is bound to the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpyadhātupratisaṃyukta*), and it is not associated with subsequent knowledge (*nānvayajñānasamprayukta*).
Because patience (*kṣānti*) is not associated with knowledge (*jñāna*),
and regarding the faculties that are associated [with it]:
this refers to the eight untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) associated with the patience of subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñānakṣānti*).
This faculty also takes as its object that which is bound to the form and formless realms;
it is not associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
because it is associated with receptivity (*kṣānti*).
The subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) is also an untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*).
This faculty also takes as its object that which is bound to the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu-saṃprayukta*),
but it does not correspond with itself, because a self-nature cannot be associated with itself.
The faculty associated with the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origin (samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti) is likewise. The subsequent knowledge of origin is also thus.
There is a faculty that is untainted (anāsrava) and associated with the subsequent knowledge of origin.
These faculties do not take as their objects those bound to the form or formless realms;
that is to say, they are the faculties associated with the subsequent knowledge of cessation and the subsequent knowledge of the path.
These are the eight untainted faculties associated with the subsequent knowledge of cessation and the subsequent knowledge of the path.
These faculties do not take the factors bound to the form and formless realms as their objects,
because they take the unbound dharmas as their objects.
There are, however, faculties that are untainted (anāsrava) and which take the factors bound to the form and formless realms as their objects.
These faculties are also associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*);
that is, the faculties associated with the subsequent knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge of origination.
These are the eight untainted faculties associated with the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origination.
These faculties have the bound states of the form and formless realms as their objects,
because they take the suffering and origin of the form and formless realms as their objects.
There are also faculties that are untainted (anāsrava) which do not have the bound states of the form and formless realms as their objects.
These faculties are also not associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

That is to say: the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), and the faculties associated with these two.
The receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*),
along with the faculties associated with these two;
as well as the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*).
And the faculties associated with those two;
the faculty associated with the acceptance of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the faculty [associated with] the subsequent knowledge of cessation;
and the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the dharma-knowledge of the path.
Furthermore, the faculties associated with the two [types of patience], as well as the faculties associated with the receptivity to the knowledge of the path and the knowledge of the path—
herein, both the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering and the knowledge of the dharma of suffering are the untainted faculty of wisdom (anāsrava-prajñendriya).
This faculty does not take as its object that which is bound to the form or formless realms,
because it takes as its object that which is bound to the desire realm;
furthermore, it is not associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Because patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are not associated with one another,
and regarding the faculties associated with both:

this refers to the eight untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) associated with the patience for the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*).
This faculty does not take as its object that which is bound to the form or formless realms,
because it takes as its object that which is bound to the desire realm;
nor is it associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Because they are associated with the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge of origination (samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti) and the dharma-knowledge of origination (samudaya-dharmajñāna),
as well as the faculties associated with these two, it is likewise.

The patience regarding the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) and the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (nirodha-dharma-jñāna) are both the untainted faculty of wisdom (anāsrava-prajñendriya).
This faculty does not take as its object that which is bound to the realms of form or formlessness,
because it takes as its object that which is unconditioned (asaṃbaddha-dharma).
Nor is it associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
because patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are not mutually associated,
and [it is] that which is associated with both faculties (*indriya*).

This refers to the eight untainted faculties associated with the acceptance of the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (dharmajñānakṣānti) and the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
These faculties do not take the phenomena bound to the form and formless realms as their objects,
because they take the unconditioned (unbound) phenomena as their objects.
Nor is it associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),

because it is associated with patience (*kṣānti*) and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*). [This applies to] the patience regarding the knowledge of phenomena concerning the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of phenomena concerning the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*).
The same applies to the two faculties associated with them.
The patience of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñānakṣānti*) is the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsravaprajñendriya*).
This faculty does not take as its object that which is bound to the form or formless realms.
Because it has as its object phenomena that are not bound [to any realm],
it is also not associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
since patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are not mutually associated.
Regarding the faculties associated [with it]:
this refers to the eight untainted faculties associated with the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).
These faculties do not take as their object that which is bound to the form or formless realms.
Because it takes non-tied phenomena as its object,
and because it is associated with the forbearances associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) is also an untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*).
This faculty does not take as its object that which is bound to the form or formless realms,
because it takes as its object that which is unconditioned (unbound).
Nor is it associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Because a self-nature does not associate with itself,
the path-knowledge-of-classification-acceptance (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and its associated faculties [do not associate with themselves].
The same applies to the path-knowledge-of-classification (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*).
"Should it be said that dharma-knowledge is simply dharma-knowledge?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: Why is the discussion here conducted solely in terms of the two knowledges, dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge?
The answer is that it is because the author of that treatise intended it so;
he composed the treatise according to his own intention.
As long as it does not contradict the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one should not hold him accountable.
If that author intends to compose a treatise based on two types of knowledge, he does so accordingly;
that is, the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) are treated as before in the *Jñānaskandha*.
Thus, according to the intention of the author, the treatise is composed based on these two knowledges.
That is to say, the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of recollecting past abodes are as explained in the subsequent *Samādhiskandha*.
Furthermore, according to the intention of the author of this treatise, the discussion is also based on two types of knowledge:
namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Thus, in this preceding *Skandhaprakaraṇa*, the author composed the treatise based on four types of knowledge—
namely, the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*),

and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). As was done previously in the *Saṃyojanaskandhaprakaraṇa*, the author composed that treatise based on eight types of knowledge according to his own intention.

These are the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. As in the *Jñeyavastu* chapter,
the author of the treatise composes this work based on these ten knowledges according to his own intention.
This refers to the aforementioned eight knowledges,
as well as the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
It is, for example, like a skilled potter who places a lump of moist clay upon a wheel.
Just as one fashions various vessels from clay according to one's will without contradicting the principles of craftsmanship, so too does a skilled author,
by means of the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection, [compose treatises].
Having practiced and clearly realized the objects of knowledge to eliminate delusion,
one may subsequently compose various treatises according to one's inclination;
these will not contradict the nature of all phenomena.
Some say that only the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) do not mutually include one another, and furthermore,
both universally take as their objects those realms that are not mutually included.
This refers to the dharmas of the four noble truths, which are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),

conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Some say that because the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) encompass all uncontaminated knowledge, they constitute its fundamental basis.
Some say that the two knowledges—
the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)— function as limited objects of cognition;
that is, the knowledge of phenomena takes the lower realms as its object, while the subsequent knowledge takes the upper realms as its object.
For these reasons, the treatise is composed based solely on these two knowledges.

Should the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) be called simply "knowledge of phenomena," or should it be called "subsequent knowledge" (*anvayajñāna*), "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*), "conventional knowledge" (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), or the "knowledge of suffering," "knowledge of origin," "knowledge of cessation," and "knowledge of the path"?
Answer: It should be said that it is dharma-knowledge, or else knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of origin, knowledge of cessation, or knowledge of the path.
Regarding what is called dharma-knowledge:
That is to say, knowing all conditioned phenomena of the desire realm,
the cause of those conditioned phenomena,
and the cessation of those conditioned phenomena.
Regarding the path that serves as the antidote to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) or the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*):
this refers to knowing the mental states and mental factors of others that constitute the path which serves as the antidote to conditioned phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Alternatively, it refers to the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*).
This refers to knowing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm possess the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. Alternatively,
for one who possesses knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*),
it means knowing that all conditioned phenomena of the desire realm possess the characteristics of cause, causal characteristic, origination characteristic, and condition characteristic.

Alternatively, knowledge of cessation refers to knowing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm possess the characteristic of cessation, the characteristic of tranquility, the characteristic of excellence, and the characteristic of detachment.
Alternatively, it is knowledge of the path.

That is to say, having already explained the knowledge of the path that serves as the antidote to the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm— namely, its aspect of the path, its aspect of tranquility, its aspect of practice,
and its aspect of emergence— one should now explain the stages (*bhūmi*).
Should the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) be said to be accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka and with only vicāra, or without both vitarka and vicāra?
Answer: It should be said that there are three types.
Namely, that which exists in the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and the first dhyāna is called "with vitarka and with vicāra.
That which exists in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is called "without vitarka and with only vicāra."
In the three higher dhyānas, they are called "without vitarka and without vicāra.
Having already explained the stages (*bhūmi*), the associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta*) shall now be explained.

Should the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) be said to be associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
Answer: It should be said that there are three types: namely, those associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in the third dhyāna;
those associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) in the first and second dhyānas;
and those in the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the fourth dhyāna.
Having already explained its association with the faculty of equanimity, one should now explain its aspects (*ākāra*).
Should it be said that the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), or signlessness (*animitta*)?
Answer: It should be said that there are three types:
namely, two associated with the aspect of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and ten associated with the aspect of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
The four aspects are associated with the signless.
Having already explained the aspects, one should now explain the objects of focus.
It should be said that dharma-knowledge takes what is bound to the desire realm as its object.
Does it have as its object that which is bound to the form realm? Does it have as its object that which is bound to the formless realm?
Or does it have as its object that which is unbound?
Answer: It should be said that it takes as its object that which is bound to the desire realm or that which is unbound.
Regarding that which takes as its object what is bound to the desire realm:
The dharma-knowledge of suffering and its origin takes that which is unconditioned as its object; the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path takes that which is unconditioned as its object.
Should subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) be called subsequent knowledge?
Or should it be called dharma-knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of origin, knowledge of cessation, or knowledge of the path?
Answer: It should be called subsequent knowledge; or it may be called knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of origin, knowledge of cessation, or knowledge of the path.
It should be said that it is "knowledge by way of category" (anvaya-jñāna),
meaning the knowledge of the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) of the form and formless realms, their causes, their cessation, and the path that serves as their antidote;
or it is the "knowledge of others' minds" (paracitta-jñāna).
This refers to knowing the formations of the form and formless realms, the untainted counteractive path, and the minds and mental factors of others; or,
for one possessing the knowledge of suffering,
it refers to knowing the four characteristics, such as impermanence, regarding the formations of the form and formless realms.
Alternatively, it is the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*),
which means knowing the four aspects of the causes of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the realms of form and formlessness, such as cause (*hetu*) and so forth;
or it is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
This refers to the knowledge of the four aspects of cessation, such as the cessation of formations in the form and formless realms;
or, regarding the knowledge of the path,
it refers to the knowledge of the four aspects of the path, such as the path that serves as the antidote to those formations in the form and formless realms.
Having already clarified the intrinsic nature, one should now clarify the stages.
Should subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) be said to involve vitarka and vicāra, to involve only vicāra without vitarka, or to be without both vitarka and vicāra?
Answer: It should be said to be of all three kinds.
That is to say, in the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and the first dhyāna, it is called "with vitarka and with vicāra";
in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), it is called "without vitarka and with vicāra only";
and in the three higher dhyānas and the lower three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), it is called "without vitarka and without vicāra."
Having explained the stages, one should now explain their associations.

Should subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) be said to be associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
Answer: It should be said to be of three kinds; that is, when it is in the third dhyāna, it is associated with the faculty of pleasure.
In the first and second dhyānas, it is associated with the faculty of joy (sukhendriya).
In the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the lower three formless attainments (ārūpya), it is associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
Having already explained the associated [factors], one should now explain the modes of activity (*ākāra*).
Should it be said that subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), or signlessness (*animitta*)?
Answer: It should be said to be associated with all three.
That is to say: two aspects are associated with emptiness;
ten aspects are associated with wishlessness;
and four aspects are associated with signlessness.
Having already explained the aspects of its activity, the objects of focus shall now be explained.
Should it be said that subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) takes as its object that which is bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta),
or that which is bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta)?
Does it have as its object that which is bound to the formless realm?
Or does it have as its object that which is unbound?
Answer: It should be said that it has as its object that which is bound to the form realm, the formless realm, or that which is unbound.

Those conditioned by the form and formless realms refer to the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origination; those not conditioned by any realm refer to the subsequent knowledge of cessation and the path.
At that time, when there is liberation of mind, should it be said that one attains the faculty of a learner (śaikṣendriya) or attains the faculty of one beyond learning (aśaikṣendriya)? ...
[and so on] up to the full explanation.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the sūtras, as the Buddha told Ānanda:
A bhikṣu should not delight in dwelling amidst clamor and bustle.
If he delights in such things, he will fail to realize for himself, in this very life,
either the liberation of mind through loving-kindness at the proper time, or the unshakable liberation of mind at any time.
It is impossible for such a person to dwell in full possession [of that state]. However,
if there is a bhikṣu who does not delight in clamor but delights in solitude, he will,
at that time, attain the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*maitrī-cetovimukti*).
Or, there is the possibility that one may personally realize the immovable liberation of mind at any time and dwell in its full perfection; although that sutra speaks of two kinds of liberation,
it does not differentiate between their respective intrinsic natures.
Nor has it yet been revealed by which faculty [this] is attained.
Although the intrinsic nature of liberation was already indicated within the preceding Section on Knowledge (*jñānaskandha*),
its attainment has not yet been revealed.
Now, desiring to reveal [the truth], this treatise is composed.
Some say it is because one wishes to refute what others have asserted.

That is to say, some maintain that the liberation of mind of one in training (śaikṣa) is subject to effort because there is still work to be done and what is to be accomplished has not yet been completed;
whereas the immovable liberation of mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is free from effort because there is no further work to be done and what was to be accomplished has already been completed.
To refute that attachment,
it is shown that both types of liberation are the work of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) who has already accomplished what was to be done.
Alternatively, there may be those who hold [the following view]:
At that time, liberation of mind through insight (*ceto-vimukti*) is with outflows (*sāsrava*),
whereas unshakable liberation of mind (*akopyā ceto-vimukti*) is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
To show that both types of liberation are indeed without outflows, he intends to stop that [previous] thought.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that occasional liberation of the mind (*sāmayikī-ceto-vimukti*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
while unshakable liberation of the mind (*akopyā-ceto-vimukti*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
To refute that attachment and to demonstrate that both types of liberation are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
this treatise was composed for such reasons.
Among all phenomena, only two dharmas constitute the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of liberation.
This means that among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there is only resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*);
among unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), there is only analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That resolute conviction is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika-caitasika*) that is always associated with the mind.
That analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is dissociation (visamyoga),
the ultimate good (paramārtha-kuśala), and the eternally abiding nirvāṇa.
There are two kinds of resolute conviction (adhimokṣa).
That is to say, it is either defiled or non-defiled.
"Defiled" refers to wrong resolve,
which is associated with the afflictions and secondary afflictions such as greed and so forth.
"Non-defilement" refers to correct resolute conviction (*samyag-adhimokṣa*),
which is associated with various wholesome factors such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth.
This correct resolute conviction is further of two kinds.

They are said to be with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*). Those with outflows refer to those associated with the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Those without outflows are further divided into two.
This refers to those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Those in training refers to the untainted resolve (anāsrava-adhimokṣa) within the bodies of the seven types of noble beings.
Those beyond training refers to...
This refers to the untainted resolve within the body of an arhat.
Furthermore, the resolve of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is of two kinds:
namely, liberation through timely mind (samayavimukti).
"Untimely liberation of mind" and "timely liberation of mind" refer to the untainted resolve within the bodies of the five types of arhats.
"Timely liberation of mind" refers to the untainted (anāsrava) resolute confidence (adhimokṣa) within the person of an Arhat of immovable dharma (akopyadharman).
These two are also termed liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
Because it is free from greed, it is called liberation of mind (*citta-vimukti*);
because it is free from ignorance, it is called liberation by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
Question: If this resolve is called liberation of mind because it is free from greed...

Regarding the statement that one is called "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*) because of being free from ignorance (*avidyā*), how should one reconcile this with what is taught in the *Saṃgītiparyāya* and other texts?
For instance, it is asked: "In what way is the mind liberated through freedom from desire? (*kathaṃ vigatarāgatvād cittaṃ vimucyate*).
Answer: Because the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*) counteracts attachment (*lobha*).
How is it that wisdom attains liberation by being separated from ignorance (*avidyā*)?
Answer: Because the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha*) counteracts delusion (*moha*).
Because of this statement, the essence of the two liberations is the wholesome root (*kuśalamūla*) and not resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
The answer is that the text should have stated it thus: [the essence of the two liberations is resolute conviction].
How is it that the mind attains liberation through the abandonment of greed?
Answer: It is the mental resolve and confirmation associated with the wholesome root of non-greed;
this is precisely what is called "timely liberation of the mind."
How is it that wisdom attains liberation by being free from ignorance?
Answer: It is the mental resolve and confirmation associated with the wholesome root of non-delusion;
this is precisely what is called the immovable liberation of mind.
What is the intention behind not making such a statement?
The answer is: this is stated in terms of the basis (*āśraya*) to manifest resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
That is to say, by relying on non-attachment (*alobha*), the mind is liberated from attachment (*lobha*).
Because of non-delusion, the mind is liberated from delusion.
However, the essence of this liberation of the mind is resolve (*adhimokṣa*).

At that time of the mind’s liberation, should it be said that it is acquired through the faculties of one in training (*śaikṣa*), the faculties of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or the faculties of both? Answer: It should be said that it is acquired through the faculties of one in training and the faculties of one beyond training.
The acquisition of the faculties of one in training refers to the faculties arising simultaneously with the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The acquisition of the faculties of one beyond training refers to the faculties arising simultaneously with the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Furthermore, the acquisition of the faculty of training refers to the faculties arising simultaneously with the path of training; the acquisition of the faculty of no-more-learning refers to [the faculties arising simultaneously with] the path of no-more-learning.
This refers to the faculties co-arising with the fruit and the path.
Furthermore, regarding the acquisition of the faculties of one in training (*śaikṣa*),
it refers to the group of faculties co-arising with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
The acquisition of the faculties of one beyond training refers to the faculties belonging to the category co-arising with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Furthermore, there is the acquisition of the faculties of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
The faculty of "one who has already known" (ājñātendriya) refers to the attainment of the faculty of "one who has fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
Furthermore, the acquisition of the faculties of those in training refers to the faculties arising together with the path of cultivation;
the acquisition of the faculties of those beyond training refers to the faculties arising together with the path of no-more-learning.
It is the same for the stage of cultivation and the stage of no-more-learning.
Regarding immovable liberation of mind,
should it be said that one attains the faculties of a learner or the faculties of one beyond learning?
Are the faculties of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) acquired?
Answer: If one originally attains the immovable [state], it should be said that the faculties of those in training and those beyond training are acquired.
If an Arhat who is liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) attains the immovable state, [the same applies].
It should be said that they are acquired by the faculties of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding their acquisition by the faculties of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training,
the detailed explanation is as previously stated.
Regarding the attainment of the faculties of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*):
because both the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) therein are comprised within the state of being beyond training,
the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarva-saṃyojana-kṣaya*) should be said to be attained through the faculties of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
Are they acquired by the faculties of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), or are they acquired by both the faculties of one in training (śaikṣa) and those of one beyond training?
Answer: It should be said that they are acquired by both the faculties of one in training and those of one beyond training.
The detailed explanation is as before.
Question: Why is this passage not stated in the same manner as the explanation of the liberation through immovable mind (*āniñjya-cetovimukti*)?
Answer: This passage should also be stated in that way.
If one first realizes the exhaustion of all fetters,
it should be said that the faculties of both the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) are attained.
When an Arhat liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) attains the realization of immovability (*akopya*), he realizes the exhaustion of all fetters.
One should say that they are acquired by the faculties of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What is the intention behind not making such a statement?
The answer is: there are two kinds of liberation.
That is to say, there are two kinds: conditioned and unconditioned. The two types of liberation of mind are conditioned;
the exhaustion of all fetters is unconditioned.
Conditioned liberation has inferior, middling, and superior grades;
it is explained as being differentiated because that which is first attained differs from that which is attained later.
Unconditioned liberation has no inferior, middling, or superior grades.
Since the subsequent attainment is identical to the first, it is not explained separately.
One realizes the fruit of stream-entry by means of the path of uninterrupted realization;
this path should be said to be associated with dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).

Are subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) associated with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), or without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*)?
They should be said to be [associated] with applied thought and sustained thought, without applied thought but with sustained thought, and without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Should it be said that it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
Should it be said that it is associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), or signlessness (*animitta*)?

Should it be said that it takes as its object that which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or that which is unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
Answer: One realizes the fruit of stream-entry by means of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).

This path should be said to be associated with patience (*kṣānti*), accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
Regarding "associated with the patience of non-attachment":

this is because it is concomitant with the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti). Regarding "with vitarka and vicāra": [this refers to its association with initial and sustained mental application].
It is solely because it relies on the stage of the threshold (anāgamya).
As for its association with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya),
this is because in the threshold stage there is only the feeling of equanimity.
Regarding that which is associated with wishlessness (*apraṇihita*): it is because the Path is conjoined with wishlessness;
and regarding its object (*ālambana*), it is because the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)—which is not bound [to any realm]—serves as its object.
When one realizes the fruit of once-returner by means of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
should this path be said to be associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*),

or is it associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), or knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)?
Should it be said that it is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, or accompanied by vicāra alone, or without both vitarka and vicāra?
Should it be said that it is associated with the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of joy, or the faculty of equanimity?
Should it be said that it is associated with emptiness, wishlessness, or signlessness?
Should it be said that [this] has as its object that which is bound to the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, or that which is unbound?
Answer: If one who has further abandoned the defilements of desire enters into the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), [then it has as its object that which is unbound].
As it was explained regarding the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*):
if one realizes the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*) from the fruit of stream-entry by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*),
this path should be said to be associated with mundane knowledge (*laukika-jñāna*).
It is associated with vitarka and vicāra, associated with the faculty of equanimity,
takes as its object that which is bound to the desire realm,
and is associated with conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
This means that because any one of the three aspects— coarseness and so forth— occurs therein,
it is not associated with emptiness and the others;
for those [latter] are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding those conditioned by the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*):
because the five aggregates of the desire realm serve as their objects of focus (*ālambana*).
The rest is as previously explained. If one realizes the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
This path should be said to be associated with either dharma-knowledge,
or knowledge of suffering,
or knowledge of origin.
It is either associated with the knowledge of cessation or the knowledge of the path;
it is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, and associated with the faculty of equanimity.
It is associated with either emptiness, wishlessness, or signlessness;
it takes as its object either that which is bound to the desire realm or that which is unbound.
"Associated with dharma-knowledge" means being associated with any one of the four dharma-knowledges; or,
"associated with the knowledge of suffering."
That which is associated with the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna),
up to that which is associated with the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna),
is associated with the dharma-knowledge of the path (mārga-dharmajñāna).
"Or associated with emptiness" means being associated with two aspects;
"or associated with wishlessness" means... [the same applies].
This refers to being associated with ten aspects,
or being associated with no aspect;
that is, being associated with four aspects.
Alternatively, those that take as their object what is bound to the desire realm refer to the dharma-knowledges of suffering and origin;
those that take as their object what is unbound refer to the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path.
The rest is as previously explained.
By means of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), one realizes the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
This path should be said to be associated with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).

Are the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) associated with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitarko vicāramātra*), or without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarko 'vicāra*)?
They should be said to be [associated] with applied thought and sustained thought, without applied thought but with sustained thought, and without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Should it be said that it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
Should it be said that it is associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), or signlessness (*animitta*)?

Should it be said that it has as its object that which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or that which is unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
Answer: If one has already become free from the defilement of desire and enters into the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma),
this path should be said to be associated with patience (kṣānti) and may be accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra.
Either with no vitarka and only vicāra,
or with neither vitarka nor vicāra;
or associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
It is associated either with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) or with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*),
and it is associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
It is conditioned by that which is not bound.
That which is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra refers to [the mind] based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya) or the first dhyāna.
Alternatively, there is that which is without vitarka and with vicāra only,
namely, that which relies on the intermediate dhyāna;
or there is that which is without both vitarka and vicāra.
This refers to those associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) based on the three higher dhyānas—
namely, the third dhyāna—
or those associated with the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya).
This refers to those based on the first and second dhyānas,
or those associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*),
which refers to those based on the *anāgamya* dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.
The remainder is as previously explained.
If one realizes the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) from the fruit of once-returner by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*),
it is as described for realizing the fruit of once-returner by means of the mundane path.
If one realizes the fruit of non-returner from the fruit of once-returner by means of the untainted path,
it is as explained regarding the realization of the fruit of once-returner by means of the untainted path; [in this case],
one realizes the fruit of arhatship by means of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Regarding this path, should it be said that it is associated with dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of origin, knowledge of cessation, or knowledge of the path?
Should it be said that it is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka and with vicāra only, or without both vitarka and vicāra?
Should it be said that it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
Should it be said that it is associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), or signlessness (*animitta*)?

Should it be said that it takes as its object that which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or that which is unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?

Answer: This path should be said to be associated either with dharma-knowledge, or with subsequent knowledge, or with the knowledge of suffering, or with the knowledge of origin, or with the knowledge of cessation, or with the knowledge of the path.
It may also be accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
Either with no vitarka and only vicāra,
or with neither vitarka nor vicāra,
or with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
It is associated with either the faculty of joy or the faculty of equanimity;
it is associated with either emptiness, wishlessness, or signlessness;
or it takes that which is bound to the formless realm as its object.
Alternatively, it takes what is unconditioned as its object;
or, it is associated with dharma-knowledge,
meaning it is associated with either the dharma-knowledge of cessation or the dharma-knowledge of the path.
"Or associated with subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)" means being associated with any one of the four subsequent knowledges;
"or associated with the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) or the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna)" means the same.
That which is associated with the subsequent knowledge of suffering and its origin (duḥkha-samudaya-anvaya-jñāna),
or associated with the knowledge of cessation and the path (nirodha-mārga-jñāna),
is associated with the dharma and subsequent knowledge of cessation and the path (nirodha-mārga-dharma-anvaya-jñāna).
There are those with both vitarka and vicāra,
namely those relying on the threshold concentration (anāgamya) or the first dhyāna;
or there are those with no vitarka and only vicāra.
This refers to relying on the intermediate dhyāna,
or being without vitarka and vicāra; that is,
relying on the [upper] three dhyānas and the [lower] three formless attainments.
Alternatively, it may be associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
which refers to its basis in the third dhyāna;
or it may be associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
This refers to those based on the first and second dhyānas,
or those associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya),
namely those based on the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), the fourth dhyāna, and the lower three formless attainments (ārūpya).
Alternatively, that which is associated with emptiness refers to being associated with two aspects;
or alternatively, that which is associated with wishlessness.
That is to say, it is associated with ten aspects;
or, being associated with the signless,
it is associated with four aspects.
Alternatively, it may take that which is bound to the formless realm as its object;
this refers to the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origination taking the suffering and origination of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as its object.
Alternatively, it may take that which is unbound as its object.

This refers to the fact that the knowledge of the dharma and subsequent knowledge regarding cessation and the path take as their objects the cessations of the three realms and the paths that serve as their antidotes.
Through how many faculties does one attain the fruit of stream-entry by means of the permanent abandonment and cessation [of defilements]?
Answer: Through the permanent abandonment of the non-roots, seven roots cease and arise.
With one ceasing and not arising while another arises and does not cease, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
Regarding the cessation and arising of the seven faculties:
"seven" refers to the mental faculty (*manas*), the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
"Cessation" means that these seven are subsumed within the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
"Arising" refers to what is subsumed under these seven paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Furthermore, "cessation" refers to what is subsumed under the path of approach (*pratipannaka-mārga*),
while "arising" refers to what is subsumed under the path of fruition (*phala-mārga*).
Furthermore, "cessation" refers to that which is subsumed under the category of the acceptance of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*);
"arising" refers to that which is subsumed under the category of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
Moreover, "cessation" refers to that which arises simultaneously with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
"Arising" refers to that which arises simultaneously with the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*).
Furthermore, "cessation" is comprised within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
while "arising" is comprised within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The same applies to the stage of seeing and the stage of cultivation.
Regarding "one ceases and does not arise":
this refers to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
That which is not extinguished together [with the path] refers to the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya).
How many faculties are permanently severed and arise when one attains the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala)?

Answer: If one enters the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) by being doubly detached from the defilements of desire, it is as explained regarding the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala).
If, however, one realizes the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala) from the fruit of stream-entry by means of the mundane path (laukika-mārga), [it is as follows].
One who has eternally severed the roots of unwholesomeness attains the fruit of a Once-Returner through the cessation and arising of seven faculties.
Regarding the cessation and arising of the seven faculties, the seven are as previously explained;
"cessation" refers to these seven being subsumed within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
"Arising" refers to what is subsumed under these seven paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
Furthermore, "cessation" refers to what is subsumed under the path of approach (*pratipannakamārga*),
while "arising" refers to what is subsumed under the path of fruition (*phalamārga*).
If one realizes the fruit of once-returner from the fruit of stream-enterer by means of the untainted path,
eight faculties are eternally abandoned and eight faculties cease and arise, whereby the fruit of once-returner is attained.
Regarding the cessation and arising of these eight faculties:
The eighth consists of the aforementioned seven faculties plus the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
The meaning of their cessation and arising is as previously explained.
How many faculties are permanently severed when one attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) through the cessation and arising [of these]?
Answer: If one has already become free from the defilement of desire and enters into rightness-in-detachment (samyaktva-niyāma), there is the permanent abandonment of the faculties;
seven faculties cease and arise, while one faculty ceases but does not arise.
Together they are extinguished;
one attains the fruit of non-returning.
Regarding the extinction and arising of the seven faculties:
The seventh consists of any one of the faculties of mind, pleasure, joy, or equanimity,
along with the five faculties beginning with faith.
The remainder is as explained in the section on attaining the fruit of stream-entry.

If one realizes the fruit of non-returner from the fruit of once-returner by means of the mundane path without entering meditative absorption, four faculties are permanently abandoned and seven faculties cease and arise upon attaining the fruit of non-returner.
Regarding "four faculties are permanently abandoned": [the faculties of suffering, grief, body, and doubt].
This refers to the female and male faculties, as well as the faculties of suffering and mental distress.
Regarding the cessation and arising of the seven faculties:
"seven" refers to the mental faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the five faculties beginning with faith.
The meaning of cessation and arising is as explained regarding the transition from the stage of stream-enterer to the stage of once-returner.
If one enters meditative absorption (dhyāna),
four faculties are permanently severed.
The six sense faculties cease and arise;
one ceases and does not arise,
while another arises and does not cease.
One attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Regarding the permanent abandonment of four faculties, it is as previously explained.
As for the cessation and arising of six faculties:
The six refer to the mind faculty and the five faculties beginning with faith.
The meaning of their cessation and arising is as previously explained.
Regarding "one ceases and does not arise":
This refers to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
That which arises but does not cease refers to the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
If one realizes the fruit of non-returner from the fruit of once-returner by means of the untainted path,
without entering dhyāna, eight faculties are permanently abandoned, eight faculties cease and arise,
and one attains the fruit of non-returner.
The eight faculties are:
the mental faculty, the equanimity faculty, the five beginning with the faith faculty, and the faculty of one who has already known;
the remainder is as previously explained.
If one enters meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), four faculties are permanently severed, seven faculties cease and arise, one faculty ceases but does not arise,
and one faculty arises but does not cease;
thus one attains the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
The seven faculties are those previously mentioned— the mental faculty and the five beginning with faith—
along with the faculty of one who has already known.
The remainder is as explained in the section on realizing the fruit of non-returner by means of the mundane path.
Question: Regarding the ninth path of liberation that abandons the defilements of the desire realm, who immediately enters meditative absorption?
Who does not enter?
Answer: Those whose supporting power is strong enter;
those whose supporting power is weak do not enter.
Some say that those with weak faculties enter [the path] in order to nourish their physical basis.
Those with a strong foundational power do not enter [the womb],
because they do not serve to nourish the foundation. Some say:
Those with a predominance of delight enter;
those with a predominance of aversion do not enter. Some say:
Those with an abundance of joy and pleasure enter;
those with an abundance of sorrow and suffering do not enter. Some say:
Those who have become free from the defilements of desire through the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path enter;
those who have become free from the defilements of desire through the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of the origin do not enter. Some say:
Those who have abandoned the defilements of desire through the path of signlessness (*animitta*) and the wishless (*apraṇihita*) enter [the attainment];
those who have abandoned the defilements of desire through emptiness (*śūnyatā*), suffering (*duḥkha*), origination (*samudaya*), and the wishless do not enter. Some say:
Those who have developed revulsion for the phenomena of the desire realm and are free from the defilement of desire enter;
those who have developed revulsion for the phenomena of the three realms and are free from the defilement of desire do not enter. Some say:
Those who have become detached through seeking meditative concentration enter it; those who have become detached through seeking liberation do not enter it.
Some say that those with sharp faculties enter it.
Those of dull faculties do not enter.
As it is with those of sharp and dull faculties,
so it is with the power of causes and the power of conditions.
The internal force and the external force;
likewise, one should understand that the force of internal right reflection and the force of externally hearing the true Dharma are also thus.
How many faculties are permanently severed, and how many arise through cessation, when one attains the fruit of arhatship?
Answer: If one realizes the fruit of arhatship based on the *anāgamya* stage, one faculty is permanently severed and seven faculties cease and arise.
When one ceases, the other does not arise;
when one arises, the other does not cease.
Thus, one attains the fruit of arhatship.
The single faculty that is eternally severed is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Regarding the seven faculties that are eternally severed, arise, and cease:
"seven" refers to the mental faculty (*manas*), the equanimity faculty (*upekṣā*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
"Permanent abandonment" refers to that which is comprised within the outflows (*āsrava*).
"Cessation" refers to that which is comprised within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*). "Arising" refers to that which is comprised within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Furthermore, "permanent abandonment" refers to that which is comprised within the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Cessation refers to that which is subsumed under the path of application;
arising refers to that which is subsumed under the path of fruition.
Furthermore, permanent abandonment refers to that which is subsumed under neither-training-nor-non-training.
Cessation refers to that which is comprised within the stage of training (śaikṣa); arising refers to that which is comprised within the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, perpetual abandonment refers to that which is comprised within the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
Cessation refers to that which is comprised within the category co-arising with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Arising refers to that which is comprised within the category co-arising with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
Furthermore, permanent abandonment refers to that which is comprised within what is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Cessation is comprised within the faculty of "one who has already known" (ājñātendriya); arising is comprised within the faculty of "one who possesses full knowledge" (ājñātāvīndriya).
Furthermore, permanent abandonment is comprised within that which is bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu);
cessation is comprised within the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
"Arising" refers to that which is subsumed within the stage of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
"One [faculty] ceases without arising" refers to the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*). "One [faculty] arises without ceasing" refers to the faculty of final knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
This refers to the faculty of one who has final knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
As it is based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), so it is also for the intermediate dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
If one realizes the fruit of arhatship based on the first dhyāna,
two faculties are permanently severed,
and six faculties are permanently severed and cease to arise.
One faculty ceases and arises;
one faculty ceases but does not arise;
one faculty arises but does not cease.
Regarding the two faculties that are permanently severed upon attaining the fruit of Arhatship, these refer to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣendriya*).

Regarding the six faculties that are permanently severed and arise [again], "six" refers to the mental faculty (*manas*) and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*); the meaning of their permanent severance and arising is as previously explained. Regarding the one faculty that ceases and arises: [it is the body-faculty].
The first refers to the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
The meaning of its cessation and arising is as previously explained. "One that ceases and does not arise" refers to the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
That which is co-existent and indestructible refers to the faculty of one who has already attained full knowledge (*ājñātāvindriya*).
This is as when relying upon the first dhyāna.
The same applies to the second and third dhyānas.
However, the distinction is that [this refers specifically] to the basis of the third dhyāna.
The arising and ceasing of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) should be explained.
