It was asked: "Why did the Wheel-Turning King, whose eye-faculty is supreme, not take it himself, but instead have his ministers take it?
The answer was: "The dharma for all noble and superior persons ought to be thus."
Just as other venerable ones, although they know where their food, clothing, and requisites are located,
do not take them for themselves, this case is also like that.
Other masters say:
The various universal monarchs have accumulated karma throughout other lifetimes that results in the service of attendants;
as that karma now ripens, whatever they may require, there are attendants who provide for and prepare it all.
If the king were to take [the fruit] for himself, his karma would be rendered futile.
Question: Following from this discussion, what is the karma by which the various Cakravartin kings bring about their attendant ministers?
Answer: To respectfully follow and not oppose the lawful instructions of one's parents, teachers, and elders constitutes this karma.
If one has previously practiced such karma, it results in having many attendants who accomplish all that one desires.
Question: It has been heard that in some places the waters of the Ganges are one *yojana* deep;
how then can the minister’s hand and the bottom of the river both reach to take up various precious jewels?
Answer: By the predominant power of the Wheel-turning King’s (*cakravartin*) karma, the jewels are caused to rise upward.
Some say that yakṣas,
gandharvas, and others bring it and bestow it.
Others say:
There were always ten thousand devas who followed the Treasurer as his attendants;
they brought forth and presented [the treasures] to him.
When asked why he did so, the Treasurer addressed the King, saying:
As for the remainder that is not needed, it should be discarded back into the water.
This answer reveals that the karmic fruits of the King’s deeds are inconceivable;
thus, whatever is required can be obtained wherever one is.
Unlike other classes of beings who might fear for their physical lives and thus accumulate [wealth] over long periods for fear of future scarcity, [the Buddha does not].
Question: How many worlds can the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas perceive?
Answer: The divine eye of a śrāvaka, without applying effort (*anabhisamskāra*), sees a small thousandfold world system;
if it applies effort, it sees a medium thousandfold world system.
The divine eye of a pratyekabuddha, without applying effort, sees a medium thousandfold world system.
If one applies effort, one sees a great trichiliocosm;
the World-Honored One’s divine eye, without applying effort, sees a great trichiliocosm,
and if he were to apply effort, he could see immeasurable and boundless worlds.
As it is with the supernormal power of the divine eye,
so it is with the supernormal power of the divine ear and others.
How many faculties (indriya) are possessed by those in the hells?
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: Why is it that here only the states of achieving the absolute minimum and maximum are mentioned, and not the other states?
Answer: Because that author of the treatise intended it to be so.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Some say this is to eliminate the fault of textual confusion.
That is to say, if one were to explain all stages in their entirety,
the text would become so disordered as to be difficult to receive and uphold; therefore,
it is explained according to the limits of their minimum and maximum extents.
How many faculties (indriya) do those in hell possess?
How many do animals, and so on up to those in the formless realms, and from those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) up to those liberated through both parts (ubhayatobhāgavimukta), possess?
Answer: Those in hell possess at most nineteen, and at least eight.
The nineteenth refers to one who possesses the seven material faculties and has not severed the roots of goodness, excluding the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
The eight [faculties] refer to the body, life, mind, and the five feeling-faculties.
This applies to those who have lost the six material faculties and whose roots of goodness are severed.
Among animals, the maximum number is nineteen and the minimum is thirteen.
The nineteenth case refers to one who possesses seven material faculties, excluding the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
The thirteenth refers to the five faculties of body, life, mind, faith,
and so forth. These are the five faculties.
Regarding those who gradually reach the end of life by first relinquishing the six material sense-faculties:
as it is said for the animal realm,
so it is for the realm of hungry ghosts as well.
Those who have severed the roots of goodness have at most thirteen and at least eight.
The thirteen refers to excluding one gender organ, the five faculties beginning with faith, and the three untainted faculties.
The eighth refers to the body, life, mind, and the five faculties of sensation; that is,
those who are gradually dying, as well as those in hell who have already lost the six material faculties.
The group of those fixed in error has at most nineteen and at least eight.
As for the nineteen,
it is as explained regarding the maximum number for those in hell.
Eighth, as it is said regarding the severance of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*):

excluding those in the hells who have lost the six material faculties (*rūpīndriya*), the maximum number for those in the stage of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*) is nineteen, and the minimum is eleven.
As for the nineteen:
This refers to those noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire and whose faculties are unimpaired, excluding one gender and two untainted faculties;
thus, they possess eleven.

That is to say, the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, the three faculties of feeling (pleasure, pain, and equanimity), the five faculties beginning with faith (faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom),
and the untainted faculties (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya, ājñendriya, and ājñātāvīndriya). For a noble one born in the formless realm,
the maximum number of faculties possessed is nineteen, and the minimum is eight.
Nineteenth: as in the case of those fixed in the wrong way, it is explained as being extremely numerous;
eighth: as in the case of those who have severed the roots of goodness, it is explained as being extremely few.
Furthermore, when born in the formless realm, an ordinary being (pṛthagjana) possesses five faculties: life, mind, equanimity, faith, and so forth.
In Jambudvīpa, the maximum number is nineteen and the minimum is eight.
Nineteenth: This refers to those with both sexual organs, who exclude the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*);
as well as noble ones (*ārya*) who have not yet abandoned desire, who exclude one sexual organ and two untainted faculties.
The eighth consists of the body, life, mind, and the five feeling-faculties;
this refers to one who has severed the roots of goodness at the stage of gradual death, as in the case of Jambudvīpa.
It is the same for the continents of Videha and Godānīya.
In Uttarakuru, the maximum is eighteen and the minimum is thirteen.
As for the eighteen:
This refers to thirteen [faculties], namely: excluding one gender faculty and the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya),
there are the body, life, mind, the five feeling faculties, and the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā).
At the stage of gradual passing away, that continent has no *śaṇḍhas*,
*paṇḍakas*, those lacking sexual organs, or those with dual sexual organs;
nor does it have those who have severed the roots of virtue, those fixed in error, those fixed in correctness, or those free from defilement.
Among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the maximum is nineteen and the minimum is seventeen.
As for the nineteen,
this refers to excluding one gender organ and two untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
This refers to noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire.
The seventeen [faculties] consist of all except for one gender faculty, the faculty of sorrow, and the three untainted faculties.
That is, an ordinary person who has already become detached from the defilements of desire,
such as those in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings or the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
The same applies up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
In the Brahmakāyika Heaven, at most there are sixteen and at least fifteen.
As for the sixteen:
Excluding the two sexual organs, the two feelings, and the two untainted faculties,
those same noble ones [possess] fifteen.
Excluding those with both sexual organs, those with two types of feeling, and the three untainted faculties;
these are the very same ordinary beings,
such as those in the Brahmakāyika heaven.
It is the same for the Ābhāsvara devas.
For the Śubhakṛtsna devas, the maximum is sixteen and the minimum is fourteen.
As for the sixteen, it is as previously explained.
Fourteenth: excluding those with both sexual organs, the three feelings, and the three untainted faculties,
they are simply ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
In the Bṛhatphala heaven, the maximum is sixteen and the minimum is thirteen.
Regarding the sixteen, it is as previously explained.
As for the thirteen:
Excluding those with both sexual organs, the four types of feeling, and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*),
those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) have at most nineteen and at least thirteen.
As for the nineteen:
This refers to those with both sexual organs,
excluding those who possess the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) as well as noble ones (ārya) who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire.
Excluding one faculty of form and two untainted faculties,
there are thirteen;
this refers to those who have severed their roots of goodness.
Excluding those with both sexual organs, the five faculties beginning with faith, and the three untainted faculties;
as well as excluding ordinary beings in the Bṛhatphala heaven,
the two sexual organs, the four feelings, and the three untainted faculties.
In the various formless realms, there are at most eleven and at least eight.
The eleven are:
the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, the three faculties of feeling, the five beginning with faith (the five spiritual faculties), and the untainted faculties.
That is to say, for those noble ones, there are eight:
the faculties of life, mind, equanimity, and the five beginning with faith;
whereas for those ordinary beings, it is as follows.
The śraddhānusārin has at most nineteen and at least thirteen.
As for the "nineteen," this excludes one gender and two untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya);
it refers to one who, not yet free from the defilements of desire, abides in the path of seeing (darśana-mārga).
Thirteenth: the four faculties of body, life, mind, and faith, etc., along with the five faculties beginning with faith, and the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*),
which belong to one who has already abandoned the defilement of desire and enters the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) at the stage of gradual death.
Question: Why is it that one can enter the path of seeing at this stage?
Answer: Because those who follow the mode of craving have, throughout their entire life, constantly felt aversion toward birth and death.
At the time of death, when touched by painful sensations,
their revulsion increases further, enabling them to enter the Path of Vision;
this is likewise true for those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).
Those with conviction and liberation (śraddhādhimukta) have at most nineteen and at least eleven.
As for the nineteen:
this excludes one gender faculty and two untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
Namely, those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire and are liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*);
the eleventh [category] consists of the faculties of life, mind, and the three feelings, the five beginning with faith, and the untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*).
These are the practitioners of the formless realm who are liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).
As it is for those liberated through faith, so it is for those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
The body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*) has at most eighteen [faculties] and at least eleven.
Eighteenth: Excluding one form of the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the two untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*),
it is the body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*) in the desire realm.
Eleventh: as it was briefly stated regarding those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*),
so it is for the body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*),
the one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), and the one liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
However, one who has attained bodily realization (kāyasākṣin) accomplishes the faculty of "having already known" (ājñātendriya);
one who has attained liberation through wisdom (prajñāvimukta) accomplishes the faculty of "one who has fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
This extends from the eye faculty up to the wisdom faculty (prajñendriya).
When one attains full knowledge (*parijñā*), how many faculties (*indriya*) attain full knowledge?
Answer: When the eye faculty attains full knowledge, up until the point of becoming free from attachment to form (*rūpa-rāga-virāga*), five faculties attain full knowledge.
In this context, "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) refers to the fruit of the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of that craving.
As for the statement that the five faculties attain the name "thorough knowledge":
it is because when the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are free from the defilement of form, that [craving] is permanently abandoned.
Although thirteen faculties are abandoned at this stage,
it is only these five faculties that achieve ultimate abandonment;
as is the case with the eye faculty.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
At the time of attaining full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the female faculty,
four faculties are attained upon reaching the state of being free from the defilement of desire.
Regarding thorough knowledge (*parijñā*): although nineteen faculties (*indriya*) are abandoned at this stage, these include both male and female faculties, as well as sorrow and suffering.
Only these four faculties attain ultimate abandonment.
As it is with the female faculty,
so it is with the male faculty, the faculty of suffering, and the faculty of grief.
When the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is fully known,
one reaches the point where eight faculties are fully known upon becoming free from the defilements of the formless realm;
these are the life-faculty, the mind-faculty (*manas*), the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣā*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
As with the life-faculty,
so it is with the mental faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the five faculties beginning with faith.
At the time when the faculty of pleasure attains full knowledge (*parijñā*), [the same applies].
Upon reaching the abandonment of the defilements of the Subhakṛtsna heaven, the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) attains full knowledge.
At the time when the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) attains full knowledge,
upon reaching the abandonment of the defilements of the Ābhāsvara heaven, the faculty of joy attains full knowledge.
When the faculty of the eye, up to the faculty of wisdom, is realized through cessation, how many faculties are realized through cessation?
Answer: When the faculty of the eye is realized through cessation...
Upon reaching the detachment from the defilements of form, five faculties are extinguished and realized.
Upon reaching the state of an Arhat, nineteen faculties are extinguished and realized.
As for the five faculties:
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—
these nineteen [elements],
excluding the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
As with the eye faculty,
so it is with the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
When the female faculty is extinguished and realized, [the same applies].
Upon reaching the detachment from the defilements of desire, four faculties are extinguished and realized;
upon reaching arhatship, nineteen faculties are extinguished and realized.
These are the four.
The nineteenth [point], concerning the sorrow and suffering of men and women,
is as previously explained.
As with the female faculty,
so it is with the male faculty, the faculty of pain, and the faculty of grief.
When the life-faculty is realized through its cessation, [it is abandoned].
Up to the stage of Arhat,
nineteen faculties are extinguished and realized, as previously explained;
this is the same as for the life-faculty.
The same applies to the faculty of equanimity and the five faculties beginning with faith.

When the faculty of pleasure is realized through cessation, one reaches the detachment from the defilements of the Subhakṛtsna realm; at that point, the faculty of pleasure is realized through cessation.
Up to the stage of arhatship, nineteen faculties are extinguished and realized,
as previously explained.
At the time of realizing the extinction of the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), [the same applies].
Upon reaching the detachment from the Ābhāsvara realm, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is extinguished and realized;
upon reaching arhatship, nineteen faculties are extinguished and realized,
as previously explained.
Question: What is the distinction between these two gates?

Answer: For those who maintain that the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) severs the acquisition of fetters (*bandhana-prāpti*), while the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) realizes the acquisition of disconnection (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
He states that just as it is with the function of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
so it is with the gate of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*);
and just as it is with the function of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The same applies to the gate of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).

This is also true for those who maintain that the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) severs the acquisition of fetters (*bandhana-prāpti*) and also realizes the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
He states that just as it is with the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) through abandonment,
so it is with the gateway of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*);
just as it is with the realization of the acquisition of disjunction.
The same applies to the gateway of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-mukha*):
just as one realizes the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) by severing the acquisition of fetters (*bandhana-prāpti*), abandons faults, cultivates virtues,
discards what is inferior, and realizes what is sublime.
One abandons what is meaningless and attains what is meaningful;
one exhausts the oil of craving and experiences the bliss of being without fever—
it should be understood that it is likewise so.
Some say: as it is with what has been abandoned and what has not yet been abandoned, so it is with the first gate;
as it is with what has been realized and what has not yet been realized, so it is with the subsequent gate.
Some say: as it is when first realizing [the fruit], so it is with the first gate;
as it is when realizing it again, so it is with the subsequent gate.
Some say: just as it is when abandoning [the defilements], so it is for the initial gateway of realization;
just as it is after having abandoned them, so it is for the subsequent gateway of realization.
This is called the distinction between thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 150.
*Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 100.
Composed by the Five Hundred Great Arhats and others;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Edict. Chapter 6: The Aggregate of Faculties (Indriya-skandha), Section 4-1: The Equalizing Mind (Samacitta-nirdeśa). The minds of all sentient beings.
Should it be said that they arise together,
abide together,
and cease together?
Having thus understood the meaning of these chapters and their exegesis,
one should proceed to analyze them in detail.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to bring certainty to those who harbor doubts.
That is to say, there are sentient beings whose physical forms are vast and expansive.
There are those whose physical forms are narrow and small,
and those whose physical forms are vast and great;
for example, there are sentient beings within the great ocean who obtain physical bodies of immense proportions.
Or one hundred yojanas;
or two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight hundred;
or even up to twenty or one hundred yojanas.
Just as the form and size of the Asura Lord Hārahutī are vast,
measuring sixteen thousand yojanas in length,
so too are the bodies of those in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; yet for those whose bodies are narrow and small, they are like mosquitoes, ants, gnats, or tiny insects in water or vinegar.
Even those with keen vision cannot see it, despite applying the utmost attention;
let there be no doubt that when the body is vast, the mind is likewise vast.
For those whose bodies are narrow and small, their minds are likewise narrow and small.
In order to bring certainty to this doubt,
it is shown that the category of sentient beings consists of matter derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Although there are differences in degree, the mind is equal in all cases; therefore, this treatise is composed.
Furthermore, among sentient beings, some move with swift agility while others move with sluggish slowness.
Those whose movements are swift and rapid include horses, deer, cats, and mongooses;
those whose movements are slow and sluggish include [the following].
Do not harbor doubts, such as thinking that because the movements of creatures like grubs and earthworms are swift,
the arising and ceasing of their minds must also be swift.
For those whose physical movements are slow, the arising and ceasing of their minds are also slow.

To resolve this doubt, it is shown that although all sentient beings are composed of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), there are variations in the speed of the movement of their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Furthermore, the arising and ceasing of the mind are entirely equal in all respects.
Moreover, among sentient beings, there are some whose deportment is light and fickle, like a gust of wind;
their awakening and wisdom are tossed about like the sun reflected upon waves.
Some possess a majestic demeanor as stable and heavy as a mountain range,
and their awakened wisdom is as serene as a lamp in a sealed chamber;
do not harbor any doubts.
For those whose deportment is frivolous and whose cognitive wisdom is unstable, the arising and ceasing of the mind occur rapidly;
for those whose deportment is dignified and whose cognitive wisdom is tranquil, the arising and ceasing of the mind occur slowly.
This is in order to bring certainty to this doubt.
This reveals that although sentient beings differ in the gravity of their deportment and the depth or shallowness of their discernment, their minds arise and cease equally without distinction.
Question: If the minds of all sentient beings arise and cease equally, [why is there such diversity?]
For what reason do deportments have degrees of lightness and heaviness, and awareness and wisdom have degrees of buoyancy and depth?
Answer: There are sentient beings who give rise to many states of mind regarding many objects;
there are sentient beings who give rise to many states of mind regarding a single object.
If sentient beings give rise to many thoughts regarding many objects,
their deportment will be fickle and their discernment will be unstable.
If sentient beings give rise to many thoughts regarding a single object, [their deportment will be steady and their discernment firm].
Thus, with dignified deportment and profound gravity, and with a tranquil and settled wisdom,
for these reasons I have composed this treatise.
Should it be said that the minds of all sentient beings arise equally, abide equally, and cease equally?
The answer is: "It is so.
Question: "Do the minds of all sentient beings arise and cease together?
Do they all arise in a single moment and cease in a single moment?"
Is it not the case that the minds of all sentient beings do not arise and cease together,
nor do they all arise and cease in a single moment? If this were so,
what fault would there be?
If the minds of all sentient beings arise and cease together,
such that they all arise in a single moment and cease in a single moment,
this may be possible during states of consciousness.
What is the state of being without mind?
It refers to the time when one enters the meditative absorption of non-perception or the absorption of cessation;
at that time, the minds of other sentient beings also arise and cease.
That mind ceases and does not arise;
yet when one emerges from the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation,
the minds of other sentient beings both cease and arise.
That mind of his arises but does not cease;
yet while he abides in the meditative attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation,
the minds of other sentient beings both arise and cease.
That mind is neither born nor extinguished.
How, then, can it be said that the birth and extinction of the mind are simultaneous with a single moment?
If it were not the case that the minds of all sentient beings arise and cease together, [this would be impossible].
Nor is it the case that one [moment] arises and another moment ceases.
How, then, should the statement made here be understood?
It refers to the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the minds and so forth of all sentient beings.
It is agreed that one should speak thus:
the minds of all sentient beings arise together and cease together;
they all arise in a single moment and cease in a single moment.
Question: It may be so in the state with mind;
how is it in the state without mind?
Answer: It may be so in the state with mind.
The same applies to the state of mindlessness; that is,
when entering the meditative attainments of non-conception or cessation,
just as with other sentient beings, the mind arises at that first moment, and the meditative absorption likewise arises.
Just as the minds of other sentient beings cease,
so too does his mind of meditative absorption cease;
yet when he emerges from the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation, [his mind arises again].
Just as the minds of other sentient beings arise,
so too does his mind arising from meditative absorption arise;
just as the minds of other sentient beings cease, [so too does his mind cease].
That final moment of meditative absorption also ceases.
While one abides in the attainment of non-conception or the attainment of cessation,
just as with other sentient beings, the mind arises and ceases moment by moment.
In that intermediate meditative absorption (*dhyānāntara*), moments arise and cease moment by moment;
therefore, this is possible in both states—those with mind and those without mind.
Other masters say that it is not the case that the minds and so forth of all sentient beings arise and cease [in this manner].
Nor is it the case that everything arises in a single moment and ceases in a single moment;
for there are sentient beings whose minds cease and do not arise,
such as those who have entered the meditative absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
There are sentient beings whose minds do not cease,
like those who have emerged from the meditative absorption of non-conception or the absorption of cessation.
There are also sentient beings whose minds neither arise nor cease.
Just as for one abiding in the meditative attainments of non-conception or cessation,
there are some sentient beings whose minds both arise and cease,
as is the case for those abiding in a state possessed of mind.
Question: How should what is stated here be understood?
Answer: This is stated in reference to their measure and so forth.
It is said that "the minds of all sentient beings are equal" so that one might not think that some minds are large while others are small.
According to this teaching,
the minds of all sentient beings arise together and cease together;
they are all born in a single moment and perish in a single moment.

Because conditioned phenomena, having arisen from conditions, all subsequently cease, should it be said that a mind possessed of greed and a mind free from greed arise together, abide together, and cease together?
Answer: It is so.
There is aversion and freedom from aversion; delusion and freedom from delusion;
contraction and distraction; depression and elevation;
smallness and greatness; agitation and non-agitation.
The non-quiescent as quiescent;
the non-concentrated as concentrated;
the uncultivated as cultivated; and the unliberated mind as liberated.
Should it be said that [the mind] arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with [the mental factors]?
Answer: It is so.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: All defiled minds are by nature heavy and sluggish, while all wholesome minds are by nature light and buoyant;
let there be no doubt about this.
Defiled minds arise and cease slowly,
whereas wholesome minds arise and cease rapidly;
this is for the purpose of resolving such doubts.
This treatise is composed because it reveals that two kinds of minds are equal in their arising and ceasing.
For two reasons, the mind is said to possess greed (*sarāga*):
first, because it is associated with greed; [and second, because it is the object of greed].
Second, regarding being bound by greed: if a "mind with greed" were defined solely as a mind associated with greed,
then states associated with hatred and so forth,
as well as contaminated wholesome and non-obscured neutral states, would have to be called "minds free from greed."
Nevertheless, that too is called a "mind with greed" because it is bound by greed; thus,
although the mind is termed "with greed" based on these two meanings, [it is so designated].
In this context, it is spoken solely on the basis of the meaning of association (*samprayoga*), so as not to cause confusion.
Furthermore, the mind is said to be "free from greed" by virtue of two meanings:
first, that it is dissociated (*viprayukta*) from greed.
Second is the antidote to greed.
If a mind that is merely dissociated from greed were called "a mind free from greed," then states associated with hatred and so forth would also have to be called "minds free from greed."
However, that [state] should not be called "a mind free from greed," because it is still defiled.
Although the mind may be termed "free from greed" in two senses,
here it is spoken of solely in terms of the antidote to greed, so as to avoid confusion.
The cases of having hatred and being free from hatred, and so forth, should all be understood according to this principle.
Therefore, it should be stated here: "One whose mind possesses greed..."
This refers to that which is associated with greed;
a mind free from greed refers to the antidote to greed.
A mind with hatred refers to that which is associated with hatred;
a mind free from hatred refers to the antidote to hatred.
A mind with delusion refers to that which is associated with delusion.
A mind free from delusion refers to that which is the antidote to delusion.
A concentrated mind refers to a virtuous mind because it collects and restrains [the faculties] with respect to their objects.
A distracted mind refers to an afflicted mind because it is heedless and unrestrained with respect to its objects.
The masters of the land of Kaśmīra say that a mind associated with sleep is called "contracted" (*saṃkṣipta*),
because the Blessed One stated that sleep is the contraction of the mind.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"What is sleep and dreaming?
It refers to the state of sleep and dreams wherein the mind is briefly concentrated or dispersed."
Question: How is the explanation given in the *Dṛṣṭiparyāya-skandha* to be interpreted?

That text states that four knowledges—namely, dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)—know the concentrated mind as it truly is; one single knowledge knows the distracted mind as it truly is.
This refers to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
The answer is that his explanation should not be accepted as a general rule, because he composed the treatise by contradicting the assertions of others.
If one wishes to resolve this contradiction, one should amend his text.
To claim that one knows contracted mind, distracted mind, and depressed mind as a single wisdom,

knowing them as they truly are— namely, that it is conventional wisdom (saṃvṛti-jñāna) and the four wisdoms beginning with "elevated mind" (uddhata-citta)— knowing them as they truly are as previously stated— is unreasonable.
If it were stated in this way, then a defiled mind in a state of torpor would also be both contracted and distracted,
because it is associated with torpor and is defiled.
To avoid such faults,
it is as previously stated that [the definition] is correct.
A "depressed mind" refers to a defiled mind because it is associated with indolence (*kausīdya*).
"Exalted mind" refers to a wholesome mind associated with diligence.
"Narrow mind" refers to an afflicted mind,
as it is that which is habitually practiced by those of inferior birth.
"Great mind" refers to a virtuous mind because it is that which has been cultivated by those of great birth.
Question: There are immeasurable sentient beings who practice various unwholesome deeds rather than sublime practices;
their defiled minds manifest before them, not their virtuous minds.
What is meant by saying that what is practiced by those with small births has a defiled mind, while what is practiced by those with great births has a virtuous mind?
Answer: The designations "small" and "great" are not established on account of the number [of beings].
In this context, those who are able to practice the white dharmas (śukladharma) are called "great," while others are called "small. Therefore,
within the three realms, there is only the Buddha who is called "great" because he possesses the white dharmas.
Therefore, although other types are numerous,
they are called "minor," because they are not fully endowed with the various pure dharmas (*śukladharma*). Some say:
A defiled mind is called "small" because it is obtained for a small price;
that is to say, a defiled mind does not require preparatory effort nor does it necessitate wealth or treasures.
However, as soon as a slight amount of improper attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) arises, it continues in succession like a great river;
thus, wholesome states of mind (*kuśala-citta*) are said to be obtained with great difficulty, meaning that all wholesome states of mind require preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, although one may renounce hundreds of thousands of precious treasures,
there are those that can manifest before one and those that cannot.
Some say that a defiled mind is called "small" because it is associated with few faculties.
That is to say, among defiled minds, some possess only one faculty,
or two in association, but never all three together;
virtuous minds are called "great."
Because they are associated with many faculties;
that is to say, all wholesome minds are associated with three faculties without any deficiency. Some say:
Defiled minds are called "small" because they have few concomitants;
that is to say, all defiled minds are accompanied by only three aggregates.
A wholesome mind is called "great" because it is frequently accompanied by concomitant factors; that is,
various wholesome minds are accompanied by either three or four aggregates.
Some say that a defiled mind is called "small" because it has few attendants.
This means that defiled minds have no cultivation in the future;
virtuous minds are called "great" because they possess many attendants.
This means that all wholesome minds possess future cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Some say that defiled minds are termed "small."
Because the counteractive forces are weak;
that is to say, when a multitude of afflictions manifest in succession,
even after a small portion of the roots of goodness has been severed, they subsequently reconnect.
A virtuous mind is called "great" because it possesses many antidotes; for example,
the arising of a single moment of the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
One suddenly severs the ten types of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) in the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, ensuring they never arise again.
Some say that a defiled mind is termed "small."
Because the leaders are inferior.
What is meant by "leaders of a defiled mind"?
It refers to all forms of ignorance (*avidyā*).
As it is said, because ignorance acts as the leader,
immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas arise.
Furthermore, it can induce the arising of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*),
just as a caravan leader who lacks both eyes and feet causes the merchants to fail in their quest.
A virtuous mind is called "great" because it is the supreme leader.
What is meant by the "supreme leader" of the virtuous mind?
This refers to the various forms of wisdom and clarity;
for it is said that wisdom and clarity serve as the foremost guide,
whereby immeasurable and sublime wholesome dharmas arise.
Furthermore, it can induce superior shame and remorse,
just as a caravan leader who possesses both eyes and feet enables the merchants to achieve their desired goals.
Some say that defiled minds are called "small" because their power is small,
while wholesome minds are called "great."
Because its power is great:
it causes all unwholesome dharmas practiced since beginningless time to be abandoned as soon as wholesome dharmas arise.
Just as when one has practiced the perception of non-salt for a long time, that perception is entirely abandoned the moment salt is tasted;
or as when darkness has accumulated in a room for a long time, that darkness is immediately dispelled the moment a lamp’s light arrives.
Furthermore, wholesome dharmas sever evil such that it never arises again,
whereas the severing of unwholesome dharmas by wholesome ones will inevitably result in their subsequent continuity.
Due to these and other such conditions, defiled minds are termed "small" and wholesome minds are termed "great."
A "distracted mind" refers to a defiled mind because it is associated with restlessness (*auddhatya*).
A "non-distracted mind" refers to...
This means that a wholesome mind is associated with equanimity.
An unpeaceful mind refers to a defiled mind because it is associated with a lack of tranquility.
All afflictions are by nature not tranquil.
A "tranquil mind" refers to a virtuous mind that is associated with tranquility.
All wholesome dharmas are by nature quiescent.
An unsettled mind refers to a defiled mind associated with distraction.
"Concentrated mind" refers to its association with the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of a wholesome mind.
"Uncultivated mind" refers to...
This refers to a mind that is neither cultivated through acquisition nor cultivated through practice.
As for "cultivated mind," it refers to a mind that is cultivated through either acquisition, practice, or both.
The "unliberated mind" refers to the mind that is not liberated from its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and not liberated from the continuity of existence (*saṃtāna*).
The "liberated mind" refers to...
That is to say, regarding the mind that is liberated by its very nature (*svabhāva-vimukta*),
liberated through the continuity of the stream (*saṃtāna-vimukta*), and liberated either individually or simultaneously.
Should it be said that life-force (āyus) turns in accordance with the mind or does not turn in accordance with the mind?
Answer: It does not turn in accordance with the mind.
Question: For what reason was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is in order to refute the positions of others and to clarify one’s own doctrine.
That is to say, the Vibhajyavādins assert that life-force (āyus) follows the mind.
One asks: for what reason do they make such a statement?
Based on the sūtras, as it is said in the sūtras:
"The triad of life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are in conjunction, not non-conjunction.
These three dharmas cannot be designated as separate or distinct."
From this it is proven that life-force (āyus) functions in accordance with the mind.
This treatise was composed to refute that claim and to demonstrate that life-force does not function in accordance with the mind.
Question: For what reason does life-force not function in accordance with the mind?
Answer: Dharmas that follow the mind (cittānuvartin) are necessarily co-arisen, co-abiding, and co-ceasing with the mind;
however, life-span (āyus) is not necessarily co-arisen, co-abiding, and co-ceasing with the mind.
Some say that those phenomena which follow the mind (cittānuvartin) are necessarily of one fruit, one outflow (niṣyanda), and one maturation (vipāka) with the mind; however,
life-span (āyus) is not necessarily of one fruit, one outflow, or one maturation with the mind.
Some say that those phenomena which follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) necessarily arise simultaneously with the mind; however,
since life-force (*jīvita*) does not necessarily arise simultaneously with the mind, it is not so classified.
Some say: it is the nature of phenomena that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) that if the mind is wholesome, they are also wholesome;
the same applies to the unwholesome and the indeterminate.
Life-force is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
If it were to follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*), then life-force could only be transformed when an indeterminate mind is present;
for if a wholesome or unwholesome mind were present, life-force would have to be severed.
Some say: regarding those phenomena that follow the mind (cittānuvartin),
it is the nature of things (dharmatā) that if the mind is bound to the desire realm, they too are bound to the desire realm.
The same applies to those bound to the realms of form and formlessness, as well as to those unbound.
Life-force (*āyus*) is bound only to the three realms, yet it follows the place of rebirth;
wherever a realm exists, there is the life-force of that realm, and not otherwise.
If it were to follow the mind, then when a mind of the desire realm manifests, the life-span of one born in the desire realm could be transformed;
yet when a mind of the form realm or other realms manifests, the life-span should be severed.
The same explanation applies even up to the case of being born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Some say that it is the nature of phenomena that follow the mind (*cittānuparivartin*) such that if the mind is in training (*śaikṣa*), those [phenomena] are also in training.
The same applies to that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Life-force (*āyus*) is exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
If it were to follow the mind in its transformation, then life-force could be transformed when a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner is present.
When a mind of training (*śaikṣa-citta*) or a mind beyond training (*aśaikṣa-citta*) manifests, life-span should be severed.
Some say: it is the nature of phenomena that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin-dharma*) that if the mind is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), [the life-span is also severed].
Those [factors] are also abandoned by seeing;
the same applies to those abandoned by cultivation and those not abandoned.
Life-force is abandoned only by cultivation.
If it were to follow the mind, then when a mind to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) manifests, the life-span could be transformed;
however, when a mind to be abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya) or other types of minds manifest, the life-span should be severed.
Some say: regarding the phenomena that follow the mind,
it is the nature of things that when the mind exists, they exist.
When the mind is absent,
that [life-force] is absent. If life were to follow the mind,
then life could be transformed while the mind exists.
If life were to be severed when the mind is absent,
then it would follow that life is severed while one abides in the meditative attainments of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*),
as well as during birth in the realm of non-conception, at times when the mind does not function.
It should be called "death" because of the absence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). To avoid such an error,
it is therefore held that life-force (*āyus*) does not follow the mind.
Question: How are the sūtras cited by the Vibhajyavādins to be reconciled?
For instance, as it is said: "The triad of life-force, warmth, and consciousness are in conjunction, not non-conjunction," and so forth, at length.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"This is stated with reference to a single basis and a single continuum;
that is to say, these three factors are all found to be present within one and the same basis and continuum."
It is not said that these three factors necessarily function in mutual coordination.
If one were to make a definitive determination as you have described,
then one should not establish the distinctions between the aggregates, elements, and bases.
For that sūtra states that these three factors cannot be established as distinct or separate from one another.
Nevertheless, vitality (*āyus*) is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*);
whereas heat (*uṣman*) is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the element of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), and the sphere of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
Consciousness is comprised within the aggregate of consciousness, the seven mind-elements, and the sphere of the mind;
therefore, one should not take this according to the literal wording.
Furthermore, if these three factors were necessarily combined, [the following would occur].
The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) should possess heat (*uṣmagata*);
insentient things should possess life-force (*jīvitendriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*);
and the state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) and other such states should possess the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of consciousness.
If one were to grant this, it would contradict both the sacred teachings and correct reasoning.
Therefore, one must not determine the meaning by following the literal phrasing;
rather, it should be understood that this passage speaks of "conjunction" and so forth based on what is possible.
Should it be said that life-force proceeds in accordance with the continuum, or does it arise once and then remain?
Answer: If sentient beings of the desire realm do not abide in the meditative attainments of non-conception or cessation, it should be said that it proceeds in accordance with the continuum.
Those who abide in the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation,
as well as sentient beings of the form and formless realms,
should be said to abide as soon as they arise.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to refute the positions of other schools and to clarify one’s own doctrine.
Specifically, it is because the Dārṣṭāntikas do not admit the existence of untimely death.
Why is this so? As it is said in the sutra:
"When one's life has ended, there is no means of rescue."
From this, it is known that there is no such thing as untimely death.
However, in order to refute that view and demonstrate that untimely passing away does indeed exist, this treatise was composed.
Question: What is meant by "proceeding in accordance with the continuity"?
Some say that calamities and misfortunes are called "continuity" (*saṃtati*),
meaning birth in the desire realm without abiding in the meditative attainments of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Life-force continues to revolve in accordance with calamities and adversities. Why is this so?
Because there are those who do not act constantly toward their life-force.
It is not constantly revolving;
it is not produced by appropriation;
it does not revolve through appropriation.
Walking at improper times,
walking in improper places,
not practicing the holy life, eating unsuitable food, and eating to excess.
That which is raw it does not cook, and that which is cooked it merely holds;
it is unable to discern what is appropriate from what is inappropriate.
They do not take medicine;
they do not follow the physician’s advice;
they do not avoid calamities or dangers.
They engage in various harmful amusements;
because of such things, their lives are cut short prematurely.

If one constantly performs and constantly turns toward [such acts] regarding life, and constantly experiences and constantly turns toward the experiencing [of their results], [the life-span will be diminished].
At that time, he practiced the holy life in his daily conduct;
he ate appropriate food in moderation,
ensuring that what was raw was cooked and discarding what was already cooked.
By being able to discern what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, by taking medicine according to the physician’s instructions,
and by avoiding calamities and dangers while staying far from harmful amusements—
for these reasons, one’s life will not be cut short prematurely.
Some say that the material body is called "continuity," meaning one who is born in the desire realm and does not abide in the meditative attainments of non-perception or cessation.
Life-force continues in succession along with the physical body.
Why is this? If the body is in a state of equilibrium, then life-force will not meet with premature death.
If the body is damaged, one's lifespan will be cut short.
Some say that another's body is what constitutes the continuum.
This refers to one born in the desire realm who does not abide in the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation,
and whose life-span continues in dependence upon the continuity of another's body. Why is this so?
If there is another body that does not cause harm to one's own lifespan, then one’s life will not be cut short;
if it does cause harm, then one’s life will be prematurely ended.
Question: What is meant by "abiding as soon as it has arisen"?
Answer: Having arisen in accordance with its causes, it continues in a stream and does not follow calamities or adversities;
it proceeds through the impairment of one's own body or the bodies of others.
That is to say, having been born in the desire realm, one currently abides in the meditative attainments of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Furthermore, for those born in the higher realms, their lifespans do not fluctuate according to external conditions.
Question: Is there also a lifespan in the desire realm that does not fluctuate according to conditions, even though one has not entered the two mindless attainments?
Why is it not stated?
One should know that when something ought to be stated but is not, the meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Some say: [text fragment].
Regarding what is said here concerning "certainty":
it means that for one abiding in the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), the life-force (*jīvita-saṃskāra*) is certain and does not follow conditions;
whereas for others, it may follow conditions, and therefore it is not mentioned [in this context].
Some say: although there are further [states] in the desire realm that do not follow conditions,
they are mentioned specifically here to demonstrate the power of the two meditative attainments.
As the Sūtra states, there are four kinds of personal existence (ātmabhāva) attained by sentient beings. First,
there is a personal existence that can be harmed by oneself but not by others.
Second, there is an apprehended self-entity that can be harmed by others but not by itself.
Third, there is an apprehended self-entity.
It may cause harm to oneself and also cause harm to others.
Fourth, that which has an acquired self-nature causes neither harm to oneself nor harm to others.
What kind of sentient being possesses a self-body that can be harmed by itself but not by another?
It refers to the gods of the Desire Realm known as the "Playful-forgetfulness" (*krīḍā-pramoṣaka*), who,
fond of adorning themselves and addicted to play, pass the time until they become exhausted, lose mindfulness, and die.
Furthermore, there are gods in the desire realm who harbor resentment in their minds;
at times, they become so enraged that they glare at one another with eyes narrowed in anger,
and when their long-standing resentment becomes unbearable, they pass away from that state.
Furthermore, there is another class of beings— whether they be nāgas,
garuḍas, pretas, humans, or others—
who may be harmed by themselves but not by others.
In what way can the physical body acquired by sentient beings be harmed by others but not by themselves?
It refers to those dwelling within an eggshell or a womb, whose sense faculties are neither fully developed nor matured.
Furthermore, there is another class of beings— whether nāgas, garuḍas, pretas, humans, or others—
who may be harmed by others but cannot harm themselves.
What is the self-body obtained by sentient beings that can be harmed both by themselves and by others?
It refers to various birds and beasts, or nāgas and garuḍas, or ghosts and humans, or again, others besides these.
Regarding those that can cause harm to oneself as well as to others:
what is the acquired body that causes neither harm to oneself nor harm to others?
It refers to all intermediate states (*antarābhava*) born within the realms of form and formlessness.
All those in the hells;

those abiding in the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*);
and those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
Finally, there is the case of a bodhisattva;
when the mother of a bodhisattva carries the bodhisattva in her womb,
and when the mother of a wheel-turning monarch carries the wheel-turning monarch in her womb.
Regarding those who are royal sages, messengers of the Buddha,
or designated by the Buddha, such as the son of the householder Ghaṭīkāra and the son of the householder Uttara.
The householder’s son Dāmilaka,
the weaver Śreṣṭha, Tiṣya, Kumāra, and others.
Those recorded by the Buddha are:
individuals in their final existence who have not yet completed what was to be done,
and the people of Uttarakuru at the beginning of the kalpa.
The Naga King Airāvaṇa, the Naga King Supratiṣṭhita,
King Yama, and others of their kind—
all such beings do not cause harm.
These are called the four kinds of acquired selfhood.
The Blessed One has taught that there is a selfhood which is neither harmed by oneself nor harmed by others.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared one shoulder,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms in reverent salutation.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What kind of sentient beings obtain a self-existence that is neither harmed by themselves nor harmed by others?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Sentient beings in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are neither harmed by themselves nor harmed by others."
Question: From this discussion, further questions arise.
Does the Venerable Śāriputra understand what has been asked?
If he understands it, why does he ask again?
If one does not understand this, how can they be called a śrāvaka who has reached the ultimate?
And why would the Blessed One rain down the rain of Dharma upon those who are neither fields nor vessels,
thereby causing the Dharma he has taught to be empty and fruitless?
Some say: "The Venerable One understood the question;
if so, why did he ask again?"
Answer: There are also cases where one knows yet asks intentionally.
As stated in the Vinaya:
"At that time, the Blessed One, though knowing [the answer], asked intentionally in order to make what was being said clear."
Furthermore, although that venerable one understood it himself,
he asked for the sake of benefiting others;
that is to say, because there were those in the assembly who did not yet understand.
Because they lack fearlessness, they are unable to question the Buddha.
The Venerable Śāriputra has attained fearlessness;
for their benefit, he asks the question even though he already knows the answer.
Some say: "The Venerable One did not understand the question.
If that were so, how could he be called a śrāvaka who has reached the ultimate? To answer "I do not know" would be incorrect; once he has spoken, he knows—what fault is there in this?
Question: Why does he rain down the rain of Dharma upon those who are neither fields nor vessels, thereby causing the Dharma he has taught to be empty and fruitless?
Answer: Although the Venerable Śāriputra did not understand this, [the Buddha] knew it.
Furthermore, within the assembly there are others capable of knowing [this],
such as the Bodhisattva Maitreya and others; thus,
it is not without fruit, for it is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
Although at that time Śāriputra was superior,
if it concerns this conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-prajñā*), then Maitreya Bodhisattva is superior;
therefore, on one occasion the Buddha engaged in a discussion with Maitreya Bodhisattva concerning conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas were unable to understand this.
They asked: "The essential nature of the lower stages is also such that it cannot be harmed by oneself or others;
why, then, is it stated only in reference to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"
Answer: Because the latter is cited to reveal the former, this statement was made.
In some instances, the Blessed One cites the latter to reveal the former, as in this passage;
in other instances, he cites the former to reveal the latter.
As it is said: "Detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states,
possessing applied thought and sustained thought, one dwells having fully attained the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and characterized by joy and bliss," and so forth.
Just as raising [the hand] reveals the end and lowering it reveals the beginning,
so too should one understand that raising [the mind] reveals entry and raising it to its culmination reveals the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Some say that because the lower stages are indeterminate, they are not mentioned; that is, the physical bodies obtained by sentient beings in the lower stages may be free from calamities and misfortunes,
as in the case of those abiding in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Alternatively, there may be calamities and misfortunes, as with the gods who forget due to their playfulness;
because the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is free from such calamities, it is specifically mentioned. Some say:
Within the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments, there are likewise occurrences such as those of the desire realm—namely, the loss of mindfulness through play and death;
however, in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, none of these things exist at all. For this reason, it is specifically mentioned [in that context].
Some say that sentient beings of the lower realms all possess the predominant power of afflictions;
if these [afflictions] manifest, they will then meet with premature death.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is devoid of these afflictions;
therefore, the Blessed One spoke only of that stage.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta offers this explanation:
In this context, that which is destroyed by itself refers to being destroyed by the path of counteraction belonging to its own level;
that which is destroyed by another refers to...
That is to say, it is destroyed by the path of counteraction belonging to a higher stage;
the essential nature of the first dhyāna is destroyed by itself;
and that which belongs to its own stage is destroyed by another, namely, the noble path.
This refers to the mundane path at the limit of the second dhyāna,
up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), which is harmed by its own nature;
that is to say, the noble path of its own level is harmed by another.
This refers to the mundane path at the limit of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The essential nature of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception itself cannot be harmed by its own [path],
because there is no noble path within its own level.
Nor is it harmed by others,
because it is the mundane path at the limit of the unsurpassed stage;
for this reason, it is called only the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The acquired personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is not destroyed by both [the cessation of perception and feeling and the attainment of cessation].
When one abides in the meditative attainments of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*),
should it be said that the life-force (*āyus*) continues to function or does it abide?
Answer: It should be said that it transforms.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.

This means that when one abides in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) do not function at all.
At that time, the dharmas of mind and mental factors neither arise nor cease.
One must not, however, assume that the life-force (*āyus-saṃskāra*) present in this state [is what sustains the person].
Just as the mind and mental factors do not arise and cease but remain in a state of quiescence,
this treatise was composed to eliminate such doubt by demonstrating that the life-force (*āyus*) in this state arises and ceases moment by moment.
Question: What is meant by "transformation" (pariṇāma)?
Answer: It is called transformation because it arises and ceases in a continuous succession from moment to moment;
that is to say, it has the sense of fluxing and flowing, not of remaining static.
As the Blessed One has said, the lifespan of humans gradually exhausts like the water of a small river.
If the lifespans of sentient beings persist once they have arisen,
how is it known that their lifespan gradually exhausts?
Answer: Because of the exhaustion of the world and the exhaustion of the kalpa.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
This refers to what was stated in the preceding text: that for those abiding in the attainment of non-conception or the attainment of cessation,
as well as for sentient beings in the form and formless realms,
their life-force should be said to abide as soon as it arises once.
Some may claim that their lifespan arises once and never ceases;
to dispel this doubt and clarify the nature of those life-formations (*āyus-saṃskāra*),
it is said that they abide from the moment they arise, because they are free from calamities and untimely deaths.
In reality, however, there is arising and ceasing moment by moment;
it is because this causes the lifespan to gradually exhaust that this treatise was composed.
Question: Do all five aggregates gradually exhaust?
"Why is it that only lifespan (*āyus*) is mentioned?
Answer: "The Blessed One, in this context, cites the gradual exhaustion of lifespan to reveal that all five [aggregates] possess the quality of gradual exhaustion. Some say:
Regarding the Buddha Jīvitasena,
because he highlights the superior to reveal the inferior within this context, he speaks only of the exhaustion of his lifespan. Some say:
Life-force (*āyus*) is able to sustain the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
If one speaks of the exhaustion of life-force, it should be understood that this already implies the exhaustion of the five aggregates. Some say:
When life-span is severed, the homogeneous group (nikāya-sabhāga) is also severed;
when the homogeneous group is severed, the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are also severed.
The Buddha follows the fundamental [principle].
It is for this reason that it is said "the lifespan is exhausted. Some say:

because the measure of lifespan increases and decreases, flourishes and declines, the Buddha specifically spoke [of exhaustion] when asked about the meaning of the gradual exhaustion of lifespan across all realms of existence (*gati*).
Why is it that only the gradual exhaustion of human lifespan is mentioned?
Answer: Because at that time, the Buddha was teaching for the sake of humans.
Some say that the Buddha’s intention was to take humans as the primary focus.
This demonstrates that the lifespans in all realms of existence gradually come to an end.
Some say this is because the Buddha is of the same category as human beings.
The Dharma taught is largely in accordance with human beings.
Some say this is because human lifespans undergo extremes of increase and decrease, as well as periods of flourishing and decline.
This refers to the time at the beginning of the kalpa when human lifespan was immeasurable;
thereafter it gradually decreased until it reached eighty thousand years,
and subsequently decreased further until it reached ten years.
In this way, the meaning that the lifespan of such beings gradually comes to an end can be clearly understood.
Since this is not the case for other realms of existence, the Buddha spoke specifically of this.
Question: The great rivers also possess the quality of gradually coming to an end.
Why is it said that they are like small rivers?
The answer is: great rivers flow constantly and their gradual exhaustion cannot be known, unlike the waters of various small rivers.
At times they overflow like during the summer rains;
at times they dry up like at the height of winter.
So too is it with the river of the lifespan of sentient beings.
At times they overflow, as at the moment of rebirth;
at other times they are completely exhausted, as at the time of death.
Therefore, the Blessed One used the simile of a small stream.
If there are sentient beings whose lifespan remains once it has begun,
this refers to those abiding in the two mindless attainments as well as sentient beings of the higher realms.
Regarding the "exhaustion of the world" and the "exhaustion of the eon":
some say that subtle impermanence is called the exhaustion of the world.
The coarse impermanence is called the end of the eon (*kalpa*).
Some say that the momentary impermanence is called the end of the world (*loka*).
The impermanence of a single kalpa is called the exhaustion of the eon (*kalpa-kṣaya*).
Some say that the impermanence of things belonging to the category of sentient beings is called the exhaustion of the world (*loka-kṣaya*).
The impermanence of things not included among sentient beings is called the end of the eon (*kalpa*).
Some say that the impermanence of internal phenomena is called the end of the world (*loka*), while the impermanence of external phenomena is called the end of the eon.
When entering the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), how many faculties (*indriya*) cease?
[The text continues] with a detailed exposition.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is in order to refute the positions of others and to clarify one’s own doctrine.
That is to say, the Dārṣṭāntikas and Vibhajyavādins maintain that in the state of non-ideational absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), the subtle mind does not cease.
He asserts this:
"If the attainment of non-conception were entirely devoid of mind,
the life-faculty would be severed and it should be called death."

It is not called "abiding in meditative concentration" (samāhita) in order to refute that intention and to demonstrate that the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is entirely devoid of mind.
Some maintain:
"Although this attainment lacks mind, it can nevertheless manifest once one is free from the defilements of desire."
Because their realms are identical,
this is intended to refute that view and demonstrate that the attainment of non-perception can only manifest after one has become free from the defilements of the Śubhakṛtsna heaven;
for it requires the fourth dhyāna as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
For this reason, the Venerable Vasumitra spoke as follows:

"What is the attainment of non-conception? It is that which belongs to one who is already free from the defilements of the Śubhakṛtsna heaven but not yet free from the defilements of the higher realms, and which is preceded by the mental attention of the perception of renunciation."
The cessation of mind and mental factors is called the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
For this reason, this treatise was composed. Question:
When entering the attainment of non-conception, how many faculties (*indriya*) cease? Answer: Seven.
That is to say, the mental faculty, equanimity, and the five faculties beginning with faith.
To what realm are the associated mind and mental factors bound that cease?
Answer: They are bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu).
This has been stated according to the general characteristics of the realms and categories;
however, it pertains specifically to the stage of the fourth dhyāna.
When emerging from the state of non-percipient attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), how many faculties (*indriya*) are manifested?
Answer: Seven, as previously stated.
Regarding which fetters the mind and mental factors are present, the answer is: those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
This is also stated in terms of the general characteristics of the realms and categories;
however, it pertains exclusively to the level of the fourth dhyāna.
From this statement, it is proven that the attainment of non-conception is definitively without mind.
When entering meditative absorption, only the cessation of the faculties, mind, and mental factors is mentioned,
while their arising is not mentioned;
when emerging from meditative absorption, only the arising of the faculties, mind, and mental factors is mentioned.
Because it does not speak of cessation.
