Question: For what reason do they necessarily pass away from the Heaven of No-Thought and arise in the desire realm?
Answer: It is because the power of the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is such;
for according to whatever power the ripening cause possesses, it causes only that specific kind of ripening to arise.
Other masters say:
because the life-span karma for other realms does not increase when the life-span of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñika*) is exhausted;
that is to say, the previously accumulated karma for the life-span of the non-conceptual state has now been fully experienced.
Because the life-span karma had not previously been increased in other realms, one who dies there is certain to be reborn in the desire realm.
Question: Did they not also previously give rise to the three lower dhyānas?
Why does it not project the life-span fruit of those [lower] stages?
Answer: Although they have previously attained the first three dhyānas, because they did not adhere to them firmly, they do not project that life-span.
It is solely because of their firm attachment to the fourth dhyāna that they draw forth that lifespan.
Some say that although they have previously given rise to the three lower dhyānas, [they do not draw forth the lifespan through them].
It is not what they seek;
they seek only the fourth dhyāna. Some say:
Although he has previously arisen in the lower three dhyānas,
they are merely like paths traversed rather than the final destination;
the fourth dhyāna is the true destination.
It is not as one might think, that the path traversed draws forth that life-span.
Some say: "If one performs karma to be experienced in the next birth (*upapadyavedanīya*) in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*),"
By the very nature of things, one also performs karma in the desire realm that is to be experienced in a subsequent life;
just as one who performs karma for birth in Uttarakuru necessarily performs karma to be experienced in a subsequent life,
by the very nature of things, one also performs karma in the heavens of the desire realm that is to be experienced in a subsequent life.
Some say that the desire realm is the place to which all sentient beings return when they fall away; that is to say,
by the power of karma and the power of cultivation, sentient beings [return there].
They go to the realms of form and formlessness;
when that karma is exhausted, they fall back into the desire realm,
just as the great earth is the place of retreat and refuge for all flying birds.
It is said that when birds fly through the air by the power of their wings,
they fall back to the earth once that wing-power is exhausted.
Some say:
The beings in the realm of non-perception remain in a state of non-perception for five hundred eons,
like one in deep sleep;
once awakened, they are unable to take up any further karmic maturation.
One then falls into the desire realm.
It is like a person at the top of a tree who, leaning against a branch while asleep, suddenly wakes after a long time;
forgetting to grasp the branch, he immediately falls to the ground.
It is the same with them. Some say that those who seek the state of non-conception (asaṃjñika) cling to the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) as the true path.
That maturation leads to nirvana,
even up to being born among those gods;
this grasping follows him until, after emerging from the perception of nothingness, he is about to die.
Upon seeing the signs of rebirth, he immediately thinks:
"There is certainly no nirvāṇa;
if it truly existed," [he would not see this].
"I have already realized it.
Why, then, do the signs of birth manifest before me now?
It is because I have slandered nirvāṇa and the noble path."
Passing away from that state, they are reborn in the miserable destinies.
The Venerable Ghosaka also stated this:
because they slander nirvāṇa and the noble ones.
Upon passing away from that state, one will certainly be reborn in an evil destination.
Question: What is the difference between the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*)?
Answer: They differ only in name.
This is called the attainment of non-conception;
this is called the state of non-conception.
Furthermore, it is because of this attainment of non-conception.
The fruit is the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*).
Furthermore, the dharma of maturation (*vipāka*) is the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*);
the maturation is the state of non-conception.
Furthermore, the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is wholesome,
whereas the state of non-conception (asaṃjñika) is indeterminate.
Furthermore, the attainment of non-conception is a meditative absorption (samādhi).
The state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) is birth.
Furthermore, the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is produced by the mental application (*manasikāra*) resulting from the effort of preparatory practice;
the state of non-conception is not produced by the effort of preparatory practice.
Furthermore, the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) exists both here [in the desire realm] and there [in the form realm],
and it manifests in both places; however,
the state of non-conception (asaṃjñika) exists only there [in the form realm], and it manifests only there.
Furthermore, the attainment of non-conception is acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*),
whereas the state of non-conception is acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*).
This is called the distinction between the attainment of non-conception and the state of non-conception.
Question: Where is the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva) included?
The masters of foreign lands say:
"Within the fourth dhyāna there are nine distinct levels; this [heaven] is one of those levels."
The masters of the Kaśmīra country say that it is subsumed under the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala),
but it is established as a separate name because of its loftiness, excellence, and tranquility.
It is like an araṇya dwelling on the outskirts of a village.
If one asks what the body size of those devas is,
the answer is five hundred yojanas.
Question: What is his lifespan?
Answer: Five hundred kalpas.
Question: In what posture does he remain?
Some say that he sat cross-legged like a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas;
others say:
He then sits in a squatting posture like a brahmin;
one who speaks thus [describes] the deportment in which he remains when first entering this meditative absorption.
Thus, by means of this deportment, one dwells there for five hundred kalpas.
When a sentient being of the non-conceptual realm is born,
should it be said that they possess conceptualization?
"Is it non-conceptualization?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is in order to refute the doctrines of others and to clarify one's own position.
That is to say, some may claim that for non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), there is no mental consciousness either at the time of birth or at the time of death.

This is to refute that intention and to demonstrate that when those sentient beings are born and when they die, they both possess mental consciousness; it is not the case that birth and death occur without mental consciousness.
Alternatively, there are those who say:
When beings in the realm of non-perception are born, they possess mind; at the time of death, they lack mind.
This is to refute that view and demonstrate that even at the time of death, they possess mental perception and are not devoid of it, because they undergo the end of life.
Alternatively, some say that although beings in the state of non-conception possess mind both at the time of birth and at the time of death,

it lasts for only a single moment and does not continue for long; this is said to refute their view and to clarify that when they are born, birth has already occurred long ago and the mind continues for a further period before they become non-conceptual, and after emerging from that state of non-conception, the mind persists for a long time before they finally relinquish their life.
Therefore, it is said thus:
Is there any instance where the mind exists for only two moments—
namely, at the time of conception and at the time of death?
Vasumitra says it does not exist,
while the Venerable Ghosaka says it does;
he identifies it as the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva).
Is there any case where the mind at rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhicitta*) arises with the mind at death (*cyuticitta*) as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
One should answer that there is not.
The Venerable Ghosaka says that there is.
That is to say, it refers to the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisattva).
Is there any place where the mind at rebirth-linking (pratisaṃdhi-citta) serves as four conditions for the arising of the mind at death (cyuti-citta)?
Some maintain that it does not exist,
while the Venerable Ghosaka maintains that it does;
he asserts that it is precisely the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisattva).
To refute these [views], this treatise is composed:
When beings in the state of non-conception (asaṃjñika) are born, should they be said to possess conception (saṃjñin) or to be without conception (asaṃjñin)?
Answer: It should be said that they possess perception (*saṃjñin*).
This is intended to refute the view that those born in the Heaven of No-Perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) are at that time without mind (*acittaka*), as the Blessed One has taught.
When those sentient beings pass away from that place due to the arising of perception,
at the time of their passing, should that perception be said to cease or not to cease?
Answer: It should be said that they cease.
This is intended to refute the view that those in the Heaven of Non-conception are without mind at the time of death.
Where, then, should it be said that they abide when those perceptions cease?
Answer: One should say that they abide in that very place.
This refutes the view held by some that non-percipient beings possess mind only at the single moment of death and the single moment of birth.
Question: Are the preceding moments of mind of non-percipient beings many?
Regarding which is more numerous, the preceding mind or the subsequent mind,
some say that the preceding mind is more numerous, not the subsequent mind.
Because, prior to entering the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*),
the force of the continuity of maturation (*vipāka-saṃtati*) is so intense,
it takes a long time for the mind to cease before one enters that state of non-conception.
Having emerged from the state of non-conception, the force of the continuity of the maturation (vipāka) becomes weakened;
therefore, when a mind arises for a brief moment, one immediately passes away. Some say:
The subsequent mind is mostly not the preceding mind,
because before entering the state of non-conception,
the mind that longs for and seeks non-conception is intense and sharp.
Therefore, when there is consciousness for a short time, one enters the state of non-conception;
having emerged from non-conception, because there is nothing further to seek or desire, there is consciousness for a long time before finally relinquishing life.
This is what is said.
This matter is not fixed;
sometimes there is much before and little after,
and sometimes there is little before and much after.
Because there is a distinction based on the difference in their underlying intentions,
should that perception be said to be wholesome or indeterminate?
Answer: It is either wholesome or indeterminate.
As for that perception, how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in accordance with it?
Question: By how many fetters (saṃyojana) is one bound by that which pertains to the form realm (rūpadhātu) and has outflows as its object?
Answer: Six.
That perception refers to the emergence from the perception of non-perception;
it is either wholesome or indeterminate.
"Wholesome" refers to that which is wholesome by birth;
"indeterminate" refers to that which is obscured-indeterminate or unobscured-indeterminate.
Regarding those with outflow that take the form realm as their object:
this refers to the latent dispositions with outflow that take the fourth dhyāna as their object.
Question: Why do the latent dispositions with outflow that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object not increase in accordance with that perception?
The answer is: They conceive of non-perception as nirvana and the attainment of non-perception as the true path,
and so on, until they are born there.
And even after passing away from that state,
this very same adherence continues to follow them;
for they do not slander the true path of cessation, claiming it does not exist.
At that time, the untainted object does not arise.
Regarding the six fetters of bondage:
with the exception of ill-will, envy, and parsimony, there are remaining fetters of bondage.
Question: Is the perception of the signless, which emerges from [the formless realm], abandoned by the five categories [of afflictions] or is it abandoned only through cultivation?
If so, what is the fault?
If it were abandoned by the five [categories],...
How should one reconcile what is stated in the Ten Gates?
For example, it is said:
"Past dharmas act as the equal-and-immediate condition for the arising of two minds."
If it is one who abandons through cultivation,
how then is this passage to be reconciled?
As it is said:
In that [state], the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with the outflows (sāsrava) and having the form realm as their object increase.
Some say that these pertain to all five stages of abandonment.
Question: How should one interpret what is stated in the Ten Gates?

Answer: That text should state that past dharmas act as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the arising of six minds, namely, the five [minds] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding the single [state] of the formless realm,
what is the intention behind not making such a statement?
It should be understood that the text merely speaks of emerging from the mind based on the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*).
It does not speak of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*). Why is this?
Because there is the mental attention (*manasikāra*) consisting of the preparatory effort for a mindless meditative absorption (*acittaka-samādhi*).
It arises; non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*) is not like this.
Other masters say:
It is abandoned solely by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Question: How should one interpret what is stated in this passage?
Answer: This passage should state that those perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are omnipresent (*sarvatraga*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
And since the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase therein,
what is the intention behind not stating this?
One should know that here, the term "conjunction" (*sāmagrī*) is used inclusively.
At the time of death, that person’s mind pertains to all five categories [of consciousness].
It is not merely that the "mind of non-perception" is mentioned;
because the mind at the moment of death is a preceding associate [of that state], it is mentioned here as well.
The critique states:
One should know that the former explanation is superior,
for there is no other principle that would preclude the occurrence of other minds.
As the Blessed One has said,
all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment.
By what nutriment do the non-percipient sentient beings subsist?
Answer: Contact, mental volition, and consciousness.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.

This means that in the Heaven of Non-perception (asaṃjñisattva), there is certainly no physical food (kavaḍīkārāhāra); contact, mental volition, and consciousness are also extinguished without remainder.

Lest one should doubt that they abide without food, [the sūtra] states that it would otherwise be impossible to reconcile this with the Blessed One’s teaching that "all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment."

To eliminate that doubt and demonstrate that although there is no edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) in the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), the other three types of nutriment do exist, this treatise was composed in accordance with the Sūtra. Question:
In that state of non-perception, the three types of nutriment are also extinguished.
How is it said that [sustenance] exists?
The answer is: there are two kinds of sustenance.
The first is that which can induce [the body] beforehand.
Second, there is sustenance by way of present maintenance.
Although in that state there is no food that maintains it in the present,
it is called "possessing food" because there is food that was previously able to project it.
Some say that there are three kinds of nutriment for that intermediate state:
first, karmic nutriment;
second, nutriment of birth.
The three types of nutriment are the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the nutriment of karma (*karma-āhāra*). As for the nutriment of karma,
it refers to the karma previously created in that stage which is capable of projecting that birth.
"Produced by nutriment" refers to the mind at the moment of linking existence (*pratisandhi-citta*) and its co-arising factors,
because they draw forth that single lifetime and cause it to continue in succession.
Regarding the equal-and-immediate condition as nutriment:
this refers to contact, volition, and cognition entering [the state] as the equal-and-immediate condition,
which are able to induce the emergence of the mind and mental factors from the state of non-conception.
Because it must necessarily arise and is not permanently severed.
For this reason, it is said that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment.
Question: How many faculties are subsumed within the eye faculty?
Up to: "How many faculties are subsumed under the faculty of final knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*)?
Answer: "The faculty of sight subsumes the faculty of sight," and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: It was composed to refute the view that all phenomena are comprised solely of other-natures (parabhāva), and to demonstrate that all phenomena possess their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Thus, this treatise was written.
Regarding the statement that "the eye faculty subsumes the eye faculty," this is spoken in terms of its general characteristic as a category.
If explained specifically, there are two kinds of eyes.
That is to say, the left and the right.
The left encompasses the left, and the right encompasses the right.
Furthermore, the left has two [aspects].
That is to say, there are those produced by nourishment and those born of maturation.
Those produced by nourishment are subsumed under what is produced by nourishment;
those born of maturation are subsumed under what is born of maturation.
Furthermore, that which is born of maturation is of two kinds:
namely, the maturation of wholesome karma and the maturation of unwholesome karma.
The maturation of wholesome karma is subsumed under the maturation of wholesome karma;
the maturation of unwholesome karma is subsumed under the maturation of unwholesome karma.
Furthermore, the maturation of wholesome karma is of two kinds.
That is to say, humans and devas;
humans comprise humans,
and devas comprise devas.
Furthermore, there are two types of heavens:
namely, those of the desire realm and those of the form realm.
The desire realm is comprised within the desire realm.
The form realm is subsumed within the form realm;
the form realm further consists of four,
namely the four dhyānas.
The first dhyāna is subsumed within the first dhyāna,
and so on, up to the fourth dhyāna being subsumed within the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, there are three types of maturation for unwholesome karma.
That which is called the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts:
the hells are subsumed within the hells, and so on,
up to the hungry ghosts being subsumed within the hungry ghosts.
In this way, the left eye and its various distinctions each possess the three periods of time:
the past includes the past,
and the future includes the future.
The present encompasses the present.
Furthermore, the past consists of immeasurable kṣaṇas,
and each individual kṣaṇa encompasses itself.
As it is with the past, so it is with the future;
as it is with the left, so it is with the right.
Here, the explanation is given in general terms based merely on their common category.
As it is with the eye faculty,
so it is with the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, life, suffering,
and mental grief; for each of these comprises only its own respective faculty.
The body faculty (kāyendriya) subsumes three faculties:
namely, the body faculty, the female faculty (strīndriya), and the male faculty (puruṣendriya).
The female faculty subsumes the female faculty and a portion of the body faculty.
As it is with the female faculty and the male faculty,
so it is with the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). The mental faculty comprises the mental faculty itself and a portion of three faculties,
namely, the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Because those three faculties have nine dharmas as their essence and include the mind-faculty (*manas*) but nothing else, they are said to be "partial.
As it is with the faculty of mind,
so it is with the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity, as well as the five faculties beginning with faith.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) subsumes the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," which consists of portions of nine faculties,
namely: the mental faculty (manas).
The three feelings and the five faculties beginning with faith—
these nine are all common to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Now, only the untainted (anāsrava) is included.
Within the untainted, there are furthermore three paths;
since only the path of seeing (darśanamārga) is included here, it is said to be "a small portion."
As it is with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," so it is with the faculty of "having known" and the faculty of "one who has fully known.
This applies likewise to the powers of faith through to the power of wisdom, and to the factors of enlightenment beginning with mindfulness.
Up to the faculty of equanimity;
the dharma-knowledge of right view up to right concentration;
and up to the path-knowledge—how many faculties are subsumed within emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness?
Answer: The power of faith subsumes one faculty and a portion of three faculties—namely, the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Each of these three has nine factors as its intrinsic nature.
Because it comprises faith and not the others, it is said to be "a small portion.
As it is with the power of faith, so it is with the other four powers. The awakening factor of mindfulness comprises a small portion of four faculties, namely:
the faculty of mindfulness and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
The faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya) encompasses both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava).
Now, it includes only the three uncontaminated faculties as its nature, consisting of nine factors;
since it includes only mindfulness here, it is said to be "a small portion."
As it is with the awakening factor of mindfulness,
so it is with the awakening factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, and concentration;
the others are not included among the faculties.
This means that the factors of enlightenment such as equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) do not encompass the characteristics of having roots or being rootless.
Right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) encompasses a portion of four roots, namely:
the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) and the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*).
As it is with right view,
so it is with right effort, mindfulness, and concentration;
the others are not included among the faculties.

This means that right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), right speech (*samyag-vāc*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*) do not include the faculties because they lack the characteristic of being faculties.
The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) includes a portion of four faculties, namely:
the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) and the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*).
As it is with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), so it is with the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
The knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) comprises a small portion of three faculties.
That is to say: the faculty of wisdom,
the faculty of "I have known," and the faculty of "one who has fully known."
How does it encompass a portion of the faculty of wisdom?
It means that the faculty of wisdom universally takes as its object one dharma or many dharmas,
whether their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
The present, the three periods of time,
other bodies and one's own body,
and objects that are associated or dissociated.
This refers exclusively to the apprehension of a single dharma,
its own-characteristic,
and the present.
Because it is the wisdom that takes as its object the states associated with other bodies,
it is said to be "partial.
The two untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) have nine factors as their intrinsic nature.
This refers exclusively to wisdom (*prajñā*).
The distinctions within wisdom are as previously described.
Because this [wisdom] encompasses only that which takes a single phenomenon (*dharma*) as its object, it is said to be "a small portion."
Conventional knowledge subsumes a small portion of one faculty,
namely the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*),
because the faculty of wisdom encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Now, because it comprises only the contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is said to be "a small portion.
Space (*ākāśa*) comprises a small portion of four faculties;
namely, the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) and the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*), which are like space.
The same applies to the wishless and the signless.
With how many faculties is the mind faculty associated?
Up to: with how many faculties is the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge associated?
The answer states: "The mind-faculty is associated with ten faculties and a portion of three faculties," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: There are those who, due to delusion, hold that associated dharmas lack real existence.
To refute their view and to demonstrate that the essence of associated dharmas is indeed substantially existent, this treatise was composed.
The mental faculty (manas-indriya) is associated with ten faculties,
namely: the five feeling faculties (vedanā-indriya),
the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā-indriya), and a portion of three faculties.
This refers to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Since those three faculties have nine factors as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
they are said to be "partial" because they exclude the substance of the mind itself and its associated mental states.
The faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are associated with nine faculties in part;
that is to say, with the mental faculty (*manas*), the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Regarding their association with the mental faculty and the five beginning with faith in part: [it refers to those instances where they arise together].
Those six faculties all arise together with the five feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*).
Now, because joy, pleasure, and equanimity each correspond only with their own respective faculties when they arise, it is said that they constitute "a small portion."

Regarding "associated with a portion of the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*)," these three faculties have nine factors as their nature and arise together with the three feelings (*vedanā*). Here,
because pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are associated only with their own respective faculties when they arise, it is said that they constitute a "portion."
The faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) and the faculty of mental distress (daurmanasyendriya) are associated with a portion of six faculties—
namely, the mind faculty (manendriya) and the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā).
In what sense are they associated with only a portion of those?
That is to say, those six faculties arise together with the five feelings (*vedanā*).
Now, because the faculty of suffering (*duḥkha-indriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya-indriya*) correspond only with their own respective faculties, they are said to be "partial.
The faculty of faith (*śraddhā-indriya*) corresponds partially with four faculties and nine faculties.
The four faculties are vigor,
mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
They correspond, in part, with nine faculties.
This refers to the mind-faculty (*manas*), the five faculties of sensation (*vedanā*), and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
As for those that are partially associated with the mind-faculty and the five faculties of sensation,
these six faculties pertain to both the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and the undefiled (*akliṣṭa*).
Because the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya) is now associated only with non-defiled wholesome states, it is said to be "partial.
Regarding its partial association with the three untainted faculties (anāsravendriya):
those three faculties have nine factors as their intrinsic nature.
Now, excluding the essential nature of faith itself, it is said to be associated with only a "partial portion" because it is associated with other [faculties].
The same applies to the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is associated with a partial portion of nine faculties, including the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" itself.
Regarding that which is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya),
this faculty has nine dharmas as its nature;
each one, excluding itself, is associated with the others, and all are termed this faculty.
Regarding the statement that "this faculty is associated with a portion of nine faculties," these refer to the mind faculty,
the pleasure, joy, and equanimity faculties, and the five faculties beginning with faith.
In what way is it associated with a portion of those?
That is to say, while those nine faculties pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
here they correspond only to the uncontaminated. Within the uncontaminated,
they pertain to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Now, it is said to be "partial" because it corresponds only with that [stage of] the path of vision (*darśanamārga*),

just as in the case of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*). The same applies to the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Because they differ only in their stages while being identical in all other respects:
from the power of faith up to the power of wisdom; from the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness up to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
Regarding the dharma-knowledge from right view up to right concentration,
and so on up to the knowledge of the path, as well as emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness—
how many faculties are associated with them?
Answer: The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is associated with four faculties and a portion of nine faculties.

As for the four faculties, they are diligence (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Regarding the association with a portion of nine faculties: [the remaining five faculties—faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—are each associated with a portion of the nine faculties].
This refers to the meaning of the mind-faculty, the five feelings, and the three untainted faculties as previously explained.
As it is with the power of faith,
so it is with the remaining four powers.

That is to say, they correspond with a portion of eleven faculties: namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth;
and the four [faculties], the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), and a portion of the four beginning with the mental faculty, the faculty of receiving (*pratigraha*), and faith.
Those eight faculties are common to both the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and the out-flow-free (*anāsrava*).
Since they are now associated only with the out-flow-free, they are said to be "partial.
To be associated with a portion of the three out-flow-free faculties means:
Those three faculties have nine factors as their nature.

Here, because mindfulness excludes its own intrinsic nature while being associated with the others, it is said to be "a partial portion," just like the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The same applies to the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, diligence, and concentration.
The enlightenment factor of joy is associated with a portion of nine faculties:
namely, the mental faculty, the five beginning with faith, and the three untainted faculties.
Regarding its association with a portion of the five faculties such as mental faith (*manas-śraddhā*) and so forth:
while those six faculties generally pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
here it is associated exclusively with their uncontaminated aspects.
Among the untainted [attainments], they generally rely upon nine stages:
namely, the threshold concentration (anāgamya),
the intermediate dhyāna, and the four dhyānas.
The lower three formless attainments are now said to be "partial" because they correspond only with those based on the first two dhyānas; likewise,
they correspond only partially with the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
Those three faculties— pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—
as well as those that arise simultaneously with them,
are all present; however, because it is now associated only with those that arise simultaneously with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), it is said to be "partial."
The enlightenment factor of equanimity is associated with three faculties and a portion of nine faculties.
The three faculties refer to the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
Regarding the nine faculties that are partially associated:
these are the mental faculty (*manas*), the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
In what way are they partially associated with those?
That is to say, those nine faculties pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Since they are now associated only with the uncontaminated, they are said to be "partial.
Right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is associated with a partial portion of eleven faculties.
This refers to the four mental faculties—desire, resolve, joy, and equanimity—and the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
Their meaning is as explained for the factors of enlightenment such as mindfulness;
they are like right view.
The same applies to right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
However, there is a slight distinction regarding right intention:
it consists of mental joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*)—namely, the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
These are called the eleven.
These eleven faculties generally rely upon all stages (*bhūmi*);
however, because they are here associated only with those relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and the first dhyāna, they are said to be "partial."
The remainder are not associated with faculties;
that is to say, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are not associated with faculties,
because they are dissociated phenomena.
The knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) is associated with a portion of eleven faculties,
as explained in the case of right view. As it is with the knowledge of phenomena, so it is [with the subsequent knowledge].
The same applies to the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
The knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) is associated with a portion of ten faculties:

namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), the four beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
The meaning is as explained in the *Saṃgīti-paryāya*.
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is associated with two faculties and a portion of eight faculties.
As for the two faculties:
This refers to the faculties of suffering and grief.
As for the partial association with eight faculties,
it refers to the mental faculty, the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity, and the four faculties beginning with faith.
In what sense do they correspond with only a portion of those?

It is because those eight faculties pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), whereas these now correspond only to their contaminated aspect; therefore, they are said to correspond with only a portion.
The emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness [samādhis] are associated with a portion of eleven faculties,
as explained in the case of the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 154.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 155,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section Six: The Aggregate of the Five Faculties; Subsection Four: The Chapter on Equanimity; Part Five. When one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the desire realm:
"How many faculties cease?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Herein, various distinctions are shown through numerous approaches.
That is to say: the distinction of elements,
the distinction of persons,
and the distinction of faculties.
There is a distinction between death-existence, intermediate existence,
and birth-existence.
The distinction between gradual death and instantaneous death;
and when one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the desire realm.
How many faculties cease?
Answer: Either four, or nine.
Either eight,
or thirteen, or nine.
Either fourteen, or ten, or fifteen.
For one who is gradually passing away,
there are four indeterminate factors:
namely, the body, life, mind, and equanimity.
There are nine types of wholesome minds;
that is, the aforementioned four plus the five beginning with faith.
This refers to those who die instantaneously.
If it is a formless, indeterminate mind, there are eight:
namely, the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, and equanimity.
If it is a wholesome mind, there are thirteen.
That is to say, the first eight plus the five beginning with faith.
If it is a single-gendered indeterminate mind, there are nine:
namely, the aforementioned eight plus one gender.
There are fourteen wholesome minds;
that is, the previous nine plus the five beginning with faith.
For one who possesses both sexual organs, there are ten neutral minds.
That is to say, the previous nine plus one form [constitute] the fifteen wholesome minds; that is,
the ten preceding ones plus the five beginning with faith.
What are the fetters of the mind and mental factors that cease?
Answer: Those bound to the desire realm.
How many faculties are present?
Answer: Either eight, or nine, or ten.
Eight are formless:
namely, the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, and equanimity.
Nine are with form.
This means that to the previous eight, one sexual organ is added,
making nine; with both sexual organs, there are ten—
meaning to the previous nine, another sexual organ is further added.
What kind of bound mind and mental factors manifest?
Answer: Those bound to the desire realm.
This occurs when one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the form realm.
How many faculties cease?
Answer: Either four or nine; or nine.
Or fourteen: for one who dies gradually, there are four indeterminate minds—
namely, those of the body, life, mind, and equanimity.
The nine [faculties] of a wholesome mind consist of the preceding four plus the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
For one who dies instantaneously, there are nine indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) minds:
namely, the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
And with either the female or male faculty,
there are fourteen wholesome [mental states],
namely the aforementioned nine plus the five beginning with faith.
What are the fetters of the mind and mental factors that cease?
Answer: Those bound to the desire realm.
How many faculties are present?
Answer: Eight.
Namely, the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, and equanimity.
Regarding which realm they are bound to when these minds and mental factors manifest: they are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
When one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the formless realm, how many faculties cease?
Answer: Either four.
Either nine, or nine,
or fourteen.
As previously stated:
"Of which fetters are the mind and mental factors that cease?
Answer: Those bound to the desire realm."
How many faculties are present?
Answer: Three;
namely, the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, and the equanimity-faculty.
To what realm are the mind and mental factors bound that manifest?
Answer: They are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This occurs when one passes away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is reborn in the form realm.
How many faculties cease?
Answer: Either eight, or thirteen.
There are eight indeterminate minds, namely:
eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life-faculty, mind, and equanimity.
There are thirteen wholesome minds.
That is to say, the preceding eight [faculties] plus the five beginning with faith.
Regarding which realm's mind and mental factors are extinguished?
The answer is: those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
How many faculties are manifested?
Answer: Eight, as previously stated.
To what fetters are the mind and mental factors bound when they are manifested?
Answer: Bound to the form realm.
When one passes away from the form realm and is born into the desire realm, how many faculties cease?
Answer: Either eight.
Alternatively, there are thirteen.
As previously stated, regarding which fetters the mind and mental factors cease:
the answer is those bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
How many faculties are present?
Answer: Either eight or nine.
Or ten, as previously explained.
Which bound mind and mental factors manifest?
Answer: When one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the formless realm,
how many faculties cease?
Answer: Either eight or thirteen,
as previously explained.
Question: To which realm are the bound mind and mental factors that cease connected? Answer: To the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Question: How many faculties (indriya) are present?
Answer: Three, as previously stated.
What kind of mind and mental factors, bound to which realm, manifest?
Answer: Those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This occurs when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the formless realm.
How many faculties cease?
Answer: Either three, or eight.
There are three indeterminate minds, namely:
life, mind, and equanimity.
There are eight wholesome minds.
That is to say, the previous three plus the five faculties beginning with faith.
As for the question of which fetters the associated mind and mental factors are extinguished from, the answer is: those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
How many faculties are present?
The answer to the three [questions] is as previously stated.
To what realm are the mind and mental factors bound that manifest?
Answer: They are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
When one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm, how many faculties cease?
Answer: Either three.
Or eight,
as previously stated.
Which fetters are extinguished when the mind and mental factors cease?
Question: How many faculties (indriya) are present for those bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)?
Answer: Either eight.
Either nine or ten,
as previously explained.
What kind of mind and mental factors belonging to which realm manifest?
Answer: Those bound to the desire realm.
This occurs when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the form realm.
How many faculties cease?
Answer: Either three, or eight, as previously explained.
To what realm are the minds and mental factors bound that cease?
Answer: They are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
How many faculties (*indriya*) are present? Answer: Eight, as previously stated.
To what realm are the mind and mental factors bound that manifest?
Answer: They are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
This occurs at the time when an Arhat enters parinirvāṇa.
How many faculties cease last?
Answer: Either four, or nine.
Either eight, or three;
for those who attain parinirvāṇa gradually in the desire realm, there are four.
That is to say: body, life, mind, and equanimity.
Those who attain parinirvāṇa instantaneously have nine [faculties]:
eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, and equanimity.
And either the female or male faculty.
There are eight in the form realm:
namely, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, and equanimity faculties.
In the formless realm, there are three:
namely, life, mind, and equanimity.
Question: By what causes and conditions do all sentient beings necessarily abide in the feeling of equanimity at the moment of death and rebirth?
Answer: Among the five feelings, there is no mental aspect as dull and weak as that of the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣāvedanā*);
among the ten periods, there is none as dull and weak as those at the time of death and birth.
Therefore, one dwells in equanimity, experiences life, and undergoes death and rebirth.
5. Section on the Single Mind, the first of five within the sixth aggregate, the Aggregate of Faculties (Indriya-skandha). All phenomena arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with the mind.
"Are those dharmas associated with the mind?
Having thus mastered the meaning of such chapters and their respective expositions, [one proceeds].
This shall be explained in detail.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to refute the views of those who claim that association (*saṃprayoga*) is not real.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, this treatise is composed:
all phenomena arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with the mind.
Is that dharma associated with the mind?
Answer: If a dharma is associated with the mind, that dharma arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the mind.
This refers to all mental factors (caitta-dharma) which arise,
abide, and cease simultaneously with the mind;
yet those factors are not associated (asamprayukta) with the mind.
This refers to matter that arises in accordance with the mind and formations dissociated from the mind.
Among these, "arising" (utpāda) means:
Arising is called birth;
abiding is called aging;
and ceasing is called impermanence.
If various phenomena arise, abide, and cease together with the mind, do those phenomena share the same object of cognition as the mind?
Answer: If a phenomenon shares the same object of cognition as the mind, [then it arises, abides, and ceases together with the mind].
Those phenomena arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with the mind;
that is to say, all mental factors (caitta-dharma).
There are phenomena that arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with the mind.
Those phenomena are not the single object of one mind;
namely, matter that evolves in accordance with the mind and formations dissociated from the mind.
Question: For what reason was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to refute the view that objects of cognition (*ālambana*) are not real, and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
There are ten meanings regarding that which evolves according to the mind:
namely, one arising, one abiding, one ceasing, one fruit, one outflow, and one maturation.
If it is wholesome, it is wholesome;
if unwholesome, it is unwholesome;
if indeterminate, it is indeterminate.
It falls within a single lifetime.
"A single fruit" refers to the fruit of dissociation (visamyoga-phala).
"Of one type" refers to the fruit of outflow;
"of one [type]" refers to the fruit of maturation.
This refers to the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
"Falling within a single world-period" means being subsumed under the same world-period.
This is the general explanation.
To explain it specifically, within the path that abandons the fetters of the tainted (*sāsrava*), there are eight aspects of concomitant occurrence (*anuvartana*):
namely, one arising, one abiding, and one ceasing.
There is one fruit, one outflow, and one maturation;
it is wholesome and falls within a single lifetime.
This occurs within the paths of preparation, liberation, and special progress for those with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, in other categories of wholesome minds associated with outflows (*sāsrava*),
there are seven aspects of concomitant functioning (*anuvartana*):
namely, one arising, one abiding, and one ceasing.
The first [type] is a single outflow (*niṣyanda*) and a single maturation (*vipāka*); it is wholesome and falls within a single lifetime.
Within the untainted path that severs the fetters (*anāsrava-saṃyojana-prahāṇa-mārga*), there is also the sense of seven concomitants (*anuvartaka*).
That is to say: one arising, one abiding, and one ceasing.
There is one fruit and one outflow;
it is wholesome and falls within a single lifetime.
Within the uncontaminated paths of preparation, liberation, and special progress, there are six meanings of concomitant occurrence.
That is to say: they arise together, abide together, cease together, and possess a common outflow;
being virtuous, they fall within a single lifetime.
Within the category of unwholesome minds, there are seven factors that function as concomitants.
That is to say: they share a single arising, a single abiding, a single cessation, a single outflow, and a single maturation;
these unwholesome [states] fall within a single time period.
Within the category of indeterminate minds, there are six meanings of concomitant transformation (anuvartana).
That is to say, they share a single arising, a single abiding, a single cessation, and a single outflow;
they are indeterminate and fall within a single time period.
Furthermore, the mind and mental factors are mutually related in this manner.
It is called "conforming" (anuvartaka) by virtue of five causes and conditions:
namely, by way of its basis (āśraya) and by way of its object (ālambana).
By way of aspect,
by way of fruit,
and by way of maturation.
The mind and the matter that arises concomitantly with the mind (cittānuvartin-rūpa),
as well as the formations dissociated from the mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra),
are said to be "concomitant" (anuvartin) when they are viewed in relation to one another by virtue of two causes.
This means: because they are results;
because they are maturation (*vipāka*);
and because they follow [the mind]—as explained at length in the *Saṃyukta-skandha*.
All phenomena arise together with the mind and are not separate from the mind;
those phenomena abide together with the mind and cease together with the mind.
"Is it not inseparable from the mind?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed once again?
Answer: Although it was explained in the preceding section on "Inclusion" (*saṃgraha*) that the mind, mental factors, and other phenomena perish moment by moment,
it did not yet distinguish the case of form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
I now wish to clarify this matter and have therefore composed this treatise; furthermore, it is to refute the position held by certain śramaṇas who maintain the doctrine of three moments.
These śramaṇas assert that all material phenomena (rūpadharma) abide for three moments.
It is taught that the mind and mental factors perish moment by moment;
these are further of two kinds,
the first being the proponents of mixed arising (*saṃsṛṣṭa-vāda*).
Regarding the *Kramasiddhi-śāstra*,
the proponents of the *Saṃkīrṇotpatti-śāstra* state as follows:
"Based on the initial visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), the initial visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*) arises."
Once they have arisen together, the eye-faculty remains while the eye-consciousness ceases;
based on a second eye-faculty, a second eye-consciousness arises.
Once they have arisen together, the eye-faculty remains while the eye-consciousness ceases.
Based on the third eye-faculty, the third eye-consciousness arises.
Once they have arisen together, while the eye-faculty remains, the eye-consciousness ceases;
it should be understood that it then ceases simultaneously with the first eye-faculty.
Question: What fault is there in that?
Answer: In that case, the initial visual consciousness arises with a basis, yet it would perish without a basis.
The second visual consciousness is likewise.
The third visual consciousness arises with a basis;
although its own basis has ceased, it nonetheless relies upon another as its basis.
This is called its fault,
because consciousness arises and ceases in accordance with its support.
Those who follow the sequential treatises speak thus:
Based on the initial eye-faculty, the initial eye-consciousness arises;
once they have arisen together,
the eye-faculty abides while the eye-consciousness ceases.
Next, again depending upon that, a second visual consciousness arises;
the visual faculty abides while the visual consciousness ceases.
Subsequently, again depending upon that, a third visual consciousness arises.
This consciousness perishes simultaneously with the eye.
Question: What fault is there in that?
Answer: That initial visual consciousness arises having a basis.
It ceases without dependence.
Second, visual consciousness arises without dependence and ceases without dependence.
Thirdly, visual consciousness arises without a basis and ceases while having a basis;
this is called its fault.
Because consciousness arises and ceases in accordance with its support,
and furthermore, those two treatises share another common error:
namely, that when one passes away from the human realm and is born in hell, [the consciousness would have to arise without a support].
If one has not yet abandoned the human realm but has already attained rebirth in hell,
then there would be a confusion of destinies and a confusion of bodies.
Regarding those of mixed destinies:
it refers to those sentient beings who belong to the destiny of hell and also to the destiny of humans.
Regarding "the body being confused":
it means that such a sentient being would possess both a hellish body and a human body,
which would constitute a great error.
According to the intent of that treatise, when one enters the meditative absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*),
the sense faculties and the primary elements arise together with the mind and are not separated from it;
nevertheless, they abide apart from the mind and cease apart from the mind.
This treatise is composed to refute that attachment. [The opponent asks:

"If all phenomena arise together with the mind and are not separate from the mind, do those phenomena also abide together with the mind and cease together with the mind, being not separate from the mind?"
Answer: For sentient beings of the desire and form realms who do not abide in the meditative attainments of non-conception or cessation,
the sense faculties and the primary elements arise together with the mind and are not separate from it.
It abides together with the mind and ceases together with the mind, never being separate from the mind.
If one abides in the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), that [attainment] is then separate from the mind.
Question: In what way is it separate from the mind?
Answer: They arise apart from the mind,
abide apart from the mind,
and cease apart from the mind.
Because the mind and mental factors sever that continuity,
as it is said:
"One does not cultivate the eye-faculty, up to and including the mind-faculty."
"What is the non-cultivation of the eye faculty?
and so forth, as explained at length.
There are four kinds of cultivation.
Namely: cultivation by acquisition,
cultivation by practice, and cultivation as an antidote.
The cultivation of elimination has been fully explained according to the *Jñānaskandha* [Abhidharma treatise].
Now, this treatise is composed based on the latter two types of cultivation.
Question: How are the faculties such as the eye not cultivated?
And how are they cultivated?
Answer: As long as the path that serves as the antidote to the faculties such as the eye has not yet arisen, it is said that the faculties are not cultivated.
This is explained in terms of cultivation as an antidote.
Furthermore, as long as the afflictions associated with the eye and so forth have not been abandoned and their nature has not been fully known,
they are said to be "uncultivated faculties."
This is explained according to the cultivation of removal (*prahāṇabhāvanā*).
If the remedial paths (*pratipakṣamārga*) for the eye and other faculties have already arisen, it is called the cultivation of the faculties (*indriyabhāvanā*);
this is explained according to the cultivation of the remedy (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*).
Furthermore, when all afflictions conditioned by the eye and so forth have been abandoned and fully understood,
this is called the cultivation of the faculties (*indriya-bhāvanā*).
This is explained according to the cultivation of elimination (*vibhāvana-bhāvanā*).
This is called the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
How does one fail to cultivate the eye-faculty, up to and including the body-faculty?
Answer: If one has not yet become free from craving for the eye-faculty.
They have not yet abandoned the moisture of desire, nor the thirst of craving.
Furthermore, regarding the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) which can exhaust attachment to the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*), they have neither cultivated nor stabilized that path.
As it is with the non-cultivation of the eye faculty, so it is for the non-cultivation of the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
If one has not yet become free from craving for the eye faculty,
this means one has not yet become free from attachment to the eye.
"One who has not yet abandoned desire" refers to one who has neither severed nor fully understood craving.
"One who has not yet abandoned moisture" refers to the same.
This refers to one who has not abandoned or fully understood the moisture of craving (*tṛṣṇā*),
and who has not yet become free from delight (*nandī*).
That is to say, it refers to one who has not abandoned or fully understood both craving and delight.
"One who has not yet abandoned craving" refers to one for whom craving has neither been severed nor fully understood. Furthermore, it refers to one who,
by means of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), is capable of exhausting attachment to the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*).
This refers to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) that is capable of exhausting craving for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
For one who has not yet cultivated or stabilized this path— that is,
who has not yet practiced it— [it is said they have not attained it].
Furthermore, there is cultivation of non-rest (aśānti) and cultivation of rest (śānti);
that is to say, habitual cultivation is called non-rest, while attainment cultivation is called rest.
Moreover, arising is termed non-rest, while cessation is termed rest.
Furthermore, that which has already arisen is called "cultivation" (bhāvanā),
and that which has already ceased is called "establishment" (sthāpanā).
It should be understood that herein, for one who has not yet abandoned craving and so forth regarding the eye-faculty:
This is explained in terms of cultivation as an antidote,
or in terms of cultivation as elimination.
Furthermore, it refers to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) which is capable of exhausting craving for form and so forth.
It is explained according to the cultivation of elimination,
or according to the cultivation of the antidote; so some say.
Regarding those who have not yet abandoned craving and so forth for the eye-faculty:
this refers to those whose attachment directed toward the eye-faculty has not been severed or fully known.
Furthermore, it refers to those for whom the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) is capable of exhausting craving for form and so forth.
This refers to the fact that other afflictions have not yet been abandoned or fully understood with respect to the eye-faculty;
some say it means that one has not yet become free from craving and so forth regarding the eye-faculty.
This refers to the non-abandonment of the acquisition of fetters (*bandhana-prāpti*).
Furthermore, regarding the statement that the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) can exhaust desire for the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*) and so forth,
this refers to the non-attainment of the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
Just as when the acquisition of fetters has not been severed,
and the acquisition of dissociation has not been realized,
so too is it when faults have not been diminished.
One has not yet cultivated merit;
one has not yet abandoned what is inferior;
one has not yet realized what is sublime.
One has not yet abandoned what is meaningless,
nor attained what is meaningful;
one has not yet eliminated the feverish affliction of craving for existence.
It should be understood that the same applies to the bliss of non-sensual pleasure (*anupādāya-sukha*). Some say:
If one has not yet abandoned craving and so forth regarding the eye faculty,
it means that the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) has not yet become operative;
furthermore, it is this path of uninterrupted transition that is capable of exhausting craving for form and so forth.
This means that the path of liberation has not yet become operative. Some say:
"If one has not yet abandoned craving for the eye faculty and so forth."
This refers to those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm up to the third dhyāna,
as well as those for whom the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) is capable of exhausting attachment to the form realm and so forth.
This means that one has not yet become free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna;
just as with the faculty of the eye,
it is the same for the other four faculties when they are not cultivated.
What is the non-cultivation of the faculty of mind?
Answer: It is when one has not yet become free from greed for the faculty of mind, and has not yet become free from the moisture of desire, delight, and craving.
Furthermore, the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) is capable of exhausting craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*).
If one has not yet cultivated or stabilized that path,
and if one has not yet become free from craving for the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), [then...]
This refers to one who has not yet abandoned craving for the mental faculty;
the remaining phrases are as before.
Furthermore, it refers to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that is capable of exhausting craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*).
This refers to the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) which is able to exhaust craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
It has not yet been cultivated or stabilized, as previously explained.
One should understand that herein, if one has not yet become free from greed and so forth regarding the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), [the aforementioned applies].
This is explained in terms of cultivation as an antidote (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*), or in terms of cultivation for elimination (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, it refers to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) that is capable of exhausting the craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*) and so forth.
This is explained according to the cultivation of elimination (*prahāṇabhāvanā*), or according to the cultivation of the antidote (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*).
The three subsequent explanations should be understood as before.
Regarding the fifth point, some say:

"If one has not yet abandoned craving for the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) and so forth" means that one has not yet been freed from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Furthermore, regarding the statement that the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*) can exhaust the craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*) and so forth:
this refers to one who has not yet become free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
As it is said:
One cultivates the eye faculty up to the mind faculty.
How does one cultivate the eye faculty up to the body faculty?
Answer: If one has already become free from craving for the eye faculty.
Having already abandoned the moisture of desire and the thirst of craving,
and since the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) can exhaust greed for the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*),
he has already cultivated and stabilized himself in this path.
Just as with the cultivation of the eye faculty,
so it is for the cultivation of the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
How is the mental faculty cultivated?
Answer: If one has already become free from greed for the faculty of mind, and has already become free from the moisture of desire and the thirst of delight;
furthermore, if the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) is capable of exhausting greed for the formless realm.
Since he has already cultivated and stabilized this path,
these phrases should be understood as being contrary to the previously mentioned state of not having cultivated it;
this is explained in detail.
"Those who do not possess the faculties of one in training (śaikṣa-indriya) obtain the faculties of one in training," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Fools who are subject to regression cling to the view that regression does not exist.
To refute their position and to demonstrate that regression truly exists, this treatise was composed.
[It concerns those] who, previously not possessing the faculties of a learner (*śaikṣa*), acquire the faculties of a learner.
Is it the case that all those who enter the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) do not possess the faculties of training (śaikṣa-indriya) and acquire the faculties of training? Answer:
If one enters the state of right determination, all such persons do not possess the faculties of training and acquire the faculties of training.
There are cases where one who was not previously accomplished in the faculties of training attains the faculties of training,
yet does not enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth;
this refers to the time when one falls away from the fruit of arhatship.
Those who previously abandoned and now obtain the faculties of training (śaikṣendriya) are those who,
not having previously possessed the faculties of training,
now acquire them.
Are all those [states] immediately followed by the "supreme mundane factors" (*laukikāgradharma*)?
Answer: If they are immediately followed by the supreme mundane factors, they all do not possess the faculties of one in training (*śaikṣendriya*), yet they attain the faculties of one in training.
There are cases where one who has not yet accomplished the faculties of training attains the faculties of training;
this is not immediately following the state of "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma),
namely at the time of falling away from the fruit of arhatship.
Those various faculties of training were previously abandoned and are now attained.
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed again?
Answer: Although the essential nature of entering into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) was previously demonstrated, [this is done here to further clarify it].
However, the entry into the immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for those [roots] has not yet been demonstrated;
wishing now to demonstrate it, this treatise is composed.
Regarding all those who abandon the untainted roots (*anāsrava-indriya*):
One attains the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
Do they all proceed from one fruit to another fruit?
Answer: If they proceed from one fruit to another fruit.
One who has abandoned all untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and attains untainted faculties refers to one who,
as a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), realizes the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*): at that time,
they abandon the untainted faculties associated with the fruit of stream-entry and the path to the superior fruit, and attain the fruit of once-returner.
It encompasses the untainted faculties.
"From fruit to fruit" means from the fruit of stream-entry to the fruit of once-returning.
It should be understood that the same applies when a Once-returner realizes the fruit of Non-returning,
and when a Non-returner realizes the fruit of Arhatship.
As it is at the time of realizing the fruit, so it is also at the time of falling away from the fruit.
There are cases where one abandons untainted faculties and acquires untainted faculties,
yet this does not constitute a transition from one fruit to another.
This refers to when the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) arises at the conclusion of the clear realization (abhisamaya),
or when an Arhat liberated by analysis (samayavimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to become one who is unshakable (akopyadharman).
Question: It may be so when the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) arises.
But how can it be so for a time-liberated Arhat (*samayavimukta-arhat*) when refining their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become unshakable (*akopyadharman*)?
Answer: This text should have stated only that it occurs when the subsequent knowledge of the path at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-mārgānvayajñāna*) arises.
One should not speak of anything else;
yet, when something else is spoken of,
it is intended to show that here one is merely speaking of the transition from a fruit of a different category to another fruit of a different category.
When an Arhat of occasional liberation (samayavimukta) refines their faculties to become unshakable (akopya),
although their nature and category differ, their fruit does not; therefore,
this is not called "proceeding from one fruit to another."
When one abandons various untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and acquires untainted faculties,
does all that [previously] ceased untainted faculty arise?
It can be answered in four propositions:
there is the case where one abandons untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and acquires untainted faculties,
yet those [faculties] do not cease and those [faculties] do not arise.
This refers to the time when one falls away from the fruits of arhatship, non-returning, or once-returning;
and when one attains the fruits of once-returning or non-returning by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
At those times, because the untainted (*anāsrava*) [path] does not manifest.
There is the case where an untainted faculty ceases and an untainted faculty arises,
yet one does not abandon the untainted faculty nor acquire an untainted faculty;
this refers to when an untainted faculty already acquired becomes manifest.

When cessation arises, it is because the continuum of the various untainted faculties previously attained during the stage of approaching all fruits arises and ceases; that [cessation] is not the arising of what was not previously attained, because the path already attained manifests in the present.
Nor is it that one abandons the noble path at only three times;
for those [three] are not the present time.
First, the time of falling back (*parihāṇi*).
Second, at the time of attaining the fruits;
third, at the time of refining the faculties (indriya).
In these cases, one abandons untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) and acquires untainted faculties.
In that case as well, untainted faculties cease and untainted faculties arise;
namely, at the time when the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) arises at the conclusion of clear realization (abhisamaya),
and when one attains the fruits of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) or non-returner (anāgāmin) by means of the untainted path.
At the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship;
at the time when an arhat liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) refines their faculties to become unshakable (akopya);
and at the time when the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) arises at the conclusion of the clear realization (abhisamaya).
Regarding the abandonment of the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya),

this refers to those subsumed within the path of seeing (darśana-mārga). Regarding the acquisition of the untainted faculties, this refers to [those subsumed within] the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).
This refers to the cessation of the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) as comprised within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga); specifically,
it refers to the category [of factors] co-arising with the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-kṣānti).
Regarding the arising of the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*):
this refers to the category co-arising with the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*),
at the time one attains the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) by means of the untainted path.
The faculty of the abandonment of outflows refers to that comprised within the fruit of stream-entry and the path to superior fruits.
Those who have attained the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) are comprised within the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
As for the cessation of the untainted faculties:
This refers to the arising of untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) subsumed under the sixth path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga);
"the arising of untainted faculties" refers to those subsumed under the sixth path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
The attainment of the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) through the untainted path (anāsravamārga) is likewise accordingly.
As for the abandonment of untainted faculties at the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala),
this refers to those subsumed under the fruit of non-returner.
And regarding the path of superior fruit:
those who have attained the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) are said to be comprised within the fruit of arhatship.
The cessation of the untainted faculties refers to the category co-arising with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
The arising of the untainted faculties refers to...

This refers to when an Arhat of the "timely liberation" (samaya-vimukta) type, at the moment of attaining the first category of knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), transforms their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) into the "unshakable" (akopya) state;
in this instance, they relinquish the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) which are comprised within the path of timely liberation.
"Attaining the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya)" refers to that which is subsumed within the path of non-periodic liberation (asamayavimukti-mārga).
"The cessation of the untainted faculties" refers to...
This refers to the arising of untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) subsumed under the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga); that is to say,
they are subsumed under the ninth path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
The refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) in other stages is not mentioned here because it is abbreviated.
There are cases where one does not abandon an untainted faculty (*anāsrava-indriya*) yet acquires an untainted faculty;
in those cases as well, it is not that an untainted faculty ceases while another untainted faculty arises.
This means excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Here, the term "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) functions in reference to that which is characterized (lakṣya);
thus, those phenomena not subsumed by the first three propositions constitute the fourth proposition.
What, then, is this? It refers to the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) up to the stage of supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).
Regarding the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), there is neither relinquishing nor acquisition,
neither cessation nor arising,
while one abides in the state of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma).
Regarding the untainted faculties, they are neither abandoned nor acquired,
and they do not arise through cessation.
This is the case when noble ones abide in the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Up until the time of the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*),
one neither abandons nor acquires any untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*);
rather, they both cease and arise.
When abiding in the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti),
one both relinquishes and acquires, and both ceases and arises, with respect to the untainted faculties (anāsravendriya).
When one realizes the fruit of a once-returner from the fruit of a stream-enterer,
if it is by means of the mundane path,
the untainted path serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
When abiding in the stage of the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*),
one does not abandon but acquires the untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*);
they cease rather than arise.
If the mundane path serves as the preparatory practice,
then while abiding in the five paths of uninterrupted transition and the five paths of liberation of that preparatory stage,
one does not abandon but rather acquires the untainted faculties.
It is neither ceasing nor arising.
At the time of abiding in the sixth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*),
