one both relinquishes and acquires the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Regarding "neither ceasing nor arising by means of the untainted path":
if the mundane path serves as the preparatory application,
it refers to the time when one abides in the stage of the path of preparation.
Regarding the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), they are neither relinquished nor acquired;
they do not cease and then arise.
If the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
When abiding in the five paths of uninterrupted transition and the five paths of liberation of the path of application,
it is not that one abandons and then acquires;
rather, it both ceases and arises.
When abiding in the sixth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one both relinquishes and acquires, and both ceases and arises, with respect to the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
The same applies accordingly for the realization of the fruit of non-returning from the fruit of once-returning.
Regarding the realization of the fruit of arhatship from the fruit of non-returning,
it occurs at the time of becoming detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
Regarding those who follow the mundane path:
if the untainted path serves as the preparatory application,
it is at the time of abiding in the stage of the path of preparation.
Regarding the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), one does not abandon them but acquires them;
they cease rather than arise.
This occurs when the mundane path (laukikamārga) serves as the preparatory application (prayoga).
When abiding in the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the nine paths of liberation of the path of preparation,
one neither abandons nor acquires the untainted faculties;
they are neither extinguished nor arise.
Regarding those who [attain it] by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*):
if the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
then while abiding in the stage of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
Regarding the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), they are neither abandoned nor acquired;
they do not arise through cessation.
If the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
When abiding in the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the nine paths of liberation of the path of preparation,
one neither abandons nor acquires the untainted faculties;
rather, they both cease and arise.
As it is with the detachment from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
so it is up to the detachment from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness.
When one is detaching from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
If the mundane path serves as the preparatory application,
then while abiding in the stage of the path of preparation,
one does not abandon but rather acquires the untainted faculties.
It does not arise through cessation.
If the untainted path serves as the preparatory application,
it occurs when one abides in the eight paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation within the stage of the preparatory application.
Regarding the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), they are not abandoned but acquired;
they both cease and arise at the time of abiding in the ninth uninterrupted path (*navama-ānantarya-mārga*).
Regarding the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), one both abandons and acquires them,
and both ceases and gives rise to them,
when one who practices through faith and understanding (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
If the mundane path serves as the preparatory practice,
then while abiding in the stage of the path of preparation,
one does not abandon but rather acquires the untainted faculties.
It does not arise through cessation.
If the untainted path serves as the preparatory application,
then while one abides in that stage of the preparatory path—
Regarding the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), they are neither abandoned nor acquired;
rather, they both cease and arise while one abides in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Regarding the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), one both relinquishes and acquires them,
and both ceases and arouses them.
This occurs when a time-liberated (*samaya-vimukta*) Arhat refines his faculties to become unshakable (*akopya*).
Just as when one is freed from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
it is said that at the very first moment of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna,
one does not abandon but rather acquires the untainted faculties.
It is extinguished rather than arising.
At the second moment,
regarding the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), they are not abandoned but are acquired.
It does not arise from cessation;
at the third moment,
it is as explained for the first moment.
When one brings forth the five supernormal powers, during the five paths of uninterrupted transition and the three paths of liberation;
or when one gives rise to the immeasurables or mundane liberations.
The bases of mastery,
the bases of totality,
and the contemplation of impurity.
Mindfulness of breathing,
mundane foundations of mindfulness,
and mundane analytical knowledges.
The knowledge of the aspiration for non-contention (*araṇāpraṇidhijñāna*),
the meditative absorption of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*),
and the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) and the wishlessness of wishlessness (*apraṇihitāpraṇihita*).
Regarding the signless-signless:
when entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) during the subtle stages of perception,
one does not abandon but rather acquires the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
It is neither ceasing nor arising.
This occurs when one gives rise to the supernormal power of the untainted knowledge of others' minds,
or when one gives rise to the untainted foundations of mindfulness.
At the time of untainted liberation and the untainted analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),
regarding the untainted faculties, they are neither abandoned nor acquired, yet they both cease and arise.
When a very subtle mind arises,
or when wisdom derived from hearing and reflection arises,
one neither abandons nor acquires the untainted faculties.
It is neither ceasing nor arising.
Within such various states, one should apply the fourth alternative as appropriate;
therefore, it is explained briefly.
Excluding the aforementioned characteristics, it says:
"The faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown,' and so forth,
as explained at length."
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the sake of enabling those who harbor doubts to attain certainty, as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?
Answer: It is that which has not yet seen the truths and has not yet realized them through direct insight.
The wisdom of those in training is the faculty of wisdom.
If these faculties consist of those who follow by faith or follow by dharma,
they are able to realize the Four Noble Truths that have not yet been realized.
This is called the faculty of "the unknown that is to be known.
That text speaks only of the present conjunction [of factors] that is capable of bearing the burden and possessing functional activity.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is neither past nor future;
let there be no doubt that it arises.
Only that which is present and in combination can bear the burden and possess functional activity;
this is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
It is not [restricted to] the past or the future.
This treatise was composed to resolve their doubts by demonstrating that [the faculty] exists throughout all three periods of time and is therefore this very faculty.
Regarding all those who possess the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya),
are they all capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths that have not yet been realized?
One should answer by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
There is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
That [faculty] does not, however, constitute the actual realization (*abhisamaya*) of the four noble truths that have not yet been realized;
that is to say, it is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
Because that which exists in the past or future possesses the characteristic of the faculty of "that which is yet to be known," it is also called the faculty of "that which is yet to be known."
However, it is not capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths that have not yet been realized,
because its past activity has already ceased and its future activity has not yet arisen.
There are those who are able to realize the Four Noble Truths that have not yet been realized,

yet they do not possess the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*). What, then, are these non-faculty dharmas that are able to realize the Four Noble Truths that have not yet been realized?
Namely: perception, volition, contact,
attention, desire, resolve, shame, dread,
non-attachment, non-hatred, and pliancy.
Equanimity, non-negligence, non-harming,
applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), those factors that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*), matter (*rūpa*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*)—
these various phenomena [arise] while the Four Noble Truths have not yet been realized.
Although one is able to realize [the truths], this is not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*),
because this faculty is constituted by the combination of nine faculties. There is,
however, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
He too is capable of realizing that which has not yet been realized regarding the Four Noble Truths;
that is to say, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is capable of realizing that which has not yet been realized regarding the Four Noble Truths.
Then, those present aggregates that are capable of functioning as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) do not constitute the faculty of "having known" (ājñendriya);
nor do they possess the capacity for clear realization (abhisamaya) regarding the Four Noble Truths that has not yet been clearly realized.
This means that, excluding the aforementioned characteristics,
those phenomena not subsumed by the first three propositions constitute the fourth proposition.
Furthermore, what are these?

This refers to all other past and future non-faculty dharmas associated with and co-existent with this faculty, excluding the intrinsic nature of the faculty "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) of the three periods of time,
as well as the non-faculty dharmas associated with and co-existent with this faculty in the present.
Furthermore, it includes the category of factors co-arising with the faculty of having known (*ājñātendriya*) and the faculty of one who has fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*),
all contaminated (*sāsrava*) mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*),
and all other matter (*rūpa*) and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
And the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) are all included in the fourth category;
therefore, it is said that "except for the aforementioned characteristics," as in the case of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
It should be understood that the same applies in detail, as appropriate, to the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), should it be said to be the knowledge of exhaustion, or even up to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
This should be explained in full detail, and so forth.
Question: Why are three types of knowledge distinguished here?
Answer: Because it is the intention of the author of this treatise (*śāstrakāra*) to do so;
and so forth, as explained at length.
Answer: It should be said that the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) is indeed the knowledge of exhaustion;
that is to say, one personally realizes: "I have fully understood suffering;
I have eternally abandoned its origin."
"I have realized cessation; I have cultivated the path.
Or there is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), which means knowing for oneself: "I have fully understood the suffering bound to the desire realm."
I have forever severed the origin associated with the desire realm.
I have realized the cessation of all conditioned phenomena associated with the desire realm.
I have cultivated the path that leads to the abandonment of all conditioned phenomena associated with the desire realm.
Alternatively, subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) refers to knowing for oneself: "I have fully understood the suffering associated with the form and formless realms;
I have eternally abandoned the origin associated with the form and formless realms;
I have realized the cessation of all conditioned formations associated with the form and formless realms."
I have already cultivated and abandoned the paths that counteract the fetters of the form and formless realms.
Alternatively, there is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), which means personally knowing: "I have fully understood the suffering bound to the three realms.
Or there is the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), which means personally knowing: "I have eternally abandoned the origin bound to the three realms."
Alternatively, the knowledge of cessation refers to personally knowing that one has realized the cessation of all conditioned phenomena bound to the three realms;
alternatively, the knowledge of the path refers to personally knowing that one has cultivated the path that severs those conditioned phenomena bound to the three realms.
Question: For what reason is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) not the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: Because the nature of the knowledge of exhaustion is not that of a vision (darśana), whereas the nature of the knowledge of others' minds is that of a vision.
Why is it not conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?
Answer: Because the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is untainted (*anāsrava*), whereas conventional knowledge is tainted (*sāsrava*).
Having explained its intrinsic nature, the stages shall now be explained.
There is that which possesses vitarka and vicāra;
this refers to the stage of *anāgamya* and the first *dhyāna*.
Or there is no vitarka and only vicāra,
namely, based on the intermediate dhyāna;
or there is neither vitarka nor vicāra.
This refers to the three higher dhyānas and the lower three formless attainments;
having already indicated the stages, their associated mental factors shall now be indicated—
namely, those associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
This means that based on the third dhyāna,
it is associated with the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya);
whereas based on the first and second dhyānas, it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
Or it may be associated with the faculty of equanimity;
that is to say, based on the preliminary concentration (anāgamya),
the intermediate dhyāna, or the fourth dhyāna.
The lower three formless attainments have already been shown to be associated [with the wish for liberation]; their specific modes of activity (ākāra) shall now be explained.
Alternatively, they are associated with the wishless (apraṇihita).
That is to say, there are ten aspects,
or it is associated with the signless,
which consists of four aspects.
Question: Why is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) not associated with emptiness (śūnyatā)?
Answer: Emptiness is the ultimate truth (paramārtha), whereas the knowledge of exhaustion pertains to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti). Therefore, it is not associated with the ultimate truth.
As it was stated, "I have fully understood that birth has been exhausted," because this involves my own realization,
it is not associated with emptiness. Having clarified the aspect of the practice (*ākāra*),
one should now clarify its object (*ālambana*).
It may take as its object that which is bound to the desire realm,
or it may take as its object that which is bound to the form and formless realms;
this is what is meant by taking suffering and its origin as objects.
Or it takes as its object that which is unconditioned;
this refers to taking cessation and the path as objects,
as in the case of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
The knowledge of non-arising is likewise.
However, there is a distinction:
it should be said that the knowledge of non-arising is the knowledge of non-arising.
That is to say, one knows for oneself: "I no longer have to fully comprehend suffering;
I no longer have to permanently abandon its origin; I no longer have to realize its cessation;
and I no longer have to cultivate the path."
The right view of one beyond training should be called the right view of one beyond training;
that is, knowing the five aggregates of clinging through four aspects,
and knowing the cause of the five aggregates of clinging through four aspects.
One knows the cessation of the five aggregates of clinging through four aspects;
one knows the path for abandoning the five aggregates of clinging through four aspects;
or it is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
That is to say, it is the knowledge of the four truths of the desire realm;
or it is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
which is the knowledge of the four truths of the form and formless realms.
Or it is the knowledge of others' minds,
which means knowing the other's untainted (anāsrava) minds and mental factors;
or it is the knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
This refers to the specific knowledge of the Four Truths within the three realms.
Question: For what reason is the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) not conventional knowledge?
Answer: Because this [right view] is untainted (anāsrava), whereas that [conventional knowledge] is tainted (sāsrava).
Having revealed the intrinsic nature, the four questions concerning the stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth are as previously explained.
The distinction is that this,
too, is associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This is also because it functions through the aspects of emptiness and non-self.
Regarding "the first moments of the knowledge of exhaustion," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: Although the three types of knowledge were explained previously, the distinctions between the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) had not yet been analyzed.
Now, wishing to resolve this matter, I have composed this treatise:
Are all those that are the first *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion) necessarily the immediate successors (*samanantara*) of the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantaryamārga*)?
Answer: It is so.
This is because the first knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) necessarily arises immediately after the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*).
However, is it the case that all instances of the knowledge of exhaustion arise immediately after the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*)? [The answer is: No.
Answer: It is so.
Because immediately following the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi), the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) necessarily arises;
[this refers to] all initial knowledges of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
Is all of that immediately preceded by the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
Answer: It is so.
This is because the initial knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) necessarily arises immediately after the knowledge of exhaustion.
If there is knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), is there necessarily knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) immediately following it?
Answer: There may be knowledge of exhaustion;
that is, for one who is liberated by occasion (samayavimukta).
Either the knowledge of non-arising—
referring to one who is liberated at any time—
or the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).

That is to say, when the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) that takes time-liberation (*samaya-vimukta*) as its object arises, does the initial knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that takes that same [liberation] as its object then arise?
Answer: If the path of immediate succession that takes arising (*jāti*) as its object arises, then the initial knowledge of exhaustion that takes that same [arising] as its object arises.
If the path of uninterrupted transition does not take that [object] as its object, then the first knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) does not arise taking it as its object;
that is to say, the diamond-like concentration (vajropamasamādhi) is associated with six knowledges, namely, the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path.
And regarding the four types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*):
those comprised within the first two types of knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) are the subsequent knowledges of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna* and *samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*).

If the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is associated with the subsequent knowledges of suffering and its origin, then it shares the same cognitive object (*ālambana*) as the first knowledge of exhaustion.
Because it arises by taking as its object the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
and because those four aggregates are designated as "birth" and are subsumed under birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). If,

however, the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) is associated with the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodhadharmajñāna*) or the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), then its objective referent differs from that of the initial knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Those [knowledges] take the cessation and the path of the three realms as their objects;

these [knowledges] take the suffering and the origin of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as their objects. Therefore, when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises taking those as its object, does the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) also arise taking them as its object?
Answer: It is so.
If the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) arises by taking something as its object, does the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) also arise by taking that same thing as its object?
Answer: It is so.
This is because both of these knowledges take the four noble truths as their objects through fourteen aspects (ākāra).

Are those factors associated with the right thought of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
One should respond by formulating four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Among these, the right view of one beyond training is obtainable in all stages (*bhūmi*).
It is not that all untainted minds (anāsrava-citta) are obtainable;
nor is it that the right thought (samyak-saṃkalpa) of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is obtainable in all stages (bhūmi).
Therefore, four great permutations (catuṣkoṭi) can be established.
There are factors associated with the right view of one beyond training,
but not with the right thought of one beyond training;
namely, the right thought associated with the right view of one beyond training.
And those factors associated with the right view of one beyond training that are dissociated from the right thought of one beyond training.
Regarding "right thought associated with the right view of one beyond training," this refers to the right thought within the aggregate of the right view of one beyond training.
This is associated only with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
and not with the right thought of one beyond training;
for a thing cannot be associated with itself due to three reasons.
First, because two natures do not arise simultaneously;
second, because preceding and succeeding moments do not coexist;
and third, because phenomena do not serve as conditions for others by observing their own intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, regarding those factors associated with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) that are dissociated from the right thought of one beyond training:
these refer to the intermediate dhyāna and the three higher dhyānas.
The three lower formless attainments and the factors associated with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are not associated with the right thought of one beyond training.
Because that stage lacks right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*),
there are factors associated with the right intention of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
but not [those] associated with the right view (*samyak-dṛṣṭi*) of one beyond training.
It refers to the right view associated with the right thought of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
as well as those factors associated with the right thought of one beyond training that are not associated with the right view of one beyond training.
Regarding "right view associated with right thought of one beyond training":
this refers to the right view within the aggregate of right thought of one beyond training; it is associated exclusively with the right thought of one beyond training.
It is not the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
because a self-nature is not associated with itself due to three causes and conditions, and furthermore,
it is not associated with the right view of one beyond training.
Regarding the factors associated with the right intention of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*):

these refer to those within the collection of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), from the threshold stage (*anāgamya*) up to the first dhyāna.
Dharmas associated with right intention:
these are not associated with the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because right view is absent from that aggregate.
There are dharmas associated with both the right view and the right intention of one beyond training.
This refers to all other factors associated with the right view and right intention of those beyond training (aśaikṣa),
excluding the right intention associated with the right view of those beyond training,
and excluding the right view associated with the right intention of those beyond training.
This means that within this aggregate, with the exception of the two intrinsic natures themselves,
the remaining minds and mental factors are associated with those two. What, then, are these?
That is to say, the nine universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*),
the ten wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*), the mind, and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
There are factors that are not associated with the right view and right intention of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This refers to right thought not associated with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
right view not associated with the right thought of one beyond training,
and those mental states and mental factors not included in the aforementioned categories.
Together with matter, the unconditioned, and the formations dissociated from mind:
"right thought dissociated from right view of one beyond training" refers to the right thought within the collection of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.
This is not associated with the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
because right view is absent within that aggregate;
nor is it associated with the right intention of one beyond training.
Because a self-nature does not associate with itself,
right view that does not associate with right thought of the stage beyond training refers to the intermediate dhyāna.
The three higher meditative absorptions (dhyānas),
the three lower formless attainments (ārūpyas),
and the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi).
This is not associated with right view,
because a self-entity is not associated with itself;
nor is it associated with the right thought of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Because right thought is absent in that stage,
as well as those mental states and mental factors not included in the aforementioned categories—
namely, the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
The three higher dhyānas,
the three lower formless attainments,
and the collection of mental states and mental factors associated with the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
Furthermore, all learned (śaikṣa) contaminated (sāsrava) minds and mental factors,
as well as matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra),
should be known as being subsumed under the fourth category.
Regarding those phenomena associated with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa):
are those phenomena also associated with the right effort of one beyond training?
One should answer by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
Among these, the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is obtainable in all stages,
but not in all untainted minds.
The right effort of one beyond training is [obtainable] in all stages.
All untainted minds can be obtained;
therefore, one may formulate four middle propositions.
There are phenomena that are associated with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), but are not associated with the right effort of one beyond training.
This refers to right effort associated with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa). It is not,
however, associated with right effort that is itself beyond training,
because a factor cannot be associated with its own self-nature.
There are phenomena associated with the right effort of one beyond training,
but not with the right view of one beyond training;
namely, the right view of one beyond training itself and those phenomena dissociated from the right view of one beyond training.
Regarding the factors associated with the right effort of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and the right view of one beyond training:
because a self-nature does not associate with itself.
Regarding those factors associated with the right effort of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that are not associated with the right view of one beyond training:
these refer to the factors associated with right effort within the collection of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
These are not associated with right view.
Because right view is absent within that aggregate,
there are factors associated with the right view and right effort of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
That is to say, excluding the right effort associated with the right view of one beyond training, it refers to all other factors associated with the right view of one beyond training.
Because right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) is predominant, it is specifically excluded from this [category].
Nevertheless, within this aggregate, with the exception of the two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), all other minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are associated with both. How is this so?
That is to say: the nine universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the nine wholesome universal factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), the mind, and vitarka and vicāra.
There are factors that do not associate with the unlearned right view (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*) and right effort (*samyag-vīrya*);
namely, the right effort that does not associate with the unlearned right view.
as well as those mental states and mental factors not previously included,
along with matter, the unconditioned, and the formations dissociated from mind—
excluding the right effort that is dissociated from the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This refers to the right effort within the collection of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.
It is not associated with right view,
because right view is absent from that collection.
Nor is it associated with right effort,
because a self-nature is not associated with itself; furthermore,
it refers to those mental states and mental factors not included among the aforementioned categories.
Among these, there are no other mind or mental factors of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) not previously included;
rather, there are only all the conditioned (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors of those in training (*śaikṣa*) that were not previously included.
It should be understood that matter, the unconditioned, and the formations dissociated from mind are all subsumed under the fourth category.
This is likewise true for the application of energy, right mindfulness, right concentration, and right liberation.
Because all these can be established within the middle four alternatives:
there are phenomena associated with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
yet those phenomena are not associated with the right knowledge of one beyond training.
Those dharmas associated with the right knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samyagjñāna) are not associated with the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi),
because these two dharmas do not arise simultaneously.
Those dharmas associated with the right intention of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-samyaksaṃkalpa)...
Are those factors associated with the right effort of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
One should respond by formulating four permutations (catuṣkoṭika).
Among these, [the case of] right intention (samyak-saṃkalpa) of one beyond training...
While all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) can be attained, they are not attainable in all stages (*bhūmi*).
However, the right effort of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyak-pradhāna*) can be attained in all stages and by all untainted minds.
Therefore, one may also formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding this.
The phrasing is as when right view is explained in relation to right effort;
it is likewise in relation to right mindfulness, right concentration, and right liberation.
All these factors are associated with the right intention of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Are those factors associated with the right knowledge of one beyond training?
One should respond by formulating four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Among these, [the first alternative concerns] the right intention of one beyond training.
All untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) can be found, but not in all stages (*bhūmi*);
the right knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagjñāna*) can be found in all stages, but not in all untainted minds.
Therefore, one may also formulate four great propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The phrasing is as when right view is explained in relation to right thought.
If a dharma is associated with the right effort of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), is that dharma also associated with the right mindfulness of one beyond training?
One should answer by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
Within this context, both right effort and right mindfulness of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are found in all stages and in all untainted minds (anāsrava-citta).
Therefore, one may formulate four minor permutations (catuṣkoṭi):
there are dharmas associated with the right effort of one beyond training.
It is not that there is no right mindfulness of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Rather, it means that while this right mindfulness of one beyond training is associated with right effort of one beyond training, it is not associated with itself;
for a self-entity is not associated with its own self-entity.
There are phenomena associated with right mindfulness of one beyond training,
but not associated with right effort of one beyond training;
namely, right effort of one beyond training itself.
This is associated with the right mindfulness of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), but not with right effort,
because a factor cannot be associated with itself.
There are factors that are associated with both the right effort and the right mindfulness of one beyond training.
This refers to all other unlearned factors associated with right effort and right mindfulness, excluding the unlearned right effort and right mindfulness themselves; that is,
within this collection, the two intrinsic natures are excluded.
Other minds and mental factors are associated with two [factors].
What are these? They are the nine universal mental factors (mahābhūmika), the nine wholesome universal mental factors (kuśalamahābhūmika), the mind itself, and vitarka and vicāra.
There are phenomena that are not associated with the right effort and right mindfulness of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

These are: those mental states and mental factors not included among the aforementioned [categories], as well as matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
In this context, there are no other mind or mental factors of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) not included among those previously mentioned;
rather, it refers exclusively to all mind and mental factors of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those with outflows (*sāsrava*),
which were not previously included.
It should be understood that form, the unconditioned, and the formations dissociated from mind are all subsumed under the fourth category.
This is likewise true for right mindfulness, right concentration, and right liberation.
Since all of these can be arranged into small fourfold propositions:
"Are those phenomena associated with the right effort of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) also associated with the right knowledge (samyagjñāna) of one beyond training?"
It is agreed that there are four lines [of verse].
Herein, right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) is obtainable in all stages and in all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*);
right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is obtainable in all stages.

the middle fourfold set of propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) is formulated in the same manner as that explained for right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) in relation to right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).

Question: For what reason is this section (skandhaka) named "Fish" (matsya)?
Answer: Because it undergoes many shifts of position and is difficult to grasp.
What are these "many positions"?
That is to say: the states of possessing faculties and lacking faculties;
the states of being formless, having one form, or having two forms;
and the states of possessing mind and lacking mind.
The stage of being fixed or unfixed;
the stage of distinctions regarding birth, realm, and level;
and the stage of having severed or not severed the roots of goodness.
The stages of being free from passion and not yet free from passion;
the stages of wholesome, defiled, and neutral mental states;
and the stages of ordinary beings and noble ones.
In the stages of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
and the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), the presence or absence of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) shifts and is not fixed.
Because they are as difficult to grasp as a fish, this name was established.
If one is endowed with the eye faculty,
among the twenty-two faculties,
how many does one possess and how many does one not possess?
The same applies even to the question regarding the faculty of full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Answer: If one possesses the eye faculty, one necessarily possesses five others; the remaining ones are not fixed.
The five that are determinate are the faculties of eye, body, life, mind, and equanimity.
The remaining seventeen faculties are indeterminate.
They may be accomplished or not accomplished;
that is to say, the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue,
and body are accomplished when they are possessed.
Those who lack [a faculty] do not possess it.
Regarding the female and male faculties, if one has only one form, one possesses that one accordingly;
if one has both forms, one possesses both.
If there is no simultaneous possession of the form,

or it is lost due to other conditions.
If the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) arises in the Subhakṛtsna [heaven] or below,

an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) born in the fourth dhyāna does not accomplish it.
If the faculty of suffering arises, it is possessed when one is born in the desire realm,
but it is not possessed when one is born in the form realm.
If the faculty of joy arises, it is possessed when one is born in the Ābhāsvara heaven or below.
If an ārya is born in the third or fourth dhyāna, they possess it;
if a pṛthagjana is born in the third or fourth dhyāna, they do not possess the faculty of sorrow (daurmanasyendriya). However, if one has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire, they possess it.
If one has already become free from the defilement of desire, these are not possessed.

If the faculties are wholesome, are those faculties caused by wholesome roots?
Conversely, if the faculties are caused by wholesome roots, are those faculties wholesome?
Answer: Those faculties that are wholesome—those faculties [are caused by wholesome roots].
The roots of goodness consist of the eight roots in their entirety and a portion of the six [other] roots;
these take the roots of goodness as their three causes.
That is to say, among those factors that are associated, co-existent, or of the same class,
there are cases where a faculty has roots as its cause and is wholesome,
yet that faculty itself is not wholesome; namely, the faculties that constitute the maturation produced by wholesome roots.
These consist of the eight faculties— vitality and the others— which are the maturation (vipāka) induced by wholesome roots,
as well as the mental, pleasure, joy, and equanimity faculties;
these take wholesome roots as their single cause.
That is to say, the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
In this context, non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion are called the wholesome roots of the cause.
If the various faculties are unwholesome, are those faculties caused by unwholesome roots?
If a faculty has an unwholesome root as its cause, is that faculty unwholesome?
Answer: All faculties that are unwholesome have unwholesome roots as their causes;
this refers to a portion of six faculties.
This takes the unwholesome roots as four causes:
namely, the associated cause, the co-existent cause, the homogeneous cause, and the universal cause.
There are thus unwholesome roots that serve as causes for other unwholesome roots.
Those faculties are not unwholesome;
that is to say, they are the life-faculty and so forth—eight faculties in total—which are the maturation (vipāka) induced by unwholesome roots.
These are the very faculties induced by unwholesome roots.
And the mental faculty and the faculty of suffering—
these have the unwholesome roots as their single cause,
namely, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Furthermore, the faculties associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm have unwholesome roots as their two causes;
namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*).
Among these, greed, hatred, and delusion are called the unwholesome roots of causes.
Are all faculties that are indeterminate caused by indeterminate roots?
And if a faculty is caused by an indeterminate root, [is it itself indeterminate]?
"Are those faculties indeterminate (avyākṛta)?
One should respond by formulating four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
This is what the Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīra say.
There are three roots of the indeterminate (avyākṛta-mūla):
namely, indeterminate craving (tṛṣṇā), wisdom (prajñā), and ignorance (avidyā).
Regarding indeterminate craving:
This refers to the five categories of craving belonging to the form and formless realms.
"Indeterminate wisdom" refers to wisdom that is obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Unobscured-neutral wisdom;
obscured-neutral wisdom— namely,
the view of a self-identity and the view of extreme attachment within the desire realm.
Furthermore, it includes the five classes of defiled wisdom in the form and formless realms,
as well as non-obscured neutral wisdom— namely,
the wisdom co-arising with the wisdom associated with the deportment, the arts and crafts, the maturation-born, and the transformation mind.
Regarding indeterminate ignorance (*avyākṛtāvidyā*):
it refers to the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme attachment (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm,
as well as the fivefold ignorance of the form and formless realms.
Among these, an indeterminate mind associated with greed is called "a mind possessing roots" because it possesses three indeterminate roots;
the remaining obscured-indeterminate minds are called "minds possessing roots" because they possess two indeterminate roots.
This refers to indeterminate wisdom (*avyākṛta-prajñā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and all unobscured-indeterminate minds (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*).
Because they possess one indeterminate root, they are called "minds with roots.
This refers to indeterminate wisdom.
To explain the meaning of the four propositions based on this:
there are faculties that are indeterminate,
yet those faculties are not indeterminate roots by way of being causes.
This refers to the eight faculties beginning with the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which lack a corresponding root.
These faculties are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) yet do not have indeterminate roots as their cause.
There are faculties that have indeterminate roots as their cause, yet those faculties themselves are not indeterminate.
This refers to the unwholesome roots,
which constitute a small portion of six [factors].
These roots are unwholesome, yet they take two neutral roots as their causes.
This refers to the homogeneous and universal [factors].
When there is a root that is indeterminate, that root is also caused by an indeterminate root;
that is to say, it refers to an indeterminate root that has an object-condition.
That is to say, five [roots] in part.
These indeterminate faculties (avyākṛta-indriya) also take indeterminate roots as their four causes:
namely, the associated (saṃprayukta), co-existent (sahabhū), similar-type (sabhāga), and universal (sarvatraga) causes.
There are faculties that are not indeterminate;
those faculties are also not causes of indeterminate roots,
namely, the wholesome roots.
That is, it consists of eight faculties in their entirety and six in part.
These faculties are not indeterminate (avyākṛta),
nor do they have indeterminate roots as their cause.
Are there any faculties that are not caused by wholesome roots,
nor caused by unwholesome roots,
nor caused by indeterminate roots?
Is it not the case that those faculties lack a cause?
Answer: Yes;
namely, the faculty that is without an object.
That is, the eight faculties beginning with life have matter and mind-dissociated formations as their causes;
these are not caused by faculties of the three natures, but rather take matter, mind, and mind-dissociated formations as their three causes.
That is to say: co-existent, homogeneous, and retributive.
The masters of the West (the Westerners) state that there are four indeterminate roots.
This refers to neutral craving, views, pride, and ignorance.
Neutral craving refers to the craving belonging to the five categories within the realms of form and formlessness.
Regarding indeterminate views:
these refer to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme attachment (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm,
as well as the five views in the form and formless realms.
"Indeterminate conceit" refers to the conceit belonging to the five categories of the form and formless realms.
"Indeterminate ignorance" refers to...
This refers to the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme attachment (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm,
as well as the ignorance of the five categories within the form and formless realms;
herein, it refers to the mind associated with neutral greed (*avyākṛta-rāga*).
It is called "a mind with roots" because it possesses two neutral roots, namely:
neutral craving and ignorance;
and a mind associated with neutral views and pride.
Furthermore, each is called "a mind with roots" because it possesses two neutral roots:
namely, those very [roots] and ignorance (*avidyā*).
This refers to all remaining obscured-neutral minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*).
Because it possesses one neutral root, it is called "a mind with roots," namely,
neutral ignorance. Based on that,
the meaning of the four propositions is explained as follows:
This passage should be stated as follows:
There are faculties that are indeterminate, yet those faculties are not indeterminate roots by way of being causes;
namely, the unobscured-indeterminate roots.
These faculties are indeterminate, yet they do not take an indeterminate faculty as their root-cause (*hetu*).
There are root-causes that are indeterminate faculties, yet those faculties are not themselves indeterminate;
namely, the unwholesome faculties (*akuśalamūla*).
This faculty is not indeterminate (avyākṛta), yet it takes two indeterminate roots as its causes—
namely, the homogeneous (sabhāga) and the universal (sarvatraga).
There are faculties that are indeterminate, and those faculties likewise take indeterminate roots as their causes.
This refers to the obscured-unspecified root (*nivṛtāvyākṛtamūla*).
This root, being unspecified, also functions as four types of causes for other unspecified phenomena:
namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
There are faculties that are not indeterminate, yet those faculties are also not caused by indeterminate roots.
That is to say, wholesome faculties are neither indeterminate nor are they caused by indeterminate roots.
Are there any faculties that are not caused by wholesome roots,
nor caused by unwholesome roots,
nor caused by indeterminate roots?
Is that faculty not without a cause?
Answer: It has one;
namely, the unobscured-neutral root (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-mūla*).
It takes form, mind, and formations dissociated from mind as its causes.
This faculty does not take faculties of the three natures as its causes;
rather, it takes form, mind, and formations dissociated from mind [as its causes].
Unobscured-neutral minds and mental factors act as four causes:
namely, the associated, co-existent, similar-type, and maturation causes.
This is a general statement; however, in terms of their specific bases, associated [factors] possess all four causes.
The non-associated faculties have only three causes, excluding the associated cause.
Question: For what reason do the masters of the West [hold this]?
Regarding the establishment of pride (*māna*) as an indeterminate root (*avyākṛta-mūla*):
the answer is that the meaning of "root" is the sense of having firm and powerful force;
because the force of pride is firm and powerful, it is established as a root.
This refers to the yogācāra.
That one falls away from hundreds of thousands of wholesome qualities is entirely due to the power of conceit (*māna*).
Question: For what reason do the masters of this land not establish it as a faculty (*indriya*)?
Answer: This teaching states that the meaning of "root" (*indriya*) is "that which is fundamental.
Because pride (*māna*) causes the mind to be uplifted and thus does not accord with what is fundamental, it is not established as a root.
Question: For what reason do the masters of this country establish non-obscured neutral wisdom (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-prajñā*) as a neutral root?
Answer: This teaching holds that the meaning of "basis" (*āśraya*) is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*).
Because wisdom that is non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) is preeminent as a basis, it is established as a faculty.
Question: For what reason do the masters of the West not establish it as a faculty?
The answer is: that which possesses the meaning of firm and strong power is the meaning of a faculty (*indriya*).
Because the power of non-obscured neutral wisdom (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-prajñā*) is weak and inferior, it is not established as a faculty.
Question: For what reason do both this [master] and that National Teacher (*rājaguru*) not establish doubt (*vicikitsā*) as a root of the indeterminate?
Answer: It is taught that the meaning of being firmly established is the meaning of a faculty (*indriya*).
Because doubt (*vicikitsā*) operates through two doors and is not firmly established, it is not established as a faculty.
Regarding this statement:
just as the wholesome and unwholesome roots each have three types,
the indeterminate roots should likewise be so.
Furthermore, just as unwholesome pride is not established as an unwholesome root,
so too should neutral pride be understood; therefore,
it is correct that there are only three neutral roots.

7. *Hetupaccaya-naya-vagga*, the seventh within the sixth *Indriya-khandha*: If various faculties (*indriya*) have the past as their cause (*hetu*), do those faculties have the past as their condition (*paccaya*)?
Having thus understood the meaning of these chapters and their exegesis,
one should proceed to analyze them in detail.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was composed to refute the views of those who deny the existence of the two time periods of the past and the future, as well as those who deny the existence of causes and conditions;
it was for these reasons, explained at length, that this treatise was written.
In this context, the treatise is composed based on two conditions:
namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Question: Why is it not composed based on the other two conditions?

If one asks why this is so, the answer is: the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) pertains to only a single moment, whereas the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) pervades all phenomena.
If one were to compose a treatise based on that [immediately preceding condition], the phrasing and meaning would not be elegant or comprehensive.
This treatise is composed based solely on two conditions.
Herein, a brief *vibhāṣā* (exegesis) should be provided regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*). Specifically:
Fourteen have an object;
eight have no object.
Among those with an object:
In the Chapter on the Association with the Five Groups of Consciousness: those [consciousnesses] associated with the past take the past as their object;
those associated with the present take the present as their object;
and those future consciousnesses that are subject to arising take the future as their object.
Dharmas that do not arise take the three periods of time as their objects.
As for those associated with the category of the mental consciousness aggregate, regardless of which period they reside in—
whether arisen or unarisen— they all take the three periods of time and unconditioned dharmas as their objects.
Furthermore, the faculties abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin take all five categories as their objects.

The faculties abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path take only their own category, as well as the unabandoned [faculties] and those abandoned through cultivation, as their objects.
The faculty of non-interruption (a-prahātavya-indriya) universally takes as its object the five categories as well as that which is not to be abandoned;
furthermore, it takes as its object both the faculties bound to the desire and form realms and those that are unbound,
as well as those bound to the three realms and those that are unbound.
The faculties associated with the formless realm take as their objects only those things associated with the form and formless realms, as well as those that are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).
The distinctions regarding their causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) should also be understood accordingly.
This is the meaning briefly explained herein.
The detailed explanation according to the text should be understood as it logically applies.
Among these, in all the first translations, the cause is abbreviated while the condition is expanded;
in all the subsequent translations, the condition is abbreviated while the cause is expanded.
In this context, the various types of patience (*kṣānti*) are designated by the name "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because they are the retinue of knowledge.
