Does he attain the past?
Having thus mastered these chapters and their respective meanings,
one should provide a detailed analysis.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is because one wishes to refute the doctrines of others and to clarify one's own position.
That is to say, there are some who hold the following view:
Since the past and future are non-existent, yet the present is described as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma,
this treatise is composed to refute that attachment and to demonstrate that the past and future exist, whereas the present is not unconditioned.
Why is this? If the past and the future did not exist,
there would be no sentient beings who possess those dharmas.
And it is not established [as a real entity], like a second head,
a third hand,
or a sixth aggregate.
Regarding the thirteenth base and the nineteenth element, etc.,
there is no one who possesses them or does not possess them.
However, because there is both the possession (*prāpti*) and non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the past and future, we know they truly exist.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain [the following].
One accomplishes that which is not a substantially existent phenomenon, as the Dārṣṭāntikas argue:
"All classes of sentient beings are not separate from those phenomena."
It is said that this lack of substantial entity is merely a conceptual designation established through dependence,
just as five fingers joined together are designated as a "fist."
Since that which is separated from [the fist] is not the fist, it does not exist substantially.
Likewise, sentient beings are said to "possess" those dharmas because they are not separated from them;
since that which is separated from them does not possess them, their substance does not exist substantially.
Question: For what reason was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is based upon the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra: "There is a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) who possesses the seven jewels."
If this accomplishment were substantially existent,
it would entail the accomplishment of other bodies and even that which is not classified as a sentient being;
that is to say, if that wheel-turning monarch were to accomplish the wheel-treasure and the jewel-treasure, then the Dharma would be destroyed.
They are both phenomena included within the category of sentient beings and phenomena not included within the category of sentient beings.
If one possesses the elephant-treasure or the horse-treasure, then it perishes.
They belong both to the realm of humans and to the realm of animals.
If one possesses the Woman-Jewel, then upon the dissolution of the body,
they may take either a male form or a female form.
If one were to possess the treasure of the minister of the treasury or the treasure of the general of the army, then karma would be destroyed;
moreover, he would be both king and minister.
To avoid such an error, possession is not truly existent.
This treatise is composed in order to refute that school’s position and to demonstrate that the essence of possession (*prāpti*) is substantially existent;
for if the essence of possession were not substantially existent, it would contradict the scriptural teachings.
As it is said, those in training (śaikṣa) accomplish eight factors,
while Arhats whose outflows are exhausted (kṣīṇāsrava) accomplish ten factors.
If these accomplishments were not real, [how could this be so?]
When that noble one’s mind with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*) is manifest,
or during the state of being without mind (*acittaka*), they do not possess the noble path of the three times.
How, then, can they be said to possess the eightfold or tenfold [path]?
This is because all its factors are untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
Furthermore, if that which is accomplished were not substantially real (*dravyasat*),
it would contradict other sūtras.
As stated in other sūtras,
this person (pudgala) accomplishes both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
If that which is accomplished were not substantially existent, [how could this be so?]
When one gives rise to wholesome dharmas, one should not be possessed of unwholesome dharmas;
when one gives rise to unwholesome dharmas, one should not be possessed of wholesome dharmas;
and when one gives rise to indeterminate dharmas, one should be possessed of neither.
Furthermore, if that which is accomplished were not substantially existent,
it would contradict other sūtras,
such as the statement: "If a bhikṣu accomplishes the seven sublime dharmas..."
Dwelling frequently in joy and happiness within this present life,
he should accomplish one sublime quality or another;
that is to say, any one of the seven sublime qualities should manifest before him.
At that time, that bhikṣu possesses only one [wisdom],
because all seven sublime dharmas have wisdom as their essential nature;
since even two instances of wisdom do not arise simultaneously, how much less could there be seven?
If other dharmas arise and manifest before one, then these seven sublime dharmas are not accomplished.
Furthermore, if their accomplishment were not substantially real,
it would contradict other sūtras.
Just as it is said that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is endowed with the ten powers,
one should instead say that he is endowed with only one power,
or that he is not endowed with them at all.
This means that whenever one power arises and manifests,
the other nine depart from the body and are no longer accomplished;
for all ten powers have wisdom as their essential nature.
Because non-dual wisdom arises simultaneously;
if other dharmas were to arise and manifest,
then the ten powers would not all be accomplished.
Furthermore, if that which is accomplished were not substantially existent,
there would be further faults: ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) should be called free from the defilements of the three realms,
and all Arhats should be called ordinary beings.
This refers to the fact that when various types of wholesome or non-obscured neutral minds arise,
as well as during states of mindlessness, no afflictions are present within the body.
Furthermore, they do not possess [the seeds] of the past or future;
how then could they not be said to be free from the defilements of the three realms?
This is because all Arhats give rise to outflow-tainted minds (*sāsrava-citta*) and exist at times when they are without mind (*acittaka*).
The noble path does not exist in the present, nor is it accomplished in the past or future.
Is it not the case that an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) lacks noble qualities? If this were so, it would lead to a great error.
Therefore, it is established that [the person] exists as a real entity.
Question: If this is established as a real entity, how do you explain the sūtra cited by the Dārṣṭāntikas?
The answer is: that [text] explains mastery (*vaśitā*) as "attainment" (*siddhi*).
That is to say, a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) exercises mastery over his own seven treasures;
this is a figurative designation for attainment, not like the actual attainment of the eightfold path of training (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*) and so forth.
Alternatively, there are those who maintain that although possession (*prāpti*) has a real substantial entity,
it does not [itself] possess [possession].
There is no substantial entity.
To refute that attachment and to demonstrate that even what is non-existent possesses a substantial entity, this treatise was composed.
If that which is non-existent lacked a substantial entity, [it would not be so].
Accomplishment also lacks substantial reality,
for accomplishment is spoken of in view of non-accomplishment,
just as one speaks of "day" in view of night.
Observing darkness and establishing light,
both are substantially existent entities. This—
It is also like this.
Furthermore, non-accomplishment is the proximate antidote to accomplishment;
they are mutually contradictory.
For example, regarding greed and non-greed, hatred and non-hatred, delusion and non-delusion, concentration and distraction, and so forth:
if these lack substantial reality, what contradiction could there be such that one would constitute the "near antidote" (pratipakṣa) to the other?
Furthermore, if they lacked substance, [the categories of] accomplishment would not be established.
One should not posit that the abandonment of all afflictions occurs through the arising of the Noble Path.

Rather, it is like cutting an object with a knife or grinding an object with a stone: one merely abandons the acquisition of bondage (*bandhana-prāpti*) and realizes the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*), such that the afflictions no longer manifest; this is what is called "abandonment."
Thus, one should know that there exists an actual nature of non-accomplishment (*asiddhatā*).
Alternatively, this treatise was composed in order to sever the web of doubt;
namely, as stated in the *Saṃyukta-skandha*: "Regarding past phenomena, their arising, aging, duration, and impermanence should be said to be past."
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Let there be no doubt that,
just as characteristics and the phenomena themselves do not belong to different time periods.
It is not different from the moment.
The same applies to the acquisition (prāpti) and the dharma:
just as the acquisition and the dharma may belong to different time periods or different moments.
The same applies to characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and phenomena (*dharma*). In order to resolve this doubt,
it is clarified that characteristics and phenomena are definitely not of different time periods (*adhvan*).
It is not different from the moment itself,
yet it can be both identical to and distinct from the dharma;
that is to say, because each and every dharma of the three periods of time possesses its own acquisition (prāpti) belonging to each of those three periods.

Question: Why is it that the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*), as well as their temporal sequence and momentariness, are determined to be without difference, whereas the attainment (*prāpti*) and the attained (*prāpya*) may be either the same or different?
Answer: Regarding the characteristics and the characterized...
They must necessarily share the same result;
they proceed together in mutual association without separation,
having no before or after.
Regarding phenomena that coexist in the same collection, one cannot abandon them;
the acquisition and that which is acquired do not share a single fruit;
they are neither necessarily concomitant nor are they inseparable.
There may be cases where [a factor] exists before or after [another],
and is capable of being discarded from a collection of dharmas that are co-existent,
just as the bark of various trees is by nature separated from the tree itself.

Therefore, in order to refute the positions of others, to manifest one's own doctrine, and to enable those who are doubtful to attain certainty, one must refute the views of others while manifesting one's own and resolving the doubts of others.
Even if one were not to refute others, it would still be necessary to manifest one's own view and resolve the doubts of those who are uncertain.
However, within the context of the meanings associated with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*),
this treatise is composed in order to clarify what is to be explained:
"Is that which acquires past phenomena itself past?"
What is intended to be revealed here by the word "attainment" (*prāpti*)?
It refers to the achievement of mastery.
How is this known to be so?
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*:
"What is attainment (*prāpti*)? It means acquisition (*lābha*) and accomplishment (*samanvāgama*). What is acquisition?"
This refers to the attainment of accomplishment.
What is accomplishment?
It is the acquisition.
Although there are differences in the terminology used for attaining accomplishment, their meaning is no different.
There are eleven types of dharmas thus attained:
four belong to the desire realm.
That is to say: wholesome,
unwholesome, obscured-neutral,
and unobscured-neutral.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are three [types of karma],
excluding the unwholesome (akuśala).
It is the same in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
And as for the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas:
the wholesome, unwholesome, and non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) [dharmas] of the desire realm each possess all five aggregates (*skandha*);
the obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) [dharmas] possess only four aggregates.
The three [realms] of the form realm each possess the five aggregates;
the three [realms] of the formless realm each possess only four aggregates;
and untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) possess all five aggregates.
And [it includes] cessation through deliberation and cessation not through deliberation;
excluding space as an unconditioned phenomenon, because it is not a dharma that can be acquired.
Among these, there are the wholesome and unwholesome forms of the desire realm.
If it occurs in the past, there is acquisition in all three time periods;
if it occurs in the future, there is acquisition only in the future;
if it occurs in the present, there is acquisition in two time periods.
That is to say: the four aggregates of the future and present that are wholesome, unwholesome, or obscured-neutral;
and among those that are unobscured-neutral—
The four aggregates co-arising with the fruition-attaining mind (abhiññā-citta) constitute its acquisition;
this is a mixture of worlds and a mixture of moments,
meaning it exists in the past, future, and present.
Because they all possess the attainment of the three times:
the entire aggregate of form that is unobscured-neutral and born of maturation, as well as the four aggregates [born of maturation],
and the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*).
Regarding the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*):
for the most part, its acquisition consists of four aggregates; it is not intermingled with worldly states and is not intermingled moment by moment.
If it belongs to the past, its acquisition is also past.
If it is acquired in the future, it is also future;
if it is acquired in the present, it is also present.
It consists of the four aggregates within the sphere of deportment (*airyāpathika*).
Those who are well-trained include, for example, the Buddha Aśvajit,
as well as other sentient beings who are well-trained,
and those who are well-trained in the four aggregates of the fields of craftsmanship.
Just as with the Buddha’s sublime deeds and those well-practiced by other sentient beings,
their attainments are likewise all mundane and momentary.
This means that for each of the three time periods, there are acquisitions (prāpti) belonging to each of those three time periods.
Therefore, within the wholesome five aggregates of the form realm,
as well as among the obscured-unspecified and unobscured-unspecified [phenomena], [this applies].
The four aggregates co-arising with the fruition-mind possess acquisitions that are both temporal and momentary; that is to say,
because they possess acquisitions belonging to each of the three time periods within any given period, they are not fixed.
The wholesome aggregate of form is like the wholesome and unwholesome aggregates of form in the desire realm;
it includes all obscured-unspecified and unobscured-unspecified aggregates of form,
as well as the four aggregates born of deportment and born of maturation.
That world is unmixed with other worlds and unmixed from moment to moment;
wherever that world exists,
there is only that world which is attained.
Therefore, the wholesome [dharmas] and the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) four aggregates of the formless realm possess acquisitions that are both temporal and momentary.
This is because, existing within the three time periods, they each possess acquisitions belonging to all three time periods.
The four aggregates born of maturation obtain [their acquisition] without being mixed with other worlds and without being mixed even for a single moment;
for wherever they exist in a particular world,
they obtain only the acquisition belonging to that very world.
The acquisition of the untainted five aggregates is both temporal and momentary; that is to say,
because for each [aggregate] belonging to the three time periods, there is an acquisition belonging to all three time periods.
This is the general explanation.
To explain it specifically:
it refers to the various previously unattained untainted (anāsrava) five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
Furthermore, those [attainments] consisting of cultivation that have been previously unobtained,
as well as those consisting of hearing and reflection that have been previously unobtained,
are obtained for the first time by them.
If that dharma is in the future, it has only a future acquisition (prāpti).
If it is in the present, it has both future and present acquisitions.
If it is in the past, it has acquisitions belonging to all three time periods.

Although the dharmas of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are not subsumed within the three time periods, their acquisitions (*prāpti*) do exist across the three time periods.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of acquisition for cessation through deliberation:
namely, those that are contaminated (*sāsrava*) and those that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of contaminated phenomena arises by means of becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm up to those of the sphere of nothingness;
it belongs to the category of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*).
If one has not yet abandoned the defilements, the acquisition (prāpti) of that cessation exists only in the past and future;
if one has already abandoned the defilements,
there is acquisition of that cessation across all three time periods.
The acquisition of untainted analytical cessation (*anāsrava-pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) arises from being freed from the defilements abandoned through seeing and meditation within the three realms.
This refers to the analytical cessation of those phenomena of the desire realm that are to be abandoned by seeing the truth of suffering, which belongs to the category of the noble path.
If the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) has not yet manifested, its cessation possesses only future acquisition (*prāpti*).
If it has manifested, its cessation possesses both future and present acquisition.
If it has already been ceased,
that cessation possesses acquisitions (prāpti) across the three time periods.
This applies likewise up to the ninth category of dharmas at the peak of existence (bhavāgra), which is their analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
If the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) has not yet manifested, one should understand this accordingly.
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Its initial acquisition occurs [at that time].
If it is in the future, its cessation has only future acquisition (*prāpti*).
If it is in the present, its cessation has both future and present acquisition. If it is in the past, its cessation has acquisition belonging to all three time periods.
Among these, the first question and answer reveals that each dharma of the three times has acquisitions (prāpti) belonging to the three times;
the second question and answer reveals that each acquisition of the three times acquires dharmas of the three times as well as those that transcend the times (lokottara).
This is called the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
Regarding those who have acquired past dharmas, do they [themselves] exist in the past?
Answer: They may exist in the past.
Whether future or present,
one attains past dharmas; as for those attained in the past:
This refers to all the aggregates of the three realms in the past,
as well as the uncontaminated aggregates and their respective past acquisitions;
it is the acquisition of past dharmas.
Regarding those obtained in the future:
this refers to the past wholesome and unwholesome five aggregates of the desire realm,
as well as the four obscured-neutral aggregates.
Within the unobscured-neutral [category], there are the factors co-arising with the mind that realizes the fruit,
as well as one portion of the four aggregates belonging to the deportment and the arts and crafts;
and the five aggregates of the wholesome [states] in the form realm.
Within the obscured-unspecified and unobscured-unspecified [categories],
there are the four aggregates co-arising with the mind that produces supernormal powers;
and within the formless realm, there are the four aggregates of the wholesome and the obscured-unspecified.
Regarding the future acquisitions (prāpti) of those untainted five aggregates,
as well as the acquisition of past dharmas and the acquisition of present [dharmas]:
This refers to the past wholesome and unwholesome five aggregates of the desire realm,
and so forth, as explained at length;
it is like their present acquisition in the future.
If one attains that which is past, does one attain past dharmas?
Answer: Those dharmas may be either past or future.
Either it is present,
or it is an unconditioned attainment of the past.
As for the attainment of past dharmas:
This refers to past acquisition (*prāpti*).
It is the acquisition of all the aggregates (*skandha*) of the three realms belonging to the past,
as well as the untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregates.
It is acquired in the past.
Regarding the acquisition of future dharmas,
this refers to their acquisition in the past.
One acquires the four aggregates of the future desire realm that are wholesome, unwholesome, or obscured-neutral;
those among the unobscured-neutral that arise simultaneously with the mind associated with the fruition of action;
and a portion of the four aggregates belonging to the deportment and the arts and crafts.
Within the wholesome five aggregates of the form realm,
as well as among the obscured-unspecified and unobscured-unspecified [states],...
The four aggregates co-arising with the fruition-mind;
the four aggregates of the wholesome and the obscured-unspecified in the formless realm;
and the five untainted aggregates.
It is acquired in the past.
Regarding the acquisition of present dharmas,
this refers to acquisition in the past.
One acquires the wholesome [dharmas] of the present desire realm,
and so forth, as explained at length regarding the acquisition of those of the future.
Regarding the acquisition of those of the past:
The attainment of unconditioned dharmas refers to past attainment;
it is the attainment of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding those acquisitions of future dharmas:
do those acquisitions themselves belong to the future?
Answer: Those acquisitions may be future.
Whether in the past or the present,
one attains future dharmas.
Those to be acquired in the future refer to all the aggregates (skandhas) of the three realms in the future,
as well as the untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha).
Whatever acquisitions he possesses in the future,
they acquire future dharmas;
as for those acquisitions in the past:
This refers to the four aggregates of the future desire realm that are wholesome, unwholesome, or obscured-neutral;
and among those that are unobscured-neutral,
it includes the category co-arising with the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-citta*).
And [this includes] one portion of the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*), consisting of four aggregates;
the wholesome five aggregates of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
and among the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) [states], [those that are associated with the mind].
The four aggregates co-arising with the fruition-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*);
the four aggregates of the formless realm that are wholesome or obscured-unspecified;
and the past acquisitions (*prāpti*) of those untainted five aggregates.
One attains future dharmas. Regarding those attained in the present,
this refers to the wholesome [dharmas] of the desire realm in the future.
...and so on, as explained at length regarding the past.
Regarding those acquisitions (prāpti) that exist in the present:
if one acquires a future dharma, does one acquire it by means of a future acquisition?
Answer: Those dharmas are either future,
or past, or present.
Or it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It is acquired in the future;
that is, one who acquires a dharma of the future.
This refers to future acquisition (*anāgata-prāpti*).
It is the future acquisition of all the aggregates (*skandha*) of the three realms as well as the untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) of the future.
Regarding the acquisition of past dharmas:
this refers to acquisition in the future.

It consists of acquiring the five aggregates of the wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas] of the desire realm, as well as the four aggregates of the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) [dharmas] of the past.
Among the non-obscured neutral states,
there are the categories co-arising with the mind of supernormal power,
as well as one portion of the four aggregates belonging to the deportment and the arts and crafts.
The five aggregates of the wholesome in the realm of form;
and, among the obscured-unspecified and unobscured-unspecified [states],
the four aggregates co-arising with the mind that produces supernormal powers.
The four aggregates of the wholesome and obscured-unspecified states of the formless realm,
as well as the five untainted aggregates,
are acquired in the future.
To "attain present dharmas" means to attain them in the future;
it refers to attaining the wholesome [dharmas] of the desire realm in the present.
...up to as extensively explained regarding the attainment of the past;
so too for the attainment of the future,
and the attainment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This refers to acquisitions in the future.
Regarding the acquisition of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): are those acquisitions of present dharmas themselves present?
Answer: That attainment may be present,
past, or future.
One attains present phenomena.
Regarding "attaining the present," this refers to all the aggregates (*skandha*) of the three realms existing in the present.
And regarding the untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*),
there is their present acquisition (*prāpti*). This acquisition of present dharmas constitutes the past acquisition.
This refers to the four aggregates of the present desire realm that are wholesome, unwholesome, or obscured-neutral;
and among those that are unobscured-neutral,
it includes the category co-arising with the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-citta*).
And [this includes] one portion of the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*), consisting of four aggregates;
the wholesome five aggregates of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
and among the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) [states], [the five aggregates].
The four aggregates co-arising with the result-of-communication mind; the four aggregates of the formless realm that are wholesome or obscured-unspecified;
the five untainted aggregates;
and their respective past acquisitions.
One attains present dharmas. Regarding those attained in the future:
this refers to the five aggregates of the wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas] of the desire realm in the present.
The four aggregates that are obscured-unspecified;
the rest are as explained regarding past acquisition.
As for their future acquisition:
If one attains [the acquisition] in the present, does one attain those dharmas in the present?
Answer: Those dharmas may be present.
Whether past, future, or unconditioned,
they are acquired in the present.
As for the acquisition of present dharmas:
This refers to present acquisition:
it is the present acquisition of all the aggregates (skandhas) of the three realms that are presently occurring,
as well as the present acquisition of the untainted (anāsrava) aggregates.
Regarding those who attain past dharmas:
this refers to attainment in the present.
It consists of attaining the five aggregates of wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas] of the desire realm, as well as the four aggregates of obscured-neutral [dharmas], which belong to the past.
Within the unobscured-neutral [states],
there are the categories co-arising with the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-citta*),
as well as a portion of the four aggregates belonging to the deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*).
The five aggregates of the wholesome in the form realm,
as well as those that are obscured-unspecified and unobscured-unspecified therein.
The four aggregates co-arising with the mind of fruition (nirmāṇa-citta),
the four aggregates of the wholesome and obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) of the formless realm,
and the five untainted (anāsrava) aggregates are acquired in the present.
Regarding "attaining future dharmas," this refers to attainment in the present.
It means attaining the four aggregates— wholesome, unwholesome, and obscured-neutral— of the future desire realm.
The rest is as explained regarding the attainment of the past.
Regarding the attainment of the present and the attainment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): [the same applies].
This refers to the present acquisition (*prāpti*) of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Are all acquisitions of wholesome phenomena themselves wholesome?
Answer: Yes; for the acquisition of a wholesome phenomenon is necessarily wholesome.
If one attains the wholesome, does one attain wholesome dharmas?
Answer: It is so.
This is because the attainment of all wholesome [dharmas] consists solely in the attainment of wholesome dharmas.
The same applies to the questions and answers regarding unwholesome and neutral states,
because the nature of that which attains and that which is attained must necessarily be identical.
This refers to all acquisitions (*prāpti*) of dharmas belonging to the desire realm.
Does that obtainment belong to the desire realm?
Answer: It does.
This is because an obtainment of a phenomenon belonging to the desire realm must necessarily itself belong to the desire realm.
If one attains [the acquisition] of the desire realm, does one attain dharmas of the desire realm?
Answer: Those dharmas are either of the desire realm or unconditioned (unbound).
The realm of desire refers to the five aggregates of the realm of desire.
Those that are unconditioned refer to all forms of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Because a person born in the desire realm attains the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of both factors bound to the three realms and those unbound to them;
all such attainments belong to the desire realm.
Regarding all those who have attained dharmas of the form realm (rūpadhātu), have they attained the form realm?
Answer: It is so.
Because that which is acquired through a dharma of the form realm must necessarily belong to the form realm.
Even if it is acquired in the form realm,
does that acquisition itself belong to a dharma of the form realm?
Answer: Those dharmas are either of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Those of the form realm refer to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of the form realm.
The unconditioned refers to both cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding cessation through deliberation:
This refers to the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the five aggregates belonging to the desire realm and the lower three dhyānas;
the acquisitions (prāpti) of these, when obtained via the mundane path (laukika-mārga), are all bound to the form realm (rūpāvacara).

Regarding the statement that "the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) pertaining to lower stages are all subsumed under the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher stages, whereas those of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are not":

this refers to a person (*pudgala*) born in the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) who attains the non-analytical cessation of phenomena associated with the three realms as well as those unconditioned by them.
Since all those acquisitions (prāpti) are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
when one acquires dharmas of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
are those acquisitions themselves of the formless realm?
Answer: It is so.
This is because all acquisitions (*prāpti*) of dharmas belonging to the formless realm are themselves bound to the formless realm.
Now, if there is an acquisition belonging to the formless realm, does that acquisition acquire a dharma of the formless realm?
The answer is: those dharmas are either of the formless realm or unconditioned.
Those of the formless realm refer to the four aggregates of the formless realm.
The unconditioned refers to both cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
As for cessation through deliberation:
This refers to the five aggregates bound to the stage of the fourth dhyāna,
as well as the four aggregates and the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) bound to the three lower formless stages;
the subsequent acquisitions (prāpti) via the conventional path (saṃvṛti-mārga) are all bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Therefore, as stated previously,
non-analytical cessation refers to a person (pudgala) born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
One attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) with respect to dharmas bound to the three realms as well as those unbound [to them].
Since all such acquisitions (*prāpti*) are themselves bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
are the acquisitions of dharmas that are "in training" (*śaikṣa*) themselves "in training"?
Answer: It is so.
Because that which is acquired through the dharmas of training (śaikṣa) is necessarily itself a dharma of training.
Now, if one acquires something through the dharmas of training, does one thereby acquire those dharmas of training?
Answer: Those dharmas are either *śaikṣa* (in training) or neither *śaikṣa* nor *aśaikṣa* (beyond training). "In training" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of one in training;
"neither in training nor beyond training" refers to [the same].
That is to say, regarding the acquisitions (prāpti) of those in training (śaikṣa) and the analytical cessations (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) they have attained:
are the acquisitions of those dharmas belonging to those beyond training (aśaikṣa) themselves [of the] beyond-training type?
Answer: It is so.
Because the acquisition (prāpti) of dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is necessarily itself a dharma of one beyond training.
However, if there is an acquisition that is a dharma of one beyond training, does it necessarily acquire a dharma of one beyond training?
Answer: Those dharmas are either beyond training (aśaikṣa) or neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
As for those that are beyond training:
The five aggregates of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
That which is neither of training nor beyond training refers to the analytical cessations (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) attained by those beyond training.
Regarding those acquisitions of factors that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner:
are those acquisitions themselves neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: Those acquisitions may be either neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Those that are either in training (*śaikṣa*) or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
as well as those that are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*),
refer to the five contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*) and four aggregates [respectively].
One attains all non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
one attains those analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) that belong to the category of the mundane path;
and one attains the state of a learner (*śaikṣa*).
This refers to the various analytical cessations (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) attained by those training in the path (śaikṣa) and by those who have become non-trainees (aśaikṣa).
That is to say, it refers to the various analytical cessations (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained through the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-mārga); even if they are obtained,
they are neither of the category of learning (śaikṣa) nor of the category of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
Does he obtain dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: Yes. This is because he obtains them by means of acquisitions that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Because one acquires only those dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Regarding all acquisitions of dharmas abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*),
are those acquisitions themselves abandoned by vision?
Answer: It is so.
This is because the acquisition (*prāpti*) of dharmas abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) must itself be abandoned by insight.
Now, if an acquisition is abandoned by insight, does that acquisition acquire a dharma abandoned by insight?
Answer: It is so.
Because that which is acquired through abandonment by seeing (darśana-heya) is acquired only as dharmas abandoned by seeing.
Are those acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all dharmas that are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) themselves to be abandoned by cultivation?
Answer: It is so.
Because the acquisition of a dharma abandoned by cultivation must itself be abandoned by cultivation.
Suppose an acquisition were abandoned by cultivation;
would that acquisition acquire a dharma abandoned by cultivation?
Answer: Those dharmas are either abandoned through cultivation or not abandoned at all.
As for those abandoned through cultivation:
This refers to the five aggregates abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
"Not abandoned" refers to all non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as well as analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) obtained by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*).
Regarding those acquisitions that are not subject to abandonment, are those acquisitions themselves not subject to abandonment?
Answer: Those acquisitions may be either not subject to abandonment or subject to abandonment.
Some are abandoned by cultivation;
those that are not abandoned refer to the acquisition of the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*).
Furthermore, there are the acquisitions of analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and the untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) refer to all acquisitions of non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, regarding the various analytical cessations (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained through the mundane path (laukika-mārga):
if their possession (prāpti) is not abandoned,
does that possession itself pertain to dharmas that are not abandoned?
The answer is: it is so.
This is because one who has attained non-interruption (anantarya-prāpti) attains only dharmas that are uninterrupted.
Having thus explained the characteristics of various attainments according to the original text.
One should further clarify various types of non-acquisition (aprāpti) according to their meaning:
if a phenomenon has acquisition,
that phenomenon has non-acquisition.
If a dharma is not attained,
that dharma is not non-attained;
the same applies to the explanations of acquisition, accomplishment, non-acquisition, and non-accomplishment.
Consequently, for all phenomena comprised within the category of sentient beings,
as well as for analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
there is acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), as well as attainment (*lābha*) and non-attainment (*alābha*).
There are those that are accomplished and those that are not accomplished:
all phenomena not included among sentient beings,
as well as space and the unconditioned.
Thus, there is neither acquisition nor non-acquisition and so forth for these;
however, with respect to phenomena within one's own continuum,
there is acquisition.
There are non-acquisitions and so forth regarding phenomena within the mental continuums of others; however,
there are no acquisitions or non-acquisitions with respect to those very phenomena in one's own continuum.
Among these, past and future dharmas each have non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) belonging to all three time periods;
present dharmas have non-acquisition only in the two time periods of the past and the future.
Because a dharma that is capable of being accomplished will necessarily be accomplished in the present life;
because "attainment" (*prāpti*) and "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*) are mutually exclusive and do not arise simultaneously;
and because non-attainment pertains to wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas.
All are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of dharmas belonging to the three realms pertains to all three realms.
This includes the non-acquisition of dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
All non-learner and non-non-learner [dharmas] are exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
The non-acquisition (aprāpti) of dharmas abandoned by seeing, abandoned by cultivation, and not abandoned,
is exclusively abandoned by cultivation.
This is called the brief *vibhāṣā* on non-acquisition (*aprāpti*). Regarding those who do not acquire past dharmas:
is their non-acquisition itself past?
Answer: That non-acquisition may be past.
Whether in the future or the present,
one does not obtain past dharmas.
Non-acquisition of the past refers to past wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified,
and unobscured-unspecified [dharmas].
Regarding the five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha),
there is a non-acquisition (aprāpti) of them in the past;
herein, one who has severed the roots of goodness (samucchinna-kuśalamūla).
The five aggregates that are wholesome and free from the defilement of desire;
the five aggregates that are unwholesome;
and the five aggregates that are obscured-unspecified for Arhats.
For the most part, all sentient beings possess the five aggregates that are non-obscured and indeterminate;
by means of these non-obscured and indeterminate phenomena,
they have already passed through moments and have not yet reached [future] moments.
Because they are for the most part unaccomplished,
the untainted five aggregates of ordinary beings are called "dharmas not obtained by way of their general characteristics."
Regarding "not obtaining past dharmas and not obtaining future ones":
this refers to the five aggregates—whether wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, unobscured-neutral, or untainted—that are past.
His non-acquisition (aprāpti) of all future [dharmas] is as explained previously.
Regarding the non-acquisition of past dharmas in the present: it is as follows.
It refers to the past wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unneutral, and unobscured-unneutral [factors],
as well as the untainted five aggregates;
it is the present non-acquisition (aprāpti) of all those.
It should be explained as before according to what is appropriate.
Suppose one does not possess the past; does that person not possess past dharmas?
Answer: Those dharmas may be past.
Either future, or present,
or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Past non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
Regarding "not acquiring past dharmas":
this refers to the fact that past non-acquisition does not acquire past wholesome [dharmas] up to the untainted (*anāsrava*) five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
As explained previously:
regarding the statement that past non-acquisition does not acquire future dharmas,
this means that past non-acquisition does not acquire future wholesome [dharmas].
Up to the untainted five aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*),
it is explained as before.
Regarding the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of past [dharmas] which does not acquire present dharmas:
This refers to the past non-acquisition (aprāpti) of the present wholesome aggregates up to the untainted (anāsrava) five aggregates, as explained previously.
Regarding the past non-acquisition of unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma): [it is as follows].

This refers to past non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) and the non-acquisition of the dharmas of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
specifically regarding cessation through deliberation for one who is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*).
Regarding all sentient beings and their non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*),
as well as those future dharmas that they have not yet attained:
do they lack the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of those future [dharmas]?
The answer is: that non-acquisition is either future or past.
Or, one may possess a present [non-acquisition] but not obtain a future dharma;
this refers to the non-acquisition of a future [dharma].
This refers to the future five aggregates, from the wholesome up to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Their respective non-acquisitions (*aprāpti*) in the future are as explained previously.
Regarding "not obtaining future dharmas through past non-acquisition":
this refers to all past non-acquisitions of the future wholesome aggregates up to the untainted (anāsrava) five aggregates.
As explained previously:
"The non-acquisition of future dharmas in the present" refers to the five aggregates of the future,
from the wholesome up to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding their present non-acquisition (*aprāpti*),
it is as explained previously;
even if the non-acquisition is future, it is likewise.
Does he not obtain future dharmas?
Answer: Those dharmas are either future or past.
It is either present,
or unconditioned; the non-acquisition of the future is likewise [unconditioned].
"Not obtaining future dharmas" refers to the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the future;
it means not obtaining future wholesome [dharmas].
Up to the untainted five aggregates,
as explained previously;
this refers to future non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
"Not obtaining past dharmas" refers to the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the future; that is,
not obtaining the past wholesome aggregates up to the untainted (*anāsrava*) five aggregates.
As explained previously:
future non-acquisition does not acquire present dharmas.
This refers to non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the future;
it is the non-acquisition of the present, from the wholesome up to the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*),
as explained previously.
Non-acquisition of the future;
that which does not acquire unconditioned dharmas refers to non-acquisition of the future.
There is no non-acquisition of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) or cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), as explained previously.
There is also no non-acquisition of present dharmas.
Is that non-acquisition not present?
Answer: That non-acquisition is either past or future.
Because it would contradict the nature of the present,
one cannot obtain a present dharma.
As for the non-acquisition of the past:
This refers to the five aggregates, from the wholesome up to the untainted,
in the present. Their past non-acquisition is as explained previously.
Regarding the non-attainment of present phenomena:
as for the non-attainment of future [phenomena],
this refers to the five aggregates, from the wholesome up to the untainted, when they are present.
His non-acquisition of all future [phenomena] is as explained previously;
even if the non-acquisition were present.
Does he not obtain present dharmas?
Answer: Those dharmas are either past or future.
Or it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
because it is incompatible with the present;
it is not an acquisition (*prāpti*) of the present.
"Non-acquisition of past dharmas" refers to the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the present;
it is the non-acquisition of past wholesome [dharmas] up to the untainted (*anāsrava*) five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
As appropriate;
as explained previously,
it is the non-acquisition of the present.
"Not obtaining future dharmas" refers to present non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
It means not obtaining the future wholesome aggregates up to the untainted (*anāsrava*) five aggregates.
As explained previously:
regarding the non-acquisition of unconditioned dharmas in the present,
this refers to non-acquisition in the present.
There is no non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) nor analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha),
as explained previously.
This refers to the non-acquisition of all wholesome dharmas (kuśala-dharma).
Is that non-acquisition not wholesome?
Answer: No. Because that non-acquisition is indeterminate (avyākṛta) and does not possess the nature of wholesomeness.
If non-acquisition is indeterminate, does that person not acquire wholesome dharmas?
Answer: Those dharmas may be either wholesome or unwholesome.
Or it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
because one does not acquire an indeterminate non-possession (*aprāpti*) of dharmas belonging to the three natures.
This applies to all cases where one does not acquire unwholesome (*akuśala*) dharmas.
Is it not the case that he has acquired non-virtue? Answer:
No, because that non-acquisition is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and not of a non-virtuous nature.
If it is the case that non-acquisition is indeterminate, must that [non-acquisition] not also be non-virtuous?
Answer: That dharma.
It may be wholesome, unwholesome,
or indeterminate;
for non-acquisition (aprāpti) is indeterminate because it does not acquire dharmas of the three natures.
Regarding those non-acquisitions of indeterminate dharmas, are they themselves indeterminate?
Answer: It is so.
Since all non-possessions (*aprāpti*) are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), if a non-possession is indeterminate, does that person not possess indeterminate dharmas? Answer: They do.
It may be wholesome, unwholesome,
or indeterminate.
Because non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it does not acquire dharmas of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).
Regarding those who do not acquire dharmas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):
is their non-acquisition itself of the desire realm?
Answer: That non-acquisition belongs either to the desire realm,
or the form realm,
or the formless realm.
One does not obtain the dharmas of the desire realm.
Non-attainment (aprāpti) of the desire realm refers to being born in the desire realm.
The non-acquisition (aprāpti) of the aggregates of the desire realm does not acquire dharmas of the desire realm.
As for the non-acquisition of the form realm:
This refers to the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the aggregates of the desire realm by one born in the form realm.
Regarding the non-acquisition of dharmas of the desire realm by one not in the form realm,
this refers to one born in the formless realm.
Regarding the non-acquisition (aprāpti) of the aggregates of the desire realm:
even if there is non-acquisition of the desire realm,
does that person not acquire the dharmas of the desire realm?
Answer: Those dharmas belong either to the desire realm,
or the form realm, or the formless realm,
or they are unconditioned (unbound).
Regarding non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) in the desire realm:
"not acquiring the dharmas of the desire realm" refers to being born in the desire realm without having acquired the various aggregates (*skandha*) of the desire realm.
Regarding non-acquisition (aprāpti) in the desire realm:
"not acquiring dharmas of the form realm" refers to one born in the desire realm who does not acquire the aggregates (skandha) of the form realm.
Regarding non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) in the desire realm:
"not obtaining the dharmas of the formless realm" refers to one born in the desire realm who has not obtained the aggregates (*skandha*) of the formless realm.
Regarding non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
"not obtaining what is not bound" refers to being born in the desire realm and not obtaining the untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregates.
And regarding analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*):
if one has not attained any phenomena (*dharma*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), does that constitute a non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the form realm?
Answer: It constitutes that non-possession.
Either the desire realm,
or the form realm,
or the formless realm.
Regarding the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of dharmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) by one who is not yet acquired [to them]:
this refers to the non-acquisition of the various aggregates (*skandha*) of the form realm by one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The non-acquisition of dharmas pertaining to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Non-acquisition pertaining to the form realm refers to the non-acquisition of the various aggregates (*skandha*) of the form realm for one born in the form realm.
Regarding the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of dharmas belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*):
this refers to the non-acquisition of the aggregates (*skandha*) of the form realm by one born in the formless realm.
If one does not acquire the form realm, does one not acquire the dharmas of the form realm?
Answer: Those dharmas may belong to the desire realm.
Either the form realm,
or the formless realm,
or that which is unconditioned.
Regarding the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of dharmas of the desire realm by one in the form realm:
this refers to the non-acquisition of the various aggregates (*skandha*) of the desire realm by one born in the form realm,
which constitutes the non-acquisition of the form realm.
"Not obtaining the dharmas of the form realm" means that one born in the form realm does not obtain the various aggregates of the form realm;
this refers to the non-acquisition (aprāpti) of the form realm.
"Not obtaining the dharmas of the formless realm" means that one born in the form realm does not obtain the aggregates of the formless realm;
this is the non-acquisition (aprāpti) of the form realm.
That which must necessarily be bound refers to those born in the form realm who do not possess the untainted aggregates, nor analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
nor non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding those who do not acquire dharmas of the formless realm, do they not possess non-acquisition (aprāpti) of the formless realm?
Answer: Their non-acquisition may belong to the desire realm.
Whether in the realm of form or the formless realm,
one does not apprehend the dharmas of the formless realm.
Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) pertaining to the desire realm refers to the non-acquisition of the aggregates (*skandha*) of the formless realm by one born in the desire realm;
it is the non-attainment of the dharmas of the formless realm.
Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the form realm refers to the non-acquisition of the aggregates of the form and formless realms when born in the form realm;
it is the failure to acquire the phenomena of the formless realm.
Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the formless realm refers to the non-acquisition of the aggregates of the formless realm for one born in the formless realm;
even if one has not acquired the formless realm [itself].
Does he not obtain the dharmas of the formless realm?
Answer: Those dharmas are either of the desire realm or of the form realm.
Either belonging to the formless realm or being unconditioned;
this refers to the non-possession (aprāpti) of the formless realm.
"Not obtaining the dharmas of the desire realm" means that one born in the formless realm does not obtain the aggregates (skandhas) of the desire realm.
Non-acquisition in the formless realm refers to one who does not acquire dharmas of the form realm; that is,
one who is born in the formless realm.
One does not obtain the aggregates of the form realm;
there is no non-possession (aprāpti) of the formless realm;
one does not obtain the dharmas of the formless realm.
This refers to one born in the formless realm who does not possess the aggregates of the formless realm;
it is the non-possession (aprāpti) of those formless realm aggregates.
Those who cannot help but be bound by phenomena refer to those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) who do not attain the untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregates.
And regarding analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
as well as all non-acquisitions of the dharmas of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*):
are those [non-acquisitions] themselves non-attainments of training?
Answer: It is not so.
Because that non-acquisition (aprāpti) is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, and it is not a learner [state].
Even if the non-acquisition were neither-learner-nor-non-learner, [it would still not be so].
Does he not obtain the dharmas of training?
Answer: Those dharmas are either of training, or beyond training, or neither of training nor beyond training.
Because there is neither acquisition nor non-acquisition of the three types of dharmas— namely, those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Regarding all those who do not acquire non-learner dharmas,
are they non-acquirers of non-learner [dharmas]?
Answer: It is not so.
Because that non-acquisition (aprāpti) is neither "neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa) nor "non-trainee" (aśaikṣa).
Even if it were a non-acquisition that is neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee, [it would still not be so].
Does he not attain the dharmas of one beyond training?
Answer: Those dharmas are either of training (śaikṣa) or beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Or it is neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
because one who is neither-learner-nor-non-learner does not acquire or fail to acquire these three kinds of dharmas.
This refers to all non-acquisitions of dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learners.
Is that non-acquisition neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: It is so.
This is because all non-acquisitions are exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
If one has not attained that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, does one not attain those dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: Those dharmas may be learner-dharmas.
It is either of the category of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) or neither of training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa),
because the non-acquisition of the three types of dharmas belongs to the category of neither of training nor beyond training.
Regarding those phenomena that are not abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), are they not abandoned by seeing? Answer: No.
Because that non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and not abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*).
Even if that non-acquisition were abandoned by cultivation,
would it not be the case that one does not acquire those factors abandoned by vision?
Answer: Those dharmas are either abandoned by insight,
or abandoned by cultivation,
or not abandoned at all.
Because one does not acquire the three types of dharmas that are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
regarding those non-acquisitions (*aprāpti*) of dharmas abandoned by cultivation:
are those non-acquisitions themselves abandoned by cultivation?
The answer is: "It is so.
This is because all non-acquisitions (*aprāpti*) are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Even if non-acquisition were abandoned through cultivation, [the same would follow].
Does he not abandon the factors to be abandoned by cultivation?
Answer: Those factors are either to be abandoned by seeing or to be abandoned by cultivation.
Or it is not abandoned,
because the non-acquisition of the three types of dharmas abandoned by cultivation results in the non-acquisition of those [dharmas] that are not abandoned.
All such non-acquisitions of dharmas that are not abandoned are themselves not abandoned.
Is that non-acquisition not abandoned?
Answer: No; because that non-acquisition is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and is not non-abandoned.
Even if non-acquisition were abandoned by cultivation...
Must those [factors] necessarily be abandoned?
Answer: Those factors are either to be abandoned by vision or to be abandoned by cultivation.
Or it is not abandoned,
because one does not acquire the non-acquisition of the three types of dharmas that are to be abandoned by cultivation.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhiskandha), Part One: The Sub-section on Attainment (Prāpti-nirdeśa), Second. Question: What is the distinction between attainment (*prāpti*) and non-attainment (*aprāpti*)?
The answer is that names themselves constitute differentiation;
namely, the name "acquisition" (prāpti) and the name "non-acquisition" (aprāpti).
Furthermore, acquisition (*prāpti*) is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
whereas non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is exclusively contaminated.
Furthermore, acquisition is wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, acquisition pertains to that which is bound to the three realms as well as that which is unbound;
non-acquisition pertains only to that which is bound to the three realms.
Furthermore, there is acquisition (*prāpti*) that is associated with training (*śaikṣa*), beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and neither-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
However, non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is exclusively neither-training-nor-beyond-training.
Furthermore, there is acquisition that is to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*).
Those to be abandoned by cultivation;
those not to be abandoned;
and non-acquisition are exclusively abandoned by cultivation.
Furthermore, acquisition may be either defiled or non-defiled;
however, non-acquisition is exclusively non-defiled.
Furthermore, acquisition may be either resultant or non-resultant.
Non-acquisition is not exclusively non-resultant.
Furthermore, acquisition may be either with resultant or without resultant;
non-acquisition is exclusively without resultant.
Furthermore, the acquisition (prāpti) and that which is acquired (prāpya-dharma) may arise simultaneously,
or they may not arise simultaneously.
Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) and the dharma that is not acquired necessarily do not arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, acquisition is subsumed under the three truths of suffering, origin, and the path;
non-acquisition is subsumed only under the truths of suffering and origin.
Through such categories as these, one should understand the distinctions between acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
Question: For what reason is acquisition of the same nature and category as the dharma that is acquired?
Is it the same or different?
Answer: There are three kinds of attainment (*prāpti*).
First, the attainment of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Second, the acquisition of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha); third, the acquisition of cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha);
and the acquisition of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma).
According to the specific categories of the dharmas as they are attained,
because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) possess functional activity that draws forth their own acquisition (*prāpti*),
the acquisition of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) follows the specific categories of the path by which it is realized.
Because analytical cessations (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) themselves possess no functional activity,
they are realized solely through the power of the Path;
it is at that time that their attainment is induced.
The acquisition of non-analytical cessation follows the specific distinctions of the nature of its own basis,
because non-analytical cessation itself possesses no functional activity.
It is not that which is sought by means of the path, because its manifestation depends solely upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Question: To what category of nature does non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) belong?
The answer is: That [consciousness] certainly does not follow along with those dharmas that have not been attained, because they are contradictory;
nor does it follow along with the path or what is sought by the non-path, because it proceeds solely in dependence upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
According to the distinctions among the categories of their respective bases.

Question: If all non-attainments (*aprāpti*) and acquisitions of analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) likewise follow the distinctions among the categories of their respective bases, [then what follows]?
The basis is either the maturation (*vipāka*) or exclusively the outflow (*niṣyanda*);
whichever of these two natures it may be, such is its specific distinction.
Answer: It follows the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*) because its meaning is universal;
it is not established as following [the nature of] maturation (*vipāka*), because that is not universal.
Question: If non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) follows the specific dharma that has not been acquired, [how is this explained]?
What fault is there in [distinguishing] the differentiation of their intrinsic natures?
Answer: One who has severed the roots of goodness would then possess wholesome [dharmas], and one who has already become free from the defilement of desire would then possess unwholesome [dharmas].
Those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa) would have to possess defilements;
ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) would have to possess the untainted dharmas (anāsravadharma) of the three vehicles;
and those who have regressed from the fruits [of the path] would have to achieve those fruits.
Otherwise, abandonment would necessarily be a path of application,
and the non-acquisition of the two cessations would necessarily be unconditioned;
such are the faults [that would follow].
Non-acquisition (aprāpti) cannot differ according to the specific nature of that which is not acquired.
Question: Is there a further acquisition of what has been described as "acquisition," or is there none?
If there were a further acquisition, then acquisition would possess a successive acquisition.
Why is it not an infinite regress?
If there were no further attainment,
by what could this attainment be said to be accomplished?
It is granted that it can be so stated;
furthermore, there is an attainment.
Question: If this were the case, it would lead to an infinite regress.
The answer is that there is no fault in this infinite regress;
it is for this reason that birth and death are difficult to sever and difficult to transcend.
Alternatively, it may be that all acquisitions arise simultaneously in a single moment,
yet their cessation does not entail the fault of infinite regress;
this is what is being stated.
Within a single moment there are only three factors:
first, that dharma;
second, its acquisition (prāpti).
There are three types of possession (prāpti).
By virtue of possession, one achieves both that dharma and the possession of possession;
by virtue of the possession of possession, one achieves the possession itself.
Because they are acquired through mutual acquisition, there is no infinite regress.
Therefore, it is said that the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) and the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) share a single acquisition (*prāpti*),
and so on up to the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) and the aggregate of formations sharing a single acquisition.
Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena have a single acquisition (prāpti).
Question: Does each individual phenomenon have its own distinct acquisition, or is it not so?
Some may say: "Co-existent dharmas have the same acquisition (prāpti).
Question: If that were so, one should not make such a statement.
Regarding the statement that the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) and the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) share the same acquisition (prāpti),
and so forth: the answer is that this is stated in order to show that there is no difference between a dharma and its acquisition of acquisition (prāptiprāpti).
However, it is not actually the case that there is no meaning of "acquisition" (prāpti) for the five aggregates, the four aggregates,
or a single [dharma]. Some say that each individual dharma has its own distinct acquisition.
Except for the acquisition of acquisition itself, it shares the same acquisition as that dharma.
Question: If that were so, there would be the fault of infinite regress.
Since acquisitions (prāpti) all possess arising, subsistence, change, and cessation,
these [characteristics] such as arising, in turn, have acquisitions and acquisitions-of-acquisitions;
and those acquisitions and acquisitions-of-acquisitions, in turn, possess arising and the other characteristics.
In this way, as they are passed on in succession, they become infinite.
[Objection: What fault is there in their being infinite? [Response:
Because of this, birth and death are difficult to sever and difficult to transcend.
Alternatively, these dharmas all arise and perish simultaneously in a single moment, so there is no fault of infinite regress.
According to this explanation,
a dharma and its [characteristics] such as arising possess the same acquisition (*prāpti*).
Because the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) are extremely closely related,

this [explanation] effectively accounts for the fact that the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), as well as their respective acquisitions and so forth, are obtained simultaneously.
Furthermore, it avoids the aforementioned fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
As it is said, "attainment" (prāpti) is the opposite of "non-attainment" (aprāpti);
this should be explained in detail accordingly.
However, there is no non-attainment that exists simultaneously with its own non-attainment.
When a phenomenon belonging to the category of sentient beings manifests, it is necessarily accompanied by its acquisition (*prāpti*).
Therefore, at the moment acquisition arises, it is not the case that non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) definitely does not arise; rather, non-acquisition and that phenomenon arise simultaneously with it.
Because these three factors are mutually contradictory, if they were said to exist at different times, this would not be a contradiction.
Question: Is there acquisition (*prāpti*) of the past and the future?
Is it accomplished?
Is it not accomplished?
If it is accomplished...
This would lead to an infinite regress;
that is to say, in a single moment, three dharmas arise together:
one dharma...
Second, the acquisition [of cessation]; third, the acquisition of that acquisition.
These three arise during the stage of cessation, making six acquisitions in total.
This refers to the three attainments and the three attainments of attainment;
these six, at the stage of cessation, give rise to twelve attainments.
That is to say, there are six acquisitions and six acquisitions of acquisitions;
twelve cessations and twenty-four arisings.
That is to say, for each of the twelve [factors], there are twelve acquisitions (prāpti), and for each of those acquisitions,

there are further acquisitions of acquisitions. In this manner, through successive progression from beginningless time until the end of the future, these acquisitions arise in every moment, doubling in number so that they become infinite.

If this is the case even when [the acquisitions] increase by multiples in the immediately succeeding moments, how much more so when they increase by multiples across intervening moments and successive prior moments?
Therefore, there would be the fault of an infinite regress.
If it were not established, it would contradict what is stated later regarding these aggregates;
as it says: "When one passes away from the formless realm and is born into the desire realm, the aggregates, elements, and bases that are acquired."
The great elements,
the roots of goodness,
and the roots of unwholesomeness.
The indeterminate roots,
fetters, bonds, latent tendencies,
secondary afflictions, and envelopments.
It should be said that one attains what has been previously attained and what has not yet been attained.
Answer: Regarding wholesome and defiled phenomena, it should be said that one attains what has been previously attained;
regarding resultant phenomena, it should be said that one attains what has not yet been attained.
If this were the case, it would not be non-accomplished, because there are both wholesome and defiled acquisitions.
One should respond by saying this: [the acquisition of the unwholesome is of three kinds].
Regarding the attainment (*prāpti*) of past and future [dharmas]:
because there are attainments belonging to the three time periods for wholesome, defiled, and other dharmas.
Question: If this were so, would it not lead to an infinite regress?
If one asks, "What fault is there in an infinite regress? [the answer is:
because of this, birth and death would be difficult to sever and difficult to transcend.
Alternatively, those various acquisitions (*prāpti*) arise for only a single moment, so there is no fault of infinite regress.
Furthermore, these various acquisitions (*prāpti*) can only be said to be numerous;
they are not infinite, as they possess limits.
Thus says another master.
There is no one who attains [the fruits] of the past or future;
therefore, there is no fault of infinite regress.
Question: How should this subsequent explanation regarding the aggregates be reconciled?
Answer: This aggregate refers to the dharmas attained, as explained in the subsequent text;
it does not refer to the "attainment" that performs the act of attaining.
What fault is there in this?
Regarding this statement:
it should be as previously explained, because one must achieve that which has been attained;
furthermore, it is called a "fruit of the śramaṇa" precisely because it is attained.
If that which has passed or not yet been attained were non-accomplished,
then the various fruits of śrāmaṇya would be abandoned moment by moment and acquired moment by moment;
however, such a thing does not occur.
Furthermore, there are three occasions for the relinquishing of the various noble paths:
namely, at the time of falling away,
and at the time of attaining a fruit.
At the time of refining the faculties,
if that which was previously attained and subsequently lost were not considered unaccomplished,
then the Noble Path would have to be abandoned moment by moment.
It is not that one intends for there to be no such fault regarding the three times;
therefore, there is the possession (*prāpti*) of past and future dharmas.
If one possesses a dharma that has been acquired, one also possesses its corresponding possession.
If one abandons a dharma that has been acquired, one also abandons that acquisition (*prāpti*),
because the dharma and its acquisition are identical in their acquisition and abandonment.
Furthermore, there are four general types of acquisition.
First, it exists prior to that phenomenon;
second, it exists subsequent to that phenomenon;
third, it exists simultaneously with that phenomenon.
The four [types of] non-dharmas are neither prior to, nor subsequent to, nor simultaneous with that [dharma].
As for the dharmas that are acquired, there are six kinds.
First, there are acquired dharmas that are acquired only simultaneously [with the dharma itself].
As in the case of those produced by maturation (*vipākaja*) and so forth,
there are two types of dharmas that possess acquisition (*prāpti*), but for these only the prior acquisition exists;
as in the case of the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*trividhānvaya-jñāna-pṛṣṭhalabdha-saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and so forth.
Some say that these [three] also possess simultaneous acquisition (*sahapratilambha*).
Regarding the dharmas acquired through the three bases, there is only simultaneous acquisition; there is no subsequent acquisition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).
As with the prātimokṣa vows and so forth,
among the four types of dharmas involving apprehension (*upalabdhi*), there are only those acquired simultaneously (*sahapratilambha*) and those acquired prior (*pūrvapratilambha*),
such as the patience associated with the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*).

5. Dharmas that are apprehended possess acquisition [of them] prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneously with [the attainment of the path], as is the case with other dharmas such as the wholesome and the defiled.
6. Dharmas that are apprehended cannot be said to have acquisition prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneously with [the attainment of the path].
Yet there are various acquisitions (*prāpti*),
namely *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) and *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation not through deliberation).
There is certainly no dharma that can be acquired solely after another dharma has arisen.
Because when [a dharma] is present before one, there must necessarily be its acquisition (*prāpti*).
There are, in total, three kinds of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*):
first, that which exists prior to the dharma in question.
Two [of these] exist subsequent to that dharma; three are neither prior to, nor subsequent to, nor simultaneous with that dharma.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of dharmas that cannot be attained:
first, those dharmas that can be attained but are not attained.
Only that aforementioned non-acquisition refers to those dharmas among the mental factors that will never arise in the future,
as well as the final moment of consciousness at the point of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and so forth.
Second, there are dharmas that cannot be acquired.
These include both the aforementioned and subsequent non-acquisitions (*aprāpti*),
namely other dharmas belonging to the category of sentient beings as appropriate.
There are three types of non-acquisition (aprāpti) of dharmas that do not exist:
there is non-acquisition without prior, posterior, or simultaneous [acquisition],
namely, analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
It is certain that non-acquisition (aprāpti) cannot coexist with a dharma;
for when a dharma is present before one,
that which is acquired must necessarily possess acquisition.
That which is not acquired is so because there is neither acquisition nor non-acquisition; furthermore,
there is no subsequent non-acquisition of that alone.
It is not the case that one has always possessed it since beginningless time;
for if it were not abandoned, that category [of non-possession] would necessarily arise until its exhaustion.
