However, because the nature of all non-possessions (*aprāpti*) is weak and inferior, [it does not persist].
It is accomplished only in the present;
having been attained in each individual moment, it is immediately relinquished.
This applies both to those dharmas not yet attained and to the state in which they have already been relinquished.
It should be understood that this non-acquisition (aprāpti) exists constantly. Furthermore,
one should know that there are fifteen categories of possession (prāpti) arising from the path of seeing (darśanamārga).

At the moment of the fifteenth mind, all the acquisitions (prāpti) that arise together with it perish simultaneously with the acquisition of its own arising at the stage of the cessation of the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
This is like the setting sun perishing simultaneously with the light it has produced.
However, the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) has fifteen acquisitions;
the dharma-knowledge of suffering has fourteen acquisitions;
and so on, until the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti), which has only one acquisition.
Question: Is the attainment of the path of vision (darśanamārga) limited to only that much, or is there something further?
Some say:
There are only that many;
some say there are further others besides these.
It is unreasonable to say that in future lives various acquisitions (*prāpti*) do not arise yet cannot be said to exist;
it would be more appropriate to say they do not exist.
One should not say that it exists yet is inexpressible;
for one who speaks thus,
there would further be other future attainments.
The patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) arises simultaneously with one acquisition (prāpti).
These patiences and acquisitions, when compared to one another, lack the status of being mutual causes.
The dharma-knowledge of suffering arises simultaneously with three acquisitions.
There are two kinds of attainment:
first, the attainment of dissociation;
second, the attainment of the path. Regarding the attainment of the path:

That is to say: the acquisition of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti), the acquisition of the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna),
and one acquisition of disjunction (visaṃyoga-prāpti).
This refers to the cessation of the ten acquisitions of the fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
and the arising of the ten acquisitions of their dissociation (*visamyoga*).
The knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) and those three acquisitions do not act as causes for one another.
The receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and its three acquisitions (*prāpti*) all possess the nature of being causes.
The receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises simultaneously with four acquisitions:
the acquisition of the path (*mārga-prāpti*) and the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
The receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*) and those four acquisitions (*prāpti*) do not serve as causes for one another.
The receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) is the cause for the four acquisitions.
The dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) is the cause for three acquisitions.

The acquisition of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is obtained [only] through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), because the wholesome dharma of the preparatory stage is superior and not an inferior cause; furthermore,
the acquisition of conditioned dharmas follows the superiority or inferiority of those dharmas.
The six acquisitions that arise simultaneously with the subsequent knowledge of suffering consist of four acquisitions of the path and two acquisitions of disjunction.

The subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*) and those six acquisitions (*prāpti*) do not act as causes for one another; however, the receptivity to the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharma-jñānakṣānti*) acts as the cause for those six acquisitions,
and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharma-jñāna*) acts as the cause for five acquisitions,
excluding the acquisition of the receptivity to the knowledge of suffering.
Because that [attainment] is inferior,
the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*) serves as the cause for the acquisition of three;
it excludes the acquisition of the previous three because that [attainment] is inferior.
Question: It may be granted that [the acquisition of a path] does not act as a cause for the acquisitions of the two preceding paths, because those [subsequent acquisitions] are inferior.
However, why does it not act as a cause for the acquisition of the dissociation from the preceding [fetters]?
How can this be so? Because that which is acquired is most excellent.
Answer: For conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), acquisition (*prāpti*) follows the excellence or inferiority of the phenomenon acquired, as it is induced by that [phenomenon].
Because the acquisition (*prāpti*) of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) follows the superiority or inferiority of the path by which it is induced,
since that path is inferior, its acquisition is not a cause [of the phenomenon].
Thus, this continues up until the twenty-two acquisitions that arise simultaneously with the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*).
There are fifteen acquisitions of the path and seven acquisitions of dissociation.
The patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) and those various acquisitions do not serve as causes for one another.
The patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) acts as the cause for twenty-two acquisitions (*prāpti*).
The dharma-knowledge of suffering acts as the cause for twenty-one acquisitions,
excluding the acquisition of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering, and so on, up to the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*).
However, it acts as a cause for three kinds of acquisition (*prāpti*):
namely, the two types of path-acquisition and the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
The first nineteen [types of outflow-free phenomena] do not obtain as causes because they are inferior.
For this reason, it is asked: Is there any previously arisen outflow-free phenomenon that is not the cause of a subsequently arisen outflow-free phenomenon?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, when the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) manifests, it is superior to that which is inferior.
One cultivates the future immeasurable patience regarding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
This present patience serves as the cause for that which is being cultivated,
and that [future patience] is its fruit.
Some say that this present patience (kṣānti) is not the cause for what is to be cultivated, nor is it the fruit of that,
because the latter never actually manifests for even a single moment.
The commentary states:
It should be said that this is the cause of that, and that is the fruit of this;
for they are subsumed within a single continuum and are not of an inferior path.
In this manner, up until the time when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests before one,
one cultivates immeasurable future diamond-like concentrations.
This present concentration serves as the cause for those that are cultivated, and they are its result.
Some say: This present concentration is certainly not the cause that is cultivated, nor is it the fruit thereof,
because it never at any time manifests for even a single moment.
The commentary states:
It should be said that this is the cause of that, and that is the fruit of this;
for they are subsumed within a single continuum and are not of an inferior path.
The patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering that has already arisen serves as the cause for the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering that has not yet arisen,
and it also serves as the cause for all paths of training and no-more-training, such as the dharma-knowledge of suffering and so forth.
The dharma-knowledge of suffering already arisen serves as the cause for the dharma-knowledge of suffering not yet arisen,
as well as for the subsequent acceptance of the inferential knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and all paths of training and no-more-training.
It does not serve as a cause for the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
In this manner, up until the already arisen knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) serves as a cause for the not-yet-arisen knowledge of exhaustion.

It also serves as the cause for all subsequently arisen and yet-to-be-arisen paths of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), but it does not serve as the cause for any paths of those still in training (śaikṣa).
For this reason, it is said: "Is there any already arisen untainted dharma (anāsrava-dharma)..."
Is it not the cause for unarisen untainted dharmas?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, the already arisen dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*).
It is not the cause for the future dharma-knowledge-patience regarding suffering,
up to and including the already arisen knowledge of exhaustion;
it is not the cause for the future diamond-like concentration.
Because a superior path does not serve as a cause for an inferior path,
the truths of suffering and origination are with outflows (*sāsrava*), and their respective acquisitions (*prāpti*) are also with outflows;
the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Those various acquisitions (prāpti) are either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
The Truth of the Path (mārgasatya) is without outflows;
those various acquisitions are also without outflows.
Furthermore, the truths of suffering and its origin are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and their respective acquisitions (prāpti) are likewise so.
The truths of cessation and the path are wholesome,
and their respective acquisitions are also wholesome.
Furthermore, the truth of suffering and the truth of origination are bound to the three realms;
their respective acquisitions (*prāpti*) are likewise so.
The truth of cessation is unbound.
Those various acquisitions are either bound to the realm of form,
or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
The Truth of the Path is unconditioned by the realms;
its acquisitions (*prāpti*) are likewise unconditioned.
Furthermore, the Truths of Suffering and Origination are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of those [dharmas] are likewise.
The Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
the acquisitions of those [dharmas] are either learner (*śaikṣa*) or non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
Some are neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
the Truth of the Path is learner or non-learner,
and their respective acquisitions (prāpti) are likewise.
Furthermore, the truths of suffering and its origin are to be abandoned by vision and by cultivation;
their respective acquisitions (prāpti) are likewise so.
The truth of cessation is not to be abandoned.
Those various acquisitions are either to be abandoned by cultivation or are not to be abandoned;
the Truth of the Path is not to be abandoned.
Those various acquisitions (*prāpti*) are also not abandoned.
Furthermore, the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and origination (*samudaya-satya*) are both defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*);
those various acquisitions are likewise so.
The truth of cessation and the truth of the path are non-defiled;
their respective acquisitions (*prāpti*) are likewise so.
Furthermore, the truths of suffering and origination possess maturation (*savipāka*).
There is no maturation;
the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of those [dharmas] are likewise.
The Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is without maturation.
Those various acquisitions (prāpti) are either with maturation (savipāka) or without maturation (avipāka).
The Truth of the Path (mārgasatya) is without maturation;
those various acquisitions thereof are likewise so.
Furthermore, the truth of suffering and the truth of origination are subsumed within the truths of suffering and origination;
their respective acquisitions (*prāpti*) are likewise so.
The truth of cessation is subsumed within the truth of cessation.
Those various acquisitions are subsumed under the three truths of suffering, origin, and the path; those that are subsumed under the truth of the path are indeed subsumed under the truth of the path.
Those various acquisitions are likewise so.
This applies to both the four truths that are acquired and the acquisition that acquires them.
There are such various categories of similarities and differences.
Question: Regarding the factors bound to the various stages (*bhūmi*), how many kinds of acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) are there?
Answer: From the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness,
all dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation possess three kinds of acquisition of dissociation—
namely, those of the learner (śaikṣa), the non-learner (aśaikṣa), and neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa).
The dharmas to be abandoned through vision regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
as well as the dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the preceding eight stages,
all possess two kinds of acquisition of dissociation.
This refers to those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Regarding the dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to that ninth category,
there is only one type of acquisition of dissociation (visaṃyoga-prāpti).
This refers to those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
It is because the initial mind of one beyond training has only now first arisen.
Question: To which stage (bhūmi) are these bound phenomena (saṃprayukta-dharma) attached?
How many stages possess the untainted acquisition of dissociation?
Some say that the acquisitions of dissociation correspond to their respective antidotes of abandonment.
He asserts this:
the untainted acquisition of dissociation from the dharmas of the desire realm abandoned through seeing and cultivation is comprised within the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration.
The untainted dissociation from the dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the first dhyāna is comprised within three stages;
[the same applies to] the dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the second dhyāna.
The untainted acquisition of dissociation (anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti) is subsumed under four stages.
The untainted acquisition of dissociation from dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the third dhyāna is subsumed under five stages.
The factors to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the fourth dhyāna,
as well as the factors to be abandoned through seeing in the formless realm,
have untainted dissociation (anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti) comprised within six stages.
The dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation in the sphere of infinite space have their untainted dissociation comprised within seven stages.
The dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation in the sphere of infinite consciousness...
The acquisition of untainted dissociation is comprised within eight stages:

the [first seven] and the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana). The acquisition of untainted dissociation is comprised within nine stages: the [eight aforementioned] and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Furthermore, there are those who say that the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) follows the counteractive agent of destruction (*bhedana-pratipakṣa*). They speak as follows:
The dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the desire and form realms,
as well as their untainted disjunctions, are all comprised within the six stages.
The dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the sphere of infinite space [are likewise].
The untainted acquisition of dissociation (anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti) pertaining to the seven stages is comprised within seven stages.

The untainted acquisition of dissociation pertaining to the dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana) is comprised within eight stages.
The sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
the dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation;
and the untainted acquisitions of disjunction are comprised within the nine stages.
Some say: if a stage possesses the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge,
that stage possesses the untainted acquisition of disjunction from the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation.
If a stage possesses the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna),
that stage includes the untainted acquisition of disjunction from those dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation within the realms of form and formlessness;
this is what they say.
The dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the desire realm,
as well as the untainted dissociation from them, are comprised within six stages.
The dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the form and formless realms [are likewise comprised within nine stages].
The untainted acquisition of dissociation is comprised within the nine stages.
The critique states:
among these, the first explanation is the correct one.
Because the attainment of all disconnections (*visamyoga-prāpti*) must necessarily be induced by the power of the antidote that abandons [the defilements].

Question: When one becomes free from the defilements of the form and formless realms to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) through the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*) or the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*), [how does this occur]?
The untainted dissociation from those dharmas of the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned through cultivation is subsumed under the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).
Is it subsumed under the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)?
If it were subsumed under the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), this would be unreasonable,
because those phenomena and their abandonment are objects of subsequent knowledge.
It is also illogical for it to be subsumed under the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
because its abandonment and attainment are realized through the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).
Some have said this:
That acquisition of disjunction is comprised within the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Question: Is it not the case that both its abandonment and its acquisition are realized by dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*)?
Answer: Although they are realized by dharma-knowledge, they are nonetheless comprised within subsequent knowledge.
Because it is known by subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Other masters say that its untainted acquisition of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) is included within the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*).
Question: Is it not the case that those dharmas and their abandonment are also known by subsequent knowledge?
Answer: Although it is known by subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), it is subsumed under dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), because it is realized by dharma-knowledge.
The critique says:
Among these, the first explanation is superior, because the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is its specific and definitive antidote. Question:
When a noble one (*ārya*) abandons the defilements of the various stages by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), [how does this occur]?
Is this one who has previously attained the Path or one who has not?
Some say: "This is one who has previously attained the Path."
Because this path has been practiced since beginningless time and was previously attained,
it now manifests before one; thus they say.
When a noble one, by means of the mundane path,
abandons the highest degree of defilement to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
[they abandon] the dharmas of the highest degree to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
One obtains two kinds of acquisition of dissociation:
first, worldly acquisition;
second, untainted acquisition.
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of this [attainment] through the mundane path is "previously acquired.
The acquisition of the untainted [attainment] belonging to the category of the Path is of the category of the Noble Path;
this occurs when the mundane path is present before one.
Furthermore, because one also cultivates the future untainted path,
one attains a single type of acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) regarding the highest-of-the-high (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) factors to be abandoned through vision within the desire realm.
This means that the conventional acquisition (*prāpti*) of this [path] is not obtained because it is a category of path already previously obtained;
as for the untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*), it has already been obtained before.
Question: If that is so, how can there be a common counteractive path (*pratipakṣa-mārga*)?
It transforms into an uncommon antidote;
that is to say, this path previously attained had already,
at an earlier time, collectively severed all phenomena of the desire realm to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation in nine grades.
At present, because this path only abandons what is to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm,
it is still called a "common path of antidote," for it constantly possesses the power to abandon both simultaneously.
Since these [defilements] abandoned through seeing have already been abandoned previously, there is nothing further to be abandoned now; it is not that they cannot be abandoned.
Therefore, this is always termed the "common path of antidote."
As it is with the abandonment of the highest-of-the-high grade,
so it is likewise for the abandonment down to the lowest-of-the-low grade;
as it is with the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
The same applies up to the abandonment through cultivation regarding the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Other masters say that this is a path not previously attained.
Because this path has not been practiced or attained since beginningless time,
and arises only through the power of the noble ones (ārya),
they speak as follows.
When a noble one, by means of the mundane path,
abandons the highest degree of defilement to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
[they abandon] the dharmas of the highest degree to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
One attains two kinds of acquisition of dissociation:
first, worldly acquisition;
second, untainted acquisition.
The mundane attainment is that which has never been attained before.
The supramundane attainment of the noble path belongs to the category of the noble path.
This is because when the mundane path is manifested, [the supramundane attainment is acquired].
Furthermore, because one is also cultivating the future untainted path,
one does not obtain the acquisition of dissociation from the highest-of-the-high (adhimātra-adhimātra) dharmas to be abandoned through vision within the desire realm.
It cannot be acquired through worldly acquisition because it is a path never before attained and is not the antidote for that [worldly state].

It cannot be acquired through untainted acquisition because it has already been previously attained. This is likewise true for the abandonment of the highest-of-the-high grade up to the abandonment of the lowest-of-the-middle grade.
As it is with the eight categories of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
so it is for the eight categories to be abandoned through cultivation in the first dhyāna,
and so on, up to the eight categories to be abandoned through cultivation in the sphere of nothingness.
At the moment of the ninth path of liberation during the cultivation for abandonment of the desire realm,
one cultivates two types of conventional paths in the future: those previously attained and those never before attained.
At that time, regarding the factors to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
one attains three kinds of acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*): first,
the worldly acquisition of what was previously attained (*laukika-pūrva-prāpta-prāpti*).
That is to say: first, the acquisition of the path-category that has already been attained;
second, the worldly acquisition of what has not yet been attained, which refers to the acquisition of the path-category not previously attained;
and third, uncontaminated acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*).
That is to say, regarding the dharmas to be abandoned through seeing in the desire realm,
the noble path acquires two kinds of acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*),
excluding the previously unobtained worldly acquisition.

Question: How is it known that at the time of the ninth liberation, one is able to cultivate both the previously attained and the never-before-attained conventional paths (saṃvṛtimārga) regarding the future?
Answer: Because it is stated that if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) in the present.
Because that [attainment] necessarily accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds regarding the past.
Question: Why is it that when one is free from the defilements of the first eight categories, one cultivates a path never before attained?
When one attains the path of liberation from the ninth grade of defilement, does one cultivate paths previously attained or paths not yet attained?
Answer: The path that abandons defilement is distinct, and the stage [of attainment] is likewise distinct.
This means that the path of detachment (*vairāgyamārga*) is exclusively something never before attained;
the future cultivation [of it] is also something never before attained.
However, at the time one attains a stage (*bhūmi*), although the present path of detachment has not been previously attained, it is attained because the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) is attained.
One cultivates universally the future paths, both those previously attained and those not yet attained.

This applies from the ninth category of the path of cultivation to be abandoned in the detachment from the desire realm, up to and including the ninth category of the path of cultivation to be abandoned in the detachment from the sphere of nothingness; it is the same for all.
The commentary states:
It should be said that when a noble one (ārya) detaches from the defilements of the various stages by means of the mundane path (laukikamārga), [the following occurs].
It should be said that this refers to the path never before attained;
for it has not been attained since time immemorial and arises solely through the power of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Nevertheless, regarding the future, one cultivates both paths previously attained and those never before attained.
Because the objects to be countered are the same,
one should state this:
the noble ones [attain it] by means of the mundane path.
When one becomes detached from the highest degree of defilement to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
one obtains three kinds of acquisition of disconnection (visamyoga-prāpti) regarding the dharmas of the highest degree to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
First, the worldly attainment of what has already been attained,
which refers to the attainment of the path-categories (mārga-anvaya) that have previously been acquired.
Second, the worldly attainment of what has not yet been attained.
This refers to the three untainted acquisitions (anāsrava-prāpti) of the path-type (mārga-jāti) that have not been previously attained; that is to say,
they belong to the category of the Noble Path (āryamārga).
Regarding the highest-of-the-high (adhimātra-adhimātra) dharmas to be abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
one attains a single acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*);
that is to say, it is the type [of acquisition] previously obtained by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*).
"One does not obtain what has never been obtained before" means that the path not yet obtained is not its antidote;
"one does not obtain an untainted attainment" means [the same].
Because it has already been attained previously.
Just as with the abandonment of the highest-of-the-high grade,
so it is for all grades down to the lowest-of-the-low.
Just as it is for those who have abandoned the defilements to be eliminated through cultivation in the desire realm,
so it is up to those who have abandoned the defilements to be eliminated through cultivation in the sphere of nothingness.
For this reason, it is said that there may be some who do not fall back.
One does not attain the fruit;
one does not transform the faculties;
and the path of seeing is not present before one.

Nor is it the case that one who is not of the class of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) can obtain the acquisition of dissociation (visamyoga-prāpti) regarding the factors to be abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya).
Answer: There is.
This refers to what was previously stated;

however, with the sole exception of the time when one abandons the sixth and ninth categories of the defilements of the desire realm, according to the meaning explained, one should state as follows: "Is there any acquisition of dissociation?"
Is it that one attains [it] but does not relinquish it?
Or is it that one relinquishes it but does not attain it?
One should respond by establishing four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the acquisition of dissociation (visamyoga-prāpti) which is acquired but not abandoned;
this refers to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) who have become detached from the desire realm.
Up until the time of being defiled by the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
as well as for noble ones (*ārya*) at the time of not yet attaining a fruit or becoming free from defilement,
there is the abandonment of the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) without its attainment.
This refers to when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) fall away from detachment ranging from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*);
when noble ones (*ārya*) do not fall away from their fruit;
and when one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the second dhyāna or above.
When one dies in the first dhyāna and is reborn in the second dhyāna or above,
up until dying in the sphere of nothingness and being reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
When one dies from the various stages of the form and formless realms and is reborn in the desire realm,
there is both the acquisition and the abandonment of the attainment of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*);
that is to say, when one advances to attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
When one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta);
or when an Arhat of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharman) and others refine their faculties to become one of the nature of mental cultivation (cetayitadharman).
When one falls away from detachment or from the spiritual lineage;
when one attains the third or fourth fruit of śramaṇaship;
or when one dies in a higher stage of the form or formless realms and is reborn in a lower stage.
There is the acquisition of dissociation that is neither [previously] non-acquisition nor abandonment;
this refers to cases other than those previously described.
Question: Suppose one has already become detached from five grades of defilement of the desire realm.
Subsequently, one enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
At the moment the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) arises,
regarding the five categories of phenomena previously abandoned through the vision of suffering:
And now, regarding the four categories of phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*),
one attains the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) up until the time when the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) arises;
this applies likewise to the five categories of phenomena previously abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, regarding the four categories of factors abandoned by the path of seeing that are now being abandoned,
one attains the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) at the moment when the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) arises.
Regarding the dharmas abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms, one obtains the untainted possession of dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*).

At what time shall one obtain the untainted possession of dissociation for those five categories of dharmas abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) in the desire realm that were previously abandoned?
The Venerable Saṅgharakṣita stated:
"It is attained at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna),
for at that moment one is designated as having entered the stream (srotāpanna)."
It is also called the "candidate for the fruit of once-returning.
That [position] is incorrect. Why is this so?

Since at that time one has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) and has not yet produced for even a single moment the path directed toward the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*),
how can one be said to be "a candidate for once-returning" (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*)?
Some say that it is acquired at the time of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) for the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*),
because it is subsumed under the stage of the candidate for once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*).
Other masters say that it is attained at the time of attaining the fruit of once-returner,
because it occurs while abiding in the sixth path of uninterrupted transition.

It can induce the acquisition of dissociation from the outflows (anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti) regarding the dharmas abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya) within the three realms, as well as the first six categories of dharmas abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the desire realm.
This is because it causes one to arise in the attainment of the fruit of once-returning.
According to this explanation,
from the fruit of stream-entry, one definitely gives rise to the path of superior progress.
It is attained when it manifests before one;
for when one arises from a lower fruit and proceeds toward the superior path of advancement,
one must necessarily cultivate the paths of counteraction that previously severed the various fetters of the higher stages.
Question: Is it possible that, for even a single moment, one might have bodily realization (*kāyasākṣātkriyā*) regarding the untainted dissociation (*anāsravavisaṃyoga*), yet wisdom does not see it;
or that wisdom sees it while the body does not realize it? [This constitutes] the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, at the time when the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti) ceases and the subsequent knowledge of the path arises.
One should formulate four propositions.
There is the acquisition of untainted dissociation which is personally realized through the body but not seen by wisdom.
This refers to the untainted acquisition of dissociation from the dharmas of the desire realm that are to be abandoned by insight;
it is an untainted acquisition of dissociation which is realized through wisdom and vision, yet not personally realized by the body.
This refers to the untainted acquisition of dissociation from those dharmas of the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned through cultivation;
there is an untainted acquisition of dissociation,
and the wisdom that realizes it through bodily witness is also seen.
This refers to the untainted acquisition of disjunction from those dharmas to be abandoned by vision in the form and formless realms.
There is an untainted acquisition of disjunction that the body does not realize and wisdom does not perceive.
This refers to the untainted acquisition of dissociation from the dharmas of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation.
Question: Is there any single moment during which one acquires, but does not lose, or loses, but does not acquire, the five faculties beginning with faith?
"Does this even extend to the four propositions?
Answer: "It does.
That is to say, when a noble one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm."
When abiding in the final path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding that which is attained but not abandoned:
This refers to the five faculties, such as faith, which are subsumed under the mundane path of the third stage and the untainted path of the second stage;
these are relinquished but not yet attained.

Regarding those that are both acquired and relinquished: these refer to the five faculties, such as faith, which arise together with regret and the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasya*) within the desire realm;
and also those five faculties, such as faith, which are subsumed under the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) of the *anāgamya* stage.
That which is comprised within the path of uninterrupted transition is abandoned;
that which is comprised within the path of liberation is acquired;
and that which is neither acquired nor abandoned is as follows.
That is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Question: If a dharma is past, is its acquisition (prāpti) also past?
Conversely, if an acquisition is past, is that dharma also past?
It can be answered in four propositions:
there are dharmas that are past,
yet their acquisition (prāpti) is not past.
That is to say, regarding dharmas that were sentient beings in the past:
their acquisition may exist in the future or the present,
or it may exist in the past.
That dharma is not past;
that is to say, it consists of the acquisition of past acquisitions, as well as future and present dharmas included within the category of sentient beings,
along with cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
There are phenomena that are past,
and their acquisition is also past;
namely, those phenomena belonging to sentient beings that are past.
That acquisition (prāpti) exists in the past;
there are dharmas that do not exist in the past,
and that acquisition likewise does not exist in the past.
This refers to the acquisition of future and present dharmas pertaining to sentient beings,
as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
These are to be treated according to the fourfold logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) as applied to past [dharmas].
One should understand, according to reason, that for the future and the present, four propositions each should be formulated.
Question: If a phenomenon exists in the past...
If a dharma has past acquisition, does that dharma exist in the past?
Furthermore, if a dharma has past acquisition,
does that dharma reside in the past?
It can be answered with four propositions:
There are dharmas that exist in the past,
yet those dharmas do not possess past acquisition (*prāpti*).
This refers to those phenomena not classified as sentient beings that exist in the past and possess past acquisition (*prāpti*),
yet those phenomena themselves do not abide in the past.
That is to say: analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*),
non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), and those phenomena belonging to sentient beings that are future or present,
which possess past acquisition (*prāpti*).
There are dharmas that exist in the past,
and those dharmas also have acquisition (prāpti) in the past;
namely, those dharmas belonging to sentient beings that are past.
There are dharmas that do not exist in the past,
and those dharmas also lack past acquisition (*prāpti*).
These refer to future and present dharmas that are not included among sentient beings (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*).
Furthermore, for space, the unconditioned, and those factors categorized as sentient beings in the future and present,
as well as for analytical cessation and non-analytical cessation, there is no past acquisition (*prāpti*).
These are treated according to the fourfold logical permutation (*catuṣkoṭika*) as in the case of the past.
Regarding the future and the present, each should be understood through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) according to reason.
Question: If a phenomenon does not exist in the past...
If that dharma has no past acquisition (*prāpti*),
does that dharma not exist in the past? And if a dharma has no past acquisition,
does that dharma not exist in the past?
I shall respond with four lines:
the second line of the former becomes the first line of this,
and the first line of the former becomes the second line of this.
The former fourth phrase becomes this third phrase;
the former third phrase becomes this fourth phrase.
As it was understood previously, one should know that as with the past, four phrases are formed for the future and four phrases are formed for the present.
This should be understood according to principle.
Question: If a dharma has an acquisition (*prāpti*), does that dharma have an acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*)?
Or, if a dharma has an acquisition of dissociation...
Is there acquisition (*prāpti*) of that dharma?
One should respond by formulating four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).
There are dharmas for which there is acquisition, yet that dharma does not possess the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
This refers to untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta-dharma*),
as well as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
these phenomena possess the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
Those dharmas for which there is no acquisition (*prāpti*) are those not included among the category of sentient beings (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*). There are dharmas for which there is acquisition;
for those dharmas, there is also the acquisition of disconnection (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
This refers to those contaminated phenomena belonging to the category of sentient beings;
there is no acquisition (prāpti) of such phenomena,
nor is there any acquisition of disconnection (visaṃyoga-prāpti) from them.
That is to say, unconditioned space (*ākāśa-asamskṛta*).
Question: If a dharma has no acquisition (*prāpti*), does that dharma have no acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*)?
Conversely, if a dharma has no acquisition of dissociation...
Is that dharma unattainable?
One should respond by formulating four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The second proposition of the former [set] constitutes the first proposition of this [set].
The first sentence of the preceding [section] becomes this second sentence; the fourth sentence of the preceding [section] becomes this third sentence;
and the third sentence of the preceding [section] becomes this fourth sentence.
It should be understood as before.
Question: If a dharma is to be cultivated, is its acquisition also to be cultivated?
Conversely, if an acquisition is to be cultivated, is that dharma also to be cultivated?
Answer: If a dharma is to be cultivated, its acquisition is also to be cultivated.
There are dharmas that ought to be cultivated,
yet those dharmas are not to be cultivated;
namely, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: If a phenomenon (*dharma*) is to be abandoned, must its acquisition (*prāpti*) also be abandoned? Conversely, if an acquisition is to be abandoned, must the phenomenon also be abandoned?
"Should that dharma be abandoned?
Answer: "If a dharma is to be abandoned, its acquisition (*prāpti*) should also be abandoned; there are dharmas whose acquisitions are to be abandoned.
That dharma which is not to be abandoned is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
One part, as well as non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: If a phenomenon is to be reviled, [how is it so?]
If a dharma is to be acquired, should that dharma be subject to revulsion?
Conversely, if a dharma is to be subject to revulsion, is that dharma necessarily to be acquired?
Answer: If a phenomenon is to be reviled, its acquisition (prāpti) should also be reviled.
There are phenomena whose acquisition should be reviled.
Those phenomena are not to be loathed;
namely, a portion of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: For what reason do all acquisitions (*prāpti*) conform to the nature of the dharmas they acquire—becoming wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth—but not become form (*rūpa*) and so forth?
Answer: Wholesomeness and so forth constitute the essential categories (*dharmatā-jāti*) of all dharmas.
The natures and categories of all phenomena may follow one another in transformation;
however, form and so forth are the intrinsic substance of these phenomena,
and the intrinsic substance of phenomena has no sense of mutual following.
Some say that the wholesome and so forth are common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) that can follow along [with other things],
whereas form and so forth are specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) that lack the sense of following along.

Question: For what reason are all acquisitions (*prāpti*) necessarily of the same moral quality as the dharmas they acquire, yet not necessarily of the same temporal status as the dharmas they acquire?
Answer: Because the movement through the time periods (*adhvan*) of the acquired dharmas is not fixed.
The acquisition of the acquisition is also not indeterminate;
because the nature of the various dharmas acquired— whether wholesome and so forth— is fixed,
the acquisition of those wholesome and other natures is likewise fixed.
Question: Regarding all acquisitions (*prāpti*), by how many consciousnesses are they cognized?
By how many knowledges (*jñāna*) are they known?
And by how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do they increase through association?

Answer: All that is cognized by a single consciousness—namely, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—is comprised within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*);
thus, it is known by eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
Because the knowledge of others' minds is conditioned and dissociated [from mind],
it is increased by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take the outflow-tainted objects of the five categories within the three realms as their objective support;
for among acquisitions (prāpti), there is no increase through association.
Question: Regarding all non-acquisitions (*aprāpti*), by how many consciousnesses are they cognized?
By how many knowledges (*jñāna*) are they known?
And by how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do they increase through association?
Answer: All those that are not "one" are cognized by a single consciousness,
namely the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
because they are also subsumed under the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
It is known by seven knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, and the knowledge of others' minds,
because it is tainted and dissociated from them.
It is increased by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through cultivation within the three realms, as well as by the universal latent dispositions;
for non-possession (aprāpti) is abandoned solely through cultivation.
Question: Is there a case where one abandons and acquires [a dharma], yet does not acquire its non-possession (*aprāpti*)?
Answer: There is;
namely, at the time of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Because one abandons all dharmas through the attainment [of them], and because the basis for non-attainment is severed, [non-attainment] is not obtained.
Question: Is there any dharma such that, once non-attainment has first arisen, it never arises again after a single attainment has occurred?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, all non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), as well as the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) and so forth.
First, because it is always accomplished from the moment of acquisition until the attainment of *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
Question: Are there any phenomena that possess acquisition (*prāpti*) from the very beginning, yet lack non-acquisition (*aprāpti*)?
Some say it does not exist, because wherever there is acquisition (*prāpti*), there must necessarily be non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
Others say: [it exists].
There are [cases where this occurs], such as the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Regarding the dharma of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), there is inherently the possession (*prāpti*) of it, but there is no non-possession (*aprāpti*).
Because that [dharma] is fundamentally and eternally non-arising.

Question: Just as there is one who attains a dharma and also attains the "attainment of attainment" (prāpti-prāpti), is there also one who, through "non-attainment" (aprāpti), abandons that dharma and also abandons the "non-attainment of non-attainment" (aprāpti-aprāpti)?
Answer: There is none.
This is because there is no non-acquisition (aprāpti) that is simultaneous with [the dharma], for there is no non-acquisition of a non-acquisition;
furthermore, because a present non-acquisition is necessarily established.
Question: Is there any phenomenon that is neither attained nor non-attained, yet when that phenomenon ceases, it is either attained or non-attained?
Answer: There is.
This refers to all phenomena not included among sentient beings.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 158; *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 100.
Composed by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (*Samādhiskandha*). First Sub-section: Attainment (*Prāpti*). Part Three. When wholesome formless states (*arūpadharma*) arise, all dharmas [attain them].
Are those dharmas associated with a wholesome mind?
[The text continues] at length. [Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
[Answer: It is intended to refute the view that there exist dissociated dharmas (viprayukta-dharma) such as birth, aging, duration, impermanence, and non-retrogression.
Furthermore, this treatise is composed in order to clearly expound the principles of our own school that are consistent with correct reasoning.
Question: Why is it that herein one asks only about the arising of the formless (*ārūpya*) and not about the material (*rūpa*)?
The answer is that it is because the author of that treatise intended it so;
this treatise was composed according to his intention.
As long as it does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one should not hold him accountable.
Some say: if a dharma pertains to all realms and all stages.
Regarding that which is obtainable within all classes and within all minds,
a question is raised herein:
This is not questioned here because material phenomena (rūpadharma) are not obtainable in all realms,
nor even in all states of mind.
Some say: If a phenomenon is for the most part coexistent with the mind,
arises through the power of the mind, and evolves in accordance with the mind.
In this regard, it is asked:
for the most part, material phenomena (rūpadharma) do not coexist with the mind,
nor are they produced by the power of the mind.
It does not follow the mind (na cittānuvartin).
For example, at the time of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti), ninety-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) arise;
however, their respective acquisitions (prāpti) do not coexist with that patience.
It is not produced by the power of patience,
nor does it follow along with patience;
although it coexists with patience, as it is likewise a formless dharma, it is still not mentioned.
Since that [mind] is accompanied by the mind of patience, how much more so are all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*)? Therefore, they are not questioned here.
What is explained in this context is that the arising of immaterial phenomena (*arūpadharma*) is accompanied by wholesome and other types of minds.
If those various formless phenomena (ārūpya-dharma) are induced by the power of that mind,
then those wholesome formless phenomena arise.
Are those phenomena concomitant with a wholesome mind?
Answer: When wholesome formless phenomena arise, those phenomena are either concomitant with a wholesome mind.
It is either associated with an unwholesome mind or associated with a neutral mind.
What is it that is associated with a wholesome mind?
Answer: All phenomena are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind;
wholesome formless states are also associated with that mind.
Wholesome formless [phenomena] refers to the wholesome mental factors that coexist with that mind.
Regarding "wholesome formless [phenomena]," this refers to their arising, aging, duration, and impermanence.
Within this context, there are likewise similar factors that arise; however, they are not mentioned here because they are abbreviated, and they should be understood by analogy.
How is it associated with an unwholesome mind?
Answer: It is as when an unwholesome mind either falls away or arises.
Regarding the arising of wholesome dharmas and the falling away from unwholesome minds:

when noble ones who have already become free from the defilements of desire fall away due to the arising of the two grades of fetters— the lowest-of-the-low and the low-of-the-middle— of the desire realm.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the four aggregates belonging to the category co-arising with the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*),
the path to the superior fruit, and both wholesome and unwholesome *kaukṛtya* (remorse) associated with the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
This occurs when one falls away due to the arising of fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the lower or upper grades.
Even those who are able to guard their application of effort,
their minds likewise arise together with the aforementioned wholesome states.
As for those who are unable to guard their application of effort, [their minds do not so arise].
Excluding the path of the superior fruit of once-returning, that mind arises together with other wholesome factors as previously described.
Question: In this context, what is meant by "application of restraint" (*saṃvara-prayoga*) and "application of non-restraint" (*asaṃvara-prayoga*)?

The answer is: because while one is capable of guarding against the power of afflictions during the preparatory stage of cultivation and abandonment, there are times when one is unable to guard against them;
thus, when one falls back due to the arising of the five grades of fetters—ranging from the middling and lower up to the upper-middling.
That mind arises simultaneously with the attainment (*prāpti*) of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), as well as the paths to higher fruits,
and the four aggregates belonging to the category of wholesome *kaukṛtya* (remorse) and the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
If, at the time of falling away due to the arising of the highest-grade fetters,
one is still able to guard the application of practice,
that mind also arises together with wholesome states as previously described.
For those who are unable to maintain the intensified practice—
excluding the path of the superior fruit of stream-entry—
their mind arises together with other wholesome states as previously described.
If it is a once-returner, whichever of the first six categories of fetters arise, he may fall away from them;
however, this excludes the category co-arising with wholesome *kaukṛtya* (remorse) and the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
His mind, according to its respective application, arises together with other wholesome acquisitions as previously described.
If an ordinary person who has already become detached from the defilement of desire falls away due to the arising of any grade of unwholesome obsession (*paryavasthāna*),

their mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the four aggregates belonging to the category that co-arises with wholesome regret (*kaukṛtya*) and the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Regarding the arising of a wholesome mind from an unwholesome mind:
this refers to one who dies in the form or formless realms and is reborn in the desire realm;
at the moment of linking existence (*pratisandhi*), an unwholesome mind arises.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the four aggregates of innate wholesome states belonging to the desire realm.
Some say that it also arises simultaneously with the acquisitions of a portion of the four aggregates consisting of those acquired through hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*).
What is associated with an indeterminate mind?
Answer: As when an indeterminate mind either regresses or arises, the acquisition of wholesome dharmas occurs.
Regarding the arising of wholesome acquisitions when the mind is indeterminate and one has regressed:
this refers to when an Arhat, having regressed from superior faculties and abiding in inferior faculties,
that indeterminate mind arises together with the wholesome acquisitions belonging to the category of inferior faculties.
The same applies to one who dwells in an inferior lineage when they fall away from a superior lineage.
Furthermore, when an Arhat falls away due to the arising of the fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
that mind [is associated] with the fruit of Non-returner and the path to a superior fruit.

It is not the case that the acquisitions (prāpti) arising simultaneously with the factors conducive to decline (*parihāṇika-bhāgīya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) arise [in this manner].
This applies likewise up to the time of falling away from the eight grades of fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the first dhyāna.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), the path of superior fruits,
and the stage conducive to decline (hānabhāgīya) of the first dhyāna.
If, when falling away from the first dhyāna due to extremely intense fetters,
one is still able to protect one's application of effort,
that mind likewise arises together with the wholesome state as previously attained.
For those who are unable to guard their intensified practice—
excluding the path of the superior fruit of the non-returner—
their mind arises together with other wholesome factors as previously described.
When non-returners and ordinary worldlings who have already abandoned the defilements of the sphere of nothingness fall away due to the arising of the active outbursts (paryavasthāna) of that sphere.
That mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the factors conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*) of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
In this manner, it continues until the time when one falls away due to the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the first dhyāna;
at that point, that mind arises together with the acquisitions of the factors conducive to decline of the first dhyāna.

Just as it is for one who has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness, so too should it be understood for one who has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of consciousness,
up to and including one who has become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna.

If an ordinary person who has already become free from the defilement of desire falls away due to the arising of the active outbursts of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) belonging to the desire realm,

that mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the four aggregates associated with the category of wholesome or unwholesome mental application and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Regarding the arising of wholesome states from an indeterminate mind:
this refers to when one dies in a higher level of the formless realm and is reborn in a lower level;
at that time, that [indeterminate] mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the four aggregates of the wholesome states belonging to that [lower] level.
If one passes away from the formless realm or from a higher dhyāna stage and is reborn in a lower dhyāna stage.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the five aggregates of the wholesome state belonging to that level.
This occurs when one dies from the form or formless realms and is reborn in the desire realm,
at the moment of linking existence (*pratisandhi*) through the fetters of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the four aggregates of innate wholesome states belonging to the desire realm.
Some say that it also arises simultaneously with the acquisitions of a portion of those states produced by hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*).
When one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the two higher realms,
or when one dies in a lower stage of the two higher realms and is reborn in a higher stage,
that mind [is associated] with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the four aggregates of the wholesome states acquired by birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) belonging to those respective stages.
They arise together.
If a dharma arises together with a wholesome mind,
is that dharma a wholesome non-material (arūpa) phenomenon?
Answer: All phenomena arise together with a wholesome mind;
those phenomena are either wholesome and formless, or they are indeterminate and formless.
What is wholesome formless [phenomena]?
Answer: Those phenomena that are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind are wholesome formless [phenomena].
The meaning is as explained previously.
What is the indeterminate formless?
Answer: It is like the advancement of a wholesome mind.
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas arises;

furthermore, while abiding in a wholesome mind, the indeterminate faculties (*indriya*), the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are nourished and augmented, as are the [characteristics] of those dharmas:
arising (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), and impermanence (*anityatā*).
Regarding the arising of a superior wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind:
this refers to the time when the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the defilements of desire ceases and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the result of the first dhyāna—
the category of neutral minds associated with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)—
up until the abandonment of the defilements of the third dhyāna.
When the ninth path of immediate succession ceases and the path of liberation arises,
that mind [attains] the fruit of the fourth dhyāna.
The acquisitions (prāpti) of the category of neutral resultant minds arise simultaneously;
they cease at the moment the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) arises and the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) emerges.

That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the various classes of neutral resultant minds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) corresponding to the respective dhyāna fruits,
for one who has already become free from the defilements of desire.
When one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) undergoes the refinement of the faculties (indriyasaṃcāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
some say this occurs during the path of preparation (prayogamārga), while others say it also occurs during the path of liberation (vimuktimārga).

That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the various types of neutral *abhijñā-phala-citta* (fruition-minds of supernormal powers) corresponding to the respective dhyāna fruits. Furthermore,
when an Arhat of the "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*) type refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become "unshakable" (*akopya*).
From the time of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) based on the *anāgamya* concentration up to the fourth *dhyāna*,

that mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the various neutral minds resulting from the supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) as appropriate for each respective *dhyāna*; and at the time of the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) based on all stages.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the four dhyāna fruits,
the indeterminate *abhijñā-phala-citta* classes,
the preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*) for inducing the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and the five uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*).
At the time of the three paths of liberation;
at the time of the uninterrupted path and the path of liberation during the initial and final stages of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna;
one gives rise to the four immeasurables.
At the time of the first three liberations,
the eight bases of mastery,
and the first eight totalities.
One gives rise to the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Furthermore,
based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) up to the fourth dhyāna,

when these are being cultivated, one gives rise to the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā*), the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), and the limit-of-reality concentration (*bhūtakoṭi-samādhi*).

Furthermore, at the time of increase, based on the *anāgamya* concentration up to the fourth *dhyāna*, one gives rise to various meritorious qualities such as emptiness-of-emptiness, wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and signlessness-of-signlessness; and at the time of their increase, that mind corresponds to the respective fruit of the *dhyāna* in which it resides.
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the categories of neutral resultant minds (*vipākaja-citta*) arise simultaneously [with those minds],
as do the [acquisitions] of one abiding in a wholesome mind, up until the point where the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of those dharmas occur.
This refers to when a stream of wholesome minds belonging to the desire or form realms has been flowing for a long time and continues in succession.
The sense faculties and the primary elements nourish and augment that mind;
it arises simultaneously with those four characteristics.
The sense faculties are nourished and the primary elements are augmented.
The question and answer explanation are as in the *Mahābhūta-skandha*.
"If various unwholesome non-material phenomena arise, do those phenomena arise together with an unwholesome mind?
Answer: "When various unwholesome non-material phenomena arise..."
Those dharmas are either associated with an unwholesome mind or associated with a neutral mind.
What is meant by being associated with an unwholesome mind?
Answer: All phenomena are associated with that mind;
they coexist with that mind. As for the meaning of "unwholesome" and "non-material," it is as explained previously.
What is it that is associated with an indeterminate mind?
Answer: It is as when an indeterminate mind either regresses or arises, and unwholesome factors arise; or when an indeterminate mind regresses and unwholesome factors arise.

This refers to when ordinary beings who have already become detached from the defilements of desire fall back due to the manifestation of the fetters of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) belonging to the desire realm; at that time,
their minds are associated with [defilements] to be abandoned through both seeing and cultivation.
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the four unwholesome aggregates arise simultaneously.
Regarding the arising of the acquisition of an unwholesome state when an indeterminate mind arises:
this refers to one who dies in the form or formless realms and is reborn in the desire realm.
When one is reborn through the fetters of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*),
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the four unwholesome aggregates (*skandha*) abandoned through both vision and cultivation;
this applies even if the factors arise together with an unwholesome mind.
Are those factors unwholesome and formless?
Answer: Those factors that arise simultaneously with an unwholesome mind may be unwholesome and formless.
Either wholesome formless states or indeterminate formless states.
What are unwholesome formless states?
Answer: Those phenomena are associated with that mind;
they are unwholesome immaterial factors coexistent with that mind.
The meaning is as explained previously.
What is wholesome formless [attainment]?
Answer: It is when, upon the falling away from or the arising of an unwholesome mind, the wholesome factors arise.
This is explained as previously in the section on the arising of wholesome formless [attainments] concomitant with an unwholesome mind.
What is the indeterminate formless?
Answer: For example, when an unwholesome mind either declines or arises, the acquisition and persistence of indeterminate dharmas occur;
furthermore, the indeterminate faculties and the great elements are nourished and augmented within that unwholesome mind.
Those dharmas undergo birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
Regarding the case where an unwholesome mind subsides and an indeterminate mind arises:
this refers to when an Arhat falls away due to the arising of the fetters of the desire realm.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the four indeterminate aggregates (*skandha*) to be abandoned through cultivation in the aforementioned eight stages.
This applies to those non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who have already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
When one falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm,
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the four indeterminate aggregates (*skandha*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) belonging to the seven stages;
this continues even until the point where one has already become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
When one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm,
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the four neutral aggregates (skandha) to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) belonging to that same level.
When ordinary beings who have already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness fall away due to the arising of unwholesome obsessions,
their minds are associated with [the afflictions] of the seven stages to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
And for those [factors] abandoned through seeing in the desire realm,
the four indeterminate aggregates arise simultaneously with their respective acquisitions (prāpti),
up until the point where one has already become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
When one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna gives rise to unwholesome obsessions and falls away,
that mind is associated with [the afflictions] of one stage to be abandoned by both insight and cultivation.

Furthermore, for those who have already become free from the defilements of the desire realm, the acquisitions (prāpti) of the four indeterminate aggregates that are abandoned through vision arise simultaneously.
When one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna falls away due to the arising of unwholesome obsessions,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the four neutral aggregates (*skandha*) to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) belonging to the desire realm.
Regarding the arising of an unwholesome mind from a neutral state:
this refers to one who dies in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and is reborn in the desire realm.
At the moment of linking existence (*pratisandhi*), that unwholesome mind is associated with the defilements to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation belonging to the seven stages.

Furthermore, the acquisitions (*prāpti*) that arise simultaneously with the four indeterminate aggregates abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm, as well as the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), are all indeterminate.
Some say: [this applies to all].
It also arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the indeterminate minds and mental factors abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm;
that is to say, with the four aggregates of the well-practiced modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*).
Even when one dies from the first dhyāna and is reborn in the desire realm,
at the moment of linking rebirth with an unwholesome mind,
that mind is associated with the four aggregates of the desire realm that are indeterminate and abandoned by vision.
The acquisitions (prāpti) of the indeterminate matter and formations aggregates abandoned through cultivation arise simultaneously with them;
some say they also arise simultaneously with the acquisitions of the indeterminate minds and mental factors abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
As previously stated,
this applies even to those who abide in an unwholesome mind,
up until the point where those phenomena undergo arising, aging, subsistence, and impermanence.
This refers to the time when the thirty-four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of ordinary beings,
or the four underlying tendencies of noble ones, flow forth continuously for a long duration; at that time,
the sense faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are nourished and increased.
That mind arises together with those four characteristics;
the rest is as previously explained.
All dharmas that are indeterminate and formless arise [in this manner].
Are those factors associated with an indeterminate mind?
Answer: When various indeterminate formless factors arise, those factors may be associated with an indeterminate mind.
It may be associated with a wholesome mind,
or it may be associated with an unwholesome mind.
What is associated with a neutral (avyākṛta) mind?
Answer: Those dharmas associated with that mind,
as well as those coexistent with that mind which are indeterminate (avyākṛta) and formless (arūpa),
are explained in meaning as previously stated.
How is it associated with a wholesome mind?
Answer: It is as when, through the advancement of a wholesome mind, unwholesome dharmas arise;
and while abiding in a wholesome mind, the unwholesome faculties are nourished and the primary elements are augmented.
Those dharmas undergo birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
This is as previously explained regarding the arising of indeterminate formless states concomitant with wholesome minds.
How is it [with] unwholesome minds?
Answer: Just as when an unwholesome mind either regresses or arises, the acquisition of indeterminate dharmas occurs;
furthermore, while abiding in an unwholesome mind, the indeterminate faculties are nourished and the great elements are augmented.
Those dharmas undergo birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
This is as previously explained regarding the indeterminate formless states (arūpa-dharma) that arise together with an unwholesome mind;
it applies even if those dharmas arise together with an indeterminate mind.
Are those factors indeterminate and formless?
Answer: Those factors that arise together with an indeterminate mind are either indeterminate and formless or wholesome and formless.
Or [it is] not unwholesome.
What is the indeterminate formless?
Answer: Those dharmas that are associated with that mind.
The indeterminate formless states coexistent with that mind are explained as before.
What are the wholesome formless states?
Answer: Just as when an indeterminate mind either regresses or arises, the acquisition of wholesome dharmas occurs;
this is explained in the same manner as the previous discussion on the arising of wholesome formless states together with an indeterminate mind.
What, then, are unwholesome formless states?
Answer: It is as in the case where, when an indeterminate mind either regresses or arises, unwholesome dharmas arise.
This is explained as before regarding the arising of unwholesome formless [dharmas] together with an indeterminate mind.
Are all those dharmas that arise from the formless realm of the desire realm accompanied by a mind of the desire realm?
Answer: When dharmas of the desire realm arise as formless,
those dharmas are either concomitant with a mind of the desire realm or concomitant with a mind of the form realm.
Or it is associated with the mind of the formless realm,
or it is associated with a mind that is unconditioned by any realm.
What is associated with the mind of the desire realm?
Answer: All phenomena that are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind are associated with the formless [factors] of the desire realm;
those which are formless of the desire realm are as follows.
This refers to the mental factors of the desire realm that coexist with that mind;
as for the "formless" [factors] of the desire realm,
it refers to the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of those phenomena.
Within this context, there is also the arising of similar types [of minds],
but it is not mentioned here due to brevity.
How does it coexist with the mind of the form realm?
Answer: Just as when a mind of the form realm arises or progresses toward excellence, the dharmas of the desire realm arise;
