and while abiding in a mind of the form realm, the sense faculties of the desire realm are nourished and the primary elements are augmented.
Those dharmas undergo birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
As for the arising of a mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) from a mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
this refers to one who passes away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
When one is born into the fourth dhyāna,
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the fruit of the fourth dhyāna and the various mind-moments of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) belonging to the desire realm.
Furthermore, when one is born into the first dhyāna,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the first dhyāna’s fruition and the various categories of supramundane supernormal powers (abhijñā-phala-citta).
Just as one who dies in the formless realm is born in the form realm,
so it is for one who dies in a higher stage and is born in a lower stage. Furthermore,
when a mind of the form realm arises through superior progress, a mind of the desire realm can also arise.
This refers to when one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm by means of the mundane path:
at the moment the ninth uninterrupted path ceases and the path of liberation arises.
That mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the fruit of the first dhyāna and the various classes of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) belonging to the desire realm;
this continues until one has abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
When the ninth path of uninterrupted realization ceases and the path of liberation arises,
that mind is associated with the fruit of the fourth dhyāna.
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the classes of minds resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) in the desire realm arise simultaneously [with those minds].

This also occurs at the time of the mundane path of preparation (*laukika-prayoga-mārga*) when one who has already abandoned the defilements of the desire realm— being one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*)— transforms their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the various categories of minds resulting from the meditative attainments (*dhyāna*) as appropriate,
as well as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the desire realm,
based upon the *anāgamya* concentration.
Up to the fourth dhyāna,
when a time-liberated arhat refines their faculties (indriya-saṃvaraṇa) to become immovable (akopya),
that mind is associated with the fruit of whichever dhyāna is appropriate.
In the category of the supernormal fruit-mind (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) of the desire realm, all acquisitions (*prāpti*) arise simultaneously;

this also applies to the five preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*), five uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), and two paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that induce the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Furthermore, at the time of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) for the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) of the minds of others in the mundane realm,
and at the time of the intermediate mind during the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, one gives rise to the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
The first three liberations, the eight bases of mastery,
and the first eight totalities arise based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) up to the fourth dhyāna. Furthermore,

when conventional analytical knowledge (*saṃvṛti-pratisaṃvid*) increases, the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), and the ultimate concentration (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*) arise.
And at the time of increase, based on the *anāgamya* concentration up to the fourth *dhyāna*,
one gives rise to mundane virtues such as the emptiness-of-emptiness, the wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and the signlessness-of-signlessness.

Furthermore, at the time of increase, that mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the various categories of minds resulting from the meditative attainments (*dhyāna*) as appropriate,
as well as the minds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
and the minds abiding in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
As for those phenomena that undergo birth, aging, subsistence, and impermanence:
this refers to when one is born into the desire realm and enters a meditative absorption of the form realm,
whereby the sense faculties and the primary elements are nourished and increased.
That mind arises together with those four characteristics.
How does it coexist with a mind of the formless realm?
Answer: As when one abides in a mind of the formless realm.
When the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that nourish the faculties of the desire realm increase,
those factors undergo arising, aging, duration, and impermanence;
that is to say, when one enters the formless meditative absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) while remaining in the desire realm.
The faculties (*indriya*) and great elements (*mahābhūta*) are nourished and increased; that mind arises together with those four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
How does it arise together with an unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*) mind?
Answer: It is as when an unconditioned mind arises through the attainment of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*) in the dharmas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, when one abides in a mind that is unbound, the faculties of the desire realm are nourished and the primary elements (mahābhūta) are augmented;
those factors undergo arising, aging, duration, and impermanence.
When there is the acquisition of a superior, unbound mind, the acquisition of factors belonging to the desire realm arises.
This refers to the time when one abides in the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

At that moment, that mind arises simultaneously with the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the category of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) pertaining to the desire realm, which are cultivated at the conclusion of the two clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) regarding suffering, origin, and cessation.
When one abandons the defilements of the desire realm by means of the untainted path,
at the moment the ninth uninterrupted path ceases and the path of liberation arises.
That mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the fruit of the first dhyāna,
as well as the various types of super-knowledge (*abhijñā*)-fruition minds of the desire realm;
this continues until one becomes free from the defilements of the third dhyāna by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
When the ninth path of immediate succession ceases and the path of liberation arises,
that mind is conjoined with the fruit of the fourth dhyāna.
The acquisitions (prāpti) of the classes of minds resulting from supernormal powers (abhijñā-phala-citta) in the desire realm arise simultaneously;
they cease at the moment the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) arises and the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) emerges.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the fruits of the respective dhyānas,
the various classes of minds resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) in the desire realm,
and the acquisitions of the wholesome dharmas of the desire realm obtained at that time.
Having already become free from the defilement of desire,
one who possesses liberation through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
At the time of the uncontaminated path of preparation (*anāsrava-prayoga-mārga*):
Some say that at the time of the path of liberation as well,
that mind is associated with the fruit of whichever dhyāna is appropriate.
The acquisitions of the classes of minds resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) in the desire realm arise simultaneously.
This occurs at the time when an Arhat liberated by occasion (*samaya-vimukta*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become one who is immovable (*akopya*),
specifically during the untainted path of preparation (*anāsrava-prayoga-mārga*) based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*) up to the fourth dhyāna.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the fruits of the respective dhyānas and the classes of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) belonging to the desire realm;
this occurs at the time of the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) based on all stages.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the fruits of the four dhyānas,
the various acquisition-sets of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the desire realm,

and the acquisitions of the wholesome dharmas of the desire realm obtained at that time; this occurs when the untainted supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñānābhijñā*) arises.
When practicing the mixed cultivation of dhyāna during the initial and final moments of mind,
or when the untainted analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and so forth increase based on the access concentration up to the fourth dhyāna,
that mind [attains] the fruit of whichever dhyāna is appropriate.

Regarding the simultaneous arising of the acquisitions (*prāpti*) associated with the classes of mind that result from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) in the desire realm, as well as those abiding in a mind not bound to any realm (*apratisaṃyukta-citta*),
up to the production, aging, duration, and impermanence of those dharmas:
this refers to when one enters the untainted (*anāsrava*) attainments of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) while born in the desire realm.
The sense faculties and the primary elements are nourished and increased;
that mind arises simultaneously with those four characteristics.
Even if the dharma arises together with a mind of the desire realm.
Are those phenomena formless (*ārūpya*) within the desire realm?
Answer: Those phenomena that arise simultaneously with the mind of the desire realm are either formless within the desire realm [or otherwise].
Either formless [states] belonging to the realm of form,
or formless [states] belonging to the formless realm,
or formless [states] that are unconditioned (unbound).
What are the formless [factors] of the desire realm?
Answer: All dharmas that are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind.
The meaning of "formless" in the desire realm is as explained previously.
What is the form realm being non-existent?
Answer: It is as with the mind of the desire realm;
whether through falling away or through rebirth, the dharmas of the form realm arise.
Regarding the arising of a mind of the form realm through the retrogression of a mind of the desire realm:
this refers to when noble ones who have already become detached from the defilements of the form realm fall away due to the arising of the fetters of the desire realm.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) belonging to the four stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
up until the point where one has already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna but has not yet become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna.
When one falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) belonging to one stage of the form realm.
This applies even if the person is an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm.
When one falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all dharmas— both those abandoned by insight and those abandoned by cultivation— belonging to the four stages of the form realm,
up until the point where one has already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
When one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna falls away due to the arising of the fetters of the desire realm,

that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all dharmas— both those to be abandoned by insight and those to be abandoned by cultivation— that belong to the single level of the form realm.
Regarding the arising of a mind of the form realm from a mind of the desire realm:
this refers to when one dies in the formless realm and is born into the desire realm;
at that time, that mind [of the desire realm] arises together with the four stages of the form realm.
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of dharmas abandoned by seeing and cultivation arise simultaneously;
this continues until the time one dies from the second dhyāna and is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
at which point that mind [is associated] with a single stage of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of dharmas abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) arise simultaneously [with those dharmas].
How is it that there are no formless [dharmas] in the formless realm?
Answer: It is like when, upon the falling away (*parihāṇi*) or the arising (*upapatti*) of a desire-realm mind, the acquisition of a formless-realm dharma arises.
Regarding the arising of a mind of the formless realm upon the regression of a mind of the desire realm:
this refers to when an Arhat regresses by giving rise to the fetters of the desire realm;
at that time, that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all the dharmas abandoned through cultivation belonging to the four stages of the formless realm.
If a non-returner who has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm,
that mind is associated with the three stages of the formless realm.
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) arise simultaneously [with them],

up until one has become detached from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) but has not yet become detached from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
When one falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the various factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) belonging to one stage of the formless realm.
When ordinary beings who have already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness fall away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm,
their minds are associated with the three stages of the formless realm.
The acquisitions (prāpti) of the dharmas to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation arise simultaneously,
up until the point where one has already become free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana),
but has not yet become free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana).
When one falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation belonging to one stage of the formless realm.
Regarding the arising of a mind of the desire realm from a mind of the formless realm:
this refers to when one dies in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and is reborn in the desire realm;
at that time, that mind is associated with the three stages of the formless realm.
The acquisitions (prāpti) of the dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation arise simultaneously;
this continues until, when one dies from the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and is reborn in the Desire Realm,
that mind [is associated] with one stage of the Formless Realm.
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of dharmas abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) arise simultaneously [with those dharmas].
How is it that there are acquisitions of non-bondage (*apratisaṃyukta*) in the formless realm?
Answer: It is like the arising of the acquisition of a non-bondage dharma when one falls away from a mind of the desire realm.
This refers to when an Arhat falls away from superior faculties and abides in inferior faculties;
at that time, his mind of the desire realm arises together with the non-bondage acquisition (*aprāpti*) belonging to the category of inferior faculties.
It is the same when one who is in training (*śaikṣa*) falls away from a superior lineage and abides in an inferior lineage.
If noble ones who have already become free from the defilements of desire fall away due to the arising of two grades of fetters— the lowest-of-the-low and the low-of-the-middle— of the desire realm,
their minds arise simultaneously with the acquisitions of the fruit of once-returner and the paths of superior fruits.
If, at the time of falling away due to the arising of lower or upper-grade fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
one is still able to maintain the application of effort (*prāyoga*),
that mind likewise arises together with the aforementioned non-bondage acquisitions (*apratisaṃyukta-prāpti*).
If there are those who are unable to protect their intensified practice,
their minds arise only together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
When they fall away due to the arising of the five grades of fetters— ranging from the middling-inferior up to the upper-middling— [they regress].
That mind arises simultaneously with the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry and the paths leading to higher fruits;
even when one falls away due to the arising of the most intense fetters,
one is still able to maintain the application of effort.
That mind also arises simultaneously with the aforementioned acquisitions (prāpti) of non-bondage; however,
for one who is unable to maintain the application of effort (prayoga),
that mind arises only simultaneously with the various acquisitions of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala).

If a once-returner regresses due to the arising of any of the six grades of fetters (*paryavasthāna*), his mind accordingly also arises together with the aforementioned acquisitions (*aprāpti*) of non-bondage.
Question: Does the acquisition of the non-bound dharmas also arise when there is progress of the mind in the desire realm?
Whether by means of generosity,
or by means of ethical discipline,
or by means of learning.
Alternatively, it may be by means of volition (*cetanā*) that one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the evil destinies and so forth.
Why is this not mentioned here?
Some say: "When something that ought to be stated is not stated,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete."
According to this explanation,
although non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is not bound,
its acquisition (prāpti) is not unbound.
In this context, it is not stated because it is said that non-tied [dharmas] can arise.
Regarding those dharmas that arise in the form realm or the formless realm,
are those dharmas concomitant with a mind of the form realm?
Answer: When phenomena of the form realm or the formless realm arise,
those phenomena are either concomitant with a mind of the form realm or concomitant with a mind of the desire realm.
Either it is concomitant with a mind of the formless realm,
or it is concomitant with a mind that is unconditioned (unbound).
What is meant by being concomitant with a mind of the form realm?
Answer: All phenomena are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind.
The meaning of "form" and "formless" is as explained previously.
How do they coexist with the mind of the desire realm?
Answer: As when a mind of the desire realm either regresses or arises, dharmas of the form realm arise.
This is as previously explained regarding the arising of form and formless [dharmas] concomitant with a mind of the desire realm.
How is it associated with the mind of the formless realm?
Answer: As when one dwells in the mind of the formless realm, the faculties of the form realm are nourished and the primary elements are augmented.
Those phenomena undergo birth, aging, duration, and impermanence;
that is to say, when one is born into the form realm or enters a meditative absorption of the formless realm,
the sense faculties and the primary elements are nurtured and increased.
That mind arises together with those four characteristics.
How does it arise together with an unconditioned (apratiṣṭhita) mind?
Answer: It is as when an unconditioned mind gives rise to the attainment of superior dharmas of the form realm.
Furthermore, when one dwells with a mind that is unbound,
the sense-faculties of the form realm are nourished and the primary elements are augmented;
those factors undergo arising, aging, subsistence, and impermanence.
Regarding the arising of unattached, superior form-sphere acquisitions:
this refers to the time when one abides in the three types of subsequent knowledge (*trividha-anvaya-jñāna*) during the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

At that time, those minds arise simultaneously with the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) belonging to the category of mundane conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) of the form realm, which are cultivated at the conclusion of the three clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, origin, and cessation.
One becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm by means of the untainted path.
If the untainted [path] serves as the preparatory application,
it includes all the paths of preparation and the nine paths of immediate succession.
At the time of the ninth path of liberation,
that mind arises together with all the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the form-realm paths being cultivated in the future.
At the time of the ninth path of liberation...
It also arises simultaneously with the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the result of the first dhyāna and the classes of minds that are the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the form realm;
for one leaves the first dhyāna by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Up to the point of being defiled by the third dhyāna,
if the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
then there are the various paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*) and the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
At the time of the nine paths of liberation,
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the various forms-realm paths cultivated for the future.
At the time of the final path of liberation, [it likewise arises].
It also arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the second through the fourth dhyānas,
as well as the mental states associated with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) in the form realm;
this occurs when one abandons the defilements of the fourth dhyāna by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
And by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*),
up to the fourth dhyāna,
one becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
When one is in the various preparatory paths (prayoga-mārga) with untainted (anāsrava) application,
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the form-realm paths (rūpāvacara-mārga) cultivated for the future;
this continues until the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) ceases.
When the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) arises,
that mind arises simultaneously with all the acquisitions (prāpti) of the wholesome states of the form realm (rūpadhātu) obtained at that time,
as well as with the fruits of the meditative concentrations (dhyāna) as appropriate.
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the classes of mind resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) in the form realm arise simultaneously [with those minds].

This also applies when one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire— being one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*)— refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*),
provided that the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*) during that path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
Some say that at the time of the path of liberation,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the various paths of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) cultivated for the future.

When one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire and possesses liberation through faith (śraddhādhimukta) undergoes the refinement of faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
if the untainted (anāsrava) serves as the preparatory application (prayoga), then at the time of that path of preparation (prayoga-mārga), some say:
And at the time of the path of liberation,
that mind [attains] the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the future paths of the form realm that are being cultivated,
as well as the fruits of the dhyānas as appropriate.
The acquisitions (prāpti) of the classes of minds resulting from supernormal powers (abhijñā-phala-citta) in the form realm arise simultaneously.
This occurs at the time when an Arhat liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) to become unshakable (akopya),
relying on the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga) that is untainted (anāsrava) and ranging from the threshold concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna) up to the fourth dhyāna.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the dhyāna-path of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to be cultivated in the future,

as well as with the acquisitions of the various classes of minds associated with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) in the form realm, which correspond to the fruits of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) as appropriate.
At the time of the ninth path of liberation in all stages,
that mind, together with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the wholesome states of the form realm obtained at that time,
as well as the fruits of the four dhyānas, [arises].
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the classes of mind associated with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) in the form realm arise simultaneously [with those minds].
This also occurs at the time of arising the untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*),
and at the time of the initial and final moments of the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas (*dhyāna-vyavakiraṇa*).
Based on the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*),
up to the untainted (*anāsrava*) states of the fourth dhyāna,
when the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) increase.
That is to say, when one gives rise to the untainted foundations of mindfulness based on those various stages,
that mind, together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the form-realm paths to be cultivated in the future,
as well as the fruits of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) as appropriate, [arise].
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the classes of minds resulting from supernatural powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) in the form realm arise simultaneously;
as do those of one abiding in a mind that is not bound (*apratisaṃyukta*),
up until the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of those dharmas.
This refers to when one born in the form realm enters the untainted *anāgamya* concentration,
up to the *ākiṃcanyāyatana* concentration; at that time,
the sense faculties and the primary elements are nourished and augmented.
That mind arises together with those four characteristics.
If a phenomenon arises together with a mind of the form realm,
is that phenomenon also of the formless realm?
Answer: All phenomena that arise simultaneously with a mind of the form realm (rūpadhātu) are either of the form realm or the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
or they are of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or the formless realm.
Or there may be no [matter] in the formless realm,
or matter that is unconditioned by the formless.
What is matter that is not in the form realm?
Answer: All phenomena are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind;
their existence as formless within the realm of form has been explained as before.
What, then, is meant by "formless in the desire realm"?
Answer: Just as when a mind of the form realm arises or progresses toward higher stages, dharmas of the desire realm arise;
and while abiding in a mind of the form realm, [dharmas of] the desire realm [arise].
The sense faculties are nourished and the primary elements (mahābhūta) are augmented;
those dharmas undergo birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
This is as previously explained regarding the arising of a form-sphere mind accompanied by an immaterial [mind] in the desire realm.
What is the formless [attainment] of the formless realm?
Answer: Just as when the mind of the form realm either regresses or arises, the acquisition of dharmas of the formless realm occurs.
Regarding the arising of a mind of the formless realm through falling away from a mind of the form realm:
this refers to when an arhat falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the form realm;
at that time, that mind [is associated] with the four stages of the formless realm.
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) arise simultaneously [with those dharmas].
When non-returners (*anāgāmin*), who have already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
fall away due to the arising of the envelopment (*paryavasthāna*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation belonging to the three stages of the formless realm,
up until the point where one has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space.
When one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness falls away due to the arising of the fetters of the Form Realm,
that mind is associated with one level of the Formless Realm.
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation arise simultaneously.
This is the case when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), who has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
falls away due to the arising of a defilement belonging to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all dharmas to be abandoned by vision and cultivation belonging to the three stages of the formless realm,
up until the point where one has already become free from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Space.
When one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness falls away due to the arising of the fetters of the Form Realm,
that mind is associated with one level of the Formless Realm.
The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation arise simultaneously [with their respective dharmas].
Regarding the case where a mind of the form realm arises and an acquisition of a dharma of the formless realm arises:
this refers to when one dies in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and is reborn in the form realm.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation belonging to the three stages of the formless realm,
up until the time one dies in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and is reborn in the form realm.

That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all dharmas belonging to one stage of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). How,
then, is it not bound to the formless realm?
Answer: Just as when the mind of the form realm undergoes either decline or progress, the arising of factors not bound [to any realm] occurs.
Regarding the case where factors not bound arise through the decline of the mind of the form realm: [it is as follows].
That is to say, when an Arhat falls away due to the arising of defilements belonging to the form realm,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions of the fruit of Non-returner and the paths of superior fruits.
Regarding the arising of a superior, unconditioned mind of the form realm:
this refers to noble ones who, by means of the mundane path, become detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the third dhyāna.
If the mundane [path] serves as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*),
then at the time of all preparatory, uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and liberation paths (*vimukti-mārga*),
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the future unconditioned dharmas (*apratisaṃyukta-dharma*) that are being cultivated.
Relying on the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) up to the fourth dhyāna,
one becomes detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
If conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) serves as the preliminary application (*prayoga*).
At the time of all paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the future unbound dharmas (*apratisaṃyukta-dharma*) that are being cultivated.
This applies when one who is resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) and becomes one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Furthermore, based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) up to the fourth dhyāna,
a time-liberated (*samaya-vimukta*) arhat refines their faculties to become unshakable (*akopya*).
If they employ the mundane path as their preparatory application (*prayoga*), [they achieve this].
At the time of all paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the future unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*) dharmas that are being cultivated.
This is also the case for noble ones (*ārya*) when they produce the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) during the paths of preparation.
The five paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and two paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
as well as the supramundane supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna-abhijñā*) at the time of the path of liberation.
When practicing the intermediate state of meditative absorption (dhyāna) in a mixed manner,
if noble beings (ārya) give rise to the four immeasurables (apramāṇa) and the first three liberations (vimokṣa).
At the time of the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the first eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
one gives rise to the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Furthermore, relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*) up to the fourth dhyāna,
when increasing the conventional analytical knowledge, one gives rise to the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā*) and the knowledge resulting from resolution (*praṇidhijñāna*).
At the time of the limit-attainments (*sīmā-vimokṣa*) and during the period of intensification,
one relies on the access concentration (*anāgamya*) up to the fourth dhyāna to give rise to the emptiness-of-emptiness, the wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and the signlessness-of-signlessness.
Furthermore, the noble one, relying upon that very stage,
gives rise to the contemplation of impurity and the mindfulness of breathing.
When mundane applications of mindfulness and other such virtues are being cultivated and increased,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃyukta-dharma*) to be cultivated in the future.
Question: When a mind of the form realm arises, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the non-bound (*apratisaṃyukta*) dharmas also arises.

For example, when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the fourth dhyāna, that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisition of the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the aggregates abandoned through vision and cultivation belonging to the third dhyāna.
Even when one dies in a higher stage and is reborn in the First Dhyāna,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the aggregates abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the Desire Realm.
Why is this not mentioned here?
Answer: Some say that when something ought to be stated but is not, one should know that this meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
This is how it should be explained.

At that time, although the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) thus attained is not bound [to any realm], its various acquisitions (*prāpti*) are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Since they are not unbound, they are not mentioned.
From the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda school, Volume 159.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 165,
composed by the [Five] Hundred Great Arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhiskandha). Chapter One: The Sub-section on Attainment (Prāpti-nirdeśa), Part Four. All phenomena that are formless arise from the formless realm.
Are those dharmas concomitant with a mind of the formless realm?
Answer: Regarding all dharmas that arise as formless within the formless realm, those dharmas are either concomitant with a mind of the formless realm or not.
Either it is concomitant with a mind of the desire realm,
or concomitant with a mind of the form realm,
or concomitant with a mind that is unconditioned (unbound).
What is associated with the mind of the formless realm?
Answer: Those phenomena that are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind;
the meaning of "formless" regarding the formless realm is as explained previously.
What is co-existent with the mind of the desire realm?
Answer: For example, when the mind of the desire realm undergoes either retrogression or arising, the acquisition of dharmas of the formless realm occurs.
This is as previously explained regarding the arising of formless-sphere [states] together with desire-sphere minds.
How do they arise together with form-sphere minds?
Answer: As when a form-sphere mind undergoes either retrogression or rebirth.
The arising of dharmas belonging to the formless realm occurs.
This is as previously explained regarding the arising of formless [dharmas] concomitant with the mind of the form realm.
How is it that they arise concomitant with a mind that is unconditioned (unbound)?
Answer: It is like the arising of dharmas of the formless realm when the mind that is unconditioned (unbound) advances;
that is to say, when one becomes detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna by means of the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga).
At the time of the nine paths of uninterrupted activity and the nine paths of liberation,
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the formless realm paths cultivated for the future.
By means of the untainted path, one becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of nothingness;
if the untainted path serves as the preparatory application.
At the time of all the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
and the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
That mind arises simultaneously with all the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the formless realm paths to be cultivated in the future;
this is the general statement.
Within this, if one relies on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
Up to the fourth dhyāna,
for one who has become detached from the defilements of the three lower formless attainments,
with the exception of the path of preparation.
Based on the lower three formless attainments, one becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
If the untainted is taken as the preparatory application,
then at the time of that path of preparation:
That mind arises simultaneously with all acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the formless realm paths to be cultivated in the future,
and it relies upon all stages (*bhūmi*),
having become free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Finally, when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises at the moment of the path of final liberation,
that mind arises together with all the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the wholesome states of the formless realm obtained at that time. At that point,
a *samayavimukta* Arhat refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) to become unshakable (*akopyadharman*).
If one relies on the three formless attainments with the untainted as the preparatory application,
at the time of that path of preparation:
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the formless realm paths cultivated in the future;
and at the time of the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) based on any stage,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions of the wholesome states of the formless realm obtained at that time.
When arising in untainted liberation;
when increasing the untainted analytical knowledges based on the formless attainments;
and when arising in the formless untainted applications of mindfulness.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the various paths of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that are to be cultivated in the future.
Suppose there is a phenomenon that arises simultaneously with a mind of the formless realm; is that phenomenon also formless?
Answer: All phenomena that arise simultaneously with a mind of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) are either formless phenomena belonging to the formless realm,
or formless phenomena belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Either formless states belonging to the realm of form,
or formless states that are unconditioned (not bound).
What are the formless states belonging to the formless realm?
Answer: All dharmas are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind;
the meaning of "formless" (*arūpa*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) has been explained as before.
What, then, is "formless" in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
Answer: Just as when the mind abides in the formless realm, the faculties of the desire realm are nourished and the primary elements are augmented;
those phenomena possess arising, aging, duration, and impermanence.
This is as previously explained regarding the arising of a formless-sphere mind from the desire realm.
What is the formless [mind] of the form realm?
Answer: It is like abiding in a formless-sphere mind.
In the form realm, the sense faculties are nourished and the primary elements are augmented;
those factors undergo birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
This is as previously explained regarding the arising of the formless mind within the form realm.
What is meant by "unconditioned [states] of the formless realm"?
Answer: It is as when the mind of the formless realm undergoes either retrogression or advancement, whereby the arising of unconditioned dharmas occurs.
Regarding the arising of non-bondage upon the regression of a mind belonging to the formless realm:
this refers to when an Arhat regresses due to the arising of the fetters (paryavasthāna) of the formless realm;
at that time, that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the fruit of Non-returner and the paths of superior fruits.
Regarding the arising of a mind of the formless realm that is superior and non-bound:
this refers to those noble ones who, by means of the mundane path,
become detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna.
If the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) serves as the application (*prayoga*),
then that path of application consists of nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*anantaryamārga*).
At the time of the nine paths of liberation,
as well as when a noble one uses the mundane path to become detached from the defilements of the lower three formless realms.
If the mundane path serves as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*),
then at the time of all preparatory, uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and liberation (*vimukti*) paths,

as well as when one relies on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) to become detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
If one practices the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) by means of the conventional [path], at the time of that path of preparation (*prayogamārga*),
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the future unconditioned dharmas (*apratisaṃyukta*). At that time,
an Arhat of occasional liberation (*samayavimukta*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become immovable (*akopyadharman*).
Based on the formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti):
when one practices the preparatory stage (prayoga-mārga) with mundane (laukika) application;
or when a noble one (ārya) gives rise to the contaminated liberations (sāsrava-vimokṣa) and the two spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) of the formless realm.
When the untainted analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) increase based on the formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti),
one gives rise to conventional mindfulness (saṃvṛti-smṛti) based on those formless absorptions;
this occurs while abiding in emptiness-of-emptiness, wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and signlessness-of-signlessness.

When one gives rise to the subtle mind associated with the perception of entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the unconditioned dharmas (*apratisaṃyukta-dharma*) cultivated for the future.
Question: When a mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) arises...
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-bound dharmas (*apratisaṃyukta-dharma*) also arises.
For example, when one dies in a higher stage of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn in a lower stage,

that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisition of the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of all defiled states to be abandoned by vision and cultivation belonging to the immediately lower stage of rebirth.
Regarding this, why is it not mentioned?
Some say that when something should have been stated but is not, one should know that the meaning is incomplete.
According to this explanation,
although the cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) attained at that time is not bound [to any realm],
its acquisition is bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and is not unbound.
Therefore, it is not stated:
"When those dharmas that are training and formless arise,
are those dharmas concomitant with the mind of training?"
Answer: When dharmas that are to-be-trained (śaikṣa) arise as formless [attainments],
those dharmas are either associated with a mind that is to-be-trained,
or they are associated with a mind that is neither-to-be-trained-nor-beyond-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
What is associated with the mind of one in training?
Answer: Those dharmas that are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind.
"Training in the formless [realms] associated with that mind":
this refers to the mental factors (caitta-dharma) of training that coexist with that mind.
Regarding the study of the formless:
it refers to the arising, aging, abiding, and impermanence of those phenomena;
herein, there is likewise the occurrence of homogeneous origination.
It is not stated because it is abbreviated.
How does it coexist with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: It is as in the case of a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Whether there is regression or advancement,
when a learner (śaikṣa) gives rise to a state that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa), there is regression from the learner state;
as for the arising [of such a state] from the learner state:
That is to say, when an Arhat arises from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
or even at the time of falling away through the eight grades of fetters following the first dhyāna,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the fruit of Non-returner and the paths of superior fruits.
If, when one falls away from the first dhyāna due to extremely intense fetters,
one is still able to guard the application of effort,
that mind likewise arises together with the previously acquired training.
As for those who are unable to guard their intensified practice,
their minds arise only together with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala).

When those non-returners fall away due to the arising of the two grades of fetters (paryavasthāna)— the lowest-of-the-low and the low-of-the-middle— of the desire realm, [their minds arise only with those acquisitions].
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions of the fruit of once-returning and the paths leading to superior fruits.
Even when one falls away due to the arising of lower-grade or upper-grade fetters,
one is still able to protect the application of practice.
That mind also arises together with the acquisitions (prāpti) of what was previously learned.
For one who is unable to maintain the preparatory effort (prayoga),
that mind arises only together with the acquisitions of the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
When one falls away due to the arising of the five grades of fetters— ranging from the middle and lower up to the upper-middle—
the mind is accompanied by the acquisitions (prāpti) of the fruit of stream-entry and the paths leading to higher fruits.
When one falls away due to the arising of the uppermost grade of fetters, [the same applies].
Even those who are able to guard their application of effort,
their minds likewise arise together with the previously acquired training;
as for those who are unable to guard their application of effort, [their minds do not].
That mind arises only together with the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
If it is a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), then whichever of the six grades of fetters (*paryavasthāna*) causes a regression,
that mind likewise arises together with the acquisitions of a trainee (*śaikṣa*) as previously described, according to its respective correspondence.
Regarding the arising of a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner through the superior progress of a learner:
this refers to those learners who, by means of the mundane path, become free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness.
If the mundane [path] serves as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*),
it occurs at all times during the preparatory, uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and liberation (*vimukti*) paths,
as well as when one is free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
If the mundane [path] serves as the preparatory application,
then at the time of that path of preparation,
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (prāpti) of all the dharmas of training that are to be cultivated in the future.
One who has attained liberation through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
When employing the mundane as the preparatory application (prayoga), at the time of that path of preparation (prayogamārga),
this learner (śaikṣa) brings forth the various supernormal powers (abhijñā).
The various paths of preparation,
the five paths of uninterrupted transition,
and the two paths of liberation.
Furthermore, at the time of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) for the supernormal knowledge of others' minds regarding the mundane;
when a learner (*śaikṣa*) practices the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) through mixed cultivation during the intermediate state of mind;
and when a learner gives rise to the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
At the time of mundane liberation,
the eight bases of mastery,
and the ten totalities.
When a practitioner gives rise to the perception of entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), when their mind becomes subtle,
when they cultivate the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) or mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), or when they practice the mundane applications of mindfulness (*laukikasmṛtyupasthāna*).

That mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the dharmas to be cultivated in the future; if those dharmas arise together with a mind that is in training (*śaikṣa*), are those dharmas immaterial (*arūpa*)?
Answer: Those dharmas that arise together with a mind that is in training.
Those dharmas are either formless states of training (śaikṣa) or formless states that are neither of training nor beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What are the formless states of training?
Answer: All phenomena are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind.
The meaning of "unconditioned" (*aśaikṣa*) in the formless realm is explained as before.
What are the non-learner and non-non-learner formless states?
Answer: They are as when, through the advancement of a learner’s mind, there arises the acquisition of non-learner and non-non-learner dharmas;
and [the states] while abiding in a learner’s mind.
Neither-learner-nor-non-learner:
the nourishment of the faculties, the increase of the primary elements,
and the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of those phenomena.
Regarding the arising of a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner through the superior progress of a learner's mind:
this refers to the time when one abides in the three types of subsequent knowledge (*trividha-anvaya-jñāna*) during the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

At that time, that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the category of conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) cultivated at the conclusion of the three clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) regarding suffering, origin, and cessation.
By means of the untainted path,
one becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness;
if the untainted [path] serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
At all times during the paths of preparation, uninterrupted transition,
and liberation; and when abandoning the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
if the path of preparation is untainted (anāsrava).
At the time of that path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all the mundane paths (*laukika-mārga*) cultivated for the future,
as one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the third dhyāna.
At the time of the ninth path of liberation,
that mind also arises together with the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the category of the result-of-attainment mind (*abhisamaya-phala-citta*).
For one who has attained liberation through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), when refining their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), they become one who has reached vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
If the untainted [state] serves as the preparatory application (prayoga),
then at the time of that path of preparation, some say:
And at the moment of the path of liberation,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the mundane paths practiced in the future,
as well as those of the classes of minds resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*).
When a trainee gives rise to the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds that is untainted;
when a trainee practices the mixed cultivation of dhyāna during the initial and final moments of mind;
and when a trainee gives rise to the foundations of mindfulness that are untainted.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the mundane paths to be cultivated in the future,
as well as those belonging to the classes of minds resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*).
When a learner (*śaikṣa*) gives rise to untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*), [it arises] together with these.
Excluding the mind that is the fruition of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*), it arises simultaneously with the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) as previously described;
furthermore, while abiding in the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*), [it arises] together with the birth, aging, duration, and impermanence of those factors (*dharma*).
This refers to those in training who are born in the desire or form realms;
while abiding in the uncontaminated meditative absorptions of the form or formless realms,
their faculties and primary elements are nourished and augmented.
That mind arises together with those four characteristics.
When various dharmas that are beyond training (aśaikṣa) and formless arise,
do those dharmas arise together with a mind that is beyond training?
Answer: When dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner arise,
those dharmas are either concomitant with a mind that is a learner,
or they are concomitant with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What is associated with the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Answer: All those phenomena that are associated with that mind, as well as those that coexist with that mind;
the meaning of "unconditioned formless [phenomena]" (*aśaikṣā arūpiṇaḥ*) is as explained previously.
What is the state associated with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: It is as when, through a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, there arises the acquisition of non-learner dharmas, whether by way of falling away or by way of spiritual progress.
Regarding the arising of a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner through the retrogression of a non-learner:
this refers to when an Arhat, having retrogressed from superior faculties, abides in inferior faculties.
That mind which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the non-learner dharmas of the inferior faculty category;
so says some.
Regarding the claim that one falls away solely because afflictions manifest:
they argue that in this context one should speak only of "progress" (viśeṣagamana) and not of "falling away."
According to those who speak thus,
since one may also fall away while abiding in an unobscured-neutral state of mind,
falling away should also be mentioned here.

That is to say, one abiding in an unobscured-neutral mind may regress from the faculty of "one who attains through penetration" (kṣāntika) to abide in the faculty of "one who abides by the dharma" (sthitākampya), and so on,
up to regressing from the faculty of "one who contemplates the dharma" (cetanādharman) to abide in the faculty of "one who regresses from the dharma" (parihāṇadharman).
Regarding the arising of a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner through the superior progress of a non-learner:
this refers to a time-liberated Arhat who refines their faculties to become immovable.
If the mundane serves as the preparatory application,
then at the time of that path of preparation,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (prāpti) of all the future unlearned dharmas (aśaikṣadharma) that are being cultivated.
The Arhat brings forth the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*),
the various paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
and the five paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The two paths of liberation,
as well as the mundane supernormal power of knowing the minds of others,
at the time of the path of liberation.
When an arhat cultivates the intermediate state of dhyāna through mixed meditation,
the arhat gives rise to the four immeasurables and the mundane liberations.
At the time of the eight bases of mastery and the ten totalities,
one gives rise to the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, when the mundane unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) increase,
one gives rise to the concentration of the limit of the wish for non-contention (*araṇā-praṇidhi-jñāna-paryanta-samādhi*),
as well as the emptiness-of-emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), the wishlessness-of-wishlessness (*apraṇihitā-apraṇihita*), and the signlessness-of-signlessness (*animittā-animitta*).
Furthermore, when [the faculties] are increasing, an Arhat may give rise to the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-saṃjñā),
mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti), or mundane applications of mindfulness (laukika-smṛtyupasthāna).
When entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) with a subtle mind accompanied by the perception [of that state],
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the various dharmas of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) to be cultivated in the future;
even if those dharmas arise together with the mind of no-more-learning.
Are those factors non-learner (aśaikṣa) and formless (arūpa)?
Answer: Those factors that arise simultaneously with a non-learner mind may be non-learner and formless.
Or, it is neither-learner-nor-non-learner formless [attainment].
What is non-learner formless [attainment]?
Answer: It consists of those dharmas that are associated with that mind.
That mind is accompanied by the formless states of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);
the meaning is as explained previously.
What are the formless states that are neither of training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
Answer: It is as when, through the advancement of an Aśaikṣa mind, the arising of dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner occurs;
and while abiding in an Aśaikṣa mind, the nourishment of the faculties that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner and the increase of the primary elements (mahābhūta) take place.
Those dharmas undergo birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
Regarding the arising of a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner through the advancement of a non-learner’s mind,
this refers to the cessation [attained] by means of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
When the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) arises,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the conventional wholesome states obtained at that time,
and also, in some cases, with the mental states associated with the supernormal powers (abhijñā).
When an Arhat of occasional liberation (samayavimukta) refines their faculties to become immovable (akopya),
if they take the untainted (anāsrava) as their preparatory practice,
then at the time of that path of preparation (prayoga-mārga):
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) to be cultivated in the future,
as well as with those belonging to the category of the supernormal powers (*abhijñāphala*).
This occurs at the time of the final path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the mundane wholesome states attained at that time,
as well as those belonging to the category of the supernormal power resulting from meditative attainment (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).
This occurs when an Arhat gives rise to the untainted supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñānābhijñā*).
When an Arhat practices the mixed cultivation of dhyāna during the initial and final moments of mind,
the Arhat, relying on the form-realm meditative absorptions (rūpadhātu-samādhi),
gives rise to untainted mindfulness-establishment (anāsrava-smṛtyupasthāna) and increases untainted analytical knowledges (anāsrava-pratisaṃvid).
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the mundane paths to be cultivated in the future,
as well as the classes of minds resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).
When an Arhat gives rise to untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*), [these arise together].
Furthermore, when one gives rise to the untainted foundations of mindfulness based on the formless absorptions,
and when the untainted analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) are increasing,
with the exception of the mind of supernormal power (abhijñā-phala-citta).
That mind arises together with the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) as previously described,
and while abiding in the state of an adept (*aśaikṣa*), until those factors— namely, birth, aging, duration, and impermanence— arise;
this refers to an Arhat born in the desire realm or the form realm.
When one dwells in the untainted meditative absorptions of the form and formless realms,
the faculties and the primary elements are nourished and increased;
that mind arises simultaneously with those four characteristics.
When various phenomena that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner arise as non-form (arūpa), are those phenomena concomitant with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: When various phenomena that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner arise as non-form...
Those dharmas are either associated with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
or associated with a learner’s mind,
or associated with a non-learner’s mind.
What is associated with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Answer: It refers to all phenomena that are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind;
the meaning of "neither-learner-nor-non-learner" regarding the formless [dharmas] is as explained previously.
What is associated with the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*)?
Answer: As when the mind of one in training advances, there arises the acquisition (*prāpti*) of dharmas that are neither of one in training nor of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, when one abides in a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, the faculties are nourished and the primary elements are augmented;
those factors undergo arising, aging, duration, and impermanence.
This is to be explained as previously described for the immaterial factors arising together with a learner’s mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What is associated with the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?

Answer: It is as when, through the advancement of the mind of one beyond training, there arises the acquisition of dharmas that are neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa), and while abiding in the mind of one beyond training.
The great elements (*mahābhūta*) that nourish the faculties which are neither-learner-nor-non-learner increase,
and those factors undergo arising, aging, duration, and impermanence.
This is as previously explained regarding the immaterial [factors] that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner arising together with a non-learner mind.
If a phenomenon arises together with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, is that phenomenon a non-learner-nor-non-learner formless state?
Answer: All phenomena that arise together with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner [are such].
Those dharmas are either neither-learner-nor-non-learner immaterial phenomena,
or learner immaterial phenomena,
or non-learner immaterial phenomena.
What are the non-learner and non-non-learner immaterial factors?
Answer: Those dharmas that are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind;
the meaning of "non-learner and non-non-learner immaterial factors" is as explained previously.
What is the acquisition of the formless states of training?
Answer: It is like the mind that is neither of training nor beyond training;
when there is falling away or advancement, the acquisition of the factors of training arises.
This is as previously explained regarding the arising of a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner from the formless realm when accompanied by a learner’s [mind].
What is the formless realm of one who is beyond training?
Answer: It is like the mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Whether through falling back or through spiritual progress,
the acquisition of the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) arises.
This is as previously explained regarding the arising of the neither-learner-nor-non-learner mind (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-citta*) together with the formless [attainments] of one beyond training.
When various phenomena that are abandoned by insight arise as non-material (arūpa), are those phenomena concomitant with a mind that is abandoned by insight?
Answer: When various phenomena that are abandoned by insight arise as non-material...
Those dharmas are either associated with a mind to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) or associated with a mind to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
What is meant by being associated with a mind to be abandoned by insight?
Answer: Those dharmas are associated with that mind;
they coexist with that mind; and those formless [dharmas] to be abandoned by seeing are associated with that mind.
These are the formless [dharmas] to be abandoned by seeing.
This refers to those mental factors abandoned by insight that coexist with that mind;
as for the formless [factors] abandoned by insight,
it refers to the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of those phenomena.
In this context, there is also the arising of similar types [of minds],
but it is not mentioned here due to brevity.
How does it coexist with the mind abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
Answer: Just as when a mind abandoned by cultivation either regresses or arises, the acquisition of factors abandoned by vision occurs;
so too when a mind abandoned by cultivation regresses.
Regarding the arising of [defilements] to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*):
this refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already become free from the defilement of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
yet fall away due to the arising of the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) belonging to that sphere which are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Or, even when falling away due to the arising of the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the factors to be abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*) belonging to one stage, or even up to those belonging to eight stages.
...up until the point where one has already become free from the defilements of the desire realm but has not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna;
at that time, when one falls away due to the arising of the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the desire realm.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all factors abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) belonging to one stage.
As for the arising of the acquisition of factors abandoned by insight from a mind abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
this refers to one who passes away from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Or one is born in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
linking rebirth with a mind abandoned through cultivation belonging to that sphere;
or even up to being born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), linking rebirth with a mind abandoned through cultivation belonging to the desire realm.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the factors to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) belonging to one stage, or even up to those belonging to the eight stages;
this continues until one dies in the first dhyāna and is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
When a mind of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) links rebirth,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all dharmas of the same stage (*eka-bhūmi*) to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*),
even if those dharmas do not arise together with a mind to be abandoned by insight.
Are those factors abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) formless (*arūpa*)?
Answer: Those factors that arise together with the mind abandoned by vision are either factors abandoned by vision that are formless.
Or [those] formless [phenomena] abandoned through cultivation.
What are the formless [phenomena] abandoned through seeing?
Answer: Those phenomena that are associated with that mind.
The meaning of the immaterial factors associated with that mind which are abandoned by seeing has been explained as before.
What are the immaterial factors abandoned by cultivation?
Answer: They are like the mind abandoned by seeing, whether it is regressed from or arises again.
The arising of dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation occurs,
as does their persistence while the mind is in a state of being abandoned by seeing;
furthermore, the nourishment of the faculties and the augmentation of the primary elements belonging to those [dharmas] to be abandoned by cultivation take place.
Those dharmas undergo arising, aging, duration, and impermanence.
Regarding the mind abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) that regresses and the mind abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) that arises:
this refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
When one falls away due to the arising of fetters to be abandoned by insight pertaining to the sphere of nothingness,
or even when one falls away due to the arising of fetters to be abandoned by insight pertaining to the desire realm,
that mind is associated with the factors to be abandoned by cultivation belonging to a single stage.
Or, up to the eighth stage, the acquisitions (prāpti) of the dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation arise together;
this continues until one has already become free from the defilements of the desire realm but has not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna.

When one falls away from the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the desire realm that are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), that mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the factors of the stage [of that desire realm] that are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
As for how the arising of a mind to be abandoned by insight brings about the arising of the acquisition of factors to be abandoned by cultivation: [it occurs as follows].
That is to say, passing away from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
one is either reborn in the sphere of nothingness,
where one links rebirth with a mind that is to be abandoned by insight regarding the sphere of nothingness.
Or even when one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) with a mind that is abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) in the desire realm,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of factors abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) belonging to either one stage or up to eight stages.
Even when one dies from the first dhyāna and is reborn in the desire realm,
at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*) with a mind abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) of the desire realm,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all dharmas abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) belonging to that same level (*ekabhūmika*).
And when abiding in a mind to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),
up until those factors undergo arising, aging, duration, and impermanence;
that is to say, when the afflictions to be abandoned by insight manifest in the desire realm or the form realm.
The sense faculties and the great elements are nourished and increased;
that mind arises simultaneously with those four characteristics.
These are the formless phenomena abandoned through cultivation that arise.
Are those phenomena associated with a mind that is abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: When formless phenomena that are abandoned through cultivation arise, those phenomena are either associated with a mind abandoned through cultivation.
It is either associated with a mind abandoned through seeing,
or associated with a mind not abandoned.
What is it that is associated with a mind abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: All dharmas that are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind—namely, the formless states (*ārūpya*) to be abandoned by cultivation—are as explained previously.
How, then, are they coexistent with the mind to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
Answer: Just as when a mind abandoned by seeing either regresses or arises, dharmas abandoned by cultivation arise;
and likewise when one abides in a mind abandoned by seeing.
The nourishment of the faculties (*indriya*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the increase of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and the arising, aging, duration,

and impermanence of those factors are to be understood as explained previously regarding the formless states (*arūpa*) that arise simultaneously with the mind abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
What is meant by "concomitant with a non-abandoned mind"?

Answer: It is as when, while abiding in a non-abandoned mind, there arises the attainment of dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) during the stage of progressive advancement (viśeṣa-bhāgīya).
And it refers to abiding in a non-abandoned mind.
The faculties to be abandoned by cultivation nourish the primary elements (mahābhūta), which in turn increase;
those factors (dharma) possess arising, aging, duration, and impermanence.
As for the attainment of those factors to be abandoned by cultivation that arise through the progressive advancement of the uninterrupted mind:
This refers to the time when one abides in the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) on the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).

At that time, that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the category of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) cultivated at the conclusion of the three clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) regarding suffering, origin, and cessation; by means of this untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
If the untainted (anāsrava) serves as the preparatory stage (prayoga),
this applies at all times during the preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,
as well as when abandoning the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
If the untainted serves as the preparatory practice,
then at the time of that path of preparation,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions of all mundane paths cultivated for the future.
When one is free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the third dhyāna,
at the moment of the ninth path of liberation,
that mind also arises together with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the category of the supernormal-resulting mind (abhijñā-phala-citta).
When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) arises and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) emerges,
