that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the conventional wholesome states attained at that time,
and also, in some cases, with the mental states associated with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
When one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
if they employ the untainted (anāsrava) as their preparatory application (prayoga),
then at the time of that path of preparation (prayogamārga):
Some say that at the time of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
that mind is associated with the mundane paths (*laukika-mārga*) cultivated in the future.
Furthermore, it may also arise simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the classes of minds resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).
When an Arhat of the "liberated by occasion" (*samaya-vimukta*) type refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become "unshakable" (*akopya*),
if they employ the untainted (*anāsrava*) as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
At the time of that path of preparation,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the mundane paths (*laukikamārga*) to be cultivated in the future,
and also, in some cases, with the categories of minds resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).
At the moment of the final path of liberation,
that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the mundane wholesome states attained at that time,
as well as those belonging to the category of the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).
When arising in the supernormal knowledge of others' minds that is untainted (*anāsrava*),
and when arising at the initial and final moments of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna,
one gives rise to the untainted foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) based on the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, when the untainted analytical knowledges (anāsravāḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ) increase,

that mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the mundane paths (laukikamārga) and the classes of minds resulting from supernormal powers (abhijñā-phala-citta) that are to be cultivated in the future.
When one gives rise to untainted liberation;
when, based on the formless attainments, one gives rise to untainted applications of mindfulness;
and when untainted analytical knowledges are being increased.
Excluding the category of the mind of supernormal fruition,
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (prāpti) of others as previously described,
and it abides in a state of non-interruption.
As for those phenomena that undergo birth, aging, duration, and impermanence:
this refers to when one is born in the desire or form realms and abides in the meditative absorptions (samādhi) of the form realm, the formless realm, or the untainted (anāsrava),
whereby the sense faculties and the primary elements (mahābhūta) are nurtured and increased.
That mind arises together with those four characteristics.
If a phenomenon arises together with a mind that is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
is that phenomenon an immaterial state (*arūpa*) to be abandoned by cultivation?
Answer: Those phenomena that arise together with a mind abandoned through cultivation may be formless phenomena abandoned through cultivation,
or they may be formless phenomena abandoned through vision.
Or, there are those that are not abandoned by the formless [attainments]. What are the formless states to be abandoned by cultivation?
Answer: Those dharmas associated with that mind.
The meaning of the immaterial factors (*ārūpya*) associated with that mind which are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) has been explained as before.
What are the immaterial factors to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*)?
Answer: Just as when the mind to be abandoned by cultivation either regresses or arises.
The arising of dharmas abandoned by seeing occurs;
this is as previously explained regarding the arising of formless states abandoned by seeing together with minds abandoned by cultivation.
What is the non-abandonment?
As with the mind abandoned through cultivation,
whether there is falling back or superior progress,
the acquisition of the dharmas not subject to abandonment arises.
Regarding the arising of the attainment of the mind abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) without abandoning [the state of being an Arhat]:
this refers to when an Arhat falls away from superior faculties (indriya) and abides in inferior faculties;
at that time, the attainment of his mind abandoned by cultivation arises together with the attainments of the non-abandonable dharmas (aheya-dharma) belonging to the category of inferior faculties.
The same applies to one who, having studied, regresses from a superior lineage and dwells in an inferior lineage.
Furthermore, when an Arhat arises in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and subsequently regresses through the eight grades of fetters down to the first dhyāna.
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) and the path to higher fruits.
Even if one falls away from the first dhyāna due to the most intense fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
one is still able to protect the practice.
That mind also arises together with the uninterrupted acquisitions (*aprāpti*) as previously described.
For one who is unable to guard their preparatory practice (*prayoga*),
that mind arises solely together with the various acquisitions of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
When those who are non-returners (anāgāmin) fall away due to the arising of the two grades of fetters— the lowest-of-the-low and the low-of-the-middle— of the desire realm,
their minds arise simultaneously with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and the path of the higher fruit.
If one falls away due to the arising of inferior or superior fetters,
yet is still able to guard the application of practice,
that mind likewise arises together with the uninterrupted acquisition as previously described.
If there is one who is unable to protect their intensified practice,
their mind arises only together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
When they fall away due to the arising of the five grades of fetters (*paryavasthāna*), ranging from the middling-inferior up to the middling-superior, [they fall back].
That mind arises simultaneously with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) and the paths leading to higher fruits.
Even if one falls away due to the arising of the most intense grades of fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
one is still able to protect the practice through application (*prayoga*).
That mind also arises together with the non-interruption of acquisition (*aprāpti*) as previously described.
For one who is unable to maintain the practice of cultivation (*bhāvanā*),
that mind arises only together with the various acquisitions of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).
Regarding the arising of uninterrupted superior progress of the mind abandoned by cultivation:
this refers to when noble ones, by means of the mundane path, become detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness.
If the mundane [path] serves as the preparatory stage,
it applies to all moments of the preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,
as well as during the abandonment of the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
If the mundane [path] serves as the preparatory practice,
then at the time of that path of preparation,
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (prāpti) of the dharmas of non-interruption (anantarya) to be cultivated in the future.
One who transforms their faculties through the liberation by faith (śraddhādhimukta) becomes one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta);
likewise, an Arhat who is liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) transforms their faculties to become immovable (akopyadharman).
If worldly [concentration] is used as the preparatory application (prayoga), [the transformation occurs].
At the time of that path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the various uninterrupted dharmas (*anantarya-dharma*) to be cultivated in the future.
This applies to the paths of preparation for the production of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) by an noble one (*ārya*).
The five paths of immediate succession,
the two paths of liberation,
and the supernormal power of conventional knowledge of others' minds.
At the time of the path of liberation,
at the time of the intermediate mind during the mixed cultivation of dhyāna,
and when noble ones give rise to the four immeasurables.
At the time of mundane liberation,
the eight bases of mastery,
and the ten totalities.
When the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the conventional analytical knowledge (*saṃvṛti-pratisaṃvid*) arise and increase;
when the concentration on the limit of the wishless (*araṇā-praṇidhijñāna-paryanta-samādhi*) arises;
and when emptiness-of-emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), the wishless-of-the-wishless (*apraṇihitā-apraṇihita*), and the signless-of-the-signless (*animittā-animitta*) arise and increase.
When a noble one practices the contemplation of impurity,
mindfulness of breathing,
or the mundane foundations of mindfulness.
When one gives rise to the subtle mind associated with the perception of entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
that mind arises together with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all dharmas that have been cultivated and remain uninterrupted in the future;
these are the various uninterrupted formless states (*ārūpya*) that arise.
Are those dharmas that are non-interrupted coexistent with a non-interrupted mind?
Answer: When various dharmas that are non-interrupted arise as formless (arūpa), those dharmas are either coexistent with a non-interrupted mind or not.
Or [they arise] together with a mind to be abandoned by cultivation.
What arises together with a mind that is not to be abandoned?
Answer: Those dharmas that are associated with that mind.
That mind is co-existent with them;
the meaning of "uninterrupted immateriality" is as explained previously.
How is it co-existent with the mind to be abandoned by cultivation?
Answer: Just as when the mind to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) undergoes either decline or advancement, the arising of the non-abandonable dharma occurs;
this is as previously explained regarding the arising of the non-abandonable formless [attainments] concomitant with the mind to be abandoned by cultivation.
If a phenomenon arises together with a non-interrupted mind, is that phenomenon a non-interrupted formless [phenomenon]?
Answer: All phenomena that arise together with a non-interrupted mind [are non-interrupted].
Those dharmas are either non-abandonable formless states or those to be abandoned by cultivation.
What are the non-abandonable formless states?
Answer: All dharmas are associated with that mind and coexist with that mind;
the meaning of "uninterrupted formlessness" is as explained previously.
What is the formless [matter] abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: It is like the arising of factors abandoned through cultivation when the mind that is not abandoned undergoes superior progress;
and it is the nourishment of the faculties and the increase of the primary elements while abiding in the mind that is not abandoned.
Those dharmas undergo birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
This is as previously explained regarding the arising of formless states abandoned through cultivation, which occur together with minds not to be abandoned.
Do all initial dhyānas possess five factors?
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed? Some say:
This is in order to refute the assertions of others;
for instance, the Vibhajyavādins maintain that the factors (aṅga) are established only in the first dhyāna and not in the others.
Why is this so? Because it is based on the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra:
The upāsaka Viśākha went to the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā and asked: "Noble Lady,
how many factors (aṅga) are there in the first dhyāna?"
He replied, "Venerable sir, there are five factors:
namely, vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā).
Since that upāsaka did not inquire about the higher dhyāna factors..."
Since that bhikṣuṇī did not speak [of them],
it is known that the branches (aṅga) are not established for the higher dhyānas.
To refute her intention and to demonstrate that the branches are indeed established for the higher dhyānas as well, this treatise was composed.
Question: If the branches are also established for the higher dhyānas,
why did Viśākhā not inquire about them,
and why did the bhikṣuṇī not explain them?
Some say:
those who have doubts ask questions, while those who have no doubts do not.
One speaks in accordance with what is asked;
one does not speak regarding what is not asked.
For this reason, one should not question why [the Buddha] remained silent.
Some say that Viśākhā wished to test whether that bhikṣuṇī was capable of knowing this matter,
so she first asked about the factors of the first dhyāna; since she spoke without hesitation, [Viśākhā concluded she did know].
The upāsaka then thought:
"Since this venerable one can explain the first dhyāna without obstruction, he must certainly also know the other dhyānas."
Therefore, she did not ask.
Because she no longer asked, the bhikṣuṇī likewise did not speak further. Some say:
Viśākhā possessed the nature of sharp faculties;
because she understood the remaining three dhyānas upon hearing about the first dhyāna, she did not ask further questions.
The bhikṣuṇī also knew that she had already realized them, and thus did not explain them to her again.
Some say that Viśākhā was of dull faculties;
by the power of intense mental attention, she was only just able to inquire about the first dhyāna.
Being incapable of asking further questions,
they therefore did not inquire.
The bhikṣuṇīs also knew that this was the extent of what they were able to receive and uphold.
It is not taught further because others are not suitable vessels for it.
Other masters say that this treatise was composed in order to bring those who harbor doubts to a state of certain understanding.
That is to say, that sutra merely states that the first dhyāna has five factors (pañcāṅga),
but does not mention the higher stages;
furthermore, it speaks only of the factors themselves, without distinguishing between those that are defiled and those that are undefiled.
Now, wishing to demonstrate that the factors of the higher stages also exist therein— existing solely within those that are non-defiled—

Do all first dhyānas possess five factors?
Answer: Those that are non-defiled possess five;

What is absent? Answer: The joy and bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha*) is absent.

that the undefiled first dhyāna possesses five factors,

Do all third dhyānas possess five factors?
Answer: There are five that are non-defiled;
there are none that are defiled.
What is absent?
Answer: Because correct mindfulness and correct awareness are absent.
Question: Since both mindfulness and wisdom are present throughout the defiled states of existence, why are they not established as factors of the defiled dhyāna?

Although these [factors] exist within the defiled [third dhyāna], they are not established as branches because they lack the characteristics of branches.
If one were to say this,
then the non-defiled third dhyāna would possess five branches.
The third dhyāna when defiled has only two factors.
Do all fourth dhyānas have four factors?
Answer: Those that are non-defiled have four.
The defiled [attainments] do not possess four [factors].
What are they lacking?
Answer: They lack the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
Question: Since mindfulness can be associated with defilement, why is it not considered a factor (*aṅga*) within defiled dhyāna? Some say:
This text should simply state that there is no equanimity (*upekṣā*),
because it is absent among the great wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) within the defiled states.
If one were to say this:
The undefiled fourth dhyāna possesses four factors;
the defiled fourth dhyāna possesses three factors. Some say:
Defiled mindfulness is termed "loss of mindfulness" (muṣitasmṛti) and is not called "purity of mindfulness.

the undefiled fourth dhyāna possesses all four factors,

Regarding this, some say:

however, it is only said that they lack joy, bliss, and so forth."
This is explained according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*);

In the second dhyāna, there is internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*),
because of the presence of the word "serene.
In the third dhyāna, there is right mindfulness and right clear comprehension (*samyaksmṛti-samyaksaṃprajanya*).
Because there is the expression "right," in the fourth dhyāna there is the purity of equanimity and mindfulness;
because there is the expression "pure."
These are all said to be "non-existent" because they are diametrically opposed to the clear manifestation of defilement;

This is explained according to their predominance:

Therefore, regarding the defiled dhyānas, it is said that [the factors] are absent according to whichever [factor] is predominant;
however, the remaining factors are likewise not established as being present in the defiled dhyānas.

Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Question: If that is so, how should one interpret the sūtra?
Answer: There are sentient beings who have previously entered that meditative absorption.

Those who are born there later include sentient beings who are born there even without having entered that meditative absorption; as for the sūtra’s statement that one is born there by entering that absorption,

The Abhidharma states that those who do not enter meditative absorption are born there;

Question: If one can be born there even without entering that meditative absorption, [how is this so?]
Why does the Blessed One state that one enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*) to be born in those realms?
Answer: Because there are certain non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) who claim that Brahmā and others do not attain their states through the cultivation of meditative absorption.
The Blessed One taught that one first enters meditative absorption here and only afterwards is born there,
so as to cause certain conviction that the fruit is obtained through its cause.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are addicted to the limited sensual pleasures of the present.
They do not delight in the supreme fruit of future freedom from desire.
For their sake, the World-Honored One censures sensual pleasure and praises the fruit of freedom from desire.
Having heard this, those sentient beings rejoice and request that he explain the reasons for it.
The Buddha explained that one first enters that meditative absorption and subsequently is born in that realm.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who,
upon hearing it said that the superior fruit of detachment from the higher realms exists, do not give rise to faith or understanding.
The Buddha intended to reveal that if one can enter that fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*), one experiences supreme bliss in the present;
thus, to make it known that its fruit is even more sublime,
the Buddha taught that one first enters this concentration and subsequently is born within that realm.
Furthermore, there are practitioners of yoga who are able to enter that meditative absorption;
although they desire to be born there,
they do not actually enter it in the present life.
The Buddha explained that one first enters meditative absorption here and only afterwards is born there.
Furthermore, there are practitioners of yoga who,
though weary of the suffering of the desire realm, seek the bliss of detachment from desire.
However, because they are indolent regarding the dharma of detachment and do not practice it,
the Buddha taught that one first enters meditative absorption and subsequently is born in that realm.
Is it possible, then, to be born in the Brahma-world without having entered the first dhyāna?
Answer: It is birth. What is birth?
It refers to being free from the defilements of the desire realm by relying on the *anāgamya* concentration.
In the final path of liberation,
as well as at a later time when one does not enter the first dhyāna— if such a person has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna and passes away,
they will necessarily be reborn in the Brahma-world.
Or, one may pass away from a higher stage and be born among those gods.
Question: Since one does not arise in that meditative absorption, how can one be born there, given that there is no cause for karmic maturation (*vipāka-hetu*)?
Answer: One is born there because karma to be experienced in a subsequent lifetime serves as the cause for maturation.
Is it possible for one who has not entered the second dhyāna to be born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven?
Answer: Yes, they are born there.

It is said to arise based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the first dhyāna,
and the intermediate dhyāna.
One may abandon the defilements of the first dhyāna through any one of the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of the second dhyāna,
yet fail to enter the second dhyāna itself.
If he dies without having abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna,
he will necessarily be reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
or else, passing away from a higher stage, he will be reborn among those gods.
Is it possible for one who has not entered the third dhyāna to be born in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven? Answer: Yes, they can be born there.
What is its arising?
It refers to that which arises based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the first dhyāna,
and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
The second dhyāna,
or any one of the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of the third dhyāna,
[is the basis for] becoming detached from the defilements of the second dhyāna.
They do not enter the third dhyāna.
If they die while still not free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
they will necessarily be reborn in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven.
Or, dying from a higher stage, one is born among those gods.
Is there, furthermore, anyone who, without entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Answer: It arises.
How does it arise?
That is to say, based on any one [level] from the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Having become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness,
but not yet having become detached from the defilements of the higher spheres,
one does not pass away while entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
One will certainly be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Herein, momentariness is excluded and continuity is excluded.
It excludes specific states and excludes the homogeneous class of beings,
but it does not exclude that which has existed from beginningless time.
If one attains the first dhyāna but not the second dhyāna, where will they be reborn at the end of life?
This is explained in detail, up to... [and so forth].
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to bring about certainty for those who harbor doubts.
As the Blessed One said: "Bhikṣus, you should know..."
I say that by relying on the first dhyāna one can exhaust all outflows;
by relying on the second dhyāna,
and so on up to the sphere of nothingness, one can exhaust all outflows.

Lest there arise the doubt that the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*) can occur only by relying on the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*) and not on the preparatory stages (*anāgamya*) and so forth,
this is stated in order to provide certainty:
it is shown that by relying on any of the nine stages, one is able to exhaust the outflows.
This refers to the seven fundamental dhyānas, the threshold (anāgamya), the intermediate (dhyānāntara), and the remaining preparatory stages (sāmantaka).
Although these cannot completely eliminate [the afflictions], they are nonetheless capable of severing them; therefore, this treatise was composed.
Furthermore, there are two types of attainment (prāpti).
There are two kinds of attainment: attainment through manifestation and attainment through possession.
Herein, the discussion is based on attainment through manifestation.
If one attains the first dhyāna but not the second dhyāna, where will they be reborn at the end of life?
Answer: Either in the Brahma-world or in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Either the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven],
or the Bṛhatphala [heaven],
or the Sphere of Infinite Space.
Either the sphere of infinite consciousness,
or the sphere of nothingness,
or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Or there may be no such case;
that is to say, one who has attained the first dhyāna in the present life, but not the second dhyāna.
Having definitely become free from the defilements of the desire realm, one is not yet fixed regarding the higher stages.
Among these, if one has not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
upon death one is reborn in the Brahma-world.
Whether it be based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya),
the first dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna,
or any one of the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of the second dhyāna.
The final path of liberation from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
as well as at a later time when one does not enter the second dhyāna and has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna.
Having passed away from there, he is reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
There, if he relies upon either the *anāgamya* (preliminary stage) or the first *dhyāna*, [he attains parinirvāṇa].
One who, while in the intermediate dhyāna,
has abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the higher stages, at the end of life is reborn in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven.
If, based on any one of the first three stages,
one becomes free from the defilements of the third dhyāna but has not yet become free from the defilements of the higher stages, then upon death, such a person is reborn in the Bṛhatphala heaven.
In this way, up to and including those who, based on any one of the first three stages,
become free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
upon their death, they have no place of rebirth.
Because he has already become free from the defilements of the three realms,
if he attains the second dhyāna,
it is not the third dhyāna.
Where is he reborn after his life ends?
Answer: Either in the Ābhāsvara Heaven or the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
...up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
or the sphere of nothingness—
namely, the actual attainment of the second dhyāna.
One who is not in the third dhyāna has certainly already become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
whereas detachment regarding the higher stages is not certain.
Among them, if one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna, they will,
at the end of life, be reborn in the Ābhāsvara heaven;
this applies if they rely on the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage].
The first dhyāna,
the intermediate dhyāna,
and the second dhyāna.
One may become detached from the defilements of the second dhyāna through any one of the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of the third dhyāna,
yet not enter the third dhyāna itself.
Not yet free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
he dies and is reborn in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven;
that same person, if relying on the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage],...
The first dhyāna,
the intermediate dhyāna,
and either one of the second dhyānas.
Having abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna but not yet having abandoned the defilements of the higher [stages],
one dies there and is reborn in the Bṛhatphala heaven.
If, based on any one of the aforementioned four stages,

one becomes free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna but has not yet become free from the defilements of the higher stages, then at the end of life, one is reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Space.
In this manner, up to:
if one relies on any one of the aforementioned four stages and becomes free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Upon the end of his life, he has no place of rebirth;
this applies if he attains the third dhyāna,
but not the fourth dhyāna.
Where is he reborn after his life ends?
The answer is: either in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven or the Bṛhatphala heaven.
Or even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
or the sphere of nothingness;
that is to say, one attains the third dhyāna in the present life.
One who is not in the fourth dhyāna has definitely already abandoned the defilements of the second dhyāna,
whereas [the state of] the higher stages is indeterminate.
In that regard, if one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna,
one will, at the end of life, be reborn in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven if one relies on the *anāgamya* concentration.
Up to the third dhyāna, having abandoned the defilements of at least one stage of the third dhyāna but not yet abandoned the defilements of the stages above, they,
upon the end of their life, are reborn in the Bṛhatphala heaven.
If one relies on any one of the first five stages and becomes free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
but has not yet become free from the defilements of the higher stages.
Upon the end of that life, he is reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Space.
In this manner, it continues until, depending on any one of the aforementioned five stages,
he becomes detached from the defilements of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception.
Upon the end of his life, he has no place of rebirth;
even if he attains the fourth dhyāna,
it is not the sphere of infinite space.
Where is he reborn after his life ends?
Answer: Either in the Bṛhatphala heaven, or even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Or there is no such place;
that is to say, one who has attained the fourth dhyāna in the present life,
but not the sphere of infinite space.
Having definitely become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
but not yet having become free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, one remains unsettled regarding the higher stages.
Upon the end of that life, he is reborn in the Bṛhatphala heaven.
This applies whether he relies on the *anāgamya* concentration or any one of the concentrations up to the fourth dhyāna.
Having abandoned the defilements of the fourth dhyāna but not yet having abandoned the defilements of the stages above it,
one dies there and is reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Space.
If one relies on any one of the preceding six stages and becomes free from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Space,
but has not yet become free from the defilements of the higher stages.
At the end of that life, he is reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.
In this manner, it continues until, depending on any one of the aforementioned six stages,
he becomes detached from the defilements of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
When he passes away from there, he has no place of rebirth.
If he attains the sphere of infinite space rather than the sphere of infinite consciousness, where will he be born after passing away?
Answer: Either the sphere of infinite space, up to and including the sphere of nothingness;
that is to say, one who has attained the sphere of infinite space in the present life.
One who is not [bound to] the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness has certainly already abandoned the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
yet the higher stages are not fixed [as such].
Among these, if one has not yet become free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space,
then at the end of life, one is reborn in the sphere of infinite space by relying on the preparatory concentration (anāgamya).
Up to and including any one of the spheres of infinite space,
one is free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space but has not yet become free from the defilements of the higher spheres.
Upon the end of that life, they are reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.
In this manner, it continues until, depending on any one of the aforementioned seven stages,
they become detached from the defilements of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.
Upon the end of his life, he has no place of rebirth;
if he attains the sphere of infinite consciousness,
it is not the sphere of nothingness.
Where is he reborn after the end of his life?
Answer: Either in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, or even up to the Sphere of Nothingness.

What is called "attaining the sphere of infinite consciousness in the present" means that one has definitely already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space, rather than [attaining] the sphere of nothingness.
However, the higher stages are not fixed.
Among them, if one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*),
upon death they will be reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.
If one relies on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*),
or any stage up to the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*),
one becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Not yet having abandoned the defilements of the higher realms,
he passes away and is reborn in the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
This continues in the same manner until, depending on any one of the aforementioned eight stages...
Having become detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
at the end of that life there is no place of rebirth;
if one attains the sphere of nothingness.
Regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
where is one reborn after death?
Answer: Either in the sphere of nothingness.
...up to, or perhaps, the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
That is to say, one attains the sphere of nothingness in the present life,
rather than the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Having definitely become detached from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness,
yet not having attained certainty regarding the higher stages;
therein, if one has not yet become detached from the defilements of the Sphere of Nothingness.
Having passed away from that state, he is reborn in the sphere of nothingness; if he relies on the threshold concentration (anāgamya) up to any one of the stages including the sphere of nothingness,
he becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness.
Without having abandoned the defilements of the higher realms,
they pass away and are reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana),
based on any one of the aforementioned nine stages.
Having become detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
there is no place for them to be reborn at the end of life.
By this principle, one should know that there are also those who attain two, three, or even up to seven [liberations].
The same applies to the prohibitions (*vāraṇa*).
The answer is that since there is no difference in principle, they are not explained in full detail.
Question: If one attains a wholesome mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), [what occurs]?
It is not the first dhyāna. Why is it not asked here:
"Where will they be reborn after their life ends?"
Some say: It should also be stated:
if one attains a wholesome mind of the desire realm that does not belong to the first dhyāna, where will they be reborn at the end of their life?
Answer: Either the desire realm,
or the Brahma world,
up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Or there is no such location;
that is to say, when one presently attains a wholesome mind of the desire realm,
it is not [the case] for those in the first dhyāna.
They are definitely situated in the desire realm, yet their detachment from passion is not fixed;
that is to say, if they have not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm,
upon the end of their life they will be reborn again in the desire realm.
If, by relying on the threshold concentration (anāgamya), one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm,
then at the final path of liberation and thereafter,
one does not enter the first dhyāna.
Not yet free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
he dies and is reborn in the Brahma-world; there,
he relies upon the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
Having become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna but not yet detached from the defilements of the higher stages,
one dies there and is reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Even up to the case where, relying on the preparatory concentration (anāgamya),
one is free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) but not yet free from the defilements of the higher [spheres].
Having passed away from that state, he is reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. If,
however, he relies on the threshold concentration (anāgamya),
he becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding the statement that "at the end of his life,
he has no place of rebirth," one should understand that this meaning is incomplete because it is not explicitly stated. Some say:
One should not inquire about or answer regarding the desire realm,
because this is the aggregate of concentration; one is properly inquiring about and answering concerning concentration and the fruits of concentration.
The desire realm is neither meditative absorption nor the fruit of absorption; therefore, it is not mentioned.
Question: One may attain the first dhyāna but not the second dhyāna and so forth;
yet upon death, such a person is also reborn in the desire realm and so on.
Why is this not mentioned here?
Some say that it should also be stated that they arise from all lower stages.
As for the fact that it is not mentioned, one should know that this meaning is incomplete [in that context].
Some say that this is because the *Skandhaprajñapti* (Treatise on the Aggregates) specifically reveals the arising in the meditative states (*dhyāna-bhūmi*).
If one were to say "arising below," there would be the fault of implying arising in the non-meditative states (*anirmita-bhūmi*) of the desire realm; therefore, it is not mentioned.
Some say: regarding the statement here that one dies and is reborn while possessing various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
those who are reborn in lower realms are not mentioned because they have fallen away from and relinquished those attainments.
Question: When those born in the higher realms pass away, they also relinquish their meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); why, then, is it said that they "progress"?
Answer: Although those born in the higher realms relinquish [attainments], they are still said to be "progressing."
How much more so for those who have something to gain?
Even those of inferior birth are called "fallen" if they have something to gain;
how much more so for those who have something to relinquish?
Now, since this aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*) specifically reveals superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*), it is not mentioned here.
Question: Why does the Sūtra state only that one can exhaust all outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) by relying on the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)?
How is it known that there is an intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) and the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), by relying upon which one exhausts the outflows?
Answer: By the Blessed One.
It is taught that there are three types of samādhi capable of exhausting all outflows (āsrava):
namely, that with vitarka and vicāra, that without vitarka but with vicāra alone, and that with neither vitarka nor vicāra.
Furthermore, another sutra states:
The first dhyāna is called "with vitarka and with vicāra.
From the second dhyāna upward, it is called "without vitarka and without vicāra.
If there is no intermediate dhyāna, what else could be designated as "without vitarka and with only vicāra"?
From this, it is known that there exists an intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara) by relying upon which one exhausts the outflows (āsrava).
Furthermore, a sūtra states that the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I do not say that [the first dhyāna] relies solely on the separation from sensual desires and unwholesome states while possessing vitarka and vicāra."
"Abiding fully in the first dhyāna, which is characterized by the joy and bliss born of seclusion, one is able to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*);
yet, through the vision of wisdom (*prajñā*), one is also able to exhaust the outflows.
This sūtra thus reveals that there is the "not-yet-attained concentration" (*anāgamya-samādhi*) which serves as a basis for exhausting the outflows.
Furthermore, for a noble one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire and has not yet attained dhyāna,
if there were no *anāgamya* concentration, upon what basis could they give rise to the Noble Path to eternally sever all outflows?
From this, it is known that there is the *anāgamya-samādhi* (preliminary concentration) by relying upon which one exhausts the outflows (*āsrava*).
Question: Why is it not stated that the first dhyāna and so forth directly exhaust the outflows, rather than stating that one relies upon them?
Some say that the dhyānas were previously attained;
if the Blessed One had said that the first dhyāna and so forth could exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*), [they would have been included].
Thus, there would be no one who possesses knowledge;
that is to say, those who have attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) would all already have exhausted their outflows (*āsrava*).
For this reason, the Buddha taught that [knowledge] relies upon meditative absorption and so forth.
Only by arising the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) can one exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*).
Some say that while all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are exclusively *śamatha*, it is only through *vipaśyanā* that one can exhaust the outflows.
Therefore, it is said that one must give rise to wisdom based upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Some say that most forms of concentration have been attained previously; thus, one might harbor attachment to them and lack the desire to progress in cultivation.
Therefore, it is said that while relying on this to advance in the quest for the superior path, one should not give rise to attachment.

Question: As stated in the Sūtra, one cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) together with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Other sūtras further state that even up to the sphere of nothingness, one can correctly penetrate and discern the noble intent.
The preceding sūtra also states that this is based on the first dhyāna.
Up to the sphere of nothingness, one can exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).
How is it that these two statements do not contradict each other?
The answer is: the first sutra speaks of their ability to induce [the attainment].
The latter two sūtras speak based on that very [practice].
Furthermore, the first sūtra speaks of the means (*upāya*),
while the latter two sūtras speak of its fulfillment (*pariniṣpatti*).
Question: If that is so, why is it said that they "occur together" (*sahagata*)?
Answer: The term "together" (*saha*) also functions in the sense of "before and after," as the Blessed One has said:
As soon as King Mandhātṛ gave rise to this thought, he immediately fell.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says that as soon as those sentient beings gave rise to this thought, they immediately perished.
Furthermore, another sutra states:
King Vemacitrin gave rise to this thought and simultaneously saw himself bound by the fivefold bonds.
In all these cases, the word "simultaneous" (*saha*) is stated with reference to what precedes and follows.
It should be understood that the *Bodhyaṅga-bhāvanā-sūtra* is likewise.
Question: If a dharma has the first dhyāna as its cause...
Is that dharma the fruit of the first dhyāna? Furthermore,
if a dharma is the fruit of the first dhyāna,
is that dharma caused by the first dhyāna?
Answer: There are phenomena for which the first dhyāna is the cause;
those phenomena are the fruit of the first dhyāna.
There are also phenomena that are the fruit of the first dhyāna.
Those dharmas do not have the first dhyāna as their cause;
namely, the abandonment of the fetters of the three realms and the fruit of the first dhyāna.
The same question and answer should be applied to the classes of mind resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) in the desire realm, up to and including the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one should speak only of the severance of fetters (*saṃyojana-prahāṇa*).
Question: When one relinquishes the mind of the first dhyāna stage and attains the mind of the second dhyāna stage,
is it the case that the mind of the first dhyāna stage ceases in all instances?
Does the mind of the second dhyāna stage arise?
It should be answered by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
Regarding the first alternative:
That is to say, it relies upon the preparatory stage (anāgamya),
or the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara),
or the access concentration (sāmantaka) of the second dhyāna.
Having become detached from the defilements of the Brahma-world and not entering the fundamental stage,
one at that time abandons the defiled mind of the first dhyāna stage.
One attains an undefiled mind of the second dhyāna stage,
yet this does not arise through the cessation of that [previous state].
This is the second case.
This refers to the case of entering meditative absorption through a sequence that is not preceded by the fading away of passion.
As for the third phrase,
it refers to the time when one dies in the first dhyāna and is reborn in the second dhyāna.
The fourth case refers to those instances excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Question: Regarding all minds that relinquish the level of the second dhyāna—
When one attains the mind of the first dhyāna stage,
does the mind of the second dhyāna stage cease and the mind of the first dhyāna stage arise?
It is answered in four propositions.
The first proposition refers to when one falls away from the second dhyāna due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm.
The second phrase refers to entering meditative absorption in reverse order.
The third phrase refers to...
This refers to the time of birth.
As for the fourth phrase,
it refers to excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Question: Do those who abandon the afflictions of the first dhyāna obtain the wholesome dharmas of the second dhyāna stage?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold permutation (catuṣkoṭi).
The first phrase refers to relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) or the first dhyāna.
In the intermediate dhyāna,
during the four moments of entering the path of seeing;
this refers to the second phrase.
This refers to when one enters the path of seeing (darśanamārga) based on the second, third, or fourth dhyāna,
as well as when a noble one (ārya) becomes free from the defilements of the seven higher stages.
As for the third phrase:
This refers to the time when one is free from the defilements of dhyāna.
As for the fourth alternative,
it refers to cases other than those previously described.
Question: Do those who abandon the virtues of the second dhyāna stage acquire the afflictions of the first dhyāna stage?
Answer: This should be treated as four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
Regarding the first phrase:
it refers to the time when one regresses from the counteractives of a higher stage,
or when one cultivates the qualities of the second dhyāna stage belonging to a higher stage.
The second phrase refers to when one dies in a higher realm and is reborn in the desire realm or the Brahma-world.
The third phrase refers to...
That is to say: when one dies in the Ābhāsvara Heaven and is reborn in the Desire Realm or the Brahma-world;
when one gives rise to afflictions of a lower stage;
and when one falls away from the second dhyāna.
The fourth phrase refers to all other concentrations,
excluding those previously mentioned,
as appropriate to each case.
One should also formulate such questions and answers for analysis.
*Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 161;
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 100.
Compiled by the six hundred and twenty-five Great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (*Samādhiskandha*). First Sub-section: Attainment (*Prāpti*). Part Six. Contemplating what is it that enters the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*)?
Answer: To bestow happiness upon sentient beings.
Question: Contemplating what does one enter the meditative absorption of compassion?
Answer: To extract the suffering of sentient beings.
What does one contemplate when entering the meditative absorption of joy?
Answer: One contemplates the celebration of all sentient beings.
What does one contemplate when entering the meditative absorption of equanimity?
Answer: It refers to equanimity toward sentient beings.

Question: In this context, is the aspect of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) being described, or is the aspect co-arising with loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others being described?
If one speaks of the aspect (*ākāra*) of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
what is the aspect when loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth are manifest?
If one speaks of the aspect co-arising (*sahaja*) with loving-kindness and so forth...
Why is this said? What does one contemplate when entering the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*)?
[The answer continues] at length.
Some say: "In this context, the aspect (*ākāra*) of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is being explained.
Question: If that is so, what is the aspect when loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others are manifested?
The answer is: one performs these four kinds of mental orientations,
namely, bestowing happiness upon sentient beings,
up to and including equanimity toward sentient beings.
Some say: "This explains the mental aspects (ākāra) that arise simultaneously with loving-kindness and the others.
Question: If this is so, for what reason was this statement made?
"What does one contemplate when entering the meditative absorption of loving-kindness?
and so forth, as explained at length.
The answer is: herein, that which has already entered is called "entry."
The expression of a distant sound regarding something near is as when one says, "From where has Your Majesty come?
This refers to the fact that [the King] has already arrived, yet it is called "coming."
As it is said that one enters into right determination by relying on the samādhi of emptiness,
this too is called "entering" because one has already entered it. Why is this so?
This is not because it is associated with the emptiness samādhi of the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
Just as it is said that one enters the state of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and attains conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamaya-anta*),
so too this [state] is called "entering" because one has already entered it.
Why is this? Because it is only at the time of the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the three categories that one attains that wisdom.
As it is said: "When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is: 'I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.
This also explains that what has already been experienced is called "feeling" (*vedanā*). Why is this so?
Because there is no self-awareness of present feeling,
as it is said: "Having abandoned pleasure and abandoned pain, with the prior disappearance of joy and grief,
one dwells in equanimity, mindful and pure, in neither-pain-nor-pleasure."
One enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, fully accomplished.
This too is called "abandoned" because it has been abandoned. Why is that?
Because the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) has already been abandoned at the time of becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is as stated:
"The mind of an Arhat is liberated from the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*)."
This too is called "liberation" because it is already liberated;
why is this so? Because at the time of being free from the defilements of the desire realm, one is already liberated from the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
In this case as well, that which has already entered is designated as "entering"; therefore, there is no fault.

Question: Does the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) and so forth also function with such a mode of activity (*ākāra*) as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
"Is it by performing other modes of activity?
The answer is: "For a beginner, only these four modes of activity can induce loving-kindness and the others."
Once it has been perfected, one may also generate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables] by means of other aspects such as suffering, according to one's desire; however,
when loving-kindness and the others arise, they function solely through the four aforementioned aspects.
What fetters and bonds does loving-kindness (*maitrī*) sever?
Answer: None.
What fetters and bonds do compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) sever?
Answer: No. Question:
For what reason do the four immeasurables not sever the afflictions?
Answer: Because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are different.
That is to say, nineteen aspects are able to sever the afflictions;
the immeasurables (apramāṇa) do not have those as their aspects.
Four aspects constitute the immeasurables.
Afflictions are not severed by means of this mode of mental engagement (*ākāra*).
Furthermore, the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are mental engagements consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika-manaskāra*);
only the mental engagement that accords with reality (*tattvārtha-manaskāra*) can sever afflictions.
Furthermore, the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are attention characterized by augmentation (*adhyāropa*).
Only attention that does not involve augmentation can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, the immeasurables take only the present as their object.
It must take the three periods of time as its object;
alternatively, the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is able to sever the afflictions.
Furthermore, it takes immeasurable sentient beings as its object.
The notion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*) is able to sever the afflictions.
Furthermore, the immeasurables take only a portion of an object as their domain;
a path that takes only a portion of an object as its domain cannot sever the afflictions.

Furthermore, the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), whereas the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are attained at the time of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Question: If the immeasurables cannot sever the afflictions, [how can they be so called]?
How is the scriptural teaching to be reconciled?
For example, as it is said: "If loving-kindness is practiced, if it is cultivated..."
If one practices it extensively,
one can sever hatred; thus,
compassion is both cultivated and developed.
If one practices it extensively,
one can eliminate harm;
if one habituates oneself to and cultivates joy, [the same result follows].
If one practices this extensively,
one can sever non-delight;
through such practice and cultivation, one attains equanimity.
If one practices this extensively, one can sever greed and anger.
Answer: There are two kinds of severance.
First, temporary abandonment;
second, ultimate abandonment.
Thus it is said in the Sūtra.
The former refers to temporary cessation,
while the Abhidharma refers to ultimate cessation;
in this way, both explanations are well-justified.
Just as there is temporary abandonment and ultimate abandonment,
so too are there abandonment with remainder and abandonment without remainder.
There is the severance of the shadowed,
the severance of the shadowless,
and the severance of that which follows and binds.
There is the severance of the binding attachment,
the severance by crushing the branches and leaves,
and the severance by uprooting the root.

It should be understood that the same applies to the abandonment of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) through suppression, and the abandonment of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) through destruction.
What fetters bound by which realm are severed by the pure first dhyāna?
Answer: None.
And so on, up to: what fetters bound by which realm are severed by the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception? Answer: None.
Answer: No. In this context, the "pure" first dhyāna and so forth refer to the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*), not the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
Question: Why do the pure (śuddha) first dhyāna and so forth not abandon the afflictions?
Answer: Although the afflictions of the lower stages are those that ought to be abandoned, it is only after they have been abandoned that these [pure states] manifest.
There are no further afflictions of one’s own level that can be abandoned.
Although they may currently be present, because they are not the specific objects of opposition [for this stage], they lack the power to be abandoned;
the same applies to those of higher levels, and thus the afflictions are not abandoned.
Question: It may be granted that [a path] cannot sever the afflictions of a higher stage;
why, however, can it not sever those of its own stage?
Answer: Because it is bound by the afflictions of its own stage.
Just as a person who has been bound cannot free themselves,
so too, because they share the same bonds as the various afflictions of their own stage,
they lack the power to overcome them.
Furthermore, because they are cherished by the craving of their own level,
just as one does not abandon an inferior friend who is dear to them;
and because they are intermingled with the afflictions of their own level.
This means that because they manifest in immediate succession to one another, [the wholesome state] cannot be severed.
Furthermore, the wholesome dharmas of a given stage and the afflictions of that same stage do not obstruct or exclude one another, being like husband and wife.
Furthermore, just as the son of a candāla and the son of a householder cannot sever their ties because they do not respect or fear one another, so too,
while the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) can sever afflictions,
the pure fundamental stages (*śuddha-mūlabhūmi*) cannot sever them, as they are not the path of immediate succession.
Furthermore, one is able to abandon [defilements] only when there is no regard for them.
Since there is not a lack of regard for the phenomena belonging to one's own level (*svabhūmi*), one cannot abandon them.
Question: For what reason is the path with outflows (*sāsravamārga*) unable to abandon [defilements] of its own level?
And can the untainted path of the higher stages then effect abandonment?
Answer: Because the untainted path is a non-tied phenomenon (*asaṃbaddha-dharma*), it is superior to all tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*); therefore, it is able to effect abandonment.

Furthermore, the contaminated path (sāsrava-mārga) performs six aspects of mental application (ākāra), because it involves weariness toward lower stages and aspiration for its own stage; thus, it only abandons [defilements].
The uncontaminated path (anāsrava-mārga) performs sixteen aspects of mental application.
Because it is averse to all stages [of existence], it is able to sever them universally.
Question: The path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*) also performs the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*);
why is it unable to sever them universally?

Answer: Although they study and practice the characteristics of the noble path, because it is not yet clear, they do not abandon the afflictions; it is like a lion cub that has not yet been able to kill wild beasts.
Regarding what fetters are abandoned by the first, second, and third liberations: the answer is none.
Question: Why do these three not abandon the afflictions?
Answer: Because their modes of activity (ākāra) differ.
That is to say, if one abandons the afflictions through a particular mode of activity, one does not perform the first three liberations through that same mode of activity.
If one practices the first three liberations through these modes of activity (*ākāra*),
yet does not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) through these modes of activity,
furthermore, these first three liberations consist of mental attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*).
Only authentic mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*) are mental attentions of superimposition (*samāropa*);
only non-superimposing mental attention can sever the afflictions.
Furthermore, the first three liberations take specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objects;
only the path that takes general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Moreover, the first three liberations take only the present as their object.
They must take the three time periods as their objects;
alternatively, the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is able to sever the afflictions.
Furthermore, the first three liberations take only a small portion of a single aggregate (*skandha*) as their object.
They must take the five aggregates or four aggregates as their object;
alternatively, the path that is not an aggregate can sever the afflictions.
Furthermore, the first three liberations take a partial object.
One cannot abandon afflictions by taking only a portion of an object as a focal point.
Furthermore, it is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons afflictions,
because the first three liberations are attained at the time of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
What fetters and bonds are severed by the liberation of the sphere of infinite space?
Answer: Either those pertaining to the sphere of infinite space, or those pertaining to the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Either the sphere of nothingness,
or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
or none at all.
Regarding the sphere of infinite space:
this refers to relying on the liberation of the sphere of infinite space and becoming free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space.
Regarding the various uninterrupted paths up to and including those of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
this refers to relying on the liberation of the sphere of infinite space to become detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding those that lack uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga) or are without them:
these are comprised within the preparatory, liberation, and special progress paths (prayoga-vimukti-viśeṣa-mārga) of the liberation of the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana-vimokṣa).
And regarding the worldly liberation of the sphere of infinite space and the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness:
what fetters and bonds are severed by the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness?
Answer: Either those pertaining to the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Either the sphere of nothingness,
or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
or none at all.
Regarding those who [attain] the sphere of infinite consciousness:
this refers to those who, relying on the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness,
become free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Regarding "all uninterrupted paths" up to "the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," this refers to relying on the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Regarding the paths of immediate succession for becoming detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
some are non-existent.
This refers to the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana-vimokṣa) and the mundane liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness,
which are subsumed within these preparatory, liberating, and progressive paths.
Regarding the liberation of the sphere of nothingness:
what fetters and bonds does it sever?
Answer: Either those pertaining to the sphere of nothingness.
Either the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
or non-existence,
or the sphere of nothingness.

This refers to the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that, based on the liberation of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), abandon the defilements of the sphere of nothingness;
or [the path] of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
This refers to the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that,
based on the liberation of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), abandon the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Alternatively, it may be non-existent.
This refers to the liberation of the sphere of nothingness, as well as the mundane liberation of the sphere of nothingness,
which are comprised within these paths of preparation, liberation, and special progress.
Regarding the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the liberation of the cessation of sensation and perception:
what fetters and bonds are severed by them?
Answer: No. Because the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception lacks the untainted (anāsrava), what fetters (saṃyojana) does the first stage of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) sever?
Answer: None.
Up to the eighth stage of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), what fetters (saṃyojana) belonging to which realm are abandoned?
Answer: None.
In this regard, the reason is as explained for the three preceding liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Regarding the question of which fetters (*saṃyojana*) are severed by the first *kṛtsnāyatana*, the answer is: none.
This applies up to the tenth *kṛtsnāyatana*.
What fetters and bonds are severed?
Answer: None.
In this context, the first eight are like the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
The latter two [knowledges] should also be understood accordingly as previously explained.
Regarding which fetters are abandoned by the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), the answer is:
those belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Either the form realm,
or the formless realm,
or none at all, or those belonging to the desire realm.
That is to say, when any one of the four dharma-knowledges (dharmajñāna) manifests,
it occurs during the uninterrupted paths (ānantaryamārga) that abandon the defilements of the desire realm,
or those of the form realm.
"Or belonging to the formless realm" means:
either when any one of the dharma-knowledges of cessation or the path is present and one is free from the form realm;
or during the various uninterrupted paths that abandon the defilements of the formless realm.
Regarding those that do not exist:
this refers to the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) comprised within the paths of preparation, liberation, and advancement;
as for which fetters they sever and from what level of bondage.
Answer: Either the form realm,
or the formless realm,
or none at all.

"Either the form realm or the formless realm" refers to any one of the four types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) manifesting as the various paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandon the defilements of the form realm or the formless realm.
Regarding "or there is none":

this refers to what kind of fetters are severed by the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) included within these paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
Answer: No. Question:
For what reason does the knowledge of others' minds not sever the afflictions? Some say:
The knowledge of others' minds takes a single object as its objective support;
it is not by taking a single object that the Path can sever the afflictions. Some say:
The knowledge of others' minds takes specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.
Only the path that takes common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object can sever the afflictions. Some say:
The knowledge of others' minds takes the present as its object;
it must take the three periods of time as its object;
or, the path of the unconditioned is able to sever the afflictions.
Some say that the knowledge of others' minds takes only mental states and their associated factors as its object;
it must take the four aggregates as its object.
Either the five aggregates or the unconditioned path can sever the afflictions.
Some say that the knowledge of others' minds takes only the mental continua of others as its object.
It must take as its object either the mental continua of oneself and others, or a non-continuous object,
in order for the path to be able to sever the afflictions.
Some say that the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) abandons the afflictions,
because the knowledge of others' minds is acquired at the time of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
By means of which fetters is mundane knowledge abandoned?
Answer: Either those belonging to the desire realm or those belonging to the form realm.
Either in the formless realm, or not at all,
or in the desire realm.
This refers to the mundane path of immediate succession (*anantarya-mārga*) for abandoning the defilements of the desire realm;
or, for those of the form realm,
it refers to the mundane path of immediate succession for abandoning the defilements of the form realm.
"Or those of the formless realm" refers to the mundane uninterrupted paths that abandon the defilements of the lower three formless realms;
"or none" refers to [the absence of such].
This refers to the conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) comprised within the paths of preparation (prayoga-mārga), liberation (vimukti-mārga), and special progress (viśeṣa-mārga),
as well as other wholesome conventional knowledge of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and all wholesome conventional knowledge of the fundamental stages (maulabhūmi).
As well as all defiled and non-obscured neutral conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Just as with conventional knowledge,
so it is with the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the samādhis of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness.
As for the distinction:
these various untainted knowledges (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and samādhis are all capable of universally severing [the afflictions] of the nine stages.
Yet they cannot universally abandon the five categories [of afflictions].
Among these, the knowledge of the four truths (*catur-āryasatya-jñāna*) can abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) across the nine stages;
the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) can abandon those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) across the nine stages.
As for the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),

the wishless concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) is able to abandon the afflictions of the nine stages that are to be abandoned through seeing suffering, origin, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation.
As for the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*):
It is able to sever the afflictions of the nine stages that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation;
this is the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*).
This is its distinction from the preceding [paths].
Among those that are either non-existent or [otherwise], only these are subsumed within the paths of preparation, liberation, and special progress, and no others.
Question: If the three samādhis are also capable of severing the afflictions, [why is this so?]
How should one interpret what is stated in the sūtras?
For example, it says:
"O bhikṣus, I say..."
"Because of knowledge and because of vision, one is able to exhaust all outflows.
It is further said:
"My noble disciples..."
One cuts the enemy of afflictions with the sword of *prajñā*.
Some say that wisdom alone is able to sever the afflictions,
while the other factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) are called "severing" because they assist in that severance.
According to this explanation,
all four or five aggregates that arise simultaneously with wisdom are capable of abandoning the afflictions,
because they abandon the afflictions through the application of mindfulness to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*).
However, the Buddha sometimes praises prajñā,
sometimes praises samādhi,
and sometimes praises others.
All are for the sake of benefiting other sentient beings.
Where is the maturation of loving-kindness experienced?
And so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is because the author of the treatise intended it to be so;
[this continues] up to the full explanation.
Furthermore, it is in order to refute what others have said;
for some say that neither wholesome nor unwholesome [actions] possess a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Alternatively, some say that all conditioned phenomena possess maturation (*vipāka*).
Or again, others say:
All unwholesome dharmas and wholesome dharmas associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) necessarily obtain maturation (*vipāka*).
This is stated in order to stop various such divergent views and to clarify that only unwholesome and wholesome dharmas associated with outflows definitely possess maturation.
Because it is indeterminate, this treatise is composed.
Now, there are two kinds of determinacy herein:
first, determinacy of maturation (*vipāka-niyama*), and second, determinacy of birth (*upapatti-niyama*).
Regarding determinate by way of maturation (*vipāka-niyata*):
this is because all unwholesome and wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena possess maturation.
Regarding determinate by way of birth (*upapatti-niyata*):...
If it arises from maturation (*vipākaja*), it is designated by names such as the Brahma-world;
if it does not so arise, it is designated as "having no location.
This is the brief *Vibhāṣā* concerning this point.
In what place is the maturation of loving-kindness experienced?
Answer: Either in the Brahma-world or in the Ābhāsvara realm.
Either in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven,
or in the Bṛhatphala Heaven,
or in a placeless realm.

"Whether in the Brahma-world or even up to the Vast Fruit [Heaven]" refers to those for whom the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) arises within the four dhyānas;
or "without a location."
This refers to the four dhyānas.

As with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of the immeasurable [state] of loving-kindness falls within the state of non-arising (*asaṃjñisattva*). As it is with loving-kindness, so it is with the others.
The same applies to compassion and equanimity,
as they all pertain to the four dhyānas.
In which place is the maturation of joy experienced?
Answer: Either the Brahma-world,
or the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
or a placeless realm.
Either the Brahma-world or the Ābhāsvara realm refers to the first and second dhyānas respectively.
Regarding the arising of the immeasurable fruit of maturation of joy,
or its being without a specific location:
this refers to the first and second dhyānas.
Regarding those who fall into non-arising as the maturation fruit of immeasurable joy:
where is the maturation of the pure first dhyāna experienced?
Answer: Either the Brahma-world, or no specific location. Regarding "either the Brahma-world":
[it refers to] the Brahma-world.
This refers to the arising of the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) of the wholesome, contaminated (*sāsrava*) first dhyāna;
or, alternatively, it refers to that which has no specific location—
namely, the ripening fruit of the wholesome, contaminated first dhyāna.
Regarding those that fall into the category of non-arising:
as is the case with the pure first dhyāna,
so it is with the pure second dhyāna.
This continues up to the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is likewise.
The distinction is that each is designated by its own name.
In what place is the maturation (vipāka) of the first and second liberations experienced?
Answer: Either the Brahma-world,
or the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
or a placeless realm.
This is as explained regarding the immeasurable state of joy (*muditā*).
Since both are situated in the stages of the first and second dhyānas,
in what location is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the pure liberation (*śuddha-vimokṣa*) experienced?
Answer: Either the Bṛhatphala [heaven], or the Placeless (Aniṣṭhā). Regarding "or the Bṛhatphala":
[it refers to those who are born there].
Regarding the statement "the maturation fruit of the pure liberation arises," or "it has no location":
this refers to the maturation fruit of the pure liberation.
Those who have fallen into non-arising are those in the liberation of the sphere of infinite space,
up to the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
In what location is the ripening [of karma] experienced?
Answer: Either in its own level, or in no specific location.
"Or from its own level" refers to the contaminated liberations (*vimokṣa*) of the four levels;
each produces its own respective matured fruit (*vipākaphala*).
"Or that which has no location" refers to the untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*) of the third stage and the tainted liberation (*sāsrava-vimukti*) of the fourth stage.
Each has its own ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
That which falls into non-arising is the liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*).
In what location is the maturation experienced?
Answer: Either in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or in no location at all.
This is as explained regarding the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
In which realm is the maturation (vipāka) of the first four spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) experienced?
Answer: Either the Brahma-world,
or the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
or a placeless realm.
This is as explained in the first and second liberations (vimokṣa).
As for the latter four spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana),
