in which realm is their maturation (vipāka) experienced?
Answer: Either the Fruit of Vast Merit (Bṛhatphala) or the Placeless (Avihā).
This is as explained regarding the pure liberation (śuddha-vimokṣa).
As with the latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
so it is with the first eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*);
the same applies to the latter two spheres of totality.
In what location is the maturation experienced?
Answer: Either in its own level or in no specific location.
This is as explained regarding the first two formless attainments of the pure class.
Where is the maturation of the knowledge of others' minds received?
Answer: Either in the Brahma-world.
Or the Ābhāsvara [heaven],
or the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven],
or the Bṛhatphala [heaven].
"Either having no specific location,
or [located] from the Brahma-world up to the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala)" refers to the tainted knowledge of others' minds belonging to the four dhyānas.
Regarding "each producing its own distinct maturation fruit" or "having no location," this refers to the untainted knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñāna*).
Furthermore, regarding the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of the outflow-tainted knowledge of others' minds (*sāsrava-paracittajñāna*),
which falls into the state of non-arising (*apravṛtti*):
where is the maturation fruit of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) experienced?
Answer: Either the desire realm,
or the form realm,
or the formless realm.
"Either having no location,
or belonging to the desire realm, up to the formless realm" refers to the contaminated wholesome states of the three realms.
As for the unwholesome mundane knowledge (*lokasamvṛtijñāna*),
when its respective matured fruit (*vipākaphala*) arises,
it may be that there is no specific location [for it].
This refers to the indeterminate conventional knowledge (*sāṃvṛtijñāna*) of the three realms,
as well as the maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*) of unwholesome and wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) conventional knowledge that have fallen into non-arising (*anutpatti*).
Other untainted knowledges (*anāsrava-jñāna*) are not mentioned here because they lack maturation (*vipāka*).

Section Two: The Section on Objects (*ālambana-varga*), being the second within the Seventh Chapter on the Aggregate of Concentration (*samādhi-skandha*). There are eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
That is to say: the four dhyānas,
the four formless attainments,
and the three meditative absorptions (samāpatti).
That is to say: associated with taste (*āsvādana*), pure (*śuddha*), and untainted (*anāsrava*).
Among these, the first seven each possess three types;
the eighth possesses only two.
That is to say, excluding the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Having thus understood these chapters and the meaning of the explanations of those chapters,
one should analyze them in detail.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is because one wishes to refute the doctrines of others and to manifest one's own position.
That is to say, some may claim:
The eight attainments do not encompass all attainments.
Some say that attainments consist only of those that are pure (*śuddha*) or untainted (*anāsrava*), and are not associated with relish (*āsvādanasamprayukta*).
Some say that there is also the untainted (anāsrava) in the desire realm and in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Others say: [there is not].
There are no phenomena such as "attainment" (prāpti) and so forth.

In order to cease such various divergent attachments and to demonstrate that the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) encompass all attainments, including even those involving attainment, this treatise was composed.
Question: If the eight attainments encompass all attainments, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the Vinaya?
As it says:
The meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) entered by the Buddha—
whose very names even all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not know—
the meditative attainments entered by the pratyekabuddhas...
All the śrāvakas do not know what Śāriputra has entered;
the other śrāvakas do not know it.
The realm entered by Mahāmaudgalyāyana was unknown to all other śrāvakas, with the exception of Śāriputra.
Why is it said that the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti) encompass all meditative attainments?
The answer is: there is no meditative attainment that is not included within the eight meditative attainments;
however, this is because there are distinctions among them based on their spiritual lineages (gotra) and wisdom (prajñā).
This causes the meditative attainments (samāpatti) entered and emerged from to also possess degrees of superiority and inferiority.
Regarding those that are inferior,
because they cannot fathom or know the superior ones, this statement was made.
For this reason, it is said that when the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa,
he entered the meditative absorption of Immovable Light (Acalābhijñā).
When Śāriputra entered parinirvāṇa, [he likewise entered this state].
When entering the meditative attainment of the lion’s boundless spring,
he entered the meditative attainment of the fragrant elephant’s yawn at the time of Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s parinirvāṇa.
When the Venerable Ānanda entered parinirvāṇa,
he did so by entering the meditative attainment of the whirlwind;
this was entirely due to the distinctions between his faculties and his wisdom.
Even up until the time of parinirvāṇa, there are distinctions among the meditative attainments (samāpatti) entered.
Question: What is the distinction between meditative concentration (samādhi) and meditative attainment?
Answer: Some say that samādhi has a single entity as its essence,
whereas samāpatti has the five aggregates as its essence.
Some say that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) consists of a single moment,
whereas meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is a continuous succession.
Some say that all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
but there are meditative attainments that are not meditative concentrations.
That is to say: the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation. Some say:
There are also cases of concentration (samādhi) that are not meditative attainments (samāpatti),
namely, concentration associated with the unconcentrated mind.
Based on this, one should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that are not meditative concentrations (*samādhi*, i.e., *cittaikāgratā*);
these refer to the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*).
There are meditative concentrations that are not meditative attainments.
This refers to meditative concentration (samādhi) associated with an unconcentrated mind.
There are also attainments (samāpatti) that are also meditative concentrations;
this refers to all meditative states involving consciousness.
There are those that are neither meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) nor meditative concentrations (*samādhi*),
namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
There are three types of the first dhyāna.
That is to say: associated with craving, pure, and untainted.
"Associated with craving" means associated with *tṛṣṇā* (thirst).
Craving is able to sustain the mind as it flows toward objects;
because its characteristic conforms to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it alone receives this name.
The remaining causes and conditions have already been explained as before.
"Pure" refers to wholesome contaminated states;
"outflow-free" refers to the noble path.
Now, regarding wholesome contaminated meditative concentration:
It is defiled, turbid, poisonous, thorny, outflowing, and faulty.
What is meant by "pure"?
The answer is: although it is not ultimate purity.
It is called "pure" by virtue of being pure in a limited sense;
that is to say, because it is unmixed with afflictions and because it is contrary to afflictions.
Because it induces the stainless ultimate purity;
because it accords with the Noble Path;
and because it is the retinue of the stainless.
Question: Since the untainted (anāsrava) attainments are the ultimate truth (paramārtha), why is the pure (śuddha) not called "pure" [in that same sense]? Some say:
Regarding that which should have been stated but was not:
one should know that there is more to be said. Some say:
That which is untainted is called "pure" (śuddha),
as is commonly understood;
that which is tainted is also called "pure."
This is not commonly known;
therefore, it is explained partially. Some say:
The designation is established based on the meaning of differentiation.
Because the wholesome, contaminated meditative absorption initially opposes defiled phenomena,
it is designated as "pure" (*śubha*) since the sense of being "clean" (*śuddha*) is predominant.
The Noble Path abandons the outflows (āsrava).
It is called "outflow-free" (anāsrava) because its meaning is superior;
it is like the three types [of wholesome states] in the first dhyāna.
This same threefold classification applies up to the sphere of nothingness.
In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are only two types,
namely, excluding the untainted (anāsrava).
Because the desire realm and the peak of existence lack the noble path.
Question: For what reason do those two stages lack the noble path?
Answer: Because they are neither a field nor a vessel.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, the desire realm is neither a stage of meditative concentration nor a stage of cultivation.
It is not a stage free from passion;
it belongs to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), which is obscure, dull, weak, and inferior,
and must be a stage of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In the stage of cultivation and the stage of freedom from defilement,
when clarity, sharpness, and intensity are present, there is the Noble Path.
Some say that restlessness predominates in the desire realm,
while tranquility predominates at the Peak of Existence.
It is said that the Noble Path exists neither where there is excessive restlessness nor where there is excessive tranquility. Some say:
The desire realm is characterized by distraction;
the Peak of Existence is characterized by hesitation.
It is only in a state of tranquility and certainty that the Noble Path can exist.
Some say that the desire realm and the peak of existence are the lower and upper limits,
and the noble path lies between them.
Because they do not exist at the extremes.
Some say that because the desire realm and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) possess a fundamental basis, the noble path does not exist there.
This refers to the tree of birth and death;
its roots are below,
while its trunk and other parts are above.
Alternatively, the roots are above while the stalks and so forth are below;
the desire realm is the root of clamor and confusion, and is thus said to be "below."
Because the faculties (indriya) exist throughout the five destinies (gati),
and because the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is the most difficult to abandon, it is designated as "superior" (ūrdhva) since it is the last to be abandoned among the faculties.
If one takes the fundamental basis of clamor and confusion as the tree of birth and death,
then the desire realm constitutes the root and the four dhyānas constitute the trunk.
The three formless realms are its branches,
and the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is its twigs and leaves.
If one relies upon this root which is so difficult to abandon, [one will not escape saṃsāra].
It constitutes the tree of birth and death:
the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is its root,
and the three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) are its trunk.
The four dhyānas constitute the branches,
while the desire realm constitutes the twigs and leaves;
therefore, it is said that the desire realm and the peak of existence (bhavāgra) possess roots.
Because this has a root, there is no noble path.
Is it possible to achieve the first dhyāna associated with relishing (āsvādana),
yet not that which is pure (śuddha) or untainted (anāsrava)?
Answer: Yes. That is to say, when desire for the realm of sensuality has not been exhausted;
specifically, when desire for the lower realms has not been exhausted.
One must necessarily achieve craving for the higher stages,
because one has not yet attained the fundamental pure and untainted [attainments] of those stages.
Is it possible to achieve the pure first dhyāna?
Is it not associated with flavor (*āsvādana*) and yet untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*).
One who has exhausted craving for the Brahma-world is born in this [present] stage or a lower stage;
however, one who has exhausted craving for this stage necessarily accomplishes the purity of this stage.
Because one necessarily does not accomplish the dhyāna associated with relish (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*) on this stage,
and because one is still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one does not accomplish the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Is it possible to accomplish the untainted first dhyāna without accomplishing that which is associated with relish or the pure (*śuddhaka*)?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to when noble ones (*ārya*) are born in the Brahma-world or above;
for when noble ones are born in a higher stage (*bhūmi*), they necessarily possess the untainted (*anāsrava*) factors of the lower stages.
It will certainly not be accomplished because the mundane (*laukika*) states associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) of the lower stage have been abandoned,
and because the pure (*śuddha*) states have been relinquished upon transcending that stage.
Question: One born in a higher realm also accomplishes the mind of supernormal power resulting from the lower realms.
Why, then, is it said that they do not accomplish the pure [mind] of the lower realms?
Answer: Some say that the unobscured-neutral is also called "pure" (śubha),
yet it is not mentioned here.
Because it is the fruit of a higher stage,
it is not termed "pure" (śuddha) of a lower stage.
Furthermore, that which is attainable in all stages is what is discussed here.
The fruition-mind (*abhiṣaṃskārika-citta*) does not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
therefore, it is not mentioned.
This is what is meant by that statement.
In this context, "pure concentration" (śuddha-samādhi) refers to wholesome states with outflows (sāsrava-kuśala).
Therefore, there is no difficulty [in the argument].
Is it possible for one to possess both the relishing-associated (āsvādana-saṃprayukta) and the pure (śuddha) first dhyāna?
Is it not the case that there are [beings] who are not untainted?
Answer: There are.
That is to say, ordinary beings born in the desire realm.
One for whom craving for the desire realm has been exhausted but craving for the Brahma-world has not yet been exhausted;
and one who is born in the Brahma-world but whose craving for the Brahma-world has not yet been exhausted;
and one who is born in this stage or a lower stage but whose craving for this stage has not yet been exhausted.
This is because one necessarily achieves the purity associated with the relish (*āsvādana*) of this stage;
furthermore, because one is still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one does not achieve the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Is it possible, however, for one to achieve both the relish-associated and the untainted first dhyāna?
"Is it not pure? Answer: "No.
Because one has accomplished the flavor-corresponding and the outflow-free states of this stage."
Because one must necessarily achieve the purity of this stage.
Is there perhaps the achievement of pure and untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna that is not associated with attachment (*āsvādana*)?
Answer: There is.
It refers to a noble one born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world who has exhausted craving for the Brahma-world.
When an Ārya is born in this stage or a lower stage and has exhausted craving for this stage,
they necessarily possess the pure (śuddhaka) and untainted (anāsrava) [attainments] of this stage,
because they do not possess those associated with relishing (āsvādana).
Is there anyone who accomplishes the first dhyāna associated with relish, the pure, and the untainted?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, a noble one born in the desire realm.
The craving for the desire realm is exhausted,
but the craving for the Brahma world is not yet exhausted;
and having been born in the Brahma world, the craving for the Brahma world is not yet exhausted.
This is because an noble one is born in this stage or a lower stage,
yet while craving for the lower stages has been exhausted,
craving for this stage has not yet been exhausted.
Because one must necessarily accomplish the three types of this stage.
Is it possible that there is one who does not accomplish the first dhyāna associated with relish,
yet does accomplish both the pure and the untainted [versions]?
Answer: There are.
That is to say, when noble ones are born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world, their craving for the Brahma-world has been exhausted.
Such passages as these are as explained in the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*).
One should explain them in detail according to their respective applications, in contrast to the characteristics of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Question: Regarding the one for whom craving for the Brahma-world has been exhausted (*brahmaloka-tṛṣṇā-kṣaya*).
Nor does one achieve the pure *parihāṇabhāgīya* first dhyāna.
Why is this not mentioned here? Some say: [omitted].
Regarding that which should have been stated but was not:
one should know that this meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*). Some say:
In this context, it is said that they are entirely unaccomplished;
although they do not accomplish the stage conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*),
they do accomplish the others.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Question: Why is it that pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*) abandons the stages by transcending them, whereas the untainted (*anāsrava*) does not?
Answer: Pure concentration is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Because it falls within the realms and stages, one generates revulsion for the lower upon arising in the upper;
furthermore, because it is no longer functional, one then abandons the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state.
Although one may fall to the ground,
one does not fall into the realms;
though born in the higher [realms], one does not loathe the lower.
Although it is useless, one does not abandon it.
Is there perhaps the attainment of the first dhyāna associated with relish that is neither pure nor untainted?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, at the time of falling back from the exhaustion of craving for the Brahma-world, and at the time of passing away from the Brahma-world above to be reborn in the desire realm.
Question: When one falls away from the exhaustion of craving for the Brahma-world, one also attains the pure "partaking of decline" (hānabhāgīya) first dhyāna.
Why is this not mentioned here?
Some say: "When something that ought to be stated is not stated,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete."
Some say: "In this context, those who are said to have attained [the path] in its entirety actually attain only a small portion."
Therefore, it is not so stated.
Is there a case where one attains the pure first dhyāna that is neither associated with relishing nor untainted?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to when an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) has exhausted craving for the desire realm;
specifically, at the time of the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) when they are free from the defilements of desire.
Because one attains the fundamental pure (*śuddha*) first dhyāna,
is it possible to attain the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna without it being associated with relish (*āsvādana*) or being the pure [dhyāna]?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, one enters into rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based upon the dhyānas or the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
Furthermore, at the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship,
it is asked: does one who enters rightness and departure from birth also attain the pure first dhyāna?
This refers to the conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) at the conclusion of clear realization (abhisamaya). Why is it not mentioned here? Some say:
Regarding that which should have been said but was not:
one should know that there is more to be said. Some say:
Regarding those mentioned here as attaining the whole,
they attain only a small portion; therefore,
they are not so described.
Some say that within the stage of entering the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), it is for the most part not obtained;
it is obtained only during three moments.
For this reason, it is not mentioned.
Some say that only the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) cease.
When the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises,
it is called "entering the state of rightness and departure from birth" (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
At that time, because one attains only the untainted (*anāsrava*), it is not described as "pure" (*śubha*).
Question: At the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship, one has already previously attained the untainted first dhyāna;
that is, at the time of entering rightness-in-detachment (samyaktva-niyāma).
Why is it further stated that one "attains the untainted" (*anāsrava*)?
The answer is: this passage should only speak of entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma-avakrānti*);
it should not speak of attaining the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*).
As for making this statement,

it is intended to show that although one had previously attained the learner’s state (*śaikṣa*) and the untainted state (*anāsrava*), one had not yet attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*);
therefore, it is stated once again.
Question: If that were so, one should also say that the fetters of the Brahma-world arise when one falls from the fruit of arhatship,
because at that time one regains the learner’s (śaikṣa) untainted [attainments].
Answer: Although the principle should also have been stated, it was not;
this is because one wishes to manifest that the untainted (*anāsrava*) is a supreme merit.
When progressing toward excellence, it is conducive to realization if [the nature] is manifested.
When one falls back [from a fruit], if it were manifested, it would not be concordant;
therefore, it is not mentioned.
Question: If that is so, at the time of attaining the fruits of training (śaikṣa-phala)...
Furthermore, when one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
they simultaneously attain superior outflow-free (anāsrava) qualities. Why, then, are these not mentioned here?
Answer: This was previously training (*śaikṣa*), and what is now attained is likewise training;
therefore, it is not mentioned. For this reason, the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is also not mentioned.
Question: When one attains the fruit of arhatship, one also attains immeasurable wholesome dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*).
Why, then, is it not said that one also attains the pure (*viśuddha*)?
Some say: "When that which ought to be stated is not stated,
one should know that there is more to be said."
Some say that in the case of the untainted (*anāsrava*), one first attains [the later state] and then relinquishes [the former]; therefore,
it is said that in the case of the tainted (*sāsrava*), one does not relinquish the former while attaining the latter.
For this reason, it is not mentioned. Some say:
"That which is obtained now..."
Together with what was previously attained, these are both termed "pure" (*śuddha*);
there is no difference in their meaning,
unlike the distinct characteristics found between those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
For this reason, it is not mentioned.
Some say that although it is attained, it is not mentioned because it is indeterminate;
that is to say, it is attained by one who is born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world and subsequently attains the fruit of arhatship.
Because those born in a higher realm do not obtain it.
Some say that "all" is mentioned here [in the context of acquisition],
but that refers only to a partial acquisition.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Is there a case where one attains the first dhyāna associated with relishing (āsvādana-samprayukta) or the pure (śuddha), but not the untainted (anāsrava)?
Answer: There is.
This refers to when one dies in the Brahma-world and is reborn in the Brahma-world;
because both [the intermediate state and the birth state] are attained at the time of birth.
Is it possible to attain the first dhyāna associated with tasting (*āsvādana-samprayukta*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), but not the pure (*śuddha*)?
Answer: No. Question:
When an Arhat falls away due to the arising of the fetters (paryavasthāna) of the Brahma-world, they obtain both types [of attainment]; why then do you say there is none?
To agree that it exists is precisely what has been explained above;
to say that it does not exist—
It should be understood that there is more to be said. Some say:
"That which was not previously accomplished is now accomplished."
This is called attaining the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna;
because it has already been accomplished previously, it is not mentioned here. Some say:
It has already been stated that the untainted (anāsrava) is a supreme merit.
When there is progress toward excellence, the manifestation of this [untainted state] is favorable;
when there is regression, its manifestation is unfavorable.
Therefore, it is not so stated.
Is there a case where one attains the pure, untainted first dhyāna that is not associated with relishing?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to when a noble one has exhausted craving for the desire realm;
at the time of attaining the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala), both are acquired simultaneously.
Is there anyone who attains the first dhyāna associated with relish, the pure, or the untainted?
Answer: No. Question:
When one falls from the fruit of arhatship due to the arising of the fetters (paryavasthāna) of the Brahma-world, [is there such attainment]?
Question: Why are the three types not said to be acquired together?
Answer: At that time, they are not mentioned because the pure [attainments] are acquired only in small measure;
the untainted ones are as previously explained.
Question: What is the difference between "attainment" (prāpti) and "possession" (samanvāgama)?
Some say that the names themselves constitute the difference.
This refers to what is called "attainment" (prāpti) and "possession" (samanvāgama).
Some say: [end of quote]
Some say that one who has not yet attained [a state] is said to have "attained" it,
and one who has already attained it is said to have "accomplished" it.
Initially it is called "attainment" (prāpti);
subsequently, when it occurs repeatedly, it is called "accomplishment" (samanvāgama). Some say:
That which was not previously accomplished but is now accomplished is called "attainment" (prāpti).
That which was previously accomplished and remains accomplished is called "possession" (samanvāgama). Some say:
That which was previously unconnected and then becomes connected is called "acquisition" (prāpti);
that which was previously connected and remains connected is called "possession" (samanvāgama).
Some say that the initial acquisition is termed "acquisition."
To obtain [the fruit] and not lose it is called "attainment" (*samanvāgama*).
Some say that its initial acquisition is called "attainment."
Having attained [it] and not losing it is called accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Therefore, attainment occurs only at the beginning,
whereas accomplishment extends through both the beginning and the end.
This is called the distinction. Is there any abandonment of the first dhyāna associated with relishing that is neither pure nor untainted?
Answer: There is.
Namely, at the time when craving for the Brahma-world is exhausted.
Such passages as these are as explained in the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*).
One should explain them in detail according to their respective applications, in opposition to the attainment (*prāpti*).
Question: At the time when craving for the Brahma-world is exhausted, does one also relinquish the pure state conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*)?
Why is it not mentioned?
The answer is: herein, all forms of relinquishment are taught, whereas there, only a limited portion of relinquishment is taught.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Question: In the cases of attaining the fruits, refining the faculties, and the state of falling away, there is always only the abandonment of the untainted first dhyāna and no others.
Regarding this, why is it not mentioned?
Some say that if something ought to be stated but is not, [it is because...]
One should know that there is more to it.
Some say that although equanimity (*upekṣā*) is mentioned here, it is not actually attained.
Because that which was abandoned is subsequently regained, it is not mentioned.
Question: What is the distinction between "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) and "non-possession" (*aprāpti*)?
The answer is that "name" refers to differentiation.
When one abandons a name, that name is no longer attained.
Such cases should be explained in detail according to the principles of attainment and non-attainment as previously established.
Is there any falling away from the first dhyāna associated with relish that is not [falling away] from the pure or the untainted? Answer: No.

Because one who has abandoned the afflictions is not said to have "fallen back," is it possible to fall back from the pure first dhyāna without falling back from the one associated with relishing (āsvādana) or the untainted (anāsrava)?
Answer: Yes.

That is to say, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) falls away from the exhaustion of craving in the desire realm, is there a falling away from the pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna that is not associated with relishing (*āsvādana*)?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, when a noble one falls away from the exhaustion of craving for the desire realm, is there any other falling away?

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Order, based on the work of the Sixty-Four Hundred Great Arhats and others. Section Seven:

The Aggregate of Concentration (*Samādhiskandha*). Second Sub-section: The Chapter on Conditions (*Pratyayavarga*). Part Three. There is cultivation of neither the pure (*śuddha*) first dhyāna nor the untainted (*anāsrava*).
That is to say, either the conventional knowledge and the untainted knowledge of the non-initial dhyāna have already been attained and are currently manifest;
or, if they have not yet been attained, [they are being sought].
When those [states] are present before him, he does not cultivate the pure first dhyāna nor the untainted [dhyāna].
This applies when any defiled mind or neutral mind is present before him.
If one dwells in the attainment of non-conception or the attainment of cessation,
is born in the heaven of non-conception,
and has already attained mundane knowledge of the first dhyāna such that it is present before them;
In this context, the remaining stages are designated by the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
These range from the desire realm and the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), excluding the first dhyāna,
up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
This means that when these various stages (*bhūmi*) previously attained mundane qualities manifest,
their momentum does not even reach their own second moment,
let alone enable the cultivation of other future qualities.
Furthermore, because it is not the first dhyāna, there is no sense of cultivation regarding either the pure or the untainted [states] associated with the first dhyāna.
This refers to one for whom an untainted knowledge that is not the first dhyāna has already been attained and is present before them.
In this context, the other stages are also designated by the name "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
This refers to everything from the *anāgamya* (preparatory stage) up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), excluding the first dhyāna.
That is to say, when the previously attained untainted (*anāsrava*) qualities manifest in these various stages.
Their functional range does not even extend beyond their own second moment,
let alone enable the cultivation of other future merits;
furthermore, it is not the first dhyāna.
Regarding the pure and untainted first dhyāna, there is no sense of cultivation [of them] together.

If one has not yet attained the mundane knowledge that is not the first dhyāna, and it manifests before one, yet one does not cultivate the pure first dhyāna and the untainted [first dhyāna], [then this is the case].
In this context, the other stages are also designated by the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
This refers to everything from the Desire Realm and the Threshold Concentration (*anāgamya*)—
excluding the First Dhyāna— up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
That is to say, an ordinary person gives rise to the previously unobtained contemplation of impurity and mindfulness of breathing belonging to the desire realm.
The foundations of mindfulness,
the contemplation of the three meanings,
and other wisdoms consisting of hearing and reflection.
At the time when it is present before one,
it refers to the various paths of preparation for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is becoming detached from the defilements of the desire realm.
At the time of the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation,
one is still an ordinary person who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire.
Based on the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi), one gives rise to the three immeasurables (apramāṇa),
the first two liberations (vimokṣa),
and the first four bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).
The contemplation of impurity,
mindfulness of breathing,
and the foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding the contemplation of the three meanings:
at the stages of Heat, Peak, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma,
one has already abandoned the defilements of desire and relies upon the preparatory concentration (anāgamya).
When the stages of Heat, Peak, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma arise,
they do so based on the intermediate dhyāna.
When the stages of Heat, Peak, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma arise, they do so based on the intermediate dhyāna.
That is to say, an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), relying on the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna as their practice (*prayoga*),
becomes detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna;
such is their path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
At the time of the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the nine paths of liberation,
an ordinary person relies upon the second dhyāna.
At the time of the preparatory paths, the five paths of uninterrupted transition,
and the three paths of liberation that induce the five supernormal powers.
The four immeasurables,
the first two liberations,
and the first four bases of mastery.
The contemplation of impurity,
the foundations of mindfulness,
and the contemplation of the three meanings.
Regarding the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas,
some say that mindfulness of breathing is also aroused at those times.
That is to say, when an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is free from the defilements of the second dhyāna,
at the time of all preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,
that ordinary person relies upon the third dhyāna.
At the time of the preparatory paths, the five uninterrupted paths,
and the three paths of liberation that induce the five supernormal powers.
The three immeasurables,
the contemplation of impurity,
and the foundations of mindfulness.
The contemplation on the three meanings:
the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas. Some say:
Furthermore, when one gives rise to mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*),
it is at the time of all preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths when an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) becomes detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
That is to say, an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), relying on the fourth dhyāna,
brings forth the preparatory paths (prayoga-mārga) and the five uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga) for the five supernormal powers (abhijñā).
At the time of the three paths of liberation,
one gives rise to the three immeasurables and the pure liberation.
The latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
the former eight bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
and the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*).
The foundations of mindfulness,
the three contemplations of meaning,
and the stages of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas.
That is, when an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
at the time of all preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,
that ordinary person gives rise to the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana).
At the time of liberation, the spheres of totality, and the foundations of mindfulness,
an ordinary person is free from the sphere of infinite space.
During the paths of preparation, uninterrupted transition, and liberation regarding the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness,
as well as during all preparatory stages.
That is, the ordinary person gives rise to the consciousness-infinity sphere,
the nothingness sphere,
and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Liberation, the foundations of mindfulness,
and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
At the time of the universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana),
if noble ones (ārya) give rise to the previously unattained contemplation of impurity (aśubhabhāvanā) pertaining to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Mindfulness of breathing,
the foundations of mindfulness,
and the contemplation of the three meanings.
Furthermore, when the wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection manifests,
the noble one then detaches from the defilements of the desire realm by means of the mundane path.
If the mundane is the preparatory effort,
it includes all paths of preparation,
as well as the nine uninterrupted paths.
At the time of the eight paths of liberation,
one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm by means of the untainted path;
if the mundane path is employed as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

At the time of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire transforms their faculty through resolute faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
If the worldly [path] serves as the preparation, [this occurs].
At the time of that path of preparation,
the noble one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire relies on the *anāgamya* concentration to give rise to the three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
The first two liberations,
the first four bases of mastery,
and the contemplation of impurity.
Mindfulness of breathing,
mundane foundations of mindfulness,
and the contemplation of the three meanings.
At the time when one enters the attainment of cessation from the state of "subtle-subtle mind" during proficiency in the seven bases, at such a time,
a conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) not previously attained arises and becomes present, though it does not belong to the first dhyāna.
One does not cultivate the pure first dhyāna nor the untainted [first dhyāna].
If one has not yet attained the untainted knowledge of the first dhyāna and it is not present before one,
yet one does not cultivate the pure first dhyāna nor the untainted [first dhyāna], [then this is the case].
In this context, other stages are also designated by the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

That is to say, for one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire, the four moments of mind during each of the clear realizations of the Four Truths (*catur-āryasatya-abhisamaya*) upon entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Furthermore, for one who has already abandoned the defilements of desire, [the same applies] when entering the state of right determination based on the *anāgamya* concentration.
The clear realizations of suffering, origin, and cessation each take four moments of mind;
the clear realization of the path takes three moments of mind.
This occurs when one abandons the defilements of the desire realm by means of the untainted path, with the untainted serving as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
At the time of all the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
and the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

When one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire and possesses liberation through faith undergoes the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*),
if the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) is untainted (*anāsrava*),
then at the time of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of that preparation:
When one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire gives rise to the untainted foundations of mindfulness,
at such a time there arises that which has never been attained before;
it is not the case that the untainted knowledge of the first dhyāna is present.
One does not cultivate the pure first dhyāna nor the untainted [dhyāna].
If any defiled mind manifests before one—
namely, a mind associated with the afflictions and secondary afflictions of the three realms— [then one does not cultivate them].
Because that which accords with decline is by nature heavy and associated with indolence,
whereas only that which accords with superior progress— being light and buoyant and associated with diligence— is capable of cultivation.
"All indeterminate minds that are present" refers to the unobscured-indeterminate minds of the three realms; because they are not firm,
not stable, and not real, their nature is weak and inferior, like a rotten seed.
This is because one must abide firmly in reality with a robust nature in order to cultivate it; furthermore,
for those who abide in the attainment of non-conception or the attainment of cessation,
since these are mindless states, cultivation can only be achieved through a state that possesses mind.
Regarding those born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*),
some say that within that heaven,
as long as the life-constituent (*nikāyasabhāga*) lasts, no wholesome mind arises.
Some say that although a wholesome mind arises in those gods, because it is not the basis for cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it lacks the sense of "cultivation. Here,
however, the text speaks only of those born in a stage of cultivation who do not cultivate.
However, there are also cases where [the cultivation] is not practiced when one is born in other places;
since these are easy to understand, they are not mentioned.
As it is said:
The same is said for the first, second, and third dhyānas.
This is because, at the time of the final path of liberation from the defilements of the lower stages, these respective levels [are attained].
Because there are those who enter the fundamental stage and those who do not.
If one cultivates the pure fourth dhyāna,
does one also cultivate the untainted (anāsrava) therein?
If one cultivates the untainted (anāsrava) fourth dhyāna,
does one also cultivate the pure (śuddha) [fourth dhyāna]?
One should respond by setting up four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the pure fourth dhyāna that is not untainted (anāsrava).
This refers to when the pure fourth dhyāna already attained is present before one,
or when the pure fourth dhyāna not yet attained is present before one.
Yet they do not cultivate the untainted [attainments].
Those for whom the already-acquired pure fourth dhyāna is present are both ordinary beings and noble ones.
Whether it be a learner (*śaikṣa*) up to a Tathāgata,
for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) and so forth,
when they bring to presence the fourth dhyāna of the mundane order (*laukika*) previously attained, [it arises].
Their influence does not even reach their own second moment,
let alone enable the cultivation of other future merits;
nevertheless, the state of being present is itself the cultivation through practice (*āsevana-bhāvanā*).
This is called the cultivation of the pure fourth dhyāna.
If one has not yet attained the pure fourth dhyāna manifest before them,
yet does not cultivate the untainted (anāsrava), [this is not so].
This refers to the final path of liberation of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who has become detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
as well as [the path] for becoming detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna.
If the fourth dhyāna serves as the preparatory practice,
then at the time of that path of preparation,
an ordinary person relies upon the fourth dhyāna.
At the time of the preparatory paths, the five uninterrupted paths,
and the three paths of liberation that induce the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā).
One gives rise to the three immeasurables,
the pure liberation,
and the latter four spheres of mastery.
The first eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*),
and the threefold contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
At the time of the stages of Heat, Peak, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma, at such times,
there arises the previously unattained,
pure fourth dhyāna, which manifests before one.
Yet one does not cultivate the untainted [meditation].
There is cultivation of the untainted fourth dhyāna that is not pure;
this refers to when the already attained untainted fourth dhyāna is present before one.
If one has not yet attained the manifestation of the untainted fourth dhyāna and does not cultivate the pure [dhyāna];
and if one has not yet attained mundane knowledge that is not the fourth dhyāna,
nor untainted knowledge that is not the fourth dhyāna.
They bring to presence and cultivate the untainted fourth dhyāna, not the pure one.
Those who have already attained the untainted fourth dhyāna and bring it to presence are the noble ones (*ārya*).
Whether it be for the sake of training, or even for the Tathāgata’s dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*),
when the previously attained untainted (*anāsrava*) fourth dhyāna arises and manifests,
its momentum does not even last beyond its own second moment.
How much more so for being able to cultivate other future merits;
since the present state itself constitutes the cultivation through practice (*āsevana-bhāvanā*),
it is termed the cultivation of the untainted fourth dhyāna.
If one has not yet attained the manifestation of the untainted fourth dhyāna,
yet does not cultivate the pure [dhyāna],
this refers to entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on the fourth dhyāna.
The clear realizations of suffering, origin, and cessation each take three moments of mind;
the clear realization of the path takes four moments of mind.
The noble one, relying upon the fourth dhyāna, becomes detached from the fourth dhyāna.
Up to the point of being defiled by the sphere of nothingness,
during all moments of the uninterrupted path and the path of liberation,
one becomes free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

During the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation, one who relies on the fourth dhyāna and possesses resolution through faith transforms their faculties to become one who has attained vision;
this occurs during the moments of the uninterrupted and liberation paths.
When an Arhat of occasional liberation (samaya-vimukta) refines their faculties to become unshakable (akopya),
during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) and the eight paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga),
at such times they give rise to the previously unattained untainted (anāsrava) fourth dhyāna as it manifests before them, yet they do not cultivate the pure (śuddha) dhyāna.
If one has not yet attained the mundane knowledge (*sāṃvṛtijñāna*) of the fourth dhyāna,
yet cultivates the untainted (*anāsrava*) fourth dhyāna rather than the pure (*śuddha*),
then in this context the remaining stages are designated by the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
That is to say, from the *anāgamya* concentration, excluding the fourth *dhyāna*,
up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; that is,
the noble ones rely upon the *anāgamya* concentration.
In order to become detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
up to those of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
if one employs the mundane [path] as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
At the time of that path of preparation,
relying on the *anāgamya* concentration and having already abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna,
one who is resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
When one who is liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) refines their faculties to become immovable (akopya),
if they employ the mundane path as the preparatory application (prayoga-mārga),
then at the time of that path of preparation, they have already abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna.
The Noble One, relying on the preparatory concentration (anāgamya),
gives rise to the three immeasurables (apramāṇa) and the first two liberations (vimokṣa).
The first four bases of mastery,
the meditation on impurity,
and mindfulness of breathing.
The mundane foundations of mindfulness consist of three types of contemplation on the meaning and the seven points of proficiency.
When the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the conventional analytical knowledge (*saṃvṛti-pratisaṃvid*) arise and increase;
and when emptiness-of-emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), wishlessness-of-wishlessness (*apraṇihita-apraṇihita*), and signlessness-of-signlessness (*animitta-animitta*) arise and increase.
That is to say, for a noble one, based on the first dhyāna, [the path serves] as the antidote to the defilements of the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
if it is a worldly [path], it serves as the preparatory application.
At the time of that path of preparation,
relying on the first dhyāna and having already become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
one who is resolved through faith transforms their faculties to become one who has attained vision.
When one who is liberated by occasion refines their faculties to become immovable,
if they employ the mundane path as the preparatory application,
then at the time of that path of preparation:
When practicing the mixed cultivation of the intermediate mind of the first dhyāna,

the noble one who has already abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna relies upon the first dhyāna to induce the preparatory paths and the five uninterrupted paths for the five supernormal powers.
During the two paths of liberation,
as well as during the mundane supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds,
one gives rise to the four immeasurables based on that very first dhyāna.
The first two liberations,
the first four bases of mastery,
and the contemplation of impurity.
The mundane foundations of mindfulness,
the contemplation of the three meanings,
and proficiency in the seven points.
Some say that it also arises at the time of practicing mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti),
and at the time of increasing the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) and conventional analytical knowledge (saṃvṛtipratisaṃvid).
When the emptiness-of-emptiness, the wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and the signlessness-of-signlessness arise and increase,
the noble ones rely upon the intermediate dhyāna.
In order to become detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
up to those of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
if one employs the mundane path as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
At the time of that path of preparation,
relying on the intermediate dhyāna and having already become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
one who is resolved through faith transforms their faculties to become one who has attained vision.
When one who is liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) refines their faculties to become immovable (akopya),
if they employ the mundane path as the preparatory application (prayoga),
then at the time of that path of preparation:
Having already become detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
the noble one gives rise to the three immeasurables based on the intermediate dhyāna.
The first two liberations,
the first four bases of mastery,
and the meditation on impurity.
Mindfulness of breathing,
the mundane foundations of mindfulness,
and the contemplation of the three meanings.
At the time of proficiency in the seven bases;
at the time of the arising and increase of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and conventional analytical knowledge;
and at the time of the arising and increase of emptiness-of-emptiness, wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and signlessness-of-signlessness.
As it was said regarding the first dhyāna,
so it is with the second dhyāna.
The same is said regarding the third dhyāna.
The difference is that, based on the third dhyāna, one excludes the immeasurables of joy (muditā).
This applies to the first two liberations (vimokṣa).
Regarding the first four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
the rest are all as previously explained; that is,
the noble ones, by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), become detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna.
If one takes the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space as the preliminary practice (*prayoga*),
then at all times during the preliminary, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,
that very person employs the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
Free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space,
the sphere of infinite consciousness,
and the sphere of nothingness.
If the mundane [path] serves as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*),
then at the time of all preparatory, uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and liberation paths (*vimukti-mārga*),
that very basis is the formless meditative absorption (*ārūpya-samādhi*).
When one abandons the defilements of the four formless realms by means of the untainted path,
if the mundane path serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
then at the time of that preparatory path, one relies upon the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
When an Arhat of occasional liberation (samaya-vimukta) refines their faculties to become unshakable (akopya),
if they employ the mundane path as the preparatory application (prayoga),
then at the time of that path of preparation (prayoga-mārga):
That is to say, when a noble one gives rise to the mundane liberations of the formless realm and the latter two spheres of totality,
they give rise to mundane applications of mindfulness based upon those very formless absorptions.
When the two conventional analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) increase,
as well as when the emptiness-of-emptiness, wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and signlessness-of-signlessness arise and increase.
When one gives rise to the subtle mind associated with the perception of entering the attainment of cessation,
at such a time there arises that which has never been attained before:
the mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the fourth dhyāna does not manifest.
And one cultivates the untainted fourth dhyāna;
it is not the case that while the pure [fourth dhyāna] has not yet been attained, or while the untainted knowledge of a non-fourth-dhyāna state is present before one,
one cultivates the untainted fourth dhyāna.
Regarding those that are not pure: herein, the remaining stages are designated by the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
These range from the *anāgamya* (preparatory concentration) up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), excluding the fourth dhyāna.
That is to say, based on the *anāgamya*, one becomes detached from the fourth dhyāna.
Up to and including the defilement of the sphere of nothingness,
if the untainted serves as the preparatory application,
then at all times during the preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths.
Regarding the detachment from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
if the uncontaminated [path] serves as the preparatory application,
that is the path of preparation.
At the time of the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation,
one relies on the *anāgamya* concentration and has already become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
When one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
if they employ the untainted (anāsrava) as their preparatory application (prayoga),
then at the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) and the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) of that preparation:
When a time-liberated arhat refines their faculties to become unshakable,
if they take the untainted as their preparatory application,
then for that path of preparation there are nine paths of uninterrupted transition.
At the time of the eighth path of liberation,
when the noble one has already become detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna and,
relying on the *anāgamya* concentration, develops the untainted foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the untainted analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
That is to say, the noble one relies upon the first dhyāna to become detached from the fourth dhyāna,
up to and including the defilements of the sphere of nothingness.
If the untainted [path] serves as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*),
then at all times during the preparatory, uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and liberation (*vimukti*) paths,
one becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
If the untainted serves as the preparatory stage,
then that preparatory path consists of nine uninterrupted paths.
At the time of the eighth path of liberation,
having relied on the first dhyāna and already become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
one who was previously resolved through faith transforms their faculties to become "attained through vision."
If the untainted [path] serves as the preparatory application,
then at the moment of the path of liberation immediately following that application,
a time-liberated arhat refines their faculties to become one who is immovable.
If the untainted serves as the preparatory application,
then that path of preparation consists of nine paths of uninterrupted transition.
At the time of the eight paths of liberation,
and at the time of the first and last moments of mind during the mixed cultivation of the first dhyāna,
the noble one has already become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
When one gives rise to the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds that is untainted by relying on the first dhyāna,
and when untainted applications of mindfulness and untainted analytical knowledges increase, [these are cultivated].
The intermediate dhyāna is as described for the preparatory stage (anāgamya).
The second and third dhyānas are as described for the first dhyāna.
That is, the noble one relies upon the sphere of infinite space.
Having emerged from the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of nothingness, it is defiled;
if it is untainted, it serves as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
At the time of all preparatory, uninterrupted,
and liberation paths when abandoning the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
if the path is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it serves as the preparatory stage.
At the time of that path of preparation,
the nine paths of uninterrupted transition,
and the eight paths of liberation.
When a time-liberated arhat, relying on the sphere of infinite space, refines their faculties to become unshakable,
if they take the untainted as their preparatory application,
that is their path of preparation.
During the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation,
one gives rise to the untainted liberation of the sphere of infinite space.
Relying on the sphere of infinite space,
when one gives rise to untainted applications of mindfulness and increases the two untainted analytical knowledges.
As it is said:
"In dependence upon the sphere of infinite space,
so too in dependence upon the sphere of infinite consciousness."
The sphere of nothingness is likewise.
The difference is that one is detached from the defilements of the stage immediately above it.
At such a time,
there arises before him an unprecedented, untainted knowledge that is not the fourth dhyāna;
he thus cultivates the untainted fourth dhyāna, not the pure one.
There is cultivation of both the pure fourth dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava).
That is to say: when one who has not yet attained the pure fourth dhyāna brings it into presence and cultivates the untainted;
or when one who has not yet attained the untainted fourth dhyāna brings it into presence and cultivates the pure.
If one has not yet attained the untainted knowledge of the fourth dhyāna,
yet cultivates the pure fourth dhyāna as well as the untainted [fourth dhyāna],
such that this untainted knowledge is present before one.
Regarding one who, without having attained the pure fourth dhyāna, brings it into presence and cultivates the untainted:
this refers to a noble one who, by means of the mundane path, has become detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
At the time of the final path of liberation,
he relies upon that very fourth dhyāna in order to become detached from the fourth dhyāna.
Up to the defilement of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
if the mundane is the preparatory application,
then at the time of that path of preparation, one relies upon the fourth dhyāna.
One who possesses faith and liberation (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta);
one who is liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) refines their faculties to become one who is immovable (akopyadharman).
If worldly [concentration] is used as the preparatory application (prayoga), [this occurs].
At the time of that path of preparation,
when one practices the mixed cultivation of the intermediate mind of the fourth dhyāna,
the noble one relies upon the fourth dhyāna.
It induces the five supernormal powers,
the various paths of preparation,
and the five paths of immediate succession.
Second, at the time of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the supramundane supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna-abhijñā*),
the noble one relies upon the fourth dhyāna.
One gives rise to the three immeasurables, the pure liberations,
the latter four bases of mastery,
and the first eight totalities.
The contemplation of impurity,
the mundane foundations of mindfulness,
and the contemplation of the three meanings.
At the time of mastery over the seven bases,
one gives rise to the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) based on the fourth dhyāna;

and at the time of increasing the conventional analytical knowledge, one gives rise to the concentration of the limit of the knowledge of vows free from contention (*araṇāpraṇidhijñānaparyantasaṃādhi*).
And at the time of increase,
based on the fourth dhyāna, one gives rise to the emptiness-of-emptiness, the wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and the signlessness-of-signlessness,
as well as at the time of their increase.
At such a time, one brings forth the previously unattained pure fourth dhyāna into the present and cultivates it as untainted (anāsrava). If, however,
one has not yet attained the untainted fourth dhyāna and brings it into the present while cultivating the pure [dhyāna], [it is likewise].
That is to say, relying on the fourth dhyāna, one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, origin, and cessation each occupy the duration of a single moment of mind,
relying upon the fourth dhyāna.
For the sake of becoming detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
if the uncontaminated [path] serves as the preparatory application.
At the time of the path of preparation,
he attains the fruit of arhatship based on the fourth dhyāna;
at the moment the first knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) arises.
Based on the fourth dhyāna,
one who possesses conviction through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
provided that the preparatory practice (prayoga) is untainted (anāsrava).
At the time of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
a time-liberated (*samaya-vimukta*) Arhat who refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) to become unshakable (*akopya*) takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as the path of preparation.
At the time of that path of preparation and the final path of liberation,
as well as at the time of the initial and final moments of the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna.
Based on the fourth dhyāna,
one gives rise to the supernormal power of uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds and the uncontaminated applications of mindfulness.
Furthermore, when the untainted (anāsrava) analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) increase, at such a time,
one brings forth the previously unattained untainted fourth dhyāna into presence and cultivates the pure (śubha).
If one has not yet attained the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the fourth dhyāna,
yet cultivates the pure fourth dhyāna and the untainted [fourth dhyāna],
then in this context the remaining stages are designated by the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
That is to say, excluding the fourth dhyāna from the threshold concentration (anāgamya) up to the sphere of nothingness; that is,
relying on the threshold concentration.
Up to the third dhyāna,
at the time of the final path of liberation when one becomes free from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
That is to say, at the moment one attains the first knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) as an arhat based on that stage,
and when an arhat of occasional liberation (*samaya-vimukta*) based on that same stage refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) to become unshakable (*akopya*).
At the moment of the final path of liberation,
when one attains the fruit of arhatship through the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) at the initial arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna),
it is precisely by relying on that same stage.
When an Arhat of occasional liberation (samayavimukta) refines their faculties to become immovable (akopya),
at the moment of the final path of liberation,
they give rise to that which has never been attained before.
It is not the case that one cultivates the pure [attainment] of the fourth dhyāna while the untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) of the fourth dhyāna is present;
rather, both the fourth dhyāna and the untainted [knowledge] are cultivated.
There is one who does not cultivate the pure fourth dhyāna,
nor the untainted; that is,
one who has already attained [a state] that is not the fourth dhyāna.
When mundane knowledge (*sāṃvṛtijñāna*) or untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) is present before one,
if it has not yet been attained and is not the fourth dhyāna,
it is mundane knowledge.
Regarding untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*):
when it is present before one, one does not cultivate the pure fourth dhyāna nor the untainted [fourth dhyāna].
This is also the case when any defiled or neutral mind (*kliṣṭa-citta* / *avyākṛta-citta*) is present before one.
If one dwells in the attainment of non-conception or the attainment of cessation and is born in the Heaven of Non-conception,
and has already attained mundane knowledge that is not of the fourth dhyāna such that it is present before them,
then in this context, the other stages are designated by the name "knowledge."
That is to say, from the sphere of nothingness— excluding the fourth dhyāna—
up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this refers to when the mundane qualities previously attained manifest in these various stages.
Its own functional range does not even extend beyond its second moment,
let alone enable the cultivation of other future merits;
furthermore, it is not the fourth dhyāna.
Therefore, regarding the pure and untainted fourth dhyāna, there is no sense of cultivation [of them].
As for that which has already been attained but whose untainted wisdom of the non-fourth dhyāna is not present before one,
here too the name "wisdom" is used to refer to other stages.
That is to say, from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) up to the fourth dhyāna, excluding the dhyāna of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
when these various stages previously attained untainted qualities (*anāsrava-guṇa*) manifest before one.
Its own functional range does not even extend to its second moment,
let alone enable the cultivation of other future merits;
furthermore, it is not the fourth dhyāna.
Therefore, in the case of the pure and untainted fourth dhyāna, there is no sense of cultivation [of them] together.
If one who has not yet attained the mundane knowledge that is not the fourth dhyāna brings it to presence, yet does not cultivate the pure fourth dhyāna and the untainted [knowledge], [then...]
In this context, it is also stated that the other stages are termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
This refers to everything from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding the fourth dhyāna, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Specifically, it concerns an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has produced the previously unobtained contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) within the desire realm.
When mindfulness of breathing,
the three types of contemplation based on the foundations of mindfulness,
and other forms of wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection are present before one.
That is to say, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm,
at all times during the preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,
that ordinary person gives rise to the three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) based on the *anāgamya* concentration.
The first two liberations,
the first four bases of mastery,
and the meditation on impurity.
Mindfulness of breathing,
the foundations of mindfulness,
and the contemplation of the three meanings.
At the stages of Heat, Peak, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma,
an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) relies on the first dhyāna in order to become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
When the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) arises, one induces the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) based on the first dhyāna.
This applies to all paths of preparation and the five paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
At the time of the three paths of liberation,
one gives rise to the four immeasurables and the first two liberations.
The first four bases of mastery,
the contemplation of impurity,
and the foundations of mindfulness.
The contemplation on the three meanings:
the stages of Heat, Peak, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma. Some say:
Furthermore, when one gives rise to mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*),
an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) relies on the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) in order to become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
When the path of preparation arises,
one relies on the intermediate dhyāna to give rise to the three immeasurables and the first two liberations.
The first four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*),
and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
The foundations of mindfulness,
the three contemplations on meaning,
and the stages of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas.
As it is said regarding the first dhyāna,
so it is regarding the second dhyāna.
The same is said for the third dhyāna.
The difference is that one is free from the defilements of those higher stages and from the third dhyāna itself;
furthermore, the liberations, the spheres of mastery, and the immeasurables of joy are excluded.
That is, an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), relying on the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of the fourth dhyāna,
abandons the defilements of the third dhyāna;
this is their path of preparation (prayoga-mārga).
During the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation,
the ordinary person relies upon the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Regarding the detachment from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna:
its path of preparation and its nine paths of uninterrupted transition.
At the time of the eight paths of liberation,
an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) relies on the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) to give rise to detachment from the defilements of the lower stages.

At the time of the ninth path of liberation, as well as at the time of generating the preparatory path (*prayogamārga*) for the sake of becoming detached from the defilements of its own stage, one gives rise to the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.

At the time of the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) relies on the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the base of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) to become detached from the defilements of the base of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
During that time of the path of preparation,
the nine paths of uninterrupted transition,
and the eight paths of liberation.
Just as it is based on the sphere of infinite space,
so it is based on the sphere of infinite consciousness;
the same applies to the sphere of nothingness.
As for the distinction: excluding the *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totality bases),

an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) relies on the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) to become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
During that time of the path of preparation,
the nine paths of uninterrupted transition,
and the eight paths of liberation.
That is to say, an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), relying on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana),
gives rise to the ninth path of liberation that abandons the defilements of the lower stages,
as well as the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception itself.
And at the time of the foundations of mindfulness,
if a noble one gives rise to the previously unobtained contemplation of impurity or mindfulness of breathing pertaining to the desire realm.
When the threefold contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness and other wisdoms produced through hearing and reflection are present,
that noble one, by means of the mundane path, [attains it].
Regarding the detachment from the defilements of the desire realm up to the second dhyāna,
if the mundane is the preparatory application,
it is all preparatory applications.
At the time of the path of immediate liberation (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the second dhyāna by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
If it is a mundane path that serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), [it is as follows].
At the time of that path of preparation, that noble one, by means of the mundane path,
becomes detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
taking the mundane as the preparatory practice.
During the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and eight paths of liberation of that path of preparation,
one becomes free from the defilements of the third dhyāna by means of the untainted path.
If the mundane serves as the preparatory application,
then at the time of that path of preparation,
one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna.

When one who relies on the stage of "resolute belief" (*adhimokṣa*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) based on the "not-yet-attained" concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*), they become a "vision-attainer" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
If they employ the mundane as their preparatory application (*prayoga*),
then at the time of that path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
That noble one, not yet free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
gives rise to the three immeasurables and the first two liberations based on the *anāgamya* concentration.
The first four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*),
and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
The mundane foundations of mindfulness,
the contemplation of the three meanings,
and the proficiency in the seven points.
One who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna,
being one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), may, based on the first dhyāna, refine their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
provided that worldly meditation serves as the preparatory application (prayoga).
At the time of that path of preparation,
those noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna induce the five supernormal powers by relying on the first dhyāna.
The various paths of preparation,
the five paths of uninterrupted transition,
and the two paths of liberation.
And at the time of the path of liberation for the mundane supernormal knowledge of others' minds,
that very [knowledge] relies upon the first dhyāna.
The four immeasurables,
the first two liberations,
and the first four bases of mastery.
The contemplation of impurity,
the mundane foundations of mindfulness,
and the contemplation of the three meanings.
Regarding proficiency in the seven bases,
some say that it also arises at the time of practicing mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti).
One who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna,
being one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), relies on the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara) to refine their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) and become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
If they employ the conventional [path] as their preparatory application (prayoga), [they achieve this].
At the time of that path of preparation,
that same noble one, not yet free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
relies upon the intermediate dhyāna.
The three immeasurables,
the first two liberations,
and the first four bases of mastery.
The contemplation of impurity,
mindfulness of breathing,
