and the mundane foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding the contemplation on the three meanings:
at the time of being well-versed in the seven points,
one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna.
When one who relies on the second dhyāna and possesses faith and resolve transforms their faculties to become a "vision-attainer" (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
if they employ the mundane path as their preparatory application,
then at the time of that path of preparation:
That noble one, not yet free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
relies upon the second dhyāna to induce the preparatory paths for the five supernormal powers.
The five paths of uninterrupted transition,
the two paths of liberation,
and the supramundane supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds.
At the time of the path of liberation,
one gives rise to the four immeasurables based on the second dhyāna.
The first two liberations,
the first four bases of mastery,
and the meditation on impurity.
The mundane foundations of mindfulness,
the contemplation of the three meanings,
and proficiency in the seven points.
Some say that even when one has initiated mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti),
one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna.
When one who relies on the third dhyāna and possesses faith-based liberation (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties to become a "one who has attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
if they employ the mundane path as their preparatory application (prayoga),
then at the time of that path of preparation:
That noble one, not yet free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
relies upon the third dhyāna to induce the five supernormal powers and their respective paths of preparation.
The five paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
the three paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
and the supramundane supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna-abhijñā*).
At the time of the path of liberation,
one gives rise to the three immeasurables based on the third dhyāna.
The contemplation of impurity,
the mundane foundations of mindfulness,
and the contemplation of the three meanings.
Regarding proficiency in the seven bases:
some say that it also arises at the time of practicing mindfulness of breathing.
When one arises from the attainment of cessation with a subtle-subtle mind,
at that time something previously unattained arises;
it is not the case that mundane knowledge belonging to the fourth dhyāna manifests and one does not cultivate the pure [knowledge].

Regarding the fourth dhyāna and the untainted [states]: when the fourth dhyāna and the untainted [states] are present, and one has not yet attained the untainted knowledge that is not the fourth dhyāna, one does not cultivate the pure [attainments].
As for "the fourth dhyāna and the untainted": [this refers to those states].
In this context, the other stages are also designated by the name "knowledge," specifically from the *anāgamya* concentration up to the third *dhyāna*.

This refers to entering the realization of the Four Noble Truths within the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma), based on the preparatory stage (anāgamya) up to the third dhyāna.
In each case, it takes four moments of mind.
One becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
If the untainted path serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), [the process is as follows].
At the time of all preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,
one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm by means of the mundane path;
if the untainted [path] serves as the preparation, [one proceeds likewise].
At the time of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), one relies on the *anāgamya* concentration to become detached from the defilements of the first and second dhyānas;
if the path of preparation is untainted (*anāsrava*),
this applies to all paths of preparation, immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Regarding the detachment from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
if the uncontaminated (anāsrava) serves as the preparatory application,
that is the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga).
During the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation,
one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna.

One who relies on the *anāgamya* concentration and possesses faith-based liberation (*śraddhādhimukta*) transforms their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
If they employ the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their preparatory application (*prayoga*),
then all such preparatory applications are [untainted].
At the time of the path of immediate liberation (*ānantarya-mārga*),
when that same noble one— who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna—
arouses the untainted application of mindfulness (*anāsrava-smṛtyupasthāna*) based upon the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
Relying on the first dhyāna, one becomes detached from the defilements of the first and second dhyānas;
this occurs during all preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths when the uncontaminated (anāsrava) serves as the application.
When one is free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
if the path of preparation consists of the untainted (anāsrava),
that is the path of preparation.
During the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation,
one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna.

When one who relies on the stage of faith and resolution (*śraddhādhimukta*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) based on the first dhyāna to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*),
if they employ the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their preparatory application (*prayoga*),
then at the time of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) immediately following that preparatory application:
That is to say, when that noble one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna,
and relies upon the first dhyāna to give rise to the untainted supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñānābhijñā) and the untainted foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Based on the intermediate dhyāna, one becomes detached from the defilements of the first and second dhyānas;
if the untainted (anāsrava) serves as the preparatory application (prayoga),
this occurs at all times during the preparatory, uninterrupted (ānantarya), and liberation paths (vimukti-mārga).
When one is free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
if the uncontaminated (anāsrava) serves as the preparatory application,
that is the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga).
During the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation,
one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna.
When one who possesses faith and liberation (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) based on the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), they become a "vision-attainer" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
If their preparatory practice (prayoga) is untainted (anāsrava),
then at the time of the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) immediately following that preparatory stage:
When that same noble one, not yet free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
gives rise to the untainted foundations of mindfulness based on the intermediate dhyāna,
they rely on the second dhyāna as the basis for becoming free from the defilements of the second dhyāna, provided that the untainted state serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
At the time of all preparatory, uninterrupted,
and liberation paths when abandoning the defilements of the third dhyāna,
if the path is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it serves as the preparatory stage.
At the time of that path of preparation,
the nine paths of uninterrupted transition,
and the eight paths of liberation.
One who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna,
being one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), may, by relying on the second dhyāna, refine their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
provided that the preparatory practice (prayoga) is untainted (anāsrava).
At the time of the path of preparation, the immediate [path], and the path of liberation,
that noble one— who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna—
arouses the supernormal power of uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds based upon the second dhyāna.
And when one dwells in the untainted foundations of mindfulness,
relying on the third dhyāna to become detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
provided that the untainted state serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
At the time of that path of preparation,
the nine paths of uninterrupted transition,
and the eight paths of liberation.
One who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna,
being one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), may, by relying on the third dhyāna, refine their faculties to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
provided that the preparatory practice (prayoga) is untainted (anāsrava).
At the time of the preparatory, uninterrupted, and path of liberation [of that attainment],
that noble one— who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna—
arouses the supernormal power of uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds based upon the third dhyāna.
And at the time of the untainted foundations of mindfulness (*anāsrava-smṛtyupasthāna*), that which has never been attained before arises;
it is not the case that when untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the fourth dhyāna is present, one does not cultivate the pure [knowledge].
The fourth dhyāna and the untainted [states],
as well as all defiled minds up to those born in the Heaven of Non-conception, are as previously explained in the section on the first dhyāna.
As it is said:
The same is said for the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). This is because,
at the time of the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) from the defilements of the lower stages, these respective levels [are attained].
Because all must necessarily enter the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*).

Question: For what reason does one rely on the path of liberation at the end of the detachment from the defilements of the desire realm up to the second dhyāna during the stage of "near-separation" (*sāmantaka*)?
Either it is the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) itself,
or one enters the fundamental [dhyāna],
excluding the third dhyāna.
Up to the defilement of the sphere of nothingness, does one necessarily enter the fundamental stage via the final path of liberation? Answer:
Because there is a difference in the experience [of meditative attainment] between the three lower preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental stages.
When seeking to attain the fundamental stage (mūlabhūmi),
there are those who are able to enter it immediately, and there are those who are not.
Because there is no difference between the experience of the five higher access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) and that of the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*),
when one seeks to attain the fundamental stage, one is necessarily able to enter it.
Thus, those practitioners of yoga who, relying on an access concentration, become detached from the defilements of a lower level [attain the fundamental stage].
One must necessarily give rise to joy within one’s own fundamental stage (*mūlabhūmi*),
because that which the power of the mind is capable of producing will necessarily arise immediately.
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 164.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 165,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhiskandha). Part Two: The Sub-section on Objects of Cognition (Ālambanavarga), Chapter Four. If one initially enters the untainted first dhyāna...
...and so on, as explained at length.
Initially, there are four kinds.
The first is the initial entry into the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
First, the initial attainment of the fruit;
second, the initial departure from defilement;
third, the initial transformation of the faculties.
In this context, the treatise is composed based on two initial conditions:
the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).
Regarding the first, the attainment of the fruit:
This refers to the moment of the initial knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) upon attaining the fruit of arhatship.
Regarding the "initial transformation of the faculties" (*indriya-saṃcāra-ādi*):
this refers to the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) when an arhat liberated by time (*samaya-vimukta*) refines their faculties to become unshakable (*akopya*).
Question: Why is it that, regarding the four [stages] of beginning, middle, and end, the treatise is composed based only on the first two beginnings?
Answer: If one is cultivating the merits of all stages at that time, this treatise is composed based upon that.
Since only these two [types of practitioners] are able to cultivate in this manner at the initial stage, the treatise is composed based upon them.
If one initially enters the untainted first dhyāna,
then all other future untainted minds and mental factors obtained at that time—
Should it be said that all of those possess both vitarka and vicāra?
Answer: Some of them possess both vitarka and vicāra;
others are without vitarka and possess only vicāra.
"Either without vitarka and vicāra,
or with vitarka and vicāra" refers to the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi) that is being cultivated.
And regarding the first dhyāna:
that which has no vitarka but only vicāra refers to the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara) that is being cultivated.
"Without vitarka and without vicāra" refers to the three higher dhyānas and the three lower formless attainments that are cultivated.
If one initially enters the second uncontaminated dhyāna,
are all other future uncontaminated mental states and mental factors obtained at that time to be said as being associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*)?
The answer is: it is associated either with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
or with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*),
or with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
That which is associated with the faculty of pleasure refers to the third dhyāna that is cultivated;
that which is associated with the faculty of joy [refers to the first two dhyānas].
This refers to the first and second dhyānas that are cultivated;
those associated with the faculty of equanimity refer to the unattained concentration (anāgamya) that is cultivated.
The intermediate dhyāna,
the fourth dhyāna,
and the three lower formless attainments.
If one initially enters the third untainted dhyāna,
are all those other future untainted minds and mental factors obtained at that time to be said as being associated with the faculty of pleasure?
Answer: It is associated either with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
or with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*),
or with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
The meaning is as explained previously.
If one initially enters the untainted fourth dhyāna,
at that time, all other future untainted minds and mental factors that are acquired—
Should it be said that all of those are associated with the faculty of equanimity?
Answer: They are either associated with the faculty of pleasure or associated with the faculty of joy.
Alternatively, it may be associated with the faculty of equanimity;
the meaning is as explained previously.
If one initially enters the untainted sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
At that time, regarding all other future untainted (anāsrava) minds and mental factors that are acquired, should it be said that they are all subsumed under the Sphere of Infinite Space?
Answer: They may be subsumed under the Sphere of Infinite Space.
It is either included within the sphere of infinite consciousness or the sphere of nothingness.
As for that which is included within the sphere of infinite space:
That which is cultivated as the sphere of infinite space is subsumed under the sphere of infinite consciousness;
that which is cultivated as the sphere of infinite consciousness is [subsumed under the sphere of nothingness].
Regarding that which is subsumed under the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*):
it refers to the sphere of nothingness that is cultivated,
or when one first enters the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

At that time, regarding all other future untainted (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are acquired, should it be said that they are all subsumed under the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*)?
Answer: They may be subsumed under the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
It is either subsumed under the sphere of infinite consciousness,
or subsumed under the sphere of nothingness;
the meaning is as explained previously.
If one initially enters the untainted sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
are all other future untainted minds and mental factors obtained at that time to be said to be included within the sphere of nothingness?
The answer is: it is either subsumed under the sphere of infinite space,
or subsumed under the sphere of infinite consciousness,
or subsumed under the sphere of nothingness.
The meaning is as explained previously.
Question: Why is it that here, regarding the dhyānas, there is a question on association, while regarding the formless attainments (ārūpya), there is a question on inclusion?
The answer is: because the intention of that author of the treatise was such, he composed the treatise according to that intention;
provided it does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one should not hold him accountable.
Some say: "The dhyānas and the formless attainments (ārūpya) should both be questioned [regarding this],
yet the fact that they are not questioned indicates that this explanation is incomplete."
Some say: it is for the purpose of manifesting various expressions and various explanations;
because of these various expressions and various explanations, the meaning is easily understood.
Some say:
it is in order to manifest two gates, two summaries, two ladders, two torches, two illuminations, two lights, and two kinds of textual reflections;
just as "conjunction" is taught in the context of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
It is the same for the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
Just as it was explained regarding inclusion in the formless realms,
so it is also for the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
Some say: Because the dhyānas are coarse, manifest, easy to see, and easy to know,
they are asked about in terms of their association.
The formless [realms] are subtle, difficult to comprehend, and difficult to realize;
therefore, one asks only about their inclusion. Some say:
The dhyānas possess various mutual dissimilarities;
therefore, their association is questioned.
The formless attainments (ārūpyas) are not like this.
Therefore, one asks only about inclusion (*saṃgraha*).
Some say that within the dhyānas there are various feelings and various faculties (*indriya*).
Therefore, it is associated with inquiry;
the formless [realms] are not so. Some say:
Meditative concentration possesses many virtues and many benefits;
therefore, it is associated with inquiry.
This is not the case for the formless attainments.
Some say that because there is wisdom with universal objects within the dhyānas,
the question concerns their association [with mental factors].
The formless [realms] possess only wisdom that takes the self and what is above as its object;
therefore, they are only asked about in terms of inclusion.
Question: Why, in this context, are the formless [realms] also included within the dhyānas?
"Is it not the case that the formless [attainments] do not include the dhyānas?
The answer is: "Because that author of the treatise intended it to be so," and so on, as explained at length.
Some say that the dhyānas and the formless attainments (ārūpya) should both be included [in this category]; however,
one should understand that the meaning of their not being mentioned as included is that the explanation is incomplete.
Some say: it is for the purpose of manifesting various expressions and various explanations;
because of these various expressions and various explanations, the meaning is easily understood.
Some say: "In order to manifest two gates, two summaries, two reflections, and two radiances," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Some say that the formless realms depend upon the dhyānas,
because one first attains the dhyānas and subsequently attains the formless realms.
The dhyānas also include the formless attainments; however,
because the dhyānas do not depend upon the formless attainments,
the formless attainments do not include the dhyānas.
Some say that the formless attainments are also not included within the dhyānas,
because statements such as "without vitarka and vicāra" have a specific intended meaning.
Regarding the phrase "without vitarka and without vicāra," this refers exclusively to the latter three dhyānas.
Regarding the phrase "associated with the faculty of equanimity":
It speaks only of the preparatory dhyāna (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the fourth dhyāna;
for since the characteristics of the dhyānas and formless attainments (*ārūpya*) differ from one another,
although they may be cultivated in relation to one another, they do not mutually include one another.
Some say that the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) should also be included among the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*);
one should state it in this way.
Whether it is included within the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-samādhi*) up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
the reason it is not mentioned is to show that the formless attainments do not involve the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for entering the dhyānas.
Because the manifestation of dhyāna does not necessarily depend on the formless realm (ārūpya).
Some say that one born in a dhyāna stage can give rise to the formless [attainments].
Those born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) are unable to give rise to dhyāna;
so some say.
For an Ārya, after being born into a dhyāna, it is possible to be born into an ārūpya;
however, after being born into an ārūpya, it is impossible to be born into a dhyāna.
Therefore, the ārūpyas are subsumed within the dhyānas.

Regarding the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) not included within the formless realm (*ārūpya*), such as the first dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādana-yoga*), and so forth as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This is to refute the intention of those who rely on analogies;
because they do not clearly understand the nature of conditions, they claim that conditions are not substantially existent.
Now, wishing to demonstrate the intrinsic nature of all conditions so that it may be known that all conditions are truly existent,
this treatise is composed.
With how many conditions is the first dhyāna associated with relish (āsvādana) related to other states associated with relish in the first dhyāna?
Answer: It is related as cause (hetu), equal-and-immediate (samanantara), object (ālambana), and predominance (adhipati) conditions to those associated with relish within its own stage (svabhūmi).
The causes are the three causes:
namely, the associated cause, the co-existent cause, and the homogeneous cause.
As for the immediately preceding condition:
That is to say, immediately following the dhyāna of the first meditative absorption associated with relishing (āsvādana),
the dhyāna of the first meditative absorption associated with relishing manifests.
As for its object (ālambana):
This means that the first dhyāna associated with relish takes the first dhyāna associated with relish as its object.
As for "predominance," it refers to the absence of obstruction to arising.
And there is merely the absence of obstruction.
Among these, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is like the nature of a seed;
the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is like the act of making way.
The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is like the method of the leaning staff;
the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is like the method of granting desire.
It serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) for the pure [states] of its own level.
Regarding the object-condition, the predominance-condition, and the immediate-condition:
this refers to when,
immediately following a dhyāna associated with relish, a pure first dhyāna manifests.
Just as with craving, views, pride, and doubt,
for one in the higher dhyānas,
pure concentration manifests immediately after the afflictions.
This is the general explanation.
To explain it specifically,
there are four kinds of purity.
That is to say: the portion conducive to decline,
the portion conducive to maintenance,
and the portion conducive to progress.
Regarding the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
some say that these arise immediately after those associated with relish (*āsvādana*).
Only the factors conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*) manifest;
some say that those conducive to maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya*) may also arise as objects of cognition.
That is to say, the first dhyāna associated with relish takes the pure first dhyāna as its object;
as for the predominant [condition]: [it is the same].
This means that it is not an obstacle to arising and is merely non-obstructive;
it is not a cause because defiled phenomena do not function as seeds for wholesome phenomena.
For this reason, regarding the states associated with relish (*āsvādana*) and those that are pure (*śuddha*) within their own stage (*svabhūmi*),
if stated generally, they are considered three conditions;
if stated specifically, they are either three or two.
That is to say, it serves as three conditions for the first two categories,
two conditions for the latter two categories,
and [one condition] for the untainted (anāsrava) states of its own level.
It acts as the dominant condition by way of being an object of focus (*ālambana*). As for the object of focus:
it refers to that which serves as the object for the category of the receptivities (*kṣānti*) and the knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding the suffering and origin [of suffering].
The "predominant" is as previously explained.
As for "not being a cause," it is because contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) do not function like seeds.
Regarding "not being an equal-and-immediate [condition]":
because the noble path does not arise as a present manifestation immediately following the afflictions.
For this reason, that which is associated with relish and the untainted of its own stage [are not mutually related as equal-and-immediate conditions].
If stated generally, there are two conditions;
if stated specifically, there are either two or one.
That is to say, with respect to the category of patience and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-anvaya-kṣānti-jñāna*), they serve as two conditions.
It shares a single object with the categories of the subsequent patience and subsequent knowledge regarding cessation and the path, as well as with all categories of patience and dharma-knowledge.
It serves as the object-condition and the dominant condition for the three higher pure and uncontaminated meditative absorptions.
As for the object-condition (*ālambana*):
it is because that [state] takes as its object the flavor-associated (*sāsvāda*) states of the lower stages.
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati*):
This means that because it does not obstruct arising and is merely non-obstructive,
it is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*);
for that which is defiled is not a seed-dharma with respect to that which is undefiled.
Regarding those that are not equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*):
because one is able to give rise to the pure or untainted states of the higher fundamental stages only after having already abandoned the defilements of the lower stages,
they serve as a single predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for others.
The remainder refers to the three higher meditative absorptions associated with taste (*āsvādanasamprayukta*) and all formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
The meaning of "predominance" (*adhipatya*) is as previously explained.
Regarding that which is not a causal condition:
because the causes and effects of dharmas belonging to different realms or stages are severed,
and because dharmas of a different category do not constitute seeds.
It is not an equal-and-immediate condition because,
having already abandoned the defilements of the lower realm, the defilements of the higher stage must first manifest;
furthermore, they are mutually contradictory.
That which is not an object-condition consists of the afflictions of the higher stages and those of the fundamental formless realms.
Because it does not take impure dharmas of a lower stage as its object.
As for pure first dhyāna, in relation to pure first dhyāna and so forth, how many conditions does it serve?

Answer: It serves as the cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate-condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant-condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for that which is pure of its own stage.
The causes are the three causes:
namely, the associated cause, the co-existent cause, and the homogeneous cause.
As for the equal-and-immediate [condition]:
That is to say, immediately following the pure first dhyāna and so forth,
the pure first dhyāna manifests.
As for its object of focus:
This means taking the pure first dhyāna as its object.
The meaning of "predominance" (adhipati) is as previously explained.
This is the general statement.
If explained individually,
the pure [states] have four parts.
The part conducive to decline serves as the four conditions for that which is conducive to decline.
The same applies to the stage conducive to stability (*anuloma-sthiti-bhāgīya*).
With respect to the other two stages, it serves as three conditions,
excluding the condition of equal and immediate antecedence (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
The stage conducive to maintenance (sthity-anuloma) serves as four conditions for the stage conducive to maintenance;
it is likewise for the stage conducive to progress (viśeṣa-anuloma).
It serves as three conditions for the stage conducive to penetration (nirvedha-anuloma).
Excluding the equal-and-immediate condition,
they serve as three conditions for the factors conducive to decline;
excluding the causal condition.
Because the superior is not the cause of the inferior,
that which is conducive to the stage of progress (viśeṣabhāgīya) serves as four conditions for that which is conducive to the stage of progress;
the same applies to its relationship with that which is conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya).
Regarding the factors conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*),
some say that it serves merely as an object of perception (*ālambana*) and a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Because the stage immediately preceding the part conducive to superior progress does not manifest when the stage immediately preceding the part conducive to decline is present.
According to this explanation,
[the latter] also manifests in the present.
Therefore, there are three conditions for the factors conducive to decline,
excluding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), because those [factors] are inferior.
The same applies to the factors conducive to abiding.
The factors conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) serve as four conditions for other factors conducive to penetration;
they serve as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) for the factors conducive to decline (hānabhāgīya).
Regarding the factor conducive to stability (*anurakṣaṇābhāgīya*),
some say it serves solely as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) by way of being an object of focus (*ālambana*).
Because the stage of abiding does not manifest immediately after the aids to penetration; however,
according to those who speak thus,
it does indeed manifest.
Therefore, it serves as three conditions for that [state],
excluding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The same applies to the factors conducive to progress (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*).
It serves as the equal-and-immediate, the object-condition, and the dominant condition for the untainted [states] of its own level.
Regarding the "equal-and-immediate":
That is to say, immediately following the pure first dhyāna and so forth,
the untainted first dhyāna manifests;
this arises solely from the levels conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya).
Some say that it also arises from the stage conducive to progress (prativedhanābhāgīya).
As for its object:
This means that it takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna as its object (*ālambana*).
As for its predominance (*adhipati*), it is as previously explained.
Regarding its not being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): [it is because]...
Because contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are not causes for uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*),
they serve as the equal-immediate (*samanantara*), objective (*ālambana*), and dominant (*adhipati*) conditions for those associated with the flavor of their own stage.
Regarding the equal-immediate condition:
Just as with attachment, views, pride, and doubt,
when an affliction manifests immediately after a pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*) for one in the higher dhyānas,
it should be understood that this arises from the stage conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*).

Alternatively, the arising of the factors conducive to stability occurs because there is a distinction between those who have already abandoned and those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of their own stage,
regarding the arising of the afflictions of that stage.
As for the object of focus (*ālambana*):
it is because one relishes the purity and tranquility of one's own stage.
The rest is as previously explained.
It serves as the equal-immediate, objective, and predominant condition for the pure and untainted second and third dhyānas.
Regarding the "equal-immediate" [condition]:
it is because one enters the second [dhyāna] in immediate succession.
Because one enters the third [dhyāna] by way of the "conducive to arising" (anuloma-utthāna),
it should be known that one enters the higher pure [dhyānas] from the "conducive to superior progress" (anuloma-viśeṣa-bhāgīya) and not from anything else.
The rest is as previously explained.
With respect to the pure and untainted fourth dhyāna as its object and dominant condition,
there is no equal and immediate condition,
because it is extremely remote.
The rest is as previously explained.
It serves as a single dominant condition for the others.
"The others" refers to the three dhyānas associated with taste (*āsvādana*).
And all formless [realms].
The meaning of "predominance" is as previously explained.
The distinction here is as follows:
That is to say, the pure and untainted formless states are not equal-and-immediate [conditions] because they are extremely remote.
The rest is as previously explained.
Question: Is there also an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
That is to say, when one dies with a wholesome mind of the first dhyāna and is reborn in a higher stage.
Why is this not mentioned here?
It should be stated that it serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for them;
yet it is not so stated.
It should be understood that the meaning here is incomplete.
Some say that within this section on meditative absorption (*samādhi-skandha*), only the wholesome states of concentration and the defilements of concentration at the time of death are discussed.
Rebirth-linking consists only of the arising of wholesome states and the arising of afflictions;
therefore, it is not mentioned. Some say:
In this Section on Concentration (*samādhiskandha*), only the fundamental wholesome states and the defilements at the moment of death are discussed.
As for the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), it abides only in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and not in the fundamental states;
therefore, it is not mentioned here.
With how many conditions does the untainted first dhyāna act as a condition for the untainted first dhyāna and its equals?
Answer: It acts as a cause, immediate antecedent, object, and predominance condition for that which belongs to its own level and is untainted.
As for the causes, there are three causes:
namely, the associated cause, the co-existent cause, and the homogeneous cause.
As for the object-condition:
This means that it takes the categories of patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*) and knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) as its object.
The rest is as explained previously;
this is the general statement.
If explained individually,
the category of dharma-knowledge acts as four conditions for the category of dharma-knowledge,
and as three conditions for the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
Excluding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) serves as four conditions for its own category,
and as three conditions for the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*).
Excluding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
The categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation are three conditions for the categories of the knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation,
excluding the object-condition.
The category of knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) acts as four conditions for its own category.
It acts as four conditions for the category of knowledge of the path.
It acts as three conditions for the categories of knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation.
Excluding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The category of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) acts as four conditions for the category of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
It is the same with respect to the category of the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*).
The category of the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya) acts as three conditions for its own category,
excluding the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya).
The category of the faculty of one who has already known acts as four conditions for its own category.
The same applies to the category of the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
With respect to the category of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), it serves as two conditions,
excluding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
As for the exclusion of causes:
that which arises later cannot be the cause of that which arose earlier, because arising does not constitute a cause [for what has already arisen].
Regarding the exclusion of the "immediately preceding" (samanantara):
because in the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
the path of seeing (darśanamārga) does not manifest as its immediately preceding condition.
The category of the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya) acts as four conditions for the category of the faculty of one who has already known.
It acts as two conditions for the categories of the faculty of one who intends to know the unknown (anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya) and the faculty of one who has already known,
excluding the cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya) and the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya).

The category of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) serves as a single predominant condition for the category of the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) of one in training (śaikṣa).
The category of the subsequent knowledge of one beyond training serves as a single predominant condition for the category of the knowledge of phenomena of one in training.
Therefore, speaking in general terms, it is said that [the defiled] acts as four conditions for the untainted (anāsrava) of its own stage. However,
if explained according to specific distinctions,
there may be four, three, two, or one such condition.
It serves as the cause, equal-and-immediate, object-condition, and dominant condition for the untainted second and third dhyānas;
this is because untainted phenomena do not fall within the realms of existence.
As previously stated, those belonging to other stages serve as causes, conditions, and so forth.
They serve as the equal-and-immediate, objective, and dominant conditions for the pure [states] of their own stage, as well as for the pure second and third dhyānas.
Regarding the pure [states] of their own level herein,
some say that,
with the exception of the stage conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*), the remaining three stages serve as the equal-and-immediate antecedents (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Some say that it serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) only for the latter two categories;
this is likewise the case for the pure states of the higher stages.
According to this explanation,
when entering [the meditative states] gradually,
it also serves as the equal-and-immediate condition for the stage of further advancement.
When entering the leap-over (*vyutkrāntaka*), it is only with the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) that they serve as immediate antecedent conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Question: Why, at the time of entering the leap-over, do only the aids to penetration and the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) mutually serve as immediate antecedent conditions?
At other times it is not so.
Answer: At the time of transcendence, there are only intense and firm roots of goodness.
The factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) that are capable of inducing [the path] are intense and firm;
the other factors are not so.
They are similar to the pure fourth dhyāna and the pure formless attainments (*śuddha-ārūpya*).
It acts as an object-condition (*ālambana*) and a dominant condition (*adhipati*).
Because the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the first dhyāna is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the formless realms,
it also serves as an object-condition for the pure formless attainments (*śuddhaka-ārūpya*).
The rest is as previously explained.
It serves as the cause, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the untainted fourth dhyāna and the untainted formless attainments;

this is because the category of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) within the formless realm also takes the category of the subsequent knowledge of the first dhyāna as its object.
The rest is as previously explained.
It serves as the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for others.
"Others" refers to all those associated with taste (*rasa*).
The meaning of "predominance" (*adhipati*) is as previously explained.
Because the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the tainted with relish (*sāsvāda*) are utterly contradictory, there is no immediate succession (*samanantara*).
Furthermore, because craving cannot take untainted phenomena as its object, they are not its objective condition (*ālambana*).
Because the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) are not seed-natures (*bīja-dharma*), they are not causes.
Question: If the untainted and the "savoring" (*āsvādana*) are utterly opposed, how can [the former] act as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)?
Answer: Although they are utterly contradictory in their immediate succession, at the very moment of arising, there is no obstruction regarding the past and future;
therefore, they are able to act as mutual predominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*) for one another.
Regarding the second dhyāna associated with relish (*āsvādana*) and its relationship to other states associated with relish:
Answer: It serves as a condition for those associated with relish within its own stage (*svabhūmi*).
It acts as the cause, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara*), the object condition (*ālambana*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati*).
It serves as the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition for the first two pure (*śuddhaka*) dhyānas;
and it serves as the object condition and the dominant condition for all untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas, as well as for the third and fourth pure dhyānas.
It serves as a single predominant condition for others.
"Others" refers to the first, third, and fourth dhyānas associated with relish,
as well as all the formless attainments.

In this context, that which serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the pure first dhyāna refers to when a practitioner of yoga gives rise to various afflictions immediately after a pure concentration of the second dhyāna.
His mind was tormented by feverish affliction as if being consumed by fire;
he then sought refuge in the pure first dhyāna.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
It is better to give rise to a mind accompanied by the first dhyāna that is associated with aversion,
rather than giving rise to a mind accompanied by the second dhyāna that is associated with inferior attention.
Question: What kind of pure first dhyāna does he produce?
Some say he produces that which is conducive to maintenance (*anurakṣaṇabhāgīya*).
Because it arises easily,
some say that its arising accords with the factors conducive to supreme progress (*viśeṣabhāgīya*).
Because it protects the higher stages.
Furthermore, what has been explained here takes the first dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) as its single predominant condition (*adhipati*).
Question: When one dies from a defiled mind of the second dhyāna and is reborn in the first dhyāna...
If there is an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
why is it not mentioned?
It should be stated that it serves as both its equal-and-immediate condition and its dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
As for the fact that it was not stated,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete. Some say:
In this section on concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), only the afflictions (*kleśa*) at the moment of death that lead to concentration are discussed;
since the afflictions at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) pertain to birth itself,
they are not mentioned here.
Some say that in this section on the aggregates (*skandha*), it is stated that at the time of death, one dies with the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*),
whereas the linking of rebirth (*pratisandhi*) occurs while abiding in the afflictions of the preparatory stages (*sāmantakabhūmi*).
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
The rest should be understood as previously explained according to what is appropriate.
How many conditions does the pure second dhyāna serve as a condition for the pure second dhyāna and so forth?
Answer: It serves as the cause, equal-immediate condition, object-condition, and dominant condition for the pure [attainments] of its own stage;
and for all untainted dhyānas, as well as the pure first, third, and fourth dhyānas.
Furthermore, that which is associated with the flavor of its own stage serves as the equal-immediate, the object-condition, and the dominant condition;
for others, it serves as a single dominant condition.
This should also be explained in detail as appropriate, as before.
How many conditions does the untainted second dhyāna serve for the untainted second dhyāna and its equals?
Answer: It serves as a condition for all untainted dhyānas.
It acts as the cause, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
It serves as the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition for all pure (*śuddha*) dhyānas;
and for the pure formless attainments (*śuddhārūpya*).
It acts as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
For the untainted (anāsrava) formless states,
it acts as the cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya), the object-condition, and the dominant condition.
It serves as a single predominant condition for the others;
this also should be understood in detail as previously explained,
starting from the third dhyāna.
This continues up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There are five, three, two, and one sets of questions and answers;
they should be understood as explained in detail in the original treatise.

Question: Just as when one becomes detached from the fourth dhyāna and the three lower formless attainments by means of the mundane path, all uninterrupted paths take the lower stages as their objects;

why then is it not stated that the [attainments] associated with the relish (*āsvādana*) and the pure (*śuddha*) states of the fourth dhyāna and the three lower formless attainments take the pure states of the higher stages as their objects?
The answer to this should also be stated;
however, since it is not stated, one should know that there is more to be said.
Some say that in this section on the aggregates (*skandha*), only the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*) are discussed,
whereas the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) belong only to the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Question: Which untainted (anāsrava) third and fourth dhyānas serve as the equal-and-immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya) for the pure (śuddha) and untainted formless attainments?
Answer: Only the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Question: Why not the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*)? Some say:
Because the category of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna-pakṣa) takes the lower realms as its object and has the lower realms as its basis;
that is to say, the category of dharma-knowledge relies solely upon the desire realm and takes only the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) of the desire realm as its object.
Furthermore, regarding their causes, their cessations, and the paths that serve as their antidotes—
since the pure, untainted, and formless [states] are not like those,
the category of dharma-knowledge is not their immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Some say that the category of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna-pakṣa) takes as its object only the desire realm and its cessation and path;
it arises immediately after taking the desire realm and its cessation and path as objects.
It cannot take objects belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) as its immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
because they are extremely remote. For this reason,
the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna-pakṣa*) is not an immediate condition for the formless realm and so forth.
Some say: because the formless stages (*ārūpyabhūmi*) are neither the basis (*āśraya*), nor the object (*ālambana*), nor the level (*bhūmi*) of the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).
That is to say, although the four dhyānas are not the basis or the object of the category of dharma-knowledge, [they are its level].
However, this is the ground of the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).
Although the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is not the ground of the category of dharma-knowledge,
it is the basis and the object of that category of dharma-knowledge.
In the various formless stages (*ārūpyabhūmi*), such a phenomenon does not exist;
therefore, it is not produced immediately after the category of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
Question: For what reason are the pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) formless [attainments] not so?

Does it take as its object only the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the lower stages, and not the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*)?
Answer: Because the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge is not the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to that stage.
Question: Is it not the case that the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) also serves as an antidote to those [defilements]?
Answer: Although it does serve as an antidote to them, it is neither fundamental nor complete;
therefore, it is not mentioned.
That is to say, although it is an antidote to those factors abandoned by cultivation,
it is not an antidote to those factors abandoned by seeing;
furthermore, although the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path is an antidote to them.
It is not, however, the dharma-knowledge of the origin of suffering.
Some say that the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is its primary antidote.

Because the category of dharma-knowledge is an adventitious antidote to those [defilements], it is not their object; however, pure or untainted dhyānas and formless attainments arise immediately before them, whether they belong to a lower or higher stage.
Arising from below is called "sequential" (anuloma) and "leaping" (vyutkrāntaka);
arising from above is called "inverse" (pratiloma) and "leaping. Arising within the same category is called "pure" (śuddha);
arising in different categories is called "mixed" (miśra).
Those without an interval between stages are called "sequential" (*anupūrva*);
those with an interval are called "leaping" (*vyutkrānta*).
Those with an interval can only leap over a single stage.
This is called the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
Question: What is the practice for the leap-concentration (*vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*) that was mentioned?
Answer: When practicing the leap-concentration:
That practitioner of meditative concentration first gives rise to a wholesome mind of the desire realm;
immediately following this, they enter the first dhyāna with outflows.
Next, he enters the second dhyāna with outflows;
proceeding in sequence, he enters up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
From there, he returns to enter the sphere of nothingness with outflows.
Proceeding in sequence until he again enters the contaminated first dhyāna,
he cycles through and cultivates these various stages until his virtue becomes as refined and mature as a royal highway.
Again, he enters the untainted first dhyāna;
next, he enters the untainted second dhyāna, proceeding in sequence until he enters the untainted sphere of nothingness.
From there, he returns to enter the untainted [attainments] once more.
From the sphere of infinite consciousness,
proceeding in sequence until returning once more to the untainted first dhyāna,
one practices these stages in a cyclical manner.
Having caused [the mind] to become well-matured like a royal road,
he again enters the contaminated first dhyāna.
From the contaminated first dhyāna...
He transcends into the contaminated third dhyāna;
from the contaminated third dhyāna,
he transcends into the contaminated sphere of infinite space.
From the contaminated sphere of infinite space,
one transcends into the contaminated sphere of nothingness;
from the contaminated sphere of nothingness...
He then transcends back into the contaminated sphere of infinite space,
and from the contaminated sphere of infinite space,
he transcends into the contaminated third dhyāna.
From the third dhyāna with outflows,
one transcends into the first dhyāna with outflows,
practicing these stages in a cyclical manner.
Having caused [the wholesome roots] to become thoroughly matured like a royal road,
he again enters the untainted first dhyāna.
From the untainted first dhyāna...
He leaps into the untainted third dhyāna.
From the untainted third dhyāna,
he leaps into the untainted sphere of infinite space.
From the untainted sphere of infinite space,
one transcends into the untainted sphere of nothingness.
From the untainted sphere of nothingness,
he again transcends into the untainted sphere of infinite space;
from the untainted sphere of infinite space...
He leaps into the untainted third dhyāna;
from the untainted third dhyāna, he leaps into the untainted first dhyāna.
He thus practices by cycling through these various stages.
He causes the wholesome [roots] to become thoroughly matured, like a royal road;
up to this point, the preparatory application for the leap-over concentration (*vyutkrāntakasamādhi*) is perfected.
From here, he again enters the contaminated first dhyāna.
From the contaminated first dhyāna,
one leaps into the uncontaminated third dhyāna;
from the uncontaminated third dhyāna...
He transcends into the contaminated sphere of infinite space;
from the contaminated sphere of infinite space,
he transcends into the uncontaminated sphere of nothingness.
From the untainted sphere of nothingness,
one again transcends to enter the tainted sphere of infinite space;
from the tainted sphere of infinite space, [one proceeds further].
He leaps into the uncontaminated third dhyāna;
from the uncontaminated third dhyāna,
he leaps into the contaminated first dhyāna.
This is called the fulfillment of the leap-concentration (*vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*).
Other masters say that when practicing the leap-concentration:
First, one arouses a wholesome mind of the desire realm;
immediately thereafter, one enters the contaminated first dhyāna,
and next enters the contaminated second dhyāna.
Proceeding in sequence up to entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
one then returns from there to enter the contaminated sphere of nothingness,
proceeding in sequence back down again until re-entering the contaminated first dhyāna.
Having become thoroughly proficient in these stages, one again enters the untainted first dhyāna;
next, one enters the untainted second dhyāna;
and so on in succession until entering the untainted sphere of nothingness.
From there, he returns again to the untainted consciousness-infinity sphere (*vijñānānantyāyatana*),
proceeding in sequence until he returns once more to the untainted first dhyāna (*prathamadhyāna*).
Having become thoroughly proficient in these various stages, he...
Again, he enters the contaminated first dhyāna;
next, he enters the uncontaminated second dhyāna;
next, he enters the contaminated third dhyāna.
Next, he enters the untainted fourth dhyāna;
next, he enters the tainted sphere of infinite space;
next, he enters the untainted sphere of infinite consciousness.
Next, one enters the contaminated sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
From there, one returns to the uncontaminated sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*),
proceeding in sequence until returning once more to the contaminated first dhyāna.
Having become thoroughly proficient in these stages,
one again enters the untainted first dhyāna,
and subsequently enters the tainted second dhyāna.
Next, he enters the untainted third dhyāna;
next, he enters the tainted fourth dhyāna;
next, he enters the untainted sphere of infinite space.
Next, one enters the contaminated sphere of infinite consciousness;
next, the uncontaminated sphere of nothingness;
and next, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
From there, he returns again to the untainted sphere of nothingness,
proceeding in sequence until he returns once more to the untainted first dhyāna.
Having become thoroughly proficient in these stages, he...
Again, he enters the contaminated first dhyāna;
from the contaminated first dhyāna,
he leaps directly into the contaminated third dhyāna.
From the third dhyāna with outflows,
one transcends into the sphere of infinite space with outflows;
from the sphere of infinite space with outflows...
He transcends into the contaminated sphere of nothingness;
from the contaminated sphere of nothingness,
he returns to the contaminated sphere of infinite space.
From the contaminated sphere of infinite space,
one transcends into the contaminated third dhyāna;
from the contaminated third dhyāna...
Having transcended into the contaminated first dhyāna and become thoroughly practiced in these stages,
one again enters the uncontaminated first dhyāna.
From the untainted first dhyāna,
one leaps into the untainted third dhyāna;
from the untainted third dhyāna...
He transcends into the untainted sphere of infinite space.
From the untainted sphere of infinite space,
he transcends into the untainted sphere of nothingness.
From the untainted sphere of nothingness,
he re-enters the untainted sphere of infinite space;
from the untainted sphere of infinite space...
He leaps into the untainted third dhyāna;
from the untainted third dhyāna,
he leaps into the untainted first dhyāna.
Having thoroughly practiced these stages, this is called the fulfillment of the preparatory application for transcending meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
From there, one again enters the contaminated (*sāsrava*) first dhyāna; from the contaminated first dhyāna...
He leaps into the uncontaminated third dhyāna;
from the uncontaminated third dhyāna,
he leaps into the contaminated sphere of infinite space.
From the contaminated sphere of infinite space,
one transcends into the uncontaminated sphere of nothingness;
from the uncontaminated sphere of nothingness...
He further transcends into the contaminated sphere of infinite space;
from the contaminated sphere of infinite space,
he transcends into the uncontaminated third dhyāna.
From the untainted third dhyāna,
one transcends into the tainted first dhyāna;
from there, one enters again into the untainted first dhyāna.
From the untainted first dhyāna,
one transcends into the tainted third dhyāna;
from the tainted third dhyāna...
He transcends into the untainted sphere of infinite space.
From the untainted sphere of infinite space,
he transcends into the tainted sphere of nothingness.
From the contaminated sphere of nothingness,
one again transcends to enter the uncontaminated sphere of infinite space;
from the uncontaminated sphere of infinite space...
He transcends into the contaminated third dhyāna;
from the contaminated third dhyāna,
he transcends into the uncontaminated first dhyāna.
This is called the perfection of the transcendental meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that all that has been explained thus far constitutes the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
From this stage onward, one circulates freely through the meditative absorptions in reverse order;
when there is no longer any obstruction, it is called "perfected.
However, one will certainly be unable to skip over and enter the fourth absorption.
Question: For what reason is it impossible to leap over and enter the fourth [dhyāna]?

Answer: This is because for all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and their noble disciples, numbering more than the sands of the Ganges, the method for leaping into the various meditative absorptions (samādhis) is exactly like this.
Therefore, one should not ask [this question].
Some say that those who practice the leap-meditations (vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti) should originally arise [the meditative states] gradually.
If one transcends those factors, one transcends only a single one,
because the momentum does not extend further;
it is like when climbing a ladder, one must also ascend step by step.
As for those who would overstep, none can do so;
it is because their power does not reach that far. Some say:
Since the subsequent paths of entry are all as described before, one merely skips one level.
That is to say, when a practitioner first enters the leap-concentration (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*),
they enter from the fifth dhyāna into the fifth, and from the fourth into the fourth.
Because the number of factors and so forth are equal, it is easy to transcend and enter [the next stage].
Since it is likewise in the subsequent [stages], one does not skip over two. Some say:
Because it is an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), one can only transcend a single [moment].
That is to say, when a practitioner does not attend with mental application (manasikāra),
they are able to transcend only a single moment with respect to the object-condition.
Question: How does a practitioner transcend the objects of focus?
Answer: By means of non-recollective attention (*amanasikāra*), he focuses individually and separately upon each of the nine stages as objects within the first dhyāna.
Within this context, one can only transcend by taking a single level as an object;
that is, immediately after taking the desire realm as an object, one can subsequently take the first dhyāna or the second dhyāna as an object, but no others.
Immediately following the first dhyāna, one is able to take the desire realm as an object below,
or the second or third dhyānas as objects above, but not anything else.
Immediately following the second dhyāna, one can take as an object the desire realm or the first dhyāna below;
or one can take as an object the third or fourth dhyāna above, but not anything else.
Immediately following the third dhyāna, one can take as an object the first dhyāna or the second dhyāna below;
or one can take as an object the fourth dhyāna or the sphere of infinite space above, but not anything else.

In this manner, even up to the consciousness that takes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its object, it can immediately take the sphere of infinite consciousness as its lower object,
or the sphere of nothingness, and no others.
This is just as in the case of relying on the first dhyāna.
In this same manner, regarding other meditative concentrations (*samādhi*),
one should explain in detail how they function with respect to their respective objects of focus (*ālambana-pratyaya*) as appropriate;
for example, just as [a lower stage] cannot transcend the objects of the two stages.
The same applies to the transcendental concentrations (*samāpatti*).
Therefore, one does not enter the fourth [dhyāna].
Question: If that is so, then...
Why is it said that after the pure liberation (śubha-vimokṣa), five moments of mind arise?
The pure liberation-mind takes the desire realm as its object,
whereas the pervasive latent tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) of the fourth dhyāna can take as their objects everything from their own level and above, up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
Is it not the case that one can transcend the objects of the two stages?
Answer: It is said that an undefiled mind cannot transcend the two;
since that mind is defiled, there is no contradiction.

Question: Just as the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) arises immediately after the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) by taking the desire realm as its object, and so on up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), why is it said that an undefiled mind cannot transcend two [realms]?
Answer: That [absorption] merely takes [the stages] as a collective object and is therefore not called "leaping" (*vyutkrānta*).
Furthermore, because it also takes other stages as its object simultaneously, this objection does not hold.
Question: In what place can one perform the leaping concentration?
Answer: It exists in the desire realm, not in the form or formless realms;
it exists among human beings, not in other destinies;
and it exists in the three continents, not in the northern continent.
Both men and women are able to leap over meditative attainments (*dhyāna*).
The Venerable Saṃghavasu said:
"Only in Jambudvīpa, and only men, are able to leap over meditative attainments."
Regarding the statement that those in other continents and women are unable [to leap] because their physical bases are inferior:
according to this explanation,
those in other continents and women are also able to leap across meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
Because he has also attained mastery over the mind regarding samādhi.
Question: What kind of *pudgala* is able to transcend meditative absorption?
Answer: It is an *ārya*, not an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
This is the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), not that of one still in training (śaikṣa).
Within the state of one beyond training, this is liberation at any time (asamayavimukti), not liberation dependent on specific times.
Within the category of liberation at any time...
One must first attain the sublime qualities such as the ultimate concentration of the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*) and so forth before one can transcend [the concentrations].
Question: For what reason is it that only those who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and are liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*) are able to transcend the concentrations?
Answer: It is necessary that within one's continuum there be no afflictions;
only when one possesses mastery over meditative concentration can one leap over it.
Within the continuum of a learner (śaikṣa), afflictions still exist.
Because those liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) do not attain mastery over meditative concentration, they are likewise unable to transcend it.
Question: Which roots of goodness (kuśala-mūla) can immediately follow [the attainment of] the transcendence of concentration?

Answer: No roots of goodness—such as the immeasurables (apramāṇa), liberations (vimokṣa), spheres of mastery (abhibhv-āyatana), spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana), or the supernormal powers (abhijñā)—can immediately follow [the attainment of] the transcendence of concentration.
Only the roots of goodness consisting of the aspects of impermanence and so forth can transcend [the meditative absorptions] immediately. Why is this?
Because it is only through roots of goodness that are intense and predominant that one is able to transcend the concentrations.
