How many formless states (*ārūpya*) and so forth are subsumed under the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and the others?

Answer: The sphere of infinite space subsumes the sphere of infinite space itself, as well as its corresponding liberation (*vimokṣa*), its corresponding totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), six knowledges (*jñāna*), and three meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).
The sphere of infinite consciousness includes the sphere of infinite consciousness, its corresponding liberation, its corresponding totalities, six knowledges, and three samādhis.
The sphere of nothingness includes the sphere of nothingness, its corresponding liberation, six knowledges, and three samādhis.

The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception includes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception itself, its liberation, the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling, and conventional knowledge.
This is because all four formless attainments therein have as their intrinsic nature the four aggregates of their own fundamental stage.
One attains all these merits. Regarding the six knowledges (jñāna),
they exclude the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
Because these two do not rely on the formless realm (*ārūpyabhūmi*).
Regarding how many liberations (*vimokṣa*) and so forth are subsumed within the first liberation and the others:
the answer is that the first, second, and third liberations subsume the first, second, and third liberations, as well as conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The liberation of the sphere of infinite space subsumes the liberation of the sphere of infinite space, its corresponding pervasive base (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the six knowledges, and the three samādhis.
The liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness subsumes the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness, its corresponding pervasive base, the six knowledges, and the three samādhis.
The liberation of the sphere of nothingness comprises six knowledges and three samādhis;
[likewise] the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) subsumes the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-vimokṣa*).
The liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-vimokṣa*) subsumes the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling.
This is because, among these, the first three liberations all have the five co-emergent aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their intrinsic nature.
It includes conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Because it is the initial general observation, it does not include the spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*) or the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
as these are contaminated (*sāsrava*).
The other three samādhis do not include the remaining types of knowledge;
because they take form as their object, they do not include the knowledge of others' minds.
Each of the four formless liberations has as its nature the four aggregates of the preparatory wholesome states belonging to its own respective level.
Therefore, it includes the latter two universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), as well as the six knowledges (*jñāna*) and the three samādhis.
As for how many bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth are included by the first base of mastery and so forth:
the answer is that the first base of mastery includes the first base of mastery, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and so on, up to the eighth base of mastery.
The eighth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) subsumes conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Since all eight spheres of mastery herein have the five co-emergent aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their intrinsic nature,
they subsume conventional knowledge within the spheres of mastery.
Because it is a form of insight (vipaśyanā), it does not include the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana).
Because it is tainted (sāsrava), it does not include other types of knowledge or the three samādhis.
Because its object is form (rūpa), it does not include the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
How many bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and so forth are subsumed within the first base of totality and so forth?

Answer: The first base of totality subsumes the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the first base of totality, and so on, up to the tenth base of totality subsuming the conventional knowledge of the tenth base of totality.
In this context, because all ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana) have as their nature the five or four aggregates that arise simultaneously,
they include conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
Because they are contaminated (sāsrava), they do not include the other types of knowledge or the three samādhis.
Because their objects and bases differ, it does not include the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Regarding how many knowledges, etc., are included within the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the answer is:
the knowledge of phenomena includes the knowledge of phenomena and a portion of five other knowledges.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Regarding the inclusion of dharma-knowledge within dharma-knowledge:
dharma-knowledge abides in six stages.
That is to say: the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*),
the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*),
and the four dhyānas.
The threshold concentration (anāgamya-samādhi) is subsumed under the threshold concentration,
up to the fourth dhyāna being subsumed under the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) exists within the three paths.
That is to say: the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning.
The path of seeing subsumes the path of seeing, and so on, up to the path of no-more-learning subsuming the path of no-more-learning.
Furthermore, the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) takes the four truths as its object.
The knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering subsumes the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering,
and so on, up to the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path subsuming the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path.
Furthermore, the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) exists within four paths:
namely, the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga), the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga), the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), and the path of excellence (viśeṣa-mārga).
The path of preparation is subsumed under the path of preparation.
Up to the point where the path of further advancement is subsumed within the path of further advancement.
Furthermore, the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) falls within the three time periods:
that which is past is subsumed within the past.
The future is subsumed by the future;
the present is subsumed by the present;
therein, even down to this very moment, it is subsumed by this very moment.

That moment subsumes that moment; because this is stated as a general rule herein, it simply says "subsumed by dharma-knowledge. As for the statement that dharma-knowledge subsumes a portion of five knowledges: [it refers to the following: dharma-knowledge subsumes a portion of conventional knowledge, a portion of subsequent knowledge, a portion of the knowledge of suffering, a portion of the knowledge of origin, and a portion of the knowledge of the path. Why? Because these five knowledges possess the nature of dharma-knowledge. Furthermore, dharma-knowledge subsumes a portion of the knowledge of cessation, because it possesses the nature of the knowledge of cessation. It does not subsume a portion of the knowledge of others' minds, because it does not possess the nature of the knowledge of others' minds. It does not subsume a portion of the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, because it does not possess the nature of those two knowledges. Subsequent knowledge subsumes a portion of dharma-knowledge, a portion of conventional knowledge, a portion of subsequent knowledge, a portion of the knowledge of suffering, a portion of the knowledge of origin, and a portion of the knowledge of the path. Why? Because these six knowledges possess the nature of subsequent knowledge. Furthermore, subsequent knowledge subsumes a portion of the knowledge of cessation, because it possesses the nature of the knowledge of cessation. It does not subsume a portion of the knowledge of others' minds, because it does not possess the nature of the knowledge of others' minds. It does not subsume a portion of the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, because it does not possess the nature of those two knowledges. The knowledge of others' minds subsumes a portion of dharma-knowledge, a portion of conventional knowledge, a portion of subsequent knowledge, a portion of the knowledge of suffering, a portion of the knowledge of origin, a portion of the knowledge of the path, and a portion of the knowledge of cessation. Why? Because these seven knowledges possess the nature of the knowledge of others' minds. Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds subsumes a portion of the knowledge of exhaustion and a portion of the knowledge of non-arising, because it possesses the nature of the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising. It does not subsume a portion of the knowledge of dharma, because it does not possess the nature of the knowledge of dharma. It does not subsume a portion of conventional knowledge, because it does not possess the nature of conventional knowledge. It does not subsume a portion of the knowledge of cessation, because it does not possess the nature of the knowledge of cessation.

The knowledge of exhaustion subsumes a portion of dharma-knowledge, a portion of conventional knowledge, a portion of subsequent knowledge, a portion of the knowledge of suffering, a portion of the knowledge of origin, a portion of the knowledge of the path, a portion of the knowledge of cessation, a portion of the knowledge of others' minds, and a portion of the knowledge of exhaustion. Why? Because these nine knowledges possess the nature of the knowledge of exhaustion. Furthermore, the knowledge of exhaustion subsumes a portion of the knowledge of non-arising, because it possesses the nature of the knowledge of non-arising. It does not subsume a portion of the knowledge of dharma, because it does not possess the nature of the knowledge of dharma. It does not subsume a portion of conventional knowledge, because it does not possess the nature of conventional knowledge. It does not subsume a portion of the knowledge of cessation, because it does not possess the nature of the knowledge of cessation. It does not subsume a portion of the knowledge of others' minds, because it does not possess the nature of the knowledge of others' minds. The knowledge of non-arising subsumes a portion of dharma-knowledge, a portion of conventional knowledge, a portion of subsequent knowledge, a portion of the knowledge of suffering, a portion of the knowledge of origin, a portion of the knowledge of the path, a portion of the knowledge of cessation, a portion of the knowledge of others' minds, a portion of the knowledge of exhaustion, and a portion of the knowledge of non-arising. Why? Because these ten knowledges possess the nature of the knowledge of non-arising. Furthermore, the knowledge of non-arising subsumes nothing else, because it does not possess the nature of any other knowledge. Therefore, it is said that dharma-knowledge subsumes a portion of five knowledges. Subsequent knowledge subsumes a portion of six knowledges. The knowledge of others' minds subsumes a portion of seven knowledges. The knowledge of exhaustion subsumes a portion of nine knowledges. The knowledge of non-arising subsumes a portion of ten knowledges. This concludes the section on subsumption. Regarding the statement that dharma-knowledge is the antidote to the three realms: it is called the antidote to the desire realm, the antidote to the form realm, and the antidote to the formless realm. Why? Because it is the antidote to the afflictions of the desire realm, the antidote to the afflictions of the form realm, and the antidote to the afflictions of the formless realm. Furthermore, it is the antidote to the view of a self, the antidote to the view of extremes, the antidote to wrong view, the antidote to the view of grasping at precepts and observances, the antidote to the view of attachment to views, the antidote to doubt, the antidote to greed, the antidote to hatred, the antidote to pride, and the antidote to ignorance. Why? Because it is the antidote to the view of a self, the antidote to the view of extremes, the antidote to wrong view, the antidote to the view of grasping at precepts and observances, the antidote to the view of attachment to views, the antidote to doubt, the antidote to greed, the antidote to hatred, the antidote to pride, and the antidote to ignorance. Furthermore, it is the antidote to the fetters of the desire realm, the antidote to the fetters of the form realm, and the antidote to the fetters of the formless realm. Why? Because it is the antidote to the fetters of the desire realm, the antidote to the fetters of the form realm, and the antidote to the fetters of the formless realm. Furthermore, it is the antidote to the outflows of the desire realm, the antidote to the outflows of the form realm, and the antidote to the outflows of the formless realm. Why? Because it is the antidote to the outflows of the desire realm, the antidote to the outflows of the form realm, and the antidote to the outflows of the formless realm. Furthermore, it is the antidote to the bonds of the desire realm, the antidote to the bonds of the form realm, and the antidote to the bonds of the formless realm. Why? Because it is the antidote to the bonds of the desire realm, the antidote to the bonds of the form realm, and the antidote to the bonds of the formless realm. Furthermore, it is the antidote to the latent tendencies of the desire realm, the antidote to the latent tendencies of the form realm, and the antidote to the latent tendencies of the formless realm. Why? Because it is the antidote to the latent tendencies of the desire realm, the antidote to the latent tendencies of the form realm, and the antidote to the latent tendencies of the formless realm. Furthermore, it is the antidote to the hindrances of the desire realm, the antidote to the hindrances of the form realm, and the antidote to the hindrances of the formless realm. Why? Because it is the antidote to the hindrances of the desire realm, the antidote to the hindrances of the form realm, and the antidote to the hindrances of the formless realm. Furthermore, it is the antidote to the perversions of the desire realm, the antidote to the perversions of the form realm, and the antidote to the perversions of the formless realm. Why? Because it is the antidote to the perversions of the desire realm, the antidote to the perversions of the form realm, and the antidote to the perversions of the formless realm. Furthermore, it is the antidote to the outflows of the past, the antidote to the outflows of the future, and the antidote to the outflows of the present. Why? Because it is the antidote to the outflows of the past, the antidote to the outflows of the future, and the antidote to the outflows of the present. Furthermore, it is the antidote to the outflows of internal phenomena, the antidote to the outflows of external phenomena, and the antidote to the outflows of both internal and external phenomena. Why? Because it is the antidote to the outflows of internal phenomena, the antidote to the outflows of external phenomena, and the antidote to the outflows of both internal and external phenomena. Furthermore, it is the antidote to the outflows of conditioned phenomena, the antidote to the outflows of unconditioned phenomena, and the antidote to the outflows of both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena. Why? Because it is the antidote to the outflows of conditioned phenomena, the antidote to the outflows of unconditioned phenomena, and
That is to say, dharma-knowledge also includes knowledge of others' minds and a portion of the knowledge of the four truths.
Knowledge of others' minds is common to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
This refers exclusively to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Within the untainted, there are both dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*);
since this [term] refers only to dharma-knowledge, it is said to be "a partial portion."

The knowledge of the four truths each encompasses both dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*). Because this [category] only includes dharma-knowledge, it is said to be "a small portion. As for subsequent knowledge encompassing a small portion of five knowledges, it is as follows: subsequent knowledge itself constitutes one; it also encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path. This is because these five knowledges each take the four noble truths as their object. Furthermore, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) also encompasses a small portion of these five knowledges, because it takes the four noble truths as its object. Thus, it is said that subsequent knowledge encompasses a small portion of five knowledges. Regarding the statement that conventional knowledge encompasses a small portion of six knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—these four—because it takes the four noble truths as its object; and it also encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of non-arising, because it takes the five aggregates belonging to the desire realm as its object. Therefore, it is said that conventional knowledge encompasses a small portion of six knowledges. Regarding the statement that the knowledge of others' minds encompasses a small portion of seven knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—these four—because it takes the four noble truths as its object; and it also encompasses a small portion of dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and conventional knowledge, because it takes the five aggregates belonging to the desire realm as its object. Therefore, it is said that the knowledge of others' minds encompasses a small portion of seven knowledges. Regarding the statement that the knowledge of non-arising encompasses a small portion of eight knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—these four—because it takes the four noble truths as its object; and it also encompasses a small portion of dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of others' minds, because it takes the five aggregates belonging to the desire realm as its object. Therefore, it is said that the knowledge of non-arising encompasses a small portion of eight knowledges. Regarding the statement that dharma-knowledge encompasses a small portion of nine knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—these four—because it takes the four noble truths as its object; and it also encompasses a small portion of subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of others' minds, because it takes the five aggregates belonging to the desire realm as its object. Therefore, it is said that dharma-knowledge encompasses a small portion of nine knowledges. Regarding the statement that the knowledge of the path encompasses a small portion of ten knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of all ten knowledges because it takes all ten knowledges as its object. Therefore, it is said that the knowledge of the path encompasses a small portion of ten knowledges. It should be understood that the same applies to the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, and the knowledge of cessation. Regarding the statement that subsequent knowledge encompasses a small portion of eleven knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—these four—because it takes the four noble truths as its object; and it also encompasses a small portion of dharma-knowledge, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge of non-arising, because it takes the five aggregates belonging to the desire realm as its object. Therefore, it is said that subsequent knowledge encompasses a small portion of eleven knowledges. It should be understood that the same applies to conventional knowledge and the knowledge of others' minds. Regarding the statement that the knowledge of non-arising does not encompass any knowledges: because it has no objects, it does not encompass any knowledges. Therefore, it is said that the knowledge of non-arising does not encompass any knowledges. It should be understood that the same applies to the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising. Regarding the statement that the knowledge of exhaustion encompasses a small portion of three knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, and the knowledge of cessation—these three—because it takes the four noble truths as its object. Therefore, it is said that the knowledge of exhaustion encompasses a small portion of three knowledges. It should be understood that the same applies to the knowledge of non-arising. Regarding the statement that the knowledge of others' minds does not encompass any knowledges:

because it has no objects, it does not encompass any knowledges. Therefore, it is said that the knowledge of others' minds does not encompass any knowledges. It should be understood that the same applies to the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising. Regarding the statement that the knowledge of suffering encompasses a small portion of four knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of others' minds—these four—because it takes the four noble truths as its object. Therefore, it is said that the knowledge of suffering encompasses a small portion of four knowledges. It should be understood that the same applies to the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path. Regarding the statement that dharma-knowledge encompasses a small portion of five knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, and conventional knowledge—these five—because it takes the four noble truths as its object. Therefore, it is said that dharma-knowledge encompasses a small portion of five knowledges. It should be understood that the same applies to subsequent knowledge. Regarding the statement that conventional knowledge encompasses a small portion of six knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, dharma-knowledge, and subsequent knowledge—these six—because it takes the four noble truths as its object. Therefore, it is said that conventional knowledge encompasses a small portion of six knowledges. It should be understood that the same applies to the knowledge of others' minds. Regarding the statement that the knowledge of others' minds encompasses a small portion of seven knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and conventional knowledge—these seven—because it takes the four noble truths as its object. Therefore, it is said that the knowledge of others' minds encompasses a small portion of seven knowledges. It should be understood that the same applies to the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising. Regarding the statement that the knowledge of exhaustion encompasses a small portion of eight knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of others' minds—these eight—because it takes the four noble truths as its object. Therefore, it is said that the knowledge of exhaustion encompasses a small portion of eight knowledges. It should be understood that the same applies to the knowledge of non-arising. Regarding the statement that the knowledge of others' minds encompasses a small portion of nine knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising—these nine—because it takes the four noble truths as its object. Therefore, it is said that the knowledge of others' minds encompasses a small portion of nine knowledges. It should be understood that the same applies to the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising. Regarding the statement that the knowledge of suffering encompasses a small portion of ten knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—these ten—because it takes the four noble truths as its object. Therefore, it is said that the knowledge of suffering encompasses a small portion of ten knowledges. It should be understood that the same applies to the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path. Regarding the statement that dharma-knowledge encompasses a small portion of eleven knowledges: it encompasses a small portion of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of suffering, and the knowledge of origination—these eleven—because it takes the four noble truths as its object. Therefore, it is said that dharma-knowledge encompasses a small portion
As explained in the *Dharmajñāna*,
the difference is that this exists in nine stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds that subsumes the knowledge of others' minds:
the knowledge of others' minds exists within the four fundamental dhyānas;
that which is in the first dhyāna subsumes the first dhyāna.
Up to the fourth dhyāna, it subsumes the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, the supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);
that which is contaminated subsumes the contaminated.
The untainted is subsumed by the untainted.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds consists of both dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge;
dharma-knowledge is subsumed by dharma-knowledge.
Subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) subsumes subsequent knowledge.

Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna) is of three types: that of those in training (śaikṣa), that of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and that which is neither in training nor beyond training (naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa). Knowledge of those in training subsumes [knowledge of] those in training.
Furthermore, that which is comprised by what is neither-learner-nor-non-learner is itself neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Moreover, the knowledge of others' minds falls within the three periods of time:
that which belongs to the past is comprised by the past.
The future is subsumed by the future;
the present is subsumed by the present;
therein, even down to this very moment, it is subsumed by this very moment.
That moment subsumes that moment;
because this is stated in general terms herein,
it simply says that the knowledge of others' minds subsumes the knowledge of others' minds.
Regarding the inclusion of portions of the four knowledges:

this means that the knowledge of others' minds also includes small portions of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
This is because both the knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge each take the four noble truths as their objects.
This [category] comprises only a small portion of the path-truth as its object;
therefore, it is said that a small portion of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) exists in eighteen stages, namely:
the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the four dhyānas.
The four formless attainments and their preparatory stages;
these include only the four dhyānas.
Within the four dhyānas,
there are states that are wholesome, afflicted, and non-obscured-neutral;
this [category] includes only the wholesome.
Within the wholesome, there are those acquired at birth, those consisting of hearing, and those consisting of cultivation;
this [category] includes only those consisting of cultivation.
Within those consisting of cultivation, there are the paths of preparation, uninterruptedness, liberation, and special progress.
This refers exclusively to the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣabhāgīya*). Within the path of superior progress,

there are the factors conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*), the factors conducive to maintenance (*sthityābhāgīya*), the factors conducive to superior progress (*viśeṣabhāgīya*), and the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
This refers exclusively to the factors conducive to abiding (*sthity-anulomika*).
Within these factors conducive to abiding,
there are those that take the past, future, present, or the supramundane (*lokottara*) as their objects.
This refers exclusively to those that take the present as their object.
Among those that take the present as their object, there are those that take one's own continuum as their object and those that take another's continuum as their object;
this [present category] refers exclusively to those that take another's continuum as their object.
Because within the mental continuum of another, there are mind and mental factors that take [an object] as their condition,
and there are [minds and mental factors] that take the five aggregates as their condition; this [definition] refers exclusively to those that take mind and mental factors as their conditions.
Among the minds and mental factors, some have one dharma as their object and some have many dharmas as their objects;
this [category] includes only those that take one dharma as their object.
Within those that take one dharma as their object:
There is that which is the knowledge of others' minds,
and there is that which is not the knowledge of others' minds;
this [category] includes only the knowledge of others' minds.
For this reason, it is said to be "partial.
The knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) exists in nine stages,
namely, the preparatory concentration (anāgamya).
The intermediate dhyāna, the four dhyānas,
and the three formless attainments—
this [category] comprises only the four dhyānas.
Within the four dhyānas,
there are the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning;
this [attainment] comprises only the path of cultivation and the path of no-more-learning.
Within these two [paths], there are the paths of preparation (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), liberation (*vimukti*), and special progress (*viśeṣa*).
This [present path] includes only the path of special progress.
Within the path of special progress, there are those that take the past, future, or present as their object.
This refers exclusively to conditions pertaining to the present.
Within those conditions pertaining to the present,
there are those that condition one's own continuum and those that condition another's continuum.
This refers exclusively to taking the mental continua of others as objects.
Among those that take the mental continua of others as objects, there are those that take the mind and mental factors as objects,
and there are those that take the five aggregates as objects.
This refers exclusively to the inclusion of those mental states and mental factors that take [other] minds and mental factors as their objects.
Among these minds and mental factors that take minds and mental factors as their objects,
some take a single phenomenon as their object, while others take multiple phenomena as their objects.
This refers exclusively to the apprehension of a single dharma as its object.
Within that apprehension of a single dharma,
there is both that which is knowledge of others' minds and that which is not knowledge of others' minds.
This refers exclusively to the knowledge of others' minds;
it is for this reason that it is said to be "partial.
As for conventional knowledge encompassing conventional knowledge: [it is because] conventional knowledge is included within conventional knowledge.
Conventional knowledge exists in eighteen stages as previously explained:
that which is subsumed under the desire realm is [restricted to] the desire realm,
and so on, up to that which is subsumed under the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is [restricted to] the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is either wholesome, defiled, or non-obscured neutral.
The wholesome is subsumed under the wholesome,
and so on, up to the non-obscured neutral being subsumed under the non-obscured neutral.

Among the wholesome [dharmas], there are those acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*), those acquired through the removal of defilements (*vairāgya-labdha*), and those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*).
Those acquired through application are subsumed under acquisition through application,
and so on, up to those acquired by birth being subsumed under acquisition by birth.
Furthermore, there are the factors conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*) up to the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*).
Those conducive to decline are subsumed under the factors conducive to decline,
and so on, up to those conducive to penetration being subsumed under the factors conducive to penetration.
Furthermore, there are the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) up to the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
The path of preparation subsumes the path of preparation,
and so on, up to the path of excellence subsuming the path of excellence.
Furthermore, there are the past, future, and present.
The past subsumes the past, and so on,
up to the present subsuming the present.
Within this context, up to the point where this moment subsumes this moment and that moment subsumes that moment—
since this is stated as a general summary herein, it is said that conventional knowledge subsumes conventional knowledge.
"A small portion of one wisdom" refers to the fact that conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) also includes a small portion of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
This knowledge of others' minds encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Because this only encompasses that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is said to be "a small portion.
Regarding the fact that the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) encompasses the knowledge of suffering:
the knowledge of suffering exists in nine stages (*bhūmi*).
They exist within the three paths and the four paths;
they fall within the three periods of time.
It falls within a single moment;
regardless of which place, which realm,
or which world it may fall into.
What is the moment?
It is that very stage and that very path.
That world is subsumed within that very moment;
because this is stated as a general summary herein, it is said that "the knowledge of suffering subsumes the knowledge of suffering."
Regarding "a small portion of two knowledges":
this means that the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) also includes a small portion of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Each of these—knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge—takes the four noble truths as its object.
This is called "a small portion" because it comprises only those [knowledges] that take the truth of suffering as their object.
The knowledge of origination comprises a small portion of two knowledges: the knowledge of origination and the knowledge of the path.
The knowledge of cessation comprises a small portion of two knowledges: the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path.
All are as explained for the knowledge of suffering.
Regarding the inclusion of the knowledge of the path within the knowledge of the path,
it is also as explained for the knowledge of suffering.
Regarding "a small portion of the three knowledges":

this means that path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*) also includes a small portion of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge each take the four noble truths as their objects.
This refers only to those [supernormal powers] that take the Truth of the Path as their object.

While the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna-abhijñā) includes both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava), this [present case] refers only to those taking the uncontaminated as their object; therefore, it is said to be "a small portion."
How many samādhis are subsumed under the emptiness samādhi and so forth?
Answer: Emptiness subsumes emptiness;
wishlessness subsumes wishlessness.
The signless concentration (animitta-samādhi) that subsumes the signless operates with respect to two aspects of the truth of suffering.
The wishless concentration (appaṇihita-samādhi) operates with respect to ten aspects of the three truths.
The signless samādhi operates by way of the four aspects of the Truth of Cessation;
within this, each individual aspect exists in nine stages and throughout the three paths.
They exist within the four paths;
they fall within the three periods of time;
they fall within a single moment.
Whichever mode of activity,
in whichever stage,
and by whichever path.
In which world-period and in which moment does it fall?
It is precisely that aspect of the formations.
That ground,
that path,
that world.
It is subsumed within that very moment.
Because this is stated as a general summary here, it says that emptiness is subsumed by emptiness,
and so on, up to signlessness being subsumed by signlessness.

Although the three samādhis can generally be associated with both the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), here they are explained in terms of the doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) and therefore include only the outflow-free.
This is because they are included in the same manner as "attainability" (*upalabdhi*): since the meaning of "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*) is that a thing is attainable within its own essence.
That is to say, the self-essence exists in relation to the self-essence;
the self-essence exists in relation to the self-essence.
This is real.
An intrinsic nature exists within itself as something presently manifest.
This is not different;
this is not external;
this is not separate.
This is non-liberation.
This is without distinction.
This is not empty.
This is not non-existent, not adventitious, not distant, not dual, and not contentious;
for all such things as these have the sense of being "attainable.
The self-essence of all phenomena encompasses its own essence.
It is not like grasping food with the hand or grasping a robe with the fingers;
rather, because all phenomena obstruct their own essence and cause it never to be relinquished, they are called "grasped."
Other masters say that this inclusion of the self-essence (svabhāva) is of four kinds,
namely, the respective realms (dhātu).
Distinct entities,
distinct moments,
and distinct continuities.
Regarding the distinct realms:
this means that the eye-realm subsumes the eye-realm,
and so on, up to the dharma-realm subsuming the dharma-realm.
Regarding "distinct entities":
this refers to the seven entities within the dharma-dhātu,
namely form, sensation, perception, mental formations, [consciousness, phenomena, and unconditioned phenomena].
And the three unconditioned phenomena:
matter is subsumed under matter,
and so on, up to non-analytical cessation being subsumed under non-analytical cessation.
Regarding "each in its own moment":
this means that within form there are the past, future, and present;
the past is subsumed under the past.
Up to "the present includes the present.
Regarding "each being a distinct continuity":
this refers to present form that falls within its own continuity.
There are those that fall into another's continuum;
those included within one's own continuum belong to one's own continuum,
and those included within another's continuum belong to another's continuum.
By this principle, other cases should be understood accordingly;
therefore it is said that "as with inclusion,
so too with apprehension," for there is no difference in meaning between inclusion and apprehension.
With how many dhyānas and so forth are the perception of impermanence and the others associated?
Answer: The perception of impermanence is associated with the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the four liberations, the four knowledges, and one samādhi.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: It was in order to stop those who are deluded regarding associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*)—those who cling to the view that associated phenomena do not truly exist—and to clearly demonstrate that associated phenomena are indeed real.
Thus this treatise is composed.
Regarding the perception of impermanence associated with the four dhyānas:
all four dhyānas have the nature of the five aggregates.
This perception is associated with two of those aggregates in their entirety and a portion of one aggregate;
it is also associated with the four formless attainments and the four liberations.
The four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) and the four formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*) all have the nature of the four aggregates (*catuḥskandha*).
This perception (*saṃjñā*) is associated with those [four aggregates] in their entirety,
as well as with a portion of one aggregate.
That which is associated with the four knowledges refers to association with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna),
conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), and the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna).
Regarding the associations:
first, association with samādhi refers to the wishless [concentration] taking suffering as its object.
Just as with the perception of impermanence, so too are there the perception of suffering in what is impermanent,
and the perception of non-self in what is suffering.
The perception of death,
the perception of cessation,
and the perception of detachment.
The same applies to the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā-nirodha*);
these all correspond to the four knowledges (*jñāna*) and a single samādhi.
Because their number is the same, the statement is likewise.
Among these, those that are entirely identical refer to cases where the perceptions of death and formations differ while the names remain the same.
That is to say, the perception of impermanence and suffering and the knowledge [of them] share the same name;
those that differ from the rest are the perception of suffering and non-self.
Because it is associated with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*),
there is only a numerical correspondence [with other concentrations], while all else differs; namely, [it possesses] the notions of abandonment (*prahāṇa*),
detachment (*virāga*), and cessation (*nirodha*).
Because it is associated with the knowledge of cessation and the signless samādhi;
as for the perception of impurity being associated with the latter two dhyānas, the first two liberations, and conventional knowledge.
This perception is associated with all four dhyānas;
however, it is said to be associated only with the latter two dhyānas,
as explained in the *Saṃgrahaṇī*.
Regarding the statement that "the perception of impurity and the perception of revulsion toward food are likewise," these perceptions do not actually correspond to the first two liberations;
yet it is said that they do correspond.
It is also as stated in the *Saṃgrahaṇī*:
the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in (*sarvaloka-anabhirati-saṃjñā*) is associated with the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) of the latter two dhyānas.
This perception is also associated with all four dhyānas;
however, the statement that it is associated only with the latter two is as explained in the *Saṃgrahaṇī*.
With how many dhyānas, and so forth, are the first dhyāna and the others associated?
Answer: The first dhyāna is associated with the four immeasurables of the first dhyāna, the first two liberations, the first four bases of mastery, the eight knowledges, and the three samādhis.
The second dhyāna is associated with the four immeasurables of the second dhyāna, the first two liberations, the first four bases of mastery, the eight knowledges, and the three samādhis.
The third dhyāna is associated with the third dhyāna, the three immeasurables, the eight knowledges, and the three samādhis.

The fourth dhyāna is associated with the fourth dhyāna, the three immeasurables, the pure liberation, the latter four spheres of mastery, the first eight spheres of totality, the eight knowledges, and the three samādhis.
Among these, all four dhyānas have the five aggregates of their own respective levels as their nature, because the four aggregates co-arising in each level are mutually associated.
Thus it is said: "the first dhyāna with the first dhyāna."
This continues up to the fourth dhyāna, which is associated with the fourth dhyāna.
There is no sense of association between a nature and itself.
Furthermore, each individual dhyāna subsumes many dharmas.
Therefore, it is associated with immeasurable and equal merits.
Regarding the three immeasurables, joy (*muditā*) is excluded because the latter two dhyānas lack the faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*).
For those who maintain that the immeasurables of sympathetic joy (*muditā*) do not have the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*) as their intrinsic nature,
it is also stated that they are associated with the feeling of joy; thus,
in those two stages, there are only three immeasurables.
With how many immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are the immeasurables such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) associated?
Answer: Loving-kindness is associated with loving-kindness and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*);
this continues up to equanimity (*upekṣā*), which is associated with equanimity and conventional knowledge.
Although loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others have non-hatred (*avyāpāda*), wholesome roots, and so forth as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
what is stated here collectively subsumes both the intrinsic nature and its associated (*samprayukta*) and co-arising (*sahabhū*) factors.
Because these constitute the essence of loving-kindness and the others, it is said that "loving-kindness is associated with loving-kindness."
"Up to the point where equanimity is associated with equanimity" means that the four co-emergent aggregates are mutually associated.
This refers to the sphere of infinite space and so forth.
With how many formless [attainments] and so forth is it associated?
Answer: The sphere of infinite space is associated with the sphere of infinite space itself, its corresponding liberation, its corresponding universal base, six knowledges, and three samādhis.
The sphere of infinite consciousness is associated with the sphere of infinite consciousness, its liberation, and its totalities—namely, six knowledges and three samādhis.
The sphere of nothingness is associated with the sphere of nothingness, its liberation, and [its totalities]—namely, six knowledges and three samādhis.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception itself, its liberation, and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Among these, all four formless attainments have the four aggregates of their own level as their intrinsic nature.
Because the four aggregates co-arising in each respective stage are mutually associated,
it is said that the sphere of infinite space is associated with the sphere of infinite space,
and so on, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception being associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, because each and every formless attainment subsumes many dharmas,
it is endowed with the other qualities as previously described.
Regarding the six knowledges, they are explained as in the section on "Subsumption."
With how many liberations, etc., are the first liberation and the others associated?
Answer: The first, second, and third liberations are associated with the first, second, and third liberations, as well as with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

The liberation of the sphere of infinite space is associated with the liberation of the sphere of infinite space, its corresponding universal base (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the six knowledges, and the three samādhis.

The liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness is associated with the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness, its corresponding universal base, the six knowledges, and the three samādhis.
The liberation of the sphere of nothingness is associated with the six knowledges and three samādhis of the sphere of nothingness.

The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is associated with the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling is not associated [with mental factors].
Although the first three liberations all have non-attachment as their essential nature (*svabhāva*),
that which is described here takes as its substance both the essential nature and the factors associated with and co-arising with it.
To say that the first, second, and third liberations are associated with the first, second,
and third liberations means that they are mutually associated with the four aggregates that arise simultaneously.
The four formless liberations are as explained in the section on the four formless [attainments].

Although the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling consists of many factors—such as the mind and mental concomitants that arise simultaneously and are inseparable—[it is nonetheless designated by its primary characteristic].
Because they lack a basis, an object of cognition, a mode of activity, or a common referent, they are not associated (*saṃprayukta*).
With how many bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth is the first base of mastery associated?
Answer: The first base of mastery is associated with the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the first base of mastery.
Up to the eighth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), it is associated with the mundane wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the eighth sphere of mastery.
Although all eight spheres of mastery have non-attachment (*alobha*) as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [they are here categorized according to their association with wisdom].
Since what is explained here generally takes the factors associated with and co-existent with intrinsic nature as its essence,
it is said that the first sphere of mastery is associated with the first sphere of mastery,
and so on, up to the eighth sphere of mastery being associated with the eighth sphere of mastery.
With how many *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totalities), etc., is the first *kṛtsnāyatana*, etc., associated?
Answer: The first *kṛtsnāyatana* is associated with the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the first *kṛtsnāyatana*;
likewise, up to the tenth *kṛtsnāyatana*, which is associated with the conventional knowledge of the tenth *kṛtsnāyatana*.
Although the first eight bases of mastery (*kṛtsnāyatana*) have non-attachment as their wholesome root for their intrinsic nature,
those mentioned here take as their essence both the intrinsic nature and the associated and co-arising factors.
The latter two universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) have, in their totality, the four co-emergent aggregates as their intrinsic nature. Therefore,
it is said that the first universal base is associated with the first universal base,
and so on, up to the tenth universal base being associated with the tenth universal base.
With how many samādhis are the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and the others associated?
Answer: The dharma-knowledge is associated with a portion of three samādhis;
and so on, as explained at length.
Regarding the statement that "dharma-knowledge is partially associated with the three samādhis":
this knowledge is said to be "partial" because it is not associated with the three samādhis in conjunction with subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) or any of the receptivities (kṣānti).
Regarding the statement "as it is for the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), so it is for the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)":
this means that because this knowledge does not correspond with the three samādhis simultaneously as the knowledge of phenomena and all the patiences (kṣānti) do, it is said to be "also thus."
Regarding the statement that "the knowledge of others' minds is partially associated with one samādhi":
this refers to the knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation, as well as the knowledge of the path not subsumed under the knowledge of others' minds.
It is associated with all forms of patience (*kṣānti*).
It is called "partial" because it is not associated with [all] samādhis;

that is to say, it is associated with only a portion of the path of a single object (*ekālambana*)—namely, the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*)—just as in the case of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
The same applies to the knowledges of origin, cessation, and the path.
This statement "the same applies" is made because they share the same number [of associated factors].
However, the knowledge of origin corresponds only with a small portion of the wishless samādhi that takes origin as its object.
The knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) corresponds only partially with the signless samādhi (animitta-samādhi);
the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) corresponds only partially with the wishless samādhi (apraṇihita-samādhi) that takes the path as its object.
This is because all [other factors] have been excluded by virtue of being associated with the three samādhis.
As for the fact that the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) is partially associated with two of the three samādhis,
this knowledge is associated exclusively with knowledge itself.
Because the emptiness samādhi and the wishless samādhi associated with the knowledge of suffering are only partially [associated], it is said that "a portion" [is associated].
As for the three gates of samādhi, they are not mentioned separately as being associated.
Because these preceding categories have already been fully explained,
and because there is no mutual correspondence within its own category,
[ends] the Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda, Volume One Hundred and Sixty-seven.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 168,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhiskandha), Part Three of the Third: The Summary Chapter (Saṃgrahavarga). If one accomplishes the first dhyāna and so forth...
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: It was composed in order to refute those who deny the existence of the natures of possession (*prāpti*) and non-possession (*aprāpti*), and to demonstrate that the natures of possession and non-possession are substantially real (*dravyasat*). Thus, this treatise was written.
If one achieves the first dhyāna and so forth,
how many of the four dhyānas and so forth does that person achieve,
and how many do they not achieve?
Answer: If one has attained the first dhyāna, one may possess one, two, three, or all four of the [subsequent] dhyānas.
"One" refers to one whose craving for the Brahma-world (brahmaloka) has not yet been exhausted.
This refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*).
If one is born in the desire realm, one possesses [the first dhyāna] solely by virtue of attaining it through the removal of defilements (*vairāgyalābha*).
If one is born in the Brahma-world, one possesses it because it is attained both through the removal of defilements and by birth (*upapattilābha*).
Because their craving for the Brahma-world has not been exhausted, they do not accomplish the three higher dhyānas.
The second case refers to those whose craving for the Brahma-world has been exhausted but whose craving for what is above it has not;
these are ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world.
Furthermore, when an Ārya is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
or if born in the Desire Realm or the first two dhyānas, they possess [the dhyāna] solely by virtue of acquisition through detachment (*vairāgyalābha*).

If born in the Brahma-world (Brahmaloka), they possess it in the first dhyāna both by acquisition through detachment and by birth (*upapattilābha*), and in the second dhyāna solely by acquisition through detachment.

If one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, one possesses only the untainted (anāsrava) [attainments] of the first dhyāna, not the tainted (sāsrava), because they have been relinquished by transcending that level;
in the second dhyāna, one possesses them only as obtained through the abandonment of defilements (vairāgya-lābhika).
Because their craving for the Ābhāsvara realm is not yet exhausted, they do not achieve the two higher dhyānas.
The third case refers to those whose craving for the Ābhāsvara realm is exhausted, but whose craving for the realms above it is not yet exhausted;
these are ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world.
Furthermore, when a noble one is born in the Ābhāsvara or Śubhakṛtsna heavens,
or if born in the desire realm, they possess [the dhyānas] because they have attained them through the mere abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya-lābha*) regarding the lower three dhyānas.
If born in the Brahma-world, they possess [them] because they have both attained them through the abandonment of defilements and attained them by birth (*upapatti-lābha*) within the first dhyāna.
In the second and third dhyānas, one achieves [the pure] solely through the attainment of freedom from defilement (*vairāgya-lābha*).
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara heaven, one achieves only the untainted (*anāsrava*) in the first dhyāna.
In the second and third dhyānas, one possesses them solely by virtue of being free from defilement (*vairāgya-lābha*).
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, one possesses only the untainted (*anāsrava*) states of the first and second dhyānas.
In the third dhyāna, one achieves [the fourth dhyāna] solely by means of detachment from defilements;
however, because craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm has not yet been exhausted, one does not achieve the fourth dhyāna.
The "fourth" refers to the exhaustion of craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm.
This refers to ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma world,
as well as noble ones born in the Ābhāsvara heaven,
up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
If one is born in the desire realm, one possesses [the dhyānas] because they are acquired solely through the abandonment of defilements (vairāgya-lābhika) with respect to all four dhyānas.
If one is born in the Brahma-world, one possesses [them] because they are acquired both through the abandonment of defilements and through birth (upapatti-lābhika) with respect to the first dhyāna.
In the three higher dhyānas, one possesses them solely through the attainment of detachment from defilements.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, one possesses only the untainted [attainments] of the first dhyāna;
in the three higher dhyānas, one possesses them solely through the attainment of detachment from defilements.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven], one accomplishes only the untainted [attainments] in the first and second dhyānas;
in the third and fourth dhyānas, one accomplishes them solely through the acquisition resulting from the abandonment of defilements.
If one is born in the Fruit of Vastness (*bṛhatphala*), one achieves only the untainted (*anāsrava*) [attainments] in the lower three dhyānas;
in the fourth dhyāna, one achieves them solely through the attainment of freedom from defilement (*vairāgya-prāpti*).
If one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one achieves only the untainted [attainments] in all four dhyānas.
Regarding the four immeasurables, there may be none, three, or all four.
"None" refers to those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This refers to noble ones (*ārya*) born in those four stages who have accomplished the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna.
It is not the four immeasurables because they are abandoned upon transcending the realm.
The third refers to those born in the Śubhakṛtsna and Bṛhatphala heavens.
These noble ones, born in those two stages, accomplish the untainted first dhyāna and three immeasurables—excluding sympathetic joy—because they have transcended that stage and abandoned them.
The fourth refers to those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*), or the Ābhāsvara heaven.
This includes ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
as well as noble ones born in the Ābhāsvara heaven.
If one is born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world, one accomplishes the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna as well as the four immeasurables.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara heaven, one accomplishes the uncontaminated first dhyāna and the four immeasurables.
Regarding the four formless attainments, there may be none, one, two, three, or all four.
"None" refers to those whose craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*) has not been exhausted;
these include both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
Because sensual desire has been exhausted but desire for the form realm has not yet been exhausted, one accomplishes the first dhyāna but not the formless [attainments].
The first case refers to those whose desire for the form realm has been exhausted but whose higher desire has not yet been exhausted;
these are both ordinary worldlings and noble ones.
Those born in the desire realm or the Brahma world,
as well as noble ones born in the Ābhāsvara heaven up to the Sphere of Infinite Space.
They all achieve the first dhyāna and one formless attainment (*ārūpya*).
If they are born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
they achieve the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna and the first formless attainment.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven up to the Sphere of Infinite Space,
one accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna as well as the tainted and untainted first formless attainment; however,
because craving for the higher realms has not been exhausted, one does not accomplish the three higher formless attainments.
The second refers to those who have exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite space but have not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
These include ordinary persons and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma world,
as well as noble ones born from the Ābhāsvara heaven up to the sphere of infinite consciousness.
They all achieve the first dhyāna and the two formless attainments.
If they are born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
they achieve the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna and the first two formless attainments.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
up to the Sphere of Infinite Space,
one accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna.
Regarding the impure and pure [attainments], in the first two formless realms:
if one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, one accomplishes the pure first dhyāna and the first formless realm;
[one accomplishes] the impure and pure second formless realm.
Because their craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted, they do not achieve the two higher formless attainments.
The third case refers to those whose craving for the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness is exhausted, but whose craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted;
these are ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma world.
Furthermore, when noble beings are born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven up to the Sphere of Nothingness,
they all achieve the first dhyāna and the three formless attainments.
If one is born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
one accomplishes the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna and the first three formless attainments;
if one is born in the Ābhāsvara heaven, [one accomplishes the same].
Up to the sphere of infinite space,
one accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna as well as the tainted and untainted first three formless attainments.
If one is born in the sphere of infinite consciousness, [one accomplishes the same].
One accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna and the first formless attainment;
the second and third formless attainments may be either tainted or untainted;
and if one is born in the sphere of nothingness, [one accomplishes the fourth formless attainment].
One accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna and the first two formless attainments;
one accomplishes both the tainted and untainted third formless attainment.
Because craving for what is above that has not been exhausted, one does not accomplish the uppermost formless attainment.
The fourth refers to the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
This pertains to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*),
as well as noble ones born in the Ābhāsvara heaven.
Up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
they all achieve the first dhyāna as well as the four formless attainments,
provided they are born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world.
One accomplishes the three formless attainments— both with and without outflows—
and one formless attainment that is with outflows,
if one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven up to the Sphere of Infinite Space.
One achieves the untainted first dhyāna;
the three formless attainments (ārūpya), both tainted and untainted;
and one formless attainment, which is tainted.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness,
one accomplishes one formless attainment that is untainted (anāsrava)— the first dhyāna—
and two formless attainments that are both tainted (sāsrava) and untainted.
There is one type of outflow-free [attainment] that is formless:
if one is born in the sphere of nothingness,
one accomplishes the first dhyāna that is free from outflows.
Two are formless.
One formless aggregate is both with outflows and without outflows.
One formless aggregate is with outflows.
If one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
one accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna and three formless attainments,
as well as one tainted formless attainment.
Regarding the eight liberations, there may be none, or one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight.
"None" refers to those born in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven who have not yet exhausted their craving for that realm.
This refers to a noble one who is born in the Śubhakṛtsna realm,
having attained the untainted first dhyāna but not yet attained liberation.
Because the first two liberations transcend their respective stages and are abandoned;
and because the latter six liberations have not yet been attained as they are still defiled by the pervasive purity (*śubhakṛtsna*) stage, it is said that they do not exist [there].
"One" refers to those born in the pervasive purity realm.
That is, craving for that [level] has been exhausted, but craving for the higher level has not yet been exhausted.
If one is born in the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) heaven, craving for that has not yet been exhausted.
Or, if one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Space (Ākāśānantyāyatana).
If craving for that [level] has not yet been exhausted,
this refers to the noble ones who, having been born in those various stages, have accomplished the untainted first dhyāna and one liberation.

Among these, if they are born in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven and craving for that has been exhausted while craving for the higher [levels] remains unexhausted, they accomplish the pure liberation (*śuddhavimokṣa*).
This is because the former two are abandoned by transcending their respective stages,
while the latter five have not yet been attained.
If one is born in the Bṛhatphala heaven, even though craving for that realm is not yet exhausted, one nevertheless accomplishes the pure liberation (śuddhavimokṣa).
It is not otherwise, as explained previously.

If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and craving for it has not yet been exhausted, that person accomplishes both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) liberations of the Sphere of Infinite Space.
This is because the former three are not lost by transcending their respective stages (*bhūmi*),
and the latter four have not yet been attained.
The second case refers to those born in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*).
If one has not yet exhausted craving for the Subhakṛtsna and Śubhakṛtsna heavens,
and is reborn in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala heavens,
then one has exhausted craving for the Bṛhatphala heaven but has not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Space, craving for that level is exhausted while craving for higher levels is not yet exhausted;
if one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, craving for that level is not yet exhausted.
This refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) born in the Desire Realm or the Brahma World.
Furthermore, from the time the Noble Ones are born in the Ābhāsvara heaven up until the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness,
they all accomplish the first dhyāna and the two liberations.
Among these, if one is born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*),
and has not yet exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, they possess the impure and pure first dhyāna as well as the first two liberations (*vimokṣa*).
This is because others have not yet attained it.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
and their craving for the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven has not been exhausted, they accomplish the untainted first dhyāna.
The rest is as previously explained.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala [heavens],
and has exhausted craving for the Bṛhatphala but not yet exhausted craving for what is above it, that person accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna and the third liberation.
The fourth liberation is both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*),
because the first two have already been abandoned and the latter four have not yet been attained.

If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Space, with craving for that level exhausted but craving for higher levels not yet exhausted, they possess the untainted first dhyāna as well as the fourth and fifth liberations, both tainted and untainted.
This is because the first three have already been abandoned by others,
and the latter three have not yet been attained.

If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and craving for that very sphere is not yet exhausted, one accomplishes the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna and the untainted fourth liberation (*vimokṣa*).
The fifth liberation is both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava);
it is not otherwise, as explained previously.
The three [types of beings] refer to those born in the desire realm and the Brahma-world.
In the Subhakṛtsna heaven, craving for the Śubhakṛtsna has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted.

If one is born in the Bṛhatphala heaven, craving for the Ākāśānantyāyatana has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted. If one is born in the Vijñānānantyāyatana...
When craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness is exhausted but craving for what is above it is not yet exhausted,
or if one is born in the sphere of nothingness and craving for that very state is not yet exhausted—
this refers to ordinary persons and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma world.
Furthermore, from the birth of noble beings in the Ābhāsvara Heaven up to the Sphere of Nothingness,
all achieve the first dhyāna and the three liberations.
Among these, if one is born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world (Brahmaloka),
having exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna heaven but not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms,
they possess the first dhyāna— both contaminated and uncontaminated— as well as the first three liberations (vimokṣa).
This is because others have not yet attained it.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara realm and has exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna realm but has not yet exhausted craving for the realms above, [one does not attain it].
He accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna;
the rest is as previously explained.
If he is born in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala [heavens], [the same applies].
When craving for the sphere of infinite space is exhausted, but craving for what is above it is not yet exhausted,
one accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna and the third liberation;
one also accomplishes the tainted and untainted fourth and fifth liberations, but not the others, because the former two have already been relinquished.
Because the latter three have not yet been attained.

If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Space and has exhausted craving for the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above that, they possess the untainted first dhyāna.
The first three formless liberations (ārūpya-vimokṣa) are both with outflows (sāsrava) and without outflows (anāsrava),
but not the others; for the former three have already been abandoned,
and the latter two have not yet been attained.

If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), with craving for that very sphere exhausted but craving for the higher spheres not yet exhausted, one accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna and the fourth liberation, as well as the tainted and untainted fifth and sixth liberations.
It is not otherwise than as previously stated.
If one is born in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and has not yet exhausted craving for that very state,
they possess the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna.
The fourth and fifth liberations are both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*); the sixth liberation is neither, as previously explained.
Regarding the four [types of beings], they are those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*), and the Ābhāsvara heaven.
When craving for the Bṛhatphala heaven has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted;
or if one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala heavens,
and craving for the Vijñānānantyāyatana has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness or the Sphere of Nothingness,
and has exhausted craving for the Sphere of Nothingness;
or if one is born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception and does not attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
This refers to ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
as well as noble ones born in the Ābhāsvara heaven,
up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception.
All have accomplished the first dhyāna and the four liberations (*vimokṣa*).

Among them, those born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world who have exhausted craving for the *Bṛhatphala* heaven but have not yet exhausted craving for what is above it, accomplish both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna, as well as the first three liberations.
The fourth liberation is both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava), because others have not yet attained it.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven...
In the case of one who has exhausted craving for the Bṛhatphala heaven but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it,
that person accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna;
the rest is as previously explained.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala [heavens],
having exhausted craving for the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness but not yet exhausted craving for what is above it,
they accomplish the untainted first dhyāna and the third liberation.
The first three formless liberations (ārūpya-vimokṣa) are both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava),
but not the others; for the former two have already been abandoned,
and the latter two have not yet been attained.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Space or the Sphere of Nothingness and has exhausted craving for them, one accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna,
as well as the tainted and untainted liberations of the first three formless attainments and the seventh liberation, but not the others, because the former three have already been abandoned.
Because the latter has not yet been attained.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness,
craving for the Sphere of Nothingness is exhausted.
He accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna and the fourth liberation,
as well as the tainted and untainted fifth and sixth liberations.
And the seventh liberation;
it is not others as previously stated.
If one is born in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), then craving for that very place is exhausted.
He achieves the untainted first dhyāna,
as well as the fourth and fifth liberations,
