and the sixth liberation, which is both tainted and untainted.
And the seventh liberation;
it is not others as previously stated.
This applies if one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He does not attain the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
He accomplishes the untainted (anāsrava) first dhyāna and the three formless liberations (ārūpyavimokṣa).
And [this applies] to the seventh liberation as well;
it does not apply to the other first three, because they have already been abandoned,
and because the last one has not yet been attained.
Or because it has already been relinquished.

The fifth refers to one born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world who has exhausted craving for the Ābhāsvara heaven and the sphere of infinite space, but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above that.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala realms,
or in the Sphere of Nothingness, and has exhausted craving for those levels but has not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti);
or if one is born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception and has attained the meditative absorption of cessation.
This refers to ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
as well as noble ones born in the Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, and Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana realms.
They have all accomplished the first dhyāna and the five liberations.
Among them, those born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world have exhausted their craving for the sphere of infinite space,
but have not yet exhausted their craving for what lies above it.
He accomplishes the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna and the first three liberations (vimokṣa),
as well as the contaminated and uncontaminated fourth and fifth liberations;
this is because he has not yet attained the others.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
having exhausted craving for the Sphere of Infinite Space but not yet exhausted craving for what is above it,
they accomplish the untainted first dhyāna.
The rest is as previously stated.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala,
or Ākiṃcanyāyatana realms and has exhausted craving for them, yet does not attain the cessation attainment (nirodhasamāpatti).
He accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna and the third liberation;
the tainted and untainted liberations of the first three formless attainments;
and the seventh liberation.
This is because the former two [types of beings] have already abandoned it,
and the latter one has not yet attained it.
If one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) and attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), [then one is such].
He accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna,
the first three formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*), and the final two liberations; it is not others,
because they have already been abandoned.

The sixth refers to those born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world who have exhausted craving for the Ābhāsvara heaven and the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, but have not yet exhausted craving for what is above;
or those born in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala heavens who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
This refers to ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
as well as noble ones born in the Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, and Bṛhatphala heavens;
all of them possess the first dhyāna and the six liberations.
Among these, if one is born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
having exhausted craving for the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness but not yet exhausted craving for what is above it,
they possess the first dhyāna— both with outflows and without outflows— as well as the first three liberations.
The first three formless liberations (ārūpya-vimokṣa) are both with outflows (sāsrava) and without outflows (anāsrava),
because the others have not yet been attained;
this applies if one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
When craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted,
one accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna;
the rest is as previously stated.
If one born in the Śubhakṛtsna or Bṛhatphala realms attains the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti),
they accomplish the untainted first dhyāna and the third liberation,
as well as the tainted and untainted liberations of the first three formless attainments, together with the latter two liberations.
This is not because others have already abandoned it.

The seventh refers to those born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world who have exhausted craving for the Ābhāsvara heaven and the sphere of nothingness, yet have not attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
This refers to ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
as well as noble ones born in the Ābhāsvara heaven;
all of them possess the first dhyāna and the seven liberations.

Among these, if one is born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world (Brahmaloka) and has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) but has not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti),
that person accomplishes both the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna.
And the first three liberations;
the first three formless liberations, whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), as well as the seventh liberation,
[are included], because the eighth has not yet been attained.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven and has exhausted craving for the Sphere of Nothingness but has not attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti),
they possess the untainted first dhyāna.
The rest is as previously explained.
The eighth refers to one born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world who attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
These are the noble ones born in the desire realm, the Brahma-world, or the Ābhāsvara heaven;
they all possess the first dhyāna and the eight liberations.
Among them, those born in the desire realm, the Brahma-world, or [the Ābhāsvara heaven] who have attained the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), [are the ones referred to].
He accomplishes the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna as well as all eight liberations.
If he is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven and attains the attainment of cessation,
he accomplishes the uncontaminated first dhyāna.
As well as all eight liberations (aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ).
Regarding the eight bases of mastery (aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni), they may be absent,
or there may be four or eight.
"Non-existence" refers to one who is born in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven but whose craving for it has not yet been exhausted;
or, if born in the formless realm,
this refers to a noble one (ārya) born in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven or the formless realm.
They both achieve the untainted first dhyāna,
but not the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), because although they are born in the Subhakṛtsna heaven, their craving for that very realm is not yet exhausted; thus,
they have already relinquished the first four [bases] and have not yet attained the latter four.
This is because those born in the formless realm have already abandoned them.
The fourth refers to those born in the desire realm, the Brahma-world,
and the Ābhāsvara heaven.
If craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm has not been exhausted,
one is born in the Subhakṛtsna realm; if that craving is exhausted,
one is born in the Bṛhatphala realm.
These are the ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire realm and the Brahma-world,
as well as the noble ones born in the Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, and Bṛhatphala heavens.
They have all accomplished the first dhyāna and the four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Among them, those born in the desire realm or the Brahma world whose craving for the Subhakṛtsna heaven has not yet been exhausted [are included].
He accomplishes the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna as well as the first four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
because he has not yet attained the others;
this applies if he is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
The craving for the Sphere of Utmost Purity is not yet exhausted.
He accomplishes the untainted first dhyāna;
the rest is as previously explained.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven], craving for that very place is exhausted;
furthermore, if one is born in the Bṛhatphala [heaven],
they accomplish the untainted first dhyāna as well as the four subsequent spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).
It is not others because they have already abandoned them.
The eighth refers to those born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world who have exhausted their craving for the Ābhāsvara and Subhakṛtsna heavens.
This refers to ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma world,
as well as noble ones born in the Ābhāsvara heaven,
all of whom possess the first dhyāna.
And regarding the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*):
if one is born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
and has exhausted all craving for the Heaven of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*).
He accomplishes the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna as well as the eight bases of mastery.
If he is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
his craving for the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven is exhausted.
He achieves the untainted first dhyāna and the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Regarding the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), he may possess none, one, two, eight, nine, or all ten.
"None" refers to those born in the desire realm, the Brahma-world, the Ābhāsvara heaven, or the Śubhakṛtsna heaven.
If one has not yet exhausted the craving for the Sphere of Universal Purity (śubhakṛtsna),
and is reborn in the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) or the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
This refers to ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
as well as noble ones born in the Ābhāsvara or Śubhakṛtsna heavens;
these latter two classes of formless beings all possess the first dhyāna but do not possess the ten universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana).
Among these, if one is born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world and has not yet exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna heaven,
they possess both the contaminated and the uncontaminated first dhyāna.
This is because the ten universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) have not yet been attained.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara or Śubhakṛtsna realms,
the craving for the Śubhakṛtsna realm has not yet been exhausted.
He achieves the untainted first dhyāna,
because he has not yet attained the ten universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana).
If he is born into either of the latter two formless realms...
He achieves the untainted first dhyāna,
but not the ten universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana), because he has already abandoned them.
The "one" refers to one who is born in the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana) and whose craving for it is not yet exhausted.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness,
this noble one, being born in those two stages,
accomplishes both the untainted first dhyāna and one base of totality.
Among these, if one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Space,
one accomplishes only the single totality-sphere (kṛtsnāyatana) of infinite space, because craving for that [sphere] has not been exhausted; it is not the other [totalities],
as the previous eight have already been relinquished.
Because the latter has not yet been attained.
If one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness,
one accomplishes one universal base (kṛtsnāyatana), namely, the universal base of infinite consciousness.
It is not others because they have already been abandoned.
Second, it refers to the sphere of infinite space;
that is, the exhaustion of craving for it.
This refers to noble ones born there who have accomplished the untainted first dhyāna and the latter two universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
It does not refer to others, because they have already abandoned them.
"Eight" refers to those born in the desire realm, the Brahma-world, the Ābhāsvara heaven, and the Śubhakṛtsna heaven.
When craving for the Śubhakṛtsna realm is exhausted, but craving for what is above it is not yet exhausted,
if one is born in the Bṛhatphala realm, then craving for that very realm is not yet exhausted.
This refers to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and noble ones (ārya) who are born in the Desire Realm or the Brahma-world.
Furthermore, when noble ones are born in the Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, or Bṛhatphala [heavens],
they all achieve the first dhyāna as well as the first eight universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana).
Among these, if they are born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world (Brahmaloka):
When craving for the Sphere of Total Purity is exhausted, but craving for what is above it is not yet exhausted,
one accomplishes the first dhyāna— both with and without outflows—
as well as the first eight universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana).
This is because others have not yet attained it.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara or Śubhakṛtsna realms,
and has exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna realm but has not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms.
Furthermore, when one is born in the Fruit of Vastness (Bṛhatphala), that craving for it is not yet exhausted;
they achieve the untainted (anāsrava) first dhyāna,
while the rest is as previously described.
The ninth refers to those born in the desire realm or the form realm who have exhausted craving for the form realm but have not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms;
these are ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world.
Furthermore, when noble ones are born in the Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, or Bṛhatphala realms,
they all achieve the first dhyāna as well as the nine preceding bases of totality (kṛtsnāyatana).
Among these, if one is born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world, [they likewise achieve them].
When attachment to the form realm (*rūparāga*) has been exhausted but attachment to the higher realms has not yet been exhausted,
one accomplishes the impure and pure first dhyāna as well as the first nine universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
because the tenth has not yet been attained.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, or Bṛhatphala realms,
having exhausted craving for the form realm but not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms,
they possess the untainted first dhyāna.
The rest is as previously explained.
"Ten" refers to those born in the desire or form realms who have exhausted their craving for the sphere of infinite space.
This refers to ordinary beings and noble ones born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
as well as noble ones born in the Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, and Bṛhatphala heavens;
all of them possess the first dhyāna and the ten universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana).
In this regard, if one is born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world and has exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite space,
they possess both the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna as well as the ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana).
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, or Bṛhatphala heavens,
or has exhausted craving for the Sphere of Infinite Space,
they accomplish the untainted first dhyāna and the ten universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana).
Regarding the eight knowledges, there may be two, four, five, six, seven, or eight.
"Two" refers to the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
Among these, [the first case applies to] ordinary persons and those who have previously abandoned the defilements of desire (*vairāgya*).

In the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) based on the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*), one accomplishes the contaminated (*sāsrava*) first dhyāna.
If based on the five higher stages, in the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering, one accomplishes both the contaminated and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna.
All of them achieve two types of knowledge:
namely, the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge.
The fourth refers to the stage of the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) and the receptivity to the subsequent [knowledge] of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*).
In this stage, if one relies on the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), one accomplishes the contaminated (*sāsrava*) first dhyāna;
if one relies on the five higher stages, one accomplishes both the contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) first dhyānas.
They all achieve four knowledges:
namely, the knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of suffering, and the dharma-knowledge.
The fifth occurs at the stage of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*).
The contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyānas accomplished by these two stages are as previously analyzed.
They both accomplish five types of knowledge;
that is, the aforementioned four, with the addition of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
The sixth refers to the stages from the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*) up to the dharma-acceptance of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*).
In these various stages, the first dhyāna that is accomplished is as previously described;
in all of them, one accomplishes six knowledges (*jñāna*).
This refers to the first five [knowledges] plus the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).
The "seven" refer to the stages from the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) up to the patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*).
The first dhyāna accomplished in these various stages is as previously described.
They all achieve seven knowledges,
namely the aforementioned six plus the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
The eighth refers to the stages from the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārgadharmajñāna*) upward.

Regarding this, the first dhyāna accomplished at the stage of the path-knowledge of the dharma (mārga-dharma-jñāna) and the path-subsequent patience (mārga-anvaya-kṣānti) is also as previously described.
At the stage of the path-subsequent knowledge (mārga-anvaya-jñāna), one necessarily accomplishes both the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyānas.
Regarding those who, within the stages subsequent to the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of that path, are born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world,
they necessarily accomplish both the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna.
As for those born in the Ābhāsvara heaven and the various stages above it:
They accomplish only the untainted first dhyāna;
all of them accomplish eight knowledges,
namely the seven previously mentioned plus the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
Regarding the three samādhis,
there may be none, two, or all three.
"None" refers to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) who have attained the contaminated first dhyāna.
Because it cannot be attained without samādhi.
Second, this refers to all the stages prior to the arising of the patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) for the noble ones.
If one relies on the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*), one achieves only the contaminated (*sāsrava*) first dhyāna.
If one accomplishes the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna based on the five higher stages,
they accomplish both the two samādhis,
namely emptiness and wishlessness.
The third refers to the arising of the patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*).

Within this context, from the patience regarding the dharma of cessation up to the knowledge of the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti-jñāna*), the first *dhyāna* achieved is as previously described.
At the stage of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna), one necessarily accomplishes both the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna.
In all stages above that subsequent knowledge of the path,
those born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world certainly accomplish both the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna.
Those born in the levels above the Ābhāsvara Heaven possess only the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna.
They all possess the three samādhis,
just as they possess the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna.
The same applies to all other cases as appropriate.
That is to say, just as it was explained regarding the attainment [of factors] by means of the first dhyāna in relation to the four dhyānas,
up to the three samādhis, so it is here.
Up to and including the fourth dhyāna,
one attains the four dhyānas;
up to and including the three samādhis, one achieves them as appropriate.
Whether they be ordinary worldlings or noble ones,
because it is acquired through the removal of defilements.
If it is because they are acquired at birth,
then whether they are with outflows or without outflows, non-existent or partial,
or complete, all such cases should be explained in detail.
There are seven types of persons (*pudgala*):

namely, those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), those liberated through resolute confidence (*śraddhādhimukta*), those attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), those who have realized the body (*kāyasākṣin*), those liberated through wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), and those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).

Question: Regarding those who follow by faith and the others, [how do they relate] to the four dhyānas associated with relish (*āsvādana*) and so forth, as well as the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*)?
How many are accomplished and how many are not accomplished?
Answer: For one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin), regarding the four dhyānas associated with relishing (āsvādana), there may be none, or one, two, three, or four.
"Non-existent" refers to those who have exhausted their craving for the form realm (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*); because they are free from passion at that time, [those factors] have all been abandoned.
"One" refers to those who have exhausted their craving for the Subhakṛtsna heaven but have not yet exhausted their craving for the higher realms;
they possess only the flavor (*āsvāda*) of the immediately superior level of dhyāna.
The second refers to one for whom craving for the Ābhāsvara realm has been exhausted, but craving for the higher realms has not yet been exhausted;
such a person possesses only the "taste" (āsvāda) belonging to the two higher dhyāna stages.
The third refers to one for whom craving for the Brahma-world has been exhausted, but craving for the higher realms has not yet been exhausted.
He achieves only the flavors of the three higher dhyāna stages.
Fourthly, one whose craving for the Brahma-world has not yet been exhausted achieves the flavors of all four dhyāna stages.
Because one who has not yet exhausted the defilements of a lower level will necessarily possess the "superior flavor" (adhimātra-rasa) of that level,
whereas one who has already exhausted the defilements of a lower level will necessarily not possess the "inferior flavor" (mṛdu-rasa) of that level;
thus, regarding the four pure dhyānas, they may be absent, or present as one, two, three, or all four.
"Non-possession" refers to one who has not yet exhausted sensual craving and has not yet attained any pure dhyānas.
"The first [category]" refers to one who has exhausted sensual craving but has not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms;
such a person accomplishes the purity of the lower stages.
The second refers to one for whom craving for the Brahma-world has been exhausted, but craving for the higher realms has not yet been exhausted;
such a person possesses only the pure [attainments] of the two lower stages.
The third refers to one for whom craving for the Ābhāsvara-realm has been exhausted, but craving for the higher realms has not yet been exhausted.
He achieves only the purity of the two lower stages.
Fourth, when craving for the Subhakṛtsna [heaven] is exhausted,
he fully achieves the purity of four stages.
One whose lower defilements are not yet exhausted will certainly not achieve the higher purity; however,
one whose upper defilements are already exhausted, even if their body remains in a lower realm,
will necessarily achieve the lower purity.
Because those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) necessarily reside in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), this statement is made:
regarding the four untainted dhyānas, they may possess none, one, two, three, or all four.
"None" refers to entering rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
In this context, some do not achieve it because they have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire;
others, though they have abandoned the defilements of desire, do not achieve it because they are unable to cultivate [the path].
The first refers to one who enters rightness-in-detachment (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the first dhyāna or the intermediate dhyāna.
They achieve the untainted [attainments] of the lower stage and none other,
because they have either not yet attained them or are unable to cultivate them.
The second case refers to those who, relying on the second dhyāna, enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
He accomplishes the untainted [attainments] of the two lower stages, but not others, as previously stated.
Thirdly, this refers to one who enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the third dhyāna;
he accomplishes the untainted [attainments] of the three lower stages.
It is not otherwise than as previously stated.
"The fourth" refers to entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the fourth dhyāna;
this is because one fully accomplishes the untainted (anāsrava) states of all four stages, having already attained them and being capable of cultivating them.
The path of seeing (darśana-mārga) necessarily does not cultivate the higher stages when based on a lower stage,
because it is the first attainment of the path. The untainted (anāsrava) [path],
however, when based on a higher stage, necessarily cultivates the lower stages, because it is autonomous and unconditioned by those levels.
Regarding the four formless attainments associated with craving for taste,
there may be one, two, three, or four [fetters].
"One" refers to one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
He has attained the flavor of the stage immediately above;
however, because he has not yet abandoned the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are two possibilities:
namely, that his craving for the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) is exhausted, while his craving for the higher stages is not yet exhausted.
He achieves the flavor of the two higher stages.
The third case refers to one for whom craving for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) has been exhausted, but craving for the higher [stages] has not yet been exhausted;
he achieves the flavor of the three higher stages.
The fourth refers to one whose craving for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) has not yet been exhausted.
Such a person fully accomplishes the flavors of four stages,
as previously explained.
Regarding the pure [attainments] of the four formless realms, there may be none, or one, two, three, or four.
"None" refers to those who have not yet exhausted craving for the form realm, because they have not yet attained any of the pure formless attainments.
"One" refers to those who have exhausted craving for the form realm but have not yet exhausted craving for the higher [realms].
He accomplishes the purity of the lower one stage.
The second case refers to one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite space but has not yet exhausted craving for the higher stages;
he accomplishes the purity of the lower two stages.
The third refers to one for whom craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) has been exhausted, but craving for the higher spheres has not yet been exhausted;
such a person accomplishes the pure [attainments] of the three lower stages.
The fourth refers to one for whom craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) has been exhausted; such a person fully accomplishes the pure [attainments] of all four stages.

Therefore, as previously stated, one does not possess any of the three untainted formless attainments because one lacks the path of vision; this is likewise true for those who follow by faith and those who follow by dharma.
Because these two types of individuals do not differ in terms of their path,
stage, meditative absorption, freedom from defilement, or basis,
they differ only in their faculties.
For those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), regarding the four dhyānas associated with relishing (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*),
there may be none, one, two, three, or all four.
"None" refers to those who have exhausted craving for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya*).
The first refers to one who has exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna realm but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The second refers to one who has exhausted craving for the Ābhāsvara realm but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The third refers to one who has exhausted craving for the Brahma-world but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The fourth refers to those who have not yet exhausted their craving for the Brahma-world;
they achieve [the meditative attainments], and the reasons for this are all as previously explained.
Regarding the four pure dhyānas, they may possess none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"Non-possession" refers to those whose craving for the realm of desire (*kāmarāga*) has not yet been exhausted.
This is because all those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) who have not yet exhausted their craving for the realm of desire have not yet attained [this state],
whereas all those born in the formless realm have already abandoned it.
The first refers to one who is born in the desire realm and has exhausted craving for the desire realm but has not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms;
or one who is born in the Brahma-world and has not yet exhausted craving for that world;
or one who is born in the Ābhāsvara heaven and has not yet exhausted craving for that world.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven], craving for that very place is not yet exhausted;
if one is born in the Bṛhatphala [heaven],
these two cases refer to being born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world.
When craving for the Brahma-world has been exhausted, but craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted,
if one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
then craving for that very realm has been exhausted, while craving for what is above it has not yet been exhausted.
If one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven], that very craving is exhausted.
The third case refers to those born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world who have exhausted their craving for the Ābhāsvara [heaven] but have not yet exhausted their craving for what is above it.
If one is born in the Ābhāsvara or Subhakṛtsna heavens and has exhausted craving for them, there are four cases;
that is, if one is born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world and has exhausted craving for the Subhakṛtsna heaven.
Among these, it is possible for faith-based liberation (*śraddhādhimukta*) to arise in all stages.
When wholesome contaminated dharmas arise in a higher stage, one necessarily abandons those of the lower stages;
therefore, it is possible to act as previously described.
Regarding the four uncontaminated dhyānas, there may be none, or one, two, three, or all four.
"Non-existence" refers to those who have not yet exhausted sensual craving.
"The first" refers to those who have exhausted sensual craving but have not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms.
"The second" refers to those who have exhausted craving for the Brahma-world but have not yet exhausted craving for the higher realms.
The third refers to one who has exhausted craving for the Ābhāsvara realm but has not yet exhausted craving for what is above it.
The fourth refers to one who has exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna realm.
This is stated with reference to those who attain the fruits and become free from defilement through gradual progression.
Alternatively, this refers to those who enter into rightness and the state beyond corruption based on whichever superior dhyāna they have attained. If it were not so,
[the following would apply].
This passage should not be stated in such a manner.
For there are those who have exhausted craving for the Brahma-world but do not possess two [attainments],
and those who have exhausted craving for the Ābhāsvara realm but do not possess three.
Because one who has exhausted craving for the Śubhakṛtsna realm does not possess four [attainments]. What are they?
They are the attainments of detachment from the Brahma-world up to the Śubhakṛtsna realm.
One enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the first dhyāna up to the third dhyāna;
however, at the time of the knowledge of the path-type (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), one does not possess the two to four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas.
Alternatively, although one does not possess two up to four [knowledges] at the time of the path-knowledge of types (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) as described here,
one will certainly possess them before long thereafter.
At that time, accomplishment is also said to occur;
this means that shortly after the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna), when the path of superior fruit is necessarily about to arise, one cultivates those [attainments] because of it.
Regarding the four formless attainments associated with relishing (āsvādana-samprayukta), one may cultivate one, two, three, or all four.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Regarding the four pure formless attainments (*ārūpya*), there may be none, one, two, three, or all four;
and so on, as explained at length.
The detailed explanation herein is as in the case of the dhyānas;
it should be understood that regarding the three untainted formless attainments,
there may be none, one, two, or all three.
"Non-existence" refers to one whose craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) is not yet exhausted.
"The first" refers to one whose craving for the realm of form is exhausted, but whose craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted.
"The second" refers to one whose craving for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is exhausted, but whose craving for the higher realms is not yet exhausted.
The third refers to the exhaustion of craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
This is also explained here with reference to those who attain the fruit and become free from defilement through gradual stages;
otherwise, it would not be so.
This text should not be explained in such a manner;
for there are those who have exhausted craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*) but do not achieve the first [attainment],
and those who have exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) but do not achieve the second.
Because one who has exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness does not accomplish three [factors]. Which are they?
They are those who, having become detached from the realm of form up to the sphere of infinite consciousness, enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Because at the time of the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) of the ultimate path, one does not yet possess the untainted (anāsrava) formless [attainments].
Alternatively, since that superior fruit-path will necessarily arise before long and one will then possess them, it is said that they are possessed even at that time.
The same applies to those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
These two types of persons are identical in terms of their path,
their stage, their meditative absorption, their freedom from passion, and their basis.
In all cases, there is no difference except for the distinction of the faculties (*indriya*).
One who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*) the four dhyānas associated with relishing (*āsvādana-samprayukta*) does not at all possess the pure (*śuddha*) four dhyānas.
"Sometimes none, sometimes one, two, three, or four," and so on,
as explained at length;
[the practitioner] achieves all four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas.
Regarding the four formless attainments associated with flavor (*sāsvāda*),
one is accomplished and three are not.
Regarding the pure (*śuddha*) four formless attainments, either one or all four are accomplished.
The first refers to those born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The fourth refers to those born in the desire realm or the form realm;
they possess all three untainted (anāsrava) formless attainments.
One liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta) does not possess any of the four dhyānas associated with relish (āsvādana).
Regarding the pure (śuddha) four dhyānas, they may have none, or one, two, three, or all four;
this is explained at length, up to... [and so forth].
One achieves all four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas.
One does not achieve any of the four formless attainments associated with relishing (āsvādana).
Regarding the four pure (śuddha) formless attainments, one may achieve one, two, three, or four.
...and so forth, as extensively explained.
They possess all three untainted formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
Those liberated through both parts (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*) do not possess any of the four dhyānas associated with relishing (*āsvādana-samprayukta*).
Regarding the four pure dhyānas, they may be absent, or one, two, three, or all four may be present;
this is explained at length.
Regarding the four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas, one achieves them all.
One does not possess any of the four formless attainments associated with relish (*āsvādana*).
Regarding the four pure (*śuddha*) formless attainments, one possesses either one or all four;
"one" refers to being born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The fourth refers to those born in the desire realm or the form realm;
they are endowed with all three types of untainted (anāsrava) formless attainments.
The detailed explanation herein should be understood as previously stated.
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School,
Fascicle 168; Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra,
Fascicle 169.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, who received the Imperial Decree. In the seventh section, the *Samgraha-vastu* (The Compendium), within the third sub-section, the fourth part: Is there anyone who accomplishes the four dhyānas associated with relish (*āsvādana-samprayukta*), which are neither pure (*śuddha*) nor untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to one whose craving for the desire realm has not yet been exhausted, because such a person has not yet attained any of the wholesome dharmas belonging to the four dhyānas.
Since there is neither the pure nor the untainted, it is for this reason that one accomplishes the four dhyānas associated with relishing (*āsvādana*).
Is it possible to accomplish the four pure dhyānas without them being either associated with relishing or untainted?
Answer: There are.
That is to say, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world who has exhausted craving for the form realm.
Because they are an ordinary person, there is no untainted [craving]; because they have exhausted craving for the form realm, there is no craving associated with relish (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*).
One born in the desire realm achieves the pure four dhyānas because craving for the Brahma-world has been exhausted.
Is there anyone who achieves the untainted (anāsrava) four dhyānas that are neither associated with relish (āsvādana) nor pure?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, when noble ones (*ārya*) are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because those noble ones are born there, they possess the four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas.
Because one is born in those [higher] realms, there is no "pure" (*śuddhaka*) attainment associated with the flavorless (*āsvādana*).

Question: If one has exhausted craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*) and enters into rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the first dhyāna, or the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), [what occurs]?
Alternatively, one may refine the faculties to become a "one-attained-by-vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Having attained that fruit, they do not give rise to the path of superior fruit;
at the end of their life, they are reborn in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Since they do not all achieve the three higher uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dhyānas,
why are four mentioned?
The answer is that some say:
This is said with reference to those who attain the fruit through gradual progression, and not others.
Some say that after one who has entered the state of rightness and departure from birth attains the fruit of non-returning, [they proceed further].
One must necessarily give rise to the path of superior fruit and cultivate the four untainted dhyānas before being born in the higher realms;
otherwise, there would be noble ones born in the Bṛhatphala heaven or above who do not possess the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
If that were so, it would contradict what is stated in the *Daśamukha-śāstra*.
Regarding those who, being of the type of "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*), refine their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) and become "attainers through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), some say:
Having attained that fruit, they will also necessarily give rise to the path of superior fruit as previously described;
after cultivating the four untainted dhyānas, they will then pass away and be reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Some say:
At the time of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*), one simultaneously cultivates the higher untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas; therefore, there is no fault.
Is it possible to possess the pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) four dhyānas without possessing those associated with relishing (*āsvādana-samprayukta*)?
Answer: There is.
It refers to a noble one born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world who has exhausted attachment to the form realm.

Question: If one enters the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the non-attainment concentration (anāgamya-samādhi) after exhausting attachment to the form realm, [is this possible]?
During the fifteen moments of mind, one does not accomplish untainted dhyāna.
Upon reaching the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*), one accomplishes only one;
that is, up to the point where, relying on the third dhyāna, one enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Question: During the interval of the sixteen moments of mind, one only accomplishes three [knowledges];
why, then, does it say four? Answer:
Some say that this is stated in reference to those who attain the fruit through gradual cultivation and become free from defilements.

Some say that once one has attained the fruit, before long one must necessarily bring forth the path of superior fruit (viśeṣamārga) so that it manifests and cultivate the higher untainted states (anāsrava). Therefore,
although [the higher paths] have not yet been accomplished at the time of the sixteen moments of mind, [they are nonetheless considered attained].
Since one must necessarily attain them, it is also said that they are accomplished. Is there anyone who accomplishes two or three of the others?
Answer: No; this refers to one who accomplishes the four dhyānas associated with tasting (*āsvādana*).
Because one necessarily does not accomplish the four pure (*śuddha*) or four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas.
Is there anyone who does not accomplish the four dhyānas associated with relish (*āsvādana*), yet neither accomplishes the pure nor the untainted?
Answer: There is.
This refers to a noble one born in the desire realm who has exhausted craving for the Brahma world and the form realm.
This is explained as the sixth case in the previous discussion on accomplishment.
Is there anyone who does not accomplish the four pure dhyānas, yet neither those associated with relish nor those that are untainted?
Answer: No. Is there anyone who does not possess the untainted (anāsrava) four dhyānas, yet neither possesses those associated with relishing (āsvādana-saṃprayukta) nor those that are pure (śuddha)?
Answer: No.
This is all as explained previously regarding the absence of the fourth and fifth phrases in the section on accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Is there anyone who does not accomplish the flavor-associated and pure (*śuddha*) four dhyānas, yet does not fail to accomplish the untainted (*anāsrava*) ones?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, when noble ones (*ārya*) are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This is explained as in the third phrase of the previous section on "possession" (*samanvāgama*).
Is there anyone who has not attained the flavor-associated and untainted (*anāsrava*) four dhyānas, yet has attained the pure (*śuddha*) ones?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, a being born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*) who has exhausted craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*).
This is as explained in the second phrase of the previous section on accomplishment.
Is there anyone who does not accomplish the pure and untainted four dhyānas, yet does not fail to accomplish those associated with relishing (*āsvādana*)?
Answer: There is.
This refers to the fact that sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) has not been exhausted;
this is explained by the first phrase in the preceding section on "attainment" (*samanvāgama*).
Is it possible for one to be non-possessed of the four dhyānas associated with relish (*āsvādana*), the pure (*śuddha*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: There are.
Specifically, those who are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because they are ordinary beings, they lack the untainted (*anāsrava*) four dhyānas.
Because one is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are no tainted (sāsrava) or pure (anāsrava) dhyānas of the four meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
Is it possible to possess the four formless attainments associated with attachment (sāmiṣa) that are neither pure nor untainted?
Answer: Yes, it is possible.
This means that because craving for form has not been exhausted, one has not yet attained any wholesome dharmas pertaining to the four formless realms.
Since there is neither pure nor untainted [attainment], for this very reason, one accomplishes the four formless attainments associated with relishing (*āsvādana*).
Is there anyone who has attained the pure and untainted four formless attainments that are not associated with relishing?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, an Arhat born in the desire realm, the form realm, or the sphere of infinite space.
Because they are Arhats, they lack the meditative attainments associated with relishing (*āsvādana-samprayukta*).
Because they are born in that stage, they fully possess the four pure (*śuddha*) and three untainted (*anāsrava*) attainments.
Is it possible for them to possess any others?
Answer: There is none.

Among these, there is no second case of one who accomplishes only the four purities, because there must necessarily be either the untainted (anāsrava) or the tainted (sāsrava), or both. Thus, there is no third case.
Only those who possess the three untainted [attainments] necessarily possess the pure [attainment], and thus there is no fourth alternative.
Those who possess the four types of mundane purity do not possess the untainted, and there is no fifth alternative.
Regarding the accomplishment of the four tastes and three untainted [factors] but not the pure ones:
this is because when one accomplishes the four tastes, one necessarily does not accomplish the four pure ones or the three untainted ones.
It is precisely for this reason that there is no seventh category.
Is there anyone who does not accomplish the flavor-associated (*sāsrava*) four formless attainments, yet neither the pure (*anāsrava*) nor the untainted (*anāsrava*) ones?
Answer: There is.
Namely, an Arhat born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
This is as explained in the sixth phrase of the previous section on accomplishment.
Is there anyone who does not accomplish the pure and untainted formless attainments, yet does not [fail to] accomplish those associated with relishing?
Answer: There is.
This refers to one who has not yet exhausted craving for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*).
This is explained as in the first phrase of the preceding section on "possession" (*samanvāgama*).
Is it possible that there is no other [craving] unaccomplished?
Answer: None.
In this context, there is no one who lacks only the four pure [faculties], because such a person necessarily also lacks the untainted [faculties].
There are none who do not achieve the three untainted [attainments].
This is explained by the fourth alternative (catuskoṭi) as it does not occur in the section on achievement.
There are none who do not achieve the four types of mundane purity that are not untainted.
As in the section on accomplishment (*siddhi*),
there is no third phrase for the explanation;
that which is not accomplished consists of the four tastes (*rasa*) and the three untainted (*anāsrava*) states, which are not pure (*aśubha*).
As explained in the second clause regarding "accomplishment," there is no case where all three are not accomplished,
because at least one or two of the three must necessarily be accomplished.
Regarding this attainment or non-attainment of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*),
one who possesses attainment is said to "possess" them;
one who possesses non-attainment is said to "not possess" them.
Furthermore, one who possesses non-attainment is said to be "non-attained.
It should be understood that one who possesses attainment is said to be "not non-attained.
Is it possible to attain the four dhyānas associated with relish (*āsvādana*) that are neither pure (*śuddha*) nor untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: Yes.
That is, when one who has exhausted craving for the form realm falls away due to the arising of the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) of the desire realm.
When one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm,
those who regress therein include both ordinary beings and noble ones; that is,
when either those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) give rise to the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of that realm.
Regarding "possessing all four tastes that are neither pure nor untainted":
this refers only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who, at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*), possess all four tastes that are neither pure nor untainted.
Is there anyone who attains the four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas that are neither associated with relish (*āsvādanasamprayukta*) nor pure (*śuddha*)?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, one who enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the fourth dhyāna.
When one attains the fruit of arhatship— specifically,
regarding the phrase "at the time of entering into rightness and departure from birth"—
this refers to the moment when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) arises.
At that time, the untainted (anāsrava) [attainments] of the four dhyānas— which were previously non-existent—
are now acquired; they are neither "tasting" (āsvādya) nor "pure" (śuddha).
Regarding the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship:
it refers to the moment when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises.
At that time, all four untainted dhyānas are relinquished.
And one attains that which is neither flavor nor purity;
even though one purifies the four dhyānas,
there are those who attain it at that time as well.
However, as for their types, there were previously none that were not abandoned;
now, one merely acquires a small portion of them.
Among the pure four dhyānas, there is not a single name that is acquired.
How much more so for four?
Therefore, it is said that they are neither flavorful nor pure. Some say:
This is stated with reference to one who attains the fruit of arhatship while being born in the formless realm.
Question: Is it not also the case that when training the faculties (indriya), one likewise relinquishes all four untainted dhyānas and acquires them anew?
Why is it not explained? One should know that when something ought to be explained but is not,
this indicates that the meaning is incomplete.
Some say that herein,
the beginning and the end are mentioned briefly to illustrate the middle; therefore,
they are not stated in full detail.
Some say that both what is abandoned and what is attained therein belong to the category of the learner (śaikṣa),
and are not entirely distinct categories.
For this reason, it is not mentioned.
For the same reason, the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) is also not mentioned.
Is there anything else that is attained?
Answer: No.
In this context, there is no second phrase;
one attains only the four purities, and the sixth phrase does not exist.
Regarding the attainment of the four pure, untainted [attainments] that are not associated with relish (*asāsvāda*):
this is because there is no simultaneous attainment of all four purities.
Question: At the time of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*trividhājñāna*) during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) based on the fourth dhyāna...
Furthermore, when one attains the fruit of arhatship,
does one not fully attain the four purities as well as the untainted state?
Why, then, are they not mentioned?
The answer is: At that time, he had already previously attained and not yet relinquished all four pure dhyānas;
although he now attains them again in part, there is not even one instance among the four pure dhyānas that constitutes a new attainment.
How much less so for four?
For this reason, it is not stated;
there is no fourth alternative.
One attains the four flavors that are pure but not untainted;
furthermore, there is no fifth category,
as one may attain the four flavors that are both untainted and pure.
Regarding "not pure":
because when one attains the four tastes, one necessarily does not attain the four purities or the four untainted states (anāsrava).
For this very reason, there is also no seventh category.
Is there any relinquishing of the four dhyānas associated with relish that is neither pure nor outflow-free? Answer: No.
Because there is no simultaneous abandonment of the defilements of four stages.
Is it possible to abandon the pure (*śuddha*) fourth dhyāna without abandoning that which is associated with relish (*āsvādana*)?
Is it not untainted?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, an ordinary person who has exhausted craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm.
When one falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm;
or when one dies in the desire realm or the Brahma-world and is reborn in the formless realm—
in these cases, those reborn in the formless realm include both ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
Is there a case where one relinquishes the pure and untainted four dhyānas, but not those associated with relishing?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, when a noble one who has exhausted craving for the Sphere of Total Purity (Śubhakṛtsna) falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the Desire Realm,
is there any other [defilement] that is abandoned?
Answer: No.
In this context, there is no third alternative;
it refers exclusively to those who abandon the four [obstacles] and are free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
This is because at the time of relinquishment, it may not be relinquished entirely;
or because it may be reacquired at that time;
or because it is relinquished together with the pure [meditation].
Because when one abandons [the path] upon attaining the fruit, it is immediately regained.
There are no fourth, fifth, or seventh cases,
because there is no simultaneous abandonment of the four types of attachment (*āsvāda*).
Is there anyone who attains the four formless attainments associated with relish (*āsvādanasamprayukta*), which are neither pure (*śuddha*) nor outflow-free (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: There is.
This refers to when an Arhat falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire or form realms;
at that time, they fully acquire the four flavors—neither-pure-nor-untainted.
Is it possible to acquire the three untainted formless attainments?
Is it not associated with flavor (*āsvādana*) and not pure (*śuddha*)?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, at the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship.
As explained previously regarding the dhyānas, is there anything else that can be attained?
Answer: No.
In this regard, there is no second alternative;
that is, one can only obtain four purities,
because it is impossible to obtain all four simultaneously.

There is no fourth, fifth, or seventh phrase because when one attains the four flavors (*āsvāda*), one necessarily does not attain the four purities (*śuddhaka*) or the three untainted states (*anāsrava*); thus, there is no sixth phrase.
One who attains the four purities and the three untainted states does not possess those associated with flavor (*āsvāda-samprayukta*).
This is because, at the time of attaining the three untainted [attainments],
although one also partially attains the pure [attainments],
they are not designated as "attained."
This is exactly as explained previously.
Is it possible to abandon the four formless attainments associated with relish (*āsvādanasamprayukta*) that are neither pure (*śuddha*) nor outflow-free (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: No. This is because there is no simultaneous abandonment of the defilements of the four stages.
Is it possible to abandon the pure [attainments] of the four formless realms?
Is it not associated with flavor (arūpa-rasa) and not untainted (anāsrava)?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, when an ordinary person who has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire or form realms,
can they abandon the pure and untainted [attainments] of the four formless spheres?
Is it not associated with relish?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, when a noble one has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
When one falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm or the form realm, is there any other [defilement] that is abandoned? Answer: No.
In this context, there is no third alternative;
it refers exclusively to those who abandon the three untainted [roots],
as explained in the section on the dhyānas.
There are no fourth, fifth, or seventh cases,
because there is no simultaneous abandonment of the four types of attachment (*āsvāda*).
This applies to the acquisition and relinquishment of these dhyānas and formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Complete acquisition is called "attainment" (prāpti);
complete non-acquisition is called "non-attainment" (aprāpti);
and complete relinquishment is called "relinquishment" (tyāga).
It should be understood that "not abandoning at all" means non-abandonment.
Is it possible to fall back from the four dhyānas associated with relish?
Is it neither pure nor untainted? Answer: No.
This is because there is retrogression regarding meritorious dharmas, but not regarding dharmas that are faults.
Furthermore, because there is no simultaneous abandonment of the four types of attachment (*āsvāda*).
Is it possible to fall away from the pure (*śuddhaka*) four dhyānas without [falling away from] those associated with attachment (*sāsvāda*) or those that are untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: Yes.
It refers to an ordinary person who, having exhausted craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm, falls away when the fetters of the desire realm arise.
Is there any falling away from the pure and untainted four dhyānas that is not associated with relishing?
Answer: Yes, there is.
That is to say, when a noble one who has exhausted craving for the Sphere of Total Purity (Śubhakṛtsna) falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the Desire Realm,
is there any other [defilement] from which they fall away?
Answer: No.
In this context, there is no third alternative;
it refers exclusively to those who have regressed from the untainted (anāsrava) four dhyānas.
Either because they may regress together with the pure [attainments],
or because they do not regress entirely,
or because they regain that stage even at the time of regression.
There are no fourth, fifth, or seventh cases because there is no falling away from the "taste" (āsvāda) [of meditative attainment].
There is no case of falling away from only the four untainted (anāsrava) attainments.
Is it possible to fall away from the four formless attainments associated with taste?
"Is it neither pure nor untainted? Answer:
"No, as previously stated."
Is there any falling away from the pure (śuddhaka) four formless attainments that is neither associated with relishing (āsvādana-samprayukta) nor untainted (anāsrava)?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, when an ordinary person who has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire or form realms,
is it possible for them to fall away from the pure or untainted [attainments] of the four formless spheres?
Is it not associated with relishing?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, when a noble one has exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness.
When one falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm or the form realm, is there any other [falling away]? Answer: No.
In this context, there is no third alternative;
for those who have only regressed from the untainted (anāsrava) states of the three formless realms do so either alone or together with the tainted (śuddha) states.
Alternatively, because there is no complete retrogression,
the fourth, fifth, and seventh cases do not exist,
as explained in the section on the dhyānas.
Question: Is there any case of falling away from untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyāna that is not [falling away] from the pure (*śuddha*)?
Answer: There is.
This refers to when a trainee (*śaikṣa*) falls away due to the arising of formless-sphere fetters (*ārūpya-bandhana*).
At that time, they fall away from that untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) which serves as the antidote, because it is not the pure [meditative absorption].
Question: Is there any case where one does not arise with formless-sphere fetters?
Is it the case that one may regress from untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyāna without it being pure (*śuddha*)?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, when one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) and has not yet reached the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
One does not regress from what has been attained by giving rise to afflictions (*kleśa*).
At the time of the path of uninterrupted liberation (*ānantarya-vimukti-mārga*), one asks:

Is there any case where one regresses from untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) without giving rise to the fetters (*paryavasthāna*), yet it is not the pure (*śuddha*) [meditative concentration]?
Answer: There are.

These are those previously mentioned, as well as those who, while training their faculties (*indriya*) in the stage of "not-yet-reached" (*anāgamya*) or the stage of "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), do not give rise to afflictions yet still fall away.
When the path of uninterrupted liberation (*ānantarya-vimukti-mārga*) is attained,
it is asked: Is there any case where one falls away from the untainted (*anāsrava*) merits subsumed under the seven stages,
yet these [merits] are not purified?
Answer: Yes.

It refers to when one has partially separated from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, yet falls away due to the arising of the fetters belonging to the category abandoned by that stage.
Question: Is there a case where one attains both the pure (*śuddhaka*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas by means of relinquishing only the untainted dhyāna?
Answer: There is;
namely, at the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship.
Question: Is there a case where one relinquishes both the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), yet acquires only the untainted?
Answer: There is.
This refers to when an arhat falls away due to the arising of the fetters of the formless realm (*ārūpya-bandhana*).
Question: Is there any case where untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyāna and pure (*śuddha*) dhyāna are acquired simultaneously, yet discarded separately?
Answer: There is.
This refers to the attainment of the fruit of arhatship;
the attainment of the fruit of non-returner based on dhyāna;
and the time when a learner (śaikṣa) refines their faculties.
Question: Is there a case where pure dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava) are acquired simultaneously, yet discarded separately?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to when a noble one (ārya) becomes detached from the defilements of their own level.
And when one is born into a higher stage.
Question: Is there any case where pure and untainted meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are acquired at different times or abandoned simultaneously?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, when a noble one, having become detached from the defilements of their own level, falls away by giving rise to the fetters of a lower level.
Question: Is there any case where both the pure (śuddha) and the untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas are acquired simultaneously and abandoned simultaneously?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, when a noble one who has already become detached from the defilements of a lower stage regresses by giving rise to the fetters of that lower stage.
This is as in the case of the question regarding dhyāna.
The same should be applied to the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) accordingly.
Furthermore, there are briefly twenty-three types of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), as previously described.
That is to say, there are twelve types of dhyāna:
namely, four associated with relishing (āsvādana), four pure (śuddha), and four untainted (anāsrava).
There are eleven types of formless attainment (ārūpya): namely, four associated with relishing, four pure, and three untainted.
If these twenty-three are established in detail, they constitute sixty-five attainments (*samāpatti*);
that is, the original twenty-three plus the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The eight liberations,
the eight bases of mastery,
and the ten totalities.
The six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) are the basis for the knowledge of non-contention (araṇā) and the knowledge resulting from resolve (praṇidhijñāna).
Question: Among these sixty-five [factors], how many take only their own level as their object?
How many take only the lower stage as their object?
How many take both their own stage and the lower stage as their objects?
How many take both their own stage and the higher stage as their objects?
How many take all stages as their objects?
Answer: Ten attainments take only their own stage as their objects;
namely, the eight associated with the flavors of pleasure (*sāsvāda*).
And the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) of infinite space and infinite consciousness;
these twenty-four attainments (samāpatti) take only the lower stages as their objects—
namely, the four immeasurables (apramāṇa).
The first three liberations,
the eight bases of mastery,
and the first eight totalities.
And regarding the absence of contention (*araṇā*):
some maintain that for those who wish to bring about the absence of contention, it takes the desire and form realms as its object;
[in this case], the absence of contention itself is excluded.
The seven attainments take their own stage and lower stages as objects;
that is to say, the two unhindered knowledges of phenomena and expression,
which serve as the basis for the five supernormal powers.
The nine attainments take as their objects both their own level and the levels above;
namely, the three pure and untainted formless attainments,
as well as the liberations of the lower three formless realms.
This is said with reference to those that have outflows (*sāsrava*) as their object.
The twelve attainments (*samāpatti*) take all stages (*bhūmi*) as their objects;

that is to say, they serve as the basis for the pure and untainted (*anāsrava*) four dhyānas, the meaning-discernment (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) and dharma-discernment (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) two analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), and the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhi-jñāna*).
This is also stated based solely on those that take contaminated (*sāsrava*) objects as their conditions.
If it were stated based on both contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) objects,
then there would be twenty-three attainments that take all stages as their objects.
This refers to the aforementioned twelve, plus eleven formless states—namely, the pure and untainted formless attainments, as well as the formless liberations.
Question: If an attainment takes whichever flavor-associated dhyāna as its cause, [what is the result?]
Is that very [attainment] its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
Furthermore, whatever dhyāna associated with relish (*āsvādana-samprayukta*) serves as the immediately preceding condition for a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*),
does that very same one serve as its cause (*hetu*)?
Answer: All meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) take that very same flavor-associated dhyāna as their cause;
they likewise take it as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
There are also meditative attainments that take that flavor-associated dhyāna as their immediately preceding condition.
Yet it does not take that as its cause.

Within this context, there are sixteen cases where an attainment takes the first dhyāna associated with relish (*āsvādanasamprayukta*) as its immediate antecedent (*samanantara*), yet does not take it as its cause.
That is to say: the pure first dhyāna,
the four immeasurables,
and the first two liberations.
The first four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are the basis for the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
If the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is that of the second dhyāna associated with attachment (*āsvādanā-samprayukta*), it serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
There are seventeen that do not take those as their cause:
namely, the pure second dhyāna and the four immeasurables.
The first two liberations,
the first four bases of mastery,
and the basis for the five supernormal powers.
And the pure first dhyāna.
If an attainment has the third dhyāna associated with relishing as its immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya),
yet does not take it as its cause (hetu-pratyaya), there are ten such cases.
That is to say, the pure third dhyāna,
the three immeasurables,
and the basis for the five supernormal powers.
And for the purification of the second dhyāna:
if an attainment has the fourth dhyāna associated with relishing as its immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya),
yet does not take it as its cause (hetu-pratyaya), there are twenty-three such cases.
That is to say: the pure fourth dhyāna,
the three immeasurables,
and the pure liberations.
The latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the first eight bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are the basis for the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
And the purification of the third dhyāna.

Question: If an attainment takes any [state] associated with relish (*āsvādana*) in the formless realm as its cause, does it take that very same state as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
If an attainment is immediately preceded by any formless state associated with a particular relish (*āsvādana*), does it necessarily have that very state as its cause?
Answer: All attainments have whatever formless state associated with relish they are immediately preceded by as their cause.
Furthermore, that very state serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
There are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) for which that flavor-associated formless attainment serves as the equal-and-immediate condition,
yet it does not serve as their cause (*hetu*).
Among these, there are four cases where an attainment associated with attachment to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) serves as its immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
yet does not serve as its cause (*hetu-pratyaya*);
namely, the pure (*śuddhaka*) sphere of infinite space.
That very liberation is that very universal base (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
as well as the pure fourth dhyāna.
If the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) has the consciousness-infinity-base associated with relishing (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*) as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
There are five instances where that [perception] is not taken as a cause:
namely, the pure consciousness of the base of infinite space, its corresponding liberation,
and its corresponding totality-sphere (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
And the pure [attainment] of the sphere of infinite space—
that is liberation.
If the meditative attainment is associated with relish, it has the sphere of nothingness as its immediately preceding condition.
There are four that do not take those as their cause:
namely, the pure sphere of nothingness,
its corresponding liberation, and the pure sphere of infinite consciousness.
That itself is liberation.
There are four cases where an attainment associated with relishing serves as the immediately preceding condition for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
yet does not serve as its cause.
That is to say: the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is its corresponding liberation;
and the pure sphere of nothingness.
That is liberation itself.
Question: If a meditative attainment takes any pure dhyāna as its cause, does it immediately follow that very same [dhyāna] as its equal-and-immediate condition?
If a meditative attainment (samāpatti) follows immediately after any pure dhyāna, does it take that very dhyāna as its cause?
Answer: All meditative attainments take that pure dhyāna as their cause.
Furthermore, that very [attainment] serves as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
There are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) for which that pure dhyāna serves as the immediately preceding condition,
yet it does not serve as their cause (*hetu*).
Among these, there are six cases where an attainment takes the pure first dhyāna as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) but does not take it as its cause (*hetu-pratyaya*):
namely, the [attainments] associated with the "taste" (*āsvādana*) of that same level and the untainted (*anāsrava*) attainments.
Regarding the pure and untainted second and third dhyānas:
there are eight cases where an attainment takes the pure second dhyāna as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
yet does not take it as its cause (*hetu-pratyaya*).
This refers to the flavor-associated, the untainted,
and the pure-untainted states of one's own level, as well as the pure and untainted first, third, and fourth dhyānas.
If an attainment has the pure third dhyāna as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), [it arises].
There are eleven [states] that do not take those as their cause:
namely, the flavor-associated and untainted states of one’s own level;
and the pure and untainted first, second, and fourth dhyānas.
The sphere of infinite space is that very liberation.
There are twelve cases where an attainment has the pure fourth dhyāna as its immediate antecedent, yet does not have it as its cause.
This refers to the liberation consisting of the associated-with-taste states of one’s own level,
as well as the pure and untainted second and third dhyānas,
and the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness.
Question: If a meditative attainment (samāpatti) takes any pure formless state as its cause, does it take that very same state as its immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya)?
Furthermore, if a meditative attainment takes any pure formless state as its immediately preceding condition, [does it take that as its cause?]
Is it that very [attainment] which serves as its cause?
Answer: Each meditative attainment (samāpatti) takes those pure formless attainments as its cause, and likewise takes them as its immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
There are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that take those pure formless states as their immediate antecedents (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
yet do not take them as their cause (*hetu*).
Among these, there are attainments that take the pure sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) as their immediate antecedent.
There are twelve that do not take those as their cause:
namely, the flavor-associated and untainted [states] of their own level,
as well as the pure and untainted third and fourth dhyānas.
The sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness;
these are the two liberations of those two spheres.

If an attainment takes the pure consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) but does not take it as its cause (*hetu-pratyaya*), there are twelve such cases:
namely, those associated with the "savoring" (*āsvādana*) of one's own level and the untainted (*anāsrava*) states.
As well as the pure and untainted fourth dhyāna,
the sphere of infinite space,
and the sphere of nothingness.
That is liberation from those two stages;
it is the purification of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
which is itself that liberation.
There are ten cases where an attainment has the pure sphere of nothingness as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) but does not have it as its cause (*hetu*):
namely, the contaminated states associated with relish (*āsvādana-samprayukta*) of its own level and the untainted (*anāsrava*) states.
And the pure and untainted [attainments] of the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness;
these are themselves liberations.
[Also] the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
That is liberation itself.
