There are seven cases where an attainment takes the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
yet does not take it as its cause (*hetu*).
That is to say: the flavor-associated [consciousness] of its own level,
as well as the pure and untainted consciousnesses of the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness,
and the Sphere of Nothingness.
This refers to liberation in those two states.
Question: If an attainment takes any given uncontaminated dhyāna as its cause, does it immediately follow that very same dhyāna as its equal-and-immediate condition?

If one enters meditative attainment (samāpatti) by means of any given untainted dhyāna as its immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), does that very same dhyāna serve as its cause (hetu)?
Answer: For each individual untainted dhyāna, one should formulate four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna:
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that have the untainted first dhyāna as their cause,
but not as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This consists of seven:
namely, the untainted fourth dhyāna and the three formless attainments.
And the three formless liberations.
There are nineteen attainments that have the untainted first dhyāna as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
but not as their cause (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That is to say: the pure first, second, and third dhyānas;
the four immeasurables;
and the first two liberations.
The first four bases of mastery,
the two analytical knowledges,
and the four supports for penetration.
There are attainments that have the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna as their cause,
and for which there are also seven immediate antecedents (*samanantara*);
namely, the untainted first, second, and third dhyānas.
The two analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),
the supernormal power of knowing others' minds, and the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) are their bases.
There are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that do not have the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna as their cause.
Nor is it an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
There are thirty-two of these, namely:
the eight pure fourth dhyānas associated with the flavor of enjoyment (*āsvādana-samprayukta*).
The four formless attainments,
the three liberations,
and the latter four bases of mastery.
The ten totalities (daśa-kṛtsnāyatana) are the basis for the knowledge resulting from the absence of conflict (araṇā-praṇidhi-jñāna).
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the untainted (anāsrava) second dhyāna:
There are attainments that have the untainted second dhyāna as their cause,
but not as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
These are six in number.
This refers to the three untainted formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and the three formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*).

There are meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) for which the second untainted dhyāna serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), but not as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
These consist of nineteen:
namely, the four pure dhyānas,
the four immeasurables, and the first two liberations.
The first four spheres of mastery,
the analytical knowledge of phenomena,
and the four bases of power are the supports for these [powers].
There are attainments that have the untainted second dhyāna as both their cause and their immediate antecedent;
these are eight in number.
This refers to the four untainted dhyānas,
the two analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid),
and the supernormal powers of knowing the minds of others and the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-abhijñā) as their bases.
There are attainments that do not have the untainted second dhyāna as their cause,
nor as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). These number thirty-two.
This refers to the eight meditative attainments associated with the flavor of the sublime, the four pure formless absorptions,
three liberations,
and the final four bases of mastery.
The ten spheres of totality,
the analytical knowledge of language,
and the basis for the absence of conflict and the knowledge resulting from aspiration.
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the untainted third dhyāna:
there are meditative attainments that have the untainted third dhyāna as their cause,
but not as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
There are four of these:
namely, the untainted consciousness of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of nothingness, [the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception].
Regarding liberation from those two stages,

there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) for which the untainted (*anāsrava*) third dhyāna serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) but not as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
These consist of thirteen types.
That is to say: the four pure dhyānas,
the sphere of infinite space,
and three of the immeasurables.
The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) is the basis for the four [analytical knowledges].
There is an attainment that has the untainted third dhyāna as its cause.
It is also equal in terms of immediate succession (*samanantara*).
This consists of eleven types, namely: the four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas.
The sphere of infinite space;
that is liberation.
The two analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
Regarding the bases for the supernormal powers of knowing others' minds and the exhaustion of outflows,
there are meditative attainments that do not take the untainted third dhyāna as their cause,
nor as their immediately preceding condition.
There are thirty-eight of these: namely, the eight associated with the flavor of existence (*sāsrava*),
and the three pure (*anāsrava*) formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
The four immeasurables of joy,
the five liberations,
and the eight bases of mastery.
The ten bases of totality,
the analytical knowledge of language,
and the basis for the absence of conflict and the knowledge resulting from aspiration.
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the untainted (*anāsrava*) fourth dhyāna:
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that have the untainted fourth dhyāna as their cause,
but not as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
There are three of these:
namely, the untainted first dhyāna and the sphere of nothingness.
And regarding the liberation of the sphere of nothingness,
there are twenty-eight attainments that have the untainted fourth dhyāna as their immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya),
but not as their cause (hetu-pratyaya).
That is to say: the pure second, third, and fourth dhyānas;
the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness;
and the three immeasurables.
The pure liberation,
the latter four bases of mastery,
and the first eight totalities.

The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) is the basis for the four types of unhindered penetration, the absence of conflict (araṇā), and the knowledge resulting from resolve (praṇidhijñāna).
It has as its cause the meditative attainments (samāpatti) based on the untainted fourth dhyāna.
It is also an equal-and-immediate [condition].
This consists of eleven types, namely:
the second, third, and fourth uncontaminated (anāsrava) dhyānas.
The sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness are themselves those liberations;
these are the two analytical knowledges of non-obstruction.
Regarding the bases for the supernormal powers of knowing others' minds and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*),
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that do not take the untainted (*anāsrava*) fourth dhyāna as their cause,
nor as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This consists of twenty-three types:
namely, the eight associated with the flavor of enjoyment (*āsvādana-samprayukta*) and the pure (*śuddha*) first dhyāna.
The sphere of nothingness,
the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and immeasurable joy.
The four liberations,
the first four bases of mastery,
and the final two totalities.
The basis for the analytical knowledge of language.
Question: If an attainment (samāpatti) takes whichever uncontaminated (anāsrava) formless state as its cause, does it immediately follow that very state as its immediate antecedent (samanantara)?

If, in the case of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), whatever untainted (*anāsrava*) formless attainment serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), does that very same one necessarily serve as its cause (*hetu*)?
Answer: With respect to each individual untainted formless attainment, one should formulate four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding the fourfold formulation based on the untainted (anāsrava) sphere of infinite space:
there are meditative attainments (samāpatti) that have the untainted sphere of infinite space as their cause,
but not as their immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya).
This is threefold:
namely, the untainted first and second dhyānas,
and that which serves as the basis for the supernormal power of knowing others' minds.

There are six types of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) but not as their cause (*hetupratyaya*).
These are the pure (*śuddha*) third and fourth dhyānas.
The lower three formless attainments,
as well as the sphere of infinite space and the [space] universal base.
There are attainments that have the untainted (anāsrava) sphere of infinite space as their cause and also as their immediate antecedent;
these are eleven in number.
This refers to the untainted third and fourth dhyānas,
the three formless attainments,
and the liberations of the lower three formless realms.
The two unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are the basis for the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).
There are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that do not have the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of infinite space as their cause.
Nor are they equal-and-immediate [conditions].
These consist of forty-five, namely:
eight associated with the pleasant.
The pure first and second dhyānas,
the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and the four immeasurables.
The five liberations,
the eight bases of mastery,
and the nine spheres of totality.
The two types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*),
the four [applications of mindfulness], and the basis for the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā*) and the knowledge resulting from resolution (*praṇidhijñāna*).
Regarding the formulation of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) based on the uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*):
There are attainments that have the untainted consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space as their cause,
but not as their immediate antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). There are four such [attainments].
This refers to the untainted (anāsrava) first, second, and third dhyānas.
The basis for the supernormal power of knowing others' minds consists of meditative attainments (samāpatti) that are untainted;
it takes the consciousness-infinity-sphere (vijñānānantyāyatana) as its immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), not as its cause (hetupratyaya).
This consists of seven:
namely, the pure fourth dhyāna and the four formless attainments.

The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the totality-sphere of infinite consciousness have meditative attainments that take the untainted (anāsrava) sphere of infinite consciousness as their cause.
It is also an equal-and-immediate [condition].
This consists of ten types, namely: the untainted fourth dhyāna.
The three formless attainments,
the liberations of the lower three formless realms,
and the two analytical knowledges.
Regarding the basis for the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-abhijñā),
there are meditative attainments (samāpatti) that do not take the untainted consciousness of the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana) as their cause,
nor as their immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
There are forty-four of these:
namely, the eight pure meditative attainments associated with the flavor of enjoyment— the first, second, and third dhyānas—
and the four immeasurables.
The four liberations,
the eight bases of mastery,
and the nine universal bases.
Regarding the two unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),
the fourfold penetration (*pratisaraṇa*), and the basis for the knowledge resulting from vows (*praṇidhijñāna*):
there are four propositions concerning that which relies on the untainted sphere of nothingness (*anāsrava-ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
There are attainments that have the untainted sphere of nothingness as their cause,
but not as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). There are five such cases.
This refers to the four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas and the basis for the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (paracittajñāna).

There is an attainment (samāpatti) which takes the untainted sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) as its immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), but not as its cause (hetu-pratyaya).
There are five of these:
namely, the four pure formless attainments and the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There are attainments that have the untainted sphere of nothingness as their cause and also as their immediately preceding condition;
these are nine in number.
That is to say: the three untainted formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*),
the liberations (*vimokṣa*) of the lower three formless realms,
and the two analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Regarding the basis for the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*):
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that do not take the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as their cause,
nor as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
There are forty-six of these:
namely, the eight pure dhyānas associated with the flavor of enjoyment,
and the four immeasurables.
The four liberations,
the eight bases of mastery,
and the ten totalities.

The two types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), the fourfold [mastery], and the basis for the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā*) and the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*).
Question: If one enters meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), by what kind of relishing-associated dhyāna (*āsvādanāsaṃprayukta-dhyāna*) is it caused?
Is that very [object] taken as the focal object?
Furthermore, if an attainment takes any dhyāna associated with relish as its focal object,
does it take that very [dhyāna] as its cause?
Answer: All meditative attainments (samāpatti) take that very same flavor-associated dhyāna as their cause, and likewise take it as their object.
There are also meditative attainments that take that flavor-associated dhyāna as their object.
Yet it does not take that as its cause.
Among these, if an attainment takes the first dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) as its object but does not take it as its cause,
there are thirteen such cases.
This refers to the pure and untainted four dhyānas,

which serve as the basis for the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid) and the three supernormal powers— clairaudience, reading others' minds, and recollection of past lives— as well as the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna).
Some maintain that the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) also takes the form realm as its object;
they state there are fourteen,
adding the absence of conflict.
Of these explanations, the first is superior,
as in the case of the first dhyāna associated with the flavor [of meditative attainment].
The same applies to the second, third, and fourth dhyānas associated with attachment (*sāsvāda*).
Question: If an attainment (*samāpatti*) takes whichever formless realm associated with attachment as its cause, does it likewise take that very same realm as its object (*ālambana*)?
If a meditative attainment takes whichever formless state associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) as its object, does it then take that very same state as its cause?
Answer: All meditative attainments take those respective formless states associated with relishing as their causes.
Furthermore, there are meditative attainments that take those flavor-associated formless states as their object,
yet do not take them as their cause.
Among these, there are fifteen cases where an attainment takes the flavor-associated sphere of infinite space as its object,
yet does not have it as its cause.
That is to say: the four pure and untainted dhyānas;
the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid); and the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayābhijñā).
The basis for the knowledge of aspiration is the pure, untainted sphere of infinite space;
it is precisely that liberation-sphere of totality.
If attainments take the consciousness-infinity-sphere associated with relishing as their object but do not have it as their cause,
there are eighteen such cases.
This refers to the pure and untainted four dhyānas,

which serve as the basis for the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid), the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayābhijñā), and the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna).
The pure, untainted sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness;
these are the liberations of that very sphere of infinite consciousness.
Regarding the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*): if an attainment has the sphere of nothingness associated with attachment as its object,
yet does not take that [sphere] as its cause.
There are twenty:
namely, the four pure and untainted dhyānas and the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid).
The supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya-abhijñā) is the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhi-jñāna);
it is pure and untainted (anāsrava), and pertains to the three lower formless attainments (ārūpya).
And as for the liberations of the three lower formless realms:
if an attainment takes the associated-with-taste sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its object,
yet does not take it as its cause.
There are twenty-two;
that is, the previous twenty plus the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and its liberation.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Volume One Hundred and Sixty-nine;
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume One Hundred and Seventy.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (Samāpatti-skandha), Part Three of the Summary of Contents (Saṃgraha-nikāya), Section Five. Question: If one enters meditative attainment (samāpatti), by what pure dhyāna as its cause does it follow?
Is that very [state] taken as its object?
Furthermore, if an attainment takes any pure dhyāna as its object,
does it take that very [dhyāna] as its cause?
Answer: Based on each individual pure dhyāna, one should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the first pure dhyāna:
There are fifteen attainments that have the pure first dhyāna as their cause,
but do not take it as their object.
That is to say: the four immeasurables,
the two liberations,
and the four bases of mastery.
The two unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),
the three supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and their bases;
there is an attainment that takes the pure first dhyāna as its object.
And there are nine that are not causes,
namely: the first dhyāna associated with the taste of meditative attainment.
The three higher pure dhyānas and the four untainted dhyānas are the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).
There are attainments that take the pure first dhyāna as their cause and also as their object;
these are six in number.
That is to say: the pure first dhyāna,
the two unhindered analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid),
and the basis for the supernormal powers (abhijñā).
There are thirty-five attainments that do not have the pure first dhyāna as their cause, nor as their object.
That is to say: the seven associated with the flavors,
the four pure formless attainments,
and the three untainted formless attainments.
The latter four spheres of mastery,
the six liberations,
and the ten totalities.
Regarding the basis for the absence of contention (*araṇā*),
concerning the four alternatives based on the pure second dhyāna:
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that have the pure second dhyāna as their cause.
It is not an object of perception (*ālambana*).
There are fourteen of these,
namely, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
The two liberations,
the four bases of mastery,
and the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
Regarding the basis for the three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*):
there is an attainment (*samāpatti*) that takes the pure second dhyāna as its object,
yet it does not have it as its cause.
There are nine of these:
namely, the first dhyāna associated with relish,
and the pure first, third, and fourth dhyānas.
The four untainted meditative absorptions (anāsrava-dhyāna) are the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna).
There are also attainments (samāpatti) that have the pure second dhyāna as their cause.
It also functions as an object of focus (ālambana).
This has six aspects, namely: the pure second dhyāna.
The two unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),
the three supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and their basis;
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that do not take the pure second dhyāna as their cause.
Nor is it an object of perception (*ālambana*).
This consists of thirty-six [factors],
namely, seven associated with the flavors (*rasa*).
The four pure formless attainments,
the three untainted formless attainments,
and the latter four spheres of mastery.
The six liberations,
the ten spheres of totality,
and the absence of conflict.
Regarding the basis for the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*),
concerning the fourfold formulation based on the pure third dhyāna:
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that have the pure third dhyāna as their cause.
It is not an object of focus.
There are seven of these,
namely, the three immeasurables.
The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) is the basis for the three supernormal knowledges;
there is an attainment that takes the pure third dhyāna as its object.
And not as a cause.
There are nine of these, namely:
those associated with the flavor of one's own level.
The first, second, and fourth meditative absorptions (dhyāna) when purified,
as well as the four untainted (anāsrava) meditative absorptions,
are the bases for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna).
There are attainments that have the pure third dhyāna as their cause and also take it as their object;
these are six in number.
That is to say: the pure third dhyāna,
the two unhindered analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid),
and the basis for the supernormal powers (abhijñā).
There are forty-three attainments that do not have the pure third dhyāna as their cause, nor as their object.
That is to say: the seven associated with the flavors,
the four pure formless attainments,
and the three untainted formless attainments.
The four immeasurables, including joy;
the eight bases of mastery;
and the eight liberations.
The ten spheres of totality,
the absence of conflict,
and the basis for the analytical knowledge of language.
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the pure fourth dhyāna:
there are meditative attainments (samāpatti) that have the pure fourth dhyāna as their cause,
but do not take it as their object.
These consist of twenty-one:
namely, the three immeasurables and the pure liberations.
The latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
the first eight totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
and the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
The third [type] is the basis for the three [types of] non-contention (*araṇā*).
There is an attainment that takes the pure fourth dhyāna as its object.
And there are eight that are not causes,
namely: the fourth dhyāna associated with the taste of attachment (āsvādanasamprayukta).
The pure attainments of the lower three dhyānas and the untainted (anāsrava) attainments of the four dhyānas have the pure fourth dhyāna as their cause.
It also serves as an object of focus.
This has seven aspects, namely: the pure fourth dhyāna.
The two analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid),
the three supernormal powers (abhijñā),

and the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) are based upon meditative attainments (samāpatti); however, there are meditative attainments that do not have the pure fourth dhyāna as their cause.
Nor are they objects of cognition.
These consist of twenty-nine,
namely, the seven associated with the flavors (*rasa*).
The four pure formless attainments,
the three untainted formless attainments,
and the immeasurable joy.
The seven liberations,
the first four spheres of mastery,
and the last two spheres of totality.
The basis for the analytical knowledge of language.
Question: If a meditative attainment takes any pure formless realm as its cause, does it necessarily take that same realm as its object?
If one enters a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) taking any pure formless state (*śuddhaka ārūpya*) as its object, does that [attainment] have that [object] as its cause?
Answer: The three lower pure formless states do.
If an attainment takes something as its cause,
it also takes that very thing as its object; however,
there are attainments that take something as their object [without taking it as their cause].
Yet, one does not take that as a cause for the purification of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; regarding this,
one should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
Among these, there are eleven cases where an attainment takes the pure sphere of infinite space as its object,
yet does not have that [sphere] as its cause.
This refers to the pure and untainted four dhyānas,
which correspond to the "savoring" (āsvādana) of their own stages and serve as the basis for the untainted knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhijñāna).
If the meditative attainments take the pure consciousness of the sphere of infinite space as their object but do not have it as their cause,
there are fourteen such cases.
This refers to the pure and untainted four dhyānas,
the untainted first two formless attainments,
and the pure sphere of infinite space.
That very liberation is the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) associated with the savor of its own stage;
if the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) takes the pure sphere of nothingness (*śuddha-ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as its object.
Those that do not take those as causes number seventeen;
namely, the four pure and untainted dhyānas.
The three formless attainments (ārūpya) that are untainted (anāsrava);
the pure (śuddha) first two formless attainments;
and the liberations (vimokṣa) of the first two formless attainments.
Regarding the fourfold logical analysis based on the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the support for the wish-fulfilling knowledge associated with its own level:
there are meditative attainments that have the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their cause.
It is not an object of focus.
There is one such [liberation]:
namely, the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa).
There are attainments that take the pure (śuddha) sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their object,
yet because of this there are not nineteen;
namely, the four pure and untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas.
The three formless [attainments] and the three formless liberations are associated with the relish of their own respective stages.

The basis for the knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) consists of meditative attainments (samāpatti) that take the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their cause and also as their object.
This consists of five:
namely, the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
as well as those two deliverances and the two analytical knowledges.
Regarding the basis for the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*),
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that do not take the pure (*śuddha*) sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as their cause,
nor as their object.
These consist of forty:
namely, the seven associated with the flavors, the four immeasurables,
and the first three liberations.
The eight bases of mastery,
the ten totalities,
and the two analytical knowledges.
It is without conflict and is the basis for the five supernormal powers.
Question: If one enters meditative attainment (samāpatti), by what kind of untainted dhyāna (anāsrava-dhyāna) is it caused?
Is that [attainment] taken as its object? Furthermore,
whatever uncontaminated dhyāna an attainment takes as its object,
does it take that very same one as its cause?
Answer: All meditative attainments (samāpatti) take those untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas as their cause and likewise take them as their object (ālambana).
There are also meditative attainments that take those untainted dhyānas as their object.
Yet it does not take that as its cause.
Within this context, if an attainment takes the untainted first dhyāna as its object,
yet does not take that as its cause:
There are ten;
namely, the four pure dhyānas and the four formless attainments.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
liberation; and the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration.
As it is with the untainted first dhyāna, so it is with the untainted second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
Question: If an attainment takes whichever untainted formless state as its cause, [what follows]?
Is that very [attainment] what serves as its object?
Furthermore, whatever uncontaminated formless attainment serves as the object of a meditative equipoise,
does that very same [attainment] serve as its cause?
Answer: In dependence on each of the untainted formless attainments (*ārūpya*), one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding the formulation of four propositions in dependence on the untainted sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*):
there is an attainment that takes the untainted sphere of infinite space as its cause.
It is not an object of cognition.
This consists of one [type],
namely, that which serves as the basis for the supernormal power of knowing others' minds.
There are attainments that take the untainted (anāsrava) sphere of infinite space as their object,
yet for which it is not the cause.
These are ten in number.
That is to say: the four pure dhyānas,
the four formless attainments,
and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

The basis for the knowledge resulting from the power of vows regarding liberation consists of meditative attainments that take the untainted sphere of infinite space as their cause and also as their object.
These consist of thirteen:
namely, the four untainted dhyānas and the three formless attainments.
The three lower formless liberations,
the two analytical knowledges,
and the basis for the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
There are meditative attainments that do not take the untainted (anāsrava) sphere of infinite space as their cause,
nor as their object;
these number forty-one.
That is to say: the eight [attainments] associated with the flavor of the sublime, the four immeasurables,
the four liberations,
and the eight bases of mastery.
The ten bases of totality,
the two analytical knowledges,
and the absence of conflict.
The basis for the fourfold [attainment] is as follows:
just as with the untainted sphere of infinite space,
so it is with the untainted spheres of infinite consciousness and nothingness.

Question: If an attainment (samāpatti) takes whichever dhyāna associated with relish (*āsvādana*) as its immediate antecedent (*samanantara*), does it necessarily take that same [dhyāna] as its object (*ālambana*)?
Conversely, if an attainment takes whichever dhyāna associated with relish as its object, does it necessarily take that as its immediate antecedent?
Is it the case that those [preceding states] are immediately contiguous (*samanantara*) to them?
Answer: With respect to each meditative absorption associated with attachment (*āsvādanasamprayukta-dhyāna*), one should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding the first meditative absorption associated with attachment, the four alternatives are as follows:
There are thirteen attainments that have the first dhyāna associated with relish as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
but not as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
That is to say: the four immeasurables,
the first two liberations,
and the first four bases of mastery.
Regarding the basis for the three types of penetration (*pratisaṃvid*):
there is an attainment (*samāpatti*) that takes the first dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*) as its object,
yet it does not serve as its immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This consists of ten:
namely, the three pure higher dhyānas and the four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas.
The analytical knowledge of meaning,
the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows,
and the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration.
There are attainments that take the first dhyāna associated with relishing as their immediate antecedent (samanantara) and also as their object (ālambana).
There are four such [attainments].
That is to say, they are based on the two types of meditative attainments— the flavor-associated (*āsvādana-samprayukta*) and the pure (*śuddha*)— of their own level.
There are meditative attainments that do not take the flavor-associated first dhyāna as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Nor are they objects of focus.
These consist of thirty-eight, namely:
the seven associated with the flavors, the pure [attainments], and the four formless [attainments].
The three untainted formless attainments,
the six liberations,
and the last four bases of mastery.
The ten spheres of totality,
the absence of conflict,
and the basis for the three analytical knowledges.
Regarding the formulation of the four propositions based on the second dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*):
there is an attainment whose immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is the second dhyāna associated with relishing,
yet it does not have that as its object (*ālambana*).
These consist of thirteen:
namely, the four immeasurables and the first two liberations.
The first four bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) serve as the basis for three [of the higher attainments].
There is an equipoise that takes the second dhyāna associated with relishing (āsvādana-samprayukta) as its object.
It is not, however, an equal-and-immediate [condition].
This consists of nine types, namely:
the pure [attainments] of the two higher dhyānas.
The four untainted dhyānas,
the analytical knowledge of meaning,
and the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.

The basis for the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) consists of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that take the second dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādanā-saṃprayukta*) as their immediate antecedent (*samanantara*) and also as their object (*ālambana*).
This consists of five:
namely, the associated-with-savor (sāsvāda) of its own level,
and the pure (śuddha) first and second dhyānas.
Regarding the second point, the basis for the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*):
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that do not take the second dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādana-samprayukta*) as their immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
nor as their object (*ālambana*).
There are thirty-eight of these:
namely, the seven associated with the flavors (sāsvāda),
the four pure (śuddha) formless attainments, and the remaining twenty-seven.
The three untainted formless attainments,
the six liberations,
and the latter four bases of mastery.
The ten bases of totality,
the absence of conflict,
and the basis for the three analytical knowledges.
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the third dhyāna associated with attachment (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*):
there are attainments (*samāpatti*) that take the third dhyāna associated with attachment as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
but do not have it as their object (*ālambana*).
This consists of six:
namely, the three immeasurables and the three bases for their attainment.
There are attainments that take the third dhyāna associated with relish as their object,
but do not have it as their immediate antecedent;
these are nine in number.
That is to say: the two pure dhyānas,
the four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas,
and the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid).
The supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayābhijñā) is the basis for the knowledge resulting from prayer (praṇidhijñāna).
There is an attainment (samāpatti) that takes the third dhyāna associated with attachment as its immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
It also functions as an object of focus (*ālambana*).
There are five such [objects]:
namely, the flavor-attendant (*āsvādana-samprayukta*) and the pure (*śuddha*) second and third dhyānas of its own stage.
Regarding the basis for the two supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*):
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that do not take the third dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) as their immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
nor as their object (*ālambana*).
There are forty-five of these:
namely, the seven associated with the flavors (sāsvāda),
and the four pure (śuddha) formless attainments.
The three untainted formless attainments,
the immeasurable joy,
and the eight liberations.
The eight bases of mastery,
the ten totalities,
and the absence of conflict.
Regarding the basis for the three analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),
concerning the formulation of four propositions based on the fourth dhyāna associated with relish (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*):
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that take the fourth dhyāna associated with relish as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
And these are not objects of focus.
There are nineteen of them,
namely, the three immeasurables.
The pure liberation,
the latter four bases of mastery,
and the first eight totalities.
Regarding the basis for the three types of supernormal knowledge:
there are meditative attainments that take the fourth dhyāna associated with relishing as their object,
yet do not have it as their immediate antecedent condition.
There are nine of these:
namely, the two pure dhyānas and the four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas.
The analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid), the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayābhijñā),
and the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna).
There are attainments that take the fourth dhyāna associated with relishing as their immediate antecedent (samanantara) and also as their object (ālambana);
these are fivefold.
That is to say: the flavor-associated [meditative attainments] of their own level,
the pure third and fourth dhyānas,
and the two bases for supernormal powers.

There are attainments for which the fourth dhyāna associated with relishing (āsvādana) is neither the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) nor the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
These consist of thirty-two.
That is to say: the seven associated with the flavors,
the four pure formless attainments,
and the three untainted formless attainments.
The four immeasurables of joy,
the seven liberations,
and the first four bases of mastery.
The latter two universal bases,
the absence of conflict,
and the three analytical knowledges are their supports.

Question: If an attainment (samāpatti) takes whichever formless state associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) as its immediate antecedent (*samanantara*), does it then take that very same state as its object (*ālambana*)?
Conversely, if an attainment takes whichever formless state associated with relishing as its object, [does it take that as its immediate antecedent?]
Is it the case that those very states serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?

Answer: For all meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), whichever flavor-associated formless state serves as the immediately preceding condition, that same state also serves as its object of focus (*ālambana*).

There are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that take those flavor-associated (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*) formless states as their object (*ālambana*) but do not take them as their immediate antecedent (*samanantara*).
Among these, there are attainments that take the flavor-associated sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) as their object.
There are eleven [minds] that do not take those as their equal-and-immediate conditions;
namely, the three pure dhyānas.
The four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas,
the untainted [states] of their own respective stages,
and the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid).
The supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows is the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration.
If the meditative attainment has the consciousness associated with relish in the sphere of infinite consciousness as its object.
There are thirteen cases in which those [minds] do not serve as equal-and-immediate conditions (samanantara-pratyaya),
namely: the pure (śuddha) and the untainted (anāsrava).
The four dhyānas,
the first two untainted formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*),
and the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) are the bases [of these].
If the meditative attainments take the "associated-with-savor" (āsvādana-samprayukta) sphere of nothingness as their object,
yet do not have it as their immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya),
there are sixteen such cases.
That is to say: the pure and untainted [states],
the four dhyānas,
and the pure sphere of infinite space.
That very liberation consists of the three untainted formless attainments;
it is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) is the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*).

If one enters meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) by taking the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception associated with relishing (*āsvādana-saṃprayukta*) as its object, yet does not take it as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), [then the aforementioned applies].
There are eighteen,
namely: the pure and the untainted [states] within the four dhyānas.
The first two pure [attainments] and the formless [attainments] are those very liberations;
the three formless [attainments] are untainted (*anāsrava*).
The analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid), the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayābhijñā),
and the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna).

Question: If a meditative attainment (samāpatti) takes whichever pure dhyāna as its immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), does it necessarily take that same [dhyāna] as its object (ālambana)?
Conversely, if a meditative attainment takes whichever pure dhyāna as its object, does it necessarily take that as its immediately preceding condition?
Is it that very [state] which serves as its equal-and-immediate condition?
Answer: In relation to each and every pure dhyāna, one should formulate four propositions.
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the pure first dhyāna:
There are fifteen attainments that have the pure first dhyāna as their immediate antecedent (samanantara),
but do not take it as their object (ālambana).
That is to say: the four immeasurables,
the first two liberations,
and the first four bases of mastery.
The two unimpeded analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid),
the three supernormal powers (abhijñā) as their basis,
and the meditative attainments (samāpatti) that take the pure first dhyāna as their object.
It is not, however, an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This consists of three types:
namely, the pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) fourth dhyāna.

The basis for the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) consists of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that take the pure first dhyāna as their immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and also as their object (*ālambana*).
There are thirteen of these:
namely, those associated with the flavor of one's own level,
as well as the pure and untainted [attainments] of the first three dhyānas.
The two analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid),
the three supernormal powers (abhijñā), and their bases;
there are meditative attainments (samāpatti) that do not take the pure first dhyāna as their immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
Nor is it an object of perception (*ālambana*).
There are thirty-five of these,
namely, seven associated with the flavors (*rasa*).
The four pure formless attainments,
the three untainted formless attainments,
and the six liberations.
The four bases of mastery,
the ten totalities,
and the basis for the absence of conflict.
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the pure second dhyāna:
there are attainments that take the pure second dhyāna as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
but do not take it as their object (*ālambana*).
These consist of fourteen:
namely, the four immeasurables and the first two liberations.
The first four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*),
and the basis for the three supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
There is one attainment that takes the pure second dhyāna as its object,
but does not serve as its immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya). This is one case.

This refers to the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) that serves as the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*). It takes the pure second dhyāna as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and also as its object (*ālambana*).
These consist of fourteen:
namely, those associated with the flavor of one's own level,
as well as the pure and the untainted.
The four dhyānas,
the two unhindered analytical knowledges,
and the basis for the [three] supernormal powers.
There are attainments that do not take the pure second dhyāna as their immediate antecedent (samanantara) nor as their object (ālambana);
these number thirty-six.
That is to say: the seven [attainments] associated with the flavors, the four pure formless attainments,
the three untainted formless attainments,
and the six liberations.
The four bases of mastery,
the ten totalities,
and the absence of conflict.
Regarding the basis for the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*),
concerning the four propositions based on the pure third dhyāna:
there is an attainment that has the pure third dhyāna as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
And it is not an object of focus.
This consists of ten types, namely: the three pure immeasurables.
The untainted sphere of infinite space is itself that liberation;
it is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid).
Regarding the basis for the three supernormal knowledges:
there is an attainment that takes the pure third dhyāna as its object,
yet it does not serve as its immediate antecedent condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
There is one such case:
namely, that which serves as the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna).
There is an attainment (samāpatti) that takes the pure third dhyāna as its immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
It also functions as an object of focus (*ālambana*).
There are fourteen such [objects], namely:
those associated with the flavor (*āsvādana*) of its own level (*svabhūmi*).
As well as the pure and untainted [states],
the four dhyānas,
and the two analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
Regarding the basis for the three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*):
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that do not take the pure third dhyāna as their immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
nor as their object (*ālambana*).
These consist of forty:
namely, the seven associated with the flavors (sāsvāda),
the pure (śuddha) states, and the three higher formless attainments (ārūpya).
The two higher formless attainments that are untainted,
the immeasurable joy,
and the seven liberations.
The eight bases of mastery,
the ten totalities,
and the absence of conflict.
Regarding the basis for the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*),
concerning the formulation of the four propositions based on the pure fourth dhyāna:
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that have the pure fourth dhyāna as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
These are not objects of focus.
There are twenty-seven of them,
namely the three immeasurables.
The pure liberation,
the latter four spheres of mastery,
and the first eight totalities.
The absence of contention,
the analytical knowledge of phenomena,
and the basis for the three supernormal knowledges.
The pure and untainted [attainments] of the first two formless realms are themselves those liberations;
there are also meditative attainments that take the pure fourth dhyāna as their object.
It is not, however, an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This [condition] is of two kinds:
namely, the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
In the first dhyāna,
there is an attainment that takes the pure fourth dhyāna as its immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) and also as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
There are thirteen of these:
namely, those associated with the flavor of one's own stage,
as well as the pure and the untainted.
The three higher dhyānas,
the two analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), and the knowledge resulting from prayer (praṇidhijñāna).
Regarding the basis for the three types of higher knowledge:
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that do not take the pure fourth dhyāna as their immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
nor as their object (*ālambana*).
There are twenty-three of these:
namely, the seven associated with the flavors (sāsvāda),
the pure (śuddha) [attainments], and the two higher formless [attainments].
In the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) superior [state], there is one formless [attainment],
the immeasurable joy (*muditā*),
and the five liberations (*vimokṣa*).
The first four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the last two totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are the bases for the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
Question: If a meditative attainment (samāpatti) takes whichever pure formless state as its immediate antecedent (samanantara), does it necessarily take that same state as its object (ālambana)?
Or, if a meditative attainment takes whichever pure formless state as its object, [does it necessarily take that as its immediate antecedent]?
Is it that very [state] which serves as its equal-and-immediate condition?
Answer: For each and every pure formless attainment, one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the pure Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*):
There are six attainments that take the pure Sphere of Infinite Space as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
but not as their object (*ālambana*).
That is to say, the pure and untainted consciousnesses of the Sphere of Infinite Space and the Sphere of Nothingness;
these are themselves the deliverances.
There are attainments that take the pure sphere of infinite space as their object,
but do not have it as their immediate antecedent; these are fivefold.
This refers to the pure and untainted first and second dhyānas,
which serve as the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna).
There is an attainment whose immediate antecedent (samanantara) is the pure sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana).
It also functions as an object of focus (ālambana).
This consists of twelve types, namely:
those associated with the flavor (āsvādana) of its own level.
And those that are pure and untainted,
as well as the two higher dhyānas and the sphere of infinite space.
That is liberation,
the spheres of totality,
and the two analytical knowledges.
Regarding the basis for the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*):
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that do not take the pure sphere of infinite space (*śuddha-ākāśānantyāyatana*) as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
nor as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
There are forty-two of these:
namely, the seven associated with the flavors (āsvādana),
and the pure (śuddha) sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
The four immeasurables,
the five liberations,
and the eight bases of mastery.
The nine bases of totality,
the four analytical knowledges,
and the absence of conflict.
Regarding the basis for the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*),
concerning the formulation of the four propositions based on the pure consciousness-infinity sphere (*viśuddha-vijñānānantyāyatana*):
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that take the pure consciousness-infinity sphere as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
And it is not an object of cognition.
This consists of five types, namely:
the pure and the untainted.
The sphere of nothingness,
the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and those two liberations.
There are attainments that take the pure consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space as their object,
yet do not have it as their immediate antecedent;
these are seven in number.
That is to say, it is pure and untainted,
belonging to the first three dhyānas,
and serves as the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration.
There are attainments that take the pure consciousness-infinity sphere as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and also as their object (*ālambana*).
These consist of thirteen [types].
This refers to the fourth dhyāna associated with the flavor of its own stage,
as well as the pure and the untainted [dhyānas].
The first two formless attainments,
as well as the liberations of the first two formless attainments,
and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The bases of totality,
the two analytical knowledges,
and the basis for the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
There are forty attainments that do not take the pure consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
nor as their object (*ālambana*).
That is to say: the seven associated with the flavors,
the four immeasurables,
and the four liberations.
The eight bases of mastery,
the nine bases of totality,
and the two analytical knowledges.
It is without dispute and is the basis for the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the pure sphere of nothingness (*śuddhākiṃcanyāyatana*):
There are attainments that take the pure sphere of nothingness as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
but not as their object (*ālambana*).
These are of two kinds.
This refers to the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
which is itself that liberation.
There is also an attainment that takes the pure sphere of nothingness as its object.
It is not, however, an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This consists of nine types:
namely, the four pure and untainted dhyānas.

The basis for the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) is an attainment that takes the pure sphere of nothingness (*śuddha-ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as its immediate antecedent (*samanantara*) and also as its object (*ālambana*).
There are thirteen of these:
namely, the [meditative attainments] associated with the flavor of one's own level,
as well as the pure and untainted [attainments] of the first three formless realms.
These are the three liberations,
the two analytical knowledges,
and the basis for the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows.

There are attainments for which the pure sphere of nothingness (*śuddhākiṃcanyāyatana*) is neither the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) nor the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
There are forty-one such cases.
That is to say: the seven associated with the flavors,
the four immeasurables,
and the four liberations.
The eight bases of mastery,
the ten totalities,
and the two analytical knowledges.
Regarding the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) as the basis for the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*):
there are four propositions concerning its reliance on the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*śuddhā naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
There is one meditative attainment that has the pure (śuddha) sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its immediately preceding condition (samanantara),
but not as its object (ālambana).

That is to say, there is an attainment of the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhavimokṣa*) which takes the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*śuddhākiṃcanyāyatana*) as its object,
yet does not stand in a relation of immediate succession (*samanantarapratyaya*) to it.
This consists of twelve [factors]:
namely, the pure and untainted [states] of the four dhyānas.
The sphere of infinite space,
as well as the liberation of the sphere of infinite space,
are the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration.

There are attainments for which the pure (śuddha) sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception serves both as the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) and as the object-condition (ālambana).
These consist of twelve [attainments].
This refers to the flavor-associated [attainments] of their own level,
as well as the pure [attainments] of the three higher formless realms;
these are precisely those three liberations.
The two higher formless attainments, the two analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid),
and the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya-abhijñā) are the bases [of these qualities]. They are untainted (anāsrava).
There are forty attainments that do not take the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
nor as their object (*ālambana*).
That is to say: the seven associated with the flavors,
the four immeasurables,
and the three liberations.
The eight bases of mastery,
the ten totalities,
and the two analytical knowledges.
It is without conflict and is the basis for the five supernormal powers.
Question: If one enters meditative attainment, by which uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dhyāna does it serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
Is that which serves as the object of focus also its immediate antecedent?
Furthermore, whichever uncontaminated dhyāna a meditative attainment takes as its object,
is that very same one its immediate antecedent?
Answer: In dependence upon each and every untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyāna, one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding the formulation of four propositions in dependence upon the first untainted dhyāna:
there are attainments (*samāpatti*) for which the first untainted dhyāna serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
These are not objects of focus.
There are sixteen of them,
namely, the four immeasurables.
The first two liberations,
the first four bases of mastery,
and the two analytical knowledges.
Regarding the basis for the fourfold penetration (*catuḥ-pratisaṃvid*):
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna as their object (*ālambana*),
yet do not stand in a relation of immediate succession (*samanantara*).
This consists of fourteen [factors],
namely: the pure and the untainted [factors] of the fourth dhyāna.
The four pure formless attainments;
the three untainted formless attainments;
the four formless [realms].
Liberation. It is the basis for the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).
There is an attainment whose immediate antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is the untainted first dhyāna.
It also functions as an object of focus (ālambana).
This consists of ten types, namely:
the pure (śubha) and the untainted (anāsrava).
The first three dhyānas,
the two types of unimpeded knowledge (pratisaṃvid),
and the basis for the two supernormal powers (abhijñā).
There are twenty-five attainments that do not take the untainted first dhyāna as their immediate antecedent (samanantara) nor as their object (ālambana).
That is to say: the eight meditative attainments associated with the flavor of the sublime, the two liberations,
and the latter four spheres of mastery.
Regarding the ten universal bases (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*) as the basis for the absence of contention (*araṇā*),
there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*) based on the untainted (*anāsrava*) second dhyāna.
There are fifteen attainments that have the untainted second dhyāna as their immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya),
but do not take it as their object (ālambana).
That is to say: the four immeasurables,
the first two liberations,
and the first four bases of mastery.
The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) is the basis for the four [analytical knowledges].
There is an attainment that takes the untainted second dhyāna as its object.
And not as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). These consist of twelve:
namely, the four pure formless attainments (*anāsrava ārūpyasamāpatti*).
The three untainted formless attainments,
the four formless liberations,
and the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration.
There are attainments that take the untainted second dhyāna as both their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and their object (*ālambana*).
These consist of twelve types, namely:
the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The four dhyānas,
the two types of unhindered knowledge,
and the basis for the two supernormal powers.
There are twenty-six attainments for which the untainted second dhyāna is neither the immediately preceding condition nor the object-condition.
That is to say: the eight liberations associated with the flavor of the beautiful, the two deliverances,
and the latter four bases of mastery.
The ten totalities,
the absence of contention,
and the basis for the analytical knowledge of language.
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the untainted third dhyāna:
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) for which the untainted third dhyāna serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
but not as an object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
This consists of eight:
namely, the three immeasurables and the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid).
Regarding the basis for the fourfold penetration:
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that take the untainted third dhyāna as their object (*ālambana*),
yet do not have it as their immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This consists of nine:
namely, the three pure formless attainments,
which are themselves the three liberations.
The two higher formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) that are untainted (anāsrava) serve as the basis for the Knowledge of Vows (praṇidhijñāna).
There is an equipoise (samāpatti) that takes the third dhyāna, being untainted, as its immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya).
It also functions as an object of focus (ālambana).
There are fifteen such [objects], namely:
the pure (śuddha) and the untainted (anāsrava).
The four dhyānas,
the sphere of infinite space,
and the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.
The two unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the basis for the two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
There are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that do not take the untainted (*anāsrava*) third dhyāna as their immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Nor is it an object of perception.
This consists of thirty-three [types],
namely, eight associated with the flavorful (rasa).
The four immeasurables of joy,
the four liberations,
and the eight bases of mastery.
The ten totalities,
the absence of conflict,
and the basis for the analytical knowledge of language.
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the untainted (anāsrava) fourth dhyāna:
there are attainments (samāpatti) for which the untainted fourth dhyāna serves as the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya),
but not as an object-condition (ālambanapratyaya).
These consist of twenty-two:
namely, the three immeasurables and the pure liberations.
The latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
the first eight bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
and the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
The absence of contention (araṇā) has four bases.
There is an attainment that takes the untainted fourth dhyāna as its object.
And it is not an equal-and-immediate condition.
This consists of seven types, namely: the pure and the untainted.
The pure [attainments] of the first dhyāna, the two higher formless attainments,
and their two corresponding liberations;
as well as the untainted [attainments] of the first dhyāna and the one higher formless attainment.
There are attainments for which the untainted fourth dhyāna serves as both the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) and the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
These consist of seventeen types.
This refers to the pure and untainted [states] of the three higher dhyānas and the first two formless attainments.
It is also the basis for the first two formless liberations,
the two analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid),
and the two supernormal powers (abhijñā) as well as the knowledge resulting from resolve (praṇidhijñāna).
There are nineteen attainments that do not take the untainted fourth dhyāna as their immediate antecedent, nor as their object.
That is to say: the eight associated with the flavor of the sublime,
the immeasurable of joy,
and the three liberations.
The first four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the last two totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are the bases for the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

Question: If an attainment (samāpatti) takes any given uncontaminated (anāsrava) formless state as its immediate antecedent (samanantara), does it necessarily take that same state as its object (ālambana)?
Conversely, if an attainment takes any given uncontaminated formless state as its object, does it necessarily take that same state as its immediate antecedent?
Is it that very [state] which serves as its equal-and-immediate condition?
Answer: Based on the first two formless attainments (ārūpya), when they are untainted (anāsrava), one should formulate four propositions for each.
Based on the last formless attainment, when it is untainted, one should formulate a proposition following the previous pattern.
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the untainted (anāsrava) sphere of infinite space:
there are meditative attainments (samāpatti) that take the untainted sphere of infinite space as their immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya),
but not as their object-condition (ālambana).
There is one such [base],
namely the sphere of totality of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-kṛtsnāyatana*).
There is an attainment that takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of infinite space as its object.
And not as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This consists of seven types, namely:
the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The first and second dhyānas,
the pure state of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and its corresponding liberation.

The basis for the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) consists of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of infinite space as their immediate antecedent (*samanantara*) and also as their object (*ālambana*).
These consist of sixteen types,
namely the pure and the untainted [states] within the latter two dhyānas.
The first three formless attainments are themselves those liberations;
they are also two of the analytical knowledges.
Regarding the basis for the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*):

there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that do not take the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
nor as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
There are forty-one of these:
namely, the eight associated with the flavors [of meditative concentration] and the four immeasurables.
The four liberations,
the eight bases of mastery,
and the nine universal bases.
The two types of unimpeded analytical knowledge,
the absence of conflict,
and the basis for the five supernormal powers.
Regarding the formulation of four propositions based on the untainted consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*):
there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that take the untainted consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
yet do not take it as their object (*ālambana*).
There is one here,
namely the sphere of totality of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-kṛtsnāyatana*).
There is an attainment that takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of infinite consciousness as its object.
And it is not an equal-and-immediate [condition].
This consists of seven types, namely: the pure and the untainted.
The first three dhyānas are the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna).
There is an attainment whose immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya) is the untainted consciousness of the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana).
It also functions as an object of focus (ālambana).
There are sixteen such objects, namely:
the pure (śuddha) and the untainted (anāsrava).
The fourth dhyāna,
the three lower formless attainments,
and the pure sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The four formless liberations,
the two analytical knowledges,
and the basis for the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
There are attainments for which the untainted consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space is neither the immediately preceding condition nor the object-condition;
these number forty-one.
That is to say: the eight attainments associated with the sublime (āsvādanasamprayukta),
the four immeasurables (apramāṇa),
and the four liberations (vimokṣa).
The eight bases of mastery,
the nine spheres of totality,
and the two analytical knowledges.
It is without conflict and is the basis for the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

Regarding the statement that it relies on the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as a "conformity to the preceding clause" (*pūrvapādaka*): [it means that] based on the untainted sphere of nothingness, one attains the five supernormal powers.
That is to say, there are meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as their immediate antecedent (*samanantara*),
and likewise take it as their object (*ālambana*).
There are also meditative attainments that take the untainted sphere of nothingness as their object.
Yet these are not taken as its equal-and-immediate [condition].
There are nine of these, namely:
the pure and the untainted.
The four dhyānas are the basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).
Question: Is there any occasion when a single meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) manifests?
In thirty-three attainments, one relinquishes but does not acquire;
in eight attainments, one acquires but does not relinquish;
in two attainments, one both relinquishes and acquires.
The second type is that which is partially relinquished and partially acquired,
while partially not relinquished and not acquired.
In the thirteen [attainments] and so forth, is it the case that one does not attain them by abandoning a portion,
nor does one fail to attain them by not abandoning a portion?
Is it the case for the seven [attainments] that they are neither abandoned nor attained?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, an arhat liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) who falls away from the first dhyāna associated with relishing (āsvādanā-samprayukta).
At that time, among the sixty-five attainments (*samāpatti*),
thirty-three are abandoned and not attained;
namely, those that are pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*).
The three higher dhyānas,
the pure and untainted formless attainments,
and the five liberations.
The latter four spheres of mastery and the ten totalities are the bases for the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
Eight are obtained and not abandoned;
namely, the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya) associated with relish (āsvādana).
Two are both abandoned and obtained.
That is to say, when one abandons the untainted pure first dhyāna,
one relinquishes that which is beyond training (aśaikṣa) as well as what was previously cultivated,
because one now attains that which pertains to training (śaikṣa) and the stage of retrogression.
Second, there is the case where a portion is relinquished and a portion is attained,
while a portion is neither relinquished nor attained;
this refers to those who maintain that there is also the supernormal power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānābhijñā) that is untainted (anāsrava).
Based on those, one may engage in this dialogue concerning the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti) and the supernormal knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).

At that time, the partial relinquishment refers to the partial attainment of the contaminated first dhyāna cultivated by all those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), as well as those in higher stages who possess both contaminated and uncontaminated states.
That is to say, a portion of the training in the first dhyāna is neither abandoned nor attained;
this refers to the remaining contaminated factors of the first dhyāna.

Furthermore, if one maintains that the supernormal power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānābhijñā*) is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), [then it would follow that]...
Based on that, one should not pose this question and answer;
for at that time, there is only a slight degree of equanimity through the supernormal power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
And because it cannot be obtained through partial relinquishment or partial non-relinquishment.
Thirteen [cases] involve neither partial relinquishment nor partial non-relinquishment, and thus they cannot be obtained.
That is to say: the four immeasurables,
the first two liberations,
and the first four bases of mastery.
Regarding the basis for the three types of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*):
one abandons and no longer attains those cultivated in all higher stages as well as in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) within one's own stage.
The remaining [qualities] belonging to one's own stage are neither relinquished nor acquired.
Seven are neither relinquished nor acquired;
namely, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The basis for the knowledge resulting from aspiration without conflict and the liberation through cessation are not attained in their fundamental form [in the lower realms].
Question: Is there any attainment of a single meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) that does not involve relinquishing anything?
Answer: There is;
namely, at the time of attaining the liberation of cessation (*nirodha-vimokṣa*).
Question: Is there a case where one attains the six meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) all at once, yet does not relinquish any of them?
Answer: There is.
This refers to when an Arhat first gives rise to the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna),
they simultaneously attain six meditative attainments (samāpatti),
namely, the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
It is the basis for the knowledge resulting from the vow of non-contention (*araṇā-praṇidhi-jñāna*).
Question: Is there any case where one relinquishes a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) such as equanimity (*upekṣā*) yet achieves nothing?
Answer: There is.
This means that when one passes away from the Śubhakṛtsna heaven and is born in the Bṛhatphala heaven, one abandons [the attainment];
although the third dhyāna is pure, there is nothing further to be attained.
Question: Regarding the individuals who are candidates for and those established in the four fruits, how many of the sixty-five attainments do they possess?
Who accomplishes how many and does not accomplish how many?
Answer: One proceeding toward the fruit of stream-entry accomplishes eight;
that is, the eight associated with the flavors.
The others are not accomplished.
As it is with the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry,
so it is also for the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning.
The minimum number of factors accomplished by one proceeding toward the stage of Non-returner is eight,
as previously explained;
this refers specifically to those who progress gradually.
At most, forty-seven are accomplished;
