that is, one who has already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness and enters into rightness and departure from birth based on the fourth dhyāna.
That is to say: the pure and the untainted [states],
the four dhyānas,
and the pure four formless attainments.
Associated with flavor;
the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
and the four immeasurables.
The seven liberations,
the eight bases of mastery,
and the ten totalities.
The basis for the five supernormal powers is,
at most, the fruit of non-returning,
as previously explained.
At minimum, twenty-five are accomplished;
namely, the eight associated with the flavor [of meditative attainment],
as well as the pure and the untainted.
The first dhyāna,
the four immeasurables,
and the first two liberations.
The first four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) serve as the basis for the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
they may be diminished by one or two flavors.
In the increase of the first two pure [attainments],
there are likewise twenty-five; those who are candidates for arhatship achieve at least thirteen,
and are immediately reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
That which cannot be attained through the liberation of cessation refers to the four untainted meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and the three formless attainments (ārūpya).
The liberation associated with relishing, the pure liberation,
and the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
these are the four liberations.
If one is born in the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) and has not yet abandoned the defilements of its own level,
one likewise accomplishes thirteen [factors],
namely, with one additional flavor.
Excluding one liberation,
at most fifty-one are accomplished; that is,
when born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world.
The body-witness refers to the one taste,
the eight pure [attainments],
and the seven untainted [attainments].
The four immeasurables,
the eight liberations,
and the eight bases of mastery.
The ten bases of totality (daśakṛtsnāyatana) are the basis for the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā).
An Arhat who has attained the fruit achieves at least thirteen [dharmas].
They are reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
As for the arhat liberated by wisdom,
they possess seven untainted [faculties].
The one purity and four liberations are the basis for the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows;
at most, fifty-seven [factors] are accomplished.
This means that for those who have attained the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā*),
and the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), all [knowledges] are possessed except for the eight associated with the flavors (*rasa*).
The Buddha has fifty-seven meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Among the Pratyekabuddhas, those who practice in groups are like the Śrāvakas of the Desire Realm;
those who are like the rhinoceros horn are like the Buddha.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Fascicle One Hundred and Seventy;
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle One Hundred and Seventy-one.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (*Samādhi-skandha*). Part Three: The Summary of Contents (*Saṃgraha-nikāya*). Part Six. Is it possible to attain all four dhyānas associated with taste (*āsvādana-samprayukta*) simultaneously?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, when one who has exhausted craving for the form realm falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm or the Brahma-world;
or when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm or the Brahma-world.
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed once again?
Answer: Although the preceding [section] clarified acquisition and relinquishment, it did not yet differentiate between the gradual and the instantaneous.
Now, I wish to demonstrate the distinction between the gradual and the sudden.
Furthermore, whereas previously the three types— taste and so forth— were distinguished in relation to one another,
I now wish to clarify only their respective categories therein.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
"Simultaneous" (頓) refers to occurring at the same time;
"gradual" (漸) refers to occurring in succession.
In this context, it is shown that the four dhyānas associated with relish (*āsvādana*) are acquired instantaneously at two times:
namely, at the time of falling away (*parihāṇi*) and at the time of rebirth (*upapatti*).
"Falling away" refers to the point when one has exhausted craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*).
One who is born dies from the formless realm;
he arises in the desire realm or the Brahma-world through the occurrence of fetters (paryavasthāna),
and likewise at the time of being born in the desire realm or the Brahma-world.
Because the four [levels] associated with taste are acquired simultaneously.
Is it possible to abandon the four dhyānas associated with taste all at once?
Answer: No.
Because it is impossible to simultaneously abandon the defilements of four stages, is it possible to gradually attain the four dhyānas associated with craving?
Answer: Yes.
This is also attained gradually at two times:
namely, through falling away and through rebirth.
Regarding falling away, it occurs from the exhaustion of desire for the form realm.
When one successively falls away from each of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) due to the influence of the fetters (paryavasthāna),
those who are being reborn pass away from the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and are successively born into each of the lower levels of the meditative absorptions.
He attains those associated with the four flavors in gradual succession.
Is it possible that he might gradually relinquish the four dhyānas associated with flavor?
Answer: Yes.
This is because one must first become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna, and so on, until finally becoming detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna.
Is it possible to attain the four pure dhyānas all at once?
Answer: No, because there is no case of not having previously accomplished the four pure dhyānas.
Because they are acquired simultaneously now.
Is it possible to abandon the four pure dhyānas all at once?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to when one has exhausted craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm and then falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm;
or when one dies in the desire realm or the Brahma-world and is reborn in the formless realm.
In this context, it is shown that the pure four dhyānas are abandoned instantaneously at two times:
namely, at the time of falling away and at the time of transcending a realm or level;
this should be applied accordingly to the explanation.
Is it possible to attain the four pure dhyānas gradually?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, when one first becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm, one attains the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, because one attains the fourth dhyāna when subsequently becoming free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
and because one sequentially descends to the lower four dhyānas after passing away from the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Although it is also called "attaining gradually," because it involves attaining one [moment] and abandoning one [moment],
it is not what is being discussed here.
Is there a gradual relinquishing of the pure four dhyānas?
Answer: There is.
This also involves gradual relinquishing at two times.
This refers to the time of falling back and the time of transcending realms and stages.
"Falling back" refers to the time of regressing due to the gradual arising of the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of a lower stage.
"Transcending realms and stages" refers to...
That is to say, when one gradually arises from a lower level to a higher level,
or when one sequentially descends from a higher dhyāna to a lower dhyāna level,
although this is also termed "gradual relinquishment," [it is distinct from the case at hand].
Since one abandons one and acquires another,
this is not what is being discussed here.
Is it possible to attain the four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas all at once?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, one who enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the fourth dhyāna, or one who attains the fruit of arhatship.
Others do not state here that one attains the fruit of arhatship,
because they have already attained the four uncontaminated dhyānas during the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).
However, it should indeed be stated here that one attains the fruit of arhatship.
Because all that was attained through training is now suddenly relinquished upon attaining the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Is it possible to suddenly relinquish the four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to when a noble one, having exhausted craving for the Sphere of Utmost Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*),
falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the Desire Realm; even though they have attained the fruit, refined their faculties,
or do not give rise to those very fetters of the Desire Realm, at the time of falling away, they also suddenly relinquish the four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas.
Yet they are immediately regained;
therefore, it is not mentioned.
Is it possible to gradually attain the four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas?
Answer: Yes.
This is because when a noble one becomes free from the defilements of the lower stages and gives rise to the path of a superior fruit, they attain them gradually.
Is it possible for the four uncontaminated dhyānas to be abandoned gradually?
Answer: Yes.

This is because when a noble one, having exhausted craving for the Sphere of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna), gradually gives rise to the fetters of the lower stages and falls away, they progressively relinquish the four untainted dhyānas.
Is there a case where the four formless attainments associated with relish are acquired simultaneously?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, when an Arhat falls away from the fetters of the sphere of infinite space belonging to the desire or form realms.
In this context, there is no possibility of obtaining [the attainments] at the moment of birth.
Is it possible to abandon the four formless attainments associated with craving all at once?
Answer: No.
As explained previously:
Is it possible to gradually attain the four formless attainments associated with taste?
Answer: Yes.
In this context, when there is falling away, one gradually attains four states of existence;
when there is birth, one gradually attains three states of existence.
Is it possible to gradually relinquish the four formless attainments associated with craving?
Answer: Yes, as explained previously.
Is it possible to attain the four pure formless attainments all at once?
Answer: No.

This is because there are no cases where one who was previously not accomplished in the four pure formless attainments attains them all simultaneously at the time of attaining the fruit or refining the faculties.
Question: At the time of attaining the fruit or refining the faculties...
Regarding the pure four dhyānas and the pure four formless attainments,
there is cultivation of them all simultaneously.
For what reason, then, is it that in the preceding dhyānas and in these formless attainments [this is not the case]?
All replied, "No. [The Master] replied:
"They all previously possessed [these qualities] and have not abandoned them;
they merely acquire a small portion anew now. Therefore, this does not constitute the meaning of 'acquisition' as explained in this context."
Is there a case where one simultaneously abandons the pure [attainments] of the four formless realms?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, when one falls away from the state of having exhausted craving for the sphere of nothingness by arising with the fetters of the desire realm or the form realm.
In this context, there is no possibility of relinquishing [the meditative attainments] by transcending the realms or stages.
Is it possible to gradually attain the four pure formless attainments?
Answer: Yes.
As explained previously:
Is it possible to gradually relinquish the four pure formless attainments?
Answer: Yes.
In this context, at the time of falling away, one gradually relinquishes four *bhavas*;
at the time of transcending a stage, one gradually relinquishes three *bhavas*.
Is it possible to acquire the three formless attainments of the untainted (*anāsrava*) all at once?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, at the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship, and at the time of refining the faculties of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Although it is also attained instantaneously, it is not a distinct category;
therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, that [attainment] is also called the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship.
Therefore, they are not explained separately.
Is it possible to abandon the three formless attainments of the untainted (*anāsrava*) all at once?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to when a noble one, having exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness,
falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire and form realms;
the explanation is as before.
Is it possible to gradually attain the three untainted formless attainments?
Answer: Yes, by means of becoming detached from the defilements of the lower stages.
Furthermore, since one attains them gradually when arising in the path of superior fruit,
is it possible to gradually abandon the three formless attainments that are untainted?
Answer: There is.
When a noble one, having exhausted craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), gradually falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to a lower stage.

Because one gradually abandons the three formless attainments that are untainted (*anāsrava*), upon which meditative concentration do the bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*) and non-intimation (*avijñapti*) depend for their cessation?
Answer: Bodily and vocal intimation depend on either the first dhyāna or the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
The unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of body and speech relies upon the four [dhyānas] or the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage].
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To refute the view that manifest and unmanifest karma are not substantially real.
It is taught that both manifest and unmanifest karma are substantially existent;
furthermore, this is to refute the claim that manifest karma of body and speech,
as well as unmanifest karma up to the fourth dhyāna, do not exist.
Up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Now, one wishes to manifest the informative acts (*vijñapti*) of body and speech, as well as the non-informative acts (*avijñapti*) up to the Brahma-world,
even unto the fourth dhyāna.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
Question: For what reason do the three higher dhyānas lack bodily and vocal informative action (*vijñapti-karman*)?
Answer: Bodily and vocal informative action is originated by *vitarka* and *vicāra*.
If vitarka and vicāra were obtainable in that stage,
then there would be bodily and vocal informative karma;
thus, the Sūtra says:
Just as speech exists subsequent to initial and sustained mental application (*vitarka-vicāra*), yet is not non-existent without them,
so too bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) must be produced subsequent to initial and sustained mental application, and cannot exist without them.
Because initial and sustained mental application have ceased in the three higher dhyānas, there is no bodily or vocal intimation therein.
Question: For what reason are there no *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) in the higher stages?
Answer: Because *vitarka* and *vicāra* are coarse, mobile, and non-quiescent, whereas the higher stages are subtle and quiescent.
Question: For what reason do the unmanifest [karmas] of body and speech exist only up to the fourth dhyāna, and not in the higher stages?
Answer: Because wholesome unmanifest karma serves as the antidote to unwholesome unmanifest karma.
There is unwholesome non-manifest karma that exists only in the desire realm and not in the formless realm;
because it is remote by way of four kinds of remoteness, it does not exist there.
Furthermore, some say:
From the realm of form up to the fourth dhyāna,
all are able to feel revulsion toward the evil karma of the desire realm;
those of the higher stages are not so.
Some say that non-informative matter (avijñapti) depends on the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the physical body;
since it lacks a physical body and primary elements, it likewise lacks non-informative matter.
Among these, bodily and vocal informative karma are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
The unwholesome is bound to the desire realm and is ceased by relying on the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The wholesome and neutral are bound to the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
Those bound to the desire realm are extinguished by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
Those bound to the first dhyāna rely on both the threshold concentration and the first dhyāna.
The intermediate dhyāna ceases the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of the second dhyāna;
the term "unattained" (anāgamya) applies generally to all eight preparatory stages.
And this includes the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*),
because neither of these has yet reached the fundamental concentrations (*mauladhyāna*).
However, the "concentration" (*samādhi*) mentioned here refers to—
Some say it is spoken in reliance on untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*). Others say: [it is spoken in reliance on tainted concentration].
This is explained based on both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). If it is said to be based on uncontaminated concentration,
that statement uses the term "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*) to indicate the not-yet-attained concentration (*anāgamyasamādhi*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
If it is said that this is explained based on both contaminated and uncontaminated meditative absorptions,
then that explanation holds that the term "not-yet-reached" (anāgamya) indicates the not-yet-reached concentration (anāgamya-samādhi),
as well as the intermediate dhyāna and the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of the second dhyāna.
Furthermore, regarding the "cessation" mentioned herein,
some say it refers generally to cessation by way of category (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Some say that this refers exclusively to cessation in its ultimate sense;
if it were said to refer generally to cessation by way of category, [it would not be so].
That [text] states that the term "not-yet-reached" (anāgamya) subsumes three stages.
Within the not-yet-reached concentration, it includes both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava),
because by means of this, one can extinguish the bodily and vocal manifest actions (vijñapti) bound to the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
If it is said that this refers exclusively to ultimate cessation,
then that statement also includes the three stages within the term "not-yet-reached" (anāgamya);
within the not-yet-reached concentration, only the untainted (anāsrava) is included.
Because this [cessation] is able to extinguish the bodily and vocal informative intimation (*vijñapti*) bound to the first dhyāna,
it is said that bodily and vocal informative intimation depends upon the first dhyāna or the *anāgamya* for its cessation.
Bodily and vocal non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*), however, may be either wholesome or unwholesome.
The unwholesome is bound to the desire realm.
The wholesome, which is extinguished by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), is bound to the four dhyānas of the desire realm and is also unbound.
That which is bound to the desire realm is extinguished by relying on the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*);
that which is bound to the first dhyāna is...
Those bound to the first dhyāna cease by means of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna;
up to those bound to the fourth dhyāna, they cease by means of the four dhyānas,
the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna, and the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
However, regarding the "concentration" (samādhi) mentioned here:

If it is said that this is explained based on both contaminated and uncontaminated meditative concentrations,

And the four aforementioned preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
Furthermore, regarding the "cessation" mentioned herein, if it is explained as cessation by way of category (*jāti-nirodha*),

That [text] states that the term "not-yet-reached" (anāgamya) includes the not-yet-reached concentration (anāgamyasamādhi),

The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) within the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) comprises exclusively the untainted (*anāsrava*). This is because,

For this reason, it is said that bodily and vocal non-informative action (*avijñapti*) ceases based on the four [dhyānas] or the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage].
The detailed explanation of informative and non-informative karma is as found in the *Karmaskandha*.
Upon which meditative concentrations do the three types of misconduct, the three types of sublime conduct, the three unwholesome roots, and the three wholesome roots cease?
Answer: They depend on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage.
Among these, the three types of unwholesome conduct (*akuśala-carita*) belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and are extinguished by relying on the *anāgamya* concentration.
The two types of sublime conduct of body and speech are associated with the four dhyānas of the desire realm and are also unassociated.
Those associated with the desire realm depend on the *anāgamya* (threshold) concentration; those associated with the first dhyāna depend on the cessation [of the first dhyāna].
Those bound to the first dhyāna cease by means of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna;
up to those bound to the fourth dhyāna, they cease by means of the four dhyānas,
the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna, and the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Wholesome mental conduct is bound to the nine stages and is also unbound.
That which is bound to the desire realm is extinguished by relying on the threshold concentration (anāgamya-samādhi).
That which is bound to the first dhyāna ceases based on the first dhyāna,
the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), and the access concentration (sāmantaka) of the second dhyāna.
Up to those bound by the sphere of nothingness,

[these are] extinguished based on the seven fundamental dhyānas, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna, and the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Those bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception cease based on the seven fundamental dhyānas, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), and the intermediate dhyāna;
however, within this context, the three wholesome courses of action are taught as the proximate antidotes to the three unwholesome courses of action.
It is simply stated that the three unwholesome roots are abandoned by relying on the *anāgamya* [preliminary concentration];
those bound to the desire realm are abandoned by relying on the *anāgamya*,
while the three wholesome roots— bound to the nine stages as well as being unbound— are abandoned in the same manner.
The meditative absorption upon which they depend ceases,
as explained in the section on sublime conduct (*manomayī sucaritā*).
Here, too, the three wholesome roots are taught based on their direct antidotes to the three unwholesome roots.
Therefore, it is also simply stated that one relies on the "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*) stage to abandon the three unwholesome courses of action,
up to the three wholesome roots, as explained at length in the *Karmaskandha* and other texts.
[This concludes] the four non-noble expressions and the four noble expressions.
The four modes of birth,
the four ways of entering the womb,
and the four stations of consciousness.

and spontaneous— and the four ways of entering the womb are based on the stage of *anāgamya*.

The consciousness-abiding of the form realm depends on the four [bases] or the threshold concentration.
Regarding the four non-noble expressions (*anāryavāda*):
That is to say: claiming to have seen what was not seen;
claiming to have heard what was not heard;
claiming to have sensed what was not sensed.
To claim knowledge of what one does not know.
Why was this treatise composed?
It is answered: because it seeks to analyze the meaning of the sūtras.
As stated in the Sūtra:
there are four non-noble modes of speech,
namely, claiming to have seen what one has not seen, and so forth, as explained at length.
Although the sūtras state this,
they do not provide a detailed analysis;
yet the sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which was not explained by him should now be analyzed; therefore,
this treatise is composed.
What is non-noble speech that claims to see what has not been seen?
Answer: That which is not obtained by the eye and is not cognized by visual consciousness.
That which is not seen is called "non-seeing.
If one forms the perception of non-seeing regarding that which is not seen, [that is what is meant].
He asked, "Have you ever seen such a thing?
Was it done by yourself or for another?"
Or, for the sake of fame and profit,
one conceals this perception, this acceptance,
and this desire, and replies, "I have seen it."
This is called "not seeing but claiming to see," which is non-noble speech.
Furthermore, there is this class of people who, regarding what they have seen, give rise to the perception that they have not seen it, yet claim to have seen it;
this also constitutes non-noble speech.
Question: For what reason is this stated again?
Answer: It is in order to manifest a rare and marvelous matter (āścaryādbhuta-dharma).
As it is said:
Is it possible that one who sees might say they see,
yet this constitutes un-Aryan speech, just as when one who does not see says they see?
Answer: There is.
For example, there is someone who does not give rise to the perception of an object they have seen.
When another asks them, "Have you ever seen this object? [they do not acknowledge it].
He may act for himself, or for others,
or for the sake of fame and profit.
He then conceals this perception, this acceptance, and this desire,
and replies, "I saw it.
At that time, by saying he saw what he did not see, he utters what is not the speech of an Arya.
This is also called "not seeing but claiming to see," which is non-noble speech.
Just as it was explained at length regarding not seeing but claiming to see being non-noble speech,
so too is it with not hearing but claiming to hear.
To claim awakening when one has not awakened,
or to claim knowledge when one does not know, is not the speech of a noble one;
the same applies in detail to all such cases.
Furthermore, there are four types of non-noble speech:
namely, claiming not to have seen what one has seen,
and claiming not to have heard what one has heard.
To say one has awakened when one has not awakened,
or to say one knows when one does not know—
how is it that saying one has seen when one has not seen is considered non-noble speech?
Answer: That which is obtained by the eye and cognized by visual consciousness is called "the seen.
This "seen" is what is termed "seeing.
If there arises the conceptualization of "seeing" with respect to that which is seen, [it is so designated].
He asks you, "Have you ever seen such a thing?
Whether he does so for himself or for another.
Or, for the sake of fame and profit,
they conceal this perception, this acceptance, and this desire,
answering that they did not see it.

When another person asks him:

To say one has not heard what was heard,

if expanded, there are eight or sixteen.

as with the general and the specific,

Answer: Its intrinsic nature is false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).

The answer is: it is called "non-noble" (anārya) because it is unwholesome (akuśala).
Furthermore, it is called "non-noble" because it manifests within the continuum of one who is non-noble.

The *Saṃgītiparyāya* states:
Why is it called "non-noble" (*anārya*)?
Answer: Because by means of this, one brings about that which is undesirable.
It is not to be delighted in,
not to be enjoyed, disagreeable, and results in what is undesirable;
therefore, it is called "non-noble."
This reveals the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Furthermore, by means of this, one brings about an undesirable, unpleasant, disagreeable, displeasing, and unsatisfactory maturation (*vipāka*).
Therefore, it is called "non-noble.
This indicates the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
This is comprised within non-noble speech or non-restraint (asaṃvara).
Or, it may be neither included within non-restraint nor included within non-non-restraint;
such a course of action (*karmapatha*) is exclusively unwholesome.
Question: Is there any speech that is neither noble (*ārya*) nor a course of action?
Is this indeterminate and bound to the form realm?
Answer: Yes.
For example, such speech as was spoken by the Great Brahmā King to the bhikṣu Aśvajit.
Although that is also termed "non-noble speech," it is not included within the non-noble speech discussed here;
for while the matters spoken of therein may be either inverted or non-inverted, they must necessarily be inverted in this context.
Arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and others may also have instances of not seeing yet claiming to see and so forth;
however, these are not included among the "un-Aryan utterances," because they are spoken without a concealing intention (*saṃvṛti-saṃjñā*).
It is like a person who, perceiving a tree stump, says they see a man;
or like the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, who predicted that a son would be born when in fact a daughter was born;
or as he said, "I abide in the meditative concentration of the sphere of nothingness."
It is heard that within the Mandākinī pond there are many nāga-elephants who trumpet with their trunks raised;
one should know that these accounts are not false, for although the objects themselves may be distorted, the perception is not.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses no such erroneous speech,
for he has forever uprooted all habitual tendencies of ignorance and directly realizes the objects of the three periods of time.
The four noble modes of speech are:
to say one has not seen when one has not seen,
and to say one has not heard when one has not heard.
To say one does not perceive when one does not perceive,
and to say one does not know when one does not know—
why do you ask this question again? Why do you further compose this treatise?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As the sūtra says regarding the four noble modes of speech:
"To say one has not seen when one has not seen."
This is explained at length, up to this point.
Although the sūtra makes this statement,
it does not provide a detailed analysis.
Now, wishing to analyze this matter, I have composed this treatise.
What is meant by the noble speech "not seeing, one says 'I do not see'"?
The answer is that the meaning of "not seeing" is as explained previously.
If one has the perception of not seeing regarding that which was not seen,
and another asks,
"Have you ever seen this matter? [one would answer accordingly].
He does not act for his own sake, nor for the sake of others,
nor for the sake of fame or profit.
Immediately, in accordance with reality, without concealing this perception, this acceptance,
or this desire, he answers, "I did not see it.

For example, it is like asking: "Is there such a thing as one who, having seen, says 'I have not seen,' and likewise, by saying 'I have not seen' regarding what was not seen, becomes one whose speech is that of an Arya?"
Answer: Yes.

Likewise, there is "not hearing and saying one does not hear."
To say "I do not perceive" when one does not perceive,

namely, to say one has seen when one has seen,

Answer: The meaning of "seeing" is as explained previously.

He does not act for his own sake, nor for the sake of others,

but answers, "I have seen.

while not seeing, give rise to the perception that they see,

Answer: It is to manifest a marvelous matter.

He replied, "I saw it.
At that time, just as the statement "I saw" constitutes a noble expression (ārya-vākya),
this too is called the noble expression "saying one has seen what was seen."
Just as it is stated at length that "seeing" refers to seeing the noble speech,
so too does "hearing" refer to hearing,
and "perceiving" refers to perceiving.
"Knowing speech, knowing noble speech.

What is meant by "entering the mother's womb with improper awareness, and likewise abiding and departing"?
The answer is that there are two types.
That is to say, one who is of little merit gives rise to perverted perceptions and perverted resolute convictions at the time of entering the womb,
seeing the celestial atmosphere as gloomy, cold, biting, windy, and rainy.
When many people were causing a commotion and the great multitude had gathered,
he thought: "I shall now enter among such thickets of grass and thorns,
or into a grass hut or a leaf hut within a dense forest."
Or, dwelling thus between walls or beneath trees to avoid wind, rain, and various disturbances,
he reflects and immediately sees his body go there.
This is when he dwells in the womb.
One also gives rise to such inverted conceptions and resolute convictions, thinking:
"I am now dwelling for a brief rest in such a thicket, a grass hut, a leaf hut, between walls, or at the foot of a tree."
When he emerges from the womb,
there likewise arises such a perverted perception and resolve,
namely: "I am now emerging from such a thicket, a grass cave, or a leaf hut."
Or they may leave behind walls or trees and depart.
Even those with merit, at the time of entering the womb,
likewise give rise to inverted perceptions and inverted resolutions.

while dwelling in the womb,

That is to say: "I am now exiting such a grove," and so on, down to "descending from the multi-storied pavilion.

What is meant by entering the mother’s womb with full awareness, but dwelling and emerging without full awareness?
The answer is: for one who possesses great merit, at the time of entering the mother’s womb, [they possess full awareness].
Without giving rise to inverted perceptions or inverted convictions, he is able to know for himself: "I am now entering my mother's womb.
However, while dwelling in the womb and upon emerging from it, he lacks correct awareness.
As explained in detail previously, this is called the second case: entering the mother’s womb with full awareness, staying therein without full awareness, and departing without full awareness.
What is meant by entering the mother’s womb with full awareness, staying therein with full awareness, and departing without full awareness?
The answer is: those with great merit do not give rise to inverted perceptions or inverted resolute convictions while entering the mother’s womb or while dwelling therein.

However, at the time of emergence, he lacks clear comprehension, as explained in detail previously.
This is called the third case: entering the mother’s womb with full awareness, remaining there with full awareness, but departing without full awareness.
What is meant by entering the mother’s womb with full awareness, and likewise remaining and departing with full awareness?
Answer: For one who possesses great merit,
at the time of entering the mother’s womb and while dwelling within the mother’s womb.
When emerging from the mother's womb,
they do not give rise to inverted perceptions or inverted resolute beliefs,
but are able to know for themselves.
"I am now entering my mother's womb;
I am now dwelling in my mother's womb;
I am now emerging from my mother's womb."
This is called the fourth [type of birth]: entering the mother’s womb with full awareness, and likewise abiding and emerging.
Question: What is it that enters the womb?
Who is it? Answer: Some say:
The fourth type of entry into the womb refers to a Bodhisattva;
the third refers to a Pratyekabuddha;
and the second refers to a Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin).
The first type of entry into the womb refers to other sentient beings;
some say that the fourth type of entry into the womb refers to the Bodhisattva.
The third type of entry into the womb refers to the Pratyekabuddhas;
the second type of entry into the womb refers to the Śrāvakas who follow the pāramitās;
and the first type of entry into the womb refers to other sentient beings.
Some say that the fourth type of entry into the womb refers to Bodhisattvas,
while the third type of entry into the womb refers to Pratyekabuddhas.
The second type of entry into the womb refers to those who are stream-enterers (srotāpanna) and once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin);
the first type of entry into the womb refers to other sentient beings. Some say:
Among sentient beings, some seek sublime wisdom while their karma is also pure;
some seek sublime wisdom but their karma is not pure;
and some have pure karma but do not seek wisdom.
There are those who do not seek the activity of wisdom nor purify it.
The first sentient being acts as the last to enter the womb;
the second sentient being acts as the third to enter the womb.
The third sentient being acts as the second to enter the womb,
and the last sentient being acts as the first to enter the womb;
that is to say, when the first sentient being enters the mother’s womb.
The mother’s womb was peaceful and free from all disturbances;
while dwelling in the womb,
the fetal chamber was spacious, pure, and without affliction.
When emerging from the mother’s womb, the birth canal remains wide open and does not cause constriction;
therefore, they do not lose mindfulness during entry, stay, or exit.
This is the second type of sentient being.
At the time of entering the womb and while dwelling in the womb,
he remains as peaceful as before and does not lose mindfulness;
it is only at the time of emerging that [he loses it].
Because the birth canal is narrow and constricted, one immediately loses mindfulness.
As for the third type of sentient being,
there is likewise no painful sensation at the time of entering the womb.
As before, he remains secure and does not lose mindfulness;
yet, while dwelling in the womb,
he is distressed by the confinement and impurities of the fetal chamber.
Furthermore, at the time of emerging from the womb,
the birth canal is narrow and extremely constricted; therefore,
it causes one to lose mindfulness both while remaining [in the womb] and while emerging.
Fourth, when a sentient being enters the mother’s womb,
the mother’s abdomen becomes agitated, and she experiences alarm and unease; likewise,
during the stages of remaining in and emerging from the womb, she suffers as previously described.
Therefore, in all three periods, they cause one to lose mindfulness.
Furthermore, these four types of entry into the womb all refer to Bodhisattvas;
regarding this, there is a teaching that says:
The fourth entry into the womb belongs to a Bodhisattva of the third asaṃkhyeya;
the third entry into the womb belongs to a Bodhisattva of the second asaṃkhyeya;
and the second entry into the womb belongs to a Bodhisattva of the first asaṃkhyeya.
The first type of entry into the womb belongs to a bodhisattva in his previous lives;
some say that the fourth type of entry into the womb belongs to a bodhisattva in his final existence.
This refers to when he passed away from Tuṣita Heaven and descended to be born in the palace of King Śuddhodana;
his third entry into the womb was that of a Bodhisattva bound to one more birth.
This refers to when he was about to pass away from Jambudvīpa and be born in Tuṣita Heaven.
The second entry into the womb refers to the Bodhisattva’s previous birth prior to this one;
that is, when he passed away from that life and was born in Jambudvīpa during the time he was practicing the holy life under the Buddha Kāśyapa.
The first entry into the womb.
This refers to the aforementioned Bodhisattva.
The commentary states:
One should not speak in such a manner.

This is because, for ninety-one kalpas, the Bodhisattva has constantly recollected his past lives; throughout the state of death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*), the state of birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*), and the state of fundamental existence (*mūla-bhava*), he has always been free from inverted perceptions and has never lost mindfulness.
For this reason, what was stated previously is correct.
Question: At the moment of linking existence (*pratisandhi*), an afflicted mind necessarily arises;
all afflicted minds are associated with lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*).
How can it be said that one enters the mother’s womb with full awareness?
The answer is: what is called "full awareness" refers to the absence of inverted perception and inverted resolve.
It is not because it is dissociated from ignorance that it is called "clear comprehension"; rather,
it is when a bodhisattva, at the moment of linking rebirth, [possesses such awareness].
Furthermore, because self-love and love for one’s parents arise, there is also a defiled mind.
Question: If that is so, [what follows]?
In what way does he differ from other sentient beings?
Answer: Just as when other sentient beings are about to enter the womb, they perceive their father not as a father and their mother not as a mother.
Because of this, a male gives rise to hatred toward his father and love toward his mother,
thereby giving rise to perverted perceptions.
That is to say, when he has intercourse with his mother,
the daughter conceives hatred toward her mother and love for her father, giving rise to perverted perceptions;
she then thinks that it is her father with whom she is having intercourse.
Due to such inverted perceptions, one undergoes rebirth;
the Bodhisattva is not so.
When about to enter the womb:
Perceiving my father as my father and my mother as my mother,
it was by depending upon them that I grew and developed my subsequent aggregates;
thus, within Jambudvīpa, I shall receive a noble and superior retribution, and based on this, I shall realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having formed the thought, "I shall perform beneficial deeds for all sentient beings," one then gives rise to affection toward one's parents and others.
Because of this, one is reborn;
therefore, it is "clear comprehension.
That is to say, non-erroneous perception does not necessarily require the absence of defilement.
These four types of entry into the womb are associated exclusively with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Therefore, they are extinguished solely by relying on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration.
Among the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), the latter three stations of consciousness are extinguished by relying on either the seven [dhyānas] or the *anāgamya*.
That is to say, the latter three consciousness-abidings are bound to nine stages.
Those bound to the desire realm cease based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya-samādhi).
That which is bound to the first dhyāna ceases by relying on the first dhyāna,
the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), and the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna.
Up to those bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
[they] depend on the seven fundamental dhyānas, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), and the intermediate dhyāna for their cessation.
However, the "concentration" mentioned here refers to...
If it is said to be based on uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) concentration,
that statement indicates that the term "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*) refers to the not-yet-attained concentration and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
If it is said to be based on both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated concentration, [then...]

That [text] states that the term "not-yet-attained" (anāgamya) indicates the not-yet-attained concentration (anāgamyasamādhi), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), and the seven proximate stages (sāmantaka) of the higher dhyānas.
Furthermore, regarding the "cessation" mentioned therein,
if it is spoken of in terms of cessation by way of category (jātinirodha):

That [text] states that the term "not-yet-attained" (anāgamya) includes the not-yet-attained concentration (anāgamya-samādhi), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), and the seven proximate stages (sāmantaka) of the higher [dhyānas].
Within the not-yet-attained concentration, both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava) are included;

for by relying on this, one is able to extinguish the three abodes of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) associated with the desire realm up to those associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
If it is said that this is spoken in terms of ultimate cessation,
then "the not-yet-attained" (anāgamya) includes the not-yet-attained concentration (anāgamyasamādhi), the dhyāna-intermediate (dhyānāntara),
and within the not-yet-attained concentration, it includes only the untainted (anāsrava).
Because by relying on this, one can extinguish the last three stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
For this reason, it is said that [the cessation] relies on the seven [stations of consciousness] or the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The station of form-consciousness (rūpavijñānasthiti) relies on four [stations] or the threshold concentration for its cessation.
That is to say, the consciousness-dwelling of form is bound to five stages.
That which is bound to the desire realm is extinguished by relying on the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
This extends up to those bound to the fourth dhyāna,
which are ceased by relying on the four dhyānas, the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), and the threshold concentration (sāmantaka) of the sphere of infinite space.
However, the "concentrations" (samādhi) mentioned here refer to—
Some say it refers to untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*). Others say: [it refers to] tainted concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*).
This is explained based on the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) meditative absorptions (*samādhi*),
and should be distinguished accordingly as previously analyzed.
Furthermore, regarding the "cessation" mentioned herein:
If it is said that this is spoken in terms of the cessation of types,

then that statement includes the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the four preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher dhyānas within the term "not-yet-arrived.
Within the *anāgamya*, both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are included.
Because by relying on this, one is able to extinguish the consciousness-abidings (vijñāna-sthiti) associated with the desire realm up to those associated with the fourth dhyāna.
If it is said that this is spoken in terms of ultimate extinction,
then that statement refers to what has not yet been reached (anāgamya).
This includes the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space.
Because by relying on these, one can eliminate the consciousness-abidings (*vijñānasthiti*) bound to the fourth dhyāna.
For this reason, it is said that one eliminates the four consciousness-abidings either by relying on the four [dhyānas] or the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*).
The detailed explanation is as in the *Mahābhūta-skandha*.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 171; *Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 100.
