Some say it is untainted (*anāsrava*);
others say it is both tainted and untainted, as previously distinguished.
Regarding what is called "cessation":
if it is said that this refers to cessation by way of category,
then that statement includes the "not-yet-attained" (anāgamya) within the term "not-yet-attained concentration" (anāgamyasamādhi).

The intermediate dhyāna and the seven higher preparatory stages (sāmantaka) are included within the threshold concentration (anāgamya), comprising both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava).

This is because, by relying on this, one is able to extinguish the mental bases (*manāyatana*) and so forth associated with the desire realm, up to those associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). If, however,
it is said that this refers to extinction in its ultimate sense, then...
That [text] states that the term "not-yet-attained" (anāgamya) includes both the not-yet-attained concentration (anāgamyasamādhi) and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara);
within the not-yet-attained concentration, it includes only the untainted (anāsrava).
Because by relying on this, one is able to extinguish the mental sphere (*manāyatana*) and so forth bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
For this reason, it is said that [cessation] occurs by relying on the seven [stages] or the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
As for the external spheres of odor and taste, as well as the nose-consciousness and tongue-consciousness bodies, [they are not present there].
Furthermore, their associated contact, feeling, perception, volition, and craving—
all being bound to the desire realm— are extinguished solely by relying on the *anāgamya* (threshold) concentration.
This applies to the groups of visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses.
And because those associated factors— the contact, feeling, perception, volition, and craving aggregates—
are all bound to two stages,
they are abandoned by relying on either the first dhyāna or the preliminary stage (anāgamya).
Among these, those bound to the desire realm are abandoned by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*);
those bound to the first dhyāna are abandoned by relying on the first dhyāna and the threshold concentration.
The intermediate dhyāna and the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna are ceased; however,
the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) spoken of here is as follows.
Some say they are untainted (*anāsrava*);
others say they are both tainted and untainted, as previously distinguished.
Regarding what was said about cessation,
some say it is spoken of in terms of the cessation of types.
Some say that this is spoken in reference to ultimate cessation;
it should also be analyzed accordingly, as was done previously.
For this reason, it is said that based on the first [dhyāna] or the threshold (anāgamya) stage,
there are the seven stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) and the eight worldly dharmas (aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ).
Regarding the nine abodes of sentient beings and the ten paths of karmic action,
by which meditative absorption are they extinguished?
Answer: The first station of consciousness,
the eight worldly dharmas,
and the first abode of sentient beings.
The ten courses of action (daśa-karmapatha) rely upon the threshold concentration (anāgamya) and the second station of consciousness (vijñānasthiti).
The abodes of sentient beings (sattvāvāsa) rely either on the first dhyāna or the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The third station of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) is also an abode of sentient beings.

The fourth station of consciousness and abode of sentient beings is based on two [dhyānas] or the threshold concentration (anāgamya). Three [stations of consciousness] or [abodes of sentient beings] are based on three [dhyānas] or the threshold concentration.
The fifth abode of sentient beings relies on either the four dhyānas or the threshold concentration (anāgamya);
this is the fifth station of consciousness.
The sixth abode of sentient beings relies on either the five [dhyānas] or the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*);
it is the sixth station of consciousness.
The seventh abode of sentient beings (sattvāvāsa) relies upon either the six [dhyānas] or the threshold concentration (anāgamya);
it is the seventh station of consciousness (vijñānasthiti).
The eighth and ninth abodes of sentient beings depend on the seven [dhyānas] or the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
The seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) are explained at length as in the *Mahābhūta-skandha*.
Among these, because the first station of consciousness is bound exclusively to the desire realm,
it ceases based solely on the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
Because the second station of consciousness is bound to the first dhyāna, [it ceases based on that].
Based on the first dhyāna,
the preparatory stage (anāgamya),
and the intermediate dhyāna.
The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna ceases;
this third station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) belongs to the second dhyāna and thus relies upon both the first and second dhyānas.
The preparatory stage (anāgamya),
the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara),
and the threshold stage (sāmantaka) of the third dhyāna are ceased.
The fourth station of consciousness is associated with the third dhyāna;
it relies upon the first three dhyānas and the preparatory concentration (anāgamya).
The intermediate dhyāna and the preparatory stage of the fourth dhyāna are excluded because they are associated with the fifth station of consciousness, the sphere of infinite space.
Based on the five fundamental [dhyānas],
the preparatory concentration (anāgamya),
and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) ceases;
because the sixth station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) is bound to the sphere of infinite consciousness,
it relies upon the six fundamental [stages].
The preparatory stage (anāgamya),
the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara),
and the threshold stage (sāmantaka) of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
The seventh station of consciousness is bound to the sphere of nothingness;
it relies upon the seven fundamental dhyānas and the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
It is the intermediate dhyāna and the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception that are ceased; however,
the "concentrations" (*samādhi*) mentioned herein are as follows.
Some say they are untainted (*anāsrava*);
others say they are both tainted and untainted, as distinguished previously.
Regarding what is called "cessation," there is no distinction between the two explanations of "cessation by type" and "ultimate cessation," because each is individually bound to only one stage.
The eight worldly dharmas are:
first, gain; second, loss; third, fame; fourth, disrepute; fifth, praise; sixth, blame; seventh, pleasure; and eighth, suffering. Question:
For what reason was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is in order to refute the doctrines of others and to clarify one's own position.
Specifically, this refers to the proponents of the *Vibhajyavāda* and the teachers of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
The Buddha’s physical body is an outflow-free (*anāsrava*) dharma.
For what reason does he speak thus?
It is based on the sūtras; as it is said in the sūtras: [text follows].
The Tathāgata is born into the world, dwells in the world, and appears in the world,
yet he is not defiled by worldly dharmas.
Because he relies upon this, it is said that the Buddha’s birth-body (janmakāya) is an outflow-free dharma (anāsravadharma).
Furthermore, since it is said that the Buddha has eternally severed all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
how could his birth-body (*janmakāya*) possibly be contaminated (*sāsrava*)?
To refute that view and to demonstrate that the Buddha’s birth-body is indeed contaminated and not an uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomenon, this treatise was composed.
Question: How is it known that the Buddha’s birth-body (janma-kāya) is a phenomenon with outflows (sāsrava-dharma)?
Answer: As stated in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know."
Enveloped by ignorance and bound by the fetter of craving,
the fool brings about the acquisition of a conscious body.
The same applies to those who possess intelligence.
Since the Buddha’s birth-body (*janmakāya*) is the fruit of ignorance and craving, it is known that it is not an outflow-free (*anāsrava*) phenomenon.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
Ten bases and a portion of two others are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
From this it is known that the Buddha’s birth-body (*janmakāya*) is certainly with outflows.
If the Buddha’s birth-body were without outflows (*anāsrava*), [it would be so].
The woman Anupamā should not give rise to desire;
Aṅgulimāla should not give rise to hatred;
and Uruvilvākāśyapa—
One should not give rise to delusion;
arrogant Brahmins should not give rise to pride.
Since the Buddha’s physical body gives rise to greed, hatred, delusion, and pride in others, it is known to be definitively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret the sūtra cited there?
Answer: That sūtra speaks with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) regarding the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*.
That is to say, it refers to the Tathāgata being born into the world and abiding in the world.
It is said that the Buddha’s birth-body appears in the world;
that which is not defiled by worldly phenomena is called the Buddha’s Dharma-body.
Furthermore, as for "worldly phenomena":
These are the eight worldly dharmas.
Because the Tathāgata is not defiled by these eight worldly dharmas, it is said that he is unstained by worldly dharmas;
this does not mean, however, that they are untainted (*anāsrava*).
That is to say, the eight worldly dharmas accord with worldly sentient beings,
and worldly sentient beings also accord with the eight worldly dharmas;
yet the eight worldly dharmas also accord with the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata does not conform to the eight worldly dharmas;
therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata is not defiled by worldly dharmas.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata is detached from the eight worldly dharmas.
Therefore, when it is said that he is "unstained," this does not mean he is without outflows (anāsrava).
Question: Since the Tathāgata also possesses the eight worldly dharmas, why is it said that he is detached from them? [The answer is:
There are those who possess gain...
For example, on a single day, the householder Uggera offered three hundred thousand garments to the Buddha;
likewise, on a single day, eighty people, including the physician-king Jīvaka and others, [made offerings].
Each offered the Buddha one hundred thousand pairs of kauseya garments.
As for those who had no profit,
it was as when the Buddha at one time put on his robes and took up his bowl.
He entered the Sāla brahmin village for alms;
he went with an empty bowl and returned with an empty bowl.
He was one who possessed a reputation.
When the Buddha was first born, his fame reached as far as the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
when he attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
his fame reached as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
When he turned the wheel of Dharma, it was said that his fame reached as far as the Brahma Heaven.
Regarding "not being praised":
for example, one day the Buddha encountered the Brahmin woman Ciñcā, who slandered him.
Furthermore, on one occasion, an evil reputation concerning the woman Sundarī spread throughout the sixteen great kingdoms;
there were those who slandered her, such as the Brahmin Akṣamālā of Vārāṇasī.
He reviled the Buddha to his face with five hundred verses.
As for those who praised him,
there was, for example, that very same brahmin.
Because the Buddha’s countenance was no different [from before], he conceived pure faith.
He further praised the Buddha in person with five hundred verses.
The Venerable Śāriputra, for his part, [praised him] with numerous verses.
In the presence [of the Buddha], he praised the unsurpassed qualities of the Buddha.
The Venerable Ānanda, with numerous verses,
praised the rare and wondrous Dharma in the presence [of the Buddha].
In this manner, the great masters of treatises, such as Upāli, Vāgīśa, Nīlabhūti, and others,
all praised the Buddha before him with hundreds of thousands of verses;
there were those who took delight in this.
The Buddha possesses a preeminent body and mind that experience bliss and the bliss of pliancy,
which no sentient being can equal;
yet he is one who still experiences suffering.
The World-Honored One likewise experienced back pain, headaches, and was wounded in the foot by a *kaṭhalla* stone;
furthermore, a flying stone injured his finger and caused it to bleed.
Such phenomena as these were all possessed by the World-Honored One.
Why is it said that he is "detached"?
The answer is: because none of those [conditions] can cause the Buddha to become defiled, he is called "detached.
This means that although the World-Honored Buddha encounters the four conditions such as gain and so forth, his mind does not become elated.
Although encountering the four conditions such as lack of gain, his mind does not sink;
furthermore, although encountering the four conditions such as gain, his mind does not rejoice;
and although encountering the four conditions such as lack of gain, his mind does not become despondent.
Furthermore, although one encounters the four conditions such as gain,
because the mind is not defiled, joy arises;
although one meets with the four conditions such as loss, because the mind does not feel aversion, sorrow arises.
Furthermore, although they encounter the four conditions such as gain, they do not give rise to attachment;
and although they meet with the four conditions such as loss, they do not give rise to aversion.
This is like Sumeru, the king of mountains, which rests upon the golden wheel.
Just as the fierce winds from the eight directions cannot shake it,
so too is the World-Honored One:
abiding upon the golden wheel of ethical discipline, he cannot be moved by the eight worldly winds.
Therefore, it is said that he is not defiled by worldly dharmas.
This does not mean that his physical body is untainted (*anāsrava*) that it is called undefiled.
Question: The Tathāgata has eternally severed all afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
How should it be said that this is "with outflows" (*sāsrava*)?
Answer: Although the various outflows within one's own person have been eternally severed, it can cause the outflows of other persons to increase.
Furthermore, they are called "with outflows" (sāsrava) because various outflows arise from them at an earlier time.
Therefore, this treatise is composed to refute the positions of others and to clarify one's own doctrine.
In this context, "benefit" (hita) refers to...
There are two kinds:
first, that which possesses life;
second, that which is devoid of life.
Benefit pertaining to life refers to obtaining elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, wives, children, servants, and so forth. Benefit not pertaining to life refers to...
[the rest of the sentence is missing from the source].
This refers to obtaining such things as gold, silver, and other treasures, as well as clothing and other articles.
"Lack of gain" means not obtaining the aforementioned two types of things.
"Gain and fame" refers to praise that is not manifest before one's eyes.
"Non-praise" refers to disparaging someone in their absence;
"praise" refers to extolling someone in their presence;
and "disparagement" refers to reviling someone in their presence.
"Bliss" refers to the physical and mental bliss of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Some say it refers exclusively to the bliss associated with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*).
"Suffering" refers to the suffering of body and mind within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Some say it refers exclusively to the suffering associated with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*).
Question: By how many elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and aggregates (skandha) are these eight worldly dharmas subsumed?
Answer: Possession of life and gain are subsumed by seventeen elements, eleven bases, and five aggregates, excluding sound.
Because sound is not constantly present and is dependent upon the body,
it is not included within the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the four elements (*dhātu*), the four bases (*āyatana*), or the one aggregate (*skandha*).
That is to say, the elements and bases of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The elements of benefit, disrepute, non-disrepute, praise, blame, pleasure, and pain, as well as the two bases, are subsumed within three aggregates:

namely, the elements of sound and mental objects (*dharmadhātu*), and the bases [of sound and mental objects], which are subsumed within the aggregates of form, feeling, and formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Among these, that which is neither beneficial nor non-beneficial is subsumed under the dharma-element, the dharma-base, and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*),
because that which is neither [beneficial nor non-beneficial] is non-accomplished (*asiddha*).
Praise, blame, fame, and ill-repute are subsumed under the sound-element and the sound-base, and are included within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Pleasure and pain are subsumed within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), and the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*).

If the eight worldly dharmas are spoken of collectively, they are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Some say that gain and loss are both subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
Because that which is attained and that which is not attained both pertain to the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth.
The rest is as previously explained. Some say:
Gain and non-gain are both subsumed under the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
This is because their essence consists in the nature of accomplishment and non-accomplishment through gain and non-gain.
The rest is as previously explained.
Question: Why are these eight called "worldly dharmas" (*loka-dharma*)?
Answer: They are called worldly dharmas because they are followed by worldly sentient beings.
When worldly sentient beings encounter the four dharmas beginning with gain (*lābha*), their minds become elated.
If one encounters the four conditions such as lack of gain, the mind becomes depressed; furthermore,
if one encounters the four conditions such as gain, joy arises in the mind,
whereas if one encounters the four conditions such as lack of gain, sorrow arises in the mind.
Furthermore, when encountering the four conditions such as gain, the mind becomes defiled and thus gives rise to joy;
when meeting the four conditions such as loss, the mind feels aversion and thus gives rise to sorrow.
Moreover, when encountering the four conditions such as gain, the mind gives rise to attachment.
If one encounters the four conditions such as disadvantage and so forth, the mind gives rise to anger;
therefore, these eight are called worldly dharmas.
Because the Tathāgata does not conform to them in his mind, [he is called the World-Honored One].
It is said that one is not defiled by worldly dharmas.
Question: Since Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have also severed craving and aversion, they likewise do not conform to these eight dharmas;
why, then, are they not mentioned?
The answer is that this is indeterminate.
That is to say, there are those who are undefiled, such as those of immovable dharma,
or there are those who are defiled, such as those of the nature to fall away.
Furthermore, because the followers of the two vehicles still possess residual phenomena that resemble [afflictions],
it is said that although Arhats have severed craving and hatred,
they still possess remaining habitual tendencies that resemble craving and hatred.
For example, there were two arhats, both of whom were liberated at all times (asamayavimukta),
who lived together in the same place; yet one received abundant offerings and a good reputation, while the other did not.
One who attains [these] seems to exalt themselves, as if possessing attachment and delight;
one who does not attain them seems to disparage themselves, as if possessing grief and sorrow.
Therefore, they are not said to be unstained by worldly dharmas.
Only the Buddha has forever uprooted the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of attachment and aversion;
even if all sentient beings were to obtain victory, honor, and renown,
the Tathāgata would not receive even a single hair’s breadth of such gain.
Ultimately, he never degrades himself; though appearing as if in sorrow or distress, he instead gives rise to joy and celebration.
Even if the Buddha alone were to obtain all victory, honor, and renown, while other sentient beings possessed not even a single hair’s breadth of it.
Ultimately, he is never self-exalting; because his compassion arises in opposition to attachment and aversion, the Buddha alone is called "unstained by worldly dharmas.
Furthermore, the World-Honored Buddha does not become arrogant upon gaining profit, for his habitual tendencies have been severed.
He does not become dejected when lacking profit, because he delights in seclusion;
he does not rejoice when gaining praise, because he has severed the habit of attachment;
he does not grieve when receiving dispraise, because he has attained fearlessness.
Praise does not give rise to joy because of the abandonment of the habit of conceit;
blame does not give rise to sorrow because of abiding in the samādhi of emptiness;
and pleasure does not give rise to craving because of abiding in the samādhi of wishlessness.
Because one does not give rise to anger toward suffering by abiding in the signless samādhi,
and because these eight worldly dharmas are bound exclusively to the desire realm,
they are extinguished solely through the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The nine abodes of sentient beings are explained in detail as in the *Mahābhūta-skandha*.
Among them, the meaning of cessation in seven cases is as explained in the *Saptavijñānasthiti*.
The fifth abode of sentient beings is associated with the fourth dhyāna.
Based on the four dhyānas,
the preparatory concentration (anāgamya),
and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space ceases;
this is because the ninth abode of sentient beings is bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
It relies upon the seven fundamental stages.
The preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) are ceased;
however, the "concentration" (*samādhi*) mentioned here refers to these.
Some say it is untainted (*anāsrava*);
others say it is both tainted and untainted, as previously distinguished.
In this context, there is no distinction between the two explanations of the cessation of the category and the ultimate cessation,
because each is individually bound to a single stage (*bhūmi*).
The ten courses of action (*karmapatha*) are explained in detail as in the *Karmaskandha*.
Among these, the ten unwholesome courses of action (akuśala-karmapatha) are bound exclusively to the desire realm (kāmadhātu);
therefore, they are extinguished only by relying on the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The first seven wholesome courses of action are bound to five stages (bhūmi) as well as being unbound.
Those bound to the desire realm are extinguished by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*),
up to and including those bound to the fourth dhyāna.
Based on the four dhyānas,
the preparatory stage (anāgamya),
and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) ceases them.
The final three wholesome courses of action (*kuśala-karmapatha*) are bound to nine stages (*bhūmi*) as well as being unbound.
Those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) cease by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
Up to those bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
they rely on the seven fundamental dhyānas and the threshold concentration (anāgamya-samādhi).
It is extinguished in the intermediate dhyāna;
however, because this discussion refers to the wholesome karmic paths of the desire realm as the immediate antidotes to unwholesome karmic paths,
it is stated that they are extinguished based on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration.
The four dhyānas,
the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments,
and the eight liberations.
Regarding the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), upon which meditative concentration do they depend for their cessation?
Answer: The first depends on either the first dhyāna or the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
The immeasurable joy (*prīti*) of the second dhyāna and the first two liberations (*vimokṣa*) rely on either the two [dhyānas] or the access concentration (*anāgamya*).
The four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) rely on either the two [dhyānas] or the access concentration.
The third dhyāna relies on three [dhyānas] or the access concentration.
The third and fourth dhyānas, the three immeasurables, the pure deliverances,
the latter four spheres of mastery, and the first eight spheres of totality rely upon either the fourth dhyāna or the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The sphere of infinite space,
as well as its corresponding liberation and all-encompassing sphere (kṛtsnāyatana),
rely upon the fifth [dhyāna] or the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The sphere of infinite consciousness,
as well as its corresponding liberation and totalities,
rely on the sixth [dhyāna] or the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The latter two formless attainments and the latter three liberations depend on the seven [dhyānas] or the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
Among these, the four dhyānas up to the ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana) are explained in detail elsewhere.
As for those four dhyānas, they are each bound to their respective stages or are unbound.
Regarding those bound to their own level:
each relies on its own fundamental level, the lower fundamental levels,
and the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
The intermediate dhyāna and the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of the successive higher levels are excluded; however,
that which is called "meditative absorption" (samādhi) is as follows:
The distinction between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) has been analyzed as previously.
Regarding what was stated as "cessation" (*nirodha*),
there is no difference here between the two explanations of cessation by way of category (*prakāra-nirodha*) and ultimate cessation (*atyanta-nirodha*).
Because each is bound to only one specific stage:
among the four immeasurables, the immeasurable joy (muditā) is bound to the first two dhyānas,
and thus relies upon either those two or the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The remaining three immeasurables are bound to four stages;
they depend on either the four dhyānas or the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
Regarding their internal distinctions, they should be understood accordingly as previously described.
However, regarding the "concentration" (samādhi) mentioned, it is either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava), as previously distinguished.
As for the "cessation" (nirodha) mentioned,
some say it is spoken of in terms of cessation by way of category (jāti-nirodha).
Some say this is spoken in reference to ultimate cessation;
it should be analyzed accordingly as previously distinguished.
However, it should be understood that within the *anāgamya* (preparatory) concentration, all instances are exclusively comprised of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Among the four formless attainments,
the first three are each bound to their own respective stages as well as being unbound.
Those bound to their own stages each rely upon the fundamental stages of their own level and those below it.
The preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*),
the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*),
and the proximate stages (*sāmantaka*) of the successive higher levels are ceased.
Subsequently, there is one formless [attainment] which is bound only to its own level;
it relies upon the seven fundamental [dhyānas] and the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
It ceases in the intermediate dhyāna.
Furthermore, as for the concentrations mentioned,
they are classified as either with-outflows (sāsrava) or without-outflows (anāsrava), as previously distinguished.
Regarding the one formless realm that follows, it should be explained solely in terms of the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*).
As for what is described as "cessation," there is no distinction here between the two doctrines of "cessation by type" (*prakāra-nirodha*) and "ultimate cessation" (*atyanta-nirodha*).
Furthermore, each of these is bound exclusively to a single level (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the first two liberations (*vimokṣa*) among the eight liberations,
they are explained in the same manner as the immeasurable joy (*muditā*).
The liberations of the lower three formless realms are as explained for the lower three formless [attainments].
The latter two liberations are as explained for the fourth formless [attainment].
The pure liberation is bound to the level of the fourth dhyāna.
Based on the four dhyānas,
the preparatory stage (anāgamya),
and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space is extinguished;
herein, both the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that has been described and the cessation (*nirodha*) that has been described [are brought to an end].
All are as explained for the fourth dhyāna.
Among the eight spheres of mastery (abhibhv-āyatana), the first four spheres of mastery are as explained for the first two liberations (vimokṣa).
The latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are as explained in the case of the pure liberations (*śubha-vimokṣa*).
Among the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the first eight totalities are as explained in the case of the latter four spheres of mastery.
This is because the totality of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-kṛtsnāyatana*) is bound exclusively to its own level.
Based on the five fundamental [dhyānas],
the threshold concentration (anāgamya),
and the intermediate dhyāna.
The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) ceases [therein],
and the totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) of the sphere of infinite consciousness is also bound exclusively to its own level; thus,
it relies upon the six fundamental [dhyānas].
The preparatory concentration (anāgamya),
the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara),
and the threshold stage (sāmantaka) of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
However, regarding the "concentration" (samādhi) mentioned here,
it is either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava), as previously distinguished.
As for the "cessation" (nirodha) that is mentioned:
Furthermore, there is no distinction between the two theories regarding the extinction of categories or ultimate extinction,
as each is exclusively bound to its own level (*svabhūmi*).
Upon which meditative concentration do the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) depend for their extinction?
Answer: The knowledge of others' minds relies on four dhyānas or the *anāgamya*;
conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) relies on seven or the *anāgamya*.
Herein, the knowledge of others' minds and conventional knowledge are explained in detail elsewhere.
However, the knowledge of others' minds is bound to four stages or is unbound;
that which is bound to the first dhyāna relies upon the first dhyāna.
The preparatory stage (*anāgamya*),
the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*),
and the threshold stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna are ceased.
Up to those bound to the fourth dhyāna,
they rely upon the four dhyānas and the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
It is extinguished in the intermediate dhyāna and in the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space; however,
the "concentration" (*samādhi*) mentioned here refers to this.
The contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [factors] are to be distinguished as previously analyzed.
Regarding what was said about "cessation" (*nirodha*), some say:
It is said that this is explained according to cessation by way of category;
others say it is explained according to ultimate cessation.
It should also be analyzed accordingly as before.
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is bound to nine stages;
that which is bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) ceases based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
Up to those bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
they rely on the seven fundamental dhyānas and the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
It ceases in the intermediate dhyāna;
however, the meditative absorptions and cessations mentioned herein are all to be analyzed as previously explained, according to their respective applicability.
For this reason, it is said that [the cessation] depends on the seven [dhyānas] or the threshold concentration (anāgamya).

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Four: The Non-Returner (Anāgāmin). Within the Seventh Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhi-skandha), Part One of Section Four: The Non-Returner. There are five types of non-returners.
That is to say: parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state,
parinirvāṇa upon rebirth,
and parinirvāṇa with exertion.
Attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin) and the upstreamer (ūrdhvasrotas) who goes to the Akaniṣṭha heaven—
these five comprise all [the types of non-returners].
Are all [factors] subsumed within the five [aggregates]?
Having thus mastered the meaning of these chapters and their respective commentaries, one should provide a detailed analysis.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As the sūtra states, there are five types of non-returners (anāgāmin), namely those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin).
This is explained at length.
Although that sutra makes this statement,
it does not explicitly clarify that these five categories encompass everything.
Although all [categories] are subsumed within the five,
their distinctions of superiority and inferiority have never been explicitly revealed.
Now, wishing to clarify them in full detail, this treatise is composed.
Does the fivefold [classification] encompass all, or do all things encompass the fivefold?
Answer: All things encompass the fivefold, but the fivefold does not encompass all.
What is not included?
Namely, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life,
and those non-returners who go to the formless realm.
In this context, because everything is for the most part not five,
everything subsumes the five, but the five do not subsume everything.
It is like a large vessel covering a small one, whereas a small vessel does not cover a large one.
"All" refers to the seven types of non-returners (anāgāmin): namely, the aforementioned five,
along with those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life (dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin),
and those who go to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Among these, the latter two are called "many" because they are not subsumed within the five [types of parinirvāṇa].
Question: Are there also those who attain parinirvāṇa without fixed certainty?
That is to say, some attain parinirvāṇa within the desire realm.
Some attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
and some attain parinirvāṇa in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Why is this not mentioned here?
Regarding the fact that he promised to speak but did not, one should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, because he is already included within the seven types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*), he is not mentioned separately;
that is to say, if he attains parinirvāṇa while in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This is subsumed under parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyī*).
Those who attain parinirvāṇa in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are subsumed under the five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
Those who attain parinirvāṇa in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are subsumed under the non-returners who go to the formless realms (*ārūpyaga-anāgāmin*).
Question: There are also those who attain parinirvāṇa after being reborn [once more].
That is to say, they may be those who are "at most seven times reborn" (saptakṛtparama) or those who go from family to family (kulaṃkula).
Either from the stage of a once-returner or from the stage of an antarābhava, one attains the fruit of non-returning;
having attained that fruit, one will necessarily attain parinirvāṇa in this very life.
He does not attain parinirvāṇa in the present life.
For a sūtra explains: "What is parinirvāṇa in the present life?
It refers to one who, in this very birth, attains the fruit of stream-entry."
By progressing to sever the remaining fetters, one attains the fruit of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat.
For this reason, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin) are not included among the seven types [of stream-enterers].
Why, then, are they not mentioned here?
One should know that there is more to be said regarding those who have promised to speak but do not.
Furthermore, because they have become weary of rebirth, once they have attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala),
they enter parinirvāṇa before very long has passed.
Because the duration of that interval is extremely brief,
it does not permit the establishment [of a distinct category], and thus it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, since it is also subsumed within parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāṇa*), it is not mentioned separately.
Since one attains the fruit of non-returner based on this very life and enters parinirvāṇa in that same life,
which is superior: parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state or parinirvāṇa upon being reborn?
Answer: If one abides in the abandonment of [the fetters] equally, then the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) is superior.
If one attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin), then he is superior because he has abandoned more fetters.
That is to say, these two types of non-returners (anāgāmin) both possess the full set of fetters belonging to the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, if one has abandoned the first eight grades of fetters of the fourth dhyāna,
then the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) is superior by virtue of three factors.
First, they undergo less suffering, as they experience the suffering of only a single existence.
Because they experience the suffering of the two types of existence,
(1) they swiftly extinguish the fire of the afflictions;
(2) they quickly cast off the burden of the aggregates.
If one attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin),
they possess the fetters of the first dhyāna up to the severing of the seven grades of fetters prior to the fourth dhyāna;
one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin) has severed the first grade of fetter of the first dhyāna.
Up to the point where one has abandoned the first eight categories of fetters of the fourth dhyāna,
one attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; this is superior by virtue of a single factor,
namely, abiding in a state of extensive abandonment.
From attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state up to the upstreamer who goes to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
What is superior? The answer is: if one abides in equal abandonment [of defilements], then parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāṇa) is superior;
if, up to the highest stream (ūrdhvasrotas), one abandons many fetters while proceeding to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, then that is superior.

This refers to one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*). Whether compared with one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*) or one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*),
it is all as explained in the case of one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*).
If one proceeds upward to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, there is a difference regarding the suffering experienced;
that is to say, this person experiences the suffering of only one existence,
whereas that person experiences the suffering of at least four existences.
The rest is as previously explained. Thus,

from those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadya-parinirvāyin) up to those who go upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven (ūrdhvasrotas), there are those who attain parinirvāṇa through application (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin).

Up to the point of the "up-streamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin*) while proceeding to Akaniṣṭha—among these up-streamers proceeding to Akaniṣṭha, which is superior?
Answer: If they abide in equal abandonment, then those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) and so forth are superior.
If there are those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) and so forth, they are superior to others because they have severed more fetters;
that is to say, among these various non-returners (*anāgāmin*), each is distinguished according to their respective counterparts.
Furthermore, if all of them are equally bound by the fetters of the first dhyāna, [they are further distinguished by other factors].
Furthermore, if one has abandoned the first eight grades of fetters of the fourth dhyāna,
then one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadya-parinirvāyin) is superior to one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin) by virtue of this single factor.
That is to say, for one who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth, there is both the path of effort and the path of swift progress.
For one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion, there is only the path of effort and no path of swift progress.
One who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion is superior by virtue of two factors.
Because he lacks both the path of diligent cultivation and the path of rapid progress,
he is superior to those who ascend to the Akaniṣṭha heaven by virtue of one factor:
namely, that he undergoes less suffering, whereas they undergo the suffering of two existences.
Because he experiences the suffering of the four existences for the shortest possible time,

the one who attains parinirvāṇa through application (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin) is superior to the one who attains parinirvāṇa without application (anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin) by virtue of a single factor:
this former one practices the path with exertion.
Because both of those are absent,
the one who goes upstream to Akaniṣṭha is superior by virtue of one factor;
likewise, the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion is superior to the one who goes upstream to Akaniṣṭha by virtue of one factor.
All is as previously explained.
If one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadya-parinirvāyin) and so forth possesses the fetters of the first dhyāna,
up to having abandoned the seven grades of fetters of the fourth dhyāna.
Those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*) and so forth, having abandoned one category of fetters of the first dhyāna,
up to having abandoned the first eight categories of fetters of the fourth dhyāna,
are those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion and so forth.
They are superior in terms of a single matter regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth and so forth;
that is to say, they abide in the abandonment of many [defilements].
Furthermore, the Saṃgītiparyāya states:
There are five types of non-returner (anāgāmin) individuals:
namely, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin),
up to those who go upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven (ūrdhvasrotas).
What is one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state?
It refers to a person (pudgala) who, in a previous life, has already abandoned and fully understood the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni),
but has not yet abandoned or fully understood the five higher fetters (pañca ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni).
He performs and accumulates karma conducive to the arising of existence (*bhava*),
but does not perform and accumulate karma conducive to birth in existence.
At the end of that life, he arises as an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
While abiding in that intermediate state (antarābhava), one attains a type of untainted path (anāsravamārga) of such a kind;
by the power of this path, one proceeds to sever the remaining fetters and enters parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu).
This is called parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*). If one asks why it is called parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, the answer is:
this *pudgala* has already transcended the desire realm but has not yet reached the form realm;
because he attains parinirvāṇa while dwelling in that intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), he is called one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Furthermore, because this person possesses sharp faculties and mild afflictions, they are able to attain parinirvāṇa within the intermediate state (antarābhava);
therefore, they are called one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Furthermore, this person first attains a state of mind with mental activity.
Immediately after a mind of training (śaikṣa), one may attain a mind of no-more-training (aśaikṣa).

Immediately after a mind of no-more-training, one may attain a mind that is neither of training nor of no-more-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa). Immediately after a mind that is neither of training nor of no-more-training, one may attain a mind of training. Immediately after a mind of training, one may attain a mind of no-more-training. Immediately after a mind of no-more-training, one may attain a mind that is neither of training nor of no-more-training.
Because one attains parinirvāṇa while remaining in that very state of mind, it is called "parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyī).
Question: By what distinction is this term intended?
Answer: It is intended to distinguish [this type of noble one] from other noble ones.
That is to say, for other noble ones (ārya), immediately after a mind of training (śaikṣa-citta),
either a mind beyond training (aśaikṣa-citta) arises, or a mind that is neither training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-citta) arises;
this is not the case here, for immediately after a mind of training, a mind beyond training must necessarily arise.
In other noble ones, there may be parinirvāṇa immediately after a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
or they may again give rise to a non-learner mind; this is not the case here.

One who attains parinirvāṇa in the meditative absorption immediately following a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner does so because other noble ones repeatedly bring the noble path into manifestation,
whereas this [attainer] does not do so repeatedly.
What is one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth?
It refers to a person (pudgala) who,
in a previous birth, has already abandoned and fully understood the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni).
While the five higher fetters have not yet been abandoned or fully understood,
one performs and accumulates karma conducive to the arising of existence and karma conducive to birth in existence.
Having passed away from that state, he arises in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the form realm and is born among the gods of the form realm.
Not long after being born, he attains such a type of untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).
By the power of this path, he further severs the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*).
One attains parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana with remainder;
this is called "parinirvāṇa upon birth.
Question: For what reason is it called "parinirvāṇa upon birth"?
Answer: This person, having been born there not long ago, attains the fruit of arhatship and enters parinirvāṇa;
therefore, they are called one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadya-parinirvāyin).
Furthermore, this person,
not long after being born there, attains the fruit of arhatship and enters parinirvāṇa at the exhaustion of his lifespan.
Therefore, they are called those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*).
Question: If they attain parinirvāṇa only at the end of their lifespan, why are they called those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth?
Answer: This is explained in terms of nirvāṇa with respect to the afflictions (*kleśa*), not in terms of nirvāṇa with respect to the aggregates (*skandha*); therefore, there is no fault.
What is "attaining parinirvāṇa through application" (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī*)?
It refers to a person who, in a previous life, relied upon the path with exertion and constant mental attention,
and through a samādhi of uninterrupted application,
had already abandoned and fully understood the five lower fetters.
While the five higher fetters (pañca-ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana) have not been abandoned or fully understood,
one performs and accumulates karma conducive to the arising of existence and karma conducive to rebirth in existence.
Having passed away from there, he arises in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm and is born among the gods of the form realm.
After having been born for a long time,
he again relies upon the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Constantly maintaining mental attention,
relying on the samādhi of uninterrupted application,
he proceeds to sever the remaining fetters and attains parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana with remainder.
This is called parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī*).
Question: Why is it called parinirvāṇa with exertion?
Answer: Because this *pudgala* [attains it] by means of the path with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-mārga*).
Having abandoned the remaining afflictions, one attains parinirvāṇa;
therefore, this is called "parinirvāṇa through exertion" (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin).
Furthermore, this person attains the fruit of arhatship by means of the path with exertion.
He attains parinirvāṇa at the exhaustion of his lifespan;
therefore, he is called one who attains parinirvāṇa through application (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin).
Furthermore, this person relies upon the path that has conditioned phenomena as its object.
One who proceeds to sever the remaining fetters and attains parinirvāṇa is therefore called one who attains parinirvāṇa through application of effort (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*).
What is one who attains parinirvāṇa without application of effort (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*)?
It refers to a person who, in a previous life, relied upon the path of non-attachment and did not constantly attend to it,
and relying on the samādhi of the practice of tranquility,
has already abandoned and fully understood the five lower fetters.
While the five fetters binding one to the higher realms have not been abandoned or fully understood,
one performs and increases karma conducive to the arising of existence and karma conducive to birth in existence.
Having passed away from that state, they arise as an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) in the form realm and are born among the gods of the form realm.
After a long time has passed since birth,
they again rely on the path of non-action and do not constantly apply mental attention.
Relying on the samādhi of the application of cessation,
one proceeds to sever the remaining fetters and attains parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana with remainder;
this is called "parinirvāṇa without exertion."
Question: Why is it called "attaining parinirvāṇa through non-application"?
Answer: Because this person attains parinirvāṇa by severing the remaining afflictions through the path of non-application.
Therefore, he is called one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion.
Furthermore, this person, by means of the path without exertion,
attains the fruit of arhatship and enters parinirvāṇa at the exhaustion of his lifespan.
Therefore, he is called one who attains parinirvāṇa through non-exertion (asaṃskāra-parinirvāyin).
Furthermore, this person, relying on the path that takes the unconditioned as its object,
proceeds to sever the remaining fetters and attains parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, this is called "attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion.
What is meant by "one who goes upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven"?
It refers to a person (pudgala) who, in a previous birth, has already abandoned and fully understood the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni).
While the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*) have not yet been abandoned or fully understood,
he attains the four mundane dhyānas; then,
at the time of death, he regresses from the upper three dhyānas and abides in the first dhyāna.
Due to that very craving and the karma conducive to the arising of existence (*bhava*)— which was performed and accumulated in that stage—
as well as the karma conducive to birth in existence,
one passes away from there and arises in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to be born among the Brahmakāyika devas.
Having been born, they are further able to enter the second dhyāna of the conventional realm;
by means of craving for that very state and through the power of that stage,
they perform and accumulate karma conducive to the arising of existence-experiencing (*bhavavedanīya*).
Because it is karma to be experienced in the next birth,
he passes away from that state and is reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
having been reborn there, he is further able to enter the third dhyāna of the mundane level.
By means of that very craving, up until the end of life there, one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
Having been born there, one is again able to enter the worldly fourth dhyāna;
by means of that very craving, up until the end of life there, one is born in the Bṛhatphala Heaven.
Having been born there, they are further able to initiate the inferior degree of mixed cultivation of the fourth mundane dhyāna;
through that very craving, they eventually pass away from there and are reborn in the Avṛha heaven.
In this manner, even up to the point where one has practiced the mixed mundane fourth dhyāna across the other four categories,
one sequentially gives rise to [the meditative states] in the other four heavens and is sequentially reborn in those other four heavens.
This is called "the upstreamer who goes to Akaniṣṭha.
Question: Why is he called "the upstreamer who goes to Akaniṣṭha"?
Answer: There are two kinds of "flowing" (srotas).
First, the craving for existence;
second, karma leading to future existence.
This person has neither abandoned nor fully understood these two types of fluxes.
By virtue of this being the condition and the cause,
one ascends and follows upward;
one goes up and follows along upward.
Because they ascend and follow along by ascending,
and flow upward and follow along by flowing upward,
they are called those who "ascend to the Akaniṣṭha heaven."
Furthermore, this person does not descend, but rather proceeds superiorly, attaining a meditative absorption that becomes increasingly higher, more sublime, and more excellent;
he is born having entered that absorption and experiences birth therein.
Therefore, they are called "those who go upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Furthermore, because this *pudgala* ascends and is reborn in higher realms, causing that upward rebirth to continue in succession, they are called "upstream-goers" (*ūrdhva-srotas*).

Question: Since ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) also undergo upward migration (*ūrdhvasrotas*) and are born in higher realms, causing their continuity to ascend, why are they not called "those who flow upwards"?
Answer: Only those who flow exclusively upward and do not flow downward are designated as "those who flow upwards."
Because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) also undergo downward-streaming (*adhogāmin*), they are not designated as "upward-streamers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
Some say that one who streams upward and is unimpeded in all places is called an upward-streamer.
Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are not called "those who go upstream" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) because they lack unimpeded movement in all places;
this is because they encounter obstructions regarding the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Question: Noble ones (*ārya*) who go upstream also encounter obstructions in two places.
This refers to the Great Brahmā King and the station of non-perception.
Why are they called "those who go upstream"?
The answer is: because they have no separate locations, being subsumed within the two stations of the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita) and Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala).
It may still be called "pervading all places.
Some say that if one who is destined to ascend (ūrdhva-srotas) can transcend the realms and attain the fruit [of Arhatship], [they are so designated].
One who has eternally severed the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni) is called an "Upstreamer" (ūrdhva-srotas).
Although ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) may transcend the realms, they do not attain the fruit [of the path];
furthermore, because they have not eternally severed the five lower fetters, they are not called Upstreamers.
Some say that one who possesses three kinds of flows is called an "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas); namely,
the flow of karma, the flow of afflictions, and the flow of the Noble Path.
Ordinary beings possess only the flow of karma and afflictions, lacking the flow of the noble path; therefore, they are not termed "those who go upstream.
Furthermore, there are two types of those who go upstream:
first, those who proceed to the form realm.
There are two types of practice:
those who practice in the realm of form, extending up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven;
and those who practice in the formless realm, extending up to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana Heaven.
Furthermore, those who proceed to the form realm (rūpadhātu) practice the meditative absorption of mixed cultivation (vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna),
whereas those who proceed to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) do not practice mixed cultivation.
Moreover, there are three types of those who ascend (ūrdhvasrotas).
There are three types: (1) the full leap, (2) the half-leap, and (3) death in every location.
Regarding the full leap: one dies in the desire realm and is born in the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude;
from the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude, one dies and is born in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Or one may be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and attain parinirvāṇa there.
Regarding the "half-leaper" (ardhapluta): having passed away from the desire realm, one is born in the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (Brahmapāriṣadya).
Having passed away from the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude, one is reborn in one, two, three, four, or five of the higher celestial abodes.
Or, having transcended even a single stage and been born universally in the remaining stages, they are subsequently born in Akaniṣṭha;
or they are born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception and there attain parinirvāṇa.
"Dying in all places" means dying in the desire realm and being born among the Brahmakāyika gods;
dying among the Brahmakāyikas and being born among the Brahmapurohita gods; and so on in succession through the higher realms up to being born among the Bṛhatphala gods.
From this point upward, there are two distinct paths:
first, entry into the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa);
second, entry into the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Those who enter the Pure Abodes pass away from the Bṛhatphala heaven and are reborn in the Avṛha heaven;
proceeding in this manner through the successive stages until they are reborn in the Akaniṣṭha heaven, they attain parinirvāṇa.
Those who enter the formless realm pass away from the Bṛhatphala heaven and are reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Space.
Proceeding in sequence up to being born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and there attaining parinirvāṇa—
just as there are two distinct paths for passing away from every stage,
one should know that this applies equally to the "complete leaper" (sakalābhisamghātī) and the "half-leaper" (ardhapluta).
Question: What kind of *ūrdhvasrotas* (one who flows upwards) enters the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), and what kind of *ūrdhvasrotas* enters the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Answer: There are two types of *ūrdhvasrotas*: those whose practice is characterized by insight (*vipaśyanā-carita*) and those whose practice is characterized by tranquility (*śamatha-carita*).
The practitioner of vipaśyanā enters the Śuddhāvāsa heavens;
the practitioner of śamatha enters the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, there are two types of "those who go upstream" (*ūrdhvasrotas*): those who delight in superior meditative concentration and those who delight in superior rebirth.
Those who delight in superior meditative concentration enter the Pure Abodes;
those who delight in superior rebirth enter the Formless Realm.
Furthermore, there are two types of "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas): those who delight in discernment and those who delight in tranquility.
Those who delight in discernment enter the Pure Abodes;
those who delight in tranquility enter the Formless Realm.
Furthermore, there are two types of "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas): those who practice mixed cultivation and those who do not.
Those who practice mixed cultivation enter the Pure Abodes;
those who do not practice mixed cultivation enter the Formless Realm.
Furthermore, in all cases, the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas) is characterized by coming from above rather than going there.
There are those manifested by going but not by coming;
there are those manifested by both coming and going;
and there are those manifested by coming but not by going.
This refers to those born in Akaniṣṭha or the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception who are manifested by going but not by coming; that is,
those born among the Brahmakāyika devas.
There are those manifested by coming and also manifested by going;
that is to say, those born in the intermediate states.
There are none that are neither manifested by coming nor manifested by going.
Question: As previously stated regarding those who proceed to Akaniṣṭha,
they first attain the four mundane dhyānas and subsequently regress to abide in the first dhyāna.
As for those who proceed to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
do they also first attain the four mundane formless attainments,
and subsequently regress to abide in the first dhyāna?
Answer: There is also such a case.
For example, one who first attains the four mundane dhyānas, later regresses and abides in the first dhyāna, and then passes away to be reborn in the Brahma-world.
Proceeding in this manner, one may even be born in the Akaniṣṭha heaven. Likewise,
there are those who first attain the four mundane dhyānas and the four formless attainments,
but later, having regressed and abiding in the first dhyāna, they pass away and are reborn in the Brahma-world.
Proceeding through successive stages up to birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), yet it is not necessarily so.
Question: Why is it not stated that one falls back from the first dhyāna?
Answer: There is no one who passes away after falling back from the first dhyāna; therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, this passage clarifies the distinctions among non-returners (anāgāmin); since one who falls back from the first dhyāna is no longer a non-returner, it is not mentioned.

Question: As it has been said that those who fall back from their attainment and dwell in the first dhyāna are born among the Brahmakāyika devas, and having passed away from all stages, they become "up-streamers" (ūrdhvasrotas)—
whether by "complete leaping over" (sakalābhisamkrama) or "half-leaping over" (ardhābhisamkrama)—
if such a person falls back from that state and dwells in the second dhyāna, they are born among the Parīttābha devas.
Falling back from the third dhyāna, one is reborn among the Parīttābha devas;
falling back from the fourth dhyāna, one is reborn among the Anabhraka devas and so forth.
These too may perform the "full leap" (kṛtsnātikrānta) or the "half-leap" (ardhātikrānta).
Is it not the case that one who dies in every location is necessarily an *ūrdhva-srotas* (one who flows upwards)? Answer:
Some say this is not so, because when one is born in the Brahma-world, there is no deficiency regarding the places where one ought to be reborn in the higher realms as a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Based on that, the "leap-over" (*pluta*) and "half-leap-over" (*ardhapluta*) are established.
Since one who dies in every location and is reborn in a higher plane would lack [the required sequence],
the leap-over and so forth are not established based on that.
Some say that this too is called "half-leaping" because one leaps over a small portion of the intermediate stage.
Others say:
They also obtain the name "complete" (sakala) in three ways;

it is said that from death in the desire realm, wherever one is reborn, one may likewise be designated as having "leaped entirely" (sakalātyudgata), "half-leaped" (ardhātyudgata), or having died in all places.
Question: If a non-returner (anāgāmin) dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the formless realm, can they also achieve the "complete leaping over" (*atyantātyaya*) and other such attainments?
Answer: Some say they cannot;
others say they can.
He is also called "Half-Transcender.
Some say that he is also fully designated by all three names; the reasons for this are all as explained previously.
Question: As with those who go upstream to Akaniṣṭha,
must they first fall away from the four dhyānas and be reborn in the Brahma world before they can proceed to the Akaniṣṭha heaven?
Regarding those who ascend to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana),
must they necessarily first attain the four formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti), fall away from them,
and be reborn in the Brahma-world before they are able to proceed to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Answer: It is not necessarily so.
Because one born in the form realm cannot initially initiate the mixed cultivation of dhyāna;
it is only when one has previously initiated it during a time in the desire realm and now cultivates it again that one is able to proceed to Akaniṣṭha.
For those born in the formless realm, there is no longer such superior class of karma;
one must have previously arisen [in the desire realm] and now cultivate it again before being able to be born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Therefore, those who go to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) are of two types:

those who first attain the formless realms and then fall back from them, and those who, having not previously attained them, die in the desire realm and are born among the Brahmakāyika gods; both are able to reach the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).

Question: Is it the case that those described as "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas) are exclusively those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), or are there also those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta)?
Answer: If one is an Upstreamer who does not fall back from the higher meditative absorptions, this applies to both types.
If one who has regressed from a higher meditative absorption is an "upward-streamer" (ūrdhvasrotas), they are exclusively those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta).
Furthermore, even those upward-streamers who have regressed from a higher absorption may belong to both types.
Question: How does that one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) regress?
The answer is: they do not attain the stage of "vision-attainment" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) by their original nature;

rather, after falling away [from a higher stage] and before death, they refine their faculties through faith-resolve (śraddhādhimukta) to attain vision-attainment, and subsequently, at the end of life, they are born in the higher realms as those who proceed upstream (ūrdhvasrotas).
Question: Is there parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāṇa) within the desire realm (kāmadhātu), just as there is in the form realm (rūpadhātu)?
Answer: No.
Question: For what reason?
Answer: The desire realm is an indeterminate realm; it is neither a stage of cultivation nor a stage of freedom from defilement. It abounds in faults, calamities, and obstacles.
Even while abiding in its state of innate existence (*sahaja-bhava*), it is difficult to attain the fruit.
How much more so for one dwelling in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) with a subtle and inferior body?
Since this is not the case in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), those dwelling in the intermediate state are able to attain parinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, if one were to attain parinirvāṇa while dwelling in the intermediate state of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), then by means of that intermediate state, one would transcend the three realms.
However, there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) body that can transcend the three realms.
Furthermore, if one were to attain parinirvāṇa while abiding in the intermediate state of the desire realm,
then one would have to sever the afflictions of the three realms within that intermediate state.
However, within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there exists a body capable of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms.

Furthermore, if one attains parinirvāṇa while abiding in the intermediate state of the desire realm, then within that intermediate state one can sever both types of afflictions: the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the neutral (*avyākṛta*).
However, within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there exists a body capable of severing the two kinds of afflictions—the unwholesome and the neutral.

Furthermore, if one attains parinirvāṇa while abiding in the intermediate state of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), then within that intermediate state one can realize either two or three fruits of the śramaṇa.
However, because one can realize either two or three fruits of the śramaṇa within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) while not yet dwelling in [the next life],
for this reason there is parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state only in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), but not in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) must have already abandoned the defilements of the desire realm in a previous birth.
One who has already abandoned the defilements of the desire realm will certainly not give rise to an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm.
Therefore, there is no parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, the afflictions and karma of the desire realm are heavy;
they cannot be eliminated and severed within the subtle and inferior body of the intermediate state.
Furthermore, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not a basis for attaining the fruit of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*),
but is rather a basis for attaining the fruit of an Arhat (*arhat*).
Furthermore, an intermediate state being of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is necessarily unable to give rise to the manifestation of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), because it is weak and inferior.
It is not so in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
For this reason, there is no parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāṇa*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Furthermore, because the intermediate state is subtle and weak, it can only bring forth the noble path (*āryamārga*) of its own fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*), and not that of the *anāgamya* stage or others, as those are difficult to arouse.
If there were those who attain parinirvāṇa within the desire realm, it would contradict this [principle], and therefore such a thing is necessarily non-existent.
Furthermore, in the desire realm, there exist afflictions that are associated with both opposition and conformity.
There are afflictions of the six external doors that are capable of inducing two fruits;
there are afflictions associated with lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*);
and there are various miscellaneous secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth.
It is difficult to shatter, difficult to sever, difficult to transcend, and difficult to abandon.
If it is already difficult to eliminate while one dwells in the fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*) despite exerting great effort,
how much more so when one is in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*)?
Therefore, there is no parinirvāṇa within the intermediate state (antarābhava) of the desire realm.
Furthermore, one must have previously fully cultivated the nine grades of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) in order to be capable of attaining parinirvāṇa within the intermediate state.
Since the intermediate state of the desire realm has not yet fully cultivated the nine grades of antidotes, one does not attain parinirvāṇa in that intermediate state.

Question: Just as one who passes away from the desire realm and receives an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm may attain parinirvāṇa, is it likewise the case that one who passes away from the form realm and receives an intermediate state of the form realm may also attain parinirvāṇa?
Answer: No. Why is this?

Because they have developed an extreme sense of revulsion toward the body in the desire realm, which is full of suffering, full of obstacles, full of calamities and misfortunes, and is utterly loathsome.
Once they have abandoned [the desire realm] and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm has arisen before them,
they also develop weariness toward the long-term maturation (*vipāka*) that is yet to be experienced, and thereby attain parinirvāṇa.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are no such calamities or extremely loathsome matters that would cause revulsion;
however, because there are objective conditions and obstructions regarding one's original existence, one does not attain parinirvāṇa there.
Now, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is likewise.
Therefore, the intermediate state that arises upon passing away from there does not attain parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, if one were to attain parinirvāṇa in that very intermediate state after passing away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), [it would follow that]...
If they were also to be called "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas), then the five types of Non-returners (anāgāmin) would become confused;
for there would be no distinguishing cause or condition [to differentiate them],

except that one who dies in the desire realm and attains parinirvāṇa while abiding in the intermediate state (antarābhava) is called an "One Who Attains Parinirvāṇa in the Intermediate State" (antarāparinirvāyin).
Furthermore, one who has not died in the form realm lacks the causes and conditions to proceed from there to a higher plane and thus is not called an "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas).
Due to this fault, such an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) does not attain parinirvāṇa.

Question: If one who dies in the desire realm and arises as an intermediate being (*antarābhava*) in the form realm attains *nirvāṇa* due to revulsion, why does one not attain *nirvāṇa* immediately within the fundamental existence (*pūrvakālabhava*) of the desire realm?
Because their revulsion increases.

The answer is: having abided in the state of "prior existence" (pūrvakālabhava) and attained the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala), they initiate the preparatory application (prayoga) for the fruit of arhatship;
since their application is perfected, they pass away immediately before the Noble Path (āryamārga) has arisen.
By the power of their previous exertion, they are able to proceed into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), sever the remaining fetters, and attain parinirvāṇa.
Question: Since their preparatory application was perfected, why do they not give rise to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) before passing away?

The answer is: it may be because their lifespan has ended, or because their karma has been exhausted, or because their merit has been exhausted, or because they were harmed by others, or for the sake of benefiting others, or because they encountered adverse conditions against their will.
He passed away before he could give rise to the Noble Path.
Some say that he attained the fruit of a Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
When the subsequent preparatory application has already been cultivated and is about to reach completion, one may encounter the causes and conditions of long-term illness,
a deficiency of requisites,
or various obstacles such as those pertaining to life itself; thus, unable to exhaust the outflows, one passes through these successive stages until the end of life.
Having attained the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the form realm, by the predominant power of the newly acquired aggregates, sense faculties, and primary elements,
one is swiftly able to bring forth the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), advance toward it, sever the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*), and enter parinirvāṇa.

Question: Is it also the case that one who passes away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) may likewise attain parinirvāṇa upon birth (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*), and so forth?
Answer: Yes.
This is because there are those who, passing away from the desire realm and being born in the two higher realms, attain parinirvāṇa without being born again.
Wherever one may be situated within those births, the three types of birth and so forth can all be established;
this is because, in every such case, one can be established as an "Upstreamer" (Urdhvasrotas).
Question: Regarding those who delight in wisdom (*prajñā-ruci*) but do not reach the Akaniṣṭha heaven,
and those who delight in meditative concentration (*samādhi-ruci*) but do not reach the Bhavāgra,
can those who attain parinirvāṇa in the lower realms also be designated as "those who stream upward" (*ūrdhva-srotas*) through either delight in wisdom or delight in concentration?
The answer is that these two names are also applied according to their respective types.
However, the statement that those who delight in wisdom reach up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven,
