while those who delight in concentration reach up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), is made in reference to the ultimate limits of those realms.
Because beyond this there is no further place for rebirth.

For example, a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) may be called "one who returns at most seven times" (*saptakṛtvah-parama*), yet one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) also receives this name; it is the same in this case. One might ask: why is it that a noble one (*ārya*) undergoes only one birth in each of the upper two realms, whereas in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) it is not so?

Answer: Because the desire realm is an indeterminate realm and a ground of confusion, where various afflictions and karmas mutually assail and intermingle without fixed boundaries or rules, it causes noble ones to be born from lower levels to higher ones, and from higher levels back down again.
Alternatively, one may undergo many births in a single location.
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) and the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) are fixed realms rather than grounds of confusion,
because the various afflictions and karmas do not intermingle there, as they possess distinct boundaries and formal regulations.
This would imply that noble ones are reborn only above and never below, or in only one place, and only once in a single lifetime.

Furthermore, a noble one born in the desire realm would not be called a "Non-returner" (anāgāmin), yet they are so designated because they are subject to at most seven more existences (*saptakṛtvah-parama*); thus, they must also be reborn both above and below, and in multiple places.
The noble ones born in the higher realms are called "Non-returners" (*anāgāmin*); thus, they are born only in the higher realms and are never born there again.
By this definition, the meaning of "Non-returner" is fulfilled, for since they do not even return to their original realm, how much less could they return to be born below?
Furthermore, there are immeasurable varieties of non-returning *pudgalas* when explained in detail.
For now, we shall distinguish the five types who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
It should be understood that these are spoken of as "one" because they are established based on the realm (*dhātu*).
They are said to be two based on the distinction between those who attain birth and those who do not;
they are said to be five based on the distinction of their specific states, namely:
those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, up to those who go upstream.
Because the Akaniṣṭha realm is established by means of these very faculties, fifteen are taught;
that is, the lower, middle,
and superior faculties each establish five stages, thus twenty are taught.
This refers to the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna;
because each is established with five types of dispositions (*gotra*), they are said to be thirty.
That is, from the disposition of one subject to retrogression (*parihāṇadharman*) up to the disposition of one who is immovable (*akopyadharman*).
They are said to be eighty because each [of the heavens] is established with five locations,
namely from the Brahmakāyika heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
They are said to be ninety because each is established with five types of spiritual faculties (indriya).
That is to say, for each of the lineages—those of the dharma-of-retrogression (parihāṇadharman) with inferior, medium, and superior faculties—there are five [types] each;
this applies likewise up to the lineage of the immovable dharma (akopyadharman).
Because they are established according to their stages and lineages, there are said to be one hundred and twenty.
This means that for each of the six types [of practitioners] in the first dhyāna there are five [levels], and so it is likewise up to the fourth dhyāna.
Because they are established according to stage (bhūmi), type (gotra), and faculty (indriya), they are said to number three hundred and sixty.
That is to say, in the first dhyāna, there are six types of natures and three faculties, each with five [subdivisions], and so it is likewise up to the fourth dhyāna.
Because they are established according to their locations, types, and natures, they are said to number four hundred and eighty.
That is to say, for each of the six classes of the Brahmakāyika devas, there are five [types], and so on up to the Akaniṣṭha devas;
because they are established according to their station, class, lineage, and faculties, one thousand four hundred and forty [types] are spoken of.
This means that for the gods of the Brahmakāyika realm, there are six types of lineage and three faculties, each with five [subdivisions], and this continues likewise up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.

Because they are established according to their place of detachment from defilement, their lineages, and their faculties, it is said that there are twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty [categories].
That is to say, each of the aforementioned one thousand four hundred and forty [types] has nine varieties of differentiation based on the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*).
Furthermore, there are also many ways to establish the distinctions among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*).
That is to say, they are spoken of as one from the perspective of their constituent elements (dhātu), as three from the perspective of their faculties (indriya),
and as four from the perspective of their stages (bhūmi).
They are said to be six by way of spiritual lineage (*gotra*);
nine by way of freedom from passion (*vairāgya*);
and sixteen by way of stage (*sthāna*).
They are said to be eighteen by way of lineage (*gotra*) and faculty (*indriya*);
twenty-four by way of stage (*bhūmi*) and lineage;
and thirty-six by way of stage and freedom from passion (*vairāgya*).
Based on the stages, lineages, and faculties, seventy-two [paths] are taught;
based on the stages and lineages, ninety-six are taught;
and based on the stages, detachment from defilements, and faculties, one hundred and eight are taught.
One hundred and forty-four are stated by way of detachment from the spheres (*dhātu*);
one hundred and sixty-two are stated by way of detachment from the lineages (*gotra*) and faculties (*indriya*);
two hundred and sixteen are stated by way of detachment from the stages (*bhūmi*) and lineages.
Based on the bases, lineages, and faculties, it is said there are two hundred and eighty-eight.
Based on the stages, detachment from defilements, lineages, and faculties, it is said there are six hundred and forty-eight.
Based on the bases, lineages, and detachment from defilements, it is said there are eight hundred and sixty-four.
Based on the distinctions of station (*sthāna*), lineage (*gotra*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and faculty (*indriya*), there are said to be two thousand five hundred and ninety-two types.
As there are this many for those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), so it is likewise for those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
Thus, there are in total twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty varieties of non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
Just as the varieties of non-returners who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are established,
so too should the varieties of non-returners who proceed to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) be established accordingly.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Fascicle One Hundred and Seventy-Four.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle One Hundred and Seventy-Five.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhiskandha), Part Four: The Sub-section on Non-returners (Anāgāmin-nirdeśa), Second. As it is stated in the Sūtra:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are seven destinations for noble persons by which one can progress to sever the remaining fetters and attain parinirvāṇa."
Question: How are the seven destinations of the superior person (satpuruṣagati) established?
Is it by way of the realms (dhātu) and the fruits of asceticism (śrāmaṇyaphala), or is it by way of the stages (bhūmi) and locations (sthāna)?
Is it established on account of the faculties (indriya) and the afflictions (kleśa)?
If so, what is the fault?
If it were established on account of the realms (dhātu) and the fruits of śrāmaṇya (śrāmaṇyaphala), then one should speak of only one [fruit].
This refers to non-returners who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
If they were established on the basis of their level (*bhūmi*) and location (*sthāna*), they would be described as being only four or sixteen;
however, if they are established on the basis of their faculties (*indriya*) and afflictions (*kleśa*), they should be described as being nine.
Because each of those has nine grades,
the answer is that they are not all established by means of these three conditions; rather,
the seven types are established solely on the basis of their superior progression through the grades of arising and non-arising.
If by this [reason] the category of "firstly produced" is established,
then by this very [reason] the category of "not first produced" is established;
if by this [reason] the category of "secondly produced" is established...
Thus, for this reason, the second category of non-arising is established;
and if for this reason the third category of arising is established,
then for this reason the third category of non-arising is established.
Furthermore, because the higher path is superior in its meaning, the *ūrdhvasrotas* (one who flows upwards) is established as a single category.
Based on this, seven destinations of the noble person (*satpuruṣagati*) are established;
that is to say, among those who are born [in the form realm], there are some who diligently cultivate the path and possess the path of rapid progress.
There may be those who practice the path with diligence but do not progress swiftly;
there may be those who practice the path without diligence and do not progress swiftly.
The first is designated as the first, the second as the second, and the last as the third.
Just as there are three types of those who are born [in the higher realms], so too are there three types of those who are not born [there].
Furthermore, based on the superior meaning of their upward progression, those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*) are established as a single category.
By means of this, the seven destinations of the noble beings (*satpuruṣagati*) are established.
Furthermore, those who are born possess superior faculties, middling faculties, and dull faculties, which correspond respectively to the three [categories].
Just as there are three types of birth, so too are there three types of non-birth.
The rest is as previously explained.
The distinctions among the afflictions (*kleśa*) are explained in the same manner as their opposites.
Furthermore, regarding those who are born, there are those with superior paths, those with middling paths, and those with inferior paths, which correspond respectively to the three [categories].
Just as there are three types of birth, so too are there three types of non-birth; the rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, regarding those who are born, there are those with superior karma, those with middling karma, and those with inferior karma, which correspond respectively to the three [types of birth].
This is explained with reference to uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma.

If explained with reference to contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma, then the latter becomes the first, the former becomes the second, and the initial one becomes the third; just as there are three types of birth, so too are there three types of non-birth.
The rest is as previously explained.
Some say that one who possesses diligence and supremacy also attains superior wisdom.
There are those for whom diligence is predominant but superior wisdom is not attained;
there are those who attain superior wisdom but for whom diligence is not predominant. These three follow the respective order.
Just as there are three types of birth, so it is with non-birth.
The rest is as previously explained.
Some say that for those who are born [in the formless realm], there is both sustained application (*sātatyaprayoga*) and instantaneous application (*tatkṣaṇaprayoga*).
There is constant preparatory application but not sudden preparatory application;
there is sudden preparatory application but not constant preparatory application;
these constitute the three cases respectively.
As there are three types of birth, so too are there three types of non-birth; the rest is as previously explained.
Some say that "birth" refers to seeing the supreme defects within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
There are those who perceive the faults of saṃsāra as being of medium degree;
there are those who perceive the faults of saṃsāra as being of inferior degree;
these constitute the three [categories] in their respective order.
As it is with the three types of birth, so it is with non-birth;
the rest is as previously explained.
It is likewise when explaining the distinctions in the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the cultivation of merit toward nirvāṇa.
Some say that among those who have attained birth, there are those with superior śamatha and vipaśyanā, those with middling,
and those with inferior; these three correspond respectively to the three [levels].
Just as there are three types of birth, so too are there three types of non-birth.
The rest is as previously explained.
The detailed explanation of the other distinctions among the wholesome roots is likewise.
Some say that the Blessed One has revealed seven stages, seven types of dispositions, seven gates, seven rungs, seven tracks, and seven paths,
by which one transcends the fetters abandoned through cultivation at the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which are difficult to sever and difficult to destroy.
Because they have attained the fruit of arhatship, these seven destinations of the virtuous persons (satpuruṣagati) are thus taught.
Question: Just as there are three types each for those who are born and those who are not born, so it is with the upper-streamers (ūrdhvasrotas), namely:
those who leap entirely (pluta), those who leap halfway (ardhapluta), and those who die in every location (sarvasthānacyuta).
Why is it said that there is only one?
Answer: Birth and non-birth each constitute a single continuity of existence (*bhava-saṃtati*).

Because the distinctions among the various stages within them are difficult to discern, and with the desire to make them known, three types of *ūrdhva-srotas* (those who flow upwards) are each described.
The distinctions among the three types of births are self-evident and easy to understand;
therefore, they are grouped together as one type according to the superior meaning of the "upward course.
Furthermore, the distinction between birth and non-birth within a single lifetime is brief in duration, and its limited scope is easily understood.
Therefore, when dividing the three types of "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas),
because the distinctions regarding their long durations and various limits are difficult to discern, they are combined and established as one.
Furthermore, there is also the sense of equality regarding birth and non-birth.
The "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas) also has a distinct meaning.
These statements were made in this way so that two textual passages might mutually clarify one another.
Furthermore, the characteristics of the destinies of superior persons (*satpuruṣa-gati*), whether already born or not yet born, are easily understood when they manifest before one.
Because they attain parinirvāṇa swiftly, each is divided into three.
As for those who "go upstream" (ūrdhva-srotas), their characteristics as a destination for noble beings (satpuruṣa-gati) are subtle, hidden, and difficult to know;
since they still undergo many births and deaths, they are described collectively as one.
Question: Why does the sūtra manifest the three kinds of non-arising through three metaphors, but not do so for the three kinds of arising?
Answer: Just as the three metaphors manifest the three kinds of non-arising, [so it is with the three kinds of arising].
It should be understood that this also demonstrates the three kinds of arising; therefore, it was stated previously:
"If by means of this the category of initial arising is established, then by means of this the category of initial non-arising is also established," and so forth in detail.
Furthermore, when one who is not yet born proceeds toward a place of birth, like a traveler on a road,
some attain parinirvāṇa before having gone far into the intermediate state (antarābhava),
while others attain parinirvāṇa after having gone a short distance.
There are those who, having already gone far and being on the verge of reaching their place of birth, attain parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, the World-Honored One used three similes to demonstrate that all three types [of non-returners] reach their place of birth.
Furthermore, because there is no destination and no distinction between near and far, there is no separate analogy.
Moreover, because the three types of non-arising are subtle, unmanifest, difficult to perceive, and difficult to comprehend, they are elucidated by means of analogies.
The three types of birth (*jāti*) are coarse, manifest, and easy to understand; therefore, they are not illustrated by analogies.
Furthermore, the three types of non-birth (*ajāti*) are subsumed under the realms (*dhātu*) rather than the destinies (*gati*).
Because the characteristics of non-birth subsumed under the destinies are incomplete, they are illustrated by analogies.
The three [types of birth] do not arise in that manner, and thus there is no illustrative analogy.
Furthermore, the Buddha foresaw that in the future there would be those with biased attachments who would slander the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
such as the Vibhajyavādins and others.
Because the Buddha wished to definitively establish the meaning of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), he manifested its distinctions through three similes;
however, since such refutations do not apply to the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) and so forth, he did not provide further similes for those three.
Furthermore, the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) excels over those who attain it upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin) and others in three respects:
first, they undergo less suffering;
second, they more swiftly extinguish the fire of the afflictions (kleśa).
Third, because of the swift abandonment of the burden of the aggregates (*skandha-bhāra*),
this is illustrated by three similes;
since birth and the other [links] are not like this, they are not illustrated by similes.
Question: From which stage does one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) arise the noble path to further sever remaining fetters and attain the fruit of arhatship?
Answer: One arises from the noble path of one's own stage.
That is to say, if one attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state while abiding in the stage of the first dhyāna, [one arises from the noble path of that same stage].
He arouses the noble path of the first dhyāna stage;
up to and including those who attain parinirvāṇa while abiding in the intermediate state of the fourth dhyāna stage,
they arouse the noble path of the fourth dhyāna stage.
Question: After one has attained those fruits, can one also give rise to the path of the noble ones belonging to the *anāgamya* concentration or the intermediate dhyāna?
Answer: Some say that there are indeed those who do so.
That is to say, if one previously attained the fruit of non-returner based on that [level], one can now also give rise to it.
Regarding such a statement,
it should be said that [the fruit] is not given rise to.
Why is this? Because it is the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, because time is short, once they have attained the fruit and swiftly entered parinirvāṇa, how could they possibly give rise again to the untainted (*anāsrava*) states of other stages?
Furthermore, the intermediate state (antarābhava) is conducive only to the noble path (āryamārga) of the fundamental stages (maulabhūmi), not that of the preparatory stages (sāmantaka).
This is because the noble path of the preparatory stages is subsumed under the "path of suffering" (duḥkhamārga) and is therefore difficult to manifest.
Furthermore, if a dhyāna stage possesses both meditative concentration (*samāpatti*) and birth (*upapatti*), one may give rise to that Noble Path while abiding within it.
The *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) concentration possesses concentration but lacks birth.
Although the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) also possesses birth, it is a birth produced by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and not by Noble Ones (*ārya*).

Because the four fundamental dhyānas consist of both meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and rebirth (*upapatti*), one abides in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and gives rise to those noble paths (*āryamārga*).
Question: Why does one not give rise to the noble paths of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)? Answer: Because they have not yet been attained at the initial stage.
Because they would be useless at a later time;
furthermore, because it is difficult for them to manifest when subsumed under other stages;
and furthermore, because they are subsumed under the path of suffering and thus one has no desire to arouse them.
Question: Why are the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) not described as "paths of the true person" (*satpuruṣagati*)?
Answer: When something should be stated but is not, one should know that this meaning is incomplete (*śeṣa*). Some say:
World-Honored One, herein the Middle Son is praised by means of the seven destinies of the virtuous person;
at other times and in other places, the Eldest Son is praised,
as stated in a verse:
The Arhat experiences supreme bliss because he has abandoned both craving and the conceit "I am," and because he has forever severed the net of delusion. Thus,
in certain instances, he may praise a young child, as is explained at length in the *Saroopama-sutta* (The Pool Simile Sūtra).
Now, this [passage] also praises the middle son;
for this reason, the stream-enterer and once-returner are not mentioned. Some say:
It was for the purpose of distinguishing between stream-enterers and once-returners that the Blessed One spoke of these seven destinations of noble persons (*satpuruṣagati*).
For although they are called "noble persons," as the Sūtra asks: "What is a noble person? [the answer follows].
That is to say, if one is endowed with the right view of a trainee,
up to and including right concentration,
how is one superior to a virtuous person?
This refers to one who has attained the right view up to the right concentration of an adept (aśaikṣa),
yet does not receive the designation of "one who proceeds as a true person" (satpuruṣagati).
This is because such a person is still far removed and is not yet able to closely approach the excellence of a true person.
Only the non-returner (anāgāmin) is called a "true person" (satpuruṣa) and is also called a "destination of the true person" (satpuruṣagati),
because he is himself a true person and can also approach the superior true persons.
For this reason, the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) are not the destination of the true person.
Some say that within the stage of training (śaikṣa), those who have already transcended the realms and attained the fruit are established as noble persons (satpuruṣagati).
Although stream-enterers (srotāpanna) and once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin) have attained the fruit, they have not yet transcended the realms.

Some say that within the stage of training (śaikṣa), if one has already transcended a realm and permanently abandoned unwholesome afflictions and karma, one is established as a "noble person" (satpuruṣagati);
this is not the case for both the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).

Some say that within the stage of training (śaikṣa), those who have already attained the fruit and have permanently abandoned unwholesome afflictions and karma are established as noble beings (satpuruṣagati).
Since stream-enterers (srotāpanna) and once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin) cannot do so, they are not established as noble beings.
Just as with unwholesome karma of the afflictions,
so too it is with karma of the afflictions associated with *āhrīkya* (lack of shame) and *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread), which possess two fruits and have maturation (*vipāka*). Some say:
Among those in the stage of training (śaikṣa),
one who has already transcended a realm and permanently severed the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana) is established as belonging to the "noble lineage" (satpuruṣagati);
this is not the case for stream-enterers (srotāpanna) or once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin).
Some say that within the stage of training (śaikṣa),
those who have already attained the fruit and have permanently abandoned the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana) are established as the destination of the noble person (satpuruṣagati).
This is not the case for stream-enterers or once-returners.

Some say that within the stage of training (śaikṣa), if one has permanently abandoned those qualities not shared with noble beings (asatpuruṣa), they are established as belonging to the destiny of noble beings (satpuruṣagati).
What are called the qualities not shared with true persons? They are:
delighting in the household life and being attached to wife and children;
and being greedily clinging to bedding, clothing, food, and drink.
They delight in adorning their bodies with various flower garlands, necklaces, and the like, as well as anointing them with perfumes and ointments.
They accumulate all kinds of impure wealth and possessions,
namely gold, silver, precious gems, storehouses, fields, houses, slaves, servants, and elephants, horses, and so forth.

Furthermore, with a defiled mind, one touches a body that is a collection of foulness—a mere skeleton where all manner of evils gather—and conceives the notion of purity, thereby indulging in the habitual practice of desire.

Or, at times, one gives rise to anger and inflicts harm upon sentient beings through acts such as striking with the fist; because such injurious and afflictive karmas still occur even for stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), these states are not said to belong to the category of "noble persons" (*satpuruṣagati*).

Some say that within the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), if one does not again enter the dark prison of the mother’s womb to receive the impurities of the various bodily parts and dwell between the receptacles of the raw and the cooked,
this is established as the "destination of the noble person" (*satpuruṣagati*).
Since even stream-enterers and once-returners still possess these [defilements], seven noble paths (satpuruṣagati) are not established.
The Venerable Ghosaka stated:
"If one in training has already abandoned sensual desire and ill-will, and does not undergo the suffering of confinement in a mother’s womb, they are established as a noble path."
The stream-enterer and once-returner are not like this.
Some say that if a learner’s mind is not disturbed by objects that are either disagreeable or agreeable, they are established as belonging to the "noble lineage" (satpuruṣagati).
This is not the case for stream-enterers or once-returners.
Some say that if one proceeds toward a higher rebirth without falling back, they are established as belonging to the "destination of the noble person" (satpuruṣagati).
The stream-enterer and once-returner are not like this. Some say:

if a learner (śaikṣa) has already attained mixed meditative concentration (dhyāna), even if they regress, they do not lose that concentration; such a person is established as belonging to the "noble lineage" (satpuruṣagati), whereas the stream-enterer and once-returner are not.

Some say: if a trainee practices only the dharmas of a virtuous person and does not practice the dharmas of a non-virtuous person, they are established as belonging to the destiny of a virtuous person (*satpuruṣagati*).
However, stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*) also practice the dharmas of a non-virtuous person.
For this reason, the *srotaāpanna* and the *sakṛdāgāmin* are not established as noble lineages (*satpuruṣagati*).
Question: A non-returner who proceeds to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) possesses five points of superiority over a non-returner who proceeds to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

That is to say: excellence of realm (*dhātu*), excellence of stage (*bhūmi*), excellence of abandoning afflictions (*kleśaprahāṇa*), excellence of the reduction of the aggregates (*skandhāpacaya*), and excellence of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

Why are these not established as the destinies of the noble person (*satpuruṣagati*)? One should know that when it is said "they ought to be explained but are not," this meaning is [intentionally] left incomplete.
Some say: if something is coarse, manifest, and easy to understand, it is established as a "destiny of a superior person" (satpuruṣagati);
since those [other destinies] are not clearly manifest, they are not so designated.
Some say that the Buddha,
in order to encourage noble ones who have not yet abandoned attachment to the desire realm— a state fraught with many defects— to quickly leave it behind,
taught that one who attains the stage of non-returner in the form realm is a "noble person's destination" (satpuruṣagati).
It is not for the purpose of exhorting noble ones who have not yet abandoned the subtle faults of the form realm to quickly leave it;
therefore, one does not describe the practice of the formless realm as the "destination of the true person" (satpuruṣagati) for those who are non-returners (anāgāmin).
Some say:

If there is a physical body that, by relying on a physical basis, possesses such movements as coming and going, and whose tranquil deportment can be made known to others as being that of a true person (*satpuruṣa*), then it is established as the "destination of the true person" (*satpuruṣagati*).
Because those who practice the formless realm do not possess such [physical] matters, the "destiny of the virtuous person" (satpuruṣagati) is not established for them. Some say:
"If there is a place where five non-returners (anāgāmin) can be designated, and seven virtuous destinies (sugati) can be established, then the destiny of the virtuous person is established."

Because those who practice the formless [attainments] do not return and do not possess the five [faculties], and because the seven destinations of the virtuous person (satpuruṣagati) cannot be established for them,
they are not mentioned.
Some say that if a realm exists where only noble ones (ārya) are born, the destination of the virtuous person is established there.
It is not so for the formless realm.

Some say that if one has already attained the meditative absorption of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna*), even if one regresses from it, one does not lose the meditative absorption; such a person is established as belonging to the "noble person's path" (*satpuruṣagati*).
This is not the case for those who practice the formless [attainments]. Some say:

if a realm has already abandoned the qualities of an unwholesome person (*asatpuruṣa-dharma*) and various wholesome persons (*satpuruṣa*) frequent it and engage in discussion therein, that realm is established as a destination for wholesome persons (*satpuruṣa-gati*).
Because it is not so in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), the "destiny of the virtuous person" (satpuruṣagati) is not established there.
Question: For what reason is an Arhat not considered a destiny of the virtuous person?
Answer: One should also say that an Arhat is indeed a destiny of the virtuous person.
That it is not mentioned should be understood as meaning that the sense is incomplete.
Furthermore, those who proceed toward higher rebirths are established as "noble beings" (*satpuruṣa-gati*);
because Arhats are subject to no further birth, they are not so established.
Furthermore, those who proceed toward a higher fruit are established as belonging to the "noble course" (*satpuruṣagati*).
Since an Arhat is already a higher fruit and there is no further fruit to be reached, they are not so established.
Question: Does an Arhat liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) also proceed toward a higher fruit?
That is to say, why is the pursuit of immovability not considered the destination of a true person (*satpuruṣagati*)?
The answer is: that pursuit pertains to a superior lineage (*gotra*), but it does not constitute a superior fruit (*phala*).
Furthermore, if an noble one (*ārya*) possesses afflictions yet does not possess the qualities of a non-true person, they are established as being on the path of a true person.
Arhats do not possess afflictions; therefore, they are not mentioned [in this context].
Furthermore, among those in the stage of training (śaikṣa), there are those who possess the qualities of non-noble persons (asatpuruṣadharma);
it is in relation to them that the seven destinies of noble persons (satpuruṣagati) are established.
The stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is not like this; therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, one does not return from the destiny of a true person (*satpuruṣagati*);
the Arhat is the supreme destiny of a true person.
If it were said that this is the "path of the virtuous person" (*satpuruṣagati*), it would be a depreciation rather than a description according to reality;
therefore, it is not so described. Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna as it has been described?
The answer is that its intrinsic nature consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Question: Why is it called "intermingled cultivation of dhyāna" (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*), and what is intended to be revealed by the term "intermingled"?
Answer: It is called "intermingled cultivation" because it thoroughly perfumes [the mind] throughout.
It is called "mixed cultivation" because it is perfumed by both;
it is called "mixed cultivation" because it causes [the meditative state] to become adorned and beautiful;
it is called "mixed cultivation" because it causes [the meditative state] to become luminous and pure.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say that it is called "mixed cultivation" (vyavakiraṇa) because it takes that [object] as its condition;
it is called "mixed cultivation" because it thoroughly perfumes [the mind], just as when a garment is placed in a chest and thoroughly perfumed with incense,
so too it is for the various practitioners of yoga.
Because the two untainted moments (anāsrava-ksana) before and after permeate the single tainted moment (sāsrava-ksana) in between,
it is called "mixed cultivation" (vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā);
this is like flowers and sesame seeds being mixed and perfumed so as to produce fragrance.
That practitioner of yoga is likewise:

by means of two moments of uncontaminated [cognition] interspersed with and perfuming a single moment of contaminated [cognition], they cause it to become refined and excellent; therefore, they are called "those who practice mixed cultivation."
Just as one scatters various flowers upon a *caitya* to make it beautiful,
so too does the practitioner scatter two moments of untainted [consciousness] upon one moment of tainted [consciousness].
It is called "mixed cultivation" because it makes [the mind] exquisite and makes it luminously pure;
this is like placing gold and other metals into a furnace to refine and melt them, thereby making them increasingly luminous and pure.
In this way, the practitioner places a single moment of contaminated [consciousness] between two moments of uncontaminated [consciousness].
By repeatedly refining it and causing it to become increasingly pure and sublime through focusing upon that [uncontaminated state], he is called one who practices mixed cultivation.
That [tradition] explains that it is called "mixed cultivation" because two moments of the untainted take one moment of the tainted as their object.
As for the realm:
that which is mixed cultivates belongs to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding the ability to practice the mixed cultivation and not falling into the realms:
both the subject that practices the mixture and the object of the mixture reside within the stages of the four fundamental dhyānas.
Question: Is there mixed cultivation of the formless realms?
Answer: Some say there is not, because it is difficult to perceive and subtle.
Some say that the Buddha practices mixed cultivation in the formless realm,
whereas this is not the case for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; furthermore, it relies on the modes of activity belonging to the desire and form realms.
Some say that both the ability to practice mixed meditation and the objects mixed therein all constitute the sixteen aspects of the noble path. Why is this so?
Because one can immediately give rise to the noble path by means of the characteristics of the noble practice,
and because one again gives rise to the characteristics of the noble practice immediately after the noble path;
thus it is said.
One is able to perform the mixed cultivation through sixteen aspects;
that which is mixed may be performed through sixteen aspects, or through other aspects.
Regarding the objects of focus for the immeasurables, liberations, spheres of mastery, and so forth,
some say that they are capable of being mixed in cultivation, taking that which is mixed as their object; however, the objects of such mixed cultivation are not fixed.
Regarding this statement:
one who is able to practice the mixed cultivation taking the four noble truths as objects,
and who practices the mixed cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness taking all phenomena as objects.

Some say that both that which is practiced through intermingling and that which is the object of such intermingling are all considered applications of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Others say:
Regarding those who maintain that the four foundations of mindfulness are cultivated in a mixed manner,
they are able to cultivate the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena alone in a mixed manner. Thus it is said.
Regarding those who are able to practice the mixed cultivation and for whom all that is mixed cultivation may serve as the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
some say that the ability to practice the mixed cultivation consists of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudayānvayajñāna*).
That which is mixed cultivation is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
According to this explanation,
that which is capable of mixed cultivation consists of the four dharma-knowledges and the four subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*).
That which is mixed cultivation is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

To state it generally, there are seven knowledges for those in training (*śaikṣa*) and nine knowledges for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Regarding "conjoined with samādhi," some say it refers to being able to intermingle [the practices] conjoined with the samādhis of emptiness and wishlessness.

Regarding the statement that "that which is mixed cultivation is not associated with samādhi," those who speak thus [assert] that what is capable of mixed cultivation is associated with the three types of samādhi, whereas that which is mixed cultivation itself is not associated with samādhi.
Regarding the association with the faculties (*indriya*), taken collectively:
both the mixed cultivation of the subject and the object are associated with the three faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Regarding the past, future, and present: both the mixed cultivation of the subject and the object pertain to all three time periods.
Regarding those that take the three periods of time as their object,
some say they are able to intermingle the cultivation of objects belonging to the past and the future.
Regarding the statement that the mixed cultivation takes as its objects those belonging to the three periods of time as well as those transcending time:
according to this explanation,
it takes as its objects both those of the three periods of time and those transcending time.
Since it was previously stated that the ability to intermingle [the meditations] takes the Four Truths as its object, it should not be explained differently.
Regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral [states],
both the agent and the object of the intermingling are wholesome objects.

Regarding "wholesome and so forth," they all take as their objects three types: those bound to the three realms and those not bound. That which is mixed with what is bound to the realm of form is itself bound;
that which is capable of mixing with what is not bound is itself not bound.
Thus, they take as their objects both what is bound to the realms and what is not bound.
Taking as objects those factors bound to the three realms as well as those unbound,
whether they be of the learner (śaikṣa), the non-learner (aśaikṣa), or neither learner nor non-learner,
one is able to perform mixed cultivation, which may be either of the learner or of the non-learner.
That which is mixed-cultivation is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.

Regarding those that take the learner and so forth as their objects, they all take all three types [of phenomena] as their objects: those abandoned by seeing, those abandoned by cultivation, and those not abandoned.
That which is mixed-cultivation is abandoned by cultivation.
Those capable of practicing the mixed cultivation (vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā) take all three types as their objects, including those abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya) and so forth.
Those taking names as their objects and those taking meanings as their objects both take both names and meanings as their objects.
Those taking their own continuum, another’s continuum, or that which is not a continuum as their objects all take all three types as their objects.
As for where it arises, it arises in the desire realm and the form realm;
however, its initial arising occurs among humans in the three continents of the human realm.
Having arisen there, one may either fall back from it or not.
They arise and manifest again when one is subsequently born in the Form Realm.
Regarding those obtained through application, obtained through detachment, and obtained through birth:
the Buddha’s are obtained through detachment, while others’ are obtained through application.
What is the preparatory application? It refers to the practitioner first entering the fourth dhyāna and arising for many moments of untainted (anāsrava) consciousness;
from this state, they then arise for many moments of tainted (sāsrava) consciousness.
Thereafter, many further moments of outflow-free (anāsrava) states arise.

Thus, as they revolve, each subsequent moment gradually diminishes until finally, immediately after the last two moments of the outflow-free state, two moments of the outflowing (sāsrava) state manifest.
Immediately after two moments of the contaminated, two further moments of the uncontaminated manifest before him.
Up to this point, it is called the completion of the preparatory stage for the mixed cultivation of dhyāna.
From this point onward, without relying on effort, he is able to produce one moment of the contaminated immediately following one moment of the uncontaminated.
Then, immediately following this, another moment of untainted [consciousness] arises.
Because these intermediate moments of tainted [consciousness] are interspersed with preceding and succeeding moments of untainted [consciousness], it is called the "mixed cultivation" of dhyāna.
At that time, it is called the fundamental accomplishment of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna.

Having thus mixed-cultivated the fourth dhyāna, by the power of this, one is also able to mix-cultivate the three lower dhyānas as appropriate. Having first relied upon the three continents of the human realm within the desire realm to thus mix-cultivate these various dhyānas, one is subsequently reborn in the form realm.
Through the power of habitual practice, one is further able to perform the mixed cultivation of dhyāna as previously described, according to what is appropriate.
Question: What kind of *pudgala* performs the mixed cultivation of dhyāna? Answer: It is an *ārya*, not an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);

it includes both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*. Specifically, those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), those liberated by time (*samayavimukta*), and those liberated at all times (*asamayavimukta*)—all are capable of performing the mixed cultivation.
Question: For what reason does one practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna?
Answer: One practices the mixed cultivation of dhyāna for three reasons:
first, for the sake of delighting in meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
Second, because of the fear of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Third, because of delighting in rebirth.
"Delighting in meditative attainment" (*samāpatti*) refers to dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Either for the sake of enjoying the wealth of the noble Dharma,
or for the sake of sporting with meritorious qualities,
or for the sake of contemplating one's original deeds.
Alternatively, it is for the sake of inducing superior qualities.
Those who fear afflictions do so because they dread the loss of superior qualities through the manifestation of arising afflictions;
or they fear that the manifestation of arising afflictions will burn their body and mind.
Those who delight in rebirth do so because they take pleasure in being born there, in the five Pure Abodes which are not shared with ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Those whose liberation is through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) cultivate the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) in a mixed manner due to three causes and conditions.
The *dṛṣṭiprāpta* (one who has attained through vision) cultivates the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) through two causes and conditions:
because they have eliminated the afflictions that cause fear and because they are of a nature not to fall back.

The *samayavimukta* (one liberated by occasion) cultivates the meditative absorptions through two causes and conditions: because they have eliminated the desire for rebirth in pleasant states and because they turn their backs on all forms of rebirth.

One who is liberated at an improper time (asamayavimukta) does so through a single causal condition: by practicing the meditative absorptions in a mixed manner (vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna), they eliminate the afflictions of fear and the arising of pleasant sensations;
because they are of the nature of non-retrogression (avaivartika) and because they turn their backs on all rebirths.
Question: How many grades of the meditative absorption of mixed cultivation (vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna) are there?
Answer: There are five: first, the inferior grade;
second, the middling grade; third, the superior grade; fourth, the superior-victorious-perfect grade; and fifth, the supreme-perfect grade.
In each of these chapters, at the stage of fulfillment, there are three types of mind:
one is with outflows (sāsrava) and two are without outflows (anāsrava).
Thus, in total, it is said that there are fifteen minds: five with outflows and ten without outflows.
Question: Do these fifteen moments of mind constitute non-arising from meditative absorption, or do they constitute arising from meditative absorption?
Answer: Some say as follows.
One does not emerge from meditative absorption;
it is, for example, like the continuous manifestation of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Some say:
Emerging from meditative absorption is like repeatedly arising from and entering into the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
According to this explanation, it is not fixed;
there may be cases where one does not emerge from absorption, yet the fifteen moments of mind continue to evolve in succession.
Furthermore, upon emerging from meditative absorption, there may be those who emerge after having generated three moments of mind,
or those who emerge after having generated six moments of mind,
or those who emerge after having generated nine moments of mind.
There are cases where, after having given rise to twelve moments of mind, one immediately enters meditative absorption.
Therefore, within those five grades [of mixed cultivation], the mixed cultivation may or may not be completed depending on whether [the intermediate moments] arise.
Question: Among these fifteen moments of mind, how many are previously attained?
How many are not yet attained?
Answer: Some say that five are not yet attained.
The tenth is "previously attained," meaning that when the first five are present before one, the remaining ten are cultivated in the future. Some say:
Ten are not previously attained, while five are previously attained;
this is because when the former ten manifest in the present, the latter five are cultivated in the future.
Thus it is said.
This is not fixed: there may be fifteen that have all never been attained;
or there may be fifteen that have all previously been attained;
or there may be some that have been attained and some that have not been attained.
Question: Among these fifteen moments of mind, how many are the primary (pravartaka) and how many are the secondary (anuvartaka)?
Answer: Some say:
The first five are the primary transformations (*pravṛtti*), and the latter ten are the secondary transformations (*anuvṛtti*).
Some say that the first ten are the primary transformations and the latter five are the secondary transformations.
Regarding this statement,
it is not fixed;
for either all [factors] are primary (pravartaka), or all are secondary (anuvartaka).
Either a small portion is the primary turning (*pravartaka*) and a small portion is the secondary turning (*anuvartaka*).
Question: If this category is the primary turning, does that same category also perform the secondary turning, or is it another category?
Answer: Some say: [it is another category].
If this category [of mental state] arises, then that category follows in its turn.

That is to say, the meditative cultivation of mixing (*miśra-bhāvanā*) is only accomplished when the objects of knowledge, the modes of activity (*ākāra*), and the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are mutually concordant from beginning to end.
Therefore, if this arises, that must necessarily follow; otherwise, it constitutes an obstacle to the meditative cultivation of mixing.
Some say:
if this category [of cultivation] proceeds and another category follows it—
meaning that the objects of knowledge, the mental aspects, and the foundations of mindfulness of different types alternate— it only then constitutes mixed cultivation.
Therefore, if this primary transformation necessarily entails a corresponding secondary transformation, otherwise it would contradict the meaning of "mixed cultivation.
According to those who speak thus,
this is not fixed.
That is to say, if dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) acts as the primary mover (pravartaka),

then either dharma-knowledge or subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) acts as the follower (anuvartaka); if subsequent knowledge acts as the primary mover, [then either dharma-knowledge or subsequent knowledge acts as the follower].
Either subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) or dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) acts as the concomitant;
the same applies to the other knowledges.
If they take the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) as their object, they act as the primary [turning].
Whether taking conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object, it functions as a conforming transformation (*anuvartaka*).
It is the same when taking other phenomena as its object.
If the aspect of impermanence (*anityākāra*) functions as the primary transformation, [the others follow].
Alternatively, the aspects of impermanence, suffering, and so forth serve as the concomitants;
the same applies to the other aspects.
If the application of mindfulness to the body serves as the primary [foundation], [the others follow].
Either the mindfulness of the body or the mindfulness of feelings acts as the concomitant (anuvartaka), and the same applies to the remaining foundations of mindfulness.
Question: If the primary (pravartaka) and the concomitant were not identical, there would be confusion regarding their aspects (ākāra) and objects (ālambana).
Why does one not encounter obstacles in the practice of mixed dhyāna?
Answer: Because it has already been thoroughly cultivated during the stage of preliminary application (*prayoga*), the path has been established;
thus, even if there is some confusion, no obstacle arises to the mixed cultivation.
Just as in the path of seeing and the mundane path,
although the aspects and objects of focus are intermingled across higher and lower levels,
there is no obstruction; this case is also like that.

Question: If the primary application (*maula*) and the subsequent application (*anuvartaka*) were identical, how could they be called "mixed cultivation of dhyāna" (*vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna*), given that the term "mixed" cannot apply to a single type of aspect (*ākāra*) or object (*ālambana*)?
Answer: It is called "mixed cultivation" (*miśrabhāvanā*) because the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states alternate and intermingle;
it does not mean that they are called "mixed" because wisdom and the other factors differ in their sequence.
Question: For what reason must the cultivation of mixed dhyāna involve the alternating arising of the contaminated and uncontaminated?
Answer: It is because one wishes to demonstrate that within these two types of dhyāna, one attains mastery over both entering and emerging from them.

Furthermore, it is because one wishes to place the untainted (anāsrava) states before and after, thereby perfuming the intermediate tainted states so that they become increasingly sublime and give rise to rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Furthermore, from time immemorial, pure dhyāna has been overwhelmed and intermingled with dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādana*).
Now, one desires to cause it to enter into and emerge from untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyāna in mutual alternation.
This causes the flavors associated with meditative absorption to no longer intermingle, as they become increasingly distant from one another.
Furthermore, when the practitioner has long entered into dhyāna, the sensations of nourishment reach their peak, pervading and saturating the entire body.
Because they wish to cause their bodies to experience temporary clarity and expansion, these arise in conjunction with the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Those who wish to practice the mixed cultivation of the four dhyānas must first practice the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna; once that is perfected, [they proceed].
Next, one further practices the mixed cultivation of the third dhyāna;
next, one further practices the mixed cultivation of the second dhyāna;
finally, one practices the mixed cultivation of the first dhyāna.
If one does not first practice the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna, one will ultimately be unable to practice the mixed cultivation of the lower stages.
Question: Following from this discussion, why must one necessarily practice the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna first?
"Then can one cultivate the three lower stages?
Answer: "Because the fourth dhyāna is the most perfect among all dhyānas, and because it is the most excellent basis for the arising of meritorious qualities."
Because it can induce the most excellent bliss of pliancy;
because it causes the body that serves as its basis to be pervaded and permeated;
and because it is the locus for many such meritorious qualities.
Because it is an immovable concentration;
because it is the most excellent among pleasant practices;
and because it possesses the greatest capability.
Furthermore, the fourth dhyāna occupies the central position among the untainted concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*),
as it lies three stages above and three stages below it.
Moreover, in the fourth dhyāna, there have appeared Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, numbering more than the sands of the Ganges.
Because all [Buddhas] rely upon it to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, the fourth dhyāna possesses five causes and five fruits.
The five kinds of causes refer to the five grades of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*); the five kinds of fruits refer to the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Question: How many grades are there in the mixed cultivation of the lower three dhyānas?
Answer: Some say there are only three grades— namely, inferior, middling, and superior—
because the lower stages lack the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Regarding this explanation, there are likewise five categories.
Question: Since those [unconditioned phenomena] lack the five fruits, for what reason are there five categories of causes?
Answer: Although there are no five fruits, those fixed dharmas nevertheless consist of five categories.
Furthermore, although the lower stages lack the five Pure Abodes as fruits, they possess five categories of faculties.

Question: Since the five grades of mixed cultivation exist in the lower three dhyānas, for what reason do the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) not exist as their fruit? Answer: Because they are neither the field nor the vessel for them.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, because the noble ones feel weary of and afflicted by the places where ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) dwell together, they seek birth in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
If there were Pure Abodes on the lower stages, they would be unable to feel such weary detachment from the places where ordinary beings dwell together.
Because they have not yet abandoned attachment to the higher realms.
Furthermore, because the noble ones seek to transcend the birthplaces of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are born in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
If the Pure Abodes were to exist on a lower level, they would be unable to transcend the birthplaces of ordinary beings.
Because there are still places for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) above;
furthermore, because noble ones (*ārya*) seek birth in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) out of weariness with the afflictions of their current state,
and because all three lower stages possess such afflictions, they do not have Pure Abodes.
Furthermore, the lifespan induced by the superior karma of the Śuddhāvāsa deities is exceedingly long.
If such beings were to exist in the lower realms, would those whose lifespans are fixed necessarily die when the three calamities arise?
If one were to die [at that time], their lifespan would certainly not be subject to premature death;
if they do not die, it should act as an obstacle to the arising of the calamity.
As it is said: "In whatever place there is even a single sentient being, down to an ant's egg, the calamity will ultimately not destroy it."
In order to prevent such faults, the Pure Abodes do not exist in the lower stages.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"For what reason do the Pure Abodes not exist in the lower stages?"
It is by means of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna that one is born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
When practicing the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, one has necessarily already become detached from the defilements of the three lower stages;
for one does not take birth in a stage from which one is already detached.
Therefore, the Śuddhāvāsa heavens do not exist in the lower stages.
Furthermore, only those of sharp faculties are able to practice the mixed cultivation (*miśra-bhāvanā*).
Since those capable of mixed cultivation can necessarily and swiftly transcend the impure lower stages to reach the purely pure realm, the Śuddhāvāsa heavens do not exist in the lower stages.
Furthermore, one must first attain the basis of the ultimate meditative absorption (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*) before being able to practice the mixed cultivation;
since only those capable of such mixed cultivation are reborn in those [Pure Abodes], there are no Pure Abodes in the lower stages.
The Venerable One said:
"Sentient beings of the lower realms are mostly born in the higher realms when the world is being destroyed, and are born in the lower realms when it is being formed.
For those born in the Śuddhāvāsa [Pure Abodes], such a thing does not occur; therefore, there are no Śuddhāvāsa heavens in the lower realms."
Question: For what reason are there exactly five Śuddhāvāsa heavens, neither more nor less?
Venerable Pārśva replied:
"This is not a question that should be asked."
Why is this? Whether they are many or few, all give rise to doubt; yet because of such doubt, it does not necessarily contradict reason.
However, regarding the true meaning of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), there should be only five, neither more nor less.
Some say: because there are only five places where ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are not born together [with the noble ones],
there are likewise only five places where noble ones (*ārya*) are born.
The five places where ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are not born together are the three evil destinies, the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*),

and the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*). Some say that because there are five grades of mixed meditative absorption (*dhyāna-vyavakīrṇa*), the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) that they induce are likewise only five.
Question: Why are there exactly five levels of mixed cultivation of dhyāna, neither more nor less?
Answer: Because the power of mixed cultivation extends only that far;
it is just as the power of the fifteen moments of the path of seeing extends only that far, neither increasing nor decreasing.
In this way, the power of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna also consists of fifteen moments of mind, neither more nor less.
Furthermore, the mixed cultivation of dhyāna is a superior merit and is not subsumed under the inferior or middling grades.
There are only five because there are the lower, the middle-lower, the upper-lower, the superior, and the supreme-upper;
thus, there are only five. Other masters say that the mixed cultivation of dhyāna is the refinement of the five faculties, such as faith and the rest.
Because each [level] is established as five grades according to the sequence of their respective predominance, there are only five.
Therefore, since the mixed cultivation consists of five grades, the Pure Abodes likewise consist of only five.
Some say that in the fourth dhyāna, nine grades of wholesome roots arise sequentially in nine locations; specifically,
the lowest-of-the-low grade of wholesome roots gives rise to the Anabhraka heaven.
From the lower and middling roots of goodness, one is reborn in the heavens that produce merit;
up to the highest of the high roots of goodness, one is reborn in Akaniṣṭha.
In these various realms, there can be neither increase nor decrease.
Therefore, there should be only five Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Some say that in the fourth dhyāna there are nine grades of afflictions.
If one has not yet subdued any of the nine grades [of afflictions], one is born in the Anabhraka Heaven;
if one has subdued the upper-upper grade, one is born in the Puṇyaprasava Heaven;
and so on, until if one has subdued the lower-middle grade, one is born in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
There is no one who, having suppressed the lower grades [of meditative concentration], is born [in the Pure Abodes]; therefore, there are only five types of Pure Abodes.
Question: Is it possible to practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna and yet not be born in the Pure Abodes?
Answer: Yes.

That is to say, having practiced the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, one either attains parinirvāṇa in the present life, or regresses to be reborn in a lower stage, or progresses to be reborn in the formless realm.
This refers to those who do not delight in the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) but practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna.
Question: Is it possible for one who has fully developed the five grades of mixed cultivation of dhyāna to be reborn in the Anabhraka Heaven and so forth?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, first there arises the "Cloudless" [heaven], and subsequently there arises the "Merit-Born" [heaven].
Next, one is born in the Bṛhatphala heaven;
thereafter, one is successively born in the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda school, Fascicle 175.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 176,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhiskandha), Chapter Four: The Sub-section on Non-returners (Anāgāmin-uddāna), Part Three. As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*, there are five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
These are the heavens of Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha.
What is the heaven of Avṛha?
It refers to the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga) of the beings belonging to the realm of Avṛha.
Based on the attainment of the object, the attainment of the location,
and the unobscured-neutral form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that have already arisen in that heaven,
this is called the Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha).
Question: For what reason is that heaven named "Free from Affliction" (Avṛha)?
Answer: It is a conventional designation, a conceptual name, an established convention, and a mental construct established according to one's inclination;
it is not necessarily the case that every meaning is fully present within the name.
Furthermore, because the bodies of those devas are free from affliction and their minds are free from affliction,
and because they experience exclusively the bliss of pure tranquility throughout their entire lifespan— bliss not possessed by those in lower realms— they are called "Free from Affliction" (Avṛha).
Furthermore, those gods clearly perceive suffering as truly suffering, the origin as truly the origin, cessation as truly cessation, and the path as truly the path.
Because they are free from the heavy, dysfunctional tendencies (*dausthulya*) arising from the lower realms, they are called "Free from Affliction" (*Abṛha*).
Furthermore, "affliction" (*prabha*) refers to the Vast Fruit Heaven (*Bṛhatphala*).
Because this heaven is the first to transcend that [level], it is called the Heaven Free from Affliction (*Abṛha*).
What is the Heaven Free from Heat (*Atapa*)?
This refers to the class of companions known as the Heaven of No Heat, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is that heaven named "No Heat"?
Answer: It is a conventional designation and a conceptual construct, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, the bodies of those devas are free from feverish distress and their minds are free from feverish distress;
because they experience exclusively pure, cooling bliss throughout their entire lifespan—something not possessed by those in lower realms—they are called "Free from Fever" (Atapa).
Furthermore, those gods clearly perceive that suffering is truly suffering, up to and including the path as truly the path.
Because they are free from the feverish heat of the afflictions arising from the lower realms, they are called "Heatless" (Atapa).
Furthermore, because the fires of the predominant afflictions arising from the neighboring lower stage still burn within the Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha), it is still called "Hot.
Because one transcends those [afflictions], it is named the Heaven of No Heat (Atapa).
What is the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven?
It refers to the class of beings belonging to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is that heaven named "Śubhakṛtsna" (Utterly Pure)?
The answer is: "They are merely conventional designations and mental constructs," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, because the physical form and appearance of those gods are upright, excellent, and surpass those of the two lower heavens, they are called Sudarśana (Good Appearance).
Furthermore, that deity clearly perceives suffering as truly suffering, up to and including the path as truly the path.
Because his mind is free from all defilements and is pure and luminous, he is named Sudarśana (Well-Seen).
Furthermore, because those who have attained the superior degree of mixed meditative absorption (dhyāna) are virtuous, coarse, and manifest, they are called the Sudṛśa devas.
What are the Sudarśana devas?
It refers to one class of companions among the Sudarśana devas, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is that deity named Sudarśana?
Answer: It is a conventional designation and a conceptual construct, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, because the form and color of that deity become increasingly exquisite and are a joy for all to behold, it is named Sudarśana.
Furthermore, those devas clearly perceive that suffering is truly suffering, and so on, up to the fact that the path is truly the path.
Because their minds have turned toward purity, being free from all defilements and turbidity, they are called "Those of Excellent Vision."

Furthermore, because those who have attained the superior and perfect meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) through the mixed cultivation of the stages obtain wholesome dharmas that become increasingly coarse and manifest, they are called the Sudarśana Heaven.
What is the Akaniṣṭha Heaven?
It refers to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
A group of companions, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is that heaven named Akaniṣṭha?
The answer is: "They are merely conventional designations and conceptual constructs," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, because the physical form (*rūpa*) of those gods is most excellent and sublime, such that no others can surpass it, they are called Akaniṣṭha (the Ultimate Form).
Furthermore, those gods clearly perceive that suffering is truly suffering, up to and including the path as truly the path.
Because they are free from all defilements and turbidity, and because no other gods of the form realm can surpass them, it is called Akaniṣṭha (the Ultimate Form).
Furthermore, because they have attained the most supreme and perfectly complete grade of mixed cultivation of dhyāna,
which no other wholesome roots of the form realm can equal, it is called Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form). Furthermore,
because those gods are the most venerable, the most excellent, and the most extreme within the realm of form, it is called Akaniṣṭha.
Furthermore, they are also called the Gods of the Culmination of Obstruction (*āvaraṇa-kṛtsna*).
"Obstruction" refers to accumulated matter (*rūpa*).
Because they are the most venerable, the most excellent, and the most supreme regarding this obstruction, they are named the Gods of the Culmination of Obstruction.
Furthermore, they are also called the "Summit of the Ultimate" (*mūrdha-paryanta*) devas, because they are both the summit of all that possesses form (*rūpin*) and the ultimate.
Question: Is the birth among the Śuddhāvāsa devas caused by karma?
Is it by means of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna?
If so, what is the fault?
If it were by means of karma, then the mixed cultivation of dhyāna would be rendered futile.
If it were by means of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, it would contradict what is stated in the Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra;
for as that text says: "By means of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna and by means of karma, one is born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens," and so forth, at length.
Answer: Some say that it is produced by karma.
Question: Would this not then render the meditative cultivation of the dhyānas futile?
Answer: Because the karma of mixed cultivation of dhyāna attains certainty, it is not in vain.

Furthermore, it is only after the preliminary mixed cultivation of dhyāna that one can bring forth the mental karma (*cetanā-karma*) that projects it; by this means, one is able to project that homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Other masters say that it is by means of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna.
As for the *Prakaraṇapāda*, how should its statement be reconciled?
Answer: It is precisely the meditative absorption of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna*) that is spoken of by means of the term "karma.
Furthermore, that treatise first mentions the one who practices mixed cultivation in order to show that they had previously entered that meditative concentration.
The subsequent statement and the phrase "born in the Śuddhāvāsa by means of karma" are spoken in order to show that at a later time,
one is born in the Śuddhāvāsa precisely through the power of that [previous practice].
Thus it is said.
It is also due to the power of karma and due to the mixed cultivation of dhyāna.
That is to say, although the volitional action may be present, if one has not cultivated dhyāna through mixing, one cannot be born there.
Even if one has cultivated the dhyānas through mixed practice, if the karma of volition (cetanā-karman) does not manifest, one still cannot be born there.
Therefore, there must be the karma of volition that draws forth the mixed cultivation of dhyāna to ensure its certainty.
Only then can one be born there.
Are all those who train training for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained?
And if they are training for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained, are they all [necessarily] training?
It is promised that this shall be explained in four verses.
Question: Why was this treatise composed?
Answer: The Śālistamba Sūtra is the fundamental basis of this treatise.
He says that one is called a "learner" (śaikṣa) because of training in what is to be learned.
Let there be no doubt that it is only when those who are learners train in what is to be learned that they are designated as "learners."
When abiding in one's original nature, one is not called a learner (*śaikṣa*).
It is only when those who are beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*) abide in their original nature that they are called "beyond learning.
When one is training in what is to be learned, one is not called "beyond learning."
In order to bring this doubt to a definitive conclusion,
and to demonstrate that those in training abide in their fundamental nature,
while those beyond training likewise train in what is to be trained in, this treatise is composed.
One in training does not train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained;
rather, it is said that there are two causes and conditions by which one who trains abides in their original nature and is called "abiding in original nature.
First, they maintain their noble and virtuous nature without falling back.
Second, there is the guarding of one's own virtues without further cultivation.
Here, it is simply said that "abiding in the original nature" refers to not cultivating the preparatory practices for the fruit of a Once-returner,
as in the case of a Stream-enterer who does not advance toward that stage.
One who is a Once-returner does not advance to cultivate the preparatory application for the fruit of Non-returning;
one who is a Non-returner does not advance to cultivate the preparatory application for the fruit of Arhatship;
and one liberated through faith does not seek to become one attained through vision.

Furthermore, those in training do not seek to give rise to the previously unattained: the meditation on impurity, mindfulness of breathing, the three types of mindfulness-stay, the seven stages of proficiency, dhyāna, the immeasurables, the formless attainments, the liberations, the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality.
They do not manifest the supernormal powers;
they do not practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna;
and they do not enter the meditative attainment of cessation.
They neither uphold, recite, or study the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, nor do they transmit them to others;
nor do they dwell in forest hermitages to contemplate and investigate the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
Nor do they attend to the affairs of the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha.
This is called training not for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained, yet training nonetheless.
Question: For what reason and by what causes and conditions does one not train in what ought to be trained?
The answer is: He may be suffering from a chronic illness, or lacking the necessary provisions;
he then reflects, "I have already transcended immeasurable cycles of birth and death."
Only seven more existences remain, or perhaps only one more existence;
or else, he reflects: "I have already emerged from the mire of desire."
Only a few remaining beings from the higher realms are currently present here;
since they now suffer from afflictions or lack the necessary provisions and conditions, they may fortunately find some respite.
Why then should one hasten to practice? For this reason, such students do not study what ought to be studied.
There are those who, having attained what was not yet attained, train therein but are not "trainers" (*śaikṣa*).
This refers to Arhats and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who further seek higher dharmas;
herein, "higher dharmas" refers to superior qualities, namely seeking immediate liberation and attaining the unshakable (*akopya*).
Furthermore, when Arhats give rise to the previously unattained contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā),
mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti),
and the threefold contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Mastery in the seven bases,
the meditative concentrations,
and the immeasurables.
The formless liberations,
the spheres of mastery, the spheres of totality,
and the manifestation of the various supernormal powers.
He practices the mixed cultivation of dhyāna and enters the meditative attainment of cessation.

He gives rise to the unhindered analytical knowledges, the knowledge of non-contention, the knowledge of aspiration, the ultimate concentration, emptiness of emptiness, wishlessness of wishlessness, and signlessness of signlessness.
One who upholds, recites, and studies the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma;
or one who transmits them to others, or dwells in a forest hermitage,
contemplating and examining the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
Or again, they may attend to matters concerning the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha;
or they may be ordinary persons seeking liberation from the defilement of desire, the defilement of form, and a portion of the defilement of the formless;
or they may give rise to the contemplation of impurity.
Mindfulness of breathing,
the foundations of mindfulness,
and the contemplation of the three characteristics.
Mastery in the seven bases;
the stages of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas;
