the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, the formless attainments, the liberations, the bases of mastery, the bases of totality, the production of the superknowledges, and entry into the attainment of non-perception.
They uphold, recite, and study the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma;
they transmit them to others; they dwell in forest hermitages;
they contemplate and investigate the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma; or they attend to the affairs of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
This is called "learning what has not yet been attained," yet that is not true learning.
Question: For what reason does an Arhat still learn what is to be learned?
Answer: Although he does not learn for the sake of abandoning afflictions (*kleśa*), [he learns for other purposes].
And because they delight in superior qualities,
those in training and those beyond training also train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained;
that is to say, they train in seeking the higher dharmas.
That is to say, a stream-enterer who advances to cultivate the preparatory practices for the fruit of a once-returner—
and so on, as explained at length, up to performing services for the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—
is said to be one in training who trains in order to attain what has not yet been attained.
There is that which is neither training (*śaikṣa*) nor training for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained;
this refers to Arhats and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) abiding in their natural state,
who are immediately liberated and do not seek to become immovable (*akopya*).
To speak at length, up to and including not even engaging in affairs pertaining to the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha; and likewise,
an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who does not seek freedom from the defilements of the desire realm—
to speak at length, up to and including not even engaging in affairs pertaining to the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha.
This is called "neither a learner nor one who trains for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained.
Are all those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa) necessarily ones who do not train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained?
Or, conversely, if one does not train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained, [is one necessarily beyond training?]
Are all those [who have attained] the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa)?
One should respond that this involves four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are those who are no-more-learners, yet for whom there is still learning for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained.

That is to say, when an Arhat seeks the higher dharma, he immediately attains liberation; or when he seeks to become unshakable; or when an Arhat gives rise to the previously unattained contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
To speak at length, this extends even to managing affairs for the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
this is called being one who has attained the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), yet it is not that they do not train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained.
There are those who do not train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained, yet they are not ones who have attained the state beyond training.

This refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who abide in their natural state— that is, stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) who do not progress toward the practice for the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*),
and so on, up to and including not engaging in activities pertaining to the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha.
Furthermore, ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) do not practice for the sake of becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm;
this applies extensively up to their not even engaging in the affairs of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
This is called "not training for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained," and they are not those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
There are those who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and do not train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained;
namely, Arhats who abide in their original nature and are liberated at that very moment, as well as Arhats who do not seek the unshakable state (*āneñja*).
One does not seek to give rise to what has not yet been attained, such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) or mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*);
this is explained at length until it is said that one does not even manage affairs for the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha.
This is called "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*) who does not train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained.
There are those who are neither non-learners (*aśaikṣa*) nor those who do not train for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained;
namely, those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who strive to seek higher dharmas,
such as a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) advancing in the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
To speak at length, up to and including those who manage affairs for the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; and likewise,
up to and including ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) seeking liberation from the defilements of the desire realm,
and those who manage affairs for the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
This is called being neither one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) nor one who trains for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained.

How should the statement in that sutra be interpreted?
The answer is: that sutra speaks only with reference to those currently training;
it does not speak of all [beings].
Furthermore, that sutra makes this statement based on the fact that the underlying intention does not cease:
namely, whether those in training give rise to a wholesome mind,

the response is that this is spoken with reference to the temporary cessation of application;

Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra:
"There are four types of persons (pudgala)."
First, flowing with the current;
second, flowing against the current;
third, abiding in the middle.
Regarding the four pāramitās,
although they are mentioned in this manner in the sūtras, they are not analyzed in detail there;
that sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which was not explained by him shall now be explained;
therefore, this treatise is composed.
Question: What is the meaning of "flowing with the stream" (anuloma)?

Answer: With respect to all births, all destinies, all states of existence, all classes of beings, and all cycles of birth and death, to serve as a limb, a gateway, a basis, a path, and a track leading toward them is the meaning of "flowing with the current."
What is the meaning of "going against the stream"?

The answer is: regarding all that arises and ceases, it is the tendency toward cessation, the category of cessation, the cessation of birth-and-death, acting as a constituent, a gateway, a basis, a path, and a track leading toward [nirvana].
This is the meaning of "going against the stream.
There are many kinds of streams;
some say that the Noble Path is called a "stream."
Some say that karma is called "flood" (ogha), some say craving is called "flood," and others say birth and death are called "flood.
Regarding these floods:
It speaks only of birth and death.
Furthermore, a sutra asks: "What is meant by 'flowing with the current'?
It refers to indulging in various desires and committing evil deeds."
What is meant by "going against the stream"?
It refers to not indulging in various sensual desires and not committing unwholesome deeds.
One should know that in that sutra, the "following the stream" and "going against the stream" are established based on a single lifetime.
What is explained here establishes "flowing with the current" and "flowing against the current" based on multiple lifetimes.
Furthermore, that sutra establishes "flowing with the current" and "flowing against the current" based on the temporary arising of desire and evil, and the abandonment of desire and evil.

Therefore, noble ones who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire are also said to be "flowing with the stream," while ordinary beings who have already abandoned the defilements of desire are also said to be "flowing against the stream.

What is described here establishes the categories of flowing with the stream and flowing against the stream based on whether one is oriented toward saṃsāra or turned away from saṃsāra over a long period of time.

Therefore, there are those who have already abandoned the defilement of form (*rūpa-rāga*) yet are called "flowing with the current," and there are those who have not yet abandoned the defilement of desire (*kāma-rāga*) yet are called "flowing against the current.
"All beings" refers to the four modes of birth (*catasro yonayaḥ*).
The various destinies refer to the five destinies.
The various existences refer to the three realms of existence.
The various types refer to the distinctions of types such as lands and locations.
"All those in birth and death" refers to the various modes of transmigration from beginningless time until the final limit.
"As branches" refers to the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-bhavāṅga*).
That which acts as a gate refers to karma and afflictions;
that which acts as a basis refers to the support;
that which acts as a path refers to the path leading toward birth and death.
One who is "tending toward the trace" refers to one tending toward the trace of the origination of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya*).
Herein, the first five phrases manifest birth and death,
while the latter five phrases manifest the nourishment of birth and death.
They are embraced by birth and death;
they are sustained by birth and death;
birth and death are without interruption.
Birth and death increase in accordance [with the flow].
Just as one draws a river so that it is never exhausted,
the five types— birth and the others— are like those previously explained in the sense of flowing against the current.
As for the distinctions: that which attains cessation therein is the "limb";
the limbs referred to are the eight branches of the Noble Path;
the gates referred to are the contemplation of impurity, mindfulness of breathing, and so forth.
That which constitutes the "task" refers to the three gates of liberation.
That which constitutes the "path" refers to the path leading to the cessation of birth and death.
That which constitutes the "track toward" refers to the track toward the cessation of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Among these, the first five phrases reveal the cessation of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);
the latter five phrases reveal that which can destroy and extinguish birth and death rather than nourishing it,
and that which can renounce and turn away from birth and death rather than grasping at it.
It can disperse and destroy birth-and-death, yet it is not that which sustains it;
it can sever birth-and-death, yet it is not without severance;
it can diminish what is contrary to birth-and-death, yet it does not increase what is compliant with it.
It is like draining a pond or a marsh, gradually causing it to dry up.
Question: At what point are they called "flowing with the current" or "flowing against the current"? Some say:
Up until the moment when the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) has not yet arisen, one is called a "follower of the stream" (*anulomika*);
once it has arisen, one is called a "counter-streamer" (*pratilomika*). Some say:
Up until the arising of the "highest mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), one is called a "follower of the stream";
once it has arisen, one is called a "counter-streamer. Some say:
Up until the arising of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one is called a "follower of the stream" (*anulomika*);
once it has arisen, one is called a "counter-streamer" (*pratilomika*). Some say:
Up to the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).
Some say up to the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*). Others say:
This continues up to the stage of Heat (ūṣmagata).
Some say it extends even to the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).

Some say that as long as the contemplation of impurity, mindfulness of breathing, and so forth have not yet arisen, one is called "flowing with the stream"; once they have arisen, [one is no longer so called].
Regarding the term "one who flows against the stream":
according to this explanation,
one who has not yet planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation is called "one who flows with the stream."
Those who have already planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation are called "those who flow against the stream. Why is this?

Because although immeasurable sentient beings are able to practice generosity toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the solitary, and those exhausted by long journeys, [they do not yet possess such roots].
As well as various foods, drinks, clothing, bedding, medicines, dwellings, lamps, incense, flowers,
and all manner of precious jewels and necessary requisites for ascetics.
Furthermore, they may establish great unrestricted sacrificial assemblies,
such as Vīramitra, Ajaṅgha, and others;
yet this is because they have not planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

Having experienced those fruits during the long night of birth and death, they are reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta), where they undergo the suffering of hunger and thirst for hundreds of thousands of years,
such that they do not even hear the names of food or drink.
Some are born among humans in states of poverty and lowliness, beset by manifold sufferings;
others, moreover, are seen to be sentient beings who uphold the prohibitive precepts and study extensively.
They uphold, recite, and study the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma;
they penetrate their words and meanings, analyzing and explaining them,
and are furthermore able to master secular treatises as well.
These include the treatises on grammar, logic, royal polity, medicine, and the arts and crafts; or alternatively,
he may also be proficient in the various non-Buddhist treatises,
such as those of the Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, Vedas, Lokāyata, and Nirgrantha schools.
Because they did not plant the roots of merit conducive to liberation,
after having experienced those fruits throughout the long night of saṃsāra,
they were reborn once again among the animals.
They take birth in the bodies of various cattle, sheep, camels, donkeys, and the like;
they are foolish and blind, even unable to speak.
Or they are born among humans as blind, deaf, mute, dull-witted, and devoid of wisdom.
Or again, he may see immeasurable sentient beings practicing various meditative concentrations or becoming free from the defilement of desire.
Either free from attachment to the realm of form,
or free from a portion of the attachment to the formless realm, they abide in the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
give rise to the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and manifest the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Because they have not planted the roots of goodness conducive to liberation,
after experiencing those fruits within the long night of saṃsāra,
they are reborn in hell to undergo various intense sufferings.
Or they may take birth in the realm of animals as great pythons,
vomiting forth blazing venom that causes crags to collapse and rocks to split;
or they may be born among humans as caṇḍālas, pukkasas, and the like, performing foul and evil deeds.
All such [actions], because they yield merit only temporarily before one subsequently falls back into decline, are called "conforming to the stream.
If sentient beings offer even a single morsel of food as a gift, [it likewise falls under this category].
Some may merely observe the precepts for a single day and night;
some may even recite a four-line verse;
or some may cultivate the preparatory practices for meditative concentration for a brief moment, thereby being able to plant the roots of merit conducive to liberation.
Consequently, even if at a later time they should, due to afflictions, commit various misdeeds of body, speech, and mind,
or perform an act of immediate retribution,
or even sever all roots of virtue.
Even if there is not the slightest seed of wholesome dharma (*śukladharma*) within their bodies,
they fall into the Avīci Hell and undergo various sufferings,
yet are still said to be "dwelling on the shore of nirvāṇa."
Because they will certainly attain parinirvāṇa.
Regarding this, there is an analogy:
it is like a fisherman who uses food as bait.
It was placed upon a hook and cast into deep water,
where a fish swallowed it;
at that time, even though the fish might sport about or enter its lair, [it remained caught].
One should know that it is already in the hands of that person,
for it will certainly reach the shore before long;
it is for this reason that it is so said.
It would be better to be Devadatta and fall into the Avīci hell than to be Udraka Rāmaputra and be born in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception. Why is this?
Although Devadatta committed the three deeds of immediate retribution, severed all roots of virtue, and fell into the Avīci hell,
he shall attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha when the human lifespan is forty thousand years.
Those of sharp faculties who surpass Śāriputra and others—
such as Udraka Rāmaputra—

though free from the defilements of the eight stages and dwelling in the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), have reached the pinnacle of *śamatha* and stand on the verge of transcending the three realms, approaching the gateway to the Deathless (*amṛta*).
Having been born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he experienced peaceful bliss for eighty thousand great kalpas.
When his life there ended,
by the power of his evil karma, he was reborn in that forest of asceticism in the wilderness.
Having grown wings, he flies as a flying raccoon-dog, preying upon birds and beasts; whether moving on land, in water, or through the air, none can escape him.
Due to these evil deeds, at the end of his life, he shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
They undergo various kinds of unbearable and intense suffering;
for this reason, the Buddha did not record the time at which they would attain liberation. Therefore, it is said.
Though dwelling in the forest of ascetic practices, one is called "one who flows with the current";
though remaining within the realm of the five desires, one is called "one who flows against the current.
There is an analogy for this.
It is like a person carrying two vessels while walking—
one of gold and one of clay—
who stumbles and falls, causing both vessels to break.
At that time, the man did not begrudge the golden vessel but instead cherished the earthenware one;
he sighed in lamentation over this.
When someone asked him the reason for it, he answered them in full detail.
The person questioned him further, saying,
"You could not bear to see your golden vessels broken;
why then do you feel such deep regret for a single earthenware pot?"
He replied again,
"You are truly foolish. Why is that?"
Once a golden vessel has been broken, although its shape as a vessel is lost, its substance as gold is not;
it can be returned to a goldsmith to be restored to its original form or even made superior to its original state.
Once a clay vessel has been broken, however, both its shape and its substance are lost.
Although it was entrusted to a potter,
it has become so fragile that it cannot even serve as a lamp-stand,
let alone function as its original vessel.
Therefore, I do not now lament for the golden vessel, but rather cherish the earthenware one.
In the same way, because Devadatta has already planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*),
although he committed many evils and was reborn in hell, [he will eventually attain liberation].
Yet he shall become a Pratyekabuddha superior even to Śāriputra and others;
just as that golden vessel was broken and then restored,
so it is with him, for the son of Maṅgala did not plant the roots of merit conducive to liberation.
Although they may leave the defilements of the eight stages and be born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
they will ultimately fall into the evil destinies and have no prospect of liberation;
they are like those earthenware vessels that, once broken, cannot be recovered.

Therefore, those who have not yet planted the roots of goodness conducive to liberation are said to be "flowing with the current," while those who have already planted the roots of goodness conducive to liberation are said to be "flowing against the current."

Question: Since the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla) within the bodies of sentient beings are subtle in their characteristics, how can it be known whether they have been planted or not?
Answer: They are known by means of their signs (liṅga).
What are its characteristics?
It is this: when one hears a virtuous friend preaching the true Dharma, the hairs on one's body stand on end and one weeps with flowing tears.
One who feels weary of birth and death and rejoices in nirvana,
and who conceives deep love and respect for the Dharma and the Dharma-preacher,
should be known as one who has certainly planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation.
If one is unable to do so, it should be known that the seeds have not been planted.
Regarding this, there is an analogy:
it is like a person who, having sown seeds in a field plot long ago, now experiences doubt.
"Did I ever sow seeds in this garden plot?
he wondered, unable to reach a decision.
A bystander said to him:
Why should you hesitate?
You need only drench it with water and cover it with dung;
if it sprouts, then you will know that it has been planted.
If it were not so, it would not be; thus, according to his words, he attains certainty.
Such is the practitioner.
He wondered to himself whether he had ever planted the seeds of liberation within his own being.
Then, that virtuous friend spoke to him, saying,
"You should now go to the place where the Dharma is being taught."
If, when listening to the Dharma, one’s body hairs stand on end and one weeps with flowing tears,
even to the point of conceiving love and reverence for the Dharma and the Dharma teacher,
it should be known that one has already planted the seeds of liberation.
Otherwise, it would not.
Therefore, by means of this characteristic, one can clearly understand what the meaning of "abiding in itself" is.
Answer: It is not a constituent of birth, nor even of the various forms of birth-and-death;
it is not even a constituent of the path leading toward [nirvana], nor is it a constituent of the cessation of birth, nor even the cessation of birth-and-death.
Even up to the stage of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry, this is the meaning of abiding in oneself.
This refers to having accomplished a small portion of what was to be done,
or having accomplished all that was to be done.
The intention (āśaya) either temporarily ceases or ceases ultimately.
Unlike those who follow the current or go against the current,
because their intention does not cease regarding what is to be done within both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, they are called "self-abiding" (svastha).
This refers to the meaning of abiding in one's own nature.
Question: Are all Arhats those who abide in their own nature?
Or, are all those who abide in their own nature Arhats?
Answer: All those Arhats abide in their own state.
In what do they abide?
They abide having abandoned the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Within the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the total exhaustion and abandonment of all fetters (*sarva-saṃyojana*) that constitutes the fruit of arhatship,
there are those who abide therein but are not yet arhats;
namely, non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
In what state does he abide?

He abides in the abandonment of the pervasive knowledge (*parijñā*) that consists in the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), which is the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) characterized by detachment from sensual desire.
As the Blessed One said:
Having eternally severed the five afflictions, perfected in training, and having attained mastery over the dharma that is not subject to further rebirth,
as well as meditative concentration and the faculties— one such as this is called a person who abides in themselves regarding the five afflictions.
This refers to the five hindrances and the five lower fetters;
because these have been exhausted by one who has attained the stage of non-returning (anāgāmin),
they are said to be "permanently severed."
"Those whose training is complete" refers to those who have perfected the fruits and perfected the faculties, but have not perfected meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
"Those who do not lead [to further rebirth]" refers to those who lack the qualities that project [a future existence].
This refers to that which cannot be induced by the karma and afflictions of the desire realm.
"Attaining mastery" means attaining mastery over the mind; it signifies the ultimate attainment of mastery through the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds.
One who has attained the faculty of concentration (samādhīndriya) refers to one who has accomplished the faculty of samādhi subsumed within dhyāna;
such a person is called one who abides in themselves.

That is to say, regarding one who dwells in the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*) within the full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) while remaining free from the defilement of desire:
are all those acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the ultimate restraint also acquisitions of the ultimate track (*pada*)?
If one attains the ultimate track (*atyantapada*), does one thereby attain all that constitutes the ultimate restraint (*atyantasaṃvara*)?
Answer: All who attain the ultimate restraint have attained the ultimate track. Why is this so?
The morality of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-śīla) is called the ultimate restraint;
the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) are called the ultimate tracks.
Those who have already attained the morality of one beyond training—
This is because they have necessarily attained the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*).
There are those who have attained the ultimate track (*atyantapada*) but have not attained the ultimate restraint (*atyantasaṃvara*);
these are the non-returners (*anāgāmin*), as the World-Honored One has said.
How does a bhikṣu attain the supreme goal?
It is by means of the permanent abandonment and thorough knowledge of the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni). Why is this so?
Regarding those who are non-returners (anāgāmin):
because they have already attained the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) but have not yet attained the ethical discipline (śīla) of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
some make this statement.
Are all those who have attained the ultimate track (atyanta-pada) necessarily those who have reached the further shore (pāra-gata)?
And are all those who have reached the further shore necessarily those who have attained the ultimate track?
Answer: All those who have attained the ultimate track are necessarily those who have reached the further shore.
Why is this so? Because the total exhaustion of all fetters is called the supreme track (atyantapada).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The "trace" refers to *nirvāṇa*.
Having eternally severed the five fetters and no longer transmigrating through birth and death is called "reaching the other shore.
When the various *arhats* have personally realized this within their own bodies, it is called "attaining the ultimate trace."
Having severed the five fetters that bind one to the higher realms, one no longer transmigrates through the birth and death of the three realms; this is called "reaching the other shore.
There is reaching the other shore that does not involve attaining the ultimate track.
This refers to the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
As the Blessed One said:
"In what way is a bhikṣu called one who has reached the further shore?"
This refers to the thorough knowledge of the permanent abandonment of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).
Because one has abandoned these, one no longer transmigrates through the cycle of birth and death in the desire realm; this is called "reaching the further shore" (*pāramitā*).
Furthermore, the Arhat reaches the further shore for a second time within the three realms.
This means that when one abandons what is to be abandoned through seeing and what is to be abandoned through cultivation within the three realms,
the non-returner (anāgāmin) reaches the further shore once more in the desire realm.
This means that when one has abandoned the defilements of the desire realm to be abandoned through seeing and those to be abandoned through cultivation,
yet has not yet attained nirvāṇa, one is not said to have "attained the supreme track.
Or, it is stated as follows:
Are all those who are arhats also those who have exhausted the very source and bottom?
And are all those who have exhausted the very source and bottom also arhats?
Answer: All those who are arhats are indeed those who have exhausted the very source and bottom.
There are those who have exhausted the source and bottom [of existence] but are not Arhats;
namely, Non-returners (anāgāmin).
As the Blessed One said:
How does a bhikṣu exhaust the source and bottom?
It refers to the permanent abandonment and full knowledge of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).
Regarding this, there are two explanations as set forth in the *Pāramitā* [treatise].
"What constitutes a bodhisattva?
and so forth, as explained at length.
[The author] asks: for what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As a sūtra says:
"There is a sentient being."
This is the class of those who are not deluded; this is the class of the wise—
namely, the bodhisattvas— who,
although they speak in this way, do not engage in conceptual discrimination.
Based on what is one called a bodhisattva?
By attaining what is one called a bodhisattva?
That sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which was not previously explained shall now be explained;
for this reason, this treatise is composed.
Furthermore, it is composed in order to sever the conceit of those who are not actually bodhisattvas yet give rise to the overweening pride of being bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Because there are sentient beings who,
by giving a single meal as an offering, [attain great merit].
Whether it be by giving a single garment or a single dwelling place,
even down to giving a single tooth-stick,
or by undertaking and observing a single precept.
Or, having recited a single verse,
or having practiced a single moment of concentrated mindfulness on impurity and so forth,
one makes a lion’s roar, speaking these words:
For this reason, I shall certainly become a Buddha.
In order to sever such overweening pride,
[the sūtra] reveals that although he passed through three incalculable eons, he fully cultivated various difficult practices and ascetic austerities.
If one has not yet cultivated the karma of the excellent marks, one should not yet claim, "I am a bodhisattva," much less so for those who are extremely inferior and possess overweening pride.
Therefore, until the completion of the first incalculable eon, the bodhisattva [remains thus].
Although he practiced various difficult ascetic disciplines,
he was not yet able to know with certainty that he would become a Buddha.
This was at the completion of the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
Although he was able to know with certainty that he would become a Buddha,
he still did not yet dare to utter the fearless words, "I shall become a Buddha.
This was during the period when, having completed the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he was cultivating the karma for the marks of excellence.
They also know with certainty that they shall become Buddhas,
and they likewise utter the fearless lion’s roar, saying:
"I shall become a Buddha."
Question: To what extent is one called a bodhisattva?
Answer: To the extent that one is able to perform and increase karma that results in the maturation of marks (*lakṣaṇa-vipāka-karman*).
Question: If all sentient beings who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are capable of non-retrogression...
From this point on, one should indeed be called a bodhisattva.
Why, then, is it that one is only designated as a bodhisattva after having performed and accumulated karma that results in the maturation of the marks?
The answer is: if one is certain regarding awakening and certain regarding the path thereto, only then is one called a true bodhisattva.
From the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the point before one has cultivated the karma for the marks of excellence,
although one is certain regarding bodhi,
one's destination remains uncertain.
One is not yet called a true bodhisattva;
it is only upon reaching the stage of cultivating the karma for the marks of excellence that one becomes certain of enlightenment.
The destiny [of such a being] is also certain;
therefore, it is only up to this point that one is called a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, when cultivating the karma for the marks of excellence:
If a person or a deva can both recognize and know that one is a bodhisattva, he is therefore called a true bodhisattva.
When he has not yet cultivated the karma for the marks of excellence, he is known only by devas;
for this reason, he is not yet called a true bodhisattva.
Furthermore, when cultivating the karma for the marks of excellence,
one abandons five inferior matters and attains five superior matters.
First, one abandons all miserable realms and is constantly reborn in the happy realms.
Second, they abandon birth in inferior families and are constantly born into noble families;
third, they abandon non-male bodies and constantly obtain male bodies;
fourth, they abandon incomplete faculties and constantly possess all faculties.
Having abandoned the five states of existence and being free from forgetfulness, mindfulness arises spontaneously and constantly;
by virtue of this, one is called a true Bodhisattva.
Prior to cultivating the karma for the marks of excellence, it was the opposite of this.
Therefore, they are not called true bodhisattvas.
Question: What benefit does a bodhisattva obtain by attaining this mindfulness of self-nature?
Answer: By attaining this mindfulness of self-nature, the bodhisattva is freed from the faults of sentient beings.
Having accumulated extensive learning and deep faith in cause and effect,
they skillfully guide their followers so that the instructions they impart are never in vain;
thus their provisions for awakening become further perfected— this is what constitutes benefit.
What is meant by "attaining the name of Bodhisattva"?
Answer: It is the attainment of karma that ripens into the marks [of a Great Being].
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed?
Answer: It is in order to bring about certainty for those who harbor doubts.
That is to say, it was previously stated that one who is capable of performing and increasing karma that results in the maturation of distinct characteristics is called a bodhisattva.
Do not give rise to doubt.
Although one is designated a bodhisattva upon reaching this stage,
the name "bodhisattva" may also arise from the realization of other superior dharmas.

This treatise is composed in order to demonstrate that one receives the name "Bodhisattva" solely through the maturation of karma characterized by specific marks, and not by means of any other factor.
Question: Is one called a "Bodhisattva" (one who possesses enlightenment) because of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Why is it that this name "follower" (anuvartaka) applies before realization, yet once realization is attained, one no longer follows [the path] and is instead called a Buddha?
The answer is: because while this sentient being has not yet attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
With a resolute intention, they constantly accord with enlightenment,
proceed toward enlightenment,
and draw near to enlightenment.
They delight in bodhi, revere bodhi,
and thirst for bodhi.
Seeking realization and desiring to realize it without slackening or ceasing,
never for a moment relinquishing the mind set on bodhi—
therefore, one is called a Bodhisattva.
Once he has realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*),
his aspiration for, and application toward, the pursuit of enlightenment both cease;
there remains only the excellence of having accomplished the meaning of awakening.
Because all defiled and non-defiled ignorance has been eternally severed; because one has fully awakened to all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) regarding both the ultimate and conventional truths;
and because one is further able to awaken immeasurable sentient beings by providing benefit according to their faculties, inclinations, and dispositions.
Because the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*) is preeminent through such factors as these,
one is called a Buddha (*buddha*),
not a Bodhisattva (*bodhisattva*).
Furthermore, "sattva" carries the meaning of one who is courageous and valiant.
Before attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
they are constantly vigorous and courageous in their pursuit of enlightenment.
Because they seek to realize [enlightenment] swiftly, they are called Bodhisattvas.
Once they have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, [they...]
Consequently, his courageous resolve for enlightenment subsides;
he is called a Buddha solely because he awakens to the supreme meaning,
as he has accomplished the most excellent awakening.

Fascicle 176; The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra,
Fascicle 177.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others, translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.

Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhiskandha), Chapter Four: The Sub-section on Non-returners (Anāgāmin-nirdeśa). Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of karma that results in maturation (*vipākakarman*)?
Is it bodily action?
Is it verbal action?
Or is it mental action?
Answer: Its intrinsic nature consists of the three types of action, yet mental action is predominant.
Some say that its intrinsic nature consists solely of mental action.
It is neither bodily nor vocal action. Why is this?
Because this karma is fierce and sharp.
Because bodily and vocal karma are dull.
Question: Is karma that has maturation as its characteristic located in the mental ground (manobhūmi), or in the five groups of consciousness (pañcavijñānakāya)?
Answer: It resides in the mental ground (manobhūmi), not in the fivefold body of consciousness (pañcavijñānakāya). Why is this so?
This karma involves conceptualization;
it must be performed after having observed [the object].
The five consciousnesses are without conceptualization.
Because it arises through the power of its objective conditions (*viṣaya*).

Question: Regarding the karma that results in the marks (*lakṣaṇa-vipāka-karman*), is it acquired through preparatory effort (*prayoga-prāpta*) or is it acquired through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya-prāpta*)?
Is it acquired through birth?
Answer: It is acquired solely through application (*prayoga*), not through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*), nor is it acquired through birth.
Why is this so? Because this karma is necessarily attained only after one has cultivated the various *pāramitās* throughout three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*),
and subsequently applied the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and mental attention (*manasikāra*) within a perfected body.
Some say that this karma is obtained through application (*prayoga*) and also obtained by birth (*upapatti-lābhika*),
but it is not obtained through the separation from defilements (*vairāgya-lābhika*).
Question: Is the karma that has the marks as its maturation produced through hearing, reflection, or cultivation?
Answer: It is produced only through reflection;
it is neither produced through hearing nor through cultivation.
Why is this? Because this karma is superior, it is not produced by hearing;
because it is bound to the desire realm, it is not produced by cultivation.
Some say that this karma is produced by both hearing and reflection,
but not by cultivation.
Question: In which realm does karma that results in marks of physical excellence arise?
Answer: It arises in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), not in any other realm.
It occurs among those in the human realm and not in other realms; it occurs in Jambudvīpa and not in other continents.
As for the physical basis upon which it arises, it arises based on a male body and not a female body or others.
As for when it arises: it arises at the time a Buddha appears in the world, not in an age without a Buddha.
As for the object upon which it arises: it arises by taking the present Buddha as its object and generating a superior thought-vow.
It does not take other objects as its focal point.
Question: Are the thirty-two marks of a great man produced by a single volition?
Is it produced by many volitions?
If so, what is the fault?
If it were projected by a single volition, [what would follow]?
How can a small amount of karma produce many fruits?
How, then, is the *Prajñapti-śāstra* to be reconciled when it says: [as follows:]
Karma of such a kind can bring about the mark of the soles of the feet being level and well-set;
and so on, up to karma of such a kind that can bring about the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance) upon the crown of the head.
If [the projection] is induced by many volitions (*cetanā*),
how is it that a single homogeneous life-span (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is projected without being differentiated?
In response, some say:
First, that which is projected by volition (*cetanā*).
Question: How can a small amount of karma produce such a vast result?
Answer: It is because it was initially drawn forth by a single volition.
Later, it is perfected through extensive reflection;
therefore, there is no fault.
It is like a painter who first uses a single color to create a sketch and subsequently fills it in with various hues.
Question: How is the statement in the *Prajñapti-śāstra* to be reconciled?
Answer: That treatise speaks of "completing karma" (*paripūraka-karma*) and does not speak of "projecting karma" (*ākṣepaka-karma*);
therefore, there is no fault.
However, the thirty-two marks of a great man are the karmic fruit of the perfection of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*),
not the karmic fruit of the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-karman*) of that homogeneous class. Some say:
It is induced by many volitions (*cetanā*).
Question: How is it that a single homogeneous life-span (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is induced through non-differentiated differentiation?
Answer: At that time, the Bodhisattva is able to focus the mind one-pointedly upon a single basis, object, and mode of activity, while many volitions proceed.
Among these, there is volition capable of producing the mark of having soles that are level, full, and well-set,
up to and including the volition capable of producing the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the head.
Thus it is said.
Thirty-two volitions induce the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, each of which is further perfected by many karmic actions.
[The text] asks: regarding the thirty-two volitions produced by a Bodhisattva—
Among all the marks, which mark is first manifested?
The answer is that some say the mark of the soles of the feet being level, full, and well-set is manifested first.
Later, other characteristics are cited;
for it is said that one first places the feet and subsequently [the rest]. Some say:
First, the mark of deep blue eyes is cited because he first gazes upon the world with eyes of loving-kindness;
thus it is said.
This is not fixed;
whichever marks are brought together by conditions, those marks are then projected.
As for the thirty-two marks of a great man:
The mark of the feet being well-placed:
this refers to the soles of the Buddha’s feet being level and full, neither concave nor convex,
such that when he steps, they press evenly against the ground.
Therefore, only the traces of the Buddha are clearly manifest;
even with an evil mind wishing to remove them, one can never destroy them.
If those who live as householders possess such signs, [they too shall attain this].
He will certainly become a king of men, to whom the lands of all under heaven submit;
and among those who have left the household life, if anyone possesses these marks,
they will certainly become a Dharma King who transforms and guides all beings.
Second is the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel.
This refers to the patterns on the soles of the Buddha’s feet which are like wheels,
complete with a thousand spokes, hubs, and rims— perfectly formed, distinct, and exquisitely crafted.
Although the Devaputra Subhakarmā applies his utmost attention, he cannot emulate or replicate that which has been separately manifested.
Why is this? Because the phenomena manifested by the Devaputra Subhakarmā are produced by an unobscured-neutral cognition (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-jñāna*).
This sign is produced by purely virtuous karma;
furthermore, the actions of those gods are produced by innate knowledge (*upapatti-pratilambhika-jñāna*),
whereas this sign is produced by superior applied knowledge (*adhika-prayoga-jñāna*).
Furthermore, the deeds performed by those gods are induced by wisdom cultivated over a single lifetime;
this mark [of the Buddha], however, is induced by wisdom cultivated over immeasurable lifetimes.
Third is the mark of long, slender fingers.
That is to say, the Buddha’s fingers are slender, long, and rounded, tapering gradually to a fine point;
the joints do not protrude,
and when held together, there are no gaps between them.

Fifth is the mark of fine and soft hands and feet;
that is to say, the Buddha’s hands and feet are as fine and soft as *tūla* cotton.
Sixth is the mark of webbed hands and feet.
This means that between all the fingers and toes of the Buddha’s hands and feet there are webbed membranes,
just like those of a king of geese;
when his fingers are joined, the webs do not appear, yet they are neither wrinkled nor lax.
When opened, it appears naturally without any constriction or tension.
Seventh is the mark of the high and broad insteps:
this refers to the Buddha’s insteps being rounded and thick, sloping toward the toes, and with both sides being straight and well-proportioned.
They are proportionate to his heels;
when he steps, they do not spread wide,
and the soles of his feet are the color of a red lotus.
The inner edges of the webbing are like the patterns of a variegated tree, and the color of the toenails is like that of red copper leaves;
the outer edges of the webbing are made of true gold,
and the fine hairs are deep blue and lustrous like vaidūrya.
The Buddha’s two feet are like precious sandals, adorned with various jewels and possessing subtle, wondrous radiance.
Eighth is the mark of the *aiṇeya* (antelope) calves;
that is to say, the Buddha’s calves are round and straight.
Gradually tapering and slender,
like the haunches of an eneya deer king;
ninth, the mark of the secret concealment of the organ.
This means that the Buddha’s secret organ is concealed within a sheath, just like that of the king of horses.
If this is so, how can those to be converted see it?
Some say: [text continues]
Out of compassion for those to be converted, the World-Honored One skillfully manifested this to them.
Some say that the World-Honored One conjured an elephant or a horse with exceptionally sublime concealed organs and addressed those to be converted, saying:
As it was with him, so it is with me. Tenth is the mark of the perfection of the body's proportions;
that is to say, the Buddha’s body is perfectly proportioned like the nyagrodha tree.
Just as from the navel to the crown of the head,
so too from the navel to the feet are the upper and lower parts proportionate.
Eleventh is the mark of body hairs that curl upward.
Twelfth is the mark of a single hair growing from each pore.
Thirteenth is the mark of body hairs curling to the right.
This means that a single hair grows from each and every pore of the Buddha’s body.
Like vaidūrya, its color is deep blue and lustrous, with the hairs curling to the right and sweeping upward from the tips;
as for why there is but a single hair in each pore,
it is because when he was a bodhisattva, he taught the Dharma without confusion.
Fourteenth is the mark of the body being the color of pure gold.
This means that the Buddha’s body is the color of pure gold,
outshining all the golden light of the world so that it no longer appears.
The brilliance and majesty of the iron and other metals used by people today do not appear before the gold used at present; likewise,
the brilliance and majesty of the gold used at present do not appear before the gold used during the time of the Buddha’s presence in the world.

When the gold used by the Buddha during his lifetime reaches the ocean, its majestic radiance does not appear before the golden sands of the path of the Cakravartin King, nor before the Jambūnada gold.
When these golden sands reach the edge of the gold of the Seven Golden Mountains, their majestic radiance does not appear.
The golden splendor and majestic radiance of the seven golden mountains do not appear when compared to the gold of Mount Sumeru;
the golden splendor and majestic radiance of the gold of Mount Sumeru does not appear when compared to the gold of the ornaments of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

In this manner, progressing successively, the majestic radiance of the golden ornaments of the Nirmāṇarati devas does not appear when compared to the golden ornaments of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas.
When the gold of the ornaments of this Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven reaches the vicinity of the Buddha’s golden body, its majestic radiance does not manifest;
therefore, the golden color of the Buddha’s body is supreme.
It outshines all the golden colors of the world.
Fifteenth is the mark of the constant light extending one fathom:
this refers to the fact that the Buddha’s body is perpetually surrounded by a radiance.
Each face is one fathom in width, constantly illuminating day and night.
Sixteenth is the mark of fine and smooth skin;
this means that the Buddha’s skin is so fine and smooth that dust and water do not adhere to it.
It is like vaidūrya or a lotus leaf;
even if a Buddha were to tread upon Mount Cakravāḍa with his feet,
and the Vairambha winds were to strike the dust therein.
It is impossible for even a single speck of dust to adhere to the Buddha’s body or beneath his feet.
Seventeenth is the mark of the seven parts being full;
that is to say, the Buddha’s seven parts are full.
In other parts of the body, these are slightly increased.
The two hands, two feet, two shoulders, and the neck constitute the seven locations.
Eighteenth is the mark of the body being broad, majestic, and straight.
That is to say, the Buddha’s body is broad, majestic, and straight;
it is neither bent nor hunched, nor does it lean to one side, but is upright, elegant, and full.
Nineteenth is the mark of the upper body being like that of a lion.
That is to say, the expanse of the Buddha’s chest is broad and majestic,
like the upper body of a lion king.
The twentieth is the mark of the fullness of the shoulders.
That is to say, the Buddha’s shoulders and upper arms are perfectly rounded,
surpassing those of any strongman or wrestler capable of physical feats.
Twenty-first is the mark of standing with his hands reaching his knees.
This means that when the Buddha stands upright with his arms extended, they reach down to touch his kneecaps.
The twenty-second is the mark of the lion’s jaw;
this means that the Buddha’s jaw is broad and well-proportioned like that of a lion king.
Twenty-third, he possesses the mark of having forty teeth.
Twenty-fourth, his teeth are even, level, and closely set.
Twenty-fifth, his teeth are bright white and radiant with light.
This means that the Buddha possesses forty teeth, all of which are perfectly even;
there is no gap between them even as much as a hair’s breadth.
Their color is a brilliant white, shining with a radiant clarity like the King of Snow Mountains.
Question: Other people have only thirty-two teeth, yet it is said that there are one hundred and three bones within their bodies;
the Buddha, however, possesses forty teeth.
Why is it said that there are one hundred and three bones in the body, and no more?
The answer is: in other persons, the skull is composed of nine parts.
The cranial bone of the World-Honored One is a single piece;
thus, he possesses one hundred and three bones in total.
Twenty-sixth is the mark of obtaining the supreme flavor.
This means that because the Buddha’s tongue faculty is pure,
whatever he consumes is transformed into a supreme flavor. Some say:
Upon the Buddha’s tongue-faculty lies the seed of all world-pleasing, exquisite, and supreme flavors.
When any bitter or sour substances reach his tongue-faculty,
these seeds undergo a transformation such that they all become superior flavors.
Some say that the tongue-faculty of the Tathāgata possesses such power that whenever any food or drink reaches it, [it is transformed into nectar].
Among these, that which is pleasant and exquisite gives rise to gustatory consciousness;
that which is coarse and vulgar does not give rise to gustatory consciousness. Some say:
Within the Buddha’s throat there are two milk springs;
when he partakes of food or drink, this milk flows forth,
and when mixed with various foods and drinks, they all become the most excellent flavor.
However, within this context, because the faculty of the tongue is pure, it causes flavors to be exceptionally sublime;
this principle ought to be so.
The twenty-seventh is the mark of the broad and long tongue.
This refers to the Buddha’s tongue being thin and soft;
when extended, it is broad and long enough to cover his face up to his ears and the hairline,
yet when retracted back into his mouth, it causes no obstruction within.
The twenty-eighth is the mark of deep blue eyes.
This means that the Buddha’s eyes are long and wide,
and their color is a pure, deep blue like the petals of the *sujāta* blue lotus flower.
Twenty-ninth is the mark of eyelashes like those of a bull king;
that is to say, the Buddha’s eyelashes are beautifully arranged, just like those of a bull king.
Thirtieth is the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa*.
That is to say, the Buddha’s uṣṇīṣa is composed of bone and flesh;
its size is like a closed fist, blue, circular, and exceptionally sublime.
Thirty-first is the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.
That is to say, the white tuft of hair between the Buddha’s eyebrows is half a fathom in length;
it curls to the right in a graceful spiral, and its radiance is pure and translucent.
The thirty-second mark is the attainment of the Brahma-voice.
This means that within the Buddha’s throat-cavity there are wondrous primary elements (*mahābhūta*) capable of producing a pleasing, harmonious, and sublime Brahma-voice,
like that of the kalaviṅka bird.
And it emits a deep, far-reaching, thunderous sound like the drum of Śakra;
such a voice possesses the eight meritorious qualities.
First, it is profound and far-reaching;
second, it is harmonious and elegant;
third, it is clear and distinct.
Fourth, it is pleasing to the ear;
fifth, it enters the heart;
sixth, it gives rise to joy.
Seventh, it is easy to understand.
Eighth, there is no weariness.
Question: What is the meaning of "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*)?
Answer: The meaning of "mark" (*cihna*) is the meaning of "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*);
the meaning of "excellence" is the meaning of "characteristic";
the meaning of "auspicious omen" is the meaning of "characteristic."
Question: For what reason are the marks of a Great Man exactly thirty-two, neither more nor less?
Venerable Tseng (Pārśva) said:
Whether there were more or fewer, both would give rise to doubt.
Only thirty-two [marks] do not contradict the characteristics of the Dharma.
Some say that thirty-two is a number universally recognized in the world as auspicious.
Therefore, they neither increase nor decrease.
Some say that if the Buddha’s body is adorned with the thirty-two marks, it is then the most supreme and peerless in the world.
If they were to be reduced, there would be deficiency;
if they were further increased, there would be confusion.
Since neither case would be sublime, they are exactly as they are.
Just as the Buddha’s teaching cannot be increased or decreased,
so too is the mark of the Buddha;
for there is nothing to be decreased that could be increased, and nothing to be increased that could be decreased.
Question: Where do the eighty secondary marks (anuvyañjana) reside?
Answer: They reside between the primary marks (lakṣaṇa), following them as they manifest, adorning the Buddha’s body so that it is exceedingly sublime and beautiful.
Question: Do the primary marks and the secondary marks not obstruct or supplant one another?
Answer: It is not so.
The primary marks and the secondary signs manifest one another, just as flowers in a forest manifest the trees.
Thus is the Buddha’s body adorned with these marks and signs.
Furthermore, just as a mountain of gold is adorned with various precious gems,
so too is the majestic radiance of the Buddha’s body extraordinary;
for the body of the Tathāgata is supremely clear and pure.
All manner of auspicious objects appeared within it,
just as when a Chinese mirror has been polished to extreme brilliance,
the reflections of all things appear according to their distance, whether near or far.
The Buddha’s body is likewise. Therefore,
when all Māras, non-Buddhists, and those harboring evil intentions come into the presence of the Buddha,
there are none who do not gaze up at him in reverence.
Beholding him, they never grew weary; they circumambulated him to the right and departed.
They asked the Bodhisattva, "Is it out of attachment or pride that you adorn yourself?
He replied, "It is not so."
Question: How is this so?

Answer: It is because the Bodhisattva, wishing to subdue those in the world who rely on their physical form and are arrogant such that they do not accept transformation, adorns his body with the various marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) in order to cause them to accept transformation.
Furthermore, it is to manifest that all qualities possessed by the Buddha are preeminent;
that is to say, his physical form, strength, lineage, retinue, reputation, wealth, sovereignty, wisdom, vision,
and meritorious virtues are all entirely preeminent.
If it were not so, then no one would believe or accept the Dharma being taught.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva adorns his body.
Furthermore, it is because one desires to serve as the vessel and support for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
For supreme qualities necessarily depend upon a supreme body.
Regarding the meaning of that future *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
he said to the bodhisattva:
"If you wish for me to abide within your body..."
First, I shall cause your body to become exceptionally pure and adorn it with the various marks and signs; were it not so,
[it would be otherwise].
I, too, cannot be born within your body.
It is like a man who wishes to marry a king’s daughter and brings her to his home;
he then secretly dispatches a messenger to say to her:
If you wish for me to come to your residence,
you should first sprinkle and sweep it to remove all filth and impurities,
hang silk banners and canopies, burn incense, scatter flowers, and adorn it in various ways.
I may then go; otherwise,
I too would be unable to reach your residence.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva adorns his body. [The text] asks:
after the Bodhisattva has performed and accumulated karma that results in the maturation of marks, during the interval—such as when he acts as a Wheel-Turning King—what occurs?
Is it the very karma of maturation that has the characteristics of what is being cultivated which brings about the fruit with those same characteristics,
or is it other karma?
Answer: Some say that it is precisely the karma of maturation (vipāka) characterized by what has been cultivated;
for the functional power (vīrya) of this karma is vast.
Even if one were to continue acting as a wheel-turning monarch until the present day,
the power of that karma would still not be exhausted;
thus it is said.
He [experiences] this through residual karma. Why is that?
Because all the karma of a bodhisattva cultivated for the maturation of the marks is intended to yield its preeminent fruit in his final body; it is not to be experienced sooner.
Nevertheless, by means of that karma acting as the dominant condition, he performs other virtuous deeds that bring about the fruit of the marks of a Wheel-Turning King.
It is like a wealthy householder who possesses many precious jewels,
yet among them, a highly valuable gem is not immediately brought out for use.
As for other items of lesser value, they may be traded as the occasion demands; it is the same with those [marks].
Question: What is the difference between the thirty-two marks obtained by a Bodhisattva and the marks of a Wheel-Turning King?
Answer: There are four ways in which that which is attained by a bodhisattva is superior:
first, it is blazing;
second, it is distinct.
Third, perfection;
fourth, attainment of the locus.
Furthermore, there are five matters of superiority.
First, the attainment of the state;
second, extreme majesty and beauty;
third, profound literary style and meaning.
Fourth, conformity with superior wisdom;
fifth, conformity with the departure from defilement.
Question: After a bodhisattva has performed and accumulated karma that results in maturation (*vipāka*), [what follows?]
"Until one reaches the final body,
is there any distinct characteristic among sentient beings that can be recognized?
He replied, "There is."
That is to say, he is born into a noble family, possesses a handsome and dignified appearance, has a male body with fully developed faculties,
attains the recollection of past lives, has deep faith in cause and effect,
delights in extensive learning, and reveres the True Dharma.
His wisdom and insight are sharp and keen, and he possesses superior eloquence.
His disposition is harmonious and supple, and his speech is gentle and refined.
In all that he undertakes, he is resolute and never retreats.
Seeing others suffer, one cannot bear it;
one must certainly deliver them.
Whatever practice one cultivates is without exception dedicated toward enlightenment.
To joyfully perform beneficial deeds for sentient beings without seeking recompense—
these are called the characteristics of that bodhisattva.
Question: As it is said in the sūtras that each of the Buddha’s marks is adorned with a hundred merits (*puṇya*), what is meant by "a hundred merits"?
Answer: In this context, one hundred volitions (*cetanā*) are called "a hundred merits."
What are the one hundred volitions?
It refers to when a bodhisattva performs and cultivates the karma that results in the mark of well-placed feet;
at that time, fifty volitions first arise.
One cultivates and purifies the vessel of the body until it is refined and pliant;
next, one generates a single volition that correctly draws forth that [attainment];
finally, one again generates fifty volitions to bring it to completion.
It is, for example, like a farmer who first prepares the furrows and ridges, next sows the seeds, and afterwards covers and irrigates them with manure and water.
He was just like that; the karma of his mark of well-placed feet was adorned by such hundreds of intentions.
The karma for the *uṣṇīṣa* mark upon the crown of the head is likewise so.
For this reason, it is said that each and every mark of the Buddha is adorned by a hundred merits.
Question: What are these fifty volitions?
Answer: There are five volitions for each of the ten paths of action.
That is to say, there are five volitions based on the path of action consisting of abstaining from killing.
First, the volition of abstaining from killing;
second, the volition of exhortation;
third, the volition of praise.
Fourth is the volition of sympathetic joy.
Fifth is the volition of dedication,
which refers to dedicating what has been cultivated toward enlightenment.
This applies up to right view as well;
these are called the fifty volitions (*cetanā*). Some say:
Based on each of the ten paths of action, there arise five grades of wholesome volition— namely, inferior, intermediate, superior, superior-superior, and supreme-superior—
just as in the case of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna. Some say:
Based on each of the ten paths of action, five types of volition arise:
first, purity of the preliminary application;
second, purity of the fundamental act.
Third, purification through subsequent action;
fourth, not being harmed by discursive thought;
fifth, being sustained by mindfulness.
Some say that fifty moments arise in dependence upon a single mark of the Buddha,
proceeding as a continuous stream of mental attention to a mark never before cultivated.
Question: What is the measure of each of these hundred merits?
Answer: Some say that it is the karma capable of inducing the status of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
To exercise sovereign power over the four great continents constitutes one measure of merit;
so it is said by some.
If there is karma capable of bringing about the status of Śakra,
Lord of the Devas, and enabling one to exercise sovereign power over the two classes of devas,
this constitutes a single unit of merit.
Some say: If karma is capable of bringing about the status of a king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods,
one exercises sovereign power over all the hosts of devas in the desire realm.
This is the measure of that merit.
Some say it is the karma capable of inducing the status of Mahābrahmā.
To exercise mastery over the first dhyāna and the devas of the desire realm constitutes one unit of merit;
so it is said by some.
The merit of the Great Brahmā King, Lord of the Sahā World,
who exhorted the Tathāgata to turn the wheel of Dharma—
this constitutes one measure of merit.
Question: At the time of that invitation to the Buddha, it was an unobscured-neutral mind bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
How can it be called merit? Answer: Some say: [The text continues: "Some say: ... (as per the provided fragment).
Dwelling in the Brahma-world,
when he wished to come and invite [the Buddha], he first gave rise to this virtuous thought:
"I shall bring great benefit to all sentient beings by requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma."
At that time, it would be called "attaining that Brahma-merit.
This is not reasonable. Why is this so?
This is not because [the goal] was already accomplished before it was performed.
According to this explanation, he,
having requested the Buddha, returned to the Brahma palace.
Later, when the World-Honored One turned the Wheel of Dharma, the earth deities first proclaimed it;
thus, by successive transmission, the sound reached the Brahma palace.
Having heard it, the Brahma King rejoiced and congratulated himself.
One generates sympathetic joy with a pure and sincere mind;
at that time, it is said that one accomplishes this merit. Some say:
When the world is formed, the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings is able to bring forth a trichiliocosm;
this constitutes one measure of merit.
Some say:
with the exception of Bodhisattvas who are close to the stage of Buddhahood,
all sentient beings possess karma capable of producing the fruits of wealth and happiness.
This is the measure of a single merit.
Some say that within this context, each individual measure of merit should be illustrated by means of a simile.
Suppose all sentient beings were born blind.
If there were one sentient being who, through great skillful means, caused them all to regain their sight,
the merit of that sentient being would constitute a single measure of merit.
Furthermore, suppose all sentient beings were to drink poisonous medicine and become dazed and on the verge of death;
yet there were one sentient being who could cause them all to have the poison removed and their minds restored to clarity.
The merit of that sentient being constitutes a single measure of merit.
Furthermore, suppose all sentient beings were bound and imprisoned, and their lives were about to be cut short;
if one were to cause them all to be liberated simultaneously and restore their lives at once—[the merit of this would equal the former].
The merit of that sentient being constitutes a single measure of merit.
Furthermore, suppose all sentient beings were to have their ethical discipline and views corrupted;
yet there were one sentient being who could cause them all simultaneously to become fully endowed with ethical discipline and views.
The merit of that sentient being constitutes a single measure of merit.
The commentary states:
All such explanations are based on a purely virtuous intention.
These are merely expedient praises of the magnitude of a bodhisattva’s merit;
however, none of them capture the actual reality.
As for the meaning according to reality:
The measure of each and every merit generated by a bodhisattva is immeasurable and boundless;
for it is through these that the bodhisattva has accumulated and perfected all the pāramitās throughout three incalculable eons.
Because the volitions and aspirations it induces are exceedingly vast,
only a Buddha can know them;
they cannot be fathomed by others.
The vast amount of merit thus described is fully sufficient to perfect one mark with its hundredfold adornments.
Successively, even up to the thirty-two marks, each is endowed with a hundred merits.
Because the Buddha adorns his body with these thirty-two marks, each embellished by a hundred merits,
as well as the eighty secondary characteristics, he is the most honored and supreme among gods and humans.
Question: Through how much time must these marks of maturation be cultivated until they are perfected?
Answer: For most, it takes one hundred great eons;
this is with the sole exception of the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni.
Because the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was of such supreme diligence, he transcended nine great eons;
thus, by completing his cultivation through only ninety-one eons,
he attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What is this matter?
As it is said in a sutra:
"In the past, there was a Buddha named Tiṣya."
Some say it was sand.
That Buddha had two bodhisattva disciples who diligently practiced the holy life;
one was named Śākyamuni.
The second was named Maitreya.
At that time, that Buddha observed which of his two disciples had first reached maturity in their faculties;
he knew, in accordance with reality, that Maitreya had matured first.
Śākyamuni’s maturation occurs later.
Furthermore, he observes which of the two types of beings to be converted has their faculties maturing first;
likewise, he knows with perfect accuracy that those to be converted by Śākyamuni are the ones whose faculties should mature first.
Having understood this, he immediately thought:
"How may I now cause their karmic conditions and my response to meet?
However, it would be easier if I were to bring a single person to swift maturity."
Not wishing to cause many people to harbor such thoughts,
he then addressed Śākyamuni.
"I wish to travel to the mountains; you may follow me.
At that time, the Buddha took up his sitting mat (niṣīdana) and proceeded ahead along the road. Having reached the mountain, he arrived first.
Entering a cave of vaidūrya, he spread out a niṣīdana,
sat down cross-legged, and entered the fire-element concentration (tejodhātu-samādhi).
For seven days and nights, he experienced sublime joy and bliss.
His majestic radiance blazed intensely.
In an instant, Śākyamuni also went to the mountain,
searching for the Buddha everywhere like a calf seeking its mother.
As they wandered on, they arrived before the niche chamber.
Suddenly, they beheld the Buddha’s majestic deportment, solemn and dignified, with his radiance shining brilliantly;
moved by single-minded sincerity, they could not contain their joy and admiration.
Without ceasing his movement, he forgot to set down a single step;
gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, he did not for a moment turn his eyes away,
continuing thus for seven days and nights.
He praised that Buddha with a single verse:
"In this world, from the heavens to the earth, throughout the realm of the learned (Śakra), in the abodes of the departed and the celestial realms of the ten directions—
nowhere is there a man, a bull among men, a Great Śramaṇa, who is equal to you, whether sought in the lands, the mountains, or the forests."
Having offered such praise, he bypassed nine kalpas and attained unsurpassed enlightenment before Maitreya.
Question: Does a bodhisattva who is close to the stage of Buddhahood necessarily [rely] upon the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes?
Having attained a marvelous mastery never before achieved,
one ought to praise the Buddha with distinct verses through various methods.
Why, then, did he praise the Buddha with only a single verse for seven days and nights?
Answer: At that time, because the Bodhisattva’s intention and vow were superior, he did not rework the prose and verse.
Had he altered the prose and verse, his intention and vow would have lacked purity.
Furthermore, at that time, the Bodhisattva feared distraction.
As it is said in the verse, "Because the mind also differs according to its distinctions," how can there be a continuous flow of a single mind?
Furthermore, it is because the Bodhisattva manifests a mind free from weariness, being able to newly and repeatedly generate superior thoughts and vows regarding even a single verse.
Question: For what reason does the Bodhisattva Maitreya first ripen his own faculties and later ripen those of those to be converted, whereas the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni acts in the opposite manner?
Answer: The Bodhisattva Maitreya primarily benefits himself and only slightly benefits others.
The Bodhisattva Śākyamuni benefits others extensively while benefiting himself little;
for this reason, he does not stand on equal footing with those he transforms.
Question: As it is said in the sūtras:
The Bodhisattva practices the four pāramitās for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas until they are fully perfected.
What kind of kalpa is this?
Answer: Some say it is an intermediate kalpa (antarakalpa);
others say it is a kalpa of formation (vivartakalpa).
Some say this is the kalpa of destruction;
those who speak thus maintain that this is a great kalpa (mahākalpa).
Accumulating these great eons until one reaches an *asaṃkhyeya*, and thus practicing until three *asaṃkhyeyas* are perfected.
Question: How can the measure of these eons and *asaṃkhyeyas* be known?
Answer: Some say that one great kalpa constitutes a single unit;
when these are accumulated from one up to one hundred thousand, it is called a lakṣa.
One hundred times one hundred thousand is called a koṭi;
one hundred thousand koṭis is called a nayuta;
one hundred thousand nayutas is called a vibhūta.
One hundred thousand *bimbara* is called a *kṛtana*.
Beyond this, it is no longer within the reach of calculable knowledge;
the stage that cannot be reached by calculation is termed the measure of one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.
The same applies to the measure of the second and third asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Some say that a mahākalpa constitutes one [asaṃkhyeya].
Accumulating these from one up to one hundred thousand is called a lakṣa;
reaching one hundred times one hundred thousand is called a koṭi;
and one hundred thousand koṭis is called a koṭikoṭi.
One hundred thousand koṭis of koṭis is called an akṣobhya-koṭi;
one hundred thousand akṣobhya-koṭis is called an aṭaṭa-koṭi;
one hundred thousand aṭaṭa-koṭis is called an ayuta.
One hundred thousand ayutas is called an ayutāṃśa;
one hundred thousand ayutāṃśas is called a nayuta;
one hundred thousand nayutas is called a nayutāṃśa.
One hundred thousand nayutas is called a *kuvya*;
one hundred thousand *kuvyas* is called a *kuvyāṃśa*;
one hundred thousand *kuvyāṃśas* is called a *padma*.
One hundred thousand padmas is called a padmāṃśa;
one hundred thousand padmāṃśas is called a kumuda;
one hundred thousand kumudas is called a kumudāṃśa.
One hundred thousand *karmara* is called a *nartana*;
one hundred thousand *nartana* is called a *nartanabhāga*;
one hundred thousand *nartanabhāga* is called a *dṛṣṭi*.
One hundred thousand koṭis is called a koṭībhāga;
one hundred thousand koṭībhāgas is called an ababa;
one hundred thousand ababas is called an ababhāga.
One hundred thousand *āpāpa* is called *ṭaṭa*;
one hundred thousand *ṭaṭa* is called *ṭaṭabhāga*;
one hundred thousand *ṭaṭabhāga* is called *udaga*.
One hundred thousand *udaka* is called an *udakabhāga*;
one hundred thousand *udakabhāga* is called a *vala*;
one hundred thousand *vala* is called a *valabhāga*.
One hundred thousand *barā* is called a *vagaḍa*.
Beyond this point, it is no longer within the reach of calculative knowledge;
the stage reached where calculation is no longer applicable is termed the measure of one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.
The same applies to the measure of the second and third asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Some say that it is called *asaṃkhyeya* because it is beyond the reach of the knowledge of calculation.
However, there is a sūtra that speaks of sixty numbers.
Among them, there is one number called *asaṃkhyeya*; when the calculation of great kalpas reaches this number, it is called one *kalpāsaṃkhyeya*.
As that sutra says:
"There is one, which is the beginning of the number 'one' without remainder;
eleven constitutes ten."
Ten tens make a hundred;
ten hundreds make a thousand;
ten thousands make a *prabheda*.
Ten *prabheda* make one *lakṣa*;
ten *lakṣa* make one *atila*kṣa*;
ten *atila*kṣa* make one *koṭi*.
Ten koṭis make one madhya;
ten madhyas make one ayuta;
ten ayutas make one mahāyuta.
Ten *ayuta*s make one *nayuta*.
Ten *nayuta*s make one *mahā-nayuta*.
Ten *mahā-nayuta*s make one *pranayuta*.
Ten *pranayuta* make one great *pranayuta*.
Ten great *pranayuta* make one *kankara*.
Ten *kankara* make one great *kankara*.
Ten *kaṅkara* make one *bimbara*;
ten *bimbara* make one *mahābimbara*;
ten *mahābimbara* make one *akṣobhya*.
Ten akṣobhya is a mahākṣobhya; ten mahākṣobhya is a vivaha;
ten vivaha is a mahāvivaha.
Ten *vibhava* make one *udgaṅga*;
ten *udgaṅga* make one *mahodgaṅga*;
ten *mahodgaṅga* make one *vahana*.
Ten *bhaṅga* make one *mahābhaṅga*.
Ten *mahābhaṅga* make one *tiṭibha*.
Ten *tiṭibha* make one *mahātiṭibha*.
Ten mahātitibhas are a hetu;
ten hetus are a mahāhetu;
ten mahāhetus are a karabha.
Ten *kṛṣṇa* make one *mahākṛṣṇa*.
Ten *mahākṛṣṇa* make one *indrala*.
Ten *indrala* make one *mahendrala*.
Ten great Indras constitute one samāpta;
thirteen samāptas constitute one mahāsamāpta;
ten great mahāsamāptas constitute one keti.
Ten koṭis are a mahākoṭi;
