ten mahākoṭis are a nayuta; ten nayutas are a mahānayuta.
Ten *niyuta* (ni-va-ra-sha) make one *muda-ra*;
ten *muda-ra* make one *mahāmuda-ra*;
ten *mahāmuda-ra* make one *balam*.
Ten *bālāna* make one great *bālāna*;
ten great *bālāna* make one *saṃjñeya*;
ten *saṃjñeya* make one great *saṃjñeya*.
Ten *saṃjñā* make one *vibhūta*;
ten *vibhūta* make one *mahāvibhūta*;
ten *mahāvibhūta* make one *balākṣa*.
Ten *vārāṇas* make one great *vārāṇa*;
ten great *vārāṇas* make one *asaṃkhyeya*. Beyond this, there are eight further numerical units;
together with the preceding ones, these constitute sixty numerical units that accumulate to form one great eon (*mahākalpa*).
Upon reaching the fifty-second asaṃkhyeya,
that duration is called one kalpa-asaṃkhyeya;
the second and third kalpa-asaṃkhyeyas are likewise.
Some say that the Venerable Śāriputra, relying on the fourth dhyāna, gave rise to the supernormal power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānābhijñā*),
taking as its object the kalpas of the past up to the extent of one *kalpāsaṃkhyeya*.
The same applies to the measure of the second and third incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
One should not say that,
for the measure of an incalculable eon is not within the range of the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) of Śāriputra and others.
In this context, some say that the measure of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is entirely within the scope of Śāriputra’s knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).
Therefore, one should not say that a single *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* is measured by the extent of what his knowledge can reach. Some have stated this.
Based on the practice of giving alone, one distinguishes the duration of the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
That is to say, at the time when a bodhisattva, although practicing generosity,
is not yet able to relinquish all things to give to all fields of merit.
This is designated as the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
It is the time when a bodhisattva is able to practice generosity and can relinquish all things,
yet has not yet been able to give to all fields of merit.
Or, one may be able to give to all fields of merit but has not yet been able to relinquish all possessions;
up to this point is called the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
At which time the bodhisattva is able to practice the giving of gifts.
Furthermore, he is able to relinquish all things and bestow them upon all fields of merit;
up to this point, it is called the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa. Some say:
Based on the Buddhas encountered, one distinguishes the duration of the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
That is to say, in the distant past, when the human lifespan was one hundred years,
there was a Buddha named Śākyamuni.
He appeared in the world,
born into the Śākya kṣatriya clan;
his mother’s name was Mahāmāyā.
His father’s name was Śuddhodana;
his son’s name was Rāhula;
the city was named Kapilavastu; and they were of the Śākya clan.
His attendant disciple was named Ānanda;
his foremost pair of disciples were named Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
At that time, the five corruptions of the world were flourishing.
Oppressed by birth, old age, and death,
they were ignorant and blind, lacking any guide; thus, that Buddha,
the World-Honored One, appeared therein through the power of his compassionate vow.
Through his superior diligence in guiding sentient beings, he never rested for even a moment;
because of this, he was overcome by wind,
and his shoulders and back became afflicted with illness.
At that time, there was a potter named Guangchi.
Knowing that the time had come, the Buddha addressed his attendant Ānanda, saying,
"I am currently unwell due to physical illness."
"You may go to the potter Vighusta’s house and request sesame oil and warm water for me to apply as an ointment and for bathing.
The attendant respectfully assented and went to the potter's house.
Having approached Guangchi and exchanged polite inquiries with affectionate words,
he skillfully praised the Buddha’s various supreme merits of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom,
as well as his thirty-two major marks, eighty minor signs, and the brilliant radiance of his halo.
His wisdom and vision were unimpeded and his eloquence was unhindered.
He then addressed Guangchi:
"If the World-Honored One had not left the household life in this manner..."
"You were destined to be a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) ruling over the four continents;
both I and all the world would have been your servants.
Yet now, you have renounced such a royal throne to go forth and practice asceticism."
They attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
possess all-encompassing wisdom and vision,
and sever the entire web of doubt.
He grants certainty to all;
he is able to exhaust the very depths of all questions and discourses;
and he regards all sentient beings as if they were his only child.
He currently resides not far from here;
however, for the sake of delivering you from suffering, he constantly travels the roads,
and his shoulders and back are worn out from being buffeted by the wind.
"I have come to you because I require oil and warm water;
would you be able to give them?
Upon hearing this, Guangchi was filled with joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
"How can there be such merit among humans?
He then replied to the Venerable One,
"Virtuous one, please return for now."
"I shall go to the Buddha's presence as you have commanded.
Not long after he had departed,
Prabhāsa prepared raw sesame oil and warm scented water, and took them to the Buddha's presence.
The Buddha saw him from afar;
in order to cause that man to plant roots of goodness, he removed his outer garments and remained sitting on a small table,
wearing only his undergarment, waiting for him.
Having arrived, Guangchi (Guṇavardhana) gave rise to a pure and sincere mind;
with the oil he had brought, he reverently and skillfully anointed the Buddha’s shoulders and back, massaging them in various ways.
He further bathed him with warm water and fragrant decoctions;
at that time, the Buddha’s wind ailment was completely cured and relieved.
With a voice of compassionate gentleness, he comforted and exhorted him extensively.
Upon hearing this, he was filled with joy and immediately made this vow:
"May I, in the future, attain Buddhahood;
may my name, retinue, time, place, and disciples be exactly as [the Buddha's]."
Now, the World-Honored One is exactly the same and no different.
You should know that the potter of that time was none other than Śākyamuni Bodhisattva;
by virtue of his original vow, his name and title are now identical to those of the past, without any change.
However, from the time he made this vow before that Buddha until he encountered and served the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin,
the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa was completed.
From this point onward until he encountered and served the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara,
this was called the fulfillment of the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
Furthermore, from that point onward until he encountered and served the Tathāgata Vipaśyin.
This is called the completion of the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
Thereafter, he again spent ninety-one kalpas cultivating the karma for the marks of excellence,
until it was finally perfected upon his encounter with and service to Kāśyapa Buddha.
Some say there are three kinds of asaṃkhyeya: first, the asaṃkhyeya of kalpas; [the second, the asaṃkhyeya of dharmas;
and the third, the asaṃkhyeya of beings].
Second, the incalculable [aeon] of births;
third, the incalculable [aeon] of sublime conduct.
Regarding the incalculable aeon (*kalpāsaṃkhyeya*):
This refers to taking a great eon (*mahākalpa*) as a single unit, accumulating them up to a *lakṣa* and *koṭi*,
continuing through successive stages until exceeding the number of *vavagra*,
which constitutes an *asaṃkhyeya*.
This means that throughout each eon, one passes through countless births.
Regarding "immeasurable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sublime practices":
this means that in each eon, one cultivates countless sublime practices.
It is unreasonable that one realizes unsurpassed enlightenment by means of these three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya*).
According to the true meaning:
In this context, it is stated that the cultivation [of the perfections] is perfected after merely three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
*Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 177.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 178,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhiskandha), Part Four of Five: The Chapter on Non-returners (Anāgāmin). Question: As it is said that a Bodhisattva [practices] for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas according to the Sūtras...
One cultivates the four pāramitās and attains their perfection;
namely, the pāramitā of generosity and the pāramitā of ethical discipline.
Regarding the perfection of diligence and the perfection of wisdom,
at what time should one practice which perfection in order to bring it to fulfillment?
Answer: Some say that when a bodhisattva practices giving,
he is not overcome by stinginess.
It should be said that the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) is fulfilled;
when maintaining pure ethical discipline, one is not overwhelmed or defiled by faulty conduct—
it should be said that the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) is fulfilled.
When exerting diligence, one is not defeated by laziness;
thus, it should be said that the perfection of diligence is fulfilled.
When cultivating wisdom, one is not disturbed or turbidified by faulty intelligence.
It should be said that the *prajñāpāramitā* is perfected. Some say:
when a bodhisattva, by means of compassion alone, is able to give all things in every way.
Even unto his body, life, head, eyes, marrow, and brain, he has not the slightest attachment;
this is defined as the perfection of the pāramitā of giving.
When a bodhisattva is suddenly struck by sentient beings and his hands and feet are severed, [he remains without attachment].
Their noses and ears were sliced off and cut away;
some had their limbs hacked apart until not even a portion the size of a mustard seed remained intact.
At that time, there was not even a single thought of anger;
how much less would he wish to retaliate?
This is defined as the perfection of the *śīla-pāramitā*.
At that time, because his mind was so courageous,
the Bodhisattva stood on one foot for seven days and nights, gazing without blinking,
praising the Buddha with a single verse.
Yet, without a single thought of weariness or indolence,
this is called the perfection of the pāramitā of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
At that time, the Bodhisattva was named Gopīndra, earnestly seeking awakening.
Possessing the foremost wisdom and being invincible in debate,
he was universally revered;
at this point, it is said that his *prajñāpāramitā* was perfected.
Or it is said:
up until sitting upon the Vajrāsana and entering the Vajropama-samādhi,
on the verge of realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The perfection of the Prajñāpāramitā is designated by this term.
Those who speak thus do so because all that has been said refers to a single moment.
It is said that they are perfected through the predominance of a single practice;
however, in terms of the ultimate meaning,
these four pāramitās are only fully perfected at the time one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
The masters of foreign lands (bahirdeśaka) say that there are six pāramitās, namely,
the four previously mentioned with the addition of patience (kṣānti) and meditative concentration (dhyāna).
The masters of the Kaśmīra school state that the latter two pāramitās are subsumed within the former four; specifically,
patience (kṣānti) is included within ethical discipline (śīla).
Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is subsumed within wisdom (*prajñā*),
because when ethical discipline (*śīla*) and wisdom are fulfilled, it is said that those [other perfections] are likewise fulfilled.
Furthermore, there is another explanation.
The six pāramitās consist of the aforementioned four,
with the addition of learning (śruta) and patience (kṣānti).
At that time, the bodhisattva is able to fully receive and uphold the twelvefold teaching (dvādaśāṅga-pravacana) spoken by the Tathāgata.
When one hears the name of this perfection of hearing, it is called "fulfillment.
At that time, when a bodhisattva declares himself patient even as King Kali cuts off his limbs,
he never harbors a single thought of anger or resentment.
Instead, one uses compassionate words to vow to benefit them;
up to this point, the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) is said to be fulfilled.
These two are also subsumed within the previous four perfections.
Patience is as previously explained; hearing is subsumed within wisdom.
Although all virtuous qualities may be termed *pāramitās*, they are designated as such here based on the sense of being predominant and manifest.
Therefore, there are only four.
Question: When practicing these four pāramitās, how many Buddhas does one encounter and serve during each asaṃkhyeya kalpa?
The answer is: During the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he encountered and served seventy-five thousand Buddhas;
the first was named Śākyamuni and the last was named Ratnaśikhin.
During the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he encountered and served seventy-six thousand Buddhas.
The first was Ratnaśikhin and the last was Dīpaṃkara.
During the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he served seventy-seven thousand Buddhas;
the first was Dīpaṃkara and the last was Vipaśyin.
During the ninety-one eons in which he performed the karma of maturation for the marks [of a Buddha], he encountered and served six Buddhas;
the first was Vipaśyin and the last was named Kāśyapa.
It should be understood that this is spoken with reference to the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni.
If other bodhisattvas are not fixed in their destiny,
it is likewise with the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni; at the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
four of the six pāramitās were already fulfilled to some extent.
His karma for the maturation of marks is now perfectly fulfilled;
he will pass away from this Jambudvīpa and be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven,
there to experience his final maturation within the celestial realm.
Question: For what reason does a bodhisattva receive the final karmic maturation (*vipāka*) of the celestial realm only in Tuṣita Heaven, and not in any other heaven?
Venerable Pārśva replied:
This should not be questioned;
for whether one considers the higher or the lower realms, doubt arises in both cases.
Nevertheless, being born in those heavens does not contradict the nature of phenomena.
Some say that among the celestial realms of the thousandfold world system, Tuṣita Heaven is like the central standard; therefore,
the Bodhisattva is born only in that heaven.
Some say that the lower heavens are characterized by negligence, while the higher heavens have dull faculties;
only the Tuṣita heaven is free from these two faults.
Because Bodhisattvas fear negligence and feel weary of dull faculties,
they are born there alone;
so says one school.
The afflictions of the lower heavens are more intense than those of the higher heavens;
the Tuṣita Heaven is free from these two types.
The Bodhisattva feels weary of these two categories of affliction.
Therefore, he is born in that heaven.
Some say that a bodhisattva performs and accumulates only those karmas that lead to rebirth in that heavenly realm.
Therefore, he is born only there.

Some say that it is because the lifespan of the Tuṣita Heaven alone corresponds to the time when the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood and when the karma for beings in Jambudvīpa to see the Buddha reaches maturity.
That is to say, fifty-seven koṭis and sixty thousand human years constitute the time required for the roots of virtue of both the emanator and those emanated to reach maturity;
this is precisely the lifespan of the Tuṣita Heaven.
Therefore, bodhisattvas are born only in those heavens:
if they are born in a higher heaven, their lifespan is not yet exhausted and their roots of goodness have already matured;
if they are born in a lower heaven, their lifespan has already been exhausted and their roots of goodness have not yet matured.
Therefore, he was not born there.
Some say it was in order to transform the immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas in Tuṣita Heaven who delight in the Dharma.
It is said that within that celestial realm there are nine courtyards,
each measuring twelve yojanas in length,
which are constantly filled with Bodhisattvas who delight in the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva in his final birth constantly preaches the Dharma throughout the six periods of the day and night;
such a thing does not occur in the higher or lower celestial realms. Some say:
Because Bodhisattvas always delight in dwelling in the middle way,
in his final birth he was born in Tuṣita Heaven, which is situated in the middle;
having passed away from there, he was born in the city of Kapilavastu in Central India.
In the middle watch of the night, he left the city by leaping over its walls and went forth into homelessness.
Relying upon the Middle Way, he attained perfect enlightenment and taught the Dharma of the Middle Way to all sentient beings.
He entered parinirvāṇa at the middle watch of the night;
for this reason, he was reborn only in Tuṣita Heaven and not in any other celestial realm.
Question: For what reason does a Bodhisattva, in his final existence, pass away only from the heavenly realm and not come from the human realm?
Answer: Some say it is because among all the realms of rebirth (*gati*), the heavenly realm is superior.
Some say it is because those who come from the heavens are held in high esteem by people.
Others say:
When coming from the heavenly realm, there are miraculous transformations;
when coming from the human realm, such things do not occur. Some say:
Among humans, there is no such lifespan as that of Tuṣita, because it is commensurate with the ripening of their roots of goodness.
Some say that it is due to the sovereign power of the karma of Bodhisattvas who delight in the Dharma in the Heaven of Tuṣita.
This causes the bodhisattva to be born in that heaven so that he may preach the Dharma for its inhabitants.
Some say it is because the bodhisattva possesses determinate karma for birth in that heaven which must necessarily be experienced.
Some say that if a Bodhisattva were to be born repeatedly among humans before attaining Buddhahood, people would become weary of and disdain him,
and thus would not accept his transformation.
Question: Why does he not attain perfect enlightenment immediately in Tuṣita Heaven, but must necessarily come to the human realm?
Answer: Because it accords with the nature of all Buddhas' dharmas.
This means that all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, numbering more than the sands of the Ganges River,
have attained perfect enlightenment among human beings.
Furthermore, the bodies belonging to the heavenly realms are not the basis for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, it is because only human beings possess sharp and keen wisdom and vision capable of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Moreover, the various devas are deeply attached to exquisite sensual desires.
Because it is not predominant with respect to such matters as entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), attaining the fruits [of the path], and becoming free from defilement;
furthermore, because those in the human realm possess sharp faculties and natures, they are for the most part able to receive the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
The heavenly realm is not like this.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva in their final existence must necessarily undergo birth from a womb,
because beings in the heavenly realm are born only through transformation.
Furthermore, there are two conditions for a Buddha’s appearance in the world:
first, the mind of renunciation;
second, sharp and penetrating wisdom.
It should be known that these two exist only within the human realm.
Furthermore, since both humans and devas are vessels for the Dharma,
he comes to the human world in order to gather them both.
If he were in the heavens, humans would have no means of going there;
furthermore, one could not allow him to attain Buddhahood in the heavens and then come to the human realm to transform others, for people would then doubt the Buddha.
Because that which is produced by illusion does not undergo the process of receiving [the dharma],
the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood in the human realm.
Nevertheless, the Bodhisattva dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven.
When his lifespan is exhausted and he is about to descend to be born again,
he first contemplates four matters;
the first is to contemplate the timing.
Second, observing the location;
third, observing the spiritual lineage;
fourth, observing the suitability of the vessel.
Regarding the observation of the time-period:
one observes at what time the Buddha should appear in the world among all the realms of existence,
and thus knows that it is from the time when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years.
"Up until the time of a hundred years, a Buddha should appear in the world;
now is precisely that time.
As for observing the location:"
That is to say, when he observes in which region of the world the Buddha should appear in the world,
he immediately knows that the Buddha should appear in the Middle Country of Jambudvīpa,
and not among the frontier regions of the barbarian Mlecchas.
Regarding the observation of the lineage:
this refers to observing within which lineage the Buddha should appear in the world;
that is, one knows that the Buddha should appear in the world either within the kṣatriya lineage or the brāhmaṇa lineage.
At that time, whoever is most powerful and superior is born therein.
As for observing the supporting vessel,
it means observing which kind of woman exists in the world.
The lineage of both his father and mother was entirely pure;
his embryonic development was spacious and free from all defects,
enabling him to sustain for ten months a body composed of the Nārāyaṇa strength of a Bodhisattva.
He then knew that among those in Jambudvīpa there was a woman named so-and-so who was a fit vessel to serve as a support.
Having thus contemplated these four matters,
the Bodhisattva addressed the Devaputra Mārgayāna, saying:
"You may go and announce to the assembly of the Tuṣita Heaven:
'Seven days hence,
the Bodhisattva who is to succeed [the Buddha] shall pass away from here and be born in the city of Kapilavastu in the land of Magadha in Central India.'"
They extensively performed Buddha-works.
Those who wished to follow them should have made vows for the future.
The Devaputra Xingdao (行道) joyfully and respectfully assented.
Riding upon his own swift supernormal power,
he addressed the assembly of Tuṣita devas, saying:
"O celestial seers, you should know!"
"Seven days hence, the Bodhisattva who is to succeed him shall descend into Jambudvīpa,
taking birth in the city of Kapilavastu in Central India,
where he will extensively perform the deeds of a Buddha."
"You virtuous ones among the host of devas who wish to follow me, you should now make a vow to be reborn [among humans].
At that time, five hundred sons of gods immediately made vows to descend and be born accordingly.
On the seventh day,
the Bodhisattva, together with five hundred devaputras,
simultaneously vanished from the Tuṣita Heaven.
They were born simultaneously in the city of Kapilavastu in Central India within Jambudvīpa;
all were of the Śākya clan and assisted in proclaiming the Buddha’s work.
It should be understood that this refers to the Śākya Bodhisattva.
If other bodhisattvas are to be addressed according to their respective needs,
it is as was said to Maitreya:
"In a future age, you shall attain buddhahood."
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing and elucidating the sūtras.
As the Blessed One has said:
when the lifespan of humans in the future reaches eighty thousand years,
this continent of Jambudvīpa will be vast and expansive.
The population was flourishing, peaceful, secure, and prosperous.
Villages, towns, and cities were so close together that their roosters crowed in succession.
Women did not marry until they were five hundred years of age.
At that time, although the bodies of those people were superior and exquisite, they still suffered from three afflictions:
first, the need for excrement and urine;
second, cold and heat, as well as hunger and thirst.
Third, regarding greed, lust, old age, and sickness:
there was a wheel-turning monarch named Śaṅkha,
who subdued the four quarters and transformed the world according to the Dharma.
He possessed the seven treasures, namely:
the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the military commander treasure.
He was also endowed with a full thousand sons.
Brave, heroic, and upright, he is able to crush his enemies.
The earth extends to the furthest limits of the great ocean, as level as the palm of a hand,
free from mounds, pits, gravel, pebbles, or poisonous thorns.
All people live in harmony, treating one another with a compassionate heart.
They do not employ weapons of war, maintaining their integrity through self-restraint.
The king possesses a precious terrace.
It was one thousand *han* in height and sixteen parts in breadth;
adorned with various ornaments, he offered it as a field of merit to generate great meritorious karma.
Not long thereafter, he shaved off his hair and beard.
Having left the household life out of faith and diligently cultivated the holy life,
one becomes an arhat in this very life and is able to know it for oneself.
"My births have been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence;
I have attained parinirvāṇa.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, [the assembly rejoiced].
Among the assembly, the bhikṣu Aśvita rose from his seat,
joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One."
"May I, in a future age, become that Cakravartin King Śaṅkha,
subduing the four quarters and transforming the world according to the Dharma,
and so forth, until finally attaining parinirvāṇa."
At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked him, saying:
"Foolish man, why do you not wish for death once, but instead seek death a second time by aspiring to become a Cakravartin King in a future life?"
...and so forth, as explained at length.
However, Āśīta, it shall be according to your wish;
in a future age, you will certainly become that Cakravartin King Śaṅkha.
Having subdued the four quarters and transformed the world according to the Dharma,
he extensively taught until finally attaining parinirvāṇa.
He then addressed the great assembly once more:
In the future, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, a Buddha will appear in the world named Maitreya Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Just as I am now endowed with the ten titles,
so too that Buddha was [endowed] among this world’s assembly of gods, Māras, Mahābrahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, and humans.
He claims for himself:
"I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat,
the Samyaksaṃbuddha," up to "the Buddha, the Bhagavān."
He fully realized and attained sovereign supernormal wisdom;

he also personally knew for himself: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence"—thus he attained Great Nirvana.
Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, he proclaimed the sublime Dharma,
revealing that which is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end;
its phrasing and meaning are exquisite, it is purely singular and complete, and it is the pure, holy life.
For the sake of all humans and devas, he correctly opens the Brahma-faring for them to practice and study extensively.
He is surrounded by a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of followers and attended by disciples of immeasurable compassionate lineage.
They bring great benefit.
Just as I do now, [I act] toward the world with its Māras, Brahmās, and Great Brahmās,
and so forth, as has been explained at length.
Innumerable disciples of the Śākya clan attended upon him, providing great benefit.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words,
the Bodhisattva Maitreya rose from his seat within the assembly.
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One,
may I in a future age attain the state of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maitreya."
The full account continues in this manner, up until:
"Just as the World-honored One now provides great benefit for the protection and service of his immeasurable disciples of the Śākya clan," at which time the World-honored One,
having heard those words, gave rise to knowledge of the past.
He carefully examines whether Maitreya has attained fulfillment through the cultivation of the four *pāramitās* over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
He knows them to be truly fulfilled as they are.
He further carefully examines whether he has attained fulfillment through the cultivation of the karma that ripens into the marks (*lakṣaṇa-vipāka-karman*) during those one hundred great eons.
He then knew, exactly as it was, that with the exception of the mark of golden complexion, all other [marks] were complete.
For this reason, the Buddha said to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"You may now offer this golden-colored robe as a gift to the Saṅgha."

If one makes offerings to the Saṃgha, know that this is also called making offerings to me. At that time, the Buddha knew in advance that after the assembly of monks had obtained these golden-colored robes, there would be a cause and condition for them to be given to Maitreya;
and once Maitreya had obtained them, he would certainly bestow them upon me.
...and so on, as explained at length.
By this cause and condition, the karma of golden color is fulfilled.
Regarding this, some say:
The Buddha, wishing to bring that karma of golden color to completion,
said to Ānanda:
"You should seek out a new garment of golden color for me."
"I wish to hold this and give it to Maitreya.
At that time, Ānanda obtained it according to his instructions and immediately knelt to present it.
The World-Honored One, having received it, commanded Maitreya, saying:
"You may take this new golden-colored robe.
Maitreya received the command, yet he did not dare to take it.
The Buddha said,
"Take them;
you may offer them as you wish to the foremost monks of the Buddha."
"Why is this? Because in the future, you shall benefit the world through this merit.
Maitreya respectfully assented, took it, and offered it to the Buddha and the foremost assembly of monks.
For this reason,
his golden karma was fulfilled;
so some say.
The karma for Maitreya’s golden-colored marks was also already fulfilled;
however, the Buddha caused him to give away a golden robe in order to demonstrate that although his merit is complete, he remains free from satiety, thereby exhorting and leading others.
The World-Honored One, having first aroused the knowledge of the past and observed the past of Maitreya,
further aroused the knowledge of the future and carefully examined whether, at a time when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years,
Maitreya would possess a physical basis for attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
He then knows that they exist.
Furthermore, he carefully examines whether, at that time, they possess the capacity to attain enlightenment;
he then knows that they are capable.
Having observed their past and future limits,
the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"It is truly excellent and virtuous that you have been able to give rise to such vast thoughts and vows for the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings.
Furthermore, he addressed Maitreya:"
"It shall be as you have wished.
In a future age, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years,
you shall become a Buddha named Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
To speak at length, up to:
"Just as I am now attended by immeasurable disciples of the Śākya clan who provide great benefit,
so too were you attended by immeasurable disciples of the Maitreya clan who provided great benefit."
Question: Both Ajita and Maitreya sought a body for the future time when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years.
Why did the World-Honored One reprimand Ajita while praising Maitreya?

The answer is: Because the bhikṣu Ajita gave rise to an intention toward existence, gave rise to resolute conviction, gave rise to longing, gave rise to aspiration, and gave rise to seeking, the Buddha rebuked him.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya, however, does not give rise to an intention toward existence.
Even up to the point of seeking,
because he gives rise to the resolute intention (*āśaya*) toward the task of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings—
even up to the point of seeking— the Buddha praised him.
Furthermore, the Buddha rebuked Ajita because he sought the worldly position of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin),
whereas he praised Maitreya because he sought the supramundane position of a Dharma-wheel-turning monarch.
The same applies to the discourse on seeking the sovereignty of saṃsāra and seeking the sovereignty of cessation (*nivṛtti*).
Furthermore, Āśvājita, because he sought his own self-interest and pleasure, the Buddha rebuked him.
Because Maitreya seeks the benefit and happiness of others, the Buddha praised him.
Likewise, it is the same when one seeks one's own benefit or seeks the benefit of others.
Although the sūtra speaks in this way, [the underlying principle remains consistent].
"Maitreya, in a future age when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, you shall attain Buddhahood,
known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maitreya," and so forth,
as extensively explained.
Yet it does not differentiate which cognition operates upon what.
Since the sūtras are the fundamental basis for this treatise,
that which was not differentiated therein should now be differentiated here.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
Question: As it is said, "Maitreya, in a future age you shall attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maitreya."
What kind of knowledge is this?
The answer is: it is the knowledge of causes and the knowledge of the path.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s knowledge that observes the prior and posterior limits of Maitreya.
Question: Upon what does this operate?
Answer: It operates upon the characteristics [of phenomena], their maturation, and karma;
by means of this, it is called the knowledge of causes.

There is the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through the untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), which is termed "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*).
This is precisely what the Tathāgata examines regarding whether Maitreya’s prior-limital characteristics (*pūrvānta-nimitta*) and the karma of their maturation (*vipāka-karma*) are complete.
Because perfect wisdom operates with respect to the cause, it is called "causal wisdom. Furthermore,
it is the observation of Maitreya’s future limit,
wherein he will attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment through the untainted faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and factors of the path.
Because wisdom operates upon the path, it is called "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*).
However, both of these knowledges are subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*),
as they do not possess the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) of the noble truths.
There may be those whose bodies possess the thirty-two marks yet lack the noble dharmas—
namely, ordinary worldlings who are universal monarchs.
Or there may be those whose bodies possess the noble dharmas yet lack the thirty-two marks.
This refers to those who are neither universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) nor śrāvakas and the like;
that is, there may be individuals whose bodies possess the thirty-two marks and who also possess the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*), yet are not Buddhas—
such as King Śaṅkha and others who have attained the noble path (*āryamārga*).
There may be those whose bodies possess neither the thirty-two marks nor the noble dharmas;
namely, other ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
All Buddha-bodies, however, necessarily possess the unsurpassed thirty-two marks and the unsurpassed noble dharmas.
This refers to perfect enlightenment.
Question: Why is it that in this context only the transformation of karma that ripens into marks is called "knowledge of the cause," whereas the transformation of the four pāramitās is not so called?
Regarding those who have promised to speak but do not speak,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, the karma of maturation is proximate.
Regarding the four *pāramitās*, this [text] speaks of their proximity here rather than their distance.
Furthermore, when the karma that results in the marks (*lakṣaṇa-vipāka-karman*) is cultivated, it becomes manifest and is commonly known by humans and devas;
the four *pāramitās* are not like that.
This is explained here according to what is manifest.
Furthermore, when one cultivates karma that has specific characteristics as its maturation,
both the certainty of enlightenment and the certainty of its attainment are established.
When practicing the four pāramitās,
although awakening is certain,
the destination is not yet certain.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, in this context, that which is known as the proximate cause of the body and the proximate cause of enlightenment is explained.
The karma that is the maturation of the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is the proximate cause of the body.
The untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), powers (*bala*), and so forth are the proximate causes of enlightenment (*bodhi*).
The four perfections (*pāramitā*) and the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and the like are not proximate causes for either [of the two].
Therefore, they are not mentioned.
As it is said:
"This bhikṣu shall, in this very life, realize the noble goal," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in the *Pavāraṇā-sūtra*:
This bhikṣu shall, in this very life, realize the noble goal and know for himself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence after this; I have attained parinirvāṇa."
Although that sūtra makes this statement,
it does not distinguish which cognition operates in relation to what.
That sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which was not previously stated shall now be explained;
therefore, this treatise is composed.
Question: Regarding the statement that "this bhikṣu shall realize the noble goal in this very life," what kind of knowledge is this?
He replied, "It is the knowledge of the path.
He asked, "In what does this operate?

He replied, "This operates toward the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*) by means of the untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*); it is for this reason that it is called the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)."

This is precisely what the Tathāgata, observing that the bhikṣus have attained the knowledge of the permanent exhaustion of all outflows through the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and factors of the path, and having turned toward the path, calls "knowledge of the path."
This is also subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), because it is not the untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) consisting of the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).
Question: Why is the knowledge of causes (*hetujñāna*) not mentioned here?
Answer: Some say that, in this context, it should be stated as follows:
"What kind of knowledge is this?"
Answer: It is based on causal knowledge (*hetu-jñāna*) and path knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*). Regarding what these operate upon:
they operate upon the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) and so forth; it is for this reason that they are called causal knowledge.

If one attains the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*) by means of the untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), this is termed "knowledge of the path" (*mārgajñāna*).
That such a statement is not made [in certain contexts] should be understood as indicating that the meaning [of those passages] is incomplete.
Some say:
"The application for unsurpassed enlightenment is vast; it is accomplished only after three incalculable eons and a hundred eons.
Since its cause is thus worthy of veneration, it is therefore said that one contemplates that wisdom."
The preparatory application for the enlightenment of a śrāvaka is narrow and limited;
that is to say, at the very fastest, it is attained in three lifetimes.
In the first lifetime, the seeds are planted.
In the second birth, there is maturation;
in the third birth, there is liberation.
Because the cause is not to be emphasized, the observation of that wisdom is not mentioned.
Some say: Because the lineage (*gotra*) and other factors upon which the maturation-karma of the marks of a Bodhisattva depend are determined, he is said to possess the knowledge of them;

because the lineage and other factors upon which the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) of a Śrāvaka depend are not determined, he is not said to possess that knowledge.
Some say that the Buddha has two matters of superiority:
first, the body upon which he relies.
Because there are two kinds of enlightenment attained, one observes their respective causes; thus, it is fully explained that the knowledge of these two types of causal wisdom exists.
While the Śrāvakas possess only the enlightenment that is attained, [the Bodhisattva's] is superior.
Because it is not the supporting body itself, only the wisdom that knows the causes of enlightenment is mentioned.
Some say that the wisdom knowing the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) and so forth was also not previously mentioned.
Therefore, one should not pose a question regarding this:
"What is the knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhijñāna)?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Although the function of the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) was previously explained, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has not yet been stated.
I now wish to explain this, and therefore I have composed this treatise.
Question: What is the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*)?
Answer: It is like an arhat who has accomplished the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and attained mastery over the mind.
Having made the correct vow to know the meaning according to his desire,
he enters the fourth dhyāna of the limit;
having arisen from that concentration, he knows everything exactly as he wished.
Regarding "knowing the meaning according to one's desire":
the question is asked, for what reason does an arhat desire to know the meaning?
The answer is: due to three causes and conditions.
First, for the sake of benefiting his disciples;
second, for the sake of maintaining and upholding the Buddha-dharma;
third, for the sake of knowing what is secure and what is insecure in the world.
Regarding "benefiting disciples":
this refers to when an Arhat is practicing contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) upon his disciples,
it is the natural law that he should contemplate how long or how recently they have entered the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
"When my life comes to an end, will [Name] be able to enter the state of rightness and transcendence? Should he be unable to enter it,
will there be another who can instruct him so that he may attain entry?"
All such things are known through the power of the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*).
These are called those who benefit their disciples and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
This refers to when an Arhat is engaged in affairs pertaining to the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha, such as constructing a stūpa, a vihāra, or a saṃghārāma;
in such cases, it is the rule that he should observe how long it will take for them to be completed.
"Will you be able to accomplish it for as long as my life lasts? If you cannot,
will there be anyone else who can continue to accomplish it after my death?"
There may be kings, ministers, elders, or merchant leaders who wish to cause the decline of the Buddha-dharma;
an arhat, mindful of this, desires to transform them.
"Even if I were to examine whether they are capable of being converted—
if they are indeed capable, will it be for long or short?
Will the task of conversion be accomplished before my life comes to an end?"
"If it does not succeed, will there be one who can continue it after my life has ended?
All such matters are known through the power of the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*).
These types of affairs are called "sustaining the Buddha-dharma" (*dharmadhāraṇa*)."
One who knows the security and insecurity of the world refers to an Arhat who,
at times, examines the countries and time periods where they reside,
foreseeing whether there will be abundance or scarcity, fear or peace, or epidemics and other such events.
Desiring to cause both oneself and others to know how to proceed toward equanimity (*upekṣā*), one gives rise to the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).
For example, in the past, there was a king named Śaka in this kingdom of Kaśmīra,
who had his territory invaded and plundered by the King of Bāhlika.
At that time, King Śrāka immediately led his troops, intending to engage in battle.
However, that king was by nature compassionate and benevolent, and he constantly feared the consequences of evil karma;
thus, he secretly thought to himself:
I do not know whether I shall certainly be victorious in battle now and preserve my royal throne.
Should I fail to achieve my purpose, I would merely be killing the people,
further inviting calamity and sin, and falling into hell after death.
"I have heard that in such-and-such a monastery there is an Arhat who has attained the wondrous knowledge of vows;
I shall go there to question him."
Having reflected thus, he immediately went there;
with sincere devotion, he paid his respects and requested a resolution for his doubts.
That arhat then replied to the king:
"Although I have previously attained this wisdom, because of a lack of supporting conditions,
my physical strength has been weak and inferior, and it has not manifested for a long time. Thereupon,
the king provided him with various kinds of food and drink, as well as excellent requisites.
Before long, the Venerable One was able to arouse his vow-knowledge (*praṇidhijñāna*) and immediately examined the matter;
he saw that the King of Bāhlīka would certainly seize the throne of King Śaka and bring about great benefit.
Having seen this, he immediately reported to King Śreṇika, saying, "Your Majesty, you shall lose your kingdom; I pray that you reflect upon this and exert yourself.
Śreṇika respectfully assented.
He immediately led his attendants and kinsmen,
abandoned the kingdom, and departed to seek refuge in another land.
For this reason, the arhats desired to understand the meaning of that matter.
Regarding one who enters the "limit" (prāntakoṭika) fourth dhyāna:
Question—Why is it called the "limit" fourth dhyāna?
Answer—Because, within this fourth dhyāna...
Because it is the pinnacle, the ultimate, and the dense forest [of meditative attainment],
it is called the "limit" (prāntakoṭika) fourth dhyāna;
this signifies that it is the most excellent grade of the fourth dhyāna.
It is like the tip of a tree; as the most excellent among trees, it is called the "limit of the tree.

Some say that this is the locus for the qualities of dharmas such as manifesting knowledge (*vijñapti-jñāna*), ultimate knowledge (*atyanta-jñāna*), and the forest of dense knowledge (*jñāna-gahana*).
Therefore, it is called the "limit" (prāntakoṭika) fourth dhyāna;
that is to say, because this meditative absorption only arises after the mental continuum has been perfumed by various meritorious qualities such as the immeasurables.
The virtues arising from this meditative concentration serve as the manifestation, the pinnacle, and the dense forest of all virtues;
they are like clarified butter, the most excellent among the flavors of cow's milk.
Some say that this should be called the "fourth dhyāna of the subsequent limit.
There are three limits.
First is the prior limit, second is the middle limit,
and third is the posterior limit; these three correspond respectively to the past, the present, and the future.
Among these, the former limit is known by two types of knowledge:
namely, the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) and the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*).
The middle limit is also known by two types of knowledge,
namely, the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge resulting from aspiration.
The subsequent limit is known solely by the knowledge resulting from aspiration.
Because this wisdom exists solely within the realm of the future,
it is called "wisdom of the posterior limit" (aparāntajñāna).
The meditative concentration that can give rise to this wisdom is termed the "fourth dhyāna of the posterior limit."
Some say that this should be called the "unreached limit" (anāgamya) of the fourth dhyāna.
There are three kinds of limits.
First, the limit of the not-yet-arrived; second, the limit of arrival; third, the limit of having already arrived.
These three correspond respectively to the future, the present, and the past.
Just as knowing the present is called the knowledge of the limit of arrival (*prāptāntajñāna*),
and knowing the past is called the knowledge of the limit already passed (*atikrāntāntajñāna*),
so too this knowledge is mostly concerned with the future, and is therefore called the knowledge of the limit not yet arrived (*aprāptāntajñāna*).
The ability to arise in this meditative absorption is called the "unattained limit" (*anāgamya*) of the fourth dhyāna.
Some say that it should instead be called the "limit" (*prāntakoṭika*) of the fourth dhyāna.
Why is this so? "Extremes" (anta) refers to the present aggregates, elements, and sense-bases;
"limits" (koṭi) refers to the past and the future.
Just as there arises a directly perceiving wisdom regarding the present aggregates, elements,
and bases, so too does such directly perceiving wisdom arise regarding the past and the future; therefore,
this wisdom is called "limit-reaching wisdom" (paryanta-jñāna).
The ability to enter this meditative absorption is called the "limit" (prāntakoṭika) fourth dhyāna.
Regarding the statement, "Having arisen from the absorption, one knows everything as desired":
does one know while remaining in the absorption, or does one know after having arisen from the absorption?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If it were known while in meditative concentration,
why is it stated here that one knows everything as desired only after arising from concentration?
If one knows while emerging from meditative absorption, why must one enter the fourth dhyāna of the limit (*prāntakoṭika*)?
The answer is: it is precisely while remaining in absorption that one is able to know.
Question: Why is it said here that after arising from meditative concentration, one knows everything according to one's wish?
Answer: At the time of speaking, this is called "knowing" because knowing is manifested through speech.
Furthermore, at that time, because one causes others to know, it is designated as "knowing."
Some say that one is able to know [the object] upon emerging from meditative absorption.
Question: For what reason does one further enter the fourth dhyāna?
The answer is: the fourth dhyāna at its limit is the skillful means for this knowledge, because this knowledge arises only when one has entered that meditative absorption.
Thus it is said.
It is initially described as wholesome because, while remaining in meditative concentration, one is able to know the circumstances for emerging from that concentration.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*)?
Answer: Its intrinsic nature is wisdom (*prajñā*).
Just as it is with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), so too are the characteristics of my things and their fundamental nature (*prakṛti*).
Having already explained intrinsic nature,
that which follows shall now be explained.
Question: For what reason is it called "knowledge resulting from resolve" (*praṇidhijñāna*)?
Answer: It is called "knowledge resulting from resolve" because one is able to know according to one's resolve.
Question: Is it that one knows according to one's own resolve?
"Is it that one can know according to the wishes of others?
Answer: "One knows according to one's own wishes, and one also knows according to the wishes of others."
Because it is able to know all aspirations as they arise.
Furthermore, it is called "aspiration-knowledge" (praṇidhijñāna) because it knows all aspirations.
There are two kinds of aspiration.
That is to say, there are the vow for enlightenment and the vow for existence.
The vow for enlightenment is, for example, the vow of Maitreya and others;
the vow for existence is, for example, the vow of Ajita and others.
Because one knows these aspirations through it, it is called "knowledge resulting from aspiration" (praṇidhijñāna).
Furthermore, because knowledge arises in accordance with the aspiration, it is called "knowledge resulting from aspiration";
that is to say, this knowledge is preeminent.
Because it must be initiated by a prior mental aspiration (*manasikāra*) and application (*prayoga*),
even though the Tathāgata lacks such mental aspiration and application,
he nonetheless necessarily has a mental vow as a prerequisite.
Some say that this should be called "knowledge through resolve" (*āśayajñāna*), because since the object of knowledge is subtle and extremely profound,
one must first form a formal resolve before being able to know it.
Some say that this should be called "sublime wisdom" (*prajñā*), because among all forms of knowledge this is the most excellent,
just as in the world one speaks of "exquisite food," "exquisite clothing," and so forth.
Just as that [sound] is a sublime voice among superior utterances,
so too is this [knowledge].
However, this is the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).
As for the realm, it is the form realm (rūpadhātu).
As for the stage, it is the level of the fourth dhyāna.
As for the basis, it relies upon a body belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
As for its aspects (*ākāra*), it consists of the sixteen aspects, or other aspects;
as for its object (*ālambana*), it takes all phenomena as its object;
as for its application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it pertains to all four applications of mindfulness.
The wise masters of the ancient Abhidharma say that there is only one conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Other teachers say that there are eight knowledges in nature, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Why is this? Because that is not of the nature of vision, whereas the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) is of the nature of vision.
Thus it is said.
The single conventional wisdom (saṃvṛtijñāna) is either associated with meditative concentration (samādhi) or not associated with meditative concentration;
it is exclusively outflow-tainted (sāsrava).
Regarding the association with faculties, it is associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Regarding time, it falls within the three times;
its objects are those belonging to the three times as well as that which is beyond time (*lokottara*).
Regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [factors], these wholesome [factors] take the three types as their objects.
As for those bound to the three realms and those not so bound, they are exclusively bound to the form realm;
they take as their objects that which is bound to the three realms as well as that which is not so bound.
That which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner is "neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
It takes three types as its object:
those abandoned by seeing, those abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned, which are abandoned by cultivation.
It takes three kinds as its objects.
Regarding "taking names as objects" and "taking meanings as objects," it takes both names and meanings as objects.
Regarding "taking one's own continuum, another's continuum, or that which is not a continuum as objects," it takes all three kinds as objects.
As for where it arises:
it arises in the desire realm, not in the form or formless realms;
within the desire realm, it arises only in the human destiny, and not in others.
Among the human realms, this occurs only in the three continents and not in the northern continent (Uttarakuru).
Within those three continents, both male and female bodies are capable of giving rise to it.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka made this statement.
It can arise only in Jambudvīpa and not in other continents;
it can arise only in men and not in women. Why is this so?
The excellence of the knowledge of aspiration requires a body that is superior, intense, and sharp;
for in the other two continents and in the female body, these qualities are all weak and inferior.
Of these explanations, the first is superior.
For in the three continents, the bodies of both men and women are all preeminent and intense,
because they are all capable of attaining mastery over the mind and mastery over meditative concentration.
If it were not so, the Sūtra should not have stated that five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, with Mahāprajāpatī as their leader,
all relinquished the life-faculties and entered parinirvāṇa on a single day.
If he had not attained the fourth dhyāna of the limit (*prāntakoṭika*), he would be unable to relinquish the formations of life-force (*jīvitasaṃskāra*);
since he has already attained this, why alone should he be unable to arouse the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*)?
Question: What kind of person (*pudgala*) is able to give rise to this knowledge?
Answer: It is a noble one (*ārya*), not an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);
among the noble ones, it is one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
It is not among those in training (śaikṣa).
Among those beyond training (aśaikṣa), it is only the one liberated at any time (asamayavimukta) and not the one liberated by time (samayavimukta).
Why is this? Because one who has attained mastery over meditative concentration and its continuity,
and is not held fast by the afflictions, is able to give rise to the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).
Ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) lack both of these matters.
Although those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) have mastery over meditative concentration,
their mental continuums remain sustained by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Although those liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) possess a continuous succession that is not held by afflictions,
they do not attain mastery over meditative concentration;
therefore, they are all unable to initiate [the path].
The knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) exists only in those who are liberated at any time (asamayavimukta),
because they have attained mastery over meditative concentration and their mental continuum is not constrained by afflictions; thus,
they are able to give rise to the knowledge of aspiration.
