translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang, who received the Imperial Decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (*Samādhiskandha*), Part Four of the Chapter on the Non-Returner (*Anāgāmī-nirdeśa*), Question Six: On the Knowledge of Aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*).
Is it acquired through preparatory effort (*prayoga*)? Or is it acquired through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*)?
Answer: It is acquired through preparatory effort.
There is that which is obtained through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya-prāpti*). Regarding this, some say that the Buddha obtains it through the abandonment of defilements.
Because it is attained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*);
because it is attained through the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
and because it manifests through preparatory application.
Some say that both Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas acquire it through the abandonment of defilements,
because they acquire it at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
It is attained through the application of effort by Śrāvakas;
it manifests through the application of effort. Some say:
The Buddha, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Śrāvaka who has reached the ultimate all acquire it through the attainment of freedom from defilement,
as they acquire it at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Other Śrāvakas acquire it through application (*prayoga*).
Regarding the statement that it manifests through application (*prayoga*):
if it is definitely obtainable, it is acquired through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya-lābhika*).
Because it is attained at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*),
it subsequently manifests only after one has applied effort (*prayoga*);
the Buddha, however, does not depend on such effort.
The preparatory application (*prayoga*) for a Pratyekabuddha is inferior;
that for a Śrāvaka is either middling or superior.
However, there is the Knowledge of Aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), which is attained through the preparatory application of the "ultimate" meditative absorption (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*).
It manifests through preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Question: What is the preparatory application for this knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*)?
Answer: It takes all stages (*bhūmi*) and the ultimate meditative concentration (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*) as its preparatory application.
That is to say, when the practitioner is about to give rise to this knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*),
they first give rise to a wholesome mind of the desire realm;
immediately following this, they enter the first dhyāna.
Next, he enters the second dhyāna;
proceeding in this manner through the stages until he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he returns to enter the sphere of nothingness.
In succession, he enters the first dhyāna;
arising from the first dhyāna, he again enters the second dhyāna;
and so on in succession until he enters the fourth dhyāna.
Having thus, through the meditative attainments of all the lower and higher stages,
entered and emerged from them in succession until they were perfectly harmonized,
he then, within the fourth dhyāna, proceeded from the lower level to the middle, and from the middle to the upper.
This superior grade is called the "limit" (prāntakoṭika) fourth dhyāna.
From this, one sequentially brings forth the knowledge resulting from resolve (praṇidhijñāna).
Therefore, the Venerable Vasumitra spoke as follows:
For the sake of benefiting others,
the various arhats enter and emerge from the higher and lower stages in a cyclical manner, making the fourth dhyāna supple and compliant;
when their preparatory application flows forth without obstruction, [they attain mastery].
At that time, it is called the fulfillment of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
From this point, one is able to bring forth the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) into manifestation.
The Venerable One said:
One understands the skillful means regarding that which arises immediately after cessation, that which arises without interval, and that which arises simultaneously.
When the flow of application proceeds without obstruction,
at that time it is called the fulfillment of application.
From this, the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) arises and becomes manifest.
Question: What is the difference between the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna) and the knowledge resulting from aspiration that takes the past as its object?
Answer: Their distinction lies in their names alone.
This is called the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
This is called the knowledge of vows directed toward the past (*atītapraṇidhijñāna*).
Furthermore, the knowledge of recollecting past lives knows the contaminated five aggregates (*sāsravapañcaskandha*) of the prior limit.
This knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) knows the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) aggregates (*skandha*).
Furthermore, the knowledge of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) knows the five aggregates of the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) within the desire and form realms (*kāmarūpadhātu*).
This knowledge of aspiration knows the aggregates belonging to the three realms as well as those that are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Furthermore, the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) cognizes the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the aggregates.
This knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) cognizes both the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the common characteristics of the aggregates.
Furthermore, regarding this knowledge of recollecting past lives, there are those who possess this dharma and those who possess external dharmas.
This knowledge resulting from aspiration exists only for those who possess this specific dharma.
Furthermore, while the knowledge of recollecting past lives exists both for ordinary beings and for noble ones,
this knowledge resulting from aspiration exists only for noble ones.

Furthermore, the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna) exists in those who are in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
This knowledge resulting from prayer (praṇidhijñāna), however, exists only in those beyond training.
Furthermore, the knowledge of recollecting past lives exists within the mental continuum of both those liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) and those not liberated by occasion (asamayavimukta).
This knowledge of aspiration exists only within the continuum of one who is liberated at times not fixed by occasion (*asamayavimukta*).
Furthermore, while the knowledge of recollecting past lives relies upon the four fundamental dhyānas,
this knowledge of aspiration relies solely upon the fourth fundamental dhyāna.

Furthermore, regarding the supernormal power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānābhijñā*), there are those previously attained and those not yet attained, those previously practiced and those not yet practiced, and those that are common and those that are uncommon.
This knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) is exclusively that which has not been previously attained, not previously practiced, and is uncommon.
Furthermore, when the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) is first induced, it can only recollect the sequence of successive births;
later, when it has reached fulfillment, it can recollect either the sequence of successive births or skip over hundreds or thousands of births and so forth.
Whatever one desires, one is able to recollect it at will.
When this knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) is first induced and when it is fully perfected,
whether in sequential or non-sequential order, one knows all things exactly as they are according to one's wish.
Furthermore, if this knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) were to operate solely upon the objects known by the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*),
it would possess six superiorities.
First, the superiority of intensity (*prabhāvaviśeṣa*).
Second, superiority in dominance;
third, superiority in subtlety;
fourth, superiority in purity.
Fifth is the excellence of clarity;
sixth is the excellence of swiftness—
how much more so for the many others?
This is called the distinction between the knowledge of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) and the knowledge of aspiration directed toward the past.
Question: What is the difference between the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledge of aspiration directed toward the present?
Answer: Their very names constitute the difference.
This is called the knowledge of others' minds;
this is called the vow-knowledge (praṇidhijñāna) that takes the present as its object.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds takes a single thing as its objective sphere.
This knowledge resulting from prayer takes as its object either a single thing or multiple things.
Furthermore, while the knowledge of others' minds takes the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object,
this knowledge resulting from prayer takes both the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its objects.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds takes the mental continuum of another as its object,
whereas this knowledge resulting from prayer takes the mental continua of both oneself and others as its objects.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds takes the mind and mental factors as its objects.
This knowledge resulting from aspiration takes the five aggregates as its object.
Furthermore, while the knowledge of others' minds relies upon the four fundamental dhyānas,
this knowledge resulting from aspiration relies solely upon the fourth fundamental dhyāna.
Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of others' minds, this dharma exists among those who possess external dharmas as well;
however, this knowledge resulting from prayer exists only among those who possess this specific dharma.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds is possessed by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
It is also possessed by noble ones (*ārya*).
This knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) belongs exclusively to noble ones.

Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is possessed by those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
This knowledge resulting from prayer exists only in those who are no longer learners (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, while the knowledge of others' minds exists within the mental continuums of both those liberated at times (*samayavimukta*) and those not liberated at times (*asamayavimukta*),
this knowledge resulting from prayer exists only within the mental continuum of one not liberated at times.
Furthermore, the supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds may have been previously attained or not yet attained, previously practiced or not yet practiced, shared or unshared;
this Knowledge through Aspiration (praṇidhijñāna), however, is exclusively that which has not been previously attained, has not been previously practiced, and is unshared.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
whereas this knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) is exclusively contaminated.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds takes as its object phenomena associated with the realms of desire and form, as well as those that are unassociated.
This knowledge resulting from prayer takes as its object both the phenomena bound to the three realms and those that are unbound.
Furthermore, this knowledge resulting from prayer functions solely with respect to the objects known by the knowledge of others' minds.
There are six matters of excellence,
namely, the excellence of intensity and so forth, as previously described;
how much more so for the many others?
This is called the differentiation of the knowledge of others' minds that takes the present as its object through the power of the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*).
Question: How can the knowledge resulting from resolve know the future?
Answer: Some say:
One infers the future by means of the past and the present;
for example, just as a farmer, having sown seeds,
infers that such a fruit will certainly arise.
It is the same for that as well. Some say:
"If that were so, then the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) would be inferential knowledge (anumānajñāna) rather than direct perceptual knowledge (pratyakṣajñāna)."
It should be stated thus:
this knowledge resulting from aspiration does not depend on contemplating the cause to know the fruit,
nor does it depend on contemplating the fruit to know the cause.
Therefore, this knowledge is direct perception (pratyakṣa-jñāna), not inferential knowledge (anumāna-jñāna).
Question: How does the knowledge resulting from resolve (praṇidhijñāna) know the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)?
Answer: Some say that it is by observing the outflow (*niṣyanda*) and the distinctions in activity (*caryā-viśeṣa*),
just as a person traveling along a path knows the destination they have reached.
Some say: "If that were so, then the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) would be inferential cognition (anumānajñāna) rather than direct perception (pratyakṣajñāna).
One should instead state it as follows:
This wisdom of aspiration does not observe the cause to know the effect,
nor does it observe the effect to know the cause;
therefore, this wisdom is a wisdom of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This is not knowledge derived from inference;
rather, because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas still possess the afflictions of residual habitual tendencies,
they must apply effort toward their objects of aspiration before they can know them.
The Tathāgata has eternally exhausted all residual habitual tendencies and afflictions;
therefore, he knows the thoughts of his aspirations as soon as they arise.
Question: How is it that the World-Honored One’s knowledge of aspirations (*praṇidhijñāna*) is able to know the distinctions among the mental states of all sentient beings?
Answer: Some say that this need not necessarily be asked. Why is that?
This is because the realm of all Buddhas is inconceivable.
Some say that although it was previously measured and weighed, one can now know it.
Some say that by perceiving the distinctions in the mental characteristics of sentient beings through one portion of what is cognized,
one can infer the rest by analogy.
Just as when the world is being destroyed, sentient beings for the most part are reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
where they inquire of one another regarding their past lives,
later coming to know them through the knowledge of recollecting former existences (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
The Buddha is also like this.
Some say that he knows it because he has thoroughly mastered dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Some say that the Buddha knows it because he possesses mastery over the knowledge resulting from his vows. Others say:
The Buddha knows because he has attained mastery over his own karma;
some say that the Buddha knows because he has attained mastery over the outflowing results (*niṣyanda*).
Some say that the Buddha knows because he has thoroughly mastered the distinctions among formations (*saṃskāra*).
The Venerable One says:
The Buddha knows the mental realms of sentient beings simply by wishing to know them;
he does so without the need for preparatory application and without the necessity of questioning.
This is because, at the very moment he first attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), [he realized this].
Because all these types of knowledge have already been attained.
Question: For what reason does one give rise to such knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*)?
Answer: It is for the sake of benefiting others.
That is to say, one first gives rise to the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) to observe the differences in the dispositions (*āśaya*) of sentient beings,
and subsequently performs beneficial deeds according to what is appropriate for each.
This is like a skilled physician who first observes the specific characteristics of a patient and only then administers medicine.
Question: Should it be said that the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) is wholesome (*kuśala*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*)?
Answer: It may be wholesome.
Or it is indeterminate.
Regarding this, some say that the knowledge resulting from aspiration is exclusively [of one kind].
That is to say, it exists only as wholesome within the fourth dhyāna.
Some say that the knowledge resulting from prayer (praṇidhijñāna) is of two kinds.
That is to say, it exists only as wholesome in the fourth dhyāna and in the desire realm.
Some say that the knowledge resulting from prayer (praṇidhijñāna) is of three types.
That is to say: the wholesome [states] of the fourth dhyāna, the wholesome of the desire realm, and the indeterminate.
Some say that the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) consists of five types.
That is to say, the four dhyānas and [the states] of the desire realm are each exclusively wholesome.
Some say that the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) consists of six [types].
That is to say: the wholesome states of the four dhyānas, the wholesome states of the desire realm, and the indeterminate states.
Some say that there are seven types of *praṇidhijñāna* (knowledge resulting from resolve).
That is to say, the three higher dhyānas are exclusively wholesome;
the first dhyāna and the desire realm each possess both wholesome and neutral [states]. Some say:
The knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) consists of ten types;
that is to say, there are both wholesome and indeterminate [states] within each of the four dhyānas and the desire realm.
This is what is taught.
It should be understood that, as previously stated, these six are wholesome.

Question: Since the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) exists only in the fourth dhyāna and is exclusively wholesome, why is it said here that it exists in the wholesomeness of the four dhyānas and the wholesomeness and indeterminate states of the desire realm?
Answer: It is true that the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*) actually exists only in the fourth dhyāna and is exclusively wholesome;
however, this is stated here with intentional meaning (*saṃdhi*).
Both the knowledge resulting from resolve and the knowledge that arises subsequently to it—sharing the same object—are referred to as "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Because all are termed "knowledge resulting from aspiration" (praṇidhijñāna).
What is the nature of this?
It means that a practitioner of yoga first relies upon the fourth dhyāna to give rise to knowledge resulting from aspiration in order to know the phenomena to be known.
Taking this very dharma as an object, he enters the third dhyāna;
proceeding in sequence, he eventually takes this very dharma as an object and gives rise to a wholesome mind of the desire realm.
Immediately following this, taking these very phenomena as its object, there arises a wholesome or neutral mind of the desire realm which is said to know all knowable phenomena (*jñeya-dharma*).
In this context, both the fundamental [state] and its subsequent activity are called the "knowledge resulting from resolve" (*praṇidhi-jñāna*).
Therefore, it is said to be either wholesome or indeterminate.
What is the practice of non-contention?
[The passage continues] at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra:
"Among my disciples, the bhikṣu Subhūti is foremost in dwelling in the practice of non-contention (*araṇā-vihāra*).
Although this was said,
it was not explained in detail.
What is the practice of non-contention (*araṇā-vihāra*), and what dharma is designated as "non-contention"?
That sutra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies;
that which was not explained therein [is now to be addressed].
This shall now be explained;
therefore, this treatise is composed.
Question: What is the practice of the "absence of contention" (*araṇā*)?
Answer: Not all arhats are well-versed in internal time; external [time] is not like this.
If one is also well-versed in external time, it is called "conduct free from contention" (*araṇā-vihāra*).
What is meant by "internal time"?
This refers to all afflictions within one's own continuum.
What is external time?
It refers to all afflictions within the continua of others.
The cessation of these afflictions is called "thorough mastery.
All Arhats have already ceased and severed all afflictions within their own mental continuums;
however, regarding the afflictions within the mental continuums of others, this is not necessarily the case.
If it can also be characterized as "preventing [conflict]," it is called the practice of non-contention (*araṇā-vihāra*).
Some say that "time" refers to the three times.
To restrain all afflictions during these three periods— the first watch of the day, the middle watch, and the last watch—
is called "thorough mastery."
All Arhats have already suppressed and severed the afflictions of their own mental continuums throughout the three times;
however, regarding the afflictions of the mental continuums of others throughout the three times, this is not certain.
If one is also able to exercise restraint, it is called "conduct free from contention" (*araṇā-vihāra*).
Some say that "time" refers to six periods.
That very night, during each of the three periods—forenoon, midday, and afternoon—one restrains the various afflictions (*kleśa*) throughout these six times; this is called "thorough mastery.
All Arhats have already restrained and severed the afflictions within their own mental continuums during these six times.
Regarding the afflictions within the mental continuums of others, these are not fixed across the six periods;
if one is also able to restrain them, it is called the practice of non-contention (*araṇā*).
The Venerable Ghosaka stated:
It is not because one lacks afflictions within one's own continuum that it is called "conduct free from strife";
rather, it is because one is able to obstruct the afflictions and strifes within the continua of others that it is called "conduct free from strife."
Why is this so? Because "dispute" is a term that refers to others;
it does not refer to oneself.
Question: Why is the restraint of afflictions called "thoroughly penetrating"?
Answer: It is because it necessarily depends upon the manifestation of skillful means and awakened wisdom.
Because one is thus able to restrain the afflictions of both oneself and others, it is called "thorough mastery.
Question: What dharma is designated as "non-contention" (*araṇā*)?
Answer: It is that which causes the mental continuum of others to proceed without defilement.
That is to say, while various afflictions (*kleśa*) act as moisture, grease, and impurity,
one who has attained the state free from contention (*araṇā*) is not moistened, greased, or defiled by the afflictions within the mental continuums of others.
This means the sense of being far removed from the various afflictions within the mental continuums of others.
Some say that this passage should state: "it functions without remainder within the mental continuums of others."
This refers to one who has attained the state of being "without strife" (araṇā).
Just as they have permanently severed the afflictions within their own continuum such that none remain,
so too are they able to restrain the afflictions within the continua of others, ensuring that none remain.
This means that it universally precludes the sense that the various afflictions which ought to arise within the mental continuums of others should be caused to arise.
Some say that this passage should read: "it functions without distinction within the mental continuums of others."
This means that just as one who has attained the state of being "without strife" (araṇā) can obstruct the afflictions within their own continuum so that they do not arise,
they likewise can obstruct the afflictions within the continua of enemies and neutral persons so that they do not arise.
This means the equal suppression of the various afflictions within the mental continuums of others.
Question: What is the difference between this and "thoroughly understanding external objects so that they do not arise as defiled"?
Answer: Thoroughly understanding external objects...
It means that wisdom proceeds without defilement;
that is, afflictions do not arise.
Furthermore, that Arhat practices five kinds of dharmas.
It causes the afflictions in the mental continuum of others not to arise. What are these five?
First, purifying the modes of deportment.
Second, speech and silence according to the occasion;
third, skillfully weighing whether to go or stay;
fourth, discriminating between what should be accepted and what should not be accepted.
Fifth, the observation of persons:
one whose deportment is purified,
that arhat first sits in a single location.
If another person approaches, one should immediately observe their mind;
by means of what deportment can one prevent the arising of fetters?
If one knows that through this [deportment] those fetters will arise, [one should avoid it].
Even if one abandons this posture and dwells in another posture,
as long as no fetters arise, one remains exactly as before;
the same applies to other postures as well.
Regarding "speaking or remaining silent at the appropriate time":
when that Arhat sees someone approaching, he observes their intention to determine whether it is appropriate to speak or to remain silent.
Having observed this, if he sees that a fetter arises through speech,
he remains silent even if he has a great desire to speak;
if he sees that a fetter arises through silence, [he speaks].
Even if one does not wish to speak, one should nevertheless engage in conversation.
If, while traveling on a road, one sees two people approaching,
one should immediately observe which of them is more suitable to speak with first.
Having observed this, if one sees that when speaking to this person, that person gives rise to fetters, then one speaks to him; and it is the same for the other.
If both give rise to fetters when spoken to, [one speaks to them].
Even if both remain silent, it is the same.
If a fetter arises whether one speaks or remains silent,
one should yield the way so that the fetter does not arise.
Regarding the one who skillfully measures going and staying:
that Arhat, wherever he dwells, immediately observes,
"I should remain here."
Should one depart?

If, while staying, one perceives that another person's fetters (saṃyojana) are arising, then even if the place is secure and provisions are abundant and conducive to wholesome qualities (kuśalapakṣa), one should abandon it and leave.
If one perceives that by departing [from this place] another fetter will arise,
then even though the location is unstable, the necessary conditions are lacking, and it is unfavorable for wholesome qualities, one nevertheless remains there by force.
One then discriminates between what should be accepted and what should not be accepted.
If a donor offers requisites to that Arhat,
he examines the donor's mind to determine whether they should accept them or not. Having examined it,
if he perceives that accepting them would give rise to fetters within him, [he does not accept].
Although it is something they need, they do not accept it;
yet if they see that by not accepting it a fetter would arise,
they will intentionally accept it even though it is something they do not need.
Regarding the observation of individuals:
when an Arhat, for the sake of alms, is about to enter a city, town, village, or the homes of others,
he observes the men, women, children, and adults therein.
Do not allow afflictions to arise on account of me.
If you know they will not arise, then enter for alms;
if you know they will arise, [do not go].
Even though they were extremely hungry, they did not enter;
such a thing could not happen because it was for the sake of making distinctions.
Even if all sentient beings...
If anyone should give rise to afflictions because of seeing me,
I shall immediately go to a place where no sentient beings dwell and die of starvation,
never allowing another to give rise to fetters on my account.
When that Arhat practices these five kinds of dharmas, he is able to obstruct the afflictions within the mental continuums of others so that they do not manifest.
Question: Why does an Arhat, having already attained liberation, practice these dharmas and thus bind himself?
The answer is: That Arhat was previously of the bodhisattva lineage.
Unable to endure sentient beings committing evil and thereby inviting suffering, for the sake of uprooting it, he constantly formed this thought:
Since beginningless time, I have been bound to all sentient beings through mutual entanglement,
wandering through the five destinies and undergoing various intense sufferings.
Now that I have fortunately escaped this fate, I ought to rescue them as well.
Furthermore, he reflects:
"Since beginningless time, I have taken the form of a dancer, a courtesan, or other such base and defiled bodies;
hundreds of thousands of sentient beings have thereby given rise to fetters toward me."
Because of this, they have suffered for a long night;
how much more so for me now, who am free from greed, hatred, and delusion and serve as a field of merit for the world?
How could giving rise to fetters toward me not result in suffering?
Therefore, I should no longer create the causes and conditions for affliction.
Thus, although an Arhat is himself liberated, he engages in the practice of non-contention for the sake of sentient beings.
Question: Are those [afflictions] to be negated as afflictions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)?
Answer: Only those of specific characteristics can be negated.
It is not a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Why is this?
Because common characteristics correspond to their respective afflictions (*kleśa*) as appropriate.
At one time, they collectively take as their object a single realm, a single level, a single location,
and a single category; thus, regarding the body they have acquired, they grasp at it as "I" and "mine," or they grasp at it as being subject to annihilation or permanence.
Some negate it as being non-existent;
some grasp it as the supreme;
and some grasp it as that which can purify.
Or, one might give rise to doubt:
that ignorance arises spontaneously and irrepressibly in all sentient beings at all times.
Therefore, [the sūtra] only prohibits afflictions in their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Question: What is the intrinsic nature of the practice of non-contention?
Is it concentration (samādhi) or is it wisdom (prajñā)?
If that were the case, what fault would there be?
If it were fixed [in its nature], how would this passage be explained:
"One who has thoroughly mastered external time is said to practice the conduct of non-contention"?
Skillful mastery is wisdom.
If this is wisdom, how are other teachings to be reconciled?
For example, as it is said: "One should practice meditative concentration and the absence of contention."
It is said that this refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). Question:
If that is so, why is it said that one should cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the absence of conflict (*araṇā*)?

The answer is: one should have stated that "one should cultivate tranquility and wisdom without conflict," yet by stating that "one should cultivate tranquility and meditative concentration (samādhi) without conflict," it is intended to show that because it coexists with concentration, it is called "concentration."
In reality, it is wisdom;
this is called the intrinsic nature of non-contention.
It is the same as [the case of] intrinsic nature, self, entity, and so forth.
The intrinsic nature has already been explained;
its purpose shall now be discussed.
Question: What is meant by "conduct free from contention"?
Answer: Because this practice can counteract the afflictions and disputes of others, it is called "the practice free from dispute" (araṇā-caryā).
Now, there are three kinds of dispute.
First, the conflict of afflictions;
second, the conflict of the aggregates;
third, the conflict of strife.
The contention of afflictions refers to the one hundred and eight afflictions.
The contention of the aggregates refers to death.
Quarreling refers to sentient beings mutually insulting one another and their verbal disagreements.
It should be understood that what is spoken of here as "the strife of afflictions" is for the purpose of preventing sentient beings from giving rise to afflictions.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Because this enables one to bring about the absence of contention between oneself and others, it is called "conduct free from contention" (*araṇā-vihāra*).
This is precisely the meaning of skillfully cultivating the practice of non-self (*anātman*).
For this reason, the Venerable Subhūti once approached a monastery at dusk, stood before its door, and knocked.
The bhikṣu inside the gate asked, "Who is this?
Because the Venerable Subhūti had long cultivated the practice of non-self while abiding in the state of non-contention (araṇā),
he remained silent and was unable to answer, saying, "I am Subhūti."
After a long silence, he said:
"This is merely a conventional designation established in the world for one named 'Sudatta.
Furthermore, that Venerable One once encountered rain while traveling on the road."
He went to the side of a non-Buddhist’s gate to avoid him.
The non-Buddhist asked,
"What is your honorable name?"
Because the Venerable Subhūti had long dwelt in the absence of contention and was thoroughly practiced in the practice of non-self,
he remained silent and could not answer, "I am Subhūti.
This was asked three times.
He then replied slowly,
"This is 'Subhūti' as a conventional designation in the world; therefore,
know that one who has well-cultivated the practice of non-self [is so called]."
Causing oneself and others to be free from dispute is called the practice of non-dispute (*araṇā-vihāra*).
Some say that because the practitioners of yoga abide in this state, they [remain unaffected] by the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Whether appropriate or inappropriate,
agreeable or disagreeable,
and amidst gain or loss, suffering or pleasure.
Because they are entirely free from contention, they are called "conduct free from contention" (*araṇā-vihāra*).
Furthermore, regarding the realm of non-contention (*araṇa-dhātu*), some say it belongs to the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*). Others say:
Regarding the statement that one falls into the desire realm and the form realm,
the former explanation is superior.
The stage [of this concentration] is in the fourth dhyāna;
some say it is in five stages.
This refers to the four dhyānas and the desire realm.
According to this explanation,
it means that the first [category] is wholesome.
As for its basis, it relies on a body belonging to the desire realm.
As for its mode of activity, it is an indistinct mode of activity.
As for its object, it takes the desire realm as its object.
Within the desire realm, it takes only the afflictions as its object;
some say it universally takes the five aggregates of the desire realm as its object.
Regarding these explanations,
the first is correct: the foundations of mindfulness refer specifically to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Some say it pertains to all four foundations of mindfulness;
this is the position of those who speak thus.
The application of mindfulness to phenomena is wholesome.
"Wisdom" refers to conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
It may be associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahagata*) or not associated with meditative concentration (*a-samādhi-sahagata*).
Regarding the faculty with which it is associated: it is associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Regarding the time period: it belongs to the three periods of time and takes the future as its object.
Regarding the moral quality: among the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, it is wholesome and takes the unwholesome as its object.
Some say that while it universally takes both the unwholesome and the neutral as its objects, it predominantly takes the unwholesome;
as for its being bound to the three realms or unbound, [it is as follows].
Those bound to the form realm that take as their object those bound to the desire realm—
whether they be trainees (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training— are,
in the case of those who are neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training, [factors] that take as their object those who are neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training.
Regarding those [factors] to be abandoned by seeing, to be abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned:
these are to be abandoned by cultivation and take what is to be abandoned by cultivation as their object. Some say:
Those that universally take as objects both what is abandoned by seeing and what is abandoned by cultivation mostly take as objects what is abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding those that take names as objects and take meanings as objects: those that take meanings as objects take as their objects [factors] within one's own continuum and the continua of others, whereas those that do not take [names] as objects do not.
It takes as its object only the mental continuum of another.
Some say that it takes as its object both one's own and others' continua, though it more frequently takes the continua of others as its object.
As for where it arises, one should say it arises in the desire realm (kāmadhātu),
not in the form or formless realms.
Within the desire realm, this arises only among the human destiny and not in other destinies;
within the human destiny, it occurs only in the three continents and not in the northern continent;
and among the three continents, both men and women are capable of giving rise to it.
The Venerable Saṃgharakṣita said:
"Only in Jambudvīpa, and only men, can [the thought of enlightenment] arise.
Of those who speak thus, the former statement is correct.
As for which type of person (pudgala) gives rise to it:
it is an noble one (ārya), not an ordinary worldling (pṛthagjana);
it is exclusively one beyond training (aśaikṣa), not one still in training (śaikṣa).
Among those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there is only the one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*), not the one liberated by time (*samayavimukta*). Why is this?
Because [the latter] can only arise when one has attained mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and when the mental continuum is no longer held fast by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Question: Do Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats who have reached the ultimate also abide in the state of non-contention (*araṇā*)?
If they do, what fault would there be [in asserting this]?
If he too dwells in the state of non-contention (*araṇā*),
which is capable of obstructing the afflictions within the mental continuums of others,
why does he still give rise to [afflictions] toward hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who take him as their object?
If he does not abide in the absence of contention (*araṇā*),
how can one reconcile this with what is stated in the sūtras?
For example, it is said that the Venerable Subhūti abides in the foremost state of the absence of contention.
If those of inferior faculties can still abide in the state of non-contention (*araṇā*),
why is it that the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas,
and others, who possess superior faculties, cannot abide in non-contention?
It is agreed that the Buddha and others also abide in the state of non-contention (*araṇā*). Question:
If this is so, why do afflictions still arise in hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who take him as their object?
Answer: Both the Buddha and the śrāvakas who have reached the ultimate, being those who preach the Dharma and transform others, all attain the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).
They observe sentient beings, thinking: "Can I now cause them to refrain from giving rise to afflictions toward me and instead plant roots of merit?"
If one knows that [the being] is capable, one should go and transform them.
If one knows they are incapable and will not give rise to those fetters, yet can still cause them to plant roots of goodness, one should think:
"It would be better even if they were to give rise to those fetters, provided that they must plant roots of goodness."
Why is this? Because if they can give rise to even a hair’s breadth of superior goodness,
they will surely be able to destroy the afflictions and various evil deeds that are as vast as mountains.
If one knows that both [options] are impossible, then one should skillfully avoid them;
this is superior to Subhūti by a hundred thousandfold. Some say:
The Buddha and the śrāvakas who have reached the ultimate do not abide in the state of non-contention (*araṇā*).
One asks: why is it that Subhūti is able to abide in non-contention, while the Buddha and others, whose faculties are superior, cannot?
Answer: The Venerable Subhūti delights in, respects, and constantly cultivates the absence of contention (*araṇā*), whereas the Buddhas and others do not;
this is because they do not give rise to the thought of regarding the absence of contention with extreme respect.
However, it is not that they are unable to abide [in such states].
Regarding this explanation:
although the Buddha and others also abide in the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), they do not abide in it extensively because they act for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Why is this? Because those who receive transformation differ in their faculties and natures;
some require consolation and encouragement.
Sometimes it is appropriate to reprimand;
sometimes it is appropriate to praise;
only then does one enter the Dharma.
Although they may occasionally give rise to greed, hatred, or pride during moments of reprimand and the like,
they necessarily do so by means of these various roots of virtue;
therefore, even though the Tathāgata’s disciples such as Śāriputra were able to dwell constantly in the practice of non-contention (*araṇā*), [they did not fall into error].
He does not dwell long [in that state] for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Question: Is the "absence of contention" (araṇā) attained through preparatory application?
Is it acquired through the abandonment of defilements?
Answer: It is both acquired through application and acquired through the abandonment of defilements.
Regarding this, some say:
"The Buddha attains it through the abandonment of defilements,
because he attains it at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)."
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attain it through application;
they bring it into manifestation through application. Some say:
Both Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas acquire it through the abandonment of defilements,
as they attain it at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*);
Śrāvakas, however, acquire it through preparatory application (*prayoga*).
It manifests through application.
Some say that Buddhas,
Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas who have reached the ultimate stage all attain it through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*).
Because it is attained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*),
whereas other śrāvakas attain it through application (*prayoga*); thus,
they bring it into manifestation through application.
Regarding this statement:
if it is definitely obtainable, it is obtained through the abandonment of defilements,
because it is obtained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Subsequently, the subsequent application (prāyogika) manifests:
for a Buddha, it is without application;
for a Pratyekabuddha, it is with inferior application.
The Śrāvakas may be of middling or superior capacity;

however, there is the "absence of conflict" (araṇā), which is attained through the application of the meditative absorption of the ultimate limit (prāntakoṭika-dhyāna) and manifests through that same application.
Question: What is the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for this absence of contention (*araṇā*)?

Answer: It takes all stages (*bhūmi*) and the meditative absorption of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*) as its preparatory practice, as explained in detail in the section on the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
"The bhikṣu Subhūti, practicing the conduct of non-contention (araṇā), has realized the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
It is asked: Does the practice of non-contention not fail to sever all afflictions?
Why did the Blessed One speak thus? The answer is:
that venerable one has, from time immemorial, delighted in and cultivated the practice of non-contention (*araṇā-vihāra*);
by means of this, he was able to successively give rise to the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).
Having severed all afflictions, he became an arhat.
From this state, he was able to manifest the "absence of strife" (*araṇā*).
It is with this underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*) that this statement was made.
It is not meant that the absence of contention can sever afflictions.
What is the matter?
It is heard that in the past, the Venerable One [attained realization] due to two conditions.
Within the state of non-contention, one generates right aspirations:
first, through seeing, and second, through hearing.
Regarding "through seeing":
This refers to having seen in the past that disciples of the Buddha, by dwelling in the state of non-contention (*araṇā*),
whenever they reached cities, towns, crossroads, or marketplaces,
would protect sentient beings so that their fetters (*saṃyojana*) would not arise.
"By way of having heard" means that in the past, one heard that the disciples of the Buddha, by abiding in the state of non-contention (*araṇā*), [attained such results];
the rest is as explained previously.
Having seen and heard this, they give rise to right mindfulness;
whatever they practice— be it generosity, ethical discipline, extensive learning, diligence, or the holy life—
they dedicate it all toward non-contention.
May I, in the future, become a disciple of the Buddha and always abide in non-contention,
protecting sentient beings just as the disciples of the Buddhas have seen and heard.

By the power of that vow, he attained a homogeneous birth (nikāyasabhāga) and became the foremost disciple in the mastery of the absence of strife (araṇāvihārin) within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha.
For the sake of non-contention, one swiftly realizes the fruit of arhatship;
this is because non-contention necessarily relies upon the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
It is with this underlying intention that [the sūtra] says so.
The Sūtra states:
"One who cultivates the practice of non-contention realizes the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
Question: What is the practice of non-contention?
Answer: He practices the conduct of tranquility for the sake of pacifying the various afflictions of others.
As it is said: "Among my disciples, Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom."
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As stated in a sutra,
the World-Honored One prophesied that among his five hundred disciples,
each would be foremost in their respective capacities, forming pairs of excellence.
Now, the Master of the Treatise, wishing to clarify the distinctions among these pairs of similars, composes this treatise.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One declare that his disciples are foremost in pairs?
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"The Blessed One wished to manifest that within this well-expounded Dharma, the teacher and disciples are harmonious and without dispute, and they do not conceal one another’s true merits."
This is not like the case of non-Buddhists who, for the sake of fame and profit, harbor jealousy in their hearts so that disciples and teachers mutually disparage one another.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One wishes to demonstrate that within the well-expounded Dharma, even the disciples possess genuine merits that can be praised and recorded.
How much more so regarding the teacher?
Within a poorly taught Dharma, there is not even a real virtue in the teacher that could be recorded,
let alone in the disciple.
Furthermore, it is to demonstrate that within the well-expounded Dharma, both teacher and disciple have eternally severed the stain of stinginess and thus mutually extol each other’s true merits,
unlike the non-Buddhists who possess such stains of stinginess.
Neither the teacher toward the disciple nor the disciple toward the teacher desires to hear others speak their praises.
How much more so when he speaks of it himself?
Furthermore, the Blessed One has manifested that all the tasks he ought to perform have been fully accomplished; having laid down the burden of instruction, he abides in peace.
Furthermore, [this is said] because he wishes to manifest that the bhikṣus are practicing correct application (*prayoga*).
It is because there is a destination to which one goes, and not because of aimless wandering.

Furthermore, the World-Honored One desires that those who take pleasure in the praised virtues and dwell extensively therein may give rise to a mind of reverent devotion, so that their aspirations may be fulfilled.
Furthermore, in order to encourage newly ordained bhikṣus to cultivate a sense of aspiration and diligent application,
the Venerable One said:
"The Blessed One proclaims the virtues of his disciples based on two causes and conditions."
First, it manifests his own dwelling in happiness in the present life;
second, it expresses compassion for sentient beings of future generations.
Furthermore, it is because the Blessed One himself manifested that among the ninety-six types of non-Buddhist sects, his own assembly is the most excellent.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One wishes to manifest that the appearance of a Buddha in the world brings great benefit;
for it is only when a Buddha appears in the world that such foremost pairs of bodhisattvas appear, and not in times when there is no Buddha.

Furthermore, the Blessed One, wishing to cause those who take delight in the various distinct categories of meritorious qualities to practice with joyful diligence, abandon all indolence, and swiftly attain realization, [taught this].
Furthermore, the Blessed One desired to show that what his disciples had realized was indeed the truth as he himself had taught it.
Furthermore, he desired to stop the slanderous claim that within the well-expounded Dharma there were no superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) personally realized.
Furthermore, the Blessed One, wishing to stop those who might look upon the bhikṣus' emaciated appearance and give rise to contempt,
revealed that they all possess extraordinary and sublime qualities.
The masters of the Abhidharma treatises say:
This is because he follows the dharmas of all Buddhas.

That is to say, regarding the dharmas of the appearance in the world of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—all of whom prophesied that among their assemblies of disciples there would be many pairs of foremost merit; now this Buddha is likewise so.
Furthermore, it is so that those in the world who individually delight in various virtues may, upon hearing this, give rise to joy;
and that they may develop a mind of reverence for the Buddha’s true Dharma, plant roots of goodness, and obtain great benefit.
Furthermore, it is because he desires to provide a retinue adorned for the Buddhas of the future.
That is to say, the Buddha prophesies that all sentient beings who see or hear his disciples will give rise to joy and initiate right aspirations.
Whatever practice they cultivate—be it generosity, ethical discipline, extensive learning, right effort, or the holy life—they dedicate all toward the supreme merit, making this aspiration:
"In a future life, may I be included among the ranks of such noble beings within the Buddha-dharma."
This serves to adorn that Buddha’s assembly.
Furthermore, it is because he wishes to cause his prophesied disciples to rejoice in the fulfillment of their vows;
that is to say, because the five hundred bhikṣus, such as Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta and others, had previously, at the sites of five hundred past Buddhas, [made offerings].
Having seen or heard that Buddha’s proclamation of the merits of his disciples, they joyfully made this vow:

"May we, through whatever giving, ethical discipline, learning, right effort, and pure conduct we possess, be included among the ranks of such great disciples within the True Dharma of a future Buddha. Now that their vow has been fulfilled.
Furthermore, having heard the Buddha’s prophecy, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, feeling deeply fortunate; hence these words were spoken.
Each and every great disciple of the Tathāgata achieved their accomplishment only after adorning themselves with great vows under five hundred past Buddhas.
For these and various other such reasons, the Buddha declared his disciples to be foremost in pairs.
It is asked: as it was said, "Among my disciples, Kauṇḍinya is foremost in wisdom."
Vahika and others were foremost in agility.
What is the difference between these two?
The answer is: the Venerable One was superior in his childlike mind, his straightforward mind, his mind free from crookedness, and his pure sincerity.
The Venerable Bhāgika and others possess minds that are tender, well-tamed, supple, and exceedingly harmonious; for these reasons, they are each called "foremost.
In this context, wisdom (*medhā*) is itself agility (*java*), and agility is itself wisdom.
Since each Buddha is praised as being foremost, it is necessary to inquire about their distinct characteristics.
The Venerable One, because his mind was like that of a child—straightforward, without crookedness, and characterized by an excellence of pure sincerity—[was thus distinguished].

"Straight" means being without crookedness; "pure and simple" refers to the difference in terminology while the meaning remains identical. Following their respective order, each subsequent term explains the preceding one.
Alternatively, "straight mind" is the general statement, while "mind without crookedness" is the specific elaboration.
To clarify that the mind is without guile and is pure and sincere is to specifically clarify that the mind is without deception.
It is like a wise horse that well understands the intentions of its master;
even if it is startled or touched, it does no harm to the person.
The Venerable Śāriputra likewise, by virtue of his wisdom, well understood the Buddha’s intention and provided a correct answer in accordance with the inquiry.
How was this? It is as described in the Sūtra.
When he was a householder, he possessed abundant wealth and treasures, and his kinsmen were noble and influential.
He had long served the Sun God, and during the prime of his youth, he was about to take a wife.
He invited a vast assembly of non-Buddhist Brahmins to his own home and prepared a grand sacrificial feast.
The Buddha never misses the proper time for his transformative deeds.
On that morning, in order to transform them, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and instructed Ānanda:
"You should follow me into the city to beg for alms."
Having received these instructions, he entered the city of Śrāvastī and stood before the gate of the house of the young brahmin.
From afar, the non-Buddhist ascetics saw him and shouted, "Today this household is hosting an auspicious ceremony; what use is there for such an inauspicious object to come here?"
Upon hearing this, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Go and tell those non-Buddhist practitioners that the Great Teacher of the Three Realms is the most auspicious among all."
"You do not wish to see auspicious things.
How could this cause be established? Today, Maṅgala will certainly abandon you all and go forth into homelessness under me.
Even if you exhaust all your skills, can you prevent him?"
Then Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s command, went among the assembly of non-Buddhist outsiders like a lion king, free from fear or hesitation, and addressed them, saying:
"The Tathāgata thoroughly understands cause and effect; what he says is true and sincere. He says to you all:"
The Great Teacher of the Three Realms, the most auspicious among the auspicious—do you not wish to see this auspicious event?
How could such a cause fail to be fulfilled? Today, the Youth (Māṇavaka) will surely abandon you all and go forth into homelessness under me.
"Can you exhaust all your skills and arts to create obstacles?
Having heard this, the non-Buddhists looked at one another and said with laughter,
"The śramaṇa Gautama speaks deceptively according to his own whims."
"How can it be that you, who are about to preside over a sacrificial assembly where our inner and outer kin have gathered in celebration, would instead return to the life of a renunciant?
How strange! This śramaṇa speaks such falsehoods."
At that time, there was a brahmin named Pañcaśikha who had previously seen the World-Honored One and, recounting the events without error, told the assembly of non-Buddhists:
"This son of a noble family will certainly renounce the household life; do not harbor any other thoughts."
The non-Buddhists all said,
"If such a thing were to happen, we would certainly be able to create obstacles.
Thereupon, they joined together, leading one another, snapping their fingers and clapping their hands.
It encircled the dwelling of the youth Jaṭila in seven layers.
In a short while, as the sun rose, this youth Jaṭila, having put on new, clean garments,
ascended to the upper story of the multi-storied pavilion.
Having burned incense and made his vow, he knelt and prostrated before the sun.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the time for conversion had arrived, transformed himself into the form of a brahmin,
wearing a black antelope skin with a golden cord draped across his body.
Holding a golden staff in his hand,
he came from the solar disc and sat upon a seat spread before the youth Jaṭila.
The youth touched his feet, returned with sincere devotion, and paid him homage by bowing his head.
The non-Buddhist rejoiced, saying, "The meritorious person, the Youth of the Confucians, has moved Great Brahmā to personally attend this ceremonial assembly; the task is now accomplished.
How fortunate! What the śramaṇa said was not true."
Then the Buddha, by means of his manifested transformation-body, addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying,
"What are you doing now that causes such commotion?
The youth, feeling ashamed, lowered his head and replied:
"Now, following worldly custom, I am about to take a wife.
The Buddha asked how much he had spent;
he replied, "I have spent three hundred thousand pieces of gold."
He asked again what was being used for it.
He replied, "One hundred thousand [pieces of gold] were used to provide ornaments for my wife,
and another hundred thousand to prepare various foods and drinks for the assembly."
"You used one hundred thousand [coins] to give as alms to the brahmins.

The Buddha said, "If you had provided food and drink as alms to the brahmins using two hundred thousand, it would be possible for you to obtain a desirable fruit; that matter might well have been so."
"Are you using the remaining hundreds of thousands to buy a wife?
Because his mind was straightforward, he immediately replied, "I am buying one.
The Buddha asked, "Is your wife worth that much?"
"Furthermore, for how much is your wife's hair worth?
Mañjuśrī replied, "It is not of great value; if it were purchased by courtesans or prostitutes, it would be worth one kārṣāpaṇa."
Or perhaps it was only half-straight.
He asked again, "How straight are those nails of yours?
Mañjuśrī replied, "These have no straightness."
The Buddha again enumerated the thirty-six components within that body one by one and questioned him about each;
the youth also answered each one, stating that none of them had any value.
However, because in the past, during the Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha,
the youth Mañjuśrī had practiced the contemplation of the elements (*dhātu-upāya*) for ten thousand years, and was subsequently questioned by that Buddha regarding impure things.
As the wholesome qualities he had previously cultivated manifested before him, he subsequently subdued his desire and greed and became free from the defilements of the desire realm.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One restored himself to his original form.
For the sake of Nyagrodha, he preached the Four Noble Truths;
upon hearing them, Nyagrodha immediately attained the realization of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Thereupon, the Buddha took Nyagrodha by the hand and ascended into the air.
He spoke in verse:
"Though adorned with the utmost splendor, he practices the Dharma; Tranquil and self-disciplined, he renounces worldly affairs to cultivate the holy life.
Having abandoned all burdens of the entire world— Such a person is a śramaṇa of pure resolve."
From this, it is known that his mind is upright and straightforward;
for if it were otherwise,
when the emanated person questioned him, he would have replied.
"You are a brahmin; why do you concern yourself with my marriage?
Is it the custom for marriage to be called 'buying'?
Because of his straightforwardness, he answered according to the question."
Through the maturation of wholesome qualities, he attained the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
For this reason, the World-Honored One praised Cūḍapanthaka as foremost among those of wise intelligence.
