By the Venerable Bhūtika and others, whose minds are supple, well-tamed, and harmonious, and who possess superior excellence.
The word "etcetera" includes Venerable Phalguna and Venerable Tishya. Among these,
"gentle mind," "pliant mind," and "harmonious mind" are different terms with the same meaning.
The subsequent [terms] explain the preceding ones in their respective order.
Alternatively, "a mind that is supple" is the general statement;
"a mind that is pliant" specifically reveals the absence of arrogance; and "a mind that is harmonious" specifically reveals the absence of pride.
How is it known that the Vāhīkas and others possess minds capable of such acts as softening?
It is heard that those three men, hearing that the Buddha had appeared in the world,
sought out his whereabouts and learned that he was staying in the city of Śrāvastī.
The three men followed [the Buddha] from Rājagṛha to Śrāvastī; however,
the World-Honored One, knowing that their roots of goodness would only ripen after they had completed the journey back and forth,
took a different route and traveled from Śrāvastī to Rājagṛha.
When the Vāhīkas and others reached Śrāvastī,
they heard that the Buddha had already departed for Rājagṛha;
they immediately set out together and returned toward Rājagṛha.
Having arrived there, they heard that the Buddha had already gone to Campā;
so they went together once more to the kingdom of Campā.
Having arrived there, they sought him out and heard that the Buddha had already gone to Vārāṇasī.
The three men followed one another and went again to that country.
Having arrived, they learned that the Buddha had already gone to the city of Kapilavastu;
they then proceeded together there and learned that the Buddha had already gone to the city of Vaiśālī.
In this manner, the World-Honored One traveled through the six great cities in six successive rounds.
Vāhīka and the others also constantly sought out the Buddha, traveling back and forth for six rounds.
When the Buddha knew that those people’s faculties had matured, [he went to them].
When he arrived at Śrāvastī and met him there,
as the Buddha was entering the city and he was leaving it, he suddenly saw the Buddha from afar; overcome with joy,
before his feet even touched the ground, he attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna).
Not long thereafter, they attained arhatship.
However, had those three men not been so gentle, harmonious, compliant, and easy to manage, they should have gone to wait for the Buddha in a single city.
How could he have been unable to seek the Buddha throughout the six great cities, circling them six times over,
without ever harboring a single thought of weariness;
for as soon as he beheld the Buddha, he immediately realized the fruit of sainthood.
The Buddha praised them, saying,
"Vahika and the others are foremost in agility.
He then asked, "As it has been said, among my disciples, Cūḍapanthaka excels in turning his mind toward the wholesome."
Regarding the distinction between Mahāpatha’s skillful turning away from perceptions and this [other method]:
the answer is that the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka dwelt frequently in the practice of contemplating the mind as the mind.
The Venerable Mahācunda dwells frequently in the mindfulness of phenomena by contemplating phenomena.
It was asked: "For what reason does the Venerable Cūḷacunda dwell frequently in the mindfulness of mind, while the Venerable Mahācunda dwells frequently in the mindfulness of phenomena?"
Answer: It is because that venerable one’s intention was different.
Furthermore, the venerable Cūḍapanthaka was one who acted out of affection;
by the power of his mind, he had experienced much suffering within saṃsāra since beginningless time.

Now, having attained the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), he constantly censures the mind; thus, he dwells frequently in the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) through contemplation.

The Venerable Mahāpanthaka was a practitioner of insight (*vipaśyanā-yogin*); by the power of his conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), he had experienced much suffering within saṃsāra since beginningless time.

Now, having attained the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), he constantly dwells in the perception of reproach (*vigarha-saṃjñā*) by means of frequently abiding in the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Question: For what reason were these two venerable ones given these names?
Answer: It was heard that in Śrāvastī there was a Brahmin’s wife who repeatedly gave birth to sons, but each time they were born, they would die.
Not long after, his wife gave birth to another son.
He immediately sent someone to abandon him on the main road;
because he did not die despite the passage of time, this name was established for him.
Later, that wife again gave birth to a son, whom she immediately sent someone to abandon on a small path.
He too did not die after a long time, and for this reason he was given this name.
The Venerable Mahāpanthaka possessed sharp faculties and was one who practiced through vision.
When he grew up, he returned to the Buddha and left the household life;
through diligent practice, he became an Arhat.
Venerable Cūḍapanthaka was of dull faculties.
Delighting in the household life, they cherish and cling to their kinsmen;
they extensively acquire wealth, property, rank, and luxury,
and their clans flourish as they enjoy various sensual pleasures, yet in the end, all these decline.
As a verse says:
Accumulated wealth must eventually be exhausted; High status must eventually decline;
Close unions must eventually part; And life must eventually end in death.
Not long after this, through that minor path, his parents passed away;
his wealth and treasures were dissipated, he was stripped of his noble status,
his kinsmen departed, and his appearance became haggard and withered.
His elder brother, Dàlù, seeing him and taking pity on him, ordained him so that he might receive the full precepts.
He was given the *Ghoṣa-gāthā* to practice and recite:
"Do not commit any evil with body, speech, or mind in this entire world."
Free from desire, mindful, and clearly comprehending, he did not experience suffering or anything meaningless;
being extremely dull-witted, he received this verse and practiced its recitation with diligent effort during the four months of the rainy season.
Those tending cattle and sheep heard it on the road and recited it all with complete fluency.
They had not yet even passed through the four months of the rainy season when monks from various places gathered together to pay their respects to the World-Honored One.
Every morning at dawn, the newly ordained bhikṣus would all go to their upādhyāyas and ācāryas to request the texts and inquire about the meanings they had forgotten.
At that time, Kṣullaka also followed their example and went out, having just stepped through the door of his cell.
The elder brother immediately asked, "Where do you wish to go?
He replied, "I wish to go to my upādhyāya and ācārya to receive their textual instruction and to request the meaning of the principles I have forgotten."
His elder brother said to him, "I am your upādhyāya;
where else could you go? However, that narrow path is one that must be entered by those who are subject to censure and expulsion."
At that moment, Dalu seized him by the nape of his neck with his hand, dragged him out of the room,
and shouted, "Fool!
During the fourth month, I bestowed a single verse upon you."
"Even those who tend cattle and sheep have mastered the recitation of these texts.
You have not yet attained this, and now you say you wish to go elsewhere to receive the texts and inquire about their meaning; do you intend to forget what you already possess?"
Having been rebuked and expelled by his elder brother, Kṣullaka went to the Jeta Grove and remained there weeping.
At that time, the Buddha entered the Jeta Grove from outside, saw him, and questioned him.
"Little Path, why are you weeping?
He then related the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha then spoke to him, saying:
"Are you able to follow my instructions without forgetting?
He replied, "I am able.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal power, removed all obstacles to his recitation of the verses and taught them to him once again.
Immediately, he was able to recite [the scriptures] with greater proficiency than the four months of prior labor.
Furthermore, [the Teacher] bestowed upon him the "Verses on Removing Dust and Impurities" and said to him:
"Today, whenever any bhikṣus come from outside, you should wipe away all the dust and impurities upon their leather sandals."
Kṣullaka respectfully assented and carried out the instructions as taught.
When evening arrived, there was a bhikṣu whose leather sandals were extremely covered in dust and grime.
Kṣudraka wiped one [pot] until it was extremely clean, yet he could not clean another no matter how hard he wiped it; he then thought:
"Even external objects cannot be cleansed when stained by dust and grime for even a brief moment."
How much more so when the mind has been defiled for a long night by internal stains such as greed, hatred, and delusion— by what means could it be purified?
When he reflects in this way,
the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) immediately appear before him.
He then attained the fruit of arhatship in successive stages.
Question: For what reason was the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka so dull-witted?
Answer: In the past, during the Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha, the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka...
Although they fully received and upheld the Tripitaka of that Buddha,
their minds were shrouded by the defilement of stinginess regarding the Dharma; consequently,
they never bestowed the transmission of the texts or the explanation of their meaning upon others, and they forgot the underlying principles.
"Due to that karma, he has now obtained such an extremely dull and obtuse result.
Some say that this Venerable One was once a pork-butcher in the city of Vārāṇasī.
He bound five hundred pigs by the mouth, transported them onto a boat, and ferried them to the other shore.
When they disembarked from the boat, the pigs had all already died because their breath was no longer circulating;
due to the power of that karma, they were thus so dull and insentient.
Some say that in a previous life,
that venerable one once blocked the entrance to a cave inhabited by *goda* deer, preventing them from escaping so that they died therein;
it is due to that karma that he is thus dull-witted.
As the Blessed One said: "Bhikṣus, you should know that I do not see a single dharma that turns as swiftly as the mind. Why is this so?"
The mind’s rapid revolution is difficult to illustrate with a simile;
therefore, you should train yourselves to understand the mind well and understand the revolution of the mind well.
Question: When it is said that the mind revolves rapidly, is this with respect to its time or its object?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If it were by way of the world, then all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) would rapidly revolve within the world.
If it were by way of the object (*ālambana*), then all minds and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) would rapidly revolve with respect to their objects.
Why is it said that [the mind] alone [is so described]?
The answer is: It is because the mind is said to be swift in its revolution both in terms of time and in terms of its objects;
however, this is said with reference to the continuum (*saṃtāna*), not with reference to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
If it were said that the mind turns rapidly based on momentary [analysis], then there would have to be some things in the world that turn rapidly and some that do not turn rapidly.
Nor is there a rapid shifting of the mind with respect to its objects;
for it is taught that if a phenomenon serves as an object for a given state of mind, there is no time when that phenomenon is not its object.
Therefore, it is only in reference to the mental continuum (*saṃtāna*) that one speaks of the rapid shifting of the mind.
That is to say, within a single body, the mind is at times wholesome, at times unwholesome, or at times indeterminate;
and it may at times rely upon the eye, and so forth, up to relying solely upon the mind.
At times it takes form as its object, and at other times it takes mental phenomena (dharma) as its object;
this is because it shifts and changes within each respective category.
Question: Do the mental factors (caitta-dharma) also possess such rapid shifting?
Why is it that only "mind" is mentioned?
The answer is: although the mental factors (*caitta*) should also have been mentioned, their omission should be understood as the Buddha’s intentional, incomplete teaching (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*).
This is also a concise explanation according to the circumstances.
Some say that the mention of "mind" (*citta*) here also includes the "mental factors" (*caitasika*), because they are gathered together in the same assembly.
Some say that what is mentioned here is the most preeminent [among its class], just as when one says, "The king has arrived. Others say:
The mental factors depend upon the mind; they are called "mental factors" (caitta) because they have the mind as their basis.
Since the mind is the universal ground (mahābhūmika), the mental factors are said to belong to that universal ground.
Therefore, when the mind is mentioned, the mental factors are also mentioned.

Some say that because the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) realized through the path of immediate succession of supernormal powers (abhijñā) takes only the mind as its object, it is mentioned specifically.
Others say:
In this context, the term "mind" (citta) collectively refers to all minds and mental factors (citta-caitta),
because they all possess the sense of accumulation (cita). Some say:
Because the mind is the precursor, only the mind is mentioned;
as a verse says: "The mind is the precursor of phenomena," and so forth. Some say:
The mind is called "far-reaching.
As a verse says: "The mind travels far, it wanders alone," and so forth. Some say:
The mind is called the king,
as stated in the verse beginning with "the sixth sovereign lord," and so forth.
Furthermore, the mind is called the basis.
As stated in the sūtras, the spheres of activity and objects of the five faculties are each distinct.
The mental faculty, however, partakes of both the spheres of activity and the objects of those five faculties, because it relies upon them.
Furthermore, the mind is called the "city-lord," as stated in the sūtras.
That which is called the city-lord is precisely the consciousness with grasping (*sopādāna-vijñāna*); it is for this reason that it is referred to simply as "mind.
Moreover, there are those who say:
The mind is able to initiate both virtuous and non-virtuous ethical discipline; therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
As stated in the Sūtra: "Virtuous and non-virtuous ethical discipline both arise in dependence upon the mind. Some say:
The mind, when treacherous, leads to rebirth in the evil realms;
the mind, when even, leads to rebirth in the good realms.
Therefore, it is said that "the mind [is the cause]," as stated in the Sūtra.
The son of the Todeyyas, the parrot, and the youth Maṇicūḍa—
because they gave rise to evil thoughts toward the Buddha— upon the dissolution of their bodies at the end of life,
shall fall into hell in the time it takes to cast a pearl shell.
Furthermore, because he gave rise to a virtuous mind toward the Buddha, at the dissolution of the body after death— like the brief moment it takes to toss a conch-shell bead—
he shall be reborn in the heavenly realms. Some say that the mind is an internal phenomenon that pervades all places.
Because it possesses an object of cognition (*ālambana*), it is specifically mentioned.
Mind is an internal phenomenon because it is subsumed under the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
It pervades all places because it exists everywhere, from the Avīci hell below up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above.
That which is capable of having an object of cognition (*ālambana*) is so because it can cognize all phenomena (*dharma*).
Some say that while the mind (*citta*) is always in a state of continuity, the mental factors (*caitta*) are not.
Furthermore, while the mind does not undergo increase or decrease, the mental factors (caitta) do not likewise remain unchanged.
Some say that when the mind operates with respect to such a basis (āśraya), object (ālambana), and mode of activity (ākāra), [the mental factors follow suit].
The mental factors follow the mind just as female fish follow wherever the male fish goes;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned [as such]. Some say:
If the mind is not tamed, not guarded closely, not protected, not restrained, and not cultivated—and thus lacks pliancy—it will quickly decay; the same applies to the mental factors.
However, if the mind is tamed, guarded closely, protected, restrained, and cultivated, such that it becomes pliant...
Thus it does not decay or perish.
The mental factors (*caitta*) are likewise; for this reason, they are mentioned specifically.
Furthermore, if the mind is not restrained, it will scatter among the five sense objects.
The mental factors are likewise.
If the mind, through restraint, does not race toward the five sense objects,
the mental factors do so as well.
Just as water leaks from a water-strainer when its top is open, but stops when the top is closed, for this reason it is said that [the analogy applies] only to the mind and not to mental factors.
Question: In another place, the Buddha stated that the mind is like a monkey.
Why is it said that the mind is so swift and rapidly shifting as to be difficult to illustrate? The answer is:

it is said to be difficult to illustrate because no one, regardless of their capacity, strength, time, or wisdom, can provide such an illustration; it does not mean that there is no illustration at all.
It is not something that follows after others;
it cannot be performed by ordinary beings who follow what they hear, by those who engage in discursive thought, or by those of inferior concentration.
It is performed only by Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble disciples.
One who well understands the specific and general characteristics of all minds is able to perform it;
it is not performed by one who merely follows their strength, nor is it produced without attention or application.
It must be performed through the application of attention and effort.
Regarding "not at all times":
it cannot be performed during a period when no Buddha exists;
it can only be performed once a Buddha has appeared in the world.
This is not something that can be accomplished by one who does not follow wisdom, nor by one with coarse or shallow wisdom;
it can only be accomplished by profound and subtle discerning wisdom. Some say:

If there is one who well knows the arising of the mind, well knows its abiding, well knows its emergence, well knows its increase, well knows its decrease, well knows the skillful means, well knows the timing, well knows the sphere of activity, and well knows its elicitation.
Because one is able to create a simile for that, it is said to be "difficult to perform.
Some say: "Who could create a simile for that? It is the Buddha."
Who could have known that the one capable of providing such a metaphor is none other than the Buddha?
Because these two do not coexist, it is said to be difficult to accomplish. Some say:
Who could provide a simile for that?
That is to say, who— knowing well that the mind arises and ceases in every moment without interval—
could know how to provide a simile for it?
This refers to one who well understands that the mind arises and ceases in uninterrupted moments;
because these two do not coexist, it is said to be difficult to perform. Some say:
That analogy is either identical or similar.
"Identical" refers to saying that the mind is like the mind;
"similar" refers to saying that the mind is like feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.
This is subsumed within the category of mental swiftness (*citta-javatva*).
Therefore, what was stated previously— that here "mind" (*citta*) and "mental factors" (*caitta*) collectively encompass all minds and mental concomitants—
is difficult to establish, because there is nothing else external that is equal to or similar to them.
Some say:
"If there were a phenomenon whose functional capacity for apprehending an object were like that of the mind, it could serve as an analogy for it;
however, since no such phenomenon exists, it is said to be difficult to perform."
Although the sūtras state that the mind is like a monkey,
yet in the interval between its letting go of one branch and grasping another, there are hundreds of thousands of moments of mind;
because it thus revolves among objects, it is said to be difficult to manage.
Some say: The Blessed One spoke only of what is difficult to do;
he did not state that there is no analogy at all, because there is no one who has directly realized it through personal experience.
This means that the Buddha’s power is able to manifest a tree in a single kṣaṇa as a metaphor for the mind;
however, because there is no one who knows this, it is said to be difficult to perform.
[The interlocutor asks: "Does the Venerable Śāriputra not know it?"
Answer: Some say it is because one does not know [the object] with extreme rapidity;
others say it is because although one can know it, one does not do so through mental attention (*manasikāra*), as there would be no purpose in doing so.
Venerable Pārśva said:
"When the World-Honored One says that the mind is like a monkey,
he is using the mind as a metaphor for the mind."
The leaping and bounding of monkeys, as well as their lightness and fickleness, are all produced by the mind.
Question: What is the difference between what is called "thoroughly knowing the mind" and "the revolving of the thoroughly known mind"?
Answer: Some say:
There is no difference.
To know the mind well is itself the turning of the mind toward thorough knowledge. Some say:
There is also a distinction:
that is to say, "name" refers to the name itself,
while "well-knowing the mind" refers to the turning of the well-knowing mind.
Furthermore, observing the self-nature of the mind is called "thoroughly knowing the mind.
Observing the modes of activity of the mind is called "thoroughly knowing the turning of the mind.
Furthermore, observing the specific distinctions of the nature of the mind is called "thoroughly knowing the mind."
To observe the distinctions within the sphere of mental activity is called "skillfully knowing the turning of the mind.

Furthermore, to observe the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the mind is called "skillfully knowing the mind," while to observe its general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is called "skillfully knowing the turning of the mind."

Some say that the contemplation of the mindfulness-establishment of mind is called "thoroughly knowing the mind," while the contemplation of the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena is called "thoroughly knowing the turning of the mind."

Furthermore, to contemplate exclusively the consciousness-food (*vijñānāhāra*), the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*), the mind-base (*manāyatana*), and the seven mind-elements (*saptamanodhātu*) is called "skillfully knowing the mind.
To contemplate collectively the four foods, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements is called "skillfully knowing the turning of the mind."
Some say that observing the mind is called "skillfully knowing the mind," and observing the mental factors is called "skillfully knowing the turning of the mind.
Others say:
To contemplate consciousness is called "skillfully knowing the mind";
to contemplate the stations of consciousness is called "skillfully knowing the turning of the mind.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
To observe a mind possessed of greed is called knowing the mind well;
to observe the transformation of a mind possessed of greed into a mind free from greed is called knowing the turning of the mind well.
Just as there is one with greed and one free from greed, so too should it be understood that there is one with hatred and free from hatred, and one with delusion and free from delusion.

The same applies to: distraction and concentration; depression and elevation; smallness and greatness; agitation and non-agitation; lack of tranquility and tranquility; non-concentration and concentration; non-cultivation and cultivation; non-liberation and liberation; the defiled and the undefiled; the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*); bondage and release; and being fettered and unfettered.
As it is said: "Among my disciples, Śāriputra possesses great wisdom and eloquence;
he upholds the Great Treasury and has attained unimpeded understanding.
What is the difference between these two?
Answer: The Venerable Śāriputra dwells frequently in the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*);
the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila dwells frequently in all four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Therefore, the Blessed One each declared them to be foremost.
Question: If that is so, does the Venerable [Mahākoṣṭhila] hold himself superior to Śāriputra?

Answer: Śāriputra is superior, because he is able to dwell at will in four *dhyānas* while dwelling in one *āśraya-parivṛtti*. Question: For what reason does Śāriputra dwell frequently in the meaning (*artha*)?
Question: Why does the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila mostly dwell in the four [erroneous] views?
Answer: The Venerable Śāriputra felt weary of names and words and cherished their meanings;
the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila, however, cherished both meanings and names and words.
Some say that while the Venerable Śāriputra had attained mastery over all four types of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*),
he dwelt at will in the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
Because he always seeks only the meaning,
the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila was not yet masterful in the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); nevertheless,
the Blessed One declared that he had attained the analytical knowledges.

He reflects thus: "May I not forget anything regarding the entry, stay, or exit of the mind in these four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), nor may my speech fail to accord with what has been recorded.
For this reason, he dwells repeatedly and extensively within these four.
It is like two bhikṣus who both recite the four Āgamas: one has mastered them thoroughly while the other is stiff and obstructed.
The one who has mastered them can chant according to his pleasure, whereas the one who is stiff and obstructed must go over the text repeatedly and in full detail; this case is also like that.
Therefore, the abodes of the two Venerable Ones are each distinct.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)?
Answer: Their intrinsic nature is wisdom (*prajñā*).
How is this known to be so? It is as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"What is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*)?
It is the non-regressive wisdom regarding the sets of names, phrases, and syllables."
What is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*)?
It is the non-retrogressive wisdom regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
What is the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*)?
What is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*)? It is the non-retrogressive wisdom regarding verbal expression,
which consists in unimpeded and appropriate speech.
And because there is non-retrogressive knowledge within sovereign concentration and wisdom,
one knows from this that wisdom is the intrinsic nature;
for knowledge is itself wisdom.
This is called the intrinsic nature of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*): it is the self, it is the thing, it is the phenomenon, it is the characteristic, and it is the fundamental nature.
Having already explained their intrinsic nature, we shall now explain the reason [for their name].
Question: For what reason are they called "analytical knowledges"?
Answer: Unimpeded comprehension (*pratisaṃvid*) is defined as the unobstructed penetration of objects of knowledge.

Specifically, the unimpeded comprehension of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) pertains to the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes; the unimpeded comprehension of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) pertains to their referents.
Regarding the ultimate truth of nirvāṇa,
it is the analytical knowledge of language;
regarding all regional dialects, it is the analytical knowledge of language.
Regarding the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*):
it is the unhindered understanding through non-retrogressive wisdom regarding correct exposition and the Path.
Some say: [text continues].
The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) is the direct perception and subsequent cognition of objects of knowledge;
it is like when people in the world, regarding a single perceived matter, say, "I understand and know this without impediment."
Some say it should be called the "Profound and Secret Explanation" (*Abhidharmasamuccaya*),
because it explains the profound and secret points of the Abhidharma.
Some say that this should be called "resolving according to the object" (*yathāyogam-avabodha*),
because it refers to resolving [the meaning] in accordance with whichever object is appropriate.
Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): the two unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of phenomena (*dharma*) and language (*nirukti*) belong to the desire realm and the form realm.
The two unhindered knowledges of meaning (*artha*) and eloquence (*pratibhāna*) belong to the three realms or do not belong to any realm at all.
Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*): the unhindered knowledge of phenomena...
Some say it exists in two stages, namely the desire realm and the first dhyāna;
others say...
It is said to exist in five stages, namely the desire realm and the four dhyānas.
Some say it exists in seven stages, namely the desire realm, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara), and the four dhyānas.
The two unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) regarding meaning and dharma that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) exist in eleven stages;
namely, the desire realm, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna, the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
The untainted [states] exist in nine stages, namely:
the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna, the four dhyānas, and the three formless attainments.
The unimpeded analytical knowledge of language exists in two stages,
namely the desire realm and the first dhyāna;
as for its basis:
The four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) all rely upon the desire realm.
As for their aspects (ākāra):
the two analytical knowledges of phenomena (dharma) and language (nirukti) possess unclear aspects.
Regarding the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*):

those who maintain that only *nirvāṇa* is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) assert that it possesses the four aspects of cessation (*nirodha*) as well as the aspect of non-manifestation (*apratibhāsana*).

Those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimate truths explain the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) as consisting of the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) and the indistinct aspects.
Some say it consists of the twelve aspects as well as the indistinct aspect.
Others say:
Regarding the four aspects of the path and the aspect of non-clarity:
as for the object of focus, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) takes the sets of names, phrases, and syllables as its object.
Regarding the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid), some maintain that it takes only the truth of cessation (nirodhasatya) as its object,
while others maintain that it takes all phenomena (sarvadharma) as its object.
The analytical knowledge of expression (niruktipratisaṃvid) takes words and speech as its object.
Regarding the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), it has as its object the path (*mārga*) and its exposition.
As for the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid), some maintain that it consists solely of the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna),
while others maintain that it comprises all four foundations of mindfulness.
The analytical knowledge of expression (niruktipratisaṃvid) consists of the mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna).
The analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid) consists of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
The analytical knowledges of phenomena (dharma) and expression (nirukti) consist of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
Regarding the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*): there are those who maintain that only nirvāṇa is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Some say:

The nature of the six knowledges consists of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Some say that they consist of four knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
Because the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) are of the nature of vision.
Regarding those who maintain that all phenomena are the ultimate truth (paramārtha), some say:
It has the nature of the ten knowledges.
Some say it has the nature of eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence.
Some say that it consists of nine types of knowledge, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). Others say:
Furthermore, regarding the nature of the seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising,
some say they consist of six knowledges.
That is to say: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, path-knowledge, knowledge of exhaustion, and knowledge of non-arising.
Some say that there are four types of knowledge by nature, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
Regarding those associated with samādhi:
the two unhindered knowledges of phenomena (*dharma*) and expression (*nirukti*) are not associated with samādhi;
as for the unhindered knowledge of meaning (*artha*), [it is].
Some maintain that it is associated only with the signless (animitta) and not with the other two samādhis;
others maintain that it is associated with all three samādhis as well as with non-samādhi.
Regarding the analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid),
some say it is associated with the samādhis of emptiness (śūnyatā), wishlessness (apranihita), and neither [of these two] (anabhisamskāra).
Some say that only the path associated with the faculties is conjoined with the wishless and non-concentrated samādhis.
In general, it is said to be associated with three faculties.
However, in the desire realm, it is associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
In the first and second dhyānas, it is associated with the faculty of joy.
In the third dhyāna, it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*);
in other stages, it is associated solely with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
The world refers to all that falls within the three periods of time;
the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) takes the three periods of time as its object.
The analytical knowledge of language (nirukti-pratisaṃvid) takes the past as its object when it pertains to the past,
the present when it pertains to the present,
and the future when it arises in relation to the future.
That which is non-arising conditions the three periods of time.
Some say that this is identical to the case of dharmas and words.
Some say that among the three unhindered knowledges of dharmas, meanings, and eloquence, those of the past and present take the past as their object,
while those of the future take all three time periods as their object.
Regarding the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*),
some maintain that it takes only that which is transcendent of time as its object,
while others maintain that it takes the three times as well as that which is transcendent of time as its object.
Those that are wholesome and so forth are all wholesome.
The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) takes the indeterminate as its object;
the analytical knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid) [is likewise].
Some maintain that they take only the wholesome as their object;
others maintain that they take all three types [wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral] as their objects.
Regarding the two analytical knowledges of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) and expression (*nirukti*), they take all three types as their objects.
Regarding those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and so forth:
the two analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of phenomena (*dharma*) and expression (*nirukti*) are bound to the desire and form realms (*kāmarūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
The two analytical knowledges of meaning (*artha*) and eloquence (*pratibhāna*) are bound to all three realms as well as being unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Regarding the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid): there are those who maintain that even in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
there exist sets of names (nāmakāya), phrases (padakāya), and phonemes (vyañjanakāya).

Those who assert that [the name-body, phrase-body, and syllable-body] pertain to all three realms state that they take as their object those things bound to the three realms. Those who maintain that the formless realm lacks the name-body, phrase-body,
and syllable-body state that they take as their object those things bound to the desire and form realms.
Regarding the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid),
some maintain that it takes only that which is unconditioned (anāpta) as its object,
while others maintain that it takes as its object both that which is conditioned by the three realms (traidhātukāpta) and that which is unconditioned.
The analytical knowledge of unimpeded eloquence (nirukti-pratisaṃvid) takes as its object that which is bound to the desire realm and the form realm.
Some say it takes as its object that which is bound to the three realms as well as that which is unbound.
Some say that [the object] consists of those bound to the desire realm and the form realm, as well as those unbound,
and [those pertaining to] the learner (śaikṣa) and so forth.
The two analytical knowledges of dharma and expression likewise have as their objects that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
The two analytical knowledges of meaning and eloquence consist of that which is non-learner and that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner; this refers to the analytical knowledge of meaning.
Some maintain that it takes as its object only that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
others maintain that it takes all three types as its object.
It is explained that the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) takes all three types as its object.
Regarding those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and so forth:
the two unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of phenomena (*dharma*) and expression (*nirukti*), when they have objects of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), are likewise [abandoned by cultivation].
As for the two unhindered knowledges of meaning (*artha*) and eloquence (*pratibhāna*), those that are contaminated (*sāsrava*) are abandoned by cultivation.
That which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is non-interruption;
this is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
Alternatively, some maintain that it takes only non-interruption as its object.
Some maintain that there are three types of objects;
they argue that the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) have as their objects both what is abandoned through cultivation and what is not abandoned,
as well as names and meanings.
The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) takes only names as its object;
the analytical knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid),
some maintain, takes only meaning as its object.
Some maintain that the two unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of meaning (*artha*) and eloquence (*pratibhāna*), which are said to take both names and meanings as their objects,
actually take only meaning as their object;
whereas those [unhindered knowledges] of phenomena (*dharma*) and eloquence (*pratibhāna*) take one's own continuum and others' continua as their objects.
Some say that the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid) takes only one's own mental continuum as its object.
Some maintain that it takes as its object only that which is not a continuum;
others maintain that it takes all three kinds [of objects].
As for those acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*) and those acquired through detachment (*vairāgya-labdha*):
It is obtained both through preparatory effort and through the abandonment of defilements.
Regarding this, some say that it is obtained by the Buddha at the moment he attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) through the abandonment of defilements.
It is manifested through the application (prayoga) of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; that is, it is manifested because they have attained it through application.
Some say that it is attained by a Buddha and a Pratyekabuddha at the moment they attain the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) upon becoming free from defilement.
It is manifested through the application of the śrāvaka; that is, it is manifested because of attaining [the fruit] through application.
Some say that it is attained when a Buddha, a pratyekabuddha, or a śrāvaka who has reached the ultimate stage attains the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) upon becoming free from defilement.
Others are attained through the application of effort by śrāvakas;
they manifest through the application of effort.
Thus it is said.
If it were necessarily to be attained through the abandonment of defilements (vairāgya-prāpti), then since it would be attained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna),
the preparatory application (prayoga) would manifest subsequently; however,
for a Buddha, no such preparatory application is required.
For Pratyekabuddhas, the preparatory application is inferior;
for Śrāvakas, it is either middling or superior.
There are unhindered analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) that are obtained through preparatory application and, by virtue of that application, are manifested in the present.
Question: What is the preparatory practice (prayoga) for the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid)?
Answer: Some say that the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) has the study of Sāṃkhya as its preparatory practice.
The analytical knowledge of meaning has the practice of the Buddha’s word as its preparatory application;
the analytical knowledge of expression has the practice of phonology (śabda-vidyā) as its preparatory application;
and the analytical knowledge of eloquence has the practice of logic (hetu-vidyā) as its preparatory application.
Because one who is not skilled in these four areas will certainly be unable to generate the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Some say that for the two analytical knowledges of phenomena (*dharma*) and expression (*nirukti*), the preparatory practice consists of studying external treatises.

According to those who say that the two unhindered analytical knowledges of meaning (*arthapratibhāna*) and expression (*nirukti*) take the study of internal treatises as their preliminary application (*prayoga*),
it is stated that all four unhindered analytical knowledges take the study of the Buddha’s word as their preliminary application.

Just as one should speak of the cultivation of those names within a single verse, such speaking of names is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).
One should understand the meaning in this way; such understanding of the meaning is the preparatory application for the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
One should train in these words in this way; such training in words is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the analytical knowledge of dharma (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
One should speak without impediment in this way;

such practice of speaking without impediment is the preparatory application for the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*). Therefore, all four analytical knowledges take the practice of the Buddha’s word as their preparatory application.
Question: By what is this unimpeded analytical knowledge (pratisaṃvid) induced?
Answer: It is induced by the wisdom of the ultimate concentration (prāntakoṭika-samādhi) of the fourth dhyāna.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
It is induced by the supernormal knowledges based on the four dhyānas.
Question: In which realm can these analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) be produced?
Answer: Only in the desire realm can they be produced.
Within the desire realm, it arises only among humans in the three continents;
it can be produced by both female and male bodies.
The Venerable Saṃgharakṣita said:
Only those in Jambudvīpa and only men can initiate it.
Of these two views, the former is superior,
because in three continents both men and women are capable of both retaining and relinquishing their life-span.
Question: What kind of person (*pudgala*) is able to give rise to the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)?
Answer: A noble one (*ārya*), not an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);
one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), not one in training (*śaikṣa*).
It is not occasional liberation, nor is it non-occasional liberation. Why is this?
Because the mental continuum must not be held by afflictions.
Furthermore, because these can only be produced by one who has attained mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
both those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) lack these two qualities.
Although those who have attained vision have attained mastery over meditative concentration, their mental continuum remains held fast by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Although those liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) possess a continuous stream that is not held by afflictions, they do not attain mastery over meditative concentration.
Only those liberated non-occasionally (asamaya-vimukta) possess both of these qualities; therefore, they are able to give rise to it.
Question: What is the sequence of the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid)?
Does one arise in accordance with how they are taught, or not?
Answer: Some say as follows.
They arise according to how they are taught.
As stated in the sūtras, the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid) is taught first; therefore, it arises first.
This continues until the analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhānapratisaṃvid), which is taught last; therefore, it arises last.
That is to say, for the sake of knowing the meaning (*artha*), the yoga practitioner first gives rise to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
Although he has already known the meaning, he has not yet skillfully arranged the names (*nāman*) and so forth;
therefore, he subsequently gives rise to the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
Although one has already well-established the names and so forth, one is not yet able to provide etymological explanations for the words;
therefore, next, the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) arises.
Although one is already able to provide etymological explanations for the words, one is not yet able to speak without impediment and in accordance with reason.
Therefore, the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) is explained last. Some say:
as it is said.
They arise as previously explained in the Abhidharma:
the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) arises first,
continuing up until the analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid), which is explained last.
Therefore, it arises subsequently;
that is to say, in order for the yoga practitioner to know the sequential arrangement of names and so forth,
the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) arises first.
Although one knows the sequential arrangement of names and so forth,
one has not yet understood the meanings they express;
therefore, next, the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid) arises.
The latter two are as previously explained.
Some say that they arise not in accordance with how they were described.
That is to say, one first gives rise to words, next gives rise to phenomena, next gives rise to meaning, and finally gives rise to eloquence. Why is this?
Because that practitioner must first thoroughly comprehend conventional terminology.
Next, one understands the names and so forth upon which speech relies;
next, one understands the meanings and intentions upon which those names and so forth rely.
Only after knowing these three things can one speak fluently and in accordance with reason.
Therefore, words can lead to the Dharma, the Dharma can lead to meaning, and meaning can lead to eloquence.
Question: Are the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) acquired one by one, or not?
Answer: If one is acquired at a single time, one necessarily possesses all four.
Just as the four noble lineages are attained simultaneously,
yet manifest in succession according to one's inclination,
[one may ask: do Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas who have reached the ultimate attainment acquire the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)?
If one has attained it, the wisdom that does not regress is called "unimpeded analytical knowledge" (*pratisaṃvid*).
This wisdom should be free from error regarding its objects of knowledge.
For what reason did the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana predict that another would give birth to a son, when in fact a daughter was later born?
He predicted that the heavens would rain, yet it did not rain at all;
he predicted that the army of Rājagṛha would be victorious, but later they were defeated by the army of Vaiśālī.
For what reason was the Pratyekabuddha unable to preach the Dharma?
How, then, is the following gāthā to be reconciled?
"Only the Buddha is called 'one beyond training,' who has attained the analytical knowledges,
reached the further shore of all virtues, and is forever free from all errors."
If it were not so, why does the Sūtra say:
"Among my disciples, Mahākauṣṭhila has attained the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid)?"
The Blessed One has stated that even though that Venerable One’s faculties were inferior, Mahāmaudgalyāyana attained them as superior;
why then could he not attain them in this case?
It should be answered:
Pratyekabuddhas and even ultimate śrāvakas also attain the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Question: Since the analytical knowledges are defined as non-retrogressive knowledge, why was the prediction made by the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana erroneous?
The answer is: In that case, his cognition does not regress with respect to the object of observation within its own domain;
it is not the case that it fails to do so with respect to a different domain that is not being observed.
Therefore, there is no fault, just as he has recorded.
Originally he was indeed male, but later he transformed into a female.
At that time, although the heavens also rained,
Rāhula, the asura king, received it and placed it in the great ocean.

Furthermore, when two nations were about to go to war, the yakṣas who protect the country first fought; those of Rājagṛha were initially victorious but later defeated, and the same was true for their people.
It was not that they were not victorious at first.
However, regarding this prediction concerning the male child and so forth,
that Venerable One considered only the preceding stage and did not consider the subsequent one;
had he considered the subsequent stage, his prediction would likewise have been unerring.
Question: If Pratyekabuddhas also attain the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), why are they unable to teach the Dharma to others?
Answer: Because they delight in the bliss of tranquility and prefer dwelling in solitude.
Because one fears clamor and feels weary of large assemblies;
because one perceives the merit of seclusion and the faults of bustle;
how could one whose mind turns away from a following possibly preach the Dharma?
Some say that all pratyekabuddhas are practitioners of śamatha;
it is only those who practice vipaśyanā who are able to preach the Dharma.
Some say that this is because all pratyekabuddhas do not delight in arranging the sets of names and so forth.
Others say:
If, upon careful examination, they were able to enter the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) when I preached the Dharma,
and were to attain the fruits, become free from passion, and exhaust their outflows (āsrava), I would likewise have taught them.
However, it cannot be so.
How could I allow my efforts to be in vain?
For this reason, I do not speak of it.
Some say that all Pratyekabuddhas can thoroughly discern that there are only two kinds of disciples to be converted in the world.
First, those transformed by the Buddha;
second, those transformed by the śrāvakas.
Because there are no sentient beings to be transformed by pratyekabuddhas, he does not preach the Dharma for them.
Some say that one who expounds the Dharma does so by means of two causes and conditions.
The first is that which is induced by power;
the second is that which arises from following the instruction of another.
A Pratyekabuddha lacks such power and does not follow the instruction of another.
Furthermore, first is the arousal of fearlessness;
second is by following the instruction of others.
Pratyekabuddhas lack fearlessness and do not follow the instruction of others.
Furthermore, there are two [causes]: first, being induced by great compassion;
second, following the instructions of others.
Pratyekabuddhas lack great compassion and do not follow the instructions of others.
Therefore, they are unable to preach the Dharma.

Question: Since the requisites for preaching the Dharma consist of all the Buddha-dharmas, why are only the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) mentioned, and not the others?
The answer is: power is able to establish one’s own doctrine;
fearlessness is able to refute the doctrines of others;
and great compassion is able to give rise to the desire to teach the Dharma without depending on anything else. Therefore, only these are mentioned.
Some say that those Pratyekabuddhas reflect as follows:
"One who is able to preach the Dharma..."
Those who are called Dharma Kings and Dharma Prince sons—I am neither a Dharma King nor a Dharma Prince son.
How could I preach the Dharma? Therefore, I do not speak.
Some say: Those pratyekabuddhas have this thought:
"Since ancient times, I have never practiced or studied the business of preaching the Dharma; therefore, I do not preach."
Some say that only one who has attained self-awakening and is skillful in the three matters of correct discipline is able to teach the Dharma;
a pratyekabuddha is not so.
Some say that only one who has attained self-awakening and is capable of possessing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is able to preach the Dharma;
the Pratyekabuddha is not so.
Some say: "The preaching of the True Dharma is always for the purpose of destroying the notion of self.
When the Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world, sentient beings' attachment to a self is so firm that it is difficult to destroy; therefore, they do not preach the Dharma."
Some say that when those who have attained self-awakening preach the Dharma, their minds must necessarily be directed toward nirvāṇa;
this is also the case when a pratyekabuddha gives rise to a mind directed toward nirvāṇa.
Because in the second moment one enters the liberation of ultimate bliss and nirvana,
the Tathāgata is not like this;
although he delights in liberation, being sustained by great compassion and great equanimity, he is able to remain for a long time to teach.
Some say that one must personally realize and achieve the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) before being able to teach the Dharma.

A Pratyekabuddha, if dwelling in a secluded forest, is able to arrange the aggregates, elements, and bases (*skandhadhātvāyatana*), as well as the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāmapadavyañjana-kāya*), by means of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
If, when entering a village to beg for alms, he should forget something previously arranged or laid out, he thinks to himself:
"Since I have not attained the quality of non-forgetfulness, what is the use of teaching the Dharma? For this reason, he does not teach.
Some say that such is the nature of the pratyekabuddha lineage:
although they have attained the unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), they do not delight in preaching the Dharma.
If one wishes to provide benefit, one may manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) alone, or simply bestow the eightfold precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*) upon others.
Question: If śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also attain the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), [why is this so?]
How then should one interpret what is stated in the gāthās?

The answer is: This was said because only that which is attained by a Buddha is ultimately perfected, supremely sovereign, and free from error; it does not mean that the two vehicles do not achieve [these qualities].
If this were not the case,
then the followers of the two vehicles would also not attain the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa),
because a verse in the Gāthā states that only the Buddha is one who has reached no-more-learning.
Other masters say that neither Śrāvakas nor Pratyekabuddhas attain the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
Question: For what reason does the Sūtra state:
Among my disciples, Mahākauṣṭhila has attained the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
His faculties are not superior;
for the Buddha has even declared that a solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*) who has reached the ultimate goal possesses superior faculties compared to a śrāvaka.
Why, in that case, is it said that "nothing is attained"? The answer is:
what he says is attained consists of roots of goodness resembling the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), but they are not the actual [attainments].
This is because that venerable one has long cherished this dharma and has diligently practiced it throughout the long night.
Because the Buddha spoke according to their inclinations, he said that they have attained it;
although others have attained similar roots of goodness,
because they do not possess extreme delight or diligent cultivation, he did not say that they have attained it.
Question: For what reason do those of the two vehicles not all attain the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)?
Answer: Non-retrogressive wisdom is called analytical knowledge.
The wisdom of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas undergoes retrogression regarding various objects.
Because there are errors in what has been declared, it is not an unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Of these two explanations,
the former is the correct one.
Because the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas does not regress regarding their own respective domains,

the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) herein subsumes the knowledge of the limit of aspiration (*praṇidhijñānaparyantajñāna*), the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇājñāna*), and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The unimpeded analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) should be understood in the same way as the knowledge of aspirations (*praṇidhijñāna*).
The knowledge of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭikajñāna*) does not include the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*);
the rest is as explained for the knowledge of aspirations.
The knowledge of non-contention subsumes the knowledge of non-contention, the knowledge of aspiration, and the knowledge of the limit;
the analytical knowledge of meaning does not subsume the three analytical knowledges of phenomena, language, and eloquence,
just as in the case of the knowledge of non-contention.
It should be understood that the three unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of phenomena, expression, and eloquence are likewise.
Each should be explained according to its respective inclusion, with the exception of the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) and the unimpeded analytical knowledge of expression.
Furthermore, they do not include the knowledge of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-jñāna*).
These seven types are all attained based on the limit-concentration (prāntakoṭika-dhyāna),
as they are induced by the power of limit-concentration.
The essence of limit-dhyāna consists of six types.
This refers to the seven [factors], excluding the word "limit" (*prāntakoṭika*).
This is because the fourth dhyāna is designated as "limit" when it is of the highest degree.
Other masters say:
The most superior grades of the four dhyānas are all termed "limit" (prāntakoṭika).
Therefore, it is said that the limit-dhyāna possesses seven types [of applications of mindfulness] and is subsumed by seven knowledges.
Its specific distinctions should also be understood according to the above.
However, that which is able to induce it is exclusively the limit of the fourth dhyāna, and nothing else.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 180. *Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 100.
