translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhiskandha), Chapter Four: The Sub-section on Non-returners (Anāgāmin-nirdeśa), Part Eight. As it has been said: "Among my disciples, Mahākāśyapa is one who possesses few desires, is content, and is endowed with the dhuta-practices."
“Bakkula has few ailments and is frugal, possessing the practice of pure precepts.
What is the difference between these two?
The answer is: “Regarding the food and drink obtained by the Venerable Mahākāśyapa...”
Whether coarse or refined, he partakes of food according to the sequence without making any distinction,
just as a noble horse eats whatever it receives. Thus,
the food and drink obtained by the Venerable Bakkula may be either coarse or refined.
He rejects the exquisite and eats the coarse.
Question: For what reason does the Venerable Mahākāśyapa eat both coarse and exquisite food, while the Venerable Bakkula rejects exquisite food and eats only the coarse?
Answer: The Venerable Mahākāśyapa possesses a sublime desire for the dharma of the śramaṇa;
because he possesses this sublime desire, he does not discriminate among exquisite foods.
Because he dwells in the dharma of a śramaṇa, he does not discriminate against coarse food;
rather, he eats whatever he obtains in its proper order.
The Venerable Bakula possesses the desire for coarse things and dwells in the dharma of a śramaṇa.
Because he possesses coarse desires, he is distinguished from those who seek the sublime.
It is for the sake of abiding in the dharma of a śramaṇa that he eats coarse food.
Furthermore, Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
One who possesses extensive knowledge and great merit easily obtains clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites;
yet, even before receiving them, such a person is able to practice the ascetic virtues (*dhūta-guṇa*).
For him, these two conditions are extremely difficult to accomplish:
namely, to refuse gains and offerings that are easily obtained,
and to be able to practice the dhūta qualities.
Venerable Bakkula,
although you did not previously receive abundant robes, alms-food, bedding, medicine, or other requisites due to your lack of great merit,
you were nevertheless able to practice and fulfill the ascetic virtues (dhūtaguṇa).
For a monk with little experience who undertakes the virtues of the dhūtas,
it is not difficult to practice them accordingly; for him,
this is not a difficult matter due to two reasons.
This refers to first accepting gains that are difficult to obtain,
and subsequently practicing the ascetic virtues (*dhūtaguṇa*) accordingly.
Regarding this passage, there is a recension that reads it contrarily.
That is to say, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was widely known for his great merit;
he easily obtained clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites,
yet he first accepted them and subsequently practiced the ascetic virtues (*dhūtaguṇa*) accordingly.
The Venerable Bakkula was not one of broad renown or great fortune;
he did not first accept robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, or other requisites that were difficult to obtain.
He followed and practiced these dhuta virtues accordingly.
A bhikṣu with little knowledge does not accept it;
the qualities of *dhūta* practice follow accordingly therein.
This is not difficult for him, because for him, due to two conditions, it is not a difficult matter.
This means that he does not first accept gains and offerings that are difficult to obtain,
but rather practices the ascetic virtues (*dhūtaguṇa*) therein;
this demonstrates that Kāśyapa is superior by virtue of three matters.
This refers to one who possesses excellent desires for joy, easily obtains gain and offerings, and practices the virtues of the dhūta austerities.
Question: For what reason did the Venerable Bakkula reject exquisite food and eat coarse food?
The answer is: by the power of intention.
Since the intentions of sentient beings differ, they eat according to their respective intentions;
one cannot be held accountable for the reason why.
Some say that because exquisite food and drink require great effort to prepare, they do not eat it out of a desire to avoid such labor and expense.
Others say:
Exquisite food and drink increase craving and mostly give rise to disputes; for this reason, he does not eat.
Some say that fine food belongs only to wealthy households, and because it would benefit the poor, he does not eat it.
Some say that fine food necessarily depends upon the harming of many living beings;
it is produced from the flesh and blood of hundreds or thousands of heads severed upon the ground.
Out of compassion for those sentient beings, he does not eat.
Some say that delicious food gives rise to many kinds of faults and afflictions; therefore, he does not eat.
Question: As it has been stated,
taking the "exclusion of the excellent" (*praṇīta-vivarjana*) as the first among the *bhadra-kula* [categories],
one does not accept what has been received and discards it once accepted.
If that were the case, what would be the fault?
If one does not accept [alms] at the very beginning, how can it be called "accepting and practicing"?
This refers to one who practices the dhuta of begging for alms in successive order.
If one accepts [an offering] and then discards it, how does this not damage the donor’s gift?
One should reply: "In the first place, one simply should not accept it."
Question: If that is so, how is he called one who practices the ascetic virtue (dhūta-guṇa) of begging for alms in successive order?
Answer: When that venerable one, having attained the divine eye and the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhi-jñāna), was about to go for alms...
First, he observes which direction, village, town, or street has only coarse food;
having known this, he proceeds to go there and beg for alms in due order,
as it is said in the Sūtra that there are four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
First, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever food one obtains;
second, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever clothing one obtains;
third, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever bedding and seating one obtains.
Regarding the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*), there are those with and without pleasure, consisting of the abandonment of pleasure and the cultivation of the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One speak this sutra?
Answer: It was for the sake of establishing the livelihood and the duties for his disciples.
This means that while the first three establish the basis of one's livelihood, the fourth establishes what is to be done.
Regarding the first three establishing the basis of livelihood:
this refers to abandoning four types of professional activities.
There is one kind of livelihood that is abandoned;
there are four kinds of livelihoods:
the first is agriculture as a livelihood.
Second, those who take trade as their livelihood;
third, those who take hired labor as their livelihood;
fourth, those who take independence as their livelihood.
In this regard, they all abandon other activities and engage in only one kind of work, which is solely the act of begging for alms.
Some say this is to demonstrate that their livelihood is inexhaustible and to show what ought to be done.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the blameless requisites for practice and what ought to be done;
furthermore, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the non-harmful requisites for practice and what ought to be done.
Furthermore, this is to demonstrate the unique provisions for practice (*sambhāra-karman*) and the tasks to be performed that distinguish [this path] from non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Herein, "provisions for practice" refers to the first three [perfections], while "tasks to be performed" refers to the fourth.
Some say: it is for the purpose of demonstrating the path and the requisites of the path;
herein, the first three demonstrate the requisites of the path, and the last one demonstrates the path.
Just as it is with the path and the requisites for the path, so too should one understand the śramaṇa and the requisites for a śramaṇa,
the brāhmaṇa and the requisites for a brāhmaṇa,
and the holy life (brahmacarya) and the requisites for the holy life.
For these reasons, the Buddha taught this Sūtra on the Noble Lineages (āryavaṃśa).
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the noble lineages?
The answer is that all have non-attachment as their wholesome root (kuśalamūla) for their intrinsic nature.
Some say that the first three are the wholesome root of non-attachment, while the last one is diligence (vīrya).
Of these explanations, the first is the most excellent, as all serve as antidotes to craving.
Question: If that is so, on what distinct basis are the four types taught?
Answer: It is for the purpose of counteracting the four kinds of craving.
That is to say, contentment with clothing counteracts craving for clothing;
contentment with food counteracts craving for food.
Contentment with bedding and seats counteracts craving for bedding and seats;
delight in abandonment and delight in cultivation counteract craving for existence and non-existence. For this reason, it is said that all [of these] have non-attachment as their essential nature.
If it also includes the associated and concomitant factors,
its nature consists of the five aggregates in the desire and form realms,
and the four aggregates in the formless realm.
This is the essential nature of the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*): it is the self, it is the thing, it is the essence, it is the characteristic, and it is the fundamental nature.
Having already explained the essential nature, that which follows shall now be explained.
Question: Why are they called "noble lineages" (āryavaṃśa)?
Some say that because they are both noble and lineages, they are called "noble lineages."
It is called "noble" (ārya) because it is wholesome and because it is untainted (anāsrava).
It is called a "seed" (bīja) because this very [state] is able to produce a continuous succession of dharmas that constitute various meritorious qualities.
Some say that they are called "noble lineages" (āryavaṃśa) because they are the lineage of the noble ones;
"noble" refers to all non-erroneous wholesome dharmas.
These four are called "lineages" (*gotra*) because they are capable of producing [wholesome states] and continue in succession.
Some say that because these operate within the continuum of a noble one (*ārya*) and cause it not to be interrupted, they are therefore called "noble lineages" (*āryagotra*).
Some say that these are called "noble lineages" (āryavaṃśa) because they can be found within the continuum of a noble one (ārya), ensuring that it remains uninterrupted.
Others say:

"Noble" (ārya) refers to fruits that are desirable, pleasing, delightful, and agreeable; because these can produce such [fruits] in an uninterrupted succession, they are called "noble lineages" (āryavaṃśa).
This is explained in terms of their outflow fruit (niṣyandaphala).
Some say that "noble" (*ārya*) refers to desirable, pleasing, delightful, and agreeable karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
Because these [four] can induce such maturation so that its continuity remains uninterrupted, they are called "noble lineages" (*āryavaṃśa*).
This is explained in terms of the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Some say that "noble ones" (*ārya*) refers specifically to Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
Because this continuity arises from that and remains uninterrupted, it is called a "noble lineage" (*āryavaṃśa*).
Some say that the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is what is called "noble."
Because these are able to sustain and maintain [the lineage] so that it continues for a long time, they are called "noble lineages" (āryavaṃśa).
Thus, the fact that the True Dharma remains in the world for a thousand years without perishing is entirely due to the power of the noble lineages.
Just as rafters and beams support a house so that it does not fall into ruin,
these conditions are therefore called the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
As for their realms, they all pertain to the three realms or to the realm that is beyond them.
Question: Since there is no food or drink in the form realm (rūpadhātu),
and none of the first three [nutriments] in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
how is it that all three realms possess all four kinds [of nutriment]?
The answer is: although those [beings] lack food and so forth, they possess the merit of contentment with those [conditions].
Some say that because the lower realm possesses all four types [of nutriment], those who successively induce birth in the higher realms also possess all four types.
The Venerable Vasumitra stated as follows:
"Although the higher realms lack food and so forth, they possess their respective antidotes.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of antidotes."

That is to say: the counteractive of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), the counteractive of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*), the counteractive of maintenance (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*), and the counteractive of remoteness (*dūribhāva-pratipakṣa*).
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) possesses all four types of counteractives regarding food and so forth;
the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) possesses three, excluding the counteractive of abandonment.
The formless realm has two [types], namely:
the sustaining and the remote.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
Just as there exist untainted noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) even though there are no untainted robes, food, and so forth,
so too there exist the noble lineages of those two realms even though there is no food and so forth in the form and formless realms.
The Venerable One said:
"If one who does not even regard the requisites for the body is still called one who dwells in the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa),
how much more so should one who does not regard the body itself be considered to possess the noble lineages?"
Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*): the contaminated (*sāsrava*) [dharmas] exist in eleven stages, while the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) exist in nine stages.
As for their bases (*āśraya*), they all rely upon the three realms (*tridhātu*).
As for their aspects (*ākāra*), they all consist of the sixteen aspects as well as other aspects.
As for their objects (*ālambana*), they all take all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) as their object.
As for the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), they are all the four applications of mindfulness.
The wise possess either eight knowledges or ten knowledges.
Those associated with meditative absorption (samādhi) are all associated with the three types of absorption, as well as those not so associated.
Regarding the faculties, it is said in general that they are all associated with the three faculties.
That is to say: pleasure, joy, and equanimity.
As for "worldly," these all pertain to the three times, taking the three times as their objects and being dissociated from the world.
As for "wholesome" and so forth, these are all wholesome, taking the three types as their objects.
The same applies to those bound to the desire realm and so forth, as well as to those conditioned by the three realms and those that are unconditioned.
Question: If this is so, how is one to reconcile this with the statement in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*:
"The four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are all neither defiled nor mixed with afflictions (*kleśa*)"?
The response is that there is no fault, because while those [factors] exclude association with afflictions, they do not exclude being tainted (*sāsrava*).
Those such as the "trainee" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth all pertain to the three types and take the three types as their objects.
Those such as "abandoned by seeing" (*darśana-heya*) and so forth are all abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) or are not abandoned (*aheya*), and they take the three types as their objects.
Those that take names as their object and those that take meanings as their object all take both names and meanings as their objects.
Those that take one's own continuum, another's continuum, or that which is not a continuum as their object all take these three types [of objects].

Those acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*), those acquired through detachment from defilement (*vairāgya-labdha*), and those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*) refer to those acquired through application and those acquired through detachment from defilement, rather than those acquired by birth.
Some say it is also acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*).
Of these two views, the former is the correct one.
If those wholesome states acquired at birth were also considered noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), then would ants, eggs, mosquitoes, and moths also possess the noble lineages?
Therefore, the noble lineages do not include those wholesome states acquired at birth.
Question: Are the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) accomplished through hearing, reflection, or cultivation?
Answer: They are comprised within all three;
they belong to the mental level (manobhūmi) as well as the five sensory consciousnesses.
Answer: It belongs only to the level of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), not to the five sensory consciousnesses.
Some say, however, that it also extends to the five sensory consciousnesses.
The critique says:
One should not speak thus. Why is that?
Because among the five consciousnesses, wholesome states are exclusively those acquired by birth (*upapatti-lābhika*).

Question: If they are wholesome through application (*prāyogika-kuśala*), then are the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) also noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*)?
The answer is: those are not the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). Why is that?
If one rejoices in liberation and feels aversion toward birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), those roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are the noble lineages.
Since all that is cherished by non-Buddhists is nothing but birth and death, their roots of goodness are not called "noble lineages" (āryavaṃśa).
Furthermore, to feel contentment with existence and the requisites for existence is what is called a noble lineage.
Because the roots of goodness of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are contrary to these, they are not noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
This is because non-Buddhists such as the Pañcaśikha also seek birth in the heavens to experience sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, the noble lineages are all roots of goodness belonging to the class of those who have gone forth (*pravrajita*).
Since the roots of goodness of non-Buddhists are all subsumed under the category of householders, they are not noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).

Question: Since both fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) and contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) have the nature of non-greed as their antidote to greed, why is contentment established as a noble lineage while fewness of desires is not?
Answer: The term "few desires" (alpeccha) involves both deficiency and augmentation, whereas "contentment" (saṃtuṣṭi) does not.
As for its deficiency, it merely speaks of having few desires without speaking of being without desire.

Because those who engage in augmentation lack actual desire [for requisites] yet are called "of few desires," the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are established within contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*), as such a thing does not exist therein. Some say:
Fewness of desires operates with respect to things not yet obtained in the future;
contentment operates with respect to things already obtained in the present.
One does not regard the acquisition of even a single *kārsāpaṇa* in the present as difficult, nor does one do so regarding the future.
The station of a wheel-turning monarch is established as a noble lineage because it is difficult to find contentment with;
some say it is for the purpose of distinguishing [the Buddhist path] from that of the non-Buddhists.
I do not say that having few desires constitutes a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).
If I were to say that having few desires constitutes a noble lineage,
then the various followers of external paths would say, "We truly are those who abide in the noble lineages."
Why is this? You still wear rag-robes, whereas we go naked and without clothing;
you still sustain yourselves by begging for alms.
"We ourselves often fast and do not eat;
you still sit beneath trees while we sometimes remain with our hands raised and our feet off the ground.
Therefore, it is we who truly deserve the name 'those who abide in the noble lineages'."
To exclude them, it is taught that contentment alone constitutes the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), because non-Buddhists lack contentment with existence and the requisites for existence.
Question: What is the difference between fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) and contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*)?
Some say that having few desires pertains only to the mental faculty,
whereas contentment extends across all six groups of consciousness.
Some say that having few desires exists only in the desire realm,
while contentment extends through both the desire and form realms.
Some say that fewness of desires pertains only to the desire realm,
while contentment extends throughout all three realms.
Some say that fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) belongs to the three realms,
while contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) is bound to the three realms as well as unbound.
Thus it is said that both fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) and contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) pertain to both the bound (*baddha*) and the unbound (*abaddha*) states across the three realms.
Question: If this is so, what is the distinction between them?
Answer: Fewness of desires operates with respect to things not yet obtained in future states.
Contentment regarding present circumstances already obtained is what constitutes the distinction. Question:
Why are the contentments arising from medicinal requisites for the sick not called noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*)?
The answer is that one should also have mentioned the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), but their omission should be understood as being due to ellipsis.
Some say they are already included within what was previously stated.
Regarding the medicinal requisites for illness, there are two kinds:
those that may be consumed and those that may not be consumed.
Those that may be consumed are included within the category of food.
Those things that are not to be consumed are included among clothing and bedding.
Some say that,
because it is for the benefit of sick bhikṣus, contentment with medicine is not mentioned as a noble lineage (āryavaṃśa).
It means that there might be a bhikṣu who, although suffering from illness, does not seek medicine because he has few duties.
If the Buddha were to establish this as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*),
he would then remain stuck with his illness and be unable to diligently cultivate the application of the noble path (*āryamārgaprayoga*).
Because they are intended to benefit others by causing them to diligently practice the path, they are not described as noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). Some say:
when their enjoyment gives rise to negligence, contentment with respect to that [enjoyment] is established as a noble lineage.
Regarding the medicinal requisites for illness, they are not mentioned because at the time of their use, they merely alleviate disease and do not increase heedlessness.
Some say that if something is used by all people, in all places, and at all times, contentment with it is established as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).
Because the medicinal requisites for illness are not enjoyed in all such ways as other objects of use, contentment with them is not established as a noble lineage (āryavaṃśa).
Therefore, the Venerable Bakula said:
I have been a renunciant within the Buddha’s Dharma for over eighty years.
I do not recall ever having experienced physical ailments, even as minor as a headache;
nor do I recall ever making use of medicines or medical requisites for the sake of illness, even as simple as *harītakī*.
If this is so even for those born in the desire realm, how much more so for those born in the form and formless realms?
Question: Why is it that, regarding the prātimokṣa restraint, only the non-informative (avijñapti) is established as a noble lineage (āryavaṃśa), and not the informative (vijñapti)?
Answer: It was stated previously that what is characterized by an uninterrupted continuity is called a "noble lineage" (āryavaṃśa).
Since these [other factors] do not possess such uninterrupted continuity, they were not mentioned. Some say:
Because the unmanifest (avijñapti) can coexist with the Noble Path, it is established as a noble lineage (āryavaṃśa);
since the manifest (vijñapti) does not coexist with the Noble Path, it is not so described.
For those who have gone forth, there are four noble lineages.
Those who live at home also possess the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
However, those who have gone forth are said to possess them due to two causes:
first, because of their intention (*āśaya*).
Second, regarding enjoyment:
those householders are said to possess the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) by virtue of a single cause,
namely, their intention (āśaya), and not by virtue of their enjoyment.
Just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, dwells upon a seat of exquisite flowers surrounded by twelve nayutas of celestial maidens and entertains himself with sixty thousand musical performances,
yet maintains a constant mental inclination toward the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) without actually partaking in their sensory enjoyments.
The same applies to kings such as Bimbisāra and elders such as Sudatta.
Question: Is each individual member of the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) itself called "one who dwells in the noble lineages"?
Answer: It is not so.
One is designated as abiding in the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) only when all four are complete;
however, at the moment one obtains a single noble lineage, one necessarily obtains all four.
Just as one who attains a single analytical knowledge necessarily possesses all four,
so too did the Buddhas of the past all praise the wearing of rag-robes (pāṃśukūla) yet not permit it;
now the Buddha Śākyamuni likewise praises the wearing of rag-robes and does permit it.
Question: Why is this so? Answer:

Because in past times, people’s greedy minds were faint; even if they obtained clothing worth hundreds of thousands in price, their mind of attachment was not like that of people today who are attached to even ordinary garments.
Some say that at that time the people were abundant in wealth and treasures;
thus, the bhikṣus desired to obtain robes worth hundreds of thousands.
Because it is difficult to find discarded rags (pāṃśukūla) in the present age,
the Venerable Vasumitra said:
"In the past, people’s aspirations were vast."
Seeing the bhikṣus possessing such excellent requisites,
he immediately gave rise to a heart of joy, faith, and reverence;
for nowadays, people’s inclinations are narrow and inferior.
Because one gives rise to a mind of joy, faith, and reverence upon seeing a bhikṣu who possesses coarse and worn-out requisites,
the Venerable Buddhadeva said:
In former times, the bodies of people were delicate and soft; if they used coarse or inferior objects, they could not survive on their own.
In the present age, the bodies of people are coarse and hard; even if they use coarse or inferior objects, they are able to survive. Therefore...
The Venerable One said:
"One should know that when the Buddhas of the past praised rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*), they were also permitting their use.
If it were not so, why would they have praised them?"
The Buddhas do not speak without a purpose.
As the World-Honored One has said, "Rags from a dust heap are few, easy to obtain, and blameless.
What does "few" mean? What does "easy to obtain" mean? And what does "blameless" mean?
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
It is called "small" because it is accomplished with little effort;
it is not called "small" because it is enjoyed by few people.
It is called "easily obtained" because it can be acquired at any time and in any place;
it is called "blameless" because it is permitted by the Buddha and thus used by the wise.
The Venerable One said:
It is called "few" because its price and measure are small;
it is called "easy to obtain" because it is not sought from others;
and it is called "blameless" because it is free from grasping.
For two reasons, the Buddha taught that contentment with robes is a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*):
first, to censure those who are discontented with robes, such as Nanda and others;
second, to praise those who are content with robes, such as Mahākāśyapa and others.
For two reasons, the Buddha taught that contentment with food is a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*):
first, to censure lack of contentment with food, as in the case of Vātūla and others;
second, to praise contentment with food, as in the case of Bakula and others.
For two reasons, the Buddha taught that contentment with bedding and seating (*śayanāsana-saṃtuṣṭi*) is a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).
First, it is to censure those who lack contentment with bedding and seating,
such as the bhikṣu Mūḍharāja and others.
As stated in a sutra, the bhikṣu Mūḍharāja said to the Buddha:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will observe how coarse and wretched my bedding is.
Second, it is for the purpose of praising contentment with bedding and seats, as in the case of Kṣemaka and others.
For two reasons, the Buddha taught that delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation are the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*):
first, to censure those who are indolent, such as Chanda and others;
and second, to praise those who are diligent, such as Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa and others.
One knows that such a person is an individual who abides in the noble lineages by four causes and conditions:
first, they do not delight in hearing others speak of their own acquisition of gains and offerings;
second, they do not delight in associating with those who crave delicious food.
Third, one possesses few requisites and maintains them with purity, giving rise to no defiled attachment;
fourth, regarding various gains and honors, whether obtained or not, one gives rise to neither love nor hatred.
As the World-Honored One said, "These four noble lineages are the most supreme knowledge."
This lineage is known to be delightful and known to be free from defilement;
it cannot be censured by anyone in the world—
whether by śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or any other beings in the world.
There is no one capable of speaking of its faults in accordance with the Dharma.
What is called "supreme knowledge"? Some say:

These four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are called "supreme" because they can induce the supreme, because they attain the supreme fruit, because they tend toward the supreme, and because they accord with the supreme.
They are said to be "known" because they were established by the Buddha and known by the Buddha.
Some say that the Buddha taught that each of the five hundred śrāvakas possesses a most excellent dharma;
these four are included among those most excellent dharmas, and are therefore called "most excellent."
Because the Buddha knows that these four constitute true contentment, it is called "knowledge.
Some say that the Buddha and his disciples are called the most excellent ones; what they praise and describe is therefore called "most excellent knowledge."
Some say:
The Buddha knows that these four are supreme treasuries capable of satisfying the aspirations of those who abide by them; therefore, they are called "supreme knowledge.
This is because most sentient beings die with their aspirations unfulfilled.
Only those who abide in the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) die without their aspirations being fulfilled.
Some say that the Buddha,
knowing these four to be inexhaustible treasuries that allow the wise to enjoy them without end, therefore knows them as the most excellent.
This means that those who dwell here do not rely on much seeking or much accumulation;
nor do they need to guard doors or secure them with locks, for they enjoy [resources] at will until the end,
and these are never exhausted.
Just as the treasures used by a wheel-turning monarch who rules over the four continents may quickly be exhausted,
yet the enjoyment of these four remains inexhaustible.
What is meant by "knowledge of the lineage" (*gotra*)?
Answer: It is called the "lineage" because all Buddhas and their disciples, numbering more than the sands of the Ganges, are born from it.
It is called "knowledge" because it is that which is realized by the wise.
Some say that "spiritual lineage" (*gotra*) has the meaning of "that which sustains. That is to say,
it is called spiritual lineage because it is able to maintain and uphold the holy teaching so that it does not perish for a long time.
Because this is what the Buddha has realized, it is called "knowledge.
Why is it called "delightful knowledge"?
The answer is: because these four are what the wise delight in and what the wise know, they are called "delightful knowledge."
Some say that the Buddha knows these four as "knowable through delight" because they can all assist in the delight of abandonment and the delight of cultivation.
Others say:
The Buddha knows that these four are to be known as "delightful" because the wise,
according to their capacity, take pleasure in and dwell peacefully within them during each of the three periods of day and night, remaining free from weariness.
Some say that the Buddha knew these four were what practitioners delight in dwelling upon for a long time; that is to say,
from the latter part of this day, they sit cross-legged and remain settled therein until the first part of the following day.
They arise from those [conditions] only when they are displaced by other causes.
Why are they called "unadulterated"?
Answer: Because these four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are not overwhelmed or intermingled with afflictions or evil karma.
What is meant by "incapable of being censured"?
The answer is: if one abides in these four [qualities], one is always praised by those who abide in the True Dharma and is never censured.
It is for this reason that among all the world—including śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, Māras, and Brahmās—[one remains beyond reproach].
No one is able to speak of its faults in accordance with the Dharma.
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke thus:
"The Buddha knows these four [knowledges] which can enter the noble womb; therefore, they are called the most supreme knowledges."
Because all noble ones arise from this, it is called the "knowledge of the lineage" (*gotra-jñāna*).
Because it is what practitioners delight in day and night, it is called the "delightful knowledge.
Because it is far removed from the four kinds of worldly activities, it is called "untainted."
The four types of livelihoods refer to agriculture, commerce, service, and sovereignty.
Because all virtues are fully realized through these, they are beyond reproach;
for they cause no harm to oneself or others.
No one in the entire world— whether śramaṇas,
brāhmaṇas, Māras, or Brahmās— is able to speak of his faults in accordance with the Dharma.
As the Bhagavān stated in a verse within a sūtra:
Those who have subdued love and hatred, Who always dwell in remote lodgings, And constantly abide in heedfulness— They uproot the latent tendency of craving for existence.
In response to the question, "What meaning is being elucidated in this verse? the answer is: "Love" (*preman*) refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
"Enmity" refers to hatred and resentment.
If the noble disciples of the Buddha subdue these two,
they dwell in secluded lodgings and remain heedful.
One is then able to forever uproot the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) toward craving for existence (*bhavarāga*).
Furthermore, within this True Dharma and Vinaya,
any mental engagement that turns toward attachment to what has been acquired is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).
The state of mental distress regarding what has not yet been attained is called aversion (*dveṣa*).
The noble disciples of the Buddha do not relish what has already been attained and do not feel distressed regarding what has not yet been attained;
therefore, they are able to subdue both.
Because they have been simultaneously subdued, one dwells in peripheral lodgings;
by abiding in heedfulness, one is then able to uproot the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) for craving for existence.
Furthermore, if there is a greedy pursuit of superior clothing, food, and drink, it is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).
If one feels aversion toward coarse and inferior clothing or food and drink, this is called "hatred.
The noble disciples of the Buddha are able to subdue both [extremes].
This phrase demonstrates the noble lineage of contentment regarding clothing and food and drink.
The second phrase indicates the noble lineage of contentment with bedding and seating.
The latter two phrases indicate the noble lineages of delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation.
Question: What is the distinction between delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation?
Answer: It is the delight in abandoning afflictions and the delight in cultivating the noble path.
Furthermore, the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) is called "delight in abandoning."
The path of liberation is called "delight in cultivation.
Furthermore, the path of seeing is called "delight in abandonment," and the path of cultivation is called "delight in cultivation."
Just as it is with the path of seeing and the path of cultivation,

so too should the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñendriya) regarding the stage of seeing and the stage of cultivation be understood.
Furthermore, those who delight in abandonment manifest the various patiences (kṣānti).
Those who delight in cultivation manifest the various knowledges.
Delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation constitute their distinction.
As it is said regarding Mahānāman: "The learner dwells much, gradually abandoning the five hindrances," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra:
The Buddha told Mahānāma:
"One who trains much dwells in the gradual abandonment of the five hindrances.
Although the sūtra states this, it does not provide a detailed analysis.
What is training? What is training in great abiding? It is the gradual abandonment of the five hindrances.
That sutra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Since that sutra has not yet explained certain matters, they shall now be explained; for this reason, this treatise is composed.
As it is said, Mahānāma trains much in the gradual abandonment of the five hindrances.
In this context, what is meant by "training"?
The answer is: one who is a stream-enterer or a once-returner.
How does one who trains frequently dwell in the gradual abandonment of the five hindrances?
Answer: By gradually abandoning, gradually detaching from, gradually subduing, and gradually turning away from them.
Question: Why are the names "one who practices through faith" (śraddhānusārī) and "one who practices through dharma" (dharmānusārī) not mentioned here as types of those who train frequently?
Does one who abides [in the first dhyāna] gradually abandon the five hindrances?
One should say "yes," yet because it is not so stated, it should be understood that this meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*). Some say:
Among those who practice through faith or through dharma, there are some for whom the five hindrances have already been abandoned,
and others for whom the five hindrances are being gradually abandoned;
because these states are not fixed, they are not mentioned here.
The stream-enterer and once-returner are not like this; they are determined to abide only in the gradual abandonment of the five hindrances, and for this reason it is so stated.
Some say that if the afflictions of the five hindrances can still manifest within their bodies...
Regarding those who gradually sever [the afflictions],

it is explained here that for those practicing in accordance with faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), even tainted wholesome minds (*sāsrava-kuśala-citta*) and unobscured-neutral minds (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) have no possibility of manifesting,
let alone the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Question: In the bodies of stream-enterers and once-returners, doubt and the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor have already been abandoned;
although remorse has not yet been abandoned, it no longer manifests.
Why is it said that one who dwells frequently [in the hindrances] gradually abandons them, yet is further said to be capable of their active manifestation?
Answer: The preceding text should have stated this as follows.
One should not say that there are five [hindrances] because a practitioner who dwells much in them gradually abandons them;
rather, they are said to be five because there are five actual entities, namely:
sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and agitation, and doubt.

Some say that the previously abandoned and the currently abandoned are collectively referred to as "abandoning five," just as it is said that by abandoning the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni), one attains the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala).
"Abiding frequently" means abiding repeatedly.
Question: What is the difference between abandoning (*prahāṇa*), detachment (*viveka*), suppression (*vibhava*), and turning away (*parāṅmukha*)? Some say:
Some say that because both are manifested as being abandoned without distinction, there is no difference;

yet others say there is a distinction: it is called "abandonment" (prahāṇa) because one abandons the fetters (bandhana) associated with them, and it is called "separation" (visamyoga) because one becomes detached from them.
It is called "subduing" (vīta) because the [defilements] do not function;
it is called "turning away" (vivarta) because one feels aversion toward them.
Furthermore, abandonment is spoken of in reference to the path of uninterrupted realization (ānantarya-mārga).
"Separation" is spoken of in reference to the path of liberation;
these two [separation and abandonment] are spoken of in reference to permanent abandonment, while "subduing" is spoken of in reference to the proximate preparatory stage,
and "aversion" is spoken of in reference to the distant preparatory stage.
These two are explained in terms of temporary abandonment.
Furthermore, abandonment is explained in terms of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
while detachment is explained in terms of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
These two are explained in terms of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).
"Subduing" is explained in terms of the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*),
and "turning away" is explained in terms of the path of excellence (*viśeṣamārga*).
These two are explained in terms of the aids to abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
Furthermore, "abandonment" is explained in terms of the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*),
while "separation" is explained in terms of the antidote of maintenance (*ādhārapratipakṣa*).
"Subduing" (*abhibhava*) is explained in terms of the antidote of distancing (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*);
"turning away" (*vimukha*) is explained in terms of the antidote of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*).
The distinction between them lies in this: subduing refers to distancing, while turning away refers to revulsion.
As it is said: "Because the Dharma is well-expounded, the Vinaya is well-expounded;
because the Vinaya is well-expounded, the Dharma is well-expounded," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
A sūtra states that in the future there will be bhikṣus who do not cultivate the body, ethical discipline, mind, or wisdom.
"He who does not cultivate the body, virtue, mind, and wisdom is a *dharmasandūṣaka*," and so forth, as explained at length.
Although the Sūtra states this, it does not analyze what "dharma" means.
What, then, is dharma?
What is the Vinaya? What is the Dharmasaṃketa?
Thus it is explained at length, and so forth.
That sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Since that sūtra does not explain certain matters, they shall now all be explained; therefore, this treatise is composed.
What is "dharma"?
Answer: The Noble Eightfold Path.
What is the Vinaya?
Answer: The cessation of greed, hatred, and delusion.
In what way is the Dharma purified by means of the Vinaya, and how is the Vinaya purified by means of the Dharma?
Answer: It is when one does not cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path.
He is unable to realize the cessation of greed, hatred, and delusion.
When he does not realize the cessation of greed, hatred, and delusion,
he is unable to cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path.
For this reason, it is said as follows.
In this context, the term *saṃtuṣṭa* (satisfied) refers to some who express contentment.
Some say it indicates destruction.

If one says it indicates contentment, how do they explain it? Because the *dharma-śāndṛśa* [is so called], the *vinaya-śāndṛśa* refers to the arising of contentment within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Consequently, one is unable to cultivate the path of cultivation;
and when one does not cultivate the path of cultivation, one is unable to realize the abandonment of those afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
In this way, because the Dharma is well-expounded (*sundara*), the Vinaya is well-expounded.
How is it that because the Vinaya is well-expounded, the Dharma is well-expounded?
It refers to the arising of contentment regarding the abandonment of those afflictions to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya-kleśa*).
Consequently, one is unable to realize the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
When one does not realize the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation,
one is unable to practice the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
In this way, because the Vinaya is corrupted, the Dharma is corrupted.
If it is said that [the Dharma] is manifested as being ruined,
that is said because the Noble Path has been ruined.
Because one cannot realize the cessation of greed, hatred, and delusion, there is the *sūtra-piṭaka*;
because [it teaches] the destruction of greed, hatred, and delusion, there is the *vinaya-piṭaka*.
Because one is then unable to cultivate the Noble Path, it is said that the *vinaya-saṃdṛṣṭa* (that which is seen in the discipline) is the *dharma-saṃdṛṣṭa* (that which is seen in the Dharma).
Question: Since the Noble Path and cessation are faultless and indestructible, how can it be said that the Noble Path and cessation are destroyed?
Answer: It is said that they are "destroyed" because their continuity is interrupted.
However, it is not that their own essence can actually be destroyed;
rather, this occurs through the manifestation of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, the continuity is destroyed;
because the continuity is destroyed,
it causes the Noble Path to become increasingly remote.
Because they have strayed far from the Noble Path and are thus unable to realize the cessation of greed, hatred, and delusion, they are said to be "ruined.
As the Sūtra says: "This is the Dharma;
this is the Vinaya."
This is the teaching of the Great Master.
Question: What is the distinction between these three?
Answer: "Dharma" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path.
The Vinaya refers to the cessation of greed, hatred, and delusion;
the Teacher’s instruction refers to the Buddha’s word. Some say:
"Dharma" refers to the Abhidharma Piṭaka;
"Vinaya" refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka;
and "the Teacher’s Instruction" refers to the Sūtra Piṭaka.
This is called the distinction between these three.
As it has been taught regarding the practice in accordance with the Dharma, and so forth at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
For example, although the sūtras speak of "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*), they do not analyze it by asking:
"What is the Dharma?"
What is "conformity with the Dharma" (anudharma)?
What is "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (dharmānudharmapratipatti)?
That sutra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which was not previously explained shall now be explained; therefore, this treatise is composed.
What is the Dharma?
The answer is: it is the quiescent Nirvana.
What is the practice in accordance with the Dharma?
The answer is: the Noble Eightfold Path.
What is the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma?

Answer: If one acts in accordance with the meaning within this context—namely, practicing the Noble Eightfold Path for the sake of seeking nirvāṇa—it is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma."
One who is able to abide in this is called a practitioner of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipanna*).
Question: Why is *nirvāṇa* alone designated as "Dharma," while the Noble Eightfold Path is designated as "in accordance with the Dharma"?
Answer: Because among all phenomena (*dharma*), nirvāṇa is supreme, and because it cannot be invaded by birth, old age, sickness, or death, it alone receives the name "Dharma.
The Noble Eightfold Path follows and accords with that [nirvāṇa], like a king’s great minister; therefore, it is called "conforming to the Dharma" (*anudharma*).
Therefore, the Sūtra states that among all phenomena, nirvāṇa is supreme;
and among conditioned phenomena, the Noble Path is supreme.
Nevertheless, in the *Śāriputra-śikṣā-anuśāsana-sūtra*, it is said: "Venerable one, this is the Dharma that accords with the Dharma."
That which is called "disjunction" (visamyoga): in that sutra,
the Noble Path is termed "Dharma."
Nirvāṇa is called "conforming to the Dharma" (dharmānudharma) because one first attains the Noble Path and subsequently realizes Nirvāṇa.
The preceding sūtra revealed the Dharma and that which conforms to the Dharma according to the sequence of superior and inferior.
Subsequently, the Sūtras reveal the Dharma and the *anudharma* according to the sequence of realization.
Furthermore, the Prātimokṣa is called "Dharma," and the Prātimokṣa restraint is called "*anudharma*."
If one acts in accordance with the meaning within this context, it is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*).
That is to say, for the sake of seeking individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*), one undertakes the vows of individual liberation;
having obtained them, to guard them accordingly without transgression is called practice in accordance with the Dharma.
One who is able to dwell securely in this is called a practitioner who acts in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharmapratipanna).
Furthermore, bodily restraint, verbal restraint, and purity of livelihood are called "receiving the Dharma" (dharma-samādāna), and this is termed "acting in accordance with the Dharma."
If one acts in accordance with the meaning within this context, it is called "practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*).

That is to say, for the sake of seeking purity of body, speech, and livelihood, one undertakes [the precepts] and, having undertaken them, guards them accordingly; this is called practice in accordance with the Dharma.
One who is able to abide in this is called a practitioner of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
Question: Since physical and verbal restraint and purity of livelihood are already subsumed within the prātimokṣa vows, why are they stated again?
The answer is: the former was an undifferentiated explanation, while the present is a differentiated explanation;
the former was a general statement, while the present is a specific statement. Some say:
The former was comprised of virtuous conduct subsumed under discipline, but not comprised of that which is apart from discipline;
the present is comprised of virtuous conduct subsumed under discipline and also comprised of that which is apart from discipline.
Some say: the former [passage] displays that which is initiated,
while the present [passage] displays that which initiates.
Previously, because it was initiated by guarding, guarding was able to initiate it;
now, because it is able to initiate guarding, it is initiated by guarding. Some say:
Previously, for the sake of protecting the fruit, one protected the cause accordingly;
now, for the sake of protecting the cause, one protects the fruit accordingly.
This is just as it is with cause and effect, or the agent and the object of action.
In this context, the informative [action] of the prātimokṣa vows and its initial moment of non-informative [action] constitute:
morality (śīla), restraint (saṃvara), excellent conduct (sucarita), prātimokṣa, the prātimokṣa restraint, karma, and the path of action (karmapatha).
From this point forward, the unmanifest [karma] is ethical discipline (śīla), restraint (saṃvara), excellent conduct (sucarita), and the prātimokṣa restraint;
it is not the prātimokṣa itself, nor is it the first liberation.
Therefore, this action is not an action-path (*karmapatha*), because the volition (*cetanā*) that brings it to completion does not operate therein.
As it is said: "Venerable sir, I shall now recite the Prātimokṣa."
Listen attentively: among these, what dharma is called *prātimokṣa*?
Is it the *śīla*, or is it the words of the one who recites the precepts?
If this were simply ethical discipline (*śīla*), it could not be so described;
why then do you say, "I shall explain the *Prātimokṣa*"?
If this is the speech of one who recites the precepts...
If he speaks with a wholesome mind,
or speaks with an unwholesome or neutral mind,
how is this reconciled with what is taught in the Vinaya?
As it is said that the Prātimokṣa is the foremost, the preeminent, and the precursor of all wholesome dharmas;
some say it is śīla. [The interlocutor] asks: Since śīla cannot be described, how can you say, "I shall explain"?
Answer: It is called "teaching" (deśanā) by virtue of being a sequential cause (*pāramparyahetu*).
This is according to the analogy of descendants: that is to say, speech is able to give rise to names, and names are able to manifest meanings. Some say:
This refers to the speech of one who recites the precepts;
when questioned, they may speak with a wholesome mind,
or they may speak with an unwholesome or neutral mind.
Why is it said that these wholesome dharmas are the foremost, the preeminent, and the precursor?
The answer is: the Vinaya makes this statement based on the cause of non-obstruction;
that is to say, the one who proclaims the precepts may do so with whatever state of mind they possess.
If those who hear [this teaching] are able to practice according to what has been taught,
they will all be able to serve as unobstructed causes for all those merits. Therefore,
it is said that *prātimokṣa* is the foremost and supreme leader of all wholesome dharmas.

Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhiskandha), Part Four: The Sub-section on Non-returners (Anāgāmin), Number Nine. What is the Wheel of Dharma? And so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed? Answer:
It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.

As it is said in a sūtra: "The World-Honored One has turned the wheel of Dharma; among all other worldlings—whether śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, or brahmās—there is none who is able to turn it in accordance with the Dharma."
Although the sūtras state this, they do not analyze it:
how is the wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra) defined, and up to what point can it be said that the wheel of Dharma is being turned?
The sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which was not previously explained shall now be explained; therefore, this treatise is composed.
What is the Wheel of Dharma?
Answer: It is the Noble Eightfold Path.
If it includes both the associated [factors] and those that arise concomitantly, its nature consists of the five aggregates.
This is the intrinsic nature of the Wheel of Dharma;
it is the self, the entity, the characteristic, the nature, and the fundamental nature.
The intrinsic nature has already been explained; now its reason for being so named shall be discussed.
Question: For what reason is it called the "Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*)?
Answer: This wheel is constituted by the Dharma, and because the Dharma is its intrinsic nature, it is called the Wheel of Dharma.
Just as a worldly wheel made of gold and so forth is called a "gold wheel" and so on because its nature consists of gold and so forth,
this is also like that.
Some say:

This wheel is called the Wheel of Dharma because it can discern and thoroughly discern, awaken and thoroughly awaken to, realize through direct intuition, and personally witness the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Some say:
This wheel is called the Wheel of Dharma because it can purify the noble wisdom and the Dharma-eye;
some say it is called the Wheel of Dharma because it can counteract that which is not the Wheel of Dharma.
Non-Dharmacakras refer to the wheels of the eightfold wrong limbs turned by the six teachers, such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others.
Question: For what reason is it called a "wheel" (cakra), and what is the meaning of "wheel"?
Answer: The meaning of "wheel" is that which moves and turns without remaining still.
The meaning of "wheel" (cakra) is the sense of abandoning this [state] and proceeding toward that;
it is the sense of being able to subdue enemies.
It is by virtue of such meanings that it is called a wheel.
As stated in the *Mahācatvāriṃśaddharmaparyāya-sūtra*:
"There are twenty categories of wholesome qualities and twenty categories of unwholesome qualities; this is called the Brahma-wheel," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: It may be so for the twenty categories of wholesome qualities;
however, why are the twenty categories of unwholesome qualities called the Brahma-wheel?
Answer: The Buddha’s intention was not to designate those as the Brahma-wheel.
It is said that when the dharmas of the categories of the wholesome and unwholesome are engaged with through patience and wisdom, it is called the Brahma-wheel (*brahmacakra*).
Question: Why is this called "Brahma"?
Answer: It is called "Brahma" because it is supremely tranquil, free from calamities and misfortunes, devoid of sinful burdens, and because it does not cause affliction or harm.
Question: Why is it called the Brahma-wheel?
Answer: Because the Brahma-world is accessible at the outset and because it is endowed with the Noble Path, it is called the Brahma-wheel.
The second and third dhyānas are not accessible at the outset, nor are they endowed with the Noble Path.
Although the fourth dhyāna is the first attained by the Buddha’s body, it is not called a "wheel" because it does not possess the noble path (*āryamārga*).
Only the Brahma-world is so named, for it is both the first to be attained and fully endowed with the path; thus, it is called the "Brahma-wheel."
Some say that it is called the "Brahma-wheel" because it can be obtained within the continuum of one who practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Others say:
It is called the "Brahma-wheel" because it serves as the antidote to non-celibacy (*abrahmacarya*).
Some say that it is called the Brahma-wheel because it serves as the antidote to the non-Brahma afflictions (*kleśa*) abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms.
Some say that because it was turned at the request of Brahmā, it is called the "Brahma-wheel.
Others say:
The Buddha is the Great Brahmā; because he proclaims, distinguishes, and elucidates [the Dharma], it is called the "Brahma-wheel" (*brahma-cakra*).
Some say it is called the "Brahma-wheel" because it is proclaimed with the Brahma-voice (*brahma-svara*).
Some say that because the noble path alone can counteract the numerous non-Brahma qualities within the Brahma-world, it is called the "Brahma-wheel.
These numerous non-Brahma qualities refer to the afflictions of the three realms that are to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
Or there are unwholesome and neutral afflictions;
or there are afflictions with maturation and without maturation;
or there are afflictions that produce two fruits or produce one fruit.
There are afflictions associated with shamelessness and lack of dread;
there are afflictions dissociated from shamelessness and lack of dread;
and there are afflictions that have an objective basis as well as those that lack an objective basis.
Or rather, it refers to the afflictions that are countered by patience (*kṣānti*) and countered by knowledge (*jñāna*).
Such things as these are called the manifold non-Brahma-factors (*abrahmacarya-dharma*). Some say:
Only in the Brahma-world is there the "Brahma-wheel" (brahmacakra), because it possesses many fruits of the holy life (brahmacarya).
These many fruits of the holy life refer to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
In the three higher dhyānas, however, there are only two fruits of śrāmaṇya.
In the formless realm, there is only one fruit of śramaṇaship;
only in the Brahma-world are all four fruits fully present,
or alternatively, the fruits of the nine thorough knowledges (parijñā).
In the three higher dhyānas, there are only five fruits of full knowledge;
in the formless realms, there are only two fruits of full knowledge;
and only in the Brahma-world are all nine fruits of full knowledge present.
Alternatively, eighty-nine fruits of śrāmaṇya exist only in the Brahma-world and not in the higher realms;
for this reason, the noble path is called the "Brahma-wheel.
Question: Why is it that only the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) is called the "Wheel of Dharma" (dharma-cakra), and not the others?
Answer: It was stated previously that the meaning of "wheel" (cakra) is the sense of moving, shifting, and not remaining still.

Because the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) is a swift path and a path that does not give rise to the intention of fixed expectation (*abhisandhi*), it is most concordant with this sense of moving, shifting, and not remaining still;
therefore, it alone is called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
Some say that the meaning of "wheel" (cakra) is the sense of abandoning this and proceeding to that;
within the path of seeing (darśanamārga), one abandons the clear realization of suffering (duḥkha-abhisamaya) and proceeds to the clear realization of origination (samudaya-abhisamaya).
Up to the clear realization of abandonment and cessation, and the clear realization of the path;
therefore, the path of seeing alone is called the Wheel of Dharma. Some say:
It is called a "wheel" (cakra) for four reasons:
first, it abandons this;
second, it proceeds toward that.
Third, those not yet subdued are subdued;
fourth, those already subdued are protected.
It is the same in the path of seeing.
To abandon this is the clear realization of suffering;
to proceed toward that is the clear realization of origination;
and to subdue what has not yet been subdued is likewise the clear realization of origination.
The guarding of those already subdued is the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of suffering;
this applies likewise up to the cessation and the path, and for this reason it is called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). Some say:
The meaning of "wheel" (*cakra*) is the sense of revolving.
Just as a chariot wheel revolves and turns around,
so too do the patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) circulate in succession.
It is called the Wheel of Dharma because after receptivity (*kṣānti*), knowledge (*jñāna*) manifests; after knowledge, receptivity manifests again;
and this cycle repeats through the categories of phenomena (*dharma*) and their types (*prakāra*).
Some say: [the rest follows].
The meaning of "upper and lower" is the meaning of "wheel.
Just as a wheel moves either upward or downward, so too does the path of seeing (darśanamārga) take its objects in an ascending and descending manner;
that is, having taken the desire realm (kāmadhātu) as its object, it immediately takes the peak of existence (bhavāgra) as its object.
Having taken the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as its object, it then takes the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) as its object;
because the antidotes for the upper and lower realms are explained in this same manner, it is called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). Some say:
The path of seeing (darśanamārga) is called a wheel because its nature is like that of spokes, a hub, and a rim.
Just as in a chariot wheel the hub is situated at the very center, the spokes rest upon the hub, and the rim encompasses the spokes; so it is here.
Thus, in the path of seeing, the patiences and knowledges regarding suffering and its origin are like the spokes;
the patience and knowledge regarding cessation are like the hub;
and the patience and knowledge regarding the path are like the rim.
Because it takes the entire path as its object.
Some say that the patiences and knowledges regarding suffering,
origin, and cessation are like the spokes, the three truths are like the hub, and the truth of the path is like the rim.
Some say that the patience and knowledge regarding the three truths are like the spokes, while the patience and knowledge regarding the path are like the rim, and the four truths are like the hub.
Others say: [the same].
Right view and right intention are like the spokes; right speech, right action, and right livelihood are like the hub; and right mindfulness and right concentration are like the rim.

Alternatively, some say that right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration are like the spokes; right speech, right action, and right livelihood are like the hub; and right view is like the rim.
Some say that only right concentration is like the rim [of a wheel], while the rest are as previously described. Others say:
The meaning of "wheel" (*cakra*) is the subduing of the four directions.
It is like the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) possessed by a universal monarch (*cakravartin*),
which subdues all enemies throughout the four continents.
In this way, because the practitioner subdues all afflictions pertaining to the Four Truths by means of the wheel of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*),
it is called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). Some say that the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) are not called the Wheel of Dharma.
Because it can give rise to the eight branches of the wrong path,
and because the Path of Seeing is its direct antidote, it is called the Wheel of Dharma.
The Venerable Ghosaka said:
The eightfold path is called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) because it is cultivated through successive harmony and simultaneously transferred into the mental continuum of another.
Since this eightfold path is preeminent at the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the Path of Seeing alone is designated as the Wheel of Dharma.
"At what point should one say that the wheel of Dharma has been turned?
Answer: "When the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya saw the Dharma.
Question: "For what reason is this further discussion undertaken?"
Answer: Although the preceding [section] revealed the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), it did not reveal its activity (*vṛtti*).
Now, desiring to reveal this, this treatise is composed. Some say:
The Mahāsāṃghika school asserts that the nature of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) consists of the Buddha’s speech.
They maintain that all words of the Buddha are the Wheel of Dharma;
if, however, one were to claim that the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) is the Wheel of Dharma, then the Wheel of Dharma would have already been turned beneath the Bodhi tree.
Why is it that only upon reaching Vārāṇasī is it called "turning the wheel of Dharma"?
It is to refute their [the heterodox] views and to demonstrate that the essence of the wheel of Dharma is solely the Noble Path, and not the nature of the Buddha’s words.
If these were the words of the Buddha, then he should have been said to have "turned the wheel of Dharma" upon preaching the Dharma to the merchants at the foot of the Bodhi tree;
why then did he only say he turned the wheel of Dharma after arriving later in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī?
Therefore, we know that at that time, it was only when the Noble Path (āryamārga) arose within the bodies of others that it was called "turning the Wheel of Dharma" (dharmacakrapravartana),
because the Wheel of Dharma has the Noble Path as its essence.
Thus, it is said that the Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma simultaneously with Ājñātakauṇḍinya’s realization of the Dharma (dharmanidhyāna).
Question: If that is so, the Buddha had already set the wheel of Dharma in motion beneath the Bodhi tree;
for what reason, then, is it said that he first set the wheel of Dharma in motion in the country of Vārāṇasī?
Answer: There are two kinds of turning the wheel of Dharma:
first, turning it within one's own continuum;
second, causing it to turn within the continua of others.
Turning the wheel of Dharma for oneself occurred beneath the Bodhi tree;
turning the wheel of Dharma for others occurred at Vārāṇasī,
because the Buddha takes the benefit of others as his primary purpose.
Based on causing others to turn [the wheel], it is said that the first turning of the wheel of Dharma occurs.
Some say there are two kinds of turning the wheel of Dharma.
There are two types: those shared with others and those not shared with others.
The wheel of Dharma turned beneath the Bodhi tree is shared with the followers of the Two Vehicles because it is a teaching for one's own benefit;
the wheel of Dharma turned in the country of Vārāṇasī is not shared with the followers of the Two Vehicles because it is a teaching for the benefit of others.
Because it was taught as being unique [to the Buddha], it is said that the Wheel of Dharma was first turned there.
Some say that what is contrary to this is called "common" or "unique," and that it turns based on a common teaching.
The same applies to whether [the turning] is shared or unshared,
and whether it has occurred before or not. Some say that if one surpasses the Pratyekabuddhas at the time of the turning, only then is it called the "first turning."
This means that while all Pratyekabuddhas are also able to turn [the wheel] for themselves,
they do not cause others to turn it;
only the Buddha is able to cause others to turn it as well.
Some say that the "first turning" is so called because it occurred when there were witnesses; that is to say,
only when the five bhikṣus realized the principle of non-self were they able to act as witnesses for the Buddha, who was thus the one who turned the wheel of Dharma.

Some say that the turning of the Wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī is called the "first turning" because it is the fruit of the meritorious labors of ascetic practices cultivated by the Buddha over three incalculable eons in the past.
Why is this? If the Buddha wished to enter parinirvāṇa in the presence of the Buddhas of the past, he could have done so at will.
This is why he spent three incalculable eons diligently practicing hundreds of thousands of ascetic austerities.
Those who seek skillfulness regarding the aggregates, bases, and elements all make this constant aspiration for the benefit of those beings to be trained:
"When I have realized unsurpassed bodhi, may I open the gate of ambrosia for sentient beings."
It causes all beings to be liberated from the prison of birth and death;
therefore, that which is now turned is precisely the fruit of former ascetic practices. Some say:
If one can subdue the afflictions of others' bodies, only then is it called the true function of the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra).
Just as the wheel-treasure of a king subdues other lands rather than merely subduing the palace where he himself resides.
The Wheel of Dharma of the Tathāgata is also like this;
it is based on this that it is said the Buddha first turned the Wheel of Dharma.
Question: If it is when the Noble Path arises within that body that it is called "turning the Wheel of Dharma," [then...]
For what reason is it said that the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma?
The answer is: this statement is made based on the cause of being able to turn [the wheel].
That is to say, regarding all the noble paths within his body, if the World-Honored One did not employ the hand of verbal expression to turn them for him, [they would not be turned].
Thus, that noble path arises without [prior] cause;
the arising of that noble path is entirely due to the power of the Buddha.
For this reason, it is said that the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma.
Just as when a Wheel-Turning King has not yet placed the wheel-treasure in his left hand and turns it with his right hand,
even the devas cannot turn it; only after the king has turned it can they do so—
therefore it is said that the Wheel-Turning King is the one who turns it, and not others— it is the same in this case.
Some say that this statement was made based on the conditions for awakening; that is to say,
although the noble path exists within that body, it cannot arise unless it is first illuminated and touched by the light of the Buddha's words.
The arising of that noble path is entirely through the power of the Buddha; therefore, it is said that the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma.
It is, for example, like the various lotuses in a pond, such as the *utpala* and others.
Even so, as long as it has not been touched by the light of the sun, it does not open, it does not expand, and it is not fragrant;
when the sun's light shines upon it, it opens, expands, and becomes fragrant—this is also like that.
Some say that this statement is made based on the condition of removing obstacles; that is to say,
although the noble path exists within that body, [it is not manifest].
If the Buddha did not eliminate all the obscurations within their bodies by means of his unprecedented skill in the sets of names, phrases,
and syllables, then that noble path would have no way to arise.
That noble path arises because the Buddha has removed its obstacles;
therefore, it is said that the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma. Some say:
This statement is made based on the condition of supportive causes;
that is to say, although the Noble Path exists within that body,
if the Buddha does not drench it with the water of the Dharma, there is no way for the sprout of the Noble Path to arise.
That he was able to give rise [to the Path] was due to the Buddha's assistance;
therefore, it is said that the Buddha first turned the Wheel of Dharma.
It is like seeds within a granary which do not sprout because they lack the necessary conditions.
One should know that the arising of a sprout is due to the power of supporting conditions;
this case is also like that. Some say:
This statement is made based on the condition of guidance through instruction;
that is to say, although the noble path exists within their bodies,
if there were no such instruction from the Tathāgata’s speech to guide them, the noble path would not proceed within those bodies.
Because the Buddha reveals and instructs, that noble path proceeds;
therefore, it is said that the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma.
It is like a lamp illuminating a dark room, whereby one can see various objects to be grasped.
This is also like that.
Some say that right view arises from two causes and two conditions.
First, hearing the Dharma from others;
second, correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
Because of hearing the Dharma from others, it is said that the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma.
Because of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), it is said that they proceed spontaneously. Some say:
"If a person is endowed with four qualities, they are said to be one who accomplishes much."
This refers to associating with virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, attending to it correctly, and practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
Because of associating with virtuous persons and hearing the true Dharma, it is said that the Buddha turns the wheel of the Dharma.
Because he practiced the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma through correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), it is said that he himself turned the wheel of Dharma.
Question: When Kauṇḍinya abided in the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), one should have said that the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma.
Why is it that one is only said to have "turned" at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)?
Answer: Although one may be said to have turned at the time of the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), it is not yet ultimate;
it is only at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path that the turning becomes ultimate.
Some say that at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), it is called "transformation" because three conditions are fulfilled:

first, the relinquishing of the previously traversed path; second, the attainment of the hitherto unattained path; and third, the realization of the single taste (*ekarasa*) in the severance of the fetters.

Some say that at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), it is called "transformation" because five causal conditions are fulfilled: first, the relinquishing of the previously traversed path;

second, the acquisition of the hitherto untraversed path; third, the simultaneous realization of the single taste (*ekarasa*) regarding the severance of the fetters; fourth, the instantaneous attainment of the eight knowledges; and fifth, the simultaneous cultivation of the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).
"Abandoning the path already traversed" refers to abandoning the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
"Attaining the path not yet attained" refers to attaining the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
"The single-taste realization of the severance of fetters" refers to the realization of the collective abandonment of what is to be severed by insight within the three realms.
"Attaining the eight knowledges all at once" means attaining the four *dharmajñānas* and the four *anvayajñānas* simultaneously.
"Cultivating the sixteen aspects at one time" means cultivating the four aspects of suffering up to the four aspects of the path simultaneously.
Some say that at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), all afflictions to be abandoned by seeing have already been abandoned;

for since the afflictions to be countered by the receptivities (*kṣānti*) regarding the [four] truths have eternally destroyed the false nature of views, there is no longer any basis for those afflictions.
It is only at that time that it is called "transformation" (āśraya-parāvṛtti).
Some say that this transformation, when reaching the stage of fruition, can be designated and enumerated.
