There are phenomena and persons that possess characteristics, can be described, and can be designated; it is with reference to these that "transformation" (pravṛtti) is spoken of, and not because they were not so named previously.
Some say that this "transformation" mentioned here refers to the states of passing away and taking rebirth.
It is not that it was not called "turning" at an earlier time;
as the sūtra says: "When the Blessed One taught this Dharma-discourse, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya and eighty thousand devas [attained realization]."
One becomes distant from dust and free from defilement, and within all phenomena, the pure Dharma-eye arises.
Herein, "distant from dust" means being distant from latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
"free from defilement" means being free from the defilements of active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
"Among all phenomena" refers to within the four noble truths.
"The pure Dharma-eye arises" means that upon seeing the four noble truths, the pure Dharma-eye arises.
When the Buddha taught this Dharma-discourse, all five bhikṣus saw the Dharma.
Why is it that only Kauṇḍinya is mentioned?
The answer is: because Kauṇḍinya was the first to see the Dharma;
that is to say, Kauṇḍinya had already entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The remaining four [disciples] were still within the stage of the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
Some say that because the Blessed One had made a prior vow regarding them, he turned the wheel of Dharma with them as the foremost; therefore, they are mentioned specifically.
For this reason, the Buddha said to Kauṇḍinya, "Have you understood?
He replied, "I have understood.
A second and a third time, it was likewise.
For this reason, he was named Ājñāta.
[The interlocutor] asked: "Why did the World-Honored One ask him three times?
[The teacher] replied: "Because that Kauṇḍinya had already seen the Noble Truths."
The Blessed One then gave rise to knowledge of the past and future limits and made this observation:
"Are the aggregates, elements, and bases of the continuity of the evil destinies that Koṇāgamana was destined to undergo more numerous,
or are the moments, lava-s, and muhūrta-s that I have passed through during my three incalculable eons of the past more numerous?"
Having observed this, he saw that the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of Koṇāgamana’s continuity in the Avīci hell were far more numerous than the moments,
lava-s, and muhūrta-s that I have passed through during my three incalculable eons in the past.

Having seen this, he then thought: "I have practiced immeasurable hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful austerities throughout three incalculable eons, and have now attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Only by causing Kauṇḍinya to abide in the state where the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of that many successions of the Avīci hell are rendered non-arising, would my labors reach fulfillment even if I were to enter parinirvāṇa immediately;
how much more so for performing other deeds to bring him joy and consolation? For this reason, I asked him three times."
Furthermore, the Buddha saw that from an unknowable beginningless limit,
Kauṇḍinya has bound all sentient beings with the fetters of afflictions,
and all sentient beings have likewise bound Kauṇḍinya with the fetters of afflictions.
Furthermore, he saw that Kātyāyana was conceived within the mental continuums of all sentient beings,
and that all sentient beings were conceived within the mental continuum of Kātyāyana.
The same applies to their accounts of mutual injury and mutual devouring.
As it is with the vision of the past limit (*pūrvānta*), so it is with the vision of the future limit (*aparānta*).
Having perceived this, the Buddha then formed this thought:

I would consider my three incalculable eons of ascetic practice to have reached their full fruition if I were to cause even a single person, Kauṇḍinya, to be free from such things as these among all sentient beings.
How much more so, then, when he benefits immeasurable sentient beings with such profound joy; for this reason, he asked three times.
Some say that he asked three times in order to prevent slander.
This refers to when the Buddha was still a bodhisattva; weary of old age, sickness, and death, he departed from the city of Kapilavastu in search of unsurpassed wisdom.
At that time, King Śuddhodana dispatched five members of the Śākya clan to follow and attend upon him.
Second is the mother and third is the father.
Two types of mothers attain purity through the practice of desire;
three types of fathers attain purity through the practice of asceticism.
While the Bodhisattva was practicing austerities,
his mother and father, unable to bear it in their hearts, departed and left him. The Bodhisattva,
realizing that these subsequent austerities were not the path, abandoned them and accepted food consisting of rice porridge, boiled rice, ghee, and milk.
Anointing his body with oil, he practiced the middle way of conduct.
His three paternal relatives all declared that the Bodhisattva was deranged and had lost his resolve, and they likewise departed.
Thereupon, the two daughters, namely Nandā and Nandabalā, both came to attend upon him.
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"If those five men do not abandon me, how could I allow a woman to come and draw near?
Having accepted the food and consumed sixteen rounds of milk-rice gruel, the Bodhisattva’s physical strength increased further.
Having received the grass from the auspicious man, he went to the Bodhi tree, spread out a seat of grass, and sat down cross-legged, making this vow:
"I shall certainly not rise from this seat."
Having subdued the hosts of Māra’s army, forever severed all outflows (*āsrava*), and realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), he made this vow;
immediately thereafter, he utterly destroyed thirty-six *koṭis* of the evil Māra armies.
By means of thirty-four minds, he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
With the Buddha-eye, he surveys all worlds to see who should first hear his True Dharma, and for whom he should preach it.
Having observed this, he knew that Udraka Rāmaputra should first hear his Dharma.
At that time, a deva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Udraka Rāmaputra passed away yesterday."
Some say it was seven days.
At that time, the World-Honored One also gave rise to knowledge and vision, and knowing that he had passed away, he uttered this lament:
"He has lost a great benefit."
"If those who hear the Dharma I teach should attain right understanding, the World-Honored One further considered:
'Aside from them, whom else should I first hear the Dharma and for whom should I preach it?'"
Having observed this, he knew that Āḷāra Kālāma should be the first to hear his Dharma.
The deva spoke again, saying: "Seven days have already passed since Āḷāra Kālāma’s life ended."
Some say it was yesterday.
At that time, the World-Honored One also gave rise to knowledge and vision, knowing that he had passed away, and uttered this lament:
"He has lost a great benefit; had he heard the Dharma I preached, he would have attained right understanding."
Question: When the Buddha first attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for what reason did he not preach the Dharma to the two individuals, allowing them to pass away without hearing the teaching?
Was it not that his instruction had missed the opportune time?
Some say that when the Blessed One first attained Buddhahood, he had not yet given rise to the intention to teach the Dharma to others,
nor had he yet taken the realm of sentient beings as his object through great compassion.
There is no fault of failing to guide and transform others at the proper time.
The Venerable Ghosaka said:
"When the Buddha first attained unsurpassed enlightenment, because he cherished the Dharma so deeply, he contemplated it for many days."
They do not even give rise to the thought of food or drink,
much less can they give rise to the thought of preaching the Dharma for others.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
At the time of his initial attainment of Buddhahood, he had not yet established the distinctions between the three categories of sentient beings;
since he did not yet know who was fit for conversion and guidance and who was not, there was no fault.
Some say that at that time, the roots of virtue of those two individuals were not yet matured and they were not yet capable of hearing the Dharma.
Why is this? After the Buddha had attained enlightenment, if that first person still had more than fifty-seven days remaining of his life, he would have been capable of hearing the Dharma.
Some say: [this is the reason].
Fifty-six days.
Some say forty-nine days.
If that second person still has remaining life-force after another fifty-one days have passed, they should be capable of hearing the Dharma.
Some say it is fifty days; others say it is forty-three days.
Therefore, it is not the case that the Buddha’s transformation of beings has missed its proper time.
At times, the Blessed One may prolong his own life-force (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) to wait for those to be transformed, as he did in the case of Subhadra and others.
However, it is impossible for him to prolong the life-force of another.
Question: For what reason does the Buddha express such sorrowful lamentation?
Answer: Previously, those two took him as their teacher and practiced mundane meditative concentrations, yet they did not attain the true Dharma.
Now, having personally realized the unsurpassed true Dharma, the Buddha wishes to cause them to know it.
Furthermore, he laments because the person for whom he wished to benefit by means of his own realization has passed away.
It was asked: "Regarding the previous statement that 'if they were to hear my Dharma, they would attain right understanding,' in what stage does one attain right understanding?"
Some say that this refers to entering the stage of the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma-avakrānti*). Others say:
Regarding the stage of abiding in the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*),
some say it refers to the stage of arising the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
Speaking in this manner,
he causes [the opponent] to eliminate all conceit regarding omniscience,
so that they may know that only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses omniscience.
At that time, it was said that they had attained right understanding.
The World-Honored One further contemplated who else, besides those two individuals, should first hear his Dharma and whom he should teach.
Having observed this, he immediately knew that the five men, including Kauṇḍinya and the others, should hear the Dharma first.
He then thought:
"They were all my parents and kinsmen who previously honored and made offerings to me;
where now can I go to repay them?"
The deva immediately replied, "He is currently at the Deer Park of the Sages in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, the World-Honored One also gave rise to knowledge and vision, knowing he was in that place;
he then left the Bodhi tree and proceeded on foot toward Vārāṇasī.
Question: Since the Buddha possesses the most supreme supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), why does he travel on foot?
Answer: Out of reverence for the Dharma, he does not employ his supernormal power.
Nevertheless, while walking, his feet are always four finger-widths above the ground.
Each footprint was marked with joyful swirls and auspicious signs, lovely to behold;
the marks of the thousand-spoked wheels were as distinct as if painted.
Wherever the shadow of his body fell, for up to seven days, it caused the sense-faculties of any sentient being who reached that place to become peaceful and joyful.
Gradually traveling on, he arrived at Vārāṇasī.
At that time, the five men suddenly saw the Buddha from afar and immediately established a rule among themselves:
"That Gautama is indolent, overly demanding, deranged, and has lost his resolve; he has gained nothing at all."
Now they have come again, wishing to summon and entice us.
We should each refrain from conversing with them or paying them respectful greetings;
we need only prepare a single ordinary seat and let them sit upon it as they please.
At that time, as the World-Honored One gradually drew near, they were overwhelmed by his majestic power;
forgetting their original intention, they rose from their seats all at once and ran forward to meet him, joining their palms in homage.
Among them, some rearranged pure seats,
some took up the Buddha’s robe, some took up the Buddha’s bowl,
and some provided water.
Some washed their feet and all addressed the Buddha, saying, "We pray that you will please take a seat.
The Buddha then thought to himself: "Such foolish people establish their own restrictions only to break them a moment later."
Then the Buddha took his seat and sat down with serene composure;
his majestic radiance was extraordinary, like Mount Sumeru.
At that time, although the five men were respectful, they still addressed the Buddha as "Venerable One" (Āyuṣmat).
Or again, they addressed the Buddha by the name Gautama.
The Buddha then said to them: "Do not address the Tathāgata as 'Venerable One' (Āyuṣmat), nor call him by his personal name.
If you persist in doing so, you shall for a long night obtain no benefit and undergo various intense sufferings."
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has already realized unsurpassed bodhi and the peace of nirvāṇa;
he has crossed over birth, old age, sickness, and death, and awakened to the nature of all dharmas.
He protects all beings and is honored as the Sovereign of the Three Realms because he has accomplished the dharmas of boundless merit.
At that time, the five men said:
"Venerable sir, you are indeed that same Gautama of old;
your physical form and conduct are no different from those of former days, yet you are indolent,
full of excessive desires, and have lost your resolve through madness."
Having abandoned ascetic practices, he partakes of fine food and anoints his body with oil, so that his skin is nourished and radiant.
Although we know that the Venerable One himself claims to have realized unsurpassed enlightenment and the peace of nirvāṇa, who would believe him?
"But you do not permit me to state my name and clan.
The World-Honored One said, "Observe now my countenance, my majestic radiance, my faculties, and my deportment; are these the same as they were in the past?"
The five men replied,
"We observe that the Venerable One is truly different from what he was before.
The Buddha said:
If I had not realized the Dharma, how could I have attained such a state?
You should know by this that I have attained unsurpassed bodhi.
Why, then, do you still harbor a lack of faith toward the Tathāgata?
The World-Honored One then gradually transformed and guided them to bring them under his influence.
During the first part of the day, he taught, exhorted, and instructed two of them, while the other three entered the village to beg for food; the alms they collected were sufficient for all six.
Later, he divided himself into three persons to preach the Dharma and provide instruction and guidance.
He sent the other two persons into the village to beg for alms,
and the food and drink thus obtained were sufficient for all five of them.
Because the World-Honored One’s nature is free from eating at improper times,
he taught and transformed them in this manner for three months—
some say four months.
Having brought those five men to maturity in their roots of goodness,
on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, the Tathāgata turned the Wheel of the True Dharma for them;
at that time, Kauṇḍinya was the first to see the Dharma.
The Buddha then asked three times, "Do you understand?

This question was intended to ask: "Do you now perceive me as one who is indolent, full of excessive desires, deranged, and lost in will—someone who fails to realize unsurpassed *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, yet deceives you?"
Therefore, he asked three times whether [the Buddha] had understood;
the other replied three times in turn, "I have already understood this meaning," saying,
"As I now observe the Buddha, he is truly not indolent or one who seeks much."
Nor am I deranged or deprived of my senses;
furthermore, I have truly realized *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, and thus I am not deceiving you.
Since I have now answered three times for the sake of being a witness for the Buddha, I am now liberated.
Therefore, he asked three questions to stop the slander against the Buddha.
Some say that he asked these three questions to manifest the fulfillment of his original vow.
What was that matter?
It is heard that in the past, during this Bhadrakalpa, there was a king named Kali.
At that time, there was a rishi known as Kṣāntivādin.
He dwelt in a forest grove, diligently practicing austerities.
At that time, King Kali had removed all the men;
accompanied by his inner palace retinue, he performed various musical performances and sported in the woods, indulging his desires for a long time until he grew weary and fell asleep.

The women of the inner palace, for the sake of flowers and fruits, were wandering among the groves when they saw from afar the rishi sitting upright and meditating peacefully at his dwelling place; they immediately hurried toward him.
Having all gathered at that place, they prostrated, circumambulated him, and sat down.
The rishi then expounded upon the faults of desire, saying:
"All desires are impure and foul-smelling phenomena."
This is censurable and this is to be loathed.
What wise person would associate with it?
Sisters, you should all give rise to a sense of revulsion and abandon it.
When the king awoke from his sleep and did not see the women, he thought to himself,
"Could it be that someone has lured them away and taken them?
He immediately drew his sharp sword and searched for them everywhere.
He then saw the women sitting in a circle around the seer.
A great rage arose within him as he thought, "What great demon is this who has enticed my daughters?
He immediately stepped forward and asked him, "Who are you?"
He replied, "I am a rishi. He asked again, "What do you do here?
He answered, "I practice the path of patience."
The king thought to himself:
"This man says that I practice patience because he sees me being angry;
I shall now test him. He then asked again:
"Have you attained the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
He replied, "I have not.
He questioned him in succession until: "Have you attained the first dhyāna?"
He replied, "I did not. The king became doubly enraged and said, "You are a man who has not yet abandoned desire;
how could you indulge your passions so as to gaze upon my daughters?"
He spoke again, saying, "I am one who practices patience.
Extend an arm and test whether you can endure it.
At that time, the rishi extended an arm.
The king struck him with a sharp sword;
he fell to the ground like a severed lotus root.
The king questioned him again, "Who are you?"
He replied, "I am a man who practices patience.
Then the king ordered him to extend his other arm, which he likewise severed as before, and questioned him again.
The seer answered as he had before: "I am a man who practices patience."
In this manner, he next cut off both feet and then severed both ears.
He also sliced off his nose, interrogating him one by one; the answers were all as before.
Once the seer’s body had been reduced to seven pieces fallen upon the ground, forming seven wounds, the king’s mind finally ceased [its violence].
The seer said:
"O King, why do you now become weary and discouraged?
Even if my entire body were cut into pieces as small as mustard seeds or even fine dust,"
I, too, did not give rise to even a single thought of anger or resentment;
my practice of patience was ultimately without duality.
Furthermore, I made this vow:
"Just as you have today, though I am truly innocent,
severed my body into seven parts and made it into seven wounds,
so shall it be for me in future lives."
When you attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
with a heart of great compassion and without waiting for your request, you will first cause you to cultivate the sevenfold path to sever the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
You should know that the seer Kṣāntivādin at that time was none other than the present World-Honored One, Śākyamuni;
and King Kali was none other than the present Venerable Kauṇḍinya.
Thus, after Kātyāyana had seen the Noble Truths, the Buddha, by means of his supernormal power,
removed his obscuration of darkness and caused him to recollect events from past lives;
he then personally saw that he himself had been King Kali and the Buddha had been a seer.
He himself used a sharp sword to sever the Buddha’s seven limbs, creating seven wounds;
yet the Buddha felt no anger or resentment, but instead sought to benefit him through his vow.
Therefore, the World-Honored One asked three times whether he understood.
This intention was to ask: "How could I have contravened my former vow?
Is it not as if my original vow has already been fulfilled?
At that time, Kauṇḍinya, filled with extreme shame and remorse, joined his palms in reverence and likewise answered three times before attaining liberation.
This mind replied: "Truly, World-Honored One, you do not contradict your former vows; as originally vowed, they have all been fulfilled.
I was formerly ignorant and committed such extreme evil."
"I only pray that you will have compassion and forgive my grave offense.
For this reason, the Buddha questioned him three times so as to fulfill his original vow. Some say:
The World-Honored One questioned him three times to demonstrate his own skillful power in expounding the Dharma, saying:
"This is my intention: throughout three incalculable eons, I have cultivated immeasurable hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful practices."
Because the Dharma realized [by him] was skillfully explained, it enabled them to attain awakening and understanding in an instant; therefore, he asked three times.
Some say that the Blessed One asked three times so that the other four would hear it, give rise to courageous exertion, and swiftly enter the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
Some say: The Blessed One wished to demonstrate that within the well-expounded Dharma,
both the teacher and his disciples have realized the Dharma with thorough certainty and truth, free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Unlike the non-Buddhists, who give rise to overweening pride regarding dharmas they have not yet attained, claiming they have already attained them,
[the Buddha] therefore asked three questions.
Question: When the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma, eighty thousand devas likewise realized the Dharma.
For what reason, then, is it said that he turned the wheel of Dharma for only the five people, including Kauṇḍinya?
The answer is that here only those who are the primary intended recipients are mentioned.
Because the various devas heard [the teaching] by means of the five persons, they were not the primary intended recipients, and therefore they are not mentioned. Some say:
Because humans first perceive the Dharma, it is explained specifically for them.
Some say that humans are directly perceived, whereas devas are not directly perceived.
Some say that while the Buddha’s physical form, deportment, and activities are entirely identical to those of the human realm, they are not so for the gods.
Others say:
If in a certain place it is said that the Dharma has perished, it is precisely in that same place that the turning of the Wheel of Dharma is said to occur.
That is to say, although there may be those among the devas who have realized the ambrosia (amṛta), if there are none among human beings, it is called the extinction of the Dharma.
Therefore, it is said that he turns the wheel of Dharma specifically for humans.
Some say that among humans, the Buddha’s disciples have the distinction of four assemblies, whereas this is not the case among the devas.
Some say that when the Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma, he took humans as witnesses,
not devas. Others say:
Among humans, there are those who can transform [the faculties] as well as those for whom they are transformed; therefore, it is taught [in their case].
Among devas, there are only those for whom [the faculties] are transformed and none who can transform them; therefore, it is not taught [in their case].
Some say that among humans one can attain various kinds of distinguished merits,
whereas this is not the case among the devas.
Therefore, it is said that he turned the wheel of Dharma for the sake of humans.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 182, of the *Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Volume 100.
Composed by the five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhiskandha), Chapter Four: The Sub-section on Non-returners (Anāgāmin), Part Ten. Regarding the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, the Earth Deities raised their voices and proclaimed it from one to another, as explained at length. Question: Were there not also other assemblies of celestial deities who raised their voices to inform one another?
For what reason is it said that only the earth deities raise their voices?
Answer: Because those earth deities were the first to utter the sound.
Question: Why do the earth deities utter the sound first?
The answer is: because he dwells closest to the Buddha’s presence;

furthermore, because he constantly follows the Buddha to serve as his protector—from the time the Bodhisattva was in the womb, his birth, his departure from the city, his renunciation, and his practice of austerities, up until his attainment of Buddhahood and his turning of the wheel of Dharma.
They have constantly followed and protected [the Buddha] so that no obstacles might arise.
Now, seeing the Tathāgata turn the wheel of Dharma, they leap for joy;
they rejoice in themselves because the merit they previously exerted has now reached its fulfillment, and thus they proclaim this first.
Furthermore, although there were other hosts of devas present in the assembly, those earth-deities (bhūmidevatā) are by nature flighty; therefore, they were the first to cry out.
Just as many among the present assembly who are flighty by nature delight in loud voices, so it was with them.
Furthermore, the nature of the earth deities is characterized by much joy and celebration;
seeing this rare phenomenon, they were filled with extreme delight and thus sounded their voices first.
Furthermore, this follows the sequential order of proximity and distance.
That is to say, first the earth deities proclaim it;
next, the space deities;
and then the gods of the Four Great Kings.
In this manner, as the sound was transmitted in succession for a brief moment, it reached the Brahma-world.
[The opponent asks: "Since sound is momentary by nature, such that it must perish at the very place where it arises, how can it be said to reach the Brahma-world?"
Answer: This statement is made based on the sense of successive transmission.

That is to say, after the earth deities have proclaimed it, the space deities proclaim it, and so on, successively announcing it up to the Brahma heavens; it is like the manner of lighting lamps, which successively increases and expands. Some say this.
When the Wheel of Dharma was turned, immeasurable hosts of devas all gathered; having heard the Dharma, they each returned to their respective abodes.
Announcing it to their own retinues, the sound was passed along in succession until it reached the Brahma world.

Some say that at that time, there was no fixed sequence of priority or posteriority in the production of sounds; rather, this statement was made because it is the conventional rule for a speaker to describe things in a specific order.
The Earth Deity first proclaimed this, and so forth, as explained at length.
As stated in the Sūtras, when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, his voice reaches as far as the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations;
when the Buddha turns the Wheel of Dharma for Kauṇḍinya and the others, his voice reaches the Brahma World.
When the Buddha attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, his voice reached the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Question: Why are there these three distinctions?
Answer: When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, he [establishes] the ten wholesome dharmas.
Instructing sentient beings,
this dharma will certainly receive its maturation fruit among the gods of the desire realm;
the hosts of the six heavens of the desire realm will all give rise to joy, thinking, "Our retinues will soon increase."
Therefore, when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, his fame reaches as far as the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations.
When the Brahma King requests the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, he hears of the Buddha turning the wheel of Dharma and rejoices with deep celebration and sympathetic joy.
Therefore, when he turns the wheel of Dharma, the sound reaches the Brahma world.
The Śuddhāvāsa devas awaken the bodhisattva, causing him to leave the city and renounce the world to seek unsurpassed wisdom.
Upon hearing that the bodhisattva has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they feel profound joy and consolation.
Therefore, when he first attained Buddhahood, his voice reached up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

Furthermore, because a Wheel-Turning King is one who experiences sensual desires, when he appears in the world, his voice reaches only as far as the Desire Realm and does not extend to the stages beyond desire.
When the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma, within a single assembly there are distinctions of honor and status, superiority and inferiority;
this matter extends as far as the Brahma world.
Therefore, when he turns the wheel of Dharma, the sound reaches the Brahma heavens.
Only the Tathāgata’s reputation is so lofty and far-reaching that there is nowhere it does not reach.
Therefore, when the Buddha attains unsurpassed bodhi, his voice pervades all places where it ought to go.
This extends even up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Even if sentient beings in the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra) were to possess auditory consciousness, sound would still penetrate there. Why is this so?
Because the Tathāgata has long cultivated the karma of renown.
Furthermore, among all classes of sentient beings, there are superior, middling, and inferior types who perform and increase the karma of great renown;
the inferior type is exemplified by a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
The middling are such as Kauṇḍinya and others;
the superior refers to the Buddha.
Therefore, there is nearness and distance regarding those sounds.
Furthermore, among the various classes of sentient beings, those who perform and cultivate pure and noble karma are categorized as superior, middling, and inferior.
The inferior are like the wheel-turning kings; the middling are like Kauṇḍinya and others.
The "superior" refers to the Buddha.
Therefore, the sound reaches [the listener] either near or far.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
All classes of sentient beings show reverence and offer praise to their parents,
teachers, elders, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas,
and the disciples of the Buddha.
The actions of body, speech, and mind are categorized as superior, middling, and inferior.
Those that are inferior are like those of a wheel-turning monarch;
those that are middling are like those of Kauṇḍinya and others.
The "highest" refers to the Buddha.
Therefore, sound reaches three different levels.
Question: Since there is also sound in the higher realms, why does the sound when turning the Wheel of Dharma reach only as far as the Brahma-world?
The answer is: because vocal informative action (vāg-vijñapti-karma) and sound reach only that [lower] level;
furthermore, because the mental formations of speech (vāk-saṃskāra)—that is to say, vitarka and vicāra—reach only that level;
and furthermore, because ear-consciousness (śrotra-vijñāna) exists only up to that level and not in the higher levels.

Some say that it is only up to the Brahma-world that one can fully give rise to wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured-neutral vocal intimation (vāgvijñapti) and sound, because these do not exist in the higher realms. Furthermore,
it is only up to the Brahma-world that the ear-consciousness (śrotravijñāna) can fully manifest as wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured-neutral, because it does not exist in the higher realms.
Some say:
if there are sentient beings in a particular place, the sound reaches them at the time the wheel of Dharma is being turned.
Furthermore, if a place is defined as the boundary of the trichiliocosm, the sound reaches that place.
Some say that the Brahma-world is the place where sentient beings of the world hold the highest esteem; therefore,
when the Wheel of Dharma was turned, the sound reached only as far as that realm.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the various devas of the higher realms are also called Brahmā; therefore,
when the Wheel of Dharma was turned, the sound reached as far as the Brahma-world.
It is not only up to the stage of the first dhyāna.
Question: Are all the teachings spoken by the Buddha called the Wheel of Dharma? Answer: No.
Only that which causes one to enter the path of seeing is called the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra).
Question: If that is so, many people hear the Buddha’s teaching and enter the path of seeing;
why are they not all called the Wheel of Dharma?
Answer: Although all of those are indeed wheels of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), it is said that the wheel of Dharma refers to that which first attains correct realization and that which attains it last.
"First" refers to Kauṇḍinya and the others.
Later, Subhadra asked:
"Is the place where all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma fixed?
If it were fixed, how would one reconcile this with the fundamental story of Dīpaṃkara Buddha?"
As it is said that the Buddha Dīpaṃkara turned the wheel of the true Dharma on Mount Kailāsa in the city of Dīpāvatī,
and so forth at length:
if [the location] were not fixed, how would one reconcile this with the verse spoken by Dharmasubhūti?
As it is said:
One should recollect the past Buddhas here at Rishipatana in Varanasi,
in the Deer Park, where they too first turned the sublime Dharma.
Some say: One should state that the place where the wheel of Dharma was turned is fixed. If this is so, how should one reconcile this with the past life story of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara?
The answer is: it is not necessary to reconcile this.
Why is this so? This is not what is taught in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma;
rather, it is merely what has been handed down by various traditions, some of which may be correct and others incorrect.
If one must reconcile this, one should know that the city of Dīpāvatī in the past was precisely the present-day Vārāṇasī,
and Mount Khadiraka in the past was precisely the present-day Ṛṣipatana Mṛgadāva.
If one were to say that the place where the Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma is fixed,
it is said that there are four fixed locations and two non-fixed locations.
The four sites of fixed [events] are: the site of the Bodhi tree,
the site of turning the wheel of Dharma,
and the sites of descending from and ascending to the heavens.
The places where he manifests great supernormal transformations.
Regarding the two places that are not fixed, these refer to the place of the Buddha’s birth and the place of his parinirvāṇa.
How is it known that the place of the Bodhi tree is fixed?
Answer: It has been heard that in the past there was a Wheel-Turning King who, leading his fourfold army, flew through the air and arrived above the Bodhi tree;
thereupon his wheel stopped, and he could not proceed further.
The king then became terrified and thought to himself,
"Could it be that I am about to lose my royal throne, or that there is danger to my life?
At that moment, the deity of the Bodhi tree addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, do not be alarmed; Your Majesty shall not lose your throne, nor shall you face any peril to your life.
Do you not see the Bodhi tree below?
Within it lies the Vajrāsana, upon which all Bodhisattvas realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
The King, wishing to pass through, was told, "You should avoid this place and proceed by another path.
Thereupon, the King made various offerings to the Bodhi tree and departed by another route.
By this matter, one knows that the location of the Bodhi tree is fixed.
Regarding the fixed location where the Wheel of Dharma was turned, it is as previously cited in the verses of Subhūti.
Furthermore, how is it known that the location for descending from and ascending to the heavens is fixed?
He replied, "I have heard that after the Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, difficulties arose in this place and all the bhikṣus abandoned it;
subsequently, non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners came to dwell there."
Later, when other bhikṣus came seeking that place, they said to the non-Buddhists:
"This is the place from which our teacher descended from the heavens; you should depart quickly."
The various non-Buddhists said,
"This is our permanent dwelling place. Because of this,
the two groups engaged in a great deal of strife and contention.
The elders, householders, and various officials of the city of Upatiṣya came to resolve the dispute, but they were unable to do so;
even when the king himself attempted to settle it, he could not reach a definitive conclusion.
Then the bhikṣus said to the non-Buddhists, "Now we shall both utter words of sincerity;
whichever side belongs to the truth shall have a portentous sign.
The non-Buddhists replied, "So be it."
He then invited [the Buddha] first, but it was in vain and there was no sign.
The bhikṣu then spoke these words of solemn truth:

"If this place is indeed where all Tathāgatas ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma to their compassionate mothers for three months and then descended, let a miraculous sign appear."
At that time, a stone lion atop a great stone pillar at that dwelling place let out a roar.
The non-Buddhists were terrified and immediately fled.
From the lion’s mouth, there further emerged various precious flower garlands that entwined and completely encircled the stone pillar.
At that time, the onlookers marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus came to dwell together.
From this, it is known that the Buddha’s descent from the heavens was to a fixed location.
Furthermore, how is it known that he dwells in meditative concentration while manifesting great supernormal transformations?

The answer is: It has been heard that once, when the Buddha was pursued through six great cities by non-Buddhist practitioners who found no place to escape him, they gathered together and requested to compete with the Tathāgata in their supernormal powers.
The Buddha did not grant permission in all cases;
it was only when he reached the city of Śrāvastī that he finally consented to manifest supernatural transformations.

Thereupon, immeasurable non-Buddhists returned to the Buddha and left the household life. From this, one knows that the manifestation of great supernatural transformations must occur at a fixed location.
Some say that the places where the Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma are not fixed. Why is this?
If Udraka Rāmaputra and Ārāḍa Kālāma had not passed away,
would the Buddha have abandoned the kingdom of Magadha to go to Vārāṇasī?
Therefore, it is known that the turning of the wheel of Dharma occurs precisely where those who first hear the Dharma happen to be, according to their needs.
Question: If this is so, how should one interpret the verse of Subhūti?
Answer: It is not necessary to provide an explanation for this. Why is that?
Because this is not what is taught in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma.
However, these are prose and verse.
Now, in composing prose and verse, there may be additions or omissions.
If one insists on reconciling this, it was because in the past there was also a Buddha who turned the wheel of Dharma here at the very beginning.
It is not because it applies to all that it is said to be non-definitive.
If one were to say this,
then the place where the wheel of Dharma was turned would be indefinite.
He states that there are three locations which are fixed and three locations which are not fixed.
The three fixed locations are: the site of the Bodhi tree, the place where he descended from the heavens, and [the place of his parinirvāṇa].
The places where great supernormal transformations are manifested.
Regarding the three places that are not fixed, these refer to the place of birth and the place where the wheel of Dharma is turned.
Regarding the place of parinirvāṇa:
as it has been said, the Buddha, at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana,
turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma for Kauṇḍinya and others.
Question: For what reason is it named Vārāṇasī?
Answer: This is the name of a river; because a royal city was established not far from it, this city is also named Vārāṇasī.
Question: For what reason is it called the "Abode of the Sages' Discourse"?
Answer: It is because it is said that all Buddhas invariably turn the wheel of Dharma at this very place.
They say that because the Buddha is the supreme ṛṣi and he first turned the wheel of Dharma at this very place, it is therefore called the "Site of the Ṛṣis' Discourse.
If one were to say that the Buddhas do not invariably turn the wheel of Dharma at this location, [then the name would not apply].
It should be said that these are "abodes of sages" (*ṛṣipatana*).
This means that when a Buddha appears in the world, they are the abodes where the Great Sage, the Buddha, and the assembly of sages who are his noble disciples reside;
when no Buddha appears in the world, they are the abodes where the pratyekabuddha-sages reside.
If there were no Pratyekabuddhas at that time, but there were worldlings who were seers possessing the five mundane supernormal powers,
this place would be called a "seer's abode" because it has always been, is now, and will continue to be inhabited by such seers.
Some say it should be called Ṛṣipatana (The Place Where the Sages Fell). Formerly,
five hundred sages were traveling through the air when they encountered the conditions for their downfall here and fell all at once.
Question: For what reason is it called the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva)?
Answer: Because deer constantly roam and dwell in this grove, it is named the Deer Park.
Formerly, there was a king named Brahmadatta.
Because this grove was given as a gift to the herd of deer, it is named Mṛgadāva (Deer Park).
It is like the householder Kalandaka, who,
within the Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha, dug a pond and gave it to the Kalandaka birds.
Because they were made to sport there, it was named the Kalandaka-nivāpa Pond.
This [grove] is likewise so named, and is thus called the Mṛgadāva (Deer Park).
What is the True Dharma?
Answer: The untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As a gāthā says:
"The Three Buddhas of the three times Are able to destroy all sorrows and poisons;
They all revere the True Dharma And constantly abide in the nature of phenomena."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"There are two types of persons capable of upholding the true Dharma:
namely, the teacher and the practitioner."
The Vinaya states that my True Dharma should remain for a thousand years, or perhaps even longer;
however, because women were permitted to go forth, it has been reduced by five hundred years.
Although the Blessed One spoke of the True Dharma in various places, [the specific duration was not stated there].
Yet one does not engage in conceptual discrimination.
What is the True Dharma?
The sūtras are the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
That which has not yet been explained therein shall now be explained; for this reason, this treatise is composed.
Question: Are the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment associated with outflows (sāsrava) the True Dharma? If they are, [then...]
Why is this not stated here?
If it is not [the case that all are the True Dharma], why is it that the untainted (anāsrava) is the True Dharma while the tainted (sāsrava) is not? Some say:
That too is the True Dharma.
Question: Why is this not mentioned here?
Answer: When that which ought to be stated is not stated, one should know that the meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, the contaminated faculties and so forth are the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for the uncontaminated.
If one speaks of the fundamental [uncontaminated states], the preparatory stages are already included therein and thus are not mentioned separately.
Furthermore, because the contaminated faculties and so forth are the preparatory stages for the uncontaminated, they are also termed "uncontaminated."
Therefore, these are already included within what was previously stated.
Some say that the contaminated faculties (*sāsrava-indriya*) and so forth are not the true Dharma (*saddharma*).
Question: Why is it that the untainted (anāsrava) is the True Dharma, while the tainted (sāsrava) is not?
Answer: Because tainted phenomena possess defects and afflictions;
only that which is free from defects and afflictions is designated as the True Dharma.
Furthermore, that which is pure and praiseworthy is called the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Because contaminated phenomena (*āsravadharma*) are contrary to this, they are not the True Dharma.
Furthermore, the True Dharma is that which can eternally bring about emergence from birth and death and attain parinirvāṇa.
Because the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) states are not so, they are not called the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

Question: Are the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) also the True Dharma? If they are, why are they not mentioned here?

If it is not so, for what reason are the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) considered the true Dharma, while the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth are not?
Answer: They too are the true Dharma.
Question: If that is so, why are they not mentioned here?
One should understand that when something promised to be explained is not explained, the meaning is incomplete.

Furthermore, if the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth were mentioned, they would accord with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) in this context, but they do not accord with the specific purpose of this particular text; therefore, they are not mentioned.
Furthermore, the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), and the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) are also all subsumed within what has been explained here.

That is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness are subsumed under the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya), the power of wisdom (prajñābala), the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicayasaṃbodhyaṅga), and right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).
The four right endeavors are subsumed under the faculty of energy, the power of energy, the awakening factor of energy, and right effort.
The four bases of psychic power are subsumed under the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the awakening factor of concentration, and right concentration.
To what extent can it be said that the True Dharma abides?
Answer: It is when those who practice the Dharma abide.
To what extent can it be said that the True Dharma perishes?
Answer: When the practitioner of the Dharma has passed away.
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that the Dharma and Vinaya realized and taught by the Tathāgata cannot be extinguished or submerged by the earth element,
the water element, the fire element, or the wind element."
However, there will arise a certain class of individuals who possess evil desires and engage in evil conduct;
they will establish what is unrighteous as righteous and what is righteous as unrighteous.
They declare what is not the Vinaya to be the Vinaya,
and they declare what is the Vinaya to be not the Vinaya;
they will cause the extinction of my True Dharma, accumulated over three incalculable eons, leaving nothing remaining.
Although the sūtras state this, they do not analyze to what extent one should say that the True Dharma (saddharma) abides,
nor to what extent one should say that the True Dharma has perished.
That sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Since that [sūtra] does not provide a detailed analysis of certain points, this treatise is now composed in order to analyze them.
Within this, there are two kinds of true dharma (*saddharma*).
First, the conventional true dharma;
second, the ultimate true dharma.
The conventional true dharma refers to the collections of names, phrases, and syllables.
These are the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
The ultimate true Dharma refers to the Noble Path, namely the untainted faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and factors of the path.
Those who practice the Dharma are also of two kinds.
First, upholding the Dharma of teaching;
second, upholding the Dharma of realization.
Upholding the Dharma of teaching refers to reading, reciting, and explaining the sūtras and so forth.
Those who uphold the realized Dharma are those capable of cultivating and realizing the untainted noble path.
Those who uphold the taught Dharma ensure that the conventional true Dharma endures for a long time by maintaining its continuity without interruption.
If those who uphold the realization maintain an uninterrupted continuity, they can cause the sublime Dharma of ultimate truth to endure for a long time;
when they cease to exist, the sublime Dharma likewise ceases.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "My sublime Dharma does not abide by means of walls, pillars, or the like."
Sentient beings abide solely by relying on the continuity of their practice of the Dharma.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One not definitively state the duration for which the Dharma would remain?
Answer: It was because he wished to demonstrate that the longevity or brevity of the True Dharma depends upon those who practice it.

That is to say, if those who practice the Dharma conduct themselves according to the right practice, they will always be as if the Buddha were present in the world, or as if it had not been long since his parinirvāṇa;
thus, the Buddha’s True Dharma will abide eternally in the world without ever perishing.
If there are no such practitioners of the True Dharma, then that True Dharma will quickly perish and disappear.
As the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Within my well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya..."
If women had not been permitted to go forth and receive ordination, my True Dharma would have remained for a thousand years,
or even longer. Because women were permitted to go forth and receive ordination, the duration of my True Dharma has been reduced by five hundred years.
Question: If the True Dharma remains for a full thousand years, why did the World-Honored One speak in such a manner?
Answer: This was spoken with the underlying intention (*samdhāya*) that liberation is firm and unshakable.
This means that if one had ordained a woman without first crossing over [the obstacles], liberation would have remained firm for a thousand years;
however, in these latter five hundred years, only the firmness of ethical discipline, learning, and meditative concentration remains, while liberation does not.
This is merely the fault of permitting women to go forth [into the religious life].
Other masters say that this was spoken with the underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*) that the eight rules of respect (*gurudharma*) were not being observed.
That is to say, if one were to ordain women as nuns without requiring them to observe the eight rules of respect, the Buddha’s True Dharma would have remained for only five hundred years.
Because the Buddha required them to observe these eight rules of respect, the True Dharma remains in the world for a full thousand years.
Question: How does the True Dharma of the Tathāgata come to extinction?
Answer: When the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is about to perish, three kings will appear in this Jambudvīpa.
There are two kinds of kings: those who possess the Dharma and those who lack the Dharma.
He who possesses the Dharma was born in the East; through his majestic virtue, compassion, and benevolence, he brought the five regions of India under his sway.
Those who lack the Dharma are born among the Ḍomba-Mlecchas;
by nature they are all stubborn and ignorant, and they harbor hatred and contempt for the Buddha-dharma.
Joining together in confederacy, they invade and plunder from the west, gradually entering India and advancing toward the east.
His resolve will cause great decline to the Buddha-dharma;
wherever he goes, he will destroy stūpas and ruin monasteries,
killing many bhikṣus— none who are widely learned or maintain the precepts shall escape him.
He burned the scriptures until not a single one remained.
At that time, the King of the East heard that the Dāxù Mièlìchē King had invaded India and was gradually advancing toward the East.
He then led his troops to engage them in battle.
The enemy king’s army immediately retreated and fled; he captured both kings and took their lives.
Thereupon, he dispatched messengers to all quarters to summon all śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya.
I invite you all to assemble and reside within my kingdom; for as long as I live,
I shall provide and offer you clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites,
as well as whatever else you may require, so that you lack for nothing.
Then, all the bhikṣus residing throughout Jambudvīpa gathered together in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the king established a five-year festival day by day, providing various kinds of offerings.
However, because the bhikṣus receive many offerings and gains,
and because many have gone forth into homelessness primarily for the sake of their livelihood,
they are unable to apply themselves diligently to the recitation and study of the sūtras.
They take no pleasure in solitary dwelling, meditative concentration, or contemplation.
By day, they gather in crowds to discuss worldly affairs, causing agitation and clamor;
by night, they are weary and indolent, indulging in sleep without any self-awareness.
Consequently, they treat all the Buddha’s instructions with negligence and fail to practice them.
At that time, there will be only two who follow the Dharma in Jambudvīpa.
The first was an arhat named Sulata;
the second was a master of the Tripitaka named Śīghra,
also known as Pan-zhu.
He became the leader of the assembly.
On that very day, as the True Dharma was about to perish,
at the first watch of the day, the king of the city of Kauśāmbī was the chief among them.
At that time, five hundred lay devotees (śraddhā-upāsaka) simultaneously established five hundred monasteries (saṃghārāma),
raising their hands in discussion because they had previously heard that the Dharma was about to perish.
When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the Dharma to his two classes of disciples:
first, those who live at home; second, those who have left the home life.
Do not say that [the Dharma] now depends solely upon the disciples who live at home.
Because you were unable to provide for and support those who have gone forth as renunciants,
causing them to fall into want, the True Dharma has perished;
it is solely due to the lack of correct practice among you, the disciples who have gone forth, that the True Dharma has been extinguished.
Some say: Just as in the custom of hosting guests, where sumptuous meals are provided both at the beginning and at the end,
so too with the True Dharma, which is provided in abundance both when it first appears and when it is about to perish.
They all provided abundant material resources and offerings for his support.
Some say that he thought:
"As long as the Buddha-dharma has not yet ceased, there are still immeasurable fields of merit in the world."
If the Buddha-dharma were to perish, the world would possess only limited fields of merit;
fortunately, as the Buddha-dharma has not yet perished,
we should together seize this opportune moment to perform what ought to be done.
Some say that when Śākyamuni was a bodhisattva, he saw that past buddhas had their True Dharma extinguished either due to a lack of material requisites or because of the occurrence of epidemics.
He immediately made this vow:
"May I attain Buddhahood, and may this matter not cause the Dharma to perish.
Thus, although the Dharma may decline, may the material requisites remain abundant and the dwelling places expand."
That night, within the saṃghārāma, for the sake of the poṣadha ceremony, immeasurable bhikṣus gathered together.
At that time, the *karmadāna* invited the community leader, the Tripiṭaka-master Śīrṣaka, to recite the Prātimokṣa for the assembly; he consented and intended to explain it in brief.
Then the Arhat Surata rose from his seat,
bared one shoulder, prostrated at the feet of the Tripitaka Master, and with palms joined, said:
"I pray that the Elder will extensively expound the Tripitaka for the sake of the assembly."
He replied,
"In this assembly, who is able to fully practice the Prātimokṣa precepts and request me to explain them in detail?
An Arhat said:
"Just as the bhikṣus and others during the Buddha's lifetime were able to practice to the very limits of all the training rules (śikṣāpada),
if this is called 'being able to practice fully,' I pray that you will explain it in detail."
When these words were spoken, a disciple of the Tripitaka Master gave rise to great anger and rebuked him, saying:
"What kind of bhikṣu is this?
To deliberately oppose my teacher before the assembly and refuse to accept his instruction!"
They then conspired together to take the life of that arhat,
whereby the ultimate True Dharma was extinguished from that point on.
At that time, there were devas, nāgas, and yakṣas who held that arhat in deep reverence.
Arising with great wrath and anger, he killed that Tripitaka master.
According to another account,
it was a disciple of that Arhat who took the life of the Tripitaka master in order to take revenge.
Some say that when the king heard that the Arhat had been killed despite being innocent, he was overcome with grief and remorse,
and consequently put the Tripitaka Master to death.
The mundane true Dharma perishes from this point on.
At that time, both the ultimate and mundane true Dharmas of the world will have vanished.
Seven days and nights having passed, heaven and earth will be shrouded in darkness, yet the world will still not know that the true Dharma has already ceased to exist.
Why is this? Because when the Buddha was formerly a bodhisattva, he delighted in concealing the faults of others and did not expose matters that others had hidden or covered up.
Due to this karma, the Dharma will perish after seven days, with no one to know it.
After the seven days have passed, the great earth will tremble, stars will fall, and fire will rain down, burning all the quarters and intermediate directions.
In the sky, celestial drums resounded with a roar so terrifying that the hosts of celestial Māras were filled with great joy;
they spread a vast white canopy across the void.
Again, a great voice resounded in the air, proclaiming:
"The True Dharma of the Great Seer Śākyamuni shall from this day forth perish forever;
henceforth, none shall again enter the state of rightness and departure from birth."
The gate of the wondrous nectar is forever closed;
great suffering and darkness pervade the world,
and there is no longer anyone to provide protection or guidance.
Some maintain this view:
"At that time, all vows, ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*), and boundary demarcations (*sīmābandha*) were abandoned.
According to those who speak thus, from that point onward there have been no further boundary demarcations, ritual procedures, or formal ordinations.
Nevertheless, that which previously existed is not abandoned at this time.
In some cases, the True Dharma of certain Buddhas perishes even before they have entered parinirvāṇa;
in other cases, the True Dharma of certain Buddhas perishes seven days after they have entered parinirvāṇa.
However, from the time after my Parinirvāṇa until the True Dharma (saddharma) is extinguished at the end of a thousand years,
there are those for whom the True Dharma is extinguished before they have entered Parinirvāṇa, as well as those for whom it is extinguished seven days after their Parinirvāṇa has already occurred.
The entry into the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) being no longer possible is called "extinction" (nirodha).
The extinction of the True Dharma of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni is called "extinction" in the sense of the severance of the realm of ambrosia (amṛta-dhātu).
Although the realm of ambrosia still exists even among the gods, it is called "extinction" because it is extinguished within the human realm.
Question: For what reason do the True Dharmas of past Buddhas undergo extinction while their Parinirvāṇa has not yet occurred?
Question: Some [Buddhas] pass away seven days after their parinirvāṇa;
why is it that the present Śākyamuni Buddha passes away only after a thousand years?
Answer: The lifespans of the Buddhas of the past were long and far-reaching.
Because much of what ought to be done regarding that True Teaching had already been accomplished during the Buddha’s lifetime, the Dharma quickly declined.
Now, at the time when the World-Honored One Śākyamuni appeared, the lifespan was short, occurring only one hundred years after his passing.
Although the work of the True Teaching may not be fully completed even after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
as long as it endures for a thousand years, there will be those among them who plant roots of goodness,
those who reach maturity, and those who attain liberation.
Therefore, it is only after a long period that the True Dharma finally perishes.
Some say that among the disciples of the Buddhas of the past, they cherished *śamatha* more than *vipaśyanā*.
Because they place excessive emphasis on śamatha, they dwell constantly in tranquility;
since they do not delight in proclaiming the twelvefold teachings such as the sūtras, the Dharma will quickly perish.
Now, the disciples of the Blessed One cherish and value vipaśyanā rather than śamatha.
Because they place great emphasis on vipaśyanā,
they dwell frequently in contemplation and delight in transmitting the twelvefold teachings, such as the sūtras;
therefore, the True Dharma will not perish for a long time.
Question: Once the True Dharma has ceased, are there no longer those who attain the state of a noble one?
Answer: There are indeed those who, from the fruit of stream-entry, attain the fruit of once-returning;
and from the fruit of once-returning, they attain the fruit of non-returning.
One attains the fruit of arhatship from the fruit of non-returning,
yet there is no one who enters the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) from the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya).
It is solely by virtue of this that the True Dharma is said to perish.
"If one first enters the untainted first dhyāna," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was composed in order to refute the doctrines of other schools and to clarify one's own position.
That is to say, some say that there is no cultivation of the future,
while others say [there is].
The Noble Path is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Some say that the Noble Path is one.
To stop that misconception and to demonstrate that there is cultivation of the future,
as well as to show that the Noble Path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and not a single unity,
this treatise was composed.
If there were no cultivation of future [dharmas], then there would be no sense of increase regarding meritorious qualities;
the Buddha, at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), would not possess all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Furthermore, if the Noble Path were unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it could not be cultivated.
Because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are not objects of cultivation,
if the Noble Path were a single entity, there would be no distinction between the three time periods. Consequently,
the Sūtra should not have spoken of Buddhas of the three time periods and so forth.
Question: If the Noble Path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and not a single entity, why does the Sūtra state:
"I have realized the ancient path, which is unique and without a second"?
Answer: This statement is made on account of five reasons.
This refers to the similarity of application (*prayoga*), the similarity of aspect (*ākāra*), and so forth, as explained in detail in the *Jñānaskandha*.

If one first enters the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna, by virtue of attaining this, one also attains all other untainted mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*). To which time period (*adhvan*) do these belong?
Answer: It belongs to the future.
From the initial entry up to the untainted sphere of nothingness, by virtue of attaining this, one also attains all other untainted minds and mental factors; to which time period do these belong?
Answer: It refers to the future.
Among these, there are four kinds of "firsts":
first, the initial entry into the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
First, the initial attainment of the fruit;
second, the initial abandonment of defilements; third, the initial transformation of the faculties.
As explained in detail in the *Jñānaskandha*,
that which arises in the future is called "acquisition" (*prāpti*),
while that which has reached the present is called "already acquired" (*prāpta*).
Therefore, what is obtained now is said to be at the time of arising.
Regarding the question of which world-period (*adhvan*) the various arisings are subsumed under, and so forth, as explained at length:
why was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is because one wishes to refute the doctrines of others and clarify one’s own position.
That is to say, the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain that conditioned phenomena exist at only two times:
first, the time prior to arising; [and second, the time after ceasing].
Regarding the second [point], at the time when [a phenomenon] has already arisen,
there is nothing further that is currently arising or currently ceasing apart from this.
Now, in order to demonstrate that the actual moments of currently arising and currently ceasing truly exist, this treatise is composed.

Furthermore, in order to stop the attachment that denies the existence of the past and future while asserting that the present is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomenon, it is now stated that the future has arising and the present has cessation.
This demonstrates that the past and future are not non-existent, whereas the present is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); for this reason, this treatise is composed.

Furthermore, in order to stop the attachment that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) merely undergo transformation through concealment and manifestation while their essence lacks arising and ceasing,
it is now stated that they arise in the future and cease in the present.
Thus, this treatise is composed to demonstrate that conditioned phenomena are not merely subject to transformation, but actually possess arising and ceasing.
To which period do all [dharmas] that arise belong?
Answer: The future.
To which period do all [dharmas] that cease belong?
Answer: It refers to the present.
That which is future is called "arising," and that which is present is called "ceasing."
The present is called "already arisen," and the past is called "already ceased. Section 5:

The Single-Practice Subsection (Ekāyana-nikāya), Part One of Five, within the Seventh Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhi-skandha): Regarding the three samādhis—namely, emptiness (śūnyatā), wishlessness (apranihita), and signlessness (animitta)—as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra, there are three types of samādhi.
Regarding what are called emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness:
although the sūtras speak thus, they do not differentiate them by asking,
"If one accomplishes emptiness, does one also possess wishlessness?"
Such are the passages.
That sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Since there are matters not explained therein that ought now to be explained, this treatise has been composed.
Furthermore, in order to stop the denial that there is a nature of non-attainment,
it was stated that the nature of attainment exists only as a designation.
This treatise is composed because one wishes to demonstrate that both the natures of attainment and non-attainment are substantially real.
Furthermore, this treatise was composed to stop the denial of the two time periods of past and future,
to refute the attachment that the present is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*),
and to demonstrate that both time periods exist and that the present is indeed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If one accomplishes emptiness, does one also accomplish wishlessness?
Answer: Yes. If one accomplishes wishlessness, does one also accomplish emptiness? Yes.
The answer is: "So it is.
This is because these three samādhis are attained simultaneously and share the same antidote.

"Attaining them simultaneously" means that if one enters the correct determination of the nature of things (*samyaktva-niyāma*) through the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), one also attains the concentration on wishlessness (*apranihita*) during the four moments of the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*);

likewise, if one enters the correct determination of the nature of things through the concentration on wishlessness, one also attains the concentration on emptiness during the four moments of the clear observation of suffering, as well as during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Within the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), if one [of the two] is attained, both are necessarily possessed.
Regarding their common counteraction (*pratipakṣa*):

it means that both are capable of counteracting the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Although one attains the wishless (apraṇihita) but not the empty (śūnya) during the four moments of the present realization of the origin (samudaya-abhisamaya) and the three moments of the present realization of the path (mārga-abhisamaya) within the path of vision (darśana-mārga),
it is at the time when one first attains what was previously unattained that [this occurs].
Because they are necessarily acquired together, they are always accomplished simultaneously. If one accomplishes emptiness (*śūnyatā*), does one also accomplish signlessness (*animitta*)?

Answer: If one acquires this—where "acquisition" means it has already been attained—specifically after the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) has arisen, one will henceforth always accomplish signlessness.
If one achieves the signless (animitta), does one achieve the empty (śūnya)?
Answer: It is so.
This is because when one achieves the signless, one must first have attained the empty.
If one accomplishes the wishless (apraṇihita), does one also accomplish the signless (animitta)?
Answer: If one has attained it.
Furthermore, if one accomplishes the signless, does one also accomplish the wishless?
Answer: It is so. Just as emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is explained in relation to signlessness (*animitta*), if one has accomplished past emptiness, has one accomplished future [emptiness] as well?
Answer: It is so.
Question: At what stage does this teaching occur?
Answer: This teaching refers to one who enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by means of the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).

It lasts for three moments of mind during the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*), and four moments of mind each during the clear realizations of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
The path of clear realization occurs during three moments of mind, as one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship.
If one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) refines their faculties to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*),
or if an arhat liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) refines their faculties to become one who is immovable (*akopyadharman*).
That emptiness samādhi, having arisen and ceased, is not lost.
If one has attained the future emptiness, has one also attained the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased and is not lost, then one has attained it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has already been extinguished but lost, then one does not possess it.
Question: In what state does this occur?
Answer: If it has already been extinguished and not lost, then one possesses it.
This refers to the various stages previously described.
As for the statement that "if it has not yet been extinguished, or even if it has been extinguished, it is lost and thus not accomplished," this refers to the case where,

by relying on the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), one enters the realization of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*) within the duration of a single moment of mind as one enters into right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
If one enters the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) by means of the concentration of wishlessness (apraṇihita-samādhi),
it takes four moments of mind for each of the clear realizations (abhisamaya) of suffering, origin, and cessation,
and three moments of mind for the clear realization of the path.
Having attained the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship,
one who is liberated through faith and resolved may refine their faculties to become one who has reached vision;
one who is liberated by occasion may refine their faculties to become one who is immovable.
The emptiness samādhi has not yet arisen or ceased;
that which has already arisen and ceased is lost due to the attainment of a fruit or the transformation of the faculties.
If one has accomplished past emptiness, has one also accomplished it in the present?

Answer: If it is manifested before one—that is, provided that one does not give rise to the wishless (*apraṇihita*), the signless (*animitta*), or a tainted (*sāsrava*) mind, nor is one in a state of non-consciousness—it is said to be "manifested before one."
Question: At what stage is this explained?

Answer: This is explained as occurring during the three moments of mind of the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*) upon entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by means of the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), as well as from the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*).
If one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra), they become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta);
if one who is liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) refines their faculties, they become one who is immovable (akopyadharman).
The concentration on emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi), having already arisen and ceased, is not lost.
And when it is present before one.
If one accomplishes the present emptiness, does one also accomplish the past?
Answer: If it has already ceased but has not been lost, then one accomplishes it.
If it has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but has been lost, then one does not possess it.
Question: In what stage does this statement apply?
Answer: If it has been extinguished and not lost, then one possesses it.
This refers to the aforementioned stages.
If [the path] has not yet been extinguished, or if it has been extinguished but lost such that it is no longer accomplished,

this refers to the moment of a single mind-instant of the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*) upon entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Having attained the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship,
one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) may refine their faculties to become one who has reached vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
and one who is temporarily liberated (samayavimukta) may refine their faculties to become one who is immovable (akopyadharman).
When the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) manifests before one,
that which has not yet been extinguished and that which has already been extinguished are lost due to the attainment of a fruit or the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).
If one accomplishes future emptiness, does one also accomplish it in the present?
Answer: Yes, provided it is present before one;
that is to say, when one does not give rise to the wishless, the signless, or a contaminated mind, nor is one in a state of non-consciousness.
Regarding the statement "if it manifests before one," the question is asked: in what stage does this refer?

The answer is: this refers to the four moments of mind during the direct realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*) upon entering the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by means of the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
And having attained the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship,
if one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*), they become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*);
if one who is liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) refines their faculties, they become one who is immovable (*akopyadharman*).
When the emptiness samādhi is present before one, if one has accomplished the present emptiness, has one also accomplished it in the future?
Answer: Yes.
Question: In what stage is this explained?
Answer: This refers to the various stages previously described.
If one has attained past emptiness, does one also possess it in the future and present?
Answer: One accomplishes the future when it is present before one.
Question: In what state does this occur?
