That is to say, when emptiness (*śūnyatā*) has not yet been attained, it manifests before one.
If one has not yet attained the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and is currently cultivating emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
or if one has not yet attained the signless (*animitta*) and the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and is currently cultivating emptiness;
or if one has not yet attained emptiness and is currently cultivating the wishless.

That is to say, it refers to the four moments of mind during the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*) upon entering the state of rightness and departure from corruption (*samyaktva-nyāma*) by relying on the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Or, it refers to becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) by relying on the concentration of emptiness.
Or, when one takes emptiness as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), all those paths of preparation, uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*),

and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)— with the exception of the final path of liberation for the abandonment of the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

If one who relies on the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) and possesses resolution through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*),

or if they take emptiness as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), then in that preparatory application, there is the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
At that time, having attained liberation and refined the faculties (indriya) to become unshakable (akopya),
with the exception of the final path of liberation,
if one relies on the concentration of emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi) during the initial and final moments of the meditative cultivation of the dhyānas.

If one relies on the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) to give rise to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*), the analytical knowledges (*artha-pratisaṃvid*),
and the two unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), some say that at such a time, the unhindered knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) alone has not yet attained the presence of emptiness.
Furthermore, one cultivates wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) but has not yet attained its manifestation in the present.
As for the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it refers to entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the concentration of wishlessness;
this occurs during the four moments of mind in the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*) and at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*).
If one relies on the wishless (*apraṇihita*) to become free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
or if the wishless serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
then all those paths of preparation, immediate succession (*ānantarya*), and liberation (*vimukti*) [are wishless].

If one who possesses faith and resolve (*śraddhādhimukta*) based on the wishless (*apraṇihita*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*), they become a "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*);
if one who is "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*) refines their faculties, they become "unshakable" (*akopyadharman*).
Alternatively, the wishless may serve as the preliminary application (*prayoga*).
Regarding all those preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths:

if one relies on the initial or final moments of the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas through the wishless [samādhi], or if one gives rise to the supranormal power of uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds; [in these cases, the path is not abandoned].

If one relies on the wishless (apraṇihita) to give rise to the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the formless liberations (ārūpyavimokṣa), the meaning-discernment (arthapratisaṃvid), and the two analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), at such a time,
although the wishless has not yet been attained and brought into presence, one also cultivates emptiness (śūnyatā), though the signless (animitta) has not yet been attained and brought into presence.
For one who cultivates emptiness and wishlessness, these are absent during the path of seeing and the path of no-more-learning;
however, if they rely on the signless, they may be free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness.

Alternatively, when the signless (*animitta*) serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), all those paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*), uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*), and paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*)—
with the exception of the final path of liberation for the abandonment of the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)— are included.
If one refines the faculties based on the signless conviction (animitta-adhimokṣa) to become a "vision-attainer" (dṛṣṭiprāpta),

or if the signless serves as the preparatory application (prayoga), then through all those paths of preparation, uninterrupted path, and liberation, as well as the path of timely liberation, one refines the faculties to become an "unshakable one" (akopyadharman).
Excluding the final path of liberation,
it refers to the initial and final moments of mind when practicing the meditative concentration of the signless,
or when, based on the signless, one gives rise to the applications of mindfulness, the formless liberations, and the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) regarding meaning.
At such a time, one has not yet attained the manifestation of the signless (*animitta*);
rather, one cultivates emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
This refers to one who, having not yet attained the manifestation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), cultivates emptiness and wishlessness.
This refers to when a noble one, by means of the mundane path, becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness;
or when the mundane path serves as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), including all those paths of preparation, immediate succession (*ānantarya*), and liberation (*vimukti*).
Furthermore, there is the abandonment of the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
the transformation of faculties through the conviction-based liberation to become one who has attained vision;
and the transformation of faculties through occasional liberation to become one who is immovable.

Taking the mundane as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), during the interval of the intermediate mind within that path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) where dhyāna is mixed, one brings forth the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*):
namely, the five paths of preparation, the five uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*), and two paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
Furthermore, there are the paths of liberation of the supernormal knowledge of others' minds with outflows;
the arising of the immeasurables, the mundane liberations, the spheres of mastery, the spheres of totality, the meditation on impurity, and mindfulness of breathing;

the mundane foundations of mindfulness, the skillfulness in the seven stations, and the contemplation of the three meanings; and the mundane unhindered knowledges, the knowledge of non-contention, the knowledge of aspiration, and the knowledge of the limit of existence.

In the state of emptiness-of-emptiness, wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and signlessness-of-signlessness, one enters the perception of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) with a subtle mind;
at such a time, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) has not yet arisen before one.
There are cases where both emptiness and wishlessness are not cultivated.
This refers to when one who has already attained the signless (animitta) brings it into manifestation;
or, if one has not yet attained the signless and brings it into manifestation, one does not cultivate emptiness or wishlessness.
If conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that has already been attained is present;
or if conventional knowledge not yet attained is present, but one does not cultivate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or wishlessness (*apranihita*);

or when all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) possess defiled or neutral minds; or when they abide in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Regarding those born in the Heaven of Non-conception who have already attained the manifestation of the signless (*animitta*), it is as explained previously.
As for those who have not yet attained the manifestation of the signless and do not cultivate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or wishlessness (*apranihita*): [the explanation follows].
This refers to the four moments of mind during the clear realization of cessation within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
During these moments, one does not cultivate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), as explained previously.
Furthermore, the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that has already been attained and is present before one is also as explained previously.
Regarding those who have not yet attained mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) manifesting before them and do not cultivate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or wishlessness (*apranihita*):

this refers to the subtle-subtle mind (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*) of noble ones (*ārya*) entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), which consists of the wisdom (*prajñā*) derived from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-bhāvanāmayī*).
"All ordinary beings" (pṛthagjana) refers to the fact that the three samādhis mentioned here are exclusively untainted (anāsrava);
since ordinary beings lack these entirely, there is no sense of "cultivation" for them.
"Defiled mind" (kliṣṭa-citta) means that a defiled mind is of the nature conducive to decline (hāna-bhāgīya).
It is associated with heaviness and indolence;
for it can only be cultivated by a mind that is compliant with superior progress, buoyant, and associated with diligence.
As for the neutral mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), this means that a neutral mind is not firm, not stable, not real, and weak—like a rotten seed.
Because one must be able to practice only by firmly abiding in a mind that is truly stable and powerful,
those who abide in the attainment of non-conception or the attainment of cessation [cannot do so].
This means that they lack a mind,
for it must be in a state where the mind is present that one can cultivate [the meditative attainment].
This refers to those born in the Heaven of Non-conception.
Some say that those born there do not give rise to wholesome states of mind at any time.
Others say:
Although those born there may give rise to wholesome states of mind, these are not the basis for cultivation.
Although all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have already been excluded previously,
they are here further excluded from the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Regarding the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), because it is esteemed by worldly people and perhaps suspected to involve cultivation,
one does not cultivate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) at such a time.
If one cultivates emptiness, is that not signlessness (*animitta*)?
If one practices the signless, is that the empty?
One should respond by establishing four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the case of practicing the empty but not the signless.
This means that when one has already attained emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it manifests before one;
if one has not yet attained emptiness, one does not cultivate the signless (*animitta*) when it manifests.
If one has not yet attained the wishless (*apraṇihita*), one cultivates emptiness when it manifests, but not the signless.
That which has already attained emptiness being present before one is explained as previously.
Regarding that which has not yet attained emptiness being present before one but does not cultivate the signless (*animitta*):

this refers to the four moments of mind during the direct realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*) when entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Regarding "not having attained the presence of wishlessness,
one cultivates emptiness but not signlessness":
this refers to the four moments of mind during the clear observation of suffering, when one enters the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) by relying on wishlessness.
There is cultivation of the signless that is not the empty.
This refers to when one who has already attained the signless brings it to manifestation;
or, if one has not yet attained the signless, when it is brought to manifestation, one does not cultivate the empty.
That which has already attained the manifestation of the signless (*animitta*) is explained as before.
Regarding that which has not yet attained the manifestation of the signless and does not cultivate emptiness (*śūnyatā*):
this refers to the four moments of mind during the contemplation of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
There is simultaneous cultivation: namely, when one who has not yet attained emptiness brings it into presence and cultivates signlessness;
or when one who has not yet attained signlessness brings it into presence and cultivates emptiness;
or when one who has not yet attained wishlessness and has not yet attained conventional knowledge brings them into presence and cultivates both emptiness and signlessness.
Regarding the cultivation of the signless when emptiness has not yet been brought before one:
this refers to abandoning the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness by relying on the concentration of emptiness.
This is explained in detail as previously stated, including the simultaneous cultivation of the wishless.
Regarding those who have not yet attained the manifestation of the signless (*animitta*) but cultivate emptiness (*śūnyatā*):
this refers to those who, relying on the signless samādhi, become detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Alternatively, it refers to all preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*), uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that take the signless as their preliminary application (*prayoga*).
And having become detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
excluding the final path of liberation—
if one refines the faculties by relying on the signless [samādhi], one becomes a "vision-attainer" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Taking the signless (*animitta*) as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) immediately following that application,
as well as the timely liberation (*samayavimukti*) when refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) to become unshakable (*akopya*)—
excluding the final path of liberation.
If, during the initial and final moments of meditative concentration practiced in a mixed manner based on the signless,
one relies on the signless to give rise to the foundations of mindfulness, the formless liberations, and the analytical knowledges regarding meaning; at such a time,
although the signless has not yet been attained as a manifest presence, one also cultivates emptiness.
When one who has not yet attained the manifestation of the wishless (*apraṇihita*) cultivates the empty (*śūnya*) and signless (*animitta*),
this refers to the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
If, relying on the wishless samādhi, one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The details are as previously explained regarding the concurrent cultivation of emptiness.
As for those who, while not yet having attained the presence of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), cultivate emptiness and signlessness:
this refers to noble ones who, by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), become detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The details are as previously explained regarding the combined cultivation of emptiness and wishlessness.
There is also the case where neither is cultivated,
namely when one who has already attained wishlessness brings it into manifestation.
If one has not yet attained the wishless (apraṇihita) and it is present before one, one does not cultivate emptiness (śūnyatā) or signlessness (animitta).
If one has already attained conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) and it is present before one,
or if one has not yet attained conventional knowledge and it is present before one, one does not cultivate emptiness or signlessness.

For all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) whose minds are defiled or neutral when they abide in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or who have been born in the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), the wishless liberation (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*) is present before them; this is explained as previously stated.

Those who have not yet attained the manifestation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) and do not cultivate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*) refer to the four moments of mind during the clear realization of accumulation (*samudaya-abhisamaya*) and the three moments of mind during the clear realization of the path (*mārga-abhisamaya*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Regarding the case where conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that has already been attained is present before one, it is explained as previously.
Regarding the case where conventional knowledge not yet attained is present before one, yet one does not cultivate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or signlessness (*animitta*):

this refers to the subtle-subtle mind (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*) of a noble one (*ārya*) who, through wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī- and cintāmayī-prajñā*), enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
All ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), up to those born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), are as explained previously.
If one cultivates wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), does one thereby cultivate signlessness (*animitta*)?

there is cultivation of the wishless that is not the signless,

There is cultivation of the signless that is not the wishless.

or when one who has not yet attained emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and has not yet attained conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) brings them into presence and cultivates both the wishless and the signless.
This should be explained in detail as previously set forth according to what is appropriate.

Answer: There are.
Specifically, the fetters abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*) are abandoned by the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
This is because they are exclusively counteracted by the wishless.
Is there any fetter that is abandoned by the signless (animitta) but not by emptiness (śūnyatā) or the wishless (apranihita)?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, the fetters to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya) are abandoned by the signless.
Because that [object] is exclusively the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) to signlessness (*animitta*).
Is there any fetter (*saṃyojana*) that is abandoned by emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), but not by signlessness?
Answer: Yes; namely, those fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) which are abandoned by emptiness and wishlessness.

Since those [fetters] are exclusively the objects to be countered by emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and wishlessness (*apranihita*), could there be any fetters that are abandoned by emptiness and signlessness (*animitta*) but not by wishlessness?
Answer: No, because there are no such classes of fetters that are exclusively the objects to be countered by emptiness and signlessness but not by wishlessness.
Is there any fetter that is abandoned by the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and the signless (*animitta*), but not by the empty (*śūnya*)? Answer: No.
Because there are no such fetters that are to be countered exclusively by the wishless and the signless, but not by the empty.
Are there any fetters that are abandoned by means of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness?
Answer: There are;
namely, those fetters to be abandoned through cultivation by one who has seen the path and is still in training (śaikṣa).
The abandonment through emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness refers to the fetters abandoned through cultivation by the noble ones within the three realms,
because those fetters are the specific objects to be countered by these three samādhis.
Are there any fetters that are not abandoned through emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness?
"And is it that which is abandoned?
Answer: "Yes.
That is to say, the fetters abandoned by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*)."

These are the fetters of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), which are to be abandoned through both vision and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*).
Since they are the objects to be counteracted by the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), one might ask:
"Are those fetters not also the objects to be counteracted by emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*)?"
The answer is: these are the objects to be countered.
However, they exist in noble ones (*ārya*) and not in ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Since those [defilements] exist in ordinary beings, it is said that they are not abandoned by means of emptiness and so forth.
Some say: the previous discussion was based on the determination of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*),
whereas the present discussion is based on the determination of function (*kāritra*).

Because the three types of samādhi have no functional activity within the continuum of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is said that those fetters (*saṃyojana*) are not abandoned by means of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth.
Question: If that is so, then...
Within the continuum of an Arya, from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness,
the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation are also severed by the mundane path. Why,
then, is it said that they are severed only by emptiness and so forth?
Answer: The preceding text should have stated that those fetters are also abandoned by the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
What is the intention behind not stating this?
It should be understood that because they are manifested by the noble ones’ untainted path (*anāsravamārga*), the mundane path is not mentioned.
Because ordinary beings lack the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), this is explained in reliance upon the conventional path (*saṃvṛti-mārga*).
Therefore, what was stated previously is without fault.
How does one apply attention (*manasikāra*) to enter into rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*)?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was composed in order to refute the doctrines of other schools and to clarify one's own position.
That is to say, some may claim that any one of the three samādhis is capable of entering the state of right determination and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Now, this [text] refutes their view to demonstrate that it is only one of the two [specific] samādhis that can enter it.
Nor was this treatise composed because of a lack of the signless (animitta).
Alternatively, some say that only the signless samādhi can enter into the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma).
As the Dharmaguptaka school explains:

they maintain that one enters the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) by means of the signless samādhi (animitta-samādhi), giving rise to the mental attention of tranquility toward nirvāṇa.
This treatise is composed to refute that attachment and to demonstrate that the samādhi of signlessness alone cannot lead one into the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
How does one enter the state of right determination through mental attention?
The answer is: it is either impermanent, or suffering, or empty, or non-self.
By means of this, the intention of one who is able to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) regarding the three samādhis and the signless alone is brought to rest.
Among these, the mental attention to impermanence and suffering is associated with the wishless concentration (*apranihita-samādhi*);
the mental attention to emptiness and selflessness is associated with the emptiness concentration (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Question: Why is it that only through these modes of activity (*ākāra*) does one enter the state of rightness and departure from corruption (*samyaktva-nyāma*), and not by others?
Answer: There are two types of those who enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
First, those whose temperament is characterized by craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*); second, those whose temperament is characterized by views (*dṛṣṭi-carita*).

Those whose conduct is characterized by craving enter through the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), while those whose conduct is characterized by views enter through the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Although a bodhisattva’s conduct is characterized by craving, they are nonetheless able to enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on emptiness.
Furthermore, there are two types of those who act out of craving:
namely, those in whom the conceit of "I am" predominates,
and those in whom indolence predominates.
Those for whom pride increases enter by means of the aspect of impermanence;
those for whom indolence increases enter by means of the aspect of suffering.
Those who practice through views are also of two kinds.
This refers to the increase of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the increase of the view of "mine" (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).
As for the increase of the view of self, one enters [the path] by means of the aspect of non-self (*anātman*).
Those for whom the view of "mine" increases enter by means of the aspect of emptiness;
therefore, only these four aspects are established.
Question: With which factors of which stage are these four aspects associated?
Some say that it is associated with the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*),
because it is said that one enters into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Some say it is associated with the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Question: If that is so, [then...]
Why is it called "entering"?
Answer: This refers to that which has already entered as being "entering";
it is a case of using a term for what is near to refer to what is distant.
It is like asking, "Great King, from where have you come?
Even though he has already come, it is called "coming";
this case is likewise.
Question: At that time, there are also other mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
Why, then, is only attention (*manasikāra*) mentioned?
Answer: Because it is attention alone that is capable of inducing the arising of the mind and its mental factors.
Some say that because attention (manasikāra) is most conducive to entering the state of rightness and departure from corruption (samyaktva-niyāma),
one should contemplate which fetters (saṃyojana) must be abandoned to enter that state.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: It is intended to refute the assertion of the Venerable Dharmatrāta, who claimed that one enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by contemplating the formations (*saṃskāra*) of the three realms all at once.

Furthermore, this treatise is composed for the purpose of addressing the intention of those who, by contemplating nirvāṇa as a means of cessation, enter the state of right determination and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Question: Contemplating which category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃyojana-prakāra*) does one enter the state of right determination and departure from birth?
Answer: It is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
By this, the two aforementioned attachments are refuted.
Question: For what reason does one enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by contemplating only those formations (*saṃskāra*) bound to the desire realm?
Answer: Because the suffering of the desire realm appears coarse and manifest, and is easy to observe.
Some say it is because the suffering of the desire realm is currently established within that continuum.
Some say that because the formations associated with the desire realm possess all three types of suffering,
this is why the Abhidharmikas [state so].
It is taught that one enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by contemplating all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being characterized by the three types of suffering;

it is not as the Dārṣṭāntikas claim, who say that one enters the state of right determination solely by contemplating conditioned phenomena as being characterized by the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Among these, disagreeable conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
agreeable conditioned phenomena are called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*);
and conditioned phenomena conducive to equanimity are called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Some say that because the suffering of the desire realm currently afflicts practitioners and is utterly detested by them,
they first contemplate it and thereby enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Question: Since nirvāṇa is also that which is most intensely desired, why do sentient beings not contemplate it and thereby enter the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma)?
Answer: Among the classes of sentient beings, their aversion to suffering is predominant, whereas their aspiration for nirvāṇa is not.
Why is this? Because they manifest as affliction and because they are not directly perceived.
Just as there are no sentient beings who do not fear suffering or who do not crave pleasure, it is asked:
upon which truth does one rely when, through patience (*kṣānti*), one subsequently enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*)? Some say:
If it is said that [the path] takes the truth of the path as its object, then it likewise takes the truth of suffering as its object.
As explained at length in the first section (*naḷaka*) of the *Saṃyuktakāya*,
should it be said that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) dwells in mindfulness by observing the body as body,
or even, should it be said that it dwells in mindfulness by observing phenomena as phenomena?

Answer: Regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), one should say that it dwells either contemplating the body as the body, or contemplating feelings, or the mind, or phenomena as phenomena.
As it is with the knowledge of exhaustion, so it is with the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the sake of enabling those who have doubts to attain certainty.
That is to say, there are those who harbor such a doubt as follows:
Because the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) do not have the nature of vision (*darśana*),
they should likewise not have the nature of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Now, I wish to definitively clarify these two types of knowledge.
Although this is not the nature of vision (*darśana*), it is a station of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); therefore, this treatise is composed.
Furthermore, within the aggregate of views (*dṛṣṭiskandha*), one analyzes the self-nature of vision as a station of mindfulness.
Now, because it is determined within the aggregates that the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) whose intrinsic nature is not [simply] "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) is being distinguished,
this treatise is composed.
Furthermore, it is for this reason that it is said in the stage of preparatory practice (*prayogabhūmi*) that one cultivates the applications of mindfulness.
It is said that the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣabhūmi) lacks the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Now, wishing to clarify that the applications of mindfulness do exist within the stage of no-more-learning, this treatise is composed.
Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Because there is a reason for this: namely, that they take only dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and future existence (*punarbhava*) as their objects.
Now, wishing to clarify that [consciousness] takes all phenomena as its objects—
excluding only space and non-analytical cessation—
I have composed this treatise.

Furthermore, there is another [proponent] who maintains that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) take only the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as their collective object.
Now, this [text] refutes that view to demonstrate the true nature of the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
This treatise is composed because [the practitioner] may take the five aggregates as a collective object or may take them as individual objects.
Regarding the statement that "one should dwell in mindfulness by contemplating the body as body," this refers to taking the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) as the object.
"Abiding in the contemplation of feelings as feelings" means taking the aggregate of feeling as the object.
"Abiding in the contemplation of the mind as mind" means taking the aggregate of consciousness as the object.
"Abiding in the contemplation of phenomena as phenomena" means taking the aggregates of perception and formations, as well as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), as the objects.
This explains the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that takes unmixed objects.
If it is the application of mindfulness to phenomena that takes mixed objects,
then it takes two at a time from among the five aggregates.
Either three [factors] as conditions for three,
or four as conditions for four,
or five as conditions collectively.
Regarding the two-by-two conditions: these refer to the condition of form and feeling;
the condition of form and perception; the condition of form and formations;
and the condition of form and consciousness.
The condition of feeling and perception;
the condition of feeling and mental formations; the condition of feeling and consciousness.

this refers to the conditions of form, feeling, perception, and mental formations.

"or the five taken collectively" means taking all five—
form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— as a collective condition.
If the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) were an object of the mindfulness foundations (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding contaminated phenomena,
it would also be associated with and take as its object other factors such as form (*rūpa*).
However, because that which is discussed here is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it takes only unmixed objects.
What is the difference between the bliss of the various untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna and the bliss of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) such as pliancy (*praśrabdhi*)?
Answer: There is no difference.
What is the difference between the bliss of the various untainted second dhyānas and the bliss of the various factors of enlightenment such as pliancy?
Answer: There is no difference.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is to refute the view that the first and second dhyānas possess the untainted faculty of pleasure (anāsrava-sukhendriya).
To demonstrate that those two stages lack the untainted faculty of pleasure, this treatise was written.
If it exists, one should not answer that there is no distinction between them.
Why is this? Because the factor of enlightenment of pliancy is pleasure (*sukha*).
Among the great wholesome mental factors (*mahākuśalabhūmika*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This is because, among the great universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the untainted faculty of pleasure (*anāsrava-sukhendriya*) has feeling (*vedanā*) as its intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, the factor of enlightenment of pliancy is subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) as the pleasant mode of practice.
The untainted faculty of pleasure is subsumed within the aggregate of feeling;
thus, these two types of pleasure differ,
yet they are described as being without distinction.
Therefore, it is known that the untainted pleasure (*anāsrava-sukha*) of those two stages is precisely the pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*).
For this reason, the untainted faculty of pleasure does not exist in those stages. [Question:
Does one emerge from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) by means of its object (*ālambana*)?
It is taught at length that there are five types of emergence:
first, the ground; second, the aspect; third, the object; fourth, the dissimilar mind; and fifth, the moment.
Herein, the treatise is composed based solely on two of these types of emergence.
That is to say, regarding the object of focus on the earth:
does one emerge from meditative concentration by emerging from that object?
Or, conversely, does one emerge from that object by emerging from the meditative concentration?
It can be answered in four propositions.
There are cases where one emerges from meditative concentration (samādhi) but not from the object of focus (ālambana).
For example, there is someone who, having contemplated this sign, enters the first dhyāna.
He further reflects on this sign and enters the second dhyāna.
Here, the object of focus is expressed by the word "sign" (*nimitta*).
It is like focusing on the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as the immediately preceding condition for the first dhyāna and so forth.
When the second dhyāna manifests,
it is likewise when taking other aggregates as its object.
This is called emerging from meditative concentration (samādhi) without [changing] the object.
Question: Since the second dhyāna is also a state of meditative concentration (samādhi), why is it said that one "emerges" from it?
Answer: Because the levels (bhūmi) are distinct.
Therefore, it was stated previously that the treatise is composed based on two types of emergence:

namely, emergence from the object of focus (*ālambana*) and emergence from meditative concentration (*samādhi*). There are cases where one emerges from the object of focus but not from meditative concentration.
That is to say, there is someone who, contemplating this sign, enters the first dhyāna and does not emerge from that first dhyāna,
but further contemplates another sign, such as the aggregate of form.
When the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) of the first dhyāna arises as the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), the first dhyāna manifests;
the same applies when other aggregates arise as conditions.
This is called emerging from the object of focus (ālambana) rather than from meditative concentration (samādhi).
There are cases where one emerges both from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and from its object (*ālambana*.
For example, suppose someone enters the first dhyāna by contemplating a certain sign;
they then enter the second dhyāna by contemplating another sign.
Just as when taking the aggregate of form as an object,
the second dhyāna manifests immediately after the aggregate of feeling of the first dhyāna.
The same applies to the remaining aggregates.
This is called that which is both emerging from meditative concentration and an object of focus.
There is also that which neither emerges from meditative concentration nor is an object of focus.
That is to say, there is one who, reflecting on this sign, enters the first dhyāna and remains therein for a long time,
as when taking the aggregate of form as an object;
the flow of the first dhyāna continues in succession and manifests for a long duration.
The same applies to the remaining aggregates (*skandha*).
As it is with the aggregates, so it is with what is not an aggregate.
As it is from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), so it is likewise.
Furthermore, there is another meaning:
if one asks whether those aspects [of the mind] emerge from meditative concentration (samādhi),
one should respond by formulating four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are cases where one emerges from meditative concentration (samādhi) without the aspect (ākāra).
For example, suppose someone enters the first dhyāna with a certain aspect,
and then again enters the second dhyāna with that same aspect.
Just as with the aspect of impermanence,
when the second dhyāna manifests immediately after the first dhyāna and the aspect of impermanence,
the same applies to the other aspects as well.
There are cases where one emerges from a mode of activity but not from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
For example, suppose someone enters the first dhyāna by means of a certain mode of activity;
they emerge from that first dhyāna and then again engage in another mode of activity.
Just as when the first dhyāna characterized by the aspect of impermanence is immediately followed by the first dhyāna characterized by the aspect of suffering,
so it is with other aspects as well.
There are also cases where one emerges from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) while still maintaining that aspect.
That is to say, for example, there is one who enters the first dhyāna by means of a certain aspect (ākāra),
and enters the second dhyāna by means of another aspect.
Just as when the aspect of suffering (duḥkha) immediately follows the aspect of impermanence (anitya) in the first dhyāna and so forth, other aspects likewise manifest in the second dhyāna.
There is that which neither emerges from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) nor consists of mental aspects (*ākāra*).
This refers, for example, to a certain person who enters the first dhyāna by means of a particular aspect and remains there for a long time;
just as the aspect of impermanence flows continuously and manifests for a long duration within the first dhyāna.
The other modes of activity are likewise;
as it is for the first dhyāna, so it is up to the sphere of nothingness.
Furthermore, there is another meaning.
If one asks whether there are cases where one emerges from the aspect (ākāra) but not from the object (ālambana),
the answer is that four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) should be formulated.
There are cases where one emerges from the aspect but not from the object.
That is to say, there is someone who contemplates a certain mental aspect (ākāra) with respect to a certain object;
they do not abandon that aspect to produce another mental aspect.

For example, when one contemplates the aspect of impermanence (*anitya-ākāra*) regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the aspect of suffering (*duḥkha-ākāra*) regarding the aggregate of form immediately follows as its equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
The same applies to other objects and other aspects.
There are cases where one emerges from the object but not from the aspect;
for example, when someone contemplates a certain aspect by means of that very aspect.
Then, by means of this very mode of activity, one further contemplates other modes:

for example, immediately following the mode of activity regarding the impermanence of the aggregate of form, one takes as an object the mode of activity regarding the impermanence of the aggregate of feeling.
It manifests before one.
It is the same for other aggregates and other aspects.
There are also cases where one emerges from an aspect and likewise from an object.
That is to say, there is someone who contemplates a certain characteristic with a particular mode of activity,
and then contemplates another characteristic with another mode of activity;
for example, immediately after taking the characteristic of impermanence in the aggregate of form as an object, the characteristic of suffering in the aggregate of feeling manifests before one.
The same applies to other aggregates and other mental aspects (*ākāra*).
There are cases that arise neither from a mental aspect nor from an object (*ālambana*);
for example, when someone dwells for a long time contemplating a particular aspect by means of that very aspect.
Just as the aspect of impermanence regarding the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) manifests for a long duration in a continuous flow,
so it is with the other aggregates and other aspects. As it is with the aggregates,
so it is with what is not an aggregate (skandhāḥ or askandhāḥ).
As it is said that bhikṣus can even reach the noble intent through the attainment of the perception-sphere of nothingness,
when a disciple of the Blessed One is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
by relying on which meditative concentration does he attain the fruit of arhatship?
Answer: It concerns the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There are seven meditative absorptions upon which one relies;
I declare that by relying on them, one can exhaust all outflows."
This refers to the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states:
"O Bhikṣus, by means of the meditative attainment of cessation, one can reach the noble intention."
"Concentrative absorptions" refers to the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments.
"Able to penetrate the noble intent" means:
This refers to being able to give rise to wisdom, abandon the afflictions, cultivate the path, and exhaust the outflows.
Alternatively, some may harbor such a doubt:
"Since there is no noble path in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," [how can one exhaust the outflows?]
If disciples of the Blessed One are born in that place,
by what means are they able to exhaust all outflows?
Could it be that such beings attain arhatship without relying on the Noble Path?
In order to resolve this doubt,
it is stated that he attained the fruit of arhatship based on the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Furthermore, it is said so as to refute the proponents of conceptual analysis (*vibhajyavādin*) who claim that arhatship is limited to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
They say that when a disciple of the Blessed One is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
at the time of death, the three factors— afflictions, karma, and life-force— all come to an end simultaneously,
and they attain the fruit of arhatship not by means of the noble path.

To stop that misconception and demonstrate that the exhaustion [of the defilements] is not simultaneous with [the attainment of cessation], but must necessarily occur through the Noble Path, this treatise is composed.
Question: Why is it stated that one relies solely on the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)?
Is it not so for other stages?
Answer: Because this is the most proximate to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Question: The lower stages are also proximate [to it].

Why is it that the untainted [attainments] of the lower stages are not said to be the basis for the exhaustion of outflows, whereas only those born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are so described? Answer:

Within the various lower stages, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of their own respective levels exist, and the noble path (*āryamārga*) of the higher stages can more easily manifest there than in the lower stages. Therefore, [the lower stages are not so designated].
Why is this? Because the wholesome states bound to the lower stages have all been abandoned, the Noble Path is difficult to arise;
for this reason, there is nothing that arises as a manifest presence.
It is not so for one born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

For them, there is no noble path (*āryamārga*) within their own stage, nor is there a higher stage upon which they could rely; thus, it is impossible for them to exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*) without the noble path.
Therefore, although it is difficult to arise in the lower stages,
that noble path arises through the power of its causes rather than the power of preparatory effort;
it manifests momentarily to sever the remaining afflictions.
Once the fruit of arhatship has been attained,
even if one were to remain for eighty thousand kalpas,
one would never again arise [in rebirth], because it would serve no purpose.
As it was said by the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Venerable friend,
I recall dwelling in the meditative concentration of the sphere of nothingness,
and I heard the sounds of many dragon-elephants roaring and so forth at the edge of the Mandākinī Lake."
"Does that venerable one hear while remaining in meditative concentration,
or does he hear after emerging from concentration?
"He hears after emerging from concentration."
It is not [the case that it occurs] only in meditative concentration.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the sake of enabling those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
As stated in the Vinaya,
the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Venerable friends,
I recall dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness."
Hearing the sounds of many dragon-elephants roaring by the side of the Mandākinī Pond,
the bhikṣus said to one another,
"Now, this Mahāmaudgalyāyana claims to have attained superhuman states; such a thing is certainly impossible."
We should together destroy it. Why is this?
Even those who dwell in the first dhyāna do not hear sounds.
How much more so for one who dwells in the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness?
He then reported this matter to the Buddha,
and the Buddha said to him at that time:
You should not disparage Mahāmaudgalyāyana. Why is this?
Mahāmaudgalyāyana speaks according to his perception.
Therefore, although the Vinaya makes this statement, it does not analyze it further.
Consequently, some may have doubts,
thinking that the Venerable One heard the sound while in meditative concentration.
In order to bring certainty to this doubt,
and to demonstrate that the Venerable One emerged from meditative absorption and heard the sound,
he composed this treatise.
Question: Since other śrāvakas also know that one does not hear sounds while in meditative concentration, they do not even make such a statement;
how much less so for Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the most eminent of śrāvakas?
Why, then, did he say what should not have been said among the assembly of bhikṣus?
Some say that this need not necessarily be explained. Why is that?
This is because it is a counterfeit Vinaya.
That is to say, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there were those who placed counterfeit sūtras within the sūtras and placed counterfeit vinayas within the vinayas.
Within the Abhidharma, spurious Abhidharma has been placed;
these various spurious passages should not be interpreted as authoritative exegesis. Some say:
The ocean of meditative concentration is profoundly deep;
śrāvakas are like rabbits who cannot reach its bottom,
for only a Buddha can exhaust it.
There is no fault even though that Venerable One spoke thus.
Question: Does that Venerable One not know that one does not hear sounds while in meditative concentration?
Why, then, did he speak in this way?
The answer is that because that venerable one enters and emerges from meditative concentration with such swiftness,
although he has emerged from concentration, he perceives himself as remaining in it.
Specifically, he first entered the first dhyāna from a wholesome mind of the desire realm.
From the first dhyāna, one enters the second dhyāna;
proceeding in this manner up to entering the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana),
and from the sphere of nothingness, one emerges and re-enters the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana).
In this manner, he even enters the first dhyāna;
from there, while a wholesome mind of the desire realm is manifest, he hears the sounds of elephants and so forth without giving rise to conceptual discrimination.
He then returns from that wholesome mind of the desire realm and enters the first dhyāna once more.
From the first dhyāna, one enters the second dhyāna;
in this manner, proceeding until entering the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana),
one then arises from the sphere of nothingness and re-enters the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana).
In this manner, up until he enters the first dhyāna,
a wholesome mind of the desire realm manifests from that state;
without careful discernment, he then speaks these words.
I recall that while in the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness, I heard the sounds of nāgas,
elephants, and other creatures by the side of the Mandākinī Lake;
yet, he (the Buddha) gave rise to discerning cognition regarding those sounds with only two moments of mind.
This refers to the mind at the initial entry into meditative absorption and the mind at the subsequent emergence from it;
because the continuity of all minds in the interval between these two is not minutely analyzed, this statement is made.
There is likewise no fault.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 185. *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 100. (of the Sarvāstivāda Jñānaprasthāna)

Section Seven: The Aggregate of Concentration (*Samādhiskandha*). Sub-section Five: The Chapter on Singlefold Categories (*Ekottarakanipāta*), Part Four. Regarding those who are indeterminate: "Are they all non-intelligent and proceeding toward ignorance? and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra:
Among the various classes of sentient beings, some are fixed and some are unfixed;
some possess wisdom and proceed toward illumination,
while others lack wisdom and proceed toward ignorance.
Although this was stated, the specific distinctions regarding their mutual inclusion were not differentiated.
That sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies;
therefore, whatever was not explained therein shall now be fully explained here.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
Question: Are all those who are indeterminate necessarily of dull wit and destined for ignorance?
Answer: All those who are indeterminate are indeed of dull wit and destined for ignorance.
There are those who are not of wise inclination toward ignorance (*avidyā-gati*), yet are not indeterminate;
namely, those of wrong determination (*mithyātva-niyata*).
Question: Are all those who are determined of wise inclination toward knowledge (*vidyā-gati*)?
Answer: All those who are wise and clear-sighted enter into all such concentrations;
however, there are concentrations that exist which are not entered by the wise and clear-sighted, namely, wrong concentration (*mithyāsamādhi*).
In this context, those who are "not wise" refer to foolish ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), because they lack noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*);
those who are "wise" refer to the noble ones (*ārya*), because they possess noble wisdom.
How is this known to be so?
Because it is stated in the sūtras.
As it is said in a sūtra,
the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
What do you think?
Those who know the noble truth of suffering as it truly is,
and [know] the noble truth of the origin of suffering and the noble truth of the cessation of suffering—
One knows the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is.
Yet, there are some who do not know this as it truly is.
In this regard, who is said to be wise?
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught,
regarding all those who [have realized] the Noble Truth of Suffering..."
One who knows, as it truly is, even the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering is called wise;
they do not know it incorrectly.
By this, it is known that the noble ones are wise, whereas ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are not wise.
The wise are those who proceed toward clear knowledge and are the basis for clear knowledge;
the unwise are those who proceed toward ignorance and are the basis for ignorance.
All those who are indeterminate are unwise.
Those who belong to the destiny of ignorance are those who are not fixed [in liberation] and are necessarily ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
All ordinary persons lack wisdom and are subsumed within the destiny of ignorance.
There are those who lack wisdom and proceed toward ignorance, yet are not "undetermined.
This refers to those who are "fixed in the wrong" (*mithyātva-niyata*); that is, all those fixed in the wrong are necessarily *pṛthagjana*s (ordinary worldlings).
Because they are fixed in their erroneous nature, they are not called "undetermined."
Regarding those who are wise and clear-sighted and who are established in all those concentrations:
it is said that the noble ones (āryas) are called "concentrated" because they are fixed in the state of rightness (*samyaktva*).
Are all those who are not concentrated unaccomplished in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: All those who are indeterminate do not possess the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
However, there are those who do not possess the factors of enlightenment who are not indeterminate;
namely, those who are fixed in error (*mithyātva-niyata*), because they are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and because their nature is fixed in error.
Are all those meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) endowed with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: All those that are endowed with the factors of enlightenment are indeed meditative concentrations;
however, there are meditative concentrations that are not endowed with the factors of enlightenment.
This refers to "wrong determination" (mithyā-niyata), as explained previously.
There are three aggregates (rāśi):
first, the aggregate of those fixed in wrong nature (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi).
2. Those fixed in the state of rightness (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi);

3. Those of the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi) and those fixed in the state of wrongness (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi), namely, those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution (pañcānantarya-karma).
The group of those fixed in the rightness [of the path] (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi) refers to those who have accomplished the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The group of those not fixed (aniyata-rāśi) refers to those who have accomplished only other remaining contaminated (sāsrava) dharmas and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
These are called the intrinsic natures (svabhāva) of the three groups.
Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): the category of those fixed in wrongness (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*) is a portion of one realm, namely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The category of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*) is a portion of the three realms.
The same applies to the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*).
As for "destinies" (*gati*), they consist of a portion of one destiny within the group fixed in wrongness (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*),
namely, humans.
A portion of two destinies within the group of those fixed in the right nature—
namely, humans and gods—
and the entirety of the three destinies within the group of those not fixed.
This refers to the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts;
and a small portion of two destinies,
namely humans and devas.
Those born as beings fixed in the state of wrongness (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*) consist of a small portion of one type of birth,
namely, womb-birth (*jarāyu-ja*).
Those fixed in the state of rightness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*) consist of a small portion of two types of birth.
That is to say: womb-birth and transformation-birth.
The two types of birth belonging entirely to the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi) are egg-birth and moisture-birth.
A small portion of the two births,
namely the other two births; so some say.
The category of those fixed in wrongness (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*) consists of a small portion of the three types of birth, excluding miraculous birth (*upapāduka*).

The category of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*) consists of a small portion of all four types of birth; the same applies to the category of those who are not fixed (*aniyata-rāśi*).
Regarding the bases (*āyatana*), some say:
they consist of a portion of three bases within the group fixed in error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*),
and the entirety of five bases within the group fixed in correctness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*).
A portion of twenty-four bases;
the five bases of the indeterminate group in their entirety;
and a portion of twenty-four bases.
According to this explanation,
there are forty locations for the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*):
the eleven locations of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*) in their entirety.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say that within a portion of twenty-four places—
from the Avīci Hell up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra)— there are all three aggregates (triskandha).
Those who are said to possess the nature of parinirvāṇa are called the group of those fixed in the rightness (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi).
Those who do not possess the nature of parinirvāṇa are called the group of those fixed in the wrongness (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi).
Those who are not determined are called the group of the undetermined (aniyata-rāśi).
The commentary states:
That which was explained previously is superior;
this [explanation] is based on the *Saṃgītiparyāya*.
According to the *Prajñapti-śāstra*,
the group of those fixed in wrongness (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*) refers to the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*),
as well as their causes, their fruits, their outflows (*niṣyanda*), their maturation (*vipāka*), and the person (*pudgala*) who possesses those dharmas.
The group of those fixed in the rightness [of the path] (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi) refers to the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa),
as well as their causes, their fruits, their outflows (niṣyanda),
and the persons (pudgala) who have attained those dharmas.
The indeterminate group refers to all other phenomena,
whether they be its causes, its effects,
its outflows, or its maturations.
Together with the individuals who have accomplished those dharmas,
these are called the three clusters (*trayaḥ rāśayaḥ*) as to their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
As for the "elements" (*dhātu*), they are as previously explained.
As for the destinies (*gati*), they consist of a portion of two destinies within the group fixed in wrongness (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*),
namely, the hells and the human realm;
the group fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*) likewise consists of a portion of two destinies.
This refers to humans and devas;
and the two destinies of the indeterminate group in their entirety,
namely animals and hungry ghosts.
A small portion of the three destinies—
namely, those born as hell-beings, humans, and gods—
and a small portion of the two births belonging to the group fixed in wrongness (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*).
This refers to the womb-born and the spontaneously born;
it comprises a portion of the four modes of birth within the group of those fixed in the right nature,
and the same applies to the group of those not fixed.
The classification of the locations should be understood as appropriate.
The Vinaya states:
"Under the Bodhi tree, the Blessed One established all sentient beings into three groups."
That is to say, up to this extent they are called the group of those fixed in error;
up to this extent they are called the group of those fixed in correctness;
and up to this extent they are called the group of those who are indeterminate.
Question: Is this established based on the limits of sentient beings, or based on the limits of phenomena?
If it is based on sentient beings, [then...]
How is it that this is not the attainment of the limit of the ocean of sentient beings?
If one relies upon the Dharma,
even a śrāvaka is able to establish it in such a manner.
What is the uncommon [quality] of the Buddha as compared to the śrāvakas?
Some say it is established based on sentient beings.
Question: If that is so, why is it not the case that one attains the limit of the ocean of sentient beings?
Answer: There is no fault in the Buddha attaining the limit of the ocean of sentient beings.
However, this is obtained by way of general characteristics, not specific characteristics;
that is to say, all sentient beings do not transcend the four modes of birth,
and it is in this manner that they are so obtained.
Some say: "It is established according to the Dharma.
Question: If that is so, then...
Śrāvakas are also able to establish [the teachings] in this way.
What, then, is the unique distinction between a Buddha and a śrāvaka?
Answer: Śrāvakas derive their cause from hearing [the Dharma] from a Buddha.
The Buddha is able to establish [the path] by himself without a teacher;
this is what constitutes his unique quality (*āveṇika*). Some say:

If [the classification] is established based on sentient beings within a trichiliocosm and for a period of one thousand years, whereas it is established based on the Dharma in other worlds and at other times;
[it is asked: if the Buddha had already established sentient beings into the three categories (tripuñja) beneath the Bodhi tree, [how is this so?]
Why, then, is it further stated that he surveys the world with the Buddha-eye during the six periods of day and night?
The answer is: although the three categories (*tri-nikāya*) were previously established, their specific distinctions of state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) had not yet been observed.
Who, at what time, enters the group of those fixed in error from the group of those not fixed?
And who, at what time, enters the group of those fixed in error or the group of those fixed in the right from the group of those not fixed?
In order to know this, he further observed day and night with his Buddha-eye.
Some say this was to demonstrate that the Buddha, at all times, constantly delights in contemplating matters that benefit others.
Some say this is to manifest that the Blessed One’s great compassion permeates his mind and is free from weariness.
The Venerable Vasumitra says:
There are sentient beings who repeatedly come from other worlds to be born in this land.
Because they had not previously been established there,
he now observes them with his Buddha-eye and establishes them once again.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"The Buddha takes the Dharma as his teacher;
it is because he wishes to reverently serve the Dharma."
Six times during the day and night, he observes the world with the Buddha-eye.
The Venerable Ghosaka says:
"The Buddha wishes to demonstrate that his actions are thoroughly examined."
Although they have established them, they further examine:
do those who have accomplished the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) also accomplish the untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma)?
Answer: Those who achieve the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) also achieve untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma), because the factors of enlightenment are themselves untainted.
However, there are those who achieve untainted phenomena but do not achieve the factors of enlightenment.
This refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
For all ordinary beings possess non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*),
and they also possess analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) in accordance with whichever category of defilement they have abandoned.
If one does not possess the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharmas), does that person not possess the untainted phenomena (anāsravadharmas)?
Answer: There is no one who does not possess the untainted phenomena.
Because non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is necessarily accomplished,
there are those who do not accomplish the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga),
namely, all ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) necessarily do not possess conditioned untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
Do those who have attained the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) necessarily attain untainted phenomena?
Answer: Those who have attained the factors of enlightenment necessarily attain untainted phenomena.
There are those who attain untainted dharmas that are not factors of enlightenment,
namely, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
[This refers to] the attainment of what is called the factors of enlightenment.
This may be so, for at the time of entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one attains what was previously unattained.
But how can it be said that untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are "attained"?
Because there is nothing that has not been non-accomplished from the beginning due to non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Some say that this passage should simply state "one attains the factors of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*).
One should not say that one attains untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*).
Some say that within this context, untainted dharmas are of two types.
The first is a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the second is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
One attains the factors of enlightenment at the time of entering rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*);
one attains analytical cessation at the time of becoming free from whichever category of defilement.
Ordinary beings attain cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding whichever category among those abandoned by seeing and cultivation in the eight stages they have detached from;
therefore, this statement was made. Some say:
Among these, there are three categories of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*):
first, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); second, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); and third, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
One attains the factors of enlightenment at the moment of entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
When one becomes detached from any category of defilement, one attains cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
At whatever time one attains it, one attains cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: Is it not the case that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) fundamentally all possess cessation not through deliberation?
Why is it said that they are "attained"?

Answer: Although they are fundamentally accomplished, they may also be said to be attained in the context of the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa-adhigama*), just as, for example, by means of giving (*dāna*).
Either by means of ethical discipline,
or by means of learning,
or by means of reflection.
Alternatively, by means of the contemplation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) while maintaining mindfulness of the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*),
or through the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*),
one causes dharmas such as those of the evil destinies to attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, if one speaks in terms of general categories (*jāti*), one should not say that [attainment] is acquired; however,
if one speaks in terms of the differentiation of specific entities (*vastu-viśeṣa*), it may be said that it is acquired,
because in each and every moment, one acquires them individually according to their respective entities.
Is one who possesses the equanimity factor of enlightenment necessarily one who possesses the untainted (anāsrava) dharma of equanimity?
Answer: There is no case of possessing the equanimity factor of enlightenment in its entirety, nor is there any case of possessing the untainted dharma of equanimity in its entirety.
This is because there is certainly no noble one who returns to being an ordinary person, nor is there any sentient being who does not possess non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
However, it is not that such cessation does not exist; rather, since there is the sense of relinquishing it only partially, it is said that there is no "complete relinquishment."
If one falls away from the factors of enlightenment, does one also fall away from the untainted dharmas?
Answer: There is no complete falling away from the factors of enlightenment, nor is there any complete falling away from the untainted dharmas.
The meaning is as explained previously.
Furthermore, it is to refute the Mahāsāṃghika school’s assertion that those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) may fall away,
and to refute the Dārṣṭāntikas’ denial of the existence of the dharma of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Therefore, this statement was made:
there is no such thing as completely abandoning or completely falling back from the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and the untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*).
Is it not the case that for all those [factors] which have not been abandoned, they have not been fully known?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Herein, the treatise is composed based on two kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*):
first, thorough knowledge by means of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*).
Regarding the two types of thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*),
among the thorough knowledges of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*), some say:
It is exclusively untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Some say it also includes both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted knowledge.
Regarding those who maintain that there is only untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*):

they say that at the time of the clear realization of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*), one is said to have "thoroughly known" (*parijñāta*) the five categories of phenomena to be abandoned by means of knowledge;
and regarding the phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, one is said to have "abandoned" them by means of the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
It is the same at the time of the full comprehension of origination (*samudaya-abhisamaya*).
The distinction is that one speaks of one's own respective truth.
At the time of the full comprehension of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya*), because one thoroughly knows the truth of cessation through knowledge, it is called "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
Regarding the phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, they are said to be "abandoned" by virtue of the complete knowledge of abandonment;
the same applies at the time of the clear realization of the path.
The distinction is that one speaks of their respective truths.

In the course of cultivating the path, whatever knowledge arises with respect to any object of focus is called "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) because it is a thorough comprehension by means of that knowledge;
likewise, with respect to any phenomenon to be abandoned.
It is called "abandoned" by virtue of being abandoned through full comprehension (*parijñā*).
This is the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
Is it the case that whatever has not been abandoned has also not been fully comprehended?
Answer: Those that have not been fully known are not yet abandoned, because it is only through knowledge that they can be abandoned.
However, there are cases where something is not yet abandoned but has already been fully known.
This means that when, by virtue of thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*), something has already been thoroughly known,

yet it has not been abandoned by virtue of the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñāna*), this refers to a case where the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen;
in this state, among the four categories of phenomena to be abandoned, those have already been thoroughly known by virtue of thorough knowledge through wisdom.
Because it is not through the full knowledge of abandonment that [the defilements] have already been abandoned.
When the knowledge of origin has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen,
regarding the three categories of phenomena to be abandoned, the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen.

Regarding the two categories of phenomena to be abandoned, since the knowledge of the path has already arisen, although one has not yet become detached from the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation,
one has already fully understood the single category of phenomena to be abandoned through the thorough comprehension of knowledge.
Because it is not through the full knowledge of abandonment that [defilements] have already been abandoned:
namely, when one has already become free from the defilements of the desire realm but is not yet free from those of the higher realms;

or when, regarding the factors to be abandoned by cultivation in the form and formless realms, one has already become free from the defilements of the form realm but is not yet free from those of the higher realms.
Regarding the factors of the formless realm to be abandoned by cultivation, they have been fully known through the full knowledge of wisdom,
but they have not been abandoned through the full knowledge of abandonment.
Are all those that have been abandoned also fully known?
Answer: Those that have already been abandoned and those that have already been fully known.

That is to say, when the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen, one has fully known a single category of phenomena to be abandoned by means of the full knowledge through knowledge.
Because of the full knowledge of abandonment, [the defilements] are already abandoned.
When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen,
regarding the two categories of phenomena to be abandoned, the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen.

Regarding the three categories of phenomena to be abandoned, since the knowledge of the path has already arisen, although one has not yet become detached from the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation,
