one has thoroughly understood the four categories of phenomena to be abandoned through the thorough understanding of them by means of knowledge.
Because it has been abandoned through full comprehension (*parijñā*), it is already severed.
That same [person], having already become detached from the defilements of the desire realm but not yet detached from those of the higher realms,
[abandons] those [defilements] of the three realms to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
And regarding the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation:
for one who has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm but not yet from those of the higher realms,
[there are] those to be abandoned by insight within the three realms.
Furthermore, when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) has arisen regarding the dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire and form realms,
one has fully understood the dharmas to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation in the three realms by means of thorough understanding through knowledge.
Because of the thorough knowledge of abandonment, [a defilement] has already been abandoned. There are cases where there is thorough knowledge but no abandonment;
that is to say, when something is thoroughly known by means of wisdom, it is thoroughly known.
It is not because of the full knowledge of abandonment that these have already been abandoned.
That is to say, when the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen;
regarding the four categories of phenomena to be abandoned, the detailed explanation is as above.
Regarding those who maintain that the knowledge of thorough comprehension (*parijñā-jñāna*) includes both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
they state that during the stage of the roots of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*),
it is called "thorough comprehension" because one thoroughly comprehends the five categories of phenomena to be abandoned by means of knowledge.
It is called "abandonment" because it is not an abandonment through thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
The stages of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation are as previously explained.
Question: Is it not the case that within the stage of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one has already attained thorough knowledge regarding all phenomena?
Answer: Although this is also called "thorough knowledge" (parijñā), it is not a "further advancement" (viśeṣagamana).
In this context, what is called "further advancement" refers to when the aspect of practice (ākāra) is identical to that of the Noble Path (āryamārga).
Some say: it refers to the wisdoms consisting of what is heard, what is reflected upon, and what is cultivated;
as well as the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas.
Because one thoroughly knows the specific and general characteristics of contaminated phenomena, all such knowledge is termed "thorough knowledge by wisdom" (*jñāna-parijñā*).
This is a brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
Is it the case that whatever has not been abandoned has not been thoroughly known?
Answer: For those that have not been fully known, they have not been abandoned;
because one first attains the full knowledge of them through wisdom and only subsequently attains the full knowledge of their abandonment.
Thus, there are cases where something has not been abandoned but has not [yet] been fully known.
This refers to the case where, because of thorough knowledge through wisdom, [the objects] have already been thoroughly known;
yet, because of the lack of thorough knowledge through abandonment, they have not been abandoned.
This refers to the stage when the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) have arisen, but the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) has not yet arisen.
Regarding the five categories of phenomena to be abandoned, they have been fully known through the thorough knowledge by wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*),
but they have not been abandoned through the abandonment by thorough knowledge (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
The rest is explained in detail as above.
"Are all those that have been abandoned also fully known?
Answer: All those that have been abandoned are also fully known.
This is explained as before."
There are cases where there is full comprehension but no abandonment;
that is to say, when something has been fully comprehended because it was fully comprehended by wisdom,
but has not been abandoned because it was not abandoned by the full comprehension of abandonment.
This refers to the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) having already arisen,
and so forth, as explained in detail above.
Although ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) may have abandonments, these are not "full knowledge through abandonment" (*prahāṇaparijñā*).
Therefore, it is not mentioned,
because it is not realized through the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñānaparijñā*).
This is because the thorough knowledge of wisdom consists exclusively of the modes of activity of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Regarding those beings who, in this life, do not see forms with their eyes—
by depending on what dharma do they bring forth the divine eye?
This is explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is because one wishes to enable those who have doubts to attain certainty, as stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*.
What is the preparatory application for the supernormal power of the knowledge and realization of death and rebirth?
How is the supernormal power of the knowledge and realization of death and rebirth induced?
It is as follows: a beginner practices within the mundane *samādhi*.
Having well cultivated and mastered [the practice] so that it manifests before him,
he first takes the reflection of his own face in a clean mirror in order to evoke the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurabhijñā*).
Or the appearance of the disks of the sun and moon, the palaces of the stars, medicinal herbs, lamps, torches, and mani-jewels;
or the appearance of a great mass of fire burning cities and towns, with flames blazing intensely for many yojanas.
Having grasped these signs, through the power of mental attention consisting of conceptualization (*parikalpa-manasikāra*),
one is able to give rise to luminosity even in the state of non-seeing;
by means of a continuous stream of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-santati*), one brings forth the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
At times, precisely within the locus of the ordinary eye, the pure divine eye— produced from the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the form realm—
arises and is able to see various forms, whether beautiful or ugly; this is explained at length.
Or perhaps someone might give rise to this doubt:
"Are all those who, being born in such a state,
do not see forms with their eyes, unable to produce the divine eye?"
In order to resolve this doubt and provide certainty,
this treatise was composed to demonstrate that although one does not see forms with the eyes of this present life, one is nonetheless able to bring forth the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Furthermore, the Prajñapti-śāstra states:
"What is the preparatory application for the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear?
How is the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear realized?"
This means that a beginner, having already well-cultivated and mastered mundane samādhi so that it manifests before them,
first takes up the sounds of elephants, horses, and chariots in order to induce the supernormal power of the divine ear.
Whether it be the sounds of bells, drums, conch shells, flutes, pipes, songs, hymns, and recitations,
or the sounds produced by the mutual striking of the four great elements—
having correctly grasped the characteristics of all such sounds—
Through the power of conceptual attention (*parikalpita-manasikāra*), one is able to produce various sounds even when separated from hearing;
by means of a continuous stream of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-santati*), the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) is induced.
At times, this occurs precisely at the location of the ordinary ear.
The pure divine ear, produced from the primary elements of the form realm,
arises and is able to hear various sounds, whether of humans or non-humans;
this is explained at length.
From this, there arises further doubt:
"How can those who do not hear sounds in this life produce the divine ear?"
In order to resolve this doubt,
it is shown that although one does not hear sounds with the ears of this present life,
they are nonetheless able to produce the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*).
Therefore, this treatise is composed.
For those who possess this birth but do not see forms with their eyes,
by means of which dharma do they bring forth the divine eye?
Answer: Suppose there is one who attains the recollection of birth by their own nature, such that in a previous life they once saw forms with their eyes;
based upon this, they bring forth the divine eye.
If there are those who, in this very life, do not hear sounds with their ears, by relying on what dharma do they bring forth the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*)?
Answer: It is as when someone attains the mindfulness of innate nature (*svabhāva-jāti-smṛti*).
Previously, in other lives, they had merely heard sounds with their ears;
based upon this, they bring forth the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*).
Question: Regarding those who have attained the knowledge of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), [how do they attain it]?
It is also capable of inducing the divine eye and the divine ear; why, then, are these not mentioned here?
One should understand that when something ought to be stated but is not, it means that the meaning [of the teaching] is incomplete.
Some say that this refers to cases where the divine eye can be induced in one born blind, and the divine ear in one born deaf;
it is in this context that the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) is discussed.
It can only induce that type of divine eye, not the divine ear.
Why is this? Because those born deaf lack the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
Because this knowledge arises through the instruction of another, it is not mentioned here.
Question: For what reason does the divine eye exist only in the four fundamental dhyānas and not in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*)?
The answer is: "It is not that field; it is not that vessel," and so on, as explained at length.
Furthermore, if the earth possesses the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that serves as the basis for supernormal powers, then there is the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Because the preparatory stages lack the meditative concentration that serves as the basis for supernormal powers, they do not possess the divine eye.
Furthermore, if a stage contains meditative concentration subsumed under its constituent factors, then it possesses the divine eye.
The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are not like this.
Some say that if a stage possesses the path of easy progress (*sukha-pratipad*), then the divine eye exists therein.
The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are not like this.
Thus, the divine eye is sometimes said to be only one,
namely, the divine eye.
Some say there are two:
namely, that which has been previously attained and that which has not yet been attained.
Others say there are three.
That is to say, the weak, medium, and superior;
or it is said there are four,
namely, the fruits of the four dhyānas.
Some say there are six,
meaning that each of the weak, medium, and superior grades is further divided into those previously acquired and those not yet acquired.
Others say there are eight.
This means that for each of the four dhyānas, there are results previously attained and those not yet attained;
alternatively, nine grades are taught,
ranging from the "soft-soft" to the "superior-superior."
Some say there are twelve, meaning that each of the four dhyānas has three grades: inferior, middling, and superior.
Others say there are eighteen.
This means that from the "soft-soft" up to the "superior-superior," each has both the previously attained and the not-yet-attained;
alternatively, twenty-four are taught,
meaning that each of the four dhyānas possesses the aforementioned six.
Some say there are thirty-two,
namely sixteen acquired at birth and sixteen acquired through cultivation.
Some say that there are twelve fruits of the four dhyānas, each having the grades of weak, medium, and superior;
furthermore, there are twenty fruits of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, each likewise having five grades.
These are called the thirty-two.
Alternatively, they are said to be thirty-six,
meaning that each fruit of the four dhyānas has nine grades, from the soft-soft up to the superior-superior.
Some say there are seventy-two,
meaning that each of the four dhyānas possesses the aforementioned eighteen [aspects].
If considered in terms of continuity (*saṃtati*) and moments (*kṣaṇa*), they are immeasurable.
Now, this is merely a general explanation regarding the single divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
It is the same for the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*) as well.
Question: Why is it that the non-homogeneous divine eyes and ears do not manifest simultaneously?
Is it not the case that the non-homogeneous (asabhāga) divine nose, tongue, and body also manifest?
Answer: The two faculties of eye and ear apprehend objects that are not in contact with them;
because they arise for the purpose of seeing and hearing from afar, the non-homogeneous divine eye and ear manifest.
The faculties of nose, tongue, and body apprehend only objects that reach them;
because they have no distinct function regarding non-homogeneous [objects], they do not arise in the presence of such. Some say:
If one were to manifest the two faculties of nose and tongue that are not currently functioning,
one would be ridiculed by the world, as it would be said:
"How is it that this person has such a prominent nose and double tongues?"
If there were different primary and secondary bodies present before one's eyes,
the world would mock it, asking:
"How can this person have two bodies like twins?"
Therefore, the nose and other [senses] do not have non-homogeneous counterparts.
Furthermore, regarding the divine eye, the categories of superiority and inferiority must be identical between the left and right;
that is, it is not the case that the left is inferior while the right is superior, and so forth.
Furthermore, when they manifest, they are necessarily complete;
they are neither blind, nor deficient, nor confused, nor are they of the same class as those [defective organs].
The rest is explained in detail in the *Indriya-skandha* and the *Sparśa-nirdeśa*.

Question: Why is it that when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) falls away, both the fetters abandoned through seeing and those abandoned through cultivation increase, whereas when a disciple of the Blessed One (*śrāvaka*) falls away, only the fetters abandoned through cultivation increase?
Answer: Because an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) uses this very path to abandon the fetters abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya),
and uses that same path to abandon the fetters abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya),
both types of fetters increase at the time of their regression.
A disciple of the Blessed One uses this path to abandon the fetters to be abandoned by vision;
he is certain not to fall back from this path.
He uses another path to abandon the fetters to be abandoned by cultivation.
Regarding other paths, there may be regression or non-regression.
If a disciple of the Blessed One uses a particular path to abandon the fetters abandoned through vision,
and uses that same path to abandon the fetters abandoned through cultivation, they likewise do not regress.
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is: in order to refute the views of those who deny the nature of retrogression (parihāṇi-dharma), and to demonstrate that retrogression truly exists, this treatise was written.
In this context, because all acquisitions (*prāpti*) are designated by the term "augmentation" (*upacaya*), they are said to be "accumulated" and "arisen.
Therefore, in some places it is said that acquisition is called "near-arising," because it arises in proximity to those dharmas.
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*,
when the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) arises in an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), five factors arise:
first, the latent tendency of sensual desire itself.
Second, the latent tendency of sensual desire is proximately produced;
third, the latent tendency of ignorance;
fourth, the latent tendency of ignorance is proximately produced.
Fifth is restlessness (*auddhatya*).
In this context, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) uses this path to abandon the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*),
they use that same path to abandon the fetters to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
This means that because one simultaneously abandons the fetters to be abandoned through seeing and those to be abandoned through cultivation by means of the nine grades of the path,
both types of fetters arise together at the time of his regression.
This refers to the disciples of the Blessed One who, by means of this path, abandon the fetters to be abandoned through seeing.
That is to say, when one uses a path of a certain grade to abandon the fetters abandoned by seeing,
one is certainly not subject to regression from that path;
whereas those who use other paths to abandon the fetters abandoned by cultivation [may regress].
That is to say, when one uses the nine grades of the path to abandon the fetters abandoned through cultivation,
there may be regression from that path or no regression.
Even if a disciple of the Blessed One uses this same path to abandon the fetters abandoned through insight.
Furthermore, those who sever the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation by means of this very path likewise do not fall away;

that is to say, even if one were to sever the fetters to be abandoned through both vision and cultivation simultaneously by means of a single grade of the path, such a person likewise does not fall away.
Because, O World-Honored One,
a disciple’s fetters abandoned through vision do not regress;
it is impossible for them to be abandoned simultaneously while regressing from others separately.

Furthermore, when a disciple of the Buddha was formerly a worldling (*pṛthagjana*), they used the nine grades of the path to simultaneously abandon the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation;
now, because they do not regress from what is stabilized by these two paths, [they remain so].

Furthermore, because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) abandon the fetters to be abandoned by both the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) simultaneously while practicing the path of cultivation,
both types of fetters arise together at the time of their regression.
The disciples of the Blessed One (*śrāvaka*), however, abandon the fetters to be abandoned by the path of seeing through the path of seeing.
He is certain not to regress from this path;
he uses the path of cultivation to abandon the fetters abandoned by cultivation.
Regarding this path, there is both regression and non-regression for him.
The rest is to be understood according to what was previously stated.

Furthermore, because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) abandon the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) simultaneously through the use of knowledge (*jñāna*),
both types of fetters arise together at the time of their regression.
The disciples of the Blessed One abandon the fetters to be abandoned by vision through patience;
they are certain not to fall back from this path.
They abandon the fetters to be abandoned by cultivation through wisdom.
In this path, some may regress while others do not;
the rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, ordinary beings do not contemplate the truths simultaneously, because they abandon the fetters to be abandoned by insight and those to be abandoned by cultivation at different times.
At the time of his falling away, two fetters arise simultaneously.
When a disciple of the Blessed One contemplates the truths and abandons the fetters to be abandoned by vision,
he is certain not to fall away from that path.
Whether one abandons the fetters to be abandoned through insight or through cultivation by contemplating the truths or not contemplating the truths,
there may be regression from that path or no regression;
the rest is to be understood according to what was previously explained.

Furthermore, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) abandons the fetters to be abandoned by seeing and those to be abandoned by cultivation simultaneously, using both the path of arising and the path of non-arising;
therefore, at the time of their falling away, the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of these two types of fetters arise together.
A disciple of the Blessed One (*bhagavataḥ śrāvaka*), however, abandons the fetters to be abandoned by seeing using only the path of non-arising.
He is certain not to regress from this path when using both the arisen and unarisen paths to abandon the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding this path, he may either regress or not regress.
The rest is to be understood according to what was stated previously.

Furthermore, because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) simultaneously abandon the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through seeing and those to be abandoned through cultivation by means of a path that is not of intense power,
both types of fetters may arise together at the time of their regression.
A disciple of the Blessed One who abandons the fetters to be abandoned by seeing through a sharp path will certainly not fall back from that path;
one who abandons the fetters to be abandoned by cultivation through a non-sharp path [will likewise not fall back].
Regarding this path, there are those who regress and those who do not;
the rest is as explained previously. Some say:

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) abandon, simultaneously by means of the contaminated path (*sāsravamārga*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through seeing and those to be abandoned through cultivation;
therefore, at the time of their falling away, both types of fetters can arise together.
The disciples of the Blessed One (*śrāvaka*), however, abandon the fetters to be abandoned through seeing by means of the uncontaminated path (*anāsravamārga*).
He is certain not to fall away from this path.
By means of both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths, he abandons the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Regarding this path, he may either fall away or not fall away.
However, it is taught that one who abandons [defilements] by means of the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) is definitely non-retrogressive.
Question: If that is so, there should be no Arhat who retrogresses from the fruit of Arhatship.
Because the fetters of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are abandoned only by the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Answer: If an Arhat has previously abandoned the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the lower eight stages by means of the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*), [then...]
He may still undergo regression,
because his fundamental attainment is not firm.
This applies to one who has previously severed the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation in the lower eight stages by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
He will certainly not fall back, because his root is firm.
Question: For what reason is there no falling back from the Path of Seeing?
The answer is: because its root is firm and stable. What is the root?
It refers to whatever acts of giving, morality, cultivation, or service to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are performed by one who seeks liberation.
Whether attending to the elderly or the sick, reciting and chanting the sacred words, expounding them for others,
engaging in correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), or practicing the meditation on impurity,
mindfulness of breathing, the four foundations of mindfulness, the seven stages of excellence, the levels of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas.
All such [states] are called the fundamental path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Some say that the path of seeing is so intense, sharp, and swift that it can sever the nine grades of fetters (*saṃyojana*) with a single grade of the path.
Therefore, there is no falling back.
Some say that in the Path of Seeing, only a single moment of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) manifests.
Therefore, there is no falling back.
Some say that if there were falling back from the path of seeing, then the holy life one has cultivated would be unreliable.
Because one who has regressed from the path of seeing is considered an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Question: Regarding the statement that noble ones (*ārya*) abandon the fetters to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) by means of other paths, there are those who regress from those other paths and those who do not. What is the distinction?
Who falls away and who does not fall away?
Answer: Those of occasional liberation (samayavimukta) fall away;
those of immovable dharma (akopyadharman) do not fall away.
Furthermore, those of dull faculties fall back,
while those of sharp faculties do not fall back.
Furthermore, those who have severed [defilements] through the power of internal causes do not fall back.
Those who fall away do so due to the power of external conditions;
some say that those who fall away do so because their practice was merely the preparatory stage of impurity meditation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
One who abandons [defilements] through the preparatory practice of mindfulness of breathing does not fall back.
Some say that if one abandons the fetters to be abandoned by cultivation in the lower eight stages by means of the mundane path, there is falling back.
If one abandons [the defilements] by means of the supramundane path, there is no falling back.
This is like a multi-storied pavilion: if its foundation is precarious, it may be toppled;
if it is firm, it is not so.
Question: For what reason do those in the three higher fruits undergo falling away (*parihāṇi*), whereas those in the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) do not?
Answer: The fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) arise based on objective entities (*savastuka*).
That is to say, they possess both pure aspects (*śubha-nimitta*) and impure aspects (*aśubha-nimitta*).
When he contemplates the sign of purity through improper attention,
he regresses from the perception of impurity,
and the fetters to be abandoned by vision arise.
It arises based on the absence of any objective entity;
there is not a single dharma that is "I" or "mine," such that one could cause them to fall away from the vision of non-self through observation.
Question: For what reason was this treatise composed?

Answer: It was composed to refute the Mahāsāṃghika school’s assertion that those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) may fall away from it, and to demonstrate that the fruit of stream-entry is definitively free from falling away. Thus, this treatise was written.
Regarding the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation that arise based on objective entities:
this refers to the fact that the hair, body hair, nails, and so forth which one grasps as objects are not entirely devoid of some degree of worldly pure appearance.
If one engages in improper mental attention at such a time, one then regresses from the perception of impurity that has been cultivated.
Regarding the previously abandoned fetters to be abandoned through cultivation and those fetters to be abandoned through vision that arise based on non-existent objects:
this refers to the fact that the characteristics of "self" and "mine" which are grasped at are ultimately non-existent.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Phenomena have no activity, nor do they possess a sentient being, a life-principle, a nourisher,
a person, an agent, or an experiencer."
Within the mere collection of conditioned formations there is no self,
just as an empty fist deceives young children;
the wise person understands this clearly, like seeing the fingers extended.
Therefore, once one has seen the selflessness of phenomena, there is necessarily no falling back;
thus, there is no retrogression from the fruit of stream-entry.
However, there is retrogression from the three higher fruits.
Regarding all the untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) that have been attained,
and so forth as explained at length:
Why was this treatise composed?

Answer: This is to refute the Venerable Śrīlāta’s assertion that when one falls away from the fruit of arhatship, one only acquires future dharmas of training previously abandoned, but does not acquire past ones.
Why is this? Because that [result] never manifests before them.
Now, I wish to clarify the occasion when one regresses from the fruit of arhatship.
One obtains those factors of training previously relinquished in the past and future;
although these past factors cannot be manifested, they can still be accomplished.
For this reason, this treatise was composed.

When one falls back from the three higher fruits, regarding all the untainted faculties (indriya), powers (bala), factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and factors of the path (mārgāṅga) that were previously acquired, should it be said that they are "previously acquired" or "previously unacquired"? Answer:
It should be said that they are "previously acquired."
This means that when one first attains a fruit, it is abandoned;
now, at the time of falling back, it is regained.
This is because all previously unattained noble paths are acquired only at the time of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*).
When one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm, regarding all the aggregates, elements, and bases that are acquired, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is that this is also to refute Śamadatta’s assertion that when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm,
one only acquires previously abandoned future dharmas and does not acquire past ones.
Why is this? Because that [form] never manifests before them.
Now, I wish to clarify the process of dying in the formless realm and being reborn in the desire realm.
This treatise was composed because one acquires dharmas previously abandoned in the past and future;
otherwise, when one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm, at the very moment of initial conception, [one would acquire them].
It should only be that one accomplishes the birth and death of two lifetimes;
however, there is no sentient being who accomplishes only the birth and death of two lifetimes,
because one definitely accomplishes the contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) of the three time periods.
When one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm,
all the aggregates, elements, and bases that are acquired, as well as the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate roots,
fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, secondary afflictions, and envelopments.
Should it be said that one acquires what has already been acquired, or that one acquires what has never before been acquired?
It should be said that wholesome and defiled dharmas are acquired by means of what has already been acquired,
whereas resultant dharmas are acquired by means of what has never before been acquired.
Regarding "wholesome and defiled dharmas that have been previously acquired":
"wholesome" refers to the four aggregates of innate wholesome [dharmas]. Some say:
One also acquires the four aggregates consisting of hearing and reflection through habitual practice.
These wholesome dharmas were previously abandoned because one had transcended that realm and stage;
now, because one has returned to that realm and stage, they are acquired as defiled.
This refers to the four contaminated aggregates— namely, those that are unwholesome or obscured-neutral—
which were previously abandoned through the removal of passion;
they are now acquired again due to returning to a particular realm or stage.
Question: Those who have practiced the four aggregates of the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the fields of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) should also attain [the fruit];
why then is this not mentioned? Answer: That which should be stated but is not stated [is because it is included within other categories].
One should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Some say that,
among the non-obscured neutral phenomena (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-dharma*), [the attainment] is for the most part not obtained.
This refers to the entirety of that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*), as well as a small portion of others;
therefore, although they are acquired to some extent, they are not mentioned.
Other masters say:
Even those who have practiced habitually do not obtain it,
because they are weak and inferior.
As for the maturation-dharmas, that which was never previously obtained is now obtained.
This means that from time immemorial, these have never been attained before, but are now accomplished for the first time in the present.
Question: Since the nourishment (*puṣṭi*) of the aggregates has also never been attained before, why is it not mentioned?
Regarding that which was promised but not yet explained:
one should know that this meaning is incomplete.
Furthermore, if maturation (*vipāka*) is discussed, it should be understood that nourishment (*aupacayika*) has also already been explained.
It nourishes and protects the maturation (vipāka),
just as a person supports another person,
or as a wall supports another wall.
Because they necessarily accompany one another, at that time there is also the acquisition of previously unobtained *niṣyanda-dharmas* (concordant phenomena).
For example, this is like the *pṛthagjanatva* (state of being an ordinary person) and so forth; however, because they are few, they are not mentioned.
When one dies in the formless realm and is born in the form realm, the aggregates, elements, and bases that are acquired are wholesome or indeterminate;
as are the faculties, fetters, bonds, latent dispositions, secondary afflictions, and envelopments.
Should it be said that one acquires what has been previously acquired, or that one acquires what has never before been acquired?
It should be said that wholesome and defiled dharmas are acquired as what has been previously acquired,
whereas resultant dharmas are acquired as what has never before been acquired.
Regarding "wholesome and defiled dharmas that have been previously acquired":
"wholesome" refers to the four aggregates of innate wholesomeness (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) and the five aggregates of applied wholesomeness (*prāyogika-kuśala*).
These wholesome dharmas were previously abandoned because one had transcended the realm and stage;
now they are acquired because one has returned to that realm and stage.
The defiled [dharmas] refer to the four aggregates of the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) type.
These defiled dharmas were previously abandoned through the separation from passion;
now, because one has returned to that realm and stage, they are acquired again.
Among the unobscured-neutral dharmas, the four aggregates of the resultant state (*vipākaja*) have also been acquired before.
They are not mentioned because they are few.
Their nourishment (*āhāra*) and their outflow (*niṣyanda*) are explained as before.
This refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth, which are acquired when one dies in the form realm and is reborn in the desire realm.
As it was explained regarding passing away from the formless realm and being reborn in the desire realm,
so too should this explanation here be understood as before.
When one induces the supernormal power of the base of miraculous power (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*) based on the first dhyāna:
How far does that extend?
The answer is: as far as the Brahma-world.
This refers to when one induces the supernormal power of the divine ear based on the first dhyāna.
How far does his hearing extend?
The answer is: up to the Brahma-world.
This occurs when one, relying on the first dhyāna, brings forth the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others.
What range of bound minds and mental factors does that supreme knowledge of the distant know?
Answer: Up to the Brahma-world.
This refers to when one, by relying on the first dhyāna, brings forth the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*).
To what extent does he recollect past lives?
Answer: Up to the Brahma-world.
This occurs when, by relying on the first dhyāna, one brings forth the supernormal power of the divine eye.
What kind of forms does that [vision] perceive from such a great distance?
Answer: Up to the Brahma-world, just as one relies on the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna.
The detailed explanations for each respective section are likewise the same.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
As stated in the Sūtras and Vinaya,
those who possess supernormal powers can exercise mastery over their bodies even as far as the Brahma-world;
yet, some may give rise to such a doubt.
Since the mastery of supernormal powers (abhijñā) extends only as far as the Brahma-world and not to the higher stages,
it is said that the supernormal powers arising from reliance upon the fourth dhyāna are intended to provide certainty regarding this doubt.
This treatise was composed because [the Buddha] exercises mastery over bodies even up to the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*) or the Ultimate of Form (*Akaniṣṭha*).
Question: If that is so, how should one reconcile this with what is taught in the Sūtras and the Vinaya?
Answer: The Blessed One taught this regarding those places where there is bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) belonging to that same level.
In the second dhyāna and above, there is no bodily intimation belonging to that same level.
For this reason, it is not mentioned.
Some say that among those [attainments], the Buddha taught that the first attainment of a higher stage is not the first attainment [of that stage].
Some say that the term "Brahma-world" subsumes all four dhyānas because they all possess pure samādhis embraced by their respective factors.
A question is raised: [this is so] because even up to the first dhyāna there exists vocal intimation (vāgvijñapti).
Based on the first dhyāna, one produces the divine ear and hears sounds from those [lower] levels;
since there is no vocal intimation (vāgvijñapti) in the higher stages, what kind of sounds does one hear when producing the divine ear based on the second dhyāna and so forth?

Answer: Just as one born in the first dhyāna initiates vocal intimation and the like by means of a mind originating from the first dhyāna when speaking, so too does one born in the three higher dhyānas initiate vocal intimation and the like by means of a mind originating from the first dhyāna when speaking.
This is what is heard by the divine ear of those in that stage.
Some say that although there is no sound of vocal intimation in the higher stages, [it is still heard].
However, there are other sounds that are heard by them;
therefore, there is no fault.
Question: If one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) relies on the first dhyāna to produce the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-abhijñā*), [how does this occur]?
Can one hear the vocal sounds of the deities in the three higher dhyāna realms?
Some say that they cannot be heard because the locations are too distant.
Alternatively, because it is subtle.
Some say that even one who applies intense attention is able to hear it.
Because these are the dharmas of this same stage.
Question: Depending on which dhyāna one manifests the supernormal power of the base of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi*), to what extent can one reach?
Answer: One who manifests it depending on the first dhyāna can reach the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*).

Up to those who have set out based on the fourth dhyāna, they can reach as far as the Bṛhatphala heaven or the Akaniṣṭha heaven; however, if a śrāvaka does not direct their attention, it extends at most to a small thousand-world system, and if they do direct their attention, it extends to a medium thousand-world system.
The Pratyekabuddha does not direct his attention beyond a medium trichiliocosm;
the Buddha does not direct his attention beyond a great trichiliocosm,
but can direct his attention as far as infinite worlds.
As it is with the supernormal power of the divine ear, so it is with the other four [supernormal powers].
A detailed explanation of the six supernormal powers is as found in the Mahābhūta-skandha.
If one contemplates suffering as suffering, one attains the fruit of arhatship.
What kind of suffering does he contemplate?
Answer: Suffering bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This is stated as a general summary of the pervasive elements (*anuśaya*).

If it follows the respective stage, one should say that the suffering associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is precisely the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).
If, while contemplating origination, one attains the fruit of arhatship, what kind of origination associated with which stage does he contemplate?
The answer is: it is the origin associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This is also stated generally according to the realms (*dhātu*).

If it were stated according to the stages (*bhūmi*), one would have to say that the origin associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is the origin known through the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvayajñāna*).
If one contemplates cessation and attains the fruit of arhatship through that contemplation, what kind of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) does one contemplate as being ceased?
Answer: Either those bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
Or, regarding the cessation of all formations associated with the form and formless realms,
there is the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (anvaya-jñāna).
If one contemplates the Path and attains the fruit of Arhatship, [the same applies].
He contemplates which fettered formations can be severed by the path.
The answer is: either those fettered to the desire realm, or those fettered to the form and formless realms.
The path that severs these formations is precisely the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (mārga-dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna).
In this way, each of these six knowledges, through four aspects,

acts as the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) to sever the lowest-of-the-low grade of afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, simultaneously with the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*).
This is the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) by which one realizes the fruit of arhatship;
it is explained in detail in the third section of the *Saṃyukta-skandha*.
Regarding the defilements abandoned through cultivation that are both variegated and formless, all take six knowledges as their path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).

That is to say, the four types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the dharma-knowledge regarding cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-dharma-jñāna*); these are said to be the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
If it is the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*), it consists solely of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Because that does not pervade [all objects], it is not what is being discussed here.
When one arises in the uninterrupted path of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) based on the first dhyāna,
there are [moments] that take only the suffering of their own level as object,

some that take only the suffering of the second dhyāna as object, and so on, up to those that take only the suffering of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as object; there is no simultaneous taking of two levels as objects.
Up to eight [objects] may be taken as conditions,
because of the difference between the coarse and the subtle, and because they are abandoned in distinct stages.
As it is with the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvaya-jñāna*), so it is also with the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*).
At the time of the uninterrupted path of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*),
there is that which takes only the cessation of the formations of its own stage as its object,
and there is that which takes only the cessation of the formations of the second dhyāna as its object.
Up to the point where there are only formations having the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their object, there are two types of cessation through association with conditions;
up to the point where there are eight,
because they are equally subtle.
Because they all oppose the defilements;
when the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) arises,
they all take as their object the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge across the nine stages, because these paths serve as mutual causes for one another.
Because of their distinct categories and so forth,
at the time of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*),
one contemplates only the cessation of the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm.
When the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) of the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) arises,
it takes as its object the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge across all six stages;
this is the case when relying on the first dhyāna.
The same applies up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

The distinction is that, based on the three formless spheres, the two types of knowledge—knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)—do not take the lower realms or cessation as their objects.
In this context, all stages do not take suffering or its origin in the lower realms as their objects.
Because it would be useless to arise [in a higher stage] once one has already abandoned the defilements of the lower stage,
when one relies on the first dhyāna to produce the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and abandons the defilements of the first dhyāna,
the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) take only the suffering and origin of the first dhyāna as their objects.
Regarding the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), some takes as its object only the cessation of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the first dhyāna;
some takes as its object the cessation of the conditioned phenomena of the first and second dhyānas;
and some takes as its object the cessation of the conditioned phenomena of the first, second, and third dhyānas.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the first dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite space.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the first dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite consciousness;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness.
There is the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) takes as its object, in its entirety, the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge across the nine stages.
The dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodhadharmajñāna*) takes as its object only the cessation of conditioned phenomena within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The path-knowledge of dharma (mārga-dharmajñāna) takes as its collective object the category of path-knowledge belonging to the six stages.
When one relies on the first dhyāna to give rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) in order to become detached from the defilements of the second dhyāna:
The subsequent knowledge of the origin of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) takes as its object only the suffering and its origin of the second dhyāna.
The subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) sometimes takes as its object the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the first dhyāna,
and sometimes takes as its object the cessation of all conditioned phenomena of the second dhyāna.
There are formations conditioned by the first and second dhyānas that cease;
there are formations conditioned by the second and third dhyānas that cease;
and there are formations conditioned by the first, second, and third dhyānas that cease.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the second, third, and fourth dhyānas;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas;
and there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the second dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite space.
There is the cessation of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) having as their object the first dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite space;
there is the cessation of conditioned phenomena having as their object the second dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite consciousness.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the first dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite consciousness;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the second dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness.
There is the cessation of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) having as their object the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness;
there is the cessation of conditioned phenomena having as their object the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There is the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Regarding the knowledge of the path as a category (*mārgānvayajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgadharmajñāna*), they are as previously explained.
When one relies on the first dhyāna to give rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and becomes detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna:
The subsequent knowledge of the origin of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) takes as its object only the suffering and its origin of the third dhyāna.
The subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) sometimes takes as its object the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the first dhyāna,
and sometimes takes as its object the cessation of all conditioned phenomena of the second dhyāna.
There are those who take as their object only the cessation of formations belonging to the third dhyāna;
there are those who take as their object the cessation of formations belonging to the first and second dhyānas;
and there are those who take as their object the cessation of formations belonging to the second and third dhyānas.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the third and fourth dhyānas;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the first, second, and third dhyānas;
and there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the third and fourth dhyānas and the sphere of infinite space;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
There is the cessation of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) having as their object the second dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite space;
there is the cessation of conditioned phenomena having as their object the third dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite consciousness.
There is the cessation of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) having as their object the first dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite space;
there is the cessation of conditioned phenomena having as their object the second dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite consciousness.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the third dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the first dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite consciousness.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the second dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the third dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There is the cessation of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) having as their object the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness;
there is the cessation of conditioned phenomena having as their object the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There is the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The knowledge of the path as a category (*mārgānvayajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path as a phenomenon (*mārgadharmajñāna*) regarding this cessation are as previously explained.
When one relies on the first dhyāna to give rise to the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) for the purpose of becoming detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna:
The subsequent knowledge of the origin of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) takes as its object only the suffering and its origin of the fourth dhyāna.
The subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) sometimes takes as its object the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the first dhyāna,
up to the point where it takes as its object the cessation of all conditioned phenomena of the fourth dhyāna.
There are formations conditioned by the first and second dhyānas that cease;
there are formations conditioned by the second and third dhyānas that cease;
and there are formations conditioned by the third and fourth dhyānas that cease.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the first, second, and third dhyānas;
and there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the third and fourth dhyānas and the sphere of infinite space;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the fourth dhyāna and the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the second dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite space;
and there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the third dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite consciousness.
There is the cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) ranging from the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The combined objects of the five, six, seven, and eight stages are as previously explained.
The knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārgadharmajñāna*) are also as previously explained.

When one relies on the first dhyāna to give rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*),
the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) takes only the suffering and origin of the sphere of infinite space as its object;
the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) takes only the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the first dhyāna as its object.
There are formations that cease having as their object only the sphere of infinite space;
there are formations that cease having as their object the first and second dhyānas;
and there are formations that cease having as their object the second and third dhyānas.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the third and fourth dhyānas;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space;
and there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the first, second, and third dhyānas;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the second, third, and fourth dhyānas;
and there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the third, fourth, and the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana).
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space, and the sphere of infinite consciousness;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness.
The combined objects of the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth stages are as previously explained.
The subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) and the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) are also as previously explained.

When one relies on the first *dhyāna* to give rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) for the purpose of becoming detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

The subsequent knowledge of the origin of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) takes as its object only the suffering and its origin of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
The subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) includes that which takes as its object only the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the first dhyāna,
up to that which takes as its object only the cessation of all conditioned phenomena of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
There are formations conditioned by the first and second dhyānas that cease;
there are formations conditioned by the second and third dhyānas that cease;
and there are formations conditioned by the third and fourth dhyānas that cease.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness;
and there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the spheres of infinite consciousness and nothingness.
There are formations conditioned by the first, second, and third dhyānas that cease;
there are formations conditioned by the second, third, and fourth dhyānas that cease;
and there are formations conditioned by the third, fourth, and the sphere of infinite space that cease.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space, and the sphere of infinite consciousness;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness.
There is the cessation of the formations associated with the consciousness of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The combined objects of the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth stages are as previously explained.
The path-subsequent knowledge (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) and the path-dharma-knowledge (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) are also as previously described.

When one relies on the first dhyāna to give rise to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) for the purpose of becoming detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
the subsequent knowledges of suffering and origination (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna* and *samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) take only the suffering and origination of the sphere of nothingness as their objects.
Regarding the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), there is that which takes only the cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the first dhyāna as its object,
up to and including that which takes only the cessation of conditioned phenomena of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as its object;
there is also that which takes the cessation of conditioned phenomena of both the first and second dhyānas as its object.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the second and third dhyānas;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the third and fourth dhyānas;
and there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space.
There is the cessation of formations conditioned by the sphere of infinite space;
there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness;
and there is the cessation of formations conditioned by the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The combined objects of the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth stages are as previously explained.
The subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) and the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) are also as previously explained.

When one relies on the first *dhyāna* to give rise to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) for the purpose of abandoning the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

The subsequent knowledge of the origin of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) takes as its object only the suffering and its origin of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
As for the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), there is that which takes as its object only the cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the first dhyāna,
up to that which takes as its object only the cessation of conditioned phenomena of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth stages collectively take [the objects] as their conditions, as previously explained.
The subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) and the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodhadharmajñāna*) are also as previously explained.

In this manner, relying on the second *dhyāna*, one gives rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) to become detached from the defilements of the second *dhyāna* up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Up to the point where one gives rise to the path of uninterrupted transition based on the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
thereby becoming free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*);
all of this should be explained in detail as appropriate.
As for the distinctions:
in the three formless stages,
two types of dharma-knowledge are excluded.
Furthermore, it cannot take the cessation of a lower stage as its object.
This refers to those born in the Desire Realm;
if one is born in the Form or Formless Realms, the knowledge of all phenomena (sarvadharma-jñāna) does not manifest at all.
When one is born in those higher stages, one does not take the cessation of lower stages as an object;
this is just like the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga).
The path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) is likewise.
Excluding only the path of liberation that is the lowest-of-the-low grade of defilement regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
it is possible for only the subsequent knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge of origin to exist. *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 186.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 187,
composed by the Five Hundred Great Arhats and Others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. 8. The Aggregate of Views (Dṛṣṭiskandha). 1. The Section on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Smṛtyupasthāna-nikāya). 1. The First of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness within the Eighth [Chapter] on the Aggregate of Views. There are four foundations of mindfulness.
This refers to the applications of mindfulness regarding body,
sensation, mind, and phenomena;
having thus mastered the meaning of such chapters and their explanations, one has attained realization.
This should be explained in detail.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the sūtras.
As stated in the sutra,
there are four foundations of mindfulness;
namely, the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
This continues up to the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Although this is stated, it is not further differentiated:
if one cultivates the application of mindfulness to the body, does one [also] cultivate that of feeling (*vedanā*)?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
That sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Regarding those points not analyzed therein:
Since all [of these] ought now to be explained, this treatise is composed.
However, the Buddha taught that there are three kinds of foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*):
first, the foundation of mindfulness by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*).
There are two types of mindfulness establishments (smṛtyupasthāna): those that are mixed and those that have objects of focus.
In what context is the mindfulness establishment as intrinsic nature (svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna) taught?
Answer: As stated in the Sūtra, there is one path leading to purification that enables sentient beings to transcend and extinguish sorrow and suffering;
namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four? They are:
dwelling in mindfulness by contemplating the body as the body, and so on, up to dwelling in mindfulness by contemplating phenomena as phenomena.
Furthermore, where is the application of mindfulness as a conjoined state (saṃsṛṣṭa-smṛtyupasthāna) taught?
Answer: As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If anyone should say..."
The collection of wholesome dharmas consists of the four foundations of mindfulness;
this is the correct teaching. Why is that?
For one who possesses the complete and perfect collection of wholesome qualities, there are only the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are these four? They are:
contemplating the body as the body.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, where is the application of mindfulness to objects (ālambanasmṛtyupasthāna) taught?
Answer: As stated in the Sūtra.
If anyone says that all phenomena are the four foundations of mindfulness,
this is the correct teaching.
Why is this? Because it is the four foundations of mindfulness alone that fully encompass and sustain all phenomena.
What are these four?
That is to say, one dwells contemplating the body as a body,
and so forth, as explained at length.
Among these, the introductory phrases of the three sūtras follow their respective order.
Regarding the distinction between the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) as having an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), being mixed, and having an object (*ālambana*):
the explanations of these terms all refer to the foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature,
because the term "contemplation" (*anupaśyanā*) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*) in both cases.
Question: For what reason does the Blessed One, in the summary verses,
sometimes speak of the foundations of mindfulness as being by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and sometimes speak of them as being by way of association (*saṃsarga*)?
If it is asked: "When the *smṛtyupasthāna* of the object (*ālambana*) is explained, why is only the *smṛtyupasthāna* of essential nature (*svabhāva*) mentioned in the explanation of the phrases?
The answer is: "It is because one wishes to ensure that the ultimate (*paramārtha*) *smṛtyupasthāna* is not lost or destroyed."
The foundations of mindfulness are of two kinds:
first, the ultimate;
second, the conventional.
The foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature is the ultimate truth;
the others are conventional.
The foundation of mindfulness as the ultimate truth can never be lost or destroyed at any time.
Therefore, the Buddha explained self-nature (*svabhāva*) in all the etymological definitions (*nirukti*).
Some say that because of the power of the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as self-nature, the mixed objects of focus are designated as "applications of mindfulness."
Some say: This is to reveal that all three applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) have wisdom (prajñā) as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva);
that is to say, a single nature of wisdom, through its association with and assistance from co-existent factors (sahabhū-dharma).
That which is capable of performing an action is called the "application of mindfulness associated with mixed objects" (*saṃsṛṣṭa-smṛtyupasthāna*).

That which, through the power of its object, is able to universally and continuously contemplate [the four truths] is called the "application of mindfulness of the object" (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*).
This is because the Buddha taught these three types of applications of mindfulness in the sūtras.
The Abhidharma also composes its treatises in various places based on the three foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
How is this known?
As it is said:
What is the application of mindfulness to the body?
It is wisdom that takes the body as its object.
... [and so on] ... What is the application of mindfulness to phenomena?
This refers to the wisdom that takes phenomena as its object;
this is what is called the station of mindfulness of intrinsic nature.
This is precisely what is taught in the sūtras.
"There is one path leading [to liberation]," and so forth, as it is said at length.
As it is asked:
"What is the foundation of mindfulness of the body?"
This refers to the wholesome, whether contaminated or uncontaminated, produced by the path having the body as its predominant condition. ...
[and so on] ... What is the application of mindfulness to phenomena?
It is the wholesome, whether contaminated or uncontaminated, produced by the path having phenomena as its predominant condition.
This refers to what is called the locus of the mixed applications of mindfulness;
this is precisely what is taught in the sūtras as "the collection of wholesome dharmas."
That is, the four foundations of mindfulness,
and so forth, as explained at length.
As it is said:
What is the application of mindfulness to the body?
It refers to the ten bases of form and the form included within the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
What is the application of mindfulness to feelings?
This refers to the six groups of feeling.
What is the application of mindfulness to the mind?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness.
What is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna)?
It refers to the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that are not comprised within the aggregate of feeling (vedanāskandha) and are non-material (arūpa).
This is said to be the basis for the application of mindfulness with respect to its objects.
This is precisely what is taught in the Sūtra:
"All phenomena" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness.
Thus, what is taught in the Abhidharma accords with the Sūtras;
for this reason, the treatise here also proceeds by means of the three kinds of foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Question: For what kind of sentient beings did the Blessed One teach the foundations of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
Furthermore, for what kind of sentient beings is the application of mindfulness regarding objects (ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna) taught?
Answer: It is taught as three applications of mindfulness for those very same three kinds of deluded sentient beings.
That is to say, for those deluded regarding intrinsic nature (svabhāva), the application of mindfulness regarding intrinsic nature is taught.

Furthermore, for those who are foolish regarding the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) with respect to their objects, he teaches the foundations of mindfulness with respect to their objects.
Moreover, there are differences in the conduct of sentient beings,
namely, those who are beginners and so forth.
For beginners, the application of mindfulness of objects is taught;
for those who have already practiced the path, the mixed application of mindfulness is taught;
and for those who have transcended mental attention, the application of mindfulness of intrinsic nature is taught.
Furthermore, there are differences in the inclinations of sentient beings.

Specifically, for those who prefer the extensive, the intermediate, or the concise—those who prefer the concise are taught the applications of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*);
those who prefer the intermediate are taught the applications of mindfulness as associated characteristics (*saṃsṛṣṭa-smṛtyupasthāna*).
For those who delight in breadth, one explains the foundations of mindfulness as objects of focus.
Furthermore, there are differences in the faculties of sentient beings—
namely, sharp, medium, and dull— for those with sharp faculties, one explains the foundations of mindfulness in terms of their intrinsic nature.
For those of middling faculties, the mixed applications of mindfulness are taught;
for those of dull faculties, the objective applications of mindfulness are taught.
Furthermore, there are differences in the intelligence of sentient beings.
That is to say: the wisdom born of development, the wisdom born of discrimination, and the wisdom born of guidance.
For the wisdom born of development, he teaches the application of mindfulness to intrinsic nature;
for the wisdom born of discrimination, he teaches the application of mindfulness to associated phenomena.
To guide them toward the arising of wisdom,
he teaches the foundations of mindfulness as objects of focus for the sake of such beings to be converted.
The Buddha taught these three types of foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Question: Among these three foundations of mindfulness, which one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*)?
Answer: Only the mixed foundation of mindfulness (*saṃsṛṣṭasmṛtyupasthāna*) can abandon the afflictions, not the others.
Question: Why is it that the application of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*) cannot sever the afflictions?
Answer: Because wisdom alone, when divorced from its auxiliary companions, cannot sever the afflictions.
Question: Why is it that the application of mindfulness as object (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*) cannot sever the afflictions?
Answer: Because that mental attention is universally dispersed;
only the mental attention directed toward a general and concise object of observation can sever the afflictions.
Question: For what reason can the application of mindfulness involving mixed objects sever the afflictions?
Answer: Because it possesses two conditions:
namely, the appropriation of auxiliary companions, and the synthesis of the object of focus through mental attention.
Question: If that is so, then the cultivation of the other foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) would be rendered useless.
Answer: They are not useless, for they are able to induce the mixed foundations of mindfulness.
Some say that there are two kinds of abandonment:
first, temporary abandonment; [second, ultimate abandonment].
Second is ultimate abandonment.
Since the cultivation of the remaining applications of mindfulness can effect temporary abandonment, they are not useless.
Furthermore, there are three types of mixed applications of mindfulness.
This refers to the distinctions among those [wisdoms] produced by hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Question: Among these three, which one is able to sever the afflictions?
Answer: That produced by cultivation is able to sever the afflictions, and not the others.
Question: Why is it that what is accomplished through hearing cannot sever the afflictions?
Answer: This necessarily proceeds toward the meaning by relying upon names;
only the path that proceeds toward the meaning without depending on names can sever the afflictions.
Question: Why is it that that which is accomplished through reflection (*cintāmayī*) cannot sever the afflictions (*kleśa*)?
Answer: Because this mental attention (*manasikāra*) is comprised within the non-concentrated stages (*anaiścarya-bhūmi*);
only the path comprised within the concentrated stages (*samādhi-bhūmi*) can sever the afflictions.
Question: For what reason is that which is produced through cultivation able to sever the afflictions?
Answer: Because it possesses two conditions;
namely, because it operates upon the object without depending on names.
Furthermore, because they are subsumed within the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*). Question:
If that is so, then the cultivation of the other two types [of wisdom] would be rendered useless.
The answer is: because they can induce that which is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*).

That is to say, that which is produced by hearing (*śruta-maya*) can induce that which is produced by reflection (*cintā-maya*), and that which is produced by reflection can induce that which is produced by cultivation.
Because that which is produced through cultivation can sever the afflictions,
it is not useless. Some say:
There are two kinds of abandonment,
as explained in detail previously.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of mindfulness establishments (smṛtyupasthāna) accomplished through cultivation (bhāvanāmayī).
That is to say: body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
Question: Among these four, which is able to sever the afflictions?
Answer: The application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) can sever the afflictions, and not the others.
Question: Why are the first three applications of mindfulness unable to abandon the afflictions?
Answer: Because they are comprised within attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*);
only the path comprised within attention to general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) can abandon the afflictions.
Some say that because each of those aggregates is a distinct object of cognition, one must take the four aggregates,
