the five aggregates, or the path dissociated from the aggregates as a collective object in order to abandon the afflictions.
Question: If that is so, then the cultivation of the first three types [of mindfulness establishments] would be rendered useless.
Answer: Because they are able to induce the mindfulness establishment of dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
That is to say, the foundation of mindfulness of the body leads to the foundation of mindfulness of feelings;
the foundation of mindfulness of feelings leads to the foundation of mindfulness of the mind;
and the foundation of mindfulness of the mind leads to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
The application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is able to sever the afflictions;
therefore, it is not useless. Some say:
One must first analyze the individual aggregates before one can subsequently take them as a collective object and thereby sever the afflictions; therefore,
it is not without purpose.
Some say that there are two kinds of abandonment,
as explained in detail previously.
The application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) is further of two kinds:
first, that which has mixed objects;
second, that which has unmixed objects.
If one takes as objects the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is called "non-mixed object.
If one takes the five aggregates as objects—either two by two, three by three, four by four, or all five together—along with the unconditioned, it is called "mixed object."
Question: Among these, which application of mindfulness of dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is able to sever the afflictions?
Answer: Both are able to sever them.
That is to say, if the path that abandons the afflictions takes as its object the truths of suffering, origin, or the path,
it is the application of mindfulness to phenomena with mixed objects;
if the path that abandons the afflictions takes as its object the truth of cessation, [it is the application of mindfulness to phenomena with pure objects].
This is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) with unmixed objects.
Within this context, it may be described collectively as a single application of mindfulness, namely:

the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and the factor of enlightenment consisting of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasaṃbodhyaṅga*), all of which belong to the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmikadharma*).
Some speak of two:
namely, the tainted and the untainted, the bound and the liberated, the fettered and the unfettered.
Or they speak of three.
That is to say, they are of weak, medium, and superior grades;
or they are those produced through hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
or they are said to be fourfold.
That is to say: body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
Alternatively, five are taught:
those bound to the three realms, the learner, and the one beyond learning.
Some say there are six,
meaning that the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) each have weak, medium, and superior grades.
Others say there are eight.
That is to say, body, sensation, mind, and phenomena each have both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) aspects.
Alternatively, they are said to be ninefold,
ranging from the "soft-soft" (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) up to the "superior-superior" (*adhimātra-adhimātra*).
Some explain twelve [factors],
meaning that body, sensation, mind, and phenomena each have weak, medium, and superior grades.
Furthermore, there is another distinct explanation of twelve.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One dwells contemplating the body in the internal body;
one dwells contemplating the body in the external body."
One dwells observing the body in the internal and external body.
As it is with the three types of bodies,
so it is likewise for the dharmas, up to and including mental objects.
Some say there are eighteen,
meaning that both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) each have nine grades, from the weakest-of-the-weak up to the strongest-of-the-strong.
Others say there are twenty-four.

This refers to the fact that body, sensation, mind, and phenomena each have weak, medium, and strong grades, and each of these is further divided into both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Alternatively, they are said to be thirty-six:
namely, body, sensation, mind, and phenomena each having weak-weak up to strong-strong grades.
Furthermore, there is another exposition of thirty-six [elements],
as stated in the Sūtra:
"One dwells with a perception of repulsion toward the internal body."
He dwells with regard to the internal body with a perception of non-disgust;
he dwells with regard to the internal body with equanimity, free from both [attraction and aversion], possessing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
As it is with the internal body, so it is [with the external body].
It is the same for the external body and for both the internal and external bodies.
Just as there are nine [applications] regarding the body,
so it is likewise for the mental objects (*dharma*), up to that point.
Some say there are seventy-two;

that is, for each of the applications of mindfulness on the body, whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), there are nine grades ranging from the soft-soft (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) up to the superior-superior (*adhimātra-adhimātra*).
Thus, as with the application of mindfulness on the body, there are eighteen [categories].
The same applies up to the application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
If one distinguishes them according to the continuity of moments (*kṣaṇa*), there are immeasurable applications of mindfulness.
Question: If that is so, then...
“World-Honored One, for what reason do you explain the four foundations of mindfulness extensively as being one, yet briefly as being immeasurable?
Answer: “It is for the sake of counteracting the four perversions.”
That is to say, the application of mindfulness to the body is taught as the antidote to the perversion of perceiving the impure as pure;
the application of mindfulness to feelings is taught as the antidote to the perversion of perceiving suffering as pleasure.
The application of mindfulness to the mind is taught as the antidote to the perversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent;
the application of mindfulness to phenomena is taught as the antidote to the perversion of perceiving the non-self as self.
Some say: It is for the purpose of counteracting the four nutriments (*āhāra*).
That is to say, in order to counteract edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is taught.
The foundation of mindfulness of feeling is taught as the antidote to the nutriment of contact;
the foundation of mindfulness of mind is taught as the antidote to the nutriment of consciousness;
and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena is taught as the antidote to the nutriment of mental volition.
Some say that it is for the purpose of counteracting the four stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*). That is to say,
in order to counteract the station of consciousness associated with the mental application to form (*rūpa-upavicāra*), the mindfulness of the body (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*) is taught.
The mindfulness of feeling is taught as the antidote to the consciousness-abiding that consists in the mental application to feelings;
the mindfulness of mind is taught as the antidote to the consciousness that abides therein;
and the mindfulness of phenomena is taught as the antidote to the consciousness-abiding that consists in the mental applications to perceptions and the mental applications to formations.
Some say: it is for the purpose of counteracting the five aggregates;
that is to say, the application of mindfulness to the body is taught as the counteragent to the aggregate of form.
The application of mindfulness to feelings is taught as the antidote to the aggregate of feeling;
the application of mindfulness to the mind is taught as the antidote to the aggregate of consciousness;
and the application of mindfulness to phenomena is taught as the antidote to the aggregates of perception and formations.
Some say that it is for the purpose of counteracting four kinds of non-cultivation; that is,
in order to counteract the non-cultivation of the body, the application of mindfulness to the body is taught.
The application of mindfulness to feelings is taught as the antidote to the failure to cultivate ethical discipline;
the application of mindfulness to the mind is taught as the antidote to the failure to cultivate concentration;
and the application of mindfulness to phenomena is taught as the antidote to the failure to cultivate wisdom.
Some say that they are called the four foundations of mindfulness because they share the same nature as the four types of cultivation.
It is said that the foundation of mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) is so called because it shares the same nature as the cultivation of the body;
the foundation of mindfulness of feelings (vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna) is so called because it shares the same nature as the cultivation of ethical discipline (śīla);
and the foundation of mindfulness of the mind (cittasmṛtyupasthāna) is so called because it shares the same nature as the cultivation of the mind (citta).
Because it shares the same nature as cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*), it is called the application of mindfulness to dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the applications of mindfulness?
Is it mindfulness (*smṛti*) or is it wisdom (*prajñā*)?
If it is by means of mindfulness,
how is this statement to be reconciled:
"One contemplates the body as a body"?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
If it is by means of wisdom,
for what reason is it called "application of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna)?
Furthermore, how should one interpret the sūtra statement:
"In what place should one practice the contemplation of the faculty of mindfulness?
It is said: in the four foundations of mindfulness"?
It is stated that wisdom (*prajñā*) is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Question:
If that is so, why is it called a "foundation of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*)?
Answer: It is called a "foundation of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna) because mindfulness abides and remains evenly established therein;
it is so named because each [object] is individually established.
This is like the places where elephants, horses, and so forth reside being called the "abodes" of elephants, horses, and so forth.
This is also like that.
Some say that by the power of mindfulness, it is able to give rise to diverse and extensive functions regarding its object of focus.
It is called a "foundation of mindfulness" because it is not lost or destroyed.
Some say that by the power of mindfulness, this practitioner of yoga clearly discerns the object of focus.
Because one remembers what was forgotten regarding the object of focus,
it is called "establishment of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna). Some say:
This practitioner first establishes mindfulness upon the object of focus and subsequently examines it;
furthermore, having first attained thorough penetration of the object, they subsequently establish mindfulness as a means of protection.
Because it is like a gatekeeper, it is called a foundation of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Some say that this practitioner, with respect to the object of focus...
First, one should sustain the mind through mindfulness;
subsequently, one should observe with wisdom and thereby sever the afflictions.
It is just as a farmer first grasps the grass and weeds with his left hand,
and subsequently uses his right hand to hold a sickle and cut them;
this case is likewise.
Therefore, it is called "application of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Some say that this practitioner of yoga is armored with the mail of mindfulness.
Upon the continuum of the mind,
wielding the sword and staff of wisdom within the battle array of saṃsāra,
one is not defeated by the enemies that are the afflictions.
Because it is able to subdue those [defilements], it is called a "foundation of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna).
Some say that it is called a foundation of mindfulness because it prevents the fault of grasping at intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
If it were called "abiding in wisdom" (*prajñā-sthiti*), there would be the fault of implying the grasping of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Some say that it is called "foundation of mindfulness" (*smṛty-upasthāna*) to show that it is not only intrinsic nature that performs the function.
For these reasons, they are called only foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and not foundations of wisdom (prajñopasthāna).
Question: How then should one interpret what is stated in the sūtras?
As it is said: "In what place should one contemplate the faculty of mindfulness? The answer is: "In the four foundations of mindfulness.
This is stated because the faculty of mindfulness exercises predominant influence regarding its function at the stage of the foundations of mindfulness.
Just as the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya) exercises predominant influence during the stage of the fourfold verified confidence (catvāri avetyaprasādāni), the Buddha further stated:
"In what respect should the faculty of faith be observed? It is to be observed in the fourfold verified confidence."
In this way, the faculty of energy corresponds to the four right efforts;
the faculty of concentration to the four dhyānas;
and likewise, the faculty of wisdom to the four noble truths.
Therefore, the World-Honored One further spoke:
"In what respect should the faculty of wisdom be contemplated with regard to the Four Noble Truths?
This case is also like that.
This is called the intrinsic nature of the foundations of mindfulness.
Having explained the intrinsic nature,
that which is its purpose shall now be explained.
Why is it called "application of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna)?
What is the meaning of "application of mindfulness"?
Answer: Mindfulness abides, abides equally, and abides individually within this.
The detailed explanation is as previously stated.
Having already provided a general exposition on the reasons for the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
the specific reasons for each one shall now be explained.
Question: Why is it called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*)?
Answer: Because this application of mindfulness takes the body as its object, it is called the application of mindfulness to the body.
Question: But other applications of mindfulness also take the body as their object.
That is to say, the mindfulness of feeling takes the six groups of feeling as its object;
the mindfulness of mind takes the six groups of consciousness as its object;
and the mindfulness of phenomena takes the six groups of perception, the six groups of volition, and so forth, as its objects.
Why are they not all called "mindfulness of the body" (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*)?
Answer: What is described here as "taking the body as an object" refers to taking the material body (*rūpakāya*) as an object.
The remaining foundations of mindfulness are not called "mindfulness of the body" because they do not take the physical body as their object.
Some say that if something is coarse, manifest, and easy to see, it is [designated as such].
That which perceives the body as it is manifested is called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The other applications of mindfulness take as their objects that which is subtle, hidden, difficult to see, and difficult to realize;
because they do not perceive the body as it is manifested, they are not called the application of mindfulness to the body.
Some say: if the body that is the object of focus is composed of an aggregation of atoms, it is called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*);
other objects of focus that are bodies are not composed of an aggregation of atoms.
That is not called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). Some say:
if one takes the body as an object and the knowledge and the known arise simultaneously, it is called the application of mindfulness to the body.
Although other [mindfulnesses] take the body as their object, they are not called "body mindfulness" because the knowing and the known do not arise simultaneously.
Although there are instances within dharma mindfulness where these arise simultaneously, they are not mentioned because they are few in number.
Just as it is called "mindfulness of the body" because it takes the body as its object,
so too it is called "mindfulness of feeling" because it takes feelings as its object,
and "mindfulness of mind" because it takes the mind as its object.
It is called the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) because it has phenomena as its object.
Question: Since everything is phenomena and everything consists solely of phenomena, why is only this one called the application of mindfulness to phenomena, and not the others?
Answer: Although all things are indeed phenomena (*dharma*), only one is established as the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
This is just as, although all eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are phenomena, [only one is designated as such].
Yet, only one is established as the *dharmadhātu*. Although all twelve bases (*āyatana*) are phenomena (*dharma*), only one is established as the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

As it is with the *dharmadhātu* and the *dharmāyatana*, so it is with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

The same applies to the recollection of the Dharma (*dharma-anusmṛti*), clear confidence in the Dharma (*dharma-avetyaprasāda*), the analytical knowledge of the Dharma (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the Dharma-jewel (*dharma-ratna*), and the refuge in the Dharma (*dharma-śaraṇa*).
Some say that the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) has only one name.
The remaining applications of mindfulness have two names.
Some say that the application of mindfulness to phenomena has a common name.
The remaining applications of mindfulness have both shared and unshared names.
Some say that all conditioned phenomena arise by means of birth (*jāti*).
Because birth has that [dharma] as its object, it is called the application of mindfulness to dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Some say that all dharmas are manifested by means of names (*nāman*).
It is called the "application of mindfulness to phenomena" (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) because its object of focus (*ālambana*) is that [name].
Some say that the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are the insignia of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Because these various signs are sealed within that object of focus, it is called the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Some say that the door of liberation of emptiness awakens to the *dharmatā* (true nature) of all phenomena.
This emptiness is subsumed within that object of focus;
therefore, it is called the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Question: If that is so, then...
The view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) also perceives the nature of phenomena (*dharma*) as a person (*pudgala*).
Why, then, is the name not established based upon that?
The answer is: because that is not a perception of reality.
This is the realization of reality;
therefore, there is no fault. Some say:
Wisdom (*prajñā*) discriminates the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena (*dharma*),
establishes the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena,
and counteracts delusion regarding harmful actions as well as delusion regarding the objects of cognition (*ālambana*).
It functions without increasing or decreasing among all phenomena;
because this wisdom falls within those objects of focus,
it is called the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Some say that the truth of cessation, nirvāṇa, is a supreme dharma that is eternally abiding and unchanging;
this dharma is included within those [mental states] that take it as their object.
Therefore, it is called the application of mindfulness to dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Some say that this application of mindfulness can take many dharmas as its object.
That is to say: form and non-form; associated and dissociated;
having a basis and lacking a basis;
having an aspect and lacking an aspect.
It has an object of focus and lacks an object of focus;
it is alert and lacks alertness.
For this reason, it is called the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
Some say: the application of mindfulness to the body takes the body as its object, but does not take the wisdom that takes the body as its object;
the application of mindfulness to feelings takes feelings as its object, but does not take the wisdom that takes feelings as its object.
Mindfulness of mind takes the mind as its object, but does not take the cognition of the mind as its object.
Mindfulness of phenomena takes the body as its object and also takes the cognition of the body as its object;
it likewise takes feeling, mind, and phenomena as its objects, and also takes the cognitions of feeling, mind, and phenomena as its objects.
Therefore, only this is called the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Some say that the application of mindfulness to the body takes the body as its object, but does not take the birth, aging, or impermanence of the body as its object.
The mindfulness-establishment of feeling takes feeling as its object, but does not take the arising, aging, or impermanence of feeling as its object.
The mindfulness-establishment of mind takes mind as its object, but does not take the arising, aging, or impermanence of mind as its object.
The mindfulness-establishment of phenomena takes the body as its object and also takes the arising, aging, and impermanence of the body as its object.

Feeling, mind, and mental factors are themselves the conditions for feeling, mind, and mental factors, and they are also the conditions for the arising, aging, and impermanence of feeling, mind, and mental factors.
For this reason, only these are called the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Some say:
In these yogācāras, the notion of a self (*ātma-saṃjñā*) and the notion of a unified whole (*piṇḍa-saṃjñā*) are both brought to cessation;
because they cultivate the notion of phenomena (*dharma-saṃjñā*) and the discernment of distinctions (*vibhakta-saṃjñā*) to perfection,
it is called the foundation of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
That is to say, when the yoga practitioner has analyzed the body, he conceives of feeling as the self;
having analyzed feeling, he conceives of the mind as the self; having analyzed the mind, he conceives of phenomena as the self;
and having analyzed phenomena, [he conceives of space as the self].
One then realizes that all sentient beings are not "mine," but are merely empty aggregates of formations.
Therefore, when the perception of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*) is perfected up to this point, it is called the foundation of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Thus, the specific reasons for each of the foundations of mindfulness have been explained.
Their sequence shall now be explained.
For what reason did the Blessed One first teach the application of mindfulness to the body,
and so on, until finally teaching the application of mindfulness to phenomena?
Answer: Because it demonstrates conformity.
That is to say, if they are demonstrated in such a sequence, it conforms to the verbal expression of the syllables. Some say:
This is because it explains the conformity of the reception.
That is to say, if one proceeds according to this sequence,
then both the teacher’s exposition and the disciple’s reception will be in conformity.
Some say: this is based on the order of their arising.
There are three kinds of order.
First, the sequence of generation;
second, the sequence of manifestation;
third, the sequence of clear realization.
Regarding the generation stage:
it consists of such things as the foundations of mindfulness,

the meditative concentrations (dhyāna), the immeasurables (apramāṇa), the formless attainments (ārūpya), the liberations (vimokṣa), the bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and the bases of totality (kṛtsnāyatana).
Regarding the demonstration of the sequence:
this refers to the right abandonments, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the factors of the path, and so forth.
Regarding the sequence of clear realization:
These refer to the Four Noble Truths.
Because the practitioner of yoga first gives rise to the mindfulness of the body, the Buddha spoke of them first;
because he eventually gives rise to the mindfulness of phenomena, the Buddha spoke of them last.
Question: Following from this discussion, a further inquiry arises:
for what reason do the practitioners of yoga first establish the application of mindfulness to the body, and so on, until finally establishing the application of mindfulness to phenomena?
Answer: It is based on the sequence of coarse to subtle.
That is to say, among the five aggregates, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is the coarsest;
therefore, one first observes it to give rise to the application of mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna).
Among the four formless aggregates, the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is the coarsest;
therefore, one next contemplates the application of mindfulness of sensation (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna).
Question: Sensation and the others have no spatial location.
How can the coarse and the subtle be established?
Answer: Although there is no spatial location for the coarse and the subtle, they can nonetheless be established by way of their modes of activity (*ākāra*).
Among these, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is coarse in its mode of apprehension,
as it is said, "I have pain in my hands and feet," and "I experience such-and-such suffering.
Although the aggregates of sensation and the others are not material, they are designated as coarse or subtle in accordance with the material form (*rūpa*).
Among the four formless aggregates, the aggregate of consciousness is the most subtle;

yet, one first observes the aggregates of perception and formations to establish mindfulness of mind because the aggregates of perception and formations are designated in conjunction with Nirvana, which is the most subtle of all phenomena.
He finally observes the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) as it arises.
Some say that from the beginningless limit of existence, men have been the objects of desire for women, and women the objects of desire for men.
This is the locus where defilement arises;
therefore, one first contemplates form to establish the application of mindfulness of the body.
Attachment to this form occurs through craving for pleasant sensation.
Therefore, one next contemplates feeling and establishes the mindfulness of feeling.
Greed for pleasure arises because the mind has not been tamed.
Therefore, next comes the application of mindfulness to the mind, which observes the arising of the mind;
because the mind is not yet tamed due to the non-abandonment of afflictions,
one finally observes phenomena through the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
Some say that because form (*rūpa*) can be conceptually established as having increase or decrease,
and because there is a similar continuity involving taking up and discarding,
one first contemplates form to establish mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
When observing form, one gives rise to physical pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and mental pliancy;
preceded by these, a feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) is induced.
Therefore, next, one observes feelings and establishes the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
When observing feelings,
one gives rise to the discernment of the ultimate object; therefore,
next, one observes consciousness and establishes mindfulness of the mind.
He thinks to himself:
"Wherever the mind arises, mental factors also arise;
therefore, as a final observation of phenomena, he establishes the application of mindfulness to phenomena."
Some say that bodily delusion can maintain the delusion regarding the aggregates (*skandha-moha*), and so on up to mental delusion maintaining the delusion regarding phenomena (*dharma-moha*);
it is not the case that bodily delusion does not function while the delusion regarding the aggregates functions.
Up to the point where delusion regarding the mind no longer functions, yet delusion regarding phenomena still functions;
thus do the four foundations of mindfulness arise in this sequence. Some say:
When the body is not deluded, it can lead to sensation that is not deluded;
this extends up to when the mind is not deluded, it can lead to phenomena that are not deluded.
It is not the case that unless the body is not deluded, it cannot give rise to sensation that is not deluded.
Furthermore, because one is not deluded regarding what is non-mental, nor deluded regarding that which does not arise or that which causes arising,
the four foundations of mindfulness arise in this sequence. Some say:
The contemplation of the body can induce the contemplation of sensation,
and so on, up to the contemplation of the mind which can induce the contemplation of phenomena.
It is not the case that the contemplation of the body does not give rise to the contemplation of sensation that is capable of arising.
The detailed explanation is as above.

Some say that the contemplation of the body is the cause, the root, the eye, the path, the gradual progression, the capacity for action, the condition for arising, the origin, and the co-arising of the contemplation of feelings.
The contemplation of feelings and the contemplation of the mind are likewise; the contemplation of the mind and the contemplation of phenomena are also thus.
The remainder is as previously explained.
Some say that the contemplation of the body and the contemplation of feeling serve as the preparatory practices, the gateways, and the bases.
The same applies to the contemplation of mind and the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā*).
The rest is as previously explained. Some say:
The contemplation of the body and the contemplation of feelings serve as the basis and the locus;
this applies likewise to the contemplation of the mind and the contemplation of phenomena.
The rest is as previously explained. Question:
If that is so, upon what basis and track does the contemplation of the body rely?
He answers by taking the previously attained characteristics of śamatha as his support and basis,
as it is said:
Because he has previously attained immovable *śamatha*,
the signs of physical lightness and pliancy accumulate throughout his body from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head; by means of this,
he is able to give rise to the application of mindfulness of the body, up to the application of mindfulness of phenomena.
Some say that within the continuum [of consciousness], one differentiates the various bases (*āyatana*) and gives rise to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
That is to say, the practitioner of yoga first desires to know the various bases of form (*rūpāyatana*).
First, one distinguishes the ten bases of form and the form included within the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Therefore, one first establishes the application of mindfulness to the body;
subsequently, one distinguishes the various feelings (*vedanā*) within that very base of mental phenomena.
Next, one arouses the application of mindfulness to feeling;
next, within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
one analytically discerns the aggregates of perception and formations, as well as the three unconditioned phenomena.
Next, he gives rise to the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). He further reflects:
"Apart from these, what else exists?"
That is to say, one knows as it truly is that there are other bases of mind (manāyatana);
by means of this, one discriminates the base of mind.
Therefore, the application of mindfulness to the mind arises last.

When practitioners of yoga contemplate according to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they first give rise to the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and subsequently give rise to the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).
When they contemplate according to general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), they first give rise to the application of mindfulness to the mind.
The application of mindfulness to phenomena arises subsequently.
Therefore, the four applications of mindfulness arise in this sequence.
Question: Does the application of mindfulness directed toward the internal arise first?
Does one first give rise to the application of mindfulness directed toward external objects?
If so, what fault is there?
If one were to first give rise to the application of mindfulness directed toward internal objects...
How is the scriptural teaching to be reconciled?
For example, it says: "If a newly ordained bhikṣu possesses pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and a perfected intention, yet wishes to swiftly eliminate sensual desire and hatred..."
One should go to a secluded road to a place where corpses are located and carefully observe their characteristics—
whether they are livid and discolored, or festering and putrid—
and so forth, as explained at length.
If one first arouses the mindfulness-establishment (smṛtyupasthāna) that takes the external as its object, how can other sūtras be reconciled? For example, there is the teaching:
"First, one dwells in the contemplation of the body with regard to the internal body."
Next, regarding the external body,
and so forth, as explained at length.
One should respond by saying this:
First, one gives rise to the application of mindfulness directed toward the internal. Why is this?
Because when there is a self, there is "what belongs to the self."
Because there is the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), there is the grasping at what belongs to a self (*ātmīya-grāha*).
Because there is the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), there is the view of what belongs to a self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).
Because there are five views of a self, there are fifteen views of what belongs to a self.
Because there is delusion regarding a self, there is delusion regarding what belongs to a self;
because there is craving for a self, there is craving for the requisites [for its sustenance].
This is because one seeks external resources in order to nourish the internal self.
Question: If that is so, how are the sūtras previously cited to be reconciled?
Answer: Those refer to the preparatory stage (prayoga) of the foundations of mindfulness, not the actual foundations of mindfulness themselves.
How is this known?
That very sutra states: "Having correctly grasped the sign, he quickly returns to his original place and recollects the sign previously grasped."
If you are able to do so, it is well;
if not, go again to the place where the corpse lies,
carefully observe its features once more, and hasten back to your original location.
Having washed his feet, he enters the dwelling, arranges his seat, and sits down.
By means of mental attention through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), he causes the sign to be grasped (*nimitta*) to appear clearly before him.
This is called the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
When one places the external signs of the apprehended object within the internal body and observes them,
this is called entering the fundamental foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Some say:
That sutra states that the attention of the superior fruit (*phala-viśeṣa-manasikāra*) does not belong to the stage of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
How is this known to be so?
That same sutra states:
Once that newly ordained bhikṣu has attained the intent of training,
if he wishes to go along the path of tranquility, he may go as he desires.
In this context, the newly ordained bhikṣu refers to one who is a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) or a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin). Therefore,

it should be understood that the aforementioned sūtra speaks of the "attention to the excellence of the fruit" (phalaviśeṣamanasikāra), and not the stage of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One dwells contemplating the body in the internal body;
one dwells contemplating the body in the external body."
"One dwells observing the body in the internal body," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: In this context, what is meant by "internal body" and so on?
What is meant by "the external body" and so forth? The answer is: matter included within one's own continuum is called the internal body;
matter included within the continua of others, as well as matter not belonging to the category of sentient beings, is called the external body.
The same applies to the explanation of internal and external phenomena.
That which is comprised within one's own continuum is called internal feeling;
that which is comprised within the continua of others is called external feeling.
The same applies to the explanation of internal and external mind.
Other masters say that matter belonging to the category of sentient beings is called the "internal body."
Matter not included among sentient beings is called the external body.
The same applies to the explanation of internal and external phenomena.
Feeling and mind are as previously described.
He addressed the Venerable One, saying:
"The present is called internal;
the past, the future, and the unconditioned are called external."
Question: Why is the present called "internal," while the past, the future, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are called "external"?
Answer: Because present phenomena largely cause sentient beings to grasp at and become attached to them.
Because it is not past, future, or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
In this context, one who dwells in the contemplation of the body with regard to the internal body dwells in the contemplation of the internal body's own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
One who dwells in the contemplation of the body with regard to the external body dwells in the contemplation of the specific characteristics of the external body.
One who dwells in the contemplation of the body with regard to both the internal and external bodies...
One dwells observing the common characteristics of the internal and external body;
this applies likewise up to the dharmas. Some say:
One who dwells in the contemplation of the body with regard to the internal body dwells observing it extensively;
one who dwells in the contemplation of the body with regard to the external body [dwells observing it extensively].
Abiding in the observation of the external body,
one practices the extensive contemplation; abiding in the observation of the internal and external body,
one practices the concise contemplation.
The same applies even to mental phenomena (*dharma*).
Some say that one who dwells observing the body in the internal body [practices mindfulness].
Abiding in the contemplation of the body with regard to the external body serves as the antidote to the grasping at a self;
it serves as the antidote to the grasping at what belongs to a self (*mamakāra*).
One who dwells in the contemplation of the body with regard to the internal and external body counteracts the grasping at "I" and "mine";
this applies likewise even to phenomena (*dharma*).
As it is with the grasping at a self and the grasping at what belongs to a self,
so too should the explanations of the view of a self and the view of what belongs to a self be understood. Some say:
One who dwells in contemplation of the body with respect to the internal body counteracts the five views of self;
one who dwells in contemplation of the body with respect to the external body...

Abiding in the contemplation of the body with respect to the internal and external body serves as the antidote to the fifteen views of "mine," and serves as the antidote to the twenty types of satkāyadṛṣṭi (view of a self-identity).
The same applies even to phenomena (*dharma*).
Just as with the view of "I" and the view of "mine," so too are the expressions "I am deluded" and "I am deluded regarding mine" likewise explained.
Some say that for one who dwells in the contemplation of the body with respect to the internal body,
it serves as an antidote to self-love.
One who dwells in the contemplation of the body with respect to the external body counteracts craving for requisites;
one who dwells in the contemplation of the body with respect to both the internal and external bodies [counteracts craving for the self].
It is the antidote to craving for both [the internal and external].
This applies even to mental phenomena (*dharma*).
Question: To what extent may one say that this constitutes the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*)?
"Up until the fulfillment of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna)?
Answer: It should be understood as fulfilled by way of two conditions:
first, the differentiation of the object of focus (ālambana)."
Second, the increase of the roots of goodness.
Regarding the analysis of the object of focus:
it refers to when one is able to analyze the object of focus by means of moments and atoms.
Alternatively, one may analyze the object of focus solely by means of moments.
For those whose roots of goodness increase, this means that based on the lower [level], they produce the middle; based on the middle, they produce the upper.
Based on this, one should know that the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are perfected.
Some say that they should be known as perfected through the transformation of the preparatory application (prayoga).
That is to say, the yoga practitioner first analyzes the body.
Having analyzed the body, he turns his cognitive wisdom toward feeling and analyzes feeling.
Having analyzed feeling, he turns his cognitive wisdom toward the mind and analyzes the mind.
Once the mind of discrimination has been transformed, the awakening wisdom discriminates phenomena,
just as a farmer leads water to irrigate his fields;
when the first furrow is full, he leads it to irrigate the second.
When the second is full, it leads to the irrigation of the third;
when the third is full, it leads to the irrigation of the fourth.
It is the same for these as well.
Some say that it should be understood as complete when the characteristics of enmity and harm are fully established.
There are two types of these characteristics of enmity and harm.
First, it causes a lack of joy;
second, it causes the arising of anger.
Here, only that which causes a lack of joy is described as the characteristic of enmity and harm.
That is to say, once the yoga practitioner has analyzed the body, they no longer find delight in the body,
but instead find delight in feeling and so forth;
having analyzed feeling, they again no longer find delight in feeling.
Having already brought about the discrimination of a mind that delights in [the mind] and so forth, one no longer generates delight in the mind itself,
but rather delights in the Dharma.
Once one has analyzed phenomena,
it should be understood that one no longer gives rise to delight toward any object of experience;
at that time, the foundations of mindfulness are perfected.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School,
Volume 187; The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume 188.
Compiled by five hundred great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Eight: The Aggregate of Views (*Dṛṣṭiskandha*), Part One of the Second Sub-section on the Applications of Mindfulness (*Smṛtyupasthāna*). Furthermore, there are three kinds of applications of mindfulness.
This refers to the distinctions among those things accomplished through hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Regarding this,
some say that it concerns the twelvefold division of the Buddha’s teachings.
The application of mindfulness consisting of reflection on what has been heard is established through upholding, reciting, and contemplating [the teachings].
Based on hearing, reflection arises;
based on reflection, cultivation arises.
By relying on cultivation, one is able to sever the afflictions,
just as gold is extracted from ore,
and diamonds are extracted from gold.
Just as a vajra can destroy hard objects such as stone,
the Venerable Pārśva stated regarding the twelvefold teachings spoken by the Buddha: [it is capable of destroying all afflictions].
To receive, uphold, recite, and contemplate with analytical discernment is the wisdom acquired through birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-prajñā*).
Based upon this wisdom acquired through birth, one gives rise to the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) formed through hearing (*śrutamaya*).
Based on hearing, one gives rise to reflection;
based on reflection, one gives rise to cultivation;
and based on cultivation, one is able to sever the afflictions.
Just as a sprout arises depending on a seed,
a stalk arises depending on a sprout,
and branches and leaves arise depending on a stalk.
Flowers and fruits grow depending on branches and leaves.
Question: What is the distinction between these three applications of mindfulness? Some say:
The distinction lies in their names;
that is to say, this is called the application of mindfulness consisting in hearing,
up to and including this being called the application of mindfulness consisting in cultivation.
Some say that the applications of mindfulness consisting of hearing always operate upon the meaning by means of names;
that is to say, as the Sūtras ask: "What is the meaning? [and then provide the explanation].
What is the meaning of *vinaya*?
What is the meaning of *abhidharma*?
What is the meaning of *upadeśa*?
What is the meaning of the Ācārya’s statement?
What is the meaning of the statements in other treatises?
The mindfulness-establishments consisting of reflection may be based on names.
Alternatively, it may function with respect to the meaning without relying on the name.
The mindfulness establishments (smṛtyupasthāna) produced by cultivation (bhāvanā-maya) at all times function with respect to the meaning while remaining detached from the name.
This is, for example, like three people bathing together in a pond.
The first person has not yet learned to swim;
the second has learned it halfway;
the third has mastered it well.
Those who have not yet learned to swim always bathe by relying on the bank.
Those who have partially learned to swim bathe either by relying on the bank or away from it.
Those who are well-trained in swimming always bathe away from the bank, remaining in the middle of the water.
As it is for the first person, so it is for that consisting of what is heard;
as it is for the second person,
so it is for that consisting of reflection.
The third person’s cultivation through meditation is likewise.
This is called the distinction between these three foundations of mindfulness.
Question: Regarding these foundations of mindfulness established through hearing, reflection, and meditation...
How many types are there in which realm?
Answer: There are two in the desire realm;
namely, those produced by hearing and reflection, but not by cultivation.
Why is this? Because the desire realm is an indeterminate realm, neither a stage of cultivation nor a stage of detachment from defilement;
when one practices through mental attention, one immediately falls into the sphere of discursive thought.
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) has two types:
those consisting of what is produced by hearing and cultivation, but not by reflection. Why is this so?
The form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is the realm of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanābhūmi*), and the stage of freedom from passion (*vītarāgabhūmi*);
for when one applies mental attention (*manasikāra*), one falls within the sphere of cultivation.
As for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is one [such category].
That is to say, it is produced by cultivation;
however, that which is produced by cultivation also does not fall within the realms (dhātu).
Other masters say:
The desire realm possesses all three types.
The rest is as previously explained. Some say:
The desire realm and the form realm each possess three types.
The rest is as previously explained. Some say:
All three realms possess all three types [of wisdom].
Only that which is produced through cultivation does not fall within any realm.
The critique states:
The first explanation is preferable.
Question: Among these foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), which serves as the cause for which?
Answer: Hearing serves as three kinds of causes.
Reflection is caused solely by reflection and not by hearing,
because the latter is inferior; nor is it caused by cultivation,
because the realms are distinct.
It is cultivated solely through the cause of cultivation and not through the cause of hearing,
because that [latter] is inferior; nor is it through the cause of reflection,
because that is both inferior and belongs to a different realm.
What serves as the cause for what fruit?
Answer: Hearing is the cause only for the fruit of hearing; reflection is the cause for the fruits of both hearing and reflection, but not for cultivation;
cultivation is the cause for the fruit of cultivation, but not for reflection.
Question: Regarding these three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), which one manifests and how many are cultivated?
Answer: When that which is produced by hearing (*śrutamaya*) manifests, only that produced by hearing is cultivated, not those produced by reflection (*cintāmaya*) or cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
When that produced by reflection manifests, only that produced by reflection is cultivated, not those produced by hearing or cultivation.
In this context, when the moments of hearing and reflection are present, they are called "cultivation" (bhāvanā) by virtue of being practiced;
they do not cultivate the future because their power is weak.
For this reason, one cultivates only oneself and does not cultivate others.
When the cultivation consisting of meditation (*bhāvanāmaya*) is present before one, one is able to cultivate three types [of wisdom].
Although the power of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*) cannot cultivate the future [wisdom] by their own force,
there is the sense of cultivating the future through the force of others.

Question: Regarding the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) accomplished through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, how many kinds does each of the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas possess?
Answer: The Buddhas possess all three kinds, yet among these, that accomplished through cultivation is preeminent.
Because they possess the quality of natural awakening as well as the powers, fearlessnesses, and other such virtues,
the Pratyekabuddhas also possess all three [types of awakening], yet their awakening is preeminent in being accomplished through reflection;
for they awaken through their own contemplation, lacking the powers, fearlessnesses, and other such virtues.
The śrāvakas also possess these three types [of wisdom], yet that which is accomplished through hearing is preeminent,
because they enter the noble path by hearing the voices of others.
As it is said:
My noble disciples, having heard this, fully abandon unwholesome states and cultivate wholesome states.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of foundations of mindfulness,
namely, the foundation of mindfulness that culminates in verbal expression.
One should know that these three— the application of mindfulness culminating in reflection and the application of mindfulness culminating in renunciation—
are the applications of mindfulness consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
According to their respective order,
however, all three types of mindfulness establishments— such as that of hearing and so forth— may be termed "consisting of what is heard" (*śrutamaya*).
As it is said:
The learned are able to know the Dharma; the learned are able to leave behind transgressions;
the learned abandon what is meaningless; the learned attain Nirvana.
All of these may be considered as accomplished through hearing.
As it is said:
"Volition is karma;
deliberation is wisdom."
The reflection spoken of therein is that which is accomplished through contemplation (*cintāmayī*);
all [such reflections] may be so named.
That which is accomplished through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*) is as has been explained.
What are the dharmas that should be cultivated?
They are all conditioned wholesome dharmas.
Question: What is meant by the application of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna)?

What is the sequence for the arising of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) that arise from hearing, reflection, and cultivation, which involve the mixed objects of the specific characteristics of the elements?
Answer: The meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti), and mental attention to the elements (dhātumanasikāra).
This is called the application of the foundations of mindfulness.
Taking this as a precursor, one enters the foundation of mindfulness of the body according to its specific characteristics and lineage;
then, taking the foundation of mindfulness of the body as a precursor, one enters the foundation of mindfulness of feelings according to their specific characteristics and lineage.
Then, preceded by the mindfulness-establishment of feelings, one enters the mindfulness-establishment of mind characterized by its own specific nature;
then, preceded by the mindfulness-establishment of mind, one enters the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena characterized by its own specific nature.
From the mindfulness of dharmas based on one's own specific characteristics and lineage, there arises the mindfulness of dharmas with mixed objects;
from the mindfulness of dharmas with mixed objects, there arises the contemplation of the three meanings;
and from the contemplation of the three meanings, there arises the mindfulness of the body produced through hearing.
First, one cultivates the aspects ranging from impermanence to non-self, taking the truth of suffering as the object;
next, one cultivates the aspect of cause, and so on, taking the truth of origination as the object;
then, one cultivates the aspect of the path, and so on, taking the truth of the path as the object.
Immediately following this, there arise the mindfulness establishments of feeling and mind acquired through hearing (*śrutamaya*),
each performing twelve aspects and arising with the three truths as their objects;
immediately following these, there arises the mindfulness establishment of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) acquired through hearing.
First, one contemplates the Truth of Suffering by means of the mental aspects ranging from impermanence up to non-self;
next, one contemplates the Truth of Origination by means of the mental aspects ranging from cause up to formation; and next, one contemplates cessation.
Proceeding until one has abandoned the aspect of observing the Truth of Cessation and gives rise to the next [aspect], which is the Truth of the Path;
continuing until one emerges from the aspect of observing the Truth of the Path.
This occurs immediately after the mindfulness-establishment consisting of the dharma derived from hearing.
There is a mindfulness of the body established through reflection that arises with twelve aspects, taking the three truths as its object.
Immediately following this, there is a mindfulness of feeling that arises with twelve aspects, taking the three truths as its object.

Immediately following this, there arises a mindfulness of mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) that takes the three truths as its object and functions through twelve aspects; immediately following that, there arises a mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that takes the four truths as its object and functions through sixteen aspects.
From the application of mindfulness on phenomena consisting of that which is produced by reflection, one proceeds to that produced by cultivation;
first, one contemplates the truth of suffering through the mental aspects ranging from impermanence to selflessness, and subsequently contemplates it as its cause.
...up to the point where, taking the aspect of origination as its object, one contemplates the truth of origination (samudaya-satya) and subsequently applies the aspect of cessation;
...up to the point where, taking the aspect of detachment as its object, one contemplates the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya) and subsequently applies the aspect of the path;
...up to the point where, taking the aspect of emergence as its object, one contemplates the truth of the path (mārga-satya).
Thus, the application of mindfulness that takes the four truths as its object and performs the sixteen aspects of contemplation is called the initial stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata).
This is known as the application of mindfulness induced by the preparatory practice, which takes both specific characteristics and a mixed range of objects as its seed-nature.
And regarding the sequence in which the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) produced through hearing, reflection, and cultivation arise:

Why is it that the applications of mindfulness produced through hearing and reflection all initially give rise to the application of mindfulness on the body, taking the three truths as their objects and performing the twelve aspects (ākāra)?
Subsequently, one then gives rise to the remaining applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Regarding the application of mindfulness consisting in cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-smṛtyupasthāna*), does one first give rise to the application of mindfulness of dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) by taking the Four Noble Truths as its object and performing the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*)?
Answer: Because the lineage (*gotra*) has not yet been attained.
Because one attains the characteristics [of the path] gradually,
one first contemplates the coarse aggregates and subsequently contemplates the subtle aggregates.
Among the five aggregates, the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is the coarsest.
Because one first observes that [body], the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) initially arises.
However, since body, sensation, and mind are all subsumed under the three truths,
the application of mindfulness to the body takes the three truths as its object and performs twelve aspects of mental attention (*ākāra*).
In this way, the application of mindfulness to the body consisting of what is produced by hearing gives rise to the application of mindfulness to feelings consisting of what is produced by hearing;
the application of mindfulness to feelings consisting of what is produced by hearing gives rise to the application of mindfulness to the mind consisting of what is produced by hearing.

The mental application of mindfulness consisting in what is heard (śrutamaya-cittasmṛtyupasthāna) gives rise to the dharma-application of mindfulness consisting in what is heard (śrutamaya-dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
This dharma-application of mindfulness consisting in what is heard takes the four noble truths as its object and performs the sixteen aspects (ṣoḍaśākāra).
Once the four foundations of mindfulness consisting of hearing have been gradually perfected,
one is then able to give rise to the four foundations of mindfulness consisting of reflection.
Once the four foundations of mindfulness consisting of reflection have been gradually perfected...
Furthermore, it can give rise to the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna produced through cultivation.
Because this has already attained the lineage (gotra), it remains firmly established in the modes of activity (ākāra) regarding all aggregates;
therefore, one first gives rise to the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna.
First, one contemplates the Truth of Suffering through its four aspects,
and so on, until finally contemplating the Truth of the Path through its four aspects,
as stated in the sūtra.
Thus, by cultivating the application of mindfulness of right aspiration, one can destroy ignorance and give rise to clear knowledge.
In this regard, it is asked:
what is meant by "cultivating the application of mindfulness of right aspiration"?
Some say: herein, the "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is taught because it can destroy ignorance;

thus, when the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm are eliminated and clear knowledge (*vidyā*) is initiated, this is the "knowledge of the dharma of suffering."
Some say that herein,
the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) is able to destroy ignorance; thus,

the fourteen proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) pertaining to the form and formless realms give rise to illumination, which is the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
Some say that in this context,
the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is so called because it can destroy ignorance; thus,

when the most subtle grade of afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) gives rise to clear knowledge (*vidyā*), there arises the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
Some say that it is stated here that all uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) are able to destroy ignorance;

thus, when the category of afflictions (*kleśa-pakṣa*) to be abandoned by them gives rise to clear knowledge (*vidyā*), that very category attains the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Thus spoke the Venerable Vaibhāṣika Śrīlāta.

In this context, it is said that the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) consisting of skillful wisdom (kauśalya-prajñā) embraced by skillful means (upāyakauśalya) is called "straight, correct,
and aspirational. Because this can destroy ignorance (avidyā),
the three unwholesome roots (akuśalamūla) give rise to the three wholesome roots (kuśalamūla) when they produce clear knowledge (vidyā).
As the Blessed One said in a verse:
"If one is caught in the thicket of craving, who can lead them?
The Buddha’s conduct is boundless; being traceless, by what trace could he be led?"
In this context, that which is practiced by the Buddha refers to the four foundations of mindfulness.
Question: Does the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa having attained the ultimate limit of the foundations of mindfulness?
Is it that one enters parinirvāṇa without having attained the limit?
If so, what fault would there be?
If you say that one does attain it, [what follows?]
For what reason is it said that the Buddha’s conduct is boundless?
If he does not attain anything,
for what reason is it said that at the time he attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), his activities were perfectly consummated?
Answer: There are causes and conditions by which one may say that a limit is reached;
there are causes and conditions by which one may say that a limit is not reached.
That is to say, based on the factor of projection (*ākṣepa*), one may say that a limit is reached.
Based on enjoyment, one may say that the limit is not reached;
furthermore, based on attainment, one may say that the limit is reached;
based on abiding in the body, one may say that the limit is not reached.
Furthermore, based on accomplishment, one may say that the limit has been reached;
based on manifestation, one may say that the limit has not been reached.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
What is meant by that which is not the sphere of activity for a bhikṣu?
It should be said: the five types of exquisite sensual pleasures.
What is meant by that which is the sphere of activity for a bhikṣu?
It should be said that the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are [the basis].
Question: Since the five objects of sensual pleasure (pañca kāmaguṇa) also enter into the foundations of mindfulness, why is it said that they are not their sphere of activity (agocara)?
Answer: This statement is made in dependence upon the one who observes.
That is to say, if one observes in an improper manner, it is called a sphere that is not within one's range;
if one observes in a proper manner, it is called a sphere that is within one's range.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There are three applications of mindfulness that noble ones should practice;
when a noble one has practiced them well, he is then fit to lead a community."
What are these three?
They are as follows: when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to his disciples, he does so with a mind of profound compassion for their welfare and benefit, declaring:
"This is for your benefit; this is for your happiness; this is for both your benefit and happiness."
If a community of disciples remains respectful and attentive, dwelling with a mind intent on following instructions,
practicing the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma without transgressing the holy teachings, and receiving and training in the points of training (śikṣāpada),
the Tathāgata does not feel celebratory joy nor does his heart leap with delight regarding them.
Abiding solely in right equanimity, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension—
this is called the first application of mindfulness.
If a noble one has well-cultivated this stage, they are then fit to guide the community.
Furthermore, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to his disciples, he gives rise to profound compassion;
out of a heart of pity for their welfare and benefit, he declares:
"This is for your benefit; this is for your happiness; this is for both your benefit and happiness."
If the assembly of disciples is not respectful, does not lend an ear, lacks a mind intent on following instructions,
does not practice in accordance with the Dharma, transgresses the holy teachings, and does not accept the training in the points of training.
The Tathāgata, toward them as well, feels no resentment; his mind is free from sorrow or distress.
He abides solely in right equanimity, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension.
This is called the second application of mindfulness.
If there is a noble one who has well cultivated this [time], then he should lead the assembly.
Furthermore, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to his disciples, he gives rise to profound compassion, even unto this:
for their benefit and happiness.
If one portion of the assembly of disciples is respectful and attentive, even to the point of training in the precepts,
while another portion of the assembly of disciples is not respectful and not attentive, even to the point of not training in the precepts either.
At that time, the Tathāgata felt no joy or elation toward those who received him with respect,
nor did he feel anger, resentment, or sorrow toward those who received him without respect.
Abiding solely in right equanimity, right mindfulness, and right clear comprehension—
this is called the third foundation of mindfulness.
If a noble one has well cultivated this stage, they are then fit to guide a community.
Question: If that is so,
there should be only two applications of mindfulness,
namely, those regarding respectful reception and those regarding disrespectful reception.
Why are three types taught?
Answer: Because there are three kinds of assemblies, three types are taught.
That is to say, there is an assembly that receives [the teaching] with total reverence and acceptance.
There are assemblies where everyone receives [the teaching] with respect;
there are assemblies where one part receives it with respect while another part does not receive it with respect.
Therefore, three applications of mindfulness are taught in accordance with that.
Question: If that is so, one should rather teach seven applications of mindfulness.
This refers to the four preceding [foundations] and these three types.
Answer: These three types are included within the four preceding ones, because both are subsumed under the foundations of mindfulness that take external phenomena as their mixed objects.
Question: If all who hear the Buddha preach the Dharma were to receive it with reverence, then there would be no need for the three stations of mindfulness (*triṣu smṛty-upasthāneṣu*).

Conversely, if there were those who did not receive it with reverence, would it not be as if the World-Honored One were raining down the rain of the True Dharma upon that which is neither a field nor a vessel?
"In that case, the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma would be in vain.
[The Buddha] replied: "The World-Honored One teaches the Dharma for people with the desire that they understand it.
Even if a person does not understand it, there may still be devas who are able to understand it."
Thus, there are three applications of mindfulness;
nor was the Buddha's teaching of the Dharma in vain. Why is this so?
Because people do not understand, there are three applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Since the gods are able to understand, they do not rain down the rain of Dharma upon those who are not fields or vessels [for it].
Some say:
When the Buddha teaches the Dharma, he intends for various sentient beings to attain the fruit of arhatship;
yet, while they do not attain the fruit of arhatship, they do attain the fruit of non-returning.
For this reason, there are three applications of mindfulness.
Nor was the Buddha's teaching in vain. Why is this?
Because they did not attain the fruit of arhatship.
There are three foundations of mindfulness.
Because he has attained the fruit of non-returning,
his teaching of the Dharma is not in vain.
Furthermore, when the Buddha teaches the Dharma, he intends for certain sentient beings to attain the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*);
yet those beings do not attain the fruit of non-returning, but instead attain the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).
The detailed explanation is as before.
In this way, one desires to attain the fruit of once-returning,
the fruit of stream-entry,
and the roots of goodness conducive to penetration.
The same detailed explanation applies in successive order to the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the roots of goodness conducive to merit (*puṇyabhāgīya*).
Furthermore, when the Buddha teaches the Dharma, he does so with the desire that various sentient beings may attain the fruits of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmaphala*).
Because although they do not obtain the fruit in the present life, they are able to plant roots of goodness for the future;
thus, the three applications of mindfulness are not taught by the Buddha in vain.
The detailed explanation is as before.
Question: Why is it that when disciples respectfully receive his teachings,
the Buddha does not experience joy,
and when they do not respectfully receive them, he does not experience sorrow?
Answer: The Buddha knows that sentient beings possess such distinctions of spiritual lineage (*gotra*):
those with evil dispositions (*āśaya*) perform evil deeds, while those with virtuous dispositions perform virtuous deeds.
If one with evil intentions were to perform good deeds, one might feel joy toward them;
if one with virtuous intentions were to perform evil deeds, one might feel sorrow toward them. But it is not so.
Because of the distinction in their essential natures (*gotra*).
Just as one knows the distinction between the essential natures of external objects—
such that iron ore yields iron and gold ore yields gold— therefore, at the time of smelting and refining, [the result corresponds to its source].
When iron is extracted from iron ore, the mind does not give rise to sorrow;
when gold is extracted from gold ore, the mind does not give rise to joy.
If it were otherwise—that is, if one were to obtain [the former] from the latter or [the latter] from the former—one might well experience sorrow or joy.
However, such a thing does not exist because their spiritual lineages (gotra) differ;
the World-Honored One is likewise,
for he knows the various spiritual lineages of sentient beings.
No mental affliction arises from differences in nature.
Some say this is because the Buddha has already thoroughly severed the dharmas of craving and aversion.
That is to say, joy resembles attachment and sorrow resembles aversion;
since the Buddha has already thoroughly severed both attachment and aversion,
he possesses neither sorrow nor joy.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the Buddha,
having already well-cultivated emptiness as the foundation, formed this thought:
"Who is it that shows me respect?"
Who is it that is disrespectful?
Since one is merely a collection of empty aggregates, one gives rise to neither sorrow nor joy amidst the assembly.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
There is one path leading to purification that enables sentient beings to become pure;
namely, the four foundations of mindfulness,
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: What is meant by the "path leading to a single destination"?
Is it called the path leading to a single destination because it is able to transcend one realm (*dhātu*), or because it is able to transcend one destination (*gati*)?
It is called the "path leading to a single destination" because it is able to transcend a single birth,
because it is able to penetrate a single truth, and because it is able to lead to a single ultimate goal.
Is it because there is only one path that it is called the "single-destination path"?
If so, what is the fault?
If it is called the single-destination path because it can transcend a single realm, [then...]
This is because the realm of the path does not consist of a single destination, as it comprises three [realms].
If one were to call it the "path of a single destination" because it can transcend a single destination,
that too would not be the case, for there are five destinations within the path.
If it is called the "path leading to a single destination" because it can transcend one birth,
this is also not correct, for there are four types of births.
If it is called the "path leading to a single destination" because it can penetrate a single truth...
Nor is it the "path leading to a single destination," because the Truth of the Path consists of four [factors].
If it were called the "path leading to a single destination" simply because it leads to one ultimate goal,
it would still not be the "path leading to a single destination."
Because there are two kinds of ultimate completion:
first, the ultimate completion of the task;
second, the ultimate completion of the effort.
If it were called the "single-path way" (ekāyana-mārga) merely because there is only one path, it would still not be the single-path way, for the paths are of many kinds:

namely, the path of those who follow by faith (śraddhānusāri-mārga), the path of those who follow by dharma (dharmānusāri-mārga), the path of those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta-mārga), the path of those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta-mārga), the path of those liberated by time (samayavimukta-mārga), and the path of those liberated independent of time (asamayavimukta-mārga). Therefore, it is not the single-path way.
How is it said that there is a single path leading to a destination?
The answer is: it is called a single path leading to a destination by virtue of the previously mentioned conditions and other conditions.
Regarding "by virtue of the previously mentioned conditions": [as follows].
This means that because it is able to transcend one realm, it is called the "path of a single destination," namely the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu);
for it is by transcending this realm [that one proceeds].
Because one will no longer be reborn within the three realms,
and because one is able to transcend a single destination, it is called the "path of a single destination," namely,
the celestial realm.
Because those who transcend this destiny do not go further to the five destinies,
and because they are able to transcend one more birth, it is called the "path of a single destiny," which is then rebirth by transformation (*upapāduka*).
Because those who transcend this birth will no longer undergo the four modes of birth,
and because they are able to penetrate the single truth, it is called the "path of a single destination"; that is,
the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Because this truth has never been attained since beginningless time,
nor has it ever been fully realized,
and because it leads to a single ultimate goal, it is called the "path leading to a single destination."
Thus, the task is brought to completion;
for it is through the ultimate perfection of cultivation that one achieves the ultimate completion of the task.
Furthermore, because there is only a single path, it is called the "path of a single destination."
Regarding the noble path:
one might ask, "Are there not many paths, such as the path of practice through faith up to the path of untimely liberation?
The answer is: because all of them are practices leading toward the cessation of suffering, they are called the "one path."
Just as there is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,
so too is there the practice leading to the cessation of existence and the cessation of the world.
Birth and death cease;
the cycle of transmigration ceases;
birth, old age, sickness, and death cease—the explanation of their cessation is likewise.
This is called the "single-path way" (ekāyana-mārga) by virtue of the aforementioned conditions,
as well as other conditions.
This means that because there is no other destination, because there is no falling back,
because one has reached non-retrogressive liberation,
and because one has reached the single destination that turns away from the five destinies.
As it is said that nirvāṇa is the destination of the arhat,
by this meaning it is called the "single-destination path.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
It is called the "path of a single direction" because it serves as the antidote to heterodox paths.
This refers to various non-Buddhist practitioners who either maintain that fasting constitutes the path,
or maintain that following the movement of the sun constitutes the path.
Some adhere to lying on ashes, drinking wind, consuming water, eating only vegetables or fruits, going naked, wearing coarse garments, or sleeping on uneven ground, each regarding these as the path.
To counteract those heterodox paths, the Buddha taught the single-path way.
The meaning of these words is that those various paths are all not the true path, but are merely evil, deviant, and false paths;
they are the paths practiced and frequented by those who are not virtuous persons.
