This is not the path practiced and pursued by true noble beings. Why is this?
Because the true path is one and only.
This refers to the four foundations of mindfulness.
Some teachers say that because they lead toward the single gateway to the palace of liberation, they are called the "path leading to a single destination."
In this regard, one should cite the analogy taught in the Udāyī-sūtra.
As it is said therein,
the Buddha addressed Udāyī:
It is like a frontier city whose walls are firm and thick,
with watchtowers, battlements, parapets, and windows all strictly prepared for defense;
there is but a single gate, entrusted to a single person for its guarding.
That man was intelligent, learned, and well-trained; he listened to those who were appropriate to enter and stopped those who were not.
As he patrolled the city and observed it, he eventually could no longer see any place where the beast came or went.
How much more so for other gates?
Udaka, you should know that those gatekeepers—
Although one does not know that on every single day so many sentient beings enter and exit the city,
one certainly knows that all who enter and exit do so through this gate and not by any other.

In this way, although the Tathāgata does not form a deliberate mental application when knowing that so many sentient beings have already attained parinirvāṇa or that so many sentient beings will attain parinirvāṇa,
he nonetheless knows with certainty which classes of sentient beings have already attained parinirvāṇa and which have not.
All [attainments] proceed by this path and not by any other path;
therefore, because it leads to the single gate of the palace of liberation, it is called the "path of a single destination" (*ekāyana-mārga*).

Question: Are the right abandonments (*samyak-prahāṇa*), bases of power (*ṛddhi-pāda*), faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) also the path of a single destination?
If this is so, for what reason does that sutra speak only of the foundations of mindfulness as the "path leading to a single destination," and not mention the others?
If this is not so, why is it that only the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are the path leading to a single destination (*ekāyana-mārga*), and not others?
One should reply: those [other factors] are also the path leading to a single destination.
Question: If that is so, why are they not mentioned in that sutra?
Regarding those who have promised to speak but do not speak,
one should know that this meaning is incomplete. Some say:
If one speaks of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), it should be understood that the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) and so forth have also been explained.
Some say that the foundations of mindfulness are both a single path (ekāyana) and the path (mārga).
The right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) and so forth constitute a single direction (*ekāyana*) but are not the path (*mārga*), because not all of them are wisdom (*prajñā*). Some say:
The application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is always superior in its function from the stage of a beginner up to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (kṣayānutpādajñāna);
this is not the case for the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) and the others. Some say:
The foundations of mindfulness can differentiate the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, establish the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena,
and eliminate delusion regarding things as well as delusion regarding objects of perception.
It functions without increase or decrease regarding all phenomena;
this is not the case for the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) and so forth. Some say:
The foundations of mindfulness are like those with eyes who can lead the rest, who are like the blind;
the factors of enlightenment proceed toward the palace of nirvāṇa without deviating to other paths,
just as one with clear vision leads the blind along the correct road so they do not travel by a wrong path.
The foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are likewise so; therefore,
that sutra mentions only the foundations of mindfulness as the "single-path way" (ekāyano mārgaḥ) and does not mention the others.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There is a single path leading to purification that enables sentient beings to transcend and extinguish sorrow and suffering,
even unto the realization of the Dharma that accords with correct principle."
This refers to noble right samādhi, as well as its causes, conditions, and requisites.
Question: For what reason does the Blessed One sometimes speak of prajñā as the single path to the goal, and sometimes speak of samādhi as the single path to the goal?
Answer: Because it is taught according to what the sentient beings being transformed have not yet attained.
That is to say, among the sentient beings being transformed, some may lack śamatha, while others may lack vipaśyanā.
If one lacks śamatha, samādhi is taught as the single path leading to the goal;
if one lacks vipaśyanā,
prajñā is taught as the single path leading to the goal.
Prajñā refers to the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) mentioned previously,
because its essential nature is the wisdom of the foundations of mindfulness.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
If one is able to accomplish the four foundations of mindfulness, then one is able to accomplish correct reasoning.
If one is able to accomplish correct reasoning, then one is able to accomplish the noble path.
If one is able to accomplish the noble path, then one is able to accomplish the deathless nectar.
If one can prepare the ambrosia, one can be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, grief, suffering, and all the afflictions of feverish distress.
Question: Is the application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) the noble path that accords with reality?
What is the distinction regarding "ambrosia" (amṛta)?
The answer is that they are distinguished by name; that is to say, they are named "foundations of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna) up to and including being named "ambrosia. Some say:
The foundations of mindfulness reveal the foundations of mindfulness;
likewise, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment are revealed by their respective names,
while the noble path reveals its own branches, and the nectar reveals its fruit.
Some say that the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) manifest the object of observation (ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna),
just as the principle manifests the mixed foundation of mindfulness (saṃsṛṣṭa-smṛtyupasthāna).
The Noble Path reveals the intrinsic nature of the foundations of mindfulness;
the Deathless reveals their fruit. Some say:
The foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) as they appear [in the scriptures] manifest those consisting of hearing;
those appearing according to reason manifest those consisting of reflection;
and those appearing as the noble path manifest those consisting of cultivation.
The "Ambrosia" (amṛta) reveals its fruit.
Some say that the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) reveal the ultimate foundation of mindfulness regarding verbal expression.
Just as "reason" (yukti) reveals the culmination of the application of mindfulness through reflection,
"the noble path" (āryamārga) reveals the culmination of the application of mindfulness through renunciation,
and "ambrosia" (amṛta) reveals its fruit.
Some say that the foundations of mindfulness manifest the path of vision,
just as correct reasoning manifests the path of cultivation.
The Noble Path reveals the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*);
the same applies to the explanations regarding the stage of vision (*darśanabhūmi*), the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanābhūmi*), and the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣabhūmi*).
The Deathless (*amṛta*) reveals its fruit.

Some say: the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) manifest the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya); the correct principle manifests the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya);
and the noble path (āryamārga) manifests the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
The nectar reveals that fruit;
this is called the distinction of the nectar of the noble path of correct principle regarding the foundations of mindfulness.
If one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of the body, does one [also] cultivate that of sensation?
...and so on, as explained at length.
There are four kinds of cultivation:

namely, cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), cultivation by practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), cultivation by counteraction (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*), and cultivation by elimination (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*).
Cultivation through practice refers to all conditioned wholesome dharmas;
cultivation as an antidote and cultivation as removal refer to all contaminated dharmas.
The masters of the West say:
There are six kinds of cultivation:
namely, the four preceding ones, along with protective cultivation (*ārakṣaṇā-bhāvanā*) and analytical cultivation (*vibhāvanā-bhāvanā*).
Regarding protective cultivation:
This refers to cultivating the faculties as described.
Thus, when the six faculties are well-tamed, well-guarded, well-preserved, and well-restrained, they can bring about the maturation of pleasant feelings in the future.
As for the detailed cultivation:

This refers to the cultivation of the body as it has been taught: "Regarding this body, [one contemplates] the hair of the head, the hair of the body, the nails, the teeth," and so forth, as explained at length.
The masters of Kaśmīr say:

The latter two cultivations are subsumed under the cultivation of removal through the preceding cultivation of counteraction; the meaning of these four cultivations is explained in detail in such places as the *Jñānaskandha*.
This treatise is composed here based on two of these cultivations.
This refers to the cultivation of attainment (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*).
Based on these two types of cultivation, there are distinctions in the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) throughout the various stages.
Specifically, in the initial stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), one takes the dharmas of the three truths as objects.
The foundations of mindfulness are cultivated in the present;
four are cultivated in the future.
One aspect is cultivated in the present.
In the future, one cultivates four;
these are cultivated as concordant, not discordant.
When the present cultivation of the mindfulness-establishment of dharmas (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) takes the Truth of Cessation as its object, then this is cultivated in the future.
One aspect is cultivated in the present;
four are cultivated in the future.
Furthermore, these are cultivated as being of the same category (sabhāga), not of a different category (tatsabhāga).
Because one cannot cultivate the path that takes the aggregates as its object by means of the contemplation of the cessation of the first aggregate,
one increases the "Heat" stage which takes the three truths as its object.
One cultivates any one of the four foundations of mindfulness in the present;
one cultivates all four in the future.
This cultivation applies to both those of the same class and those of a different class.
One aspect is cultivated in the present;
sixteen are cultivated in the future.
When the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna takes the truth of cessation as its object, it is cultivated in the present.
Regarding the future, one cultivates four;
regarding the present, one cultivates one aspect,
while in the future, one cultivates sixteen.

Question: Why is it that at the initial stage of *ūṣmagata* there is cultivation only of the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and not the heterogeneous (*visabhāga*), whereas at the stage of increased *ūṣmagata* there is cultivation of both the homogeneous and the heterogeneous?
Answer: Because the initial *ūṣmagata* is a lineage (*gotra*) that has never been attained before.

Because the power of the aspectual activity (*ākāra*) arising from the initial application to the Truths is weak, it consists only of cultivation that is "of the same class" (*sabhāga*) and not "of a different class" (*visabhāga*).

However, when the "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) stage increases—being a lineage already previously attained—the power of the aspectual activity arising from the application to the Truths becomes strong and superior; therefore, it is capable of both cultivation that is of the same class and of a different class.
In the initial stage of the Peak (mūrdhan), one cultivates the present mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) taking the four truths as its object;
one cultivates all four [foundations of mindfulness] in the future,
both those of the same category (sabhāga) and those of a different category (visabhāga).
One aspect is cultivated in the present;
sixteen are cultivated in the future.

In the stage of increase (*vṛddha*) and the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*), one cultivates in the present any one of the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) that takes the three truths as its object.
In the future, one cultivates four;
these are cultivated as both homogeneous and heterogeneous.
Regarding the aspect (*ākāra*), one cultivates it in the present.
In the future, one cultivates sixteen.
When the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna that takes the truth of cessation as its object is cultivated in the present,
four are cultivated in the future.
One aspect is cultivated in the present;
sixteen are cultivated in the future.

During both the initial stage of patience (*kṣānti*) and the stage of increase (*vṛddhi*), the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) takes the four truths as its object and is cultivated in the present.
In the future, one cultivates four;
these are cultivated as both homogeneous and heterogeneous.
Regarding the single mode of activity, it is cultivated in the present.
In the future, one cultivates sixteen [aspects].

Question: Why is it that during the initial stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) and the stage of increase (*vṛddhi*), only the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is cultivated in the present?
Answer: Because Patience is proximate to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is similar to the Path of Seeing.
Just as in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), only the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is cultivated in the present, so it is with patience (*kṣānti*).
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
"The roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) exist in two [realms], namely, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)."

That is to say, the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata) and Peak (mūrdhan) exist in both realms; the two stages of Patience (kṣānti) and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma) exist only in the form realm.

According to that teaching, when one relies on the first Patience, one takes the dharmas of the three truths as objects and cultivates the present application of mindfulness to dharmas (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
Regarding the future, one cultivates four.
As for the present cultivation of aspects, one cultivates four in the future;
this is cultivation of the homogeneous, not of the non-homogeneous.

When one cultivates the present mindfulness-establishment on phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) with the truth of cessation as its object, one does not cultivate it in the future; for the contemplation of the cessation of the aggregates cannot cultivate a path that has the aggregates as its object.
Therefore, only one aspect (ākāra) is cultivated in the present.
In the future, one cultivates four;
these are cultivated as concordant, not discordant.
When increasing patience, one takes three truths as objects and cultivates any one of the four foundations of mindfulness in the present.
In the future, one cultivates four;
these are cultivated as both homogeneous and heterogeneous.
Regarding the mode of activity (*ākāra*), one cultivates them in the present.
In the future, one cultivates sixteen.
Regarding the present cultivation of the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna that takes the truth of cessation as its object,
one cultivates four in the future.
One aspect is cultivated in the present;
sixteen are cultivated in the future.
Question: Why is it that, at the initial stage of *kṣānti*, cultivation is restricted to those of the same category (*sabhāga*)?
Is the cultivation of increased patience also of a dissimilar nature?
Answer: As explained extensively above.
The critique says:
The previous explanation was excellent because the roots of goodness of the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) accord with the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
In the stage of initial arising, one currently cultivates only the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*);
in the stage of increase, any one of the four mindfulness-establishments manifests.

Because the stage of initial patience (*kṣānti*) is proximate to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), at all times one currently cultivates only the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
At the stage of the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), one likewise currently cultivates only the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
Regarding the future, one cultivates four.
One aspect is cultivated in the present;
four aspects are cultivated in the future.
It is cultivated through its own class (*sabhāga*), not through a different class (*visabhāga*).

Question: Since the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) also arises as an aspect directed toward the Truths based on a previously acquired lineage (*gotra*), why is it said to be only of its own class?
Is it not that one cultivates what is non-homogeneous?
Answer: The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is the most proximate root of goodness to the Path of Seeing; it most closely resembles the Path of Seeing.
Just as within the Path of Seeing one cultivates only what is homogeneous and not what is non-homogeneous, so it is here.
The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is likewise.
Some say that the Supreme Mundane Dharma is the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) which serves as the precursor to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Just as on the Path of Seeing one cultivates only the homogeneous [aspects],
some say that for the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), there are only so many aspects (*ākāra*) that can be cultivated.
Just as one who is naked has no clothing to be stripped away,
it should be understood that the same applies to *adhimātra-kṣānti* (superior patience).

In the other stages of patience (*kṣānti*), as the objects of focus (*ālambana*) are progressively reduced, one does not cultivate the mental abiding or the aspects (*ākāra*) associated with those [objects].
It should be understood as such.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 188, of the *Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Volume 100.
Compiled by eight hundred and ninety-five great Arhats and others;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section One of the First Sub-section on the Foundations of Mindfulness within the Eighth Aggregate of Views: Part Three. If one enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) through the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of suffering and its origin, each taking four moments of mind.

During the three moments of mind of the clear realization of the path (*mārgābhisamaya*), one cultivates the present and future applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). There is one aspect (*ākāra*) in the present cultivation and four in the future cultivation.
In the present cultivation and future cultivation, one cultivates those of the same category (*sabhāga*), not those of a different category (*visabhāga*).

During the four moments of mind of the clear realization of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya*), one cultivates the present mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and simultaneously cultivates it in the future.

This is because the initial observation of the cessation of the untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) cannot yet cultivate the path that takes those aggregates as its object. Thus, one aspect (*ākāra*) is cultivated in the present and four aspects are cultivated in the future; these are cultivated as being of the same type (*sabhāga*), not of a different type (*visabhāga*).

Because the power of the initially acquired uncontaminated lineage has not yet expanded, one cultivates the present and future applications of mindfulness regarding phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) within the path-knowledge of subsequent realization (*mārgānvayajñāna*).

One cultivates four aspects—both those of the same category and those of different categories—and cultivates one aspect in the present and sixteen aspects in the future, because the force of the already acquired uncontaminated lineage has increased and expanded.
From this point onward, whenever all noble beings bring forth previously unattained roots of goodness into the present,
they cultivate all four foundations of mindfulness and sixteen aspects in the future.
Except for the wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection,
and at the time of the extremely subtle mind upon entering the meditative absorption of cessation,
all other ordinary beings likewise lack the characteristics of noble conduct.
Therefore, from this point forward, only the extent of the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) will be discussed, and not their specific modes of activity (ākāra).
This applies when ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are practicing the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga) for detachment from the defilements of the desire realm.
In the cultivation of any one of the four foundations of mindfulness in the present, one cultivates all four in the future.
During the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the nine paths of liberation, one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena in the present and cultivates all four in the future.
As it is for becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm, so it is up to becoming free from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
Regarding becoming free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
one takes the fourth dhyāna itself as the preparatory application (prayoga).
At the time of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), one of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is cultivated in the present, and all four are cultivated for the future.
If there are those who maintain that the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the Sphere of Infinite Space has a distinct object of focus, then at the time of their path of preparation:
When practicing any one of the four foundations of mindfulness in the present, one practices all four in the future.
During the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation,
when the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena is practiced in the present, one practices all four in the future.

At the time of the ninth path of liberation, one cultivates the present application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and cultivates the three [applications of mindfulness] excluding the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) for the future.
This applies to those who maintain that the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of those [formless attainments] take only a composite object (*samastālambana*).
During the nine paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the eight paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the [first] eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
when the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) is cultivated in the present,

it is also cultivated in the future. During the ninth path of liberation, when the application of mindfulness to phenomena is cultivated in the present, it is cultivated in the future along with three others, excluding the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*).
It is the same for those who have become free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna up to those who have become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The difference is that the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is excluded;
thus, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) give rise to the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).

During the cultivation of the first three applications of mindfulness (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*), the first eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the first eight totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
and when manifesting the supernormal powers of the base of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*),
one cultivates four future applications of mindfulness in the present.
When one arises from [the attainment of] any one of the last three applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), one cultivates it in the present and cultivates all four in the future.
When one arises from the four immeasurables (apramāṇa) or induces the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā),
one cultivates the application of mindfulness to dharmas (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) in the present and cultivates all four in the future.

When inducing the supernormal power of knowing others' minds, one cultivates either the mindfulness of mind or one of the mindfulnesses of feeling, mind, or phenomena in the present, and all four in the future.
This is also the case when arising the formless liberations and the latter three applications of mindfulness.
Regarding any one of the latter three applications of mindfulness, when cultivated in the present, there is cultivation of the future; this excludes the application of mindfulness to the body.
This is the case when the sphere of infinite space or the sphere of infinite consciousness arises.

When practicing the present cultivation of the application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and the future cultivation of the three [other applications]— excluding the application of mindfulness of the body—
this is called the distinction in what is cultivated during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Furthermore, when noble ones (*ārya*) are on the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) for the sake of becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), [they cultivate these].
When any one of the four foundations of mindfulness is cultivated in the present, all four are cultivated for the future.
At the time of every uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation path (*vimukti-mārga*),
the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) is cultivated in the present, and all four are cultivated for the future.
One who transforms their faculties through resolute faith becomes a "vision-attainer" (dṛṣṭiprāpta);
one who transforms their faculties while liberated by time becomes "immovable" (akopya).
During all stages of the preparatory path (prayoga-mārga), one of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is cultivated in the present, and all four are cultivated for the future.

At all times during the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one cultivates the present and future applications of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Furthermore, when noble ones (*ārya*) give rise to the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), the application of mindfulness of the body (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*), the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the first eight totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), [they likewise cultivate these].
Furthermore, when one brings forth the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear,

or when one gives rise to the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), one cultivates the present mindfulness of the body and the future cultivation of the [remaining] four [foundations of mindfulness].
This is also the case for those who practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, as well as for those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimately real (*paramārtha*).
When one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) with a subtle mind characterized by perception,

one cultivates any one of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) in the present and cultivates all four in the future. This applies to the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), the limit of concentration (*samādhiparyanta*), and the formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*).
When one gives rise to the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*),
or those who maintain that only *nirvāṇa* is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), as well as when one gives rise to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*),

the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), the two latter universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), the wishlessness of wishlessness (*apranihitā-praṇihita*), and the signlessness of signlessness (*animittā-animitta*).
When cultivating the present foundation of mindfulness of dharmas, one cultivates the four future ones.

When inducing the supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds, one cultivates either the foundation of mindfulness of mind, or the foundations of mindfulness of feeling, mind, and dharmas; and when arising any one of the latter three foundations of mindfulness, one cultivates the four future ones.
This is called the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
If one cultivates the application of mindfulness to the body, does one [also] cultivate that of sensation?
And if one cultivates the application of mindfulness to sensation, does one [also] cultivate that of the body?
It can be answered in four propositions.
There is the case of establishing mindfulness on the body that is not [established] on feeling:
this refers to when one who has already attained the establishment of mindfulness on the body brings it to presence.
Because when a previously attained dharma manifests in the present,
one lacks the power to extend it to the future, one does not cultivate the application of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
However, since this manifestation constitutes cultivation through practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), it is said that one cultivates the application of mindfulness of the body (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Question: Is it also the case that one may have the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) manifest before one without yet having cultivated the mindfulness of feelings (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*), such as when the mindfulness of the body consisting of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*) has manifested for the first time?
Why is this not mentioned here?
One should know that when something ought to be stated but is not, the meaning is incomplete (sāvaśeṣa).
Some say: [text continues]
This treatise is composed based on the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) produced by cultivation (bhāvanāmaya).

There is no case where one who has not yet attained the foundation of mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) produced by cultivation can have it manifest without simultaneously cultivating the foundation of mindfulness of feelings (vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna); therefore, this is not mentioned.
There is the cultivation of the mindfulness of feeling but not of the body;
that is to say, when one who has already attained the mindfulness of feeling brings it to presence,
or when one who has not yet attained the mindfulness of feeling brings it to presence without cultivating the mindfulness of the body.
If one has not yet attained the mindfulness of mental factors (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) present before them, one cultivates feeling but not the body;
if one has already attained the mindfulness of feeling present before them, it is explained as previously stated;
if one has not yet attained the mindfulness of feeling present before them and does not cultivate the body [it is as follows].
This refers to ordinary beings who are free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of nothingness.
If they take the application of mindfulness of feeling as their preparatory practice,
then at the time of that path of preparation, when those ordinary beings give rise to the application of mindfulness of feeling and the formless deliverances:
At such a time, when one has not yet attained the application of mindfulness to feelings (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna), one cultivates feelings rather than the body;
and when one has not yet attained the application of mindfulness to the mind (citta-smṛtyupasthāna), one cultivates feelings rather than the body.
This refers to ordinary persons who are free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of nothingness.
If they take the application of mindfulness of mind as their preparatory practice,
then at the time of that path of preparation— when those ordinary persons give rise to the application of mindfulness of mind and the formless liberations.
At such a time, when one has not yet attained the presence of mindfulness of mind (cittasmṛtyupasthāna), one cultivates feeling but not the body;
and when one has not yet attained the presence of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna), one cultivates feeling but not the body.
This refers to when ordinary beings, at the time of the final path of liberation from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
become free from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of nothingness.
If one relies on a lower fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) to give rise to the application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) as a preparatory practice (*prayoga*),
and during that path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) one relies on a higher preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) as the basis for that practice—
this applies to those who maintain that the preparatory stages of the formless realm (*ārūpyasāmantaka*) possess distinct objects of focus.
If one takes the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) as the preparatory application,
then during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the nine paths of liberation of that path of preparation—
specifically for those who maintain that the access concentrations (sāmantaka) of the formless realm take only a collective object— it is only at the time of the ninth path of liberation.
When ordinary beings give rise to the application of mindfulness of dharmas,
the formless liberations, and the latter two totalities,
at such times they have not yet attained the manifestation of the application of mindfulness of dharmas; they cultivate feeling and non-self, but not the body.
There is simultaneous cultivation: when the mindfulness of body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) has not yet been attained but is present before one;
or when the mindfulness of feeling (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*) has not yet been attained but is present while cultivating the body;
or when the mindfulness of mind and phenomena (*cittadharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) has not yet been attained but is present while cultivating the body and feelings.

"Not having yet attained the present manifestation of the application of mindfulness to the body" refers to the present manifestation of the application of mindfulness to the body during the stages of Increasing Heat and Summits; or,
when one is free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
When the application of the mindfulness of the body serves as the preparatory path— that is, during the time of that preparatory path—
if one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra), they become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta);
if one who is liberated by time (samayavimukta) refines their faculties, they become one who is immovable (akopyadharman).
When the mindfulness of the body serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*) and that path of preparation (*prayogamārga*),
if one generates the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), or the mindfulness of the body;

or if one brings forth the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the first eight totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-vidhi*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*).
When arising the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*),
if one practices the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) by means of the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*),
for those who maintain that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*):

When he gives rise to the analytical knowledge of the meaning of the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna-artha-pratisaṃvid*) and the analytical knowledge of eloquence regarding the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna-nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), at the limit of the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna-paryanta-samādhi*), during the formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*), and when entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—at such times, his mind is subtle.

At such a time, when one has not yet attained the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) and is cultivating the body while the application of mindfulness to sensation (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*) is present before them;

that is to say, when one who has not yet attained the application of mindfulness to sensation is cultivating the body at the time the application of mindfulness to sensation is present during the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*.
If one is free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and takes the application of mindfulness of feelings as the preparatory practice during that path of preparation; or if,
being one liberated through faith, one refines the faculties to become one who has attained vision.
When one who is liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) refines their faculties to become unshakable (akopya),
they take the application of mindfulness of feeling (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna) as the preparatory practice (prayoga).

At the time of that path of preparation, if they induce the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (paracittajñāna-abhijñā), the application of mindfulness of feeling is present before them.
When one cultivates dhyāna by means of the application of mindfulness to feeling (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna),
those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimate reality give rise to the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid) regarding the application of mindfulness to feeling,
as well as the analytical knowledge of eloquence (niruktipratisaṃvid) regarding the application of mindfulness to feeling.

When one enters the meditative absorption on the limit of knowledge (*jñānaparyantadhyāna*), the formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*), or the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), at which time the perception is subtle and the mind is faint— during such a time,

when the mindfulness of feelings (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*) has not yet been attained and is present, one cultivates the mindfulness of the body and feelings, but the mindfulness of the mind has not yet been attained and is present while cultivating the mindfulness of the body and feelings.
This refers to when the application of mindfulness of mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) is present during the stages of Increasing Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*),

taking as its preparatory practice the application of mindfulness of mind directed toward the defiled states of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

At the time of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), if one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*),
or if one who is temporarily liberated (*samayavimukta*) refines their faculties to become one who is unshakable (*akopyadharman*),
the application of mindfulness regarding the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) serves as the preparatory practice during that path of preparation.
When the mental application of mindfulness (cittasmṛtyupasthāna) is present during the manifestation of the supernormal power of knowing others' minds,
or when one practices the meditative absorption (dhyāna) by intermingling it with the mental application of mindfulness—
those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimately real (paramārtha).
The analytical knowledge of meaning regarding the application of mindfulness to the mind,

as well as the analytical knowledge of eloquence regarding the application of mindfulness to the mind, occur at the limit of the knowledge of aspiration, during the formless liberations, and when entering the meditative attainment of cessation, at which time the mind is subtle.
At such a time, one has not yet attained the presence of mindfulness of the mind,
nor has one attained the presence of mindfulness of phenomena, while cultivating the body and feelings.

That is to say: when the stage of initial "warmth" (ūṣmagata) takes the three truths as its object and increases, and the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) taking the four truths as its object is present;
and when the stage of "summit" (mūrdhan), both in its initial and increased states, takes the four truths as its object and the mindfulness of phenomena is present.
Whether it be at the time of all the patiences (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*),

or during the four moments of mind for each of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, origin, and the path upon entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*),

if one takes the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) as the preparatory application (*prayoga*) to become free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
At the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,
if one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties, they become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta);
if one who is liberated by time (samayavimukta) refines their faculties, they become one who is immovable (akopyadharman).
The application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) serves as the preparatory practice (*prayoga*).

At the time of all those uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) of the preparatory stage, when one brings forth the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñānābhijñā*), the application of mindfulness to phenomena is present; and when one brings forth the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtyabhijñā*) or gives rise to the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
When one practices the meditative absorptions by means of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*),
for those who maintain that all phenomena are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
at the time they give rise to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena:
For those who maintain that only nirvāṇa is the ultimate truth, when they give rise to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*),
the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the latter two universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), wishlessness of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-apraṇihita*), and signlessness of signlessness (*animitta-animitta*), [they do not perceive it].

When one gives rise to the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the limit of meditative concentration (*samādhiparyanta*), the formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or when the mind is extremely subtle during the perception [of these states], at such times,
although the application of mindfulness to phenomena has not yet been attained, the cultivation of the body and feelings is present.
There is the case where neither is cultivated:
namely, when the mindfulness of mental states (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that has already been attained is present before one,
or when the mindfulness of mental states not yet attained is present before one.

One who does not cultivate the mindfulness of body dwells with all defiled minds or with neutral minds while in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or when born in the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-deva*).
As for the mindfulness of mental objects (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) that has already been attained and is present before one, it is explained as previously stated.
Regarding those who have not yet attained the application of mindfulness to dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) being present, but have cultivated neither the body nor feelings:

this refers to the initial stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), when one takes the Truth of Cessation as an object, or during the four moments of mind when entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and realizing the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of cessation.
If ordinary beings are free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness,
and if there are those who maintain that the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the formless realms only take the aggregate as their object in general;

If the proximate stage of a higher level serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), then during all such times— the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)—
the mindfulness of dharmas (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) has not yet been attained and does not manifest in the present.
One does not cultivate bodily feeling.
"All defiled minds" refers to those defiled minds that are of a nature conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*), being heavy and associated with indolence.
Because the mind can only engage in cultivation when it is compliant with the nature of progressive advancement,
buoyant, and associated with diligence;
as for the indeterminate mind:

That is to say, because the nature of the indeterminate mind is weak, corrupt, and withered, one must abide in a mind that is powerful, firm, and superior before one can cultivate [the meditative attainments].
This applies to those who dwell in the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation.
This means that since one must possess a mind in order to cultivate [the state],
those born into the realm of non-conception (asaṃjñika) cannot do so. Regarding this, some say:
For those born there, wholesome minds do not arise at any time.
Some say that although they may arise, they are not the basis for cultivation, because one cannot cultivate future dharmas [in that state].
At such a time, one does not cultivate the body or feelings.
Question: Is there also a case where the mental application of mindfulness has not yet been attained, yet it is present before one, while the body and feelings are not being cultivated?
For example, as when the mental application of mindfulness consisting of hearing and reflection, which has not been previously attained, is present before one.
Why is this not mentioned here?
One should understand that when something ought to be stated but is not, it means the meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Some say: [text fragment]
In this context, it is said that when the mindfulness foundations (smṛtyupasthāna) not previously attained manifest,
one is able to cultivate those of the future, yet one does not cultivate the body or feelings;
however, there is no time when the mindfulness foundation of mind (cittasmṛtyupasthāna) not previously attained manifests.
Because one can cultivate future [states] without cultivating the body or feelings, they are not mentioned.
Question: If that is so, then all distracted wholesome minds (*kuśalacitta*) should also be mentioned; why are only defiled minds (*kliṣṭacitta*) and indeterminate minds (*avyākṛtacitta*) mentioned?
Regarding those who agree to speak but do not speak, one should know that this meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Some say that because it is not definitive, it cannot be easily expressed.
That is to say, if one speaks in terms of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), they lack the power to cultivate what is future;
if one speaks in terms of non-cultivation, then at the time it is present, it is subsumed under the category of habitual cultivation (*vāsanā-bhāvanā*).
Therefore, it is not mentioned in either the context of cultivation or non-cultivation here.
Just as with the mindfulness of the body and the mindfulness of feelings,
one should know that the mindfulness of the body and the mindfulness of the mind are likewise.
Because the future applications of mindfulness regarding feelings and the application of mindfulness regarding the mind must necessarily be cultivated together.
If one cultivates the application of mindfulness regarding the body, does one also cultivate that dharma?
And if one cultivates the application of mindfulness regarding dharmas, does one also cultivate that body?
It can be explained in four propositions. There is the case where the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is practiced, yet it is not in accordance with the Dharma;
this refers to when one who has already attained the application of mindfulness to the body brings it into manifestation, as explained previously.
There are those who cultivate the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena but not that of the body;
namely, those for whom the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena already attained is present,
or those for whom the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena not yet attained is present but they do not cultivate the body.

If one who has not yet attained [the mindfulness of] mental objects brings the present manifestation of the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) but does not cultivate the body, it is as previously explained.
If one who has already attained the mindfulness of phenomena brings it to present manifestation but does not cultivate the body, it is also as previously explained.
If one who has not yet attained the mindfulness of phenomena brings it to present manifestation but does not cultivate the body, [it is likewise].
This refers to when one takes the Truth of Cessation as an object during the initial stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*);
or for a duration of four moments of mind when entering the realization of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya*) within the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*);
or when various ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) become free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna.
For those who maintain that the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) only takes a collective object (*saṃgraha-ālambana*),

if they take that [sphere] as their preliminary application (*prayoga*), then during its nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*anantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), [the object would be the same].
When ordinary beings free themselves from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of nothingness,
and take the mindfulness of dharmas as their preliminary application (*prayoga*), then during all those preliminary, uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and liberation paths (*vimukti-mārga*).
When ordinary beings give rise to the application of mindfulness on phenomena,
the formless liberations, and the latter two universal bases, at such a time:
When the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) has not yet been attained and is brought into presence, one does not cultivate the body.
When the mindfulness of feeling (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*) has not yet been attained and is brought into presence, one cultivates the phenomenon but not the body;
this is as previously explained regarding the case where, when the mindfulness of feeling has not yet been attained and is brought into presence, one does not cultivate the body.

When one who has not yet attained the mindfulness of mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) brings it to presence and cultivates the dharma-foundation but not the body-foundation, there is simultaneous cultivation as explained in the case of feeling;
that is, when one who has not yet attained the mindfulness of body brings it to presence.
If one has not yet attained the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and is currently cultivating the body,
or if one has not yet attained the mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā*) or mind (*citta*) and is currently cultivating the body and phenomena;

and regarding those who have not yet attained the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) and are currently cultivating it— this is as previously explained for those who have not yet attained the mindfulness of the body and are currently cultivating it.

Regarding one who has not yet attained the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) present before them and cultivates the body: this is as previously explained for one who has not yet attained the application of mindfulness to phenomena present before them and cultivates the body and feelings.
Regarding one who has not yet attained the applications of mindfulness to feelings and mind present before them and cultivates the body and phenomena: [it is the same].
This refers to when the applications of mindfulness regarding feeling and mind are present during the stages of increasing heat (*uṣmagata*) and summits (*mūrdhan*);
or when, having abandoned the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
the applications of mindfulness regarding feeling and mind serve as the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for those paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
If one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
or if one liberated by time (samayavimukta) refines their faculties to become one who is unshakable (akopyadharman),

the application of mindfulness to feelings and mind (vedanā-citta-smṛtyupasthāna) serves as the preparatory practice (prayoga). At the time of that path of preparation (prayogamārga), when one brings forth the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (paracittajñānābhijñā), the application of mindfulness to feelings and mind is present before them.
When one practices the meditative absorptions in a mixed manner through the application of mindfulness to feelings and the mind,
those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimate reality give rise to the analytical knowledge of meaning regarding the application of mindfulness to feelings and the mind.

Furthermore, when one is abiding in the mindfulness of feeling and mind, when exercising the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the limit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-paryanta*), the formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*), the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), or when the mind is subtle during the perception of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
at such times, although the mindfulness of feeling and mind has not yet been attained, the mindfulness of body and phenomena are present before one.
There is the case where neither is cultivated.

This refers to when the mindfulness of feelings and the mindfulness of mind have already been attained and are present; all defiled minds and indeterminate minds; and when one is in the attainment of non-conception, the attainment of cessation, or born in the realm of non-conceptual beings—all as explained previously.
If one cultivates the mindfulness of feelings, does one also cultivate that mind?
Or, if one cultivates the mindfulness of mind, does one also cultivate those feelings?
One should respond by establishing four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There is the cultivation of the mindfulness of feeling but not of the mind;
that is, when one who has already attained the mindfulness of feeling brings it into manifestation.
There is the cultivation of the mindfulness of mind but not of feeling.
This means that when the mindfulness of mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) has already been attained and is present before one, it is all explained as previously stated.
There is "cultivation of both" (*ubhayabhāvanā*) when the mindfulness of body, sensation, and mind have not yet been attained and are now present;
or when the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) has not yet been attained and is now present, one cultivates sensation and mind.

Regarding those who have not yet attained the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) as being present before them, it is as previously explained for all those who have not yet attained the application of mindfulness to the body as being present before them.

Regarding those who have not yet attained the applications of mindfulness to feeling (*vedanā*) and mind (*citta*) as being present before them, it is as previously explained for all those who have not yet attained the applications of mindfulness to feeling and mind as being present before them.

Regarding those who have not yet attained the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and are currently cultivating the applications of mindfulness to feeling (*vedanā*) and mind (*citta*), it is as previously explained for those who have not yet attained the application of mindfulness to phenomena and are currently cultivating the other applications of mindfulness.
There are cases where neither is cultivated, namely when one has already attained the applications of mindfulness to the body (*kāya*) and phenomena and they are currently present.

If one has not yet attained the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and it is present before one, one does not cultivate [the applications of mindfulness to] feeling or mind;

this occurs when all defiled or neutral minds are present, or during the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or when born in the heaven of non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñisattva*).

Regarding those who have not yet attained the application of mindfulness to dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and do not cultivate the applications of mindfulness to feeling or mind when it is present before them:

as previously explained for those who have not yet attained the application of mindfulness to dharmas and do not cultivate the other applications of mindfulness when they are present before them, the rest is to be explained as before.
If one cultivates the mindfulness-establishment of feeling, does one also cultivate those factors?
And if one cultivates the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena, does one also cultivate feeling?
One should respond by setting forth four permutations.
There is the cultivation of the mindfulness of feeling that is not the Dharma [foundation of mindfulness];
this refers to when one has already attained the mindfulness of feeling and brings it into manifestation, as explained previously.
There is also the cultivation of the mindfulness of phenomena that is not the mindfulness of feeling.
This refers to when the already-attained application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is present before one.
If the not-yet-attained application of mindfulness to phenomena is present before one, one does not cultivate [the application of mindfulness to] feeling.
Regarding "when the already-attained application of mindfulness to phenomena is present before one," it is explained as previously stated.

Regarding those who have not yet attained the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and do not cultivate the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*) when it is present before them:

this is as previously explained for those who, having not yet attained the application of mindfulness to phenomena when it is present before them, do not cultivate the other applications of mindfulness.
There is simultaneous cultivation, which refers to when the mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind has not yet been attained but is now present;
or when the mindfulness of feeling has not yet been attained but is being cultivated as it becomes present,
while the mindfulness of body has not yet been attained and is becoming present.
As previously stated regarding those who have not yet attained the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) being present before them,
so too it is as previously stated regarding those who have not yet attained the applications of mindfulness to feeling (*vedanā*) and mind (*citta*) being present before them.

Regarding one who has not yet attained the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and is currently cultivating the application of mindfulness to feeling (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*):
this is as previously explained for those who have not yet attained the application of mindfulness to phenomena and are currently cultivating the other applications of mindfulness.
There are cases where neither is cultivated: namely, when the mindfulness of body and mind already attained is present;
when all defiled or neutral minds are present; and during the attainment of non-conceptualization, the attainment of cessation, or when born in the Heaven of No-Thought.
All are as explained previously.
It should be understood that this applies to the application of mindfulness of feelings and the application of mindfulness of phenomena;
the same holds true for the application of mindfulness of the mind and the application of mindfulness of phenomena.
Because the cultivation or non-cultivation of the future foundations of mindfulness of feeling and mind must necessarily occur together,
one should say that the application of mindfulness consisting of the contemplation of the body as a body is "dharma-knowledge," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Question: This text should have been explained after first discussing cultivation. Why is this?
Because cultivation is only possible once intrinsic nature exists; what, then, is the intention behind not explaining it first?
Answer: The Abhidharma should be sought by way of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), not by way of sequential order.

This is because the Abhidharma intends precisely to analyze the intrinsic natures and characteristics (*dharmasvabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, provided that it does not contradict their underlying meaning.
Whether they are explained first or later, there is no fault.
Other masters say that this is intended to show that,

among these, only the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) produced by cultivation (bhāvanā-maya) are meant, and not those produced by hearing (śruta-maya) or reflection (cintā-maya), and so forth.
First, the cultivation is explained, followed by the clarification of its intrinsic nature:
when one dwells contemplating the body as a body within the body,
it should be called "knowledge of phenomena" (dharmajñāna).
That is to say, knowledge of matter bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and a portion of untainted (*anāsrava*) matter should be called subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
This refers to knowledge of matter bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and a portion of untainted matter.
The "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*) is not mentioned here because the knowledge of others' minds knows [only] minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Because the mindfulness of the dharma-body knows only material phenomena (rūpa-dharma),
it should be said to be conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna);
that is, it knows all material phenomena.
It should be called the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*),
meaning that one knows conditioned form (*sāsrava-rūpa*) through the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
It should be called the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).
This means knowing the aspects of the causes, origins, arising, and conditions of contaminated form;
as for what is not called the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*),
the knowledge of cessation knows only unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
The foundation of mindfulness of the body is called the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) because it knows conditioned phenomena;
that is to say, it knows uncontaminated form as the path, characterized by the aspects of proceeding and emerging.

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are not mentioned here because these belong to the aggregate of views (*dṛṣṭiskandha*); only those types of knowledge that are of the nature of views are discussed.
Since that knowledge is not of the nature of a view, it is not mentioned.
Having already manifested its intrinsic nature,
the stages shall now be manifested;
it should be said that they possess vitarka and vicāra.
That is to say, based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and the first dhyāna,
it should be said that there is no vitarka and only vicāra;
this refers to the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
It should be said that they are without vitarka and without vicāra;
that is to say, based on the three higher dhyānas and the four formless attainments.
Having already explained the levels, the associated mental factors will now be explained.
It should be said that it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
namely when based on the third dhyāna;
it should be said that it is associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
This means that based on the first and second dhyānas,
it should be said to be associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).

This means that based on the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), the fourth dhyāna, and the four formless attainments (ārūpya), [it is associated with the faculty of equanimity].
Having already explained the associated [factors], one should now explain the aspects (ākāra).
It should be said that it is accompanied by the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi),
namely, two aspects.
It should be said that it is associated with the wishless concentration (*apranihita-samādhi*),
namely, the ten aspects (*ākāra*).
As for why it is not said to be associated with the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*), it is as when [the text] does not mention the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
Having explained the mode of activity,
one should now explain the object of focus;
it should be said that it takes as its object that which is bound to the desire realm and the form realm.
That is to say, taking suffering and its origin as objects;
it should be said that when taking the unconditioned as an object,
one dwells contemplating feelings in feelings while taking the Path as an object.
It should be called "dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna*),
meaning that it knows the [suffering] associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and a portion of the untainted (*anāsrava*) feeling.
It should be called "subsequent knowledge" (*anvayajñāna*).
That is to say, knowing the feeling associated with the form and formless realms, as well as a portion of the untainted (anāsrava) feeling,
should be called the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
That is to say, knowing the feeling currently manifesting in the mental continua of others that is associated with the desire and form realms, as well as a portion of the untainted feeling.
It should be said that this is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*),
namely, the knowledge of all feelings;
it should also be said that this is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*).
This means that knowing tainted feeling (sāsrava-vedanā) through the four aspects such as impermanence (anitya) is called the knowledge of suffering;
knowing it through the four aspects such as cause (hetu) is called the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna).
The knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) is not mentioned here.
Because the application of mindfulness to feeling knows only conditioned phenomena,
it should be called the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*);
that is to say, it knows untainted feeling through the four aspects of the path and so forth.
Regarding "not teaching other knowledges," it is explained as before.
Having thus clarified its intrinsic nature, [the text continues:]
The aspects of the practice corresponding to the stages are all as previously explained.
Now the objects of focus shall be clarified:
it should be said that they take the factors bound to the three realms as their objects.
That is to say, when taking suffering and its origin as objects,
it should be said that they take what is unconditioned as their object; when taking the path as an object, it is likewise so.
As it is with regard to feeling, so it is with regard to the mind,
for these two are always associated in their objects.
One dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena.
It should be called "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna),

meaning the knowledge of all factors belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge regarding the formations bound to the desire realm, as well as their causes, their cessation, and the path leading to that cessation.
It should also be called "subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna).
That is to say, knowing the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) pertaining to the form and formless realms, as well as their causes, their cessation, and all categories of knowledge regarding them,
should be called the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). That is to say,
knowing those [phenomena] pertaining to the desire and form realms, as well as a portion of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) [phenomena], as they manifest within the mental continuums of others.
Excluding feeling and mind, the remaining mental factors should be said to be conventional knowledge;
that is to say, knowing all phenomena.
It should be called the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*),
meaning that one knows the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*) through the four aspects (*ākāra*) such as impermanence (*anitya*).
It should be called the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).
That is to say, knowing the outflowing causes through the four aspects of "cause" and so forth should be called the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
That is to say, knowing the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) through the four aspects of "cessation" and so forth.
One should speak of "knowledge of the path" (mārgajñāna),
which refers to knowing the five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha) through the four aspects of being the path and so forth.
As for the other types of knowledge not mentioned here, they are also explained as previously stated.
Having already manifested the intrinsic nature,
the correspondence with the stages is as previously explained;
now the modes of activity shall be manifested.
It should be said that [the mind] is also associated with the samādhis of emptiness and wishlessness, as explained previously;
it should be said that it is associated with the samādhi of signlessness,
namely, by way of its four aspects.
Having explained the mode of activity,
one should now explain the object of focus;
it should be said that it takes as its object that which is bound to the three realms.
That is to say, taking suffering and its origin as objects,
one should say they take what is unconditioned as their object;
that is to say, taking cessation and the path as objects.
As it is said: "When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is: 'I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.
These are the four knowledges.
...and so on, as explained at length.

Question: Why is it that within this [section], the applications of mindfulness regarding feelings, mind, and phenomena (*vedanā-citta-dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) are analyzed twice, whereas the application of mindfulness regarding the body (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*) is analyzed only once?
The answer is: because that is the intention of the author of the treatise, and so forth, as explained at length. Some say:
In this regard, the Blessed One should also have stated:
"When walking, standing, and so forth, he knows as it truly is: 'I am walking,' 'I am standing,' and so forth. These four knowledges [are to be understood], and so on, as explained at length.
What is the intention behind not explaining [this]?

The answer is: if a phenomenon is subtle, difficult to see, difficult to realize, unclear, and not directly perceived, then one extensively analyzes the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), which is coarse and manifest.
It is not repeated because it is already clearly evident. Some say:
"If various dissimilar and distinct phrases arise based upon that [basis], [they are considered different]."
Furthermore, for one who possesses wisdom regarding distinct characteristics, they then further analyze the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Since when analyzing [it], the phrasing does not differ and the wisdom does not differ, it is not stated again.
Question: When one experiences a pleasant feeling, one does not know it as it truly is;
when one knows it as it truly is, one does not experience the pleasant feeling. Why is this so?
When experiencing a pleasant feeling, that feeling exists in the present, yet at that time one is unable to know it as it truly is;
this is because it is not associated with [the knowledge of] non-cognition, and because two mental states do not function simultaneously.
When one knows them as they truly are, those feelings exist in the past or the future;
at that time, they are not called "feeling" because they lack functional activity (*kāritra*).
The same applies to the explanations regarding painful feelings and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
For what reason did the Buddha say, "When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is: 'I am experiencing a pleasant feeling,'" and so forth?
Some say that this should be explained in this way:

Having experienced a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is: "I have experienced a pleasant feeling"; having experienced a painful feeling or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is: "I have experienced a painful feeling or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
What is the intention behind not making such a statement?

It should be understood that here, the term "feeling" (*vedita*) refers to what has already been felt; it uses a past designation for the present, just as one says, "From which direction does Your Majesty come?
when referring to someone who is currently arriving.
Since this has been stated, it is called "coming.

Furthermore, as it is said that when a bodhisattva enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma), they attain the conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (abhisamaya-antika-saṃvṛti-jñāna), so too is it said that they have "entered" therein. It is the same in this case.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"Feelings that exist in the past or the future cannot be felt;
even when they exist in the present, they cannot be felt as they merely proceed by way of their own intrinsic nature."
How is it that one speaks of experiencing pleasure or experiencing pain?
It should be understood that this is said in reference to the continuity of the conditions for pleasure and pain;
that is, observing the continuity of the conditions for pleasure, one says, "I experience pleasure."
Observing the continuity of the conditions for suffering, one says, "I experience suffering.
Furthermore, observing the continuity of the causes and conditions for pleasure and suffering, one speaks thus:
that is, observing the continuity of the causes and conditions for appropriation, one says, "I experience pleasure."
Observing the continuity of the causes and conditions of harm, one says, "I am experiencing suffering.
Furthermore, while those sensations continue to arise in succession, the mental consciousness directed toward those objects repeatedly arises in the interim.
One might think that because this [feeling] benefits or harms its basis, one says, "I now experience pleasure" or "I now experience pain.
The Venerable One said:

Because one refers to the transformation within the continuity of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as the basis for pleasant and painful feelings as "feeling," one says, "I now experience pleasure" or "I now experience pain."
As it is said: "When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is: 'I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.
These four knowledges consist of the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and path knowledge (mārga-jñāna).
Question: Why is the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna) not mentioned here?
Answer: The knowledge of others' minds knows the mental states and mental factors within the continuums of others.
Since the knowledge of reality as it is (yathābhūta-jñāna) knows the mental states and mental factors within one's own continuum, it is not mentioned here.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds knows present minds and mental factors;
herein, the knowledge of reality as it is knows past minds and mental factors.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds knows only minds and mental factors.
In this context, the knowledge of things as they truly are (yathābhūta-jñāna) also cognizes the bases and objects of the mind and mental factors.

Furthermore, while the knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna) takes each individual phenomenon as its object, the knowledge of things as they truly are takes many phenomena collectively as its object; for this reason, the knowledge of others' minds is not mentioned here.
Question: For what reason, moreover, are the knowledges of suffering and its origin not mentioned here?
Some say: although the knowledges of suffering and its origin should also have been mentioned here, their omission indicates that this explanation is incomplete.
Some say that the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of its origin are knowledges characterized by the aspect of revulsion;
