the knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) among these is not mentioned here because it is characterized by the aspect of aspiration.
Some say that the knowledge of suffering and its origin takes as its object things to be loathed,
whereas the knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) therein takes as its object things to be delighted in.
Some say that the knowledge of suffering and its origin proceeds by way of aversion toward its object, whereas in this context,
the knowledge of reality proceeds by way of delighting in its object.
Some say: "In this context, it is taught that one knows as they truly are the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
However, contaminated minds and mental factors have been known repeatedly since beginningless time."

Furthermore, because coarse and proximate objects are easily understood, one can comprehend them by giving rise to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) without depending on the arising of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

Therefore, there is no case where one abandons conventional knowledge and instead knows those objects through the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) or the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).
The untainted (anāsrava) mind and mental factors have been unknown from time immemorial;
furthermore, because they are subtle and difficult to discern, it is only by giving rise to untainted wisdom that one can know them.
Therefore, herein one knows the tainted (sāsrava) mind and mental factors as they truly are.
Only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) knows the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind and mental factors as they truly are;
that is to say, because the other three knowledges do not [know them], it is not said that there are knowledges of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) or origin (*samudaya-jñāna*). Some say:

In this context, it is explained that one knows, as they truly are, the distinct characteristics of the phenomena of contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors. Regarding those contaminated [phenomena], when conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) arises, one knows them;
however, the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) and the knowledge of its origin (*samudayajñāna*) do not arise [simultaneously], because they are difficult to arouse.

Furthermore, because at the time of its arising one knows only the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), that uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [wisdom] cannot know [the conventional]; thus, conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) arises.
However, although the path-wisdom (*mārga-jñāna*) arises, it does not—unlike the former case—consist of knowing only the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*).
However, because one knows specific phenomena through general characteristics, there is knowledge of the path but no knowledge of suffering or its origin.
Some say that this is what is being stated here.
One knows, as they truly are, the distinctions between the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
However, most tainted minds and mental factors do not have the noble truths as their objects of cognition (*ālambana*).
Even if such things exist, they have not yet been perfectly accomplished;
therefore, by means of conventional knowledge, one forms a non-ultimate mode of activity and knows the distinctions between those modes of activity as they truly are.
Because all untainted minds and mental factors are perfectly accomplished in their aspect of taking the Truths as objects,
they further employ the knowledge of the path to take the Truths as objects and know, in accordance with reality, the distinctions among those aspects.
Therefore, within this [aggregate], there is no knowledge of suffering or its origin, nor is the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising mentioned.
This is because it is the aggregate of views (*dṛṣṭi-skandha*), which speaks only of those knowledges whose nature is that of views;
since those [other knowledges] do not have the nature of views, they are not mentioned.
In this context, "knowledge of phenomena" (dharmajñāna) refers to knowing the category of pleasant feeling; "subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna) refers to [knowing] that same category.
This refers to conventional knowledge that knows the category of pleasant feeling within the class of subsequent knowledge;
it refers to knowing tainted pleasant feeling.
Regarding the knowledge of the path:
this refers to knowing untainted pleasant feeling.
Although there is not a single pleasant feeling that is known by all four knowledges.
That is to say, that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is known by one wisdom,
while that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is known by three wisdoms.
However, because it is stated in general terms, it is said that the four wisdoms know pleasant feeling as it truly is.
Some say that untainted pleasant feeling is known by four knowledges; when experiencing a painful feeling,
knowing it as it truly is— that one knows "this is a painful feeling"— is known by a single knowledge, namely, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Because painful feeling is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is known by conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
When experiencing neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one knows "I am experiencing neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling" as it truly is.
These four knowledges are the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
As it was explained regarding the knowledge of pleasant feeling,
so it is stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda, Volume 189.

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section Eight: The Aggregate of Views (*Dṛṣṭiskandha*). First Sub-section: The Application of Mindfulness (*Smṛtyupasthāna*). Part Four: The experience of pleasant bodily sensation, painful bodily sensation, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant bodily sensation.
Furthermore, when experiencing a painful mental feeling, one knows it as it truly is.
This is one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), because all bodily feelings and painful mental feelings are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
When conventional knowledge arises, one knows as it truly is the experience of a pleasant mental feeling and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant mental feeling; these constitute four types of knowledge.

This refers to the Dharma-knowledge, the Subsequent-knowledge, and the conventional knowledge; these two types of mental feeling (citta-vedanā) pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
They are known through the four knowledges, as explained in detail above.
Question: Among these, what is called bodily feeling (*kāya-vedanā*) and what is called mental feeling?
Answer: If feeling occurs within the five bodies of consciousness, it is called bodily feeling;
if it occurs in the sphere of the mind, it is called mental feeling.
Furthermore, if feeling is non-conceptual, it is called bodily feeling.
That which is accompanied by conceptual discrimination is called mental feeling (*caitasika-vedanā*).
Furthermore, if a feeling apprehends an object characterized by its specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is called bodily feeling (*kāyikī vedanā*);

if it apprehends an object characterized by its general commonality (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it is called mental feeling. Furthermore, if a feeling apprehends a present object, it is called bodily feeling.
Taking as its object the three times and that which is non-temporal is called mental feeling (*cittavedanā*).
Furthermore, if feeling takes a distinct object as its referent, it is called bodily feeling (*kāyavedanā*);
taking both a distinct referent and a composite object is called mental feeling.
Furthermore, if one experiences an object that causes a single lapse, it is called bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*);
if one repeatedly lapses regarding an object, it is called mental sensation (*caitasikī vedanā*).
Furthermore, if a sensation arises suddenly toward an object, it is called bodily sensation.
That which involves conceptualization and deliberation is called mental feeling (*cittavedanā*).
Furthermore, if a feeling has matter as its basis (*āśraya*) and matter as its object (*ālambana*), it is called bodily feeling (*kāyikavedanā*);
if it has non-matter as its basis and both matter and non-matter as its object, it is called mental feeling.
As it is with "form" and "non-form," so too for "resistant" and "non-resistant," "accumulated" and "non-accumulated," "conjoined" and "non-conjoined"— the detailed exposition is likewise.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
As the Buddha has taught,
at that time one experiences two types of feeling:
namely, bodily feeling and mental feeling.
What is bodily feeling?
What is mental feeling?
Answer: There is no feeling that is bodily feeling; all feelings are exclusively mental feelings.
Why is this? Because they are associated with the mind.
However, when various feelings arise in dependence upon the five sense faculties, these feelings are called "bodily feelings" (kāyikī vedanā).
Because it always has the body as its predominant condition,
when this feeling arises based on the mental faculty (manas), it is called "mental feeling" (caitasikī vedanā),
because it always has the mind as its predominant condition.
Furthermore, it is said:
there is no feeling that is bodily feeling;
all feelings are mental feelings, because they are associated with the mind.

However, those sensations that arise based on the three faculties [of eye, ear, and body] which grasp their objects through direct contact are called "bodily sensations" (*kāyikī-vedanā*), because they constantly produce perception.

Those sensations that arise based on the three faculties [of nose, tongue, and mind] which grasp their objects without direct contact are called "mental sensations" (*caitasikī-vedanā*), because they do not constantly produce perception.
The Venerable said:
"If it is experienced by the body, is it also experienced by the mind?
He replied: "If it is experienced by the body, it is also experienced by the mind."
There is mental feeling that is not bodily feeling;
this refers to when one conceptualizes external objects, grasps signs internally, and grasps persons (*pudgala*) as well as the matter included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
The characteristics of formations dissociated from mind and of the unconditioned—
sensations of this kind are all termed "mental sensations," because they arise through conceptualization directed toward objects that do not truly exist.
This is called the distinction between bodily feeling and mental feeling.
Feeling pleasure is a feeling associated with attachment;
feeling pain is a feeling associated with attachment.
When one knows, as it truly is, the pleasant-feeling sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant,
as well as the unpleasant-feeling sensation that lacks such flavor,
this constitutes one type of knowledge.
This refers to the conventional [truth].
Because all pleasant feelings and all unpleasant feelings associated with suffering are tainted (*sāsrava*),
when one gives rise to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), one knows them as they truly are.
When experiencing a pleasant feeling as being without savor, or an unpleasant or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as being without savor, one knows it as it truly is.

These four knowledges—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)—are employed;
for these two types of unsavored feelings pertain to both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava), and are therefore known by means of these four knowledges.
The detailed explanation is as above.
In this context, "taste" (*āsvāda*) refers to the nature of craving and attachment;
if feeling serves as the basis for that [craving], it is called "feeling with taste" (*sāsvāda-vedanā*).
Some say that "savor" (āsvāda) refers to the nature of attachment inherent in all afflictions;
if feeling serves as a basis for that [attachment], it is called "feeling with savor" (sāsvāda-vedanā).
If feeling that does not provide a basis for craving or any other afflictions is called "flavorless feeling," then one might ask:
if that were so, would it not follow that all painful feelings are "flavored"?
Because they all serve as a basis for craving or for all afflictions.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"What are the phenomena associated with relish (*sāsvāda*)?"
That is to say, they are contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*). What are phenomena without flavor? They are uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*).
Why, then, is it said here that there is a feeling of suffering that is without flavor?

Answer: Although painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*) is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), it possesses a small degree of the nature of being "without flavor" (*arasa*). Because it relies upon that [nature], it is said that painful feeling is without flavor.
This is because it has a nature that is contrary to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and is unmixed with the afflictions.
Other masters say:

although all painful feelings (duḥkhā vedanā) are with-outflows (sāsrava), there are those capable of inducing and conforming to the outflow-free (anāsrava) feeling that is flavorless (arasa) in the ultimate sense;
it is in reference to these that it is said that painful feeling is flavorless.
Because they can temporarily suppress all flavors,
they serve as the basis for indulgence in the experience of pleasure and the basis for indulgence in the experience of suffering.
One knows feelings as they truly are: feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant and based on attachment, and feelings that are painful and based on renunciation.
This one wisdom is called conventional (saṃvṛti),
because all feelings based on worldly attachment,
as well as feelings based on the transcendence of suffering, are with outflows (sāsrava).

When conventional knowledge arises, one knows, in accordance with reality, the basis for the renunciation of pleasant feeling, the basis for the renunciation of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and the experience of those feelings; thus one knows these four knowledges as they truly are.
The Dharma-knowledge, Subsequent-knowledge, and conventional knowledge are as explained previously.
In this context, "attachment" (*gardha*) refers to the nature of craving and clinging;
if feeling serves as the basis for that attachment, it is called "feeling that is the support of attachment."
Some say that "addiction" (gardha) refers to the nature of attachment inherent in all afflictions;
if feeling serves as the basis for that [attachment], it is called "feeling that is the basis for addiction."
Painful feeling that does not serve as a basis for craving or any other afflictions is called "feeling based on renunciation.
Question: If that is so, then all painful feelings should be termed "feelings based on worldly attachment" (*gardhāśrita*).
Because they all serve as a basis for craving or for all afflictions.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"What is the dharma based on which there is indulgence? It refers to contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas."
What is the basis for renunciation? It refers to untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
Why, then, is it said here that there is a basis for renunciation from suffering within the category of feeling (*vedanā*)?
The answer is: although painful feeling is tainted (*sāsrava*), it possesses a slight degree of the nature of being a basis for renunciation.
Based on that, it is said that the departure from suffering relies upon feeling (*vedanā*);
that is to say, it possesses a nature that is contrary to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and unmixed with the afflictions.
Other masters state:

Although all painful feelings (*duḥkhā vedanā*) are with-outflows (*sāsrava*), there are those that can induce and accord with the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) feeling that serves as the basis for transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*) in the ultimate sense.
It is in dependence upon these that painful feelings are said to be the basis for transcendence, because they are able to temporarily suppress all forms of craving (*pariṣkāra-tṛṣṇā*).
As it is said: "One knows a mind with greed as a mind with greed," and so forth in detail;
this is because there are two meanings.
The mind is called "possessing greed" (sarāga) because it is associated with greed and because it is bound by greed. Some say:
In this context, the treatise is composed based on "attachment through association.
Some say that in this context,
the treatise is composed based on two kinds of attachment.
Why is this? If one were to formulate the treatise based solely on the presence of greed through association,
then even tainted wholesome states and non-obscured neutral states of mind would have to be called "minds free from greed."
However, that too is a mind "possessing greed" because it is bound by greed;
one should know that minds possessing hatred and so forth are likewise.
In this context, it is called a "mind possessing greed" because it is bound by greed.
It is well said that it is called "a mind free from greed" because it is the antidote to greed; conversely,
it is called "a mind possessed by greed" because it is bound by greed.
It is called a "mind free from greed" because it is the antidote to greed.
If one were to say that it is called a "mind with greed" because it is associated with greed,
and a "mind free from greed" because it is dissociated from greed, then other minds associated with afflictions that are dissociated from greed would also have to be called "minds free from greed."
Nevertheless, that mind is also "possessing greed" because it is bound by greed.
If one says that a mind is "possessing greed" because it is associated with greed, and "free from greed" because it is the antidote to greed; [then...]
In that case, the defiled mind dissociated from greed and one portion of the non-obscured neutral and wholesome minds would neither be "minds with greed" nor "minds free from greed.
However, those too are "minds with greed," because they are bound by greed.
One knows a mind with greed as it truly is: a mind with greed.
This is one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
One knows a mind free from greed as it truly is: a mind free from greed.

These four knowledges—the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the path knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*)—are all explained as previously stated.
Because it is bound by hatred, it is called a "mind with hatred";
because it is the antidote to hatred, it is called a "mind free from hatred," as explained at length regarding greed.
When there is a mind of hatred, one knows "there is a mind of hatred" as it truly is.
This is one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge, as explained previously.
When there is a mind free from hatred, one knows "there is a mind free from hatred" as it truly is.
These three knowledges refer to the dharma-knowledge and the conventional knowledge.
Within this context, because the explanation is based on the immediate antidote (*pratipakṣa*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is not mentioned;
this is because the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge is not the immediate antidote for the desire realm. The remainder is explained as previously stated.
It is called "a mind with delusion" because it is bound by delusion;
it is called "a mind free from delusion" because it is the antidote to delusion.
This explanation is excellent.
This means that it is called "a mind with delusion" because it is bound by delusion;
it is called "a mind free from delusion" because it is the antidote to delusion.
Alternatively, if one says it is called "a mind with delusion" because it is associated with delusion.
If it were called "a mind free from delusion" simply because it is dissociated from delusion,
then a portion of the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) and wholesome (*kuśala*) minds would also have to be called "minds free from delusion."
However, that [mind] is also called "a mind with delusion" because it is bound by delusion.
If one says it is called "a mind with delusion" because it is associated with delusion,
and "a mind free from delusion" because it is the antidote to delusion— then [the same logic applies].
Then, a portion of non-obscured neutral minds and wholesome minds would neither be "minds with delusion" nor "minds free from delusion.
However, they too are "minds with delusion" because they are bound by delusion.
When there is a mind with delusion, one knows as it truly is that there is a mind with delusion;
this is one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
When there is a mind free from delusion, one knows as it truly is that there is a mind free from delusion.
These four knowledges—the dharma, subsequent, conventional, and path—are explained as previously stated.
"Defiled mind" refers to a defiled state of consciousness because it is associated with afflictions;
"non-defiled mind" refers to a wholesome state of consciousness because it is contrary to afflictions.
Some say that both wholesome minds and non-obscured neutral minds are called "non-defiled minds" because they are dissociated from afflictions.
To know a defiled mind as a defiled mind— this one type of knowledge is called conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
One knows an unstained mind as it truly is: an unstained mind.

These four knowledges—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the path knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*)—are to be explained as previously done for the minds with delusion and free from delusion.
Regarding the "contracted mind":
This means that a wholesome mind is "withdrawn" because it briefly collects [its objects], whereas a distracted mind is so called because it scatters toward its objects due to being afflicted.
One knows a withdrawn mind as it truly is: "the mind is withdrawn."

These four knowledges refer to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of subsequent categories (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
When one knows a distracted mind as it truly is—a distracted mind—this is one knowledge, namely conventional knowledge.
This should be explained accordingly, as previously set forth.
The masters outside of Kaśmīra say:
"A contracted mind" refers to a mind associated with sleep (*middha*), because the term "contraction of the mind" is used as a designation for sleep.
As it is said: "What is sleep?"
It refers to the nature of sleepiness, characterized by the inability of one who is sleeping to maintain the body and mind, and by mental contraction.
Question: If that is so, how can what is stated here be reconciled?
As it is said: "One knows the contracted mind as it truly is as a contracted mind"—these are the four knowledges.
This should be explained in detail up to that point.
To this, the answer should be stated as follows:

One knows the concentrated mind, the distracted mind, and the inferior mind as they truly are; this knowledge of the concentrated, distracted, and inferior minds is called conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
One knows the uplifted mind as it truly is; these four knowledges are as previously explained.
The critique states:
He should not make such a statement;
for if he were to do so, then a defiled mind associated with torpor would also have to be called a "contracted mind," because it is associated with torpor.
It is also called a "distracted mind" because it is afflicted.
By this, one should know that the previous explanation is correct.
A "depressed mind" refers to an afflicted mind because it is associated with laziness.
"Uplifted mind" refers to a wholesome mind associated with diligence.
"Dull mind" is known as it truly is; this one knowledge is conventional (saṃvṛti).
"Uplifted mind" is known as it truly is; these four knowledges—namely, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge—are explained as before.
The "small mind" refers to the defiled mind, because it is practiced by those of inferior birth.
The "great mind" refers to the virtuous mind, because it is practiced by those of superior birth.
Question: We now clearly see immeasurable sentient beings committing evil deeds.
Question: Few sentient beings practice virtue;
why then is it said that the defiled mind is practiced by "few"?
Answer: In this context, "few" does not refer to the smallness of their number.
It is called "small" merely because it consists of a small amount of pure dharmas;

that is to say, the mental state practiced by one in whom a small amount of pure dharmas has arisen is called a "small mind," whereas the mental state practiced by one in whom a great amount of pure dharmas has arisen is called a "great mind."
Therefore, throughout the ocean of birth and death, only the Buddha is called "Great" because he has cultivated wholesome dharmas to the utmost,
unlike all other sentient beings. Some say:
The defiled mind is called "small" because it is acquired at a low price;
the wholesome mind is called "great" because it is acquired at a high price.
This is because a defiled mind gives rise to immeasurable improper mental attentions (ayoniśomanasikāra) for the sake of even a minor cause.
It causes afflictions and unwholesome conduct to arise like a flowing river;
wholesome states of mind do not do so.
Even when one gives away hundreds of thousands of precious treasures, some [afflictions] may still arise while others may not.
Some say that because a defiled mind possesses few faculties,
it is called "small," whereas because a wholesome mind possesses many faculties, it is called "great."
That is to say, whether it be a defiled mind— possessing either one or two faculties— or a wholesome mind,
all are fully endowed with three faculties. Some say:
The defiled mind is called "small" because it has few concomitants;
the wholesome mind is called "great" because it has many concomitants.
That is to say, the defiled mind is accompanied by only three aggregates.
A wholesome mind is accompanied by either three or four aggregates as its concomitants.
Some say that a defiled mind is called "small" because it has few attendants.
A virtuous mind is called "great" because it has many attendants;
that is to say, while defiled minds lack cultivation in the future,
virtuous minds possess cultivation in the future.
Some say that the defiled mind is called "small" because its antidotes are few,
while the wholesome mind is called "great" because its antidotes are many.
For example, when the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises in a single moment,
it can suddenly and permanently sever the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
This single power is superior to all of them, just as a single strong man can subdue a thousand men.
Yet no single moment of defiled mind possesses such power.
Furthermore, within a defiled mind, its primary leaders lack eyes and feet;
that which serves as the leader therein is ignorance (*avidyā*).

As it is said: because ignorance is the foremost and the primary cause, immeasurable kinds of evil and unwholesome dharmas arise, as well as their various types such as shamelessness and lack of dread.
Within the wholesome mind, that which serves as the foremost and possesses both eyes and feet is precisely clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
Just as clarity is the foremost and primary cause for the arising of immeasurable kinds of wholesome dharmas and their corresponding types of shame and remorse;
furthermore, regarding the unwholesome dharmas practiced since beginningless time.
Practicing virtue for a brief moment causes [afflictions] to be severed forever;
it is just as when a room has been filled with darkness for a long time—
a lamp’s light illuminates it for a moment, and the darkness is immediately dispelled.
Just as when one has long practiced the perception of saltlessness, that perception is immediately abandoned upon tasting salt even for a moment,
so it is here; however, there is no such thing regarding the severance of the wholesome by means of the unwholesome.
Furthermore, the wholesome can ultimately subdue or ultimately sever the unwholesome,
whereas the unwholesome cannot do so for the wholesome.
Due to these conditions, a defiled mind is called "small" and a virtuous mind is called "great.
To know a small mind as it truly is a small mind is one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

To know a great mind as it truly is a great mind involves four types of knowledge—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)—all of which are explained as before.
A "distracted mind" refers to a defiled mind because it is associated with restlessness (*auddhatya*).
A "non-distracted mind" refers to a wholesome mind because it is associated with calm abiding (*śamatha*).
One knows a distracted mind as a distracted mind, according to reality.
This one wisdom is called conventional (saṃvṛti).

Knowing an unperturbed mind as it truly is—that an unperturbed mind is unperturbed—these four wisdoms are the dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), and conventional knowledge; all are explained as before.
The non-quiescent mind refers to the defiled mind because it is constantly agitated;
the quiescent mind refers to the virtuous mind because it turns away from agitation.
To know an unpacified mind as it truly is—an unpacified mind—is one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
To know a pacified mind as it truly is—a pacified mind—constitutes four types of knowledge:
dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge, and path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*). All these are explained as before.
The unconcentrated mind refers to an afflicted mind because it is associated with distraction.
The concentrated mind refers to a wholesome mind because it turns away from distraction.
To know an unconcentrated mind as it truly is—an unconcentrated mind—this is one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

To know a concentrated mind as it truly is—a concentrated mind—these are four types of knowledge, namely the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); all are explained as before.
One who does not cultivate the mind refers to one who cultivates neither the cultivation of acquisition nor the cultivation of practice regarding the mind.
One who cultivates the mind refers to one who cultivates either the cultivation of acquisition, the cultivation of practice, both, or at least one of these two regarding the mind.
To know the uncultivated mind as it truly is—that is one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

To know the cultivated mind as it truly is—that is four types of knowledge, namely the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge, and path knowledge (*mārgajñāna*). All these are explained as previously stated.
The "unliberated mind" refers to a mind that is neither liberated by nature (*svabhāva-vimukta*) nor liberated through continuity (*saṃtāna-vimukta*).
The "liberated mind" refers to a mind that is both liberated by nature and liberated through continuity.

Whether both [minds] are liberated or only one is liberated, he knows the unliberated mind as it truly is—an unliberated mind. This is one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

He knows the liberated mind as it truly is—a liberated mind. These are four types of knowledge, namely dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and conventional knowledge; all are explained as previously stated.
As it is said: "There is the internal hindrance of sensual desire," and so forth, at length.
Within this sacred teaching, the "internal" is of two kinds.
It is called "internal" because it is comprised within the internal bases (*āyatana*).
As it is said: "These six internal bases," and so forth, as explained at length.
Second, it is called "internal" because it is comprised within one's own continuum (*saṃtāna*).
As it is said: "One contemplates the body in the internal body," and so forth, as explained at length.
In this context, the discussion is based on the internal continuum and not on the internal location.
Why is that? Because if the discussion were based on the internal location, [it would be as follows].
In that case, one should not say that there is an internal hindrance such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*),
because hindrances like sensual desire are all subsumed under the external sense-bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
Nevertheless, although they are external bases, they are designated as "internal" because they are comprised within one's own continuum (*svasaṃtāna*).
As it is said, when there is the internal hindrance of sensual desire,
one knows as it truly is that there is the internal hindrance of sensual desire;
this single knowledge is called conventional (saṃvṛti).
In this context, "existence" refers to the manifestation of the hindrance of sensual desire within one's own continuum;
or it refers to its acquisition and possession by one who has not yet abandoned it;
or it refers to the fact that the path which serves as its antidote has not yet arisen.
This wise person, by means of mundane knowledge arising from the presence of outflows,
knows as it truly is that there is no internal hindrance of sensual desire;
he knows as it truly is that there is no internal hindrance of sensual desire.
These three knowledges refer to the mundane path of the Dharma.
"Non-existent" herein means that within one's own continuum, the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) is not found as an active manifestation;
or, having already abandoned it, its attainment has been realized.
Alternatively, the path that serves as their antidote has already arisen;
these three knowledges refer to the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), which belongs exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Therefore, its immediate antidote does not belong to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
When the internal hindrance of sensual desire has not yet arisen but does arise, one knows this as it truly is;
this single knowledge is called conventional (saṃvṛti).
In this context, "that which has not arisen but arises" refers to the following:
That is to say, through this or that cause and this or that condition, the internal hindrance of sensual desire arises.
Regarding this, the wise person is as previously explained:
having arisen, it is immediately abandoned; once abandoned, it does not arise again.
To know these three knowledges as they truly are— namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*),
and the path (*mārga-jñāna*)— in this context, "having arisen,
it is then abandoned" means that once the counteractive path has arisen, the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) is abandoned.
"Having been severed, it does not arise again" means that it either never arises at all,
or it does not arise until its counteractive path has degenerated.
These three knowledges are explained as before.

It should be understood that the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), lethargy-and-drowsiness (*styāna-middha*), restlessness-and-regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are likewise [to be abandoned],
because they are all bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As it is said that there is an internal eye-fetter (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyojana*),
knowing as it truly is that there is an internal eye-fetter— this is one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Here, too, the discussion is made with reference to the internal continuum (*saṃtāna*).
It does not depend on the internal locus;
the detailed explanation is as previously stated.
Furthermore, "existence" refers to the fact that the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of eye-affliction (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyojana*) can be found within one's own continuum.
Or, they have not yet attained accomplishment because they have not abandoned those [defilements],
or because their counteractive path has not yet arisen;
this "one wise person" is explained as before.
One knows as it truly is the absence of internal eye-fetters when there is no internal eye-fetters.
These four knowledges consist of the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the path (mārga-jñāna).
Herein, "absence" refers to the fact that within one's own continuum, the eye-fetters are not found to be manifest.
Either one has already become detached from them and attained their accomplishment,
or the path that serves as their antidote has already arisen.
These four types of knowledge are so called because they internally perceive the fetters of desire and form-realm attachment.
That immediate antidote pertains to both the category of dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Just as one knows as it truly is when internal eye-fetters that have not yet arisen come to arise,
this single knowledge is called conventional (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Regarding that which has not yet arisen but does arise:
this refers to the arising of internal eye-fetters through various causes and various conditions.
This one wise person is explained as before.
Having arisen, it is immediately severed; having been severed, it does not arise again.

One knows these four knowledges as they truly are—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*).
Among these, "having arisen, it is immediately severed" means:
This refers to the fact that once the path of counteraction has arisen, the internal fetters of the eye are severed;
having been severed, they do not arise again,
meaning they either never arise at all or arise only until the end.
Or even until one has not yet abandoned that path of counteraction;
these four knowledges are as explained previously.
As it is with the fetter of the eye, so should the fetters of the ear, body, and mind be understood.
Because their respective direct antidotes (pratipakṣa) both pertain to the categories of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna),
and because the fetters of nose and tongue are explained as being like a lid,
as they are all exclusively bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
As it is said that there is the internal factor of enlightenment consisting of mindfulness,
one knows as it truly is that there is the internal factor of enlightenment consisting of mindfulness.
These four knowledges are the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
In this context, "possessing" means that the awakening factor of mindfulness is found to be manifest within one's own continuum;
or that it has already been attained and accomplished;
or that the obstacles which are its direct adversaries have already been abandoned.
Regarding these four knowledges,

some say that among them, the three knowledges— namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)— know the factor of enlightenment of true mindfulness.
The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness that is similar [to its mundane counterpart] is known by one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Some say that since this context refers exclusively to the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness that is ultimate (*tattvika*), it is therefore known by four types of knowledge.
That is to say, conventional knowledge does not know with clarity;
the knowledge of phenomena, the knowledge of types, and the knowledge of the path know with clarity.
One knows as it truly is that there is no factor of enlightenment consisting of mindfulness internally, and that there is no factor of enlightenment consisting of mindfulness internally.
This single wisdom is called conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
"Non-existent therein" means that within one's own continuum, the factors of enlightenment such as mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) are not found to be manifest,
or that they have not yet been attained or accomplished.
Alternatively, because the obstacles to be countered have not yet been severed,
the first type of wisdom is as previously described;
it is like the awakening factor of mindfulness arising when it has not yet arisen.
Having arisen, they abide without being forgotten, leading to their fulfillment, increase, expansion, and realization through wisdom.

These four types of wisdom are the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
Among these, that which has not yet arisen but does arise refers to the internal awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) arising through various causes and various conditions.
Regarding the phrase "having arisen, it abides and is not forgotten," etc.: A question is raised as follows— since there is as much arising as there is ceasing,
and because [a phenomenon] certainly does not abide after a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), how can it be said that "having arisen, it abides and is not forgotten," and so forth?
Answer: Herein, two kinds of wholesome roots are taught, namely, those conducive to maintenance (*sthity-anugata*) and those conducive to progress (*viśeṣa-anugata*).
That which, having arisen, remains without being forgotten is said to be the wholesome root conducive to maintenance.
The roots of goodness conducive to the stage of progress (*viśeṣabhāgīya*) are those which, once arisen, cause [the factors] to become perfected, increased, and expanded.
The four knowledges are as explained previously.

Just as it should be understood for the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*), so it is for the awakening factors of discrimination of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
Because they belong to the same category.
Question: Since the factors of enlightenment such as joy (*prīti*) are sensations (*vedanā*), they have already been examined within the previous mindfulness of sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Why is he now observing again?
Answer: Previously, he observed by means of the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*);
now, he observes by means of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Furthermore, previously one observed alone;
now one observes together with the other factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Furthermore, previously one observed their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Now one observes their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, previously one observed the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);
now one observes the uncontaminated.
Some say that within this [context], both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are observed,
because it universally observes both the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) that are ultimate reality and those that are merely similar to them.
As it is said: "One observes, as they truly are, the increase of one's own greed, hatred, and delusion," and so forth, at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the Buddha’s sūtras.
As it is said in a sutra:
"When bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others observe that their own greed is increasing," and so forth.
One should understand that when the Buddha speaks of "retrogression" regarding various wholesome dharmas, the same applies to retrogression from hatred and delusion.
Although the sūtra makes this statement, it does not provide a detailed analysis as to how greed increases,
up to and including how delusion increases.
That sūtra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Since that [sūtra] does not analyze certain matters, this treatise is now composed in order to provide such analysis.
How do greed, hatred, and delusion increase?
Answer: Because there are the fetters of inferior greed, hatred, and delusion, it is middling;
because there are middling [fetters], it is superior—this is what is meant by "increase."
Regarding this, some say that the treatise is composed based on what is observed in the world as an increase in greed, hatred, and delusion.
As for the increase of greed, it is like men who, while in their youth, give rise to the fetters of inferior greed.
In his youth, he gives rise to middling bonds of craving;
in his prime, he gives rise to superior bonds of craving;
and it is the same regarding his wife.
Regarding those in whom hatred increases: it is like men who engage in mutual strife;
when they have not yet uttered harsh words, a minor fetter of hatred arises;
when they do utter harsh words, a middling fetter of hatred arises.
One who harbors resentment and plots harm gives rise to the upper fetter of hatred (*dveṣa-saṃyojana*).
As for the increase of delusion (*moha*): it is like a man born into a non-Buddhist sect who, having not yet studied their scriptures and treatises, gives rise to the lower fetter of delusion.
If one studies but has not yet mastered its meaning, the fetter of delusion arises at a moderate level;
if one has attained ultimate and thorough mastery, the fetter of delusion arises at a superior level. Some say:
In this context, the discussion is conducted based on the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*).
That is to say, by observing the inferior grade of the fetters of greed (*rāga-paryavasthāna*), the middling grade is designated;
by observing the middling, the superior grade is designated.
The same applies to hatred and delusion.
Some say that this discussion is based on the occurrence of retrogression.
This means that one falls away from the middling [level] due to retreating from the inferior level of the fetters of greed;
one falls away from the superior [level] due to retreating from the middling.
The same applies to hatred and delusion.
As it is said: "One observes with equal contemplation the diminution of one's own greed, hatred, and delusion," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is this treatise further composed?
Answer: Because the analysis of desire refers to other meanings explained in the preceding sutra.
As it is said therein:
"When monks, nuns, and others observe for themselves that their greed is diminishing..."
One should understand that he does not regress from wholesome dharmas;
the Buddha stated that this applies equally to non-regression from hatred and delusion.
Although that sutra makes this statement, it does not provide a detailed analysis.
What is the diminution of greed, up to the diminution of delusion?
That sutra is the fundamental basis upon which this treatise relies.
Since it does not explain certain points, they shall now all be explained; for this reason, this treatise is composed.
How are greed, hatred, and delusion diminished?
Answer: Because the fetters of supreme greed, hatred, and delusion are absent, there is the middle;
because the middle is absent, there is the lower—this is called diminution.
Some say that this discourse is based on what is observed in the world regarding the diminution of greed, hatred, and delusion.
As for the diminution of greed, it is like [the case of] men.
In the stage of youth, one gives rise to the superior fetter of greed;
in the stage of middle age, one gives rise to the middling fetter of greed;
and in the stage of old age, one gives rise to the inferior fetter of greed.
It is the same regarding one's wife.
As for the reduction of anger: when men harbor mutual resentment and plot to harm one another, they give rise to the highest entanglement of anger;
when they engage in strife and dispatch messengers back and forth, they give rise to the middling entanglement of anger.
While in the midst of a quarrel, he gives rise to the lower fetter of malice.
As for those whose delusion has diminished,
they are like certain men who have joined a non-Buddhist sect and studied its scriptures and treatises.
When one has already attained thorough penetration, the superior fetter of delusion arises;
when the Buddha’s words abide within the mind, the middling fetter of delusion arises;
and when one develops even a slight degree of faith in the Buddha’s words, the inferior fetter of delusion arises.
Some say that this discussion is based on the principle of relative dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*); that is,
it is by observing the superior degree of the entanglement of greed (*rāga-paryavasthāna*) that the middling degree is established.
Because they are observed within [the mind], the designation "inferior" is applied;
the same applies to hatred and delusion. Some say:
In this context, the treatise is composed based on the abandonment of defilements: [feeling] is "middling" because the intense fetters of greed have diminished;
it is "inferior" because the middling [fetters] have diminished.
What is feeling at the limit of death?
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It was for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the sūtras.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Ānanda, you should know that in the past there was a wheel-turning monarch named Sudarśana,
who experienced such a death-bound state."
It is just as when a strong man eats much fine food and momentarily becomes dazed and faint.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"I have now given rise to intense, harmful sensations at the limit of death."
Although the sūtra states this, it does not analyze it:
what is "feeling at the limit of death," and up to what point should one say that it is feeling at the limit of death?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, this treatise is composed. Some say:
The reason for composing this treatise is to stop the world from giving rise to the perception and notion of the "limit of death" regarding what is not the limit of death,
as the world commonly says: [insert common worldly saying here].
"I have already experienced sensations pertaining to the limit of death.

Now I experience them, and in the future I shall experience them; yet regarding those sensations which do not pertain to the limit of death, I give rise to the perception that they pertain to the limit of death. Why is this so?"
If one experiences this feeling and passes away before long, it is called the "feeling at the limit of death.
What is the feeling at the limit of death?
The answer is: it is that by which the vital points (*marman*) are severed and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) ceases.
Question: For what reason is this feeling called "the limit of death"?
Answer: Because it leads one to the state that is the limit of death, it is called the feeling of the limit of death.
Question: If that is so, then the final feeling itself should be called the feeling of the limit of death.
One should not say that life ends because of the severance of these vital points (marman). Why is this?
Because even after the vital points have been severed, one may still live for a day or a night before finally passing away.

The answer is that the sensation experienced at the moment of the severance of the vital points (*marmaccheda*) is also called the "final sensation," because death will inevitably occur shortly after the severance of the vital points. Some say:
Within a single homogeneous class of beings (nikāya-sabhāga), there are two kinds of sensation (vedanā):
first, bodily sensation;
second, mental sensation.
The feeling associated with the destruction of the vital points (*marmaccheda*) is the final among bodily feelings;
the feeling associated with the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the final among mental feelings.
Up to what point should one say that these are the feelings at the limit of death?
Answer: Up to this point, the vital points (*marmans*) are severed and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) ceases.
Question: For what reason is this treatise further composed?
Answer: To explain the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the experience at the limit of death, as previously stated.
Since its status has not yet been clarified and one now wishes to clarify it, this treatise is composed.
Under which aggregate is the experience at the limit of death subsumed? Answer: It is subsumed under the aggregate of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
With how many consciousnesses is it associated?
Answer: With body-consciousness and mental-consciousness.
That is to say, when the *marmaccheda* (vital point) is first severed, it is associated with body-consciousness.
Finally, it is associated with the consciousness of the final moment of existence.
Question: How many primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are capable of severing the vital points (*marmans*)?
Answer: Three, namely earth, water, and wind.
Question: For what reason cannot the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*) sever the vital points (*marmāṇi*)?
Answer: Because it is not a field (*kṣetra*), nor is it a vessel (*bhājana*);
and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that while the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) capable of severing the vital points (*marmasthāna*) are intense, the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*) is not intense.
Others say:

If the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) were capable of destroying external objects such that they could serve as external calamities, they would likewise be capable of destroying internal objects and severing the vital points (*marmaccheda*). However, because the earth element cannot destroy external objects and cannot serve as an external calamity, it does not do so.
Furthermore, it cannot destroy the internal constituents nor sever the vital points (*marmāṇi*).
In this context, the severing of the vital points by the water element occurs within the internal body at the time of death.
The water element increases in intensity;
by this soaking, all the sinews are caused to rot.
Because the sinews rot, the joints and limbs fall apart.
Because the joints and limbs fall apart, one’s life does not last long.
Regarding the terminal destruction by the fire element:
at the time of death, the fire element within the internal body becomes excessively intense.
Because of this, he is scorched and oppressed, causing all his sinews to wither.
Because the sinews wither, his limbs and joints fall apart.
Because his limbs and joints fall apart, he does not long survive and meets his end.
Regarding the terminal destruction of the wind element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*):
it refers to the time when one is about to die, when the wind element within the internal body becomes excessively aggravated;
by this agitation, all the tendons are shattered.
Because the various tendons are shattered, the joints and limbs fall apart;
because the joints and limbs fall apart, one does not survive long and meets their end.
Furthermore, there are those who maintain that the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is what severs the vital points (*marmāṇi*).
He says this: at the time of death,
the earth element within the body increases and causes all the orifices to become obstructed.
Because the various orifices are blocked, the limbs and joints become detached.
Because the limbs and joints are detached, one does not live long and passes away.
Question: Where do the fatal moments (maranāntika-kṣaṇa) occur?
Answer: They exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), not in the form or formless realms.
Within the desire realm, beings in the hells do not have "fatal points" (*marman*) because they are constantly severed;
however, animals and hungry ghosts do possess fatal points.
Among humans, this occurs in the three continents but not in Uttarakuru;
likewise, the gods of the desire realm do not experience the cessation of the vital points (*marmaccheda*),
because they do not possess the karmic fruit of such affliction.
Question: Which types of persons (*pudgala*) possess the "vital points" (*marmaccheda*)?
Answer: Both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) possess them.
Among the noble ones, they are present in stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), arhats, and pratyekabuddhas.
Except for the Blessed One, who possesses no karma that causes affliction or disturbance,
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not undergo the severance of the vital points (*marman*);
their voices do not fail, and they do not pass away gradually.
Because the faculties of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, have been suddenly extinguished;
or because Arhats possess the "vital points" (marman) that can be severed,
whereas butchers and the like do not.
Because the severance of the vital points (*marmaccheda*) is the fruit of karma that causes affliction and disturbance,
those who possess such karma will experience the severance of their vital points even if they are Arhats;
whereas those who lack such karma will not experience the severance of their vital points, even if they are sheep-slaughterers and the like.
Question: How are the vital points (*marmāṇi*) arranged within the intervals?
Answer: In great powerful animals such as elephants, horses, and oxen, the bones and joints within the intervals of the vital points support one another and are moreover firm and solid.
The joints of a mahānagna are connected like planks joined together;
the joints of a praskandhin are interlocked like iron hooks.
The joints of Nārāyaṇa’s body are linked together like iron chains;
the joints of the Buddha’s body are coiled and interlaced like a coiling dragon;
the joints of all other sentient beings are separated from one another and lack solidity.
Therefore, those types are of the weakest power.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 190. *Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 100.
Composed by the ninety-one [disciples] and five hundred great Arhats, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.

Section Eight: The Aggregate of Views; First Sub-section: The Application of Mindfulness (Smṛtyupasthāna); Part Five. Regarding the mind of an Arhat at the moment of Parinirvāṇa, should it be said to be wholesome (*kuśala*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Answer: It should be said that it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
This refers to an arhat who has already abandoned unwholesome states and accomplished wholesome states.
Someone might then doubt:
"If that is so, an arhat must abide in a wholesome state of mind when entering parinirvāṇa."
In order to resolve this doubt,
it is clarified that although an Arhat has abandoned unwholesome dharmas and accomplished wholesome dharmas,
he enters parinirvāṇa while abiding in an indeterminate state of mind, which is not itself wholesome.
If this treatise had not been composed previously, then even up to the present day, were such a question to be asked:
"Regarding the mind of an Arhat at the moment of parinirvāṇa, should it be described as wholesome or as indeterminate?"
Because they do not understand,
they may answer:
"It is wholesome, not indeterminate."
Because Arhats have already severed all unwholesome dharmas and accomplished wholesome dharmas,
and because this treatise was composed previously,
they have attained correct understanding up to the present day.
For this reason, this treatise is composed.
Question: Why does an Arhat enter parinirvāṇa while abiding solely in a neutral (avyākṛta) state of mind?
Answer: Because only the neutral state of mind is conducive to the cessation of the mind.

That is to say, a wholesome mind is powerful, firmly established, and difficult to destroy; it can cause other minds to arise in succession for a long duration and is not conducive to the interruption of the mental continuum.
A neutral mind, however, is weak and inferior, like a rotten seed; it is not firmly established and is easily destroyed.
Because it cannot cause other minds to arise in succession for a long duration,
it is most conducive to the cessation of the mind.
Some say:
This is because the arising of neutral states (*avyākṛta-citta*) involves fewer faults.
That is to say, wholesome and unwholesome states give rise to many faults within saṃsāra by way of two doors:
first, by way of the door of ripened results (*vipāka-phala*).
Second, by way of the flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*):
a neutral mind gives rise to faults solely by way of the flow-on fruit, not by way of the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
Some say:
Because an Arhat has turned his back on all rebirth, whereas other sentient beings,
when their lives are about to end, exert the power of intense mental attention for the sake of being born again,
thereby causing a wholesome mind to arise.
"May I not fall into any undesirable realms of existence.
Because an Arhat has turned his back on all rebirth, he no longer applies such mental attention;
rather, abiding in an indeterminate state of mind, he enters parinirvāṇa.
Some say that because an Arhat does not seek to enter a future vessel of karmic maturation—
unlike other sentient beings who, seeking to enter a future vessel of maturation, give rise to a wholesome mind through intense application at the time of death.
Because an arhat does not seek such a vessel for the ripening of karmic fruition, he enters parinirvāṇa while abiding in a neutral state of mind (*avyākṛta-citta*).
Some say that the arhat enters nirvāṇa while abiding in his natural state of mind (*prakṛti-citta*).
The mind of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-citta*) is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind,
because it has never been absent throughout successive births.
Alternatively, within a certain homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*), no wholesome mind may arise.
This refers to those who have severed their roots of goodness but have not yet reconnected them; or,
within a certain homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*), there is no arising of unwholesome minds,
such as those who have already become detached from the defilements of the desire realm.
There is not a single being within any homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) who does not give rise to a neutral mind (*avyākṛta-citta*).
For this reason, the neutral mind is called the "mind of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-citta*),
and it is by abiding solely in this mind that one enters *nirvāṇa*.
Some say that an Arhat enters parinirvāṇa while abiding in the aforementioned mind of a kinsman and friend;
this is like a person wishing to travel to another land who is escorted by a kinsman and friend, with the close kinsman returning at the gate.
From the village boundary in the middle up to the national border at the top—
likewise, when an Arhat proceeds toward Nirvana, the unwholesome and defiled mind is like an inferior friend;
it is immediately abandoned upon becoming detached from the desire realm and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
A virtuous mind is like a middle friend;
when an indeterminate state of mind arises, it immediately departs.
An indeterminate mind is like a superior friend.
It is only at the time of parinirvāṇa that one finally abandons them.
Some say this is because an arhat gradually relinquishes the phenomena of birth and death.
That is to say: at the time of becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm, one abandons all unwholesome minds;
at the time of becoming free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one abandons all defiled minds;
and when an indeterminate mind arises, one abandons all wholesome minds.
At the time of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, one abandons all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) minds.
The Venerable Ghosaka states:
"All wholesome minds arise through the application of effort; at the time of death, one can no longer apply such effort."
Therefore, one enters parinirvāṇa abiding solely in a mind of moral neutrality (*avyākṛta-citta*).
Question: What is the object of the final mind of an Arhat? Some say:
It takes as its object the sense faculties and the primary elements within one's own continuum;
some say it takes the six internal bases as its object.
Some say it takes the six external bases as its object;
others say...
Taking the twelve sense bases as its object,
the Venerable One said:
"What is the object of the final mind of an Arhat?"
Answer: Taking himself as the object, he forms the perception of himself as being without life or as being devoid of life;
then, with the door of liberation of emptiness manifesting before him, he enters parinirvāṇa. Some say:
With that mind taking all conditioned phenomena as its object, having deeply perceived the faults within all conditioned phenomena,
the door of liberation of wishlessness manifests, and he attains parinirvāṇa. Some say:
That mind takes nirvāṇa as its object; by contemplating the quality of tranquility within nirvāṇa, the door of signless liberation (animitta-vimokṣamukha) manifests, and one attains parinirvāṇa.
It should be understood that this refers to the final dying thought within the continuum of an arhat.
The final mind of the non-momentary [state] is not [the object], because that mind is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The Venerable One says:
"The final mind of an Arhat takes as its object the realms of what is seen, heard, sensed, and known."
Because that mind is comprised within an entity born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
it ceases spontaneously once the force of prior karmic formations is exhausted,
just as a potter’s wheel stops when its momentum is spent.
Why did the two noble disciples enter parinirvāṇa first, and the Buddha afterwards?

The answer is: because those two venerable ones had previously, throughout the long night, performed and accumulated karma that would result in uninterrupted maturation; therefore, it was not to be empty or without fruit.
Those two venerable ones sought such a place and initiated this karma due to two causes and conditions:
first, because they were preceded by seeing;
second, because they were preceded by hearing.
Regarding those for whom vision comes first: those two venerable ones had previously seen the two foremost disciples of a past Samyaksaṃbuddha enter parinirvāṇa before that Buddha himself did.

Regarding those for whom hearing comes first: in the past, those two venerable ones heard that the two foremost disciples of a previous Samyak-saṃbuddha entered parinirvāṇa first, and only then did that Buddha [pass away].
Having seen and heard this, they then give rise to and follow that cause,
dedicating all their practices— whether precepts, prohibitions, asceticism, or the holy life— toward it.
May I, in the future, become one who acts as a virtuous person of such a kind,
and may I always enjoy the Dharma-pleasure together with the Great Master without interruption.
If the Buddha were to enter parinirvāṇa first, followed later by the two excellent disciples.
In that case, the ripening of the karma created, accumulated, and experienced by those who have not severed the continuity [of their practice] would be empty and fruitless.
Question: There is no one who creates, accumulates, and experiences karma that has not been severed like the Buddha.
If the two noble disciples were to enter parinirvāṇa first, then the Buddha’s uninterrupted karma would become empty and without fruition.
Could it be that the uninterrupted karma produced by the two noble disciples is superior to that of the Buddha?
Answer: A disciple has two kinds of superior utilization toward a teacher:
first, the utilization of material wealth;
second, the utilization of the Dharma.
The teacher has one kind of superior utilization regarding the disciple, namely, that which pertains to both material wealth and the Dharma.

However, when performing and increasing actions that induce uninterrupted karma, it is solely for the sake of the Dharma and not for the sake of material wealth; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
Question: Among the two noble disciples, why did the one superior in *prajñā* enter *parinirvāṇa* first rather than the one superior in supernatural powers (*abhijñā*)?
If the one superior in supernatural powers has already lost the opportunity to enjoy the Dharma there [in that world], what is the purpose?
Why is it that the karma of those who have attained the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) does not result in an empty fruition of maturation?
The answer is: there is no one superior to the Blessed One in wisdom.
Although he has entered parinirvāṇa, because the Blessed One still exists, the enjoyment of the Dharma is not empty and does not lack fruit.
Furthermore, by the nature of things (*dharmatā*), the two noble disciples enter *parinirvāṇa* before the Buddha.
What is meant by "the nature of things"?
It means that the Dharma ought to be thus; it cannot be altered nor can it be questioned—this is the meaning of "the nature of things."
This demonstrates that for all Buddhas, it is the established principle that their two noble disciples must enter parinirvāṇa before the Buddha; there is no difference in this logic.
Some say it is because they share a similar dharma with the wheel-turning kings (cakravartin).
Just as a wheel-turning monarch, when wishing to travel to various regions he has not yet reached, must have his brave generals lead the way for him;
so too does the Ten-Powered Dharma-Wheel-Turning Monarch, when wishing to travel to the realm of nirvana without remainder which he has not yet reached.
He also caused the two noble disciples, the brave generals of his former army, to go ahead as guides,
just as before. Some say this was because he wished to lead the sentient beings to be converted into the Buddha-dharma.
This refers to those sentient beings to be converted who, although dwelling near the Buddha for the duration of their entire life-span (*nikāya-sabhāga*),
have no desire to come before the Buddha to practice the Buddha-dharma;
rather, it is when they see the two noble disciples enter parinirvāṇa that they become weary of and terrified by birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
They come to the presence of the Buddha to practice the Buddha-dharma.
Some say it is for the sake of dispelling the sorrowful minds of the sentient beings to be converted.
That is to say, if the Buddha were to enter parinirvāṇa first, there would be no one capable of dispelling the sorrowful minds of the sentient beings to be converted.
If the two excellent disciples were to enter parinirvāṇa first, there would still be the Tathāgata who, during the four months of the rainy season, [could provide such guidance].
Based on those [teachings] and his own teaching on impermanence, he dispels their sorrow and causes them to cultivate superior practice.
Some say that he intends to cause the sentient beings to be converted to dwell in mindfulness in anticipation of the Buddha’s imminent parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is said that because the two most excellent disciples entered parinirvāṇa first,
the sentient beings they had converted thought:
"The Buddha, too, will soon enter parinirvāṇa."
Because the two noble disciples have already entered parinirvāṇa,
it is like the heavens that must first flash lightning before thundering.
If the thunder were to strike without lightning preceding it, it would cause those who are timid and weak to faint.
When sentient beings hear it, they are struck with terror or even die.
Therefore, when the devas wish to send thunder, out of compassion for sentient beings, they first flash lightning.
Once they have perceived this, the beings wait for it with open hearts.
Just as one hears a clap of thunder yet remains without alarm or terror, so too,
if the Buddha were to enter parinirvāṇa first, it would cause certain classes of sentient beings who cherish and yearn for him to be struck with such shock and distress that they faint away.
If the two most excellent disciples were to enter parinirvāṇa first,
it would cause their followers to prematurely conceive the notion that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa; thus,
when the Buddha actually enters nirvāṇa, they would not fall into despair.
There is a verse that says:
"By constantly cultivating the perception of impermanence, one will have no sorrow when things change and decay.
Just as one who first sees lightning is not startled or terrified by the thunder."
Some say it is for the purpose of quelling slander; that is to say,
there are non-Buddhists who constantly slander the Buddha, saying:
Because the Śramaṇa Gautama has taken Upatiṣya and Kolita under his care,
he receives their instructions at night and expounds them to others during the day. If,
after those two have passed into parinirvāṇa, the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma remains no different from before, then all the slanders of the non-Buddhists will cease.
Some say that it was to manifest that the World-Honored One would not remain long in the world and would certainly enter parinirvāṇa,
just as when a world is about to undergo destruction.
When Mount Sumeru is abandoned by the two great nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, after having coiled around it,
the devas, upon seeing this, immediately know that the world will soon be destroyed.
In this way, as the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered parinirvāṇa first,
the world came to know that the Buddha would soon pass into extinction due to various causes and conditions such as these.
The two excellent disciples entered parinirvāṇa first, and only then did the Buddha pass away.
Question: For what reason did the Venerable Subhadra enter parinirvāṇa before the Buddha?
The answer is: it is also due to the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
That is to say, it is the nature of all Buddhas that their final disciple attains parinirvāṇa first, and only then does the Buddha [attain it].
Question: What is meant by "the nature of things"?
Answer: The Dharma should be thus; because it cannot be altered, it is called "dharmatā" (the nature of things).
This reveals that for all Buddhas, the principle is without exception: they must enter parinirvāṇa after their very last disciple.
Some say it is because it possesses qualities similar to those of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
For example, when a wheel-turning monarch wishes to enter a garden or a superior location for recreation:
He must first cause the youngest prince to enter, adorned with all manner of ornaments, and only then proceed himself;
such is the Unsurpassed Dharma King endowed with the Ten Powers.
When he was about to enter the garden-like ground of the realm of nirvana without remainder,
he likewise first adorned his final disciple with the factors of enlightenment, causing him to enter nirvana beforehand.
After that, he went there himself.
Some say that the Venerable Subhadra had this thought:
"All my fellow practitioners of the holy life shall enter the realm of nirvana with remainder before me;
I, in turn, shall enter the realm of nirvana without remainder before all my fellow practitioners of the holy life."
Due to his aspiration, he entered parinirvāṇa before those previous Buddhas.
Some say that the Venerable One had this thought:
Just as one receives such merit from the holy teachings,
so too does one receive such suffering and affliction from birth and death;
since I am unable to receive the manifold merits of the holy teachings, [I shall not accept this].
"Why should he remain for long and undergo the manifold afflictions of birth and death?
Therefore, those former Buddhas entered parinirvāṇa.
So it is said.
Because that venerable one feared receiving excessive offerings and honor,
the Mallas of Kuśinagara had previously regarded him as their Great Teacher.
Furthermore, he knew that [the Blessed One] had attained the fruit of arhatship.
That venerable one thought:
"After the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa, he will surely make a grand offering to me."
"Fortunately, because the Buddha has not yet entered parinirvāṇa, the Mallas and others are occupied with making offerings to the World-Honored One;
they have no leisure to attend to me. I shall enter parinirvāṇa before the Buddha.
Some say: [End of quote].
Because he wished to sever the very root of contention,
that venerable one thought to himself:
"If I were to pass away after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa..."
The non-Buddhists claimed,
"I am of their kind," while the bhikṣus in turn said, "I am of their kind.
Because of this, various disputes and quarrels arose.
He perceived that such events would occur in the future; therefore, the previous Buddha entered parinirvāṇa.
Some say this was intended to demonstrate that even at his final stage, the Blessed One’s merit in teaching beings remained undiminished.
That is to say, some may think:
"The World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa because his merits have declined.
Those venerable ones wish to demonstrate that even in his final state, the World-Honored One was still able to teach and transform sentient beings, causing their merits to reach perfection.
That is to say, it causes them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Due to various causes and conditions such as these, they attain parinirvāṇa prior to the previous Buddha.
As it is said: "The World-Honored One, relying upon the immovable and tranquil samādhi, has attained parinirvāṇa; the Eye of the World has been extinguished."
"Is this while in meditative absorption or after emerging from it?
Answer: "After emerging.
Question: "For what purpose was this treatise composed?"
Answer: It is in order to bring about certainty for those who harbor doubts.
For a sūtra states that the Blessed One entered parinirvāṇa while abiding in the immovable, tranquil meditative absorption, and thus the Eye of the World was extinguished.
There may be those who doubt that the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa while remaining in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In order to resolve this doubt and clarify that the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa after emerging from concentration, this treatise was composed.
In this context, "the immovable,
tranquil concentration" refers to a concentration associated with a desire-realm mind that is non-obscured and neutral;
it is called "immovable and tranquil" because it resembles the fourth dhyāna.
The Buddha attained parinirvāṇa based on this.
The masters of the Gandhāra country in the western regions speak thus:
