"As it is said, the World-Honored One entered the fourth dhyāna and attained parinirvāṇa; the Eye of the World has been extinguished."
"Is this while remaining in meditative absorption or after emerging from it?
Answer: "After emerging.
Question: "Since the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa having attained all four dhyānas, why is it said that he entered only the fourth dhyāna?"
Answer: Although one also enters the first three dhyānas, one does not remain attached to them;
however, upon entering the fourth dhyāna, one becomes firmly attached, and for this reason it is specifically mentioned. Some say:
Because one enters the first three dhyānas in order to enter the fourth dhyāna, the fourth is specifically mentioned.
Some say that the first three dhyānas are like being on the road, while the fourth dhyāna is the actual destination; therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
Some say that when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he arose from the fourth dhyāna and entered the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of the third dhyāna;
from the preparatory stage of the third dhyāna, he arose and entered the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna.
Emerging from the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna, one enters the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna;
emerging from the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna, a wholesome mind of the desire realm manifests before one.
Immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm, an unobscured-neutral mind of the desire realm manifests;
one then attains parinirvāṇa while abiding in this very mind.
This is because the first three dhyānas involve entry and emergence only through their preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), and not from the fundamental states (*maula*).
The fourth dhyāna is mentioned specifically because it is the basis for both entering and emerging from the fundamental state.
The Venerable Ghosaka said:
"When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa..."
Immediately after the fourth dhyāna, a wholesome mind of the desire realm manifests;
immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm, an unobscured-neutral mind of the desire realm manifests.
Then, abiding in this mind, one enters parinirvāṇa.
Question: Is it possible for a wholesome mind of the desire realm to arise immediately after the fourth dhyāna?
Answer: Yes.
This refers to the Buddha and no one else.
Question: For what reason does the Buddha enter the fourth dhyāna at the time of his final parinirvāṇa?
Answer: Because [beings] exceeding the sands of the Ganges in number [rely upon it].
The dharmas of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, are all likewise.
He enters meditative absorption in successive order and attains parinirvāṇa;
that is to say, at the time of the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, as the final natural law (*dharmatā*), they enter the fourth dhyāna.
Having emerged from that [samādhi], he entered parinirvāṇa.
Some say this was to demonstrate that the Buddha possesses supreme mastery over that samādhi, such that even as he was about to enter nirvāṇa, he still manifested its entry.
If it were not so, [the Buddha] would be unable to manifest [them] before his eyes.
Some say that the Buddha did so out of a desire to have compassion for those born in future generations.
This means that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there will be sentient beings who will think:
"The World-Honored One, who possesses all-encompassing wisdom, even when approaching nirvāṇa, still entered the fourth dhyāna."
"How much more so for us, who do not fail to apply ourselves diligently to the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)?
By virtue of this diligent cultivation of all attainments," some say.
Because it shares similar characteristics with a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
For example, if a wheel-turning monarch first receives his consecration and assumes the royal throne in this very place,
he subsequently passes away in that same place.
Thus, the Dharma King endowed with the ten powers first assumed the rank of Dharma King based upon the fourth dhyāna,
and later entered parinirvāṇa by relying again upon this same stage. Some say:
Because it shares a similar quality with a great merchant lord:
just as a great merchant lord, at the very end, exchanges [his goods] for precious jewels of great value without any attachment,
so too the Blessed One, at the very end, relinquishes the preeminent fourth dhyāna without any attachment.
When the Blessed One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he first gave rise to a wholesome mind of the desire realm;
from that, he immediately entered the first dhyāna,
and from the first dhyāna, he entered the second dhyāna.
In this manner, proceeding in succession, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception from the sphere of nothingness;
and immediately after emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Immediately after emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, one enters the sphere of nothingness;
from the sphere of nothingness, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
and from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness.
From the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness;
from the sphere of nothingness, one enters the sphere of infinite space;
from the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness; and from the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the fourth dhyāna.
From the fourth dhyāna, one enters the sphere of infinite space;
from the sphere of infinite space, one enters the third dhyāna;
from the third dhyāna, one enters the fourth dhyāna.
From the fourth dhyāna, he enters the second dhyāna;
from the second dhyāna, he enters the third dhyāna;
from the third dhyāna, he enters the first dhyāna.
From the first dhyāna, one enters the second dhyāna;
from the second dhyāna, one enters the third dhyāna;
from the third dhyāna, one enters the fourth dhyāna.
Having arisen from the fourth dhyāna, he entered parinirvāṇa.
Thus, at the time of his final nirvāṇa, the Blessed One entered the fourth dhyāna four times;
during the first three entries, it was not yet called the "immovable, peaceful concentration."
The entry into the fourth [dhyāna] is called the immovable, tranquil concentration.
Why is this? Because during the entries into the three preceding [dhyānas], one does not take nirvāṇa as an object.
Because at the time of the fourth entry, one takes *nirvāṇa* as the object.

Question: For what reason did the Blessed One, when approaching his own *parinirvāṇa*, not enter the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) by ascending in regular order, but instead entered them only by ascending in reverse order?
Answer: The dharmas of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, numbering more than the sands of the Ganges, all likewise transcendently enter these meditative absorptions.
Some say this is to demonstrate that the World-Honored One has attained mastery over all meditative absorptions.
Why is this? Because if one has attained mastery over meditative concentration,
one is then able to enter the reverse order of transcendence directly, without relying on the forward order of transcendence.
If one lacks mastery over the various meditative absorptions, one cannot even enter them by ascending in regular order,
much less by skipping levels in reverse order. Some say:
This is to demonstrate that the Blessed One is capable of performing what is difficult to perform;
namely, that it is difficult to enter the various meditative absorptions by skipping them in reverse order without first entering them in forward order,
as opposed to those who skip them in reverse only after having already entered them in forward order.
Some say:
it is in order to manifest the great majesty of the World-Honored One that the World-Honored One’s power is able to skip [the stages] not in forward order, but in reverse order.
If śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not enter [the meditative attainments] by ascending in order, they cannot enter them by descending;
some say this is because they wish to enter the attainment of cessation as well.

This means that if the Buddha were to enter the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna) by way of progressive or skipping entry at that time, there would be no possibility of him entering the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). Why is this?

Because the attainment of cessation must necessarily manifest immediately after the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), following a gradual sequence.

If it were so, then at the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he would not manifest entry into all the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti).
Yet, at the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he certainly manifests entry into all the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
Therefore, rather than entering the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) in direct order, he enters them in reverse order.
Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, manifest entry into all the dhyānas, liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti)?
The answer is: because the dharmas of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, numbering more than the sands of the Ganges, are likewise.
That is to say, when all Buddhas approach parinirvāṇa, their dharmas invariably manifest entry into all dhyānas, samādhis, and samāpattis.
Some say:
This is to demonstrate that the Blessed One has attained mastery over all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
That is to say, one who has attained mastery over all absorptions is still able to manifest entry into them even at the time of his final *parinirvāṇa*.
If one does not attain mastery over the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), one is unable to enter them even at other times, let alone at the time of *parinirvāṇa*.
Some say that the Buddha did so out of compassion for sentient beings of future times.
It means that after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, there will be sentient beings who think:

"The World-Honored One, possessing all-knowledge, even as he was approaching parinirvāṇa, still manifested entry into all meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti)."
"How much less would we fail to apply ourselves with diligent effort toward them?
It is for this reason that one diligently cultivates the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*). Some say:
It was for the purpose of re-consecrating the stūpas containing the remaining śarīra relics;
furthermore, it was to nourish those whose bodies were emaciated and weak;
and also, it was so that Cunda, the son of a craftsman, might increase his field of merit.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of ceasing the various bodily painful sensations arising from the disintegration of the body.
Some say it is because it possesses a quality similar to that of a great and wealthy merchant leader.
Just as a great and wealthy merchant lord, at the time of his death, opens all his storehouses, inspects his treasures, and entrusts them to his sons and grandsons before passing away,
so too is the Blessed One the supreme merchant lord of the True Dharma.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, he opened the treasury of merit and examined all the treasures of the dharmas— such as the dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis—
and having entrusted them to his disciples, he then entered nirvāṇa.
The Venerable Ghosaka said:
"Because the Blessed One himself manifested the quality of non-retrogression;
that is to say, the Buddha, having accomplished all merits and attained mastery over all objects and cognitions, even as he approaches parinirvāṇa."
He was still able to manifest all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments.
As stated in the sūtra:
"The Blessed One attained parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees in the Malla birthplace at Kuśinagara."
Question: Why did the World-Honored One enter parinirvāṇa in the city of Kuśinagara?
Answer: It was because he wished to transform and deliver the Mallas within the city of Kuśinagara;
furthermore, it was to gather and convert the non-Buddhist Subhadra, and also for the sake of the great Malla Puṣkasa.
Because it plants the seeds for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha,
and furthermore causes his wife to plant the seeds for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Some say:
This was to prevent the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara from being subjected to contempt;
for had the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa in any other great city,
the Mallas of this small city would have been held in derision.
Because no single portion of the Tathāgata’s physical remains could be obtained, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa at this place.
Some say it was so that the relics of the Buddha’s body might be widely disseminated.
If the Buddha were to attain parinirvāṇa in some other great city, those people there would be difficult to subdue;
they might develop a sense of possessiveness toward the Buddha’s bodily relics and thus prevent their distribution.

If he were to attain parinirvāṇa in the city of Kuśinagara, the Mallas and others would possess both physical and mental vigor; because their minds are vigorous, they would delight in distributing [the relics];
and because their bodies are vigorous, they could not be overcome by others, and thus, delighting in distribution, they would ensure it.
It causes the Buddha’s *dharmadhātu* (body-relics) to be widely disseminated.
Some say it is intended to show that although the Buddha is approaching *parinirvāṇa*, he still continues to experience the fruits of supreme sovereignty and prosperity within the world.
That is to say, if the Buddha were to attain parinirvāṇa in any other great city,
the offerings he would receive, though exceeding those of a wheel-turning monarch by many hundreds of thousands of times, would not be considered extraordinary.

Even if one enters nirvana in such a remote and small frontier city, the offerings received therein still exceed those of a universal monarch by many hundreds of thousands of times; this is truly extraordinary.
Some say that because the Buddha repeatedly sacrificed his own life at this place,
as stated in that sutra.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "From here to the city of Kuśinagara, there is the Golden River and the pair of Śāla groves.
The territory of the Makuṭabandhana Caitya of the Mallas extends for exactly twelve yojanas all around."
The Tathāgata has relinquished his life as a wheel-turning monarch on six such occasions;
now, for the seventh time, he relinquishes his life as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Ānanda, you should know that I have never seen such a place before.
Whether to the east, south, west, or north, the Tathāgata further relinquishes his eighth life-essence.
Why is this? Because for the Tathāgata, all paths of existence have been severed, birth and death are forever exhausted, and there is no further existence hereafter.
As it is said: The Buddha addressed Ānanda, "You should go to the twin *śāla* grove and prepare for the Tathāgata a bed with the head to the north;
today at midnight, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa in the realm of non-abiding. This is explained at length.
Question: Why did the Blessed One command that a bed with the head toward the north be prepared and lie upon it?
Answer: It was because he wished to demonstrate that such is the proper practice for the masters of logic (*tārkika*) in that country;
that is to say, all the masters of logic in that country prepare a bed with the head toward the north and lie upon it.
The World-Honored One is likewise.
Because the Buddha is able to subdue all masters of debate, he is the unsurpassed and foremost among them;
yet as a master of debate, he allowed himself to lie down according to the bedding prepared by them.
Some say that this is intended to demonstrate the avoidance of what the world falsely clings to as auspicious; for instance,
in that country, when someone dies, they are made to lie on their bed with their head toward the north.
The Buddha, in order to shatter their false attachment to auspiciousness, commanded that his bed be prepared with the head toward the north for him to lie upon before entering parinirvāṇa.
Some say it was because he wished to quell the impure thoughts of the Mallas within the city of Kuśinagara.
It is said that according to the customs of that country, they all establish shrines for the gods in the northern direction;
if the Buddha were to lie with his feet toward the north,
the Mallas would give rise to impure thoughts.
"Why do you insult us by lying on your north foot, which we serve?
Some say this was said because he wished to manifest his reverence for the True Dharma.

This means that because the Buddha knew in advance that after his parinirvāṇa the unsurpassed torch of the Dharma would blaze intensely in the north for a long time without extinguishing, he lay upon his bed with his head toward the north.
Some say:
The Buddha wishes to manifest that his own activities are progressively superior at all times;
that is to say, because the roots of goodness he has cultivated over three incalculable eons have gradually increased and become more excellent, without ever declining or ceasing.
He causes [the deceased] to lie with the head directed toward the superior direction,
because the north is the superior direction.
Some say:
The Buddha wished to manifest that the population in the northern regions would gradually increase;

that is to say, because the Buddha foresaw that after his parinirvāṇa the people of the north would steadily multiply, he directed that a bed with the head toward the north be prepared and lay upon it.
As it is said: "At that time, the Blessed One approached the prepared bed and lay down on his right side with one foot upon the other, facing west with his head toward the north;
he dwelt in the perception of light, possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension," and so forth, as extensively described.
Question: Why does the World-Honored One lie on his right side?
Answer: To manifest that the Buddha lies like a lion king.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
There are four ways of lying down: the lion’s posture, the celestial posture, the ghostly posture, and the posture of those addicted to desire.
The lion king lies on his right side;
the celestial beings lie with their faces turned upward.
The ghosts lie with their faces turned downward.
Those addicted to desire lie on their left sides touching the ground;
because the Buddha is the unsurpassed lion among men, he lies on his right side.
Some say that this is to demonstrate that the Blessed One acts exactly as he speaks;
for it is said in the Sūtra:
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You all should learn the lion’s posture for lying down.
Since the Buddha is one who acts according to his word, and having already exhorted others to lie on their right side, he himself likewise did so.
Question: World-Honored One, for what reason do you enter parinirvāṇa lying down rather than sitting?
Answer: It is because I wish to enable the great assembly to easily perceive and understand all parts of the Buddha’s body.
Some say:
"If the Buddha were to enter nirvāṇa while lying down, his physical dimensions would be directly perceivable without depending on conceptual analysis.
Others say: [as follows].
This is to demonstrate that the Tathāgata is free from deceit.
If the Buddha were to sit in parinirvāṇa, those who lack faith would say:
"This is a deception; how could a dead person remain sitting upright?"
Some say: it is in order to prevent people from slandering the noble ones in the future;
for if those who attain parinirvāṇa while sitting were to do so now, the arhats would have their physical strength diminished and enter nirvāṇa while lying down.
The world then slandered him, saying: "He is not an Arhat; if he were, why does he not sit in parinirvāṇa together with the Buddha?
Some say it was to sever the prideful mind of those who rely on their own power.
That is to say, when they saw the Buddha lying down in parinirvāṇa, they all thought:
"The World-Honored One’s every limb possessed the strength of Nārāyaṇa, yet he was unable to sit upright, being pressed by impermanence."
"How much less, then, should we—ordinary beings of inferior capacity and meager strength—rely on our slight power to give rise to arrogance?
[The disciples] asked, "World-Honored One, for what reason did you enter parinirvāṇa during the middle watch of the night?"
The answer is that at this time it is most tranquil.
That is to say, because the heat in that land makes it impossible to perform tasks during the day,
most activities are carried out during the first and last watches of the night.
Only during the middle watch of the night is all perfectly still;
because the Tathāgata always delights in and praises tranquility, he entered parinirvāṇa during the middle watch of the night.
Some say that this is intended to show that the Buddha did not for even a moment depart from the proper moderation regarding matters of increase and decrease; that is to say,
the Buddha retained his life-force during the first watch of the night and relinquished it during the final watch of the night.
Furthermore, during the middle watch of the night, he left what preceded and abandoned what followed, entering parinirvāṇa at that midpoint.
Some say this was because the Buddha wished to cause the great assembly to give rise to profound revulsion and fear toward the dark abyss of saṃsāra.
It is said that on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, at midnight, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the lunar disc set behind the mountain peak;
likewise, when the moon of the Buddha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, vanished behind the mountain of the great nirvāṇa of meditative concentration, two kinds of darkness arose simultaneously.
This refers to the darkness of the nature of form and the darkness of ignorance.
When the great assembly witnessed this event,
they immediately gave rise to a profound sense of revulsion and fear toward birth and death.
Therefore, he entered parinirvāṇa at midnight.
Some say it was because the Buddha always delights in practicing the Middle Way.
This refers to when the Buddha was formerly a bodhisattva, being born in his final existence among the gods in the Tuṣita heaven, which is situated in the center;
and being born in his final existence among humans in the city of Kapilavastu in Central India.
In the middle watch of the night,
he left the city to renounce the world, practiced the Middle Way,
and realized unsurpassed enlightenment for the benefit of sentient beings.
He taught the sublime Dharma that is free from existence and non-existence and abides in the middle way,
and at the middle watch of the night, he entered parinirvāṇa.
As it is said, at that time Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
in this city of Kuśinagara there are such and such Mallas,
including all their men and women, great and small, servants, laborers, friends, and kinsmen."
"I take refuge in the Blessed One, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus;
I accept the various precepts," and so forth, as explained at length.
It is asked: Is the prātimokṣa restraint obtained through its own informative [action]?
How is it that the precepts received by those Mallas were obtained through the communication of another?
The answer is: by the Buddha’s supernormal power. That is to say, precepts are generally obtained through one's own communication;
however, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, the Buddha, through his majestic power, caused the precepts of the Mallas and others to be obtained through the communication of another.
Some say that the Venerable Ānanda had previously entered the city of Kuśinagara and conferred upon the Mallas the three refuges and the precepts;
now he merely informs the Buddha so that they may know he wishes to demonstrate that the Mallas are the true disciples of the Buddha.
Furthermore, it demonstrates that even at the final stage, the Tathāgata is still able to sustain his newly initiated disciples.
Therefore, the World-Honored One’s disciples are fully endowed [with stability], unlike those of the non-Buddhists whose followers disperse at the time of their death.
Some say that the prātimokṣa restraint can also be obtained from the informative act of another in other cases. For example,
although the informative act of the women of the Vaṅga country was not very clear, they nevertheless obtained the prātimokṣa restraint through the power of the informative act of others.
As it is said, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, and even after my parinirvāṇa, you must not arbitrarily ordain non-Buddhists as renunciants or grant them full ordination (upasampadā),
with the sole exception of those of the Śākya clan and those non-Buddhists with matted hair who serve the fire."
If there is anyone of the Śākya clan who comes wearing the robes of an outsider seeking to go forth,
you should immediately ordain him, allow him to go forth,
and confer the full precepts upon him. Why is this?
"Because my own retinue should be granted permission," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: Since the Blessed One possesses all-pervading great compassion, for what reason does he grant permission only to his own retinue?
Answer: There were members of the Śākya clan who had previously taken refuge in non-Buddhist paths but had not yet taken refuge in the Buddha.
Now, for the sake of skillfully gathering them in, this statement was made;
that is to say, it was because of the evil king Virūḍhaka Śākya.

Because the Śākyas of the city of Kapilavastu had been slaughtered, some remaining Śākyas, out of fear, went forth as renunciants among non-Buddhist sects merely to preserve their lives. For their sake, the Buddha spoke these words of meaning: "Out of fear, you [have done this]."
Having left the household life according to the non-Buddhist paths and donned their religious robes, they now have no fear and will surely return to take refuge in the Buddha’s Dharma.
Therefore, I have commanded my disciples to ordain them; thus, these immeasurable members of the Śākya clan who were formerly non-Buddhists have come to take refuge in the Buddha’s Dharma.
Some say: It was in order to entice those of the Śākya clan who had not yet entered the Buddha-dharma and possessed overweening pride (adhimāna), so that they might enter the Buddha-dharma.

That is to say, because there were members of the Śākya clan whose minds were bound by the fetter of overweening pride, they did not come to see the Buddha for as long as their life-span (nikāya-sabhāga) lasted.
After the Tathāgata had spoken these words, he entered parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing this later, they will think:
"Did the Buddha not, out of regard for us as his kinsmen, manifest compassion even as he approached parinirvāṇa?"
Consequently, there was not one who did not give rise to a pure mind, come to take refuge in the Buddha and Dharma, and leave the household life to receive the precepts.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"The Tathāgata, in order to cause the kinsmen of the Śākya clan to accumulate and expand their sublime roots of goodness, made this their final entrustment at the time of his parinirvāṇa."
As it is said in the Sūtra:
At that time, the Blessed One bared his upper body and addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:
"You should contemplate me; you should examine me."
Why is this? Because the appearance of a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha,
is difficult to encounter.
It is difficult to behold, surpassing even the *utpala* flower.
He asked the World-Honored One: "For what reason did you expose your upper body and address the assembly of bhikṣus, saying, 'You should contemplate me,' and so forth, as explained at length?"
Answer: Suppose there were someone who practiced śamatha for a full twelve years;
the wholesome qualities produced by that person would not equal the merit obtained by contemplating the Buddha’s body of marks and signs for even a single moment.

Regarding this, the meaning of the Buddha’s words is as follows: "Until the mass of merit I have accumulated over three incalculable eons has been reduced to ashes, you should all attentively look up and observe, seeking the firm and enduring Dharma."
Question: "You should observe me; you should examine me—what is the difference between these?
Answer: "To observe me means by means of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*);
to examine me means by means of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)."
Furthermore, "one should contemplate the self" means by means of a non-conceptual mind;
"one should examine the self" means by means of a conceptual mind.
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the self:
it means that one should examine the self in the present.
That is to say, regarding the future;
furthermore, "one should contemplate the self" refers to the body born of birth.
"One who should examine the self" refers to the dharmakāya.
Furthermore, "one who contemplates the self" [refers to this].
"Contemplating what has been accumulated" means examining that which has been realized. "Examining the self" means examining that which has been realized.
Furthermore, "contemplating the self" refers to contemplating that which is to be reviled;
"examining the self" refers to...
That is to say, it refers to examining what one delights in.
Furthermore, "observing the self" refers to observing the primary and secondary marks of physical excellence.
"To examine oneself" means to examine one's own merits;
this is called "examining the distinctions."
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"O Bhikṣus, you should maintain silence for a while and contemplate that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are of a nature to perish and cease.
This was the final instruction of the Blessed One.
Question: Why did the World-Honored One speak these words?
Answer: Because the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣus were overcome with profound grief and lamented one after another.
The Buddha spoke these words because he wished to quell their sorrow and cause them to give rise to contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).

In this context, "you bhikṣus should for now maintain silence" means to abide in right mindfulness; "you should contemplate that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are of a nature to perish" means to arouse right knowledge (*saṃprajanya*).
Furthermore, those who are capable of being silenced should be made to cultivate śamatha,
while those practitioners who are capable of discernment should be made to cultivate vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, those who are capable of being silenced...
He causes those who are grieving to cease their sorrow and causes practitioners to give rise to contemplative practice.
The Venerable Ghosaka said:
"O Bhikṣus, you should for now maintain silence."

The statement that one who wishes to stop the sorrow of others should contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being subject to exhaustion and cessation demonstrates that he has personally accomplished the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharman*).
Herein, the meaning of the Buddha’s words is: "Not long after I attained Buddhahood, I already made this declaration."
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
they are subject to arising and ceasing, for they originate and pass away. Their stillness is bliss.
Now, furthermore, based on that, it is said: "All conditioned phenomena are subject to exhaustion and cessation."
Is it not that I have accomplished the quality of non-forgetfulness?

translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section One of the First Sub-section on the Foundations of Mindfulness within the Eighth Chapter, the Aggregate of Views (Dṛṣṭiskandha), Part Six. At that time, having spoken these words, the Blessed One entered the first dhyāna.
Proceeding in succession until he had entered the meditative attainment of cessation,
the Venerable Ānanda then asked the Venerable Aniruddha:
"Has the World-Honored One now entered parinirvāṇa?"
He replied, "Not yet;
he has merely entered the meditative attainment of cessation.
He asked again, "How do you know this?"
He replied, "I have heard directly from the Buddha:
'The World-Honored One has entered the fourth dhyāna and, relying on the immovable and tranquil concentration, has passed into parinirvāṇa; the Eye of the World has been extinguished.'"
Question: Does the Venerable Ānanda ask because he knows, or because he does not know?
If he knows, why does he ask again?
If he does not know, how can he be said to know the Buddha’s mind?
Some say that the Venerable One knew it.
[The interlocutor] asks: "If that is so, why did he ask again?"
Answer: There are also cases where one knows yet asks intentionally for the purpose of initiating a discourse.
As it is said: "The Blessed One, knowing, asked intentionally.
Furthermore, the Venerable Ānanda, wishing to manifest the superior virtues of the Venerable Aniruddha, asked even though he already knew.
It is said that although that venerable one possessed superior virtues, the assembly was unaware of them;
therefore, he asked this question so that they might know.
Some say:
That venerable one did not know it.
[The interlocutor] asks: "If that is so, how can he be said to know the Buddha's mind?

[The respondent] answers: "After the Buddha has emerged from meditative absorption, Ānanda knows his preceding state of mind; yet at that time [the venerable one] did not know it because the Buddha was still in absorption."
Furthermore, when that venerable one dwells in a state of mind characterized by permanence, he is able to know the Buddha’s mind;
however, at that time, because his own mind is shrouded and overwhelmed by two kinds of distress, he does not know the Buddha’s mind.
First is the sorrow and distress of losing one's kinsmen;
second is the sorrow and distress of losing the Great Teacher.
One asks: "Venerable Aniruddha, how do you know this?"
Some say:
"Because the Blessed One entered a meditative attainment (samāpatti) shared with the śrāvakas at the time of his parinirvāṇa, they were able to know it.
The critique states:
One should not speak thus;

for at that time, the Buddha was manifesting entry into meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti) that are unique and not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Question: If that is so, how does he know?
Answer: At that time, the Blessed One gives rise to a mind that enters and emerges from meditative absorption in common with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
he knows it by virtue of the fact that it is an object within their domain.
It is just as when a king of elephants crosses a deep river:
while he is actually in the middle of the river, no one knows [his whereabouts];
yet by observing the tracks of his entering and emerging from the water, one knows the places where the king of elephants has entered and emerged.
In this way, when the Blessed One abides in the river of profound meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*),
he cannot be seen directly by any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
they can only know his mind as it enters and emerges from concentration by observing the traces of his entry and emergence, like the footprints left in water.
Entering such a meditative absorption and emerging from such a meditative absorption—as it was said:
"At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa had this thought:
'By what means shall I extinguish the fire burning the Tathāgata’s body?'"
He then thought to himself,
"I should now extinguish this with fragrant milk.
As soon as he gave rise to this thought, four streams of fragrant milk descended from the sky, whereby the fire burning the Tathāgata’s body was extinguished all at once.
Question: Why must fragrant milk be used to extinguish the fire that cremates the Tathāgata’s body?
Answer: It is because one wishes to manifest a practice similar to that of the various *ṛṣis*.
That is to say, according to the custom of that country, when an *ṛṣi* passes away, the fire of his cremation is extinguished with milk.
If those who indulge in sensual desires die, they extinguish the fire of their bodies with wine.
Since the Buddha is the most excellent among all sages, he is the foremost of sages;
therefore, even now, he extinguishes the fire with fragrant milk.
Furthermore, because one wishes to make the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) utterly pure, one bathes them with milk.
Moreover, because the Buddha’s physical body was nurtured by milk,
his *śarīra* are now likewise bathed with milk.
Furthermore, the nature of milk is nourishing and yet it can extinguish fire;
whereas there are things whose nature is nourishing yet cannot extinguish fire,
but instead cause it to blaze more fiercely, such as ghee and oil.
There are substances that, although capable of extinguishing fire, are not inherently nourishing by nature—such as water, wine, and the like.
Only milk is both inherently nourishing and capable of extinguishing fire; therefore, milk alone is used.
For this reason, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa...
He manifested four streams of fragrant milk to extinguish the fire of the Tathāgata’s cremation.
As it is said: "At that time, seven days and nights after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Ānanda circumambulated the funeral pyre of the Tathāgata to the right."
He spoke these verses:
"A thousand robes were wrapped around the Buddha for his funeral;
only two robes did not burn—namely, the outer robe and the one next to his body. This is a most marvelous thing."
Question: For what reason were only the two robes of the World-Honored One not burned?
Answer: Because they were sustained by the majestic power of various devas and others who possessed faith and reverence for the Buddha, they were prevented from burning.
Some say that this is because it is sustained by the power of the Buddha’s vow, which causes both the internal and external to be pure.
That is to say, a single garment remains within, sustaining the Tathāgata’s *dhātu* so that it does not become scattered or defiled.
One garment is worn outside to prevent the ashes he carries from scattering and defiling others.
Some say this signifies that the Tathāgata’s True Dharma has two kinds of protection: internal and external.
Internal protection refers to pure bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others;
external protection refers to kings, ministers, and others who possess pure faith.
It is through the majestic power of the True Dharma that these are not consumed by fire.
Some say that this manifestation [indicates] that both the Tathāgata’s inner mind and outer body are pure. As for the purity of the mind,
it means that he has forever abandoned all afflictions along with their residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
"Purity of body" means being produced by the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma characterized by the most excellent marks.

This is as explained regarding the four states of existence (*bhava*): namely, the state of prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*), the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the state of birth (*upapattibhava*), and the state of death (*maraṇabhava*).
The term "existence" (*bhava*) has many meanings, as explained extensively above.
Here, the term "existence" refers to the five aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings within a commonality of type (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
What is "prior existence" (*pūrvabhava*)?
Answer: It refers to the various states of existence (*bhava*) between the aggregates of the phase of birth and the phase of death.
This [existence] has the five or four aggregates as its nature.
Question: Why is this existence called "fundamental existence" (*mūlabhava*)?
Answer: This is called "existence at birth" (*pūrvakālabhava*) because it is produced by karma created during the preceding period.
Question: If that is so, then the other forms of existence (*bhava*) would also be "existence at birth," since they too are produced by karma created during the preceding period.
Answer: If that which is produced by karma created in a previous time is coarse, manifest, easy to perceive, clear, and directly visible, it is called "existence from the beginning" (pūrvakālabhava).
Other things, although produced by karma created in a previous time, are subtle, hidden, difficult to perceive, and not clearly or directly visible; therefore, they are not so designated.
What is death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*)?
Answer: It consists of the aggregates at the stage of death; that is, its nature is the five aggregates or four aggregates at the time of passing away.
What is intermediate existence (*antarābhava*)?
Answer: Excluding the aggregates of the death-moment and the birth-moment, the intermediate states consist of the five aggregates existing between those two existences.
Question: For what reason is this existence called "intermediate existence" (antarābhava)?
Answer: Because this arises in the interval between two existences, it is called the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Question: If that is so, then other existences would also be intermediate existences, as they all arise in the interval between two existences.
Answer: If there is a birth between two existences that is not included within a realm of rebirth (*gati*), it is called the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Others, though born between two existences, are included within a realm of rebirth and are therefore not called the intermediate existence.
What is birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*)?
Answer: It consists of the aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), having the nature of five or four aggregates.
Question: How many moments and how many continuities do these four existences possess?
Answer: Two moments refer to death and birth; two continuities refer to the remaining forms of existence (*bhava*).
Question: Among these four existences, how many are defiled and how many are undefiled?
Answer: All are common to both types.
Question: Among these four types of minds associated with existence (*sattvabhava*), how many are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and how many are non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*)?
Answer: The mind at the moment of birth is exclusively defiled;
the remaining minds may be either defiled or non-defiled.
Question: Among these four [existences], how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
Answer: All are exclusively with outflows.
Question: At the time of these four existences, how many minds are with outflows and how many are without outflows?
Answer: Two are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), namely the mind at the time of death and the mind at the time of birth;
two are both contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), namely the remaining minds at other times.
Question: Among these four types of minds at specific times, how many arise as minds of the same class (*sabhāga*) and how many arise as minds of a different class (*tatsabhāga*)?
Answer: There are two cases where only minds of the same category (*sabhāga-citta*) arise: namely, at the time of death and at the time of birth.
There are two cases where both minds of the same category and minds of a different category (*tatsabhāga-citta*) arise: namely, at all other times.
Regarding the statement, "Do all those who possess desire possess all five modes of existence? and so forth, it is explained in detail.
In this context, the aggregates (skandhas) are spoken of by the term "formations" (saṃskāra).
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha of the past spoke of the aggregates as formations;
now the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, speaks of formations as the aggregates.
Because the former Buddha taught the five elements (*pañca-dhātu*) and the present Buddha teaches the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*),
this Abhidharma explains the five elements in order to show that the five aggregates taught by the present Buddha are identical to the five elements taught by the former Buddha.
Question: Why did previous Buddhas speak of the aggregates (*skandha*) as formations (*saṃskāra*), while the present Buddha speaks of formations as aggregates?
Answer: Because the Buddha teaches in accordance with the needs of the sentient beings he seeks to transform.

This means that those converted by previous Buddhas attain correct understanding upon hearing teachings on the "formations" (*saṃskāra*), whereas those converted by the present Buddha attain correct understanding upon hearing teachings on the "aggregates" (*skandha*).
Question: For what reason are they called "formations"?

Answer: They are called "formations" (*saṃskāra*) because they involve a process of flowing and turning. That is to say, the aggregates (*skandha*) of a preceding birth flow and turn by means of the aggregates of a succeeding birth, or the aggregates of a succeeding birth flow and turn by means of the aggregates of a preceding birth.

If one is born in the desire realm, a mind of the desire realm is a "concordant mind" (sabhāga-citta) because it shares the same category as that life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and its homogeneous class;
minds of the form realm, the formless realm, and the outflow-free (anāsrava) mind are "discordant minds" (tatsabhāga-citta).
Because it does not share the same life-faculty or the same group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) with them.
If one is born in the form realm, a mind of the form realm is its homogeneous mind (*sabhāga-citta*),
while minds of the desire realm, the formless realm, and the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind are its non-homogeneous minds (*visabhāga-citta*).
If one is born in the formless realm, taking a formless-realm mind as a homogeneous mind and an untainted mind as a non-homogeneous mind,
are all those in the desire realm of fivefold activity?
If one posits the five aggregates (skandhas), are they all the existence of desire (kāmadhātu)?
One should respond that there are four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are cases of the existence of desire that are not the five aggregates.

This refers to sentient beings of the desire realm who abide in a mind of a different category (*asabhāga-citta*) or who abide in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
At those times, because the existence of the desire realm consists of only two formations (*saṃskāra*),
there are five formations that do not constitute the existence of the desire realm.

This refers to those dwelling in the heavens of the form realm who possess perception and abide in a mind of homogeneous character (*sabhāga-citta*), as well as those in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) who have not yet attained the state of non-perception;
at that time, they all possess the five formations (*saṃskāra*). This refers to the state of possessing mind within that heaven of non-perception.
Because they certainly do not give rise to a mind of a different category (*asabhāga-citta*), those formations do not belong to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, there are five types of formations belonging to the realm of desire;
that is, sentient beings of the desire realm who abide in a mind of the same category (*sabhāga-citta*).
At that time, because the existence of desire (kāmadhātu-bhava) possesses the five aggregates,
there is an existence that is neither the existence of desire nor possessed of the five aggregates;

namely, the existence of the gods of the realm of form (rūpadhātu) who abide in a mind of a different category (visabhāga-citta), as well as those abiding in the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) or the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
If one attains the state of non-conception in the Heaven of Non-conception, or is born into the Formless Realm,
at that time there are only two, four, or one of the formations;
furthermore, those formations do not belong to the realm of desire.
Are all those belonging to the realm of form (rūpadhātu) who possess perception (saṃjñin) necessarily of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha)?
And are all those of the five aggregates necessarily those belonging to the realm of form who possess perception?
One should answer that this involves four permutations (catuṣkoṭika).
There are beings with form and with perception who do not possess the five aggregates;
namely, those gods of the form realm who abide in a dissimilar state of mind,
as well as those abiding in the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation.
At that time, because the gods of the realm of form who possess perception (rūpāvacara-saṃjñin) possess only two modes of activity,
there are five modes of activity that do not belong to the gods of the realm of form who possess perception;
namely, sentient beings of the desire realm who abide in a mind of homogeneous character (nikāya-sabhāga).
If those in the Heaven of Non-conception do not attain non-conception,
then although they all possess the five aggregates at that time,
those aggregates do not constitute the existence of form, because they are in the Heaven of Having Conception.
There are also form-sphere gods with perception who possess five factors; that is,
when a god in the form realm with perception abides in a mind of homogeneous character (*sabhāgata-citta*),
at that time the form-sphere god with perception is endowed with five factors.
There are those who possess neither form nor perception, and who also do not belong to the five aggregates;
namely, sentient beings of the desire realm who abide in a dissimilar state of mind,
as well as those abiding in the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation.
If one attains the state of non-perception in the Heaven of Non-perception, or is born in the Formless Realm,
at that time there are only two, four, or one of these formations. Furthermore,
those formations do not exist in the realm of form, nor among beings who possess perception.
Are all those who possess form in the Heaven of Non-perception (asaṃjñisattva) necessarily of both types of formations?
And are all those who are of both types of formations necessarily those who possess form in the Heaven of Non-perception?
One should answer by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).
There is a case where there is matter and the realm of non-perception (asaṃjñisattva), yet it does not possess both modes of activity.
This refers to when those in the realm of non-perception have not yet attained non-perception;
at that time, because they possess the five modes of activity, it is as previously stated.
There are two types of beings who possess the two [mental] courses but do not exist within the realm of form or the heaven of non-perception:
namely, sentient beings of the desire realm who abide in a dissimilar state of mind,
and those who abide in the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation.
If beings in the form realm who possess perception abide in a mind of a different category,
or abide in the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation,
then although both types of formations exist at that time, those formations do not belong to the form realm because they are [the realm of] non-perception.
There is a realm of form with non-percipient gods that also possesses two formations;
namely, when one attains non-perception in the non-percipient heaven,
at that time, that realm of form with non-percipient gods possesses only these two formations.
There are those who possess neither form nor the heaven of non-perception (asaṃjñika), nor do they possess both types of formations;

these are sentient beings of the desire realm, as well as those of the heaven of perception in the form realm abiding in a mind of homogeneous character (sabhāgata-citta), or those born in the formless realm.
At that time, there may be five modes of conduct, or four, or one.
Furthermore, those modes of conduct do not exist among the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu), because they are the realm of non-perception (asaṃjñisattva).
Are all those in the formless realms possessed of all four modes of conduct?
If one posits four modes of conduct, are they all present in the formless realm?
Answer: All those four modes of conduct are present in the formless realm;
it is not that sentient beings in the desire and form realms possess these four modes of conduct.
There is a formless existence that does not consist of the four modes of conduct;
namely, when sentient beings of the formless realm abide in a mind of a different category,
at that time, that formless existence consists of only one mode of conduct.
"Is there perhaps a fivefold [set of] elements?
and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is this treatise further composed?

Answer: Although the preceding text established that there is existence through two courses of action, it did not preclude the existence of three courses of action, nor did it establish the existence of one course of action.
Now, for the purpose of precluding the existence of three courses of action, [this is stated].
Furthermore, wishing to establish that there is an existence consisting of five modes of being (*pañca-bhava*), this treatise is composed.
Is there such an existence consisting of five modes of being?
Answer: There is.
This refers to sentient beings of the desire realm and those in the heavens of the form realm who possess perception, abiding in a mind of homogeneous character (*sabhāga-citta*).

Furthermore, if those in the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) do not attain the state of non-perception, they must necessarily possess the five present formations (*saṃskāra*) belonging to their own level.
Is there a fourfold classification?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, sentient beings of the formless realm abide in a mind of homogeneous character (*sabhāga-citta*).
Is there perhaps a triad of formations?
Answer: No, because no sentient being is established by means of three aggregates.

Why is this so? Because the mind and its mental factors are necessarily inseparable; since feeling, perception, volition, and so forth are always associated with one another, can there ever be two [mental states] that possess two distinct modes of activity?
Answer: Yes.

This refers to sentient beings of the desire realm, as well as those in the heavens of the form realm who possess perception and abide in a state of dissimilar mind (*visabhāga-citta*), or those abiding in the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
If those in the Heaven of Non-conception attain non-conception, it is because they possess only two types of formations (*saṃskāra*).
Is there perhaps anyone who possesses only one type?
Answer: There is.
This refers to sentient beings in the formless realm who abide in a mind of a different category;
they possess only one type of formation. Is there any case where there is no formation? Answer: No.
Because there is no sentient being that is not constituted by the aggregates (*skandha*),
and because all sentient beings necessarily possess the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth belonging to their own level (*svabhūmi*).

**The Second Section of the Eighth Chapter, the Aggregate of Views (*Dṛṣṭiskandha*), entitled "The Section on the Three Existences" (Part One):** Regarding those who abandon the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu-bhava*) and continue [their existence] within the existence of desire:
When all phenomena of the desire realm cease,
do phenomena of the desire realm manifest?
Having thus mastered these chapters and the meaning of their explanations, [one should proceed].
This should be explained in detail; however, the term "existence" (*bhava*) refers to many meanings.
Here, it refers to the five aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings within a common destiny (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
This is as when it is said, "dying in the desire realm and being reborn in the desire realm."
"Is all that a continuity of desire-existence (*kāmadhātu-bhava*)?
and so forth, as explained at length.

He also states that "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) belonging to the category of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*) within a particular homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
As it is said, for those in the hells who are bound by the various *paryavasthānas*, there is a continuity;

the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and primary elements (*mahābhūta*) first acquired therein serve as the single dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for these mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, as it is said, when there is the continuity of existence (*bhava*),
how many sense-faculties produced by karma (*karmaja-indriya*) are first obtained?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, it is as when the four types of existence (*bhava*) are taught:
namely, existence at birth (*upapatti-bhava*), existence at death (*maraṇa-bhava*), intermediate existence (*antarā-bhava*), and fundamental existence (*pūrva-kāla-bhava*).
One should know that those passages all explain that the five aggregates belonging to the category of sentient beings within a common destiny (*nikāya-sabhāga*) are called "existence" (*bhava*).
For example, it is said that the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*), induced by the *phalguṇa* [seed], is capable of bringing about the manifestation of future existence.
He explains that at the time of rebirth, the mind and its attendants are called "existence" (bhava).
As it was said to Ānanda:
"In this way, karmic existence is able to draw forth future existence."
He explains that the volition which draws one toward future existence is called "existence" (*bhava*).
As it is said, "with grasping as condition, there is existence," he explains that existence refers to the five aggregates in their specific state.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka states:
That [text] explains that karma which draws one toward future existence is called "existence" (*bhava*).
As it says: "What is the dharma of existence? It refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas.
That [text] explains that all contaminated dharmas are called "existence."

As it is said, there are seven types of existence (*bhava*): existence in the hells, existence as animals, existence in the realm of hungry ghosts, existence as humans, existence as gods, existence as karma, and intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
These are called "existence" because they comprise the five destinies (*gati*), the causes of the five destinies, and the means for reaching the five destinies.
As it is said: "What is the existence of desire?
It refers to karma that can induce rebirth in the desire realm," and so forth, as explained at length.
They state that karma and its maturation (vipāka) are called "existence" (bhava), but they do not say that the object of grasping (ālambana-upādāna) is existence.
Question: If this is so, how should one interpret what they later state?
As it is said: "In the desire realm, all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with the desires," and so forth, at length.

Since there are five categories of karma in the desire realm that are all capable of producing maturation (*vipāka*), one may say that all latent dispositions of the desire realm increase in accordance with them.
In the realms of form and formlessness, only karma to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) can produce maturation (*vipāka*).
How, then, can it be said that all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the realms of form and formlessness increase in association with them?
The answer should be stated as follows in the subsequent text:
"In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), all latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) increase;
in the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are the universal [proclivities] of the realms of form and formlessness."
Furthermore, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase therein; this is how it should be stated.
That it is not so stated should be understood as meaning that "existence" (*bhava*) and its attendants (*saparivāra*) are both designated by the term "existence."
Because that which is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) through its combination [of causes] is also called "existence" (*bhava*). Other masters say:
"What was previously described as karma and its maturation (*vipāka*) is called existence."
It is not said that the existence of the object of grasping (*ālambana-bhava*) is [the same as] existence;
later, it is said that karma and its maturation (*vipāka*) are called existence,
and it is also said that the existence of the object of grasping is [existence].
They should not speak in this way:
"For those who compose treatises,
when they establish gates based on chapters, it is not the case that what is stated in one chapter must differ from what is stated in another gate."
Therefore, that which was stated previously is correct.
Question: For what reason is it called "existence" (bhava)?
Answer: It is called existence because it can be existent and can be non-existent.
Question: If that were so, the Noble Path should be called "existent," because the Noble Path is both capable of being existent and capable of being non-existent.
Answer: That which is capable of being existent and capable of being non-existent, yet which nourishes, benefits, and sustains all forms of existence (*bhava*), is called "existent."
Although the Noble Path is capable of existence and yet is not existence itself, it is not called "existence" because it destroys, damages, and disperses all forms of existence (*bhava*).

Furthermore, if that which is capable of existence and yet is not existence can cause the continuity of all existences to flow on, such that the path of old age and death is not severed, it is called "existence."
Although the Noble Path has the capacity to cause various forms of existence (*bhava*) not to continue or to circulate,
because it is the path that severs old age and death, it is not called "existence. Furthermore,
if that which has the capacity to cause existence were itself an existence, it would be a course toward the origin of suffering, a course toward existence, and the world.
The practice that accumulates birth-and-death and old age-and-death within the cycle of transmigration is called "existence" (*bhava*).
Although the Noble Path possesses the capacity [to bring about cessation], it is not "existence";

rather, because it is the practice that leads toward the cessation of suffering and the cessation of the cycle of transmigration, birth-anddeath, and old-age-and-death within the world of existence, it is not called "existence."
Furthermore, if there were both existence and non-existence,
that would be the basis for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the basis for perversion, the basis for latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
and the basis for craving; it would be the ground upon which greed, hatred, and delusion take their stand.

That which is accompanied by defilement (*sāsrava*), possessed of poison (*saviṣa*), and subsumed under all [phenomena], falling within the truths of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-satya*), is called "existence" (*bhava*).

Although the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) possesses the capacity [to lead to cessation], it is not "existence"; nor is it the objective basis for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) up to the objective basis for craving (*tṛṣṇā*), nor is it the locus for the settling of greed, hatred, and delusion.
It is stainless, undefiled, unclouded, and non-toxic; it is not comprised within the realms of existence (*bhava*).
Because it does not fall under the truths of suffering and its origin, it is not called "existence" (*bhava*).
Other masters say:
Because it is an instrument of suffering, it is called "existence" (*bhava*).
Question: If that is so, this too is an instrument of pleasure.
As it is said: "O Mahānāman, if form were exclusively suffering—not pleasure, nor conducive to pleasure, nor increasing joy and happiness..."
If it were solely the cause for the departure from pleasure, then sentient beings would not give rise to craving or defilement toward form.
Mahānāman, because form is not exclusively suffering, but is also pleasure, conducive to pleasure, and increases joy and happiness.
It is not merely because they lack the causes of pleasure that sentient beings give rise to craving and defilement toward form;
furthermore, the Buddha has definitively established that the three feelings are distinct and non-confounded.
That is to say, there are pleasant feelings, painful feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
Since such tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are likewise instruments of pleasure,
why are they called "tainted" (*sāsrava*) solely on account of being instruments of suffering?
The answer is that suffering is predominant.
That is to say, within the cycle of birth and death, suffering is abundant while happiness is scarce; factors conducive to suffering are many, whereas factors conducive to happiness are few.
Because happiness is so scarce, it is categorized under the heading of suffering.
Just as a single drop of honey falling into a vessel of poison does not cause it to be called a vessel of honey,
but is still called a vessel of poison because the poison is predominant, so too is this case.
Furthermore, there are those who say that it is called "existence" (bhava) because it is to be feared.
Question: If that were so, then nirvāṇa should also be called [existence].
As it has been said: "There are certain classes of foolish persons, unlearned worldlings among the bhikṣus, who conceive a great fear regarding nirvāṇa, thinking:
'I shall not exist; mine shall not exist; I will not be; mine will not be.'"
If one has already conceived fear toward nirvāṇa, then nirvāṇa should also be called "existent.
Answer: To have fear toward existence is correct;
to conceive fear toward nirvāṇa is erroneous.
Because nirvāṇa is not something to be feared,
it is therefore not called "existence" (bhava).
Furthermore, that which causes both ordinary beings and noble ones to feel fear is what is called "existence."
Nirvāṇa is not said to have five types of continuity because it causes ordinary beings to feel fear. These five are:
first, the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*);
second, the continuity of birth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
Third, the continuity of stages;
fourth, the continuity of dharmas;
fifth, the continuity of moments.
Regarding the continuity within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*):
it refers to the cessation of the aggregates of the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) and the arising of the aggregates of the intermediate existence.
Because the aggregates of the death-existence are said to form a continuity by means of the aggregates of the intermediate existence, it is called the "continuity of the intermediate state."
Regarding the continuity of the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*):
this refers to the cessation of the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the arising of the aggregates of the existence of birth.
Because the aggregates of the intermediate state are said to form a continuity by means of the aggregates of the existence of birth, it is called the "continuity of the existence of birth."
Regarding the continuity of stages:
this refers to the cessation of the stage of the *kalala* and the arising of the stage of the *arbuda*.
The stage of the *kalala* is said to be continuous by way of the stage of the *arbuda*.
Thus, up until the stage of middle age ceases and the stage of old age arises,
the stage of middle age is designated as "continuity" by virtue of the stage of old age; therefore,
it is called the continuity of states (*avasthā-saṃtati*).
Regarding the continuity of phenomena (*dharmasaṃtati*):
it refers to the manifestation of defiled or indeterminate phenomena immediately following wholesome phenomena.
Wholesome phenomena are said to be "continuous" by virtue of being followed by defiled or indeterminate phenomena.
When defiled dharmas and indeterminate dharmas each manifest immediately after one another in two ways, and the detailed explanation is likewise,
it is therefore called the "continuity of dharmas.
As for the "continuity of moments," a subsequent moment manifests immediately after a preceding moment.
Because a preceding moment is designated as a "continuity" by virtue of the succeeding moment, it is called a "momentary continuity.
These five continuities are all subsumed within two types of continuity:
namely, the continuity of phenomena (*dharma-saṃtati*) and the continuity of moments (*kṣaṇa-saṃtati*).
Because the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*), the states (*avasthā*), and the continuity (*saṃtati*) are all termed "dharmas" and "moments" (*kṣaṇa*).
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all five types of continuity are present;
in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are four, excluding the state of existence.
In the formless realm, there are three [types of birth], excluding intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and birth by transformation (*aupapāduka*);
in the heavens, the hells, and among those born by transformation, there are four, excluding birth by transformation;
in all other cases, all five are present.
Some say that gods and those born by transformation also possess the five continuities;
among these five continuities:
In this context, the discussion is based on two continuums,
namely the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*). This refers to those who abandon the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
If there is a continuity of desire-existence,
does all that which is a phenomenon of the desire realm cease,
and do phenomena of the desire realm manifest?
Answer: For all those who abandon existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-bhava*),
when that existence is continuous, all phenomena (*dharma*) of the desire realm cease and phenomena of the desire realm manifest before them.
This refers to one who, having died in the desire realm and being reborn again in the desire realm,
relinquishes the existence of the desire realm at the moment of passing from the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
The "death-existence" (maranabhava) refers to the death-existence of the desire realm.
The "intermediate existence" (antarābhava) that continues the stream of existence in the desire realm refers to the intermediate existence of the desire realm.
The "cessation of phenomena" of the desire realm refers to the aggregates (skandhas) of the death-existence in the desire realm.
Dharmas of the desire realm that are present refers to the various aggregates within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm.
As for "when one transmigrates from the intermediate state and abandons existence in the desire realm," this refers to the intermediate state of the desire realm.
The continuity of existence in the desire realm refers to the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) of the desire realm.
The cessation of phenomena in the desire realm refers to the various aggregates (*skandha*) within the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm.
The phenomena of the desire realm that appear before one refers to the aggregates of the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) within the desire realm.

Question: If one who dwells in the desire realm dies while abiding in an unobscured-neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*), at the time of abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), [what occurs]?
One does not possess the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) while abiding in the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*).
One cannot be said to "abandon" the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) while abiding in it.
However, if one dies while abiding in a wholesome or defiled state of mind, [one abandons it] while abiding in the intermediate existence.
One possesses the existence at death;
while abiding in the existence at birth,
one possesses the intermediate existence.
What is meant by "equanimity"?
Some say that,
in this context, it refers specifically to those who pass away while abiding in an unobscured-neutral state of mind.
Therefore, there is no fault. Some say that here it is spoken in reference to the abandonment of active manifestation (*samudācāra*);

although one abides in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), one possesses the death-existence (*cyuty-bhava*), and while abiding in the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*), one possesses the intermediate existence.
Because they do not manifest, it is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Some say that in this context,
turning away from the preceding aggregates is what is termed equanimity.
It does not speak of the meaning of accomplishment or non-accomplishment.
There are dharmas of the desire realm that cease and dharmas of the desire realm that manifest,
yet there is neither the relinquishing of the existence of desire nor the continuity of the existence of desire.
What is meant by the cessation of dharmas of the desire realm and the manifestation of dharmas of the desire realm without one’s life having ended?
It refers to the immediate succession of the *arbuda* stage following the *kalala* stage.
Up until the stage of middle age, the stage of old age manifests immediately thereafter.
Immediately after wholesome states, defiled or indeterminate states manifest;
immediately after defiled states, wholesome or indeterminate states manifest.
Immediately after an indeterminate dharma, wholesome or defiled dharmas manifest;
immediately after a preceding moment, the subsequent moment manifests;
and the continuity of the form realm arises from the relinquishing of the desire realm.
When all dharmas of the desire realm cease and dharmas of the form realm manifest, is that so?

Answer: For all those who, having abandoned the existence of the desire realm, continue in the existence of the form realm, when all dharmas of the desire realm cease, dharmas of the form realm manifest.
This refers to one who dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the form realm;
at the moment of passing from the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), one abandons the existence of the desire realm—
that is, the death-existence of the desire realm.
The continuity of form refers to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The cessation of dharmas of the desire realm refers to the aggregates (*skandha*) of the death-existence (*maraṇabhava*) in the desire realm.
The manifestation of dharmas of the form realm refers to the aggregates of the intermediate existence in the form realm.
There are cases where dharmas of the desire realm cease and dharmas of the form realm manifest,
yet there is no relinquishing of the existence of desire and the continuity of the existence of form.
What is the manner of this, wherein one does not die, dharmas of the desire realm cease, and dharmas of the form realm manifest?
Regarding this, some say that immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm, the preparatory concentration (anāgamya) manifests. Others say:
Immediately following a wholesome mind of the desire realm, the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*),
the first dhyāna, or— according to some— the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) manifests.
The Venerable Ghosaka stated:
"Immediately following a wholesome mind of the desire realm, the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*), the first dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna, or the second dhyāna may manifest."
Why is this? Just as when one transcends the meditative absorptions,
the third dhyāna manifests immediately after the first dhyāna, so too should it be here.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) in the desire realm, namely:
those that are the fruits of the first dhyāna up to those that are the fruits of the fourth dhyāna.
Immediately following a transformative mind that is the fruit of the first dhyāna within the desire realm, a pure (*śuddha*) first dhyāna manifests before one.
Up to the point where, immediately after a mind of transformation that is the fruit of the fourth dhyāna of the desire realm, a pure fourth dhyāna manifests;
[this applies to] all those who abandon the continuity of existence in the desire realm and the formless realm.
When all dharmas of the desire realm cease, do dharmas of the formless realm manifest?
Answer: It is so.
Furthermore, when dharmas of the desire realm cease, do dharmas of the formless realm manifest?
Does that [person] abandon all continuity of existence in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Answer: It is so.
Question: Why is it not stated here that "without dying, the phenomena of the realm of desire cease"?
Is it possible for a dharma of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) to manifest while one is currently in the formless realm?

Answer: Logically, this is impossible; for there is no case where one does not pass away from the formless realm and yet causes a dharma of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to cease while a dharma of the formless realm manifests.

Question: Is it not possible that one does not die while remaining in the desire realm, yet an attainment of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) manifests while an attainment of the desire realm is present?
Answer: In this context, it is stated that when a homogeneous dharma ceases, a homogeneous dharma manifests.
There is no case where, while remaining in the desire realm,
one’s homogeneous dharmas of the desire realm cease without passing away,
yet the homogeneous dharmas of the formless realm arise and manifest; therefore, this is not mentioned.
Some say: "In this context, it is said that the mind and mental factors cease.

Since there are no mind and mental factors present [in the intermediate state], there is no case where one has not yet died in the desire realm and yet the mind and mental factors of the desire realm cease."
Because the mind and mental factors of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are not present [in those states], they are not mentioned.
Regarding all those who abandon the form existence (*rūpabhava*) and continue in the form existence:
do all of them have the phenomena of the form realm (*rūpadharmas*) cease and the phenomena of the form realm manifest?
Answer: All those who abandon form yet possess form and possess continuity, for them all dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the form realm manifest;
that is to say, one dies in the form realm and is reborn again in the form realm.
When proceeding from the existence at death (*cyuty-bhava*) to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*),
that which abandons the existence of form (*rūpa-bhava*) refers to the existence at death in the realm of form;
that which continues the succession of the existence of form refers to the intermediate existence in the realm of form.
The cessation of the dharmas of the form realm refers to the aggregates of the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) in the form realm.
