The manifestation of the dharmas of the form realm refers to the aggregates of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) in the form realm.
From this intermediate existence, there is the transition to the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*).
"Abandoning the existence of form" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the realm of form.
"The continuity of the existence of form" refers to the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) of the realm of form.
"The cessation of the phenomena of the realm of form" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*) within the intermediate state of the realm of form.
The phenomena of the form realm that appear before one refers to the aggregates of the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) within the form realm.
Among these, whether one dies while abiding in an unobscured-neutral mind,
or while abiding in a wholesome or defiled mind, it is in all such cases termed "abandoning the existence of form" (*rūpabhava*).
The distinctions between the questions and answers should be understood as previously explained.
There are cases where dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the form realm manifest,
yet there is no relinquishing of the possession of form, and the continuity of form exists.
This refers to the cessation of dharmas of the form realm without passing away, and the manifestation of dharmas of the form realm being present before one. What is the process of this?
It is that immediately after the first dhyāna, the second and third dhyānas manifest.
Immediately following the second dhyāna, the first, third, and fourth dhyānas manifest.
Immediately following the third dhyāna, the first, second, and fourth dhyānas manifest.
Immediately after the fourth dhyāna, the second and third dhyānas manifest.
Immediately after wholesome dharmas, defiled or neutral dharmas manifest.
The same applies to the manifestation of defiled and neutral dharmas.
The subsequent moment arises immediately after the preceding moment.
When the continuity of those who have abandoned existence in the form realm (*rūpabhava*) and existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) occurs,
is it the case that all dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the desire realm arise?
Answer: For all those who, having abandoned form, continue their existence with desire, there is the cessation of all dharmas of the form realm and the manifestation of dharmas of the desire realm;
that is to say, when one dies in the form realm and is reborn in the desire realm.
When proceeding from the existence at death (*cyuty-bhava*) to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*),
"abandoning the existence of form" refers to the existence at death in the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*),
while "the continuity of the existence of desire" refers to the intermediate existence in the realm of desire (*kāma-dhātu*).
The cessation of dharmas of the form realm refers to the aggregates of the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) in the form realm.
The manifestation of dharmas of the desire realm refers to the aggregates of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) in the desire realm.
Thus, there is the cessation of dharmas of the form realm and the manifestation of dharmas of the desire realm.
It is not that the continuity of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is abandoned;
rather, how is it that without passing away, the phenomena of the form realm cease and the phenomena of the desire realm manifest? What is the manner of this occurrence?
Regarding this, some say that immediately after the *anāgamya* concentration, a wholesome mind of the desire realm manifests; others say:
The wholesome mind of the desire realm manifests immediately after the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*) and the first dhyāna;
some say that it also manifests immediately after the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
The Venerable Ghosaka stated:

"In the access concentration (*anāgamya*), the first dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the second dhyāna, the wholesome mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) manifests immediately after [the cessation of the meditative state]."
Why is this so? It is because when one transcends meditative absorption, the first dhyāna manifests immediately after the third dhyāna; this case should be understood in the same way.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) in the desire realm.
This refers to the fruits of the first dhyāna up to the fruits of the fourth dhyāna.
Immediately following the pure (śuddha) first dhyāna, the transformation mind (nirmāṇacitta) that is the fruit of the first dhyāna belonging to the desire realm manifests.
Up until the point when, immediately after the pure fourth dhyāna, the transformation mind (nirmāṇacitta) which is the fruit of the fourth dhyāna of the desire realm manifests before one;
[this occurs] for those who are abandoning the existence of form and continuing the existence of the formless.
Do all those for whom dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the formless realm manifest?

Answer: For all those who relinquish existence in the form realm and take up continuity in existence in the formless realm, all dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the formless realm manifest.
This refers to the transition from death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) in the form realm to birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) in the formless realm.
"Abandoning the existence of form" refers to death-existence in the form realm;
"the continuity of formless existence" refers to birth-existence in the formless realm.
The cessation of dharmas of the form realm refers to the aggregates of the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) in the form realm.
The manifestation of dharmas of the formless realm refers to the aggregates of the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) in the formless realm.
There are cases where dharmas of the form realm cease and dharmas of the formless realm manifest,
yet there is no relinquishing of existence in the form realm and no continuity of existence in the formless realm;
that is to say, one does not die while the dharmas of the form realm are ceasing.
What is the manner in which the dharmas of the formless realm manifest?
It is as follows: immediately after the third dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space manifests;
immediately after the fourth dhyāna, the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness manifest.
Regarding all those who relinquish existence in the formless realm and take up a continuity of existence in the formless realm:
do all such individuals have dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the formless realm manifest?
Answer: Regarding all those who relinquish existence in the formless realm and take up a continuity of existence in the formless realm...
All those dharmas of the formless realm cease,
and dharmas of the formless realm manifest before them; that is to say,
one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn again in the formless realm.
From the moment of death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) until the moment of birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*):
"abandoning formless existence" refers to the death-existence of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*);
"the continuity of formless existence" refers to the birth-existence of the formless realm.
The cessation of dharmas of the formless realm refers to the aggregates of the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) in the formless realm.
The manifestation of dharmas of the formless realm refers to the aggregates of the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) in the formless realm.

There are cases where dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the formless realm manifest in the present, yet there is no relinquishing of the existence of the formless realm and no continuation of the existence of the formless realm.
That is to say, without passing away, dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the formless realm manifest in the present; what is the nature of this occurrence?
That is to say: immediately after the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception manifest.
Immediately after the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception manifest.
The sphere of nothingness immediately precedes the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception as they manifest.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception immediately precedes the spheres of infinite consciousness and nothingness as they manifest.
Immediately after wholesome dharmas, defiled or neutral dharmas manifest.
The same is said for defiled and neutral dharmas.
Immediately following the preceding moment, the succeeding moment manifests.
Is it the case that for all those who abandon the formless existence and continue in the existence with desire, all formless-realm dharmas cease and desire-realm dharmas manifest?
Answer: It is so.

If the dharmas of the formless realm cease and the dharmas of the desire realm manifest before one, does all that relinquishing of existence in the formless realm result in the continuity of existence in the desire realm?
Answer: It is so.
Question: Why is it not stated here that, without dying, the dharmas of the formless realm cease and the dharmas of the desire realm manifest?
Answer: By principle, it is necessarily impossible to remain in the formless realm without dying.
However, because there are dharmas of the formless realm that cease and dharmas of the desire realm manifest in the present,
the remaining questions and answers are as before.
In all cases, there is a continuity of both the formless and the formed.

When all dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the form realm manifest, is it the case that for all those who abandon the formless and possess the form with continuity, all dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the form realm manifest? Answer:
For all those who abandon the formless and possess the form with continuity, all dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the form realm manifest.
This refers to one who dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the form realm.

At the moment of passing from the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), one abandons the formless existence; that is to say, the death-existence of the formless realm.
The continuity of form refers to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the form realm.
The cessation of phenomena of the formless realm refers to the aggregates of the death-existence (*maraṇabhava*) in the formless realm.
The manifestation of phenomena of the form realm refers to the aggregates of the intermediate existence in the form realm.
There are cases where dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the form realm manifest in the present, yet there is no abandonment of the continuity of the formless or the form.
That is to say, how is it that one does not die, yet dharmas of the formless realm cease and dharmas of the form realm manifest? What is the nature of this occurrence?
That is to say, the fourth dhyāna manifests immediately after the sphere of infinite consciousness;
the third and fourth dhyānas manifest immediately after the sphere of infinite space.
Having already analyzed the meaning according to the root text, one should now further analyze it extensively in accordance with that meaning.
Question: If one dies in the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm, what does that person relinquish, what does he obtain, what dharmas cease, and what dharmas manifest?
Furthermore, if one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the form realm, what does that person relinquish, what do they obtain, what dharmas cease, and what dharmas manifest?
Answer: This applies to those who die in the desire realm and are reborn again in the desire realm.
If one who abides in the Prātimokṣa restraint has no unwholesome bodily or vocal intimation,
or even if such intimation existed but has already been lost, and he dies while abiding in a wholesome state of mind,
he abandons two wholesome aggregates and two neutral aggregates.
When the indeterminate aggregates arise,
two [sets] occur: at that very moment, the five wholesome aggregates and one defiled aggregate cease,
while one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
If one dies while abiding in a defiled state of mind,
they relinquish two wholesome aggregates and two neutral aggregates,
and acquire two neutral aggregates.
At that very moment, two wholesome aggregates, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
If one passes away while abiding in a neutral state of mind,
they relinquish two neutral aggregates and five wholesome aggregates,
and acquire two neutral aggregates.
At that very moment, two wholesome aggregates, one defiled aggregate, and five indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest in the present.
If, moreover, one who possesses unwholesome bodily or vocal intimation does not lose it,
and then passes away while abiding in a wholesome state of mind,
they relinquish two wholesome aggregates, two defiled aggregates, and two neutral aggregates.
When the two neutral aggregates are attained,
at that time the five wholesome aggregates and the two defiled aggregates cease,
while one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two neutral aggregates manifest.
If one dies while abiding in a defiled state of mind,
they relinquish two aggregates of the wholesome, two aggregates of the defiled, and two aggregates of the indeterminate;
they acquire two aggregates of the indeterminate.
At that time, the two wholesome aggregates, the five defiled aggregates, and the two indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
If one passes away while abiding in a neutral state of mind,
one relinquishes five aggregates— two wholesome, two defiled,
and two neutral— and acquires two neutral aggregates.
At that time, the two wholesome aggregates, the two defiled aggregates, and the five indeterminate aggregates cease;
the one wholesome aggregate, the four defiled aggregates, and the two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
If one who originally abided in non-restraint lacks virtuous bodily or vocal intimation,
or even if such intimation was previously present but has been lost,
should they die while abiding in a virtuous state of mind.
He abandons two defiled aggregates and two indeterminate aggregates,
and acquires two indeterminate aggregates.
Thus, at that time, four wholesome aggregates, two defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates cease.
One wholesome aggregate and four indeterminate defiled aggregates are present.
If one passes away while abiding in a defiled mind, [these aggregates are present].
He abandons two defiled aggregates and two neutral aggregates;
he acquires two neutral aggregates.
Thus, at that time, there is one wholesome aggregate.
The five defiled aggregates and two neutral aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two neutral aggregates manifest.
This occurs when one passes away while abiding in a neutral state of mind.
He abandons two defiled aggregates and five neutral aggregates,
and acquires two neutral aggregates.
Thus, at that time, one wholesome aggregate, two defiled aggregates, and five neutral aggregates cease.
One wholesome aggregate and four defiled aggregates, along with two neutral aggregates, are manifested.
If those [defiled states] possess unimpaired wholesome bodily or vocal intimation (*kāya-vāk-vijñapti*),
and if one passes away while abiding in a wholesome mind, the details are as extensively explained in the section on abiding in the Prātimokṣa vows.
There is an explanation regarding unwholesome bodily and vocal intimation:
if one originally abides in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, and possesses unwholesome bodily or vocal intimations which have already been lost.
If one dies while abiding in a wholesome state of mind,
they relinquish two neutral aggregates and acquire two neutral aggregates.
At that time, four wholesome aggregates and one defiled aggregate cease,
while one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
If one passes away while abiding in a defiled mind,
they relinquish two acquisitions of the indeterminate aggregates and [attain] two acquisitions of the indeterminate aggregates;
at that time, one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates cease.
When one in whom a wholesome aggregate is present has the four defiled aggregates and two indeterminate aggregates manifest before them; or,
if one passes away while abiding in an indeterminate state of mind,
they relinquish five indeterminate aggregates.
When two indeterminate aggregates are attained,
at that time one wholesome aggregate and one defiled aggregate cease,
while one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
If that person possesses wholesome bodily and vocal intimation which has not been lost,
or if they lack unwholesome bodily and vocal intimation even if it has already been lost,
and they die while abiding in a wholesome, defiled, or neutral state of mind; [then...]
Just as in the case of one abiding in the prātimokṣa restraint,
it is taught that if there are no unwholesome bodily or vocal intimation (*vijñapti*), or if those already lost, one dies while abiding in any of the three types of mind; likewise,
if there are unwholesome bodily or vocal intimations that have not been lost, or if wholesome bodily or vocal intimations are absent or already lost.
If one dies while abiding in a wholesome, defiled, or neutral state of mind—
just as it was explained for one who dies while abiding in non-restraint (asamvara) where wholesome bodily and vocal informative acts (*vijñapti*) may have been lost—
it is said that one dies while abiding in these three types of minds.
If, moreover, one has not lost the virtuous or non-virtuous bodily and vocal intimation,
then even if one dies while abiding in a virtuous, defiled, or neutral state of mind,
it is just as in the case of one abiding in the prātimokṣa vows.
It is said that one who possesses non-virtuous bodily or vocal informative action (*vijñapti*) without losing it,
as well as one who abides in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) and possesses virtuous bodily or vocal informative action without losing it,
dies while abiding in any of the three types of mind.
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School,
Volume 192; Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume 193.
Compiled by the Five Hundred Great Arhats and others;

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section Eight: The Aggregate of Views (Dṛṣṭiskandha), Part Two of the Second Sub-section on the Three Existences (Trisaṃyojananirdeśa). Those who die in the Desire Realm and are reborn in the First Dhyāna.
Whether one originally abides in the prātimokṣa vows or does not abide in the prātimokṣa vows,
provided that there is a wholesome bodily or vocal intimation (vijñapti) that has not been lost.
If one dies while abiding in a wholesome state of mind,
they relinquish five wholesome aggregates and two indeterminate aggregates;
some say this.
Five are wholesome aggregates and four are indeterminate aggregates.
At that very time, five wholesome aggregates and one defiled aggregate, as well as two indeterminate aggregates, cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest in the present.
If one dies while abiding in an indeterminate state of mind,
they relinquish five aggregates of the wholesome and five aggregates of the indeterminate;
they acquire four aggregates of the wholesome and two aggregates of the indeterminate.
At that very moment, two wholesome aggregates, one defiled aggregate, and five indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest in the present.
If one has not originally abided in the prātimokṣa restraint,
and lacks virtuous bodily or vocal intimation— or even if such intimation was previously present but has been lost—
if one dies while abiding in a virtuous state of mind.
He abandons four aggregates of the wholesome and two aggregates of the indeterminate.
Some say that five [aggregates] are obtained: four of the wholesome and two of the indeterminate.
At that time, four wholesome aggregates and one defiled aggregate cease,
while one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
If one dies while abiding in an indeterminate state of mind,
they relinquish four aggregates of the wholesome and five aggregates of the indeterminate;
they acquire four aggregates of the wholesome and two aggregates of the indeterminate.
At that very time, one wholesome aggregate, one defiled aggregate, and five indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
Those who die in the desire realm and are born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna—
whether they originally abide in the prātimokṣa vows or do not abide in the prātimokṣa vows.
There are those who do not lose their wholesome bodily and verbal intimation:
if one dies while abiding in a wholesome state of mind,
they relinquish five wholesome aggregates and five neutral aggregates.
One acquires four wholesome aggregates and two neutral aggregates.
At that very moment, the five wholesome aggregates and one defiled aggregate cease, while one wholesome aggregate,
four defiled aggregates, and two neutral aggregates manifest in the present.
If one passes away while abiding in a neutral state of mind,
they relinquish five wholesome aggregates and five neutral aggregates,
and acquire four wholesome aggregates and two neutral aggregates.
At that very moment, two wholesome aggregates, one defiled aggregate, and five indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
If one has not originally abided in the prātimokṣa vows,
and lacks wholesome bodily or vocal intimation— or even if such intimation was previously present but has since been lost—
and yet dies while abiding in a wholesome state of mind.
He abandons five wholesome aggregates and five indeterminate aggregates;
he acquires four wholesome aggregates and two indeterminate aggregates.
At that very moment, four wholesome aggregates, one defiled aggregate, and two indeterminate aggregates cease.
When the one wholesome aggregate and the four defiled aggregates are present, along with the two indeterminate aggregates—
if one dies while abiding in an indeterminate state of mind—
one relinquishes the five wholesome aggregates and the five indeterminate aggregates.
One acquires four wholesome aggregates and two neutral aggregates.
At that very moment, one wholesome aggregate, one defiled aggregate, and five neutral aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two neutral aggregates manifest in the present.
Those who die in the desire realm and are reborn in the formless realm—
whether they originally abided in the prātimokṣa vows or did not abide in the prātimokṣa vows.
There is one who possesses wholesome bodily and vocal intimation that is not lost.
If such a person passes away while abiding in a wholesome state of mind,
they relinquish five wholesome aggregates and five indeterminate aggregates.
One acquires four wholesome aggregates and one indeterminate aggregate.
At that very moment, the five wholesome aggregates and one defiled aggregate cease, while one wholesome aggregate,
four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate manifest in the present.
If one passes away while abiding in a neutral state of mind,
one relinquishes five aggregates of the wholesome and five aggregates of the neutral;
one acquires four aggregates of the wholesome and one aggregate of the neutral.
At that very moment, two wholesome aggregates, one defiled aggregate, and five indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate manifest in the present.
If one has not originally abided in the prātimokṣa restraint,
and lacks virtuous bodily or vocal intimation— or even if such intimation was previously present but has been lost—
if one dies while abiding in a virtuous mind.
He abandons five aggregates of the wholesome and five aggregates of the indeterminate;
he acquires four aggregates of the wholesome and one aggregate of the indeterminate.
At that very moment, four wholesome aggregates and one defiled aggregate of the indeterminate cease.
When one wholesome aggregate and four defiled aggregates of the indeterminate class are present,
if one passes away while abiding in an indeterminate state of mind,
one relinquishes five wholesome aggregates and five indeterminate aggregates.
One acquires four wholesome aggregates and one indeterminate aggregate.
At that very time, one wholesome aggregate, one defiled aggregate, and five indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate manifest in the present.
Regarding those who die in the various realms of form and are reborn again in the realms of form—
specifically those who pass away from this very stage and are reborn in this very stage—
if they die while abiding in a wholesome state of mind:
He abandons two neutral aggregates and acquires two neutral aggregates;
at that very moment, four wholesome aggregates and one defiled aggregate cease, while two neutral aggregates arise.
When one with a wholesome mind manifests one defiled aggregate and four indeterminate aggregates,
or when one dies while abiding in a defiled mind,
they relinquish two indeterminate aggregates.
Regarding the acquisition of the two indeterminate aggregates:
at that very moment, one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates cease;
and one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
If one dies while abiding in a neutral state of mind,
one abandons five neutral aggregates and acquires two neutral aggregates.
At that very time, one wholesome aggregate, one defiled aggregate, and five indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
Regarding one who passes away from a lower level of the form realm and is reborn in a higher level:
if they die while abiding in a wholesome state of mind,
they relinquish five wholesome aggregates and five neutral aggregates.
One acquires four wholesome aggregates and two indeterminate aggregates.
At that very moment, four wholesome aggregates, one defiled aggregate, and two indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
If one passes away while abiding in a neutral state of mind,
they relinquish five wholesome aggregates and five neutral aggregates,
and acquire four wholesome aggregates and two neutral aggregates.
At that time, one wholesome aggregate, one defiled aggregate, and five indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
Regarding those who pass away from a higher level of the form realm and are reborn in a lower level:
if they die while abiding in a wholesome state of mind,
they relinquish five wholesome aggregates and five neutral aggregates.
There are five wholesome aggregates, four defiled aggregates, and five indeterminate aggregates.
At that very moment, four wholesome aggregates, one defiled aggregate, and two indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest in the present.
If one dies while abiding in a defiled state of mind,
they relinquish five aggregates of the wholesome and five aggregates of the indeterminate;
they acquire five aggregates of the wholesome, four aggregates of the defiled, and five aggregates of the indeterminate.
At that time, one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
If one dies while abiding in an indeterminate state of mind,
they relinquish five aggregates of the wholesome and five aggregates of the indeterminate;
they acquire five aggregates of the wholesome, four aggregates of the defiled, and five aggregates of the indeterminate.
At that very moment, one wholesome aggregate, one defiled aggregate, and five indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
Regarding those who die in the form realm and are reborn in the desire realm:
if they die while abiding in a wholesome state of mind, they relinquish five wholesome aggregates and five indeterminate aggregates,
and acquire four wholesome aggregates, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates.
Some say there are five:
at that time, four wholesome aggregates and one defiled aggregate cease,
while one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
If one dies while abiding in a defiled state of mind,
they relinquish five aggregates of the wholesome and five aggregates of the neutral;
they acquire four aggregates of the wholesome, four aggregates of the defiled, and two aggregates of the neutral.
Some say there are five:
at that very moment, one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates cease;
and one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
If one dies while abiding in a neutral state of mind,
they relinquish five aggregates of the wholesome and five aggregates of the neutral;
they acquire four aggregates of the wholesome, four aggregates of the defiled, and two aggregates of the neutral.
Some say there are five:
at that very time, one wholesome aggregate, one defiled aggregate, and five indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
When those who pass away from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and are reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) die while abiding in a wholesome state of mind,
they relinquish five wholesome aggregates (*skandha*) and five neutral (*avyākṛta*) aggregates.
One attains four wholesome aggregates and one indeterminate aggregate.
At that very time, four wholesome aggregates and one defiled aggregate cease, while one wholesome aggregate,
four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate manifest in the present.
If one passes away while abiding in an indeterminate state of mind,
they relinquish five aggregates of the wholesome and five aggregates of the indeterminate;
they acquire four aggregates of the wholesome and one aggregate of the indeterminate.
At that very moment, one wholesome aggregate, one defiled aggregate, and five indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate manifest in the present.
Regarding those who die in the formless realms and are reborn in the formless realms—
specifically those who pass away from this very level and are reborn again in this same level—
if they die while abiding in a wholesome state of mind:
He abandons one indeterminate aggregate and acquires one indeterminate aggregate.
At that very moment, four wholesome aggregates, one defiled aggregate, and one indeterminate aggregate cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate manifest in the present.
If one dies while abiding in a defiled state of mind,
they relinquish one neutral aggregate and acquire one neutral aggregate.
At that very time, one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate manifest. If one dies while abiding in an indeterminate state of mind, [the same applies].
He abandons four indeterminate aggregates and acquires one indeterminate aggregate;
at that very moment, one wholesome aggregate, one defiled aggregate, and four indeterminate aggregates cease.
One wholesome aggregate and four defiled aggregates, as well as one indeterminate aggregate, manifest.
This applies to one who dies in a lower stage of the formless realm and is reborn in a higher stage,
provided they pass away while abiding in a wholesome state of mind.
He abandons four wholesome aggregates and one neutral aggregate;
he acquires four wholesome aggregates and one neutral aggregate.
At that very moment, the four wholesome aggregates and the defiled aggregate cease, while the neutral aggregate remains.
When a wholesome aggregate is present, four defiled aggregates and one indeterminate aggregate are manifested.
If one passes away while abiding in an indeterminate state of mind,
they relinquish the wholesome aggregates and the four indeterminate aggregates.
One acquires four wholesome aggregates and one indeterminate aggregate.
At that very moment, one wholesome aggregate, one defiled aggregate, and four indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate manifest in the present.
For one who dies from a higher level of the formless realm and is reborn in a lower level:
if they pass away while abiding in a wholesome state of mind,
they relinquish four wholesome aggregates and one neutral aggregate.
When there are four wholesome aggregates, four defiled aggregates, and one neutral aggregate, then at that time,
the four wholesome aggregates, the one defiled aggregate, and the one neutral aggregate cease;
and one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and one neutral aggregate manifest in the present.
If one dies while abiding in a defiled state of mind,
they relinquish four aggregates of the wholesome and one aggregate of the neutral;
they acquire four aggregates of the wholesome, four aggregates of the defiled, and one aggregate of the neutral.
At that time, one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate manifest.
If one passes away while abiding in a neutral state of mind,
one relinquishes four aggregates of the wholesome and four aggregates of the neutral;
one acquires four aggregates of the wholesome, four aggregates of the defiled, and one aggregate of the neutral.
At that time, one wholesome aggregate, one defiled aggregate, and four indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate manifest in the present.
Regarding those who die in the formless realm and are reborn in the desire realm:
if they die while abiding in a wholesome state of mind,
they relinquish four wholesome aggregates and one indeterminate aggregate.
One acquires four wholesome aggregates, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates.
Some say there are five;
according to that view, at that time, four wholesome aggregates, one defiled aggregate, and one indeterminate aggregate cease.
When one with a wholesome mind has the four defiled aggregates and two indeterminate aggregates present before them,
if they die while abiding in a defiled mind,
they relinquish the wholesome aggregates and one of the four indeterminate aggregates.
One acquires four virtuous aggregates, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates.
Some say five;
that is, at that very time, one virtuous aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate cease.
When one with a wholesome mind manifests four defiled aggregates and two neutral aggregates,
or when one dies while abiding in a neutral mind,
they relinquish the wholesome aggregates and four neutral aggregates.
One acquires four wholesome aggregates, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates.
Some say five;
that is, at that very moment, one wholesome aggregate, one defiled aggregate, and four indeterminate aggregates cease.
One wholesome aggregate and four defiled aggregates, along with two neutral aggregates, are present.
For those who pass away from the formless realm and are reborn in the form realm,
if they pass away while abiding in a wholesome state of mind:
He abandons four wholesome aggregates and one neutral aggregate;
he acquires five wholesome aggregates, four defiled aggregates, and five neutral aggregates.
At that very moment, four wholesome aggregates, one defiled aggregate, and one neutral aggregate cease.
When one with a wholesome mind has the four defiled aggregates and two indeterminate aggregates manifest,
or when one dies while abiding in a defiled mind,
they relinquish the wholesome aggregates, the four indeterminate aggregates, and one [aggregate].
There are five wholesome aggregates, four defiled aggregates, and five indeterminate aggregates.
At that very moment, one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and one indeterminate aggregate cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest in the present.
If one passes away while abiding in a neutral state of mind,
they relinquish four wholesome aggregates and four neutral aggregates;
they acquire five wholesome aggregates, four defiled aggregates, and five neutral aggregates.
At that very time, one wholesome aggregate, one defiled aggregate, and four indeterminate aggregates cease;
one wholesome aggregate, four defiled aggregates, and two indeterminate aggregates manifest.
For what reason do the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm not increase with respect to the phenomena (*dharma*) of the form realm?
This is explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is in order to bring certainty to those who harbor doubts.
Specifically, it was stated in the previous section on the "Aggregates of Bondage" (*saṃyojana-skandha*) and the "Fettering of Sentient Beings" (*sattva-nikāya*):
"In the desire realm, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that increase, and they are bound by nine fetters (*saṃyojana*)."
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have sixty-two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that increase and are bound by six fetters (*saṃyojana*).
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), ordinary beings have thirty-one underlying tendencies that increase and are bound by six fetters.
Some may harbor doubts:
do the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the form and formless realms increase in ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) of the desire realm?
And do the latent dispositions of the formless realm increase in ordinary beings of the form realm?
In order to resolve this doubt, it is shown that while one achieves those [attainments], they do not increase therein;

that is to say, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm is subject only to the increase of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm, and not those of the form or formless realms.
Ordinary beings in the form realm are subject only to the increase of latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the form realm, not those of the formless realm.
For this reason, this treatise was composed.
Why is it that the latent dispositions of the desire realm do not increase with respect to the phenomena of the form realm?
Answer: Because the realms would become confused and it would be impossible to designate them as being free from desire and defilement.
As for the confusion of realms, it means that they would be both the desire realm and the form realm.
Thus, it cannot be said that the desire realm and the form realm are distinct,
nor can one designate someone as "free from the defilement of desire";
for when one is free from greed for the desire realm, one is not yet called "free from the defilement of the desire realm."
To claim that one is called "detached from the defilements of the desire realm" only at the time of becoming detached from the greed of the form realm is unreasonable.
For what reason do the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the desire realm not increase with respect to the dharmas of the formless realm?
Answer: It would follow that the realms (dhātu) would become confused, and it would be impossible to designate [a state] as being free from desire and defilement.
As for the confusion of the realms:
That is to say, if that [state] were both the desire realm and the formless realm,
then one could not say that the desire realm and the formless realm are distinct,
nor could one designate anyone as being free from the defilement of desire.
To claim that when one is free from craving for the desire realm, one is not said to be free from the defilements of the desire realm,
whereas only when one is free from craving for the formless realm is one said to be free from the defilements of the desire realm—
this is unreasonable.
Why do the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) not increase with respect to the phenomena (*dharma*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
Answer: Because it would result in a confusion of realms, and because those [phenomena] are not the objects (*ālambana*) of these [dispositions].
Regarding the confusion of realms (*dhātu-saṃkara*):
it means that if something were both of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
one could not say that the form realm is distinct from the desire realm, nor that it is not an object of perception (*ālambana*) for the latter.
This means that the afflictions of a higher stage take the phenomena of a lower stage as their objects.
Why, then, do the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) not increase in relation to the phenomena of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
The answer is: because it would result in a confusion of the realms.
Furthermore, it cannot be designated because it is free from attachment to form (*rūpa-rāga*).
As for the confusion of realms (*dhātu-saṃkara*),
this means that it belongs both to the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) and to the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
Thus, it cannot be said that the form realm and the formless realm are distinct,
nor can one designate anyone as being free from passion for the form realm;
that is to say, when one is free from craving for the form realm, it is not termed "being free from passion for the form realm."
To claim that one is called "detached from the defilements of the form realm" only at the time of becoming detached from the craving for the formless realm is unreasonable.
Why is it that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the formless realm do not increase in relation to the phenomena of the desire realm?
Answer: It would result in confusion between the realms (*dhātu*), and because those [unconditioned phenomena] are not the objects of perception (*ālambana*) for this [realm].
Why, then, do the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) not increase with respect to the phenomena of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
Answer: The realms would become confused,
and furthermore, because those [objects] are not the objects of this [consciousness],
all should be understood as previously explained.
Question: How are the three realms (dhātus) established as described?
Is it by way of the levels (bhūmi), by way of the locations (sthāna), or by way of the abandonment of craving (tṛṣṇā-prahāṇa)?
If it were so, what would be the fault?
If categorized by way of the levels (*bhūmi*), one should speak of nine elements (*dhātu*), because there are nine levels:
namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
If categorized by way of the bases (*āyatana*), [one should speak of eighteen].
It should be said that there are forty realms because there are forty locations:
namely, twenty locations in the desire realm and sixteen locations in the form realm.
Regarding the four bases of the formless realm,
if they are abandoned through craving,
one should also speak of nine elements.
This refers to craving for the desire realm up to craving for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
because each has its own distinct limit,
it should be said that the three realms are established by means of the abandonment of craving.
Question: If that is so, there should be nine realms established.
Answer: Because craving for similar types [of existence] is severed, only three realms are established.
That is to say, from the Avīci Hell up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, all are established as the Desire Realm because they are differentiated by desire and attachment;
from the Brahmakāyika Heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven [is the Form Realm].
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) is established because it is differentiated by craving for form;
the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), from the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, is established because it is differentiated by craving for the formless.
Furthermore, wherever there is form and desire, the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu) is established;
where there is form but no desire, the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) is established;
and where there is neither form nor desire, the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) is established.
Furthermore, where there is form and a second [form], it is established as the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*);
where there is form but no second [form], it is established as the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*);
and where there is no form and no second [form], it is established as the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, wherever there is form and an objective sphere, the desire realm is established;
where there is form but no objective sphere, the form realm is established;
and where there is neither form nor an objective sphere, the formless realm is established.
Furthermore, wherever there is form and there are material requisites, it is established as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
where there is form but no material requisites, it is established as the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
and where there is neither form nor material requisites, it is established as the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, wherever there is form and desire, yet there is the grasping at a self, it is established as the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
Where there is form but no desire, yet there is the grasping at a self, it is established as the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
Where there is neither form nor desire, yet there is the grasping at a self, it is established as the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Furthermore, wherever there is form and the grasping at a second self exists, that is established as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Where there is form but no grasping at a second self exists, that is established as the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Where there is no form and no grasping at a second self exists, that is established as the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The same applies to the explanation of objects and requisites.

Furthermore, wherever there is form associated with shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), it is established as the Form Realm with form; wherever there is form dissociated from shamelessness and lack of dread, it is established as the Form Realm without form.
The formless realm is established as being dissociated from both shamelessness and lack of dread.
Furthermore, wherever there is form associated with stinginess and envy, it is established as the desire realm;
wherever there is form dissociated from stinginess and envy, it is established as the form realm.
The formless realm is established as being dissociated from stinginess and envy.
Furthermore, a place where there is form associated with the faculties of grief and suffering is established as the desire realm;
a place where there is form dissociated from the faculties of grief and suffering is established as the form realm.
The formless realm is established as being dissociated from the faculties of sorrow and suffering.
Furthermore, that place where there is material food and which is associated with sensual desire is established as the desire realm;
that place where there is material food but which is dissociated from sensual desire is established as the form realm.
The formless realm is established as being dissociated from edible food in morsels and from sensual desire.
Furthermore, wherever there are the five aggregates as the ripening cause and the five aggregates as the ripening fruit, that is [the formless realm].
The desire realm is established based on the fact that unwholesome and neutral proclivities increase therein;
it consists of the five aggregates as the ripening cause and the five aggregates as the ripening fruit.
The form realm is established based solely on the fact that neutral proclivities increase therein.
There are four aggregates as the cause of maturation and four aggregates as the fruit of maturation;
because only indeterminate latent dispositions increase therein, it is established as the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, wherever there is a cause of maturation for the four aggregates that results in a single fruit, [it is the formless realm].
The desire realm (kāmadhātu) is established by the presence of unwholesome and neutral proclivities (anuśaya) that increase;
it consists of the five aggregates (skandha) which, as a ripening cause (vipāka-hetu), yield a single fruit.
The form realm (rūpadhātu) is established solely by the presence of neutral proclivities that increase.
There are four aggregates that constitute a ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) which yields a single fruit;
these are established as belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) because they are characterized solely by the increase of neutral latent dispositions (anivṛtāvyākṛta-anuśaya).
Furthermore, wherever there are three types of feelings as ripening causes and three types of feelings as ripening fruits, [that is the formless realm].
The desire realm is established based on the increase of unwholesome and neutral proclivities (*anuśaya*);
it possesses two types of feelings as its maturation cause and two types of feelings as its maturation fruit.
The form realm is established based solely on the increase of neutral proclivities.
There is one type of cause for the maturation of feeling that results in one type of fruit of the maturation of feeling;
it is established as the formless realm solely because the indeterminate latent dispositions (anivṛtāvyākṛta-anuśaya) increase therein.
Furthermore, there are places where there are five causes for the maturation of feeling and four fruits of the maturation of feeling.
The desire realm is established based on the increase of unwholesome and neutral proclivities;
it possesses three types of feeling as its ripening cause and three types of feeling as its ripening fruit.
The form realm is established based solely on the increase of neutral proclivities.
There is one type of cause for the ripening of sensation that results in one type of ripened fruit;
it is established as the formless realm solely because the indeterminate latent dispositions (anivṛtāvyākṛta-anuśaya) increase therein.
Furthermore, wherever there is both a material and an immaterial cause for ripening, there is also both a material and an immaterial ripened fruit.
The desire realm is established based on the fact that it is accompanied by the increase of unwholesome and neutral proclivities (*anuśaya*),
possesses both material and immaterial retributive causes, and yields both material and immaterial retributive fruits.
The form realm is established based on the fact that it is accompanied solely by the increase of neutral proclivities.
There is an immaterial retributive cause and an immaterial retributive fruit;
it is established as the immaterial realm solely because the indeterminate latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.
As it is with the material [realm], so it is with the immaterial.
The same applies to the explanations of "with vision" and "without vision," and "with resistance" and "without resistance.
Question: How are the three realms mentioned above established?
Are they arranged as upper and lower layers?
If it were distributed laterally to adjacent areas,
or vertically above and below,
how could one establish the complete abandonment of those defilements?
How can supernormal power reach there?
If it were to spread laterally,
how would one reconcile this with what Dāruddhara taught?
As it is said that the worlds of the lower direction are infinite and the worlds of the upper direction are infinite,
some among them say that they are stacked one above the other.
This means that from this world-system, far below the wind-circle in the void, there is the Akaniṣṭha Heaven of the lower direction;
further down from there, continuing successively, there is yet another Akaniṣṭha Heaven below the wind-circle.
Descending successively in this manner down to the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*),
it continues thus through successive worlds below until reaching the infinite.
Furthermore, from this world, far above the Akaniṣṭha heaven in the void, there exists a wind-circle of the upper direction.
From that point, they extend upward in succession up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Above that, there is further a wind-circle extending upward in succession up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
In this manner, they extend upward through the world-systems until they are infinite.
Question: If that is so, how is it established that one is completely free from defilement regarding them?
And how can supernormal powers reach them everywhere?
Answer: If one becomes detached from the defilements of even a single part of the desire realm,
it is said that one has become detached from all the defilements of the desire realm,
because their characteristics are identical.
However, the supernormal powers (abhijñā) produced based on the first dhyāna can only reach one desire realm— the Brahma world— and no others,
because their locations are distinct.

In this same way, it should also be understood accordingly for those who have become free from the defilements of the form realm and who manifest supernormal powers based on other meditative concentrations.
Other masters say:
[The opponent] replies: "It is contiguous and extends alongside.
[The proponent] asks:
"If that is so, how do you explain what Dharmatrāta has said?"
The answer should be stated as follows:
the desire realm below is boundless,
and the form realm above is boundless.

Among these, the various locations of the desire realm share a single underlying tendency (*anuśaya*), whereas those of the form and formless realms have distinct underlying tendencies according to their respective levels.
Question: For what reason do the various locations of the desire realm share a single underlying tendency?
In the form and formless realms, [the afflictions] vary according to each respective level.
Answer: The desire realm is an indeterminate realm; it is neither a stage of cultivation nor a stage of freedom from defilement.
Within this realm, the afflictions run wild and unrestrained, like horses without bridles.
Therefore, in all instances, the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are identical.
The form and formless realms are the realm of meditative concentration, the stage of cultivation, and the stage of freedom from passion;
herein, the afflictions operate without autonomy, like a horse restrained by a bridle.
Therefore, the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the upper and lower stages are each distinct.
Furthermore, because the unwholesome roots (akuśalamūla) in the desire realm are powerful and the wholesome roots (kuśalamūla) are weak,
this applies to all cases.
The underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are identical [in nature].
Because there are no unwholesome roots in the form and formless realms and wholesome roots are predominant,
the underlying tendencies of the upper and lower stages are each distinct.
Furthermore, in the desire realm, unwholesome states increase while wholesome dharmas decline;
in the form and formless realms, there are no unwholesome states and wholesome dharmas increase.
Furthermore, in the desire realm, unwholesomeness is like a sovereign.
Wholesome dharmas are like guests;
in the form and formless realms, there are no unwholesome dharmas.
Wholesome dharmas are like the host.
Furthermore, in the desire realm there are unwholesome roots capable of severing the wholesome roots,
whereas in the form and formless realms there are no unwholesome roots capable of severing the wholesome roots.
Furthermore, the social decorum in the desire realm lacks restraint, being like that between husband and wife.
Therefore, in all cases, the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are identical.
Although there is a separation of etiquette between the form and formless realms— much like that between a mother and her child—
the underlying tendencies of the upper and lower stages are each distinct.
Furthermore, the wholesome dharmas of the desire realm and those of formal deportment (airyāpathika) are intermingled,
just as a prince and the son of a caṇḍāla might be confined together in the same prison; therefore,
they share the same underlying tendencies (anuśaya) in all instances.
The wholesome dharmas of the form and formless realms are unmixed with those of the *airyāpathika* (demeanor) class;
they are like a prince and the son of a householder confined together in a prison.
Therefore, the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the upper and lower stages are each distinct.
Question: Is there a substance that intervenes between the three realms?
If there were, those two realms would become five realms because of that intervening substance.
Furthermore, within those five intermediate [factors], there would again be four entities;
thus, the elements (dhātus) would amount to nine.
In this manner, through successive extension, they would become infinite.
If it does not exist,
why do the three realms not merge into one?
One should answer that within them there is no intervening substance whatsoever.
Question: If that is so, why do the three realms not become one?
Answer: Although there is no intervening substance between them, they do not become one.
Just as the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, the five aggregates, the three periods of time, the four great elements, and so forth,
do not become one despite having no intervening substance,
this case is also like that.

Furthermore, because their intrinsic natures and characteristics differ and because they belong to distinct categories of entities, even though there is no intervening space between them, they do not constitute a single unity.
Question: If that is so, then...
Between the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations and the lower stage of the first dhyāna,
there is an immense distance and an immeasurable realm of space and form.
How can one know the distinction between the limits of what constitutes the desire realm and what constitutes the form realm?
Answer: Both the wheel-boundaries of the two realms possess networks of light.
Because the extent and quality of these two lights differ—being coarse in one and subtle in the other—one thereby discerns that "this is the desire realm" and "this is the form realm."
Furthermore, if a place visible to the divine eye obtained by birth in the desire realm is the desire realm,
and a place not visible to it is the form realm;
furthermore, if a place reachable by the supernormal powers obtained by birth in the desire realm is the desire realm.
Not all locations constitute the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, if a location is the object of craving for the desire realm, it is the desire realm;
if it is the object of craving for the form realm, it is the form realm.
This is called the distinction between the limits of the two realms.
Why is it that the non-universal proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm do not increase (*anuśerate*) with respect to all phenomena of the desire realm?
Answer: Because they would [otherwise] become universal, and because those [phenomena] are not their objects (*ālambana*).
This would then entail that [the defilements] are universal;
that is to say, if these non-universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the desire realm were to increase in accordance with all phenomena of the desire realm.
Furthermore, it would follow that [the affliction] is omnipresent;
thus, one could not establish the distinction between the characteristics and functions of omnipresent latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and non-omnipresent latent dispositions,
nor [could one maintain] that "because it is not its object, it is not [an object] of this."
This means that those dharmas belonging to other categories are not the objects of these non-universal latent dispositions (*anubandha*),
because these [dispositions] take only the dharmas of their own category as their objects. Why is this so?
The distinction between the five categories of phenomena is established by the power of non-universal latent dispositions (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-anuśaya*).
If non-universal latent dispositions were also to universally take all five categories as their object, [the distinction would not hold].
In that case, they would necessarily increase pervasively across all five categories.
Thus, there would be a confusion of the five categories;
and because the five categories are confused, their antidotes would likewise be confused.
Because of the confusion regarding the antidotes, there is confusion regarding the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*).

Because of the confusion regarding the clear realizations, it is impossible to establish the distinctions between the thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) and the distinctions between the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
In order to avoid such a fault,
it is held that the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm do not increase in relation to all phenomena of the desire realm. For what reason, then,
do the non-universal latent dispositions of the form realm [not increase in relation to all phenomena of the form realm]?
Do they not increase in accordance with [those] dharmas that are not pervasive within the form realm?
Answer: This would entail that they are pervasive, and furthermore, because those [dharmas] are not the objects of these [defilements].
Why do the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm not increase with respect to all phenomena of the formless realm?
Answer: Because they would [otherwise] become universal, and because those [phenomena] are not their objects (*ālambana*).
All of these are explained as previously stated.
The meaning of the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is explained in detail in the *Jñāna-nirdeśa* section of the *Prakaraṇapāda* and the *Akusala-nirdeśa* section of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.
There are ten perceptions, namely, the perception of impermanence up to the perception of cessation.
These have already been analyzed in detail within the *Śaikṣa-varga* (Chapter on the Disciples) of the *Samādhiskandha* (Section on Concentration).
If one cultivates the perception of impermanence, does one contemplate the perception of impermanence?
...and so on, as explained at length.
There are four kinds of cultivation:

namely, cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), cultivation by practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), cultivation by counteraction (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*), and cultivation by elimination (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*).
The meaning of the four cultivations is explained in detail in the *Jñānaskandha*, in the section on the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Regarding this, some say that the treatise is composed based solely upon cultivation through practice (*āsevana-bhāvanā*).
Some say that this treatise is composed based on both acquisition-cultivation (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and practice-cultivation (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*). However,
there are those who maintain that within this context, the treatise is composed based solely on practice-cultivation.
When he says, "if one cultivates the perception of impermanence," it means that the perception of impermanence is present before one;
he is one who contemplates the perception of impermanence.
That is to say, taking the perception of impermanence as its object means that when the perception of impermanence is present, it takes the meaning of the perception of impermanence as its object.
If one cultivates the perception of impermanence, does one then contemplate the perception of impermanence?
It can be answered with four propositions.
There is the cultivation of the perception of impermanence without contemplating the perception of impermanence;
that is, cultivating the perception of impermanence by taking other phenomena as its object.

Just as one takes the aggregates of form, feeling, formations, and consciousness as objects, so too, setting aside the perception of impermanence, one gives rise to the perception of impermanence by taking other aggregates of perception as objects.
Question: At what stage does this occur?

Answer: They occur during the stages of increasing heat (*uṣmagata*) and summits (*mūrdhan*), consisting of the applications of mindfulness regarding the body, feelings, and mind through the aspect of impermanence, as well as the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) taking other phenomena as its object, when one is free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The applications of mindfulness regarding body, sensation, and mind consist of the aspect of impermanence;
the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena, which takes other phenomena as its object, serves as the preparatory practice (*prayoga*).

During that stage of the path of preparation, if one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*), they become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
When one who is liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to become unshakable (akopyadharman),
they take the contemplation of impermanence (anityākāra) as their practice, employing the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding body, sensation, and mind,
as well as the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) taking other phenomena as its object, as the preparatory exercises (prayoga).
At the time of that path of preparation,
when one gives rise to the application of the aspect of impermanence through the applications of mindfulness of body, sensation, and mind,
or when one practices the application of mindfulness of phenomena by taking other phenomena as the object;
If one practices the meditative absorptions by means of these very same types of applications of mindfulness,
then for those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimate reality,
at the moment they give rise to this kind of analytical knowledge of meaning regarding the applications of mindfulness, [the following occurs].

Furthermore, when one gives rise to such applications of mindfulness, the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), the knowledge resulting from prayer (praṇidhijñāna), the limit of meditative concentration (samādhi-paryanta), the formless liberations (ārūpyavimokṣa), the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti),
or a subtle state of mind involving perception— at such times as these, one cultivates the perception of impermanence (anityasaṃjñā).
Because the perception of impermanence has manifested before one,
yet one does not contemplate that perception of impermanence while taking other phenomena as its object; thus,
there is contemplation of the perception of impermanence without the cultivation of the perception of impermanence.
This refers to cultivating other perceptions by taking the perception of impermanence as their object.
These "other perceptions" refer to the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, and other wholesome, afflicted, or neutral perceptions.
Among these, "wholesome perceptions" refers to both acquired wholesome perceptions and innate wholesome perceptions;
that is, the perception of acquired wholesomeness.
This refers to that which is produced through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Regarding that produced through hearing:
it is the perception produced through hearing that takes impermanence as its object and gives rise to the mental aspect of "not being non-impermanent."

That which is accomplished through reflection refers to the perception accomplished through reflection that takes the arising of the notion of impermanence as its object and contemplates the mental aspect of non-impermanence.
That which is accomplished through cultivation refers to...
That is to say, taking impermanence as the object, one gives rise to the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of "not being non-impermanent.
Question: At what stage is this perception (*saṃjñā*) produced through cultivation said to exist?
Answer: It exists at the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and their initial development and increase.
The application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) characterized by the aspect of non-permanence arises based on the perception of impermanence;
the application of mindfulness to phenomena characterized by three aspects arises at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*);

and [the application of mindfulness to phenomena characterized by four aspects] arises during the four moments of mind within the direct realization of suffering (*duḥkhābhisamaya*) upon having entered into the state of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
One arouses the application of mindfulness on phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) with four aspects during the four moments of mind of the clear observation (abhisamaya) of the origin and the path;
one arouses the application of mindfulness on phenomena with sixteen aspects [during the clear observation of suffering].
If, by means of the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) that takes the perception of impermanence as its object but not its aspect of impermanent activity,
one becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and if one employs this very [practice] as the preparatory application (prayoga).
At the time of all those paths of preparation, uninterrupted paths, and paths of liberation,
if one employs the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) with the perception of impermanence as its object, but not with the aspect of non-impermanence,
and if one is a believer resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta) who refines their faculties to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).

When one who is liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to become immovable (akopyadharman), if they employ this very [attainment] as the preparatory effort (prayoga),
then at the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted (ānantarya), and liberation paths (vimukti-mārga):

If one takes as an object the perception of impermanence, rather than the aspect of the practice of impermanence, during the time of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, the arising of the supernormal knowledge of others' minds, or the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives; [at those times, the application of mindfulness to phenomena occurs].
When one gives rise to the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) based on the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*), yet not through the aspect of impermanence (*anityākāra*);
and when one gives rise to the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
For those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimate reality (*paramārtha*):
That is to say, at the time of arising the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) regarding this kind of application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*),
as well as the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*) regarding this kind of application of mindfulness to phenomena;

and at the time of the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), the limit of meditative concentration (*samādhiparyanta*), the formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*), the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness (*ākāśavijñānānantyāyatana*), the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), when the mind is subtle through the perception [of these states].
This is called wholesome perception (*samyag-saṃjñā*).
As for defiled perception (*kliṣṭa-saṃjñā*),
it refers to the arising of the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) based upon a perception of impermanence.
Grasping at "self" and "what belongs to self," one gives rise to the view of extremes.
Grasping at annihilationism or eternalism, one gives rise to false views.
Grasping at the absence of cause, the absence of action, and the denial of reality, one gives rise to the adherence to views.
One clings to what is superior, excellent, and foremost, giving rise to the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
One clings to [what is] pure, liberation, and renunciation, giving rise to doubt, hesitation, and indecision.
One gives rise to ignorance, lack of knowledge, darkness, and delusion.
One gives rise to greed, which is characterized by fondness and delight;
one gives rise to anger, which is characterized by lack of fondness and lack of delight;
and one gives rise to pride, which is characterized by haughtiness.
Such times as these are called defiled perceptions (*saṃkliṣṭa-saṃjñā*).
As for neutral perceptions (*avyākṛta-saṃjñā*),
they refer to perceptions arising from the object of impermanence that are neither appropriate nor inappropriate perceptions.
This is called contemplating the perception of impermanence.
Because one contemplates the perception of impermanence, one does not cultivate the perception of impermanence due to the arising of other perceptions.
There is cultivation of the perception of impermanence as well as contemplation of the perception of impermanence.
This refers to cultivating the perception of impermanence by taking impermanence as its object.
Just as when the perception of impermanence manifests in a long-lasting continuity,
it takes one's own continuum— both past and future— as its object.
And the perception of the impermanence of the three times regarding the mental continuums of others.
Question: In what stage is this said to reside?
Answer: It resides in the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and their initial increase (*vṛddhi*).
The application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) characterized by the aspect of impermanence arises conditioned by the thought of impermanence;
or, the application of mindfulness to phenomena characterized by the aspect of impermanence arises at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*);
or, it arises during the four moments of mind within the direct realization of suffering (*duḥkhābhisamaya*) once one has entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktvaniyāma*).
One arouses the application of mindfulness to phenomena through the aspect of impermanence;
if one does so by means of the application of mindfulness to phenomena through the aspect of impermanence based on the perception of impermanence,
one becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
If one employs this very [dharma-smṛtyupasthāna] as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*),
then at the time of all those uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the preparatory stage,

if one applies such dharmas through the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the resolution of faith (*śraddhādhimokṣa*), one refines the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) and becomes one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).

When one who is liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to become unshakable (akopyadharman), if they employ this very [attainment] as the preparatory stage (prayoga),
then during all those preparatory, uninterrupted (ānantarya), and liberation paths (vimukti-mārga):
If one cultivates dhyāna by means of such applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding phenomena,
and if one wishes to maintain that all phenomena are the ultimate truth (paramārtha),
one gives rise to the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid).

Furthermore, it is said that when one gives rise to the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), the limit of meditative concentration (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*), the formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or the subtle mind associated with perception;
and when one gives rise to the "wishless-of-the-wishless" (*apraṇihitāpraṇihita*) samādhi.
At such times as these, because one cultivates the perception of impermanence and the perception of impermanence is present before one,
and because one also contemplates the perception of impermanence and takes the perception of impermanence as its object,
there are instances where one neither cultivates the perception of impermanence nor contemplates the perception of impermanence.
This means excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Question: At what stage is this said to occur?
Answer: It occurs at the initial stages of *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and the further development of *kṣānti*.
One gives rise to the application of mindfulness on phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) conditioned by the truth of cessation.

This occurs when one increases the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata) and Summits (mūrdhan), at which time the applications of mindfulness do not take impermanence as their object, nor do they give rise to the mental aspect of non-impermanence;
or when one has already entered the correct nature of liberation (samyaktvaniyāma) for the duration of the four moments of the clear realization of cessation (nirodha-abhisamaya).
If, during the stages of cultivation or the stage of no-more-learning,
one gives rise to any of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) that do not take impermanence as their object and do not have the aspect of impermanence (*anityākāra*),
then at such times, one does not cultivate the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*).
Because the perception of impermanence does not manifest before him,
he does not contemplate the perception of impermanence,
nor does he take the perception of impermanence as an object of cognition.
The masters outside of Kaśmīra say this:
there are those who neither cultivate the perception of impermanence nor contemplate the perception of impermanence;
