that is to say, they cultivate other perceptions by taking other phenomena as their objects.
Just as, with the exception of the perception of impermanence, other perceptions arise within the aggregates of feeling,
formations, and consciousness when taking form as their object;
so too do other perceptions arise when taking the unconditioned as their object.
"Other perceptions" refers to the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, and the perception of non-self in suffering,
as well as all other perceptions that are not the perception of impermanence.
The detailed exposition should be understood as being like that of the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*).
The same applies to the perception of suffering in what is impermanent (*anicce dukkhasaññā*) and the perception of non-self in what is suffering (*dukkhe anattasaññā*).
The difference is as follows:
One should state one's own name;

furthermore, in the third phrase, one should exclude the perception of wishlessness-within-wishlessness, the perception of impurity, the perception of revulsion toward food, the perception that all worlds are not delightful, the perception of death, the perception of abandonment, the perception of detachment, and the perception of cessation.
Regarding "it should be understood according to the circumstances":
this means that if one cultivates the perception of impurity,
one does not mentally attend to that perception of impurity.
Because when the perception of impurity manifests, it takes as its object both color and shape; therefore,
if one contemplates the perception of impurity while [focusing on these],
one is not cultivating the perception of impurity.
Because when one attends to the perception of impurity, other perceptions arise in the present moment.
These "other perceptions" refer to the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, and the perception of non-self in what is suffering.
The same applies to other wholesome, defiled, and neutral perceptions (*saṃjñā*),

such as the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*), the perception of revulsion toward food (*āhāre pratikūla-saṃjñā*), the perception that all worldly things are not to be delighted in (*sarvaloke 'nabhirati-saṃjñā*), the perception of death (*maraṇa-saṃjñā*), the perception of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃjñā*), the perception of detachment (*virāga-saṃjñā*), and the perception of cessation (*nirodha-saṃjñā*).
As for the distinction:
it refers to speaking of one's own object of focus;
that is, if one cultivates the perception of revulsion toward food.
He does not contemplate the perception of revulsion toward food,
because when that perception manifests, it takes fragrance, flavor, and tangibility as its objects.
If he were to contemplate the perception of revulsion toward food...
He does not cultivate the perception of revulsion toward food because,
when that perception is being attended to, other perceptions manifest.
These "other perceptions" are as previously described.
If one cultivates the perception of the unattractiveness of all worlds,
yet does not contemplate that perception of the unattractiveness of all worlds,
it is because when the perception of the unattractiveness of all worlds manifests, it takes as its object the desirable things within those worlds.
If one contemplates the perception that all worlds are not to be relished,
yet does not cultivate that perception of the non-relishability of all worlds,
it is because when that perception of the non-relishability of the world is being taken as an object, other perceptions manifest before the mind.
The other perceptions are as previously explained.
If one cultivates the perception of death, one does not conceptualize the perception of death itself;
for when the perception of death manifests, it takes as its object the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the impermanence co-arising with that life-faculty.
If one contemplates the perception of death but does not cultivate that perception of death,
it is because when that perception of death is the object of focus, other perceptions manifest.
These "other perceptions" are as previously described.
If one cultivates the perception of abandonment, one does not contemplate the perception of abandonment,
because when the perception of abandonment is present, it takes nirvāṇa as its object.
If one contemplates the perception of abandonment, one does not cultivate the perception of abandonment.
Because when one contemplates the perception of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃjñā*), other perceptions arise in the present.
These "other perceptions" are as previously explained,
just as with the perception of abandonment and the perception of detachment (*virāgasaṃjñā*).
The same applies to the cessation of perception.
*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 193. *Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 100.
Compiled by nine hundred and fifty great Arhats and others;

translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Eight: The Aggregate of Views (*Dṛṣṭi-skandha*), Part Two of the Sub-section on the Three Existences (*Tri-bhava-nirdeśa*). For those who wish to establish a treatise herein concerning the cultivation of acquisition (*prāpti*) and the cultivation of practice (*bhāvanā*) based upon these [categories]:
Regarding that statement, "if one cultivates the perception of impermanence," it means that whether the perception of impermanence is manifest or unmanifest,
one cultivates it by contemplating that perception of impermanence.
That is to say, taking the perception of impermanence as its object is itself the perception of impermanence;
when it is cultivated, it takes the meaning of the perception of impermanence as its object.
If one cultivates the perception of impermanence, does one then contemplate the perception of impermanence?
It can be answered with four propositions.
There is the cultivation of the perception of impermanence without contemplating the perception of impermanence;
that is, cultivating the perception of impermanence by taking other phenomena as its object.
Just as one takes the aggregates of form, feeling, formations, and consciousness as objects,
so too, setting aside the aggregate of perception other than the perception of impermanence,
one cultivates the perception of impermanence by taking the unconditioned as its object while cultivating the perception of impermanence.
Question: At which stage is this taught?

Answer: This is taught as occurring at the stages of *uṣmagata* (heat) and *mūrdhan* (summit), where one gives rise to the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding body, sensation, and mind.
And the application of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that takes other phenomena as its object;
or when the initial stages of "summits" (*mūrdhan*) and "patience" (*kṣānti*), as well as the increasing stages of patience, arise taking the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) as their object;
or when one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) by means of the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
The application consists of the mindfulness of body, the mindfulness of feelings, the mindfulness of mind, and the mindfulness of phenomena as objects other than those;
it is likewise stated that at the time of all such uninterrupted paths and paths of liberation,
one becomes detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Except at the time of the ninth path of liberation;

if one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) develops the faculty-sharpening (indriya-saṃcāra) by taking the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna that has the truth of cessation as its object, they become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
If one takes the mindfulness of body and the mindfulness of mind as the preliminary practice,
or the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) having other phenomena as its object as the preliminary practice,
then at the moment of the path of liberation immediately following that preliminary practice:
The explanation for the training of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) by one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is likewise,
with the sole exception of the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
This applies when [the practitioner] employs the foundations of mindfulness of body and mind (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna* and *citta-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Furthermore, when one practices the mixed cultivation of dhyāna through the application of mindfulness to other dharmas;
when one brings forth the supernormal powers of the divine eye, the divine ear, and the power of psychic travel;
or when one brings forth the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds by means of the applications of mindfulness to feeling, to mind, and to other dharmas.

When one gives rise to the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhā-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the first eight bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the two unhindered knowledges of phenomena and language (*dharmapada-pratisaṃvid*), or when one gives rise to the absence of contention (*araṇā*),
emptiness-of-emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), wishlessness-of-wishlessness (*apranihitā-apranihita*), or signlessness-of-signlessness (*animittā-animitta*).
Some say:

except when one gives rise to the "wishless-of-the-wishless" (apraṇihitāpraṇihita), at that time one establishes mindfulness of the body, feelings, and mind; and when one takes other dharmas as objects, one establishes mindfulness of dharmas.
For those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimate reality,

there arises the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) regarding the applications of mindfulness of body, feeling, mind, and the application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) taking other phenomena as its object.
Furthermore, for one who maintains that only *nirvāṇa* is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),

when giving rise to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), they give rise to the applications of mindfulness regarding body, feeling, and mind; and when giving rise to the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) taking other phenomena as its object,

or when giving rise to the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*), the limit of concentration (*samādhikotībhāva*), the formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*), or the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they do so with a subtle mind characterized by perception (*saṃjñā*).
At such a time, there is the cultivation of the perception of impermanence without reflecting upon the perception of impermanence;
and there is the reflection upon the perception of impermanence without cultivating the perception of impermanence—
namely, when one cultivates other perceptions while taking the perception of impermanence as an object.
As for "other perceptions," these refer to the perception of impermanence and suffering, the perception of suffering and non-self, as well as other wholesome, afflicted, and neutral perceptions.
Among these, the wholesome perceptions are:

This refers to the wholesome [states] acquired through application (*prāyogika*) and those acquired by birth (*upapattilābhika*). Regarding the wholesome states acquired through application, there are the notions of application and the notions of the wholesome.
These consist of what is accomplished through hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
What is accomplished through hearing and reflection is as previously explained.
Regarding that which is produced through cultivation:

it refers to the perception produced through cultivation that takes impermanence as its object and gives rise to the mental aspect of "not being non-impermanent," yet does not cultivate the perception of impermanence itself.
Question: At what stage is this said to occur?
Answer: It occurs at the initial stage of "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) when one takes the truths of Origination (*samudaya*) and the Path (*mārga*) as objects.
Alternatively, it occurs during the four moments of mind within the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of Origination once one has entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
During the three moments of mind of the clear realization of the Path,
if an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness,
and takes as their preparatory practice the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) focused on the perception of impermanence;
At the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,

as well as at the time of the supernormal knowledges of the knowledge of others' minds and the recollection of past lives, an ordinary person induces the application of mindfulness on phenomena based on the perception of impermanence.
That is to say, when an ordinary person gives rise to the four immeasurables and the mindfulness of phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) taking impermanence as its object,
they simultaneously give rise to the formless liberation (ārūpya-vimokṣa) which takes impermanence as its object.
Furthermore, when one gives rise to the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) of infinite space and infinite consciousness,
these are called wholesome perceptions, defiled perceptions, and neutral perceptions,
as previously explained.
This is called contemplating the perception of impermanence without cultivating the perception of impermanence.
There is also the cultivation of the perception of impermanence while contemplating the perception of impermanence;
that is, taking the perception of impermanence as an object and cultivating the perception of impermanence.

Just as when the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā) arises in continuous succession, one takes as its object the perception of impermanence regarding one's own continuum in the past and future, as well as the three times of another's continuum.
Question: In what stage is this said to occur?
Answer: This refers to the initial stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata).

At this point, one develops the application of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) taking the Truth of Suffering as its object. As "Heat" and "Summit" (mūrdhan) increase, one develops the application of mindfulness of phenomena taking the perception of impermanence as its object. At the initial stage of "Patience" (kṣānti), which arises from the Summit, [the same applies].
Furthermore, as the stage of increasing patience develops,
one gives rise to the application of mindfulness on phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) taking the three truths as its object;
subsequently, if one gives rise to the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma).
If, during the four moments of mind of the present observation of suffering upon entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
or at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*),
one practices the application of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) by taking impermanence as the object; [this constitutes the attainment of the fruit].
Regarding the detachment from the defilements of the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
if one employs these very [attainments] as the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
then at the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and liberation paths (*vimukti-mārga*):
If one practices the application of mindfulness on phenomena by taking impermanence as the object,
those resolved through faith refine their faculties to become "attainers-by-sight," while those liberated by occasion refine their faculties to become "unshakables."
If one takes this very [contemplation] as the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
then at the time of all those uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the preparatory application;
or if one practices the mixed cultivation of dhyāna through the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) that takes impermanent phenomena as its object.

When one gives rise to the supernormal knowledge of the mind of others (*paracittajñāna*) conditioned by the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*), or when one gives rise to the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*),
or when one gives rise to the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*),
for those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimate reality (*paramārtha*):
The analytical knowledge of the meaning of the conditioned origination of the perception of impermanence and the analytical knowledge of eloquence;
the knowledge resulting from prayer, the limit of meditative concentration, the formless liberations,
and the entry into the attainment of cessation at the time of the subtle mind of perception.
When one gives rise to the universal sphere (kṛtsnāyatana) of infinite space and consciousness,
some say that one also gives rise to the wishless-of-the-wishless (apraṇihitāpraṇihita).
At such a time, one may cultivate the perception of impermanence and also contemplate the perception of impermanence;
or one may neither cultivate the perception of impermanence nor contemplate the perception of impermanence—
namely, excluding the aforementioned cases.
Question: At what stage is this said to occur?

Answer: This is said to occur at the initial stage of *uṣmagata* (heat), when one gives rise to the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) on phenomena (*dharma*) with the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) as its object.
If one has already entered the state of correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and, for the duration of the four moments of mind during the realization of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya*),
as well as in all other states, does not take impermanence as an object nor cultivate the perception of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*).
One should understand all [applications] according to what is appropriate.
The recitation by the masters of foreign lands should also be understood as before.
As it is with the perception of impermanence, so it is with the perception of suffering in the impermanent, and the perception of non-self in suffering.
As for the distinctions:

one mentions their own names; furthermore, in the third sentence, one excludes the mention of "the wishless regarding the wishless," the perception of impurity, the perception of revulsion toward food, the perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in, the perception of death, the perception of abandonment, the perception of detachment, and the perception of cessation.
Regarding "it should be understood accordingly":
this means that the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) and so forth should also be treated in fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*),
though with certain distinctions.
That is to say: if one cultivates the perception of impurity, does one contemplate that perception of impurity?
One should answer this by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are cases where one cultivates the perception of impurity but does not contemplate that perception of impurity.
This refers to cultivating the perception of impurity by taking other phenomena as its object.
Question: At what stage is this said to occur?
Answer: This is said to occur when one becomes detached from the desire realm through the knowledge of cessation or the knowledge of the path.
Up to the defiled third dhyāna,
one takes the mindfulness of body and mind as well as the mindfulness of phenomena directed toward other phenomena as the preparatory application.
Regarding that, some say it occurs at the time of the final path of liberation within all paths of preparation;
others say it occurs at the time of every path of liberation.
If, relying on a form-sphere concentration, one becomes detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
one employs the mindfulness of body and the mindfulness of mind as well as the mindfulness of phenomena directed toward other phenomena as the preliminary application.
At all times during the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),

or at the time of the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) when attaining the fruit of Arhatship while born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one employs either the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
One who transforms their faculties from the stage of "resolute belief" (śraddhādhimukta) to "attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) employs the mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind,
as well as the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) taking other phenomena as its object, as the preparatory application (prayoga).
At the time of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is not necessarily fixed as previously described.
One who is liberated by time (*samaya-vimukta*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) to become immovable (*akopya*).
This occurs if they rely on a meditative absorption with form (*rūpa-dhyāna*).
Taking the mindfulness of body, feelings, and mind,
as well as the mindfulness of phenomena regarding other phenomena as the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
at the time of that path of preparation and the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
When one practices the mixed cultivation of dhyāna through the mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind,
as well as the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) directed toward other phenomena;

or when one brings forth the supernormal powers of the base of psychic power, the divine eye, the divine ear, and the knowledge of others' minds— during the four paths of immediate succession and the single path of liberation.
Furthermore, when one attains the supernormal knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*) by taking other dharmas as its object;

or when one gives rise to the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the first eight bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), or the two analytical knowledges of phenomena and language (*dharmapada-pratisaṃvid*); at these times [the aforementioned faculties are present].
When one dwells in the mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind based on a meditative absorption with form,
or when one dwells in the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) taking other phenomena as its object— at that time,
for those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimate reality (paramārtha), [this would be untenable].
When one establishes the mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind based on the meditative concentrations of the form realm;
when one attains the analytical knowledge of meaning regarding the mindfulness of phenomena that takes other phenomena as its object;
and when there are those who maintain that only nirvana is the ultimate truth.
When arising the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*),
if one relies on a material meditative concentration (*rūpadhyāna*) to give rise to the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*),
as well as the applications of mindfulness regarding body, sensation, and mind (*kāyavedanācittasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Furthermore, when one dwells in the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) taking other phenomena as objects, or during the knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) and the meditative absorption of the ultimate limit (prāntakoṭika-samādhi);
when one gives rise to the state of non-contention (araṇā);

or when, relying on a meditative concentration with form, one gives rise to the emptiness-of-emptiness (śūnyatā-śūnyatā), the wishlessness-of-wishlessness (apraṇihitā-apraṇihita), and the signlessness-of-signlessness (animittā-animitta).
At such a time, there is the cultivation of the perception of impurity without mentally attending to the perception of impurity;
and there is the mental attention to the perception of impurity without cultivating the perception of impurity—
namely, when one attends to other perceptions while taking the perception of impurity as an object.
"Other perceptions" refers to the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of non-self in suffering,
as well as other wholesome, defiled, and indeterminate perceptions.

Among these, "wholesome perceptions" refers to both wholesome perceptions acquired through application (*prāyogika*) and those acquired by birth (*upapattilābhika*). Wholesome perceptions acquired through application refer to those produced by hearing,
reflection, and cultivation (*śrutamayī*, *cintāmayī*, and *bhāvanāmayī*).
That which is produced through hearing refers to the perception produced through hearing that takes impurity as its object.
That which is produced through reflection refers to...
That is to say, the perception accomplished through reflection arises by taking impurity as its object;
the perception accomplished through cultivation arises by taking impurity as its object.
Yet one does not cultivate the perception of impurity.
Question: In what stage is this said to occur?

Answer: This is said to occur in the stages of Initial Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and Increasing Patience (*vṛddhakṣānti*), wherein one takes the truths of Suffering (*duḥkha*) and Origination (*samudaya*) as objects.
One increases the applications of mindfulness on the perception of impurity during the stages of Heat and Summits;
if one gives rise to the Supreme Mundane Dharmas,
or has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma), then for four moments of mind each during the clear realizations of suffering and origin.
When one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm up to the third dhyāna by means of the mundane path or through the knowledge of suffering and its origin—
at all times during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the eight paths of liberation— this applies.

Some say that it occurs only at the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) when one becomes free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna by means of the mundane path (laukika-mārga).
Taking the perception of impurity as the object of the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space,
one employs the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) as the preliminary practice.
At the time of all those preliminary practices and the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), [one proceeds].

If, by means of the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin, one abandons the defilements of the fourth dhyāna during the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the nine paths of liberation; or if,
by means of the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin,
one who is resolved through faith refines their faculties to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Regarding that, it is not fixed whether they occur during the path of uninterrupted transition or the path of liberation, as previously stated. If,
relying on the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space,
one gives rise to the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) that takes impure phenomena as its object, then:
This is called wholesome perception (*saṃjñā*).
Defiled and neutral perceptions are as previously explained.
The distinction is that it takes the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) as its object.
At such a time, there is one who contemplates the perception of impurity but does not cultivate the perception of impurity;
and there is one who both cultivates the perception of impurity and contemplates the perception of impurity—
namely, one who, taking the perception of impurity as an object, cultivates the perception of impurity.
Question: In what stage is this taught?

Answer: This is taught in the case of one who, by means of the mundane path or through the knowledge of suffering and its origin, becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the third dhyāna.
Taking the mindfulness of mental objects (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) focused on impure phenomena as its preparatory application (prayoga),
it is said by some that at the time of the final path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) of all those paths of preparation (prayoga-mārga):
And at the time of all paths of liberation,
if one relies on a form-sphere concentration to become detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
or if one relies on that very same concentration with the application of the mindfulness foundation of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) taking impure things as its object.
At the time of all those paths of preparation,
if one employs the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) having the truths of suffering and its origin as its object,
and transforms the faculties through resolute faith, one becomes one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Taking the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) focused on impure objects as the preparatory practice (*prayoga*),
at the time of that path of preparation, the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is not necessarily fixed as previously described.
This applies if one relies upon a meditative concentration (*samādhi*) associated with form.
When one who is liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) refines their faculties to become unshakable (akopya),
they take the application of mindfulness on phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) focused on the perception of impurity as their preparatory practice.
At the time of that path of preparation, when they practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna while focusing on the perception of impurity through the application of mindfulness on phenomena:
When one gives rise to the supernormal knowledge of the knowledge of others' minds by taking the perception of impurity as its object;
when one gives rise to the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives;
or when one gives rise to the four immeasurables.

When one, relying on a material meditative absorption (*rūpadhyāna*), gives rise to the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) that takes the perception of impurity as its object— at that time,
for those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimate reality (*paramārtha*),
when they give rise to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) based on that material absorption which takes the perception of impurity as its object—
When one gives rise to the perception of impurity and enters the *pranidhijñāna-paryantaka-samādhi*,
at such a time, one may both cultivate the perception of impurity and contemplate the perception of impurity;
or one may neither cultivate the perception of impurity nor contemplate the perception of impurity.
This means excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Question: In what stage is this said to occur?

Answer: This refers to the initial stages of *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti*, as well as the intensification of *kṣānti*, wherein one establishes mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) by taking the truths of cessation and the path as objects.
If one increases the stages of Heat and Peak, there are the applications of mindfulness regarding bodily sensations and the mind,
as well as the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena when taking other phenomena as objects;
and if one has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and attained the clear realization of the path of cessation, each lasting for four moments of mind.
If one becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm up to the third dhyāna by means of the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path,
it is said by some that during all those nine paths of uninterrupted transition and eight paths of liberation,
[the following occurs].
Only at the time of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*):

when one abandons the defilements of the fourth dhyāna through the nine paths of immediate succession and nine paths of liberation using the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*;
or when one abandons the defilements of the fourth dhyāna by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*).
That is to say, based on the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space,
one employs the application of mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind,
as well as the application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) taking other phenomena as its object, as the preliminary practice (*prayoga*).
At the time of the nine paths of liberation of that path of preparation,
if one relies on a form-sphere concentration to become detached from the defilements of the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.
At all times during the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation paths (*vimukti-mārga*),
with the sole exception of the final liberation path for abandoning the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*),
if one relies on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) to abandon the defilements of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
With the mindfulness establishments of body, feeling, and mind,
as well as the mindfulness establishment of phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) taking other phenomena as its object, these serve as the preparatory practices (prayoga).
At the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted (ānantarya), and liberation paths (vimukti-mārga):
If one relies on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) to become free from the defilements of the upper three formless realms,
then during all those paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),

this applies with the sole exception of the final path of liberation for becoming free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) when one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
If one practices the application of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) by taking the truth of the cessation of the path as an object,
and attains the stage of "one who has reached vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) through the refinement of faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*) based on faith and resolve (*śraddhādhimukta*),
then at the time of the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*), the liberation path (*vimuktimārga*) is not fixed, as previously explained.
When one who is liberated by occasion sharpens their faculties to become unshakable,
they take the mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind based on the formless realms as their preparation,
as well as the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) which takes other phenomena as its object.
At the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths—
excluding only the final liberation path—
and when one gives rise to the formless liberations or the latter two universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana), [the same applies].
When one relies on the formless realm to give rise to the mindfulness of body, feelings, and mind,
or when one gives rise to the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) taking other phenomena as its object;

and when one relies on the formless realm to give rise to the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) of meaning and eloquence, or the concentrations of emptiness-of-emptiness and wishlessness-of-wishlessness.
Regarding the signless and the signless-less:
when one gives rise to the subtle mind that perceives the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti),
such is the case during the state of wholesomeness.
If one is in a state of defilement or neutrality, one does not take impurity as an object;
likewise, in all states of mindlessness,
during such times one neither cultivates the perception of impurity nor contemplates the perception of impurity.
The same applies to the perception of impurity, the perception of revulsion toward food, and so on, up to the perception of cessation;
each of these also forms four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
One should reflect upon the distinctions among them as appropriate to reason.
If one gives rise to a thought of sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*), does one then contemplate that thought of sensual desire?
One should respond by establishing four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is the case where one gives rise to a thought of sensual desire but does not contemplate that thought of sensual desire.
This refers to the arising of sensual thought (*kāma-vitarka*) by taking other phenomena as its object—
such as the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and consciousness.

When sensual thought arises with respect to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), excluding the sensual thought itself, this is called "the arising of sensual thought without reflecting upon that sensual thought."
Because one takes other phenomena as objects,
there is contemplation that gives rise to no thoughts of sensual desire;
that is to say, taking thoughts of sensual desire as an object, one gives rise to other thoughts.
This is of three kinds:
namely, wholesome, defiled, and neutral.
As for the wholesome:
That is to say, there are the virtues acquired through application (*prayoga-kuśala*) and those acquired by birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*).
Within the virtues acquired through application, there are those consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Regarding those consisting of hearing:
That which arises with discursive thought regarding desire as its object refers to that which is produced through hearing;
that which arises with discursive thought regarding desire as its object refers to that which is produced through reflection.
Regarding that which is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*):
this refers to that which arises from the cultivation based on the investigation of desire.
Question: In what stage is this said to exist?

Answer: This explains that at the initial stages of Heat, Peak, and Patience, as well as when Patience is increasing, one develops the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) taking dharmas of the desire realm as its object;
whereas when Heat and Peak are increasing, one develops the application of mindfulness to phenomena taking thoughts of the desire realm as their object.
If one gives rise to the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*),
or if one has already entered the correct nature of departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) during the two moments of the clear observation of suffering (*duḥkha-abhisamaya*),

namely the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*), or during the two moments of the clear observation of origination (*samudaya-abhisamaya*).
This refers to the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*).
If one becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm through the knowledge of suffering and origination,
one employs the mindfulness-establishment on phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) concerning thoughts of the desire realm as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
During the nine paths of preparation, nine uninterrupted paths, and nine paths of liberation,
if one abandons the defilements of the desire realm by means of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*),
one takes the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that has thoughts of desire as its object as the path of preparation.
During those nine paths of uninterrupted transition within the path of preparation,
if one relies on the *anāgamya* concentration to become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
Taking the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) associated with desire and discursive thought as the preliminary application (prayoga),
throughout all those stages of the path of preparation,

up until one relies upon the fourth dhyāna to become detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, and so on, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Taking the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) associated with desire and discursive thought as the preparatory practice (*prayoga*),
at the time of all those paths of preparation,

if one refines the faculties through the dharma-knowledge of suffering and origination (*duḥkha-samudaya-dharmajñāna*) by means of resolute faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), one becomes one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Taking the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) associated with desire and discursive thought as the preparatory application (prayoga),
at the moment of the path of liberation immediately following that application—
when one who is liberated-by-faculties (samayavimukta) refines their faculties to become unshakable (akopya).
If one takes the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) that has desire and discursive thought as its object as the preparatory application,
then at the time of that path of preparation;
or if one takes the mindfulness of phenomena that has desire and discursive thought as its object when practicing the mixed cultivation of dhyāna.
When arising with desire as the object through the supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds;
when arising with the recollection of past lives in the desire realm as the object through the supernormal power of knowledge of past abodes;
and when arising with the four immeasurables.
When one gives rise to the application of mindfulness on phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) that takes desire and discursive thought as its object,
for those who maintain that all phenomena are of ultimate reality (paramārtha),
there arises the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid) regarding the application of mindfulness on phenomena that takes desire and discursive thought as its object.

If, when arising, one establishes the application of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) through thoughts conditioned by desire, or during the concentration of non-contention (*araṇasamādhi*), the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*),
or the ultimate concentration (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*), it is called wholesome. As for that which is defiled:
This refers to the arising of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which clings to "I" and "mine," conditioned by discursive thoughts regarding desire;
the full explanation is as previously stated.
Regarding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*): it refers to the arising of attention that is neither appropriate nor inappropriate, conditioned by discursive thoughts regarding desire.
At such a time, while contemplating sensual thoughts, no sensual thought arises;
yet there are occasions when a sensual thought does arise even while one is contemplating sensual thoughts—
namely, when a sensual thought arises taking another sensual thought as its object.
Just as when sensual desire (*kāma-vitarka*) manifests in a long-term continuous succession,
one may take as objects sensual desire within one's own continuum across the past and future, or sensual desire within the three periods of time in the continua of others;
there are instances where sensual desire does not arise, nor does one mentally attend to sensual desire.
This refers to what is recited by masters outside [this school], namely:
"When one conditions other phenomena, other discursive thoughts arise.
In this context, it is as when one conditions the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and consciousness.
Excluding the state of desire-thoughts, when other formations of the aggregate of volitional formations arise,
when thoughts directed toward the unconditioned arise,
and in all other instances where desire-thoughts do not arise and one does not contemplate desire-thoughts.
It is the same for the thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, and the thought of harmfulness;
the difference is that they are referred to by their own names.
This also applies when the thought of renunciation arises.
Does he contemplate the search for renunciation?
One should respond that this involves four permutations: there may be the arising of a search for renunciation without contemplating the search for renunciation;
that is, the arising of a search for renunciation by taking other phenomena as its object.
Just as with the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and consciousness, so too,
with the exception of the thought of renunciation,
other formations arise taking the thought of renunciation as their object; and the thought of renunciation arises taking the unconditioned as its object.
Question: In what stage does this teaching occur?

Answer: This teaching refers to when, based on the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and the first *dhyāna*, during the stages of initial *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and the intensification of *kṣānti*, one gives rise to the mindfulness-establishment (*smṛtyupasthāna*) of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) having the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) as its object.

If one increases the applications of mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind that arise during the stages of Heat and Summits, as well as the application of mindfulness of phenomena that takes other phenomena as its object;

or if one has already entered the state of rightness and the departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma), and for the duration of the four moments of mind during the realization of cessation (nirodha-abhisamaya).

If, by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm and the first dhyāna through the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*);
or if, by relying on the first dhyāna, one becomes free from the defilements of the first dhyāna through the knowledge of cessation.
If one takes the mindfulness of body, the mindfulness of feeling, the mindfulness of mind, and the mindfulness of phenomena regarding other phenomena as the preliminary application (*prayoga*),
then at the time of all those paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) resulting from that application:
Relying on those two stages, one abandons the defilements of the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception through the knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation.
This is done by employing the mindfulness of body and the mindfulness of mind as preparatory practices, as well as the mindfulness of phenomena that takes other phenomena as its object.

At the time of all those paths of preparation, uninterrupted paths, and paths of liberation, one relies on that very stage to refine the faculties through the conviction of the knowledge of cessation, thereby becoming a "one who has attained vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).

If one employs the mindfulness of body, the mindfulness of feeling, the mindfulness of mind, and the mindfulness of phenomena—taking other phenomena as its object—as the path of preparation; [then one becomes a dṛṣṭiprāpta].
At the time of the path of preparation, the immediate path, and the path of liberation,
one relies on that very stage to attain liberation through the knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation, and to refine the faculties (indriya-saṃskāra) to become unshakable (akopya).

If one takes the mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind as the path of preparation, or the mindfulness of phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) taking other phenomena as its object, [one proceeds accordingly].
At the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,

when one practices the mixed cultivation of the first dhyāna through the mindfulness of body and mind, as well as the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) taking other phenomena as its object.
If one induces the supernormal powers of the divine eye, the divine ear, and the knowledge of others' minds based on the first dhyāna,
there are four paths of uninterrupted transition and one path of liberation; furthermore,
this applies at the time of the path of liberation for the knowledge of others' minds when taking other phenomena as its object.
If one practices mindfulness of breathing based on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage,
or if one practices the first two liberations,

the first four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), and the applications of mindfulness regarding body, feeling, mind, and phenomena based on either the *anāgamya* or the first *dhyāna*:
Furthermore, regarding the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that takes other phenomena as its object:
for those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimate reality (*paramārtha*),

there arises the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) concerning the applications of mindfulness to body, feeling, and mind, as well as the application of mindfulness to phenomena that takes other phenomena as its object.
Furthermore, for those who maintain that only nirvāṇa is the ultimate truth,
when they give rise to the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid),
they simultaneously give rise to the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid) and the analytical knowledge of language (niruktipratisaṃvid) based on those two stages.

When one explains the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) regarding the applications of mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind, as well as the application of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) that takes other phenomena as its object,
it is then based upon those two stages that one gives rise to the emptiness-of-emptiness, the wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and the signlessness-of-signlessness.
Some say that when one gives rise to the signless-signless,
at such a time one gives rise to the thought of renunciation because one does not contemplate the thought of renunciation by taking other phenomena as its object.
There are cases where, although one contemplates the search for renunciation (*naiṣkramya-vitarka*), the search for renunciation does not arise;
that is, while taking the search for renunciation as its object, other searches arise.
These are of three kinds.
That is to say: wholesome, defiled, and indeterminate.
Regarding the wholesome, with the exception of that produced through reflection (*cintāmayī*), the rest is as previously explained.
Within the category of that which is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), in what stage is this said to reside?
Answer: This is said to depend on the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) and the initial stages of heat (*uṣmagata*), summits (*mūrdhan*), and patiences (*kṣānti*) within the three higher dhyānas.
Furthermore, when increasing the stage of patience (*kṣānti*),
one gives rise to the application of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) taking the three truths as its object;

when increasing the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "summit" (*mūrdhan*), one gives rise to the application of mindfulness on phenomena taking the search for renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-paryeṣaṇā*) as its object.
If one gives rise to the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*),
or if one has already entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
there are four moments of mind each for the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, origin, and the path.
If, relying on the intermediate dhyāna,
one becomes detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna through the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path,

and if one employs as the preparatory application (prayoga) precisely these [knowledges] along with the investigation of renunciation and the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) directed toward conventional dharmas.
At the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,
he relies on the intermediate dhyāna to abandon the defilements of the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

If one takes these very factors, as well as the mundane dharma-smṛtyupasthāna consisting of the knowledge of suffering and its origin through the investigation of renunciation, as the preparatory practice (prayoga),
then at the time of all those uninterrupted paths of liberation following the preparatory stage:
Except for the final path of liberation that abandons the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
if one relies on the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna to abandon the defilements of the first dhyāna,

or if one relies on this very same stage with the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*)— characterized by thoughts of renunciation— as the preliminary practice (*prayoga*).
At the time of all those preparatory and uninterrupted paths,
if one relies on the second dhyāna to abandon the defilements of the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).

If one takes these very [factors], as well as the investigation of renunciation, the knowledge of suffering and its origin, and the mundane mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), as the preparatory practice (*prayoga*),
then at the time of all those uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) of that preparatory practice:
This excludes the final path of liberation that is free from the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
As it is with the second dhyāna,
so it is with the third and fourth dhyānas as well.

If, relying on the sphere of infinite space, one uses the knowledge of the path to become detached from the defilements of the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and if one employs as the preliminary practice (prayoga) this very [knowledge] as well as the mindfulness-establishment (smṛtyupasthāna) focused on mundane phenomena associated with the investigation of renunciation; [then...]
At the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths—
excluding only the final liberation path that abandons the defilements of the Peak of Existence—
it is as when relying on the sphere of infinite space.
The same applies to the sphere of nothingness based on the sphere of infinite consciousness.
If one relies on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to become free from its defilements,
one takes the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) associated with the investigation of renunciation as the preliminary application.
At the time of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
if one relies on the intermediate dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna,

and through the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path, together with faith-resolve (*śraddhādhimukta*), refines the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become a "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
If one takes these very [applications] and the mundane mindfulness-establishments (smṛtyupasthāna) associated with the investigation of renunciation as the preparatory practice (prayoga),
then at the moment of the path of liberation immediately following that preparation,
by relying on those very stages, through the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), one who is liberated by occasion refines their faculties to become immovable (akopya).

If one takes these very [states], as well as the mundane mindfulness-establishment on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) consisting of the knowledge of suffering and its origin (*duḥkhasamudayajñāna*) associated with the search for renunciation (*naiṣkramyavitarka*), as the preparatory practice (*prayoga*);
then, during that path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), at the time of the nine paths of non-interruption (*ānantaryamārga*) and the eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
If, relying on the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), one refines the faculties (*indriya*) of one liberated by way of the path (*mārga-jñāna-vimukta*) to become immovable (*akopya*),

one takes these very [attainments] as well as the mundane mindfulness-establishment (*laukika-dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that has renunciation-seeking (*naiṣkramyavitarka*) as its object as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
At the time of the nine paths of preparation, the eight uninterrupted paths, and the eight paths of liberation;
or when one employs the wisdom of suffering, origin, and the path that takes renunciation as its object;
or when one practices the mundane application of mindfulness of dharmas while interspersing the cultivation of the upper three dhyānas.
If one relies on the three higher dhyānas to induce the supernormal knowledge of the minds of others conditioned by thoughts of renunciation, or the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives;
or if one relies on the intermediate dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna to give rise to the immeasurables (apramāṇa).
When one gives rise to the investigation of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) directed toward the formless liberations (ārūpya-vimokkha),

or when one gives rise to the application of mindfulness of phenomena (dhammā-satipaṭṭhāna) directed toward renunciation while relying on the intermediate dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana).
For those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimate reality,
when they— relying on the intermediate dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna—

give rise to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) regarding the mundane application of mindfulness (*laukika-dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) consisting of the wisdom that takes renunciation as its object and the wisdoms of suffering, origin, and the path; at that time:

When, based on the formless attainments, one gives rise to the analytical knowledge of the meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) regarding the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) that takes renunciation as its object during the path-knowledge of investigation,
it occurs whether one is based on the intermediate dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
When one gives rise to the analytical knowledge of unimpeded eloquence (pratisaṃvid) based on the thought of renunciation,
or when one gives rise to the wish-fulfilling knowledge (praṇidhijñāna) at the limit of concentration based on the thought of renunciation,
as well as when entering the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) during moments of subtle consciousness; at those times—
This is called wholesome.
As for the defiled,
it refers to the arising of the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which grasps at a self and what belongs to a self, based upon thoughts of renunciation.
The detailed explanation is as before.
Regarding the indeterminate [state]:
it refers to the mental attention that is neither appropriate nor inappropriate, which arises based on thoughts of renunciation.
At such a time, one who contemplates the thought of renunciation does not give rise to the thought of renunciation;
yet there is one who gives rise to the thought of renunciation while also contemplating the thought of renunciation—
namely, one who gives rise to the thought of renunciation by taking the thought of renunciation as its object.
Just as when the investigation of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) manifests in a long-lasting continuum,
it takes as its object the investigation of renunciation regarding one's own continuum across the past and future, as well as that of others' continua throughout the three times.
Question: At which stage is this explained?
Answer: This explanation refers to the stages of "Heat," "Summits," "Patience," and "Increased Patience" within the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna;
therein, one gives rise to the application of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) taking the three truths as its object.
If one increases the stages of *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, there arises the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) associated with the thought of renunciation;

if one gives rise to the *laukikāgradharma*, or has already entered the state of correctness and departure from birth (*samyaktvaniyāma*), there are four moments of mind for each of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, origin, and the path.
If one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm through the mundane path by means of the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path,
and if one employs these very knowledges as the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
then at the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and liberation (*vimukti*) paths:
If, relying on the "not-yet-attained" (anāgamya) stage or the first dhyāna,
one becomes detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna through the knowledge of suffering,

origin, and the path, using precisely these, as well as the mindfulness foundations (smṛtyupasthāna) directed toward worldly phenomena associated with the thought of renunciation, as the preparatory application (prayoga).
At the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,
one relies on those two stages to abandon the defilements of the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

If one employs as the preparatory application (*prayoga*) this very [contemplation] along with the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) regarding conventional dharmas that seek liberation from suffering and its origin,
then at the time of all those uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) of the preparatory application:
Except for the final path of liberation that abandons the defilements of the Peak of Existence,
one relies on those two stages to refine the faculties through the knowledge of suffering, origin, and the path, and through faith-resolve, becoming a "one who has attained vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
If one takes these very [factors] and the mundane applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) associated with the investigation of renunciation as the preparatory practice (prayoga),
then at the time of all those uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga) and paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) of that preparatory practice:
That is to say, based on those two stages, one transforms the faculties from "timely liberation" to "unshakable" through the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

If one employs as the preparatory application (*prayoga*) both this [knowledge of the path] and the mundane mindfulness-establishment (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) consisting of the knowledge of suffering and its origin (*duḥkhasamudayajñāna*) which takes renunciation as its object, [one attains the unshakable state].
At the time of the nine paths of preparation, the eight paths of uninterrupted transition, and the eight paths of liberation;

or when one cultivates the first dhyāna through the mixed cultivation of the mundane mindfulness of dharmas, which is associated with the knowledge of suffering, origin, and path, and has renunciation as its object; at such times [the faculty of knowledge arises].

If, relying on the first dhyāna, one brings forth the supernormal knowledge of the knowledge of others' minds and the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives by means of thoughts of renunciation;
or if, relying on the threshold concentration (anāgamya) of the first dhyāna, one gives rise to the immeasurables (apramāṇa).
Furthermore, when one dwells in the application of mindfulness to phenomena by taking renunciation as the object of thought,
those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimate reality do so based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) or the first dhyāna.

When one attains the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) during the moment of the knowledge of suffering, origin, path, and conventional phenomena (*saṃvṛtidharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) that takes renunciation as its object,
at that very time, based on those two stages, one attains the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*) that takes renunciation as its object.
Some say that when one gives rise to the emptiness-of-emptiness and the wishlessness-of-wishlessness based on those two stages, at such times as these,
one also gives rise to the thought of renunciation and contemplates the thought of renunciation.
There is one who neither gives rise to the thought of renunciation nor contemplates the thought of renunciation;
that is to say, excluding the aforementioned cases.
Question: In what stage does this refer?
Answer: This explanation refers to the intermediate dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna;

during the initial stages of heat (*uṣmagata*), summits (*mūrdhan*), patience (*kṣānti*), and the increase of patience (*kṣānty-vṛddhi*), one gives rise to the application of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) taking the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) as its object.

If one increases the stages of *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, giving rise to the mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind, as well as the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) taking other phenomena as its object;
or if one has already entered the state of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*) and is in the four moments of mind during the realization of cessation (*nirodha-abhisamaya*).
If, relying on the intermediate dhyāna,
one becomes detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna through the knowledge of cessation,
one employs the application of mindfulness of bodily sensations and the application of mindfulness of phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) taking other phenomena as objects as the preparatory practice.
At the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,
one relies on the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara) and employs the knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation.

One becomes detached from the defilements of the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by employing the mindfulness of body and the mindfulness of mind as the preliminary application, as well as the mindfulness of phenomena that takes other phenomena as its object.
At the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,
if one relies on the threshold stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna to become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
one employs the mindfulness of body and the mindfulness of mind as the preparatory path, along with the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) taking other phenomena as its object.
At the time of the path of preparation and the path of liberation,
if one relies on the second dhyāna,
[one employs] the knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation.

One becomes detached from the defilements of the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by employing the mindfulness of body and the mindfulness of mind as the preparatory application, as well as the mindfulness of phenomena directed toward other phenomena.
In all those cases of the preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths,
it is the same whether one relies on the second dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
If one relies on the preparatory stage of the third dhyāna, one becomes detached from the defilements of the second dhyāna.

If one relies precisely upon this body-reception mindfulness-abiding (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), mind-reception mindfulness-abiding (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*), and the remaining dharma-dharma mindfulness-abiding (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) as the preparatory practice (*prayoga*),
then at the time of all those preparatory, uninterrupted (*anantarya*), and liberation paths (*vimuktimārga*):
As it is in dependence upon the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the third dhyāna,
so it is in dependence upon the preparatory stage of the fourth dhyāna.
If one relies on the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one becomes detached from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding those who maintain that the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the formless realms have distinct objects,

they say that if one relies on this very [stage] as the basis for the application of mindfulness of body, feelings, and mind, and takes other phenomena as the object for the application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), these serve as the preliminary practice (*prayoga*).
Regarding those who claim that there is no distinct object for the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the formless realms:

they say that if one takes this very basis as the support while using other phenomena as the object, with the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) serving as the preliminary application (*prayoga*),
then at the time of all such preliminary applications, the paths of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) and liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
As it is with the preliminary stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space,
so it is for all stages up to the preliminary stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

If one relies on the preliminary stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to give rise to the applications of mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind in order to become detached from its defilements.
And when the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) directed toward other phenomena serves as the preparatory practice (prayoga),
at the time of that path of preparation,
if one relies upon the intermediate dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna.
By means of the faculty of conviction (*adhimokṣendriya*) associated with the knowledge of cessation, one refines the faculties to become a "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Taking the mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind, as well as the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) having other phenomena as its object, as the preparatory practice (*prayoga*),
at the moment of the path of liberation immediately following that preparatory practice:
If, relying on the intermediate dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness,
one employs the knowledge of suffering, origin,
and cessation to refine the faculties of one liberated by time so as to become immovable.
Taking the mindfulness of body, feelings, and mind, as well as the mindfulness of phenomena regarding other objects, as the preliminary application (*prayoga*),
at the time of all those uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
if one relies upon the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
At that time, one who is liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta) practices the application of the mindfulness of body,
feeling, and mind, as well as the mindfulness of phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) taking other phenomena as its object, in order to transform their faculties into those of the immovable (akopya).
During that stage of the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga),...

When one practices the mixed cultivation of the upper three dhyānas through the mindfulness of body, the mindfulness of feeling, the mindfulness of mind, and the mindfulness of phenomena directed toward other dharmas;
or when, based on the upper three dhyānas, one brings forth the supernormal power of psychic travel, the divine eye, and the divine ear.
And when one exercises the supernormal knowledge of the minds of others taking other phenomena as its object, or the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives;
or when, relying on the intermediate dhyāna or the second dhyāna,
one gives rise to the first two liberations and the first four bases of mastery.
When one gives rise to the third and eighth liberations, the four subsequent bases of mastery, and the ten totalities;
or when one gives rise to the mindfulness of body, feelings, and mind, as well as the mindfulness of phenomena directed toward other phenomena; or during the four formless liberations.
When one gives rise to the contemplation of impurity based on the intermediate dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna,
or when one practices mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) based on the intermediate dhyāna or the access concentrations (sāmantaka) of the second and third dhyānas.
If, relying on the intermediate dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
one gives rise to the application of mindfulness of body, feeling, and mind, as well as the application of mindfulness of phenomena taking other phenomena as objects;
For those who maintain that all phenomena are ultimate reality, there is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) regarding the applications of mindfulness of body,

feeling, and mind, as well as the application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) taking other phenomena as its object, based upon the intermediate dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, for those who maintain that only nirvāṇa is the ultimate truth,
when they give rise to the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid) based on those various stages,
they simultaneously give rise to the applications of mindfulness regarding body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (kāya-vedanā-citta-dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) based on those very same stages.
And when one explains the analytical knowledge of dharma (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) by means of the mindfulness of dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) taking other dharmas as its object;
and when one gives rise to the analytical knowledge of dharma based on the intermediate dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna.
Some say that when one gives rise to the analytical knowledge of language (nirukti-pratisaṃvid) based on the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara),
if one arouses the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding bodily sensations and the mind, [they are present].
Furthermore, when one is dwelling in the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) taking other phenomena as its object, or in the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*),
or in the meditative absorption of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*), or when entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) during which thought is subtle,
or when arising in the state of non-contention (*araṇā*).
When, relying on the intermediate dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
one gives rise to the emptiness-of-emptiness, the wishlessness-of-wishlessness, or the signlessness-of-signlessness— at such times as these,
one does not give rise to the thought of renunciation.
Nor does one contemplate the thought of renunciation;
as with the thought of renunciation,
so it is with the thought of non-ill will and the thought of non-harming.
The three unwholesome thoughts and the three wholesome thoughts are explained in detail as in the *Vitarkavicāra-nirdeśa* of the *Saṃgītiparyāya*.
