translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Eight: The Aggregate of Views (Dṛṣṭiskandha), Part Two of the Second Sub-section on the Appropriation of the Three Existences (Trabhavopādāna). Question: Are all phenomena that have ignorance as their cause also conditioned by ignorance?
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: Why is the discussion here conducted in reliance upon clarity (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)?
Answer: It is because the intention of the author of that treatise was such.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that these two are the fundamental dharmas of both affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*).
This means that all defilements have ignorance as their root,
as it is said:
"Whatever various evil and unwholesome dharmas there may be."
Whether arising or growing,
all have ignorance as their root,
as their origin, as their source, and as their condition.
All purity has clarity as its root.
As it is said: "Whatever various wholesome dharmas there may be, whether they arise or increase [they all have clarity as their root]."
There is nothing that does not have clarity as its root, its origin, its category,
and its source. Some say that this is because these two are both preeminent dharmas.
That is to say, the Blessed One stated in the sūtras that these two kinds are the foremost dharmas,
as it is said:
"O bhikṣus..."
With ignorance as the primary factor and ignorance as the precursor,
various kinds of evil and unwholesome states all arise.
Furthermore, for one who has thereby become shameless and unscrupulous, this serves as the primary cause and the preceding sign that various wholesome qualities will fail to arise;
conversely, for one who has thereby become possessed of shame and scruple, [various wholesome qualities] do arise.
Some say that these two are the remedial dharmas for the immediate obstacles to clarity; that is to say,
ignorance is the immediate obstacle to clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the direct antidote to ignorance (*avidyā*).
Some say this is because these two are mutually exclusive phenomena commonly known to all.
That is to say, ignorance is the opposite of clear knowledge,
and clear knowledge is the opposite of ignorance. Some say:
These two both take as their objects the four noble truths, whether they are mutually inclusive or not;
both take as their objects contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena that are mutually exclusive;
and both take as their objects conditioned and unconditioned phenomena that are mutually exclusive.
For these various reasons,
the author of this treatise has composed it based on clarity (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). Now,
as for the categories of the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of clarity and ignorance, there are eleven types.
Those bound to the desire realm are of four kinds:
namely, wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and unobscured-neutral.
Those bound to the form realm are of three kinds, excluding the unwholesome.
The same applies to those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-baddha*) as well as to untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*). Herein,

wholesome phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-baddha-kuśala-dharma*), whether accompanied by clarity (*vidyā*) or ignorance (*avidyā*), are not causes for one another, yet they all function as three conditions (*pratyaya*).
That is to say, with respect to the equal-and-immediate, the object-condition, and the dominant condition:
unwholesome dharmas have ignorance as their four causes— namely, association, coexistence, similar-type, and universal—
and they likewise function as the four conditions.
To clarify that ignorance is not their cause, two conditions are established, namely:
the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Ignorance serves as the four causes for obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
That is to say, those that are associated, co-existent, of the same class,
and universal also function as four conditions; furthermore,
it is clarified that what is not its cause functions as one condition, namely, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Excluding the maturation of ignorance, the unobscured-neutral dharmas of the desire realm do not have ignorance as their cause;
rather, ignorance acts as three conditions for them— namely, the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Ignorance acts as a dominant condition for that which is not its cause;
ignorance acts as a ripening cause for the ripening of ignorance,
thereby acting as three conditions.
This refers to the causes of equality, immediate succession, and predominance,
but not the objective cause (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
because that maturation (*vipāka*) exists within the five sensory consciousnesses.
Clear knowledge (*vidyā*) is not its cause, but acts as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Wholesome factors associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśala-dharma*) are neither clear knowledge nor ignorance;
they act as all three conditions.
That is to say, with regard to the equal-immediate, the object-condition, and the dominant condition:
obscured-unspecified phenomena of the form realm have ignorance as their four causes—
namely, the associated, the co-existent, the homogeneous, and the universal causes.
It also acts as four conditions;
it is explained that while it is not its cause, it serves as two conditions,
namely, the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
Unobscured-neutral dharmas bound to the form realm do not have ignorance as their cause, but serve as three conditions for it— namely, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Clear knowledge (*vidyā*) does not have them as its cause, but serves as one condition for it— the dominant condition.
Just as there are three types in the form realm,
so it is with the three types in the formless realm.
Ignorance is not the cause of untainted phenomena.
It acts as two conditions;
that is, it serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
With the exception of the first untainted dharma (*anāsrava*), all other untainted dharmas serve as its three causes (*hetu*).
That is to say, associated, co-existent, and homogeneous [factors] act as four conditions.
With the exception of the initial light,
all other initial untainted factors act as two causes for that light.
That is to say, they are associated and co-existent;
or there is one cause, namely the co-existent cause,
which acts as two conditions, namely the causal condition and the sovereign condition.
Initially, clear illumination is not its cause;
it acts as a single dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
This is the brief *vibhāṣā* on this point.
If all phenomena have ignorance as their cause, do those phenomena have ignorance as their condition?
Answer: If a phenomenon has ignorance as its cause, that phenomenon has ignorance as its condition.
Herein, "all phenomena having ignorance as their cause" is stated by way of their general category.
Those phenomena have ignorance as their five causes:
namely, associated, co-existent, homogeneous, pervasive, and retributive.
Regarding those conditioned by ignorance, this refers to the phenomena caused by ignorance when categorized by their types.
Ignorance serves as its four conditions.
There are phenomena that take ignorance as their condition but do not have ignorance as their cause;
namely, excluding the maturation of ignorance.
Regarding all other non-obscured neutral formations and wholesome formations,
ignorance serves as three conditions, two conditions, or one condition for those phenomena, but it is not their cause.
If all phenomena have clarity as their cause, do those phenomena have clarity as their condition?
Answer: If a phenomenon has clarity as its cause, that phenomenon has clarity as its condition.
Herein, "phenomena having clarity as their cause" is stated in terms of their general category.
Those dharmas take clarity as their three causes—
namely, the associated, the co-existent, and the similar.
As for those that take clarity as their object-condition, they are dharmas that take clarity as their cause when spoken of in terms of their category.
Wisdom (*vidyā*) serves as its four conditions; there are dharmas for which wisdom is a condition, yet wisdom is not their cause.
This refers to initial wisdom and all contaminated (*sāsrava*) formations (*saṃskāra*).
For those dharmas, wisdom acts either as three conditions, two conditions, or one condition, but it is not their cause.
If phenomena have ignorance as their cause, do those phenomena have clarity as their condition?
Answer: If phenomena have ignorance as their cause, those phenomena have clarity as their condition.
Herein, "phenomena that have ignorance as their cause" is stated in terms of their general category.
Those dharmas take ignorance as their five causes, as previously explained.
Regarding those that take clarity as a condition, if one speaks in terms of their categories,
clarity serves as two conditions for those dharmas that take ignorance as their cause.
This refers to the predominance of the object of focus (*ālambana-adhipati*).
There are phenomena that take light as their object and do not depend on ignorance (*avidyā*),
namely, excluding the maturation (*vipāka*) of ignorance.
As for other non-obscured-neutral formations and wholesome formations,
they serve as four conditions, three conditions, two conditions, or one condition for those dharmas.
Ignorance is not its cause.
Are those phenomena that have clarity as their cause conditioned by ignorance?
Answer: If a phenomenon has clarity as its cause, that phenomenon is conditioned by ignorance.
In this context, when all phenomena are discussed in terms of their categories,
those phenomena have three types of causes:
namely, the associated cause, the co-existent cause, and the homogeneous cause.
That which is conditioned by ignorance takes the factors of knowledge as its cause; speaking in terms of their categories,
ignorance serves as two conditions for them,
namely, the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the sovereign condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
There are dharmas that take ignorance as their object but do not have clarity as their cause;
namely, initial clarity and all contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*).
For those dharmas, ignorance acts as either four conditions, three conditions, two conditions, or one condition.
It is clear that ignorance is not its cause.
Are those phenomena which have ignorance as their cause necessarily unwholesome?
Answer: If a phenomenon...
Unwholesome states have ignorance as their cause;
herein, ignorance is the cause of unwholesome states when considered by way of category.
Those phenomena have ignorance as their four causes—
namely, the associated, co-existent, similar-type, and universal causes—
and there are phenomena that, though caused by ignorance, are not unwholesome.
This refers to the maturation of ignorance (*avidyā-vipāka*) and obscured-unspecified formations (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-saṃskāra*).
Among these, the maturation of ignorance has ignorance as its single ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*),
while the obscured-unspecified formations [have other causes].
Speaking in terms of categories,
ignorance serves as four types of causes:
namely, the associated cause, the co-existent cause, the homogeneous cause, and the pervasive cause.
Yet that phenomenon is not unwholesome,
because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Is a phenomenon wholesome simply because its causes are luminous?
Answer: If a phenomenon is wholesome because its cause is clear,
then herein the wholesome phenomena are explained by way of their general category.
Those dharmas have clarity (*vidyā*) as their three causes—
namely, association, coexistence, and homogeneity.
There are also dharmas that are wholesome but do not have clarity as their cause.
This refers to initial clarity (*āloka*) and wholesome contaminated formations (*sāsrava-kuśala-saṃskāra*).
Among these, initial clarity is wholesome but does not have clarity as its cause,
because there is no preceding or simultaneous clarity.
Wholesome contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) likewise do not have clear knowledge (*vidyā*) as their cause,
because they lack the nature of having no cause.
Is there any phenomenon that neither has clear knowledge as its cause nor has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its cause, yet is not itself causeless?
Answer: There are.

Specifically, with the exception of the maturation of ignorance (*avidyā-vipāka*), all other non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) formations (*saṃskāra*) as well as the wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) formations of initial illumination.
Thus, these phenomena do not arise from clarity (*vidyā*) nor from ignorance (*avidyā*), yet they are not without cause.
Among them, with the exception of the maturation (*vipāka*) of ignorance,
all other unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) formations (*saṃskāra*) [are so].

In terms of their categories, there are four causes: namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Regarding the first [the associated cause], it is explained that there are two types of causes.
That is to say, they are associated and co-existent.
When wholesome contaminated formations are categorized by their types, they have three causes:
namely, the associated cause, the co-existent cause, and the similar-type cause.
Question: At the beginning, it was explained that there is acquisition (prāpti) of both the untainted (anāsrava).
This [acquisition] is neither caused by clarity (vidyā) nor caused by ignorance (avidyā), yet it is not without a cause.
Why is this not mentioned here?
Answer: This passage should have stated that it also clarifies their initial untainted acquisitions (*anāsrava-prāpti*).
That it does not so state should be understood as indicating that the meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*). Some say:
This [acquisition] is included within the first explanation of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and for that reason it is not mentioned [separately].
One should not say that;
for acquisition is not a co-existent cause in the sense of the first explanation.
It should be said that they are subsumed within the first chapter on "Illumination" (*āloka*).
If one speaks of illumination, it should be understood that its associated aggregates have already been explained.

The meaning of illumination and non-illumination among all phenomena is explained at length as in the *Pratītyasamutpādavarga* (Chapter on Dependent Origination) of the *Saṃyuktaskandha* (Miscellaneous Aggregates).

3. Saṃjñā-varga, Part One of the Third Section on the Aggregate of Perception within the Eighth Chapter on the Aggregate of Views: Regarding all phenomena, when the perception of impermanence arises, are those phenomena associated with that perception of impermanence?
Having thus mastered these chapters and the meaning of their expositions, one should analyze them in detail.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This treatise was composed to refute the view that associated phenomena (saṃprayukta-dharma) are not real because they are associated with the delusion of grasping at phenomena;
it demonstrates that associated phenomena definitely exist as real entities.
Thus, this discussion was made.
When various phenomena arise from the perception of impermanence, are those phenomena associated with the perception of impermanence?
One should answer that this involves four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are phenomena that arise from the perception of impermanence but are not associated with the perception of impermanence.
This means that when the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*) manifests, other perceptions must necessarily cease, and those mental factors associated with it must necessarily arise.
In this context, it is said that immediately following the perception of impermanence is the perception of suffering in what is impermanent (*anicce dukkhasaññā*).
Up to the point where any one of the [states] associated with the cessation of perception manifests:
those factors associated with it refer to the nine universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma), excluding perception itself.
The ten great wholesome mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma),
the stage with vitarka and vicāra,
and the stage without vitarka and vicāra.
Only the investigation (*vitarka*) of the stage of investigation and the mind [are involved].
Thus, these dharmas arise because the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*) functions as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
It is not the case that the perception of suffering and non-self (*duḥkha-anātmasaṃjñā*), up to the perception of cessation (*nirodhasaṃjñā*), are associated with the perception of impermanence.
Because of association with one [of the two],
there is a phenomenon that is associated with the perception of impermanence but not produced by the perception of impermanence;
namely, when other perceptions are present and must cease, while the perception of impermanence is present and must arise.
Regarding those associated dharmas:

herein it is said that from among the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, up to the perception of cessation, one [perception] arises uninterruptedly, and the perception of impermanence manifests in the present;
these are the associated dharmas.
This refers to the other nine universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) excluding perception (*saṃjñā*),
as explained in detail above.
Such dharmas are associated with the perception of impermanence, yet they do not arise from the perception of impermanence.
Because it arises with any one of the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, up to the perception of cessation, as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
there are cases where the perception of impermanence arises and is also associated with the perception of impermanence.
That is to say, when the perception of impermanence manifests, that which is destined to cease necessarily ceases;
when the perception of impermanence manifests, that which is destined to arise necessarily arises,
along with its associated mental factors.
In this context, within the subsequent cluster of the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*),
the remaining mental states and mental factors (*cittacetasika*)— excluding the perception of impermanence itself—
are explained in detail as above.
Thus, because these various phenomena arise with the perception of impermanence as their equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
they are also associated with the perception of impermanence,
since that [perception] exists within that collection.
Although the perception of impermanence arises from the perception of impermanence,
it is not associated with the perception of impermanence;
for a nature is not associated with itself due to the three conditions of association.
As previously stated:
there are phenomena that are neither produced by the perception of impermanence nor associated with the perception of impermanence;
namely, those cases where one perception must necessarily cease while another perception must necessarily arise.
Regarding those associated dharmas,
it is said herein that the perception of impermanence and suffering,
up to the perception of cessation, manifest one after another in immediate succession.
Those phenomena associated with that perception are explained in detail as above. Thus,
these phenomena do not arise from the perception of impermanence.
Because other perceptions arise with it as their equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
it is also not associated with the perception of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*),
since it is associated with other perceptions.
As it is with the perception of impermanence, so it is with the perceptions up to the perception of cessation;
for each, four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be formulated as appropriate.
Thus, there are ten sets of four propositions.
"When the perception of impermanence arises regarding all phenomena, does that perception of impermanence have a single object?
Thus it is stated at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This treatise was composed because one wishes to stop the delusion that clings to the nature of the object of cognition as being a real entity;
it demonstrates that the nature of the object of cognition is definitely and truly existent.
Thus, this treatise was written.
When the perception of impermanence arises regarding all phenomena, does that perception of impermanence have a single object?
It should be answered by means of four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
There are phenomena for which the perception of impermanence arises, yet it does not have a single object as its condition.
That is to say, when the perception of impermanence manifests, it must necessarily cease;
when other perceptions manifest, they must necessarily arise,
for there are other conditions present.
In this context, it is said that immediately following the perception of the impermanence of the aggregate of form, one of the perceptions— namely, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent,
or the perception of non-self in what is suffering— manifests with respect to the aggregates of feeling and so forth.
The same applies to the explanations concerning the remaining aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).
Those phenomena arise from the perception of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*), but they do not have the perception of impermanence as their sole object (*ālambana*),
because they take other phenomena as their objects.
There are phenomena that possess the perception of impermanence as their single object, yet are not produced by the perception of impermanence;
namely, those wherein other perceptions must necessarily cease upon becoming manifest, while the perception of impermanence must necessarily arise upon becoming manifest,
and such [phenomena] possess this object.
In this context, it is taught that one contemplates the aggregates, such as form, through the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, and the non-selfhood of suffering.
Immediately following any one of these, the perception of impermanence regarding those very aggregates manifests before one.
The same applies to the explanation regarding the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*).
Those factors do not arise from the perception of impermanence (*anicca-saññā*) as their single object;

rather, they arise with either the perception of suffering in what is impermanent (*anicce dukkha-saññā*) or the perception of non-self in what is suffering (*dukkhe anatta-saññā*) serving as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-paccaya*).
Question: What is meant here by saying that one perception shares the same object as another perception?
Is it said that the perception of impermanence shares the same object as the perception of impermanence, or is it said that the perception of impermanence shares the same object as other perceptions?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
Both positions entail errors.
If it is asserted that the perception of impermanence and the perception of impermanence share the same object, [then...]
How is this passage to be reconciled?
It says, "He possesses this object-condition.
If it is said that the perception of impermanence shares the same object-condition as other perceptions, [how is this to be understood?]
How, then, is this passage to be reconciled?
It says that those phenomena do not arise from the perception of impermanence,
because at times those perceptions do indeed arise from the perception of impermanence.
Answer: Here it is stated that the perception of impermanence and the perception of impermanence share the same object; therefore, it says "the perception of impermanence has a single object.
Question: If that is so, how is this passage to be reconciled?
As it is said that "this has that as its condition," some say that this passage should be stated as follows:
This means that when other perceptions are present, the perception of impermanence must necessarily cease, and when [the perception of impermanence] is present, it must necessarily arise.
Regarding those associated phenomena (*saṃprayuktadharma*),
this refers to the phenomena associated with the perception of impermanence being associated with the perception of impermanence.
Regarding this explanation,
it includes three types of perception therein;
namely, the perception of impermanence followed by the arising of other perceptions.
After other perceptions, the perception of impermanence arises again.

Within this context, it is said that because the subsequently arising perception of impermanence shares the same object as the preceding perception of impermanence, the perception of impermanence is said to have a single object.
In this way, both textual passages are well-explained.
Alternatively, some may raise such a question regarding this matter;
now it should be investigated and analyzed.
In this context, what is being said regarding which perception shares the same object as which other perception?
Is it saying that the perception of impermanence shares the same object as other perceptions,
or is it saying that other perceptions share the same object as the perception of impermanence?
Yes. What is the distinction between these two?
If it is said that the perception of impermanence shares the same object as other perceptions, [then what is the difference]?
How is this passage to be reconciled?
For it says that there is a single object for the perception of impermanence regarding phenomena;
and that if the perception of non-self regarding suffering arises immediately after [the perception of suffering], the perception of impermanence arises [subsequently].
That [perception] shares the same object as the perception of suffering and the perception of non-self,
but it is not the perception of impermanence. If one says that other perceptions share the same object as the perception of impermanence,
then at times those phenomena arise from the perception of impermanence.
Then it should not be said that it does not arise from the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*). Some say:
"In this context, it is stated that the perception of impermanence shares the same object (*ālambana*) as other perceptions."
Question: If that is so, how is this passage to be reconciled?
As it is said: "There is a phenomenon (dharma) which is impermanent, a perception, and has a single object."
It is agreed that one should speak thus:
when other perceptions manifest, the perception of impermanence necessarily ceases; when [the perception of impermanence] manifests, it necessarily arises along with its associated mental factors.
If that were so, those dharmas would arise from the perception of impermanence and would share the same object as the perception of impermanence.
Thus it is said.
In this context, it should be stated that the perception of impermanence and the perception of the perception of impermanence share the same object.
Therefore, these three perceptions are here subsumed collectively;
namely, the initial perception of impermanence.
Next, other perceptions arise.
Immediately following those other perceptions, the perception of impermanence arises again.
In this context, it is said that the subsequently arisen perception of impermanence shares the same object as the previously arisen perception of impermanence.
In this way, both faults are avoided.
There is a phenomenon where the perception of impermanence arises and the perception of impermanence shares a single object;
that is to say, when the perception of impermanence is present, it must necessarily cease.
The perception of impermanence necessarily arises when it is present before one; such is its condition.

In this context, it is said that immediately after the perception of the impermanence of the aggregates such as form, the perception of the impermanence of those very same aggregates becomes manifest.
The same applies to the explanation regarding the elements (dhātu) and bases (āyatana).
Those phenomena arise from the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā) and share the same object (ālambana) as that perception of impermanence.
There are also phenomena that do not arise from the perception of impermanence and do not share the same object as that perception of impermanence.
This means that when one perception manifests, another must necessarily cease; when another manifests, it must necessarily arise.
There are other conditions for this.
Here, the "perception of impermanence and suffering" regarding the remaining aggregates and the "perception of suffering and non-self" are explained as those conditions.
Whichever one of the notions of impermanence, suffering, or non-self regarding the aggregates arises immediately following another [notion], whichever one manifests in the present.
The same applies to the elements and bases.
Those phenomena do not arise from the notion of impermanence.
Because other perceptions arise with the perception of equality as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
the perception of impermanence is not a single object;
for it consists of various perceptions and various conditions.
It is the same for the perception of impermanence up to the perception of cessation.
Question: Among those perceptions mentioned here, it may be so for the others;
however, regarding the perception of impurity and the perception of revulsion toward food—
The past conditions the past;
the present conditions the present;
that which arises in the future conditions the future.
How is the third case established?
The answer is: there is no fault in speaking according to similarity.
That is to say, the preceding perception of impurity ceases while taking a skeleton as its object, and the subsequent perception of impurity arises again by taking a skeleton as its object.
Because the characteristics of the objects are similar, it is also called "the single perception of revulsion toward food," and so forth.
All phenomena arise from the mind and not without the mind; this is explained at length.
In the preceding aggregate of karma, the distinctions of states arising from the mind that result in desirable and undesirable fruits were demonstrated;
here, the distinctions of states arising from the mind regarding the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—are demonstrated.
The mind is of two kinds:
namely, the primary (pravartaka) and the concomitant (anuvartaka).
The primary refers to that which can induce the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—and arises prior to them.
"Concomitant turning" (anuvartaka) refers to that which assists the two types of action— bodily and vocal—
and arises simultaneously with them.
Here, "turning" (vartaka) is mentioned, but "concomitant turning" is not.
Question: What are these "dharmas" that have been mentioned?
Some say they are the prātimokṣa restraint.
If one were to say that all phenomena constitute the prātimokṣa restraint,
then it would follow that those phenomena arise from the mind.
This means that the prātimokṣa restraint is produced by the power of the mind;
it does not arise without the mind,
for there is no obtaining of that restraint apart from the power of the mind.
If at the time the mind arises, do those phenomena arise at that same time?
Answer: The mind arises first, and those phenomena arise later;
that is to say, such a mind arises first.
"After I have received the Prātimokṣa restraint, I then correctly initiate the informative karma (vijñapti-karman) of that restraint.
When the mind ceases, does that dharma [the informative karma] also cease at that time?
Answer: "The mind ceases first; afterwards, that dharma ceases."
This means that the mind has already arisen and ceased,
and subsequently the informative action (vijñapti-karman) of that restraint has also arisen and ceased. Why is this so?
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are swallowed by impermanence; having arisen, they lack the power to remain even for a moment, as they must necessarily perish without interval in each instant.
When the mind attains such a state, do those phenomena likewise attain it?
Answer: The mind is acquired first, and those dharmas afterwards.
That is to say, that wholesome mind is acquired by virtue of two conditions:
first, the continuity of the roots of goodness.
Regarding the discipline obtained from the two realms or stages, it is acquired through the manifest action (*vijñapti*).
When the mind abandons it, at that time is that dharma also abandoned?
Answer: That dharma is abandoned first, and only afterwards is the mind [abandoned].
That is to say, that restraint is relinquished due to four conditions:
first, the relinquishing of the training rules;
second, the arising of both sexual organs.
Third, the severance of the three roots of goodness;
fourth, the relinquishing of the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga). Some say:
It is also relinquished at the time of committing a root offense.
That mind is relinquished due to two conditions:
first, the severance of the roots of goodness; [and second, the arising of a contrary thought].
Second, transcending the realm and the stage.
Question: If one dies in the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm, it is possible that one first abandons those factors and only thereafter [the mind].
If one who has passed away from the desire realm is reborn in the form or formless realms, or attains parinirvāṇa,
those factors are abandoned simultaneously with the mind. How,
then, can it be said that those factors are abandoned first and the mind afterwards?
Yes. The answer is that this passage speaks only of those who die in the desire realm and are reborn again in the desire realm;
because they relinquish their *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous class) at the time of death, they also relinquish the *prātimokṣa-saṃvara* (vow of individual liberation).
Although one abandons the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), one does not abandon the mind.
Some say that this applies to those who,
at the end of life in the desire realm, are reborn in the form or formless realms, or attain parinirvāṇa.
This is also what is explained herein:
at the time of death, one’s physical strength is weak and diminished,
either because the vital points (*marmaccheda*) have been severed or because one is afflicted by suffering.
One would then lose the restraint of body and speech that has been undertaken, and it would only be at the time of death that the mind finally relinquishes it. [Objection:
If this is so, how can it be said that "a certain bhikṣu has passed away"?
Answer: Since their original names are retained, there is no fault;
it is like a king who has lost his throne yet is still called "king.
Question: How are items such as robes and alms bowls to be divided among those who have left the household life?
The answer is: In the past, he also once divided such wealth belonging to others;
now that he has passed away, others divide it again.
Furthermore, this is what has been permitted through successive tradition from of old.
It has been heard that in the past, when a certain seer passed away,
his fellow practitioners of the holy life delivered his property to the king and spoke thus:
"This is the wealth and assets belonging to such-and-such a seer."
"He has no heir.
I now offer this to Your Majesty; I pray that you will accept it.
The king had it returned and said to him:
"The articles used by those who have gone forth should not be used by us laypeople.
From this day forward, if any among those who have gone forth should pass away,"
All requisites should be shared equally among those practicing the holy life (*brahmacārin*).
Since this has been permitted, there is no fault.
The commentary states:
What was stated previously is preferable. Why is this so?
Because painful contact is not a condition for the relinquishing of the precepts.
The intended purpose here is that even until the end of life— and not before the life has ended—
one abandons the precepts by severing the roots of goodness and so forth;
it is at the final moment of death that the mind and the restraint are lost simultaneously.
If at the time the mind experiences maturation (vipāka), does it [experience] those factors at that same time?
Answer: Either at that time or at another time.
"At that time" means:
This refers to a single moment, a single continuum, a single stage, or a single homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
"At other times" refers to different moments, different continua, different stages, or different homogeneous classes of beings.
Because there are four types [of non-restraint] in the present time.
Furthermore, some say that "all phenomena" refers to non-discipline (*asaṃvara*). If one speaks thus:
Regarding those phenomena that constitute non-restraint:
when it is said that these phenomena arise from the mind,
it means they are produced by the power of the mind of non-restraint.
"It is not that it does not arise from the mind" means that there is no way to obtain non-restraint apart from the power of the mind. When the mind arises,
at that very moment do those factors [of non-restraint] also arise?
Answer: The mind arises first, and subsequently that phenomenon [arises].
That is to say, one first gives rise to such a thought:
"I shall undertake and perform such a task," and only afterwards does one correctly initiate the non-restraint (*avirati*) manifest action (*vijñapti-karma*).
If at the time the mind ceases, does that phenomenon [cease] as well?
Answer: The mind ceases first, and subsequently that phenomenon [ceases].
That is to say, that mind arises first and then ceases.
Once non-restraint has arisen, it subsequently ceases;
the explanation is as before.
At the time when the mind attains [it], does that dharma [also] attain it at that time?
Answer: The mind is acquired first, and those factors later.
That is to say, that unwholesome mind is acquired by way of two conditions:
first, through falling away from detachment; second, through returning to a particular realm or stage, whereby that non-restraint is acquired by means of informative action (*vijñapti*).
If at the time the mind is relinquished, is that dharma also relinquished at that time?
Answer: That dharma is relinquished first, and only afterwards is the mind.
That is to say, non-restraint (asamvara) is relinquished due to four conditions.
First, receiving the vows of discipline;
second, attaining meditative concentration;
third, the arising of both sexual organs.
Fourth, the relinquishing of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
That unwholesome mind is relinquished through a single condition:
namely, at the time of becoming free from the defilement of desire (*kāmarāga*).
If at the time the mind experiences maturation, is it also at that time those factors?
Answer: It may be at that time, or it may be at another time, as explained previously.
Furthermore, there are those who say that "all phenomena" refers to the wholesome and unwholesome conduct of body and speech that belongs neither to formal restraint nor to non-restraint.
If one speaks in this way:
Regarding those phenomena that are neither discipline nor non-discipline—
namely, all virtuous and non-virtuous actions of body and speech—
it is said that these phenomena arise from the mind.
This means that those virtuous and non-virtuous actions of body and speech are produced by the power of the mind;
they do not arise without the mind.
There is no way for those virtuous and non-virtuous actions of body and speech to occur apart from the power of the mind.
If at the time the mind arises, do those phenomena arise at that same time?
Answer: The mind arises first, and those phenomena arise later;
that is to say, such a mind arises first.
"I shall perform such and such an action.
Subsequently, one correctly initiates the informative intimation (vijñapti) of body and speech.
At the moment when the mind ceases, at that time does that dharma [also cease]?
Answer: The mind ceases first, and those factors [cease] afterwards;
this is as explained previously.
Is it the case that when the mind exists, those factors exist at that same time?
Answer: The mind is acquired first, and those dharmas are acquired later;
that is, that wholesome mind is acquired by way of two conditions.
First, the continuity of a single root of goodness;
second, returning from another realm or level.
That unwholesome mind is also acquired due to two conditions.
First, from falling away from detachment;
second, when returning from another realm or level, one acquires those bodily and vocal sublime or unwholesome actions by means of informative intimation (*vijñapti*).
At the moment the mind abandons them, at that time those dharmas [are also abandoned].
The answer is that those factors are first abandoned and only thereafter the mind;

that is to say, they are abandoned due to three conditions: first, the cessation of the intention. Regarding bodily and vocal wholesome or unwholesome conduct, they are abandoned through these three causes.
First, the cessation of the intention.
Second, the relinquishing of application;
third, the exhaustion of power.
That wholesome mind is relinquished due to these two conditions.
They are abandoned because of the single object of an unwholesome mind,
as explained previously.
At what time does the mind receive its maturation (vipāka), and at that same time do those factors?
Answer: Either at that time or at another time, as explained previously.
Is there any phenomenon that is both thoroughly penetrated and fully understood?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: To refute the doctrines of other schools and to clarify one's own position.
That is to say, some may say that what is thoroughly penetrated and what is fully known are not substantially existent dharmas;
or again, others may say:
Uncontaminated conditioned phenomena are also objects of abandonment;
alternatively, some say that even unobscured-neutral states arising from application are objects of cultivation.
Alternatively, some may say that only nirvāṇa is that which is to be realized.
To stop such views, it is clarified that what is thoroughly penetrated and fully known is a truly existent phenomenon (*dravyasat*).
That which is abandoned is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*);
that which is cultivated is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).
That which is realized as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) pertains to all that is wholesome.
Furthermore, because it arises based on meditative concentration and is non-obscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta),
I have composed this treatise.
That which is thoroughly penetrated is as follows:
This means that all phenomena are thoroughly penetrated by sublime wisdom (*saddhī*).
As for "that which is to be fully known," it means that all phenomena are that which is to be fully known by primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).
As it is said, what is that which is thoroughly understood?
It refers to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
What is that which is fully known?
This refers to all phenomena (*dharma*).
That which is to be abandoned refers to all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), because they are to be abandoned by the path of antidotes (*pratipakṣamārga*).
As it is said: "What are the phenomena that are to be abandoned?"
This refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
That which is "cultivated" (*bhāvita*) refers to all conditioned wholesome (*kuśala-saṃskṛta*) phenomena,
because they are cultivated through either the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) or the cultivation of practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), or both.
As it is said, what are the dharmas to be cultivated?
They are all conditioned wholesome dharmas.
What is that which is to be realized?
This refers to all that is wholesome and the non-obscured neutral states arising from meditative concentration, which are to be delighted in and sought after because one desires to attain them.
As it is said: "What is the dharma to be realized through practice?"
This refers to all wholesome dharmas and the unobscured-neutral divine eye and divine ear that arise based on meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Is there any dharma that is both thoroughly penetrated and fully known?
Is it not that which is to be abandoned, not that which is to be cultivated, and not that which is to be realized?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, space and non-analytical cessation.
These two dharmas are that which is to be thoroughly penetrated,
because they are what is thoroughly penetrated by skillful wisdom;
they are also that which is to be fully known, because they are what is fully known by the knowledge of thorough penetration.
Because it is untainted (*anāsrava*) and thus not something to be abandoned;
because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and thus not something to be cultivated;
and because it is not something to be realized through effort, nor is it a dharma to be sought after with longing.
Is there any phenomenon that is to be thoroughly penetrated and fully known, yet is neither to be abandoned nor to be cultivated, and is instead to be realized?
Answer: There is.
This refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because it is that which is realized, that which is to be aspired to, and that which is to be sought after.
The rest is as explained previously.
Is there any phenomenon that is both thoroughly penetrated (*parijñeya*) and fully known (*parijñāta*)?
Are there those which are not to be abandoned, yet are to be cultivated and realized?
Answer: There are;
namely, uncontaminated conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta-dharma*).
This is because it is a conditioned phenomenon that is wholesome and cultivated.
The rest is as explained previously.
Is there any dharma that is both thoroughly penetrated and fully known, that is abandoned, that is cultivated, and that is realized?
Answer: There are.
They are wholesome contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*), because these are contaminated phenomena that are to be abandoned.
The remainder is as explained previously.
Is there any phenomenon that is what is thoroughly penetrated, what is fully known, and what is abandoned, yet is neither what is cultivated nor what is realized?
Answer: There is.
This refers to the divine eye and ear produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
These are not [the objects of cultivation] because they are outflowing (*sāsrava*) states that are to be abandoned,
and because they are non-defined (*avyākṛta*) states that are not to be cultivated.
This is the realization of what has been accomplished;
because one seeks that [realization] by relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that has arisen,
the rest is as explained previously.
Is there any phenomenon that is to be thoroughly penetrated, to be fully known, and to be abandoned, yet is neither to be cultivated nor to be realized?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, with the exception of the divine eye and divine ear produced by meditative concentration.
The remaining indeterminate formations and unwholesome dharmas are explained in meaning as previously stated.
Question: The masters of foreign lands say:
There are eight types of dharmas that are unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) and produced through cultivation:
namely, the divine eye and divine ear arising based on meditative concentration;

the two types of consciousness associated with those [faculties] which are unobscured-neutral; the two analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of dharma and meaning; the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*); and the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*).
In this context, why are only the divine eye and the divine ear mentioned, and not other dharmas?
The answer is that the textual recitations of the masters of foreign lands state as follows:
"What are the dharmas that serve as proof?"
This refers to all wholesome dharmas and the non-obscured, neutral dharmas arising from meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
The masters of Kaśmīra should also maintain this view.
The reason they are not mentioned is that there is a specific underlying intention:
the visual and auditory consciousnesses arising from meditative concentration (dhyāna) are included within the "divine eye and ear" that have been described.

If one speaks of their bases, it should be understood that this already includes the two unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of dharma and expression, as well as the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*);
these are exclusively wholesome, are cultivated through practice, and are not included herein [among the aforementioned categories].
One should not question this;
the mind of transformation functions like a craft and is not something to be greatly esteemed,
so it is not discussed here.
For this reason, one does not follow what they say.
Furthermore, that which is sought through the application of effort (*prayoga*) is superior because it is correctly attained;
therefore, it is explained here.
The divine eye and divine ear consciousnesses have no distinct preparatory application;
they are obtained simply through the pursuit of what is sought by means of the divine eye and divine ear.
All minds of transformation arise due to preparatory application, and those obtained through the pursuit of freedom from defilement are all not predominant.
Therefore, these are not mentioned here.
Furthermore, the divine eye and divine ear require extensive preparatory application (*prayoga*) to achieve them even for a brief moment; because they are rare, they are spoken of.

Those consciousnesses and the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*), however, are obtained without effort when one is free from the defilement of desire or when returning from a higher realm or stage.
Having attained them, they are constantly accomplished throughout the three periods of time and are not considered rare;
therefore, they are not mentioned here.
Furthermore, the divine eye and divine ear are the fruits of meditative cultivation.
Because it is the fruit of the concentration that comprises the factors of support;
because it can be manifested after the defilement of desire has been abandoned;
and because consciousness is never empty at any time.
Arising necessarily does not exist,
because it is of the same nature as that [non-arisen state];
however, one who possesses [the faculty] must necessarily exercise its function.
Because it is the basis for the supernormal powers of the eye and ear,
and because it is the supreme root for wearying of birth and death,
it is explained here.
Other dharmas are not like this;
therefore, they are not mentioned here. That which is called "cessation not through deliberation" (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) in this context is as follows:

This means that when certain persons attain a cessation that is not a dissociation and is not obtained through the analytical discernment of dharmas, they do not become dissociated from their fetters.

As for what is called "cessation through analytical discernment," it refers to a cessation that is a dissociation and is obtained through the analytical discernment of dharmas; when such persons attain it, they immediately become dissociated from their fetters.
These two cessations are explained in detail as in the *Vibhaṅga-skandha*, in the section on *chanda* and *gaurava*.

Is there any dharma that has no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), yet arises together with a cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) that has no object, and with object-conditions that have no object? ... [and so forth,] as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is because one wishes to refute the doctrines of others and to clarify one’s own position.
That is to say, some may assert as follows:
The characteristics of all conditioned phenomena lack intrinsic reality,
as the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain. Why is this so?
They assert that the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are included within the aggregate of formations dissociated from thought (*viprayuktasaṃskāra-skandha*),
and that all formations dissociated from thought lack any substantial reality (*dravya*).
Alternatively, some say that the characteristics of the conditioned are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
As it is said by the Vibhajyavādins. Why is this?
They speak as follows:
If that which possesses the characteristics of the conditioned were itself conditioned,
its power would be weak and inferior; how then could it produce anything else,
or even cause it to cease?
Because of this unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta*), one is able to give rise to dharmas, up to and including the cessation of dharmas. Alternatively,
there are those who say that among the conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*), birth, aging, and abiding are what constitute the conditioned.
Cessation is unconditioned.
Why is this? Because it is said that it is easy to cause those phenomena to arise, age, and abide.
To cause [them] to cease would be difficult.
If the characteristic of impermanence were itself conditioned,
its nature being weak and inferior, how could it cause others to cease?
Because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), its nature is powerful and capable of extinguishing all phenomena.
Alternatively, some say that the very essence of the conditioned factors of matter— namely arising, aging, duration, and impermanence— is itself matter.
The others are also like this.
Alternatively, some say that the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are associated phenomena (*saṃprayuktadharma*).
To stop such various heterodox attachments,
it is shown that the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are of a real nature and not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
they are neither identical to form (*rūpa*) and so forth, nor are they dissociated (*viprayukta*).
Therefore, this treatise is composed.

Is there any phenomenon that has no object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), yet arises together with a phenomenon that has no object-condition as its causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), and which is a phenomenon that has an object-condition?
This is what possesses the nature of existence.
Is it not the case that what is non-existent and lacks intrinsic nature is distinct from form, distinct from feeling, perception, and consciousness, and distinct from the associated formations?
Answer: It is so.

This refers to the five groups of sensory consciousness and their associated mental factors, as well as the mind-dissociated formations conditioned by form and the unconditioned; and the group of mental consciousness and its associated mental factors, along with all their arising, aging, duration, and impermanence—all these phenomena are without an object-condition (*anālambana*).
This is because these dissociated formations lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
This causal condition consists of non-objective phenomena taking non-objective phenomena as their objects,
arising simultaneously with the previously mentioned six groups of consciousness and their associated mental factors as its cause.
Because it arises simultaneously with that [conditioned phenomenon],
this already refutes the position that holds the characteristics of the conditioned to be unconditioned;
for unconditioned phenomena do not arise from causes.
This is because it is a phenomenon that exists as a non-existent;
it is an existent nature, not a provisional phenomenon;
it is not non-existent, nor is it a non-existent nature.
This is the definitive meaning of what was previously stated.
Furthermore, the first two phrases establish one's own doctrine,
while the latter two phrases refute the doctrines of others.
Regarding the establishment of one's own doctrine:
it is like a teacher of the well-spoken Dharma establishing the thesis of the well-spoken Dharma,
or a teacher of the ill-spoken Dharma establishing the thesis of the ill-spoken Dharma.
The proponents of the *Yuktivāda* establish the tenets of the *Yuktivāda*,
while the proponents of the *Vibhajyavāda* establish the tenets of the *Vibhajyavāda*.
As for those who refute the doctrines of others:
Just as those who propound the Dharma well refute the tenets of those who propound it poorly,
and those who propound it poorly refute the tenets of those who propound it well,
so too do those who rely on reasoned argument refute the tenets of those who engage in mere conceptual proliferation.
The Vaibhāṣikas refute the Sautrāntika tenets;
here, too, it is the same:
the first two lines establish our own position.
The latter two lines refute the positions of other schools.
If one were to refute others without establishing one's own position,
it would be a futile argument.
Because there is nothing upon which to rely.
If one were to establish only one's own position without refuting that of others,
then one's own position would not be well-established.
Therefore, having first established one's own position, one subsequently refutes the arguments of others.
The meaning is that this arising, aging, abiding, and impermanence possess such a logical principle;
by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), they exist and possess the quality of existence.
It is neither non-existent nor of a non-existent nature.
By this, the intention of those who maintain that the characteristics of the conditioned are not truly existent has already been refuted,
because these are dharmas distinct from both form and non-form.
Because they are distinct from feeling, perception, and consciousness, and because they are not of the nature of feeling, perception, or consciousness; by this,
the attachment to the characteristics of form and so forth as being identical to form and so forth is already refuted, since these associated mental factors are not dissociated phenomena.
By this, the attachment to the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) as associated phenomena (*saṃprayuktadharma*) has already been refuted.
Should it be said that these factors are causes for those factors, or should they be said to be conditions?
Answer: They should be said to be causes, and they should be said to be conditions.
In this context, what is meant by "this dharma" and what is meant by "that dharma"?
Some say that birth,
aging, duration, and impermanence are "this dharma."
If one were to say that the six groups of consciousness and their associated mental factors arising simultaneously with this [primary] dharma are themselves that dharma,
then according to such a statement, if this dharma arises simultaneously with that dharma, it should be called its cause and it should be called its condition.
As for causes, there is one cause, namely the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
As for conditions, there are two conditions, namely the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
If this dharma arises prior to that dharma, it should also be called its cause and its condition.
As for the causes, there are three: namely, the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Regarding conditions, there are three conditions, excluding the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
If a given dharma arises prior to another dharma, it should be called a condition, but it should not be called a cause (*hetu*).
Regarding conditions, there are two conditions: namely, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
If this dharma is generally [the cause] of that dharma, it should be called a cause and it should be called a condition.
The causes are four causes, namely:
co-existent, similar-type, pervasive, and retributive.
The conditions are three conditions.
Excluding the immediately preceding conditions (samanantara-pratyaya),
there are others who say that the aforementioned six groups of consciousness (ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya) and their associated mental factors (saṃprayukta-dharma) [are so designated].
If one were to say that "this phenomenon, along with its co-arising aging, duration, and impermanence,
is that phenomenon," then according to such a statement,
if this phenomenon arises simultaneously with that phenomenon, it should be called a cause and it should be called a condition.
The cause is one cause,
namely the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
The conditions are two conditions.
This refers to the predominance of the cause (*hetu-adhipati*).
If, with respect to a subsequent arising, this dharma is said to be the cause and the condition for that dharma,
the "cause" consists of three causes.
This refers to the similar-type (sabhāga), universal (sarvatraga), and retributive (vipāka) [causes].
As for the conditions, there are two: namely, the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
If this dharma arises prior to that dharma, it should be called a condition (*pratyaya*), but not a cause (*hetu*).
As for the condition, there is only one:
namely, the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
If this dharma is generally [the cause] of that dharma, it should be called a cause and it should be called a condition.
As for causes, there are four causes:
namely, the co-existent, the similar-type, the universal, and the maturation.
Regarding conditions, there are two conditions:
namely, the causal condition and the predominant condition.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
If one were to say that the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of this dharma are the same as the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of that dharma,
then according to such a statement,
if this dharma arises simultaneously with that dharma, it should be called its cause and it should be called its condition.
The cause is a single cause,
namely the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
The conditions are two conditions.
This refers to the predominance of the cause (*adhipati-hetu*).
If, with respect to a subsequent arising, this dharma is said to be the cause and the condition for that dharma,
then as for the cause, there are three causes.
This refers to the similar-type, pervasive, and retributive [causes].
As for the conditions, there are two:
namely, the causal condition and the dominant condition.
If this dharma arises prior to that dharma, it should be called a condition (*pratyaya*) but not a cause (*hetu*).
As for conditions, there is only one:
namely, the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
If this dharma is generally [considered] with respect to that dharma, it should be called a cause and it should be called a condition.
As for causes, there are four causes:
namely, co-existent, similar-type, pervasive, and retributive.
Regarding conditions, there are two conditions, namely: the causal condition and the predominant condition.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
That which was previously described as arising, aging, abiding, and impermanence constitutes this phenomenon (*dharma*).
That which is the arising of its own kind, up to and including the impermanence of its own kind, constitutes that phenomenon.
If one were to speak thus,
it would mean that if this dharma arises simultaneously with that dharma, it should be called both a cause and a condition.
As for the cause, it is a single cause.
That is to say, they are co-existent.
As for the conditions, there are two conditions:
namely, the causal condition and the dominant condition.
If this dharma arises prior to that dharma, it should be called its cause and its condition.
As for the causes, there are three: namely, the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Regarding conditions, there are two conditions: namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
If this dharma arises prior to that dharma, it should be called a condition, but it should not be called a cause.
As for conditions, there is one condition,
namely the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
If a given dharma is considered a cause with respect to another dharma in its entirety, it should be called both a cause and a condition.
As for causes, there are four causes:
namely, the co-existent, the similar-type, the universal, and the retributive.
As for conditions, there are two conditions.
That is to say, with respect to the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Should this dharma be called wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
Answer: With respect to wholesome dharmas, it should be called wholesome.
Regarding unwholesome phenomena, they should be said to be unwholesome;
regarding indeterminate phenomena, they should be said to be indeterminate.
This is because the nature and category of that which produces must necessarily be the same as that which is produced, and likewise for that which ceases and that which is ceased.
How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase in relation to this dharma, and by how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) is it bound?
Answer: The underlying tendencies that take the contaminated (*sāsrava*) objects of the three realms as their condition increase in relation to it, and it is bound by nine fetters.
Question: For what reason is it not said that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in relation to this dharma as having the untainted (anāsrava) as their object?
Answer: Because latent dispositions increase by way of two conditions.
First, because of having a single object;
second, because of association;
and because the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have untainted objects lack such an object.
Because they increase in accordance with their objects and because they are liberated from them;
and although there is increase through association, in this case there is nothing that is not associated with it.

Here, speaking in terms of general categories, it is said that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) which have the outflows of the three realms as their object increase, and that there is bondage by the nine fetters (saṃyojana).

If explained individually, [this refers to] everything abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and everything abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) that is pervasive (*sarvatraga*), within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) relative to the desire realm, and so on, up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) relative to the formless realm.
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of suffering,
all those abandoned through the vision of origination,
and the universal [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya),
it consists of those with outflow-conditions (sāsrava-ālambana) and the universal [defilements] (sarvatraga) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya).
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of cessation...
Those [defilements] with outflow that take [other] outflowing things as their object and the universal [defilements], which are to be abandoned by the path of seeing,
[act as conditions] for those to be abandoned by the path of seeing;
and all [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation and the universal [defilements], which are to be abandoned by cultivation, [act as conditions] for those to be abandoned by cultivation.
There are nine fetters in the desire realm;
in the form realm, there are six fetters.
Regarding the form realm and the formless realm,
there are six fetters in the formless realm.
Regarding the formless realm.

Thus, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) conditioned by the outflows within the three realms and the nine fetters (saṃyojana) all increase and bind with respect to these phenomena solely by way of the object (ālambana), and not by way of association (samprayoga).
The detailed explanation of the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) is as set forth in the *Rūpa-āyatanavarga* of the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
