translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under imperial decree. Section Eight: The Aggregate of Views (Dṛṣṭi-skandha), Part Three of the Second Sub-section on Perception (Saṃjñā-nirdeśa). Regarding how many latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in association with feeling (vedanā) that is associated with views, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: It is to refute the views of those who deny the existence of conventional right view, and to demonstrate that conventional right view truly exists and is subject to increase through the influence of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) as well as the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
Furthermore, this treatise was composed to refute the claim that there exists an underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
thereby demonstrating that the underlying tendency of doubt is abandoned solely through vision (*darśana-heya*).
Question: When one sees an object at night and wonders, "Is it a tree stump or a person?
is this doubt not something to be abandoned through cultivation?
Answer: Doubt arises because one has not yet understood that matter;
once it is understood, the doubt is severed and no longer possesses the nature of a latent tendency (*anuśaya*).
Question: Why is the discussion here based solely on views and doubt?
The answer is that this is because the intention of the author of that treatise was such;
this is explained at length.
Furthermore, it is only these two types [of consciousness] that do not correspond with one another while both taking the Four Truths as their object.
Both are pervasive mental factors;
both take both the contaminated and the uncontaminated as their objects;
both take both the conditioned and the unconditioned as their objects.
Among the other afflictions, it is superior;
for although greed, hatred, and pride are mutually dissociated,
they cannot universally take the Four Noble Truths as their objects.
It is exclusively non-universal;
it takes only the contaminated as its object and only the conditioned as its object.
Although ignorance takes all four truths as its objects, [it is still classified as non-universal].
Furthermore, these universal [factors] take as their objects all conditioned and unconditioned, contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena;
yet, while they are associated with all afflictions, they are not predominant in any of them.
Therefore, in this context, the treatise is composed based solely on view and doubt.
How many latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in association with the feeling associated with views?

Answer: The latent disposition of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) that is associated with those [views] increases, whether they have objects that are tainted (sāsrava) or untainted (anāsrava) across the three realms. This is the general explanation.
If explained separately, there are five distinctions of feeling associated with views, namely:
those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, up to those to be abandoned by cultivation.
Among these, the feelings associated with views that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering include all [feelings] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
Furthermore, the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) increase [in association] with them.
The feeling associated with the views abandoned through the vision of the origin is itself abandoned through the vision of the origin;
all pervasive latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) increase [in association] with it.
The feeling associated with the views to be abandoned by the vision of cessation;
the view that takes the untainted as its object and is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation; the ignorance associated with that [view];
and all [factors] that take the tainted as their object.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [in association with them].

There are feelings associated with views abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya), as well as the untainted objects (anāsrava-ālambana) abandoned by the path of seeing, and the ignorance (avidyā) associated with those views abandoned by the path of seeing.
All latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take contaminated objects as their condition and all pervasive latent dispositions increase [in association] with them.
Furthermore, all latent dispositions that are abandoned through cultivation and are associated with views,
as well as all pervasive latent dispositions, increase [in association] with feelings abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding this, the distinctions of how [the latent dispositions] increase should be formulated as four propositions.
There may be a latent disposition that increases by way of being an object (*ālambana*) with respect to a feeling associated with views, but not by way of association (*samprayoga*).
There are some latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase by way of association with the feelings associated with views, but not by way of being their object;
there are others that increase both by way of being the object of the feelings associated with views and by way of association with them.

There are some latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that increase neither by way of being an object (*ālambana*) nor by way of association (*samprayoga*) with feeling (*vedanā*) associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the first case: this refers to all outflow-tainted objects of views, excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with them.
Regarding the other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have contaminated objects (*sāsravālambana*):
the second phrase refers to the view (*dṛṣṭi*) that has uncontaminated objects (*anāsravālambana*) and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with it;
the third phrase refers to...
The first [category] consists of the outflow-tainted views that take those [factors] as their object,

along with the ignorance associated with them. The fourth category refers to all other outflow-free latent dispositions (anuśaya), excluding the outflow-free views that take those [factors] as their object and the ignorance associated with them.
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in association with the feeling dissociated from [wrong] view?
Answer: With the exception of those underlying tendencies that have the untainted as their object and the ignorance associated with them, the remaining underlying tendencies increase.
This is the general explanation.
To explain it specifically,
it is dissociated from views.
There are five distinctions of feeling, namely:
those to be abandoned by seeing suffering, up to those to be abandoned by cultivation.
Among these, the feeling dissociated from views is that which is to be abandoned by seeing suffering.

All [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering, as well as the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through the vision of the origin, increase in association with the feeling dissociated from views that is abandoned through the vision of the origin,
and all [defilements] abandoned through the vision of the origin.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering increase [in relation to this].
Regarding the feeling dissociated from views that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation:

with the exception of the false view to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and its associated ignorance, all other remaining latent dispositions to be abandoned by the vision of cessation as well as the universal latent dispositions increase [in relation to it].
The feeling dissociated from views that is to be abandoned by the path of seeing,
excluding the wrong view to be abandoned by the path of seeing and its associated ignorance,
as well as all other [factors] to be abandoned by the path of seeing.
Furthermore, the universal proclivities increase in association with it.
Regarding feeling dissociated from views that is abandoned by cultivation,
all [proclivities] abandoned by cultivation as well as the universal proclivities increase in association with it.
Within this context, the distinctions of "increase" (anuśaya) are also formulated as four propositions.
There are some latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase with respect to feelings dissociated from views by way of the object (ālambana), but not by way of association (samprayoga).
This is expanded into four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first proposition refers to the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) views that take those [factors] as their object, along with the ignorance associated with them.
The second proposition refers to the exception of the untainted (*anāsrava*) views that take those [factors] as their object, along with the ignorance associated with them.
Regarding the remaining latent dispositions (anuśaya) that have uncontaminated objects:
the third phrase refers to all other latent dispositions with contaminated objects, excluding those views that have contaminated objects and the ignorance associated with them.
Regarding the fourth clause, it refers to the untainted object-conditioned view and the ignorance associated with it.
As for how many latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in association with the feeling associated with doubt:
the answer is the tainted object-conditioned [dispositions] abandoned through vision within the three realms.
Furthermore, the latent tendencies of doubt and the ignorance associated with it increase in relation to the untainted objects.
This is the general explanation.
To explain them specifically, there are four distinct types of feeling associated with doubt.
This refers to those [afflictions] abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Among these, those abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin are as previously explained.
Those abandoned through the vision of cessation are the feeling associated with doubt.
The doubt to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, its associated ignorance, all outflow-tainted objects conditioned by the vision of cessation,
and the pervasive latent dispositions increase [therein]. Also,
the feeling associated with the doubt to be abandoned by the vision of the path.
Doubt abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*), the ignorance associated with it,
all outflow-tainted objects (*sāsravālambana*) abandoned through the path of seeing,
and the pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) increase [therein].
Within this context, the distinctions of "increasing along with" (anuśaya) are also formulated as four propositions.
There are some latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase along with feelings associated with doubt.
It increases by way of the object of focus (*ālambana*), not by way of association (*samprayoga*).
This is explained at length through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first permutation refers to doubt (*vicikitsā*) that takes the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) as its object, excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with it.
Regarding the other latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned by insight that have impure objects:
the second phrase refers to doubt with pure objects and the ignorance associated with it;
the third phrase refers to doubt with impure objects and the ignorance associated with it.
Regarding the fourth phrase: setting aside the doubt that takes the untainted as its object and the ignorance associated with it,
how many latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in association with the remaining latent dispositions that take the untainted as their object, which are not associated with doubt?
Answer: With the exception of doubt that takes the untainted as its object and the ignorance associated with it, the remaining latent dispositions increase [in relation to it].
This is the general statement.
If explained individually, there are five distinctions in the types of sensations associated with doubt:
namely, those abandoned through the vision of suffering, up to those abandoned through cultivation.
Among these, those abandoned through the vision of suffering and those abandoned through the vision of the origin are as previously described.
The feeling dissociated from doubt that is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation;
with the exception of the ignorance associated with that doubt which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation,
all other [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [in association with it].
This includes the feeling dissociated from doubt that is abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya),
excluding the ignorance (avidyā) associated with that doubt which is abandoned by the path of seeing.
The remaining [afflictions] abandoned through the path of seeing,
as well as the pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya), increase [in association];
the doubt abandoned through cultivation is dissociated from feeling.
All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) ones, increase [in association] with it.
Regarding the distinctions of this increase (*anuśayana*), four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are also established.
There may be a latent disposition that increases by way of being the object (*ālambana*) of feeling (*vedanā*) dissociated from doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Because they increase through association rather than by way of being concomitant,
one should elaborate the four permutations at length.
The first permutation refers to doubt that has outflowing objects and the ignorance associated with it.

The second phrase refers to all other latent dispositions (anuśaya) with uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*), excluding doubt with uncontaminated objects and the ignorance associated with it.
The third phrase refers to [all latent dispositions] with contaminated objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*), excluding doubt with contaminated objects and the ignorance associated with it.

Regarding the other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have impure objects (*sāsravālambana*), the fourth category consists of doubt (*vicikitsā*) with pure objects (*anāsravālambana*) and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with it.

As for the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharma*) pertaining to the cause and the path: how many elements (*dhātu*), how many bases (*āyatana*), and how many aggregates (*skandha*) do they comprise?
Answer: The eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
Among these, the causes are the six causes, namely:
association (saṃprayuktaka) up to the efficient cause (kāraṇa).
The Path is the Noble Eightfold Path,
namely right view up to right concentration.
Dependent Origination is the twelve-linked dependent origination.
That is to say, from ignorance up to old age and death.
This causal dependent origination fully encompasses all realms, bases, aggregates, and phenomena.
Question: It may be so for the cause and dependent origination.
How is it that the Path is also fully subsumed?
The answer is: this passage should be stated as follows:
"The causes and dependent originations are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas)."
The Path is subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates; yet,
because it is not stated as such [in the specific context],

one should know that here the Path is explained in general terms as being subsumed by the dependent origination of causes, and thus subsumes all realms, bases, and aggregates, rather than being subsumed by each one individually.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the factors of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) are all called "six causes" (*ṣaḍ-hetu*), as these are all specific designations for causes.
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*:
Because [the categories of] "paths" and so forth all share the same meaning,
they are therefore all subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and so on.
Some have said this:
"Causes" refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"What are causal phenomena?"
This means that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are fully subsumed by this within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth.
The path (*mārga*) is precisely this cause; with respect to whom does it serve as a path, and for what attained fruit?
By this, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth are also subsumed;
dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is likewise all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*),
as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
What is the dharma of dependent origination?
It refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
By this, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth are also subsumed.
Excluding the phenomena associated with perception, feeling, and mind arising from eye-contact, as well as the phenomena dissociated from perception,
feeling, and mind arising from ear-contact, by how many elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and aggregates (skandha) are the remaining phenomena subsumed?
Answer: The arising of the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates is of two kinds, namely, causal arising (*hetu-samutthāna*) and momentary arising (*kṣaṇa-samutthāna*).
Here, only momentary arising is discussed.
Because of the explanation regarding the associated and the dissociated:
[the author] asks, among those things explained here, which associated and dissociated phenomena are excluded,
and what remaining phenomena are included within the elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and aggregates (*skandha*)?
Answer: Herein, excluding from the eye-contact aggregate the non-contact phenomena of perception, feeling, and mind, as well as the [conditioned characteristics of] birth,
aging, subsistence, and impermanence within the ear-contact aggregate— the remaining associated phenomena and the [characteristics of] birth, aging, subsistence, and impermanence—
are included within the remainder of the dharma-element, dharma-base, and dharma-aggregate.
Why is this so? Because among those things thus described, there are dharmas that arise from eye-contact and are associated with perception, feeling, and mind,
as well as those that arise from ear-contact and are dissociated from perception, feeling, and mind.
Regarding that which is to be excluded: although contact within the aggregate of eye-contact is associated with perception, feeling, and mind,
it is not the self-substance (svabhāva) that arises from eye-contact,
because the sense of "arising" does not apply to its own self-substance.
Although perception arises from eye-contact and so forth, and is associated with feeling and mind,
it is not itself associated with its own self-entity;
for there is no sense of association within a self-entity.
The same applies to feeling, mind, and so forth.
Therefore, within the aggregate of eye-contact (*cakṣuḥ-saṃsparśa*), contact, perception, feeling, and mind are not to be excluded.
Rather, it is the other associated factors that arise from eye-contact and are associated with perception, feeling, and mind that are indeed to be excluded.
Within the aggregate of ear-contact, contact does not arise from ear-contact itself,
nor is it dissociated from perception and feeling;
although perception arises from ear-contact, it is dissociated from perception.
Yet it is associated with the mind of feeling;
the same applies to the teaching regarding the mind of feeling.
Although other mental factors arise from ear-contact and so forth, [they are likewise associated].
And because it is associated with perception,
feeling, and mind, therefore, within the aggregate of ear-contact, all mental states and mental factors are not excluded.
Those [factors] arising together with it— namely, birth, aging, duration, and impermanence— arise simultaneously with the ear-contact.
Furthermore, because they are dissociated from perception, feeling, and mind, these are what are to be excluded; this is called the "dharmas to be excluded.
What are the remaining dharmas?
They are the six groups of contact, the six groups of perception, the six groups of feeling, and the six groups of consciousness.
And the remaining associated formations within the aggregates of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental contact;
all dissociated formations, excluding those of aging, abiding, and impermanence within the aggregate of auditory contact;
and all matter and unconditioned phenomena.
In this way, the remaining phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
This continues until one excludes those phenomena associated with perception, feeling, and mind that arise from body-contact,
as well as those dissociated from perception, feeling, and mind that arise from mental-contact.
By how many elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and aggregates (skandha) are the remaining phenomena subsumed?
Answer: By eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
Within this, the mutual exclusion and inclusion of these factors should be explained in detail according to the previous method.
Others provide a specific distinction here, stating that one must exclude the mental factors dissociated from mind—
such as perception and feeling— that arise from eye-contact, as well as the mental factors associated with mind—
such as perception and feeling— that arise from ear-contact and so forth.

Other phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates, excluding those phenomena arising from body-contact that are dissociated from perception, feeling, and mind,
as well as those phenomena arising from mind-contact that are associated with perception, feeling, and mind.
The inclusion of the remaining factors is as previously explained; furthermore, there is a specific distinction made here, namely:

excluding those factors associated with perception, feeling, and mind arising from eye-contact, as well as those factors associated with perception, feeling, and mind arising from ear-contact, and so forth.
The inclusion of the remaining factors is as previously explained.

This continues until: with the exception of the factors associated with perception, feeling, and mind arising from body-contact, and the factors associated with perception, feeling, and mind arising from mind-contact—the inclusion of the remaining factors is as previously explained.
Furthermore, there is another formulation of distinctions here,
which states: excluding those mental factors dissociated from mind— namely, perception and feeling— that arise from eye-contact,
as well as those mental factors dissociated from mind— namely, perception and feeling— that arise from ear-contact, and so forth.
The inclusion of other dharmas is as previously explained,
up to the exclusion of the mental factors dissociated from mind that arise from body-contact,
as well as the mental factors dissociated from mind that arise from mind-contact.
The inclusion of other factors is as previously explained. 4.

The Section on Knowledge (Jñāna-nirdeśa), the Fourth Part of the First Sub-section within the Eighth Chapter, the Aggregate of Views (Dṛṣṭi-skandha): If a given thing can be thoroughly penetrated, can that thing also be fully known?
Having thus understood these chapters and the meaning of the explanations within them, one should next provide a detailed exposition.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This response intends to refute the claim that patience (*kṣānti*) is itself the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*).

It demonstrates that while various patiences arise simultaneously with the attainment of the doubt to be abandoned by themselves, they cannot be termed "knowledge" because they have not yet reached a state of repeated critical examination and definitive resolution.
Therefore, this treatise is composed.

There are five kinds of entities (*vastu*): first, the entity of intrinsic nature; second, the entity of bondage; third, the entity of the object of cognition; fourth, the entity of cause; and fifth, the entity of appropriation.
Regarding the entity of intrinsic nature, as the Blessed One said:
I shall explain to you forty-four matters of knowledge and seventy-seven matters of knowledge; that is to say,
the knowledge of the factors of existence (bhavāṅga) is expressed by the term "matter" (vastu).
The Venerable Ghosaka spoke thus:
that sutra speaks of the "thing" (vastu) as the object of focus;
because all the members of existence (bhavāṅga) are the objects of wisdom, they are called "things."
However, that sūtra states that "matter" (vastu) refers to knowledge (*jñāna*), not to the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
This is because in the subsequent explanation, only knowledge is mentioned.
As for the matter that is bound, it is as explained previously in the first section.
If a thing is bound by the fetter of attachment (*rāga-saṃyojana*), is that same thing also bound by the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?

This refers to how the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the five categories are bound to the phenomena of the five categories either by way of being an object (*ālambana*) or by way of association (*samprayoga*).
Those five categories of phenomena are explained by way of their objective entities (*vastu*).
As for the objective entities that serve as objects of focus, they are as described in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"All phenomena are known by wisdom according to their respective entities."
What is meant by "according to its object" (*vastu*)?
It means according to its activity, according to its sphere (*gocara*), and according to its objective support (*ālambana*).
The spheres and objective supports of all types of knowledge are expressed by the term "object" (*vastu*).
Regarding "factors with a cause," it is as explained in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.

Factors with a basis (*savastuka*) and factors without a basis (*avastuka*) are precisely factors with a cause (*sahetuka*) and factors without a cause (*ahetuka*), as also stated by the Blessed One in a verse:
The bhikṣu whose mind is tranquil is able to sever all conditioned activities forever;
birth and death are ultimately extinguished, and he shall no longer undergo further existence.
Herein, the term "activity" (*saṃskāra*) is used to denote these various causes.
There is nothing in all of birth and death that does not arise from causes.
If those causes are severed, birth and death are extinguished; one no longer undergoes further existence and attains parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the grasping of things, it is as stated in the sūtra:
One abandons the matters of fields, houses, wealth, treasures, and so forth.
Furthermore, as the Blessed One said in a verse:
"Regarding a person's matters of fields, wealth, cattle, horses, servants, and so on..."
Men and women, as well as their various relatives, each separately indulge in and crave [their objects].
Furthermore, householders speak thus:
"I have already taken so many things from her."
He still owes me that much of his service.
Such matters as these are called "matters of inclusion.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of matters.

There are ten types of matters: first, the matter of the elements; second, the matter of the sense bases; third, the matter of the aggregates; fourth, the matter of the worlds; fifth, the matter of moments.
Among these ten types of matters, the present discussion is based on the matter of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That is to say, the intrinsic natures of patience (*kṣānti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and so forth are designated by the names of their objects.
If an object can be penetrated, can that object also be fully known?
One should respond that this constitutes four permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*).
Among these, because it is said that one can "know as it truly is" through the wisdom that penetrates based on the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), this is called "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).

Because it is said that one can "permanently abandon the afflictions" by realizing the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) based on the untainted path, this is called "permanent abandonment."
Therefore, because these two possess mutual variations in length, one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is a case where there is penetration (*prativedha*) but not thorough knowledge (*parijñā*);
namely, when the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path does not abandon the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
This refers to all the wisdoms within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
as well as the wisdoms regarding the four truths— excluding those on the path that directly abandons afflictions— within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and so forth.
Because such wisdoms are capable of penetrating the nature of reality as it truly is, they do not constitute thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
Because they do not abandon the afflictions,
there are instances where one can have thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) but lacks penetrative realization (*abhisamaya*.
This refers to the abandonment of various afflictions through the patiences (*kṣānti*) regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
These are the various patiences (*kṣānti*) that abandon the afflictions within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
For one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire, they comprise both the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) and the subsequent patience (*anvayakṣānti*);
for one who has already abandoned the defilement of desire, they consist solely of the subsequent patience.

These various patiences (*kṣānti*) are capable of thoroughly knowing and permanently severing the afflictions; however, they are not capable of penetrating [the truth], because their nature is not that of "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
Question: If these various patiences are not capable of penetrating [the truth], how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
As it was said, what is that which is able to penetrate?
It is wholesome wisdom.
What is that which is penetrated?
That is to say, the patience regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma-kṣānti*) is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of wholesome wisdom (*kuśala-prajñā*).
Why, then, is it said here that it is not capable of thorough penetration?
The answer is that this passage should be stated as follows:
If a given thing is capable of penetrating that object, it is also capable of fully knowing it;
and if a given thing is capable of fully knowing that object, it is also capable of penetrating it.
That such a statement was not made has a specific underlying intention.
That is to say, herein, one is said to be "able to penetrate" based on the thorough knowledge through wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*),
and one is said to be "able to fully know" based on the thorough knowledge of abandonment through realization (*prahāṇa-parijñā*). Therefore,
it should not be objected that there is a case where one can penetrate but cannot fully know.

This means that through the knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, one abandons all afflictions; this constitutes the abandonment of afflictions within the cultivation of the path.

Because the four knowledges of the path, suffering, and so forth possess the nature of wisdom that penetrates reality as it is (*yathābhūta*), they are also able to fully comprehend and permanently sever the afflictions.
There are instances where there is neither penetration nor thorough knowledge;
that is to say, when the patiences (*kṣānti*) regarding suffering, origin, cessation, and the path do not abandon the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
This refers to the four patiences regarding the dharmas within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of one who has already abandoned the defilement of desire.
It is not of the nature of knowledge as it truly is;
nor is it capable of thoroughly knowing and permanently abandoning all afflictions,
because the afflictions that are its counteragents have already been abandoned.
If a phenomenon can cause weariness toward an object, can that same phenomenon also lead to detachment from it?
One should respond by formulating four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
In this context, "weariness" (*nirveda*) refers to the mental application that proceeds with the aspect of weariness toward contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
"Detachment" (*virāga*) refers to that which is able to abandon the afflictions to be eliminated.
Since these two [detachment and revulsion] possess mutual variations in their scope, one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are cases where there is revulsion toward an object but no detachment.
This refers to the patience and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-kṣānti-jñāna*) which do not sever the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
This pertains to one who has already abandoned the defilement of desire and entered the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*);
specifically, it concerns the dharma-patience regarding suffering and its origin within that path of seeing.
And as for all knowledge of the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudayajñāna*):
within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and so forth, excluding the path of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) that abandons afflictions,
the remaining knowledge of the origin of suffering functions by taking the objects of aversion as its conditions for the purpose of generating revulsion.
This is because it is not capable of abandoning [the afflictions] by means of non-abandonment.
There are cases where one is capable of abandoning them but not capable of becoming weary of them;
that is to say, the patience and knowledge regarding cessation and the path abandon all afflictions.
This refers to those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire: specifically,
the dharma-forbearances regarding cessation and the path within the path of vision,
as well as all subsequent forbearances regarding cessation and the path.
On the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one correctly abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The two knowledges (*jñāna*) of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*),
as well as the corresponding patiences (*kṣānti*), are capable of detaching from and severing the afflictions.
This is because it does not function by taking a desirable object as its object of aversion.
There are, however, entities that can both be objects of aversion and lead to detachment;
namely, the patience and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin which abandon all afflictions.
This refers to those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire:
specifically, the dharmakṣāntis of suffering and origin within the path of seeing,
as well as all the anvayakṣāntis of suffering and origin.
Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the two knowledges of suffering and its origin constitute the path of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Thus, these patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) function by taking as their objects that which is to be reviled, thereby inducing weariness;
furthermore, they are capable of abandoning and severing all afflictions (*kleśa*).
There are matters that are neither capable of being weary of nor capable of being detached from;
namely, when the patience and knowledge regarding the cessation and the path do not abandon the various afflictions.
This refers to one who has already become free from the defilement of desire.

Within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it consists of the dharma-patience regarding cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgadharmakṣānti*) and all cognitions of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgajñāna*).

Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and so forth, it consists of all cognitions of cessation and the path, excluding the paths that consist of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) for the purpose of eradicating afflictions.
Thus, this patience and wisdom do not function by taking objects of delight as their objects of aversion;
nor do they function to abandon afflictions through detachment.
If an object can be viewed with aversion, is that object itself cultivated as an object of aversion?
Answer: If a phenomenon is capable of inducing revulsion, that phenomenon is also cultivated as revulsion.
Herein, "cultivation" refers to both acquisition-cultivation (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and practice-cultivation (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*).
This occurs during the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) through the patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding suffering and its origin.
Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and so forth, there is only the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*).
Thus, these patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges are able to function by taking as their object that which is to be reviled, because they are capable of cultivating revulsion;
for they cultivate revulsion through the aspect of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇākāra*) in both the present and the future, either individually or simultaneously.
There is a case where one cultivates revulsion but is not capable of revulsion.
This refers to the abandonment of all afflictions through the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path.
This occurs when, during the path of cultivation, one becomes detached from the defilements of the three realms by means of the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path.
Because one cultivates the aspect of weariness through the knowledge of suffering and its origin regarding future existences, it is called "cultivating weariness.
Because it functions toward the objects of delight found in the truths of cessation and the path, it is not called "able to weary."
Question: When the knowledge of the path to cessation (*nirodhamārgajñāna*) is present,
one does not abandon the afflictions, yet one is still able to cultivate revulsion (*nirveda*),

as occurs during all paths of application (*prayogamārga*), liberation (*vimuktimārga*), and advancement (*viśeṣamārga*) in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
The two knowledges of cessation and the path, as well as these two knowledges, refine the faculties, practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna,
and bring forth the various supernormal powers, the analytical knowledges, and the formless liberations.
Furthermore, when one cultivates various virtues such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
one is also able to cultivate revulsion (*nirveda*) but is not yet capable of being fully revulsed. Why is this not mentioned here?
The answer should also have been stated; that it was not stated means one should know that this meaning is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Some say that what is stated here is definitive (*niyata*).
This means that when the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path eliminate all afflictions,
during the stage of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), one is necessarily able to cultivate the two knowledges of suffering and its origin;
this is because these alone are being manifested for the first time.
At other times, it is indeterminate, being either previously attained or not yet attained.
If it has been previously attained, one cannot cultivate it; therefore, it is not mentioned. Some say:
In this context, the initial stage is described, while other stages are not.
Some say that here,
the explanation follows the manifest characteristics and is stated in summary.
Therefore, it is not said that one cultivates revulsion in other stages.
If a thing can lead to detachment, does one cultivate revulsion toward it?
One should respond by establishing four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
There are cases where one is able to abandon [defilements] without having cultivated revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā*).

This refers to the abandonment of all afflictions through the patiences (*kṣānti*) regarding cessation and the path; this is the case for one who has not yet abandoned the taint of desire (*kāmarāga*) during the dharma-patiences regarding cessation and the path within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
And all the patiences (*kṣānti*) regarding the cessation and the path categories (*nirodha-mārga-ākāra*).
Since these various patiences are capable of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*), they do not constitute the cultivation of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā*);
at that time, one cultivates only the aspect of delight (*abhirati*).
There is a cultivation of revulsion that is not capable of detachment;
this refers to the patience and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-kṣānti-jñāna*) which do not sever the various afflictions (*kleśa*).

This, then, is the patience regarding the dharma of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*) within the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) for one who has already become detached from the defilements of desire (*kāma-rāga-virakta*).
And all knowledge of the origin of suffering (*samudaya-jñāna*).

Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and so forth, this refers to the knowledge of the origin of suffering, excluding the path of right abandonment (*samyak-prahāṇa*) that abandons afflictions.
Such patience and knowledge constitute the cultivation of revulsion (*nirveda-bhāvanā*).
At that time, because one is able to cultivate the aspect of the practice of revulsion (*nirveda*), it is not because one is able to abandon or sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Question: When the knowledge of the path leading to cessation (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*) is present before one, [what occurs]?
One does not sever the afflictions, nor does one cultivate revulsion without detachment,
as occurs during the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) and the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga),
at all times when practicing the preparatory, liberation, and special progress paths for the sake of becoming free from defilement.
Through the two knowledges of cessation and the path, as well as by means of these two knowledges, one refines the faculties, practices the mixed cultivation of dhyāna,
and brings forth the various supernormal powers, the analytical knowledges, and the formless liberations.

When one contemplates the various virtues such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one likewise cultivates revulsion (*nirveda*) yet does not become detached from them. Why, then, is this not mentioned here?
Answer: It should indeed have been mentioned.
One should know that the meaning is not fully stated here; it is incomplete.
Some say that what is taught herein refers to the definitive [teaching].
This means that in those various stages, the two knowledges of suffering and origin are fixed;
however, the cultivation of the two knowledges of cessation and the path is not fixed,
because when what has already been attained manifests, one does not cultivate revulsion.
There are instances where one is both able to become detached and cultivates revulsion;
namely, when the patience and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin, as well as the knowledge regarding cessation and the path, sever the various afflictions.
This refers specifically to the dharma-patience regarding suffering and its origin within the path of vision for one who has not yet abandoned the defilement of desire.
Furthermore, there are the patiences regarding the origin of all suffering and the knowledges of the path,
the origin, cessation, and the path during the cultivation of the path (bhāvanāmārga) which correctly abandons the afflictions.
Since these patiences and knowledges are capable of abandoning and severing all afflictions, they are also cultivated as revulsion (nirveda).
At that time, because one is able to cultivate the aspect of revulsion (*nirveda*),
there are instances where an object is neither capable of being abandoned nor is revulsion cultivated;
namely, when the forbearances (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding cessation and the path do not abandon the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
This refers to those who have already abandoned the defilements of desire: during the path of seeing, at the moments of the dharma-patiences of cessation and the path;
and during the path of cultivation and so forth, whenever the previously attained knowledges of cessation and the path manifest before them.
Thus, this patience and wisdom are neither free from nor do they involve the non-abandonment of afflictions, nor do they constitute the cultivation of revulsion (*nirveda*).
This is because at that time, one does not cultivate the mental aspect of revulsion.
The various distinctions among the phrases concerning revulsion and abandonment previously explained [apply here].
All of these depend on the distinctions in the stages of the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*),
and not on others, because they rely on the preceding thorough comprehension (*parijñā*) of the objects of penetration;
for thorough comprehension consists exclusively of the untainted.
Question: As it has been stated, what is the essential nature of "disenchantment" (nirveda)?
Is it non-attachment (alobha), or is it wisdom (prajñā)?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If this were non-greed, how would one account for what is stated here?
For example, it says: "There are things that can both cause revulsion and lead to detachment;
namely, the patience and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin abandon the various afflictions."
How, then, is what is stated in the *Saṃgītiparyāya* to be reconciled?
For it says: "What is the cultivation of revulsion, dispassion, and freedom from greed?
It is the non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion associated with the revulsion of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)."
Non-greed cannot be said to be associated with non-greed,
because a self-nature is not associated with itself.
If it were wisdom (*prajñā*), how would the aforementioned statement be reconciled?
As it is said: "How does one cultivate weary detachment and freedom from greed?
It refers to the non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion associated with the weariness of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Since non-delusion is wisdom (*prajñā*), it cannot be said that wisdom is associated with wisdom."
Therefore, it is as stated previously. Regarding this,
some say that the essential nature of revulsion (*nirveda*) is non-attachment (*alobha*).
Question: If that is so, how should one interpret the statement made in this text?
For example, it says: "There is a thing which can both cause weariness and lead to detachment," and so forth, as explained at length.
Answer: In that context, the term "weariness" (*nirveda*) refers to phenomena that are associated with weariness.
That is to say, non-attachment associated with patience and wisdom is termed "patience-wisdom.
[Objection: How then is the statement in the *Saṃyukta-skandha* to be reconciled?
For example, it says: "What is the cultivation of revulsion? It is the fading away of greed," and so forth, at length.
The answer to that passage should be stated as follows:
"It is the wholesome roots of non-hatred and non-delusion associated with disenchantment;
one should not say it is non-attachment. As for its being so stated, one should know that this is merely an augmentation by the reciter following the momentum of the words.
Some say that the essence of revulsion (*nirveda*) is wisdom (*prajñā*). If this were so,
how would one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Saṃgītiparyāya*?
As it is said: "How does one cultivate revulsion, become dispassionate, and abandon greed? and so forth, at length.
The answer in that passage should have been stated as follows:
"It is non-greed and non-hatred associated with revulsion; it should not be said to be non-delusion."
Furthermore, the proponent should know that this reciter increases [the affliction] according to the force of the words.
The critique states:
one must explain that the essential nature of revulsion (*nirveda*) is distinct; it is neither non-greed (*alobha*) nor wisdom (*prajñā*).
There exists a distinct mental factor (caitta-dharma) called "aversion" (nirveda) that is associated with the mind;
this is included among the remaining mental factors mentioned [in the previous list].
Here, it refers to untainted (anāsrava) aversion.
Nevertheless, there is also that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and characterized by weariness (*nirveda*).
This refers to the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*),
the three types of application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the threefold contemplation (*trividhā vipaśyanā*), and the seven points of excellence (*saptasthānasuvidhi*).
It is associated with the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas;
with the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realizations within the Path of Seeing;

and with the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, the formless attainments, the liberations, the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality, which possess the aspects of viewing [existence] as a disease, an abscess, or an arrow, within the Path of Cultivation and so forth.
Having explained at length that which exceeds the four great oceans, I shall now briefly state that much.
In this way, regarding the object of aversion (*nirvidya*) and the act of aversion (*nirvid*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is that which is aversion but not an object of aversion.

That which is untainted aversion (*anāsrava-nirveda*) is aversion but not the object of aversion; that which is the object of aversion but not aversion refers to all other tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) excluding untainted aversion;
that which is both aversion and the object of aversion refers to mundane aversion (*laukika-nirveda*).
There is that which is neither aversion nor the object of aversion; this refers to all untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) excluding the untainted aversion itself.

Question: If one takes all phenomena as an object and forms the mental aspect (ākāra) of non-self, should this be called an attention characterized by delight (abhinandanīya-manasikāra) or an attention characterized by aversion (nirvedanīya-manasikāra)?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If it were an attention characterized by delight,
how could it also proceed by taking an object of revulsion as its focal point?
If it is an attention characterized by aversion (*vidūṣaṇā-manasikāra*), how can it also proceed by taking a pleasing object as its focal point?
One should answer: It is an attention characterized by delight (*abhipramodana-manasikāra*).
Question: If that is so, how can it also proceed by taking an object of aversion as its focal point?
Answer: That practitioner of meditation deeply delights in observing things that are inspiring;
thus, even when taking as an object immeasurable things that are loathsome, they still give rise to inspiration.
It is like placing a single gold coin upon a heap of copper coins.
Just as one develops a mind of delight toward a certain collection for the sake of money,
so it is here: if a phenomenon acts as a cause for another phenomenon.
Is there ever a time when this dharma does not act as a cause for that dharma?
Answer: There is no time when it is not a cause.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: It was composed to refute the views of those who, being ignorant of the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), cling to the notion that the nature of dependent origination is not truly existent, and to demonstrate that the essential nature of dependently originated phenomena is indeed truly existent. Thus, this treatise was written.
Some say that in this context,
the treatise is composed based on a single cause,
namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
Because all minds and mental factors, by virtue of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), apprehend the same object, are always inseparable, and pertain to all three time periods.
Some say that in this context,
the treatise is composed based on two causes.

This refers to the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), because these two causes both pertain to all three time periods and are never dissociated from one another. Some say:
In this context, the treatise is composed based on three types of causes:
namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
These three possess superior efficacy regarding their effects because they operate throughout the three periods of time.
Some say that the treatise herein is composed based on four causes—
namely, association (*samprayoga*), coexistence (*sahabhū*), maturation (*vipāka*),
and functional capacity (*kāraṇa*)— because these four causes pertain to all three time periods.
Some say that,
in this context, the treatise is composed based on five causes,
namely, excluding the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Some say that this treatise is composed based on the six causes. Question:
If a dharma has not yet reached the stage of having already arisen, it cannot function as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) or a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Only upon reaching the stage of having already arisen can [a dharma] function as a cause.
How is it that, based on the six causes, the treatise states that there is no time when something is not a cause?
Answer: This is stated with reference to the final stage.
This means that future dharmas, upon reaching the stage of actual arising (*jāti*), are certainly able to function as causes.
Since there is no time thereafter when they are not a cause, this statement is made.
Question: If that is so, why is it not stated in the same way for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?

As it is said: "If a dharma acts as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for another dharma, is there ever a time when this dharma does not act as the equal-and-immediate condition for that dharma?
Answer: "When this dharma has not yet reached the state of having already arisen."
However, regarding the fact that minds and mental factors should function as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*):
once they reach the stage of being about to arise (*upapadyamāna*), they are certainly able to function as such conditions.
Why, then, is it not stated that there is never a time when they are not an equal-and-immediate condition?
The answer is: He should have made that statement as well, yet he did not;
one should know that this was intended to manifest various literary styles and various modes of exposition to adorn the meaning and make it easy to understand.

Furthermore, it is because one wishes to manifest two gates, two summaries, two staircases, two shadows, two lights, and two torches that display one another: as it is here, so it is there; as it is there, so it is here.
The remaining meanings are explained in detail as in the *Jñānanirdeśa* section of the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
If a dharma acts as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for another dharma,
is there ever a time when this dharma does not act as the equal-and-immediate condition for that dharma?
Answer: When this dharma has not yet reached the state of having already arisen.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: To stop the misconception of those who, being ignorant regarding the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), hold that the equal-and-immediate condition is not substantially real.
This treatise is composed because the nature of the dharmas that constitute the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is substantially real (*dravyasat*).
Question: At the time when this dharma has not yet reached the state of having already arisen, what is this dharma?
Does a preceding dharma act as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for a subsequent dharma while it has not yet reached the stage of having arisen,
or does it act as such only when it has reached that stage?
Does a subsequent dharma not act as an equal-and-immediate condition for a preceding dharma during its states of being "not yet arrived" (*anāgata*) or "already arisen" (*utpanna*),
but rather acts as an equal-and-immediate condition only when it has actually arrived?

Just as when the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) gives rise to the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), because the supreme mundane dharma has not yet reached the state of having already arisen,
it does not serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering.
Does it become its equal-and-immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) as soon as it arrives?

Or does the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) not become the equal-and-immediate antecedent of the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*) while it is still in the state of being unarisen, and only become so once it has arrived?
If a preceding dharma has not yet reached the stage of having already arisen, it does not act as the equal-and-immediate condition for a subsequent dharma;
if it has reached that stage, it does so. This may be the case when there is a state of mind.
How could this be possible in the state of mindlessness?
For example, when one enters the attainment of non-conception or the attainment of cessation for seven days and nights, or even for a longer period,
if the mind that entered the meditative absorption were to reach the stage of having already arisen [at the end of that time], [it would follow that it is not truly ceased].
In that case, the mind emerging from meditative absorption (vyutthānacitta) would necessarily arise in the second moment as its equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya). Why is this?
Because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that, while serving as an equal-and-immediate condition for another phenomenon, does not take that [condition] as its fruit.
Or suppose there were sentient beings— whether they be medicinal herbs, incantations, Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Arhats who have reached the ultimate—
who could obstruct it such that a second moment could not arise.
In that case, the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) would never arise again.

If a subsequent dharma does not function as the equal-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for a preceding dharma when it has not yet reached the state of having arisen, yet does so once it has reached that state,

then would it not be the case that the "patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) also [functions as such] before it has reached the state of having arisen?
Is it also the equal-and-immediate condition for the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*)?
Regarding this, some say:
if the preceding dharma has not yet reached the state of having already arisen.
It does not act as an equal-and-immediate condition for a subsequent dharma unless it reaches that state;
if it reaches it, then it acts as such.
Question: If this is so, it may be possible in the state of having consciousness, but how can it be possible in the state of being without consciousness?
Answer: Here it is said that this refers to the state of possessing mind (*sacittaka*), not other states.
Some say that even if it were explained based on the state of being without mind (*acittaka*), there would be no fault.
This means that when the mind entering meditative absorption is present, it simultaneously grasps all the absorptions as well as the results of the emerging mind;
it also [grasps] the subsequent moments of the absorption's result following the first moment of that absorption.
Furthermore, when the mind emerges from meditative absorption and arises, it gives rise to its fruit but does not grasp [it], because it has already been grasped previously.
The critique states:
One should not make such a statement.

Why is this so? Because there is no equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) that takes up its fruit at one time and gives its fruit at another; if it were to take up its fruit at this time, [it would have to give it at that same time].
This is because [the subsequent dharma] coexists with the fruit at that time. Some say:
"If a subsequent dharma has not yet reached the state of having already arisen, it does not act as the equal-and-immediate condition for the preceding dharma."
If it occurs as soon as one arrives [at that stage], one might ask:

"Is it not the case that the *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*, even while it has not yet reached the state of having already arisen, also serves as the immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*)?
The answer is: "At that time, although it does serve as the immediate antecedent for the Supreme Mundane Dharma," [it is not yet considered fully arisen].
It is not, however, an immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Once it has reached the state of having already arisen, it is called both "immediately antecedent" and "immediately antecedent condition," just as with the term "immediately antecedent" and the term "immediately antecedent condition."
The same applies to the existence of immediate succession (*samanantara*) and the continuity of that which follows immediately;
the remaining meanings are explained in detail as in the *Jñānaprasthāna* chapter on Knowledge within the *Prakaraṇapāda*.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section Four, Part Two of the Fourth Sub-section on Knowledge within the Eighth Aggregate of Views: If a phenomenon serves as an object-condition for another phenomenon, is there ever a time when this phenomenon does not serve as an object-condition for that phenomenon?
Answer: There is no time when [an object] is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: To stop the delusion regarding the object-condition—that is, the grasping at the object-condition as having a substantial reality—and to show that the object-condition lacks any intrinsic nature.
This treatise is composed because the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is established as a substantially existent phenomenon (*dravyasat*).
In this context, there is no time when something is not an object-condition, because the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are necessarily fixed upon their objects.
Question: How are the mind and mental factors determined with respect to their objects?
Is it determined by way of location, or is it determined by way of blue and so forth?
Is it fixed by location, or is it fixed by moment? Regarding this,
some say that mental states and their concomitants are fixed only by location, and not by color such as blue, nor are they fixed by moment.
Why is this? If one were fixed upon [objects] such as blue or upon moments, then immeasurable minds and mental factors would abide in a state of non-arising;
since we wish to avoid such an error, [the mind] is fixed only upon the location.
Question: If it were restricted solely to the sense-base (āyatana), then within that base of form (rūpāyatana) there would be various natures of color, such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
If it were not restricted to these, then the cognition that perceives blue would perceive [all of them].
The same applies to yellow and the other [colors].
It is impossible for a single cognition to possess multiple cognizing natures, because there is no certainty regarding two [distinct objects]. Some say:
The mind and mental factors are fixed with respect to their bases and are also fixed with respect to blue and so forth,
but they are not fixed with respect to moments. Why is this?
If it were fixed to a single moment, then immeasurable minds and mental factors would abide in a state of non-arising;
to avoid this error, it is not said to be fixed to a single moment.

Question: If that is so, it is like the case where within the color blue there are many kinds of blue—namely, the blue root, the blue stem, the blue branch, the blue leaf, the blue flower, and the blue fruit.
If one were not to specify [the particular type] therein, then the cognition perceiving the root would simply perceive [blue].
The same applies to the stalk and other parts.
It is impossible for a single cognition to possess multiple cognizing natures, because there is no certainty that two [distinct natures] could exist within one.
Thus it is said.
The mind and mental factors are fixed with respect to three things.
Question: If that were so, then immeasurable minds and mental factors would abide in a state of non-arising.
Answer: What fault is there in immeasurable minds and mental factors abiding in a state of non-arising?
Is there no room in the future world?
Yet, they have always possessed their own abodes from the very beginning.
Question: Just as the mind and mental factors are fixed with respect to their objects, are they also fixed with respect to their bases?
Answer: They are also fixed with respect to their supports (*āśraya*).

That is to say, the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, along with their associated mental factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*), are distant from their supports when they exist in the future.
The present is both [distant from] the past and distant from the future;
some say that the future is distant from its basis.
The present and the past coexist with their bases.
The remaining meanings are explained in detail as in the *Jñāna-nirdeśa* section of the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
If a dharma acts as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for another dharma...
"Is there ever a time when this dharma is not the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for that dharma?
Answer: "There is no time when it is not the dominant condition.
Question: "For what purpose was this treatise composed?"

Answer: This treatise was composed to stop the delusion of those who, regarding the nature of the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), hold that the sovereign condition is not substantially real, and to demonstrate that the essence of the sovereign condition is indeed substantially real.
Question: Since all phenomena arise and cease due to the conjunction of conditions,
and there is never a time when these conditions are not in conjunction,
why do all phenomena not arise and cease at all times?
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke thus:
"The arising and ceasing of all phenomena are distinct from their conjunction;
that is to say, phenomena arise due to the conjunction of other conditions."
Because other conditions come together, all phenomena cease;
therefore, they do not arise and perish at every moment.
Furthermore, once this phenomenon has arisen, other phenomena arise in succession, following it through many moments in close temporal proximity.
Therefore, there is no capacity for rebirth; it is like a person who has fallen over a precipice and is crushed by a collapsing mound of earth—though he wishes to rise, he is crushed again.
At such a time, that person cannot even move, let alone rise up.
All phenomena are likewise thus;
therefore, there is no fault of perpetual arising and ceasing.
The remaining meanings are explained in detail as in the *Jñānaprasthāna* section on the *Vijñānakāya* within the *Saṃyuktāgama*.
"Is all that which is contact through mental consciousness contact arising from the conjunction of the three?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is in order to refute the positions of others and to clarify one's own doctrine.
That is to say, there are some who maintain that mental factors (caitta) are identical to the mind (citta).
Some say that "contact" (sparśa) refers to the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness;
this is said in order to refute that view and to demonstrate that mental factors (caitta) are not the mind itself, but rather that contact exists as a distinct entity associated with the mind.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of dispelling the doubts of others.
That is to say, some may doubt: "It is reasonable that the contact of the eye up to the contact of the body is called 'the conjunction of the three' (*trikasamnipāta*).
However, since those faculties, objects, and consciousnesses arise simultaneously, how can mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*) also be called 'contact of the conjunction of the three'?"

Why is this? Because the mental faculty (*manas*) is past, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is present, and the phenomena (*dharma*) are either of the three time periods or transcendent of time.
Now, it is intended to definitively demonstrate that mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) is also called the "conjunction of the three."

Contact (*sparśa*) is defined as "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*) because it arises from mutually non-contradictory factors to produce a single result; it is not merely their simultaneous arising that constitutes conjunction.
For this reason, this treatise was composed.
Are all instances of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*) necessarily contacts resulting from the conjunction of the three?
Answer: All instances of mental contact are contacts resulting from the conjunction of the three;
there is no contact that does not arise from the conjunction of the three.
There is contact through the conjunction of the three that is not mental contact;
namely, contact associated with the five groups of consciousness.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikṣus, you should know."
There is the element of mind, the element of phenomena, and the element of ignorance.
From contact with ignorance arises feeling;
because they are touched by this feeling, unlearned fools then grasp at existence or grasp at non-existence.
Some maintain that there is both existence and non-existence.
In this context, "the mind-element" refers to the past mind-element;
"the phenomena-element" refers to the phenomena-element of the three periods of time.
The "element of ignorance" refers to the element of ignorance in the present.
"Ignorance-contact" and so forth refer to delusion regarding the fact of non-self,
whereby one then clings to the existence of a self.
That is to say, one who gives rise to the view of eternalism clings to non-existence; one who gives rise to the view of annihilationism clings to existence;
and one who clings to both existence and non-existence gives rise to the views of both eternalism and annihilationism.
The Venerable Pārśva said:
"The meaning intended here is that ignorance regarding one's own nature is called the element of ignorance (avidyā-dhātu)."
The six groups of consciousness that have ceased without interval are called the mind-element (manodhātu).
At that time, the mental states and mental factors that arise in dependence upon it are called the phenomenon-element (dharmadhātu).
Ignorance-contact and so forth are as previously explained.

Question: It is acceptable to say that the contact associated with the five consciousnesses is called "contact through the triad" because it arises from the present sense faculty, object, and consciousness.

However, regarding the contact associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), since the sense faculty is past, the object may be future, and the consciousness is present, how can it be called "contact through the triad"?
Answer: There are two kinds of conjunction (*sāmagrī*).
First, that which arises simultaneously and is inseparable is called conjunction.
Second, that which is non-contradictory and accomplishes a single purpose together is called conjunction.
Contact associated with the five consciousnesses is called "conjunction" (saṃnipāta) because it arises from the conjunction of two factors;
contact associated with the mental consciousness is called "conjunction" because it arises from the conjunction of various factors performing a single function.
Why is this so? Just as the functioning of the five consciousnesses occurs when their faculties and objects are present,
so too does the functioning of the mental consciousness occur across different time periods.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghosaka stated:
"The sense faculty, the object, and consciousness are termed 'conjunction' (saṃnipāta) because they collectively perform a single function;
it is not because they arise simultaneously and are inseparable that they are called a conjunction."
Thus, these three factors, at whatever time they may occur, are all capable of collectively accomplishing a single task; therefore, they are all termed "conjunction" (*sāmagrī*).
Others have added explanatory elaborations to this point.
Are all eye-contact instances, up to and including body-contact instances, contact through the conjunction of the three?
Answer: All eye-contact instances, up to and including body-contact instances, are contact through the conjunction of the three.
There is a contact arising from the conjunction of the three that is neither eye-contact nor even body-contact;
namely, contact associated with the group of mental consciousnesses (*manovijñānakāya*). What is the intention behind not stating it in this way here?
To demonstrate that herein only those meanings not yet established are being proven,
the fact that the designations "eye-contact" through to "body-contact" signify the meaning of contact as the conjunction of the three is self-evident, and thus it is not explicitly stated.
The term "contact of the mind" (manas-saṃsparśa) refers to the meaning of contact as the conjunction of the three;
this is not universally established. Therefore, it is better to say, as previously recited, "by means of which.
Are all those [types of] pride instances of self-grasping?
...and so on, as explained at length.
Question: Within this aggregate of views (*dṛṣṭiskandha*), one should only analyze views; why then is pride (*māna*) also analyzed?
Answer: It is because the author of that treatise intended it to be so, and so on, as explained at length.
Some say that because they are similar, among all afflictions there is no affliction that does not have the nature of a view;
rather, it functions as if it were a view, just like pride.
Some say: "It has already been stated that all phenomena are analyzed within each individual aggregate (*skandha*).
If pride were not analyzed within this [feeling] aggregate," [it would be incomplete].
How is it that each individual aggregate (skandha) analytically discerns all phenomena?
For this reason, herein one also analytically discerns pride, all forms of pride, and all instances of self-clinging.
Answer: All forms of pride (*māna*) involve self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*), because pride is a phenomenon characterized by self-exaltation, self-reliance, and competitive grasping.
However, there is self-clinging that is not pride.
This refers to various speculative views.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikṣus, you should know that one clings to a self and clings to what belongs to a self."
In this context, "clinging to a self" indicates the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*),
while "clinging to what belongs to a self" indicates the view of what belongs to a self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, "clinging to a self" indicates the five views of a self.
The grasping at "mine" demonstrates the fifteen views of "mine.
Furthermore, the grasping at a self demonstrates the characteristic of the conduct of the self-view,
while the grasping at "mine" demonstrates the characteristic of the conduct of the view of "mine."
Some say this: one who clings to a self manifests craving for the self (*ātmasneha*);
one who clings to what belongs to the self manifests craving for what belongs to the self (*ātmīyasneha*).
Other masters say:
one who clings to a self manifests delusion regarding the self;
one who clings to what belongs to the self manifests delusion regarding what belongs to the self.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) that clings to a self reveals a non-distinct entity;
the view of a personal identity that clings to what belongs to a self reveals a distinct entity.
Among all afflictions, there is no affliction that does not have pride as its intrinsic nature yet manifests as if it were something other than pride;
because it is like a "viewer," the self-clinging of the views is said to be [a form of] pride.
Are all forms of conceit (*māna*) entirely non-quiescent?
Why was this further inquiry posed? The answer is:
previously, one merely analyzed the conceits that have modes of activity similar to those of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
The modes of activity similar to all afflictions have not yet been analyzed;
wishing now to analyze them, this treatise is composed.
Are all forms of pride entirely non-quiescent?
Answer: All forms of pride (*māna*) are entirely non-quiescent, because pride is a dharma characterized by self-exaltation, self-reliance, and contentious grasping.
There are, however, states that are non-quiescent which are not pride.
This refers to the manifestation of other afflictions.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikṣus, you should know that those who waver are bound by Māra;
those who do not waver are liberated from evil."
Among these, "other afflictions" refers to the views,
doubt, ignorance, attachment, aversion, the envelopments,
and the stains that manifest before one; their manifestation reveals the characteristic of lack of tranquility.
Question: For what reason do present afflictions possess the characteristic of non-quiescence, whereas those of the past and future do not?
Answer: Present afflictions obstruct the Noble Path and the preparatory practices for the Noble Path within one's own continuum.
The afflictions of the past and future are not like this.
Furthermore, present afflictions are able to take up and give forth results within one's own continuum,
whereas the afflictions of the past and future are not.
Furthermore, present afflictions within one's own continuum can produce both outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) and ripening fruits (*vipāka-phala*),
whereas past and future afflictions do not.
Moreover, present afflictions cause one's own continuum to become subject to censure, loathing, and avoidance.
Past and future afflictions are not like this.
Furthermore, present afflictions burn the self, destroy the self, and oppress the self;
past and future afflictions are not like this.
Furthermore, present afflictions harm oneself,
harm others, or harm both;
past and future afflictions do not do so.
Furthermore, present afflictions are of a non-quiescent nature;
they are so described because they possess a non-quiescent function.
Past and future afflictions are also of a non-quiescent nature.
Because there is nothing that is not tranquil, it is not so described.
Regarding the phrase "movement is bound by Māra" and so forth:
