here, the first clause reveals that those who are not tranquil are bound by the Māra of the afflictions (*kleśa-māra*).
The latter phrase reveals that those who have attained tranquility are liberated from the celestial Māras,
because those whose nature is corrupt and evil are exclusively celestial Māras.
Other masters say:
In this context, both phrases reveal the nature of the māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*).
Because various afflictions harm wholesome dharmas, they are called "māras";
because they give rise to unwholesome karma, they are further termed "evil ones."
If sentient beings are not at peace, they are bound by afflictions;
if they can attain tranquility and cultivate the remedies, they will then achieve liberation from those afflictions.
Are all karmas non-restraint?
One should respond that there are four permutations.
There are karmas that are not non-restraint.
That is to say, there is restraint of body and speech;
there is non-restraint that is not karma, namely the non-restraint of the faculties;
and there is that which is both karma and non-restraint, namely the non-restraint of body and speech.
There are things that are neither karma nor non-restraint, namely, restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*).
Are all those that are karma also restraint?
One should answer by means of four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There is action that is not restraint, namely bodily and vocal non-restraint.
There is restraint that is not action, namely sense-faculty restraint.
There is action that is also restraint, namely bodily and vocal restraint.
There is that which is neither karma nor restraint, namely, non-restraint of the faculties (*indriya-asaṃvara*).
Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of restraint of the faculties and non-restraint of the faculties herein?
Some say as follows:
Restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) has mindfulness and clear comprehension (*smṛti-samprajanya*) as its intrinsic nature;
lack of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-asaṃvara*) has forgetfulness and lack of clear comprehension (*muṣitasmṛty-asamprajanya*) as its intrinsic nature.
How is this known to be so?
Because the sūtras are authoritative,
as it is said in a sūtra:
At one time, a deva addressed a bhikṣu, saying:
"O Bhikṣu, do not let sores and tumors arise!
The Bhikṣu replied, "I shall cover them.
The Deva asked again, "Since the sores and tumors are so large, how can you possibly cover them?"
The bhikṣu replied, "I shall cover it with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
The deva then praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
To be able to cover it in this way is true skillful covering."

From this, it is known that restraint of the sense faculties has mindfulness and clear comprehension as its intrinsic nature, while non-restraint of the sense faculties has forgetfulness and lack of clear comprehension as its intrinsic nature.
Question: If this is so, how are the sūtras to be reconciled?
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Because mindfulness and clear comprehension are fulfilled, one is able to fulfill the restraint of the sense faculties.
How could a nature fulfill itself by its own nature?
The answer is: mindfulness and clear comprehension possess both causal nature and resultant nature.
The causal nature is designated by the term "right mindfulness," while the resultant nature is designated by the term "restraint.
Because the cause is fulfilled, the result is brought to completion; therefore, there is no fault.
Some say that restraint of the sense faculties has heedfulness as its intrinsic nature,
while non-restraint of the sense faculties has heedlessness as its intrinsic nature.
Some say that restraint of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) has the six constant abidings (*ṣaḍ-āveṇika-dharmāḥ*) as its intrinsic nature,
while non-restraint of the faculties (*indriyāsaṃvara*) has the arising of various afflictions (*kleśa*) based upon the six faculties as its intrinsic nature.

Some say that sense-faculty restraint (indriya-saṃvara) has as its intrinsic nature the permanent abandonment and thorough knowledge of the sense faculties, as well as all excellent conduct and roots of virtue;

whereas lack of sense-faculty restraint (indriya-asaṃvara) has as its intrinsic nature the non-abandonment and lack of thorough knowledge of the sense faculties, as well as the afflictions, unwholesome conduct, and roots of non-virtue.
Thus, wholesome and unwholesome conduct constitute the basis for restraint of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) and non-restraint of the faculties (*indriyāsaṃvara*),

respectively. Some say that restraint of the faculties consists in the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of non-restraint of the faculties, its non-abandonment (*aprahāṇa*), and its lack of full comprehension (*aparijñāna*).
Furthermore, the nature of the restraint of the faculties consists in the accomplishment of the path that serves as their antidote;
whereas the non-restraint of the faculties consists in the non-cessation and non-thorough knowledge of the faculties,
as well as the non-accomplishment of the path that serves as their antidote.
Thus, both restraint of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) and non-restraint of the faculties (*indriyāsaṃvara*) have fulfillment and non-fulfillment as their essential nature.
Some say that restraint of the faculties has non-defiled phenomena (*akliṣṭadharma*) as its intrinsic nature.
Non-restraint of the faculties has defiled phenomena as its intrinsic nature.
Thus, both restraint of the faculties and non-restraint of the faculties have the five aggregates as their essential substance.
Formerly, in the monastery of Śrīvijaya in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there were two brothers who were both arhats and Dharma masters,
renowned in the world as the sons of Nandika.
That [text] explains that both faculty-restraint (*indriya-saṃvara*) and non-faculty-restraint (*indriyāsaṃvara*) have as their intrinsic nature faculty-restraint and non-faculty-restraint,
which are included within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*) and are unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
This establishment of intrinsic nature means that its essence is substantially existent.
This is subsumed within the category of "other formations dissociated from mind" (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Question: If there are restraint of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*) and non-restraint of the faculties (*indriya-asaṃvara*), [how are they categorized]?
If both have as their intrinsic nature the unobscured-neutral aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), what is the distinction between them?
Answer: Among these unobscured-neutral aggregates of formations, there are those that accord with the wholesome category (*kuśala-pakṣa*).
That which conforms to the category of afflictions is called lack of restraint of the faculties;
that which conforms to the category of the wholesome is called restraint of the faculties.
That which conforms to the category of afflictions is called non-restraint of the faculties.
"If a thing has not been attained, is it not accomplished? and so forth, as explained at length.
Among the five kinds and ten kinds of things previously mentioned, the discussion here is based on the category of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

The intention behind wishing to stop the discussion regarding the nature of non-accomplishment is to demonstrate that the natures of accomplishment and non-accomplishment are substantially real. [Objection:
Is it not the case that when a thing has not yet been acquired, there is non-accomplishment of it?
Answer: If a thing has not yet been attained, it is not accomplished;

that is to say, the contemplation of impurity, mindfulness of breathing, the three types of mental abiding, the seven stages of proficiency, and the levels of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
Regarding the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning:
in such matters as these, if one has not yet attained them, they are not accomplished;
however, there are cases where something is not accomplished even though it has been attained.
This refers to having attained [a state] and then losing it; this is what was previously called the "contemplation of impurity" and so forth.
It is not the case that one fails to achieve it simply because it has not yet been attained.
If a matter has already been attained, is that then its achievement?
Answer: If a thing is accomplished, it has already been attained;
that is to say, one has already attained and not lost the previously mentioned impurity meditation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth.
There are, however, cases where a thing has been attained but is not yet accomplished.
This refers to having attained [a state] and then losing it; that is to say, the previously attained *asubha-bhāvanā* (contemplation of impurity) and so forth have been lost.
This excludes the Noble Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-āryasatya*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), and so on, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This is for the purpose of refuting the positions of others and clarifying one’s own doctrine.
That is to say, some may claim that all phenomena include the nature of others but do not include their own nature.
The truth of origination is exclusively craving;
the truth of the path is exclusively the Noble Eightfold Path.
Alternatively, it is said that the locus of phenomena (dharmāyatana) encompasses all phenomena.
Some say that the locus of dharmas is exclusively non-material;
others say that the two time periods of the past and future do not exist;
and still others say that the five consciousnesses are exclusively indeterminate in nature.
This treatise is composed in order to refute these various erroneous attachments and to reveal the meaning that accords with the characteristics of phenomena;
it contains two intended purposes for its expression.
First, for the purpose of establishing;
second, for the purpose of excluding.

Herein, the word "excluding" is intended to exclude those factors other than the Noble Truth of Suffering and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), which are subsumed under two elements, one sphere, and one aggregate.
In this context, the noble truth of suffering refers to all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), namely: fifteen elements (*dhātu*),
a portion of three elements,
ten bases (*āyatana*), and a portion of two bases.
A portion of the five aggregates;

the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) refers to the seven categories of phenomena, namely the aggregates of perception, feeling, and formations, non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa), and the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
"Other phenomena" refers to untainted (anāsrava) consciousness.
Therefore, this dharma comprises two elements—namely, the mind element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*);
one base—namely, the mind base (*manāyatana*);
and one aggregate—namely, it is subsumed within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
The same applies to the explanation regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin [of Suffering] and the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
This is because, although the meanings of suffering and its origin differ, their substance is not different.
Excluding the Noble Truth of Cessation and the sphere of phenomena, the remaining factors are subsumed within seventeen elements (dhātus), eleven spheres (āyatanas), and two aggregates (skandhas).
Among these, the noble truth of cessation refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It constitutes a small portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*).
As for the dharma-base, it consists of the seven types of dharmas as previously described.

The remaining factors refer to resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) and all mind (*citta*); therefore, these factors are subsumed under seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
The same explanation applies when excluding the noble truth of the path (*mārga-āryasatya*) and the base of mental objects (*dharma-āyatana*).
In this context, it is stated that "it is likewise" because the measure of what is subsumed is the same.
However, the Noble Truth of the Path refers to untainted (anāsrava) conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma), namely:
the mental element (manodhātu), the mental-consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu), and the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) belonging to the three realms.
The two bases are the mind base (*manāyatana*) and the phenomena base (*dharmāyatana*).
A portion of the five aggregates belongs to the phenomena base, as previously explained.
The remaining phenomena consist of obstructive matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*) and contaminated mind (*sāsrava-citta*).
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha).
Excluding phenomena that possess form and the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
the remaining phenomena are subsumed within seven elements, one base, and one aggregate.
Among these, the dharmas with form refer to the four great elements and their derivatives, namely ten elements, a portion of one element,
ten bases, a portion of one base, and one aggregate— the dharma-base— as previously explained.
As for the remaining phenomena, they refer to all minds; therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within seven mind-elements, one base, and one aggregate.
Excluding formless phenomena and the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), the remaining phenomena are subsumed within ten elements, ten bases, and one aggregate.
Among these, the formless dharmas refer to the mind and mental factors,
the non-associated formations, and the unconditioned; these constitute seven mind-elements (*citta-dhātu*),
a portion of one element, one base (*āyatana*), and a portion of another base.
The four aggregates, excluding the aggregate of form, and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are as previously explained.

As for the remaining phenomena, they refer to all obstructive forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*); therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within ten elements (*dhātu*), ten spheres (*āyatana*), and one aggregate.

Excluding the visible phenomena (*sanidarśana-dharma*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), the remaining phenomena are subsumed within sixteen elements (*dhātu*), ten spheres (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
Among these, "visible phenomena" refers to that which is the range of the eye; it consists of one element, one sphere, and a portion of one aggregate.
The sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is as previously explained.
The remaining phenomena consist of invisible and impinging matter (*rūpa*) and all mental states (*citta*).
Therefore, these phenomena comprise sixteen elements (*dhātu*), excluding the element of visible form (*rūpadhātu*) and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Excluding the sense-base of form and the sense-base of mental objects from the ten sense-bases,
there are the two aggregates of form and consciousness;
excluding the invisible phenomena and the sense-base of mental objects.
The remaining phenomena are subsumed within one element, one base, and one aggregate.
Among these, "non-visible phenomena" refers to all phenomena except those within the range of the eye;
these consist of seventeen elements.
Eleven bases, four aggregates, and a portion of one aggregate.

As previously stated regarding the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), the remaining dharmas are those that are the objects of the eye; therefore, these dharmas are subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base, and one aggregate.
Excluding the obstructive dharmas (*sapratigha-dharma*) and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining dharmas are subsumed within seven elements (*dhātu*), one sphere, and one aggregate (*skandha*).
Among these, "obstructive dharmas" refers to all except for non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
All other forms consist of ten elements (dhātus), ten bases (āyatanas), and a portion of one aggregate (skandha).
As for the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana), it has been explained previously.
"Other phenomena" refers to all states of mind; therefore, these phenomena are subsumed under seven mental elements, one base, and one aggregate.
Excluding the non-resistant phenomena (*apratigha-dharma*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining phenomena are subsumed within ten elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*).
Herein, "non-resistant phenomena" refers to all things except for resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*).
All other phenomena consist of eight elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and a portion of one aggregate (skandha).
The base of phenomena (dharmāyatana) is as previously explained.
The remaining phenomena refer to all resistant forms (sapratigha-rūpa); therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within ten elements, ten bases, and one aggregate.
Excluding the contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining dharmas are subsumed under two elements (*dhātu*), one base, and one aggregate (*skandha*).
Herein, "contaminated dharmas" refers to the truths of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and its origin (*samudayasatya*).
Thus, there are fifteen elements (dhātu):
a portion of three elements, ten bases (āyatana), a portion of two bases, and a portion of five aggregates (skandha).
The sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) is as previously explained.
The remaining dharmas refer to the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*). Therefore,
these dharmas are subsumed under two elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*),
excluding the untainted dharmas and the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The remaining phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
Among these, untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) refer to the truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the path (*mārga-satya*), as well as the two unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*);
they constitute a portion of three elements, two bases, and five aggregates.
The sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is as previously explained.
The remaining phenomena consist of resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) and contaminated mind (*sāsrava-citta*).
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven spheres (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
Excluding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
To ask about other phenomena while excluding all phenomena is a baseless and empty argument.
Herein, "conditioned phenomena" refers to the truths of suffering, origin, and the path, which comprise seventeen elements (*dhātu*).
A portion of one element, eleven bases, a portion of one base, and the five aggregates;
as for the dharma-base, it has been explained previously.
Apart from these, there are no other phenomena that can be included.
Therefore, this is called a "void discourse on non-entities.
With the exception of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
all other phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven spheres (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).

Among these, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) refer to space (*ākāśa*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); they constitute a portion of one element and one base.
The base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is as previously explained.
The remaining phenomena consist of resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) and all mental states (*citta*).
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha).
Excluding past phenomena and the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
the remaining phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements, eleven bases, and two aggregates.

Among these, past phenomena refer to those phenomena that have already arisen and already ceased; they constitute a portion of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
The base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is as previously explained.
The remaining dharmas refer to future and present resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) as well as mind (*citta*).
Therefore, these dharmas are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
The same explanation applies when excluding future dharmas, present dharmas, and the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Since there is no distinction among the different types at that time, with the exception of wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*). Among these,
"wholesome phenomena" refers to those phenomena whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is secure and which can obtain desirable fruits.
This consists of a portion of the ten realms, four bases, and five aggregates.
The *dharmāyatana* is as previously explained;
the remaining factors refer to unwholesome, neutral, and resistant matter, as well as the mind.
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed under seventeen elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha).
The same applies when excluding unwholesome phenomena and the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Because they are subsumed by their categories rather than individually,
with the exception of indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*) and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining phenomena are subsumed within nine elements (*dhātu*), three spheres (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
In this context, "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) dharmas refer to those that do not yield desirable or undesirable fruits,
as well as those that are not by nature states of security.
That is to say: a portion of eight elements and ten elements; a portion of eight bases and four bases;
five aggregates;
and a portion of the dharma-base, as previously explained.
The remaining factors refer to wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, resistant form, and the mind. Therefore,
these factors are subsumed within nine elements, three bases, and two aggregates,
excluding the factors bound to the desire realm and the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The remaining phenomena are subsumed within thirteen elements (*dhātu*), nine bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).

Among these, phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) refer to those in which desire-craving (*kāmarāga*) increases; that is, four elements, a portion of fourteen elements, two bases, a portion of ten bases, and a portion of five aggregates.
The sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is as previously explained.

The remaining phenomena consist of the resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), as well as the mind (*citta*) bound to the realm of form, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), or unbound.
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed under thirteen elements (*dhātu*), nine bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
Excluding the factors associated with the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*) and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining factors are subsumed under seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven spheres (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
Among these, "factors associated with the realm of form" refers to those in which craving for form (*rūpatṛṣṇā*) increases by way of latent proclivity (*anuśaya*).
These consist of a portion of fourteen elements, ten bases, and five aggregates.
As for the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), it has been explained previously.
The remaining phenomena refer to the resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) bound to the desire realm, as well as the minds bound to the desire and formless realms and those that are unbound.
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha).

The same explanation applies to the phenomena associated with the formless realm, the phenomena of those in training (śaikṣa), the phenomena of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and the base of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
This is because the number of factors included therein is the same.
Excluding the dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner and the dharma-base (dharmāyatana),
the remaining dharmas are subsumed under two elements (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha).
Among these, the dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner refer to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas.
These consist of fifteen elements (*dhātu*), a portion of three elements; ten bases (*āyatana*), a portion of two bases; and a portion of five aggregates (*skandha*).
The sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is as previously explained.
The remaining phenomena refer to the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*).
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed under two elements (*dhātu*), one sphere (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*).
Excluding the factors abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining factors are subsumed under seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
Herein, "factors abandoned by insight" refers to those which are the objects of opposition for the receptive patiences (*kṣānti*).
This consists of a portion of the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates.
The dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) is as previously explained;
the remaining factors refer to all obstructive matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*).
And because it includes the mind that is abandoned through cultivation as well as the mind that is not abandoned,
these factors are subsumed within seventeen elements, eleven bases, and two aggregates;
excluding the factors abandoned through cultivation and the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The remaining dharmas are subsumed under two elements (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha).
Among these, the dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) refer to those counteracted by knowledge (jñāna);
they consist of fifteen elements, a portion of three elements, a portion of ten bases, a portion of two bases, and a portion of five aggregates.
The sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is as previously explained.
The remaining phenomena refer to the minds that are to be abandoned by vision and those that are not to be abandoned;
therefore, these phenomena are subsumed under two elements, one sphere, and one aggregate.
Excluding the non-interruption dharmas (*anuccheda-dharma*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*),
the remaining dharmas are subsumed under seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
Herein, "non-interruption dharmas" refers to all untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
This consists of a portion of the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates.
The base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is as previously explained;
the remaining phenomena refer to all obstructive matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*) and all contaminated mind (*sāsrava-citta*).
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within seventeen elements (dhātu), eleven bases (āyatana), and two aggregates (skandha).
With the exception of phenomena that have already arisen and those that are destined never to arise,
all other phenomena are subsumed within eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
Among these, "already arisen phenomena" refers to the past and present, which constitute a portion of the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
"Phenomena certain not to arise" refers to past and present phenomena.

Furthermore, there are those dharmas destined never to arise in the future, as well as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, because they have already arisen, because they will not arise, and because they are non-arising by nature. These are definitely non-arising;
they also constitute a portion of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
The remaining phenomena refer to those that are currently arising and those that are capable of arising;
therefore, these phenomena are also subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
This excludes phenomena that have already arisen and those that are determined never to arise.
This excludes all phenomena (*dharma*).
Question: Are other phenomena merely empty discourses on non-entities? Answer:
Among these, "non-arisen phenomena" refers to future phenomena and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
These consist of a portion of the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha).
As previously stated, they include those phenomena that are determined not to arise;
apart from these, there are no other phenomena to be included.
Therefore, it is said that this is a groundless and empty discourse.
Excluding material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) and those phenomena that are necessarily non-arising,
all other phenomena are subsumed within eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and four aggregates (*skandha*).
Among these, the material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) and those phenomena that are necessarily non-arising are as previously explained.
The remaining phenomena refer to all currently arising and potentially arising minds (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within eight elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha).
With the exception of formless phenomena and those phenomena that are definitively non-arising,
all other phenomena are subsumed within eleven elements, eleven bases, and one aggregate.
Among these, the formless dharmas and those dharmas that are definitely not to arise are as previously explained.
The remaining dharmas refer to all material dharmas that are currently arising or are capable of arising.
Therefore, these dharmas are subsumed within eleven elements (dhātus), eleven bases (āyatanas), and one aggregate (skandha).
Excluding the dharmas that are visible (*sanidarśana*) and those that are necessarily non-arising (*anutpattidharman*),
the remaining dharmas are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*).
Among these, the dharmas that are visible and those that are necessarily non-arising are as previously explained.
The remaining factors refer to those factors that are currently arising, those that are capable of arising,
and all invisible factors (*anidarśana*). Therefore, these factors are subsumed within seventeen elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*),
excluding invisible factors and those factors that are definitively non-arising.
The remaining dharmas are subsumed under one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha).
Among these, the dharmas that are non-visible (anidarśana) and those that are necessarily non-arising (anutpattidharmin) are as previously explained.
The remaining dharmas refer to all visible forms (rūpa) that are currently arising or are capable of arising.
Therefore, this dharma is subsumed under one element, one base, and one aggregate.
With the exception of obstructive dharmas and dharmas that are necessarily non-arising,
all other dharmas are subsumed under eight elements, two bases, and five aggregates.
Among these, the dharmas that possess resistance (*sapratigha*) and those that are necessarily non-arising (*aniyatotpāda*) are as previously explained.
The remaining dharmas refer to all non-resistant (*apratigha*) dharmas that are currently arising or capable of arising.
Therefore, these dharmas are subsumed within eight elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*).
Excluding the non-obstructive (*apratigha*) dharmas and those dharmas that are definitely not to arise,
the remaining dharmas are subsumed within ten elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*),
and one aggregate (*skandha*). Among these, the non-obstructive dharmas and those definitely not to arise are as previously explained.
The remaining dharmas refer to those material forms (*rūpa*) that are currently arising or are capable of arising and are characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*). Therefore,
these dharmas are subsumed within ten elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*),
excluding the tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas and those dharmas that are definitely not to arise.
The remaining dharmas are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates.
Among these, the contaminated dharmas (*sāsrava-dharma*) and those dharmas destined never to arise (*anutpatti-dharmin*) are as previously explained.
The "remaining dharmas" refer to all uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas that are currently arising or are capable of arising.
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates.
With the exception of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) and phenomena that are necessarily non-arising,
all other phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*).
Among these, the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas and those dharmas that will never arise have been explained as before.
The remaining dharmas refer to all tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas that are currently arising or are capable of arising.
Therefore, these dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
Excluding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and those phenomena that are necessarily non-arising (*anutpattidharman*), this excludes all phenomena.
Question: Are the remaining phenomena merely empty talk regarding non-existent entities?
Answer: Within this context, conditioned phenomena and those that are necessarily non-arising are as previously explained.
Apart from these, there are no other dharmas that can be subsumed;
therefore, it is called a "baseless empty discourse," with the exception of unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and those dharmas that are determined never to arise.
Other phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
Among these, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and those phenomena that are necessarily non-arising have been explained as before.
"Other phenomena" refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that are currently arising or are capable of arising.
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu), the twelve bases (āyatana), and the five aggregates (skandha).
The same explanation applies to past phenomena, present phenomena, and those phenomena that are determined never to arise.
In this context, "other phenomena" refers to all conditioned phenomena that are currently arising or are capable of arising.
Therefore, these phenomena are all subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).

Excluding future phenomena and those phenomena that are destined never to arise—this excludes all phenomena. [Objection: Is it not a groundless and empty argument to claim that the remaining phenomena are "without a basis" (*avastuka*)?
[Response: Within this context, future phenomena and those destined never to arise fully encompass all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
Apart from these, there are no other phenomena that can be subsumed; therefore, they are called "empty discourses on non-entities.

With the exception of wholesome phenomena and those phenomena that are necessarily non-arising, all other phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
Among these, wholesome dharmas and those dharmas that are not destined to arise are as previously explained.
The remaining dharmas refer to all unwholesome and neutral dharmas that are currently arising or are capable of arising.
Therefore, these dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
The same explanation applies to the exclusion of unwholesome dharmas and dharmas that are definitely not to arise,
because they are included within the same categories as the remaining dharmas.
This excludes indeterminate dharmas and dharmas that are definitely not to arise.
Other dharmas are subsumed within ten bases (*āyatana*), four spheres (*dhātu*), and five aggregates (*skandha*).
Among these, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas and those dharmas that are necessarily non-arising have been explained as before.
"Other dharmas" refers to wholesome and unwholesome dharmas that are currently arising or are capable of arising.
Therefore, this dharma is subsumed within ten elements (dhātus), four bases (āyatanas), and five aggregates (skandhas).
With the exception of dharmas bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) and dharmas that will certainly not arise,
the remaining dharmas are subsumed within fourteen elements, ten bases, and five aggregates.
Among these, the factors bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and those that are definitely not to arise (*anutpattidharman*) are as previously explained.

The remaining factors refer to those bound to the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and those unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*), which are currently arising or are capable of arising.
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within fourteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*).
With the exception of phenomena bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and those that are necessarily non-arising,
all other phenomena are subsumed within eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
Among these, the factors bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and those that are definitely not to arise are as previously explained.

The remaining factors refer to those currently arising, those capable of arising, and those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), or those that are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).

This also applies to the exclusion of phenomena bound to the formless realm, phenomena of those in training (śaikṣa), phenomena of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and phenomena that are determined not to arise.
It is stated in the same way for these as well.
Because they are subsumed under the same numerical categories as other phenomena,
with the exception of those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*) dharmas and those dharmas that are definitely not to arise;
all remaining dharmas are subsumed within the three realms (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*).
Among these, the dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
as well as the dharmas that are definitely not to arise, are as previously explained.
The remaining dharmas refer to those learner and non-learner dharmas that are currently arising or are capable of arising.
Therefore, these dharmas are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates.
With the exception of the dharmas abandoned through seeing and those dharmas that are definitively non-arising,
all other dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates.
Among these, the factors abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and those that are necessarily non-arising are as previously explained.
The remaining factors— namely, those currently arising, those yet to arise, and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) or not to be abandoned—
are comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
Excluding the factors abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and those factors that are definitively non-arising,
all remaining factors are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates.
Among these, the factors abandoned through cultivation and the definitively non-arising factors are as previously explained.
The remaining dharmas refer to those that are currently arising, those capable of arising, and those to be abandoned by vision as well as those not to be abandoned.
Therefore, these dharmas are subsumed within the three realms, two bases, and five aggregates,
excluding the dharmas not to be abandoned and those that are definitely non-arising.
The remaining dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
Among these, the dharmas that are non-interrupted and those that are necessarily non-arising are as previously explained.
The remaining dharmas refer to those that are currently arising, those that are capable of arising, and those dharmas to be abandoned through vision (darśana-heya) and cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Therefore, these phenomena are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
Is there any single element, single base, or single aggregate that subsumes all phenomena?
Answer: Yes.
One element refers to the dharma-element;
one base refers to the mind-base;
and one aggregate refers to the form-aggregate.
In this way, all phenomena are fully subsumed.
Why is this? Because no phenomenon exists outside of these five categories.

That is to say: matter (rūpa) comprises the aggregate of form; mind (citta) is comprised within the sense-base of mind (manāyatana); and the remaining factors—mental concomitants (caitta), non-associated formations (viprayuktasaṃskāra), and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta)—are comprised within the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Therefore, all phenomena are subsumed.
Furthermore, no phenomenon transcends the eighteen elements (*dhātus*).
Among these, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) subsumes the ten material elements.
The mind base (manāyatana) comprises the seven consciousness elements (cittadhātu).
Because the dharma element (dharmadhātu) comprises the dharma element itself, it comprises all phenomena (sarvadharma).
Furthermore, all phenomena are included within the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana).
These three are mutually inclusive:
that is to say, the aggregate of form includes the ten material elements, the ten material bases, and a small portion of the element of phenomena and the base of phenomena;
the base of mind includes the seven mental elements.

The aggregate of consciousness is subsumed within the dharma-element and the dharma-base; the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, as well as a portion of the aggregate of form, are likewise included.
Therefore, these three [bases] encompass all phenomena. *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra-vibhāṣā*, Fascicle 197.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 198,
composed by five hundred great arhats and others.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Section 5: The Chapter on Views (Dṛṣṭivarga). Within the Eighth Aggregate of Views (Dṛṣṭiskandha), Part One of the Fifth Section on the Chapter on Views: Regarding those who hold this view that "there is no giving," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is intended to explain the views (dṛṣṭigata) mentioned in the sūtras so that they may be known as things to be abandoned. Why is this so?
Within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), there is no greater source of great attachment that leads to great harm,
nor any greater basis for grasping (*upādāna*) than the various views (*dṛṣṭigata*).
These points are explained in detail in the *Pañcavastuka-vibhāga* of the *Jñānaskandha*.
All those who hold the view that there is no giving, no offering, no sacrifice, and no wholesome or unwholesome conduct—
this is a wrong view of denial (*abhyākhyāna-mithyādṛṣṭi*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
"There is no giving" and so forth are explained as above.
This false view reveals its intrinsic nature;
that which is abandoned through the vision of the origin reveals its antidote.

That is to say, when the forbearance and knowledge regarding the Truth of Origin have already arisen, all improper investigations and improper conceptualizations directed toward that [origin] are eliminated.
Perverse views and unbalanced grasping are then forever severed, extinguished, and vanish.
Furthermore, because these views arise based on the station of origination (*samudaya*), they are severed at the time of seeing origination;
they are like dew on the tip of a blade of grass that dries up when the sun rises.

This is likewise: the denial that there are fruits of wholesome and unwholesome conduct is a wrong view regarding the fruit, which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
"Wrong view" indicates its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), while "abandoned through the vision of suffering" indicates its antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
This means that when patience and knowledge regarding the truth of suffering have arisen,
all improper investigation, improper discrimination, inverted views, and unbalanced grasping concerning it are forever severed, extinguished, and vanish.
Furthermore, because this view operates based upon the locus of suffering, it is severed at the very moment suffering is seen.
It is just as dew on the tip of a blade of grass dries up when the sun rises;
so too is this case.
However, this merely explains the intrinsic nature of that view and its antidote;
it does not explain its origination.
What is its origination?
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"There are certain non-Buddhists who observe in the world that there are those who kill and live long lives, and those who refrain from killing and have short lives;
there are those who steal and possess abundant wealth, and those who refrain from stealing and lack wealth."
There are those who are stingy yet wealthy, and those who are generous yet poor.
There are those who harm others yet remain free from illness and enjoy peace and happiness,
while there are those who do not harm others yet suffer much sickness and pain.
Having observed such contradictory phenomena, they then form this thought:
"There is no giving, no affection, nor even any fruit of good or evil conduct.
If there were such things, then all those who kill living beings would necessarily have short lifespans."
"Even up to 'not harming others' leads to being free from illness and dwelling in peace and happiness.
Because this is seen to be contradicted by what is actually manifest, one knows for certain that there is no such thing as giving, and so forth, as explained at length.
However, those non-Buddhists do not properly understand that the fruits of virtuous and non-virtuous conduct may be either distant or immediate.
Regarding perceptible phenomena, one gives rise to this view through improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).

Some say that non-Buddhists who have attained mundane meditative concentration (*laukikasamādhi*) perceive only a small portion of time and do not understand the distinctions between causes and effects throughout the beginning and end.
Seeing those who practice evil attain birth in heaven,
and seeing those who perform good deeds fall into the miserable realms,
they then form this thought: "There is no giving, there is no offering," and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say: there are certain non-Buddhists who,
neither based on direct perception nor based on meditative concentration,
but merely following the instructions of evil friends, assert that there is no giving, and so forth, as explained at length.
"There is no this world, there is no other world, and there are no beings born by transformation.
This is a false view that denies causes, which is either abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering],
or it is a false view that denies results, which is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Question: It may be appropriate to say that the next world does not exist because it is not perceived;
however, why do you say this world does not exist when it is directly perceived?
Answer: Those non-Buddhists are blinded by ignorance, and thus they even deny things that are directly perceived.
One should not blame the ignorant and blind for falling into a pit.
Furthermore, some say that those non-Buddhists merely repudiate cause and effect, but do not repudiate the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
To say "there is no this world" means that there is no this world as a cause for another world,
or that there is no this world as an effect of another world.
To say "there is no other world" means that there is no other world as a cause for this world.
Or there may be no future world as the fruit of this present world,
and no beings born by transformation; thus do certain non-Buddhists (tīrthika) speak,
asserting that the birth of all sentient beings is caused solely by present factors such as semen and blood.
There is nothing that arises suddenly without a cause.
For example, the growth of a sprout necessarily depends upon the seed, soil, water, and the proper season; there is nothing that can arise without these conditions.
Therefore, it is certain that there are no beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
This [denial] either negates the karma that produces birth by transformation,
or it negates the birth by transformation that is produced.
Some may say that the beings born by transformation— namely those in the intermediate state (antarābhava)—
are those who do not exist in this world or the next; such [a view] slanders the existence of rebirth.
Those who deny that there are beings born by transformation slander the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
There are certain non-Buddhists who claim that the intermediate state does not exist;
they assert that from this world one goes directly to that world, and no third world can be found between them.
This may either deny the karma that brings about the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*),
or deny the intermediate existence itself that is brought about by such karma,
or deny that the intermediate existence is the cause of the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*).
Alternatively, some deny that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is the fruit of the existence at death (*mṛtyubhava*).
This false view reveals its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Whether it is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), this reveals its antidote (*pratipakṣa*), as explained in detail previously.
"There is no father and no mother"—this slander arises from wrong view and is abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
Question: Since parents are directly perceived by everyone in the world, for what reason do they slander them, saying they do not exist?
The answer is: "Those various non-Buddhists are blinded by ignorance," and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that those non-Buddhists deny the existence of parents and the karma that brings about a child, but they do not deny the substantial reality of the child itself.
They argue that it is not because the parents, out of their own hearts of affection and attachment, act for the sake of the child;
rather, due to the causal condition of the union of semen and blood, that class of being arises spontaneously, and it is not said that the parents possess the karma to produce a child.
Just as various insects arise because of damp leaves, dung, soil, and so forth—
yet it is not the case that the damp leaves and such possess karma that produces those insects— so too is this [the case here].
Therefore, those non-Buddhists have this verse:
When man and woman unite with染心 (a mind of passion), and the woman encounters her fertile period and is free from illness, [the man thinks:
"From this, I shall possess [an offspring] myself; what does he have to do with me?
Or, as some say: [the woman thinks: "What does he have to do with me?"
Those non-Buddhists slander the meaning of "parents" but do not slander their substance.
It is like how worms arise from damp leaves, dung, and so forth;
for the worms, the leaves and such are neither father nor mother.
Thus, they are produced from that impurity.
For what reason, then, are those who give birth alone accorded the profound debt of gratitude known as "father and mother"?
It is for this reason that such classes of beings claim to have no parents.
This false view reveals its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); that which is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) reveals its antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
As explained extensively above, here only its intrinsic nature and its antidote are stated, while its motivating cause (*samutthāna*) is not mentioned.
Regarding their origin,
the Venerable Vasumitra said:
"When certain non-Buddhist practitioners see bubbles on the surface of the water during a heavy rain, they form this thought:"
From where does this come, and to what place does it go when it ceases?
It merely arises and ceases suddenly due to water and rain.
In the same way, sentient beings arise through the convergence of conditions.
Death occurs due to the dissociation of conditions.
One does not come from a previous life to this present birth, nor does one go from this life to a future world; thus, it is definitively taught that there is neither this world nor another world.
Furthermore, seeing that parents give birth to children in the world and water and soil produce sprouts—all such things exist only through the conjunction of conditions—he then reflects:
"Where could there possibly be spontaneously born sentient beings?"
Furthermore, one sees insects born from moisture, such as leaves and the like, as described in detail previously.
Yet those non-Buddhists do not understand that there is a distinction between sentient and insentient origins, nor do they recognize the four modes of birth for sentient beings.
Because the conditions are unequal— internal phenomena and external phenomena having distinct natures as conditions—
one improperly conceptualizes even upon matters that are only slightly similar, thereby giving rise to these various views.

Furthermore, there are those who say that those non-Buddhists who have attained mundane meditative concentration perceive sentient beings passing away from higher realms and other worlds to be born here in this world.
Or, having passed away from this world, they are born in a higher plane or another world;
because they do not perceive the place from which they came or the place to which they have gone,
they give rise to the view that "this world does not exist, nor does another world."
Furthermore, because they have attained only a coarse and shallow meditative concentration, when observing the past and future lives, they see only the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*),
and do not perceive the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) because it is so subtle.
For this reason, it is said that there are no beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
Furthermore, through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one may observe that various sentient beings come from enemies to become their parents,
or come from wives, children, brothers, or sisters to become their parents.
Even down to cases where they come from the bodies of various animals such as camels, donkeys, or dogs to become their parents;
having again become those specific forms through their parents, they then form this thought:
This is like a guest house; what certainty is there in it?
For this reason, it is said that there is neither father nor mother.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Those non-Buddhists do not rely on direct perception, nor do they rely on meditative concentration;
rather, it is solely because they follow the instructions of evil friends that they claim this world does not exist, and so forth, as explained at length.
The view that "there are no arhats in the world" is a false view that slanders the path;
it is abandoned through the vision of the path (*darśanamārga*).
This [statement] regarding the false view that slanders the path clarifies its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That which is to be abandoned by the path of seeing reveals its antidote;
that is to say, once the patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding the Truth of the Path have arisen,
all improper investigation, improper conceptualization, inverted views, and unbalanced grasping pertaining thereto are forever severed, extinguished, and vanish.
Furthermore, because this view operates within the sphere of the Path, it is abandoned at the very moment of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Just as dew on the tip of a blade of grass dries up when the sun rises, so too is this [view];
there is no further progress toward its cessation.
This false view that slanders cessation is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).
"Rightly reached" (*samyakprāpta*) refers to nirvāṇa, because it is that which is to be reached by the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
This false view that slanders cessation reveals its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That which is abandoned through the vision of cessation reveals its antidote;
that is to say, when the receptivities and knowledges regarding the Truth of Cessation have arisen,
all improper investigation, improper discrimination, perverted views, and unbalanced grasping directed toward those [defilements] are forever severed, extinguished, and vanish.

Furthermore, because this view operates regarding the place of cessation, it is abandoned at the very moment cessation is seen—just as dew on the tip of a blade of grass dries up when the sun rises. This is also like that.
Without right practice in this world or the next, one then, in this very life, knows for oneself, attains realization, and dwells in its fulfillment.
"I have exhausted birth, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence"—
to know this as it truly is constitutes the false view that slanders the path, which is abandoned through the vision of the path.
"Those who lack right practice in this world and the next" refers to those who deny the four kinds of right practice;
this constitutes a denial of the path of one in training (*śaikṣa*),
while the remainder constitutes a denial of the path of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This [passage] on the false view that slanders the Path reveals its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The statement that it is "abandoned by the vision of the Path" (*darśana-heya*) reveals its antidote (*pratipakṣa*), as explained at length previously.
Here, however, only its intrinsic nature and its antidote are stated.
The origination [of these] was not explained. What is their origination?
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
There are certain non-Buddhists who, seeing that arhats undergo old age, sickness, death,
and various sufferings just like other sentient beings, claim that there are no arhats in the world.
This is precisely to slander the dharma of the arhats as being non-existent.
Furthermore, upon hearing that in nirvāṇa all faculties are eternally extinguished, one forms the thought: "That must be suffering.
Again, upon hearing that in nirvāṇa all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are stilled and extinguished, one forms the thought: "That must be non-existence."

Furthermore, seeing that the physical appearance, diet, and conduct of the Noble Ones are identical to those of other sentient beings, they claim that those Noble Ones possess no noble path whatsoever.
Yet these non-Buddhists do not understand that the Noble Ones' contaminated body is distinct from their uncontaminated body, nor do they understand the tranquility and bliss of Nirvana.
Because it is neither suffering nor non-existent, such a differentiated false view arises.
Some say that non-Buddhists who have attained mundane meditative concentration are unable to perceive the Noble Path and Nirvana.
He then spoke these words: "There are no Arhats," and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that the non-Buddhists neither rely on direct perception nor on meditative concentration [to reach this conclusion].
However, it is solely due to following the instructions of evil friends that one says,
"There are no arhats in the world," and so forth, as explained at length. Some say:
In this context, the matter of Śrīkṛṣṇa should be explained;
that matter is precisely the origination of these views.
All those who possess such views [should be understood in this way].
"Even until such a living being has died, been cut off, destroyed, and no longer exists—
this person consisting of the four great elements," and so on,
as explained at length, up to...
This is an extreme view categorized as nihilism,
abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Within this context, it refers to the notion that from the time a living being exists until after death, they are annihilated, destroyed, and no longer exist.
They maintain that there is a self called the "life-principle" (*jīva*).
This life-principle exists continuously from birth until death;
once dead, it no longer continues, being termed "annihilated," "destroyed," and "non-existent."
Regarding this body of a person composed of the four great elements:
although that aforementioned body of a person is also constituted by other phenomena, it is spoken of as consisting only of the four great elements because they are coarse and manifest.
Regarding the statement that "at the time of death, the earth-body returns to earth, the water-body returns to water, the fire-body returns to fire, the wind-body returns to wind,
and the sense-faculties follow into space," this refers to the teaching that when sentient beings die, their internal primary elements (mahābhūta) return to the external earth and so forth.
Because the sense faculties lack the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as their support, they follow along with space,
just as birds fly through the air when a tree falls. This form of extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*),
categorized as the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Because they cling to the notion that "mine" is permanent.
Regarding the palanquin as the fifth:
this refers to a palanquin measuring four and a half cubits, carried by four men.
Because one carries the corpse away,
it is said that "carrying" constitutes the fifth [stage].
One takes that corpse and goes to discard it among the burial mounds.
The place where the body was given away or where the corpse was cremated is called "the charnel ground" (śmaśāna).
"While it is not yet cremated and can still be recognized" means that as long as the distinct features [of the body] are still visible before cremation.
"Having been burned, they have become ash" refers to those pigeon-colored bones which,
once burned, have turned into charred remains.
In this context, if one says that "burning" refers to the burning of fuel and so forth, this is correct vision (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).
If one says it is the fire itself that burns, this is false knowledge (*mithyā-jñāna*) and not vision.

If one says it is the burning of contaminated karma (*sāsrava-karma*), this is a false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) that denies the cause; it is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
If one claims that untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) is burned away, this is a false view that slanders the Path, abandoned through the vision of the Path (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*).
"Fools" praise giving, while "the wise" praise receiving;
"fools" refers to those who lack wisdom or possess corrupted discernment (*kuprajñā*).
"Wisdom" refers to those who possess knowledge and those with excellent discernment.
Those non-Buddhists say that fools praise the act of giving,
while the wise praise receiving gifts.
Yet the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, noble disciples, and all those possessed of wisdom praise the practice of giving;
he rejects this as foolishness,
which is to slander the dharma of those who have attained wisdom.
This is the false view that slanders the Path;
it is abandoned by the vision of the Path.

It is the claim of all those who argue that everything is empty and a false speech, even down to those who say that both the foolish and the wise, while alive, are annihilated and cease to exist after death.
Those who maintain that there is a future life are called proponents of existence (vādins).
They all slander [the Buddha’s teaching] as empty and false speech, saying:
"From the living state until death, whether one is a fool or a wise person, once dead, everything is annihilated and ceases to exist."
However, the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble disciples teach that there is a future life;
he rejects this as false.
This is precisely to slander the Dharma of those who speak words of truth.
This is the false view that slanders the Path;
it is abandoned by the vision of the Path.
As for this extreme view, it is subsumed under the category of nihilistic views (ucchedadṛṣṭi).
This reveals its intrinsic nature;
although other wrong views and so forth exist herein,
it specifically indicates [the view of] annihilationism and non-existence.
Regarding those included within the view of nihilism that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),
their antidotes are explained in detail as previously stated.
This merely explains their antidotes by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-pratipakṣa*), but does not explain their origins (*samutthāna*). What, then, are their origins?
The Venerable Vasumitra says:
There are certain non-Buddhists who do not recollect the past nor perceive the future,
and they reckon that for all sentient beings, this birth is the beginning and death is the end.
Furthermore, because there is no one who returns after life has ended, it is said that "even while living, there are those with life.
Once dead, they are severed and destroyed;
they do not exist, just as grass and trees have no future world.
Some say that non-Buddhists attain mundane concentration (*laukika-samādhi*),
or that there are sentient beings who, passing away from this world, are reborn in higher realms or other worlds.
Observing these beings and not knowing where they had gone, he spoke thus:
"As long as there are living beings with life," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Some say that non-Buddhists,
without relying on any other cause but solely due to evil friends and false instructions, speak as follows:
"As long as there are living beings with life," and so forth, as explained at length.
Any such view as "there is no cause and no condition that brings about the defilement of sentient beings;
rather, it is without cause and without condition that sentient beings become defiled" is a false view that denies causality (*hetu-apavāda-dṛṣṭi*),
and it is abandoned through the vision of the origin of suffering (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
This slander is due to wrong view; this reveals its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That it is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) reveals its antidote (*pratipakṣa*), as explained in detail previously. How does it arise?
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"There are certain non-Buddhists who, while directly observing the world,
see that some who dwell in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka) give rise to defilements."
There are those who dwell in cities and towns yet do not give rise to defilement;
they then form this thought: "Sentient beings undergo defilement without cause and without condition;
it is neither through a cause nor through a condition that sentient beings become defiled."
If such a thing existed, then those dwelling in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*) would not give rise to defilements, whereas those dwelling in towns and cities would all give rise to defilements;
this is contradicted by what is directly perceived.
Therefore, it is certain that there is no cause and no condition, and so forth, as explained at length.
However, sentient beings undergo defilement due to three factors:
first, by the power of causes;
second, by the power of application.
Third, by the power of the object (*viṣaya-bala*):

although those who dwell in forest hermitages (*araṇya*) lack such objects, various defilements (*saṃkleśa*) arise due to the power of the cause (*hetu-bala*) and the power of application (*prayoga-bala*).
Although those dwelling in cities possess causes and objective conditions,
because they lack the power of application (*prayoga*), afflictions do not arise.
Failing to penetrate this matter, they give rise to the view that there are no causes and no conditions, and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that because non-Buddhists have attained worldly, coarse, and shallow meditative concentration,
they perceive sentient beings as giving rise to various defilements.
Failing to perceive the distinctions among causes and conditions,
they give rise to the view that there are no causes and no conditions, and so forth,
as explained at length. Some say:
The non-Buddhists do not rely on direct perception, nor do they rely on meditative concentration;
rather, it is due to evil friends that they give rise to this view that sentient beings attain purification without cause and without condition,
and that sentient beings attain purification through neither cause nor condition.
This false view that slanders the path is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
"This false view that slanders the path" reveals its intrinsic nature;
"abandoned through the path of seeing" reveals its antidote, as explained in detail previously.
Regarding their origin,
the Venerable Vasumitra said:
"There are certain non-Buddhists who observe that those dwelling in cities and towns can attain purification."
There are those who dwell in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka) yet are not pure;
they then form this thought: "There is no cause and no condition for the purification of sentient beings;
it is neither through a cause nor through a condition that sentient beings are purified."
If it were so, then those dwelling in *āraṇya* (forest hermitages) would all be pure,
whereas those dwelling in towns and cities would all be impure;
this is clearly contradicted by what is observed.
Therefore, it is definitively established that there are no causes and no conditions, and so forth, as explained at length.
Nevertheless, sentient beings attain purification through three factors:
first, by the power of causes.
Second, by the power of application;
third, by the power of conditions.
Although one dwelling in an araṇya may have the necessary causes and conditions, they may fail to attain purity due to a deficiency in application.
Although those dwelling in cities may lack certain conditions, they attain purification through the power of causes and preparatory application;
yet, failing to penetrate this matter, they give rise to the following view:
"Without cause and without condition," and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that this is because non-Buddhists have attained mundane, coarse, and shallow meditative concentration.
One perceives sentient beings attaining purity, yet does not perceive the causes and conditions by which they attain that purity;
thus one gives rise to the view that there is no cause and no condition, and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that these non-Buddhists do not give rise to this view based on direct perception, nor do they base it on meditative concentration; rather, they do so due to evil friends.
They maintain that there is neither cause nor condition for sentient beings to lack wisdom and vision.
The view that sentient beings lack wisdom and insight despite there being neither cause nor condition is a false view that denies causality;
it is abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
This "false view that denies causality" reveals its own intrinsic nature.
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), their antidotes are explained at length as previously stated.
As for how they arise, the Venerable Vasumitra says:
There are certain non-Buddhists who, observing the world directly,
do not engage in spiritual practices for the sake of seeking the absence of knowledge and vision;
yet those sentient beings, being naturally devoid of knowledge and vision, form this thought that there is no cause and no condition, and so forth, as explained at length.
If it were existent, one would have to apply effort to seek that which lacks wisdom and vision;
yet that which lacks wisdom and vision does not arise for one who does not seek it.
Since this contradicts what is directly perceived, we know with certainty that there is no cause and no condition, and so forth, as explained at length.
However, sentient beings lack wisdom and vision due to three factors:
first, because they are attached to the ālayavijñāna;
second, because they harbor much doubt regarding what is to be done.
Third, because of a lack of humility and respect toward sentient beings.
Some say it is due to five factors.
Three are as previously explained.
Fourth, because of a lack of diligent seeking;
fifth, because of a lack of skillful means.
Not thoroughly understanding this matter, they give rise to the view that there is no cause and no condition, and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that non-Buddhists attain a mundane, coarse, and shallow meditative concentration through which they perceive sentient beings as lacking wisdom and lacking vision.
Not perceiving the distinctions among causes and conditions, they give rise to this view that there is no cause and no condition, and so forth,
as explained at length.
Some say that these non-Buddhists neither rely on direct perception nor on meditative concentration.
However, due to evil friends, one gives rise to this view that the cognition and vision of sentient beings arise without cause and without condition,
and that the cognition and vision of sentient beings exist neither through causes nor conditions.
This is a false view that slanders the path, and it is abandoned by the vision of the path (*darśanamārga*).
This [statement] "this is a false view that slanders the path" reveals its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Abandoned by the vision of the path" (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*) reveals its antidote (*pratipakṣa*), as explained in detail previously.
What is its origination (*samutthāna*)?
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"There are certain non-Buddhists who, despite directly perceiving the world and applying great effort in their pursuit of knowledge and vision, do not give rise to such knowledge and vision."
There are those who produce knowledge and vision without applying effort, and they then think:
"It is without cause and without condition," and so forth, as explained at length.
If such were the case, then knowledge and vision would arise for one who applies effort in seeking them, while they would not arise for one who does not apply effort.
Because it is contradicted by what is directly perceived, one knows that there is certainly no cause and no condition, and so forth, as explained at length.
Nevertheless, sentient beings perceive through four factors:
first, by correctly grasping the name.
Second, they do not correctly grasp the meaning;
third, they delight in excessive speculative searching;

fourth, they delight in discriminating between what is logical and what is illogical. Without properly understanding these matters, they claim that there are no causes and no conditions, and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that non-Buddhists, having attained a mundane, coarse, and shallow meditative concentration, perceive sentient beings as possessing superior knowledge and vision;
yet, failing to see the distinctions among their causes and conditions, they give rise to this view.
"Without cause and without condition," and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that non-Buddhists [assert this] neither based on direct perception nor based on meditative concentration.
However, it is due to evil friends that this view arises.
Those who hold such a view lack power and energy;
they lack power and energy, they lack manly vigor and majesty, and they lack manly vigor and majesty.
There is no self-creation, no creation by another, and no creation by both self and another.
All sentient beings, in all births and in every way, lack power, lack sovereignty, lack diligence, and lack majesty; they are subject to the transformation of fixed nature.
Regarding the experience of various sufferings and pleasures within the six superior births,
if one slanders the existence of the power of outflows (*āsrava*), vigor (*vīrya*), and so forth,
this constitutes wrong view that slanders the cause, which is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
If one slanders the untainted powers, such as diligence and so forth, this constitutes the wrong view that slanders the Path, which is abandoned through the vision of the Path (*darśana-mārga*).
In this context, "power" (*bala*) and "diligence" (*vīrya*) are identical in essence but differ in meaning.
All these refer to the specific functional capacities of phenomena.
"Power" (*bala*) means a force that is difficult to subdue;
"vigor" (*vīrya*) means the sense of setting out [toward a goal].
A "kṣatriya" (śi) signifies one who is heroic and fierce;
"majesty and power" (vibhūti) signifies the ability to subdue others.
Those [phenomena] you speak of do not possess such characteristics.
This is a general denial of the functional efficacy of all phenomena (*dharma*).
To say there is "no self-agent" is to deny the functional efficacy of the phenomena within one's own continuum;
to say there is "no other-agent" is to deny the functional efficacy of the phenomena within the continua of others.
To deny both self and other as agents is called "denying both.
This refers to the view of the naked Kāśyapīyas, as will be explained later.
"All sentient beings" refers to those classes possessing consciousness.
"All that is born" refers to sentient beings, who are termed "living beings.
"All kinds" refers to the continuity of the seeds of those very living beings.
