Furthermore, although "power," "mastery," and so forth are identical in essence, they differ in their specific meanings.
This refers to the differentiation of the functional capacities (*śakti*) of sentient beings.
"Mastery" (*vaśitā*) means the ability to employ others.
"Power" (*bala*) and so forth are explained as before.
That [opponent] asserts that sentient beings do not possess such distinctions of merit.
"Certainty" (niyata) means that it is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); "conjunction" (sāmagrī) means the coming together of conditions.
"Nature" refers to the fundamental nature;
"transformation" refers to change.
They say that for sentient beings there is this principle: when conditions naturally converge, their fundamental nature undergoes transformation.

Regarding the experience of various sufferings and pleasures within the six superior births, it is not by the power of those [gods], such as their sovereign mastery, that one experiences such pleasure and pain; this will be explained later in the section on the six superior births.
To hold otherwise is the wrong view of either denying the cause or denying the path.
This reveals their intrinsic nature.
That which is abandoned through the vision of origin or the vision of the path reveals their antidote;
the detailed explanation is as previously stated.
Regarding their arising,
the Venerable Vasumitra said: "There are certain non-Buddhists who, observing the world,
exert great effort in pursuit of wealth and status yet are unable to obtain them."
There are things that are obtained spontaneously without being sought after;
yet one might think, "I lack power and diligence," and so forth, as explained at length.
If something exists, it should be sought and then obtained; if one does not seek it, one will not obtain it.
It is known that [the self] does not exist because it contradicts what is directly perceived.

However, worldly merit and happiness necessarily arise from past determinate or indeterminate karma; as for those who exert effort yet do not obtain results, this is because they lack such prior karma.
There are those who obtain [results] without exerting effort because of a previously established determinate cause;
yet, failing to understand this matter correctly, they claim they lack power and lack diligence, and so forth, as explained at length.
The cases of [overestimation] due to meditative concentration and due to evil friends should be understood according to what was previously stated.
In the previous *Saṃgītiparyāya*, regarding the section on perversions (*viparyāsa*),
it was explained that because they exclusively negate the causes of the contaminated (*sāsrava*), they are abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

In this context, because it clearly elucidates the causes for slandering both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), all those who hold such views—whether they personally perform acts of killing, command others to kill, or incite others to cook [beings] or harm them—are severed from the truths of the origin (*samudaya*) and the path (*mārga*). These are abandoned through the vision of the origin and the vision of the path.
All such individuals who harbor these views—those who commit acts of killing, instruct others to kill, or incite others to cook, to boil, or to harm—are [thus characterized].
Killing sentient beings,
taking what is not given,
and sexual misconduct.
They speak falsehoods despite knowing the truth;
they drink various liquors;
they breach walls and untie knots to seize all that is possessed; and they guard narrow passes and block the roads.

One who harms villages, cities, and nations, taking the lives of living beings with swords and wheels and seizing the great earth—should know that all sentient beings therein are severed, cut apart, and piled up into a single mass of flesh; by this, there is no evil, nor any cause for evil.
One should know that whether one cuts, severs, beats, or strikes on the south bank of the Gaṅgā,
or practices generosity and cultivates merit on the north bank of the Gaṅgā, there is neither sin nor merit,
nor any causal condition for sin or merit.

The view that there is no merit in gathering sentient beings through the four means of attraction—generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—is a false view regarding causes, abandoned by the vision of the origin [of suffering]. In this context, "absence of evil" means the absence of an intrinsic nature of evil.
One who lacks the conditions for evil cannot experience an evil result.
It should be understood that this is likewise true for the absence of merit and demerit, as well as the absence of the conditions for merit and demerit.
Regarding those who cut, sever, or beat [trees] on the banks of the Gaṅgā, it is because there are many yakṣa shrines along the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Because among them there is the killing of sentient beings;
and because those who practice giving and cultivate merit north of the Gaṅgā do so in a place where there are many deva-shrines, practicing giving and cultivating merit therein.
The statement that "this slander arises from false view" reveals its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That it "is abandoned by the vision of the origin [of suffering]" reveals its antidote (*pratipakṣa*), as explained in detail previously.
What is its origination (*samutthāna*)?
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"There are certain non-Buddhists who observe in the world that those who commit evil deeds experience various forms of happiness."
There are those who practice virtue yet encounter much sorrow and suffering;
they then think: "If one creates [merit], teaches it, and explains it extensively... [as previously stated] ...there is ultimately no merit at all.
If there were such a thing, those who commit evil would instead have to undergo suffering."
One attains happiness by practicing virtue;
yet, because this is contradicted by what is currently perceived, they conclude that there is definitely no merit in performing or teaching [virtuous] actions, and so forth.
However, since the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma have both distant and near results, those who do not understand this give rise to such a view.
This should be understood according to what was previously stated regarding meditative concentration and evil companions.
Those who hold this view— that these seven bodies of the person (saptapuruṣapudgalāḥ) do not act nor cause action, are not transformed nor cause transformation,
cannot be harmed, are eternally abiding like a *iṣikā* reed, remain motionless and unchanging, and do not interact with one another— [hold such a view].
What are the seven?
They are earth, water, fire, wind, suffering, pleasure, and life-force.
These seven constituents of the person are uncreated and remain as stable and immovable as an *īṣāka* pillar.
Whether it be demerit, merit, both demerit and merit, suffering, pleasure, or both suffering and pleasure, these cannot be transformed,
nor can they cause mutual obstruction or interference.
Even if a person were to sever the head of another person, this would not be called "harming the arising of the world."
Whether walking or standing, even as the blades of swords rotate between the seven parts of the body, they do not take life.
In this state, there is no one who can harm and no one who is harmed;
there is no one who can strike and no one who is struck.
Non-manifestation and the sphere of non-manifestation are included within the view of eternalism among the views of extreme attachment, and are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
The seven bases of the person refer to that which is grasped as "mine."
The seven types of persons are non-doers;
that is to say, there is no agent who can act.
Regarding this body, "an agent" means that although there is no actual acting, it appears as if acting.
"Non-transformative" means that there is no transformer who can transform this body.
"Transformative" means that although there is no actual transformation, it appears as if transformed.
"Like the *iṣīkā*" means like the *iṣīkā* wood,
or like Mount *Iṣīkā*, which is firm and difficult to destroy.
"Without transformation" means that although the self is eternal and undergoes concealment and manifestation, it remains without transformation.
Regarding "not mutually touching," there is nothing that can cause mutual contact or obstruction.
As for "whether moving or stationary," "moving" refers to humans and the like, while "stationary" refers to trees and the like;
it is said that trees and such are also called *puruṣa* (persons).
Since it is reckoned that there is a life-span within those classes of beings,
even though there may be gaps between the seven bodies large enough for a blade to pass through,
they do not harm the life-force; for the life-force, which is constantly sustained by the maintenance of "mine," cannot be harmed.
"Non-manifestation" (*avijñapti*) refers to the absence of the capacity to harm or strike;
"the locus of non-manifestation" refers to the absence of an object that is harmed or struck.
That this [view] is subsumed under the eternalist extreme (*śāśvatānta-grāha-dṛṣṭi*) reveals its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of suffering, their antidotes have been explained at length as before.
As for how they arise,
the Venerable Vasumitra says:
There are certain non-Buddhists who, regarding the four great elements, as well as suffering, pleasure, and the continuity of life,
fail to properly understand that these exist through the conjunction of causes and conditions and do not abide for even a single moment.
One then conceives of a self within that [continuum], grasping at it so as to prevent its harm.
What they call "life" is the continuity of consciousness;
however, they do not perceive the continuity of body and mind.
Within the intervals of the causal process that unfolds moment by moment,
they falsely grasp at a self that maintains it as permanent;
yet when this body is abandoned and another body is received, [that self is not found].
Just as when a tree falls, birds flock to other trees, so it is said regarding these seven bases of human existence, and so forth at length.
This should be understood according to what was previously explained, both in terms of meditative concentration and through the influence of evil companions.
There are fourteen billion, sixty thousand, six hundred gateways of birth for those who hold these views;
there are five types of karma, three types of karma, two types of karma, half-karma, and sixty-two modes of conduct.
Sixty-two intermediate kalpas;
one hundred and thirty-six hells;
one hundred and twenty faculties.
There are thirty-six realms of dust,
forty-nine thousand families of nāgas,
and forty-nine thousand families of garuḍas.
Forty-nine thousand heterodox practitioners,
forty-nine thousand livelihood-seekers,
and seven treasuries of perception.
The seven non-percipient treasuries,
the seven dissociated treasuries,
and the seven asuras.

Seven piśācas, seven heavens, seven persons, seven dreams, seven hundred dreams, seven awakenings, seven hundred awakenings, seven ponds, seven hundred ponds, seven precipices, seven hundred precipices, seven decreases, seven hundred decreases, seven increases, seven hundred increases, six superior classes of beings, and the eight stages of the Great Beings.
In such a place, for eighty-four thousand great eons,
whether foolish or wise, one wanders through the cycle of rebirth until one is finally able to bring an end to suffering.
Like a ball of thread that comes to rest once the thread is exhausted, there is no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa within this [state].
One can say: "By means of my ethical discipline (*śīla*), or my diligence (*vīrya*), or my holy life (*brahmacarya*), I cause all karma that has not yet ripened to ripen;
and once it has ripened, upon contact, I immediately eject it."
By means of such measures as the *droṇa*, the limits of the suffering and pleasure of birth and death cannot be established;
it cannot be said that they increase or decrease, nor can it be said that they are thus or otherwise.

This [view] is the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) which regards what is not a cause as a cause, and is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding the fourteen billion, sixty thousand, and six hundred "gateways of birth":
just as within the True Dharma there are four gateways of birth—
namely, viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, and transformation-born— which all sentient beings collectively undergo and experience.
Their measure is fixed, neither exceeding nor falling short.
Likewise, regarding the various classes of birth-gates as reckoned by the non-Buddhist Nirgrantha Jñātiputra,
the number of times each sentient being must pass through them is fixed, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Regarding those who perform five types of karma up to half a type of karma, as in the True Dharma, they experience the four modes of birth;
furthermore, the karmas created within these modes of birth do not exceed the five types of karma and so forth.
Thus, regarding the gateways for producing such births as taught by the non-Buddhists,
and the karma created within those gateways for producing such births, it does not exceed the five types of karma and so forth.
These five types of karma are as they are described in the True Dharma.
It is said that these result in the five destinies, the five preparatory actions for the five destinies, and the locations of the five destinies.
Such are the five types of action taught by the non-Buddhists:
namely, lifting, lowering, contracting, extending, and movement as the fifth.
Alternatively, there are five [categories] regarding speech, hands, feet, and the large and small gates.
Regarding the three types of action (*karmapatha*), as in the *Saddharma* [treatise], they consist of bodily, vocal, and mental actions;
their explanation here is likewise, with the exception that speech is mentioned first.
Regarding the two types of karma: as in the True Dharma, there is the karma of volition (*cetanā*) and the karma that follows having willed (*cetayitvā*).
These are said to be black karma and white karma.
Regarding the half-karma: as in the True Dharma, the karma of projection (*ākṣepaka-karman*) is called karma.
A completed action is called a "half-action" (*ardhakarma*).
Alternatively, that which possesses both [aspects] is called an "action.
That which possesses only one [aspect] is called a "half-action" accordingly.
Thus, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) speak of two types of karma:
first, dual karma, and second, single karma.
Projecting karma (ākṣepaka-karma) is called dual karma.
A completed action is called a "single action" (*eka-karman*);
alternatively, that which possesses both [aspects] is called a "dual action" (*ubhaya-karman*).
Depending on whether it possesses only one [aspect], it is termed a "single action."
Those that occur in pairs are called full karma, while those that occur singly are called half-karma.
Furthermore, those non-Buddhists assert two types of karma:
namely, falling karma (*pātakakarma*) and near-falling karma (*upapātakakarma*).
If one harms a brahmin, or commits [sexual misconduct with] one's mother, father, teacher, friend, or woman, or steals gold,
or drinks alcohol, these are called *pārājika* offenses (offenses involving expulsion).
All other evil karmas are called *sthūlātyaya* offenses (near-expulsion offenses).
The former is called "action" (*karman*) and the latter is called "half-action.
Furthermore, it is said that vocal and bodily actions are termed "action" because they cause benefit or harm to both oneself and others;
mental action is termed "half-action" because it causes benefit or harm to oneself alone.

Furthermore, it is said that karma which brings about birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) is called "karma," while karma which brings about intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) is called "half-karma.
Moreover, it is said that karma which brings about the acquisition of a homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) prior to birth is called "karma."
Regarding karma that has already arisen and is undergoing its maturation, it is called "half-karma.
Furthermore, it is said that karma performed in its entirety is called "karma," whereas that performed only partially is called "half-karma."
Regarding the sixty-two types of conduct:
just as within the True Dharma four types of conduct are taught and called the path of purification,
so too do the non-Buddhists teach sixty-two types of conduct and call them the path of purification.
Regarding the sixty-two intermediate kalpas:
just as it is taught in the True Dharma that eighty intermediate kalpas constitute one period,
so too do the non-Buddhists teach that sixty-two intermediate kalpas constitute one period.
During this time, one cultivates the sixty-two modes of practice to bring an end to suffering.
Regarding the one hundred and thirty-six hells:
as stated in the True Dharma, each of the eight great hells has sixteen subsidiary hells.
The teachings of the non-Buddhists are likewise thus;
however, they claim that sentient beings are born pervasively within these realms before attaining liberation.
Regarding the "one hundred and twenty faculties," as taught in the True Dharma, there are twenty-two faculties.
Thus, the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) assert that there are one hundred and twenty faculties (indriya).
That is to say: the eyes, ears, and nose each have two, making six;
the tongue, body, mind, life, and the five feeling faculties (vedanendriya), together with the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā), total twenty.
The twenty faculties for each of the six destinies constitute one hundred and twenty.
Regarding the six destinies, the asuras are designated as the sixth.
It is taught that sentient beings must experience exactly this number of faculties within the six destinies, neither more nor less.
Some say that "root" (*mūla*) has the sense of "predominance" (*adhipatya*); sentient beings must first exercise sovereignty over one hundred and twenty locations before they attain liberation.

Regarding the thirty-six realms of objects (*viṣaya-dhātu*), as explained in the True Dharma (*saddharma*), there are ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) which serve as the basis for all defilements (*saṃkleśa*).
Thus, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) teach that there are thirty-six realms of dust (*dhātu*) which serve as the basis for defilement.
Regarding the "forty-nine thousand dragon families" (*nāga-kula*):
"family" (*kula*) refers to a genus or species; as in the True Dharma (*saddharma*), dragons have four lineages, namely: those born from a womb, from an egg, from moisture, and by transformation.
Thus, the non-Buddhists say there are forty-nine thousand families of nāgas;
not a single sentient being fails to undergo experience within those lineages.
As for the forty-nine thousand families of garuḍas:
Just as within the True Dharma there are four lineages of garuḍas— namely, those born from the womb, from eggs, from moisture,
and by transformation— so too the non-Buddhists speak of forty-nine thousand families of garuḍas.
Not a single sentient being among those classes has failed to undergo [this experience].
As for the forty-nine thousand heterodox practitioners (*tīrthika*),
this refers to that many types of renunciant outsiders.
He states that every single sentient being within those classes ought to go forth into homelessness;
as for the "forty-nine thousand livelihoods," this refers to the various types of occupations through which one sustains oneself by practicing crafts and skills.
They say that sentient beings should thoroughly train in all those locations.
Regarding the "seven repositories of perception," they say there are seven meditative attainments of perception (*saṃjñā-samāpatti*).
Regarding the "seven repositories of non-perception," they say there are seven meditative attainments of non-perception (*asaṃjñā-samāpatti*).
In this way, each and every sentient being should give rise to all these meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).
Regarding the "seven treasuries of dissociation" (*visaṃyoga-kośa*), these are the preparatory applications (*prayoga*) for the aforementioned meditative absorptions.
It is said that sentient beings should, through those preparatory applications, dissociate themselves from all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and cultivate them with a concentrated mind.
Regarding the "seven asuras and seven piśācas," it is said that sentient beings must pass through seven cycles of rebirth within the realms of the asuras and piśācas before they attain liberation.
Regarding "seven times and seven persons," it is said that sentient beings, after wandering back and forth seven times among the realms of gods and humans, finally attain liberation.
Regarding "seven dreams and seven hundred dreams," it is said that there are seven great dreams corresponding to the various distinctions of the places where sentient beings are born.
There are seven hundred minor dreams;
what is undergone and what is seen in each is different,
and every sentient being experiences them all.
Regarding the seven awakenings and seven hundred awakenings:
it is said that according to the distinctions in the birthplaces of sentient beings, for as many large or small dreams as there may be,
there are likewise that many large or small awakenings.
What is experienced and what is seen also differ for each;
every single sentient being undergoes these experiences.
As for the seven ponds and seven hundred ponds:
According to his teaching, there are seven great springs and pools in the world for the destruction of sins,
and seven hundred smaller ones;
every sentient being must bathe in each of them before they can attain liberation.
Regarding the "seven perils" and the "seven hundred perils":
"peril" refers to pits, valleys, mountain crags, and riverbanks.
They explain it thus as the perilous places for the extinction of offenses.
The large ones number seven,
and the small ones seven hundred.
Within each of them, every sentient being must pass through the exhaustion of body and life before attaining liberation.
Regarding "the seven decreases" and "the decrease of seven hundred":
"decrease" refers to the loss of meritorious qualities (*guṇa*).
This explains the states in which sentient beings fall away from their acquired virtues.
There are seven great ones and seven hundred small ones;
every single sentient being should, within these, fall away from their attained virtues.
Regarding the "seven increases" and the "increase of seven hundred": "increase" refers to the advancement of merit.
It is said that there are seven great instances where sentient beings advance in merit.
There are seven hundred minor [realms].
In each of these, every sentient being must pass through them in succession, withdrawing and advancing, before finally attaining liberation.
Regarding the six superior classes of beings (*ṣaḍ abhijātayaḥ*): this refers to the six superior classes of beings established by the non-Buddhist teacher Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.
These are black, blue, yellow, red, white, and extremely white.
Regarding the distinctions among classes of beings, those who are "black" and superior among such classes are those whose livelihood is defiled, namely butchers and the like.
Those who are "blue" and superior among such classes are other householders who maintain their lives [through worldly occupations].
The yellow class of superior beings refers to other renunciants who sustain their lives;
the red class of superior beings refers to the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas;
and the white class of superior beings refers to the various Nirgranthas.
The most excellent among the white class of beings refers to Nanda, Upananda, Vatsa, Maśaka, Kṛkī, Gautamīputra, and others.
They maintain that sentient beings must fully undergo all six of these [rebirths] before they can attain liberation.
The Buddha has also established six types of superior lineages (*gotra*).
First, there is the person (*pudgala*) of a black superior lineage who produces and grows black dharmas.
Second, there is the person of a black superior lineage who produces and grows white dharmas.
Third, there is the person (pudgala) of the black-superior class who grows in a state that is neither black nor white and attains the dharma of nirvāṇa.
Fourth, there is the person of the white-superior class who grows in white dharmas.
Fifth, there is the person of superior white birth who produces black dharmas.
Sixth, there is the person of superior white birth who produces neither black nor white dharmas and attains the dharma of nirvāṇa.
Regarding the "Stages of the Eight Great Beings" (*aṣṭamahāpuruṣabhūmi*):
just as within the True Dharma there are the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments which are bases for the possession of merit,
so too do the non-Buddhists speak of eight Brahma-victorious abodes, which they call the "Eight Stages of the Great Beings."

Within this, all sentient beings— whether foolish or wise— must pass through eighty-four thousand great kalpas of coming and going in transmigration before they can definitively bring an end to suffering.
According to that teaching, one transmigrates through the black superior class for fourteen thousand great kalpas before entering the blue superior class; then,
one transmigrates through the blue superior class for fourteen thousand great kalpas.
Thereafter, one enters the superior class of yellow beings;
having remained in the superior class of yellow beings for another fourteen thousand great kalpas of coming and going in saṃsāra,
one then enters the superior class of red beings.
Then, having again undergone the cycle of coming and going for fourteen thousand great kalpas within the red superior birth-class,
one subsequently enters the white superior birth-class.
Within that white superior birth-class, one again undergoes the cycle of coming and going for fourteen thousand great kalpas.
Thereafter, one enters the most pure and superior class of beings.
Having spent fourteen thousand great kalpas wandering through the cycle of coming and going within that most pure and superior class of beings,
one is finally able to bring an end to suffering.
It is like throwing a ball of thread; once the thread is exhausted, it stops.

Just as when one throws a large ball of thread from a mountain, it continues until the thread is completely spent before finally coming to rest, so too do sentient beings pass through eighty-four thousand great kalpas, wandering and transmigrating through various places of birth, only then able to bring an end to suffering.

When measured by such a *hu* (a dry measure), the limits of the suffering and pleasure of birth and death cannot be established as having increase or decrease, nor can they be described as either so or not so;
it is like measuring rice, wheat, and the like with a *hu*-sized container.
Having known the number, one neither increases nor decreases it, nor does one give rise to doubt.
Thus, it is said that those sentient beings wander and transmigrate through the aforementioned locations for eighty-four thousand great kalpas.
Thereafter, one attains liberation neither by excess nor by deficiency, and one should not harbor doubt regarding this.
Some say that one must transmigrate through a number of births twice that which has been described before finally attaining liberation.
Because that [view] speaks of coming and going, it is a case of regarding what is not a cause as a cause.
The "clinging to rules and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa) reveals its intrinsic nature;
its abandonment through the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya) reveals its antidote, as explained in detail previously.
How do they arise?
It is said that there are non-Buddhists who do so either due to improper reflection or due to attaining mundane meditative concentration.
Or, one may give rise to this view due to associating with evil friends, as should be understood from what was stated previously.
For all those persons and individuals who hold such a view, whatever they experience—
There is nothing that does not have past karma as its cause.
This [view] is the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which falsely regards what is not a cause as a cause.
All that is appropriated (*upādāna*) is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), namely, all present sensations of pleasure and pain.
"There is nothing that does not have past action as its cause" means that all these have past karma as their cause.
Question: In this True Dharma, it is also taught that the suffering and pleasure one experiences have past karma as their cause; is this not a wrong view?
Those non-Buddhists also say this:
"For what reason is it called a wrong view?
The answer is: In this True Dharma, it is taught that the existence currently experienced has past karma as its cause.
Regarding those who maintain that there is a present result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*),
they assert that everything has as its cause what was performed in the past;
because they do not claim that a present result of human effort exists [independently], this is not called a wrong view.
Question: Since they deny the existence of present causes and effects, this should be called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*);
why then is it called the grasping of rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?
Answer: We do not say that their denial of present causes and effects is what constitutes the grasping of rules and observances.

It is simply stated that those views which conceive of phenomena produced by other causes as having other factors as their cause are subsumed under the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
This [definition]—conceiving what is not a cause to be a cause—is intended to reveal its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding those [afflictions] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), their antidotes have been explained at length as before. How do they arise?
It is said that those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) directly perceive in the world that there are cases where effort is exerted yet no fruit is obtained.
There are things that are obtained spontaneously without being sought after;
one might then think, "One should know that all these have past actions as their cause, rather than the power of present effort.
However, such a person does not understand the categories of wholesome and unwholesome karma, nor whether they are determinate or indeterminate.
This attachment arises due to the differentiation of temporal divisions.
Some say that non-Buddhists who have attained mundane meditative concentration can recollect and know the various karmas they previously performed.
They then claim that everything is caused by past actions (*pūrvakṛta*).
Others say that it is due to evil friends that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) propound these views extensively, as described before.

Section Eight: The Aggregate of Views; Sub-section Five: The Chapter on Views, Part Two. Regarding those who hold this view: "All persons and *pudgalas*..."
All that is experienced has the transformation of mastery as its cause.

This [view] which takes what is not a cause to be a cause is the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
The phrase "clinging to rules and observances which takes what is not a cause to be a cause" reveals its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of suffering, their antidotes have been explained at length as previously stated.
How do they arise? It is said that there are non-Buddhists who, either due to improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) or other causes, [give rise to them].
This view arises either through the attainment of meditative concentration or due to evil companions; it should be understood as previously explained.
However, the arising of all phenomena does not occur gradually by means of a creator god (*īśvara*).
That is to say, if all things in the world were produced through the transformations of Īśvara as their cause, then they should all arise simultaneously;
for that cause would possess no power to obstruct them and prevent their arising.
If it is argued that Īśvara can only produce [effects] by depending on further causes, then he is not truly independent (anīśvara), because he is like other causes.
If it is argued that all phenomena arise from the will of Īśvara and therefore do not arise simultaneously; [we reply: ...

If Īśvara possesses mastery over desire and pleasure, why do they not arise instantaneously? Since he possesses constant mastery over their arising and nothing can obstruct it, they ought to appear at once.
If you claim that Īśvara must await other causes before producing desire and pleasure, then he is no longer sovereign.
Furthermore, this would lead to an infinite regress, because that cause would itself depend on another cause for its arising.
Moreover, if the Lord were the creator of all phenomena, then since his causes would not differ, the phenomena produced should likewise be without distinction.
If it is claimed that the Lord produces a single primary phenomenon, and subsequently, from that phenomenon, many more are produced in turn, how can that single phenomenon produce many?
For it is just like the Lord himself, whose essence is one.
Furthermore, the phenomena produced [by Ishvara] should also be eternal, because their effects resemble their cause.
Moreover, the essence of Ishvara should be incapable of producing [anything], because that essence is eternal, like space.
The view that all experiences undergone by every man and person (pudgala) are entirely without cause and without condition is a false view that denies causality;
it is abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
This slander is due to false view; this reveals its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That it is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) reveals its antidote (*pratipakṣa*), as explained in detail previously. How does it arise?
It refers to certain non-Buddhists who observe that the causal characteristics of the world are not invariably similar;
when their efforts to achieve something do not succeed, they consequently repudiate what they have experienced, claiming it is without cause and without condition.
However, that which is experienced does not arise without causes and conditions.
This is because we observe that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, and because not all phenomena arise simultaneously.
If there were no causes and conditions, everything would arise all at once, and all phenomena would be without distinction.
If there were no causes and conditions, by what distinction could the various experiences not be without causes and conditions? [Who would hold] such views as:
"suffering and pleasure are created by oneself," "suffering and pleasure are created by another," or "suffering and pleasure are created by both oneself and another"?
This is the view of grasping at precepts and observances as causes when they are not causes, which is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
It is the view held by those who think that the pleasure and pain experienced here are neither self-created nor created by another, but arise without cause.
This denial [of causes] is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), as it is a false view.
This adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) which regards what is not a cause as a cause,
along with the false view that denies causes, reveals their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Those abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin are explained in detail as previously described regarding their respective antidotes.
What is their origination?
It is said that the causal conditions involving the naked ascetic Kāśyapa constitute the origination of these views.
That naked Kāśyapa was formerly a merchant leader during his time as a householder.
Having frequently entered the ocean to gather treasures, on his very first entry he encountered various maritime perils; having emerged with great hardship, he then had this thought:
"This hardship was caused by my own actions, for when I first entered the sea, I did not bathe.
On my second entry, I bathed myself.
Having entered the sea and encountered the same calamities as before, I returned with great difficulty and thought to myself:"
"This misfortune was caused by another; it occurred because he did not offer sacrifices to the gods when setting out upon the sea.
On his third voyage, he bathed himself and also offered sacrifices to the gods, yet once he reached the middle of the sea, he encountered the same disaster as before."
Having narrowly escaped his predicament, he thought to himself:
"Such hardships were brought about by my own actions and the actions of others;
they resulted from my lack of reverence when I bathed and made offerings to the gods upon entering the sea."
At the very end, he performed an extremely solemn ablution and worship of the deities before entering the sea.
Having entered, he encountered perils just as before; barely managing to return, he then thought to himself:
This suffering that is encountered does not arise from oneself or others;
it occurs without cause.
Because of this, he perceives the faults inherent in the attachments of household life.
He immediately went forth into the religious life among the Nirgrantha outsiders.
Later, in Rājagṛha, he saw the Buddha and asked, "By whom is suffering created?
At that time, the World-Honored One subdued him by means of the method of the four types of categorical discourse (*caturvidha-vyākaraṇa*).
The detailed explanation is as given in the *Nirgrantha-Kāśyapa Sūtra*.
Therefore, those causes and conditions are the origin (*samutthāna*) of this view.
All instances of the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) previously mentioned are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Because it arises based on the perversion of regarding the self as permanent and operates with respect to the fruit,
although it is not a cause, it is conceived of as a cause and is thus abandoned through the vision of suffering.
That is to say, the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) consists of two general categories.
First, regarding what is not a cause, one conceives it as a cause;
second, regarding what is not the path, one conceives it as the path.
Furthermore, there are two categories within the conception of what is not a cause as being a cause.
First, it arises from the delusion that clings to a self and eternal dharmas;
second, it arises from the delusion regarding past actions, ascetic practices, and so forth.
The former is based on the inversion of the self and the eternal, as it also operates with respect to the fruit.
Following these two inverted views, which are abandoned through the vision of suffering, [the other views] subsequently operate only with respect to the fruit,
because the characteristics of the fruit are coarse and manifest, making them easy to perceive; furthermore,
the estimation of causes as causes is not entirely erroneous.
Since it is deluded regarding the characteristics of the fruit, it is also abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding the misapprehension of what is not the path as the path (*amārga-mārga-saṃjñā*), there are also two types:
first, the attachment to tainted precepts and so forth as being the path.
Because this delusion arises from the coarse and manifest characteristics of the fruit, it can be permanently severed upon seeing the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Second, there is the grasping at and slandering of wrong views regarding the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) as being the path;
because this directly opposes the path by failing to distinguish between the characteristics of cause and effect, it can only be permanently severed upon seeing the Truth of the Path.
When one slanders the time of the accumulation and cessation [of suffering], one negates the characteristics of the phenomena that are to be abandoned and those that are to be realized.
If one then clings to [the path] as being the path, it becomes useless;
for the path is established precisely by depending upon the phenomena that are to be abandoned and those that are to be realized.
Furthermore, regarding that which they negate as being distinct from the path, there can never be a case where one clings to it as the path immediately after [realizing its difference].
If at a later time one were to cling to it as the path, one would necessarily give rise to the clinging to it as the path at the very point where the fruit is attained.

Because this view is abandoned at the time of seeing the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not abandoned by the seeing of the Truths of Origination (*samudaya*) or Cessation (*nirodha*).

As for the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), since that which is grasped has no counter-correlative and is merely clung to as supreme, all false views subsequently manifest before it; therefore, it pervades all four categories [of abandonments].

Among those [wrong views] mentioned here, the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) consists solely in regarding what is not a cause as a cause; therefore, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
There are those who hold this view: "The self and the world are eternal, stable, enduring, unchanging phenomena, remaining exactly as they are."
This view of extremes, categorized as the view of eternalism, is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
The phrase "this view of extremes, categorized as the view of eternalism" reveals its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
while "abandoned through the vision of suffering" reveals its antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
The detailed explanation is as before.
How do they arise?
It refers to certain non-Buddhists who, due to improper reflection, [give rise to such views].
This view may arise either through the attainment of meditative concentration or due to evil companions;
this should be understood as previously explained.
However, the self and the world that they grasp are both not eternal.
Because a real self and what belongs to a self cannot be found;
because it is directly perceived that all things in the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world undergo transformation;
and because they arise from causes and conditions.
Since all that is born must eventually undergo destruction,
one should not cling to the notions that the self and the world are eternal, stable, or otherwise permanent.
The statement "all" reveals the meaning of permanence; because those who hold this view [assert] that "I exist" and "there is a self" due to the truth of their abiding,
this is an extreme view (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) subsumed under the view of permanence (śāśvatadṛṣṭi).
"Because it is the truth to be abandoned by seeing suffering" means because it is the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*).
"Because it abides" means...
This refers to the fact that it is the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
To say "I have a self" means that the self exists eternally;
this view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), categorized as the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), reveals its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
That which is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering reveals its antidote,
as explained in detail previously.
What is their origination?
This refers to certain non-Buddhists who, due to improper reflection and so forth—
as explained at length—
hold the view that "because of this [self], because of its persistence, there is a self or there is no self."
This view of extremes is subsumed under the view of nihilism; it is abandoned through the vision of suffering and is explained as abiding [in its object] as previously described.
Regarding "I shall not exist," this refers to the thought that "I will cease to exist."
Question: Within this True Dharma, it is also taught that there is no-self (*anātman*), yet it is not considered a wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also teach no-self; for what reason, then, is theirs called a wrong view?
Answer: In this True Dharma, regarding the collection of practices on emptiness and no-self—
Seeing emptiness and non-self, one speaks of non-self; therefore, this is not a wrong view.
Those non-Buddhists falsely claim there is a self within the collection of formations that are empty of self.
Because we merely state that such a self will not exist in the future, [our position] is not a wrong view.
That this view of extremes is subsumed under the view of nihilism reveals its intrinsic nature;
that it is abandoned through the vision of suffering reveals its antidote.
The detailed explanation is as previously stated.
What is their origination?
It refers to non-Buddhists who, due to improper reflection,
and so forth, as explained at length.

All those who hold the view that "I perceive the self; my eye and form are the self" possess the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
The phrase "I perceive the self" refers to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who cling to a self as being pervasive throughout both internal and external phenomena.
When seeing forms with the eye, one thinks, "I am observing," because both the eye-faculty and the forms are considered to be the self.
Those who hold this view maintain that the self observes the non-self eye, which is itself the self, while the forms serve as its instruments.
This view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
When I observe that there is no self, I mean that certain non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*),
because the eye is unique [to each individual] and is an internal phenomenon (*ādhyātmikadharma*), cling to it as being the self.
Form is the opposite of this, being merely my equipment;
thus, when the eye sees form, one thinks, "I am observing what is non-self," or holds the view that "I am observing what is non-self," or "form is I," or "the eye is mine as my equipment."
This view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Regarding those who perceive a self where there is no self:
it refers to certain non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who observe that the great earth and the various mountains in the world remain unchanged over long periods of time.
That is to say, when something accords with the principle of "self," one clings to it as being the self.
Since the eye is the opposite of this—being merely an instrument—when the eye sees forms, one regards it as a "non-self" while observing the self.
Question: Why is it not said that one contemplates non-self by means of non-self?
Answer: Because all phenomena are in reality without self.
If one were to say that one contemplates non-self by means of non-self, that would constitute right view; therefore, this is not stated.

Question: If there are non-Buddhists who cling to the view that the ear, sound, and so forth are the self and nothing else, yet when the eye sees forms they say, "I observe non-self, I observe non-self"—is this not correct view?

The answer is: although the attachment to the ear, sound, and so forth as being the self is a wrong view, if one speaks of non-self and contemplates non-self, that is right view; therefore, it is not mentioned here.
In this context, "all those with the view of a self-existent body" (satkāyadṛṣṭi) indicates its intrinsic nature.
Those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering reveal their respective antidotes;
as explained extensively before,
the distinctions in their origination should also be understood as previously described.

Those who hold such views as: "This is my self, this is a sentient being, a living soul, a creature, a nourisher, a person (*pudgala*), a mind-born one (*manuja*), a youth (*māṇava*), an agent, an instigator, a producer, a procreator, an originator, a progenitor, a speaker, a cognizer, or an experiencer."
It is not that they have not existed before,
nor that they will not exist in the future;
in various places, they perform wholesome and unwholesome deeds.
In various places, one experiences the ripening of the fruit;
abandoning these aggregates, one continues into other aggregates.
This form of extreme view, which is the view of eternalism, is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
That this extreme view is subsumed under the view of eternalism reveals its intrinsic nature;
that it is abandoned through the vision of suffering reveals its antidote.
The detailed explanation is as previously stated.
The distinctions regarding their origination (*samutthāna*) should also be understood as previously explained.
Question: What is the difference between the doctrine of eternalism (*śāśvatavāda*) mentioned at the outset and that which is discussed here? Some say:
"Initial" refers to that which relies on meditative concentration (samādhi), while this [latter] relies on discursive investigation (vitarka).
Some say that "initial" refers to the teacher and the latter to the disciple.
Some say that the former is the *ācāra* (proper conduct) and the latter is the *upavāsa* (fasting observance). Others say:
The former refers to those who are venerable, while the latter refers to those who are practitioners.
Some say that the former refers to both those who have realized [the truth] and those who teach it.
Subsequently, they are those who realize [the truth] rather than those who teach it. Some say:
the former hold that the self exists eternally from the past limit to the present limit, while the latter hold that the self exists eternally from the present limit to the future limit.
This is called the distinction between the theories of eternalism regarding the beginning and the end.
Question: How are these six views established?
Is it by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or by way of their basis (*āśraya*) and object (*ālambana*)?
If that were the case, what fault would there be?
If they were established by way of their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva), there would have to be only two:
namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extreme adherence (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
If categorized by way of their bases (*āśraya*) and objects (*ālambana*), there would be eighteen—
namely, three for each from the eye and forms up to the mind and mental phenomena—
or they would amount to thirty-six.
That is to say, there are six based on the eye and visible forms, and so on up to six based on the mind and mental objects.
Answer: In this context, the sixfold division is established by way of the basis (*āśraya*) and the object (*ālambana*).
Question: Has it not already been stated that there should be eighteen or thirty-six?
Answer: It is not so.
Why is this? Because herein [the analysis] is based generally upon the perceiver (grāhaka), the perceived (grāhya), and the sense-faculties (indriya).
The meaning of the faculties (*indriya*) is established by way of their objects (*viṣaya*), the distinctions among those objects, and their modes of activity (*ākāra*).
If one were to rely on the distinctions between moments (*kṣaṇa*) within the continuum (*saṃtati*), they would be infinite;
however, for now, only this much has been briefly explained.
Those who hold the view that experiencing the five excellent sensual pleasures constitutes attaining the supreme *nirvāṇa* in the present life—
this adherence to inferior phenomena as superior is a form of *parāmarśadṛṣṭi* (clinging view) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Those who hold this view— that by being secluded from sensual desires and unwholesome states,

with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, they enter and dwell in the first dhyāna in its full perfection— claim to have attained the first *nirvāṇa in the present life*.
With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, his mind becomes internally serene and unified, free from applied and sustained thought, and born of concentration,
he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is characterized by joy and bliss; this is called attaining the first nirvāṇa in the present life.
Detached from joy, dwelling in equanimity, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, one experiences happiness with the body;
as the Noble Ones declare, "one who dwells happily, possessing equanimity and mindfulness," he enters and abides in the third dhyāna.
This is called attaining the first nirvāṇa in the present life.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, one enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness;
this is called attaining the first nirvāṇa in the present life.
This grasping at inferior dharmas as superior is the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Those who experience the five excellent sensual desires are humans and the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Some say that it is only the devas of the desire realm [who attain this], because their five sensory pleasures are extremely superior and sublime.
"Nirvāṇa in the present life" refers to the nirvāṇa attained within one's current physical existence.
Question: Why does this constitute the clinging to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa)?

Answer: Because the five objects of sensual pleasure are tainted, defiled, poisonous, and turbid—being base and inferior phenomena—and yet one clings to them as being equivalent to the bliss of renunciation or the bliss of nirvāṇa; therefore, it constitutes the clinging to views.
Question: Entering and abiding fully in the four dhyānas is a supreme merit.
Why, then, is taking this as "nirvāṇa in the present life" also called *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views)?
Answer: Worldly dhyāna is stained, defiled, poisonous, and turbid; it is a base and inferior phenomenon.
Because they grasp at that [state] as being identical to the bliss of freedom from defilement or the bliss of nirvāṇa, it constitutes the view of clinging to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
Question: Are there not also non-Buddhists who grasp at the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) as being nirvāṇa?
Why is this not mentioned here?
The answer is: those non-Buddhists mostly cling to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) as nirvāṇa, while only a few cling to the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
Since this teaching is based on what is prevalent among them, there is no fault.
Furthermore, they hold that the formless realms constitute ultimate nirvāṇa;
however, since this [text] speaks of nirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇa*), it does not refer to them.
Moreover, the four fundamental dhyānas are subsumed under the path of bliss.
The various non-Buddhists reckon these as nirvana in the present life;
however, because the four formless attainments are subsumed under the path of suffering,
they do not cling to them as nirvana in the present life.
Furthermore, because the various non-Buddhists do not understand the subtlety of the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*),
and because they harbor deep fear of what they perceive as annihilation, [the Buddha] did not speak of them as being *nirvāṇa* in the present life.
For this reason, the formless [realms] are not mentioned.
This grasping at inferior dharmas as superior is the view of holding to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa);
this explains its essential nature.
That which is abandoned through the vision of suffering reveals its antidote,
as explained in detail previously.
What is their origination?
This refers to certain non-Buddhists who, upon hearing it said that nirvāṇa is the supreme and wondrous bliss,
claim that if one attains the pleasures of the five stages— the desire realm and the form realm—
one has already attained *dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa in the present life); thus they give rise to this view.
Some say that non-Buddhists who have attained mundane meditative concentration see sentient beings in the five stages experiencing various forms of happiness,
and because they believe they have thereby attained *nirvāṇa* in the present life, they give rise to this view.
Some say that non-Buddhists give rise to this view because they associate with evil friends.
Question: For what reason is this adherence to views abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*)?
Answer: This view arises based on the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because it clings to the existence of a self-substance that experiences the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, it arises in relation to the fruit, because it clings to contaminated fruits as being nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, because this delusion regarding the truth of suffering takes what is actually suffering as being pleasure, there are nine types of pride, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of analyzing the meaning of the sūtras.
This refers to the fact that although the sūtras speak of the nine types of pride (*māna*), they do not provide a detailed analysis thereof;
since we now wish to analyze them, this treatise is composed.
Question: Within this section on "Views" (*dṛṣṭi-nirdeśa*), one should only analyze the various views.
Why are the various types of pride (*māna*) analyzed?
Answer: It has already been stated previously that all phenomena (*dharma*) are explained within each aggregate (*skandha*).
Therefore, there is no fault in explaining many phenomena within each individual section (*śikṣāpada* or *nāśika*).
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"In this *naya* (chapter), various wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are correctly analyzed;
likewise, among the afflictions that resemble wrong views, those such as the various types of pride (*māna*) are analyzed, for there are no [afflictions] resembling wrong views other than these."
Therefore, within this context, pride is also analyzed.
The Venerable One said:
"The various types of pride depend upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)."
This is nurtured by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and manifests subsequent to that view;
for one who has already seen the truths, it does not arise again.
For this reason, within this context, both the view of correct discrimination (*samyag-vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*) and the pride of discrimination (*vikalpa-māna*) are [included].
The Venerable Buddhadeva stated:
"Because all types of views and pride alike cause sentient beings to find it difficult to enter the Buddha-dharma, they are all taught."
That is to say, if sentient beings were free from wrong views and all forms of pride,
they would be able to take refuge in the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, practice the holy life, transcend the suffering of birth and death, and attain the bliss of nirvana.
Because of the presence of views and pride, one does not take refuge in the Tathāgata’s True Dharma and thus loses its supreme benefit.
The Venerable Ghosaka stated:
"The categories of wrong views and pride both obstruct sentient beings from approaching virtuous persons, hearing the True Dharma, and engaging in correct mental attention."
Because the fault of practicing contrary to the Dharma is particularly grave, both are mentioned together.
As for "I am superior," when one who is actually equal considers oneself superior,
this is the pride of superiority (abhimāna) arising based on views.
This is based on the pride arising from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
for considering oneself superior to those who are equal is subsumed under the category of "excessive pride" (*atimāna*).
As for "those who consider themselves equal," they consider themselves equal to those who are their equals.
"Arising from views" refers to the pride that arises based on the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Regarding "equal," one considers oneself equal [to others] and thus exalts oneself; this is subsumed under pride.
Regarding "inferior," one considers oneself inferior to those who are superior.
This statement that "inferiority-pride (ūnamāna) arises based on views" means that inferiority-pride arises based on the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi);
for it is subsumed under inferiority-pride when one considers oneself slightly inferior in relation to those who are largely superior.
"There is one who surpasses me" means that he considers another to be superior to himself;
this is to claim inferiority for oneself regarding that which is superior.
The rest is as previously explained.
Regarding those who say "there is a self equal [to others]," they mean that there exists another who is equal to oneself.
That is to say, regarding those who are equal, they consider themselves equal to others as previously described.

Regarding those who possess an inferior self, they consider others to be inferior to themselves; this is equivalent to considering oneself superior to others when one is actually equal, as previously described. Regarding those who possess no superior self...
Regarding "he thinks there is no one superior to himself," this refers to those who are equal; regarding "he considers himself equal to others," it is as previously explained.
Regarding "he thinks there is no one equal to himself," this refers to those who are equal; regarding "he considers himself superior [to them]," this refers to those who are equal.
The rest is as previously explained.
Regarding "the absence of an inferior self," this means that the absence of another who is inferior to oneself is itself the state of regarding oneself as inferior to one who is superior.
The rest is as previously explained.
These nine types of pride are subsumed under three of the seven types of pride, namely:
pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), and inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*).
It is explained in this manner according to this treatise (*Mūlaśāstra*).
According to the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, three types of conceit are subsumed within the category of "conceit of superiority" (*mānottaramāna*):
if one regards oneself as superior when one is actually inferior, that is conceit.
If one considers oneself superior to those who are equal, this is the pride of overestimation (*atimāna*).
If one considers oneself superior to those who are actually superior, this is the pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*).
The remaining eight types of pride should be explained accordingly according to their logical application.
Although these nine are all subject to abandonment through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation,
they are not mentioned here; some say this is because they are incidental discussions.
Some say: Because that [view] is not similar to a [correct] view,

those who hold such a view as "the wind does not blow, rivers do not flow, fire does not burn, milk does not curdle, the womb is not impregnated, and the sun and moon neither rise nor set" [are not to be considered holders of right view].
The nature of affliction and purification abides without increase or decrease.
This view of extremes, categorized as the view of permanence, is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
The statement that this view of extremes is categorized as the view of permanence reveals its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), their antidotes have been explained in detail as previously stated.
As for how they arise,
the Venerable Vasumitra says:
There are certain non-Buddhists who, due to improper reflection, cling to the existence of a real self that is subtle, permanent, and omnipresent.
Amidst all phenomena, it lies latent and exerts activity; when they perceive winds, rivers, and so forth blowing or flowing, they claim, "This is created by me."
It is not that they can do so in such a manner as when one sees a tree move and knows it is caused by the wind,
or when a mechanical device moves and knows it is the work of a person.
The Venerable One said:
There are certain non-Buddhists who, due to unwholesome reflection,
cling to the notion of a real self that is subtle, permanent, possesses superior activity,
and undergoes transformation when they see things such as wind and rivers blowing and flowing.
That is to say, I cause them to manifest such signs:
just as when a tree or similar object moves, its shadow is seen to move;
when the master of the transformation speaks, the transformed body also speaks.
Some say that non-Buddhists who have attained mundane meditative concentration perceive the continuous and uninterrupted flow of sentient beings through the various realms of existence;
they also perceive things such as whirlwinds and rivers as being indeterminate in their presence or absence according to place and time.
It is then asserted that there exists a self (ātman) which is subtle, permanent, and possesses superior agency,
causing various transformations— such as those of wind and rivers— to either exist or not exist. Some say:
The non-Buddhists, having associated with evil friends and followed the instructions of those evil friends,
gave rise to this view:
that sentient beings grasp at a self as the agent.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Herein, the meaning of the verses in various sūtras that censure wrong views is briefly explained.
Regarding those who cling to the notion of a "self" as the agent and so forth:
To cling to the idea that within one's own body there exists an ultimate self that can create, produce, and transform various things,
and to cling to the idea that another can create them, is to cling to the notion that within the external body there exists an ultimate self.
It is capable of acting, producing, and transforming various things.
That which acts produces internal, eternally existing dharmas;
that which produces generates external, eternally existing dharmas.
The transformer transforms internal and external phenomena that are not permanently existent.
Furthermore, the agent produces the various phenomena of its own body,
while the producer generates the various phenomena of other bodies.
When the transformer transforms them into insentient phenomena,
such that each is considered individual rather than universal,
this reveals that the various non-Buddhists hold distinct, individual attachments to what is not universal.
Regarding the phrase "the same arrow" (*tulya-śalya*), it means that wrong views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) are able to inflict injury;
this indicates that the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of these wrong views is so fierce and sharp that they cause harm from afar,
just like a poisoned arrow.
Those non-Buddhists are blinded by ignorance and are unable to observe and know faults as they truly are;
one should regard this as an arrow.
...and so on, as explained at length.
In this context, he exhorts them that they should regard wrong views as true poisonous arrows,
for they serve as the precursors to old age, sickness, and death.
Just as worldly poisoned arrows give rise to manifold sufferings,
so too do wrong views give rise to various afflictions such as old age and sickness for sentient beings possessed of pride;
this is explained at length.
This passage demonstrates that those possessed of the seven types of pride, being bound and attached by pride,
are unable to transcend the boundless cycle of birth and death due to their mutual opposition regarding the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
The seven types of pride are as explained above.
"Attachment" refers to slight attachment;
"excessive attachment" refers to extensive attachment.
"Universal attachment" (*pari-graha*) means pervasive attachment;
the same applies to "bondage" (*bandhana*) and so forth.
Question: What is the difference between attachment and bondage?
The answer is that the names themselves are the distinctions.
Furthermore, there is also a difference in meaning:
"attachment" (*saṅga*) means firm attachment, in the sense of being difficult to wash away.
"Binding" (bandhana) means being entangled; it signifies the state of being difficult to liberate.
Furthermore, "attachment" (sakti) refers to the binding of association (samprayoga-bandhana), while "binding" refers to the binding of the object (ālambana-bandhana).
This means that because the seven types of pride possess both forms of bondage,
they are able to cause attachment to and bind those sentient beings.
Furthermore, "attachment" refers to attaching to their minds, while "bondage" refers to binding their bodies.
This is called the distinction between the two meanings of "bondage" (*bandhana*) and "attachment" (*abhiniveśa*).
Regarding those of the views of eternalism and nihilism who oppose one another:
it is like householders who, due to the bondage of craving, oppose one another over what they have appropriated.
Because those who have gone forth are bound by and attached to pride, they contradict one another regarding the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
That which flows on unceasingly through various destinies and various births throughout the beginningless cycle of birth and death is the meaning of *saṃsāra*.
In this way, saṃsāra has no prior limit because it is unknowable;
yet it has a subsequent limit because it exists due to preceding causes and takes parinirvāṇa as its final boundary.
Furthermore, because the duration of birth and death is so vast and long that one does not know the time when liberation will be attained, it is called "boundless" (ananta).
It is said that both what has been attained and what is yet to be attained are defiled,
and so forth, as explained at length.
This shows that because non-Buddhists are defiled by the dust of greed, hatred, and delusion regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense bases they have already acquired or will acquire,
they do not see, as they truly are, the faults of the two extremes of the practices of suffering and pleasure.
Because they do not see [the goal], they either sink too deeply or rush too far.
"Sinking" refers to being overly lax and unable to advance;
"rushing" refers to being overly hurried and unable to reach the destination.
The remaining meanings within the verse are explained in detail as in the treatise.
As stated in the Sūtra, various śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas,
and others each give rise to various disputes based on their respective resolute convictions (*adhimukti*).
All [of these views] revolve around five points. What are the five?
First, they cling to the notion that after death there is perception.
Only this is true and real, while all else is foolish and false.
Second, they cling to the view that after death there is no perception.
Third, they cling to the view that after death there is neither perception nor non-perception.
Fourth, they hold that the self is annihilated after death.
Fifth, they claim there is nirvana in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇa*).
Those five are identical to those three, and those three are identical to those five.
Those five views are subsumed within three:
namely, the theories of having perception, having no perception, and neither having perception nor being without perception correspond to this view of eternalism;
the theory of annihilation corresponds to this view of nihilism.
The doctrine of parinirvāṇa in the present life is precisely this adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Regarding "the third consists of those five":
this means that the view of eternalism (*śāśvatavāda*) is identical to those [five] theories of existence with perception (*saṃjñivāda*) and non-existence with perception (*asaṃjñivāda*).
The doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is this view of annihilationism;
this adherence to views is that doctrine of nirvana in the present life.
Furthermore, the Brahmajāla Sūtra states that all sixty-two types of evil views have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their root.
As for these sixty-two types of views:
That is to say, there are eighteen speculative views regarding the past and forty-four speculative views regarding the future.
As for the eighteen speculative views regarding the past:
That is to say: the four theories of universal eternalism,
the four theories of partial eternalism,
and the two theories of causeless origination.
The four theories of finitude and so forth;
the four evasive doctrines of the immortals;
and the forty-four views concerning the discrimination of the posterior limit.
That is to say: sixteen theorists who maintain the existence of perception,
eight theorists who maintain the non-existence of perception,
and eight theorists who maintain that perception is neither existent nor non-existent.
The seven theories of annihilationism and the five theories of nirvana in this very life: herein,
the speculative views arising in dependence upon the past are called "speculative views regarding the prior limit" (*pūrvānta-vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*).
The conceptual view arising in dependence on the future is called the "conceptual view of the posterior limit.
If a conceptual view arises in dependence on the present, it is indeterminate;
it may be termed either the "conceptual view of the anterior limit" or the "conceptual view of the posterior limit."
Because the present age is prior to the future and posterior to the past;
or because the future is the cause and the past is the effect.
Among the views concerning the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), there are four types of eternalist theories (*sarvatraga-śāśvata-vāda*).
First, by being able to recollect one eon of destruction and formation,
or two, three, or even up to eighty,
they then maintain that both the self and the world are eternal.
Question: For what reason do they hold this position?
Answer: Because they postulate either transformation (*pariṇāma*) or manifestation and concealment (*tirobhāva-āvirbhāva*).
As for those who maintain the theory of transformation:
One forms such attachments as that milk transforms into curd,
a seed transforms into a sprout,
and firewood transforms into ash.
All such categories as these,
which arise in continuity with that [preceding state], are all transformations of it;
for it is not the case that this dharma arises because that dharma has ceased.
The proponents of the theory of concealment and manifestation maintain this adherence: that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is eternally abiding.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is either hidden or manifest.

There, he sees that the previously existing earth, continents, Mount Sumeru, other mountains, great oceans, trees, and so forth—possessing such shapes, colors, dimensions, and proportions—have all been destroyed.
Later, at this very place, there again comes to be the formation of the great earth and so forth, with such shapes, appearances, and dimensions;
then one forms this thought:
"That which was previously invisible during the interval has not perished by way of its intrinsic nature."
However, during the kalpa of destruction, that nature remains latent and hidden; when the kalpa of formation arrives, that nature manifests once again.

Furthermore, because the seven constituent elements of a person (saptapuruṣapudgala) are eternally immovable, do not touch one another, and cannot have their life-force harmed, they form this thought: [that these are permanent].
Both "I" and that which is remembered are eternal;
by this, one perceives that both the self and the world are eternally abiding.
Second, because one is able to remember events from one, two, three, or even up to hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
They thus maintain that both the self and the world are eternal,
based on their reckoning of transformation or of concealment and manifestation.
If they were able to remember the destruction and formation of the external vessel-world, [they would realize this is not so].
Because one perceives that this place previously possessed such shapes, colors, dimensions, great earths, and continents—
as described before up until "life cannot be harmed"—
if one is unable to recollect the destruction and formation of the external vessel-world, then the principle that the world is eternal need not even be mentioned.
Thus he forms this thought:
"Both I and that which I recollect are both eternal.
From this, he perceives that both the self and the world are eternally abiding.
Question: What is the difference between this and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
Answer: Although previously one recalled many [lives], one had not yet attained mastery over the uninterrupted succession of those births that could be recalled;
now, although one recalls few, one has attained mastery over those that can be recalled.
Having already attained mastery over the various births in the intermediate state,
he perceives through the divine eye the continuity of the aggregates of sentient beings at the time of death and the time of birth;
that is to say, he sees the aggregates of the death-existence (cyuti-bhava) immediately followed by the manifestation of the intermediate existence (antarābhava).
Furthermore, one sees that the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arise without interruption, manifesting as the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*).
One also sees that the aggregates of the existence at birth arise without interruption, manifesting as the fundamental existence (*pūrvakālabhava*).
The aggregates of this fundamental existence continue through their various states until the existence at death (*maraṇabhava*).
For example, it is like the continuity of a stream of water or a succession of lamp-flames;
because one fails to perceive the subtle arising and ceasing within the aggregates, the notion of permanence arises,
and one consequently clings to the view that both the self and the world are eternal.
Because they conceive of transformation or of concealment and manifestation—
just as a sword enters or exits its scabbard, a snake its hole, or a person a dark room, thus appearing and disappearing—
they form this thought.
Both "I" and "that which is seen" are eternal;
by this, one perceives that both the self and the world are eternally abiding.
Fourth, it is due to not knowing vitarka and vicāra as they truly are.
That is to say, they hold that both the self and the world are eternal.
They conceive this thought:
"There exists a phenomenon that is permanent."
It is impossible for non-existence to be eternally non-existent, nor can existence be produced from nothing, nor can it be extinguished.
They maintain that cause and effect, from beginningless time, are in their nature solely one—neither ceasing nor arising.
Therefore, this is subsumed under the speculative views regarding the past.
If one clings to form as the self,
because the visible shape appears to be constantly similar, one consequently clings to it as permanent.
If one maintains that the mind and its concomitants constitute the self,
