[this is untenable] because these mental phenomena arise without interruption, arise in a similar succession, and arise at all times;
thus, one is unable to perceive their subtle arising and ceasing.
Because one can recollect events experienced in the past,
because preceding and succeeding activities resemble one another, and because they are not obstructed by others,
one consequently clings to them as being permanent.
Due to such false conceptualization and discursive thought,
they cling to the view that both the self and the world are eternal.
These four types of views regarding the past are the doctrines of universal eternalism.
These arise from four factors: the kalpa, birth and death, and discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*).
Regarding those who maintain the doctrine that one part is eternal:
first, there are those who pass away from the Brahma-world and are reborn in this realm.
Because they have attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), they hold this view:
"We were all emanated by Mahābrahmā;
Brahmā is capable of such emanation and abides there eternally."
Because they are what we have transformed, they are impermanent.
Second, having heard that the Brahmā King holds such a view and establishes such a doctrine, [it is said]:
"The great elements are impermanent."
The mind is permanent;
alternatively, it may be said that the mind is impermanent while the great elements are permanent. Those who possess such patience as this either dwell in the Brahma-world or are born in this world.
Or, having heard such principles through successive transmission, they form this attachment:
"I take Mahābrahmādeva as my authority;
therefore, one portion of the world is eternal and another portion is impermanent."
Those who previously passed away from the Heaven of Forgetfulness through Play (*krīḍā-pramoṣaka*) and were reborn here,
having attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*),
formed this conviction: "Those in that heaven whose existence does not involve extreme play and who do not lose mindfulness remain there eternally."
"We were previously impermanent because we passed away from that realm due to extreme playfulness and forgetfulness.
Furthermore, four of us previously passed away from the Heaven of Mental Anger (*manah-pradoṣa*) and were reborn here."
Because they have attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, they form this conviction:
"Those gods, in their various states of existence, do not harbor extreme resentment or glare at one another with hostile eyes; they remain there eternally."
Because we previously died from that place due to our minds being extremely agitated by mutual resentment and our eyes glaring at one another, it is impermanent.
Question: In what location do such devas reside?
Some say they dwell on the terraces of Mount Sumeru;
others say...
Those are the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
Thus, these four types of views concerning the past that assert partial eternalism arise from clinging to four things:
Mahābrahmā, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), the mind, or forgetfulness and anger.
Regarding the second group, those who propound the theory of causeless origination: there is one who,
having passed away from the Heaven of Non-percipient Beings (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*) and been reborn in this world,
is able— by means of attaining the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtyabhijñā*)— to remember both the mind that emerged from non-perception and the subsequent states.
Being unable to recollect any states prior to that point in his mental continuum,
he then forms this thought:
"At that time, I originally did not exist and then arose."
Just as all phenomena, so too should the self be held to have arisen from being originally non-existent.
From this, one then clings to the view that both the self and the world are entirely without cause and arise spontaneously.
Second, because of the false investigation through vitarka and vicāra:
since one can now recall everything experienced by this present body,
if there were experiences from a previous life, one should also be able to recall them within this present body.
Since they cannot be recollected, one knows that they do not exist.
Furthermore, one reflects:
"If sentient beings were to arise depending upon them, they would necessarily resemble them."
Just as a worm within curd resembles curd,
a worm within cow dung resembles cow dung,
and a worm within a green leaf resembles a green leaf.
Parents give birth to children who resemble them;
yet curd and the like are not themselves the cause of worms and such.
Therefore, one knows that all phenomena—bodies, sense faculties, cognition, wisdom, and so forth—arise without a cause.
Furthermore, they form this thought:
"We see directly that the various distinctions of color and shape among peacocks, pheasants, phoenixes, chickens, mountains, rocks, grasses, trees, flowers, fruits, thorns, and so forth,
all exist spontaneously without depending on a cause."
They speak thus: "Who sharpens the thorns?
Who paints the birds and beasts? Who accumulates the mountains and plains? Who carves the ravines and valleys? And who again fashions and carves the grasses, trees, flowers, and fruits?"

Since all these things are not produced by causes and there is no sovereign creator of the world, they consequently maintain that both the self and the world arise without cause and exist spontaneously.
These two types of views concerning the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) that maintain the theory of causeless arising arise from two things:
false conceptualization and discursive thought regarding the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*).
As for those who hold the four views on the finite nature [of the world] and so forth:
First, by means of the divine eye, one sees downward only as far as the Avīci hell,
and upward only as far as the gods of the first dhyāna;
one then conceives that the self completely pervades all within this range.
He thinks to himself:
"If there were a self or a world beyond this, I should also perceive it;
since I do not perceive anything further, I know they do not exist."
From this, one then clings to the view that both the self and the world are finite;
this refers to the meaning of having two kinds of spatial limits.

Second, by relying on the superior meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of the "excellent portion" (*viśeṣabhāgīya*), one develops the pure divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and perceives the boundless [world] in its lateral extent, thereby clinging to the notion that the self completely pervades all within it.
From this, one then maintains that both the self and the world are infinite;
this refers to the meaning of being devoid of the two kinds of spatial limitations.
Third, by means of the divine eye and the supernormal power of psychic travel.
By means of the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*), one sees downward only as far as the Avīci Hell,
and upward only as far as the gods of the First Dhyāna Heaven.
By means of the supernormal power of the basis of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-viṣaya-abhijñā*), one moves the body sideways but cannot reach its limit.
Consequently, they give rise to the notion of finitude regarding the zenith and nadir,
and the notion of infinitude regarding the lateral worlds,
clinging to the idea that the self completely pervades all within them.
From this, one then maintains that both the self and the world are both finite and infinite;
this refers to the two aspects of having and not having limits.
Fourth, "neither finite nor infinite" is the negation of the third [position], serving as the fourth.
He thinks thus:
"Both myself and the world cannot be definitively said to be either finite or infinite;
nevertheless, both are truly existent."
Some say that because they perceive the world to be horizontally boundless,
they maintain that both the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite.

Because he perceives that the world has a vertical limit, he maintains that both the self and the world are not infinite; although this is not definitive, he nonetheless holds that there truly is a self.
Furthermore, there are others who say:
They maintain that the substance of the self is sometimes expanded and sometimes contracted, such that it cannot be definitively described:
because it is expanded without limit, it is said to be not finite;
because it is contracted with limits, it is said to be not infinite.
Question: Since these four types [of discrimination] take the present as their object, why are they called "discrimination regarding the prior limit" (*pūrvānta-vikalpa*)?
Answer: They are also termed "prior limit" insofar as they refer to the future.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because these four are established through the recollection of the kalpas of formation and destruction,
they are all to be designated as "discrimination regarding the past limit" (*pūrvānta-vikalpa*).

That is to say, the first proponent, by recollecting the time of the past eon of formation, perceives that both the self and the world possess vertical limits; thus, they give rise to the notion of finitude.
As for the second proponent, by recollecting the time of the past eon of formation...
Because I and the world are limitless in their horizontal extent, the notion of being infinite arises.
According to the third treatise, by recollecting the time of the past eon of formation (*vivartakalpa*),
it is established that I and the world are limited in their vertical extent but limitless in their horizontal extent.
Upon arising, there is also the perception that [the world] is both finite and infinite.
This is because, according to the fourth discourse, when recollecting the time of the past eon of destruction,
although the measure of myself and the world could not be distinguished as either narrow or broad.
However, there is indeed the arising of the perception that things are neither finite nor infinite.
Some say: "To cling to the view that things are finite is itself the nihilistic view (ucchedadṛṣṭi)."
To cling to [the world] as having no limit is the view of eternalism.
To cling to it as both having a limit and having no limit is the view of partial annihilationism and partial eternalism.
Those who maintain that there is neither finitude nor infinitude merely give rise to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
These four types of speculative theories concerning the prior limit, such as the existence of finitude and so forth, [are thus explained].
Based on what was previously stated, it arises from four matters.
Regarding the "fourfold equivocation concerning immortality" (*amarā-vikkhepikā*):
"immortality" (*amara*) refers to the devas.
Because non-Buddhist practitioners such as the Tīrthikas cling to the notion that the heavens are eternal and deathless,
some among them seek rebirth in those celestial realms;
having heard the doctrines of these non-Buddhists, they speak in this manner.
If one is able to answer those questions posed by the Immortal Deva without confusion, one will be reborn in that heaven;
if one cannot answer them, one will not.
For one who asks without confusion, there can be no arising of [erroneous] meaning.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of non-confusion:
first, that which possesses signs and conceptual differentiation; [and second, that which is free from both].
Second, there is the signless and non-conceptual.
For those who possess true vision, there is no sign and no conceptualization because they have nothing upon which to rely;
for those who lack true vision, there is sign and conceptualization because they have something upon which to rely.
Regarding those questions concerning immortality and non-confusion, those followers of external paths resort to evasive speech;
they think to themselves: "First, let me do this."
I did not know, as they truly are, what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, nor the Four Noble Truths.
There were other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who sought to know such matters as they truly are.
If he were to ask me such a question,
for me to give a definitive answer to his inquiry would constitute a falsehood.
Because of false speech, I would not have been born in that heaven. Out of fear of false speech, when asked a question regarding the deathless that was not confused, he spoke evasively, saying this:

[The Buddha said: "Ānanda, what do you think? When a person is asked a question regarding the deathless that is not confused, and they speak evasively, saying: 'I do not say so; I do not say it is not so; I do not say it is both so and not so; I do not say it is neither so nor not so,' would that person, by means of such speech, be able to know the deathless, or see the deathless, or attain the deathless? "Venerable sir, no. "Therefore, Ānanda, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall not utter even a single word that is false, whether in jest or in earnest. Thus, Ānanda, should you train yourselves."
I should not speak of all the secret meanings of the devas;
whether it be that which is personally realized or the path of purification, I have this thought:
"I do not know as they truly are what is wholesome or unwholesome, nor the Four Noble Truths."
There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who seek to know such matters as they truly are.
If they were to ask me about such matters, and if I were to deny the meaning of what they asked, that would constitute a false view.
"Because of my wrong view, I shall not be reborn in that heaven.
Out of fear of wrong view, he evades with equivocal speech when asked about deathlessness and non-confusion, as previously described.
Third, he reflects:
"I do not know as they truly are what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, nor the Four Noble Truths.
There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas..."
Regarding such a matter, one seeks to know it as it truly is.
If someone were to ask me about such a matter,
and if I were not to truthfully confirm what they have asked, [I would be at fault].
If they were to question me,
I would say, "I do not know.
Because of this ignorance, I would not be able to be reborn in that celestial realm.
Fearing ignorance, he resorts to evasive speech regarding questions concerning the deathless that are not confused;
the rest is as previously explained.
Fourth, he thinks thus:
My nature is dull and inferior, such that I am unable to compose or gather deceptive and confused words.
Furthermore, I have this thought:
if one adheres exclusively to [the view that] "it is not," it is not excellent or wholesome.
Because one-sided adherence does not accord with the minds of all sentient beings,
if I were to act in opposition to the minds of others,
I would not be able to be reborn in that celestial realm.
Therefore, I should rely on the principle of non-contradiction.
If someone asks me, "Is there a future life?
I should respond by asking a counter-question:
What do you intend?
If you say that there must be existence, then I shall confirm your statement:
I also allow that there is existence in future lives.

If one asks whether it is "both existent and non-existent" or "neither existent nor non-existent," or asks whether it is "thus" or "not thus," or "different" or "not different," in all such cases one should respond with a counter-question;
according to what the other desires, I shall then confirm it for them.
Furthermore, one should think:
"I am by nature foolish;
if I were to reject or oppose another, they would then separate from me."
Out of fear of appearing foolish, one resorts to evasive speech regarding questions concerning immortality that do not lead to confusion.
To which of these four views are such [evasive] questions subsumed?
Answer: Those four [views] arise regarding the heavens with the notion of immortality and are all subsumed under the view of permanence (*śāśvatavāda*).
To reckon that answering the questions of others is the cause for rebirth in heaven constitutes the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Question: Are these four not rather "speculations concerning the past" (*pūrvāntakalpa*)?
Answer: These four all operate with respect to present phenomena;
however, because they depend upon the future, they are designated by the term "prior limit" (*pūrvānta*).
Alternatively, some say:
These four all take as their object the teachings previously heard;

that is to say, those non-Buddhists previously heard from their own teachers the supreme teaching stating that one must answer the questions of others in such a manner to be reborn in the Immortal Heaven.
That immortal heaven is attained precisely through answering questions in such a manner;
therefore, these four types are all subsumed under views that conceptualize the past (*pūrvānta-vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*).
Such are the four types of conceptualization regarding the past.
The "Immortality-Confounding" [view] arises based on fear, false speech, wrong view, ignorance, and dullness.
*Sarvāstivāda-jñānaprasthāna-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 199; this fascicle, line 16 of the twenty-third leaf.

Regarding the passage of one hundred and forty-six characters beginning with "Under the inquiry into the clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it states that from the wholesome and the defiled up to "therefore it is said that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) conditions consciousness, and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the four categories in the three realms increase therein."
This is merely the concluding text of the eighteenth fascicle of this treatise;
it was erroneously transcribed in the Song edition of the Tripiṭaka.
In this regard, both editions state:
"Are these four indeed conceptualizations of the past?
Answer: These four all operate with respect to present phenomena."
The term "prior limit" (*pūrvānta*) is established because it refers to the future;
some teachers say that all four of these take as their object the teachings previously heard.
That is to say, those non-Buddhists previously heard the authoritative teaching spoken by their own teacher,
stating that it is only by means of such [practices] that one answers the questions of others and is reborn in the Immortal Heaven.
That immortal deity is attained precisely through such answers to questions; therefore,
these four types are all subsumed under views concerning the past (*pūrvānta-vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*).
These four types of speculations concerning the past arise based on fear, false speech, wrong views, ignorance, dullness, and delusion; the above consists of one hundred and nine characters.
This is the main text.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 205,
composed by the Great Arhats and others.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Section Eight: The Aggregate of Views; Sub-section Five: The Exposition on Views—Part Three. Within the Analysis of Views Concerning the Future Limit, there are those who maintain sixteen theories regarding the existence of perception.
This means that the first four types are established based on three views.
As it is said: "A certain class of persons gives rise to such a view and establishes such a doctrine."
"The life-principle is identical to the body.
Furthermore, there is a class of persons who give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine.
The life-principle is different from the body.
Furthermore, there is a class of persons who give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine.
"This 'self' in its totality is all-pervading,
non-dual, undifferentiated, and without deficiency.
Based on this primary view, one establishes the first theory of a self that possesses form and has perception after death."
That is to say, those non-Buddhists cling to form as the self and cling to the other four aggregates as "belonging to the self" (ātmīya).
The self they thus conceive has form as its essential nature.
Therefore, it is called "possessing form.
Grasping the characteristics of various phenomena is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*).
Because this self possessing form has that perception, it is called "possessing perception."
Because they grasp the four aggregates as "mine," they form this thought: "This self,
which possesses form, exists with perception after death."
This exists throughout the desire realm and one portion of the form realm,
excluding the Heaven of Non-conception;
it is also admitted that there is form within the formless realm.
This [view] also resides within the first three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Because it involves perception (*saṃjñā*), it does not reside in the final one.
Based on the second type of view, the second theory—that the self is formless and possesses perception after death—is established.
This refers to those non-Buddhists who cling to formlessness as the self,
or cling to form or the other four aggregates as "mine.
That is to say, they may exclude perception and cling to the remaining three aggregates— either collectively or individually— as the self.
One grasps the aggregate of perception and the aggregate of form as "mine.
If one grasps the aggregate of perception as the self,
one then grasps the remaining aggregates as "mine."
That which they grasp as the self has formlessness as its nature; therefore, it is called "formless.
Grasping the characteristics of phenomena is termed "perception" (*saṃjñā*).
This formless self would thus have perception as its nature.
Either it is called "possessing perception" because of the activity of perception,
or it is called "possessing perception" because of that perception itself,
since one clings to the aggregate of perception as "mine."
He forms this thought:
"This formless self exists with perception after death;
it exists within the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness."
Excluding the Heaven of Non-conception,
based on the third view, one establishes the third type of self-theory:
the doctrine that after death there is consciousness, and that the self is both with form and without form.
This refers to those non-Buddhists who grasp at form and formlessness as the self,
such as the Tīrthikas of True Speech (Satyavādin) and others,
who collectively give rise to the notion of a single self with respect to the five aggregates.
Because one cannot find a real self by analyzing each of the aggregates individually—
just as one cannot find a single, real, composite taste when analyzing sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and bland tastes separately.
Having conceived a single notion regarding the aggregates, they grasp them collectively as a self.
That self which they grasp has both form and formlessness as its nature;
therefore, it is called "both with form and without form."
The grasping of the characteristics of all phenomena is called perception (*saṃjñā*).
This [perception] also has a self that is both with form and without form;
or, it takes perception as its intrinsic nature.
Either it is called "having perception" because there is the act of perceiving,
or it is called "having perception" because there is that perception;
this is due to grasping one's own aggregates as a self.
Because they grasp at the aggregates of others as "mine," there are other non-Buddhists who,
having recognized the fault in the view of a material self, [proceed further].
He dwells depending on a formless self.
Having seen the faults in a formless self,
he dwells again depending on a material self.
Those non-Buddhists have not yet severed the view of a self;
although they cling to the existence of a self, they do so without certainty,
asserting that the self they grasp is either exclusively material or exclusively immaterial.
However, one forms this thought:
"This is both with form and without form;
after my death, there is perception. This applies entirely to the desire realm as appropriate to each case.
...and so on, as explained at length.
The fourth [view], the doctrine that the self is neither material nor immaterial and possesses perception after death,
serves to negate the third [view], which lacks a distinct basis for its assertion.
He thinks to himself:
"Although the self truly exists, it cannot be definitively said to be both with form and without form.
He perceives the real self as being definitively both with form and without form.
Because both [positions] entail faults, it is said:
"This self is neither material nor immaterial; after death, it possesses perception."
The rest is as previously explained.
Thus, these four types [of views] may arise based either on vitarka and vicāra or on meditative attainment (samāpatti).
This refers to those who maintain the thesis that the self is finite and possesses perception after death.
If one holds form (*rūpa*) to be the self (*ātman*),
that self as conceived by them has spatial limitations;
or it is within the mind, the size of a finger joint, blazing with radiant light.
Or else, within the body, it takes on the dimensions of the physical form, being transparent both internally and externally.
As it is said: "I, I—my form is handsome, radiant, blazing, and supremely pure."
The Venerable Gautama would rather say that there is no self;
for if one were to grasp that which is non-material as the self,
that self grasped by him would likewise have limits.
Because non-material phenomena have limits in terms of their basis and their objects,
they are also called "finite.
Based on vitarka and vicāra, they give rise to such a misconception.
If one gives rise to this attachment based on meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), one has certainly not yet attained the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Thus, both of these types [of beings] think:
"I am certainly finite; after death, there is perception."
This exists throughout the entire Desire Realm and a portion of the Form Realm,
excluding the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*).
For those who maintain that the Formless Realm also possesses form, this [form] likewise exists in the first three of those Formless Realms.
Regarding those who hold the view that the self is infinite and possesses perception after death:
if they hold form (*rūpa*) to be the self,
then the self as they conceive it must be omnipresent.
As stated in the *Vidyā-śāstra*:
"There exists a self (*ātman*) or person (*puruṣa*), vast in measure and its limits difficult to fathom,
with a radiance like that of the sun."
Those who are shrouded in darkness cannot see it even when standing before it;
only by knowing this "self" can one transcend birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Apart from this, there is no other way to transcend them.
Furthermore, as it is said:
"The earth is the self, and the self is the earth;
its measure is boundless."
If one clings to formlessness as the self, they think:
"Just as that which does not reach fire can never be burned."
If it does not reach the blade, it can never cut;
if it does not reach the water, it can never moisten.
In the same way, if there is nothing that reaches me, I can never grasp that which is of boundless measure.
They give rise to such attachments based on vitarka and vicāra.
If they were to give rise to this attachment based on meditative attainment (samāpatti), they would necessarily have already attained the universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana).
Thus, both of these types [of practitioners] entertain this thought.
"I am certainly infinite and possess perception after death.
This applies throughout the entire desire realm as appropriate,
and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding those who hold the view that the self is both finite and infinite, and who maintain the doctrine that there is perception after death:
if they hold form (*rūpa*) to be the self,
then that self of theirs conforms to the body upon which it depends.
Whether coiled or extended, its measure is not fixed.
He thinks to himself:
"If the body has a limit, then I must have a boundary."
If the body were immeasurable, then the self would be boundless.
If one clings to formlessness as the self,
they conceive this thought:
If the self is finite according to its finite basis and object,
and if the self is infinite according to its infinite basis and object,
both of these two types [of persons] conceive this thought.
"I am both finite and infinite, and possess perception after death.
This applies throughout the entire desire realm (kāmadhātu) as appropriate,
and so on, as explained at length.
Those who hold the view that the self neither has an end nor is endless, and who maintain that there is perception after death,
are excluded from the third [category] and constitute this fourth.
One should understand that the three alternative formulations are as previously explained.
These four types may arise based either on vitarka and vicāra or on meditative attainment (samāpatti);
they are described in this way because they differ in their modes of perception (saṃjñā) and feeling (vedanā).
"I have a single perception; I have manifold perceptions; I have a limited perception; I have an immeasurable perception.
I am purely happy; I am purely suffering;
I am both suffering and happy; I am neither suffering nor happy. After death, there is perception."
Regarding the phrase "in this regard, there is the perception of unity":
this refers to the three preceding formless attainments.
Because those various perceptions arise through a single gateway, they are designated as "the perception of unity."
When I possess various perceptions,
this refers to those in the desire realm and the form realm,
excluding the Heaven of Non-perception.
Because those various perceptions (saṃjñā) operate through six or four doors,
and because they take various objects as their conditions, they are called "various perceptions. Furthermore,
there are also distinctions among those who rely on vitarka and vicāra.
That is to say, one who possesses a single kind of skillful knowledge is said to have "a single perception.
One who possesses various kinds of skillful knowledge is said to have "various perceptions.
As for my statement, "I have a small perception": [it refers to this].
This refers to grasping a limited amount of form as self,
or grasping a limited amount of the formless as self.
If one grasps a limited amount of form as self:
They grasp at form as the self, and its dimension is narrow and small,
like that of a finger joint and so forth;
they grasp at perception as the self.
Because its basis is a small body and because it takes a limited object as its condition,
it is called "small perception.
When the self is conjoined with that, it is termed "possessing small perception."
This exists throughout the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and a portion of the form realm (rūpadhātu),
excluding the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva).
For those who maintain that the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) also possesses form, [it exists there as well].
This also occurs within those aforementioned three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
If one clings to a limited formless state as the self,
one may then grasp it as the notion of "I" or as "mine."
Because it relies on a small body and takes a limited object as its condition,
it is called "small perception."
The combination of "I" and "that" is called "possessing limited ideation.
To take conditioned activities as the self and consciousness as the self is explained at length in the same manner.
If one grasps perception as the self,
because that perception relies upon a small body and takes a limited object as its condition,
it is called "small perception."
Because they grasp limited perception (*parītta-saṃjñā*) as being the nature of the self,
or because there is the activity of perception, it is called "having limited perception.
This exists from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Excluding the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*),
those who possess the notion of the immeasurable (*apramāṇasaṃjñin*) are those who grasp at immeasurable form as self, or grasp at immeasurable formless [states] as self.
If one clings to immeasurable form as the self,
that person clings to a self of form that is omnipresent.
That person clings to perception as the self.
Because its basis is an immeasurable body and it takes an immeasurable object as its domain, it is called the "perception of the immeasurable.
When the self is conjoined with that [perception], it is termed "possessing the perception of the immeasurable.
This exists throughout the entire Desire Realm and a portion of the Form Realm.
Excluding the Heaven of Non-conception,
those who maintain that the formless realm also possesses form assert that this [form] likewise exists within those three aforementioned formless states.
If one clings to the immeasurable formless realms as the self,
they may then grasp at them as "I" or as "mine.
Because that perception relies upon immeasurable bodies and takes immeasurable objects as its domain, it is called the "immeasurable perception."
Because I am conjoined with that, it is called "having immeasurable perceptions.
Taking formations as the self and taking consciousness as the self—
the detailed explanation is likewise so.
If one clings to perception as the self,
that perception is called "immeasurable perception" because it relies upon immeasurable bodies and takes immeasurable objects as its domain;
since one clings to that immeasurable perception as being the nature of the self.
Alternatively, because it involves the mental application of perception, it is called "having immeasurable perception.
This exists from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness,
excluding the heaven of non-perception.
These four types may arise either based on vitarka and vicāra or based on meditative attainments (samāpatti).
"I possess pure bliss" refers to being in the first three dhyānas.
Those who have attained meditative concentration see, by means of the supernormal power of the divine eye, that those in the three dhyānas constantly experience pleasure.
Later, when they pass away from there and are reborn in this world, they think: "I possess nothing but pleasure."
Those who engage in discursive thought perceive all sentient beings as being at all times conjoined with happiness,
and they form this thought: "I possess nothing but happiness," just as it is in this world,
so it is in other worlds as well.
Those who possess nothing but suffering are those in the hells.
Those who have attained meditative concentration see, by means of the supernormal power of the divine eye, that those in the hells are constantly undergoing suffering.
Later, having passed away from that realm and come to be born in this world, one forms this thought: "I am possessed of nothing but suffering.
Those who engage in discursive investigation see that all sentient beings are, at all times, joined with suffering.
He then forms this thought: "I have only suffering.
As it is in this world, so it is in other worlds as well.
"I have both suffering and pleasure."
This refers to those in the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and the gods of the desire realm.
Those who have attained meditative concentration perceive, through the supernormal power of the divine eye, that these sentient beings experience a mixture of suffering and pleasure;
subsequently, they pass away from those realms and are reborn here in this world.
Then one forms this thought: "I have suffering and I have pleasure.
Those who engage in discursive investigation see that sentient beings are at times conjoined with suffering and at times conjoined with pleasure.
Then he thinks: "I have suffering and I have pleasure;
as it is in this world, so it is in other worlds.
I am without suffering and without pleasure."
This refers to those who have attained meditative absorption in the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness;
these beings are known to be without suffering and without pleasure,
and subsequently, passing away from there, they are reborn in this world.
He then forms this thought: "I have neither suffering nor pleasure.
Those who engage in discursive thought and investigation form this thought:
"My essence is permanent and does not function with clarity."
Although there may be a temporary association with suffering or pleasure, that [association] is adventitious and does not belong to the self;
these are the sixteen types of discrimination regarding the future limit (*aparānta*).
All proponents of the existence of consciousness (*saṃjñā-vādin*) give rise to their views based on the sixteen matters previously described.
The eight proponents of non-perception (asaṃjñika) are those who maintain that there is form and so forth, and those who maintain the four positions regarding being finite and so forth.
Regarding the four positions that there is form and so forth:
First, there is the adherence that the self possesses form and is without perception after death;
that is to say, they hold that the self possesses form and attains the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*),
and seeing others attain that attainment and be born among the gods of the Heaven of Non-perceiving Beings (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), they then form this thought.
"I possess form and am non-percipient after death;
I shall be reborn among the non-percipient beings (asaṃjñisattva) because perception does not arise.
Thus do those who engage in discursive thought (vitarka-vicāra) cling to form as the self.
Seeing one who is afflicted by wind-disorder (vāta), deep sleep, fainting, or the intensity of painful sensation, appearing as if entirely without perception, one then forms this thought:
"Although I possess form, I lack that perception."
As it is in this world, so it is in the next world.
There are two who hold the view that the self is formless and that there is no perception after death;
that is to say, they hold that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) constitutes the self and that they have attained the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Furthermore, seeing others who have attained that concentration and are reborn among the non-percipient beings in the Heaven of Non-percipient Beings, he thinks:
"After I die here in the formless realm, I shall be reborn among the non-percipient beings in the Heaven of Non-percipient Beings."
Because they do not perceive [the mind],
those who engage in discursive thought and investigation (vitarka-vicāra) cling to the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) as the self.
They observe that during states such as epilepsy, deep sleep, fainting, or when one is overwhelmed by painful sensations, it appears as if there were no perception at all.
He then forms this thought:
"I am formless and without perception;
as it is in this world, so it is in other worlds."
Those who possess vitarka and vicāra exclude the aggregate of perception and grasp the remaining three aggregates as the self;
they may also grasp that the self is formless and non-perceptual after death.
There are also those who grasp the self as being both with form and without form, and non-perceptual after death.
This means that they grasp at form and the life-faculty as the self;
they give rise to a single notion of "self" with respect to these two,
yet because they cannot find a real self through their individual analysis of these two, [they do not perceive one].
Just as one cannot obtain a collective taste from individual distinctions such as sweetness and so forth,
they maintain that these two are a single self, having attained the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*),
and seeing others attain that attainment, they are born into the heaven of non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*).
He then thinks:
"I am both with form and without form; after death, I shall be without perception and will be reborn among the gods of the realm of non-perception."
Because they do not perceive [the self],
those who engage in discursive thought and investigation (vitarka-vicāra) grasp at the physical form and the life-faculty as the self.
They observe that during states such as epilepsy, deep sleep, fainting, or when one is overwhelmed by painful sensations, there appears to be a total absence of perception.
Then he forms this thought:
"I am both with form and without form, yet entirely without perception;
as it is in this world, so it is in other worlds."

Those who possess vitarka and vicāra may conceive of the four aggregates—excluding perception—as the self; they may also conceive of the self as being both with form and without form, or as being without perception after death.
They may also conceive of the self as being neither with form nor without form, and as being without perception after death.
This immediately excludes the third [option] as being this fourth.
One should understand that the different explanations regarding the three gateways are as previously stated.
As for the four [views] beginning with "having an end":
First, there is the adherence that the self is finite and that after death there is no perception;
this refers to those who adhere to form (*rūpa*) as the self,
and who thus conceive of the self consisting of form as being limited in extent.
Just as with the finger-joints and so forth;
if one clings to formlessness as the self,
that person clings to the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) as the self.
Pervading the entire body in accordance with its physical dimensions,
having thus grasped it, one attains the meditative absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*),
as well as seeing others who have attained that absorption and are born among the gods of the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).
He then had this thought:
"I am finite; after death there will be no perception.
I shall be reborn among the non-percipient beings in the Heaven of Non-percipient Beings."
Because they cannot be recollected; furthermore,
those who engage in discursive thought and investigation also grasp them as a self, and there are cases of wind-disorders (vāta) such as epilepsy,
according to their respective circumstances.
As explained in detail previously,
the second [type] clings to the self as being infinite and without perception after death;
that is, if one clings to form (*rūpa*) as the self.
They maintain that the self consisting of form pervades all places;
if they maintain the formless as the self,
they maintain the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as the self.
It also pervades all places.
Having thus grasped this, they attain the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*),
and they see others who have attained that meditative state being born among the non-conceptualizing beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) in the Heaven of Non-conception.
He then thought: "After my death, which is boundless, I shall be without perception;
I shall be reborn among the non-percipient beings in the Heaven of Non-percipient Beings."
Because it cannot be conceptualized,
those who engage in discursive thought also grasp it as the self,
seeing it as a wind-disorder (vāta-vyādhi).
The details should be understood as previously explained according to what is appropriate.
Third is the adherence to the view that the self is both finite and infinite, and that there is no consciousness after death;
this refers to those who maintain that form (*rūpa*) is the self.
They conceive of the self as material, either contracted or expanded;
if they conceive of it as immaterial,
they conceive of the life-faculty as the self.
Just as the body’s form may be either contracted or extended, so too,
having grasped [the view] in this way, one attains the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*),
and sees others who have attained that attainment being born among the beings of the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).
Then he thinks:
"I am both finite and infinite; after death, I shall be without perception and will be reborn among the non-percipient beings in the Heaven of Non-percipient Beings."
Because it cannot be perceived as such,
those who engage in discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) also grasp it as the self;
this should be understood in detail according to the context, as explained previously.
The fourth [view] is the grasping that the self is neither finite nor infinite and that there is no consciousness after death;
this immediately excludes the third [view], which serves as the basis for this fourth.
One should understand that the different explanations regarding these three gateways are as previously stated.
These eight types of discrimination regarding the future arise based on the eight matters previously described by those who maintain the doctrine of non-perception (asaṃjñika).
The eight proponents of the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" doctrine refer to the four views concerning form and so forth,
and the four views concerning finitude and so forth.
Regarding the four views concerning form and so forth:
First, there is the adherence that the self possesses form and that after death it is neither percipient nor non-percipient;
this refers to those who employ vitarka and vicāra and who grasp form as the self,
perceiving that the perception of sentient beings is not clear.
He then forms this thought:
"I have form, which is neither with perception nor without perception;
as it is in this world, so it is in other worlds."
One who has not attained that meditative absorption cannot possibly hold this view.
Why is this? Because it requires one who has already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Only then could one grasp the aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as a self.
Since that [sphere] is devoid of form, such a grasping would lack a rational basis; it is spoken of in this way by way of a distinct sense.
Even those who have attained that meditative absorption possess this grasping.
This refers to those born in the desire or form realms who have already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),
yet grasp at the aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as a self.
Although the essence of the self they grasp is not material (*arūpa*).
Yet, because it is conjoined with form, it is called a "self possessing form.
This is like saying there is a person with a topknot, even though the human body itself is not the topknot;
although such a person does not grasp form as "mine," [they still possess it].
However, because the self they grasp has not yet been separated from the physical body and still follows it until the end of life, they say that the self possesses form. This is because,
due to the entry into the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, their perception is not clear.
They maintain that the self exists neither as possessing perception nor as lacking perception in the present, and that it is likewise after death.

Those who assert that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) also possesses form maintain that there is indeed a grasping of the self as having form in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
It is neither with perception nor without perception.
Second, the attachment to a self that is formless after death and is neither with perception nor without perception:
this refers to those who have attained that meditative absorption and cling to the various formless aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as being the self.
Or it is the self as my possession;
that self which they grasp has formlessness (*arūpa*) as its nature,
or because it is without form, it is called the "formless self" (*arūpyātmā*).
Because the perception associated with the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception entered by them is not clear,
they maintain that the self exists as neither possessing perception nor lacking perception in the present, and likewise after death.
Those who engage in discursive thought and investigation cling to the formless as the self.
Seeing that the perception of sentient beings is not clear, they conceive this thought:
"I am formless, neither possessing perception nor lacking perception."
As it is in this world, so it is in the next world.
There are three types of grasping at a self that is both with form and without form, and which, after death, is neither percipient nor non-percipient;
namely, those who engage in discursive thought and investigation grasp at both form and formlessness as the self.
Seeing that his perception of sentient beings was not clear,
he then thought: "I am both with form and without form, neither percipient nor non-percipient."
As it is in this world, so it is in other worlds as well.
It is impossible for one who has not attained that meditative absorption (samādhi) to hold such a view. Why is this?
Only one who has already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness can grasp the aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as a self;
since that [sphere] is devoid of form, such a grasping is logically impossible.
According to another interpretation,
those who have attained that meditative absorption also possess this grasping;
namely, those born in the desire or form realms who have already abandoned the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
They grasp the aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the self.
Although the essence of the self they grasp is not material, it is called a "material self" because it is conjoined with matter.
This is like saying there is a person with a topknot; although the person's body is not the topknot itself, even though they do not grasp matter as "mine," [the designation still applies].
Furthermore, because the self they grasp has not yet departed from the physical body and still follows it until the end of life, they say that the self also possesses form;
because they grasp the formless as the self, they say that the self also lacks form.
Because the perception associated with his attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is not clear,
he clings to the notion that the self exists as neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving in the present, and likewise after death.

Those who maintain that the formless realm also possesses form assert that there exists a self in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception which is both truly possessed of form and devoid of form,
yet is neither percipient nor non-percipient.
The fourth [view] is the grasping that the self is neither material nor immaterial,
and after death it is neither percipient nor non-percipient;
this immediately excludes the third [view] as being the fourth.
The divergent explanations regarding the three gates should be understood as previously stated.
Regarding the four [views] such as "having limits":
the first is the attachment to the self as having limits, [asserting that] after death it is neither percipient nor non-percipient.
Second, they cling to the view that the self is infinite and that after death it is neither percipient nor non-percipient.
Third, they cling to the view that the self is both finite and infinite and that after death it is neither percipient nor non-percipient.
The four [views] are: holding that the self is neither finite nor infinite;
and that after death it is neither percipient nor non-percipient.
All such views as these take the formless as the self.
Those who have attained the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception may all harbor this misconception;
furthermore, all of these may likewise misconceive the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception [as being the ultimate state].
They regard the four formless aggregates as self and what belongs to the self.
First, because their duration is necessarily brief and because they take each individual aggregate as an object of perception, they cling to the notion that the self is finite.
Second, because the duration of that meditative absorption is long and it takes the four aggregates as its object in their entirety, one clings to the self as being infinite.
Third, because the duration of that meditative absorption is either short or long...
Because they take either each individual aggregate or the four aggregates collectively as their object,
they cling to the view that the self is both finite and infinite;
this immediately excludes the third [alternative] as its fourth.
The divergent explanations regarding the three gates should be understood as previously stated.
In this context, all [of these] arise because the perception (saṃjñā) of the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) is not clear.
Those who maintain that the self exists neither as possessing perception nor as lacking perception in the present, and likewise after death;

those who engage in discursive thought (vitarka and vicāra); and those who assert that there is form even in the formless realm—all of them maintain that both the realm of form and the formless realm constitute the self.
These should be understood in detail according to their respective applications, as extensively explained previously.
Thus, these eight types of speculations concerning the future regarding the state that is neither-perception-nor-non-perception arise based on the eight matters previously mentioned.

Question: Why is it that in the discourse on non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) and the discourse on neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), the eight positions such as "I have perception" are not mentioned?
Answer: If they were also mentioned, all of them would necessarily be called the discourse on perception (*saṃjñāvāda*).
Because those who possess perception and feeling are not those without perception and so forth;
thus, all such theories concerning perception and so forth that speak of what occurs after death are subsumed under the speculative views regarding the future limit (*aparānta-vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the seven proponents of annihilationism:
first, one forms this thought:
"This self possesses form; it is coarse, composed of the four great elements, and has them as its nature."
"After death there is annihilation; it is absolutely non-existent.
This is what I call the ultimate annihilation.
Such a person views this life as beginning with conception and ending at the time of death, and then forms this thought:
"When I was conceived, that which did not originally exist came to be.
If, upon reaching the stage of death, that which existed returns to non-existence, this is called 'wholesome severance and extinction.
The two [teachers] thought thus."
"This self, after death in the heavens of the desire realm, is annihilated and will never exist again;
up to this point, I am said to have attained perfect annihilation. Thus they think.
I was not born from the birth canal;
I existed where there was originally nothing,
and having existed, I have returned to non-existence.
They regard things such as comets as being "wholly annihilated.
They conceive this threefold thought:
"This self, after death, is annihilated in the realm of the gods of the form realm; it is utterly non-existent."
He reflects upon this, thinking: "This is what I call the right abandonment and cessation.
Since I am not born through the birth canal, [I have attained it]."
That which was originally non-existent comes into being through the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); that which,
having existed, returns to non-existence is called "wholesome abandonment and cessation" (*kuśala-prahāṇa-nirodha*).
Some say that these three types of annihilationist views all arise in relation to sentient beings who have already become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna.
As for those who hold such annihilationist views:
Although he has attained meditative concentration, he has not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna;
thus, the divine eye produced by him perceives only those beings of the lower realms.
As for the aforementioned three types of sentient beings, once they have passed away, they are all reborn in the higher realms.
The bodies of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) that one has received are not within their range; thus, they form this thought:
"For those who have attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), once life has ended, all [phenomena] are completely extinguished."
Fourth, he thinks:
"This self, having died as a deity in the Sphere of Infinite Space, will be annihilated and will never exist again;
up to this point, it is called my 'right annihilation.'"
Fifth, he thinks:
"This self, having died as a deva of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, will be annihilated and will absolutely cease to exist.
Up to this point, it is called my 'right annihilation.'"
Sixth, they form this thought:
"This self, having died after passing from the Heaven of Nothingness, will be annihilated and will never exist again;
up to this point, it is called my 'right annihilation.'"
Seventh, he thinks:
"This god of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception will, after death, be annihilated and will ultimately cease to exist.
Up to this point, I shall be completely annihilated."
Among these, the latter four hold that the sphere of infinite space is the pinnacle of saṃsāra,
up to those who hold that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the pinnacle of saṃsāra.
If one holds that the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is the pinnacle of birth and death,
they hold that after death in the sphere of infinite space there is no further existence, which is a complete and utter cessation;
and so on, up to if one holds that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is the pinnacle of birth and death.
They maintain that after death there is no designation for the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which they call "wholesome utter annihilation.
These are the seven types of theories concerning annihilation based on speculations regarding the future limit.
It arises based on the seven matters previously mentioned.
Since all seven of these refer to what occurs after death,
they are subsumed under the speculative views concerning the future limit (*aparānta-vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*).
Fifth, those who propound the doctrine of nirvana in the present life (dr̥ṣṭadharma-nirvāṇavāda):
this refers to non-Buddhists who maintain that if one experiences peace and happiness in the present life, it is called attaining nirvana.
If I were to possess suffering at that time, I would not be said to have attained nirvāṇa, because it would not be peaceful and blissful.
Thus, one first forms this thought:
"This self is pure, liberated, and has emerged from all calamities and misfortunes."
That is to say, when one currently enjoys the exquisite pleasures of the five sensory desires, at that time it is called attaining *nirvāṇa* in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇa*).
Second, one is able to see the faults of all desires and thinks as follows:
The pleasure born of desire is accompanied by manifold sufferings and beset by many harms;
the pleasure born of meditative concentration is subtle, serene, free from accompanying sufferings, and devoid of all harms.
Again, he thinks:
"This self is pure, liberated, and has emerged from all calamities and misfortunes," meaning that he currently dwells in the first dhyāna.
At that time, having attained what is called "nirvāṇa in the present life," he is the third [type of person] who can perceive the faults inherent in both desire and discursive thought. He reflects:
"This is my purity, liberation, and deliverance from all calamities and misfortunes."
That is to say, when one currently dwells in the second dhyāna, at that time it is called attaining nirvāṇa in the present life;
for in the fourth [dhyāna], one is able to see the faults of sensual desires, applied and sustained thought, and joy.
He forms this thought:
"This is my purity, liberation, and deliverance from all calamities and misfortunes.
That is to say, when he presently dwells in the third dhyāna, at that time it is called attaining nirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa*).
Fifth, one is able to see that sensual desires, discursive thoughts, joy, and inhalation and exhalation all possess faults.
One then reflects:
"This is my purity, liberation, and renunciation from all calamities and misfortunes."
This refers to being currently established in the fourth dhyāna; at that time, it is called "attaining nirvāṇa in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa*). Question:

How is it that these five theories of nirvāṇa in the present life are subsumed under the speculative views regarding the future limit (*aparāntakalpakadṛṣṭi*)? Answer: Although these five take the present as their object, they are called "future" because they depend upon the past.
Therefore, this is called the discrimination regarding the future limit (*aparānta-vikalpa*).
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"This self, which clings to these five [aggregates], possesses happiness both in the present and will possess happiness in the future."
Therefore, this is subsumed under the speculative view concerning the future limit (*aparānta-vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*). Question:
If that is so, why is it called the doctrine of "nirvāṇa in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇavāda*)?
Answer: Because one first seeks happiness in the present and then clings to happiness in the future.
Because it refers to what is presently existing, it is used to designate the title of this treatise.
These five kinds of discrimination regarding the future limit arise based on the five matters previously explained in the *Nirvāṇa-vibhaṅga*.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that among the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the world..."
All views based upon these [factors] are subsumed within two types of view:
namely, the view of existence and the view of non-existence.
This shall now be analyzed.
How is it that all views are included within these two views?
Answer: This term "included" does not indicate that their essential nature is subsumed [within them];
rather, it indicates that they are included within the categories of these two views.
Why is this? Those who hold the view that things exist fall into the view of eternalism;
those who hold the view that nothing exists fall into the view of nihilism.
Although there are many varieties of erroneous views, none fail to fall within these two categories.
For example, at the beginning of this section, Pūraṇa asserted that there is no giving and so forth.
The five types of wrong views are included in the category of the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*),
because they grasp at non-existence. Some say:
It is included in two categories.
Because it involves clinging to a self as permanent and slandering causes and so forth, it is included in the category of eternalism (*śāśvatavāda*).

Next, because it includes views such as "the living being, the soul, or the person is annihilated and destroyed after death and does not exist," it is included in the category of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Thus, it is subsumed under the category of nihilism.
Some say: "This refers to the body of a person composed of these four great elements, up to what is praised and accepted by the wise; it is included within the two categories [of views].
Next, the teaching of 'without cause and without condition' and so forth is the view of Makkhali Gosāla."
Next, it is taught that the views of "the creator" (*kartṛ*) and "the teaching" (*śāsana*), and so forth, belong to the Sañjayīya school.
Both of these fall within the category of nihilistic views (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*),
because they maintain the doctrine of non-existence.
Some say that they enter two categories because,
by clinging to a self as permanent and by slandering causes and so forth, they fall into these states.
Next, it is explained that these seven types of persons (sapta-puruṣa-pudgalāḥ) and so forth are subsumed under the view of eternalism; thus, they belong to the category of eternalism.
Next, it is explained that the fourteen billion [heretics] and so forth hold the views of Aśvajita and the hair-matted ascetics (jaṭila).
Next, it is taught that "all that is experienced by every person has no cause other than past karma," and so forth;
this is the view of the Son of the One Free from Bonds (Vātsīputrīya).
Both of these [views] fall into two categories.
Because they hold that the self is annihilated after death,
they next assert that everything experienced by a person is without cause and without condition;
this is the view of the Vātsīputrīyas.
Entering the Chapter on the View of Annihilation.
Because of the adherence to non-existence, some say:
It falls into two categories.
Because they slander [the idea of] causelessness by clinging to a permanent self, it is next stated that suffering, pleasure, and so forth are self-created; this also falls into two categories.
Because they hold that there is a self which subsequently undergoes annihilation,
it is next explained that the suffering and pleasure experienced are not created by oneself and so forth; this enters the category of the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*),
because they hold that [the self] does not exist.
Some say that they enter two categories,
because they cling to a permanent self and slander the absence of a cause.
Next, it is taught that because [the views] such as "the self and the world are eternal" are subsumed under the category of eternalism, they constitute the section on eternalism.

Next, it is taught that because [the views] such as "there is a self," "I exist," and so forth, are subsumed under the category of eternalism due to their adherence to truth and persistence, they constitute the section on eternalism.

Next, because it speaks of the truths (*satya*), abiding, and the selflessness of the self (*anātman-ātmā*), which are subsumed under the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), it belongs to the category of the view of annihilation.
Next, because it speaks of the contemplation of a self and the like, it enters the category of the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
Next, the section on entering the view of permanence by experiencing the five sublime sensual pleasures is explained.
This is because they cling to a self that eternally attains nirvāṇa.
Regarding this, some say:
It is included in two categories.
Because they hold that there is a self which subsequently undergoes annihilation, they are included in the category of the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, because the subsequent teaching on "the wind does not blow" and so forth is subsumed under the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), it is included in the category of eternalism.
Next, it is explained that sentient beings’ grasping at a self as an agent and so forth leads them into the category of the two views [of eternalism and nihilism].
Because they grasp at a self that subsequently undergoes annihilation,
this is followed by the explanation that the enjoyment of various desires as pure, exquisite, and pleasant, while being free from fault, leads them into the category of the view of eternalism.
Because they cling to a self and constantly experience superior desires,
some say that they enter two categories.
Because they hold that there is a self which subsequently undergoes annihilation, the Sūtra says:

"I have the view that I have perception; I have the view that I am without perception; I have the view that I have neither perception nor non-perception; I have the view of annihilation; and I have the view of nirvāṇa in the present life."
These five enter into two categories of views:
namely, the first three enter the category of the view of eternalism,
and the fourth enters the category of the view of nihilism.
Fifth, some say that one enters the category of those with eternalist views.
Some say that they enter into two categories:
the sixty-two views as explained in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
They are also all included within these two categories of views:
namely, among the views of discrimination regarding the past, the four theories of universal permanence enter the category of eternalism,
as do the four theories of partial permanence.
Some say that they enter the category of those with eternalist views;
others say...
The two [types of] proponents of existence enter the category of those who hold that there is permanence and impermanence.
The two proponents of causelessness enter the category of those with the view of annihilationism. Some say:
They fall into two categories.
Because they cling to a permanent self and slander the absence of a cause,
there are the four views concerning finitude and so forth.
Furthermore, the four theories of the "Evasion of the Immortal" (amarā-vikkhepa) are included in the category of the eternalist view (*śāśvata-vāda*).
Some say they are included in two categories, because while they hold to the self as eternal, they later also assert its annihilation.

The subsequent speculative views concerning the intermediate state— namely, the theories of having perception, having no perception, and neither having nor not having perception— are all subsumed under the view of eternalism,
and thus belong to the category of the eternalist school.
The seven theories of annihilation are subsumed under the view of nihilism, and thus belong to the category of the nihilist school.
The fifth section, the Chapter on Entering the View of Permanence within the Treatise on Nirvāṇa in the Present Life,
is so called because it maintains that there exists a self which eternally attains nirvāṇa. Some say:
They enter into two categories,
because they hold that there is a self which attains nirvāṇa in the present life and subsequently undergoes annihilation.
This is stated in the Kātyāyanāvavāda-sūtra.
In the world there are two views:
first, the view of existence;
second, the view of non-existence.
These are, respectively, subsumed within the categories of the views of eternalism and nihilism.
The *Siṃhanāda Sūtra* states:
"All views are based upon these two views."
That is to say, there is the view of existence and the view of non-existence.
Those who rely on the view of existence are attached to the view of existence and hostile toward the view of non-existence;
those who rely on the view of non-existence are attached to the view of non-existence and hostile toward the view of existence.
These two are, respectively, also subsumed within the categories of the views of eternalism and nihilism.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"The eternalist non-Buddhists either cling to transformation..."
Some maintain that there is concealment and manifestation;
others maintain that the mental faculty (manodhātu) is eternal, comes and goes, and so forth.
Since all such views are subsumed under the view of permanence, they belong to the category of eternalism.
As stated in the Sūtra:
there are non-Buddhists who maintain that the life-principle is identical to the body,
and others who maintain that the life-principle is distinct from the body.
The life-principle is not identical to the body;
the life-principle is not distinct from the body.
Question: For what reason do the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain that the life-principle is identical to the body?
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke thus:
"When one observes that the body arises in the world, one speaks of the birth of a sentient being;
when the body perishes, one speaks of the death of a sentient being."
Furthermore, he observes that the world speaks of there being a "living being" (jīva) in a physical body endowed with sense faculties,
whereas it speaks of there being no living being in a body devoid of sense faculties.
Furthermore, he observes that the world gives rise to the notions of "male" and "female" based on the distinctions between bodily characteristics.
Furthermore, he observes that in the world, people speak of being strong or weak based on the strength or weakness of their physical power.

Furthermore, he observes that in the world, people speak of being tall or short, coarse or fine, fat or thin, white or black, and so forth, based on the differences in the length, shortness, coarseness, fineness, stoutness, leanness, fairness, or darkness of their physical forms.
Furthermore, he perceives that when even a single part of the body in the world is afflicted,
the entire body experiences the suffering of insecurity.
Furthermore, he perceives that when there is sorrow or joy in the world...
Because [he] sheds tears, his hair stands on end, and his countenance is joyful.
Furthermore, because he perceives that all in the world give rise to the designation "self" with respect to the body,
other masters say:
Having observed that the tails of creatures such as lizards and chameleons in the world can each still move and twitch when severed,
the Venerable One said:
He perceives that in this world, regarding the physical body endowed with sense faculties, there is the designation of "sentient being" (sattva),
as well as the speech of sentient beings and the beauty or ugliness of sentient beings.
Because of the deportment of sentient beings,
their activities, and so forth;
through such various causes and conditions as these.
The various non-Buddhists (tīrthika) claim that the life-principle (jīva) is identical to the body.
One asks: for what reason do the non-Buddhists maintain that the life-principle is distinct from the body?
The Venerable Vasumitra explains as follows:
Those non-Buddhists maintain that form constitutes the body,
and they maintain that the mind and its mental factors constitute the life-principle;
yet form and mind are each distinct in their continuity.
They perceive the transformation of the body’s form before and after, yet they do not perceive the differing characteristics of the mind and mental factors before and after;
thus they give rise to this view. Furthermore, they regard the body as coarse while the mind and mental factors are subtle.
The life-principle (jīva) is distinct from the body because it is subtle;
furthermore, they perceive that its postures and movements turn according to its own volition,
and thus they grasp this volition as being the life-principle.
Dignified deportment (īryāpatha) is simply a differentiation in the transformation of the body.
Furthermore, seeing that the physical appearance of a dead person is no different [from when they were alive],
he then forms this thought:
Because it is taught that the departure of the life-principle from the body is called death, [the self] is distinct from the body.
Furthermore, they perceive that the physical body and the various states of the mind and mental factors undergo different transformations throughout their successive stages.
Because they maintain that the mind and so forth are themselves the life-principle (*jīva*),
it is distinct from the body. Furthermore, because they perceive the physical body as having many parts while the life-principle is a single unity, it is distinct from the body.
Furthermore, those non-Buddhists observe that one abandons the previous body to receive an intermediate body (*antarābhava*),
and then abandons the intermediate body to receive the present body.
Thus, although the bodies differ as they transmigrate, because the life-principle (*jīva*) is one, it is distinct from the body.
Other masters say:
Since they observe that the body continues to move even during sleep,
they know that there is a distinct "vitality" (jīva) within it.
Furthermore, when one sees a dream,
the body remains in its original location while the life-principle (jīva) travels to other regions; therefore,
it is known that there is a life-principle distinct from and separate from the body.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
seeing that one can rely on meditative concentration to recollect the past and know the distinctions among many bodies in the future, they then form this thought.
Although the body is manifold, the life-principle (jīva) is one;
therefore, we know they are distinct from one another.
Furthermore, he perceives that in the world the body is devoid of movement or transition.
Because one can recollect the past and know the future,
it is known that there exists a life-principle distinct from the body.
Some have said this:
He perceives the world,
recollecting his former deeds and experiences,
yet his body remains unmoving.
Thus, one knows that there is a life-principle distinct from the body.
Some say that they perceive the body's form to be different across its preceding and succeeding states.
Since the wisdom of craftsmanship and so forth function without distinction [from the body],
we know that there exists a life-principle (jīva) separate from the body.
The Venerable One said:
He observes that both those in the world who lack self-mastery and those who possess mastery have bodies that move and shake together; therefore,
he knows that their bodies are moved by a life-principle (jīva).
Question: For what reason do the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) maintain that the life-principle (jīva) is not identical to the body?
Venerable Vasumitra says:
They observe that, for the most part, the bodies in the world are different [from one another].
Because the life-principle (*jīva*) is not different [from the body], it is not identical with the body.
Furthermore, that [proponent] observes that the worldly body evolves according to conditions, whereas the life-principle does not;
therefore, it is not identical with the body.
Furthermore, he observes that the body in the world undergoes various changes such as increase and decrease, or loss and gain;
the life-principle (jīva), however, does not do so, and therefore it is not identical to the body.
The Venerable One said:
He observes that in the world, a single body possesses various different characteristics, whereas the life-principle (*jīva*) is not like this;
therefore, it is not identical to the body.
Question: For what reason do the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) maintain that the life-principle is not different from the body?
The Venerable Vasumitra stated as follows:
"Since he perceives no distinct, substantial entity called a 'life-principle' (jīva) apart from the body,
he maintains that the life-principle is not different from the body."
The remainder is as previously stated in the section on the body itself.
The Venerable One said:
"One perceives that worldly beings give rise to self-love (*ātmasneha*) toward their own bodies."
It is not because of any other dharma that one clings to the idea that the life-principle is not different from the body;
the rest is as previously explained in the discussion on the body itself.
However, foolish worldlings do not properly understand the momentary continuity of form, mind, and so forth.
To say that the possessor of life is identical to the body and so forth leads to the category of annihilationism;
to say it is the body itself and not different from the body leads to the category of annihilationism;
to say it is different from the body and not identical to the body leads to the category of eternalism.
Therefore, there are no wrong views or heterodox paths among the various non-Buddhists that do not fall within the categories of eternalism or nihilism;
for the sake of counteracting these, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas proclaim the Middle Way.
This means that form, mind, and so forth are neither annihilated nor eternal.
Question: How should one know that after death there is no annihilation?
The Venerable Vasumitra spoke as follows:
