One observes that at present, the mind consists of many thoughts in continuous succession;
because each preceding thought ceases, each succeeding one arises,
and thus the subsequent mind necessarily arises in dependence upon the preceding mind.
The preceding mind possesses power that necessarily induces the succeeding mind;
it is only when encountering conditions of extreme aversion that the succeeding mind does not arise.
Consequently, the initial mind of rebirth in this life must certainly have a preceding mind as its cause for its induction.
At the stage of approaching death, there is no object of extreme aversion;
at the very moment of death, the mind is certainly able to project the subsequent body,
just as the preceding body was able to project the arising of the present body.
Why does the present body not project a subsequent body?
From this, one should know that there is no annihilation after death.

Furthermore, it is observed that the present sensory cognition arises based on the sense faculties; once these faculties have arisen, they can again act as causes to project the arising of mental cognition.
Therefore, one should know that the initial mental cognition within the womb must necessarily be induced by the sensory cognitions of the past.
Since the preceding life was able to induce the arising of the present life,
why should the present life not likewise induce the subsequent life?
From this, it should be understood that there is no annihilation after death.
The Venerable One said:
"It is not the case that one mind arises independently of other minds."
One also perceives that there is form which arises following the mind,
and one further perceives that there is mind which arises depending upon form.
Because form and mind arise due to afflictions, it should be understood from this that after death there is no annihilation.
Furthermore, it is directly observed that a body possessing afflictions in a preceding moment is necessarily able to project the arising of mind and matter in a succeeding moment.
Thus, one knows that for one who possesses afflictions at the point of death, these must certainly project the subsequent mind and matter so that they arise.
From this, one should know that after death there is no annihilation.
Question: Why are form, mind, and so forth not eternal?
Answer: Because they undergo transformation and are not constant.
How could it be eternally abiding?
One might ask: how do we know that transformation does not occur through the concealment and manifestation [of a single essence], yet you insist that its substance undergoes arising and ceasing?
The Venerable Vasumitra speaks thus:
If that transformation were merely due to concealment and manifestation,
then the stages of being in the womb, an infant, a child, a youth, an adult, and an elder should all arise simultaneously;
however, they arise gradually.
Therefore, one should know that the essence of transformation possesses arising and ceasing,
rather than being dependent on concealment and manifestation. Furthermore, if that transformation were merely due to concealment and manifestation,
then the stages of being in the womb, an embryo, an infant, a child, a youth, an adult, and an elder would necessarily be subject to interruption.
Nevertheless, it is uninterrupted;
thus we know that the substance of transformation possesses arising and ceasing, rather than depending on concealment and manifestation.
The Venerable One said:
In the world, it is directly perceived that when various conditions combine, phenomena arise;
if those conditions diverge, the phenomena perish.
This distinction does not belong to something that is merely hidden or manifest.
Therefore, one should know that transformation does not depend on concealment or manifestation;
rather, it depends solely on the fact that the substance itself undergoes arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, when a phenomenon undergoes transformation, if its preceding and succeeding characteristics are distinct, its substance must also be distinct.
Because the characteristic and the substance are one,
even if a phenomenon is eternally abiding and possesses distinctions in its states of concealment and manifestation, there is no difference in its characteristic.
Therefore, it is known that the intended meaning of the verse and the summary section regarding transformation is that the substance itself undergoes arising and ceasing.
As the text is easily understood, it is not further explained.
When the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang had finished translating this treatise, he spoke these two verses:
Four hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, King Kaniṣka [ruled] over Jambudvīpa.
Having convened five hundred arhats, the Tripiṭaka Master of Kaśmīra composed this Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra.
Having fully obtained the original text, the translation is now complete.
May it nourish all sentient beings, so that they may swiftly realize the wondrous Bodhi of parinirvāṇa.
The Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra of the Sarvāstivāda School, Fascicle Two Hundred.
